output_text: A weekend flash flood in Vietnam’s mountainous north killed five people and left one person missing, authorities said Tuesday. Heavy rains triggered the flooding Saturday night in Son La province, destroying 22 houses, damaging many others, and forcing dozens of families to evacuate. The agriculture ministry said three bodies were recovered on Monday, adding to two others found earlier in the aftermath. The flood also swept away more than 445 acres of crops and 2,600 cattle and poultry. Vietnam is highly vulnerable to tropical storms, flash floods, and landslides, and officials noted that climate change is making destructive flooding more likely. The disaster came after Tropical Storm Wipha killed three people and flooded nearly 4,000 homes in central Nghe An province last week.

# Vietnam Flash Flood Summary A weekend flash flood in Vietnam's mountainous Son La province killed five people, with one person still missing. Heavy rains on Saturday night destroyed 22 houses, damaged numerous others, and forced dozens of families to evacuate. Three bodies were recovered Monday, adding to two previously found. The disaster destroyed over 445 acres of crops and swept away 2,600 cattle and poultry. Vietnam frequently experiences tropical storms causing deadly flash floods and landslides. Climate change intensifies these weather patterns, increasing flood likelihood. Recent disasters include Tropical Storm Wipha, which killed three people and flooded nearly 4,000 homes in Nghe An province last week. In July, a whirlwind capsized a tourist boat in Ha Long Bay, killing 39 people. September's Typhoon Yagi devastated northern Vietnam, causing 345 deaths and $3.3 billion in economic losses.

Australia’s Muslim community leaders have condemned Prime Minister Tony Abbott for remaining largely silent amid a wave of Islamophobic attacks that followed recent anti-terror raids, arguing that government rhetoric has helped encourage hostility toward Muslims. According to the London-based *Muslim News*, which cited the Sydney-based Muslim Legal Network (MLN), 30 attacks on Muslims had been reported by October 9, beginning after anti-terror raids in Sydney on September 18. Many of the victims were women wearing hijabs. The raids, involving more than 800 police officers in Sydney and Brisbane, were said to have disrupted a terrorist plot to publicly behead a member of the public. In response to the broader security threat, the Australian government has committed forces against the Islamic State of Iraq and the Levant (ISIL/Daesh) in Iraq, raised the domestic alert level to “high,” and planned new laws to give intelligence officials greater powers. National security agencies have also received nearly $650 million in additional funding. Muslim leaders, however, say far less attention has been given to protecting Muslims from street-level hate crimes. The article describes a series of incidents: a Muslim woman was threatened with having her hijab torn off and set alight; coffee was thrown through the car window of another woman wearing a hijab; and a pig’s head and a cross were thrown into the grounds of a Brisbane mosque. In Melbourne, a 26-year-old Muslim woman was abused, assaulted, and thrown from a moving train, suffering injuries after an unknown woman repeatedly bashed her head against the train wall while shouting abuse. Police described the attack as “totally unacceptable” and said it had a “massive effect” on the victim. Other incidents included a mother in western Sydney being spat on and having her baby’s pram kicked, a Muslim mother in Melbourne being told to remove her child from play with non-Muslim children, and two separate shooting attacks in Brisbane on September 26, one targeting a Muslim family’s home in Mount Gravatt East and another firing into a car on nearby Dunbar Street. Threats have also reportedly been made against the Grand Mufti of Australia and mosques in Lakemba and Auburn. A note appearing to threaten Muslims with death was left near a mosque in Doncaster, Victoria. In Queensland, the word “evil” was sprayed on a mosque in Mareeba, while anti-Muslim slogans were painted on a car in Liverpool, New South Wales. Online abuse on Twitter and Facebook has included calls for Muslims to be beheaded, deported, or blown up. The Islamic Council of Victoria met with government ministers to demand a public condemnation of the attacks. Executive member Almir Colan said Muslims had been told privately that the government supported them, but wanted public backing instead. He urged Abbott to lower the rhetoric and say that “an attack on Muslims is an attack on all of us,” arguing that such a message would isolate extremists and reassure Muslims. Colan also criticized remarks by Palmer United Party senator Jacqui Lambie, who had described supporters of Islamic Shari’a law as “maniacs and depraved humans.” Abbott has said Australians are on “team Australia” and called Muslims “absolutely first-class Australians,” but he also criticized Muslim protesters in Lakemba and called the ICV “foolish” for not meeting him after his comments. Muslim leaders warned that without stronger public condemnation, anti-Muslim bigots would feel emboldened. Co-founder of the Australian Arabic Council Joseph Wakim said Abbott needed to make a “clear and bold statement” that “team Australia” must include Muslims, not target them.

# Australia's Muslim Leaders Call for PM to Condemn Rising Islamophobic Attacks Australia's Muslim community leaders are demanding that Prime Minister Tony Abbott publicly denounce a surge in Islamophobic attacks occurring across the country, accusing him of fueling the violence through inflammatory rhetoric. ## The Rising Violence According to the Muslim Legal Network (MLN) in Sydney, at least 30 attacks against Muslims have been reported since anti-terrorism raids began on September 18. The raids, involving over 800 police officers in Sydney and Brisbane, were conducted to disrupt an alleged terrorist plot. Most of the reported attacks have targeted women wearing the hijab. The incidents documented are deeply disturbing. They include a woman threatened with having her hijab torn off and set alight, coffee thrown through a car window, and a pig's head and cross thrown into a Brisbane mosque's grounds. In one particularly severe incident, a 26-year-old Muslim woman was assaulted and thrown from a moving train in Melbourne, suffering head injuries when her head was bashed against the train wall multiple times. A mother in western Sydney was spat upon and had her baby's pram kicked. In another case, a Brisbane mother was told to remove her child from playing with non-Muslim children at a playground. Shootings have also occurred, with two separate Muslim families' homes targeted on September 26—one house shot with a shotgun and a car fired upon several hundred meters away. Additionally, threatening notes and death threats have been left near mosques in Victoria, with threats made against the Grand Mufti of Australia and several major mosques. ## Government Response and Context The Australian Government has committed military forces against the Islamic State of Iraq and Levant (ISIL) in Iraq and raised the domestic terror alert level to "high." New legislation is being introduced to grant intelligence officials greater powers, and national security agencies have received nearly $650 million in additional funding. However, Muslim leaders criticize the disparity in resources, arguing that insufficient police resources are devoted to stopping street-level Islamophobic crimes. They contend that Abbott's "team Australia" rhetoric and provocative statements by other government ministers are inadvertently encouraging attacks. ## Community Demands The Islamic Council of Victoria (ICV) met with government ministers demanding public condemnation of the attacks. Executive member Almir Colan stated: "We want the Prime Minister to lower the rhetoric and concentrate on responsible, productive language." Colan expressed particular concern about comments from Palmer United Party Senator Jacqui Lambie, who called Islamic Sharia law supporters "maniacs and depraved humans," yet questioned why Abbott failed to condemn such statements. He argued that Abbott's "team Australia" phrase creates a citizenship test requiring Muslims to constantly prove themselves, effectively excluding them from the national community. Joseph Wakim, co-founder of the Australian Arabic Council, echoed these concerns, calling for Abbott to make a "clear and bold statement" against Islamophobia and clarify that "team Australia isn't about the kicking of Muslims." ## Social Media Amplification Islamophobic comments have proliferated on social media platforms, with Twitter and Facebook users calling for Muslims to be beheaded, deported, or killed. Colan warned that without stronger government support, more Australians may become radicalized against Muslims, as inflammatory rhetoric provides "cover" for bigots. While Abbott has stressed that Muslims are "absolutely first-class Australians," Muslim leaders maintain that private assurances are insufficient—they demand public, vocal support to counter the rising tide of Islamophobic violence.

Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania closed their borders Monday to most Russian citizens in response to Russia’s war in Ukraine and what the Baltic governments described as broad Russian public support for the invasion. Under the coordinated travel ban, Russians traveling to the Baltic states or to Poland for tourism, business, sports or cultural reasons will be denied entry even if they hold valid Schengen visas, which normally allow travel across much of Europe without border checks. The move was agreed earlier this month by the prime ministers of the three Baltic countries and Poland, who said limiting Russian entry was necessary to protect the security of EU states bordering Russia. Lithuanian Interior Minister Agne Bilotaite said Russia was “an unpredictable and aggressive state” and argued that it was unacceptable for people who support the war to move freely into Lithuania and the European Union. She said three-quarters of Russians back the war and that such support could threaten both Lithuania and the EU as a whole. The ban includes several exceptions. Humanitarian cases, family members of EU citizens, Russian dissidents, serving diplomats, transport workers, and Russians who already have residence permits or long-stay national visas from Schengen countries are still permitted to enter. The restrictions are aimed mainly at land travel, and the Baltic states cannot stop Russian citizens from entering through another Schengen country. In Poland, there were no immediate signs of new restrictions taking effect Monday, even though the country had agreed with the Baltic states to adopt the ban by Sept. 19. Poland already has tight limits on Russian travelers that date back to the COVID-19 pandemic. A member of the Russian Culture and Education Association in Poland said in Bialystok that a new ban would have been more disruptive if the pandemic-era restrictions had not already sharply reduced travel and contact with Russia. He said the lack of any sign of improvement after more than two years of restrictions was the worst part. Lithuania said 11 Russian citizens were stopped from entering the country starting at midnight, most of them attempting to cross by land from Kaliningrad or Belarus. No incidents were reported. Estonian Foreign Minister Urmas Reinsalu said last week that Russian travelers posed security concerns because Russian spies had allegedly used fake identities and tourist visas to conduct activities in Europe. He also referred to reports that Ukrainian refugees in Europe had been forced to serve wealthy Russian clients in spas and similar establishments, calling the situation “perverse.” Estonia, with a population of about 1.3 million, has recorded hundreds of thousands of border crossings by Russian citizens since the start of the war. The Baltic governments want all 27 EU members to adopt similar restrictions, but that has not happened. Some limits already exist, including restrictions on flights from Russia into the EU. The Czech Republic, which does not border Russia, was among the first EU countries to stop issuing visas to Russians, doing so the day after the Feb. 24 invasion. The article notes that the Baltic states, once Soviet republics, and Poland and the Czech lands, once Soviet satellites, remain especially sensitive to Moscow’s aggressive behavior because of their history.

# Baltic Nations Close Borders to Russians Over Ukraine War Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, and Poland implemented a coordinated travel ban on Monday, closing their borders to most Russian citizens in response to widespread domestic support for Russia's invasion of Ukraine. The measure prevents Russian nationals from entering these countries even if they hold valid European Union Schengen Area visas, regardless of their stated purpose—whether tourism, business, sports, or cultural activities. The four nations' prime ministers had agreed earlier in the month to implement this security measure, arguing it was necessary to protect EU member states neighboring Russia. Lithuanian Interior Minister Agne Bilotaite emphasized the rationale, stating that approximately three-quarters of Russian citizens support the war in Ukraine, making it unacceptable for these individuals to freely travel through Europe and into Lithuania. She further noted that such support for hostilities poses security threats to both individual countries and the EU as a whole. The ban includes several humanitarian exceptions. Russian citizens may still enter under specific circumstances: for humanitarian reasons, as family members of EU citizens, as political dissidents fleeing persecution, as serving diplomats, as transportation employees, or if they hold residence permits or long-stay national visas from Schengen countries. While Poland agreed to implement the ban by September 19, no new restrictions were reported on Monday, as existing COVID-19 pandemic travel restrictions already significantly limited Russian travel to the country. Poland shares a border with Russia's Kaliningrad exclave, making it particularly sensitive to security concerns. On the first night of enforcement, Lithuania's Interior Ministry reported that eleven Russian citizens were prevented from entering the country. Most attempted to cross by land from Kaliningrad or Belarus without incident. Estonian Foreign Minister Urmas Reinsalu cited additional security concerns, noting that Russian intelligence services have historically used fake identification documents and tourist visas to conduct operations in Europe. He also raised concerns about reports of Ukrainian refugees in Europe being exploited by wealthy Russian clients in spas and other establishments. Estonia, with a population of approximately 1.3 million, had registered hundreds of thousands of Russian border crossings since the war began, making the security measure particularly relevant for the nation. However, the effectiveness of these national bans is limited by EU structure. Russian citizens can theoretically enter the Baltic nations and Poland by first traveling through other Schengen countries without border controls. The nations are advocating for all 27 EU member states to implement similar measures, though this has not yet been agreed upon. The EU has already introduced flight restrictions from Russia, but the new ban primarily targets land travel. The Czech Republic, which shares no border with Russia, was among the first EU nations to stop issuing visas to Russian citizens, implementing this policy immediately after Russia's February 24 invasion of Ukraine. The Baltic nations' heightened sensitivity to Russian aggression stems from their history as former Soviet republics, while Poland and the Czech Republic, previously under Soviet influence, remain acutely aware of Moscow's aggressive policies toward neighboring states.

Venezuela’s government has issued an arrest warrant for opposition leader Juan Guaidó and said it has asked Interpol to circulate a red alert, accusing him of misusing state oil money for personal gain. The announcement was made Thursday night by Attorney General Tarek William Saab. Guaidó, who once had recognition from the United States and more than 50 other countries as Venezuela’s legitimate leader, is now living in Miami after leaving Venezuela earlier this year. He said he fled because he feared arrest. After the warrant was announced, Guaidó rejected the accusations as false and said they were part of a “machine of promoting lies.” He also accused the Maduro government of using justice as a political weapon, saying the regime was again attacking him through “the kidnapping of justice.” Guaidó rose to prominence in 2019, when he declared himself interim president after Nicolás Maduro was sworn in for a second term in an election widely denounced as fraudulent. At the time, Guaidó was the democratically elected head of Venezuela’s National Assembly and argued that Maduro’s presidency was illegitimate. The Maduro government never arrested him, even as he led mass protests and backed a failed uprising aimed at removing Maduro from power. The political context has changed significantly since then. In April, months after other opposition leaders voted to dissolve Guaidó’s interim government, Guaidó said he received phone calls from two senior Maduro officials warning that his arrest was imminent. Analysts say the government’s decision to move against him now, after he has lost much of his domestic support and is outside Venezuela, suggests Maduro no longer sees him as a serious threat. Geoff Ramsey of the Atlantic Council said the government is effectively placing Guaidó in the same category as other exiled opposition figures: barred from returning, but no longer considered untouchable. Saab said the warrant was requested over alleged crimes including treason, usurping authority, and profiting from public funds. He accused Guaidó of using money tied to Venezuela’s state oil company for his own benefit, including legal expenses, and said the actions of Guaidó’s interim government caused the country to lose $19 billion. Saab specifically cited two entities that were under the interim government’s control: Citgo, the Houston-based oil refiner formerly controlled by Maduro’s government, and Monómeros, a Venezuelan fertilizer company in Colombia. Those institutions have long been controversial. Maduro’s government, and even some independent observers, have accused Guaidó’s team of mismanaging them. Venezuela expert David Smilde of Tulane University said the handling of Citgo undermined its legal autonomy and exposed it to creditors. He noted that a federal appeals court in Delaware recently echoed that criticism, suggesting the interim government used funds from the state oil company, Petróleos de Venezuela, S.A., to cover its own debts. Appeals are now before the U.S. Supreme Court, though Smilde doubts the justices will take the case. Interpol has not appeared to act on similar requests against other Venezuelan opposition figures, including Julio Borges. Interpol’s rules prohibit involvement in political matters. The warrant also comes amid sensitive political negotiations. Maduro’s government is in talks with the Biden administration about possible relief from U.S. sanctions on Venezuela’s oil industry in exchange for promises of free and fair elections next year. The move also comes just before the opposition’s primary vote to choose a candidate for the 2024 presidential election. Guaidó is not running, while the frontrunner, Maria Corina Machado, has been disqualified by the Maduro government, drawing strong criticism from U.S. officials. Smilde said the Interpol request is largely symbolic and unlikely to affect Guaidó while he remains in the United States. He said it mainly allows Maduro to blame the interim government for damage to Venezuela’s assets and economic crisis, while deflecting attention from the government’s own failures.

# Venezuela Issues Arrest Warrant Against Opposition Leader Juan Guaidó Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro's government has issued an arrest warrant for opposition leader Juan Guaidó, requesting an Interpol red alert and accusing him of misusing state oil money. Guaidó, who fled to Miami earlier this year citing threats of arrest, currently resides in the United States where he maintains support from some Washington and Florida allies. Attorney General Tarek William Saab announced the warrant on Thursday, charging Guaidó with treason, usurping functions, and profiting from public money. Guaidó dismissed the allegations as false, characterizing them as part of the regime's "machine of promoting lies." ## Background on Guaidó's Rise and Fall In 2019, following Maduro's widely-condemned fraudulent reelection, Guaidó declared himself interim president as the democratically-elected leader of Venezuela's National Assembly. Once recognized by the United States and over 50 countries as Venezuela's rightful leader, Guaidó attempted to unseat Maduro through mass protests and a failed uprising. However, the Maduro government never arrested him during this period. By April 2024, after fellow opposition leaders voted to dissolve his interim government and his popularity plummeted domestically, Guaidó received warnings from high-ranking Maduro officials that his arrest was imminent, prompting his departure. ## Charges and Financial Allegations Saab accused Guaidó of using money from Venezuela's state-owned oil company for personal benefit, including legal expenses. The government claims the interim government's decisions caused Venezuela to lose $19 billion. The charges specifically reference the interim government's management of Monómeros, a Venezuelan fertilizer company in Colombia, and Citgo Petroleum, a Houston-based oil refiner. A federal appeals court in Delaware confirmed that the interim government used funds from Petróleos de Venezuela to finance its own debts. Legal representatives are appealing to the U.S. Supreme Court, though experts consider this unlikely to succeed. ## Limited Practical Impact Experts note the arrest warrant carries primarily symbolic value. Geoff Ramsey from the Atlantic Council suggests the timing—after Guaidó lost popular support and left the country—indicates Maduro no longer views him as a genuine threat. David Smilde, a Venezuela expert at Tulane University, states the Interpol action has little chance of affecting Guaidó in the United States. Interpol's constitution explicitly prohibits engaging in matters of political character, and the organization has not acted on previous red alerts against opposition politicians, including Julio Borges. ## Political Context The announcement comes as Maduro's government pursues talks with the Biden administration regarding potential sanctions relief on Venezuela's oil sector in exchange for promises of free elections. It also precedes opposition primary elections to select a 2024 presidential candidate. Notably, Guaidó is not running, and the government has disqualified frontrunner Maria Corina Machado—a move condemned by U.S. officials. Smilde suggests the warrant allows Maduro to deflect blame for Venezuela's economic crisis while undermining Guaidó's credibility regarding the interim government's financial mismanagement.

Kenya Airways has dismissed 140 engineers and aircraft maintenance staff after they took part in what management described as an illegal strike that began on Tuesday, November 28. Managing Director and Chief Executive Sebastian Mikosz said the airline would not tolerate actions that undermine its recovery after two years of losses. He said management had issued three written instructions to the workers, but some remained defiant and continued the strike. In a memo to staff, Mikosz said all employees who participated in the action had been terminated with immediate effect and that their airport passes had been revoked. The affected workers, however, rejected the dismissals and said they would challenge them in court. Speaking to journalists on Thursday, they said they would not back down until their grievances were addressed, with the main issue being a salary increase they claim has not been implemented. Joseph Oyuga said their lawyers would file a suit by Friday afternoon, arguing that the airline had unlawfully terminated them. Management says the technical staff received a 60 percent salary increase in February 2017. According to the airline, the board approved a pay review for the department despite the company’s difficult financial position, and the new salaries were implemented in April and backdated to March 2017. KQ said a technical assistant’s pay rose from Sh120,000 to Sh200,000, while duty control engineers and production engineers moved to Sh340,000. The workers dispute that account, saying the increment never reached them. Oyuga said technical assistants currently earn about Sh36,000, which he argued is below industry standards. The staff are demanding much higher pay, including a basic salary of Sh340,000 for technical assistants, Sh1.2 million for duty control and production engineers, Sh500,000 for technicians, and Sh600,000 for senior technicians. Management said the technical team numbers more than 600, with about 15 percent participating in the strike, but the workers disputed those figures, saying there are 220 engineers and aircraft technicians and that 169 were fired on Wednesday. They also said they were not trying to force management, only seeking a meeting to air their concerns. The dispute comes as Kenya Airways continues to face labor tensions, including earlier strike threats from pilots. In August, the airline signed a new collective bargaining agreement with pilots that ended three years of negotiations, though it did not include a salary increase. The airline has also recently completed a major capital restructuring involving government and local banks.

# Kenya Airways Fires 140 Engineers Over Illegal Strike Kenya Airways has terminated 140 engineers and aircraft maintenance technicians for participating in an illegal strike that began on November 28. Managing Director Sebastian Mikosz stated the airline would not tolerate actions undermining its recovery after two years of losses. Despite three written warnings, employees continued the strike, leading to immediate termination and revocation of their facility passes. The dismissed workers have rejected the termination as unlawful and vowed to pursue legal action, with lawyer Joseph Oyuga announcing a lawsuit would be filed by Friday. The core dispute centers on salary increases, with technicians demanding raises of up to 844 percent. Management claims it approved a 60 percent salary increase in February 2017, implemented in April with backdated payments to March. For example, technical assistants' salaries supposedly increased from 120,000 to 200,000 shillings. However, striking employees dispute receiving these increases, citing current technical assistant wages of only 36,000 shillings—below standards for smaller aircraft operations. The workers are requesting technical assistants earn 340,000 shillings, with duty control and production engineers earning 1.2 million shillings. Additionally, technicians seek 500,000 shillings (from 62,000) and senior technicians want 600,000 shillings (from 90,000). Oyuga characterized their action as a request for dialogue rather than a demand, questioning why management responded harshly to reasonable grievances. Management disputes the number of striking employees, claiming 15 percent of over 600 technical staff participated. However, technicians assert only 220 engineers and aircraft technicians exist, with 169 fired on Wednesday. This represents the latest labor conflict at Kenya Airways, following pilot strikes. In August, the airline signed a one-year Collective Bargaining Agreement with the Kenya Airlines Pilot Association, offering no salary increases but productivity allowances for extra hours worked. Kenya Airways recently underwent capital restructuring, with the government increasing its shareholding to 48.9 percent and local banks owning 38.1 percent after converting 17 billion shillings in debt to equity.

Grünenthal, the Aachen, Germany-based global pharmaceutical company focused on pain management, announced on April 7, 2021, that it had received a favorable environmental, social and governance assessment from Sustainalytics, a Morningstar company and a major ESG research provider. Sustainalytics rated Grünenthal as having “overall medium ESG risk” and said the company demonstrates “strong management” of those risks. That result placed Grünenthal in the top five percent of the global pharmaceuticals subsector. CEO Gabriel Baertschi said the rating reflected the company’s efforts to make a “net-positive impact on society,” but he also stressed that the company saw the recognition as only one step in a longer process. He said Grünenthal intended to integrate sustainability more closely into its core strategy while building on its existing foundation as a responsible business. The assessment was based on Sustainalytics’ ESG Risk Ratings framework, which examines both a company’s exposure to material ESG issues and how well it manages them. In this framework, exposure refers to how much a company’s enterprise value is vulnerable to issues such as ethical marketing, clinical trial transparency, whistleblowing, corruption and bribery. Management refers to the company’s preparedness and past performance in handling those risks through policies, training, programs and management systems. Grünenthal said its ESG work is organized around four main pillars. The first is educating health care professionals and others about pain treatment and the responsible use of opioids. The company said it has reached about 65,000 health care professionals with efforts to improve pain management and patient outcomes. Because Grünenthal is both a pain specialist and an opioid manufacturer, it said it places particular emphasis on ensuring that employees, customers, patients and partners understand its position on responsible medical use of opioids. It has required opioid-related materials to include its statement on responsible use, highlighting both the risks and benefits of these medicines. The company also said it has created a dedicated governance body to provide guidance, promote consistent behavior, support training and oversee control mechanisms. The second pillar is ensuring access to medicine. Grünenthal said it is committed to making key medicines available where there are unmet medical needs. It cited the United States, where about 5 million patients need treatment for neuropathic pain associated with diabetes. The company said a U.S. FDA label extension for one of its non-opioid pain medicines for diabetic peripheral neuropathy of the feet helped expand patient access to treatment. It also said it is working to meet unmet therapeutic needs in underserved markets by offering specialized non-opioid pain medicines. The third pillar is innovation in pain management. Grünenthal said its research and development strategy aims to address major unmet needs in pain, including through partnerships. It supports young scientists through the EFIC-Grünenthal Grant, a biennial program that awards €200,000. Since the grant’s creation in 2004, about €1.6 million has been distributed to fund 65 projects. The company also backs the Brain, Mind, and Pain Patient-Centered Innovation Grant, which awards €90,000 every two years to encourage research that is both scientifically strong and focused on patient needs, especially in chronic pain and neurological disorders. The fourth pillar is raising awareness of “pain as a disease.” Grünenthal said chronic pain affects around 10% of the world’s population and is a major global health issue. To promote better pain policy, it supports the Societal Impact of Pain platform, a multi-stakeholder initiative that helps develop national-level pain policies. It also created the Pain Toolkit, a practical resource for patients that includes explanations, infographics and videos to help them manage pain themselves. In addition, the company highlighted the Grünenthal Foundation for Palliative Care, which supports research and science in palliative care for seriously or terminally ill people in Europe and Latin America. Beyond these four pillars, Grünenthal said its ESG efforts also extend across the environmental, social and governance spectrum. On the environmental side, it said it has set concrete goals for its five production sites, supply chain and affiliates worldwide, following international standards for environment, health and safety. It collects and analyzes production data to improve efficiency, reduce energy use and minimize waste through a zero-waste-to-landfill approach. On the social side, Grünenthal said it prioritizes employee well-being and community responsibility. It described its workplace as one that offers development opportunities and seeks to maintain high engagement, with the goal of being a Great Place to Work®. It said its culture is based on shared values and behaviors, and it recognizes outstanding contributions through the annual Grünenthal Global Excellence Award. On governance, the company said strong oversight is essential to maintaining its license to operate and continue supplying medicines to patients. It described a comprehensive compliance and ethics system, employee Code of Conduct, business partner Code of Conduct, and a 24/7 external Ethics Helpline for anonymous reporting. It also said it commits to full disclosure of transfers of value to health care professionals, health care organizations and patient organizations. Grünenthal closed by describing itself as a privately owned, science-based global leader in pain management and related diseases, with affiliates in 29 countries, products in more than 100 countries, about 4,500 employees in 2020, and annual sales of €1.3 billion.

The article argues that Donald Trump’s return to the White House could have major consequences for exchange rates, especially for Southeast Asian and other regional currencies versus the US dollar. It begins by noting that Trump’s political and policy views are polarizing, but some of his economic ideas are still seen as relevant models for development. The author says that one of the biggest concerns for people in the region is whether local currencies will rise or fall against the dollar during Trump’s next term, and perhaps for years afterward, given the possibility that Trump’s ideas will shape both American and global politics and economics. The piece says the US dollar rose sharply when news of Trump’s re-election broke. This initial surge is attributed to optimism in the United States and among global business communities, who expect Trump to pursue pro-business policies. The article points to Trump’s business background and recalls that his first-term tax cuts were widely welcomed. By contrast, the author says Kamala Harris, Trump’s Democratic opponent, was seen as focusing more on domestic social and ideological issues than on economic management, and often avoided direct answers on economic problems. This contrast, the article argues, helped fuel business confidence in Trump. However, after the first wave of enthusiasm, the article asks whether Trump would actually want a persistently strong dollar. It answers that he likely would not. Trump’s “Make America Great Again” agenda, according to the article, is tied to reviving domestic manufacturing so the United States can produce enough for its own needs, reduce dependence on imports, and generate surpluses for export. A BBC investigation describes how Russia has expanded wartime recruitment beyond convicted prisoners to include people who have only been charged with crimes and are awaiting trial. Under laws passed in March 2024, both prosecutors and defense lawyers must tell many accused people that they can enlist in the military instead of going through the court process. If they sign up, the criminal investigation and prosecution are suspended, and the case is usually closed once the war ends. The article opens with the case of Andrey Perlov, a 62-year-old Olympic gold medallist in race walking and former managing director of a football club near Novosibirsk in Siberia. Police came to his home at about 6:45 a.m. on 28 March and accused him of stealing around three million roubles from the club, an allegation he and his family deny. Perlov has been detained for more than six months. His family says authorities are pressuring him to agree to fight in Ukraine, promising that the embezzlement case would be frozen and might be dropped after the war. His daughter, Alina, says he has repeatedly refused, but the pressure has continued. After his refusal, she says, he was sent to a strict punishment cell and later barred from seeing or calling his family. When she last saw him in court in mid-July, he had lost a lot of weight. The BBC says this practice has become widespread. Olga Romanova, head of the NGO Russia Behind Bars, says the legal system has been “turned upside down,” because even someone caught after committing a violent crime can now be offered the chance to go to war instead of facing justice. The BBC cites a leaked recording in which an investigator tells the wife of a man already sentenced for theft that he could receive a longer sentence for a new offense, but that signing a military contract would stop the case. Three lawyers in Russia confirmed that offering suspects this choice is now routine. The article also highlights the case of Yaroslav Lipavsky, a teenager accused of causing serious bodily harm. He signed up for the army as soon as he turned 18, hoping to avoid prosecution, after learning his girlfriend was pregnant. He left for Ukraine and died a week later, becoming one of the youngest soldiers killed in the war. This shift reflects Russia’s need to replenish manpower while limiting broader civilian mobilization, according to military analyst Michael Koffman. He says the authorities may view accused people and prisoners as expendable and unlikely to have a major impact on the economy. The BBC notes that the original prisoner recruitment effort began with Wagner, whose late leader Yevgeny Prigozhin recruited inmates from high-security prisons, offering pardons in exchange for service. Using confidential documents, dog tags, and family payment records verified with Mediazona, the BBC says Wagner recruited nearly 50,000 prisoners and suffered huge losses, including more than 17,000 killed in the battle for Bakhmut between July 2022 and June 2023. As Wagner’s losses mounted, recruitment broadened further, and later the Ministry of Defence adopted similar methods. Some accused people refuse because they oppose the war, fear being killed or wounded, or want to stay and defend themselves in court. But the article says many face severe pressure from authorities to accept the deal.

# Russians Accused of Crimes Offered Choice: Go to War Instead of Court Russia has implemented a controversial policy allowing individuals accused of crimes to enlist in the military as an alternative to facing prosecution, according to BBC analysis. This system represents a significant shift in how Russia's law enforcement operates and reflects the country's urgent need for military reinforcements in Ukraine. ## The Policy and Its Implementation Legislation passed in March 2024 requires both prosecution and defense lawyers to inform accused individuals of their option to join the military. If someone signs up, their prosecution is halted and their criminal case is typically closed entirely when the war ends. This applies to people yet to face trial, marking an expansion from the initial focus on convicted prisoners. The process moves rapidly: once someone signs a military contract, their criminal case is suspended within days, and they deploy to the front line almost immediately. Three Russian lawyers confirmed this has become standard practice across the country. ## Pressures and Consequences Olga Romanova, director of Russia Behind Bars, an NGO providing legal assistance to detainees, describes the system as having "turned Russia's law enforcement system upside down." She illustrates the absurdity with an extreme example: police could arrest someone at a crime scene, only to have them escape prosecution by volunteering for military service. Not everyone accepts this offer willingly. Some refuse on principle, opposing the war itself, while others fear the extreme danger of combat. However, those who decline face severe pressure. Andrey Perlov, a 62-year-old Olympic gold medalist accused of embezzlement, refused the military option and was placed in strict punishment cells and forbidden from contacting his family. His daughter reports he has lost significant weight under the strain. ## The Human Cost The consequences can be fatal. Yaroslav Lipavsky, a teenager accused of assault, signed up immediately upon turning 18 to avoid prosecution after learning his girlfriend was pregnant. He died in Ukraine a week later, becoming one of the war's youngest casualties. ## Historical Context and Scale This expansion builds on earlier recruitment practices. Wagner, the mercenary group led by the late Yevgeny Prigozhin, initially recruited from high-security prisons, offering pardons in exchange for service. Prisoners are identified by dog tags beginning with "K" (kolonya, or prison colony), with numbers indicating their origin and recruitment sequence. ## Strategic Rationale The government's motivation appears clear: maintain military troop levels while minimizing civilian mobilization. The policy continues despite resistance from some accused persons and their families, who struggle against enormous institutional pressure. Cases like Perlov's demonstrate that those refusing the military option face significant hardship, raising concerns about whether the choice is genuinely voluntary or coerced through intimidation and isolation.

On exploration, Learmonth said a management shake-up in late 2014 had increased spending on resource development and improved inferred and indicated resources. Blanket’s measured and indicated resource stands at 638,000 oz grading 4.18 g/t in 4.74-million tonnes, while inferred resources total 419,000 oz grading 5.03 g/t in 2.59-million tonnes. The company also expects upside from satellite exploration properties. Following the announcement, Caledonia’s AIM-listed shares rose 11.71% to a new 52-week high of £0.85, bringing year-to-date gains to 121%.

The article surveys the main peace initiatives proposed for ending the war in Ukraine and contrasts them with the positions of Russia and Ukraine. Russia says it is open to considering all incoming settlement proposals, according to Deputy Foreign Minister Andrey Rudenko, and welcomes mediation efforts from any country. But Moscow also insists that any serious peace plan must take account of what it calls the “new regions” that joined Russia, and it rejects Ukrainian proposals that do not recognize those territorial changes. Russia says the accession of the four regions is not negotiable. The newest initiative mentioned is Indonesia’s, presented in early June. It resembles ideas used after the Korean War: both sides would immediately cease fire, withdraw forces 15 km from current positions, and create a demilitarized zone. UN peacekeepers would be stationed there, and the UN would supervise referendums to “objectively confirm the will of the majority.” The proposal does not specify which territories would be covered. Indonesia has said it is ready to participate in the process and even contribute troops to a peacekeeping mission. Defense Minister Prabowo Subianto has argued that the Korean precedent shows such measures can work. China’s 12-point peace plan, published in February, calls for de-escalation, a ceasefire, an end to hostilities, and negotiations. Beijing says the security concerns of all sides must be respected and that regional peace should not be pursued through the expansion of military blocs. Its plan also includes humanitarian measures, such as helping resolve the crisis, exchanging prisoners, and keeping grain exports flowing through the grain corridor. China also urges prevention of biological, chemical, and nuclear weapons use or proliferation, opposes unilateral sanctions not approved by the UN Security Council, and says it is ready to help rebuild Ukraine after the war. Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva is also pushing for talks. He wants a new international format involving countries willing to mediate between Moscow and Kiev, and he has called for a UN summit with both Vladimir Putin and Volodymyr Zelensky. The precise details of Brazil’s proposal have not been made public, but Lula says Moscow should be given some “minimal preconditions.” France has also floated diplomatic ideas. According to Bloomberg, President Emmanuel Macron wanted to develop a plan with China, though so far he has only suggested a summit in Paris with Zelensky. Macron has called for reliable security guarantees for Ukraine, a position backed by Germany. Denmark and Sweden have said they are ready to provide a venue for such an alliance-related effort. The Vatican has proposed its own peace mission and mediation role. Pope Francis said he would be willing to travel to both Kiev and Moscow. The current Vatican initiative is being led by Matteo Zuppi, head of the Italian Episcopal Conference. The mission’s exact terms are not public, but its stated aim is a ceasefire. South Africa and other African states announced in mid-May that they were working to persuade Russia and Ukraine to begin peace talks. Their initiative is not a single detailed plan but a collection of ideas drawn from other proposals, including a ceasefire and making the UN the main settlement platform. African states are also interested in restoring some Russian banks’ access to SWIFT. Their delegation to Moscow and Kiev is being prepared for late June or early July. The article also recalls Russia’s own negotiating position from talks in Belarus and Turkey in 2022: Ukraine should become neutral and non-bloc, renounce nuclear weapons, demilitarize and “denazify,” settle language issues, and recognize the independence of the DPR and LPR as well as Russia’s sovereignty over Crimea and Sevastopol. # Summary: Peace Plans for Ukraine Multiple countries have proposed various peace initiatives to resolve the conflict in Ukraine, though significant disagreements persist between Russia and Ukraine regarding their fundamental terms. ## International Peace Proposals **Indonesia's Plan**: Introduced in early June, Indonesia's proposal mirrors the Korean Peninsula settlement model, calling for an immediate ceasefire, mutual withdrawal of forces 15 kilometers from current positions, and establishment of a demilitarized zone (DMZ). The plan includes UN peacekeeping forces in the DMZ and UN-supervised referendums to confirm territorial preferences, though it lacks territorial specificity. Indonesian Defense Minister Prabowo Subianto advocates for this approach based on Korea's successful precedent. **China's Initiative**: Beijing's 12-point peace plan from February emphasizes de-escalation, ceasefire, and peace talks while considering all parties' security concerns. It addresses humanitarian crises, prisoner exchanges, grain corridor access, and prevention of biological, chemical, and nuclear weapons proliferation. China opposes unilateral sanctions and military bloc expansion, offering post-war reconstruction assistance. **Other Proposals**: Brazil's President Lula da Silva advocates for negotiations through a new international format excluding conflict participants, potentially including a UN Summit with both Putin and Zelensky. France's Macron proposed a Paris summit and security guarantees, supported by Germany, with Denmark and Sweden offering platforms. The Vatican initiated a peace mission led by Pope Francis, who expressed willingness to visit both capitals. South Africa announced African states are developing a multi-faceted approach combining ceasefire proposals with UN involvement and SWIFT banking system restoration for Russian banks. ## Russian Position Russia demands Ukraine's neutral, non-bloc constitutional status and nuclear disarmament. Additional requirements include Ukraine's demilitarization and denazification, language issue resolution, and recognition of the Donbas People's Republics' independence and Russia's sovereignty over Crimea and Sevastopol. Critically, Russia insists that recognition of the four newly annexed regions' accession is non-negotiable in any peace agreement. Moscow stated it welcomes settlement efforts but expects specific proposals and noted China's plan could serve as a treaty basis once Western nations and Kyiv accept it. ## Ukrainian Position Ukraine categorically rejects proposals calling for immediate ceasefires, viewing them as advantageous to Russia. Kyiv will only discuss initiatives from President Zelensky, who proposed his own ten-point peace plan in November 2022. This plan requires complete Russian force withdrawal, restoration of Ukrainian territorial integrity, and prisoner exchanges under "all for all" formulas. Ukraine demands international security guarantees and Russian compensation for war damages. Notably, Kyiv declared "the time for mediators is over," dismissing China, Brazil, and Vatican efforts, while viewing Indonesia's initiative as merely buying time for Russia. However, Ukraine expressed openness to African proposals while refusing to freeze the conflict. ## Current Status Negotiations stalled by late April 2022 when Ukraine failed to respond with clearly formulated peace agreement language. Russia continues welcoming peaceful resolution efforts but maintains that territorial concessions regarding the four annexed regions remain non-negotiable. The fundamental disconnect—Ukraine's demand for territorial restoration versus Russia's insistence on territorial recognition—remains the central obstacle to resolution, making compromise extremely difficult despite numerous international mediation attempts.

Beginning June 6, Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Customs and Border Protection conducted enforcement operations in the sanctuary city. Border Patrol arrest data shows 5,414 apprehensions between June 1-22, compared to 9,577 in May. Gotaways decreased from 2,123 in May to 986 in June. DHS stated that sanctuary cities are "no longer a safe haven" and emphasized commitment to community security despite political opposition and assaults on officers. The agency highlighted larger comparative statistics: from February 1 to June 22, 2025 recorded 37,518 apprehensions versus approximately 600,000 during the same period in 2024, demonstrating significantly reduced border crossings under the current administration.

Complexo do Alemão, a cluster of favelas in Rio de Janeiro’s north zone, stood in stark contrast to the city’s beaches and Olympic showcase projects as the 2016 Games approached. Home to about 60,000 people, the area had seen little of the improved quality of life promised when Rio was awarded the Olympics in 2009. Instead, it remained one of the city’s most troubled neighborhoods, with the lowest Human Development Index in Rio, reflecting poor education, short life expectancy and low income. In the weeks before the opening ceremony, Alemão was marked by near-daily shootings, including one in which a 16-year-old was killed. A frightening image had circulated of children ducking for cover during gunfire inside the cable car that runs across the community. Violence was only part of the crisis: many residents still lacked garbage collection and sewer services, and in some places toilet waste flowed directly into the streets. Rio’s authorities were preparing to deploy more than 15,000 Army soldiers to help ensure peaceful Olympic Games, but residents of Alemão were unlikely to be the focus of that security effort. The Brazilian government’s main attempt to curb violence in Rio’s favelas had been the Pacifying Police Units, or UPP, which entered Alemão in 2010 in a large operation aimed at pushing out drug gangs ahead of the 2014 World Cup. Police remained there as an occupying force, but the intervention did not bring the intended peace. Instead, the operation sparked criticism from residents and human rights observers, who accused police of excessive violence. The article cites data showing that in 2015, for every Rio police officer killed on duty, security forces killed 24.8 people—more than twice the rate in South Africa and three times the rate in the United States. The problem worsened as Rio de Janeiro state’s economic crisis forced a $600 million cut in the security budget. Silvia Ramos, who coordinates the Security Studies and Citizenship Center at Cândido Mendes University, said police violence was one of the main reasons violence in Rio’s favelas had reached such extreme levels. She argued that decades of state presence in these neighborhoods had been defined mainly by arresting people, creating a tradition in which police believed they could do whatever they wanted in the favelas. “To end violence, you don’t need more shooting,” she said. Official figures underscored the severity of the situation. The Public Security Institute reported that 40 people were killed by on-duty Rio officers in May alone, compared with 17 in the same month the previous year. At the same time, social deprivation continued to feed the cycle of crime. Researchers and security specialists pointed out that the lack of basic services and opportunities pushed many young people toward drug trafficking. A study by Federal University of Rio de Janeiro professor Felicia Shrike found that Alemão residents had far worse access to education and sanitation than the city average. Illiteracy among people over 15 was nearly three times higher than in Rio overall. More than 60 percent of the population lived on the equivalent of the minimum wage or less—about $280 a month—and about 6.5 percent had no income at all. Shrike’s report described a mother of six who said three of her children had become involved in trafficking because the family could not support them. She wondered whether she had failed them, and said that where they came from, respect seemed to come only through that life. The violence also took a heavy psychological toll on residents not involved in crime. Sociologist Natalia Fazzioni Helou said the armed conflict tied to trafficking had become everyday life in Alemão since the mid-1990s, contributing to depression and panic disorders. She noted that tensions increased further after the arrival of the Pacifying Police Units in 2012. Doctors Without Borders had identified similar problems even earlier, in 2007, when psychologist Milena Osório found panic, anxiety and depression were already common. She said grief was especially difficult because people could not openly process deaths or the loss of children and future prospects. Poor health conditions added to the sense of abandonment. Diseases associated with inadequate sanitation, such as scabies and diarrhea, remained more common in Alemão than elsewhere in Rio. More than 8 percent of residents had their garbage uncollected, compared with less than 1 percent citywide. Resident Cátia Souza said it was hard for people to feel hopeful when sewage ran beneath their windows.

# Rio's Alemão Favelas: Violence and Neglect Overshadow Olympic Promise As Rio de Janeiro prepared to host the 2014 World Cup and 2016 Olympics, city officials promised transformative improvements to the Complexo do Alemão, a sprawling favela in the city's north zone home to approximately 60,000 residents. However, instead of experiencing enhanced quality of life, the area has become synonymous with violence and social neglect, presenting a stark contrast to Rio's glamorous beaches and Olympic facilities. Located just miles from the upscale neighborhoods of Ipanema and Copacabana, Alemão occupies roughly one square mile and has earned the city's worst Human Development Index—a United Nations metric measuring education, life expectancy, and income. Just one month before the Olympic opening ceremony, the favela experienced nearly daily shootings, including an incident involving a 16-year-old. These violent episodes, such as children cowering during gunfire in the area's cable car, have become disturbingly routine. ## The Failed Pacification Effort In 2010, the Brazilian government launched an ambitious security initiative called UPP (Pacifying Police Units) to combat drug trafficking in Rio's favelas ahead of the World Cup. However, this effort failed to produce meaningful peace in Alemão. Despite the police presence remaining in the area, violence has intensified rather than diminished. The complexity of drug trafficking networks and the favela's size have proven too challenging for the pacification strategy. More troublingly, police tactics have drawn widespread criticism for excessive violence. Data reveals the severity of the problem: in 2015, Rio security forces killed 24.8 people for every officer killed on duty—more than double South Africa's rate and triple that of the United States. By May 2016, police had killed 40 people compared to 17 the previous year. ## Economic Crisis Compounds Problems Rio de Janeiro's severe economic crisis has exacerbated the situation, forcing $600 million in security budget cuts. According to Silvia Ramos, coordinator of the Security Studies and Citizenship Center at Cândido Mendes University, police violence is a primary driver of the favela's escalating violence. She explains that the state's presence in these areas historically involves only arrests, creating a tradition where police operate without accountability—a dynamic absent in other city neighborhoods. ## Systemic Poverty and Limited Opportunities Beyond violence, Alemão residents face desperate poverty and inadequate services. More than 60 percent earn minimum wage (approximately $280 monthly) or less, while 6.5 percent have no income. Illiteracy rates for people over 15 are nearly triple the city average. Additionally, shockingly large portions of the population lack access to garbage collection and sewer services, with human waste flowing directly onto streets. These conditions create a vicious cycle. Research by UFRJ professor Felicia Shrike demonstrates that lack of opportunity drives young people toward drug trafficking as their only path to respect and survival. One mother of six told Shrike that three of her children became involved in trafficking, leading her to question whether she had failed them. ## Mental Health Consequences The chronic violence takes severe psychological tolls on residents. Sociologist Natalia Fazzioni Helou notes that residents experience elevated rates of depression and panic disorders. Doctors Without Borders identified these mental health issues as early as 2007, with psychologist Milena Osório reporting that anxiety disorders and depression were prevalent because residents couldn't openly process grief and loss. ## The Broader Picture While over 15,000 Army soldiers were deployed to secure Olympic venues, Alemão residents remained largely neglected. The favela's situation illustrates how inadequate government services, police violence, poverty, and limited opportunities create interconnected crises that security measures alone cannot resolve. As resident Cátia Souza poignantly observed, it's difficult for people to envision better futures when sewage flows beneath their windows.

Kazakhstan’s GDP grew 2.5 percent from January to October, Minister of National Economy Alibek Kuantyrov said at a Nov. 15 government meeting. Foreign trade turnover rose 35 percent in January-September to $98.4 billion, driven by a 47.5 percent increase in exports to $63.8 billion, including a 37.5 percent rise in processed goods exports. Imports climbed 16.5 percent to $34.6 billion. Finance Minister Yerulan Zhamaubayev said the state budget collected 12.4 trillion tenge, or 104 percent of plan. Prime Minister Alikhan Smailov said the economy is growing moderately, with manufacturing, engineering, agriculture, and fixed-asset investment all up.

# Kazakhstan's Economic Growth Summary Kazakhstan's GDP grew 2.5 percent from January to October, according to Minister of National Economy Alibek Kuantyrov. Foreign trade turnover increased 35 percent to $98.4 billion in January-September, with exports rising 47.5 percent to $63.8 billion and imports reaching $34.6 billion. The state budget received 12.4 trillion tenge, exceeding targets by 4 percent. Manufacturing production increased 4.3 percent, mechanical engineering grew 7.7 percent, and agriculture expanded 8 percent. Prime Minister Alikhan Smailov noted the economy maintains moderate growth, with fixed asset investments rising 6.7 percent during the reporting period.

Ethiopia has emerged from a difficult period through determined diplomatic efforts and the support of friendly countries, according to Ambassador Taye Atseke Selassie in an interview with the Ethiopian News Agency on December 29, 2022. He said the past two years were especially hard for the country because of an unexpected internal conflict, but Ethiopia was able to withstand the pressure through perseverance, national unity, and international backing. Taye said many African nations and other countries recognized that the conflict was an internal matter that should first be resolved by Ethiopians themselves. He criticized some international institutions and leaders who, in his view, doubted Ethiopia’s ability to solve its own problems. Despite those predictions, he said Ethiopia demonstrated resilience, wisdom, and commitment, and ultimately “the country has prevailed and our people have triumphed.” He explained that although the conflict in the northern part of the country was domestic, it was taken directly to the UN Security Council, forcing Ethiopia to defend itself in the international arena. This, he said, required major diplomatic effort to correct misunderstandings, explain Ethiopia’s position, and defend the country’s sovereignty and territorial integrity. He added that some in the international community feared the conflict could spill over into neighboring countries and destabilize Ethiopian politics. The ambassador also pointed to reforms over the past four years as evidence that Ethiopia’s differences can be addressed through civilized political dialogue. He said the country now has strong relations with many nations, despite previous misunderstandings and misrepresentations of facts. Looking ahead, Taye said Ethiopia is in a better position to rebuild and strengthen bilateral ties. He noted goodwill from several countries, especially the United States and some European states, and called for renewed, rejuvenated, and reinvigorated relations through cooperation and other diplomatic mechanisms.

The visit comes as the two countries deepen long-standing ties built on history, culture, and economics and formalized in the 2003 Strategic Partnership Agreement. Cooperation is expanding in technology, pharmaceuticals, and cultural exchanges, with Indian tourism to Iran rising 30% in 2022. North Carolina Attorney General Jeff Jackson has sued the U.S. Department of Education over its decision to terminate nearly $50 million in federal school funding, saying the move was unlawful and would harm students and staff across the state. The lawsuit claims the department violated the Administrative Procedure Act, federal education rules, and the Constitution by trying to control federal spending, which the complaint says is Congress’s authority, not an executive agency’s. The funding was awarded through the Full-Service Community Schools (FSCS) program, which supports about 23,000 students in North Carolina, including in counties heavily affected by Hurricane Helene. Jackson’s office said the U.S. Department of Education notified the state on Dec. 12 that the grants would end on Dec. 31. The lawsuit argues that such a sudden cutoff would force schools to shut down programs and possibly lay off staff in the middle of the school year. Jackson said the department had already approved the schools’ plans and that districts relied on that approval to hire staff and build programs. “Our kids deserve better,” he said, calling the cut “a surprise” and saying it came with “virtually no notice and no allegation of misuse.” According to the attorney general’s office, the grants help rural and under-resourced schools expand learning opportunities, address adverse childhood experiences, retain teachers, and improve student achievement. They also fund early childhood education, literacy efforts, family programming, and college- and career-exposure activities such as college tours and trade presentations. Congress authorized the FSCS program under the Elementary and Secondary Education Act and the Every Student Succeeds Act. North Carolina received more than $49.8 million through the program for the North Carolina Community Schools Coalition, which planned to serve 55 schools in 18 districts over five years. Jackson’s office said the funding also helped schools respond to Hurricane Helene by securing temporary housing and transportation for families and students.

# North Carolina Sues U.S. Department of Education Over Funding Termination North Carolina Attorney General Jeff Jackson filed a lawsuit against the U.S. Department of Education for unlawfully terminating nearly $50 million in federal education funding for public schools. The department notified North Carolina on December 12 that grants would be terminated effective December 31. The lawsuit alleges the department's actions violate the Administrative Procedure Act, federal education regulations, and the Constitution, which grants Congress—not executive agencies—authority over federal spending. The funding was awarded through the Full-Service Community Schools (FSCS) program, which supports approximately 23,000 students, including those in areas impacted by Hurricane Helene. Jackson argues the abrupt cuts would force schools to shut down programs and potentially lay off staff mid-school year without warning or allegations of misuse. He stated: "Our kids deserve better. A surprise cut of nearly $50 million from rural schools, with virtually no notice and no allegation of misuse, is unlawful and harmful." The $49.8 million in grants was distributed to the North Carolina Community Schools Coalition, which planned to serve 55 schools across 18 school districts over five years. The program supports rural and under-resourced communities by expanding learning opportunities, addressing childhood trauma, improving literacy, and providing college and career exposure. Schools used flexibility granted by the program to address diverse community needs, including food insecurity, after-school programs, health services, and housing assistance. Following Hurricane Helene, funds helped secure temporary housing and transportation for displaced students. Jackson emphasized that the Department of Education had already reviewed and approved how schools would use the funding when grants were awarded, and schools relied on that approval to hire staff and develop programs.

Sunrise New Energy Co., Ltd. (NASDAQ: EPOW) announced that it has been selected to supply anode materials for a 2.5 GW Integrated Generation, Grid, and Energy Storage (IGGES) project, securing an order valued at about $16 million. The signing ceremony took place on September 16 at the 20th China-ASEAN Expo and China-ASEAN Business and Investment Summit, which was attended by Chinese Premier Li Qiang. Participants included Shenzhen Zhuhai New Energy Co., Ltd., Guangxi Longyuan Power Group Corporation Limited, China Railway Construction Corporation Limited, and the People’s Government of Tiandong County, Baise, Guangxi. The IGGES project is designed to improve energy system efficiency, increase renewable energy use, reduce dependence on fossil fuels, and boost grid flexibility and reliability. Sunrise (Guizhou) New Energy Materials Co., Ltd. will supply 3,000 tons of anode materials for the initial phase. The 2.5 GW project is a pilot for a larger 50 GW IGGES rollout planned over the next five years, during which Sunrise expects to provide a total of 60,000 tons of anode materials. Chairman Haiping Hu said the contract represents a substantial and stable order and strengthens Sunrise’s role in the energy storage industry.

On May 14, 2025, Fulani ethnic militias carried out coordinated attacks in Nigeria’s Plateau state that killed eight Christians and destroyed large areas of farmland, according to International Christian Concern. The assaults hit predominantly Christian farming communities in two counties and were described by local leaders as part of an ongoing campaign to drive Christians off their ancestral lands. In Wereng camp, Riyom County, gunmen reportedly entered the area around midnight and opened fire on sleeping families. A survivor told ICC that the attackers “shot anyone they saw,” with many of the victims being children and elderly people. The raid left eight Christians dead, while homes were torched, food supplies looted, and survivors injured, traumatized, and displaced. Local witnesses said the attack was unprovoked and deliberate. That same day in Kpachudu village, Bassa County, Fulani herdsmen reportedly moved into cultivated fields under armed protection and unleashed cattle to destroy crops. More than 300 hectares, or roughly 740 acres, of farmland were damaged, including maize, cabbage, potatoes, and hot peppers that were near harvest. Farmers said the destruction deepened already severe poverty and threatened their ability to survive. Officials and community leaders condemned the attacks as more than ordinary farmer-herder conflict. Dr. Joshua Riti, a local administrator, called it a “genocidal campaign” and said communities were being systematically wiped out. Farmers described heavy financial losses and claimed attackers often return at night after reports are made. One farmer said no Fulani attackers were arrested, while another accused the military of siding with them and arresting Christians when cattle die, but not holding anyone accountable for burning homes and food stores. Ezekiel Bini of the Irigwe Youth Movement said local youth are regularly detained while attackers go free, and he urged a ban on open grazing. A Nigeria Civil Defense Corps Agro Rangers member confirmed security forces were present but offered no details. Hon. John Araye, a former Bassa County official, said the attacks are a strategic effort to displace Christian communities and warned that without government intervention, the people have no future. Local leaders are calling for diplomatic pressure, humanitarian aid, advocacy, and prayer for Christians in Nigeria.

# Summary: Christian Persecution in Nigeria's Middle Belt On May 14, 2025, Fulani ethnic militias launched coordinated attacks against Christian farming communities in Nigeria's Plateau state, killing eight people and destroying over 740 acres of farmland. The violence represents an escalating campaign of persecution targeting Christian communities through killings, arson, and economic sabotage. ## The Attacks In Wereng camp, Riyom County, gunmen attacked sleeping families around midnight, killing mostly elderly people and children. Survivors reported no provocation preceded the assault. Attackers torched homes and looted food supplies, leaving survivors injured and displaced. Simultaneously, in Kpachudu village, Bassa County, armed Fulani herdsmen deliberately destroyed cultivated farmland by allowing cattle to trample crops including maize, cabbage, potatoes, and peppers—most near harvest. The destruction devastated over 300 hectares, pushing vulnerable farming families deeper into poverty. ## Economic and Humanitarian Impact Farmers reported catastrophic losses. Ibrahim Danjuma lost over 10 million naira, while others described deliberate destruction patterns followed by retaliatory killings when communities report incidents. The destruction of farmland threatens the survival of the Irigwe, a predominantly Christian indigenous agrarian group in Plateau and Kaduna states. ## Accountability Concerns Local leaders allege security force complicity or indifference. Youth movement leaders report that Christian community members face detention while Fulani attackers remain unpunished. Military personnel allegedly side with attackers, arresting Christians over livestock deaths while ignoring village burnings. Nigeria Civil Defense Corps representatives declined substantive comment despite their presence in affected areas. ## Calls for Action Local administrators characterize the violence as "genocidal campaign" rather than farmer-herder conflict. Leaders demand international intervention, humanitarian aid, advocacy, and a government ban on open grazing. The Irigwe Youth Movement and community representatives emphasize that without government intervention, Christian communities face existential threats and displacement from ancestral lands.

The article recounts difficult consular duties faced by U.S. diplomat Sundwall while serving in Panama. He says he once had to inform a family in the United States that their relative had died, but they declined to travel for the burial, though they sent money. Because no one else was willing to attend, Sundwall arranged the cremation and honored the woman’s wish to have her ashes scattered over the graves of her two husbands. That same year, he also visited two U.S. citizens in a Panamanian jail, described as Satanist killers, to check that they were being treated humanely and to pass messages to their families. The most painful case, however, involved an Indiana couple who had adopted a severely burned and abandoned Panamanian girl. When they tried to fly her to the United States, the airline refused to let her board because she had no U.S. visa. Although the child was now the daughter of American citizens, she remained a Panamanian national and could not enter under humanitarian parole. Sundwall explained that the couple had completed the adoption process in Panama but had not done the required American paperwork. He told them they would need to return home, complete the full adoption process with social-worker review, and then apply for an immigrant visa so the girl could later become a permanent resident and eventually a U.S. citizen.

# Summary Diplomat Sundwall recounts challenging experiences from his tour in Panama, illustrating the complex responsibilities of consular officials. He describes arranging the cremation and burial of an elderly American woman whose family refused to participate, demonstrating his commitment to serving citizens abroad. Sundwall also visited U.S. citizens imprisoned in Panama, including two Satanist killers, to ensure humane treatment and facilitate family communication. Another significant case involved an American couple who adopted a burned and abandoned Panamanian girl but were unable to bring her home because she lacked a U.S. entry visa. Though the adoptive parents had completed Panamanian paperwork and scheduled critical medical treatment including reconstructive surgery, they had neglected U.S. immigration procedures. Sundwall faced the difficult task of explaining that the Immigration and Naturalization Service would not grant humanitarian parole without proper documentation. He advised them that they must return home, complete a formal adoption application involving social worker home visits, and file an immigrant visa petition to establish the girl as a permanent resident and eventual citizen. These episodes exemplify the demanding situations diplomats navigate while balancing humanitarian concerns with legal requirements.
