Ethiopian police said Sunday they had arrested 364 people suspected of involvement in recent ethnic violence that killed at least 26 people. In a joint statement, the Addis Ababa and Oromia police said the arrests were tied to last weekend’s unrest in Burayu, a town on the outskirts of the capital, where violence between local ethnic Oromos and other communities also displaced about 4,500 people. Police said 219 of the suspects were brought before Ethiopia’s Federal High Court on Saturday for preliminary hearings. The detainees are suspected of crimes including murder, assault, arson, rape and robbery. The Burayu attack followed earlier clashes in Addis Ababa between local residents and youth from surrounding Oromo areas who came to celebrate the return of the exiled leader of the Oromo Liberation Front, a rebel group that has long fought for Oromo self-determination. Addis Ababa is ethnically mixed but lies within Oromia regional state. On Monday, thousands protested the killings and property damage, demanding government protection for civilians. Five people were later shot dead during confrontations between police and demonstrators. Police commissioner Zeynu Jemal said some people tried to loot under the cover of protests and attempted to seize officers’ weapons.

# Summary Ethiopian police arrested 364 individuals suspected of involvement in ethnic violence that killed at least 26 people in Burayu town, near Addis Ababa, last weekend. The suspects face charges including murder, assault, arson, rape, and robbery, with 219 brought before the Federal High Court for preliminary hearings. The violence erupted between local Oromos and other ethnic groups, displacing approximately 4,500 people. The clashes followed recent tensions in Addis Ababa triggered by celebrations surrounding the return of an exiled Oromo Liberation Front (OLF) leader. The OLF has been fighting for Oromo self-determination. Addis Ababa, a 4-million-person ethnically-mixed city located within the Oromo-dominated Oromia region, subsequently experienced mass protests on Monday. Demonstrators demanded government action to protect civilians and prevent property damage. During the protests, police confrontations resulted in five deaths. Police Commissioner Zeynu Jemal claimed some protesters attempted to loot property and disarm officers.

The article reports several international developments. In Libya, a senior U.S. diplomat made the first visit by an American official of that rank since the U.N.-backed interim government was chosen in February. Acting Assistant Secretary of State for Near Eastern Affairs Joey Hood traveled to Tripoli and said the United States fully supports Libya’s transitional authorities and wants an end to foreign military interference in the country. Hood said the visit showed Washington’s commitment to helping Libya move toward an inclusive political settlement. He met with Prime Minister Abdul Hamid Dbeibah, Presidential Council head Mohammad Younes Menfi, and Foreign Minister Najla al-Manqoush. The government of national unity is expected to uphold a cease-fire signed in October and prepare Libya for elections planned for December 2021. In North Macedonia, the government ordered a Russian diplomat to leave the country, though it did not explain why. The Foreign Ministry said it had summoned the Russian ambassador last Friday and informed him that one of the senior diplomats at the Russian embassy had been declared persona non grata under Article 9 of the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations. The unnamed diplomat was given seven days to depart. A spokeswoman for the Russian Embassy in Skopje confirmed the expulsion and said Russian authorities were considering reciprocal measures. This was the second time North Macedonia has expelled a Russian diplomat; the first was in 2018, when it cited domestic security concerns and solidarity with Britain after the poisoning of former Russian spy Sergei Skripal. In Germany, police arrested a fifth suspect in the 2019 theft of historic jewels from Dresden’s Green Vault Museum. Prosecutors said the 22-year-old man, the twin brother of one of the men already in custody, was detained in Berlin on Monday evening. Four other suspects had been arrested earlier in Berlin in November and December. The men are accused of organized robbery and arson in connection with the Nov. 25, 2019, theft of a diamond brooch, a diamond epaulette and other treasures. Despite searches at more than a dozen locations, the stolen items have not been recovered. The Green Vault, founded in 1723, houses the treasury of Augustus the Strong of Saxony. The report also noted that relatives of the twins were convicted last year in the theft of the “Big Maple Leaf,” a giant Canadian gold coin stolen from Berlin’s Bode Museum in 2017. Off the coast of Tunisia, more than 50 migrants drowned or went missing when their boat capsized near Sfax, according to the Tunisian Defense Ministry. Thirty-three others were rescued by workers on an oil platform who saw the vessel sinking and alerted authorities. Navy units searched the area for survivors. The International Organization for Migration said the rescued migrants were all from Bangladesh and that the boat had departed from Zawara, Libya, on Sunday. The nationalities of those who died were not immediately known.

The 22-year-old man, the twin brother of an already-detained suspect, was arrested in Berlin on Monday evening. Four suspects were previously arrested in November and December for the November 25, 2019 theft of a large diamond brooch, epaulette, and other treasures. The arrested man had evaded capture twice previously. Investigators have searched over a dozen locations but have not recovered the stolen items. The suspects face charges of organized robbery and arson. Notably, relatives of the twin brothers were convicted in 2017 for stealing a 220-pound Canadian gold coin from Berlin's Bode Museum. ## Oil Rig Crew Rescues Migrants Off Tunisia Over 50 migrants drowned or disappeared when their boat capsized off Tunisia's southeast coast on Monday, while 33 others were rescued by workers from an oil platform. The Tunisian Defense Ministry reported that platform personnel witnessed the boat going under and alerted authorities, prompting navy search operations. According to the International Organization for Migration, all 33 survivors were from Bangladesh. The vessel had departed from Zawara, Libya, on Sunday. The nationalities of the deceased remain unclear.

A new Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) report says Somalia has the world’s worst record for solving journalist murders, ranking first on its annual global impunity index for the third year in a row. The index measures unsolved, work-related murders of journalists over the previous 10 years as a share of each country’s population. In the decade ending August 31, 2017, Somalia had 26 unsolved cases, while South Sudan and Nigeria also appeared among the 12 worst countries, with five unsolved cases each. South Sudan ranked fourth and Nigeria 11th. The CPJ says impunity is especially common in conflict zones, where armed groups and weak institutions make attacks on journalists more likely and accountability less likely. The 12 countries on the list account for nearly 80 percent of all unsolved journalist murders worldwide during the period studied. The other countries on the index are Syria, Iraq, the Philippines, Mexico, Pakistan, Brazil, Russia, Bangladesh, and India. In Somalia, the killings are linked to the country’s long civil war and the insurgency by al-Shabaab. CPJ says both militants and government officials are implicated in the unresolved murders. The report notes that at least one journalist, Abdiaziz Ali, was killed since the previous index. He was shot in Mogadishu in September 2016 while walking home from his parents’ house, after reporting on civilian suffering in the conflict between government forces and al-Shabaab. Somalia has issued death sentences against at least three people accused of murdering journalists, but CPJ says President Mohamed Abdullahi Mohamed has not advanced justice in these cases despite voicing support for media freedom. In South Sudan, all five documented journalist murders remain unsolved. CPJ says no suspects have been identified or convicted. The report highlights a January 2015 ambush in Western Bahr al Ghazal state, where five journalists traveling in a politician’s convoy were shot, attacked with machetes, and burned. CPJ also says journalists there have faced detention, harassment, and physical attacks, and that the government has not responded to UNESCO inquiries about the cases. In Nigeria, CPJ attributes the five unsolved murders to Boko Haram and unknown attackers. The report also cites continuing threats against journalists, including the June abduction and beating of editor Charles Otu after critical reporting on the Ebonyi state government. One example of an earlier killing is Zakariya Isa, a reporter and cameraman for state-run Nigeria Television Authority, whom Boko Haram said it killed in 2011.

# Africa's Crisis: Journalists Murdered With Impunity Somalia has the world's worst record for unsolved journalist murders, according to the Committee to Protect Journalists' annual "global impunity index." The country leads for the third consecutive year with 26 unsolved cases spanning a decade ending August 31, 2017. Three African nations appear among the 12 countries worldwide with at least five unsolved work-related journalist murders. Besides Somalia, South Sudan ranks fourth with five cases, and Nigeria ranks 11th, also with five cases. Rankings are calculated by comparing unsolved cases over ten years against each country's population. **Root Causes** Somalia's killings stem from prolonged civil war and Al-Shabaab insurgency, with murders attributed to both militants and government officials. South Sudan's five journalists were killed in a 2015 ambush during factional fighting following independence. Nigeria's murders were perpetrated by Boko Haram militants and unknown assailants. The CPJ notes that "impunity thrives in conflict environments, where powerful actors use violent intimidation to control media coverage, while weak law enforcement increases attack likelihood." **Specific Cases** In Somalia, journalist Abdiaziz Ali was shot multiple times by motorbike-riding gunmen in September 2016 after reporting on civilian casualties in government-militant conflicts. Eight journalists from his outlet, Shabelle Media Network, have been murdered in the past decade. South Sudan has convicted no one for the five journalist murders documented by CPJ. In January 2015, five journalists were shot, attacked with machetes, and burned alive in an ambush while accompanying a politician's convoy. In Nigeria, Boko Haram claimed responsibility for murdering reporter Zakariya Isa in October 2011. Additional attacks include the 2018 abduction and beating of editor Charles Otu by thugs demanding he cease critical reporting. **Global Context** The twelve countries on the impunity index account for nearly 80 percent of worldwide unsolved journalist murders during the ten-year period. Non-African countries on the list include Syria, Iraq, Mexico, Pakistan, and others, highlighting this as a global crisis threatening press freedom and accountability.

Firefighters in Cape Town are battling an out-of-control wildfire on Table Mountain that began early Sunday on the slopes of Devil’s Peak and was driven by strong winds toward the city. On Monday, emergency workers started evacuating three 17-storey residential towers at Disa Park, while schools in nearby Vredehoek were also told to leave and homes housing travelling cabinet ministers in Walmer Estate were being cleared. About 250 firefighters are trying to contain the blaze, but helicopters have been grounded by the wind. Thick smoke has reduced visibility across the city centre. The fire has already damaged several properties, including parts of the University of Cape Town, where students evacuated residences after flames reached campus buildings, among them a library storing historic books and manuscripts. Other damaged sites include the hikers’ restaurant at Rhodes Memorial and Mostert Mill, South Africa’s oldest working mill. Two firefighters were hospitalized with burn injuries. City officials said one suspect was detained on Devil’s Peak amid concerns the fire may have been deliberately set.

# Wildfire Threatens Cape Town Residential Areas A wildfire burning on Table Mountain in Cape Town, South Africa, has forced emergency evacuations of three high-rise residential buildings and multiple other properties. The fire began Sunday morning on Devils' Peak slopes, spreading rapidly due to strong winds that have grounded firefighting helicopters. Approximately 250 firefighters are battling the uncontrolled blaze, which has damaged several significant structures, including a University of Cape Town library containing historic books and scripts, a historic restaurant, and South Africa's oldest working mill. Two firefighters sustained burn injuries requiring hospitalization. The fire has prompted evacuations of residential areas including Disa Park and Vredehoek, with all local schools ordered to evacuate. Heavy smoke obscures city visibility. Officials have detained one suspect on Devils' Peak, investigating whether the original fire was deliberately set and if additional fires were intentionally started.

Japan’s Finance Ministry has announced a larger-than-expected cut in super-long bond issuance, a move that could ease upward pressure on yields ahead of key auctions this week and help calm a market that has been under strain. The reduction may also be timely given the weekend U.S. strikes on Iranian nuclear sites, which have heightened geopolitical risk and could push oil prices and inflation higher, adding further pressure on long-dated Japanese government bond yields. Under the revised plan, sales of 20-, 30- and 40-year Japanese government bonds will be reduced by a total of 3.2 trillion yen, or about US$21.9 billion, through March next year. Officials presented the changes late Friday in a meeting with primary dealers. Market participants initially viewed the shift as supportive for super-long bonds, especially after a poorly received 20-year bond auction last month triggered a sharp rise in yields in Japan and spilled over into global markets. The 20-year maturity saw the biggest surprise: the planned cut is twice as large as earlier draft proposals seen by Bloomberg and other media. Strategists said the move was designed in part to reduce the risk of another weak 20-year auction on June 24 and to avoid a repeat of the volatility seen in May. The next 30-year bond auction is scheduled for July 3. Despite the favorable supply adjustment, analysts warned that Japan’s bond market still faces major headwinds. Consumer prices are rising at the fastest pace in several years, and an election this summer could increase pressure for more government spending. Some of the issuance cut is also being offset by a shift toward shorter-dated debt. Strategists at firms including Nomura and Sumitomo Mitsui Trust Asset Management said the key question is whether demand at the upcoming 20- and 30-year auctions is strong enough to stabilize liquidity and reduce volatility. The Finance Ministry’s move was the second policy response in a week to market stress, following the Bank of Japan’s decision to slow the pace of its market withdrawal from next year. An official approval of the revised issuance plan is expected early this week.

# Japan Cuts Long-End Bond Issuance to Stabilize Market Japan's Finance Ministry announced a significant reduction in super-long bond issuance totaling 3.2 trillion yen (approximately $21.9 billion) through March 2020, aimed at easing upward pressure on yields before an upcoming auction that could trigger market turmoil. The plan reduces sales of 20-, 30-, and 40-year bonds, with the 20-year reduction being twice larger than previously suggested in draft documents. This move comes after a poorly received 20-year bond auction in May caused volatility in both Japanese and global markets. The ministry presented the revised plan to primary dealers on Friday, with the 20-year auction scheduled for June 24 and the 30-year auction for July 3. Bond market strategists largely welcomed the announcement as a stabilizing factor. Analysts noted that the decision clarifies supply and demand dynamics for super-long government bonds. Naoya Hasegawa from Okasan Securities stated the revised plan would help calm trading in this key sector, while Shoki Omori from Mizuho Securities suggested the announcement was timed to prevent another failed auction and avert market volatility. However, challenges remain. Rising consumer prices at their fastest pace in several years, combined with an upcoming summer election likely to encourage government spending, continue to weigh on the bond market. Additionally, escalating military tensions in the Middle East pose risks through higher oil prices and inflation, potentially pressuring super-long yields. Concerns exist that the issuance cuts may shift rather than eliminate problems by increasing shorter-dated debt issuance. Some strategists questioned why the ministry aggressively reduced 20-year bonds rather than 30-year bonds, where supply and demand issues also exist. The revision represents the second policy response in a week. The Bank of Japan previously announced it would slow its market withdrawal from next year to ensure stability. Officials indicated the revised issuance plan would likely receive official approval early in the week following the announcement.

A South Korean appellate court on Thursday overturned a lower court ruling and rejected a request to publicly release diplomatic documents related to South Korea’s 2015 agreement with Japan over wartime sex slaves. The Seoul High Court said keeping the records confidential was appropriate because disclosing the behind-the-scenes negotiations could harm relations between Seoul and Tokyo. The lower court had previously ordered the documents released, citing the public’s right to know and the need for transparency in state affairs. But the appellate court said that if the documents were made public, Japan’s positions could be exposed without its consent, potentially causing serious damage to bilateral ties, diplomatic friction, and conflicts of interest. The court also warned that disclosure could undermine the South Korean government’s credibility and weaken its ability to negotiate in the future. It added that revealing only part of the negotiations could distort the overall intent of the consultations. The ruling comes at a time when South Korea and Japan are already facing strained relations, including tensions over a South Korean court decision involving Japanese wartime forced labor. The 2015 deal, reached under President Park Geun Hye, said the issue of Japan’s sexual enslavement of Korean women during World War II would be resolved “finally and irreversibly.” Under the agreement, Japanese Prime Minister Shinzo Abe issued an indirect apology and Japan provided 1 billion yen, or about $8.9 million, to support a foundation for surviving victims. However, the deal has been heavily criticized in South Korea for failing to secure a clear legal admission of responsibility from Japan and for being reached without consulting victims. The Moon Jae In government later called it seriously flawed and dissolved the foundation, which Japan viewed as a breach of the agreement. Lawyer Song Ki Ho, who sought disclosure of the documents, said he would consult victims before deciding whether to appeal.

# South Korean Court Blocks Disclosure of Sex Slave Deal Documents A South Korean appellate court rejected a request to publicly release diplomatic documents related to the 2015 agreement between South Korea and Japan regarding wartime sex slaves, overturning a lower court's decision. The Seoul High Court ruled that maintaining confidentiality of the documents was appropriate, arguing that revealing behind-the-scenes negotiation details could damage bilateral relations. The lower court had previously ordered disclosure to guarantee public transparency and the right to know. The 2015 agreement, negotiated under President Park Geun Hye's administration, aimed to "finally and irreversibly" resolve the issue of Japan's sexual enslavement of Korean women during World War II. The deal included an indirect apology from Japanese Prime Minister Shinzo Abe and Japan's contribution of 1 billion yen ($8.9 million) to a foundation supporting victims. However, the accord faced significant criticism in South Korea for failing to secure Japan's acknowledgment of legal responsibility and for not consulting victims before implementation. The subsequent liberal Moon Jae In government denounced the agreement as "seriously flawed" and dissolved the foundation last year—a move Japan viewed as a breach. Lawyer Song Ki Ho, who requested document disclosure in 2016, expressed disappointment with the court's decision, stating the court prioritized diplomatic ties over accountability. He pledged to continue pursuing Japan's formal acknowledgment of wrongdoing, apology, and compensation, pending consultation with sex slave victims. The ruling comes amid escalating tensions between Seoul and Tokyo over wartime forced labor issues.

Mingtang Hall in Luoyang, Henan Province, was one of the grandest wooden structures in ancient China and a symbol of imperial authority. Built in AD 688 by Wu Zetian, China’s only female emperor of the Tang Dynasty, the hall was also known as the “Palace of the God of Everything.” At 98 meters tall and covering 12,000 square meters, it was said to be the largest wooden structure in the world at the time and a peak achievement of Tang-era architecture. The hall served as a ritual center where rulers announced policies and expressed political doctrine. Wu designed it as a three-tiered structure with symbolic meanings: the square lower level represented the four seasons and was used for issuing laws; the 12-sided middle level symbolized the 12 hours of ancient Chinese timekeeping and was used for ancestor worship; and the circular top level, supported by nine dragons, functioned as a pavilion from which Wu could survey her realm. A massive central wooden pillar, 15 meters in circumference, acted as the building’s backbone, and Tang records say more than 1,000 workers were needed to move and raise it. Wu ordered the hall built shortly after taking power, seeking to legitimize her rule in a society where female emperors were unprecedented. She changed the reign title, created new words, promoted myths about herself, and placed Buddha images bearing her face across the empire. Despite officials’ objections, Mingtang Hall became her most ambitious statement of authority. She also commissioned her favored court companion, Xue Huaiyi, to build a nearby Sky Hall, or Tiantang Hall, to house a giant Buddha for religious ceremonies. Xue, once a street vendor selling medicine, rose to prominence after Wu had him shaved and disguised as a monk so he could enter the palace. Their relationship later soured. In AD 695, Xue Huaiyi, enraged and feeling sidelined as Wu took on increasingly younger favorites, set fire to both Mingtang Hall and Sky Hall, destroying them completely. More than 1,300 years later, the site was rediscovered during a construction project at the junction of Zhongzhou Road North and Dingding Road. Workers uncovered unusual bricks and an ancient wall, prompting excavation and a halt to the development. Archaeologists identified the remains as Mingtang Hall, confirming a monumental relic first linked to the nearby discovery of Sky Hall in 1975. The preserved site now features a glass cover over the octagonal foundation, and the local government has reconstructed Mingtang Hall and Sky Hall nearby at full scale, allowing visitors to view the ancient site and climb the rebuilt tower for panoramic views of modern Luoyang.

# Summary: China's Only Empress' Wooden Palace Mingtang Hall, built by Wu Zetian, China's only empress of the Tang Dynasty (AD 618-907), stands as a remarkable architectural achievement and symbol of her unprecedented rise to power. Constructed in AD 688 in Luoyang City, this wooden structure was the world's largest at the time, reaching 98 meters tall and covering 12,000 square meters. The hall's design reflected ancient Chinese cosmology and served as a ritual center for declaring political doctrines. Its three levels represented different concepts: the square base symbolized the four seasons and was used for issuing laws; the middle dodecagon level represented the twelve hours of ancient timekeeping and served as an ancestor worship site; and the round top level, supported by nine dragons, provided Wu a vantage point to observe her territory. A massive wooden post with a 15-meter circumference formed the structure's backbone, requiring over 1,000 workers to position. Wu's construction of Mingtang Hall was a bold political statement. As a woman assuming supreme power in feudal China, she employed various strategies to gain acceptance, including changing the reign's name, inventing new words, and spreading myths about herself. Despite officials' objections, she pursued this ambitious project as a cornerstone of her new era. The hall's fate became intertwined with court scandal. Wu commissioned her favored companion, Xue Huaiyi—a former medicine vendor disguised as a monk—to build the nearby Sky Hall for religious ceremonies. However, as Wu's attention shifted to younger men, the jealous Xue set fire to both structures in AD 695, destroying them completely. Approximately 1,300 years later, modern archaeology rediscovered the site when workers uncovered unusual bricks during a construction project. Subsequent excavations revealed an octagonal stylobate—the foundation of the giant wooden post—confirming the historical records. The discovery of Sky Hall's remains in 1975 further validated the accounts. Today, the original relic site is protected by a glass shield, allowing visitors to walk directly over the ancient foundation. The local government has reconstructed both Mingtang Hall and Sky Hall at their original size, enabling visitors to experience the structures as Wu did centuries ago and enjoy panoramic views of modern Luoyang City.

A New South Wales government inquiry has concluded that Australia’s devastating 2019-2020 bushfires were “clearly” fueled by climate change, while warning that extreme fire seasons are likely to become more frequent. The 436-page report was released Tuesday after months of consultation and expert testimony, following a disaster that burned for nine months until March and became one of the largest forest-fire events ever recorded. The fires were especially severe in New South Wales, where about 11,000 fires burned more than 5.5 million hectares, destroyed over 2,400 homes, and killed 26 people. The report said climate change, driven by increased greenhouse gas emissions, “clearly played a role” in creating the conditions that led to the fires and in sustaining the intense, prolonged burning. However, it also said it was impossible to determine the exact contribution of climate change because the crisis arose from a complex mix of factors, including years of drought, high winds, thunderstorms, and low humidity. The inquiry rejected claims that arson or poor forest management were the main causes. It found only 11 fires in New South Wales were deliberately lit by arsonists, and said many of the largest blazes were sparked by lightning in remote areas. The report also criticized those who dismissed climate change as irrelevant, saying the conditions were consistent with climate projections. Its recommendations focused on improving disaster preparedness and response, including better technology to detect remote fires sooner and more aerial water-bombing capacity to prevent fires from growing out of control. Officials said the scale of the disaster overwhelmed firefighting systems and warned Australians may need to adapt to “new extreme” conditions. The report comes as this year’s fire season is already underway, and a national Royal Commission is due to release its findings later this month.

# Summary Australia's devastating 2019-2020 bushfires were "clearly" fuelled by climate change, according to a government inquiry released Tuesday. The fires, among the largest ever recorded globally, burned for nine months through March 2020, destroying over 2,400 homes in New South Wales and killing 26 people. The blazes consumed 5.5 million hectares across the state. A comprehensive 436-page report by the New South Wales government explicitly linked climate change to the fires' severity, stating that increased greenhouse gas emissions "clearly played a role in the conditions that lead up to the fires." The report identified contributing factors including a years-long drought, high winds, thunderstorms, and low humidity. While acknowledging that climate change "does not explain everything," the authors noted that catastrophic conditions aligned with climate change projections. The inquiry rejected alternative explanations promoted by climate change skeptics. Only 11 of New South Wales' 11,000 fires were deliberately set by arsonists, while many major blazes resulted from lightning strikes in remote areas. With fire season already underway, authorities warned that extreme fires are "likely to become more frequent" and urged urgent action to limit future impacts. Recommendations focused on disaster response and mitigation, including improved detection technology for remote fires and increased aerial water-bombing capabilities. The report noted that fire authorities' systems were stretched beyond capacity during the crisis. Australia faces a broader challenge: many bushfire mitigation measures recommended in inquiries dating back to the 1930s remain unimplemented. A national Royal Commission is expected to release additional findings by month's end.

Dunedin City Council says it was not told in advance about a private Six60 concert in a Castle Street student accommodation courtyard where a balcony collapsed and injured 18 people. About 20 people were standing on the first-floor balcony when it gave way during the Friday night event, which drew around 1,500 attendees. Council inspectors had previously visited the site and found the building structurally sound and free of maintenance issues, but general manager of services and development Simon Pickford said the balcony was designed for only six or seven people. He said the concert was organized at very short notice, without the council, police, or the University of Otago being involved, and that the venue was not suitable for such a large crowd. WorkSafe said its investigators had also inspected the building and would decide early next week whether the incident fell within its jurisdiction. Councillor David Benson-Pope said students should not be blamed for the accident and argued it was a random event, while noting that recent bad behaviour in the area had often come from people with no connection to the university or Dunedin. He also said the university and authorities were working well together and that student behaviour had improved in recent years.

# Concert Balcony Collapse Raises Safety Concerns A balcony collapsed during a private Six60 concert at a Dunedin student accommodation block on Friday night, injuring 18 people. Approximately 20 people were standing on the first-floor balcony when it gave way, though the venue had hosted around 1,500 attendees total. The Dunedin City Council expressed concern that no advance notice was given to council staff, police, or Otago University. Council inspectors confirmed the building was structurally sound with no maintenance issues. However, the balcony was designed to hold only six or seven people maximum, making it unsuitable for the crowd size. Council general manager Simon Pickford attributed the accident partly to the event's last-minute organization and the inappropriate venue choice. Worksafe investigators also examined the building and will decide early next week whether the incident falls within their jurisdiction. Councillor David Benson-Pope defended students, characterizing the collapse as a random accident rather than reflecting broader safety issues. He noted that previous incidents in the city involved outsiders unconnected to the university.

At the sixth hearing in the Kyoto District Court, Shinji Aoba, the 45-year-old suspect in the 2019 Kyoto Animation arson attack, said he modeled the crime on a 2001 arson attack on a Takefuji Corp. branch in Hirosaki, Aomori Prefecture. He testified that he used gasoline to start the fire after learning from that earlier case. Aoba is facing murder and other charges. He said he targeted Kyoto Animation’s No. 1 studio in Kyoto’s Fushimi Ward because he believed that attacking a building where many people were working would cause many deaths. He also said he brought six knives to the scene because he expected someone might attack him after he poured the gasoline or try to stop him. Aoba added that he felt sympathy for former death-row inmate Tomohiro Kato, who carried out the 2008 Akihabara stabbing spree, and said he could not dismiss Kato’s misfortune as someone else’s problem. The July 18, 2019 attack killed 36 people, including leading animators, and injured 32 others. Aoba was also severely burned. He admitted he hesitated at the last moment because he knew what he was doing was wrong, saying, “Even a villain like me has a scruple.” He also said he acted out of resentment because Kyoto Animation allegedly rejected his novel and stole its content. The trial is now centered on his criminal responsibility and mental state.

# Summary Shinji Aoba, 45, the suspect in the July 2019 arson attack on Kyoto Animation's Studio No. 1, revealed during his sixth court hearing that he used gasoline as a weapon after referencing a 2001 arson attack on a Takefuji Corp. branch in Hirosaki. He deliberately targeted the studio because he believed many people would die in the crowded building, and brought six knives anticipating potential confrontation. Aoba expressed sympathy for Tomohiro Kato, a death-row inmate who committed a 2008 stabbing spree in Tokyo's Akihabara district, stating he identified with Kato's unsuccessful life. The attack killed 36 people, including leading animators, and injured 32 others. Aoba himself sustained severe burns. Aoba claimed he harbored malice toward KyoAni for rejecting his award-seeking novel and allegedly stealing its content. He acknowledged last-minute hesitation, saying even he possessed some moral conscience. The trial now focuses on criminal liability and sentencing. The prosecution argues Aoba bears full responsibility, while the defense contends he should be acquitted or receive a lighter sentence due to mental incompetence or diminished capacity.

At least three people died and 97 were injured when a fire broke out Saturday in a 10-story apartment building in a northern Seoul suburb. Five were critically hurt. Investigators had not ruled out arson, with the blaze apparently starting in a mailbox. Some residents were rescued by helicopter.

# Apartment Fire in South Korea Kills Three A fire at a 10-story apartment building in Seoul's northern suburbs killed at least three people and injured 97 others on Saturday. Five injured victims remained in critical condition. The fire allegedly started in a mailbox, with arson not ruled out. Authorities rescued several people by helicopter from the building's roof.

After the anti-terrorism court sentenced Imran Ali to death for the rape and murder of seven-year-old Zainab, the victim’s mother, Nusrat Bibi, demanded that the punishment be carried out publicly at the place where her daughter was taken. Zainab’s brother also urged the government to amend the constitution to allow a public hanging. Her father, Haji Ameen, said he was satisfied with the court’s verdict. Zainab’s killing last month triggered nationwide outrage, including riots in Kasur and widespread demands for justice on social media. Officials said DNA evidence linked Ali to the crime and similar cases. At least 12 rape-and-murder cases have been reported in Kasur over two years.

# Summary An anti-terrorism court sentenced Imran Ali to death for the murder of 7-year-old Zainab in Pakistan. The victim's mother, Nusrat Bibi, demanded his public execution at the location where he killed her daughter. Her brother requested constitutional amendments to enable public hanging, while her father expressed satisfaction with the verdict. Zainab's murder sparked widespread outrage across Pakistan, triggering riots in Kasur, with thousands storming police stations and setting fires to politicians' homes. DNA evidence linked Ali to the crime and connected him to multiple similar cases. Ali confessed to eight rape and murder cases, though at least twelve such crimes have occurred in the Kasur region over two years.

G20 delegates attending the Tourism Working Group meeting in Siliguri, West Bengal, took part in a cultural night and gala dinner on Sunday, where they danced after earlier joining a yoga session. Around 130 participants are attending the three-day meeting, held from April 1 to 3, 2023, in Siliguri and nearby Darjeeling, a major tourist destination in the Himalayan foothills. On the first day, delegates also experienced tea plucking, highlighting the region’s tourism and cultural attractions. The meeting is focused on discussing ways to revive the tourism sector, which was badly affected by the COVID-19 pandemic. Harshvardhan Shringla, the G20 chief coordinator, said Prime Minister Narendra Modi wanted India to be showcased to the world ahead of the G20 summit in September and emphasized that G20 meetings should not be limited to New Delhi because every part of India has its own heritage, beauty, and culture.

# G20 Tourism Working Group Celebrates in West Bengal The G20 Tourism Working Group held its second meeting in Siliguri, West Bengal from April 1-3, 2023, with approximately 130 delegates attending. On the first day, participants engaged in tea plucking activities. The second day featured a yoga session followed by a cultural night and gala dinner where delegates danced together. The meeting focuses on reviving the tourism sector following the COVID-19 pandemic's impact. Darjeeling and Siliguri, located in the Himalayan foothills, were selected as hosts due to their significance as major tourist destinations. G20 Chief-coordinator Harshvardhan Shringla emphasized Prime Minister Narendra Modi's directive to showcase India's diverse regions and cultures during G20 meetings, rather than limiting events to New Delhi, ahead of India's hosting of the G20 summit in September 2023.

Odessa police responded early Saturday morning to a disturbance at Billy’s Zodiac Club, 400 S. Dixie Blvd., where they found 26-year-old Lester Starling III dead from a gunshot wound. Two other men, 22-year-old Tyrone Davis and 18-year-old Kevin Shorter, were taken to Medical Center Hospital with gunshot wounds, though an MCH employee later said neither was listed as a patient Monday afternoon. On Sunday evening, police were called back to the club for a possible structure fire, but officers did not see flames when they arrived. City spokeswoman Andrea Goodson said fire marshal investigators later found evidence of fire in several small areas of the roof, but the cause remains under investigation and arson has not been ruled out. Police spokesman Cpl. Steve LeSueur said there is no reason to believe the shooting and fire are connected, though investigators are monitoring the fire marshal’s findings. Police have issued an arrest warrant for 29-year-old Kortney Lynn Powell in connection with the shooting, but he has not been found. The club has previously been the scene of fatal shootings in 2006 and 2008.

# Club Shooting and Fire Summary Early Saturday morning, Odessa police responded to Billy's Zodiac Club after a disturbance call. Officers discovered 26-year-old Lester Starling III dead from a gunshot wound, while two other men—Tyrone Davis, 22, and Kevin Shorter, 18—were hospitalized with gunshot injuries. Both injured men were later discharged from Medical Center Hospital. The following evening, police were called about a potential structure fire at the same club. While no active fire was visible upon arrival, fire marshal investigators found evidence of small fires on the roof. Authorities have not ruled out arson as the cause and continue investigating. Police obtained an arrest warrant for 29-year-old Kortney Lynn Powell in connection with the shooting. Powell remains at large with no leads on his whereabouts. He has an extensive criminal history including drug possession, reckless driving, and aggravated assault charges. Police stated they have no reason to believe the shooting and fire are connected, though they're monitoring the fire investigation. The club has a violent history, with two previous fatal shootings in its parking lot in 2006 and 2008.

Poland’s ruling conservative Law and Justice party blamed “hooligans” and provocateurs for violence at Warsaw’s annual Independence Day march, which it has long supported as a patriotic event. During Wednesday’s far-right-organized rally, dozens of riot police and a photographer were injured in clashes, and an apartment, a shop, and an office door were set on fire. City officials estimated the damage at tens of thousands of zlotys. The events prompted widespread condemnation and renewed calls to ban the march. Although the city had prohibited this year’s event because of pandemic restrictions, participants still gathered. The government defended freedom of assembly while distancing itself from the violence. The unrest came amid daily nationwide protests against the government over a tightened abortion law. Nov. 11 marks Poland’s restoration of sovereignty after World War I.

# Poland Blames Violence at Far-Right March on Hooligans During Warsaw's Independence Day march organized by far-right groups, violence erupted Wednesday, injuring dozens of riot police and a photographer. Participants set fire to an apartment, shop, and office door, causing tens of thousands of zlotys in damage. The incident drew widespread condemnation and calls to ban the march. Poland's ruling Law and Justice party, which promotes these annual marches despite their history of violence, defended them as patriotic while condemning the specific violent acts. Government spokesman Piotr Mueller attributed the incidents to hooligans and emphasized Poland's commitment to freedom of assembly and expression. City authorities had banned this year's march due to pandemic restrictions. The violence occurred amid ongoing nationwide protests demanding the government's resignation, sparked by Poland's newly tightened abortion law—among Europe's strictest. November 11 commemorates Poland's post-World War I independence.

Hungary booked its place at Euro 2024 in dramatic fashion on Thursday, qualifying for its third consecutive European Championship after a stoppage-time own goal in a 2-2 draw with Bulgaria in a match overshadowed by violent unrest outside the stadium in Sofia. The result left Hungary two points clear of Serbia in Group G after seven matches and secured the point it needed to advance. The match was played in an empty stadium, but thousands of Bulgarian fans gathered outside to protest the national federation and its handling of the team’s poor results. Anger over Bulgaria’s recent humiliating defeats, including losses to Albania in a friendly and Lithuania in qualifying, had already fueled calls for a nationwide protest and demands for resignations. The decision to stage the game behind closed doors made the situation worse. Outside the stadium, Bulgarian fans threw makeshift bombs, stones and plastic bottles at police. Officers responded with a water cannon after trash cans were set on fire in Sofia. Emergency services said more than 20 fans and five police officers were injured, and four fans were hospitalized with serious injuries. Police detained about 40 people and seized pyrotechnics, signal pistols, metal pipes and other prohibited items. On the field, Bulgaria appeared to be on course for its first qualifying win. Martin Ádám gave Hungary an early lead in the 10th minute, but Bulgaria came back through Spas Delev in the 24th minute and Kiril Despodov from the penalty spot in the 79th. With Bulgaria leading late, defender Alex Petkov turned the ball into his own net seven minutes into stoppage time, handing Hungary the equalizer and the decisive point. Both teams finished with 10 men. Bulgaria’s Valentin Antov was sent off in the 37th minute after a second yellow card, and Hungary’s Milos Kerkez was also dismissed in the 57th for a second booking. Hungary, coached by Marco Rossi, had also failed to clinch qualification in its previous match, drawing 2-2 in Lithuania after falling two goals behind. The team’s unbeaten run extended to 11 matches, with its last defeat coming against Italy in the Nations League in September 2022. Bulgaria remained last in the group with two points. Elsewhere, Slovakia also qualified for Euro 2024 by finishing second in Group J after a 4-2 home win over Iceland. Lukas Haraslin scored twice, and Slovakia advanced to its third straight European Championship. Portugal, already qualified, beat Liechtenstein 2-0, with Cristiano Ronaldo scoring his 128th international goal and fifth in his last three matches. He now has 10 goals in qualifying, tied with Belgium’s Romelu Lukaku. Spain, already through, stayed atop Group A with a 3-1 win over Cyprus, while Scotland, also already qualified, drew 2-2 at Georgia. Austria beat Estonia 2-0 to move two points ahead of Belgium in Group F, though both had already secured Euro 2024 spots.

Swiss investigators are set to question the French owners of the Le Constellation bar in Crans-Montana, where a New Year’s Eve fire killed 40 people and injured 116. Jacques and Jessica Moretti, who owned and managed the bar, will be interviewed Friday by the public prosecutor’s office in Sion, according to sources close to the case. This will be the first time they are formally questioned since charges were announced Saturday. The couple face allegations of manslaughter by negligence, bodily harm by negligence and arson by negligence. They have not been detained and said in a statement Tuesday that they were “devastated and overwhelmed with grief” and would fully cooperate with investigators, insisting they would not try to evade the matter. Prosecutors believe the fire may have started when champagne bottles fitted with sparklers were raised too close to sound-insulating foam on the ceiling in the bar’s basement area. Questions have also emerged about fire safety compliance: municipal authorities admitted on Tuesday that the bar had not undergone fire safety inspections since 2019. The case has drawn further scrutiny because of the Morettis’ background and property holdings. French newspaper Le Parisien reported that Jacques Moretti had previously served jail time in southern France on charges linked to prostitution and kidnapping. Lawyers for victims’ families welcomed the planned questioning, saying it could mark a renewed push in the investigation. After the inquiry ends, the Wallis regional prosecutor will decide whether to bring an indictment or close the case.

Patrick County officials and state and federal leaders announced an ambitious plan to reopen the long-closed Stuart hospital in 2023 and to bring two mobile medical units to the county in the near future, using a $600,000 federal grant to expand local health care access. The announcement drew more than 30 people to the Stuart site where Pioneer Community Hospital of Patrick once operated before closing in 2017 after filing for bankruptcy the year before because of financial troubles. County leaders described the announcement as a major turning point. Patrick County Director of Economic Development Sean Adkins said that just a year earlier the county had no hospital and no clear path toward one, leaving residents, visitors and local businesses with very limited access to adequate medical care. He said the county had now reached the point where the future Foresight Hospital of Patrick County was expected to open in 2023. Adkins also credited U.S. Sen. Mark Warner and U.S. Rep. Morgan Griffith for helping make the project possible, saying the county would receive a $600,000 federal grant check and two mobile health units. Patrick County Emergency Management Services Director Scottie Cassell explained that the mobile units could begin operating once staff training is complete. He described them as “a doctor’s office on wheels” that could travel wherever care is needed. If a patient’s condition is more serious than the staff can treat, the patient would be transferred to another facility. William Clark, chairman of the Patrick County Economic Development Authority, said the effort to bring the hospital back had been underway for years and gained momentum after the original hospital closed. He said that without congressional support and earmarked federal spending, the county would not have reached this point. Nancy Bell, a population health manager with the Virginia Department of Health, described how the county’s broader health planning effort began from almost nothing. She said that when she started working on community health assessments and improvement plans, she found that other nearby localities already had established processes, but Patrick County did not even know what those processes were. Bell said she had to start from scratch, meeting with county leaders, economic development officials, tourism representatives and others to build a team. She said the county later worked with Community Health Solutions of Richmond on a telehealth demand study and launched telehealth in rescue squad stations. Bell compared the county’s health care system to Legos, saying the hospital and mobile units were major pieces that would make a big difference. Foresight Health CEO and General Counsel Joseph Hylak-Reinholtz said reopening the hospital sooner would benefit the community more than waiting through regulatory delays. He said the company looked forward to a long partnership with Patrick County to restore quality health care. Hylak-Reinholtz said Foresight’s mission had been to serve areas of need and underserved communities, and that it had expanded that mission into rural health care, bringing back services lost when the hospital closed in 2017. County Board of Supervisors Chairman Clyde DeLoach called the announcement a day to celebrate and said he looked forward to celebrating again when the hospital actually opens. He said he was excited about the future of health care in the county. Griffith said rural health care is difficult everywhere, and Patrick County is no exception. He noted the challenges of attracting and keeping providers and securing enough resources. He said those burdens require action from elected officials at every level, and that the mobile health units were the result of bipartisan cooperation and seizing available opportunities. He also emphasized that party affiliation should not matter when it comes to meeting Patrick County’s health care needs. Warner echoed that bipartisan message, calling the effort a team project and praising Delegate Wren Williams for helping expedite the process. Warner said reopening hospitals is extraordinarily difficult, noting that nearly 1,000 rural hospitals have closed across the country over the past 25 years and almost none have reopened. He said the timeline for reopening the Stuart hospital was very aggressive, but he pledged federal support to help the county meet the goal of reopening by 2023. Overall, the announcement marked a significant step toward restoring hospital services in Patrick County after years without a local hospital, while also adding mobile and telehealth options to address ongoing rural health care challenges.

# Stuart Hospital to Reopen in 2023 with Federal Support and Mobile Health Units Patrick County celebrated a significant milestone in addressing its healthcare crisis as officials announced plans to reopen Stuart's Pioneer Community Hospital by 2023, alongside the arrival of two mobile health units funded by a $600,000 federal grant. ## Background and Current Situation Pioneer Community Hospital of Patrick in Stuart closed in 2017 after filing for bankruptcy the previous year due to financial hardships. Taunton is moving ahead with an effort to clear out blighted downtown properties and return them to productive use, with city officials saying the work is part of a broader central business revitalization strategy tied to the long-delayed renovation of City Hall. City Solicitor Jason D. Buffington said the removal of a white GMC flatbed truck that had been sitting behind 73 Main St. for years was another small but useful step. The truck, which had a toilet and trash on its bed and was described as an eyesore, disappeared before the city’s planned towing date. Buffington said the city had been preparing to remove it legally because it was parked on municipal property and appeared abandoned, but by the time the tow company was ready, it was already gone. The truck was connected in some way to former Taunton property owner Michael O’Donnell, who Buffington said had been involved with a number of problem properties that were eventually seized and cleaned up. In a Feb. 12 certified letter, Buffington notified Steven Simpson of 145 Winthrop St. that police records identified him as the last registered and titled owner of the GMC truck and gave him 10 days to remove it. Buffington then sent another letter on Feb. 20 to attorney and former city councilor Sherry Costa Hanlon, after someone in her office was contacted by Juanita Gallagher, who said that years earlier she or Simpson had hired Costa Hanlon to transfer the truck to O’Donnell. Buffington said no such transfer had been recorded, meaning Simpson remained the official owner of record. He said he never heard back from Costa Hanlon. The city’s efforts are part of a larger push to reclaim and redevelop several downtown buildings. One example is the former Rainforest Gardens Floral Shop at 65 Main St. The city took possession of that property in 2015 over unpaid back taxes and auctioned it off last summer. Buffington said city officials had done everything they could to work with the owner before taking action. Another nearby building, 73 Main St., formerly Main Street Pizzeria, is also headed for public auction after the state Land Court issued a judgment in February allowing the city to foreclose. Buffington said O’Donnell was the owner of record for 73 Main St., even though he never registered the deed of sale at the registry of deeds. O’Donnell had bought the site at public auction in 2012 for $115,000. A 2013 newspaper story had reported that two women signed a lease with O’Donnell to open a Dominican-style restaurant called Mama King there, but they later said they moved to another location because of disputes with him. Downtown redevelopment is also tied to the city’s plans for a renovated City Hall, which has been closed since an arson fire in 2010. Mayor Thomas Hoye Jr. has said he wants to acquire or take ownership of three adjoining apartment buildings behind and below Main Street, along Allans Avenue between Spring and Weir streets. He said demolishing them would help create parking and improve the look of the area around the future City Hall. The City Council approved the City Hall renovation in 2017, with the project expected to cost between $25 million and $26 million. One of the apartment buildings, at 27 Leonard Court, was owned by O’Donnell before the city seized it in December 2016 for unpaid taxes. Another, at 29 Leonard Court, was bought by the city in February for $255,000 from a Quincy couple after the council authorized the mayor to spend up to $262,000. The assessed value of that property is $224,300. Buffington said the city is hopeful it can reach an agreement with the owners of the third building, 30 Leonard Court, which registry records show belongs to Eduardo and Olga Almeida. He described them as responsible and said the city is trying to resolve the matter amicably, though he did not rule out eminent domain if necessary. Local business owners welcomed the cleanup. Jose Bejarano, owner of Tux Towne on Main Street, said he was happy when Taunton resident Ming Luc bought 65 Main St. last June. Bejarano said the property had become an eyesore, with junk stored there, and he hopes it will become a useful business again, perhaps a pizza shop or roast beef restaurant. Buffington said that is exactly the goal: to put these downtown properties back into productive commercial use.

Paris 2024 organizers have unveiled an unusual Olympic and Paralympic medal design: each medal will contain a small piece of iron from the Eiffel Tower. The medals, which will be awarded at the July 26-Aug. 11 Olympic Games and the Paralympics that follow, will feature a hexagonal, polished chunk of the landmark embedded in the center of each gold, silver, and bronze medal. Organizers say the design is meant to give athletes not only a prize for their achievements, but also a tangible piece of French history to take home. The idea was described Thursday by Paris Games officials as a “monumental” way to make the medals unique. While many Olympic champions, including Simone Biles and LeBron James, have accumulated multiple medals over the years, none of the roughly 36,600 medalists from previous Summer Games dating back to 1896 has owned one quite like these. Paris is aiming to make history through the competition itself and through the awards handed out afterward. The iron pieces are genuine fragments of the Eiffel Tower. The 330-meter-tall structure, built for the 1889 World’s Fair and originally intended to last only 20 years, has instead become one of the world’s most recognizable symbols and a long-standing emblem of Paris. The tower, which has been renovated and maintained over time, has also been part of Olympic history before, having appeared during the 1900 and 1924 Paris Games. According to Joachim Roncin, head of design for the Paris Games organizing committee, the metal pieces were taken from girders and other parts removed from the tower during renovation work and kept in storage. The concept came after organizers decided that the Eiffel Tower was the most universally recognized symbol of France. They approached the Eiffel Tower Operating Co. to ask whether a piece of the monument could be incorporated into the medals, and the company agreed. Roncin said the idea “became reality,” adding that “it’s really a bit of metal from the Eiffel Tower.” Before being used, the fragments were stripped of paint, polished, and varnished. Each piece weighs 18 grams, or about two-thirds of an ounce. The hexagonal shape was chosen as a reference to France itself, which is often nicknamed “L’Hexagone” because of its outline. The medals were designed by Paris jewelry house Chaumet. Six small clasps holding the Eiffel Tower piece in place are meant to echo the tower’s 2.5 million rivets. The medals are made from recycled metal, not newly mined material. Around the central iron insert are disks of gold, silver, or bronze with a crinkled surface designed to catch the light. The Olympic medals are stamped with “Paris 2024,” the Games logo, and the five Olympic rings. The Paralympic medals will carry the Paralympic logo, known as the Agitos, and the other side will show the Eiffel Tower from below. For visually impaired athletes, the medals include Braille text reading “Paris 2024” and distinct edge notches indicating gold, silver, or bronze. Paris organizers say the design is unprecedented. Olympic medals have often been relatively traditional, though the 2008 Beijing medals included inlaid jade disks. Paris is the first host city to place pieces of a famous monument inside the medals themselves. Roncin said the Eiffel Tower was chosen as “the cherry on the top” of the medal design and called the fragment “a piece of history.” The Paris Mint is producing 5,084 medals in total, including about 2,600 for the Olympics and 2,400 for the Paralympics, with extra medals held in reserve in case replacements are needed later, such as if medals are stripped after doping violations. Some extras may be sent to museums, while others could be destroyed. The medals vary by type. Gold medals weigh 529 grams and are not solid gold; they are made of silver plated with 6 grams of gold. Silver medals weigh 525 grams, and bronze medals weigh 455 grams and are made from a copper, tin, and zinc alloy. All medals measure 85 millimeters across and 9.2 millimeters thick. They will be presented in a dark-blue box from Chaumet and accompanied by a certificate from the Eiffel Tower Operating Co. verifying that the embedded iron came from the monument. Paris organizers did not disclose the medals’ monetary value.

# Paris 2024 Olympic Medals Feature Pieces of the Eiffel Tower The Paris 2024 Olympic Games will award medals unlike any in Olympic history. Each gold, silver, and bronze medal presented to athletes will contain a hexagonal, polished chunk of iron extracted from the iconic Eiffel Tower. Games organizers unveiled this revolutionary design on Thursday, creating medals that no athlete in the 29 previous Summer Olympics dating back to 1896 has ever received. ## The Eiffel Tower Connection The 135-year-old Eiffel Tower, built for the 1889 World's Fair celebrating the 100th anniversary of the French Revolution, is composed of 18,038 iron parts. Originally designed by engineer Gustave Eiffel to stand for only 20 years, the tower has endured through constant maintenance and periodic renovations. It previously hosted the Olympics in 1900 and 1924, making it a fitting symbol for Paris's return as an Olympic host city. The iron pieces embedded in the medals' centers each weigh 18 grams (approximately two-thirds of an ounce). These chunks were carefully cut from girders and other components removed during the tower's renovations and subsequently stored for safekeeping. According to Joachim Roncin, head of design for the Paris Games organizing committee, the concept emerged from discussions recognizing the Eiffel Tower as a symbol known worldwide. After approaching the Eiffel Tower Operating Company, organizers successfully incorporated pieces of the monument into the medal design. ## Medal Design and Preparation The iron pieces underwent careful preparation for their new purpose. Workers stripped away paint, polished the metal, and applied varnish. Each piece is stamped with "Paris 2024" and the Games logo, which resembles either a flame or a woman's face with a chic bob haircut. The five Olympic rings are stamped on Olympic medals, while the Paralympic Agitos—three swooshes—appear on Paralympic medals. The hexagonal shape of the iron pieces represents France, which French citizens sometimes refer to as "L'Hexagone" due to its geographic shape. Paris jewelry house Chaumet designed the medals, incorporating six small clasps that reference the 2.5 million rivets binding the Eiffel Tower together. Surrounding the iron pieces are disks of gold, silver, or bronze with a crinkled surface that reflects light, creating a distinctive shine. All metal used is recycled rather than newly mined. ## Unique Design Elements Paris is the first Olympic host city to incorporate chunks of a famous monument into medals, making them genuinely unique. While the 2008 Beijing Olympics included inlaid jade disks in their medals, Paris distinguishes itself with this unprecedented approach. "Having a piece of it is a piece of history," Roncin explained, noting that the Eiffel Tower addition provides "this cherry on the top" to an already incredible achievement. The medals feature the ancient Greek goddess of victory, Nike, on one side—continuing a tradition since 1928. However, Paris breaks with convention by adding a small representation of the Eiffel Tower on that same side. Paralympic medals display a view of the tower as if viewed from underneath, and include Braille text and notched edges for visually impaired athletes—one notch for gold, two for silver, three for bronze. ## By the Numbers The Paris Mint is manufacturing 5,084 medals: approximately 2,600 for the Olympics and 2,400 for the Paralympics. Gold medals weigh 529 grams and consist of silver plated with 6 grams of gold. Silver medals weigh 525 grams, while bronze medals weigh 455 grams and are made from a copper, tin, and zinc alloy. All medals measure 85 millimeters across and 9.2 millimeters thick. Medals will arrive in dark-blue boxes from Chaumet, accompanied by certificates from the Eiffel Tower Operating Company authenticating the iron pieces. Some manufactured medals will be stored for potential reassignment if winners are later stripped of medals for doping violations, while others may go to museums or be destroyed.

Rick DeMorgan Jr., a flight engineer from Navarre, Florida, was identified as one of three Americans killed Wednesday in a Large Air Tanker crash while fighting wildfires in Australia. DeMorgan served 18 years in the U.S. Air Force and, according to Coulson Aviation, loved flying and his children. He is survived by two children, his parents, and his sister. The other crew members killed were Captain Ian H. McBeth and First Officer Paul Clyde Hudson. Coulson Aviation said one of its Lockheed large air tankers was lost after departing Richmond, New South Wales, with retardant for a firebombing mission. The company grounded other aircraft as a precaution while investigators examine the cause. A memorial service is scheduled in Australia on February 23. The crash came as the bushfire crisis intensified, with at least 31 deaths, more than 2,600 homes destroyed, and over 25.7 million acres burned.

In a December 30 interview with state-run ILNA, Hamid Reza Tahsili, executive director for Organizing Jobs in Tehran, claimed some peddlers had “taken over” city streets and had effectively “rented out all the streets.” He said officials had identified these people and would “definitely deal with force” against them. Tahsili argued that vendors not connected to what he called mafia groups should move to designated areas in Tehran, where they must pay for booths, tables, tents, and other equipment. The article notes that many street vendors earn barely enough to survive and turn to this work only as a last resort. He tied his accusations to recent self-immolations by street vendors, saying a truly needy vendor would not set himself on fire and that such acts must be “coordinated” by mafia members trying to pressure the municipality. The article rejects that claim, comparing the deaths to the self-immolation of a Tunisian fruit seller whose death helped spark the Arab Spring, and describing such acts as the desperate response of people in severe economic distress. # Summary: Iran Official Accuses Street Vendors of Mafia Connections In a December 30 interview with Iran's state-run ILNA news agency, Hamid Reza Tahsili, executive director for Organizing Jobs in Tehran, made controversial claims that street peddlers in the capital are associated with organized crime. He threatened to use force against them, stating that some vendors have been "hired by some people" and have "taken over our streets." Tahsili argued that legitimate peddlers should relocate to designated areas where they must pay for booths and tables. However, he attributed recent self-immolations by street vendors to coordinated mafia actions designed to pressure the municipality into backing down, rather than acknowledging them as desperate acts by economically struggling individuals. This characterization contradicts statistical evidence from Iran's Sociological Association, which reveals that street vendors are predominantly impoverished workers: 76% support children, 90% lack alternative employment, and 98% have no other income sources. The article criticizes the Iranian government for scapegoating street vendors instead of addressing underlying economic problems. It documents systematic harassment, including arrests, exorbitant fines, confiscation of merchandise, and allegations of authorities demanding sexual favors for goods' return. Videos show vendors injured during interactions with Tehran's "Urban Disciplinary Team." The article notes that street vending has increased as Iran's economy deteriorated, forcing job losses.
