Rather than confronting actual economic issues, the government continues profiting from vendor fines while characterizing vulnerable workers as criminals.

Tunisia’s former president Zine El Abidine Ben Ali was buried on Saturday in Medina, Saudi Arabia, after dying in exile in Jeddah on Thursday, an AFP photographer reported. He was laid to rest in Al-Baqi cemetery beside the Prophet Mohammed’s mosque, one of the holiest sites in Islam. His body, wrapped in a green shroud, was carried by a procession of about a dozen men across a marble forecourt near the mosque’s green dome before entering the cemetery. A small notice in Tunisia’s La Presse newspaper said some of Ben Ali’s family would receive condolences on Sunday in an upscale suburb of Tunis. Saudi authorities and media did not comment on his death. Ben Ali died at 83, having ruled Tunisia from 1987 until 2011. He was seen by some as a barrier against Islamist extremism, but he was widely criticized for suppressing opposition and resisting democratic reform. Public anger over unemployment and rising prices eventually boiled over. In late 2010, the self-immolation of a young street vendor in Sidi Bouzid, following police humiliation, ignited protests that spread nationwide and triggered a violent crackdown. The protests ultimately forced Ben Ali to flee to Saudi Arabia on January 14, 2011, helping spark the Arab Spring uprisings that later toppled leaders in Egypt and Libya. Ben Ali’s wife and children remained in exile, while he himself had been sentenced multiple times to life in prison, including for the deadly repression of anti-government protests.

# Tunisia's Ex-President Ben Ali Buried in Saudi Arabia Tunisia's former president Zine El Abidine Ben Ali, who died Thursday in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, was buried Saturday in Medina's Al-Baqi cemetery near the Prophet Mohammed's mosque. His body, wrapped in a green shroud, was carried by approximately a dozen men across the cemetery's marble forecourt. Ben Ali, 83, ruled Tunisia from 1987 until 2011, when he became the first leader toppled by the Arab Spring. Though some viewed him as a bulwark against Islamist extremism, he faced criticism for suppressing opposition and resisting democratic reforms. His downfall began in late 2010 when a young trader in Sidi Bouzid set himself on fire to protest police humiliation. This sparked widespread protests and a violent government crackdown that killed over 300 people. On January 14, 2011, Ben Ali fled to Saudi Arabia, where he remained until his death. His departure triggered similar uprisings across the Middle East, toppling Egyptian president Hosni Mubarak and Libyan leader Moamer Kadhafi. Ben Ali's family, including wife Leila Trabesli and their three children, remained in exile. Trabesli faces heavy sentences for embezzlement and possession of weapons, drugs, and archaeological artifacts. Ben Ali himself received multiple life sentences, including for the violent suppression of final-weeks protests.

Iraqi government troops have withdrawn from the Heet training camp in western Anbar province, leaving the city of Heet fully under Islamic State control, security sources said Monday. IS fighters had already seized the city center on the Euphrates River, while government forces remained at a nearby base. A senior police official in Ramadi said the evacuation was ordered by military command so the troops would not remain exposed to IS attacks and could instead reinforce the defense of Asad air base, one of the last government-held positions in the province. Ahmed Hamid, head of the Anbar provincial council’s security committee, said about 300 security personnel left the camp, located a few kilometers northwest of Heet. Some senior officers were airlifted out, while the rest traveled by convoy to Asad after burning trailers and other equipment. Witnesses said IS fighters moved into the abandoned camp Monday morning. Officials warned that government forces in Anbar have suffered repeated losses and that their hold on Ramadi, the provincial capital, was becoming increasingly fragile.

# Summary Iraqi government troops have withdrawn from Heet, a city in Anbar province, leaving it entirely under Islamic State control. According to security officials, approximately 300 military personnel evacuated the Heet training camp on Sunday night on orders from military command. The military leadership decided that maintaining exposed forces in the city was untenable, and instead relocated them to reinforce Asad air base, a larger, more defensible position located northwest of Heet and surrounded by desert. Before departing, soldiers set fire to trailers and infrastructure at the training camp. IS fighters subsequently occupied the abandoned base on Monday morning. This withdrawal represents another significant setback for Iraqi forces in Anbar province, with officials expressing concern about the government's weakening control over the provincial capital, Ramadi.

Federal authorities have identified 19-year-old Stephen Spencer Pittman as the suspect in the Jan. 10 fire at Beth Israel Congregation, Jackson’s oldest synagogue, and say he told investigators he set the blaze because of “the building’s Jewish ties.” A criminal complaint charges him with arson of property used in interstate commerce. Mississippi Gov. Tate Reeves said in a Jan. 12 news release that additional charges could still be filed as the investigation continues. According to a federal affidavit, Pittman was interviewed by law enforcement on the day of the fire and referred to the synagogue as the “synagogue of Satan.” He also allegedly told his father that he had “finally got them.” Authorities say the fire began around 3 a.m. and that Pittman later texted his father photos and messages from the scene, including, “There’s a furnace in the back,” “BTW, my plate is off,” “Hoodie is on,” and “And they have the best cameras.” Security footage released by the synagogue showed a masked, hooded person using a gas container to pour liquid on the lobby floor and a couch before the fire. Investigators allege Pittman drove from Madison County, about 30 miles north of Jackson, and stopped at a gas station in Ridgeland to buy the fuel used in the arson. The affidavit says he removed his license plate before heading to the synagogue. Once there, he allegedly broke a window with an axe, poured gas inside, and used a torch lighter to ignite the fire. The Jackson Fire Department responded quickly and contained and extinguished the blaze. No injuries were reported, but an administrative office and library were charred, and several Torahs were damaged or ruined. The case took a turn when Pittman’s father noticed burns on his son’s ankles, hands, and face later that day. After confronting him, the father allegedly heard Pittman confess and laugh about what he had done, saying again that he had “finally got them.” The father then contacted the FBI and reported the confession. The affidavit says cellphone data and the burn injuries corroborated the account. Agents later recovered a burned cellphone believed to belong to Pittman, along with a hand torch turned over by a congregation member. Reeves said Pittman was admitted to the University of Mississippi Medical Center with non-life-threatening burn injuries before being taken into custody. Pittman had previously attended St. Joseph Catholic School in Madison and played baseball there and at Coahoma Community College. The Catholic Diocese of Jackson condemned the alleged actions as “senseless, reprehensible, and wholly incompatible” with Catholic values. Beth Israel’s history gives the attack added weight: the synagogue dates to before the Civil War and was previously targeted in a 1967 Ku Klux Klan bombing that damaged its office and the home of Rabbi Perry Nussbaum. Reeves said Mississippi stands with Beth Israel Congregation and that the perpetrator should face the full consequences of the crime.

# Summary: Beth Israel Synagogue Fire Suspect Identified On January 10, around 3 a.m., a fire broke out at Beth Israel Congregation synagogue in Jackson, Mississippi, a historic institution dating back before the Civil War. Security camera footage captured a masked and hooded individual pouring liquid from a gas container onto the floor and furniture in the building's lobby before igniting the blaze. The Jackson Fire Department successfully contained and extinguished the fire, with no injuries reported, though an administrative office and library were charred, and several Torahs—Jewish holy texts—were ruined or damaged. Federal authorities have identified the suspect as Stephen Spencer Pittman, 19, who has been charged with arson of property used in interstate commerce. According to a federal affidavit filed January 12, Pittman told authorities he lit the fire due to "the building's Jewish ties" and referred to the synagogue as the "synagogue of Satan." Mississippi Governor Tate Reeves indicated that additional charges may be filed as the investigation continues. The affidavit details Pittman's alleged actions leading up to the fire. He traveled from his residence in Madison County, approximately 30 miles north of Jackson, and purchased gasoline at a gas station in Ridgeland. At the station, he removed his license plate. Before entering the synagogue, Pittman texted his father a photo of the building's rear, mentioning the furnace, his removed plate, and hooded appearance. When his father urged him to return home, Pittman allegedly responded that he was "due for a homerun" and had "done his research." At the synagogue, Pittman allegedly used an axe to break a window, poured gasoline inside, and used a torch lighter to start the fire. Later that day, his father noticed burns on Pittman's ankles, hands, and face. When confronted, Pittman allegedly confessed to the crime, laughing as he told his father "he finally got them." His father then contacted the FBI, reporting his son's confession. Evidence corroborating the confession includes cell phone data, burn marks on Pittman's body, a recovered burned cell phone believed to be his, and a hand torch found by a congregation member. Pittman was admitted to the University of Mississippi Medical Center with non-life-threatening burn injuries before being taken into custody. Pittman was a former student and baseball player at St. Joseph Catholic School in Madison and played for Coahoma Community College, a historically Black institution. The Catholic Diocese of Jackson condemned the alleged actions as "senseless, reprehensible, and wholly incompatible" with church values. Beth Israel's history includes a 1967 Ku Klux Klan bombing that damaged the temple's office and Rabbi Perry Nussbaum's home, making this incident a troubling repeat of the synagogue's experience with violence.

Several Palestinian detainees burned uniforms they say Israeli authorities forced them to wear before release as part of the sixth batch freed under the ceasefire and prisoner-exchange agreement with Gaza. The clothes reportedly displayed the Star of David and the Arabic slogan, “We will not forgive, we will not forget.” According to the report, prison officials used the uniforms to humiliate the detainees, and some freed prisoners responded by setting the clothes on fire immediately after release. Israeli media confirmed the uniforms were used, with Yedioth Ahronoth noting similar tactics in earlier releases and Maariv describing the move as a “surprise.” Photos showed detainees wearing the uniforms in Ketziot Prison. Hamas condemned the treatment as racist and illegal, praised the detainees’ freedom as a national achievement, and urged Israel to proceed with the next exchange phase without delay.

# Summary Israeli authorities released the sixth batch of Palestinian detainees under a ceasefire agreement with Gaza resistance groups. However, prison officials forced detainees to wear uniforms bearing the Star of David and the Arabic phrase "We will not forgive, we will not forget." Upon release, some prisoners burned the uniforms in protest. Israeli media confirmed the tactic, noting similar humiliating practices in previous releases, including marked bracelets. A monument has been inaugurated in Kabul to honor Farkhunda Malikzada, the 27-year-old woman who was lynched and burned by a mob in March 2015 after being falsely accused of burning the Quran. The memorial stands near the Kabul River, where her body was thrown after the attack. Farkhunda’s killing shocked Afghanistan and triggered mass protests. In the aftermath, several of the attackers were arrested, tried, and sentenced. But the article says the legal outcome disappointed many: death sentences were later overturned and reduced, and some defendants were released, deepening public anger and distrust in the justice system. The monument was unveiled on March 17, nearly a year after her death, during a commemoration organized by the Solidarity Party of Afghanistan. Hundreds of people attended the event, gathering to demand justice and to affirm that Farkhunda’s case should not be forgotten. The party described the monument as a symbol of resistance against “ignorance, bigotry, misogyny and obscurantism.” Al Jazeera spoke with attendees who expressed grief, rage, and fear about women’s safety in Afghanistan. Many said the case showed that the government and courts cannot be trusted to protect women or punish violence against them. Several speakers said they no longer believed the judicial system would work in women’s favor, and some said women in Afghanistan live in constant fear of rape, stoning, silencing, and murder. Others said they attended because Farkhunda reminded them of their own daughters and the vulnerability of women more broadly. One participant said the case raised terrifying questions about whether a family could save a daughter if she were targeted. Another called for the killers to be punished in the same brutal way Farkhunda was killed, reflecting the depth of anger still felt a year later. Despite the passage of time, attendees said they were still crying over the lack of justice for Farkhunda and her family. The article concludes that she has become a lasting symbol of women’s suffering in Afghanistan and a rallying point for those determined to keep fighting for women’s rights.

# Summary: Afghanistan Commemorates Farkhunda Malikzada A monument was inaugurated in Kabul, Afghanistan, commemorating Farkhunda Malikzada, a 27-year-old woman killed by a mob in March 2015. Malikzada was falsely accused of burning the Quran and brutally attacked by a group of mostly men who beat her, set her body on fire, and threw it into the Kabul River. Following her death, mass protests erupted and some attackers were prosecuted and sentenced. However, those initially given death sentences had their punishments overturned and reduced, while others were released entirely. This failure of justice sparked widespread outrage. On March 17, nearly a year after the killing, the Solidarity Party of Afghanistan organized a commemoration event that drew hundreds of attendees. The party stated that the monument would serve as "a testimonial to the pledge of those who have vowed to fight relentlessly against the ignominy of ignorance, bigotry, misogyny and obscurantism." Attendees expressed deep frustration with Afghanistan's government and judicial system. Many speakers criticized the failure to adequately punish Farkhunda's killers and highlighted broader concerns about women's safety in Afghanistan. Participants described living in fear and losing trust in government institutions designed to protect them. Speakers emphasized that Farkhunda's case represents a systemic problem affecting Afghan women, with some noting that women face stoning, rape, and murder with little governmental accountability. One attendee expressed personal terror, fearing for her daughter's safety in such an environment. Another demanded that Farkhunda's killers receive the same brutal punishment she endured. Despite the grim circumstances, attendees demonstrated solidarity and commitment to continued advocacy. They vowed to keep fighting for women's rights and justice, viewing Farkhunda as a symbol of both the brutality women face and the necessity of sustained resistance. The gathering underscored both the tragedy of Farkhunda's death and Afghans' determination to ensure her memory inspires ongoing efforts for justice and women's safety.

The blazes broke out in the southwestern countryside and spread to houses in the villages of al-Hwaish, al-Salihyia, and al-A’li. The report said similar fires in mid-June near al-Jawadyia killed six people, including a woman and a child, and injured others. It accused US-backed Qasad and Asayish militias of deliberately setting fires to pressure farmers not to deliver crops to state grain centers.

# Summary A child and two women died from severe burns while fighting agricultural fires in Hasaka's southwestern countryside near Ras al-Ain. Turkish authorities detained nine people on Sunday after a night of attacks on offices of the main pro-Kurdish Peoples’ Democratic Party (HDP), in what appeared to be reprisals for a deadly bombing blamed on Kurdish militants. The arrests were linked to violence in Istanbul, according to the Dogan news agency. The HDP said its offices in 20 locations across Turkey were targeted after a suicide car bombing in the central city of Kayseri on Saturday killed 14 soldiers. According to the party, several offices were burned, ransacked, or shot at by nationalist protesters. The attacks raised fears of escalating tensions and possible street clashes in a country already shaken by repeated assaults blamed on the outlawed Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK) and its affiliates. In Istanbul, a policeman died after falling from a balcony while trying to persuade protesters to stay away from an HDP office in the Umraniye district. Police said the officer had gone onto the balcony during the attempted raid and accidentally fell. HDP spokesman Ayhan Bilgen accused the authorities of ignoring the attacks, while saying the party had urged supporters not to be provoked. He said efforts were under way to create “the conditions for conflict.” The government said the PKK was likely responsible for the Kayseri bombing. The HDP denies any ties to the group, though the government accuses it of acting as the militants’ political wing. Several HDP lawmakers, including its co-leaders, are already under arrest over alleged PKK links. In Kayseri, protesters broke into the HDP building, removed its sign, scattered papers and furniture, and set a fire while displaying the flag of the nationalist MHP. Turkish media said some protesters were linked to the Grey Wolves, an MHP-aligned militant group.

# Summary Turkish authorities detained nine people on Sunday suspected of involvement in reprisal attacks against offices of the pro-Kurdish Peoples' Democratic Party (HDP). The violence followed a Saturday suicide car bombing in Kayseri that killed 14 soldiers, which the government blamed on the outlawed Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK). The HDP reported that 20 of its offices nationwide were attacked by nationalist protesters. Several offices were destroyed by fire and ransacking, while others were shot at. In Istanbul's Umraniye district, a policeman died in an accidental fall while attempting to prevent protesters from raiding an HDP office. HDP spokesman Ayhan Bilgen accused authorities of ignoring the attacks and claimed the party urged supporters to avoid provocations. He alleged the violence was designed to create conflict and destabilize Turkey. All nine detainees are suspected of attacking HDP buildings in Istanbul. The government maintains the PKK orchestrated the Kayseri bombing, though the HDP denies links to the militant group. Turkish media reported that right-wing Grey Wolves supporters participated in the Saturday protests, displaying nationalist symbols at the Kayseri office. The incidents heightened tensions in Turkey amid ongoing PKK insurgency in the southeast. The HDP condemned the Kayseri attack while facing government accusations of being the political front for Kurdish militants, with several party leaders currently arrested on alleged PKK-related charges.

# Summary Montreal police released surveillance video of two suspects in connection with a firebombing at Cavalli restaurant on Peel Street. In January 2015, the U.S. Supreme Court agreed to review the lethal injection protocol used in Oklahoma after a series of troubled executions raised questions about whether the method amounted to unconstitutional cruel and unusual punishment. The controversy centered on the drug midazolam, which was used as the first sedative in the three-drug combination given to Clayton Lockett before his botched execution. Lockett later died of a heart attack, and the same protocol was also used in the execution of Charles Warner. The article says the debate over the drug mixture has intensified concerns about whether capital punishment can still be considered humane. It notes that sodium thiopental, once the standard sedative for lethal injections, became unavailable after European manufacturer Hospira stopped producing it in 2011, reportedly because of its use in U.S. executions. Midazolam was used as a substitute, but critics argue it lacks analgesic properties and therefore cannot prevent severe pain during execution. The article describes the combination of midazolam, vecuronium bromide, and potassium chloride as an untested mixture that may effectively torture inmates. An independent autopsy of Lockett, led by forensic pathologist Joseph Cohen, found that the execution team had failed to properly place the IV line. As a result, the drugs reportedly entered tissue rather than the bloodstream, causing Lockett to twitch, convulse, exhale loudly, and attempt to rise from the table. Ryan Kiesel, executive director of the American Civil Liberties Union, described the execution as a “science experiment” and said Lockett died in pain over about 40 minutes. The article presents the Supreme Court’s decision to review the protocol as a potentially important step that could open the door to broader death penalty abolition efforts, including those being pursued in Washington State. It suggests that life imprisonment without parole and hard labor could be considered as alternatives to execution, offering a form of restitution to victims’ families without using lethal injection.

# Supreme Court Reviews Lethal Injection Protocols Following Execution Controversies The U.S. Supreme Court has announced a review of lethal injection protocols used in executions, prompted by controversial cases involving Clayton Lockett and Charles Warner in Oklahoma. Both executions raised serious concerns about whether the drug mixture constitutes cruel and unusual punishment under the Constitution. ## The Failed Execution and Drug Concerns Clayton Lockett's execution in 2014 was marked by significant complications. The execution team failed to properly insert the intravenous line, causing drugs to be absorbed into muscle tissue rather than administered intravenously. Lockett experienced visible distress—twitching, convulsing, and attempting to rise from the table—over approximately 40 minutes before dying of a heart attack. Charles Warner was subsequently executed using the same problematic protocol. ## The Drug Mixture Problem The executions employed midazolam, vecuronium bromide, and potassium chloride as a substitute for sodium thiopental, the traditional sedative used in lethal injections. Sodium thiopental became unavailable after European manufacturer Hospira ceased production in 2011 due to its association with American executions. The primary issue is that midazolam lacks analgesic properties—meaning it cannot prevent pain—making the three-drug combination potentially torturous. An independent autopsy by forensic pathologist Joseph Cohen confirmed the IV administration failure, supporting claims that Lockett died in agony. ## Implications for Capital Punishment The American Civil Liberties Union characterized Lockett's execution as a "science experiment" that violated basic humane standards. The Supreme Court's review is viewed as a potential pathway toward abolishing capital punishment entirely. Some advocates, including Washington State legislators, propose replacing the death penalty with life imprisonment without parole as an alternative that provides restitution to victims' families without the risks associated with lethal injection protocols. This review represents a significant moment in the ongoing debate about capital punishment in America, questioning both the constitutionality and humanity of current execution methods.

A Dollard-des-Ormeaux family called 911 around 11 p.m. Friday after returning home to find a bullet hole in their house on Brahms Street near Mozart Avenue. # Summary A Dollard-des-Ormeaux family discovered a bullet hole in their home on Brahms Street near Mozart Avenue and called 911 Friday night. The family was absent during the apparent shooting. A former foster child is mourning the death of Gord Parmenter, the 78-year-old man killed in a shooting Sunday at the Salmon Arm Church of Christ in British Columbia. Parmenter and his wife, Peggy, had long cared for foster children in the Interior B.C. community, and the former foster son said they treated him “like their own kin.” In an email, the man said Parmenter’s faith guided his life and that helping others was his way of serving God. He described Parmenter as especially skilled at supporting difficult cases and said he helped him find confidence and purpose. The former foster child said he cried for an hour after learning of Parmenter’s death. According to Salmon Arm RCMP, a second man was seriously injured in the shooting before churchgoers tackled the 25-year-old suspect and held him down until police arrived. The B.C. prosecution service says the accused, Matrix Savage Gathergood, has been charged with first-degree murder, aggravated assault, and disguise with intent to commit an indictable offence. He appeared in court Tuesday and is scheduled to return on April 23. The former foster son said the Parmenters had opened their home as an emergency placement for children who had nowhere else to go. He recalled spending time in Parmenter’s woodworking shop and said Parmenter’s stories helped him and other youth cope with hardship. He credited Parmenter with helping him stay in school and ultimately reach college. The statement also mentioned a suspicious fire in mid-March that heavily damaged a trailer home owned by the Parmenters, though police have not linked it to the shooting. Salmon Arm Mayor Alan Harrison said the small community is seeking ways to support the family and described Parmenter as a respected elder in the congregation and community.

# Summary Gord Parmenter, a 78-year-old British Columbia resident, was fatally shot while attending services at the Salmon Arm Church of Christ on Sunday. A second parishioner was seriously injured in the attack before church members subdued the 25-year-old suspect, Matrix Savage Gathergood, until police arrived. Gathergood has been charged with first-degree murder, aggravated assault, and disguise with intent to commit an indictable offence. He appeared in court Tuesday and will next appear on April 23. However, police have not connected this fire to the shooting. Salmon Arm's mayor noted that the community of under 20,000 people is deeply affected by the loss of the well-respected church elder and is seeking ways to support the Parmenter family.

A Holtsville man has been indicted on felony charges after prosecutors said he intentionally set fire to a Wading River pizzeria weeks after being fired from the business. Suffolk County District Attorney Raymond A. Tierney announced that 59-year-old Constantine Sackos was charged with third-degree arson, along with burglary, criminal mischief, and petit larceny, in connection with a fire at Pazzo Ristorante and Wood Fired Pizzeria on November 18. According to investigators, a 911 call reporting the blaze came in at about 1:57 a.m., bringing Riverhead Town police and multiple fire departments to the scene. Firefighters contained the blaze after roughly two hours, limiting damage beyond the restaurant. A later joint investigation by local police, fire marshals, the Suffolk County Police Department Arson Squad, and the district attorney’s office concluded the fire was deliberately set. Authorities said they found seven points of origin and recovered a bottle of charcoal lighter fluid from inside the restaurant. Prosecutors said Sackos became a suspect after investigators learned he had recently been terminated and had allegedly gone to the owner’s home multiple times before and after the fire demanding payment for back wages. Surveillance footage allegedly shows him buying Kingsford charcoal lighter fluid hours before the fire and transporting a bicycle in his Jeep. Video also reportedly places him in the Mount Sinai area, where he left his vehicle near the North Shore Rail Trail and rode a bicycle toward the pizzeria before the fire. Footage allegedly shows a person matching Sackos leaving the rear of the restaurant as smoke filled the building, fleeing on a bicycle, briefly returning, and leaving again. A search of his Holtsville home on November 20 led to the seizure of clothing consistent with what was seen on video, and a K9 accelerant dog indicated accelerants on the items. Sackos was arraigned Wednesday, released under supervised conditions with GPS monitoring, and is due back in court on February 26. If convicted on the top charge, he faces 5 to 15 years in prison.

A New York court has dismissed a lawsuit accusing Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi of crimes against humanity over the 2002 Gujarat riots, ruling that he was protected by immunity as a sitting foreign head of government, in line with the Obama administration’s position. The case had been filed last September by the American Justice Centre, which alleged that Modi failed to stop the violence and was responsible for crimes including extrajudicial killings, torture, and severe mental and physical abuse, largely against Muslims. The article recounts that the violence began on 27 February 2002, when a group of Muslims attacked and set fire to the Sabarmati Express, killing 58 passengers, most of them Hindu pilgrims returning from Ayodhya. The attack triggered widespread sectarian riots across Gujarat. More than 1,000 people were confirmed dead, including 790 Muslims and 254 Hindus, and at least 253 others were reported missing. The unrest also damaged 523 places of worship and led to thousands of arrests. Modi, then chief minister of Gujarat, has long denied wrongdoing and never apologized. After years of Western boycott and a visa revocation under President George W. Bush, attitudes shifted following the BJP’s election victory, and Obama later invited Modi to visit the United States.

At a sentencing hearing in Montreal, the Crown argued that Richard Henry Bain should serve 25 years in prison with no chance of parole for the deadly 2012 shooting at the Parti Québécois election victory celebration. Prosecutor Dennis Galiatsatos described the attack as a politically motivated attempt at a “massacre” and said Bain should be treated as a mass murderer because he planned the assault in advance and intended to kill as many separatists as possible. Bain, now 66, was convicted of second-degree murder in the death of lighting technician Denis Blanchette, 48. Another man, Dave Courage, was struck by the same bullet but survived. The hearing was not about guilt, but about how much of Bain’s 25-year sentence he must serve before becoming eligible for parole. The Crown urged the judge to deny parole eligibility entirely, emphasizing the scale of the planning: Bain stocked his vehicle with weapons, drove two hours to Montreal, and carried out surveillance at the nightclub where newly elected sovereigntist premier Pauline Marois was celebrating with supporters. In a letter to a psychiatrist written two months after his arrest, Bain said he had spent three weeks planning the attack. Although his rifle jammed after the first shot, he also set fire to a garbage bin outside the nightclub before police detained him. Bain’s lawyer, Alan Guttman, asked the court to ignore the written confession, arguing that the psychiatrist who received it believed Bain was psychotic at the time. He said Bain should be eligible for parole after 10 years, drawing a comparison to Denis Lortie, who attacked Quebec’s legislature in 1984 and killed three employees. Guttman argued the cases were similar because both involved armed attacks intended to kill political targets. Victim impact statements painted a picture of lasting trauma. Diane Blanchette, the victim’s sister, said Bain violated her brother’s right to life and deprived a young girl of growing up with her father. Other witnesses described Bain as a terrorist who used violence to pursue a political agenda. Some said the shooting left them with nightmares, depression, post-traumatic stress disorder, drug abuse, and suicidal thoughts years later. One colleague, Jonathan Dubé, said Bain’s claim that he was carrying out God’s plan was false, calling the attack a “personal terrorist crusade.” Bain himself expressed regret at the hearing, saying the tragedy was “terrible” and that he had “great regrets about it.” Judge Guy Cournoyer is to decide the parole eligibility period.

Victims and witnesses submitted impact statements describing lasting trauma, including nightmares, depression, PTSD, drug abuse, and suicidal thoughts. Several characterized Bain as a terrorist advancing a political agenda. Diane Blanchette, the victim's sister, emphasized how the shooting robbed a young girl of her father. Judge Guy Cournoyer will determine the final sentencing decision.

A former Wisconsin police officer was charged Thursday with first-degree reckless homicide in the fatal shooting of Sylville Smith, an African American man whose death sparked two nights of unrest in Milwaukee. Dominique Heaggan-Brown, who is also black, faces up to 60 years in prison if convicted. According to a criminal complaint based largely on body-camera footage, Heaggan-Brown shot Smith twice after a foot chase. Police said the first shot hit Smith in the arm while he was raising his right hand, which held a semi-automatic pistol. Smith then fell to the ground and was no longer armed, but Heaggan-Brown fired a second shot into Smith’s chest. Authorities said no officer searched Smith afterward for another weapon. Smith, 23, died at the scene. The complaint focused on the second shot as the basis for the homicide charge. Smith’s mother, Mildred Haynes, said the officer should have faced a more serious charge, telling the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel that he “shot to kill.” Police had initially noticed Smith because he was in a car with an out-of-state license plate and someone was leaning into the passenger window. Heaggan-Brown later said he believed the situation could have involved drug activity. Heaggan-Brown had already been fired from the Milwaukee Police Department in October over unrelated sexual assault charges. The shooting triggered two days of violent protests in Milwaukee, during which cars and businesses were set on fire and police were attacked with gunfire, rocks and bottles. The unrest came amid national outrage over police killings of black Americans and the killing of five officers in Dallas. The article also noted a mistrial in Charleston in the case of former officer Michael Slager, who shot Walter Scott in the back.

Sen. Mike Lee of Utah is being portrayed as moving from a confrontational conservative activist to a more pragmatic consensus builder as Senate Republicans struggle to craft a replacement for the Affordable Care Act. Four years ago, Lee and Sen. Ted Cruz helped drive a failed effort to block funding for President Barack Obama’s health care law, a fight that ended in a 16-day federal government shutdown and earned them a reputation among GOP leaders as “bomb throwers” willing to blow up negotiations. Now, Lee and Cruz are again central players in the health care debate, but in a different role: they are working behind the scenes on a conservative alternative to Obamacare while Republicans try to unite behind a repeal-and-replace plan. Lee’s spokesman, Conn Carroll, rejected comparisons to the 2013 shutdown fight, saying the circumstances are “night and day different.” He argued that Lee’s strategy has not changed, only the political environment, because President Donald Trump now wants to repeal Obamacare and Lee is “building consensus to reform health care.” The pair’s involvement has drawn national attention. Politico warned that the two conservative senators, once known for hardline tactics, were now trying to build consensus but could push the GOP bill so far to the right that it collapses. At the same time, a conservative website, The Resurgent, suggested that the Trump administration may believe Lee and Cruz could actually help save the repeal effort. The article cited White House legislative affairs director Marc Short, who said the administration supported their efforts and praised a provision in their plan that would remove Obamacare’s protections for people with pre-existing conditions. Supporters of Lee say his role has evolved into that of a policy architect. Boyd Matheson, a former Lee chief of staff and head of the conservative Sutherland Institute, said Lee is in regular contact with the White House and is viewed as the “policy idea guy.” Matheson compared Lee’s early opposition to Obamacare with Mitt Romney’s warnings about Russia during the 2012 campaign, arguing that Lee was ahead of his time in predicting the harm the law would cause, especially to working-class Americans. Others see the shift as a lesson learned from the failures of 2013. University of Utah political science professor Matthew Burbank said Republicans now understand the political cost of failing to act, and that Lee appears more willing to engage in serious negotiation than before. Burbank said Lee’s current tone is more measured and less like an uncompromising refusal to accept any deal. The broader context is one of deep Republican division despite control of the White House and both chambers of Congress. The House had passed one health care plan, but the Senate postponed its vote after objections from Lee, Cruz, and other Republicans. Critics of Majority Leader Mitch McConnell’s proposal said it did not give states enough control over health care funding and cut Medicaid too aggressively. President Trump added pressure by tweeting that if Senate Republicans could not pass their current bill, they should repeal Obamacare immediately and replace it later. On CBS’s “Face the Nation,” Lee said that if the Senate cannot agree on a replacement, Republicans may need to repeal the law with a delayed implementation date, calling that consistent with what Republicans have promised voters for years.

A shooting at the Chabad of Poway synagogue near San Diego on the final day of Passover left one woman dead and three other people injured, authorities said. Police identified the suspect as 19-year-old John T. Earnest of San Diego, a student at California State University San Marcos. He was taken into custody after the attack. According to San Diego County Sheriff Bill Gore, Earnest entered the synagogue armed with an AR-type assault weapon and began firing at people inside during an 11 a.m. Passover holiday celebration. Witnesses described chaos as congregants dropped to the floor and tried to protect children. Danny Almog, who was inside, said he saw a man wearing glasses and a vest standing near the entrance and “shooting, shooting, shooting everybody.” Almog said he screamed for his children, who were in another room, while family members and friends rushed them toward an exit. He described one friend, Almog Peretz, as a hero for grabbing the children and running out with them. Peretz was later reported shot in the leg while escaping. As the suspect fled the synagogue, an off-duty Border Patrol agent in the area fired at him and struck his vehicle, Gore and San Diego Police Chief David Nisleit said. A San Diego police officer responding to the scene then heard on a scanner that the suspect had called the California Highway Patrol to report his involvement and give his location. The officer found the suspect in his vehicle nearby. Nisleit said Earnest pulled over, got out with his hands up, and was immediately arrested. Police found a rifle on the front passenger seat. Authorities said investigators were examining whether Earnest may also have been involved in a March 24 arson at a mosque in Escondido, north of Poway. Graffiti at that scene had referenced the March 15 massacre of 50 Muslim worshippers in New Zealand, and sheriff’s detectives were working with the Escondido Police Department and the FBI to determine any connection. At the hospital, Michael Katz, a trauma surgeon at Palomar Medical Center, said the victims included a 61-year-old woman who died. A girl and two men, including a rabbi shot in the hand, were reported stable. Gore called the attack a “senseless act of tragedy” but declined to discuss a motive while the suspect was being questioned by police and the FBI. Poway Mayor Steve Vaus said he believed it was a hate crime and thanked congregants who confronted the shooter and helped prevent a larger massacre. President Donald Trump also called the attack a hate crime in comments on Saturday and offered condolences. Vaus said Trump phoned him from Air Force One and offered assistance. The synagogue, Chabad of Poway, serves as a community center for ultra-Orthodox Jews and is part of the Chabad movement, which also reaches out to less observant Jews. The attack drew concern from law enforcement in major cities across the country, and the U.S. Holocaust Memorial Museum said it was shocked and alarmed by what it described as the second armed attack on a synagogue in the United States in six months. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu condemned the shooting as an attack on the Jewish people and urged a stronger international fight against antisemitism. Witnesses said there were many people in the synagogue at the time, including children. Almog said the gunman appeared to know the congregation was holding Passover services, noting that families often bring children who play while adults pray.

# Summary: Shooting at Chabad Synagogue Near San Diego On Saturday, April 27, 2019—the final day of Passover—a gunman opened fire at the Chabad of Poway synagogue near San Diego, killing one woman and injuring three others. The suspect, 19-year-old John T. Earnest, a student at California State University San Marcos, was quickly apprehended and taken into custody. ## The Attack Earnest entered the synagogue armed with an AR-type assault weapon and began shooting indiscriminately at worshippers. Eyewitness Danny Almog described seeing a white man, approximately 5'6" to 5'7" tall, wearing glasses and a vest, firing repeatedly at people inside. When gunfire erupted, congregants immediately dropped to the floor. Almog's friend Almog Peretz heroically gathered children and rushed them toward the exit, suffering a gunshot wound to the leg in the process. The group escaped through a back door. ## Apprehension As the gunman fled the synagogue, an off-duty Border Patrol agent in the area fired at his vehicle, striking it. Police received a crucial break when the suspect himself called the California Highway Patrol to report his involvement and provide his location. A San Diego police officer responding to the call spotted the suspect in his vehicle. When the officer approached, Earnest immediately pulled over, exited with his hands raised, and was taken into custody. Police discovered a rifle on the front passenger seat. ## Victims and Injuries A 61-year-old woman was killed in the shooting. Among the injured were a girl and two men, including a rabbi shot in the hand. All three injured individuals were reported to be in stable condition at Palomar Medical Center. ## Investigation and Possible Links Sheriff's detectives and FBI investigators are examining a potential connection between Earnest and a March 24 arson fire at a mosque in nearby Escondido. Graffiti at the mosque fire scene referenced the March 15 terrorist attack in Christchurch, New Zealand, that killed 50 Muslim worshippers. Authorities are working to determine Earnest's possible involvement in that incident. ## Official Responses Sheriff Bill Gore called the shooting a "senseless act of tragedy," while Poway Mayor Steve Vaus explicitly characterized it as a hate crime. President Trump, speaking from Air Force One, stated the attack "looks like a hate crime" and offered assistance. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu condemned the shooting as "an attack on the heart of the Jewish people." ## Broader Context The incident occurred during Passover services, when the synagogue was hosting a community celebration with many families and children present. The shooting represents the second armed attack on a U.S. synagogue in six months, prompting the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum to call it a "wake-up call" regarding growing antisemitism. Law enforcement agencies in major cities including Los Angeles, San Francisco, and New York closely monitored the situation. Community leaders emphasized unity, with Mayor Vaus stating that Poway would walk through the tragedy together.

Russia’s airstrike on a children’s and maternity hospital in Mariupol marked the latest in a string of attacks in Ukraine that have destroyed apartment buildings and killed civilians in their homes or on the street. The strike, which killed at least three people including a child, has intensified accusations of war crimes, though such claims remain unproven, and the International Criminal Court has opened an investigation. The assault has prompted comparisons to Russia’s earlier wars in Chechnya and Syria, where overwhelming force and heavy aerial bombardment devastated cities such as Grozny and Aleppo. But the article argues that, for now, Ukraine is not yet on that scale of destruction. The invasion is still in its third week, and military analysts say Russia has increased its use of airpower but has not yet fully exploited its aerial superiority. After the Mariupol strike, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky denounced Russia for targeting hospitals and maternity wards. Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov dismissed such criticism as “pathetic shrieks” from the enemy. The article recalls how Grozny was flattened during Russia’s two wars in Chechnya from 1994 to 2000. In late 1999, Russian planes dropped leaflets warning people to leave the city or be destroyed. Russia had entered Chechnya after rebel fighters crossed into Dagestan, and militants were also blamed for deadly apartment bombings in Russian cities. Russian forces bombarded Grozny for weeks, using airpower heavily because commanders feared the casualties that street fighting had caused in the earlier Chechen war. Moscow had initially predicted a quick victory, much as it has in Ukraine, but the conflict became prolonged and brutal. British Prime Minister Boris Johnson warned in January that an invasion of Ukraine could become “a painful, violent and bloody business” and could produce “a new Chechnya.” Russia’s airpower also played a decisive role in Syria, helping Bashar Assad’s government in the civil war. In Aleppo, hundreds of civilians died, and by 2016 the city’s destruction was vast: tens of thousands of homes were uninhabitable, factories had been looted or destroyed, and historic landmarks had been reduced to rubble. Rebuilding was expected to cost tens of billions of dollars and take years. The article notes that while other countries, including the United States, have also faced criticism for disproportionate force in wars such as Vietnam, Iraq, and Afghanistan, Russia’s tactics in Grozny and Aleppo were especially relentless. In Ukraine, the war is still early, but if Russia turns to prolonged siege and close-quarters fighting, analysts warn the devastation could become even worse.

# Summary: Russia's Destructive Tactics in Ukraine Russia's invasion of Ukraine has already resulted in devastating attacks on civilian infrastructure, including a recent airstrike on a children's and maternity hospital in Mariupol that killed at least three people, including a child. These attacks have prompted allegations of war crimes under investigation by the International Criminal Court, and comparisons to Russia's previous military campaigns in Chechnya and Syria. However, military analysts caution that while the destruction is severe, comparisons to the complete devastation of cities like Grozny and Aleppo may be premature. The Ukraine invasion is only three weeks old, and Russia has not yet fully deployed its aerial advantage, suggesting the potential for escalation. Russia's assault on Grozny, the Chechen capital, during wars from 1994 to 2000 provides a sobering precedent. After initial optimistic forecasts of quick victory proved wrong, Russian forces relied heavily on airpower rather than risking street battles that had caused heavy casualties in earlier fighting. The city was systematically bombed and shelled for weeks, ultimately leaving it devastated. Similarly, in Syria's civil war, Russian airpower supported President Bashar Assad's forces in the siege of Aleppo. The 2016 bombardments destroyed tens of thousands of homes, factories, and ancient landmarks, reducing the former industrial and cultural hub to ruins. Rebuilding costs were estimated in the tens of billions of dollars, with recovery taking years. The parallels are striking: Russian military doctrine appears to favor overwhelming aerial bombardment to avoid costly street combat and minimize troop casualties. This strategy, while tactically advantageous for Russia, inflicts catastrophic civilian harm. British Prime Minister Boris Johnson warned before the invasion that Ukraine could face "a new Chechnya" with prolonged street fighting and heavy casualties. Military experts now suggest that if Russian forces encounter sustained urban resistance, the destruction could resemble medieval-style city sieges with "extraordinary misery" and "indiscriminate shelling." While the United States has also faced criticism for disproportionate force in Vietnam, Iraq, and Afghanistan, Russia's established pattern of using relentless aerial bombardment to achieve military objectives without risking ground troops raises serious concerns about Ukraine's future. The invasion's trajectory suggests that if street fighting ensues, Ukrainian cities could suffer devastation comparable to Grozny or Aleppo, with similarly catastrophic long-term consequences.

Ukrainian filmmaker Oleg Sentsov, imprisoned in Russia, is entering the most dangerous phase of his hunger strike just as Russia hosts the World Cup. By Thursday, when the tournament begins, he will have gone a month without food. Sentsov says he is prepared to die unless Moscow releases dozens of Ukrainian political prisoners, and he deliberately timed the protest to maximize pressure on the Kremlin during its moment of global visibility. Sentsov, 41, is serving a 20-year sentence in a Russian prison in the far north after being convicted on charges of masterminding arson attacks in Crimea, accusations he denies. A prominent critic of the Kremlin, he was detained in 2014 after Russia annexed Crimea from Ukraine. Supporters say the severe sentence was meant to make an example of him. His film “Gamer” had earlier won acclaim at the Rotterdam Film Festival in 2012. The hunger strike began on May 14, after Sentsov had already spent weeks gradually reducing his food intake. In a letter published Saturday, he said, “I will not back down.” Doctors have warned that his kidneys may soon fail and that the effects of the strike are becoming irreversible. He has agreed to receive a glucose drip, but doctors have also threatened to force-feed him through a stomach tube, a practice activists often describe as torture. He has already lost about eight kilograms. There has been some speculation that Sentsov might be included in a prisoner exchange with Ukraine. President Vladimir Putin has recently suggested that back-channel talks may be taking place, raising hopes for Sentsov and other Ukrainians held in Russian prisons. But there are no firm details, and it remains unclear whether any swap will happen, or whether it would come in time to save his life. A Carnegie Moscow Center analyst said it would be damaging for Putin if the issue became major international news during the World Cup. Sentsov’s cousin, Natalya Kaplan, has appealed to the West to intervene, noting that he is the father of two children, one of whom has autism, and that he has long struggled with health problems but always shown determination. His case has prompted a broad campaign: protests have been held in cities across Europe, the United States and the Middle East, and several activists attempted solidarity fasts but later stopped. Prominent writers including Margaret Atwood and Ian McEwan also signed a letter to Putin urging Sentsov’s release “in the spirit of this unifying global event.” Still, many observers doubt the Kremlin is prepared to free all Ukrainian political prisoners. The article also places Sentsov’s case in a wider human rights context. Activists say Russia’s crackdown on dissent continues, and they are urging FIFA to use its influence. Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch both criticized Russia’s rights record, with Human Rights Watch calling the World Cup the start of the worst human rights crisis in Russia since the Soviet era. FIFA has at least criticized the detention of another activist, Oyub Titiyev, though his detention was later extended. Some critics, including Ukrainian artist Andriy Yermolenko, have called for a boycott and used graphic artwork to highlight the war in eastern Ukraine, arguing that celebrations of football should not obscure what they see as ongoing violence and repression.

A new study presented at the annual European Emergency Medicine Congress in Barcelona found that women who suffer out-of-hospital cardiac arrest in public places are significantly less likely than men to receive bystander CPR. The research, led by Sylvie Cossette, Ph.D., of the University of Montreal, examined how age, gender, and location affect the likelihood of receiving bystander cardiopulmonary resuscitation (BCPR) in adult, nontraumatic, bystander-witnessed out-of-hospital cardiac arrest cases. The analysis included 39,391 patients. Overall, 54% received BCPR, 23% of arrests occurred in public locations, 39% involved an initial shockable heart rhythm, and 18% of patients survived to hospital discharge. The key finding was a three-way interaction between gender, arrest location, and age. In public settings, women were less likely than men to receive BCPR, with an adjusted odds ratio of 0.72, meaning their odds were about 28% lower. In private locations, there was no meaningful difference between men and women in the likelihood of receiving CPR. The study also found that age mattered differently depending on location and gender. In public places, there was no significant age-gender interaction. In private settings, however, older age was associated with lower odds of receiving BCPR, especially for men. For men experiencing cardiac arrest in private locations, each 10-year increase in age was linked to a 9% reduction in the odds of receiving CPR. The decline with age was weaker for women in private locations. The researchers said they do not yet know why women in public are less likely to receive CPR. Coauthor Alexis Cournoyer, M.D., suggested possible explanations include bystanders’ fear of touching or hurting women, or the mistaken belief that women are less likely to be in cardiac arrest.

Coauthor Dr. Alexis Cournoyer suggested possible explanations: bystanders may hesitate to touch women due to concerns about causing harm, or they may incorrectly assume women are less likely to experience cardiac arrest. This study highlights an important public health concern, suggesting that awareness campaigns and CPR training programs may need to address potential gender biases to ensure equitable emergency care for all cardiac arrest patients.

One man, Alik Blbuyan, said his son had served in the army in Artsakh, the name used by Karabakh Armenians for their breakaway region. # The Kursk Disaster: Russia's Nuclear Submarine Tragedy The August 2000 sinking of the Russian nuclear-powered submarine Kursk stands as one of the most significant naval disasters of the post-Cold War era. The incident resulted in the deaths of all 118 crew members and exposed serious flaws in Russian naval operations, safety procedures, and government transparency that would have lasting implications for the nation. ## The Incident and Initial Response On August 12, 2000, at 11:28 local time, a catastrophic explosion occurred in the torpedo room of the Kursk as the crew prepared to fire torpedoes during a major naval exercise in the Barents Sea. The exercise marked the first major Russian naval operation since the Soviet Union's dissolution nine years earlier. The explosion killed most of the 118-person crew instantly. However, 23 sailors managed to escape to a rear compartment of the submarine, which had sunk in relatively shallow waters approximately 350 feet deep, and they awaited rescue. The Russian Navy's response proved tragically inadequate. Moscow declined offers of Western assistance and instead deployed mini-submarines to attempt rescue operations. These vessels made repeated but unsuccessful attempts to hook onto the Kursk's escape hatch. Only after a week of futile efforts did the Kremlin finally invite Norwegian divers to assist. These professionals were able to open the hatches within hours, but by then all 23 surviving sailors had perished. Russian officials later suggested that some crew members could have survived for at least three days, but an official investigation claimed all would have died from carbon monoxide poisoning within eight hours. This discrepancy fueled accusations that the slow response resulted in unnecessary deaths. ## The Kursk Submarine The Kursk was one of eleven Project 949A Antey (Oscar II) class nuclear-powered cruise missile submarines built at Seveorvinsk. Named after the July 1943 Battle of Kursk—history's largest tank engagement—the submarine featured advanced engineering for its time. It had a distinctive outer hull made of high-nickel, high-chrome stainless steel measuring 8.5 millimeters thick, providing excellent corrosion resistance and a weak magnetic signature. The vessel was powered by two pressurized water-cooled reactors that drove two steam turbines, delivering approximately 98,000 shaft horsepower. The submarine featured at least ten separate compartments that could be sealed off from each other during emergencies. ## The Cause: A Faulty Torpedo Following the wreck's recovery—a massive salvage operation that cost approximately $65 million and required Dutch marine companies Smit International and Mammoet—the explosion was traced to a Type-65-76A torpedo. Despite its power to destroy an aircraft carrier with a single hit, the Soviet Union had inexplicably designed this weapon to run on hydrogen peroxide fuel, an extremely volatile substance requiring careful handling. Multiple reports indicated that the crew had not received adequate training to operate these torpedoes or manage the dangerous fuel. ## Recovery and Salvage The recovery operation represented the largest salvage effort of its kind at that time. Dutch salvage experts lifted the Kursk using steel cables lowered from a Giant 4 barge, employing specially designed clamps and fitted holes for the submarine's protruding conning tower and tail fins. The operation, completed in just over 15 hours in October 2001, was hailed as a success by salvage company officials. ## NATO Collision Theory and Political Fallout In November 2021, retired Russian Admiral Vyacheslav Popov, who commanded the Northern Fleet when the disaster occurred, claimed that a NATO submarine had collided with the Kursk. However, Popov provided no evidence and acknowledged he could not identify the Western submarine. U.S. and NATO officials denied any collision, though they acknowledged that an American submarine was in the area. This unproven allegation directly contradicted the official investigation's findings and appeared motivated by Popov's desire to deflect blame from his own bungled response. ## Long-term Consequences The Kursk disaster had profound consequences for Russia. The government's cover-up and mishandling damaged President Vladimir Putin's prestige and is widely considered a "turning point" for modern Russia. Russian lawyer Boris Kuznetsov, who represented families of 55 crew members, described the incident as Putin's "first lie" and noted that "the lies began with the sinking of the Kursk." The government subsequently consolidated media control and began undermining democratic institutions.
