Venezuela is set to close November with 36 consecutive months of hyperinflation, a condition experts interviewed by EFE describe not simply as an economic problem, but as the clearest sign of the deep distortions in the country’s economy. Although specialists do not agree on exactly when Venezuela will emerge from this period, they largely blame President Nicolás Maduro’s government and its fiscal policies for the collapse in the value of the bolivar. The article organizes the situation into five main points. First, it traces the origins of the crisis to a chain of fiscal mistakes. Venezuela entered hyperinflation in November 2017, but prices had already been rising sharply since 2014, when the fall in oil prices sharply reduced state income and imports declined. That led to severe shortages of food and medicine. Economist Luis Bárcenas said the real trigger was the government’s decision, beginning in 2014, to finance enormous public spending through the Central Bank. Venezuelan economists describe this as “inorganic money,” meaning the money supply expands without any real assets or services supporting it. In Bárcenas’s view, the government lost the ability to sustain cheap imports, which had been a central part of its economic model during the commodities boom, and instead turned to the “money-making machine.” The Maduro administration responded to rising inflation with more money creation and strict price controls, but analysts say those measures only worsened the situation. Bárcenas compared price controls to “controlling gangrene by hiding the blood,” arguing that they do not address the root causes and instead produce shortages and “hidden inflation.” Second, the article explains what hyperinflation has done to workers’ incomes. Real wages have been reduced to almost nothing, even though nominal salaries may be in the millions of bolivars. Economist and opposition lawmaker Ángel Alvarado said the minimum wage, which once was roughly equivalent to $200 to $300 a month and comparable to wages in other Latin American countries, is now less than one dollar. He noted that the minimum wage of 400,000 bolivars, or about $0.51, paid to pensioners and public employees, buys only 0.72% of the basic food basket. This has condemned millions of Venezuelans to poverty. As the bolivar loses credibility, people increasingly reject it in favor of foreign currency, especially the U.S. dollar. Economist Jesús Casique said the bolivar no longer functions as a unit of account, a means of payment, or a store of value, because prices are already defined in dollars and people no longer save in bolivars. Third, the article addresses how long hyperinflation may last. Experts disagree, but they note that monthly inflation no longer reaches the three-digit figures seen in 2018. Casique said Venezuela may be on the way out of hyperinflation, but warned that the economy is so volatile that it is too early to be certain. He said the key will be inflation data for the first half of 2021. Still, he believes Venezuela will exit this phase before June 2021, and therefore will not reach the 44 months of hyperinflation experienced by Greece after World War II or the 63 months of very high inflation recorded in Nicaragua between 1986 and 1991. Fourth, the article says the broader crisis has intensified inflation. The collapse of the bolivar pushes people to buy dollars, which weakens the local currency further. Bárcenas explained that when people hold bolivars, they lose value quickly, but spending rises rapidly, feeding hyperinflation. Ronald Balza, dean of economics and social sciences at Andrés Bello Catholic University, added that the collapse of public services, fuel shortages, and difficulty obtaining raw materials have all pushed up the cost of producing and distributing goods. Transportation problems, electricity failures, and telecommunications breakdowns have all raised business costs. He also said the mass exodus of professionals has damaged the country’s productive capacity, making it harder and more expensive for firms to remain open. Finally, experts agree on the main steps needed to leave hyperinflation behind. The government must stop issuing inorganic money and cut public spending, something Maduro promised when he announced an economic package in August 2018. But Alvarado said those measures have been timid, late, and insufficient because they do not address the real causes. Balza argued that Venezuela needs to restore institutional checks and balances so government branches can supervise one another and the executive must account for its spending. He noted that since 2016, the opposition-controlled National Assembly has been declared in contempt by the Supreme Court, which critics say supports Maduro. As a result, Maduro has not presented a budget to the legislature for four years, as the constitution requires, and the legislature has not been informed about how public resources are used. Alvarado added that Venezuelans’ economic rights must be restored, saying the economy has been devastated during Maduro’s seven years in power and that hyperinflation was deliberately used to destroy workers’ wages and keep him in office.

# Venezuela's 36 Months of Hyperinflation: A Comprehensive Overview Venezuela is concluding November 2020 with 36 consecutive months of hyperinflation, a crisis that economists view not merely as an inflation problem but as a critical symptom of deep structural distortions in the Caribbean nation's economy. While experts disagree on when the country will exit this state, they unanimously attribute the currency's severe devaluation to the fiscal policies of President Nicolás Maduro's government. ## The Root Causes Venezuela's hyperinflation crisis traces back to 2014, when collapsing oil prices reduced the country's cash flow and caused imports to plummet, creating severe shortages of basic food and medicine. However, the actual hyperinflation began in November 2017, triggered by the government's financing of massive public spending through the Central Bank since 2014. Economist Luis Bárcenas identifies this practice as the primary fuel for hyperinflation: the creation of "inorganic money" or a "money-making machine." This phenomenon involves expanding the monetary mass without corresponding assets or services to support the new currency issuance. Rather than addressing the root causes, the Maduro Administration responded with more money issuance and strict price controls—measures economists compare to fighting fire with gasoline. Price controls, in particular, create shortages that produce "hidden inflation" by driving prices upward. ## Devastating Impact on Workers Hyperinflation has catastrophically reduced Venezuelan workers' real income. The minimum wage, once equivalent to $200-300 USD—comparable to other Latin American countries—has plummeted to less than one dollar. Currently, the minimum wage of 400,000 bolivars (approximately $0.51) provides only 0.72% of the food basket, condemning millions to poverty. This crisis has fundamentally undermined the bolivar's function as currency. According to economist Jesús Casique, the bolivar no longer serves as a unit of account (prices are quoted in foreign currency), a means of payment (dollars are preferred), or a store of value (citizens avoid saving in bolivars). This rejection of the local currency perpetuates the crisis, as citizens purchasing dollars further devalues the bolivar. ## Timeline for Recovery Experts disagree on when Venezuela will exit hyperinflation, though they note that monthly inflation rates no longer reach the three-digit figures recorded in 2018. Casique suggests that conclusive data won't emerge until mid-2021. He predicts Venezuela will exit hyperinflation before June 2021, avoiding the 44 months Greece endured post-World War II or Nicaragua's 63 months of very high inflation between 1986-1991. ## Compounding Factors Beyond fiscal mismanagement, Venezuela's broader crisis accelerates inflation. Collapsed public services, fuel shortages, and raw material scarcity increase production and distribution costs. The massive exodus of professionals has destroyed productive capacity, forcing remaining companies to operate with higher expenses. These systemic failures make Venezuelan products and services notably more expensive than regional counterparts. ## Path Forward Economists unanimously agree the government must immediately cease inorganic money creation and reduce fiscal spending. However, opposition deputy Ángel Alvarado criticizes Maduro's August 2018 economic measures as "timid, late and completely insufficient," failing to address hyperinflation's root causes. Institutional reform is equally critical. Since 2016, the opposition-controlled Parliament has been declared in "contempt" by the Supreme Court, allegedly aligned with Maduro. Consequently, the president has not presented budgets to the Legislature for four years, violating constitutional requirements and preventing oversight of resource use. Economist Ronald Balza emphasizes that restoring institutional checks and balances is essential for economic recovery. Alvarado further argues that restoring Venezuelans' "economic rights" is necessary, rights he claims were curtailed under both Maduro and his predecessor, Hugo Chávez. He contends that Maduro has destroyed 92% of the Venezuelan economy since assuming power in 2013, suggesting the hyperinflation was deliberately engineered to suppress worker salaries and maintain political control.

Connor Kerner, an 18-year-old Valparaiso man already charged with murdering two Lake County teenagers, faced additional accusations Monday in a crowded Porter County courtroom filled with relatives and supporters of the victims. He was formally arraigned on two new felony counts: intimidation and arson. Pleas of not guilty were entered on his behalf. The new charges stem from allegations that, shortly after the killings, Kerner told an acquaintance what had happened and then threatened her and her family if she disclosed it. According to the filing, he warned that if she told anyone he had committed the murders, “he would kill her and her family.” The arson charge alleges Kerner burned the 2012 Honda Civic belonging to the victims, Thomas Grill Jr., 18, of Cedar Lake, and Molley R. Lanham, 19, of St. John. Police said the two were in the car when it was set on fire. Kerner already faced two counts of murder in connection with the Feb. 25 deaths. Court records say he has claimed the killings occurred during a drug deal gone bad in his grandparents’ garage in Boone Township. Investigators say Kerner told a confidential informant that he shot Grill after Grill tried to rob him during the deal. When Grill fell to the ground and begged for his life, police records say Kerner admitted he panicked because he was out of bullets and then beat Grill with a pipe wrench until he died. Authorities allege Kerner then showed Grill’s body to Lanham and warned her not to say anything. As she turned to leave, he allegedly shot her in the head. Police say an informant reported that around midnight after the killings, Kerner loaded both bodies into the trunk of the teens’ Honda Civic, added several containers of flammable liquid, drove the car to an area near County Roads 550 South and 250 West in Porter Township, and set the vehicle and bodies on fire. The burned car and the victims’ remains were discovered March 2 and later identified as Grill and Lanham. According to the informant, Kerner later said he had done something “really bad,” and when pressed, replied, “I killed someone, and I killed an innocent girl.”

# Summary: Valparaiso Double Murder Case An 18-year-old Valparaiso man, Connor Kerner, appeared in court Monday to face two additional felony charges of intimidation and arson, in connection with the February murders of two Lake County youths. The courtroom was packed with family and supporters of the victims: Thomas Grill Jr., 18, of Cedar Lake, and Molley R. Lanham, 19, of St. John. According to police allegations, Kerner killed both victims on February 25 in his grandparents' garage in Boone Township during what he claims was a drug deal gone wrong. Court records indicate Kerner shot Grill after alleging the victim tried to rob him. When Grill fell to the ground begging for his life, Kerner—claiming to be out of bullets—beat him to death with a pipe wrench. Kerner then allegedly showed Grill's body to Lanham and warned her to remain silent. As she attempted to leave, Kerner shot her in the head, police said. Hours after the killings, Kerner allegedly confessed details to an acquaintance, threatening to kill her and her family if she revealed what happened. He told her he had "done something really bad" and admitted to killing "someone, and an innocent girl." According to the informant, Kerner loaded both bodies into the victims' 2012 Honda Civic around midnight and filled the vehicle with flammable liquids. He then drove the car to Porter Township near the intersection of County Roads 550 South and 250 West, where he set it ablaze. The burned vehicle and bodies were discovered March 2 and identified as Grill and Lanham. The new arson charges specifically allege Kerner burned the vehicle while the victims were inside it. Kerner, who was 17 at the time of the killings, already faced two murder counts. Not guilty pleas were entered on his behalf for the additional intimidation and arson charges.

Argentina’s 2012 Gender Identity Law has transformed the lives of many transgender people by giving them legal recognition and a path toward greater social inclusion, though deep discrimination and economic exclusion remain widespread. The article opens with the story of Florencia Guimaraes, a transgender woman who says the law changed her life. At age 35, after obtaining a national identity document that reflected her true gender, she returned to school and eventually completed the studies she had abandoned at 14 because of bullying and mistreatment. Born male but feeling from childhood that she was a girl, Florencia says she was pushed away from education and the formal labor market, forcing her into sex work to survive. She argues that exclusion, not choice, drove many transgender people into prostitution, often at a very young age, because they lacked opportunities. For her, the law and the new identity documents were tools of empowerment, allowing transgender people to stop being treated as “sick” or abnormal and to re-enter institutions that had effectively expelled them. Argentina’s Gender Identity Law, approved by Congress in May 2012, was pioneering because it allows people to change their gender, name, and photograph on their identity documents without requiring medical examinations, surgery, or hormone therapy. Over the past decade, 12,665 people have changed their DNI national identity card under the law. Of those, 62 percent chose to be registered as female and 35 percent as male. A smaller group—354 people, or nearly 3 percent—recently selected an “X” marker for sex on their documents after President Alberto Fernández signed a 2021 decree recognizing non-binary gender identities. Diego Watkins, a 28-year-old trans man and a prominent figure in ATTTA, the Association of Transvestites, Transsexuals and Transgenders of Argentina, described the legal recognition as a turning point. He said that before being recognized, he felt like a person without identity, future, or life plan, and that even ordinary complaints were treated as psychological issues. Being able to know and be known for who he is, he said, gave meaning to his life. The article also notes a shift in language and identity politics within the community. The term “transvestite,” long used as an insult in Argentina, has been reclaimed by many as a political identity and a banner of pride and resistance in defense of trans rights. Despite legal progress, exclusion remains severe. Florencia Guimaraes, who studied Gender and Politics at the National University of General Sarmiento, now leads the Access to Rights Program for Transvestites, Transsexuals and/or Transgendered Persons at the Magistrates Council of Buenos Aires. It is the first formal job she has ever had, and she says it would not have been possible without the law. She also heads Casa de Lohana y Diana, a self-managed center in Laferrere, a poor and populous suburb of Buenos Aires, where training workshops are offered with the hope of creating job opportunities. She says many trans people still survive through prostitution. A 2019 study by the Public Defense of Buenos Aires, titled *The Butterfly Revolution*, found that only 9 percent of the trans population is in the formal labor market, and most have never even had a job interview. Rights groups estimate that the actual transgender population is 10 to 15 percent larger than the 12,665 people officially registered. Esteban Paulón, head of the Institute for LGTB+ Public Policy, says the law made the trans community visible after years of discrimination and invisibility, but the change is still recent. He previously served as undersecretary for Sexual Diversity Policies in Santa Fe province and led a vulnerability survey there in 2019, reaching nearly one-third of the 1,200 trans people estimated to live in the province. That survey found that only 46 percent had finished high school and only 5 percent had completed tertiary or university studies. It also revealed alarming levels of distress: 75 percent reported self-harm and problematic alcohol use, 77 percent had used other substances, and 79 percent had eating disorders. LGTB organizations estimate the average life expectancy of trans people in Argentina is only 35 to 41 years. In Santa Fe, only 30 of the 1,200 trans people are over 50. Paulón said the long chain of exclusion often prevents trans people from taking care of their health, with many reaching hospitals only when illnesses such as AIDS are already advanced. Valeria Licciardi, a trans woman who became well known after appearing on the television show *Big Brother* and now owns a lingerie brand designed for transvestites, said the law marked a beginning for social change by recognizing trans people as citizens with a right to identity. But she also warned of a backlash: as rights advance, hatred and discrimination can intensify. She pointed to a recent arson attack on Hotel Gondolín, a shelter for transvestite people in Buenos Aires’ Villa Crespo neighborhood. A board member, Solange Fabián, said police told them surveillance footage showed two men setting the fire from the street. The government has also taken steps to improve employment access. A 2020 presidential decree required that 1 percent of jobs in the national public administration be reserved for trans people, and a registry of applicants was created. Greta Peña, the undersecretary for Diversity Policies at the Ministry of Women, Genders and Diversity, said around 300 trans people are now working in the public sector, about 0.2 percent of all public positions, and 6,007 people are registered as applicants, showing strong demand for work opportunities. This year, the government also launched a one-time economic aid program for trans people over 50, offering six minimum wages, since older trans people face the greatest barriers to entering the labor market. Peña concluded that no regulation can by itself end structural violence, but said the Gender Identity Law has been a milestone in Argentina’s democratic history, affecting not only trans people but society as a whole.

# Transgender People Gain Their Place in Argentine Society Argentina's pioneering Gender Identity Law, passed by Congress in May 2012, has fundamentally transformed the lives of transgender individuals in the country by allowing them to change their gender, name, and photo on identity documents without requiring medical tests, surgeries, or hormone treatments. This groundbreaking legislation has enabled over 12,665 people to legally align their documents with their gender identity, marking a significant shift toward inclusion and recognition in Argentine society. Florencia Guimaraes exemplifies the law's transformative impact. At age 35, she obtained a document reflecting her true identity and returned to school to complete her studies, which she had abandoned at age 14 due to severe bullying and mistreatment. Born male but identifying as female since childhood, Florencia spent years in sex work due to the barriers she faced in accessing education and employment. Now 42 years old and holding a degree in Gender and Politics, she heads the Access to Rights Program for Transvestites, Transsexuals and Transgendered Persons at the Magistrates Council of Buenos Aires—a position she credits entirely to the law's passage. Statistics from the law's implementation reveal that 62 percent of those who changed their identity documents chose to be female, while 35 percent chose to be male. Additionally, a decree signed in July 2021 by President Alberto Fernández introduced a non-binary gender option marked with an "X," which 354 people have selected. These developments represent crucial recognition of diverse gender identities. Diego Watkins, a 28-year-old trans man and visible spokesperson for the Association of Transvestites, Transsexuals and Transgenders of Argentina (ATTTA), describes the law's impact as marking a "before" and "after" in his life. He emphasizes that obtaining legal recognition of his identity provided him with a sense of purpose and future previously denied to him. The community has reclaimed the term "transvestite," traditionally used as a derogatory insult in Argentina, transforming it into a political identity and banner for asserting transgender rights. Despite these advances, significant challenges persist. A 2019 study by the Public Defense of Buenos Aires found that only nine percent of the trans population is employed in the formal labor market, with most trans individuals never receiving job interviews. Many continue relying on sex work for survival. LGBTQI+ rights organizations estimate the actual transgender population is 10 to 15 percent higher than the officially registered 12,665 people, suggesting many remain undocumented. Research conducted in Santa Fe province in 2019 revealed stark disparities: only 46 percent of trans people completed high school, and merely five percent achieved tertiary education. Mental health statistics are deeply troubling, with 75 percent reporting self-harm, 77 percent having consumed drugs, and 79 percent experiencing eating disorders. Most alarming is that LGBTQI+ organizations estimate the average lifespan for trans people is between 35 and 41 years—a devastating figure that reflects the cumulative impact of exclusion, poverty, and limited healthcare access. The government has implemented measures to address employment discrimination. A 2020 presidential decree mandated that one percent of national public administration jobs be filled by trans people. Currently, approximately 300 trans individuals are employed through this initiative, with 6,007 registered applicants expressing strong desire to work. Additionally, the Undersecretariat for Diversity Policies launched an economic assistance program providing six minimum wages to trans people over 50 years old, acknowledging this group's particular vulnerability in the labor market. However, progress brings complications. Valeria Licciardi, a trans woman and entrepreneur, warns that increased rights recognition has simultaneously sparked greater hatred and discrimination from certain sectors. Recent incidents, including an arson attack at Hotel Gondolín, a transvestite community shelter, illustrate ongoing violence and hostility. Greta Peña, undersecretary for Diversity Policies at the Ministry of Women, Genders and Diversity, acknowledges that while no regulation alone resolves structural violence, Argentina's Gender Identity Law represents "a milestone in the democratic history of this country" with impacts extending beyond the trans community to the entire population. The law has provided visibility to a historically marginalized group and established a foundation for continued progress, though activists recognize that genuine social transformation remains an ongoing process requiring sustained commitment and resources.

Chile’s unrest erupted on October 18 after student protests against higher Santiago subway fares sparked mass fare evasion. Violence quickly escalated: 118 of 136 subway stations were damaged, 25 were set on fire, and seven were completely burned, causing major losses.

# Summary Social unrest erupted in Chile on October 18th, beginning with student protests against Santiago's subway fare increases. Violence quickly escalated, destroying 118 of 136 subway stations within hours, with 25 damaged by fire and seven completely burned.

A car chase and gun battle near Mexico’s northern border killed four people on Friday evening, officials in Tamaulipas said. Three of the dead were members of the Gulf Cartel, and one was a bystander. The violence began in Matamoros when military and police tried to stop several suspicious vehicles. Cartel gunmen opened fire on the security forces, then set up 15 blockades across the city, burned several cars, and some fled on foot into downtown Matamoros. Officials said it was the second major violent incident in Matamoros in less than a week. Last Sunday, social media videos showed a separate episode of vehicles speeding through the city amid gunfire. Matamoros has also been a major destination for migrants under the Trump-era Migrant Protection Protocols, which required many asylum seekers to wait in Mexico while their U.S. cases were processed. The policy has been widely criticized for leaving migrants in dangerous border cities, and the Biden administration has moved to end it while complying with a court order to keep it in place for now.

# Summary A shootout between gang members and law enforcement in Matamoros, Mexico, near the northern border, resulted in four deaths on Friday evening: three Gulf Cartel members and one bystander. The incident began when military and police attempted to stop suspicious vehicles. Gang members responded by firing on security forces, establishing 15 blockades across the city, and setting cars ablaze. Some suspects fled on foot into downtown Matamoros. This was the second major violent incident in the city within a week. The article notes that Matamoros previously housed a large migrant camp from 2019 to March 2021, where asylum seekers waited under the Trump-era Migrant Protection Protocols policy. The program has faced criticism from migrant advocates for placing asylum seekers in crime-ridden border cities like Matamoros for extended periods.

January was the hottest month in a decade in Colombia’s Amazon region, fueling a sharp rise in forest fires in the southeast and likely worsening air quality in Bogota, according to a report from the Environment Ministry seen by AFP. The ministry said January registered the highest number of “hot spots” in 10 years in the Colombian Amazon, a sign linked to the dry season and to human activity, especially deforestation. A ministry spokesman said at least 80 percent of the hot spots were forest fires. By the end of January, officials had identified more than 3,300 hot spots across the six departments that make up the Colombian Amazon, including about 1,300 in Guaviare alone. AFP had previously reported that during the dry season, from January to April, peasants and landowners often burn or clear forest to plant coca or create pasture for cattle. The fires threaten sensitive areas such as Serrania del Chiribiquete National Park, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and the Nukak National Nature Reserve, home to Colombia’s last nomadic indigenous people. The Foundation for Conservation and Sustainable Development said it recorded at least 938 forest fires, the highest January total since 2012. Its director, Rodrigo Botero, warned that thousands of hectares of recently cut Amazon forest were burning and that the smoke was reaching Bogota. Bogota Mayor Claudia Lopez criticized the government’s inability to control the territory, calling the blazes arson attacks that, carried by the wind, degrade air quality nearly 500 kilometers away. Medellin authorities also warned of harmful air pollution for children and the elderly. The article notes that deforestation has surged in Amazonian Colombia in recent years, especially after the 2016 peace deal with the FARC, which left large areas without guerrilla control.

# Record Heat and Forest Fires Impact Colombia's Amazon and Beyond January 2023 marked the hottest month in Colombia's Amazon region in a decade, triggering a surge in forest fires across the southeastern region, according to an Environment Ministry report. The ministry recorded the "highest hot spot values in the last 10 years," with over 3,300 hot spots identified across six Amazonian departments, including 1,300 in Guaviare alone. At least 80 percent of these hot spots were forest fires. The phenomenon stems from seasonal low rainfall combined with human activity, particularly deforestation. During the dry season from January to April, peasants and landowners deliberately burn or clear trees to plant coca crops or establish cattle grazing areas. The Foundation for Conservation and Sustainable Development recorded 938 forest fires in January—the highest monthly figure since 2012. The fires threaten UNESCO World Heritage sites, including Serrania del Chiribiquete National Park and the Nukak National Nature Reserve, home to Colombia's last nomadic indigenous people. The impacts extend far beyond the Amazon. Smoke has reached Bogota, nearly 500 kilometers away, degrading air quality. Medellin officials warned of air quality levels "harmful to the health" of children and the elderly. Bogota Mayor Claudia Lopez criticized the government's inability to control the territory and described the fires as deliberate arson attacks. Experts attribute the crisis partly to the 2016 peace deal with FARC guerrillas, which left vast territories previously under their control now vulnerable to illegal deforestation.

U.N. experts on women’s rights called on Chilean police to drop a criminal complaint against the feminist collective Lastesis, whose anti-violence performance “A Rapist In Your Path” became a global symbol of protest against gender violence. Police in Valparaiso filed the case in June against four named members after a YouTube video allegedly showed them saying “fire for the cops.” Authorities said the masked women, filmed outside a police station, were inciting violence against the police. The U.N. working group on discrimination against women and girls said Lastesis has played an important role in denouncing police and gender violence in Chile. It warned that prosecuting the group could discourage women in other countries from defending their rights. The experts said they had already raised the issue with the Chilean government and were awaiting a reply. The song gained international prominence during Chile’s 2019 social unrest over inequality, which included mass marches, clashes with police, looting and arson. That unrest left at least 31 people dead, 3,000 injured and 30,000 detained. Prosecutors are also investigating more than 5,000 complaints of abuse against security forces. Support for Lastesis has included a statement with Pussy Riot and an open letter from 30 Hollywood actresses.

# Summary UN human rights experts have urged Chilean police to drop a criminal case against feminist collective Lastesis. Police in Valparaiso filed a complaint in June against four group members over a YouTube video where they allegedly said "fire for the cops" while standing outside a police station, claiming they incited violence. The UN experts, part of the Human Rights Council's working group on discrimination against women, argue that Lastesis has been instrumental in denouncing police and gender violence in Chile. They warn that prosecuting the group could discourage women worldwide from advocating for human rights. Lastesis gained international prominence in November with their anti-violence song and dance routine "A Rapist In Your Path," which inspired global performances during Chilean social protests against inequality. Those protests resulted in 31 deaths, 3,000 injuries, and 30,000 detentions, with prosecutors investigating over 5,000 abuse allegations against security forces. Thirty Hollywood actresses, including Natalie Portman and Julianne Moore, have signed an open letter supporting the group's case dismissal.

Sergio Moro, the former Brazilian judge who led the sweeping “Car Wash” corruption investigation, said Thursday that he will no longer run for president in this year’s election. Moro had tried to present himself as a centrist alternative to what he described as the extremes of leftist former President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and far-right President Jair Bolsonaro, but his campaign never gained momentum. Opinion polls consistently showed him far behind the leading contenders, with support stuck in the single digits. Moro rose to national prominence as the judge who jailed powerful figures once seen as untouchable, including Lula. In 2018, he sentenced Lula to prison on corruption charges, a ruling that removed the then-front-runner from that year’s presidential race and helped clear the way for Bolsonaro’s victory. Bolsonaro later appointed Moro as his justice minister, but the two fell out publicly. Lula was released from prison in 2019, and his convictions were later overturned after Brazil’s Supreme Court ruled that Moro had acted with bias. Moro’s reputation was further damaged by leaked messages published by The Intercept Brazil, which suggested he had coordinated with prosecutors to secure Lula’s conviction. Moro has denied wrongdoing, arguing that the messages do not show improper conduct. In announcing his decision not to seek the presidency, Moro said Brazil needed “an alternative to get rid of the extremes, of instability and radicalization.” Brazilian media reported that he now plans to run for a seat in the lower house of Congress in October’s elections instead. Moro said he would continue serving, calling himself “a soldier of democracy” working to “reclaim the dream of a better Brazil.”

# Summary Sergio Moro, the former judge who led Brazil's prominent "Car Wash" corruption investigation, announced Thursday that he will not run for president in the upcoming October election. Moro had positioned himself as a moderate alternative to the expected frontrunners—leftist former President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and far-right incumbent Jair Bolsonaro—but failed to gain significant public support, with polling consistently placing him in single digits. Moro gained prominence as a corruption-fighting crusader, securing convictions against numerous business leaders and politicians previously considered untouchable. His most notable case involved sentencing da Silva to prison on corruption charges in 2018, effectively removing the then-frontrunner from that year's presidential race, which Bolsonaro subsequently won. However, Moro's reputation has since been significantly damaged. After serving as Bolsonaro's justice minister before a public falling out, da Silva was released from jail in 2019. The Supreme Court later overturned his convictions after determining that Moro had ruled with bias. Leaked messages published by The Intercept Brazil revealed that Moro had colluded with prosecutors to secure da Silva's conviction, though Moro has consistently denied any wrongdoing. Rather than pursuing the presidency, Brazilian media reports indicate that Moro will seek a seat in Congress's lower house during the October elections. In his statement announcing the decision, Moro stated: "Brazil needs an alternative to get rid of the extremes, of instability and radicalization," and pledged to be "a soldier of democracy to reclaim the dream of a better Brazil."

Mexico is heading into what officials fear could be a severe wildfire season in 2024. The National Forestry Commission (Conafor) says the country had already recorded 55 forest fires in the first 18 days of January, matching the total number reported in all of 2020. Those early fires had burned 643 hectares, far more than the 421 hectares consumed during all of 2020. Officials say the risk is being driven by unusually dry conditions across much of the country. The National Meteorological Service reported that 55% of Mexico was in drought at the end of 2023, and authorities even carried out cloud-seeding efforts near Mexico City last year to try to induce rain. In Durango, one of the hardest-hit states, Civil Protection coordinator Arturo Galindo Cabada said dry mountains and strong winds were helping fires spread. He noted that winds reached up to 90 kilometers per hour in some cases and contributed to five fires in the state during the first three weeks of January. Although some parks had to close, he said the overall impact there was limited. Other states also saw early activity, including nine fires in Mexico state, eight in Veracruz and seven in Jalisco between Jan. 1 and Jan. 18. Galindo said the fires were starting much earlier than usual; last year they did not begin in earnest until late February. Mexico had 138 wildfires in 2023, which burned 3,111 hectares, making it one of the more active years of the past decade. Experts say the dry season, winter cold that leaves grass and shrubs brittle, and rising temperatures in February and March are all increasing fire risk. Still, authorities emphasize that many fires are caused by human negligence or arson. Climate patterns such as El Niño also matter, and researchers warn that if it persists, Mexico could face drought and heightened wildfire danger through spring and into June.

# Mexico Faces Severe Wildfire Risk in 2024 Mexico's National Forestry Commission (Conafor) is preparing for an exceptionally dangerous wildfire season in 2024. Early indicators suggest unprecedented activity, with 55 forest fires reported in just the first 18 days of January—matching the entire 2020 total. More alarmingly, these early fires have already consumed 643 hectares compared to only 421 hectares for all of 2020. The primary culprits are extreme drought conditions and high winds. Approximately 55% of Mexico experienced drought at the end of 2023, with some areas experiencing winds exceeding 90 kilometers per hour. States like Durango, México, Veracruz, and Jalisco have been particularly affected. Officials note that fires are starting unusually early; last year they didn't begin until late February. According to researchers, multiple factors contribute to the risk. Cold January temperatures are creating extensive dry grass accumulation, while rising temperatures in February and March will increase fire probability. The El Niño phenomenon, responsible for reduced precipitation in 2023, may prolong drought conditions through June if it continues. However, experts emphasize that human activity significantly exacerbates the problem. Many wildfires result from human negligence or arson rather than purely climatic factors. Last year, Mexico experienced 138 wildfires consuming 3,111 hectares—fewer than 2021 and 2017, which saw 176 and 153 fires respectively. University of Guadalajara researcher Valentina Davydova warns that if El Niño persists, Mexico will face a prolonged spring with delayed rains and poor rainfall development, extending fire risk through June. Authorities are mobilizing resources, though the combination of drought, wind, and human factors presents a formidable challenge for 2024.

A Sydney man has been charged after a shocking unprovoked attack on a 31-year-old pregnant woman at a cafe in western Sydney. Security footage showed the 43-year-old man lunging over a table where three women wearing headscarves were seated, punching the woman, who was 38 weeks pregnant, and stomping on her after she fell. Bystanders pulled him away. Police charged him with assault occasioning actual bodily harm and affray, and denied him bail, while saying more charges were possible. The Australian Federation of Islamic Councils called the incident a racist, Islamophobic attack and said the man had shouted anti-Islamic hate speech.

# Summary A 43-year-old Sydney man has been charged with assault after attacking a heavily pregnant woman at a café in an incident described as "Islamophobic." Security footage shows him unprovoked punching and stomping on the 31-year-old victim, who is 38 weeks pregnant, as she sat with two other women wearing headscarves. Bystanders intervened to stop the assault. The suspect was charged with assault and affray, and bail was denied. While police haven't confirmed motives, the Australian Federation of Islamic Councils stated the attacker yelled anti-Islamic hate speech and called it a racist, Islamophobic attack.

The article is a personal and political reflection by a Chinese South African writer who argues that Asian people in South Africa and elsewhere need to respond more forcefully to racism and xenophobia. The piece begins with the author describing his own complicated sense of belonging. He says that although he lives in South Africa and holds a green passport, he has long doubted that he will ever be fully accepted as South African. He recalls a moment of joy after returning from China, when landing in Cape Town and hearing a passport officer greet him with “Welcome home, Sammy.” For him, that moment symbolized the possibility of belonging in the “rainbow nation.” He argues that if being South African means holding the passport, contributing to the country’s economic growth, social harmony, and the upliftment of vulnerable people, then he qualifies. Even if one defines South African identity by participation in the country’s struggles and harsh realities, he says he would still fit that description. Despite this, he says that in everyday life he is not seen as South African. He recounts repeated experiences of racism and humiliation over about 10 years in the country. As a university student, he says he was mocked and excluded in nightclubs by people of all racial groups. He describes being called slurs such as “Ching Chong,” “Kung fu,” and even “Chinese p*ssies” by strangers and acquaintances. He also recalls being publicly humiliated when a social worker at a school where he was volunteering called him “Jackie Chan” in front of students, prompting laughter from the crowd. These experiences left him anxious about walking past groups of young people, fearing they might shove, shout at, jeer at, or laugh at him. He also describes an incident in which a white man told him to “go back to China” while he was simply walking with his parents. His concern has extended to his family, especially his mother, whom he now accompanies on short errands for safety. Since the pandemic, he says he has become increasingly wary of reading online comments or using social media because he feels attacked from all sides. The author argues that anti-Asian prejudice has been amplified during the pandemic by media coverage, social media, and political discourse. He criticizes news outlets for disguising anti-Asian bias as “journalistic freedom,” and says that articles ostracizing Asians have spread widely online. He points to conspiracy theories and xenophobic rhetoric in South Africa, including claims that the country is under Chinese neocolonial control and social media campaigns such as #NoChineseInParliament when Dr Xiaomei Harvard of the ANC became an MP. Because of this atmosphere, he says he withdrew from public debates and felt unable to respond. What pushed him to write again, he says, was a wave of anti-Asian violence in the United States. He references several attacks: an 84-year-old Thai immigrant who died after being shoved during a morning walk in San Francisco; a 91-year-old Asian man assaulted in Oakland; a 61-year-old Filipino American who had his face slashed on the New York subway; and, most notably, six Asian women shot dead in Atlanta in what was described as a racist attack. He presents these incidents as evidence that anti-Asian hatred is longstanding and deeply rooted, comparing it to other forms of racism and white supremacy. In his view, the pandemic merely provided racists with a new excuse to target Asians. He then offers three reasons why he believes anti-Asian hatred has become so widespread. First, he says Asians are often targeted not only because of generic xenophobia but also because people confuse cultural identity with political identity. Asians, especially Chinese people, are frequently treated as if they are personally responsible for the actions of the Chinese government. He argues that political anger toward China has become entangled with racism against Chinese people, and that this hatred often spreads to other Asian groups because many people cannot distinguish among different Asian ethnicities. Second, he says Asian cultural values, especially those associated with Confucianism, emphasize harmony, tolerance, and subservience. He argues that Asian children often grow up being told to endure racism quietly rather than to assert anger or resistance. Third, he says Asians are often a small minority in places like South Africa, the United States, and Europe, which means they have less political power and less public attention. This also helps explain why Asians are underrepresented in politics outside Asia, he says. The author concludes that he does not expect major top-down change to come soon. He believes anti-Asian discrimination will continue even after the pandemic ends, unless Asians themselves change how they respond. He proposes two steps. First, Asians should separate their political identity from their cultural and ethnic identity. He argues that Chinese people should not be expected to answer for the Chinese government, just as Koreans should not be forced to explain relations between North and South Korea. He says that, just as Afrikaans-speaking South Africans are not asked about politics in the Netherlands or Germany, Asians should not be made to bear political responsibility for distant governments. He also urges East Asians to put aside political tensions among themselves and recognize a shared cultural and ethnic bond, especially because racists will not distinguish among Chinese, Korean, Japanese, Indonesian, or Thai people anyway. Second, he says Asians must be willing to “fight back.” While condemning violence in principle, he argues that violence is sometimes an unavoidable part of struggle and can serve as a deterrent when all other options fail. He acknowledges the importance of peaceful leaders such as Nelson Mandela and Martin Luther King Jr., but says that history shows peace and violence coexist, and that the threat of force can be necessary to defend human rights. Citing Malcolm X, he suggests that both “bullet and ballot” have a role in political struggle. He clarifies that he is mainly calling for a violent mindset, not necessarily violence itself: a mindset that rejects passivity, responds strongly to hate crimes, and signals that Asians are not weak, submissive, or powerless.

Tetyana Chornovol, a former Ukrainian lawmaker and investigative journalist long celebrated by many as a heroine of the 2014 Revolution of Dignity, has been charged with arson and premeditated murder over a fire that killed a man during the uprising. The case has revived deep political tensions in Ukraine, where anti-Russian revolutionaries, far-right activists, and current political rivals all remain entangled in the legacy of 2014. Chornovol, now 40, became a prominent anti-Kremlin figure over the past two decades through aggressive reporting and provocative political activism. She has repeatedly faced violence and punishment for her activism, including beatings, paint attacks, fines, and arrests. Her past protests included chaining herself to railway tracks in 2001 to oppose arrests of nationalist activists and being detained in 2012 for graffiti criticizing then-president Viktor Yanukovych’s move to grant Russian official status in parts of Ukraine. During the 2014 revolution, she took part in clashes with pro-Russian figures, helped lead protesters in seizing Kyiv’s city hall, and, according to investigators, encouraged protesters to throw Molotov cocktails into the office of Yanukovych’s Party of Regions. That fire led to the death of 57-year-old IT specialist Volodymyr Zakharov, who suffocated in smoke. The death had not been investigated until April 10, when investigators searched Chornovol’s home near Kyiv and charged her. She admitted setting the fire but denied wrongdoing, saying the charges were an attack on the revolution’s achievements. On Facebook and in court, she insisted that she had supervised the evacuation of the office and that investigators had no evidence linking her to Zakharov’s death. She said the case file itself indicated that Zakharov entered the smoke-filled building after protesters had left. If convicted, she could face life in prison, though for now she has been placed under house arrest. The punishment has stirred debate because Ukraine often allows suspects in politically sensitive murder cases to remain free while awaiting trial. Critics say authorities fear that arrests could provoke protests or anger powerful nationalist groups. The article cites several examples: the 2015 killing of pro-Russian publicist Oles Buzina, in which two suspects from the ultra-nationalist C14 group were arrested and later released pending trial; and the 2018 stabbing death in Odesa linked to far-right activist Serhiy Sternenko, who remains on trial while free. The broader context is the rise of ultra-nationalist groups after Russia-backed separatists launched the war in eastern Ukraine, a conflict that has killed about 13,000 people and displaced millions. Many volunteers who fought in the war later entered the armed forces, police, or politics, gaining legitimacy as defenders of Ukrainian independence. Human rights and hate-crime experts say some have used that status to attack pro-Russian figures, liberals, feminists, LGBTQ activists, and artists, often without serious consequences. Interior Minister Arsen Avakov quickly defended Chornovol, portraying the case as revenge by supporters of Yanukovych and urging investigators not to distract President Volodymyr Zelenskyy from rebuilding the country. But analysts quoted in the article argued that the case is part of a broader political struggle. Some said Zelenskyy’s camp may be using investigations to pressure former president Petro Poroshenko, whose party still holds a significant bloc in parliament and whose support is important for passing controversial legislation. Others said there is an unwritten elite pact to avoid seriously investigating revolutionary violence, and that cases are often revived mainly to pressure political opponents. Despite the seriousness of the charge, some Ukrainians expressed doubt that Chornovol would actually go to prison, suggesting that she, like other politically connected figures, would likely avoid real jail time.

The case exemplifies how investigations into revolutionary-era violence serve as political tools rather than genuine justice pursuits. Whether Chornovol faces real jail time remains uncertain, reflecting Ukraine's inconsistent approach to accountability for violence committed during the 2014 uprising.

Centro Civico, a Division of Ibero, will hold its own Pride flag-raising ceremony in Amsterdam after Mayor Michael Cinquanti denied a request to fly the Pride flag outside City Hall during Pride month. Jennifer Vallejo, Centro Civico’s community mobilization program coordinator, said the flag would have been a visible sign of support for an LGBTQ community she described as present in Amsterdam but largely hidden out of fear. She said the goal was to show that the city is a safe and inclusive place and to encourage more safe spaces throughout the community. The organization, working with In Our Own Voices, asked permission to raise the Pride flag at City Hall in June. Cinquanti rejected the request, saying City Hall should display only government flags because they represent all residents. He noted that the American, New York state, and Amsterdam flags already fly there and said the city has no formal policy on which flags may be displayed. He also argued that allowing non-governmental flags could create legal problems if the city were later asked to fly a symbol associated with a hate group. Cinquanti said he is proud to be mayor of a city with an active LGBTQ community and that he wants all residents to feel included. Vallejo said the explanation was disappointing and made little sense, especially because the city had previously raised the Ukrainian flag outside City Hall after Russia invaded Ukraine as a gesture of solidarity. She said the refusal to fly the Pride flag contradicted the mayor’s message of support and reflected a long pattern of local failure to embrace the gay community. Vallejo said the issue was not simply about one flag, but about recognition, safety, and belonging for people who are often afraid to be open about their identity. In response, Centro Civico will host a Pride event at its building at 143 E. Main St. on Friday at 4 p.m. The event will include music and guest speakers from local nonprofits that support the LGBTQ community. Vallejo said the ceremony is meant to show love, build bonds, and demonstrate that Centro Civico is an ally and a safe space for everyone. Vallejo also described the personal stakes, saying she has heard from young people who were forced to leave home because their parents rejected them. After leaving Amsterdam for college in New York City, where she studied psychology and sociology, she returned home determined to help create a more inclusive environment. She said she plans to start a petition and work with local organizations to push the city to adopt a policy allowing the Pride flag to be flown at City Hall in the future. For now, she said, the focus is on celebrating Pride in a welcoming setting and showing support for the community.

Poland’s ambassador to Israel, Marek Magierowski, was spat at while sitting in his car in Tel Aviv, an incident that Israeli police said is under investigation and which has intensified already strained relations between Warsaw and Jerusalem. Israeli police said a 65-year-old Israeli architect was arrested on Tuesday in connection with the episode and, after a court hearing on Wednesday, was placed under house arrest until the inquiry is completed. Both governments condemned the attack. Israeli Foreign Ministry spokesman Emmanuel Nahshon said the ministry expressed “fullest sympathy” to the ambassador and shock at the assault. In Warsaw, Poland’s Foreign Ministry summoned Israel’s ambassador, Anna Azari, over the matter. Polish Prime Minister Mateusz Morawiecki denounced the incident on Twitter as a “racist attack” and “xenophobic act of aggression,” saying violence against diplomats or any citizens should never be tolerated. The spat came amid worsening Polish-Israeli ties, which have been strained by disputes over anti-Semitism and, especially, restitution of Jewish property seized during or after World War Two. Poland’s nationalist Law and Justice (PiS) government has been accused of tolerating a resurgence of anti-Semitic behavior, a charge it rejects. The issue has also fueled domestic politics in Poland, where hundreds of far-right supporters marched in Warsaw on Saturday to protest a U.S. law related to Jewish property restitution. According to police, the suspect, identified as Erik Lederman, had first gone to the Polish Embassy in Tel Aviv on Tuesday to ask about restitution, but was turned away. He then approached the ambassador’s vehicle outside the embassy, opened the door, and spat at him. His lawyer said the incident was not premeditated, claiming an embassy car honked at him. Lederman later said he had been upset after an embassy employee allegedly used an anti-Semitic slur against him, though Magierowski denied on Twitter that any such language or inappropriate behavior had occurred. The World Jewish Congress called on Polish leaders to condemn anti-Semitism unequivocally. On Monday, Poland had already canceled a planned visit by an Israeli delegation after learning it intended to raise the restitution issue.

A Paris court has sentenced Lebanese-Canadian academic Hassan Diab to life in prison, in absentia, for the 1980 bombing outside the Rue Copernic synagogue that killed four people and wounded dozens. The verdict came more than 42 years after the attack, which was widely regarded as the first fatal antisemitic assault in France since the Holocaust and prompted huge protests at the time. Diab, now a Canadian citizen, had been the subject of a long and winding legal saga. French authorities initially suspected neo-Nazis, but later issued an arrest warrant for Diab in 2008, alleging he had ties to the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine-Special Operations. He was extradited from Canada in 2014, indicted in Paris, and imprisoned. In 2018, however, the case was dismissed and he returned to Canada. Prosecutors appealed, and in 2021 a court revived the case and ordered him to stand trial. At Friday’s hearing, prosecutor Benjamin Chambre praised French judicial and police persistence and said the ruling sent a message that France does not give in to terrorism. Diab’s lawyer, William Bourdon, argued that there was no material evidence and no proof Diab was in France at the time of the bombing, calling the case a possible miscarriage of justice. Lawyers for victims’ families said the trial still had to happen, even after 43 years. The bombing and later antisemitic attacks contributed to a deep sense of fear among French Jews and encouraged increased emigration to Israel.

The conviction comes during a period of increased antisemitic violence in France, prompting significant Jewish emigration to Israel, particularly following the 2015 attack on a kosher supermarket in Paris. Community leaders emphasized the bombing's enduring significance in Jewish French history.

Hundreds of protesters clashed with Lebanese security forces Sunday near the U.S. Embassy in Beirut during demonstrations against President Donald Trump’s decision to recognize Jerusalem as Israel’s capital. Authorities had sealed off roads leading to the heavily guarded embassy and erected barbed wire about half a mile away to keep the crowd from getting close. When demonstrators tried to break through the barrier and reach a closed road toward the compound, security forces fired tear gas. Protesters answered by throwing stones, burning garbage bins, and, in one case, drop-kicking an officer to the ground. Witnesses said several people were injured, including some hit directly by tear gas canisters and one man who appeared to have birdshot wounds in his back. Lebanon’s Health Ministry later said eight people were hospitalized and 43 treated at the scene. The official National News Agency said security forces dispersed the rally after protesters attempted to breach the security cordon, and Lebanese television reported that several people suffered temporary breathing problems from tear gas. The Beirut protest drew Lebanese and Palestinian participants bused in from across the city. They waved Palestinian flags, along with banners from Lebanese parties, Arab nationalist groups, and Hezbollah. Chants included “Jerusalem is Arab! Palestine is Arab!” and “God Bless Jerusalem,” while some protesters burned an effigy of Trump and shouted, “America is the head of terrorism.” The crowd’s anger reflected the broader regional reaction to the White House announcement earlier in the week. Lebanon, which hosts more than 500,000 Palestinian refugees and their descendants, has long imposed restrictions on Palestinians, including bans from more than 30 professions, in an effort to avoid formally integrating them. At the edge of the Beirut rally, Palestinian protester Faraj Shahin denounced Arab leaders as “traitors” who had sold out Palestinians, saying, “Arab leaders sold al-Aqsa for dollars.” An 18-year-old protester, his face covered against the tear gas, said the clashes were an attempt to “liberate” al-Aqsa Mosque from Israel. Across the region, the Jerusalem decision had sparked widespread outrage and demonstrations, though in Jerusalem itself violence remained limited to smaller confrontations. In the occupied West Bank and Gaza, the larger protests had mostly subsided by Sunday, though clashes were still reported in Ramallah and near Hebron. The article also describes major protests in Indonesia, where about 10,000 people rallied Sunday outside the U.S. Embassy in Jakarta, making it the third and largest demonstration there since Trump’s announcement. The protests, many organized by the Islamist Prosperous Justice Party, also took place in at least 10 provincial capitals and cities. Demonstrators carried signs reading “U.S. Embassy, Get Out from Al Quds,” “Free Jerusalem and Palestinians,” and “We are with the Palestinians,” while waving Indonesian and Palestinian flags. The party called Trump’s move “a form of humiliation and provocation against Muslims all over the world.” Indonesian President Joko Widodo condemned the decision as a violation of U.N. resolutions. In Sweden, the backlash took a different and more violent form. Police in Gothenburg arrested three people after a masked group threw Molotov cocktails at a synagogue during an event on Saturday night. The attack set the synagogue’s yard on fire, but the building itself did not burn and no one was injured; people inside escaped to the basement. Police said the case could become a hate crime, though it was initially investigated as attempted arson. Officials said the threat level against Jewish targets had risen after Trump’s Jerusalem announcement. Türkiye strongly condemned repeated attacks on the Quran and urged Denmark to prevent further “hate crimes.” In a statement Tuesday, the Turkish Foreign Ministry said Danish authorities had failed to grasp the seriousness of the consequences by tolerating and protecting such provocations. It said the incidents offend billions of Muslims and threaten social peace and coexistence. The ministry called on Denmark to take necessary measures so the abuse would not recur. The statement followed Quran burnings in Copenhagen by the far-right Danish Patriots, first outside the Egyptian and then Turkish embassies, after similar protests near the Iraqi embassy in recent days.

# Summary Türkiye strongly condemned repeated attacks on the Quran, urging Denmark to take preventive measures. The Turkish Foreign Ministry criticized Danish authorities for allegedly condoning these incidents and providing protection to provocateurs. The ministry stated such actions offend billions of Muslims and undermine social peace and coexistence. On Tuesday, far-right Danish Patriots burned the Quran outside Egyptian and Turkish embassies in Copenhagen. Similar demonstrations occurred recently at the Iraqi embassy. Türkiye demanded Danish authorities take necessary steps to prevent further "hate crimes."

Eight people were injured in an attack on a pro-Israel rally in Boulder, Colorado, Reuters reported. Police said a man shouted “Free Palestine” and threw several firebombs at the group, which had gathered near a shopping mall and close to the University of Colorado to commemorate hostages in Gaza. The victims included four men and four women, aged 52 to 88; one remained in critical condition. Authorities initially reported six injuries before revising the toll to eight. The FBI said early evidence suggested a targeted act of violence and opened a terrorism investigation. The suspect was identified as Mohamed Suleiman, an Egyptian immigrant and citizen who was hospitalized after the attack. FBI Director Kash Patel called it a “targeted terrorist attack,” and Colorado’s attorney general said it appeared to be a targeted hate crime. The attack came amid heightened tensions over the Gaza war and rising anti-Semitic violence in the U.S. Deputy White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller said Suleiman had overstayed his visa and had been allowed to work under the previous administration.

# Summary Eight people aged 52 to 88 were injured when a man shouting "Free Palestine" threw firebombs at a pro-Israel rally near a Colorado shopping mall and the University of Colorado. The victims were taken to hospital, with one in critical condition. The suspect, Mohamed Suleiman, an Egyptian immigrant and citizen, was hospitalized after the attack. The FBI is investigating the incident as an act of terrorism and a targeted hate crime. FBI Director Kesh Patel and the Colorado Attorney General both characterized it as a targeted attack. The incident occurs amid escalating tensions over the Gaza war and rising anti-Semitic violence. The Trump administration has been cracking down on pro-Palestinian demonstrations, arresting protesters and cutting university funding. Deputy White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller noted that Suleiman had overstayed his visa.

JinNews reporter Öznur Değer is under investigation in Turkey for her reporting and social media posts about the killing of seven members of the Kurdish Dedeoğulları family in Konya’s Meram district. The Kızıltepe Chief Public Prosecutor’s Office opened the case on charges of “inciting the public to hatred and hostility or humiliation.” Değer was questioned on September 1 about posts she shared online after the July 30, 2021 massacre, which left seven family members dead, including four women. Prosecutors also cited the news articles she shared as evidence. Among the posts used against her were statements such as “I am Kurd too,” “Kurds are being massacred in Konya,” and comments describing the incident as a “racist attack” and “massacre,” rather than “hostility” or “killing.” In her statement to prosecutors, Değer said the content she shared came from the news agency she works for and argued that her posts fall under freedom of expression. She rejected the accusation. The case has drawn attention because it links a journalist’s coverage of a violent attack on a Kurdish family to criminal charges over the language she used to describe it.

# Summary JinNews reporter Öznur Değer faces investigation by Turkish authorities for reporting on the July 30, 2021 massacre of seven Kurdish family members in Konya's Meram district. The Kızıltepe Chief Public Prosecutor's Office charged her with "inciting the public to hatred and hostility or humiliation." Değer was questioned on September 1, 2021, regarding her social media posts about the Dedeoğulları family killings, which included four women. Her news reports and digital posts serve as evidence against her in the investigation. The journalist defended her statements as legitimate news reporting from her employer and as protected freedom of expression. Her posts included statements such as "I am Kurd too," "Kurds are being massacred in Konya," and criticisms of racism and state complicity in targeting Kurds. She characterized the killings as a "racist attack" rather than mere "killing." Değer rejected the charges, arguing her posts fell within acceptable bounds of free speech and journalistic reporting. The case highlights concerns about press freedom and the targeting of journalists who report on violence affecting Kurdish populations in Turkey.

A young nurse from Bnei Brak says she was humiliated during a job interview at Ichilov Hospital’s operating room on Monday morning because of her religious appearance. According to her account, the interviewer asked where she was from, and after hearing “Bnei Brak” replied that she would not be suitable because she would want more children. The nurse said she was shocked by what she described as a racist and degrading attack. When she objected and asked whether other women with children worked in the operating room, she was told, “It’s not the same thing.” She said the interviewer continued in a contemptuous tone, asking why she wanted to work at Ichilov when there are “hospitals for religious people,” such as Maayanei Hayeshua. The interviewer then reportedly called her supervisor, referred to her as “some religious woman,” and said she was unsuitable. The interview ended shortly afterward. The nurse contacted hospital administration and was promised an investigation. Later, her supervisor apologized on behalf of the hospital and offered her an interview for another department. The nurse said she was unsure she could work in a place that had treated her so badly and said she may sue the hospital. She also said steps must be taken to prevent similar incidents. Ichilov Hospital responded that its operating theatre and all departments include staff from across Israeli society, including religious and chareidi employees. The hospital said the supervising nurse had asked standard questions about family status and availability for extra hours, and concluded that the candidate’s availability did not match the job’s demands. It added that the candidate could apply for future openings. After the story was published by B’Chadrei Chareidim, other chareidi nurses reported similar humiliating experiences in their own job searches. Professor Gimzu, who directs Ichilov Hospital, ordered nursing administration to give the woman another interview and offer her a position that would suit her, but she remained dissatisfied with the response.

# Summary A young nurse from Bnei Brak attended a job interview at Ichilov Hospital's operating room on Monday morning and experienced what she described as discriminatory treatment based on her religious appearance. During the interview, the interviewer questioned her origin and, upon learning she was from Bnei Brak, stated this would be unsuitable because "you'll want to have more children." The interviewer made inappropriate references to her family situation and personal life, suggesting she wouldn't be able to meet the operating room's work hour requirements. When the nurse questioned whether other women with children worked there, she was told "it's not the same thing." The interviewer further suggested she work at religious hospitals like Maayanei Hayeshua instead of Ichilov. The interviewer subsequently contacted the nurse's supervisor, dismissing her as "some religious woman" and deeming her unsuitable for the position. The nurse complained to hospital administration, which promised an investigation. The supervisor later apologized and offered an interview for another department, though the woman questioned whether she could work at a facility that had humiliated her so severely. She is considering legal action and demanding measures to prevent future incidents. The hospital's response claimed the supervisor was simply inquiring about family status and availability for extra hours, stating the job's demands didn't match the candidate's availability. However, following the story's publication, other chareidi nurses reported similar discriminatory experiences. Hospital director Professor Gimzu ordered the nursing administration to grant the woman another interview and offer suitable employment, though the woman remained unsatisfied by the gesture.

Canadian authorities have approved terrorism charges against Nathaniel Veltman, 20, in connection with the killings of four members of a Muslim family in London, Ontario. Prosecutors said in a brief hearing that terrorism charges were being added to four counts of premeditated murder and one count of attempted murder. The Royal Canadian Mounted Police said federal and provincial attorneys general consented to begin terrorism proceedings, alleging that the murders and attempted murder also constituted terrorist activity. Authorities say Veltman deliberately drove his truck into the family because of their faith. He faces four counts of first-degree murder, terrorism charges, and one count of attempted murder. Police said he has no criminal record and no known links to extremist groups. Appearing by video in court, he said he did not have a lawyer. He has not yet entered a plea and is due back in court on June 21. The attack took place on June 6, when Salman Afzaal, 46, Madiha Salman, 44, Yumna Afzaal, 15, and Afzaal’s mother, 74, were killed during an evening walk. The couple’s nine-year-old son survived but remains hospitalized with serious injuries. The case has intensified concern about Islamophobia in Canada and fears among Muslims that visible signs of faith may make them targets. Pakistani Prime Minister Imran Khan condemned the attack and urged Western countries to take stronger action against hate crimes and anti-Muslim extremism.

# Summary Canadian authorities have charged 20-year-old Nathaniel Veltman with terrorism following a vehicle attack that killed four members of a Pakistani-origin Muslim family in London, Ontario. On June 6, Veltman deliberately struck the family with his truck during an evening walk, killing Salman Afzaal (46), Madiha Salman (44), Yumna Afzaal (15), and Salman's mother (74). The family's nine-year-old son survived with serious injuries. Veltman faces four counts of first-degree murder, one count of attempted murder, and terrorism charges. Prosecutors confirmed the murders were premeditated and religiously motivated. Despite having no criminal background or known extremist affiliations, Veltman appeared via video link and indicated he lacks legal representation. He has not entered a plea and will reappear in court on June 21. The attack has intensified discussions about Islamophobia in Canada and sparked concerns within the Muslim community about safety. Pakistani Prime Minister Imran Khan condemned the attack and called for international action against hate crimes targeting Muslims, urging world leaders to combat hate-inciting content and extremism more effectively.

Two arts institutions in North America have reversed course after backlash tied to the Israel-Hamas war, underscoring how cultural organizations have become flashpoints in the conflict. In Vancouver, the Comic Arts Festival apologized to Jewish-American-Israeli comics artist Miriam Libicki after banning her over her past service in the Israeli military. The festival had initially announced the ban after activist complaints, citing concerns that her presence would create a “volatile atmosphere” because of pro-Palestinian backlash at previous festivals. That statement was quickly removed from social media, but the decision drew sharp criticism from Libicki and from leaders of major Canadian Jewish organizations. In its new apology, posted late Sunday, VanCAF said it had “lost and continues to lose the trust” of many people it serves. It acknowledged that “conflating the political with the practical safety of those attending our festival was the wrong stance to take.” The group said the “vast majority” of those involved in the ban had resigned from its board and that it was entering a transition period. VanCAF also noted that it has no paid staff and is run entirely by volunteers. The apology did not name Libicki, but it referred to one of her works, “But I Live,” a collaboration with Holocaust survivors. The controversy came amid heightened concern in the Jewish community after a synagogue in Vancouver was targeted in an arson attack last week, which authorities are investigating as a hate crime. Separately, Seattle’s Wing Luke Museum said it would proceed with an exhibition on how Asian, Jewish, and Black communities in the region have responded together to hate. The museum had temporarily closed after several staff members walked out, objecting to what they called “Zionist perspectives” in the exhibit. In a joint statement with the Washington State Jewish Historical Society and the Black Heritage Society, the museum said it remained committed to the exhibit’s “core message of confronting hate” and would make unspecified changes to add framing about the exhibit’s origins, the public reaction, and the history of intercommunity cooperation. The exhibit is scheduled to reopen June 30.

# Vancouver Festival and Seattle Museum Reverse Israel-Related Sanctions Two arts institutions have reversed controversial decisions related to the Israel-Hamas war following significant backlash. The Vancouver Comic Arts Festival (VanCAF) apologized for banning Jewish-American artist Miriam Libicki over her past Israeli military service. The festival initially removed the ban from social media after facing criticism from Libicki and Canadian Jewish leaders. In a lengthy apology, VanCAF acknowledged that "the vast majority" of board members involved in the ban have resigned. The festival stated it had imposed the ban due to safety concerns, claiming pro-Palestinian backlash had created a "volatile atmosphere." However, the apology noted that "conflating the political with the practical safety" was "the wrong stance to take." VanCAF is entirely volunteer-run with no full-time staff and said it is entering a transition period following the fallout. The festival's decision referenced Libicki's IDF service, which she has documented in comics, though the apology highlighted her collaborative work "But I Live" with Holocaust survivors. Meanwhile, the Wing Luke Museum in Seattle announced it would proceed with an exhibition on how the region's Asian, Jewish, and Black communities have jointly responded to hate. The announcement followed a staff walkout, with employees objecting to "Zionist perspectives" in the exhibit and demanding acknowledgment of Palestinian perspectives. The museum, along with partner organizations the Washington State Jewish Historical Society and Black Heritage Society, released a joint statement reaffirming commitment to the exhibit's "core message of confronting hate." They acknowledged the complexity of the work and pledged to make unspecified content changes, including additional framing on the exhibit's genesis and community history before reopening June 30. Staff had objected to descriptions of modern antisemitism, including references to campus protests following October 7. The exhibit predates the current conflict. Both reversals reflect growing turmoil in arts institutions over the war, leaving some Jewish artists and community members uncertain about their place in the cultural sphere.

The graffiti at Wilma Hansen School also contained racist remarks targeting Syrian refugees, including a message calling for violence against Syrians and mosques. Prime Minister Justin Trudeau responded via Twitter, affirming Canada's commitment to welcoming refugees and stating that the spirit of acceptance won't be diminished by fear and hate.
