Canada’s proposed Bill C-9 is drawing attention from Christians and other faith groups because of possible effects on religious freedom. The bill would amend the Criminal Code to address hate propaganda, hate-motivated offenses, and intimidation or obstruction at community places. While hate-crime laws are often criticized for vague language, the article notes they do not always target the Church and should be examined carefully. Floyd Brobbel of the Voice of the Martyrs Canada says one major concern is the possible removal of a “good faith” religious belief defense. He argues that eliminating that protection could affect not only Christians, but other religious communities as well. He also warns that, under expanded provisions, some faith-based teachings could be interpreted as “hate,” potentially restricting religious speech. At the same time, Brobbel urges Christians not to assume the bill is meant to attack the church. He says religious freedom is broad, and limits on it do not always harm believers; in some cases, they can protect religious minorities. He points out that some Jewish groups support Bill C-9 as a safeguard against antisemitic hate. He also notes that Canada already limits religious claims when they involve harm. Brobbel encourages Christians to study the bill carefully, follow guidance from groups such as the Evangelical Fellowship of Canada and the Christian Legal Fellowship, and respond with wisdom rather than fear. Since the bill has not yet passed, he says believers should stay informed, speak up if needed, and remain grounded in Scripture.

# Summary Canada's Bill C-9 proposes amendments to the Criminal Code addressing hate propaganda, hate-motivated offences, and obstruction of access to community places. However, some faith leaders express concerns about potential negative impacts on religious freedom. Floyd Brobbel of Voice of the Martyrs Canada warns that the bill could eliminate the "good faith" religious belief defence, which currently protects people of faith. Additionally, expanded Criminal Code provisions might interpret some faith-based teachings as "hate," potentially restricting religious speech. Despite these concerns, Brobbel cautions against assuming the bill is designed to attack churches. He notes that religious freedom limitations do not always harm Christians and can sometimes protect religious communities. For example, Jewish groups support Bill C-9 as protection against antisemitic hate. Brobbel emphasizes that society already establishes boundaries when religious practices cause harm. He stresses the importance of careful study before drawing conclusions about the bill's implications. Brobbel recommends that Canadian Christians consult trusted faith and legal voices, including the Evangelical Fellowship of Canada and Christian Legal Fellowship, to understand the law's practical effects. Since Bill C-9 has not yet passed, believers should become informed and speak up if risks emerge, responding with both wisdom and biblical faithfulness.

President Joe Biden used the first-ever White House summit on hate-motivated violence to announce what he called a historic package of new federal actions aimed at combating hate, alongside civic, faith, philanthropic, and business leaders. The announcement came during a sharp rise in antisemitism across the United States. The Anti-Defamation League has recorded the highest number of antisemitic incidents since it began tracking them in 1979. Biden said the timing was especially painful as the Jewish high holidays approach and families prepare to reflect under the shadow of rising antisemitism, four years after the Tree of Life synagogue attack in Pittsburgh, which he described as the deadliest antisemitic attack in U.S. history. He argued that hate-fueled violence is not new in America and reflects a long pattern of violence against religious and minority communities. The president pointed to existing steps his administration has already taken, including legislation to help local law enforcement combat hate crimes and gun safety measures. He called for a “whole-of-government” response, saying the White House would use every federal resource available to fight violence. He also said his budget had increased funding to protect nonprofits and houses of worship from hate-driven attacks. Biden urged Congress to support a broader national service agenda, including raising the living allowance for service positions, which he said could help strengthen communities and bridge divisions. He also pressed lawmakers to curb the special legal immunity enjoyed by social media companies and require greater transparency from them. The White House highlighted several related efforts. A bipartisan group of former White House officials is launching a new initiative to promote dialogue, while a cross-partisan coalition of philanthropic leaders is mobilizing $1 billion in investments to help build bridges across communities. Biden also praised Rabbi David Saperstein and Rabbi Rachel Schmelkin as “uniters” for their efforts to connect people across identity lines. The summit featured personal accounts from people affected by hate violence. Rabbi Charlie Cytron-Walker, who was held hostage with congregants at Congregation Beth Israel in Colleyville, Texas, described how Catholic and Muslim neighbors supported his community during and after the ordeal. ADL President Jonathan Greenblatt said he was hopeful because people in communities are stepping up and taking the threat seriously. Joseph Borgen, who was attacked in New York during the May 2021 Gaza conflict, said his experience pushed him to work with Asian-American, Muslim, and Christian communities. Maggie Feinstein of the 10.27 Healing Project, created after the Tree of Life shooting, said her group seeks to honor victims through Jewish traditions while recognizing the multifaith support that followed the tragedy. The summit included a wide range of participants, including federal, state and local officials, civil rights advocates, faith and community leaders, technology and business representatives, law enforcement, former hate group members, gun violence prevention advocates, media figures, and cultural leaders.

His budget increases funding for protecting nonprofits and houses of worship, while he urged Congress to raise living allowances for national service positions and eliminate special immunity protections for social media companies while imposing stricter transparency requirements. Beyond government action, bipartisan former White House officials are launching a dialogue initiative, while philanthropic leaders are mobilizing $1 billion in bridge-building investments. The summit featured powerful testimonies from community leaders. Maggie Feinstein, director of the 10.27 Healing Project founded after the Tree of Life shooting, explained how the Jewish faith honors victims through service and remembrance while acknowledging multifaith support. The diverse summit included federal, state, and local officials; civil rights groups; faith leaders; business and technology representatives; law enforcement; former hate group members now preventing violence; gun violence prevention advocates; and cultural figures, reflecting a broad coalition united against hate-motivated violence.

The federal trial of Robert Bowers, the man who killed 11 worshippers at Pittsburgh’s Tree of Life synagogue in 2018, is proceeding as a detailed but largely uncontested proof of what happened that October morning, even though nearly everyone already agrees on the basic facts. Over the past two weeks, members of Jewish congregations, police officers, investigators, and other witnesses have testified in a Pittsburgh courtroom about the deadliest antisemitic attack in U.S. history. Jurors and alternates have also been shown hundreds of exhibits documenting the aftermath: a prayer book torn by gunfire, a bullet-scarred glass door, a prayer shawl and yarmulke left behind on the floor and stairway, and other evidence from the violent invasion of the synagogue building. The most graphic photos, including images of bodies, have not been made public. The central issue is not who carried out the attack, but whether Bowers should be sentenced to death. Defense attorney Judy Clarke acknowledged in her opening statement on May 30 that there was “no dispute and there will be no doubt” that her client entered the synagogue and “shot every person he saw.” She then posed the question that frames the case: why is there a trial at all? The answer, according to legal observers, is that the proceedings are necessary to establish the record before the trial moves to a separate penalty phase, which could last six more weeks. Judge Robert Colville has made clear that discussion of the death penalty must wait until that phase. University of Pittsburgh law professor David Harris, who has closely followed the case, said the only real issue is whether Bowers will be sentenced to death, and that this affects every tactical decision in the trial. That was evident during jury selection, when defense lawyers focused less on whether jurors could consider acquittal and more on whether they could seriously weigh a life sentence without parole instead of execution. Both sides succeeded in removing some prospective jurors who held rigid views for or against the death penalty. The second week of testimony ended Thursday with evidence ranging from DNA samples to lease documents showing how congregations that once worshipped at Tree of Life had to find new places to meet. Friday was a scheduled day off. Clarke, who has represented several high-profile defendants in death-penalty cases, including Boston Marathon bomber Dzhokhar Tsarnaev, Unabomber Ted Kaczynski, and Eric Rudolph, is trying to lay the groundwork for avoiding execution. In this case, federal prosecutors rejected a defense offer for Bowers to plead guilty in exchange for a life sentence. Many families of the victims support seeking the death penalty, though some relatives and synagogue members would have preferred a guilty plea and life imprisonment to spare survivors the trauma of reliving the massacre in court. The attack occurred on Oct. 27, 2018, a Sabbath morning when Bowers opened fire on members of the Dor Hadash, New Light, and Tree of Life congregations, all of whom met in the synagogue building. He killed 11 people and injured seven others, including five police officers who responded to the scene and were also fired upon. The trial began about four and a half years later. Although Clarke has not mounted a full insanity defense, she has tried to show that Bowers acted under delusional, irrational beliefs rather than because of straightforward hatred alone. She focused on the hate-crime charges, explaining that Bowers believed, in a distorted and nonsensical way, that killing Jews would stop what he imagined was a Jewish-backed effort to bring immigrants into the country and harm children. She argued that he was motivated by an “unthinkable, nonsensical, irrational thought” that murdering Jews would achieve that goal. Legal experts note that this is not the same as an insanity defense, which requires proving not only mental impairment but also its effect on the defendant’s ability to understand and act rationally. Bowers’ lawyers have already said they are not pursuing insanity, though they plan to introduce evidence in the penalty phase that he has schizophrenia, epilepsy, and brain impairments. Prosecutors conducted their own mental health evaluation, but the results have not been made public. Harris said Clarke’s approach may be less about winning acquittal than about shaping the death-penalty debate in advance. He noted that the prosecution must prove beyond a reasonable doubt that Bowers killed because the victims were Jewish or to prevent them from worshipping, while the defense is trying to suggest that the evidence will show a disturbed and irrational man driven by extremist online beliefs, including racist “great replacement” ideas about immigrants and Jews. Clarke also portrayed Bowers as a socially awkward loner who did not live independently until age 44, had few friends, spent much of his time online, and became absorbed in extremist material. By contrast, the prosecution is not yet discussing punishment, but its evidence—guns, antisemitic statements, and testimony about prayers violently interrupted—is steadily building toward a guilty verdict on charges that could lead to death.

# Pittsburgh Synagogue Trial Summary On October 27, 2018, Robert Bowers opened fire at the Tree of Life synagogue in Pittsburgh, killing 11 worshippers and injuring seven others, including five police officers. The attack remains the deadliest antisemitic incident in U.S. history. More than four years later, Bowers faces federal trial in a case where the central question is not guilt or innocence, but whether he will receive the death penalty. ## The Trial's Unusual Focus The trial, which began in late May and was anticipated to last approximately nine weeks total, presents an unusual legal situation. Both the defense and prosecution agree on the fundamental facts: Bowers committed the attack, entered the synagogue, and shot every person he encountered. Defense attorney Judy Clarke, representing Bowers, explicitly acknowledged in her opening statement that "there is no dispute and there will be no doubt" regarding her client's actions. This prompted Clarke herself to pose the question observers might naturally ask: "Why are we here?" The answer lies in the trial's structure. Rather than determining guilt, the trial focuses entirely on sentencing. The guilt phase, lasting approximately three weeks, will be followed by a penalty phase potentially lasting six additional weeks, during which the jury will decide whether Bowers receives a death sentence or life imprisonment without parole. ## Strategic Defense Approach Clarke's strategy reveals the trial's true purpose. Rather than focusing jury selection on the possibility of acquittal, the defense team concentrated almost exclusively on identifying jurors willing to consider life sentences as an alternative to execution. This approach demonstrates that the defense has essentially conceded the guilt phase to focus resources on preventing capital punishment. Clarke brings significant experience in high-profile death penalty cases, having previously represented Boston Marathon bomber Dzhokhar Tsarnaev, Unabomber Ted Kaczynski, and 1996 Olympics bomber Eric Rudolph. However, unlike these prior cases, federal prosecutors rejected Bowers' defense team's offer to plead guilty in exchange for a life sentence. This prosecution decision forced the trial to proceed despite the certainty of conviction. ## Evidence and Testimony Over two weeks of trial, members of Jewish congregations relived the attack's horrors through witness testimony. Police officers described responding to horrific carnage while coming under fire themselves. Hundreds of exhibits documented the violence's aftermath: a prayer book torn by gunfire, a bullet-damaged glass door, prayer shawls and yarmulkes left where they fell, and photographs of bodies so disturbing the court kept them from public view. This meticulous documentation serves the prosecution's goal of establishing guilt on charges carrying capital punishment, including 11 counts each of hate crimes resulting in death, obstruction of religious practice resulting in death, and use of a firearm to commit murder. ## The Defense's Argument on Motivation Clarke's defense strategy, while not challenging the facts, focuses on Bowers' mental state and motivation. She argued that Bowers acted from delusional thinking rather than hatred based on victims' religion. According to Clarke, Bowers believed he was preventing genocide by killing Jews who he thought were facilitating immigrant resettlement—reflecting the "great replacement theory" conspiracy narrative. However, Clarke explicitly stated that the defense would not mount an insanity defense, despite planning to introduce evidence during the penalty phase that Bowers suffers from schizophrenia, epilepsy, and brain impairments. This distinction is legally significant; proving mental illness differs substantially from proving insanity, which requires demonstrating that mental impairment prevented the defendant from understanding their actions' nature or wrongfulness. ## Community Perspective and Trial Rationale Most families of slain worshippers support pursuing the death penalty, though some family members and synagogue members preferred a guilty plea resulting in a life sentence to spare survivors from reliving the attack in court testimony. University of Pittsburgh law professor David Harris noted that the trial's sole issue is whether Bowers receives execution or life imprisonment. However, this focus profoundly influences every strategic decision and tactical move throughout the proceedings, even during the guilt phase when the outcome seems predetermined. Clarke's description of Bowers as a socially awkward loner who didn't live independently until age 44, who cared for relatives but had few friends and spent excessive time absorbing extremist online content, establishes groundwork for the penalty phase argument against capital punishment. The trial represents a legal proceeding where established facts give way to questions of culpability, responsibility, and appropriate punishment for horrific crimes motivated by hatred and conspiracy theories.

The National Council of Canadian Muslims abruptly cancelled a planned Monday meeting with Prime Minister Justin Trudeau, saying his government has failed both to protect Palestinians and to take meaningful action against hate crimes in Canada. At a news conference, council chief executive Stephen Brown said the group no longer believed it was productive to speak with the prime minister because, in his view, the government has repeatedly ignored promises made to Muslim Canadians. Brown said the meeting had been intended as a check-in on efforts to combat anti-Muslim hate, but he pulled out because Trudeau has not followed through on commitments made during the 2015 election campaign. Those promises, Brown said, included stronger prosecution of hate crimes and better funding for prevention measures such as security cameras at places of worship. He argued that the government has delivered only limited reform and only after serious harm has already occurred. “It has become clear that we seem to only get a sliver of policy reform when our lives, or our safety, is destroyed,” he said. Brown also criticized the Liberal government’s response to the war in Gaza. He said there is no sign Ottawa is willing to pressure Israel to ease its bombardment of the Gaza Strip or to address the broader humanitarian crisis triggered by Hamas’s Oct. 7 attack on Israel and Israel’s subsequent military campaign. He said the group wants “real tangible action” both to reduce Islamophobia in Canada and to help stop the fighting in the Middle East. Brown pointed specifically to Canada’s decision last week not to join allies in calling on Israel to comply with International Court of Justice orders aimed at preventing genocide in Gaza. He said the government’s position undermines international institutions and shows selective support for justice. Trudeau did not directly address the cancellation before question period, instead speaking only about the national day of action against Islamophobia. His office later said it had “nothing to add.” Brown said the disappointment runs deep because many Muslims once viewed Trudeau as a defender of equality and tolerance. A suburban Seattle man accused of making racist threats to businesses nationwide has been ordered detained pending trial. Joey George, 37, of Lynnwood, appeared in U.S. District Court in Seattle on Monday after being arrested last week. Prosecutors said he carried out a months-long campaign of threatening phone calls, including twice calling a Buffalo, New York grocery store in July and threatening to shoot Black people while ranting about a “race war.” Although he did not call the same Tops Friendly Supermarket where a white supremacist-inspired gunman killed 10 Black people on May 14, he referenced that massacre in his threats. Assistant U.S. Attorney Thomas Woods argued the calls were part of an escalating “campaign of terror” meant to instill fear and tell people of different races they do not belong. He said there was no indication George had weapons. George’s lawyer said he had no criminal history and cared for his mother, opposing detention. Judge Brian Tsuchida sided with prosecutors, calling the allegations “spectacularly concerning” and ruling that detention was warranted. Investigators said George also threatened businesses in Texas, Georgia, California, Washington, New York, Connecticut, Maryland and Michigan, and admitted making the calls after his arrest.

# Summary A 37-year-old Lynnwood man, Joey George, has been ordered detained pending trial after being accused of making racist threats to businesses nationwide over several months. George allegedly called a Buffalo grocery store twice in July, threatening to shoot Black customers and referencing a May mass shooting at a different Buffalo supermarket that killed 10 Black people. Prosecutors argued George conducted a deliberate "campaign of terror" designed to instill fear and tell people of different races they don't belong. They noted he made similar threatening calls to businesses across eight states including Texas, Georgia, and California. When arrested, George acknowledged making the calls and admitted to additional calls investigators were unaware of. George's defense attorney argued against detention, noting his client has no criminal history and serves as a caretaker for his mother. However, the court agreed with prosecutors that the case constitutes a "crime of violence" warranting detention, with the judge calling the allegations "spectacularly concerning." Prosecutors confirmed no evidence indicated George possessed weapons.

A North Carolina woman was arrested Monday evening after police say she drove into protesters who were blocking a roadway in Elizabeth City during a demonstration over the police shooting death of Andrew Brown Jr. Authorities are investigating the incident as a possible hate crime. According to the Elizabeth City Police Department, the driver was identified as Lisa O’Quinn, 41, of Greenville. Police say she struck two protesters, Michelle Morris, 42, and Valerie Lindsey, 42, both of Elizabeth City, at about 6:45 p.m. at an intersection roughly 90 miles northeast of Greenville. The protesters were part of a group demonstrating over the death of Brown, a local resident whose fatal shooting by police had sparked ongoing protests in the city. Both victims were treated and released from Sentara Albemarle Medical Center. Lindsey later said that when she and two other protesters approached O’Quinn’s car to confront her, O’Quinn used racial slurs, including the n-word. Police said two other witnesses corroborated that slurs were spoken. O’Quinn is white, while the two victims are black, and police said that factor is part of why they are examining the case for possible hate-crime enhancements. O’Quinn has been charged with two counts of assault with a deadly weapon with intent to kill by use of a motor vehicle, along with one count each of careless and reckless driving and unsafe movement. She was being held at the Albemarle District Jail on a $40,000 secured bond, and police said her first court appearance took place Thursday. The incident was captured on video and posted to social media. In the footage, O’Quinn’s white car is seen stopped at a stop sign while protesters walk in front of it. As she slowly begins to move forward into the intersection, one protester steps in front of the vehicle. Protesters then surround the front of the car and bang on the hood. O’Quinn then accelerates and turns right, knocking at least one protester down. The person hit was able to get back up immediately. In a Tuesday statement, police said they were still investigating and would present facts and findings, including possible aggravating factors for criminal enhancements tied to a hate crime. The department said it was considering whether the event met the criteria for such an enhancement. The article also places the Elizabeth City incident in the broader context of protests that have blocked roadways in response to police violence and the political backlash that has followed. It notes that blocking roads has become common in Elizabeth City since Brown was shot and killed on April 21, 2021. Prosecutors later ruled Brown’s shooting justified. Beyond the North Carolina case, the article describes a wave of Republican-backed laws in several states aimed at punishing protesters who block roads or obstruct vehicles. In Florida, Gov. Ron DeSantis signed an “anti-riot” law in April that grants civil immunity to people who drive through protesters blocking a road. DeSantis said the law was meant to prevent roadway shutdowns and ensure “swift penalties” for such actions. In Oklahoma, Gov. Kevin Stitt signed a law in April that protects drivers who unintentionally injure or kill demonstrators from liability while imposing jail time and fines on protesters who block roadways. The article then turns to Texas, where legislation increasing penalties for blocking roads or emergency vehicles was moving to Gov. Greg Abbott’s desk. Abbott said he planned to sign the measure and tweeted support for it after the Texas Senate passed it 25-5. House Bill 9, which had already passed the Texas House 90-55, would make it a state jail felony to intentionally, knowingly, or recklessly block an emergency vehicle with lights and sirens on, or to obstruct a hospital entrance. The bill would also require at least 10 days in jail as a condition of community supervision. Abbott framed the legislation as necessary to protect access to emergency services and to stop “chaos” on Texas roads. The article says these efforts followed the nationwide protests over police brutality that erupted after George Floyd’s death in Minneapolis. It also notes that Texas lawmakers separately advanced another bill to punish cities that cut police funding, reflecting broader GOP efforts to strengthen penalties against protest activity and to support law enforcement.

Israel’s Diaspora Affairs Ministry released its 2017 annual report on anti-Semitism ahead of International Holocaust Remembrance Day, and the document highlighted Ukraine as an unusual case in Eastern Europe, saying anti-Semitic incidents there had risen sharply even as they declined elsewhere in the region. The report said Ukraine was “a striking exception” to the broader regional trend, with recorded anti-Semitic attacks doubling from the previous year and exceeding the total number of incidents reported across the rest of Eastern Europe combined. The ministry did not give a precise total in the report itself, but a spokesperson later told JTA that more than 130 anti-Semitic incidents, including violent assaults, were reported in Ukraine during 2017. The figures were compiled from Jewish communities and from Nativ, an Israeli government agency now focused on Jewish immigration to Israel. The report also said 2017 was the second year in a row that Ukraine had the highest number of anti-Semitic incidents among countries of the former Soviet Union. The findings prompted sharp criticism in Ukraine. In an article published by Radio Liberty, Ukrainian historian Vladimir Vyatrovich dismissed the report as anti-Ukrainian propaganda, while anti-Semitism researcher Vyacheslav Likhachev called it flawed and amateurish. Likhachev, who is affiliated with the Va’ad Association of Jewish Communities and Organizations of Ukraine, argued that the report’s authors appeared to have simply counted incidents found online, which he said showed a “blatant lack of professionalism” and ignored accepted standards for documenting hate crimes. The ministry rejected that criticism. Spokesperson Reut Moshonov said the report relied only on credible sources and expressed hope that the trend would reverse in the following year. The report described the kinds of incidents it said were increasing in Ukraine: anti-Semitic propaganda in public discourse, vandalism at Jewish cemeteries, Holocaust memorials and communal institutions, and repeated attacks on the same sites because authorities failed to catch perpetrators. It also said many incidents were treated by police as ordinary vandalism or hooliganism rather than hate crimes. According to the report, after Ukraine’s 2014 revolution there was initially an impression that the country had moved beyond the anti-Semitic rhetoric that had sometimes been used for political purposes. But over the past two years, the report said, scapegoating Jews in public discourse had become “very prevalent.” It also claimed that the Jewish backgrounds of prominent officials, including Prime Minister Volodymyr Groysman, were increasingly seen as part of Ukraine’s political difficulties, and that even non-Jewish leaders such as President Petro Poroshenko were sometimes assumed on the street to be secretly Jewish. The report cited comments by nationalist politician Nadiya Savchenko, who had described Poroshenko’s government as “non-Ukrainian.” The issue is politically sensitive because Russia has long used allegations of anti-Semitism in anti-Ukrainian propaganda. Since annexing Crimea in 2014 and backing separatists in eastern Ukraine, Moscow has portrayed its actions as protecting minorities. Israel, which maintains ties with both Russia and Ukraine, has publicly stayed neutral. By contrast, the report’s section on Russia was notably milder. It said anti-Semitic attacks there continued their downward trend, though it cited 11 incidents, including firebombs thrown at the Moscow offices of the Federation of Jewish Communities and broken synagogue windows.

Armenian lawmaker Mkhitar Hayrapetyan of the ruling My Step bloc strongly condemned the arson attack on the St. Gregory Armenian Apostolic Church in San Francisco during a September 18 parliamentary session. Hayrapetyan said the suspects had not yet been arrested, but suggested the attack may have been carried out with pro-Azerbaijani motives. He linked it to an earlier incident in San Francisco in July, when anti-Armenian and pro-Azerbaijani graffiti was sprayed on the Krouzian-Zekarian Vasbouragan Armenian School and adjacent community center. Parliament Speaker Ararat Mirzoyan said all lawmakers would surely support this position. This was the second attack on an Armenian institution in San Francisco in two months. In July, vandals targeted the Armenian school and community center with hate-filled graffiti. Police classified that case as a hate crime, and the suspects remain unidentified. The Armenian National Committee of America’s San Francisco Bay Area chapter also condemned the latest attack, calling it part of an emerging pattern of hate crimes against the Armenian-American community. The church board said it was working with fire and police officials to assess the damage and investigate the incident.

In this opinion column, Fabiola Santiago argues that Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis deserved the hostile reception he received when he visited Jacksonville after a racist mass shooting that killed three Black people. Santiago says it took the deaths of Anolt “AJ” Laguerre Jr., 19, Jerrald De’Shaun Gallion, 29, and Angela Michelle Carr, 52, along with the shooter’s racist manifestos and the national spotlight of DeSantis’ presidential campaign, to force him to confront Jacksonville’s African American community. Even then, she writes, his appearance was met with boos, jeers, and shouts such as “You have blood on your hands!” Santiago calls DeSantis’ reaction hypocritical, saying he had spent the previous two years advancing policies that harmed Black Floridians. She points to his efforts to make voting harder, his support for redistricting that diluted Black political power, and his push to erase or soften the teaching of African American history and slavery. She also criticizes his support for permitless carry gun laws, arguing that these policies helped create an environment where a white supremacist like 21-year-old Ryan Christopher Palmeter could legally arm himself. Palmeter bought an AR-15 rifle and Glock handgun legally, despite having been Baker Acted in 2017. The column says DeSantis’ response to the shooting was especially troubling because he pledged $1.1 million for security at Edward Waters University, a historically Black college near the Dollar General store where the gunman killed the victims. Santiago says money cannot compensate for lost lives or undo hate. She quotes former state Sen. Audrey Gibson, who called it “blood money” and said the funds were “our money” being returned after years of oppression. Santiago notes that Jacksonville Councilwoman Ju’Coby Pittman, a Democrat, tried to calm the crowd and let DeSantis speak, arguing the university needed the security funding. But Santiago says Black residents have good reason to distrust promises from state leaders because Jacksonville’s Black neighborhoods have long been neglected on infrastructure and other needs. The column concludes that DeSantis’ visit would not earn him political credit because only his actions matter. Santiago says there was no justification for further militarizing Florida or for deepening racial resentment through policies that target minority groups and suppress truthful teaching about racism. In her view, Jacksonville’s Black community stood up to DeSantis in grief and justified anger, and the culture wars he has waged have damaged Florida more than any hurricane.

# Summary: DeSantis Deserves Criticism from Jacksonville's Black Community Governor Ron DeSantis faced significant backlash when he visited Jacksonville's African American community following a mass shooting at a Dollar General store that killed three people: Anolt "AJ" Laguerre Jr., 19; Jerrald De'Shaun Gallion, 29; and Angela Michelle Carr, 52. The shooter, 21-year-old Ryan Christopher Palmeter, was a white supremacist who had legally purchased his weapons despite a 2017 Baker Act commitment. Columnist Fabiola Santiago argues that DeSantis deserved the booing and jeering he received, given his record on racial issues. She contends that his apparent outrage over the hate crime rings hollow considering his anti-Black policies. DeSantis has spent the past two years implementing policies that Santiago characterizes as discriminatory, including making voting more difficult for Black citizens, gerrymandering to dilute African American political power, and whitewashing the teaching of slavery in Black studies curricula. Santiago also criticizes DeSantis for loosening gun laws through permitless carry legislation, which she argues enabled dangerous individuals like Palmeter to obtain weapons easily. She notes that his response to the shooting—pledging $1.1 million for security at nearby historically Black college Edward Waters University—is insufficient and somewhat offensive, as money cannot restore lost lives or change hateful ideologies. Former state Senator Audrey Gibson echoed this sentiment on social media, calling the funding "blood money" and noting it represents taxpayer money anyway. She highlighted DeSantis's opposition to diversity initiatives, including the "Stop WOKE Act," which she views as suppressing discussions of racial divisions. However, Jacksonville Councilwoman Ju'Coby Pittman, a Democrat, defended accepting the security funding while acknowledging the governor's problematic history. Santiago notes this reflects the difficult position of Black communities—needing resources while remaining skeptical of broken promises from state leadership. Santiago concludes that DeSantis's actions matter more than his public appearances at crisis moments. She criticizes his cultural wars and divisive policies as deeply harmful to Florida, arguing they promote hatred and erase historical truth. She commends Jacksonville's Black community for standing firm against the governor, suggesting his visit accomplished nothing politically and only reinforced existing grievances about systematic discrimination and neglect of Black neighborhoods.

Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla unveiled the first statue of Swami Vivekananda in Latin America during a visit to Mexico on Saturday, calling the philosopher’s teachings timeless and universal. In a post on X, Birla said the statue would inspire people, especially young people in the region, to work for positive change and help their countries reach “new prime.” He added that Swami Vivekananda’s message “transcend[s] geographical barriers and time” and was meant for all humanity. Birla is leading an Indian parliamentary delegation to Mexico. During the visit, he also unveiled a bust of freedom fighter Dr. Pandurang Khankhoje at Chapingo University, the oldest agricultural university in Latin America. He toured the university as well. The Speaker met Santiago Creel, President of the Chamber of Deputies in Mexico, and the two discussed issues of mutual importance. Birla noted the long-standing closeness of India-Mexico ties, pointing out that Mexico was the first country to recognize India as an independent nation in 1947. He also said the historical discovery of Mexico by the modern world was linked to an expedition originally launched to explore India, underscoring the deep connections between the two countries in trade, economy, and culture. Earlier, Birla inaugurated the India-Mexico Friendship Garden in the Mexican Parliament complex. He said the garden symbolized the vitality of bilateral relations and hoped it would spread the “energy and fragrance of democracy” worldwide. Concluding his trip, Birla thanked the Mexican Parliament and government for their support and expressed confidence that India-Mexico relations would continue to grow.

Eighty-two Nigerian schoolgirls freed after more than three years in Boko Haram captivity were reunited with their families in Abuja on Saturday, in scenes marked by tears, dancing, prayers, and relief. Parents searched the crowd for signs of how the abduction and captivity had changed their daughters, many of whom were taken in the 2014 mass kidnapping from Chibok that drew worldwide attention and inspired the “Bring Back Our Girls” campaign. One mother, Godiya Joshua, said she was overwhelmed with joy after seeing her daughter Esther again. The release of the 82 girls was the largest since the original abduction of 276 Chibok schoolgirls. It followed the October release of 21 others, and Nigeria has said it may continue prisoner exchanges to secure the return of the 113 girls still missing. Officials acknowledged that five Boko Haram commanders were exchanged for the girls’ freedom, with mediation help from the Swiss government and the International Committee of the Red Cross. Families expressed gratitude but said their happiness remained incomplete until all the remaining girls were returned. Many of the freed girls, most of them Christians, were reportedly forced to marry militants and have children, while some may have been radicalized or even used in suicide bombings. The 2014 abduction helped expose Boko Haram’s wider insurgency, which has kidnapped thousands and killed more than 20,000 people over eight years. The freed girls have been kept in government care in Abuja as part of a nine-month reintegration program overseen by President Muhammadu Buhari, a policy criticized by human rights groups for separating them from their home communities.

# Nigeria's Chibok Girls: Families Reunite After Years in Captivity Eighty-two Nigerian schoolgirls recently released after more than three years in Boko Haram captivity were reunited with their families Saturday in Abuja, Nigeria. The emotional reunion featured families embracing, dancing, and celebrating their daughters' return. This month's release represents the largest hostage liberation since 276 Chibok schoolgirls were abducted from their boarding school in April 2014. The government exchanged five extremist commanders for the girls' freedom and pledged to make further exchanges to recover the remaining 113 captives. The 2014 abduction sparked international outrage and launched the global "Bring Back Our Girls" campaign, supported by celebrities including former U.S. First Lady Michelle Obama. Boko Haram's eight-year insurgency has resulted in over 20,000 deaths and thousands of kidnappings. Many freed girls, predominantly Christian, were forced into marriages with extremists and had children. Some have been radicalized and refused to return, while others are feared to have been used in suicide bombings. The current release follows an initial group of 21 girls freed in October. UNICEF says more than 10,000 children were killed in wars over the past year, while thousands more were forcibly recruited by government and rebel forces in conflict zones including the Central African Republic, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Somalia, South Sudan, Syria and Yemen. The agency warned that tens of thousands of girls and boys are being used in conflicts worldwide, often under coercion or because poverty and social pressure leave them vulnerable. It reported a 70% rise in child abductions, with Somalia especially hard hit: Al-Shabaab alone abducted more than 1,600 children to expand its ranks. UNICEF said children are being used as fighters, cooks, porters, messengers, spies and for sexual exploitation. It also noted that attacks on schools and hospitals are compounding the suffering of children in war-torn areas.

# Summary Over 10,000 children have been killed in conflicts across Africa and the Middle East during the past year, with thousands more forcibly recruited into armed forces. Affected regions include the Central African Republic, Democratic Republic of Congo, Somalia, South Sudan, Syria, and Yemen. UNICEF reports a 70 percent increase in child abductions, with Somalia's Al-Shabaab group alone abducting over 1,600 children for combat and support roles. Children are recruited through force, economic pressure, or social circumstances, serving as fighters, cooks, porters, messengers, spies, or victims of sexual exploitation. The organization warns that displaced and impoverished children face heightened vulnerability. Additionally, warring parties continue attacking schools and hospitals, further endangering children's safety and access to education and healthcare.

A United Nations-supported food and nutrition assessment has warned that 4.4 million people in three northeastern Nigerian states could face food insecurity between June and August 2023 if urgent action is not taken. The report, titled *October 2022 Cadre Harmonisé*, said nearly 25 million Nigerians may be at risk of hunger during the 2023 lean season, up from the 17 million currently estimated to be food insecure. The analysis, conducted twice a year, identified conflict, climate change, inflation, and rising food prices as the main drivers of the worsening situation. In the northeast, persistent violence in Borno, Adamawa, and Yobe states has severely reduced access to food. Elsewhere, armed banditry and kidnappings in states including Katsina, Sokoto, Kaduna, Benue, and Niger have also disrupted livelihoods and food supplies. Flooding during the 2022 rainy season made the crisis worse. The National Emergency Management Agency said more than 676,000 hectares of farmland were damaged, reducing harvests and increasing food insecurity nationwide. The report noted that climate change is likely to bring more extreme weather events that will further threaten food production. Of the 17 million Nigerians currently food insecure, about 3 million are in the northeastern BAY states. That number is projected to rise to 4.4 million during the lean season. The report said many of these are displaced people and returnees already living through a major humanitarian crisis that affects 8.3 million people in the region. Matthias Schmale, the UN Resident and Humanitarian Coordinator for Nigeria, said the situation was “deeply concerning” and described visiting nutrition stabilization centres filled with children fighting for survival. He urged immediate action to provide life-saving support. Children are especially vulnerable. Around 6 million of the 17 million food-insecure Nigerians are children under five in Borno, Adamawa, Yobe, Sokoto, Katsina, and Zamfara states. In the BAY states alone, acute malnutrition among children is expected to rise from 1.74 million in 2022 to 2 million in 2023. UNICEF said it is working with the government and partners such as MSF and ALIMA to expand nutrition interventions. In 2022, it reached about 650,000 children with life-saving services in the six affected states. The northwest, especially Katsina, Zamfara, and Sokoto, is also emerging as a major hotspot, with 2.9 million people already critically food insecure and 4.3 million projected to be affected in the lean season. FAO said it is helping restore livelihoods through livestock, crops, gardening, value chains, and aquaculture. The UN called on the government, donors, and other stakeholders to urgently mobilize resources and act now.

# Summary: Food Insecurity Crisis in Nigeria A United Nations report warns that approximately 25 million Nigerians face hunger risk during the June-August 2023 lean season without urgent intervention, representing a significant increase from the current 17 million people experiencing food insecurity. The situation is particularly dire in Nigeria's northeast, where 4.4 million people in Borno, Adamawa, and Yobe states are projected to face food and nutrition insecurity during the lean season, up from three million currently affected. The northwest region around Katsina, Zamfara, and Sokoto states also faces escalating crisis, with 4.3 million people expected to be critically food insecure by the lean season. Multiple factors drive this humanitarian emergency. Persistent armed conflict in the northeast, widespread banditry and kidnapping in northern states, climate change impacts, inflation, and rising food prices collectively threaten food security. The 2022 rainy season caused severe flooding that damaged over 676,000 hectares of farmland, diminishing harvests and exacerbating the crisis. Children represent the most vulnerable population. Approximately six million of the 17 million currently food-insecure Nigerians are children under five in affected states. Acute malnutrition among children in the BAY states is projected to increase from 1.74 million in 2022 to two million in 2023, with serious mortality risks. The humanitarian crisis extends beyond food insecurity, with 8.3 million people overall requiring assistance, including displaced populations and returnees already struggling to survive. UN Humanitarian Coordinator Matthias Schmale emphasized the urgency, citing nutrition stabilization centers filled with children fighting for survival. UNICEF and partners including MSF and ALIMA are scaling up preventive nutrition interventions and life-saving services, having reached approximately 650,000 children in 2022. The FAO supports livelihood restoration through livestock production, crop development, gardening, value chains, and aquaculture initiatives. The UN appeals to the Federal Government, donors, and public-private stakeholders to urgently commit resources and implement mitigation measures to prevent catastrophic consequences.

Twenty-eight bodies were found on Saturday near Alhira, about 60 kilometres southwest of Tripoli, in an area west of Libya’s capital that has recently been hit by clashes between rival armed groups. The National Commission for Human Rights in Libya said the victims had bullet wounds and signs of torture, including injuries to the chest and head. Ahmad Hamza of the NCHR said the dead were fighters opposed to government-aligned coalition forces and had been arrested before being killed. Locals discovered the bodies by a road in the Wershafana region, where fighting erupted last week after a coalition of forces nominally aligned with Libya’s internationally recognised Tripoli government launched an offensive against rival armed factions, including supporters of former leader Muammar Gaddafi. Hamza said the families were not allowed to receive the bodies for reasons that were unclear. The Wershafana area has long been isolated and known for violence and crime. The recent fighting displaced about 480 families, though roughly 100 have returned home. Libya remains unstable after Gaddafi’s 2011 ouster.

# Summary Twenty-eight bodies bearing bullet wounds and torture marks were discovered Saturday in Alhira, a town 60 kilometers southwest of Tripoli, Libya. According to the National Commission for Human Rights, the victims were fighters opposed to government-aligned coalition forces who had been arrested before their deaths. The bodies were found near a road in the Wershafana area, where fighting erupted when forces supporting Libya's internationally recognized government launched a campaign against rival armed groups, including former leader Muammar Gaddafi's loyalists. The victims' families were prevented from receiving the bodies for unknown reasons. The Wershafana region, largely isolated for years, has become notorious for violence and criminal activity. The military council of Zintan, participating in the campaign, stated it aimed to address "murder, kidnapping and acts of barbarism." The recent clashes displaced approximately 480 families, though about 100 have returned home. Libya remains unstable following Gaddafi's 2011 ouster, with competing armed factions and rival governments struggling for control.

Comair has told passengers that it is operating as normal after securing a court interdict preventing the Air Services Licensing Council (ASLC) from immediately revoking its domestic air services licence. The interdict will remain in force until a hearing on Tuesday 17 May, after which Comair may challenge any ASLC decision on review. The dispute came to a head at a meeting in Pretoria on Wednesday, where the ASLC said it could not clarify its intentions and was still undecided about whether to suspend Comair’s Domestic Air Services License. Comair CEO Erik Venter said the airline had taken “extra-ordinary and urgent measures” to protect thousands of travellers from possible disruption and to ensure the matter would be decided by a court rather than by administrative uncertainty. He said Comair would have a fair chance to argue that it complies with the law. The row began after FlySafair lodged a complaint with the ASLC questioning Comair’s foreign shareholding. Under the Air Services Licensing Act, foreign ownership of voting rights in a domestic airline may not exceed 25%. Comair says it is within that limit. Venter added that although FlySafair later said it no longer wished to pursue the complaint, the ASLC still was not satisfied with Comair’s compliance, which Comair strongly disputes.

# Summary Comair has secured a court interdict preventing the Air Services Licensing Council (ASLC) from revoking its license pending a hearing on May 17. The dispute stems from a complaint by competitor Flysafair questioning Comair's foreign ownership levels, which the Air Services Licensing Act limits to 25% of voting rights. At a recent ASLC meeting, officials indicated indecision about suspending Comair's Domestic Air Services License without providing clarity on their intentions. CEO Erik Venter stated the airline sought urgent legal measures to ensure operational certainty for thousands of passengers affected by potential disruption. He expressed confidence in Comair's compliance with regulations and gratitude for customer support. Notably, while Flysafair has withdrawn its complaint, the ASLC remains unsatisfied regarding Comair's compliance. Comair disputes this assessment and will have the opportunity to present its case in court, where the decision can subsequently be reviewed.

The article argues that the Pretoria peace agreement has ended active fighting in Tigray but has not ended the broader crisis facing the region, and it calls on U.S. Secretary of State Antony Blinken to pressure both the Ethiopian federal government and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) to fully implement the deal. It begins by crediting the United States, through its special envoy to the Horn of Africa, with playing a central role in stopping what it describes as the deadliest war of the twenty-first century. The war in Tigray is portrayed as having caused massive human suffering: about one million deaths, four million displaced people, hundreds of thousands of rape victims, and the destruction of livelihoods and local economies. The article also accuses forces involved in the war of committing severe war crimes, including ethnic cleansing of Tigrayans through mass killings, systematic rape, economic devastation, and the use of hunger as a weapon. The Pretoria agreement, formally a permanent cessation of hostilities signed by Abiy Ahmed’s administration and the TPLF, is presented as having raised hopes that the siege on Tigray would end and peace would return to both Tigray and Ethiopia. However, the article says that four months later, Tigray remains under siege despite some limited improvements in access to food aid and basic services. It states that more than three million internally displaced people cannot return home because their houses are occupied by Amhara militias and Eritrean troops. It also says land transport is blocked, air travel remains limited, and essential services such as telecommunications and electricity are still intermittent. According to the article, arrests of Tigrayans and ethnic profiling have declined, but more than 17,000 Tigrayan officers are still being held in concentration camps, and many civilians detained because of their ethnicity remain in prison. It further claims that Western Tigray and parts of Southern Tigray are still occupied by Amhara forces, while pockets of Northern Tigray remain under Eritrean control, with ethnic cleansing continuing in those areas. The article places the blame for the lack of progress on both sides, though it says Abiy Ahmed’s government bears the greater responsibility. It argues that Abiy’s administration is using every possible excuse to keep Tigray under siege, including limiting air transportation, imposing discriminatory travel controls, restricting financial flows into the region, and maintaining banking hurdles. It says the government has shown no willingness to release detained Tigrayans or to remove non-Ethiopian National Defense Force troops, including Amhara forces and Eritrean troops, from areas of Tigray that the agreement recognizes as constitutionally belonging to the region. At the same time, the article criticizes the TPLF for helping create the conditions for continued stalemate. It says the TPLF is more interested in preserving its authoritarian dominance over Tigray than in alleviating the suffering of the population. Instead of speeding the creation of an inclusive interim regional administration, as required by the Pretoria deal, the TPLF is accused of proposing an interim arrangement that would preserve its old monopoly on power. The article says the TPLF wants to keep the regional parliament that emerged from an election described in the agreement as illegal, and it wants to control half of the cabinet seats in the interim administration, leaving only 15 percent to other political parties and 35 percent to military leaders and scholars chosen in ways that would still leave the TPLF with the real power. The article dismisses this as a cosmetic attempt to preserve authoritarian rule. The article says the TPLF’s proposal gives Abiy’s government another reason to continue the siege, creating a cycle in which both sides contribute to the suffering of ordinary people. It argues that, although the guns have fallen silent, the economic and humanitarian blockade is still “silently suffocating” Tigrayans. Against this backdrop, Blinken’s visit is framed as a possible chance to break the deadlock. Because the U.S. helped bring the two sides to the table and is a guarantor of the agreement, the article says it has a responsibility to ensure compliance. It urges Blinken to pressure Abiy Ahmed to withdraw all non-ENDF forces from Tigray, restore full access to public services, release civilians detained on ethnic grounds, free the 17,000 officers in camps, unblock federal budgets and salaries once the interim administration is established, and remove all travel restrictions, including by securing safe land routes to and from Tigray. The article also says Blinken should pressure the TPLF to stop trying to monopolize power in Tigray. It calls for the voices of Tigrayans to be heard in favor of a democratic transition. It cites recommendations from groups such as the Global Society of Tigrayan Scholars and the Global Coalition of Tigrayans, as well as individuals including Professor Mehari Taddele Maru and Lieutenant General Tsadkan Gebretinsae. These recommendations, the article says, share several core ideas: the regional parliament created through the disputed election should be dissolved; a nonpartisan committee should convene a conference to establish an interim regional council; that council should choose an interim administrator, who would then select a cabinet subject to council approval; and the head of the interim authority should be nonpartisan and barred from running in the election that would follow. The article also calls for an independent monitoring body, similar to African experts involved in DDR processes, to ensure the inclusiveness and transparency of the interim administration’s formation. The article concludes that the Pretoria agreement has stopped the fighting but not the suffering, and it urges the U.S. and other signatories to act to end both the federal siege and the TPLF’s attempt to hold Tigray hostage.

# Commentary Analysis: Blinken's Role in Enforcing the Pretoria Agreement ## Background and Current Situation The United States, through its special envoy to the Horn of Africa, played a crucial role in negotiating an end to what has been described as the bloodiest war of the twenty-first century—the conflict in Tigray. The war has resulted in catastrophic humanitarian consequences: approximately one million deaths, displacement of four million people, hundreds of thousands of sexual violence victims, and widespread economic devastation. The conflict was marked by horrific war crimes including ethnic cleansing, systematic rape, economic destruction, and the weaponization of hunger against the Tigrayan population. The Pretoria agreement, signed by Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's administration and the Tigray Peoples Liberation Front (TPLF), initially sparked hope that the siege on Tigray would end and peace would return to Ethiopia. However, four months after the agreement's signing, the situation remains dire, with only meager improvements in humanitarian access. ## Ongoing Violations and Siege Conditions Despite the cessation of hostilities, Tigray continues to suffer under what amounts to a continued siege. More than three million internally displaced persons cannot return home because their residences are occupied by Amhara militias and Eritrean troops. Land transportation remains blocked, air transport is severely limited, and basic services including telecommunications and electrical power remain intermittent. Over seventeen thousand Tigrayan military officers remain detained in concentration camps, while many civilians arrested during the war based on their ethnicity languish in prisons. Significant portions of Western Tigray and parts of Southern Tigray remain occupied by Amhara forces, with some pockets of Northern Tigray still under Eritrean control. Independent sources document that systematic ethnic cleansing continues in occupied territories, contradicting the spirit and letter of the peace agreement. ## Abiy's Strategy and Violations The commentary argues that Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's strategy appears designed to perpetuate the siege on Tigray under various pretexts. His administration continues restricting Tigrayan movement through discriminatory transportation controls, limiting air transport access, and restricting financial flows into the region through restrictive banking policies. The federal government has not fulfilled its responsibility to remove all non-ENDF (Ethiopian National Defense Force) forces from Tigrayan territory, and there is no indication of willingness to release the tens of thousands of detained Tigrayans. ## TPLF's Obstructionist Role While Abiy's administration bears primary responsibility, the TPLF also impedes implementation of the agreement. Rather than establishing an inclusive interim regional administration as specified in the Pretoria agreement, the TPLF proposes maintaining its authoritarian control through what the commentary characterizes as an "TPLF for TPLF" approach. The TPLF's proposal contradicts the agreement by proposing to continue the regional parliament, which was formed through elections the Pretoria agreement deemed illegal. The TPLF controls all but one parliamentary seat and proposes maintaining this dominance while allocating only 15 percent of cabinet positions to other political parties, with 35 percent going to TPLF-handpicked military leaders and scholars with minimal political influence. ## Recommendations for Secretary Blinken The commentary argues that Secretary of State Blinken's visit presents an opportunity to break the stalemate. As a guarantor and major architect of the Pretoria agreement, the United States bears responsibility for ensuring both parties' commitment to implementation. The commentary recommends that Blinken pressure Abiy Ahmed to: immediately remove non-ENDF forces from Tigrayan territory, cease restricting public services access, release ethnically detained civilians and the seventeen thousand imprisoned officers, release withheld federal budgets and salaries, and remove travel restrictions including ensuring safe land passage to and from Tigray. Two South African families are desperately hoping to bring their loved ones home after long and traumatic captivity in Mali and Equatorial Guinea, and both are urging that their relatives be released safely before Christmas. Their fears were sharpened by the death of fellow hostage Pierre Korkie, who was buried on Friday after being killed during a failed rescue operation in Yemen. Daniel Janse van Rensburg, a 48-year-old businessman from the Southern Cape, has been held for a year in Equatorial Guinea’s notorious Black Beach prison. His family says he is being detained over a failed business deal with a prominent businessman and politician, and that a ransom of R1 million has been demanded for his release. So far, they have managed to raise only R27 000. His wife, Melanie Janse van Rensburg, said hearing about Korkie’s death made her realize how grave her own husband’s situation is. She described the uncertainty of waiting for news as unbearable, saying she knows what Korkie’s widow meant when she compared the experience to “drinking poison” slowly. Melanie said Daniel has had malaria seven times and that the family is not allowed to speak to him, receiving only weekly government updates on his condition. She said she feels helpless and abandoned, while their 21-year-old daughter Abigail, a law student at Stellenbosch University, said the family is “living a nightmare” and fears her father may never come home alive. The other family is holding onto hope for Stephen Malcolm McGown, a South African banker with dual British citizenship who has been held by militants in northern Mali for 1 120 days. His father, Malcolm McGown, said the family is praying that Stephen’s mother, Beverley, who suffers from chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, will live long enough to see her son freed. Malcolm said he still believes Stephen will be released “very soon” and remains optimistic because his son has survived captivity for so long. The McGowns were encouraged by the recent release of French hostage Serge Lazarevic, who had been held in Mali since November 2011 and was freed in a controversial deal in which three al-Qaeda members were exchanged for him. Another hostage, Dutch citizen Sjaak Rijke, appeared with Lazarevic in a proof-of-life video last month. Rijke had been kidnapped in Timbuktu in 2011 along with McGown, Swedish national Johan Gustafsson, and a German friend who was killed immediately. Malcolm McGown said he believes Stephen may be next to be freed. The families of McGown and Korkie have been in contact and share their grief. The McGowns said they were devastated by Korkie’s death, especially because he had been expected to be released. They also expressed sympathy for Yolande Korkie and the difficult position faced by rescuers. Despite the danger and the lack of recent contact, both families say they are still waiting and hoping for a breakthrough, while trying to keep negotiations quiet so as not to increase ransom demands.

# Families Plead for Safe Return of Hostages Held in Mali and Equatorial Guinea Two South African families are desperately hoping their loved ones will return home safely for Christmas after being held captive in West Africa and Central Africa. Their hopes were shaken following the death of Pierre Korkie, a hostage killed during a failed US military rescue operation in Yemen. **Daniel Janse van Rensburg's Plight** Daniel Janse van Rensburg, a 48-year-old Southern Cape businessman, has been imprisoned in Equatorial Guinea's notorious Black Beach prison for one year. His wife, Melanie, expressed her anguish after hearing about Korkie's death, saying the news "shook me to my core" and made her realize they must act immediately to bring her husband home. They have no direct contact with him. Melanie has received telephonic threats that if the ransom isn't paid, her husband "would not make it out of prison alive." Their 21-year-old daughter, Abigail, expressed fear that her father might not survive and lamented that diplomatic efforts have failed. **Stephen McGown's Captivity** Stephen McGown, a banker holding dual British and South African citizenship, has been held in Mali's desert by militants for 1,120 days. McGown's father, Malcolm, is cautiously optimistic about his son's release, particularly following the recent exchange of French hostage Serge Lazarevic for three al-Qaeda members. Initially demanding astronomical sums, the militants' demands have gradually decreased over time. Sudan’s Armed Forces said Tuesday that they have fully liberated Jebel Marra and taken control of the Sorong area in Darfur, describing it as the last stronghold of the rebel movement led by Abdul-Wahid Mohamed Nour. Military spokesman Brig. Dr. Ahmed Khalifa Al-Shami said the army had advanced on all fronts and imposed full control over the area. The statement added that the forces are also carrying out humanitarian duties in Jebel Marra, protecting civilians and property and helping residents return home after what it called abuses by the rebels, including forced recruitment of children, banditry, kidnapping, obstruction of movement, and attacks on locations and trade convoys. It accused the rebels of serving foreign agendas and undermining peace and stability. The Armed Forces said they, along with police, Rapid Support Forces, and Border Guards, will continue fighting the rebels and defending the country and its people.

# Summary On April 12, Sudan's Armed Forces announced the complete liberation of Jebel Marra and control of Sorong area, the last stronghold of Abdul-Wahid Mohamed Nour's rebel movement in Darfur. Armed Forces spokesman Brigadier Dr. Ahmed Khalifa Al-Shami stated that forces have advanced across all fronts and axes, securing the region. The statement emphasized humanitarian efforts, including protecting citizens' lives and property while encouraging displaced residents to return home. It accused rebels of forcible recruitment, banditry, kidnapping, and obstructing development projects. The Armed Forces characterized the rebel movements as foreign-agenda-driven obstacles to peace and stability, rejecting the government's peace initiatives. The statement reaffirmed commitment from the Armed Forces, Security forces, Police, Rapid Support Forces, and Border Guards to continue fighting insurgents and defending Sudan and its citizens.

The Kenya Kwanza side in the bipartisan talks has called on Azimio la Umoja to return to the negotiating table, saying dialogue remains the best way to resolve the long-running dispute between the two coalitions. Led by co-chair George Murugara, the team said the talks were not terminated but only suspended after Azimio’s anti-government protests and subsequent withdrawal from the process. Murugara urged Azimio’s team, led by Rarieda MP Otiende Amollo, to confirm its readiness to resume discussions. He said Kenya Kwanza had remained willing to continue negotiations and expected Azimio to “show leadership” by bringing its members back to the table. The reconstitution of the Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC) remains the main issue Kenya Kwanza wants addressed. Murugara said the current vacancy at the commission has left some wards and constituencies without full representation and warned that further delays could trigger a crisis, especially with boundary review work expected ahead. At the same time, Kenya Kwanza stressed that any discussion on the poll body must remain within the law. Murugara said the coalition was ready for resumed talks, but would not engage in anything “extrajudicial or extralegal.” Last month, Kenya Kwanza had told the IEBC Selection Panel to proceed with hiring commissioners after Azimio declined to return to negotiations. Murugara said if Azimio again fails to attend, the law should be allowed to take its course, insisting the IEBC matter is urgent and cannot be delayed indefinitely.

# Summary Kenya Kwanza's bi-partisan team has called for renewed dialogue with the Azimio La Umoja Coalition to resolve outstanding disputes between the two political sides. Led by co-chair George Murugara, the team clarified that previous talks were suspended rather than dissolved, following opposition-led anti-government protests. Murugara emphasized that Kenya Kwanza remains ready to engage and has invited Azimio's lead negotiator Otiende Amollo to return to the negotiating table. He stressed that Amollo must demonstrate leadership by bringing his team back to talks. The reconstitution of the Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC) will be a primary agenda item. Murugara noted that several wards and constituencies currently lack representation due to IEBC vacancies, and delays in reconstitution could create a crisis related to boundary limitations. President William Ruto's team warned that IEBC reconstitution discussions will proceed strictly within legal parameters, rejecting any extrajudicial or extralegal approaches. The Kenya Kwanza team previously instructed the IEBC Selection Panel to proceed with commissioner hiring after Azimio declined to return to negotiations. Murugara warned that if Azimio continues snubbing meetings, the law will take its course, as the IEBC reconstitution issue is urgent and Kenyans cannot remain indefinitely held at ransom. Kenya Kwanza proposed a meeting for Tuesday, July 4.

Beijing police have launched a six-month high-intensity training programme for about 1,350 officers and 150 armoured vehicles to strengthen their response to terrorism and extreme violence, the municipal public security bureau said. Starting Monday, the officers will undergo five-day intensive courses led by experienced veterans who have handled recent violent incidents on the mainland, including a hostage case in Beijing last May. The drills are meant to help officers identify suspects in crowds and fire accurately without endangering bystanders, according to deputy criminal police chief Li Qiang. Trainees must learn to fire within 1 to 1.5 seconds from different angles, and for the first time they are also using paintball guns to improve accuracy. Each officer is required to shoot 120 pistol rounds and 30 rifle rounds daily. Training will also take place in simulated settings such as schools, hospitals, bus stops, train stations, shopping malls and residential compounds. The move comes amid stepped-up anti-terrorism efforts, including inspections of fuel stations and helicopter monitoring of key city routes.

# Summary Beijing police officers are undergoing intensive six-month training to prepare for potential terrorist attacks and extreme behavior. Approximately 1,350 officers and 150 armored vehicles began the program on Monday, designed by veterans experienced with recent mainland violent incidents, including a May hostage situation in Beijing. The training features five-day intensive courses where officers practice locating suspects in crowds and firing accurately without harming bystanders. Officers must fire bullets within 1-1.5 seconds from various angles, using paintball guns for the first time to improve accuracy. Daily requirements include firing 120 pistol bullets and 30 rifle bullets per officer. Tactical training occurs in simulated environments such as schools, hospitals, bus stops, train stations, shopping malls, and residential complexes. Additionally, Beijing police have intensified counterterrorism efforts following nationwide terrorist attacks, including sending 100 inspection teams to check approximately 1,000 filling stations for safety compliance. The city has also designated eight air routes for helicopter surveillance, focusing on high-traffic areas, parks, and highway exits.

Global stock markets were mixed Tuesday after China confirmed that Vice Premier Liu He would travel to Washington for trade talks, even as U.S. President Donald Trump threatened to sharply escalate the tariff fight with Beijing. The announcement briefly supported hopes that a deal could still be reached soon, but investors remained uneasy about the risk of a widening trade war and its impact on global growth. Chinese shares led gains in Asia, with the Shanghai Composite rising 0.7%, while Hong Kong’s Hang Seng added 0.5%. Several other Asian markets also recovered, including Sydney, New Zealand, Taiwan and Singapore. But Japan’s Nikkei 225 fell 1.5% after reopening from a weeklong holiday, and India’s Sensex slipped slightly. In Europe, markets declined: London’s FTSE 100 dropped more than 1%, France’s CAC 40 fell more than 0.7%, and Germany’s DAX lost 0.6%. U.S. stock futures also pointed lower. Trump’s Sunday threat revived tensions after earlier signs that negotiations were progressing. He accused China of backtracking and said tariffs on $200 billion in Chinese goods would rise to 25% from 10% on Friday, while duties on another $325 billion of imports could also be imposed. Analysts said the market still sees a framework agreement as possible, but the deadline and tariff threats have increased uncertainty. Elsewhere, U.S. crude and Brent oil prices fell, while the dollar was slightly weaker against the yen and the euro was little changed.

# Global Markets React to China Trade Talk Developments Global stock markets showed mixed results Tuesday as China confirmed its economy czar will attend trade negotiations in Washington, despite U.S. President Donald Trump's recent threats to escalate tariffs. China's main stock index rose 0.7%, and most Asian markets rebounded following the announcement that Vice Premier Liu He will proceed with planned talks. However, European shares declined and Wall Street futures indicated a lower opening. The news provided some relief after Trump threatened Sunday to raise tariffs on $200 billion of Chinese goods from 10% to 25% effective Friday, with additional increases on $325 billion more in imports. Asian market performance was mixed. Tokyo's Nikkei 225 plunged 1.5% after a holiday break, while Hong Kong's Hang Seng added 0.5%. Sydney's S&P-ASX 200 and benchmarks in New Zealand, Taiwan, and Singapore advanced, though India's Sensex declined. European markets fell significantly. London's FTSE 100 dropped over 1%, France's CAC 40 fell more than 0.7%, and Germany's DAX declined 0.6%. U.S. futures for the S&P 500 and Dow Jones Industrial Average each fell approximately 0.6%.
