Police in North Aceh, Aceh, arrested four men suspected of carrying out an armed kidnapping ring. The suspects, identified as S (60), N (31), G (35), and B (36), were detained in Kuta Makmur Sub-district after officers first captured S and then tracked down the other three in separate locations. North Aceh Police Criminal Investigation Unit head First Inspector Reski Kholiddiansyah said the men were suspected of kidnapping M Azwani, also referred to as M Azni, a resident of Cot Girek Sub-district. The kidnapping occurred on September 7, 2018, in Alue Seumambu Village, Cot Girek, when the victim was riding a motorcycle with a friend. Four unidentified men in a Toyota Avanza intercepted them, and two reportedly used firearms to force the victim into the vehicle. The suspects covered the victim’s face, taped his eyes, and left his friend behind with the motorcycle. During the arrests, police also found four packages of methamphetamine weighing 9.29 grams and inhalers. Investigators are still probing the motive and the firearms used.

# Summary North Aceh police arrested four men suspected of kidnapping M Azwani on September 7, 2018. The suspects, identified as S (60), N (31), G (35), and B (36), were apprehended in Kuta Makmur Sub-district. According to police, the victim was intercepted while riding his motorcycle in Alue Seumambu Village. Two perpetrators allegedly used firearms to force Azwani into their Toyota Avanza minibus, covering his face and taping his eyes while his companion was left behind. Police initially arrested suspect S, then apprehended the three others separately. During the arrests, officers recovered four methamphetamine packages weighing 9.29 grams and drug paraphernalia. The suspects remain detained at police headquarters pending investigation into both the kidnapping and drug charges. Police are continuing their investigation to determine the kidnapping motive and locate the firearms used.

Two South Koreans abducted in southern Nigeria nearly three weeks ago were released and are now in good health, South Korea’s foreign ministry said Saturday. The men were taken on December 12 by an unidentified armed group and were employees of Daewoo Engineering & Construction, according to Yonhap. South Korean authorities secured their custody on Friday, then moved them to a safe location after a medical checkup, where they were able to call their families. The ministry said the release came through close cooperation between the South Korean government and the company, along with collaboration from Nigerian military, police and intelligence officials. It did not say whether a ransom was paid. During the abduction, the armed group killed four bodyguards, identified by Seoul as Nigerian soldiers, and two local drivers. South Korea said it would continue reviewing protection measures for its nationals in Nigeria and work with government agencies, businesses and overseas Koreans to help prevent future kidnappings. Kidnapping for ransom is common in Nigeria, where foreign workers, including those in construction and mining, have often been targeted.

# Two South Koreans Released After Nigerian Abduction Two South Korean employees of Daewoo Engineering & Construction Co. were released after being abducted nearly three weeks ago in southern Nigeria on December 12. South Korean authorities secured their custody on Friday, and both men are reported to be in good health. The kidnapping was carried out by an unidentified armed group. During the incident, four Nigerian bodyguards and two local drivers were killed. The abductees have been moved to a safe area following medical examination and have contacted their families. South Korea's foreign ministry credited the release to close cooperation between the Seoul government, the company, and Nigerian military, police, and intelligence authorities. The statement did not confirm whether ransom was paid. Kidnapping for ransom is common in Nigeria, with criminal gangs frequently targeting foreign workers in remote areas. The South Korean government pledged to strengthen protective measures for its nationals in Nigeria and collaborate with relevant agencies to prevent future incidents.

Australian filmmaker James Ricketson, 68, remains in detention in Cambodia on espionage charges after a court session in Phnom Penh examined emails found on his seized computer. Ricketson was arrested in June last year after flying a drone without a permit over an opposition rally. Prosecutors later charged him under Cambodia’s espionage laws, accusing him of gathering information for a foreign power that could harm national security. If convicted, he could face up to 10 years in prison. He has repeatedly denied the accusation, and critics say the case is politically driven. On Tuesday, a judge questioned Ricketson for two hours in a closed hearing at Phnom Penh Municipal Court. According to his lawyer, Peung Yok Hiep, the judge focused on three emails, which were the first pieces of evidence Ricketson had been shown during his eight months of pre-trial detention. The Australian is expected to be questioned again next week. One email, sent in 2013 to self-exiled former opposition leader Sam Rainsy, allegedly asked for confirmation about whether Rainsy was subject to a new arrest warrant. Ricketson acknowledged sending that email, and his lawyer argued that such contact was normal for a journalist. Rainsy also defended him, saying the correspondence was similar to what he received from many foreign reporters and calling Ricketson a “scapegoat” and “hostage” used to intimidate journalists critical of the Hun Sen government. Another email discussed in court involved Ricketson allegedly replying to a foreign friend who asked about the number of bodyguards protecting Prime Minister Hun Sen and the number of water cannon trucks available to break up protests. His lawyer said Ricketson answered that the number of bodyguards was about 10,000. A third email involved an Indian woman asking him to help a Cambodian film team with an NGO-related project. Separately, the Australian Broadcasting Corporation reported that Australian Foreign Minister Julie Bishop had formally intervened by writing to Cambodian Foreign Minister Prak Sokhonn, raising concerns about Ricketson’s detention. Australia has already been providing consular assistance, but this was said to be the first direct diplomatic representation on the case. Ricketson’s prosecution comes amid a wider crackdown ahead of Cambodia’s elections, targeting the opposition Cambodia National Rescue Party, independent media, and foreign journalists. Radio Free Asia journalists have also been arrested on espionage charges, radio frequencies carrying RFA and Voice of America content were shut down, and the Cambodia Daily newspaper was forced to close after a disputed tax bill. Ricketson is currently held in the overcrowded Prey Sar prison, where he was recently moved into a cell with 140 inmates.

# Australian Filmmaker Faces Espionage Charges in Cambodia Australian filmmaker James Ricketson, 68, is being prosecuted in Cambodia on espionage charges that could result in a 10-year prison sentence. Arrested in June 2017 after flying a drone without a permit over an opposition rally, Ricketson has repeatedly denied the charges, which critics argue are politically motivated. During a two-hour court questioning on February 6, judges examined emails from Ricketson's seized computer, marking the first evidence presented during his eight months of pre-trial detention. The emails, sent to self-exiled opposition leader Sam Rainsy, form the basis of the prosecution's case. One email from 2013 shows Ricketson asking Rainsy to confirm whether the politician faced a new arrest warrant. Ricketson's lawyer, Peung Yok Hiep, argued this constituted normal journalistic work, stating: "It is normal, because he is a journalist, to meet politicians." Rainsy defended Ricketson, characterizing the correspondence as routine communication with foreign journalists and describing Ricketson as "a scapegoat and a hostage held by the government to frighten other foreign journalists." A second email discussed in court involved Ricketson responding to inquiries about Prime Minister Hun Sen's security detail, which he indicated numbered approximately 10,000 bodyguards, and the government's water cannon trucks used for crowd control. A third email concerned an Indian woman requesting assistance with a Cambodian film project for an unidentified NGO. Ricketson's case reflects Cambodia's broader pre-election crackdown targeting opposition parties and independent media. The opposition Cambodia National Rescue Party (CNRP) was dissolved in November 2017 following the arrest of leader Kem Sokha on disputed treason charges. Additionally, two Radio Free Asia journalists were arrested on espionage charges, multiple radio frequencies carrying critical content were shut down, and the Cambodia Daily newspaper was forced to close after receiving an exorbitant tax bill. In a significant development, Australian Foreign Minister Julie Bishop formally intervened by writing to her Cambodian counterpart, Prak Sokhonn, expressing concerns about Ricketson's detention. This marked the first formal diplomatic representation on his behalf, though Australia had previously provided consular support. Ricketson is currently detained in Phnom Penh's overcrowded Prey Sar prison, recently moved to a cell containing 140 inmates. He is expected to face additional questioning the following week.

New Zealand’s intelligence agency has confirmed for the first time that a 17-year-old tried to assassinate Queen Elizabeth II during her 1981 visit to Dunedin, prompting a police review of how the case was handled. Declassified documents from the New Zealand Security Intelligence Service (SIS) say Christopher Lewis fired at the Queen on 14 October as she stepped from her vehicle on the way to a science fair during her eight-day tour of the country. A 1997 SIS memo said Lewis had intended to kill the Queen but lacked a suitable firing position and a powerful enough rifle to hit her from the distance involved. Lewis was not charged with attempted murder or treason. Instead, he faced charges of unlawful possession and discharge of a firearm, which has fueled suggestions that authorities downplayed the incident to avoid embarrassing New Zealand while hosting the royal visit. Witnesses in Dunedin, including members of the crowd and reporters, heard the shot, but police initially said the sound may have come from a falling sign, a car backfiring, or later a firework. Another SIS memo from November 1981 said the police inquiry had been conducted discreetly and that most media likely believed the noise was a firework. The revelations have led the police commissioner to order an examination of the case file. Intelligence records also show police monitored Lewis closely during Queen Elizabeth’s 1986 visit, fearing he remained a threat. Lewis was later charged with the murder of an Auckland mother and the abduction of her baby daughter, and he died in prison in 1997 while awaiting trial.

# Summary New Zealand's Security Intelligence Service confirmed Thursday that a 17-year-old named Christopher Lewis attempted to assassinate Queen Elizabeth II during her 1981 visit to Dunedin. According to declassified documents, Lewis fired a shot at the Queen as she exited her vehicle en route to a science fair on October 14, 1981. Intelligence memos revealed that while Lewis intended to kill the Queen, he lacked an adequate vantage point and a sufficiently powerful rifle for the distance. Despite this assassination attempt, Lewis was not charged with attempted murder or treason—only with unlawful possession and discharge of a firearm. This lenient treatment has prompted claims that authorities downplayed the incident to avoid embarrassing the country during the royal visit. Witnesses heard the gunshot, but police initially told the public it was a falling sign or car backfiring. An SIS memo noted that media representatives likely believed it was a firework. During the Queen's 1986 return visit, police monitored Lewis closely due to continued concerns about his threat level. Over a decade later, Lewis was charged with murdering an Auckland mother and abducting her baby. He electrocuted himself in prison in 1997 while awaiting trial, denying the murder charge in a suicide note. The revelations have triggered a police inquiry into how the assassination attempt was handled.

Malacañang on Friday accused communist rebels of using their holiday ceasefire declaration to lull government troops into complacency, following an NPA attack in Agusan del Sur that left two soldiers and 12 militiamen hostage. Presidential Spokesperson Salvador Panelo said the rebels appeared to be taking advantage of the truce to catch soldiers off guard. He noted that CPP founder Jose Maria Sison had earlier announced a five-day holiday ceasefire despite President Rodrigo Duterte’s order for a full-scale war against the communists. Defense Secretary Delfin Lorenzana had already admitted the military was caught unprepared by the Agusan del Sur attack. Panelo said the rebels’ repeated ceasefire announcements may have led troops on the ground to believe there would be no attack, but he stressed that complacency was “not prudent.” He said soldiers should always be prepared because the NPA could strike “like a thief in the night.” While welcoming Sison’s statement that the hostages would be released, Panelo said the government would continue military operations against the rebels. Executive Secretary Salvador Medialdea earlier said Duterte would not declare a holiday ceasefire.

# Summary The Philippine Palace accused communist rebels of exploiting a holiday ceasefire declaration to ambush military forces. The New People's Army (NPA) recently captured two soldiers and 12 militiamen in Agusan del Sur, prompting accusations that they were using the truce deceptively. Presidential Spokesperson Salvador Panelo stated that soldiers were caught off guard, believing the declared five-day ceasefire was genuine. Defense Secretary Delfin Lorenzana acknowledged the military was unprepared for the attack. Panelo criticized the military's complacency, emphasizing that soldiers should remain vigilant despite ceasefire declarations. He warned that the NPA operates unpredictably, like "a thief in the night." While the Palace welcomed the NPA's statement about releasing hostages, it rejected any formal ceasefire agreement. Executive Secretary Salvador Medialdea confirmed President Rodrigo Duterte would not declare a holiday ceasefire with the rebels, and the government vowed to continue pursuing communist forces despite the declared truce.

A Reuters report said a U.S. official claimed China would still be able to buy Venezuelan oil after the United States became involved in Venezuela’s oil industry, but that Beijing would no longer get what the official described as “unfair, undercut” prices. The comment came amid a major shift in Venezuela’s political and economic situation after President Donald Trump announced that American oil experts would cooperate with Venezuela’s new leadership to restore production and sales. According to the article, Trump approved a Delta Force mission to enter Caracas and arrest deposed dictator Nicolás Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, on narco-trafficking charges. The operation reportedly caused no significant American losses, but led to the deaths of at least 32 Cuban state security agents who were guarding Maduro. After Maduro’s arrest, control of the socialist regime passed to his vice president, Delcy Rodríguez, who publicly signaled willingness to work with the United States. Trump has praised Rodríguez, describing her as “terrific,” and said she is in regular contact with Secretary of State Marco Rubio. He also mocked the situation on social media, joking that he—not Rodríguez—was the “acting” president of Venezuela. The article presents this as part of a broader U.S. effort to reshape Venezuela’s oil sector and political alignment. China stood to lose the most geopolitically from Maduro’s removal, the article said, because Beijing had long supported the Chávez-Maduro government. A major source of China’s financial exposure in Venezuela was a 2018 agreement in which the Chinese Communist Party extended Maduro a $5 billion loan, apparently to be repaid in oil. After the first Trump administration sanctioned Petróleos de Venezuela (PDVSA), Venezuela’s state oil company, oil shipments to China reportedly increased because fewer countries were willing to defy U.S. sanctions and buy from Maduro. Oil analysts viewed Maduro’s arrest as a serious blow to China. The article said some initially thought China could replace Venezuelan crude with Iranian oil, but that option became less attractive after the United States imposed new sanctions on Iran in response to violent repression of protesters there. Under the new arrangement described by the U.S. official, China could still purchase Venezuelan oil, but it would no longer receive what was effectively oil at a steep discount in repayment for the 2018 loan. The official said Trump’s operation would ensure Venezuela received a “fair price” from China and other buyers. Trump also announced that the United States would soon begin drilling for oil in Venezuela, saying American companies were already negotiating and would help rebuild the country’s crippled PDVSA. He argued that Venezuela would earn more money and that the United States would also benefit financially. The article says PDVSA had been left in a state of minimal production after the socialist government forced out many of the country’s most skilled engineers and chemists, contributing to plunging crude output, weak refining capacity, and fuel shortages despite Venezuela’s vast oil reserves. China’s Foreign Ministry responded by saying Venezuela had the right to choose its partners and that Washington would not block Chinese purchases as long as they were made at a fair price. Beijing has long been one of Maduro’s closest allies, and the article notes that Maduro’s last public engagement before his arrest was a meeting with Chinese officials in Caracas. Rodríguez also met with the Chinese ambassador soon after, thanking China for condemning Maduro’s arrest and criticizing what she called violations of Venezuelan sovereignty. Despite its public support, China had not taken concrete action to aid the new regime, and reports suggested Beijing was instead pressing Rodríguez to repay debts that Bloomberg estimated could total as much as $20 billion.

# Summary: U.S. Oil Strategy in Venezuela Following Maduro's Arrest The Trump administration has announced a significant shift in U.S. policy toward Venezuelan oil following the arrest of former dictator Nicolás Maduro. According to an unnamed U.S. official, China will still be permitted to purchase Venezuelan oil, but will no longer receive the heavily discounted prices it previously enjoyed under Maduro's regime. ## Maduro's Arrest and Regime Change President Trump approved a Delta Force mission that successfully arrested Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, on narco-trafficking charges. The operation resulted in at least 32 Cuban security agent deaths but minimal American casualties. Following Maduro's removal, his vice president, Delcy Rodríguez, assumed control and has publicly committed to cooperating with the United States. Trump has praised Rodríguez as "terrific" and claims she maintains regular communication with Secretary of State Marco Rubio. ## Geopolitical Implications for China Maduro's arrest represents a major geopolitical setback for China, which had been a primary supporter of Venezuela's socialist regime for decades. China's financial stake in Venezuela is substantial, stemming from a 2018 agreement in which Beijing loaned Maduro $5 billion, ostensibly payable in oil. When the Trump administration previously sanctioned Venezuela's state oil company (PDVSA), China became Venezuela's primary oil buyer, receiving what was essentially discounted or free oil as loan repayment. ## New U.S. Oil Initiative The Trump administration plans to actively develop Venezuelan oil resources, with U.S. oil industry experts helping to rehabilitate PDVSA's deteriorated infrastructure. Venezuelan production has collapsed due to the exodus of skilled engineers and chemists under socialist policies, leaving the country unable to maximize extraction and refining despite possessing some of the world's largest known oil reserves. Trump announced that major American oil companies are currently negotiating to begin drilling operations in the near future. The administration's strategy requires Venezuela to sell most of its oil to the United States in exchange for American technical expertise and investment. This arrangement would generate revenue for Venezuela while providing the U.S. with significant financial returns. ## China's Response and Debt Obligations A U.S. official stated that the new arrangement ensures Venezuelans receive "fair prices" for their oil rather than the "corrupt, cheap price" offered by Maduro's regime. China's Foreign Ministry responded cautiously, asserting Venezuela's sovereignty to choose its cooperation partners and reiterating that Washington should not impede Chinese oil purchases. However, China now faces a critical challenge: Venezuela owes the country approximately $20 billion in outstanding obligations, according to Bloomberg News. Reports indicate that Beijing is pressuring Rodríguez to repay these debts. While China has vocally condemned Maduro's arrest as a violation of international law and Venezuelan sovereignty, it has taken no concrete measures to support the remaining socialist government. Rodríguez has attempted to maintain Chinese relations, meeting with China's ambassador to Venezuela shortly after Maduro's arrest to express appreciation for China's rhetorical support and condemnation of what she characterized as an "abduction." The situation reflects a dramatic reversal of fortune for China's Venezuelan interests, transforming it from a primary beneficiary of discounted oil into a creditor seeking debt repayment from a new government aligned with the United States.

A South Korean appellate court on Friday upheld the life sentence of former elementary school teacher Myeong Jae-wan for murdering her first-grade student, Kim Ha-neul, at a school in Daejeon. The court affirmed the earlier ruling that she was guilty of murder by kidnapping under the Act on the Aggravated Punishment of Specific Crimes. Although medical exams showed she had mental illness, judges said her cognitive ability was not significantly impaired. Prosecutors said Myeong lured the seven-year-old with a promise of a book, killed her inside the school on Feb. 10, 2025, then injured herself and confessed before emergency surgery. Police believed repressed emotions may have driven the attack. The case prompted calls for legal reforms on teachers with severe mental illness.

# Summary A South Korean appellate court upheld a life sentence for Myeong Jae-wan, a former elementary school teacher convicted of murdering her first-grade student. On February 10, 2025, Myeong lured seven-year-old Kim Ha-neul with a book promise and killed her at school, inflicting injuries to the victim's neck and arm. Though psychiatric evaluations revealed Myeong suffered mental illness, the court determined her cognitive abilities remained intact. The teacher, who had been depressed with workplace difficulties and had attacked a colleague days prior, confessed to the murder. Police attributed the crime to repressed emotions. Following the incident, lawmakers proposed legal revisions to prevent mentally ill teachers from classroom positions.

As the Islamic State’s deadline for two Japanese hostages in Syria expired, the group posted a message saying the “countdown has begun” and threatened to execute them, accusing the Japanese government of lying about efforts to secure their release. The hostages are Kenji Goto and another Japanese man abducted in Syria. In Tokyo, Goto’s mother, 78-year-old Junko Ishido, made an emotional appeal for her son’s freedom before the ultimatum ended. Speaking at the Foreign Correspondents’ Club of Japan, she said Goto was “not an enemy of the Islamic State” and pleaded, “Please free him,” adding that she had been overwhelmed by sadness and tears over the previous three days. Goto’s pastor also defended him, describing him as a man with a strong sense of justice who cared deeply about vulnerable people, including children. Japan’s Muslim community, estimated at about 100,000 people, also called for the hostages’ release. Around 600 Muslims gathered at Tokyo Camii, the country’s largest mosque, for prayers, where a Turkish envoy preached about the “dignity of life.” Meanwhile, the Japanese government faced criticism for its handling of the crisis. Chief Cabinet Secretary Yoshihide Suga said officials were trying to contact the captors but would not yield to terrorism.

# Summary As a deadline for two Japanese hostages held by the Islamic State in Syria expired, the militant group posted a message indicating a "countdown has begun" toward their execution. The hostage-takers accused the Japanese government of lying about rescue efforts. One hostage, Kenji Goto's mother, made an emotional public appeal for her son's release, expressing her distress over the three-day crisis. Religious figures attested to Goto's character, describing him as having a strong sense of justice. Japan's Muslim community, numbering approximately 100,000, responded by condemning the abduction. About 600 Muslims gathered at Tokyo's largest mosque for a prayer service focused on "the dignity of life." The Japanese government faced criticism for insufficient rescue efforts. The Islamic State claimed Prime Minister Shinzo Abe had lied about his actions, prompting media calls for transparency. The government denied these accusations while asserting it would neither negotiate with terrorists nor abandon rescue attempts. Cabinet Secretary Yoshihide Suga confirmed efforts to contact the hostage-takers.

A UN human rights report has accused South Sudan’s government of allowing soldiers and allied militias to commit widespread rape, torture, murder and forced displacement during the country’s civil war, often in exchange for wages or as a form of payment. Published by the Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR), the report says the abuses, which began after fighting broke out in December 2013, may amount to war crimes or crimes against humanity. It concludes that while all sides committed serious violations, the government appears to bear responsibility for the most systematic abuses. The report describes deliberate attacks on civilians rather than accidental harm from combat. In Unity state, an oil-rich region in the north that saw some of the worst violence between April and September last year, the UN recorded more than 1,300 rape reports. It says opposition forces also carried out abuses in 2014, harassing towns and turning churches, mosques and hospitals into traps for civilians. Even after those forces scattered in 2015 under a government offensive by the Sudan People’s Liberation Army (SPLA), civilians continued to be deliberately targeted. The UN says the scale of sexual violence suggests rape had become an “acceptable practice” among SPLA soldiers and affiliated militias. Investigators were told that youth militias fighting alongside the SPLA operated under an informal agreement to “do what you can and take what you can.” According to the report, these groups raided cattle, stole property, raped and abducted women and girls as part of their compensation. UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Zeid Ra’ad Al Hussein said South Sudan was facing one of the world’s most horrific human rights crises, but one that had struggled to attract international attention. He said the report’s descriptions of sexual violence, gang rape, and the calculated destruction of civilians’ lives and property were devastating, though likely only a fraction of the true total. The South Sudanese government rejected the findings, insisting SPLA troops were not responsible. A spokesman for President Salva Kiir said any crimes against civilians were condemned, and suggested the abuses may have been committed by militias wearing SPLA uniforms. He said government forces were bound by strict rules of engagement. South Sudan, the world’s youngest nation, has been at war since Kiir accused former vice-president Riek Machar of plotting a coup. The conflict has split the country along ethnic lines, killed at least 50,000 people and displaced 2.2 million more.

# Summary: UN Report Documents Systematic Sexual Violence in South Sudan's Civil War A United Nations report released Friday documents severe human rights abuses committed during South Sudan's civil war, which began in December 2013. The Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights found that the government systematically allowed soldiers and militias to rape women as an alternative form of payment, torture suspected opponents, and deliberately displace civilians. The report attributes most atrocities to government forces, though it acknowledges that all sides committed serious violations. While characterizing many acts as potential war crimes or crimes against humanity, the UN emphasized that most civilian casualties resulted from deliberate attacks rather than combat operations. In Unity state alone, an oil-rich northern region that experienced severe violence, the UN recorded over 1,300 rape reports between April and September of the previous year. The report indicates that sexual violence became an "acceptable practice" among SPLA (Sudan People's Liberation Army) soldiers and affiliated militias. Youth militias operated under an informal agreement to "do what you can and take what you can," leading them to raid cattle, steal property, and rape women and girls as compensation. UN High Commissioner Zeid Ra'ad Al Hussein emphasized that while the documented sexual violence was extensive and devastating, the reported figures likely represent only a fraction of actual crimes. He noted that South Sudan's human rights situation ranks among the world's worst yet struggles to gain international attention. The South Sudanese government rejected the findings, with presidential spokesman Ateny Wek Ateny condemning crimes against civilians while suggesting that perpetrators may have worn SPLA uniforms without authorization. He maintained that government troops operated under strict rules prohibiting civilian targeting. The conflict, rooted in ethnic tensions between President Salva Kiir's Dinka supporters and former Vice President Riek Machar's Nuer followers, has killed at least 50,000 people and displaced 2.2 million others since its outbreak.

The Defense Department has said that U.S. troops who took part in the hunt for Ugandan rebel leader Joseph Kony and his Lord’s Resistance Army in central Africa are eligible for medals tied to the global war on terror. In a Feb. 28 memo, the Pentagon designated Operation Observant Compass as an approved operation for both the Global War on Terrorism Expeditionary Medal and the Global War on Terrorism Service Medal. To qualify for the expeditionary medal, service members must have deployed to the operation’s area between October 2011, when the mission was formally launched, and its end in September 2017. The operation covered border regions of the Democratic Republic of Congo, South Sudan, the Central African Republic and Uganda. Kony, who styled himself a messiah, led the LRA for more than two decades. The group kidnapped children, forced them into combat or slavery, and drove tens of thousands of civilians from their homes. U.S. special operations forces, including Green Berets and Navy SEALs, supported the mission, while African Union troops led the actual manhunt. President Barack Obama ordered U.S. forces into the region in 2011 to assist with intelligence and logistics. According to AFRICOM, LRA strength fell from about 2,000 fighters to fewer than 100 during the six years of U.S. involvement. A major factor was a campaign encouraging fighters to defect and surrender to international authorities. The Kony operation now joins other missions recognized under the broader war on terror, including Enduring Freedom, Iraqi Freedom, and Inherent Resolve.

# Summary The U.S. Defense Department announced that troops participating in Operation Observant Compass are eligible for Global War on Terrorism medals. This operation, which ran from October 2011 to September 2017, aimed to capture warlord Joseph Kony and neutralize his Lord's Resistance Army (LRA) in central Africa. To qualify for the expeditionary medal, soldiers must have deployed to the operation's area of operations spanning the Democratic Republic of Congo, South Sudan, Central African Republic, and Uganda during the specified timeframe. The LRA, led by self-proclaimed messiah Kony, terrorized central Africa for over two decades through kidnapping, forced recruitment, and enslavement. President Obama authorized U.S. special operations forces, including Green Berets and Navy SEALs, to assist African Union troops in the hunt. American forces provided intelligence and logistical support rather than direct combat operations. The campaign proved effective, reducing LRA fighters from approximately 2,000 to fewer than 100 by 2017. A significant factor in this success was a campaign encouraging LRA fighters to defect and surrender to international authorities. Operation Observant Compass joins a growing list of designated global war on terror operations eligible for these medals, which date back to the September 11, 2001 terrorist attacks.

At least 43 migrants died and 80 others survived after an overcrowded wooden boat broke apart on rocky reefs just off southern Italy early Sunday, according to the Italian Coast Guard. The vessel smashed near the coast of Calabria, close to the beach at Steccato di Cutro on the Ionian Sea, in rough weather conditions. Some survivors managed to reach shore on their own after the shipwreck, while others were pulled from the water by rescue crews. The Coast Guard said shortly before noon that 80 people had been recovered alive and 43 bodies found along the shore. Search-and-rescue operations continued through the day, with helicopters, motorboats, state firefighters, border police, and coast guard vessels all involved. A Coast Guard motorboat rescued two men suffering from hypothermia and recovered the body of a boy in rough seas. Firefighter boats, including rescue divers, recovered 28 bodies, and three more were found farther from the wreckage after being carried by a strong current. Italian news agency AGI reported that one of the dead was a baby just a few months old. Italian Premier Giorgia Meloni said the migrants had been crowded into a 20-meter, or 66-foot, boat and blamed human traffickers for the tragedy. In a statement from her office, she expressed “deep sorrow” for the lives lost and called it inhumane to trade men, women, and children’s lives for the price of a ticket sold under the false promise of a safe journey. Meloni, whose government includes the anti-migrant League party, said she would use her leadership to push for tougher action against departures organized by smugglers and to urge other European Union leaders to help Italy. The wreckage left splintered wood scattered across the beach, where some survivors wrapped themselves in blankets or sheets to stay warm. Crotone Mayor Vincenzo Voce called the disaster “an enormous tragedy” and said the city would provide cemetery space for the dead. Pope Francis also expressed grief during his Sunday address in St. Peter’s Square, saying he prayed for the victims, the missing, the survivors, and the rescuers. He lamented that children were among those who died. Authorities did not immediately identify the nationalities of the migrants or confirm where the boat had departed from. However, migrant boats reaching Calabria often come from Turkish or Egyptian shores, sometimes landing on remote parts of Italy’s southern coastline without being intercepted. The article also noted other dangerous migration routes to Italy, including the central Mediterranean crossing from Libya and departures from Tunisia toward Lampedusa or Sardinia. Many migrants on these routes are fleeing poverty rather than war, and some face rejection of asylum claims. Meloni’s government has also sought to make it harder for humanitarian rescue boats to carry out multiple rescues in the central Mediterranean by assigning them distant disembarkation ports in northern Italy.

# Migrant Boat Disaster Off Italy Kills 43 A tragic maritime disaster occurred off the coast of southern Italy when an overcrowded wooden boat broke apart on rocky reefs at dawn on Sunday. The Italian Coast Guard reported that at least 43 migrants died in the incident, while 80 survivors were recovered, some of whom managed to reach shore after the shipwreck. The vessel, a 20-meter wooden boat, was dangerously overcrowded with migrants attempting to reach Europe. According to Italian Premier Giorgia Meloni, the migrants were packed into the boat under adverse weather conditions. Meloni condemned human traffickers in a statement, calling it "inhumane to exchange the lives of men, women and children for the 'price' of a ticket paid by them in the false prospect for a safe voyage." As a far-right leader whose coalition includes the anti-migrant League party, Meloni pledged to intensify crackdowns on smuggler operations and seek greater support from European Union leaders. The disaster occurred at Steccato di Cutro in Calabria, along the Ionian Sea. The beach was littered with boat debris and splintered wood, with survivors wrapped in blankets attempting to stay warm. Rescue operations were extensive, involving Coast Guard motorboats, helicopters, firefighter vessels, and border police. The recovery efforts revealed the tragedy's scope. The Coast Guard rescued two hypothermic men and recovered a boy's body from rough seas. Firefighter rescue divers recovered 28 additional bodies, including three swept far from the wreck by strong currents. French police arrested seven Italians in France on Wednesday after Italy sought their extradition for left-wing terrorist crimes committed decades ago, the French presidency said. The suspects, several of them former members of the Red Brigades, had fled Italy before serving prison sentences imposed for acts including murder and kidnapping. Police were also searching for three additional suspects who were not at home. Among those detained were people convicted in Italy for the 1980 killing of a Carabinieri paramilitary general and the 1980 kidnapping of a judge. Italian police said the arrests were carried out under an operation code-named “Red Shadows.” Five of the detainees had belonged to the Red Brigades, the far-left group that was active in the 1970s and 1980s and carried out killings, kidnappings, and “kneecappings,” or attacks in which victims were shot in the legs. The organization later became dormant. One of the best-known figures arrested was Giorgio Petrostefani, 77, a militant from Lotta Continua, another far-left group. He had been convicted in Italy of the 1972 murder of Milan Police Chief Luigi Calabresi and sentenced to 22 years in prison. Calabresi’s death was one of the emblematic crimes of Italy’s “Years of Lead,” a period of political violence by both the extreme left and extreme right in the 1970s and 1980s. Calabresi had been investigating Giuseppe Pinelli, a suspected anarchist linked to the 1969 Milan bank bombing that killed 17 people. Pinelli later fell from a fourth-floor window at police headquarters, and the bombing itself remains unsolved. Another arrested suspect, Narciso Manenti, had belonged to Armed Cells Against Territorial Power, which Italian police described as a subversive group. He was convicted of the 1979 killing of a Carabinieri officer and, according to Italian police, married a French citizen in 1985. The French presidency said the arrests followed extensive bilateral work and a decision to focus on the most serious cases. Italy had initially identified about 200 people. French Interior Minister Gérald Darmanin said a French court will decide whether the suspects are extradited, and the process could take two to three years because of appeals. A Paris court is expected soon to decide whether the detainees remain in custody or are released under judicial supervision. The case also touches on France’s 1985 “Mitterrand doctrine,” under which Italian far-left fugitives in France were generally not extradited unless accused of “crimes of blood.” The policy long angered Italian right-wing politicians. Italian Prime Minister Mario Draghi welcomed France’s decision to begin judicial proceedings, saying the crimes had “left an open wound” and that their memory remains vivid in Italy.

The Gulf of Guinea is a large and strategically important maritime region stretching from Senegal to Angola and covering about 6,000 kilometers of coastline. It serves as a major shipping corridor for oil, gas, and other goods moving to and from central and southern Africa, with roughly 1,500 fishing vessels, tankers, and cargo ships in its waters on any given day. Because of this heavy traffic, the region faces serious maritime security threats, including piracy, armed robbery at sea, kidnapping of seafarers, illegal fishing, smuggling, trafficking, and broader transnational organized crime. These problems endanger seafarers and shipping, but also threaten economic development across the region. The European Union has developed a policy framework to respond to these challenges. Its Maritime Security Strategy Action Plan includes a regional focus on the Gulf of Guinea and calls for continued support for the Gulf of Guinea Strategy and Action Plan, as well as national and regional efforts under the Yaoundé architecture. The EU adopted its own Strategy for the Gulf of Guinea in 2014 to support the objectives of this regional framework. That framework, known as the Yaoundé Architecture, was created through an intra-regional commitment among the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS), the Economic Community of Central African States (ECCAS), and the Gulf of Guinea Commission (GGC). It was signed at the Yaoundé Heads of State Summit in June 2013 in response to maritime crime in all its forms. To help implement this strategy, the EU later launched a Gulf of Guinea Action Plan. Through the strategy and action plan, the EU says it aims to assist regional efforts against maritime insecurity and transnational crime as part of its broader engagement with West and Central Africa. The plan emphasizes raising awareness of maritime threats, strengthening institutions at both regional and national levels, improving cooperation among national, regional, and international actors, and encouraging more resilient and prosperous coastal economies and communities. The article highlights the severity of the security situation by citing 2020 figures from the International Maritime Bureau. That year, the Gulf of Guinea recorded 84 attacks on ships and 135 seafarers kidnapped for ransom. Kidnapping for ransom in the region rose by nearly 50 percent between 2018 and 2019, and by about 10 percent between 2019 and 2020. As a result, the Gulf of Guinea now accounts for just over 95 percent of all kidnappings for ransom at sea worldwide. The article argues that stronger cooperation among regional states and organizations is essential to reduce these threats, both at sea and onshore. The EU works with coastal states and regional bodies such as ECOWAS and ECCAS, and also cooperates with international partners including Interpol and UNODC’s Global Maritime Crime Programme. Another important multilateral effort is the G7++ Friends of the Gulf of Guinea (G7++ FOGG), which brings together coastal states, private actors, and regional and international stakeholders to advance maritime security cooperation. A key part of the regional response is the Yaoundé Code of Conduct, signed in June 2013 by governments in and around the Gulf of Guinea. Officially titled the “Code of Conduct concerning the Repression of Piracy, Armed Robbery against Ships, and Illicit Maritime Activity in West and Central Africa,” it is intended to promote regional maritime cooperation and create a stable maritime environment that supports prosperity. Under this agreement, signatories established regional information-sharing and coordination centers: the Interregional Coordination Centre (ICC) in Yaoundé, Cameroon; the Regional Centre for Maritime Security of West Africa (CRESMAO) in Abidjan, Côte d’Ivoire; and the Regional Centre for Maritime Security of Central Africa (CRESMAC) in Pointe Noire, Congo. The EU says it is actively helping coastal states build maritime security capacity through a range of programs and projects focused on legal frameworks, operational rules, information sharing, training, and institutional strengthening. Funding comes from the Instrument contributing to Security and Peace (IcSP) and the European Development Fund (EDF). Several specific initiatives are listed. CRIMSON is a €2 million project that monitors and supports the broader Critical Maritime Routes Programme in the Gulf of Guinea and the Indian Ocean, providing coherence, visibility, communications, monitoring and evaluation, policy analysis, and expert recommendations. GoGIN, launched in December 2016 with €9.3 million and co-financed by Denmark with €1.8 million, aims to improve maritime safety and security in 19 countries by supporting training and the YARIS information-sharing network, which is meant to improve maritime domain awareness. SWAIMS, started in 2019 with €28 million, supports the ECOWAS Integrated Maritime Strategy and seeks to improve maritime security and safety, especially through stronger law enforcement and governance. PASSMAR, also launched in 2019, provides €10 million to Central Africa to reinforce institutional, legal, and operational frameworks for cross-border maritime cooperation. Other projects address fisheries, ports, customs, and trafficking. PESCAO, launched in 2018 with €15 million, promotes sustainable fisheries governance and combats illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing, with ECOWAS managing the project alongside regional fisheries bodies and support from the European Fisheries Control Agency. WeCAPS, begun in 2019 with €8.5 million, works to improve port security and help countries meet International Ship and Port Facility Security standards. IPCOEA, also starting in 2019 with €1.88 million, seeks to improve customs and clearance efficiency through Single Window Systems in several ECOWAS ports. SEACOP, running since 2015 with €6 million, strengthens cooperation against maritime trafficking and drug smuggling along the trans-Atlantic cocaine route by supporting Joint Maritime Control Units in ports across West Africa, Latin America, and the Caribbean. Finally, CRIMJUST, a €12 million UNODC-led project launched in 2016, works to strengthen criminal justice institutions and cooperation against drug trafficking and transnational organized crime in West Africa and beyond.

He suggested the U.S. should instead respect American victims killed by IS rather than making unfounded claims. Psaki reiterated the U.S. commitment to condemning the Assad regime's violence against civilians and human rights violations, while pledging support for Syrian opposition and a political solution. Al-Zoubi countered that the Syrian military does not target civilians and accused the U.S. of deliberately misleading public opinion.

Security forces in Deir Ezzor arrested the leader of a kidnapping gang and several accomplices after they abducted local resident Mohammed Jamal Alloush on Monday evening. According to the Public Security Department, the gang contacted the victim’s family and demanded a $35,000 ransom for his release, while also sending photos showing his torture to pressure them. After receiving the report, security services collected information, investigated the case, and identified the gang leader. Two security units then carried out a precise raid on the place where Alloush was being held, freeing him safely. The leader and several accomplices were detained, while efforts continue to arrest the remaining gang members. The suspects have been referred to investigators for legal proceedings.

# Summary Security forces in Deir Ezzor arrested a kidnap gang leader and accomplices after abducting citizen Mohammed Jamal Alloush on Monday evening. At the World Economic Forum in Davos, US officials unveiled an ambitious and highly controversial vision for rebuilding Gaza into what they described as a “New Gaza” — a modern, seaside destination of skyscrapers, promenades and large-scale investment that could supposedly emerge within three years. President Donald Trump, speaking as he introduced his “Board of Peace” conflict-resolution initiative, said the territory could become “a great thing to watch,” describing it in real-estate terms as “a beautiful piece of property” on the sea. His son-in-law and envoy Jared Kushner, who has no formal government title, went further, saying the plan aimed for “catastrophic success.” Kushner presented slides showing gleaming terraced apartment towers and a tree-lined waterfront, arguing that rebuilding Gaza could be “very doable” if implemented quickly. He said the plan envisioned at least $25 billion in investment to restore infrastructure and public services, and projected that within 10 years Gaza’s GDP could reach $10 billion, with average household income rising to $13,000 a year. He said the goal was to create “opportunity for everybody” and turn Gaza into a place where people could “thrive.” He also said the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza had enlisted Israeli real estate developer Yakir Gabay, whom Kushner described as volunteering “not for profit.” The presentation echoed Trump’s earlier suggestion during the conflict that Gaza could become the “Riviera of the Middle East,” a remark that drew international outrage. Egypt’s President Abdel Fattah El-Sisi, whose government had led an Arab-backed Gaza reconstruction proposal in 2025, was notably absent from Kushner’s presentation. Egypt’s plan had also been welcomed by the European Union. A statement from El-Sisi’s office said he returned home early Thursday after meeting Trump, who praised him as “a great leader, a great guy.” The article also notes that Gaza remains in a severe humanitarian crisis despite a US-brokered ceasefire that took effect last October. A UN official recently described conditions as “inhumane.” Entire neighborhoods, hospitals and schools have been damaged or destroyed, and hundreds of thousands of people are living in makeshift shelters. Kushner argued that Gaza’s economy had long been dependent on aid — he said 85 percent of output came from it — and insisted that disarming Hamas, as required by the ceasefire, was essential to attracting donors and companies. The war began with Hamas’s October 7, 2023 attack on Israel, which killed 1,221 people and saw 251 hostages taken. Israel’s response has killed at least 71,562 people in Gaza, according to the territory’s health ministry, which the UN considers reliable. Since the ceasefire began on October 10, the ministry says 477 Palestinians have still been killed.

# Summary: US Presents Vision for Gaza Reconstruction at Davos At the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, US officials unveiled an ambitious plan to transform Gaza into a modern Mediterranean resort destination within three years following the October 2023 war between Israel and Hamas. German Chancellor Angela Merkel sharply criticized Russia’s air campaign in Syria on Monday, saying in Ankara that she was “horrified in the face of this human suffering,” in comments that marked some of her strongest public criticism of Moscow’s role in the conflict. Russia responded by telling Merkel to choose her words carefully. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said everyone should be “very careful and responsible” in their language because of the already fragile situation in Syria and the peace process. Peskov rejected Western and opposition accusations that Russian airstrikes had killed civilians, saying Moscow had not received any credible evidence of such deaths. He also complained that no one had protested what he called the “barbaric actions of terrorists” when they attacked Syrian government forces earlier in the war. When asked whether Russia would continue bombing if Syria peace talks resumed, he declined to comment. The exchange came as Syria peace talks in Switzerland had been suspended the previous week after the West and the Syrian opposition accused Russia of targeting civilians and pursuing a military solution to the nearly five-year war. Concerns were also growing that mainstream rebel forces could face collapse after a Russian-backed government advance cut their main supply route to Aleppo. The article also notes worsening Russia-Germany tensions beyond Syria. Moscow had recently turned a reported rape case involving a 13-year-old girl with Russian-German citizenship into a diplomatic dispute, accusing Berlin of a cover-up. German prosecutors later said the girl had not been abducted. Meanwhile, some German media urged a tougher stance on Moscow, arguing Russia’s Syria bombing was intended to deepen Europe’s refugee crisis and weaken EU unity.

# Summary German Chancellor Angela Merkel criticized Russian airstrikes in Syria during a visit to Ankara on Monday, expressing horror at the resulting human suffering. This represented her sharpest rebuke of Russia's aerial campaign to date. In response, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov warned Merkel to choose her words carefully regarding the Syrian crisis, citing the delicate situation. Peskov countered that Russia had received no credible evidence of civilian deaths from its airstrikes and criticized the West for remaining silent about alleged terrorist attacks on Syrian regime forces. The comments came as Syria peace talks in Switzerland were suspended last week, with Western nations and Syrian opposition groups accusing Russia of targeting civilians and pursuing a military solution to the nearly five-year conflict. Russian-backed regime advances have severed the main supply line to Aleppo, threatening the collapse of mainstream opposition rebels. The exchange reflects deteriorating Russia-Germany relations. Previously, Moscow sparked a diplomatic row by amplifying allegations of a Russian-German girl's abduction by migrants—claims later disproven by Berlin prosecutors. This incident was widely viewed as an attempt to inflame anti-refugee sentiment among Germany's Russian immigrant population. German media outlets have pressured the government to adopt a harder stance on Moscow, with some suggesting Russian bombing aims to worsen Germany's refugee crisis. International observers believe Putin seeks to deepen divisions within the EU, which has imposed sanctions on Russia since its 2014 annexation of Crimea from Ukraine.

Human Rights Watch says Lebanese authorities should immediately release Hannibal Gaddafi, the son of former Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi, after eight years in pretrial detention on what it calls spurious charges. Gaddafi was arrested in December 2015 and has remained in custody ever since, even though the case against him is tied to events in 1978, when he was only two years old and held no official role. The case centers on the disappearance of Lebanese Shiite cleric Moussa al-Sadr and two companions during an official visit to Libya in August 1978. Lebanese authorities have long blamed Libya’s former regime for the disappearance, which severely damaged relations between Lebanon and Libya. Hannibal Gaddafi was detained by Lebanon’s Internal Security Forces in 2015 on allegations that he had some connection to the case. Authorities charged him with “withholding information and subsequently interfering in the crime of continued kidnapping” of Sadr, according to one of his lawyers, despite the fact that he was a child at the time of the disappearance. According to the article, Gaddafi’s ordeal began when unidentified armed men kidnapped him in Syria near the Lebanese border in 2015. He had been living in Syria with his family after fleeing Libya following the 2011 uprising that overthrew his father’s government, after earlier periods in Algeria and Oman. The kidnappers reportedly told him he would be interviewed by a newspaper, but instead took him to Lebanon, where they tortured him, demanded information about Sadr’s disappearance, and sought a ransom. Lebanese authorities later freed him from those captors, but then arrested him themselves within days. Judge Zaher Hamadeh issued an arrest warrant accusing him of concealing information about Sadr, and Gaddafi was formally charged in 2016. Human Rights Watch says the detention is arbitrary and has dragged on without adequate legal justification. In July 2023, the group wrote to both the Internal Security Forces director-general, Major General Imad Othman, and Judge Hamadeh, asking for information about Gaddafi’s legal status and health, but received no response. One of Gaddafi’s lawyers told the organization that he went on a hunger strike from June to October 2023 to protest his continued detention and the prison conditions, which led to significant weight loss and repeated hospitalizations. The article notes that prison conditions across Lebanon have worsened sharply since the country’s economic collapse began in 2019. Facilities face poor health care, inadequate and low-quality food, and severe overcrowding. Authorities have blamed rising crime, slow court procedures, and the inability of some prisoners to pay release fees. The broader judicial picture is also troubling. Human Rights Watch says nearly 80 percent of Lebanon’s prison population is held in pretrial detention, in some cases for years and without charge. Gaddafi’s case is presented as one example of a system in which detainees can remain imprisoned for long periods with little public information about their status. The article says it is unclear which judicial body periodically approves his continued detention or how often he is brought before a judge. Gaddafi’s lawyers deny Lebanese claims that he knew where Sadr and his companions were held between 1978 and 1982. Lebanese authorities have said he signed an affidavit providing information during detention, but his lawyer said in 2022 that any such document was signed under duress and without a lawyer present. In 2018, Gaddafi also received a separate 15-month sentence for insulting the Lebanese judiciary, along with a one-year travel ban. The article places the case in the context of the unresolved disappearance of Sadr, founder of the Amal movement, and the longstanding accusations against the Gaddafi regime. Muammar Gaddafi maintained that Sadr and the two companions left Tripoli for Rome in 1978, but Italian authorities rejected that account. Sadr’s followers have accused the former Libyan ruler of abducting and killing them over disputes involving payments to militias in Lebanon. Human Rights Watch argues that under international law, detention must meet strict due process standards, including prompt judicial review and a speedy trial or release. It says Lebanon has failed to meet those standards in Gaddafi’s case and should drop the charges and free him.

# Summary: Lebanon Wrongfully Detains Hannibal Gaddafi for Eight Years Human Rights Watch has called for the immediate release of Hannibal Gaddafi, son of Libya's former leader Muammar Gaddafi, who has been held in Lebanese pretrial detention since December 2015 on what the organization characterizes as spurious charges. The case highlights systemic problems within Lebanon's judicial system, where nearly 80 percent of the prison population languishes in pretrial detention, some for years without formal charges. ## The Charges and Their Basis Lebanese authorities arrested Gaddafi on allegations connecting him to the 1978 disappearance of Moussa al-Sadr, a prominent Lebanese Shiite Imam, and two companions during an official visit to Libya. However, the charges appear fundamentally flawed: Gaddafi was only two years old when Sadr disappeared and held no senior official position as an adult. He was formally charged in 2016 with "withholding information and subsequently interfering in the crime of continued kidnapping" based on claims that he possessed knowledge of Sadr's whereabouts between 1978 and 1982—allegations both Gaddafi and his lawyer have consistently denied. ## Circumstances of Detention Gaddafi's detention began when unidentified armed men kidnapped him in Syria near the Lebanese border in 2015, allegedly deceiving him about meeting a newspaper interviewer. The captors transferred him to Lebanon, where they tortured him, demanded ransom, and sought information about Imam Sadr. Lebanese authorities subsequently freed him from these captors but arrested him within days, issuing a warrant through Judge Zaher Hamadeh. This pattern suggests potential coordination between his initial kidnappers and state authorities. ## Detention Conditions and Health Concerns Prison conditions in Lebanon have severely deteriorated since the country's 2019 economic crisis. Gaddafi reportedly endured inadequate healthcare, insufficient food, and severe overcrowding. In protest of his arbitrary detention and harsh conditions, he conducted a hunger strike from June to October 2023, resulting in significant weight loss and repeated hospitalizations. The broader Lebanese prison system faces challenges including slow trial proceedings, inability of released prisoners to pay required fees, and increased crime rates. ## Legal and Procedural Violations Throughout his imprisonment, Lebanese authorities have provided minimal information regarding Gaddafi's judicial status and the legal justification for continued detention. It remains unclear which judicial entity authorizes his ongoing detention or how frequently he appears before a judge. In 2022, Gaddafi's lawyer claimed he was forced to sign a document under duress without legal representation, contradicting Lebanese authorities' assertions that he provided an affidavit about Sadr's detention. ## International Concerns In January 2019, Lebanese Justice Minister Selim Jreissati requested an assessment of whether Gaddafi's continued pretrial detention remained judicially relevant, but results were never publicized. In August 2023, Libyan authorities questioned the legality of his detention and called for his release and return to Syria to his family—a request Lebanon ignored. ## Broader Context The disappearance of Imam Sadr, founder of the Lebanese Shiite political party Amal, damaged Lebanon-Libya relations. Muammar Gaddafi claimed Sadr departed Libya for Rome, but Italian authorities denied this, and Sadr's followers accused Gaddafi of orchestrating their disappearance and deaths over militia payment disputes. Human Rights Watch emphasizes that Gaddafi's detention violates international law, including the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, which Lebanon ratified in 1972. The organization argues that prolonged pretrial detention for mere possible association with wrongdoing is unlawful, regardless of public interest in resolving Sadr's disappearance.

An opposition-backed government in Syria’s Idlib province has introduced one of Islamic law’s harshest punishments for kidnappers and armed robbers, citing worsening insecurity and a rise in violent crime. The Syrian Salvation Government, an opposition administration formed last year as an alternative to the Syrian Interim Government and backed by Hayat Tahrir al-Sham, announced through its Ministry of Justice that it would begin enforcing the Sharia principle of hirabah on Dec. 10. Mohammed Kabakbaji, the attorney general in Idlib under the Salvation Government, said the measure would be applied in the ministry’s courts. Under hirabah, people convicted of abduction or armed robbery can face execution, amputation of hands and feet, or exile, depending on the offense. The ministry said its decree was based on a Quranic verse describing the punishment of those who “wage war against Allah and His Prophet and strive to spread disorder in the land,” and argued that the law is meant to restore security, reassure residents and deter attacks on people’s property and dignity. The decision comes amid what officials describe as a surge in kidnappings and robberies across Idlib province. Relief and humanitarian workers have increasingly been abducted by unidentified gunmen, forcing some organizations to suspend operations. Wealthy residents have also been targeted in ransom kidnappings. Opposition activists in Idlib blame armed factions for many of the crimes, noting that most occur in areas under their control. They argue that outsiders would have difficulty escaping because the factions have established security checkpoints throughout the region. Kabakbaji defended the new policy by describing hirabah as the Islamic legal concept for violent highway robbery or gang crime. He said it covers attacks on passersby by armed groups that overwhelm victims through fear and coercion, and he compared it to robbery by violence and organized kidnapping gangs. He argued that criminals have taken advantage of Syria’s war, the spread of weapons among civilians and the distraction of rebel forces fighting regime troops and allied militias. According to him, some gangs began with isolated crimes before escalating to kidnapping for ransom and robbery. He said some abductors even filmed themselves torturing victims, sent the videos to relatives to demand payment, and in some cases killed victims when ransom was not paid or cut off fingers, later posting the footage on social media. Those videos are reportedly no longer available and are being removed for their violent content. Kabakbaji said severe punishment is justified because criminals used such brutality themselves, and he argued that adopting hirabah would protect lives and property while deterring further crimes. Not everyone agreed. Opposition-affiliated judge Hussein Hamadeh criticized the ministry’s decision, saying such cruelty is inappropriate given Idlib’s unemployment, low living standards and chaotic conditions. Lawyer Marwan Kaid also opposed the move, saying hirabah does not fit the current situation and that long prison sentences would be more suitable. Others supported the measure. Lawyer Issam Khatib, who works in the Justice Ministry courts, said the timing was right because armed groups, including Islamic State-linked cells, were hiding in Idlib, looting to survive and justifying their crimes with distorted interpretations of Sharia. He argued that hirabah’s punishments — including execution, amputation and exile — could reduce the security chaos and deter gangs from abducting, robbing and killing civilians.

# Opposition Group in Idlib Imposes Severe Islamic Punishments The Syrian Salvation Government, an opposition administration in Idlib backed by Hayat Tahrir al-Sham, an Islamist coalition, has implemented hirabah law beginning December 10. This Islamic Sharia provision prescribes extreme penalties for serious crimes including armed robbery and abduction. Under hirabah law, perpetrators of abductions and armed robberies face execution, amputation of hands and feet, or exile depending on the severity of their crimes. The decree applies to both civilians and military personnel found guilty of leading or participating in criminal gangs. The government based this decision on a Quranic verse describing punishments for those who "wage war against Allah and His Prophet and strive to spread disorder in the land." Mohammed Kabakbaji, the attorney general of Idlib, explained the rationale behind the decision to Al-Monitor. He defined hirabah as attacking passersby to steal money through intimidation and force. According to Kabakbaji, the measure was necessary because criminals have exploited Syria's ongoing conflict and widespread civilian weapons to form organized gangs engaged in abductions, armed robberies, and ransom demands. He noted that some perpetrators have filmed themselves torturing victims and posted videos on social media to pressure families into paying ransoms, sometimes murdering victims when payments weren't received. The decision was prompted by escalating security concerns in Idlib province. Officials and workers from relief and humanitarian organizations have become frequent abduction targets, forcing some organizations to suspend operations. Additionally, unidentified armed groups have been kidnapping wealthy individuals for ransom. Opposition activists attribute many of these crimes to armed factions controlling areas in Idlib, though these groups maintain security checkpoints throughout the region. Kabakbaji argued that severe punishment is justified given the circumstances. He stated that punishment should match the brutality of the crimes and that the country's wartime status necessitates deterrent measures. He contended that hirabah implementation would protect people's lives and property while carrying minimal disadvantages. However, the decision has generated significant opposition among legal professionals in Idlib. Judge Hussein Hamadeh criticized the Justice Ministry's adoption of hirabah, arguing that such cruel punishment is inappropriate given the region's high unemployment, low living standards, and chaotic environment. Lawyer Marwan Kaid similarly opposed the decision, suggesting that long-term imprisonment would serve as a more appropriate deterrent than hirabah punishments. Conversely, Issam Khatib, a lawyer working in Justice Ministry courts, supported the measure. He argued that hirabah came at an opportune time, noting that armed groups and gangs, including those affiliated with ISIS, hide in Idlib and commit crimes to survive. Khatib contended that hirabah's multiple punishment options—execution, amputation, and exile—could effectively reduce security chaos and deter criminal activity. The implementation of hirabah reflects the Syrian Salvation Government's attempt to address persistent security challenges in Idlib province through Islamic legal frameworks, though the decision remains controversial among local legal experts and opposition activists who question its appropriateness and effectiveness.

Amid reports that a new nuclear agreement with Iran could be reached within weeks and Iran’s announcement of a new hypersonic missile said to evade air defenses, the article says Tehran has continued a pattern of coercive behavior. It reports that Azerbaijani student Farid Safarli, 27, was arrested in Tehran on what are described as false espionage charges. Safarli, a University of Jena student, had traveled to Iran to visit his girlfriend and was expected to return to Germany in March, but is now said to be held hostage in Tehran. The article argues that Iran may be using Safarli as leverage against Azerbaijan. It points to recent tensions between the two countries, including Azerbaijan’s opening of an embassy in Tel Aviv and Iran’s anger over that move. In recent years, Iran allegedly attempted to execute Azerbaijani-Iranian dissident Ahmad Obali and his son Deniz, tried to assassinate an Azerbaijani member of parliament, and killed an Azerbaijani security guard during an attack on the Azerbaijani Embassy in Tehran on International Holocaust Memorial Day earlier this year. The article also recalls the detention of British-Iranian aid worker Nazanin Zaghari-Ratcliffe, who was held from 2016 until 2022 on espionage charges Amnesty International called fabricated, and who was released only after the British government paid what the article calls a bribe. It similarly mentions British-Iranian engineer Anoosheh Ashoori, who was released at the same time. Another case highlighted is Swedish-Iranian academic Ahmadreza Djalali, who remains imprisoned and faces execution, with Amnesty International warning that Iran is using him as a hostage to pressure other states. The article further references the 1979-81 U.S. embassy hostage crisis and concludes that, given Iran’s support for armed groups across the Middle East and its advances in weapons technology, a new nuclear deal would be dangerous and would not stop such abuses.

# Summary As negotiations for a new Iranian nuclear deal progress toward completion within weeks, concerns mount over Iran's continued hostile actions. The article highlights the arrest of Azerbaijani student Farid Safarli, 27, in Tehran on fabricated espionage charges. Safarli, a University of Jena student who traveled to meet his girlfriend, was expected to return to Germany in March but remains detained.
