The author argues that given Iran's demonstrated hostage-taking practices, support for terrorist organizations across Yemen, Lebanon, Syria, Gaza, and Iraq, and advances in weapons technology including nuclear capabilities despite sanctions, negotiating a new nuclear deal would be counterproductive and likely worsen conditions for current hostages.

Emad Mishko Tamo, a 14-year-old Yazidi refugee in Winnipeg, has become the inspiration behind an effort to provide bicycles to Yazidi children in his community. For Emad, a bright-green mountain bike represents freedom and hope after years of trauma under Islamic State captivity. Emad lived with his family in an Iraqi village until the summer of 2014, when Islamic State militants attacked and displaced thousands of Yazidis. He was separated from his mother, Nofa Mihlo Zaghla, during the chaos. She was held captive for two years before escaping with four of her children during an attack on the compound where they were being kept. She eventually made her way to Canada and settled in Winnipeg, believing Emad had died. Emad, meanwhile, endured three years as a captive. He later described witnessing horrific violence and suffering among children taken by ISIS. Speaking through translator Khalil Hesso, president of the Yazidi Association of Manitoba, he said he had seen many children crying and dead, and vowed that if he ever had the chance, he would help other children. That chance began to emerge after some Yazidis were freed in Mosul in 2017, when a photo surfaced online of a dusty young boy sitting in a vehicle. The boy was Emad. Efforts were quickly made to reunite him with his surviving family in Winnipeg. When he arrived in Canada, a bicycle was waiting for him, donated by Steve Maman, founder of the Liberation of Christian and Yazidi Children of Iraq (CYCI). Maman said Emad had come from years of captivity without possessions such as a bike, basketball, or soccer ball, and that the bicycle symbolized a dream for a child who had lost so much. Emad and his family have tried to build a new life in Winnipeg, but they continue to carry the pain of what happened in Iraq. His uncle, Hadji Tamo Rafo Zaghler, pointed to a wall poster showing 12 family members, including Emad’s father, whom he says was found in a mass grave. The fate of many others remains unknown. Last summer, Maman learned that Emad’s bicycle had been stolen. Wanting to replace it, he contacted Emad, who made an unexpected request: he would only accept another bike if all Yazidi refugee children in Winnipeg could also receive bicycles. Maman was moved by Emad’s desire to help other victims of genocide. The effort gained momentum after Maman connected with Bryan Phillips, a car enthusiast from Indiana. Phillips offered to sell a Bentley he had purchased through Maman, and the proceeds were used to buy 100 bicycles. The bikes are set to be delivered to Yazidi refugee children during a special Eid celebration on Friday. Maman said fulfilling Emad’s wish was important both to encourage him and to show him he can help others and achieve great things.

# Summary: From Captive to Advocate Emad Mishko Tamo, a 14-year-old Yazidi refugee now living in Winnipeg, has become the driving force behind a movement to provide bicycles to all Yazidi refugee children in his community. His journey from captivity to advocacy is remarkable. In summer 2014, Emad's Iraqi village was attacked by Islamic State militants. He was separated from his mother, Nofa Mihlo Zaghla, during the displacement of thousands of Yazidis, a Kurdish minority. While his mother was held captive for two years before escaping during a compound attack, Emad remained missing for three years. His mother feared he was dead. In 2017, after some Yazidis were freed in Mosul, a photograph of a dust-covered boy emerged online—it was Emad. He was quickly reunited with his surviving family in Winnipeg. Upon his arrival, a bicycle was waiting for him, donated by Steve Maman, founder of the Liberation of Christian and Yazidi Children of Iraq (CYCI). For Emad, who had endured three years of captivity, the bicycle represented freedom and hope—something he never expected to own. The bicycle held deep significance, but when it was stolen the following year, Maman offered to replace it. However, Emad insisted on a condition: he would only accept another bicycle if they could find a way to provide bikes to all Yazidi refugee children in Winnipeg. This generous stipulation reflected Emad's desire to help other genocide victims and children suffering like he had suffered. The initiative gained momentum through an unexpected connection. Bryan Phillips, a car enthusiast from Indiana, learned of Emad's goal while discussing vehicle parts with Maman. Without hesitation, Phillips offered to sell his Bentley to support the cause. Maman used the profits to purchase 100 bicycles for Yazidi refugee children. The bicycles were scheduled to be distributed during a special Yazidi Eid celebration. For Emad, the initiative represents more than material gifts; it symbolizes hope and the possibility of helping others despite personal trauma. Community leaders emphasize that these bicycles will mean everything to the children and represent the Yazidi community's determination not to forget their suffering. Emad's story demonstrates how a young person who experienced unimaginable hardship has channeled his experiences into compassion for others, transforming his own symbol of freedom into a gift for his entire community.

Ontario Education Minister Liz Sandals is releasing a report on the troubled Toronto District School Board, after describing a “culture of fear” among staff. The board, Canada’s largest, has faced repeated public infighting, including a police call to one meeting last year after accusations that a trustee held education director Donna Quan hostage in her office. Tensions escalated when board chair requested government intervention following a standoff over Quan’s refusal to release her employment contract. Staff also reported intimidation by some trustees. Earlier external audits found capital and structural deficits and issues with trustee expenses, but the government focused on the ongoing disputes and governance problems. Former Ontario College of Teachers registrar Margaret Wilson was appointed to conduct the review.

# Summary Education Minister Liz Sandals released a report into Canada's largest school board, the Toronto District School Board (TDSB), which faced significant governance problems. The board experienced a "culture of fear" among staff, marked by public disputes and confrontations between trustees and leadership. A notable incident involved police intervention when a trustee allegedly held education director Donna Quan hostage over her employment contract. External audits revealed financial deficits and inappropriate trustee expenses. Margaret Wilson, former Ontario College of Teachers registrar, conducted an external review examining operational and governance issues. The TDSB serves 246,000 students across nearly 600 schools and had been plagued by daily confrontations and poor communication.

Two people were arrested after a human trafficking investigation led to the rescue of a missing woman in New Hanover County, North Carolina. On January 30, the Coastal Carolina Human Trafficking Task Force, which includes local, state, and federal agencies, arrested Dartez Faulk, 31, and Rosalind Comfort, 48. Deputies said a missing person report had been filed for a woman last seen in the Wilmington area. Investigators found commercial sex ads involving the victim and said she was being held for ransom and forced into sex dates. Both suspects face kidnapping and trafficking charges and are jailed on $2 million bond.

# Summary On January 30, the Coastal Carolina Human Trafficking Task Force arrested Dartez Faulk, 31, and Rosalind Comfort, 48, following a human trafficking investigation in New Hanover County, North Carolina. A missing woman from the Wilmington area was discovered being held for ransom and forced into commercial sex work for her captors' financial gain. Commercial sex advertisements featuring the victim were found online. The task force, comprising the Sheriff's Office, FBI, Homeland Security, and NCIS, rescued the victim. Faulk faces charges including first-degree kidnapping, five counts of human trafficking, and eighteen counts of promoting prostitution. Comfort faces first-degree kidnapping, five counts of human trafficking, and two counts of promoting prostitution. Both are held on $2 million bonds.

Edmonton police have arrested Nikita Sandra Cook, who is charged with first-degree murder and kidnapping in the death of 25-year-old Tiki Brook-Lyn Laverdiere. RCMP say Cook was taken into custody Thursday in Edmonton and is scheduled to appear in court in North Battleford, Sask., on Monday. Laverdiere disappeared in April after attending a funeral for Tristen Cook-Buckle, another alleged homicide victim. Her body was found last month near North Battleford. In total, eight people, including Cook, have now been charged in the case.

# Summary Edmonton police arrested Nikita Sandra Cook on Thursday, charged with first-degree murder and kidnapping in the death of Tiki Brook-Lyn Laverdiere, a 25-year-old Edmonton woman. Laverdiere's body was discovered near North Battleford, Saskatchewan last month after she disappeared in April following a funeral service. New Brunswick Premier Blaine Higgs said Tuesday that he was hopeful he would not need to call an early election and could instead move ahead with his government’s agenda, despite continued internal dissent over his controversial changes to the province’s school gender-identity policy. The possibility of a snap election had been hanging over the province for weeks after six Progressive Conservative members broke ranks with Higgs over his decision to require parental consent before teachers can use students’ preferred first names and pronouns. The issue, tied to changes to Policy 713, sparked widespread criticism across Canada, including from Prime Minister Justin Trudeau and the province’s child and youth advocate, who argued the policy violated the rights of non-binary and transgender students. The unrest became serious enough that six Tory cabinet members openly rebelled, and two of them — Dorothy Shephard, then social development minister, and Trevor Holder, then labour minister — resigned from cabinet. Higgs said over the summer that he could not govern while members of his caucus were publicly criticizing him, leaving open the possibility of an election. On Tuesday, however, after the lieutenant-governor’s throne speech opened a new legislative session, Higgs struck a more conciliatory tone and said he was ready to govern. “I’m hopeful, this is a good start,” he said, adding that the province should focus on “the greater good” and “the bigger prize.” Higgs said he had contacted the six dissenting MLAs and that one of them, Daniel Allain, agreed to meet. Still, the premier suggested not all divisions had been resolved. “We have to recognize that there will be differences, but we have to find a way to manage them,” he said. Allain said it was time for someone to “budge.” He said Higgs had not spoken to some of the six dissidents over the summer, but later reached out to him. Allain said no deals were made, but the two found they agreed on more issues than they disagreed on. He also said caucus meetings over the previous three days had become “more structured” and that discussion was moving “in a right direction.” That shift appeared to be reflected in the throne speech, which emphasized improving education, building inclusive and safe communities, increasing police visibility, disrupting the illegal sale of drugs, cannabis and tobacco, and limiting property-tax increases. The government made only a brief reference to the gender policy, saying it remained committed to a safe and welcoming learning environment while respecting parents’ role. However, the speech did not directly address New Brunswick’s health-care or housing crises. Opposition leaders sharply criticized the government’s agenda. Liberal Leader Susan Holt said the throne speech had “absolutely nothing” to help make life affordable or address housing and health care, accusing Higgs of focusing on his own ambitions. Green Leader David Coon said it was “devoid of any content” and lacked any real vision. University of New Brunswick political scientist J.P. Lewis described the speech as confident and not reflective of a government on the verge of collapse, noting that its lack of detail could also give the premier flexibility later. Andrea Anderson-Mason, one of the six dissenting Tories, said she would vote for the throne speech but declined to say whether she still disagreed with Higgs on Policy 713. While Higgs is not required to call an election until Oct. 21, 2024, he said he would remain prepared, insisting the government could not be “held at ransom.” He also joked that the fate of his campaign bus remained uncertain.

# New Brunswick Premier Expresses Hope for Stability Despite Party Divisions New Brunswick Premier Blaine Higgs stated Tuesday that he hopes to avoid calling an early election, expressing optimism about his government's ability to move forward on its agenda despite ongoing internal party conflict. The province has faced political uncertainty for weeks following a significant revolt within Higgs's Progressive Conservative caucus. Six cabinet members broke ranks over the premier's decision to modify Policy 713, requiring parental consent before teachers can use students' preferred first names and pronouns. This policy change sparked widespread criticism across Canada, including from Prime Minister Justin Trudeau and the province's child and youth advocate, who argued it violates Charter rights for non-binary and transgender students. The conflict escalated when two dissenting cabinet ministers—Dorothy Shephard and Trevor Holder—resigned from their positions. Higgs subsequently suggested he might call an early election, stating he couldn't govern effectively with public criticism from caucus members. He indicated he had reached out to the dissident members and confirmed that Daniel Allain, one of the six rebels, had agreed to meet with him. Allain confirmed this outreach and suggested progress was being made, noting that discussions revealed more areas of agreement than disagreement between himself and the premier. He indicated recent caucus meetings had become "more structured" and were moving "in a right direction." The throne speech itself appeared to reflect some compromise, emphasizing education system improvements and inclusive, safe communities while making only passing reference to the gender policy controversy. It pledged to increase police visibility, combat illegal drug sales, and limit property-tax increases, though it noticeably avoided addressing healthcare and housing crises. Liberal Leader Susan Holt claimed it contained "absolutely nothing" to help with affordability, housing, or healthcare needs, suggesting the premier was focused on personal ambitions rather than governance. Victor Duarte, a 44-year-old father of three who was born and raised in Canada, has won a temporary reprieve from removal to Mexico after a Federal Court judge in Toronto found an immigration decision to be unreasonable. Duarte had been ordered to leave Canada even though he has never lived in Mexico, the country of his citizenship at birth. The case arose because Duarte’s father was a Mexican diplomat, which made Duarte a Mexican citizen when he was born in Canada. He never acquired Canadian citizenship and, according to his lawyer, did not realize he lacked Canadian status until immigration authorities moved to deport him. He is married to a Canadian and all three of his children were born in Canada. Duarte challenged the removal order, arguing that being sent to Mexico would expose him to serious danger and cruel or inhumane treatment. He said he had never been there, had no family, no job prospects, and no support network, leaving him homeless and vulnerable. His lawyer argued that, as a person who would be seen as a foreigner and possibly as someone with money, Duarte could be targeted by criminals for kidnapping, ransom, or disappearance. A senior immigration officer rejected that claim last August, concluding that homelessness and lack of prospects did not amount to a protected “risk” under immigration law. The officer also said the danger Duarte described was a general one faced by people in Mexico and therefore did not qualify for protection. Federal Court Judge Douglas Campbell disagreed. He said the officer failed to consider whether Duarte’s complete lack of familiarity with Mexico made him uniquely vulnerable, turning a general risk of crime into a personal one. Campbell ruled that the officer’s failure to address that issue made the decision unreasonable, set it aside, and sent the matter back for reconsideration by another immigration officer.

# Summary Victor Duarte, a 44-year-old man born and raised in Canada, has won a legal reprieve from deportation to Mexico on a technicality. A Federal Court judge ruled that an immigration official acted unreasonably in dismissing his protection claim. Duarte's situation stems from his birth circumstances: his father was a Mexican diplomat, making Duarte a Mexican citizen by birth despite being born in Canada. He never acquired Canadian citizenship and was unaware of his lack of legal status throughout his life in Canada. He married a Canadian woman and fathered three Canadian-born children. When immigration authorities ordered his removal, Duarte challenged the decision, arguing he faced serious risks if deported to Mexico—a country he has never visited. He claimed he would have no job prospects, relatives, or housing, making him vulnerable to criminals. He specifically feared abduction, kidnapping for ransom, and forced disappearance by criminal elements. A senior immigration officer rejected his appeal in August, ruling that homelessness and joblessness don't constitute sufficient "risks" under immigration law. The officer determined that since crime affects all Mexican citizens generally, Duarte didn't qualify for protection. However, Judge Douglas Campbell disagreed with this reasoning. He noted that Duarte's unique circumstances—never having lived in Mexico and lacking any support network there—could personalize the generalized crime risk faced by Mexicans. The judge found the immigration officer's failure to address whether Duarte's "unique ineptitude" created personalized vulnerability rendered the decision unreasonable. Campbell set aside the deportation order and referred the matter to another immigration officer for reconsideration, giving Duarte another opportunity to make his case.

Joshua Sullivan, a 34-year-old Tennessee pastor from Maryville, remains missing after being kidnapped at gunpoint in South Africa last week. Sullivan, his wife Meagan, and their six children have lived in South Africa for the past 10 years, where they have been planting churches and serving as missionaries. The kidnapping happened Wednesday during a prayer service at Fellowship Baptist Church in Motherwell, in South Africa’s Eastern Cape. According to police, four armed and masked men entered the church, seized Sullivan, and forced him into his truck. The vehicle was later found abandoned nearby. Sullivan’s family says the incident was witnessed by Meagan and the children, who were also present at the service. His father-in-law, David Witt, said the family remains focused on prayer and is asking the public to continue praying for Joshua’s safe return. He described Sullivan and Meagan’s work as a response to what they believed was God’s call to serve and spread Christianity in other countries. Witt said the family is in contact with U.S. authorities and that officials have been cooperative, though he could not share many details. A retired FBI agent and hostage negotiator, Jason Pack, said there is still hope because no other family members were harmed, suggesting the possibility of communication with the kidnappers. Meagan Sullivan also posted online, thanking people for their support and urging continued prayers until her husband comes home safely. Thousands have responded with prayers and messages of support. South Africa’s Anti-Gang Unit has now taken over the investigation.

Toronto Star’s roundup of its most-read 2017 stories highlighted investigations that drew the most reader attention, including pieces on Donald Trump, workplace deaths, and a Toronto case of alleged slavery and child theft. The article explains that the stories were ranked by the total time readers spent on each page, and that many of the top items reflected the Star’s focus on exposing injustice. One featured investigation followed reporter Sara Mojtehedzadeh, who went undercover for a month at a GTA industrial bakery after 23-year-old temp worker Amina Diaby died in an accident there. The company had said worker safety was its top priority, but the investigation examined the risks faced by temporary workers, who often receive low pay, little training, and dangerous assignments. After the story was published, the company launched an independent review of its health and safety practices and use of temp agencies. It was later convicted under Ontario’s Occupational Health and Safety Act and fined $300,000. The provincial government also moved to strengthen protections for temp agency workers, including curbing unequal pay for the same work.

# Summary The Toronto Star's 2017 most-read stories included investigations into workplace safety, political coverage, and social injustice. A prominent case involved the death of 23-year-old temp worker Amina Diaby at a GTA industrial bakery. Star journalist Sara Mojtehedzadeh went undercover for a month at the facility, exposing dangerous conditions and inadequate training for temporary workers. Following the investigation's publication, the company underwent an independent health and safety audit and was convicted under the Occupational Health and Safety Act, receiving a $300,000 fine. The story prompted Ontario's provincial government to strengthen protections for temp agency workers, including preventing employers from paying temps less than permanent employees for identical work. Other highly-read stories covered alleged slavery and child theft in Toronto, Trump-related news, and a hostage situation at the newsroom.

U.S. Senators Marco Rubio, Jim Risch, Susan Collins, and Mike Crapo wrote to President Joe Biden urging him to take immediate steps to protect Americans and vulnerable Afghans as the Taliban rapidly expanded its control across Afghanistan. Their letter said the United States has a responsibility to evacuate citizens, allies, and partners who now face danger because of the withdrawal and the way it was carried out. They argued that safeguarding people from hostage-taking or Taliban reprisals should be the administration’s top priority in the coming weeks and months. The senators first called for a clear, public plan for the orderly evacuation of all American citizens and vulnerable Afghans who want to leave. They said that announcing a firm U.S. commitment to continued evacuations would reassure people that departing flights would not be their last chance to escape. They also insisted that U.S. forces at Hamid Karzai International Airport ensure the Taliban do not block access to the airport and, if necessary, retaliate against attempts to stop evacuations. The letter emphasized that troops should secure the airport so people can reach it safely. A major focus of the letter was Mark Freichs, a U.S. Navy veteran who was working as a civil engineer in Kabul when the Taliban abducted him in January 2020. The senators urged Biden to use “any and all tools” to secure his release, saying that leaving him behind while withdrawing U.S. troops would be a disgrace to the country’s commitment to those who served in uniform. They also warned that while U.S. forces remained in Kabul, they must prevent the Taliban from abducting any additional Americans before the evacuation ends. The senators described Freichs as the last American hostage held by the Taliban, according to public reporting. The letter also pressed the administration to broaden evacuation efforts beyond American citizens. The senators said the operation should include not only the roughly 22,000 Afghan Special Immigrant Visa applicants, but also those eligible for Priority 1 and Priority 2 refugee status. They pointed to the Taliban’s past rule in the 1990s, describing it as a reign of terror marked by harsh Sharia-based abuses and human rights violations. The senators said reports were already emerging that Taliban fighters were going door to door searching for people who had assisted the United States, as well as vulnerable groups such as Afghan women and religious minorities. Because of these risks, they urged the administration to reconsider requirements that Afghans bring paper documentation to the airport, arguing that such papers could expose them to danger at Taliban checkpoints. The senators further asked Biden to ensure that the State Department and the Department of Homeland Security have enough resources to process and resettle refugees. They said part of the $500 million Biden had announced for Afghan refugees should be used for housing, health care, and other support for Afghans relocated to third countries for processing. They also suggested deploying more personnel to U.S. embassies in those countries to handle applications. The letter acknowledged reports that the State Department destroyed Afghan passports and applications during the urgent evacuation from Kabul to prevent the Taliban from using them to identify and target people, but the senators said this could delay asylum processing. They requested information on how the administration planned to handle destroyed applications and keep congressional offices updated on relocation and resettlement efforts. Finally, the senators rejected Biden’s August 16, 2021 statement that all Afghans had not shown the will to fight. They said many Afghans had bravely fought alongside U.S. troops, diplomats, and NGOs, and that the United States owed it to them and their families to ensure their loyalty to America would not put them at further risk.

# Summary: Senators Urge Biden to Prioritize Safe Afghanistan Evacuation Four U.S. senators—Marco Rubio (R-FL), Jim Risch (R-ID), Susan Collins (R-ME), and Mike Crapo (R-ID)—have sent a letter to President Joe Biden expressing grave concerns about the safety of American citizens and vulnerable Afghans remaining in the country following the Taliban's takeover of major urban centers. The senators emphasize that regardless of the merits of the withdrawal decision, the United States bears responsibility for those now at risk and must prioritize their safety from potential hostage situations and Taliban reprisals. The letter outlines several specific demands. First, the senators call for a clear, publicly stated plan for orderly evacuation of all American citizens and vulnerable Afghans wishing to leave. They stress that U.S. troops must secure Hamid Karzai International Airport and prevent Taliban obstruction of airport access, with authority to retaliate against any interference attempts. Second, the senators urge the administration to secure the release of Mark Freichs, described as the last American hostage held by the Taliban. Freichs, a U.S. Navy veteran and civil engineer, was abducted in January 2020. The senators argue that leaving him behind would betray the nation's commitment to those who served in uniform. Third, the letter advocates for expanding evacuation eligibility beyond the approximately 22,000 Special Immigrant Visa applicants to include those qualified for Priority 1 and Priority 2 refugee status. This expansion specifically targets women and religious minorities, groups deemed most vulnerable under Taliban rule. The senators reference the Taliban's brutal 1990s regime, when strict Sharia law interpretations resulted in systematic human rights violations. They note reports indicating Taliban fighters are already conducting door-to-door searches for individuals who assisted the United States and targeting vulnerable populations, despite recent Taliban amnesty announcements. The senators criticize the administration's requirement that Afghans present paper documentation at airports, arguing such documents could endanger individuals at Taliban checkpoints. They emphasize that Afghan soldiers, NGO leaders, women, and others who trusted the United States must not be abandoned. Finally, the letter addresses resettlement logistics, urging the administration to ensure the State Department and Department of Homeland Security have adequate resources for processing and resettling refugees. The senators recommend allocating a portion of the announced $500 million in Afghan refugee assistance toward housing, healthcare, and other support services. They also suggest deploying additional personnel to U.S. embassies in third countries to expedite application processing. The senators acknowledge the State Department's decision to destroy Afghan passports and applications to prevent Taliban misuse but express concern this will delay asylum processing. They request detailed plans for processing destroyed applications and maintaining updates on relocation and resettlement efforts. The letter concludes by rejecting Biden's August 16, 2021 statement that all Afghans lacked the will to fight. The senators assert that thousands of Afghans bravely fought alongside American troops and worked with American diplomats and NGOs, with countless sacrificing their lives. They argue the nation owes these individuals and their families protection from the consequences of their decision to support the United States.

The US Justice Department has unsealed an indictment charging Haji Najibullah, an Afghan national, with six counts tied to the 2008 kidnapping of an American journalist and two Afghan men. Najibullah, 44, was arrested in Ukraine and transferred to the United States, where he will stand trial. Although the indictment does not name the journalist, a law enforcement official told Reuters the case concerns David Rohde, then a Reuters and New York Times correspondent and now a New Yorker journalist. Rohde was kidnapped by the Taliban in 2008 while traveling with Afghan colleagues to interview a Taliban leader. According to the indictment, in November 2008 Najibullah “caused” a group of armed men carrying machine guns to detain Rohde and the two Afghans. It says Najibullah and about six armed guards later forced the captives to hike from Afghanistan into Pakistan. The victims were held in a Taliban-controlled compound in Pakistan’s tribal areas for more than seven months before Rohde and Afghan journalist Tahir Ludin escaped dramatically. Their driver, Asadullah Mangal, escaped a few weeks later. Najibullah faces charges including hostage taking, conspiracy to commit hostage taking, kidnapping, conspiracy to commit kidnapping, and two counts of using and possessing a machine gun in furtherance of crimes of violence. The indictment says the kidnappers forced the victims to make repeated calls and videos pleading for help while demanding ransom from Rohde’s family and the release of Taliban prisoners by the US. It also alleges that in April 2009 Najibullah recorded at least three videos of Rohde while pointing a machine gun at his face.

# Summary The US Justice Department unsealed an indictment on October 28, 2020, charging Haji Najibullah, an Afghan national, with six counts related to a 2008 kidnapping. Najibullah was arrested in Ukraine and transferred to the United States to face trial. The indictment does not name the journalist involved, but law enforcement officials confirmed the case concerns David Rohde, a former Reuters and New York Times correspondent now working for the New Yorker, who was kidnapped by the Taliban in 2008. Najibullah faces multiple charges including hostage-taking, conspiracy to commit hostage-taking, kidnapping, conspiracy to commit kidnapping, and two counts of using and possessing a machine gun in furtherance of violent crimes. According to the indictment, in November 2008, Najibullah coordinated the detention of Rohde and two Afghan nationals assisting him. Armed guards then forced the victims to hike across the border from Afghanistan into Pakistan. The victims were identified as Rohde, Afghan journalist Tahir Ludin, and driver Asadullah Mangal. After more than seven months in captivity at a Taliban-controlled compound in Pakistan's tribal areas, Rohde and Ludin made a dramatic escape, with Mangal escaping weeks later. During their captivity, Najibullah and other kidnappers forced the victims to make calls and videos demanding ransom from Rohde's family and the release of Taliban prisoners by the US. In April 2009, Najibullah recorded at least three videos of Rohde pleading for help while a machine gun was pointed at his face.

Russia said on Thursday that Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov will chair a UN Security Council meeting in April, when Moscow takes the body’s rotating presidency. The Russian Foreign Ministry said a major event will be an open debate on “effective multilateralism through the defence of the principles of the UN Charter.” Spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said Russia’s presidency is largely ceremonial and that no legal path exists to remove Russia from its permanent seat, despite Ukraine’s demand that Moscow be expelled over the war launched in February 2022. Ukraine’s Foreign Minister Dmytro Kuleba called the presidency “a bad joke” and accused Russia of usurping its seat and waging a colonial war. The presidency rotates monthly among the 15 council members, and Russia last chaired the council in February 2022.

# Summary Russia announced that its foreign minister will chair the UN Security Council in April during Russia's rotating monthly presidency. Russia has faced criticism from Western nations at the UN since launching its military operation in Ukraine in February 2022. Ukraine has called for Russia's removal from the Security Council, though Russia, as a permanent member, cannot be removed through international legal means. Russia plans to hold a high-level debate on "effective multilateralism" during its presidency, which the foreign ministry describes as largely ceremonial. Ukrainian Foreign Minister Dmytro Kuleba criticized the presidency on Twitter, calling it "a bad joke" and accusing Russia of usurping its seat and waging colonial war. The Security Council presidency rotates monthly among its 15 member states.

In Chechnya, three Islamic insurgents and two police officers were killed in a shoot-out after an overnight attack on a police post in Chali, about 30 kilometers south of Grozny, according to regional leader Ramzan Kadyrov. Kadyrov said the attackers struck during the night, triggering a firefight in which two policemen and three assailants died. Two civilians were also wounded. The region has been largely pacified under Kadyrov after two brutal separatist wars, but a small Islamist insurgency still carries out sporadic attacks across Chechnya and the broader North Caucasus. The article also notes criticism of Kadyrov’s rule and recent Russian security operations against suspected Islamic State figures in the region.

# Summary Three Islamic insurgents and two policemen were killed in a shoot-out in Chechnya's Chali town, according to leader Ramzan Kadyrov. The clash followed a jihadist attack on a police post located 30 kilometers south of Grozny. Two civilians were also wounded in the firefight. Though Russia fought two brutal separatist wars in Chechnya over the past two decades, the region has been largely pacified under Kadyrov's authoritarian rule. However, a dwindling group of Islamist insurgents continues sporadic attacks. A notable 2014 incident killed fourteen security officers during Grozny raids. Rights activists criticize Kadyrov's governance, citing widespread kidnapping and torture with minimal Moscow oversight. The North Caucasus remains a significant source of foreign jihadists fighting in Syria and Iraq.

Pirates hijacked the Malta-flagged crude oil tanker Kalamos off Nigeria on Tuesday while it was anchored near ExxonMobil’s Qua Iboe terminal awaiting cargo, the Greek coastguard said. The attackers took three hostages and killed the ship’s Greek deputy commander. Two of the hostages are Greek, and Greeks make up 10 of the 23 crew members. The 15-year-old tanker was seized in the Gulf of Guinea, now a major piracy hotspot. The International Maritime Bureau reported 33 piracy and armed robbery incidents there from January to September last year.

# Summary Pirates hijacked the Malta-flagged oil tanker Kalamos off Nigeria's coast on Tuesday, killing the Greek deputy commander and taking three hostages, including two Greeks. The vessel was anchored near ExxonMobil's Qua Iboe terminal awaiting cargo when attacked. The 23-crew ship operates in the Gulf of Guinea, now considered Africa's piracy epicenter. Between January and September last year, the region experienced 33 piracy incidents. Pirates in this area are heavily armed, violent, and frequently hold crews hostage for extended periods.

Kyrgyzstan’s president, Sooronbai Jeenbekov, announced on Thursday that he intended to resign after more than a week in hiding following a disputed parliamentary election and mass protests. In a statement issued from an undisclosed location, Jeenbekov said he did not want to be remembered as a leader “who shed blood and shot at his own citizens.” He did not say whether he had already formally left office. Jeenbekov disappeared after protesters angry over the Oct. 4 election, which was widely tainted by vote-buying, stormed the president’s office and other government buildings in Bishkek. His whereabouts were unclear, though there were rumors he had taken shelter at a Russian military air base in Kant, near the capital. His expected departure marks the third time in 15 years that violent unrest has forced out a president in Kyrgyzstan, the only Central Asian state with a relatively open political system, active civil society and competitive elections. Under the constitution, the speaker of parliament would become acting head of state and commander in chief, though the speaker himself was also under pressure to resign. Real power, however, appeared to rest with Sadyr Japarov, a convicted kidnapper who was freed from prison by protesters last week and then named prime minister by lawmakers at a disputed session held without a quorum. Jeenbekov urged Japarov and rival politicians to withdraw their supporters from Bishkek and restore peace. Tensions had risen after Japarov’s supporters clashed with those backing another would-be prime minister, fueling fears that Japarov might mobilize his followers again if Jeenbekov stayed in office. Jeenbekov had earlier said he would step down once calm returned to the capital. Japarov has long claimed his 2017 conviction for organizing the kidnapping of a regional governor was politically motivated. Jeenbekov, meanwhile, had previously jailed his own predecessor, Almazbek Atambayev, on corruption charges. Atambayev was among those freed during the unrest and later rearrested.

# Kyrgyzstan's President Announces Resignation Following Disputed Election Sooronbai Jeenbekov, president of Kyrgyzstan—Central Asia's only democracy—announced his resignation on Thursday from an undisclosed location after more than a week in hiding. He stated he did not wish to be remembered as a leader "who shed blood and shot at his own citizens." The announcement followed violent protests triggered by October 4 parliamentary elections marred by widespread vote-buying. Demonstrators stormed government buildings in the capital, Bishkek, forcing Jeenbekov to disappear. He reportedly took refuge at a Russian military air base near the city. This marks the third time in 15 years that violent protests have toppled a Kyrgyzstan president, despite the country's reputation as the region's most democratic with a vibrant civil society, relatively free press, and competitive elections. Jeenbekov's departure creates significant uncertainty. Parliamentary speaker Sadyr Japarov will assume the presidency's formal duties, though he has also faced pressure to resign. In reality, governing authority rests with Japarov, a convicted kidnapper released by protesters last week. Lawmakers appointed him prime minister during a controversial, reportedly illegal parliamentary session held without a quorum. Japarov's rise is contentious. Critics view him as a nationalist rabble-rouser, while supporters claim his 2017 kidnapping conviction was politically motivated. The country has a troubling pattern of new governments jailing predecessors and rivals; Jeenbekov arrested his predecessor Almazbek Atambayev on corruption charges, though Atambayev was freed during last week's unrest and subsequently rearrested. Jeenbekov called on Japarov and rival politicians to withdraw supporters from Bishkek and restore peace. Recent clashes between Japarov's followers and rival political supporters had raised concerns about further violence if the president refused to step down.

Kazakh paediatric orthopaedist Roza Karabekova has created knitted panties for newborns, up to three months old, to help prevent hip joint dislocation and related deformities. She says the device is meant to support early prevention of hip dysplasia, a condition that can be treated much more effectively if detected before a child turns one. Karabekova said she first came up with the idea after the birth of her fifth child, a girl, in January 2009. As an orthopaedist, she noticed signs such as asymmetry in the hip creases and a “flick” sound, which suggested dysplasia. Knowing that treatment works best when hip joints are positioned correctly early in life, she initially tried to use baby linen to keep the legs apart, but found that method uncomfortable and impractical. She later adapted the idea after seeing boxing shorts with an inserted plastic piece, prompting her to design panties with a pocket for a similar plastic element. The panties are intended to keep a baby’s legs from coming together and help the hip joints develop properly. Karabekova later turned the idea into a broader preventive product for children at risk of hip deformities. She said the project took years to develop, supported by grants, including two million tenge from Astana Medical University in 2010 and one million tenge from the SANTO Company. These funds also allowed her to travel abroad for study and conferences. During a visit to Lithuania, she observed that trauma orthopaedists there use ultrasound machines directly in their offices, allowing early screening of children in one place without extra referrals. She contrasted this with Kazakhstan, where hip deformities are often detected late, making treatment after age one more difficult and expensive. Karabekova is now writing a business plan and improving the plastic bar used in the panties. The bar is certified and safe, and costs about 1,000 tenge. She envisions selling sets that could include panties, a blanket and a cap. She stresses that the panties are only preventive, not a cure, and parents should still take babies to an orthopaedist at three months. A recent $1,350 grant from the Ambassadors Spouses Association is helping fund the work. Karabekova has begun working with clinics Nos. 4 and 10, seeing patients every Saturday and giving the panties free of charge. So far, she has examined nine children and distributed three pairs. She is an associate professor at Astana Medical University and founder of the Karabekov Public Fund, named after her father.

# Summary: Kazakh Paediatric Orthopaedist Develops Innovation for Hip Dysplasia Prevention Kazakh paediatric orthopaedist Roza Karabekova has invented specialized knitted panties for newborns up to three months old designed to prevent hip joint dislocation. The innovation addresses a significant health issue, as early diagnosis and treatment of hip dysplasia before age one produces superior outcomes and avoids the need for expensive gypsum and splinting treatments later. The panties contain a small plastic element that prevents infants from bringing their legs together, promoting correct hip joint development. Karabekova developed this solution after noticing dysplasia symptoms in her fifth child born in 2009, including hip crease asymmetry and abnormal sounds. After experimenting with various approaches, she adapted the concept from her son's boxing pants, creating a pocket within knitted panties to hold the plastic piece. Developing and refining the product required substantial effort and funding. Karabekova received a two-million tenge grant from Astana Medical University in 2010, followed by a one-million tenge grant from SANTO Company. These funds enabled her to travel internationally for professional development and study. During a research visit to Lithuania, she observed how trauma orthopaedists there conduct early hip joint diagnostics using ultrasound machines in their offices, allowing mass screening without requiring separate specialist appointments. In Kazakhstan, hip deformities are frequently diagnosed late, making treatment expensive and complicated after age one. Karabekova's initiative aims to address this problem through prevention and early detection. Currently, she is developing a business plan and modifying the plastic components, sourced from certified orthopaedic manufacturers. She proposes packaging the panties with blankets and caps for new mothers. A recent $1,350 grant from the Ambassadors Spouses Association supports her work. Karabekova emphasizes that the panties serve as preventative measures, not cures. She established free clinics at two healthcare facilities where she examines patients and distributes panties without charge. An Associate Professor at Astana Medical University, Karabekova continues her father's legacy of paediatric orthopaedic innovation through her public health fund.

The article argues that a society must confront its history honestly rather than try to erase or ignore it. Using a Russian proverb about the danger of dwelling on the past or forgetting it entirely, the writer suggests that the past remains powerful and will continue to shape people unless it is properly addressed. Avoiding history, the article says, only deepens pain, distortion, and moral harm. Quoting the idea that “the struggle of people against power is the struggle of memory against forgetting,” the author insists that no one has the moral right to say “let bygones be bygones” when injustice has occurred. This understanding, the writer says, is important because people may become discouraged if they expect immediate or linear progress. Public institutions such as the media, schools, and other educational bodies are urged to play an active role in building awareness and creating democratic space for open discussion about reconciliation. While the success of reconciliation depends mainly on the sincerity and willingness of the main parties involved, the article argues that its long-term sustainability also depends on how public institutions support the process. These institutions can help communities understand that reconciliation involves both looking back and moving ahead, and that it can still reach its goal if there is genuine participation. Ultimately, the article presents national reconciliation as both an individual and collective duty. It says the process requires courage, political will, and a vision of a shared and respectful future. It also leaves room for spiritual transformation, suggesting that true change requires not only reason but grace from God.

Belarusian senator Yekaterina Serafinovich said criticism of Belarus for bringing children from Donbass to the country only reinforces support for the effort. Speaking to BelTA in Grodno on July 31, she said the children interviewed by Belarusian and Russian media described their holidays in Belarus positively and expressed a wish to return. According to her, stays in Belarusian sanatoriums and health camps give children from Donbass a chance to rest, recover physically and emotionally, and briefly experience a peaceful childhood they do not have at home. Serafinovich said Belarus has never concealed that it hosts these children or the reasons for doing so. She rejected accusations from some foreign media and politicians that Belarus is “kidnapping” children, arguing that the same voices ignore the deaths and suffering of children in Donbass caused by shelling, mines, life in basements, and separation from parents. She described this as “European cynicism” and compared it to a thief shouting “catch the thief.” Her remarks came in response to what she called another anti-Belarusian report by the European Parliament’s Committee on Foreign Affairs, which she said again denigrated the country. She noted that a final decision is expected in September but insisted that, whatever happens, Belarus will continue policies based on the interests of its people and national security, including support for those in need. She said this stance reflects not only the work of philanthropist Aleksei Talai and his charitable foundation, but also the position of President Aleksandr Lukashenko and the Belarusian public. Serafinovich also accused self-exiled opposition figures of hypocrisy, saying their statements exposed the “deceitful inhumane face” of Western propaganda. She added that such pressure can also unite Belarusians around shared values and goals. Drawing on Belarus’s wartime memory, she said the country understands the suffering of children and will continue helping those affected by what she called the cruelty of the “democratic” West.

Russian President Vladimir Putin said Friday that Russia will continue its war against Ukraine despite Ukraine’s recent battlefield gains, and he warned that Moscow could intensify attacks on Ukrainian infrastructure if Kyiv keeps striking targets inside Russia. Speaking to reporters after a summit of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization in Samarkand, Uzbekistan, Putin said the main objective of Russia’s military campaign remains the “liberation” of Ukraine’s entire eastern Donbas region, and he said there is no reason to change that goal. He added that Moscow was “not in a rush” and claimed that Russia has relied only on volunteer soldiers in the war, even as some Russian hard-liners have called for a wider mobilization to address manpower shortages. Putin’s comments came after Russia suffered a major setback in northeastern Ukraine. Ukrainian forces had forced Russian troops to withdraw from large areas of the region in a rapid counteroffensive the previous week, reclaiming several Russian-occupied cities and villages. That advance marked Moscow’s biggest military reversal since Russian forces retreated from areas near Kyiv early in the war. Putin’s first public reaction to the counteroffensive was cautious, saying, “Let’s see how it develops and how it ends.” He also accused Ukraine of trying to strike civilian infrastructure in Russia. Putin said Moscow had so far responded with restraint, but warned that any further attacks could trigger a much stronger Russian response. He said Russian forces had recently carried out what he called “impactful strikes,” apparently referring to attacks earlier in the week on power plants in northern Ukraine and a dam in the south. He described those as “warning strikes.” Putin further alleged, without providing details, that Ukraine had attempted attacks near Russian nuclear facilities and nuclear power plants, and said Russia would retaliate if such tactics continued. The article noted that Russia has reported explosions and fires at civilian infrastructure near Ukraine, as well as at ammunition depots and other sites, while Ukraine has claimed some of the attacks and declined to comment on others. In his diplomatic outreach, Putin also used the summit to reassure India about Russia’s position on the war. In a meeting with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, he said Moscow wanted the fighting to end quickly and blamed Ukraine for refusing negotiations. Putin told Modi that he knew India’s concerns and said Russia would do all it could to bring the conflict to a close, but he claimed the Ukrainian leadership had rejected talks and chosen to pursue its goals on the battlefield. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, by contrast, has argued that Russia is the side unwilling to negotiate seriously and has insisted that Russian troops withdraw from occupied territory before meaningful talks can begin. Putin’s remarks to Modi echoed what he had said a day earlier in talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping. On Thursday, Putin thanked Xi for China’s “balanced position” on the war and said he was prepared to discuss China’s concerns about Ukraine. On Friday, Putin said he and Xi had discussed how to respond effectively to what he called unlawful Western restrictions. The European Union, the United States and other Western governments have imposed sanctions on Russian energy and other sectors because of the war. China’s government issued a statement saying Xi supported Russia’s “core interests” while also expressing interest in working together to “inject stability” into world affairs. An international relations expert quoted in the article said the reference to stability was likely aimed at China-U.S. relations, arguing that U.S. efforts to pressure China had pushed Beijing toward closer cooperation with Moscow. China and India have both refused to join Western sanctions on Russia and have increased purchases of Russian oil and gas, helping Moscow cushion the economic impact of sanctions. Putin also met with Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan on Friday to discuss economic cooperation and regional issues, including a July agreement brokered by Turkey and the United Nations that reopened Ukrainian grain exports through Black Sea ports. Meanwhile, Xi used the summit in Uzbekistan to warn Central Asian countries against outside interference. He said they should prevent “external forces” from instigating a “color revolution,” a term used for popular uprisings that topple governments. Xi offered to train 2,000 police officers, establish a regional counterterrorism training center, and strengthen law enforcement capabilities. His remarks reflected Beijing’s concern that Western support for democracy and human rights activists could destabilize authoritarian governments. The comments also echoed longstanding Russian suspicions of democratic uprisings in former Soviet states. Xi’s broader message fit into China’s “Global Security Initiative,” announced in April, which Beijing presents as an alternative framework for international security. The article noted that U.S. officials see parallels between that initiative and Russian arguments supporting Moscow’s actions in Ukraine. Central Asia is also a major part of China’s Belt and Road Initiative, which seeks to expand trade and influence through infrastructure projects across Asia, the Middle East, Europe and Africa. The Shanghai Cooperation Organization, the regional bloc meeting in Uzbekistan, was formed by Russia and China as a counterweight to U.S. influence. Its members include India, Pakistan, and four Central Asian ex-Soviet republics, with Iran expected to become a full member.

Reynaldo Bignone, Argentina’s last dictator, has died at age 90, officials said. The retired army general, who ruled from 1982 to 1983, died Wednesday from complications after hip surgery at the Buenos Aires Central Military Hospital. Bignone took power on July 1, 1982, after Gen. Leopoldo Galtieri was ousted following Argentina’s defeat in the Falklands War. One of his first actions was to call general elections, but he also ordered the destruction of records related to detentions, torture, abductions and killings. Bignone later received several life sentences for crimes against humanity, including torture, unlawful detention, conspiracy and the theft of 34 babies. He handed power to democratically elected President Raúl Alfonsín in December 1983, ending seven years of military dictatorship. Alfonsín later overturned Bignone’s amnesty for military human rights violators. Bignone was briefly detained in 1984 over disappearances and murders, but was later released. Argentina’s 1976-1983 dictatorship is blamed for the abduction, torture and killing of an estimated 10,000 to 30,000 people, many of whom remain missing.

# Summary Gen. Reynaldo Bignone, Argentina's last dictator, died Wednesday at age 90 from complications following hip surgery. He governed Argentina from 1982-1983, assuming power after the nation's defeat in the Falkland Islands War. During his brief presidency, Bignone held general elections but simultaneously ordered the destruction of records documenting detentions, torture, abductions, and murders. He was convicted in 2010 and sentenced to life imprisonment for crimes against humanity, including torture, unlawful detention, and the theft of 34 babies. In December 1983, after seven years of military dictatorship, Bignone transferred power to democratically elected President Raul Alfonsin, who reversed an amnesty protecting military human rights violators. Argentina's 1976-1983 military regime is responsible for the abduction, torture, and execution of between 10,000 and 30,000 people, many remaining "disappeared."

At the World Trade Organization’s 11th biennial ministerial conference in Buenos Aires, Donald Trump reshaped the institution largely by not intervening aggressively. Many participants had arrived fearing the Trump administration would try to blow up the global trading system, but U.S. officials did not deliver such a confrontation. Instead, the conference ended on Wednesday with a sense of disappointment and very few concrete results. The meeting had been expected to produce progress on issues such as e-commerce and agricultural stockpiles, but negotiators were unable to reach broad agreements. Officials offered several explanations for the failure. Some said the issues were not mature enough for final deals, while others argued that members were too rigid and unwilling to compromise. No one blamed Washington alone, but many agreed that the WTO lacked the kind of strong leadership that the United States had historically supplied. That absence, they said, left a vacuum at the top of the organization. WTO Director-General Roberto Azevêdo said the U.S. role mattered because it is such a major player in trade talks. When the United States takes a different view, he said, it introduces uncertainty and changes the dynamics of negotiations. For many attendees, the U.S. presence in Buenos Aires was reassuring in one sense: U.S. Trade Representative Robert Lighthizer chose to attend the ministerial, signaling measured support for the WTO rather than outright hostility. His decision to come was welcomed by other countries and WTO supporters, even though he left Tuesday night before the conference ended. Many other U.S. officials stayed for the full four days, avoiding a dramatic rupture while still making clear that Washington was not going to play along simply for the sake of consensus. Lighthizer later framed the outcome positively, saying the Buenos Aires meeting “will be remembered as the moment when the impasse at the WTO was broken.” In his view, many members had recognized that the WTO needed a “fresh start” in key areas, so that countries willing to move ahead would not be held back by those unwilling to act. But not everyone shared that assessment. Some participants were frustrated by what they saw as the Trump administration’s tactics, and one senior attendee remarked that it is difficult to “hold someone hostage when they don’t want to pay ransom,” suggesting the U.S. was not vulnerable to pressure in the way some had hoped. The article also describes how the United States had already been retreating from its traditional leadership role for months. In Geneva, where much of the preparatory work was done, the U.S. mission lacked a political appointee at the top because the White House nominee for WTO ambassador had not been confirmed. Without a strong U.S. broker to push compromises, no one else fully filled the gap. That absence changed the tone of the talks. Some negotiators said the atmosphere in Buenos Aires was actually less tense than in previous rounds because many members had already accepted that no major deals would be reached. Meetings often ended earlier than in past ministerials, in part because Azevêdo was not conducting the kind of late-night, closed-door rescue efforts he had used in earlier gatherings to try to force agreements. Other players tried to step up. The European Union, especially EU Trade Commissioner Cecilia Malmström, attempted to take a leading role and present itself as a defender of multilateral trade. But Malmström acknowledged that the EU could not do the job alone. Even working with Japan and others, she said, the bloc could not force agreement when other major partners were unwilling to cooperate. She called that “the sad truth.” Beyond the lack of U.S. leadership, the WTO’s own consensus rule made progress difficult. Because any member can block an agreement, one country can stall the entire process. India was widely seen as the main obstruction in several rooms, especially because it refused to accept any outcome that did not also include a permanent deal on public food stockpiles. Critics described this as a hostage-taking approach that ultimately contributed to the breakdown of negotiations. European officials were particularly vocal in expressing disappointment. Bernd Lange, chair of the European Parliament’s trade committee, said the problem was not the EU’s leadership but the stubbornness of many countries that were determined to push their own interests no matter what. Malmström, closing the talks, said the outcome should prompt delegations to think carefully about what message they were sending to citizens, stakeholders, and future generations. In the end, the Buenos Aires conference produced almost nothing tangible: no negotiated outcomes and no unified ministerial declaration to guide future work. Yet the failure also exposed the deeper structural problems of the WTO, especially the difficulty of reaching unanimous consensus among 164 members with competing priorities. Some observers suggested that the organization may increasingly rely on smaller plurilateral agreements among willing countries, especially on e-commerce, investment facilitation, and support for micro-, small-, and medium-sized enterprises. The article’s final judgment is blunt: the WTO may not need Trump to destroy it, because it is already struggling under its own weight to accomplish much at all.

# Summary: Trump's Absence Reshapes the WTO The World Trade Organization's 11th biennial ministerial conference in Buenos Aires concluded on Wednesday with minimal accomplishments, marking a significant shift in the organization's dynamics. Rather than the anticipated confrontational approach many feared, the Trump administration's subdued presence and reduced leadership role fundamentally altered the conference's trajectory and outcomes. ## Initial Expectations vs. Reality Many attendees arrived in Argentina expecting the Trump administration to aggressively dismantle the global trading system. However, U.S. officials, led by Trade Representative Robert Lighthizer, took a measured approach. While Lighthizer departed early on Tuesday evening before the conference's conclusion, the U.S. delegation's participation throughout most of the four-day summit was viewed as a gesture of measured support for the struggling institution. This unexpected restraint surprised many trading partners and prevented the anticipated systemic shock to global commerce. ## The Leadership Vacuum The conference's disappointing results stemmed largely from the absence of traditional American leadership at the WTO. WTO Director-General Roberto Azevêdo acknowledged that the lack of strong leadership at the organization's helm hindered negotiations. Historically, the United States filled this role, but the Trump administration's withdrawal from this position created a vacuum that other nations struggled to fill. The U.S. mission's lack of a confirmed political appointee as ambassador to the WTO exacerbated this leadership gap. Without effective American direction, no strong-armed compromise broker emerged to drive negotiations and facilitate agreements on critical issues ranging from e-commerce to agricultural stockpiles. ## Attempted Leadership Replacements The European Union, under Trade Commissioner Cecilia Malmström, attempted to assume the role of "multilateral leader" in the U.S.'s absence, with support from Japan and other nations. However, Malmström acknowledged the EU's limitations, noting that while the 28-member bloc carries significant weight, it cannot achieve agreements alone without cooperation from other major trading partners. Her frustration was evident as she emphasized that the EU could not accomplish its objectives without support from larger partners. ## Structural and Political Obstacles The conference revealed fundamental challenges within the WTO's consensus-based structure, which requires unanimous agreement from all 164 member nations. This mechanism proved particularly problematic when individual countries blocked progress. India emerged as a primary obstructionist, refusing to consider any negotiated outcome that didn't include a permanent agreement on public food stockpiles—a position critics described as "hostage-taking." Multiple countries pursued inflexible stances on their individual interests, prioritizing national concerns over collective progress. This widespread unwillingness to compromise demonstrated the difficulties inherent in achieving consensus among such a diverse group of nations. ## Tangible Results and Future Implications The conference produced no negotiated outcomes and no cohesive ministerial declaration charting the organization's path forward. The atmosphere in negotiating rooms reflected resigned acceptance that no deals could be reached, with talks ending at reasonable hours rather than extending into early morning sessions as in previous ministerials. However, the conference did identify potential pathways forward. WTO members recognized the possibility of pursuing plurilateral agreements—arrangements among willing members rather than requiring universal consensus—on topics including e-commerce, investment facilitation, and support for micro-, small, and medium-sized enterprises. ## Conclusion Lighthizer declared the conference successful, claiming it represented "the moment when the impasse at the WTO was broken." Yet the reality revealed a struggling organization facing existential challenges beyond Trump's influence. As one U.S. source observed, "The WTO doesn't need Trump to blow it up because the WTO is already struggling under its own weight to accomplish anything." The conference ultimately demonstrated that the WTO's fundamental structural limitations and competing national interests pose greater obstacles to progress than any single nation's policies. The organization faces uncertain prospects as it attempts to adapt to a multipolar world where consensus-based decision-making increasingly proves inadequate.

Venezuelan authorities said two suspects in the murder of retired General Félix Velázquez are police officers. Interior Minister Gustavo González stated that Kendinyers García and Yaemil Brito acted with a criminal gang linked to extortion, kidnapping, and murder. After their arrest, investigators found the weapon used in the killing in their possession. González said the probe would continue to dismantle “paramilitary bands” seeking to destabilize the country. President Nicolás Maduro posthumously awarded Velázquez the First Class Order of Liberator and personally expressed condolences to his family. Maduro also promised justice and said the investigation would continue until those responsible were identified. Velázquez, shot last Saturday while traveling in his car, had served as commander of the Bolivarian National Militia under Hugo Chávez and later headed the Military House. His remains will be viewed at the Military Academy in Caracas.
