Teaching students in Mexico’s western state of Michoacán held Chilchota municipality police chief Alfredo Lucio Rios Chávez hostage on Tuesday after he approached them during a confrontation in the indigenous village of Carapan, authorities said. The students were burning vehicles, including a passenger bus, a tractor-trailer and a pickup truck, when Rios tried to calm the situation and was seized, according to Mayor Mario Silva. Earlier that day, security forces had arrested 49 students from the Indigenous Normal School in Cherán. The students have been protesting for months, stealing more than 100 vehicles and burning some of them to pressure authorities to guarantee them automatic jobs after graduation. After taking Rios hostage, they moved him first to the community of Tacuro and then to Turicuaro, where they maintain their base of operations. Silva said he had no direct contact with the students, who were negotiating through the state Interior Secretariat. He added that Rios was not seriously injured, though he had been beaten. The latest vehicle burnings followed earlier protests in Paracho, where students torched three other vehicles to demand the release of detained classmates.

# Summary Teaching students from an Indigenous Normal School in Michoacán, Mexico, are holding police chief Alfredo Lucio Rios Chávez hostage to demand the release of 49 arrested fellow students. The incident began Tuesday afternoon in Carapan village when Rios approached students who were burning vehicles and confronting security forces. The students seized him and transported him to Turicuaro, where they currently hold him at their operational base. The students have been protesting for three months, stealing and burning vehicles to demand automatic job placement upon graduation. On Tuesday alone, they burned six vehicles—three in Carapan and three earlier in Paracho. The mayor reported that Rios was beaten but not seriously injured, and that state authorities are negotiating directly with the students. Officials expressed hope for his release during the day.

Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro recently agreed to meet with a top Republican congressional staffer to discuss the possible release of Joshua Holt, a Utah man who has been jailed in Venezuela for more than 20 months, according to six U.S. congressional and administration aides cited by The Associated Press. The talks are informal and their results are unclear, but officials say the fact that Maduro accepted the meeting — and then sent one of his own allies to Washington — suggests there may be movement in a case that has become a growing source of friction between Caracas and Washington. The backchannel began in February, when Caleb McCarry, a Republican aide on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, traveled to Caracas and met with Maduro and first lady Cilia Flores. The aides said McCarry made the trip at the request of Sen. Orrin Hatch of Utah, and that while in Venezuela he also visited Holt in jail and delivered a letter from Hatch. McCarry has known Maduro for more than 15 years through a small bipartisan network called the Boston Group, which once brought together Democrats, Republicans, socialists and capitalists from the United States and Venezuela in an effort to improve relations after the failed 2002 coup against Hugo Chávez. The Trump administration is aware of McCarry’s efforts, though there is no sign it has formally backed them. State Department spokeswoman Heather Nauert declined to discuss the talks, saying only that the United States is “disappointed Mr. Holt has still not been released on humanitarian grounds.” The behind-the-scenes diplomacy prompted a surprise visit to Washington this week by Rafael Lacava, the governor of Carabobo state and a trusted Maduro ally, three congressional aides said. Lacava arrived in the United States on Sunday after receiving a visa, but his visit immediately drew criticism from Sen. Marco Rubio, a leading Republican critic of Maduro. In an email to fellow Republicans on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, Rubio accused Lacava of trying to negotiate Holt’s freedom in exchange for sanctions relief or the release of Maduro’s relatives, including the first lady’s two nephews, who were convicted in New York federal court on drug-trafficking charges. Rubio also cited press reports linking Lacava to money laundering and other criminal activity and said he had been assured that no Trump administration official would meet with him. One congressional aide disputed that account, saying Lacava had only requested meetings on Capitol Hill and that his sole purpose was to press for Holt’s release, not to strike any broader deal. Any discussion of sanctions relief, the aide said, would be beyond Lacava’s authority and would have to be decided by the U.S. administration. Holt, 25, went to Caracas in June 2016 to marry a fellow Mormon he met online while learning Spanish. The couple were waiting for her U.S. visa when Venezuelan police raided the housing complex where they lived and arrested them. Authorities accused Holt of stockpiling “weapons of war,” charges U.S. officials have repeatedly called politically motivated and false. He has remained in a Caracas jail awaiting trial, even as Washington has demanded his release on humanitarian grounds. His detention has intensified already strained U.S.-Venezuela relations, which are marked by sanctions, mutual accusations, and recent warnings from Secretary of State Rex Tillerson that the U.S. could impose tough oil sanctions. Rubio’s office said the mere possibility of a “sanctions-for-hostage” deal shows Holt is being used as leverage by Maduro.

# US Opens Backchannel Talks with Venezuela Over Jailed American Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro has welcomed diplomatic discussions regarding Joshua Holt, a 25-year-old Utah man imprisoned in Venezuela for over 20 months, according to six U.S. congressional and administration officials. While the progress of these negotiations remains unclear, the fact that high-level talks are occurring suggests potential movement in a case that has become a significant source of tension between the two nations. The informal discussions began in February when Caleb McCarry, a Republican aide on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, traveled unannounced to Caracas at the request of Senator Orrin Hatch, a Utah Republican. During his visit, McCarry met with President Maduro and First Lady Cilia Flores to discuss Holt's case. McCarry, who has known Maduro for over 15 years through their shared work on the Boston Group—an informal diplomatic initiative aimed at improving U.S.-Venezuelan relations—also visited Holt in jail and delivered him a letter from Hatch. In response to McCarry's efforts, a Venezuelan envoy traveled to Washington this week. Rafael Lacava, governor of Carabobo state and a trusted Maduro ally, visited the capital to discuss Holt's release, according to congressional aides. However, the Trump administration has not formally endorsed these backchannel efforts, with State Department spokeswoman Heather Nauert only stating that the U.S. remains "disappointed" Holt has not been released on humanitarian grounds. Holt arrived in Caracas in June 2016 to marry a fellow Mormon he met online. The couple was arrested during a police raid on their apartment, with Venezuelan authorities claiming Holt was stockpiling weapons. U.S. officials consider these charges politically motivated and have repeatedly demanded his release. The case has become increasingly contentious amid broader U.S.-Venezuelan tensions. Secretary of State Rex Tillerson recently warned of potential oil sanctions against Venezuela and expressed support for military intervention to remove Maduro from power. These developments have further strained the relationship between the two countries. Senator Marco Rubio, a Florida Republican and harsh Maduro critic with the president's ear on Venezuelan policy, has strongly opposed Lacava's visit. In an email to fellow Republicans, Rubio characterized the visit as an attempt to negotiate Holt's freedom in exchange for sanctions relief or the release of the First Lady's two nephews, convicted in New York for drug trafficking. Rubio has received assurances from the White House and State Department that no Trump administration officials will meet with Lacava. However, a congressional aide countered that Lacava's meetings are solely focused on urging Holt's release, not negotiating sanctions relief, which would be an administration matter rather than a congressional one. The aide emphasized that the purpose of the visit is humanitarian rather than transactional. The situation remains delicate, with diplomatic channels quietly operating while public positions harden, reflecting the complex dynamics between Washington and Caracas.

Nearly five years after San Diego teen Miguel Anthony Rendon was abducted, tortured and killed in Tijuana for stealing methamphetamine he had agreed to smuggle into the U.S., a jury convicted Tijuana resident Brian Alexis Patron Lopez on multiple charges. Prosecutors said Patron shot Rendon five times in the head and dumped his body in a ravine.

# Summary A Tijuana man, Brian Alexis Patron Lopez, was convicted this week for the May 2020 killing of 19-year-old San Diego teen Miguel Anthony Rendon. Rendon was abducted and tortured in Tijuana after stealing methamphetamine he was supposed to smuggle into the U.S. Patron shot Rendon five times in the head and abandoned his body in a ravine.

Chile announced new anti-crime laws and an additional $1.5 billion in security spending on Thursday, one day after a third police officer was killed on duty in less than a month. President Gabriel Boric said the country faces a serious challenge from organized crime and that unity is needed to confront it, speaking at La Moneda palace. The government signed four new laws aimed at tackling organized crime, drug trafficking and general crime. They include making extortion a criminal offense, raising penalties for kidnapping and some firearm possession offenses, and increasing punishments for crimes against police officers. The new police law also gives officers more latitude to use force when their lives or others’ lives are at risk. Human rights groups, including Amnesty International, criticized the measure, warning it could increase police abuse and impunity and represent a setback for police reform. Chile’s police have long faced abuse allegations, especially after the violent crackdown on 2019 anti-inequality protests. Interior Minister Carolina Toha said the government would accelerate an intervention plan in 30 districts after the killing of officer Daniel Palma in downtown Santiago. His death triggered public backlash amid rising insecurity and falling approval of Boric’s handling of crime.

# Summary Chile enacted new laws and allocated $1.5 billion toward crime-fighting efforts on Thursday, following a surge in crime perceptions and the third police officer killing in less than a month. President Gabriel Boric announced the measures from the presidential palace, emphasizing national unity against organized crime. The government signed four new laws designed to combat organized crime, drug trafficking, and extortion. The measures include increased penalties for kidnapping, firearm possession, and crimes against police, while granting officers greater latitude in using force when lives are at risk. However, human rights organizations, including Amnesty International, criticized one law, arguing it could increase police abuse and impunity. This criticism reflects concerns about Chile's police force, which faced human rights abuse accusations following a violent 2019 crackdown on inequality protests. The Interior Minister announced an accelerated intervention plan in 30 districts following the death of police officer Daniel Palma. Notably, Boric, a former student protest leader and vocal police critic, has hardened his stance on crime as polls show public disapproval of his government's crime handling.

Opposition supporters filled the streets of Caracas and other Venezuelan cities on Saturday to protest President Nicolas Maduro’s government as the country’s political and humanitarian crises deepened under widespread blackouts and water shortages. The demonstrations came after opposition leader Juan Guaido, recognized by about 50 countries as Venezuela’s interim president, urged supporters late Friday to join what he called “the greatest escalation of pressure we have seen in our history.” In the western city of Maracaibo, two opposition lawmakers were detained during an anti-government protest, according to legislator Adriana Pichardo, who said the arrests violated parliamentary immunity. Another deputy, Elimar Diaz, said the Maracaibo rally faced “brutal repression,” including tanks and tear gas fired from helicopters. He said residents were enduring days without electricity and what he described as “inhumane rationing” by the government. Maduro, who has blamed US-backed sabotage for the blackouts that left millions without power, organized a pro-government march in Caracas “in defence of peace,” which drew hundreds. His administration has been trying to weaken Guaido’s position amid mounting pressure. It has stripped him of parliamentary immunity, authorized prosecution over his self-declaration as acting president in January, and banned him from public office for 15 years. Guaido said earlier in the week that he feared being abducted by government agents. The United States intensified pressure on Maduro as well. Vice President Mike Pence announced new sanctions against 34 vessels belonging to Venezuela’s state oil company and two firms that transport crude to Cuba. Speaking in Houston, Pence said Washington would continue to apply diplomatic and economic pressure for a peaceful democratic transition and warned that “all options are on the table.” National security adviser John Bolton called the sanctions “only a first step” and warned Defence Minister Vladimir Padrino to protect peaceful demonstrators from violence by Cuban personnel or pro-government “colectivos,” armed paramilitary groups accused by the opposition of attacking protesters. Maduro retains support from the military and from allies such as China and Russia, which sent two military planes to Caracas on March 23. The US and its partners regard him as illegitimate after a disputed second-term inauguration in January. Meanwhile, Venezuela’s economy has collapsed as oil exports fall and sanctions mount, worsening malnutrition and disease. A US-requested UN Security Council meeting was scheduled for Wednesday to address the crisis. Since the major blackout on March 7, power cuts have continued, water supplies and communications have been disrupted, and many Venezuelans have shortened workdays. “We are tired,” said one protester, but added that people had to take to the streets because it was the only way to remove the government.

# Summary: Venezuelan Political Crisis Intensifies Venezuela faces escalating political turmoil as opposition supporters staged massive protests in Caracas and other cities on Saturday against President Nicolás Maduro's government. The demonstrations were triggered by opposition leader Juan Guaidó's call for a "greatest escalation of pressure" against the regime, supported by approximately 50 nations that recognize him as the legitimate interim leader. The crisis is compounded by severe infrastructure failures, including massive blackouts and collapsed water supplies that have devastated the country since March 7. These utility failures have disrupted transportation and communications, forcing many residents to work shortened days. Citizens express exhaustion with deteriorating living conditions marked by malnutrition and disease. Government crackdowns have intensified, with two opposition deputies detained during protests in Maracaibo, where authorities reportedly used tanks and fired tear gas from helicopters. The Maduro government has systematically weakened Guaidó's position by stripping his parliamentary immunity, authorizing his prosecution, and banning him from public office for 15 years. Guaidó has expressed fears of abduction by government agents. The United States has escalated pressure on Maduro through additional economic sanctions, with Vice President Mike Pence announcing penalties against 34 vessels from Venezuela's state oil company and firms shipping crude to Cuba. National Security Advisor John Bolton warned Venezuela's Defense Minister of his "constitutional responsibility" to protect peaceful demonstrators and cautioned against violence by armed paramilitary groups known as "colectivos." Maduro, blaming US-backed sabotage for infrastructure failures, organized a counter pro-government march "in defence of peace." His government maintains strong support from the military, China, and Russia, which sent military planes to Caracas on March 23. Venezuela's economic collapse stems from plummeting crude exports combined with international sanctions. The socialist president's January inauguration for a second term followed deeply flawed elections widely viewed as illegitimate by the US and allies. The humanitarian crisis has become critical, with the UN Security Council convening Wednesday to address the situation. Citizens like Verony Mendez, facing two months without water, remain determined to protest, viewing street demonstrations as the only viable path to political change.

The West African Action Network on Small Arms (WAANSA) Nigeria has called on the federal government to give special packages to security personnel who helped make the COVID-19 lockdown in the country largely effective. The civil society group said the officers played a major role in enforcing restrictions and maintaining order during the pandemic. WAANSA made the appeal in a statement issued on Monday, May 25, and signed by Temitope Lamidi. The statement came after the group inaugurated its Global Wear Orange Against Gun Violence campaign, scheduled for Friday, June 5. The campaign is part of a global effort to honour victims of gun violence and promote a future free of armed conflict. As part of the campaign, WAANSA asked Nigeria’s Vice President, Professor Yemi Osinbajo, and the National Security Adviser, Major-General Babagana Monguno (retd), to show solidarity by wearing orange shirts on June 5. The group also called on heads of security agencies, members of the presidential committee on small arms and light weapons, and officials of the ministry of justice to identify with the one-week event. In its statement, WAANSA said Nigeria’s current challenges, including unemployment, food insecurity, poverty, the coronavirus pandemic and wider insecurity, make the fight against gun violence even more urgent. It warned that the unchecked spread of small arms and light weapons continues to worsen violence, displacement and vulnerability across communities. The group argued that Nigeria’s role in promoting peace and stability in West Africa gives added weight to its participation in the campaign. WAANSA said political actors and security stakeholders must work together to prevent conflict and protect development, since no society can achieve genuine progress amid insecurity. WAANSA Nigeria is led by Jephthah Asimole, a peacebuilder and security stakeholder.

# Summary West African Action Network on Small Arms (WAANSA) Nigeria has called on the federal government to provide special packages for security personnel who helped enforce the COVID-19 lockdown successfully across the country. American rapper Darryl Dwayne Granberry Jr., known as DDG, has criticized Western media portrayals of Nigeria as “fake” while holidaying in Lagos. In a video, he said Nigeria is “nowhere near” as dangerous as the United States, which he described as the most dangerous country. He acknowledged insecurity in Nigeria but argued that gun violence and gangsterism are far less common there than in America, urging foreigners to visit and judge for themselves. DDG also said he had been warned Nigerian food was unhealthy and water unsafe, but he found the food, especially jollof, very healthy.

# Summary American rapper DDG, currently vacationing in Lagos, Nigeria, criticized Western media coverage of the country as "fake." He argued that Nigeria is significantly safer than the United States, stating that while Nigeria experiences some insecurity, gun violence and gangsterism are far more prevalent in America. DDG encouraged foreigners to visit Nigeria firsthand rather than rely on Western propaganda. He also debunked misconceptions about Nigerian food safety, revealing he was warned against local cuisine but found Nigerian dishes, particularly jollof rice, to be healthy and nutritious.

Gunmen stormed a room at a men’s hostel in the Umlazi township near Durban, South Africa, killing eight people and injuring two others, police said. Seven men were found dead immediately after the pre-dawn attack on Saturday, and an eighth died in hospital on Sunday. Police said 12 men were drinking alcohol in the room when several gunmen entered, opened fire, and fled. Two men were not hurt, while one injured victim escaped by jumping out of a window. The shooting is the latest mass killing in South Africa, a country with one of the world’s highest homicide rates. Earlier this year, at least two other mass shootings were reported, including killings at a house in April and at a birthday party in January. Last year, 22 people were killed in three bar shootings over one weekend. Although South Africa has strict gun laws, officials and activists say illegal firearms remain a major problem. Official statistics show an average of 30 firearm-related deaths per day in the first three months of this year.

# Summary A mass shooting at a men's hostel near Durban, South Africa killed eight people and injured two others in the pre-dawn hours of Saturday. Gunmen burst into a room where 12 men were drinking alcohol, opened fire, and fled. Seven victims died immediately; an eighth died on Sunday. Two injured men are hospitalized, including one who escaped by jumping from a window. This shooting is the latest in a series of mass killings in South Africa, which ranks among the world's top 10 countries for homicide rates. Earlier this year alone, 10 family members were killed in April and eight people at a birthday party in January. Last year, 22 people died in three separate bar shootings over one weekend. Despite reasonably strict gun laws, South Africa struggles with illegal firearms. Official statistics show an average of 30 people killed daily by firearms in the first quarter of this year, with over 4,000 cases of illegal gun possession recorded during the same period.

Gun Free SA says South Africa’s rising murder rate is being driven largely by firearm violence, blaming weak regulation and poor compliance. Police Minister Bheki Cele’s annual crime statistics, covering April 2019 to March this year, showed more than 21,000 people were killed, 303 more than the previous year, a 1.4% increase overall. Guns were again the most common weapon used in murders and attempted murders, with 7,351 killings committed using firearms such as pistols, revolvers, high-calibre weapons and homemade guns. Claire Taylor of Gun Free SA said the figures were unsurprising because guns are widely available in communities and homes, and argued that gun availability closely tracks gun violence. She called for better reporting, mandatory notification of gunshot wounds by health centres, and action to prevent new guns entering the market. Parliament has also approved a new firearms amnesty period, due to begin on Saturday.

# Summary South Africa is experiencing a surge in firearm-related deaths, according to advocacy group Gun Free SA. Police Minister Bheki Cele released annual crime statistics showing over 21,000 murders between April 2019 and March 2020—a 1.4% increase from the previous year. Firearms were the most common murder weapon, accounting for 7,351 murders, representing 45% of killings where the weapon is known. Gun Free SA attributes this surge to poor regulations and inadequate compliance. The organization's Claire Taylor emphasized that gun availability directly correlates with gun violence and urged accurate reporting, prohibition of new firearms entering the market, and mandatory reporting of gunshot wounds by health centers to track violence in real-time. Parliament has approved a new firearms amnesty period beginning Saturday.

Kenya says its priorities on the United Nations Security Council will be fighting terrorism and radicalization, and promoting regional peace and stability, after defeating Djibouti for a two-year non-permanent seat. Foreign Affairs Chief Administrative Secretary Ababu Namwamba said Kenya’s experience with terror attacks gives it a strong basis to push an anti-terrorism agenda that would benefit the wider region. He described Kenya as a peace maker with a record of involvement in conflict resolution in Liberia, Sierra Leone, and Somalia, and said the country would bring that “pedigree” to the council. Kenya won the 2021–22 seat on Thursday night at UN headquarters in New York after receiving 129 votes in a second-round ballot, compared with Djibouti’s 62. The two countries had both emphasized their roles in promoting peace in the Horn of Africa and their contributions to UN peacekeeping. Kenya entered the race as the African Union’s endorsed candidate. The victory came after Kenya failed to secure the required two-thirds majority in an initial vote on Wednesday, when it received 113 votes and Djibouti got 78, leading to a rerun. Namwamba said Kenya would use the seat to represent African security concerns and rally global and regional support against terrorism on the continent. He added that Kenya’s position would help advance Africa’s peace aspirations at the Security Council. The article also notes Kenya’s own experience with major attacks, including the 2013 Westgate Mall attack, the 2015 Garissa University attack, and the 2019 Riverside attack. Kenya’s support for refugees from Somalia and South Sudan, and its backing of their fragile governments, also helped strengthen its candidacy.

# Kenya Wins UN Security Council Seat, Pledges Focus on Counterterrorism Kenya has secured a non-permanent seat on the United Nations Security Council for 2021-22, defeating Djibouti in voting held at UN headquarters in New York. Kenya garnered 129 votes compared to Djibouti's 62 in the second round of voting on Thursday, after initially failing to achieve the required two-thirds majority with 113 votes in Wednesday's first round. Foreign Affairs Chief Administrative Secretary Ababu Namwamba stated that combating terrorism, radicalization, and promoting regional peace and stability will form the cornerstone of Kenya's agenda. He emphasized Kenya's credentials as a peacemaker, citing the country's peacekeeping contributions in Liberia, Sierra Leone, and Somalia. Kenya's commitment to counterterrorism is rooted in its own tragic experiences. The country has endured several major terror attacks, including the 2015 Garissa University assault that killed 147 students, the 2013 Westgate Mall shooting that claimed 71 lives and wounded approximately 200 others, and the 2019 Riverside attack that killed 21 people. Namwamba assured African nations that Kenya would champion the continent's security interests at the global council, rallying international consensus around counterterrorism initiatives. Kenya's victory was supported by its role as the African Union's endorsed candidate and recognition of its support for refugees and fragile governments in Somalia and South Sudan.

A gunman was shot dead after carrying out an hour-long shooting spree in western Sydney on Wednesday night, firing at a home and then two police stations. New South Wales police said the first shots were fired into a suburban house in Marayong, in western Sydney, before the attacker moved on to St Marys Police Station and then Penrith Police Station. At St Marys, several shots were fired into the front of the station, prompting NSW Police to declare the incident a critical one. Multiple officers were injured, including one who was taken to hospital with a pellet wound to the head. Police said the gunman, armed with a pump-action 12-gauge shotgun, then fired at officers at Penrith Police Station. Officers returned fire, fatally injuring him at the scene. NSW Police said in an overnight statement that the man died where he was shot. Deputy Police Commissioner Jeff Loy said police had “no choice” but to shoot back, describing the man’s actions as “extreme” criminality. Local media identified the gunman as 32-year-old bodybuilder Daniel King. Reports said the home in Marayong belonged to his estranged girlfriend, who is seven months pregnant with his child. The attack has renewed concern among gun-control advocates in Australia, where strict gun laws were introduced after the 1996 mass shooting but are said to have been weakened over time. Gun ownership has risen in recent years, with about 3.2 million firearms now in circulation. Although mass shootings remain rare, recent deadly incidents in Darwin and elsewhere have raised alarm. NSW, which includes Sydney, is often seen as the least restrictive Australian state on firearms, allowing silencers and fewer limits on gun ownership and ammunition.

# Summary A 32-year-old gunman was fatally shot by police after an hour-long shooting spree in western Sydney on Wednesday night. The man, identified as bodybuilder Daniel King, fired shots at a residential home in Marayong belonging to his estranged girlfriend who is seven months pregnant with his child. He then opened fire on St Marys Police Station and subsequently on Penrith Police Station, injuring multiple officers, including one treated for a pellet wound to the head. Police returned fire at Penrith, fatally wounding the gunman at the scene. Deputy Police Commissioner Jeff Loy stated officers had "no choice" but to return fire, describing the incident as "very unusual" with "extreme criminality." The shooting reignites debate among gun control advocates about Australia's firearms regulations. Despite strict gun laws implemented following a 1996 mass shooting, gun ownership has increased significantly over the past two decades. Approximately 3.2 million firearms now circulate in Australia, with individual gun owners possessing an average of 3.9 firearms compared to 2.1 in 1997. While indiscriminate gun violence remains rare in Australia, recent incidents suggest a concerning trend. A June shooting in Darwin killed four people, and last year saw the country's worst mass shooting in over 20 years, with seven deaths including four children. New South Wales, where this incident occurred, has relatively lenient gun regulations, permitting silencers and unlimited ammunition purchases.

A new U.S. Senate report on the Jan. 6 Capitol riot said intelligence and communication failures helped lead to the attack, which the article says exposes glaring U.S. double standards. It contrasts Washington’s condemnation of the Capitol violence as a “riot” by “thugs” with U.S. politicians’ 2019 praise of violent protests in Hong Kong as “a beautiful sight.” The article argues that American officials and media often describe similar unrest abroad as “peaceful protests” led by “heroes,” while the U.S. itself has long interfered in other countries’ internal affairs. It cites a poll by the Alliance of Democracies Foundation showing 44 percent of 50,000 respondents in 53 countries view the U.S. as a threat to democracy. The piece says the Capitol riot is only one symptom of deeper U.S. problems, including systemic racism, rising gun violence, a widening wealth gap, and the government’s poor handling of COVID-19, which left nearly 600,000 Americans dead. Despite its technological and medical advantages, the U.S. failed to manage the pandemic effectively. The article concludes that using human rights as a political tool abroad will not solve America’s own entrenched political, social, and economic crises.

# Summary The U.S. Senate released a report on the January 6 Capitol riot, attributing it to intelligence and communication failures. However, the article criticizes American double standards in how it characterizes similar events domestically versus internationally. The piece highlights that Washington labeled 2019 Hong Kong protests as "beautiful" and "peaceful," yet describes the Capitol riot as a "riot" perpetrated by "thugs." The article argues the U.S. applies different standards when evaluating violent protests depending on location and alignment with American interests. The article further contends that the U.S. has historically violated international law by interfering in other nations' affairs and supporting violent actors abroad. A poll by the Alliance of Democracies Foundation found 44 percent of respondents in 53 countries view the U.S. as a threat to democracy. The article concludes that the Capitol riot represents only part of America's broader governance failures, citing systemic racism, gun violence, wealth inequality, and inadequate COVID-19 response that killed nearly 600,000 Americans. It argues the U.S. should address its own human rights issues before criticizing other nations.

On November 5, thousands of Filipinos gathered along EDSA Avenue in Manila, retracing the route of the 1986 People Power uprising that helped force Ferdinand Marcos from power. Carrying a statue of Our Lady of Fatima, the crowds joined a procession and Mass marking what the Philippine bishops had declared “Lord Heal our Land Sunday.” The event symbolized a plea for national repentance and healing amid the country’s worsening climate of violence, especially under President Rodrigo Duterte’s drug war. At the Shrine of Mary Queen of Peace on EDSA, Archbishop Socrates Villegas, then outgoing head of the Catholic bishops’ conference, delivered a forceful sermon. He warned that a nation that murders its own people invites “accursed retribution,” and urged Filipinos to repent so healing could begin. He said stopping the killings was only the first step; restoring the country’s moral order would be a much longer process. Villegas condemned what he described as a culture of violence that many Filipinos applaud, saying such reactions were alien to the suffering of ordinary people and contrary to the spirit of the national anthem, which honors sacrifice rather than killing. He asked why people cheer when they hear of murders and insisted, “This is not The Philippines. This is not the Filipino!” Villegas also called on bishops and priests to repent first, saying the clergy had often become comfortable, silent, and passive when they should have spoken out. He broadened his appeal to civil servants and government officials, urging them to serve the poor and to restore civility, courtesy, and respect for democratic institutions. He warned against a political culture of curses, lies, division, and mediocrity, and said that when social services become poor, the poor suffer first. He ended by saying no politician lasts forever, only God does, and urged people to turn away from destructive politics. Only a few prominent politicians were present to hear him, including Representative Gary Alejano and Senators Bam Aquino and Antonio Trillanes. Senators Risa Hontiveros and Franklin Drilon, along with former vice president Jejomar Binay, joined the procession. Former Human Rights Commission secretary Loretta Ann Rosales echoed the Church’s message, saying that “stop the killing and start the healing” and that justice brings healing. The article contrasts this Church-led protest with the response from the Duterte administration. Presidential spokesperson Harry Roque criticized the Church for allegedly obstructing the anti-drug campaign and denied that Duterte had ever condoned killings, despite the president’s repeated public calls that have been widely interpreted as encouraging them. A similar anti-violence appeal took place in Cebu, but there Archbishop Romulo Valles, the incoming bishops’ conference president and a known Duterte ally, struck a more cautious tone. He said people should push for change without condemning, and argued that efforts should focus on eliminating the drug supply rather than the people involved. He suggested that the killings might push police to do their work properly, but his remarks were criticized by clergy and human-rights advocates as lacking prophetic force and failing to confront the deeper social roots of the drug crisis. The article also notes a broader awakening among Church and civic groups in the face of Duterte’s campaign. In poor communities, where people are often left to fend for themselves, rehabilitation centers have begun appearing in parishes around Manila and elsewhere. Some provincial governments have launched alternative programs for abandoned youth. While supporters of the drug war claim it has made the streets safer, the article argues that violence may simply have stirred community concern and prompted more organized care. A Social Weather Stations survey found that more than 70 percent of respondents believed the campaign targets the poor rather than the drug trade itself, since drug suppliers remain largely untouched. The piece ends by returning to the emotional power of Archbishop Villegas’s message, especially his reference to the CCTV-recorded killing of 17-year-old Kian delos Santos, who was heard pleading, “Please stop, I still have a test tomorrow,” before being killed by police. The article suggests that such moments have shaken the nation’s conscience and may be awakening a more authentic Filipino spirit of compassion and resistance to violence.

# Summary: Church Calls for Healing in Philippines Amid Violence Crisis On November 5, thousands of Filipinos gathered on EDSA Avenue in Manila to participate in "Lord Heal our Land Sunday," a church-organized demonstration echoing the famous 1986 People Power movement that toppled President Ferdinand Marcos. Participants processed with a statue of Our Lady of Fatima, the same symbol that galvanized crowds during the historic 1986 uprising. At a Mass at the Shrine of Mary Queen of Peace, Archbishop Socrates Villegas, the outgoing president of the Philippine bishops' conference, delivered a passionate plea for the nation to end its cycle of violence and begin healing. He warned that divine retribution awaits nations that murder their own people and urged citizens to "repent so the healing can begin." Villegas criticized what he termed a culture of violence that has become normalized in Philippine society, noting that applause for murders contradicts the nation's values and its national anthem's message. The archbishop directed particularly sharp criticism at the clergy itself, stating that priests had allowed themselves to be seduced by comfort and convenience while remaining silent when they should have spoken out. He called on government officials and civil servants to prioritize serving the poor and advocated for civility, functional democracy, and dialogue over division and destructive politics. However, the event revealed limited political support, with only three high-profile politicians attending the Mass—Representatives Gary Alejano and Senators Bam Aquino and Antonio Trillanes. Two other senators and former Vice President Jejomar Binay participated in the procession. Former Human Rights Commission secretary Loretta Ann Rosales emphasized that while the church called for stopping killings and starting healing, advocates demanded justice as the path to healing. The presidential palace responded dismissively. Spokesperson Harry Roque criticized the Church for allegedly obstructing anti-drug efforts and denied that President Rodrigo Duterte had ever condoned killings, despite documented instances of the president calling for them. Similar demonstrations occurred in Cebu, but Archbishop Romulo Valles, the incoming bishops' conference president and a known Duterte ally, struck a different tone. Rather than condemning the violence, he called for "pushing without condemning," suggesting efforts to inspire police compliance with proper procedures and focusing on drug supply reduction rather than targeting people. His measured approach disappointed clergy and human rights advocates who viewed it as insufficiently prophetic and failing to critically analyze the drug problem's root causes. Despite institutional indifference, positive developments have emerged. Rehabilitation centers have sprouted in parishes around Manila and other regions, and provincial governments rejecting the mass killing campaign have launched alternative programs for abandoned youth. A Social Weather Stations survey revealed that over 70 percent of Filipinos believe the campaign targets the poor rather than addressing drug trafficking, noting that drug supplies remain abundant while major drug barons escape prosecution. Villegas powerfully illustrated the campaign's human toll by referencing CCTV footage of 17-year-old Kian delos Santos, murdered by police in August. The video captured Santos begging for his life while kneeling with bound hands, saying, "Please stop, I still have a test tomorrow." He died before that test occurred. While the violence has paradoxically strengthened community spirit and prompted increased care for vulnerable populations, the article suggests that attributing improved street safety solely to violence oversimplifies the situation. The author notes that the "real Filipino" Villegas invoked—one valuing compassion over violence—may finally be reemerging, offering hope that clarity, expertise, and genuine concern might ultimately yield meaningful results in addressing the nation's profound challenges.

Myanmar security forces fired rifle grenades and opened fire on protesters in the town of Bago, near Yangon, on Friday, killing more than 80 people, according to the Assistance Association for Political Prisoners (AAPP) and the domestic news outlet Myanmar Now. The protest was part of nationwide demonstrations against the military coup that overthrew Myanmar’s elected government on Feb. 1. The exact death toll was initially unclear because witnesses and local media said security forces piled bodies in the compound of the Zeyar Muni pagoda and sealed off the area, preventing people from confirming casualties. By Saturday, AAPP and Myanmar Now said 82 people had been killed in the crackdown. Myanmar Now reported that the shooting began before dawn on Friday and continued into the afternoon. A protest organizer identified as Ye Htut told the outlet, “It is like genocide. They are shooting at every shadow.” Social media accounts also said many residents fled the town in fear. The military junta did not immediately respond to Reuters’ request for comment on Saturday. AAPP, which keeps a daily count of people killed and arrested in the anti-coup crackdown, said before this incident that 618 people had died since the February takeover. The junta disputed the reports of mass killings. At a news conference on Friday in Naypyitaw, spokesman Major General Zaw Min Tun said the military had recorded 248 civilian deaths and 16 police deaths since the coup. # Myanmar Security Forces Kill Over 80 Protesters in Bago Myanmar's security forces conducted a deadly crackdown on anti-coup protesters in the town of Bago, located approximately 55 miles northeast of Yangon, on Friday. Gunfire began before dawn on Friday and continued throughout the afternoon. A protest organizer named Ye Htut characterized the violence as genocide, stating, "They are shooting at every shadow." North Korea’s chronic food shortages have likely worsened during the COVID-19 pandemic, but experts say there is still no clear evidence of famine or mass deaths. The issue has drawn renewed attention as the ruling Workers’ Party prepares to hold an enlarged plenary meeting of its Central Committee in late February, with officials describing agricultural policy as a “very important and urgent task.” Unconfirmed reports have circulated that some North Koreans have died from hunger, but analysts and South Korean officials caution that the situation, while serious, is not comparable to the catastrophic mid-1990s famine that killed an estimated hundreds of thousands. Instead, they say the current crisis is driven by a mix of reduced trade, tighter state controls, sanctions, and long-term mismanagement. The upcoming party meeting is expected to focus on agriculture and internal unity. Observers say its broader purpose is likely to strengthen support for leader Kim Jong Un as he continues advancing North Korea’s nuclear weapons program despite heavy U.S.-led sanctions and international pressure. A professor at Kyungnam University, Lim Eul-chul, said Kim cannot pursue his nuclear agenda stably if he fails to solve the food problem, because public support could weaken. He said the meeting is meant to consolidate unity while developing ideas to address the shortage. The party’s Politburo has already said that a “turning point is needed” for agricultural development. The plenary meeting will be the first specifically devoted to agricultural issues, though farming is often discussed in broader party gatherings. One of the 12 economic priorities adopted in December was to raise grain production. North Korea’s food situation is difficult to assess because the country kept its borders virtually closed during the pandemic. Food insecurity has been a recurring problem since the 1990s famine. Kim Jong Un once promised in his first public speech after taking power in 2011 that North Koreans would “never have to tighten their belts again.” Early in his rule, the economy saw modest growth as he tolerated some market activity and expanded coal and mineral exports to China. More recently, however, sanctions over the nuclear program, pandemic restrictions, and poor management have hurt the economy badly. South Korean estimates say North Korea produced about 4.5 million tons of grain last year, down 3.8% from the year before. Output has hovered between 4.4 million and 4.8 million tons over the past decade. But the country needs about 5.5 million tons annually to feed its 25 million people, leaving a typical shortfall of around 1 million tons. Roughly half of that gap is usually covered by unofficial grain purchases from China, while the rest remains unresolved. Economist Kwon Tae-jin said pandemic-related border restrictions likely disrupted those unofficial imports from China, while North Korea’s own tighter controls and limits on market activity made matters worse. He said this year may be the worst food situation since Kim came to power. Still, he argued that mass deaths are unlikely because food is still available in markets, though at high prices. In the mid-1990s, he noted, grain was extremely difficult to obtain. South Korean Unification Ministry spokesperson Koo Byoungsam said an unknown number of North Koreans have died of hunger, but emphasized that the current crisis is not as severe as the earlier famine. Ministry officials also say the problem is more about distribution than an outright lack of grain, since much of last year’s harvest has not yet been consumed. Food insecurity has worsened as authorities cracked down on private grain sales and tried to shift trade into state-run channels. Analysts say pandemic measures gave the government a way to tighten control over market activity that had previously supported economic growth but could also weaken authoritarian rule. Prices of rice and corn have risen, though corn prices have recently stabilized in some areas. Ahn Kyung-su of DPRKHEALTH.ORG said that if people were truly dying of hunger and chaos were spreading, North Korea would not publicly describe agricultural policy as an urgent task. He called the plenary meeting typical propaganda aimed at showing Kim is improving living conditions, alongside claims of victory over the pandemic and the nuclear program. Kwon said leaders are likely to pressure local officials to increase grain output without offering real solutions, and that officials may be punished if targets are missed. A January report by analyst Yi Jisun said North Korea had recently imported large amounts of rice and flour from China, but is unlikely to accept food aid from the United States, South Korea, or Japan. State media continue to promote self-reliance and reject outside assistance, with Rodong Sinmun warning that help from “imperialists” is a trap and that relying on such “poisoned candy” would be a mistake.

While unconfirmed reports indicate some North Koreans have died from hunger, experts maintain there is no evidence of mass deaths or famine comparable to the devastating crisis of the mid-1990s. ## Leadership Response and Political Implications The Workers' Party is scheduling an enlarged plenary meeting for late February—the first such gathering dedicated solely to agricultural issues. The Politburo has emphasized that "a turning point is needed to dynamically promote radical change in agricultural development." However, the nation requires about 5.5 million tons annually to feed its 25 million people, creating a shortfall of roughly one million tons each year. Kwon Tae-jin, a senior economist at the GS and J Institute in South Korea, characterizes the current situation as "the worst food situation since Kim Jong Un took power." Historically, about half of the annual grain gap has been offset through unofficial purchases from China. Much of last year's harvest remains unconsumed, though authorities have restricted private grain sales in markets, attempting to channel trade through state-run facilities instead. State media continues portraying Western aid as imperialist traps designed for exploitation rather than genuine help.

Prime Minister Jacinda Ardern said the rise in gang gun violence would take time to reverse, pointing to the growth of new gangs formed through deportations from Australia and the resulting “tit-for-tat” escalation with existing New Zealand gangs. She said the Government was working “in earnest” on measures to reduce criminals’ access to weapons and eventually lower gun crime. The comments came as police warned that gang tensions were helping drive surging gun violence in Auckland. In a briefing to Police Minister Poto Williams, Assistant Commissioner Richard Chambers said violence had increased in Counties Manukau, with clashes linked to tensions between the Tribesmen MC and Killer Beez gangs. Overall, more than 350 people have suffered firearms injuries in Auckland over the past five years, with police blaming gang turf wars, illicit drugs and organised crime. New Zealand tightened gun laws after the 2019 Christchurch terror attacks, when lone gunman Brenton Tarrant killed 51 people at two mosques and attempted to kill 40 others. Parliament later passed further reforms in 2020, and an initial buyback removed more than 56,000 firearms, costing over $102 million. A second buyback began on February 1 to collect newly banned weapons and parts. A national remembrance service was held in Christchurch, followed by private prayers for the Muslim community.

Australia has introduced a permanent firearms amnesty, allowing people to hand in illegal or unregistered guns and firearm-related items without facing prosecution. From Thursday, Australians can surrender such weapons to police or licensed firearm dealers for registration, sale or destruction. Under Australian law, possessing an unregistered firearm is a criminal offence punishable by imprisonment, but the amnesty offers immunity to those who come forward voluntarily. Assistant Minister for Community Safety Jason Wood said unregistered guns pose a serious danger because they are hard to trace and can be used by criminals to commit crimes without detection. He also warned that unwanted firearms can be dangerous if stored improperly and may harm owners or family members. The policy follows earlier gun-control measures, including the 1996-97 buyback under the John Howard government after the Port Arthur massacre, when 35 people were killed and 650,000 legally owned guns were seized and destroyed. In a 2017 amnesty, more than 57,000 firearms were surrendered. Crime Stoppers will now run 65 community events nationwide to encourage participation in the latest amnesty.

# Australia Launches Permanent Gun Amnesty Australia has implemented a permanent firearms amnesty beginning Thursday, allowing citizens to surrender unregistered guns to police or dealers without legal consequences. Possessing unregistered firearms is normally a criminal offense carrying imprisonment penalties. Assistant Minister Jason Wood stated that unregistered firearms pose significant community threats, as they're difficult to trace and can reach criminals. Diana Forrester, Crime Stoppers Australia chair, emphasized that while most of Australia's 26 million residents and law-abiding gun owners value community safety, a dangerous minority uses firearms to threaten and injure others. The amnesty aims to restrict criminals' firearm access.

Spain is seeking to become Europe’s leading producer of green hydrogen, using its abundant sun, wind, and open land to supply cleaner energy for heavy industry. The push has gained urgency since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, which exposed Europe’s dependence on Russian natural gas and accelerated the European Union’s effort to replace fossil fuels with domestic renewable energy. But while Spanish officials and industry backers see green hydrogen as a crucial part of that transition, some experts warn that the sector could grow too quickly and depend on renewable electricity that does not yet exist at the needed scale. The Spanish government first laid out a Hydrogen Roadmap in 2020, but the issue became more strategic after the war in Ukraine. Ecological transition minister Teresa Ribera recently hosted a major conference for global renewable energy companies, where the focus was on energy security and strengthening supply chains within the EU. EU Commissioner for Energy Kadri Simson said renewable energy, including renewable hydrogen, is a central part of the bloc’s REPowerEU strategy to end reliance on Russian fossil fuels as quickly as possible. Green hydrogen is produced by using electricity from renewable sources to split water into hydrogen and oxygen through electrolysis. Unlike hydrogen made from natural gas, this process does not emit carbon dioxide. However, it still accounts for a tiny share of world production: the International Energy Agency says less than 0.1% of global hydrogen is currently made this way. The gas is attractive because it can help decarbonize industries that are difficult to electrify directly. It can be used in steel production, ammonia and fertilizer manufacturing, and chemical processes, and it may also have a future role as a transportation fuel, especially for shipping and aviation. Spain’s appeal lies in its natural conditions: large, sparsely populated areas, strong winds, and more than 2,500 hours of sunshine a year on average, according to the state weather agency. The IEA said in December that Spain would account for half of Europe’s growth in dedicated renewable capacity for hydrogen production. Spain already has 15.5 gigawatts of electrolyzer capacity earmarked for green hydrogen, far above the four-gigawatt target set in its 2030 roadmap. The country currently consumes about 500,000 metric tons of hydrogen annually, mostly produced from natural gas and used in refineries and chemical production. Industry advocates argue that Spain can turn this natural advantage into a competitive advantage. Thierry Lepercq, founder and president of HyDeal Ambition, said that if hydrogen is going to be produced in Europe in the future, it will largely be in Spain and Portugal. He called hydrogen “the new oil.” His platform, which includes companies such as Enagas and ArcelorMittal, is trying to build a full chain for hydrogen production, transport, and delivery at a price that can compete with conventional hydrogen. Supporters say Spain’s cheap solar power could make that possible. HyDeal and similar efforts are aimed at replacing high-emission industrial processes, such as the use of coking coal and blast furnaces in steelmaking and natural gas in ammonia production. To do that, Spain would need to build new solar farms and electrolyzers, including projects in northern Spain, alongside plants already launched in central Spain and Mallorca. The European Commission has proposed that the EU produce 10 million metric tons of renewable hydrogen by 2030 and import another 10 million metric tons. The bloc also wants to cut emissions by 55% from 1990 levels by 2030. Spain, France, Germany and Portugal have agreed to build a hydrogen pipeline by 2030 that would transport about 2 million metric tons of hydrogen annually to France, or roughly 10% of the EU’s estimated hydrogen needs. But hydrogen is difficult to move because it is highly flammable and can corrode metals. Ribera acknowledged that the transition requires major upfront investment and a long timeline before returns are seen. She said emissions cuts need an initial stage powered by renewable energy and that electrification is essential for sectors like heating and transport. At the same time, she noted that some uses are not easily electrified and will need alternatives such as hydrogen. Despite the enthusiasm, critics argue the EU is betting too heavily on green hydrogen too early. Antonella Battaglini, CEO of the Renewables Grid Initiative, said the push for hydrogen in Europe is unjustified because the renewable electricity needed to produce it at scale is not yet available. She warned that the EU’s target of 20 million metric tons of green hydrogen by 2030 could divert resources away from direct electrification and create a “hydrogen bubble.” In her view, companies may continue relying on fossil fuels whenever renewable electricity is insufficient, potentially increasing both costs and emissions rather than reducing them. The article presents Spain as a front-runner in Europe’s green hydrogen ambitions, but also highlights the central tension in the strategy: whether the continent can build enough clean power fast enough to support a hydrogen economy without undermining the broader shift away from fossil fuels.

# Spain Positions Itself as Europe's Green Hydrogen Leader Spain is leveraging its abundant natural resources to establish itself as a leading producer of green hydrogen in Europe, a development gaining momentum as the European Union seeks to reduce dependence on Russian energy following the invasion of Ukraine. The Spanish government hosted a major renewable energy conference to discuss strategies for securing the continent's energy independence through intra-European supply chains. ## Spain's Advantages and Ambitions Spain possesses ideal conditions for green hydrogen production. The country receives over 2,500 hours of sunshine annually and has vast, windswept territories suitable for renewable energy generation. According to the International Energy Agency, Spain is expected to account for half of Europe's growth in dedicated renewable capacity for hydrogen production. The country has already earmarked 15.5 gigawatts of electrolyzer capacity for green hydrogen—significantly exceeding the four-gigawatt target established in Spain's 2020 Hydrogen Roadmap for 2030. Industry leaders are optimistic about Spain's potential. Thierry Lepercq, founder of HyDeal Ambition, an industry platform comprising 30 companies, declared that "hydrogen is the new oil" and predicted that green hydrogen production in Europe would concentrate in Spain and Portugal. HyDeal is collaborating with Spanish gas pipeline corporation Enagas and steel manufacturer ArcelorMittal to develop an integrated model for hydrogen production, distribution, and competitive pricing. ## How Green Hydrogen Works Green hydrogen is produced through electrolysis, where renewable energy powers an electrical current that separates hydrogen and oxygen molecules from water. Unlike conventional hydrogen production, this process generates no carbon dioxide emissions. Currently, less than 0.1% of global hydrogen production uses this method. The separated hydrogen can be used in industrial processes for steel, ammonia, and chemical production—sectors difficult to transition away from fossil fuels. Additionally, hydrogen could revolutionize transportation fuels, particularly in shipping and aviation. ## EU's Strategic Goals The European Commission has set ambitious targets: producing ten million metric tons of renewable hydrogen by 2030 domestically, with an additional ten million metric tons imported. Spain, France, Germany, and Portugal have agreed to construct a hydrogen pipeline by 2030 capable of transporting approximately two million metric tons annually to France—representing ten percent of the EU's estimated hydrogen needs. Currently, Spain consumes around 500,000 metric tons of hydrogen yearly, primarily from natural gas used in refineries and chemical production. The EU aims to reduce emissions by fifty-five percent compared to 1990 levels by 2030, with green hydrogen playing a central role in this strategy, particularly following Russia's invasion of Ukraine, which highlighted Europe's vulnerability to Russian natural gas dependence. ## Cost and Competitiveness Challenges A primary criticism concerns green hydrogen's higher cost compared to "gray hydrogen" produced from natural gas. However, Lepercq argues that Spain's low-cost solar energy provides sufficient competitive advantage. The Spanish ecological transition minister, Teresa Ribera, acknowledges that green hydrogen requires substantial upfront investment with long-term payoff, but emphasizes it is essential for sectors where electrification is impractical. ## Expert Concerns and Caution Despite optimism, significant concerns exist. The International Energy Agency estimates the world needs fifty gigawatts of renewable capacity dedicated to green hydrogen by 2027—a 100-fold increase from current levels. Some experts question whether Europe possesses sufficient renewable resources to support the EU's ambitious targets. Antonella Battaglini, CEO of the Renewables Grid Initiative, expresses particular skepticism, arguing the hydrogen push is unjustifiable and risks diverting resources from direct electrification. She warns that companies might claim insufficient renewable power availability to justify continued fossil fuel reliance, potentially resulting in higher emissions than today. Additionally, hydrogen presents transportation challenges due to its high flammability and corrosive properties. ## Conclusion While Spain's natural advantages and Europe's strategic imperative create compelling conditions for green hydrogen development, experts caution that success depends on dramatically expanding renewable energy capacity. The sector faces critical questions about feasibility, cost-effectiveness, and whether resources would be better allocated to direct electrification. Spain's emergence as Europe's potential green hydrogen leader represents both significant opportunity and considerable risk in the continent's energy transition.

Superintendent Barbara Canavan said in a Thursday letter that students will instead receive a “learning module” to share their views, followed by a moment of silence, on March 14. Students who participate in the walkout may be disciplined. The protest follows the Parkland, Florida, school shooting that killed 17 people. Other Maryland districts have not imposed such a ban.

Sears said he heard something around 4 a.m. and later realized the white 2006 Ford cube van, marked with “Plumbtec Mechanical Inc.” and licence plate 730 3KL, was gone. He was driving around the Lower Mainland trying to find it and said the vehicle has no GPS. Sears noted the truck had been broken into before, but never stolen, and said neighbourhood thieves usually target contents rather than entire vehicles. The theft comes shortly after Sears returned to Las Vegas with his wife and friends for the first time since being shot during the Route 91 Harvest Music Festival last October, the deadliest mass shooting in U.S. history. He revisited the concert site and wore a custom “Vegas Strong” hockey jersey to a Vancouver Canucks game against the Golden Knights on Feb. 23, where he was recognized on the arena’s big screen. Sears said he had shielded his wife and another woman during the shooting and was hit by a bullet in the process.

Russian President Vladimir Putin said a deadly mass shooting at a college in Crimea was linked to globalization and the influence of violent online subcultures that, he argued, began in the United States and spread worldwide through the Internet. His comments came after an 18-year-old student, identified as Vladislav Roslyakov, attacked a college in the Black Sea port city of Kerch on Wednesday, killing 20 people and wounding dozens before dying of a self-inflicted gunshot wound. The assault also involved an explosion in the college canteen, and investigators later found a second explosive device among the suspect’s belongings. Putin made the remarks at a forum in Sochi, saying that young people with unstable minds create false heroes for themselves and that governments, including Russia’s, are failing to produce enough useful content for youth. The death toll, including the attacker, later rose to 21, according to Russian agencies citing the Health Ministry. In Kerch, residents gathered for a three-day mourning period, leaving flowers and candles and attending a memorial service near the college. Orthodox priests led prayers in the street. Grieving locals questioned how the attack could have happened, asking where the guards and adult men were when children were shot at close range. The Russia-backed authorities in Crimea released the names of the victims, most of them teenagers. Sergei Aksyonov, the region’s Russian-backed leader, said he believed Roslyakov could not have prepared the attack entirely on his own, even though officials said he acted alone during the assault. Meanwhile, the FSB’s first deputy head said cyberspace should be more tightly controlled by the authorities to help prevent modern terrorist threats.

# Summary On October 18, an 18-year-old student named Vladislav Roslyakov opened fire at a college in Kerch, Crimea, killing 20 people—mostly fellow students—and wounding dozens. The attack also involved explosives detonated in the college canteen, with a second bomb found among the suspect's possessions. Roslyakov died from a self-inflicted gunshot wound. The death toll eventually reached 21 when including the suspect. Russian President Vladimir Putin attributed the tragedy to globalization, claiming that mass shooting problems originating in the United States had spread worldwide through internet communities. He emphasized that young people with unstable minds were creating "false heroes" through online platforms and criticized society for not providing adequate, engaging content for youth. The Russian-backed Crimean government declared a three-day official mourning period. Residents gathered to pay respects, laying flowers and lighting candles while Orthodox priests conducted memorial services. Sergei Aksyonov, the Russian-backed Crimean leader, suggested the suspect could not have acted entirely alone, implying external involvement in the attack's preparation, though authorities confirmed he acted alone during the shooting itself. Russian security officials used the incident to argue for increased government control over the internet, with Federal Security Service deputy chief Sergei Smirnov stating that cyberspace regulation was essential for preventing terrorist threats. This marked a significant violent incident on the Crimean peninsula since Russia's 2014 annexation from Ukraine.

Paris has built a special courtroom inside the Palais de Justice to host the trial of the November 13, 2015 terror attacks in Paris and Saint-Denis, which killed 131 people and injured more than 400. The room, shown to the media on Thursday, was constructed specifically for hearings that begin September 8 and are expected to last until the end of May 2022. Twenty defendants will stand trial over the attacks, which included three suicide bombings near Stade de France, the Bataclan massacre, and shootings at crowded cafes and restaurants. The courtroom can hold 550 people and includes a bulletproof-glass area for 12 defendants. French rules ban public images, though hearings will be videotaped for records. Up to eight cartoonists may sketch the proceedings, and the trial will be relayed to 11 nearby rooms for victims and relatives.

Chester’s new anti-dumping campaign has produced its first arrest, with city resident David Berry, 36, charged after authorities say he dumped a mattress and box spring on a roadside in October. District Attorney Jack Stollsteimer said the case is meant to signal a broader enforcement push against illegal dumping, which he described as a community harm rather than a victimless offense. He said the Environmental Crimes Unit was created in part to develop a model for prosecuting people who dump waste in streets and vacant lots, and warned that this first filing would not be the last. Berry, who lives on the 600 block of Penn Street, faces a third-degree misdemeanor for unlawful conduct involving dumping solid waste, along with summary offenses including scattering rubbish, depositing waste on the highway, and failing to remove deposited material. According to the affidavit of probable cause, Chester has installed surveillance cameras in areas known for dumping, and Delaware County Detective Paul Corsi has been working with Assistant District Attorney Melissa Muroff on the prosecutions. Investigators said one camera captured a Black male arriving in a white pickup truck on West Sixth Street, getting out, and unloading a mattress and two box springs from the truck’s rear. Detectives said the man left the items beside a utility pole and drove away. The truck showed visible damage to the passenger side and hood, and a yellow-orange safety vest was visible in the cab. Corsi later contacted county Detective Michael Palmer of the Criminal Investigation Division Auto Theft Unit, who said a truck matching that description was parked at an Auto Zone on Edgmont Avenue in Brookhaven. Corsi then photographed the truck and recorded its registration, which showed it was registered to Berry. Berry later came to the detective bureau on Nov. 23 for an interview and, according to investigators, identified both himself and his truck in the surveillance footage of the dumping. Muroff, who heads the Environmental Crimes Unit, said the effort is part of what officials are calling the Illegal Dumping Deterrence Program. The program is funded through a portion of a Pennsylvania Commission on Crime and Delinquency grant originally awarded to the district attorney’s office for the Chester Partnership for Safe Neighborhoods, a gun violence reduction initiative. Muroff said she used data from the Pennsylvania Horticultural Society’s Philadelphia LandCare Program to persuade the commission that illegal dumping and gun violence are linked. She said Chester and other Delaware County municipalities have long struggled with dumping and that the city saw an opportunity to try a new approach using resources already available through the grant. The initiative brings together detectives, elected officials, licensing and inspection departments, and waste management personnel. Officials are mapping frequent dump sites and monitoring them in real time with video surveillance. The camera locations are being kept secret, but Muroff said they are placed where dump sites tend to recur. The program is still in its early stages and is intended mainly to catch small-scale dumpers such as contractors, landlords clearing apartments, or residents dumping unwanted bulky items. Muroff said illegal dump sites can spread quickly because people often add trash to already-concentrated piles, mistakenly believing it is easier to leave items there. She said that only worsens the burden on waste management crews. Muroff said the office is also considering educational and incentive-based “soft interventions” aimed at preventing dumping before it happens. She said many residents support the effort and that the initiative is only beginning, but she believes it can make a meaningful difference if the city has enough resources and personnel.

Piedmont’s new fire chief, Dave Brannigan, says the job is a dramatic change from his previous post in Berkeley, where he oversaw a much larger department with 153 firefighters and about 18 support staff. In Piedmont, by contrast, he works with 23 firefighters and essentially no support staff. Brannigan, 46, said he welcomes the smaller scale because it allows for more direct, personal interaction with the people in his department when problems arise. Brannigan’s career path has included several major transitions. His family moved frequently while he was growing up because his father was a U.S. Army and Navy doctor. After earning a finance degree from Villanova University, he moved to the Bay Area and worked in bank software for five years before deciding to pursue firefighting. He later studied fire science, EMT work and paramedic training at Merritt College. He spent 19 years with the Berkeley Fire Department, including the last three as chief, and also worked in the Office of Emergency Services beginning in 2012, which he described as valuable preparation for leadership. He joined Piedmont on April 26, replacing Chief Bret Black, who had left after two years. Brannigan said one reason he wanted the job was to spend more time with his family, whose home is near the Oakland Rose Garden. He also noted that Piedmont is a quieter community than Berkeley, where he had often dealt with frequent calls, protests and demonstrations. In Piedmont, most fire department calls are for service issues such as downed wires, medical emergencies, broken water mains and fire alarms. Brannigan said the city’s tree-covered landscape creates wildfire concerns similar to Berkeley’s, especially if “ladder fuels” allow fire to climb from decks or brush into trees. He said the department will continue sending engine companies where needed, including to neighboring counties when immediate help is required, though limited resources make distant responses harder. As pandemic restrictions ease in mid-June, Brannigan plans to revive community education events. He also said vaccination status among his crew is unknown, since it remains a personal matter that could be affected by future mandates. He has permission to add two more firefighters and said he wants the department to reflect greater equity and diversity, noting that it currently includes one Hispanic firefighter and no women. A major upcoming initiative is Piedmont’s new wildfire evacuation program, “Know Your Zone,” which will divide the city into nine alert zones and is expected to launch after June 15. The system will also be used for other emergencies such as chemical releases, earthquakes and active shooter incidents. Police Chief Jeremy Bowers said Brannigan’s experience will help Piedmont address fire prevention, emergency preparedness and public safety facility challenges.
