The Kyle Police Department is offering CRASE, or Civilian Response to Active Shooter Events, a free training program designed to help people survive an active shooter situation. Built around the “Avoid, Deny, Defend” strategy developed by ALERRT in 2004, the course teaches civilians practical ways to respond if law enforcement cannot arrive immediately. KPD Capt. Pedro Hernandez said the department has five CRASE instructors, all trained through ALERRT to teach the program. The training is available to a wide range of groups, including businesses, hospitals, places of worship, community organizations and schools. It is normally a four-hour class, but it can be adjusted to fit the needs of the participants, and instructors typically travel to the location where the training is requested. The course does not include hands-on exercises. Instead, it uses PowerPoint presentations and training videos to explain the history and frequency of active shooter incidents, possible civilian responses, medical concerns and guidance for conducting drills. Hernandez emphasized that these events unfold quickly, and officers may need minutes to reach the scene, making immediate civilian action critical. The ADD strategy focuses on three steps: avoid the attacker by staying aware of surroundings, deny access by creating distance and barriers, and defend yourself if escape or concealment are not possible. Hernandez also noted that one upcoming session will include a medical component called Self-Aid Buddy Aid, which teaches participants how to use tourniquets, pack wounds and apply bandages. He said this is important because police’ first priority is stopping the killing, which may delay care for the wounded. There are no age restrictions, though Hernandez said parents should decide what is appropriate for their children. Some materials may be disturbing, including audio such as a 911 call from the Columbine High School shooting. Hernandez said younger children and teens should still be introduced to survival training, since the lessons can apply in many settings, not just schools. Those interested in scheduling CRASE in Kyle or Buda can contact local officials or visit the ALERRT website.

# Summary: CRASE Active Shooter Training Program The Kyle Police Department offers CRASE (Civilian Response to Active Shooter Events), a free training program designed to help people survive active shooter incidents. The program is based on the "Avoid, Deny, Defend" strategy developed by ALERRT (Advance Law Enforcement Rapid Response Training) in 2004. The four-hour course, which can be customized based on participants' needs, covers the history and prevalence of active shooter events, civilian response options, medical considerations, and drill procedures. The Kyle Police Department has five certified CRASE instructors who have completed ALERRT training and can travel to organizations to deliver the program. The core strategy teaches participants to avoid the attacker while remaining aware of surroundings, deny the attacker access by maintaining distance and creating barriers, and defend themselves when avoidance and denial are impossible. This approach is critical because active shooter events develop rapidly, and law enforcement may take several minutes to arrive—time that could be lifesaving. The program utilizes PowerPoint presentations and training videos rather than hands-on exercises. Some upcoming sessions include a medical component called Self-Aid Buddy Aid, which teaches practical skills like applying tourniquets, packing wounds, and bandaging. This addition recognizes that law enforcement's initial priority is stopping the shooter, leaving wounded victims without immediate medical assistance. While the program has no age restrictions, Captain Pedro Hernandez notes that parents should determine appropriateness for their children, as some audio and video content—including a 911 call from the 1999 Columbine shooting—may be disturbing. Hernandez emphasizes that these survival strategies apply universally to any location, not just schools. Interested Kyle residents can contact Captain Hernandez, while Buda residents should reach out to Community Affairs Officer Freddy Erdman. Additional information is available at www.alerrt.org.

No arrests have been made. Prosecutor Julien Moinil said the shootings appeared tied to rival drug gangs. Local media report Brussels had 89 shooting incidents last year, leaving nine dead, as Belgium remains a major narcotics-smuggling hub.

At Indian River State College, FERTES is already built into the future-teacher curriculum through modules embedded in different courses. Some parts of the instruction are general, while others are tailored to classroom conditions. Hard corners are areas not visible through the classroom door that could serve as shelter points if furniture is moved out of the way. The training also includes a live simulation. In the exercise, an instructor acts as the teacher while students sit as if they were in class. During the simulation, they hear gunfire and someone attempts to enter the room. Zgonc said this hands-on component is important because it gives future teachers a realistic sense of what such a crisis could be like and allows them to ask questions and practice responses, even though the hope is they never have to use those skills. The curriculum also teaches students how to fortify a classroom and how to respond if an armed intruder enters. According to Zgonc, future teachers learn options for using available tools to secure the room and, in the rarest circumstances, techniques to protect themselves and possibly fight off an attacker. The bill’s sponsor, Rep. Dan Daley, a Democrat from Coral Springs, said he introduced the legislation because he believes statewide training is necessary in the aftermath of Parkland. Daley, who was a student at Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School, said he has personal ties to victims such as Aaron Feis and wants to help prevent another tragedy like the one that killed 17 students and staff members on Valentine’s Day six years ago. Daley said it is better to reach future educators before they are overwhelmed by the demands of a teaching job. He also said the goal is to better prepare educators and help save students’ lives. The bill is in its final committee and could soon reach the House floor. If passed and signed by Governor Ron DeSantis, it would take effect on July 1, 2024.

After the mass shooting at a gay nightclub in Orlando, Fla., that left 49 people dead, the debate over assault-style weapons intensified again. The article examines whether local, state, and former federal bans on such weapons actually work, drawing on the experience of seven states, several municipalities, and the federal assault-weapons ban that lasted from 1994 to 2004. The overall conclusion from the available evidence is discouraging for supporters of these bans: they have had little measurable effect on the number of assault-style weapons in circulation and no clear impact on crime. One major reason is that guns move easily across borders. Experts say state and local laws are hard to enforce because weapons can be purchased in neighboring states with weaker restrictions and then trafficked into places with bans. This creates a persistent challenge for states trying to control assault weapons without a federal law. Another problem is that gun manufacturers can adapt quickly. When laws ban certain features, manufacturers often redesign weapons so they remain legal while still resembling the banned models. As a result, bans can be circumvented without eliminating the underlying type of firearm. The article notes that many bans also include “grandfathering” provisions, meaning people who already own assault weapons can keep them and sometimes pass them down. That limits the laws’ long-term effect. New York State is presented as a partial exception because it does not allow assault weapon owners to sell or give their guns to other New Yorkers or leave them to heirs in the state. Instead, the weapons must be sold out of state. If enforced over time, this could gradually reduce the number of assault weapons in the state. But New York faces another obstacle: registration compliance appears to be very low. James Jacobs of New York University estimates that perhaps only about 5 percent of owners have registered their weapons, making the law difficult to enforce. Chicago provides another example of the limits of local bans. Cook County adopted a strict assault-weapons ban in 1993, and in Chicago only police officers and military personnel may possess such weapons. There is no grandfathering in of guns. Even so, police say assault weapons continue to enter the city illegally from states like Indiana, where gun laws are looser. Chicago authorities acknowledge that most shootings involve handguns, but they say assault weapons still play a role in violence. In one recent year, police confiscated 104 assault weapons, about 3 percent of all guns seized. The article also explains how manufacturers exploit loopholes in the law. Assault-weapon definitions usually depend on a gun having one or two military-style features, such as detachable magazines, folding or telescoping stocks, pistol grips, thumbhole stocks, or barrel shrouds. Manufacturers can alter designs to avoid those exact features while keeping the weapons functionally similar. In California, for example, companies created “bullet buttons,” which require a tool such as a bullet to remove the magazine, allowing the gun to comply with state law. California is now trying to close that loophole. The federal assault-weapons ban offers a similar lesson. Although it was intended to restrict these guns, manufacturers were still able to produce assault-style weapons during the ban, according to critics. A Violence Policy Center study found that there were more assault-weapons manufacturers at the end of the ban than at the beginning, and more than one million new assault weapons were manufactured for sale in the United States during that period. Despite the ban, researchers have found no clear evidence that gun violence either rose or fell because of it. The article ends with the divide between gun-control advocates and gun-rights supporters. Advocates like Josh Sugarmann argue that stronger laws are needed. Chicago police commander Ronald Holt, whose teenage son Blair was killed by gun violence and for whom Cook County’s ban is named, says assault weapons should be reserved for military and law enforcement use and kept away from criminals and unstable individuals.

# Do Local Bans on Assault Weapons Work? Following the tragic mass shooting at an Orlando nightclub in which 49 people were killed with an assault-style semiautomatic rifle, the nation renewed its debate over whether such weapons should be banned. Seven states and several municipalities have already implemented assault weapon bans, providing data on their effectiveness. However, research suggests these bans have been largely ineffective at reducing the number of assault weapons in circulation or preventing crime. ## Limited Effectiveness of Current Bans The primary challenge facing assault weapon bans is their limited scope. Most state and local bans allow "grandfathering," permitting current owners to keep their weapons and sometimes pass them to heirs. New York State represents an exception, prohibiting owners from selling or transferring their assault weapons to New Yorkers and requiring they be sold out of state. While this approach could theoretically reduce the state's assault weapon inventory over time, it faces significant implementation obstacles. Registration requirements, intended to track existing weapons, have proven largely unsuccessful. In New York, despite mandatory registration laws, only approximately 5 percent of assault weapon owners registered their guns, making it extremely difficult to track and enforce regulations. ## The Interstate Gun Trafficking Problem A fundamental problem undermining local and state bans is the ease with which guns cross borders. Chicago has maintained a strict assault weapon ban since 1993, prohibiting civilian ownership entirely. Yet police consistently report illegal trafficking of assault weapons from neighboring states with less restrictive laws, particularly Indiana. This interstate movement of weapons significantly hampers local enforcement efforts. As UCLA law professor Adam Winkler explains, "State and local gun control laws always face the problem of the easy transportability of guns. They easily cross city, state, and other borders." ## Industry Adaptation Gun manufacturers have proven adept at circumventing ban legislation by modifying weapon designs. Since assault weapon definitions typically specify certain military features—such as detachable magazines, folding stocks, pistol grips, and barrel shrouds—manufacturers simply remove these features while maintaining the weapon's fundamental functionality. California's experience illustrates this problem: when the state restricted detachable magazines, manufacturers developed "bullet buttons" that allow magazine removal only with tools like bullets, technically complying with the law while preserving the weapon's practical utility. During the federal assault weapon ban (1994-2004), manufacturers continued producing assault weapons throughout the ban period. A 2004 study found more assault weapon manufacturers at the ban's end than at its beginning, with over one million new assault weapons manufactured for sale during the ban. ## Minimal Impact on Crime Data reveals no clear connection between local assault weapon bans and reduced gun violence. While assault weapons account for a small fraction of overall gun deaths, police data shows mixed results. Chicago confiscated 104 assault weapons in one year, representing only 3 percent of total gun confiscations, though authorities acknowledge assault weapons do play some role in crime. ## Conclusion and Future Outlook The evidence suggests that simply enacting assault weapon bans produces minimal substantive change without additional measures. Gun control advocates argue for much stricter legislation with comprehensive enforcement mechanisms, while others contend that assault weapons' small contribution to overall gun deaths makes them an ineffective policy focus. Experts and law enforcement officials, including Chicago police commander Ronald Holt, whose teenage son was killed by gun violence, continue advocating for stricter bans limiting assault weapons to military and law enforcement use. However, the experience of existing bans demonstrates that effective regulation requires federal coordination to prevent interstate trafficking, comprehensive registration and enforcement mechanisms, and continual legal adaptation to address industry workarounds.

In the rural Quebec municipality of Saint-Apollinaire, just 49 eligible voters will decide in a Sunday referendum whether a parcel of land can become a Muslim-run cemetery serving the Quebec City area. The vote will determine whether the town keeps or overturns zoning changes approved by the municipal council to allow the land’s use as a cemetery operating according to Islamic faith requirements. The land is currently used for burying ashes in urns and is being sold by Harmonia funeral home director Sylvain Roy to the Centre Culturel Islamique de Québec. Roy said the outcome could carry symbolic weight far beyond the town, warning that Saint-Apollinaire could be seen as a symbol of social exclusion in Canada and possibly beyond. The issue first arose in October 2016, when Roy met a Muslim family that had no nearby burial option that met their religious customs. At present, the only Muslim-run cemetery in Quebec is in Laval, about 250 kilometres away from Saint-Apollinaire. The matter gained broader attention after the deadly January shooting at the Quebec City mosque, which killed six men and wounded others during Sunday prayers. One of the victims was buried in Laval, while the others were returned to their countries of origin. Mohamed Kesri said ownership would ensure families have a burial place “for eternity.” Létourneau also raised concerns about long-term maintenance and the financial impact of tax breaks for religious groups. Jury selection begins Tuesday in Denver in the trial of James Holmes, the man accused of carrying out the 20 July 2012 mass shooting at a Colorado movie theatre that killed 12 people and wounded 70. The case will force a courtroom re-examination of one of the deadliest mass shootings in U.S. history and may offer a rare glimpse into the mind of a gunman who survived the attack. Holmes’ lawyers do not dispute that he was the shooter, but argue that he was suffering a psychotic episode at the time and should be found not guilty by reason of insanity. A jury pool of 9,000 people must be reduced to a small panel that will decide whether Holmes was legally insane when he opened fire during a midnight screening of a new Batman film in Aurora, a suburb of Denver. The case has provoked intense emotion. Holmes’ parents have urged a plea deal that could spare his life, while many survivors and relatives of victims want him tried and, if convicted, sentenced to death. Because many mass shooters are killed or die by suicide, Holmes’ survival has made the case unusually public and controversial. Holmes, then 24 and recently dropped out of a neuroscience PhD program at the University of Colorado Denver, was arrested in the theatre parking lot as he removed his combat gear. He has pleaded not guilty by reason of insanity to multiple murder and attempted murder charges. If convicted, jurors must then decide whether to recommend the death penalty; if acquitted on insanity grounds, he would be committed indefinitely to a state mental hospital. Colorado law says defendants are not responsible if their minds are so “diseased” they cannot tell right from wrong. The long delay in the case stems partly from disputes over Holmes’ mental state, much of which remains sealed under a gag order. Prosecutors and defense lawyers have also clashed over prior psychiatric evaluations and over an earlier plea offer.

He did not inform Superintendent Samuel Mijares until later that evening. After reviewing the note, Mijares concluded it was not an “imminent threat,” and he and Eagle Pass ISD Police Chief Cristino Ynosencio decided not to contact Eagle Pass Police Chief Amy Gonzalez. Mijares said they did not believe outside help was necessary. The next morning, September 23, Ynosencio assigned an investigator to examine the note. Officials determined there was no active shooter or immediate danger from that first message. Later, however, Leija informed Mijares that a second note had been found, this one containing a “kill list,” which was treated as an imminent threat. At about 8:47 a.m., the Eagle Pass ISD police chief received a call from a city police dispatcher asking whether there was an active shooter at Armando Cerna Elementary. Ynosencio again said outside assistance was not needed, stating the district had enough resources to protect students and staff. Meanwhile, Chief Gonzalez, unaware of the district’s internal investigation, said she began receiving 911 calls from worried parents at 8:59 a.m. about threats at the campus. An Eagle Pass police sergeant was sent to the school, where Principal Leija confirmed there was no active threat. Gonzalez later stressed the importance of cooperation between agencies and the community. Additional threats followed at other campuses. On September 29, a student at Juan N. Seguin Elementary warned classmates about a possible shooting and told them not to come to school. The student was identified and disciplined. On September 30, an eight-year-old student at Glass Elementary told a classmate on the bus that he planned to bring a gun the next day. Eagle Pass ISD police investigated, visited the child’s home, found no weapons, and disciplined the student after the parent called the remark a joke. In response, Eagle Pass ISD and the City of Eagle Pass held a meeting at City Hall on September 29 to improve coordination and establish procedures for handling school threats.

The fatal shooting of Green Bay native Alex Pretti by federal agents in Minneapolis has become a flashpoint not only in the political debate over immigration enforcement, but also among gun owners, many of whom say Trump administration officials distorted what happened and unfairly attacked lawful firearm possession. Pretti, 37, was a U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs nurse and concealed-carry license holder. During a protest against immigration enforcement operations in Minneapolis, he had a semi-automatic handgun concealed in a holster at the back of his waist. According to video described in the article, Pretti was tackled by agents, his gun was taken by one agent, and then he was shot by another. The footage indicates he did not draw his weapon before being taken down and was holding a cellphone at the time. After the shooting, Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem said, “I don't know of any peaceful protester that shows up with a gun and ammunition rather than a sign.” FBI Director Kash Patel said, “You cannot bring a firearm, loaded, with multiple magazines, to any sort of protest that you want. It's that simple.” President Donald Trump also weighed in on Jan. 27, saying, “You can't walk in with guns.” Those remarks drew immediate backlash from gun owners, trainers and advocacy groups in Wisconsin and beyond. Eddie Silas, a firearms instructor and co-owner of Prolific Arms in West Allis, argued that carrying a concealed weapon to a protest is not unusual for gun owners. He said many people do so for protection and pointed out that gun-rights activists have openly carried firearms at demonstrations, including a pro-Second Amendment rally in Virginia the week before, without similar criticism from the administration. Several gun trainers said the administration’s comments mischaracterized the Second Amendment and the legality of concealed carry, including at protests. Rob Pincus, who runs the Personal Defense Network in North Carolina, called it “criminal” for Noem, Patel and other officials to demonize what he described as defensive firearm ownership. Gun owners also objected to Noem’s suggestion that Pretti may have been planning to attack law enforcement because he had more than one magazine, noting that carrying a spare magazine is common. Silas said that if Pretti had intended to harm police, he could have drawn his gun at any point. “The facts — through my eyes, my lens, and no agendas involved — he was murdered, killed unjustly,” he said. The article also places the Minneapolis shooting in the context of the 2020 Kenosha unrest and the Kyle Rittenhouse case, which continues to fuel debate over armed civilians at protests. Social media users have compared Pretti’s death to the Kenosha shootings, where Rittenhouse, then 17, shot three people, killing two, during unrest after the police shooting of Jacob Blake. Rittenhouse was later acquitted. Attorney Kimberley Motley, who represents Gaige Grosskreutz, the man Rittenhouse wounded, said both Grosskreutz and Pretti were lawful gun owners. She argued that the central question often becomes not whether someone had a legal right to carry, but whether observers agree with that person’s politics or presence at the protest. Grosskreutz, a medic, had carried a concealed gun in Kenosha and pointed it at Rittenhouse before being shot; he and others have a pending lawsuit against Rittenhouse and Kenosha law enforcement. The episode has also revived long-standing doubts among some gun owners about Trump’s commitment to gun rights. Critics pointed to his 2018 remark after the Parkland school shooting that suggested taking guns first and sorting out due process later, as well as his ban on bump stocks after the 2017 Las Vegas massacre, a policy later struck down by the U.S. Supreme Court. Nik Clark, head of Wisconsin Carry, said gun rights activists are usually fighting Democrats over gun restrictions, and he found it ironic that Democrats were appearing more supportive of concealed-carry rights in this moment. Still, he said he does not trust Republicans either and described Noem, Patel and others in the administration as “country club gun owners” who support gun rights in theory but do not live like ordinary armed citizens. Clayton Schlosser, a gun trainer west of Minneapolis, called the administration’s statements a “backstab” to legal gun owners and said the rhetoric was especially jarring coming from what is supposed to be the nation’s most pro-Second Amendment administration. At the same time, some gun instructors said the situation should not be reduced solely to a gun-rights issue. Clark said it is legal to attend a peaceful protest armed, but he viewed the Minneapolis incident as involving interference with law enforcement and a highly dangerous proximity to officers. Pincus, however, focused blame on the federal agents, saying they appeared to escalate rather than calm the situation. He pointed to what he described as basic failures in Minneapolis and another shooting involving Renee Good, saying agents seemed irrational and confrontational. Pincus noted that one agent had earlier crossed the street and shoved a female protester who was yelling at him. He said that if an officer cannot handle verbal confrontation, “go home, call in sick.” He added that Pretti made a mistake by getting pulled into the confrontation and advised caution in Minneapolis, where he said immigration agents and protesters are creating an “incredibly volatile situation.”

Cartier has come under criticism after its website used a photograph of Yanomami children playing in a green field to promote the French luxury brand’s supposed support for the Amazon rainforest and the Indigenous people who live there. The image appeared on Cartier’s site until about two months before the article was published, alongside a description suggesting the company was helping protect Yanomami culture and the forest in their territory, which spans parts of Brazil and Venezuela. But the project described on the website never actually took place, and the photo was posted without the approval of Yanomami leadership, according to Indigenous representatives. Critics say the episode shows a contradiction: a gold jewelry company using the image of a people devastated by illegal gold mining. The Yanomami, who lived in near-total isolation until contact with outsiders in the 1970s, have long suffered from the impact of illegal mining in their territory. Thousands of miners have brought disease, violence, prostitution, drugs and alcohol into the region. Brazilian statistics cited in the article say 570 Yanomami children died from malnutrition, diarrhea and malaria between 2019 and 2022. The mercury used in illegal mining poisons people and ecosystems, and Indigenous leaders say the demand for gold itself fuels the invasions. Júnior Hekurari, a Yanomami member and head of the group’s health council, asked how a gold jewelry company could use the Yanomami image when the community opposes gold jewelry. Cartier says it does not buy illegally mined gold, but Yanomami leaders argue that even legal gold purchases help drive the market and encourage mining in Indigenous lands. Cartier and other jewelry brands owned by the Swiss conglomerate Richemont reported combined sales of 11 billion euros, or $11.7 billion, in the fiscal year ending March 31, 2022. Some Cartier pieces sold on its U.S. website were priced as high as $341,000. Cartier’s relationship with the Yanomami goes back around 20 years, mainly through Fondation Cartier, the company-funded philanthropic and arts foundation created in 1984. The foundation has supported exhibits featuring Yanomami photographs and Indigenous art, including a show in Manhattan and earlier in Paris. Those exhibits have been praised in the press as examples of Indigenous support through art sponsorship. But critics, including artists and some Yanomami, see a more self-serving motive, accusing Cartier of greenwashing: using philanthropy and cultural sponsorship to improve its brand image while benefiting from an industry tied to environmental destruction. One such critique comes from Barbara Navarro, a French multimedia artist, whose exhibit “Pas de Cartier” (“Not Cartier”) in Nemours, France, directly attacks the luxury brand’s relationship to gold and the damage caused by illegal mining. Her show includes sculptures, drawings and a photo montage placing a large Amazon gold mine beside a Cartier store. Navarro argues that the Yanomami are paying with their health and lives for society’s appetite for gold, and that Cartier’s support for Yanomami causes helps burnish its image. The use of the children’s photo on Cartier’s website also raised concerns about consent. The Roraima Indigenous Council said the image violated the Yanomami’s right to prior, free and informed consent, a principle recognized under International Labour Organization Convention 169, which Brazil has signed. Many Indigenous groups require formal permission before corporations or institutions use their images. Hekurari said his people need international cooperation, but would never accept money from a jewelry company. His organization, Urihi, has launched an online campaign against the gold trade, including a video in which he calls on Oscar winners to replace gold statuettes with wooden figures of Omama, a mythical entity in Yanomami tradition. In March, after the Associated Press contacted Cartier, the company removed the photo and the project description from its website. Cartier said the description was inaccurate and called it a “regrettable oversight” that was corrected once it was brought to its attention. The company also said the funds mentioned on the site had been allocated to a forest-preservation project but were instead used to buy medical equipment to fight COVID-19 among the Yanomami. Cartier said a donation of $74,200 was made in June 2020. Still, the controversy goes beyond one mistaken webpage, according to Indigenous leaders and advocates. Dário Kopenawa, vice-president of the Hutukara Yanomami Association, said anyone who buys a gold ring is participating in the crime. He distinguished between Cartier as a luxury brand and Fondation Cartier as a separate cultural branch, saying the foundation supports Yanomami protection even if the company itself buys gold around the world. Kopenawa has participated in Fondation Cartier-sponsored events, including a February exhibition in New York titled “Yanomami Struggle - Art and Activism in the Amazon,” where he appeared alongside Yanomami artists and UN Secretary-General António Guterres attended the opening. Fondation Cartier says it is run by an independent team of art professionals, and its leadership has openly acknowledged the corporate value of patronage. Its head, Alain Dominique Perrin, a former top executive at Richemont, once said that sponsorship benefits both artists and the company because the foundation receives praise from the press, media and social networks. Richemont itself wrote in a 1994 annual report that the foundation would become a focal point for managing Cartier’s image. The article also notes the role of French anthropologist Bruce Albert, who has worked with the Yanomami for decades and helped secure land demarcation in the 1990s. He connected Fondation Cartier with the Yanomami in 2003 and curated the first foundation-sponsored Yanomami art and photo exhibit that year. Albert later praised the foundation as independent, but criticized Cartier’s website use of the Yanomami children’s image and said the tribe had not granted permission. He also said Cartier was not funding any reforestation project. Cartier says most of the gold it acquires is recycled and that it follows standards set by the Responsible Jewelry Council. But the article emphasizes that tracing gold provenance is extremely difficult because illegal gold can enter global supply chains. For Yanomami leaders, that makes the issue not just one of sourcing, but of the broader harm caused by the gold trade itself. As lawyer Ivo Makuxi put it, the central questions are whether there is responsibility in buying this gold and whether the company truly respects Indigenous rights.

# Cartier's Controversial Use of Yanomami Images Sparks Accusations of Hypocrisy The French luxury jewelry brand Cartier has faced significant criticism for using images of the Yanomami Indigenous people in promotional materials while the tribe faces devastation from illegal gold mining—the very industry that produces the company's primary product. ## The Image and the Deception Until recently, Cartier's website featured photographs of Yanomami children playing in a green field. The company claimed it was working to promote Yanomami culture and protect the Amazon rainforest where approximately 40,000 Yanomami live across territories in Brazil and Venezuela. However, the project described on the website never actually took place, and Cartier published the photographs without obtaining approval from Yanomami leadership, violating the beliefs of a people who lived in near-total isolation until contact with outsiders in the 1970s. ## The Humanitarian Crisis The Yanomami have been devastated by the influx of thousands of illegal gold miners into their territory. Between 2019 and 2022, 570 Yanomami children died from malnutrition, diarrhea, and malaria. The illegal mining operations have brought disease, killing, prostitution, and widespread social destruction fueled by imported drugs and alcohol. Additionally, the poisonous mercury used in illegal mining causes birth defects and ecological damage. ## Accusations of Greenwashing While some Yanomami appreciate Cartier's promotion of their causes, many view the company's advertising as greenwashing—using support for a cause to improve corporate image while ignoring contradictions. Júnior Hekurari, a member of the Yanomami health council, posed a pointed question: "How can a gold jewelry company, which we, the Yanomami people, are against, use the image of the Yanomami?" Yanomami leaders have urged people to stop buying gold jewelry entirely, regardless of its source, because increased demand drives up gold prices and attracts miners to their territory. Cartier and other brands under the Swiss conglomerate Richemont generated combined sales of 11 billion euros in fiscal year 2022, with some pieces costing as much as $341,000. ## Corporate Sponsorship and Exhibits Cartier's relationship with the Yanomami dates back 20 years, primarily through Fondation Cartier, a corporate philanthropy created in 1984. Recently, the foundation sponsored an acclaimed exhibit displaying Yanomami photographs and Indigenous artwork at a Manhattan arts center. While outlets like The New York Times praised the exhibit, critics like French multimedia artist Barbara Navarro organized counter-exhibitions titled "Not Cartier," highlighting the contradiction between luxury brand sponsorship and the humanitarian crisis affecting the Yanomami. ## Permission and Consent Issues The Roraima Indigenous Council argued that using the children's photograph violated the Yanomami's right to prior, free, and informed consent under the International Labour Organization's Convention 169 on Indigenous and Tribal Peoples, which Brazil has signed. ## Cartier's Response After being contacted by the Associated Press in late March, Cartier removed the photograph and project description from its website. The company explained that funds allocated for a forest-preservation project were instead used to acquire medical equipment to fight COVID-19 among the Yanomami, with a donation of $74,200 made in June 2020. Cartier called the inaccurate website description "a regrettable oversight" that was addressed immediately. ## The Broader Debate The controversy extends beyond the website incident. Dário Kopenawa, vice-president of the Hutukara Yanomami Association, stated that "anyone who buys a gold ring is part of the crime." However, some Yanomami leaders distinguish between Cartier the jewelry company and Fondation Cartier, viewing the foundation as genuinely supportive of Yanomami protection despite their concerns about the parent company's gold business. Cartier claims to purchase the vast majority of its gold recycled and conforms to Responsible Jewelry Council standards. However, proving gold's provenance is nearly impossible, as illegal material regularly seeps into global supply chains. Yanomami leaders maintain that gold demand itself—regardless of source—is the root cause of their suffering. The controversy raises fundamental questions about corporate responsibility and Indigenous rights in the luxury goods industry.

Medellin, Colombia, long known around the world as the home base of Pablo Escobar and the Medellin Cartel, is being reimagined by a growing number of American retirees as a livable, affordable, and even welcoming place to settle. The article centers on Cindy Crawford Thomas and her husband, David, former South Florida residents who moved to Medellin to retire after deciding that life in Florida had become too hectic and isolating. In Medellin, they say they have found a friendlier community, lower costs, good weather, and health care that they consider superior to what they had in the United States. The Thomases are part of a broader trend of foreigners, especially retirees, choosing Colombia’s second-largest city as a destination. A key indicator of that trend is data from the U.S. Social Security Administration, which sent 6,704 retirement checks to Colombia in 2017, an 85 percent increase from 2010. While that number does not capture everyone who has retired there, it reflects Medellin’s rising profile among expats. The city has also gained attention in retirement magazines and on television programs such as “House Hunters International.” That popularity is striking given Medellin’s violent history. For decades, it was synonymous with bombs, assassinations, and cartel warfare. In the 1990s, it was considered a no-go zone and at one point had the highest murder rate in the world, peaking in 1995 at 225 homicides per 100,000 residents. But the city has changed dramatically. Its homicide rate is now about 20 per 100,000, much lower than several major U.S. cities including St. Louis, Baltimore, New Orleans, and Detroit. Officials say improved safety has helped bring in more visitors and new residents. In 2017, Medellin welcomed more than 735,000 foreign visitors, a 5 percent increase from the previous year. Juliana Cardona Quiros, Medellin’s undersecretary of tourism, said that while younger digital nomads are visible in the city’s cafes, older people are also discovering its appeal. She pointed to Medellin’s springlike climate, public transportation, and mix of urban life and nature as major draws. Still, the city’s image remains complicated by pop-culture portrayals such as Netflix’s “Narcos” and Colombia’s “El Patron del Mal,” which focus heavily on the city’s violent past and can reinforce old stereotypes. For some retirees, those stereotypes initially made Medellin seem unthinkable. Nancy Kiernan, a 59-year-old health care executive from Maine, recalled meeting someone years earlier who praised the city and thinking he must be foolish. But after moving there nearly six years ago, she found that the city was increasingly attracting expats, including retirees who had previously settled in Ecuador and Panama. She joked that in some neighborhoods there are now so many foreigners that “you can’t spit without hitting a gringo.” The Thomases’ own path to Medellin included a stop in Boquete, Panama, where they had lived for five years. They liked Boquete’s small-town charm and weather, but eventually found it too quiet. Cindy Thomas said she wanted something less boring, so they decided to try Medellin. They moved there just six weeks before the article was written. In their new city, they rent a three-bedroom, 4.5-bath apartment shared with their three dogs and three cats for about $1,400 a month. They say their total monthly spending, including gym memberships and eating out often, is well under $3,000. Affordability is a major part of Medellin’s appeal. Kiernan said many people can live comfortably there for under $2,000 a month. She described the city as a place with a good balance of cost, climate, infrastructure, and quality of life. Medellin also benefits from an international airport that gives it quick access to the U.S. East Coast. Health care is another major selling point. A 2017 survey by América Economía found that Medellin had seven of the top 49 hospitals in Latin America. Permanent residents can buy into the state-run health system for as little as $30 a month. He said those experiences changed people’s perceptions of the city. At the same time, the article emphasizes that Medellin is not an ideal destination for everyone. Brad Hinkelman, founder of the property development company Casacol, said the media often oversells the city by portraying it either as a deadly drug haven or as “the Paris of Latin America.” He said some prospective retirees arrive with unrealistic expectations, imagining they can live lavishly on Social Security alone, and need to be reminded of the practical realities. Colombia also continues to face serious problems, including its status as the world’s top cocaine producer, ongoing conflict with leftist guerrillas, and frequent political assassinations. Even with those issues, Colombia ranked No. 6 on International Living’s 2018 list of best places to retire. Kiernan, who writes for the publication, said the country is still considered an emerging destination, which means it does not yet offer the dense expat networks or English-language services found in more established retirement hubs. Most newcomers need at least some Spanish to get by. The article closes by contrasting Medellin’s reputation with events in the United States that have made some retirees rethink where they feel safe. The Thomases, both former teachers in Broward County, mentioned the Parkland school shooting near where they once worked and the deaths at a Florida nursing home after Hurricane Irma. Against that backdrop, Cindy Thomas said she cannot imagine moving back to Florida. She and her husband are already thinking about other countries, including Peru, Spain, and Portugal. “The world is open,” she said. “There’s no sense in staying in one place.”

The article is an opinion piece reacting to the May 2022 mass shooting in Buffalo, New York, in which 18-year-old Payton Gendron drove from Conklin to a supermarket in a predominantly African-American, low-income neighborhood and opened fire on shoppers and employees. The attack killed at least 10 people and injured three others; 11 of the 13 victims were Black. Gendron also livestreamed the massacre on Twitch, intensifying the horror and public outrage. Buffalo Mayor Byron Brown described the event as the “worst nightmare” a community could face, while President Joe Biden called for unity against racial hatred and condemned violence fueled by the belief that one group is inherently inferior to another. The article links the shooting to what it describes as the “Great Replacement Theory,” the idea that immigrants and people of color are replacing white Americans. It says this belief has been spread and magnified by media, the internet, political commentators, and politicians, causing some alienated individuals to become radicalized and violent. In the article’s telling, the Buffalo attack is not an isolated event but one of many hate crimes that reflect deeper problems in American society. From there, the piece broadens into a critique of the United States as a “critical society.” It argues that Americans are trained from an early age to be highly critical, especially through education that emphasizes critical thinking, writing, and analysis. According to the author, this habit extends beyond schools into books, movies, television, newspapers, fashion, and public culture, where criticism is portrayed as constant and pervasive. However, the article says this critical mindset is not balanced by constructive force, respect for tradition, or appreciation for the classics. Instead, it claims, American culture tends to tear down the past and treat nearly everything as flawed or suspect. The article also criticizes higher education, saying universities have become places that promote radical critical thinking rather than preserve classical learning. It presents non-technical academic fields as especially problematic, describing them in highly dismissive terms. In the author’s view, this has produced a polarized and destructive intellectual environment that makes the United States more hateful and despairing. A central theme of the piece is that in an overly critical society, people can no longer see what is positive or stable. If everything is open to criticism, the article argues, then everything appears problematic and imperfect. It claims that in such an atmosphere, no one is seen as normal and everyone can be turned into a target of suspicion or condemnation. The result, the article says, is not healthy debate but hopelessness. It suggests that young people like Payton Gendron are products of this environment—lost, despairing individuals shaped by a society that leaves them with no constructive direction. The article also blames the internet and political culture for amplifying anger and disappointment. It says modern information flows make hatred easier to spread and harder to manage, and it accuses politicians of constantly exposing, creating, and magnifying the flaws of their opponents. In this account, political conflict reinforces a broader national mood of resentment and despair. Toward the end, the piece contrasts the United States with China, claiming that Chinese academia has at least one think tank capable of combining critical and empirical analysis. It argues that technology alone cannot solve the problem of excessive criticism, because technology can clarify issues but can also create new ones. The article concludes that the only way for the United States to help people “see the light” is for society itself to change and move away from being an overly critical society.

Pupy, a 35-year-old African elephant, has arrived safely at a sanctuary in Mato Grosso, Brazil, after a 2,700-kilometer overland trip from Buenos Aires, Argentina, where she had lived for 30 years in a zoo later converted into an ecological park. Buenos Aires city officials said she reached Elephant Sanctuary Brazil in “perfect health” after a five-day journey and did not need sedation. Pupy was transported in a large iron crate strapped to a truck and accompanied by vans carrying caretakers and veterinarians. She had been trained for the move over several months. The sanctuary, located in Chapadas dos Guimarães in Brazil’s Amazon region, is the first elephant refuge in Latin America. When the veterinary team opened the crate door, Pupy was initially reluctant to step out. To help her settle, caregivers offered her sugarcane and watermelon, one of her favorite foods, and gave her a bath to cool her off. Officials said she will stay in an outdoor shed at first while she gradually adjusts to her new surroundings, with the process guided by her own pace. Buenos Aires began transforming its century-old zoo in the Palermo neighborhood into an ecological park in 2016, with the stated goal of preserving biodiversity and conserving native species. Since then, more than 1,000 animals, including lions, tigers, bears and apes, have been relocated to better conditions in other countries. One well-known example was Sandra, an orangutan now living at a great ape center in Florida. Pupy arrived at the Palermo zoo in 1993 and was the last elephant remaining in the Buenos Aires Ecopark. She joins five Asian elephants already living at the Brazilian sanctuary, including Mara, a former circus elephant who made a similar journey five years ago and now walks at least 10 kilometers a day. Officials said Pupy will not be housed with Mara because the sanctuary keeps the species separate in accordance with their biological and behavioral needs. The Buenos Aires Ecopark will continue to care for animals that cannot be moved because of age or logistical limits.

# Libya: 16 Civilians Killed in Derna Airstrikes On October 30, 2017, unidentified aircraft conducted airstrikes on several locations in Derna, Libya's eastern city, resulting in the deaths of 16 civilians and critical injuries to four children. According to medical sources, the majority of victims were members of the same extended family, with 12 of the 16 deceased being children ranging in age from 2 to 16 years old. Notably, no fighters were reported killed or injured in the attack. The Libyan National Army (LNA), which has previously conducted airstrikes on Derna, denied responsibility through a televised statement, instead blaming "terrorists" and pledging to investigate. The DMSC, which opposes the LNA, took control of the city after helping to oust the extremist group ISIS in April 2016. The militant alliance continues to resist the LNA's efforts to reclaim the city. ## Details of the Attack Dr. Mansour Ben Fayed, director of Derna's main hospital, reported that the October 30 airstrikes targeted two distinct locations: the al-Fatayeh neighborhood and the rural al-Arqam area. The first strike hit a family farm in al-Fatayeh shortly after 7 p.m., coinciding with the call for Isha prayers. Thirteen of the 16 victims were brought to the main hospital, all women and children who had been attending an event at a private house. The remaining three victims died in their home in al-Arqam and were buried without hospital treatment due to the LNA's siege restricting vehicle access to that area. Ambulance driver Moncef al-Bazouti described the horrific scene, explaining that as emergency responders arrived at al-Fatayeh to collect bodies, a second strike hit the same area, damaging his ambulance. The victims were extracted from collapsed rubble, with some bodies charred, others suffering severed limbs and heads, and severe facial injuries. The youngest victim was only three years old, while one injured child was merely three months old. A second series of airstrikes struck the city's western entrance between midnight and 1 a.m., damaging a building but causing no reported casualties. ## Pattern of Previous Incidents This attack is not an isolated incident. Previous airstrikes on Derna have gone uninvestigated, according to Human Rights Watch. In February 2015, joint Libyan and Egyptian airstrikes killed at least seven civilians and damaged civilian structures. In February 2016, unidentified aircraft attacked a hospital, killing at least two civilians and causing extensive damage. In May 2017, the Egyptian air force reportedly conducted retaliatory strikes following the killing of 28 Egyptian Christian Copts, though no civilian casualties were reported from those operations. ## Broader Conflict Context Libya's conflict since 2014 has resulted in two rival governments claiming legitimacy. The United Nations-backed Government of National Accord controls western Libya and Tripoli, while the Interim Government controls eastern regions except Derna, along with southern areas. The LNA's siege has severely restricted humanitarian access, causing shortages of medical supplies and medications while limiting civilian movement. ## Legal Implications Under international humanitarian law, all attacks must target military objectives, and deliberate, indiscriminate, or disproportionate attacks against civilians are prohibited. Warring parties must take feasible precautions to minimize civilian harm and allow unimpeded humanitarian aid passage. Serious violations constitute war crimes subject to prosecution by domestic courts or the International Criminal Court, which has jurisdiction over crimes committed in Libya since February 2011 under UN Security Council Resolution 1970. Human Rights Watch emphasized that warring factions should impartially investigate possible war crimes, noting that too many civilian wartime deaths have been ignored without accountability.

Rwanda has made striking gains 20 years after the 1994 genocide, even as questions remain about the government’s political direction and the limits of international efforts to prevent mass atrocities elsewhere. In villages across Rwanda’s steep green hills, some of the people who took part in the killing of their neighbors now live beside relatives of the dead. Speech that stokes ethnic division has been banned, and local gacaca courts have helped reduce prison populations by allowing many offenders to win release in exchange for confessions and remorse. A younger generation, born after the massacres, has grown up identifying more as Rwandan than as Hutu or Tutsi. The genocide was one of the worst crimes of the 20th century. More than 800,000 Tutsis and moderate Hutus were slaughtered by Hutu extremists over roughly 100 days, and some estimates place the death toll at as many as one million. The violence began on April 7, 1994, after a plane carrying Rwandan President Juvenal Habyarimana and Burundian President Cyprien Ntaryamira was shot down near Kigali. The cause of the attack remains disputed. Kagame’s government says Hutu extremists in Habyarimana’s own military assassinated him to create a pretext for exterminating Tutsis. Kagame’s Rwandan Patriotic Front had already invaded from Uganda in 1990, and after nearly three years of civil war, the Arusha accords had established a peace deal and power-sharing plan. The plane crash destroyed that agreement and unleashed the killings. The violence was carried out with horrifying brutality. Radio broadcasters called Tutsis “cockroaches” who should be exterminated. Neighbors killed neighbors, entire families were wiped out, and many victims were murdered in Roman Catholic churches where they had sought refuge. Several Catholic clergy members later were convicted as perpetrators. The United Nations Assistance Mission for Rwanda, sent to support the peace deal, failed to stop the slaughter, saying its mandate was too limited. Western governments also did not intervene. Former President Bill Clinton later apologized, saying as many as 300,000 lives might have been saved if the United States had acted. Kagame’s forces eventually won the war after three months, taking Kigali and driving the Rwandan army and government-backed militias from power. But some perpetrators fled to eastern Congo, where the Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda continues to operate and conduct cross-border raids. Rwanda itself has been accused of backing rebel forces in Congo, including M23, which has been accused of atrocities and using child soldiers. Rwanda has denied the allegations, though the United States froze military aid in 2012 over Kigali’s support for the group. Despite the unresolved regional tensions, Rwanda’s domestic progress has been impressive. Life expectancy has more than doubled since 1994 to over 60 years. The economy has grown at about 8% a year. Child mortality has fallen sharply, from 230 deaths per 1,000 children under age 5 to 55. The government spends heavily on health and education, and the country is ranked by the World Bank as one of the easiest places to do business in Africa. Rwanda is also self-sufficient in staple crops despite being Africa’s most densely populated country, and acute malnutrition among young children is relatively low. Kagame argues that education, poverty reduction, and hard work are the best safeguards against a return to violence. He portrays external criticism as a form of Western control and says Rwanda must rely primarily on its own efforts. His government has also attracted criticism from human rights advocates, who say his rule is becoming increasingly authoritarian. Still, Rwanda’s order, cleanliness, and economic momentum have made it a model for some observers, even as the country’s experience stands in contrast to the failures of the international community in places such as the Central African Republic, South Sudan, and the Democratic Republic of Congo.

# Rwanda's Remarkable Recovery Two Decades After Genocide Twenty years after the 1994 genocide that claimed over 800,000 lives, Rwanda has achieved remarkable progress in rebuilding its society and economy, though challenges and criticisms remain. ## The Genocide and Its Aftermath The Rwandan genocide began on April 7, 1994, when a plane carrying President Juvenal Habyarimana was shot down, triggering a hundred-day massacre orchestrated by Hutu extremists against Tutsis and moderate Hutus. Radio hosts incited violence by calling Tutsis "cockroaches," and neighbors killed neighbors in churches and villages. The United Nations peacekeeping mission failed to intervene, and Western powers did not act—a failure for which President Clinton later apologized, acknowledging that 300,000 lives could have been saved with U.S. intervention. The killing stopped only when President Paul Kagame's Rwandan Patriotic Front military forces reached Kigali after three months of fighting. ## Remarkable Economic and Social Progress Rwanda's recovery has been stunning. Life expectancy has doubled from 30 to over 60 years. The country maintains consistent 8% annual economic growth and has significantly reduced child mortality, dropping deaths of children under five from 230 per 1,000 to 55 per 1,000. The government prioritizes development, spending 25% of its budget on health and 17% on education. Rwanda is now ranked by the World Bank as one of Africa's easiest places to do business. Despite being Africa's most densely populated nation with 11 million people, it is self-sufficient in staple crops and maintains low malnutrition rates of 3.6% among young children. ## Reconciliation Efforts Rwanda has implemented innovative reconciliation mechanisms. Speech creating ethnic divisions has been outlawed. Local gacaca courts have allowed many perpetrators to be released from prison in exchange for confessions and expressions of remorse. A new generation of young Rwandans who grew up after the genocide identifies by nationality rather than ethnicity, embodying hope for the nation's future. Survivors and perpetrators now live side by side in villages across the country. ## International Context and Criticism Rwanda's progress contrasts sharply with the international community's failures elsewhere. Following the Rwanda and Yugoslav tragedies, the world established the International Criminal Court in 2002 and adopted the "responsibility to protect" doctrine in 2005. However, recent crises demonstrate these commitments remain inconsistent. The Central African Republic has experienced ongoing sectarian killings without adequate international response, while UN peacekeepers in the Democratic Republic of Congo and South Sudan have had mixed success preventing atrocities. ## Political Tensions and Controversies President Kagame has drawn criticism from human rights advocates for increasingly authoritarian governance. He views such criticism as Western attempts to control Africa, framing human rights lectures as perpetuations of colonial-era predatory relationships. The U.S. froze military aid to Rwanda in 2012 over its support for M23 rebels in eastern Congo, accused of using child soldiers and committing atrocities—charges Rwanda denies. ## Kagame's Vision Forward Kagame emphasizes that improved education and poverty reduction are the most effective violence prevention measures. He frequently exhorts citizens to work hard, remember the genocide, and move forward, promoting Rwandan self-reliance and democracy. Mandatory Saturday community cleanups have made Rwanda notably clean and orderly, though critics note their somewhat authoritarian character. Kagame insists that external assistance should supplement, not replace, Rwandan efforts. His philosophy—"if we wait for others to develop our country, we will not make progress"—guides national policy and reflects Rwanda's determination to chart its own course forward while building on the remarkable progress achieved since the devastating genocide of 1994.

# Summary: Nigeria's Insecurity Crisis Rooted in Weak Statehood A US military strike on Christmas Day targeting Islamic State militants in northwest Nigeria has failed to resolve the country's escalating security crisis, highlighting that military solutions alone cannot address such complex problems. While President Trump framed the operation as combating "Christian genocide," analysts dispute this characterization. Nigeria faces multifaceted security challenges: jihadist insurgencies in the northeast, separatist tensions in the southeast, herder-farmer conflicts in central regions, and criminal gang violence in the northwest. The underlying issue connecting all these crises is the fundamental weakness of Nigeria's security architecture and administrative systems. Early warning mechanisms are inadequate, community liaison efforts are minimal, and the police and judicial systems are deeply flawed and distrusted. This institutional failure drives citizens toward alternative protection sources, including vigilantes and criminal organizations. The military, despite containing capable personnel, suffers from poor command structure, low morale, reactive strategies, and weak intelligence analysis—exemplified by intelligence officers in the northeast who don't speak local languages like Hausa or Kanuri. However, improved security responses alone cannot solve Nigeria's problems. The fundamental issue is the breakdown of the social contract between the state and its citizens. The Nigerian state must work harder to earn public legitimacy and allegiance. In the northeast, ISWAP—the largest jihadist group—exploits state failure by positioning itself as an alternative to the Nigerian government. Unlike its brutal rival Boko Haram, ISWAP employs public relations campaigns emphasizing social justice and offers basic services to those joining its caliphate, contrasting sharply with the corruption and exploitation most Nigerians experience. The northwest exemplifies state collapse, with bandit gangs controlling entire districts and extorting communities. Paradoxically, some gangs' core grievance stems from state authorities' failure to fairly mediate communal tensions between politically connected farmers and pastoralist communities. Rather than addressing root causes, state governments have appeased bandits through stipends and amnesties—a counterproductive approach that encourages further violence while ignoring victims' suffering. The solution requires Nigerian authorities to tackle underlying conditions creating insecurity by more effectively serving their populations, though implementing such reforms remains challenging.

A Sudanese court on Saturday accepted corruption-related charges against ousted former President Omar al-Bashir, who appeared in court in a cage for the third time this month. Al-Bashir, who was removed by the military in April after months of mass protests against his 30-year authoritarian rule, remains in custody. The court said it would reconvene in a week. After hearing al-Bashir’s statement and testimony from other witnesses, the court agreed to proceed on prosecutors’ allegations that he illegally possessed foreign currency. He is also accused of money laundering after millions of dollars, euros, and Sudanese pounds were seized from his home shortly after his fall from power. During the hearing, al-Bashir said he had received $25 million through his office manager from Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman. He claimed the money was intended as donations and not for his personal use, saying the source was meant to remain undisclosed and that depositing it in the central bank would have exposed where it came from. He said some of the funds went to a military hospital, a Sudanese university, and the Rapid Support Forces, a paramilitary group led by Gen. Mohammed Hamdan Dagalo, also known as Hemedti, who sits on the new Sovereign Council. Al-Bashir provided no documents to support his account. The court rejected his lawyers’ request for bail. If convicted on the corruption charge, he could face up to 10 years in prison. This case is separate from charges over the killing of protesters during the uprising that helped topple him. Al-Bashir also remains wanted by the International Criminal Court for war crimes and genocide linked to the Darfur conflict, though Sudan’s military says it will not extradite him.

Chinese wartime thriller *Dead to Rights* is dominating the domestic box office as China intensifies its nationwide campaign to commemorate 80 years since the end of World War II. Since its July 25 release, the film has earned 1.5 billion yuan (about US$208 million), according to state broadcaster CCTV citing Maoyan ticketing data. Set during the 1937 Nanjing Massacre, it follows civilians hiding in a photo studio who discover disturbing images of atrocities while developing photos for Japanese troops, and then risk their lives to keep the evidence. The film has been strongly received by Chinese audiences, scoring 9.7 on Maoyan and 8.6 on Douban. Viewers praised its emotional impact and its use of personal stories to reflect broader history. *Dead to Rights* has already opened in Macau, is due in Hong Kong this month, and is also scheduled for release in Australia, New Zealand, the United States, Malaysia and Singapore.

The Cambodia International Film Festival (CIFF) will return for its 11th edition from June 28 to July 3 after being canceled for the previous two years because of the Covid-19 pandemic. Organizers say the festival’s comeback is meant to symbolize the recovery and “rebirth” of Cambodia’s film sector after a period in which cultural life and the cinema industry were badly disrupted. The festival’s poster features an original painting, Just Born, by Battambang-based artist Khchao Touch. The artwork is intended to represent the revival of the film industry in Cambodia after two difficult years in which the pandemic “shattered” much of the sector. CIFF director Cedric Eloy said at a press conference on May 25 at Rosewood Phnom Penh that the last two years had been hard on the creative sector, artists and cultural organizations, and that the festival wanted to acknowledge those losses while encouraging greater support. Organized by the Cambodia Film Commission and the Bophana Audiovisual Resource Centre, with support from the Ministry of Culture and Fine Arts, this year’s festival will screen 140 films from more than 40 countries across six continents. The program includes feature films, short films, documentaries and animated works. The festival website says there will be more than 160 screenings of over 130 films at 10 venues in Phnom Penh. The full schedule will be released later. CIFF was launched in 2010 as a way to help develop Cambodia’s film industry and has since become one of the country’s largest international cultural events. Eloy said the festival began 12 years ago at a time when the local film industry was still very small, with Bophana Centre the only film organization and the Cambodia Film Commission just newly created. Since then, CIFF has drawn more than 20,000 attendees and has served as a bridge between Cambodia and the wider world by presenting Cambodian films alongside international works and helping local productions circulate regionally and beyond. Eloy said the festival has played an important role in showing the progress of the industry and in developing film education. In his view, it has helped inspire the opening of modern cinemas and encouraged hundreds of young Cambodians to become involved in filmmaking. He also said it has had a direct impact on attracting foreign films to Cambodia. The festival has regularly brought notable films and guests from Cambodia and abroad, with an emphasis on diverse cinema, innovative filmmaking in different formats and high-quality productions made in and about Cambodia by both local and international filmmakers. Since 2015, CIFF has also included a special environmental and climate-action film selection, and that focus will continue this year. The festival stresses that it has secured permission or rights for all of the films it shows, noting that copyright has historically been a concern in Cambodia but that CIFF fully respects film rights. This year, audiences in Phnom Penh will again be able to attend screenings free of charge. Venues include Legend Cinemas, Major Cineplex at Aeon 1 and Sorya, the French Institute, Bophana Centre, Chaktomuk Conference Hall, Rosewood Phnom Penh, Java Creative, and Factory Phnom Penh. Eloy said the festival had been growing in popularity before the pandemic and now, as it restarts, it will need additional backing to continue expanding. He said organizers are seeking more sponsors from both the private and non-profit sectors, alongside support already received from UNESCO and the Australian embassy, as well as cooperation from the ministries of tourism, information and education. He described CIFF as difficult to organize but said it would not have been possible without the support, love and advice of the festival team, partners and friends. The Bophana Centre said this year’s edition will also place special emphasis on Australian cinema to mark the 70th anniversary of diplomatic relations between Australia and Cambodia. At the press conference, Bophana Centre director Sopheap Chea traced cinema culture in Cambodia back to the 1940s and 1950s, when it began taking root in society, and said it became an important part of modern Cambodian culture in the 1960s and early 1970s before being destroyed under the Khmer Rouge’s “Year Zero” policy, which sought to erase existing culture and civilization and led to genocide. He said cinema was devastated during that era, but young people have since rediscovered filmmaking as a form of expression. Sopheap added that Covid-19 had caused major damage to cinema and cultural activity in Cambodia and around the world, with cinemas and cultural venues in Cambodia closed or restricted for almost two years. He said organizers were excited to bring back the country’s biggest film event. The article also notes the broader recovery of Cambodia’s cinema sector. After conditions improved, movie theaters were allowed to operate at 50 percent capacity in March 2022 under stricter health measures, following a two-year closure. Pok Borak, director of the Ministry of Culture and Fine Arts’ Cinema and Cultural Diffusion Department, said this was the result of the government’s efforts to control the virus and the fact that Cambodia had reached periods with zero new infections. He said the government, through the culture ministry, had tried to support the film industry during the crisis by suspending tax obligations, exempting monthly taxes for three months, and providing salary allowances for cinema staff over the past two years. In early May, the culture ministry asked national leaders to allow cinemas to operate at full capacity, and this was approved after a long stretch of very low or zero infections. Borak said he was pleased that CIFF was returning and hoped the festival would help revive the spirit of Cambodia’s film industry. The complete program for the 11th CIFF will be announced later in June, with more information available through the festival’s Facebook page and website.

Australia’s most populous state has reversed its decision to ban greyhound racing, with New South Wales Premier Mike Baird saying the government “got it wrong” after heavy public, political and industry pressure. In July, Baird had announced the sport would be shut down from July 1 next year following a series of scandals, including live baiting and the slaughter of tens of thousands of dogs. The move was widely criticized as a rushed response and raised fears that regional communities dependent on the industry would be badly hurt. On Tuesday, Baird said he had listened to feedback and that the greyhound industry would be given “one last chance” to reform. He said the government would impose the toughest possible animal welfare standards and create a new regulatory body to oversee the sport. “We are not returning to the status quo,” he said, stressing that “barbaric practices” must end. The reversal comes after Australia’s greyhound industry was rocked by revelations from the national broadcaster ABC that live animals — including piglets, rabbits and possums — had been used as bait in training. Subsequent raids across New South Wales, Victoria and Queensland followed, and a New South Wales inquiry found widespread live baiting, the mass killing of dogs deemed too slow, and systematic deception about deaths and injuries in races, including skull fractures and broken backs. Greyhound racing remains a major industry in Australia, but no other state had proposed a ban as sweeping as New South Wales’ original plan.

India’s government is facing accusations that it is using bulldozers to destroy Muslim-owned properties as a form of collective punishment after communal violence. In New Delhi’s Jehangirpuri suburb, Haneefa, a 38-year-old barbecue shop owner, said she was working when bulldozers suddenly arrived and demolished her shop, along with several other stalls, kiosks, and part of a mosque. She said the authorities gave no notice. Her livelihood was destroyed, and she lost her cooking stove and skewers. The demolition was broadcast live by Indian media and defended by the government as an operation against “illegal encroachments,” but local residents and critics saw it as part of a broader campaign targeting Muslims. Similar “anti-encroachment” drives have been carried out in recent weeks in New Delhi and in the BJP-ruled states of Madhya Pradesh and Gujarat, where dozens of Muslim properties were razed. These actions followed outbreaks of Hindu-Muslim violence during Hindu festivals. In several cities, processions of Hindu devotees reportedly marched through Muslim neighborhoods carrying sticks and knives, playing provocative music, and shouting anti-Muslim slogans. In one account, Dilshad, a 25-year-old factory worker, said the violence began during iftar time, when a mob entered his neighborhood shouting abuse and then clashes broke out, with both sides throwing stones. Critics of India’s ruling Bharatiya Janata Party say the demolitions are part of a wider pattern of hostility toward Muslims, who make up about 14 percent of the population. Pawan Khera of the opposition Indian National Congress said the aim has long been to normalize hatred by demonizing a community. The BJP-led state governments, however, blamed Muslims for the unrest and defended the demolitions. Madhya Pradesh home minister Narottam Mishra said that if Muslims carried out attacks, they should not expect justice, and he warned that homes from which stones were thrown would be turned into rubble. In Madhya Pradesh alone, at least 45 Muslim properties were demolished. Opposition figures and activists described the bulldozer operations as arbitrary and punitive, especially in areas already experiencing communal tension. Krishnan of CPIML Liberation argued that bringing bulldozers into such neighborhoods only deepens conflict and amounts to extrajudicial punishment. The article places these demolitions in the context of a broader rise in attacks, hate speech, and discrimination against Muslims since Narendra Modi and the BJP came to power in 2014. It cites controversial laws seen as anti-Muslim, lynchings over accusations involving cows, arrests tied to the “love jihad” conspiracy theory, calls by Hindu religious leaders for violence against Muslims, and the recent banning of Muslim girls wearing hijabs from classrooms in Karnataka, a decision upheld by courts. Some experts have gone further, warning of the possibility of genocide. Gregory Stanton of Genocide Watch said in a U.S. congressional briefing that genocide could “very well happen” in India. Muslim researcher Maaz Rashid said even the judiciary appeared indifferent, and warned that state institutions seemed complicit in violence against Muslims.
