Krismon, an orangutan once kept as a family pet in North Sumatra, is now a symbol of Indonesia’s illegal orangutan trade and the damage it has done to the species. The article begins in Kabanjahe, where 55-year-old Zulbaidah recalls how her family used to treat the orangutan almost like a child. When Krismon was young, he rode in the back of the family car on road trips and played with the children. Zulbaidah said, “He was like my own son.” But as he grew older, stronger, and harder to control, the family kept him in a cage, eventually locking him away so long that by the time authorities seized him in June 2016, he was so weak and immobile that his legs had wasted away and he could no longer stand. Krismon, estimated to be about 20 years old when confiscated, is now at a rehabilitation center near Medan, the capital of North Sumatra. There, he is relearning basic movement and climbing, but caretakers say he has been in captivity so long that he no longer has the skills needed to survive in the wild. Zulbaidah said the family had not understood how large he would become. The man who gave the baby orangutan to her husband had told them he would stay small forever. His case is presented as one example of a broader black-market trade in orangutans that has brought the species close to extinction. Baby orangutans are highly prized because they are cute and can confer status on their owners. But obtaining them usually involves a brutal process: poachers often kill the mother to take the infant. The trade is intensified by deforestation, which destroys orangutans’ forest habitat and forces them into contact with people. Indonesia has lost more rainforest than any other country since the start of the century, largely because of the expansion of plantations, especially for palm oil, which is used in products ranging from ice cream to laundry detergent. As forests disappear, orangutans wander into farmland and conflict with farmers, who may use pellet guns to protect crops. Orphaned animals can then be captured and sold through trafficking networks that operate across Indonesia and beyond. The article notes that orangutans have appeared in tourist attractions in Thailand, where they have been dressed up and forced to perform, and that in the late 1980s more than 1,000 orangutans were illegally imported into Taiwan after a TV character made the animals fashionable there. Indonesia’s laws formally protect orangutans, with a maximum penalty of five years in prison for anyone who transports, sells, keeps, or kills them. Both Sumatran and Bornean orangutans are listed as Critically Endangered. Yet enforcement is weak. According to the Orangutan Information Center (OIC), since 2012 it has helped authorities confiscate 114 orangutans, including 39 kept as pets. But no one has been prosecuted simply for owning one as a pet. Conservationists say the reason is that many owners are wealthy or influential figures — soldiers, politicians, police officers, or other powerful people who can keep such animals and avoid consequences. OIC founder Panut Hadisiswoyo describes repeated encounters with people who know the law but ignore it. He recounts trying to recover an orangutan from a high-ranking police officer in Aceh, where the species mainly lives. The officer brushed him off, saying, “Don’t teach me about the law — the law is in my head.” In another case, the OIC found a baby orangutan on display in a park in Aceh and discovered it belonged to the city’s mayor, who surrendered it. The group also helped seize two orangutans from a former commander of Aceh’s separatist GAM movement. Although that man said he had bought the animals to save them from villagers, police let him go, only for the OIC to later discover he was preparing to send five more orangutans by bus to a buyer in Medan. The animals were recovered, but the man remains free. Hadisiswoyo argues that both traders and owners are criminals, while stressing that rescued orangutans are only the lucky ones. Krismon’s own history helps explain how the trade works and how ordinary pet ownership can lead to animal suffering. According to Zulbaidah, her late husband, who ran a military base, received Krismon as a baby in 1998 while stationed near the Leuser Ecosystem, one of Indonesia’s richest rainforests. That year was marked by turmoil in Aceh and by the Asian financial crisis, known in Indonesia as Krisis Moneter. The family named the ape Krismon in memory of the crisis. The children grew up with him, watching television with him and playing with him in the living room. He made a laughing sound, described as “hhk hhk hhk.” Because of their military connections, the family felt safe taking him on trips, even across provincial lines. But as Krismon matured, he became harder to manage. His teeth sharpened, his body enlarged, and he sometimes became aggressive. Zulbaidah let him wander outside, where neighbors fed him cakes, but when he misbehaved she locked him in a chicken cage with a tiny doorway. Over time, he was kept there more and more often. Eventually he became so large that he could barely squeeze in or out, and finally the family simply left the cage door open because he was too big to escape. By the time the OIC responded to an anonymous tip and arrived at the house, Krismon was severely weakened. His muscles had atrophied from years of confinement and a poor diet of table scraps. The cage was so small that rescuers had to cut it open to remove him. At the Sumatran Orangutan Conservation Program’s rescue center outside Medan, staff found him shaking uncontrollably from prediabetes and unable even to lift food to his mouth. He was quarantined, then gradually shifted from rice and bread to a normal orangutan diet. After four months, he was able to walk again, though awkwardly, and later began climbing the bars of his enclosure. Still, he remains frightened by unstable surfaces. Caretakers disagree about his future. Jennifer Draiss says he will never be able to return to the wild because he has spent too long around humans and lacks the knowledge needed to live in the forest. Ian Singleton, who runs the center, is more hopeful and believes Krismon may recover more strength. The rescue center was never intended to house animals permanently, but that is the likely fate for some of its residents unless the SOCP can build a planned orangutan haven nearby. The project would create a series of islands in a reclaimed rice paddy for orangutans that cannot be released. Visitors would be able to see them and learn why keeping orangutans as pets is harmful and why conserving Indonesia’s rainforests matters. The animals would still be fed by caretakers and sleep in a night house, but they would have outdoor space instead of cages. The haven is planned to open in about three years if funding is secured. For now, Krismon’s progress is slow, but there are small signs of improvement. One morning, Draiss saw him sitting on a high pole in the sun — something she had never seen him do before.

# The Orangutan Who Escaped Indonesia's Blackmarket Pet Trade Krismon's story begins with a gift. In 1998, a soldier stationed near one of Indonesia's most biodiverse rainforests received a baby orangutan as a present. The soldier, Zulbaidah's late husband, brought the ape home to their family in Kabanjahe, North Sumatra. Named after "Krisis Moneter," the Asian financial crisis occurring that year, Krismon initially seemed like a beloved family member. Zulbaidah recalls him as being "like my own son," riding in the back of family vehicles on road trips and enjoying television shows and tickle fights with the children in the living room. The young ape would laugh with a distinctive sound—"hhk hhk hhk"—that endeared him further to the family. However, as Krismon matured, the reality of keeping a wild primate became apparent. His teeth grew longer and sharper, his body swelled dramatically, and his temperament became increasingly unpredictable. When he grew angry and threw things, the family's solution was confinement. They placed him in a cage originally designed for chickens, with a doorway barely large enough for a bird. Over the years, as Krismon continued growing, the family used the cage more frequently, eventually throwing away the key. By June 2016, when authorities confiscated him at approximately age 20, Krismon had been confined to this tiny enclosure for so long that his legs had wasted away to the point where he could no longer stand. Krismon represents one of thousands of victims of Indonesia's illegal orangutan trade, a blackmarket that has pushed these great apes toward extinction. The trade operates through a ruthless system: poachers slaughter mother orangutans to capture their babies, who are prized for their cuteness and the prestige an exotic pet brings to its owner. This demand is fueled by deforestation, which has devastated Indonesia's rainforests more severely than any other country since the turn of the century. As palm oil plantations expanded to make Indonesia the world's leading producer, orangutans lost their forest homes and were forced into dangerous encounters with farmers protecting their crops. Orphaned and displaced apes enter trafficking networks that extend throughout Indonesia and beyond, reaching destinations like Thailand, where orangutans are dressed in silk shorts and forced to box like fighters for tourist entertainment. Despite Indonesia having laws that impose maximum five-year prison sentences for transporting, trading, keeping, or killing protected species like the Sumatran or Bornean orangutan—both classified as Critically Endangered—not a single citizen has ever been prosecuted for keeping an orangutan as a pet. This legal failure stems from a troubling pattern: orangutan owners tend to be influential figures such as soldiers or politicians who can afford the animals' upkeep and leverage their status to avoid prosecution. Panut Hadisiswoyo, founder of the Orangutan Information Center, has encountered this impunity repeatedly. When attempting to recover an ape from a high-ranking police officer in Aceh province, the officer dismissed him, saying "the law is in my head." Another case involved a former commander of a separatist movement who claimed he purchased orangutans to save them from villagers, yet was later discovered preparing to ship five more by bus to a buyer in Medan. The man was never charged. Since 2012, the OIC has assisted authorities in confiscating 114 orangutans, including 39 pets. Burma’s government is considering new legislation that could place tighter control on the work of international nongovernmental organizations, including potentially the United Nations, at a moment when the country is already under intense criticism for its treatment of Rohingya Muslims and for a broader rollback of democratic freedoms. The proposed measure, called the Draft Law on International Non-Governmental Organizations, was reviewed by The Washington Post. It gives the government broad authority over aid groups, but critics say it is vague and offers little protection against arbitrary interference. The draft would allow Burmese staff to monitor the work of foreign aid organizations and would give the government wide discretion to suspend their activities. Aid groups fear it could be used to limit their operations in Burma, also known as Myanmar. The draft comes as the government of Nobel laureate Aung San Suu Kyi faces mounting backlash over military operations in Rakhine state that have driven nearly 700,000 Rohingya across the border into Bangladesh since August. Human rights advocates say the new law fits a larger pattern of shrinking space for civil society. In a February presentation, the INGO Forum, a coalition of dozens of aid organizations operating in Burma, warned that the law’s stated purpose would let the government suppress activities it does not favor and weaken efforts to advance democracy and human rights. International aid groups and diplomats have been lobbying members of the parliamentary committee reviewing the draft, asking them either to revise the wording or withdraw the bill entirely. It remains unclear whether the legislation will advance or what form it might take if it does. It is also unclear who authored the draft or whether it was written at the direction of the president’s office or Suu Kyi’s state counselor’s office. Government spokesman Zaw Htay referred questions to the Ministry of Planning and Finance, whose deputy minister did not respond to requests for comment. Tin Maung Oo, a member of the commission working on the legislation, said the committee is consulting with ministries, nongovernmental groups, and experts. He said the government recognizes the importance of international aid groups and wants them to “flourish,” but believes a law is needed to oversee their work. Critics say the proposal reflects a broader regional trend. Richard Weir of Human Rights Watch said laws and policies across Southeast Asia have increasingly reduced the space for civil society and critical speech, and that Myanmar has been especially affected. He noted that civil society space opened rapidly after 2011 but has narrowed again since the National League for Democracy came to power in 2016. The NLD government has also proposed changes to the country’s protest law, including provisions that would impose prison sentences on people whose demonstrations could endanger the “security, rule of law and stability of the state.” Hundreds of protesters marched in downtown Rangoon in early March against those amendments, even standing for a time before a large portrait of Suu Kyi. Two days later, the NLD-dominated upper house approved the changes, which now move to the lower house, where the party also holds a majority. A Western diplomat in Rangoon said the protest-law amendments and the draft NGO law were the first two active steps he had seen by the NLD to make Myanmar less democratic. Aid organizations say they are already facing more practical obstacles, including greater difficulty obtaining visas and travel permissions. Some participants at the February INGO Forum meeting believed the draft law could be a precursor to broader restrictions on civil society, similar to developments in other countries. One especially controversial section would require Burmese citizens employed by international NGOs to report their “cooperation” with the law to the government. The INGO Forum warned that this would create another layer of monitoring, could damage trust, and might undermine partnerships. The Washington-based International Center for Not-for-Profit Law said in its analysis that it could not find comparable provisions in other laws. Tin Maung Oo said the draft would also apply to the United Nations’ work in Burma. That possibility is especially sensitive because the government has blocked a U.N. fact-finding mission from entering the country, barred a U.N. human rights investigator, and denounced U.N. statements about the Rohingya crisis, which it has dismissed as a “textbook example of ethnic cleansing.” In Rakhine state, where ethnic Rakhine Buddhists have long accused aid groups and the U.N. of favoring the Rohingya, hostility toward international organizations is particularly strong. Still, it is unclear whether the government could legally apply the new law to the U.N. itself. Stanislav Saling, spokesman for the U.N. Resident and Humanitarian Coordinator’s office in Burma, said the country is already bound by international conventions and agreements governing U.N. activities. He added that U.N. agencies and other development partners are concerned that the draft’s provisions are arbitrary and excessive and could hinder the humanitarian and development work of INGOs. He said the proposal would not help the government regulate or manage aid groups effectively or transparently. The article also notes that the NLD-led government has continued to use punitive existing laws, including the controversial Telecommunications Law, often used to punish criticism of authorities. Although amended last year to reduce possible prison terms and narrow who could be charged, activists say the changes did not go far enough. Free Expression Myanmar reported nine criminal complaints under the law between August and November 2017. Activist and poet Maung Saungkha, who spent six months in jail under the law during the previous government, said the changes were largely cosmetic and that authorities still want to control free speech.

Vietnam and Cambodia inaugurated the Long Binh–Chrey Thom Bridge on April 24, linking Vietnam’s An Giang province with Cambodia’s Kandal province. The ceremony in Kandal was attended by Vietnamese Prime Minister Nguyen Xuan Phuc, Cambodian Prime Minister Hun Sen, and large numbers of border residents. Phuc said the bridge reflects strong bilateral cooperation in trade, investment, security, defense, culture, education, and tourism, and will create the shortest route between Phnom Penh and Vietnam’s border area, helping boost trade and reduce poverty in disadvantaged border communities. Both leaders said the bridge has economic, political, cultural, social, security, and defense significance, calling it a symbol of friendship and solidarity between the two countries. Hun Sen thanked Vietnam for its past support in Cambodia’s struggle against the Khmer Rouge and for its continued assistance in national development. Construction began in January 2014, financed in part by an 18.76 million USD Vietnamese government credit package. It is Cambodia’s second-largest transport project funded through Vietnamese preferential credit and also reflects progress on border demarcation and marker planting.

A junior high school in Oita, Kyushu, received a mass-killing threat after a video of one student acting violently toward another spread on social media. The threatening email was sent around 11 p.m. on Jan. 11 through the Oita municipal government website’s inquiry form and warned that on Jan. 15 the sender and several accomplices would enter the school and “carry out a mass killing of students and teachers.” The sender is unknown. The city education board confirmed the message on Jan. 13 after the holiday weekend and informed police, who are investigating the case as intimidation and have placed officers inside and around the school. Classes on Jan. 15 will continue as usual, but after-school club activities are canceled and students will leave together. The education board said the threat is unacceptable and vowed to ensure student safety.

# Summary A junior high school in Oita, Japan received a mass-killing threat via email following the online spread of a video depicting student-on-student violence. The threatening email, received January 11, warned of an intrusion and attack planned for January 15 involving multiple perpetrators. School authorities discovered the message on January 13 after a holiday weekend and immediately notified prefectural police, who are investigating for intimidation. Police have deployed officers at the school to enhance security. While regular classes will proceed on January 15, all after-school club activities have been canceled and students will be dismissed together. School officials have condemned the threat and pledged cooperation with law enforcement to protect students and staff.

Indonesia’s biggest Muslim organization, Nahdlatul Ulama (NU), has urged Google to restore Palestine to Google Maps after the company removed the Palestine label and replaced it with Israel. NU chairman Said Aqil Siroj said the issue should be resolved quickly to avoid inflaming religious sentiment, warning that “if not put back, we will fight.” The call came amid an online petition on change.org that had gathered more than 300,000 signatures demanding Google recognize Palestine and clearly identify the Palestinian territories occupied by Israel. Petition organizer Zak Martin said the omission insulted Palestinians and made Google complicit in Israeli “ethnic cleansing,” while one supporter said he had boycotted Google over the issue. In response, a Google spokeswoman told the Guardian that there had never been a Palestine label on Google Maps, but a bug had removed the West Bank and Gaza Strip labels, and the company was working to restore them.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky traveled to Warsaw on Friday for his first in-person meeting with Poland’s new president, Karol Nawrocki, in what is expected to be a difficult encounter. The two leaders had spoken by phone after Nawrocki’s election victory, but it took four months for them to meet face to face. The visit comes amid growing tension between Kyiv and Warsaw, despite Poland remaining one of Ukraine’s most important allies since Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022. Poland has hosted more than a million Ukrainian refugees and has been a major transit route for Western military and humanitarian aid to Ukraine. Yet Nawrocki, a nationalist historian, has signaled a tougher line than his predecessor Andrzej Duda. According to Polish media, he rejected at least three invitations to visit Kyiv, apparently expecting Zelensky to come to Warsaw instead. Ukrainian analysts described that stance as contemptuous, while an EU official said Nawrocki’s approach to Ukraine is more hardline than Duda’s. Nawrocki has criticized Kyiv for what he sees as a failure to treat Poland as an equal partner and for insufficient gratitude for Poland’s support. He has also drawn support from the Polish far right by stressing historical grievances, especially the Volhynia massacres of 1943-1945, when an estimated 100,000 Poles were killed. He has called those killings a genocide and vowed to press the issue, though he says this does not alter Poland’s strategic backing for Ukraine. At the same time, Nawrocki opposes “unconditional” Ukrainian membership in the European Union and NATO and has ruled out sending Polish troops to Ukraine after the war. His positions reflect a rise in anti-Ukrainian sentiment in Poland. Opinion polls in Ukraine show trust in Nawrocki at 44%, about 20 points lower than trust in Duda during his presidency. Analysts say the political situation in Warsaw complicates relations further because Nawrocki often clashes with Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s centrist government. Tusk recently warned on X that if the president cannot help, he should at least not obstruct. Ukrainian observers say Zelensky’s trip will not be easy, but they stress that direct dialogue is necessary to prevent future disputes and maintain cooperation, even if relations are strained.

In Paris, the attack on a kosher supermarket that killed four Jews has deepened an already widespread sense of fear among France’s Jewish community, which many say has been growing more vulnerable amid a broader rise in anti-Semitism. Outside the Beth Hanna primary school, where armed soldiers now patrol, anxious mothers describe a new normal in which Jewish schools and institutions require military protection. “I’m scared,” says Vanessa Ganum, while another mother, Sarah, says the ease with which attackers can reach Jewish lives and businesses has become terrifyingly clear. The article describes the supermarket killings as the latest and most shocking episode in a series of anti-Jewish incidents that have intensified in recent months. France, home to more than 500,000 Jews—the largest Jewish population outside Israel and the United States—has seen arson, vandalism, rape, gunfire directed at a synagogue, and attacks on schools, cemeteries, and grocery stores. In the first seven months of the previous year, the Jewish Community Protection Service recorded 527 anti-Semitic acts, nearly twice the number from the same period in 2013. Jewish leaders say the attacks have made many in the community feel that the country is deteriorating and that Jews may be only the first target in a wider wave of hatred. Yonathan Arfi of the Representative Council of Jewish Institutions says the assaults on Jewish sites should make ordinary French citizens recognize that they have a responsibility to confront the problem. He argues that once France’s own core values were attacked, people began to see that “Jews are only the first target on a longer list.” Police and officials attribute most of the recent violence not to the traditional far right, but to radical Islamist young men from Muslim backgrounds. The article notes that anti-Semitic violence often spikes when tensions rise in the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. During last summer’s Israeli bombardment of Gaza, anti-Israel demonstrations in Paris reportedly turned into anti-Semitic attacks on synagogues and grocery stores. The 2012 killing of three Jewish children and a teacher by Mohammed Merah in Toulouse is cited as an earlier example of jihadist violence against Jews in France. Amedy Coulibaly, who attacked the kosher market, was not the first such attacker. The article also captures a shift in Jewish attitudes. Some, like journalist Mickaelle Bensussan, say the supermarket attack made them personally feel fear for the first time, even if the feeling of wanting to leave France passed quickly. Others are more pessimistic. David Cohen, a plumber, says many around him believe their future is no longer in France and are considering emigration to Israel. That trend is already visible: nearly 7,000 French Jews left permanently last year, twice as many as in 2013. A poll found that 74 percent of respondents had considered emigrating, and one-third cited rising anti-Semitism. Some Jewish observers say the link between the supermarket attack and the Charlie Hebdo killings made the threat feel larger and more political. Shimon Samuels of the Simon Wiesenthal Center argues that the attacks show Jews may be the first targets of jihadist terrorism, but not the last. French Prime Minister Manuel Valls acknowledged the seriousness of the crisis, calling anti-Semitism a symptom of a crisis of democracy and saying the national community had not reacted strongly enough. Yet leaders and activists agree that words must now be matched by broader public awareness and action.

# Rising Anti-Semitism in France: A Community in Crisis France's Jewish community faces an unprecedented wave of anti-Semitic violence, intensified by recent terrorist attacks that have left many contemplating emigration. The attacks on Charlie Hebdo magazine and a kosher supermarket in Paris have brought this escalating problem into sharp focus. ## The Current Climate The atmosphere among French Jews is one of palpable fear. Armed soldiers now patrol Jewish schools, and parents express anxiety about the safety of their children and their community establishments. This heightened security reflects the vulnerability felt by France's 500,000-strong Jewish population, the largest outside Israel and the United States. ## Rising Violence and Statistics Anti-Semitic incidents have surged dramatically. In the first seven months of 2014, the Jewish Community Protection Service reported 527 attacks—nearly double the 2013 figure for the same period. These incidents range from arson and vandalism targeting Jewish schools, cemeteries, and stores to serious crimes including rape and armed assault on synagogues. The violence appears linked to tensions surrounding the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. The Israeli bombardment of Gaza last summer, for example, sparked anti-Israel demonstrations in Paris that devolved into anti-Semitic attacks on Jewish institutions. ## Perpetrators and Pattern While classical anti-Semitism still exists among far-right supporters, police attribute most recent violence to radical Islamist young men from Muslim backgrounds. This represents a shift in the nature of anti-Semitic threats facing French Jews. ## The Emigration Trend Many Jews now view France as unsafe. In 2014, nearly 7,000 Jews emigrated—double the 2013 figure. A poll by Siona, a French Jewish organization, found that 74 percent of respondents had considered emigrating, with one-third citing rising anti-Semitism as their reason. Some community members express resignation. David Cohen, a plumber, describes France as "a boat that is sinking" and considers following his parents to Israel. Others, like journalist Mickaelle Bensussan, initially experienced panic but ultimately rejected fear as a reason to abandon their country. ## Historical Context This is not the first such attack. In 2012, Mohammed Merah killed three Jewish children and a teacher at a Toulouse school, but the incident received limited public attention and even some Jews dismissed it as an isolated event. The recent kosher supermarket attack by Amedy Coulibaly, however, has galvanized broader awareness. ## Broader Implications Community leaders argue that the attacks reveal a wider threat. Shimon Samuels of the Simon Wiesenthal Center notes that "what starts with the Jews never ends with them," suggesting that anti-Semitic terrorism signals deeper dangers to Western democracy itself. ## Government Response French Prime Minister Manuel Valls acknowledged the severity of anti-Semitism, calling it "a symptom of a crisis of democracy, a crisis of the Republic." He suggested the national community had not reacted sufficiently to previous incidents, stating, "We were not indignant enough." ## Conclusion France's Jewish community stands at a crossroads. While some maintain faith in their country, many others view emigration as necessary for their safety and future. The challenge now lies in whether government acknowledgment of the problem will translate into meaningful action to protect this vulnerable population and preserve France's democratic values.

A Rwandan genocide fugitive, Phénéas Munyarugarama, has been confirmed dead, according to Serge Brammertz, chief prosecutor for the U.N. International Residual Mechanism for Criminal Tribunals. Munyarugarama, one of the last major suspects indicted by the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda, is said to have died of natural causes around Feb. 28, 2002, in Kankwala in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, where he was buried. His death follows confirmation less than a week earlier that another major fugitive, Protais Mpiranya, died in Zimbabwe in 2006. Munyarugarama had been charged with genocide, direct and public incitement to commit genocide, and crimes against humanity. Prosecutors accused him of helping direct mass killings, attacks and sexual violence against Tutsi civilians in Rwanda’s Bugesera region. The 1994 genocide began after President Juvénal Habyarimana’s plane was shot down on April 6, triggering Hutu extremist violence against Tutsis with support from the army, police and militias. Brammertz said the confirmation may offer some closure to victims’ families. He said the top remaining priority is locating Fulgence Kayishema, previously found in South Africa.

The article examines the tension in France and across Europe over freedom of speech, hate speech, and accusations of unequal treatment of Muslims and Jews after the January attacks in Paris. The killings at the Charlie Hebdo offices, where cartoonists were shot dead after publishing material mocking the Prophet Muhammad, were widely seen as an assault on free expression. But in the aftermath, French authorities arrested more than 70 people for allegedly praising or defending the attackers, prompting debate over whether free speech is being applied unevenly. The most prominent case highlighted is that of French comedian Dieudonne M'bala M'bala, who was charged after posting on Facebook, “I feel like Charlie Coulibaly,” a phrase that merged the name of Charlie Hebdo with that of Amedy Coulibaly, the gunman who killed four hostages at a kosher supermarket. Dieudonne, who has a history of anti-Semitic prosecutions, argued that he was being punished under a hypocritical system that protects some forms of provocative speech while targeting others. In an open letter to French Interior Minister Bernard Cazeneuve, he claimed he was being treated like a terrorist despite seeing himself as no different from Charlie Hebdo’s satirists. The article explains that France’s legal framework bans promoting racial or religious hatred and also prohibits inciting or defending terrorism or crimes against humanity. Prosecutors said Dieudonne’s comment crossed that line. At the same time, blasphemy itself is not illegal in France, which is why Charlie Hebdo’s mocking of religion is treated differently from speech that directly targets a protected group. Still, the boundary between satire and hate speech can be difficult to define. Charlie Hebdo was sued by Muslim groups in 2006 over cartoons that allegedly abused people because of their religion, but the paper was acquitted when a court ruled the cartoons were aimed at extremists rather than Islam as a whole. The magazine has also faced suits from Roman Catholic groups, underscoring that its satire has offended multiple faith communities. Human rights groups have criticized the French response. Amnesty International expressed concern about a new French law allowing prison sentences of up to seven years for defending or inciting terrorism, arguing that some prosecutions have been excessive. One example cited was a drunk man who praised the Kouachi brothers, the Charlie Hebdo attackers, and told police, “I hope you will be next.” He received a four-year sentence. Amnesty’s Europe director, John Dalhuisen, said France was understandably under pressure to defend freedom of expression after the attacks, but warned that punishing people too harshly could undermine that principle. The article places the French debate in a wider European context. In Britain, hate-speech laws have been used against people across different backgrounds: a white supremacist was convicted for an anti-Semitic tweet to a lawmaker, a Muslim teenager was tried for posting that “all soldiers should die and go to hell,” and a 22-year-old man was jailed for anti-Muslim Facebook comments after the murder of soldier Lee Rigby by al-Qaida-inspired attackers. These examples are used to show that, at least in law, restrictions on hateful expression are not supposed to discriminate by faith. Yet many Muslims in Europe feel they are not treated equally. Political scientist John Keane said the arrests in France reinforce a perception among Muslims that insulting Jewish people is not tolerated under French law, while insulting Muslims is effectively treated differently. Muslims, he noted, often feel like second-class citizens and believe they are blamed for extremist violence committed by others. Jewish communities, meanwhile, also fear rising hatred and feel that authorities are not doing enough to protect them. The article contrasts the historical position of the two communities. Jewish populations in Britain and elsewhere have lived in Europe for centuries, and the Holocaust has made governments especially alert to anti-Semitism; Holocaust denial is illegal in several countries, including France. Muslim communities are more recent arrivals, often poorer on average, and many feel they are unfairly associated with terrorism. Jonathan Romain, a British Reform rabbi, said Jews have had long experience adapting to life as a minority, while Muslims are still navigating that process. The piece also highlights efforts to respond to hate through organization and humor. Fiyaz Mughal, who runs the British anti-Muslim monitoring project Tell MAMA, said fear among Muslims has grown since the 2013 murder of Lee Rigby and intensified after the Paris attacks. He urged social media companies such as Facebook and Twitter to respond more quickly to hateful content. Jonathan Sacerdoti of Britain’s Campaign Against Anti-Semitism said many Jews also feel unsafe amid rising abuse, citing anti-Israel demonstrations where banners praised Hitler. Despite the tensions, the article ends on examples of solidarity and satire. Mughal described a humorous Twitter campaign, #foxnewsfacts, that mocked a Fox News claim that Birmingham was “totally Muslim” by turning absurd images into jokes about Islamic domination. He saw that as communities using humor to address prejudice. Romain offered another example: the Mormon church’s calm response to the musical “The Book of Mormon,” suggesting that offended groups can answer mockery not with outrage but with confident engagement.

# French Arrests Raise Question: Is Free Speech for All? Following the January 2015 terrorist attacks in Paris that killed 12 people at Charlie Hebdo magazine and four at a kosher supermarket, French authorities arrested more than 70 individuals for allegedly praising terrorists or encouraging further attacks. While many globally viewed the attack on the satirical publication as an assault on freedom of expression, the subsequent arrests have sparked significant debate about whether free speech protections apply equally to all groups in France. The most prominent arrest involved comedian Dieudonne M'bala M'bala, who faced charges for a Facebook post stating "I feel like Charlie Coulibaly"—combining the names of Charlie Hebdo and Amedy Coulibaly, the supermarket attacker. Dieudonne, who has faced repeated prosecutions for anti-Semitism, later claimed he was being silenced by free-speech hypocrisy in an open letter to French Interior Minister Bernard Cazeneuve, arguing he was being treated like a terrorist despite merely expressing an opinion. These arrests have fueled accusations of a double standard in French law. Critics argue that while Charlie Hebdo's mockery of the Prophet Muhammad receives protection as religious satire, Muslims face prosecution for expressing provocative views. Many Muslims contend that France aggressively prosecutes anti-Semitic speech but fails to extend similar protections against racist speech targeting Muslims. French law prohibits promoting racial or religious hatred and defending terrorism, but blasphemy remains legal, creating a distinction between religious satire and hate speech that is not always clear. Charlie Hebdo itself has faced lawsuits from Muslim groups for "publicly abusing a group of people because of their religion" over 2006 cartoons. However, courts ruled the cartoons targeted extremists rather than Islam itself. The publication has also been sued by Roman Catholic groups, indicating its provocative approach extends beyond Islam. Defenders argue the cartoonists are motivated by satire rather than hatred or discrimination. International human rights organizations have criticized the arrests. Amnesty International expressed concern about a new French law permitting sentences up to seven years for defending or inciting terrorism, arguing some prosecutions have been excessive. One case involved a drunk man sentenced to four years for praising the Kouachi brothers attackers. Amnesty Europe Director John Dalhuisen warned that while authorities must attack criminals, they should not undermine freedom of expression itself. The perception of unequal treatment reflects Europe's complex relationship with religious minorities. Australian political scientist John Keane noted that many Muslims believe satirizing Jewish people is prohibited under French law while similar protections do not apply to Muslims. This perception of a double standard stems from Europe's historical context: Jewish communities have been established for centuries, and the Holocaust's legacy has prompted strong anti-Semitism laws in several European countries, including France, where Holocaust denial is criminal. Muslims, who arrived in larger numbers more recently and often face economic disadvantages, feel treated as second-class citizens. Despite occupying different positions in European society, both Muslim and Jewish communities share concerns about rising hatred. British Jewish leaders report alarming incidents, including protest banners reading "Hitler was right" and "Hitler should have finished the job" during Gaza war demonstrations. Muslim communities report "cumulative fear" following the 2013 killing of soldier Lee Rigby and subsequent mosque attacks and social media abuse. The language of anti-Muslim rhetoric is increasingly shifting toward targeted threats. Some Muslims look to Jewish communities for guidance on combating hatred. Tell Mama, a British project monitoring anti-Muslim incidents, is modeled on the Community Security Trust, a Jewish charity combating anti-Semitism. Tell Mama director Fiyaz Mughal noted that "the Jewish community has been far more vocal and far more organized" in responding to hatred. However, some observers suggest alternative approaches to offensive speech. Rabbi Jonathan Romain highlighted the Mormon church's response to the satirical musical "The Book of Mormon," which involved taking out a full-page advertisement inviting audiences to visit churches rather than protesting or harassing actors. Similarly, when Fox News claimed Birmingham was "totally Muslim," British Muslims and non-Muslims united in satirical Twitter responses under #foxnewsfacts, with humorous false claims about Islamic domination. Mughal saw this as communities "coming together and having a laugh about stupidity, but also about some of the sensitive issues" regarding difference and integration. The Paris arrests ultimately reveal tensions between protecting freedom of expression and preventing hatred, with significant disagreement about whether current French law applies these protections equally across religious groups.

Félicien Kabuga, an 85-year-old former radio station owner accused of helping fuel Rwanda’s 1994 genocide, appeared Wednesday before a United Nations court in The Hague, where his lawyer entered not guilty pleas on his behalf. It was Kabuga’s first appearance before the U.N.’s International Residual Mechanism for Criminal Tribunals since he was transferred to the Netherlands after his arrest outside Paris in May. Kabuga, who was seated in a wheelchair and guarded by two officers, did not speak in court. His lawyer, Emmanuel Altit, asked Presiding Judge Iain Bonomy to treat Kabuga’s silence as a plea of not guilty on all counts, which the judge formally entered. Kabuga listened as the court read an 18-page indictment, occasionally fidgeting with his blue medical face mask. He faces charges including genocide, complicity in genocide, incitement to genocide, persecution and extermination, and could receive a life sentence if convicted. Prosecutor Serge Brammertz said the prosecution plans to file a shorter amended indictment by mid-January as it tries to locate witnesses during the coronavirus pandemic. Kabuga was sent to The Hague rather than the tribunal’s Arusha branch so he could undergo a detailed medical assessment because of concerns about his health. The mechanism was created to handle remaining cases from the tribunals for Rwanda and the former Yugoslavia. According to the indictment, Kabuga and others used the RTLM radio station to spread ethnic hatred against Tutsis and allegedly helped arm and support Interahamwe militias with machetes and other weapons. He is also accused of creating a National Defense Fund to support the militias financially and logistically. The genocide, which began after President Juvénal Habyarimana’s plane was shot down on April 6, 1994, left about 800,000 Tutsis and moderate Hutus dead.

In the aftermath of the deadly synagogue attack in Jerusalem’s Har Nof neighborhood, religious Jews in Israel responded by turning to faith, prayer, and scripture for comfort and meaning. The Tuesday massacre, in which four rabbis and a policeman were killed by two Palestinians armed with a meat cleaver, knives, and a gun, deeply shocked the Jewish community. But many worshippers and religious leaders said the proper response was not despair, but a renewed commitment to Torah study, good deeds, and spiritual resilience. Rabbi Avi Berman, executive director of the Orthodox Union’s Israel office, described the attack as a devastating and horrific shock, but said believers try to respond to tragedy by bringing more “light” into the world. Speaking from his Jerusalem office, he said Jews ask God “why” when tragedy strikes, but ultimately conclude that their task is to do more good, help others, and connect more deeply to God. In his view, the attack was aimed not just at people, but at a place of worship and the values it represents. He argued that synagogues and yeshivas produce light, happiness, and insight, and that this goodness is precisely what terrorists seek to destroy. The synagogue itself resumed morning prayer on Wednesday, just one day after the attack, and dozens of worshippers returned before dawn to the same service where the killings had occurred. Security was visibly tighter: the synagogue now had two armed guards, unlike the day before. Several people said that returning to pray there was an act of defiance and faith. Akiva Pollack, a paramedic who had responded to the attack, said that seeing the synagogue full made him believe the community would not close the place down but would instead strengthen it. He said the response should be to come back and pray. The families of the victims also drew comfort from the fact that their loved ones died while engaged in prayer. Meshulam Twersky, son of Rabbi Mosheh Twersky, said at his father’s funeral that his only solace was knowing his father was praying when he was killed. Another worshipper, Gavriel Cohen, said simply that the future depends on God. Religious leaders across the ultra-Orthodox world echoed the message of spiritual strengthening. Rabbi Aharon Leib Steinman, a prominent leader, published a letter in Yated Neeman urging Jews to respond to the tragedy by increasing Torah study and acts of kindness. He cited the Talmud and said that in difficult times, especially as redemption approaches, one should learn more Torah and do more good deeds. His message reflected a broader theme among mourners: that the response to violence should be humility, introspection, and greater devotion. The article also highlighted the personal and intellectual loss of Rabbi Mosheh Twersky, one of the victims. Twersky, originally from Boston, was remembered by people who knew him as exceptionally brilliant, patient, and compassionate. An anonymous blogger from the pro-Israel site Israel Matzav said he had grown up with Twersky in Boston and recalled that Twersky was placed in advanced classes years ahead of his age because of his intellect. Despite his brilliance, he was known for patiently helping others understand difficult Talmud passages and for showing kindness to those who felt left out. Twersky was the grandson of Rabbi Joseph Soloveitchik, a major modern Jewish philosopher, and the son of Rabbi Isadore Twersky, who founded Harvard’s Center for Jewish Studies. After graduating from Harvard, he moved to Israel in 1990 and became a senior figure at Yeshivas Toras Moshe. Rabbi Menachem Genack of OU Kosher also remembered Twersky as a child and described him as a great scholar and exceptionally humble man. Twersky’s son Meshulam, speaking at the funeral, stressed that his father was someone people could always confide in and “pour your heart out to.” Throughout the article, the central theme is that the massacre, intended to spread fear and destroy a sacred space, instead prompted a response of faith, solidarity, and renewed commitment to Jewish learning and worship. Religious Jews and leaders insisted that they would answer violence with more prayer, more charity, and more Torah, believing that this would transform grief into spiritual strength.

The Embassy of Israel in Kathmandu marked the United Nations International Day for the Commemoration of the Victims of the Holocaust on January 27 with a memorial event titled “Zikaron Bassalon- Memory in the Living Room.” Held under the global theme “Holocaust Remembrance for Dignity and Human Rights,” the program honored the six million Jewish people murdered during the Holocaust and highlighted the importance of remembrance, dignity, and resistance to hatred and antisemitism. The event drew high-level government officials, diplomats, media representatives, and friends of Israel. Israeli Ambassador Shmulik Arie Bass said racial discrimination and the attempt to exterminate a people must never happen again, calling the Holocaust a black mark on human history. Top Bahadur Magar, chairperson of the National Human Rights Commission, said the Holocaust profoundly influenced international human rights law and led to the adoption in 1948 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and the Genocide Convention, to which Nepal is a state party. He called for a world of hope, tolerance, social justice, dignity, and equality. Germany’s ambassador Udo Volz and Australia’s ambassador-designate Simon Ernst also shared reflections. Holocaust survivor Sophia Geller gave a moving personal testimony, while Nepali students performed music. A video of survivor Dugo was screened, recounting his tradition of eating falafel every January 18 to celebrate freedom and life. The embassy reaffirmed its commitment to Holocaust education, peace, tolerance, and mutual respect.

On September 16, 1969, the Chaldean-Syriac-Assyrian village of Sorya in Iraq’s Zakho district was the site of a deadly massacre under the Ba’ath regime of President Ahmed Hassan al-Bakr. According to the article, the Iraqi Army, led by Lieutenant Abdul Karim al-Juhaishi, attacked the remote village after claiming its residents had detonated a landmine against his convoy four kilometers away. Soldiers gathered villagers in an animal pen and opened fire, killing 38 people and seriously injuring about 25 others. Among those killed were Father Hanna Qasha, the village priest, and Khammo Marawge, the mayor, along with his daughter. The article says the victims’ bodies were left in the streets and squares, reflecting the brutality of the attack. It argues that the stated punishment for a supposed attack the villagers did not commit masked a deeper aim: the destruction of the village’s 40 Chaldean-Syriac-Assyrian families. More than 56 years later, the article says successive Iraqi governments have failed to provide justice or official recognition for the massacre. Chaldean-Syriac-Assyrian groups, including the Beth Nahrain Patriotic Union, in Iraq and abroad continue to demand acknowledgment and accountability, insisting they will not stop pressing for recognition of the victims.

# Summary: The Forgotten Massacre of Assyrians in Iraq On September 16, 1969, the remote village of Sorya in Iraq's Zakho district experienced a devastating massacre during the Ba'ath regime. Iraqi Army forces, led by Lieutenant Abdul Karim al-Juhaishi, attacked the predominantly Chaldean-Syriac-Assyrian village, killing 38 people and injuring approximately 25 others. The military justified the attack by claiming villagers had detonated a landmine against a nearby convoy, though the residents were allegedly uninvolved. Soldiers gathered villagers in an animal pen and opened fire indiscriminately, killing the village priest, mayor, and his daughter, among others. Bodies were left scattered throughout the village. The massacre represented the latest tragedy in a long history of violence against the Chaldean-Syriac-Assyrian people, following the 1915 Genocide and the 1933 Simmele Massacre. The unstated objective appeared to be the complete elimination of the village's 40 families. Despite 56 years passing and multiple Iraqi governments claiming democratic principles, no official recognition or justice has been provided. The Chaldean-Syriac-Assyrian community and political organizations continue demanding accountability and official acknowledgment of this historical atrocity.

Yemen’s Houthi militia executed nine civilians, including a 17-year-old minor, in Sanaa on Sunday after accusing them of involvement in the 2018 killing of Saleh Al-Samad, the Houthi-appointed president of the administration that controls much of northern Yemen. Al-Samad was killed in an airstrike in Hodeidah, on Yemen’s west coast, in April 2018. The executions drew sharp condemnation from Yemen’s internationally recognized government, which called them a war crime, and triggered widespread outrage among human rights activists. Hundreds of activists denounced the Houthis on social media, saying the killings were intended to terrorize civilians living in areas under militia control and urging human rights organizations to intervene. Yemen’s Minister of Information, Moammar Al-Eryani, described the executions as a “terrorist crime” committed by the Iran-backed Houthis. He said the nine civilians had been subjected to years of enforced disappearance and torture, then tried in a mock trial that stripped them of basic rights. Al-Eryani said the killings reflected the Houthis’ disregard for Yemeni lives and compared the move to political executions by Iran’s clerical leadership. He also warned that the perpetrators would not escape punishment and would eventually be brought to justice. At the same time, he criticized what he described as the silence and inaction of the international community, including the United Nations and its envoys, over continuing Houthi abuses.

# Summary The Houthi militia executed nine civilians, including a 17-year-old minor, in Sanaa on Sunday, allegedly in connection with the April 2018 killing of Saleh Al-Samad, the Houthi-controlled administration's president, who died in an airstrike in Hodeidah. The executions have sparked widespread outrage among human rights activists and Yemen's internationally recognized government, which condemned the killings as a war crime. Hundreds of activists used social media to protest the Iran-backed militia's actions, calling on human rights organizations to intervene and demanding an end to civilian violence. Yemen's Minister of Information Moammar Al-Eryani characterized the executions as a terrorist crime, noting the victims had endured years of enforced disappearance, torture, and mock trials. He compared the Houthis' conduct to Iranian practices of executing political opponents and using controlled judiciary systems to settle scores. The article reflects on the author’s personal connection to Kanczuga, Poland, the town where his grandmother was born before fleeing the country and surviving the Holocaust. He describes an encouraging relationship with a young Polish man, referred to as “P,” who has become deeply committed to documenting the history of Kanczuga’s once-thriving Jewish community. As a child, P knew Jews had lived there, but after visiting the U.S. Holocaust Museum he became determined to learn everything he could about the town’s Jewish past, including details many locals would rather forget. The author says P has helped him see that some form of reconciliation may be possible, even if he is unsure what reconciliation really means in practical terms. He appreciates P’s efforts to preserve the Jewish cemetery where many of his relatives are buried and recognizes that P has also drawn hostility from people who do not want Kanczuga’s Jewish history remembered. For the author, the relationship offers a rare and meaningful form of remembrance, especially because his family’s history there is now so distant and painful. But the article argues that recent Polish government actions have undermined any broader hope for reconciliation. The author focuses especially on a new law passed by the Polish parliament that effectively blocks descendants of Holocaust victims and other former Jewish property owners from reclaiming property seized, confiscated, or nationalized during and after World War II. He sees this as a near-total denial of justice for Jews whose homes and possessions were taken while they were deported or murdered. He illustrates the issue with a photograph of his great-aunt Rachel and her children standing in front of a house that still exists today. He does not know whether it was their home or a neighboring one, but he is sure the family did not sell it before being deported and shot. He suggests the property was likely taken over by neighbors or by people resettled there from elsewhere after the war. The author acknowledges that many Poles were also victims of Nazi occupation, and he says P has helped him better understand that reality. But he insists that Polish suffering does not excuse the looting of Jewish property or the participation of some Poles in the murder of Jews. He criticizes Poland’s broader approach to memory, including a law that makes it illegal to refer to Nazi camps on Polish territory as “Polish death camps.” While he agrees that the camps were Nazi crimes, he argues that refusing to acknowledge the role of some Poles in facilitating or participating in the killings distorts history and blocks genuine national reconciliation. He points to the story of Bennie Schanzer, a survivor from Kanczuga whom he knew decades ago. Schanzer told him that during the deportation of the town’s Jews, it was the author’s great-grandmother who urged him to flee, saving his life. Schanzer also recalled that the man driving the horse-drawn cart carrying Jews to their deaths was a young man he had gone to school with, raising the question of whether local participation was coerced, paid, or voluntary. The author notes that the massacre of Kanczuga’s Jewish community, about 1,000 people, occurred 79 years earlier that week. The article ends on a note of paradox. Poland benefits economically from Jewish tourism and now allows descendants of Polish Jews to obtain citizenship, which can seem like a gesture of welcome or reconciliation. Yet the author remains skeptical, seeing these policies alongside laws that deny restitution and suppress uncomfortable truths. He concludes that Poland may appear to love Jews in some ways, but its actions suggest something far more conflicted.

# They Love Us, They Love Us Not: Poland's Complicated Relationship with Jewish History Jonathan Feldstein reflects on his complicated relationship with Poland, specifically the town of Kanczuga where his grandmother was born before fleeing to escape persecution. Through his connection with "P," a young Polish man dedicated to documenting the town's once-thriving Jewish community, Feldstein explores themes of reconciliation, historical responsibility, and Poland's conflicting signals toward Jewish descendants. Feldstein's relationship with "P" represents a hopeful possibility for reconciliation. "P" became passionate about preserving Jewish history after visiting the U.S. Holocaust Museum, driven to document everything about Kanczuga's Jewish past—a past that many locals preferred to ignore or obscure. Notably, "P" maintains the Jewish cemetery where Feldstein's relatives are buried, and he has become a target for those unwilling to acknowledge the town's Jewish heritage. While Feldstein admits uncertainty about what reconciliation truly means, he recognizes something redemptive in "P's" efforts. However, recent Polish legislation has shattered any optimism about widespread reconciliation. The Polish parliament passed a law effectively preventing Holocaust survivors' descendants from reclaiming property seized, confiscated, or nationalized during the Nazi era. This legislation is particularly significant given the historical context. Feldstein shares a photograph of his great aunt Rachel standing before a house that still stands today, over eighty years later. He is confident she did not voluntarily sell this property before being deported and murdered. Either neighbors took the house, or it was occupied by people "resettled from the east." Either way, no legitimate transactions likely exist. The new law allows current Polish residents to sleep peacefully in homes they have occupied for decades, knowing Jewish descendants cannot reclaim them. This stands in stark contrast to other European nations with formerly thriving Jewish populations, many of which have facilitated property reclamation. RCMP in Saskatchewan have released a detailed timeline of the mass killing at James Smith Cree Nation and nearby Weldon, describing a chaotic and unpredictable series of attacks by Myles Sanderson in the days leading up to and during the Sept. 4, 2022 rampage. According to investigators, Sanderson, 32, was selling cocaine and causing trouble on the First Nation northeast of Saskatoon on Sept. 1, along with his brother, Damien Sanderson. The brothers attacked some residents and stole a vehicle. Police investigating the theft were searching for Damien Sanderson and entered a home where he was believed to be staying, but officers were given a false name and did not realize they were dealing with him. RCMP said they had no knowledge of the earlier assaults and no indication that a mass killing was about to unfold. On Sept. 3, Damien Sanderson told people at a bar in Kinistino that he and his brother had a “mission” and that “people would hear all about it in the next few hours.” He was among the first people killed the next morning. Police said the brothers attacked a man in his home, and Myles Sanderson stole a kitchen knife before the two fought. Damien Sanderson, injured, fled into a wooded area and was found dead the next day. Myles Sanderson then moved from house to house on the First Nation, killing and injuring people with the knife. He first killed Robert Sanderson, 49. At another home, he killed Christian Head, 54, and Lana Head, 49. At another residence, he killed Gregory Burns, 28, and attacked Gregory’s mother, Bonnie Burns, 48, and two young boys. Sanderson later returned and killed Bonnie Burns as well as Lydia Gloria Burns, 61, who had come to help. Witnesses told RCMP that Sanderson was covered in blood and carrying a knife, and one said he asked, “Want to know how many bodies I got tonight?” He also threatened others, telling some they were lucky. Police arrived at James Smith Cree Nation around 6:18 a.m., but did not locate him. Assistant Commissioner Rhonda Blackmore said his movements were erratic: he abandoned vehicles, stole others, and moved on foot, making the situation “very rapidly unfolding, very dynamic and chaotic.” Almost an hour into the rampage, Sanderson attacked Earl Burns, 66, his former father-in-law. Despite his injuries, Earl Burns got into his school bus and tried to chase Sanderson before later dying in the bus. Sanderson then killed Thomas Burns, 23, and Carol Burns, 46, who were visiting family. He left the community shortly before 7 a.m., stopped in Kinistino, and then went to Weldon, where he killed Wesley Petterson, 78, at his home. In total, 11 people were killed and 17 were injured. RCMP had previously said 18 were wounded but later corrected the number. Sanderson was found days later after police sightings in Regina and back on the First Nation. On Sept. 7, he broke into a home and stole a vehicle near Crystal Springs. RCMP pursued him by road and helicopter until the vehicle crashed into a ditch and trees near Rosthern. He was taken into custody but soon went into medical distress and died. Blackmore said the investigation was extremely complex, involving 42 crime scenes, about 700 exhibits, and more than 250 witnesses. She said some questions may never be answered. Families and survivors received the update before the public presentation, and some said the added details brought a small measure of healing. Joyce Burns, widow of Earl Burns, called him her hero for trying to save his family. Some information was withheld because of two coroner’s inquests scheduled for early next year, one on the killings and one on Sanderson’s death in custody.

Two days after being acquitted by the Senate in his impeachment trial, President Donald Trump moved swiftly on Friday to remove two officials who had testified against him, signaling a retaliatory response to the witnesses who had helped build the Democratic case against him. Rep. Jackie Speier of California called it “the Friday Night Massacre,” comparing it to the “Saturday night massacre” under President Richard Nixon, when Justice Department officials resigned after refusing to carry out Nixon’s orders in the Watergate era. Republicans in the Senate, who had acquitted Trump just two days earlier, largely stayed silent Friday evening, even though many had objected during the trial when Democrats warned that Trump would seek revenge against his critics. Joe Manchin, the West Virginia Democrat whom Trump had hoped might side with Republicans. Trump supporters, by contrast, applauded the move. Rep. Lee Zeldin of New York said Vindman should not remain on the National Security Council, arguing it was not retaliation but a matter of trust and his term ending anyway. Rep. Paul Gosar of Arizona joked on Twitter that the White House was offering “a two for one special today on deep state leakers.” Defense Secretary Mark Esper said the Pentagon would protect service members from retaliation and had already addressed such protections through policy and other means. According to two officials speaking anonymously, Alexander Vindman was expected to attend a military college in Washington later in the summer, while his brother was slated for assignment to the Army General Counsel’s Office.
