As pro-democracy protests in Hong Kong stretched into their 10th week, President Donald Trump responded in a way that critics said showed indifference to democratic aspirations and a fixation on trade with China. Demonstrators in Hong Kong had been waving American flags, singing the U.S. national anthem, and using the symbols of the United States to highlight their demands for democratic reforms, protection of Hong Kong’s autonomy, and an investigation into alleged police brutality. But Trump’s public comments focused far more on Chinese President Xi Jinping and on the trade war between Washington and Beijing than on the protesters themselves. Trump praised Xi as “a good man in a ‘tough business,’” and at one point suggested on Twitter that if Xi met directly with the protesters, the crisis could end “happily and enlightened.” He also tied the Hong Kong unrest to trade negotiations, writing, “Of course China wants to make a deal,” and adding, “Let them work humanely with Hong Kong first!” That linkage made Hong Kong a new bargaining chip in already tense trade talks, even as the protests were becoming increasingly volatile and at times violent. The article describes Trump’s stance as muddled at best and indifferent at worst. Unlike many Democratic and Republican lawmakers, as well as State Department officials, who publicly backed the protesters’ demands or warned against a harsh Chinese crackdown, Trump was reluctant to clearly support the Hong Kong movement. When asked by reporters, he said the situation was “very tricky” and expressed hope that it would work out “for liberty” and “for everybody, including China.” Before that, he had praised Xi for acting “very responsibly” by allowing the protests to continue. Human rights advocates and former diplomats sharply criticized Trump’s approach. Nicholas Burns, a former U.S. diplomat now at Harvard, said the United States had a responsibility to speak up and accused Trump of “opening the door to Chinese intervention.” Yaqiu Wang of Human Rights Watch called Trump’s praise for Xi “very disturbing” and said it was unclear whether he was signaling a crackdown or simply avoiding the issue. She urged him to publicly and consistently support the peaceful activism of Hong Kong residents. The Trump administration’s official posture remained cautious and vague. Commerce Secretary Wilbur Ross described the Hong Kong protests as an “internal matter” for China and suggested the United States would not intervene militarily, saying, “What would we do? Invade Hong Kong?” A senior administration official said the U.S. was monitoring the situation and urging all sides to remain calm, safe and peaceful. The official also said freedoms of expression and assembly are “core values” shared with the people of Hong Kong, though the administration did not explain what it was doing to protect those freedoms. The article places Trump’s response in a broader pattern. Previous presidents often balanced support for human rights with strategic interests, but Trump has frequently shown a preference for strongmen, praising leaders such as Vladimir Putin and Kim Jong Un and expressing respect for Xi even while criticizing China’s economic policies. Critics worry that he may look the other way if Chinese paramilitary forces, which had been massing outside Hong Kong, are used to crush the protests. The article recalls Trump’s 1990 comments to Playboy, in which he praised China’s violent suppression of the 1989 Tiananmen Square protests as an example of “the power of strength.” Former officials also noted the diplomatic bind. If Trump openly supports the protesters, Beijing could accuse Washington of fomenting unrest; if he stays silent, it could be seen as a green light for intervention. The article compares the situation to President Barack Obama’s handling of Iran’s 2009 Green Movement, when he initially downplayed the protests and later hardened his rhetoric after a crackdown. Some analysts argued that Trump’s trade focus could still affect Beijing’s calculations. Dean Cheng of the Heritage Foundation said a violent crackdown could make a trade deal politically impossible for Trump. But Jude Blanchette of the Center for Strategic and International Studies warned that if mainland forces entered Hong Kong, it would be a major geopolitical event requiring a careful and coordinated U.S. response.

# Trump's Indifference to Hong Kong Protests Reflects His Prioritization of Trade Over Democracy Over the past ten weeks, Hong Kong has witnessed massive anti-government demonstrations, with protesters waving American flags and singing the U.S. national anthem as they advocate for democratic reforms and investigation into alleged police brutality. These demonstrations reflect widespread fears that Beijing is threatening Hong Kong's limited autonomy. However, President Donald Trump's response has been notably muted and contradictory, revealing his reluctance to champion democracy globally—a responsibility many of his predecessors considered central to the presidency. Rather than supporting the protesters, Trump has lavished praise on Chinese President Xi Jinping, describing him as "a good man in a 'tough business.'" Trump suggested that if Xi would meet personally with protesters, there would be a "happy and enlightened ending" to the Hong Kong crisis. This stance contrasts sharply with Democratic and Republican lawmakers, as well as State Department officials, who have consistently backed the protesters' demands or opposed a harsh Beijing crackdown. Trump's response has been further complicated by his fixation on trade negotiations with China. He tweeted that China should "work humanely with Hong Kong first" before reaching a trade deal, essentially leveraging the protest crisis as a bargaining chip in already volatile negotiations. When addressing reporters, Trump offered only vague platitudes, stating he hoped the situation would work out "for liberty" and "for everybody, including China," while earlier praising Xi for "acting very responsibly" by allowing protests to continue. Human rights experts have criticized this approach. Yaqiu Wang from Human Rights Watch called Trump's praise for Xi "very disturbing," urging the president to consistently and publicly support Hong Kong's peaceful activism through Twitter or other channels. The ambiguity of Trump's position leaves unclear whether he is signaling approval for a crackdown or attempting some diplomatic strategy. Commerce Secretary Wilbur Ross characterized the protests as an "internal matter" for China, echoing Beijing's standard defense against human rights accusations. When asked whether previous administrations would have responded differently, Ross dismissively asked, "What would we do? Invade Hong Kong?" A senior administration official offered only generic language about valuing freedoms of expression and assembly, without specifying any concrete actions to protect these rights. Trump's approach reflects a broader pattern. Unlike previous presidents who worked with authoritarian leaders while maintaining rhetorical support for democracy, Trump has openly embraced strongmen including Vladimir Putin, Kim Jong Un, and various autocrats worldwide. Notably, in 1990, Trump praised China's violent 1989 Tiananmen Square crackdown, telling Playboy that military strength was necessary to suppress the student protests, despite the deaths of hundreds or thousands. This historical context deeply concerns critics. They fear Trump will ignore potential Chinese military intervention in Hong Kong, particularly given massing paramilitary forces outside the city. President George H.W. Bush, who had led the U.S. Liaison Office in China, publicly denounced Tiananmen Square while privately signaling willingness to strengthen U.S.-China ties—a delicate balance Trump appears unwilling to attempt. Chinese diplomats have reportedly expressed private confidence that Trump has minimal interest in Hong Kong and remains narrowly focused on trade disputes. Doug Paal, formerly on the National Security Council, notes that Trump "skipped" the traditional political process of positioning America as a democratic beacon, instead becoming fixated on trade deficits. Some analysts suggest Trump's trade linkage might actually constrain Beijing's response. Dean Cheng from the Heritage Foundation argues that a violent crackdown could make it politically untenable for Trump to finalize a trade agreement, as no president could sign such a deal following "a replay of Tiananmen Square." The White House faces a genuine dilemma: supporting protesters risks accusations of fomenting dissent, while silence could green-light intervention. President Obama faced similar challenges during Iran's 2009 Green Movement protests, ultimately downplaying the uprising before hardening his rhetoric after violent crackdowns—an approach that satisfied neither critics nor protesters. China scholar Jude Blanchette warns that the Trump administration appears unprepared for potential mainland military intervention in Hong Kong, which he describes as "the single most significant geopolitical event in recent memory" if it occurs. Such an event would require sophisticated, coordinated response—precisely what Trump's administration has not demonstrated regarding this crisis.

About 50 residents of Debert, N.S., attended the first of four community open houses held by the commission of inquiry into the Nova Scotia mass killing that left 22 people dead last year. The two-hour session took place Sunday at a local community centre and was designed as an informal way for investigators to meet members of the public, hear their experiences, and gather information relevant to the inquiry. The open house format involved small-group and one-on-one conversations with about 20 inquiry staff, rather than a formal presentation or question-and-answer period. Barbara McLean, the commission’s director of investigations, said the goal was to bring the inquiry into the community, allow people to speak directly with investigators, and help the commission build connections with local leaders who may later be important in carrying out its recommendations. She said attendees could simply share what they went through or provide documents and other information useful to the investigation. Some participants said the session was helpful. Victoria Dickie of nearby Meaghers Grant, whose nephew Joey Webber was among the gunman’s victims, said she found the meeting “a little bit reassuring.” She brought a list of questions for investigators and left it with them, including questions about how the commission decides whom to interview and what documents to subpoena. She said the process is still ongoing. Others were frustrated by the lack of a formal forum. Joy McCabe, who lives next to the Onslow firehall where Mounties fired shots during the search for the gunman, said the meeting was “nothing but noise.” She said she had witnessed the incident from her kitchen window and felt there had been too little information about what happened. McCabe said people in the area are still dealing with trauma, including PTSD and anxiety, and need answers. The inquiry is examining the events of April 18, 2020, when a gunman disguised as a Mountie set fire to homes in Portapique, N.S., and killed 13 people there. Over the next 13 hours, he moved across about 100 kilometres of central and northern Nova Scotia, killing more people he knew and others at random before being fatally shot by police at a gas station in Enfield, north of Halifax. The commission, chaired by former Nova Scotia chief justice Michael MacDonald, is scheduled to begin public hearings in Halifax next month. An interim report is expected by May, and a final report by November 2022. MacDonald has said the inquiry will not determine criminal or civil liability, but will instead focus on facts and on preventing a similar tragedy. The commission can, however, make findings of misconduct. No witness list has been released yet. As part of its work, inquiry staff visited Portapique in early June to better understand the geography of the killings and the routes taken by survivors fleeing through wooded areas as homes burned. After Sunday’s Debert session, the commission planned open houses in Truro on Monday, Millbrook on Tuesday, and Wentworth on Wednesday.

# Summary: Nova Scotia Mass Killing Inquiry Holds Community Open House A commission of inquiry investigating Nova Scotia's mass shooting that killed 22 people held its first community open house in Debert, N.S., on Sunday, drawing approximately 50 residents. The gathering was one of four scheduled open houses this week designed to engage with affected communities and gather information relevant to the investigation. The informal format featured small group discussions and one-on-one conversations between community members and approximately 20 inquiry investigators at tables throughout the venue. According to Barbara McLean, the commission's director of investigations, this approach allows residents to share experiences and provide relevant information while enabling the inquiry to explain its work and connect with community leaders who will help implement future recommendations. The April 2020 rampage began when a gunman disguised as a Royal Canadian Mounted Police officer set fires and killed 13 people in Portapique, N.S. Over the next 13 hours, he evaded police while killing additional victims across a 100-kilometer area before being fatally shot by police at a gas station in Enfield, north of Halifax. Responses to the open house format were mixed. Victoria Dickie, whose nephew was among the victims, found the meeting helpful and "reassuring." She submitted questions to investigators regarding their interview criteria and document subpoena processes. However, some attendees criticized the lack of formal presentations or structured question-and-answer sessions. Joy McCabe, who witnessed officers firing shots at a firehall near her home in Onslow, expressed frustration about insufficient information and the ongoing psychological toll on survivors, stating residents "have to have answers" given widespread PTSD and anxiety. The commission, chaired by former Nova Scotia Chief Justice Michael MacDonald, has emphasized its role is fact-finding rather than assigning blame or establishing criminal or civil liability. However, it can make misconduct findings. The inquiry began work 11 months ago and plans to conduct public hearings next month in Halifax, with an interim report expected by May and a final report due by November 2022. Additional open houses are scheduled for Truro, Millbrook, and Wentworth throughout the week. Earlier in June, inquiry staff visited Portapique to understand the geography where killings occurred and where survivors hid or fled through wooded areas.

As Canada approaches the ninth anniversary of the 2017 Quebec City mosque attack, Muslim leaders are renewing calls to confront Islamophobia and anti-Muslim fearmongering. Stephen Brown, CEO of the National Council of Canadian Muslims, said the anniversary is a reminder that Islamophobia in Canada “is not benign” and can have deadly consequences. The attack at the Quebec Islamic Cultural Centre on January 29, 2017, killed six Muslim men and remains the deadliest assault on a house of worship in Canadian history. It shocked Quebec City’s Muslim community, prompted vigils and condemnation nationwide, and drew attention to rising anti-Muslim hate globally. The Canadian government called it a terrorist attack and later, in 2021, designated January 29 as the National Day of Remembrance of the Quebec City Mosque Attack and Action against Islamophobia. Brown said the post-attack effort to heal and build bridges has faded, and many Muslims in Quebec now see a renewed use of Islamophobia and fear of Muslims for political gain.

# Summary Canadian Muslim leaders are calling for an end to Islamophobic rhetoric as the country marks the nine-year anniversary of a deadly mosque attack in Quebec City. On January 29, 2017, a gunman killed six Muslim men at the Quebec Islamic Cultural Centre, marking Canada's deadliest attack on a house of worship. Stephen Brown, CEO of the National Council of Canadian Muslims, emphasized that Islamophobia "kills people" and has real consequences. The attack devastated Quebec City's Muslim community, sparked national condemnation, and highlighted the global rise in anti-Muslim hate. The Canadian government designated January 29 as a National Day of Remembrance and pledged to address underlying issues. However, Brown expressed concern that lessons learned have not been fully retained, noting a troubling return to using Islamophobia for political purposes, particularly in Quebec.

The national chief of the Assembly of First Nations is urging Ottawa to restart stalled talks on long-promised legislation that would recognize Indigenous policing as an essential service, saying a coroner’s inquest into the 2022 James Smith Cree Nation mass stabbing exposed deep failures in the police and justice system. Cindy Woodhouse said in Saskatoon that the tragedy showed what can happen when First Nations police services are not adequately funded. She argued that if James Smith Cree Nation had been equitably supported, the killings might have been prevented. Myles Sanderson killed 11 people and injured 17 others on the First Nation and in nearby Weldon, northeast of Saskatoon, on Sept. 4, 2022. He later died in police custody. On Wednesday, the inquest into the deaths issued more than two dozen recommendations, including a call for the First Nation to establish a local police force as soon as possible. Testimony at the inquest showed that the Melfort RCMP detachment, about 50 kilometres away, received the first stabbing report at 5:40 a.m. that day and did not arrive until 6:18 a.m. Woodhouse said that delay was tragic and underscored the need for local policing. Prime Minister Justin Trudeau promised in 2020 that his government would introduce First Nations policing legislation, and the issue gained renewed attention after the attack. But Woodhouse said the file remains stalled. She said she has met with Public Safety Minister Dominic LeBlanc, but there has been no progress, while jurisdictional disputes over whether provinces or First Nations should lead remain the main obstacle. Former public safety minister Marco Mendicino had previously said the legislation would be tabled in fall 2022, but later backed away from that commitment. Public Safety Canada did not comment Thursday. James Smith Band Chief Wally Burns said the situation has become repetitive and frustrating, and that the community needs officers on the ground soon. Woodhouse said she is seeking $3.6 billion in the upcoming federal budget to begin addressing policing problems in First Nations communities. The article also notes that chronic underfunding has long troubled Indigenous police services. There were 36 Indigenous police services in Canada as of October, funded through a 1991 federal-provincial cost-sharing program. Last year, police organizations in Ontario and Quebec filed human rights complaints alleging systemic discrimination through underfunding.

# Summary Following a coroner's inquest into a mass stabbing in Saskatchewan, the Assembly of First Nations' national chief Cindy Woodhouse is urging the federal government to resume negotiations on legislation declaring Indigenous policing an essential service. On September 4, 2022, Myles Sanderson killed 11 people and injured 17 others on James Smith Cree Nation and in nearby Weldon, northeast of Saskatoon, before dying in police custody days later. The inquest released over two dozen recommendations, including one for the First Nation to establish a local police force promptly. Woodhouse argues the tragedy demonstrates a systemic failure. She contends that adequate funding for a First Nations police service could have prevented the massacre. The inquest revealed that the Melfort RCMP detachment, located 50 kilometers away, received the initial stabbing report at 5:40 a.m. but didn't arrive until 6:18 a.m.—a critical delay Woodhouse says proved fatal. Prime Minister Justin Trudeau promised in 2020 that his government would introduce new First Nations policing legislation, a commitment reiterated after the stabbing rampage. However, the legislation remains stalled, with jurisdiction disputes between provinces and First Nations remaining the primary obstacle. Former Public Safety Minister Marco Mendicino pledged to table the legislation in fall 2022 but later withdrew that commitment. Current Minister Dominic LeBlanc has met with Woodhouse, but no progress has occurred. Woodhouse is seeking $3.6 billion in the March federal budget to address First Nations policing issues. Currently, 36 Indigenous police services operate across Canada, with only five in Western Canada. These services are funded through the First Nations and Inuit Policing Program, established in 1991, where Ottawa covers 52 percent of costs and provinces or territories pay 48 percent. Chief Wally Burns of James Smith Band emphasized the community needs immediate action, stating they are "spinning our wheels" without results. Last year, Indigenous police chiefs from Ontario and Quebec filed separate human rights complaints alleging systemic discrimination due to underfunding.

New Democrat Leader Jagmeet Singh made the federal election campaign’s central focus on Friday the suffering of Indigenous communities and the grim legacy of residential schools, following the discovery of unmarked graves at former school sites. Singh began the day with a visit to Cowessess First Nation in Saskatchewan, where a preliminary finding of 751 unmarked graves was announced in June at the site of a former residential school. After seeing the grave site, Singh called the revelations a genocide and said the crimes were especially devastating because they were carried out by the state and by institutions meant to protect people. Singh was the first federal leader to visit the site of the former Kamloops Indian Residential School after the discovery of what are believed to be the remains of more than 200 children. His campaign stop underscored how the issue of reconciliation had become unavoidable for all major party leaders. In Winnipeg, Liberal Leader Justin Trudeau and Conservative Leader Erin O’Toole were also pressed to address the issue while they made campaign announcements on other topics. Trudeau reiterated support for reconciliation and said Justice Minister David Lametti was working with Indigenous stakeholders “to look for consequences and to seek accountability in every possible way” for the abuses at residential schools. He emphasized that police and prosecutors are independent of politics. Trudeau also defended the pace of progress, saying the damage done over generations or even centuries would take more than a few years to repair. He said the government still needed to improve education for Indigenous children, settle land claims, and address the crisis of missing and murdered Indigenous women and girls. Earlier in the week, his government had announced $321 million in new funding to help communities search burial sites and support residential school survivors. Trudeau met Friday with three Manitoba chiefs. O’Toole, meanwhile, pointed to his own visit to Cowessess the previous month and criticized Trudeau for not acting decisively enough. He argued that a Conservative government would deliver action rather than just promises and said restoring trust with Indigenous people would be central to reconciliation. He also used his Winnipeg appearance to promote a hiring incentive in his party’s platform. Indigenous leaders in Manitoba welcomed attention to the issue but said much more is needed. Grand Chief Arlen Dumas of the Assembly of Manitoba Chiefs called the federal funding a “good gesture” but said more resources were necessary and that the response should be accelerated. He said the discoveries could create an opportunity for healing. Assembly of First Nations Regional Chief Cindy Woodhouse urged Canadians to use the campaign to learn more about First Nations suffering, especially as COVID-19 has limited travel and direct engagement. Garrison Settee, grand chief of Manitoba Keewatinowi Okimakanak, said the pandemic had exposed major gaps in infrastructure, health care, and other systems, and that Indigenous people needed to “catch up to the rest of Canada.” Dumas said he had a brief but positive discussion with Trudeau about First Nations-led COVID-19 responses, along with ongoing water and housing problems on reserves. He also noted that Manitoba chiefs had received an informal invitation from the Liberals, but not from the Conservatives. He said he had received a letter from O’Toole when the Conservative leader first took office, but no meaningful follow-up. Dumas was especially critical of a group of Conservative MPs who wrote demanding that two statues of British queens be restored after they were toppled on Canada Day in Winnipeg, calling it evidence that the party was not listening to the concerns behind the protests. O’Toole said his party would work with Indigenous leaders to restore trust, which he described as the foundation of reconciliation.

Russian peacekeepers were deployed to Nagorno-Karabakh on Tuesday after Armenia and Azerbaijan signed a Russian-brokered agreement to end a six-week war that had already killed thousands and dramatically altered the balance of power in the South Caucasus. The deal, announced overnight by Russian President Vladimir V. Putin, requires Armenia to accept major territorial losses to Azerbaijan, including a broad swath of land and several important towns that had been under Armenian control since the early 1990s. The agreement triggered immediate fury in Armenia. Many Armenians saw it as a humiliating defeat and blamed Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan for signing it. Opposition politicians demanded his resignation, and protesters in Yerevan stormed the Parliament, where they beat the speaker, Ararat Mirzoyan, who later required surgery. Demonstrators also broke into the prime minister’s office; Mr. Pashinyan later said a computer and a wristwatch were stolen. In a Facebook post during the turmoil, he said he was in Armenia and continuing to work as prime minister. Armenian officials tried to explain that the country had little choice but to stop the fighting because of mounting losses in both lives and territory. Armenia’s Defense Ministry said that while the country had shown the bravery of its soldiers, officers, and generals, “it is time to stop the bloodshed.” Yet the mood on the streets was deeply emotional. Richard Giragosian, director of the Regional Studies Center in Yerevan, said he was awakened at 3 a.m. by shouting and car horns, but also sensed resignation among many Armenians. He said people felt the deal was the best available way to preserve what remained of Nagorno-Karabakh. For Armenians, the loss carried profound symbolic weight. Nagorno-Karabakh, known to Armenians as Artsakh, has long been tied to national identity, and the defeat was being compared to some of the darkest moments in Armenian history, including the slaughter and expulsion of Armenians from Turkey a century ago. Giragosian said many felt abandoned by the world and the West. The war began on Sept. 27, when Azerbaijan launched an offensive to retake Nagorno-Karabakh and surrounding regions that are internationally recognized as part of Azerbaijan but had been controlled by Armenian forces since the early 1990s. Azerbaijan lost that earlier war, and about a million people, mostly Azerbaijanis, were displaced. This time, however, Azerbaijan’s military advantage proved decisive. Backed by oil wealth and modern drones and other weaponry, Azerbaijani forces killed more than 1,300 Armenians, according to the Nagorno-Karabakh Defense Ministry. Journalists and observers described the situation as increasingly desperate for the Armenians. Tatul Hakobyan, an Armenian journalist who has covered the conflict for more than 30 years, said the reality was simply that Armenia had lost the war. He said gunfire could still be heard near Stepanakert, the enclave’s capital, as Azerbaijani forces closed in. Azerbaijan had also captured Shusha, a strategically important hilltop town just six miles from Stepanakert and a place of great historical significance to both sides. The new cease-fire differs from earlier failed attempts because it formally accepts Azerbaijan’s gains and is backed by Russian peacekeepers, who are to remain for at least five years. Under the deal, about 1,960 Russian troops and 90 armored personnel carriers will patrol the line of contact and the road linking Armenian-controlled Nagorno-Karabakh to Armenia. Russian television showed military vehicles heading toward the region from the Armenian border city of Goris. Armenia’s Defense Ministry said combat had been suspended and peacekeepers were being deployed. Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev celebrated the agreement as a major victory, calling it one of his country’s greatest triumphs. Turkey, which supported Azerbaijan throughout the war, also welcomed the settlement, with Foreign Minister Mevlut Cavusoglu calling it a “great success and victory for Azerbaijan.” The outcome underscored both Turkey’s growing role and Russia’s continuing dominance in the region. Although some Armenians had hoped Moscow would intervene more forcefully because of Armenia’s defense ties with Russia, the deployment of peacekeepers likely prevented even more of Nagorno-Karabakh, including Stepanakert, from falling to Azerbaijan.

# Armenians Erupt in Fury Over Bitter Defeat in Nagorno-Karabakh War Armenia and Azerbaijan have ended their six-week war over the disputed territory of Nagorno-Karabakh through a Russian-brokered peace agreement signed on Tuesday. However, the deal has sparked widespread outrage among Armenians, who view it as a humiliating defeat and territorial loss. ## The Agreement and Deployment Under the accord, Armenia has agreed to cede significant territory to Azerbaijan, including several key towns that Armenia had controlled since 1994. Russian peacekeeping forces—approximately 1,960 armed personnel and 90 armored vehicles—have been deployed to monitor the ceasefire and guard the line of contact between the two nations for at least five years. The deployment marks a significant reassertion of Russian influence in the southern Caucasus region. ## Armenian Anger and Protests Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan's decision to sign the agreement has provoked fierce domestic opposition. Angry protesters stormed Armenia's Parliament, where they beat Speaker Ararat Mirzoyan so severely that he required surgery. Demonstrators also invaded the prime minister's office, where items including a computer and wristwatch were stolen. Opposition politicians have called for Pashinyan's resignation, while the prime minister posted on Facebook that he remained in the country and would continue his duties. ## The Military Situation Azerbaijan launched its offensive on September 27 to recapture Nagorno-Karabakh and surrounding regions, areas that belong to Azerbaijan under international law but have been under Armenian control since the early 1990s. Azerbaijan's superior military firepower, funded by oil wealth and including a fleet of modern drones, proved decisive. The conflict resulted in over 1,300 Armenian deaths, according to the Nagorno-Karabakh Defense Ministry. Azerbaijan captured the strategically important hilltop town of Shusha, located just six miles from Stepanakert, the capital of Nagorno-Karabakh. ## Armenian Perspective While some Armenians acknowledge the agreement was necessary to prevent further losses, the territorial concession carries profound emotional weight. Nagorno-Karabakh, known to Armenians as Artsakh, has long been central to Armenian national and ethnic identity. The loss is being compared to historical Armenian traumas, including the expulsion and slaughter by Turkey a century ago, widely recognized as the first genocide of the twentieth century. Regional analyst Richard Giragosian noted that while there is a sense of resignation among Armenians—understanding that the agreement prevented worse outcomes—there is also widespread pain and a perception that the West and international community have abandoned Armenia. ## Regional Implications The agreement reshapes the security landscape of the southern Caucasus, a volatile region bordered by Turkey, Russia, and Iran. Turkey, which supported Azerbaijan throughout the conflict, has hailed the agreement as a major victory. Russia's role as peacemaker reinforces Moscow's continued dominance in the region, despite some Armenian disappointment that Russia did not provide more active military support despite their mutual-defense treaty. According to journalist Tatul Hakobyan, who has covered the region for over thirty years, Russia's decision to deploy peacekeepers ultimately prevented Azerbaijan from capturing additional territory, including Stepanakert itself. However, for many Armenians, the agreement represents a tragic defeat and a painful chapter in their nation's history.

Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan will travel to Turkey on Friday for talks with President Tayyip Erdogan, in a rare bilateral visit that Armenia hopes could help reset strained relations and eventually reopen the countries’ shared land border after decades of hostility. The two neighbours have no formal diplomatic ties, largely because of the legacy of the World War One mass killing of Armenians by Ottoman forces, which Armenia and many other countries recognize as genocide. Turkey also has long backed Armenia’s rival, Azerbaijan. Armenpress quoted Pashinyan on Wednesday confirming the trip. Armenian parliamentary speaker Alen Simonyan called the visit “historic” and said it was partly intended to reduce the risk of renewed fighting with Azerbaijan. Pashinyan has pushed normalization with both Turkey and Azerbaijan after several military defeats to Baku, and he has portrayed better ties with Ankara as a way for Armenia to strengthen its international position as relations with Russia have worsened. Earlier this year, he said Armenia would stop lobbying for international recognition of the Ottoman-era killings as genocide, a highly controversial concession at home. A senior Armenian diplomat said the talks would focus on the Armenia-Azerbaijan peace process and could also touch on the Israel-Iran conflict and possible evacuations of foreign nationals from Iran. Turkey closed its border with Armenia in 1993 over the Nagorno-Karabakh conflict. Ankara says it will reopen the border only if Armenia signs a peace deal with Azerbaijan. Armenia has said it wants the border reopened and refurbished a crossing point last year. The day before Pashinyan’s visit, Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev is also due to meet Erdogan in Turkey.

# Summary Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan will visit Turkey on Friday to meet President Tayyip Erdogan in a rare bilateral meeting aimed at normalizing relations and reopening their shared border after decades of hostility. Armenia and Turkey lack formal diplomatic relations due to historical tensions, including the World War One mass killing of Armenians by Ottoman forces, which Armenia considers genocide. Turkey has also supported Azerbaijan in its longstanding conflict with Armenia. Pashinyan has prioritized normalizing relations with both Turkey and Azerbaijan, framing it as an opportunity to strengthen ties with Western countries as Armenia's relationship with traditional ally Russia deteriorates. Controversially, he has agreed to stop lobbying for international recognition of the Armenian genocide—a deeply unpopular concession among many Armenians. The visit aims to discuss the Armenia-Azerbaijan peace process and potentially address the Israeli-Iranian conflict and evacuating foreign citizens from Iran. Armenia police have arrested Telman Kalashyan, the suspect in a deadly shooting in Shamiram village, Aragatsotn Province. Police said he was found Friday in Armavir village after being wanted for the August 1 attack. According to earlier reports, Kalashyan entered a funeral home at the village cemetery and opened fire, killing three people immediately and injuring eight others. One injured victim later died during surgery. Police opened a criminal case, named Kalashyan as the accused, and detained his uncle on suspicion of hiding the crime.

# Armenia Village Tragedy Suspect Arrested Armenian police arrested Telman Kalashyan, accused of a mass shooting in Shamiram village on August 1. Kalashyan was found Friday in Armavir village after being declared wanted. He allegedly burst into a funeral home in the Yazidi-populated village and opened fire, killing three people immediately and injuring eight others. One injured person died during surgery. In 2017, livestock and poultry sales totaled 1.68 million tonnes, nearly unchanged overall, though poultry sales rose 5.6% and pork sales 2%.

# Belarus Milk Production Increases in 2017 Belarus produced 7.32 million tonnes of milk in 2017, a 2.5% increase from 2016. The cattle population grew to 4.4 million head, including 1.5 million cows. Hog and poultry populations also increased slightly. Agricultural enterprises sold 1.68 million tonnes of livestock and poultry, with poultry sales rising 5.6% and pork sales up 2%. Armenian Deputy Foreign Minister Shavarsh Kocharyan said Baku, not Armenia, had created the conditions for war in Nagorno-Karabakh rather than for a settlement. His remarks followed Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev’s claim that Azerbaijan had already laid the necessary diplomatic and legal foundations for resolving the conflict. Kocharyan accused Azerbaijan of pursuing a genocidal and aggressive policy, saying it had enabled mass killings of Armenians in Azerbaijan, ethnic cleansing in and around Nagorno-Karabakh, and large-scale military aggression against the Nagorno-Karabakh Republic. He argued that the only meaningful step toward peace came in 1993, when then-President Heydar Aliyev instructed officials to arrange contact with Nagorno-Karabakh leaders. Kocharyan said the Moscow meeting between Heydar Aliyev and the Nagorno-Karabakh leader on September 25, 1993, helped pave the way for the ceasefire agreement later signed by Nagorno-Karabakh and Azerbaijan, with Armenia joining it. He added that the current Azerbaijani leadership was undermining the OSCE Minsk Group mediation process by making territorial claims against Armenia, which he said could trigger a new conflict. Kocharyan claimed such rhetoric was meant to preserve an authoritarian and corrupt regime by mobilizing society through anti-Armenian hatred. He warned that renewed adventurism would have tragic consequences, especially for Azerbaijan, and said real state strength comes from love for one’s own people, not hatred of a neighbor.

# Summary Armenian Deputy Foreign Minister Shavarsh Kocharyan disputed Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev's claim that Baku has established grounds for resolving the Nagorno Karabakh conflict. Kocharyan argued that Azerbaijan instead laid the foundation for military conflict through genocidal policies, mass killings of Armenians, ethnic cleansing, and large-scale military aggression against Nagorno Karabakh. Kocharyan identified only one genuine step toward resolution: a 1993 meeting between former Azerbaijani President Heydar Aliyev and Nagorno Karabakh's leader in Moscow, which led to a ceasefire agreement. He emphasized that Aliyev's recognition of Nagorno Karabakh as a negotiating party represented real progress. The Deputy Foreign Minister criticized the current Azerbaijani president for undermining the OSCE Minsk Group mediation process and making territorial claims on Armenian lands, which he characterized as laying groundwork for new conflict. Kocharyan attributed this aggressive stance to efforts to maintain the authoritarian regime by uniting Azerbaijani society through anti-Armenian sentiment. He warned that such bellicose policies would have tragic consequences, particularly for Azerbaijan, and concluded that state strength derives from citizens' welfare, not hatred toward neighbors.

Colombian officials had been quietly working for months to open a channel to U.S. President Donald Trump, even as President Gustavo Petro publicly traded harsh remarks with him, Colombia’s foreign minister Rosa Yolanda Villavicencio told the Mainichi Shimbun in an exclusive interview in Bogota. The backdrop was highly tense. Petro, a former leftist guerrilla member who took office in 2022, had repeatedly clashed with Trump over immigration, Gaza, and U.S. pressure on Venezuela. At the U.N. General Assembly last year, Petro called Trump an “accomplice to genocide” over the war in Gaza. Washington answered by revoking Petro’s U.S. visa and sanctioning him and his family, accusing them of worsening drug trafficking. In January, after the U.S. launched an operation against Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro on drugs and weapons charges, Trump called Petro a “sick man” tied to drug production and sales and suggested military action was possible. Petro responded that he would “take up arms for the homeland.” Despite the public confrontation, Colombia sought mediation through a wide network of intermediaries. Villavicencio said the effort involved contacts in the Vatican who could speak directly to Trump, as well as repeated trips to Europe and the Middle East. From October onward, Colombian officials also reached out to the United Arab Emirates, Egypt and Qatar, countries with ties to Trump. At the same time, the Colombian Embassy in Washington contacted influential Republicans close to the president. Those efforts culminated in a Jan. 7 phone call between Trump and Petro that lasted about an hour. Villavicencio said Colombia carefully explained its anti-drug efforts and seizures, countering accusations that it was ignoring cocaine production. Petro later said Trump acknowledged that false stories had been spread about him, just as they had about Trump himself. Villavicencio said dialogue was essential to changing Trump’s view. The two leaders are scheduled to meet in Washington on Feb. 3, with coca eradication expected to be a major topic.

# Colombia's Behind-the-Scenes Diplomacy Eases Tensions with Trump Colombia's President Gustavo Petro and U.S. President Donald Trump recently softened their hostile stances following months of quiet diplomatic efforts, according to Foreign Affairs Minister Rosa Yolanda Villavicencio in an exclusive interview. The two leaders had engaged in heated public exchanges over multiple issues, including forced deportation of immigrants and Trump's military operation targeting Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro. Petro, a former leftist guerrilla member, had criticized Trump as an "accomplice to genocide" regarding Gaza and condemned U.S. actions against Venezuela. Trump responded by revoking Petro's visa, imposing sanctions, and accusing him of drug trafficking. In January, Trump called Petro a "sick man" and threatened military action, while Petro countered by pledging to "take up arms for the homeland." Behind the scenes, however, Colombia pursued resolution through multiple channels. Villavicencio revealed that intermediaries included a papal aide with direct Trump access and influential Republicans. Colombia also conducted diplomatic missions across Europe, the Middle East, and countries with Trump connections, including the United Arab Emirates, Egypt, and Qatar. The strategy focused on clarifying misunderstandings about Colombia's drug-fighting efforts. A January 7 phone call between the leaders lasted approximately one hour, with Colombia detailing drug seizures and other counter-narcotics initiatives. Trump acknowledged that fabricated claims had been made about both himself and Petro, reportedly understanding the Colombian president's position. The diplomatic breakthrough appears to have succeeded because "Mr. Trump ultimately understood that easing tensions was important for the U.S. as well," Villavicencio explained. The leaders are scheduled to meet in Washington on February 3, with U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio coordinating the agenda. Eradicating coca leaf production is expected to be a central discussion point.

The article is a personal travel reflection by the author, who is in Madrid on a book tour for *Live Not By Lies* and has spent the day speaking with Spaniards about political and cultural trends in their country. The central focus is a conversation he had with a Venezuelan refugee, whom he calls “Ana” to protect her identity because her mother still lives in Caracas. Ana told him that reading the book deeply resonated with her because she sees similar warning signs in Spain that she once saw in socialist Venezuela. Ana said that the author’s discussion of “soft totalitarianism” reminded her of the way ideological movements ignore reality when it conflicts with their beliefs. She described how, in Venezuela, when people were seen eating from garbage bins, the socialist authorities did not address the poverty causing the problem; instead, they removed the garbage bins so the scene would disappear. To her, this reflected a deeper pattern: ideological purity mattered more than human suffering or practical solutions. The author connected this to his own criticism of woke ideology, citing an example of a columnist condemning Tom Hanks for not being “antiracist,” and Ana agreed that such ideologues create impossible standards that cannot be satisfied. In her view, the logic of this kind of thinking can become extreme enough to treat people as inherently wrong simply because they exist and do not fit the ideological ideal. As they walked and later stopped for coffee, Ana became visibly emotional. She trembled and cried while describing the psychological toll of having fled Venezuela and the fear that the same kind of collapse could happen again. She said she was exhausted from “running” and just wanted a normal life: marriage, a house, children, and stability. But she could not relax because she feared that the political and social dangers she escaped might follow her to Spain. She emphasized that she was among the fortunate ones because she could afford to leave by plane, whereas many others could not escape. Ana also told the author that many Spaniards do not believe their country could ever slide into dictatorship because Spain is part of the European Union. In her view, that confidence is dangerously naive. She believes liberty is eroding in Spain under a Socialist-Communist coalition government that includes actual Communists, and that people are too passive because they assume “it can’t happen here.” The author says this attitude mirrors the disbelief he has encountered among Americans when exiles from Communist regimes warn that current trends resemble the early stages of authoritarianism. Later, when he repeated Ana’s story to a larger group over coffee, a young woman said her husband works with two Venezuelans who say the same thing. The article ends by broadening the point: the author wonders whether Spanish media have paid attention to such warnings, just as he believes American media have largely ignored exiles from Communist countries who see parallels between their past and contemporary “woke” politics. He closes by urging readers to ask immigrants from Communist nations whether today’s developments in America remind them of what they left behind, and he references Yeonmi Park, a North Korean defector, as another example of someone warning that woke culture can resemble the oppressive logic of totalitarian systems.

# Summary: The Long Shadow of Hugo Chavez Rod Dreher, author of "Live Not By Lies," recounts a meaningful conversation with a Venezuelan refugee named "Ana" during a book tour in Madrid. The encounter highlights striking parallels between the ideological rigidity that destroyed Venezuela under socialism and the emergence of "woke" ideology in Western democracies. Ana fled Venezuela several years ago and escaped to Spain seeking refuge. She resonated deeply with Dreher's book because she recognizes the same patterns of soft totalitarianism developing in Spain that Eastern European émigrés have warned about in America. Like those refugees from Communist countries, Ana struggles with the fact that Spaniards dismiss her warnings about creeping authoritarianism, believing their EU membership and democratic institutions provide adequate protection. Ana identified a crucial characteristic of ideological extremism: its refusal to accommodate reality that contradicts its worldview. She illustrated this through Venezuela's response to widespread hunger—rather than adjusting their socialist policies to address starvation, the government removed garbage bins where desperate people were scavenging for food. The ideology remained pure while people suffered. This pattern, she argues, now manifests in Western wokeness, where ideological purity supersedes human welfare and practical reality. Dreher shared an example of Eric Deggans criticizing actor Tom Hanks for insufficient "antiracism." Ana recognized this as characteristic of totalitarian thinking: the demands are impossible to satisfy. No action can prove adequate because the problem isn't behavioral—it's existential. The person themselves becomes the problem simply by existing, making elimination the logical ideological conclusion. The conversation grew emotional as Ana discussed her exhaustion from fleeing and her desperate desire for normalcy—marriage, a house, children. She trembled while expressing her fear that the totalitarianism she escaped might follow her to Spain. Though she considers herself fortunate to have afforded escape, she emphasized that millions of Venezuelans lacked such resources. Ana expressed frustration with Spanish complacency. Citizens believe their European Union membership and democratic traditions immunize them against leftist dictatorship, failing to recognize how fragile democracy truly is. She observed that liberty is eroding daily under Spain's Socialist-Communist coalition government, yet people remain passively confident that such collapse "can't happen here." Later, Dreher mentioned Ana's story to a larger group, and a young woman immediately reported that her husband works with two Venezuelans who express identical concerns. This convergence suggests a pattern the author believes deserves greater media attention. Dreher concludes by urging readers to seek out and listen to immigrants from Communist countries. Their firsthand experience with totalitarian systems provides invaluable perspective on current Western developments. He references Yeonmi Park, a North Korean escapee who testified that Columbia University's woke ideology rivaled totalitarianism she experienced in her home country, arguing that dismissing such warnings represents dangerous foolishness.

Eladio Mena once lived a stable, prosperous life in Michoacan, Mexico. He owned a 200-acre ranch with 50 head of cattle, grew crops, and his wife sold cheese. His son also had begun building a separate income through a successful seafood restaurant. That life ended when the Jalisco New Generation Cartel moved into the area and tried to pull local residents into its conflict with rival groups, especially the Viagras. Mena said the cartel sought to recruit him and others as armed muscle, while also extorting money and stealing from people in the community. Mena refused to cooperate. He would not allow his land to be used for illegal crops or take up arms for the cartel. In response, the traffickers gave his family a deadline to leave. He said they fled at night to avoid cartel roadblocks. Now Mena, his wife, son, daughter-in-law, and two grandsons are staying in a migrant shelter in Juarez, waiting for a chance to seek asylum in the United States. He said they do not want to return to Michoacan because they have been threatened. Their case reflects a broader trend of Mexican families leaving rural areas increasingly dominated by cartel violence. U.S. Customs and Border Protection reported that encounters with Mexican citizens rose by more than 10,000 in February, reaching 71,210, compared with the previous month. By contrast, encounters involving citizens from Guatemala, Honduras, and El Salvador rose by 7,500 to 39,178. Overall unauthorized migration increased 7 percent in February, totaling 164,973. Mena said he is not willing to make an unauthorized and potentially dangerous crossing into the United States, especially since the government is not currently processing asylum claims at ports of entry. Instead, he remains in Juarez, where he has relatives in Sacramento who he hopes can help support the family once they are able to enter legally. He also fears telling too many details about his hometown or shelter location, because he still worries about cartel retaliation. He described Michoacan as a state torn apart over the past four years by multiple armed groups, including the Jalisco cartel, Familia Michoacana, Guerreros Unidos, Los Viagras, and vigilantes who have also become involved in profit-making violence. He said mayors and journalists have been killed, drones carrying explosives have been used in attacks, and cartels have extorted avocado growers. The Mexican army has even been sent to clear land mines planted by criminals near Aguililla. Mena said he has no faith in local authorities, whom he believes are colluding with criminals and warning cartels about complaints. He said the pressure on his family escalated from recruitment attempts to extortion demands, then threats against his son. Eventually, he said, the cartel took everything they had: their cattle, land, and livelihood. A relative drove them out in the middle of the night, and they left their home and possessions behind.

# Cartel Violence Drives Prosperous Mexican Families North Eladio Mena's story exemplifies a growing crisis in Mexico: drug cartel violence is displacing not just the poor, but successful farmers, ranchers, and business owners from the Mexican countryside. Mena previously lived a comfortable life in Michoacan, operating a 200-acre ranch with 50 cattle and diverse crops. His wife made and sold cheese while his son ran a successful seafood restaurant. This stability ended when the Jalisco New Generation Cartel arrived, seeking to recruit fighters for territorial battles against rival gangs like the Viagras and to extort money through forced "taxes" and theft. When Mena refused to allow the cartel to use his property for illegal crop cultivation or permit his son to join their violent operations, he faced immediate consequences. The cartel gave him limited time to leave and forced his family to flee at night to avoid roadblocks. Today, Mena, his wife, son, daughter-in-law, and two grandsons await asylum processing at a Juarez migrant shelter, having abandoned their entire livelihood. Their departure reflects a broader trend. According to U.S. Customs and Border Protection, encounters with Mexican citizens increased by over 10,000 in February to 71,210—surpassing the combined numbers from Guatemala, Honduras, and El Salvador. Overall unauthorized migration rose 7 percent that month, totaling 164,973 encounters. Mena prefers filing for asylum through official channels rather than crossing illegally, hoping to join relatives in Sacramento, California who can sponsor his family. However, U.S. ports of entry currently are not processing asylum claims, leaving him in limbo. Michoacan has become particularly violent. Over four years, the Jalisco cartel has fought multiple rival organizations including Familia Michoacana, Guerreros Unidos, and Los Viagras. The violence includes assassinations of mayors and journalists, drone attacks carrying explosives, and systematic extortion of avocado growers. The Mexican army recently deployed to remove land mines planted by criminals near Aguililla. Mena's distrust of Mexican authorities runs deep. He believes officials collaborate with criminals, sharing information with cartels and protecting their operations. He cannot safely report crimes without risking cartel retaliation. The cartel's control proved inescapable. Initial recruitment attempts were followed by extortion demands. When Mena resisted, enforcers—reportedly five or six local brothers paid by the cartel—threatened his son. Witnessing community members attacked and facing explicit warnings that he no longer had a place in his hometown, Mena concluded escape was his only option. In his final night, a relative drove the family away in darkness, leaving behind their cattle, land, and decades of accumulated wealth. Mena now waits for the U.S. border to reopen to asylum seekers, unwilling and unable to return to Michoacan due to ongoing threats.

In Guayaquil, Ecuador, the family of 23-year-old Jonathan Burbano is still searching for answers after he was killed in a prison massacre at Litoral Penitentiary in September 2021. Jonathan, who was serving a two-year sentence, died in one of the deadliest prison riots in Ecuador last year, when violence across the country’s prisons left 119 inmates dead in that single wave of unrest. His brother Alex Burbano said the family first learned of trouble on the morning of September 28, when they received an email warning that riots had broken out at Litoral. They spent the day waiting anxiously for news. Around 9 p.m., Jonathan managed to call them on WhatsApp, a common way prisoners communicate in Ecuador. He said he was safe, but his family could hear explosions and gunshots in the background. They never heard from him again. Later, witnesses told Alex that a grenade had exploded near Jonathan’s cell. An autopsy concluded that he died from a traumatic brain injury. Alex said it took authorities two days to confirm his brother’s death, in part because prison officials did not have accurate records of which inmates were held in which cells. He said armed groups inside the prison effectively controlled placement and movement, underscoring the state’s lack of authority. “The state has no control over anything,” he said, arguing that weapons and explosives entering prisons showed how little control officials had. Ecuador’s prison management system and interior ministry did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Unable to identify who directly killed his brother, Alex places responsibility on the Ecuadorian state. He has joined with relatives of other prisoners who died in the massacres to create the Committee of Families for Justice in Prisons, which is demanding reforms and accountability for what they describe as years of neglect. Alex said he is fighting because Jonathan, as a person in state custody, had rights that were violated. The government has acknowledged that around 400 prisoners have died in prison riots in Ecuador since February of last year, but families believe the real toll is higher because of continuing reports of violence and inmate assassinations. Billy Navarrete, director of the Committee for the Defense of Human Rights in Guayaquil, said the families’ organizing is an important step toward demanding accountability, restitution, and reparations. He said the crisis stems from decades of neglect, including a failure to invest in rehabilitation programs or train guards, allowing corruption to flourish in overcrowded prisons. Another family member, Kimberley, whose last name was withheld for safety, said she had been forced to pay more than $100 a month to criminal groups controlling her husband’s prison wing at Litoral for food, phone access, and other fees. Despite being unemployed and raising four children alone, she paid out of fear. Her husband was later strangled to death during a February 2021 riot. She said she hoped the killings would not go unpunished and urged President Guillermo Lasso to act. Lasso has blamed criminal groups controlling prisons and promised to strengthen intelligence and remove weapons, explosives, and other contraband. But rights groups including the UN, Amnesty International, and the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights have called for deeper reforms. Ecuador’s National Assembly and human rights secretariat have also issued extensive recommendations, but Navarrete said they have not been turned into action. Alex said families fear the violence has become routine and that no one is stopping it.

# Summary: Ecuador's Prison Crisis and Families Demanding Justice Ecuador faces a severe prison crisis marked by deadly riots and widespread violence, with grieving families now organizing to demand accountability from the state. The situation came into sharp focus through the story of Jonathan Burbano, a 23-year-old inmate killed during a September 2021 massacre at Guayaquil's Litoral Penitentiary that claimed 119 lives—one of the deadliest in a series of riots that year. Jonathan's brother Alex received an email warning of the riot and spoke briefly with Jonathan via WhatsApp that evening, but heard explosions and gunshots in the background. Jonathan never called again. Witnesses reported a grenade detonated near his cell, and an autopsy confirmed he died from traumatic brain injury. Authorities took two days to confirm his death because prison records were inadequate—armed groups inside the prison control cell assignments, not the state. The broader crisis is staggering. Ecuador's government acknowledges approximately 400 prisoner deaths from riots since February of the previous year, though families believe the actual number is significantly higher. The violence reflects decades of systemic failure: government neglect, inadequate investment in rehabilitation programs and guard training, overcrowding, and rampant corruption. In response, Alex Burbano and other families of deceased prisoners formed the Committee of Families for Justice in Prisons to demand reforms and state accountability. Another member, Kimberley, revealed the desperation families face—she paid criminal groups controlling her husband's prison wing over $100 monthly for basic necessities, despite being unemployed and raising four children alone. Her husband was strangled to death during a February 2021 riot. Human rights advocates support these families' efforts. Billy Navarrete, director of the Committee for the Defense of Human Rights in Guayaquil, emphasized that such advocacy is crucial for demanding accountability, restitution, and reparations. He attributes the crisis to long-standing government neglect and corruption flourishing in overcrowded facilities. President Guillermo Lasso has blamed criminal groups controlling prisons for the massacres and announced plans to strengthen prison intelligence and remove weapons and explosives. However, human rights organizations—including the United Nations, Amnesty International, and the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights—have called for comprehensive reforms. Ecuador's National Assembly special committee presented over 70 urgent recommendations, including rehabilitation system restructuring and dismantling criminal gangs. The human rights secretariat issued a nearly 200-page reform report in February. Yet these recommendations have not translated into meaningful action. Alex Burbano expressed the frustration felt by many: the prison riots have become normalized with no decisive leadership to stop the cycle. Families continue fighting for justice, accountability, and systemic change to prevent further tragedies in Ecuador's failing prison system.

Eight Brazilian food equipment and ingredient companies will take part in Gulfood Manufacturing, a food and beverage processing and packaging trade show in Dubai from November 8 to 10, through the Brasil Food Service project run by ApexBrasil and Abiepan. The companies selected are Ariete, Bralyx, IMG Brasil, Fortfrio, Glasart, G. Paniz, Prática and Skymsen. To prepare them for the event, the two organizations held an online warm-up session on Tuesday (25) with presentations from ApexBrasil business analyst Antonio Braga, Arab Brazilian Chamber of Commerce economist Sotirios Ghinis, and halal specialist Omar Chahine. Braga outlined business opportunities in Arab countries, describing the population and GDP of the 22 Middle East and North Africa nations and reviewing trade between Brazil and the region. He said trade with the Arab bloc reached USD 24.25 billion in 2021, the highest since 2014, with Brazilian exports totaling USD 14.42 billion, up 26%. That made the bloc Brazil’s third-largest export destination. He also noted strong regional demand for food-processing machinery, including ice cream equipment, baking machines, autoclaves, and similar products. He added that, while the United Arab Emirates is a relatively small market, it has become the main distribution and re-export hub in the region. Ghinis offered advice on doing business with Arab partners, stressing that negotiations should ideally involve executives of similar rank and that final decisions often rest with the Arab side. He also suggested culturally relevant conversation topics, such as the Arab diaspora in Brazil and football, and mentioned that consumption patterns change during periods such as Ramadan. Chahine focused on halal certification and the Muslim consumer market, which he said represents 24% of the world’s population. He explained that halal covers more than slaughter rules and includes broader ethical and legal standards. He said certification requires traceability, proper labeling and storage, and compliance with legislation and good manufacturing practices.
