Alan García, one of Peru’s most prominent and controversial political figures, died on Wednesday in Lima after shooting himself in the head as police arrived to arrest him over allegations of money laundering linked to a corruption investigation. He was 69. García’s political career spanned more than three decades. Born in 1949, he studied law at the University of San Marcos in Lima and earned a doctorate in Madrid. After returning to Peru in 1978, he joined the Constituent Assembly that helped draft the 1979 constitution, later served as a Lima deputy, and became secretary general of the Peruvian Aprista Party in 1982. That party carried him to the presidency in 1985. His first administration, from 1985 to 1990, was widely viewed as disastrous. Peru faced a severe economic collapse, inflation soared above 7,000 percent annually, and the Maoist Shining Path insurgency intensified. His government was also marked by the 1986 killing of more than 200 prisoners in three Lima prisons after a prison riot. In 1987, his attempt to nationalize the banking system triggered mass protests led by Mario Vargas Llosa. By the end of his term, García had become deeply discredited. In 1992, he sought refuge in the Colombian Embassy in Lima after being accused of illicit enrichment and ordering prisoner massacres. He then lived in exile in Colombia and France until 2001, when Peru’s Supreme Court ruled those alleged crimes had expired under the statute of limitations. Despite that past, García returned to power in 2006 after a strong ideological shift to the center-right. His later political decline continued, and in 2016 he won only 5% of the vote when seeking a third term. The corruption probe that ultimately led to his death centered on alleged Odebrecht payments.

# Summary Alan Garcia, a prominent Peruvian politician for 35 years, died on Wednesday from a self-inflicted gunshot wound as police arrived at his home to arrest him on money laundering charges. He was 69. Garcia's political career began in 1978 when he joined the Constituent Assembly drafting Peru's 1979 constitution. He became secretary general of the Peruvian Aprista Party in 1982 and was elected president in 1985 at age 36, earning the nickname "Crazy Horse." His first presidency (1985-1990) was widely considered disastrous. Peru faced severe economic crisis and terrorist attacks from Shining Path. In 1986, over 200 prisoners were massacinated in three Lima prisons during a riot response. A 1987 bank nationalization attempt sparked massive protests led by future Nobel laureate Mario Vargas Llosa. By 1990, hyperinflation exceeded 7,000 percent annually, destroying Garcia's credibility. Accused of illicit enrichment and ordering the prison massacre, Garcia fled to Colombia's embassy in Lima in 1992, then went into exile in Colombia and France until 2001, when Peru's Supreme Court declared the crimes prescribed. Garcia was reelected in 2006, shifting ideologically from left to right-wing economics. His 2016 presidential bid garnered only five percent of votes, prompting his resignation from the party and relocation to Spain. He returned to Peru in November to face corruption investigations regarding alleged payments from Brazilian construction company Odebrecht, leading to his fatal decision Wednesday.

Two Peruvian filmmakers, Miguel Araoz Cartagena and Stephanie Boyd, used their film *Karuara, People of the River* at the 55th IFFI in Goa to draw parallels between the struggle of Peru’s Kukama people to protect the Maranon river and Goa’s fight to save the Mhadei. While walking along Panaji’s Mandovi waterfront, the filmmakers said they “meet the river of every country” they visit and urged Goans to consider a legal strategy similar to the one used in Peru: seeking recognition of the Mhadei as a legal person with rights. Araoz said such recognition could help secure the river’s right to flow freely and shield it from dams and pollution. He also stressed that river protection is not only about water needs but about spirituality and cultural identity, saying the Kukama view natural places as mothers and wondering whether the Mhadei holds a similar significance for Goans. The film focuses on the Kukama community’s struggle to defend the Maranon river and its spiritual world from modern threats. Boyd described it as the story of a brave indigenous woman and her community resisting what she called cultural genocide. The filmmakers worked closely with Peru’s indigenous women’s federation, which filed four lawsuits to protect the river, including the key case seeking legal personhood for the Maranon. The documentary’s creation involved collecting elders’ stories, compiling 500 children’s paintings into a book, and using testimonies from indigenous people as legal evidence. The team chose traditional hand-drawn animation over computer graphics, requiring 24 drawings per second of film. The pandemic disrupted production, especially in the Amazon, where healthcare was limited and indigenous communities had to isolate themselves. Boyd said filming became impossible, but the pause allowed the team to continue animation work. Despite the setbacks, the filmmakers persevered over a decade, beginning in 2015 and completing the film after a victory in the appeal process this year. Through the documentary, they hope to strengthen the global movement for rivers to be recognized as living entities with rights.

# Peruvian Filmmakers Advocate for River Rights in Goa Two Peruvian filmmakers have suggested that Goa adopt legal strategies used by indigenous communities in Peru to protect their rivers. Miguel Araoz Cartagena and Stephanie Boyd created a documentary exploring the Kukama people's efforts to protect Peru's Maranon river in the Amazon. The filmmakers worked with an indigenous women's federation that filed four lawsuits, with the most significant seeking legal personhood for the Maranon river. This status would grant the river rights to flow freely and protection from dams and pollution. Cartagena recommended that Goans pursue similar legal recognition for the Mhadei river. Their film, "Karuara, People of the River," screened at the 55th International Film Festival of India, documents the indigenous community's struggle against cultural genocide and environmental threats. The filmmakers emphasized the spiritual significance of rivers to indigenous peoples, suggesting the Mhadei may hold similar sacred meaning. The documentary's production was unconventional, utilizing hand-drawn animation instead of computer graphics, requiring 24 drawings per second. The team gathered stories from community elders and collected 500 paintings by children, which served as evidence in the lawsuits alongside indigenous testimonies. The pandemic significantly impacted production, particularly affecting the Amazon region through healthcare shortages and high death rates. These challenges forced the team to focus on animation work rather than documentary filming. Despite beginning in 2015, the filmmakers completed the project after ten years and achieved a legal victory in an appeal this year. Through their film, Cartagena and Boyd aim to amplify voices advocating for rivers to be recognized as living entities with legal rights, offering a model for environmental protection worldwide.

A Court of Appeal hearing in Buenos Aires has taken place in a landmark universal jurisdiction case brought in Argentina over alleged repression, genocide and crimes against humanity committed against the Uyghur people by the Chinese government. The case was filed by Lawyers for Uyghur Rights, the Uyghur Human Rights Project (UHRP) and the World Uyghur Congress (WUC), after a prosecutor had previously decided to stay the proceedings on the mistaken belief that a related case was already underway in Turkey. According to Justice Abroad, the hearing marked the first time the Uyghur case had come before a criminal court. The complaint was first filed on August 16, 2022, in Buenos Aires under Article 118 of the Argentine Constitution, which allows Argentine courts to hear complaints involving international crimes. On August 4, 2023, the prosecutor concluded that because press reports suggested victims in Turkey were “filing a case” through a lawyer there, the Argentine proceedings should be paused. The victims then appealed that decision on November 14, 2023, challenging the stay ordered by the investigating judge on the basis of the prosecutor’s view. At the appeal hearing on Thursday, the victims’ side argued that there was no evidence the allegations raised in Argentina were actually being examined in Turkey. They also said that, under Turkish law, only the Justice Minister can initiate a case involving international crimes such as genocide and crimes against humanity, and that this had not happened. The argument was that the supposed Turkish proceedings were not a real or available alternative, so the Argentine case should be allowed to proceed. WUC President Dolkun Isa said on social media that he had testified at the Court of Appeal hearing on December 21, 2023, in the universal jurisdiction case in Argentina. In his opening statement, he emphasized Argentina’s unique role as a place where victims of international crimes can seek justice without political interference. He said the atrocities against Uyghurs are based on ethnicity and religion, and stressed that the victims in this case do not have a case before Turkish courts. He concluded by saying that when Argentina’s people and judiciary say “never again,” Uyghurs believe them, which is why they brought the complaint there. The release said this was the first time a Uyghur had addressed a court about the international crimes being committed against the group. The victims’ argument was backed by an amicus brief from Turkish constitutional lawyer Ali Yiildiz, who explained that Turkish legal rules give only the Justice Minister authority to bring such cases, that there was no evidence this had been done, and that any case was unlikely because of the close relationship between China and Turkey. Additional supporting amicus submissions were filed by the International Bar Association’s Human Rights Institute, represented by Ewelina Ochab and Argentine lawyer Roberto Durrieu, and by the Italian international justice NGO STRALI, represented by President Benedetta Perego and Head of International Criminal Law Tomas Manguel. Earlier, the University of Notre Dame’s Religious Liberty Initiative also submitted an amicus brief prepared by Lord Alton, former U.S. officials Sam Brownback and Kelley Currie, Uyghur American advocate Nury Turkel, and Frank Wolf. The lawyers representing WUC and UHRP include international law barrister Michael Polak, director of Justice Abroad and chair of Lawyers for Uyghur Rights, along with Argentine lawyers Gabriel Cavallo and Juan Nieto, both experienced in cases involving victims of international crimes in Argentina. They expressed hope that the Court of Appeal would find there were no open cases elsewhere and order the complaint to proceed, consistent with the prosecutor’s earlier determination that the complaint contained prima facie evidence of genocide and crimes against humanity. Polak said Dolkun Isa’s testimony was the first time a Uyghur had addressed a criminal court about the persecution of the Uyghur people. He said the case should be opened because the evidence and the prosecutor’s prior findings supported it, and argued that a decision to move forward would send a message that states and officials cannot rely on power or influence to escape accountability for the gravest crimes. Isa described the day as important in the history of accountability for Uyghurs, saying that two Uyghurs had addressed a criminal court for the first time in relation to the ongoing genocide in East Turkistan. UHRP Executive Director Omer Kanat added that Uyghurs deserve to have their case heard in court and said the proceedings showed there is nowhere to hide for regimes responsible for atrocity crimes. If some parts of the international community will not examine the evidence, he said, national courts must do so.

# Argentina Court Hears Appeal in Universal Jurisdiction Case Against Chinese Repression of Uyghurs On December 21, 2023, Argentina's Court of Appeal in Buenos Aires held a significant hearing in a universal jurisdiction case addressing allegations of repression and crimes against humanity committed against the Uyghur people by the Chinese government. This marked the first time a Uyghur case involving allegations of genocide and crimes against humanity came before a criminal court. ## Background and Legal Framework The case was filed by three organizations—Lawyers for Uyghur Rights, the Uyghur Human Rights Project (UHRP), and the World Uyghur Congress—under Argentina's universal jurisdiction provisions outlined in Article 118 of the Argentine Constitution. This constitutional provision allows Argentine courts to try cases involving international crimes regardless of where they occurred. The original criminal complaint was filed on August 16, 2022. ## Prosecutor's Decision and Appeal The case encountered a significant setback when the Prosecutor decided on August 4, 2023, to stay proceedings. The Prosecutor's reasoning was based on press reports suggesting that victims had filed a case in Turkey through their lawyer. However, on November 14, 2023, the victims appealed this decision, challenging the Prosecutor's grounds for dismissal. ## Arguments Presented at Hearing During the December 21 hearing, the victims' legal team argued that there was no concrete evidence that facts presented in the Argentine case were being considered in Turkish courts. They emphasized that under Turkish law, only the Justice Minister can initiate cases involving international crimes such as crimes against humanity and genocide, and no such action had occurred. This argument was bolstered by an amicus brief from Turkish Constitutional lawyer Ali Yilldiz, who explained Turkey's legal requirements and noted that it was highly unlikely Turkey would pursue such a case given China and Turkey's close diplomatic relationship. ## Historic Testimony A particularly significant moment came when Dolkun Isa, President of the World Uyghur Congress, testified before the court. In his opening statement, he emphasized Argentina's unique position as a place where victims of international crimes could seek justice against dictatorial regimes without political obstacles. He stressed that the atrocities against Uyghurs were motivated by ethnicity and religion, and concluded by invoking Argentina's historical commitment to accountability: "When the people and judiciary of Argentina say never again, we believe them. That is why we filed a complaint, and why we did so in Argentina." This testimony was historic—the first time a Uyghur had addressed a criminal court regarding international crimes committed against their people. ## Supporting Evidence The case received substantial international support through multiple amicus briefs. The International Bar Association's Human Rights Institute, the Italian international justice NGO STRALI, and the University of Notre Dame's Religious Liberty Initiative all submitted briefs supporting the case. The Notre Dame brief was signed by prominent figures including Lord Alton, former US Ambassador Sam Brownback, and Nury Turkel, a Uyghur American human rights advocate. ## Legal Representation and Expectations The victims' legal team included international law barrister Michael Polak, Director of Justice Abroad, alongside experienced Argentine lawyers Gabriel Cavallo and Juan Nieto, who have previously secured justice for victims of international crimes in Argentine courts. The legal team expressed hope that the Court of Appeal would determine no open cases exist on this matter and order the case's opening, consistent with the Prosecutor's earlier finding that the complaint contained prima facie evidence of crimes against humanity and genocide. ## Significance and Future Outlook Both Dolkun Isa and UHRP Executive Director Omer Kanat characterized the hearing as an important step toward accountability. Kanat emphasized that if parts of the international community remain unwilling to examine evidence, national courts must adjudicate atrocity crimes. The case represents a potential avenue for justice when international mechanisms prove insufficient, with the Court of Appeal's decision pending.

A major police raid in Rio de Janeiro’s Complexo do Alemao favela left at least 18 people dead and triggered fresh accusations that authorities are using excessive force in poor, predominantly Black communities. Rio officials said the dead included 16 suspected criminals, one police officer, and one woman. The operation targeted a criminal gang accused of stealing cars, robbing banks, and moving into nearby neighborhoods. The raid unfolded in one of Rio’s largest and most densely populated favela complexes, home to about 70,000 people across 13 communities. Social media videos showed heavy gunfire and a police helicopter flying low over rows of small brick houses. Police in Rio have often used helicopters during raids, including in residential areas, and video from the scene showed shots being fired from the favela toward the aircraft. At the scene, AP reporters saw residents carrying about 10 bodies while people shouted, “We want peace!” One woman, speaking anonymously for fear of retaliation, described the event as “a massacre inside, which police are calling an operation.” She said residents were being prevented from helping the wounded and claimed one man was arrested for trying to do so. Police investigator Ronaldo Oliveira said officers would have preferred to make arrests, but the suspects allegedly opened fire on police first. The operation began before dawn and ended around 4 p.m., with nearly 400 officers involved, including Rio’s tactical police unit. The raid quickly became a political flashpoint. Rio Governor Cláudio Castro, who is seeking reelection in October, expressed grief over the slain police officer and vowed to continue fighting crime. He also attacked his main election rival, leftist Marcelo Freixo, accusing him of defending criminals. Freixo replied that Castro was using police violence for political gain. Federal lawmaker Talíria Petrone condemned what she called a “genocidal policy,” arguing that the current public security strategy is leaving both residents and police dead. The incident renewed criticism of Rio’s long-running, militarized approach to crime, which frequently involves deadly raids in favelas. In May, a similar operation in Rio’s Vila Cruzeiro favela killed more than 20 people. The issue is especially sensitive ahead of Brazil’s October elections, when security is a major theme and President Jair Bolsonaro is campaigning on a tough-on-crime message. Security experts also condemned the raid. Robert Muggah of the Igarapé Institute said the operation reflected “failed leadership” and an institutional culture that tolerates excessive force. He argued such raids are ineffective, counterproductive, and disproportionately harm low-income Black residents while damaging trust between communities and police. The raid also comes after Brazil’s Supreme Court imposed conditions earlier this year on police operations in Rio favelas, requiring lethal force only when all other options are exhausted and only to protect life. Those restrictions followed the 2021 Jacarezinho raid, in which 28 people were killed and an officer died. Community outlet Voz da Comunidade showed residents waving white cloths and calling for peace from windows and rooftops. Police official Fabrício Oliveira warned that Friday could bring more violence, saying raids often lead to retaliatory attacks on police. Amnesty International called for an immediate investigation into the officers involved and denounced the operation as brutal and rights-violating.

# Police Raid in Rio Favela Kills 18, Sparks Violence Debate A police raid on Rio de Janeiro's Complexo do Alemao favela resulted in at least 18 deaths, reigniting controversy over excessive police force in Brazil's largest slum complex and intensifying debate ahead of state and presidential elections scheduled for October. Rio authorities reported that 16 suspected criminals were killed during confrontations with police, along with one police officer and one civilian woman. The operation targeted a criminal organization responsible for car thefts, bank robberies, and invasions of neighboring communities. Nearly 400 police officers, including tactical units, conducted the raid, which lasted from dawn until approximately 4 p.m. Social media videos documented intense gunfire exchanges and a police helicopter flying low over the densely populated residential area. The helicopter engaged in direct fire, with footage showing shots being returned from the favela. Associated Press reporters witnessed residents carrying approximately 10 bodies while bystanders pleaded for peace. Residents disputed official accounts, with one woman describing the operation as "a massacre" and reporting that authorities prevented people from assisting victims. Police investigator Ronaldo Oliveira justified the violence, stating that suspects "chose to fire at our policemen" rather than submit to arrest. The raid has become a political flashpoint. Governor Cláudio Castro, seeking reelection, used the incident to attack his leftist rival Marcelo Freixo, accusing him of defending criminals who attack police. Freixo countered that Castro "uses police to make politics." Federal lawmaker Talíria Petrone condemned the operation as part of a "genocidal policy" that disproportionately affects Black residents and favela communities. This operation mirrors a May raid on Vila Cruzeiro favela that killed over 20 people, reflecting Rio's militarized policing strategy. The approach has drawn substantial criticism from human rights organizations and security experts. Robert Muggah, co-founder of the Igarapé Institute think tank, characterized the raid as "a symptom of failed leadership" and warned that militarized policing is "not only ineffective, it is counterproductive." Amnesty International called for immediate prosecution of officers involved and demanded an end to Castro's "rights violating public security policies." The raid occurred despite Brazil's Supreme Court establishing conditions for favela operations in response to a 2021 Jacarezinho raid that killed 28 people. The court mandated that lethal force be used only as a last resort when necessary to protect life. Observers questioned whether Thursday's operation adhered to these guidelines. Complexo do Alemao comprises 13 favelas housing approximately 70,000 residents, nearly three-quarters of whom are Black or biracial. Police coordinator Fabrício Oliveira warned that Friday could bring additional violence, citing patterns of retaliation following such operations. The incident underscores tensions between security concerns and human rights protections, with security becoming a central election issue as President Jair Bolsonaro campaigns on tough-on-crime policies.

Hundreds of residents marched in one of Rio de Janeiro’s poorest neighborhoods over the weekend to protest violence in the city after an 8-year-old girl was killed by a stray bullet during a police operation. The Saturday rally in Complexo do Alemao included chants of “Justice! Justice!” and followed the death of Agatha Sales Felix, who was shot on Friday amid what police described as a shootout with suspected criminals. Police said officers were in a corner when they came under attack from several directions and returned fire. Officials confirmed the girl’s death and said an investigation had been opened. According to the police account cited by the Associated Press, no one else was reported injured or arrested in the incident. Many residents, however, blamed police for Felix’s death. One resident, Renata Trajana, told AP that there was no shootout when Agatha was hit and said people in the community know the violence taking place there. Amnesty International also condemned the killing, accusing Rio’s authorities of failing to protect life and questioning a public security policy that, it said, violates the right to life, especially for poor and Black residents. The case comes amid a sharp rise in police killings in Rio de Janeiro state under Governor Wilson Witzel. Police killed 1,249 people in the first seven months of the year, more than five a day, according to the state’s Public Security Institute, marking a more than 16 percent increase from the same period in 2018 and the highest level since records began in 2003. The article also notes a growing number of stray-bullet deaths, with 225 last year and more than 100 this year so far, according to violence monitor Crossfire. Witzel has previously vowed a hardline crackdown on crime and drug gangs.

# Summary Hundreds of residents in Rio de Janeiro's Complexo do Alemao favela protested Saturday following the death of eight-year-old Agatha Sales Felix, who was killed by a stray bullet during a police operation on Friday. The girl's death has intensified concerns about violence in Brazil's poorest neighborhoods. Police claimed officers were attacked from multiple directions and returned fire, with no other injuries or arrests reported. However, residents disputed this account, with some asserting there was no actual shootout when Agatha was struck. Local resident Renata Trajana criticized police conduct, citing ongoing atrocities in the community. Amnesty International condemned the killing, accusing Rio's authorities of failing their constitutional duty to protect life and questioning the state's public security policy that has allegedly violated citizens' right to life. The incident reflects a broader crisis in Rio de Janeiro state, where police killings have surged dramatically under Governor Wilson Witzel. In the first seven months of 2019, police killed 1,249 people—more than five daily—representing a 16 percent increase compared to the same 2018 period. This marks the highest police lethality rate since records began in 2003. Poor and Black citizens are disproportionately affected by these killings. Additionally, stray bullet deaths—fired by both criminals and police—have increased, with 225 deaths recorded last year and over 100 so far in 2019. Witzel, who took office in January, promised aggressive action against criminals, including using helicopter-mounted snipers, though critics argue his policies have intensified violence rather than reduced it.

A senior UN human rights official said Wednesday that rape, killings and other violence are still affecting Darfur, despite Sudanese claims that the conflict there has ended. Aristide Nononsi, the UN expert on Sudan, said after visiting parts of Darfur that the region remains troubled by banditry, armed robbery, assaults, killings, rape and clashes between communities over farmland. He said the overall situation may appear calm, but incidents continue and are worsened by impunity, weak rule of law and fragile justice institutions. Nononsi cited reports of nine rapes in the Sortoni displaced persons’ camp between January 27 and February 18, noting that many more cases likely go unreported because victims fear retaliation. He said inter-communal violence has become a major feature of the conflict. Darfur’s war began in 2003 when rebel groups rose up against President Omar al-Bashir’s government, accusing it of marginalization. The conflict has displaced more than 2.5 million people and killed about 300,000, according to the UN. Nononsi also urged Sudan to free activists detained without charge, including university professor Mudawi Ibrahim Adam, who is on hunger strike. He expressed concern over arrests and prolonged detention of civil society members by Sudan’s intelligence service.

# Summary A UN human rights expert reported that rape and inter-communal killings continue in Sudan's Darfur region despite claims by Sudanese officials that the conflict has ended. After touring parts of Darfur, Aristide Nononsi documented ongoing violent incidents including banditry, armed robbery, assault, and rape, with nine cases reported in one displaced persons' camp between January and February. He attributed the persistence of violence to weak rule of law and widespread impunity. The Darfur conflict began in 2003 when ethnic minority rebels rebelled against the Arab-dominated government, citing marginalization. The war has displaced over 2.5 million people and killed approximately 300,000 according to UN figures. Nononsi criticized Sudan's government for arbitrary detentions of activists and civil society members, including a university professor held without charge since December. He urged authorities to release detainees and address harassment by the National Intelligence and Security Service. These arrests followed a government crackdown on protests against fuel price increases.

Congolese women and children have been raped and otherwise abused during a new wave of mass expulsions of migrant workers from Angola into the Democratic Republic of Congo, according to a doctor, local officials, and the United Nations. The exact scale of the latest crackdown is unclear, but UN migration agency figures show that 12,000 workers passed through a border crossing near Kamako in the past six months. Angola has deported thousands of workers in recent months, continuing a pattern of periodic mass expulsions that rights groups and the UN say have repeatedly been accompanied by abuse. A preliminary internal UN report, seen by Reuters, said that women and girls were being arrested, detained without basic needs, separated from their families, and sometimes raped. The report did not identify the perpetrators. A doctor working in Kamako blamed both civilians in Congo and Angolan security forces for the violence. The Angolan migration authority rejected the allegations. Spokesman Simão Milagres said there had been a recent increase in expulsions but denied that rapes or other abuses were occurring. He insisted there was no institutional policy encouraging violence against migrants. In Kamako, however, Dr. Victor Mikobi, who treats sexual violence victims, said local clinics had recorded 122 rape cases this year, an unprecedented number for the town. He said many of the victims were women and girls expelled from Angola, some younger than 10, left without resources and highly vulnerable. He added that gang rape had caused serious medical complications. Based on patient accounts, he estimated that at least 14 rapes were committed by Angolan security forces and dozens more by civilians in Congo. A Congolese immigration official, speaking anonymously, said officials had discussed dozens of rapes on both sides of the border. The governor of Kasai region, Dieudonne Pieme Tutokot, said he was aware of the allegations and had launched an investigation. Angola’s Lunda Norte region, rich in diamonds, has long drawn migrant workers from Congo’s impoverished south, many of them undocumented. The UN report said only 20% of those expelled had permits. The IOM’s Congo mission described Kamako as an “open-air migrant camp,” while civil society leaders said Congolese workers often occupy villages in Angola, fueling resentment. Angola says it is trying to encourage legal migration through an online visa system. Mass deportations have recurred for years: in 2018, 330,000 workers were expelled, and in 2010 the UN estimated that more than 650 people suffered sexual violence during similar operations.

# Summary: Migrant Workers Face Abuse During Angola's Mass Expulsion Angola has been deporting thousands of migrant workers to the Democratic Republic of Congo in recent months, with reports documenting widespread sexual violence and abuse against women and children during the process. Approximately 12,000 workers have crossed through a single border crossing near Kamako in the past six months, according to the International Organization for Migration (IOM). A preliminary UN report, based on staff visits to the area, documented cases of girls and women being arrested without proper procedures, separated from families, subjected to inhuman treatment, and raped. However, the report did not specify perpetrators. A local doctor treating sexual violence victims blamed both Congolese civilians and Angolan security forces. Dr. Victor Mikobi, who works at a health center in Kamako, reported an unprecedented 122 rape cases this year, many involving girls under 10 years old. He estimated at least 14 rapes were committed by Angolan security forces, with dozens more perpetrated by Congolese civilians. Gang rapes have caused serious medical complications for victims. Angola's migration authority spokesperson Simão Milagres denied that institutional violence occurred, attributing the expulsion increase to efforts promoting legal migration through an online visa system. He noted that only 20% of deported workers had proper permits. The Congolese governor of Kasai region acknowledged awareness of rape incidents and opened an investigation. A Congolese immigration official reported that officials discussed dozens of rapes on both sides of the border but lacked resources to respond effectively. This pattern reflects historical precedent: Angola conducted mass deportations in 2018, expelling 330,000 workers, and in 2010, the UN documented over 650 sexual violence cases during a two-month expulsion period. The IOM's Congo mission head described Kamako as an "open-air migrant camp." Local civil society leaders attributed the crackdowns to Angolan concerns about population displacement, as many Congolese illegally occupy villages in Angola's diamond-rich Lunda Norte region, seeking economic opportunities in the wealthier country.

Rwanda on Thursday rejected criticism from the Democratic Republic of Congo over its sponsorship deals with Arsenal, Bayern Munich and Paris Saint-Germain, saying the attacks threatened regional peace and stability. Earlier this month, Congolese foreign minister Therese Kayikwamba Wagner urged the three clubs to end what she called “blood-stained” partnerships with Rwanda’s “Visit Rwanda” campaign, arguing that the deals were morally unacceptable while fighting continued in eastern Congo. The dispute comes amid a major escalation in the long-running conflict in eastern DRC, where Rwanda-backed M23 rebels have captured key territory in recent weeks. The war is rooted in the spillover of Rwanda’s 1994 genocide into Congo and the struggle over the region’s mineral wealth. Rwanda’s Development Board, which oversees the sponsorships, said Congo was trying to damage Rwanda’s international partnerships through “misinformation and political pressure.” It said such efforts misrepresented the situation and undermined peace, stability and economic cooperation. The conflict has been linked by the United Nations to serious abuses, including summary executions, attacks on displacement camps, and rape and other sexual violence. Rwanda says it is acting in self-defense and accuses Congo’s army of working with Hutu militias hostile to Tutsis. “Visit Rwanda” has sponsored Arsenal since 2018, Bayern since 2023, and PSG since 2019.

# Summary Rwanda has rejected criticism from the Democratic Republic of Congo regarding sponsorship deals between Rwanda's tourism board "Visit Rwanda" and three major football clubs: Arsenal, Bayern Munich, and Paris St Germain. The DRC's foreign minister recently called these agreements "blood-stained," questioning their morality amid ongoing conflict in eastern Congo. The dispute occurs against a backdrop of escalating violence in eastern Congo, where Rwanda-backed M23 rebels have made significant territorial gains in recent weeks—marking the worst escalation in over a decade. The conflict stems from Rwanda's 1994 genocide spillover and competition for Congo's mineral resources. Rwanda's Development Board stated that the DRC's criticism misrepresents facts and threatens regional peace and stability. Meanwhile, the UN has documented serious human rights violations in the fighting, including summary executions, camp bombings, and sexual violence. Rwanda claims it is defending itself against Congo's military and ethnic Hutu militias threatening Tutsis. The sponsorships began in 2018 (Arsenal), 2019 (PSG), and 2023 (Bayern Munich), with Arsenal's deal reportedly worth over $12 million annually.

A major blackout struck most of Tanzania on Saturday as Cyclone Hidaya brought heavy rain and strong winds to the country’s coast. Ferry services between Dar es Salaam and Zanzibar were suspended as the storm approached with maximum winds of 120 kph and powerful gusts. Authorities urged residents to stay cautious as the cyclone intensified, while the weather service reported unusually heavy overnight rainfall in coastal areas. The Tanzania Red Cross Society had been running preparedness campaigns along the coast. The storm came after weeks of flooding across Tanzania and East Africa that have killed about 155 people and affected more than 200,000 others, officials said.

# Summary Cyclone Hidaya has severely impacted Tanzania, causing widespread power blackouts across the country on Saturday. The storm brings maximum winds of 120 kph and heavy rainfall to the East African coast. Ferry services between Dar es Salaam and Zanzibar have been suspended as authorities warn residents to exercise caution. This cyclone follows weeks of regional flooding that have already claimed 155 lives and affected over 200,000 people. The Roman Catholic Diocese of Alexandria in central Louisiana has filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection, citing the financial strain of clergy sexual abuse claims. In a statement released Friday, the diocese said it has joined more than 40 Catholic institutions in the United States that have sought bankruptcy protection amid the broader church abuse scandal. Penn State Law has noted that 28 of those cases have already been resolved, underscoring how common bankruptcy has become as a result of abuse-related liabilities. Bishop Robert W. Marshall, who has led the diocese since August 2020, said the filing was necessary because claims tied to past priest-perpetrators “exceed our means.” In a letter to the faithful, he described the abuse as “evil” and “sinful,” and said the diocese has two main goals in filing: to compensate survivors as fairly as possible and to preserve essential church ministries for parishes and people who depend on diocesan support. The move follows earlier reporting that Alexandria was considering bankruptcy, especially after the neighboring Archdiocese of New Orleans filed for protection in 2020. That New Orleans case recently reached a major milestone: on Thursday, victims of clergy sexual abuse overwhelmingly approved a $230 million settlement. Although the official results were not due until November 6, court filings showed 99.63% of voting claimants backed the deal. The New Orleans settlement also includes the release of files on certain abusive priests and deacons and new safeguards for children and vulnerable adults. A small group of bond investors opposed the settlement, alleging securities fraud over unpaid interest on church bonds.

# Louisiana Diocese Files for Bankruptcy Over Clergy Abuse Claims The Diocese of Alexandria in central Louisiana has filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection, becoming part of a growing trend among U.S. Catholic institutions facing clergy sexual abuse claims. This filing brings the total number of American Catholic dioceses that have declared federal bankruptcy to over 40, with 28 having already concluded their proceedings, according to Penn State's law school. Bishop Robert W. Marshall announced the decision Friday, stating that the diocese filed due to numerous clergy sexual abuse claims exceeding its financial capacity. In his statement, Marshall acknowledged that past priests sexually abused minors, describing these actions as "evil" and contrary to church values. The diocese aims to compensate victims fairly while maintaining essential ministries. The Alexandria diocese joins the Archdiocese of New Orleans, which filed for bankruptcy in 2020. Recently, New Orleans achieved a significant milestone when victims overwhelmingly approved a $230 million bankruptcy settlement on Thursday. Though official results were not scheduled for announcement until November 6, unofficial returns showed approximately 99.63% acceptance among voters. The New Orleans settlement includes provisions to release files on abusive priests and deacons and establishes protections for children and vulnerable adults. However, a small group of bond investors opposed the settlement, alleging the archdiocese committed securities fraud by withholding promised interest payments.

A Libyan court in Tripoli postponed the trial of 23 former Gaddafi-era officials after the first defendant, Saif Al-Gaddafi, failed to appear at Sunday’s session in al-Hadba prison. The judge rescheduled proceedings for Nov. 16. The defendants face charges including corruption, genocide, incitement to rape, and ordering attacks on protesters.

# Trial of Gaddafi Officials Postponed A Libyan court postponed the trial of 23 officials who served under former leader Muammar Gaddafi. The proceeding, held at Tripoli's al-Hadba prison, was rescheduled to November 16 after Saif Al-Gaddafi failed to appear. Defendants face charges including crimes against humanity, corruption, genocide, and incitement to rape related to the 2011 uprising.

A Bangkok Criminal Court sentenced 43-year-old Samruai Chitchuen to 10 years and 8 months in prison after he confessed to raping a 12-year-old girl in an abandoned building earlier this year. He had originally received a 21-year-and-4-month sentence, which was reduced because of his admission. The attack took place on the night of Feb. 13, when Samruai approached the girl and her younger sister near their apartment and lured them out by offering to buy snacks. He sent the younger sister home, took the victim to a vacant seven-storey building, and raped her after she tried to escape. He later dropped her off near Ramkhamhaeng Soi 68. Police arrested him on Feb. 17 after a three-day search.

# Summary A 43-year-old Thai man, Samruai Chitchuen, has been sentenced to 10 years and eight months in prison for raping a 12-year-old girl in Bangkok. The attack occurred on February 13 in an abandoned seven-storey building. Samruai lured the girl away from her younger sister under the pretense of buying snacks, then took her to the building where he assaulted her. When she attempted to escape, he recaptured her. He later abandoned her near her apartment. Police arrested him three days later on February 17 after a medical examination confirmed sexual assault. His initial sentence of 21 years and four months was reduced due to his confession.

An International Kashmir Seminar opened in Islamabad on a strong note, with participants urging the world to stop remaining silent on Kashmir and to support the people’s right to self-determination. The two-day event was organized by the Mirpur University of Science and Technology to discuss the global dimensions of the Kashmir dispute and what speakers described as Indian efforts to suppress the liberation movement. Speakers said Kashmir is the oldest dispute on the UN agenda and accused the United Nations of failing to implement its resolutions. They argued that resolving the issue according to the wishes of the Kashmiri people is essential for peace and stability in South Asia. They also voiced alarm over India’s reported plans to alter the demographic makeup of occupied Kashmir. The seminar condemned the continued detention of prominent Hurriyet leaders, including Syed Ali Gilani, Mirwaiz Umar Farooq, and Muhammad Yasin Malik, and paid tribute to Kashmiri martyrs. Among the participants were Azad Jammu and Kashmir President Sardar Muhammad Yaqoob Khan, Raja Zafarul Haq, Sheikh Tajammul-ul-Islam, Dr Habibur Rehman, Dr Atia Anayatullah, Dr Muhammad Khan, Mushaal Malick, Abdur Rasheed Turabi, Agha Syed Hassan Al-Moosvi Al-Safvi, Zafar Akbar Butt, Ghulam Muhammad Safi, and MEP Amjad Bashir. Syed Ali Gilani addressed the gathering from Srinagar via video link, and the university awarded him an honorary Doctorate of Letters. The participants also prayed for the recovery of Pakistani Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif. Separately, Kashmir Media Service reported that Indian troops killed 21 Kashmiris in May, injured 71, arrested 591 civilians, disgraced four women, and destroyed four homes. A shutdown was observed in Doda, while authorities blocked Kashmir University students from holding a seminar on the Shopian rape and murder victims. In Baltimore, Dr Ghulam Nabi Fai told a Kashmir panel that Kashmiris alone would decide their political future.

An Australian church committee is preparing to recommend major governance changes that would give lay professionals control over key administrative areas of the Catholic Church in Australia. Jack de Groot, a member of the six-person review committee, said the draft plan would shift authority over financial, human resources and governance functions from bishops to laity with professional expertise. The committee was created in May 2018 by the Australian Catholic Bishops’ Conference and Catholic Religious Australia and is expected to present its recommendations by late March. The proposal is part of the Catholic Church’s response to Australia’s Royal Commission Into Institutional Child Sexual Abuse, which documented widespread abuse in religious and secular institutions, including Catholic schools and orphanages. The commission concluded that the Catholic Church was the worst offender among Australian denominations. Since then, the church has paid hundreds of millions of dollars in compensation, and many offenders, including clergy, have been jailed. The government also launched a National Redress Scheme in June 2018 to support and compensate survivors. Church leaders say they are acting on the commission’s recommendations issued in August 2017. In a mid-December progress report, Archbishop Mark Coleridge said the past year had brought “steady and significant progress” in education, governance reform and responding to victims, while stressing the need for strong safeguarding systems and swift action on allegations. De Groot said governance reform is now the church’s top priority. The review was delayed from an earlier October target because the church had to complete an update to the Australian government on its response to the commission. The committee is chaired by Justice Neville Owen, a former senior Western Australian judge and former chair of the Truth, Justice and Healing Council.

# Summary A six-person committee in Australia is preparing to recommend significant governance reforms to the country's Catholic bishops. The plan would transfer control of financial, human resources, and governance functions from church leadership to professional lay members, according to committee member Jack de Groot. Established in May 2018 by the Australian Catholic Bishops' Conference and Catholic Religious Australia, the committee expects to present its recommendations by late March. The governance review, chaired by former judge Justice Neville Owen, represents the church's key priority. These reforms are part of the Australian Catholic Church's broader response to the Royal Commission Into Institutional Child Sexual Abuse, which documented extensive abuse in religious and secular organizations. The commission identified the Catholic Church as the worst offender among Australian institutions, leading to hundreds of millions in victim compensation and dozens of imprisoned offenders, including clergy members. Since the commission's recommendations in August 2017, the church has implemented various reforms across education, governance, and victim support. The government established the National Redress Scheme in June 2018 to provide compensation to survivors, though many continue pursuing legal action. Archbishop Mark Coleridge, president of the bishops' conference, acknowledged progress while emphasizing the need for continued vigilance and strong protocols. The governance review was originally scheduled for October but was delayed to allow completion of an update to the government on the church's compliance with Royal Commission recommendations.

Thailand reported only two new Covid-19 cases on May 12, raising the national total to 3,017, with no new deaths and the toll remaining at 56. The new infections were a 19-year-old woman in Bangkok and a 51-year-old Thai woman from Narathiwat; both had been living with previously confirmed cases. One of the more unusual stories involved a Phuket bus driver who returned to Trang after leaving the holiday island in the mass exodus of about 50,000 people seeking work elsewhere. When he was placed in a government quarantine facility at a temple, he discovered that a coffin was being kept in the same room beside his bed. Officials said the monks had long stored the coffin there because the temple lacked space. After he posted about the situation on social media, authorities allowed him to complete his quarantine at home. In Mukdahan province, a 16-year-old girl has now come forward in a school rape investigation, adding to allegations against teachers already accused in the assault of a 14-year-old student. Three teachers may also face charges over the sexual assault of the older girl. Both victims were reportedly abused repeatedly over a one-year period beginning in March 2019. The school has suspended five teachers accused of repeated sexual assaults against the younger girl. The 16-year-old, from the same school, is serving as a witness in the first gang rape case. Police say they have already gathered incriminating evidence, and the girls’ accounts are said to corroborate one another. On Koh Samui, police arrested 24 people during a raid on the La Bohemia bar, including 22 foreigners and two Thai nationals. They were charged with violating the emergency decree, which bans alcohol sales in restaurants and prohibits gatherings. Among those detained was a 24-year-old Frenchman identified as the bar owner, along with three Burmese men working as waiters, only one of whom had a work permit. Thailand is also preparing for its next round of business reopenings, expected on Sunday. The provisional list includes shopping malls, community malls, bowling alleys, fitness clubs, amusement parks, beauty salons offering hair-curling, dyeing and nail services, eateries in office buildings, beauty and weight loss clinics, outdoor team sports without spectators, public gardens, galleries and Thai foot massage parlours. Movie theatres and beaches are not included yet. Finally, a dog rescued from Thailand’s illegal meat trade won attention on Britain’s Got Talent. Miracle, once shown crushed in a cage with other dogs, is now healthy and energetic six years after being rescued. His owner, Scottish woman Amanda Leask, now cares for 40 dogs, including 19 rescues. During the performance, Miracle performed a magic trick, but it was his backstory that moved the audience and even prompted judge Simon Cowell to tear up.

The Philippines, through the Maritime Industry Authority (Marina), joined the 9th Session of the Sub-Committee on Human Element, Training and Watchkeeping (HTW) at the International Maritime Organization headquarters in London from Feb. 6 to 10. Marina said the conference focused on maritime training, certification, and the updating of IMO model courses, while also addressing exhaustion, bullying, harassment, sexual assault, and sexual harassment in the maritime sector. Marina Administrator Hernani Fabia represented the country in discussions on several agenda items, including implementation of the 1978 STCW Convention, the comprehensive review of the STCW Convention and Code, the review of the 1995 STCW-F Convention, and Philippine measures against fraudulent certificates. In a separate meeting with IMO Secretary-General Kitack Lim, Fabia discussed Philippine efforts to protect Filipino seafarers’ interests under the STCW Convention and thanked the IMO for its technical cooperation. Lim said the organization would continue assisting the Philippines and encouraged its support for IMO work on maritime safety and marine environmental protection.

# Summary The Philippines' Maritime Industry Authority (Marina) led a delegation to the 9th Session of the Sub-Committee on Human Element, Training and Watchkeeping at the International Maritime Organization headquarters in London from February 6-10. The conference provided maritime training and certification updates while addressing workplace issues including harassment, bullying, and sexual assault in the maritime sector. Marina Administrator Hernani Fabia discussed the nation's positions on several agenda items, including the Standards of Training, Certification and Watchkeeping Convention implementation and measures to combat fraudulent certificates. During a separate meeting with IMO Secretary-General Kitack Lim, Fabia highlighted the Philippines' support for Filipino seafarers and expressed gratitude for the organization's technical assistance through its Integrated Technical Cooperation Programme. The IMO committed to continuing support for maritime safety and environmental protection efforts.

Authorities said six of 10 suspects were taken into custody Tuesday, and criminal proceedings have been initiated, though it is unclear how many will be charged. Police said the suspects include nine students and one young man. The attack allegedly happened Sunday evening after the girl left home for a friend’s birthday party. Ten suspects—nine students and one young man—were summoned for questioning. Six were taken into custody on Tuesday. A Christchurch woman, Lee Howden, says she is speaking publicly about an alleged sexual assault by Rolf Harris in the hope that other victims will also come forward, despite feeling vulnerable under the media spotlight. Howden, a former Television New Zealand makeup artist, alleges Harris assaulted her during an interview break in a Christchurch studio in the 1980s. She says she told no one at the time except a few friends, partly because of the celebrity culture of the era and because she was so upset she did not want to dwell on it. Police are due to take a formal video statement from her next week. Harris, 84, was this week sentenced in London to five years and nine months in prison after being convicted on 12 counts of indecent assault against four girls spanning nearly 20 years from 1968. Although witnesses from New Zealand and Australia gave evidence at his trial, he was not charged over those allegations because British courts had no jurisdiction over incidents outside the UK. Howden said she was motivated to speak out after National MP Maggie Barry revealed she had been groped by Harris during a radio interview in the mid-1980s. She said the publicity has made her feel exposed, but she believes it will be worth it if it encourages others to report abuse. She also said she was appalled by Harris’s apparent arrogance during the trial and sentencing, and praised police for their support. Detective Senior Sergeant Darryl Sweeney said police would not comment further because the matter remains under active investigation.

# Summary A Christchurch woman has come forward with allegations of sexual assault by disgraced entertainer Rolf Harris, despite acknowledging the media attention has made her feel vulnerable. Lee Howden, a former Television New Zealand makeup artist, alleges Harris sexually assaulted her during an interview break in a Christchurch studio in the 1980s. She did not report the incident at the time, citing the celebrity culture of that era and her reluctance to confront the traumatic experience. Lawyers for the woman who accused late Seoul Mayor Park Won-soon of sexual harassment urged the Seoul city council on Monday to investigate the allegations, saying the council must uncover the truth. Their demand was supported by the Korea Sexual Violence Relief Center, whose spokesperson said the alleged victim’s workplace should formally examine the claims. Park’s body was found on a hill in Seoul on Friday, hours after he left home. Before disappearing, he left a note apologizing “to everyone,” especially his family, for “causing only pain.” His death followed a sexual harassment complaint filed by a female public official, a claim later confirmed by authorities after media reports. Police closed the case because South Korean law requires cases to end when a suspect dies. The woman, identified only as “A” and now seeking police protection, has also filed a separate complaint over “secondary damages” caused by Park’s death. Her lawyer, Kim Jae-ryun, said the alleged harassment began four years ago. While some reports described her as Park’s former secretary, Kim clarified that she worked in another department and still remains employed. Kim said the client first consulted her on May 12, before the formal complaint was filed on July 8. She alleged Park sent sexually suggestive messages and photos of himself in underwear, which she shared with friends and police. She also claims he made unwanted physical advances and inappropriate contact in his office and an adjoining bedroom. In a letter read by her lawyer, “A” said she hoped to one day return to normal life and wanted a humane apology and legal judgment.

# Summary Seoul City Council has been asked to investigate sexual harassment allegations against the late Mayor Park Won-soon, who died in an apparent suicide on Friday. The woman who filed the complaint, identified only as "A," and her legal representatives are demanding an official inquiry. Park, a popular and twice-re-elected mayor, disappeared after leaving a note apologizing to his family. His death occurred days after the female public official filed a harassment complaint against him. Under South Korean law, police were required to close the case following his death. According to the victim's lawyer, the alleged abuse began four years ago. The woman, who works in city departments but was not Park's direct secretary, first sought legal counsel in May before formally filing her complaint in July. The lawyer presented evidence including sexually explicit messages and photographs that Park allegedly sent to the victim. The allegations include inappropriate physical contact and sexual advances in Park's office and adjoining bedroom. The victim has applied for police protection and filed an additional complaint for "secondary damages" resulting from Park's death. The Korea Sexual Violence Relief Center has supported the investigation request, emphasizing the city council's responsibility to uncover the truth. In her statement, the victim expressed her desire for legal judgment and a sincere apology, rather than the outcome that occurred.

China’s LGBT community won a rare, if limited, victory after Sina Weibo, one of the country’s largest social media platforms, reversed a ban on “homosexual” content following a public backlash. The episode highlighted both the growing ability of LGBT activists and supporters to push back online and the many restrictions that still shape gay life and representation in China. The controversy began when Weibo abruptly announced that it was removing “illegal content,” including videos with “pornographic implications, promoting violence or (related to) homosexuality.” The wording angered users, who argued that it singled out a community rather than specific kinds of harmful content. An #IamGay campaign quickly spread on the platform, and some users called for a boycott. Even the Communist Party’s People’s Daily weighed in with an essay supporting LGBT acceptance, while noting that gay content was still subject to censorship rules on pornography and violence. Activists called the reversal encouraging but incomplete. Xiao Tie, director of the Beijing LGBT Centre, said it was an “incremental victory” and a positive sign, but suggested Weibo may have been motivated partly by concern over its share price. She also noted that the company had not deleted its original notice and had not apologized, meaning the issue was far from resolved. Raymond Phang, co-founder of Shanghai Pride, said people were offended by the insensitive language, which seemed to target people rather than content. He also pointed out that, unlike past censorship orders from authorities, this case involved a listed company, giving users some channels to complain. Despite the backlash, the article said mainstream LGBT representation in China remains heavily constrained. In 2016, regulators banned gay characters from television, declaring that dramas must not show “abnormal sexual relationships and behaviours,” including same-sex relationships. Last year, authorities banned gay content from online streaming platforms. Oscar-winning Call Me by Your Name was also removed from the Beijing International Film Festival last month. The release of Looking for Rohmer, described as China’s first gay film, showed how limited that openness remains. After a two-year delay, the film finally opened in Chinese theatres, but it had been cut so heavily that the romance between the two male leads was barely visible. They never kiss and hardly touch, with their relationship conveyed only indirectly. The Chinese version runs 83 minutes, far shorter than the two-hour version listed by a Sydney festival. Ticket sales also appeared weak, with only eight advance purchases for screenings in central Beijing on Tuesday evening. The article also described broader legal and social barriers. China lacks comprehensive sex education and has no anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation or gender identity. Homosexuality was decriminalized only in 1997 and removed from the list of mental illnesses in 2001, yet clinics still offer abusive “conversion” treatments. Same-sex marriage remains illegal, and a Hunan court rejected a marriage lawsuit by two men in 2016. Still, there have been some legal gains: a court in Guizhou ruled that a transgender man had been unfairly dismissed, and another court ordered a psychiatric hospital to compensate a gay man forced into conversion therapy.

# China's LGBT Community Scores Rare Victory Against Censorship China's gay community achieved an unexpected win when Sina Weibo, a major social media platform with 400 million active monthly users, reversed its ban on homosexual content following significant public backlash. The controversy began when Weibo abruptly announced it would remove "illegal content," explicitly listing material "related to homosexuality" alongside pornography and violent content. This sparked the #IamGay campaign, with users calling for boycotts and demanding the platform reconsider. The backlash was so substantial that even the Communist Party's official newspaper, People's Daily, published an essay on Weibo promoting LGBT acceptance, though it noted that gays should still face censorship regarding pornography and violence. Xiao Tie, director of the Beijing LGBT Centre, characterized the reversal as "an incremental victory and quite a positive signal," but noted that Weibo's original notice remained undeleted and no apology was issued. Raymond Phang, co-founder of Shanghai Pride, criticized Weibo's insensitive language, which targeted a specific community rather than problematic content. He highlighted that this platform's corporate status made it possible to protest, unlike government censorship where citizens have limited recourse. Despite this victory, significant challenges persist for China's LGBT community. Since 2016, government censors have banned gay characters from television dramas entirely. Last year, authorities banned gay content from all online streaming platforms. The Oscar-winning film "Call Me by Your Name" was pulled from the Beijing International Film Festival, and "Looking for Rohmer," released as China's first gay movie, was heavily censored—cut from two hours to 83 minutes, with romantic scenes virtually eliminated. Broader societal obstacles remain entrenched. China lacks comprehensive sex education about LGBT issues, and deeply rooted traditional values pressure people toward marriage and children. The country has no anti-discrimination laws protecting gender identity or sexual orientation. Though homosexuality was decriminalized in 1997 and removed from mental illness classifications in 2001, conversion therapy clinics still operate nationwide, employing electroshocks, confinement, and chemical castration. Taiwan's vibrant pride parades contrast sharply with mainland China, where mass mobilizations are restricted to cultural activities due to government concerns about social stability. Same-sex marriage remains illegal; a 2016 lawsuit by two men seeking marriage rights was rejected. However, some progress has emerged. A Guizhou court ruled that a transgender man was illegally fired in China's first unfair dismissal case. Additionally, courts have ordered compensation and apologies in conversion therapy cases, condemning the practice. The Weibo reversal represents a meaningful but limited victory, demonstrating that public pressure can influence corporate decisions while systemic discrimination and legal barriers continue constraining LGBT rights in China.

A special court in Kota on Monday sentenced a young man, Jugraj, to life imprisonment for raping a 16-year-old girl last year and fined him Rs 45,000. The court convicted him under relevant provisions of the Indian Penal Code and the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act, public prosecutor Lalit Sharma said. According to the complaint, the survivor filed a report at Budhadeet police station on April 25, 2022, alleging that Jugraj entered her home on April 14 while her parents were away, raped her, and threatened her. Police registered a case, arrested him after preliminary investigation, and later added a gang-rape charge after Jugraj claimed a minor aide had guarded the gate during the crime. That minor was detained, and a charge sheet was filed. The juvenile’s case is still pending before the juvenile justice board.

# Summary A special court in Kota convicted a man named Jugraj of raping a 16-year-old girl and sentenced him to life imprisonment. The court found him guilty under the Indian Penal Code and the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act, imposing a fine of Rs 45,000. The victim filed a complaint on April 25, 2022, alleging that Jugraj forcibly entered her home on April 14 while her parents were away, raped her, and threatened her. Police arrested Jugraj following initial investigations. During interrogation, Jugraj revealed that a minor accomplice guarded the gate during the crime. Consequently, police added gang rape charges and detained the minor accomplice. The case against the juvenile is currently under trial at a juvenile justice board.

Polish police said Thursday they arrested 100 men, aged 18 to 75, in a major cybercrime operation targeting child sex abuse material. Two suspects were charged with raping minors, and one was described as among Poland’s 10 most active producers and distributors of paedophile content. Officers seized at least 600,000 files containing child sex abuse and bestiality. The operation, codenamed “Game Over,” led to 37 people being held in custody. Police said it was their largest such operation in three years, with 477 people charged overall and possible sentences of three months to 15 years.

# Summary Polish police arrested 100 men in a major cybercrime operation called "Game Over," suspected of producing, distributing, or possessing child sexual abuse material. The suspects range from 18 to 75 years old; two faced rape charges and one was identified as among Poland's ten most prolific producers of such content. Officers seized approximately 600,000 illegal files. Thirty-seven men were held in custody. This operation represents the largest of seven conducted over three years, resulting in 477 total charges. Convicted offenders face sentences ranging from three months to 15 years imprisonment.

U.S. Army Garrison Benelux marked National Sexual Assault Awareness and Prevention Month by hosting “Got Your Back” training on April 23 and 24 at several locations across USAG Benelux. The sessions were organized by the garrison’s Sexual Harassment/Assault Response and Prevention program, or SHARP, and led by Catharsis Productions, a group that uses humor and audience participation to challenge harmful beliefs about sex, relationships, and gender stereotypes. The program, described by the company as “fight fire with funny,” is research-based and designed to help participants distinguish healthy intimacy from sexual violence. Educator Anne Dufault said humor makes it easier to discuss topics people often avoid and helps break down cultural assumptions that can contribute to sexual assault. During the training, she encouraged attendees to reflect on healthy and unhealthy relationship behaviors and to work together on ways to prevent violence in their communities. Dufault said she values speaking to military audiences because the armed forces have historically helped drive broader social change. She suggested that conversations in the military can influence culture beyond the service itself. Stephanie Jones, the sexual assault response coordinator at USAG Benelux Army Community Service, said she hoped participants would leave ready to support others, intervene when needed, and make use of resources such as SHARP to help survivors. The article notes that SHARP training is an annual requirement for U.S. service members and civilian employees. In addition to special programs like “Got Your Back,” the Army provides SHARP and SAPR training throughout the year to keep people informed about reporting options, bystander intervention, and available support services. Sexual assault response coordinators are stationed throughout USAG Benelux communities. The piece also provided contact information for SHARP offices and the U.S. Army Europe 24/7 Sexual Assault Hotline, along with emergency instructions to contact military police or dial 112 if immediate help is needed.

# Sexual Assault Prevention Training Comes to Benelux Community U.S. Army Garrison Benelux hosted "Got Your Back," a research-based sexual assault prevention training program on April 23-24 across multiple locations in recognition of National Sexual Assault Awareness and Prevention Month. The program was facilitated by Catharsis Productions, an organization known for using humor and interaction to address serious topics. Participants actively contributed to conversations about intervention techniques and support resources. She highlighted that community resources like SHARP exist to support survivors and help people intervene effectively. The Sexual Harassment/Assault Response and Prevention (SHARP) program requires annual training for all U.S. service members and civilian employees. Additional training opportunities occur throughout the year to keep personnel informed about available resources and reporting procedures. ROME — The abuse case of Slovene priest and artist Father Marko Ivan Rupnik has drawn renewed attention to a possible gap in canon law surrounding so-called “false mysticism,” with legal experts warning that the absence of a clearly defined offense may be making it harder for the Vatican to prosecute him and others accused of similar abuses. Rupnik, 68, is one of contemporary Catholicism’s best-known muralists. He is accused of sexual, psychological, and spiritual abuse involving at least 25 adult women over a period of 30 years. The case has troubled Catholics for more than a year, not only because of the allegations themselves but also because of the confusing and apparently shifting way church authorities have responded, including Pope Francis. The Vatican’s Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith (DDF) initially refused to open canonical proceedings beyond a brief excommunication Rupnik received in 2020. That excommunication was linked to allegations that he had used the confessional to absolve a woman with whom he had had sexual relations. The DDF said it would not proceed further because the abuse allegations involving adults were beyond the statute of limitations under the Code of Canon Law. That decision stood out because in other cases the Vatican has waived the time limit. Meanwhile, an internal Jesuit investigation concluded that the accusations against Rupnik were “highly credible.” That inquiry ended with Rupnik’s expulsion from the Jesuits in June, not for the abuse allegations directly, but for disobedience: he had refused to cooperate with the investigation and had ignored orders from his superiors. Critics say Pope Francis’s response appeared inconsistent. He granted an audience on Sept. 15 to a longtime Rupnik ally who has publicly dismissed the accusations as a “lynching.” Three days later, the Diocese of Rome issued a statement giving the Centro Aletti, the artistic and spiritual center founded by Rupnik, a clean bill of health. That statement also questioned the legitimacy of Rupnik’s 2020 excommunication, calling the procedures behind it “gravely anomalous” and expressing “well-founded doubts” about the decision. Then, a month later, the Diocese of Koper in Slovenia announced that Rupnik had been incardinated there, meaning he had been formally accepted into that diocese because he had not been charged with any crime. Many observers believed such a move would not have happened without at least tacit approval from Vatican officials. The practical effect was to leave Rupnik a priest in good standing, able to continue his ministry and art with little restriction. Soon after, however, Francis seemed to reverse course. According to a Vatican statement, he had decided to lift the statute of limitations after an appeal from the Pontifical Commission for the Protection of Minors, allowing a canonical trial to go forward. Experts say part of the difficulty lies in the nature of the alleged abuse itself. Rupnik, like some other notorious abusers in recent decades, is said to have wrapped sexual abuse in spiritual language, presenting sexual acts as part of a mystical experience. This kind of conduct is traditionally described as “false mysticism.” It is treated as a crime against the faith, but one without a clearly defined legal standard. For centuries, the DDF — formerly known as the Holy Office — has been responsible for prosecuting crimes against the faith. A 1995 DDF rulebook, signed by then-prefect Cardinal Joseph Ratzinger, later Pope Benedict XVI, says the dicastery handles crimes against the faith and the most serious crimes against morality and the sacraments. It also lists “cases of pseudo-mysticism,” alleged apparitions, visions, messages claimed to be supernatural, spiritism, magic, and simony. But canon lawyers say the problem is that these categories are not precisely defined. That lack of specificity has created what some describe as an “eye of the beholder” standard, making investigators wary of opening cases that could become legally tangled. Canonical experts acknowledge that no specific rule in canon law — including the revised penal code — directly addresses crimes against the faith such as false mysticism. Even so, some experts argue that such conduct can still be pursued under broader charges such as abuse of power. Critics of the Vatican’s handling of cases like Rupnik’s say the issue is not simply a legal gap, but a lack of will to act decisively. Spanish canon lawyer Father Fernando Puig told Crux that crimes such as false mysticism fall under the DDF’s competence and said the hope is that the dicastery will soon prosecute such cases so a precedent can be set. A recent case from Spain may help. Last week, 82-year-old Franciscan Father Francisco Javier Garrido Goitia was convicted by the tribunal of the Apostolic Nunciature in Spain on two counts of “false mysticism and request for confession,” involving abuse of power, abuse of conscience, and sexual abuse of nuns. He was barred from ministry, including spiritual direction, and forbidden to publish books or articles. The decree said he had no right of appeal. The Rupnik affair also underscores a broader inconsistency in the Church’s response to abuse: it has developed a relatively clear and firm approach to abuse of minors, but its handling of abuse involving adults and “vulnerable persons” remains uneven and less defined. One of Garrido Goitia’s victims told Spanish media that adult abuse is often not understood and is wrongly assumed to be consensual. She said the victims are actually in vulnerable positions and are manipulated “in the name of God” in abuses of power, conscience, and sexual and spiritual abuse. Questions also remain about the apparent contradiction between the Jesuits’ investigation and the Diocese of Rome’s later statement clearing Rupnik and Centro Aletti. Some Vatican and diocesan officials have suggested that politics may have played a role, pointing to a long-running rift between Pope Francis and Cardinal Angelo De Donatis, the vicar of Rome, dating back to the COVID-19 pandemic. An official in the vicariate, speaking anonymously, said the Sept. 18 statement was issued personally by De Donatis, ordered to be published immediately, and not shared in advance with others who might have reviewed it. Some observers say De Donatis has long supported Rupnik and the Centro Aletti, raising concerns about his impartiality. Similar questions have been raised about Archbishop Giacomo Morandi, the former second-ranking official in the Vatican’s Dicastery for Bishops, who was later removed from that role. For now, Rupnik’s whereabouts are unclear. He is believed to divide his time between Italy and Slovenia, including Koper, Rome, and Udine, where many of his supporters are based. It remains uncertain what charges, if any, the DDF will ultimately pursue — including whether “false mysticism” will be among them.
