Poland’s prime minister, Mateusz Morawiecki, tried on Friday to calm public anxiety over energy shortages and rising prices, telling parliament that the government is assembling enough natural gas and coal to get through the coming months. He blamed the strain on Russia’s nearly five-month war in Ukraine and said the ruling Law and Justice party would “do everything to adjust the energy strategy to the times of war.” Morawiecki’s comments came as Poland faces mounting public anger over high inflation and a shortage of coal for heating. He said, “We will cope with the effects of the war in Ukraine; we will cope with inflation.” The issue is politically important for the right-wing governing coalition, which opinion polls suggest could lose its parliamentary majority in next year’s election if dissatisfaction continues to grow. Inflation in Poland reached 15.5% year-on-year in June, the highest level in 25 years. Gas prices and especially coal prices have risen sharply. The price of quality coal, used by millions of households for heating, has tripled in recent months after imports from Russia were cut off because of sanctions imposed over Moscow’s invasion of Ukraine. Poland had relied heavily on Russian coal before the war. In response, the government has introduced lower, regulated prices for households and ordered some state-owned energy companies to make urgent purchases of coal for individual consumers. Most of the coal Poland produces domestically is used by industry, not households. Morawiecki said the government had bought coal from many countries and that gas storage facilities would be full before winter. He insisted that supplies would be sufficient despite the disruption caused by the war. But opposition politicians and some economists criticized his assurances as too optimistic, warning that the country still faces serious risks of shortages and continued price pressure. The AP article portrays the government’s message as an effort to reassure citizens while Poland grapples with the economic fallout of the war next door.

The article marks World Press Freedom Day, observed by the UN on Friday, and uses the occasion to highlight both the dangers journalists face and the importance of protecting press freedom, especially in a time when “fake news” and distrust of the media are widespread. It begins with the global context: according to the International Federation of Journalists, at least 95 journalists were killed in 2018, and 2019 was already proving no safer. On the eve of Press Freedom Day, a journalist in southern Mexico who founded a community radio station in an indigenous region was shot dead after reportedly receiving death threats on the air. Mexico remains one of the world’s most dangerous countries for journalists, with more than 100 murdered since 2000 amid violence tied to drug trafficking and political corruption. The article notes that Telesforo Santiago Enriquez was shot in the heart and mouth. The piece then broadens the picture, pointing to journalists in countries such as Turkey, Brazil, the Philippines, and Myanmar who are imprisoned, harassed, or threatened for trying to report stories powerful people want suppressed. While Catholic journalists have not faced comparable physical threats, the article says the Church has seen its own form of pressure on the press. In Peru, Archbishop Jose Antonio Eguren Anselmi of Piura filed defamation charges against two journalists, Pedro Salinas and Paola Ugaz, after they reported on a sexual abuse scandal involving the powerful Catholic group Sodalitium Christianae Vitae and alleged financial misconduct. Eguren argued that he had been defamed and, under Peruvian law, had the right to bring a criminal complaint. Those charges led to Salinas being convicted in early April. A Piura court gave him a one-year suspended sentence and imposed a $24,000 fine. The article says the Peruvian bishops’ conference quickly distanced itself from the ruling, issuing a statement that effectively sided with Salinas and suggesting that Pope Francis did as well. The bishops quoted the pope praising journalists who investigate abuses, help punish perpetrators, and assist victims, saying the Church needs their help in fighting evil. Eguren initially defended his decision to sue. In an April 15 statement, he argued that freedom of expression, while valuable, is not absolute and must respect people’s honor and good name. He insisted the Salinas verdict did not amount to a gag on free expression. But about ten days later, after mounting criticism, Eguren withdrew the charge against Salinas, which effectively nullified the conviction, and then did the same for Ugaz. He said he was doing so to preserve Church unity. Although that brought relief to the journalists, the article warns that the damage may already have been done: other reporters in Peru may now hesitate to publish sensitive stories about Church leaders if they cannot count on public support. The article then turns to the broader challenge of defending press freedom in an era when many people distrust the media. Citing a 2018 Gallup poll, it says 62 percent of Americans believed mainstream media news was biased, while 80 percent said social media news was biased. Eight in ten said they were angry about biased information, and nine in ten were angry about inaccurate reporting. Another Gallup poll found that newspapers and television news ranked among the least trusted major institutions, surpassed only by Congress. The author acknowledges that the media often deserves criticism, citing opinion presented as news, sloppy reporting, and careless journalism that can damage reputations without basis. Still, the article argues that abuse does not invalidate legitimate use. Freedom of the press remains essential, especially for Catholics who have seen how independent journalism helped expose clerical sexual abuse and force the Church to confront it. The piece ends by quoting Pope Francis, who said on Press Freedom Day: “We need a journalism that is free, at the service of truth, goodness and justice; a journalism that helps build a culture of encounter.” The article concludes that freedom alone does not guarantee such journalism, but without freedom, it cannot exist at all.

Pope Francis articulated the ideal on Press Freedom Day: "We need a journalism that is free, at the service of truth, goodness and justice; a journalism that helps build a culture of encounter." Defending press freedom remains essential despite current credibility challenges and documented abuses.

A large new mural in Roubaix, France, has drawn international attention for its pointed criticism of President Donald Trump’s immigration and deportation policies. The article describes how Israeli women have joined the global #MeToo wave, while also showing that in Israel the conversation about sexual harassment and assault has been building for years. Among those who spoke out were fashion model Maayan Keret, who said she was raped at age 12 and later harassed or assaulted so often that she “stopped counting”; Olympic silver medalist Yael Arad, who said that despite her strength and public image, men had tried three times to take advantage of or harass her; and Knesset member Merav Ben-Ari, who said male soldiers on her army base verbally harassed her and touched her inappropriately. Their stories were part of a larger wave of testimonies from both famous and ordinary Israeli women. The Israeli press gave the issue prominent coverage. On Monday, one of the country’s major newspapers, Yediot Acharonot, put the accounts of six well-known Israeli women on its front page under the headline “Also Us.” But the article emphasizes that this was not the first time Israeli women had said “Me Too,” or “Gam Ani” in Hebrew. A Facebook page called “One Out of One,” created in 2013, had already gathered nearly 2,500 testimonies, most of them anonymous, and had become a significant platform for survivors. The page was started by attorney Gal Shargill and feminist activist Shlomit Havron. Their goal was to raise awareness about how widespread sexual harassment and assault are in Israel. Shargill explained that the name reflected the idea that nearly every Israeli woman has a story. She said they did not want to be victims, but felt compelled to speak because silence only hides the reality. Over time, the Facebook page grew to more than 40,000 followers, and the pair also created a nonprofit with the same name to provide guidance, legal counsel, and public education. Shargill and Havron themselves had shared their own experiences; Shargill said she had been raped once and repeatedly harassed at work. In the wake of #MeToo going viral, the pair saw a surge in submissions to their page, receiving about 30 to 40 in a short period, compared with 10 to 20 in a typical week. The article also places the campaign in the context of several major Israeli sex scandals in recent years, including a Tel Aviv nightclub owner charged with rape or other sex crimes against six women, a respected army general who avoided rape charges through a plea deal, and former president Moshe Katsav, who had recently been released from prison after serving five years for rape and other sex offenses. Sulitzeanu said sexual harassment and assault remain pervasive in Israel and partly blamed mandatory military service, arguing that young men in the army can learn a sense of entitlement. She cited an internal Israel Defense Forces study finding that one in six female soldiers are sexually harassed during service, and said the rape crisis centers in her network receive around 40,000 calls a year. At the same time, she said attitudes are improving and described the public embrace of #MeToo as “a mini-revolution.” The campaign, she said, has broken the code of silence and made many survivors feel less alone, though she stressed the need to support those who are not ready to speak publicly. Shargill said One Out of One would continue collecting testimonies even after the global #MeToo moment passes.

# Israeli Women Join Global #MeToo Movement, Though Movement Already Existed Locally The #MeToo campaign, launched on Twitter by American actress Alyssa Milano in response to sexual abuse allegations against Harvey Weinstein, has resonated powerfully in Israel, where high-profile women have publicly shared their experiences of sexual harassment and assault. International fashion model Maayan Keret revealed she was raped at age 12 and has experienced countless subsequent assaults. The campaign spread rapidly, generating over 12 million Facebook posts, reactions, and comments within 24 hours. Israeli media gave the movement significant coverage, with Yediot Acharonot, one of Israel's most widely read newspapers, featuring six prominent women's accounts on its front page under the headline "Also Us." However, Israeli women have been sharing such testimonies for years through "One Out of One," a Facebook page launched in 2013 by attorney Gal Shargill and feminist activist Shlomit Havron. The page has collected nearly 2,500 anonymous testimonies designed to raise awareness about the prevalence of sexual harassment and assault in Israel. The Hebrew name "Gam Ani" parallels the English "Me Too," reflecting the reality that nearly every Israeli woman has experienced such abuse. The One Out of One Facebook page now has over 40,000 followers and has evolved into a nonprofit organization providing legal counsel and guidance to victims while creating awareness-raising content. Orit Sulitzeanu, executive director of the Association of Rape Crisis Centers of Israel, credited the organization with "paving the way" for the #MeToo campaign by normalizing testimony-sharing on social media. The #MeToo campaign differs from One Out of One primarily in its emphasis on public identification. While One Out of One collected mostly anonymous stories, #MeToo encourages women to attach their names and identities to their accounts. Sulitzeanu noted that #MeToo "took what they did one step further with women saying 'here, this is my name, this is my identity, and I'm talking.'" Both Shargill and Havron shared their own experiences—Shargill disclosed being raped and repeatedly harassed at work—and have participated in the #MeToo campaign while managing the surge of new submissions. Typically receiving 10 to 20 submissions weekly, they received 30 to 40 following #MeToo's viral spread. Sexual harassment and assault appear particularly pervasive in Israel. An internal Israel Defense Forces study found one in six female soldiers experience sexual harassment during service. The nine rape crisis centers under Sulitzeanu's umbrella organization receive approximately 40,000 phone calls annually. The World Health Organization reports that one in three women worldwide experiences physical or sexual violence during their lifetime. Recent high-profile Israeli cases include a Tel Aviv nightclub owner charged with rape against six women and a revered army general who pleaded guilty to sex crimes. In December, President Moshe Katsav was released from prison after serving five years of a seven-year sentence for rape. Sulitzeanu partially attributes the prevalence of sexual assault to Israel's mandatory military service, suggesting young men learn they are "entitled to anything." However, she has observed improving societal attitudes in recent years. The prominent media coverage of #MeToo represents what she calls a "mini-revolution," breaking the silence surrounding sexual abuse in ways previously unseen in Israeli media. Despite this progress, Sulitzeanu emphasizes the importance of legitimizing those unable to speak publicly, including men and children. Shargill commits to continuing One Out of One's work beyond the campaign's inevitable decline, ensuring ongoing support for victims seeking to share their stories.

Nobel Peace Prize laureates Denis Mukwege and Nadia Murad used their acceptance speeches in Oslo to call on the world to do far more to protect victims of sexual violence in war and conflict, denouncing global indifference to the suffering of women and children. Mukwege, a Congolese gynecologist whose work at Panzi hospital in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo has made him one of the world’s leading experts on rape in conflict, said the violence in his country “shames our common humanity.” He argued that the real fight should be against indifference, not only against armed conflict itself. Speaking before an emotional audience that repeatedly gave standing ovations, he described how, for 20 years, he had seen the consequences of what he called the country’s gross mismanagement: babies, girls, young women, mothers, grandmothers, and also men and boys being raped, often publicly and collectively, with brutal methods. He blamed much of the violence on those in power in Congo, saying the country’s natural-resource wealth fuels predatory corruption and that profits from minerals often end up in the hands of an oligarchy while children mine them in inhuman conditions. Mukwege also said responsibility lies not only with perpetrators but with those who choose to look away. He called for a global fund to compensate victims and for economic and political sanctions against those behind the violence. Murad, a Yazidi activist and survivor of Islamic State sexual slavery, appealed for urgent action to free the women and girls still held by jihadists. She said that more than 6,500 women and girls from her community had been kidnapped, raped, and traded “in the 21st century, in the age of globalisation and human rights.” She noted that the fate of around 3,000 women and girls remains unknown. Murad said it was “inconceivable” that the conscience of the leaders of 195 countries had not been mobilized to rescue them, and she compared their situation to what would happen if they were a commercial deal, oil field, or weapons shipment—suggesting that in those cases, governments would act immediately. She said all victims deserve a safe haven until justice is done, and added that justice and prosecution of criminals are the only things that can truly restore dignity. The Nobel committee said the prize was awarded to Mukwege and Murad for their efforts to end the use of sexual violence as a weapon of war and armed conflict, calling them two of the strongest voices in the world today. The pair received gold medals, diplomas, and a shared prize of nine million Swedish kronor, about $1 million. Murad, who was captured by IS in 2014, beaten, gang-raped, and later escaped, said older Yazidi men and women were executed during the assault, which the UN has described as a possible genocide. She said steps toward justice had given her some hope, including a UN team expected to begin fieldwork in Iraq next year. No jihadist has yet been tried for atrocities against the Yazidis. Murad, the first Iraqi to win the Nobel Peace Prize, was supported in her justice campaign by human rights lawyer Amal Clooney, who attended the ceremony.

# Nobel Laureates Call for Action Against Sexual Violence in Conflict Denis Mukwege, a Congolese gynecologist, and Nadia Murad, a Yazidi activist and survivor of Islamic State sexual slavery, jointly received the 2018 Nobel Peace Prize for their efforts to end sexual violence as a weapon of war. At the emotional Oslo ceremony, both laureates delivered powerful speeches urging the world to address the widespread indifference to victims' suffering. Mukwege, 63, has dedicated his career to treating victims of sexual assault at his Panzi hospital in the Democratic Republic of Congo's conflict-ridden east, where tens of thousands of women and children have received care. He emphasized that sexual violence has become a "new reality" in the region, describing the brutality inflicted on civilians—including babies, girls, young women, mothers, and men—as shameful to humanity. He attributed much of the violence to governmental mismanagement and the exploitation of the country's natural resources, noting that minerals extracted under inhumane conditions often end up funding the violence while enriching corrupt oligarchs. Mukwege called for a global fund to provide reparations for victims and economic and political sanctions against perpetrators. He stressed that responsibility extends beyond direct perpetrators to those who choose indifference, declaring: "If there is a war to be waged, it is the war against the indifference which is eating away at our societies." Murad, 25, survived capture by ISIS in 2014, enduring beatings and gang rape before escaping. She implored the global community to help free hundreds of women and girls still held by jihadists. According to her account, over 6,500 women and girls from her Kurdish-speaking community were kidnapped, raped, and trafficked, with approximately 3,000 still missing. She highlighted the stark disparity in how the world prioritizes commercial interests over human suffering, asking rhetorically what response would occur if these women were "a commercial deal, an oil field or a shipment of weapons." Murad emphasized that true justice—not merely recognition—would restore dignity to her people. She noted that no jihadist has yet faced trial for atrocities against the Yazidis, though a UN investigation team is scheduled to begin fieldwork in Iraq next year. President Donald Trump said Tuesday that he would ease sanctions on Syria and move to normalize relations with the country’s new government, saying he wanted to give Syria “a chance at peace.” He made the announcement in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, shortly before he was scheduled to meet Syrian President Ahmad al-Sharaa, the former insurgent leader who helped overthrow longtime ruler Bashar Assad last year. Trump’s comments came during the first stop of a four-day Middle East trip and marked a major shift in U.S. policy toward Syria. The United States has not formally recognized the new Syrian government, and sanctions imposed during Assad’s rule remain in place. Trump said the move toward rapprochement was encouraged by Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan. “There is a new government that will hopefully succeed,” Trump said of Syria. “I say, good luck, Syria. Show us something special.” The planned meeting with al-Sharaa is especially notable because of the Syrian leader’s past. Al-Sharaa, once known by the nom de guerre Abu Mohammed al-Golani, was imprisoned in Iraq for his role in the insurgency after the 2003 U.S.-led invasion. He later joined al-Qaida-linked fighters in Iraq, then returned to Syria in 2011, where he led al-Qaida’s Syrian branch, formerly known as the Nusra Front. He eventually renamed the group Hayat Tahrir al-Sham, or HTS, and severed ties with al-Qaida. The U.S. once offered $10 million for information leading to his capture, and he still faces an arrest warrant on terrorism charges in Iraq. Al-Sharaa was named Syria’s president in January, after insurgent groups led by HTS launched a surprise offensive in December that took Damascus and ended 54 years of Assad family rule. If the meeting goes ahead, he will become the first Syrian leader to meet an American president since Hafez Assad met Bill Clinton in Geneva in 2000. Gulf states have been urging Washington to engage the new Syrian leadership, arguing that it can help block Iran from regaining influence in Syria after years of backing Assad during the civil war. Israel, by contrast, has warned against quickly embracing al-Sharaa because of his militant background. Trump’s Syria announcement was paired with a broader message to Iran. Speaking at the U.S.-Saudi investment conference, he said he wanted to avoid conflict with Tehran and urged its leaders to take “a new and a better path” toward a nuclear deal. But he also warned that if Iran rejects his offer, the United States would impose “massive maximum pressure” and drive Iranian oil exports to zero. Trump said time is running out as Iran advances its nuclear program. His latest warning came after his envoy, Steve Witkoff, held a fourth round of talks with Iranian officials aimed at persuading Tehran to abandon its nuclear ambitions. Trump also said he hoped Saudi Arabia would eventually join the Abraham Accords and recognize Israel “in your own time.” Saudi Arabia has long said any recognition of Israel depends on the creation of a Palestinian state along the 1967 borders. Under President Joe Biden, the United States had tried to broker a Saudi-Israeli deal, but the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas attack on Israel upended those efforts and intensified regional conflict. The White House said before Trump’s remarks that he had agreed to greet al-Sharaa during his time in Saudi Arabia. Trump’s planned engagement with the Syrian leader represents a dramatic change in tone and a potential diplomatic opening after years of hostility between Washington and Damascus. A Syrian analyst described the meeting as a “strategic shift” that could open the door to constructive talks between the two countries.

U.S. Defense Secretary James Mattis made a surprise visit to Kabul on Friday, arriving in Afghanistan’s capital just days after a deadly suicide bombing killed 21 people and wounded 90 others. He was accompanied by Gen. Joseph Dunford, chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, and was expected to meet with President Ashraf Ghani as well as Afghan, U.S., and NATO military commanders, according to Afghan officials and the U.S. command in Afghanistan. The visit came amid a surge in violence across the country, including brutal attacks targeting Afghanistan’s Shiite minority and a series of insider attacks this week that killed one American service member and eight local police officers. Mattis was expected to discuss the worsening security situation, especially the rising toll on both civilians and military personnel. The Islamic State group’s affiliate in Afghanistan has continued to stage high-profile attacks in Kabul despite an aggressive U.S.-backed campaign against its fighters in eastern Nangarhar province. The group has frequently targeted Shiite Muslims, whom it considers apostates. On Wednesday, a suicide bomber attacked a wrestling center in Kabul, killing 21 people and injuring 90. Two of the dead were journalists who were killed when a second blast hit as first responders and reporters rushed to the scene. On Friday, the Islamic State affiliate claimed responsibility for the attack, saying it was carried out by a suicide bomber identified as Saber al-Khorasani. The group also said the second explosion was caused by a vehicle packed with explosives, though that account could not be independently verified and differed from the Afghan government’s initial report that two suicide bombers were involved. Mattis’ trip also took place against the backdrop of a renewed U.S. push for a negotiated end to Afghanistan’s long war. Earlier in the week, Secretary of State Mike Pompeo announced the appointment of Zalmay Khalilzad as Washington’s new envoy for Afghan reconciliation. Khalilzad, a former envoy to Afghanistan, is a controversial figure in the region. The defense secretary arrived in Afghanistan after meetings in Pakistan, where Pompeo said the U.S. wanted to “reset” its relationship with Islamabad. Newly elected Prime Minister Imran Khan voiced cautious optimism about working with Washington for peace, but also declared that Pakistan would no longer fight “someone else’s war.” Pakistan remains central to any peace effort because of its ties to the Taliban, even as Washington and Kabul accuse it of harboring Taliban safe havens, a charge Pakistan denies. Khalilzad’s appointment has been especially unwelcome in Pakistan because of his criticism of its military and intelligence services. Last weekend, Washington also canceled a $300 million Coalition Support Fund payment to Pakistan.

Yemen’s Houthi rebels escalated their campaign against maritime traffic in the Middle East on Friday by firing a missile at the U.S. destroyer USS Carney in the Gulf of Aden, according to the U.S. military. The warship intercepted and shot down the projectile, and Central Command said there were no injuries or damage. A U.S. official, speaking anonymously, said this was the first time the Houthis had directly targeted a U.S. warship since their attacks on shipping began in October, though Central Command described the missile as having been fired “toward” the ship and said it was difficult to know exactly what the rebels intended to hit. The attack came amid an intensifying wave of Houthi strikes on commercial and military shipping linked to the Israel-Hamas war. Later Friday night, another vessel was set ablaze after being hit by Houthi missile fire, underscoring the continuing danger to ships in the Red Sea and nearby waters. Houthi military spokesman Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree did not mention the USS Carney incident, but he claimed responsibility for a missile strike on a commercial ship that he identified as the Marshall Islands-flagged tanker Marlin Luanda. The Associated Press could not immediately reach the ship’s British managers. The British military’s United Kingdom Maritime Operations also reported that a vessel had been struck by a missile and was on fire in the Gulf of Aden, though it was not immediately clear whether anyone was hurt. The USS Carney, an Arleigh Burke-class destroyer, has been involved in U.S. efforts since November to counter Houthi attacks on shipping. Friday’s incident marked a notable shift because it was the first acknowledged direct attack on an American warship. The U.S. has generally used cautious language in describing earlier incidents, partly to avoid broadening the conflict into a wider regional war. But analysts said publicly recognizing this as a direct attack on U.S. forces was important. Brad Bowman of the Foundation for the Defense of Democracies said the United States was “finally calling a spade a spade” by acknowledging that the Houthis were trying to attack and kill U.S. personnel. The Houthis have been attacking ships in the Red Sea and surrounding waters since November, saying they were acting in solidarity with Palestinians and retaliating against Israel’s war on Hamas in Gaza. In practice, however, they have often targeted vessels with only tenuous or no clear connection to Israel, threatening a major global trade route linking Asia, the Middle East, and Europe. After U.S. and British airstrikes began hitting Houthi missile depots and launcher sites in Yemen, the rebels said they would also target American and British ships. The United States and Britain have responded with repeated airstrikes against Houthi military sites in Yemen, where the rebels seized the capital, Sanaa, in 2014 and have since fought a long civil war. The latest attacks have drawn comparisons to the “Tanker War” of the 1980s. The U.S. Navy’s top commander in the Middle East told the AP earlier in the week that the current Houthi campaign is the worst sea conflict the region has seen in decades, evoking the 1980s confrontation between the United States and Iran that culminated in a naval battle and the accidental U.S. shootdown of an Iranian passenger jet in 1988, killing 290 people. The Houthi campaign has already disrupted global shipping and raised fears of a broader conflict, and Friday’s missile attack on a U.S. warship marked another sharp escalation.

Human Rights Watch said Monday that Daesh fighters are also raping and torturing Sunni Arab women, not only Yazidis. Oklahoma enters the 2016 Big 12 season as the league’s most decorated program, already holding a record nine conference titles and coming off the Big 12’s first appearance in the College Football Playoff. Since winning its last national championship in 2000, Oklahoma has returned to the title stage once, in the 2008 BCS Championship Game, and last season reached the Orange Bowl before losing a playoff semifinal to Clemson. Baylor still has major offensive talent, but depth is a concern following the offseason dismissal of coach Art Briles amid allegations the program mishandled sexual assault complaints. The article highlights several top players: Mayfield, a Heisman contender who threw for 3,700 yards and 43 total touchdowns last season; Texas linebacker Malik Jefferson; Texas Tech quarterback Patrick Mahomes, now focused solely on football after quitting baseball; Perine, who is closing in on Oklahoma’s career rushing record; Baylor quarterback Seth Russell, returning from a neck injury; TCU pass rusher Josh Carraway; and Oklahoma State receiver James Washington. New York Democratic Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand said Monday that “affirmative consent” laws should become the national standard for addressing sexual assault. Speaking at an MSNBC-hosted panel on sexual assault at the Fashion Institute of Technology in New York, Gillibrand praised the State University of New York system for recently adopting the “yes means yes” standard after urging from Gov. Andrew Cuomo. Asked whether the approach could be expanded nationwide, she said she had been “studying it and looking at it” and believed “that is where our debate needs to go.” Affirmative consent requires explicit prior consent for each sexual act. It differs from the traditional “no means no” framework, under which sexual assault generally depends on an explicit refusal or incapacity to consent. California already requires the standard at colleges that receive state funding, and some other schools have adopted it voluntarily. Gillibrand did not outline how a national version would work, but the article notes that the federal government could potentially impose it broadly through Title IX, which governs sex discrimination at schools receiving federal funds. The proposal has drawn criticism from civil liberties advocates, who argue it can create a presumption of guilt and does not reflect how young people actually behave in sexual relationships. Supporters counter that it would better protect victims, especially in cases involving dating relationships or alcohol use, where obtaining justice can be difficult. Gillibrand also used the event to push back against recent setbacks in the campus sexual assault debate. Activists have faced scrutiny after Rolling Stone’s disputed report on an alleged University of Virginia gang rape and a Justice Department report suggesting campus sexual assault rates are lower than advocates claim. Gillibrand insisted that, by any measure, too many rapes are still occurring on college campuses and too little justice is being delivered. Sexual assault has been one of Gillibrand’s signature issues in the Senate, including her recent effort to remove military sexual assault investigations from the chain of command.

She also pointed to social media as an increasingly important contributor, citing online sexual exploitation and bullying as reasons more people are seeking counselling. Bishop Michael Hoeppner of Crookston, Minnesota, has denied allegations that he pressured a man who says he was sexually abused as a teen by a diocesan priest to withdraw or recant his claim. The dispute is at the center of a lawsuit filed by Ronald Vasek against Hoeppner and the Diocese of Crookston. Vasek is seeking more than $50,000 in damages, along with the release of diocesan records related to priest abuse, according to Reuters. Vasek alleges that in 1971, when he was 16, he was molested during a trip to Cincinnati by Msgr. Roger Grundhaus, then a priest of the diocese who later became vicar general. He says he first reported the abuse to a priest in 2009 or 2010, while considering becoming a deacon, and that the information was then passed along to Bishop Hoeppner. The diocese says the allegation was reported to law enforcement in 2011. Grundhaus, who retired in July 2010, is currently suspended from active ministry. According to the lawsuit, Hoeppner later pressured Vasek in 2015 to sign a letter withdrawing his earlier abuse allegations. Vasek claims the bishop told him he would have difficulty being ordained a deacon unless he recanted, and suggested that his son’s priesthood career could also be harmed. Vasek says he signed the letter after being told the bishop would keep it in his vault if needed, and he describes the situation as blackmail. The diocese strongly rejected the accusation, saying Hoeppner “categorically denies” forcing, coercing, or encouraging Vasek not to pursue his allegations. It said the bishop and other leaders are saddened and troubled by the claims and plan a thorough investigation, declining further comment until that is complete. Vasek’s son was ordained a priest for the diocese in 2010, and Vasek entered the diaconate program the following year. The lawsuit also claims a 2015 court order required the abuse allegation against Grundhaus to be made public, but that did not happen. Jeff Anderson, a lawyer known for church abuse litigation, represents Vasek. At a May 9 news conference, Father Bob Schreiner, who oversees the diocesan deacon program and has known Vasek for decades, said he believed Vasek’s account.

University of Minnesota leaders punished 10 Black football players in 2016 to make themselves look like “heroes of the fight against sexual violence,” the players’ lawyer argued Friday in federal court. The university rejected that claim, saying its student discipline process worked properly and produced different outcomes based on the evidence in each case. The dispute stems from a September 2016 allegation by a white female student that between 10 and 20 football players gang-raped her. No criminal charges were filed, but the accusation triggered major fallout on campus and within the football program. Head coach Tracy Claeys was eventually dismissed, and the team briefly boycotted the Holiday Bowl after all 10 accused players were suspended. The players are suing the university in U.S. District Court, alleging due process violations and discrimination based on race and sex. They seek damages and want the four expelled players reinstated with clean records. Judge Donovan Frank heard arguments on the university’s motion to dismiss but did not say when he would rule. Plaintiffs’ attorney David Madgett pointed to a July 2015 email from Kim Hewitt, the university’s director of Equal Opportunity and Affirmative Action, which warned of a “potential pattern” of sexual misconduct by Gopher football players. He argued that after the 2016 complaint, President Eric Kaler and Title IX Coordinator Tina Marisam saw an opportunity to show the university was taking sexual violence seriously. Madgett said the white student’s account was accepted while the accounts of the Black players were “universally discredited.” Marisam’s investigation led to suspensions for all 10 players after three months. Five were later cleared in student conduct hearings, a sixth had his suspension overturned on appeal, and four were expelled. University lawyer Carrie Ryan Gallia said those varied outcomes show there was no discrimination. She argued the process involved “fair, nuanced, careful consideration” and noted the expelled players could have pursued further appeals in state court but did not.

Canada’s sport minister, Pascale St-Onge, has announced a broad package of safe sport reforms aimed at making national sports organizations more accountable for the federal money they receive and at changing a culture that has been rocked by abuse and maltreatment allegations. The measures include the creation of a public registry of people sanctioned or suspended under the Universal Code of Conduct to Prevent and Address Maltreatment in Sport. St-Onge also said non-disclosure agreements and non-disparagement clauses will no longer be allowed to stop athletes and other participants from speaking about abuse or harassment they experienced or witnessed. National sport organizations will be required to adopt AthletesCAN’s athlete agreement template. Governance changes are also part of the plan. Athletes must have representation on national sport organization boards, at least 40 per cent of board members must be independent from the organization, no staff member may sit on the board, and directors will be limited to nine-year terms. In addition, organizations will have to publish annual audited financial statements, board meeting minutes and annual reports on board diversity online. The reforms are backed by $13.8 million in federal budget funding for safe sport this year. A new Sport Canada compliance unit will work with national sport organizations and outside experts to fix problems, monitor progress and connect compliance to federal funding. The government says those plans must be in place by 2024. Sport Canada and the Canadian Olympic Committee will also spend a combined $2 million on education and promotion of the UCCMS and the tools available to fight abuse. The Coaching Association of Canada will receive $250,000 to ensure all national and developmental team coaches are screened and certified, including background checks and training on the code. St-Onge said athlete well-being is her top priority and argued that sport should not be judged only by medals and podium results. She described the reforms as part of a long-term shift toward culture change, saying the new requirements will improve accountability, governance and athlete representation. The announcement comes after more than a year of upheaval in Canadian sport. Soon after St-Onge took over the sport portfolio in October 2021, she was confronted by what she called a safe sport crisis. In her first five months, accusations of maltreatment, sexual abuse or financial misuse were raised against at least eight national sport organizations. Tensions were already rising before the 2022 Winter Olympics and Paralympics, and after Beijing athletes in bobsled, skeleton, boxing, gymnastics, rugby, rowing and artistic swimming publicly demanded change. Their complaints covered abuse, harassment, bullying, opaque selection decisions and the handling of misconduct complaints. The crisis deepened with revelations about Hockey Canada’s response to an alleged gang rape involving members of the 2018 junior men’s team, and with public backlash over the use of minor hockey registration fees to settle sexual assault lawsuits. That sparked broader scrutiny of how Canadian sport measures success and allocates funding, especially given that taxpayers provide more than $200 million annually to high-performance sport. Athletes and executives continue to appear before parliamentary committees in Ottawa. Canada Soccer has also come under scrutiny, including for financial mismanagement and how it handled a coach convicted of sexual assault. St-Onge has used funding as leverage before: she suspended Hockey Canada’s money and later restored it, and she froze Gymnastics Canada’s funding until it became a signatory to the Office of the Sport Integrity Commissioner, which it did in October. OSIC, led by lawyer and former artistic swimmer Sarah-Eve Pelletier, was created as an independent body to handle abuse complaints. All national sport organizations were required to join by April 1 or risk losing federal funding. Some critics have called for a national inquiry into the crisis, including St-Onge’s predecessor Kirsty Duncan, but St-Onge has so far resisted that call.

Russian activist Ildar Dadin, who is serving a two-and-a-half-year prison sentence in Karelia for repeated participation in unsanctioned anti-government protests, said in a letter published Tuesday that he was beaten, threatened with rape, and warned he could be killed if he complained about abuse. Dadin, 34, was the first person jailed under a new law that imposes prison terms for repeated solo or unsanctioned demonstrations. In the letter to his wife, published by the independent Latvia-based news site Meduza and transcribed by his lawyer Alexei Liptser, Dadin said the abuse began on the second day of his detention in September. He alleged that the prison governor and three other staff members came to his cell and beat him repeatedly, sometimes with 10 to 12 people participating, and that after one beating his head was forced into a toilet bowl in an isolation cell. He also claimed prison workers hung him by his handcuffs for half an hour, pulled down his underwear, and threatened him with rape unless he ended a hunger strike. Dadin said he had begun the strike after being denied basic necessities such as soap and toilet paper. He added that other inmates were also suffering constant beatings, humiliation, and harsh detention conditions. The allegations prompted official reactions. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said President Vladimir Putin would be informed. Russia’s regional investigative committee said it would open a probe. Dadin asked the Committee Against Torture, a rights group under pressure from authorities, to help protect him and other prisoners. The group’s head, Igor Kalyapin, said he was seeking permission to visit the prison. However, a regional penitentiary official told Novaya Gazeta that guards used physical force only after Dadin refused to leave his cell for a search and tugged at guards’ uniforms. Russia’s human rights ombudsman Tatyana Moskalkova said Dadin had not confirmed the abuse and that photographs showed no visible injuries. International rights groups have long criticized prison conditions in Russia as overcrowded and corrupt.

In Kazakhstan, a recent rape case and the public backlash around it have pushed sexual violence to the center of national debate, with activists now pressing for legal reform. On August 18, four activists gathered in central Almaty with handmade signs reading “I’m against rape culture” and “No to sexual violence!” to protest the country’s handling of rape cases and demand changes to Article 120 of the criminal code, which governs punishment for rape. The protest was organized by 25-year-old Fariza Ospan and others, even though they did not have permission to assemble. Ospan said city bureaucracy would not stop them from speaking out. Their demonstration was aimed at changing Article 120 so that rape would again be classified as a “serious” crime rather than a “moderate” one. Activists argue that the current legal framework is too weak and reflects a broader failure to treat sexual violence seriously. The immediate catalyst for the outcry was a case involving two train conductors who raped and beat a passenger on a Talgo train in November 2018. After the case reached court this summer, prosecutors sought six-year prison sentences, but the judge instead sentenced each man to two and a half years. One sentence was reduced by three months because the defendant had already spent that time under house arrest. Activists noted that even the prosecutor’s requested sentence would have fallen below what many consider adequate, and the final punishment was especially shocking given the severity of the crime. News of the ruling spread rapidly across social media, where women began sharing their own experiences and fears using hashtags such as #MeTooTalgo and #NeMolchiKZ, meaning “Don’t Stay Quiet.” These online conversations quickly moved from grief and outrage to calls for action, with many focusing on the legal status of rape in Kazakhstan. Human rights activist Dina Smailova criticized the law’s classification of rape as less serious than crimes such as cattle theft, highlighting what she sees as a deeply distorted legal hierarchy. Article 120 has been controversial since its introduction in 1997. At first, rape was classified as a serious offense, but lawmakers later downgraded it to a moderate crime. Activists say this change has helped normalize weak punishment and inadequate protection for survivors. Ospan and fellow activist Moldir Aban tried to hold an authorized protest by submitting a request on August 8, but local authorities rejected it, citing sudden pipe maintenance at the planned location and time. After debating the risks of protesting without permission, they went ahead anyway. Their brief 40-minute demonstration drew attention from both supporters and opponents, including members of an anti-feminist, anti-LGBT group who came to disrupt it. Police arrived but made no arrests. The Talgo case has become a turning point in Kazakhstan’s public conversation about sexual violence. Activists now see reform as increasingly likely, especially after President Kasym-Jomart Tokayev signaled plans to tell parliament to strengthen penalties for sexual violence in his September 2 State of the Nation address.

However, they subsequently downgraded rape to moderate severity, a decision activists now seek to reverse. Members of an anti-feminist group attempted to disrupt the protest by calling police, but authorities made no arrests, suggesting they either recognized the legitimacy of the activists' cause or acknowledged the political sensitivity of interrupting a protest against sexual violence. President Kasym-Jomart Tokayev indicated he would use his State of the Nation address on September 2 to instruct parliament to toughen penalties for sexual violence, signaling that legal reform—once seemingly impossible—now appears inevitable.

Aiman Omarova, a prominent Kazakh human rights lawyer, says her dog was likely poisoned in what she believes was a warning tied to her work. Omarova found the 5-year-old dog dead in the backyard of her Almaty home early on June 5. She said the animal had been healthy, friendly, and had never caused problems with neighbors. Believing the death was intentional, she filed a police complaint. Omarova, who has represented victims of sexual abuse and people she says are politically persecuted in Kazakhstan, said this was not the first apparent threat against her. Earlier this year, she said someone hung a dead cat on the gate of her home, which she also interpreted as intimidation. She suspects the attack is connected to her recent role in helping Sairagul Sauytbay, a woman who fled China in 2018 and later left Kazakhstan for Sweden after being denied asylum. Sauytbay testified in Kazakhstan that thousands of ethnic Kazakhs, Uyghurs, and other Muslims in China’s Xinjiang region were being subjected to “political indoctrination” in reeducation camps. The revelations have complicated Kazakhstan’s relations with China.

Dunja Mijatović, the Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights, said after a recent visit to Armenia that the country’s new government should put human rights at the centre of its policies and focus on the needs of the most vulnerable people. In an article published by the Council of Europe, she praised Armenia’s peaceful transfer of power in May 2018 as “truly remarkable,” but warned that public expectations for real improvements in daily life are high and must be met with concrete action. Mijatović visited Armenia from September 15 to 20, with attention on women’s rights, gender equality, domestic violence, the rights of disadvantaged and vulnerable groups, and accountability for past human rights violations. She said the government should use this period of political transition to strengthen rights protections and avoid neglecting groups that have long been overlooked. A major focus of her remarks was women’s participation in public life. She said women in Armenia should be more effectively promoted in politics, especially at the highest levels of decision-making and at the local level, where their representation is particularly low. She said temporary special measures such as mandatory quotas can help create a more level playing field, and urged the authorities to set ambitious targets for women’s participation, including in local elections. She also called for greater efforts to encourage women and girls to engage in politics, promote role models of gender equality, and create an education environment free of discriminatory stereotypes. On employment, the Commissioner said Armenia should take decisive steps to ensure equal pay and equal access to the labor market for women. She pointed to the country’s high gender pay gap and said the list of professions considered hazardous for women should be abolished. She also recommended measures to help women return to work after maternity leave and called for stronger activity by the Council on Ensuring Equal Rights and Equal Opportunities for Women and Men under the Prime Minister. Mijatović welcomed Armenia’s adoption in December 2017 of a law on preventing domestic violence and protecting victims, as well as the country’s signature of the Council of Europe Convention on preventing and combating violence against women and domestic violence. But she said legal reforms must be matched by effective implementation once the law fully enters into force in January 2019. She stressed the need to train law enforcement officers, investigators, social workers, and judges so they can better protect victims and prevent re-victimization. During her visit, she saw Armenia’s only shelter for domestic violence victims, which was housing just five women with children. She said this was far from sufficient and welcomed the government’s plan to open new shelters in 2019, stressing that they should exist not only in Yerevan but also in other regions and remote areas. She also urged authorities to protect the right to education of children living in shelters. The Commissioner also addressed the rights of persons with disabilities. While welcoming Armenia’s efforts to move away from institutional care, she said the legal framework for state support still needs revision. She called for an end to plenary guardianship for people with psycho-social disabilities and urged a shift toward supported decision-making. She said confining such people to large state institutions is not the right approach and praised a small care home in Spitak as a better model for empowerment and self-reliance. On education, Mijatović commended the government’s commitment to make all education inclusive by 2025 and urged it to continue working toward that goal, with special attention to preschool education and equal de-institutionalization for children with and without disabilities. At the Nork children’s care home in Yerevan, she praised the quality of care and the dedication of staff but expressed concern that many children, including those without disabilities, had been placed there temporarily or abandoned by parents, often because of poverty. She said all children have the right to grow up in a family and that neither poverty nor disability should justify institutional placement. She urged Armenia to invest in community support for biological parents and continue promoting foster care. She also said ratifying the Lanzarote Convention would strengthen protection against child sexual exploitation and abuse. Mijatović said social protection for older persons in Armenia is still largely inadequate. She called for a comprehensive strategy to ensure dignity and welfare, including higher old-age benefits, the right to live in the community, and affordable healthcare, including for those in nursing homes. She also urged Armenia to adopt a comprehensive anti-discrimination law so that no one is discriminated against in public or private life. Regarding the legacy of the March 2008 violence that left ten people dead, she welcomed steps to establish responsibility but said this must be done carefully, with rule of law, judicial independence, transparency, and fair trial guarantees to avoid accusations of revenge politics or selective justice. Mijatović concluded by calling on politicians and opinion leaders to help build a cohesive society and avoid polarizing, stigmatizing, or inflammatory language during Armenia’s transition.

Police in Shymkent, Kazakhstan, are investigating allegations that a 22-year-old hearing-impaired woman was repeatedly raped and blackmailed, according to local reports and the #Nemolchikz fund. The case allegedly began in August last year, when she accepted a ride while trying to get home from work. The fund says one man later lured her outside, raped her, and another filmed the assault, which was then used for blackmail. In March, a suspect allegedly threatened to burn her family’s house, forcing her to leave home. She was later taken to a secluded place and assaulted by two men.

# Summary Police in Shymkent, Kazakhstan are investigating allegations of group rape and blackmail against a 22-year-old hearing-impaired woman. The #Nemolchikz fund reported that the victim's ordeal began in August when she accepted a ride from a taxi, leading to her rape by one suspect while another recorded video. The perpetrators subsequently blackmailed her using the footage. In March, escalating threats—including burning down her house—forced her to flee home. She was then allegedly taken to a secluded location where two men assaulted her again. The case involves multiple alleged incidents spanning several months.

Russia reported another one-day high in COVID-19 infections as the country continued to battle a surge that began in mid-September and has lasted more than a month. On Saturday, the national coronavirus task force said there were 41,335 new cases in the previous 24 hours, topping the prior record of 40,993 set on Oct. 31. It also reported 1,188 deaths, only seven fewer than the daily record announced Thursday. Officials have blamed Russia’s low vaccination rate for much of the sharp rise. The task force said about 57.2 million people had received full-course vaccinations, which is less than 40% of Russia’s 146 million population. The country has one of the world’s largest outbreaks, with more than 8.75 million confirmed cases and 245,635 deaths recorded by the task force since the start of the pandemic. However, Russia’s state statistics agency, which uses broader criteria for virus-related deaths, has said the real toll is much higher; its latest report put virus-connected deaths at about 462,000 through the end of September. In response to the worsening situation, President Vladimir Putin ordered many Russians to stay off work from Oct. 30 through Nov. 7 and allowed regional authorities to extend the nonworking period if needed. Several regions, including Novgorod in the northwest, Tomsk in Siberia, Chelyabinsk in the Ural Mountains, and Kursk and Bryansk southwest of Moscow, have extended the shutdown through the end of next week. At the same time, Moscow’s mayor said conditions in the capital had improved enough for residents to return to work on Monday. People in Crimea, the Russia-annexed peninsula, are also set to resume working next week. Even as some areas reopen, restrictions remain in Moscow. Older adults are still under a stay-at-home order, businesses must keep 30% of staff working from home, and access to theaters and museums is limited to people who are fully vaccinated, recently recovered from COVID-19, or able to show a negative test.

# Russia Battles Record COVID-19 Surge Russia reached a new daily infection record as it continues struggling with a persistent coronavirus wave that began in mid-September. The national coronavirus task force reported 41,335 new cases on Saturday, surpassing the previous record of 40,993 cases from October 31. Additionally, 1,188 deaths were recorded, nearly matching the daily death record of 1,195 reported Thursday. Officials attribute the sharp rise in cases primarily to Russia's low vaccination rate. Fewer than 40% of the country's 146 million people have completed vaccination courses, with approximately 57.2 million full-course vaccinations administered to date. In response to the crisis, President Vladimir Putin previously ordered many Russians to take time off work between October 30 and November 7. Regional governments were authorized to extend these nonworking days as needed. Several regions, including Novgorod, Tomsk, Chelyabinsk, Kursk, and Bryansk, have extended the shutdown through the following week. Moscow's situation has reportedly stabilized enough to allow workers to return Monday, though certain restrictions will remain. These include a stay-at-home order for older adults and a requirement that businesses maintain 30% remote work. Access to cultural venues like theaters and museums is restricted to those who are fully vaccinated, recovered within the past six months, or possess a negative coronavirus test. Crimea will also resume normal work schedules next week. According to the national task force, Russia has recorded over 8.75 million confirmed cases and 245,635 deaths. However, state statistical services report significantly higher figures, tallying approximately 462,000 virus-connected deaths through September's end when counting deaths where the virus was a contributing factor or suspected but unconfirmed. This discrepancy highlights the pandemic's potentially greater impact than official confirmed case numbers suggest.

The Aurora Prize for Awakening Humanity Selection Committee has announced three humanitarian activists as finalists for the 2018 Aurora Prize, a $1.1 million award presented by the Aurora Humanitarian Initiative in gratitude to the rescuers of Armenians during the Genocide. The three nominees were selected for what the committee described as exceptional courage, broad impact and an unwavering commitment to saving lives and advancing humanitarian causes under difficult and dangerous conditions. The finalists are Kyaw Hla Aung of Myanmar, Fr. Héctor Tomás González Castillo of Mexico, and Sunitha Krishnan of India. One of them will be named the 2018 Aurora Prize Laureate at a ceremony in Yerevan, Armenia, on June 10, 2018, following a ceremonial honoring of the three humanitarians on June 9. The Laureate will receive a $100,000 grant and, more significantly, a $1 million award to support organizations that have inspired and supported their work. Kyaw Hla Aung is a lawyer and Rohingya leader in Myanmar. He has spent years advocating for equality, education and human rights for the Rohingya Muslim community, despite being imprisoned for a total of 12 years for participating in peaceful protests against discrimination and violence. He has used his legal training to defend his community and has nominated Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) International, the Malaysian Medical Relief Society and the International Catholic Migration Commission for the award funds. These organizations provide medical aid and refugee assistance in Myanmar. Fr. Héctor Tomás González Castillo, a Franciscan friar and founder of La 72 in Mexico, has spent years helping migrants traveling through Mexico from Central America. He has provided shelter, food, water, counseling and legal assistance to more than 50,000 immigrants along journeys often marked by attacks, attempted kidnappings and forced expulsions. His nominated organizations are El Oasis San Juan de Dios and La Escuela de Agricultura Ecológica U Yits Ka'an, both of which work on human rights and cultural support. Sunitha Krishnan, co-founder of Prajwala in India, is a survivor of gang rape who transformed her experience into activism against sex trafficking and forced prostitution. Through Prajwala, she has helped rescue, rehabilitate and reintegrate victims back into society, with the organization benefiting more than 17,800 women and children. She nominated Prajwala, Stop Trafficking & Oppression of Children & Women (STOP), and Sanlaap India, all of which work against gender violence, trafficking and related abuses. The Selection Committee is co-chaired by actor and humanitarian George Clooney and includes prominent figures such as Nobel laureates Oscar Arias, Shirin Ebadi and Leymah Gbowee; former Irish president Mary Robinson; human rights advocate Hina Jilani; former Australian foreign minister Gareth Evans; former Mexican president Ernesto Zedillo; Lord Ara Darzi; Médecins Sans Frontières founder Bernard Kouchner; and former U.S. ambassador to the United Nations Samantha Power. The committee shortlisted the three finalists from 750 nominations representing 509 unique candidates submitted in 12 languages from 115 countries. Vartan Gregorian, speaking for the committee, said the nominees embody the kind of frontline humanitarian sacrifice that Aurora seeks to recognize, linking their work to the historical experience of Armenians who were saved during the Genocide. He said the prize is meant to honor those who protect the vulnerable and continue the cycle of gratitude and giving. The article also notes the previous Aurora Prize laureates. In 2017, the prize went to Dr. Tom Catena, an American Catholic missionary and the sole surgeon at the Mother of Mercy Catholic Hospital in Sudan’s war-ravaged Nuba Mountains, where he treats patients around the clock despite severe restrictions on aid. Catena said the prize not only supported his work but also drew international attention to crises that are often overlooked. The first Aurora Prize Laureate, in 2016, was Marguerite Barankitse of Burundi, who created safe haven for orphans and refugees during her country’s civil war and later supported multiple initiatives across several countries. The 2018 Laureate will be announced at the end of a weekend of Aurora events that also includes the annual Aurora Dialogues, a forum bringing together humanitarian and business leaders to discuss solutions to pressing global problems. This year’s Dialogues will feature the three finalists sharing their experiences and personal stories.

Francisco José Cox, a former influential Chilean archbishop who was removed from the priesthood by Pope Francis in 2018 over sexual abuse allegations, died on Aug. 12 at age 86 without ever standing trial. His death was announced by the Schoenstatt Fathers, the religious community connected to him later in life. According to the statement, he died early in the morning from respiratory failure and multisystemic failure and was buried the same day, with only his four brothers present. Cox had a prominent career in the Chilean Catholic hierarchy. He served as bishop of Chillán from 1975 to 1981 and as archbishop of La Serena from 1990 to 1997. Between those posts, he worked at the Vatican’s former Pontifical Council for the Family. In 1987, he was chosen to help organize Pope John Paul II’s visit to Chile, which brought him into close contact with Archbishop Angelo Sodano, then the papal representative in Chile. Sodano later became Vatican secretary of state, and many observers have since described him as a central figure in the broader abuse crisis that has engulfed the Chilean Church. The allegations against Cox emerged years before his removal from ministry. In 1992, a priest filed a formal complaint with the bishops’ conference claiming he had caught Cox having sex with a young man. Despite this, Cox remained active in church roles for years. His resignation from La Serena was quietly accepted by the Vatican in 1997, but he continued to hold positions in the Latin American bishops’ conference and at the Vatican until 2002. That year, the Vatican’s Congregation for Bishops ordered him to live a life of “penance and prayer,” first in Switzerland and then in Germany under Schoenstatt Fathers’ care. Public acknowledgment of the accusations came in 2002, when Cardinal Francisco Javier Errázuriz initially dismissed them as “rumors” but soon afterward issued a statement asking forgiveness for those harmed by Cox’s actions. Cox himself wrote to the faithful of La Serena, saying: “I ask forgiveness for this dark side within me and which is against the Gospel.” Later, in 2018, he declined to answer questions from Chilean media and said the allegations in Chile and Germany were “not my problem at this moment.” The Schoenstatt Fathers said Cox had been investigated in penal cases and expressed pain for the victims, while reaffirming cooperation with authorities. His removal from the clerical state in 2018 was described by survivors as overdue, though unprecedented. The same day, another Chilean bishop, Marco Antonio Ordenes Fernandez, was also laicized.

# Ex-Archbishop Dies Without Trial in Chilean Sex Abuse Case Francisco José Cox, a former powerful Chilean archbishop, died on August 12 at age 86 without ever facing trial for allegations of sexually abusing minors. The Schoenstatt Fathers, his religious order, announced his death from respiratory and multisystemic failure. He was buried the same day with only his four brothers present. Cox served as bishop of Chillan from 1975 to 1981 and archbishop of La Serena from 1990 to 1997. Between these positions, he worked at the Vatican and organized Pope John Paul II's 1987 visit to Chile, developing a close relationship with papal representative Angelo Sodano, who would later become Vatican Secretary of State and is widely regarded as instrumental in enabling Chile's abuse crisis. Cox's resignation from La Serena in 1997 followed a 1992 complaint from a priest who discovered Cox engaging in sexual activity with a young man. Despite this, Cox remained semi-active in various positions until 2002, when he was ordered to live a life of "penance and prayer" in Switzerland and later Germany. In 2002, Cardinal Francisco Javier Errazuriz initially dismissed allegations against Cox as "rumors" but subsequently requested forgiveness for those harmed by the archbishop's actions. Cox himself issued a public statement admitting "this dark side within me" but later refused to address the allegations, claiming they were "not my problem." Pope Francis removed Cox from the priesthood in 2018 following a Vatican investigation, allowing him to remain a lay member of Schoenstatt for continued care. The Schoenstatt Fathers acknowledged Cox "was investigated in causes of a penal character" and expressed solidarity with victims, reaffirming their cooperation with the justice system. Allegations against Cox were lodged in the two Chilean dioceses he served and in Germany, where he lived from 2002 until 2019, when he was forced to return to Chile. The 2018 Vatican ruling was unprecedented but labeled "too late" by survivors. On the same day, Pope Francis also removed another bishop from the clerical state.

Chile’s Senate has rejected a bill that would have legalized abortion up to 14 weeks of pregnancy. The measure failed narrowly, with 65 votes in favor, 62 against and one abstention. Abortion is currently allowed only in limited cases, including rape, danger to the mother’s life, or fetal nonviability. Despite the restrictions, thousands of abortions are believed to occur clandestinely each year. Under current law, both doctors and patients can be prosecuted. The vote contrasts with neighboring Argentina, which legalized abortion up to 14 weeks late last year.

# Summary Chile's Senate rejected a bill legalizing abortion up to 14 weeks, with 65 votes for and 62 against. Currently, abortion is only permitted in exceptional cases: after rape, when the mother's life is endangered, or if the fetus is nonviable. Both doctors and patients face prosecution for illegal abortions, though thousands occur secretly annually in private clinics. Argentina recently legalized abortion up to 14 weeks, while most Latin American countries restrict it to exceptional circumstances. Uruguay, Cuba, Guyana, and parts of Mexico permit abortion more broadly, whereas El Salvador bans it entirely, with severe penalties including imprisonment even for miscarriages.

Brazilian footballer Dani Alves is awaiting a decision from the Barcelona Court of Appeal on Tuesday over whether he can leave prison while his sexual assault case continues. Alves has spent a month in Brians 2 prison after being ordered held without bail over an allegation that he sexually assaulted a 23-year-old woman in a bathroom at Barcelona’s Sutton nightclub on December 30. His lawyer, Cristóbal Martell, appealed the detention order and asked for provisional release, arguing Alves should be allowed to defend himself from outside prison. Alves insists the encounter was consensual and says he is innocent, though he has changed his account several times. If the court grants release, he would likely face precautionary measures such as posting bail, surrendering his passport, wearing a tracking bracelet, regularly appearing in court, and having no contact with the alleged victim. The original judge ordered preventive detention because of what she saw as a high risk that Alves might flee, citing his financial resources and the fact that Spain has no extradition treaty with Brazil. At a hearing last Thursday, both the prosecution and the private prosecution representing the victim opposed his release, saying the circumstances had not changed since the detention order and that evidence contradicts Alves’ latest version of events. The court has spent several days reviewing the arguments and will announce its ruling Tuesday.

# Summary Dani Alves, a Brazilian footballer, awaits a Barcelona Court of Appeal decision on Tuesday regarding his release from Brians 2 prison, where he has been held for one month. He is accused of sexually assaulting a 23-year-old woman in a nightclub bathroom on December 30. A judge initially remanded Alves in custody without bail, citing his high risk of absconding due to his wealth and the absence of an extradition treaty between Spain and Brazil. His lawyer, Cristobal Martell, appealed this decision, requesting the footballer's release on four-month measures. Alves maintains the encounter was consensual, though he has changed his account multiple times. If released, he would face conditions including bail payment, passport surrender, electronic monitoring, and regular court appearances. He would also be prohibited from contacting the victim. Both the prosecution and the victim's representative oppose his release, arguing that the original detention conditions remain valid. They claim substantial evidence contradicts Alves' current version of events. The court heard arguments from both parties last Thursday and will announce its decision on Tuesday. Despite his imprisonment, Alves continues asserting his innocence through his legal team.

Brazil’s Supreme Court ruled on Nov. 29 that abortion cannot be criminally punished during the first three months of pregnancy, a decision that immediately drew strong criticism from church and political leaders. The ruling came while the court reviewed a habeas corpus petition involving five employees of a clandestine abortion clinic in Duque de Caxias, in Rio de Janeiro state. The justices said Brazil’s Penal Code, by criminalizing abortion in early pregnancy, violates women’s fundamental rights, including autonomy, physical and psychological integrity, sexual and reproductive rights, and gender equality. They also argued that “democratic and developed countries” such as the United States, Germany and France do not penalize abortion in the first trimester. Bishop Antonio Carlos Rossi Keller called the decision a “death sentence for the unborn” and said the Supreme Court should uphold Brazil’s Constitution, which does not allow the death penalty. He also condemned what he saw as hypocrisy in protecting animals while allowing abortion. In response, the House of Representatives announced it would create a special commission to review the ruling. Representative Evandro Gussi said the court had overstepped its authority and violated the separation of powers, insisting abortion remains a crime under the Criminal Code except in limited cases such as rape, danger to the mother’s life, or microcephaly. The vote was supported by judges Luis Roberto Barroso, Rosa Weber and Edson Fachin.

# Summary On November 29, 2016, Brazil's Supreme Court ruled that abortion cannot be legally penalized during the first three months of pregnancy, citing women's rights to autonomy, physical and psychological integrity, and reproductive rights. The justices referenced examples from Western democracies like the United States, Germany, and France that do not criminalize early-stage abortion. The controversial decision emerged from a habeas corpus petition involving five employees of an underground abortion clinic in Rio de Janeiro. The ruling immediately sparked significant opposition. Bishop Antonio Carlos Rossi Keller condemned the decision as a "death sentence for the unborn," arguing it contradicted Brazil's constitutional prohibition on capital punishment and represented societal hypocrisy. In response, the House of Representatives announced plans to establish a special commission to review the court's decision. Mexican actress Adriana Barraza will receive the 2018 Platino Prize of Honor for Ibero-American Cinema this week in Mexico, and says she is approaching the award “with my heart full of joy.” In an interview with EFE in Buenos Aires, Barraza said she feels “very proud” and “honored” because she has taken part in several Platino galas and now feels like part of the event itself. The honor will be presented at the fifth edition of the Platino Awards, to be held next Sunday in Xcaret, on Mexico’s Riviera Maya. The award recognizes her “impressive and multifaceted professional career” as an actress, director, producer and teacher, as well as her commitment to the Ibero-American film industry. Barraza, 62, said she does not favor one of those roles over another and feels comfortable working both in front of and behind the camera. She said the variety helps her “discover, experiment and do research,” and keeps her from “getting old” on set. She also praised the Platino Awards as one of the few prizes that brings together both European and Latin American artists, calling them a “delight” and a “blessing” for filmmakers with stories to tell. In her view, Ibero-America is a large and diverse region, and its unity strengthens the industry. Often described as the “grande dame of Ibero-American cinema,” Barraza has spent four decades in acting and appeared in about 50 films. Among her best-known work are two films by Mexican director Alejandro González Iñárritu: “Amores perros” (2000) and “Babel” (2006). She said “Amores perros” showed her a new way of acting, explaining that Iñárritu’s method makes performances less melodramatic and more rooted in real life. With “Babel,” she gained worldwide recognition and received major nominations and awards, including a Golden Globe and an Oscar nomination. She said that film marked “the most wonderful thing” because it launched a new phase in her career after years of working mainly behind the camera. Barraza said she never dreamed of becoming an actress as a child and originally wanted to be a ballerina. At 16, when she had to choose between basketball, theater and ballet, she ended up in theater because the ballet class was full. She recalled that her first stage experience brought her together with other disadvantaged teenagers looking for acceptance. She also spoke candidly about discrimination early in her career, especially while working behind the scenes, where she said she faced mistreatment “all the time.” She noted that abuse and harassment have long existed in the film world, and said many victims were not listened to because they were not famous. Born in Toluca, Mexico, Barraza now lives in Miami, where she teaches at the acting school she founded in 2011 with her husband and manager, actor Arnaldo Pinke. She also has a home in Buenos Aires, where her daughter and grandson live.

Ecuador has cut off Julian Assange’s internet access at its embassy in London, saying he violated a written agreement not to comment on other countries’ affairs. The National Communications Secretariat said Wednesday that the systems allowing Assange to communicate with the outside world were suspended on Tuesday. President Lenín Moreno’s government said the decision followed Assange’s failure to comply with a December 2017 pledge not to make social media posts that could be seen as interference in other nations’ politics. Ecuador said Assange had already irritated officials last year by expressing support for Catalonia’s independence movement in Spain. More recently, he criticized the United Kingdom’s expulsion of 23 Russian diplomats after the poisoning of former Russian double agent Sergei Skripal and his daughter in Salisbury. On Monday, Assange tweeted that while Theresa May was reasonable to suspect the Russian state, the evidence was still circumstantial. Ecuador said his posts threatened the country’s “good relations” with the UK, the European Union, and other nations. Assange has lived in Ecuador’s London embassy since June 2012, after seeking refuge there to avoid extradition to Sweden over sexual assault allegations. Ecuador granted him asylum in August 2012. Although Sweden later dropped its rape investigation, Assange cannot leave the embassy without risking arrest by UK authorities for allegedly breaching bail conditions in 2012. Assange denies the accusations and says he fears the UK will extradite him to the United States over WikiLeaks’ publication of classified material.
