An Argentine court on Tuesday dismissed aggravated rape charges against French international rugby players Hugo Auradou and Oscar Jegou, ending a case that had cast a shadow over French rugby. The two 21-year-olds had been under investigation since July 12 after a 39-year-old woman accused them of rape in Mendoza province, where they had just made their international debuts. They denied any wrongdoing throughout, saying the encounter was consensual. Argentina’s judiciary said Judge Eleonora Arenas ruled that “the facts investigated do not constitute a crime.” The case had been classified as “sexual abuse with carnal access aggravated by the participation of two or more people,” according to court documents seen by Reuters. In September, psychological and psychiatric evaluations found “a series of inconsistencies and contradictions” in the woman’s account. The players were detained in Mendoza shortly after the complaint, spent several days in preventive detention, and nearly a month under house arrest before being allowed to leave Argentina in early September and return to France. Since then, both have resumed club rugby: Auradou has played for Section Paloise and Jegou for Stade Rochelais. Their lawyer, Rafael Cuneo Libarona, welcomed the ruling and said he had always believed in their innocence. The French Rugby Federation also said it was relieved and that the players are now eligible for national team selection again.

The dismissal concludes what the judiciary described as a difficult period for France's rugby community.

A man was detained Thursday night after reportedly pointing a handgun at close range at Argentine Vice President Cristina Fernández outside her home in Buenos Aires, authorities said. Video aired by local television showed Fernández getting out of her vehicle in the Recoleta neighborhood, surrounded by supporters, when a man extended his hand with what appeared to be a pistol. Fernández ducked as the crowd around her reacted in shock. Security Minister Aníbal Fernández told the cable news channel C5N that the man was identified by people nearby as carrying a gun and was quickly restrained by the vice president’s security team. According to the minister, guards separated the suspect from the crowd, found the weapon, and turned it over for analysis. He said officials were being cautious about releasing further information until investigators learned more. At the time of the report, there was no official confirmation about whether the weapon was real. Unverified footage posted on social media appeared to show the pistol coming very close to Fernández’s face. The incident prompted concern because it occurred in front of supporters gathered outside her residence, creating a tense scene in one of the city’s most prominent neighborhoods. Authorities had not yet provided additional details about the suspect, the motive, or the condition of the weapon as the investigation continued.

La ONU informó este martes de un aumento significativo de las denuncias por supuestos abusos sexuales cometidos por personal de la organización o por entidades asociadas en 2021. En total, recibió 445 denuncias, frente a 387 en 2020. De ellas, 194 se referían a presuntos casos atribuidos a empleados de la ONU y sus agencias, mientras que 251 involucraban a grupos e instituciones con los que coopera, pero sobre los que no tiene autoridad directa. El incremento se enmarca en la política de transparencia adoptada por Naciones Unidas tras el escándalo de abusos cometidos por cascos azules en varios países africanos. En el caso de las misiones de paz, se registraron 75 acusaciones en 2021, por encima de las 66 de 2020 y de la media de 69 de la última década. Estas denuncias se vinculan a 190 víctimas, muchas de ellas relacionadas con un mismo contingente de la misión de paz en la República Centroafricana (Minusca). Ante esos hechos, la ONU anunció en septiembre la repatriación de todos los soldados gaboneses desplegados en esa operación. También aumentaron las acusaciones de abuso sexual contra menores por parte de cascos azules: hubo 25 denuncias y 51 víctimas. Casi el 90% de los casos contra fuerzas de paz se concentraron en dos misiones: la Minusca y la Monusco, en la República Democrática del Congo. De las 75 acusaciones contra personal de paz, 25 habrían ocurrido en 2021 y las otras 50 corresponden a años anteriores, algo que la ONU atribuye en parte a sus campañas para animar a las víctimas a denunciar. En paralelo, las denuncias contra personal de agencias, fondos y programas de la ONU subieron a 115, y las vinculadas a entidades colaboradoras alcanzaron 251. António Guterres reconoció en el informe que aún no se ha logrado un éxito claro y admitió que sigue siendo necesario hacer más para erradicar la explotación y los abusos sexuales.

Somali security forces have arrested Abdinasir Mohamed Hassan, a mechanical engineer accused of helping Al-Shabaab prepare vehicles for suicide bombings in Mogadishu, according to Somalia’s intelligence agency. The agency said Hassan inspected and modified vehicles that were turned into Vehicle-Borne Improvised Explosive Devices (VBIEDs) used to attack hotels and other key sites in the capital. He is alleged to have altered at least nine vehicles that were later used in bombings that killed dozens of civilians in Mogadishu and elsewhere. Officials said Hassan handed over the most recent vehicle he worked on to Abdinasir Dahir Nur Jim’ale, also known as Guri Ma Leedahay, and that vehicle was later used in the March 14 attack on the SYL Hotel, only a short distance from Somalia’s presidential compound. The assault on the hotel involved both a suicide bombing and a prolonged armed siege. Fighters stormed the building in gunfire late on Thursday, and the 13-hour attack left at least three soldiers and six attackers dead, while 27 people were wounded. Al-Shabaab claimed responsibility for the attack. The intelligence agency said Jim’ale, described as a notorious figure in the Elasha area near Mogadishu, has been captured, sentenced, and is now in prison. The arrest comes just two days after authorities detained two medical professionals, Koshin Mohamed Ahmed and Keyse Farah Hassan, for alleged links to the militant group. Ahmed is accused of managing hospitals and treating wounded Al-Shabaab fighters brought to Mogadishu, while Hassan allegedly treated members in Jilib, a stronghold in Middle Jubba. The agency also said Hassan is related to Hussein Ali Fidow, a senior Al-Shabaab leader. Last week, security forces also detained a Somali National Army first lieutenant, Abdullahi Ahmed Hassan, on suspicion of serving as an Al-Shabaab informant. Al-Shabaab has not responded to the arrests. The group, driven from Mogadishu in 2011, continues to wage attacks across Somalia and still controls parts of the south.

As South Africa prepares to host the 25th African Union Summit in Johannesburg, more than 50 African heads of state and government are expected to arrive at Waterkloof Air Force Base in Pretoria for the June 14–15 ordinary assembly. Zimbabwe, under President Robert Mugabe, holds the AU chairmanship for 2015, and Mugabe is set to preside over a packed and difficult agenda. The crisis in Burundi is expected to dominate discussions. AU leaders face the challenge of helping to resolve the country’s political turmoil and persuading President Pierre Nkurunziza to abandon plans to seek a third term, despite constitutional limits of two terms. Burundi’s instability is likely to be the summit’s most pressing political issue. Security and terrorism will also feature prominently. The AU is expected to mount a stronger campaign against extremist groups such as Boko Haram in Nigeria and al-Shabaab in Kenya and the wider region. These groups have killed hundreds, displaced thousands and devastated communities. Boko Haram’s abduction of hundreds of schoolgirls in Nigeria remains one of the most alarming examples, with fears that some may have been trained as suicide bombers. The threat posed by these groups may add urgency to efforts to operationalise the African Standby Force, a continental security force that has been delayed for years. Economic integration will be another major topic. Leaders are expected to review progress toward the Continental Free Trade Area (CFTA), which the AU wants in place by 2017. The plan, endorsed at the 2012 Addis Ababa summit under the theme of boosting intra-African trade, is intended to increase trade within Africa by 25 to 30 percent over the next decade. The summit will also focus on Agenda 2063, the AU’s long-term development vision. Leaders are expected to outline the first 10-year implementation plan for the initiative, which aims to guide the continent toward a prosperous Africa by 2063, the centenary of the Organisation of African Unity. Other agenda items include women’s empowerment, with calls for greater female participation in economic leadership, and a report from a 10-member committee working on reform of the United Nations Security Council. The AU wants permanent African representation on the council. Finally, funding remains a major concern. The AU has long depended on foreign donors, and Commission Chair Nkosazana Dlamini Zuma is pushing for greater financial self-reliance through contributions from member states, though many remain too poor to easily provide substantial support.

On International Women’s Day, Judy Chepsoi, the widow of slain Administration Police officer Arnold Kipyegon Kenei, had little reason to celebrate. Her husband, 33, was killed in what investigators say was part of a plot to conceal a Sh39 billion fake military equipment tender linked to former Sports Cabinet Secretary Rashid Echesa. According to Directorate of Criminal Investigations (DCI) chief George Kinoti, Kenei was targeted because he knew too much about the scheme. He had reportedly ushered Echesa into Deputy President William Ruto’s office, where Kenei worked as a security officer, as Echesa sought to advance the fake arms deal with foreign dealers. Ruto was not in the office at the time and has denied ever having an appointment with Echesa, whom he considers a close ally. Kenei was found dead on February 20, 2020, in his Villa Franca home in Nairobi, with a bullet wound under his chin, his pistol beside him, and a suicide note on the table. However, detectives later concluded the scene had been staged. Kinoti said CCTV footage showed events surrounding Echesa’s visit to the Deputy President’s office and confirmed that Kenei’s death was tied to the arms scandal. Kenei had been scheduled to record a statement with investigators two days before his body was discovered. At Kenei’s burial in Chemasis village, Solai, Rongai sub-county, on Saturday, Chepsoi was overcome with grief. The funeral was attended by Deputy President Ruto. Chepsoi said the year and a few days she spent with Kenei were far too short, but described them as the happiest and most fulfilling of her life. She remembered him as a devoted father and the best husband any woman could wish for. The couple had a one-month-old baby boy, and Kenei also left behind a 13-year-old son from a previous relationship. Chepsoi vowed to preserve his legacy for their children and demanded justice for his killing. Kenei’s son also paid tribute, calling his father his best friend and saying he would always cherish their time together. Ruto, meanwhile, has called for a thorough investigation and accused the DCI of being used to implicate his office in the murder.

# Summary On International Women's Day, Judy Chepsoi, 27, mourned her husband Arnold Kipyegon Kenei, a 33-year-old Administration Police officer who was killed in connection with a Sh39 billion fake military equipment tender scandal. According to DCI head George Kinoti, Kenei was murdered by individuals linked to former Sports Cabinet Secretary Rashid Echesa. Chepsoi and Kenei had been married for only one year and ten days before his death on February 20, 2020. They met on Valentine's Day 2019 and shared 372 days together. Their one-month-old son was left orphaned, and Kenei also had a 13-year-old son from a previous relationship. Kenei was targeted because he possessed sensitive information about the fraudulent arms deal. As a security officer at Deputy President William Ruto's office, he had escorted Echesa to meet with the DP to arrange the fake deal with foreign arms dealers. Ruto was reportedly absent during this meeting and has denied any appointment with Echesa. The official account suggested suicide—Kenei's body was found in his Villa Franca home with a bullet wound to his chin, his pistol nearby, and a suicide note on the table. However, detectives concluded the scene was staged and classified it as murder. Kenei had been scheduled to give a statement to investigators two days before his death. At his funeral in Solai, Rongai sub-county, attended by Deputy President Ruto, Chepsoi delivered an emotional eulogy, describing their year together as fulfilling and joyful. She vowed to care for their sons and preserve Kenei's legacy while demanding justice for his death. Ruto subsequently called for a thorough investigation, accusing the DCI of misusing its authority to implicate his office in the murder.

The Democratic Republic of Congo’s Supreme Court opened a new hearing on Friday in the long-running case over the 2010 murder of leading human rights activist Floribert Chebeya, with judges considering a request from civil parties linked to Chebeya and his organization, La Voix des sans Voix (VSV), to prevent any final verdict from later being overturned. Chebeya, a prominent and increasingly outspoken critic of President Joseph Kabila in his later years, disappeared after being summoned on 1 June 2010 by then national police chief General John Numbi. Numbi denied arranging any meeting, but he was later suspended and eventually formally dismissed in December because of the case. The next day, Chebeya was found dead in the back seat of his car, with signs that he had been handcuffed. His driver, Fidèle Bazana, also vanished and is presumed to have been killed as well. A military court in Kinshasa convicted Deputy Chief of Police Special Services Colonel Daniel Mukalay of murder in 2011 and sentenced him to death, along with three other officers. A fifth policeman received a life sentence. However, three of the convicted men fled and remain at large. The defendants appealed, and a military court of appeal reopened the case in June 2012. That process was suspended in May of the previous year after civil parties denounced procedural irregularities, and Chebeya’s family and VSV have argued from the start that the trial was flawed. The activist’s supporters want Numbi prosecuted when the proceedings resume, saying he is the prime suspect in the deaths of both Chebeya and Bazana. VSV deputy director Rostin Maketa said Numbi’s name had been raised from the first day of the disappearance and discovery of the body, and the group wants him arrested and made a suspect. In the original proceedings, Numbi told the court he had never met Chebeya or summoned him to police headquarters. One defendant who fled to Senegal directly implicated Numbi, but the court rejected that testimony. Whatever the Supreme Court decides, the appeal by the five convicted officers is expected to continue in the coming weeks. The case has drawn international attention and criticism. French President François Hollande honored Chebeya’s memory in Kinshasa in 2012, prompting a diplomatic stir. UN and Human Rights Watch officials said justice still has not been done and expressed hope that the resumed trial will finally hold the real culprits accountable. Meanwhile, Senegal’s judiciary has agreed to investigate one of the convicted officers, Paul Mwilambwe, after a lawsuit filed by the victims’ families through FIDH.

# DRC Court Reopens Hearing in Activist's Murder Case The Democratic Republic of Congo's Supreme Court prepared Friday for a new hearing regarding the 2010 murder of Floribert Chebeya, the country's most prominent human rights activist. Civil parties and the organization Chebeya founded, La Voix des sans Voix (Voice of the Voiceless), requested that the court ensure any final verdict cannot be overruled, following prior legal irregularities. Chebeya was summoned by then-police chief General John Numbi on June 1, 2010, though Numbi later denied arranging the meeting. The following day, Chebeya was discovered dead in his car with signs of handcuffing. His driver, Fidele Bazana, disappeared and is presumed murdered. A military court convicted Colonel Daniel Mukalay and three other officers of murder in 2011, sentencing them to death. A fifth officer received a life sentence, though three remain at large. The case was retried in 2012, but proceedings suspended in May 2013 due to irregularities. Chebeya's relatives and supporters consider ex-police chief Numbi the prime suspect, demanding his arrest and prosecution. One defendant who fled to Senegal directly implicated Numbi, but the court disallowed his testimony. Numbi was formally dismissed last December after being suspended from duties. International observers express skepticism about the justice process. Abdoul Aziz Thioye of the UN office for human rights stated "the general feeling is that justice has not been done" and "the real culprits have not yet been punished." Human Rights Watch's Ida Sawyer expressed hope that "justice will finally be handed down" with the trial's resumption. Chebeya had become an increasingly outspoken critic of President Joseph Kabila before his death. His murder caused diplomatic tension when French President François Hollande honored his memory at the 2012 Francophonie summit in Kinshasa. Recently, Senegal agreed to investigate one convicted officer, Paul Mwilambwe, who fled there, following a lawsuit by the International Federation for Human Rights on behalf of the victims' families.

More than 1,000 pilgrims died during this year’s Hajj in Saudi Arabia as record-breaking heat swept across the holy sites, according to officials and a Reuters tally. The death toll included nearly 100 Indians, with India’s Ministry of External Affairs saying 98 Indian pilgrims had died. MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said India had sent 175,000 pilgrims, and the reported Indian deaths were attributed to natural illness, chronic conditions, old age, and a few accidents. He noted that six Indians died on Arafat Day and four in accidents, adding that 187 Indians died during last year’s Hajj. The overall toll was especially high among Egyptians. Reuters reported that Egypt’s death count rose to 672, with 25 pilgrims still missing. Tunisia, Jordan, Iran, Senegal, and two pilgrims from the United States also reported deaths, bringing the total to at least 1,114. Saudi Arabia has not publicly commented on the fatalities. The Hajj, one of Islam’s five pillars, draws millions of Muslims to Saudi Arabia each year for a five-day pilgrimage. Deaths are not unusual at the event, which has previously seen deadly stampedes and disease outbreaks. The article recalled the 2015 Mina stampede, which killed more than 2,400 people, and the 1990 stampede, which killed 1,426. The extreme heat was central to this year’s tragedy. Temperatures in Mecca and surrounding sacred sites reportedly exceeded 46°C (117°F) and reached 49°C (120°F), according to Saudi meteorological authorities. Some pilgrims fainted while performing rituals, including the symbolic stoning of the devil. The article linked the heatwave to broader climate conditions affecting multiple continents and noted that climate change may be intensifying record temperatures. In Egypt, a crisis unit investigating the deaths said it suspended the licenses of 16 tourism companies and referred them to prosecutors, accusing them of facilitating travel for pilgrims outside the official system. The Egyptian government said 31 authorized pilgrims died from chronic illnesses, but a Cabinet official said at least 630 more Egyptians died, many at a medical complex in Mecca’s Al-Muaisem district. Authorities said many of the deceased had already been buried in Saudi Arabia. Officials also said Saudi authorities had expelled tens of thousands of unauthorized travelers, but many Egyptians still reached the holy sites without access to hotel shelter from the heat. The government blamed travel agencies for failing to provide proper services and for using visas that did not permit entry to Mecca. More than 1.83 million Muslims performed Hajj in 2024, including over 1.6 million from abroad and about 222,000 Saudi citizens and residents. Because the Islamic lunar calendar shifts the timing of the pilgrimage earlier each year, Hajj will fall in April by 2029. A 2019 MIT study warned that Hajj would face “extreme danger” temperature thresholds in future decades even under climate mitigation efforts.

# Over 1,000 Pilgrims Die During 2024 Hajj Due to Extreme Heat More than 1,000 people died during this year's annual Hajj pilgrimage in Saudi Arabia, with record-breaking heatwaves identified as the primary cause. According to a Reuters tally, the death toll reached at least 1,114 people, making this one of the deadliest Hajj seasons in recent history. Egypt suffered the highest casualties, with 672 confirmed deaths and 25 pilgrims still missing. Indonesia reported 236 deaths, while India confirmed 98 fatalities among its 175,000 pilgrims. Additional deaths were reported by Tunisia, Jordan, Iran, Senegal, and the United States. The Indian Ministry of External Affairs attributed most deaths to natural causes, chronic illnesses, and old age, with only six deaths occurring on the Day of Arafat and four from accidents. The extreme heat proved devastating, with temperatures in Mecca and surrounding sacred sites soaring above 46 degrees Celsius (117 degrees Fahrenheit) and reaching 49 degrees Celsius (120 degrees Fahrenheit) in some areas. These record temperatures caused pilgrims to faint while performing religious rituals, particularly during the symbolic stoning of the devil. Egyptian authorities launched an investigation into the crisis, suspending licenses of 16 tourism companies and referring them to prosecutors. The government alleged these companies were responsible for deaths among unregistered pilgrims lacking adequate accommodations. Many Egyptian pilgrims lacked hotels to escape the scorching heat, having been illegally transported using inappropriate visas. Saudi Arabia expelled tens of thousands of people but many Egyptian pilgrims still reached holy sites unprepared for the conditions. The government blamed travel agencies for failing to provide adequate services and facilitating illegal travel arrangements. Over 1.83 million Muslims participated in the 2024 Hajj, including more than 1.6 million from 22 countries and approximately 222,000 Saudi citizens and residents. Deaths at the Hajj are not uncommon due to the massive crowds, though this year's toll reflects the severe heat impact. The pilgrimage's timing continues shifting earlier each year due to the lunar Islamic calendar, meaning it will occur in April by 2029. A 2019 MIT study warned that even with climate change mitigation efforts, Hajj temperatures will exceed "extreme danger thresholds" during 2047-2052 and 2079-2086. The deadly heatwaves extended beyond Saudi Arabia, affecting multiple continents as the Northern Hemisphere entered summer. Record temperatures across Asia and Europe have caused hundreds to thousands of additional deaths, while Mediterranean countries experienced severe heatwaves triggering forest fires from Portugal to Greece and North Africa.

The Abia State Police Command has arrested 26-year-old Chinazaekpere Uwadineke for allegedly killing a six-month-old baby in Umuahia, reportedly the child of her ex-lover. Police said a missing-child report was first filed, prompting an investigation that led officers, acting on a tip-off, to find the baby’s body in a drainage channel in the city. According to police sources, Uwadineke had visited the family compound a day earlier and noticed that the child’s mother had left the baby in the care of other children. She allegedly tricked the babysitter by claiming the mother had sent her to collect the child. The babysitter then handed the baby over to her, after which the child disappeared. The baby was later discovered dead in a gutter. Investigators said Uwadineke later confessed that she had been dating the child’s father and only later learned he was married with children. Police said she claimed the man had hidden his marital status from her and that she had undergone several abortions for him. The dead child has been deposited in the morgue, while the suspect remains in custody at the State Criminal Investigation Department. Commissioner of Police Ene Okon confirmed the arrest and said she would be charged to court after investigations are completed.

# Summary The Abia State Police Command arrested 26-year-old Chinazaekpere Uwadineke for allegedly killing a six-month-old baby in Umuahia. After a missing child report was filed, police discovered the infant dead in a drainage channel. According to police sources, Uwadineke, the ex-lover of the baby's father, visited the family residence and deceived a babysitter into handing over the child by claiming the mother had sent her. The baby was subsequently found dead in a gutter. During interrogation, Uwadineke confessed to dating the child's father, unaware he was married with children. She allegedly had multiple abortions for him. Police suspect she killed the baby out of provocation upon discovering his true marital status. The Abia State Commissioner of Police confirmed the arrest and stated that Uwadineke has been transferred to the State Criminal Investigation Department (SCID). She will be charged to court once the investigation concludes. The deceased child's body has been deposited at the morgue.

Libya’s prime minister, Fayez Al Sarraj, has rejected an EU proposal to establish asylum processing centres in Libya, dealing another blow to European efforts to reduce migrant arrivals. In an interview with the German newspaper *Bild*, Sarraj said Libya would not allow Europe to place migrants who are “no longer wanted in the EU” in his country, and he ruled out any arrangement funded by EU money to take in more migrants. Instead, he argued that European leaders should pressure migrants’ countries of origin to prevent departures in the first place. The EU agreed at a tense summit in June to create so-called “disembarkation platforms” outside the bloc where migrants could be processed in cooperation with the UN refugee agency and the International Organisation for Migration. These centres would be used to separate irregular migrants from asylum seekers who might be eligible to enter the EU. However, no country has yet volunteered to host such a facility. Morocco has already refused, Tunisia has also rejected the idea, and Albania’s prime minister, Edi Rama, said such centres would amount to “dumping desperate people somewhere like toxic waste that no one wants.” The issue has also strained relations within the EU. Italian Prime Minister Giuseppe Conte has said Italy will no longer take in migrants rescued in the Mediterranean unless other EU states agree to accept some of them. European Commission President Jean-Claude Juncker responded that such ad hoc arrangements would not be sustainable long term, though he said efforts would continue to find countries willing to temporarily host rescued migrants. The article also notes that June was the deadliest month in the Mediterranean in recent years, with the IOM reporting about 564 deaths or disappearances, even as overall migrant departures have fallen sharply since summer 2017. Separately, Sarraj rejected accusations from the Spanish rescue group Proactiva Open Arms that Libya’s coastguard failed to save two women and a child on a dinghy. He said the claims were false and insisted Libyan forces rescue hundreds of people daily, while also calling for more international technical and financial support. The UN and the European Court of Human Rights have criticized Libya’s migrant return policy, citing abuse and horrific detention conditions.

# Libya Rejects EU Asylum Processing Plan Libya's Prime Minister Fayez Al Sarraj has rejected a European Union proposal to establish asylum processing centres in his country, dealing another blow to EU efforts to manage migrant arrivals. Sarraj stated Libya would not accept "illegal migrants who are no longer wanted in the EU" and refused any EU-funded deals to accommodate additional migrants. He argued instead that European leaders should pressure origin countries to prevent migrants from departing in the first place. During a June summit, EU leaders agreed to create "disembarkation platforms" outside Europe to process migrants in cooperation with UN and international organizations. However, no country has volunteered to host such centres. Morocco and Tunisia have already rejected the plan, while Albania's Prime Minister Edi Rama compared it to "dumping desperate people somewhere like toxic waste." The initiative faces mounting pressure. Italian Prime Minister Giuseppe Conte warned Italy would cease accepting Mediterranean rescue migrants unless other EU members shared responsibility. EU Commission President Jean-Claude Juncker acknowledged that temporary solutions are unsustainable but agreed to identify nations willing to shelter rescued migrants pending a permanent framework. Most migrants originate from the Middle East, Africa, and South Asia. Sarraj also denied accusations from Spanish rescue group Proactiva Open Arms that Libyan coastguards selectively rescued migrants, leaving two women and a child, two of whom were later found dead. He emphasized Libya's daily rescue efforts and requested increased technical and financial aid. The EU's controversial arrangement with Libya involves Libyan coastguards intercepting migrants, though the UN has condemned this as "inhuman," citing horrific detention conditions and rights abuses.

The African Union is urging African communities to strengthen communal values as a key strategy for addressing the continent’s growing mental health crisis. Speaking on World Mental Health Day 2025, Dr. Adamu Isah, the AU’s Director of Medical and Health Services, said prevention must be rooted in families, neighborhoods, and public policy rather than viewed only as a clinical issue. He stressed that communication, understanding, and respect within households are the foundations of mental health protection. Isah said that many mental health problems are fueled by unmet basic needs, including food insecurity, economic hardship, and limited access to medical care. He warned that increasing Western-style individualism is weakening Africa’s traditional support networks, contributing to isolation, especially among young people. In response, he called for a renewed embrace of African cultural values such as extended family ties, mutual aid, brotherhood, spiritual support, and collective responsibility. The AU’s warning comes amid the death of Kenyan journalist Kimani Mbugua, 29, who had publicly discussed living with bipolar disorder, depression, and psychosis. Mbugua died in a suspected suicide at a mental health rescue center in Mombasa. His death, confirmed by former Nairobi Governor Mike Sonko, has drawn attention to major gaps in mental health care and the need for stronger family-based prevention and support systems. The article also places Africa’s situation in a global context. The World Health Organization’s 2025 Mental Health Atlas reports that global spending on mental health remains low, with a median of just 2.1 percent of health budgets. Low-income countries spend less than 1 USD per person, there is a shortage of specialists, and only 9 percent of people with depression receive adequate treatment. Isah said prevention should begin at home through stable livelihoods, peaceful family relationships, early recognition of symptoms, and community support. He urged governments to create policies that give families the resources to care for loved ones. He concluded that Africa’s social cohesion and cultural heritage can help the continent respond to mental illness with resilience and collective healing.

# Summary The African Union is urging African communities to embrace traditional communal values as a strategy to address the continent's growing mental health crisis. Speaking on World Mental Health Day 2025, Dr. Adamu Isah, Director of Medical and Health Services at the AU, emphasized that mental health prevention must be family-centered and rooted in African cultural traditions rather than relying solely on clinical interventions. Isah stressed that mental health begins at home and extends into neighborhoods, requiring communication, understanding, and respect within families. He identified unmet basic needs—including food insecurity, economic hardship, and lack of medical access—as key stressors contributing to mental health disorders. He also warned that Western individualism is eroding Africa's traditional communal support systems, leading to increased isolation, particularly among youth. The AU director called for Africans to embrace cultural values emphasizing social bonds, extended family, and mutual aid, advocating for a return to principles like brotherhood and collective care. The urgency of this message was underscored by the recent death of Kenyan journalist Kimani Mbugua, 29, who died in a suspected suicide at a mental health facility in Mombasa. Mbugua, who had publicly battled bipolar disorder, depression, and psychosis, highlighted dangerous gaps in mental health care across the continent. According to the WHO's 2025 Mental Health Atlas, mental health remains severely underfunded globally, with low-income countries investing less than $1 per capita. Only 9 percent of individuals with depression receive adequate treatment. Isah urged African governments to invest in policies empowering families with resources needed for care and support. He concluded that Africa's cultural heritage and emphasis on social cohesion provide a powerful foundation to combat mental illness and promote collective well-being.

A meeting in Hanoi on May 31 marked World No Tobacco Day and National No Tobacco Week, jointly organized by the Ministry of Home Affairs and the Ministry of Health. The event supported this year’s WHO theme, “Tobacco: A Threat to Our Environment,” which calls on countries to raise awareness of tobacco’s harm to the environment as well as to human health. At the opening, Vu Dang Minh, Chief of the Office and Deputy Head of the Ministry of Home Affairs’ Tobacco Control Steering Committee, said the ministry has already implemented practical measures to promote a smoke-free living environment. He urged agencies and units to intensify communications on the dangers of tobacco use, the Law on Tobacco Harm Prevention and Control, and responsibilities of leaders and smokers, especially in smoke-free places. Associate Professor Dr. Luong Ngoc Khue, head of the Ministry of Health’s Department of Medical Examination and Treatment and director of the Vietnam Tobacco Control Fund, noted that smoking is a major cause of non-communicable diseases such as cancer, hypertension, stroke and heart disease. He called for collective action to fight smoking for community health and a cleaner environment. Vietnam’s tobacco control program says about 40,000 people die each year from tobacco-related diseases.

# Summary On May 31, Vietnam's Ministry of Home Affairs and Ministry of Health jointly held a meeting to commemorate World No Tobacco Day and the National No Tobacco Week (May 25-31). The event's theme, "Tobacco: A Threat to Our Environment," aligned with the World Health Organization's message to raise public awareness about tobacco's environmental and health impacts. Officials emphasized the need for stronger communications campaigns about tobacco's harmful effects and enforcement of the Law on Tobacco Harm Prevention and Control. They highlighted that smoking is a major cause of non-communicable diseases including cancer, high blood pressure, stroke, and heart disease. According to the national tobacco harm prevention program, approximately 40,000 Vietnamese people die annually from tobacco-related diseases. In 2021, tobacco-related deaths exceeded combined deaths from HIV/AIDS, tuberculosis, traffic accidents, and suicide. Officials called for collective action to combat smoking for community health and environmental protection.

A man believed to be 30 to 40 years old was found dead around 5:30 a.m. Sunday on the ground outside a condominium building at Camella Northpoint along J.P. Laurel Avenue in Bajada, Davao City. Police initially received reports of a possible suicide inside the building, but investigators later found the unidentified victim had nine stab wounds on different parts of his body. Captain Hazel Tuazon of the Davao City Police Office said authorities are still trying to establish the victim’s identity and determine whether he fell from an upper floor. A 25-year-old call center agent living in the same building saw the man face down and alerted security guards. An autopsy is planned, and police are also searching for the assailant and motive.

# Summary A dead man with stab wounds was discovered outside a condominium building at Camella Northpoint in Davao City on Sunday at approximately 5:30 a.m. The male victim, estimated to be between 30 and 40 years old, had nine stab wounds on different parts of his body. Police initially received reports of a suicide, but investigation revealed the death was a homicide. A 25-year-old call center resident discovered the victim lying face down and alerted security guards. Authorities are investigating to identify the victim, locate the assailant, and determine the motive. An autopsy will be conducted to confirm the cause of death. In Myanmar, a growing number of biologically female people who present in a masculine way are beginning to speak more openly about their identities as “tomboys” or trans men, even as they continue to face legal, social, religious and workplace discrimination. The article follows several of them, especially Jel Li and Paing Soe San, and shows how internet access, online communities and public advocacy have helped some move out of isolation. Jel Li’s story begins in seventh grade in a small town about five hours north of Yangon, where he developed a crush on another girl. Confused and ashamed, he wrote his feelings down and then burned the paper. At the time, he believed he was “abnormal” and hoped each day that he would change. His understanding shifted in 2012, when he was 19 and the internet became more widely available after years of military suppression. Searching online, he found people like himself and began to accept his identity. He now identifies as a transgender male. The article explains that in Myanmar, “tomboy” refers to people born female who wear short hair and masculine clothing, and often prefer masculine pronouns. Some also identify as transgender men or lesbians. The term is about gender identity rather than sexual orientation, though most of the tomboys interviewed said they are attracted to women. Their visibility appears to be increasing: a Burmese-language online chat group for tomboys and trans men drew 1,400 members in just six weeks after launching in early August. Activist Htar Htar Thet said the number of people identifying this way is likely much larger. LGBT awareness in Myanmar has improved, according to Hla Myat Tun, deputy director of the LGBT group Colors Rainbow, but the language remains limited and often derogatory. The legal environment is still highly conservative. Myanmar does not allow legal gender changes, and a colonial-era law criminalizes “carnal intercourse against the order of nature,” though it is rarely enforced. A 2018 National Youth Policy includes anti-discrimination language for LGBT youth, but there is no broad anti-discrimination law naming LGBT people as a protected class. The article notes that public attention to LGBT issues has been uneven. In June, a 26-year-old gay librarian at a public university died by suicide after posting evidence of harassment from coworkers. A government investigation cleared the university and described the librarian as “mentally weak,” drawing attention to the discrimination gay men still face. Trans women have also received some visibility, often through stereotypes tied to beauty work, fashion and spirit-medium roles. Tomboys and trans men, however, have remained less visible, which is one reason Jel Li and three others created Rainbow Six in 2018 to advocate for their community. Several tomboys interviewed said Myanmar society is gradually becoming more accepting. Thar Thar, a 26-year-old private hospital employee, said more people now understand what tomboys are. Min Min, 26, who works at a media company, said open prejudice has declined and bigots are increasingly seen as being in the wrong. Some families accept their identities, even calling them “son.” Thar Thar said his family gave little resistance and allowed him to live as he wanted. Others, though, are treated as if their identities are temporary phases. Jel Li said his mother still expects him to “act like a man” only temporarily, while 17-year-old Ah Theint said his mother hopes he will return to identifying as female and gave him women’s clothes and cosmetics as a graduation gift. Because acceptance is inconsistent, many tomboys adjust their presentation depending on where they are. Thar Thar uses a female identity at work but a male identity at home and socially. Min Min is called “son” at home and “brother” at work, but attended a state-run girls’ high school. When questioned, he sometimes answers, “Yes, I am a girl, so what?” and at times continues to identify as a girl simply to avoid conflict. Workplace rules remain a major obstacle. Government schools and many jobs require gendered uniforms, forcing tomboys to wear fitted female blouses, often hidden under jackets. Paing Soe San left his first office job because he was required to wear a female uniform. He said some employers refuse to let tomboys apply for male-designated positions, while others expect male workloads but pay female wages. Medical transition is also difficult. Some trans men use testosterone to align their bodies with their identities, and in Myanmar many tomboys buy the hormone online and learn from friends how to inject it. Paing Soe San, who began injecting at 20, said he struggled with the decision but ultimately chose to live in a way that made him happy. Still, he said it is hard to find doctors in Myanmar who are both LGBT-sensitive and knowledgeable about hormone treatment, leaving people to rely on uncertain online information and peer advice. Religion adds another layer of pressure. Min Min, who is Muslim, is accepted as male by his family but prays at home with his mother instead of at the neighborhood mosque with men. In Buddhism, serving briefly as a monk is a rite of passage for most males, while some females become nuns. Thar Thar wears a male longyi when visiting pagodas but served as a nun. Paing Soe San, who always wanted to be a monk, said strict religious rules forced him to serve as a nun instead. He also rejected the belief held by some Buddhists that being LGBT is punishment for a past-life transgression, arguing instead for compassion and “loving kindness.” Paing Soe San had his breasts removed in 2017 in Yangon and later became a model and video interview subject, gaining more than 30,000 Facebook followers. He says he is open about being a trans man because there is nothing shameful about gender identity or sexual orientation.

# Myanmar's 'Tomboys' Stride Out of the Shadows Myanmar's LGBT community is experiencing gradual social acceptance, but a particular group—tomboys and transgender men—has remained largely invisible despite their growing numbers. These biologically female individuals who adopt masculine gender identities through short hair, masculine clothing, and masculine pronouns are increasingly claiming visibility and advocating for their rights in a conservative society. Jel Li's journey exemplifies the transformative power of internet access for Myanmar's LGBT community. In seventh grade, Jel Li developed romantic feelings for another girl but felt confused and abnormal, burning written records of these emotions. This changed dramatically in 2012 when widespread internet access became available after years of military suppression. "I searched on Google and I saw people like me," Jel Li recalled. This discovery enabled self-acceptance and eventually led him to establish Rainbow Six in 2018, an organization dedicated to advocating for tomboys and trans men alongside three other activists. The term "tomboy" in Myanmar relates to gender identity rather than sexual orientation, though most tomboys interviewed indicated attraction to women. A Burmese-language online chat group for tomboys and trans men attracted 1,400 members within six weeks of its August establishment, suggesting significantly larger numbers of people identifying this way. However, tomboys remain less visible than other LGBT groups, according to Hla Myat Tun, deputy director of the LGBT organization Colors Rainbow. Myanmar's legal and social framework remains among Southeast Asia's most conservative regarding LGBT rights. Changes of legal gender are prohibited, and a colonial-era law criminalizing "carnal intercourse against the order of nature" remains on the books, though rarely enforced. A 2018 National Youth Policy includes anti-discrimination clauses protecting LGBT youth, but Myanmar lacks comprehensive anti-discrimination legislation specifically protecting LGBT people. The suicide of a 26-year-old gay university librarian in June following workplace harassment highlighted institutional challenges, though a government investigation controversially exonerated the university and characterized the librarian as "mentally weak." Despite these obstacles, interviewed tomboys expressed optimism about societal progress. Thar Thar, a 26-year-old hospital employee, noted that increased visibility has improved acceptance: "There are many of us going this way; now people know what tomboys are." Min Min, a 26-year-old media company worker, observed that "people who look down on us have decreased." Family acceptance varies considerably. Some parents embrace their children's identities, even using masculine pronouns and calling them "son." However, others view tomboy identities as temporary phases. Jel Li's mother expressed hope he would change upon maturation, while 17-year-old Ah Theint's mother continued offering feminine gifts and clothing, hoping for a return to female identification. Tomboys navigate daily life through constant adaptation, adjusting their gender presentation across different contexts. Some use female identities at work while maintaining male identities socially or at home. Practical challenges include gendered school uniforms and workplace requirements; Paing Soe San, a 24-year-old LGBT trainer, quit his first office job rather than wear mandatory female uniforms. Some employers prevent tomboys from applying for male positions while assigning male workloads at female wages. Many trans men use testosterone to align physical characteristics with gender identities. In Myanmar's unregulated environment, tomboys purchase testosterone online and learn injection techniques from friends, lacking access to qualified medical professionals. Paing Soe San, who began injecting at age 20, emphasized the difficulty: "People search online but information is not exactly sure, so people listen to each other. ... No one exactly knows the details about the benefits and risks." Religious identity presents additional complications. Muslim Min Min prays at home rather than at the mosque, while Buddhist tomboys face restrictions: most males serve briefly as monks as a rite of passage, but tomboys typically serve as nuns instead. Some Buddhists attribute LGBT identity to sexual transgressions in previous lives—an interpretation Paing Soe San considers harmful, advocating instead for Buddhist concepts of loving-kindness. Heavy rain triggered a deadly landslide late Friday in Jemblung village in Banjarnegara district, Central Java, Indonesia, killing eight people and leaving more than 100 others missing, officials said. National Disaster Mitigation Agency spokesman Sutopo Purwo Nugroho said the mudslide swept away nearly 105 houses in the hill area, about 460 kilometers east of Jakarta. Rescue teams made up of residents, police, and soldiers searched through mud and rubble using hoes, shovels, and their bare hands before bulldozers and tractors were brought in. By Saturday, eight bodies had been recovered, including that of an 8-year-old boy, while about 100 people remained unaccounted for. Another 38 villagers were injured and taken to a nearby hospital, with four in critical condition. Around 370 residents were moved to temporary shelters. Nugroho said bad weather, thick mud, and difficult terrain were slowing the operation and that more heavy equipment was needed. The disaster was the second landslide in Java in just a few days, following another in Wonosobo district that killed one person. Seasonal torrential rains have caused widespread flooding and landslides across Indonesia.

# Indonesia Landslide Summary A devastating mudslide struck the village of Jemblung in Banjarnegara district, Central Java, on Friday night, killing eight people and leaving approximately 100 missing. Heavy rainfall triggered the disaster, which destroyed nearly 105 houses in the lower hill areas. Rescue operations involved residents, police, and soldiers who searched through rubble and mud using basic tools and heavy equipment like bulldozers and tractors. Among the confirmed dead was an 8-year-old boy. Thirty-eight injured villagers were hospitalized, with four in critical condition, while around 370 residents were displaced to temporary shelters. Rescue efforts faced significant challenges from adverse weather, mud, and difficult terrain, prompting officials to request additional heavy equipment. This was the second major landslide in days on Java; another in Wonosobo district killed one person on Thursday. The incidents resulted from seasonal torrential rains causing widespread flooding and multiple landslides across Indonesia's densely populated regions, where millions live in mountainous areas and flood-prone plains.

A Myanmar couple suspected of murdering an Iranian restaurateur and his Thai wife surrendered to police in Nakhon Pathom and said they wanted to be sent back to Myanmar. Chon Buri police commander Pol Maj Gen Thawatkiat Jindakhuansanong said arrest warrants were being prepared for Kyaw Myint Oo, 23, and Ei December, 19, who had entered Thailand through Tak using border passes. Police believe they targeted the victims for valuables and are still investigating what was taken. The victims, Mojtaba Ghanbariazad, 64, and his wife Thanaporn Poonprakhon, 49, were found dead Tuesday in a commercial building on Soi Day-Night in South Pattaya, where their Banoo Iranian Restaurant operates on the ground floor. Their bodies were discovered in an upstairs bedroom. The man was naked from the waist down and is believed to have been strangled with trousers. The woman was found naked, bound with plastic rope and a charger wire. A hammer suspected in the killings was also recovered. Police said the suspects left the restaurant on the victims’ motorcycle after an argument on July 11, later abandoned it, took a taxi to Bangkok, and traveled to Nakhon Pathom. They were fined for illegal immigration and sent to Mae Sot, while Thai police sought help from Myanmar authorities.

# Summary A Myanmar couple surrendered to Thai police in Nakhon Pathom after allegedly murdering an Iranian restaurateur and his Thai wife in Pattaya. Kyaw Myint Oo, 23, and Ei December, 19, are suspected of killing Mojtaba Ghanbariazad, 64, and Thanaporn Poonprakhon, 49, in their commercial building on July 11. The victims were discovered in a second-floor bedroom; the man was strangled with trousers, while the woman was found bound with plastic rope and charger wire. Police believe the couple targeted them for valuables and discovered a hammer suspected as the murder weapon. Following an argument at the Banoo Iranian Restaurant, the suspects fled on the victims' motorcycle, later abandoning it to travel by taxi to Bangkok and then Nakhon Pathom. The couple surrendered citing illegal immigration concerns. Police fined them and transferred them to Mae Sot district near the Myanmar border. The victims' daughter revealed the Myanmar employee and his wife lived upstairs, and the Iranian man had recently scolded the employee over missing money.

Panasonic has asked its employees in Japan to leave work by 8 p.m. as part of a broader push to reduce Japan’s notoriously long working hours. The new rule, which took effect on February 1, applies even to executive positions but not to the board of directors. Company president Kazuhiro Tsuga personally emailed the policy to Panasonic’s 100,000 Japan-based employees, a spokeswoman said. The move comes as Japan reexamines work-life balance after the 2015 suicide of Matsuri Takahashi, a young employee at advertising giant Dentsu who had logged more than 100 hours of overtime a month. Her death renewed concern over “karoshi,” or death from overwork, and prompted scrutiny of company labor practices. Other firms, including Daiwa Securities Group and Unicharm, have also introduced earlier departure or overtime limits. Panasonic has a history of such reforms, including banning a six-day workweek in 1965.

# Panasonic Urges Employees to Leave by 8 P.M. Electronics giant Panasonic has implemented a policy requiring employees to leave the office by 8 p.m., effective February 1st. President Kazuhiro Tsuga personally emailed 100,000 Japanese employees about this decision, which applies to all staff except board directors. This move reflects Japan's growing focus on work-life balance, prompted by the 2015 suicide of Matsuri Takahashi, a young advertising executive who worked over 100 hours of overtime monthly. Other companies like Daiwa Securities and Unicharm have implemented similar measures. Panasonic has historically led such initiatives; it prohibited six-day work weeks in 1965, decades before other firms. The Takahashi case has renewed attention on "karoshi"—death by overwork—in Japan. The labour ministry is pursuing legal action against Dentsu, Takahashi's former employer, for failing to comply with labour standards and falsifying overtime records.

Police Regional Office-7 Director Brigadier General Debold Sinas said investigators are “in the right path” in the killing of 16-year-old Christine Lee Silawan, after evidence pointed to self-confessed killer Renato Llenes. Sinas said the testimony of Llenes, 42, of Lapu-Lapu City, was accurate and that police are convinced he is the prime suspect in the case. The Philippine National Police earlier announced that DNA samples taken from the scissors allegedly used in the murder matched Llenes. According to Llenes’ confession, he used a pair of scissors to stab Silawan in several parts of her body and to peel the skin from her face. Sinas said the scissors tested positive for Christine’s DNA and for fluid DNA belonging to Llenes. He also noted that Llenes underwent a polygraph test and passed, suggesting he was telling the truth, and that a psychological test found no mental problems. Sinas said he had already spoken with Lapu-Lapu City Police Chief Limuel Obon to help turn over the evidence to the City Prosecutor’s Office. Still, he stressed that investigators are continuing to gather more evidence. Silawan was found dead on March 11, 2019, in Barangay Bankal, Lapu-Lapu City, with her body half-naked and her face skinned to the bone.

# Summary Police Regional Office in Central Visayas Director Brigadier General Debold Sinas confirmed that self-confessed killer Renato Llenes is the prime suspect in the murder of 16-year-old Christine Lee Silawan. DNA samples extracted from scissors allegedly used in the crime matched both Silawan and Llenes, supporting the suspect's confession that he used the scissors to stab Silawan multiple times and remove skin from her face. Llenes, 42, from Lapu-Lapu City, passed a polygraph test indicating truthfulness in his testimony and a psychological evaluation found no mental health issues. Sinas stated these findings confirm they are "on the right path" in the investigation. Silawan's body was discovered on March 11, 2019, in Barangay Bankal, Lapu-Lapu City, with 20 stab wounds and her face severely mutilated. Sinas indicated that evidence would be delivered to the City Prosecutor's Office, though additional evidence remains under investigation.

The New Zealand College of Public Health Medicine (NZCPHM) has condemned proposed staff cuts at the Public Health Agency (PHA), warning they would weaken New Zealand’s ability to respond to current and future health threats. Under a restructure now out for consultation, the agency would lose a net 21 roles. The largest reduction would be in emergency management, where staffing would fall from 11 roles to just 2. The Māori Public Health team would also be cut from six staff to two, and further reductions are proposed in the unit responsible for mental health, addiction, and suicide prevention. NZCPHM President Sir Collin Tukuitonga said cutting the PHA to save money would be “seriously misguided,” especially given the growing frequency of public health threats such as extreme weather events and pandemics. He argued that Cyclone Gabrielle showed the importance of embedding public health expertise in civil defence responses, while COVID-19 highlighted the need for stronger pandemic preparedness. In his view, Aotearoa should be strengthening, not reducing, its emergency management and preparedness capacity. Tukuitonga also strongly criticised the proposed cuts to the Māori Public Health team, saying they were “appalling” given the persistent and entrenched inequities in Māori health. He said the Government had previously promised to retain the functions and expertise of Te Aka Whai Ora after disestablishing the Māori Health Authority, but the current proposal suggested that commitment was not being met. He added that public health delivers high value for money, citing evidence that every $1 invested can return up to $14 in health benefits.

# Summary The New Zealand College of Public Health Medicine (NZCPHM) has expressed serious concern about proposed staff cuts at the Public Health Agency (PHA), which is currently undergoing restructuring consultation. The reorganization would result in a net loss of 21 roles, with the most significant cuts affecting the emergency management team, which would be reduced from 11 to 2 positions, and the Māori Public Health team, shrinking from six to two staff members. Additional reductions are planned for the unit managing mental health, addiction, and suicide prevention. College President Sir Collin Tukuitonga argues that these cuts are fundamentally misguided. He emphasizes that the PHA serves as the government's primary advisor on public health and mental health matters, with responsibility for disease prevention and addressing health inequities. Tukuitonga points out that recent events like Cyclone Gabrielle and the COVID-19 pandemic demonstrate the critical importance of robust emergency management and pandemic preparedness capabilities—making cuts to these areas particularly counterproductive. He also criticizes the proposed reductions to the Māori Public Health team, noting that Māori face substantial health inequities requiring increased, not decreased, resources. Tukuitonga highlights that the government committed to retaining the Māori Health Authority's functions when it was disestablished, suggesting these cuts represent a failure of that commitment. Additionally, Tukuitonga stresses that public health represents sound fiscal policy, with evidence showing every dollar invested returns up to fourteen dollars in health benefits.

British mother-of-three Victoria Hart, 33, was killed on Saturday in her home in Alhaurín el Grande, Málaga, in what Spanish authorities are treating as a case of gender violence. Hart was found dead around 11:40 a.m. in the La Paca residential area with stab wounds to the neck, and a knife was found beside her. Police were alerted after neighbours heard screams from the property and her 11-year-old son ran out into the street to seek help. Hart’s twin daughters, aged seven, were also in the house at the time. Hart was a hairdresser and beautician who worked from a salon in her home. She had moved to Spain from the West Midlands as a teenager with her mother and sister. Neighbours described her as kind and hardworking, especially devoted to her children. Police arrested her ex-partner and the father of her children, Spaniard Juan Antonio Rueda, after he handed himself in at the nearby Alhaurín de la Torre prison. According to reports, he told officers he had “done something very bad,” had “taken a knife,” “gone mad,” and stabbed the mother of his children. The couple had reportedly been married for about ten years before separating last year. The children allegedly witnessed the attack and told police what happened when officers arrived. Hart’s son is said to have phoned his grandmother to say that his father had killed his mother, and her eldest child reportedly shouted in the street that his father had killed his mother and left the knife. The case is now awaiting judicial proceedings. Rueda, who is originally from Alhaurín el Grande and ran a chicken rotisserie in town, had been under restraining orders. Hart had previously reported him in October 2025, saying she had suffered death threats and manipulation. She was already listed in Spain’s VioGén system, which assesses the risk of gender-based violence, but her case had been classified as low risk. Although contact and approach were prohibited, he was still allowed contact with the children. Neighbours also said they had seen psychological abuse and derogatory comments directed at Hart. The killing has prompted strong reactions locally and nationally. Andalusian Equality Minister Loles López condemned the murder as another example of gender-based violence. In Alhaurín el Grande, the town council declared a day of mourning on Monday, January 26, and held a vigil with a minute’s silence in the town hall square. Hart’s children, mother, sister, and other relatives attended, and white balloons were released in her memory. Her funeral is scheduled for Wednesday, January 28, at San Gaudencio cemetery. Friends and family have also launched a GoFundMe campaign to help support her children and cover urgent needs such as food, clothing, and daily care. Hart’s death is the first femicide in Málaga province this year, the fifth in Spain, and the third in Andalusia.

European Union leaders met in Brussels on Thursday for an emergency summit aimed at reassessing strained ties with the Trump administration after a week of threats from U.S. President Donald Trump. The immediate trigger was Trump’s dramatic rhetoric over Greenland, which included demands that Denmark and NATO step aside and let the United States “acquire” the semiautonomous Danish territory. He had also threatened tariffs on European countries that supported Denmark. By the eve of the summit, however, Trump had backed down, saying for the first time that he would not use force to seize Greenland and dropping the tariff threat as well. EU Council President António Costa welcomed Trump’s retreat and said the bloc still wanted to preserve the transatlantic relationship. He stressed that EU leaders believe it is “very important to preserve and cherish our transatlantic partnership” and that the priority now should be implementing the EU-U.S. trade deal agreed last July. Costa said the goal remained “effective stability of the trade relations,” while also making clear that the EU would defend itself, its member states, citizens, and companies against coercion. The tone at the summit varied. French President Emmanuel Macron took a firmer line, saying Europe can make itself respected and that using the tools available had produced respect “this week.” Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk also emphasized the importance of the United States as Europe’s key security partner, but said there is a difference between “domination and leadership,” and that leadership is acceptable. Despite Trump’s reversal, European officials remained wary because his positions have shifted repeatedly. The details of the hastily arranged “framework” deal that appeared to prompt Trump’s change of heart were not made public, and Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen insisted her country would not negotiate over Greenland’s sovereignty. She said Denmark is a sovereign state and cannot bargain over that, though she was open to strengthening cooperation on Arctic security. Frederiksen called for a permanent NATO presence in the Arctic, including around Greenland. Macron said French troops would take part in NATO exercises in the region. Meanwhile, U.S. Lt. Gen. Alexus Grynkewich, NATO’s top military officer, said no Arctic operation had yet been planned and no political guidance had been given. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the EU should deepen ties with Greenland and promised a forthcoming package of investments, though she did not give details. The summit also focused on Trump’s proposed “Board of Peace,” an expanded international body originally tied to the Gaza ceasefire but now described by Trump in broader terms, including replacing some United Nations functions. Several European countries have declined to join, including Norway, Slovenia, and Sweden. Germany has responded cautiously, while Hungary and Bulgaria accepted. Costa said most EU leaders had serious doubts about the board’s scope, governance, and compatibility with the U.N. Charter. At the same time, the broader security backdrop remained dominated by Russia’s war in Ukraine. Speaking in Switzerland, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy criticized Europe for what he called a slow, fragmented, and inadequate response to Russia’s invasion and ongoing aggression. He said “Europe looks lost” and urged it to become a stronger global force. Von der Leyen responded that the EU has already spent more than 193 billion euros on Ukraine over four years and plans to provide another 90 billion euros over the next two years to help cover most of Ukraine’s economic and military needs.

# EU Leaders Work to Stabilize Relations with Trump Administration European Union leaders held an emergency summit Thursday to address escalating tensions with the Trump administration following a turbulent week of threats and controversial proposals. The meeting reflected deep concerns about preserving transatlantic partnerships while maintaining European sovereignty and interests. ## Greenland Crisis Resolution The immediate trigger for the summit was Trump's extraordinary threats to acquire Greenland, a Danish territory. On the eve of the EU meeting, Trump dramatically reversed course, stating he would not use military force to seize the island and dropped threats of tariffs against European nations supporting Denmark. However, EU leaders remain cautious, recognizing Trump's unpredictability and the possibility of future reversals. Before backing down, Trump had pressured Denmark and NATO to cede Greenland, warning that cooperation would be "appreciated" while non-compliance would be "remembered"—language interpreted as veiled threats. ## EU Response and Strategy EU Council President António Costa struck a measured tone, emphasizing the importance of preserving transatlantic partnership and implementing the EU-U.S. trade deal agreed last July. He stated the bloc would "stand up for its interests" and "defend itself" against coercion, though the language remained diplomatic. French President Emmanuel Macron adopted a more assertive stance, claiming that Europe had earned respect by using its available tools. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk distinguished between "domination and leadership," suggesting concerns about American pressure tactics. Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen firmly insisted that Denmark would not negotiate its sovereignty, though she expressed openness to strengthening Arctic security cooperation. She called for permanent NATO presence in the Arctic region, including around Greenland. Macron pledged French participation in NATO military exercises. ## The "Board of Peace" Controversy EU leaders expressed significant skepticism about Trump's proposed "Board of Peace," originally conceived as oversight for Gaza ceasefire negotiations but expanded into a more ambitious structure that Trump suggested could replace some UN functions. Multiple European nations declined invitations, including Norway, Slovenia, and Sweden. Germany offered only a guarded response, while Hungary and Bulgaria accepted. Trump responded to Macron's apparent reluctance by threatening 200% tariffs on French wines and champagne. EU Commission President Ursula von der Leyen articulated widespread concerns, noting that leaders had "serious doubts" about the Board's scope, governance, and compatibility with the UN Charter. ## Ukraine Concerns Amid these discussions, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy criticized European allies for slow, fragmented responses to Russia's invasion. Speaking at the World Economic Forum, Zelenskyy characterized Europe as "lost" and urged the continent to become a global force comparable to American assertiveness in other regions. In response, von der Leyen highlighted the EU's substantial commitment, noting the bloc has spent 193 billion euros on Ukraine over four years of war, with plans to provide an additional 90 billion euros over the next two years. She emphasized Europe's steadfast support despite inability to match Ukrainian sacrifices. ## Outlook The summit revealed a fractured European response to Trump's unpredictability, ranging from Costa's diplomatic caution to Macron's more confrontational approach. While welcoming Trump's retreat on Greenland, EU leaders remain wary of his volatility and determined to protect European interests while maintaining critical transatlantic security relationships.

Police found the husband and daughter dead Saturday morning at an upscale hotel in central Reykjavik, while the woman was found alive with stab wounds. Reykjavik police said the victims had injuries including stab wounds, but the exact cause of death is still under investigation. Icelandic authorities have not publicly confirmed the suspect’s relationship to the deceased, though police said she was traveling with the two people who died. The Reykjavik district court remanded her in custody until June 20 as part of the investigation into the deaths of two French tourists. Murders are rare in Iceland, which is generally considered one of the world’s safest countries.

Only his family and closest friends attended. Avicii was found dead on April 20 in Muscat, Oman, while on holiday with friends. In an open letter released after his death, his family said he “wanted peace” and “could not go on any longer,” adding that he struggled with thoughts about meaning, life and happiness. His spokesman declined to confirm the cause of death, despite media reports suggesting suicide. Avicii had previously spoken openly about health problems, including pancreatitis linked partly to heavy drinking and his party lifestyle. NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte said Wednesday that four U.S. soldiers who went missing during training in Lithuania have died, though he said the details were still unclear. Speaking in Warsaw, Rutte said he had been informed of the deaths and expressed sympathy for the soldiers’ families and for the United States. “This is still early news so we do not know the details,” he told reporters, calling it “really terrible news.” A U.S. official, speaking anonymously, said only that the four soldiers were involved in a training accident and declined to confirm their status. U.S. Army Europe and Africa later said in a statement from Wiesbaden, Germany, that the soldiers had been taking part in scheduled tactical training when the incident occurred. Lithuanian public broadcaster LRT reported that four U.S. soldiers and a vehicle were reported missing Tuesday afternoon during an exercise at the General Silvestras Žukauskas training ground in Pabradė, a town less than six miles from Lithuania’s border with Belarus. The report indicated the search began after the soldiers disappeared during the drill. The incident took place in a country that is a NATO member and one of the Baltic states, along with Latvia and Estonia. These nations have long had strained relations with Russia and its ally Belarus, especially since Lithuania and the other Baltic states declared independence from the Soviet Union in 1990. Tensions rose further after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda has been among Europe’s strongest supporters of Ukraine in its war against Russian President Vladimir Putin’s forces. The article did not provide further details about the accident, the condition of the vehicle, or how the soldiers died.

Sweden’s I Break Horses, the project of Maria Lindén, has shared a new song and video, “I’ll Be the Death of You,” from her upcoming album *Warnings*, due May 8 on Bella Union. The track follows the album’s first single, “Death Engine,” which was previously released with a video and was named the #1 Song of the Week. The new video was directed by Douglas Hart. *Warnings* will be I Break Horses’ first album in six years and the follow-up to 2014’s *Chiaroscuro*. Lindén said the record took about six years to complete and went through several false starts: work in multiple studios, failed collaborations, a crashed hard drive that wiped out about two years of material, and a return to writing new songs after trying to salvage the lost work. Much of the album was eventually recorded by Lindén herself at home. She said she initially focused on instrumental music, but only realized she was making a new I Break Horses album once she began adding vocals and lyrics. Producer and mixing engineer Chris Coady, known for work with Beach House and TV on the Radio, later mixed the album. Lindén said she chose him because of his interest in slowing sounds down to reveal new textures. According to Lindén, *Warnings* reflects the anxious climate of the present day, though she described it as not overtly political. She said each song serves as a subtle warning that something is not quite right. She also noted that “Death Engine” was inspired by a close friend’s suicide attempt and broader concerns about mental health among Generation Z. Lindén said she wanted the album to resist today’s shorter attention spans and be heard as a full journey.

Iraqi forces renewed their offensive against the Daesh group around Mosul on Saturday, following a major breakthrough in Fallujah, where government troops had driven militants out of most of the city. Defense Minister Khaled Al-Obeidi said the new operation marked the “second phase of the liberation of Nineveh” and began at 5:00 a.m. The immediate goal, he said, was to seize Qayyarah, a town about 60 kilometers south of Mosul with an airfield that could serve as a launchpad for the assault on the Islamic State’s last major urban stronghold in Iraq. Mosul had been the original target of an Iraqi offensive announced in March, but the government shifted its forces to Fallujah, west of Baghdad, under domestic political pressure. That diversion now appears to be ending as attention returns to Nineveh province. The Mosul push has been strongly backed by the United States, including through a US Marine artillery position near Makhmur in the Kurdish-controlled area south of Mosul. Prime Minister Haider Al-Abadi said on Friday that the liberation of Mosul was “very near” after declaring victory in the Fallujah campaign. He said only small pockets of resistance remained, though Daesh still held northern neighborhoods of Fallujah and was believed to be using civilians as human shields. In Fallujah, Iraqi forces spent Saturday clearing mines and explosives left behind by retreating militants. Air strikes continued, including attacks on Daesh snipers near the main hospital. Troops advanced cautiously toward the hospital because of fears that patients could be used as human shields. Iraqi special forces had entered Fallujah the previous day, causing Daesh’s two-year hold on the city to collapse rapidly. On Friday, officials said government forces controlled about 80 percent of Fallujah, with militants concentrated in four districts on the northern edge. The battle displaced large numbers of civilians. Aid groups estimated that 50,000 people were trapped when the offensive began, and between 30,000 and 42,000 have since fled, many to camps nearby. Thousands more escaped during Friday’s final push, some by swimming across the Euphrates River. Iraq’s wider conflict has now displaced more than 3.3 million people, while the country also hosts up to 300,000 Syrian refugees. Elsewhere, government forces advanced north in Salahuddin province toward Daesh-held territory near the Beiji oil refinery, while militants retaliated with a suicide truck bombing near a Kurdish group’s office in northern Iraq.

Syrian priest George Rafiq Housh, 65, was found dead on April 6 at St. George’s Greek Orthodox Cathedral in Latakia, Syria. Early reports, including a statement from Syria’s Ministry of Interior, said he had shot himself with his own pistol because of “psychological and social pressures.” The Greek Orthodox Archdiocese of Latakia also referred to his “surprising behavior.” Housh was reportedly discovered sitting in a chair with multiple gunshot wounds, a pistol nearby, and a handwritten note. However, the suicide account has been questioned. Syrian researcher Dr. Samira Moubayed said the claim was “naive” and accused the regime of using false narratives to intimidate Christians and drive them from the region. The death has renewed concerns about persecution and suspicious attacks on Christian leaders in Syria.
