Two people were killed and 11 others were injured in a mass shooting at a Madden video game tournament in Jacksonville, Florida, authorities said. The suspected gunman also died at the scene after apparently taking his own life. Police said three bodies were found at the location, including the suspect. Of the injured, 11 were taken to area hospitals by Jacksonville Fire and Rescue Department crews, and nine of them had gunshot wounds; all were reported in stable condition. Officers responded to Chicago Pizza at 1:36 p.m., about two minutes after the first reports of gunfire during the Madden 2019 gaming tournament. The business was locked down, and evacuations followed. Bomb squad and SWAT units later swept the area. Jacksonville Sheriff Mike Williams said investigators believe the suspect was 24-year-old David Katz of Baltimore, Maryland, pending confirmation. He said the FBI was assisting with the investigation in Baltimore, and that police had recovered and impounded the suspect’s vehicle. Witnesses said the shooter was a tournament participant who had lost. Authorities said they had not yet determined the exact motive, though they confirmed the suspect was there for the competition. Police also sought additional videos from the scene and tried to determine where the suspect had stayed the night before. As the attack unfolded, the sheriff’s office warned people hiding in locked areas at The Landing to stay calm and remain hidden until officers could reach them. Florida Governor Rick Scott and President Trump were briefed on the shooting. The attack occurred at Jacksonville Landing, an entertainment complex on the St. Johns River, just two days after another deadly shooting in Jacksonville.

Iran’s Forensic Medicine Organization says the cause of fugitive judge Gholamreza Mansouri’s death in Romania will be announced within two weeks, pending final genetic identification tests. Abbas Masjedi Arani said the body will then be handed over to Mansouri’s family under judicial orders. Mansouri was found dead in a hotel in Romania in June, and Tehran confirmed his death on June 19. He had been accused of corruption and of receiving more than $500,000 in bribes, and was a co-defendant in a major financial corruption case involving several senior judges accused of embezzlement and bribery. Iranian officials have repeatedly sought clarification from Romanian authorities. Foreign Ministry spokesman Abbas Mousavi said Iran was awaiting an official explanation of the cause of death. Prosecutor General Mohammad Jafar Montazeri also asked his Romanian counterpart to carry out a serious investigation, noting that Mansouri had been wanted by Iran’s judiciary and was pursued through Interpol before his arrest. A later Bucharest prosecutor’s office report, released on June 23, said an autopsy indicated Mansouri died from violence, specifically a blow from a hard object rather than a natural cause. Meanwhile, a Nour News report said Iran had received the body, but that Romanian police had not sent hotel CCTV footage, leaving doubts about the case.

# Summary Iranian judge Gholamreza Mansouri, a fugitive accused of corruption and bribery, was found dead in a Romanian hotel in June. Iran's Forensic Medicine Organization head Abbas Masjedi Arani announced that the cause of death would be revealed within two weeks, pending genetic identification tests. Mansouri was wanted by Iranian authorities for allegedly accepting over $500,000 in bribes and was a co-defendant in a major financial corruption trial involving senior judges. Though initially reported as an apparent suicide, Romania's prosecutor's office later stated he died from blows by a hard object in non-natural circumstances. Iran's government expressed skepticism about the investigation, noting that while Romania provided a 29-page police report, crucial closed-circuit camera footage was withheld. Iran's Prosecutor General requested a serious investigation from Romanian authorities, questioning the circumstances surrounding Mansouri's death. The body was reportedly returned to Iran in July for identification and family delivery.

Yemen’s recent flooding has killed at least 30 people and displaced hundreds, according to a Yemeni official, as heavy seasonal rains battered several western and northwestern areas of the country. Hodeidah governor Mugammad Qahim said Wednesday that floods in the southern city of Hodeidah displaced residents from about 500 homes and left five people missing. He also said the city was among the hardest hit, alongside Taiz and Hajjah. The exact nationwide death toll has not been confirmed by authorities, who have also not released a full count of the injured or missing. But the UN humanitarian office in Yemen said Friday’s flooding in Taiz’s Maqbnah district killed 15 people, destroyed agricultural land, and damaged homes and infrastructure. More severe weather was expected later Wednesday in Hodeidah, where residents in Al-Mansuriyah district were reportedly stranded in their homes after roads were blocked. Witnesses told The Associated Press that local authorities had not reached heavily affected areas for two days, leaving some people trapped. Mahdi Al-Mashat, chairman of the Houthi-led Supreme Political Council, ordered local authorities to respond to the damaged areas, according to Masirah TV. The station said the floods caused major damage to property, farmland, and roads in Hodeidah. Residents described devastating losses in the Tihamah coastal plain, part of Hodeidah province. Mohamed Rassam said livestock drowned in mud, while food supplies and drinking water were washed away. “The floods swept away everything,” he said. Other residents said they had received no assistance despite repeated hardship. Ahmed Ayesh said wind damage and rain destroyed the hut where he lived with his seven children. Khaled Meswat said the community often hears about aid and emergency services but never receives them, and claimed at least three people were swept away while elderly people died from hunger and cold. Faree Hamdan said hundreds of straw-built houses and livestock were washed away in the past 24 hours. The UN Population Fund said floods affected more than 28,000 people in four districts in Hajjah, and said rapid response teams had identified about 4,112 families needing emergency relief. Yemen’s rainy season begins in late March and peaks from July to mid-August. The floods have hit a country already devastated by civil war, which began in 2014 when the Houthis seized Sanaa and much of the north.

A major wildfire in Greece killed one person and continued burning on the outskirts of Athens on Tuesday, though officials said lighter winds and firefighting efforts had reduced its intensity. The blaze began on Sunday near the village of Varnavas, about 35 kilometers north of the capital, and quickly spread through dry forest, destroying homes, vehicles and land. Fueled by gale-force winds, it moved from a wooded, hilly area into Athens suburbs on Monday, covering the city in smoke and ash and causing panic in neighborhoods that had not faced such a fire so close to the center in decades. The fire reached Vrilissia, about 14 kilometers from central Athens, where the body of one person was found, according to the fire brigade. Hundreds of firefighters, supported by fire engines and waterbombing aircraft, were battling the blaze. The cause had not yet been determined. Authorities warned that winds could strengthen again later Tuesday, while Greece remained on high fire alert until Thursday, with temperatures expected to reach 40 degrees Celsius. More than 30 areas were evacuated, along with at least three hospitals, and power cuts hit parts of the Athens region. Police helped evacuate more than 250 people, some of whom spent the night in shelters.

Princess Leila Pahlavi, the youngest daughter of Iran’s last Shah, Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, and Empress Farah Pahlavi, was born in Tehran on March 27, 1970, into extraordinary privilege. She spent her early childhood inside the protected world of the Pahlavi court, surrounded by protocol, private tutors, Persian tradition and Western influence. Family members remembered her as gentle, introspective and close to her parents and siblings. That life ended abruptly when the Iranian Revolution gathered force in January 1979. At age nine, Leila fled Tehran with her family as protests against the Shah escalated and the monarchy collapsed. The royal family then entered a long period of exile, moving from country to country, including Egypt, Morocco, the Bahamas, Mexico, the United States and Panama. Their stays were temporary and often politically complicated, and the instability was compounded by the Shah’s worsening health as he battled advanced lymphoma. For Leila, exile meant losing the routines, security and identity of her early life. She would never return to Iran. Her father died in Cairo on July 27, 1980, when Leila was 10. His death ended any realistic hope of a return home and deepened the family’s sense of loss. Empress Farah eventually settled in Greenwich, Connecticut, giving the family a more permanent base in the United States. Leila attended the United Nations International School in New York and graduated from Rye Country Day School in 1988. She later divided her time between the United States and Paris and became fluent in Persian, English and French. Although her life looked comfortable from the outside, those close to her said she struggled deeply with identity, belonging and the absence of a homeland. In adulthood, she faced serious health problems, including chronic fatigue syndrome, depression and severe anorexia, and she received repeated treatment in medical facilities in the United States and the United Kingdom. She also became dependent on prescription medication, especially sleeping pills, which family and friends said was tied to insomnia, anxiety and emotional isolation. Her mother remained closely involved in her care. Leila largely avoided public life. She briefly worked as a model in Paris and was known for her elegance and restraint, but she was uncomfortable with attention and did not embrace the public role that her elder brother, Reza Pahlavi, accepted as crown prince in exile. On June 10, 2001, Leila was found dead in her room at London’s Leonard Hotel at the age of 31. An inquest concluded that she died from an overdose of prescription barbiturates, with cocaine also in her system, and her death was ruled a probable suicide. She was buried in Paris, far from Iran. A decade later, tragedy struck again when her brother Ali Reza died in exile by suicide in 2011. Leila’s life is remembered as a heartbreaking example of how exile, loss and history shaped a royal life marked by loneliness rather than privilege.

Police in Houston charged 19-year-old Isaac Tiharihondi, the son of Uganda-born Episcopal priest Israel Ahimbisibwe, with two counts of capital murder after his parents and 5-year-old brother were found dead in their apartment Monday morning. Authorities say the victims were Israel Ahimbisibwe, 51; his wife, Dorcus Ahimbisibwe, 47; and their young son, Israel Ahimbisibwe Jr. Court documents and an affidavit allege that Tiharihondi had told his family he had joined the Marines and was due to report for duty on Friday, but his parents believed he was lying and planned to confront him. Police said the U.S. Marine Corps had no record of his enlistment. Investigators allege he killed his parents with a lamp, baseball bat and hammer, causing blunt force trauma to their heads. The boy was stabbed in the neck and back. Autopsies had not yet been completed. The couple’s 17-year-old son was away at boarding school in California when the killings occurred. # Summary In Houston, 19-year-old Isaac Tiharihondi has been charged with the brutal murders of his parents and younger brother. Israel Ahimbisibwe, 51, his wife Dorcus, 47, and their 5-year-old son Israel Jr. were discovered dead in their apartment Monday morning. Tiharihondi was arrested Wednesday morning in Jackson, Mississippi, and faces two counts of capital murder pending extradition to Houston. According to court documents, Tiharihondi claimed he had enlisted in the Marines and would report for duty Friday. However, his parents suspected he was lying and planned to confront him—shortly before they were killed. The Marine Corps confirmed no record of his enlistment. A provincial fatality inquiry in Nova Scotia heard that a lack of collaboration among health-care professionals was a central factor in the case of Lionel Desmond, the former soldier who killed three family members and then himself in 2017. Dr. Peter Jaffe, a psychologist at Western University and co-founder of the Centre for Research and Education on Violence Against Women and Children, testified that Desmond’s mental-health care was fragmented, with psychiatrists, psychologists, social workers and others failing to share key information about his worsening condition after his release from the military in June 2015. Desmond, 33, bought a Soviet-era SKS 7.62 semi-automatic carbine on Jan. 3, 2017, and later shot and killed his mother Brenda, 52, his wife Shanna, 31, and their 10-year-old daughter Aaliya in their home in Upper Big Tracadie, N.S. Jaffe said the case reflected a recurring pattern seen in fatality reviews: professionals working in silos, not communicating, and not coordinating care. The inquiry, which began hearings in January 2020 and has heard 49 days of testimony, has repeatedly returned to the issue of poor collaboration. Jaffe told the inquiry that Desmond had contact with about 40 mental-health professionals from the time he was diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder and major depression in 2011 until his death in 2017. He said there was no reason why earlier providers could not have prepared a summary of his history and passed along contact information for follow-up. Jaffe pointed to Desmond’s desperate attempts, along with his wife, to obtain help in eastern Nova Scotia in the fall of 2016. A psychiatrist at St. Martha’s Regional Hospital in Antigonish, Dr. Ian Slayter, took Desmond as a patient and quickly realized he was in serious trouble, but he could not get federal medical records needed for a full assessment. Judge Warren Zimmer noted that Desmond had requested a discharge summary from Veterans Affairs Canada on Oct. 11, 2016, after treatment at Ste. Anne’s Hospital in Montreal, but he still did not have it when he arrived at St. Martha’s on Oct. 24. Jaffe said that with access to that document, Slayter would have been much better positioned to understand the severity of the situation and act quickly. He also said many providers focused too heavily on Desmond’s risk of suicide and missed warning signs that he might commit domestic violence. Jaffe made eight recommendations, including more domestic-violence education for front-line professionals, better flagging and sharing of high-risk cases by the military and Veterans Affairs, a domestic violence death review committee in Nova Scotia, and improved police risk-assessment tools.

# Summary: Desmond Inquiry Highlights Health Professional Communication Failures A provincial fatality inquiry in Nova Scotia heard Thursday that inadequate information sharing among health-care professionals contributed to a tragedy in which ex-soldier Lionel Desmond killed three family members and himself in 2017. Dr. Peter Jaffe, a psychologist from Western University, testified that lack of collaboration was an "overwhelming theme" in the case. Desmond, 33, fatally shot his mother Brenda (52), wife Shanna (31), and daughter Aaliya (10) on January 3, 2017, after purchasing a semi-automatic rifle. Jaffe noted that psychiatrists, psychologists, social workers, and other professionals failed to share critical information about Desmond's mental decline following his military discharge in June 2015. The Afghanistan veteran had contact with 40 mental-health professionals between his 2011 PTSD diagnosis and his death in 2017, yet crucial information remained siloed among providers. A significant gap emerged when Desmond and his wife sought help in fall 2016. When Dr. Ian Slayter at St. Martha's Regional Hospital in Antigonish agreed to treat Desmond in October 2016, he could not access federal medical records necessary for proper assessment. Desmond had requested a discharge summary from his treatment at Ste. Anne's Hospital in Montreal on October 11, but did not receive it before arriving at St. Martha's on October 24—limiting Slayter's ability to understand the severity of Desmond's condition. Jaffe emphasized that accessible prior assessments would have positioned Slayter "in a much better position to understand the depth of the issue and the need for immediate planning." The inquiry, which began in January 2020 and has heard 49 days of testimony, is expected to conclude before year's end. Jaffe submitted eight recommendations, including expanded domestic violence education for front-line professionals, better information sharing between the Canadian Armed Forces and Veterans Affairs Canada, establishment of a domestic violence death review committee in Nova Scotia, and improved police risk assessment tools. Notably, Jaffe indicated that most professionals focused on Desmond's suicide risk while overlooking warning signs of potential violence toward family members.

Five years after the July 7 ambush in Dallas that killed five police officers, the families of two of the victims, Brent Thompson and Patrick Zamarripa, are still living with the loss while also reflecting on their sons’ bravery. The article recounts how a peaceful protest turned deadly when a gunman opened fire on officers assigned to protect the crowd. Paulette and Sam Thompson, in Corsicana, and Valeria Zamarripa, in Fort Worth, were watching the events unfold on television that night. As reports came in that officers were being shot, both mothers frantically tried to reach their sons. Paulette said she kept texting Brent, asking if he was safe, while Valeria described hearing the terrifying updates and feeling in her heart that Patrick was gone. Sam Thompson remembered the moment he and Paulette silently understood Brent had been killed before it was officially confirmed. Newly released video, shown five years later, reveals the final moments of the officers and highlights their heroism. In footage from Patrick Zamarripa’s cruiser, the Navy veteran is seen listening to a Rangers game as the protest passes by. When gunfire erupts, he immediately exits his vehicle and runs toward the shots. He is struck within seconds. Fellow officers rush to help him, but they too come under fire. The video also shows Brent Thompson, a DART officer, confronting the gunman, Micah Johnson, only feet away from where Zamarripa was shot. Thompson fires at Johnson, wounds him, and forces him into El Centro College. DART Officer Misty McBride, who was injured that night, said Thompson’s actions likely saved lives by preventing the attack from becoming even worse. Brent’s brother, Darryll Thompson, said remembering Brent’s courage is essential because of the lives his actions helped protect. The families also described the painful moments when they learned their sons had died. Valeria recalled being told at Parkland Hospital that Patrick had been shot and killed, while Brent’s father described walking into Baylor and hearing officers snapping their heels together in salute as the family passed by. The years since have brought more tragedy for the Thompson family: Brent’s brother Lowell died of pneumonia, and Brent’s 19-year-old son William died by suicide a year after Brent’s death. Sam Thompson said all three are buried together in the family cemetery. Despite the grief, the families say they find comfort in memories and symbols of honor, including a statue of Brent in downtown Corsicana. Valeria treasures the last words Patrick said to her: “I love you mom.” Both families want the public to remember their sons as heroes when reflecting on the tragedy.

# Five Years After Dallas Police Ambush: Families Remember Fallen Heroes On July 7, 2016, a peaceful protest in Dallas turned tragic when a gunman ambushed police officers, killing five officers in what became one of the deadliest attacks on law enforcement in U.S. history. Five years later, the families of those killed continue to honor their memory and reflect on that fateful night. Among those killed were Brent Thompson, a DART officer, and Patrick Zamarripa, a police officer and Navy veteran. Their families watched the events unfold from afar—Paulette and Sam Thompson from their home in Corsicana, and Valeria Zamarripa from Fort Worth. Despite hoping for good news, their maternal instincts told them their sons were gone. Newly released video footage reveals the heroism displayed by the fallen officers during their final moments. Officer Zamarripa was shot within seconds of leaving his vehicle to run toward the gunfire. Officer Thompson engaged the shooter, Micah Johnson, wounding him and forcing him into El Centro College. His actions prevented further casualties. Fellow officer Misty McBride, injured that night, credited Thompson's heroism with saving lives, noting that "a lot more citizens could have died; more could have been injured." The grief has been profound for the families. The Thompson family experienced compounded tragedy: Brent's brother Lowell died of pneumonia, and Brent's 19-year-old son William died by suicide a year after his father's death. Sam Thompson explained that William "couldn't live without his dad. They were inseparable." All three are now buried together at the family's cemetery. Despite their pain, the families find ways to honor their sons' memory. A statue honoring Brent stands in downtown Corsicana, serving as a reminder of his sacrifice. Valeria finds comfort in her last words with Patrick: "I love you mom." As the city marks the five-year anniversary, both families emphasize that this day should be remembered for the heroism displayed by their sons and fellow officers. They want people to recognize that on that tragic night, "they were all heroes," working together to protect their community even at the ultimate cost. The families' strength and resilience serve as a testament to the sacrifice made by these fallen officers.

A Terre Haute, Indiana, woman named Marlene became suspicious after receiving repeated phone calls offering a “free” cancer screening through Medicare. The caller told her that Medicare and her primary insurance would cover the test and that all she had to do was swab the inside of her mouth and mail it in. To determine whether she “qualified,” Marlene gave the telemarketer her Medicare identification number. Because she has a family history of cancer and the pitch sounded convincing, she initially believed the offer might be legitimate. Three days later, a bright red envelope arrived in her mailbox marked “URGENT” and “TIME SENSITIVE.” Inside was a DNA testing kit containing a cotton swab, a test tube, a biohazard specimen bag, and a return envelope. More calls followed, urging her to complete the test and mail it back immediately. That pressure made her uneasy. Marlene said she began to suspect something was wrong because a legitimate medical provider would not keep calling to ask whether she had mailed the test in yet. She reported the matter to 13 Investigates but asked that her last name not be published because she feared becoming a target for more telemarketers. Her concern is consistent with warnings from state and federal officials, who say genetic testing kits are becoming a new Medicare fraud scam. Nancy Moore, director of Indiana’s Senior Medicare Patrol program, called it a relatively new scheme that can begin through phone calls, Facebook solicitations, postcards, and appearances at senior fairs or health fairs. She said reports of these offers have been increasing. The article notes that several states have issued warnings in recent months. In Kentucky, Attorney General Andy Beshear opened an investigation after Louisville residents said men in a van paid Medicaid recipients $20 for DNA samples and insurance information. Beshear said scammers appeared to be trying to steal personal and insurance data in order to bill Medicare for unnecessary tests. In Nebraska, scam artists targeted senior centers and assisted living facilities, prompting warnings from the state Department of Insurance. In New Jersey, a man was sentenced to 50 months in prison after using DNA test kits to defraud Medicare out of $430,000 by telling seniors in low-income housing they were at risk for serious diseases if they did not agree to genetic testing. Marlene reported her kit to her local Area Agency on Aging and to Indiana’s Senior Medicare Patrol coordinator, who has already filed a complaint with the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Office of Inspector General. Moore said investigators are paying close attention because the kits can generate large bills to Medicare, often between $6,000 and $11,000. If Medicare approves the test, the program typically pays 80%, which can leave the beneficiary responsible for the rest. The article explains that Medicare changed its policy last year to cover certain next-generation DNA sequencing tests for people with advanced cancer or a family history of specific cancers, but only when the test is medically necessary and ordered by a physician. Officials say scammers are exploiting that policy change by aggressively soliciting seniors and, in some cases, offering kickbacks to doctors willing to authorize tests without ever seeing patients. When 13 Investigates contacted the company that sent Marlene the kit, a customer service representative said the test would show whether she has “the cancer gene” and would list possible cancers. When asked why the kit was mailed without a doctor’s approval, the representative said her doctor did not need to approve it and that she would receive a call from a licensed doctor with the results. The company also said it had not yet set up a website or signs, describing itself as “very new,” even though the kit directed Marlene to send her sample to “Hudson Cancer Testing Center,” which turned out to be a call center in a strip mall with a disconnected phone number. Follow-up calls to the company were repeatedly put on hold and then disconnected. Marlene said she has decided not to mail the kit to Florida until her doctor investigates further. She said the most troubling part is that the callers already had her Medicare number and personal details. Federal and state authorities continue investigating these DNA swab solicitations, and the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services has issued consumer warnings. Indiana residents who suspect Medicare fraud can report it to the Senior Medicare Patrol or their local Area Agency on Aging.

Notably, the representative stated that physician approval was unnecessary, contradicting Medicare's requirement that tests be doctor-ordered. The company lacks a website or proper signage and claims to be "very new." Multiple follow-up calls went unanswered. Marlene decided not to mail her DNA sample until her physician could investigate further. She expressed concern about the company's access to her Medicare number and personal information, stating, "It's kind of scary." The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services has also posted consumer warnings about genetic testing kits to protect vulnerable populations from exploitation.

Toronto Transit Commission subway riders lost 26 hours of service last year because people repeatedly went down onto the tracks, including one person who chased a train to retrieve a forgotten bag. TTC spokesman Stuart Green said there is never a reason to enter track level because the third rail carries 600 volts, trains move quickly, and the act is both dangerous and illegal. He added that if someone drops an item, they should leave it and notify a uniformed TTC employee instead. Going onto the tracks can also bring a $425 fine. In 2016, the TTC recorded 167 incidents of people descending to track level, causing delays on subway lines including Line 3 in Scarborough. Among them, eight people went down to recover belongings, causing 32 minutes of delay, and 16 people crossed the tracks to reach the opposite platform. The tally also included 12 accidental falls and three suicide attempts in which no one was injured. It did not include 23 other incidents involving injuries or deaths from suicide attempts, or cases where no delay resulted. Green said about one-third of people who go onto the tracks flee before being caught. Montreal has responded to similar problems with warning signs after losing 14.5 hours of service to riders retrieving dropped items.

# Subway Track Jumpers Cause Delays in Toronto In 2016, Toronto's TTC subway system experienced 26 hours of service delays due to 167 incidents of people jumping onto track level. These incidents included someone attempting to chase down a train to retrieve a forgotten bag and eight people retrieving personal belongings, which caused 32 minutes of delays alone. The TTC warns that the third rail carries 600 volts of electricity and poses extreme danger. Jumping to track level is illegal and results in a $425 fine. Additionally, power must be cut when someone is on the tracks, disrupting service for other customers. TTC spokesman Stuart Green notes that approximately one-third of track-level trespassers flee before being caught, making the actual number of incidents difficult to determine. The TTC advises passengers to notify uniformed employees if items are dropped rather than attempting retrieval themselves.

Political scientist Armen Hovhannisyan told Armenpress that the South Caucasus has become more tense and geopolitically unstable amid what he described as a broader erosion of stable borders, relationships, and international rules. He said Donald Trump’s post-election remarks are troubling and unacceptable even under international law, warning that such rhetoric, though aimed at a domestic audience, weakens global security norms. Hovhannisyan argued that if a U.S. president can make unsupported territorial claims against NATO member Denmark, then countries such as Azerbaijan or Turkey may feel emboldened to behave similarly toward their neighbors. He pointed to Turkey’s actions in Syria as evidence of a growing pattern, saying an entire country is being turned into a Turkish satellite through local forces tied to Ankara. For Armenia, he said, this makes vigilance essential and increases the importance of building military-political alliances. In his view, remaining isolated and weak in such an environment could be “similar to suicide.” Turning to Armenia’s Crossroads of Peace initiative, Hovhannisyan said Trump’s approach suggests a new era in which major powers will negotiate deals and decide the routes of regional transport and connectivity. Because the region contains competing interests, he said it is still unclear whether the superpowers are ready to compromise. The real test of Armenia’s initiatives, he added, will come only after those decisions are made. Hovhannisyan urged Armenia’s leadership to clearly define the country’s security orientation and stop relying on the old argument that breaking with one power or another will bring punishment. Instead, he said Armenia should focus on countries that share its interests and are willing to defend them, including in the military sphere. He named France and India as examples. He concluded that geopolitical rivalry could produce rational outcomes, but only after possible escalations and clashes. Citing the 20th century and the long path toward the Helsinki security architecture, he said Armenia must remain cautious and take calculated security steps.

Uzbekistan President Shavkat Mirziyoyev is expected to win another term in Sunday’s election by a wide margin, facing only weak, little-known challengers in a race that offers little real competition. Mirziyoyev came to power in 2016 after the death of longtime authoritarian ruler Islam Karimov, and while he has loosened many of the harsh controls associated with that era, he has made limited progress on political reform. The four candidates running against him were low-profile and did not even participate directly in televised debates, instead sending proxies who avoided substantive exchanges. Independent candidates were not permitted. Political analyst Akhmed Rahmonov said the rivals were offering vague promises about issues such as social security without presenting concrete programs, because it was already clear who would win. Among the challengers, Alisher Qodirov drew the most attention for proposing that Uzbeks working abroad should pay taxes in Uzbekistan. That idea was widely unpopular in a country where many families rely on remittances from relatives overseas. Mirziyoyev publicly rejected the proposal, and some observers speculated that Qodirov’s campaign may have been designed to help the incumbent by steering votes his way; his party is in coalition with Mirziyoyev’s in parliament. Despite the lack of political competition, Mirziyoyev has changed Uzbekistan significantly compared with Karimov’s rule. Freedom of speech has expanded somewhat, with independent news outlets and bloggers emerging. He has also eased restrictions on Islam, which had been tightly controlled under Karimov as a way to suppress dissent. In the economic sphere, Mirziyoyev lifted controls on hard currency to encourage foreign investment and worked to improve relations with other countries after the isolation that marked the previous era. Andrey Kazantsev of the Moscow State Institute of Foreign Relations said Mirziyoyev has strengthened ties with major powers including Russia, China and Western countries, while also improving relations with neighboring states. He has also sought peaceful engagement with Afghanistan, which shares a border with Uzbekistan and has long been a concern because of the risk that instability could spread. Uzbekistan’s foreign minister became the first foreign official to visit Afghanistan after the Taliban seized control there in August.

At a meeting of the Council of Heads of Security Agencies and Intelligence Services of CIS member states in Tashkent on November 7, Russia’s FSB director Alexander Bortnikov warned that at least 2,000 spouses and children of militants of Russian origin have been identified in Middle Eastern conflict zones. He said these women and children, who are family members of militants, may become part of terrorist networks after returning home, noting that extremist leaders often view such “returnees” as potential suicide bombers, recruiters, agitators, or links to clandestine cells. Bortnikov said humanitarian corridors used to bring back wives, widows, and children from war zones have become one of the main channels for terrorist groups to deploy personnel. He also argued that militants moving through CIS countries often rely on illegal migration routes organized by transnational criminal groups and corrupt officials. Once in places of settlement, he said, they are supported by ethnic organized crime groups involved in drug and arms trafficking, which help create underground cells and recruit vulnerable people. The FSB chief stressed that protecting the southern borders of the CIS remains a top priority for member states’ security services. He called for stronger joint efforts against the Islamic State group and Al Qaeda, which he said are entrenched in Afghanistan. He also highlighted the need to step up countermeasures against online propaganda promoting terrorism and extremism. Bortnikov reviewed cooperation among CIS security agencies, saying joint work with partners in Azerbaijan, Tajikistan, Kyrgyzstan, and Uzbekistan had uncovered and disrupted 13 cells of international terrorist organizations and led to the detention of 138 militants. He added that from May to October, partner services removed more than 200 CIS citizens from border guard blacklists tied to suspected terrorist and extremist activity. He also cited a joint operation with Belarus’s KGB that dismantled an illegal weapons-trafficking channel, resulting in the seizure of more than 40 small arms and 9,000 rounds of ammunition. In addition, security services from Russia, Belarus, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, and Uzbekistan seized large quantities of narcotic and psychotropic substances in anti-drug operations. Finally, Bortnikov said the West had intensified efforts to interfere in CIS countries through non-governmental organizations, which he described as a traditional tool for meddling in the domestic affairs of sovereign states.

# Summary: FSB Chief Addresses Security Threats in CIS Nations Russian Federal Security Service (FSB) Director Alexander Bortnikov addressed the 47th Council of Heads of Security Agencies and Intelligence Services of CIS Member-States in Tashkent on November 7, highlighting multiple security challenges facing the region. Bortnikov reported that at least 2,000 spouses and children of militants with Russian citizenship have been identified in Middle Eastern conflict zones. He characterized these foreign and international NGOs as conventional tools for external meddling in the domestic affairs of CIS member-states, calling for increased scrutiny of such activities as they pose threats to regional stability and sovereignty.

Leading Russian independent media have mounted a public campaign for the release of Abdulmumin Gadzhiev, the religious affairs editor of the Dagestan weekly *Chernovik*, who has been jailed on terrorism charges that supporters say are meant to silence an independent journalist in Russia’s North Caucasus. Russian fitness coach and influencer Dmitry Nuyanzin, 30, has died after taking part in an extreme binge-eating experiment meant to promote his weight-loss programme. Reports say he died in his sleep while following a diet of more than 10,000 calories a day for several weeks, with the aim of quickly gaining weight before publicly losing it to demonstrate the effectiveness of his plan. Nuyanzin had set out to gain 25 kilograms and had already put on 13 kilograms in a month, reaching 105 kg. His social media posts documented the dramatic transformation, showing his once muscular frame becoming noticeably larger, especially around his abdomen. In one video, he displayed his belly fat while holding a packet of chips. His daily intake reportedly included pastries and half a cake for breakfast, nearly 800 grams of dumplings with mayonnaise for lunch, and a burger plus two small pizzas for dinner, along with constant snacking on crisps. He had spoken openly about the junk-food routine as part of the challenge. A day before his death, Nuyanzin told friends he felt unwell and planned to see a doctor. He also cancelled his training sessions, but died before getting medical help. A graduate of the Orenburg Olympic Reserve School and the National Fitness University in St Petersburg, he had coached elite Russians for more than a decade. His death has raised concern about the dangers of extreme fitness stunts.

Seven people were found dead after a fire destroyed a wooden house in Ono, Fukushima prefecture, Japanese police said. Firefighters got an emergency call at about 11:05 p.m. Wednesday, and the blaze was extinguished roughly an hour later. The two-story home, along with an adjacent warehouse, burned down. Nine people, including four children, lived in the house owned by 61-year-old Tsuneyoshi Shiota. Shiota’s 57-year-old wife and 33-year-old son-in-law survived; his wife suffered minor hand injuries. The dead were believed to include Shiota’s mother, daughter, and four grandchildren aged 3 to 8. Neighbors reported hearing barking, then flames and explosions.

Images showed debris and dust in the upscale Dionisio Torres neighborhood near Iracema Beach, an unusual site for such a collapse in Brazil.

Peru has entered another period of crisis after an assassination attempt on a cumbia band in Lima on October 8 helped ignite a new wave of unrest. Two days later, President Dina Boluarte was removed from office, and Congressman José Jerí was sworn in as Peru’s eighth president in ten years. In the days that followed, Peruvians launched the country’s largest protests in five years, with clashes between demonstrators and police leaving at least one person dead and dozens injured. The protests were directed not only at Jerí, who has faced accusations of corruption and sexual assault, but also at a deeper breakdown in public life: the spread of organized crime and the collapse of trust in the state’s ability to protect citizens. The article argues that the security crisis is now central to Peru’s politics as the country heads toward April 2026 elections. Organized crime has expanded dramatically over the past three years. Reported extortion cases rose sixfold between 2019 and 2024, and this year one in three Peruvians said they knew someone who had been extorted, often a small business owner. Homicides have also surged, doubling since 2019, and in January alone there were 203 percent more homicides than in January 2017. What had long been viewed as a problem limited to border areas or drug-trafficking routes has become a daily reality for small and medium-sized businesses, which are described as the backbone of Peru’s economy. In cities such as Trujillo and Chiclayo, bus operators and construction companies now pay weekly “quotas” to criminal groups. In Lima, even market vendors are receiving extortion calls demanding payments through digital wallets. Many of those affected work in Peru’s huge informal sector, which employs nearly seven in ten Peruvians. As extortion and killings have become routine, strikes and street protests have followed, driven by anger at a government widely seen as absent or complicit. The article traces this deterioration to a decade of institutional erosion and political instability. Since 2016, Congress — dominated by the fujimorismo movement — has repeatedly used impeachment and oversight powers as political weapons, a practice described as “constitutional hardball.” This has turned impeachment into a tool for leverage rather than accountability, as seen in the removals of Boluarte and former President Martín Vizcarra. At the same time, Peru underwent the fallout of Operation Car Wash, the sweeping anti-corruption investigations that began in Brazil and spread across the region. Peruvian prosecutors aggressively pursued corruption cases against the political class that governed before 2016. Four former presidents were convicted, former President Alan García killed himself as police arrived to arrest him, and ministers, presidential candidates, business figures, and mayors were also investigated. Although this appeared to cleanse politics, the article says it instead left behind a more fragmented and self-interested elite that was easier for organized crime to infiltrate. Congress has increasingly acted as a shield for illicit interests, the article says, advancing laws that reduced penalties for some crimes, weakened political finance controls, and blocked efforts to vet local officials for corruption. Meanwhile, prosecutors remain underfunded and police leadership is frequently reshuffled, creating favorable conditions for criminal economies to grow. With national elections less than six months away, Peru faces an uncertain future. Citizens are exhausted and distrustful, and the party system is in disarray. The article warns that if democracy cannot provide security and stability, it loses legitimacy. Yet there is still a democratic impulse: Peruvians continue to protest corruption and demand a capable state. The danger is that this frustration could instead empower populist candidates promising “order at any cost,” potentially further weakening democracy. The article concludes that Peru’s old model of political chaos without immediate economic collapse may have reached its breaking point, and that without restored security and institutional credibility, the country’s democracy could become unrecognizable.

# Peru at a Breaking Point: Organized Crime and Political Collapse Peru faces an unprecedented crisis as political instability and surging organized crime threaten the nation's democratic future. Following an assassination attempt against a cumbia band in Lima on October 8, President Dina Boluarte was removed from office on October 10, making José Jerí the eighth president in ten years. The subsequent protests—the largest in five years—reflect deeper concerns than political leadership changes: citizens are demanding protection from escalating criminal violence that has infiltrated everyday life and eroded faith in state institutions. The organized crime crisis has reached alarming proportions. Between 2019 and 2024, reported extortions increased sixfold, with one in three Peruvians now knowing an extortion victim. Homicides have doubled since 2019, and January 2024 saw 203 percent more homicides than January 2017. What was once confined to border regions now affects Peru's economic backbone—small and medium-sized businesses. In cities like Trujillo and Chiclayo, bus operators and construction firms pay weekly extortion quotas to criminal groups. Even Lima's market vendors receive digital wallet extortion demands. This criminality has driven strikes and protests from Peru's informal sector, which employs seven of ten Peruvians. This crime explosion stems from a decade of institutional decay caused by self-interested politicians. Beginning in 2016, Congress dominated by the fujimorismo movement exploited procedural rules in what legal scholars call "constitutional hardball," weaponizing impeachment for political leverage rather than accountability. Simultaneously, Operation Car Wash—investigations originating from Brazil—targeted Peru's pre-2016 political class, resulting in four former presidents convicted of corruption. Former President Alan García committed suicide as police arrived to arrest him. However, rather than producing cleaner leadership, these purges created a more fragmented, parochial, and self-interested political class vulnerable to criminal penetration. Congress, now one of the hemisphere's least trusted institutions, has shielded illicit interests by quietly advancing legislation reducing penalties for certain crimes, weakening political financing controls, and obstructing corruption vetting of local authorities. Many current lawmakers face criminal investigations themselves. With hollowed-out institutions, underfunded prosecutors, and constantly reshuffled police leadership, criminal economies have flourished unchecked. Citizens feel abandoned by government and terrorized by crime, making democracy's legitimacy precarious. When democratic systems cannot guarantee security or stability, they lose moral and practical authority. As Peru approaches April 2026 elections, the outcome remains uncertain. Two trajectories are possible. Citizens retain democratic reflexes—they protest, reject corruption, and demand competent governance. A reformist leader could rebuild institutions and salvage democracy. Alternatively, populism offers fertile ground. Candidates promising "order at any cost" will find receptive audiences among desperate voters. An opportunistic leader could exploit security concerns to dismantle remaining democratic structures. The October protests signal that Peru's old model—political chaos isolated from economic collapse—has reached its breaking point. Unless the next government restores both security and institutional credibility, Peru's democracy risks becoming unrecognizable. The nation stands at a crossroads where democratic renewal or democratic destruction are equally plausible outcomes.

Héctor Timerman, Argentina’s former foreign minister and a central figure in the long-running controversy over the country’s agreement with Iran on the 1994 AMIA bombing, died Sunday at his home in Buenos Aires at age 65. His lawyer, Graciana Peñafort, said he died of respiratory failure while being treated for liver cancer. She said he had been in very poor physical condition and that his heart could no longer withstand the strain of his illness. Timerman served as foreign minister under President Cristina Fernández de Kirchner from 2010 to 2015, after previously serving as Argentina’s ambassador to Washington from 2007 to 2010. His time in office was marked by growing friction between Argentina and the United States. The most controversial episode was his signing in 2013 of a memorandum of understanding with Iran over the AMIA bombing, which killed 85 people and injured about 300 in the attack on the Jewish community center in Buenos Aires. The agreement, approved by Argentina’s Congress, called for the two countries to create a joint commission to investigate the bombing. Supporters said it was meant to help obtain answers from Iranian officials accused of involvement in the attack. Critics argued it was an effort to shield suspects from justice. The deal was later ruled unconstitutional. Iran has consistently denied responsibility, and no one has ever been convicted for the bombing. In 2006, Argentine prosecutors had already accused several top Iranian officials, including former President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani, and Imad Mugniyah, a senior Hezbollah commander, of involvement in the attack. Mugniyah was killed in 2008, and Rafsanjani died in 2017. Federal prosecutor Alberto Nisman later accused Fernández, Timerman, and others of taking part in a cover-up intended to prevent Iranians from facing justice. He said the memorandum was the first step toward canceling Interpol red notices that had restricted the movement of the suspects. Shortly after making those allegations, Nisman was found dead in his apartment in January 2015 with a gunshot wound to the head. His death remains unresolved. In December 2017, Judge Claudio Bonadio ordered Timerman and several former officials detained over their role in the Iran agreement. Because of his illness, Timerman was placed under home detention. Bonadio said there was enough evidence to indict Fernández and her allies for treason, arguing they had sought impunity for the Iranian suspects and aimed to normalize relations with Iran. Timerman later described himself in a New York Times opinion piece as a “political prisoner.” Bonadio also alleged that Ronald K. Noble, former head of Interpol, had been part of the cover-up, an accusation Noble denied. After Timerman’s death, Noble wrote that he had died “under a cloud of false accusations” because Argentina’s judiciary had not thoroughly investigated the case. Fernández said Timerman, who was Jewish, had been deeply committed to bringing the AMIA attackers to justice. His efforts to seek treatment in the United States were complicated when his U.S. visa was canceled after the indictment, though it was later restored. His lawyer said the delay cost him precious time and worsened his condition. Before entering government, Timerman was a journalist and human-rights activist, following in the footsteps of his father, Jacobo Timerman, a prominent journalist imprisoned and tortured by Argentina’s military dictatorship. Born in Buenos Aires in 1953, Héctor Timerman worked for publications his father helped found, lived in exile in the United States from 1978 to 1984, earned a master’s degree from Columbia University, and later renounced his U.S. citizenship. He is survived by his wife and two daughters.

# Argentine Ex-Foreign Minister Héctor Timerman Dies at 65 Héctor Timerman, Argentina's former foreign minister, died Sunday at his home in Buenos Aires from respiratory failure while undergoing treatment for liver cancer. He was 65. Timerman served as foreign minister from 2010 to 2015 under President Cristina Fernández and previously held the position of Argentine ambassador to the United States. His tenure was marked by escalating tensions between Argentina and the U.S. ## The Iran Controversy Timerman's most significant and controversial act was negotiating a 2013 memorandum of understanding with Iran regarding the 1994 bombing of the Argentine Israeli Mutual Association (AMIA), a Jewish community center in Buenos Aires that killed 85 people and injured approximately 300. The agreement aimed to establish a joint commission to investigate the attack. Though Congress approved it, the agreement was later declared unconstitutional. The deal became highly contentious. Federal prosecutor Alberto Nisman accused Timerman and Fernández of orchestrating a cover-up to shield Iranians from justice. Nisman alleged the memorandum was designed to eventually cancel Interpol red notices against the suspects, allowing them to travel freely. Nisman died from a gunshot wound to the head in January 2015, just days after making his accusations. His death remains unsolved. ## Legal Troubles In December 2017, federal judge Claudio Bonadio ordered Timerman and other officials taken into custody, charging them with treason. Bonadio concluded there was sufficient evidence that they sought "impunity for the Iranian nationals accused of the attack on the AMIA headquarters." Due to his illness, Timerman was granted home detention rather than imprisonment. Timerman subsequently called himself a "political prisoner" in a New York Times opinion piece. His legal troubles had serious health consequences: his U.S. visa was canceled following the indictment, delaying his ability to receive medical treatment in America. Though the visa was later reinstated, his lawyer contended that the delay cost him critical time for treatment that could have improved his condition. ## Background and Legacy Before entering government, Timerman was a journalist like his father, Jacobo Timerman, a prominent newsman imprisoned and tortured during Argentina's military dictatorship from 1976 to 1981. Héctor lived in exile in the United States from 1978 to 1984, earning a master's degree in international relations from Columbia University in 1981. He became a naturalized U.S. citizen but renounced his citizenship in 2006. Beyond journalism, Timerman was a human rights activist and co-founder of Americas Watch. He is survived by his wife, Anabel Sielecki, and two daughters, Amanda and Jordana.

Hector Timerman, Argentina’s foreign minister, is at the center of a major scandal involving the 1994 bombing of the AMIA Jewish community center in Buenos Aires, which killed 85 people and wounded hundreds. The controversy has intensified after the mysterious death of federal prosecutor Alberto Nisman, who had spent more than a decade investigating the attack. The article recalls the Timerman family’s history under Argentina’s military dictatorship. In 1977, during the “dirty war,” soldiers abducted Hector Timerman’s father, the Jewish newspaper editor Jacobo Timerman, and took him to a torture center. Hector later went into exile in the United States, where he became a human rights activist and co-founded a group that later became Human Rights Watch. That background makes the current accusations especially explosive within Argentina’s Jewish community, where some now accuse him of betraying his own people. Nisman had accused Timerman and President Cristina Fernández de Kirchner of helping to cover up Iran’s alleged role in the AMIA bombing. In a complaint he was scheduled to present to Congress the day after he died, Nisman alleged that Timerman sought to shield Iranian officials suspected of masterminding the attack. According to Nisman, Argentina was willing to help remove those officials from Interpol’s wanted list, and in return Iran would provide Argentina with a favorable trade deal. His claims were based on intercepted phone calls between people believed to be involved in secret Argentine-Iranian negotiations. Nisman was found dead on January 18 in his apartment with a bullet in his head and a pistol beneath him. Investigators later found drafts of arrest warrants for Timerman, Kirchner, and others in his garbage. The investigation into his death continues, and it is still unclear whether he was murdered or took his own life. Timerman, 61, has strongly denied wrongdoing. In interviews after Nisman’s death, he said he never asked Interpol to lift the warrants and produced an email from Interpol’s former secretary general supporting that claim. He argued that only the judge in charge of the case could request such a move. Timerman also said Argentina never could have received the refined oil it needed from Iran, and that private companies, not the government, controlled grain exports. He insists that he and the president have done everything possible to bring justice to the victims of the bombing.

# Summary In 1977, Hector Timerman's father, Jacobo Timerman, a Jewish newspaper editor, was tortured by Argentina's military dictatorship. The younger Timerman subsequently became a prominent human rights activist in the United States and co-founded what became Human Rights Watch. However, as Argentina's current foreign minister, he now faces accusations of the opposite: allegedly covering up a terrorist attack that devastated Argentina's Jewish community. The controversy centers on the 1994 bombing of the Argentine Israelite Mutual Association (AMIA), a Jewish community center in Buenos Aires that killed 85 people and injured hundreds. Federal prosecutor Alberto Nisman had led the investigation for over a decade but was found dead in his apartment on January 18 with a bullet in his head—under circumstances still unclear as to whether it was murder or suicide. Days before his death, Nisman filed charges against Timerman and President Cristina Fernández de Kirchner, alleging that Timerman sought to shield Iranian officials allegedly responsible for the bombing. According to Nisman's complaint, based on intercepted phone calls, Timerman allegedly negotiated to remove these officials from Interpol's wanted list in exchange for favorable trade deals between Argentina and Iran. The agreement reportedly fell apart because Timerman could not secure Interpol's cooperation, with an Iranian intermediary stating that Timerman had "messed up." Some members of Argentina's Jewish community have called for Timerman to face a communal tribunal or expulsion. However, Timerman denies any wrongdoing and has defended his actions, asserting that his primary duty as foreign minister is to Argentina. He provided evidence from Interpol's former secretary general confirming he never requested the removal of arrest warrants. Timerman also argued that only the Argentine judge overseeing the case could request such removal, and that Iran lacked the economic capacity to fulfill proposed trade agreements anyway. The scandal remains contentious, with Timerman insisting his government has done everything possible to help achieve justice for the bombing victims.

Residents of northern Chile, especially in the border town of Colchane, say the national government has failed to contain a worsening migrant crisis. Mayor Javier Garcia told Efe that the area continues to see a “massive, uncontrolled influx” of migrants and that the measures announced by President Sebastian Piñera’s administration have not worked. He said a woman migrant found dead in Colchane on Wednesday, near an unoccupied guard post on the Bolivian border, raised the year’s death toll in the area to 19. For years, undocumented migrants have crossed into Chile’s remote northern desert from Bolivia and Peru, but the flow surged sharply over the past year during the Covid-19 pandemic. Garcia criticized the government’s response, including migrant shelters, as of doubtful effectiveness. He also said there appears to be no real state will to stop indiscriminate entries, arguing that the increased presence of soldiers and Carabineros is focused more on humanitarian assistance than on protecting local residents. He further objected to the continued closure of the area’s only legal border crossing because of the pandemic. Most of the migrants arriving in Colchane each day are Venezuelans fleeing their country’s economic collapse. One 21-year-old Venezuelan woman said she hoped to reach Santiago, find work, and save enough to buy a house in Venezuela for herself and her daughter. Another Venezuelan migrant rejected a proposal by right-wing presidential candidate Jose Antonio Kast to dig a trench along the northern border, saying Kast was not treating migrants as human beings. The article also notes growing tension elsewhere in northern Chile, including camps of migrants in city streets and an anti-immigration attack in Iquique in late September, when tents and belongings were burned. In April, Chile enacted a new immigration law requiring visas before entry and allowing large-scale deportations. Human Rights Watch later reported abuses against Venezuelan migrants, including family separations and summary deportations. Chile now hosts about 1.4 million migrants, more than 7% of its population.

Mexican immigration agents detained 213 Central American migrants on Wednesday from a fourth caravan that had recently entered Mexico on its way toward the United States. The National Immigration Institute said the migrants were taken to a processing center and could be repatriated if they lacked proper documents. The group was stopped on a highway between the Guatemalan border and Tapachula in southern Mexico. It included 186 Salvadorans, 16 Guatemalans, 10 Hondurans, and one Nicaraguan. The caravan left El Salvador on Nov. 18 and appears to have crossed from Guatemala into Mexico on Tuesday, following the same route used by three larger caravans that entered Mexico beginning Oct. 19. Mexican authorities have generally avoided confronting the larger caravans, which ranged from about 1,500 to 6,000 people, but have detained smaller groups that split away. Mexico has offered migrants residency and other visas, though most have refused because they want to continue to the United States. Also on Wednesday, prosecutors in Baja California confirmed that a 17-year-old Honduran migrant, Oscar Baudiel Cruz Alcerro, was killed after being struck by a vehicle on a highway between Mexicali and Tijuana. Another migrant died earlier after falling from a truck in Chiapas.

Sudan’s government says FBI agents have arrived in Khartoum to assist with the investigation into Monday’s assassination attempt on Prime Minister Abdallah Hamdok. The attack targeted Hamdok’s motorcade in the capital with a car bomb, but he escaped unharmed, and no group has claimed responsibility. Information Minister Faisal Mohammed Saleh said security forces have arrested several people, including both Sudanese and foreign nationals, in connection with the bombing, though he gave no details about their identities or number. Interior Minister Attarifi Iddris Dafallah said after an emergency government meeting that Sudan welcomes outside help in identifying the attackers. He condemned the attack as an effort to damage Sudan’s reputation and said the government wants those responsible brought to justice. Hamdok, who leads a transitional government formed after the military ousted President Omar al-Bashir in April, said on Twitter that he was in “good shape” and described the attack as a possible boost to Sudan’s reform process. The top prosecutor, General Taj Al Ser Ali al-Hibr, called the bombing a “professionally plotted” attempt to destroy the transitional government and promised to pursue those behind it. A member of the Sovereign Council, Mohamed Al Fekki Suleiman, said a new security team would be empowered to closely monitor people linked to terrorist and banned organizations. Retired police general Awad Al Nil Dhahiya said Sudanese security services lack sufficient experience dealing with terrorist threats and welcomed FBI involvement. Journalist Mohammed Fazari said opponents of the transitional government may be trying to undermine the political transition, warning that Islamists still have influence and could destabilize the situation. Bashir’s 30-year rule was marked by Islamist laws, and his government still has support in some security circles. Sudan has also indicated it may transfer Bashir to the International Criminal Court over war crimes and genocide charges related to Darfur.

Libya’s decade since the fall of Moamer Kadhafi has been marked by repeated political fragmentation, armed conflict, and failed attempts at reconciliation. After protests inspired by the Arab Spring broke out in February 2011, the United States, France and Britain backed an armed revolt against Kadhafi’s 42-year rule. Kadhafi fled Tripoli, but rebels captured and killed him on October 20, 2011. A transitional authority, the General National Congress, took power in August 2012. Soon after, violence worsened: in September 2012, US ambassador Chris Stevens and three other Americans were killed in an attack on the US consulate in Benghazi, blamed on an Al-Qaeda-linked group. In April 2013, a car bomb struck France’s embassy in Tripoli, injuring two guards and prompting many foreign diplomats to leave. The country split further in 2014 when eastern commander Khalifa Haftar launched an offensive against jihadists in Benghazi and formed the Libyan National Army. Parliamentary elections in June produced the House of Representatives, dominated by anti-Islamists, but Islamist-led militias rejected the result and seized Tripoli in August, restoring the GNC there. The elected parliament relocated to Tobruk, leaving Libya with two rival governments and two parliaments. In December 2015, the rivals signed a UN-backed accord in Morocco creating a Government of National Accord. Fayez al-Sarraj arrived in Tripoli in March 2016 to lead it, but Haftar refused to recognize the new administration. Haftar later declared Benghazi “totally liberated” in July 2017 after a long battle, gaining support from Egypt and the United Arab Emirates and later ties with Russia. In 2019, Haftar expanded his campaign into southern Libya, capturing Sebha and a major oil field before ordering an assault on Tripoli in April. Russia reportedly sent mercenaries to assist him in November, while Turkey deployed troops to support the Tripoli government the next month. Fighting continued until Tripoli’s forces overran Haftar’s last western stronghold in June 2020. A ceasefire was signed in October 2020, and in November the sides agreed to hold elections in December 2021. A unity government led by Abdulhamid Dbeibah was formed in March 2021, but political disputes soon returned. By September, disagreement over election laws, budgets, and authority had deepened, and the eastern parliament even passed a no-confidence vote against the unity government. Haftar then stepped back from the military, apparently clearing the way for a presidential bid, while the Tobruk parliament approved a December 24 vote and delayed legislative elections. Tripoli’s chamber rejected the postponement.

# Libya's Decade of Chaos Since Kadhafi's Fall Libya has experienced ten years of civil conflict and institutional breakdown following the 2011 overthrow of dictator Moamer Kadhafi. Inspired by Arab Spring movements, Libyan protests erupted in February 2011 with military support from the United States, France, and Britain. Kadhafi was captured and killed in October 2011 after 42 years in power. The transitional government, the General National Congress (GNC), took control in August 2012. However, stability proved elusive. A September 2012 attack on the U.S. consulate in Benghazi killed Ambassador Chris Stevens and three staff members, attributed to an Al-Qaeda-linked group. Diplomatic presence subsequently diminished. In 2014, Eastern military strongman Khalifa Haftar launched operations against jihadist groups in Benghazi. Legislative elections produced an anti-Islamist House of Representatives, but Islamist militias rejected results, storming Tripoli and reinstalling the GNC. This created a fractured state with two competing governments—the House of Representatives retreating to eastern Tobruk while a rival administration controlled Tripoli. A December 2015 agreement established a Government of National Accord, but Haftar refused recognition. By 2019, Haftar launched major offensives into southern Libya and toward Tripoli, backed by Egypt, the UAE, and later Russia. Turkey countered by sending troops to support the Tripoli government. After years of fighting, rival governments signed a ceasefire in October 2020 and agreed to elections. A unity government led by interim Prime Minister Abdulhamid Dbeibah was approved in March 2021, tasked with organizing elections. However, progress stalled. The UN warned of political and security deadlocks in July 2021. In September, the eastern parliament controversially ratified a presidential election law favoring Haftar, who announced stepping back from military command to pursue candidacy. The Tobruk parliament scheduled presidential elections for December 24, postponing legislative elections to January, but this postponement was rejected by Tripoli's upper chamber, deepening institutional divisions.

With Nigeria’s presidential election less than two weeks away, analyst Roux argued that the country was “definitely” not ready to hold what was expected to be one of its fiercest contests in years. The vote was scheduled for 14 February, but major doubts had emerged over both security and logistics, and Roux said those problems made a free and fair election highly unlikely on that date. The biggest concern, he said, was the security situation in the north-east, where Boko Haram’s insurgency continued to destabilize large areas of the country. Although the African Union summit in Addis Ababa had recently authorized a 7,500-strong regional force to fight the militants, Roux stressed that such a deployment would take time to organize and could not immediately remove the threat. He noted that more than one million people had already been internally displaced by Boko Haram violence, meaning many citizens would be unable to vote even if they wanted to. Others, he said, would be too frightened to go to polling stations, which he warned would be attractive targets for suicide bombers. Roux explained that Boko Haram remained a serious threat because the group was highly mobile and capable of striking quickly and disappearing. He said the militants could “swarm” a village, attack it, and then vanish using trucks, buses, motorcycles, cars, and other transport. In his view, election rallies would be especially vulnerable to vehicle bombs and individual suicide attacks, since Boko Haram’s goal would be to spread fear and intimidate voters. He also said that protecting fixed sites such as polling stations and rallies would tie down Nigerian security forces, reducing the pressure on Boko Haram and allowing the group to continue attacking towns and cities in the north-east. The analyst pointed out that a rapid deployment by Chadian troops, operating under an earlier Status of Forces Agreement as part of a multinational task force, had already had some impact. Even so, he said the broader challenge of defeating Boko Haram was a long-term one and could not be solved before the election. Beyond security, Roux identified the voter card issue as another major obstacle. He said only about 30 million Nigerians had received their cards in the previous year, roughly half of the electorate. Expecting the remaining 30 million to receive theirs within two weeks, he said, was unrealistic. In his assessment, this technical failure alone made the 14 February election date implausible and undermined the possibility of a credible vote. Roux said President Goodluck Jonathan was aware of the problem, but that the political stakes made postponement difficult. He explained that Jonathan faced strong opposition from Muhammadu Buhari’s coalition, the All Progressives Congress (APC), and that any delay would be portrayed by opponents as a political tactic to benefit the ruling party. As a result, Roux said, Jonathan would likely have to rely on the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) to admit that the election could not technically be held on time and recommend a postponement. Asked about the possibility of a peaceful transfer of power if the opposition won, Roux said Nigeria’s democratic culture was now more deeply rooted than in the past, making a military coup or unconstitutional retention of power less likely to be accepted. He argued that social media had increased transparency and made national mobilization easier, comparing the potential public response to the Arab Spring. He suggested that key political actors understood that an attempt to subvert the election would provoke widespread unrest. Roux also addressed reports that foreign journalists were being blocked from covering the elections. He said the decision could be seen as an attempt by the ruling party and government to control information and prevent sensitive issues such as Boko Haram and the economy from becoming major election topics. He added that there could also be security, governance, perception-management, and political concerns behind the move, especially given the strength and visibility of the opposition. Overall, Roux said the central worries were Nigeria’s economic and security stability. He described the country as deeply divided along religious, ethnic, and economic lines, with only fragile ties holding it together as a democratic state. Public dissatisfaction with the ruling party over service delivery, the economy, and Boko Haram, combined with a broader opposition base, meant the election was likely to be very close. He warned that election violence was a real possibility and that some areas might become too dangerous for normal campaigning. If the elections were postponed, he said, the political struggle would only intensify and distract the government further from Boko Haram, the economy, governance, and development.

# Nigeria 'Definitely' Not Ready for Elections, Analyst Says With Nigeria's presidential elections scheduled for February 14, analysts warn the country faces significant obstacles to holding a free and fair vote. An analyst interviewed by News24 stated unequivocally that despite Nigerians' desire for democratic elections, the nation is fundamentally unprepared for the upcoming polls. ## Security Concerns Dominate The primary concern centers on security threats posed by Boko Haram, the militant Islamist group that has destabilized the country's northeastern regions. The violence has internally displaced over one million people, preventing many from voting and creating fear among potential voters. Polling stations are vulnerable to attacks, with analysts warning that election rallies represent prime targets for vehicle bombings and suicide attacks that Boko Haram has previously employed. While the African Union recently mandated a 7,500-member regional force to combat the insurgency, deployment will take weeks. Chad has already deployed military forces under an earlier agreement, achieving some impact, but the challenge remains substantial. Boko Haram operates across an area the size of Belgium with considerable mobility, using various vehicles to attack villages before disappearing. Analysts suggest this reflects the ruling party's desire to control information flow and prevent critical issues—such as Boko Haram and economic mismanagement—from becoming prominent campaign topics where balanced viewpoints might emerge. Security concerns and perception management also likely influenced this decision. ## Democratic Prospects and Potential Violence Despite Nigeria's history of political instability and military coups, the analyst expresses cautious optimism about democratic transition. The electorate is unlikely to accept being denied democratic outcomes, and democracy appears more entrenched than previously. Social media and increased transparency make mobilizing opposition to unconstitutional power seizures easier, as demonstrated by the Arab Spring. Key stakeholders are reportedly aware of these implications. However, significant risks remain. Deep societal divisions along religious, ethnic, and economic lines create fragile bonds holding Nigeria together. Election violence is a genuine concern, with certain regions potentially becoming inaccessible to opposition campaigners. ## Long-term Implications The analyst warns that postponing elections would intensify political struggle, diverting government attention from critical issues including combating Boko Haram, economic management, governance, and development—areas already suffering from neglect. Overall, Nigeria's economic and security stability represents the paramount concern. The election occurs amid multiple crises, with fundamental readiness issues likely to persist regardless of whether voting proceeds on schedule.

Magloire Paluku Kavunga, a former journalist, cultural figure, and adviser to the AFC/M23 rebel movement, was shot dead on Wednesday evening in Goma, eastern Democratic Republic of Congo. Authorities confirmed the killing but have not yet provided details about the attackers or the exact circumstances. He was reportedly returning from an evening engagement when unknown gunmen opened fire, killing him instantly. Paluku, 58, was born in Butembo on 12 December 1966 and was long regarded as one of North Kivu’s most influential media entrepreneurs. He founded Radio Kivu 1 and Kivu 1 Television, outlets that played a major role in shaping political debate and cultural identity in the region. He was also known as a writer, poet, actor, and musician. Before joining the rebel administration, he had served in the DRC Ministry of Culture. In 2025, Paluku made a controversial move by becoming a Communications and Cultural Adviser for AFC/M23, placing him within one of eastern Congo’s most divisive political movements. According to sources in Goma, he had increasingly clashed with the rebel leadership in recent months, especially over communication strategy and influence within the civil administration. He reportedly felt unsafe and asked for an armed escort, which the rebel authorities allegedly denied. His death has sparked shock and concern in North Kivu, especially among the Nande community, where many see the killing as tied to deeper inter-communal tensions and power struggles. AFC/M23 condemned the killing and said it would investigate and punish those responsible, though no evidence has been made public. The assassination could further damage the group’s legitimacy in areas such as Butembo, Beni, and Lubero, where Paluku had served as a rare bridge between the rebels and skeptical local communities. He died two days before his 59th birthday.
