Việt Nam has completed its term as a non-permanent member of the United Nations Security Council, with officials saying the country fulfilled all its goals despite an exceptionally difficult global environment. A review meeting in Hà Nội on Tuesday marked the final session of the inter-sectoral working group overseeing Việt Nam’s UNSC work, chaired by Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs Đặng Hoàng Giang. During the tenure, the Security Council held about 840 ambassador-level meetings and adopted more than 240 documents across 60 agenda items. Việt Nam served as Council president twice, in January 2020 and April 2021. It also successfully advanced several initiatives, including two resolutions: one on reappointing the prosecutor and reviewing the two-year operation of the International Residual Mechanism for Criminal Tribunals, and another on protecting essential infrastructure. Other outcomes included three presidential statements on respect for the UN Charter, cooperation between the UN and regional organizations, and mine action, as well as a press statement on a terrorist attack in Indonesia and the Hà Nội Declaration on women, peace and security. Giang credited the success to coordinated efforts across the political system, careful preparation, policy consistency, flexibility, public support, and international backing. He urged the working group to draw lessons and propose measures to strengthen Việt Nam’s external relations and multilateral diplomacy.

# Summary Việt Nam has successfully completed its tenure as a non-permanent member of the United Nations Security Council for 2020-21, achieving all established objectives despite challenging global conditions. During the tenure, the Security Council held approximately 840 ambassador-level meetings and approved over 240 documents addressing 60 agenda items. Việt Nam served as Council President twice, in January 2020 and April 2021. The country's approved proposals included two resolutions on the International Residual Mechanism for Criminal Tribunals and critical infrastructure protection; three presidential statements on UN Charter compliance and mine-related issues; one press statement regarding an Indonesian terrorist attack; and the Hà Nội declaration on women, peace, and security. Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs Đặng Hoàng Giang attributed the successful tenure to coordinated efforts across Vietnam's political system, strategic consistency combined with tactical flexibility, and strong inter-ministerial cooperation. He emphasized the crucial support from the Vietnamese people and international partners, and called for extracting lessons to strengthen future multilateral diplomacy efforts aligned with the nation's development goals.

A Philippine Army officer was killed and nine soldiers were wounded in clashes with Abu Sayyaf Group militants in Sulu province, according to the Armed Forces of the Philippines-Western Mindanao Command. Lt. Gen. Cirilito Sobejana said the fighting broke out Monday in Barangay Pansul, Patikul town, after troops launched an assault on an ASG hideout. Corleto Vinluan, commander of the 11th Infantry Division, said forces in other towns had been alerted and ordered to remain vigilant. He said troops were balancing anti-terror operations with efforts to help prevent the spread of Covid-19. The clash followed a June 13 attack in Parang town, where gunmen raided a police station, killing two policemen and wounding two others before escaping.

China strongly condemned the suicide bombing at the Wagah border crossing in Pakistan, which killed 61 people and injured about 200, and urged joint efforts against terrorism. In Beijing, Zhang Dejiang, chairman of China’s National People’s Congress, told Pakistan’s Joint Chiefs of Staff Committee chairman Rashad Mahmood that China strongly opposes terrorism and wants closer cooperation with Pakistan, its “all-weather strategic partner.” Zhang said both sides should implement the consensus reached by their leaders, expand cooperation, support major projects, and strengthen trade and cultural exchanges. Mahmood said Pakistan-China friendship is central to Pakistan’s foreign policy and pledged support for China’s fight against militants, including the East Turkestan Islamic Movement, which Beijing blames for attacks in Xinjiang and says has bases in Pakistan’s tribal areas. Earlier, Chinese foreign ministry spokeswoman Hua Chunying also expressed shock, offered condolences to the victims, and said China would continue supporting Pakistan’s efforts to protect national security and stability.

# Summary China condemned a suicide bombing at the Wagah border crossing in Pakistan, calling for joint counterterrorism efforts. China's National People's Congress Chairman Zhang Dejiang met with Pakistan's Joint Chiefs of Staff Committee Chairman Rashad Mahmood, pledging stronger bilateral ties between the "all-weather strategic partners." Rashad affirmed Pakistan's commitment to supporting China's counterterrorism operations against groups like the East Turkestan Islamic Movement (ETIM), which operates from Pakistan's tribal areas and conducts attacks in China's Xinjiang province. Zhang emphasized enhancing cooperation across legislatures, armed forces, trade, and cultural exchanges. The attack killed 61 people and injured 200 at the India-Pakistan border. China's foreign ministry spokesperson expressed condolences to victims and families, reaffirming China's support for Pakistan's security and stability efforts.

Police in Karachi said three alleged terrorists were killed in an exchange of fire during an operation in Khuda Baksh Goth near the Super Highway on Monday, after acting on a tip-off. Two suspects escaped. Officers recovered a suicide jacket, hand grenades and a large cache of weapons, and said the group was planning an attack.

# Summary Three alleged terrorists were killed in a firefight with law enforcement in Karachi's Khuda Baksh Goth area on Monday. Acting on a tip-off, police conducted an operation where three suspects were eliminated while two escaped. Authorities recovered a suicide jacket, hand grenades, and weapons from the scene. Police claim the group was planning a terrorist attack, with ongoing search efforts for the fugitives.

A video published by Japanese media appears to show Japanese freelance journalist Jumpei Yasuda, who has been held by militants in Syria for three years, pleading for help. In the clip, a bearded man in an orange jumpsuit kneels between two hooded gunmen and says in Japanese, “My name is Umar. I am South Korean... Please help me immediately.” It is unclear why he identified himself that way. Japan’s Chief Cabinet Secretary Yoshihide Suga said the government believes the man is Yasuda and is making every effort to secure his safety, though he declined further comment. A Foreign Ministry official also said Yasuda is believed to be Japanese. Yasuda reportedly entered Syria from Turkey in 2015 and was captured by an al Qaeda affiliate. He has appeared in earlier online videos.

# Summary A video released by Japanese media on Wednesday appears to show Jumpei Yasuda, a Japanese freelance journalist missing for three years, pleading for help from Syrian militants. In the footage, a bearded man in an orange jumpsuit, surrounded by armed gunmen, identifies himself as "Umar," a South Korean, and requests immediate assistance. The Japanese government confirmed it believes the man is Yasuda, who was reportedly captured by an al Qaeda affiliate after entering Syria from Turkey in 2015. He has periodically appeared in online videos showing physical deterioration over time. Japan's top government spokesman pledged the government would make utmost efforts to protect its citizens using available information networks. The case recalls similar incidents involving Japanese nationals captured in Syria, including journalist Kenji Goto and soldier Haruna Yukawa, both of whom were killed by ISIS in early 2015.

President Rodrigo Duterte issued a fresh ultimatum to Communist Party of the Philippines founder Jose Maria Sison, giving him only two months to return to the Philippines and help restart stalled peace talks with communist rebels. Speaking at the inauguration of the Davao River bridge widening project, Duterte said that if nothing comes of the negotiations, he would tell Sison never to return and would even “kill” him, blaming him for the deaths of soldiers and policemen. Duterte said the offer was a “make-or-break” deal and warned that if the talks fail, he would personally escort Sison to the airport so he could leave the country permanently rather than be arrested and jailed. He stressed that Sison would not be allowed back. Sison, however, dismissed Duterte’s repeated threats, saying they had become almost a “term of endearment.” In a statement posted on the National Democratic Front website, Sison said Duterte’s strong language suggested he was now eager to resume negotiations rather than obstruct them. Sison urged both sides to let their negotiating panels continue preparing for the formal reopening of talks and to make substantial progress as soon as possible. He said he was prepared to return home once there is meaningful progress in the process and expressed optimism that backchannel discussions were moving in the right direction. He also said an interim peace agreement was expected to be signed when formal talks resume on June 28, with both sides likely to announce a stand-down agreement two weeks earlier, by June 14. The peace process collapsed in November of the previous year after clashes between government forces and communist rebels. Duterte said the government was winning against the New People’s Army, the armed wing of the communist movement, apparently referring to the arrest of Elizalde “Ka Jinggoy” Cañete, whom authorities regard as the top NPA commander in Mindanao and successor to Leonardo “Kumander Parago” Pitao. Meanwhile, presidential peace process adviser Jesus Dureza told the media at the 22nd National Press Forum in Pasay City that journalists have a key role in peace building. He said the public would better appreciate peace milestones if they were informed during the process, not only after agreements are signed. The article also reported continuing rebel violence in several provinces. In Negros Oriental, the military said the NPA burned three heavy equipment units—a roller, backhoe, and bulldozer—used for farm-to-market road construction in Mabinay town, causing at least P14 million in damage. Police said two suspects were arrested. In Quezon province, one soldier was killed and two rebels were captured after a week of clashes in General Nakar town. In Cagayan province, rebels shot dead Allacapan town councilor Ronel Millare, a former police officer accused by the insurgents of spying.

# Duterte Issues Two-Month Ultimatum to Communist Leader Sison President Duterte has given Communist Party of the Philippines founder Jose Ma. Sison a two-month window to return to the Philippines and resume peace negotiations with leftist guerrillas, or face permanent exile. During the inauguration of a Davao River bridge project, Duterte threatened that if Sison fails to return and resume talks, he would tell him never to return, stating "I will kill you. He pledged that if negotiations produce no significant results, he would personally escort Sison to the airport rather than arrest him, while ensuring he cannot return to the country. Sison, who has lived in Europe since fleeing after failed peace talks in 1987, responded dismissively to the threats. Through a statement on the National Democratic Front website, he suggested Duterte's repeated death threats have become "a term of endearment," comparing them to expressions in American comedies. Sison interpreted Duterte's strong language as evidence of eagerness to resume negotiations rather than obstruct them. Sison indicated he is prepared to return once "substantial progress" occurs in negotiations. He expressed optimism about backchannel consultations and revealed expectations for an interim peace agreement to be signed on June 28, with a stand-down agreement announcement anticipated by June 14. Peace talks collapsed in November following clashes between government troops and communist rebels. Duterte claimed the government is winning the conflict against the New People's Army (NPA), the communist party's armed unit, citing the arrest of Elizalde "Ka Jinggoy" Cañete, considered the overall NPA commander in Mindanao. Presidential adviser on the peace process Jesus Dureza urged media to engage the country in pursuing peace, emphasizing the media's unique role in peace building. He stressed that the public should be informed about peace process milestones as they occur, not only after agreements are finalized. Violence continued despite peace efforts. In Negros Oriental, the military reported that NPA rebels burned three heavy equipment units used for farm-to-market road construction, causing P14 million in damage. Two suspects were arrested. In Quezon province, fighting between government troops and communist guerrillas in General Nakar town resulted in one soldier killed and two NPA rebels captured. A rebel camp was abandoned after approximately 20 minutes of combat. In Cagayan province, NPA rebels killed Allacapan town councilor Ronel Millare, a former police officer, while he worked at his welding shop. Police condemned the attack as terrorism, noting rebels accused Millare of spying.

Bangkok authorities conducted a crisis response drill as part of the national C-MEX 17 program to build public confidence and improve preparedness. The exercise simulated a bombing at the Thai-Japan Youth Stadium with multiple casualties and radiation contamination, and also included a terrorist attack on the subway at Thai Cultural Center station. City officials set up a command center at Bangkok City Hall and held a video conference with the Prime Minister. Military, police, and the Office of Atoms for Peace practiced coordinated response. Officials said the annual drill helps prepare for attacks involving radioactive materials.

# Bangkok Crisis Response Drill Summary Bangkok authorities conducted a comprehensive crisis response drill on June 27, 2017, simulating a bombing at Thai-Japan Youth Stadium with radiation contamination and a subway terrorist attack. The exercise, part of the C-MEX 17 program by Bangkok's Office of Disaster Prevention and Mitigation, aimed to boost public confidence in emergency preparedness. Military personnel, police, and the Office of Atoms for Peace coordinated responses through a command center at city hall, with Prime Minister participation via video conference. Officials stated the annual drill, which included radiation response protocols, would prepare authorities for modern attack scenarios involving radioactive elements.

Pakistan authorities faced intense outrage after body parts of some victims of Thursday night’s suicide bombing at the Lal Shahbaz Qalandar Sufi shrine in Sehwan, Sindh, were reportedly found dumped in garbage. The attack, claimed by ISIS, killed at least 88 people and injured more than 200. Sindh Chief Minister Syed Murad Ali Shah condemned the desecration and promised strict action against those responsible. He said he had ordered an inquiry and directed Hyderabad Commissioner Qazi Shahid Pervez to investigate the negligence and identify those involved. “Whoever is responsible for behaving inhumanely and desecrating body parts will be dealt very strongly,” he said. Television footage showing officials recovering body parts from garbage and taking them for burial triggered protests, which spread further on social media. Relatives of the dead also criticized the ruling Pakistan Peoples Party, accusing authorities of mishandling the tragedy and providing inadequate medical care to the injured. Local municipal official Syed Asif Shah said two sanitary workers had been suspended and further investigations were underway. Angry protesters later forced the Jamshoro deputy commissioner, who had come to inspect the situation, to leave without carrying out his visit. Senior Superintendent of Police Qadir Jatoi said preliminary investigations confirmed security lapses at the shrine during the attack. He added that investigators had not yet identified the bomber’s facilitators, but evidence suggested the attacker was a man who entered the shrine wearing a burqa. The article also noted a broader wave of militant violence in Pakistan, including a February 13 bombing in Lahore that killed 13 people.

# Summary A suicide bombing at the Lal Shahbaz Qalandar shrine in Sehwan, southern Pakistan, killed 88 people and injured over 200 on Thursday night. The attack, claimed by ISIS, was followed by a disturbing discovery that body parts of victims were found dumped in garbage, sparking outrage among relatives and widespread protests. Sindh Chief Minister Syed Murad Ali Shah condemned the desecration and ordered an inquiry, vowing strict action against those responsible for the negligent handling of the bodies. The ruling Pakistan Peoples Party faced severe criticism for inadequate medical treatment of the injured and mismanagement of the tragedy. Two sanitary officials were suspended following the incident. Initial investigations revealed security lapses at the shrine during the attack. Police confirmed the suicide bomber was male and entered the shrine wearing a burqa, though facilitators remain unidentified. Angry protesters forced the Deputy Commissioner of Jamshoro to leave without completing his inquiry work, demonstrating public frustration with authorities' response. This attack is part of a series of terrorist incidents in Pakistan. Just five days earlier on February 13, a suicide bomber struck a protest outside Punjab's Provincial Assembly in Lahore, killing 13 and injuring 85—also claimed by the Afghanistan-based Jamat-ul-Ahrar group.

During Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s visit to Japan for the 15th India-Japan Annual Summit, India and Japan issued a strong joint condemnation of the April 22, 2025 terror attack in Pahalgam, Jammu and Kashmir. In the official statement released by the Prime Minister’s Office, Modi and Japanese Prime Minister Shigeru Ishiba “unequivocally and strongly” denounced the attack and called for coordinated action against all UN-listed terrorist groups and entities, including Lashkar-e-Tayyiba (LeT), Jaish-e-Mohammad (JeM), Al Qaeda, ISIS/Daesh, and their proxies. The two leaders said the perpetrators, organisers, and financiers of the attack must be brought to justice without delay. They also called for stronger efforts to eliminate terrorist safe havens, cut off terror financing networks, disrupt links between terrorism and transnational crime, and stop the cross-border movement of terrorists. The statement noted the United Nations Security Council Monitoring Team report of July 29, which referred to The Resistance Front (TRF), and said Modi explained that TRF had claimed responsibility for the attack. Ishiba, according to the release, took note of this with concern. The attack killed 26 civilians. The summit statement also covered several other major international issues. On Myanmar, both leaders urged an immediate end to violence, called for a return to democracy through inclusive dialogue and free and fair elections, and supported ASEAN’s efforts to implement the Five Point Consensus for a peaceful resolution. They also welcomed the recent announcement ending the state of emergency and plans for elections, while urging the release of detainees. In the Indo-Pacific, India and Japan reaffirmed the importance of their collaborative projects, including in Africa. They welcomed the launch of the Japan-India Cooperation Initiative for Sustainable Economic Development in Africa, aimed at building industrial concentration in India to support trade and investment links with Africa. The two prime ministers also reiterated support for a just and lasting peace in Ukraine in line with international law and the UN Charter, and welcomed diplomatic efforts by various countries. They condemned North Korea’s ballistic missile launches and nuclear weapons program, reaffirmed support for complete denuclearisation, and urged Pyongyang to return to dialogue. Modi invited Ishiba to India for the Quad Leaders’ Summit later this year. Modi’s Japan visit ran from August 29 to 30, after which he was scheduled to travel to China for the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation Summit in Tianjin.

The leaders welcomed the launch of the Japan-India Cooperation Initiative for Sustainable Economic Development in Africa, designed to establish India as an industrial hub for African trade and investment. They reaffirmed the importance of collaborative Indo-Pacific projects. Additionally, Modi invited Prime Minister Ishiba to visit India for the Quad Leaders' Summit scheduled later in the year. Following his Japan visit, Modi is proceeding to China to attend the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation Summit in Tianjin, continuing India's diplomatic engagements across Asia.

Yannis Behrakis, one of Reuters’ most celebrated photographers, has died at the age of 58 after a long battle with cancer. Over a career spanning three decades at the news agency, he built a reputation as a fearless, deeply committed photojournalist whose images from conflict zones and crises around the world won admiration, major awards, and the respect of colleagues and rivals alike. Behrakis joined Reuters as a freelancer in Athens in 1987, after a formative period that shaped his passion for photography and journalism. As a young man, he encountered a Time-Life photography book, which inspired him to enroll in a private photography course. He later worked in a photographic studio in the mid-1980s, but found the environment too restrictive. A 1983 film, “Under Fire,” about reporters in Nicaragua in the years before the 1979 revolution, convinced him to pursue journalism instead. His first foreign assignment for Reuters came in January 1989, when he was sent to Libya under Muammar Gaddafi. He quickly showed an instinct for finding the decisive moment, recalling how he managed to slip beside Gaddafi during a hotel visit and capture wide-angle pictures that appeared on front pages around the world the next day. From then on, Behrakis spent much of his life on the road, covering violence and upheaval across Europe, Russia, the Middle East, Africa, and Asia. His assignments included the wars in Afghanistan and Chechnya, the 2005 earthquake in Kashmir, and the Egyptian uprising in 2011. His photographs were noted for their ability to capture terror, death, fear, starvation, homelessness, anger, despair, and courage, while still finding moments of beauty and humanity amid chaos. Colleagues described his style as both artistic and intensely purposeful. Reuters photographer Goran Tomasevic said Behrakis believed in “clearly telling the story in the most artistic way possible,” and praised his dedication and willingness to sacrifice everything for the most important image. Senior producer Vassilis Triandafyllou, a friend for 30 years, called him a “hurricane” who worked around the clock and often took great personal risks to get the shot he wanted. Behrakis’ work was not only admired but also highly decorated. He helped lead Reuters’ team to a Pulitzer Prize in 2016 for coverage of the refugee crisis. U.S. general news editor Dina Kyriakidou Contini described him as “one of the best news photographers of his generation,” calling his pictures iconic and saying his empathy made him a great photojournalist. Behrakis himself saw his mission as bearing witness so that no one could claim ignorance about what was happening in the world. Speaking about the refugee crisis, he said his job was to tell the story and ensure that nobody could say, “I didn’t know.” Several of his most memorable images came from war zones. One photograph from the former Yugoslavia in 1998 showed an ethnic Albanian man lowering the body of a two-year-old boy into a tiny coffin. Behrakis took the picture from above using a slow-speed zoom technique, creating a disorienting, emotional effect. He described the image as making the child appear to be floating, as if his spirit were leaving for the heavens. His work from other conflicts similarly conveyed the human cost of war. A defining tragedy in Behrakis’ life came in Sierra Leone in 2000, when a convoy carrying Reuters colleagues Kurt Schork and Mark Chisholm, along with AP cameraman Miguel Gil Moreno, was ambushed by gunmen believed to be rebels. Schork, one of Behrakis’ closest friends, was killed instantly, as was Moreno. Behrakis and Chisholm escaped by crawling into the undergrowth and hiding for hours until the attackers left. Behrakis later photographed himself after the ordeal, looking dazed and stunned. Chisholm said the attack and Schork’s death changed him deeply. The four men had become close during the siege of Sarajevo and called themselves a “band of brothers.” Behrakis said he hated war, but the danger, travel, and camaraderie drew him back to it, and Schork’s memory helped push him to return to war photography. In later years, Behrakis spent more time in his native Greece, where he documented the effects of the financial crisis and the arrival of hundreds of thousands of refugees into Europe. In 2015, he and a team of photographers and cameramen worked in relay for months covering people fleeing wars in Syria, Afghanistan, and elsewhere. During that period he mentored younger photographer Alkis Konstantinidis, who later joined the Pulitzer-winning team. Konstantinidis described Behrakis as demanding but generous, someone from whom others could learn a great deal once he opened up. The refugee crisis affected Behrakis personally as a proud Greek and father of a young daughter, causing him guilt, insomnia, and nightmares. Yet it also brought out his strongest humanitarian instincts. He focused on the dignity of people in distress rather than treating them as objects of pity. One of his most famous images showed a Syrian refugee carrying and kissing his daughter while walking in the rain. Triandafyllou recalled that Behrakis insisted he had not yet captured “the picture” and kept searching until he found it. Behrakis described the father as a kind of superhero, wearing a “black plastic cape” made from garbage bags, and said the image represented universal fatherhood and unconditional love. In 2017, Behrakis launched a project to help Reuters build a more diverse team of news photographers. He continued appearing at photo festivals and events, inspiring younger journalists and encouraging applications for Reuters bursaries. At the time of his death, he was still looking for new talent. He is survived by his wife Elisavet and their children, Rebecca and Dimitri.

Stanislav Aseev, a 27-year-old undercover journalist working in separatist-held eastern Ukraine, disappeared on June 2 while returning to Donetsk, the breakaway city where he had continued to live and write throughout three years of war. Aseev had reported under a pseudonym because freedom of expression is tightly suppressed in the self-proclaimed Donetsk People’s Republic (DNR). He had called his mother to say he would visit the next day, but he never arrived. When friends and relatives went to his apartment after repeated unanswered calls, they found his front door smashed open and his belongings, including his work laptop, gone. DNR authorities refused to tell them what had happened. It later emerged that DNR security agents were holding him incommunicado at an unknown location, and friends feared he had been beaten or tortured. Human rights investigators say such treatment is routine in detention in Donetsk. Aseev’s case is one among many in eastern Ukraine’s “dirty war,” where the front lines have settled into a grim stalemate but abductions, secret detentions, torture, and killings continue across the wider conflict zone. The article says hundreds, and possibly thousands, of people are missing or being held as prisoners of war. The United Nations has documented arbitrary detention and enforced disappearances, especially in areas controlled by Russian-backed separatists. Captives are often hidden in secret prisons, basements, and other improvised facilities, denied access to relatives or lawyers. The International Committee of the Red Cross has estimated that as many as 2,000 people may be missing. Human rights monitors also describe abuses by both sides. A recent U.N. report suggested that both Ukrainian forces and separatist forces have carried out extrajudicial executions. In one case, the body of a missing man was found near a government-held front-line town, and an SBU officer was arrested and later released on bail. In another, Ukrainian soldiers allegedly looted a house, set it on fire, shot the occupant, and buried the body in a forest. In rebel-held Horlivka, two civilians were allegedly killed by pro-Russian gunmen, and separatist authorities reportedly blocked relatives from identifying the bodies. The article highlights another prominent victim, theologian Igor Kozlovsky, who became one of the most well-known detainees in the wave of clandestine wartime arrests. Kozlovsky, who was described by his nephew as charismatic, scholarly, and deeply patriotic, stayed in Donetsk after separatists seized power in 2014 to care for his disabled older son. He lived quietly, practicing yoga, writing poetry, and looking after his family. In January 2016, he was seized by armed men. While in custody, he called his nephew to say he had been held in a basement and tortured. A military tribunal later convicted him of “illegal possession of weapons,” and he was sent to one of Donetsk’s notorious prisons, where tuberculosis is common. His health worsened during roughly a year in a damp, dark cell before he was moved to another prison in Horlivka. Relatives have tried desperately to secure his release, but efforts have been frustrated by corrupt intermediaries and a chaotic prisoner-swap system. The article says some people have even demanded $100,000 to arrange his freedom, though his nephew believes these are scams. The broader detention system in the region is portrayed as arbitrary and brutal. The warring sides have failed to exchange DNA data about detainees, making it difficult to identify remains or locate missing people, and leaving families in prolonged uncertainty and anguish. Civilians in front-line areas also live under severe pressure: troops have looted and occupied homes belonging to displaced residents, and those who remain are often isolated and dependent on soldiers for water, food, and fuel. Abuse in custody, indefinite detention, and solitary confinement are described as common on both sides, but the scale is said to be worse in separatist territory. Even teenagers have been detained; last August, five were taken by DNR security agents and remained in custody. The article also alleges that Ukrainian law enforcement has systematically used torture to force confessions from suspected separatists. Methods include beatings, waterboarding, suffocation, and electric shocks, and detainees are often forced to sign statements they have not read. Complaints are rarely investigated effectively, creating a climate of impunity. One tortured detainee said reporting injuries would be dangerous because authorities could then harm him further or target his family. Aseev’s fate remains unknown. His last article, “Between Heaven and Hell,” was published from the war zone on the same day he disappeared. In an earlier interview, he said he worked there not just out of duty but for personal growth, describing war as a place where the old saying that there are no winners becomes a lived reality.

# Hundreds Missing in Eastern Ukraine's Dirty War Eastern Ukraine's three-year conflict has evolved beyond conventional front-line combat into a shadowy "dirty war" characterized by arbitrary detention, torture, and enforced disappearances. Hundreds—possibly thousands—of people have vanished in the lawless region, caught between government forces and Russian-backed separatists accused of systematic human rights abuses. ## A Journalist Disappears The crisis is exemplified by Stanislav Aseev, a 27-year-old undercover journalist who remained in Donetsk, the separatist stronghold, despite most colleagues fleeing. Publishing under a pseudonym to avoid repercussions in a city where freedom of expression is harshly suppressed, Aseev documented the conflict through three years of war. On June 2, after promising his mother a visit, he vanished near his apartment. Friends discovered his front door smashed and his possessions, including his work laptop, seized. Security agents from the self-proclaimed Donetsk People's Republic (DNR) provided no information about his whereabouts. Aseev is now held incommunicado in an unspecified facility, with friends fearing he has endured beatings and torture—standard practice for detainees in Donetsk according to human rights investigators. His former university friend and former parliamentarian Egor Firsov stated grimly, "No one can guarantee that he will survive." ## Scale of the Crisis The International Committee of the Red Cross estimates up to 2,000 people may be missing or held as prisoners of war in eastern Ukraine. The United Nations has documented systematic war crimes including arbitrary detention, enforced disappearances, torture, sexual abuse, and summary executions, particularly in separatist-controlled territory. Captives are held in secret prisons, basements, and improvised detention areas, denied access to relatives or legal counsel. A U.N. report suggests both warring parties conduct extrajudicial executions. In one case, an SBU officer was arrested and released on bail after a missing man's body was found near a government-held town. Ukrainian soldiers allegedly looted a house, set it ablaze, shot the occupant, and buried the body in a forest. In rebel-held Horlivka, pro-Russian gunmen allegedly shot two civilians dead, and separatist authorities prevented relatives from identifying the bodies. ## High-Profile Victims Igor Kozlovsky, a 63-year-old theologian and former regional religious affairs head, represents the crisis's human toll. When separatists took power in 2014, he remained in Donetsk to care for his disabled older son while his wife and younger son fled. In January 2016, armed men grabbed him from the street. In custody, he called his nephew Denis to report basement detention and torture. A military tribunal convicted Kozlovsky—a confirmed pacifist—of illegal weapons possession. He was imprisoned in Donetsk's notorious tuberculosis-ridden prisons, then transferred to Horlivka. His health deteriorated in damp, dark cells. Sudan entered 2026 with little reason for optimism, despite a brief moment of hope earlier in the war when the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) recaptured Khartoum from the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) in late March. Many soldiers and residents celebrated the RSF’s expulsion from the capital, which the group had seized soon after fighting began in April 2023. Some believed the army’s victory might mark a turning point and eventually help end the conflict. Instead, the war intensified elsewhere. Seven months after Khartoum was retaken, the RSF launched a new wave of brutality in El-Fasher, the capital of North Darfur, 800 kilometers away. The city’s fall on Oct. 26, after an 18-month siege, became one of the darkest episodes in Sudan’s modern history. Fighters carried out mass executions, torture and rape, with abuses echoing the 2003-05 Darfur genocide committed by the Janjaweed, the RSF’s predecessor. Rather than moving toward peace, Sudan appeared to be hardening into a split country, with the SAF controlling the east, north and central areas, and the RSF dominating the west. El-Fasher was the SAF’s last major holdout in Darfur, so its capture gave the RSF control over most of western Sudan and large parts of Kordofan. The International Crisis Group warned that the war could settle into a prolonged stalemate that would become a durable partition, raising fears among neighboring states that Sudan could become a failed state whose instability spreads across borders. The country had already been divided once before, when South Sudan became independent in 2011. The focus of fighting has now shifted to Kordofan, a large agricultural region of three states and a vital area because it contains Sudan’s oil fields and key supply routes to the west. Violence there escalated sharply in recent weeks. The UN said hundreds of civilians had been killed since late October. On Dec. 4, a drone strike hit a children’s nursery and a hospital in Kalogi, killing 114 people, including 63 children. Nine days later, another drone strike killed six Bangladeshi UN peacekeepers who had been deployed to South Kordofan to monitor disputed territory between Sudan and South Sudan. Sudan’s largest oil field, Heglig, near the border and important to both countries, has also fallen to the RSF. As major global attention remained fixed on Gaza and Ukraine, Sudan’s humanitarian catastrophe worsened throughout 2025. UN agencies describe it as the world’s largest humanitarian and displacement crisis, and the International Rescue Committee calls it the largest humanitarian crisis ever recorded. Tens of thousands have been killed, more than 12 million people displaced, and about 30 million—two-thirds of the population—now need aid. Half the country faces acute hunger, and parts of Darfur and Kordofan are already experiencing famine. Chatham House researcher Ahmed Soliman said the war is “the most devastating” in Sudan’s history and the worst humanitarian crisis in the world. The fall of El-Fasher exposed the scale of the violence in stark detail. Around 260,000 people were trapped in the city when it was overrun, after the RSF built an earth barrier to prevent escape. Fighters filmed themselves shooting residents in the city and as they fled. One massacre at the Saudi Maternity Hospital left more than 460 men, women and children dead. Satellite imagery analyzed by the Yale Humanitarian Research Lab showed blood and bodies at the hospital. Survivors and witnesses described killings and sexual violence, including a woman raped along with her 14-year-old daughter, who later died, and a man who said RSF fighters killed 17 of 20 men after forcing them to lie down. The International Criminal Court said it was taking urgent steps to preserve evidence for future prosecutions. Even before El-Fasher, the RSF had been accused of war crimes and crimes against humanity, and the US had determined it committed ethnic cleansing and genocide. The atrocities have renewed diplomatic efforts to stop the war. The conflict traces back to the collapse of Omar Bashir’s rule, the sidelining of civilians in the 2021 transition, and the power struggle between SAF commander Abdel Fattah Al-Burhan and RSF chief Mohammed Hamdan Dagalo, which erupted into war in April 2023. Since El-Fasher fell, mediators from Saudi Arabia, the US, Egypt and the UAE have stepped up ceasefire efforts. Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman urged US President Donald Trump to help end the war, while the RSF said it would accept the mediators’ roadmap, beginning with a three-month humanitarian truce and moving toward a permanent ceasefire and civilian rule. On Dec. 16, Al-Burhan said he was ready to work with the Trump administration. For Sudanese civilians, it offers only a faint hope after a year of immense suffering.

Travellers were also told to ensure their documents are valid and that they have any visas needed for onward travel. Kosovo Prime Minister Albin Kurti warned in an interview Thursday that a Russian victory in Ukraine could destabilize the Balkans and threaten what he called 25 years of peace, freedom and democracy in the region. Speaking at Kosovo’s diplomatic mission in Warsaw, he said the West must remain united behind Ukraine because a stronger Russia would encourage Serbia and revive what he described as Serbian expansionist ambitions. Kurti argued that if Russia prevails, Serbia could act as a “regional hegemon and Russian proxy,” putting not only Kosovo at risk but also Bosnia, Montenegro and possibly North Macedonia. He said President Vladimir Putin would be emboldened to continue destabilizing efforts if he believed Russia was succeeding in Ukraine. The remarks came amid continuing tensions between Kosovo and Serbia. The two sides have been in EU-facilitated normalization talks for 13 years with little progress, and relations worsened after a September shootout last year between masked Serb gunmen and Kosovo police killed four people. NATO-led peacekeepers have since increased their presence along the Kosovo-Serbia border. Kurti recalled the wars that accompanied the breakup of the former Yugoslavia in the 1990s and said the Balkans had enjoyed an unprecedented period of stability since then. Kosovo was formerly a Serbian province, and NATO’s 1999 bombing campaign ended a war between Serbian forces and ethnic Albanian separatists that left about 13,000 dead, mostly ethnic Albanians. Serbia still does not recognize Kosovo’s 2008 declaration of independence, and thousands of international peacekeepers remain in the country. Kurti was in Poland as the country prepares to assume the rotating presidency of the European Union next January. Kosovo seeks eventual EU membership, but five EU states still do not recognize it. Kurti said some small steps, such as Spain’s recognition of Kosovo passports for travelers, are not enough without full recognition. Kosovo, whose population is about 90% Albanian, will hold parliamentary elections next February, a contest expected to test Kurti and his governing party.

Syrian regime security services have completed new reconciliation arrangements in Kanaker, a town west of Damascus, according to the Syrian Observatory for Human Rights. Reliable sources said the deal was reached between the Interior Ministry, town dignitaries, and security services. As part of the agreement, regime forces withdrew from two checkpoints inside the town, while police were given authority to carry out security raids and arrest suspects in criminal cases. Security forces, however, kept checkpoints at Kanaker’s entrances and promised not to harass residents traveling in or out. The deal followed weeks of tension, including a tight siege, demonstrations, and a military buildup that had raised fears of a storming of the town. On October 8, SOHR sources said women arrested in Kanaker on September 19 were released. The regime also lifted the siege, restoring movement into and out of the town. According to the report, reconciliation was reached with local gunmen except those accused by the regime of involvement in the Damascus bombings. Those who refused the new terms would later be allowed to leave for northern Syria.

Iraq’s prime minister, Mohammed al-Sudani, is confronting a delicate political and economic challenge as his government cracks down on dollar smuggling to Iran under pressure from the United States. On Saturday, elite Iraqi counter-terrorism forces raided dealers in Baghdad’s currency markets, an operation more typical of campaigns against Islamist militants than financial crime. The move is an early test for Sudani, who took office in October after more than a year of political deadlock and now must balance relations with both Washington and Tehran. The crackdown comes after the New York Federal Reserve imposed tighter controls in November on international dollar transfers by commercial Iraqi banks. The new rules were intended to block the illegal diversion of dollars to Iran and increase pressure on Tehran, which is already under heavy U.S. sanctions over its nuclear program and other disputes. Iranian access to dollars has become more difficult as a result, and the restrictions have also affected Iraqi banking and currency markets. A senior banking official said Washington made its position clear to Iraqi authorities: comply with the new regulations or risk fines on Iraq’s central bank. That puts Sudani in a difficult position. He depends on U.S. cooperation to protect Iraq’s oil revenues and financial system from American censure, and he also needs U.S. assistance in the fight against Islamic State remnants. At the same time, his political base includes powerful militias backed by Iran, making it dangerous for him to be seen as hostile to Tehran. Aqeel al-Fatlawi, a Shi’ite lawmaker, accused Washington of using the dollar restrictions as a political lever, warning that the message to Sudani was essentially: stay aligned with American interests or risk losing power. Political analyst Ahmed Younis described the prime minister as walking a “tightrope” between two rival powers that both have influence in Iraq. Iran itself badly needs dollars to stabilize its weakening economy, which has been hit by U.S. sanctions since 2018, when President Donald Trump withdrew from the nuclear deal. Its currency has fallen sharply, losing about 30% of its value amid domestic unrest after the death of Mahsa Amini in police custody in September. For years, Iranian networks have used front companies in Iraq and Turkey to obtain dollars for international transactions and to fund regional proxies. Two advisers to Iraqi private banks said Iran receives about $100 million a month from Iraqi traders. Iraqi security officials said they had strong evidence that smugglers have been buying large amounts of dollars in Baghdad and moving them across the border to Iran, especially since mid-January. A border police colonel at the Shalamcheh crossing near Basra said smugglers often transport the cash in school backpacks, then load it into four-wheel-drive vehicles guarded by armed men. During Saturday’s operation, the counter-terrorism forces came under pistol fire from unknown gunmen in the Kifah market. The new U.S.-backed system requires Iraqi banks to use an online platform that discloses details of dollar transactions, including senders and beneficiaries, and allows U.S. officials to block suspicious transfers. Economists say this has slowed transactions, but it has also created shortages in Baghdad’s currency market as some banks avoid the platform and turn to the free market to buy dollars. That has pushed up consumer prices and weakened the Iraqi dinar. The dinar had traded at about 1,470 per dollar before the restrictions, then fell to around 1,620 in December. In response, Sudani replaced the central bank governor, Mustafa Ghaleb Mukheef, after the currency’s slide. Sudani has tried to calm public concern, saying the government has taken “bold decisions” to stabilize the dinar and warning against exploiting the crisis. But bankers remain skeptical, saying the new rules make transfers slow and burdensome, while much of the dollar flow still appears to benefit Iran-linked businesses.

# Iraqi PM Navigates Complex Diplomatic Challenge Over Dollar Smuggling to Iran Prime Minister Mohammed al-Sudani faces a delicate balancing act between U.S. pressure to halt dollar smuggling to Iran and maintaining relationships with Tehran-backed militias who supported his October rise to power. Recent raids in Baghdad represent an early test of his ability to walk this diplomatic tightrope. ## The U.S. Pressure Campaign The New York Federal Reserve introduced stricter controls on international dollar transactions by Iraqi commercial banks in November, specifically targeting the illegal flow of currency to Iran. These measures aim to complement existing U.S. sanctions against Tehran over its nuclear program. American officials have made clear that Iraqi compliance is mandatory—non-compliance could result in fines against the Iraqi central bank. Sudani's vulnerability to American pressure is significant. Iraq depends on Washington's goodwill to protect its oil revenues and finances from U.S. sanctions, while simultaneously requiring American military assistance against Islamic State militants. However, this dependence creates tension with his power base. ## The Smuggling Operations According to banking advisers and security officials, Iran receives approximately $100 million monthly from Iraqi traders. Smugglers operate systematically from Baghdad's currency markets, using school backpacks to transport dollars before packing them into four-wheel drive vehicles at border crossings, often protected by armed guards. The Shalamcheh crossing near Basra has been a particular hotspot. Saturday's counter-terrorism raids in Baghdad targeted currency dealers, though forces faced gunfire from unknown assailants in Kifah, one of three major currency markets, complicating the operation. ## Iran's Desperation for Dollars Iran urgently needs dollars to stabilize its economy, severely damaged by sanctions reimposed after President Trump withdrew from the 2015 nuclear deal. The Iranian currency has lost approximately 30% of its value since September, following nationwide protests triggered by the death of 22-year-old Mahsa Amini in police custody. For years, Iran has relied on front companies across Iraq, Turkey, and other nations to obtain necessary dollars for international transactions and funding regional proxies. ## Domestic Consequences The new regulations have created significant economic disruption within Iraq. Banks avoiding the mandatory online platform—which requires disclosure of transaction details and allows U.S. officials to object to suspicious transfers—have turned to Baghdad's free markets to purchase dollars. This has created shortages as demand exceeds supply, driving up consumer goods prices and weakening the Iraqi dinar. The dinar deteriorated from 1,470 per dollar before the Fed restrictions to approximately 1,620 per dollar by December. This currency collapse prompted Sudani to replace the central bank governor on Monday. ## Political Backlash Shi'ite lawmaker Aqeel al-Fatlawi characterized U.S. actions as deliberately weaponized politics, accusing Washington of using restrictions as threats to ensure Sudani's compliance. Political analyst Ahmed Younis notes that Sudani faces an "interlocking challenge" managing competing interests between two nations that are simultaneously Iraq's adversaries and partners. The crackdown has deepened anti-American sentiment among Iraqi politicians, particularly given Iraq's instability following the 2003 U.S.-led invasion. Bank official Hadi Ali expressed skepticism about Sudani's reassurances, noting that lengthy approval delays for transfers harm legitimate business operations. Sudani has attempted to calm public concerns, declaring bold decisions to strengthen the dinar while warning against exploitation of the crisis. Nevertheless, the underlying tensions between American pressure and Iranian interests suggest his diplomatic balancing act will remain precarious.

Lebanon’s long-delayed parliamentary election is bringing a wave of fresh candidates, but many of them carry some of the country’s oldest political names. The article describes how, in Lebanon’s confessional political system, power has often passed informally from one generation to the next within the same families, despite the country’s official parliamentary democracy. As Lebanon prepares for its first legislative vote in nine years, candidates from third- and even fourth-generation political dynasties are appearing across nearly all of the country’s 18 religious communities. Several of these candidates are defending themselves against accusations of nepotism and “feudalism,” arguing that family background does not automatically make them anti-reform. Nadim Gemayel, already a parliament member since 2009, is one of the best-known examples. He is the youngest son of Bachir Gemayel, the president-elect assassinated in 1982, and the grandson of Pierre Gemayel, founder of the Phalangist, or Kataeb, Party. Gemayel says his political involvement is tied both to his father’s assassination and to frustration with Lebanon’s poor governance. He insists that being someone’s son can also be a positive force if younger generations adapt their forefathers’ ideas to modern needs. Another first-time candidate, Zaher Eido, rejects the idea that his family name has simply opened doors for him. Running in Beirut, he comes from a family marked by tragedy: his father, a former lawmaker, and his older brother were killed in a car bombing in the capital. Eido, a banker and member of the Future Movement like his father, says he has built his own career over more than a decade and wants to use his professional experience to help pass laws against money laundering. The pattern extends well beyond these two. Michelle Tueini, whose father Gebran was assassinated in 2005, is running for parliament after following him into journalism and after her sister Nayla served as a lawmaker for nine years. Prime Minister Saad Hariri rose to power after the assassination of his father Rafik, and his campaign materials prominently feature his father’s image. Other examples include Taymour Jumblatt, son of Druze leader Walid Jumblatt and grandson of party founder Kamal Jumblatt; Tony Franjieh, representing the fourth generation of his political family; and even relatives of President Michel Aoun, including a nephew and two sons-in-law, who are also seeking seats. Political scientists say this hereditary system persists because patriarchy and leader worship remain deeply rooted in Lebanese society. Some dynasties stem from older feudal traditions, while others grew out of armed factions during the civil war. The practice has long angered voters, and reformist groups such as Kulluna Watani are fielding dozens of candidates to challenge it. Yet even critics acknowledge that Lebanon’s politics remain a mix of cronyism and confessionalism, making real change slow.

# Lebanon's Political Dynasties Dominate Upcoming Elections Lebanon is preparing for parliamentary elections after a nine-year gap, but the candidate pool reveals a striking pattern: the same influential families continue to dominate the country's political landscape. Despite Lebanon's official parliamentary democratic system, political power remains informally inherited across generations within religious communities that comprise the nation's complex confessional structure. Multiple candidates represent third or fourth generations of the same political families. Nadim Gemayel, an incumbent, descends from his grandfather Pierre Gemayel, who founded the Phalangist Party, and his father Bachir Gemayel, who was assassinated while president-elect in 1982. Now 36, Nadim defends his candidacy as driven by genuine reform desires and frustration with national mismanagement, arguing that "being someone's son is not necessarily something negative or anti-reform." Similarly, Zaher Eido, a first-time candidate and banker, is running in Beirut over a decade after his father and older brother died in a car bomb attack. Though inheriting a political legacy through the Future Movement, Eido claims to have forged his own career path and promises to resign if unable to advance reform, particularly regarding money-laundering legislation. Michelle Tueini, 31, is following her father Gebran's footsteps as both a journalist and parliamentary candidate, taking over from her sister Nayla. Prime Minister Saad Hariri ascended to power following his father Rafik's assassination in 2005, with campaign posters featuring his father's portrait. Other examples include Taymour Jumblatt, son of Druze leader Walid and grandson of party founder Kamal, and Tony Franjieh, representing the fourth generation of his family—his great-grandfather served as head of state in 1970. Critics attribute this pattern to deeply ingrained patriarchal traditions and personality cults within Lebanese society. Saint Joseph University professor Fadia Kiwan explains that while some families practice "strict centuries-old feudalism," a "pseudo-feudal system" has emerged in other communities since modern Lebanon's founding. Many current political dynasties originated when their founders led armed groups during the 1975-1990 civil war. The hereditary political system has long frustrated Lebanese voters. The reformist coalition Kulluni Watani has responded by fielding 70 candidates nationwide, pledging to break the dynastic pattern. Coalition strategist Wadih al-Asmar denounces the system as "sclerotic and out-of-breath," criticizing the "blend of inherited power and nepotism" across all ruling parties as "simply unacceptable." However, some dynastic candidates acknowledge systemic limitations. Gemayel admits Lebanon's system is "not meritocratic" but rather "a blend of cronyism and confessionalism," arguing that traditional families must modernize to remain relevant. Despite defenders' reform rhetoric, the persistence of political dynasties continues to challenge Lebanon's democratic principles and frustrate voters seeking genuine change.

Yemeni Information Minister Muammar Al-Eryani said the coalition’s interception of two explosives-laden boats shows again how dangerous Houthi control of Hodeidah’s coastline is to international shipping, oil tankers and maritime navigation. He said the Houthis are using Hodeidah ports, including Salif and Ras Isa, to prepare and launch remote-controlled explosive boats, and argued this proves they are exploiting the Sweden Agreement to advance terrorist acts that threaten Yemen, the region and international interests. It also called on the Southern Transitional Council to stop violations against state institutions, halt military mobilization, and end actions that worsen crises and undermine the state and army.

# Summary Yemeni Information Minister Muammar Al-Eryani stated that the coalition's successful foiling of a Houthi attack involving two explosives-laden boats demonstrates the serious threat the militia poses to international maritime security. The UN Security Council has demanded that armed groups in the Central African Republic stop fighting immediately and join peace talks after UN attack helicopters struck rebel fighters near Bambari over the weekend. UN peacekeeping chief Herve Ladsous said about 300 gunmen were advancing on the central city in pickup trucks mounted with machine guns, and at least four of seven vehicles were destroyed. After meeting, the council urged armed groups to enter the peace and reconciliation dialogue, citing the country’s fragile security situation and severe humanitarian crisis. UN attack helicopters targeted approximately 300 fighters advancing on Bambari in pickup trucks equipped with machine guns, destroying at least four vehicles. The number of casualties remains unclear. The council urged armed groups to halt hostilities and engage in peace and reconciliation dialogue. Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau condemned a deadly extremist attack in Somalia that killed 26 people, including Somali-Canadian journalist Hodan Nalayeh and her husband, Farid Jama Suleiman. In a statement on Sunday, Trudeau offered condolences to Nalayeh’s family, friends, and colleagues, and said Canada strongly denounces the “heinous attack.” He added that Canada would continue working with Somalia and international partners to confront terrorism and violent extremism, and stressed the importance of media freedom in healthy democracies. According to Somali officials, the attack took place Friday in the port city of Kismayo, where Nalayeh, 43, and her husband were staying at a hotel. The assault began with a suicide car bomb, followed by gunmen storming the building. Somali authorities said 56 people were injured. The al-Shabab Islamist militant group later claimed responsibility. Nalayeh was a former Toronto-based journalist known for highlighting positive stories about the Somali community in Canada. Canada’s immigration minister, Ahmed Hussen, wrote on Twitter that she “became a voice for many” through her work. Nalayeh launched Integration TV in 2014 and interviewed a range of guests, including former Ontario premier Kathleen Wynne. She also founded the Somali Refugees Awareness Project, a nonprofit advocating for Somali refugees worldwide. Trudeau described her work as a testament to the role of a free press in broadening perspectives and supporting diversity and inclusion. Friends and family remembered Nalayeh as a loving wife, mother, dependable friend, and storyteller. She is survived by two sons. The Somali Journalists Syndicate also confirmed that another journalist, Mohamed Omar Sahal, was killed in the attack. The group said Sahal is survived by his wife and four children, and its secretary general, Abdalle Ahmed Mumin, said the deaths of both journalists were devastating.

# Summary Prime Minister Justin Trudeau condemned a terrorist attack in Kismayo, Somalia, on Friday that killed 26 people, including prominent Somali-Canadian journalist Hodan Nalayeh and her husband Farid Jama Suleiman. In his Sunday statement, Trudeau offered condolences to the victims' families and pledged Canada's commitment to working with Somalia and international partners to combat terrorism and violent extremism. The Syndicate's secretary general expressed shock at losing both journalists in the tragedy.

As the 101st anniversary of the Armenian genocide approached, Armenian filmmakers and musicians in Los Angeles sought to draw attention to an atrocity they say remains largely unknown to the wider American public. The article describes how, beginning in 1915, the Ottoman Turkish government arrested Armenian community leaders and launched a campaign of mass killing and deportation that left an estimated 1.5 million Christian Armenians dead by the early 1920s. Victims were forced from their homes on death marches across the Mesopotamian desert, where many died of thirst, exhaustion, or were shot. The ruling Young Turks also organized death squads that carried out brutal killings by drowning, cliff-throwing, crucifixion, and burning, while women were raped, enslaved, or forced into harems. The trauma, the article notes, has been passed down through generations of Armenians who later settled in Europe and the United States. In Los Angeles, home to the world’s largest Armenian diaspora community, thousands were expected to rally on Sunday to press Turkey to formally recognize the massacres as genocide. Campaigners, however, expressed frustration that many Californians and other Western audiences have little or no knowledge of the events, known in Armenian as “Medz Yeghern,” or “The Great Crime.” One effort to change that is French-Armenian filmmaker Robert Guediguian’s movie “Don’t Don’t Tell Me The Boy Was Mad,” which had its U.S. premiere at COLCOA, a major French film festival in Los Angeles. Guediguian said he believed much of America, and even Europe, remained unaware of the genocide, arguing that cinema can educate audiences about overlooked history. His film, set among the Armenian diaspora in 1970s and 1980s Marseille, follows the wave of bombings and assassinations by Armenian radicals targeting Turkish interests in Europe, acts carried out in response to the genocide. The story was inspired by Jose Antonio Gurriaran’s autobiographical novel “The Bomb”; Gurriaran was left semi-paralyzed by an Armenian attack in Madrid but later became an advocate for genocide recognition. The article also notes that despite past support for recognition measures, President Barack Obama never used the term “genocide” for the killings while in office, something critics saw as a concession to Turkish sensitivities. Guediguian drew on his own family history for parts of the film, including a story of a raped relative who survived and reached France. He said audience reactions had been very warm, and he was seeking a U.S. distributor. A second film, “Armenia, My Love,” also premiered in the Los Angeles area. Written and directed by Romanian American Diana Angelson, it depicts an Armenian family in 1915 in eastern Turkey. Angelson said she wanted the film’s themes of hope, love, faith, perseverance, and strength to stand alongside its depiction of the massacres.

# Armenians Confront Hollywood with 'Forgotten Genocide' As the 101st anniversary of the Armenian genocide approaches, filmmakers and musicians in Los Angeles are working to educate Americans about a largely unknown historical tragedy. On Sunday, thousands of Armenians are expected to gather in Los Angeles—home to the world's largest Armenian diaspora—to commemorate the massacres and demand Turkish recognition of the genocide. Beginning in 1915, Turkey's Ottoman government systematically slaughtered approximately 1.5 million Christian Armenians through mass executions, death marches through the desert, drowning, crucifixion, and burning. Women were raped, enslaved, or forced into harems. The trauma has persisted across generations, with descendants carrying their ancestors' unresolved suffering. However, many Americans remain unaware of these events, referred to by Armenians as "Medz Yeghern" or "The Great Crime." French-Armenian filmmaker Robert Guediguian is attempting to address this ignorance through cinema. His film "Don't Tell Me The Boy Was Mad" premiered at COLCOA, the world's largest French film festival held annually in Los Angeles, and will receive wider U.S. distribution. Guediguian emphasized that awareness of the genocide exists primarily in communities with large Armenian populations. He believes cinema can educate the public about historical atrocities. The film, set in 1970s and 1980s Marseille, explores the Armenian diaspora and follows radical Armenian responses to the genocide, including bombings and assassinations targeting Turkish interests across Europe. The story draws inspiration from "The Bomb," an autobiographical novel by Jose Antonio Gurriaran, a Spanish man semi-paralyzed by an Armenian terrorist attack who became an advocate for international recognition of the "forgotten genocide." Many scenes in Guediguian's film reflect his own family history, including accounts of rape and suffering passed down from his grandparents' generation. President Barack Obama has faced criticism for refusing to use the term "genocide" regarding the Armenian killings, despite earlier campaign promises to recognize it. Guediguian noted that politicians typically pledge support for genocide recognition while campaigning but abandon these commitments once elected. A second film, "Armenia, My Love," directed by Romanian-American Diana Angelson, also premiered recently in Pasadena. Set in occupied Armenian homeland territory in 1915, the film depicts the massacres' horrors while emphasizing messages of hope, love, faith, and perseverance. These cinematic efforts represent attempts to ensure the Armenian genocide is no longer forgotten by mainstream American audiences.

The United States said Friday it will conduct additional interviews related to the deadly August 26, 2021 suicide bombing at Kabul’s Abbey Gate, which killed more than 170 people, including 13 US service members, during the chaotic withdrawal from Afghanistan. The bombing struck crowds gathered outside Kabul airport, where many Afghans were trying to flee as the Taliban seized power. According to Central Command spokesman Michael Lawhorn, the new review will include 19 interviews, with more possible if needed. The decision follows a review of public testimony that found former Marine Sgt. Tyler Vargas-Andrews, who was wounded in the attack and later testified before lawmakers, provided information not previously shared by any other witness. The review also identified additional wounded service members who were not interviewed because they were immediately medically evacuated after the blast. Lawhorn said the purpose of the new interviews is to ensure due diligence, hear all relevant voices, and thoroughly examine the new information so the facts are clear. A US investigation had previously concluded the bombing could not have been prevented. The attack was claimed by the Islamic State group, and the White House said earlier this year that the Taliban killed the attack’s mastermind. The renewed scrutiny comes amid continued Republican criticism of President Joe Biden over both the bombing and the broader end of the US war in Afghanistan.

# Summary The United States announced Friday that it will conduct additional witness interviews regarding the August 26, 2021 Abbey Gate bombing in Kabul that killed over 170 people, including 13 US troops. Although a prior US investigation concluded the attack could not have been prevented, Republican lawmakers have continued pressuring President Biden's administration over both the bombing and the chaotic Afghanistan withdrawal. A new Kansas City nonprofit is trying to solve a shortage of poll workers by recruiting veterans. With Election Day 26 days away, election offices across the region say they are struggling to find enough workers, especially because many current poll workers are older or retired and concerned about COVID-19. The effort is being led by former Army Sergeant First Class Vincent Morales, who served overseas and helped secure Iraq’s first democratic election in 2005. Morales said his unit protected voters during that election, and he wants veterans who have returned home to continue serving democracy by staffing polling places in the United States. Through his group, Mentoring the Force, he is encouraging veterans to help with elections and “secure our elections” in a different way. So far, Morales says about 20 veterans have signed up to work polls on both sides of the Kansas-Missouri state line. Election officials say the help is badly needed. Johnson County, Kansas election commissioner Connie Schmidt called poll workers the “foot soldiers of democracy” and said veterans are a strong fit for the job. She also noted that cancellations are common this year because of pandemic fears. Jackson County, Missouri’s Election Board said it especially needs poll workers who are comfortable using computers. Morales also urged people who cannot work the polls to still vote, saying it is a right people often take for granted.

# Summary With Election Day 26 days away, jurisdictions nationwide face a critical shortage of poll workers. This problem is particularly acute in the Kansas City area, where most election workers are older or retired individuals at higher COVID-19 risk. The United States on Friday renewed its criticism of Afghanistan’s Taliban rulers, saying they must follow through on their promises before seeking international legitimacy. John Kirby, the U.S. National Security Council coordinator for strategic communications, told Voice of America that the Taliban will remain isolated unless they reverse their restrictions on women and girls. He said that if the Taliban want recognition, financial aid, and investment, they must “meet their promises, meet their obligations, and behave accordingly.” The Taliban took power in Afghanistan in August 2021 and have since imposed sweeping restrictions that sharply limit women’s participation in social, economic, and political life. Afghanistan is now the only country in the world where girls are barred from secondary school and university education. The Taliban have also prohibited Afghan women from working for national and international nongovernmental organizations that deliver humanitarian assistance to millions of people in the war-torn country. In addition, women have been ordered to stay away from parks, gyms, and public bathhouses. These policies have prevented the global community from formally recognizing the Taliban as Afghanistan’s legitimate government. The Taliban reject the criticism, arguing that they are governing according to Afghan culture and their interpretation of Islamic Sharia law. However, scholars in Muslim-majority countries dispute that claim, saying Islam grants women full rights to work and pursue education. Kirby also raised concerns about the Taliban’s counterterrorism efforts against Islamic State militants in Afghanistan. He said the Taliban remain under threat from ISIS, which he described as a credible danger not only in Afghanistan but elsewhere. The group’s Afghan branch, Islamic State Khorasan, has carried out repeated high-profile attacks in Kabul and other parts of the country in recent months, killing scores of people. The discussion also touched on growing tensions between Afghanistan and Pakistan. Pakistani officials have increasingly accused Afghan authorities of allowing leaders of the banned Pakistani Taliban, or Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), to stage cross-border attacks. The latest major attack occurred Monday, when a suicide bombing at a crowded mosque in Peshawar killed more than 100 people and wounded 225, most of them police officers. Taliban leaders deny the accusations, saying they do not allow any group to use Afghan territory for such attacks. Kirby said people in Pakistan remain under threat from the Pakistani Taliban and noted that the U.S. would stay in contact with Islamabad about possible responses. Separately, the United Nations called on Friday for the immediate release of Ismail Mashal, a university lecturer and education activist detained by Taliban security forces in Kabul. Mashal had reportedly been handing out books after publicly tearing up his diploma in protest against the ban on female higher education. U.N. spokesman Stephane Dujarric called the arrest deeply concerning and another sign of backsliding, especially on women’s and girls’ education. A Taliban official said Mashal was detained for gathering journalists and spreading “propaganda against the government,” while another official said he was being held in good conditions and had contacted his family.

A U.S. citizen was shot to death in Managua, Nicaragua, on Saturday amid escalating violence and social unrest. Medical authorities said Sixto Henry Vera’s body was found in the street beside two burned vehicles, with a bullet wound to the head. Employees at the Managua bar he owned said Vera had left late Friday to help a friend who was under attack. U.S. Ambassador Laura Dogu expressed condolences on Twitter and said the death of a U.S. citizen was of “great concern” to the embassy. Vera’s killing came during a period of intense turmoil in Nicaragua. Since mid-April, more than 110 people have been killed in clashes between supporters of President Daniel Ortega and opposition groups demanding his removal. Streets are often empty after dark as armed groups travel in unmarked vehicles, shooting and robbing. Violence also flared on Wednesday during Mothers’ Day protests, when gunmen fired into crowds and killed more than a dozen people. Civil society groups blamed paramilitary forces loyal to Ortega, while government officials blamed the opposition. As insecurity spreads, residents in some cities have formed neighborhood watch groups. The Red Cross said two people manning barricades in Masaya were killed Saturday.

Vera, who owned a local bar, was discovered with a bullet wound to the head beside two burned vehicles. According to bar employees, he had left Friday night to assist a friend being attacked.
