Some Nicaraguan business leaders have proposed accelerating the presidential election currently scheduled for 2021.

The Louisiana National Guard’s 256th Infantry Brigade Combat Team, the “Tiger Brigade,” is marking the 20th anniversary of its return from a major deployment to Iraq during Operation Iraqi Freedom III. A central part of that story is the 3rd Battalion, 156th Infantry Regiment, which became known as Task Force Bandit. The article explains that the 3-156th was not originally included in the brigade’s mobilization because of Army organizational procedures at the time. Brig. Gen. John Basilica, then commander of the 256th, worked to make sure the battalion’s Soldiers were brought along. At first, many of them were cross-leveled into other units. During the train-up period, roughly 20 Soldiers from the battalion formed an improvised group called Task Force Bandit. By the time the brigade deployed to Iraq, that group had expanded to about 400 Soldiers. Though smaller than the brigade’s other battalions, Task Force Bandit played an outsized role in the mission. One of its most notable actions came on May 29, 2005, during the Battle of Al Quabasey Mosque. Insurgents firing from the mosque and a nearby swimming pool complex attacked the unit with small arms, and a car bomb exploded nearby, intensifying the fight. Despite the danger, the Soldiers pressed on. After the firefight, they searched the area and detained two enemy snipers. They also uncovered a significant weapons cache, including bomb-making materials and military uniforms. The operation helped eliminate an enemy stronghold that had been used to support attacks on U.S. troops and Iraqi civilians. Two of the captured uniforms are now displayed at the Louisiana National Guard Museum at Jackson Barracks in New Orleans. Another major incident involved Specialist Steven Tschiderer, a medic with E Troop, 101st Cavalry of the New York National Guard, which was attached to Task Force Bandit. During a routine patrol, the unit came under sniper fire. As Soldiers secured the area and searched nearby buildings, Tschiderer was hit in the chest while reporting the situation up the chain of command. His body armor saved his life. He took cover and then indicated the sniper’s location. The attackers fled in a van, but Task Force Bandit pursued them through Baghdad, disabled the vehicle, and captured the insurgents. Tschiderer was later required, as a medic, to treat the wounded sniper who had shot him. Evidence gathered by the unit and testimony from local civilians helped the 256th’s legal team ensure the insurgents were prosecuted in Iraqi Criminal Court. Beyond these battles, Task Force Bandit secured key infrastructure, including a bridge over the Grand Canal and a major Iraqi government compound, and helped provide security during Iraq’s 2005 national elections. Basilica later succeeded in getting the 3-156th officially added to the brigade’s order of battle so the Soldiers would receive proper campaign credit. As he said in 2007, their flag was present, and Soldiers died under it, so they deserved recognition.

# Louisiana National Guard's Tiger Brigade Marks 20 Years Since Iraq Deployment This November, Louisiana's 256th Infantry Brigade Combat Team, known as the Tiger Brigade, will commemorate the 20th anniversary of its return from Operation Iraqi Freedom III in Iraq. The deployment is particularly notable for the formation and achievements of Task Force Bandit, an ad hoc unit composed primarily of soldiers from the 3rd Battalion, 156th Infantry Regiment. ## Formation of Task Force Bandit Initially, the 3rd Battalion was excluded from the brigade's mobilization due to Army organizational procedures at the time. However, Brigadier General John Basilica, commander of the 256th, ensured these soldiers were included in the deployment. During the training phase, approximately 20 soldiers from the 3-156th were cross-leveled into other battalions but formed an informal task force called Task Force Bandit. By the time the unit reached Iraq, Task Force Bandit had grown to roughly 400 soldiers, making it smaller than other battalions but highly impactful. ## Combat Operations On May 29, 2005, Task Force Bandit engaged in the Battle of Al Quabasey Mosque. Insurgents fired from the mosque and an adjacent swimming pool complex using small arms, while a nearby car bomb added to the intensity. Despite these attacks, the unit persevered, ultimately detaining two enemy snipers and seizing a substantial weapons cache containing bomb-making materials and military uniforms. Two of these uniforms are now displayed at the Louisiana National Guard Museum in Jackson Barracks, New Orleans. ## Notable Incident During routine patrol operations, Specialist Steven Tschiderer, a medic attached to E Troop, 101st Cavalry of the New York National Guard, was shot by a sniper in the chest. His body armor proved lifesaving. Tschiderer quickly took cover and directed his unit toward the sniper's position. Task Force Bandit pursued the attackers' van through Baghdad, disabled the vehicle, and captured the insurgents. Remarkably, Tschiderer, as the unit's medic, provided medical treatment to the sniper who had shot him. Evidence collected by the unit and civilian testimony enabled the 256th's legal team to ensure the insurgents faced prosecution in the Iraqi Criminal Court system. ## Additional Contributions Beyond these major operations, Task Force Bandit secured critical infrastructure, including a bridge over the Grand Canal and a major Iraqi government compound. The unit also provided essential security during Iraq's 2005 national elections. ## Recognition General Basilica eventually succeeded in officially adding the 3-156th to the order of battle, ensuring the Bandits received proper campaign credit. As Basilica stated in 2007, "Their flag was present, and there were Soldiers who died under that flag. It was only right that they be recognized."

Former NHL players Daniel Carcillo and Nick Boynton have sued the league in U.S. District Court in Minnesota, alleging it failed to warn them about the long-term risk of brain damage from fighting. The lawsuit says both men kept playing despite repeated head injuries and now suffer from degenerative brain damage. Carcillo played nine seasons for five teams and won a 2013 Stanley Cup with Chicago; Boynton played 12 years for six teams. A similar suit already includes dozens of former players.

Armenian President Serzh Sarkisian on Tuesday appointed Karen Karapetyan, a Kremlin-friendly technocrat, as the country’s new prime minister after Hovik Abrahamian resigned amid public anger over a hostage crisis. Sarkisian’s office said the decree was signed Tuesday morning. Karapetyan, 53, is a former mayor of Yerevan and has held senior roles at Gazprom’s subsidiary Mezhregiongaz and Gazprombank in Moscow. His appointment follows a two-week standoff in July, when armed anti-government gunmen seized a police compound in Yerevan, killed two police officers and took senior officers hostage before surrendering on July 31 after clashes and negotiations. The crisis triggered anti-government protests and prompted Sarkisian to promise a cabinet reshuffle. Armenia, Russia’s closest ally in the Caucasus, hosts a Russian military base, belongs to a Moscow-led economic union and depends on Russian weapons supplies in its conflict with Azerbaijan over Nagorny Karabakh. Political analyst Stefan Safaryan said Karapetyan is widely seen as “Russia’s protege.” The appointment comes as Armenia faces economic strain from Russia’s downturn, while poverty remains high, with about 30 percent of the population living below the official poverty line.

# Summary Armenian President Serzh Sarkisian appointed Karen Karapetyan, a pro-Russian technocrat, as the nation's new prime minister on Tuesday. Kazakhstan’s longtime leader Nursultan Nazarbayev abruptly resigned Tuesday after nearly three decades in power, creating uncertainty about the country’s political future. In a televised address, the 78-year-old president said he had made the “difficult” decision to end his authority effective immediately. He gave no specific reason for stepping down, but said he would have marked 30 years in office later this year and emphasized that his role was to ensure a smooth transfer of power. Although he is leaving the presidency, Nazarbayev will keep significant influence. He will retain the honorary title of “Elbasy,” or “leader of the nation,” and continue as chairman of the Security Council and head of the ruling Nur Otan party. He said upper house Speaker Kassym-Jomart Tokayev would serve as interim president under the constitution until a new election is held. In Rome, U.S. and Russian officials said they remained divided over how to resolve Venezuela’s political crisis after talks between U.S. special envoy Elliott Abrams and Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Sergei Ryabkov. Abrams said the two sides did not reach agreement, though the meeting was constructive and gave both sides a better understanding of each other’s positions. Russia continues to support Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and accuses the United States of interfering by pressuring him to step down in favor of opposition leader Juan Guaido. Ryabkov told Russian media that dialogue with Washington is necessary but warned against military intervention. He said Russia interprets President Donald Trump’s statement that “all options are on the table” as leaving open the possibility of force. Abrams said the United States is still keeping its options open, but has chosen to rely on political, financial and diplomatic pressure on Maduro’s government. In Bangladesh, gunmen attacked two cars carrying ballot boxes as they returned from a polling station in the southeastern district of Rangamati, killing at least seven people and wounding 15. Police said the attack happened Monday evening in Baghaichhari, a region known for tribal communities and tourism and once affected by insurgency. The dead included election and security officials. Eleven critically injured people were flown by military helicopter to a hospital in Chittagong. Authorities tightened security after the attack. Voting in Rangamati was being held to elect local government officials, though some candidates boycotted the election over alleged irregularities. In Germany, a court ruled that the government has partial responsibility to ensure that U.S. drone strikes linked to the Ramstein air base comply with international law, but it stopped short of ordering the ban sought by human-rights activists. The case was brought on behalf of three Yemeni plaintiffs whose relatives were killed in a 2012 drone strike. It ordered the German government to take appropriate measures to determine whether such use is lawful and, if necessary, to press Washington to comply.

The source said Russian helicopters are conducting air patrols over Tajikistan, and in some cases resources from Russia’s air base in Kyrgyzstan are also being used. The comments came after an armed attack on a Tajik border post on November 6, which the source linked to militants of the Islamic State terrorist group, outlawed in Russia. Moscow on Monday blamed Ukraine for helping trigger an anti-Israel riot at Makhachkala airport in Russia’s Dagestan region, while Kyiv rejected the accusation and said the violence reflected deep-rooted anti-Semitism in Russia. The unrest erupted on Sunday evening when a crowd of angry men stormed the airport in the Muslim-majority region, broke through barriers, and ran onto the runway in an attempt to reach a plane that had arrived from Israel. Russian officials said the disorder was fueled by “external interference” and by anger over images from the war in Gaza. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the airport events were “to a large extent” the result of outside meddling, arguing that footage of suffering in Gaza made it easy for “enemies” to provoke unrest. He said President Vladimir Putin would meet top advisers and intelligence chiefs to discuss what the Kremlin described as the West’s attempts to exploit Middle East tensions to divide Russian society. Russia’s foreign ministry later went further, accusing the “criminal Kyiv regime” of playing a direct and central role in the riot. Ukraine denied involvement. Foreign ministry spokesman Oleg Nikolenko said the events in Makhachkala showed the “deep-rooted anti-Semitism of Russian elites and society.” Moscow has often blamed domestic unrest on foreign forces, usually the West. Authorities said 60 people were arrested after the airport was overrun by demonstrators allegedly trying to attack Jews. Russia’s Orthodox leader, Patriarch Kirill, condemned the violence as an attempt to “sow discord” between Jews and Muslims in Russia, warning that those behind it would continue trying to create disorder. The airport reopened on Monday, though damage was reported and an airline cancelled flights to Israel in the coming days. The riot came amid broader tensions in the North Caucasus. On the same day, Russian state media reported that a Jewish center in Kabardino-Balkaria had been set on fire. AFP also saw police outside Makhachkala’s synagogue the next day. Israel urged Russia to protect its citizens and Jewish communities. In Moscow, people outside a synagogue said they were shaken but not surprised by the events, given the global fallout from the Israel-Hamas war. Dagestan’s leaders have publicly supported the Palestinians since Hamas’s October 7 attack on Israel, which Israeli officials said killed 1,400 people and led to 239 hostages being taken. Israel’s subsequent bombardment of Gaza has killed more than 8,300 people, according to the Hamas-run health ministry. Russian officials also focused on a Telegram channel linked to former Russian lawmaker Ilya Ponomarev, now in Ukraine, saying it helped organize the protests. Dagestan governor Sergei Melikov blamed social media posts from Utro Dagestan, which he said was run by “traitors” in Ukraine. He called the riot a “stab in the back” to Dagestani soldiers fighting in Ukraine and urged residents not to fall for provocations.

# Moscow Blames Ukraine for Dagestan Airport Riot A violent riot erupted Sunday evening at Makhachkala airport in Russia's Muslim-majority Dagestan region, when crowds of angry men stormed the facility searching for Jewish passengers on a plane arriving from Israel. The mob breached barriers and took over the runway in an attempt to encircle the aircraft. Moscow immediately blamed Ukraine for orchestrating the disturbance, claiming "external interference" was responsible. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov stated the riot resulted from enemies exploiting footage of Gaza Strip violence to provoke unrest and split Russian society. Russia's foreign ministry specifically accused Kyiv's "criminal regime" of orchestrating the "destructive act." President Putin convened top advisers and spy chiefs to discuss what Moscow characterized as "the West's attempts to use the events in the Middle East to split Russian society." Ukraine firmly rejected these allegations. The Ukrainian foreign ministry spokesman declared that the events "reflect the deep-rooted anti-Semitism of Russian elites and society," directly contradicting Moscow's narrative. Authorities arrested 60 people suspected of violently storming the airport and targeting Jewish passengers. The incident prompted damage to the facility, though it reopened Monday. Several airlines cancelled upcoming flights to Israel. Additionally, a Jewish center in the nearby Kabardino-Balkaria region was set on fire the same day. Israel called upon Russia to protect its citizens and Jewish communities. Police were stationed outside Makhachkala's synagogue, and people in Moscow synagogues expressed concern, though some acknowledged the violence was unsurprising given escalating global tensions over the Israel-Hamas conflict. Russian Orthodox Patriarch Kirill condemned the violence as an attempt to "sow discord" between Russia's Jewish and Muslim populations, suggesting external forces orchestrated the incident. Investigators traced the riot's organization to a Telegram channel called Utro Dagestan (Dagestan Morning), allegedly connected to Ilya Ponomarev, a former Russian lawmaker now living in Ukraine who was granted Ukrainian citizenship in 2019. Dagestan's governor, Sergei Melikov, called the riot a "stab in the back" of Dagestani soldiers fighting in Ukraine, noting that Dagestan has proportionately sent more men to the conflict than many Russian regions. The underlying tensions reflect broader Middle East conflicts. Hamas's October 7 attacks killed approximately 1,400 Israelis, prompting Israel's retaliatory bombardment that has killed over 8,300 Palestinians, according to Hamas health officials. Prominent Dagestani figures have publicly supported Palestinians since these attacks, contributing to the volatile atmosphere that preceded the airport violence.

Armenian national security forces detained the third gunman after an attack on a police station in Yerevan’s Nor-Nork district, Russian state media reported. Armenia’s interior ministry said three armed men tried to storm the station on Sunday. Two were wounded when grenades they were carrying exploded and were taken to hospital. No one was injured in the arrest of the third suspect. Earlier reports linked the men to the Combat Brotherhood group, which denied involvement.

# Summary Armenian security forces detained a gunman who attacked a police station in Yerevan's Nor-Nork district on Sunday. Three armed men attempted the assault; two were wounded when their hand grenades detonated and were hospitalized. The third was detained without injuries. Reports suggested the attackers might belong to the Combat Brotherhood organization, approximately 50 of whose members were detained earlier that day. However, the organization denied involvement in the incident.

Heavy fighting between Armenia and Azerbaijan over the separatist region of Nagorno-Karabakh continued on Saturday, marking the worst violence in the area since the 1994 ceasefire that ended a war over the territory. The clashes, which began on September 27, have spread across the front line and surrounding areas. Armenian Defence Ministry spokeswoman Shushan Stepanian said “intensive fighting is taking place along the entire front line” and claimed Armenian forces had shot down three aircraft. Azerbaijan’s defence ministry did not address that claim, but said Armenian forces had shelled civilian areas inside Azerbaijan, including the city of Terter. Casualty figures remained unclear. Nagorno-Karabakh officials said more than 150 of their servicemen had been killed. Azerbaijan has not released military casualty numbers, but said 19 civilians have been killed and 55 others wounded. The conflict dates back to the Soviet era, when Nagorno-Karabakh was an autonomous region within Azerbaijan. It declared independence in 1991, before the Soviet Union collapsed, and a full-scale war in 1992 killed an estimated 30,000 people. By the 1994 end of fighting, Armenian forces controlled Nagorno-Karabakh and nearby territories outside its formal borders. Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev said the occupied areas must be returned before fighting can stop. In a television interview with al-Jazeera, he also criticized the OSCE Minsk Group mediators, saying they had failed to pressure Armenia to implement UN Security Council resolutions. “We have no time to wait another 30 years,” he said.

# Summary Heavy fighting between Armenia and Azerbaijan resumed on Saturday over the disputed territory of Nagorno-Karabakh, marking the worst violence since a 1994 war ended. The conflict began on September 27. Armenian Defence Ministry spokeswoman Shushan Stepanian reported intensive fighting along the entire front line and claimed Armenian forces shot down three Azerbaijani planes. Azerbaijan's defence ministry did not address the plane claims but accused Armenian forces of shelling Azerbaijani civilian areas, including the city of Terter. Casualty reports show Nagorno-Karabakh officials stating over 150 servicemen killed on their side, while Azerbaijan reported 19 civilian deaths and 55 wounded, without disclosing military casualties. The disputed territory was an autonomous region within Azerbaijan during the Soviet era. It declared independence in 1991 and became the center of a devastating 1992-1994 war that killed approximately 30,000 people. Armenian forces currently control not only Nagorno-Karabakh but also substantial surrounding areas, contrary to UN Security Council resolutions demanding withdrawal. Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev criticized international mediators, particularly the Minsk Group of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe, for failing to enforce UN resolutions. He stated that Armenian forces must withdraw from occupied areas before fighting can cease and emphasized the need for immediate conflict resolution rather than waiting another 30 years.

Russia’s Federal Security Service said Wednesday that it had arrested eight suspects in the October 8 bombing of the strategic bridge to Crimea, including an Armenian citizen identified as Artur Terchanian, born in 1985. Moscow blames Ukraine for the attack, which killed at least four people and destroyed part of the 19-kilometer road bridge, a crucial supply route for Russian forces in southern Ukraine. In its statement, the FSB said the blast was organized by Ukraine’s military intelligence service and its director, Kyrylo Budanov. It claimed the explosive device had been hidden in plastic film rolls shipped from Odesa in August and moved through Bulgaria, Georgia, and Armenia before entering Russia on October 4. The agency said the cargo was cleared by customs in Yerevan between September 29 and October 3. The FSB also said the customs process was handled by GURG Group, a brokerage firm registered in the northern Armenian town of Alaverdi. The company’s listed address and that of its owner, Gurgen Shlepchyan, are tied to an apartment occupied by a Russian national and owned by Shlepchyan’s sister. She told RFE/RL’s Armenian Service that her brother works in Georgia and is involved in trade, but declined to provide more details. Armenia’s Prosecutor-General’s Office said it was examining Russia’s claims and had ordered the National Security Service to investigate. It said it would seek to fully establish the facts. Terchanyan is not listed in Armenia’s voter registry, suggesting he may not be a permanent resident. Ukraine has not officially admitted involvement, though some Ukrainian officials have praised the damage, and an unnamed Ukrainian official told the New York Times that Kyiv was responsible.

# Summary Russia's Federal Security Service arrested eight suspects, including Armenian citizen Artur Terchanian, in connection with the October 8 bombing of the Crimea Bridge, a critical supply route for Russian forces in Ukraine. The explosion killed at least four people and damaged a section of the 19-kilometer bridge. The FSB claimed the attack was organized by Ukrainian military intelligence and its director Kyrylo Budanov. According to Russian authorities, the explosive device was concealed in plastic film rolls that departed from the Ukrainian port of Odesa in August, traveling through Bulgaria, Georgia, and Armenia before reaching Russia on October 4. The cargo underwent customs clearance in Yerevan from September 29 to October 3, facilitated by a customs brokerage firm called GURG Group registered in the Armenian town of Alaverdi. Investigators discovered that GURG Group's registered address and its owner, Gurgen Shlepchyan, were connected to an apartment rented by a Russian national, though the apartment actually belongs to Shlepchyan's sister. When contacted, she claimed her brother works in Georgia in the trade business but provided no additional details. Armenia's Prosecutor-General's Office announced it would investigate the Russian claims and instructed the National Security Service to launch an inquiry. Terchanian does not appear on Armenia's voter registry, suggesting he may not have been a permanent resident. Ukraine has not officially confirmed involvement in the attack, though some officials have celebrated the damage.

Hundreds of Argentines gathered in Buenos Aires on Friday to mark the 31st anniversary of the 1994 bombing of the AMIA Jewish cultural center, the deadliest attack in Argentina’s history, and to demand justice in a case that still has not gone to trial. The car bomb destroyed the seven-story Argentine Israelite Mutual Association building on July 18, 1994, killing 85 people and injuring more than 300. The commemoration came two years after an earlier bombing of the Israeli embassy in Buenos Aires killed 29 and wounded 200. The event, held under the slogan “Impunity persists, terrorism too,” was attended for the second time by President Javier Milei, a strong supporter of Israel. Survivors and victims’ relatives have expressed hope that his administration may bring progress, noting his repeated visits to Israel and his interest in Judaism. In April 2024, an Argentine court ruled that Iran and Hezbollah were responsible for the attack, describing it as a crime against humanity and saying the likely motive was Argentina’s cancellation of nuclear contracts with Iran under former president Carlos Menem. In June, a judge approved a trial in absentia for ten Iranian and Lebanese defendants, including former ministers and diplomats, though no date has been set. Iran denies involvement and has refused to surrender suspects. Victims’ groups remain divided over the in absentia trial. Memoria Activa opposes it, while AMIA supports it but warns against a process that could later be invalidated. Both have sharply criticized the state’s handling of the case. Last year, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights held Argentina responsible for failing to prevent and properly investigate the bombing and for attempts to cover up and obstruct the inquiry.

# Summary On Friday, hundreds of Argentines commemorated the 1994 bombing of the Argentine Israelite Mutual Association (AMIA) building in Buenos Aires, demanding justice for the attack that killed 85 people and injured over 300. This marked the 31st anniversary of the July 18, 1994 bombing, Argentina's worst such attack. A similar 1992 Israeli embassy bombing killed 29 and wounded 200. President Javier Milei, a staunch Israel supporter who has visited twice since taking office in December 2023, attended the commemoration. Survivors and relatives hope his administration will advance the stalled case. In April 2024, an Argentine court determined Iran and Hezbollah were responsible for the attacks, ruling the likely motive was Argentina's cancellation of nuclear contracts with Iran under then-president Carlos Menem. A judge authorized a trial in absentia in June against ten Iranian and Lebanese defendants, though no trial date has been set. However, victim advocacy groups remain skeptical. Memoria Activa believes accused parties must participate for full truth-telling, while the AMIA fears an in absentia trial could be nullified. Both organizations have criticized the Argentine state's handling of the case. The Inter-American Court of Human Rights previously found Argentina responsible for failing to prevent and properly investigate the attack, and for obstructing the investigation. Prosecutor Alberto Nisman, investigating cover-up allegations, was later murdered with no charges filed.

Police in Argentina detained a man suspected in the killing of 11-year-old Máximo Jerez, who died early Sunday after gunmen attacked a birthday party in Rosario. Three other children, including a 2-year-old, were wounded. The arrest came amid outrage in the city, where drug-related violence has sharply escalated. After Máximo was buried Monday, angry neighbors in the northern Rosario area where the suspect lived attacked his home. Local television showed people throwing rocks, setting fires, and destroying the house. At one point, the suspect reportedly held a gun and appeared to fire it before police detained him and protected him from being lynched. Once he was taken away, residents wrecked the home and stole belongings. Neighbors also destroyed at least three other houses they said were used by drug dealers. Máximo’s aunt, Antonia Jerez, said the neighborhood was tired of violence and did not want “another Máximo.” Prosecutor Adrián Spelta said the killing was linked to a turf war between rival drug gangs, noting that even children’s presence no longer stops attacks. The case follows other recent violence in Rosario, including a threat to soccer star Lionel Messi after gunmen attacked a supermarket owned by his in-laws.

# Summary Police in Rosario, Argentina arrested a suspect in the killing of 11-year-old Máximo Jerez, who was shot during a birthday party attack early Sunday. Three other children, including a 2-year-old, were also injured in the incident. Following Máximo's burial Monday, angry neighbors attacked the suspect's home, setting fires and throwing rocks while police worked to protect him from the mob. After his arrest, residents destroyed at least three houses they claimed were used by drug dealers, expressing frustration over escalating violence in their community. Prosecutor Adrián Spelta attributed the killing to a turf war between rival drug gangs, noting that traditional boundaries protecting minors from gang violence have been crossed. The incident reflects a troubling pattern of drug-related violence in Rosario, which has become increasingly common despite being rare for Argentina overall. The city gained international attention when gunmen threatened soccer superstar Lionel Messi in a written message after firing at a supermarket owned by his in-laws the previous week.

Argentine President Mauricio Macri met Tuesday with Organization of American States Secretary-General Luis Almagro at the Olivos residence outside Buenos Aires. Almagro was in Argentina to attend commemorations marking the 24th anniversary of the AMIA Jewish community center bombing, which killed 85 people and injured 300. On Twitter, he honored the victims’ families and said all countries are responsible for eradicating terrorism and anti-Semitism. He also spoke at a World Jewish Congress event for survivors of terrorist attacks, saying anti-Semitism has no place in the Americas and that truth is needed for justice.

# Summary Argentine President Mauricio Macri met with Organization of American States Secretary-General Luis Almagro at the presidential residence in Buenos Aires. Almagro visited Argentina to commemorate the 24th anniversary of the 1994 AMIA attack, which killed 85 people and injured 300. At an event organized by the World Jewish Congress honoring terrorism survivors, Almagro emphasized that every country must combat terrorism and anti-Semitism. He stated that anti-Semitism has no place in the Americas and that truth is essential for justice.

At least five police officers were injured when a bomb sent in a package exploded at the 54th Police Station in Huechuraba, Santiago, Chile, authorities said Thursday. The parcel was addressed to the police commissioner, and two officers suffered serious injuries. Three nearby offices were also damaged. Police later identified the woman who sent the package. President Sebastian Pinera called the blast a terrorist attack, saying it was intended to spread fear.

# Summary A bomb-laden package exploded at a police station in Santiago, Chile on July 26, injuring five officers, including the police commissioner. Two officers sustained serious injuries. The parcel was addressed to the commissioner, and authorities identified the woman who sent it. Three nearby offices were damaged. Chilean President Sebastian Pinera classified the incident as a terrorist attack, stating that sending an explosive package to a police station is intended to cause terror.

Ecuadorian authorities said Friday that 57 prison guards and police officers who had been held hostage for more than a day in six prisons were released safely, after a wave of violence that officials blamed on criminal groups resisting government attempts to retake control of the country’s jails. The National Service for Attention to Persons Deprived of Liberty said the 50 guards and seven police officers were safe, but did not explain how they were freed. Earlier in the day, provincial officials had reported partial releases, including 44 hostages at a prison in Cuenca, before confirming that all 57 had been released. The hostage crisis came amid a coordinated series of explosions and attacks across Ecuador. In less than 48 hours, four car bombs and three other explosive devices detonated in different parts of the country. Early Friday, a bridge in the coastal province of El Oro was damaged by dynamite, though no one was injured. Hours earlier, another bridge in Napo province, in Ecuador’s Amazon region, was struck by an explosive device made from a gas tank packed with dynamite. Police said the attacks were part of a broader response by gangs to government efforts to regain control of prisons by relocating inmates, seizing weapons, and taking other security measures. The violence began Wednesday night with a car bomb in Quito near a former corrections office, followed by two more car bombs in El Oro. Another vehicle exploded Thursday outside the current offices of the prison agency in Quito, and an explosive device also went off in Cuenca. Authorities arrested several suspects in connection with the blasts: six people were ordered held in the Quito case, and police said four suspects, including a minor, were detained in Napo after dynamite was found in a taxi. Security analyst Daniel Pontón called the attacks “systematic and clearly planned,” saying they showed the state’s failure to prevent violence and suggesting the orders likely came from prisons via cellphones. He said the attacks appeared intended to spread fear and influence politics ahead of Ecuador’s Oct. 15 presidential runoff. Officials say Ecuador’s recent surge in violence stems from a power vacuum after the 2020 killing of Jorge Zambrano, leader of Los Choneros. Rival gangs linked to Mexican and Colombian cartels have since fought for control of drug routes and territory, including prisons, where authorities say at least 400 inmates have died since 2021. The unrest comes just three weeks after the assassination of presidential candidate Fernando Villavicencio, who had campaigned against organized crime and accused Los Choneros leader Adolfo Macías, known as “Fito,” of threatening him.

# Ecuador Releases 57 Hostages After Criminal Gang Violence Ecuador's government announced Friday that 57 law enforcement officers—50 guards and seven police officers—held hostage across six prisons for more than a day have been safely released. The government attributed the hostage-taking to criminal groups retaliating against authorities' efforts to regain control of several large correctional facilities through inmate relocation, weapon seizures, and other measures. The hostage release followed an escalating wave of violence orchestrated by criminal gangs with imprisoned members. Early Friday, explosives damaged a bridge in El Oro province, part of a series of attacks that included four car bombs and three explosive devices detonated across the country within 48 hours. No injuries were reported from the bridge explosion, but the coordinated attacks raised alarm about the state's ability to maintain security. The violence began Wednesday night with a car bomb in Quito near a corrections office, followed by two additional car bombs in El Oro province. Another vehicle exploded Thursday outside the corrections system's current offices in Quito, and an explosive device detonated in Cuenca. A judge ordered six suspects arrested in connection with the capital blasts to remain in custody pending investigation. Police arrested four additional suspects—three adults and a minor—in Napo province while traveling in a taxi containing dynamite blocks synchronized to an explosive device with a slow fuse. Authorities performed two controlled detonations. Security analyst Daniel Pontón characterized the attacks as "systematic and clearly planned," criticizing the state's ineffectiveness in preventing violence. He expressed concern that the escalating violence aims to generate fear and influence politics ahead of Ecuador's October 15 presidential runoff election. Pontón warned that without intervention, attacks against the general population could follow. The violence stems from gang conflicts over drug-trafficking routes and territorial control, particularly within prisons. Since 2021, at least 400 inmates have died in Ecuador's detention facilities. The Los Choneros gang and similar groups linked to Mexican and Colombian cartels dominate these conflicts. The escalation intensified following the August 9 assassination of presidential candidate Fernando Villavicencio, a vocal organized crime opponent. Villavicencio had accused Los Choneros and imprisoned leader Adolfo Macías ("Fito") of threatening him days before his death. Authorities attribute the broader three-year violence spike to a power vacuum created by the 2020 killing of previous Los Choneros leader Jorge Zambrano ("Rasquiña").

Argentine football star Angel Di Maria said he will not end his career in Rosario, his hometown, because of repeated threats against his family. The 36-year-old World Cup winner had previously hoped to return to Rosario Central, but said a recent attack made that impossible. According to Di Maria, a box containing a pig’s head and a bullet in the forehead was left at his sister’s business, along with a note warning that if he returned to Rosario Central, the next head would be that of his daughter Pia. Di Maria told Rosario3 that he would not return “in this way” and would not allow his family to be targeted, saying his priority is their “peace and happiness.” He said the threats followed earlier intimidation, including a note thrown onto a family property in March warning that he and his family would be killed if he joined a club in Rosario. Authorities had described that earlier threat as the work of “criminal organizations” showing force. While Santa Fe Governor Maximiliano Pullaro said security protocols existed for public figures, Di Maria rejected that claim, arguing that ordinary Rosario residents already face severe violence and insecurity. The article notes that Rosario has seen a surge in gang-related crime and that other South American footballers have also faced threats, including Lionel Messi’s family and Luis Diaz’s father.

# Summary Argentine soccer star Ángel Di María has abandoned plans to finish his career with his boyhood club, Rosario Central, citing safety concerns for his family. The 36-year-old World Cup winner revealed that a pig's head with a bullet through its forehead was thrown at his sister's business, accompanied by a threatening note warning that his daughter would be next if he returned to Rosario. This incident follows a previous threat in March, when a note was thrown into a family property warning against him joining any Rosario club. Argentine authorities attributed these threats to criminal organizations attempting to demonstrate their power. Di María expressed frustration with government claims about security protocols, arguing it was disrespectful to discuss his protection when ordinary Rosario residents cannot safely work or use public transportation without fear of robbery or violence. The situation reflects a broader pattern of criminal threats targeting high-profile South American footballers. Similar incidents include an attack on a shop owned by Lionel Messi's wife's family in Rosario and the kidnapping of Liverpool player Luis Díaz's father in Colombia last year.

Volunteers delivering earthquake relief in Mexico’s southern Oaxaca state were attacked and robbed, the Roman Catholic Archdiocese said. Unidentified gunmen ambushed a pickup carrying young aid workers on Tuesday. According to foundation administrator Carlos Arvizu, one person was shot, another beaten, and a woman raped. The attackers also stole cellphones and about $2,000. The aid effort followed the September 7 magnitude 8.1 quake and a September 23 aftershock that devastated the region.

# Summary Young Catholic volunteers delivering earthquake relief supplies in Oaxaca, Mexico were attacked and robbed by unidentified gunmen on Tuesday. One volunteer was shot, another beaten, and a woman was raped during the incident. The attackers stole cellphones and approximately $2,000. The region suffered two earthquakes in September—magnitude 8.1 and 6.1—prompting church groups to distribute aid throughout affected communities.

Colombian authorities say they have arrested a Cuban man accused of plotting to kill U.S. diplomats in Bogotá in the name of the Islamic State. The suspect, Raul Gutierrez, was brought in handcuffs to a Bogotá courtroom on Thursday, where a judge ordered him held without bail on terrorism and conspiracy charges. He had been arrested earlier in the week in Pereira, in western Colombia, during a coordinated investigation involving Colombian police, Spanish police, and the FBI. Authorities said they intercepted communications from late February in which Gutierrez allegedly discussed building and detonating a homemade explosive in a Bogotá restaurant where he had applied for work as a dishwasher. The restaurant was reportedly frequented by U.S. diplomats. In another Telegram message, he allegedly said he was willing to blow himself up for Allah and ISIS. Colombia’s police chief, Gen. Jorge Nieto, said investigators seized electronic devices that support the suspicion he was preparing a terrorist attack, but he declined to give more details. Gutierrez pleaded not guilty at his first court appearance Wednesday. Officials said he had been expelled from Colombia twice before. He first entered legally in 2015 on a visa, reportedly intending to eventually reach the United States, but authorities later discovered he had obtained the visa through false statements and deported him to Cuba. He returned in 2016 by crossing overland from Ecuador, which does not require visas for Cubans, and was expelled again in 2017. He is believed to have re-entered Colombia for a third time at the start of this year. Spanish police said they had monitored Gutierrez online for weeks and saw signs of radicalization, including his use of “jihadist” on social media and militant clothing. Prosecutors also said he had received detailed instructions from people in Spain and Morocco on how to carry out an attack against Americans. The U.S. Embassy and FBI declined to comment.

# Colombia Arrests Cuban Man in Plot to Kill US Diplomats Colombian police arrested Raul Gutierrez, a Cuban national, on terrorism and conspiracy charges after intercepting communications revealing an alleged plot to kill American diplomats. Gutierrez appeared in a Bogota courtroom Thursday and was ordered held without bail. He pleaded not guilty at his initial court appearance Wednesday. The investigation, coordinated with Spanish police and the FBI, uncovered intercepted messages from late February in which Gutierrez allegedly discussed plans to construct and detonate a homemade explosive device at a Bogota restaurant where he sought employment as a dishwasher. The restaurant was frequented by U.S. diplomats. Messages sent via Telegram also allegedly showed Gutierrez expressing willingness to commit suicide bombing for ISIS and Allah. Police seized electronic devices supporting the terrorism hypothesis, though authorities declined to discuss specific evidence details. Gutierrez had been expelled from Colombia twice previously. He initially entered legally in 2015 on a visa obtained through false statements, intending to reach the United States. After deportation to Cuba, he illegally re-entered Colombia in 2016 from Ecuador, which doesn't require Cuban visas. He was expelled again in 2017 but reportedly returned at the start of 2019. Spanish police monitored Gutierrez's online activities over several weeks, observing signs of radical Islamic indoctrination, including adding "jihadist" to social media accounts and wearing militant-identifying clothing. Prosecutors stated he received precise attack instructions from contacts in Spain and Morocco targeting Americans. The U.S. Embassy in Colombia, one of the world's largest, serves as a crucial hub for U.S.-Colombian anti-narcotics and counterinsurgency cooperation. Despite security improvements following Colombia's decades-long conflict, U.S. diplomats face movement restrictions reflecting ongoing dangers from terrorism and crime.

U.S. President Donald Trump said Wednesday that American and Iranian officials will hold talks next week, as a fragile ceasefire between Israel and Iran appears to be holding. Speaking at a NATO summit in The Hague, Trump said the fighting between Israel and Iran had ended and that discussions would focus on Iran’s nuclear program. He added that he was not especially interested in reopening negotiations over Tehran’s nuclear ambitions, saying he did not know whether a formal agreement would be necessary at all. The planned talks come after U.S. strikes on three Iranian nuclear sites on Sunday. A leaked U.S. intelligence assessment reportedly concluded that the core elements of Iran’s nuclear program were likely not destroyed, but instead set back by only several months. Trump rejected that assessment and repeated his claim that the sites were “obliterated.” He said the strikes had pushed Iran’s nuclear-weapons capability back “for many years to come,” and argued that this result could last indefinitely if Iran does not regain access to nuclear material. Trump also defended the strikes by comparing them to the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, saying the attack “ended the war.” Separately, Axios reported that Trump’s push to end the conflict began soon after the U.S. bombing. According to the report, Trump instructed Special Envoy Steve Witkoff to tell Iran he wanted a deal to stop the fighting. Iran reportedly refused to engage until it retaliated against U.S. targets. Before launching missiles at a U.S. base in Qatar, Iran informed the Trump administration through Qatar about the timing and targets of the strike. Afterward, Iran told the White House it would not carry out further attacks, and the U.S. said it would not retaliate and was ready to resume talks. Axios also reported that Trump called Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Monday and urged an end to the conflict. Netanyahu reportedly agreed to the ceasefire on the condition that Iran stop firing missiles.

# Summary President Donald Trump announced on Wednesday at a NATO summit in The Hague that American and Iranian officials would hold talks next week to discuss Iran's nuclear program, as a fragile ceasefire between Israel and Iran appears to hold. Trump stated he was not particularly interested in reaching a formal nuclear agreement, saying: "I don't care if I have an agreement or not." He indicated the talks would follow U.S. strikes on three Iranian nuclear sites conducted on Sunday. According to leaked U.S. intelligence, those strikes likely only delayed Iran's nuclear program by several months rather than destroying it completely. However, Trump dismissed these reports, claiming the targets were "obliterated" and asserting the strikes have set back Iran's nuclear weapons development for "many years to come." Trump justified the strikes by comparing them to the atomic bombings that ended World War Two, stating the Iranian strikes were "essentially the same thing." According to reporting by Axios, Trump's ceasefire efforts began immediately after Sunday's strikes. Trump instructed his Middle East Special Envoy Steve Witkoff to convey his willingness to negotiate with Iran. Initially, Iran refused diplomacy, insisting on retaliatory action first. However, Iran notified the Trump administration in advance of its missile strike on a U.S. base in Qatar. After launching this attack, Iran immediately informed the White House it would conduct no further strikes against U.S. targets. The U.S. responded that it would not retaliate and expressed readiness to resume negotiations. Trump also called Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who agreed to a ceasefire, with Israel promising to refrain from further strikes if Iran did likewise.

American and British citizens have been caught up in Ethiopia’s sweeping detentions of ethnic Tigrayans under a new state of emergency, according to an Associated Press report from Nairobi. The detentions are taking place as Ethiopia’s war intensifies and Tigrayan forces advance toward Addis Ababa, prompting fears of a wider crackdown. Thousands of Tigrayans have already been detained in the capital and elsewhere in the country. On Thursday, those fears grew after authorities ordered landlords to register tenants’ identities with police. In some neighborhoods, men carrying sticks were seen on the streets as volunteer “community policing” groups searched for Tigrayans to report to authorities. The Ethiopian government says it is arresting people suspected of backing the Tigray forces, which are moving closer to the capital after a year-long conflict that began with a political dispute. But human rights groups, lawyers, relatives of detainees, and even the government-backed Ethiopian Human Rights Commission say the arrests appear to be based largely on ethnicity. Children and elderly people have also been detained. Among those affected is a British national, Kiros Amdemariam Gebreab, whose daughter said he was arrested at his home in Addis Ababa on Nov. 1. The 55-year-old had lived in the U.K. for more than 25 years and was in Ethiopia working on PhD studies. His daughter said he had no political involvement and was detained “purely for being a Tigrayan human being.” She said the family has not been allowed to communicate with him. The British government said it has raised his case with Ethiopian authorities and believes only a very small number of U.K. nationals have been detained. At least two U.S. citizens are also among those detained. One case involves a hotelier and his son, who were arrested at their home on Nov. 2, the night the state of emergency was declared. Police accused them of supporting Tigrayan forces, according to another family member. The father, who is in his late 70s, was released after three days, but his son remains in custody and has not been charged. The U.S. Embassy had not responded to questions at the time of the report. Most detainees are Ethiopian citizens, including some prominent figures. A lawyer said the CEO of Lion Bank and seven colleagues, along with a customer, were detained Monday morning and later released that evening. An Ethiopian Orthodox Church official said dozens of priests, monks, deacons, and others had also been detained because they are Tigrayan, including an assistant to the patriarch. A city civil servant said two friends were arrested in a cafe after police overheard them speaking Tigrinya; he has not heard from them since and fears he may be next. Federal police spokesman Jeylan Abdi said he did not know how many people had been detained since the emergency was imposed, and claimed the arrests were not ethnically motivated. He said searches had uncovered weapons and military uniforms. He also confirmed the presence of volunteer neighborhood patrols but said they were not new and were helping police protect local security. The crackdown comes amid a devastating war that has killed thousands, displaced hundreds of thousands, and left millions in Tigray under blockade. The African Union and the United States have recently pushed for an immediate cease-fire and talks, while U.S. Secretary of State Antony Blinken warned that the conflict could spread beyond Ethiopia and destabilize the region.

# Summary: Ethiopia's Mass Detentions of Tigrayans Ensnare Foreign Citizens Ethiopia's government has declared a state of emergency and initiated mass detentions of ethnic Tigrayans as Tigray regional forces advance toward the capital, Addis Ababa. The detentions have swept up thousands of people, including American and British citizens, raising international concerns about the escalating conflict. ## Scale and Methods of Detentions According to the Associated Press investigation, detentions have occurred across Ethiopia's capital and throughout the country. Authorities have ordered landlords to register tenants' identities with police, while volunteer groups armed with sticks patrol streets searching for Tigrayans to report. Federal police spokesman Jeylan Abdi acknowledged he doesn't know the total number detained since the emergency was declared, as detainees are held at various police stations without a unified count. ## Government Claims vs. Human Rights Concerns Ethiopian authorities claim they are detaining suspected supporters of Tigray forces. However, human rights groups, lawyers, relatives, and Ethiopia's government-created Human Rights Commission assert that detentions are ethnically motivated, affecting children and elderly people regardless of political involvement. ## Foreign Citizens Affected At least two American citizens have been detained. A hotelier in his late seventies and his son were arrested on November 2; the father was released after three days, but the son remains in custody without charges. The family believes the arrests stem from supporting Tigray forces, though they deny this claim. A British national, Kiros Amdemariam Gebreab, 55, was detained at his home on November 1. His daughter told the AP he had lived in the United Kingdom for over 25 years and was visiting to pursue PhD studies. She emphasized his lack of political involvement and attributed his detention solely to his Tigrayan ethnicity. The British government has raised his case with Ethiopian authorities and believes a small number of UK nationals have been detained. ## Broader Detention Pattern Beyond foreign citizens, thousands of local Tigrayans have been arrested, including high-profile figures. The CEO of Lion Bank and seven colleagues were detained, along with dozens of Orthodox Church officials, priests, monks, and deacons. A civil servant reported that two friends were arrested at a café after plainclothes officers overheard them speaking Tigrinya, the Tigray language. ## Government Defense Police spokesman Jeylan Abdi dismissed allegations of ethnic targeting as "propaganda," claiming searches discovered weapons including assault rifles, heavy machine guns, and military uniforms in detainees' possession. He characterized volunteer patrols as community policing efforts, not new initiatives. ## Broader Conflict Context The detentions occur amid an ongoing year-long war triggered by political conflict between Ethiopia's government and Tigray forces. Thousands have been killed, millions in Tigray face government blockades, and hundreds of thousands in the Amhara region are displaced. International envoys from the African Union and United States have held urgent discussions seeking a ceasefire, though warring sides indicate negotiations will be difficult. An Ethiopian government airstrike struck Mekelle, the capital of the volatile Tigray region, on Friday, reportedly killing several people. The attack came after the collapse of a humanitarian cease-fire in northern Ethiopia that had paused fighting for five months. According to AFP, the Ethiopian Air Force bombed targets in Mekelle just before 3 p.m. local time. The article offers few additional details, but the strike marks a renewed escalation in the conflict following the breakdown of the truce.

# Summary The Ethiopian government launched an airstrike on Mekelle, the capital of the Tigray region, on Friday, reportedly killing several people. The U.S. military is investigating whether an airstrike against al-Shabaab in Somalia on Feb. 15 killed two Cuban doctors who had been held hostage by the militant group since 2019, AFRICOM said Tuesday. A spokesperson confirmed that a strike was carried out near the town of Jilib, but said the command was aware only of reports alleging two civilians were killed and had no further information yet. AFRICOM said it takes all claims of civilian casualties seriously and will continue assessing the operation. The inquiry follows an al-Shabaab statement on Saturday claiming that the airstrike killed the two doctors, identified as Assel Herrera Correa and Landy Rodriguez Hernandez. The group said the bombardment struck a house in Jilib around 12:10 a.m. and included an alleged photo of one of the men. Herrera, a general medicine specialist, and Rodriguez, a surgeon, were abducted on April 12, 2019, in the Kenyan border town of Mandera while traveling to work at Mandera hospital. A police officer escorting their convoy was killed in the attack. The two were among about 100 Cuban medical professionals sent to Kenya in 2018 under a bilateral agreement to expand specialized healthcare access. In May 2019, mediators from Kenya and Somalia said they had seen the doctors treating local residents in al-Shabaab-held Jubaland, and later reported that the militants were demanding a $1.5 million ransom for their release. The United States has carried out strikes against al-Shabaab in support of Somali forces since 2007. Violence has intensified since Somali President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud declared “total war” on the group in August 2022. Al-Shabaab, an al-Qaeda affiliate, controls rural areas in central and southern Somalia and continues attacks in Somalia, Kenya and Ethiopia.

Reports from Arab media say relations between Iran and Syria have become strained, mainly over economic issues and growing security suspicions, though analysts quoted in the article say the alliance is still likely intact. The immediate trigger appears to be Tehran’s decision to stop supplying subsidized petroleum products to Damascus. That move has deepened Syria’s already severe economic crisis and angered many Syrians, according to Middle East experts. At the same time, repeated Israeli strikes on pro-Iranian militia targets in Syria have prompted concern in Tehran and among its allies that some Syrian military figures may be passing information to Israel about the movements of Iranian-linked forces. The tensions intensified after a drone strike in late January hit a pro-Iranian militia truck convoy near the Syrian-Iraqi border. Following that attack, some reports claimed Syrian sources had been informing Israel about Iranian weapons shipments inside Syria. London-based Syrian analyst Ramy Abdel Rahman said Iran, Hezbollah, and Iraqi militia allies quickly changed personnel at the Boukamel border post and nearby positions after the strike. It was unclear whether Syrian government forces were included in those changes. Abdel Rahman rejected the idea that Syrians were responsible for leaking information, saying instead that people working for Israel were likely Lebanese or Iranian, not Syrian. He also argued that the pattern of some convoys being hit and others not suggested leaks from inside Iran about what the convoys were carrying. The Saudi-owned newspaper Asharq Alawsat similarly reported that Tehran and Damascus were tense because Iran feared Syrian sources might be helping Israel track Iranian and allied movements inside Syria. Joshua Landis of the University of Oklahoma said many Syrians, including some in the military, are unhappy with Iran’s conduct in the country and worry that Israeli attacks are hurting morale in President Bashar al-Assad’s forces. Still, he said the friction is unlikely to produce a major break because Iran, Syria, and Hezbollah are deeply intertwined. He added that Iran’s cutoff of subsidized fuel has worsened Syria’s economic collapse and left the country in a downward spiral, especially amid sanctions on Russia and Iran and continued military pressure. Khattar Abou Diab of the University of Paris said Iran has been Syria’s main benefactor since 2011, supplying most of the aid to Assad’s government in exchange for economic and political influence, including interests in land, buildings, and phosphate mines. He acknowledged friction, including the cancellation of an expected visit by Iranian President Ebrahim Raisi in December, but said cooperation remains strong. He pointed to a recent visit by Syrian Defense Minister Ali Abbas to Iran, where the two sides reportedly agreed to deepen intelligence and electronic cooperation and install a new air-defense system near Damascus. Iran analyst Mehrdad Khonsari said Tehran’s reduced support to Syria is tied to money being constrained by the stalemate over reviving the 2015 nuclear deal, the JCPOA. Even so, he too doubted a serious rupture, arguing that Assad has few better options than Iran, which he described as his most reliable partner over the past decade.

# Iran-Syria Relations Strained Over Economic and Security Issues Relations between Iran and Syria have deteriorated following Tehran's decision to halt subsidized petroleum shipments to Damascus, according to Arab media reports. The economic pressure comes alongside growing security concerns that have created friction between the longtime allies. Following this attack, both Iran and Syria grew suspicious that Syrian military sources might be leaking information about Iranian weapons shipments and militia movements to Israel. In response, Iran and its allies quickly replaced personnel at the Boukamel border crossing between Syria and Iraq. However, London-based Syrian analyst Ramy Abdel Rahman disputes claims of Syrian government involvement in intelligence sharing. He argues that Israeli informants are instead Lebanese and Iranian nationals working within pro-Iranian forces, with information likely coming from inside Iran regarding convoy contents rather than from Syrian sources. The economic dimension of the crisis is particularly severe. Joshua Landis, who directs the Middle East studies program at the University of Oklahoma, emphasizes that Iran's decision to stop selling subsidized petroleum has exacerbated Syria's already critical economic crisis, leaving the country with "no foreseeable way to get out of the downward spiral." Many Syrians, including military personnel, resent Iran's presence and worry that Israeli strikes are destroying morale within Assad's forces. Despite these tensions, Landis believes they are unlikely to cause a serious breach between the allied nations, as "Iran and Syria are connected at the hip." Khattar Abou Diab, a political science professor at the University of Paris, notes that Iran has been Syria's primary benefactor since 2011, providing substantial aid to President Assad's government in exchange for economic and political influence, including access to natural resources and government assets. He argues that cooperation remains strong despite friction, citing recent visits by Syrian Defense Minister Ali Abbas to Iran, where agreements were reached to strengthen electronic, intelligence, and air defense ties. Iran analyst Mehrdad Khonsari attributes Iran's reduced aid to financial constraints resulting from the stalled nuclear deal negotiations. He suggests that Iran's Revolutionary Guard views reviving the 2015 JCPOA nuclear agreement as essential to freeing resources for Syria and other regional priorities. Despite current tensions, analysts remain skeptical of a serious rift. Khonsari points out that Assad has few alternatives, noting that "Iran has been the most reliable partner that he's had" over the past 10-15 years. The South African National Editors’ Forum (SANEF) has condemned the killing of journalists in Gaza and urged an end to attacks on media workers. Its statement came after two more journalists were killed, raising the total number of journalists and media workers killed in Gaza since October 2023 to 208. Palestine TV correspondent Mohammed Mansour, his wife and child were killed in an Israeli airstrike on their home in Khan Younis. The attack was reported on social media by Al Jazeera journalist Hossam Shabat, 23, who was then killed more than an hour later in Beit Lahia when a drone strike hit his car. SANEF said these killings are part of broader war crimes and an assault on press freedom, with project manager Hopewell Radebe saying the attacks appear deliberate and violate international law.

# Summary The South African National Editors' Forum (SANEF) has condemned the killing of journalists in Gaza, with 208 journalists and media workers killed since October 2023. Recent deaths include Palestine TV correspondent Mohammed Mansour, killed alongside his wife and child in an Israeli airstrike in Khan Younis, and Al Jazeera journalist Hossam Shabat, killed by a drone strike in Beit Lahia. SANEF characterizes these killings as deliberate war crimes and violations of international law. Project manager Hopewell Radebe stated the attacks represent an assault on press freedom, noting journalists have documented drones targeting them, suggesting a deliberate Israeli policy.

The Nigerian Air Force (NAF) said it has completed its special air operation, “Operation Ruwan Wuta,” after carrying out further strikes on Boko Haram terrorist structures in the North East. According to a statement by NAF Director of Public Relations and Information, Air Commodore Olatukunbo Adesanya, the operation involved intensive day-and-night aerial bombardments of areas where Boko Haram fighters were reportedly trying to re-establish themselves. On the final day of the operation, 16 September 2017, NAF aircraft attacked structures in Kote, near Bama, where terrorists were suspected of holding a meeting. The location had been identified through intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance platforms as a Boko Haram-infested area with significant terrorist activity. Alpha Jet and F-7Ni aircraft carried out the air interdiction, dropping bombs on the target. A subsequent battle damage assessment showed that the structures were destroyed. The Air Force said the aim of the 10-day operation, which ran from 7 to 16 September, was to “rain significant fire” on Boko Haram hideouts, weaken the group’s ability to operate freely, and help ground forces gain momentum. Other locations successfully attacked included Parisu, Njimia, Zanari, Garin Maloma, Yale Market, Mungusum, Arra and Kote. A comprehensive assessment after the operation reportedly found no remaining Boko Haram activity in the targeted areas. Overall, the NAF said it flew 129 missions in 180 sorties, totaling more than 208 flying hours. The operation also included a medical outreach for internally displaced persons in camps near Maiduguri, the Sambisa general area and Rann. The Air Force provided free treatment and surgeries, including airlifting some patients to its medical centre in Maiduguri. In Rann alone, 700 IDPs received free treatment, while 146 of 1,032 screened across the camps underwent surgery. These included 90 eye surgeries and 56 general surgeries, with 60 others receiving medicated eyeglasses.

# Nigerian Air Force Completes Operation Against Boko Haram The Nigerian Air Force concluded "Operation Ruwan Weta," an intensive aerial bombardment campaign targeting Boko Haram terrorist hideouts in the North East, on September 16, 2017. The operation successfully destroyed multiple terrorist structures across eight locations, including Parisu, Njimia, Zanari, Garin Maloma, Yale Market, Mungusum, Arra, and Kote. During the final day of operations, the Air Force attacked suspected Boko Haram meeting locations in Kote near Bama using Alpha Jet and F-7Ni aircraft. Battle damage assessments confirmed the complete destruction of targeted structures and revealed the absence of terrorist activities in all attacked locations following the 10-day operation. To execute the campaign, the Air Force conducted 129 missions in 180 sorties, accumulating over 208 flying hours between September 7-16. The operation aimed to degrade Boko Haram's operational capabilities and provide support to ground forces. Beyond combat operations, the Air Force integrated a humanitarian medical outreach program serving internally displaced persons (IDPs) in camps near Maiduguri, Sambisa, and Rann. The initiative provided free medical treatment to 700 IDPs in Rann alone and screened 1,032 people across all beneficiary camps. Medical teams performed 90 eye surgeries, 56 general surgeries, and distributed 60 free medicated eyeglasses. The surgical interventions were scheduled to conclude on September 21, 2017.

Japan is preparing for possible pressure from President Donald Trump on defense issues when Prime Minister Shinzo Abe meets him at Mar-a-Lago in Florida beginning Tuesday. Tokyo is also watching closely for signs of Trump’s next move in Syria after last week’s U.S.-led airstrike with Britain and France, because past American military actions in the Middle East have often influenced Japanese security policy. The summit is already expected to be difficult, with trade disputes and North Korea on the agenda. Trump has also been pushing Japan to purchase more U.S. defense equipment. Japanese officials say it is hard to predict Trump’s intentions because his statements are often unclear or contradictory, leaving Tokyo uncertain about what demands may come next. Abe has publicly backed the “resolve” behind the strike on Syrian government facilities, which followed an alleged chemical attack on civilians by Bashar Assad’s regime on April 7. But a Defense Ministry official said Japan has little it can do directly at the moment, though it is gathering information and remains highly concerned. The article notes that Japan’s defense policy has repeatedly shifted in response to U.S. conflicts. During the 1991 Persian Gulf War, Japan provided about $13 billion in financial support but could not contribute troops, prompting criticism and leading to a 1992 law allowing Self-Defense Forces participation in U.N. peacekeeping. After the Sept. 11 attacks, Koizumi’s government enabled logistical support for U.S. forces, including naval refueling. In 2003, Japan expanded its role again to allow Ground Self-Defense Force humanitarian deployment to Iraq. Abe’s 2015 security legislation further broadened Japan’s ability to aid other countries’ militaries. As Washington increasingly expects allies to share more defense burdens, developments in Syria could affect both Japan’s budget and its security policy.

# Japan Prepares for Defense Discussions at Trump Summit Japan is bracing for potential defense demands from President Trump during Prime Minister Shinzo Abe's visit to Mar-a-Lago beginning Tuesday. The summit comes amid heightened concerns about U.S. military involvement in Syria following last week's Western airstrikes on Assad regime facilities, which Japan's leadership has cautiously supported. The meeting will address multiple pressing issues, including bilateral trade and North Korea diplomacy, but Trump's push for Japan to purchase substantial American defense equipment remains a central concern. Japanese policymakers face challenges interpreting Trump's sometimes contradictory statements regarding U.S. foreign policy intentions. Japan's defense involvement has historically been shaped by American military actions. During the 1991 Persian Gulf War, Japan provided $13 billion in economic support but faced criticism for lacking on-the-ground presence. This prompted a 1992 law permitting Self-Defense Forces deployment in UN peacekeeping operations. The September 11 attacks further expanded Japanese military capabilities. The Koizumi administration authorized naval refueling support for American forces and later deployed Ground Self-Defense Forces to Iraq for humanitarian operations. The 2015 security legislation under Abe enabled Japan to support allied militaries without special measures. As the U.S. shifts away from its "global policeman" role, American officials increasingly expect Japan to assume greater defense responsibilities and costs. The escalating Syrian conflict and resulting tensions between Russia, the U.S., France, and Britain could significantly impact Japan's defense budget and military policies going forward.

Hà Nội’s education sector has undergone a dramatic transformation over the 70 years since the capital was liberated, growing from a system that served only a small fraction of children into one of the country’s largest and strongest educational hubs. According to Trần Thế Cương, director of the municipal Education and Training Department, the city now has 2,913 public schools, nearly 2.3 million students and about 130,000 teachers. Among these are one institution for training educational staff and 29 centres for vocational and education work. Nearly 80 per cent of public schools have met national standards, while 23 schools have been recognised as high-quality institutions. Hà Nội is also preparing to invest in seven advanced, modern multi-level schools, each covering more than five hectares. The city’s recent academic results reflect this progress. In the 2023–24 school year, Hà Nội led the country with 184 students winning awards at the National Excellent Student Selection Exam, 43 more than in 2023. Three students won prizes at the National Science and Technology Competition, and 35 were recognised in the national student entrepreneurship contest. Hà Nội students also achieved success internationally, with two earning gold medals at the International Biology Olympiad and the International Chemistry Olympiad. At the National High School Graduation Exam, Hà Nội improved significantly, rising five places to 11th nationally, while recording the highest number of perfect scores in the country, with 915 full marks. In sports, Hà Nội students won 339 medals and placed second overall at the 2024 National Phù Đổng Sports Festival. The article contrasts these achievements with the city’s condition in 1954, when Hà Nội had only three kindergartens, 96 primary schools, four secondary schools and one vocational school, serving fewer than 10,000 students. At that time, education met only about 20 per cent of demand, leaving 80 per cent of children from working-class families without schooling. In the years immediately after liberation, the city launched efforts to expand literacy and mobilised teachers and volunteers to support education. Despite great difficulty, Hà Nội schools opened their first academic year just ten days after the capital was fully liberated. Primary schools began on October 15, 1954, and secondary schools on October 18, 1954. The decade from 1954 to 1965 was a crucial period in which the education sector worked to recover from war damage while contributing to economic revival and broader development. From 1965 to 1975, the sector faced severe challenges as the country supported the southern front while enduring American bombing in the north. Teachers and students were evacuated to rural areas to continue learning, but schools, classes and enrolment continued to grow. After national reunification in 1975, Hà Nội shifted its focus toward improving quality, with greater attention to holistic education, vocational training and career guidance. During the reform era from 1986 to 2007, the city’s education system expanded rapidly and modernised its curriculum and teaching methods. Hà Nội became the first locality in the country to achieve universal primary education in 1990 and universal lower secondary education in 1999. Public, semi-public and private schools all developed, reinforcing the capital’s role as a national education centre. Since 2008, after administrative boundary expansion under National Assembly Resolution No. 15, Hà Nội’s education system has continued to grow in scale and diversity. It now leads the country in the number of schools, teachers and students, while also developing new educational models to meet increasingly varied learning needs. Generations of Hà Nội students have become a high-quality workforce contributing to the capital’s and the nation’s industrialisation and modernisation. The article also highlights the importance of the revised Capital Law, passed in June 2024 and effective from January 1, 2025. Article 22 sets out strategies to make Hà Nội a leading centre for high-quality education aligned with digital transformation, innovation and international integration. It calls for investment in high-quality public schools and multi-level institutions, and encourages cooperation between public schools and foreign educational institutions to narrow the gap with private schools. Nguyễn Tùng Lâm, vice president of the Việt Nam Psychological and Educational Science Association, said the law gives Hà Nội room to innovate and reinforces the need for the city’s education sector to lead nationally, with schools built on autonomy, democracy, humanity and creativity.

The system includes one teacher training institution and 29 vocational and education centers, with nearly 80 percent of public schools meeting national standards. International success included two gold medals at the International Biology and Chemistry Olympiads. Hà Nội students also achieved 339 medals at the 2024 National Phù Đổng Sports Festival, placing second overall. ## Historical Context The contrast with 1954 is striking. Diverse educational institutions flourished, including public, semi-public, and private schools.
