Article 22 outlines strategies for advancing education, aiming to make Hà Nội a prominent center for high-quality education adaptable to digital transformation and international integration. The law mandates investing in high-quality public schools and requires public institutions to collaborate with foreign educational establishments. According to Nguyễn Tùng Lâm, Vice President of the Việt Nam Psychological and Educational Science Association, the education sector must maintain its position as the nation's locomotive. He emphasized schools should center on autonomy, democracy, humanity, and creativity, allowing independence in selecting educational methods and developing curricula tailored to students' needs, thereby maximizing their potential and qualities.

At the G20 summit in Osaka, Japan, President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin projected a strikingly friendly image, laughing together, joking about election interference, and openly showing their personal rapport on a global stage. Their meeting on Friday came one day after Putin had praised Trump’s nationalist politics and declared that liberalism in the West had become obsolete. During their first face-to-face meeting in nearly a year, a reporter asked Trump whether he would warn Putin not to meddle in the 2020 U.S. election. Trump answered, “Of course,” but then turned to Putin and jokingly said, “Don’t meddle in the election,” repeating the remark while pointing at him. Putin laughed. The exchange recalled the Helsinki summit in 2018, when Trump did not publicly rebuke Putin over Russian election interference and did not side clearly with U.S. intelligence agencies. Putin continues to deny the conclusion reached by special counsel Robert Mueller that Russia interfered in the 2016 election to help Trump win. In an interview with the Financial Times this week, Putin called the allegation “mythical interference” and suggested Trump had simply recognized changes in American society and capitalized on them. Putin also praised Trump’s efforts to curb migration and drugs from Mexico, tying those themes to his broader argument that liberalism has outlived its usefulness. He said the liberal idea had become “obsolete,” arguing that it wrongly assumes migrants can “kill, plunder and rape with impunity” because their rights must be protected. The two leaders also mocked the news media. During a photo opportunity, Trump told Putin, “Get rid of them, fake news. You don’t have the problem in Russia. We have it; you don’t have it.” Putin replied, “Yes, yes, we have it. The same.” They then laughed before sitting down for their first substantive discussion since the Mueller report was issued in April. Mueller concluded that Moscow extensively interfered in the 2016 campaign, though he did not establish a criminal conspiracy between Russia and the Trump campaign. Trump’s joking about interference drew sharp criticism in the United States. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer said the joke was on America and that “Putin’s the only one laughing.” He accused Trump of giving Putin a “green light” to interfere in 2020. Former President Jimmy Carter was even more direct, saying he believed Russian interference helped put Trump in the White House. Carter said there was “no doubt” Russia interfered and suggested a full investigation would show Trump did not actually win the 2016 election. Despite the controversy, Trump said in Japan that “many positive things” would come from his relationship with Putin, who invited him to visit Russia next year for the 75th anniversary of the Allied victory in World War II. Their warm tone stood in contrast to Putin’s tense meeting the same day with outgoing British Prime Minister Theresa May. May confronted him again over the March 2018 nerve-agent attack on former Russian spy Sergei Skripal and his daughter Yulia in Salisbury, England. Britain blames Russia for the poisoning with Novichok, which Moscow denies. May said there could be no normalization of relations until Russia stopped “irresponsible and destabilizing activity.” Trump’s relationship with Putin has been unusually close, but the two countries remain at odds on several major issues. The Trump administration has imposed sanctions and other pressure on Russia. Washington and Moscow are also on opposite sides of the crisis with Iran, after the U.S. accused Tehran of shooting down an American drone. Trump canceled a retaliatory strike but said Iran must not obtain nuclear weapons or support militant groups. Trump had previously canceled a planned meeting with Putin at the G20 summit in Argentina in November after Russia seized Ukrainian vessels and crews in the Sea of Azov. Those sailors remain detained, and Trump said in Osaka that their fate had not yet been discussed. The two leaders also face a deteriorating arms-control landscape: both have announced withdrawal from the 1987 Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty, which is set to end this summer, and the New START treaty expires in 2021 unless extended. After the meeting, the White House said both men agreed to continue discussing a “21st century model of arms control,” which Trump said should include China. They also discussed Syria, Venezuela and Ukraine, where the U.S. and Russia remain on opposing sides.

# Trump and Putin Make Light of Election Interference at G20 Summit At the Group of 20 summit in Osaka, Japan, President Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin met for their first face-to-face discussion in nearly a year, displaying a notably friendly rapport while dismissing concerns about Russian election interference and expressing shared criticism of the media. ## The Light-Hearted Exchange When a reporter asked Trump whether he would warn Putin against meddling in the 2020 election, the president responded affirmatively but then turned to Putin and jokingly said, "Don't meddle in the election," while pointing at him playfully. Putin laughed at the exchange. This moment recalled a similarly controversial meeting between the two leaders in Helsinki a year earlier, where Trump notably failed to admonish Putin regarding 2016 election interference and sided with him over U.S. intelligence agencies. ## Putin's Defense and Political Views Putin has consistently disputed special counsel Robert Mueller's findings that Russia interfered in the 2016 election to help Trump win, calling it "mythical interference." After their meeting, the White House announced the leaders agreed to discuss a "21st century model of arms control," with Trump insisting it include China. ## Putin's Other Meetings In contrast to his warm exchange with Trump, Putin had a frosty meeting with outgoing British Prime Minister Theresa May, who confronted him over the 2018 nerve agent poisoning of former Russian double agent Sergei Skripal and his daughter in Salisbury. Britain accused Russia of using the nerve agent Novichok, which Russia denied. May demanded that the Russian military officers accused of involvement face justice and stated that bilateral relations cannot normalize until Russia ceases destabilizing activities. The summit illustrated Trump's prioritization of personal relationships with Putin while highlighting deepening partisan divisions over Russia policy within the United States.

Saudi Arabia remained China’s biggest crude oil supplier in September, supported by demand from new Chinese refineries, while imports from Iran and Venezuela continued to decline under the pressure of U.S. sanctions, according to Chinese customs data released on Friday. Saudi crude arrivals totaled 7.17 million tonnes in September, or about 1.74 million barrels per day. That was down from 7.79 million tonnes in August, but far above the 3.784 million tonnes imported in September 2018. Over the first nine months of the year, China imported 59.7 million tonnes of Saudi crude, up 55.4% from the same period a year earlier. The September figures came before the major Sept. 14 drone and missile attack on Saudi oil-processing facilities, which cut half of the kingdom’s production. That disruption is expected to affect October deliveries. During the incident, Saudi Aramco asked customers to switch crude grades for cargoes scheduled in the second half of September and early October, and it delayed some crude and product shipments by several days. Imports from Iran remained weak under tightened U.S. sanctions. China bought 538,878 tonnes of Iranian crude in September, down from 787,657 tonnes in August and far below 2.13 million tonnes a year earlier. Refinitiv said cargoes lifted after sanctions were tightened in May were routed into China’s strategic petroleum reserve sites in Tianjin, Jinzhou, Huizhou and Zhoushan. Venezuelan shipments also fell sharply to 588,698 tonnes from 1.45 million tonnes in August. Refinitiv said the September arrivals came from a single shipment loaded in late July. China National Petroleum Corp skipped Venezuelan loadings for a second straight month, aiming to avoid violating U.S. sanctions. Venezuelan crude was instead diverted to Malaysia’s Tanjung Bruas transshipment hub and then shipped to China under new grade names such as Singma. China’s imports of Malaysian crude rose to 1.97 million tonnes in September. U.S. crude imports dropped to 517,982 tonnes from 1.01 million tonnes in August amid a new 5% Chinese tariff. Russia remained China’s No. 2 supplier, with shipments rising to 6.31 million tonnes.

# Summary Saudi Arabia maintained its position as China's largest crude oil supplier in September 2019, delivering 7.17 million tonnes (1.74 million barrels per day), despite a significant decline from August's 7.79 million tonnes. The year-to-date imports reached 59.7 million tonnes, up 55.4% compared to the same period in 2018. The September 14 drone and missile attack on Saudi oil-processing facilities, which disabled half of the country's production capacity, necessitated grade switching and delivery delays for customers. This disruption is expected to impact October shipments. Imports from Iran and Venezuela continued declining due to US sanctions. Iranian crude arrivals fell to 538,878 tonnes in September from 787,657 tonnes in August and 2.13 million tonnes a year earlier. All post-May Iranian oil entered China's strategic petroleum reserves at designated sites. Venezuelan shipments plummeted to 588,698 tonnes from 1.45 million tonnes in August. Chinese state oil company CNPC skipped Venezuelan loadings for the second consecutive month to avoid breaching US sanctions. Notably, Venezuelan crude was diverted to Malaysia's Tanjung Bruas transshipment hub, rebranded as new grades like Singma, then shipped to China. Malaysian crude imports surged to 1.97 million tonnes in September from 646,236 tonnes in August, reflecting this rerouting strategy. US crude oil imports dropped to 517,982 tonnes from 1.01 million tonnes in August as China imposed a 5% tariff amid escalating trade tensions. Russia, China's second-largest supplier, provided 6.31 million tonnes in September, slightly up from August's 6.02 million tonnes.

Members of Taiwan’s Presbyterian Church met in southern Taiwan on Aug. 12 to discuss how their congregations could strengthen community resilience through civil defense. The gathering took place at Tavadran Presbyterian Church in Rinari, a Paiwan village in Pingtung County at the foot of the mountains dividing Taiwan’s east and west coasts. About 200 elders, ministers, and members of the Paiwan Presbytery attended the event to hear proposals on how the church’s existing networks could be used to prepare communities for emergencies. The main speaker was Ljavakaw Tjaljimaraw (謝易宏), founder and leader of the civil defense group Academia Formosana, which he launched in July after leaving Academia Sinica to work on the project full time. Its central initiative is the “Noah’s Ark Plan,” which Tjaljimaraw hopes to implement through the Presbyterian Church’s broad network of congregations across Taiwan. He described the idea as organizing Taiwan’s 1,200 Presbyterian congregations into a kind of ark so that, in the event of flood or war, communities can help and protect one another. Tjaljimaraw said Academia Formosana’s mission is to promote community-based civil defense rooted in a strong attachment to Taiwan. He emphasized that the purpose is not abstract political theory but practical preparation for emergencies. Under the Ark Plan, each congregation would serve as a basic unit for disaster management. This would include practical training to ensure the stability of supplies, emergency healthcare, leadership structures, and planning for different kinds of disaster scenarios. During his presentation, Tjaljimaraw showed maps of Presbyterian congregations in Pingtung in relation to military bases, schools, police stations, and beaches to illustrate the kinds of threats communities might face. He urged attendees to think through local safety plans based on their specific surroundings, including possible airstrike locations, likely enemy landing sites, and where essential resources could be found. He also asked them to consider how Indigenous villages might respond if outsiders sought shelter there during a conflict, whether there would be enough supplies if church members working in cities returned home suddenly, and how communities might deal with looting if resources ran short. He made clear that Saturday’s talk was only an initial presentation, and that more hands-on training would come later. He asked pastors, elders, and deacons to bring the idea back to their congregations for discussion and decision-making, and said practical skills would be provided to communities that chose to join the project. The article notes that civil defense has become a prominent topic in Taiwan, especially when it involves civilian training for armed resistance. Tjaljimaraw, however, stressed that Academia Formosana’s approach is not about weapons. He said the focus is “purely civil defense” and concerns how people should prepare themselves for shortages of food, water, and electricity, as well as the possibility of looting. In his view, the issue is the coherent organization of communities, not guns or combat. Tjaljimaraw explained that the Presbyterian Church is a natural starting point because of its long history and strong communal structure. The church has existed for nearly 160 years, surviving Japanese colonial rule and the era of Kuomintang authoritarianism. It reports nearly 260,000 members in more than 1,200 congregations, with around 500 congregations led by Indigenous Taiwanese. He said the church is especially important in Indigenous society because it is already a strong community network. He also invoked Corinthians 12:25-27, which speaks of one member suffering with all and one member being honored with all, as a biblical example of shared responsibility and unity. Tjaljimaraw argued that each congregation already has its own decision-making structure and that pastors and elders are natural local leaders. He said what is needed is coherent leadership that can work together to defend land and people. Pastor Aravas Talalang (李耀光), who leads Tavadran Presbyterian Church, said concern for community defense is not new. Although media coverage has heightened public awareness of cross-strait tensions, he said Indigenous communities have long thought about protecting themselves. He referred to historical oppression of Indigenous people by Taiwan’s government and said Paiwan people have shed blood in the pursuit of freedom and democracy. He said he wants his people to be able to train to protect their lives and help themselves. While he acknowledged that training all Taiwanese people or all Presbyterian congregations is beyond his reach, he noted that about one-third of Paiwan people belong to the Presbyterian Church. If the church is well prepared, he said, that could influence a large portion of the wider community. The discussion also touched on politics, especially Taiwan’s January 2024 presidential election. Paiwan Presbytery General Secretary Ljegean Tudalimaw (樂歌安督達里茂) asked whether the election outcome would affect the likelihood of conflict. Tjaljimaraw replied that war, like a typhoon, is not determined by who is president and that broader trends suggest conflict could eventually come regardless of the leader in office. Afterward, he said his answer was not meant to avoid politics or take a neutral stance. Rather, he said it reflected his belief that it is unrealistic to treat politicians as idols capable of preventing war. He openly said he has political views and partisan preferences, including dissatisfaction with the Democratic Progressive Party and disdain for other parties he considers worse. He added that he believed the question reflected “anti-DPP” framing that presents the election as a false choice between voting for Lai Ching-te and risking war or voting for another candidate and securing peace. Tjaljimaraw said this was misleading and argued that war would happen regardless of who is elected because it results from broader systemic changes and disturbances.

# Summary South Korea's foreign ministry expressed "deep concerns" on Thursday regarding Myanmar's military airstrikes targeting civilians. China’s AG600, believed to be the world’s largest amphibious aircraft, may soon enter operational service after completing its first water takeoff and landing, according to China’s state-run Xinhua news agency. Xinhua said the aircraft took off at about 8:51 a.m. from a reservoir near Zhanghe Airport in Jingmen under the command of captain Zhao Sheng and landed safely on the water after a 14-minute flight. China presents the AG600, developed by the Aviation Industry Corporation of China, as a large civil special-purpose aircraft intended for forest firefighting and water rescue missions. It is part of a broader push by China to develop major domestically designed aircraft, alongside the Y-20 military transport and the C919 passenger jet. The AG600 has four turboprop engines and a maximum takeoff weight of 54 tons. Its hull is shaped with a “V” design to improve performance in rough water. Xinhua says it can scoop up 12 tons of water for firefighting, operate in complex weather, withstand waves up to two meters high, carry as many as 50 people in maritime search-and-rescue missions, and support marine monitoring and safety patrols. The article notes that Xinhua repeatedly emphasized that the aircraft and its engines are domestically produced, which is significant given China’s long reliance on Soviet and Russian aircraft designs. That suggests China’s aviation industry is becoming more self-sufficient. However, the article also argues that the AG600 has clear strategic implications beyond civilian rescue work. In the tense geopolitical environment of the South China Sea, where China and several other countries dispute sovereignty over islands and waters, a large amphibious aircraft could help China supply island bases, transport troops, and conduct operations without depending on vulnerable airfields. It could also allow Chinese aircraft to appear over disputed areas under the cover of rescue or patrol missions. The piece concludes by noting that amphibious aircraft have been used elsewhere, including in Russia and in World War II Japan, but that their water-landing capability comes with performance tradeoffs compared with conventional aircraft.

# Summary: China's AG600 Amphibious Aircraft China has successfully tested the AG600, believed to be the world's largest amphibious aircraft, completing its first water takeoff and landing near Jingmen. The aircraft, roughly the size of a Boeing 737, flew for fourteen minutes before landing smoothly on a reservoir's surface. Built by the Aviation Industry Corporation of China, the AG600 is officially described as a civil aircraft designed for forest firefighting and water rescue operations. The plane features four turboprop engines, weighs fifty-four tons at maximum takeoff, and has a V-shaped fuselage designed to withstand two-meter waves. It can collect twelve tons of water for firefighting and carry fifty people during maritime rescue missions. The aircraft represents China's growing indigenous aviation capabilities, as state media emphasized its domestically-produced engines and components—a notable shift from China's historical reliance on Soviet and Russian aircraft designs. However, military analysts view the AG600 with strategic concern. Located in the contested South China Sea, where multiple nations claim sovereignty over disputed islands, the aircraft's amphibious capabilities have obvious military applications. Its ability to transport an infantry platoon and land on water without requiring airfields makes it valuable for supporting Chinese island bases and operations in disputed territories. The "maritime rescue" designation may provide cover for Chinese aircraft to operate over contested areas. While amphibious aircraft are not unique to China—Russia operates several Soviet-era models—their dual-use potential troubles the region. Historical precedent suggests amphibious aircraft sacrifice performance for water-landing capability, though their utility in remote areas with limited airfields remains valuable. The AG600's true significance may lie less in firefighting than in its potential to project Chinese military power across the South China Sea.

The United States and the Philippines have reached an agreement to create a new temporary relocation pathway for Afghan allies who helped the U.S. war effort, according to U.S. and Philippine officials. Under the plan, Afghans approved for the program will be sent to the Philippines while they wait for U.S. special immigrant visas and eventual resettlement in the United States. The deal is expected to be announced as early as Tuesday, just days after the third anniversary of the collapse of the U.S.-backed government in Kabul on Aug. 15, 2021. The arrangement is part of the Biden administration’s Operation Enduring Welcome, which is meant to help resettle Afghans who supported the U.S. mission. Officials said the Philippines will initially process about 300 Afghans, though they expect the program could continue and possibly expand, turning the country into another temporary “way station” for Afghan applicants. The Afghans selected for the first group have already been vetted and received initial U.S. approval. They are expected to stay only a few months, and the U.S. government will provide food, housing, security, medical care and transportation at a facility outside Manila. It was not immediately clear where the Afghans approved for transfer are currently located. Tens of thousands of Afghans who may qualify for U.S. visas are scattered around the world, often waiting in whatever country will accept them temporarily. Since the Taliban returned to power, Afghanistan has seen a severe rollback of rights, especially for women and girls, and reports of Taliban reprisals against people who worked with Americans have continued. Human rights workers say revenge killings remain a serious and ongoing danger. The new plan comes three years after the chaotic U.S. withdrawal from Afghanistan, which remains one of the Biden administration’s most damaging political liabilities and a frequent target of Republican criticism. In August 2021, a U.S.-led evacuation airlifted 124,000 people from Kabul in 17 days, but tens of thousands who were eligible for relocation were left behind. The evacuation was marred by tragedy, including an Islamic State suicide bombing near the airport that killed 13 U.S. service members and more than 170 Afghans, followed days later by an errant U.S. drone strike that killed seven children and three adult civilians. U.S. officials said President Joe Biden, Vice President Kamala Harris, Secretary of State Antony Blinken and White House national security adviser Jake Sullivan all played roles in securing the agreement with Manila. Biden raised the issue several times, including during an Oval Office meeting on April 11. Harris, now the Democratic presidential nominee, first suggested the idea to Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. during a visit to Manila in November 2022 and later raised it again during Marcos’s visits to Washington in May 2023 and San Francisco in November 2023. Supporters of Afghan resettlement said Harris’s involvement helped restart a process that had stalled. Shawn VanDiver, who leads the #AfghanEvac coalition, said her engagement was important and noted that the effort is still continuing three years after the fall of Kabul. Philippine officials described the agreement as significant and said it could be extended if it proves successful. Philippine Ambassador to the United States Jose Manuel Romualdez said the arrangement reflects a long humanitarian tradition in the Philippines, citing the country’s acceptance of more than 1,200 Jewish refugees before World War II and the processing of 30,000 Vietnamese refugees during the Vietnam War under Ferdinand Marcos Sr. The deal also reflects the broader strengthening of U.S.-Philippine ties under Marcos Jr., who has moved Manila closer to Washington since taking office in 2022. The two countries have a mutual defense treaty, and the Biden administration has recently announced plans to deepen defense cooperation and provide $500 million to modernize the Philippine armed forces. Marcos has visited the United States four times, most recently in April. Officials emphasized that the Philippines was making a notable commitment by agreeing to host the Afghans, especially given domestic concerns that a temporary program could become permanent. The country has long struggled with Islamist insurgencies, particularly in the south. U.S. officials said they worked to reassure Manila that the process would be fast and secure, and that the Afghans involved had already undergone extensive screening, including pre-travel security checks and medical exams. Analysts said the agreement underscores the depth of trust between Washington and Manila, extending beyond military cooperation into political and humanitarian collaboration. The two nations have also expanded ties through trade and regional diplomacy, including a U.S. trade mission that brought $1 billion in investments and a trilateral summit with Japan aimed at boosting economic growth. At the same time, Manila remains wary of China, whose military and coast guard have increasingly challenged Philippine vessels in disputed waters. The new Afghan resettlement deal, officials said, is another sign of how closely the two allies are working together at a moment of heightened strategic alignment.

# U.S. and Philippines Reach Agreement to Help Afghan Allies The United States and Philippine governments have announced a new agreement to create an additional pathway for Afghan allies who assisted American forces during the war in Afghanistan to reach the United States. The deal establishes a temporary relocation program in Southeast Asia, where Afghans will wait while their visa and resettlement applications are processed. The announcement comes three years after the collapse of the U.S.-backed Afghan government on August 15, 2021, following President Joe Biden's April 2021 order to withdraw American troops. The evacuation crisis remains one of the lowest points of the Biden administration and continues to be used as a political weapon by Republicans. ## Program Details Under the new arrangement, part of Operation Enduring Welcome—the Biden administration's ongoing Afghan resettlement initiative—approximately 300 Afghans will be processed for resettlement through the Philippines. These individuals have already undergone vetting and received initial approval from U.S. officials. The U.S. government will provide comprehensive support including food, housing, security, medical services, and transportation at a facility outside Manila. The program is designed to be temporary, with Afghans expected to remain in the Philippines for no more than a few months while awaiting final visa approval and resettlement in the United States. U.S. officials anticipate the program could expand after the initial cohort, effectively making the Philippines another temporary "way station" for Afghan refugees. ## Broader Resettlement Efforts Over the past three years, the United States has successfully resettled more than 160,000 Afghans, including those who directly supported the U.S. government and their families. These individuals arrived through multiple pathways, including Qatar and Albania. The current initiative builds upon the dramatic 2021 evacuation from Kabul, which airlifted 124,000 people to safety in just 17 days from a single runway. However, that evacuation was marked by tragedy and desperation, with tens of thousands of eligible individuals left behind. During the chaotic withdrawal, an Islamic State suicide bombing near the airport killed 13 U.S. troops and more than 170 Afghans. Additionally, a U.S. drone strike days later killed seven children and three adult civilians. ## High-Level Negotiations Senior U.S. leaders played crucial roles in securing the agreement. President Biden, Vice President Kamala Harris, Secretary of State Antony Blinken, and White House National Security Adviser Jake Sullivan all contributed to closing the deal. Harris, now the Democratic presidential nominee, was particularly instrumental, having first suggested the idea to Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. during a November 2022 Manila visit and raising it again in subsequent meetings in May 2023 and November 2023. ## Philippine Perspective and Historical Context Philippine Ambassador Jose Manuel Romualdez called the agreement "very significant" and noted it could be extended if successful. He connected the current effort to the Philippines' historical humanitarian traditions, citing President Manuel Quezon's acceptance of more than 1,200 Jewish refugees between the late 1930s and 1941—when even the United States was not accepting Jews fleeing Nazi Germany. During the Vietnam War, former President Ferdinand Marcos Sr., the current president's father, opened a processing center in northern Luzon that handled 30,000 Vietnamese refugees. ## Strategic Considerations The agreement reflects strengthened U.S.-Philippine diplomatic and military ties. The deal was framed as a "big ask" of Manila, given domestic concerns about security and fears that a temporary program could become permanent. The Philippines has battled Islamist insurgencies for decades, particularly in its southern regions. However, the arrangement demonstrates deep trust between the nations. Beyond military cooperation, the U.S. and Philippines have expanded economic and diplomatic partnerships, including a $500 million commitment to modernize Philippine armed forces and a presidential trade mission resulting in $1 billion in investments. ## Regional Context The Philippines' willingness to cooperate also reflects its strategic positioning amid rising tensions with China. Recent confrontations between Philippine and Chinese vessels have heightened security concerns for Manila, making the strengthened U.S. relationship increasingly valuable. ## Ongoing Crisis in Afghanistan Meanwhile, the situation in Afghanistan remains dire. Since the Taliban regained control, the regime has reimposed strict religious controls, curtailing nearly all rights for women and girls. Human rights workers warn that revenge killings of those who assisted Americans remain a persistent problem, making resettlement efforts critical for the safety of Afghan allies.

Salesian missionaries in Cambodia are providing humanitarian assistance after renewed clashes along the Cambodia-Thailand border forced mass displacement and disrupted life in several provinces. Don Bosco School in Poipet closed on Dec. 9 as fighting intensified, and it remains shut amid one of the most serious flare-ups in recent years. Cambodian authorities say border provinces including Banteay Meanchey and Oddar Meanchey have seen large-scale evacuations as families fled artillery fire and aerial strikes. Current estimates put the number of displaced people at nearly 500,000 nationwide. A Salesian team visited families of students and staff affected by the violence. Many have spent weeks in makeshift shelters, government school buildings, or overcrowded camps after leaving homes near the border. The displacement has interrupted schooling, livelihoods, and access to basic services, while host communities are under pressure from rising food prices, limited water supplies, and growing health concerns. During the visit, the Salesians distributed food, household necessities, hygiene items, and small treats for children. The aid was intended not only to meet urgent needs but also to offer reassurance and emotional support to families facing uncertainty and loss. Conditions in the camps remain difficult. Families reported having little access to safe drinking water and often must buy it at high cost. Safety problems, including snakes entering shelters at night, have added to fear, especially among children and the elderly. Poor sanitation, overcrowding, and limited medical access have increased health risks. Don Bosco Cambodia is appealing to the international community, partner organizations, and benefactors for help for displaced students and their families, especially those in temporary camps or without stable housing. It says support is urgently needed for food, shelter, transportation, school materials, and psychosocial care. The Salesians also renewed their call for peace, urging all sides to protect civilians, especially children, and resolve the conflict through dialogue. Salesian houses in Phnom Penh, Kep, Sihanoukville, Battambang, and Poipet have begun raising funds for relief efforts. Local Don Bosco institutions are also preparing contingency plans to help students whose education may be disrupted, including meals, transportation, and pastoral care.

# Salesian Missionaries Provide Aid After Cambodia Border Clashes Salesian missionaries are responding to a humanitarian crisis in Cambodia following escalating clashes along the Cambodia-Thailand border. Don Bosco School in Poipet closed on December 9 as fighting intensified, marking one of the most serious flare-ups in recent years. The conflict has caused severe displacement across the region. Border provinces including Banteay Meanchey and Oddar Meanchey have experienced large-scale evacuations, with approximately 500,000 people displaced nationwide. Families fled artillery fire and aerial strikes, with some seeking shelter near the border while others moved inland seeking security and assistance. The humanitarian impact is substantial. Displaced families are living in makeshift shelters, government school buildings, and overcrowded camps. Host communities face strained resources, including rising food prices, limited water supplies, and growing health concerns. Education, livelihoods, and access to basic services have been severely disrupted. A Salesian team visited affected families, distributing food, household supplies, hygiene materials, and treats for children. However, conditions in camps remain challenging. Families report limited access to safe drinking water, often forcing them to purchase it at high costs. Safety concerns include snakes entering shelters at night, while poor sanitation and overcrowding create significant health risks with restricted medical access. In response, Salesian communities across Cambodia—in Phnom Penh, Kep, Sihanoukville, Battambang, and Poipet—have begun mobilizing support. They are raising funds for food, shelter, and essential supplies while preparing contingency plans for displaced students, including meals, transportation, and pastoral care. The Salesians are appealing to the international community for urgent assistance with food, shelter, transportation, school materials, and psychosocial support. They are also calling for peace, urging all parties to protect civilians, especially children, and pursue dialogue to end the violence. The organization emphasizes that education, safety, and human dignity must remain priorities above conflict.

The European Union is preparing to make major decisions on Ukraine funding at a summit on Thursday, with leaders seeking to secure Kyiv’s finances for the next few years. EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said negotiations over frozen Russian assets are still difficult but continuing. The main proposal is a 90-billion-euro “reparations loan” for Ukraine, backed by several countries that want the frozen Russian funds used to fill Ukraine’s budget gaps. Belgium, which holds most of the assets, opposes the plan unless other EU states share the legal and financial risks. Italy and some others also have concerns. The European Commission has suggested protections for Belgium and Euroclear, but no deal has been reached. Tensions increased after Russia’s central bank threatened legal action. EU leaders say they remain committed to finding a solution.

# Summary The European Union will make critical decisions Thursday on funding Ukraine, aiming to secure Kyiv's finances long-term. EU leaders plan to discuss a 90-billion-euro "reparations loan" using frozen Russian assets to cover Ukraine's budget gaps. However, Belgium, which holds most assets, opposes the plan due to legal and financial risks, demanding strong guarantees from other EU nations before releasing funds. Italy and others share similar concerns. Russia's central bank has threatened legal action against Euroclear, complicating matters further. The EU proposed a "three-tier defence" but hasn't reached agreement. European leaders worry the United States might attempt to free assets during peace negotiations. EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas confirmed leaders remain committed to finding a solution, emphasizing the summit will produce results.

Tensions over Ukraine rose sharply on Thursday amid contradictory claims about whether Russia had begun pulling back troops from the border region, while fighting intensified in eastern Ukraine and diplomacy accelerated at the United Nations and in Europe. President Joe Biden warned that the risk of a Russian invasion remains “very high” and could come within “several days.” At the same time, Russia expelled a senior U.S. diplomat in Moscow, which Washington called an unprovoked escalation. The move added to the sense of crisis as NATO allies said Russia was not actually withdrawing forces, but instead continuing to build up its military presence near Ukraine. Russia had announced a day earlier that some troops were returning to their bases after large-scale exercises, but NATO officials disputed that claim. They said Moscow was moving forces around in ways that obscured its real intentions. Commercial satellite imagery from Maxar Technologies, which has been tracking the buildup, showed continued military activity near Ukraine, including a new pontoon bridge and a new field hospital in Belarus. NATO estimates that Russia has amassed more than 150,000 troops on three sides of Ukraine. Russia denies it is preparing an invasion. NATO Secretary-General Jens Stoltenberg said Russia has “enough troops, enough capabilities, to launch a full-fledged invasion of Ukraine with very little or no warning time,” calling that the reason the situation is so dangerous. He argued that moving tanks onto trains or shifting units around does not amount to a real withdrawal unless it is a meaningful de-escalation. Violence in eastern Ukraine further heightened fears that Russia might be looking for a pretext to intervene. Ukrainian government forces and Russia-backed separatists accused each other of heavy shelling along the line of contact in the Donetsk and Luhansk regions. In the latest reported incident, separatist authorities in Luhansk said Ukrainian shelling increased, while Ukraine’s military said it had not returned fire after being shelled. Ukrainian officials also said shells hit a kindergarten and wounded two civilians. The article notes that satellite images, while useful, cannot alone prove whether Russian forces are truly increasing or decreasing, or predict exactly when or if an invasion will happen. High-resolution commercial imagery can show units positioned close to Ukraine and reveal visible military infrastructure, but it may miss rapid changes on the ground. U.S. military and intelligence agencies can combine such imagery with live video, intercepted electronic signals, aircraft surveillance such as RC-135 Rivet Joint flights, and human intelligence to build a fuller picture. Diplomatically, the crisis remained active. U.S. Secretary of State Antony Blinken changed his travel plans and went to the United Nations instead of heading directly to a security conference in Germany, in order to press for a diplomatic solution. While EU and NATO officials insisted there was still room for talks, Russia expelled Bart Gorman, the second-highest-ranking U.S. diplomat in Moscow. The State Department called the expulsion an unprovoked escalation and said it was weighing a response. At the U.N. Security Council, Blinken laid out the U.S. view of how a Russian invasion could unfold. He said Washington believes Moscow may first stage a violent or dramatic incident to justify military action, such as a fake terrorist bombing, a staged drone strike, or even a fabricated chemical weapons attack. According to Blinken, the assault itself would begin with cyberattacks and missile strikes, followed by Russian troops moving into Ukraine and advancing toward Kyiv and other key targets. He said U.S. intelligence suggests Russia has already identified and mapped out those targets and may also target specific groups of Ukrainians, though he did not provide details. Blinken stressed, “I am here today not to start a war, but to prevent one.” Later on Thursday, the State Department said Blinken and Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov had agreed to meet in Europe the following week, as long as there was no further Russian invasion. Russia’s formal response to U.S. and NATO security proposals was also published Thursday. According to a 218-page dossier obtained by *The Sunday Times*, Ture moved from Portugal to Newham, east London, in 2005 and later registered as unemployed. The report says he became adept at fraudulently accessing government support and used the system to help IS sympathisers, including girls seeking to become “jihadi brides,” travel from the UK to Syria by exploiting student subsidies. Russia’s attacks on Ukraine continued to cause civilian deaths and injuries across several regions, while Kyiv highlighted progress in domestic weapons production and the country’s cultural resilience. In the Kharkiv region, Russian shelling struck the town of Bohodukhiv early on Aug. 27, according to Ukraine’s prosecutor general’s office. The attack hit a bus stop and killed a 71-year-old man, while six other people were wounded. Among the injured were a 15-year-old boy and his pregnant sister. Preliminary reports said the strike involved guided missiles launched from a Tornado-S multiple launch rocket system. In the Donetsk region, Russian forces dropped an aerial bomb on the village of Izmailivka overnight into Aug. 28, killing an entire family. Emergency responders recovered the bodies of a 45-year-old father, a 53-year-old mother, their 24-year-old daughter, and their 17-year-old son from the ruins of their home. Earlier that same day, an Iskander ballistic missile attack injured four people in the village of Andriivka. Regional governor Oleh Synehubov said the target was an operating infrastructure facility. Central Ukraine was also hit. In Kryvyi Rih, the hometown of President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Russian missiles struck several locations, including residential areas and a hotel. Regional officials said at least five people were killed in the attack. Zelenskyy also announced an important military development: Ukraine has successfully tested its first domestically produced ballistic missile. Speaking at a press conference on Aug. 27, he said he had initially considered keeping the information secret but wanted to recognize the specialists involved in Ukraine’s defense industry. A few days earlier, he had also praised the first combat use of the new Ukrainian-made “Palianytsia” drone missile, which was developed over the past year and a half and can be launched from a ground-based installation. No additional details about the weapon were released. Ukraine’s prosecutor general, Andriy Kostin, said that since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion, more than 130,000 war crimes have been recorded. Law enforcement has identified 660 suspects, and 126 have been convicted. Kostin noted that the true number is likely much higher because Ukraine lacks access to temporarily occupied territories where Russian forces operate. He said more than 100 Russian military officers, including generals, have already been brought to justice. The investigations also include ecocide and cybercrimes. The article also highlighted cultural developments. Ukraine’s installation at the 2024 Burning Man festival features a large sculpture reading “I’M FINE” with a smiley face, using irony to express wartime resilience. Built from bullet-riddled road signs and other war debris, the 32-meter-long artwork includes pedestrian-crossing signs commemorating civilians killed by Russian attacks and “Attention! Children!” signs from a destroyed Kherson school. The piece was created by 25 volunteers, some of them veterans, and will remain on display in Nevada through Sep. 2. Finally, the documentary “Yaremchuk: Incomparable World of Beauty” became Ukraine’s highest-grossing documentary, earning 9.9 million hryvnias and drawing 63,000 viewers in under three weeks. The film about singer Nazar Yaremchuk surpassed “20 Days in Mariupol” in box-office revenue, though Chernov’s film still leads in attendance.

Sweden said Thursday that Iran has agreed to compensate the families of those killed when a Ukrainian passenger jet was shot down near Tehran in January. Foreign Minister Ann Linde said the deal followed negotiations between Iran and the countries whose citizens died in the crash, and that Sweden had signed a mutual understanding to begin talks with Iran on compensation for victims’ next of kin. She said she had no doubt Iran would carry out the agreement, though the amount and terms remain unclear. The Boeing 737, bound for Kyiv, was hit by two ground-to-air missiles and crashed on Jan. 8, killing all 176 people aboard. Iran first denied responsibility, then three days later admitted that Revolutionary Guard forces had accidentally downed the plane during heightened tensions with the United States, calling it a “disastrous mistake.” The crash came shortly after Iran fired ballistic missiles at U.S. bases in Iraq in retaliation for the U.S. drone strike that killed Gen. Qassim Suleimani. Victims included citizens of Canada, Sweden, the U.K., Afghanistan and Ukraine. Canada had 57 victims. Iran has also said it will send the plane’s black boxes to France for analysis.

# Summary Sweden announced Thursday that Iran has agreed to compensate families of victims killed when Iranian forces shot down a Ukrainian airliner near Tehran on January 8. Iran initially denied responsibility but later admitted the Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps accidentally shot down the plane, calling it a "disastrous mistake." European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen will travel to Egypt and Jordan on Saturday as the Israel-Hamas war continues, her spokesman said. She is scheduled to meet Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi first, then go to Sinai near the Israeli border to attend the arrival of an EU humanitarian convoy. After that, she will meet Jordan’s King Abdullah II. Von der Leyen previously visited Israel on October 13, one week after Hamas launched its deadly attack that killed about 1,200 people, mostly civilians, and took roughly 240 hostages, according to Israeli officials. Since then, Israel’s aerial bombardment and ground offensive in Gaza have killed more than 11,500 people, mostly civilians, according to health officials in the Hamas-run territory. At the beginning of November, von der Leyen told EU diplomats that the bloc would increase humanitarian aid to Gaza by 25 million euros. She reiterated strong support for Israel, while saying it must avoid civilian casualties. She also said Hamas was using civilians and hostages as human shields, and that Gaza should not remain a safe haven for terrorists after the war. She added that a two-state solution still needs a future perspective. EU foreign policy chief Josep Borrell is also traveling to the region for talks.

She will meet Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi and attend the arrival of an EU humanitarian convoy in Sinai near the Israeli border, before meeting King Abdullah II in Jordan. British Foreign Secretary Boris Johnson addressed the House of Commons on Brexit, relations with Russia, and the Iran nuclear deal. On Brexit, he said some of the figures being discussed for the UK’s final settlement with the European Union were “eye-watering,” citing a reported demand of up to 100 billion euros, which he described as far too high. He said it was now up to the EU to consider Britain’s offer and move the negotiations forward. Brexit talks began in June and were expected to conclude by late March 2019. After the fourth round of negotiations in late September, UK Brexit Secretary David Davis said both sides had made substantial progress on issues including greater certainty for citizens and businesses, as well as matters concerning Northern Ireland and the Republic of Ireland. Johnson also commented on relations with Moscow, saying Russia was acting as though a new Cold War existed. He said the UK’s goal was to prevent tensions from worsening by constraining Russia, penalizing it for “malign and destructive activities,” and engaging where possible. He added that Britain could not have normal relations with Russia, but should still maintain dialogue. The UK Foreign Office had recently said Johnson would visit Russia later in the year, following an invitation from Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov. A planned April visit had been canceled after the US missile strike on the Syrian base of Ash Sha’irat. On the Iran nuclear deal, Johnson responded to the US decision on October 13 not to certify the agreement. He said the JCPOA “remains alive” and “intact,” and that Britain would work with its allies, including China, Russia, and the European Union, to keep the accord in place. The US move drew criticism from other members of the P5+1, who reiterated that Iran was complying with the deal.

# Summary British Foreign Secretary Boris Johnson addressed Parliament on three major international issues in October 2017. **Brexit Negotiations** Johnson criticized the European Union's reported demand of 100 billion euros ($119 billion) as a final payment from the United Kingdom, calling the figure "eye-watering" and "far too high." He stated it was the EU's responsibility to review the UK's offer and make progress. Brexit talks, which officially began in June, are scheduled for completion by late March 2019. Following the fourth round of negotiations in late September, UK Brexit Secretary David Davis reported considerable progress on several issues, including citizen and business certainty and matters concerning Northern Ireland and the Republic of Ireland. **Russia Relations** Johnson characterized Russia's behavior as resembling a "new cold war," stating Britain's objective is to prevent escalation by constraining Russia, penalizing its "malign and destructive activities," while maintaining dialogue where possible. He acknowledged the UK cannot maintain normal relations with Russia but emphasized the importance of keeping communication channels open. Johnson announced plans to visit Russia toward year's end following an invitation from Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov, though a previously scheduled April visit had been canceled following US missile strikes on Syria. **Iran Nuclear Deal** Johnson affirmed that the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA) "remains alive" and "remains intact" following the US administration's October 13 decision not to certify the agreement. He pledged the UK government, working with China, Russia, and the European Union, would maintain the deal, noting Iran's continued compliance.

Earlier, the Iraqi Joint Operations Command said fighter jets had struck the area after reports that senior IS figures were there. Iraqi forces have stepped up operations in recent months as IS remnants continue guerrilla attacks from urban, desert, and mountainous areas despite the group’s 2017 defeat.

Islamic State militants posted photos online that appeared to show a captured Jordanian pilot after his warplane was shot down over Syria’s northern Raqqa province on Wednesday. The pilot was identified as First Lieutenant Muaz Kasasbeh. According to the images described by pro-government media, one photo showed him being pulled from what looked like a lake by four IS fighters while conscious and wearing only underwear. Two other images showed him being dragged along a dirt road by militants, some of whom were looking upward, apparently fearing an airstrike. Opposition reports said the Jordanian jet was hit by a thermal missile while flying at low altitude. The aircraft had been taking part in U.S.-led coalition strikes against IS in Raqqa, alongside Arab allies including Jordan, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates. IS later claimed online that Kasasbeh had ejected, landed in the area, and threatened a shepherd to surrender his clothes as a disguise, though the group did not explain how he ended up in the lake. The incident was the first downing of a foreign coalition warplane by IS in Syria since airstrikes began last September. Jordan’s military confirmed both the jet’s downing and the pilot’s capture, and his relatives urged authorities to work for his release.

According to opposition reports, IS used a thermal missile to shoot down the Jordanian warplane, which was conducting strikes against IS as part of the U.S.-led anti-terror coalition that includes Jordan, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates. IS claimed Kasasbeh ejected and initially disguised himself using a shepherd's clothing before being captured. According to an Iraqi security source quoted by Sputnik, five Katyusha rockets were fired at the area around the base, which lies about 160 kilometers west of Baghdad. The source said the rockets landed on the outskirts of the facility and caused no casualties. Sabereen News, a Telegram channel linked to Iraq’s Popular Mobilization Units (PMU), gave a slightly different account, saying six 122mm BM-21 Grad rockets struck Ain al-Asad. It also reported explosions heard near the city of Haditha, roughly 240 kilometers northwest of Baghdad. In the aftermath, US military helicopters and reconnaissance drones were said to have flown over the Khan al-Baghdadi area in western Anbar, between Haditha and Heet. The article links this broader hostility to the US drone strike that killed Iranian commander Qassem Soleimani and PMU deputy chief Abu Mahdi al-Muhandis near Baghdad International Airport in January 2020. Iran also retaliated in January 2020 by striking Ain al-Asad with missiles, an attack the Pentagon said left more than 100 US personnel with traumatic brain injuries.

A large car bombing struck Syria’s rebel-held city of Idlib on Sunday evening, killing at least 23 people and injuring dozens, activists said. The blast caused fires, damaged buildings, and overturned several cars along a major avenue, with ambulances and fire crews rushing to the scene. According to the Britain-based Syrian Observatory for Human Rights and a local activist, the explosion happened outside the office of Ajnad al-Koukaz, an insurgent group made up largely of foreign fighters from the Caucasus and Russia. The group is allied with an al-Qaida-linked faction that dominates Idlib province. It was not immediately clear who carried out the attack. Residents and activists said they believed it was a car bomb, and one activist noted there were no signs of an airstrike. The death toll rose quickly from an initial report of 18 killed to 23. At least 35 wounded people were taken to one city hospital, according to a medical technician. The bombing came hours after the Syrian military announced it had recaptured Sinjar, a strategically important town in eastern Idlib. The Observatory said that advance could open the way for government forces to move toward the nearby Abu Zuhour air base. Idlib remains the last major rebel stronghold in northern Syria, with more than 2.5 million people living there, including over 1 million displaced civilians.

Yemen’s Houthi rebels said they fired a short-range ballistic missile at a military camp in the Buko desert of Saudi Arabia’s southern Najran region on Friday, claiming it was retaliation for overnight Saudi-led coalition airstrikes on Sanaa International Airport. The rebels said the Badr-1-P missile hit its target accurately. Earlier, more than 30 airstrikes struck the airport and surrounding areas in the rebel-held capital, with residents reporting powerful blasts that shook the city. Saudi-owned Al Arabiya quoted coalition spokesman Turki al-Maliki as saying the strikes targeted ballistic missile launchpads at the airport. Saudi Arabia had no immediate comment on the rebel missile launch. Buko is a border crossing area near Yemen’s Saada province, the Houthis’ main stronghold, and has been controlled by Saudi border forces since 2016. # Yemen's Rebels Fire Missile at Saudi Border Camp Yemen's Houthi rebels fired a short-range ballistic missile at a military camp in Saudi Arabia's Najran region on Friday, retaliating for coalition airstrikes on Sanaa airport. Over 30 airstrikes hit the rebel-held capital's airport pre-dawn, targeting ballistic missile launchpads according to coalition spokesman Turki al-Maliki. The Houthis claimed their Badr-1-P missile accurately struck the Buko desert camp, a shared Saudi-Yemeni border crossing under Saudi control since 2016. The attack represents the latest escalation in Yemen's ongoing conflict, which began in 2015 when the Saudi-led coalition intervened to support President Abd-Rabbu Mansour Hadi after Houthi rebels forced him into exile. Most Houthi missiles are typically intercepted. The fresh military escalation occurs ahead of upcoming UN-proposed peace talks.

The article profiles Chris, a 26-year-old who runs the Instagram archive @ToyotasOfWar, a page devoted to documenting Toyota vehicles used in combat around the world. What began as an obsession while he worked for a defense company building out Toyotas became a broader project of collecting photos, stories, and historical context from veterans and others with firsthand experience. Over time, the account evolved into a kind of photojournalism archive focused on how Toyotas are used in conflict, rather than on the trendy “overlander” or “mall crawler” culture common in car social media. Chris argues that Toyota’s reputation in war comes from a mix of reliability, availability, and adaptability. He notes that the company’s military connections stretch back to the Korean War, when Toyota received design influence from U.S. Army vehicles such as the Model BM truck and the Willys Jeep. That lineage eventually helped shape the modern LandCruiser. He says the page often prompts reactions from followers, including people who say they are now convinced to buy a Toyota after seeing stories about how much punishment the vehicles can survive. The article also explains why the white Toyota pickup became so closely associated with the War on Terror. According to Chris, the association is partly coincidental and partly practical: white vehicles are common worldwide, remain cooler in hot climates, are easier to maintain visually, and can be camouflaged with mud. He emphasizes that combat use is not limited to pickups; the archive includes sedans, vans, scooters, and even a forklift. One of the most serious examples mentioned is a U.S. drone strike on Aug. 29, when commanders believed they had identified a white Toyota sedan carrying explosives and driven by an Islamic State operative. In reality, the vehicle belonged to an aid worker transporting water for his family. The strike killed seven children and three adults. On Nov. 3, the Defense Department said a review found no misconduct. The review, conducted by Air Force Lt. Gen. Sami Said, identified communication failures and problems in target identification and confirmation, but concluded that the mistaken strike occurred despite efforts intended to avoid civilian casualties. The U.S. is now moving toward financial reparations for the family and may also help them seek asylum outside Afghanistan.

The Canadian Department of National Defence said Wednesday that all Canadian service members were safe after a deadly rocket attack on Camp Taji, a military base north of Baghdad in Iraq that has hosted Canadian troops as part of NATO’s mission to train Iraqi forces against the Islamic State group. The attack killed at least two Americans and one British soldier and wounded about a dozen other military personnel. U.S. officials said one of five injured service members was seriously wounded and evacuated from the base, while seven others were still being assessed. Buildings on the base were reported to be burning after the strike. Defence Department spokesman Daniel Le Bouthillier said in a statement that the Canadian Armed Forces was aware of the attack and that all Canadian personnel in the area were “confirmed safe and accounted for.” He declined to give details about the number or location of Canadian troops for operational security reasons. Canada has about 500 military personnel in Iraq supporting local forces and the fight against ISIL. U.S. military officials said more than 15 small rockets hit Camp Taji, and one official said as many as 30 rockets may have been fired from a truck launcher, with 18 reaching the base. No group immediately claimed responsibility, but officials said Kataib Hezbollah or another Iranian-backed Shia militia was likely behind the attack. Kataib Hezbollah was blamed for a late-December rocket attack on a base in Kirkuk that killed a U.S. contractor, triggering American retaliatory strikes. Those strikes led to protests at the U.S. Embassy in Baghdad and were followed on Jan. 3 by a U.S. airstrike that killed Iranian Gen. Qassem Soleimani and Abu Mahdi al-Muhandis, a militia leader in Iraq. The attack came days after Lt.-Gen. Mike Rouleau, commander of Canadian Joint Operations Command, told Parliament that Iranian-backed Shia militias posed a greater threat to Canadian troops than ISIL because they were well armed with artillery, rockets and armed drones. Later Wednesday, Syrian opposition activists and a war monitor reported a separate airstrike on Iranian militia positions near the Iraq-Syria border. The Syrian Observatory for Human Rights said 10 airstrikes hit the Boukamal region in eastern Syria, causing several explosions, though no casualties were immediately reported. U.S. officials said that strike was not connected to the Camp Taji attack.

The article marks the first anniversary of the assassination of Lt. Gen. Qasem Soleimani, who was killed along with Abu Mahdi al-Muhandis, the deputy commander of Iraq’s Popular Mobilization Units, in a US airstrike ordered by President Donald Trump at Baghdad International Airport on January 3, 2020. It presents Soleimani as a central figure in the fight against terrorism in Syria and Iraq, and as a widely admired commander in Iran and across the region. According to the article, Soleimani is regarded in Iran as a national hero because he devoted his life to defending the country’s interests in the region. He is also described as a hero to “freedom-seeking” people around the world for his role in defeating ISIL, which the article calls the world’s most notorious terrorist group. On the anniversary of his killing, Mehr News Agency interviewed Sayyed Tahir al-Hashemi, an Egyptian member of the Ahl Al-Bayt World Assembly, to discuss Soleimani’s influence in West Asia. Al-Hashemi says the assassination deeply angered Arab and Islamic nations and hurt their feelings, calling Trump’s decision “stupid.” In response to a question about whether the killing weakened the Resistance, he argues that the opposite occurred. He says the Islamic Republic of Iran is becoming stronger every day and describes it as a “great university” that produces commanders, leaders, and scholars like Soleimani. In his view, Soleimani represented one of the greatest schools of anti-terrorism struggle in his era and fought terrorist groups and their supporters with all his strength. The interview emphasizes Soleimani’s role in the battles against ISIL in Syria and Iraq. Al-Hashemi calls him a “heroic commander” and says he became the number one figure in the fight against ISIL terrorism. He claims Soleimani not only defended Islam and Muslims but also “rescued humanity,” because ISIL threatened everyone, not just specific communities. He says Soleimani’s efforts helped defeat the group and thereby ruined the conspiracies and plans of the United States, Israel, and their regional allies. When asked about the assassination’s impact on Egypt and world public opinion, Al-Hashemi says the killing of Soleimani, al-Muhandis, and others shocked their friends and also affected the Egyptian people. He says the event angered Arab and Islamic nations and reinforced the view that the United States is a “terrorist state,” one that even its Arab and Islamic allies cannot trust. In his telling, the assassination made the Axis of Resistance more determined to confront colonialism, arrogance, and terrorism, and inspired many young people in the Islamic world to seek revenge against terrorists and their backers. The interview closes by stressing Soleimani’s strategic role in supporting resistance groups and uniting the Islamic ummah. Al-Hashemi says Soleimani’s popularity came from his services to Muslims and his leadership in the struggle against terrorism. He concludes that many honorable people and nations continue to see him as a role model and beacon in defending truth and resisting terrorism.

# Summary: Lt. General Qasem Soleimani's Legacy in the Fight Against Terrorism On January 3, 2020, the United States conducted an airstrike at Baghdad's international airport that killed Lt. General Qasem Soleimani, a prominent Iranian military commander, and Abu Mahdi al-Muhandis, deputy leader of Iraq's Popular Mobilization Units. Canada updated its travel advisory for Ethiopia on November 14, warning citizens to avoid non-essential travel because of civil unrest, violence, armed conflict and crime. The advisory says the security situation can deteriorate without warning and cites reports of protests and rising tensions between Ethiopia and Eritrea as additional concerns. The Canadian government said travelers should exercise a high degree of caution in Addis Ababa, where it warned that crime is increasing and spontaneous demonstrations could turn violent. It also said fighting in the Amhara and Oromia regions could spread to the capital. Several parts of the country were placed on the “avoid travel” list. In northern Ethiopia, the advisory names Amhara, Benishangul and Tigray, citing ongoing armed conflict, possible civil unrest and an unpredictable security environment. The article notes that Benishangul is actually in western Ethiopia, not the north, and says there have been no recent reports of active conflict there. The advisory’s concern in the north is reinforced by recent developments involving the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), which fought a devastating war against the federal government from 2020 to 2022. According to the article, the TPLF has recently made incursions into northern Afar, prompting a reported drone strike by federal forces. The TPLF confirmed the strike and said there were unspecified casualties. The advisory also warns against travel to parts of central Ethiopia, including Gambella, Sidama, North Shewa, West Shewa, West Wollega, East Wollega, Kellem Wollega and Horo Gudru Wollega, due to violent crime, kidnapping, armed conflict and civil unrest. The article says the advisory mentions airstrikes there, though most recorded strikes have been in Amhara. Border areas with Eritrea, Somalia and Kenya were also listed as no-travel zones because of instability, military activity, banditry, terrorism risks, kidnapping, violence and landmines.

# Canada Updates Travel Advisory for Ethiopia On November 14, the Canadian government issued an updated travel advisory for Ethiopia, citing civil unrest, armed conflict, and crime as primary concerns. The advisory recommends that Canadian citizens avoid non-essential travel to the country due to the unpredictable security situation, which can deteriorate without warning. **Key Risk Areas:** The capital, Addis Ababa, requires "a high degree of caution" due to rising crime and potential spontaneous demonstrations that could escalate to violence. The advisory warns that regional conflicts could spread to the capital. Northern regions including Amhara, Benishangul, and Tigray are designated as areas to avoid entirely. The ongoing armed conflict in Amhara, which has persisted for approximately two and a half years, poses significant risks. Additionally, recent military tensions between the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) and Federal government forces have escalated, with confirmed drone strikes and unspecified casualties reported. Central Ethiopian zones—including Gambella, Sidama, North Shewa, and various Wollega regions—are flagged due to violent crime, kidnapping, armed conflict, and civil unrest, with potential airstrikes noted as concerns. **Border Regions:** Areas bordering Eritrea, Somalia, and Kenya are classified as "avoid travel" zones due to instability, military activity, banditry, terrorist attack risks, kidnapping, violence, and landmines. The advisory reflects growing tensions between Ethiopia and Eritrea and the unpredictable nature of the security environment. The Canadian government's recommendations emphasize the volatile conditions affecting multiple regions simultaneously, making travel throughout much of Ethiopia inadvisable for non-essential purposes.

The United States and several allies called for an immediate 21-day ceasefire along the Lebanon-Israel border as fighting between Israel and Iran-backed Hezbollah sharply escalated and raised fears of a wider war. The appeal came as Israeli airstrikes hit Hezbollah positions across Lebanon, killing hundreds this week, while Hezbollah responded with rocket barrages and said it had fired a ballistic missile toward Tel Aviv. The joint statement, issued by US President Joe Biden, French President Emmanuel Macron and other partners including Japan, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, said the situation in Lebanon was “intolerable” and in “nobody’s interest.” It urged a temporary halt to fighting to create space for diplomacy and a longer-term settlement. The announcement was made as leaders gathered on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York. On the ground, the violence intensified. Lebanon’s National News Agency said Israeli strikes near Baalbek in eastern Lebanon were the “most violent” of recent days. Residents described extreme fear; one 22-year-old student, Nour Hamad, said people had spent days without sleep, unsure whether they would survive the night. The UN said about 90,000 people had fled homes in Hezbollah strongholds for safer areas elsewhere in Lebanon. The ceasefire appeal followed warnings from both sides. Israel’s army chief, Lieutenant General Herzi Halevi, told troops to prepare for the possibility of a ground operation in Lebanon, saying the military was attacking to prepare for a potential entry and to keep striking Hezbollah. Israel’s UN envoy Danny Danon welcomed diplomatic efforts but stopped short of agreeing to a ceasefire, saying Israel would use all means available, within international law, to achieve its goals of weakening Hezbollah. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, speaking before his planned trip to New York, said Israel would not stop until displaced Israelis could return home. Hezbollah escalated its own attacks by targeting what it said was Israel’s Mossad headquarters near Tel Aviv, marking the first claimed ballistic missile launch in nearly a year of cross-border clashes that began after the Gaza war. UN Secretary-General António Guterres warned that “hell is breaking loose,” while many in both countries recalled the devastation of the 2006 Israel-Hezbollah war.

# US and Allies Call for 21-Day Ceasefire in Lebanon-Israel Conflict The United States and its allies are pressing for a 21-day ceasefire to halt escalating violence between Israel and Iran-backed Hezbollah that threatens to ignite a full-scale war in Lebanon. ## Current Situation Israeli aerial bombardment of Hezbollah strongholds has killed hundreds of people this week, with the militant group retaliating with rocket barrages and ballistic missiles targeting Tel Aviv. Israeli army leadership has instructed soldiers to prepare for a potential ground offensive, raising concerns about further escalation. Lebanon's National News Agency described recent bombardment near Baalbek in eastern Lebanon as "the most violent" in recent days. ## Diplomatic Response A joint statement from US President Joe Biden, French President Emmanuel Macron, and other Western allies, along with Japan and Gulf Arab states—Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates—called for an immediate 21-day ceasefire to allow diplomatic negotiations. UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres warned that "hell is breaking loose" and urged an immediate ceasefire. ## Israeli Position Israel welcomed diplomatic efforts but stopped short of committing to a ceasefire, vowing to continue degrading Hezbollah using all available means within international law. Israeli envoy Danny Danon stated Israel is "grateful" for diplomatic efforts but remains focused on its military objectives. Prime Minister Netanyahu promised to continue striking Hezbollah "with full force" until displaced Israeli residents can return home. ## Human Impact The violence has displaced approximately 90,000 people from Hezbollah strongholds seeking safer areas. Residents on both sides report living under extreme stress and tension. The situation evokes memories of the devastating 2006 war that killed 1,200 people in Lebanon, mostly civilians, and 160 Israelis, mostly soldiers. ## Escalation Triggers The conflict intensified after Hezbollah claimed responsibility for firing a ballistic missile at Israel's Mossad headquarters in Tel Aviv—the first such attack in nearly a year of cross-border clashes stemming from the Gaza war.

A tornado struck near Didsbury, Alberta, on Saturday afternoon, damaging homes and killing some livestock but causing no serious injuries, officials said. Environment and Climate Change Canada issued a tornado warning at 1:50 p.m. local time for the area about 145 miles south of Edmonton after reports came in of a large twister along a major highway. RCMP said the tornado was about one-half mile to 1.2 miles wide. The warning was later lifted. Authorities reported widespread damage, though no confirmed deaths. Cpl. Gina Slaney said numerous homes were damaged and there were no known injuries. Deputy mayor Dean Allan of nearby Carstairs said the tornado passed between Didsbury and Carstairs, damaging 12 homes, with a couple destroyed and some livestock lost. Carstairs fire chief Jordan Schaffer said five homes were destroyed, including one where rescuers pulled a woman from a basement without injury. Storm chaser Aaron Jayjack posted video showing the tornado crossing a highway and apparently damaging two rural homes, while downed power lines blocked access. Prime Minister Justin Trudeau expressed support for those injured or displaced and said Canadians “are here for you.”

# Alberta Tornado Summary A tornado struck near Didsbury, Alberta, approximately 145 miles south of Edmonton on Saturday afternoon, damaging numerous homes and killing livestock but causing no serious injuries. Environment and Climate Change Canada issued a tornado warning at 1:50 p.m. local time. The tornado, measuring between half a mile and 1.2 miles wide, crossed a major highway in the region. According to authorities, the tornado passed between Didsbury and nearby Carstairs, located 8 miles south. While reports varied on damage extent, at least 12 homes were damaged, with some completely destroyed. Carstairs Fire Chief Jordan Schaffer reported five homes destroyed, including one where rescuers successfully extracted a woman from her basement without injury. Deputy Mayor Dean Allan confirmed minor injuries but no deaths. Storm chaser Aaron Jayjack posted video footage showing the tornado crossing the highway and damaging rural homes. Prime Minister Justin Trudeau expressed support for affected residents on Twitter, stating Canadians "are here for you" and urging people to stay safe as officials monitored the situation.

Senior U.S. peace envoy Zalmay Khalilzad has arrived in Kabul for talks with Afghan leaders, marking his first visit to the Afghan capital since being appointed to lead U.S. efforts to negotiate with the Taliban. An Afghan presidential spokesman said Khalilzad was expected to dine with President Ashraf Ghani and other officials, though no further details were given. The U.S. embassy in Kabul did not immediately comment. Khalilzad, a former U.S. ambassador to Afghanistan, Iraq and the United Nations, is on a 10-day regional trip that will also take him to Pakistan, the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia and Qatar. According to the State Department, the purpose of the trip is to coordinate and lead U.S. efforts to bring the Taliban to the negotiating table. His arrival comes amid a sharp escalation in violence across Afghanistan as the Taliban and Islamic State intensify attacks ahead of this month’s long-delayed parliamentary elections, which are viewed as a rehearsal for next year’s presidential vote. In one of the latest attacks, Taliban fighters killed 14 members of the security forces in Sayedabad district in eastern Wardak province, which lies along the strategic Kabul-Kandahar highway. The district police chief was among the dead, and seven others were wounded, officials said. The Taliban claimed to have killed dozens of security personnel, while Afghan officials said the insurgents also suffered heavy casualties. The fighting damaged an electricity cable, cutting power to several provinces. The attack followed the destruction of bridges on the same highway in neighboring Ghazni province, briefly closing the route. Separately, the defense ministry is investigating possible civilian casualties in Paktia province after an air strike reportedly killed 10 civilians and wounded 20. U.S. Forces denied carrying out that strike.
