Canada has announced a temporary withdrawal of non-essential personnel and family members from its embassy in Haiti as the country’s security situation worsens. Global Affairs Canada said the move was prompted by rapidly deteriorating conditions, especially a severe fuel shortage caused by armed gangs blocking oil terminals. Essential embassy staff will remain in place to continue assisting Canadian citizens in Haiti. The foreign ministry also urged Canadians to avoid traveling to Haiti unless absolutely necessary. The fuel crisis has persisted for months and has disrupted much of the economy, affecting private businesses and state institutions alike. Meanwhile, gang violence has intensified, with armed groups controlling large parts of Port-au-Prince and other areas. Their activity since June 2021 has forced more than 19,000 people to flee their homes.

The U.S. carried out an airstrike in Somalia on Sunday in support of Somali National Army forces that were under attack by al-Shabab near Buulobarde, more than 124 miles north of Mogadishu, U.S. Africa Command said Tuesday. AFRICOM said the strike killed two al-Shabab fighters and caused no civilian casualties. The attack appears to have been the 10th U.S. strike in Somalia this year, according to the Long War Journal tracker, compared with 11 in 2021 and 44 in 2020. AFRICOM described al-Shabab as the “largest and most kinetically active al-Qaeda network in the world” and said U.S. forces, alongside partners, continue working to stop the group from planning and carrying out attacks on civilians and U.S. interests. The strike followed recent Somali government claims of battlefield gains. A week earlier, Somalia’s Ministry of Information said government forces had retaken territory in the Hiiraan and Middle Shabelle regions of Hirshabelle State and killed numerous militants, though it did not provide a precise number. The U.S. action was part of a broader pattern of recent airstrikes against al-Shabab. In September, AFRICOM said a U.S. strike near the same area killed more than 27 militants and helped Somali and African Union Transition Mission in Somalia forces regain the initiative in what it called the largest combined Somali and ATMIS offensive in five years. In August, U.S. strikes reportedly killed about 13 militants. The renewed air campaign comes as hundreds of U.S. troops resumed rotations in Somalia after the Biden administration reversed a Trump-era plan to remove all troops by early 2021. The U.S. military has been operating in Somalia since 2007.

# US Airstrike in Somalia Against Al-Shabab The U.S. conducted an airstrike in Somalia on Sunday against al-Shabab militants who were attacking Somali National Army forces near Buulobarde, approximately 124 miles north of Mogadishu, according to AFRICOM. The strike killed two al-Shabab fighters with no civilian casualties reported. This marks the 10th U.S. airstrike in Somalia in 2022, a decrease from 11 strikes in 2021 and 44 in 2020. AFRICOM characterized al-Shabab as "the largest and most kinetically active al-Qaeda network in the world," emphasizing the group's threat to U.S. forces and security interests. The airstrike follows recent territorial gains by Somali government forces in the Hiiraan and Middle Shabelle regions, where they claimed to have killed numerous al-Shabab militants. Similar operations occurred in September, when a U.S. airstrike killed an estimated 27 al-Shabab fighters in the same region, and in August, when strikes killed approximately 13 militants. These operations represent part of a broader military campaign. The Biden administration reversed a Trump-era decision to withdraw all U.S. troops from Somalia, restarting regular troop rotations in the country. The U.S. has maintained a military presence in Somalia since 2007 as part of the Global War on Terror. However, AFRICOM has faced previous accusations from human rights organizations like Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch of killing civilians in strikes, despite the command's denials.

World leaders broadly welcomed the inauguration of Joe Biden as U.S. president and Kamala Harris as vice president, using the occasion to signal hopes for closer cooperation with Washington and, in some cases, to criticize the Trump administration. British Prime Minister Boris Johnson congratulated Biden and Harris, calling Harris’s swearing-in historic and saying U.S. leadership is vital on issues such as climate change and COVID-19. Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau said he looked forward to working with the new administration and Congress to make both countries safer, more prosperous and more resilient, while advancing climate action, clean economic growth, inclusion and diversity. Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi also offered congratulations and highlighted Harris’s heritage, calling her success “pathbreaking” and a source of pride for Indian-Americans. China’s ambassador to the United States, Cui Tiankai, said Beijing looked forward to working with the new administration on stable China-U.S. relations and on global challenges including public health, climate change and economic growth. But shortly after Biden took office, China imposed sanctions on several former Trump officials, including Mike Pompeo, Robert O’Brien and Peter Navarro. European leaders emphasized renewed transatlantic ties and Biden’s climate moves. French President Emmanuel Macron welcomed the United States back to the Paris Agreement, which Biden rejoined through one of more than a dozen executive orders he signed on his first day. German Chancellor Angela Merkel called the inauguration “a true celebration of American democracy.” European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the Paris decision was “a very strong starting point” for renewed cooperation and described the moment as “a new dawn in America.” Israeli President Benjamin Netanyahu said he and Biden share a long personal friendship and expressed hope for stronger U.S.-Israel ties, continued Arab-Israeli peace efforts and a united front against Iran. Iranian Foreign Minister Javad Zarif, meanwhile, criticized the Trump administration, pointing to the U.S. airstrike that killed Iranian commander Qasem Soleimani.

# World Leaders Welcome Biden and Harris Inauguration World leaders offered widespread congratulations following the inauguration of President Joe Biden and Vice President Kamala Harris on Wednesday, with reactions ranging from simple congratulations to statements positioning their countries for enhanced cooperation with the new administration. British Prime Minister Boris Johnson emphasized America's vital leadership on global issues including climate change and COVID-19. Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau expressed eagerness to collaborate on making both nations safer and more prosperous, highlighting climate action and economic growth as priorities. Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi congratulated both leaders and specifically noted Harris's historic significance as the daughter of an Indian mother and Jamaican father, calling her success "pathbreaking" for Indian-Americans. China's ambassador to the U.S. signaled openness to improved relations, expressing hope for cooperation on public health, climate change, and economic growth. However, China simultaneously imposed sanctions on several Trump administration officials, including former Secretary of State Mike Pompeo. European leaders particularly welcomed Biden's immediate executive action rejoining the Paris Climate Agreement. French President Emmanuel Macron and German Chancellor Angela Merkel both praised the move, with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen calling it "a new dawn in America" and describing Europe as ready for a fresh start with its "oldest and most trusted partner." Israeli President Benjamin Netanyahu highlighted his personal friendship with Biden and expressed optimism about strengthening U.S.-Israel relations while advancing Middle Eastern peace and confronting Iran. Iran's Foreign Minister Javad Zarif used the occasion to criticize the Trump administration's authorization of the airstrike that killed Iranian commander General Qasem Soleimani. Overall, the international response reflected optimism about renewed American engagement on climate, diplomacy, and global cooperation.

Russian Ambassador to Tehran Levan Dzhagaryan said Russia has made its strongest efforts to preserve the 2015 nuclear agreement, the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA), while criticizing Europe for what he described as passivity in supporting the deal. In an interview with ILNA published on Sunday, he said Europe publicly backs the accord but has not acted decisively to keep it alive. His comments came amid renewed European efforts to prevent the agreement from collapsing. EU foreign policy chief Josep Borrell has argued that Iran must again receive the benefits promised under the deal if it is to survive. He has also said the EU should keep the dispute-resolution process open-ended rather than allow it to end in a way that could send the issue to the UN Security Council or trigger fresh sanctions. Borrell said in January that more time would be given for discussions because of the complexity of the issues. He later met President Hassan Rouhani in Tehran on February 3, where Rouhani criticized the EU for failing to meet its commitments after the United States withdrew from the JCPOA and reimposed sanctions. Rouhani nevertheless said Iran remained ready to cooperate with the European Union and would return to its own commitments if the other side fully honored its obligations. The article also recalls that in May 2019 Iran began reducing its JCPOA commitments in stages, citing Washington’s withdrawal from the deal and Europe’s inability to protect Iran’s economy from U.S. sanctions. Dzhagaryan also warned that Iran would face problems if it refuses to join the Financial Action Task Force (FATF). He said Russia had shared its view with Tehran as a friendly country, but that the final decision was Iran’s internal matter. The FATF had set a February 2020 deadline for Iran to strengthen anti-money-laundering laws and adopt the Palermo and Terrorist Financing conventions or face the full return of countermeasures. The Iranian government is seeking approval to join the body. Parliament approved the move in October 2018, but the Guardian Council rejected it, leaving the matter to the Expediency Council for final arbitration. Finally, Dzhagaryan condemned the U.S. assassination of Major General Qassem Soleimani, saying it would have negative consequences for the West Asia region. Soleimani was killed in a U.S. drone strike in Baghdad on January 3, prompting Iran to launch missile attacks on a U.S. base in Iraq on January 8. The ambassador urged both Iran and the United States to show restraint and resolve disputes through dialogue.

Russia has expressed regret over damage to Azerbaijan’s embassy in Kyiv after reviewing Baku’s complaint, according to the Russian Foreign Ministry. The issue was discussed at a meeting between Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Mikhail Galuzin and Azerbaijan’s Ambassador to Russia, Rahman Mustafayev. Russia said its competent authorities carefully examined Azerbaijan’s November appeal concerning damage to the embassy’s buildings, property, and grounds, and conveyed “sincere regret” over the incident. The damage followed a Russian missile and drone attack on Kyiv around 1:00 a.m. on November 14, 2025, when an Iskander-type missile struck the Azerbaijani diplomatic mission. Azerbaijan later summoned Russian Ambassador Mikhail Yevdokimov to its Foreign Ministry and delivered a formal protest note. Baku said the blast destroyed part of the embassy’s perimeter wall and damaged structures, service vehicles, the administrative building, the consular section, and the compound itself, though no one was injured. Azerbaijan also said the attack was not an isolated case, citing a March 10, 2022 airstrike that damaged its honorary consulate in Kharkiv.

# Summary On November 21, Russia expressed regret over damage sustained by the Azerbaijani Embassy in Kyiv, Ukraine. Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Mikhail Galuzin conveyed this sentiment during a meeting with Azerbaijan's Ambassador to Russia, Rahman Mustafayev, after reviewing Azerbaijan's November appeal about the incident. The damage occurred on November 14 when an Iskander-type missile struck the embassy during missile and drone attacks on Kyiv. The strike destroyed a section of the perimeter wall and severely damaged multiple structures, including the administrative building and Consular Section, though no casualties resulted. A Ukrainian air force Antonov-26 transport plane crashed and burst into flames while approaching landing at Chuhuiv airport, about 250 miles east of Kyiv, killing 26 people and leaving one survivor. The aircraft was carrying seven crew members and 20 cadets from a military aviation school when it went down Friday night. Two people were initially reported alive, but one later died in hospital. Search teams later recovered two more bodies, raising the death toll to 26. No cause has yet been determined. President Volodymyr Zelenskiy declared Saturday a day of mourning, ordered all An-26 flights suspended pending investigation, and visited the crash site. He called for a full review of the condition of Ukraine’s military equipment, saying the country had lost “young cadets and experienced military men” with their futures ahead of them. Prime Minister Denis Shygal requested an official report by Oct. 25. Deputy Defense Minister Igor Starobinsky said families of the dead would receive compensation of about $56,000 each. Defense Minister Andrei Taran said the crashed plane was built in 1977. The An-26 is a widely used transport aircraft, and this was the second major aviation disaster in Ukraine this year, following the January downing of a Ukraine International Airlines Boeing 737 in Tehran that killed all 176 aboard.

# Ukraine Military Plane Crash Summary A Ukrainian military aircraft crashed Friday night near Chuhuiv, approximately 250 miles east of Kyiv, killing 26 people with one survivor. The twin-turboprop Antonov-26 was carrying seven crew members and 20 military aviation cadets when it burst into flames while attempting to land at the airport. Two people initially survived the crash, but one died later in the hospital. The cause remains undetermined. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy declared Saturday a national day of mourning and immediately halted all An-26 flights pending investigation. He visited the crash site and called for a comprehensive assessment of the country's military equipment. Prime Minister Denis Shygal requested an official crash report by October 25. The government announced compensation of approximately $56,000 for each victim's family. The aircraft, built in 1977, was one of nearly 1,400 An-26 transport planes manufactured between 1969 and 1986. This represents Ukraine's second major aviation disaster in 2020. In January, a Boeing 737 belonging to Ukraine International Airlines was shot down near Tehran by Iran's Revolutionary Guards, killing all 176 people aboard during escalated U.S.-Iran tensions.

In the central Russian village of Kedrovoye, the family of 37-year-old Ruslan Gavrilov is mourning after learning that he was among the Russians killed in a U.S. airstrike in Syria. His mother, Farkhanur Gavrilova, said an acquaintance alerted her a week after the strike that her son had died. She later said a colleague of his called on the morning of Feb. 8 to report that an unidentified caller had told him Ruslan was killed in the Feb. 7 attack. Gavrilova believes her son would have contacted her himself if he had survived. The strike marked the first time Russian and U.S. combatants were directly pitted against each other in the Syrian war. The Russian Foreign Ministry later acknowledged that five Russians had been killed, while stressing they were not on active military duty. Before that, both Russian and U.S. officials said they had no information confirming Russian casualties. The clash was widely attributed to poor coordination between the Russian military and private military contractors operating in Syria. Gavrilov was one of several men from Kedrovoye who are believed to have joined Wagner, a private military company. Residents and relatives say the village, home to about 2,300 people and located roughly 1,400 kilometers east of Moscow, is now piecing together who went to Syria and what became of them. The men reportedly traveled first to Krasnodar in southern Russia, where social media evidence and family testimony indicate Wagner has a training base on the grounds of a Russian Defense Ministry facility. The company itself could not be found for comment. Gavrilova said she tried to discourage her son from going, but he was persuaded by the promise of high pay. He had been remodeling apartments and had not even completed military service. She said he was not formally prepared for combat and was not given the kind of medical screening one might expect. Her comments reflect the economic desperation she believes drove many of the men to Syria. “Why did they leave? Because of poverty, to make money,” she said. Russian law prohibits mercenary activity, yet private contractors have reportedly played a significant role in Syria alongside Russian forces. Their presence has allowed the Kremlin to keep its official military death toll lower and avoid negative publicity as President Vladimir Putin campaigned for re-election ahead of the March 18 vote. Putin had declared victory in Syria during a December visit to a Russian base there and ordered a partial troop withdrawal, but critics have long accused the government of denying or obscuring the role of contractors. The article says the Russian private fighters’ mission in Syria appears to have focused heavily on oil assets. The Associated Press previously reported on a contract giving Russian interests a 25 percent share of proceeds from oil fields they captured and guarded. Other Kedrovoye families are also waiting for news. One local, Yevgeny Berdyshev, said his half brother Alexander Potapov went to Syria out of “patriotic sentiment,” believing Putin was fighting Islamic State militants. Potapov, 54, had prior combat experience in Chechnya but struggled to find work because of his age, an injury, and a criminal conviction. He left in October with Gavrilov. Local residents, lacking reliable information, have begun compiling lists of men who went to Syria and sharing scraps of news from associates. One more man, Igor Kosoturov, originally from nearby Asbest, is also believed to have died in the U.S. strike. A local legislator confirmed his death, and a paramilitary Cossack leader said it was evident that Kosoturov and another Asbest resident were killed, though he did not elaborate. Kosoturov had previously fought alongside Russia-backed separatists in eastern Ukraine and had received a town award for a “humanitarian mission” there. For the families left behind, the hardest part is the uncertainty. Gavrilova said the grief initially overwhelmed everyone, but now they are waiting for survivors to return with details. She expressed confusion and anger over why Russian men were sent to Syria if they were not officially part of the army. Her neighbor, Berdyshev, criticized the government’s refusal to acknowledge the contractors at all, saying they clearly exist and that the state remains responsible for what happened to them.

Russian troops stationed in the Nagorno-Karabakh area were reportedly fired on in the Zangilan region near the Azerbaijani-Armenian border, according to sources close to Russia’s Defense Ministry. The article says the targets included positions of Russia’s FSB border service and Azerbaijani border units in the village of Seyidlyar. No casualties have been reported. Azerbaijan has officially denied that the incident took place, while Russian military sources claim commanders ordered Russian personnel not to return fire in order to avoid deaths and a wider escalation. The alleged shooting came only days after Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev accused Russia of trying to strike Baku with an Iskander-M ballistic missile. The Russian peacekeepers’ command in Nagorno-Karabakh issued a statement saying that units of the state border service and Russian border service positions in the area had come under fire. The article presents this as the first serious incident in the region since the end of last year’s war between Armenia and Azerbaijan, warning that the conflict could resume and potentially involve Russia directly. The piece then reviews the long history of the Nagorno-Karabakh conflict. Tensions began in 1988, when the Nagorno-Karabakh Autonomous Region declared it would leave the Azerbaijan SSR. During the 1992-1994 war, Azerbaijan lost control of Nagorno-Karabakh and seven surrounding districts. Peace talks were later held under the OSCE Minsk Group, co-chaired by Russia, the United States, and France. A ceasefire was signed in 1994 through Russian mediation, but fighting periodically resumed, including the 2016 four-day war. It also recalls the large-scale war that began on September 27, 2020, when both sides introduced martial law and mobilized. After six weeks of fighting, Azerbaijan gained major territorial advantages. A trilateral agreement signed on November 9-10, 2020, ended the fighting, deployed Russian peacekeepers for at least five years, and required Armenia to hand over occupied territories. Russian troops now guard the road linking Armenia with Stepanakert.

# Summary The military situation in Nagorno-Karabakh remains precarious despite last year's ceasefire agreement. According to Russian Defense Ministry sources, Azerbaijani soldiers fired upon Russian border patrols in the Zangilan region along the Azerbaijani-Armenian border, marking the first serious incident since the conflict's end. No casualties were reported. While Azerbaijan officially denies the incident, Russia has documented it, and Russian commanders reportedly prohibited return fire to prevent escalation and further conflict. This incident follows Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev's recent threats accusing Russia of planning a missile attack on Baku using Iskander-M ballistic missiles. A Russian peacekeepers' command press release confirmed that border service units in the village of Seyidlyar and FSB positions in the area were fired upon. The Nagorno-Karabakh conflict has deep historical roots, beginning in February 1988 when the region announced withdrawal from Azerbaijan. The 1992-1994 armed conflict resulted in Azerbaijan losing control of Nagorno-Karabakh and seven surrounding areas. Multiple ceasefires followed, with the most significant escalation occurring in 2016 during a four-day war that killed hundreds. The most recent conflict erupted on September 27, 2020, resulting in six weeks of intensive fighting. Azerbaijan gained significant territorial advantages before a trilateral peace agreement was signed on November 9-10, 2020. This agreement established a ceasefire, deployed Russian peacekeepers for at least five years, and required Armenia to transfer occupied territories to Azerbaijan. Russian troops now protect the road connecting Armenia to the separatist region's capital, Stepanakert. The current incident demonstrates the fragility of the ceasefire arrangement and raises concerns about potential renewed conflict involving Russian forces, despite diplomatic efforts by Russia, the USA, and France through the OSCE Minsk Group to achieve a lasting political settlement.

WTO Director-General Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala warned at the Astana International Forum in Kazakhstan that rising geopolitical tensions are threatening the stability of the global trading system. Speaking during a high-level special session on June 9, she said the combination of decoupling, deglobalization, and fragmentation poses one of the biggest risks to world trade. She linked these pressures to the vulnerabilities exposed by the COVID-19 pandemic and the Russia-Ukraine war, both of which disrupted supply chains and highlighted weaknesses in the international trading order. Okonjo-Iweala cautioned that if the global trading system were to split into competing blocs, the economic damage would be substantial. According to WTO estimates, a world divided into two trading blocs could lead to a 5 percent loss in real global GDP over the long term, a hit greater than the 3.5 percent loss experienced by OECD countries during the 2008-2009 financial crisis. She urged countries to avoid retreating into protectionism or inward-looking trade policies, arguing that the open trading system has delivered major benefits over the past 75 years, including lifting about one billion people out of poverty. At the same time, she acknowledged the need for resilience. She welcomed the G7’s May statement that it was not pursuing decoupling, but instead seeking “de-risking” and diversification. In her view, this was a more constructive response to current global tensions than outright separation from trading partners. The WTO chief also pointed to areas of growth and opportunity. She said services are now the fastest-growing segment of trade, especially digitally delivered services, which are expanding at around 8 percent annually, compared with goods trade growth of 5.6 percent. “The future of trade is services,” she said, describing it as digital, green, and inclusive. She stressed the importance of reaching a plurilateral agreement among all WTO members on e-commerce so that digital trade can operate under clear rules that support stability, fairness, and competition. The session also reviewed the outcomes of the WTO’s 12th Ministerial Conference (MC-12), held in June 2022 and chaired on Kazakhstan’s side by Timur Suleimenov, who moderated the Astana forum discussion. One major MC-12 achievement was a long-negotiated agreement to eliminate $22 billion in harmful fishery subsidies that contribute to illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing. Okonjo-Iweala said overfishing is a serious threat, with 38 percent to 50 percent of ocean stocks affected, and noted that 260 million people worldwide depend on fisheries for their livelihoods. The goal is to ratify the Fisheries Subsidies Agreement within 18 months. She also pointed out that Kazakhstan spends about USD 100 million importing fish and expressed hope the landlocked country would ratify the agreement. Other MC-12 outcomes mentioned included a declaration on food security aimed at addressing high food prices, volatility, and export restrictions, as well as the extension of the moratorium on customs duties on electronic transmissions and a TRIPS decision related to COVID-19 therapeutics and diagnostics, which helped improve vaccine access. Looking ahead to the 13th Ministerial Conference, scheduled for February next year in the United Arab Emirates, Okonjo-Iweala said WTO reform remains a major priority. She said the organization wants to strengthen its negotiating, monitoring, transparency, and dispute settlement functions so it can meet 21st-century challenges, with reform expected to be completed by 2024. She also highlighted Kazakhstan’s WTO membership as important for the wider Central Asian region, saying it can help encourage accession by countries such as Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan and support reforms that boost growth, development, and integration into global value chains. Finally, she raised concerns about harmful trade-distorting subsidies, climate change’s impact on agriculture, support for least-developed countries’ graduation, and an investment facilitation agreement intended to reduce bureaucratic barriers and make investment easier.

# WTO Director-General Warns of Global Trading System Fragmentation Risks At the Astana International Forum in Kazakhstan on June 9, World Trade Organization (WTO) Director-General Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala highlighted geopolitical tensions as a major threat to global economic stability, warning that decoupling and deglobalization could fragment the world's trading system with severe consequences. ## Economic Impact of Fragmentation Okonjo-Iweala emphasized the potential economic damage of a fractured global trading system. According to WTO estimates, if the world splits into two competing trading blocs, it would result in a 5 percent loss in real global GDP over the long term—exceeding the 3.5 percent loss experienced by OECD countries during the 2008-2009 financial crisis. She cautioned that such fragmentation "could be very costly for the entire global economy." The Director-General attributed current vulnerabilities to the COVID-19 pandemic and the Russia-Ukraine conflict, which exposed weaknesses in supply chains and the trading system. However, she noted positively that G7 countries stated in May they are not decoupling but rather pursuing de-risking and diversification strategies. ## Trade Protection Concerns Okonjo-Iweala urged countries to resist protectionism and maintain the stability and openness of the global trading system. She highlighted that this approach has successfully lifted one billion people out of poverty over the past 75 years, demonstrating the benefits of open trade. ## Future of Trade: Services and Digital Economy The Director-General identified services as the fastest-growing trade segment, with digitally delivered services expanding at 8 percent annually compared to goods trade growth of 5.6 percent. She declared that "the future of trade is services. It is digital, it is green, and it should be inclusive." Okonjo-Iweala emphasized the need for a plurilateral agreement involving all WTO members on e-commerce to establish rules for digital trade ensuring stability, fairness, and competition. ## Recent WTO Achievements The discussion covered significant outcomes from the WTO's 12th Ministerial Conference (MC-12) in June 2022. A landmark achievement was an agreement to eliminate $22 billion in harmful fishery subsidies—a goal pursued for over two decades. With 260 million people depending on fisheries worldwide and overfishing occurring at 38-50 percent of ocean capacity, the agreement aims for ratification within 18 months. Another important outcome was a declaration on food security, responding to the United Nations World Food Program's request to remove export restrictions that could control food prices and volatility. ## WTO Reform and Expansion Okonjo-Iweala outlined three key WTO reform priorities: strengthening negotiating functions, monitoring and transparency, and dispute settlement mechanisms to address 21st-century challenges. The organization pledges to complete reforms by 2024. She highlighted Kazakhstan's WTO membership and encouraged other Central Asian nations, including Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan, to join, noting that WTO access enables fundamental economic reforms and integration into global value chains. ## Additional Priorities The WTO extended its moratorium on customs duties for electronic transmissions and expanded the TRIPS Decision to cover COVID-19 therapeutics and diagnostics, advancing vaccine accessibility. Okonjo-Iweala also raised concerns about trade-distorting agricultural subsidies disadvantaging smaller nations, particularly in cotton production, and stressed the need to address climate change impacts on agricultural regions. She advocated for helping least-developed countries graduate from LDC status to industrialize and create jobs, and promoted an investment facilitation agreement to reduce bureaucratic barriers.

A Venezuelan judge has granted six jailed U.S. oil executives, known as the “Citgo 6,” an appeals hearing, a rare move in a judicial system widely seen as aligned with President Nicolás Maduro. According to a court document seen by The Associated Press, the hearing was scheduled for Tuesday before a three-judge panel. The men — Tomeu Vadell, José Luis Zambrano, Alirio Zambrano, Jorge Toledo, Gustavo Cárdenas and José Pereira — have been detained for four years on corruption charges. They were arrested in 2017 after being lured to Caracas for a meeting at the headquarters of Citgo’s parent company, the state-run oil giant PDVSA. Masked security agents took them away during the meeting, just before Thanksgiving. Last year, the six were convicted of embezzlement in a trial marked by delays and irregularities. They received prison sentences ranging from eight to 13 years for their involvement in a never-executed plan to refinance billions in oil company bonds. Maduro accused them of “treason,” while the executives have maintained their innocence. The hearing comes the same week the U.N. Working Group on Arbitrary Detention is set to consider the case of Tomeu Vadell. The men have twice been granted house arrest. The first time, in December 2019, they were returned to jail two months later on the same day Donald Trump hosted Venezuelan opposition leader Juan Guaidó at the White House. They were granted house arrest again in April, but that ended on Oct. 16, the same day a Maduro ally was extradited from Cape Verde to the United States.

# Summary Six U.S. oil executives, known as the Citgo 6, have been granted an appeals court hearing after four years of detention in Venezuela on corruption charges. A Venezuelan judge scheduled the hearing before a three-judge panel for Tuesday, marking a rare judicial decision in the country. The six Houston-based Citgo employees—Tomeu Vadell, Jose Luis Zambrano, Alirio Zambrano, Jorge Toledo, Gustavo Cardenas, and Jose Pereira—were arrested in November 2017 after being lured to a meeting at PDVSA headquarters in Caracas. They were convicted of embezzlement last year and sentenced to 8-13 years in prison for proposing to refinance the oil company's bonds, a plan never executed. All six pleaded innocence, while Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro accused them of "treason." The timing of the appeal hearing coincides with the UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention taking up Vadell's case. The executives have been granted house arrest twice previously—in December 2019 and April 2024—but both arrangements were terminated following politically sensitive events, including Trump's meeting with Venezuelan opposition leader Juan Guaidó and an ally of Maduro's extradition to the U.S. on money laundering charges.

Mexico’s President Andrés Manuel López Obrador called for the United States and Iran to resolve their confrontation peacefully through dialogue, urging both sides to “say no to war” during his morning press conference. His appeal came after Iran launched more than a dozen ballistic missiles at two Iraqi military bases housing U.S. troops. No casualties were reported, but the attack signaled Iran’s refusal to back down after the killing of a top Iranian general in a U.S. airstrike last week. Iranian Foreign Minister Mohammad Javad Zarif said Iran did not “seek escalation or war” and described the strikes as a proportional response to U.S. actions. President Donald Trump responded on Twitter, saying, “All is well!” while the U.S. and other parties took precautions, including diverting flights away from Iranian airspace and telling embassy personnel in Jordan to stay home. The missile attack directly challenged Trump, who had warned Iran hours earlier that it would face severe consequences if it acted against U.S. interests. The article says López Obrador’s call for peace, though well intentioned, is unlikely to be enough to defuse the crisis.

# Summary Mexico's President Andres Manuel Lopez Obrador called for peaceful dialogue to resolve escalating tensions between the United States and Iran, urging both parties to reject war. Iran launched over a dozen ballistic missiles at two Iraqi military bases housing U.S. troops, resulting in no reported casualties. Iranian Foreign Minister Mohammad Javad Zarif claimed the attacks were a proportional response to a U.S. airstrike that killed a top Iranian general. Zarif stated Iran does not seek escalation or war. President Trump responded via tweet, saying "All is well!" but precautionary measures were implemented, including airlines diverting flights from Iranian airspace and the U.S. Embassy in Jordan requesting staff maintain low profiles. The Iranian attacks directly challenge Trump's previous threats against Iran. While Trump had emphasized the drone strike aimed to reduce violence and warned of "disproportionate" consequences for Iranian retaliation, Iran proceeded with its military response anyway, making Obrador's peaceful appeals unlikely to succeed.

Venezuelan Foreign Minister Jorge Arreaza on Tuesday condemned the U.S. killing of Iranian Lt. Gen. Qassem Soleimani, calling it a “treacherous” act and saying Soleimani was targeted because he fought terrorism. Speaking in Tehran, Arreaza praised Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and other military branches for helping stabilize the region. He also defended Iran’s January 8 missile strike on a major U.S. base in Iraq as a necessary act of self-defense and sovereignty, saying it helped prevent a wider regional escalation. Arreaza argued that without retaliation, the United States would likely have taken further actions against Iran. Soleimani was killed in a U.S. airstrike in Baghdad on January 3, prompting vows of “harsh revenge” from Iranian leaders. Iran responded by firing dozens of ballistic missiles at the Iraqi base. Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei later said U.S. forces must leave the region and described the strike on the base as a “Day of Allah,” calling Soleimani’s assassination a cowardly and disgraceful act.

# Summary Venezuelan Foreign Minister Jorge Arreaza condemned the U.S. assassination of Iranian Lieutenant General Qassem Soleimani on January 3 as a "treacherous" act, praising Soleimani's counter-terrorism efforts. He commended Iran's military for regional stabilization and justified Iran's retaliatory missile strike against a U.S. military base in Iraq on January 8, arguing it prevented further American aggression and was necessary to defend Iranian sovereignty. Arreaza predicted that without Iran's response, the U.S. would have escalated military actions. Iranian leaders, including Ayatollah Khamenei, vowed "harsh revenge" and demanded complete U.S. withdrawal from the region. Khamenei later characterized the missile strike as a "Day of Allah," representing societies ridding themselves of oppressors, and described Soleimani's assassination as a cowardly act that disgraced the United States.

Chileans marked the 46th anniversary of the Sept. 11, 1973 coup that overthrew Socialist President Salvador Allende by honoring both Allende and the victims of Gen. Augusto Pinochet’s dictatorship. Across Santiago, people laid flowers and wreaths at memorials, Allende’s tomb, mass graves, and at Villa Grimaldi, a former secret police detention and torture site. The day also included a commemoration at the Morande Street gate of La Moneda palace, where Allende made his final entrance and where his last stand was remembered with red carnations and a wreath. President Sebastián Piñera, a conservative billionaire, spoke at the official government ceremony but did not mention Allende by name. He described the coup as a “breakdown of democracy” and urged Chileans to reflect calmly on the causes and consequences of Sept. 11, 1973, so that such mistakes would not be repeated. Allende’s granddaughter, Socialist lawmaker Maya Fernández, said the anniversary should also honor the families of those who suffered under Pinochet, noting that many still do not know the fate of their loved ones and cannot bury or visit them. Nearly 1,200 of the roughly 3,200 people killed by the military regime remain missing. The article recalls that Allende died by suicide as Pinochet’s troops stormed La Moneda after an aerial bombardment and tank attack. Pinochet later rebuilt the palace without the Morande gate, which was restored in 2003 under President Ricardo Lagos. At Villa Grimaldi, the ceremony featured a recording of Allende’s final radio address. In total, the Pinochet regime killed more than 3,000 people and arbitrarily detained and tortured about 40,000 political opponents.

# Chile Commemorates 1973 Coup Anniversary Chile observed the 46th anniversary of the September 11, 1973 military coup that overthrew Socialist President Salvador Allende and led to General Augusto Pinochet's 17-year dictatorship. While political divisions between right and left persist, Chileans broadly agree on preventing such violence from recurring. President Sebastian Piñera, a conservative billionaire, acknowledged the "breakdown of democracy" but notably omitted mention of Allende during the official ceremony. He called for reflection on the coup's causes and consequences to learn from past errors. Allende died during the coup when he took his own life as Pinochet's forces stormed La Moneda palace following aerial bombardment and tank attacks. His final stand was commemorated at the Morande Street gate he regularly used to enter and exit the palace. Though Pinochet had the gate removed during palace reconstruction, President Ricardo Lagos ordered its restoration in 2003. Tributes included red carnations and wreaths at the gate and Allende's statue. Allende's granddaughter, Socialist lawmaker Maya Fernandez, emphasized honoring not only her grandfather but all dictatorship victims. She highlighted that nearly 1,200 of the approximately 3,200 people killed by the military regime remain missing, leaving families unable to locate or properly mourn their loved ones. Chileans gathered at Santiago's General Cemetery and Villa Grimaldi, a former secret police torture center, to pay respects. At Villa Grimaldi, Allende's final radio address was broadcast. Beyond the 3,200 deaths, Pinochet's regime arbitrarily detained and tortured 40,000 political opponents.

Kenya’s government on Thursday condemned nationwide protests that left at least 16 people dead and caused widespread destruction, calling the unrest “terrorism disguised as dissent.” The demonstrations, held on Wednesday, marked the first anniversary of anti-tax protests that had previously escalated into deadly clashes when a large crowd stormed parliament and security forces used lethal force. The latest protests began peacefully but later turned violent, according to AFP, as young men fought police, set fires and tore up pavements to use as weapons. In a televised address, Interior Cabinet Secretary Kipchumba Murkomen said the violence was not a legitimate protest but an “attempted coup.” He accused “criminal anarchists” of unleashing “violence, looting, sexual assault, and destruction.” The worst damage was reported in Nairobi’s business district, where entire shopping centers and thousands of businesses were reportedly destroyed. Emergency responders said they treated multiple gunshot injuries, while some local media outlets, though unconfirmed, reported that police fired on protesters, especially outside the capital. Rights group Vocal Africa said at least four bodies had been brought to the Nairobi morgue, all of them dead from gunshot wounds. A coalition of rights groups said around 400 people had been injured, including 83 in intensive care. The protests were reported in 23 counties. The United Nations said it was “deeply concerned” and called attention to reports of deaths and injuries among both protesters and police officers.

# Kenya Protests Leave 16 Dead, Government Condemns as "Terrorism" Kenya's government has condemned nationwide protests that resulted in at least 16 deaths and extensive damage to thousands of businesses, characterizing the unrest as "terrorism disguised as dissent." The demonstrations on Wednesday commemorated the one-year anniversary of anti-tax protests that culminated in crowds storming parliament. What began as peaceful protests escalated into violence as young men clashed with police, set fires, and used torn-up pavements as projectiles. Interior Cabinet Secretary Kipchumba Murkomen delivered a televised statement denouncing the violence, looting, sexual assault, and destruction, describing events as an "attempted coup." The unrest was particularly severe in Nairobi's business district, where entire shopping centers were destroyed. According to the rights group Vocal Africa, at least four bodies have been brought to the Nairobi Morgue, all killed in gunfights. A coalition of rights groups reported approximately 400 injuries, with 83 people in serious condition requiring intensive care. Police reportedly fired on protesters, particularly in towns outside the capital. The protests occurred across 23 counties throughout Kenya. The United Nations expressed deep concern over the situation, with UN human rights spokeswoman Elizabeth Throssell acknowledging reports of multiple protester deaths and numerous injuries among both demonstrators and police officers.

The Stormers have reached a point where every remaining Super Rugby match is effectively a must-win if they want to finish top of Africa 1 and secure a home quarter-final. They face the Cheetahs at Newlands on Saturday, then travel to play the Rebels and Force before ending the season against the Kings. A few weeks ago, the Cape Town side appeared to be cruising toward the playoffs, but recent setbacks have made their path much harder. Losses to the Waratahs and Bulls, combined with a 17-17 draw against the Sunwolves in Singapore, have left coach Robbie Fleck’s team under pressure. With the Bulls improving and the Sharks and Lions collecting points in Africa 2, the playoff race has become extremely tight. Fleck said the Stormers still want to win every game, but admitted the pressure has increased. He described the remaining fixtures as “cup final stuff,” while stressing that the team must stay focused on its own process and not be distracted by the stakes. Captain Frans Malherbe also acknowledged the disappointing recent results, but said the upcoming break would help the squad reset and concentrate fully on the Cheetahs. Despite their difficult position, the Stormers still control their own destiny. Winning four matches would almost certainly be enough to secure a playoff place, either by topping the conference or through a wildcard spot.

# Summary The Stormers face a critical period in their Super Rugby season, needing to win their remaining matches to secure top spot in Africa 1 and a home quarter-final. After recent defeats to the Waratahs and Bulls, plus a draw against the Sunwolves, the team's playoff position has become precarious with no room for error. Coach Robbie Fleck and captain Frans Malherbe have adopted a "cup final mentality" for their upcoming fixtures, starting with the Cheetahs at home on Saturday. The Stormers must also face the Rebels and Force away before closing against the Kings at Newlands. While acknowledging the increased pressure, Fleck emphasized the team won't become distracted by the need to win every game and will maintain focus on their established processes. The team remains confident they can turn their season around.

The article examines how the COVID-19 pandemic is compounding existing crises across Africa, especially conflict, displacement, gender-based violence, and economic insecurity for women and girls. It begins with the global spread of the new coronavirus, noting that more than one million people had been infected worldwide and that Algeria had become the African country with the highest COVID-19 death toll at the time. In response, governments introduced sweeping measures to slow transmission. But the article stresses that these measures have created new dangers for women, particularly those trapped at home with abusive partners during mandatory lockdowns. South Africa is presented as one of the clearest examples of the surge in gender-based violence during lockdown. Police Minister Bheki Cele announced that 2,230 gender-based violence cases were reported in the first week of the national lockdown alone. In Zimbabwe, several organizations moved quickly to respond. The Musasa Project, Adult Rape Clinic, and the Zimbabwe Women Lawyers Association opened dedicated hotlines for women seeking help with domestic violence and related legal problems. Another rights organization, Veritas, urged the government to intensify community awareness campaigns and distribute information about available support nationwide through official channels. Veritas warned that the government must recognize the increase in domestic violence during lockdown and expand facilities and public information accordingly. The Musasa Project, an NGO and member of Zimbabwe’s Peacebuilding Network, reported that between March 30 and April 9 it received 764 gender-based violence complaints across all platforms. The organization said the spike in just two weeks revealed the scale of the problem across the country. The article links this rise not only to lockdown confinement but also to the reduced ability of survivors to access services, legal help, and life-saving support. The pandemic’s impact is described as especially severe in countries already affected by armed conflict, instability, and humanitarian emergencies. In such settings, refugees and internally displaced people face heightened risk because social distancing is often impossible. The article notes that conflict zones are frequently inaccessible, dangerous, and beyond state control, which undermines peacebuilding and protection efforts. It cites violations of human rights such as restrictions on free speech and press freedom, attacks on women human rights defenders, increased state surveillance, and militarized responses. Mark Suzman, CEO of the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation, is quoted saying that most frontline healthcare workers in Africa and globally are women and therefore face greater exposure to the virus. He said they should be prioritized for protective equipment. Suzman also pointed to anecdotal evidence that social isolation is increasing gender-based violence, adding that the foundation is trying to gather better data and resources on the issue. The Gates Foundation’s 2020 priorities include expanding its focus on gender equality. The article then turns to displaced women and girls. Gillian Triggs, Assistant High Commissioner for Protection at UNHCR, warns that COVID-19 is creating massive protection risks for women and girls forced to flee their homes. UNHCR says millions of people across 21 countries in West and Central Africa face a potential humanitarian catastrophe because of the combined pressures of armed conflict and the pandemic. The region already has one of Africa’s largest displaced populations, with more than nine million people forcibly displaced by conflict and climate-related extreme weather. South Sudan is highlighted as a particularly vulnerable case. The pandemic is expected to delay implementation of the Revitalized Agreement on the Resolution of the Conflict, which could worsen pre-existing gender inequalities. The country hosts 1.5 million displaced people, most of them living in camps. Triggs urges urgent attention to the protection of refugee, displaced, and stateless women and girls, saying they are among those most at risk and that no help should be spared for survivors of abuse. The article also describes how women peacebuilders and grassroots organizations are responding. The Global Network of Women Peacebuilders is creating a COVID-19 and Women Peace and Security database to track the pandemic’s effects on conflict-affected communities and on women’s peacebuilding work. Using information from more than 100 organizations worldwide, the database is intended as a living document to support gender-responsive and conflict-sensitive responses. In Kenya, Rural Women Peace Link is using short radio messages translated into local languages to teach safe practices and hygiene to women in rural areas, especially because women are often primary caregivers for the sick and elderly. Economic consequences are another major concern. The article says the pandemic is expected to hit Africa’s informal sector especially hard, and women make up the majority of informal workers. In Uganda, restrictions included a ban on the sale of non-food items in markets, which is likely to hurt women market sellers and other informal workers disproportionately. The article also reports police brutality against informal workers, including women, who continued selling goods. Movement restrictions have further limited access to sexual and reproductive health clinics. The UN refugee agency warns that lockdowns and quarantines are worsening intimate partner violence because reduced movement and social isolation trap women with abusers. The article also warns of a possible food security crisis in vulnerable communities, driven in part by reduced food imports. Finally, the article outlines recommended responses. The World Health Organization says governments should include essential services for violence against women in COVID-19 preparedness and response plans, fund them, and ensure they remain accessible despite physical distancing. Health facilities should provide information on local hotlines, shelters, rape crisis centers, and counselling services. UN Secretary-General António Guterres has urged governments to make the prevention and redress of violence against women a central part of national COVID-19 plans. UN Women Executive Director Phumzile Mlambo-Ngcuka says shelters and helplines must be treated as essential services, backed by dedicated funding and broad public awareness campaigns. Overall, the article argues that COVID-19 is not only a health crisis but also a driver of deeper gender inequality, violence, displacement, and economic hardship across Africa, especially for women and girls in conflict-affected and impoverished communities.

# Africa Navigating Conflict, Gender-Based Violence, and COVID-19 As the COVID-19 pandemic spreads globally, infecting over one million people worldwide, Africa faces a compounded crisis. Algeria has emerged as the African nation with the highest COVID-19 death toll, prompting governments to implement stringent containment measures. However, these lockdowns have created an unintended consequence: a dramatic surge in gender-based violence, particularly domestic abuse, as women are confined with their abusers. ## The Domestic Violence Crisis The pandemic's impact on gender-based violence has been immediately apparent across the continent. In South Africa, Police Minister Bheki Cele reported that 2,230 gender-based violence cases were documented during just the first week of the national lockdown. Zimbabwe has experienced similarly alarming trends, with the Musasa Project recording 764 gender-based violence reports between March 30 and April 9 alone. In response, women's rights organizations have mobilized quickly. Groups including the Musasa Project, Adult Rape Clinic, and Zimbabwe Women Lawyers Association have established dedicated hotlines to assist domestic violence survivors. Veritas, a Zimbabwe-based women's rights watchdog, has called on the government to increase awareness campaigns about domestic violence and distribute information about available support services through official channels. ## Vulnerable Populations Face Heightened Risks The pandemic poses particularly severe threats to displaced persons and refugees. The UN Refugee Agency (UNHCR) warns that millions of people across 21 countries in West and Central Africa face potential humanitarian catastrophe due to armed conflict combined with coronavirus spread. The region hosts over nine million internally displaced persons fleeing conflict and climate-related disasters. In these conflict zones, social distancing is impossible, making virus transmission inevitable. Additionally, these areas are often inaccessible and beyond government reach, limiting humanitarian assistance. Gillian Triggs, Assistant High Commissioner for Protection at UNHCR, emphasized the heightened vulnerability of displaced women and girls, stating that "doors should not be left open for abusers and no help spared for women surviving abuse and violence." South Sudan exemplifies this crisis, hosting 1.5 million displaced persons in camps while facing potential delays in implementing peace agreements due to COVID-19, which could worsen existing gender inequalities. ## Healthcare Worker Disparities Women comprise 70 percent of frontline healthcare workers globally, yet hold only 25 percent of global leadership positions. Mark Suzman, CEO of the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation, highlighted this disparity while announcing $150 million in additional COVID-19 funding. He emphasized that female healthcare workers require prioritized access to protective equipment to prevent illness and enable continued service delivery. The Gates Foundation has identified expanding gender equality focus as a key 2020 goal. ## Women Peacebuilders' Response Despite challenges, women and youth peacebuilders continue their essential work. The Global Network of Women Peacebuilders is developing a COVID-19 and Women Peace and Security database, utilizing over 100 organizations worldwide to document the pandemic's impacts on conflict-affected communities and women's peacebuilding efforts. This living document will inform gender-responsive and conflict-sensitive interventions. In Kenya, the Rural Women Peace Link organization conducts hygiene and safety sensitization through radio messages translated into local languages, specifically targeting rural women who face elevated risks as primary caregivers for the sick and elderly. ## Economic Impact on Women The informal economy, where women constitute the majority of workers in most African countries, faces devastating impacts. Uganda's COVID-19 response includes banning non-food item sales in markets, disproportionately affecting women vendors. Police brutality against informal workers, including women, has been documented. Movement restrictions have also limited access to sexual and reproductive health services, while potential food security crises loom in vulnerable communities. ## Recommended Solutions International health and development organizations have provided specific recommendations. The World Health Organization urges governments to include essential violence-against-women services in COVID-19 response plans, fund them adequately, and ensure accessibility despite physical distancing measures. Services should include hotlines, shelters, rape crisis centers, and counseling. UN Secretary-General António Guterres called for governments to prioritize violence prevention in national COVID-19 response plans. Phumzile Mlambo-Ngcuka, Executive Director of UN Women, stressed that addressing increased violence against women requires measures embedded in economic support packages, with shelters and helplines designated as essential services receiving dedicated funding and awareness campaigns. The pandemic has exposed existing inequalities while creating new vulnerabilities for African women and girls, demanding urgent, comprehensive, and gender-responsive policy responses.

Somalia’s drought crisis is worsening as government officials and aid agencies warn of rising humanitarian needs and a severe funding shortfall. More than 116,000 people have been displaced since October 2020 because of extreme water shortages, and over 50 districts are facing moderate to severe drought. Forecasts show little or no rain for most of the country until at least the third week of April. Humanitarian Affairs Minister Khadija Diriye said urgent funding is needed to prevent catastrophe amid food insecurity, malnutrition, displacement and disease. The situation is compounded by COVID-19, desert locusts, conflict and instability. Water prices have risen sharply, while the Humanitarian Response Plan is only 4.1% funded.

# Somalia's Worsening Drought Crisis Somalia faces a severe drought exacerbated by financial constraints. Since October 2020, over 116,000 people have been displaced by extreme water shortages, with more than 50 districts experiencing moderate to severe drought. Forecasts predict minimal rainfall through mid-April. The government and humanitarian organizations warn that the situation is critical, as communities already struggle with COVID-19, desert locust infestation, armed conflict, and food insecurity. Water costs have surged over 50 percent in some areas. The Humanitarian Response Plan is only 4.1 percent funded, prompting urgent appeals for immediate financial support to prevent catastrophic consequences and save lives.

Sudan announced on Tuesday that it has recovered 570 antiquities looted during the country’s ongoing armed conflict, calling the return a major step in protecting its cultural heritage and historical identity. The announcement was made at a ceremony in Port Sudan by Graham Abdel Qader, undersecretary of the Ministry of Culture, Information and Tourism and head of the National Committee for the Protection of Sudanese Culture and Antiquities. Abdel Qader said the recovered objects cover a broad span of history, from prehistoric times to the modern era. He said the effort is part of a wider national campaign to safeguard Sudan’s heritage. Recent inventory checks showed losses at several museums. The Gezira Museum lost 68 items out of 408, and the Ethnographic Museum reported the same number missing from a collection of 4,600. About 200 artifacts were also missing from the Khalifa House Museum, while some items remain with private citizens. He added that the National Museum in Khartoum was heavily looted, including its main exhibition hall and secure storage area, with around 4,000 artifacts lost. He said remaining collections have since been catalogued and reorganized for future display. UNESCO representative Ahmed Junaid Sorosh-Wali described the recovery as an example of international cooperation in protecting cultural property during war. Since April 2025, Sudan has worked with INTERPOL and UNESCO to recover artifacts allegedly smuggled out through neighboring countries. The conflict, which began on April 15, 2023 between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the Rapid Support Forces, has caused widespread looting and damage at museums and archaeological sites nationwide.

# Sudan Recovers 570 Looted Antiquities During Conflict Sudan's government announced the recovery of 570 antiquities that were looted during the country's ongoing armed conflict, representing a significant achievement in protecting the nation's cultural heritage. The announcement was made at a ceremony in Port Sudan by Graham Abdel Qader, undersecretary of the Ministry of Culture, Information and Tourism. The recovered artifacts span from prehistoric times to the modern era. Recent inventory reviews revealed substantial losses across multiple museums: the Gezira Museum lost 68 of 408 items, the Ethnographic Museum lost 68 of 4,600 items, the Khalifa House Museum lost approximately 200 artifacts, and the National Museum in Khartoum suffered the most severe damage, losing an estimated 4,000 artifacts from its main exhibition hall and secure storage facility. Since April 2025, Sudan has collaborated with INTERPOL and UNESCO to recover artifacts smuggled through neighboring countries. UNESCO's Sudan representative praised the recovery as a model of international cooperation in protecting cultural heritage during armed conflicts. Numerous museums and archaeological sites across Sudan have been damaged or looted since the conflict began in April 2023 between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces, resulting in tens of thousands of deaths and millions displaced.

Northern Ethiopia’s Tigray region remains highly dangerous for journalists nearly three years after the end of Ethiopia’s civil war, according to the Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ). Reporters there have been detained, threatened with guns, raided by armed men, and caught in a worsening political struggle inside the region’s dominant party, the Tigray Peoples’ Liberation Front (TPLF). The article says the turmoil has revived fears that the region, which was the center of the 2020–2022 war, could again slide toward conflict. The tensions are unfolding as Ethiopia’s foreign minister, Gedion Timothewos, warned the United Nations this month that a faction in Tigray was collaborating with Eritrea, Ethiopia’s historic enemy, in an attempt to overthrow the government. Although the 2022 Pretoria peace agreement formally ended the war, many of its provisions have not been fully implemented. Armed groups remain active, a million civilians are still displaced, and the TPLF itself has fractured into rival camps competing for power, territory, institutions, and control of the media. One of the most alarming recent incidents took place on July 27 in Adi Gudem town, where journalists were covering a protest by residents. Merhawi Birhane, who was traveling with other reporters, said local militia members detained the journalists for several hours after fighters stormed the protest, beat people, and fired into the crowd, killing one man. As the violence unfolded, Merhawi texted Abel Guesh, chief executive of privately owned Tigray Broadcasting Services (TBS), saying they could not continue filming. Abel told them to leave and save themselves. During the confrontation, one militiaman pointed a gun at TBS camera operator Meaza Wubete, while another shouted at Tigray Public Media camera operator Sirak Assefa: “Stop filming or I will shoot you!” Merhawi, Meaza, Sirak, and TPM reporter Eyerusalem Birhanu hid until evening and then returned to Mekelle, the regional capital, disguised in villagers’ clothes to avoid the militia. They left behind their equipment and carried only memory cards so they could still broadcast the story. Both TBS and TPM later condemned the attack as a deliberate effort to suppress press freedom and keep Tigray under authoritarian control. The article says the July attack came after earlier pressure on TBS. In the previous month, police detained two of its camera operators, Bereket Teklegerima and Ermias Gebrekidan, for three days in Axum. The local office of the ruling party accused them of lacking authorization and trying to create “chaos,” while Abel said the station had been reporting on complaints about poor governance. These incidents are tied to the broader power struggle inside Tigray. The article traces the TPLF’s long history: it began as a guerrilla movement in 1975, helped overthrow dictator Mengistu Haile Mariam in 1991, and then dominated Ethiopian politics for 27 years. But after mass protests in 2018, Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed removed several TPLF leaders, and tensions between the TPLF and Abiy later escalated into war. Under the peace deal, Getachew Reda became interim president of Tigray, but in March he and Mekelle’s mayor were ousted by a faction loyal to veteran TPLF leader Debretsion Gebremichael. Getachew fled to Addis Ababa and formed an opposition party. In April, the federal government replaced him with military general Tadesse Worede, who then used Tigray Defence Forces troops to remove pro-Getachew officials and install Debretsion supporters. That move helped spark the July 27 protests. Journalists and media workers say the environment remains perilous. CPJ said nine journalists in Tigray described press freedom as precarious after a war that crippled the national media landscape. During the war, at least 63 journalists were detained, often on accusations of links to or sympathy for the TPLF, and at least 54 went into exile between 2020 and 2024. Mathewos Gebrehiwot, a journalism lecturer at Mekelle University, told CPJ that many reporters had quit and that untrained activists were filling the information vacuum online. He said what remains can barely be called journalism, adding that many journalists now side with one political faction or another, deepening polarization and hopelessness. The article highlights the March 13 takeover of the state-owned Mekelle FM 104.4 radio station as a stark example of the struggle to control the narrative. About 20 armed men stormed the station, pulled programs off air, deleted Facebook posts critical of the faction, and installed their own manager. Station head Halefom Nerea, who later left Tigray, said staff were stunned and some challenged the armed men, asking why they needed guns. One employee called it the saddest day of his life. The station had already faced a similar armed attack in January, though police had intervened then. Later, on September 19, Fetlewerk Gebregziabher, a senior administrative party official, delivered an hour-long speech warning of a “zero tolerance” policy toward media that pushed the “enemies’ agenda.” She accused unnamed outlets of calling for violence, spreading poison, and being paid by outsiders. Abel of TBS told CPJ that journalists now fear “death or detention,” saying the media has become the first victim of the region’s political crisis. CPJ said its requests for comment to regional communication officials and a TPLF deputy chair went unanswered.

# Ethiopian Journalists Face Dangerous Conditions in Post-War Tigray Nearly three years after Ethiopia's civil war concluded, the northern Tigray region remains a perilous environment for journalists. Despite the 2020-2022 conflict's end, reporters continue to face violence, detention, equipment confiscation, and intimidation as they navigate a complex power struggle that threatens to reignite conflict. ## Recent Threats and Violence In July 2025, journalists covering a protest in Adi Gudem town experienced direct threats to their safety. Camera operators from Tigray Broadcasting Services (TBS) and Tigray Public Media (TPM) were confronted by armed militiamen who explicitly threatened to shoot them if they continued filming. The journalists witnessed fighters attacking protesters and firing into the crowd, killing one person. Unable to safely continue reporting, the journalists abandoned their equipment and fled, disguised in villagers' clothes, carrying only memory cards to preserve their footage. Both news organizations condemned the incident as a deliberate attack on press freedom designed to suppress truth and maintain authoritarian control. This incident followed an earlier June incident where TBS camera operators were detained for three days in Axum, accused by the ruling party of lacking proper authorization and attempting to create chaos. The journalists had been reporting on governance complaints. ## The Power Struggle Context The violence against journalists reflects a broader battle for control of the Tigray Peoples' Liberation Front (TPLF), which has fractured since the civil war's end. The TPLF, founded as a guerrilla movement in 1975, played a crucial role in overthrowing Ethiopia's dictator in 1991 and dominated national politics for 27 years before mass protests removed it from power in 2018. Following the 2022 peace agreement signed in Pretoria, South Africa, tensions escalated within the TPLF itself. Federal-backed interim president Getachew Reda was ousted in March by a faction loyal to TPLF veteran Debretsion Gebremichael, who accused the federal government of violating the peace agreement. When the federal government replaced Getachew with military general Tadesse Worede in April, he used Tigray Defence Forces troops to install Debretsion's supporters, triggering the July 27 protests. ## Systematic Media Control The competing factions have attempted to control media narratives through force. Most notably, around 20 armed men stormed state-owned Mekelle FM radio station on March 13, pulling news programs off air, deleting critical Facebook posts, and installing their own manager. This represented the second assault in two months, following a January attack that police had intervened to stop. Station head Halefom Nerea, who has since left Tigray, called it the saddest day of his career. A senior TPLF administrative official, Fetlewerk Gebregziabher, delivered a September speech threatening "zero tolerance" against media pushing the "enemies' agenda," accusing unnamed outlets of calling for violence and accepting foreign payments. These threats have created a chilling effect across the region's media landscape. ## Deteriorating Press Freedom The broader picture of press freedom in Tigray is dire. During the civil war, at least 63 journalists were detained, often accused of TPLF sympathies, and at least 54 journalists went into exile between 2020 and 2024. Many experienced reporters have abandoned journalism entirely, leaving untrained activists to fill the news vacuum online. Mathewos Gebrehiwot, a Mekelle University journalism lecturer, told the Committee to Protect Journalists that the current state of reporting is "difficult to even call journalism." He noted that journalists lack fundamental skills, many side with political factions, and there is widespread hopelessness in the profession. The Ethiopian foreign minister warned the United Nations that Tigray remains unstable, with one faction allegedly colluding with Eritrea to overthrow the government. As tensions persist and armed groups retain weapons despite peace agreement provisions, journalists remain vulnerable targets caught between competing powers determined to control information and suppress dissenting voices.

Malik Ambar’s life is presented as one of the most remarkable examples of the deep historical links between India and Ethiopia, connections that Prime Minister Narendra Modi highlighted during a speech in the Ethiopian Parliament. Modi said the two regions have been tied across the Indian Ocean for nearly 2,000 years, with merchants exchanging not only spices and gold but also ideas, customs, and ways of life. Within that long relationship, the article says, stands the extraordinary story of Malik Ambar, an Ethiopian-born slave who rose to become one of the most powerful figures in the Deccan and helped shape resistance to Mughal expansion. Born as Chapu in 1548 in Harar, in present-day Ethiopia, Malik Ambar belonged to an ethnic community linked to the Oromo or possibly the now-extinct Maya tribe. He was captured as a child during regional conflict and sold for 20 ducats to Arab traders in Yemen. From there, he was taken to Baghdad, where he was converted to Islam and renamed Ambar by his owner, Mir Qasim al-Baghdadi, who reportedly recognized his intelligence. More than 170 peace-building organizations from around the world have issued a renewed appeal for governments to recommit to peace ahead of the International Day of Peace, arguing that war, the COVID-19 pandemic, and the resulting economic crisis are deepening inequality, hardship, and instability. In a joint statement, the groups said that while the pandemic has exposed the scale of global vulnerability, some government responses and other actions are making conditions worse rather than better. The appeal follows earlier efforts by UN Secretary-General António Guterres, who in March called for an immediate global ceasefire so the world could focus on defeating COVID-19. He urged armed conflict to be “put on lockdown,” but later told the UN Security Council that not all parties had responded. Guterres has since warned that the pandemic could intensify existing conflicts or create new ones, and that public trust, socio-economic conditions, and the social fabric are all under strain. The new statement, backed by faith-based groups, development agencies, policy organizations, and other civil society actors, says crisis responses that increase violence, injustice, and exclusion will only deepen human suffering. Instead, it calls for policies centered on peace, justice, and inclusion both during emergencies and in the longer term. The signatories urge governments to use the pandemic response to mainstream peace by applying conflict-sensitive and risk-informed planning when distributing resources for health and economic recovery. They also call for greater inclusion, including the elimination of gendered and racialized violence and the protection of civic participation. In addition, they say governments should reject violent coercion as a shortcut to political or economic goals, and should reinforce multilateralism and international norms by reducing arms flows and supporting investment, taxation, and trade practices that uphold human rights and humanitarian law. The statement also presses for a reduction in military spending and the elimination of nuclear weapons, arguing that these measures would free up resources to save lives and support the most vulnerable. It explicitly rejects the use of state violence to respond to large-scale unemployment and displacement. Looking beyond the current crisis, the groups warn that climate change, environmental degradation, inequality, and exclusion may bring further disruption in the years ahead. Their message is clear: if the world is to meet tomorrow’s challenges, it must recommit to peace today. Events marking International Peace Day are planned globally, with activities spanning education, the arts, social justice, sports, health, the environment, and community service, alongside a Minute of Silence at noon local time.

Cambodian activist Youk Chhang and Indian psychiatrist Bharat Vatwani were among the recipients of the Ramon Magsaysay Award, announced Friday in Manila. Often called Asia’s Nobel Prize, the award recognized Chhang for documenting the crimes of Cambodia’s Khmer Rouge regime and Vatwani for rescuing mentally ill people from Indian streets. Chhang, a survivor of Khmer Rouge violence and oppression, returned from exile to lead the Documentation Center in Cambodia. Since 1995, the center has collected and digitized about one million documents from roughly 23,000 forced-labor camps, where an estimated two million people were killed, and has recorded the testimonies of about 10,000 victims and perpetrators. Vatwani has spent decades helping homeless people with mental illness through his Shraddha Rehabilitation Foundation. Since 1988, he has assisted around 7,000 patients, providing shelter and treatment and often reuniting them with their families. Estimates suggest about 400,000 mentally ill people live on India’s streets. Other honorees included Filipino Howard Dee, Indian educator Sonam Wangchuk, Vietnamese disability advocate Vo Thi Hoang Yen, and East Timorese humanitarian Maria de Lourdes Martins Cruz. The foundation praised all the winners for taking on major causes despite limited resources, adversity, and opposition. Dee was recognized for peace and poverty-reduction work in conflict areas, Martins Cruz for social service projects, Yen for improving life for people with disabilities, and Wangchuk for education and cultural development in Jammu and Kashmir.
