Cambodian activist Youk Chhang, a Khmer Rouge survivor, was recognized for documenting the regime's crimes against humanity through his Documentation Center. Since 1995, the center has collected approximately one million digitalized documents from 23,000 forced-labor camps where two million people were killed, and recorded testimonies from 10,000 victims and perpetrators. Indian psychiatrist Bharat Vatwani was honored for rescuing mentally ill individuals from Indian streets. Since 1988, he has assisted around 7,000 mental patients through his Shraddha Rehabilitation Foundation, reuniting many with their families. The other winners included Filipino Howard Dee, former Philippine ambassador who founded the Assisi Development Foundation in 1975, implementing over 4,100 projects benefiting 10.5 million Filipinos through sustainable development and poverty reduction initiatives. Indian educator Sonam Wangchuk was awarded for promoting education and cultural development in Jammu and Kashmir. Foundation president Carmencita Abella praised the winners for their courage in pursuing significant causes despite limited resources and opposition.

China has accused organizers of a Bangkok art exhibition of distorting its policies on Tibet, Xinjiang and Hong Kong after the show’s co-curator said artworks were removed or altered at Beijing’s request. The exhibition, **“Constellation of Complicity: Visualising the Global Machinery of Authoritarian Solidarity,”** opened on July 24 at the Bangkok Arts and Cultural Centre, one of Thailand’s leading galleries. According to Reuters, works dealing with Hong Kong and China’s treatment of ethnic minorities in Tibet and Xinjiang were later removed or modified after pressure from the Chinese Embassy in Bangkok. The Chinese foreign ministry did not clearly confirm or deny that the embassy had ordered the changes, but it strongly defended the action, saying the exhibition promoted “fallacies” about “Tibetan independence,” the “East Turkestan Islamic Movement,” and “Hong Kong independence,” and undermined China’s “core interests and political dignity.” When Reuters visited the exhibition on Thursday, several pieces that had been publicly advertised or photographed were no longer on display. These included a multimedia installation by a Tibetan artist. Other works had been edited so that the words “Hong Kong,” “Tibet,” and “Uyghur” were blacked out, along with the names of the artists. Sai, a Myanmar artist who goes by one name and co-curated the show, said Chinese embassy staff, accompanied by Bangkok city officials, entered the exhibition three days after it opened and demanded it be shut down. In an email dated July 30 and seen by Reuters, the gallery said it had received pressure from the Chinese Embassy, relayed through Thailand’s foreign ministry and the Bangkok Metropolitan Administration, and had been warned the show could create diplomatic tensions between Thailand and China. The gallery said it had “no choice” but to make adjustments, including obscuring the names of Hong Kong, Tibetan and Uyghur artists. Sai said the embassy later demanded further removals. China said the intervention showed the “fallacies” in the exhibition had “no market internationally” and were unpopular. It also reiterated its opposition to anyone using culture or art as a cover for political interference in China’s internal affairs. Sai and other organizers described the episode as an example of authoritarian pressure crossing borders. He said removed items included Tibetan and Uyghur flags, postcards featuring Chinese President Xi Jinping, and a postcard linking China and Israel. He called it “tragically ironic” that an exhibition about authoritarian cooperation had itself been censored. Sai also said he was speaking from overseas after Thai police sought him, though a Bangkok police official said no such report had been received. The article notes that China has been expanding its influence in Southeast Asia, where governments often try to balance economic ties with Beijing against sovereignty concerns. It also recalls Thailand’s recent deportation of 40 Uyghurs to China, despite UN warnings they could face torture or harm. The Bangkok exhibition also includes work by exiled artists from Xinjiang, Russia, Iran and Syria.

Oil prices held near US$70 a barrel on July 31 as a series of supply risks from the Middle East to the North Sea offset broader bearish pressure from trade tensions and rising US production. In New York, West Texas Intermediate futures were little changed after rising 2.1% the previous day, their biggest gain in more than a month. Brent also eased only slightly in London. The market has been pulled in opposite directions. On one hand, crude is heading for its biggest monthly loss in a year because the US-China trade dispute has weighed on demand expectations while American shale output continues to climb. On the other hand, traders are increasingly worried about tightening supplies from several major producers. Output in Venezuela has slumped because of economic collapse, Libya remains unstable amid civil conflict, and US sanctions on Iranian oil are expected to curb exports further. Barclays warned of “significant upside risk” to prices once those sanctions begin to bite. Additional supply concerns emerged in Saudi Arabia and the UK. Saudi tankers altered course after the kingdom temporarily suspended oil shipments through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a crucial route at the southern end of the Red Sea, following reported attacks on two tankers by Yemen’s Houthi rebels. In the North Sea, a strike forced workers to start shutting down production at Total SA’s Alwyn, Dunbar and Elgin fields. Union officials said no talks with the company were planned. Prices were also influenced by shifting US-Iran rhetoric. President Donald Trump said he would be willing to meet Iranian President Hassan Rouhani without preconditions, but the White House quickly tempered that message. Secretary of State Michael Pompeo later outlined conditions for any meeting and said sanctions would remain unless Iran changed its behavior. At 8:19 a.m. in London, WTI for September delivery traded at US$69.87 a barrel, down 26 cents, and was on track for a 5.8% monthly decline. Brent for September settlement fell 24 cents to US$74.73, while the more actively traded October contract slipped to US$74.72. Shanghai crude futures rose 0.7% to 513.2 yuan a barrel.

The article describes how some Buddhist monks in Myanmar have aligned themselves with the military junta that seized power in the 2021 coup, despite Buddhism’s association with peace and nonviolence. Disarmament Week, observed from October 24, is intended to raise awareness and improve public understanding of disarmament and its importance across many global issues. Disarmament refers to reducing or fully eliminating a state’s military capabilities. The article says it is essential to prevent arms races, reduce threats to humanity, protect civilians from suffering, and ease the burden of military spending on states. The United Nations places top priority on reducing and ultimately eliminating nuclear weapons, destroying chemical weapons, and strengthening the ban on biological weapons. The observance of Disarmament Week dates back to the 1978 special session of the UN General Assembly on disarmament, which called for it in its final document. In 1995, the General Assembly encouraged governments and non-governmental organizations to continue participating actively in the week so the public could better understand disarmament issues. The article notes that, throughout history, countries have pursued disarmament to create a safer world and protect people from harm. Since the UN was founded, disarmament and arms control have been central to preventing and ending crises and armed conflict. It argues that rising tensions should be addressed through political dialogue and negotiation rather than by acquiring more weapons. The piece also highlights the UN’s Agenda for Disarmament, which is built around four key pillars and practical measures meant to be achieved through stronger partnerships and firm commitment. It says the agenda addresses six Sustainable Development Goals through nine actions, showing that disarmament and arms control are closely linked to development. This connection, the article argues, creates an opportunity to advance both the SDGs and disarmament goals together. A major focus is conventional arms, especially small arms and light weapons. These remain central to many conflicts, with civilians bearing the greatest burden of armed violence. Their widespread availability enables violence, worsens insecurity, facilitates human rights abuses, and blocks humanitarian access. The article links this directly to the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, especially Goal 16, which calls for a significant reduction in illicit arms flows to support peaceful, just, and inclusive societies. It adds that fighting the illegal trade in small arms is also important for progress on poverty reduction, economic growth, health, gender equality, and safer cities. In discussing the need for disarmament in the 21st century, the article says it is a tool to prevent conflict and reduce harm when conflict does occur. It points to renewed Cold War-style tensions in a more complex multipolar world, along with more frequent and deadlier wars due to modern weaponry. Conflicts in Syria, Yemen, Iraq, Afghanistan, and Palestine are described as being tied to regional and global rivalries involving extremists, terrorists, militias, and criminal groups. Global military spending is rising, having doubled in inflation-adjusted terms since the end of the Cold War. # Summary: Disarmament Week and Global Arms Control Challenges Disarmament Week, beginning October 24, aims to raise awareness about disarmament issues and their critical importance in maintaining global peace and security. Disarmament refers to the reduction or complete elimination of a nation's military capabilities, serving as a crucial mechanism for preventing arms races, reducing threats to humanity, minimizing civilian suffering, and alleviating the financial burden of military expenditure on states. ## Historical Context and UN Priorities The United Nations established Disarmament Week following a 1978 special General Assembly session on disarmament. By 1995, the UN formally invited governments and non-governmental organizations to actively participate in promoting public understanding of disarmament issues. The UN has prioritized reducing and eliminating nuclear weapons, destroying chemical weapons, and strengthening prohibitions on biological weapons. Throughout history, countries have pursued disarmament to create safer, more secure worlds, recognizing that political dialogue and negotiation are more effective than military buildup in resolving tensions. ## The Disarmament Agenda The Disarmament Agenda addresses six Sustainable Development Goals through nine specific actions, establishing four key pillars for practical implementation. Notably, disarmament and arms control are intrinsically linked to sustainable development, offering opportunities to advance both the Agenda for Disarmament and the 2030 Sustainable Development Goals. Conventional arms remain a significant threat, with civilians bearing the brunt of armed violence. Small arms and light weapons proliferation facilitates armed conflict, human rights violations, and humanitarian access impediments. Reducing illicit arms flows is essential for achieving peaceful, just, and inclusive societies, as well as goals related to poverty reduction, economic growth, health, gender equality, and safe communities. ## Contemporary Challenges The 21st century presents complex disarmament challenges. Although Cold War tensions have diminished, the multipolar world environment has become more dangerous. Modern weaponry has made armed conflicts more frequent and deadly for civilians. Regional conflicts in Syria, Yemen, Iraq, Afghanistan, and Palestine involve multiple actors including violent extremists, terrorists, organized militias, and criminal elements, interconnected with global rivalries. Global military spending has doubled since the Cold War's end, with 12.6 percent of gross world product devoted to containing violence. According to Uppsala Conflict Data, over 2.7 million people have died in armed conflicts since 1989. Critically, 12,700 nuclear weapons remain an existential threat, while strategic arms control negotiations remain stalled. ## Rising Regional Arms Races Global defense spending reached a record $2.2 trillion in 2023, with multiple regional arms races intensifying. China increases its arsenal to counter the USA, while India expands its military capabilities to address threats from both China and Pakistan. Pakistan, facing conventional warfare disadvantages, has increased its nuclear arsenal beyond India's capabilities. Japan counters China's growing military power through increased defense spending. The Middle East witnesses an arms race between Iran, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE, with potential Iranian nuclear weapons acquisition threatening further escalation. The International Institute for Strategic Studies predicts continued budget increases throughout 2024, indicating that the volatile security environment will likely persist, emphasizing the urgent need for renewed disarmament efforts and international cooperation to prevent catastrophic global conflict.

Amnesty International has accused the U.S.-led coalition’s 2017 assault on Raqqa, Syria, of causing massive destruction and civilian deaths through what it described as “disproportionate or indiscriminate” attacks that may amount to war crimes. The report, released Tuesday in London, examines the five-month campaign to retake the city from ISIS, which ran from June to October last year and relied on tens of thousands of U.S. and allied air and artillery strikes in support of the Syrian Democratic Forces, a U.S.-backed coalition dominated by the Kurdish YPG militia. According to Amnesty, the overwhelming majority of the bombardment was carried out by U.S. forces: about 90 percent of airstrikes and all artillery strikes. British and French forces conducted the remaining airstrikes, while other members of the 70-nation coalition provided support such as aerial refueling and target identification. The report quotes U.S. Army Sergeant-Major John Wayne Troxell boasting that Marines fired 30,000 artillery rounds on ISIS targets in five months, and that coalition forces were striking Raqqa continuously with mortars, artillery, rockets, Hellfires, and armed drones. Amnesty senior crisis response adviser Donatella Rovera said the use of artillery shells, which can miss by more than 100 meters, made mass civilian casualties unsurprising. The report sharply contrasts with U.S. military claims that the campaign was highly precise. U.S. Lieutenant General Stephen Townsend had called the offensive “the most precise air campaign in the history,” but Amnesty said the reality on the ground was widespread devastation. Journalists and rights monitors had already warned during and after the battle that entire civilian neighborhoods were being destroyed. Raqqa, which had served as the administrative capital of ISIS’s self-declared “caliphate” since 2014, was left in ruins, and thousands of civilians were killed or displaced. Amnesty documented the experiences of four families as examples of the broader civilian toll. The Aswad family lost eight members in one airstrike, the Badran family lost 39, the Fayad family lost 16, and the Hashish family lost 18. In each case, powerful bombs struck buildings where civilians had been living long-term. Based on interviews with 112 civilians in February, Amnesty said these cases provided “prima facie evidence” that several coalition attacks violated international humanitarian law. The coalition responded by arguing that ISIS had used civilians as human shields and that its forces were fighting an enemy unconstrained by laws or norms. Speaking to the BBC, coalition spokesman U.S. Army Colonel Sean Ryan criticized Amnesty staff and accused them of ignoring the realities of combat. Amnesty acknowledged that ISIS also endangered civilians by hiding among them and placing them in harm’s way, but said that did not excuse the scale of destruction inflicted on the city. The report concludes by demanding that the coalition publicly acknowledge civilian deaths in Raqqa, release strike information such as dates, times, locations, weapons used, and intended targets, and provide reparations to survivors whose families, homes, and neighborhoods were destroyed.

The campaign also involved widespread deployment of white phosphorus, a chemical weapon, despite coalition criticism of the Syrian government's use of chemical agents. Journalists and rights monitors documented massive destruction throughout the city, with entire civilian districts reduced to rubble. The Aswad family lost eight members in a single airstrike; the Badran family lost 39 members; the Fayad family lost 16; and the Hashish family lost 18. Amnesty argues that the coalition's belief in precision airstrikes minimizing civilian casualties represents "wishful thinking" contradicted by evidence from Raqqa and the Iraqi city of Mosul.

ASM International N.V. reported strong third-quarter 2020 results, saying performance was supported by continued high demand in logic/foundry markets and an exceptionally strong gross margin. The company, based in Almere, the Netherlands, released its unaudited IFRS results on October 28, 2020. New orders in Q3 2020 totaled €303.4 million, up 2% from the previous quarter and 4% from the same period a year earlier. Revenue came in at €314.6 million, down 8% from Q2 2020, though ASM said about half of that decline was due to foreign exchange translation effects. Even so, revenue remained 16% higher than in Q3 2019 and was at the high end of the company’s guidance range of €300 million to €320 million. Gross profit margin improved to 49.9% in the third quarter from 48.3% in Q2, which ASM attributed to an exceptionally strong product mix. Operating result was €83.9 million, slightly below the €87.6 million recorded in the prior quarter, mainly because of lower sales, partly offset by the stronger margin and lower costs. Net earnings were €58.1 million, compared with €74.1 million in Q2 and €53.5 million in Q3 2019. Normalized net earnings, which exclude certain amortization and sale-related items tied to ASMPT, fell to €61.2 million from €77.4 million in the second quarter. Chief Executive Officer Benjamin Loh said the company continued to deliver strong results in Q3 and noted that supply chain and logistics conditions had largely returned to normal. He emphasized that the quarter’s sales were driven by sustained demand in the logic/foundry segment. He also said order intake slightly exceeded the company’s guidance range, and that the stronger-than-expected gross margin reflected the favorable mix of business. Looking ahead, ASM said it expected fourth-quarter 2020 revenue of €330 million to €350 million on a currency-comparable basis, and bookings of €340 million to €360 million. Based on market conditions in the second half of the year, the company now expected the wafer fab equipment (WFE) market to grow by a high single-digit to low double-digit percentage in 2020, and it said it expected to outperform the broader WFE market for the full year. ASM also updated investors on its share buyback program, which had been announced on June 2, 2020. By September 30, 2020, 35.5% of the €100 million program had been completed, at an average share price of €124.18. The company included standard forward-looking statement warnings about risks such as semiconductor industry cycles, exchange-rate movements, competition, regulation, and broader economic disruptions. It also said the release contained inside information under EU market rules and announced an investor conference call and webcast for October 29, 2020.

Kashmir Council Europe (KC-EU) announced that it will hold a one-day protest camp in Brussels on Tuesday, 13 July 2021, to commemorate the martyrs of 13 July 1931 in Srinagar. The event will take place at 11:30 a.m. in front of the EU External Action Service (EEAS) at Schuman Place, near the European headquarters. The article recalls that on 13 July 1931, thousands of Kashmiris gathered outside Srinagar’s central jail to witness the trial of Abdul Qadeer. According to the report, Dogra ruler forces opened fire on the crowd, killing 22 Kashmiris. KC-EU said the protest camp is meant to honor those martyrs and all Kashmiri victims. In a statement from Brussels, KC-EU Chairman Ali Raza Syed paid tribute to the martyrs and accused Indian forces of continuing abuses against Kashmiris. He cited a recent United Nations report that, he said, exposed the targeting of a large number of children in occupied Kashmir in recent years. At the end of the protest camp, participants will hand a petition to EEAS officials urging the European Union to help stop violations of children’s rights by Indian forces in occupied Kashmir. The article also quotes UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres, who expressed concern over “grave violations” against children in Indian-occupied Kashmir and called on India to end the use of shotgun pellets against children. He urged preventive measures to protect children and endorsed the Safe Schools Declaration. Ali Raza Syed called on the UN Security Council to act immediately to protect children in conflict zones, especially in Indian-administered Kashmir, and urged the EU to use its influence to pressure India to stop human rights violations. He said the EU, as a champion of human rights, has a moral duty to act under its guidelines on children and armed conflict. KC-EU also plans a protest in front of the Indian embassy in Brussels on 5 August 2021, marking the second anniversary of India’s revocation of Jammu and Kashmir’s special constitutional status in 2019.

In eastern Ukraine’s Donbas region, the war often looks very different from the intense urban combat seen in places like Bakhmut. In most sectors of the front, Ukrainian soldiers spend long stretches waiting in trenches, bunkers, and forest positions, watching for Russian movement, occasional shelling, or drone activity. A reporter visiting the trenches near Velyka Novosilka and nearby positions in southern Donbas found a war defined as much by boredom, cold, and routine as by danger. Near Velyka Novosilka, a small town close to the front, a Ukrainian lieutenant named Sergey commands a trench system less than 2 kilometers from Russian forces. The two sides are separated by a mine-filled open field. On a snowy day, Sergey says the weather makes things calmer because neither side can see clearly. From his observation point, he and his men can only watch and wait. He describes the front there as quiet compared with Bakhmut, where fighting has been close-range and relentless. In this sector, he says, the war is more often about surveillance, tension, and the possibility of sudden fire than constant combat. Inside the trench complex, soldiers move through narrow corridors in a repetitive pattern: checking a camouflaged .50-caliber machine gun, scanning the field with binoculars, looking for drones, then repeating the same route to another observation post. Sergey says many people imagine war as nonstop explosions and gunfire, but that is not the reality here. In the bunker where he and his men spend their spare time, the conditions are dark and cold, lit only by a candle. One soldier sleeps while a cat nurses three kittens born in the trench. Sergey explains that his unit has been in this position for three months. Before that, they were 800 meters farther forward, but in December they had to retreat because Russian artillery was too accurate. Since then, they have mostly been watching and waiting, with only occasional enemy fire or threats of an advance. The article contrasts this quieter front with Bakhmut, which has become a symbol of the war’s second year. There, Russian and Ukrainian troops fight street by street and house by house, and tens of thousands of soldiers on both sides have been killed or wounded in months of brutal combat. But Bakhmut is presented as an exception. Across the rest of the roughly 1,000-kilometer front stretching from northern Donbas to Kherson in the south, the fighting has largely been static for months. Trenches, rivers, and other barriers hold the line, and while skirmishes happen daily, there are few major advances or retreats. A few kilometers away, another Ukrainian unit experiences the same mix of tension and inactivity. In a forest near Vuhledar, Ivan, a young former book editor from Kharkiv, leads a group of six soldiers responsible for one of three artillery pieces in the area. On snowy days, he says, they rarely receive orders to fire because drones cannot see across the battlefield well enough. Most of the time, the crew simply waits in a bunker about a kilometer from their Soviet-era 2S3 Akatsiya self-propelled gun. When a command does come, they can be ready to fire in less than two minutes. Ivan says the soldiers usually do not know exactly what they are shooting at or whether they have hit the target. At their range, only the command center can see the full picture. Inside the bunker, the men pass time playing offline games on their phones and warming socks near ovens, since their phones are kept disconnected to prevent Russian interception or geolocation. As the weather shifts, radio messages begin relaying fire orders to other Ukrainian artillery crews. Ivan notes that neighboring units equipped with Western guns have longer range. Sensing that an order is near, he moves his men closer to the Akatsiya. Soon, cannon booms echo through the forest, the command arrives, and the crew rushes to make final adjustments. Ivan warns the reporter to open his mouth to equalize the pressure from the blast. The gun fires with a burst of flame and smoke, and Ivan immediately tells the reporter to leave because their position may now be known. Another soldier, Sasha, a 36-year-old farmer from near Dnipro, has spent nine months in Velyka Novosilka. He stands watch in one of the few remaining intact houses at the edge of the ghost town, where only about 150 civilians still live. Sasha and a colleague are tasked with reporting who enters and exits through the town’s western access point. Their work is monotonous, interrupted by the constant fear of nearby shelling. He says they keep digging deeper into the ground because they never know when they will be hit. Sasha joined the war after his stepfather was killed at the start of the Russian invasion. His stepfather had fought in Donbas since 2015, but never really explained what war was like. Sasha says he now understands that war is very different from what people are told from afar, and he tries to pass that lesson on to younger people in his village when he is home. Back in Sergey’s trench system, the snowy calm is broken when a soldier thinks he hears a drone. A brief firefight erupts, bullets crack through the air, and then the silence returns almost immediately. Sergey says mortars may follow, but he treats the exchange as only a provocation and expects the front to settle back into its normal rhythm. He carries a small burned candle tucked between his uniform and body armor as an amulet. It was given to him by his father’s best friend, a former Soviet soldier who fought in Afghanistan and survived the war, though he lost both legs. Sergey believes the candle will protect him too. When asked whether survival alone is enough, he answers simply that the main thing is to come home alive, no matter how.

At Paris Fashion Week on Saturday, Loewe presented one of the season’s most striking and unsettling menswear shows, imagining a bleak future in which nature has been largely reduced to something humans exploit or view only through technology. The runway itself reinforced that vision: a stripped-down deck was framed by a descending white wall, while models moved in a rigid, almost mechanical way through misty white light, creating the impression of a sterile, lifeless world. Designer Jonathan Anderson used the concept as more than a theatrical backdrop. His collection, described as a “nature morte,” or still life, carried a pointed ecological message about humanity’s contempt for the natural world. He suggested that if current behavior continues, the natural environment could be destroyed, and living creatures such as bees may exist only on screens. That idea appeared throughout the show in surreal details: models wore plates displaying television images of deep-sea fish, while plasma-like visor screens projected blooming chrysanthemums. In one of the most unusual touches, grass seemed to grow out of shoes, with green blades quivering as the models walked. The collection balanced organic and artificial elements in deliberately odd ways. A white minimalist sweater was cut with extra sleeves that hung limply at the sides, paired with white sports leggings and loafers sprouting clumps of grass. Bare chests and exposed legs added vulnerability, while square-shouldered bags introduced a harder, more severe note. Perhaps the most memorable footwear was a pair of oversized mustard-colored toggle shoes that resembled horse hooves, though they also suggested something from a science-fiction set. The overall effect was both conceptual and highly accomplished, with Anderson using the dystopian theme to support inventive tailoring and design. The article also noted the continued importance of invitation design in the luxury fashion world. Houses compete to send the most original and extravagant invites, often at odds with climate concerns because they are delivered physically to guests. Some invitations hint at the themes of the show, while others are simply eccentric. Louis Vuitton sent a large board-game-style invitation for a show linked to the late Virgil Abloh’s creative world. Dior mailed out flower seeds, which one fashion journalist reportedly planted and saw sprout. Loewe’s invitation was perhaps the strangest: a limp box of real watercress growing in soil. Another standout on the day was British designer Craig Green, who continued to earn praise for his forward-thinking approach to menswear. Recently appointed an MBE by Queen Elizabeth II for services to fashion, Green returned to the Paris runway with a collection centered on uniforms and utilitarian wear. Drawing on influences from internships with designers such as Walter van Beirendonck and Henrik Vibskov, and on past collaborations with Moncler, Green presented deconstructed looks featuring straps, pockets, stirrups and accessories. His pastel equestrian and fencing-inspired pieces had a transgressive, almost aggressive edge, blurring the line between art and fashion. One especially inventive look resembled an upside-down sink with a builder’s ladder attached to the back, evoking both DIY construction and armor.

The Azov Battalion, a far-right group within Ukrainian Armed Forces, has faced long-standing accusations of neo-Nazi ideology due to its use of Nazi symbols and extremist rhetoric. The group remains controversial, with differing interpretations of whether it represents Ukrainian nationalism or dangerous extremism. According to Russian presidential press secretary Dmitry Peskov, Ukraine's de-Nazification can only occur after the war ends through military or diplomatic means. President Putin previously outlined Moscow's preconditions for conflict resolution, including Ukrainian military withdrawal from Donbass and Novorossia, abandoning NATO aspirations, and adopting non-aligned, non-nuclear status.

Syrian Foreign Minister Walid Muallem said on Sunday that Russia’s delivery of S-300 air defense systems to Syria was a “timely step” and a defensive measure meant to protect Syrian airspace. In an interview with RT, he praised President Vladimir Putin’s decision and said the system was intended to support security and stability rather than war. Muallem’s comments came after Russia decided to supply the systems following the downing of a Russian Il-20 aircraft earlier in the month during a Syrian air defense response to Israeli F-16 strikes near the province of Latakia. According to the Russian Defense Ministry, Israel informed Russia of the operation only one minute before the attack. Muallem also addressed the situation in Idlib, the last major province outside full government control. He said Damascus hoped the recent agreement to establish a demilitarized zone there would be implemented and that the issue could be resolved through peaceful means or national reconciliation. At the same time, he said the Syrian state had the legal right to use force if necessary, though it did not want to do so. He added that the process of implementing the Idlib deal had already begun, while Moscow has emphasized that the withdrawal of terrorists from the province is a key issue. Turning to northeast Syria, Muallem said Damascus did not want to use military force against the Kurds, but would do so if they pursued secession. He argued that the real complication was the US military presence, which he said encouraged Kurdish groups to ignore Damascus’s authority. According to him, early talks between the Syrian government and the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces were promising but were disrupted when the United States increased military support to the Kurds and attacked Syrian forces in the area. Muallem also accused the United States of trying to prolong the war by retraining Daesh (ISIS/ISIL) militants at the al-Tanf base in southeastern Syria. He claimed Washington was gathering remnants of the group to send them against the Syrian army and said this was being done in Israel’s interests. The US maintains a 34-mile zone around al-Tanf and has trained Syrian opposition forces there since 2016. Damascus and Moscow have repeatedly criticized the base, alleging that it is being used to move militant groups that carry out attacks on Syrian troops and civilians.

In Kabul, about 30 men sit in a classroom as the first student group at a Taliban-run institute created to train tourism and hospitality workers. The class is an unusual mix: one student is a model, another is 17 and unemployed, and others have different ages, educational backgrounds, and work histories. None has formal experience in tourism or hospitality, and all are men because Afghan women are barred from studying beyond sixth grade. Still, the students say they want to help present a different image of Afghanistan, and the Taliban is encouraging that effort. The push to develop tourism comes despite Afghanistan’s deep problems. The Taliban government remains isolated internationally, mainly because of its severe restrictions on women and girls. The economy is weak, poverty is widespread, and infrastructure is in poor shape. Yet foreign visitors are still coming in increasing numbers, drawn by improved security, easier travel links from places such as Dubai, and the appeal of visiting an unusual destination. Tourism numbers remain small, but they have risen sharply: 691 foreign tourists came in 2021, 2,300 in 2022, and about 7,000 last year. Mohammad Saeed, who heads Kabul’s Tourism Directorate, said China is the largest foreign market because of its population and proximity. He also argued that Afghanistan has an advantage over some neighboring countries because some travelers consider Pakistan dangerous. Saeed said he had heard similar concerns from Japanese travelers. He sees this as an opportunity for Afghanistan. At the same time, major obstacles remain. Obtaining visas is difficult and expensive. Many countries cut ties with Afghanistan after the Taliban returned to power, and no country formally recognizes the Taliban as the country’s legitimate government. Afghan embassies have either closed or suspended operations, and there is an ongoing struggle between diplomatic missions controlled by former Western-backed officials and those now under Taliban control. Saeed acknowledged these barriers but said he was working with ministries to address them. His long-term goal is to establish visa-on-arrival access for tourists, though he said that could take years. Transportation is another major problem. Large parts of Afghanistan’s road network are half-paved or nonexistent, and many airlines avoid Afghan airspace. Kabul has the most international flights, but no Afghan airport has direct service to major tourist markets such as China, Europe, or India. Even so, Saeed said the Taliban leadership supports his ambition to turn Afghanistan into a tourism powerhouse. He said he had been appointed to the post on the instructions of senior officials and believed they trusted him with the role. The students at the institute have their own reasons for joining. Ahmed Massoud Talash, a model, said he wants to learn enough about Afghanistan’s scenic sites to promote them on Instagram and to speak about the country’s history in media appearances. Samir Ahmadzai, a business school graduate, hopes to open a hotel but first wants to understand tourism and hospitality better. He said Afghanistan is often described as backward and defined by poverty and war, but he wants people to remember that it has 5,000 years of history and deserves “a new page.” The curriculum includes Afghan handicrafts and basic anthropology. It also includes an unofficial lesson on how to deal with foreign women and possible clashes between their behavior and local customs or Taliban edicts. Examples mentioned include women smoking or eating in public and mixing with unrelated men. Under Taliban rule, women must follow strict dress codes and are required to travel with a male guardian, or mahram. It has become harder for them to dine alone, travel alone, or socialize publicly with other women. With gyms closed to women and beauty salons banned, their public spaces have narrowed further. Signs of a modest tourism revival are already visible. Kabul’s Serena Hotel, the country’s only five-star hotel, has reopened its women’s spa and salon for foreign women after being closed for months. Visitors must show passports to use the services, and Afghan women whose IDs list them as born in Afghanistan are not allowed in. Travel companies say Afghanistan’s treatment of women complicates their business, so some try to emphasize constructive engagement by donating to local causes, supporting community projects, or using family-run businesses. Shane Horan, founder of Rocky Road Travel, said traveling to Afghanistan should not be interpreted as support for any government or political regime. Notably, there are no women enrolled at the Institute of Tourism & Hotel Management. The students do not discuss the absence, but an official at the Tourism Directorate called it heartbreaking. The official said even female relatives have asked to study there, but policy changed after the Taliban takeover, and women who had been studying before then never returned or graduated.

# The Taliban's Push to Develop Afghanistan's Tourism Industry The Taliban government is actively working to establish Afghanistan as a tourism destination, despite significant obstacles and international criticism. This effort is exemplified by a new Taliban-run institute in Kabul that recently opened its doors to train tourism and hospitality professionals. ## The Training Program The debut cohort at the Institute of Tourism & Hotel Management consists of approximately 30 male students with diverse backgrounds and varying levels of education and experience. The group includes a model, a 17-year-old with no job history, and a business school graduate. Despite their lack of tourism knowledge, all students share enthusiasm for promoting a different image of Afghanistan. Notably, no women attend the program, as the Taliban has banned Afghan women from studying beyond sixth grade. ## Growing Tourism Numbers Despite Afghanistan's status as a pariah state due to Taliban restrictions on women and girls, foreign tourism is increasing. The numbers remain modest but show significant growth: 691 foreign tourists visited in 2021, rising to 2,300 in 2022, and reaching 7,000 in 2023. This growth is attributed to reduced violence, improved flight connections through hubs like Dubai, and the appeal of visiting an unusual destination. Mohammad Saeed, head of the Tourism Directorate in Kabul, reports that China represents the largest foreign visitor market due to proximity and population size. Some international travelers also choose Afghanistan over neighboring countries like Pakistan, citing safety concerns. ## Significant Obstacles Despite these encouraging signs, substantial challenges impede tourism development. Visas are difficult and expensive to obtain, as many countries severed ties with Afghanistan after the Taliban's return to power and no nation officially recognizes the Taliban as legitimate rulers. Afghan embassies have either closed or suspended operations, creating additional complications. An ongoing power struggle exists between embassies staffed by the former Western-backed administration and those controlled by the Taliban. Infrastructure problems also hinder tourism growth. Road networks are partially unpaved or nonexistent in many regions, and airlines largely avoid Afghan airspace. Kabul is the only Afghan airport with significant international flights, and no Afghan airport offers direct routes to major tourist markets such as China, Europe, or India. ## Future Aspirations Despite these challenges, Saeed envisions Afghanistan becoming a tourism powerhouse, with support from Taliban leadership. His long-term goal includes implementing visa-on-arrival policies, though this remains years away. The students themselves harbor ambitions aligned with this vision. Ahmed Massoud Talash, the model, wants to learn about Afghanistan's scenic locations for social media and historical content. Samir Ahmadzai, the business graduate, aspires to open a hotel and believes further tourism education will help him achieve this goal. Both students emphasize Afghanistan's rich 5,000-year history, hoping to create "a new page" beyond the country's reputation for poverty and conflict. ## The Women's Question The exclusion of women from tourism training reflects broader Taliban restrictions. Afghan women face severe limitations, including dress codes, requirements for male guardians when traveling, and restrictions on accessing gyms and beauty salons. The government has, however, reopened the Serena Hotel's women's spa and salon for foreign female guests, though Afghan women with "born in Afghanistan" on their identification are barred from these services. An anonymous Tourism Directorate official acknowledged this situation as "heartbreaking," noting that female students who studied before the Taliban takeover never returned to complete their education. ## International Perspectives International travel companies acknowledge the challenges posed by Taliban restrictions on women. Some operators attempt to focus on positive cultural interactions through donations and supporting local projects, while others argue that visiting Afghanistan should not be interpreted as endorsing the Taliban government. The Taliban's tourism initiative represents an ambitious attempt to diversify Afghanistan's economy and improve its international image, yet significant political, infrastructural, and humanitarian obstacles remain.

Yemen’s Houthi rebels have accused the United States of striking a prison for African migrants in Saada governorate on Monday, April 28, 2025, killing and wounding people among roughly 100 detainees held there. The allegation has triggered outrage from migrant rights advocates and renewed scrutiny of the US military campaign in Yemen. The US military has not commented directly on the reported incident, and it remains unclear whether American forces were responsible. US Central Command said it withholds details of its ongoing airstrike operations for operational security reasons. A spokesperson said the command would not disclose specifics about what it has done or plans to do, even as it continues what it calls a broad campaign against the Houthis. According to the Houthis, armed men first tried to storm the detention facility, leading to a gunfight and then an explosion that damaged the building and caused casualties. Houthi-run al-Masirah television aired graphic footage showing bodies, wounded people, and damaged walls, with gunfire and cries for help audible in the background. The casualty toll has not yet been independently confirmed, but the images suggested severe destruction. The incident has drawn attention to the long-running suffering of African migrants in Yemen, many of whom, especially Ethiopians, travel through the country in hopes of reaching Saudi Arabia for work. Along the way, they often face abuse, detention, and exploitation by smugglers, armed groups, and security forces. The article notes that migrants have also been killed in past attacks near the Saudi border, and that the UN reported in 2022 that as many as 430 migrants may have died in an attack blamed by the Houthis on Saudi forces, which Saudi Arabia denied. The alleged strike comes amid the US “Operation Rough Rider,” under which Central Command says it has carried out more than 800 airstrikes against the Houthis, targeting missile and drone capabilities in response to Houthi attacks on Red Sea shipping and strikes against Israel.

Two staff members of Afghanistan’s independent human rights commission were killed in Kabul on Saturday when a bomb attached to their vehicle exploded, according to the commission and police. The victims were identified as 24-year-old donor coordinator Fatima Khalil and 41-year-old driver Ahmad Jawed Folad, who were traveling to the AIHRC office when the device detonated. Kabul police confirmed two deaths in the blast. No one immediately claimed responsibility, and a Taliban spokesman denied any involvement. The AIHRC condemned the attack, saying assassinating human rights defenders is a war crime and noting that its staff had been targeted before. The killings occurred amid a surge in violence across Afghanistan, including attacks on officials in urban areas, even as the United States and other international actors push the Taliban and the Afghan government toward peace talks. Those efforts follow a February US-Taliban troop withdrawal agreement aimed at ending more than 18 years of war. Diplomatic sources said the rising violence could threaten the talks. The UN, Britain, and Turkey condemned the attack and called for an immediate investigation and accountability.

In Aleppo, Syria, a 16-year-old rebel named Hussein Mansour sits in a prayer room inside a 12th-century mosque that has been turned into a makeshift headquarters. The room, cluttered with tea cups, coffee, ashtrays, and weapons, reflects the strange normalcy of war for young fighters. Hussein, lanky and grinning, casually handles a grenade and a small bag of pretzels, even pretending to pull the grenade’s ring, prompting an older rebel, Abu Musab, to remark that the boy is too young for such a role. Hussein is one of many teenagers increasingly filling the ranks of rebel forces as the Syrian civil war grinds on. With hundreds of exhausted fighters deserting and many others being killed each day, opposition groups are relying more heavily on boys like him. Hussein has already lost 13 uncles and cousins in combat against government forces. He now carries the Kalashnikov of a deceased cousin and handles it with the familiarity of a toy. He dismisses the weapons around him as ordinary rifles, saying even his six-year-old brother could use them. The article places Hussein’s story in the broader context of a devastating conflict that has killed more than 190,000 people and continues to claim civilian lives daily. Human rights groups estimate there are about 5,300 child fighters on the opposition side, excluding extremist groups, and around 2,000 fighting for pro-government forces, most between 14 and 17 years old. Human Rights Watch has condemned the recruitment of children, warning that armed groups are violating international law by enlisting vulnerable minors, especially those whose families have been killed. Despite formal bans by major rebel groups such as the Western-backed Free Syrian Army and the Islamic Front on recruiting fighters under 18, battlefield desperation means willing young recruits are rarely turned away. One fighter, Hassan Suwaas, serves alongside his 14-year-old son, Omar, believing it is better than letting the boy join extremist Islamist factions. He argues that children who grow up under shelling and death will inevitably want to fight. The article closes by describing the Umayyad Mosque front line, where the rebel-held position has remained largely unchanged for more than a year. The mosque’s damaged stone walls, pillars, and carpets show the wear of prolonged conflict, while clashes there have become sporadic.

# Syrian Civil War: Young Fighters on the Front Lines In Aleppo, Syria, teenagers are increasingly joining rebel forces in the ongoing civil war, filling positions left by deserting or killed fighters. Hussein Mansour, a 16-year-old, exemplifies this troubling trend. The lanky teenager casually handles weapons in a 12th-century mosque serving as rebel headquarters, carrying a grenade alongside snacks. He inherited the Kalashnikov rifle of a deceased cousin and has lost 13 family members to the conflict. With over 190,000 lives already claimed by the war, child soldiers have become a significant presence on both sides. The Syrian Network for Human Rights estimates approximately 5,300 child fighters among opposition forces and 2,000 with pro-government forces, mostly aged 14-17. In June, Human Rights Watch released a report accusing Syrian armed groups of violating international law by recruiting vulnerable children, particularly those whose families were killed. Mainstream rebel groups like the Western-backed Free Syrian Army and Islamic Front officially prohibit enlisting fighters under 18. However, the desperate situation on the ground means willing fighters, regardless of age, are not turned away. Hassan Suwaas, an Islamic Front fighter, justifies his 14-year-old son Omar's participation by reasoning it's preferable to his joining extremist Islamist groups. Suwaas believes exposure to violence will naturally drive children toward fighting. The psychological toll is evident in the fatalistic attitude pervading rebel areas, summarized in the phrase "It's all one death." Young fighters appear resigned to a grim fate, treating weapons casually and displaying a disturbing acceptance of their circumstances. Experts worry that institutionalizing violence through child soldiers will cause lasting damage to Syrian society. Human Rights Watch researcher Priyanka Motaparthy stated: "The horrors of Syria's armed conflict are only made worse by throwing children into the front lines." At the Umayyad Mosque front line in Aleppo, where clashes have been sparse for over a year, these young fighters wait and train, representing a generation marked by war and loss.

UN Secretary-General António Guterres visited the King Salman Humanitarian Aid and Relief Center (KSrelief) headquarters in Riyadh on Tuesday to discuss expanding cooperation between the United Nations and Saudi Arabia’s main humanitarian body. He met KSrelief Supervisor General Dr. Abdullah bin Abdulaziz Al-Rabeeah, senior officials, and Saudi Arabia’s UN representative Abdulaziz bin Mohammed Al-Wasil. According to the Saudi Press Agency, the talks focused on humanitarian priorities and ways to deepen collaboration with UN agencies. Officials also presented KSrelief’s growing international work, saying it has carried out 3,881 projects in 109 countries worth more than $8 billion. They highlighted initiatives including the artificial limbs programme, the Masam demining project in Yemen, the Kafak scheme for reintegrating Yemeni children affected by conflict, voluntary medical missions, and the conjoined twins programme. Guterres toured KSrelief’s exhibition, tried virtual-reality headsets showing refugee experiences, met Saudi medical volunteers, and visited partner organizations’ offices inside the center.

Militants launched a deadly attack on a Save the Children office in Jalalabad, eastern Afghanistan, on Wednesday, according to Afghan officials. The assault began with a suicide car bomb outside the agency’s compound, after which four gunmen entered the site and exchanged fire with Afghan special forces who surrounded the building. Officials said at least one person was killed and 11 others were wounded. Provincial spokesman Attaullah Khogyani said the target was Save the Children and that the attackers had entered the compound after the blast. He said fighting was still ongoing and that at least one gunman remained active inside the building. The provincial health department director reported that 11 wounded people had been taken to hospital. Security forces also recovered one body from inside the compound, though the person’s identity was not immediately known. Witnesses described a powerful explosion, a vehicle catching fire, and people fleeing the area. Some said the attackers appeared to be wearing police uniforms, a tactic militants in Afghanistan have used before, but officials did not confirm that detail. The Islamic State group claimed responsibility through its Amaq news agency, though it offered no immediate evidence. Jalalabad, the capital of Nangarhar province near the Pakistani border, has become a stronghold for Islamic State, which has expanded in Afghanistan since 2015. The attack came days after Taliban gunmen stormed the Intercontinental Hotel in Kabul, killing at least 20 people, including 13 foreigners. It also highlighted the growing danger faced by humanitarian organizations in Afghanistan, where aid groups have been under intense pressure from militants and kidnappers.

# Summary Four gunmen attacked the Save the Children office in Jalalabad, Afghanistan on Wednesday, initiating the assault with a suicide car bomb outside the compound before entering and engaging Afghan security forces. The attack resulted in at least one death and 11 wounded individuals who were transported to hospitals. The gunmen, who some witnesses claimed wore police uniforms—a common militant tactic—fought with Afghan special forces inside the compound. Security forces surrounded the building and engaged in an ongoing firefight to neutralize the attackers. At least one gunman continued fighting as forces worked to secure the area. Authorities recovered one body inside the compound, though the person's identity remained unclear. Islamic State claimed responsibility for the attack through its news agency Amaq, though no immediate evidence was provided. The attack occurred in Jalalabad, capital of Nangarhar province on the Pakistan border, which has become a stronghold for Islamic State since the group emerged around 2015. The assault highlighted the increasing dangers faced by humanitarian organizations operating in Afghanistan. This attack followed a Taliban assault on Kabul's Hotel Intercontinental just days earlier, which killed at least 20 people, including 13 foreigners. Despite U.S. air support and reported Afghan military successes against militants, attacks on civilian targets continue causing heavy casualties. The security situation has prompted organizations like the Red Cross to drastically reduce operations in the country.

A gunman who attacked the U.S. Embassy near Beirut on Wednesday morning was shot and captured by Lebanese soldiers after a shootout that injured an embassy security guard, according to Lebanese military and embassy officials. The attack unfolded in Aukar, a Christian suburb north of Beirut, amid heightened regional and domestic tensions tied to months of fighting between Hezbollah and Israeli forces along Lebanon’s border, as well as Lebanon’s prolonged political and economic crisis. Local media said the gunbattle involved at least one attacker and lasted nearly half an hour. A nearby gas station worker, Joe Abdo, said he heard “around 15 to 20 rounds of gunfire” before the army sealed off the area. Authorities said the motive was not immediately clear. However, Lebanese media published photos that appeared to show a bloodied attacker wearing a black vest marked with the Arabic words for “Islamic State” and the English initials “I” and “S.” A Lebanese security official and two judicial officials, speaking anonymously because they were not authorized to brief the press, said the suspect appeared to have acted alone. They identified him as a resident of Majdal Anjar, a border town in eastern Lebanon near Syria, though the Lebanese military initially said he was a Syrian national. The army later raided Majdal Anjar and nearby Suweiri, arresting three relatives of the suspect and two other people believed to be linked to him. The officials said no other gunmen or signs of an extremist cell were found. The suspect was shot in the stomach and leg before being taken to a military hospital in Beirut. The U.S. Embassy said one security guard was injured and wished him a full recovery. Lebanese caretaker Prime Minister Najib Mikati said the situation was stable and that serious investigations were underway. Troops were deployed around the embassy and nearby areas. The embassy has a long history of attacks, including the 1983 bombing that killed 63 people and a 1984 bombing at its current site.

# Beirut Embassy Gunman Arrested A gunman attacked the U.S. embassy near Beirut on Wednesday morning, resulting in a shootout with Lebanese soldiers that lasted approximately 30 minutes. The attacker was shot and captured, while an embassy security guard sustained injuries. The incident occurred amid escalating tensions in Lebanon, where months of conflict between Hezbollah militants and Israeli troops have displaced thousands along the border. According to witnesses, approximately 15 to 20 rounds of gunfire were exchanged during the attack. Lebanese media published photos appearing to show a bloodied attacker wearing a black vest marked with "Islamic State" in Arabic and English initials. However, the gunman's exact motive remained unclear. Officials identified the suspect as a resident of Majdal Anjar, an eastern Lebanese border town near Syria, though the military initially described him as a Syrian national. Three security officials stated the attacker appeared to be acting alone, with no evidence of an extremist cell. The gunman sustained gunshot wounds to the stomach and leg before being captured and transported to a military hospital in Beirut. Following the incident, the Lebanese military raided both Majdal Anjar and nearby Suweiri, arresting three relatives of the suspect and two additional individuals believed to be associated with him. Prime Minister Najib Mikati's office stated that the situation had stabilized and serious investigations were underway. The Lebanese military deployed troops around the embassy and surrounding areas. This attack represents the latest security incident at the embassy. In 1983, a bombing killed 63 people, leading to the embassy's relocation to Aukar. Similar incidents occurred in September 2023, when a gunman opened fire near the embassy without casualties, and in October 2023, when protesters clashed with security forces near the compound.

Canadian stocks edged higher on Wednesday, extending the previous session’s gains, as investors weighed the Bank of Canada’s latest policy decision and outlook against rising geopolitical risks in the Middle East. The benchmark S&P/TSX Composite Index opened above the prior close, traded unevenly through the day, and finished at 33,176.07, up 79.67 points, or 0.24%. The Bank of Canada left interest rates unchanged for a second straight meeting, a move that had been widely expected. The central bank kept its target for the overnight rate at 2.25%, with the Bank Rate at 2.50% and the deposit rate at 2.20%. In its statement, the Governing Council said it still considers the current policy rate appropriate. It also said the Canadian economy is likely to see modest growth in the near term, partly because population growth is slowing as Canada adjusts to U.S. protectionist policies. Inflation is expected to remain close to the 2% target. While the Bank noted that uncertainty has increased, it said it stands ready to respond if conditions change. A major source of uncertainty remains trade relations with the United States. Since August 2025, Canada has been dealing with 35% U.S. tariffs on most exports to the American market. Some goods have been shielded by the Canada-United States-Mexico Agreement, but the future of that pact is also in question, with U.S. President Donald Trump suggesting it may or may not be renewed. The Bank of Canada specifically identified the “review of CUSMA” as an important source of trade uncertainty. The article also noted that Prime Minister Mark Carney has recently pursued efforts to broaden trade ties with India and to improve relations with China. In global markets, fears of a U.S.-Iran conflict pushed investors toward safe-haven assets such as gold. Gold prices surged to a record high of $5,301.60 per troy ounce for January delivery, helping lift Canadian gold-related shares. Only three of the 11 TSX sectors advanced, led by Materials, which rose 1.91%. Energy gained 1.03% and Information Technology added 0.34%. Declining sectors included Financials, Consumer Staples, Consumer Discretionary, and Healthcare. Notable gainers included Aya Gold and Silver, Oceanagold, Skeena Resources, Parex Resources, and Firan Technology Group. Among the day’s notable losers were Curaleaf Holdings, Aritzia, Magna International, and Alimentation Couche-Tard. Energy Fuels, Denison Mines, and NexGen Energy were among the most active market movers.

As the pandemic forced schools to close and parents to balance remote work with at-home schooling, one Los Angeles family found help from an unexpected source: a grandfather’s improvised “grandparent school.” Jason Smith, a television editor, has two daughters, ages 8 and 4. Before the shutdown, his parents often helped by picking up his older daughter from school, but stay-at-home orders kept them from visiting. With his wife teaching her own students online and Smith trying to keep both children learning and occupied, the household became increasingly strained. Smith said he was essentially running homeschool without any experience, while also working from home. Seeing how exhausted his son and daughter-in-law were becoming, David Smith, Jason’s father, decided to step in. A retired university professor who once taught marketing, he spent more than six hours preparing a history lesson for his granddaughters. He chose the battle at the Old North Bridge in Concord, Massachusetts, a key event on the first day of the American Revolution. To make the lesson engaging, David Smith drew on a diorama he had built years earlier showing British soldiers on one side of the bridge and colonists on the other. He created notes, a PowerPoint presentation, and a map, then delivered the lesson through video conferencing. He said he likes using something tangible, like the diorama, so he can point to real objects while teaching. He also adapted his explanation to the children’s world, using language from “Star Wars” to help them understand the idea of a long-ago conflict between an “evil empire” and “rebels.” The lesson proved successful: both girls stayed engaged, asking questions and making comments. David Smith said they were especially fascinated by the bayonets on the British soldiers’ guns and even wanted one themselves. Encouraged by the response, David Smith said he is already preparing his next 20-minute lesson, this time on riverboats. For that session, he plans to use two model boats, including one he built during the pandemic while stuck at home.

The Wyoming Cowgirl tennis team closed its season with a dramatic comeback win Sunday at Utah State, rallying from an early deficit to defeat the Aggies 4-3 in Logan, Utah. The victory extended Wyoming’s winning streak to seven matches, tying the third-longest streak in program history. Utah State earned the doubles point by winning two of three matches, though Wyoming’s No. 1 pair of Noesjka Brink and Maria Oreshkina delivered the Cowgirls’ lone doubles victory, 6-4. That left Wyoming needing to win four of the six singles matches to complete the comeback. The Cowgirls answered by winning the final two singles matches of the day. Brink opened the singles rally with a straight-set 6-4, 6-2 win over Gabrielle Dekkers at No. 5, and Mihaela Kaftanova clinched the team victory at No. 6 by beating Naya Tillitt 6-2, 7-6 (7-3). Wyoming also picked up singles wins from Sophie Zehender at No. 2, 7-5, 6-3, and Lucia Malinak at No. 4, who earned her seventh consecutive win, 7-6 (7-2), 7-5. Wyoming finished the year 13-6 overall and 7-2 in Mountain West play, technically placing third in the standings, though it played one fewer conference match than Fresno State and UNLV because of COVID-19. Head coach Dean Clower praised the team’s improvement and said the future looks promising with everyone returning for the next two years.

Canada’s military has reportedly modelled how it would respond to a hypothetical U.S. invasion, amid growing tensions sparked by President Donald Trump’s comments about Canada as a possible “51st state.” According to the Globe and Mail, Canadian defence planners have examined scenarios in which American forces attack from the south and quickly overwhelm Canadian positions on land and at sea, potentially within a week and in some cases as little as two days. The officials cited in the report stressed that such an invasion is considered highly unlikely. The preparations, however, reflect how sharply relations between the two longtime allies have deteriorated during Mr. Trump’s second term. The reports follow earlier coverage from The Economist, which said Canada’s military has been discussing worst-case scenarios that could now include incursions by the United States. Canada and the U.S. have not fought each other since the War of 1812, when Canada, then a British colony, repelled American advances. In the scenario described by the Globe, Canada’s response would not rely on conventional battlefield strength, which would be far outmatched by the far larger and more powerful U.S. military. Instead, Canadian planners envision small groups of irregular fighters or armed civilians conducting ambushes, sabotage, and drone attacks. Those tactics would resemble “hit-and-run” operations, including improvised explosive device attacks similar to those used by the Taliban against U.S. and allied forces in Afghanistan, where Canada also fought. Wesley Wark, a senior fellow at the Centre for International Governance Innovation, said a direct U.S. invasion is “extremely unlikely,” but added that defence contacts had told him contingency planning was underway as a worst-case measure. He said these plans were prompted by Mr. Trump’s second administration and were not in place under President Joe Biden. Wark argued that Canada’s more realistic concerns are economic coercion and political pressure, including possible U.S. attempts to exploit separatist sentiment in Alberta and Quebec, demand greater access to Canadian energy, minerals and water, or press for more control in the Arctic and over the Northwest Passage. If a full-scale assault ever occurred, Wark said Canada would likely turn to partisan warfare and withdraw to “northern fortresses” to preserve military and government functions, noting that occupying such a vast country would be extremely difficult. Separately, Foreign Minister Anita Anand said Canada is strengthening its Arctic presence and plans to spend 2% of GDP on defence this year, with a goal of reaching NATO’s 5% target by 2035. Prime Minister Mark Carney is also considering sending a small troop contingent to Greenland for NATO exercises. Anand said, “Canada will never be the 51st state.”

The article argues that federal prosecutors in Washington, D.C., are relying on a Project Veritas sting video in the case against people arrested for protesting at Donald Trump’s inauguration, even though Project Veritas and its founder, James O’Keefe, are presented as deeply deceptive and politically motivated. That video, the court learned, had been filmed by a Project Veritas operative. The article stresses that the video’s editing history is unknown, and that neither the prosecutor nor the court could say who supplied it beyond describing the source as “a third party.” The author argues that this creates serious evidentiary problems. Because the Project Veritas footage may have been edited, and because there may have been multiple operatives in the room influencing events, the video could have shaped the undercover officer’s perception and therefore tainted his testimony. Wood is quoted saying he did nothing wrong and that the world can judge his actions because his footage was available from beginning to end. It frames the prosecution as senseless and suggests that right-wing figures defend such behavior as long as it serves their side.

# Summary: Project Falsitas Federal prosecutors in Washington, D.C. have introduced a Project Veritas video as evidence in the trial of six inauguration protesters charged under the federal Riot Act, raising serious concerns about the credibility and authenticity of the material being used. Project Veritas, the undercover sting operation run by James O'Keefe, has a documented history of deceptive practices. Most notably, the organization spent months attempting to infiltrate The Washington Post with false accusations against Roy Moore, a former Alabama judge running for Senate. The scheme involved a woman claiming Moore had impregnated her as a minor and pressured her to abort. Post reporters discovered the operative walking into Project Veritas offices and exposed the operation, though O'Keefe dismissed their investigative work dismissively. On the same day the Post exposed Project Veritas's deception, prosecutor Jennifer Kerkhoff introduced a Project Veritas video during testimony from an undercover officer who had infiltrated a January 8 church meeting where protest organizers coordinated Inauguration Day activities. The officer testified that his supervisors prohibited him from recording, but that MPD later obtained a video of the same meeting filmed by Project Veritas operatives. Multiple red flags undermine the video's reliability. Kerkhoff admitted in court she was "not aware of any edits or anything," and when asked who provided the video to MPD, she vaguely responded "a third party." Critically, the number of Project Veritas operatives present in the room remains unknown, meaning their statements and actions could have influenced the undercover officer's perception and testimony. The contrast between this approach and the transparency of defendant Alexei Wood, a photojournalist, is striking. Wood livestreamed his entire presence at the protest, explicitly inviting public scrutiny: "I didn't do anything wrong. I livestreamed myself from beginning to end, and the entire world can decide whether I incited a riot." The government's handling of the Project Veritas video is particularly troubling. Federal prosecutors not only used the unauthenticated footage but actually edited it to obscure the identity of the unknown Project Veritas operative, treating him as though he were a law enforcement officer. This represents a deeper problem: evidence of close connections between law enforcement, government officials, and right-wing movements. An MPD communications officer previously provided defendant names to far-right conspiracy site Got News, and video shows a U.S. Park Police officer directing a protester to follow a militia member's orders. O'Keefe's organization, despite its name invoking "Veritas" (truth), is fundamentally built on deception. The group faces potential loss of nonprofit status in New York due to O'Keefe's failure to disclose a criminal record from attempting to enter a federal building under false pretenses. O'Keefe's previous failed sting operations have included the infamous boat incident involving a CNN reporter. The article argues this represents broader patterns within the far right: defending allies regardless of conduct, as evidenced by Roy Moore's campaign. The prosecution of inauguration protesters appears "senseless," driven by ideological alignment rather than justice. The article concludes by noting Trump's apparent endorsement of this approach, suggesting the administration views mass prosecution of protesters as politically advantageous.

Gen. Jonathan Vance says he is focused on leading Canada’s military through current and future challenges, not on his own career prospects, despite persistent speculation that he could be nominated for NATO’s top military post. In an interview with The Canadian Press, the chief of the defence staff said he has no plans to step down and will continue serving “at the pleasure of the government.” He emphasized that his attention is on the pandemic, overseas deployments, and preparing the Canadian Armed Forces to remain effective in warfare well into the 21st century. Vance has served as Canada’s top military commander for nearly five years, making him one of the longest-serving chiefs in Canadian history. Appointed by former prime minister Stephen Harper in 2015, he has overseen a period of wide-ranging military activity and institutional strain. During his tenure, Canadian Forces have fought the Islamic State group in Iraq, helped train Ukrainian troops after Russia’s annexation of Crimea, led a NATO battlegroup in Latvia, contributed to a NATO training mission in Iraq, participated in peacekeeping in Mali, and responded to natural disasters in Canada. At the same time, the military has faced major internal problems, including sexual misconduct scandals, aging equipment such as fighter jets, and upheaval in senior leadership. One of Vance’s first major moves after taking command in July 2015 was launching Operation Honour, the military’s campaign to eliminate sexual misconduct. The initiative was meant to repair damage caused by comments from his predecessor, Gen. Tom Lawson, and restore public trust. It also formed part of a broader effort to make the Forces more diverse and better suited to modern warfare. Vance set a goal of having women make up one-quarter of the military by 2026, reached out to the LGBTQ community, and relaxed rules on beards, ponytails, boots, and cannabis use. Vance has also been the public face of the military during a period of changing government policy. After the Liberals came to power, they developed a defence policy promising tens of billions of dollars in future equipment spending and laying out a long-term vision for the Forces. Vance said he has provided continuity through these shifts and wants to remain involved in major ongoing work, including the modernization of NORAD and broader continental defence planning. He said he wants to help ensure the military is “the right force for the future.” Although he has received praise from the government for his leadership, Vance has also faced criticism. Early in his tenure, some questioned whether he was adjusting the definition of “combat” to fit the government’s messaging on Canada’s mission in Iraq. Others objected when he appeared alongside Liberal ministers in 2016 as the government delayed a competition to replace Canada’s aging CF-18 fighter jets and instead bought 18 Super Hornets. More recently, Vance has been tied to the controversy surrounding Vice-Admiral Mark Norman. Norman was suspended in January 2017 after an RCMP investigation into allegations that he leaked cabinet secrets about a shipbuilding project. He was later charged with breach of trust, but prosecutors dropped the case in May 2019, and Norman eventually received a settlement and retired. Supporters of Norman have strongly criticized Vance’s role, but Vance said he does not regret his decision and acted according to military rules. The article also notes the sudden retirement of Lt.-Gen. Jean-Marc Lanthier, who stepped down as vice-chief of the defence staff after less than a year, citing family reasons. He was the latest in a series of officers to hold the military’s second-in-command position since Norman’s suspension. Despite speculation that Vance could eventually become chairman of NATO’s military committee, a post last held by a Canadian from 2005 to 2008, he declined to discuss it. He said that until the government makes a decision, the possibility is not real to him. With Russia and China asserting themselves, instability in Iraq, disaster response at home, and the COVID-19 outbreak all demanding attention, he said he has enough to focus on in his current role and is not thinking about his legacy.
