Tony Sanchez’s arrival as UNLV’s head football coach is presented as one of the most unusual hires in modern college football: he was taken directly from the high school ranks, after eight dominant seasons at Bishop Gorman High School in Las Vegas, rather than from another college program. The article centers on his first National Signing Day as a college coach and uses that moment to show both the novelty of his background and the style he brings to a struggling UNLV program. The scene opens in the Rebels’ locker room, where Sanchez casually pulls up a chair in front of a small group of parents whose sons he is recruiting. He invites them to ask anything, and he means it literally. Rather than delivering a polished sales pitch, he speaks like a familiar, approachable local coach, joking and answering questions directly. When the topic turns to UNLV’s modest facilities, including an unimpressive weight room, Sanchez does not pretend otherwise. Instead, he argues that winning depends on effort and toughness, not on flashy surroundings. His remark that he just needs “some junkyard dogs” resonates with the parents, who seem to appreciate his bluntness. The article emphasizes that Sanchez appears unusually comfortable because, only 45 days earlier, he was sitting in the same position as these parents, listening to recruiters talk about their own sons. That perspective matters because Sanchez is one of only a handful of coaches in the modern era hired directly from high school football. The article lists the small group of predecessors who made similar jumps, noting that none lasted long in college coaching. UNLV’s decision to hire him is framed as a gamble by a program that has long struggled. The Rebels are described as one of the nation’s worst programs, with only eight two-win seasons in the past 11 years and just four bowl appearances in school history. Previous attempts to fix the program by hiring former stars, promising assistants, or successful lower-division coaches have all failed. Against that backdrop, Sanchez’s appeal lies partly in his ordinariness. He does not act like a celebrity coach. He has no big-time pedigree, no famous coaching tree, and no past as a major college or NFL assistant. Yet he is now a Division I head coach, a peer of figures such as Nick Saban and Urban Meyer, which he acknowledges with amazement. He says, “I’m 41 years old and I’m a Division-I football coach. I don’t know how it gets any better than this.” The article suggests that his lack of grandiosity is refreshing in a sport often built on image and hierarchy. He does not surround himself with a large entourage, and he even seems amused by small conveniences, like no longer having to reserve a bus. Sanchez’s high school background shaped the way he recruits. At Bishop Gorman, he regularly sent players to major college programs and saw virtually every major college coach and assistant pass through his office. He also spent time around national all-star events and built relationships with coaches across the country. From that experience, he developed a simple philosophy: be genuine. He describes the best recruiting style as “raw and real,” meaning that a coach should be true to his actual personality rather than trying to invent a polished persona. He believes players and parents can immediately detect dishonesty. He says UNLV will recruit with passion, positivity, and honesty, and he intends to be unusually direct with families about where their sons stand in the process, including their place on the recruiting board. That openness is presented as a deliberate contrast to what Sanchez sees as the deception common in recruiting. He says too many coaches make promises they cannot keep or mislead families who are unfamiliar with how the process works. His own approach, he says, is to tell the truth and build trust. The article backs up this claim by recounting a period earlier in his life when he sold photocopiers after graduating from New Mexico State. Even then, he says, he succeeded by being honest with customers. He would tell them the machines would break down eventually, but he and his company would be there to help. That strategy worked so well that he once made the biggest sale in company history by convincing the warden of the Southern New Mexico Correctional Facility to buy 13 copiers. Still, he missed football and eventually returned to coaching. Kazakhstan announced that it will no longer host the Syria peace talks known as the Astana process, marking the 20th meeting held this week as the last one in its capital. Kazakh Deputy Foreign Minister Kanat Tumysh said the gradual end of Syria’s isolation showed that the Astana process had “honorably fulfilled its mission.” He pointed to Syria’s return to the Arab League as evidence of progress. The Astana format, launched by Russia, Iran, and Turkey, was created to promote negotiations between the Syrian opposition and the Damascus government, and Kazakhstan has hosted the meetings since 2017. Russia’s special envoy for Syria, Alexandr Lavrentiev, said the participants were surprised by Kazakhstan’s decision, but stressed that the format would continue in another location. He suggested possible future venues including Moscow, Tehran, Ankara, or Damascus. He also said that if Kazakhstan no longer wishes to host the talks, the parties will consult and choose a new site. In a joint statement, Russia, Turkey, and Iran agreed to hold the 21st international Syria meeting in the second half of 2023, though they did not specify the country. The statement also emphasized efforts to improve relations between Damascus and Ankara, which were severed in 2011 when the Syrian war began and Turkey backed the rebels. Since last year, Turkey has shown signs of rapprochement with the Assad government, including meetings between intelligence chiefs, defense ministers, and deputy foreign ministers. Lavrentiev said a Russian roadmap for normalization still needs more work before being sent to the presidents, and only then could a summit between Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Syrian President Bashar al-Assad be considered. The statement also called for continued humanitarian aid to Syria under UN Resolution 2672, the removal of obstacles to aid delivery, support for the voluntary return of Syrians, and backing for the Syrian Constitutional Committee tasked with drafting a new constitution.

Chile’s new left-leaning government has moved to eliminate the traditional office of first lady, saying it is outdated and should be transformed into a new institutional role. Under the change announced Wednesday, the first lady will now be called the “sociocultural coordinator of the republic’s presidency.” The decision came after the administration of President Gabriel Boric initially drew backlash for trying to rename the office’s internal structure as “Irina Karamanos’ Cabinet,” referring to Boric’s partner. That wording became public Tuesday and immediately prompted criticism from opposition figures, who accused the government of personalizing what should be an institutional function. Government spokesperson Camila Vallejo later said the naming was an “administrative error.” By Wednesday morning, the reference to “Irina Karamanos’ Cabinet” had been removed from the presidential website. The administration then clarified that the goal was not to personalize the office, but to redefine it. Karamanos said on Twitter that the administration’s “main interest is to move forward with our commitment to transform the role.” Boric and Karamanos had both previously spoken openly about their desire to remake the position. In January, Karamanos said she had agreed to take on the role, “traditionally called first lady,” with the commitment to reformulate it. Boric, who was sworn in in March at age 36, is Chile’s youngest-ever president. His government’s effort to reshape the first lady’s office reflects its broader left-leaning agenda and its stated intention to modernize a role that both the president and his partner have described as archaic. The controversy centered less on the reform itself than on the initial way it was presented, which opponents said blurred the line between public office and personal identity.

# Chile Transforms the Role of First Lady Chile's new left-leaning government, led by President Gabriel Boric, is overhauling the traditional role of first lady as part of broader efforts to modernize institutional positions. The office will now be called the "sociocultural coordinator of the republic's presidency" rather than maintaining its historical title. Irina Karamanos, the president's partner, will assume this newly renamed position. Both Boric and Karamanos have characterized the traditional first lady role as archaic and have publicly committed to transforming it. The initiative encountered controversy when the government initially attempted to rebrand the office as "Irina Karamanos' Cabinet." This move quickly sparked backlash from opposition members, who accused the administration of personalizing an institutional government role rather than maintaining its formal, impersonal nature. Facing criticism, the government reversed course on Wednesday. Government spokesperson Camila Vallejo dismissed the personalized naming as an "administrative error," and the reference to "Irina Karamanos' Cabinet" was removed from the executive's website the following morning. Karamanos responded to the controversy via Twitter, reaffirming the government's commitment to transforming the first lady role despite the setback. She had previously stated in January that she agreed to take on the position with a commitment to reformulate it. At 36 years old, Boric became Chile's youngest-ever president when sworn in during March. The government's effort to reshape the first lady position reflects its broader left-leaning agenda to modernize traditional governmental structures, though the initial implementation revealed the sensitive nature of altering long-established institutional roles.

Leonardo Fossati grew up in La Plata in the 1980s with a vague but persistent feeling that something about his life was hidden from him. As a child, he would look in the mirror and imagine that reality existed “on the other side,” sensing that his life was like a movie he could not fully see. Years later, that intuition proved true: the people who raised him were not his biological parents. In 2005, a DNA test identified him as one of Argentina’s “stolen grandchildren,” babies born in captivity during the military dictatorship of 1976 to 1983 and then handed to other families. Fossati’s biological parents, Ines Beatriz Ortega and Rubén Leonardo Fossati, were among an estimated 30,000 people disappeared by security forces during the dictatorship, and their remains have never been found. He said that learning the truth, however painful, gave him a foundation for his life. His case is one of many uncovered by the Abuelas de Plaza de Mayo, or Grandmothers of the Plaza de Mayo, the human rights group that for decades has demanded answers about the disappeared and their children. So far, the identities of 130 stolen grandchildren have been restored through DNA testing, but the organization says about 300 more remain missing. To reach them, Abuelas has launched a new campaign that uses Argentina’s COVID-19 vaccination drive. Because people in their 40s are now being vaccinated, the group sees an opportunity to catch the attention of the age cohort most likely to include the missing grandchildren. Supporters are being asked to post photos of their vaccinations on social media using the hashtag #UnaDosisDeIdentidad, or “One Dose of Identity,” along with messages urging anyone born between 1975 and 1980 who has doubts about their identity to contact the organization. Belen Altamiranda Taranto, the 88th identified grandchild, said the campaign was timed carefully because many of the people Abuelas is searching for will soon be focused on vaccination. Taranto now works with the group in Cordoba. The effort is part of a broader push to keep the search alive and adapt it to new circumstances. The Argentine government has also joined the effort with its own campaign aimed at citizens living abroad, called “Argentina Te Busca” (“Argentina is Looking For You”). Foreign minister Felipe Sola appeared in a video message telling people with questions about their identity to contact an Argentine consulate. The government said some people have discovered their true identities after moving overseas to places such as Holland, the United States and Spain, while others were identified earlier in Chile and Uruguay. The reason so many grandchildren are still unaccounted for lies in the dictatorship’s systematic repression. Under the claim of fighting leftist rebels, security forces carried out a broad campaign of state terror against political dissidents, students, activists, union organizers, journalists and others. Victims were abducted, tortured, murdered, thrown from planes into the sea, or buried in unmarked graves. Pregnant women who disappeared often gave birth in clandestine detention centers, and their babies were then placed with military-supporting families or others who did not ask questions. An Argentine court ruled in 2012 that this appropriation of children was not random abuse but a systematic plan amounting to a crime against humanity. More than 1,000 people have since been sentenced for crimes linked to that period. The article highlights how the search for the missing grandchildren remains deeply personal for families still waiting. Anna Carriquiriborde, 41, said her aunt Gabriela disappeared in La Plata in 1976, and the family believes Gabriela gave birth to a baby boy in captivity that December. One woman who thinks she may be Gabriela’s daughter is awaiting DNA results, while two other suspected matches were ruled out. Carriquiriborde, who lives in La Plata but was raised in Sweden after her parents received asylum there, said the family continues to hope for closure. She described the dictatorship as having stolen both the present and the future of her family. Time, however, is working against the search. Taranto said there are very few grandmothers left, and it is painful to see them die without finding their grandchildren or recovering their children’s bodies. Still, both Taranto and Fossati said that discovering their identities gave them a sense of freedom and empowerment. Taranto said she was able to meet both sets of grandparents before they died. Fossati now runs a memorial space in La Plata at a former clandestine detention center where his parents were held and where he himself was born. He emphasized that adoption was not what happened to him; it was appropriation. Both urged anyone with doubts to seek answers, saying that identity is a right and that the truth, though difficult, can provide a firm basis for life.

Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro issued an open letter to the people of the United States, delivered Sunday by Foreign Minister Jorge Arreaza, warning the Trump administration against taking military action against Venezuela. The letter came amid recent U.S. threats toward the Bolivarian Republic. Maduro said Venezuela does not want armed conflict and cannot accept war threats, blockades, or any attempt to impose an international guardianship that would violate the country’s sovereignty. He also rejected Trump’s claims that any action would be justified by fighting drug trafficking, calling those arguments false and unfounded. Maduro urged Americans not to believe those explanations and instead to pressure their leaders to focus on the urgent battle against the COVID-19 pandemic. He expressed solidarity with the U.S. public, which was suffering from the virus, and said the United States should direct its resources toward public health rather than confrontation abroad. He also called for an end to military threats, illegal sanctions, and the blockade that he said restricts access to humanitarian supplies needed to fight the pandemic. Maduro said Venezuela seeks fraternal relations, cooperation, exchange, and respect, and he warned Americans not to let their country be drawn into “another Vietnam or another Iraq,” this time closer to home.

# Summary Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro issued an open letter to the American people on Sunday, warning against potential U.S. military intervention. Read by Foreign Minister Jorge Arreaza, the letter responded to recent Trump administration threats toward Venezuela. Maduro stated that Venezuela opposes armed conflict and rejected Trump's justifications for military action, particularly claims about fighting drug trafficking, which he called false and unfounded. He emphasized Venezuela's desire for fraternal relationships, cooperation, and respect rather than war threats, blockades, or violations of sovereignty. The letter also referenced ongoing political dialogue between the government and opposition, urging preservation of these advances. Maduro expressed solidarity with Americans suffering from COVID-19, calling on U.S. citizens to hold their leaders accountable and redirect resources toward combating the pandemic rather than military conflicts. He specifically requested the cessation of military threats, removal of illegal sanctions, and lifting of the blockade restricting humanitarian supplies needed to fight the virus. Maduro concluded by appealing to Americans not to allow their country to enter another endless conflict, comparing potential intervention to Vietnam or Iraq.

Ecuadorian President Rafael Correa said Colombia’s ELN rebels have contacted the government in Bogotá about opening peace talks. He told Canal Capital that representatives from both sides met a few months ago in Ecuador and that his country could host future negotiations. The ELN is Colombia’s second-largest guerrilla group. Meanwhile, the larger FARC has been in peace talks with the Colombian government in Cuba since late 2012. Correa spoke in Bogotá at President Juan Manuel Santos’s inauguration.

# Summary Colombia's second-largest guerrilla group, the ELN, has initiated contact with the government about peace talks, according to Ecuador's president Rafael Correa. Representatives from both sides met in Ecuador months ago, and Correa offered his country as a venue for future negotiations. Meanwhile, Colombia's largest guerrilla group, the FARC, continues ongoing peace talks with the government in Cuba since late 2012. President Juan Manuel Santos, recently re-elected, prioritizes reaching a peace agreement with the FARC during his second term.

Colombian prosecutors announced that former president Álvaro Uribe will face trial for alleged witness tampering, marking the first time in Colombia’s history that a former head of state has been brought to trial. Uribe, who governed from 2002 to 2010, is accused of bribery of witnesses and procedural fraud in connection with an investigation into possible ties between him and right-wing paramilitary groups. Prosecutors did not say when the trial would begin, but the charges carry possible prison sentences of up to eight years. The case dates back to 2012, when Uribe, then a senator, filed a complaint against leftist senator Iván Cepeda, accusing him of orchestrating a scheme to falsely link him to paramilitaries. Instead, Colombia’s Supreme Court turned its attention to Uribe, concluding that he may have tried to manipulate witnesses in order to discredit Cepeda. Uribe has consistently denied wrongdoing, saying that his contacts with jailed paramilitaries were meant to obtain the truth about his alleged involvement with the far-right armed groups. The prosecution said its decision was based on new evidence, including testimony from jailed former militia member Juan Guillermo Monsalve, who says he received messages from Uribe asking him to alter his account. The indictment follows an October court ruling that rejected prosecutors’ latest request to close the case, after years of legal twists in a highly politicized investigation. A new attorney general, Luz Camargo, took office in March after being selected from a shortlist proposed by President Gustavo Petro, a longtime political rival of Uribe. Uribe was briefly placed under house arrest in 2020 before being released two months later while the inquiry continued. The former president remains a powerful figure on Colombia’s right. During his presidency, he pursued a hardline campaign against the leftist FARC guerrillas and opposed the 2016 peace agreement that led the rebels to disarm. Petro, who took office in 2022, has sought to end Colombia’s decades of conflict through his “total peace” policy. Reaction to the indictment was sharply divided. Cepeda welcomed the move to trial, while Uribe’s allies insisted he was only defending himself against false testimony. One of Uribe’s former lawyers, Diego Cadena, is also set to stand trial for allegedly offering money to a former paramilitary to retract testimony against him. Uribe faces other investigations as well, including a probe into a 1997 paramilitary massacre in Antioquia, where he was governor, and a complaint filed in Argentina over alleged abuses during his anti-guerrilla campaign.

Furthermore, Argentina has filed a complaint against Uribe under universal jurisdiction laws, alleging his involvement in over 6,000 executions and forced disappearances of civilians by the military during his 2002-2008 presidency's anti-guerrilla crackdown. Victims' relatives filed the complaint seeking "serious and impartial investigation" they claim was unavailable domestically. Argentina's courts have not yet ruled on the case.

Thousands of Venezuelans marched in Caracas on Wednesday to mark the 20th anniversary of Hugo Chavez’s return to power after the brief April 11, 2002 coup that removed him from office for two days. The Chavista government described the event as the “rescue of national dignity.” Supporters dressed in red shirts and militia uniforms marched from downtown Caracas squares to the Miraflores presidential palace. They were received by President Nicolas Maduro, Chavez’s political heir, along with senior leaders of the ruling Socialist Party of Venezuela (PSUV), including First Vice President Diosdado Cabello. Cabello told the crowd that “the betrayals were left behind” and that those who had overthrown Chavismo were gone. Maduro then addressed the rally, saying that 20 years earlier Venezuela had given “an historic lesson” to the “national oligarchy,” imperialism, and the international right. He led the crowd in an oath to work for the construction of “the socialism of the 21st century.” In remarks broadcast by state television, Maduro recalled those killed during the coup period and said that Bolivarian civil-military unity now exists. He argued that the country’s rebuilding has been shaped by the events of April 13, 2002, and warned not to underestimate the “revolutionary capacity” and courage of the Venezuelan people. Maduro also urged citizens to continue in the spirit of April 13 in order to restore prosperity and condemned corruption within state institutions. He called on the public to support efforts against bureaucrats, corrupt officials, and “lazy ones” wherever they may be. The government had been organizing commemorative events since Monday for the April 11-13, 2002 events, which Chavistas call a “shameful deed.” Chavez ruled Venezuela from 1999 until his death in 2013, after which Maduro assumed power and has remained president.

# Summary On April 13, thousands of Venezuelans marched in Caracas to commemorate the 20th anniversary of Hugo Chavez's return to power following a two-day coup on April 11, 2002. Supporters dressed in red shirts and militia uniforms proceeded from downtown squares to the Miraflores presidential palace, where they were welcomed by President Nicolas Maduro and Socialist Party leaders, including Diosdado Cabello. Cabello declared that "the betrayals were left behind" and those responsible for overthrowing Chavism had been defeated. Maduro characterized the 2002 events as "an historic lesson" delivered to Venezuela's oligarchy and imperialism, describing the occasion as demonstrating "Bolivarian civil-military unity" and continued "rebellion against neoliberalism." In his nationally broadcast speech, Maduro honored coup victims and emphasized the government's ongoing construction of "the socialism of the 21st century." He urged citizens not to underestimate the revolutionary capacity and collective courage of the Venezuelan people, attributing the nation's development to the April 2002 victory. Maduro called for continued commitment to the spirit of April 13 to restore national prosperity. He specifically condemned institutional corruption, demanding action against corrupt bureaucrats and lazy officials, appealing to the public for support in pursuing those responsible. The government organized multiple commemorative events beginning April 11, labeling the 2002 coup a "shameful deed." Chavez led Venezuela from 1999 until his 2013 death, after which Maduro assumed the presidency and has remained in power since.

Motorists have been urged to avoid roads near Nancefield Metrorail Station in Soweto after protesting residents began stoning passing vehicles. The unrest escalated on Monday when the protest moved to the station, where an altercation between Prasa security guards and community members left two people dead. Residents are demanding government housing for the nearby informal settlement. Police said roads to the station and toward Holomisa informal settlement were closed, while other routes remained open. Metrorail has suspended services at Nancefield until further notice.

# Summary Motorists are advised to avoid roads near Nancefield Metrorail Station in Soweto, where protesting residents are throwing stones at vehicles. Two people died Monday during a clash between Prasa security guards and angry community members. The residents are demanding government-provided housing for their informal settlement. Police have closed roads leading to the station and Holomisa informal settlement, though other routes remain accessible. Metrorail has suspended services at Nancefield Station indefinitely while authorities monitor the situation.

A man died in south-western Khartoum on Sunday after police fired tear gas to disperse a protest in Kalakla El Laffa. On Monday, local resistance committees said Mohamed Tembel, who already had breathing problems, was in the market when the gas was used nearby. Bystanders took him to Turkish Hospital, but the facility reportedly lacked emergency equipment, oxygen, and qualified staff, so he was transferred by ambulance to another hospital. His companions then unsuccessfully searched for an intensive care bed in a better-equipped facility. His condition worsened and he died. The committees said the protest was peacefully demanding basic rights and local services, and they blamed Sudanese police fully for Tembel’s death, saying tear gas was unnecessary.

# Summary A man died in Khartoum after police fired tear gas to disperse demonstrators. Mohamed Tembel, who had pre-existing breathing problems, was at a market in Kalakla El Laffa when police deployed tear gas Sunday. Witnesses rushed him to a nearby Turkish Hospital, but lacking emergency equipment and oxygen, he was transferred to another facility. Despite efforts to find an intensive care bed, his condition deteriorated and he died. Local resistance committees organized the peaceful demonstration demanding basic rights and local services. They claim the police use of tear gas was unnecessary and hold authorities fully responsible for Tembel's death.

At least seven people were killed in eastern Congo’s North Kivu province as anger over a surge of attacks by suspected Islamist rebels triggered protests and clashes, local officials said Saturday. The unrest followed a wave of violence blamed on the Allied Democratic Forces (ADF), a rebel group aligned with the Islamic State. Officials said the ADF killed more than 40 people in Mayikengo village earlier in the week and more than 80 people in other villages the week before. Public frustration boiled over on Friday night in Lubero territory, where a crowd killed two soldiers and their driver and set their vehicle on fire, according to local official Julio Mabanga. On Saturday, further confrontations between security forces and residents left three more dead: a civilian, a soldier, and an agent of the national intelligence service. In Butembo, hundreds of youths also marched with sticks, chanting and singing to denounce insecurity. Protester Daniel Sivanzire Paluku said residents were blocking roads to monitor movement in the area. Butembo’s mayor confirmed that one civilian died during clashes there. The ADF, originally from Uganda but now based in eastern Congo, has repeatedly attacked the region. SITE Intelligence Group said Islamic State communiques claimed responsibility for killing 51 people in North Kivu that week and beheading more than 60 in a June 7 attack.

# Summary At least seven people were killed in eastern Congo's North Kivu province during unrest triggered by escalating attacks from the Allied Democratic Forces (ADF), an Islamic State-affiliated rebel group. The ADF allegedly killed over 40 people in Mayikengo village and more than 80 in other villages during recent weeks, sparking public outrage and protests. The violence intensified when angry residents killed two soldiers and their driver in Lubero territory on Friday, burning their vehicle. On Saturday, clashes between security forces and local residents resulted in three additional deaths—a civilian, soldier, and intelligence agent. Hundreds of youths protested in the city of Butembo on Saturday, blocking roads and chanting against the widespread insecurity. One civilian died during clashes between security forces and protesters there. Demonstrators stated they needed to monitor movement in the area to protect themselves. The ADF, originally from Uganda but now based in mineral-rich eastern Congo, frequently conducts attacks that destabilize the region where multiple militant groups compete for resources. The U.S.-based SITE Intelligence Group reported that the Islamic State claimed responsibility for killing 51 people in North Kivu and beheading over 60 in a single June 7 attack.

Sudan on Saturday summoned Ethiopia’s charge d’affaires to lodge an official protest over what it said was an incursion by Ethiopian army-backed militias into Sudanese territory. According to Sudan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the militias attacked Sudanese citizens and armed forces inside Sudan, killing several officers, soldiers and civilians, including children. The ministry said it conveyed the government’s condemnation and rejection of the “heinous attack,” noting that it came as Khartoum was preparing to host the second meeting of a high-level joint border committee, to be co-chaired by Sudan’s Minister of Cabinet Affairs and Ethiopia’s deputy prime minister. Sudan demanded action to stop such attacks and warned that cooperation between the two countries must rest on mutual respect for sovereignty, independence and borders, and on the right of both peoples to live safely and use their resources without aggression.

# Sudan Protests Ethiopian Military Incursion Sudan summoned Ethiopia's Charge d'Affaires on Saturday to formally protest an alleged incursion by Ethiopian army-backed militias into Sudanese territory. According to Sudan's Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the attack resulted in deaths among Sudanese military officers, armed forces members, and civilians, including children. The protest comes at a particularly sensitive time, as Khartoum was preparing to host the second meeting of a high-level joint committee on border issues, scheduled to be co-chaired by Sudan's Minister of Cabinet Affairs and Ethiopia's Deputy Prime Minister. Sudan's government condemned the attack and demanded it cease immediately. The ministry warned that future cooperation between the two nations must be based on mutual respect for sovereignty, independence, and borders, emphasizing both countries' rights to security, peace, and unimpeded use of their natural and economic resources.

Gibson said the atmosphere felt like a revival and that many people came to Christ. He added that he attended the “Save America Rally” on Jan. 6 and described it as peaceful. Gibson, founder of peaceablygather.com, claims he has been falsely accused of involvement in the violence that occurred and has consequently relocated to an undisclosed location under 24/7 security protection. He stated that President Trump did not incite violence and that he never heard the president call for storming the Capitol. Gibson emphasized that he condemns all violent acts that occurred that day, asserting he was not involved in any rioting.

Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, joined by First Lady Zinash Tayachew and senior officials, inaugurated the integrated Tulu Arara Model Village in Addis Ababa, presenting it as a new stage in Ethiopia’s rainy season volunteer and charity program. Abiy said the 7,000-square-meter village was designed to offer dignified, comfortable housing and can accommodate 150 people at the household level. Each housing unit has five rooms, including two bedrooms. The site is equipped with internal roads, electricity, solar power, a fitness and recreation area, and green development features. It also follows an integrated development model that links production to market value chains. Residents are expected to benefit from dairy cattle and poultry farming, backyard gardening, and a commercial chain connecting output to markets, creating sustainable income and improving self-sufficiency.

# Summary Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed inaugurated the integrated Tulu Arara Model Village in Addis Ababa, accompanied by the First Lady and government officials. The 7,000-square-meter village represents an advancement in Ethiopia's rainy season volunteer and charity program. Designed to house 150 households, each unit contains five rooms including two bedrooms. The village features comprehensive infrastructure including roads, electricity, solar power, fitness facilities, and green initiatives. The development employs an integrated approach combining dairy and poultry farming with backyard gardening, directly linking production to market outlets. This creates sustainable income opportunities and promotes self-sufficiency, demonstrating community-centered development focused on improving residents' living standards and livelihoods.

Rangers at Kahuzi-Biega National Park in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo protested for a sixth straight day over months of unpaid wages, witnesses said. The eco-guards at the UN-listed sanctuary blocked the park entrance with barricades, preventing employees from entering while allowing residents to pass. The protest began on December 24, when the rangers said they had gone unpaid for 10 months. Over the next four days, witnesses said, some demonstrators fired warning shots at the gate. Kahuzi-Biega is a UNESCO World Heritage site covering 600,000 hectares of rainforest and is home to the world’s largest population of eastern lowland gorillas. The dispute has raised concern among local civil society leaders, who warned it could escalate and urged a quick, lasting solution, while also criticizing the way the protest was being conducted. Park spokesman Hubert Mulongoy said the back-pay issue affects all workers at Kahuzi-Biega, not only the rangers, and said those responsible would face military justice. An army spokesman said forces would work to restore order. The unrest also forced Gorilla FM, an environmental radio station based at park headquarters, to stop broadcasting after armed demonstrators intimidated staff. The park has long faced illegal activities, including armed groups and charcoal burning.

# Summary Rangers at Kahuzi-Biega National Park in eastern DR Congo protested for the sixth consecutive day over unpaid salaries, claiming they haven't been paid for 10 months. Osaka craft beer Nishinari Riot Ale is more than a catchy brand name: it draws on the history of the Airin district in Nishinari Ward, where riots by disaffected day laborers broke out in the 1990s. The beer is produced by Derailleur Brew Works, a brewery run by Cyclo, a company that originally started as a nursing care provider and still focuses on employment support for people with disabilities. The brewery’s workers, many of whom have disabilities, are involved in every stage of production and distribution, including brewing, bottling, labeling, sales, and delivery. One worker, 54-year-old Shoichi Nishizawa, who has a mental disability, said he works with enthusiasm and finds the job enjoyable. Cyclo chief Masanobu Yamazaki launched its disability employment support program in 2014, initially offering jobs such as bagging screws. But workers wanted to create something of their own, and the idea of making craft beer emerged. Yamazaki said the concept made sense because beer could sell well, and many workers were themselves beer fans. The history of illegal beer brewing in Nishinari during the 1990s also became part of the inspiration. In 2017, Yamazaki rented brewery space in Osaka and began test brewing with workers. After obtaining a brewing license, he opened Derailleur Brew Works in April 2018. Nishinari Riot Ale was then released after extensive testing and tasting. Since then, the brewery has produced 23 varieties of beer, and Nishinari Riot has gained popularity nationwide. Demand has grown so much that production is struggling to keep up. Over the past two years, the number of disabled employees at the brewery has increased from about 16 to 65. Yamazaki said there are also more workers with perfect attendance than before, joking that alcoholic beverages may have a unifying effect. To expand capacity, Cyclo bought a roughly 265-square-meter property in Osaka’s Haginochaya area in June. A new brewery is planned there for next year or later, which would quadruple production capacity and allow the company to hire about 40 more people with disabilities. Yamazaki said he hopes to create a highly motivating workplace while expanding opportunities for disabled workers.

In response, some growers have begun using XAG’s agricultural drones to improve productivity. One example is Chhay Thi, an early adopter who owns 20 hectares of land in Varin District, Siem Reap Province. In May 2022, he arranged for a demonstration through XAG’s local partner, Red Sparrow Cambodia, on his 10-hectare cassava field. The drone was used for autonomous weeding and herbicide spraying. After the tank was filled, the drone took off automatically following simple commands from a mobile app. It flew over the cassava ridges, sprayed precisely along a preset route, and completed herbicide application on 8 hectares without human control. Because it sprays from above, it avoids the need for tractors or backpack sprayers to enter tall cassava fields, where plants can exceed human height. Averil Pooten-Watan, a 46-year-old community leader in Waltham Forest, east London, had been told to keep her meeting with King Charles III brief: give him a quick, firm handshake, make a curtsy, and let him move on. But when the King visited Waltham Forest Town Hall on December 20, the encounter became more personal than protocol suggested. Watan, who was born in the UK to Igorot parents from the Mountain Province, wore a tapis and joined about 20 other local community leaders at the reception. She introduced herself as chair of Igorot UK charity and greeted the King with, “Hello, Your Majesty.” According to her account, Charles responded by saying that Britain “would be nothing without the Filipinos,” especially in the National Health Service. He also mentioned that he had recently undergone cancer treatment and had received excellent care from a Filipino nurse. The two spoke for several minutes, during which the King asked about Filipino rice varieties and Watan showed him a hamper she had prepared, including champorado mix. She said Charles seemed genuinely interested, stayed longer than expected, and came across as warm and sincere. The royal visit, which came five days before Christmas, was set against the backdrop of unrest earlier in the year. In the summer, riots erupted in parts of the UK after the stabbing deaths of three girls. False online claims blaming a Muslim immigrant helped fuel Islamophobia and anti-immigrant anger. In Walthamstow, local residents mobilized in response, organizing anti-racism demonstrations and preventing far-right groups from targeting the area. Watan described the community response as extraordinary, saying more than a thousand people gathered in central Walthamstow to resist political hate. She believes the royal household wanted to thank the local community for standing together. A few months later, Watan received a message from the mayor of Waltham Forest inviting her to a reception with King Charles III. At first, she thought it was a mistake, but a follow-up email asking her to prepare a Filipino hamper convinced her it was real. Watan’s own story reflects the long history of Filipino migration to the UK. Her mother went to Britain in the early 1970s to train as a nurse at Claybury Hospital, part of a major NHS recruitment drive. After marrying in the Philippines, her mother returned to the UK in 1978 with Watan’s father, who is from Sagada, Mountain Province. Watan was born that same year. Growing up in the 1980s, she said there were only a few Filipino families in the area, so her parents made a deliberate effort to instill pride in their Igorot identity. She later married another second-generation Igorot, Mark Sapaen Watan, and they have two daughters. Her parents have since retired to Baguio, which she described as the “immigrant dream.” Watan said the Filipino community in the UK has grown dramatically since her childhood. There are now more than 200,000 Filipinos in the country, many working in healthcare, education, and hospitality, and at least 200 Filipino groups and societies registered with the Philippine embassy in the UK and Ireland. In Walthamstow alone, she estimated there are now more than 1,000 Filipinos. Despite that growth, she said Filipinos still need greater representation in mainstream media, politics, and business, and she continues working toward stronger integration and visibility for the community.

# Summary: The Day an Igorot Woman Met King Charles Averil Pooten-Watan, a 46-year-old community leader of Igorot descent living in Waltham Forest, London, recently met King Charles III at a royal reception on December 20. The encounter proved far more meaningful than the brief protocol handshake she had been instructed to give. Watan, born to two Igorot parents from the Philippines' Mountain Province, grew up in Walthamstow, east London. She now chairs Igorot UK, a grassroots charity organization dedicated to integrating Filipinos in the United Kingdom. Preparing for the royal meeting, she practiced her curtsy and assembled a hamper of Filipino items, including champorado mix and Ding Dong snacks, to showcase Philippine culture. When King Charles III arrived at the town hall wearing traditional Filipino attire, she introduced herself and was surprised by the King's genuine interest and extended conversation. Charles shared that the country relies heavily on Filipino healthcare workers and mentioned receiving excellent care from a Filipino nurse during his recent cancer treatment. He engaged with her about Philippine agriculture and showed authentic interest in the champorado she displayed, lingering much longer than protocol typically allows. Watan's presence at this event reflected the broader context of community solidarity in Waltham Forest. During summer 2024, anti-immigrant riots erupted across the UK following false social media posts blaming a Muslim immigrant for murders committed in July. However, Walthamstow residents mobilized impressively, with over 1,000 community members gathering to demonstrate against hatred and prevent far-right groups from targeting the area. This unprecedented show of solidarity—bringing together neighbors, friends, and grassroots organizations—ultimately deterred extremist demonstrations. The Royal Household recognized this community resilience, and the mayor of Waltham Forest invited Watan to meet the King as a way of thanking local residents for their anti-racism stance. Watan's personal journey exemplifies the Filipino diaspora experience in Britain. Her mother arrived in the early 1970s as part of the National Health Service's massive recruitment drive for nurses. Her father followed after they married in the Philippines, and Watan was born in 1978. Despite being a small minority in 1980s London—with only a handful of Filipino families present—her parents deliberately instilled pride in their Igorot heritage in Watan and her sister. The Filipino presence in the UK has grown dramatically since then. Currently, over 200,000 Filipinos live in Britain, working across healthcare, education, hospitality, and other sectors. Walthamstow alone now hosts approximately 1,000 Filipinos, with at least 200 Filipino community groups and societies registered with the Philippine embassy across the UK and Ireland. Watan's own family expanded this community when she married fellow second-generation Igorot Mark Sapaen Watan in 2004; they are raising two daughters together. Despite this growth, Watan emphasizes that Filipino communities need greater representation in mainstream media, politics, and business—areas where Indian, Pakistani, and Chinese communities have achieved greater visibility and influence. Her work continues to focus on facilitating Filipino integration while preserving cultural identity and community pride.

The latest National Crime Records Bureau (NCRB) report has drawn mixed reactions in West Bengal. While the Trinamool Congress has highlighted Kolkata’s ranking as the safest metro city in India, opposition leaders and legal experts say the same report exposes a troubling picture of crimes against women across the state. According to the NCRB data cited in the article, India recorded 174 acid attacks against women in 2021, and West Bengal accounted for the highest number, with 34 cases. Senior advocate Kaushik Gupta of the Calcutta High Court argued that these figures are likely understated. He said acid attacks in remote parts of the state often never reach the police because of political and social pressure on victims and their families. Gupta also noted that despite a Supreme Court order restricting open sale of acid, it can still often be bought from hardware stores without receipts, while the police remain silent. Even Kolkata’s “safest city” tag was questioned. Gupta pointed out that the number of serious offences in the city rose to 1,080 in 2021, up from 981 in 2020 and 961 in 2019. Criminal lawyer Jyoti Prakash Khan said West Bengal does not present a favorable picture overall on crimes against women. He said the state ranked fourth in India for total crimes against women, with 35,884 cases, behind Uttar Pradesh, Rajasthan and Maharashtra. He added that this category includes rape, murder after rape, dowry-related crimes, acid attacks, abetment to suicide, kidnapping, forced marriage, human trafficking and online harassment. BJP leader Amit Malviya attacked Chief Minister Mamata Banerjee on social media, calling the NCRB findings her “report card.” In response, state minister Sashi Panja accused the BJP of mud-slinging and urged it to focus on crime in BJP-ruled states, especially Uttar Pradesh. CPI(M) leader Sujan Chakraborty said the NCRB figures are based on data submitted by the state government, suggesting the real numbers may be even higher.

France was hit by a third consecutive day of strikes and demonstrations on Thursday as anger over President François Hollande’s labour reforms continued to disrupt transport and public services. Dozens of flights and trains were cancelled after rail workers and air traffic controllers joined the walkouts, part of two months of protests against the government’s plan to make the labour market more flexible. Prime Minister Manuel Valls took a harder line, warning that protesters blocking ports, refineries and airports could face forceful intervention. His strongest comments were aimed at those who attacked a police car in Paris on Wednesday during a rare rally by police officers protesting what they called “anti-cop hatred.” In that incident, a small group of masked demonstrators beat the vehicle with iron bars and threw in an explosive device while a policeman and policewoman were inside. Both escaped unharmed. Valls said the punishment should be “harsh,” and police said five suspects had been arrested. A video of the attack quickly spread online, drawing millions of views. Tensions were still high on Thursday, when police estimated that up to 14,000 people marched in Paris. Masked protesters again sought confrontation with riot police, and officials said violence in recent weeks had increasingly been driven by small groups of troublemakers infiltrating the wider rallies. Paris police chief Michel Cadot responded by banning 19 more people identified as hardcore activists from taking part in demonstrations. He urged ordinary marchers to keep their distance from violent participants. He had already issued about 40 such bans, though some have been suspended by the courts. The unions rejected Valls’s warning that organisers should think twice before calling protests. CGT union leader Philippe Martinez said demonstrations were a democratic right and should not be prevented because of problems on the margins. Security marshals deployed by unions were said to have left clubs and batons at home after police urged restraint. Over the past two months, about 350 security officers have been injured in protests over the reforms, which were pushed through the lower house of parliament last week without a vote. On Thursday, SNCF said about 14 percent of its staff were striking, while Orly airport cancelled 15 percent of flights. The government argues the reforms will boost employment, but critics say they will weaken job protection without reducing unemployment, which stands at 10 percent overall and nearly 25 percent among young people.

The article argues that Europe is undergoing a deep political and social crisis marked by xenophobia, inequality, corruption, and demographic decline, and that these pressures have caused the continent to “lose its compass.” It opens with Sweden, long presented as a model of democracy, civic responsibility, and social justice. The author presents this as evidence that the “Nordic myth” of a progressive, humane northern Europe has collapsed. Similar nationalist and anti-immigrant parties, the article notes, are influential across Finland, Norway, and Denmark. The piece then turns to Germany, where a new anti-immigrant movement gained rapid momentum in Dresden, Saxony. Thousands marched under the slogan “Wir sind das Volk,” a phrase associated with the 1989 protests against East Germany’s communist regime, but now used against immigrants. The demonstrations were organized around “Patriotic Europeans Against the Islamisation of the West,” a group created by Lutz Bachmann, a 41-year-old activist who had previously been little known. In only seven weeks, Bachmann was able to mobilize thousands. The article says local reporting revealed that he had multiple criminal convictions, including burglary, cocaine dealing, and driving without a license or while drunk, but that these facts did not deter supporters. They spoke of missing their country, demanded protection of the homeland, and applauded Bachmann’s call for a “clean and pure Germany.” The immediate trigger for the protests was the plan to house about 2,000 Syrian refugees in Dresden, even though foreigners made up only 2 percent of Saxony’s population and Muslims were only a tiny fraction of that group. The rise of the Alternative for Germany, which won nearly 10 percent in the last state election, is presented as part of the same trend. The author says a comparable irrational fear of immigrants is spreading across Europe. Italy is used as a central example. There, the Northern League and the Five Star Movement together account for around 35 percent of the vote, both with xenophobic overtones, while Silvio Berlusconi’s Forza Italia is described as leaning toward anti-European positions. The three parties, the article says, more or less openly advocate leaving the euro. Yet the author argues that Italy’s real problems are demographic and social, not caused by immigration. In 2013, only 514,308 children were born, 20,000 fewer than the previous year. Between 2001 and 2011, single-person households increased sharply while families with children declined. Nearly half of families with children had only one child, and only about 10 percent had three or more. With a replacement rate of 2.1 children per woman, the article concludes that Italy, like Europe generally, is on a steep demographic decline. The author links this demographic weakness to austerity and insecurity. Italy’s budget for social interventions was cut from 2.5 billion euros in 2009 to about one-third of that four years later, while the Family Policies Fund fell from 186.5 million euros to less than 21 million. As a result, 60 percent of Italians reportedly fear becoming poor. Youth unemployment and exclusion are reflected in the rise of NEETs, from 1.8 million in 2007 to 2.5 million in 2013. At the same time, elderly citizens are also struggling, with 41.3 percent of pensions below 1,000 euros a month. The article also challenges claims of massive immigration. It notes that 83,000 Italians emigrated in 2013, including more than 3,000 university graduates heading to the UK, while 44,000 foreigners left Italy in the same year. Immigration to Italy fell from nearly 355,000 in 2011 to 280,000 two years later, despite public rhetoric suggesting the opposite. Beyond Italy, the article says social decline is occurring in different forms across Europe. In Germany, it claims, 25 percent of the population lives in the Hartz IV welfare category. The piece then broadens into a critique of rising inequality, citing a study by François Bourguignon and Christian Morrisson that tracks the world’s inequality index from 1820 to 2002 and shows a steep long-term rise. The author summarizes the gap starkly: the “small guy” must work 80 years to earn what the “big guy” makes in a year. Corruption is presented as another symptom of this broader decay. The article says social comparison and “catching up” can encourage corruption, and notes that southern Europe is more affected than the north. It cites several scandals: former Portuguese prime minister José Sócrates jailed, Nicolas Sarkozy returning to politics amid accusations, corruption revelations in Spain, and criminal infiltration of local government in Rome and Milan. The article concludes that in times of crisis and fear, scapegoating immigrants becomes politically convenient. Yet, it argues, Europe depends on immigrants economically and would struggle without them. Still, politicians continue to exploit fear rather than address reality. The final judgment is bleak: Europe has lost its compass, and no recovery is visible soon.

# Europe Has Lost Its Compass: A Summary This opinion piece by Roberto Savio examines Europe's troubling political and social trajectory, arguing that the continent has fundamentally lost direction amid economic decline, rising inequality, and xenophobic politics. ## Political Upheaval and the Rise of Xenophobia The article opens with Sweden's government collapse in December, triggered by the far-right Sweden Democrats—now parliament's third-largest party—siding with the opposition. This development is particularly symbolic, as Sweden has long represented European democracy, social justice, and refuge for those fleeing dictatorship. The Sweden Democrats' anti-immigrant stance demonstrates how quickly xenophobic parties have gained influence across Nordic countries, shattering the myth of progressive northern Europe. Similar concerning trends appear elsewhere. In Dresden, Germany, thousands marched against immigration under the slogan "Wir sind das Volk"—the same cry used against East Germany's communist regime 25 years earlier. A previously unknown activist, Lutz Bachmann, established the Patriotic Europeans Against the Islamisation of the West and rallied thousands within seven weeks, despite his criminal convictions for burglary, cocaine dealing, and drunk driving. Notably, Saxony has only two percent foreign immigrants and minimal Muslim populations, yet the announcement of facilities for 2,000 Syrian refugees triggered this backlash. The populist Alternative for Germany party captured nearly 10 percent in recent state elections. Italy presents another alarming case, with two major xenophobic parties—the Northern League and Five Star Movement—accounting for approximately 35 percent of votes, while Silvio Berlusconi's Forza Italia flirts with anti-European policies. All three advocate Euro withdrawal. ## Demographic and Economic Crisis However, Savio argues this xenophobia is fundamentally irrational given Europe's actual demographic situation. Italy's birth rate has plummeted, with only 514,308 children born in 2013—20,000 fewer than the previous year. Between 2001 and 2011, single-person families increased 41.3 percent while families with children declined five percent. With Italy's demographic replacement rate requiring 2.1 children per family, the population faces steep decline. The economic context makes childbearing increasingly untenable. Italy's social intervention budget collapsed from 2.5 billion euros in 2009 to less than one-third that amount by 2013. The Family Policies Fund plummeted from 186.5 million to just 21 million euros. Consequently, 60 percent of Italians fear poverty. Youth unemployment is devastating, with NEET (Not in Education, Employment or Training) individuals rising from 1.8 million in 2007 to 2.5 million in 2013. Pensioners suffer equally, with 41.3 percent receiving less than 1,000 euros monthly. Immigration data contradicts xenophobic narratives. While 83,000 Italians emigrated in 2013 and 44,000 foreigners also left Italy, immigration actually declined from 355,000 in 2011 to 280,000 in 2013. Yet xenophobic campaigns persist in claiming dramatic immigrant increases. ## Systemic Inequality and Corruption Savio highlights unprecedented social inequality across Europe. Using the Gini inequality index, he notes it rose from 50 in 1820 to 70 by 2002, meaning minimum-wage workers must labor 80 years to earn what executives earn in one year. This inequality drives corruption, particularly in southern Europe, where numerous scandals have emerged: Portugal's former prime minister José Socrates jailed, France's Nicolas Sarkozy returning to politics amid accusations, and Spain's massive government corruption revelations. Rome discovered criminal organizations controlling the town council, while Milan saw previously convicted corruption offenders return to public works contracts. ## Conclusion Savio concludes that Europe has lost its compass entirely. The continent's political leaders escape reality by scapegoating immigrants rather than addressing genuine crises. Ironically, Europe would economically collapse without immigrant labor, yet politicians exploit fear and uncertainty to pursue xenophobic agendas. With no visible solutions emerging from those in power, Savio questions who will address Europe's profound anguish as the continent spirals deeper into crisis.

Spain is facing intense scrutiny over the condition of its rail network after a deadly week of accidents raised questions about whether maintenance spending has kept pace with booming passenger demand. The country’s high-speed rail system, the largest in Europe, carried nearly 40 million passengers in 2024, almost twice as many as in 2019, while total rail usage reached a record 549 million trips, according to competition authority data. Experts say that surge has increased wear and tear on the system, exposing a long-running emphasis on expansion over upkeep. The crisis was triggered by a series of incidents. Last Sunday, a high-speed collision in Andalusia killed 45 people in one of Europe’s deadliest rail accidents. Two days later, a commuter train near Barcelona derailed after a containment wall collapsed onto the tracks following heavy rain, killing the driver and seriously injuring four passengers. Another train derailed near Barcelona after a rock fell onto the line, and a fourth train struck a crane arm in southeastern Spain, leaving six passengers with minor injuries. Preliminary findings from the Andalusia crash suggested that a fracture in the rail may have occurred before the derailment, according to the rail accident investigation body CIAF. Transport Minister Oscar Puente said after the accident that there should be a debate about whether more money is needed for maintenance, but he urged that this discussion be kept separate from the Andalusia crash itself, noting that the track had been renovated in May and inspected on January 7. Data from the European Commission show Spain has spent heavily on its rail system overall, averaging about 1.5 billion euros a year from 2018 to 2022 on its high-speed network alone. But only around 16% of that went to maintenance, renewal and upgrades, compared with 34% to 39% in France, Germany and Italy. Spain has built out its roughly 4,000-kilometer high-speed network aggressively, but critics say upkeep has not matched that pace. Jose Trigueros, head of the Association of Roads and Civil Engineers, argued that maintenance spending on high-speed lines should rise to 150,000 euros per kilometer from the current 110,000 euros, with conventional lines also needing more funding. Union leaders say the situation is worsening. SEMAF, the main train drivers’ union, called a three-day nationwide strike to protest what it described as the “constant deterioration” of the railway system and to demand stronger safety and maintenance guarantees. In an August letter to infrastructure operator Adif, the union had already warned of severe wear on several lines, including the one involved in Sunday’s crash. Official data show reported rail problems such as deterioration and rail breaks rose from 440 in 2015 to 716 in 2024, while accidents including derailments increased from 42 to 57. The government says Spain’s rail problems remain proportionally below the EU average and points to rising investment since Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez took office in 2018, including a tripling of infrastructure spending and a 58% increase in maintenance spending per kilometer to 71,000 euros last year. Still, a BBVA and Ivie report says rail investment remains far below pre-2008 crisis levels, with 2024 gross investment less than a third of its 2009 peak.

# Spain's Rail Crisis: Success Creates Maintenance Challenges Spain's railway system faces a critical juncture following a series of devastating accidents in one week that have exposed a dangerous gap between network expansion and maintenance investment. ## The Accidents A high-speed collision in Andalusia killed 45 people, making it one of Europe's deadliest rail accidents. Within days, additional incidents occurred near Barcelona, including a derailment caused by a fallen containment wall and another derailment from a rock on the line. A fourth accident involved a train colliding with a crane arm. Preliminary investigations into the Andalusia crash revealed a pre-existing rail fracture, raising questions about track condition. ## Explosive Growth Strains Infrastructure Spain's rail system has experienced unprecedented success. Nearly 40 million passengers used high-speed trains in 2024—almost double the 2019 figure—bringing total railway usage to a record 549 million passengers. This growth on Europe's largest high-speed network has created significant wear and tear, yet investment priorities haven't adjusted accordingly. ## Investment Imbalance The core problem is structural: Spain prioritizes expansion over maintenance. From 2018 to 2022, Spain spent an average of 1.5 billion euros annually on high-speed rail—more than any other country. However, only 16% went to maintenance, renewal, and upgrades. By contrast, France, Germany, and Italy allocated 34-39% to maintenance despite having far smaller networks. Experts argue maintenance spending must increase from the current 110,000 euros per kilometer to 150,000 euros. Official data reveals the consequences: rail deterioration and breaks increased from 440 cases in 2015 to 716 in 2024, while accidents rose from 42 to 57 over the same period. ## Government Response and Debate Transport Minister Oscar Puerte acknowledged the maintenance debate while noting that the Andalusia track had been renovated in May and inspected in January. The government contends that Spain's accident rates remain proportionally below EU averages and comparable to Germany and France. It also highlighted that maintenance spending has increased 58-71% per kilometer since 2018 and overall infrastructure investment has tripled. However, these gains remain insufficient. A 2024 infrastructure report found that gross rail investment in 2024 was less than one-third of its 2009 peak when adjusted for inflation. Investment only became consistently adequate again in 2021. ## Union Response Spain's main train drivers' union, SEMAF, called a three-day nationwide strike, demanding safety guarantees and maintenance improvements. The union had warned Adif, the state rail operator, about severe wear on multiple lines, including the crash site. ## The Core Issue As one expert observed, Spain's rail system is "dying from its own success." Like maintaining a Ferrari, operating a world-class rail network requires continuous investment beyond initial construction. Spain's failure to adequately fund maintenance while dramatically increasing usage has created a dangerous mismatch between demand and infrastructure condition, necessitating urgent policy realignment.

Iran’s top police chief on Monday gave protesters accused of taking part in “riots” three days to surrender, warning that those who do not turn themselves in will face the full force of the law. National police chief Ahmad-Reza Radan said young people who were “deceived” into joining the unrest would be treated more leniently and not as “enemy soldiers,” and urged them to hand themselves over for lighter punishment. The warning came as Iran’s leadership also promised to address the economic grievances that helped trigger the demonstrations. In a joint statement carried by state television, the heads of the executive, legislative and judicial branches — President Masoud Pezeshkian, parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf and judiciary chief Gholamhossein Mohseni Ejei — said they would work “around the clock” to solve “livelihood and economic problems,” while also pledging to “decisively punish” those behind what they called “terrorist incidents.” The protests have become the biggest challenge to Iran’s leadership in years, but the full extent of the violence remains unclear because of an unprecedented internet blackout that has lasted 11 days. Rights groups say the crackdown has killed thousands. The Iran Human Rights NGO said it has verified 3,428 protesters killed by security forces, and warned the real toll could be much higher. Its director, Mahmood Amiry-Moghaddam, said evidence from eyewitnesses, families and others suggested the number of deaths may exceed the highest media estimates, calling it one of the largest mass killings of protesters in modern times. There is growing concern that authorities may use capital punishment against detainees. The United Nations said Monday that Iran is using executions as “a tool of state intimidation.” UN human rights chief Volker Turk noted that Iran reportedly executed 1,500 people last year, making it the world’s most prolific executioner after China, according to rights groups. Iranian officials said around 3,000 people had been arrested, though rights groups believe the figure could be as high as 20,000. Supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei said Saturday that authorities must “break the back of the seditionists.” Officials also said internet access would gradually return this week. President Pezeshkian criticized the restrictions and called for better cyberspace governance. Damage from the unrest has been reported in Tehran and Mashhad, where the mayor said public infrastructure losses exceeded $15 million. Outside Iran, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan called the unrest a “new test” for Tehran and said Turkey would oppose any move that could plunge the region into chaos.

Poland’s main political forces are both trying to turn migration into an election-winning issue ahead of the country’s parliamentary vote this fall. The nationalist ruling party, Law and Justice (PiS), and the centrist opposition led by former European Council President Donald Tusk are each warning about Muslim immigration, even though their arguments are often contradictory and, in some cases, aimed more at political advantage than policy clarity. PiS has recently made the issue central to its campaign. The government refused to back an EU agreement on relocating migrants, angering other member states and the European Commission, and party leader Jarosław Kaczyński called for a referendum on the question to be held at the same time as the election. At a rally on Saturday, Kaczyński said Poland would not accept the EU relocation plan and insisted that “the people of Poland also do not agree to this.” The move appears designed to recreate the political conditions that helped PiS win power in 2015, during the height of Europe’s migration crisis. Back then, Kaczyński warned that migrants coming to Europe carried “all sorts of parasites and protozoa,” and he attacked the then-government of Tusk’s Civic Platform for agreeing to accept some asylum seekers under an EU scheme. This year, however, Tusk is responding with rhetoric that borrows heavily from PiS. In a series of social media videos that have gone viral in Poland, he accused PiS of using the EU migration plan as a distraction, arguing that the plan would not actually bring people into Poland while the government was simultaneously opening the country to mass migration from Muslim countries. He began by referring to the riots in France, echoing language used by Prime Minister Mateusz Morawiecki at a recent European leaders’ summit on migration. Morawiecki had angered France by tweeting: “We don’t want such scenes in any city in Europe ... stop illegal migration. Safety first.” Tusk then claimed Kaczyński was preparing a document that would allow even more migrants to come from countries including Saudi Arabia, India, Iran, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates, Nigeria and Pakistan. He alleged that the government brought in 130,000 people from those countries last year, far more than under his own party in 2015. Tusk accused Kaczyński of scapegoating foreigners while allowing large-scale immigration at the same time, suggesting that the goal was to create internal conflict and fear, because “that’s when it’s easier for him to rule.” He ended by saying Poles must regain control of the country and its borders. Tusk’s approach reflects a broader trend among center-right politicians in Europe who are trying to appeal to public concern over migration to compete with populist rivals. But his language has drawn criticism from the Left and from human rights groups, which called it borderline racist and xenophobic. Adrian Zandberg, one of the Left’s leaders, said that competing with the far right is not a “vote on migration policy” but “wrestling with a pig in the mud.” Tusk’s attack has nevertheless exposed confusion inside PiS. The party is still moving ahead with its referendum plan, but it has backed away from an earlier push to loosen migration rules. Kaczyński admitted to the state news agency that “the initiative was clearly a mistake and has been stopped.” The debate is taking place against the backdrop of major demographic change in Poland. The country was once one of Europe’s most homogeneous societies, with only 0.3 percent of residents born abroad a decade ago. But Poland has become more diverse as its economy has grown, attracting migrants from around the world. It now hosts over a million Ukrainian refugees, in addition to hundreds of thousands already living there before the war. The social security agency says about 6.5 percent of working people in Poland are foreign. Despite PiS’s anti-migration rhetoric, the party has overseen a sharp rise in foreign workers. In 2021, the government issued just over 500,000 work visas to foreign nationals, 24 percent more than in 2020 and eight times the number in 2015. Last year the figure was still nearly 470,000. At the same time, Poland’s birth rate is falling sharply, with April recording only 21,000 births, the lowest monthly total ever. The population is expected to shrink from 38 million today to 33 million by 2050 and 28 million by 2080. The article concludes that Poland’s strong economy will continue to need migrant labor, meaning future governments of any political stripe will likely face pressure to allow more immigration, even as politicians continue to exploit the issue for votes. After criticism of his first video, Tusk softened slightly, saying everyone should enjoy full respect and rights regardless of birthplace, religion, skin color or worldview. But he still insisted on tighter, more “pragmatic” control over migration from Muslim countries and Africa.

# Polish Politicians Attack Migrants for Electoral Gain As Poland approaches its fall parliamentary election, both major political parties are capitalizing on migration fears to gain electoral advantage, despite the country's actual need for immigrant workers. ## The Ruling Party's Strategy The nationalist Law and Justice (PiS) party, led by Jarosław Kaczyński, has aggressively opposed an EU migration relocation plan and called for a referendum on the issue. Kaczyński is attempting to replay the successful strategy that brought PiS to power in 2015, when he warned darkly about migrants carrying "parasites and protozoa." The party held firm against EU pressure to accept migrant relocations, drawing criticism from fellow member states and the European Commission. ## Opposition Counterattack Centrist opposition leader Donald Tusk, a former European Council President, has fought back using similar anti-migration rhetoric. In viral social media videos, Tusk accused PiS of hypocrisy—scapegoating migrants while simultaneously allowing mass immigration. He claimed the government brought in 130,000 people from Muslim-majority and African countries last year, fifty times more than during Tusk's tenure in power. Tusk referenced recent French riots while warning that Kaczyński's policies would enable immigration from countries like Saudi Arabia, Iran, and Pakistan. Tusk concluded by calling for Polish citizens to "regain control" of their country and borders. However, after facing criticism from the Left opposition and human rights organizations who labeled his language "borderline racist and xenophobic," Tusk moderated his tone in subsequent videos, emphasizing respect for people regardless of "place of birth, religion, color of their skin or worldview." ## The Contradiction Despite PiS's anti-migration rhetoric, the party has presided over a dramatic increase in immigration. In 2021, the government issued over 500,000 work visas to foreign nationals—24 percent more than 2020 and eight times more than 2015. Last year's figure reached nearly 470,000. This contradiction has thrown PiS into disarray; Kaczyński eventually acknowledged that an earlier effort to ease migration rules "was clearly a mistake and has been stopped." ## Poland's Demographic Reality Poland faces a demographic crisis that necessitates immigration regardless of political rhetoric. A decade ago, only 0.3 percent of Poland's population was foreign-born, making it one of Europe's most homogenous nations. However, Poland's growing prosperity has attracted migrants worldwide. The country now hosts over a million Ukrainian refugees plus hundreds of thousands of other foreign residents. The social security agency estimates that 6.5 percent of working people in Poland are foreign-born. Meanwhile, Poland's birth rate has collapsed. April 2023 recorded only 21,000 births—the lowest monthly total ever. The social security agency projects Poland's population will shrink from 38 million currently to 33 million by 2050 and 28 million by 2080. ## Economic Necessity Poland's robust economy requires continued worker immigration to sustain growth. Any future government, regardless of political orientation, will face pressure to maintain or increase immigration levels. This creates an unavoidable tension between electoral posturing against migrants and the economic reality that Poland desperately needs them to maintain prosperity and fund social welfare systems—ironically, programs that PiS has expanded through generous family payments.

SPGPrints announced that it will introduce its new Nebula Sublimation Ink Range at FESPA Digital 2016, held from 8–11 March in Amsterdam. At its stand in Hall 5, Stand 41, the company will also showcase information about its PIKE digital printer and its broader textile ink portfolio. The new Nebula Sublimation inks are designed to expand high-quality digital textile printing by offering a wider colour gamut, lower manufacturing costs and strong print quality. SPGPrints said sublimation printing has gained a firm place in digital textile production over the past two years, especially for fashion applications. This growth has been supported by improvements in polyester fabrics, which now better suit fashion garments and meet the expectations of major brands. Sublimation has also benefited from its environmental advantages, since it does not require post-processing steps such as steaming and washing. Although some limitations remain, brands have increasingly accepted the quality of sublimation-printed fashion items. The new ink set is described as producing bright, vivid colours along with what SPGPrints calls the best deep black currently available in the market. It joins the broader Nebula family, which already includes Nebula Direct Disperse inks, launched at FESPA Digital in Munich, and Nebula Reactive HD inks, launched at FESPA in Cologne. Formulated for Kyocera print heads, the Nebula range is intended to help printers using equipment with those heads achieve improved gamut, vibrance, image quality, runnability and productivity. SPGPrints also highlighted its own ink manufacturing capabilities. The company develops and produces its inks at its Boxmeer plant in the Netherlands, which has recently completed the latest of three expansion projects, adding new equipment and doubling production space. The PIKE uses specially formulated Reactive inks and Archer technology to jet up to 4mm between the substrate and print head, reducing the risk of head damage and allowing a wide range of substrates to be printed in a single pass.
