Saudi Arabia is portrayed in the article as entering a new and more openly confrontational phase, not only in its foreign policy but also inside the royal family itself. The piece describes a sweeping anti-corruption crackdown that, in practice, has become a purge of political and economic rivals by Crown Prince Mohammad bin Salman (MBS), who chairs a newly created Supreme Organ for the Fight Against Corruption. The body was established by King Salman only two hours before the arrests, giving MBS the authority to move immediately against prominent princes, ministers, businessmen, and media figures. According to the article, 11 princes, 38 ministers and businessmen were detained, with bank accounts frozen and assets seized before any court proceedings. Those targeted included people close to the late King Abdullah as well as influential figures in Saudi and pan-Arab media. Among the best-known names were Prince Al Walid bin Talal, owner of Rotana; Sheikh Walid Al Ibrahim, owner of MBC; and Saleh Kamel, owner of ART. The article argues that MBS is seeking not only to neutralize political opposition but also to centralize media power, especially through control of Al Arabiya and other outlets. The arrests also included former senior officials and members of the security establishment: Prince Fahd, former deputy minister of defense; Prince Turki, former governor of Riyadh; Khaled al-Tuwaijri, former head of the royal chancery; Adel Fakih, minister of planning; Ibrahim Assaf, former finance minister; Abdallah Al Sultan, chief of the naval forces; Bakr Bin Laden, owner of Bin Laden Industries; Mohammad Al Tobeishi, former head of royal protocol; and Prince Turki bin Nasser, former environment minister, among others. One of the most significant detainees was Prince Miteb bin Abdullah, the third son of the late King Abdullah and head of the National Guard. He was seen as a major obstacle to MBS’s rise. The article also says Prince Ahmad bin Abdulaziz, brother of King Salman, had been placed under house arrest for four days, suggesting the purge extended even to senior members of the ruling family. The author presents MBS as seeking to secure succession by overcoming two essential sources of legitimacy in Saudi Arabia: the royal family and the Wahhabite religious establishment. The article notes that he has distanced himself from the Wahhabites through reforms such as appointing a woman ambassador and allowing women to drive, while simultaneously asserting control over rivals within the family. This raises questions, the article says, about where his confidence and power come from if he loses support from both the family and the clerics. Prince Al Walid bin Talal is presented as a particularly insidious rival because of his wealth and political positions. His estimated fortune is put at about $18 billion. The article says he supported former crown prince Mohammad bin Nayef and publicly urged MBS to release him. It also claims bin Talal refused to invest in Neom, the futuristic city project that MBS wants to build. His past public clash with Donald Trump is also recalled, including bin Talal’s insult of Trump’s candidacy and Trump’s retaliatory remarks. The article further mentions the arrest of Saudi Telecommunications chairman Saud Dweish and reports an “accident” in which a helicopter carrying Prince Mansur bin Muqrin crashed in the southwest of the kingdom, with rumors that the passengers were trying to flee. Turkish prosecutors have opened an investigation into whether a provocative protest sign displayed at a rally in Switzerland violated laws against inciting violence, police said Monday. Swiss authorities have also begun a parallel inquiry. The rally took place on Saturday in Bern, where several thousand people, including Kurdish protesters, gathered to oppose Turkey’s April 16 referendum that could expand President Tayyip Erdogan’s powers through a constitutional overhaul. During the demonstration, some participants held a banner reading “Kill Erdogan with his own weapons,” accompanied by an image of a pistol aimed at his head. Turkey reacted sharply. Its foreign ministry summoned Swiss diplomats in Ankara and demanded legal action against those responsible. Erdogan, already angry over restrictions placed by Germany and the Netherlands on Turkish ministers campaigning abroad for a “Yes” vote, accused Switzerland of going even further. In a speech in Istanbul on Sunday, he said European media were effectively campaigning for a “No” vote and claimed Swiss leftist parties and “terrorists” had joined forces in the march. He also said his image had been displayed in the Swiss parliament with a gun to his head, while Swiss officials remained silent. Swiss foreign ministry spokesman declined to comment on Erdogan’s accusations. Bern police spokesman Dominik Jaeggi said prosecutors would decide whether Swiss law had been broken, noting that police did not confiscate the banner and did not actively intervene in the demonstration. Turkey said the protest was organized by the outlawed Kurdistan Workers Party (PKK), which it, the EU and the United States classify as a terrorist organization, though Switzerland does not. Organizers, including the Swiss Green party and the Social Democrats, rejected responsibility for the sign, saying it came from a splinter group and was not part of the planned event. The Greens said the rally was intended to promote peace and dialogue and called the banner counterproductive.

On Election Day in the U.S. midterm elections, officials and voters across the country reported a wide range of problems, from malfunctioning machines and long lines to security scares and allegations of misconduct at polling places. By Tuesday afternoon, the nonpartisan Election Protection hotline had logged about 17,500 calls from voters who were having trouble at their polling places. Kristen Clarke, president of the Lawyers’ Committee for Civil Rights Under Law, which helps operate the hotline, said that total was roughly comparable to the volume usually seen in a presidential election and far above the about 10,400 calls received by the same point in the 2014 midterms. Clarke said most of the complaints involved malfunctioning voting machines. In New York City, broken ballot scanners caused long waits at multiple polling locations. On Manhattan’s Upper West Side, heavy turnout led to a line that stretched around a junior high school gym, and poll workers told voters that two of the roughly half-dozen scanners were not working. In Brooklyn, voters at two polling places found that most of the scanners had broken down. One voter, Veronica Vela, said half the scanners were broken at a Crown Heights site and that she waited two hours before being forced to place her ballot in an emergency ballot box after all the machines stopped working. Georgia also saw significant delays. In Atlanta, voters arrived at a library they had used as a polling place for years only to find signs on a car in the parking lot saying “NOT A VOTING LOCATION.” Jessica Olson, who had voted there for nearly a decade, said she was suddenly told to go to a church nearly two miles away. Fulton County said the move had been made earlier in 2018 because the library was closing for renovations. At the new site, one voter, Mylandria Ponder, said she waited an hour and 20 minutes before leaving. Across the state, some polling places reported waits of up to three hours. In Porter County, Indiana, a judge ordered 12 polling places to remain open up to 2 1/2 hours past their scheduled closing time after voting failed to start on time at several sites. County Clerk Karen Martin said some locations opened as much as 90 minutes late because some expected poll workers quit, some workers failed to pick up election supplies, and some polling places were not open when workers arrived. Democratic Portage City Councilman Collin Czilli called the situation unacceptable. Rhode Island experienced a brief disruption on Prudence Island, which is only accessible by ferry, when the island’s sole voting machine malfunctioned. The state board of elections said the machine had a technical problem early Tuesday, but a replacement machine was ferried over and voting resumed normally. The board said all ballots had been counted and statewide turnout had already surpassed 135,000 voters by late morning. Security concerns also surfaced in Florida, where a polling place in Palm Bay was put on lockdown for about 40 minutes after a man with a gun was reported in a nearby parking lot. Police said bystanders saw the man sitting in his vehicle with a gun on his lap and called 911. Officers arrived as the man was driving away. Authorities said the man, who was in his mid-80s, did not threaten anyone and the gun was unloaded. He was taken for a mental health evaluation and was not arrested. Election officials said voters were not sent elsewhere because the incident ended quickly. In Texas, a deputy in Harris County cited a poll worker for misdemeanor assault after an argument with a voter escalated. According to the sheriff’s office and local reporting, the dispute began over an address discrepancy. The worker, who is white, allegedly made a racist remark to a Black woman voter, saying, “Maybe if I’d worn my blackface makeup today you could comprehend what I’m saying to you.” The election judge separated the two, and Harris County authorities said they were investigating. Also in Pennsylvania, a man was charged after allegedly threatening to shoot poll workers at a western Pennsylvania voting site when he was told he was not registered to vote. Authorities said 48-year-old Christopher Thomas Queen of Claysville came to the South Franklin Volunteer Fire Department polling place around 9 a.m. and became angry after being informed of the registration problem. He allegedly said he would go get a gun and return to shoot the workers. He was charged with terroristic threats and disorderly conduct. Federal officials were also focused on election security. Homeland Security Secretary Kirstjen Nielsen said cybersecurity officials were preparing for the worst while hoping for the best, and she described the election as likely to be the most secure in the modern era. She spoke at a command center where federal, state, and local officials were coordinating on possible foreign or domestic interference. Nielsen said no voting machines had been compromised, though foreign groups had been spreading misinformation in an effort to sow discord. Another federal issue arose in Texas when the U.S. Border Patrol canceled a planned “crowd control exercise” in a Latino neighborhood of El Paso after criticism from civil liberties groups, who argued it could discourage voting. A Border Patrol agent confirmed the cancellation but did not say why. Taken together, the day’s reporting showed that while election officials were working to protect the vote from cyber threats and interference, many of the most immediate problems were more ordinary but still serious: broken equipment, delayed openings, long lines, confusing polling-place changes, and isolated but alarming confrontations at the polls.

# Summary: Voting Problems Reported Across Nation During Midterm Election The 2018 midterm election saw widespread voting problems reported across the United States, with the nonpartisan Election Protection hotline receiving approximately 17,500 calls from voters experiencing difficulties at polling places by Tuesday afternoon. According to Kristen Clarke, president of the Lawyers' Committee for Civil Rights Under Law, which helps operate the hotline, this call volume matched the number received during a presidential election and significantly exceeded the 10,400 calls logged during the 2014 midterm election at the same time. The majority of reported problems involved malfunctioning voting machines. Technical issues plagued polling locations nationwide. In New York City, broken ballot scanners created substantial delays, with some voters waiting in extremely long lines. At one Manhattan precinct on the Upper West Side, the line to scan ballots stretched around a junior high school gymnasium after two of roughly half-dozen scanners malfunctioned. In Brooklyn, most scanners broke down at two separate polling stations, with one voter, Veronica Vela, waiting two hours to vote only to find all machines non-functional, forcing her to use an emergency ballot box. Rhode Island experienced a unique technical challenge when the sole voting machine on Prudence Island, an island community accessible only by ferry, malfunctioned. Election officials quickly ferried a replacement machine to restore service. Beyond technical failures, voters encountered significant logistical problems. In northwestern Indiana's Porter County, twelve polling places were ordered to stay open up to two-and-a-half hours past the scheduled 6 p.m. closing time after some sites opened as much as 90 minutes late. The county clerk attributed delays to expected poll workers quitting, workers failing to pick up election supplies, and sites not being open when poll workers arrived. In Atlanta, voters discovered that a long-time polling location at a library had been moved to a church nearly two miles away without adequate notification, creating hardship for pedestrians accustomed to walking to vote. Across Georgia, multiple polling stations reported lengthy waits, with some exceeding three hours. The election day saw several incidents involving voter intimidation and misconduct. In Harris County, Texas, a white poll worker was cited for misdemeanor assault after she allegedly bumped a black female voter during an argument and made a racist comment, stating, "Maybe if I'd worn my blackface makeup today you could comprehend what I'm saying to you." The dispute began over a discrepancy with the voter's address. In western Pennsylvania, a man named Christopher Thomas Queen was charged with terroristic threats and disorderly conduct after becoming irate upon learning he wasn't registered to vote and allegedly threatened to retrieve a gun and shoot poll workers. Additionally, the U.S. Border Patrol canceled a "crowd control exercise" scheduled in a Latino neighborhood of El Paso after civil liberties groups criticized it as potentially discouraging voting. A Florida polling place was temporarily locked down for approximately 40 minutes after an elderly man was reported sitting in a nearby parking lot with a gun on his lap. Police determined the gun was unloaded and the man made no threats; he was taken for mental health evaluation but not arrested. Federal officials emphasized cybersecurity preparations for the election. Homeland Security Secretary Kirstjen Nielsen stated that cybersecurity officials were "hoping for the best but preparing for the worst," noting that the election would be the most secure in the modern era. However, Nielsen confirmed that no voting machines had been compromised, though foreign groups had engaged in misinformation efforts designed to sow discord. Federal and state officials had spent nearly two years strengthening election infrastructure against cyberattacks. Despite extensive cybersecurity preparations, election officials and voting rights groups expressed concern that widespread technical and logistical problems could undermine voter confidence in election results if issues became more prevalent on Election Day as millions of Americans voted in pivotal races for Congress and governor positions.

Manitoba’s Progressive Conservatives are facing growing criticism over a series of attack ads tied to the province’s decision not to search the Prairie Green Landfill for the remains of two missing First Nations women, Morgan Harris and Marcedes Myran. The party placed a digital billboard in Winnipeg and a full-page ad in the Winnipeg Free Press defending its position against a landfill search, citing safety concerns and describing it as an “unsafe $184-million landfill dig.” The ads have drawn anger from the families of the women, Indigenous leaders, and opposition politicians, who say the Tories are exploiting a painful tragedy during an election campaign. The controversy escalated Wednesday when Harris and Myran’s families, along with a small group of supporters, protested outside a Progressive Conservative announcement. They drummed and shouted slogans such as “search the landfill” and “bring them home.” The day before, police were called to Tory leader Heather Stefanson’s constituency office after what authorities described as a traffic disturbance. Protesters had left signs demanding a landfill search and painted red handprints on the office windows. At Wednesday’s event, Tory cabinet minister Kevin Klein tried to defend the party’s messaging while also acknowledging the issue is highly sensitive. He said Stefanson wants the party to be “clear and transparent” about its position, but admitted the question has become divisive. Klein said the issue should not be treated as partisan, though he conceded it has become one. Indigenous leaders strongly condemned the ads. Assembly of Manitoba Chiefs Grand Chief Cathy Merrick said Stefanson had missed an opportunity in a crucial election period to use her platform to amplify First Nations women’s voices and instead had lost the trust of Indigenous people. Long Plain First Nation Chief Kyra Wilson, whose community includes Harris and Myran, said Stefanson’s campaign shows why change is needed and called her insensitivity toward grieving families unacceptable. Political analyst Paul Thomas said the Progressive Conservatives appear to be “pulling out all stops” as polls show them trailing. He argued the party is leaning into emotional and controversial Indigenous issues to energize its base and hold onto seats it may have once considered secure. The same day, the Tories ran another full-page ad in the Winnipeg Free Press aimed at the New Democrats. Titled “Don’t Gamble on the NDP,” it used playing-card imagery and criticized NDP candidates, including leader Wab Kinew, who has prior charges of drunk driving and assault, and Thompson candidate Eric Redhead, who faces domestic assault charges. Kinew called the ad “desperate” and said it reflected an American-style reliance on negative campaigning. He said he was glad the Tories were attacking him instead of the families of the women believed to be in the landfill. Liberal Leader Dougald Lamont was equally harsh, calling it “one of the most disgusting campaigns” he had ever seen and saying the Tories were willing to stoop to anything to win. The NDP and Liberals both support searching the landfill. Harris and Myran are believed to have been dumped there last year. Jeremy Skibicki has been charged with first-degree murder in their deaths, as well as in the killings of Rebecca Contois and an unidentified Indigenous woman known by some leaders as Mashkode Bizhiki'ikwe, or Buffalo Woman.

Before Team USA’s game against Finland at the NHL 4 Nations Face-Off in Montreal, the U.S. national anthem was booed by much of the crowd at the Bell Centre. The reaction, which had been expected, followed similar incidents at other NHL games in Canadian cities. Although the arena announcer asked fans in English and French to respect both anthems, loud booing began almost immediately after the singer started “Oh say can you see,” especially from the upper sections. Finland’s anthem was performed without disruption. The booing comes amid rising tensions tied to Donald Trump’s return to office last month, including tariff threats against Canadian goods and his repeated suggestion that Canada should become the 51st state. Trump reiterated that claim on Thursday and referred to Prime Minister Justin Trudeau as “Governor Trudeau” while discussing tariffs. The crowd, heavily Canadian, also cheered for Finland throughout the game, though that was likely influenced by Team USA being seen as a stronger threat to Canada’s chances in the tournament. NHL commissioner Gary Bettman had addressed the issue beforehand, saying the league wanted hockey to bring people together and expected fans to show respect. He noted that booing had stopped at a previous game after an announcement from the arena. Bruins forward Brad Marchand, speaking on a podcast before the event, also criticized anthem booing, saying the songs are meant to honor veterans and that politics should be kept separate from hockey.

Dalhousie University and the faculty association have ratified a new three-year collective agreement, ending a labour dispute that lasted nearly a month and disrupted the start of the academic term. The Dalhousie Faculty Association said members voted overwhelmingly in favour of the deal: 899 of 939 voting members supported it, with turnout close to 95 per cent. DFA president David Westwood said the membership remained “strong and unified” throughout the dispute. He acknowledged the union did not secure everything it wanted, but said it achieved major gains on several issues important to faculty. The agreement provides more than a 10 per cent salary increase over three years, improved parental leave benefits, and a requirement that each faculty develop workload policies aimed at creating a “more fair and equitable distribution of workload.” It also includes five days of paid leave for Indigenous faculty to observe cultural or traditional days of significance. For early-career faculty hired at ranks other than full professor, the deal adds salary adjustments ranging from $1,500 to $5,000. The university’s faculty are expected to return to work on Thursday, while classes are scheduled to resume on Sept. 23. However, some details of the academic calendar, including final exam dates and possible other schedule changes, have not yet been finalized. Students expressed uncertainty about how the semester will be adjusted, with some wondering whether time will be made up by shortening vacation periods or extending the term. The dispute began after Dalhousie locked out faculty on Aug. 20, followed by a strike two days later. The union had argued that pay had not kept pace with inflation and noted wide salary differences across faculty ranks and departments, with some senior professors earning about $240,000 annually while some technology instructors start around $56,000. Before the lockout, the university had offered a six per cent raise over three years, while the faculty association had sought 14.25 per cent. Meanwhile, some students are planning a sit-in on campus to demand tuition refunds, arguing they should not pay full tuition for a semester they believe will be significantly disrupted.

Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev pardoned 625 people on March 18, including 38 identified by rights groups as political prisoners. Those pardoned included four members of the opposition Azerbaijan Popular Front Party, 28 people jailed over the deadly 2015 Nardaran clashes with police, one person convicted in the Ganca clashes case, one Islamic party member punished for protesting school hijab bans, and one person allegedly targeted because of a relative’s activism abroad. The decree will release 475 inmates, reduce 98 prison terms by half, and shorten three life sentences to 25 years. Rights groups say Azerbaijan has about 150 political prisoners, a claim the government denies.

# Summary On March 18, Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev pardoned 625 individuals, including 38 identified as political prisoners by human rights groups. The pardoned political prisoners included four opposition party members, 28 from the 2015 Nardaran village clashes, one from Ganca clashes, one Islamic party member convicted for protesting hijab bans, and one person related to a political activist abroad. The clemency decree releases 475 inmates, reduces sentences for 98 convicts by half, and shortens three life sentences to 25 years. Rights activists estimate 150 political prisoners remain in Azerbaijan, while the government denies any exist.

Sayfullo Saipov, the Uzbek national accused of killing eight people and injuring at least 12 in a truck attack in Lower Manhattan on October 31, was once seen as the promising son of an affluent family in Uzbekistan. The attack, the deadliest in New York since September 11, 2001, was described by US officials, including the president, as a terrorist incident. Saipov, 29, was charged with 22 counts, including attempted murder and providing material support to the Islamic State of Iraq and the Levant (ISIL, also known as ISIS). Nine of the charges could carry the death penalty. On Tuesday, he pleaded not guilty in a New York court. The article contrasts the image of Saipov in Uzbekistan with the man accused in the US case. He was the only son in a well-off family, grew up with three younger sisters, attended a private school and the prestigious Financial Studies university, played football, and was remembered by his sister Umida Saipova as someone who wore polished shoes and “looked like a gentleman.” She said the family was shocked by the attack and described it as “an unexpected blow” and “a nightmare.” In their home area of Uch Tepa, or Three Hills, his father owns a store at a construction materials market, and the family lives in a house that stands out as luxurious in an otherwise poor former Soviet country. Uch Tepa is portrayed as a traditional neighborhood where men typically wear jeans or suits rather than shorts, women dress modestly, and religious behavior is closely watched. A local makhalla official, Bakhtiyor Yunuskhodjayev, said he would quickly learn of any signs of radicalism, including pro-Sharia rhetoric or unusual clothing styles. In Central Asia, full beards, no moustaches, and shorter trousers are often associated with Salafism, which is viewed as extreme. Neighbors insisted that neither Saipov nor his family showed any such signs. One nearby woman said he was not the kind of boy who would hurt or kill people. The article places Saipov’s story in the broader context of Uzbekistan’s long struggle with religion and state control. Under former president Islam Karimov, the government harshly suppressed independent Muslim activity and sought to eliminate “extremism” through repressive measures. Human rights groups say thousands of mostly ordinary, peaceful Muslims were jailed as alleged radicals. Some fled abroad, including to Afghanistan, Turkey, and Syria. The article says that although Saipov’s apparent radicalization seems to have taken place in the United States, he would likely have been aware of the persecution of Muslims in his home country. It cites years of abuses, including torture, beatings, asphyxiation, electrocution, rape, and other forms of mistreatment. It also mentions a 2002 case in which two jailed Muslims allegedly were boiled to death, and the 2005 crackdown in Andijan, where Karimov ordered troops to shoot protesters he branded as Islamist conspirators. After Karimov’s death in 2016, Shavkat Mirziyoyev took over and introduced reforms that some described as Uzbekistan’s “perestroika.” Following Saipov’s attack, Mirziyoyev expressed condolences to the United States and said Uzbekistan was ready to assist fully in the investigation. Yet rights advocates say the system remains harsh. Nadejda Atayeva, who heads the Association for Human Rights in Central Asia, said at least 10,000 people remain blacklisted as alleged radicals, and that the list is not shrinking. She said Uzbek authorities still refuse to change their attitude toward religious communities that do not fit the government’s prescribed model, and she warned that emigration among believers is increasing. The article adds that abuse continues in prison, citing a report that a prisoner’s genitals were doused with boiling water after guards saw inmates praying. Against this background, Saipov himself appears to have been far from a religious extremist in his youth. His sister said he was a diligent student who worked as an accountant at a hotel starting in 2009, studied constantly, and never wore a beard or spent much time at the mosque. In 2010 he won a US Green Card, an outcome seen in Uzbekistan as a major achievement because many citizens live on low incomes and millions work abroad. Saipov reportedly did not even plan to move to the United States; his sister said he copied a friend’s lottery application. Once in the United States, however, the dream unraveled. Saipov worked as a long-haul truck driver, registered two transport companies that never became successful, and lived in several states including Ohio, Florida, and New Jersey. He married an Uzbek woman, had three children, and eventually grew a full beard. In 2015, federal agents interviewed him about possible links to suspected fighters, according to ABC News. Six months before the attack, he became an Uber driver. The article explores possible explanations for his radicalization and notes that observers disagree. Uzbek journalist Khusniddin Kutbiddinov, who fled to the US, argued that Saipov was “manipulated” into pledging allegiance to ISIL and suggested that decades of propaganda under Communist rule and Karimov had left Uzbeks vulnerable to manipulation. Another commentator, Vladimir Chernomorsky, said immigrant men may become more conservative when their status declines and they lose the role of family breadwinner, making radicalization a way to regain authority and self-respect. Saipov is described as the fourth Uzbek linked to an attack in 2017. The article recalls three others: Abdulkadir Marsharipov, who killed 39 people at an Istanbul nightclub in January; Akbarjon Jalilov, who bombed a St. Petersburg subway train in April, killing 15; and Rakhmat Akilov, who drove a truck into a crowd in Stockholm, killing four and injuring 15. The article says these men, unlike homegrown fighters, converted to hardline ideology after living abroad and were influenced by online propaganda. Central Asia expert Daniil Kislov said the important issue is the social and psychological reasons why Uzbek men in emigration become susceptible to extremist ideas, stressing that in Uzbekistan they were not religious radicals or enemies of the state. The article ends by noting the anger many Uzbeks feel over what Saipov has done not only to victims in New York but also to the reputation of his homeland and the honor of his family.

# Summary Armenia's Supreme Judicial Council chairman Ruben Vardazaryan criticized a meeting between Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan and judges, stating it presented an impermissible agenda. A political expert in Azerbaijan said Hamas’s resilience in confronting Israel has strengthened unity and sympathy among Palestinians and many Muslim countries. Samid Pasha, a senior expert at the Institute of Oriental Studies of Azerbaijan’s National Academy of Sciences, told IRNA that Hamas entered what he described as an exhausting war and still retained the support of the Islamic world. He said Israeli airstrikes caused heavy damage to homes and infrastructure in Gaza, and although Hamas suffered casualties, it also delivered serious blows to Israel. Pasha argued that Hamas joined the conflict in response to Israeli violence at al-Aqsa Mosque and to defend Palestinian rights. He added that people in the West Bank welcomed the resistance movement’s sacrifices, and protests spread across the territory against Israeli actions. According to Pasha, solidarity also appeared beyond Palestine, with people in Lebanon and Jordan moving toward border areas to support Palestinians. He said Israel’s continued settlement expansion in East Jerusalem and the West Bank, along with efforts to expel Palestinians from their homes, provoked strong reactions. Restrictions on Palestinian access to al-Quds during Ramadan, crackdowns on protesters, and violence by extremist Jews at al-Aqsa also angered Muslim nations. Pasha further noted that Palestinian rockets now reach up to 220 kilometers, surprising Israel’s military, and said the Iron Dome intercepted only about half of them despite Gaza’s long siege.

# Summary According to an Azerbaijani political expert, Hamas's resistance against Israel has strengthened unity among Palestinians and Islamic nations. Senior analyst Samid Pasha stated that despite Israeli airstrikes causing significant damage to Gaza's infrastructure and civilian areas, Hamas has maintained the Islamic world's support and inflicted considerable damage on Israeli forces. The conflict escalated following Israeli actions at al-Aqsa Mosque and restrictions on Palestinian access during Ramadan, prompting widespread protests across the West Bank and neighboring regions. Citizens from Lebanon and Jordan demonstrated solidarity at border areas. Pasha attributed the escalation to Israel's continued settlement expansion in East Jerusalem and the West Bank, which fueled Palestinian grievances and reactions. A notable development, according to the expert, is the increased range of Palestinian rockets—expanding from 40 to 220 kilometers—which has shocked the Israeli military. He noted that Israel's Iron Dome defense system destroyed only half of the Palestinian rockets in this conflict round. Despite Gaza's 14-year blockade, Pasha emphasized that Hamas has successfully expanded its military capabilities, contributing to heightened regional tensions and broader Muslim world solidarity with Palestinians.

The Baku Court of Appeal has upheld the 30-day arrest of Popular Front Party of Azerbaijan activist Orkhan Salimzade. He was detained on August 18 and sentenced for allegedly disobeying police orders. The PFPA says the case was politically motivated, linking it to his participation in the July 15 unsanctioned march in Baku in support of the Azerbaijani Army. That rally ended in clashes with police, after which dozens of PFPA activists were arrested; by August 1, the number had reached 48. PFPA press representative Tezekhan Miralamli said the court only formally reviewed the case and refused to request video footage. The defense plans to appeal to the European Court of Human Rights.

# Summary The Baku Court of Appeal upheld the arrest of Orkhan Salimzade, a Popular Front Party of Azerbaijan activist, who was detained on August 18 for allegedly disobeying police orders. The party claims the arrest is politically motivated, stemming from Salimzade's participation in an unsanctioned July 15 pro-Army march that resulted in police clashes. As a forced migrant, Salimzade participated to support swift conflict resolution and his return home. Following the July 15 demonstration, approximately 48 PFPA activists were arrested. The defense plans to appeal to the European Court of Human Rights, criticizing the court's refusal to examine surveillance footage from Salimzade's detention.

The article says the unrest had serious political consequences, including the cancellation of President Prabowo Subianto’s planned trip to China for the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit. Giuliano alleged that two external actors may have been involved: the National Endowment for Democracy, which he said has supported Indonesian media since the 1990s, and George Soros’s Open Society Foundations. Jeff J. Brown, author of *The China Trilogy* and founder of the Seek Truth From Facts Foundation, echoed the claim that the situation resembled unrest in Serbia. Brown also described Indonesia as strategically important because of its large economy, its role as ASEAN’s biggest economy, and its population of nearly 300 million.
