Belarus is preparing for parliamentary elections on September 11, but opposition figures and many analysts say the vote is unlikely to produce meaningful change because the political system remains tightly controlled by President Alexander Lukashenko and his administration. In Minsk, a small coalition of opposition politicians has turned a sparsely furnished apartment in a Soviet-era housing block into both an office and, at times, living quarters. From there, they are coordinating a campaign to observe the election and document irregularities. Their group, Right to Choose, plans to deploy more than 1,000 observers and use a phone application to report problems on election day. Right to Choose issued an early assessment in July that was blunt in its judgment: Belarus’s political and legal environment, it said, remains unchanged and does not allow free, fair, or competitive elections with equal opportunities for all candidates. Dzianis Sadouski, the group’s national coordinator and general secretary of the Belarusian Christian Democracy party, said that for the vote to inspire confidence, both local and international observers would need full access to polling stations, including the actual vote count and turnout figures. The opposition says the results are effectively predetermined. Lukashenko, who has ruled Belarus for 22 years, has long faced accusations of authoritarian rule, human rights abuses, and election fraud. After he won a fifth term in October of the previous year, observers from the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe concluded that the election process once again showed how far Belarus still is from meeting democratic commitments. The parliamentary elections are the last major national vote before 2020, when presidential and parliamentary elections will be held together, making them an important test of Belarus’s political direction and its relations with the West. The government has introduced some limited changes, such as allowing candidates five minutes on state television and giving observers slightly better access at polling stations. But opposition leaders and analysts dismiss these steps as merely cosmetic. They also point to early voting as a major source of possible manipulation. About 30 percent of the population is believed to take part in early voting, and critics argue that the lack of transparency in this process makes it easier to falsify results. Western governments are watching closely. Yauheni Preiherman, policy director at the Liberal Club in Minsk, said the election will be a gauge of Belarus’s future relationship with Lukashenko and with the West. He noted that the Central Elections Committee has implemented only three of 30 recommendations made by the OSCE after last year’s presidential election, which he sees as at least a small sign of progress and a willingness to keep dialogue open. The chairwoman of the committee, Lidia Yermoshina, who was previously banned from entering the United States and the European Union over fraud allegations, rejected the criticism on state television. She said the opposition was preparing for defeat and trying to discredit the election authorities, and argued that it is the opposition, not the system, that threatens free and fair elections by provoking disobedience. Despite growing public frustration with a struggling economy and Lukashenko’s historically low approval ratings, the opposition has struggled to mobilize ordinary Belarusians. Preiherman said opposition parties are in their weakest state in years, partly because the regime has long worked to marginalize them and partly because they have failed to offer society anything new or compelling. After Lukashenko’s re-election, opposition groups that had been divided over whether to take part in elections they consider unfair made renewed efforts to unite. One major initiative is the Belarus National Congress, an alliance of eight parties and trade unions led by Mikhail Statkevich, a veteran opposition figure who was imprisoned after the 2010 presidential election. Statkevich has already called for street protests on September 12, the day after the results are announced, saying that as long as Lukashenko remains in power there can be no free elections. He described protest as the only peaceful option available. Not all opposition voices agree on tactics. Political analyst Siarhei Bohdan said the parties in the Congress are politically unsophisticated and have little to offer beyond repeating what the public already knows: that elections are unfair and non-transparent. In his view, coalitions without a stronger public mandate cannot gain traction. By contrast, independent candidate Tatyana Korotkevich, who ran a notable grassroots campaign in the previous presidential election, sees participation as a way to build trust and encourage peaceful change over time. She described her approach as a long-term political marathon that will continue beyond the 2020 elections. An international observer familiar with Belarusian politics said that if the vote count were fair, some opposition candidates would probably win, especially in districts where candidates have spent time building local support between elections. For Sadouski, however, democratic change remains a distant but possible goal. He said he stays in Belarus because he feels responsible for helping bring that change, adding that even powerful systems can collapse quickly, just as the Soviet Union once did.

# Belarus: Will New Elections Yield New Results? As Belarus prepares for parliamentary elections on September 11, opposition groups remain deeply skeptical about the electoral process, despite some cosmetic reforms. The upcoming vote comes amid widespread concerns about democratic freedoms and a history of alleged election fraud under President Alexander Lukashenko's 22-year rule. ## Opposition Monitoring Efforts From a modest Soviet-era apartment in Minsk, opposition coalition Right to Choose is coordinating an extensive election observation campaign. The group plans to deploy over a thousand observers and utilize a phone application to document irregularities on election day. In their July assessment, Right to Choose concluded that "the political and legal environment in Belarus remains unchanged and doesn't enable the conduct of free, fair and competitive elections that offers equal opportunities for all competing candidates." Campaign coordinator Dzianis Sadouski emphasized that for the opposition to have confidence in the results, local and international observers must have complete access to polling stations to oversee vote counting and monitor turnout rates. ## Lukashenko's Controversial Record Lukashenko's tenure has been marked by persistent accusations of human rights abuses and election fraud from international observers. Following his re-election to a fifth term last October, the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe reported that Belarus "still has a considerable way to go in meeting its OSCE commitments for democratic elections." The Central Elections Committee has implemented limited reforms this year, including allowing candidates five minutes of television airtime and providing observers marginally better polling station access. However, opposition groups and analysts dismiss these measures as merely cosmetic changes that fail to address fundamental concerns. ## Systemic Concerns Opposition groups identify several mechanisms they believe facilitate ballot falsification, including an early voting system in which approximately 30 percent of the population participates. The lack of meaningful observer access during vote counting remains a central concern. Elections Committee Chairwoman Lidia Yermoshina, who was banned from entering the United States and European Union in 2006 over election fraud allegations, defended the system on state television. She accused the opposition of preparing to "spoil" the election's reputation rather than acknowledging systemic problems. ## Western Scrutiny and Strategic Implications Policy analyst Yauheni Preiherman notes that Western nations will closely scrutinize these elections as a gauge for future relations with Lukashenko. The fact that the Central Elections Committee implemented only three of thirty OSCE recommendations demonstrates minimal progress, though Preiherman suggests it indicates willingness to maintain dialogue with the West. ## Weakened Opposition Movement Despite historically low approval ratings for Lukashenko and public dissatisfaction with the struggling economy, the opposition remains fragmented and weak. Political analyst Siarhei Bohdan describes opposition parties as "politically unsophisticated" with little beyond repeating known criticisms. He argues that "zero plus zero still equals zero"—coalitions cannot gain traction without developing platforms that attract genuine popular support. ## Divided Opposition Strategy Following Lukashenko's October re-election, opposition groups made efforts to unite, including the Belarus National Congress—an alliance of eight parties and trade unions led by former presidential candidate Mikhail Statkevich. Though public appetite for protest has been minimal since 2011's violently repressed demonstrations, Statkevich has called for street protests on September 12, arguing that "there can be no free elections while Lukashenko is in power." Some opposition figures, like independent candidate Tatyana Korotkevich, view participation as an opportunity to build voter trust and promote dialogue, framing change as a "long-term strategy" extending to 2020 elections. ## Conclusion An international observer suggested that opposition candidates could win in districts where grassroots civic engagement has been strong, if vote counting were fair. However, without fundamental systemic reforms, most observers expect predetermined outcomes. For committed activists like Sadouski, democratic change remains a long-term commitment, comparing Belarus's potential transformation to the Soviet Union's unexpected collapse.

The article argues that the authoritarian turn in Cuba and Venezuela was not simply the result of ideology from the start, but of how power was consolidated under Fidel Castro and Hugo Chávez. It opens by asking whether regimes become radical because events push them in that direction or because leaders had hidden ambitions all along. In Cuba, Castro’s 1959 victory over Fulgencio Batista did not initially come with an open declaration of communism. After entering Havana, he said the revolution was not communist. Only later did he explicitly describe it as Marxist-Leninist and vow to remain a communist. The article suggests several events may have pushed his government toward radicalization: U.S. sanctions in 1960 after Cuba nationalized American companies, the full trade embargo that followed, the failed Bay of Pigs invasion in 1961, and the 1962 Missile Crisis. After that, Cuba increasingly aligned itself with leftist movements abroad, in part as a response to U.S. hostility, support for anti-communist dictatorships, and CIA assassination attempts against Castro. A similar pattern is described in Venezuela. In 1998, Chávez told journalists he did not support socialism and even said he considered Cuba a dictatorship. The article identifies the decisive turning point as the 2002 strike at the state oil company PDVSA, followed by a failed coup attempt against Chávez. According to the article, nearly all subsequent government efforts to concentrate power came after that moment. It cites later developments under Chávez: the 2003 expropriations and controls that helped destroy Venezuela’s manufacturing base, proposals to keep Chávez in office until 2021, the 2004 Organic Law that enabled control over the Supreme Court, and restrictions on free expression noted by Human Rights Watch. The article acknowledges that some later critics of Chávez, including María Corina Machado and Leopoldo López, had supported the failed coup. Still, it concludes that while crises can radicalize regimes, in democracies they usually lead to elections or resignations. In authoritarian systems, however, riots or coups can be used as excuses for repression, suggesting that the leaders’ true ambitions emerge only once they are securely in power.

# Summary This article examines whether Cuba and Venezuela's communist regimes were predetermined or radicalized by events. Both Fidel Castro and Hugo Chávez initially denied communist intentions. In 1959, Castro stated his revolution was not communist, later qualifying it as Marxist-Leninist. In 1998, Chávez told reporters he opposed Cuban-style dictatorship and wasn't leading a socialist movement, eventually coining "21st-Century Socialism" to describe his system. The article presents two explanations for this transformation: deliberate deception or radicalization through adverse circumstances. For Cuba, external pressures may explain the shift. The U.S. imposed sanctions in 1960 following nationalization of American companies, organized the failed 1961 Bay of Pigs invasion, and faced the 1962 Missile Crisis. These events prompted Cuba to support leftist revolts abroad in response to American anti-communist interventions. Venezuela's radicalization had a clearer catalyst: the 2002 strike at state oil company PDVSA and a subsequent failed coup attempt against Chávez. Following these events, the government systematically accumulated power. The 2003 wave of expropriations and controls devastated manufacturing. The 2004 Organic Law allowed Chávez's system to control the Supreme Court, while freedom of expression was curtailed. However, the article suggests a critical distinction: while democracies typically respond to crises through resignations or elections, these regimes used such events as pretexts for authoritarian crackdowns. This pattern indicates that charismatic leaders' true authoritarian ambitions may have existed from the beginning, only revealed once they consolidated power. The article concludes that while circumstances may contribute to regime mutation, the suspicious timing and nature of power consolidation suggests deliberate intent rather than reactive radicalization.

Argentinian researchers have published a new study in *Archives of Toxicology* reporting that glyphosate, the herbicide sold by Monsanto and now Bayer as RoundUp, caused significant harm in pregnant laboratory rats and their offspring even at relatively low doses. The findings, the article says, add to growing concerns about the chemical’s effects on fertility, fetal development, and health across generations. In the experiment, pregnant female rats were given a glyphosate-based chemical at two doses. The higher dose was 200 mg per kg of bodyweight per day, selected in relation to the agrochemical industry’s claimed no-observed adverse effect level (NOAEL) of 1000 mg/kg/day for maternal toxicity. The lower dose was 2 mg/kg/day, only slightly above the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency’s reference dose, which is considered safe for lifetime daily ingestion. The researchers argued that this lower amount is relevant because it matches glyphosate residues found on soybeans and levels detected in Argentina. The study found that the doses did not produce obvious embryo toxicity or abnormal maternal behavior. However, they did impair female fertility in the first-generation offspring: females exposed to glyphosate later had fewer fertilized egg implantations than control animals. The most serious effects appeared in the second generation. Offspring from both the low-dose and high-dose groups showed delayed growth, lower fetal weight and length, and a significantly higher number of abnormally small fetuses. At the higher dose, the researchers observed severe malformations they described as unexpected, including conjoined fetuses and abnormal limbs. These defects were found in three out of 117 second-generation fetuses, with each affected fetus coming from a different mother in the first-generation group. The authors said the results showed a significant statistical link between glyphosate exposure and the fetal abnormalities. Based on these findings, the researchers argued that the industry’s NOAEL for maternal toxicity is unreliable, since the dose that produced abnormalities was far below the 1000 mg/kg level cited as safe. They also noted that the industry studies used to establish the NOAEL relied on aminomethylphosphonic acid (AMPA), a breakdown product of glyphosate, rather than glyphosate itself. The article places the study within a broader debate over glyphosate, citing prior research linking it to cancer, digestive problems, reduced fertility, and disruptions to sexual development, gene health, and gut bacteria. It also notes that the European Union renewed glyphosate’s approval for five more years despite opposition, and points to a 2019 JAMA study reporting a sharp rise in RoundUp detected in the blood of southern Californians since the early 1990s.

# Study Links RoundUp Herbicide to Fetal Defects Argentine researchers have published a study in Archives of Toxicology revealing that glyphosate, the herbicide marketed as RoundUp by Monsanto (now Bayer), causes significant damage to pregnant rats and their offspring at relatively low doses. The findings raise serious concerns about the chemical's safety standards. The study examined glyphosate exposure in pregnant female rats using two dosage levels. The higher dose of 200 mg per kilogram of body weight daily was based on the industry's claimed safe level of 1,000 mg/kg. The lower dose of 2 mg/kg was only slightly above the EPA's reference dose considered safe for lifetime daily consumption and matches glyphosate residue levels found on soybeans and throughout Argentina. While the tested doses did not cause embryonic toxicity or abnormal maternal behavior, the results were concerning across generations. First-generation female offspring exposed to glyphosate showed significantly reduced fertility, with fewer fertilized egg implantations than control groups. The most alarming findings appeared in second-generation offspring. All rats exposed to glyphosate—at both low and high doses—exhibited delayed growth, lower fetal weight and length, and higher rates of abnormally small fetuses. The high-dose group showed severe malformations including conjoined fetuses and abnormal limbs in three of 117 fetuses, with each affected fetus having a different mother from the first-generation group. The researchers concluded that the industry's established safety threshold is unreliable, since the high dose causing abnormalities (200 mg) was significantly lower than the claimed safe level (1,000 mg). Notably, industry studies determining safety used AMPA, a glyphosate degradation product, rather than glyphosate itself. This study adds to mounting evidence linking glyphosate to various health problems including cancer, digestive issues, and reduced fertility. A recent May study found the herbicide disrupts mammalian sexual development, gene health, and beneficial gut bacteria even at supposedly safe doses. These findings are particularly troubling given glyphosate's increasing environmental presence and presence in human bodies. A 2017 JAMA study found glyphosate levels in southern Californians' blood had spiked over 1,200 percent since the early 1990s. The research comes despite the European Union's late approval of glyphosate for another five years, despite widespread opposition. The multigenerational effects documented in this latest study suggest that widespread glyphosate exposure poses significant health risks not only to current populations but to future generations.

Peruvian authorities on Saturday demolished a mausoleum in Lima that held the remains of eight Shining Path rebels killed more than three decades ago during prison massacres, then moved the bodies to a cemetery in the city’s northern Comas district. Prosecutor Javier Zapata said more than 50 police officers and dozens of cemetery workers took part in the operation. The rebels will be buried in separate niches. The men died in June 1986 riots at three prisons in Lima, where security forces killed 250 suspected Shining Path inmates. Prisoners also killed three soldiers and one police officer. In 2013, prosecutors accused 35 navy members of homicide and extrajudicial executions in the massacres, seeking prison terms of 25 to 28 years; that case is still pending. The bodies were originally burned and buried clandestinely, then recovered by forensic experts beginning in 2012. The eight rebels were the first remains returned to families. Their mausoleum, built by relatives in 2016 and intended for up to 51 niches, drew criticism from conservatives and the military, who called it an apology for terrorism. Authorities also said it lacked permits. A few relatives protested outside the cemetery, while one father denounced the demolition as denying the dead peace.

# Peru Demolishes Shining Path Rebel Mausoleum Peruvian authorities demolished a mausoleum containing eight Shining Path rebels on Saturday and relocated their remains to a cemetery in Lima's Comas district. The operation involved over 50 police officers and cemetery workers. The rebels died during June 1986 prison riots in which security forces killed approximately 250 suspected Shining Path inmates, while prisoners killed three soldiers and one police officer. In 2013, prosecutors accused 35 navy members of homicide and extrajudicial executions during these riots. The inmates' bodies were initially burned and buried clandestinely but were exhumed by forensic teams beginning in 2012. The eight remains were the first returned to families. The mausoleum, built in 2016 by relatives without proper permits, faced opposition from conservative parties and military members who viewed it as justifying terrorism. A handful of relatives protested at the cemetery gates but arrived after demolition was complete. Peru has approximately 6,462 clandestine cemeteries, remnants of its brutal 1980-2000 internal conflict that killed up to 70,000 people.

Venezuela’s oil workers have launched a series of protests and walkouts in recent days to demand better wages, restored labor rights, and access to health insurance. Since June 1, employees at the Puerto La Cruz refinery in Anzoátegui state have been holding demonstrations at company headquarters, other oil facilities, and in the streets. Although the refinery has been the main center of mobilization, workers and union representatives from other subsidiaries of state oil company PDVSA have also joined in. José Bodas Lugo, secretary-general of the Unitary Federation of Oil Workers (FUTPV), said the refinery workers had placed themselves in “permanent assembly” until industry authorities respond. He said the protesters want to be heard by Oil Minister Rafael Tellechea. During a protest on Monday at PDVSA’s Eastern Venezuela Refining headquarters, workers were told that Tellechea was in Vienna attending OPEC meetings. Bodas described the situation of oil workers and pensioners as “very precarious,” saying their collective contract expired 18 months ago and negotiations for a new one have made no progress. He said wages are insufficient. According to various sources, rank-and-file PDVSA workers earn between US$100 and US$200 a month, though only part of that amount is considered salary for calculating benefits. Additional payments may be given for night shifts, transportation, or at the discretion of some companies. Bodas, who belongs to the Trotskyist CCURA union current, also said workers have lost several benefits in recent years, including access to favorable PDVSA-backed mortgage programs. The central demand in the current protests is the restoration of SICOPROSA, PDVSA’s health insurance system. Bodas accused the company of failing to fulfill promises to reactivate it. He said only PDVSA’s board and top managers currently have access, leaving most workers dependent on Venezuela’s deteriorating public health system. He said two long-serving workers recently died in state hospitals because of poor care. SICOPROSA previously covered workers and their immediate families, allowing treatment at private clinics in Venezuela and abroad. It was financed through wage contributions and company payments. Bodas urged oil workers nationwide and the broader working class to join the mobilizations, while criticizing efforts to criminalize union leaders and weaken the right to strike. The protests come amid a wider wave of public-sector demands for higher wages and collective bargaining rights. The Maduro government has responded to sanctions-driven economic collapse with a more liberal economic approach and slower wage adjustments. On May 1, it raised the minimum income for public employees to US$70 through bonuses rather than salary increases, which unions say reduces benefits tied to wages. The oil sector has also been hit hard by U.S. sanctions, brain drain, and corruption, including a recent embezzlement probe that led to dozens of arrests.

# Venezuela Oil Workers Protest for Better Wages and Health Insurance Oil industry workers in Venezuela have staged ongoing protests since June 1, demanding improved wages and labor rights. The demonstrations, centered at the Puerto La Cruz refinery in Anzoátegui state, have expanded to include workers from other state oil company PDVSA affiliates across the country. José Bodas Lugo, secretary-general of the Unitary Federation of Oil Workers (FUTPV), explained that workers declared themselves in "permanent assembly" until authorities address their grievances. The protesters seek a meeting with Oil Minister Rafael Tellechea, though he was unavailable, attending OPEC meetings in Vienna. The workers face dire economic conditions. PDVSA employees earn between $100 and $200 monthly, with only a portion constituting base salary for calculating benefits. The collective contract expired 18 months ago with no progress toward negotiation. The primary demand is reinstating SICOPROSA, the industry's health insurance program, which previously offered generous coverage at private clinics throughout Venezuela and abroad. Currently, only top-level managers access the program, leaving workers dependent on Venezuela's deteriorating public healthcare system. Bodas noted that two veteran workers recently died in state hospitals due to inadequate care. Beyond healthcare, workers have lost other benefits, including favorable mortgage programs previously backed by PDVSA. These protests reflect broader labor unrest across Venezuela's public sector, as workers demand wage increases and restoration of collective bargaining rights. The government's May 1 minimum wage increase to $70 for public employees came through non-wage bonuses, which trade unionists criticized as benefiting employers by reducing social security contributions and severance compensations. Venezuela's oil sector, the country's economic foundation, has deteriorated significantly under nearly six years of US sanctions that blocked financial markets and exports. The industry has also suffered from brain drain and corruption, with recent investigations resulting in dozens of arrests for alleged embezzlement of at least $3 billion.

Venezuelans across the country staged protests on Saturday in “Operation Freedom,” a campaign called by opposition leader Juan Guaido to force President Nicolas Maduro to resign. Speaking at the main rally in Caracas, Guaido said people were demanding not only water and electricity, but also democracy and a future, pointing to recent blackouts that have caused water shortages. He argued Maduro remains in power only because of support from armed paramilitary groups and said more than 90% of Venezuelans want a change of government. Guaido, recognized by more than 50 countries as interim president, said the opposition’s long-running demonstrations were entering a “definitive phase.” The protests were met with unrest in several cities. In Maracaibo, two opposition politicians were briefly detained, according to lawmakers. In northwestern Venezuela, about 30 protesters were injured in clashes with police, and in the coastal city of Valencia, two VPItv journalists were struck by the National Guard, the journalists’ union said. The rallies came days after the pro-Maduro Constituent Assembly stripped Guaido of parliamentary immunity, raising the possibility of his arrest. The United States and Colombia warned Maduro against detaining him. Maduro, who won a second term in a boycotted election in May, continues to rely on the army as Venezuela’s economic crisis deepens.

# Summary Venezuelan opposition leader Juan Guaidó organized nationwide "Operation Freedom" protests on Saturday to pressure President Nicolás Maduro to resign. Guaidó, recognized as interim president by over 50 countries, addressed the main rally in Caracas, demanding democracy and solutions to widespread blackouts and water shortages. He claimed over 90% of the population supports regime change and that Maduro relies on armed paramilitary groups to maintain power. The demonstrations turned violent in some areas. In Maracaibo, two opposition politicians were temporarily arrested, approximately 30 demonstrators were injured during police clashes, and journalists were attacked by the national guard. The protests follow the pro-Maduro Constituent Assembly's recent decision to strip Guaidó of parliamentary immunity, raising arrest concerns. The United States and Colombia warned Maduro against detaining Guaidó, threatening a "firm multilateral response." Despite Venezuela's severe economic collapse, Maduro retains power because the military continues supporting him. Maduro won his second term in a May election boycotted by most opposition parties.

Brazil’s prisons, already notorious for overcrowding, poor sanitation and violence, have become even more dangerous as Covid-19 spreads through the system. Inmates are held in poorly ventilated cells, often with limited food and water, and some prisons operate at up to four times their intended capacity. The pandemic has intensified these long-standing conditions, leaving prisoners and their families increasingly fearful. Brazil has the world’s third-largest prison population, with nearly 750,000 inmates in facilities designed for about 440,000. The country is also among the hardest hit by the pandemic overall, with more than 3.5 million infections and 112,000 deaths at the time of the report. Since the first confirmed prison case in Rio de Janeiro in April, the virus has spread rapidly despite suspended visits and transfers. Official figures say more than 17,300 inmates have been infected and nearly 100 have died, but experts believe the true toll is far higher because only 7.8% of prisoners have been tested. Researchers and relatives describe a system under severe strain. Alexandra Sanchez of the Fiocruz public health institute said there is no clear picture of the outbreak inside prisons, warning that inmates’ already fragile health situation has become even more uncertain. In one study at Sorocaba II prison in Sao Paulo, 38% of the 2,095 inmates tested positive for the virus, a rate Sanchez said was even higher than in Rio de Janeiro’s worst-affected slums. The pandemic has also worsened emotional distress. A paper co-authored by Sanchez said fear of illness and death, combined with restrictions on movement and the suspension of work, education and religious activities, is increasing tension and causing serious psychological harm. Families have echoed these concerns. One woman said she feared losing her husband because medical care had always been inadequate and the coronavirus made the situation worse. Another relative shared a letter from her 29-year-old son, who said he was sick and that several cellmates had symptoms while the infirmary did nothing. Authorities suspended prison visits in March and removed day-release privileges for some low-security inmates, but those measures triggered riots and escape attempts, especially amid fears that guards would bring the virus inside. In fact, prison staff have been a major source of infection: of 110,000 employees, 7,143 have been infected and 75 have died, according to the National Justice Council. Human rights bodies, including the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights, have urged Brazil to reduce overcrowding and expand parole. The justice ministry says nearly 49,747 prisoners have been released during the pandemic, but experts believe more should be freed, including pregnant and nursing mothers.

# Brazil's Prisons Face Worsening Crisis as COVID-19 Spreads Brazil's already dire prison conditions have deteriorated further as the coronavirus pandemic spreads rapidly through the country's overcrowded facilities. With the third-largest prison population globally—nearly 750,000 inmates against a capacity of 440,000—Brazil's jails now confront a public health catastrophe. Since the first confirmed COVID-19 case in a Rio de Janeiro prison in April, the virus has spread swiftly despite suspended visits and inmate transfers. Official figures report over 17,300 infected inmates and nearly 100 deaths, though experts believe actual numbers are substantially higher, with only 7.8 percent of prisoners tested. A comprehensive study at Sorocaba II prison in São Paulo found 38 percent of 2,095 tested inmates were positive—significantly higher than infection rates in Rio's hardest-hit slums. Brazil's prisons were already notoriously bleak before the pandemic. Cells are dingy and poorly ventilated, food and water rations are limited, and overcrowding can reach four times capacity. The addition of COVID-19 has created an "invisible enemy," as one inmate's wife described it, pushing already inadequate medical services to the brink while increasing isolation from families. The authorities' preventive measures have proven ineffective and counterproductive. When authorities suspended all prison visits in March and revoked work-release privileges at minimum-security prisons, inmates responded with riots and mass escape attempts. The virus likely spread through prison employees; of 110,000 system workers, 7,143 have been infected and 75 have died. Inspections reveal alarming conditions. Inmates with confirmed and probable COVID-19 cases share cells with apparently uninfected prisoners. One inmate's letter described sharing a cell with 41 others, stating: "Mom, I'm sick. Several of us have symptoms, and the infirmary isn't doing anything." The psychological toll is severe. Restrictions on movement, work, education, and religious activities have aggravated tensions and caused serious emotional distress among prisoners already fearful for their lives. International concern is mounting. The Inter-American Commission on Human Rights recently called on Brazilian authorities to reduce overcrowding and grant parole whenever possible. The justice ministry claims to have released 49,747 prisoners during the pandemic, following recommendations to parole non-violent offenders. However, experts argue this number should be much higher, potentially including approximately 2,000 pregnant or nursing mothers currently incarcerated.

Thousands of Ecuadorians marched in Quito and other cities on Monday to protest President Lenin Moreno’s austerity measures as the country struggled with the economic fallout from Covid-19. Demonstrators opposed government-backed layoffs and pay cuts, chanting “Out Moreno, Out” in the capital. Many wore masks and tried to keep social distance, even as Ecuador’s official coronavirus death toll exceeded 3,200. However, many believe the real number is far higher, citing “excess deaths” in Guayaquil and nearby areas. In downtown Quito, police confronted student protesters who had burned tires near a square. The students were demanding the withdrawal of bills that would cut the education budget and the dismissal of Economy Minister Richard Martinez. Union leaders also criticized Martinez for authorizing a $324 million payment to foreign creditors during a public health emergency. The protest movement drew support from medical unions, which condemned the government’s handling of the crisis and its failure to punish officials accused of profiting from the pandemic. Critics also pointed out that Moreno had promised to avoid layoffs but did little as at least 150,000 people lost their jobs. Truckers joined the protests over a new fuel distribution system that effectively removes subsidies, reviving anger over a similar policy that had previously sparked nationwide unrest. The demonstrations reflected broader frustration with Moreno’s government, with signs accusing officials, banks, bosses, and police of exploitation and mistreatment. Local officials and opposition figures warned that rising political anger could worsen the pandemic by forcing people into the streets.

# Summary Thousands of Ecuadorians protested across the country on Monday against the government's austerity measures, including layoffs and pay cuts implemented in response to the Covid-19 economic crisis. Demonstrators in Quito chanted "Out Moreno, Out," targeting President Lenin Moreno, who has delegated significant powers to unelected aides despite having a year remaining in his term. Despite coronavirus concerns—which have killed over 3,200 officially, though excess death figures suggest much higher tolls—protesters wore masks and maintained social distancing. Police confronted students who set tires ablaze near downtown Quito, with demonstrators criticizing officers' aggressive tactics on social media. Key protest demands included withdrawing education budget cuts and firing Economy Minister Richard Martinez, who faced criticism for paying $324 million to foreign creditors during the health emergency. Students and unions also condemned the government's prior dismissal of 2,500 healthcare workers, including 300 epidemic specialists, in March 2019. Additional grievances included Moreno's broken promise to prevent layoffs—at least 150,000 jobs were lost—and a new fuel distribution system eliminating subsidies that previously sparked nationwide unrest. Medical unions protested the government's failure to punish officials who exploited the pandemic for personal gain. Provincial Governor Paola Pabon warned that Moreno's policies force people to protest, amplifying pandemic risks through increased contagion exposure.

Libya’s UN-recognised authorities said they carried out air strikes on drug trafficking and fuel smuggling hubs in Zawiya, west of Tripoli. The military gave no casualty details, and it was unclear whether anyone was killed or injured in the attacks.

# Summary Libya's UN-recognized authorities conducted air strikes on drug trafficking and fuel smuggling sites west of Tripoli in Zawiya on the Mediterranean coast. Casualty reports remain unclear. The operation targeted criminal smuggling operations in the war-torn nation.

Sudan’s Prime Minister Kamal Idris has publicly appealed to Colombia and other Spanish-speaking countries to stop the recruitment and deployment of Colombian mercenaries to fight in Sudan. In a video message written in Spanish and circulated in Arabic, French, and other languages, Idris linked his appeal to a broader message of solidarity from the Spanish-speaking world, citing figures such as Picasso, Neruda, García Márquez, and Vargas Llosa. He urged Colombians to help end the siege of El Fasher, the capital of North Darfur and the last major stronghold of the Sudanese Armed Forces, which has been besieged for more than a year by the Rapid Support Forces. Idris said the RSF is reportedly receiving support from Colombian mercenaries hired by the United Arab Emirates. He called on the Colombian government to investigate the recruitment networks, warning that such practices deepen the humanitarian crisis and undermine peace. Colombian President Gustavo Petro responded on X, telling former soldiers and officers not to “sell yourselves” and to fight for their own country rather than die in foreign wars. The article cites an investigation by the Colombian newspaper La Silla Vacía, which says the deployment is part of a transnational operation involving four countries. It reports that at least 300 former Colombian soldiers have been sent to Sudan, and about 40 were allegedly detained by recruiters after refusing to fight and saying they had been misled. According to the report, they were hired through the Colombian company International Services Agency A4SI, officially for security work tied to Emirati oil infrastructure, but later sent into the Sudan conflict in partnership with an Emirati firm. The article notes that retired Colombian soldiers are often sought after because of their combat experience.

# Sudan Appeals to Colombia Over Mercenary Deployment Sudanese Prime Minister Kamal Idris has issued a video appeal to Colombian authorities and citizens, urging them to stop sending mercenaries to fight in Sudan's ongoing conflict. In his multilingual message, Idris praised Spanish-speaking cultures' contributions to humanities before calling for Colombian support in ending the siege of El Fasher, North Darfur's capital and the last stronghold of the Sudan Armed Forces (SAF). The city has been besieged for over a year by the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) militias, who reportedly employ Colombian mercenaries hired by the United Arab Emirates. Idris demanded that Colombia investigate recruitment networks deploying fighters to Sudan, arguing these practices threaten peace and worsen the humanitarian crisis. The Colombian president responded via social media, discouraging soldiers from fighting in foreign wars. According to Colombian newspaper "La Silla Vacía," at least 300 former Colombian soldiers have been deployed to Sudan as part of a transnational operation involving four countries. Approximately 40 have been imprisoned by recruiters for refusing to fight, claiming they were recruited under false pretenses. The investigation revealed that Colombian company "International Services Agency A4SI" officially contracted to provide oil infrastructure security in the UAE, secretly deployed mercenaries in partnership with an Emirati company. The company's leadership includes a former Bogotá army officer who left in 2007 amid alleged drug cartel connections. Colombia's experienced military professionals, many retiring at age 40, are highly sought by international security firms due to their combat experience.

The Kenyan High Court has extended until Wednesday an order suspending the release on bond of Briton Jack Marrian and Kenyan Francis Mwanthi, who face drug trafficking charges involving 100 kilos of cocaine worth Sh598 million seized at the Port of Mombasa. High Court Judge Luka Kimaru made the decision after it emerged that neither suspect had filed a response to an affidavit by the Director of Public Prosecutions, which opposed their bail. Marrian had briefly been freed by Kibera Senior Resident Magistrate Derrick Kuto on a Sh70 million bond with two Kenyan sureties, but the High Court immediately suspended that release after the DPP objected. Mwanthi had also been granted a Sh60 million bond with two sureties. Both men were charged separately in connection with the cocaine shipment, and if convicted they could face life sentences. Their lawyer, Sheetal Kapila, argued the case was part of efforts to prevent Kenya from becoming a drug transit route, but insisted his client was innocent and that “unknown people” had smuggled the drugs into the consignment. The case has drawn attention in Britain because of Marrian’s aristocratic family background and elite schooling. His family says it believes he will be cleared, and both his father and employer have publicly backed him, saying they will support him until the facts are fully presented.

# Summary Kenya's High Court extended an order suspending bail for Jack Marrian, a British national, and Francis Mwanthi, a Kenyan, who face drug trafficking charges. High Court Judge Luka Kimaru extended the suspension until Wednesday after the defendants failed to respond to the Director of Public Prosecutions' opposition to their release. Marrian's Sh70 million bond and Mwanthi's Sh60 million bond were both suspended shortly after a magistrate initially granted them bail. The two men were separately charged with trafficking 100 kilos of cocaine worth Sh598 million, seized at the Port of Mombasa. Conviction could result in life sentences. Defence lawyer Sheetal Kapila argued the case targets the wrong individuals and that unknown parties smuggled the drugs into the consignment. He suggested authorities aim to prevent Kenya from serving as a drug transit point. The case has attracted significant British media attention due to Marrian's aristocratic background—his mother is Lady Emma Clare Campbell of Cawdor, and he attended elite private schools. His family has deep historical ties to Kenya, with his grandfather serving as a colonial minister before independence in 1963. Marrian's employers, including Mshale Commodities and ED&F Man, expressed full support and confidence in his eventual exoneration.

Kenya has called for stronger cross-border cooperation among African states to confront the continent’s worsening drug trafficking problem, warning that African countries are increasingly becoming not just transit points but also consumer markets for illicit drugs. The appeal was made in Abuja, Nigeria, during the 31st meeting of the Heads of Drug Law Enforcement Agencies in Africa (HONLAF), where Kenya’s Secretary for National Administration in the State Department of Internal Security, Beverly Opwora, led the Kenyan delegation. Opwora said the rising demand for psychotropic and narcotic substances, along with the misuse of precursor chemicals, requires a coordinated regional response. She argued that continued illicit cultivation and trafficking across borders can only be curbed through closer cooperation among African governments. Kenya was represented at the meeting by officials from the Ministry of Interior and National Administration, the National Authority for the Campaign Against Alcohol and Drug Abuse (NACADA), the Pharmacy and Poisons Board, and the Financial Reporting Centre. Participants noted that drug cultivation, trafficking and consumption are placing additional pressure on African economies already burdened by drought, poverty, disease and corruption. Opwora reaffirmed Kenya’s opposition to the global push to commercialize controlled substances such as cannabis for non-medical use. She also stressed that drug users should be treated rather than punished, saying they need rehabilitation and support instead of discrimination or incarceration. She added that Kenya is pursuing a two-pronged drug control strategy focused on both reducing demand and suppressing supply. At the forum, NACADA acting Chief Executive Officer John Muteti outlined Kenya’s demand-reduction measures, including mass media campaigns, life-skills training for children and youth, positive parenting programs, strong-family initiatives, workplace prevention efforts, and treatment and rehabilitation services for people with substance use disorders. On the supply side, Muteti said Kenya has strengthened enforcement agencies and coordination with criminal justice stakeholders to improve surveillance, investigations, enforcement and prosecution of drug offenses. He said the drug threat is complex and constantly changing, requiring greater investment in technical and infrastructure capacity, as well as stronger international collaboration grounded in the three international drug control conventions. The article also notes that in March, the UNODC reported that Nigeria’s market ranks highest in Africa for cocaine smuggling. Kenya had hosted the previous HONLAF meeting in November 2022. This year’s meeting was opened by Nigerian Vice President Kashim Shettima, and leadership of HONLAF has now passed from Kenya to Nigeria.

# Kenya Calls for African Unity Against Drug Trafficking Kenya has urged African nations to strengthen cross-border cooperation to combat the continent's escalating drug trafficking crisis. Beverly Opwora, Kenya's Secretary for National Administration, made this appeal at the 31st meeting of the Heads of Drug Law Enforcement Agencies in Africa (HONLAF) held in Abuja, Nigeria on September 27. Opwora highlighted alarming trends showing that African countries have transitioned from being merely transit routes for illicit drugs to experiencing significant domestic consumption. The surge in demand for psychotropic and narcotic drugs, along with the misuse of precursor chemicals, demands coordinated regional action. Kenya's delegation includes representatives from the Ministry of Interior and National Administration, the National Authority for the Campaign Against Alcohol and Drug Abuse (NACADA), the Pharmacy and Poisons Board, and the Financial Reporting Centre. Participants noted that drug cultivation, trafficking, and consumption exacerbate Africa's existing socio-economic challenges, including drought, poverty, disease, and corruption. Kenya opposes the global commercialization of controlled substances like cannabis for non-medical purposes and advocates for treating drug users through rehabilitation rather than incarceration. Kenya implements a two-pronged strategy combining demand reduction and supply suppression. NACADA's Chief Executive Officer John Muteti outlined demand reduction efforts including mass media campaigns, youth empowerment programs, parenting initiatives, and workplace prevention programs alongside treatment services. For supply reduction, Kenya has enhanced law enforcement coordination across the criminal justice system, improving surveillance, investigations, and prosecutions of drug offenses. Muteti emphasized the need for substantial investments in technical and infrastructural capacity building to support effective criminal justice processes. He stressed that drug control requires enhanced international cooperation anchored to three international drug control conventions. The UN Office on Drugs and Crime's 2023 Global Report on Cocaine identified Nigeria as Africa's leading cocaine smuggling region, underscoring the urgency of regional cooperation. Kenya chaired HONLAF for the past year and has now passed leadership to Nigeria, which officially opened the meeting through Vice President Kashim Shettima. The previous HONLAF meeting, held in Kenya in November 2022, similarly addressed trafficking trends, concealment methods, and regional cooperation strategies.

An Isiolo County Assembly member, Abdullahi Golicha Maje, 27, has been arrested alongside Nura Abdi Diba, 25, over suspected marijuana trafficking. The Directorate of Criminal Investigations said the two were intercepted Thursday in Isiolo town by officers from the Transnational Organized Crimes Unit and a multi-agency team. They were later linked to a house at Kambi Garba Estate, where six gunny bags containing 57 stones of bhang were recovered. The suspects and the seized exhibits were taken to DCI headquarters in Kiambu Road as investigations continue.

# Summary An Isiolo County Assembly Member, Abdullahi Golicha Maje (27), was arrested Thursday alongside Nura Abdi Diba (25) for marijuana trafficking. The Directorate of Criminal Investigations, working with a multi-agency team, apprehended the suspects after flagging down their Toyota Land Cruiser in Isiolo town. Officers subsequently searched Diba's residence at Kambi Garba Estate, recovering 57 stones of bhang stored in six gunny bags. The confiscated drugs were transported to DCI headquarters for processing, and detectives have launched an investigation into their alleged involvement in illegal drug trafficking.

South African customs and law-enforcement authorities have confiscated smuggled goods worth more than R2.3 billion over the past year, with most of the seizures taking place at the country’s airports. The figures, released by the South African Revenue Service (Sars), cover illicit flows into and out of South Africa from April 2017 until the end of the previous month. The haul included rhino horn, hard drugs, counterfeit clothing, illegal cigarettes, endangered wildlife products, gold and large sums of undeclared cash. The report showed that the scale of the busts was significant, but experts cautioned that the numbers only reflect what was intercepted, not the true size of the illegal market. Eric Pelser, head of the Trans-National Organised Crime in Africa programme at the Institute of Security Studies, said the figures should not be celebrated because they do not reveal the growing volume of illicit trade. He pointed out that heroin seizures, for example, have risen sharply over the past two decades. The latest seizures also included a major counterfeit clothing bust in KwaZulu-Natal, where the Hawks raided a container depot on the Bluff. Hawks spokesperson Captain Simphiwe Mhlongo said investigators already knew who the suspects were and that they would be summoned to appear in the Durban Specialised Commercial Crime Court once procedures were completed. In another KwaZulu-Natal case, King Shaka International Airport was mentioned in a currency-smuggling incident in which more than R6 million in rand and US dollars was being sent to Dubai. Sars said there had been 46 busts in total. The biggest involved a truck that arrived in Cape Town from Johannesburg on March 1 and 2, carrying uncut crystal methamphetamine, or tik, valued at about R30 million hidden inside fridges. The same truck also contained a large quantity of suspected counterfeit clothing, and the driver was arrested. Among the most notable cases listed by Sars were several high-value cocaine interceptions, rhino horn seizures, and multiple currency-smuggling incidents. These included rhino horn worth R5.75 million bound for Hong Kong from South Africa at OR Tambo International Airport; cocaine worth R56.7 million travelling from Brazil to Australia via South Africa; and another cocaine shipment worth more than R10 million moving from Brazil to Namibia via South Africa. Other cases involved tik from Nigeria and Rwanda, ecstasy from Cameroon via Kenya, ephedrine from Kenya, sexual-enhancement tablets from India, Viagra and Kamagra shipments, and cash headed for Dubai, Canada and South Africa. Additional recent busts included 108kg of drugs hidden in boxes falsely declared as calcium carbonate. Officials checked the cargo after it arrived from Kenya at OR Tambo Airport and found a white powder and a brown sand-like substance. Laboratory tests confirmed the substances were ketamine and acetylanthranil, an ingredient used to make mandrax. The case was handed over to the Hawks. On Thursday, Sars also seized 6,000kg of cannabis worth more than R9 million at the Ficksburg border crossing from Lesotho, and the driver was taken into police custody. According to Sars chief officer for Customs and Excise Teboho Mokoena, counterfeit clothing, footwear and similar goods accounted for the biggest share of the busts, totaling R1.8 billion. Drugs, including tik and cocaine, made up more than R326 million of the seizures.

# Customs Confiscates R2.3 Billion in Smuggled Goods South African customs officials have seized smuggled goods worth more than R2.3 billion over the past year, according to a statement released by the South African Revenue Service (Sars). The confiscated items, primarily intercepted at the country's airports, include rhino horn, hardcore drugs, and counterfeit clothing. The seizures occurred between April 2017 and the end of the previous month and comprised 46 major busts. However, Eric Pelser, head of the Trans-National Organised Crime in Africa programme at the Institute of Security Studies, cautioned against celebrating these figures. He noted that the busts do not reflect the actual size of the illicit market or the escalating flow of illegal goods, pointing to exponential increases in heroin trafficking over the past two decades. Recent enforcement actions in KwaZulu-Natal have intensified. The Hawks raided a Bluff container depot this week, seizing counterfeit clothing, while King Shaka International Airport featured in the Sars report for a currency smuggling case involving over R6 million in rand and US dollars destined for Dubai. Additional KwaZulu-Natal seizures within two weeks included R27 million in illegal cigarettes, drugs, endangered wildlife products, gold, and counterfeit items. Hawks spokesperson Captain Simphiwe Mhlongo indicated that suspects have been identified and will be summoned to the Durban Specialised Commercial Crime Court. The largest single bust occurred on March 1-2 when uncut crystal methamphetamine (tik) valued at R30 million was discovered hidden in refrigerators on a truck traveling from Johannesburg to Cape Town. The same truck contained counterfeit clothing, and the driver was arrested. Currency smuggling registered the highest number of individual busts—six cases totaling over R57 million—while cocaine smuggling involved the highest-value contraband, exceeding R73 million across three cases. Notable seizures included rhino horn valued at R5.75 million destined for Hong Kong and cocaine worth R56.67 million intended for Australia via South Africa, both intercepted at OR Tambo International Airport. Other significant confiscations at OR Tambo included cocaine valued at R10.07 million and R7.48 million destined for Namibia and Congo respectively, tik worth R7.2 million from Nigeria, ecstasy valued at R33.6 million from Cameroon, and various pharmaceutical products including sexual enhancement tablets and Viagra totaling millions of rands. Additional recent busts revealed 108 kilograms of drugs hidden in boxes declared as "calcium carbonate" at OR Tambo Airport, containing ketamine and acetylanthranil, a base ingredient for methaqualone. The Hawks assumed investigation responsibility. At the Ficksburg border crossing with Lesotho, authorities discovered 6,000 kilograms of cannabis worth over R9 million, with the driver taken into custody. According to Teboho Mokoena, chief officer for Customs and Excise, counterfeit clothing, footwear, and related goods constituted the largest smuggling category at R1.8 billion. Drugs, including tik and cocaine, accounted for over R326 million of the total seizures, highlighting the diverse nature of South Africa's smuggling challenges and the critical role of customs enforcement in combating transnational organized crime.

The African Union (AU) has voiced deep concern over the rising threat to peace and security in Africa from terrorism, radicalization, violent extremism, and the influx of foreign terrorist fighters. In a statement issued after a meeting of the AU Peace and Security Council, the 55-member bloc said it had discussed the impact of foreign terrorist fighters on the continent’s stability. The council warned that it would not hesitate to “name and shame” any non-African states found to be sponsoring or promoting terrorism. It said the growing threat is undermining AU efforts to end violent conflicts and achieve lasting peace and security across Africa. The AU also highlighted the increasing links between terrorism and transnational organized crime, including money laundering, illicit financial flows, arms proliferation, human and drug trafficking, cybercrime, and the risk of weapons of mass destruction reaching terrorist groups. It condemned ongoing indiscriminate terrorist attacks in several parts of the continent, as well as the continued recruitment and state sponsorship of foreign terrorist fighters. Without naming countries, the council said some non-African states are behind the rising influx of such fighters into Africa. It urged AU members and other stakeholders to fully comply with UN Security Council Resolution 2170, which outlines a comprehensive approach to combating foreign terrorist fighters. The council also called on international partners to strengthen cooperation and information-sharing, and urged African states to cut off terrorist financing, stop ransom payments, and develop common standards for tracking terrorism-related financial networks.

# AU Expresses Concern Over Foreign Terrorist Fighters in Africa The African Union's Peace and Security Council has expressed deep concern over the escalating threat posed by terrorism, radicalization, and violent extremism across Africa, particularly the influx of foreign terrorist fighters (FTFs) into the continent. During its latest meeting, the council warned it would publicly identify and shame non-African states sponsoring terrorism. The council emphasized that these threats undermine AU efforts to achieve sustainable peace and stability across the 55-member organization. The council highlighted growing connections between terrorism and transnational organized crime, including money laundering, illicit weapons trafficking, human and drug smuggling, cyber crimes, and potential access to weapons of mass destruction. It condemned ongoing indiscriminate terrorist attacks and the continued recruitment and state sponsorship of FTFs. In response, the council urged AU members to comply with UN Security Council Resolution 2170 and called for international partners to enhance collaboration through intelligence sharing and assistance. The council also advocated for destroying terrorist financial networks and combating transnational organized crime through coordinated efforts. Additionally, the council discouraged member states from paying ransoms to terrorists and called for developing common standards to track terrorism financing networks in accordance with AU and international instruments.

Cambodia and the Philippines have pledged to expand cooperation across a wide range of fields in the post-Covid-19 period, according to Cambodia’s Foreign Ministry. The commitment came after the third meeting of the Cambodia-Philippines Joint Commission for Bilateral Cooperation, held virtually on December 1-2 and co-chaired by Cambodian Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Prak Sokhonn and Philippine Foreign Secretary Teodoro Locsin. During the talks, both sides discussed shared interests and ways to deepen existing cooperation in political-security affairs, defense, trade and investment, agriculture and agribusiness, tourism, air connectivity, culture, labor, education and vocational training, science and technology, health, and environmental protection. On security, they agreed to strengthen law enforcement cooperation to confront regional threats including terrorism, drug trafficking, human trafficking, arms smuggling, money laundering, piracy, cybercrime, identity fraud, and illegal wildlife trade. The two countries also highlighted strong economic potential and pledged to boost two-way trade and investment through more joint trade events. They welcomed the virtual signing of a memorandum of understanding between the Cambodia Chamber of Commerce and the Philippine Chamber of Commerce and Industry to promote business ties. In tourism, they emphasized the importance of the ASEAN Tourism Forum 2022 in Cambodia’s Preah Sihanouk province. The Philippine side also announced that Philippine Airlines will begin weekly direct flights between Phnom Penh and Manila next month. Both sides reaffirmed their commitment to coordinate closely in ASEAN and the UN.

# Cambodia and Philippines Pledge Expanded Cooperation Cambodia and the Philippines have committed to broadening cooperation across multiple sectors during the post-Covid-19 era, according to a statement from Cambodia's Foreign Ministry issued on Friday. Former Delhi law minister and AAP leader Somnath Bharti has approached the Delhi High Court challenging a National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) order directing the Delhi government to pay Rs. 25,000 each to African women whom the commission described as victims of racial prejudice and unlawful acts. The women were allegedly targeted during Bharti’s controversial midnight anti-crime campaign in Khirki Extension, south Delhi, in January, when he is said to have barged into their homes after complaints about a suspected prostitution and drug racket. Bharti’s petition seeks to set aside the NHRC’s September 29 order, arguing that the commission lacked jurisdiction and that he was denied a reasonable opportunity to defend himself or present evidence. The plea claims he was not given notice of certain suo motu proceedings initiated by the NHRC in January 2014, even though he was treated as a principal actor in the matter. It also says the NHRC order wrongly creates the impression that the allegations against him were prima facie established. Filed through advocate Deepak Khosla, the petition asks the court to direct the NHRC to produce its records and declare them incorrect, while also seeking Rs. 100 crore in damages jointly from the NHRC, the central government, and Delhi Police for allegedly defaming Bharti. Justice Manmohan recused himself from hearing the case, which was then transferred to another bench and listed for hearing the next day.

# Summary Former Delhi law minister Somnath Bharti filed a petition in the Delhi High Court challenging a National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) order requiring the Delhi government to compensate African women with Rs. 25,000 each for alleged racial prejudice and unlawful treatment. The controversy stems from January 2014, when Bharti, then an Aam Aadmi Party leader, allegedly raided homes in south Delhi's Khirki Extension area following complaints about prostitution and drug trafficking. According to the NHRC, Bharti and his supporters humiliated the African women, wrongfully confined them in a vehicle, and subjected them to racial abuse. An illegal search by a doctor at AIIMS found no drugs. Bharti's petition argues that the September 29 NHRC order violated his rights by failing to provide him reasonable opportunity to be heard or present evidence in his defense. He seeks to nullify the order and claims it implies the allegations were "prima facie proved." The plea also demands Rs. 100 crore in damages from the NHRC, central government, and Delhi Police for defamation. The Delhi High Court transferred the case to another bench for hearing on Wednesday.

Jammu and Kashmir Police on Wednesday issued an advisory warning the public against investing in cryptocurrencies such as bitcoin, citing the “heightened risk” involved. The crime branch inspector general said people should avoid putting money into virtual currencies because they are not backed as legal tender by the government or central financial institutions. The advisory cautioned that such investments could suffer a sudden and prolonged crash, leaving especially retail investors to lose their hard-earned money. It also warned that the public should stay alert and avoid fraudulent schemes. According to the police, the Reserve Bank of India has not licensed or authorized any entity to operate cryptocurrency schemes in India, and these currencies have no regulatory permission or protection. The advisory further said the lack of oversight over blockchain-based transactions makes them vulnerable to misuse for subversive activities, smuggling, drug and human trafficking, terror funding, and money laundering.

# Summary On January 2, Jammu and Kashmir Police issued an advisory warning citizens against investing in cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin, citing heightened risks. The police emphasized that cryptocurrencies are not recognized as legal tender by the government or central financial institutions. The advisory cautioned that such investments could result in sudden market crashes, causing retail investors to lose their savings. The Inspector General noted that the Reserve Bank of India has not authorized any entity to operate cryptocurrency schemes in India, and these currencies lack regulatory protection. The police highlighted that the lack of regulatory oversight makes cryptocurrencies vulnerable to misuse for illegal activities including smuggling, drug trafficking, human trafficking, terror funding, and money laundering. The public was urged to remain alert and avoid fraudulent schemes involving virtual currencies.

Assam Rifles and other law-enforcement agencies seized drugs worth more than Rs 18.33 crore, recovered a large amount of Myanmar currency, and arrested seven suspected drug peddlers in separate operations in Mizoram and Manipur on Wednesday, officials said. With these actions, total seizures in Assam, Mizoram and Manipur over the past 24 hours rose to more than Rs 57.33 crore, with ten drug peddlers arrested. In Mizoram’s Champhai district, Assam Rifles acted on intelligence about narcotics trafficking in the Diltlang area and set up a Mobile Vehicle Check Post. Personnel intercepted a suspicious two-wheeler, but the rider and pillion rider fled. A search of the abandoned bike led to the recovery of 2.057 kg of heroin valued at around Rs 15.42 crore, along with a mobile phone. In a second operation in the same district, troops stopped a Chinese-made Kenbo bike at Tlangsam and found 87.6 grams of heroin worth about Rs 68.25 lakh. The rider, identified as Tlana, was apprehended and handed over with the contraband and vehicle to the Excise and Narcotics Department in Champhai for further legal action. In another Mizoram operation, Assam Rifles intercepted two vehicles at Laki in Siaha district and recovered Myanmar currency worth Kyat 3,46,07,000. Five people were detained, including three Myanmar nationals and two Indians. They were handed over to Tuipang Police Station for further proceedings. In Manipur, Assam Rifles, working with state police, conducted an anti-narcotics operation in the Maram area of Senapati district and arrested one person with 268 grams of brown sugar valued at about Rs 53.60 lakh. Separately, in Noney district, Assam Rifles seized 560 bags of illegal areca nuts, totaling 56,000 kg and valued at roughly Rs 1.7 crore. The consignment was handed over to the Divisional Forest Officer for legal action. The operations underscore the continuing role of Myanmar’s unfenced 1,643-km border with northeastern states as a transit route for heroin, methamphetamine tablets and other contraband entering India.

# Summary Law enforcement agencies, including the Assam Rifles, conducted multiple operations across northeastern India on Wednesday, resulting in significant seizures and arrests. In the 24-hour period, agencies confiscated drugs worth over Rs 57.33 crore and arrested ten drug peddlers across Assam, Mizoram, and Manipur. In Mizoram's Champhai district, Assam Rifles established a mobile checkpoint in Diltlang following intelligence about narcotics trafficking. Officers intercepted a two-wheeler whose riders fled, leading to the discovery of 2.057 kg of heroin valued at approximately Rs 15.42 crore. In a separate operation in the same district, personnel recovered 87.6 grams of heroin worth Rs 68.25 lakh from a Kenbo bike, apprehending the peddler identified as Tlana. At Laki in Siaha district, Assam Rifles intercepted two vehicles and recovered Myanmar currency totaling Kyat 3,46,07,000. Five individuals were arrested—three Myanmar nationals and two Indians—and handed over to local police. In Manipur's Senapati district, coordinated operations between Assam Rifles and state police resulted in the apprehension of one individual and seizure of 268 grams of brown sugar valued at approximately Rs 53.60 lakh. Additionally, Assam Rifles seized 56,000 kg of illegal areca nuts (betel nuts) in Noney district, valued at approximately Rs 1.7 crore, based on intelligence regarding illicit movement along a state highway. The operations underscore ongoing efforts to combat drug trafficking and contraband smuggling. Myanmar shares a 1,643-kilometer unfenced border with four northeastern states—Arunachal Pradesh, Manipur, Nagaland, and Mizoram—serving as a major transit route for heroin, methamphetamine tablets, and other illegal goods entering India. Officials stated that the Assam Rifles remain committed to securing the border and establishing a drug-free society in the region.

A city council candidate in Hualien, Taiwan, Chen Renzhi, has drawn attention with an anti-drug campaign poster featuring Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte. The poster follows a similar eyebrow-raising campaign tactic seen last month in Kaohsiung, where a North Korean leader image appeared on a poster. Chen is running in local elections later this year and is using Duterte’s hardline anti-drug reputation to reinforce his message. The poster says “Cherish Life, Refuse Drugs” and shows Chen alongside a stern-looking Duterte, with the Chinese character for “drug” crossed out. Duterte is internationally known for his brutal anti-drug war, which has involved thousands of killings of suspected dealers and users since he took office. Photos of the campaign truck were taken during the Dragon Boat Festival weekend and posted on Facebook by user Nieviv Sucuaje.

# Summary A Taiwanese city council candidate in Hualien has created an unconventional campaign poster featuring Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte to promote an anti-drug message ahead of local elections. Chen Renzhi chose this approach to emphasize his stance against drug use and trafficking. The poster, which reads "Cherish Life, Refuse Drugs," displays Duterte alongside a cartoon character with the Chinese character for "drug" crossed out. The Embassy of India in Phnom Penh hosted a sending-off programme at India House for 40 Cambodian officials who will travel to India for customised training courses. The event was attended by Senior Minister H.E. Chhay Sinarith, president of the National Information Technology Centre, and opened with remarks by Indian Ambassador H.E. Vanlalvawna Bawitlung, who highlighted the value of international cooperation and knowledge-sharing in building government capacity. The participants are split into two groups. Twenty officials from the Ministry of Interior will take part in a “Cyber Crime Investigation and Cyber Forensic” course from January 28 to February 3, 2026. That training aims to help Cambodian officials use administrative data to produce reliable, timely, and policy-relevant subnational statistics. In his closing remarks, Senior Minister Chhay Sinarith thanked the Indian government for its support in strengthening Cambodia’s technological capabilities. The embassy also noted that other Cambodian officials have recently completed or are currently undergoing training in India in areas such as drug trafficking prevention, good governance, public policy, and judicial studies.

Four senior Western Australian Police officers with a combined service of more than 140 years have been recognised in the Australia Day Honours with the Australian Police Medal for distinguished service. Commander Michael James Bell, Detective Senior Sergeant Stephen John Cleal, Inspector Jodie Lee Di Lallo and Detective Superintendent John Andrew Hutchison will all receive the award. Bell, WA’s top traffic officer, has served for almost 40 years. He was praised for giving “clear directions” to road policing efforts and for playing a key role in the Infringement Reform Project, which modernised the system for issuing safety camera-detected infringements. His work involved close cooperation with the Road Safety Commission and the Department of Transport. Cleal, who led the investigation into the death of 15-year-old Cassius Turvey, was recognised after nearly 30 years in the force. He was commended for supporting the Turvey family and for encouraging Cassius’ mother, Mechelle, to take an active role in police-related initiatives. She later created TAKE 5, a victim engagement program aimed at improving police-community relations. Cleal was praised for his ability to drive change and bridge the gap between police and the community. Di Lallo, a former specialist interviewer in the Child Abuse Unit, received the medal for her work with victims of sexual and physical abuse, which was described as having a “profound effect.” She also helped implement facial recognition capability and the Police Force Covert Re-Assimilation Program within WA Police. Hutchison, with 38 years of service, was honoured for his leadership in major investigations, including Operation Beech, which intercepted 24 tonnes of cocaine bound for WA, worth about $1 billion. The operation led to charges against 12 people linked to the Mexican cartel, and further arrests in Africa, the UK and Mexico. He also worked on high-profile homicide cases, including the Daniel Morcombe case.
