He played a pivotal role in the Infringement Reform Project, which modernised the system for safety camera-detected infringements through partnerships with the Road Safety Commission and Department of Transport. **Detective Senior Sergeant Stephen John Cleal**, with almost 30 years' service, led the investigation into 15-year-old Cassius Turvey's death. He was commended for supporting the Turvey family and empowering Cassius' mother, Mechelle, to establish TAKE 5—a victim engagement program improving police-community relations. Sgt Cleal was praised for his remarkable capacity to drive change and bridge community-police gaps. **Inspector Jodie Lee Di Lallo**, a former Child Abuse Unit specialist interviewer, was recognised for profoundly affecting sexual and physical abuse victims. She implemented the Facial Recognition Capability and Police Force Covert Re-Assimilation Program into WA Police. **Detective Superintendent John Andrew Hutchison**, with 38 years' service, led Operation Beech—a covert international operation that intercepted 24 tonnes of cocaine worth $1 billion destined for WA. This represented one of Australia's biggest drug busts. His leadership resulted in arrests of cartel members across Africa, the United Kingdom, and Mexico. Supt. Hutchison has also been involved in high-profile homicide cases, including Daniel Morcombe's.

South Korean police are expanding their crackdown on criminal activity on the Dark Web, the hidden part of the internet that is not indexed by search engines and can be accessed only with special software. Until now, the investigation had been handled by a six-member task force at the National Police Agency, but it will now be carried out jointly by cybercrime units at police agencies nationwide. On Sunday, the National Police Agency said it would also cooperate with investigative authorities in the United States and Britain to fight a recent rise in Dark Web crimes, including child pornography, drug trafficking, and the sale of personal information. Police said their main priority would be child pornography cases. Seized illegal content reportedly included videos of sexual acts involving children, toddlers, and infants. Under South Korean law, producing or distributing child or adolescent pornography can bring at least five years in prison, while possession can lead to up to one year in jail or a fine of 20 million won. Police data showed that about 13,000 South Koreans visited the Dark Web daily in September, down from 20,000 in August after a crackdown. The article also recalled the 2018 arrest of Son Jong-woo, who ran a child porn site and earned about 400 million won in cryptocurrency before being sentenced to 1.5 years in prison.

# South Korean Police Launch Expanded Dark Web Investigation South Korean police have escalated their efforts against Dark Web crimes, expanding from a six-member task force to a nationwide operation involving cyber investigation squads across district agencies. The Dark Web, an unindexed internet section requiring special software and offering user anonymity, facilitates illegal activities including child pornography, drug trafficking, and personal information trading. The National Police Agency announced on November 10 that it would collaborate with investigative bodies in the United States and United Kingdom to combat the surge in Dark Web crimes, with particular focus on child pornography. Seized illegal content included videos of sexual acts involving children, toddlers, and infants. Generating or distributing such material carries sentences of five years or more, while possession carries up to one year imprisonment or fines of 20 million won. Police data revealed approximately 13,000 South Koreans visited the Dark Web daily in September, declining from 20,000 in August following enforcement actions. In a notable case, police arrested 23-year-old Son Jong-woo, operator of a child pornography site, in a 32-country joint operation. Of 310 arrested users worldwide, 223 were Korean. Son earned approximately 400 million won in cryptocurrency profits over 2.8 years of operation before receiving a 1.5-year sentence.

Italy, the European country hardest hit by coronavirus, has responded to the outbreak not only with concern but also with humor. Instead of giving in to fear, many Italians have turned to parody, jokes, and absurd stunts to cope with the crisis. In Milan, bars near the main outbreak area have rebranded the traditional “happy hour” as “aperitiviruses,” offering discounted drinks and snacks. Near Cremona, at the Gelateria Infinito shop, customers can buy a “Corona Cake,” an ice cream cake decorated with virus-like crown spikes. The owners said they understand the seriousness of the situation, but believe problems should be faced calmly rather than with sadness. Humor has also flourished online, including among people confined to Italy’s red zones under mandatory isolation. Many jokes play on familiar Italian themes such as public transport, crime, and bureaucracy. One joke features a mayor claiming metro delays are actually protective because the wait is longer than the virus’s 14-day incubation period. Another shows a drug dealer offering hard drugs, only for the customer to ask for Amuchina, Italy’s best-known hand sanitizer. The shortage and rising price of Amuchina have become a major source of satire, with mock ads treating the sanitizer as “transparent gold” and even joking about trading liters of it for a luxury car. Other jokes mock the government’s containment measures, including a video in which a sneeze triggers a dramatic special forces raid on an elderly woman’s home. However, not all of the humor has been harmless. Police in northern Italy were investigating a man who falsely claimed on social media that he had the virus and told acquaintances to get tested, before later admitting it was meant as a joke.

# Italians Combat Coronavirus Fear with Humor Italy, facing Europe's highest coronavirus cases and death toll, has responded with widespread jokes and parodies rather than panic. Despite the serious situation, Italians are using humor as a coping mechanism. In Milan, bars have rebranded "happy hour" as "aperitiviruses," offering discounted aperitifs and snacks. Meanwhile, the Gelateria Infinito shop in Cremona's Lombardy region sells a "Corona Cake" decorated with the virus's characteristic crown-like spikes. Shop owners Andrea Schirali and his wife Daniela explained their approach: "We know this is serious, but problems can't be solved with sadness and fear. The important thing is following instructions and staying calm." Virus-related jokes have proliferated on social media, often targeting Italy's cultural stereotypes. One joke depicts a city mayor claiming metro delays actually protect citizens since waiting times exceed the virus's 14-day incubation period. Another features a drug dealer's client requesting hand sanitizer instead of drugs. The mafia has become a popular joke target, with mock videos showing gangsters switching from cocaine smuggling to selling Amuchina, Italy's most famous hand sanitizer gel, which they call "transparent gold" due to skyrocketing demand. Humorous advertisements joke about trading five liters of Amuchina for luxury vehicles worth €100,000. Jokes have also mocked preventive measures, including a video showing special forces dramatically raiding an elderly woman's home after she sneezes. However, not all coronavirus humor has been welcomed. Police investigated a man in northern Italy who falsely claimed on social media to have the virus, advising contacts to get tested before admitting it was a hoax.

UK Border Force and the National Crime Agency have dismantled a Ghanaian cocaine-smuggling network after intercepting four suspects at Heathrow Airport. The group had tried to bring nearly $4 million worth of cocaine into the UK from Ghana using airline luggage. In total, officers recovered 36 kilograms of cocaine hidden in suitcases and food containers. Albert Gyamfi, 52, and Jennifer Agyemang, 38, were found with 15 kilograms of cocaine in Agyemang’s suitcase. They initially denied knowing each other, but investigators later found evidence that they had been rearranging items in the suitcase together before check-in at Kotoka International Airport in Accra. Gyamfi received a nine-year sentence, while Agyemang was jailed for six years and nine months. Eric Appaih, 50, was caught with 15 kilograms of cocaine concealed in food boxes in his luggage. Court records cited by local media said he had made six trips between Ghana and the UK since November 2019. He was sentenced to six years in prison in a separate trial. Julius Tetteh Puplampu, 56, was intercepted after arriving from Accra with six kilograms of cocaine hidden in his suitcase lining. He pleaded guilty and received a six-year sentence. The NCA said the suspects knew one another, and officials in Ghana have also made related arrests as the investigation continues.

# UK Border Force Dismantles Ghanaian Drug Trafficking Operation UK Border Force arrested four members of a Ghanaian cocaine smuggling ring at Heathrow Airport for attempting to import nearly $4 million worth of cocaine concealed in luggage on flights from Ghana to London. Albert Gyamfi, 52, and Jennifer Agyemang, 38, were found with 15 kilograms of cocaine in a suitcase. Despite initially claiming ignorance of each other, evidence showed them rearranging items before check-in in Ghana. Gyamfi received nine years imprisonment; Agyemang received six years and nine months. Eric Appaih, 50, had 15 kilos of cocaine valued at $1.63 million hidden in food boxes. Court records indicated he made six trips to Ghana since November 2019. He was sentenced to six years. Julius Tetteh Puplampu, 56, was intercepted with six kilos of cocaine in his suitcase lining and received six years after pleading guilty. The National Crime Agency investigation revealed all suspects knew each other. The operation successfully prevented the smuggling group from distributing drugs on the UK market. When the Berlin Wall fell in 1989, there were 16 major border walls worldwide; by 2016, that number had risen to 66, according to University of Quebec researcher Elisabeth Vallet. The article uses that trend as backdrop to Donald Trump’s first steps toward fulfilling his campaign promise to build a wall on the US-Mexico border. It then surveys some of the world’s most significant frontier barriers. In Europe, Hungary erected a 110-mile fence along its border with Serbia in 2015, later extending barriers to Croatia, as part of a broader regional response to the continent’s migrant crisis. Greece built the seven-mile Evros wall on its border with Turkey in 2012 after becoming a major entry point for migrants. Northern Ireland remains divided by 99 “peace lines,” first built in 1969 to separate Protestant and Catholic communities during The Troubles, and their number and size have continued to grow despite the 1998 Good Friday Agreement. Cyprus is still split by a wall dating to Turkey’s 1974 invasion. In the Middle East, the Moroccan-occupied Western Sahara is separated from Polisario-controlled territory by a 1,700-mile sand berm, described as the world’s oldest functioning security barrier. Saudi Arabia reinforced its border with Iraq with a 560-mile fence, watchtowers, command centres and surveillance systems in response to the Islamic State threat. Israel began building its West Bank barrier in 2002, saying it was meant to stop Palestinian attacks, while critics argue it amounts to land seizure and a de facto border. The United States has already built more than 1,000 km of barriers along the Mexican border since the 2006 Secure Fence Act, following earlier tightening in the 1990s and after 9/11-era security fears. Elsewhere, Spain’s enclaves of Ceuta and Melilla in North Africa are protected by high-tech fences, and India has gradually fenced much of its border with Bangladesh since 1993, creating disputed frontier zones and leaving tens of thousands in limbo.

# Summary: World's Major Border Walls The number of major walls protecting borders worldwide has increased dramatically from 16 in 1989 to 66 by 2016, according to researcher Elisabeth Vallet. As President Trump initiated steps toward building a wall on the US-Mexico border, the article examines ten significant frontier barriers globally. Hungary constructed a 110-mile fence along its Serbian border in response to Europe's worst migrant crisis since World War II, with neighboring countries following suit. The Moroccan-occupied Western Sahara features the world's oldest functioning security barrier—a 1,700-mile sand wall separating Moroccan territory from Polisario rebel-controlled land since the 1970s. Saudi Arabia responded to the Islamic State threat by adding a 560-mile fence to its Iraqi border, complete with watchtowers and surveillance infrastructure. Israel began constructing its West Bank security barrier in 2002, citing Palestinian attacks, though critics argue it illegally seizes land. The US-Mexico barrier exceeds 1,000 kilometers, developed following the 1990s border-tightening initiatives and post-9/11 security concerns about illegal immigration and drug trafficking. Greece built the seven-mile Evros wall in 2012 when it became Europe's primary migrant entry point amid economic collapse. Northern Ireland contains 99 "peace lines" separating Protestant and Catholic communities, with origins dating to 1969 during "The Troubles." These barriers have increased despite the 1998 ceasefire. Spain's North African enclaves of Ceuta and Melilla employ high-tech border fences, with deaths occurring during crossing attempts. India has gradually surrounded Bangladesh with a barbed-wire fence since 1993 to restrict immigration, leaving approximately 100,000 people stranded in no-man's land. Finally, Cyprus remains divided between Turkish and Greek Cypriot halves by a wall established following Turkey's 1974 invasion, splitting the capital Nicosia.

Former Netherlands international Quincy Promes has been extradited from the United Arab Emirates to the Netherlands to begin serving prison sentences for drug trafficking and assault, Dutch prosecutors said. The 33-year-old, capped 50 times by the Netherlands, was sentenced in absentia last year to six years for involvement in two cocaine shipments from Brazil via Antwerp to the Netherlands in 2020. In 2023, he also received an 18-month sentence for stabbing a cousin in the knee during a 2020 fight. Promes denies the charges and has appealed both cases. He was arrested in Dubai in March 2024, later released under travel restrictions, and subsequently lost his Spartak Moscow contract.

# Summary Former Dutch international Quincy Promes has been extradited from the United Arab Emirates to the Netherlands to serve jail sentences for drug trafficking and assault. A Dutch court sentenced the 33-year-old former Ajax and Spartak Moscow forward to six years for involvement in cocaine shipments from Brazil through Antwerp to the Netherlands in 2020. He also received an 18-month sentence for assaulting his cousin in 2020. Promes has denied all charges and filed appeals. Spain is moving quickly to protect its gas supplies amid worsening tensions between Algeria and Morocco. Algeria provides about half of Spain’s LNG imports, and after diplomatic fallout with its southern neighbor, it announced that gas for Spain would be routed through a direct pipeline across the Mediterranean rather than the existing line through Morocco. After meeting Algerian officials, he said he was “reassured about the continuity of natural gas supplies” and called Algeria a “first-rate partner.” The timing is sensitive because a 25-year distribution agreement among Spain, Algeria, and Morocco is set to expire at the end of the month, making future gas transport arrangements uncertain. Meanwhile, Spain is also trying to repair ties with Rabat. The rupture with Morocco earlier this year left Madrid in a difficult position, since Morocco is Spain’s key security partner in North Africa on migration, trafficking, and organized crime.

# Summary Spain is securing natural gas supplies amid diplomatic tensions in North Africa. Algeria supplies half of Spain's liquefied natural gas (LNG) imports, traditionally through a pipeline crossing Morocco. Following diplomatic friction between Algeria and Morocco, Algeria announced plans to redirect Spanish-bound gas through a separate Mediterranean pipeline, bypassing Morocco entirely. The article describes how Israeli-made Pegasus spyware, developed by NSO Group Technologies, has been used around the world to monitor journalists, activists, politicians and other public figures, raising fears that it has helped silence critics and enable abuses. It begins with the case of Mexican journalist Cecilio Pineda, who on March 2, 2017, used a Facebook Live broadcast to accuse state and local police of colluding with the leader of a drug cartel. Two hours later, he was shot dead by two men on a motorcycle. Later, the investigative network Forbidden Stories confirmed that both Pineda and the state prosecutor investigating his murder, Xavier Olea Pelaez, had been targeted by Pegasus in the weeks and months before the killing. Pineda’s phone was also missing from the crime scene when authorities arrived. The article then turns to the murder of Washington Post columnist Jamal Khashoggi. Two weeks after Khashoggi was killed inside the Saudi Consulate in Istanbul in October 2018, the digital rights group Citizen Lab reported that his close friend Omar Abdulaziz had been targeted with Pegasus. New findings from Forbidden Stories and its partners say Pegasus was also successfully installed on the phone of Khashoggi’s fiancée, Hatice Cengiz, just four days after his murder. His son Abdullah’s phone was also selected as a target, according to the leaked data analyzed by the consortium. In total, the investigation says the phones of 180 journalists worldwide were selected as targets by NSO clients. Forbidden Stories, working with Amnesty International’s Security Lab, said it had access to a leak of more than 50,000 phone numbers belonging to journalists, politicians, officials, activists and judges that NSO clients had chosen for surveillance. Forensic analysis of phones, carried out by Amnesty’s Security Lab and peer-reviewed by Citizen Lab, confirmed infection or attempted infection in 85% of the cases examined. Amnesty Secretary-General Agnes Callamard said the numbers show abuse is widespread, endangering journalists and their families, undermining press freedom and silencing critical media. NSO Group rejected the findings, saying the reporting was based on “wrong assumptions” and “uncorroborated theories.” It insisted that it was on a “life-saving mission” and argued that the alleged list of more than 50,000 phone numbers could not simply be a list of government targets. NSO says its technology is used only by intelligence agencies against criminals and terrorists. Its transparency report says it has 60 clients in 40 countries and that Pegasus is not a mass-surveillance tool but one that is supposed to collect data only from specific individuals suspected of serious crime or terror. The article also highlights India. Investigative journalist Paranjoy Guha Thakurta said his phone was hacked in 2018 while he was working on a story about the finances of the Ambani business group. He said access to his phone would have allowed attackers to identify his sources. Forbidden Stories says Thakurta is one of at least 40 Indian journalists selected as targets by an NSO client. The phones of two cofounders of The Wire, Siddharth Varadarajan and MK Venu, were infected, with Venu’s phone hacked as recently as July. Other journalists linked to The Wire, including Prem Shankar Jha, Rohini Singh, Devirupa Mitra and Swati Chaturvedi, were also listed as targets. Varadarajan said it was alarming to see so many names connected to the outlet, though many more names not linked to The Wire also appeared in the records. India’s Information Technology Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw dismissed the allegations in parliament, calling them sensational and saying illegal surveillance is not possible because of existing checks and balances. He said the timing of the reports, just before the monsoon session of parliament, was not a coincidence and suggested the story was meant to malign Indian democracy. The article places these revelations in a broader historical context. The Committee to Protect Journalists had previously documented 38 cases since 2011 in which spyware from companies in four countries was used against journalists in nine countries. Cybersecurity expert Eva Galperin of the Electronic Frontier Foundation said early spyware attacks in the 2010s often relied on phishing emails, but Pegasus changed the game by enabling “zero-click” exploits that can infect smartphones without any action by the target. Once installed, Pegasus can give operators full access to a device, including encrypted messaging apps such as Signal, WhatsApp and Telegram. It can record audio and video, track GPS location, retrieve passwords and authentication keys, and be reactivated whenever the phone is turned back on. Galperin said governments have increasingly adopted a “hit and run” approach: infect the phone, extract the data quickly and leave before detection. She also noted that governments once built such tools themselves, but private companies like NSO Group, FinFisher and Hacking Team now sell spyware to states. The article mentions a June 2021 case in which French spyware company Amesys was charged with complicity in torture for selling spyware to Libya between 2007 and 2011; plaintiffs said the surveillance helped identify opponents of Muammar Gaddafi who were later tortured. Overall, the investigation concludes that the Pegasus revelations cast serious doubt on the safeguards meant to prevent misuse of cyberweapons and on NSO Group’s claim that it is helping create “a better, safer world.”

A report says Afghanistan’s drug economy continues to thrive under Taliban rule, sustained by a close relationship between drug cartels and the militant regime. According to Khaama Press, cartels provide farmers with advance payments to grow ephedra and opium, while also supplying financial support that helps keep the Taliban’s “jihadist proto-state” functioning. Drug trafficking has become a major source of revenue in the country, and cartels reportedly use Pakistani channels to obtain the chemicals needed for drug production. Hamid Pakteen, cited by the Afghan Diaspora Network, said traffickers also rely on diverse nationalities as hostages until their groups can pay for drug deliveries, while terrorist groups provide security services in exchange for money. The report traces the roots of the trade back to 1979, when Pakistan’s Inter-Services Intelligence allegedly supported jihadist groups using drug profits. It also says heroin trafficking expanded under General Muhammad Zia-ul-Haq, with officials benefiting from the trade and heroin syndicates gaining political influence. During the first Taliban emirate, cartels reportedly became more institutionalized, threatening farmers who refused to grow poppies and using routes through Iran, eastern Turkey, Central Asia and Russia. The article says trafficking from Afghanistan into Pakistan remains largely unchecked because of weak investigations and lenient court decisions. It also notes that Afghanistan has become a major crystal meth supplier since 2017, when traffickers realized ephedra could be used to make ephedrine, a key meth ingredient. Despite the Taliban’s public ban on poppy cultivation, opium production continues, driven by poverty and the regime’s financial dependence on the trade. Khaama Press said opium accounted for 12% to 14% of Afghanistan’s GDP in 2021, and output has risen 34% despite the ban.

# Summary Afghanistan's drug trade has flourished under Taliban rule through a symbiotic relationship between drug cartels and the regime. Cartels provide farmers with advances to plant opium and ephedra while offering financial support to sustain the Taliban government. Pakistani sources supply chemicals needed for drug production, and diverse nationalities are held hostage until cartels can afford drug deliveries. In exchange, terrorist groups provide security services for payment. This arrangement traces back to 1979 when Pakistan's Inter-Services Intelligence supported jihadist groups to fund drug trafficking, leading to increased heroin production. During the first Taliban emirate, cartels institutionalized their control, forcing farmers to cultivate poppies under threat. Trafficking routes extended through Iran, Turkey, Central Asia, and Russia to Europe. The drug trade from Afghanistan to Pakistan remains largely unchecked due to weak investigations and lenient court sentences. Since 2017, Afghanistan has become a major crystal meth supplier after traffickers discovered native ephedra could produce ephedrine, a key meth ingredient. Despite announcing a ban on poppy cultivation, the Taliban has not enforced it, as opium remains the primary income source for both farmers and the cash-strapped government. Opium production contributed 12-14 percent of Afghanistan's GDP in 2021, worth USD 1.8-2.7 billion. Production has increased 34 percent despite the official cultivation ban.

Na’ama Issachar, a 27-year-old dual American-Israeli citizen, returned to Israel this week after spending 10 months in a Russian prison, ending a case that drew intense public attention and political speculation in Israel. Her ordeal began during a layover in Moscow while she was flying on Aeroflot from India to Israel. According to the article, she was arrested on drug-trafficking charges after Russian authorities said she had less than 10 grams of cannabis in her possession. The article emphasizes that the drugs were allegedly found not on her person or in her carry-on luggage, but in checked baggage that she was not planning to retrieve in Moscow and that was supposed to be checked through to Tel Aviv. Despite this, Russia arrested and prosecuted her, ultimately sentencing her to 7.5 years in prison, a punishment described as wildly disproportionate for what would be a misdemeanor in many other places and, the article suggests, even under Russian law. Russia maintained that she had the drugs, but there were also reports that the case may have been staged, with Issachar unknowingly forced to collect her luggage and leave the airport so she could be caught with planted drugs. Her arrest quickly became a major story in Israel. The public reaction was one of outrage and disbelief, with many Israelis viewing the case as fabricated and unjust. It also raised concerns about whether traveling through Russia was safe, not because of the airline itself, but because of the possibility of politically motivated Russian arrests. The article then explores possible reasons Russia might have targeted Issachar. At first, some believed her detention was meant to pressure Israel not to extradite a Russian man accused of massive internet fraud to the United States; that man has since been extradited and pleaded guilty. Another theory was that Russia was trying to gain leverage over Israel regarding a parcel of land in central Jerusalem that Israel had purchased from Russia in 1964 for $3.5 million. The article notes that many Israelis oppose any move that would give Russia a greater presence in Jerusalem. Issachar’s release this week came through a pardon from Russian President Vladimir Putin, but the article says there is widespread speculation about what Israel may have agreed to in return. One factor likely involved in the background is the complicated relationship between Israel and Russia over Syria. Russia effectively controls much of Syrian airspace and territory, while Israel has been able to carry out strikes against Iranian and other military targets there with relative freedom. The article suggests that this arrangement likely depends on a tacit understanding between the two countries, and that Russia may be expecting something in exchange for allowing Israel that operational freedom. The writer argues that it is implausible to think Putin acted purely out of humanitarian concern. Instead, he suggests that some kind of political or strategic compensation likely played a role, though it may never be made public, especially before Israel’s March election. This leaves many Israelis asking whether the price of Issachar’s freedom was worth it. The article then broadens into a reflection on the Jewish obligation to redeem captives, drawing on the author’s personal experience with efforts to free captives from Russia in the Soviet era. It notes that Jewish tradition strongly supports redeeming captives, but not at any cost. If paying a ransom or making concessions would encourage more kidnappings, redemption may be discouraged or even forbidden. A historical example is Rabbi Meir of Rothenburg, who was said to have refused efforts to free him because he feared it would encourage similar hostage-taking of others. The same dilemma appears in modern Israel, the article says, especially in cases involving captured soldiers or even the return of their remains. Israel has often paid very high prices, including releasing terrorists with blood on their hands, in order to bring Israelis home. At the same time, officials worry that soldiers might fight less boldly if they believed the state would not try to retrieve them. This tension has led some religious soldiers to sign documents stating they should not be exchanged for terrorists if captured. In concluding, the article acknowledges the relief and joy felt by Issachar and her family, but says Israelis will continue to wonder what Russia received in return, whether the bargain was justified, and whether a government should devote so much effort and political capital to securing the release of one civilian imprisoned abroad.

# Politics, Diplomacy, and Redeeming Captives in Israel On January 31, 2020, Na'ama Issachar, a 27-year-old dual American-Israeli citizen, returned home to Israel after enduring a 10-month ordeal in Russia's judicial system. Issachar had been arrested during a layover in Moscow while traveling on Aeroflot from India to Israel—a popular route for Israeli tourists and businesspeople seeking affordable international connections. During this routine layover, Russian authorities arrested her for drug trafficking, claiming she possessed less than 10 grams of cannabis. The circumstances surrounding her arrest appeared highly suspicious to many observers. The alleged drugs were not found on her person or in her carry-on luggage; rather, they were purportedly discovered in her checked baggage—luggage to which she had no access during the layover and which she had not intended to retrieve in Moscow, as it was meant to be checked through to Tel Aviv. Despite these questionable circumstances, Russia sentenced Issachar to an extraordinarily harsh 7.5 years in prison for what would constitute merely a misdemeanor in most countries, including Russia itself. Some observers suspected the drugs may have been planted, with reports suggesting Issachar was forced to retrieve her luggage to be caught with the contraband. The case generated widespread attention in Israeli media and sparked public outcry, raising serious concerns about the safety of flying through Russian territory. Israelis questioned whether the arrest was politically motivated rather than based on genuine criminal conduct, prompting broader concerns about potential Russian leverage against Israel. Initial speculation about Russia's motivations varied considerably. One theory suggested Russia sought to pressure Israel not to extradite a Russian citizen arrested for massive internet fraud to America—though this individual was subsequently extradited and pleaded guilty. Another theory proposed Russia was using Issachar as a bargaining chip to pressure Israel into returning land in central Jerusalem that Israel had purchased from Russia in 1964 for $3.5 million, a proposal Israelis widely opposed. When Russian President Vladimir Putin pardoned Issachar this week, widespread speculation erupted regarding what reciprocal concessions Israel had committed to in return. Analysts focused particularly on Israel's military operations in Syria, where Russia maintains significant control. Israel has reportedly enjoyed relative freedom to strike Iranian and other military targets in Syrian territory, presumably with tacit Russian approval or facilitation. Many observers found it implausible that Putin would release Issachar purely from humanitarian motives without receiving substantial benefits, likely related to Israel's operational latitude in Syria or other strategic considerations. The author, Jonathan Feldstein, draws parallels to Jewish historical experiences with captive redemption. Jewish tradition mandates redeeming captives, but not unconditionally. The tradition prohibits redemption if doing so would encourage future kidnappings or create dangerous precedents. A famous medieval example involved Rabbi Meir of Rothenburg, who reportedly forbade his community from ransoming him to prevent establishing a pattern of targeting Jewish leaders. Modern Israel faces similar dilemmas regarding captive soldiers and prisoners. Israel has historically paid substantial prices—including releasing numerous imprisoned terrorists—to recover captured soldiers and remains, though this practice remains contentious. Some religious soldiers have even signed documents prohibiting their exchange for terrorists should they be captured. The fundamental question raised by Issachar's case concerns the appropriate extent to which nations should expend resources and diplomatic capital to redeem civilians held captive in foreign countries for alleged civil crimes, particularly when sentences appear disproportionately harsh and circumstances seem fabricated. While Israelis celebrate Issachar's return and the end of her ordeal, many continue questioning whether the unknown price paid to Putin justified the redemption, and whether securing her release set a dangerous precedent encouraging future Russian exploitation of Israeli civilians.

Drug use is rising among Iraqi youth, prompting authorities in Wasit province to launch a broad campaign against hallucinogen dealers and addicts. The problem is visible in several parts of the country: in Baghdad’s Mansour district, young women have been seen smoking hallucinogenic drugs in coffee shops, while in Basra, abuse is widespread among young boys, students and unemployed people who can easily buy drugs from street peddlers. Basra recorded 31 overdose deaths in the first half of the year. Pharmacists and officials say the substances being abused are not limited to illegal street drugs. Hussein Abu Laban, a pharmacist, said young people are misusing a wide range of medicines, including pills for schizophrenia, severe depression, Parkinson’s tremors, arthritis pain and inflammation, as well as tranquilizers and hallucinogens such as LSD. He said addicts often use them for excitement in the same way others use marijuana, cocaine or heroin. He also highlighted Tramadol, a highly addictive painkiller that acts as a nervous system tranquilizer, noting that users quickly develop tolerance and keep increasing the dose until they cannot stop. A Baghdad pharmacist, speaking anonymously, said drug trafficking is profitable for some pharmacy owners and drugstores, and corruption helps narcotics reach the streets through middlemen. There are also accusations that government officials are involved in covering up trafficking. In January, the parliamentary Health and Environment Committee said expired medications, unlicensed drugs and hallucinogens were spreading after authorities seized a vehicle in Baghdad carrying 70 cartons of unauthorized medicines. Another growing concern is local production. Judges revealed late last year that traffickers in crystal methamphetamine were trying to expand into Iraq by setting up local labs. While smuggling through Iraq’s porous border with Iran has long been a major source of narcotics, reports now say Iraq has become not just a transit route but also a distribution point for neighboring countries, with traffickers from East Asia increasingly targeting the Iraqi market. Experts and lawmakers link addiction to social pressures. A University of Wasit sociologist said field research found many teenagers turn to drugs to escape romantic, family or psychological problems. A parliamentary labor committee member said there are no official addiction statistics, but the number has risen sharply in the past five years, driven by unemployment and poverty. Iraq’s 2016 drug law imposes severe penalties, including confiscation of property and, in some cases, life imprisonment or the death penalty. But psychologists argue that punishment alone will not solve the problem. They call for treatment centers, psychological care, social support, and better border control, along with sports and recreational programs to help young people and the unemployed find healthier outlets.

# Drug Abuse Epidemic Among Iraqi Youth Iraq is experiencing a growing crisis of drug abuse among its young population, with narcotics and hallucinogens becoming increasingly prevalent across major cities. The Wasit Crime Combating Directorate has launched a campaign to address both drug trafficking and addiction in east-central Iraq. ## Scope of the Problem Drug abuse is widespread in urban areas, with young women smoking hallucinogenic drugs in Baghdad's coffee shops and young men, students, and unemployed individuals in Basra easily obtaining substances from street peddlers. Basra alone recorded 31 drug overdose deaths in the first half of this year. Experts acknowledge that accurate addiction statistics don't exist, but numbers have increased significantly over the past five years. ## Types of Drugs Beyond traditional narcotics like marijuana, cocaine, and heroin, young Iraqis are abusing prescription medications intended for serious conditions—antipsychotics, antidepressants, Parkinson's treatments, and arthritis pain relievers. Tramadol, a highly addictive narcotic painkiller, is particularly problematic due to its rapid addiction potential. LSD and crystal methamphetamine are also emerging threats, with traffickers establishing local methamphetamine labs. ## Sources and Trafficking Narcotics reach Iraqi streets through multiple channels: smuggling across porous borders with Iran, local pharmaceutical corruption, unauthorized medication distribution, and increasingly, local drug manufacturing. Iraq has transitioned from merely a transit point to a primary distribution hub for East Asian drug traffickers. ## Root Causes Experts identify multiple factors driving addiction. Sociologist Maged Murhac al-Sultani notes that teenagers use drugs to escape romantic, family, and psychological problems. Rising unemployment and poverty exacerbate the issue, with young people seeking excitement and escape from meaningless lives. ## Government Response Iraq implemented a 2016 Drugs and Mental Stimulants law imposing severe penalties, including property confiscation, life sentences, and death penalties for trafficking offenses. However, experts argue punitive measures alone are insufficient. ## Proposed Solutions Parliamentary officials advocate a comprehensive national strategy focusing on rehabilitation rather than punishment. Proposed measures include establishing advanced treatment centers offering psychological counseling and social research, stricter border control, and creating sports and entertainment centers to engage unemployed youth in positive activities. According to psychologist Qassem Hussein Saleh, addressing underlying social and psychological problems is essential to genuinely solving Iraq's drug crisis.

output_text: The RCMP has launched a major round of arrests in the Montreal area as part of what it says is the third and final phase of Project Clemenza, a long-running investigation into Mafia-linked drug trafficking. The operation targeted 15 people and focused on cocaine smuggling and trafficking networks tied to organized crime in Greater Montreal. Among those arrested was Liborio “Pancho” Cuntrera, 47, who police sources have described as a possible leader in what remains of the Rizzuto organization. Cuntrera is the son of Agostino Cuntrera, a Rizzuto associate who was killed in St-Leonard in 2010 during a period when the Montreal Mafia was under pressure from rivals. Liborio Cuntrera also represents the second generation of the Cuntrera-Caruana family, a wealthy and internationally known drug-smuggling group. He was not taken into custody Wednesday because he is on vacation in Italy, but sources said he has been in contact with the RCMP and has agreed to surrender when he returns to Canada in a few days. Another target was Martino Caputo, 42, who is already serving a 12-year sentence in Kingston for his role in a cocaine-smuggling conspiracy involving an attempt to bring in a tonne of cocaine into Canada every month. Caputo also faces separate murder charges in Ontario related to a 2012 killing. The article also notes the case history of another figure, Crivello, who in 2004 received a three-year sentence for unlawful confinement and aggravated assault after hiring men to recover $60,000 he believed had been stolen. Three victims were held, beaten, and one required surgery. While before the Parole Board in 2005, Crivello admitted he had been involved in drug trafficking since the age of 17. Frank Iaconetti, 48, was also arrested Wednesday. He previously served time in a federal penitentiary after pleading guilty in 1999 in U.S. District Court in Massachusetts to participating in a cocaine-distribution conspiracy. Court records say he delivered $250,000 in cash to undercover agents as a down payment on 100 kilograms of cocaine intended for Canada. At sentencing, a judge was told there was little evidence he knew the full details of the deal. Iaconetti said at the time that he had agreed to deliver the money because of a severe gambling addiction and had even asked to be banned from the Montreal casino. RCMP said Project Clemenza was delayed after investigators uncovered evidence connected to the murder of Salvatore Montagna, a New York Mafia figure involved in efforts to wrest control from the Rizzuto organization about six years earlier. Because of that delay, some charges filed in Montreal date back to 2011, including allegations against Liborio Cuntrera and Marco Pizzi, 46, of Montreal North, for cocaine trafficking between Sept. 28 and Oct. 6, 2011. Police say the drug network brought cocaine in through the United States and relied on commercial ground-transport contacts. Authorities in Canada and the United States have seized more than 220 kilograms of cocaine and more than $2 million in connection with the investigation. The RCMP said the operation would have a significant impact on organized crime and drug-smuggling activity in the Greater Montreal region. Among those arrested was also Hansley Joseph, 36, a well-known Montreal street-gang member who was often seen with Mafia-linked traffickers during Project Colisee, a major earlier investigation that severely weakened the Rizzuto organization. Joseph had already served two years in prison for his role in a northern Montreal drug-trafficking network. In 2005, he was among about two dozen men charged in one of Canada’s first gangsterism cases against street-gang members. Court findings later said he was part of the “Dope Squad” and regularly supplied cocaine to the Pelletier St. gang, which sold crack in north Montreal.

Hamilton Mayor Fred Eisenberger says Canadian municipalities can no longer wait for federal or provincial governments to create international economic opportunities, especially as U.S. President Donald Trump threatens to upend NAFTA. Speaking from Bogotá, Eisenberger said Hamilton and the nearby Niagara region are strengthening ties with Colombia, a relationship that began during the Pan Am Games in the Greater Toronto Area two years earlier. Trump has repeatedly said he wants to renegotiate NAFTA, arguing the trade pact disadvantages the United States. On Aug. 27, he again tweeted that the U.S. was in a renegotiation process with Canada and Mexico and suggested the agreement might have to be terminated. Eisenberger responded sharply on Twitter, saying the only thing that should be terminated was Trump’s presidency. In comments to The Canadian Press, he said his reaction reflected growing frustration with what he described as Trump’s divisive politics, misogyny and racism. Although he believes NAFTA will survive because of its importance to the U.S., he said the president’s rhetoric is “ridiculous.” The mayor is leading a 12-day delegation to three Colombian cities: Bogotá, Barranquilla and Medellin. Business and institutional representatives from the Hamilton area are joining him, including Air Canada Cargo, Kubes Steel, McMaster University and Mohawk College. The trip is aimed at building direct business links and exploring opportunities in sectors such as agribusiness, information and communications, and advanced manufacturing. Eisenberger said Colombia has become an especially attractive partner because it has moved beyond years of insurgency tied to drug cartels and is now seen as more stable and open to growth. The relationship was initially sparked by contacts made during the Pan Am Games, when Hamilton hosted visitors from the Americas, including Colombians. Local business leaders say Trump’s comments are already affecting decisions. Justin Avery, CEO of Hamilton-based Xeist Inc., said he recently returned from Colombia looking for a manufacturer to produce sportswear for his company. He said the uncertainty around NAFTA and possible tariff hikes makes it necessary to consider alternative markets and suppliers. Among the concrete outcomes expected from the trip, McMaster Innovation Park is set to sign a memorandum of understanding with a Colombian counterpart.

Ohio’s Organized Crime Investigations Commission (OOCIC), a statewide drug enforcement effort that brings together federal, state and local agencies, reported that its major drug interdiction task forces seized more than $42 million in illegal narcotics in 2021. That total was up from $29 million in seizures in 2020, according to an announcement made Wednesday, Dec. 22, by Ohio Attorney General Dave Yost, Gov. Mike DeWine and Homeland Security Investigations Special Agent-in-Charge Vance Callender. Officials said the sharp increase in seizure totals was driven by several factors: the addition of a new OOCIC task force, the expansion of existing task forces, higher levels of drug trafficking in Ohio and the completion of long-running investigations. In addition to the large narcotics seizures, task forces also confiscated 7,906 opioid pain pills and 1,205 other prescription pain pills during the year. Yost praised the officers involved, describing them as “guardians on the wall” who protect Ohio residents from overdoses and death by intercepting drugs before they reach communities. He said the larger quantities of heroin, fentanyl and methamphetamine seized in 2021 showed that the task forces were staying ahead of traffickers, and he expressed optimism about continued success in 2022. The task forces operate through partnerships between Homeland Security Investigations and local law enforcement agencies across Ohio. They are funded through RecoveryOhio, working alongside the Ohio Department of Public Safety and Ohio Criminal Justice Services. Callender said the task forces’ success was due to the “tireless efforts” of police officers and special agents working together to arrest and prosecute people who profit from addiction. He noted that HSI contributes national and international resources so that investigations can reach beyond street-level dealers to the organizers and suppliers behind larger criminal networks. The article highlighted several major seizures and investigations from 2021: In Hamilton County, the Major Drug Interdiction Task Force made four significant seizures in April of narcotics headed to southwest Ohio from California, including more than 5 pounds of heroin and 43 pounds of methamphetamine. In November, after a long investigation that ended in the federal felony indictment of four people, the task force seized 25 pounds of fentanyl, 1.2 pounds of cocaine, 38 pounds of marijuana, 13 firearms and $43,701. The task force includes the Hamilton County Sheriff’s Office, Regional Narcotics Unit, HSI and the Hamilton County Prosecutor’s Office. The Licking, Muskingum and Guernsey Major Drug Interdiction Task Force, known as CODE, seized 2,350 grams of methamphetamine and 2,718 counterfeit Oxycodone pills containing fentanyl in June, leading to the arrest of two Licking County men. In September, the same task force seized 24.5 pounds of methamphetamine worth more than $500,000. Its members include sheriff’s offices from several counties, the Ohio State Highway Patrol, the U.S. Postal Inspector, HSI and the Licking County Prosecutor’s Office. The Medina and Summit task force, ONSET, seized 13 kilograms of cocaine and a loaded handgun in September from suspects tied to a vehicle linked to the Southwest border. Its partners include law enforcement agencies from Medina and Summit counties, the Copley Township Police Department, HSI, the DEA, highway patrol and county drug task forces and prosecutors. In Belmont County, the task force seized 9 pounds of methamphetamine, 6 ounces of cocaine, $3,861 and a loaded firearm in March during the arrest of a Bellaire man. In October, multiple search warrants led to the seizure of more than 1 pound of methamphetamine and other narcotics, along with paraphernalia and packaging materials. The Miami Valley Bulk Smuggling Task Force identified a suspected trafficker in Montgomery County in November and seized 10 kilograms of cocaine and 1 pound of marijuana. In December, it arrested Jose Noriega-Rodriquez of Sinaloa, Mexico, on narcotics trafficking charges. Over the course of that investigation, detectives seized 10 kilograms of fentanyl, 2 kilograms of cocaine, 1 kilogram of heroin, 336 grams of methamphetamine, 4 pounds of marijuana and about $150,000. In Central Ohio, a February investigation disrupted a trafficking operation connecting Columbus and Las Vegas. Three people were indicted on federal cocaine-distribution charges after investigators determined the group used short-term rentals in Columbus and other East Coast cities as mailing locations to bring in smuggled cocaine from Mexico. After the drugs were sold locally, the cash was sent back to Las Vegas. Authorities said the network had shipped and distributed more than 100 kilograms of cocaine and over $1 million. In Toledo, a task force working with police gang and SWAT units executed a search warrant in April tied to California-based drug trafficking. Brandon Moore was arrested and charged with multiple trafficking and weapons offenses after authorities seized more than 20 pounds of marijuana, other drugs, a loaded pistol and $48,000. Together, the examples illustrated how OOCIC task forces used coordinated intelligence, local policing and federal support to target drug trafficking networks across Ohio in 2021.

A Waterloo restaurant manager who sold cocaine during the pandemic has been sentenced to 30 months in prison after police found nearly a pound of the drug in her home. Nicole Kopiasz, 31, of Kitchener, pleaded guilty this week to possession of cocaine for the purpose of trafficking. In March 2021, police searching her Bankside Crescent house seized 454 grams of cocaine, about $12,000 in cash, and 14 cellphones. They also found four legally owned firearms that were locked up in the home. Kopiasz was arrested later when she arrived at a Husky gas station on Highland Road West in Kitchener. Court heard that Kopiasz had studied culinary arts at Conestoga College, started at the restaurant as a waitress, and eventually became a manager. She was also close to obtaining her real estate licence. Her lawyer, Daniel Mulak, told the court that the pandemic left her in a “very dire” financial position and she turned to drug dealing to support her lifestyle and schooling. Justice Matthew Stanley noted her skills and abilities, but accepted the joint sentencing recommendation from the defence and Crown. Prosecutor Andrew Nisker said the operation was unsophisticated and described Kopiasz as a street-level dealer. He said her car being registered in her name was the kind of mistake an experienced trafficker would avoid. The Crown agreed to the 30-month sentence partly because of possible Charter issues at trial and because Kopiasz pleaded guilty, showing remorse. Kopiasz has no prior criminal record. The conviction means she cannot work as a real estate agent, though her restaurant job will be waiting when she is released, her lawyer said. The judge also imposed a weapons ban, ordered the firearms and cash forfeited, and required her to provide a DNA sample. Stanley said she has good prospects for rehabilitation.

# Restaurant Manager Sentenced for Cocaine Trafficking Nicole Kopiasz, a 31-year-old manager at a Waterloo restaurant, was sentenced to 30 months in prison after pleading guilty to possession of cocaine for trafficking purposes. In March 2021, police executed a search warrant at Kopiasz's home following a tip about drug sales. Officers discovered approximately 454 grams of cocaine, $12,000 in cash, fourteen cellphones, and four legally-owned firearms. She was arrested at a nearby gas station. Kopiasz had worked her way up from waitress to manager at the restaurant while completing a culinary arts program at Conestoga College. She was also pursuing a real estate license. According to her defense lawyer, financial hardship during the COVID-19 pandemic motivated her to turn to drug trafficking to fund her lifestyle and education. The Crown described it as an unsophisticated operation, noting that Kopiasz made amateur mistakes, such as registering her car in her own name—something experienced dealers would avoid. She was characterized as a street-level dealer rather than a major trafficker. Justice Matthew Stanley accepted the joint recommendation from both the defense and Crown prosecutor for the 30-month sentence, which he noted is at the low end of the typical range. The Crown agreed to this lighter sentence due to potential Charter issues at trial, Kopiasz's guilty plea demonstrating remorse, and the significance of imprisonment for someone with no prior criminal record. The judge imposed a weapons ban, ordered forfeiture of the firearms and cash, and required a DNA sample. Kopiasz's restaurant employer has promised to rehire her upon release. The judge expressed confidence in her rehabilitation prospects.

British Columbia Premier David Eby plans to ask Prime Minister Mark Carney to designate the Lawrence Bishnoi gang as a terrorist group, according to the Vancouver Sun. Eby said the issue is not limited to British Columbia but also affects Alberta and Ontario, where South Asian community members have reportedly faced extortion, threats, and violence linked to the gang. He said he would write to Carney to seek the designation so police would have stronger tools to investigate the group’s activities. Eby described the move as serious and said it was not being made lightly, arguing that the gang’s actions undermine public confidence in the justice system and democracy. He pointed to a previous federal action against a Mexican drug cartel as an example of similar steps taken before. The article also noted a case involving Satish Kumar, president of the Lakshmi Narayan Mandir Temple and owner of Reflections Banquet Halls, who said he was threatened after refusing to pay USD 2 million to an extortionist. Separately, India’s NIA recently arrested Rahul Sarkar, described as a key aide to the Bishnoi gang, for helping members obtain fake passports to evade arrest.

# Summary British Columbia Premier David Eby plans to request that Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney designate the Lawrence Bishnoi gang as a "terrorist group." This move aims to provide law enforcement with enhanced investigative tools to combat the gang's activities. The Bishnoi gang has been linked to extortion and crimes targeting South Asian communities across British Columbia, Alberta, and Ontario. Victims are being threatened with violence or death to extort cash payments. Eby emphasized this is a serious concern affecting public confidence in the justice system and democracy. A notable victim, Satish Kumar, president of Lakshmi Narayan Mandir Temple, received death threats after refusing to pay $2 million to an extortionist. Eby referenced the Canadian government's previous action against a Mexican drug cartel to justify the recommendation. In related developments, India's National Investigation Agency arrested Rahul Sarkar in May, a key aide managing the gang's fake passport operation, which helped members evade arrest by fleeing the country.

Alberta police and U.S. authorities say they have dismantled a major international drug network after seizing more than $15 million in drugs, about $4.5 million in cash and assets, and 13 firearms in a two-year investigation called Project Coyote. Dwayne Lakusta, head of Alberta Law Enforcement Response Teams (ALERT), said the haul includes what is believed to be the largest fentanyl seizure in Canada. ALERT alleges the network was led by Warren Lowe, 53, of Calgary, who now faces 23 charges related to organized crime, drugs and firearms. Police say the operation stretched from British Columbia to Ontario and also involved cocaine importation routes extending into the United States. The investigation began in February 2018 after a tip led police to 250,000 fentanyl pills in a downtown Calgary apartment. No one was home and no arrests were made at the time. Investigators later uncovered a major cocaine distribution and importation scheme. A key break came on May 18, when Calgary police, the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration and the Harris County Sheriff’s Office intercepted an 81-kilogram cocaine shipment in Houston. Calgary woman Elizabeth Fisher, 49, was arrested and remains in a Texas prison; a Canadian warrant has also been issued for her arrest. Police said that seizure prompted search warrants and arrests in Canada. Officials stressed they were targeting the people running the network, not just couriers. More than 30 search warrants were executed, with the latest arrest on Oct. 3. In total, seven people have been arrested and face 77 charges. The investigation involved multiple agencies, including the Calgary Police Service, RCMP, Canada Revenue Agency, U.S. Department of Homeland Security, and other Canadian law enforcement partners.

# Calgary Drug Bust Targets Alleged International Crime Kingpin Alberta police and U.S. officials have dismantled a major international drug network through Project Coyote, a two-year investigation resulting in significant seizures and multiple arrests. The operation netted over $15 million in drugs, approximately $4.5 million in cash and assets, and 13 firearms. Most notably, it includes Canada's largest fentanyl seizure. In February 2018, police discovered 250,000 fentanyl pills in a downtown Calgary apartment.
