This seizure prompted Canadian authorities to execute search warrants and arrests domestically, targeting the network's leadership rather than low-level couriers. Seven individuals total have been arrested and face 77 criminal charges, including Lowe, the Fishers, Emanuel Amha, Olivier Kenge, Cole Leblanc, and Victoria Pon from Vancouver. The investigation involved unprecedented coordination between the Calgary Police Service, RCMP, DEA, Canada Revenue Agency, U.S. Department of Homeland Security, and multiple regional Canadian law enforcement agencies. The investigation remains ongoing.

Pablo Garcia Ortiz, a 50-year-old man from Orange, Texas, was sentenced to three years in federal prison after pleading guilty to possession with intent to distribute cocaine. U.S. District Judge David S. Morales also ordered five years of supervised release. Ortiz may remain on bond for now but must later surrender to the Bureau of Prisons. According to court records, on Nov. 1, 2024, Ortiz drove a Freightliner tractor to the Sarita Border Patrol checkpoint in South Texas, where a K-9 alerted officers to the vehicle. Investigators said Ortiz tried to hide the smell of narcotics by pouring urine inside the cab and later claimed officers had planted evidence. Agents then found 22 bundles of cocaine, weighing about 24 kilograms, concealed in a blue toolbox under the truck bed. The drugs were wrapped in a trash bag and cardboard box and tested positive for cocaine. Officers also found chili powder in the vehicle, which is sometimes used to evade detection dogs. A search of Ortiz’s phone revealed evidence of another cocaine-smuggling attempt in September 2024. The case was investigated by the DEA and Border Patrol and prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorney Izaak Bruce.

# Summary A 50-year-old man from Orange, Texas, Pablo Garcia Ortiz, has been sentenced to three years in federal prison for attempting to smuggle cocaine through a South Texas checkpoint. On November 1, 2024, Ortiz drove a Freightliner truck to the Sarita Border Patrol checkpoint, where a drug-detection dog alerted officers to the vehicle. Agents discovered approximately 24 kilograms of cocaine hidden in a blue toolbox beneath the truck's bed, packaged in a trash bag and cardboard box. Ortiz pleaded guilty to possession with intent to distribute cocaine on April 2. In addition to his 36-month prison sentence, he received five years of supervised release. Investigators found chili powder in the vehicle, a substance commonly used to mask narcotics from detection dogs. Evidence from Ortiz's phone also revealed an earlier smuggling attempt in September 2024. The Drug Enforcement Administration and U.S. Border Patrol investigated the case.

Antonio Reynoso Gonzalez, 72, a Mexican businessman extradited to the U.S. two decades after a 1995 indictment, pleaded guilty in San Diego federal court to conspiracy to import cocaine for distribution. Prosecutors said he helped arrange Sinaloa cartel shipments and that his family’s food-import business lent legitimacy to El Chapo Guzman’s operations. Though the charge carries a 10-year minimum, prosecutors will recommend about eight years because of his age, health and acceptance of responsibility.

# Summary Seventy-two-year-old Mexican businessman Antonio Reynoso Gonzalez was extradited to the U.S. and pleaded guilty in San Diego federal court to conspiring to import cocaine for the Sinaloa cartel. Charged in 1995, he used his family's food importation business to legitimize drug operations for "El Chapo" Guzman. The conspiracy charge carries a mandatory ten-year minimum sentence, though prosecutors recommend eight years considering his age and health.

On 6 November in Washington, President Donald Trump and Uzbekistan’s President Shavkat Mirziyoyev announced a broad package of planned economic, security, and humanitarian cooperation, according to the U.S. State Department. Uzbekistan said it intends to invest billions of dollars in the United States and in U.S. companies, while both governments said the agreements are meant to support stability and prosperity. The deal set includes joint development of mineral deposits and up to $400 million in investments in the United States and Uzbekistan to strengthen supply chains for strategic and rare-earth materials. Uzbekistan also committed to purchasing small modular reactors from American energy companies. In a major aviation agreement, contracts were signed for 22 Boeing 787 Dreamliner aircraft worth $8.5 billion, which the U.S. said will support the American aviation industry. Agriculture was another major focus. Uzbekistan pledged to buy up to $2 billion in agricultural machinery, along with up to two million tons of soybeans and 100,000 tons of cotton from the United States over three years, benefiting American farmers. The country also plans to import $5 billion worth of automotive components and deepen cooperation around the privatization of UzAuto Motors. Separately, Air Products plans to invest up to $3 billion in a methanol plant in Uzbekistan. The two sides also want to expand work on methanol-to-olefins and carbon-chemical projects. Uzbekistan said it will introduce a 30-day visa-free regime for U.S. citizens starting in 2026. The countries also agreed to expand security cooperation, including information sharing against criminal groups and drug cartels, and stronger border protection using American equipment.

# Summary On November 6, President Donald Trump and Uzbekistan's President Shavkat Mirziyoyev announced major bilateral agreements involving billions of dollars in investments and purchases. **Key Economic Agreements:** Uzbekistan committed to purchasing 22 Boeing 787 Dreamliner aircraft valued at $8.5 billion. The country also pledged to buy up to 2 million tons of soybeans and 100,000 tons of cotton from the United States over three years, along with $2 billion in agricultural machinery. Additional commitments include acquiring $5 billion in automotive components and developing partnerships related to UzAuto Motors privatization. Uzbekistan will invest up to $400 million in U.S. and domestic supply chains for strategic and rare-earth elements, and purchase small modular reactors from American energy companies. **Industrial Development:** Air Products plans a $3 billion investment in a methanol production plant in Uzbekistan, with expansion into methanol-to-olefins and carbon-chemical industries. **Other Initiatives:** The agreements also address security cooperation, including law enforcement information sharing and border protection enhancement. Uzbekistan will introduce a 30-day visa-free regime for U.S. citizens starting in 2026 to promote economic and business opportunities. Both nations emphasized strengthening comprehensive economic, security, and humanitarian cooperation for regional stability and mutual prosperity.

St. Petersburg customs officers, working with Russia’s FSB, intercepted two cocaine smuggling attempts totaling more than 100 kilograms, the Northwestern Customs Administration said. The drugs were found in 100 identical briquettes wrapped in plastic and hidden in the technological cavities of banana containers that arrived by ship from Belgium at the port of St. Petersburg. Two criminal cases have been opened for large-scale drug smuggling.

# Cocaine Seizure at St. Petersburg Port St. Petersburg customs officers discovered over 100 kilograms of cocaine hidden among banana shipments from Belgium. Working with Russia's Federal Security Service, they found 100 identical drug-filled briquettes concealed in container cavities. The operation prevented two major smuggling incidents. Two criminal cases were filed under Russian law for large-scale drug smuggling.

Armenian law-enforcement authorities have arrested a Turkish citizen accused of smuggling 97 kilograms of heroin from Iran into Armenia. The State Revenue Committee (SRC) said the unidentified man was driving a truck that was searched at a customs checkpoint on the Armenian-Iranian border, where officers discovered the drugs hidden in makeshift metal containers attached to the vehicle. According to the SRC, the heroin was packed into 119 plastic boxes. Vartan Vartanian, head of the SRC’s anti-smuggling unit, estimated the seized narcotics were worth between $10 million and $11 million on the market. Vartanian said investigators expect more arrests and are working intensively with Armenia’s National Security Service and police to identify everyone connected to the case. He described the seizure as the second major heroin bust reported in Armenia this year. In late February and early March, authorities said they had confiscated more than 365 kilograms of heroin smuggled from Iran and arrested at least six Armenian and foreign nationals in connection with that case. Officials said those drugs were also intended for Europe. The article notes that Armenia has seen large heroin seizures before, including a record 850-kilogram bust in 2014 tied to a Turkish-led trafficking ring. Iran is widely considered the main source of drug trafficking through Armenia, with many Iranians and local accomplices imprisoned there on related charges.

# Turkish Citizen Arrested in Armenia After Massive Heroin Seizure Armenian law enforcement authorities arrested a Turkish citizen accused of smuggling 97 kilograms of heroin from Iran. The State Revenue Committee (SRC) discovered the Class A drug hidden in plastic boxes within a truck at an Armenian-Iranian border customs checkpoint. The seizure, valued at $10-11 million, consisted of 119 packs of heroin. This represents the second major heroin seizure in Armenia this year. Authorities indicated that additional arrests are likely as investigations continue into all individuals potentially connected to the smuggling operation. In late February and early March, Armenian officials seized over 365 kilograms of heroin smuggled from Iran, resulting in arrests of six Armenian and foreign nationals. The drugs were reportedly destined for Europe. Similar drug trafficking incidents have occurred regionally. In February, Bulgarian authorities seized 400 kilograms of Iranian heroin and arrested two Turkish citizens. Armenia's largest drug bust occurred in 2014, when authorities confiscated 850 kilograms of heroin allegedly smuggled by a Turkish-led trafficking ring. The leader received a 19-year prison sentence. Iran remains the primary source of drug trafficking through Armenia. Since the 1990s, hundreds of Iranians and local accomplices have been imprisoned there on drug charges. Iran faces significant drug trafficking challenges due to its borders with Afghanistan, the world's largest opium producer, and Pakistan, a major drug transit country.

An Ecuadorian court on Monday sentenced 11 soldiers to 34 years in prison for the forced disappearance of four children whose deaths last year shocked the country and intensified scrutiny of President Daniel Noboa’s decision to deploy the military in cities to combat drug violence. The court also ordered each soldier to pay $10,000 to the victims’ families and to publicly ask for forgiveness. The convicted soldiers are expected to face a separate murder trial next year over the children’s deaths. The victims were brothers Ismael and Josué Arroyo, and their friends Saúl Arboleda and Steven Medina, who were ages 11 to 15. They were reported missing on Dec. 8, 2024, after failing to return home from a soccer game in Guayaquil, Ecuador’s main port city. Days later, security camera footage obtained by local journalists showed the boys being detained by a military patrol and forced into the back of a pickup truck. Later that month, investigators found the charred remains of the children near a military base outside Guayaquil. A judge then ordered several soldiers detained as suspects. The military later acknowledged the boys had been in its custody and were taken by the patrol after reports of a robbery, but it initially tried to blame drug gangs, saying the children had been killed after being released. Judge José Suárez said Monday that the boys were killed by soldiers who failed to tell their superiors or police that they had detained them. He said the children were “executed in a cruel fashion” after being forced to move a fallen tree in a wooded area near a military base. According to the judge, they were beaten with rifles, ordered to undress, and then killed. Investigators used the children’s remains and testimony from about 100 witnesses to show they had been beaten in the head before execution. Five other soldiers who cooperated with investigators received reduced sentences of 2 1/2 years. The ruling also required Ecuador’s military to hold a ceremony acknowledging the state’s and military’s responsibility and to install a plaque honoring the children at the base where the soldiers were stationed. The Defense Ministry said it would comply, declaring, “Justice has been delivered today.”

# Ecuador Court Sentences 11 Soldiers for Abduction and Murder of Four Children An Ecuadorian court sentenced eleven soldiers to 34 years in prison Monday for the forced disappearance and torture of four children aged 11 to 15. The soldiers must also pay $10,000 fines to the victims' families and publicly apologize. They face additional murder charges next year. The case involves brothers Ismael and Josué Arroyo and their friends Saúl Arboleda and Steven Medina, who disappeared on December 8, 2024, after failing to return from a soccer game in the port city of Guayaquil. Security camera footage revealed military personnel detained the children and forced them into a pickup truck. Their charred remains were discovered weeks later outside a military base. Judge José Suárez determined soldiers executed the children "in a cruel fashion" after forcing them to move a fallen tree near the base. The children were beaten with rifles, ordered to strip, and then killed. Approximately 100 witnesses testified, and forensic evidence confirmed head trauma from beatings. The military initially claimed drug gangs killed the children after soldiers released them, but later acknowledged the children had been in custody. The military reportedly detained them following robbery reports but failed to report their arrest to police or inform superiors. Five soldiers who cooperated with investigators received reduced sentences of 2½ years. The case has intensified scrutiny of President Daniel Noboa's militarization policies. Since January 2024, the military has patrolled city streets following Noboa's declaration of an "internal armed conflict" aimed at combating drug-related violence. Ecuador's homicide rate has tripled since 2021 as gangs battle for control of ports and cocaine smuggling routes. Human rights groups have criticized these measures, alleging military and police committed abuses including extrajudicial killings and thousands of arrests without due process. The court ordered the military to conduct a ceremony acknowledging state and military responsibility in the crime and install a memorial plaque at the base. Ecuador's Defense Ministry pledged compliance, stating "Justice has been delivered today."

La Pintana, a poor and crime-hit suburb on the outskirts of Santiago, Chile, has become an unexpected model for recycling. Despite its harsh social conditions, residents regularly separate household waste and hand it over to municipal collectors, who gather large amounts of organic material each week. One resident, Marina Ortiz, said she carefully sorts vegetable scraps, paper, cardboard and food waste, following instructions taught by the municipality years ago. She was told the waste would later be turned into earth. Her routine reflects a wider habit in the neighborhood, where the municipality now collects about 140 tons of plant waste from homes every week, a notably high amount compared with similar areas. La Pintana has some of Chile’s worst socioeconomic indicators. About 42% of its 177,000 residents live in poverty, far above the national average of 17%. The area has few medical centers, little formal employment and is often associated in the news with drug trafficking, delinquency and violence. Mayor Claudia Pizarro said residents have long been neglected by the state, with poor access to services, health care and education, and high levels of inequality. She said the recycling program is one of the community’s positive achievements and that the municipality has worked to be recognized for environmental care. The recycling effort began in 2005, when local officials looked for ways to reduce spending on waste management. Felipe Marchant, who heads the municipality’s environmental management division, said the initiative also saves money because it reduces the amount of garbage sent to landfill, where disposal is costly for municipalities. Chile as a whole has been expanding environmental policies, including efforts to cut single-use plastics, reduce emissions and raise recycling rates ahead of hosting the COP25 climate conference in December. But La Pintana stands out as a particularly successful example. Gonzalo Muñoz, Chile’s COP25 environmental “champion,” said no other municipality had achieved the same level of reach and effectiveness, and he expressed surprise that others had not copied it. Beyond its financial and environmental benefits, the program has also strengthened community ties. Environmental educator Carol Valdebenito said residents often talk not only about recycling, but also about social problems and personal concerns during visits by the green truck. The collected waste is taken to a composting and vermiculture facility, where worms help break it down into dark earth. That compost is then used as fertilizer for a municipal nursery, where trees are grown for local green spaces and species are tested for climate and drought resilience. Officials describe this as a practical example of the circular economy.

# La Pintana's Recycling Success Story La Pintana, an impoverished Santiago suburb plagued by crime and poverty, has emerged as an unlikely environmental leader through an innovative recycling program that has become a model for Chile. ## The Program Residents like Marina Ortiz participate in a well-established waste separation system, collecting food scraps, paper, and cardboard for municipal trucks that visit regularly. The municipality now collects 140 tons of plant waste weekly—significantly higher than comparable neighborhoods. The program, which began in 2005, teaches residents to separate waste at the source, with collected materials transported to a composting and vermiculture facility where they transform into nutrient-rich soil. ## Community Context Despite its environmental achievements, La Pintana faces severe socioeconomic challenges. The neighborhood has a 42 percent poverty rate—far exceeding Chile's 17 percent national average—with limited medical centers, minimal employment opportunities, and persistent issues of drug trafficking and violence. These conditions stem from the area's history of receiving families displaced during Chile's 1973-1990 military dictatorship. ## Multiple Benefits The initiative provides both environmental and economic advantages. By reducing landfill waste, the municipality saves significant money on disposal fees, which represents their largest financial burden. The composting process produces fertilizer for a municipal nursery that grows trees for community green spaces while researching climate-resilient species. Beyond environmental gains, the program strengthens community bonds. Environmental educator Carol Valdebenito noted that residents use interactions with recycling workers to discuss broader social concerns and problems. ## Recognition and Expansion La Pintana mayor Claudia Pizarro emphasized the program's significance for a community historically neglected by the state. Environmental champion Gonzalo Muñoz called it exceptional, noting that "no one has done this with the level of penetration and perfection that La Pintana has," expressing surprise that other municipalities haven't replicated it. As Chile prepares to host the COP25 climate conference in December, the country is expanding environmental initiatives including reducing single-use plastics and increasing recycling rates. La Pintana's success demonstrates how waste management can simultaneously address environmental, economic, and social challenges while embodying circular economy principles.

Ecuador’s most notorious drug lord, Adolfo Macias, known as “Fito,” has agreed to be extradited to the United States to face cocaine and weapons-smuggling charges, a court in Quito said Friday. Macias, the leader of the powerful Los Choneros gang, was recaptured in June after escaping from a maximum-security prison last year. His jailbreak triggered a major surge in gang violence across Ecuador, including car bombings, hostage-taking of prison guards and an armed attack on a television station during a live broadcast. He had been on the run since escaping from prison in Guayaquil, where he had been serving a 34-year sentence since 2011 for organized crime, drug trafficking and murder. Once a taxi driver, Macias became Ecuador’s top criminal target after the escape. President Daniel Noboa’s government issued wanted posters and offered a $1 million reward for information leading to his arrest. After months of pursuit, he was found hiding in a bunker beneath floor tiles in a luxury home in the port city of Manta during a military and police operation in which no shots were fired. Noboa then said he wanted Macias extradited “the sooner the better,” adding that Ecuador would “gladly send him” to face U.S. justice. At a court hearing Friday, Macias appeared by video from a high-security prison in Guayaquil and, when asked by a judge, said: “Yes, I accept (extradition).” The court said the formal transfer process would now proceed, but Noboa must sign the official handover documents. If completed, Macias will become the first Ecuadoran extradited by his country since extradition was approved in law last year through a referendum aimed at strengthening the fight against criminal gangs. Ecuador, once relatively peaceful between Colombia and Peru, has been shaken by escalating violence as gangs linked to Mexican and Colombian cartels battle for control, often inside prisons where Macias wielded significant influence. Authorities found images glorifying him, weapons and U.S. dollars in his prison area, and videos showed him hosting parties with fireworks and a mariachi band. He was also being investigated as a suspect in the 2023 assassination of presidential candidate Fernando Villavicencio.

# Ecuador Drug Lord Agrees to US Extradition Adolfo Macias, alias "Fito," Ecuador's most notorious drug lord and leader of the "Los Choneros" gang, has agreed to extradition to the United States to face cocaine and weapons smuggling charges, according to a Quito court announcement Friday. Macias was captured in June following his escape from a maximum-security prison in Guayaquil last year. The jailbreak triggered a severe wave of gang violence across Ecuador. The former taxi driver was serving a 34-year sentence since 2011 for organized crime, drug trafficking, and murder. President Daniel Noboa must now sign official handover papers to complete the process. This would make Macias the first Ecuadoran extradited since extradition was written into law following a 2023 referendum. He is also suspected in the 2023 assassination of presidential candidate Fernando Villavicencio. Los Choneros maintains ties to Mexico's Sinaloa cartel, Colombia's Gulf Clan, and Balkan mafias. Ecuador, once peaceful, has experienced recent violence as gangs vie for control of cocaine trafficking routes. The country now serves as a major drug transit hub, with over 70 percent of world cocaine production passing through its ports. In 2024, Ecuador seized a record 294 tons of drugs, primarily cocaine.

Two months after 43 students disappeared in Mexico, the case has triggered a national crisis that is forcing President Enrique Peña Nieto to confront corruption, police brutality, and the weakness of the country’s justice system. The students vanished in September in the southern state of Guerrero after police attacked busloads of college students in Iguala, abducted 43 young men, and handed them over to members of a drug gang. The gang later said it had killed the captives. The case has become a stark symbol of collusion between criminal groups and corrupt officials in a drug war that has killed tens of thousands since 2006. The outrage has sparked protests across Mexico and what analysts describe as a “civil awakening,” with the political class now under intense scrutiny. Peña Nieto, facing the biggest crisis of his two-year presidency, said the government must take “profound actions” with Congress and society to prevent such a tragedy from happening again. On Thursday, he is expected to announce a new strategy aimed at repairing the country’s dysfunctional justice system. The Iguala case has also damaged the main leftist opposition party, the Democratic Revolution Party (PRD), because the city’s mayor belonged to it. Prosecutors say the mayor ordered police to act against the students out of fear they would disrupt a speech by his wife, who is alleged to have ties to a drug cartel. The PRD’s founder, Cuauhtemoc Cardenas, resigned from the party amid internal disputes over how to restore public trust. The president’s new plan is expected to include placing Mexico’s often ineffective and sometimes gang-infiltrated municipal police forces under federal control, creating a national commission to oversee judicial reforms, and pushing a long-stalled national anti-corruption law through Congress. Security experts say Peña Nieto has lacked a coherent response and now must address corruption and violence directly. The depth of the problem was underscored by a report from Common Cause showing that 42,214 police officers at the federal, state, and municipal levels remain on the job despite failing vetting tests designed to purge corruption. Peña Nieto had come into office in December 2012 promising to reduce violence, but he kept the militarized anti-cartel strategy of his predecessor, Felipe Calderón, while also launching crime-prevention programs and a new gendarmerie. Before the Iguala case, he had claimed progress based on falling murder rates. Now, however, protesters are demanding his resignation, and students from Ayotzinapa have given him until December 1 to step down.

# Mexico's President Faces Crisis Over 43 Missing Students Two months after 43 college students disappeared in Mexico's southern Guerrero state, President Enrique Pena Nieto faces unprecedented pressure to address corruption and police brutality. The disappearance has triggered nationwide protests and forced the government into action. In September, police in Iguala attacked buses carrying students from Ayotzinapa teacher-training college, abducting 43 young men and handing them to drug gang members, who later claimed to have killed them. Investigations revealed that Iguala's mayor, a member of the leftist Democratic Revolution Party (PRD), allegedly ordered the police attack to prevent the students from protesting his wife's speech—a woman prosecutors say has drug cartel connections. This case exemplifies the deep collusion between criminals and corrupt officials plaguing Mexico's drug war, which has killed tens of thousands since 2006. The incident triggered a "civil awakening," according to political analysts. The PRD's founder, Cuauhtemoc Cardenas, resigned from the party Tuesday over internal disputes about restoring public trust. Students from the college have demanded Pena Nieto's resignation by December 1, the anniversary of his presidency, while protesters across the nation voice similar demands. Facing the biggest crisis of his two-year administration, Pena Nieto announced plans to address systemic failures. On Thursday, he will unveil a new strategy targeting the dysfunctional justice system. Key proposals include placing Mexico's notoriously corrupt and gang-infiltrated municipal police forces under federal control, creating a national commission for judicial oversight, and pushing for a national anti-corruption law stalled in Congress. However, experts question whether these measures suffice. A report released Monday revealed that 42,214 police officers remain employed despite failing vetting processes designed to purge the corrupt. Security expert Alejandro Hope emphasized that Pena Nieto "must find an escape strategy, handling what he has not handled so far: corruption and violence." Pena Nieto previously focused on internationally-acclaimed economic reforms while maintaining his predecessor's militarized drug war strategy. He launched crime prevention programs and created a 5,000-strong militarized police force, the gendarmerie. Before the Iguala case, he cited murder rate statistics suggesting progress. Political analysts warn this is a critical turning point. Professor Jose Antonio Crespo argued the government should enact "deeper measures against corruption, whether the entire political class accepts it, wants it, or not." Columnist Ciro Gomez Leyva cautioned that Pena Nieto "will not get a second chance."

Venezuela’s military and police on Wednesday publicly pledged loyalty to interim president Delcy Rodriguez, in a major show of support for the government after the United States removed Nicolas Maduro from power and kept Rodriguez in place. The ceremony underscored the continued importance of the armed forces, long viewed as a central pillar of Maduro’s rule since he succeeded Hugo Chavez in 2013. At the event in Caracas, Defense Minister Vladimir Padrino declared, “We swear absolute loyalty and subordination,” while presenting Rodriguez with the ceremonial baton and sword associated with independence hero Simon Bolivar. Interior Minister Diosdado Cabello, a major figure in the Maduro era, spoke for the police and said backing Rodriguez was necessary to protect the continuity of government and the integrity of the Venezuelan people. More than 3,000 troops and police in uniform marched past Rodriguez, Venezuela’s first female leader and commander in chief. Rodriguez is trying to balance competing pressures: appeasing Maduro loyalists while also dealing with U.S. President Donald Trump, who has said she may remain in office if she follows Washington’s demands, especially granting the United States access to Venezuela’s oil reserves. Trump reportedly chose to pressure Rodriguez rather than empower the opposition after Maduro and his wife were seized in a January 3 U.S. raid in Caracas and taken to New York on drug-trafficking charges. Opposition leader Maria Corina Machado, visiting Washington, dismissed Rodriguez as untrustworthy and accused the Maduro camp of repression and state terrorism. Rodriguez responded at the ceremony by saying those who want to harm Venezuela should remain in Washington.

# Summary Venezuela's military and police formally pledged loyalty to interim president Delcy Rodriguez on January 29, 2026, following the United States' removal of Nicolas Maduro from power. Defense Minister Vladimir Padrino and Interior Minister Diosdado Cabello led the pledge ceremony, presenting Rodriguez with symbolic artifacts and declaring "absolute loyalty and subordination" as over 3,000 uniformed troops and police filed past the country's first female leader. Rodriguez faces a delicate balancing act, attempting to satisfy both Maduro loyalists and U.S. President Donald Trump. The U.S. captured Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores in a January 3 raid on Caracas and transported them to New York to face drug trafficking charges. Trump has indicated Rodriguez can remain in power as long as she complies with American interests, particularly granting the U.S. access to Venezuela's vast oil reserves. Rather than empowering the opposition, Trump has chosen to pressure Rodriguez, dismissing opposition leader Maria Corina Machado as lacking sufficient "respect." Machado, a Nobel peace laureate visiting Washington, strongly criticized Rodriguez, declaring "no one has faith in Delcy Rodriguez" and characterizing her as part of a criminal regime responsible for deaths, mass emigration, and systematic torture. Rodriguez responded sarcastically during the ceremony, suggesting Machado should remain in Washington rather than return to Venezuela.

Chile and the Central American Integration System (SICA) countries agreed at a summit in Santiago to pursue joint action against violence and drug trafficking. At the 1st Forum of Political Dialogue and Cooperation of SICA and Chile, the presidents of Panama and Honduras praised Chile’s strong security system, calling it one of the safest places in Latin America and the Caribbean. Chilean President Michelle Bachelet acknowledged the praise but noted that security remains a major concern for many Chileans. Panamanian President Juan Carlos Varela, who chairs SICA, said Panama and Chile will develop a regional cooperation program to help reduce insecurity in Central America, especially in the “northern triangle” of Honduras, Guatemala, and El Salvador, where violence and drug trafficking remain serious problems despite falling crime rates. Chile has been a SICA observer since 2008.

# Summary Chile and Central American countries met at a summit in Santiago to address violence and drug trafficking. During the 1st Forum of Political Dialogue and Cooperation between SICA (Central American Integration System) and Chile, leaders committed to joint action against these issues. While Panama's President Varela and Honduras's President Hernandez praised Chile's security system, Chilean President Bachelet acknowledged this contradicts public concerns about safety in her country. Varela noted Chile is among Latin America's safest nations, contrasting sharply with Central America's situation. Panama and Chile agreed to create a regional cooperation program targeting the "northern triangle" (Honduras, Guatemala, and El Salvador), which faces severe violence and drug trafficking despite recent crime reductions.

Former combatants from Colombia’s once-largest rebel movement have suspended their political campaign activities because of growing security fears. Leaders of the Common Alternative Revolutionary Force, the party formed by ex-guerrillas, said Friday they would stop holding campaign events until the government can better guarantee their safety. Speaking from behind armed police protection, former rebel leader Jorge Torres, also known as Pablo Catatumbo, urged authorities to protect their right to participate in politics. The decision comes less than two weeks after the former fighters began campaigning and have already faced hostile crowds and protests, highlighting the difficult reconciliation process that has followed Colombia’s 2016 peace accord. That agreement ended a five-decade conflict among leftist rebels, paramilitaries and government forces that left at least 250,000 dead, 60,000 missing and 7 million displaced. In Mexico, authorities said they arrested Jose Maria Guizar Valencia, a dual U.S.-Mexican citizen accused of leading the Zetas drug cartel. Mexican National Security Commissioner Renato Sales announced Friday that Guizar Valencia, known by the alias “Z 43,” was detained Thursday in Mexico City’s Roma neighborhood. A federal official confirmed his last name. The United States had offered a $5 million reward for his capture. Sales said he was one of the main drivers of violence and had overseen the cartel’s drug trafficking and other operations in southern Mexico. U.S. officials say he is responsible for moving large quantities of cocaine and methamphetamine into the United States each year and faces separate drug trafficking indictments in Texas and Virginia. Egypt launched a major security operation Friday involving land, sea and air forces in areas including the northern Sinai Peninsula, where militants linked to the Islamic State have waged an insurgency. Army spokesman Col. Tamer el-Rifaai said the operation also covers central Sinai, the Nile Delta and the Western Desert, and targets “terrorist and criminal elements and organizations.” Officials said at least 20 militants were killed in Bir al-Abd in northern Sinai. In France, an appeals court upheld the far-right National Front’s expulsion of founder Jean-Marie Le Pen over anti-Semitic comments, while also confirming that he remains honorary party president for life. The ruling was a setback and partial win for the 89-year-old, and it sets up another clash with his daughter, Marine Le Pen, who has tried to reshape the party’s image. The party may vote in March to eliminate the honorary title altogether.

President William Ruto has committed Sh100 million to support a 16-day, women-led campaign against femicide and gender-based violence in Kenya. Speaking at State House on Wednesday alongside women leaders, he said the funding will back the “Safe Home, Safe Space” campaign, launched through the Women’s Rights Advisor as part of the 16 Days of Activism Against Gender-Based Violence, which begins on November 25. Ruto described the rise in femicide as a national crisis requiring urgent action and pledged that his administration would protect women’s lives and dignity while ensuring perpetrators are held accountable. He said four out of every five women killed in Kenya are victims of intimate-partner violence, adding that many are murdered in places they should feel safe. The president also warned that social media is increasingly being used to lure women and called for stronger regulation to protect them from online predators. He expressed condolences to bereaved families and urged a united response from government, religious leaders, parents, civil society, teachers, and the public. The announcement comes after Kenya recorded 97 femicide cases since August, with police reporting a steady rise in murder and manslaughter cases over the past two years.

# Summary President William Ruto announced a Sh100 million commitment to support a 16-day women-led campaign against femicide in Kenya. Speaking at State House on November 20, flanked by women leaders, Ruto emphasized the urgent need to address the rising crisis of gender-based violence (GBV) and femicide. The "Safe Home, Safe Space" campaign launches November 25 as part of the 16 Days of Activism Against Gender-Based Violence. Ruto highlighted alarming statistics: four of every five women murdered in Kenya are victims of intimate-partner violence, often in places considered safe. Since August, Kenya has recorded 97 femicide cases. The President called for comprehensive action, urging government agencies, religious leaders, parents, civil society organizations, teachers, and the public to unite against the crisis. He also raised concerns about social media exploitation and the need to regulate online spaces to protect women from predators. The National Police Service and its Directorate of Criminal Investigations pledged to intensify efforts to curb the increasing murder and manslaughter cases over the past two years.

A major rescue operation was underway Thursday evening after a 12-story condominium building in Surfside, Miami, collapsed around 1:30 a.m., leaving at least one person dead, 10 injured, and 99 people unaccounted for, according to Miami-Dade police chief Alfredo Ramirez. Authorities said 53 residents had been rescued or otherwise accounted for, and that about 55 of the building’s 130 apartments were affected. The cause of the collapse was still unknown, though police launched a homicide inquiry, county commissioner Sally Heyman said. Crews from more than 80 fire-rescue units worked through the rubble of Champlain Towers South, and responders reported hearing noises from inside the debris as they searched for survivors. Early video from the scene showed a boy being pulled alive from the wreckage, one of 35 people rescued, according to the Miami-Dade commission. Miami-Dade Mayor Daniella Levine Cava described the disaster as “unimaginable” and pledged that officials would do everything possible to identify and rescue those trapped. Search teams also brought in dogs trained to detect survivors, though commissioner Eliana Salzhauer said they were not finding much and that no one was celebrating the rescues because the situation remained grim. Salzhauer confirmed that roof construction work had recently taken place and said residents reported that a building inspector had visited the property on Wednesday, but she cautioned against speculation about the cause. Florida fire marshal Jimmy Patronis said rescuers continued to hear sounds from the rubble, describing the operation as intense and emotionally driven. Earlier, county emergency management director Frank Rollason said workers believed all reachable survivors had been rescued. On Friday morning, President Joe Biden approved an emergency declaration for Florida, authorizing federal assistance and directing FEMA and the Department of Homeland Security to coordinate disaster relief efforts.

# Miami Building Collapse Summary On June 24, 2021, the Champlain Towers South, a 12-story condominium building in Surfside, Miami, collapsed at approximately 1:30 a.m., triggering a massive rescue operation. At least one person was confirmed dead, 10 were injured, and 99 remained unaccounted for, while 53 residents were rescued or accounted for. The collapse affected approximately 55 of the building's 130 apartments. Rescue crews reported hearing noises from within the rubble, offering some hope for finding survivors among the debris. More than 80 fire-rescue crews, along with search dogs, were deployed to the oceanfront site. Thirty-five people were rescued alive, including a boy pulled from the wreckage early in the operation. Authorities indicated the death toll would likely increase but declined to specify numbers. The cause of the collapse remained unknown at the time, though recent roof construction work and a building inspection on Wednesday were noted as potential factors requiring investigation. A homicide inquiry was launched by Miami-Dade police. President Joe Biden approved an emergency declaration for Florida and authorized federal assistance through the Department of Homeland Security and FEMA to coordinate disaster relief efforts. Miami-Dade Mayor Daniella Levine Cava described the situation as "unimaginable" and emphasized the ongoing search and rescue mission. However, rescue officials cautiously noted that easily accessible survivors had likely been recovered, and search dogs were not yielding significant results, dampening hopes for finding additional survivors in the rubble.

An Egyptian police officer opened fire on a group of Israeli tourists in Alexandria on Sunday, killing at least two Israelis and injuring several others, according to security sources. The shooting occurred in the Al Mansheya district at Pompeo’s Column, where the officer was reportedly assigned to security duties. The motive was not immediately known, but the attack came amid rising violence in the Middle East between Israel and the Palestinians. Security sources said the officer has been arrested. Local media, including Cairo24, reported that an Egyptian man was also killed and another person wounded. The Egyptian government had not commented on the incident. The attack is unusual in Egypt, which regularly receives many Israeli visitors, especially in Sinai. It also follows a rare June incident last year, when an Egyptian police officer crossed into Israel and killed three soldiers before being shot dead.

# Summary An Egyptian police officer opened fire on Israeli tourists in Alexandria on October 8, killing at least two and injuring several others. The shooting occurred in the Al Mansheya district at Pompeo's Column, with the officer firing indiscriminately without apparent cause. An Egyptian bystander was also killed and another injured in the attack. The responsible officer was apprehended by security forces. While the motive remains unclear, the incident coincided with escalating Israeli-Palestinian conflict. Such violence against Israeli tourists is rare in Egypt, a popular destination for Israeli visitors. The Egyptian government has not commented. This incident echoes a similar June incident when an Egyptian officer crossed into Israel and killed three soldiers before being neutralized, prompting Israeli security reviews but no diplomatic tensions between the two nations.

A forensic report aimed at explaining why Andrew Chimboza killed a man and allegedly ate his heart will be presented to the Western Cape High Court next month. On Wednesday, Judge Ashley Binns-Ward was told that Major Hayden Knibbs, a clinical psychologist with the SA Police Service’s investigative psychology unit in Pretoria, had agreed to assist. Prosecutor Jacqueline Sibiya said Knibbs needed time to consult the relevant parties and prepare a report, and also required a transcript of the proceedings for his analysis. The judge ordered the transcript urgently. The defence did not oppose the report, and Chimboza, 35, will remain in custody until the report is heard on 16 February. Chimboza, who moved from Zimbabwe to Cape Town six years ago, pleaded guilty on Monday to murdering 62-year-old Mbuyiselo Manona as part of a plea agreement. In his explanation, he said he stabbed Manona at the home of a former client after an argument. He claimed Manona attacked him with a knife, and that he fought back by kicking him in the groin, stabbing him with a fork, then repeatedly stabbing him in the neck, chest and abdomen. Manona was the lover of Chimboza’s former client and had accused him of having sex with his partner. Chimboza expressed remorse. The State called witnesses in aggravation of sentence, but the judge criticised prosecutors for not initially calling a mental health expert. Evidence from the arresting officer, a forensic pathologist and a Gugulethu resident suggested Chimboza removed Manona’s heart, cut it up and ate it. Manona died from severe stab wounds and blunt force injuries.

# Summary Andrew Chimboza, a 35-year-old Zimbabwean resident of Cape Town, pleaded guilty to murdering 62-year-old Mbuyiselo Manona in June under a plea agreement. According to Chimboza's account, he stabbed Manona to death after a disagreement at a former client's home, claiming Manona had attacked him with a knife first. The case has drawn significant attention due to allegations that Chimboza ate his victim's heart. Evidence from an arresting officer, forensic pathologist, and a Gugulethu resident suggests Chimboza removed, dismembered, and consumed Manona's heart. Manona died from severe incisions to his neck, chest, and abdomen, along with blunt force injuries. The victim was the lover of Chimboza's ex-client, who had accused Chimboza of infidelity. Judge Ashley Binns-Ward criticized the State for failing to present mental health expert evidence, stating in nearly 40 years he had never encountered such a case. A forensic report from Major Hayden Knibbs, a clinical psychologist with the SA Police Service's investigative psychology unit, will be presented on February 16 to provide psychological insight into Chimboza's actions. Chimboza remains in custody pending the report's presentation.

Sudan has announced that it will hand over former ruler Omar al-Bashir to the International Criminal Court, along with two other former officials wanted in connection with the Darfur conflict. The decision was reported by Foreign Minister Mariam al-Mahdi after a cabinet meeting, but it still requires approval from Sudan’s ruling sovereign council, which includes both military and civilian leaders. The announcement came during a visit to Khartoum by ICC chief prosecutor Karim Khan. Al-Bashir, now 77, has been wanted by the ICC for more than a decade on charges of genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity. The court issued an arrest warrant in 2009, later adding genocide. He is currently imprisoned in Khartoum’s high-security Kober prison, where he is also held alongside former Defence Minister Abdel Rahim Mohamed Hussein and former South Kordofan governor Ahmed Haroun, both of whom face ICC charges as well. The Darfur conflict began in 2003, when non-Arab rebel groups rose up against what they described as systematic discrimination by al-Bashir’s Arab-dominated government. Khartoum responded by deploying the Janjaweed militia, and human rights groups have long accused al-Bashir and his allies of carrying out a scorched-earth campaign involving rape, murder, looting and the burning of villages. The United Nations estimates that 300,000 people were killed and 2.5 million displaced. Sudan’s transitional authorities have said previously that they would transfer al-Bashir to the ICC, but one obstacle was that Sudan had not been a party to the court’s founding Rome Statute. That changed last week, when Sudan’s cabinet voted to ratify the treaty, a move seen as an important step toward possible prosecution. Prime Minister Abdalla Hamdok said the decision reflected both Sudan’s international commitments and the demands of the Sudanese people for justice. Mohamed Hamdan Daglo, deputy chair of the sovereign council, said Sudan was prepared to cooperate with the ICC. It remains unclear whether al-Bashir would be extradited to The Hague or kept in Sudan for trial. UN Special Representative Volker Perthes said the ICC could help establish a special court for Darfur. ICC spokesman Fadi El Abdallah declined to comment in detail, saying only that Khan was in Khartoum to discuss cooperation. The announcement was welcomed by the United States, with State Department spokesman Ned Price calling it a major step in ending decades of impunity. Sudan has recently received other signs of Western support, including removal from the US list of state sponsors of terrorism. Meanwhile, violence in Darfur has continued despite a peace deal signed last October, and a former militia leader, Ali Kushayb, surrendered to the ICC last year.

# Sudan Agrees to Hand Over Al-Bashir to International Criminal Court Sudan's cabinet has decided to extradite longtime ruler Omar al-Bashir, 77, to the International Criminal Court (ICC) in The Hague, along with two other officials implicated in the Darfur conflict. Foreign Minister Mariam al-Mahdi announced the decision, though it requires approval from Sudan's sovereign council before proceeding. The Darfur conflict, which erupted in 2003, resulted in approximately 300,000 deaths and displaced 2.5 million people according to UN estimates. This announcement follows Sudan's removal from the US terrorism sponsors list in December and pledges to clear World Bank arrears. Recently, militia leader Ali Kushayb surrendered to the ICC and faces charges of murder, rape, and torture.

Police are searching for suspects who hijacked a Cape Town truck carrying large appliances worth about R70,000. Officers in Strandfontein were alerted by a member of the public on Tuesday, spotted the vehicle, and chased it before losing sight of it. Working with the tracking company, they located it in Samora Machel, where it was found with the keys still inside but the appliances missing. Separately, Gauteng police praised a swift response to a Midrand double-truck hijacking that left one suspect dead and another arrested.

# Summary Cape Town police launched a manhunt for suspects who hijacked a truck carrying large appliances worth approximately R70,000. Law Enforcement officers spotted the vehicle in Strandfontein on Tuesday after receiving a public alert but lost sight during pursuit. Using the vehicle's tracking company, officers located it in Samora Machel, discovering all appliances had been stolen while the keys remained inside. Separately, Gauteng's acting police commissioner praised officers' response to a double-truck hijacking in Midrand that resulted in one suspect's death and another's arrest.

Sudan’s government has declared the U.N. special envoy to the country, Volker Perthes, persona non grata, escalating tensions with the international body even as Sudan’s warring factions agreed to another brief cease-fire. The Foreign Ministry announced late Thursday that U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres had been informed that Perthes was no longer welcome. The move came weeks after Sudan’s military leader, Gen. Abdel Fattah Burhan, had written to demand Perthes’ removal. The U.N. rejected Sudan’s action, saying a member of U.N. personnel cannot be declared persona non grata and that the decision violates the U.N. Charter. U.N. spokesperson Stéphane Dujarric said Perthes would remain the organization’s envoy to Sudan, though he did not say whether the German diplomat would return to the country. Germany also condemned the announcement. Perthes has served as a major mediator in Sudan since 2021, first during the country’s troubled transition toward democracy and later as relations worsened between the military and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces. The expulsion announcement came as Sudan’s army and the Rapid Support Forces agreed to a new 24-hour truce beginning at 6 a.m. Friday. The cease-fire was announced in a joint statement by Saudi Arabia and the United States and then confirmed by both Sudanese sides on social media. It is the eighth cease-fire attempt since fighting erupted in mid-April, but previous truces have repeatedly collapsed. Washington and Riyadh have been leading mediation efforts in the conflict, including peace talks in Jeddah that began in late May. Those talks were suspended last week after repeated cease-fire violations by both sides. On the same day, the United States imposed sanctions on defense companies linked to both the military and the Rapid Support Forces, along with visa restrictions. Despite the suspension, the mediators said they remain in contact with both sides in hopes of restarting negotiations. The conflict between Burhan’s army and the forces led by Gen. Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo has devastated Khartoum, leaving many neighborhoods without water or electricity and bringing widespread looting and sexual violence, including reported rapes in Khartoum and Darfur. Sudan’s Doctors’ Syndicate says more than 860 civilians have been killed, though the real toll is believed to be much higher. The article also reported deadly violence in South Sudan, where clashes in a U.N. site in Malakal left more than 20 people dead and over 50 wounded, according to MSF. The fighting involved displaced people from the Shilluk and Nuer ethnic groups.

# Sudan Declares U.N. Envoy Persona Non Grata Amid Ongoing Conflict Sudan's government has declared the United Nations envoy to the country unwelcome, marking an escalation in tensions even as warring factions agreed to a new 24-hour ceasefire. Sudan's Foreign Ministry announced Thursday that envoy Volker Perthes has been declared persona non grata, a designation typically meaning a diplomat is unacceptable to the host government. The move follows weeks after Sudan's military chief, General Abdel Fattah Burhan, demanded Perthes's removal in a letter. The U.N. has rejected the declaration, stating that U.N. personnel cannot be designated persona non grata and that doing so violates the U.N. charter. U.N. spokesperson Stephane Dujarric confirmed Perthes will remain the organization's envoy but did not clarify whether he would return to Sudan. A precedent exists: when Somalia declared a U.N. envoy persona non grata in 2019, that diplomat never returned. Perthes has served as a key mediator since 2021, initially during Sudan's failed democratic transition and later as military-paramilitary tensions escalated. Germany has condemned Sudan's announcement. The conflict between Sudan's military and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces has devastated the nation since mid-April. More than 860 civilians have been killed according to Sudan's Doctors' Syndicate, though actual casualties are likely higher. The fighting has reduced Khartoum to an urban battlefield, with widespread reports of sexual violence, particularly in Darfur, blamed primarily on the Rapid Support Forces. On Friday, Saudi Arabia and the United States jointly announced an eighth ceasefire agreement, effective for 24 hours starting at 6 a.m. However, all previous seven ceasefires have collapsed. Last week, Washington and Riyadh suspended formal peace talks in Jeddah, citing repeated violations by both sides. The U.S. subsequently imposed sanctions against defense companies and military officials from both factions. Despite setbacks, mediators remain engaged with both sides, hoping to resume negotiations. In related developments, violence erupted at a U.N. site in South Sudan's Malakal camp between Shilluk and Nuer ethnic groups, killing over 20 people and wounding more than 50. The clash reportedly began with a stabbing. Medical charity MSF reported that two of its staff were injured, with some patients airlifted to the capital Juba. Many women and children who fled the camp remain fearful of escalation.

The FCT Police Command has arrested multiple suspects in connection with the murder of a school nurse and a 14-month-old pupil at Clear Hope Foundation Academy in Dawaki, Abuja, after a ransom of ₦3 million was collected. Commissioner of Police Saka Adewale Ajao said the case involved the killing of 55-year-old nurse Chinyere Anaene and toddler Nanenter Asher Yese, both reported missing on July 23, 2025. Police said the main suspect, David Moses, a security guard posted to the school, confessed that he planned the kidnapping and murder with an accomplice, Sunday Irimiya, who is still at large. According to Moses’ confession, the nurse was lured into a trap and strangled by Sunday, who had been hiding in a toilet. Moses then brought the baby, who was also killed after Sunday insisted the child had to die so the ransom would be “worth it.” On the same day the victims disappeared, the nurse’s husband received a phone call demanding ₦250 million, later reduced to ₦3 million. The suspects allegedly collected the money while falsely assuring the family that the victims were still alive, even though they had already been killed. A further twist came after the ransom was shared: Sunday reportedly stabbed Moses and fled with the money. Injured and fearful of mob action, Moses sought medical help and later confessed to police. Authorities have also arrested the school principal, two other guards, and the chief security officer of the private security company that deployed Moses. A company representative admitted serious negligence, saying the firm failed to properly document Moses’ employment or obtain guarantor details.

# Summary The Federal Capital Territory Police Command has arrested multiple suspects in connection with the murder of a school nurse and a 14-month-old child at Clear Hope Foundation Academy in Abuja's Dawaki area. Security guard David Moses and his accomplice Sunday Irimiya plotted the kidnapping and murder. On July 23, 2025, both victims—55-year-old nurse Chinyere Anaene and toddler Nanenter Asher Yese—went missing. The perpetrators then contacted the nurse's husband demanding ₦250 million, later reduced to ₦3 million, falsely claiming the victims were alive. Moses confessed that Irimiya strangled the nurse after luring her into a trap near a toilet, then pressured Moses to also kill the baby to justify the ransom amount. The ransom was collected despite the victims already being dead. Following the handover, a dispute over the money led Irimiya to stab Moses, who subsequently fled with the funds. The injured Moses eventually sought police help and made a full confession after receiving medical treatment. Authorities have also arrested the school principal, two additional guards, and the Chief Security Officer of the private security company that deployed Moses. The security firm's representative admitted to gross negligence, acknowledging failures in employment documentation, guarantor verification, and supervisory oversight at the school.

Myanmar security forces killed at least 82 people in a single day during a crackdown on pro-democracy protesters in the city of Bago, according to reports Saturday from independent local media and the Assistance Association for Political Prisoners, a group that tracks casualties and arrests after the Feb. 1 coup. The reported death toll from Friday’s violence was the highest in one city since March 14, when more than 100 people were killed in Yangon. Bago is about 100 kilometers northeast of Yangon. The Associated Press said it could not independently verify the figures. The Assistance Association for Political Prisoners described the 82 deaths as a preliminary count and said the number was likely to rise as more cases were confirmed. The group’s tallies are widely regarded as credible because it does not add cases until they have been verified. Myanmar Now, an online news outlet, also reported 82 deaths, citing an unnamed source involved in charity rescue work. Local media said the bodies had been collected by the military and dumped on the grounds of a Buddhist pagoda. The latest violence brought the total number of people killed by security forces since the army’s takeover to at least 701, according to the same monitoring group. The Bago assault was the third major use of force in a week as the junta sought to crush opposition to military rule. Earlier attacks on Wednesday targeted anti-junta strongholds in the northern towns of Kalay and Taze, where at least 11 people were reported killed, possibly including bystanders. Security forces were accused of using heavy weapons such as rocket-propelled grenades and mortars, though those claims could not be independently confirmed. Photos from Bago circulating on social media appeared to show mortar fragments. While most anti-coup demonstrations across Myanmar have remained nonviolent and part of a civil disobedience movement, some hardened protesters have taken up homemade weapons in self-defense as the military has escalated lethal force. In Kalay, activists described themselves as a “civil army,” and some used rudimentary hunting rifles common in the region. Myanmar Now reported that residents of Tamu, another town in the area, ambushed a military convoy with hunting rifles and claimed to have killed three soldiers. The junta has also intensified repression through arrests and legal threats. It recently issued a wanted list of 140 people in the arts and journalism accused of spreading destabilizing information, with penalties of up to three years in prison. State television also reported that a military court sentenced 19 people to death, 17 of them in absentia, for allegedly killing an army officer in Yangon. The case appeared to be the first death sentence imposed under junta rule. Meanwhile, U.N. special envoy Christine Schraner Burgener arrived in Bangkok on a regional mission but was denied permission to enter Myanmar.

# Myanmar Security Forces Kill 82 in Single Day Myanmar's security forces killed at least 82 people in a single day during a brutal crackdown on pro-democracy protesters in the city of Bago, according to reports from independent local media and the Assistance Association for Political Prisoners (AAPP). The Friday massacre represents the largest one-day death toll for any city since the military coup on February 1, which ousted elected leader Aung San Suu Kyi. Bago, located approximately 100 kilometers northeast of the capital Yangon, experienced unprecedented violence as security forces launched a major assault. The AAPP, a highly credible organization that tracks casualties, issued a preliminary count of 82 deaths and indicated the figure would likely increase as more cases were verified. Myanmar Now, a local news outlet, corroborated this death toll, reporting that military forces collected bodies and dumped them at a Buddhist pagoda. Since the coup, at least 701 protesters and bystanders have been killed by security forces. The Bago attack represents the third major offensive in a week, following assaults Wednesday on opposition strongholds in Kalay and Taze in northern Myanmar, where at least 11 people were reportedly killed in each location. Security forces have allegedly deployed heavy weapons including rocket-propelled grenades and mortars, though these claims remain unconfirmed by independent sources. Social media photographs from Bago appeared to show mortar shell fragments, suggesting the use of military-grade weaponry against civilians. As the military escalates lethal force, protest tactics have evolved. While most demonstrations remain nonviolent civil disobedience, armed resistance factions have emerged, using homemade weapons and firebombs for self-defense. In Kalay, activists formed a "civil army" equipped with traditional hunting rifles. Reports indicate residents of nearby Tamu ambushed a military convoy Saturday, claiming to kill three soldiers. The junta has implemented additional suppressive measures, publishing a wanted list of 140 artists and journalists accused of spreading destabilizing information. The offense carries penalties up to three years imprisonment. Additionally, a military court sentenced 19 people to death—17 in absentia—for allegedly killing an army officer in Yangon on March 27, marking the first death sentences imposed under the current junta rule. Meanwhile, the UN special envoy for Myanmar, Christine Schraner Burgener, arrived in Bangkok Friday to consult regional governments about resolving the crisis, though she was denied permission to visit Myanmar itself.

A SWAT team on Monday took a person of interest into custody for questioning in the fatal Sunday shooting of 22-year-old Jake Gengelbach outside Hire’s Big H restaurant in West Valley. Gengelbach was shot and killed in the parking lot at 4700 S. 2900 West after police were first called to the nearby Overlook Point apartments, where residents reported hearing multiple gunshots. Detectives later gathered information that led them to a house at 2125 E. Newcastle Drive in Sandy. Because of the circumstances of the homicide and the belief that a weapon was involved, police used a heavy show of force, including an armored BearCat vehicle and officers in tactical gear, to approach the home. Nearby streets were blocked off during the operation. West Valley Police Lt. Bill Merritt said the occupants of the house had a history of hostility toward police, so a robot was used to clear the residence and ensure no one was hiding inside. Three other people were in the home at the time. Merritt said the man surrendered without incident once SWAT arrived. Police were also serving a search warrant to look for additional evidence. Meanwhile, social media filled with condolences and tributes to Gengelbach from friends and acquaintances. The investigation remained ongoing.

# Summary A SWAT team arrested a person of interest on Monday in connection with Sunday's fatal shooting at a West Valley restaurant parking lot. Jake Gengelbach, 22, was killed early Sunday in the parking lot of Hire's Big H. Police initially responded to nearby Overlook Point apartments after residents reported hearing gunshots. Detectives' investigation led them to a house in Sandy on Newcastle Drive Monday afternoon. Law enforcement deployed an armored BearCat and a full tactical SWAT team to execute a search warrant, citing the dangerous nature of the homicide and the presence of a weapon. Because the house's occupants had a history of hostility toward police, a robot was used to search the interior and ensure no one was hiding inside. The suspect surrendered without incident once SWAT arrived. Three other people were present in the home during the arrest. Nearby streets were blocked off during the operation. Police served the search warrant to collect additional evidence. Social media posts expressed condolences to Gengelbach, with friends describing him as a loyal and good-hearted person.

Southeast Asian leaders are gathering in Jakarta for ASEAN’s final summit of the year, facing a crowded agenda dominated by unresolved crises and rivalries. Indonesian President Joko Widodo is hosting the meetings, which open Tuesday under tight security, but the usual atmosphere of unity is muted by the absence of U.S. President Joe Biden, who typically attends the annual gathering. The 10-member Association of Southeast Asian Nations is struggling with several major challenges at once, especially Myanmar’s continuing civil conflict, renewed tensions in the disputed South China Sea, and the broader U.S.-China competition. At a Monday meeting of ASEAN foreign ministers, Indonesian coordinating minister Mohammad Mahfud said the region’s “community’s strength is being challenged by one crisis after another.” He warned that the lack of progress on Myanmar had “left a negative mark on ASEAN” and said rising geopolitical tensions “could lead to open conflict” that Southeast Asia might be forced to confront. Indonesia’s Foreign Minister Retno Marsudi said the bloc would review the five-point peace plan agreed in 2021 to help restore stability in Myanmar. That plan has made little visible progress, and ASEAN has faced criticism for its limited ability to influence the situation. After the leaders’ summit begins Tuesday, ASEAN will hold broader meetings Wednesday and Thursday with Asian and Western counterparts. Those sessions are often used for discussions on trade, climate change, and global security. Chinese Premier Li Qiang is expected to attend, along with U.S. Vice President Kamala Harris, who will represent the United States in Biden’s place, and Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov. Biden’s absence comes as he travels to India for the G20 summit and then on to Vietnam to strengthen bilateral ties. The White House said his decision not to attend ASEAN should not be seen as downgrading the bloc, emphasizing his administration’s efforts to deepen U.S. engagement in the region. Overall, the summit reflects ASEAN’s difficult balancing act as it seeks to preserve regional unity while navigating internal conflict and intensifying great-power competition.

Thai officials have detained a 22-year-old Dutch man, Roslan Bendenia, after a TikTok video showed him illegally spearfishing in Phuket. The video sparked online outrage because it appeared to show him catching endangered parrotfish and stabbing a sea eel. According to Thailand’s National Parks service and the Department of Marine and Coastal Resources, the arrest took place Monday afternoon, and Bendenia was taken to Chalong police station for questioning. Officials said Bendenia had hired a boat in Hat Noppharat Thara-Mu Koh Phi Phi National Park to travel from Koh Phi Phi Don to Koh Phi Phi Leh, where he went fishing around 1 p.m. on Aug. 9. He also reportedly rented a speargun from a local operator on Koh Phi Phi Don. Bendenia told authorities he did not know the area was inside a national park and was unaware the fishing was illegal. Police said they would pursue legal action not only against him, but also against the boat owner and the person who supplied the speargun. Tourist police confirmed he lives in Phuket and said he apologized for both his actions and for posting the video on his TikTok account, @roslanofficial.

# Summary A 22-year-old Dutch man, Roslan Bendenia, was arrested in Phuket for illegal spearfishing after a TikTok video of him catching endangered parrotfish sparked online outrage. Detained on Monday by Thailand's National Parks officials, Bendenia had hired a boat and rented a speargun to fish at Koh Phi Phi Leh on August 9. The video showed him holding multiple parrotfish and other fish while stabbing a sea eel. Bendenia claimed he was unaware the area was part of a protected national park and didn't know catching parrotfish was illegal. He has apologized for his actions and the social media post. Authorities plan to take legal action not only against Bendenia but also against the boat captain, Krisana Thodthing, and the person who supplied the speargun.

Police in Uttar Pradesh have arrested two constables after the fatal shooting of Vivek Tiwari, an Apple sales manager, during a routine night patrol in Lucknow’s Gomti Nagar area on Saturday. Tiwari was shot dead by a constable on a motorbike patrol about 13 km from the state capital. The officer involved said he fired by mistake and claimed self-defense, while state police chief O.P. Singh said that was the constable’s explanation. Police spokesman Vivek Tripathi said both constables were arrested on suspicion of murder. Uttar Pradesh Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath said the state would investigate and, if needed, hand the case to federal police. Apple expressed shock and condolences. Tiwari, who leaves behind two daughters, was described by his family as the victim of a serious injustice; they have demanded a special inquiry, compensation, and employment for his widow. The state has promised 250,000 rupees and a municipal job for her.

# Summary An Apple employee, Vivek Tiwari, a sales manager, was fatally shot by a police constable in Uttar Pradesh's Gomti Nagar neighborhood early Saturday morning during a routine night patrol. The officer claimed the shooting was accidental and fired in self-defense. Two constables were arrested on suspicion of murder. The state's top police officer said the shooting occurred during a standard patrol operation.
