The state offered 250,000 rupees ($3,448) and a municipal job for his widow.

When President Donald Trump meets Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte in Manila, the most explosive issue between them will likely be left untouched: Duterte’s anti-drug campaign, which has left thousands dead in killings widely condemned by human rights groups, the U.S. Congress, the European Union, and the United Nations. The article says Trump is unlikely to raise the subject, despite the scale of the violence and despite calls from some lawmakers and rights advocates for him to do so. Duterte’s “war on drugs,” carried out by police with his explicit backing, has involved suspected dealers and users being shot without due process, including people killed in jail, at home, or while asleep. Among the examples cited are a 17-year-old allegedly shot while in custody and dumped in an alley, and a 4-year-old child identified as the youngest victim. Yet the White House has signaled no intention of pressing Duterte, saying Trump enjoys a “warm rapport” with him. The two leaders are scheduled to meet at the Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit in Manila, the final stop on Trump’s 12-day, five-country Asia tour, which also included Japan, South Korea, China, and Vietnam. Duterte appears to welcome the encounter. He was in Vietnam on Friday for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, where he made headlines by saying he had killed someone when he was 16. In remarks in Da Nang, he described his youth as marked by fights and stabbings and said, “At the age of 16, I already killed someone - a real person.” He added that if that was the case as a teenager, “How much more now that I am president?” The White House did not immediately respond to the admission. Human Rights Watch’s Phelim Kine said Duterte is “notably thin-skinned” and reacts strongly to criticism, so what he wants from Trump is not confrontation but “international acceptance and recognition,” something he has been denied because of the bloodshed in his anti-drug campaign. According to the Philippine foreign ministry, Trump and Duterte are expected to discuss trade and investment, innovation, cybercrime, countering radicalization, humanitarian aid, disaster relief, and the protection of migrant workers’ rights. They will also be joined by U.N. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres, European Council President Donald Tusk, and Russian Prime Minister Dmitry Medvedev. Trump has already shown little appetite for criticizing Duterte’s campaign. In an April phone call, he reportedly congratulated Duterte for doing an “unbelievable job on the drug problem.” Duterte nonetheless warned Trump not to bring it up, telling reporters, “Lay off. That is not your business. That is my business.” Observers say the relationship fits a broader pattern of solidarity among authoritarian-leaning populists. Richard Javad Heydarian described it as a “strongman populist internationale,” arguing that Trump feels more comfortable with leaders like Duterte than with Western allies. Duterte has also used increasingly hostile language toward critics. He threatened U.N. special rapporteur Agnes Callamard, saying he would “slap her” if she investigated the killings. But despite his bluster, he faces growing domestic pressure. Public support has weakened after a series of high-profile deaths, including the August killing of 17-year-old Kian Loyd Delos Santos. Police said Delos Santos drew a gun, but witness accounts and surveillance footage suggested he was unarmed and in custody when shot. Another case that shocked the country was the death of 14-year-old Reynaldo de Guzman, whose body was found in September with stab wounds and packing tape wrapped around his head. He had last been seen with a 19-year-old friend who was also killed by police. Duterte dismissed the death as part of a plot to “sabotage” the police, but the incidents contributed to a sharp drop in his approval ratings. Social Weather Stations reported in October that his net satisfaction rating had fallen to 48 percent, down 18 points from June. Two U.S. congressmen, Randy Hultgren and James McGovern, urged Trump to raise human rights concerns and reaffirm U.S. commitments to due process and the rule of law. Duterte responded by threatening to ban them from Manila. Even so, the article suggests the Trump-Duterte meeting is more likely to focus on security issues than on human rights. Marawi, where Philippine forces battled Islamic State militants for five months before ending the siege in September, may be a central topic. So may the South China Sea, where the Philippines has become important in resisting China’s territorial claims. Despite Duterte’s anti-U.S. rhetoric and his efforts to cultivate ties with Beijing, analysts say he has not fundamentally broken the long-standing U.S.-Philippines alliance. Andrew Shearer noted that China’s practical security assistance has been limited, while the U.S. continues to provide more substantial support, including Coast Guard vessels, modern equipment, intelligence help, and crucial assistance during the Marawi crisis. That, he said, reminded Duterte that the United States remains an indispensable security partner. Duterte has clearly tried to rebalance toward China, encouraged by Chinese investment and angered by U.S. criticism of his drug war. He has spoken more softly toward Beijing than his predecessor did. In August, the Philippines did not challenge Chinese boats near a contested island. Duterte said then, “Why should I defend a sandbar and kill the Filipinos because of a sandbar?” He said he would ask Chinese President Xi Jinping about South China Sea issues, but Philippine trade secretary Ramon Lopez later described Duterte and Xi as having a “very strong, close relationship like brothers,” suggesting any challenge to China may remain restrained.

# Trump and Duterte Meeting Unlikely to Address Philippine Drug War Killings President Donald Trump is set to meet with Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte in Manila during the Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit on Monday, marking the final stop of Trump's 12-day Asian tour. The South China Sea may also be addressed, where the Philippines plays a central role in resisting China's territorial assertions. ## The U.S.-Philippines Alliance Despite Duterte's harsh rhetoric toward Washington, experts note he has not fundamentally altered the U.S.-Philippines alliance, which dates back over six decades. The U.S. provides more advanced military equipment and training than China, whose security assistance has been limited to second-hand assault rifles. Ukraine is increasingly turning to its prison population to reinforce its depleted front-line forces, using a new legal framework that allows certain convicts to be released on parole in exchange for military service. The article follows several inmates in Zhytomyr and Kyiv oblasts as they weigh whether to trade prison life for combat, and it shows how the policy is being implemented across the country. At the center of the story is Taras Netavrovanyi, an inmate at Zhytomyr medium-security prison. He is serving a two-and-a-half-year sentence for illegal possession of ammunition, but he sees the new law as a chance not only to leave prison early, but also to redeem himself. Under the legislation, prisoners convicted of some felonies, including manslaughter, may join the Armed Forces, receive parole, monthly pay, and the social benefits available to soldiers. Netavrovanyi, a chiropractor with 15 years of experience, has applied to serve as a combat medic in the 153rd Infantry Brigade, where five former fellow inmates already serve. He says his skills would be more useful in the army than in prison. The new mobilization law is part of Ukraine’s broader effort to replenish manpower as the war drags on. The government has said it hopes to recruit 20,000 convicts, and the first wave has already drawn around 5,000 inmates out of cells and into military pipelines. Some 300 prisoners with previous combat experience had already been recruited since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion. The law excludes people serving sentences for premeditated murder, killing two or more people, sexual violence, drug production, and crimes against national security. It also comes with a strict penalty: if a parolee violates the terms of release, including by desertion, they can receive five additional years on top of their original sentence. The Justice Ministry has played a major role in designing the system and says demand has been strong. Deputy Justice Minister Olena Vysotska said the ministry was flooded with applications after the law took effect in May, with the number of requests matching what officials had expected for the entire campaign. Recruiters are now visiting prisons nationwide, presenting military service as a way for inmates to change their lives and, in the words of one brigade recruiter, “cleanse their sins with their blood, or the blood of invaders.” The Zhytomyr prison is one of 86 facilities included in these recruitment tours. Inmates are gathered for presentations about training and service, and recruiters from units such as the 5th Assault Brigade are trying to identify men they consider motivated and physically strong enough for a separate battalion made up entirely of prisoners. That battalion would undergo two months of boot camp before deployment to the eastern front in Donetsk Oblast, where the brigade is fighting in the long and brutal Battle of Donbas. Brigade captain Vladyslav Shahan says the effort should strengthen the defense line and encourage other prisoners to consider joining. The process is structured and bureaucratic. Prisoners submit a written request for parole and for military service. Military doctors then assess whether they are fit. If they pass, a prison commission and an army officer decide whether to suspend the sentence, after which the case goes to court for parole hearings. Once parole is approved, the National Guard escorts the former inmate to an enlistment office, where he signs a contract with the brigade. The article also highlights the limits and moral tensions of the policy. In Boryspil prison, Andrii Fetisov, 28, is eager to enlist but cannot because he was convicted of double homicide and therefore falls under the law’s exclusions. Serving a 14-year sentence, he says it would be good to help his country and argues that war is about killing, not guarding fields. Vysotska says the law was written with victims and their families in mind, but she does not rule out future changes if the military requests them. For now, however, any amendment would require strong arguments in parliament. Ukraine’s prison recruitment program is explicitly contrasted with Russia’s use of inmates in the war. The article notes that Moscow, through Wagner boss Yevgeniy Prigozhin, recruited tens of thousands of prisoners in 2022 for violent assaults on Ukrainian positions, later continuing inmate recruitment through the Defense Ministry and offering pardons after six months of fighting. Vysotska insists Ukraine is avoiding that model, saying the country is focusing on the legal status of recruits and on monitoring their training to prevent “meat grinder” tactics. Not all prisoners are ready to sign up. Maksym Kryvenko, 26, is considering enlistment but remains cautious. He is serving a sentence for drug offenses after a business decision gone wrong during the Covid-era delivery boom led him to deliver amphetamines instead of food. He was caught quickly, confessed, and received a reduced five-year sentence instead of 12. Now he spends his days cleaning, cooking, reading, and taking technical courses. He says he would consider joining if recruiters were looking for tech-oriented roles, but for now he is waiting to see how the first prisoners fare and whether the program proves worthwhile. Overall, the article presents Ukraine’s prison recruitment drive as a pragmatic but carefully regulated attempt to address battlefield shortages, while also offering inmates a path to redemption and early release.

# Ukraine's Prison Recruitment: Offering Redemption Through Military Service As Ukraine faces mounting casualties in its ongoing conflict with Russia, the government has implemented an innovative and controversial strategy to bolster its military forces: recruiting convicted prisoners to serve on the front lines. This new mobilization law represents a significant shift in Ukrainian military recruitment policy and has already generated substantial interest among the incarcerated population. ## The New Legislation and Its Scope Ukraine's revised mobilization law, which came into effect in May, permits prisoners convicted of certain felonies to exchange their sentences for military service. The government aims to recruit approximately 20,000 convicts, with an initial campaign targeting around 5,000 inmates. The military had previously recruited some 300 inmates with combat experience since Russia's full-scale invasion began, but this new legislation dramatically expands the eligible pool. The law excludes convicts serving sentences for premeditated murder, murders of multiple victims, sexual violence, drug production, and crimes against national security. However, it permits recruitment of those convicted of manslaughter and other serious felonies. Prisoners who violate their parole through desertion or other infractions face an additional five years added to their original sentences. The Justice Ministry, which developed the legislation, was overwhelmed by applications immediately after implementation. Deputy Justice Minister Olena Vysotska reported that the number of applications received equaled the anticipated total for the entire recruitment campaign, demonstrating unexpected enthusiasm among the prison population. ## Motivations and Personal Stories The article profiles several inmates considering military service, each with distinct motivations. Taras Netavrovanyi, a chiropractor serving a two-and-a-half-year sentence for illegal ammunition possession, emphasizes redemption as his primary motivation. He has applied to serve as a combat medic with the 153rd Infantry Brigade and has already survived two failed attempts to join the military. Netavrovanyi views military service as an opportunity to apply his medical knowledge more meaningfully than his current prison role allows. Andrii Fetisov, 28, represents a different perspective. Serving a 14-year sentence for double homicide, he is ineligible under current law but expressed frustration at being excluded. He argues that his violent crime actually qualifies him for combat, reasoning that soldiers inevitably kill in warfare. Vysotska acknowledged the possibility of expanding eligibility criteria if the military requests it, though such changes would require substantial parliamentary justification. Maksym Kryvenko, a 26-year-old drug offender, represents the hesitant category. Imprisoned for drug delivery following a pandemic-era economic crisis, Kryvenko is cautiously considering enlistment. Rather than rushing into combat, he prefers to observe the experiences of fellow former inmates and develop technical skills through prison courses, hoping to contribute to the military in tech-related roles rather than frontline combat. ## Recruitment Operations and Military Integration The 5th Assault Brigade actively recruits at 86 prison facilities throughout Ukraine, organizing recruitment presentations for inmates. The brigade aims to establish a separate battalion comprising 600 motivated prisoners, who will undergo two months of boot camp before deployment to the eastern front in Donetsk Oblast. The recruitment process involves multiple stages: inmates submit written parole pleas and military applications, undergo fitness assessments by military medics, receive sentence suspension decisions from prison commissions and army officers, attend parole hearings before courts, and finally sign military contracts with the National Guard's oversight. ## Distinguishing Ukraine's Approach from Russian Tactics Ukraine's prisoner recruitment strategy deliberately contrasts with Russia's indiscriminate methods. Russia, under the late Wagner Group commander Yevgeniy Prigozhin, recruited tens of thousands of inmates regardless of their crimes, offering pardons for six months of service and deploying them in costly, poorly-trained assault waves. Deputy Justice Minister Vysotska emphasizes that Ukraine focuses on legal mechanisms and monitored training, avoiding what she calls "meat grinder assaults." Ukraine claims to be the first country implementing a legal framework allowing convicts to join the armed forces, suggesting a more structured and accountable approach than Russia's chaotic recruitment. ## Uncertain Outcomes and Cautious Optimism As the program gains momentum, questions remain about long-term outcomes. Many prisoners await news from fellow inmates who have already deployed to assess whether military service genuinely offers redemption or merely different dangers. The success of this recruitment strategy will ultimately depend on how these former convicts perform in combat and whether the program achieves its dual objectives of strengthening military capacity while providing rehabilitation opportunities for Ukraine's incarcerated population.

New Hampshire authorities reported three separate incidents. A Rotterdam foster parent has been indicted on murder charges in the death of a 4-year-old boy who was in his care, according to Schenectady County District Attorney’s officials. Dequan Greene, 27, of Broadway, appeared in Schenectady County Court on Friday morning after a grand jury indictment charged him with second-degree murder, first-degree manslaughter, second-degree assault, and child endangerment offenses. Prosecutors said he is accused of causing the December 20 death of the boy, identified by authorities as Charlie, and of assaulting Charlie’s 5-year-old brother, who was also living in the home. Greene’s wife, Latrisha Greene, was also charged, but not in connection with Charlie’s death. Prosecutors said she faces evidence tampering and misdemeanor child endangerment charges. The evidence tampering allegation stems from claims that she texted her husband from Ellis Hospital after speaking with police and asked him to clean the house. She was not charged in the child’s death itself. According to prosecutors, emergency responders were called to the couple’s home at 2734 Broadway after a 911 report that Charlie was in respiratory distress. Paramedics found him not breathing and tried unsuccessfully to revive him. Greene initially told first responders that Charlie had fallen out of a child’s chair, began slurring his speech, and then passed out. He later told others the child had choked. Prosecutors said he did not call 911 himself; instead, he called his wife, who was out shopping, and she later made the emergency call when she returned home. A medical investigation found that Charlie’s death was caused by “extensive internal injury to his liver and intestines caused by blunt force trauma,” prosecutors said. Charlie’s older brother was also removed from the home and taken to Albany Medical Center, where he was treated for bruises, abrasions, and a torn frenulum. The brothers had been placed with the Greenes in September by Child Protective Services of the Albany County Department of Social Services after an Albany County Family Court order removed them from their biological parents. Prosecutors said the Greenes had been certified as foster parents by the Schenectady County Department of Social Services, though they had only fostered one child before, and only for one day. The couple also have three young daughters of their own. District Attorney Robert Carney said his office will prosecute the case and emphasized that questions about how the tragedy occurred are legitimate areas for investigation. He said the children had been placed in the foster home in a well-intentioned effort to keep them safe, but instead were subjected to cruelty and violence. Carney added that Charlie’s brother is now in a safe and caring environment. Dequan Greene pleaded not guilty and was ordered held. He is represented by attorney James Tyner. Prosecutors said the investigation was led jointly by Carney and Rotterdam Police Chief William Manikas, with the case developed through a grand jury investigation.

Dartmouth’s men’s basketball team voted Tuesday to unionize in a landmark move that could become the first labor union for college athletes in the United States, though several legal and procedural steps still stand between the vote and an actual contract. In an election overseen by the National Labor Relations Board in Dartmouth’s human resources offices in Hanover, New Hampshire, the players voted 13-2 to join Service Employees International Union Local 560, which already represents some Dartmouth workers. Every player on the roster took part in the vote. Team members Cade Haskins and Romeo Myrthil called the result “a big day” for the team and said they had stayed united through the season to win the election. They argued that student-athletes can also be campus workers and union members, and said Dartmouth was “stuck in the past” and that “the age of amateurism” should end. The vote is not yet the final step. Dartmouth has five business days to object to the NLRB’s handling of the election and could also challenge the matter in federal court. Those actions could delay any collective bargaining negotiations until long after the current players have graduated, meaning the team that voted to unionize may not be the team that actually negotiates a first agreement. Dartmouth responded with a statement rejecting the players’ claim that they are employees. The school said it supports the five unions it already negotiates with on campus, including SEIU Local 560, but argued that this situation is different. According to Dartmouth, the men’s basketball players are “not in any way employed by Dartmouth,” and, as Ivy League students, their academics are primary while athletics are part of the educational experience. The school said classifying them as employees “simply because they play basketball” is unprecedented and inaccurate, and said it does not believe unionization is appropriate. The case comes as the NCAA’s long-standing amateur model has been steadily weakened by court decisions and policy changes. For decades, college athletes were treated as unpaid amateurs while coaches, schools, and athletic departments generated huge revenue. More recently, athletes have been allowed to earn money from their name, image, and likeness, and to receive limited stipends for living expenses beyond the cost of attendance. Last month’s NLRB decision that the Dartmouth players are employees with the right to form a union represented a major challenge to that model. The Dartmouth players said they plan to keep pushing beyond their own team. Haskins and Myrthil said they want to speak with other athletes at Dartmouth and across the Ivy League about organizing and advocating for athletes’ rights and well-being. They also said they understand the effort may not help them personally if the process takes too long. The team’s roster includes four seniors, five juniors, three sophomores, and three freshmen. Myrthil said after a game at Harvard last month, following the NLRB ruling, that the team has teammates they love and support and that future players who join the program are part of the same “Dartmouth family.” He said they would support those players as much as possible. The union’s national president, Mary Kay Henry of SEIU, praised the players, saying they “will go down as one of the greatest basketball teams in all of history.” She added that the Ivy League, in her view, is where the “scandalous model” of nearly free labor in college sports began and where it will end. The Dartmouth vote is considered unprecedented in American sports. A prior effort to unionize Northwestern football players failed partly because Northwestern competes in the Big Ten, which includes public universities outside the NLRB’s jurisdiction. The Dartmouth case is seen as especially significant because it comes from the Ivy League, where athletes do not receive athletic scholarships, games are played in largely empty gyms, and contests are often streamed online rather than shown on major television networks.

Belgium’s national Holocaust museum, Kazerne Dossin near Antwerp, has become the center of a political and historical dispute after nine historians resigned from its scientific council, later joined by a tenth, in protest over the cancellation of an event honoring a prominent critic of Israel. The episode has raised concerns among Belgian lawmakers about the museum’s future and whether its mission is being pulled into broader arguments over the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. Kazerne Dossin opened in 2012 as a major step for Holocaust commemoration in Belgium, a country where remembrance has long been complicated. During the Nazi occupation, local police helped in the murder of about a quarter of Belgium’s Jews, and the country’s two main regions have often disputed how much responsibility each should bear for that history. The museum was meant to focus on the Holocaust in the Belgian context, especially the persecution of Jews and Roma, while also reflecting on racism and discrimination more broadly. The current controversy began when the museum agreed in November to host an event organized by Pax Christi, a Catholic aid group, to honor Brigitte Herremans as an “ambassador of peace.” Herremans is known as an outspoken critic of Israel who has called for European Union sanctions against Israel and its citizens and has accused Israel’s supporters of exaggerating anti-Semitism to deflect criticism. Pax Christi itself has previously urged the EU to suspend economic relations with Israel until it respects international law. After Belgium’s Jewish community protested strongly, the museum canceled the event within days. In response, the historians resigned. Herman Van Goethem, rector of Antwerp University and one of those who stepped down, told VRT that Herremans had been “thrown outside the museum like a dog.” He also pointed to the earlier resignation of the museum’s former director, Christophe Busch, in November, saying Busch had wanted to broaden the museum’s scope beyond the Holocaust to include current human rights issues, but that the board resisted. The museum’s board, which is funded by the Flemish region’s center-right, pro-Israel government, did not mention Herremans directly in its statement, but defended its overall mission. It said Kazerne Dossin operates within the Flemish government’s vision of preserving the historical story of Jewish persecution and the Holocaust while also considering modern forms of racism and discrimination. The resignations prompted debate in the Flemish parliament, where lawmakers from different parties worried about the museum’s standing. Tom de Meester of the Labor Party said the cancellation showed that Kazerne Dossin was being “weaponized” by a political wing to legitimize Israel’s policies. Others defended the museum’s decision. Mia Doornaert, a Belgian baroness and former journalist group president, called the planned honor for Herremans “pure provocation” and said anti-Israel activism should not be mixed with Holocaust remembrance. Jewish lawmaker Michael Freilich initially dismissed the resignations, saying “Good riddance,” but also told JTA he is concerned the museum debate is becoming politicized. He said the resignations may help restore calm and allow the museum to move forward without drawing what he sees as inappropriate parallels between the Israeli-Palestinian conflict and the Nazi genocide of Belgian Jews.

Hezbollah fired about 250 rockets and other projectiles into Israel on Sunday in one of its heaviest barrages in months, wounding seven people and sending some rockets as far as the Tel Aviv area. The attack came in response to deadly Israeli strikes in Beirut as cease-fire negotiations continued in an effort to stop the widening war between Israel and Hezbollah. The Israeli military said roughly 250 projectiles were launched, with some intercepted by air defenses. Israel’s emergency service, Magen David Adom, said it treated seven injured people. Among them were a 60-year-old man in severe condition from rocket fire in northern Israel, a 23-year-old man lightly wounded by a blast in Petah Tikva near Tel Aviv, and a 70-year-old woman who inhaled smoke after a car caught fire there. In Haifa, a rocket struck a residential building that police said was at risk of collapsing. The Palestine Red Crescent also reported 13 injuries in Tulkarem in the West Bank, saying an interceptor missile had hit several homes there, though it was not immediately clear whether injuries and damage were caused by rockets or interceptors. Sirens sounded again later in central and northern Israel. The exchange marked a sharp escalation after Israeli airstrikes without warning on Saturday hit central Beirut, killing at least 29 people and wounding 67, according to Lebanon’s Health Ministry. Smoke rose over Beirut again on Sunday after new Israeli strikes. Israel said it had targeted Hezbollah command centers and the group’s intelligence unit in the southern suburbs of Dahiyeh, where Hezbollah has a major presence. A separate Israeli strike hit an army center in southwest Lebanon between Tyre and Naqoura, killing a Lebanese soldier and wounding 18 others, Lebanon’s military said. The Israeli military said it regretted the incident, saying the strike occurred in an area where it was fighting Hezbollah and that its operations are aimed only at militants. Still, Israeli strikes have killed more than 40 Lebanese soldiers since the war began, even though Lebanon’s army has largely stayed out of the conflict. Lebanon’s caretaker prime minister, Najib Mikati, condemned the Beirut strike as an attack on U.S.-led cease-fire efforts, calling it a “direct, bloody message rejecting all efforts and ongoing contacts” to end the war. The fighting began after Hezbollah started firing rockets, missiles and drones into Israel following Hamas’ Oct. 7, 2023, attack from Gaza, saying it was acting in solidarity with the Palestinians and Hamas. Iran supports both armed groups. Israel responded with retaliatory airstrikes, and in September the conflict escalated into all-out war after Israel launched broad airstrikes across Lebanon and killed Hezbollah leader Hassan Nasrallah. The toll has been severe on both sides. Lebanon’s Health Ministry says Israeli attacks have killed more than 3,700 people there and displaced about 1.2 million people, or roughly a quarter of the country’s population. On the Israeli side, about 90 soldiers and nearly 50 civilians have been killed by bombardment in northern Israel and in fighting after Israel’s ground invasion in early October. About 60,000 Israelis have been displaced from the north. Diplomatic efforts continued even as the violence intensified. European Union foreign policy chief Josep Borrell called for an immediate cease-fire and said more pressure was needed on both sides to reach a deal. After meeting Mikati and Lebanese Parliament Speaker Nabih Berri, who has been mediating with Hezbollah, Borrell said the EU was ready to provide $208 million to support the Lebanese military. He later said he did not see the Israeli government clearly interested in a cease-fire and suggested Israel was seeking new conditions. The emerging cease-fire plan would reportedly include the withdrawal of Hezbollah fighters and Israeli troops from southern Lebanon below the Litani River, in line with a U.N. Security Council resolution from the 2006 war. Lebanese troops would patrol the area alongside U.N. peacekeepers. The broader regional war also remained tied to stalled efforts to secure a Gaza cease-fire and hostage release deal. Around 100 hostages are still held in Gaza, and at least a third are believed dead. Families marked a year since the only hostage-release deal of the war, while talks for another agreement have suffered setbacks, including the firing of Israeli Defense Minister Yoav Gallant and Qatar’s suspension of mediation. Hamas wants a full Israeli withdrawal and an end to the war, while Israel has offered only a temporary pause. Meanwhile, Gaza’s Health Ministry said the Palestinian death toll had passed 44,000, and AP journalists reported that six people were killed in strikes in central Gaza on Sunday.

Zeinab Sekaanvand, a young Iranian Kurdish woman, is facing execution in Iran after being convicted of murdering her husband, despite claims that he had repeatedly abused her since she was a minor. Human rights groups and activists have urged Iranian authorities to halt the execution, but it is reportedly scheduled for tomorrow. Sekaanvand ran away from her poor, conservative family at age 15 to marry Hossein Sarmadi. According to her account, the marriage quickly turned violent: she said her husband beat and verbally abused her, and she filed several police complaints, none of which were investigated. When she tried to leave him and return to her parents, they disowned her for eloping. Her case took a fatal turn in 2012, when she was charged with her husband’s murder. She allegedly confessed to stabbing him, but later said that confession was made after 20 days of detention at a police station, where she claims she was tortured and denied access to a lawyer. She did not meet a state-appointed lawyer until her final trial session in October 2014. Before her conviction in West Azerbaijan Province, Sekaanvand retracted her confession and told the judge that her husband’s brother, whom she accused of repeatedly raping her, had killed Sarmadi. She said the brother had promised to pardon her if she accepted blame, invoking a legal practice that allows a victim’s family to accept compensation instead of execution. Her retraction and accusations were ignored, and the brother-in-law was not prosecuted. Her execution was previously postponed because she remarried in prison and became pregnant. She gave birth to a stillborn baby on 30 September after doctors said the fetus died two days earlier, reportedly following the shock of her cellmate’s execution. The article also notes that Iranian law can spare juvenile offenders if they did not understand their crime, but this was not examined in her case. An official assessment found she had a depressive disorder, and she was denied medical care in prison. Iran continues to execute people for crimes committed as minors and reportedly has many more child offenders on death row.

# Summary Zeinab Sekaanvand, a young Iranian woman, faces execution despite being a victim of domestic violence. Married at 15 to Hossein Sarmadi, she endured repeated physical and verbal abuse. Despite filing police complaints, authorities took no action, and her husband refused to grant a divorce. When she attempted to return home, her family disowned her. In 2012, Sekaanvand was charged with her husband's murder after allegedly stabbing him. She was tortured during 20 days of police detention and denied legal representation until her trial in October 2014. She initially confessed but later retracted, claiming her husband's brother—who had repeatedly raped her—committed the murder. The brother-in-law reportedly promised to ensure her pardon if she accepted blame, as Islamic law permits victim's families to accept compensation instead of execution. However, her retraction and accusations were dismissed, and the brother-in-law faced no charges. Sekaanvand's execution was previously postponed after she remarried in prison and became pregnant in 2015. She delivered a stillborn child on September 30, which doctors attributed to trauma from witnessing her cellmate's execution. Despite pleas from human rights organizations, her execution was scheduled to proceed. A psychological evaluation found she suffered from depression with insomnia and decision-making difficulties, yet she was denied medical care in prison. Iranian law permits judges to spare those under 18 if they lack understanding of their offense—a provision never investigated in her case. This year, Iran has executed at least one child offender and maintains approximately 49 more on death row.

Pope Francis used the final day of his historic visit to Iraq to urge Christians in the country’s battered north to forgive the abuses committed by Islamic State militants, to resist despair, and to rebuild their communities. Visiting towns and cities that were once at the center of IS violence, he encountered jubilant crowds of Iraq’s remaining Christians, many of whom saw his presence as proof that they had not been abandoned. In Qaraqosh, one of the main Christian towns on the Nineveh Plains, church bells rang as the pope arrived at the Church of the Immaculate Conception. The town had been overrun by IS in 2014, when Christians and many Muslims fled the group’s advance. Most of the Christian population has still not returned. Francis told the congregation that forgiveness is essential for Christians and said the road to recovery would be long. He urged them not to lose hope and not to give up on their homes, faith, or future. The church he visited had been vandalized by IS militants but was later extensively renovated, making it a visible sign of recovery. The pope’s message was aimed not only at the Christian minority but also at encouraging Iraq’s broader religious coexistence. The Vatican sees the continued presence of Christians in Iraq as crucial to preserving a community that dates back to the time of Christ. Before the 2003 U.S.-led invasion, Iraq’s Christian population was about 1.5 million; today it has fallen to only a few hundred thousand, many of them scattered inside Iraq or abroad. Francis’s visit was meant to strengthen their resolve to remain and help restore the country’s “intricately designed carpet” of faiths and ethnicities. Earlier in the day, Francis visited Mosul, Iraq’s second-largest city and once the center of IS’s self-declared “caliphate.” There, he stood on a red-carpeted stage in a square surrounded by the hollowed-out shells of four destroyed churches. The scene symbolized the devastation left behind after years of extremist rule and war. Francis denounced the cruelty that had befallen Iraq, calling it the cradle of civilization, and lamented the destruction of ancient places of worship and the killing or displacement of thousands of people, including Muslims, Christians, and Yazidis. He specifically spoke out about the suffering of Yazidis, who endured mass killings, kidnappings, and sexual slavery under IS. The square in Mosul where he spoke contained four ruined churches belonging to different Christian denominations: Syriac Catholic, Armenian Orthodox, Syriac Orthodox, and Chaldean. The city had been one of IS’s administrative and financial strongholds, and it was from Mosul’s al-Nuri mosque that IS leader Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi declared himself caliph in his only public appearance. Mosul was liberated only after a brutal nine-month battle in 2017, during which an estimated 9,000 to 11,000 civilians were killed. The war left much of the city and the surrounding north in ruins, and reconstruction has been slow because of Iraq’s ongoing financial crisis. Francis’s visit also highlighted moments of reconciliation. In Mosul, Father Raed Kallo, one of the few Christians who returned after IS’s defeat, told the pope that his Muslim neighbors welcomed him back with hospitality and love. He said that before IS, he had 500 Christian families in his parish, but now only 70 remain. A Muslim civic leader, Gutayba Aagha, used the occasion to invite Christians to come back to Mosul, their properties, and their businesses. Throughout the four-day trip, Francis emphasized interreligious tolerance and fraternity, including in a notable Saturday meeting with Grand Ayatollah Ali al-Sistani, Iraq’s top Shiite cleric. In Qaraqosh, he repeated that forgiveness is necessary to remain Christian and to remain in love. His words followed a testimony from Doha Sabah Abdallah, a resident who said her son and two other young people were killed in a mortar strike in August 2014 as IS approached the town. Their deaths, she said, warned the town to flee; Francis described them as martyrs whose sacrifice saved the city. Before leaving Qaraqosh, Francis signed the book of honor, calling the rebuilt church a symbol of hope for Qaraqosh and all Iraq and praying for peace. He was then scheduled to conclude the day with Mass in a stadium in Irbil, in the Kurdish region, where as many as 10,000 people were expected. The visit drew public health concerns because Iraq was experiencing a worsening coronavirus outbreak and vaccination rates were low, though the Vatican said precautions were being taken, including an outdoor service with limited attendance. Despite that, large crowds gathered throughout the trip, often closely packed and frequently without masks. Francis and his delegation had been vaccinated, but most Iraqis had not.

# Pope Francis Calls for Forgiveness and Rebuilding in Iraq's Christian Communities Pope Francis visited Iraq's devastated Christian heartland, calling on the nation's remaining Christians to forgive the atrocities committed by the Islamic State group and to rebuild their communities. The historic four-day papal visit highlighted the desperate situation facing an ancient faith community struggling to survive in a country where their population has dramatically declined. ## The Scale of Christian Displacement Iraq's Christian population has collapsed from approximately 1.5 million before the 2003 U.S.-led invasion to just a few hundred thousand today. The Islamic State's brutal three-year reign beginning in 2014 accelerated this exodus dramatically. Traditionally Christian towns across the Nineveh Plains were emptied as residents fled the extremists' violence. Four years after IS's military defeat, only a small fraction have returned to their homes, with the majority scattered throughout Iraq or living abroad. ## Pope's Message of Forgiveness and Hope In the town of Qaraqosh, Francis addressed a packed Church of the Immaculate Conception, emphasizing that forgiveness represents a crucial element of Christian recovery. "The road to a full recovery may still be long, but I ask you, please, not to grow discouraged," he stated. "What is needed is the ability to forgive, but also the courage not to give up." The church itself symbolized recovery efforts, having been extensively renovated after IS militants vandalized it during their occupation. Francis also spoke in Mosul, Iraq's second-largest city and the former bureaucratic center of the IS caliphate. Standing on a red carpet stage surrounded by the grey, hollowed-out shells of four destroyed churches—Syriac Catholic, Armenian-Orthodox, Syriac Orthodox, and Chaldean—the pontiff delivered a striking visual message about both devastation and potential renewal. ## Acknowledging Widespread Suffering Francis acknowledged that IS atrocities extended beyond Christians to include Muslims, Yazidis, and other communities. He deviated from his prepared remarks to specifically address the Yazidi minority, which suffered mass killings, abductions, and sexual slavery. "How cruel it is that this country, the cradle of civilization, should have been afflicted by so barbarous a blow," he said, referencing the destruction of ancient places of worship and the deaths of thousands. The nine-month battle to liberate Mosul in 2017 claimed between 9,000 and 11,000 civilian lives. IS leader Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi, who made his only public appearance at Mosul's al-Nuri mosque, was later killed in a U.S. raid in Syria in 2019. ## Signs of Interfaith Reconciliation Despite the trauma, some positive signs emerged. Rev. Raed Kallo, one of the few Christians who returned to Mosul, reported that his Muslim neighbors received him "with great hospitality and love" after liberation. Though his parish dwindled from 500 families to just 70, he now ministers to 2 million Muslims. Gutayba Aagha, the Muslim head of the Independent Social and Cultural Council for Families of Mosul, publicly invited Christians to return to their city, properties, and businesses. ## Broader Papal Objectives Francis's visit aimed to encourage Christians to remain in Iraq and help rebuild the country's "intricately designed carpet" of faith and ethnic groups. Throughout his journey, he delivered messages of interreligious tolerance and fraternity to Muslim leaders, including an historic meeting with Iraq's top Shiite cleric, Grand Ayatollah Ali al-Sistani. The visit concluded with a Mass in Irbil's stadium, expected to draw approximately 10,000 people in the semi-autonomous Kurdish region. ## Health Concerns Public health experts expressed concerns that large gatherings could accelerate coronavirus transmission in Iraq, where vaccination rates remain low and cases are rising. While the Vatican implemented precautions, including holding outdoor events with limited capacity, crowds frequently gathered in close proximity with minimal mask usage. The pope and his delegation were vaccinated, but most Iraqis were not, creating potential transmission risks throughout the visit.

The RCMP’s top officer in British Columbia warned the provincial government last year that budget cuts to a major missing-and-murdered women investigation would weaken its ability to solve cases along the Highway of Tears. The warning came amid reductions to Project E-PANA, the RCMP task force created in 2006 to investigate whether a serial killer was responsible for disappearances and deaths along Highway 16 in northern B.C. E-PANA was eventually assigned 18 cases involving women and girls who vanished or were found dead in the region. The RCMP and the B.C. government confirmed last year that six officers had been removed from the investigation, on top of earlier funding cuts. In a June 4 memo released through a freedom-of-information request, Deputy Commissioner Craig Callens, the commanding officer for B.C., told the province’s director of police services that ending or reducing E-PANA funding would seriously damage historical homicide investigations in the province. Callens wrote that if the force lost more resources, “no other Highway of Tears historical homicide investigations” would be undertaken for the foreseeable future. Sgt. Annie Linteau later said in a written statement that 12 officers were still assigned to the probe, along with support staff, and that the unit still had enough resources to meet current investigative needs. She noted, however, that the task force had once had about 70 officers at its peak. The B.C. government said Justice Minister Suzanne Anton was unavailable for an interview. The ministry said the RCMP had been consulted about the cuts and that it was up to the force to decide how to distribute its resources. A separate freedom-of-information release showed E-PANA’s budget had dropped to $1.8 million for 2012-13, down from about $5 million in earlier years. The investigation has produced some notable developments. In 2012, police said they believed a dead American convict may have killed as many as three of the women. In December, Mounties announced murder charges against a 67-year-old Ontario man in the 1978 death of 12-year-old Monica Jack, who disappeared from Merritt, B.C. The Highway of Tears has been a major focus of the public inquiry into the Robert Pickton case and is often raised by advocates calling for a national inquiry into missing and murdered Aboriginal women. In a draft version of his memo, Callens warned that cuts could also damage public confidence and undermine B.C.’s reputation for improving these investigations. The opposition NDP criticized the government, urging it to reverse the cuts.

# RCMP Warned B.C. Budget Cuts Would Harm Highway of Tears Investigation The RCMP's top-ranking officer in British Columbia warned the provincial government that budget cuts would compromise investigations into missing and murdered women along Highway 16, known as the Highway of Tears. The E-PANA task force was established in 2006 to investigate whether a serial killer operated in the northern B.C. corridor. The investigation eventually encompassed 18 cases of missing or deceased women and girls. In a June 4 memo obtained through freedom-of-information request, RCMP Deputy Commissioner Craig Callens informed the province's director of police services that eliminating E-PANA funding "would impair the ability to effectively conduct historical homicide investigations" and result in no further Highway of Tears investigations "for the foreseeable future." The RCMP and B.C. government confirmed that six officers were cut from the investigation, which had previously experienced budget reductions. The task force, which once employed approximately 70 officers, now has 12 investigators plus support staff. The budget dropped from roughly $5 million to $1.8 million for 2012-2013. Despite the warnings, Justice Minister Suzanne Anton declined to comment. The ministry stated that the RCMP was consulted about cuts and retains responsibility for resource allocation. An RCMP sergeant countered that remaining resources are sufficient for current investigative needs. The investigation has produced results despite reduced funding. In 2012, investigators identified a deceased American convict as potentially responsible for three murders. Last December, the RCMP charged a 67-year-old Ontario man in the 1978 death of 12-year-old Monica Jack from Merritt, B.C. A draft version of Callens' memo included additional concerns absent from other versions. Callens warned that budget cuts could damage British Columbia's reputation as committed to serious investigation of murdered and missing women cases, potentially eroding public confidence and causing loss of best practices. It remains unclear whether this passage appeared in the final memo. The Highway of Tears case gained prominence through the Robert Pickton missing women inquiry, with commissioner Wally Oppal recommending safety improvements. The case is frequently cited by advocacy groups demanding a national inquiry into murdered and missing Indigenous women. Opposition NDP public safety critic Mike Farnworth criticized the cuts, stating it was inappropriate to reduce funding for such a high-profile investigation while claiming to take the issue seriously.

At Richard Henry Bain’s first-degree murder trial in Montreal, the defence tried Friday to undermine the Crown’s psychiatric expert and support its claim that Bain was not criminally responsible because of mental disorder. Bain is accused of shooting a man dead outside the Parti Québécois election-night victory rally on Sept. 4, 2012, and faces charges of murder, attempted murder and arson-related offences. Defence lawyer Alan Guttman argued that Bain suffered a psychotic episode after taking the antidepressant Cymbalta in 2009 and never fully recovered. He said Bain resumed the drug in 2012, without his doctor’s knowledge, which triggered another psychotic episode before the shooting. Bain has told the jury that the medication caused his symptoms. During cross-examination, Guttman pressed Crown forensic psychiatrist Joel Watts on his report and got him to acknowledge that Bain had shown signs of psychosis in the past, contrary to what Watts had written. Defence psychiatrist Marie-Frederique Allard had already testified that Bain displayed mania and psychosis in 2009, including stockpiling about $75,000 in food, medicine and other supplies because of a delusional fear of H1N1 flu. Watts, however, maintained that Bain’s actions in 2012 did not necessarily prove another manic episode. He pointed to evidence of organized planning on the night of the shooting, including Bain wearing a mask and removing the license plate from his vehicle. The Crown argues Bain acted out of anger over the PQ’s election win, not mental illness.

# Summary Richard Henry Bain's defence team attempted to discredit the Crown's psychiatric expert during his first-degree murder trial in Montreal on Friday. Defence lawyer Alan Guttman argued that Bain suffered a psychotic episode caused by the anti-depressant Cymbalta in 2009 and never fully recovered. Bain allegedly resumed taking the drug in 2012, triggering another episode that led to the shooting death of a man outside a Parti Québécois election rally on September 4, 2012. Guttman successfully pressured Crown forensic psychiatrist Joel Watts into acknowledging that Bain had previously shown psychotic symptoms, contradicting Watts's written report. The defence psychiatrist testified that Bain displayed mania and psychosis in 2009, including delusional fears about H1N1 flu, leading him to stockpile $75,000 in supplies. The defence claims Bain's symptoms resurfaced in May 2012 when he resumed Cymbalta without medical supervision, manifesting as erratic behaviour and irrational beliefs. Guttman questioned whether Bain's spending of $400 on sex workers and champagne before the shooting indicated a manic episode, though Watts disagreed. The 65-year-old has pleaded not guilty to first-degree murder, three counts of attempted murder, and arson charges. The defence argues Bain is not criminally responsible due to mental disorder, while the Crown claims he acted from anger over the election results.

A man and woman from Whittier, a Los Angeles suburb, were arrested on suspicion of murder after trying to enter Mexico with the body of a 2-year-old girl hidden in a duffel bag, San Diego police said. The suspects were identified as Johnny Lewis Hartley, 39, and Mercy Mary Becerra, 43. Police said the pair were stopped Tuesday at the San Ysidro Port of Entry while attempting to cross the pedestrian bridge into Tijuana. Mexican authorities contacted San Diego police after customs agents stopped them. During the stop, Becerra allegedly ran off, while Hartley was detained with the bag. An X-ray of the duffel bag revealed a child’s body inside. Authorities said the girl was about 2 years old and that Hartley and Becerra were not her parents. Becerra was later taken into custody by Mexican authorities, and both suspects were turned over to U.S. investigators, interviewed by homicide detectives, and booked into San Diego County jails. Police said the case may have originated in Whittier, and San Diego investigators are working with Whittier police. Hartley was booked on suspicion of first-degree murder and child cruelty, and Becerra was booked on the same charges. Both were scheduled for arraignment Friday.

# Summary On Tuesday, Johnny Lewis Hartley, 39, and Mercy Mary Becerra, 43, from Whittier, California, were arrested at the San Ysidro Port of Entry while attempting to cross into Tijuana with the body of a 2-year-old girl concealed in a duffel bag. Mexican customs agents stopped them at the pedestrian bridge, and when X-rayed, the bag revealed the child's body inside. Becerra fled but was quickly apprehended by Mexican authorities, while Hartley was initially detained with the duffel bag. Both individuals were turned over to U.S. investigators and interviewed by homicide detectives. Neither suspect is the girl's parent. Police determined the incident likely occurred in Whittier, prompting coordination between San Diego and Whittier police departments. Both suspects were booked into San Diego County jails on Wednesday—Hartley at San Diego Central Jail and Becerra at Las Colinas Detention and Reentry Facility—on suspicion of first-degree murder and child cruelty. Both were scheduled for arraignment on Friday.

Ontario Premier Kathleen Wynne sharply criticized Prime Minister Stephen Harper on Friday for rejecting calls for a national inquiry into missing and murdered aboriginal women. In an interview with The Canadian Press, Wynne said Harper was wrong to argue that police investigations, rather than a public inquiry, are the best response. She called his dismissal of a systemic problem “outrageous,” saying there is clearly a broader pattern behind the violence. Her comments came amid renewed public pressure following the death of 15-year-old Tina Fontaine, whose body was found wrapped in a bag and dumped in Winnipeg’s Red River. Fontaine had been in Winnipeg for less than a month after running away from foster care. Police are treating her death as a homicide. The case has intensified demands for an inquiry into the larger crisis affecting Indigenous women and girls. Harper and the federal Conservatives have repeatedly rejected that approach, saying the issue should be addressed through existing measures such as aboriginal justice programs and a national DNA missing-persons index. Harper said Thursday that most cases are solved by police and should be treated as crimes, not as a “sociological phenomenon.” He pointed to an RCMP report released in May that documented 1,181 cases since 1980 and showed that aboriginal women, while representing 4.3 per cent of Canada’s population, accounted for 16 per cent of female homicides and 11.3 per cent of missing women. Wynne said the premiers will continue pushing for an inquiry. She noted that all provinces and territories already endorsed the idea at last year’s Council of the Federation meeting, and they are expected to discuss the issue again at next week’s meeting in Charlottetown with aboriginal leaders. She argued that Indigenous communities face deep systemic problems that go beyond individual crimes, including poor education outcomes and inadequate infrastructure. In Ontario, she said, high-school graduation rates for aboriginal youth can be as low as 40 per cent, compared with 83 per cent for other students, and some northern communities still lack safe drinking water. Wynne also accused Harper of avoiding serious engagement with provinces and territories on national issues, saying his approach is polarizing and counterproductive. She said Ottawa’s refusal to work collectively risks repeating past conflicts, such as the dispute over job training funding, which eventually forced the federal government to compromise.

# Summary Ontario Premier Kathleen Wynne criticized Prime Minister Stephen Harper's position on addressing crimes involving missing and murdered aboriginal women, calling his stance "outrageous." Harper has rejected calls for a national public inquiry, arguing that police investigations are the most effective approach to solving these crimes. The dispute centers on whether systemic issues contribute to these crimes. Harper contends that these cases should be viewed as individual crimes requiring police investigation rather than as a sociological phenomenon. The federal Conservatives prefer addressing the issue through aboriginal justice programs and establishing a national DNA missing person's index. Wynne countered that systemic problems clearly exist within aboriginal communities. She cited RCMP statistics showing that aboriginal women comprise only 4.3 percent of Canada's population but account for 16 percent of female homicides and 11.3 percent of missing women cases. She also highlighted other systemic disparities: aboriginal high school graduation rates in Ontario reach only 40 percent compared to 83 percent among mainstream students, and some northern Ontario communities lack safe drinking water. The renewed debate was prompted by the death of 15-year-old Tina Fontaine, whose body was discovered in the Red River wrapped in a bag. She had been in Winnipeg less than a month after running away from foster care, and police are treating her death as a homicide. All Canadian provinces and territories previously endorsed calls for a public inquiry at last year's Council of the Federation conference. They plan to discuss the issue again at an upcoming meeting in Charlottetown, P.E.I., with aboriginal leaders present. Wynne argued that while Ontario has made efforts to improve conditions in aboriginal communities, the constitutional responsibility for addressing these systemic issues rests with the federal government. She suggested Ottawa opposes an inquiry because it would expose these broader societal failures. She also criticized Harper's general approach to federalism, arguing his preference for dealing with provinces separately rather than collectively is polarizing and counterproductive.

The Winnipeg Police Service is mourning Banner, a K-9 officer who died Wednesday from aggressive cancer at Bridgewater Veterinary Hospital. Police shared the news on Twitter Thursday and said Banner, who had been with the K-9 unit since 2014, passed away suddenly and will be missed. Banner’s handler, Const. Justin Casavant, said the dog had more than 200 tracking arrests and took part in hundreds of high-risk operations with the Tactical Support Team. Winnipeg police Const. Jay Murray said Banner was instrumental in helping capture Bryan Kyle Thomas, who was later convicted of second-degree murder in the 2017 stabbing death of Winnipeg Transit driver Ivrine Jubal Fraser. Casavant said Banner remained active until the end of his life. Less than 24 hours before he died, on what became his last official shift, Banner tracked from a stolen vehicle to a residence, leading to the arrest of two people. He began showing signs of illness on Tuesday, was taken to the veterinary hospital, and by Wednesday morning veterinarians determined the cancer was advancing rapidly. Casavant and his wife thanked supporters and the veterinary staff, and he also credited retired Sgt. Dave Bessason and Const. Dennis Robert for training him and Banner. Winnipeg police said their K-9 unit supports officers in suspect searches and other operations, and the service maintains its own breeding program.

# Summary The Winnipeg Police Service announced the death of Banner, a K-9 unit officer who died from cancer on Wednesday at Bridgewater Veterinary Hospital. Banner had served in the police force since 2014 and was instrumental in capturing Bryan Kyle Thomas, who was convicted of second-degree murder in the 2017 stabbing death of Winnipeg Transit driver Ivrine Jubal Fraser. According to Banner's handler, Constable Justin Casavant, the dog achieved over 200 tracking arrests and participated in hundreds of high-risk operations with the Tactical Support Team. Notably, Banner completed a tracking arrest just 24 hours before his death, locating suspects from a stolen vehicle. Banner became ill on Tuesday and was hospitalized, where aggressive cancer was diagnosed. The disease caused rapid deterioration, leading to his death the following morning. Casavant expressed gratitude to the veterinary hospital staff and colleagues who supported Banner's training and development. The Winnipeg Police Service operates one of Canada's few in-house K-9 breeding programs, primarily using Belgian Malinois, German Shepherds, and Labrador Retrievers.

Keshaudas Spence, a 29-year-old Brockton, Massachusetts native and former Sacred Heart University football standout, was identified Monday as the victim of a fatal weekend shooting in Pawtucket, Rhode Island. Police said Spence was found around 4:45 a.m. Saturday in the passenger seat of a car with a gunshot wound. He was rushed to a hospital, where he was pronounced dead. Authorities have not released details about the driver, and no arrests have been announced. His death was ruled a homicide. Spence starred as a running back at Sacred Heart from 2011 to 2014, finishing as the program’s all-time leading rusher with 3,745 yards and earning a communications degree in 2015. Head coach Mark Nofri called him one of the greatest players to wear a Sacred Heart jersey and praised him as a great teammate and person. After college, Spence played in the Indoor Football League for the Green Bay Blizzard and Iowa Barnstormers, both of which issued tributes following his death.

# Summary Keshaudas Spence, a 29-year-old from Brockton, Massachusetts, was fatally shot in Pawtucket, Rhode Island early Saturday morning. He was discovered in a car's passenger seat with a gunshot wound at approximately 4:45 a.m. and pronounced dead at the hospital. Police have not identified the driver or made any arrests, though the death was ruled a homicide. Spence was a standout running back at Sacred Heart University in Connecticut from 2011 to 2014, finishing as the program's career rushing leader with 3,745 yards. After graduating in 2015 with a communications degree, he played professionally in the Indoor Football League for the Green Bay Blizzard and Iowa Barnstormers. Both his university and professional teams released statements mourning his loss, praising his athletic abilities and character.

Armenia and Azerbaijan reported renewed fighting on Tuesday over the separatist territory of Nagorno-Karabakh, despite two recent attempts to secure a cease-fire. The latest clashes have continued for more than three weeks, making this the worst escalation in the decades-old conflict since fighting broke out again on Sept. 27. Azerbaijan’s Defense Ministry said hostilities continued overnight and accused Armenian forces of shelling the Terter and Agdam regions in the morning. Azerbaijani authorities said two civilians were killed and one wounded in Terter. In response, Armenian Defense Ministry spokeswoman Shushan Stepanian said there were “intensive fierce battles” in the southern part of the conflict zone and alleged that Azerbaijani forces were using aviation and artillery in the north. The two sides had announced a cease-fire on Saturday, following an earlier Russian-brokered truce a week before. Both agreements quickly unraveled amid mutual accusations of violations, and the fighting resumed almost immediately. Nagorno-Karabakh is internationally recognized as part of Azerbaijan, but it has been controlled by ethnic Armenian forces backed by Armenia since a war ended in 1994. That earlier war left Armenian forces in control of Nagorno-Karabakh itself and also in possession of significant surrounding territory. Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev said his military had retaken several towns and villages in the Jabrayil and Fizuli regions, which are among the Azerbaijani districts outside Nagorno-Karabakh seized in the early 1990s. He also said Azerbaijani forces captured the town of Zangilan and nearby villages south of Nagorno-Karabakh. Casualty figures remain disputed. Nagorno-Karabakh officials say 773 of their troops and more than 30 civilians have been killed since Sept. 27. Azerbaijan has not disclosed military losses, but says 61 civilians have died and 291 have been wounded. The fighting has drawn international concern over the risk of a broader regional conflict, especially given Turkey’s support for Azerbaijan and Russia’s security ties to Armenia. A Russian-hosted meeting on Oct. 9 produced a cease-fire that collapsed within minutes. The latest truce followed calls by Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov, but new attacks were again reported. Armenian and Azerbaijani foreign ministers are scheduled to meet U.S. Secretary of State Mike Pompeo in Washington on Friday.

Armenia's Defence Ministry spokeswoman countered with reports of "intensive fierce battles" in the southern conflict zone and allegations that Azerbaijan was using aviation and artillery in the north. The latest outbreak of violence began September 27, representing the worst escalation of a decades-long dispute. Nagorno-Karabakh, located within Azerbaijan's borders, has been controlled by ethnic Armenian forces backed by Armenia since a 1994 war ended. Armenian and Azerbaijani foreign ministers are scheduled to meet U.S. Secretary of State Mike Pompeo in Washington on Friday. Pompeo has called on both countries to "implement their agreed-upon commitments to a cease-fire" and stated that Washington is pursuing diplomatic efforts toward a sustainable settlement.

Iran’s judiciary said several people convicted of terror-related crimes were executed on Aug. 2 in western Kurdistan province. Officials said the men belonged to the extremist group “Tohid and Jihad” and had been sentenced to death after a six-year trial for killing and injuring civilians, wildlife guards, security forces and Sunni clerics. The statement also linked them to armed robbery. The number executed was not given, though human rights groups said at least seven were killed. Iran allows the death penalty for several crimes and ranks second globally in executions.

# Summary Iran's judiciary announced the execution of several individuals charged with terrorism in Kurdistan province on August 2. The executed were members of the extremist group "Tohid and Jihad." While the exact number remains unspecified, human rights groups claim at least seven were executed. Following a six-year trial, they were sentenced to death for killing and injuring civilians, security forces, and wildlife guards, plus armed robbery. Iran ranks second globally in execution numbers after China.

Belarusian President Aleksandr Lukashenko has signed an amnesty law timed to the 75th anniversary of Belarus’ liberation from Nazi occupation, the presidential press service said. The measure is presented as an act of “humanity” linked to the historic anniversary. It covers people convicted of minor offenses, including minors, mothers and single fathers with underage children, pregnant women, pensioners, people with disabilities in groups 1 and 2, cancer patients, foreign war veterans, those injured on duty, and people affected by the Chernobyl disaster. The law also provides sentence reductions for some drug-related convictions under Article 328: one year off for those convicted under Part 1 and Parts 2-3, while minors may receive a two-year reduction. However, it excludes people previously amnestied or pardoned between 2014 and 2019 who reoffended, those who failed to compensate damages, serious prison rule violators, and people convicted of grave crimes such as murder, serious bodily harm, sex crimes, terrorism, civil unrest, drunk driving causing injury or death, and illegal drug trafficking. About 6,000 convicts, including roughly 2,000 prisoners, are expected to benefit. The law takes effect upon publication and must be implemented within nine months.

# Summary Belarusian President Aleksandr Lukashenko signed an amnesty bill into law on July 22, commemorating the 75th anniversary of Belarus' liberation from Nazi occupation. The amnesty applies to approximately 6,000 convicts, including roughly 2,000 prisoners convicted of minor crimes. Eligible beneficiaries include minors, mothers and single fathers with underage children, pregnant women, pensioners, disabled individuals, cancer patients, foreign war veterans, and Chernobyl victims. The law provides one-year sentence reductions for most eligible convicts and two-year reductions for minors. However, the amnesty excludes individuals previously amnestied between 2014-2019 who committed subsequent crimes, those who failed to compensate victims, serious prison rule violators, and those convicted of grave offenses including homicide, sexual crimes, terrorism, and drug trafficking. The law takes effect upon official publication and must be executed within nine months.

Darya Ageny was 18 when, in June 2018, she stabbed a stranger who she says sexually assaulted her on a street in Tuapse, a Russian resort town. Ageny, an aspiring artist from Moscow who was working at a children’s camp for the summer, said a drunk man followed her as she walked back to her hostel, shouted lewd remarks, grabbed her by the arm, and then pushed her against a wall and thrust his hand down her pants. She said she screamed for help, but no one intervened. Fearing for herself, she reached into her bag for a small pocketknife she used for sharpening pencils and swung it until the man backed off and left. After the attack, Ageny gathered her scattered belongings and was escorted home by a group of teenagers she encountered nearby. They examined the knife and threw it into a stream, something Ageny later said hurt her case. Investigators eventually recovered the blade from the water. The man, later identified as 38-year-old married father Igor Storozhev, ended up in hospital after the knife pierced his intestine, and doctors were required by law to alert police. Ageny, meanwhile, left Tuapse and assumed the matter would fade; she said she did not remember what her attacker looked like and was certain she had not stabbed him. But a month later, police came to her workplace in Moscow and arrested her. She now faces up to 10 years in prison on a charge of grievous bodily harm. Her case has become one of the most closely watched examples in Russia of the struggle over self-defense, sexual violence, and victim-blaming. Human rights advocates and feminist activists say Russian women are often left to fend for themselves when assaulted, with the state failing to protect them and courts applying a rigid idea of “proportionality” that can punish victims for using force to escape danger. Alyona Popova, a prominent women’s rights activist, said cases like Ageny’s, as well as other recent high-profile trials, show that victims are often forced to grab whatever weapon is available because they are abandoned by the system. Several other cases have intensified public attention. In the Krasnodar region, 28-year-old Kristina Shidukova was sentenced to eight years in prison after stabbing her husband to death when, according to her account, he tried to push her off a fourth-floor balcony. Her case prompted an online petition that gathered more than 150,000 signatures. Even more attention has focused on the Khachaturyan sisters—Maria, Angelina, and Krestina—who stabbed their father to death in a Moscow suburb after years of alleged humiliation and sexual abuse. Their trial has fueled broader debate about domestic violence and self-defense in Russia. Ageny says she knew from the beginning that if she told anyone about the assault, she would be blamed. After her arrest, she was taken back to Tuapse for questioning and placed in a lineup with two women who, she said, looked nothing like her. Storozhev identified her as the attacker. Ageny described the scene as absurd, saying it felt like a second violation: the man she says tried to rape her was now accusing her of being the criminal. During a joint interview with investigators, Storozhev reportedly claimed he had merely been reciting poetry to her and that she stabbed him only after he took her hand. According to Ageny and her lawyer, Yevgeny Salomatov, he was asked to recite the Sergei Yesenin poems he said he had been reading to her, but declined, saying he no longer remembered them. Salomatov urged Ageny to make her story public, and once she did, she began hearing from other women who had been assaulted or raped. Many told her they had never gone to police or spoken to relatives because they feared being disbelieved or blamed. Ageny said one woman contacted her after locking herself in a room during a first-date assault and asked for urgent help; Ageny later traveled to help her file a police report. She launched a website and the Instagram hashtag #саманевиновата, or “it’s not my fault,” to encourage survivors to share their stories and to connect them with resources. Her case has become a symbol not only of self-defense but also of the wider culture of silence and shame surrounding sexual violence in Russia. Ageny’s trial has not yet begun, and investigators are still assembling the case. Her lawyer says the central problem is that there is little physical evidence of assault: she has no obvious injuries and no witnesses, so it becomes her word against Storozhev’s. He argues that Russian law offers no clear guidance for self-defense when an attacker leaves no visible marks, and that cases like hers need publicity or they may never reach court fairly. Ageny says she should not have to campaign publicly to defend herself. “There should be fair courts,” she said, while adding that she does not want to be remembered simply as “the girl who stabbed someone.”

Belarusian President Administration head Igor Sergeyenko said anyone in Belarus or abroad who tries to “stage a revolution” will be held accountable, following the killing of a KGB officer in Minsk. He described the officer’s death as a tragedy, saying the officer died in the line of duty during special anti-terrorism and anti-extremism operations, and expressed condolences to the family and friends. Sergeyenko also addressed people he accused of supporting extremism, including shop owners allegedly selling “battle leaflets,” social media users, self-styled reporters, and others who, in his words, glorified the suspect or mocked the victim’s family. He warned them not to delete online accounts and said those involved would be found and made answerable. He portrayed their actions as immoral and said there would be “no forgiveness and no justification” for them.

# Summary A Belarusian KGB officer was killed in Minsk during special operations against terrorism and extremism. Igor Sergeyenko, head of the Belarus President Administration, announced that all those involved in attempting to stage a "revolution" in Belarus and abroad will face justice. Sergeyenko condemned those who celebrate the officer's death, including activists, media figures, and opposition supporters. He warned shop owners selling materials advocating extremism and violence, as well as social media users promoting revolutionary activity. Sergeyenko stated that authorities will identify and prosecute all perpetrators and their supporters, declaring there is "no forgiveness and no justification" for the incident. He characterized opposition figures as unprincipled and immoral, equating them with criminals.

The article argues that a recent wave of terrorist attacks in the West Bank and Jerusalem has sharply increased internal tensions in Israel at a sensitive political moment. It says the violence, which killed soldiers and civilians, has reignited public anger and sharpened divisions between supporters of tougher military action and those favoring a more restrained approach. The atmosphere became especially heated after the attack in Givat Assaf, with thousands of people demonstrating in Jerusalem near the prime minister’s residence and demanding a firm response to the violence. The Associated Press report, datelined Astana, Kazakhstan, describes the growing number of Russian soldiers who have fled the war in Ukraine but have found that escape brings no clear safety or future. All now face criminal charges in Russia, where desertion can bring prison terms of 10 years or more. Their situation highlights a wider dilemma for Western governments: Russian soldiers on the run may be seen as potential refugees, antiwar dissidents, or security threats. Are they spies, war criminals, or men who refused to participate in the invasion?
