Policymakers remain split over whether exiled Russians should be treated as assets who weaken Putin’s war effort or as risks to national security. One advocate for engagement is Andrius Kubilius, a former Lithuanian prime minister now in the European Parliament. He argues that the West should cultivate Russians who oppose Vladimir Putin because each soldier who leaves the front weakens Russia’s army. He rejected the idea that all Russians are guilty and said it is a mistake not to believe in the possibility of Russian democracy. The activist group Idite Lesom, or “Get Lost,” based in Georgia, says more than 500 people contacted it in the first two months of this year alone to ask about desertion. In Germany, fewer than 10% of the 5,246 asylum applications processed last year resulted in some kind of protection. Still, Russians continue to leave in large numbers. U.S. border authorities encountered more than 57,000 Russians in fiscal year 2023, up from about 13,000 in fiscal year 2021. Affirmative asylum requests nearly quadrupled to almost 9,000 in the year ending September 2022. France saw Russian asylum requests rise more than 50% from 2022 to 2023, reaching about 3,400. The article notes that these figures do not specify how many applicants were soldiers. The piece closes with another deserter, nicknamed Sportsmaster, who documented his escape in a video diary. After crossing the border with only a small backpack, he said the worst had already happened and that only good things were left ahead.

A Chilean judge on Tuesday moved proceedings to a house in Santiago’s San Miguel neighborhood to stage a re-enactment of the 1974 killing of leftist militant Miguel Enriquez Espinosa, leader of the Movement of the Revolutionary Left (MIR). Judge Mario Carroza said the goal was to clarify whether Enriquez was killed during a gunfight with Augusto Pinochet’s secret police, the DINA, or executed after the confrontation ended. The re-enactment involved former DINA agent Miguel Krassnoff, who led the operation, and Carmen Castillo, Enriquez’s partner, who was six months pregnant at the time. Carroza said he was satisfied to hear Krassnoff describe his own actions and those of his subordinates. Krassnoff was later returned to Punta Peuco prison, where he is serving what amounts to a life sentence for dozens of convictions linked to the Pinochet era. According to the article, Enriquez, Castillo, and two other MIR militants were in the house when DINA agents, backed by tanks and helicopters, attacked. Enriquez was hit 10 times in a 25-minute battle that wounded Castillo; two other militants escaped. Plaintiffs argue Enriquez was still alive when agents entered and was then finished off. More than 1,250 MIR activists died under Pinochet’s rule.

# Summary A Chilean judge conducted a re-enactment on Tuesday at the Santiago home where leftist militant Miguel Enriquez Espinosa was killed on October 5, 1974, by Augusto Pinochet's secret police. The re-enactment included former DINA agent Miguel Krassnoff, who led the operation, and Carmen Castillo, Enriquez's pregnant partner who was present during the original incident. Krassnoff, currently serving a de-facto life sentence for crimes under the 1973-1990 Pinochet regime, was returned to prison following the session. Heavy rain at Interlagos forced organizers to postpone qualifying for the Brazilian Grand Prix on Saturday after a two-hour delay, pushing the session to Sunday at the Sao Paulo circuit. More than 60,000 fans began leaving the stands once the postponement was announced. The weather also delayed a tribute to legendary three-time Formula 1 champion Ayrton Senna, whose title-winning McLaren was scheduled to be driven by Mercedes’ Lewis Hamilton, one of Senna’s biggest admirers. The rain interruption came after a dramatic day in which McLaren’s Lando Norris won the sprint race and reduced his championship deficit to Red Bull’s Max Verstappen. Norris, who started second on the grid, benefited from a late-race decision by teammate Oscar Piastri, who yielded the lead to him during the 24-lap sprint. Norris said over team radio that he was confused by Piastri’s pace and asked, “I am not sure what I am doing here, mate. I thought we spoke about this.” Afterward, Norris acknowledged the team’s strategy and thanked Piastri, saying McLaren had worked well together. “I am not proud about it but we worked well as a team together so I thank Oscar,” he said. “Oscar deserved (a win) but we did what we had to do.” Piastri later said it was “not as fun as winning,” but noted the team had been discussing the arrangement for months. Verstappen finished third in the sprint, but a stewards’ ruling changed the result after the race. Officials said he had been “above the minimum time at the virtual safety car end,” which led to a five-second penalty and dropped him to fourth. The penalty also added one point to his license total, bringing him to seven for the 12-month period. Ferrari’s Charles Leclerc, who remains a long-shot contender for the title, finished fourth on track and was promoted to third after Verstappen’s penalty. Carlos Sainz Jr. was fifth, followed by Mercedes’ George Russell, Alpine’s Pierre Gasly and Red Bull’s Sergio Perez in the points. With four grands prix and one sprint race remaining in the season, Norris has cut Verstappen’s lead to 44 points. Verstappen also faces an added setback for Sunday’s race after taking a five-place grid penalty for using his sixth engine of the season, exceeding the allowed four.

At least 18 people were killed Saturday at the illegal Cicapra gold mine in southern Venezuela when army troops moved in to seize control of the area, an official said. An army officer, speaking anonymously, said the operation began after the military received reports that an armed gang was threatening wildcat miners. During the clash, soldiers seized four assault weapons, grenades and several light firearms. Officials said no troops were killed. The dead were not identified, though one victim is believed to be a woman known locally as “the boss,” who allegedly took over after her brother, suspected gang leader Anderson Rodriguez, was killed last year. The violence was the deadliest mine incident in Bolivar state since 17 miners were found in a mass grave in 2016, underscoring the worsening turf war between criminal gangs and the military.

# Summary At least 18 people died during clashes between Venezuelan security forces and armed individuals at an illegal gold mine in southern Venezuela on Saturday. The army intervened at the Cicapra mine after receiving reports that an armed gang was threatening wildcat miners in the remote area. Four assault weapons, grenades, and several firearms were seized during the confrontation. No soldiers were killed. Officials believe one of the deceased is a woman suspected of controlling the area following her brother's murder last year. The incident marks the most violent mine clash in Bolivar state since 2016, when 17 wildcat miners were discovered in a mass grave. Violence has escalated in the resource-rich region as Venezuela's government seeks foreign investment while criminal gangs and military forces battle for control.

In Buenos Aires’s largest slum, Villa 21-24, the coronavirus pandemic has intensified an already harsh daily struggle marked by poverty, overcrowding, drug use, violence, poor sanitation, and unreliable water and electricity. The neighborhood, located beside the heavily polluted Matanza Riachuelo River, is home to about 70,000 people and has four public health centers, but its dense living conditions make infection risk especially high. Against this backdrop, residents, parish workers, and local organizations have turned the neighborhood into a tightly knit support network. Liliana, a Paraguayan resident recovering from dengue, continues helping elderly neighbors during quarantine by delivering food. She said she feels compelled to keep fighting despite having a fever herself. Along with Leonida, who has been emotionally affected since her 25-year-old son was killed by police in 2017, she works with the Corriente Villera Independiente and the parish led by Father Lorenzo de Vedia, known locally as Father Toto. At the Church of the Virgin of Miracles of Caacupe, long lines form as people wait for food to take home. The church and parish kitchens are feeding large numbers of families, with Father Toto saying they cook for 900 families in one area and 500 in another, while also supporting eight dining halls. Because many elderly residents cannot risk leaving home, volunteers deliver meals and medications directly to their doors. Carolina, a health coordinator with the MP La Dignidad organization, said volunteers already know where vulnerable older residents live and go door to door to check on them. The quarantine began on March 20, and while it initially caused panic, some residents say government aid has eased the situation somewhat. Norma, who owns a small grocery store, said the food card system has made people a little calmer. Still, the neighborhood remains under pressure, and authorities have not made it mandatory for residents to stay inside their homes, though they have said people cannot leave their neighborhoods. Community efforts are also being led by younger residents. Lucas, 22, coordinates friends who cook donated meals from neighbors and businesses and distribute them to needy families. He said the church dining halls are full and that more than 150 people come to one of their food distributions each time. Beyond these grassroots efforts, the Pilares Foundation has spent more than a decade supporting around 500 families in Villa 21-24 and Villa 1-11-14, the city’s second-largest slum. Backed by donations and cooperation with companies and the state, it has delivered more than 1,000 bags of food and hygiene supplies, with special attention to children. Religion remains a central part of life in the neighborhood, where many residents are Paraguayan and devoted to the Virgin of Caacupe. Father Toto said the state has expanded its presence over the past two decades, but the area still needs better organization and infrastructure. Despite ongoing problems with drugs, violence, and poverty, he said the people still maintain a spirit of progress.

Peru’s southern city of Juliaca held a day of mourning Wednesday for 17 people killed by police two days earlier during protests against President Dina Boluarte’s transitional government. Thousands of residents, many wearing black, joined a funeral procession carrying the coffins of the dead through the city’s main streets. Among the victims were a medical student and a street vendor. Juliaca, about 1,300 kilometers from Lima, has become the main center of anti-government unrest since demonstrations resumed after a holiday pause. The protests began on Dec. 7, when Congress removed leftist President Pedro Castillo after he attempted to dissolve the legislature and rule by decree while calling for elections within nine months. Since then, the first three weeks of unrest left 28 people dead, 22 of them from gunfire by police and soldiers, bringing the overall death toll to 47. Many of the fatalities occurred after the government declared a state of emergency and suspended some constitutional rights. The protest movement is demanding Boluarte’s resignation, the dissolution of Congress, early elections this year and a constituent assembly to replace Peru’s 1993 constitution. During Wednesday’s procession, the coffins were accompanied by photographs, flowers, donation boxes and signs demanding justice. One message attached to a coffin read, “Dina murdered me with bullets.” The Attorney General’s Office has opened a preliminary investigation into Boluarte and several members of her new administration on suspicion of mass murder. After a funeral Mass in Juliaca’s main square, some coffins were taken to the city airport, where some of the fiercest clashes with security forces had occurred. Tensions also remained high elsewhere in the country. In Cuzco, hundreds marched toward the airport under heavy police guard. In Ayacucho, protesters observed a moment of silence during a general strike. In Tacna, demonstrators burned toll booths on the Panamericana Sur highway and police used tear gas to break up an attempted attack on a shopping center. The article also recalled Castillo’s rise from schoolteacher and union leader to president in 2021, when he defeated Keiko Fujimori in the runoff.

# Summary On January 11, Juliaca, a southern Peruvian city of 280,000 residents, held a funeral procession honoring 17 people killed by police two days earlier during anti-government protests. Thousands attended the ceremony, which included a funeral Mass and procession through the city's main streets. The protests began December 7 after Congress removed leftist President Pedro Castillo following his attempt to dissolve the legislature and rule by decree. Vice President Dina Boluarte assumed the presidency, becoming Peru's sixth leader since 2016. The demonstrations have since intensified, with the death toll now reaching 47, including 22 attributed to police and military gunfire. Most fatalities occurred after the government declared a state of emergency, suspending certain constitutional rights. Protesters demand Boluarte's resignation, Congress's dissolution, immediate general elections, and a new constitution to replace the 1993 document enacted under Alberto Fujimori, now imprisoned for massacres and embezzlement. The victims included a medical student and street vendor, with some coffins bearing messages like "Dina murdered me with bullets." The Peruvian Attorney General's Office has launched a preliminary investigation into Boluarte and administration members on suspicion of mass murder. Juliaca has remained the protest epicenter, located approximately 1,300 kilometers from Lima. Tensions continued spreading across southern Peru on January 11, with hundreds marching to Cuzco's airport and clashes occurring in other cities. Ayacucho observed a moment of silence during its general strike, while Tacna province saw protesters burn toll-booths and police deploy tear gas against demonstrators. Castillo, a former schoolteacher and union leader, unexpectedly reached the 2021 presidential runoff and defeated Keiko Fujimori, daughter of the disgraced former president.

A Brazilian former au pair testified in Fairfax, Virginia, that she turned against her ex-lover, Brendan Banfield, because she “wanted the truth to come out” in a double homicide case involving his wife and another man. Juliana Peres Magalhães said she had stayed silent for more than a year about the 2023 killings of Christine Banfield and Joseph Ryan, as well as Banfield’s alleged role, but changed course just days before her own criminal trial. Prosecutors say Banfield and Magalhães lured Ryan to the Banfield home, then shot him and staged the scene to make it appear that Ryan had attacked Christine Banfield as a predator. Banfield has pleaded not guilty to aggravated murder and could face life in prison if convicted. He is also charged with child abuse and felony child cruelty because his 4-year-old daughter was in the house that morning. Magalhães is a central witness for the prosecution. She testified that she and Banfield created a social media account in Christine Banfield’s name on a site used by people interested in sexual fetishes. Through that account, Ryan allegedly connected with the pair, and they arranged to meet for a sexual encounter involving a knife. She also described Banfield’s alleged months-long plan to kill his wife and then live with her, saying he had carefully worked to create alibis and cover his tracks. During cross-examination, Banfield’s attorney, John Carroll, challenged Magalhães’ credibility and her motives for pleading guilty. He pressed her on details about who created the account, where she and Banfield were when it was set up, and the specific messages exchanged. Magalhães often said she could not remember and at one point told him, “I am not going to do this.” Carroll also questioned her about jail letters in which she expressed despair, including writing, “No strength. No courage. No hope.” Magalhães said her poor health in jail and isolation from loved ones also influenced her decision to cooperate. She will be sentenced after Banfield’s trial, and her lawyers say she could receive time already served depending on her assistance to prosecutors.

# Summary A Brazilian au pair testified in a Virginia court that her ex-lover, Brendan Banfield, plotted to kill his wife Christine and another man, Joseph Ryan, in 2023. Juliana Peres Magalhães, who had remained silent for over a year, decided to cooperate with prosecutors days before her own trial, stating she "wanted the truth to come out." According to prosecutors' account, Banfield and Magalhães lured Ryan to their home under false pretenses. They allegedly created a fake social media account in Christine's name on a platform for people interested in sexual fetishes, where Ryan connected with them and arranged a meeting involving a knife. The pair then shot Ryan and staged the scene to appear as though he had attacked Christine. Magalhães testified that Banfield planned to kill his wife so he could spend his life with her, with whom he was having an affair. She described months of plotting and efforts to manufacture alibis. However, Banfield's defense attorney, John Carroll, challenged her credibility throughout Wednesday's testimony. He questioned specific details about the social media account's creation, their whereabouts when it was established, and who sent particular messages. Magalhães repeatedly stated she couldn't remember crucial details, at one point telling Carroll, "I am not going to do this." Carroll also presented letters Magalhães wrote from jail expressing depression and hopelessness, suggesting her cooperation might be motivated by desperation rather than truthfulness. She testified that jail conditions and isolation from loved ones influenced her decision to testify against Banfield. Banfield has pleaded not guilty to aggravated murder charges and faces life imprisonment if convicted. He also faces child abuse and felony child cruelty charges, as his 4-year-old daughter was present during the killings. Magalhães' sentencing will depend on her cooperation; she could potentially serve only the time already spent in jail.

Ethiopia will launch a community mobilization campaign this Ethiopian year to curb human trafficking from the grassroots, Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Demeke Mekonnen said at the annual National Council for Prevention and Suppression of Trafficking in Persons and Smuggling of Migrants. He said trafficking has risen because COVID-19 has weakened border security and reduced foreign employment opportunities, pushing more people toward illegal migration. The meeting noted that border controls had previously helped reduce trafficking, but relaxed enforcement during the pandemic created new risks. High school students under 18 were identified as the most frequent victims. Council leaders said community mobilization is needed to stop the crime against citizens, citing past successes in campaigns against HIV/AIDS and COVID-19. Demeke urged the use of elders, religious leaders, associations, and other trusted community figures, and stressed that the effort must be planned, practical, and results-oriented. He also warned regions to coordinate closely and said officials who fail to carry out their duties will be held accountable. The council was established in 2015.

# Summary Deputy Prime Minister Demeke Mekonnen announced that Ethiopia will launch a community mobilization campaign this year to combat human trafficking from grassroots level. During the annual National Council for Prevention and Suppression of Trafficking in Persons and Smuggling of Migrants meeting, he attributed the increase in human trafficking to relaxed border security resulting from the COVID-19 pandemic. Many countries' border closures and reduced foreign employment opportunities have driven illegal immigration. High school students under 18 are identified as the most vulnerable victims. Mekonnen emphasized the need for community engagement through respected figures like elders and religious leaders, citing successful mobilization efforts against HIV/AIDS and COVID-19. He stressed that regional authorities must collaborate and be held accountable for fulfilling their responsibilities. The council, established in 2015, works to prevent trafficking and migrant smuggling through coordinated efforts.

The Lamidi Apapa-led faction of the Labour Party has criticized Peter Obi, the party’s 2023 presidential candidate, over his recent comments attacking President Bola Tinubu’s administration. The dispute followed a series of posts Obi made on X in which he faulted actions of the federal government. In a statement issued on Tuesday, the faction’s Publicity Secretary, Abayomi Arabambi, accused Obi of still being unable to accept his defeat in the 2023 presidential election. He said Obi was “basking on the euphoria” of that loss and engaging in what he described as deceptive politics by circulating “fictitious and unfounded figures and indices” on national issues. Arabambi specifically rejected Obi’s claim that a federal government-sponsored delegation to Dubai numbered 1,411, insisting the actual figure was 422. He also said Obi’s criticism of Nigeria on the International Day for the Abolition of Slavery showed a lack of understanding of global and domestic issues. According to him, Obi’s comments about the 2023 Global Slavery Index published by Walk Free were misleading and reflected “shallow intellectual capacity” and a campaign of character assassination against President Tinubu. The faction urged Nigerians to verify information through independent research instead of relying on what it called falsehoods. Arabambi argued that Obi had become a frustrated opposition figure who routinely invents figures and data to mislead the public and his supporters. He cited the 2023 Global Slavery Index to support his own position, saying North Korea had the highest rate of modern slavery in the world, while Eritrea, Mauritania, and South Sudan were the African countries with the highest prevalence. He added that Nigeria was among countries with minimal cases of modern slavery. He also listed what he described as the top ten countries globally with the highest prevalence of modern slavery: North Korea, Eritrea, Mauritania, Saudi Arabia, Turkiye, Tajikistan, the UAE, Russia, Afghanistan, and Kuwait. Arabambi concluded by saying the Apapa faction, through its national chairman, Bashiru Lamidi Apapa, distanced the party from Obi’s remarks and urged Nigerians to disregard his comments, which it described as false and malicious.

# Summary The Lamidi Apapa faction of Nigeria's Labour Party has publicly criticized Peter Obi, the party's 2023 presidential candidate, for his recent criticisms of President Bola Tinubu's administration. In a statement released Tuesday, Abayomi Arabambi, the factional Publicity Secretary, accused Obi of engaging in "deceptive politics" by spreading "fictitious and unfounded figures." Arabambi specifically cited Obi's claim about a federal government delegation to Dubai, asserting that Obi stated the delegation comprised 1,411 members when the actual number was 422. The faction also challenged Obi's recent comments made on International Day for the Abolition of Slavery, claiming his statements about modern slavery in Nigeria were misleading and reflected "shallow intellectual capacity." Arabambi suggested that Obi was attempting to damage President Tinubu's reputation through character assassination to gain undeserved sympathy. To counter Obi's assertions, the Labour Party faction provided data from the Walk Free Organisation's 2023 Global Slavery Index, which ranks countries by modern slavery prevalence. According to this report, North Korea has the highest rate globally, followed by Eritrea, Mauritania, and Saudi Arabia. In Africa, Eritrea, Mauritania, and South Sudan lead, while Nigeria is described as experiencing "minimal cases of modern slavery." Arabambi emphasized that Nigeria eliminated slavery in 1945 and urged Nigerians to conduct independent research rather than relying on what he characterized as Obi's falsehoods. He accused Obi of "cooking up figures, data and indices to deceive gullible Nigerians." The statement concluded by distancing LP National Chairman Bashiru Lamidi Apapa from Obi's "unguided utterances," describing him as known for fabricating statistics and appealing to his supporters through ethnic rhetoric. The faction called on Nigerians to disregard what it deemed Obi's malicious and false statements about slavery in Nigeria.

In North Kivu, in the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, escalating conflict has turned childbirth into a life-threatening ordeal for many displaced women. The article centers on Francine Toyata, who went into labour at 2 a.m. while sheltering in an overcrowded camp amid fighting between the Congolese national armed forces and M23 rebels near Goma, the provincial capital. Already displaced twice since January, she and her mother traveled through darkness and chaos, with bombs echoing nearby, to reach a UNFPA-supported mobile health clinic. Toyata is originally from Kabati in Rutshuru territory. She had first fled with her husband in February 2023 as clashes spread through their area. In the current crisis, she managed to reach the clinic just in time. Two hours after arriving, she gave birth safely to a baby girl. Looking at her newborn, she said she would name her Amani, meaning “Peace,” because the child was born in war but symbolized hope. The article explains that the region was already facing severe pressure from displacement before the latest surge in violence. Fighting that erupted in January 2025 forced hundreds of thousands more people from their homes, adding to the population living in formal and informal camps around Goma. Access to reproductive health care had been scarce even before the escalation, and the Democratic Republic of the Congo already had one of the world’s highest maternal mortality rates. Now, with only about one-third of hospitals and one-fifth of health centres in the region functioning, UNFPA’s mobile teams are often the only way women can receive skilled care during pregnancy and delivery. The situation for women and girls is described as especially dangerous. Of an estimated 220,000 pregnant women in North and South Kivu, more than 12,000 are displaced and lack reliable access to medical services. More than 88,000 women and girls are at risk of gender-based violence, while unintended pregnancies are expected to increase as health services collapse. The article says cases of rape, assault, coercion, forced marriage, trafficking, and survival sex have risen sharply, particularly in eastern provinces such as Ituri, North Kivu, and South Kivu. Overcrowded camps, hunger, insecurity, and few income opportunities have left many women and girls exposed to exploitation. The conflict has also directly damaged humanitarian operations. Bombs have struck displacement camps, forcing more people to flee again and destroying fragile safety nets. Several UNFPA-supported mobile clinics and listening centres have been looted or destroyed, causing services to stop temporarily. Despite these dangers, UNFPA continues to operate eight mobile health clinics in the region, staffed by 27 midwives. Three health facilities serving eight camps provide safe deliveries, prenatal care, and family planning for more than 8,000 people. The agency is also distributing contraceptives and other supplies, running a hotline for survivors of gender-based violence, and maintaining five safe spaces for women and girls. UNFPA says it is working with the government and humanitarian partners, but the needs are growing faster than available resources.

# Childbirth in Crisis: Maternal Health Struggles in Congo's War Zone The Democratic Republic of the Congo faces a humanitarian catastrophe as intense fighting between national armed forces and the M23 rebel group has devastated maternal healthcare in North Kivu. The conflict, which erupted in January 2025 near Goma, has displaced hundreds of thousands of people and created dire conditions for pregnant women and girls. Francine Toyata's story exemplifies this crisis. Already displaced twice since January and living in an overcrowded camp, she went into labor at 2 a.m. amid bomb explosions. Despite the harrowing circumstances, she managed to reach a UNFPA-supported mobile health clinic, where she safely delivered a baby girl she named Amani—meaning "peace"—as a symbol of hope amid conflict. The scale of the crisis is staggering. Approximately 220,000 pregnant women live in North and South Kivu combined, with over 12,000 currently displaced and lacking assured access to medical care. The Democratic Republic of the Congo already had one of the world's highest maternal mortality rates before this escalation, and conditions have dramatically worsened. Healthcare infrastructure has collapsed across the region. Only one-third of hospitals and one in five health centers remain functional, leaving UNFPA's mobile health clinics as often the only option for women to deliver with skilled assistance. These fragile tent facilities offer minimal protection from ongoing bombardment, yet they serve as critical lifelines for vulnerable populations. Beyond maternal health, women and girls face compounding dangers. Over 88,000 are at risk of gender-based violence, with two-thirds of reported incidents occurring in eastern provinces including North Kivu. The conflict has created conditions ripe for exploitation: minimal security in displacement camps, widespread hunger, and lack of income opportunities have increased risks of forced marriage, human trafficking, and survival sex. The deteriorating security situation has directly impacted humanitarian response. Several UNFPA-supported mobile clinics and listening centers have been looted or destroyed, forcing temporary service suspensions. Blocked humanitarian corridors prevent supply deliveries, and displacement camps themselves have become targets, forcing residents to flee repeatedly. Currently, UNFPA operates eight mobile health clinics staffed by 27 midwives across the region. Three health facilities support eight camps, providing safe deliveries, prenatal care, and family planning to over 8,000 people. Additionally, a hotline offers support to gender-based violence survivors, and five safe spaces provide refuge and psychosocial care for women and girls. Despite these efforts, needs vastly exceed available resources. UNFPA continues distributing contraceptives and reproductive health supplies under treacherous conditions and remains committed to supporting the government and humanitarian partners. However, as Francine's experience demonstrates, thousands of women remain trapped in tents, facing bombardment, uncertain whether they and their babies will survive childbirth. The organization urgently calls for increased support to meet the escalating humanitarian crisis affecting the region's most vulnerable populations.

During a major awareness campaign held in Mwene-Ditu from July 8 to 10, 2022, the Agency for the Prevention and Fight against Trafficking in Persons (APLTP), a specialized service under President Félix-Antoine Tshisekedi’s office, urged residents to denounce and help combat human trafficking, which it described as a human rights violation. The campaign also trained 75 civil society and institutional contractors in methods for supporting victims and sensitizing the public. Residents were encouraged to contact local authorities or call the toll-free number 129 to report cases and obtain medical, psychological, legal and social assistance. Mrs. Sylvie Ntumba Kabeya, the service’s awareness officer, said the population responded positively to prevention messages. She cited forms of trafficking and exploitation seen in the region, including forced labor, child trafficking and exploitation in mines and artisanal quarries, prostitution of minors, organ trafficking and begging, all of which can lead to trauma, disability, illness or death. The campaign also explained the basic definition of trafficking and was carried out in public places such as roads, markets and churches.

# Summary From July 8-10, 2022, the Congolese agency for preventing and combating human trafficking (APLTP) conducted a major awareness campaign in Mwene-Ditu, Lomami province. The initiative, operating under President Felix-Antoine Tshisekedi's human rights promotion policy, urged residents to report and fight human trafficking as a human rights violation. Seventy-five civil society and institutional contractors participated, educating the population about reporting mechanisms, including a toll-free hotline (129), and available medical, psychological, legal, and social support services. Agency representative Sylvie Ntumba Kabeya noted the community's receptiveness to prevention messages. The campaign addressed trafficking forms prevalent in the region: forced labor, child exploitation in mining, child prostitution, organ trafficking, and forced begging—all causing severe harm including trauma, disability, illness, and death. The campaign, held in public spaces like markets, churches, and roads, educated residents on trafficking definitions: recruitment, transport, and harboring of persons through force, threats, or deception for exploitation purposes.

Eastern Libyan authorities have rounded up thousands of migrants, mostly Egyptians, in a widening crackdown on trafficking networks and people trying to reach Europe, according to activists and local groups. The detentions took place over the past two days in raids on trafficking warehouses in the border town of Musaid and other eastern areas, said Tarik Lamloum of the Belaady Organization for Human Rights. Libya remains a major transit route for migrants from Africa and the Middle East heading toward Europe, especially across the dangerous Central Mediterranean Sea. Since the 2011 NATO-backed uprising that overthrew and killed Moammar Gadhafi, the country has been fragmented between rival eastern and western authorities backed by militias and foreign powers. That instability has allowed human traffickers to flourish, smuggling migrants across Libya’s long borders and sending them out in overloaded rubber boats and other unsafe vessels. Lamloum and the migrant-aid group al-Abreen estimated that more than 6,000 migrants were being held at the border, most of them Egyptians taken to the customs hangar at the Musaid crossing point to await deportation. The Security Directorate of Benghazi confirmed raids in Musaid but gave no details. It also said five suspected traffickers were detained, including four Libyans and one Bangladeshi, after a Europe-bound boat carrying eight other Bangladeshi migrants was intercepted. Footage posted by al-Abreen showed large groups of migrants escorted by security officers and marched on foot to the border crossing, along with images of migrants said to have been freed from a traffickers’ warehouse. Esreiwa Salah of al-Abreen called conditions at the hangar “tragic,” saying the site was not equipped to hold detained migrants. Some Egyptian migrants were released and sent back to Egypt on Friday after tribal elders from the Egyptian city of Matrouh mediated with Libyan authorities, according to former Egyptian lawmaker Mahdi el-Omda. Lamloum said the detained migrants also include Syrians, Sudanese, Pakistanis and Bangladeshis who had legally entered Libya over the years through Benghazi’s Benina airport. He added that at least 400 more migrants from Pakistan and Bangladesh were taken to the Qanfouda detention center for deportation. The eastern campaign mirrors similar raids in western Libya, where clashes in Zuwara and a video showing migrants torturing and killing a Libyan man helped fuel anti-migrant sentiment. The U.N. refugee agency said 1,800 migrants have been detained in the west over the past month, and warned the crackdown is likely to expand further. U.N.-commissioned investigators have said detention centers in Libya are marked by abuse, including forced labor, beatings, rape and torture.

# Eastern Libya Conducts Major Crackdown on Migrants Libyan authorities have rounded up thousands of migrants, predominantly Egyptian, in an intensified crackdown across the country. Over two days, security forces conducted raids on trafficking warehouses in the border town of Musaid and other eastern areas, according to human rights activists Tarik Lamloum of Belaady Organization for Human Rights and the al-Abreen group. More than 6,000 migrants were detained and held at the Musaid customs crossing, awaiting deportation to Egypt. The detainees include Egyptians, Syrians, Sudanese, Pakistanis, and Bengalis who had legally entered Libya through Benghazi airport. Authorities also transferred at least 400 Pakistani and Bangladeshi migrants to the Qanfouda detention center for deportation. Five suspected traffickers, including four Libyans and one Bengali, were arrested during operations. Libya serves as the primary transit point for African and Middle Eastern migrants attempting to reach Europe. The country has descended into chaos since a 2011 NATO-backed uprising toppled Moammar Gadhafi, leaving it divided between rival governments in eastern and western regions, each supported by militias and foreign powers. This instability has enabled human traffickers to exploit vulnerable migrants, transporting them through Libya's porous borders and onto dangerous Mediterranean Sea crossings. The crackdown extends beyond eastern Libya. In the western capital of Tripoli and surrounding towns, drone raids targeted alleged trafficking warehouses in Zawiya and Maya—major migrant smuggling hubs. These operations resulted in 1,800 migrant detentions over the past month, with detainees transferred to government facilities. The intensified campaign follows several triggering incidents: clashes between Nigerien and Sudanese migrants in Zuwara, and an April video showing migrants torturing and killing a Libyan national, which fueled anti-migrant sentiment. Activists describe conditions at detention facilities as dire. Al-Abreen spokesman Esreiwa Salah characterized the Musaid hangar as "tragic," noting inadequate infrastructure for housing detainees. A UN report documented systematic abuses in detention centers, including forced labor, beatings, rapes, and torture—practices classified as crimes against humanity by UN-commissioned investigators. The UNHCR expects the crackdown to continue expanding throughout Tripoli and beyond, raising concerns about migrant welfare during the ongoing campaign.

Egyptian activists and rights groups are condemning the prison sentences handed to two young women with large social media followings, saying the case reflects a widening crackdown on online expression rather than a legitimate criminal prosecution. The two women, Haneen Hossam, 20, a student, and Mawada al-Adham, 22, a model, were first among at least nine people prosecuted last year on accusations of violating “family values” after posting TikTok and Likee videos in which they danced, sang, and encouraged followers to make money by becoming influencers. Those initial charges were later dropped on appeal, but prosecutors then brought new human trafficking charges against them. Last month, Hossam was sentenced to 10 years in prison and Adham to six years. Both were accused of exploiting children for profit because some minors appeared in the videos. Two employees of social media platforms and a blogger were also sentenced to six years, and all were fined 200,000 Egyptian pounds, or about $12,800. Judge Mohamed al-Guindy said in court that social media platforms were using “debauchery” to lure people and posed a moral threat to family life. He argued that the absence of family oversight and negligence in some households were contributing to “moral collapse.” The case has triggered alarm among activists, who say prosecutors are misusing a 2010 human trafficking law, originally intended mainly to combat child marriage, to create moral panic and suppress internet freedoms. Lobna Darwish of the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights said the case was part of a broader moral campaign by the prosecution against society. Amnesty International has also accused Egyptian authorities of using “repressive new tactics” to control cyberspace. The prosecution had previously described itself as a defender of “social national security” and a “guardian of social morals,” saying it was protecting Egypt’s cyber border from “forces of evil.” Officials have also said they are trying to protect women from violence and help them become economically empowered. The court has not yet published the full reasoning behind the trafficking convictions. Meanwhile, some Egyptians online have called for the platforms to be banned, while others said the women were being treated unfairly and were no different from celebrities in advertising or film. Lawyers for both women say they will appeal. Hossam, who was tried in absentia, was later arrested after posting a video protesting her innocence and asking President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi for a pardon. Adham’s lawyer said she was a minor when some of the videos were made and that even if there had been wrongdoing, the trafficking charge was excessive.

# Summary: Egyptian Influencers Sentenced on Human Trafficking Charges Two popular Egyptian social media influencers have been sentenced to prison on human trafficking charges, sparking alarm among human rights activists who dispute the accusations and view them as part of a broader government crackdown on internet freedoms. Haneen Hossam, a 20-year-old student, received a 10-year sentence, while 22-year-old model Mawada al-Adham was sentenced to six years in jail. Both were accused of exploiting children for profit because minors appeared in their videos, which promoted influencer careers on platforms like TikTok and Likee. Two social media platform employees and a blogger also received six-year sentences. All defendants were fined 200,000 Egyptian pounds ($12,800). The case represents an escalation in prosecution. Initially, the women faced charges of violating family values after posting dance and singing videos. When those charges were dropped on appeal, authorities brought the human trafficking charges instead—an unprecedented application of a 2010 law originally designed to combat child marriage. Judge Mohamed al-Guindy justified the sentences by characterizing social media as a "moral threat" to family life, citing "debauchery" as a concern. The prosecution framed itself as a "guardian of social morals" protecting "social national security." However, human rights organizations strongly contest these convictions. Amnesty International accused authorities of deploying "repressive new tactics to control cyber space." The Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights argues the prosecution is stoking "moral panic" rather than addressing genuine crimes. Lawyers note that minors appeared in videos with family consent and there was no intention of abuse. Activists express frustration that resources are directed toward prosecuting influencers rather than investigating sexual assault cases, which gained attention through Egypt's #MeToo movement. Legal representatives for both women plan to appeal. Hossam was tried in absentia after her arrest and can claim a retrial. Her lawyer notes that Adham was a minor when the original videos were made, and argues the trafficking charge and sentence are disproportionate. Some Egyptians have called for banning the platforms, while others view the verdicts as unjust, comparing the influencers to celebrities in advertisements and films.

Qaumi Watan Party (QWP) Provincial Chairman Sikandar Hayat Khan Sherpao on Wednesday accused the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KP) government of ignoring the province’s worsening security situation and warned that his party would launch protests if immediate action was not taken. Speaking at a press conference at Watan Kor, he urged both the provincial and federal governments to cooperate in restoring law and order, according to The News International. Sherpao cited a recent Counter-Terrorism Department (CTD) report showing 636 incidents of subversion in KP in 2024 so far, resulting in 257 deaths, including security personnel. He said the province has seen an average of 57 attacks a month, or roughly two a day, and noted that the scale of violence was comparable to 2009. He added that 2023 had also been highly unstable, with 631 such incidents recorded. He blamed the PTI-led provincial government, in power since 2013, for poor governance and failure to protect the rights and security of the people. He said lawlessness was especially severe in Bannu, Dera Ismail Khan, and Malakand, but stressed that the problem was no longer confined to southern districts or Kurram and had spread across the province. According to him, nearly half of KP’s population is now exposed to terrorist threats, while in many areas the government’s authority has weakened and militants move freely after dark. Sherpao praised the governor for convening a multi-party conference on law and order but criticized the provincial government for not holding a similar special meeting. He also condemned rising extortion, saying residents were being threatened through phone calls, and accused the government of even paying extortion money to kidnappers, which he said had deepened public anxiety. Responding to remarks by Chief Minister’s Information Adviser Barrister Mohammad Ali Saif, Sherpao said peace could not be achieved through words alone and required concrete action. He questioned how the government could protect ordinary citizens when judges and officials were also unsafe. He further criticized what he described as unequal compensation, saying PTI workers’ families received Rs 10 million while ordinary citizens were given far less. He also highlighted the worsening humanitarian crisis in Kurram, where road blockades have led to shortages of food and medicine.

# Summary Sikandar Hayat Khan Sherpao, Provincial Chairman of the Qaumi Watan Party (QWP), publicly criticized the PTI provincial government in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KP) for failing to address the region's deteriorating security situation during a press conference on December 12. Sherpao warned that the QWP would initiate protests against the provincial government if immediate steps were not taken to improve law and order. He called for collaboration between federal and provincial authorities to tackle the crisis. Drawing from a Counter-Terrorism Department report, Sherpao highlighted alarming statistics: 636 subversion incidents occurred in KP during 2024, resulting in 257 deaths including security personnel. This averages approximately two attacks daily, with 57 incidents monthly. He noted these figures matched 2009 levels, with 2023 also experiencing 631 acts of subversion. An Australian expert has sharply criticized several high-profile reports alleging “forced labor” in Xinjiang, saying they lack transparent methods, reliable evidence, and a sound legal basis. In two working papers released by CO-WEST-Pro Consultancy, Jaq James, co-founder of the research body and described as a Western propaganda analyst, examined reports by Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch, and the Australian Strategic Policy Institute (ASPI) from an international law perspective. James said ASPI’s widely cited “Uyghurs for Sale” report could not withstand scrutiny on legal, evidentiary, or merit grounds. She argued that the institute used misleading Chinese-to-English translations to heighten sensationalism, relied on weak or questionable sources, and presented dubious claims as fact. She also suggested there may have been some form of cooperation, or even collusion, between ASPI and The Washington Post, pointing to the report’s publication date being revised to appear later than Washington Post stories it cited, without informing readers. According to James, ASPI and similar organizations exploit the emotionally charged term “forced labor” to advance geopolitical aims and further discredit China. She said that if such organizations face no legal or reputational consequences, they will continue to act arbitrarily or maliciously. In a separate paper on Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch, James said those organizations also misused the legal category of forced labor for propagandistic purposes. She criticized Amnesty for relying on anonymous, unsworn, and uncorroborated testimony without proper cross-examination, saying this amounted to little more than asking readers to “trust us.” She said Human Rights Watch likewise relied on hearsay, anonymous evidence, and lay opinions presented as expert analysis, while failing to provide enough context to determine whether the legal criteria for forced labor had actually been met. James concluded that both groups were seeking evidence that confirmed pre-existing beliefs while ignoring contrary information. She described their work as “junk science” and urged professionals in human rights and labor rights, as well as the public, to scrutinize such claims carefully. Her central message was that evidence-based judgment should be preferred over accusation-based narratives, especially when assessing allegations about China’s human rights situation.

Vietnam is facing a severe human-trafficking crisis in which young women and girls are being sold into prostitution or forced marriages in China, according to the article. The victims are often described as “modern sex slaves,” and the problem is especially acute along the Vietnam-China border. The article says that traffickers target girls from poor, remote regions with little education, though young women from urban, middle- and lower-middle-class families are also increasingly at risk because of the Internet and modern communication tools. Traffickers commonly promise legitimate jobs that would help support the victim’s family, but once the women cross into China, they are forced into brothels or sold as brides to Chinese men who have paid for them. Before departure, victims are often made to sign fake employment contracts in foreign languages, such as Chinese, which they cannot understand. The article also says the trafficking networks exploit weak border controls and, in some cases, the complicity or negligence of officials. Young Vietnamese men and women of Chinese origin are sometimes used to recruit victims by gaining their trust and persuading them to move for work. Recent figures highlight the scale of the problem. In 2014, thousands of young Vietnamese women crossed the border and were reduced to slavery in the sex trade. In November, police in China’s Guangxi and Yunnan provinces rescued about 100 young Vietnamese women who had been held in semi-slavery. Earlier, in 2013, sources in Hanoi said at least 982 young women were sold in China, including 871 identified as victims of human trafficking. Authorities have also carried out major crackdowns. In Lai Châu province, with support from border guards in Ma Lu Thang, a trafficking ring was dismantled on 14 December, leading to trials of about 512 people and prison sentences of at least three years for 420 of them. The article notes that trafficking is not limited to Vietnamese women; victims also come from Myanmar, Laos, Thailand, and Cambodia. Among the traffickers are young Vietnamese men from border villages who see the trade as easy money. One case involved two men, Văn Pan Tao Lu and Lò Thị Chom, who were reportedly paid US$4,000 per woman. Another trafficker, Bùi Đ. Giang from Hanoi, allegedly deceived more than 50 young women, many from ethnic minority communities, into prostitution. His father said the family was shocked and did not know about his crimes. Catholic groups and social workers are actively involved in rescuing and supporting victims. One social worker described helping a woman rescued from a Chinese brothel, who was later trafficked again, abused, forced to take drugs, and made to serve Chinese customers.

This modern form of slavery represents one of Asia-Pacific's largest sex trafficking issues, prompting the Church to designate February 8 as a day of prayer and reflection against human trafficking. ## Vulnerable Populations and Recruitment Methods Trafficking victims primarily come from Vietnam's remote, impoverished regions with limited educational opportunities. However, urban middle and lower-middle-class women increasingly fall victim through internet and modern communication technologies. Traffickers employ deceptive tactics, promising legitimate employment that would help victims support their families. Once across the border into China, women are forced into brothels or sold as wives to Chinese men. ## Exploitation Mechanisms Victims are coerced into signing employment contracts in foreign languages they cannot understand. Unscrupulous traders exploit administrative corruption and government official complicity to move hundreds of women across borders. Notably, Vietnamese men and women of Chinese origin also participate in trafficking, gaining victims' trust before relocating them to prostitution-related work. ## Scale and Impact In 2014 alone, thousands of young Vietnamese women crossed into China for sexual exploitation. In November, authorities rescued approximately 100 women from semi-slavery conditions in Quang Tây and Vân Nam provinces. Data from 2013 showed at least 982 women were sold in China, with 871 classified as trafficking victims. Trafficking also involves women from Myanmar, Laos, Thailand, and Cambodia. ## Criminal Involvement and Prosecution Young Vietnamese men, particularly those in border villages, view trafficking as profitable. For example, two traffickers earned $4,000 per woman. In another case, a Hanoi native trafficked over 50 women from ethnic minority border communities. A major 2014 operation in Lai Châu resulted in 512 people being tried, with 420 sentenced to at least three years imprisonment. ## Systemic Challenges Legal and cultural obstacles hinder anti-trafficking efforts. Governments often conflate smuggling and trafficking, preventing proper victim identification and perpetrator prosecution. This confusion leaves many victims unrecognized and criminals unpunished. ## Root Causes and Response Activist groups attribute rising trafficking to pervasive consumerism and materialism undermining Vietnamese family values. Catholic organizations, both clerical and lay, lead anti-trafficking efforts, providing counseling and support to survivors. However, recovery remains difficult; one social worker documented a victim rescued from a Chinese brothel who was trafficked again after three years, suffering drug addiction and sexual abuse. The crisis demands comprehensive legal reform, better victim protection, and stronger enforcement to combat this persistent form of modern slavery affecting Vietnam's most vulnerable populations.

Vietnam’s prime minister has ordered an investigation into whether the 39 people found dead in a truck in the United Kingdom last month were trafficked illegally from Vietnam, a move that may ease public anger but does little to solve a deeper problem: the country’s long-running inability to stop risky migration to richer countries. The deaths in southeastern England drew attention to human trafficking from Vietnam to Europe, where wages are much higher. British police have made several arrests, and one man has been charged with conspiracy to traffic people. Vietnamese officials have also responded diplomatically. Prime Minister Nguyen Xuan Phuc directed the Ministry of Public Security and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs to investigate human smuggling and consider “citizen protection measures.” Vietnamese and British officials have already signed a memorandum of understanding to combat modern slavery, and in a recent phone call, both sides agreed to call on the international community to strengthen cooperation against the crime. Experts, however, say the problem is deeply entrenched. Carl Thayer, an emeritus professor at the University of New South Wales, said the battle against trafficking is “never-ending” because smugglers make too much money and lure desperate people with the promise of a better life. He argued that officials may be able to publicize the issue more aggressively and occasionally arrest organizers, but they are unlikely to dismantle the networks entirely. Victims often cannot identify the leaders of trafficking rings, and porous borders, especially in Vietnam’s special economic zones near neighboring countries, make movement easy. Human trafficking has existed in Vietnam for generations. A 2015 book on colonial Vietnam describes networks that trafficked women and children to Hong Kong and mainland China for marriage or prostitution. Today, the government closely checks marriage applications to prevent women from entering abusive marriages with wealthier foreign men, said lawyer Frederick Burke. He noted that the UK case has renewed attention on trafficking and “sale of wives,” though many ordinary Vietnamese view the deaths mainly as people being deceived by a group leader. He also said many still believe in a “grass is greener” mentality when it comes to working abroad. Vietnam’s economy has grown strongly, helped by foreign investment and export manufacturing, with growth projected at up to 6.8% this year after 7.1% in 2018. But blue-collar wages remain below $200 a month, far less than what migrants can earn in Britain, Russia, Libya, or other destinations. About 10% of Vietnam’s 95 million people live in poverty, including pockets of extreme poverty in remote mountain areas. Economists say these isolated communities are hardest to reach, and addressing their lack of access to industrial work will remain a major challenge.

# Summary: Vietnam's Struggle Against Human Trafficking Vietnam faces significant challenges in combating human trafficking to wealthier nations, despite government efforts following the discovery of 39 Vietnamese nationals dead in a truck in the United Kingdom. Prime Minister Nguyen Xuan Phuc ordered an investigation and pledged citizen protection measures, while British and Vietnamese governments reaffirmed their commitment to tackling modern slavery through a previously signed memorandum of understanding. However, experts warn that these responses mask deeper structural problems making trafficking difficult to stop. According to Carl Thayer, a Southeast Asia specialist at the University of New South Wales, the smuggling networks have become too sophisticated and profitable for authorities to effectively dismantle. The rewards for smugglers and the perceived opportunities for desperate Vietnamese citizens create what Thayer calls "a never-ending fight." Several barriers complicate enforcement efforts. Vietnam's porous borders and special economic zones with neighboring countries facilitate illegal emigration. Trafficking victims rarely possess information about smuggling ring leaders, limiting law enforcement's ability to target higher-level organizers. Additionally, trafficking networks have deep historical roots in Vietnam, dating back centuries, and have evolved into mature international operations. The economic disparity between Vietnam and destination countries fuels continued migration attempts. Despite Vietnam's robust economic growth—projected at 6.8% this year—blue-collar wages remain below $200 monthly, far less than wages in Russia, Libya, and the United Kingdom where trafficked workers often end up. Approximately 10% of Vietnam's 95 million people live in poverty, with some concentrated in remote mountain areas lacking access to industrial employment opportunities. While government efforts have successfully implemented rigorous background checks on marriage applications to prevent trafficking of women into abusive marriages, broader trafficking for labor continues largely unchecked. Many Vietnamese citizens view emigration through an optimistic lens, maintaining a "grass is greener" mentality about overseas opportunities. Experts suggest the Vietnamese government could improve outcomes by publicizing trafficking dangers and targeting smuggling organizers more aggressively. However, addressing extreme poverty in remote regions remains challenging due to geographical isolation and limited access to industrial jobs. Ultimately, stopping human trafficking requires simultaneous efforts to improve domestic economic conditions, strengthen border enforcement, and enhance international cooperation—a complex task that authorities acknowledge will require sustained, multifaceted approaches.

A new UN report says opium poppy cultivation in Southeast Asia’s “Golden Triangle” — the border region of Myanmar, Laos and Thailand — has nearly tripled since 2006. According to the UN Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC), poppy cultivation in Myanmar and Laos reached 63,800 hectares in 2014, up from 21,600 hectares in 2006. That marks the eighth straight year of increases and supports an illicit drug economy the UN estimates is worth about $16 billion annually in the region. Myanmar and Laos produced 762 tons of opium this year, much of which would be refined into about 76 tons of mixed-grade heroin for trafficking into regional and global markets. UNODC regional representative Jeremy Douglas said the two countries must do more to stop the “two-way flow” of drugs across their borders and warned that corruption is widespread at border crossings. He also said the trade threatens development in the ASEAN Economic Community. The growth in cultivation comes despite Myanmar’s earlier promises to eliminate the crop. In 1999, the government pledged to eradicate all opium cultivation within 15 years, and production fell sharply, dropping 86 percent between 1998 and 2006. But demand for opium and heroin has risen again, leading to a resurgence driven largely by transnational criminal networks operating in areas where the government is still fighting armed rebels. Most cultivation remains concentrated in Myanmar. The report says 80 percent of the total area, or 51,400 hectares, was in Shan State, which has seen civil conflict for more than 50 years. Northern Laos accounted for just under 10 percent of the total. Myanmar’s government has tried to respond: in the 2013-14 poppy season it eradicated 15,188 hectares, a 19 percent increase from the previous year, according to government data. However, Myanmar has limited ability to control its borders, especially along its frontier with China, where illegal trade in drugs, human trafficking and precious stones is common. U Nyan Win, spokesman for the opposition National League for Democracy, said the problem is worsening because there are no laws in these border areas and argued that peace is essential to reducing drug production. The report also highlights rising drug use in China, the world’s largest heroin market. Heroin users there increased by 500,000 between 2007 and 2013, reaching 1.3 million. Across Asia, China now accounts for nearly 58 percent of the estimated 3.33 million opiate users. In Myanmar, opiate use is among the highest in Southeast Asia, and preliminary findings suggest heroin and methamphetamine use has tripled since 2012 in some villages in Shan and Kayah states.

The Council of the European Union on Friday formally extended Operation Sophia, formerly known as EUNavForMed, until September 30. At the same time, it instructed the operation’s commander to temporarily suspend the deployment of naval units for the entire extension period, citing operational reasons. EU member states will continue seeking a solution to the disembarkation issue, in line with European Council conclusions from June 2018. The extension was approved through a written procedure, confirming the agreement EU ambassadors had reached on Tuesday in the Political and Security Committee. The Council said the mission will keep carrying out its mandate by increasing aerial surveillance, strengthening support for the Libyan coast guard and navy, expanding monitoring on land, and continuing training activities. Operation Sophia’s main goal is to help dismantle migrant smuggling and human trafficking networks in the south-central Mediterranean. It also supports the Libyan coast guard and navy, monitors the long-term effectiveness of that training, helps enforce the EU arms embargo off Libya, and tracks illegal oil exports from Libya under UN Security Council resolutions. Launched on June 22, 2015, the mission is led by Italian Division Admiral Enrico Credendino and is based in Rome.

Sex workers in Hamburg protested on 11 July against Germany’s continued closure of brothels, which have remained shut for months since the coronavirus outbreak. As the country’s streets, shops, restaurants, and bars have largely returned to normal despite ongoing daily infections, the sex industry remains restricted. The protest filled Hamburg’s red-light district with licensed sex workers, some wearing lingerie or theatrical masks, alongside inflatable sex dolls. Many carried signs demanding financial support and warning that the industry is being “driven into illegality.” Others used more playful slogans, including “We are attracting tourists to our dear Germany.” The demonstration was organized by Germany’s Association of Sex Workers, which argued that keeping brothels closed pushes sex workers onto the streets, where they are less safe and operating illegally. The group said prostitution should be treated like other close-contact services that have reopened under hygiene rules, such as massages, cosmetics, dancing, or contact sports. Human Rights Watch says Central Asia is experiencing a rare opening for rights reform, especially in Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan, and that leaders across the region should use political change to end repression. In releasing its World Report 2018, the group urged governments in Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, Tajikistan, and Turkmenistan to abandon abusive policies, allow free speech, stop torture in detention, and free critics held in jail. In Uzbekistan, President Shavkat Mirziyoyev, who took office in 2016, has made several encouraging moves. HRW said he released at least 16 political prisoners, eased some restrictions on free expression, removed citizens from the security services’ “black list,” and made government institutions somewhat more accountable. But the organization stressed that serious abuses remain. Security services brought new charges against journalists including Bobomurod Abdullaev, Hayot Nasreddinov, and Nurullo Otahonov. Torture, politically motivated imprisonment, and forced labor in the cotton sector continue. Kyrgyzstan also has an opportunity for change under newly elected President Sooronbai Jeenbekov. International observers described the October 2017 presidential election as competitive, but they also pointed to abuse of public resources and pressure on voters. Before the vote, authorities banned public assemblies in central Bishkek. HRW highlighted the continued imprisonment of human rights defender Azimjon Askarov, who is serving a life sentence. It also said media freedom has worsened, with the Prosecutor General’s office filing lawsuits against critical media outlets and a human rights defender. Several foreign human rights workers, including HRW staff, are barred from entering the country. The report describes Kazakhstan as having further deteriorated in 2017, despite the government’s efforts to improve its international image through high-profile events. Authorities silenced critics, used politically motivated criminal charges and other harassment against journalists and activists, and continued a crackdown on independent trade unions, including the closure of the Confederation of Independent Trade Unions of Kazakhstan. Several activists and union leaders remain in prison. Freedom of religion, expression, and peaceful assembly remain tightly restricted. Tajikistan’s situation worsened as well, with an intensified crackdown on free expression, political opposition, the independent legal profession, and religious practice. More than 150 political activists, including lawyers and journalists, remain unjustly jailed. Authorities have also retaliated violently against relatives of dissidents who criticize the government from abroad. Turkmenistan remains one of the world’s most closed and repressive states, effectively banning independent religious and political expression, tightly controlling media, and blocking outside monitoring. Dozens remain forcibly disappeared. Hosting the 2017 Asian Indoor and Martial Arts Games briefly opened the country, but HRW said it led to even harsher repression.

# Central Asia: Window of Opportunity on Rights Human Rights Watch's 2018 World Report urges political leaders in Central Asia to prioritize human rights improvements, particularly highlighting opportunities in Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan amid recent political transitions. **Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan's Opportunities** Since becoming president in 2016, Uzbekistan's Shavkat Mirziyoyev has implemented positive reforms, including releasing at least 16 political prisoners, relaxing free expression restrictions, and removing citizens from security blacklists. However, serious abuses persist, including torture and forced labor in cotton fields. Kyrgyzstan's newly elected president, Sooronbai Jeenbekov, has an opportunity to reverse recent negative trends concerning freedom of expression and assembly, though the October 2017 elections raised concerns about voter pressure and resource abuse. **Deteriorating Conditions Elsewhere** Kazakhstan, Tajikistan, and Turkmenistan continue implementing repressive policies. In Kazakhstan, authorities silenced critics and cracked down on independent trade unions, closing the Confederation of Independent Trade Unions. The government suppressed freedom of religion, expression, and assembly while maintaining tight controls despite hosting international events. Tajikistan's human rights record significantly worsened with a severe crackdown on free expression, political opposition, and religious practice. Over 150 political activists, including lawyers and journalists, remain unjustly imprisoned. Authorities orchestrate violent retaliation against relatives of dissidents living abroad. Turkmenistan remains among the world's most repressive countries. The government effectively bans all unapproved religious and political expression, tightly controls media, and prohibits independent monitoring. Dozens remain victims of enforced disappearance. Despite hosting the 5th Asian Indoor and Martial Arts Games in 2017—a rare international engagement—the government intensified suppression of expression and rights. **Key Recommendations** Human Rights Watch's Executive Director Kenneth Roth emphasizes that political leaders can limit authoritarian agendas when combined with mobilized publics and effective multilateral actors. The organization calls for Central Asian leaders to abandon repressive policies, allow free speech, end torture in detention, and release imprisoned critics. The 643-page World Report, reviewing human rights in over 90 countries, demonstrates that while authoritarian governments present challenges, determined leadership committed to human rights principles can create meaningful change. The current political transitions in Central Asia represent critical moments for advancing fundamental freedoms and establishing more accountable governance.

Human Rights Watch says Libya’s civilians are being placed in grave danger by reckless fighting between rival armed groups and by the foreign powers backing them. In its World Report 2020, the organization urges the UN Human Rights Council to create a Commission of Inquiry to document abuses and identify those responsible, arguing that impunity has allowed violations to continue. The conflict escalated in April 2019 when fighters affiliated with the eastern-based Libyan National Army (LNA), led by Khalifa Hiftar and aligned with the interim authorities in the east, launched an offensive against armed groups loyal to the Tripoli-based, internationally recognized Government of National Accord (GNA). Since then, Tripoli and surrounding areas have been hit by hundreds of drone and air strikes. Human Rights Watch says these attacks have killed and displaced civilians and reflect a broader pattern of indiscriminate violence. Foreign involvement has intensified the conflict. A leaked UN report in November said the United Arab Emirates, Turkey, Sudan, and Jordan repeatedly violated the UN arms embargo by supplying weapons, drones, and fighters to the warring sides. The article says the UAE and Jordan supported the LNA, while Turkey backed the GNA with armed drones. Foreign fighters from Sudan, Chad, and reportedly Russia also took part in the fighting. The UN estimates that by December the Tripoli conflict had killed at least 284 civilians and displaced more than 128,000 people. Among the deadliest incidents was a June airstrike on a migrant detention center in Tajoura, on the outskirts of Tripoli, which also housed militias and killed more than 43 civilians. Another apparent unlawful strike on October 14, attributed to the LNA or its allies, killed three small children in their home in Tripoli. Human Rights Watch also highlights other abuses linked to the conflict. Parliament member Seham Sergewa remains missing after being abducted from her home in Benghazi in July by an armed group tied to the LNA. Meanwhile, thousands of migrants and asylum seekers remain trapped in abusive detention centers, facing forced labor, beatings, and sexual violence. The report says European Union support for Libyan authorities to intercept and return migrants helps sustain these abuses. The ICC, which has investigated Libya since 2011, has issued an arrest warrant for LNA commander Mahmoud al-Werfalli for unlawful killings, but he remains free.

At least 49 migrants have died and 140 others are still missing after a boat carrying 260 people capsized off Yemen’s coast near Alghareef Point in Shabwah governorate on 10 June, according to the International Organization for Migration (IOM). The dead include 31 women and six children. Survivors said the vessel had left Bossaso, Somalia, around 3:00 a.m. on Sunday. It was carrying 115 Somali nationals and 145 Ethiopians, including 90 women. The IOM said the disaster reflects the continuing rise in migration from the Horn of Africa to Yemen, driven by political and economic instability as well as drought and other extreme weather in countries such as Ethiopia and Somalia. The IOM has deployed two mobile medical teams to assist survivors, including six children. Of the 71 survivors, eight were taken to hospital for further treatment, while 63 received first aid, trauma care, and wound dressing from an on-site mobile clinic. IOM psychologists are also providing mental health support to 38 survivors. Search and rescue operations are continuing, though they face major difficulties because of a shortage of operational patrol boats and the effects of Yemen’s conflict. Local fishermen and other community members helped recover bodies and bury the dead at Ayn-Bamaabed cemetery. More bodies are still washing ashore in different locations, and authorities are exploring additional search and rescue options. The tragedy follows two other shipwrecks on the same route near Djibouti that killed at least 62 migrants. Since 2014, IOM’s Missing Migrants Project has recorded 1,860 deaths and disappearances along the Eastern Route from the Horn of Africa to the Gulf, including 480 drownings. The agency described the Eastern Horn of Africa–Yemen route as one of the world’s busiest and most dangerous migration corridors. Despite Yemen’s conflict, thousands continue to travel there in hopes of reaching Saudi Arabia and other Gulf states. In 2023, more than 97,200 migrants arrived in Yemen, up from just over 73,000 the previous year.
