The article explains that San Diego police, like many law-enforcement agencies, may be using secretive cell-phone surveillance tools, but the public has limited information about how they work or how often they are deployed. A lawsuit over the San Diego Police Department’s use of “StingRay” technology is beginning to pry open that secrecy, and journalists have been piecing together how these devices function and what legal rules apply. The first key point is that police cell-phone tracking is not new. For years, officers have been able to obtain location information from phone records and use it to infer where a user was at a particular time. One common method is called a “tower dump,” in which police examine carrier data to identify all phones that connected to a specific cell tower during a certain period. That can help investigators narrow down suspects or reconstruct movements after the fact. StingRay-style technology is different because it works in real time. Instead of relying on phone-company records, the device sends out a signal that tricks nearby phones into believing it is a cell tower. Phones then connect to it automatically, allowing police to collect information from all devices in range. Depending on how it is used, the technology can potentially track a person as they move, even inside private buildings. A unit hidden in a police van would cover a limited area, but reports have said the devices have also been placed in small planes to monitor much larger regions. The Wall Street Journal has reported that at least five metropolitan areas have been targeted. The article notes that the legal rules are murky. In most states, police can obtain many kinds of cell-phone data without a warrant, unlike the warrant required to search a home or car. Civil liberties advocates argue that this creates a dangerous form of mass surveillance. David Loy of the local ACLU said the public has a right to know whether the San Diego Police Department is using the technology in that way. The FBI has told senators that law enforcement does not need warrants to use these devices in public. States can impose their own restrictions, and nine reportedly have limited live cell-phone spying without a warrant, but California is not among them. At the same time, the Supreme Court has ruled that police cannot search the contents of a cell phone without a warrant, underscoring the distinction between a device’s data and the phone’s stored contents. The article also describes the technology itself and the secrecy surrounding it. Harris Corporation, which makes StingRay devices, has refused to provide details and has warned that people could face prosecution for disclosing certain information about them. ArsTechnica described StingRay as a portable box-shaped device that gathers information by fooling phones into connecting to it, allowing police to locate specific targets or log all phones in an area. StingRays can also eavesdrop on conversations, according to that report. In 2013, the devices were said to cost between about $68,000 and $135,000, while a related Harris device called Gossamer cost about $19,700. The FBI reportedly spent more than $1.3 million on such technology in the 2000s. Harris also sells a “Hailstorm” system, which can cost up to about $169,600, though its exact capabilities remain unclear. Public records show that the San Diego Police Department spent $33,000 “on the possession or use” of StingRay technology and had sought $738,000 in grant money for it in 2009. What exactly the department bought, how it uses the equipment, and why the spending figure is so much lower than the reported price of the devices remain unknown. The article concludes with the growing pushback. An Android app called “SnoopSnitch” claims it can detect StingRay-style surveillance, though it cannot stop it; to avoid tracking, a user would need to turn off the phone, and removing the battery may help. Meanwhile, the First Amendment Coalition sued the San Diego Police Department on Dec. 15, arguing that the department had refused journalists’ records requests and asking a court to order disclosure of documents about its possession and use of “International Mobile Subscriber Identity Catchers.” The lawsuit could reveal how the technology is being used in practice. The article cites a separate example from Los Angeles, where the First Amendment Coalition learned that police used such devices 21 times in four months in 2012 in cases involving homicide, kidnapping, suicide, rape, human trafficking, robbery, fugitives, and narcotics. No hearing date had been set, and after the city challenged Judge Richard E. L. Strauss, the case was transferred to Judge Judith Hayes.

# Five Things to Know About Police Cell-Phone Spying Law enforcement agencies across the United States possess sophisticated technology that allows them to monitor citizens' cell phone locations and communications, often without public knowledge or judicial oversight. A pending lawsuit against the San Diego Police Department has begun to illuminate this secretive practice, revealing significant concerns about privacy rights and government surveillance. ## Traditional Cell Phone Tracking Police have utilized cell phone location data since the late 1990s when mobile phones became widespread. The most basic method, called a "Tower Dump," involves examining phone company records to identify which cell phones connected to specific cell towers at particular times. While this approach provides historical location data, it requires cooperation from telecommunications companies and typically demands a warrant for detailed information about individual phones. ## Advanced StingRay Technology The StingRay device represents a more invasive surveillance method. Unlike tower dumps that access existing phone company data, StingRays operate in real-time by impersonating cell towers, forcing nearby phones to connect to the device. This technology can track individuals as they move through both public spaces and private buildings. Law enforcement has deployed these devices in police vans for localized monitoring and in small aircraft to cover broader geographic areas. According to the Wall Street Journal, at least five metropolitan areas have been targeted by this technology. ## Minimal Legal Restrictions A significant concern is that police can obtain most cell phone data without warrants in most states, despite the fact that warrants are required to search homes or vehicles. The FBI has informed U.S. senators that law enforcement does not need warrants to use surveillance devices in public spaces. Only nine states have implemented laws restricting live cell phone surveillance without warrants, and California is notably absent from this list. However, the Supreme Court unanimously ruled that police cannot search data stored on individual phones without a warrant, establishing at least one privacy protection. ## Equipment and Costs Harris Corporation manufactures the primary surveillance devices used by law enforcement. StingRays, which can eavesdrop on conversations and track locations, cost between $68,479 and $134,952 depending on the model. The company also produces less expensive alternatives like Gossamer ($19,696) and Hailstorm systems (up to $169,602). The FBI spent over $1.3 million on this technology during the 2000s. The San Diego Police Department spent $33,000 on StingRay technology and sought $738,000 in grant funding in 2009, though the exact equipment and usage remain unclear. ## Legal Challenges and Public Response Civil liberties organizations, including the American Civil Liberties Union, argue that this surveillance constitutes mass surveillance without public accountability. In December, the First Amendment Coalition sued the San Diego Police Department demanding disclosure of documents regarding its use of cell phone surveillance technology. The lawsuit was transferred to Judge Judith Hayes after the city challenged the initial judge assignment. The Los Angeles Police Department used similar devices 21 times in a four-month period in 2012 to aid in various criminal investigations. While such applications suggest law enforcement value, critics contend the public has a right to know how extensively this technology is deployed. ## Limited Protective Measures An Android app called "SnoopSnitch" can detect StingRay surveillance, but it cannot prevent tracking. Disabling cell phones entirely, preferably by removing the battery, remains the only reliable protection. Privacy cases and other strategies offer minimal defense against determined surveillance. The lawsuit against San Diego Police may eventually reveal more details about how law enforcement agencies utilize this powerful technology, potentially influencing future privacy protections and surveillance regulations.

Lawmakers and experts from Canada, the U.S. and Europe met in Ottawa for the “Bringing Responsibility Home” symposium to assess government progress on human rights protections in transnational business. Hosted by members of Parliament from all major Canadian parties and two senators, and organized by Above Ground and the International Corporate Accountability Roundtable, the event focused on international developments and how Canada could lead on corporate accountability as it prepares for the G7 presidency. Former UN special representative John Ruggie said business and human rights align with Prime Minister Justin Trudeau’s priorities on sustainability, gender and Indigenous rights, and urged Canada to engage fully. Participants examined Europe’s move toward making human-rights respect by multinationals a legal obligation. Above Ground’s Karyn Keenan said laws should require all corporations to respect human rights wherever they operate, citing France’s new law on preventing harm in global operations and supply chains. ICAR’s Amol Mehra said stronger home-state laws are needed to address abuses such as land grabs, pollution, trafficking and forced labor.

Gavin Daley, 23, was found dead on Dec. 17, 2015, in his apartment at 123 Westwood Dr. after a fire was reported there. Waterloo Regional Police ruled the death a homicide because of signs of trauma to his body. Police have said the attack was targeted, but have not publicly released or confirmed further details. Veronica Daley says her son was shot in the back of the head and then his apartment was set on fire. Since then, she has spent years trying to understand what happened to him, including who he was associating with and how he ended up in Kitchener while on the run from drug-related charges in Kingston. In 2016, police released photos of two people connected to the investigation: Sarah Poole, then 23, who was wanted on a Canada-wide warrant for human trafficking and fraud, and Devon Victor, then 28, who was described as armed and dangerous and was also wanted by Toronto police. This summer, Victor was arrested in Toronto and charged with possession of a loaded firearm and trafficking illicit drugs. Veronica Daley said his arrest gave her hope that police might finally obtain the information needed to make arrests in her son’s killing. She said she had repeatedly been told by police and the Crown that they could not move forward until they spoke with Victor. Staff Sgt. Kyle Lambert said he could not comment on whether police had interviewed Poole or Victor, but confirmed they were aware of Victor’s arrest last June. He said police want future conversations with both people, whom he described as persons of interest. Lambert stressed that the case is not being treated as a cold case and that investigators still hope to hold people accountable. He said the investigation has been complicated and resource-intensive, with more than 300 people interviewed or providing statements, more than 50 judicial authorizations obtained, and 23 full-time investigators assigned over the years. He added that the pandemic made the work even harder. Police believe the case is tied to criminal subculture and street gang activity, and that some witnesses are unwilling to come forward. Investigators think they know who was involved, but believe other people still have information they are not sharing. Gavin Daley had been in Kitchener for less than two months when he was killed. In April 2015, he and Victor were jointly charged with three counts of possession for the purpose of trafficking after Kingston police seized methamphetamine, heroin and cocaine worth about $90,000. When Gavin was killed, the trafficking charges against Victor were withdrawn because the evidence was considered strongest against Gavin. Veronica Daley described her son as a good kid whose life changed after a traumatic Grade 8 incident. He lost respect for authority, refused counselling, stopped attending school regularly, and began petty theft before getting involved with drugs and crime. He spent time at Brookside youth correctional facility and eventually told his mother he was addicted to money. Despite his troubled path, she said he was loved by family and respected by teachers. Now, she says Victor’s arrest may encourage others to speak up, but she no longer expects justice. Waterloo Regional Police are asking anyone with information to contact their major crime tip line or Crime Stoppers anonymously.

Gavin had spent less than two months in Kitchener before his death. The Florida Legislature returned to Tallahassee for one extra day on Saturday, approved a $91.1 billion state budget, and then adjourned quickly, formally ending a 61-day session that had been extended because lawmakers could not reach a spending deal on time. The final vote took only minutes, with the House and Senate passing the budget without debate after having already worked through the differences in the previous two days. Afterward, Republican leaders celebrated the session as a success and praised one another from the floor. Senate President Bill Galvano told senators to “give yourselves a round of applause,” and they did. House Speaker Jose Oliva followed by saying, “Here we are 61 days later, and we have done what we said we would do. We should all go home tremendously proud.” The House chamber responded with loud applause. Much of the Legislature’s work came late in the session. Early on, lawmakers fulfilled one of Gov. Ron DeSantis’ major requests by repealing Florida’s ban on medical marijuana. After that, however, relatively little significant legislation reached the governor for weeks. In the final days, activity accelerated sharply, with many bills passing in a rush and some appearing unexpectedly at the end. Among the last-minute measures was a human trafficking bill approved at 11:19 p.m. on the final day for considering bills other than the budget. That measure includes a publicly accessible database of people who solicit prostitutes and requires training for hotel and massage parlor workers to help them identify and report trafficking. Although most of the roughly 3,500 bills filed this year died, the state’s three most powerful Republican leaders each claimed important victories. Galvano won approval for rural toll roads he says would support economic development, reduce congestion on Interstate 75, and create new hurricane evacuation routes. Oliva secured health care changes, including a bill that makes it easier to build new hospitals. DeSantis largely got what he wanted as well, including a bill intended to help students prepare for careers without needing a four-year college degree and an expansion of the state’s voucher program that uses taxpayer money to send students to private schools. Republicans also agreed to spend more than either chamber had initially proposed. The Senate had advanced a $90.3 billion budget and the House had suggested $89.9 billion, but negotiators settled on $91.1 billion. DeSantis had originally asked for $91.3 billion, though on Saturday he joked that he would trim the final number further when he reviews it. Standing with Galvano and Oliva, he said the budget would end up “under 91” billion dollars after his changes and argued that Florida remained fiscally stable. Some legislation drew bipartisan support, including bills expanding benefits for firefighters with cancer, increasing penalties for people who kill police dogs, banning child-like sex dolls, and protecting front-yard vegetable gardens from local ordinances. But several of the session’s most contentious issues involved immigration, voting rights, guns in schools, and constitutional changes. Advocates for immigrants had protested for weeks against a proposal barring local governments from adopting sanctuary policies. In the final week, lawmakers passed a bill requiring local governments to cooperate with federal immigration authorities. Democrats also fought a bill requiring felons to pay court-imposed financial obligations before regaining voting rights, and it passed on the session’s 60th day. Another controversial measure expanded a program allowing school districts to train teachers to carry guns in classrooms. Republicans also inserted language on the final day making it harder for citizens to amend the state constitution through petition drives. While Republicans celebrated, Democrats said the session produced troubling outcomes. Rep. Anna Eskamani said, “Democracy died a little this session,” criticizing the teacher-gun measure, the lack of environmental legislation, and the restrictions on the constitutional amendment process.

Paola Guzman, a 41-year-old housekeeper who has lived in Alaska for 20 years, is fighting deportation after being arrested during a federal workplace immigration audit this summer. Guzman, who lacks permanent legal status, was detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement during an I-9 inspection. She has two U.S. citizen sons and no criminal record. After spending several months at the Tacoma Detention Center, she was released on bond. A federal judge ruled that Guzman’s continued detention was not justified because ICE had not shown she was a flight risk or a danger to the community. Even so, she still faces possible deportation and remains in legal limbo while awaiting a court decision. Speaking from Anchorage, Guzman said she is fighting to stay in the United States for her children and her family, most of whom are in Alaska. “I wanna fight for my kids. The article notes that workplace audits, or I-9 inspections, have increased significantly under the Trump administration as part of a broader enforcement strategy. Border Czar Tom Homan said work-site enforcement is meant to target undocumented workers, employers, and trafficking cases. Immigration advocates, however, argue the approach unfairly sweeps up workers like Guzman who do not pose a public safety threat.

The Trump administration on Wednesday announced that part of Louisiana State Penitentiary, the notorious prison known as Angola, will be converted into a federal migrant detention center called “Camp 57.” The facility is intended to hold migrants the administration considers the most serious offenders and is part of President Donald Trump’s broader mass deportation effort. Officials said Camp 57 will initially provide about 400 beds and help expand ICE detention capacity nationwide. The move comes as the administration has added more than 60 new federal, state, and local detention sites this year in an effort to keep pace with Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s intensified arrest operations. The Justice Department has denied in court filings that ICE is operating under a formal quota of 3,000 arrests per day, though the administration has publicly tied the expansion to its aggressive enforcement goals. Louisiana Gov. Jeff Landry, a Republican, said the new site would “fulfill the president’s promise of making America safe again” and allow ICE to “consolidate the most violent offenders into a single deportation and holding facility.” Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem said the government needs more detention space because arrests and deportations are occurring at a very high rate. Angola’s selection carries heavy symbolism. Located in northwestern Louisiana near the Mississippi River, the prison has long been called the “Alcatraz of the South.” It currently houses more than 4,300 inmates, about 70 percent of whom are serving life sentences, and more than 90 percent have been convicted of violent crimes, a higher share than any other prison in the state. Angola’s history is marked by brutality and forced labor: inmates once worked the cotton fields under guard, and in 1951 dozens of men cut their Achilles tendons in protest against that labor, becoming known as the “Heel String Gang.” By the 1970s, violence there was so common that the prison was described as the bloodiest in America. It is also known today for its prison rodeo and public tours, which the prison says now reflect its rehabilitation and vocational programs. The conversion became possible after Landry issued an emergency order in July for Camp J, a unit that had been closed since 2018 and had deteriorated badly enough to pose a safety threat. Emergency repairs were authorized, paving the way for the unit’s use as a federal detention site. Officials said Angola offers a faster solution than building a new prison from scratch because it already has fortified infrastructure, including razor wire, armed towers, and lockdown units. Landry said the facility will hold 208 “criminal illegal aliens” by mid-September, including 51 already present, and should reach more than 400 in the coming months. The expansion is part of a much larger immigration crackdown backed by Congress in July, when lawmakers approved more than $150 billion for Trump’s immigration agenda. The package tripled ICE’s budget, funded new detention centers and border barriers, and created incentives to hire more enforcement personnel. Critics say using Angola for immigration detention blurs the line between civil and criminal custody. ICE policy describes detention as “non-punitive,” but the ACLU argued that placing civil detainees in a prison built for violent offenders violates that principle. The announcement comes amid a sharp rise in arrests: migrant arrests more than doubled in the first six months of Trump’s second term, and in July, 37 percent of ICE arrests involved people with no U.S. criminal convictions or pending charges.

The 2025 St. Petersburg Conference on World Affairs opened Tuesday evening at the Palladium Theater with a keynote address that reflected the event’s theme, “The Ties That Bind Us.” Former ambassador Stuart Eizenstat, who served under six presidential administrations, launched the three-day conference with remarks focused on diplomacy, negotiation and the importance of international engagement. Eizenstat is widely regarded as one of the country’s leading diplomatic experts. Over the course of his career, he helped negotiate major agreements with Germany, Austria, France and other European nations involving restitution for property, compensation for slave and forced labor, and the recovery of looted art and bank accounts. His keynote drew on those experiences as well as on his 2024 book, *The Art of Diplomacy: How American Negotiators Reached Historic Agreements That Changed the World*, published by Rowman & Littlefield. The conference, which began in 2013, is designed to explore the overlap between global and local issues through civil, nonpartisan conversation. City Councilmember Gina Driscoll, who spoke at the event, said the theme was especially timely and urged attendees to use the conference as a chance to learn, connect and grow together. She said the goal should be to focus not only on what divides people, but on what unites them. In his address, Eizenstat said he wrote his book during a time of seemingly unsolvable problems in order to show that leaders have overcome equally difficult challenges in the past. He contrasted diplomacy with military force, noting that presidents have increasingly relied on force, often with “very mixed results.” He also warned against an isolationist mindset, saying the United States cannot simply rely on its oceans for protection while leaving room for countries such as Russia, China and Iran to shape global affairs according to their own interests and values. Eizenstat argued that diplomacy must produce “win-win” outcomes and emphasized the importance of appointing the right people to the right jobs at the right time, citing Henry Kissinger as an example. He also told the audience that effective negotiators must listen carefully to opposing views, not just present their own arguments, and must be creative, persistent and prepared for unexpected costs. He recalled sleeping only three or four hours a night while helping negotiate the Kyoto Protocol with 190 countries. He concluded that diplomacy remains essential to solving today’s problems and that progress depends on the right people working with creativity and determination. Willi Rudowsky, board president of organizer St. Petersburg in the World, said the nonprofit has joined the World Affairs Councils of America and will now host at least 12 annual events. The next program is scheduled for March 20 at The Studio@620, where James Ketterer of Bard College will speak about jazz as a diplomatic tool. The conference runs through Thursday at 5 p.m.

Kazakhstan marked May 31 as the Day of Remembrance of Victims of Political Repressions and Famine, honoring what President Kassym-Jomat Tokayev called one of the darkest chapters in the country’s history. In a message to the nation, delivered through the Akorda press service, Tokayev said the day commemorates the victims of two catastrophic periods: Stalin-era political repression and the 1931–1933 famine. He said political repression in the first half of the 20th century devastated millions across the former Soviet Union, and that in Kazakhstan more than 100,000 people were unjustly convicted, with about a quarter sentenced to death. He also noted that some estimates say more than 40% of Kazakhstan’s population died in the famine, which was caused by Stalin’s collectivization policies. Tokayev recalled that the 1930s repressions killed thousands of Kazakhs and wiped out much of the country’s intellectual elite, naming figures such as Akhmet Baitursynov, Alikhan Bokeikhanov, Mirzhakyp Dulatov, Mukhametzhan Tynyshbayev, Magzhan Zhumabayev, Saken Seifullin, Ilyas Zhansugirov, Beimbet Mailin, Sanzhar Asfendiyarov and Turar Ryskulov. Some were executed, others died in labor camps, and thousands more were imprisoned. He also said 11 Soviet forced labor camps were established on Kazakh territory, including ALZHIR and Karlag, both now memorial complexes. Despite the suffering, he said Kazakh people sheltered deported populations, with around five million people eventually finding refuge there. Tokayev emphasized that independence enabled Kazakhstan to begin rehabilitating victims’ names. He said a state commission was created last year to complete this work and restore historical justice, describing it as both a state responsibility and a moral duty of society.

# Kazakhstan Commemorates Victims of Stalinist Repression and Famine Kazakhstan observed May 31st as the Day of Remembrance of Victims of Political Repressions and Famine, honoring millions who perished during two catastrophic periods in the nation's history. President Kassym-Jomat Tokayev addressed the nation, emphasizing the historical significance of this dark chapter. During Stalin's political repressions in the early 20th century, over 100,000 people were unjustly convicted in Kazakhstan, with approximately 25 percent receiving death sentences. The subsequent 1931-1933 famine, caused by Stalin's brutal collectivization policies, claimed the lives of more than 40 percent of the Kazakh population. The 1930s repressions particularly devastated Kazakh intellectuals, including renowned writer Akhmet Baitursynov, poet Magzhan Zhumabayev, and political figure Turar Ryskulov. Some were executed; others perished in labor camps or received prison sentences. Eleven Soviet forced labor camps operated on Kazakh territory under inhumane conditions, including ALZHIR and Karaganda labor camp (Karlag). These sites now function as historical memorials. Despite these atrocities, the Kazakh people demonstrated resilience and compassion, providing shelter to approximately five million deported people on the steppes. President Tokayev highlighted that the nation's suffering strengthened unity and solidarity. Following independence, Kazakhstan initiated rehabilitation efforts for repression victims. Last year, a state commission was established to complete this process and restore historical justice, fulfilling both the state's and society's moral obligations to innocent victims.

The campaign was introduced in Minsk on February 20 and features stickers designed by Belarusian illustrator Mitya Pislyak, showing a cat in different travel settings, including the Brooklyn Bridge and snowy downtown Minsk. The project builds on an existing partnership between IOM and Viber, one of the world’s leading free messaging platforms. Its main purpose is to warn Belarusians about the risks of trafficking and to provide guidance on safe travel and safe stays abroad. People who download the sticker pack are automatically added for three months to the IOM Belarus Viber community, where they can access practical safety advice. IOM Belarus Chief of Mission Mahym Orazhammuhammedova said the organization hopes the campaign will use Viber’s large audience to spread useful information about safe migration more widely. Pislyak said his own experience of traveling and recently moving to New York made him appreciate the importance of having reliable information throughout a journey, and he hopes the stickers will remind users to take safety measures when traveling. Viber Communications Director for the CIS and France Yana Rozhkova said the company prioritizes security and is pleased to support IOM’s efforts. The cooperation is intended to raise awareness of modern slavery and reduce vulnerability, while complementing an existing IOM/Viber hotline and related campaigns.

Belarus’s Interior Ministry has denied online claims that an Indian national was trapped in forced labor and unable to leave the country. According to the ministry, the 38-year-old woman arrived in Belarus last November for work and, under a contract with an agricultural enterprise, received a temporary residence permit and housing in a brick house with basic amenities. Her employment contract was terminated just eight days later, which led to the cancellation of her residence permit. After that, she traveled to Russia and later returned to Belarus. The woman told authorities that an agent in India had promised her a different job, but after she arrived, the agent stopped answering her calls. The ministry said she is now receiving all necessary assistance, including help with returning home. Police and migration officials are investigating the circumstances of her stay and are identifying everyone involved, including employers and intermediaries, whose actions will be legally assessed. The Interior Ministry said the online reports have not been confirmed and warned that spreading false information can carry legal consequences. It added that Belarus welcomes law-abiding visitors, while violations involving foreign labor recruitment will not be ignored.

According to the ministry, a 38-year-old Indian woman arrived in Belarus in November for employment with an agricultural enterprise and received temporary residence and housing. However, her employment contract was terminated just eight days later, resulting in the annulment of her permit. The woman subsequently traveled to Russia before returning to Belarus. She acknowledged that an Indian employment agent had promised her different work but became uncontactable after her arrival. The ministry stated the woman is currently receiving assistance for her return home. Authorities are investigating the circumstances of her stay and assessing the legal actions of all involved parties, including employers and intermediaries. The ministry warned that spreading false information carries legal consequences and emphasized that Belarus welcomes law-abiding visitors while maintaining strict oversight of its labor market and worker protections.

Ten anti-slavery NGOs have criticized the UK Home Office for detaining victims of human trafficking and modern slavery, saying immigration detention has no place in a fair and progressive system. The criticism follows accusations that the Home Office has been sending slavery survivors to detention centres, which groups such as the Labour Exploitation Advisory Group say can harm their mental health. The Home Office says it is committed to protecting survivors and identifying them in detention. Scottish Refugee Council data show 255 identified slavery survivors were detained between 2016 and 2018, while LEAG says there is no effective mechanism for spotting victims before removal.

An estimated 10 million migrants are moving across Central Asia, many heading to construction sites in Russia, oilfields in Kazakhstan, or destinations such as Turkey and the Middle East. Most are vulnerable to traffickers who profit from exploiting people in construction, agriculture and entertainment. In Uzbekistan, where about 600,000 new workers enter the labor force each year, officials say traffickers are increasingly using online recruitment to target aspiring migrants, avoiding face-to-face contact and making victims easier to reach. Sanjar Toshbaev, IOM’s country manager in Uzbekistan, said traffickers once traveled physically from countries such as Turkey and Russia, but now can ensnare victims online. He said the rise in online trafficking over the past two years makes it necessary to fight back on the same platforms. This week, the International Organization for Migration brought together 20 anti-trafficking organizations near Tashkent to plan how to integrate online information campaigns into their work. Joe Lowry of IOM’s Vienna Regional Office, who led the USAID-funded workshop, said traffickers constantly adapt to protect their lucrative business model, so anti-trafficking efforts must do the same. The two-day workshop focused on using social media to spread safe migration messages and on improving participants’ skills in writing for online and traditional media and producing audio-visual content. Ravshan, a former Uzbek migrant worker in Moscow, said better information is essential because corruption and exploitation are common, and migrants need to know the risks before leaving.

# Summary Central Asia faces a significant human trafficking crisis, with an estimated ten million migrants vulnerable to exploitation as they seek work in Russia, Kazakhstan, Turkey, and the Middle East. Uzbekistan is particularly affected, with 600,000 new workers entering the labor force annually. Traffickers have increasingly shifted their recruitment tactics online, exploiting migrants through digital platforms rather than face-to-face interactions. This trend has accelerated dramatically over the past two years, making it more difficult for authorities to combat trafficking. In response, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) convened 20 anti-trafficking organizations near Tashkent to develop online countermeasures. The two-day workshop, funded by USAID, aimed to integrate behavioral change components into digital campaigns and educate migrants about the dangers of irregular migration and fraudulent job offers. Participants received training on crafting effective social media messages, writing for traditional and digital media, and producing audio-visual content. Experts emphasized that knowledge is crucial for safe migration experiences, noting that migrants face corruption, fees, and exploitation throughout their journey. The initiative recognizes that traffickers continuously adapt their methods, requiring anti-trafficking efforts to similarly evolve and meet them in the digital space where recruitment now occurs.

On 10 November, the Third Committee of the 78th UN General Assembly adopted by consensus Belarus’s annual resolution, “Improving the coordination of efforts against trafficking in persons,” according to Belarus’s Foreign Ministry. The resolution has been adopted by the UN since 2006 and is presented as a practical follow-up to an initiative Belarusian President Aleksandr Lukashenko proposed at the 2005 UN summit to create a global partnership against human trafficking. The text drew more than 40 co-sponsors from all regions, which Belarus said shows the continuing relevance of its initiative and the confidence placed in Minsk to help coordinate international anti-trafficking efforts. The resolution is described as a universal umbrella document that keeps the UN focused on trafficking and brings together separate thematic efforts previously scattered across the organization. It also highlights the role of universal and regional bodies in anti-trafficking work, including the Inter-Agency Coordination Group against Trafficking in Persons, UN agencies such as the Commission on Crime Prevention and Criminal Justice and the UN Office on Drugs and Crime, as well as the OSCE. The resolution addresses current challenges, including the growing use of information and communication technologies by traffickers and the rising number of migrants among victims. It also urges stronger international action to support trafficking victims.

# UN Adopts Belarus-Sponsored Resolution on Combating Human Trafficking On November 10, the UN General Assembly's Third Committee unanimously adopted Belarus's resolution titled "Improving the Coordination of Efforts Against Trafficking in Persons." This marks the continuation of an annual resolution that has been adopted since 2006, stemming from an initiative proposed by Belarusian President Aleksandr Lukashenko at a 2005 UN summit to establish global partnership against human trafficking. The resolution garnered support from over 40 co-sponsoring nations across all world regions, demonstrating widespread international confidence in Belarus's leadership on this issue. The document serves as a comprehensive, universal framework that consolidates individual anti-trafficking initiatives promoted by various states within the UN, reducing previous fragmentation in efforts. The resolution acknowledges contributions from universal and regional organizations, including the Inter-Agency Coordination Group Against Trafficking in Persons and UN entities like the Office on Drugs and Crime. It addresses contemporary challenges, including the increasing use of information and communication technologies for trafficking purposes and the rising number of migrants among trafficking victims. The resolution also emphasizes strengthening international measures to support trafficking victims.

A U.N. report released Friday says Ecuador must do more than rely on policing to confront its worsening security crisis, arguing that crime is closely tied to poverty, weak labor protections, and lack of opportunity. The report, issued by U.N. special rapporteur on extreme poverty and human rights Olivier De Schutter, urges the government to strengthen enforcement of labor laws, end slavery-like bonded labor, and redirect money from fuel subsidies toward social programs. De Schutter told The Associated Press that insecurity in Ecuador should be treated as a poverty problem as much as a law-enforcement problem. He said the answer “cannot be just law enforcement,” and pointed to the country’s large youth poverty rate. The report says about 34% of Ecuadorians ages 15 to 24 live in poverty. According to De Schutter, many young people who left school during the COVID-19 pandemic never returned and have become easy recruits for gangs. The report was released nearly a month after the assassination of presidential candidate Fernando Villavicencio, an anti-corruption figure who was shot dead in broad daylight on Aug. 9 despite having police and bodyguard protection. Since then, at least two other political leaders have been killed, and last week several car bombs and other explosive devices detonated in different cities, including Quito. Ecuadorian officials say the surge in violence over the past three years stems from a power vacuum created after the 2020 killing of Jorge Zambrano, alias “Rasquiña” or “JL,” leader of the Los Choneros gang. De Schutter met with President Guillermo Lasso, government officials, Afro-Ecuadorian leaders, and indigenous representatives. The report criticizes Ecuador for underenforcing labor laws, saying the country has only 140 labor inspectors, a number De Schutter called far too low and too poorly resourced to stop modern slavery. It says some Afro-Ecuadorian families, including children as young as 12, are working for pay far below the minimum wage in debt-bondage conditions. De Schutter said Lasso and labor vice minister Henry Valencia committed to sending inspectors to three large plantations to help “rescue” about 170 families from bonded labor. With Lasso’s presidency ending in December, the report calls on his successor to pursue gradual fiscal reform that would reduce fuel subsidies, which totaled $4.5 billion last year, and shift those funds to health, education, and social assistance for poor indigenous and Afro-Ecuadorian communities. The report acknowledges that such reform will be politically difficult, recalling the violent 2019 protests that forced President Lenin Moreno to abandon a subsidy-cutting austerity plan.

# UN Report Links Ecuador's Crime Crisis to Poverty and Labor Violations A United Nations special rapporteur has issued a report urging Ecuador's government to enforce labor laws more strictly and eliminate fuel subsidies as part of broader policy reforms to address the country's escalating crime problem. The report, released by UN envoy Olivier De Schutter, criticizes Ecuador's government for failing to combat slavery-like bonded labor, particularly affecting minority communities. De Schutter emphasized that insecurity should be addressed as a poverty and economic opportunity issue, not solely through law enforcement. He noted that approximately 34% of Ecuadorians aged 15-24 live in poverty, with many youth who left school during the COVID-19 pandemic becoming easy recruits for criminal gangs. The report arrives amid Ecuador's security crisis, highlighted by the assassination of anti-corruption presidential candidate Fernando Villavicencio on August 9. Despite having police and bodyguard protection, Villavicencio was fatally shot in broad daylight. Since then, two additional political leaders have been killed, and multiple car bombs and explosive devices have detonated across the country, including the capital. Authorities attribute the three-year violence surge to a power vacuum created by the 2020 death of Los Choneros gang leader Jorge Zambrano. The gang engages in contract killings, extortion, drug trafficking, and prison control. The report criticizes Ecuador's labor law enforcement, noting only 140 inspectors—described as inadequately resourced—oversee the country's labor sector. Some Afro-Ecuadorian families, including children as young as 12, work for significantly below minimum wage in debt bondage conditions. President Guillermo Lasso committed to sending inspectors to three plantations to rescue approximately 170 families from bonded labor. The UN recommends redirecting Ecuador's $4.5 billion annual fuel subsidy—equivalent to the Education Ministry's budget and four times social assistance spending—toward social programs benefiting indigenous and Afro-Ecuadorian communities. However, this faces significant political obstacles. In 2019, an austerity package cutting fuel subsidies triggered violent protests, looting, highway blockades, and clashes with security forces, ultimately forcing the government to withdraw the measure. The report advocates for gradual subsidy phase-out combined with increased social assistance and investments in health and education for impoverished communities, benefiting both vulnerable populations and the nation overall.

The Archdiocese of Bogotá has sharply criticized Colombian President Gustavo Petro after he announced what he described as a bilateral cease-fire with armed groups, only for the ELN guerrilla movement to quickly deny that any agreement had been reached. In an editorial published Jan. 11 in the archdiocese’s newspaper, *El Catolicismo*, the Church described the episode as “a first great defeat” for the Petro government. Petro, a leftist president who took office in August 2022 and once belonged to the now-defunct M-19 guerrilla group, announced on Dec. 31, 2022, via Twitter that a cease-fire would begin Jan. 1, 2023, and last six months. He said the arrangement involved several armed groups, including the ELN, a dissident faction of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC) that rejected the 2016 peace deal, and the Gaitanista Self-Defense Forces of Colombia, also known as the Clan del Golfo. But soon after the announcement, the ELN publicly rejected Petro’s statement, saying there was “still no agreement on this matter.” The archdiocese said the government had made the announcement “with fanfare,” but that the denial came even faster than the claim itself. It argued that what the government wants to present and what armed groups are actually thinking are very different things. The editorial portrayed these groups as driven by power, money, drug trafficking, human trafficking, illegal mining, and territorial control, rather than by the social conflict often cited to explain Colombia’s violence. It called it “absolutely naïve” to believe such organizations would abandon their activities simply because the president declared a “total peace.” At the same time, the archdiocese said the Colombian bishops remain willing to help mediate efforts toward peace. However, it warned that they must not allow themselves to be used politically or lose their moral credibility. The editorial also expressed distrust of the current government, saying its words often do not match reality and are more rhetorical than substantive. The article concluded with a caution against rushing toward supposedly easy solutions. According to the archdiocese, peace is a long and difficult process, and any government announcement should be carefully verified before being taken at face value.

# Church Criticizes Colombian President's Failed Cease-Fire Announcement The Archdiocese of Bogotá has published a scathing editorial condemning President Gustavo Petro for announcing a cease-fire agreement that armed groups subsequently denied agreeing to, calling it "a first great defeat" for his government. On December 31, 2022, Petro announced via Twitter that a bilateral cease-fire had been agreed upon with multiple armed groups, effective January 1, 2023, for six months. The supposed agreement included the ELN (National Liberation Army), a Marxist-Leninist guerrilla group founded in 1964, a FARC faction that rejected the 2016 peace accord, and the Gaitanista Self-Defense Forces of Colombia. However, the ELN quickly denied any agreement existed, stating "there is still no agreement on this matter." The archdiocese's January 11 editorial, titled "There is no easy peace," criticized the government's announcement as hasty and poorly coordinated, noting that "the announcement took longer [to make] than the denial." The church argues that armed groups are driven by desires for power, wealth, and exploitation—not by social grievances—making them unlikely to abandon lucrative illegal activities like drug trafficking, human trafficking, and mining. The editorial expresses skepticism about Petro's credibility, noting that his words "rarely correspond to reality" and are "more rhetorical and political than anything else." The archdiocese warns against being manipulated by the government and recommends scrutinizing all official announcements carefully. While offering to mediate peace efforts, the bishops caution against lending moral authority to politically motivated initiatives. They emphasize that genuine peace requires patience and realistic expectations, warning against "magical or extraordinarily quick solutions." The criticism is particularly significant given Petro's own history as a former member of the M-19 guerrilla group, which dissolved decades ago. The archdiocese's statement reflects broader skepticism about the government's peace strategy and its ability to negotiate with armed groups operating entrenched criminal enterprises across Colombian territory.

Police and prosecutors from Brazil, French Guiana, Guyana and Suriname have arrested nearly 200 people in a first-ever joint cross-border crackdown on illegal gold mining in the Amazon, authorities said Thursday. Backed by Interpol, the European Union and Dutch environmental crime police, the December operation—called Operation Guyana Shield—carried out more than 24,500 checks on people and vehicles in remote border areas. The sweep led to seizures of cash, unprocessed gold, mercury, firearms, drugs and mining equipment. In Guyana, officers detained three men on suspicion of gold smuggling and money laundering after finding unprocessed gold and about $590,000 in cash. Investigators believe they may belong to an organized crime group and may have ties to a major gold-exporting company in Guyana. Authorities also confiscated mercury valued at more than $60,000 in Guyana and Suriname. The toxic metal, widely used in illegal mining to separate gold from sediment, had been hidden inside solar panels and moved by bus, Interpol said. Police searched vehicles, boats and riverside shops that supply fuel, tools and other items used by miners, some of which are suspected of helping smuggle gold and mercury across borders. The operation also uncovered counterfeit medicines, alcohol and cigarettes worth more than $40,000, as well as mining pumps, gold-collecting mats, mobile phones and firearms. Officers stopped a bus carrying undocumented migrants, including several minors; some children are suspected of being victims of forced labor or sexual exploitation. Illegal gold mining has become a major source of deforestation, river pollution and mercury contamination in the Amazon, especially in Indigenous territories. It has expanded rapidly as gold prices have climbed, making it highly profitable for transnational criminal networks. Interpol Secretary General Valdecy Urquiza said the activity is causing serious harm to the environment and local communities, and called the operation an important step in regional cooperation against a crime that has long been difficult to police because of the Amazon’s vast, porous borders.

# Interpol-Led Amazon Gold Mining Crackdown Results in Nearly 200 Arrests Police from Brazil, French Guiana, Guyana, and Suriname conducted their first-ever joint cross-border operation in December targeting illegal gold mining in the Amazon region, resulting in nearly 200 arrests. The operation, called Operation Guyana Shield, was supported by Interpol, the European Union, and Dutch environmental crime specialists. The coordinated effort involved over 24,500 vehicle and person checks across remote border areas. Officers searched vehicles, boats, and riverside shops suspected of facilitating illegal mining operations. The sweep led to significant seizures including cash, unprocessed gold, mercury, firearms, drugs, and mining equipment. Notable arrests included three men in Guyana suspected of gold smuggling and money laundering. Police seized unprocessed gold and approximately $590,000 in cash from the suspects, believed to be connected to organized crime with links to a major Guyanese gold exporting company. Authorities also confiscated cylinders of mercury worth over $60,000, which had been hidden inside solar panels and transported by bus. Illegal gold mining has become a major environmental threat in the Amazon, driving deforestation and river pollution. Mercury contamination poisons waterways and damages lands relied upon by Indigenous communities. The activity has expanded rapidly due to climbing global gold prices, making it increasingly profitable for organized crime networks. The operation also uncovered human trafficking concerns, with police stopping a bus carrying undocumented migrants, including children suspected of being victims of forced labor or sexual exploitation. Interpol Secretary General Valdecy Urquiza emphasized the operation's significance, noting that illegal gold mining causes serious environmental and community harm. The coordinated effort demonstrates progress in regional cooperation to combat illegal mining across the Amazon's challenging terrain and porous borders.

Ecuador’s National Assembly has approved a constitutional change that would allow foreign military bases in the country, a proposal backed by President Daniel Noboa to strengthen cooperation against transnational crime. The measure passed its final vote on Tuesday with 82 lawmakers in favor, supported by Noboa’s ruling bloc and allied parties. It now must be approved by voters in a national referendum before taking effect, as required for partial constitutional reforms. Noboa introduced the proposal in October 2024 to amend Article 5 of the constitution, which currently bans foreign military bases or military facilities on Ecuadorian soil. Lawmakers said the reform would improve national security through intelligence sharing, technology transfer and strategic cooperation. The move comes amid a severe security crisis, with the government fighting criminal gangs and more than 3,000 homicides reported in the first four months of 2025.

# Summary Ecuador's National Assembly approved a constitutional amendment on June 3 allowing foreign military bases in the country. The bill passed with 82 votes, supported by President Daniel Noboa's ruling coalition, to combat transnational crime through enhanced international cooperation and intelligence sharing. The amendment must be ratified through public referendum to take effect. Noboa originally proposed the measure in October 2024 to revise Article 5 of the Constitution, which currently prohibits foreign military bases. Lawmakers argue the reform is essential for addressing organized crime, drug trafficking, illegal mining, and human trafficking. This action reflects Ecuador's deepening security crisis, following the government's January 2024 declaration of "internal armed conflict" against criminal gangs. Early 2025 saw over 3,000 homicides in the first four months.

The article argues that the Trump administration’s January 3, 2026 operation in Venezuela marks a major turning point in U.S. foreign policy. It says the United States completed “Operation Absolute Resolve,” captured Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro, and severely weakened his socialist government. The piece presents the action as a bold and justified strike against dictatorship, while noting that it immediately drew criticism from political leaders and commentators. Among those cited are New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who condemned the operation as a unilateral attack on a sovereign country, and Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez, who said Spain would not recognize a U.S. intervention that violated international law. The United States and Argentina said they will work more closely to disrupt Hezbollah’s funding networks in Latin America. U.S. Secretary of State Rex Tillerson discussed the issue Sunday in Buenos Aires with Argentine Foreign Minister Jorge Faurie, and both said they agreed on the need to intensify cooperation against transnational criminal groups. Tillerson said the talks covered narcotics trafficking, human trafficking, smuggling and money laundering, which the U.S. believes are linked to terrorist financing. He specifically said Lebanese Hezbollah has a presence in the hemisphere and is raising funds to support its terrorist activities. Faurie echoed that view, saying South America should remain a “zone of peace” and that outside groups must not be allowed to undermine it. He called for greater exchange of information and dialogue about criminal networks that exploit transnational crime. The concern is rooted in Argentina’s history and its Lebanese expatriate population. U.S. authorities suspect some individuals in that community of using organized crime to raise money for Hezbollah, the Iranian-backed armed group. Argentina was hit by major anti-Jewish attacks in 1992 and 1994, including bombings of the Israeli embassy and a Jewish community center in Buenos Aires that killed 114 people combined. Although no bombers were convicted, investigators traced the attacks to Hezbollah and senior Iranian officials. U.S. experts believe Hezbollah has since built a Latin American fundraising network tied to drug smuggling.

# Summary US Secretary of State Rex Tillerson and Argentine Foreign Minister Jorge Faurie announced plans for increased cooperation to disrupt Hezbollah's funding networks in Latin America during talks in Buenos Aires. The Iranian-backed militant group allegedly raises funds through organized crime activities within Argentina's large Lebanese expatriate community. Tillerson emphasized the need to target transnational criminal organizations, including drug trafficking, human trafficking, smuggling, and money laundering, which he connected to terrorist financing. Both officials agreed that such external groups threaten the region's stability and must be eliminated. This initiative follows a violent history in Argentina. In 1992, bombers attacked the Israeli embassy, killing 29 people, and in 1994, a Jewish community center attack resulted in 85 deaths. While no bombers were convicted, international investigators linked the attacks to Hezbollah and Iranian officials. Though the bombings ceased, US experts believe Hezbollah has since established a sophisticated fund-raising network in Latin America under Iranian supervision, leveraging drug smuggling profits to finance its political and military operations. The US and Argentina's enhanced cooperation aims to dismantle these financial mechanisms.

Brazilian brewery Kaiser, owned by Heineken, has been added to the Brazilian government’s list of companies linked to labor conditions analogous to slavery. The inclusion stems from Kaiser’s subcontracting of Sider, a trucking firm that delivered beer in São Paulo. Sider was accused in 2021 of subjecting 23 drivers — 22 Venezuelans and one Haitian — to “slavery-like conditions.” Labor inspectors said the drivers worked illegally long hours, sometimes up to 18 hours a day, with no paid time off. Although Sider had promised lodging, it failed to provide it, and many workers slept in their trucks. The Venezuelan workers had been hired through Operacao Acolhida, a federal program that helps resettle migrants and connect them with employers. Heineken said it had not known about the situation at Sider and no longer works with the company. It added that it has created a tool to monitor labor issues involving subcontractors and is working to resolve Kaiser’s inclusion on the list. In Brazil, the “slave labor” list is updated every six months, and companies on it face restrictions on government contracts and loans.

# Summary Brazilian brewery Kaiser, owned by Heineken, has been added to the government's "slave labor" list due to labor violations by its subcontractor, trucking company Sider. In 2021, labor inspectors found that Sider subjected 23 drivers—22 Venezuelans and one Haitian—to slavery-like conditions, including illegal 18-hour workdays without paid time off and promised but undelivered lodging, forcing workers to sleep in trucks. Heineken stated it was unaware of the situation and no longer works with Sider, adding it has created monitoring tools for subcontractor labor issues. Brazil legally defines slavery as forced labor, debt bondage, degrading conditions, and excessive hours posing health risks. The Venezuelan workers were hired through a federal government resettlement initiative. Companies on Brazil's "slave labor" list remain for two years if no new violations occur, and face consequences including ineligibility for federal contracts, state loans, and potential credit restrictions from private banks and international buyers.

Millions of Ethiopian Orthodox Christians marked Epiphany, known locally as Timkat, on Monday in celebrations honoring the baptism of Jesus Christ by John the Baptist. In Batu, on the western shore of Lake Dambal in Oromia, thousands of pilgrims entered the water after priests blessed it, reenacting baptism and reflecting the festival’s themes of purification, renewal, and faith. In Addis Ababa, worshippers gathered to await the tabots, sacred replicas symbolizing the Ark of the Covenant and used to consecrate churches. The tabots were carried in ritual processions to public spaces for overnight prayers before being returned to their churches the next day, drawing huge crowds of the faithful. Similar observances took place nationwide, including at the 17th-century Fasilides Fortress in Gondar, in the conflict-hit Amhara region. Timkat is regarded as one of Ethiopia’s most important religious holidays, nearly as significant as Easter and Christmas, and was designated a UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage in 2019. Participants described the day as joyful and also as a moment of generosity toward those in need. The celebrations came amid rising tensions with Eritrea and worsening famine, with aid groups warning that millions of Ethiopians need emergency food assistance as Western support declines.

# Summary Millions of Ethiopian Orthodox Christians celebrated Epiphany, known locally as Timkat, on Monday, commemorating Jesus Christ's baptism by John the Baptist. In Batu, a western Lake Dambal town, thousands of pilgrims entered blessed waters in symbolic baptism reenactments, emphasizing purification, renewal, and faith. In Addis Ababa, sacred tabots—symbols of the Ark of the Covenant—were ceremonially carried to public spaces for overnight prayers before returning to churches, drawing millions of devoted followers. Similar celebrations occurred nationwide, including at Gondar's 17th-century Fasilides Fortress in the war-torn Amhara region. UNESCO recognized Timkat as Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2019, reflecting its significance as a major religious holiday rivaling Easter and Christmas. Priests in colorful robes carried ceremonial umbrellas while chanting and singing during processions. Participants emphasized the holiday's charitable aspects. The celebrations occur amid challenging circumstances for Ethiopia, including escalating tensions with Eritrea and worsening famine conditions, with humanitarian organizations warning that millions require emergency food aid as Western support declines.

A Federal University Lokoja lecturer, Professor Mohammed Nasirudeen Suleiman, has called for greater use of natural plant-based remedies to preserve food and control crop diseases, warning against the misuse of chemical pesticides and fungicides by farmers. Speaking at his inaugural lecture titled *“Pathogenic Fungi and Food Deprivation: The Challenges of Plants Pathologists,”* held on Wednesday at the university’s Adankolo Campus in Lokoja, he recommended **Azadirachta indica (neem) leaves** and **rice chaff** for preserving rice and cowpeas. He said many farmers lack the financial resources and technical knowledge needed to safely handle imported agrochemicals, which can also lose effectiveness in tropical heat. According to him, fungi remain a major threat to Nigerian agriculture, damaging crops such as yams, potatoes, beans, maize, cocoa and groundnuts. He argued that plant diseases, especially those caused by pathogenic fungi during transit and storage, contribute significantly to food deprivation, hunger, malnutrition and related cognitive problems. Professor Suleiman highlighted the success recorded four years earlier in the FUL Biological Science Laboratory with bio-pesticides and fungicides derived from plants such as neem, tobacco and chrysanthemum. He said this experience had encouraged further research into plant compounds including alkaloids, flavonoids, terpenoids and other secondary metabolites, which plants naturally produce to defend themselves against fungi and bacteria. He added that many tropical plants possess medicinal properties that could be harnessed to protect crops and prevent food shortages. The lecturer also urged the global introduction of intensive mycology studies in secondary schools, lamenting that fungi are largely ignored in school curricula despite their importance. In his view, studying fungi is essential because “the secret of our living may be there.” He stressed that natural compounds used as fungicides have proven effective, environmentally safe and biodegradable. Suleiman further noted that no plant is useless, since plants can serve as food, medicine or shelter, and he called for support to equip the university laboratory for the manufacture of herbal drugs. He said all stakeholders should work toward making Federal University Lokoja a hub for herbal medicine production. He thanked his parents for their sacrifices, appreciated his wife and children for their support, and commended Vice Chancellor Professor Olayemi Olarotimi Akinwumi and the university management for the opportunity to deliver the 10th inaugural lecture series.

# Summary: Herbal Remedies for Food Preservation and Herbal Medicine Development Professor Nasirudeen Suleiman of Federal University Lokoja (FUL) has advocated for natural herbal remedies to replace harmful pesticides in food preservation. During his inaugural lecture titled "Pathogenic Fungi and Food Deprivation: The Challenges of Plants Pathologists," he recommended using Azadirachta Indica (neem) leaves and rice chaff to preserve rice and cowpeas. The professor highlighted serious concerns about current agricultural practices, noting that farmers misuse chemical pesticides and fungicides. He explained that many farmers lack adequate resources and technical expertise to properly handle imported chemicals, which often deteriorate in tropical climates. These pesticides pose environmental and health risks while failing to effectively address crop diseases. Suleiman emphasized that pathogenic fungi cause significant damage to major crops including yams, potatoes, beans, maize, cocoa, and groundnuts, contributing to global food deprivation. He cited successful historical experiments conducted at FUL's Biological Science Laboratory four years ago, where naturally-derived compounds like azadirachtin, nicotine from tobacco, and pyrethrin from chrysanthemum flowers effectively functioned as bio-pesticides and fungicides. The lecturer noted that plants have naturally evolved secondary metabolites—alkaloids, flavonoids, and terpenoids—to protect themselves against fungal and bacterial damage. He pointed out that approximately 400,000 tropical flowering plant species possess medicinal properties applicable to crop disease control. Examples include Vernonia amygdalina, which treats malaria, and Cymbopogon citratus, which contains anti-malarial compounds. Suleiman called for funding to equip university laboratories for manufacturing herbal medicines and urged FUL to become a hub for herbal drug production. He also advocated for intensive mycology education in secondary schools globally, arguing that fungi are currently marginalized in curricula despite their importance. The professor emphasized that natural compounds used as fungicides are environmentally safe, easily biodegradable, and effective. He stressed that disease control during crop transit and storage is crucial for preventing food deprivation, hunger, malnutrition, and related cognitive impacts. Suleiman concluded that every plant has potential uses for food, medicine, or shelter, with only 10 percent of Earth's estimated 500,000 plant species currently utilized.

A new UNICEF report says the COVID-19 pandemic caused a major setback in childhood immunization across Africa, leaving the continent at heightened risk of disease outbreaks and what the agency calls a “child survival crisis.” Between 2019 and 2021, 12.7 million children in Africa missed one or more vaccinations, and 8.7 million received no vaccine at all, according to *The State of the World’s Children 2023*. UNICEF said this was part of the worst decline in childhood vaccination in 30 years. The report says the pandemic “interrupted childhood vaccination almost everywhere,” but Africa has the largest number of unvaccinated and under-vaccinated children. Half of the world’s 20 countries with the most “zero-dose” children are in Africa. Nigeria has 2.2 million children who have never been vaccinated, while Ethiopia has 1.1 million. UNICEF linked the decline to strained health systems, diversion of immunization resources to COVID-19 vaccination, health worker shortages, and stay-at-home measures. It also cited conflicts, climate change, and vaccine hesitancy. In Africa, the pandemic worsened long-standing weaknesses in primary health care and health system resilience. The consequences are already visible. UNICEF said 34 of Africa’s 54 countries experienced outbreaks of diseases such as measles, cholera, and poliovirus last year. # UNICEF Report: 12.7 Million African Children Missed Vaccinations During COVID-19 Pandemic A UNICEF report released Thursday reveals that approximately 12.7 million children in Africa missed one or more vaccinations between 2019 and 2021 due to COVID-19's disruptive impact. Of these, 8.7 million children received no vaccinations whatsoever during this period, representing the worst regression in childhood immunization in 30 years globally. Africa faces the highest number of unvaccinated children worldwide, with half of the world's 20 countries having the largest populations of "zero-dose" children located on the continent. Nigeria accounts for 2.2 million unvaccinated children, while Ethiopia has 1.1 million. The pandemic's interruption of vaccination programs has already produced severe consequences. Malawi experienced its worst cholera outbreak in 20 years, killing over 1,000 people early this year. Zimbabwe recorded nearly 700 child deaths from measles, with most victims unvaccinated. Last year, 34 of Africa's 54 countries reported disease outbreaks including measles, cholera, and poliovirus. Contributing factors to missed vaccinations include overwhelming demands on health systems, resource diversion to COVID-19 vaccination efforts, health worker shortages, stay-at-home measures, conflicts, climate change, and vaccine hesitancy. In Africa specifically, the pandemic exposed weaknesses in health systems and primary care infrastructure. UNICEF emphasizes an urgent "child survival crisis" on the continent and calls for immediate action from African leaders. Children born during the pandemic are now aging past their critical vaccination window, necessitating catch-up immunization efforts. The World Health Organization estimates Africa must vaccinate 33 million children by 2025 to recover from the pandemic's disruptions and restore vaccination progress.

Sudan’s government, business community, banks, and ordinary citizens were left uncertain after the United States delayed a final decision on whether to permanently lift long-standing trade sanctions on the country. Many Sudanese had hoped the decision, expected on Tuesday, would mark the end of restrictions first imposed in 1997 over accusations that Khartoum supported terrorism, and would help reintegrate Sudan into the global economy. Instead, the US State Department announced a three-month postponement, extending the period of limbo and dampening hopes for immediate relief. The delay was especially disappointing for Sudanese expatriates who had been waiting to send money home through normal banking channels. Mohammed Saad, a Sudanese living in Boston, said he had expected to be able to transfer funds directly to his family without relying on intermediaries or informal routes. He described banks as the most reliable way to send money and said he had waited six months for the sanctions decision. Another expatriate, Hussam Greishi, who was back in Khartoum on leave from work in Saudi Arabia, said he hoped eventually to return home and invest in a small business or farmland, but argued that the current situation was still not suitable for business. The sanctions had already been partially eased by former president Barack Obama in one of his final executive orders. That temporary measure relaxed restrictions on Sudan’s oil and gas sector, unfroze some Sudanese assets in the United States, and allowed certain approved imports and exports. However, many Sudanese said that the banking system remained effectively isolated, making it difficult to transfer money or conduct normal business. The global banking sector remained wary of Sudan because of the heavy $8.9 billion penalty imposed on BNP Paribas in 2015 for violating sanctions involving Sudan, Cuba, and Iran. As a result, many international banks continued to avoid dealings with Sudan even after the temporary easing. The sanctions also affected professionals and consumers in everyday ways. Software engineer Mohammed Abd Alaziz said he could not buy original software versions because of the sanctions and had to rely on alternatives. Translator Azza Mubarak said she often had to buy reference materials in expensive hard-copy form because online versions were unavailable or inaccessible. She explained that such books often cost two or three times more than regular versions because they had to be obtained through intermediary countries rather than directly from the US or Europe. The three-month delay followed pressure from human rights activists and members of the US Congress, who urged President Donald Trump to keep the sanctions in place because of Sudan’s human rights record. Sudanese political analyst Mohammed Humma said he had expected a delay and predicted the sanctions might be extended for six months or a year while the US monitored Sudan’s progress under the agreed review framework. That framework, known as the “five tracks,” included improving humanitarian access in war zones, cooperating with the US on counterterrorism, ending hostilities against armed groups inside Sudan, and stopping support for rebels in neighboring South Sudan. Senior US officials said Sudan had made substantial progress on all five tracks, but the new administration needed more time to review the situation. The extension also placed greater emphasis on human rights, religious freedom, and Sudan’s support for UN Security Council resolutions on North Korea. One US official said North Korea had become the Trump administration’s top security concern, framing it as a global threat. Sudan reacted angrily to the delay and froze talks with Washington on sanctions until October, when the three-month extension would expire. Foreign Minister Ibrahim Ghandour called the US decision “illogical and unacceptable,” insisting that Sudan had fully met its commitments under the engagement plan and expressing hope that sanctions would eventually be lifted so Sudan could remain a partner in regional security. A January 2017 report by the US State Department had already said Sudan had made “significant progress” in each of the five areas before Obama’s partial easing of restrictions. United Nations agencies in Sudan also said humanitarian access had improved markedly over the previous six months. Even so, many Sudanese businesses remained frustrated. Shop owners in Khartoum said they hoped sanctions relief would bring more tourists and customers, while a tea seller named Hadiya Adam questioned whether another delay would make any real difference to prices or daily life. Journalist Mohammed Amin said people were eager for sanctions to end, but many did not believe their removal would quickly improve living conditions or produce a dramatic change in everyday life.

Prime Minister Justin Trudeau met face-to-face on Friday with Myanmar leader Aung San Suu Kyi in Danang, Vietnam, and used the 45-minute discussion to confront her with evidence of the state-led violence that has driven a massive Rohingya refugee crisis. The meeting took place on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation leaders’ summit and was Trudeau’s first in-person encounter with Suu Kyi since Myanmar’s security forces launched a crackdown in late August. The violence has forced more than 600,000 Rohingya Muslims to flee into neighboring Bangladesh, creating what Canadian officials and the United Nations have described as ethnic cleansing. The crisis has severely damaged Suu Kyi’s international reputation, once celebrated because of her Nobel Peace Prize and pro-democracy legacy. Canada’s special envoy on the Rohingya crisis, Bob Rae, attended the meeting with Trudeau and later said the prime minister was “very direct” with Suu Kyi and that the two sides did not immediately agree. Rae said Trudeau and Canadian officials believe “more needs to be done and more could be done,” emphasizing that the situation is both a humanitarian and political emergency. He had just briefed Trudeau on a recent visit to the region and told reporters that Canada remains committed to staying engaged with Myanmar and helping create conditions for the refugees to return safely to their homes. He also acknowledged that repatriation would be difficult, given the overcrowded and dire conditions in refugee camps in Bangladesh. During the meeting, Rae said Suu Kyi acknowledged the country’s history of oppression and fear, and expressed willingness to work with Bangladesh to facilitate refugee returns and rebuild in line with a plan associated with former UN secretary general Kofi Annan. Still, Rae stressed that Canada’s concern is not just what leaders say but what they do, and that Ottawa will continue pressing for concrete implementation of necessary steps. Trudeau opened the meeting by saying it was a pleasure to meet Suu Kyi again and that they would discuss the refugee situation and ways Canada could help. Foreign Affairs Minister Chrystia Freeland also attended. Rae said Suu Kyi faces a difficult political reality: she has limited control in a country long dominated by the military, yet she also risks a domestic backlash if she speaks out too forcefully on behalf of the Rohingya, who have been targeted by anti-Muslim rhetoric. Canadian officials, speaking anonymously, said Ottawa has been cautious about directly blaming Suu Kyi because it believes Myanmar’s military is trying to undermine her standing. But criticism of her has grown internationally, including from other Nobel Peace Prize winners. Trudeau had already raised the issue with her in September and sent a letter outlining what Myanmar must do to protect innocent lives and meet Canada’s expectations. The Liberal government has also faced pressure to revoke Suu Kyi’s honorary Canadian citizenship, which she received in 2007.

# Trudeau Confronts Myanmar Leader Over Rohingya Violence Prime Minister Justin Trudeau held a direct 45-minute meeting with Myanmar's leader Aung San Suu Kyi on Friday during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Danang, Vietnam, to discuss the state-led violence against the Rohingya Muslim minority.
