Signs of renewed friendship between Rohingya Muslims and Rakhine Buddhists are being seen in Myanmar’s Rakhine State, offering hope amid a severe humanitarian crisis. Although many people view tensions between the two communities as the main cause of the August 2017 sectarian violence, many Rohingya did not flee to Bangladesh and remain in internally displaced persons camps set up before the latest conflict. A member of the Capacity Development Foundation, speaking anonymously for security reasons, said humanitarian groups are now recruiting both Rakhine and Rohingya locals for their projects. These include hiring teachers and launching education programs ranging from elementary school to university level for both communities. The source said mistrust and political tensions remain widespread, but there are many initiatives underway from Sittwe to the Bangladesh border, despite international pressure such as the European Union’s threat of economic sanctions. Following a memorandum of understanding signed by Myanmar and two UN agencies, UNDP and UNHRC, aid programs have expanded in Rakhine. The World Food Programme is distributing food in refugee camps, while other efforts focus on housing construction and renovation, as well as maintenance and infrastructure development. Assistance also extends to other minorities, including the Myo and Kamar, to promote integration and reconciliation. In the coming months, UN agencies and civil society groups plan to launch a Cash for Work program after public consultations that brought Rohingya and Rakhine together.

Despite widespread ethnic tensions, many Rohingya chose to remain in Myanmar rather than flee to Bangladesh and now live in internally displaced persons camps. Humanitarian organizations are actively recruiting from both communities to implement development projects, including education programs from elementary to university level. A Capacity Development Foundation representative noted that while mistrust and political tensions persist, numerous initiatives are underway across the state. Following a Memorandum of Understanding between Myanmar and UN agencies (UNDP and UNHCR), assistance programs have expanded significantly. Support extends beyond Rohingya and Rakhine to other ethnic minorities like the Myo and Kamar, aiming to promote integration and reconciliation. The article argues that India’s debate over its rank in the Global Hunger Index misses the larger issue: starvation and malnutrition are widespread, deeper, and more complex than a single international ranking can capture. It opens by recalling the UN Sustainable Development Goals, especially Goal 2, under which world leaders pledged to eliminate hunger by 2030 and to prioritize food and nutrition security for children, women, and the elderly. Yet, the author says, the real scale of hunger is still not being honestly acknowledged. Rather than focusing only on whether India is placed 50th, 100th, or somewhere else in the Global Hunger Index, the article says attention should be directed to the structural causes of starvation. It describes the index, developed by the International Food Policy Research Institute, as useful because it highlights child nutrition, unlike many other reports. The index is based on indicators such as undernutrition, wasting, stunting, and under-five mortality. However, the article also says this is only a partial measure and that hunger should be understood across a full life cycle. That broader view includes gender discrimination, child marriage, violence, education, safe childbirth, reproductive rights, breastfeeding, maternal rights, protection of natural resources, and the rights of farmers and laborers. The article links India’s poor standing in hunger-related measures to the condition of backward and tribal communities. It notes that India has about 10.4 million tribal people, who have historically relied on forests, water, and local ecological systems for survival. According to the article, global economic policies have weakened those systems by taking away access to land, forests, and culturally rooted livelihoods. It cites a UNICEF report from 2016-17 on nutrition among tribal children, which says that prolonged food insecurity in families and communities leads to stunted growth in children. Such children are more likely to remain ill, struggle in school, and be unable to grow into healthy citizens. The article attributes this condition to poverty, food insecurity, inadequate nutrition for women, poor breastfeeding practices, and unhealthy living conditions. The article then points to National Family Health Survey data, noting that NFHS-4 did not provide specific figures for malnutrition among tribal children. But it says NFHS-3 from 2005-06 showed that 54%, or about 6.2 million tribal children, suffered malnutrition and stunted growth due to persistent hunger. In a list of states including Andhra Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Gujarat, Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Odisha, Rajasthan, and Telangana, it says 4.7 million tribal children were found to have stunted growth. To address this, the article says the state has a constitutional duty to protect tribal communities from starvation. It recalls the Forest Rights Act passed by Parliament in 2006, which was intended to free tribals from encroachment on forest land and grant legal rights over land and forest produce such as wood, medicines, water, fruits, and vegetables. But the article says implementation has been poor. According to a Tribal Development Ministry report, by February 2017, 41.65 lakh claims had been filed for individual and community rights, and 18.47 lakh were rejected, often without reasons being communicated to the applicants. The article concludes that hunger is ultimately a governance issue, not just a statistical one. It criticizes systems that turn crises into opportunities for profit, whether through corporate control of nutrition programs or bureaucratic dependence on Aadhaar-linked ration access. As an alternative, it calls for drawing on India’s own long-standing experience with food security, agriculture, child-rearing, and natural resource management, while also using modern technology appropriately. The author says that if these approaches are followed in order, eliminating hunger by 2030 is possible.

# Summary: "Starvation' is larger than the hunger index" The article addresses the gap between India's commitment to eliminating hunger by 2030 under the Sustainable Development Goals and the reality of widespread malnutrition in the country. Rather than engaging in substantive debate about hunger solutions, the author argues that discussions have become fixated on India's ranking in the Global Hunger Index—whether 50th or 100th—rather than addressing root causes. The International Food Policy Research Institute measures global starvation through the Global Hunger Index, which evaluates nutrition status, malnutrition rates, and child mortality under five years. While this metric may seem limited, the author contends it should be understood through a life cycle perspective encompassing gender discrimination, child marriage, education, reproductive rights, and access to natural resources. India's poor ranking particularly reflects the conditions of backward and tribal communities. With 10.4 million tribal people in India, these populations have traditionally managed food security through sustainable use of natural resources. However, global economic policies have stripped them of access to water, forests, and their culture-based systems. According to a 2016-17 UNICEF report on tribal nutrition, sustained food insecurity leads to stunted child growth, chronic illness, poor school performance, and inability to become healthy citizens. Data reveals the severity of the problem: NFHS 3 (2005-06) showed 54 percent—approximately 6.2 million—tribal children suffered malnutrition and stunted growth due to persistent hunger. In nine selected states, 4.7 million tribal children experienced stunted growth. The government's response through the 2006 Forest Rights Act attempted to address this by granting tribal and forest dwellers legal rights to up to 10 acres of land and collective rights to forest resources including wood, medicines, water, fruits, and vegetables. However, implementation has been inadequate. By February 2017, while 41.65 lakh claims were filed for personal and community interests, 18.47 lakh were rejected—often without explanation to claimants. The author criticizes the approach to hunger as a governance commitment failure. Rather than viewing hunger as a crisis requiring immediate action, some stakeholders treat it as a profit opportunity. Nutritious food companies secure government contracts, while international organizations complicate the issue by presenting hunger as a disease, shifting focus from systemic solutions. Meanwhile, poor citizens must repeatedly prove identity through Aadhaar cards to access basic rations of rice, wheat, or sugar. The article proposes that India's solution lies not in Western models but in traditional Indian food security systems and practices. The author advocates integrating conventional agricultural technologies with modern scientific approaches—methods that European and American civilizations have already adopted. By implementing these traditional systems sequentially across farming, child nutrition, and natural resource management, the author contends that eliminating hunger by 2030 is entirely achievable. The piece ultimately argues that genuine hunger elimination requires political will, proper implementation of existing laws, respect for tribal rights and traditional knowledge systems, and prioritizing food security over profit motives.

The Balochistan High Court has warned that Quetta’s drinking water crisis has become extremely serious and said the provincial government appears unprepared to address it. A two-member bench headed by Chief Justice Jamal Khan Mandokhail and Justice Muhammad Kamran Khan Mullahkhail heard a petition on Saturday concerning the city’s water shortage. Chief Justice Mandokhail described the condition reported by the managing director of the Water and Sanitation Agency (Wasa) as “horrible and very serious.” He noted that Quetta’s groundwater level has fallen to around 1,200 feet, and even at that depth water is not always found. The court ordered the deputy commissioner of Quetta, the chief engineers of the Public Health Engineering and irrigation departments, and the Wasa managing director to meet and prepare a report on what policy and mechanism are needed to recharge groundwater and ensure alternative supplies of clean drinking water for the city’s residents. The bench also said the committee may recommend any necessary amendments to the Wasa Act’s rules and regulations. It directed the irrigation secretary and the PHE secretary to fully support the committee. During the hearing, Wasa’s managing director told the court that many tube wells in Quetta had been installed without feasibility studies, allegedly on the orders of some members of the Provincial Assembly, and without a detailed survey of suitable locations. He said a proper policy to remove some tube wells and recharge others could partly solve the crisis; otherwise, he warned, the city could face a famine-like situation. He added that many tube wells, including the one under discussion, had already dried up. He also informed the court that a sewage treatment plant built in 2010 had stopped working because of funding shortages and would need Rs100 million to become operational again. The bench ordered the committee members to appear in person at the next hearing with a detailed progress report.

# Summary: Balochistan High Court Addresses Quetta's Water Crisis The Balochistan High Court has expressed concern that the provincial government lacks a concrete strategy to address Quetta's severe drinking water shortage. During a hearing on Saturday, a two-member bench led by Chief Justice Jamal Khan Mandokhail described the situation as "horrible and very serious." The court heard that groundwater levels in Quetta have dropped critically to 1,200 feet, with wells often failing to strike water even at that depth. The Water and Sanitation Agency (Wasa) managing director revealed that most tube wells were installed without proper feasibility studies, based solely on directives from Provincial Assembly members, contributing to the crisis. To address the problem, the court directed officials from multiple departments—including the deputy commissioner, chief engineers from public health and irrigation departments, and Wasa's managing director—to form a committee. This committee must develop a comprehensive policy for groundwater recharging and alternative water supply mechanisms, and submit a detailed report to the court. The Wasa MD suggested that removing some tube wells and recharging existing ones could partially alleviate the problem. He warned of a potential famine-like situation without proper intervention. He also noted that a sewage treatment plant, closed since 2010 due to insufficient funding, could be reopened with Rs100 million to recycle water for industrial, agricultural, and construction purposes. The International Rescue Committee’s annual Emergency Watchlist identifies the countries most likely to face new or worsening humanitarian crises in the coming year, based on conflict, climate change, and political instability. Its 2025 list highlights 10 countries where war, displacement, hunger, and environmental shocks are driving severe risk. Sudan tops the list for the second year in a row. The country remains engulfed in civil war between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), producing what the IRC describes as the world’s largest and fastest-growing humanitarian and displacement crisis. The fighting has been marked by widespread violations of international law, sexual violence, child soldier recruitment, and attacks on civilians, hospitals, and aid workers. Myanmar ranks second. Since the military takeover in 2021, violence has intensified and spread as insurgent groups have expanded the conflict. More than 3 million people have been displaced. The situation is worsened by cyclones and floods, while damaged water and health systems are struggling to meet basic needs. Syria remains in crisis after 14 years of war. Rebel forces overthrew Bashar al-Assad’s government in late 2024 and now control Damascus, but the country’s future is uncertain. The conflict has displaced more than 13.8 million Syrians and left widespread poverty in its wake. South Sudan is also on the list for a second consecutive year, facing conflict linked to Sudan, political instability, violence, and climate emergencies. It is hosting large numbers of Sudanese refugees, while severe flooding has damaged the economy and food production, deepening the crisis. Lebanon enters the top 10 for the first time. Since October 7, 2023, Hezbollah and Israel have been locked in fierce conflict, although a 60-day ceasefire has been in place since November 27, 2024. Even so, the war displaced more than 1.4 million civilians. Burkina Faso has seen armed clashes involving ISGS and JNIM displace millions. Nearly 40 towns have been isolated, up from just one in 2021, cutting off around 2 million people from the rest of the country and disrupting aid. Haiti continues to suffer from gang violence, the 2021 assassination of President Jovenel Moïse, and a weakened government, with nearly half the population facing severe hunger and poverty. Mali’s 12-year conflict, involving the military, Russian Wagner Group, Tuareg forces, ISGS, and JNIM, has worsened food insecurity. The withdrawal of UN and French support has increased civilian casualties and allowed blockades to expand. Somalia remains highly unstable as al-Shabaab carried out more than 120 attacks in 2024. The country is still recovering from drought, hunger, and malnutrition. Yemen rounds out the list, where civil war since 2015 has left the country in turmoil, with famine, disease, and collapsing infrastructure adding to the suffering.

The European Union has announced an additional €500,000 in humanitarian aid to support victims of the earthquakes that hit Indonesia’s Lombok island in late July and early August. This new funding comes on top of an earlier €150,000 contribution, bringing the EU’s total assistance to €650,000. The aid is intended to complement the Indonesian government’s response and will focus on the most vulnerable people and communities in the affected areas. The funding will be used through the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC) to provide relief and protection services, and it is expected to directly assist about 80,000 vulnerable people in some of the hardest-hit localities in North East and West Lombok districts. It will also help reunite families separated by the earthquakes. EU Commissioner for Humanitarian Aid and Crisis Management Christos Stylianides said the EU stood by the Indonesian people and that the additional contribution would provide crucial support to those in need during a difficult time. By 13 August, the disaster had killed at least 390 people and injured more than 1,300 after two major quakes, measuring 6.4 and 6.9, struck the popular tourist island within a week. The tremors destroyed more than 67,000 homes and displaced over 300,000 people. Severe damage to public facilities and infrastructure, including health centers, power lines, and main roads, also hampered access to some affected areas. The EU aid is being provided through the European Commission’s ECHO emergency tool. The Netherlands and Spain have also contributed €500,000 and €100,000 respectively, bringing total EU support to €1.25 million. The funds are being channeled to the Indonesian Red Cross Society (PMI) through the IFRC.

# EU Increases Humanitarian Aid for Lombok Earthquake Victims The European Union has announced an additional €500,000 in emergency assistance for victims of devastating earthquakes that struck Indonesia's Lombok island in late July and early August. Combined with an initial €150,000 contribution, the EU's total commitment reaches €650,000. Two major earthquakes measuring 6.4 and 6.9 magnitude struck the popular resort island within one week, killing at least 390 people and injuring over 1,300. The tremors destroyed more than 67,000 homes and displaced over 300,000 residents. Significant damage to critical infrastructure, including health facilities, power lines, and roads, has hindered access to affected areas. EU Commissioner Christos Stylianides stated the funding demonstrates solidarity with affected Indonesian citizens, emphasizing support for the most vulnerable populations during this difficult period. The EU aid, administered through the European Commission's Civil Protection and Humanitarian Aid Operations (ECHO), will support the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC) in delivering relief assistance and protection. The funding is expected to directly benefit 80,000 vulnerable people in the worst-hit North East and West Lombok districts, including family reunification services. Additional contributions from the Netherlands (€500,000) and Spain (€100,000) bring total EU collective support to €1,250,000. The Indonesian Red Cross Society will serve as the beneficiary, channeling funds through the IFRC.

The article describes the European Union’s response to the conflict in South Sudan one year after violence erupted on 15 December 2013, plunging the newly independent country into armed conflict only two and a half years after it gained independence. It argues that the war has severely damaged the country’s prospects and that there is little basis for optimism, despite a year of negotiations mediated by IGAD, the regional body. The warring parties have not reached any meaningful political settlement, and civilians remain trapped in a highly insecure environment that may deteriorate further as the rainy season ends and fears grow of renewed offensives. The conflict has caused immense human suffering. According to the article, tens of thousands have been killed and around two million people displaced. It has also led to serious violations of international humanitarian law and human rights. Although famine among the most vulnerable was avoided in 2014 thanks to international aid, the humanitarian situation remains desperate. The article says that at least 2.5 million people are expected to face severe food shortages in the coming months, making the crisis one of the worst man-made humanitarian emergencies in the world. It also warns that the conflict could destabilize an already fragile region. The EU says it remains committed to supporting international efforts to end the violence and is urging the international community to take tougher measures to pressure South Sudan’s leaders to resolve their disputes peacefully and democratically. The EU frames its policy through its broader Horn of Africa strategy, under which it has worked since South Sudan’s independence in 2011 to help stabilize the country. From the beginning of the crisis, the EU, through its Special Representative for the Horn of Africa and alongside other international actors, has tried to prevent the violence from escalating into a full-scale ethnic civil war. The EU’s main goals have been to keep neighboring states from being drawn into the conflict, end the fighting immediately, and support a political transition. The article says the EU has pursued a comprehensive peace strategy, but that these efforts have so far failed. EU foreign affairs ministers met to reaffirm their commitment to South Sudan and called for stronger international action to press all sides to negotiate in the South Sudanese people’s interest. They urged the parties to stop fighting immediately and reach a political settlement quickly. The article criticizes both sides for undermining the process by failing to honor commitments, excluding others from negotiations, and continuing hostilities on the ground. It stresses that they must respect their promises and abandon planned offensives. Because of the lack of progress, the ministers called for restrictive measures by IGAD and the African Union, in coordination with the UN Security Council. The EU has already imposed an arms embargo and urged other international partners to consider the same step. It also wants measures to ensure the country’s wealth is used for the benefit of the people rather than to stockpile weapons. The EU says it is ready to consider further targeted sanctions against individuals who obstruct peace. It emphasizes that leaders on both sides bear responsibility for the conflict and have the power to end it. The humanitarian situation is described as critical. Nearly two million people have been forced from their homes, including about 470,000 who have fled to neighboring countries. By the end of the year, an estimated 3.8 million people were expected to need humanitarian assistance, and 1.5 million were at immediate risk of food insecurity. The UN has classified South Sudan as a Level 3 emergency, its highest category for humanitarian crises. South Sudan also ranks second in the European Commission’s Global Vulnerability and Crisis Assessment index, behind the Central African Republic. The most urgent needs include food, clean water, medical care, shelter, sanitation, hygiene, protection, and epidemic response. Seasonal flooding and other natural disasters further aggravate the crisis. Humanitarian access remains difficult, with aid workers harassed, assets commandeered, and aid diverted in some areas despite the obligation of all parties to allow free movement of humanitarian personnel and supplies. The crisis also places strain on countries hosting refugees, especially Ethiopia, Uganda, Kenya, and Sudan. In response, the European Commission provided more than €110 million in humanitarian aid in 2014 for the crisis inside South Sudan and another €20 million for refugees in neighboring countries. Overall, the EU and its Member States had provided more than €267 million in humanitarian assistance that year. The article also outlines the EU’s development assistance. In 2011 and 2013, it approved projects worth €85 million and €185 million in agriculture, education, health, and rule of law. As the conflict worsened, the EU adjusted its approach. It supported IGAD’s mediation efforts with €1.1 million from the African Peace Facility to establish peace talks and a monitoring and verification mechanism, and planned to add another €1.1 million for that purpose. It also mobilized an additional €45 million from the European Development Fund, including €30 million for the humanitarian crisis in South Sudan and €15 million for refugees in neighboring states. The EU further reprogrammed its development aid under agreed principles. Since January 2014, it suspended an €80 million State Building Contract that had been intended as budget support, redirected that support toward education and health with partners such as EU Member States, NGOs, and international organizations, and contracted €68 million for related support. It also shifted some rule-of-law programs toward direct support for the population, including increased access to justice and reconciliation efforts, and began helping local authorities across the country improve service delivery and budget implementation. Finally, a €23.5 million crisis-response package under the 2014 Instrument contributing to Stability and Peace was to be implemented in both South Sudan and Sudan.

# Summary: South Sudan and the European Union's Response to Crisis ## Background and Conflict Overview South Sudan descended into armed conflict on December 15, 2013, merely two and a half years after gaining independence, fundamentally altering the prospects for the world's newest nation. As the international community marked the one-year anniversary of this conflict, optimism remained scarce. Despite extensive negotiations under the Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD), the warring parties had failed to reach any meaningful political agreement while civilians endured extreme insecurity with conditions threatening to deteriorate further. ## Humanitarian Catastrophe The conflict has created one of the world's worst humanitarian crises. Tens of thousands have died, approximately two million people have been displaced, and widespread violations of international humanitarian law and human rights have occurred. While international assistance prevented famine in 2014, the humanitarian situation remains dire, with at least 2.5 million people facing severe food shortages in the coming months. This man-made crisis threatens regional stability, particularly as the rainy season ends and warring parties are reportedly preparing major military offensives. ## EU's Strategic Response The European Union, guided by its Horn of Africa Strategy, has been committed to stabilizing South Sudan since its 2011 independence. The EU's primary objectives include preventing neighboring countries from becoming involved in the conflict, ending immediate hostilities, and initiating political transition. Through its Special Representative for the Horn of Africa and in coordination with the international community, the EU has pursued a comprehensive crisis response strategy. ## Diplomatic and Sanctions Measures Frustrated by the failure of previous efforts, EU Foreign Affairs Ministers reaffirmed their commitment to pressing all conflict parties toward peaceful negotiation. They emphasized the essential need for parties to respect their commitments and abandon planned offensives. Recognizing the lack of progress, the EU Ministers called for restrictive measures through IGAD and the African Union in coordination with the UN Security Council. The EU has already imposed an arms embargo and invited international partners to adopt similar measures. Additionally, the EU expressed readiness to implement further targeted sanctions against individuals obstructing peace efforts. ## Humanitarian Assistance The humanitarian situation remains critical, with nearly two million internally displaced persons and approximately 470,000 South Sudanese refugees in neighboring countries. An estimated 3.8 million people require humanitarian assistance, with 1.5 million facing immediate food insecurity risks. The UN designated South Sudan a Level 3 emergency, its most serious classification. Primary humanitarian needs include food, clean water, healthcare, shelter, sanitation, hygiene, and protection against epidemics. The country also faces seasonal flooding and natural disasters. Access challenges persist, as warring parties continue harassing aid workers and diverting humanitarian assistance despite their obligations to allow unhindered access. The humanitarian crisis extends regionally, straining resources in host countries including Ethiopia, Uganda, Kenya, and Sudan. The European Commission allocated over €110 million in 2014 for humanitarian response, with an additional €20 million for refugee assistance. Overall, the EU and its Member States provided more than €267 million in humanitarian aid during 2014. ## Development Assistance Adaptations The EU adopted development projects worth €85 million in 2011 and €185 million in 2013 across agriculture, education, health, and rule of law sectors. However, the conflict necessitated substantial program adjustments. The EU mobilized €1.1 million from the African Peace Facility to support IGAD's mediation efforts and peace talks platforms, with plans to increase this support by another €1.1 million. An additional €45 million from the European Development Fund was allocated: €30 million for humanitarian crisis response and €15 million for refugee assistance. Development program modifications included suspending an €80 million State Building Contract initially intended as budget support, subsequently reprogrammed to address education and health needs through partnerships with Member States, NGOs, and international organizations. The EU contracted €68 million to support humanitarian needs and redirected rule of law programs toward direct population support for justice access and reconciliation processes. Additionally, the EU strengthened local authorities' capacity to deliver services nationwide through budget implementation support. ## Conclusion The EU's response demonstrates comprehensive engagement addressing immediate humanitarian needs, diplomatic pressure for peaceful resolution, and long-term development support adjusted to crisis conditions. The EU remains committed to supporting South Sudan's people while calling for international community cooperation to pressure conflicting parties toward peaceful, democratic solutions.

The article reports on the launch in Rome, on 11 May, of a new FAO partnership with five Nobel Peace Laureates to advance food security, peace, and stability. The alliance, called the FAO–Nobel Peace Laureates for Food Security and Peace Alliance, brings together the Food and Agriculture Organization with Muhammad Yunus, Oscar Arias Sánchez, Tawakkol Karman, Betty Williams, and Kofi Annan. The initiative reflects FAO Director-General José Graziano da Silva’s view that food security can help create stability and that food and agriculture should be treated as pathways to peace, especially as the world works toward the 2030 Development Agenda. The event centered on the idea that hunger, poverty, conflict, and environmental degradation are deeply connected. Each Laureate used the occasion to argue that lasting peace cannot be separated from access to food, livelihoods, and dignity. Muhammad Yunus opened the series of remarks by emphasizing that hunger is a cause close to the Laureates’ hearts, but he rejected the idea that simply distributing free food is a durable answer. Instead, he promoted the microcredit model he pioneered in Bangladesh more than forty years ago, arguing that small loans can give poor people financial independence and the means to secure food for themselves. Yunus described this approach as part of a broader “social business” model that combines charity’s goals with business efficiency. He said such a model could improve the lives of rural communities excluded from the mainstream economy and encourage young people to become entrepreneurs in agriculture rather than leaving for cities in search of jobs. He framed this in terms of “job creators” rather than “job seekers,” and said the alliance could help move the world toward his vision of “three zeros”: zero hunger, malnutrition and poverty; zero unemployment; and zero net carbon emissions. Oscar Arias Sánchez followed by linking peace, conflict, and environmental protection. He warned of a looming conflict between humanity and nature, saying “the earth is complaining, and it is calling for peace.” Arias argued that armed forces are major polluters and that violence takes many forms beyond war. In his view, the absence of open conflict does not mean true peace if people still suffer from hunger, lack of medical care, or other forms of deprivation. He called for greater efforts to protect the environment, resolve conflicts, and use the FAO’s influence and resources to consolidate peace. He also stressed that there can be no sustainable development without peace, and no peace without sustainable development. Tawakkol Karman built on that message by urging action toward the Sustainable Development Goals with both effort and moral commitment. She said the world must pursue a fairer form of globalization in which the benefits are shared by all, rather than a system where the poor bear the negative consequences. For Karman, fighting hunger and poverty is the first step toward sustainable development and a more just world. She argued that conflict is the root of hunger, famine, misery, and poverty, and said that building peace is inseparable from achieving food security. She also stressed that freedom must mean more than freedom from want; it must include political freedom as well. Karman said transitional justice can help communities recover from conflict and move toward peace, and she insisted that by 2030 the world must have lifted the burdens of poverty and hunger through collective commitment and cooperation. Betty Williams spoke next, reflecting on her own experiences as a peace activist in Northern Ireland during the sectarian violence of the early 1970s. She recalled initially wanting to keep her door closed out of fear for her family’s safety, but said her response changed after witnessing the deaths of three children on a Belfast street. That tragedy pushed her into action and helped inspire a wider peace movement led by “ordinary extraordinary people.” Williams also described her later work in places including Africa, Afghanistan, Nicaragua, Argentina, Chile, and even impoverished communities in developed countries such as the United States, where she came to understand hunger more directly. She said the suffering often made her physically ill, but she believed action was necessary because “tears without action are wasted sentiment.” She then recounted her work in Basilicata, in southern Italy, where she opposed plans for nuclear waste disposal and later helped create a foundation that builds inexpensive, ecologically sound housing for refugees. Williams said her deepest commitment remains the protection of children, and she closed by reading from the Universal Declaration of the Rights of the Child, which she vowed to defend for the rest of her life. Kofi Annan contributed by video message. He said that a stable and peaceful environment is the foundation for lasting food security and livelihoods. Like the others, he emphasized the links among food security, peace, and sustainable development. Annan expressed optimism that hunger could be eradicated within a generation if political leaders and political will were mobilized. In the discussion that followed, Yunus returned to the practical question of how to make anti-poverty finance sustainable. He argued that a banking system and supporting legislation are needed to serve poor people directly. In his view, NGO-based microcredit is limited because it depends on scarce external funding, and what is needed instead are self-sustaining financial systems that can lift individuals and communities out of poverty over the long term. Although the alliance’s goals are ambitious, the article presents the first meeting as hopeful and energized. Yunus described himself as a “compulsive optimist” and told young people they have the power to change the world. Williams echoed that optimism, saying everyone must remain hopeful in the struggle for sustainable development, and even suggested opening a bank for the poor in Basilicata. The article concludes that if this first gathering is any indication, the partnership may have a promising future in linking food security with peace.

Angola is participating in the 39th Session of the Governing Council of the International Fund for Agricultural Development (IFAD), which opened on Wednesday at IFAD’s headquarters in Rome. Speaking on Thursday, Angola’s Permanent Representative to IFAD, Ambassador Florêncio de Almeida, said the forum is important because it allows Angola to share its own experience while learning from other countries’ practices, challenges and successes, helping to modernize national agriculture and raise productivity. Addressing the council on behalf of Angola’s Agriculture Minister, the ambassador said the country’s economic crisis, triggered by the sharp fall in oil prices, has led the government to adopt austerity and public spending containment measures. These policies are intended to speed up economic diversification, with agriculture, livestock, fisheries and aquaculture identified as priorities. The aim is to meet domestic food needs, support manufacturing and increase exports. The ambassador also called on IFAD to continue mobilizing funds and seeking alternative financing sources in line with its mandate, so it can attract more co-financing and steadily improve the quality of its projects and programmes. He used the occasion to announce that Angola intends to contribute to IFAD’s 10th replenishment, despite current economic difficulties. Angola previously contributed $1.9 million to the fund. In the country, IFAD-financed initiatives are already under way in the agriculture and fisheries sectors. In agriculture, one major project is MOSAP, a family-farming initiative aimed at market orientation and co-financed by the Angolan government, the World Bank and the Japanese government, with IFAD contributing $8 million. The project is being implemented in the provinces of Malanje, Huambo and Bié. The article also recalls that IFAD was created in 1977 as a UN specialized agency, following the 1974 World Food Conference, to finance agricultural development projects in developing countries, especially to improve food production and address rural poverty.

British Ambassador to Zimbabwe Melanie Robinson yesterday paid a courtesy call on Vice President Constantino Chiwenga in Harare, where they discussed government reforms and the country’s humanitarian challenges. Robinson, who was accompanied by the head of the Department for International Development, Cate Turton, said the United Kingdom wants Zimbabwe to succeed and to see it move toward a “more prosperous democratic and peaceful future.” She said this required vigorous pursuit of both political and economic reforms. The ambassador noted that the government’s reform agenda has already led to new legislation in Parliament, including the Maintenance of Peace and Order Act, the Zimbabwe Development Agency Bill and the Companies and Other Entities Act. She said the Maintenance of Peace and Order Act replaced the Public Order and Security Act as part of efforts to broaden democratic space and regulate public gatherings and demonstrations. Robinson also said Britain has committed £54 million in humanitarian support to Zimbabwe. Of this, £49 million is earmarked for food assistance and £5 million for health support to help prevent a cholera outbreak. She said the two sides discussed the food-insecure population, as well as difficulties affecting health and education, and that the UK wanted to coordinate its assistance with government information on grain stocks. According to Robinson, Chiwenga expressed concern about the situation and arranged for a further meeting in the coming days to share the relevant information. She also reiterated Britain’s wish for Zimbabwe to rejoin the Commonwealth, saying this would be considered once the government’s reform programme is completed and progress is evident.

Seven local and national organizations have asked the U.S. Department of Justice to investigate the death of Jamycheal Mitchell, who was found dead in his cell at Hampton Roads Regional Jail on Aug. 19, 2015. A state investigation concluded that Mitchell died of starvation while waiting to be transferred to Eastern State Hospital for a mental health evaluation. His family filed a $60 million wrongful death lawsuit on May 11. In a letter to DOJ official Steven Rosenbaum, the groups cited a State Office of the Inspector General report that described “systematic failures” leading to Mitchell’s death and warned that similar deaths could happen again if problems are not fixed. According to the UK Prime Minister’s Office, the funding will provide urgent life-saving humanitarian assistance to about 2.5 million Afghans, most of them women and girls. The money comes from the UK’s broader £286 million aid commitment to Afghanistan announced in September. It will be delivered through UN agencies and the International Committee of the Red Cross. The aid is meant to address immediate winter needs, including food, nutrition, shelter and medicine, while also strengthening the UN’s wider humanitarian response. The government said protection from gender-based violence will also be a priority. The announcement comes amid a worsening crisis in Afghanistan following the collapse of the elected government and the Taliban’s takeover in August. The UK said at least 18 million people, around half the population, are now affected. The Taliban has also restricted girls’ education and kept women teachers from returning to work. Syrian government forces and the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) were locked in a tense standoff in northeastern Syria after the deadline passed on a weeklong ceasefire, raising the possibility that fighting could resume. The truce, agreed to on Jan. 18, was already widely viewed as a major setback for the SDF, which had lost much of the leverage it previously held in negotiations with Damascus. In recent weeks, Syrian government troops have advanced into large areas of territory formerly controlled by Kurdish forces in the east and north of the country, including important oil fields and dams. Under the ceasefire deal, the SDF was to accept the full integration of its forces into the Syrian national army, a long-standing demand of the government, and hand over administrative control of much of northeastern Syria. SANA, Syria’s state news agency, reported that the government had given the SDF four days to submit a detailed plan for integrating Hasakah province, the last province still under militia authority. It was unclear whether such a plan had been submitted, and the SDF did not immediately comment on the deadline or the ceasefire’s status. On Saturday night, SANA cited an unnamed government source saying the ceasefire had ended and that officials were considering their next steps. Earlier, Syria’s Foreign Ministry rejected social media reports that the deadline would be extended. A ministry official, Mohammad Taha al-Ahmad, said, “All options remain on the table, alongside calm and dialogue, to enforce the law, preserve Syria’s unity and safeguard the rights of the Syrian people.” The SDF, meanwhile, accused the government of moving troops in violation of the truce, saying Damascus was trying to “undermine de-escalation and steer the situation toward war instead of political solutions.” The confrontation is part of President Ahmad al-Sharaa’s effort to consolidate control over Syria after his rebel forces overthrew Bashar Assad more than a year earlier. Al-Sharaa has tried to bring the country’s many ethnic and religious communities under centralized rule from Damascus, while also promising protection for minorities. This month, he signed a decree affirming Kurdish rights, including a call to restore citizenship to Kurds who had been stripped of it after a 1962 census. The SDF remains the main obstacle to that centralization effort. For years, the Kurdish-led force has governed northeastern Syria as a de facto autonomous region and has resisted full incorporation into the national army, insisting on autonomy and local security control. At the same time, the SDF has been one of the U.S. military’s most important partners in the fight against ISIS, guarding American bases and overseeing prisons and detention camps holding thousands of militants and their families. That relationship appeared to weaken this week. U.S. special envoy Tom Barrack said Washington no longer regarded the Kurdish-led forces as its primary partner against ISIS and believed the Syrian government could now take on that role. The shift reflected growing U.S. confidence in al-Sharaa, who has a close relationship with President Donald Trump. The ceasefire remained fragile throughout the week. Fighting broke out near two prisons in northeastern Syria holding ISIS members, underscoring fears that detainees could escape during any transfer of authority. U.S. Central Command said Wednesday that American forces had already moved 150 ISIS fighters from a detention center in northeastern Syria to a “secure location” in Iraq, and that as many as 7,000 detainees could eventually be transferred to Iraqi facilities. As part of the deal, the SDF agreed to hand over control of Raqqa and Deir el-Zour to the government. But the United Nations warned that Kurdish-held cities faced a worsening humanitarian crisis. In Kobani, a Kurdish stronghold, roads were closed and electricity, water, and internet service were disrupted during bitter winter weather. The U.N. said food, medicine, and other essentials were increasingly scarce, and it was working to assess needs and improve access.

A report from Zakho describes the desperate situation of Yazidi refugees in northern Kurdistan, where many have fled Islamic State attacks and now face winter cold, hunger, and uncertainty. He lives among Yazidis sheltered by Our Lady Parish in Khanik, a mostly Christian village near the border with Turkey and Syria. Only his “uncle,” Bashar, speaks for him. Hassan is believed to be the only surviving member of his immediate family. His parents, siblings, and other relatives disappeared after ISIS advanced on their village of Tal Afar, where Yazidis had lived peacefully alongside Sunni Muslims. Hassan fled at night as the militants approached, but lost contact with his family, including three unmarried women. Bashar says they were likely seized, raped, or killed. The article emphasizes that ISIS’s campaign against Yazidis is especially brutal. Unlike Christians, who may be spared if they convert or pay the jizya tax, Yazidis are viewed by ISIS as pagans to be exterminated. One escaped woman said she was raped by 20 ISIS men in a single day. Some women, the report says, have killed themselves to avoid such abuse. Bashar recounts how his own family fled to Mount Sinjar in early August when ISIS advanced. They stayed there for five days, then tried to return after hearing that the militants had withdrawn. The article quotes Chaldean Patriarch Louis Sako, who says Christians and especially Yazidis are suffering what amounts to “physical and cultural genocide.” It also notes that Pope Francis had recently met Tahsin Said Ali Beg, the Yazidi supreme spiritual leader. A United Nations-led operation is underway to remove nearly a million barrels of crude oil from the FSO Safer, a decaying supertanker moored about five miles off Yemen’s coast in the Red Sea. The 47-year-old vessel has been abandoned since 2015, when Yemen’s civil war began, and for years the UN has warned that it could break apart, catch fire, or leak its highly flammable cargo, creating one of the worst environmental disasters in decades. The ship is being treated as a “ticking time bomb” because of its age, deteriorating condition, and the enormous volume of oil it holds. Experts are carefully pumping the crude off the tanker in an effort to prevent the vessel from collapsing, the oil exploding, or a major spill occurring during the transfer. The UN says the operation is complex and dangerous, but necessary to avert a catastrophe in the strategically important Red Sea. According to UN Resident and Humanitarian Coordinator for Yemen David Gressly, the overall mission is expected to cost about USD 141 million and is being carried out with the help of SMIT, a dredging and offshore contractor that also helped remove the Ever Given container ship after it blocked the Suez Canal in 2021. The effort is financed by 23 UN member states, along with USD 16 million from private donors. Among those private contributors is Yemen’s largest private company, HSA Group, which donated USD 1.2 million in August 2022. Gressly also said the UN took part in a crowdfunding campaign that helped build the fund over the course of a year. The replacement tanker, the Nautica, is receiving the oil. The transfer is proceeding at a rate of roughly 4,000 to 5,000 barrels per hour, and more than 120,000 barrels had already been moved at the time of reporting. The full transfer is expected to take about 19 days. Once the Safer is emptied, it still must be cleaned so that no oil residue remains, and then a giant buoy will be attached to the replacement vessel while decisions are made about the oil’s final disposition. The oil aboard the Safer is estimated to be worth around USD 80 million, but its ownership remains politically and legally disputed. That dispute is tied to Yemen’s broader civil war. The tanker sits in waters controlled by the Houthi rebels, while the internationally recognized Yemeni government rejects Houthi control. Experts say the oil technically belongs to the Yemeni state company Safer Exploration & Production Operations Company (SEPOC), though other energy entities may have interests as well. Discussions are ongoing to determine who can claim or sell the oil once it is removed. The vessel’s cargo is enormous: nearly one million barrels, enough to power about 83,333 cars or 50,000 U.S. homes for a year. If released into the sea, the spill could rank as the fifth-largest tanker spill in history, according to a UN website, and cleanup costs have been estimated at USD 20 billion. The Safer contains about four times as much oil as was spilled in the Exxon Valdez disaster in Alaska in 1989, which polluted 1,300 miles of coastline. The Red Sea makes the operation especially urgent. It is a major global trade route, and at its southern end lies the Bab el-Mandeb strait, through which about 9 percent of all seaborne-traded petroleum passes. At the northern end is the Suez Canal, a critical link between Africa and Asia. Much of the oil and natural gas exported from the Persian Gulf that reaches global markets passes through this corridor. The sea is also ecologically and economically important, with a rich marine ecosystem, diving tourism, coastal resorts, and major Saudi development projects along its eastern shore. Before the oil transfer could begin, the first task was to stabilize and secure the Safer so it would not collapse. Gressly said that step has already been completed over recent weeks. Crews also had to remove gases from each of the tanker’s 13 compartments to reduce the risk of explosion. Pumping systems were rebuilt, some lighting was repaired, and floating booms were placed around the vessel to contain any leaks. Even after the oil is removed, the UN warns that the ship will still pose a danger because of sticky residue left inside its tanks and because the weakened hull remains vulnerable to collapse. For that reason, the UN says an additional USD 22 million is urgently needed to finish the job. The consequences of a spill would be severe. Yemeni ports that are essential for food and fuel imports could be shut down, affecting as many as 17 million people amid an already dire humanitarian crisis caused by war and a Saudi-led military campaign. Oil could spread toward the African coast, damage fish stocks for up to 25 years, and threaten as many as 200,000 jobs. A Stanford University study cited by CNN said the health effects could be “catastrophic” in Yemen and neighboring countries, especially Yemen, Saudi Arabia, and Eritrea. The study found that air pollution from a spill of this size could raise hospitalization risk for cardiovascular or respiratory disease by 530 percent among those directly exposed, while also contributing to other health problems, including psychiatric and neurological effects. Stanford professor David Rehkopf said the region’s lack of water and food means such a spill could become one of the most disastrous in history in terms of human impact. The study estimated that up to 10 million people could struggle to obtain clean water and 8 million could face threats to food access, while Yemen’s fisheries in the Red Sea could be almost completely wiped out. Despite the technical progress, the Safer remains a political flashpoint in Yemen. Many Yemenis have welcomed the removal effort, viewing the tanker as a long-standing threat hanging over them. But the question of who owns the oil, and what should happen to it after offloading, is still unresolved. The UN hopes the time gained by transferring the oil will allow political and legal discussions to continue before any sale is considered.

Eight Israeli soldiers were killed in Lebanon on Wednesday, the first Israeli fatalities in the ground campaign against Hezbollah, underscoring how costly and potentially expansive the offensive could become. The Israel Defense Forces said the soldiers died in three separate incidents and that seven others were seriously wounded, but it provided no further details. The announcement came only hours after the military said its troops were engaged in “close-range” firefights inside Lebanese territory. The deaths immediately raised questions about how far Israel intends to push its operation and how much territory it is prepared to clear and hold. Israeli officials have described the ground activity so far as “limited, localized and targeted” raids just a few miles inside Lebanon near the border. Yet the scale of the military buildup in northern Israel suggests planning for something larger than the public description implies. Tanks and thousands of troops have been massed in the area, and analysts say the level of resistance Israeli forces encounter in the coming days and weeks could determine the depth and duration of the offensive. For Israel, the deaths also recalled the 2006 Lebanon war, when the first tank to cross the border struck a roadside bomb and four soldiers were killed. That conflict remains a cautionary memory for Israeli leaders and the public alike, especially because it began with expectations of a limited campaign and ended with a prolonged and costly war. Yaakov Amidror, a former major general and Israeli national security adviser, said the extent of the current invasion is still unclear and will depend on what is achieved on the ground. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has kept his plans vague, but he has said Israel will continue striking Hezbollah with “full force” until more than 60,000 residents displaced from Israel’s northern border can return home. Hezbollah began firing rockets into northern Israel on Oct. 8, a day after the Hamas-led assault in southern Israel that killed about 1,200 people and saw more than 250 taken hostage. Since then, Israel has broadened its campaign against Iran-backed groups across the region, aiming to restore deterrence, alter regional dynamics, and prevent further attacks. Netanyahu now faces competing pressures. Domestically, there are calls for decisive action against Hezbollah. At the same time, there are concerns that Israeli troops could become bogged down in guerrilla-style fighting and fail to deliver the larger strategic results the government seeks. Far-right voices in the government have pushed for a more permanent “buffer zone” inside Lebanese territory. The United States and other allies, meanwhile, have tried to discourage Israel from escalating into a full-scale war because of the risk of regional spillover and worsening humanitarian consequences. Lebanon has already suffered heavily from the air campaign. The Israeli military has carried out more than 3,600 airstrikes there, and Lebanese Prime Minister Najib Mikati said as many as 1 million people have been displaced. Israeli officials say the main goal of the ground operation is to stop Hezbollah from mounting an Oct. 7-style attack in northern Israel, something the group has threatened for years. It is not clear whether Hezbollah had an imminent attack planned, but Israeli intelligence believes the group spent years building border infrastructure, including attack tunnels. According to an Israeli military official, Hezbollah had between 2,000 and 3,000 elite Radwan Force fighters operating roughly two miles from the border, with another 6,000 to 8,000 militants stationed about six miles away. The official said it would take “a few weeks” to destroy the infrastructure in the area. The military also said it had already dismantled some attack tunnels and materiel. On Tuesday, it said Israeli commandos had conducted more than 70 raids in Lebanon in recent months, sometimes remaining undetected for several nights. The current ground push, however, is a new phase and could inflict greater damage on Hezbollah, the official said. Still, senior former Israeli security figures warned that the operation could become bogged down in southern Lebanon, where Hezbollah fighters know the terrain and have prepared booby traps and hiding places. Miri Eisin, a former senior intelligence officer, said the military may ultimately shift to night operations, where it would have an advantage. She also noted that the Lebanese operation has more limited and measurable objectives than the war in Gaza, where Israel has sought to destroy Hamas as both a governing authority and a military force. The Israeli military has publicly denied plans to advance on Beirut or deep into southern Lebanon. Spokesman Daniel Hagari said Tuesday, “We’re not going to Beirut. We’re not going to the cities in southern Lebanon.” But the military has also ordered residents of 30 villages in southern Lebanon to move farther north, posting instructions on X that told people to go above the Awwali River, more than 30 miles from the border line. On Wednesday, the IDF announced that infantry and armored units were joining the fight, a sign that the operation may be broadening. Israel has long insisted that Hezbollah should pull back north of the Litani River, about 18 miles from the border, in line with the U.N.-backed arrangement that ended the 2006 war. Yet the military’s insistence that it does not want a full invasion has not stopped discussion of a larger occupation or buffer zone. Michael Horowitz of Le Beck risk consultancy said Israel does not want to be trapped in a long campaign that could ultimately strengthen Hezbollah, but warned that such outcomes are hard to avoid once fighting begins. History offers a sobering precedent. Israel invaded Lebanon in 1978 and initially intended to occupy only a narrow strip of land, but the mission expanded to the Litani River and Israeli forces did not leave for 22 years. Israel later invaded again in 1982, reaching Beirut before withdrawing in 1985 to a security zone along the border that lasted until 2000. The idea of a buffer zone is now being promoted by far-right Israeli politicians. Diaspora Affairs Minister Amichai Chikli called for a “renewed buffer zone, free of enemy population,” and posted maps depicting a redefined border inside Lebanese territory. National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir has also threatened to leave the government if Netanyahu agrees to a cease-fire in Lebanon. Some experts say Israel may be able to enforce a border zone without formally occupying it, through a strict policy of targeting anyone who enters. Ephraim Sneh, a former defense minister and former commander in the southern Lebanon security zone, said the ideal solution would be an effective Lebanese or international force preventing Hezbollah from rebuilding. But others warned that without a diplomatic track, military gains could prove temporary. Michael Horowitz said that eventually a political settlement would be necessary if Israel wants to avoid becoming stuck in Lebanon.

The ground campaign was officially announced early Tuesday, with stated objectives focused on destroying Hezbollah infrastructure near the border. ## Implications for the Campaign Military experts suggest that if Israeli casualty rates continue at the current pace, they could significantly influence the depth and scope of the offensive. Samaritan’s Purse is responding to catastrophic flooding in Pakistan by delivering emergency food, drinking water, and shelter materials through a local partner organization. The floods, driven by unusually heavy monsoon rains, have killed more than 1,100 people, injured at least 3,500, and inundated millions of acres of land, destroying homes, roads, and livestock. The disaster is among the worst in Pakistan’s recent history, with about 33 million people estimated to have been affected and at least 6.4 million in urgent need of assistance. Jason Martens, a Samaritan’s Purse project manager, said millions are suffering from the “worst flooding in decades,” and emphasized that the organization is able to respond quickly despite damaged infrastructure. He said the goal is to provide food, shelter, and clean water to thousands of families and offer hope amid despair. A local partner described the hardship facing many of the affected people, noting that many work in brickyard factories or on farms and now cannot obtain food, water, or other necessities because of the rain and flooding.

# Summary Pakistan faces its worst flooding in decades, with overwhelming monsoon rains killing over 1,100 people, injuring at least 3,500, and flooding millions of acres. Approximately 33 million people have been affected, with 6.4 million requiring assistance. The disaster has destroyed homes, roads, and livestock while damaging critical infrastructure. Samaritan's Purse and its local partner organization are responding to the crisis by distributing emergency relief supplies including food rations, drinking water, and shelter materials to thousands of affected families. According to reports, many victims are workers from brickyard factories and farms who currently lack access to food, water, and basic necessities due to the flooding and heavy rainfall. Project manager Jason Martens emphasized the organization's commitment to providing hope and assistance during this humanitarian emergency. The relief efforts aim to support survivors in despair as they face the catastrophic aftermath of these unprecedented floods.

The UN Support Mission in Libya (UNSMIL) strongly condemned a terrorist attack on a hotel in Tobruk where the country’s House of Representatives was meeting. According to media reports, a suicide bomber drove a car packed with explosives into the site on Tuesday, wounding at least 11 people. The blast was apparently the largest attack on the Libyan parliament since it relocated to Tobruk near the Egyptian border to avoid the intense violence elsewhere in the country. UNSMIL said the “despicable act” would only strengthen Libyans committed to a political solution and to restoring stability and security. The attack came shortly after the mission warned that further violence could push Libya into “all-out war.” The bombing is the latest in a series of violent incidents since Libya’s civil war began in 2011 and led to the ouster of Muammar Gaddafi. It follows militant attacks on an oil facility in Sidra that set storage tanks ablaze and killed at least 20 soldiers, as well as government air strikes on militant positions in Misrata. Elsewhere, fighting in the Nafusa mountains has killed 170 people and displaced at least 120,000, creating shortages of food and medicine. In Benghazi, 450 people have been killed since October, and about 90,000 people have been displaced. UNSMIL urged all sides to stop fighting and pursue dialogue.

# Summary The United Nations Support Mission in Libya (UNSMIL) has condemned a terrorist bombing at a Tobruk hotel housing the country's Parliament, which wounded at least 11 people. This marks the most significant attack against Libya's legislature since it relocated to the eastern city to escape widespread violence. The attack represents the latest escalation in Libya's ongoing civil war, which began in 2011 following Muammar Gaddafi's ouster. Recent violence includes a militant attack on an oil installation in Sidra that killed 20 soldiers and destroyed storage tanks, government airstrikes in Misrata, and fighting in the Nafusa mountains that claimed 170 lives. The conflict has created a severe humanitarian crisis, displacing approximately 120,000 people and causing critical shortages of food and medical supplies. In Benghazi, 450 people have been killed since October, with 90,000 residents displaced and facing medical care shortages. UNSMIL warned that further violence risks triggering "all-out war" and urged all Libyans to abandon violence and pursue political resolution through dialogue rather than continued armed conflict.

The federal government has pledged $10.8 million to extend a program that helps the Canadian Red Cross rapidly deliver emergency supplies overseas. International Development Minister Christian Paradis announced the funding in Vancouver, two years after Ottawa and the Red Cross agreed to work more closely on disaster response. The Enhanced Emergency Disaster Assistance Fund, created in 2012, has already been used for 14 emergencies. Paradis said the program is continuing because it has worked and because Canada should not ignore crises abroad. The Red Cross manages the fund and distributes Canada’s relief stockpile, which is stored in Mississauga and Dubai so supplies can reach crises within 48 hours. Secretary general Conrad Sauve said the fund is especially important for disasters that receive little media attention and attract fewer donations. He cited current Red Cross work in Ghana, Kenya and Ethiopia. The fund supplements Ottawa’s separate policy of matching Red Cross donations for international emergencies.

# Summary The Canadian federal government has pledged $10.8 million to continue the Enhanced Emergency Disaster Assistance Fund, which enables the Canadian Red Cross to rapidly distribute emergency supplies internationally. International Development Minister Christian Paradis announced the funding in Vancouver, two years after the government and Red Cross established a closer partnership. Since 2012, the fund has responded to 14 emergencies. The Red Cross manages the program and maintains relief supply stockpiles in Mississauga, Ontario, and Dubai to ensure 48-hour response capabilities. According to Red Cross CEO Conrad Sauve, the fund specifically addresses disasters that receive limited international attention and charitable donations, such as cholera outbreaks, droughts, and refugee crises in Africa. This initiative supplements the government's existing practice of matching Canadian donations to international Red Cross relief efforts at a three-to-one ratio.

The Chicago Police Department is investigating allegations that an unspecified number of officers engaged in improper sexual relations with newly arrived migrants, according to officials. CPD said the matter is being reviewed by its Bureau of Internal Affairs and the Civilian Office of Police Accountability (COPA). It is not yet clear how many officers are involved or whether any disciplinary action has been taken. The allegations were first reported by the Chicago Sun-Times. COPA later confirmed it had learned of a sexual misconduct allegation involving CPD members assigned to the 10th District and a migrant temporarily housed at the police station. COPA said investigators are still determining whether the claims are substantiated, but emphasized that allegations of this kind are being treated as a top priority. The case comes amid Chicago’s ongoing struggle to house thousands of migrants who have arrived from the southern border after being bused to the city from Texas. Over the past several months, hundreds of migrants have been staying in city buildings, including police stations, while officials search for longer-term housing. At one point, more than 70 migrant families were sleeping at the city’s 12th District police station. Mayor Brandon Johnson’s office said the city is aware of the investigation and is monitoring it closely, but declined to comment further because it remains active. The city said it takes the allegations, and the care of both residents and new arrivals, seriously. Advocates and police leaders reacted sharply. Karina Ayala-Bermejo, head of the nonprofit Instituto del Progreso Latino, said housing migrants and asylum seekers in police stations was “never a long-term solution” and urged officials to accelerate resettlement efforts. She said these families need “stability, safety, dignity and respect,” especially because many have experienced trauma and persecution. John J. Catanzara Jr., president of the Chicago Fraternal Order of Police, dismissed the allegations as baseless and said there was “no validity” to the complaints. He argued the migrant situation has turned police stations into “playgrounds” and said the real solution is to move migrants into proper shelters where their needs can be addressed. The city has spent nearly a year trying to find permanent housing for migrants, many of whom traveled thousands of miles from countries across Central and South America and Mexico. Efforts to place migrants in community colleges and high schools have faced strong neighborhood opposition. Former Mayor Lori Lightfoot also struggled with the influx and declared an emergency before leaving office, calling the situation a “national humanitarian crisis.”

A report by the Center for International Policy says that Saudi-linked lobbying and campaign money helped shape opposition in the U.S. Senate to ending American military support for the Saudi-led war in Yemen. The report, *The Saudi Lobby: How the Kingdom Wins in Washington*, examined major U.S. lobbying firms registered under the Foreign Agents Registration Act as working for the Saudi government and compared their activities with campaign contributions to members of Congress. The report came out before a Senate vote on Wednesday in which lawmakers voted 63-37 to advance S.J.R. 54, a measure that would require President Trump to withdraw U.S. troops in or affecting Yemen. The final vote was set for the following week. Although the measure advanced, 37 Republican senators voted against it. According to the CIP report, at least five of those 37—Tim Scott of South Carolina, John Boozman of Arkansas, Roy Blunt of Missouri, Richard Burr of North Carolina, and Mike Crapo of Idaho—had received campaign contributions from lobbying firms representing Saudi interests in 2016 and 2017. The report says some donations arrived on the same day the senators were contacted by Saudi lobbyists. Blunt received the most among them, with $19,200 in 2017. The report also shows that Saudi-linked political contributions were not limited to Republicans. It says the donations were bipartisan, and that Hillary Clinton’s failed presidential campaign received the largest amount of money from Saudi-connected firms during the 2016–2017 period. Among Democratic senators, Bill Nelson of Florida, Tim Kaine of Virginia, and Heidi Heitkamp of North Dakota each received more than $20,000 from lobbying firms representing Saudi interests. The Podesta Group, one of the Saudi government’s top lobbying firms in the United States, is tied to John Podesta, Clinton’s former campaign chair. The findings renewed scrutiny of the Saudi lobbying network, which had already drawn criticism the previous year. Some of the same firms were accused of exploiting U.S. military veterans by paying for luxurious trips to Washington, including stays at the Trump International Hotel, in an effort to use veterans to oppose the Justice Against Sponsors of Terrorism Act, or JASTA. That law allows Americans to sue Saudi Arabia and other countries linked to terrorist attacks on U.S. soil that caused American deaths. The article says some senators may have voted against advancing the Yemen resolution not only because of Saudi influence, but also to align themselves with President Trump. Trump strongly opposed the bill and threatened to veto it. Reports said his administration sent Defense Secretary James Mattis and Secretary of State Mike Pompeo to Capitol Hill to lobby senators against allowing the measure to reach the floor. Still, the Senate’s decision to move the bill forward was widely seen as a rebuke of Trump’s handling of Saudi Arabia, especially after the October killing of journalist and U.S. resident Jamal Khashoggi. Even senators usually friendly to Saudi interests, such as Lindsey Graham of South Carolina, supported advancing the bill because of the administration’s response to Khashoggi’s death. The article emphasizes that, beyond the Khashoggi controversy, the humanitarian catastrophe in Yemen itself is reason enough to oppose U.S. support for the war. Since 2015, the conflict has killed an estimated 50,000 people, driven a famine threatening more than two-thirds of the population, and helped fuel the world’s worst cholera outbreak. The Saudi-led blockade of food, medicine, and other essentials has worsened the crisis.
