These senators included Tim Scott (R-SC), John Boozman (R-AR), Roy Blunt (R-MO), Richard Burr (R-NC), and Mike Crapo (R-ID). Senator Blunt received the most funding, taking in $19,200 in 2017. Notably, some senators received campaign contributions on the same day they were contacted by Saudi lobbyists. The report examined top U.S. lobbying firms registered as foreign agents under the Foreign Agents Registration Act (FARA), which were paid by the Saudi government to represent its interests. Importantly, Saudi-linked campaign contributions were bipartisan, with Hillary Clinton's failed presidential campaign receiving the greatest contributions. Democratic senators Bill Nelson (D-FL), Tim Kaine (D-VA), and Heidi Heitkamp (D-ND) each received over $20,000 from Saudi-interest lobbying firms. The Podesta Group, linked to Clinton's former campaign chair John Podesta, was identified as one of the top Saudi lobbying firms. Beyond financial contributions, the Trump administration actively lobbied against the bill, with Secretary of Defense James Mattis and Secretary of State Mike Pompeo visiting Capitol Hill to persuade senators to oppose it. Trump himself threatened to veto any measure that passed. The Senate's passage of the bill represented a sharp rebuke of Trump's handling of recent Saudi Arabia controversies, particularly the murder of Saudi journalist and U.S. resident Jamal Khashoggi in October. Some senators who typically support Saudi Arabia, including Lindsey Graham (R-SC), voted to advance the bill specifically in response to this incident. However, the humanitarian crisis in Yemen provides substantial justification for ending U.S. support independent of recent controversies. Since the war began in 2015, an estimated 50,000 people have been killed, and over two-thirds of the population faces famine threats. The Saudi-led coalition's years-long blockade has prevented food, medicine, and essential goods from entering the country, exacerbating the world's worst cholera outbreak. The article concludes by suggesting that for some senators, Saudi campaign funding appears to have been prioritized over preventing the deaths of millions of innocent Yemenis. The final vote on S.J.R. 54 is scheduled for the following week, with the outcome uncertain given the administration's strong opposition and the apparent influence of Saudi lobbying efforts on certain lawmakers.

The UN Security Council has unanimously approved a resolution aimed at addressing the worsening humanitarian crisis in Aleppo, where thousands of civilians are believed to remain trapped in the eastern districts. The measure requests the United Nations and other relevant institutions to carry out “adequate, neutral monitoring and direct observation” of evacuations from those areas and calls for additional UN staff to be deployed as needed to monitor and report on the process. The Council also demanded that all parties to the conflict provide monitors with safe, immediate and unimpeded access. It said urgent humanitarian evacuations and assistance are needed for many residents of Aleppo and insisted that aid agencies and their partners be allowed to reach civilians through the most direct routes so that basic needs, including medical care, can be met. The resolution further calls on all sides to respect and protect medical and humanitarian workers, their vehicles and equipment, as well as hospitals and other medical facilities across Syria. The Secretary-General was asked to take urgent steps, including making security arrangements in consultation with interested parties, so that the UN and other institutions can observe the well-being of civilians. He must report back to the Security Council within five days. This decision followed two recent failed attempts by the Council to act on Syria. On October 8, Russia vetoed a resolution that would have demanded an end to military flights over Aleppo. On December 5, a proposed seven-day ceasefire in the city failed after negative votes from China and Russia. Overall, Russia has vetoed six Syria-related texts, while China has vetoed five of those six. Top UN officials welcomed the resolution. Stephen O’Brien, the UN Emergency Relief Coordinator and head of OCHA, said the challenge now is to turn the words into action and noted that the UN stands ready to expand its presence across Aleppo if the parties comply. UN Special Envoy Staffan de Mistura said the vote could mark the beginning of renewed unity in the Security Council and urged further steps. Meanwhile, the World Food Programme has expanded operations in Aleppo, distributing hot meals, bread and rations to more than 20,000 displaced people each day and mobilizing supplies for up to 150,000. Across Syria, WFP supports more than four million people, while nearly one million remain in besieged areas it cannot regularly reach. OCHA says 13.5 million Syrians need humanitarian aid, including 4.9 million trapped in besieged or hard-to-reach areas.

# UN Security Council Approves Monitors for Aleppo Evacuation The United Nations Security Council has unanimously adopted a resolution to address the humanitarian crisis in Aleppo, Syria, where thousands of civilians remain trapped. The measure requests the UN and other relevant institutions to conduct neutral monitoring and direct observation of evacuations from eastern districts of the war-torn city. The Council emphasized the urgent need for humanitarian evacuations and assistance for large numbers of Aleppo inhabitants, calling for protection of medical and humanitarian personnel, their equipment, and medical facilities throughout the country. This decision follows two failed attempts by the Security Council to address Syria's crisis. In October, Russia vetoed a resolution calling for an end to military flights over Aleppo, and in December, a measure proposing a seven-day ceasefire failed after negative votes from China and Russia. Russia has now vetoed six texts on the Syrian conflict, while China has vetoed five. UN officials have welcomed the resolution's adoption. Stephen O'Brien, the UN's Emergency Relief Coordinator, stated: "Our task now is to turn these words into meaningful action," while cautioning that implementation depends on parties honoring the resolution. UN Special Envoy Staffan de Mistura expressed hope that the decision signals restored unity in the Security Council. The World Food Programme has intensified operations in Aleppo, providing meals and rations to over 20,000 displaced people daily and mobilizing stocks to support up to 150,000 people. A study highlighted by the New York Times followed season eight contestants of *The Biggest Loser* for six years after the show ended. Researchers from the National Institutes of Health found that 13 of the 14 contestants regained much or all of the weight they had lost. They believe rapid weight loss slowed the contestants’ metabolism, and that it never fully returned to normal, making long-term maintenance difficult. Gundersen Health System dietitian Marisa Pruitt said the body responds to famine by increasing fat storage and hunger signals. Dietitians say weight loss should be viewed as a lifelong commitment, not a short-term fix.

# Study: The Biggest Loser Contestants Regain Weight Researchers from the National Institutes of Health followed 14 contestants from season eight of The Biggest Loser for six years. Results showed that 13 of the 14 participants regained most or all of their lost weight. Scientists attribute this to metabolic slowdown during rapid weight loss, which never normalized afterward. The body's survival mechanisms make fat storage easier and increase hunger signals during extreme weight loss. Dietitians recommend treating weight loss as a lifelong lifestyle approach rather than a short-term program focused on quick results.

RCMP traffic investigators say a wrong-way driver caused a multi-vehicle crash in the Massey Tunnel area on Highway 99 in Delta on Sunday, sending three people to hospital. Police say a 26-year-old Vancouver man driving a southbound Volkswagen Golf collided head-on with a Toyota RAV4 travelling northbound just south of the Highway 17 overpass. The Golf driver suffered life-threatening injuries. In the Toyota, a 19-year-old passenger was seriously injured and the 48-year-old driver had unknown injuries; both were taken to hospital. A Honda Pilot was also involved, and its driver and passenger were treated at the scene for minor injuries. No names were released. RCMP said investigators are still trying to determine how the Golf ended up going the wrong way. The northbound lane of Highway 99 was closed for several hours during the investigation, and police are asking witnesses to contact Deas Island Traffic Services.

# Summary A multi-vehicle collision occurred Sunday in the Massey Tunnel on Highway 99 in Delta, British Columbia, when a 26-year-old Vancouver man drove his Volkswagen Golf southbound in the northbound lane. His vehicle collided head-on with a Toyota RAV4, resulting in life-threatening injuries for the Golf driver and serious injuries for the RAV4's 19-year-old passenger. The RAV4's 48-year-old driver sustained unknown injuries. A third vehicle, a Honda Pilot, was also involved, with its occupants suffering minor injuries. Three people were hospitalized. Police are investigating how the driver ended up traveling in the wrong direction. The northbound lane remained closed for several hours during the investigation. The RCMP is seeking witness accounts from anyone who observed the crash.

The announcement followed the Saudi-led coalition’s decision to halt its offensive on the key port city of Hodeidah. Facing growing international pressure to end a war that has killed over 10,000 people, the Houthis said they were ready for a broader ceasefire if the coalition seeks peace.

Scientists in Russia have revived a microscopic Arctic rotifer that had been frozen in Siberian permafrost for about 24,000 years, and the tiny animal has since reproduced. The creature was recovered from subsurface sediments in Yakutia, northeastern Siberia, more than 11 feet below the surface of a frozen riverbed near the Alazeya River. Researchers say the sediments froze rapidly after forming and never thawed, creating conditions that preserved the organism in a state of suspended animation. The rotifer, a bdelloid species nicknamed a “wheel animal,” is less than a millimeter long but has a surprisingly complex body, including a gut and a brain. After being thawed in the lab, it resumed normal activity and reproduced through parthenogenesis, a clonal form of reproduction in which eggs develop without fertilization. Scientists say the animal’s survival for millennia is the strongest evidence yet that a multicellular organism can remain viable in cryptobiosis, a near-total shutdown of metabolism, for tens of thousands of years. The study, published in the journal Current Biology, was led by researchers from Russia’s Institute of Physicochemical and Biological Problems in Soil Science and the Soil Cryology Lab, which specializes in extracting ancient microorganisms from permafrost. The team has previously revived single-celled microbes, a 30,000-year-old nematode worm, and ancient mosses and plants from Siberian ice. In this case, they thawed dozens of rotifers in the laboratory and found that the animals could survive slow freezing and the formation of ice crystals, suggesting they possess a protective system that shields cells and organs from damage at extremely low temperatures. The discovery has broader implications beyond the rotifer itself. Scientists say it could help improve cryopreservation methods for animal cells, tissues, and organs, especially for mammals, where long-term freezing remains difficult. Dr. Stas Malavin, a co-author of the study, said the finding supports the idea that multicellular organisms can be frozen and later return to life, a concept long imagined by science fiction writers. He added that understanding the mechanism behind this survival may also help researchers learn how to prolong life. The article notes that there are already more than 350 people cryogenically frozen in hopes of future revival, with thousands more signed up at facilities in the United States and Russia. While bringing mammals back from the dead is not currently possible, the rotifer’s revival is being seen as an important step forward because it moves from single-celled life to an organism with a gut and brain, however tiny. Researchers say the species has been asexual for about 80 million years and is remarkably resilient, able to survive drying, freezing, starvation, and low oxygen. They are continuing to search Siberian permafrost for other long-preserved organisms and to learn what biological traits allow such extreme survival. The article also mentions that another Russian-South Korean project is aiming to revive a 42,000-year-old foal, with hopes of eventually contributing to efforts to bring back extinct animals such as the woolly mammoth.

# Ancient Rotifer Revived After 24,000 Years in Siberian Permafrost Scientists in Russia have successfully revived a microscopic water animal that spent 24,000 years frozen in Siberian permafrost, marking a significant breakthrough in cryobiology. The creature, an Arctic rotifer measuring less than one millimeter in length, was extracted from deep within frozen soil in a state of "suspended animation" and has even reproduced since being thawed. The rotifer, belonging to a group called Bdelloids, represents the most complex organism yet to be revived from ancient ice. Despite its microscopic size, it possesses a functional gut and brain, making this discovery far more significant than previous revivals of single-celled organisms. Scientists from Russia's Institute of Physicochemical and Biological Problems in Soil Science, led by Dr. Stas Malavin, published their findings in the journal Current Biology. The specimens were collected from the Alazeya River in Yakutia, northeastern Siberia, at depths exceeding 11 feet below the surface. This region has yielded numerous naturally mummified prehistoric creatures, including woolly mammoths, woolly rhinos, and ancient bison. The frozen sediment layers in this area have remained continuously frozen since their formation, providing ideal preservation conditions. Rotifers are particularly remarkable organisms. They are entirely female and have reproduced asexually through parthenogenesis—a clonal process requiring no fertilization—for approximately 80 million years. These creatures are renowned for their extraordinary resilience, capable of surviving drying, freezing, starvation, and oxygen deprivation. However, the discovery that they can persist for tens of thousands of years in cryptobiosis—a state of nearly arrested metabolism—represents unprecedented evidence of multicellular animal survival. Laboratory experiments revealed that the revived rotifers could withstand ice crystal formation during slow freezing, suggesting they possess biological mechanisms that shield cells and organs from damage at extremely low temperatures. Researchers froze and thawed dozens of specimens to confirm this capability. This breakthrough carries profound implications for cryobiology and biotechnology. Over 350 people are currently cryogenically preserved, with thousands more enrolled in programs at facilities in the United States and Russia, awaiting potential future resurrection. The research offers hope for understanding cellular preservation mechanisms that could extend life and preserve organs and tissues for medical purposes. However, Dr. Malavin acknowledges significant challenges ahead. While this represents a major step forward in understanding cryo-preservation, resurrecting more complex organisms, particularly mammals, remains impossible with current technology. The biological mechanisms enabling such long-term survival require further investigation. The discovery has inspired related projects, including a Russian-South Korean initiative to resurrect an extinct horse breed using blood extracted from a 42,000-year-old foal discovered in 2018. This "Jurassic Park"-style effort could eventually enable the resurrection of the woolly mammoth. Researchers continue exploring Siberian permafrost to identify other organisms capable of long-term cryo-preservation, seeking to understand the evolutionary and biological foundations of this remarkable phenomenon that could revolutionize medicine and paleontology.

Experts quoted by Armenpress said that recent moves by some countries to reconsider arms sales to Turkey are unlikely to stop President Recep Tayyip Erdogan from continuing the military offensive in northern Syria. Turkish studies expert Hayk Gabrielyan argued that an arms embargo by countries such as France and Germany would have little practical effect because Turkey has significantly developed its own military industry under Erdogan. He added that whenever tensions open up between Turkey and the West, Russia tends to fill the resulting vacuum, making sanctions more effective than weapons restrictions. In his view, Turkey is most vulnerable economically, so financial pressure would matter most. Arabic studies expert Armen Petrosyan said the strong statements from Arab states against Turkey are understandable because Arab countries have lost influence in Syria to Turkey and Iran. However, he said these declarations are mostly situational and would not stop Turkey’s operation in practice. He suggested that only the presence of joint armed forces on the ground could halt Turkish advances. She called on Canada to follow the United States in imposing sanctions on key Venezuelan officials and to work with international partners to deliver humanitarian aid and help stop the violence. Venezuelan-Canadians say they are trying to support relatives back home as best they can. Nereida Coello, who moved to Montreal eight years ago, said she is sending supplies to her sister in Venezuela, a retired lawyer living on a pension of just $12 a month. Peru said Friday it would declare a state of emergency along its southern border and send more armed forces there as a growing number of Venezuelan migrants move north from Chile. The move comes amid rising anti-immigrant sentiment in Chile during a tense presidential campaign. For years, migrants fleeing hardship in their home countries or seeking better opportunities have crossed into Chile, one of the region’s more stable and prosperous countries. Now, however, many people without legal status in Chile, mostly Venezuelans, are heading back toward Peru as Chile prepares to toughen its immigration policies. The shift has been fueled by ultraconservative presidential frontrunner José Antonio Kast, who has centered his campaign on fears about immigration and organized crime. Kast recently filmed a campaign video at the porous desert border with Peru, warning undocumented migrants to leave Chile before a new administration takes power on Dec. 14. He said those who remain would be detained and expelled. Peruvian media soon showed migrant families rushing north, carrying belongings in backpacks and garbage bags. President José Jerí traveled to the border area to inspect controls and ordered armed forces to strengthen security. By Friday, he convened his Cabinet to approve the emergency declaration after reports that people leaving Chile were stranded because they could not enter Peru. Officials said there is no clear estimate of how many migrants have left Chile in response to Kast’s threats and what lawyers describe as a broader rise in xenophobia. Kast issued another warning Friday, while Peru’s foreign minister rejected his remarks as not speaking for the Chilean government. Chilean Security Minister Luis Cordero said rhetoric can have consequences and stressed that the government’s goal is to avoid a humanitarian crisis.

Border towns reported growing chaos as migrants lacking permission to enter Peru remained stranded. While no precise figures exist for total departures, Chilean Security Minister Luis Cordero acknowledged that "rhetoric sometimes has consequences," emphasizing the government's priority to prevent a humanitarian crisis.

Brazilians mourned the death of samba legend Elza Soares on Friday, a day after she died at home in Rio de Janeiro at age 91. Her body was taken to Rio’s Municipal Theater, where family and friends first gathered for a private viewing before the venue opened to the public. Her granddaughter, Vanessa Soares, said in a TV Globo interview that Elza died “the way she wanted, without suffering, and surrounded by family.” Tributes poured in from across Brazil and abroad, spanning generations and genres. Singer Maria Rita called Soares “one of our country’s greatest” and a symbol of “resistance and resilience,” while Beyoncé thanked her for inspiring “so many from Brazil and around the world.” Rio Mayor Eduardo Paes declared three days of mourning and posted: “Woman! Warrior! Elza Lives!” Soares’ life story was central to her legend. Born Elza Gomes da Conceição in June 1930 into poverty in Rio’s Vila Vintem favela, she endured extreme hardship from an early age. Forced to marry at 12, she had her first child at 13 and was widowed by 21 with several children to support. Brazilian media also reported that she lost two children to starvation. Her 2019 album, “Planet Hunger,” referenced the poverty that shaped her youth. She often explained her distinctive raspy voice by recalling childhood chores carrying water jugs on her head through the favela. “I picked up a jug, and I groaned,” she once said, describing how the sound became part of her singing style. To survive, she worked odd jobs, including in a soap factory, before becoming a samba singer in the early 1960s. Her career later expanded beyond samba, and in 1999 BBC London named her “singer of the millennium,” cementing her international stature. She recorded more than 30 albums and remained intensely active throughout her life. Soares also became a fashion icon, known for bold clothing, elaborate headdresses, and heavy makeup. Her relationship with famed soccer player Mané Garrincha made headlines and drew public criticism, but Soares rejected being defined by the men in her life. She insisted on her independence and identified as a feminist ahead of her time, saying in 2017 that she was herself, not “Garrincha’s wife.” In recent years, her influence remained strong. She was featured in Rio’s 2020 Carnival parade and appeared in a documentary series honoring pioneering Black women singers. After her death, younger Brazilian artists shared photos with her as a tribute to her enduring impact. She was to be buried Friday near the Vila Vintem favela where she grew up.

Venezuela and Colombia moved toward restoring diplomatic relations on Monday when Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro received Colombia’s newly appointed ambassador, Armando Benedetti, at the Miraflores Palace in Caracas. The appointment filled a post that had been vacant since February 2019, when the two countries broke off ambassador-level ties amid a bitter political dispute. Benedetti arrived in Venezuela a day earlier, following his designation by Colombia’s new president, Gustavo Petro. Petro, Colombia’s first leftist president, has reversed the hard line taken by his conservative predecessor, Iván Duque, and has pledged to rebuild relations with Maduro’s government. Colombia had been among the countries that withdrew recognition of Maduro as Venezuela’s legitimate leader after his disputed 2018 re-election, which critics said was fraudulent. The meeting between Maduro and Benedetti was held in the Venezuelan capital, but neither man made public remarks afterward. Benedetti had previously said he intended to discuss the possibility of a future presidential meeting between Petro and Maduro. Venezuela’s ambassador to Colombia, Félix Plasencia, also arrived in his post on Sunday, signaling a reciprocal diplomatic thaw. Both governments have expressed interest in a broader reset that could include reopening border bridges to commercial traffic, renewing military cooperation, and restoring Colombian consular services in Venezuela. The border between the two countries stretches about 1,370 miles, and for years it has been a zone of intense smuggling, with armed groups, traffickers, guerrillas and paramilitaries operating in remote areas. Maduro shut down official border crossings in 2015 after an attack on soldiers and a civilian during anti-smuggling operations, though limited foot traffic and some cargo movement later resumed. Despite the closure, illegal trade has continued across dirt routes, often with the involvement or tolerance of authorities on both sides. Legal commerce, however, has been sharply reduced. Trade between the two countries, which reached $2.4 billion in 2014, fell to about $406 million last year, according to the Chamber of Venezuelan-Colombian Economic Integration. The group said trade could rise to $800 million this year if the border remains closed, or to as much as $1.2 billion if crossings reopen to vehicles. Venezuela’s government has said a fully reopened border could push commerce above $4 billion within a year. The article also noted the political sensitivities surrounding any high-level meeting between Petro and Maduro. A researcher at Rosario University warned that such a visit in Colombia could trigger protests from Venezuelans living there. More than 6 million Venezuelans have left their country amid a prolonged crisis, and about 2 million of them live in Colombia. Juan Guaidó, the U.S.-backed opposition leader who had Duque’s support, criticized Benedetti for not addressing Venezuela’s humanitarian crisis, migration and electoral conditions upon arrival. Still, he acknowledged that the ambassador had been appointed by a democratically elected president.
