In Chile’s Putaendo Valley, a severe drought is devastating ranchers and their livestock, leaving hundreds of cows, horses and sheep dead from thirst and starvation. The valley in the Valparaiso region has seen rainfall drop by more than 70 percent, prompting authorities to declare a state of catastrophe and warning of possible desertification. Across the plains and hillsides, animal carcasses have become common, with flies and scavengers among the few creatures benefiting from the crisis. Local ranchers say they have run out of options. Fernando Enriquez, 82, once owned nearly 200 beef cattle and more than 10 horses, but has been forced to bury dead animals in mass graves because he cannot save them. Standing over a grave containing 15 cows and three mares, he said there was “nothing else we can do,” explaining that there is no water or grass left in the countryside. His remaining cattle are severely weakened, eating dried vine shoots and even rocks, with ribs and hip bones visible, hair falling out, and cows unable to produce milk for their calves. Enriquez said livestock that once sold for strong prices are now too underweight to fetch much of anything. Traditionally, ranchers in Putaendo relied on hillsides and streams to feed and water animals that roamed freely and returned healthy after summer. Now, many farmers release their animals to die in the hills, knowing there is no feed available and that burying carcasses on their land would be costly. Another rancher, 59-year-old Luis Manzano, described a similar struggle. He keeps only the cattle he believes he can still save, while sending the rest to the hillsides where they once grazed. He said another dry year has left all the livestock dying and that he feels powerless as a lifetime’s work slips away. The drought is not limited to Putaendo. Chile’s central zone, including Santiago, and parts of the north are experiencing their worst rainfall deficit in 60 years. The Agriculture Ministry says 34,000 animals are affected from Atacama to Maule. Over the past decade, rainfall has fallen by about 38 percent below historical averages, making it increasingly unlikely that cattle ranchers and goat farmers in the valley can continue supporting their families from livestock alone.

# Chile Drought Devastates Putaendo Valley Ranchers A severe drought in Chile's Putaendo Valley has caused catastrophic losses for local ranchers, with hundreds of livestock dying from thirst and starvation. Rainfall in the Valparaiso region has plunged over 70 percent, prompting authorities to declare the area a state of catastrophe and warn of potential desertification. The situation has become dire for ranchers like 82-year-old Fernando Enriquez, who once owned nearly 200 beef cattle and over 10 horses. He has been forced to bury his animals in mass graves, including 15 cows and three mares. His remaining cattle are severely malnourished, reduced to chewing dried vine shoots and rocks, with visible bones and inability to produce milk. Enriquez lamented that he once earned approximately $500 per animal, but now cannot sell his underweight livestock at any price. The drought has fundamentally altered traditional grazing patterns. Historically, ranchers released their animals to hillsides and streams during the Southern Hemisphere winter through summer, where they found abundant grass and water. Now, many ranchers release their livestock to the hillsides knowing they will likely die, as keeping them on private property would require expensive burial costs. Luis Manzano, a 59-year-old rancher, represents the resigned attitude of local farmers. He selectively cares for cattle he believes can survive while releasing others to the hillsides, accepting that some or all may perish. He expressed despair over losing a lifetime's work. The agricultural crisis extends beyond Putaendo. Central Chile, including Santiago, and northern regions face their worst rain shortfall in 60 years. The Agriculture Ministry reports the drought is affecting 34,000 animals across regions from Atacama to Maule. Over the past decade, rainfall has declined approximately 38 percent below historical averages. Both cattle ranchers and goat farmers agree that continuing their livelihoods in Putaendo Valley has become virtually impossible, marking a devastating blow to the region's agricultural heritage.

At the UN General Assembly in New York on 25 September 2025, Colombian President Gustavo Petro urged countries of the global south to “unite armies and weapons” to “liberate Palestine” amid the war in Gaza. In what he said would be his final speech before the UNGA, Petro condemned the continuing destruction in Gaza and accused Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, along with allies in the United States and Europe, of allowing genocide to continue. “We heard too many words already; it is the hour of the sword,” he said, calling on nations and peoples to act. His remarks came as the war, which began in October 2023, has left more than 65,400 people dead, displaced most of Gaza’s 2.2 million residents, and reduced much of the enclave to rubble. The article says ongoing Israeli strikes and aid restrictions have pushed Gaza into famine. Israel has recently intensified bombardment of Gaza City, home to nearly one million people, and ordered residents to evacuate south. A UN commission of inquiry last week said Israeli forces and authorities had committed four of the five genocidal acts defined under the Genocide Convention, citing mass killings, serious harm, and deliberately unlivable conditions, and describing Israeli officials’ statements as evidence of genocidal intent. A separate UN-backed food security analysis in August confirmed famine in Gaza City. Meanwhile, Israel has continued to restrict aid and block activist flotillas. The Global Sumud Flotilla accused Israel this week of drone attacks on its aid boats, prompting Italy and Spain to send vessels in support.

# Colombia Calls for Military Action to "Liberate Palestine" Colombian President Gustavo Petro delivered a controversial speech at the United Nations General Assembly on September 25, 2025, urging the global south to unite militaries and weapons to "liberate Palestine" amid the ongoing Gaza conflict. He condemned the war as genocide and called for accountability for Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu and his international allies, stating "it is the hour of the sword" rather than continued diplomatic dialogue. Since October 2023, the Israeli military has killed over 65,400 people in Gaza, displaced most of its 2.2 million residents, and devastated much of the territory. The enclave faces severe famine conditions due to ongoing strikes and aid restrictions. Israel recently intensified bombardment of Gaza City, ordering evacuations southward. A UN commission of inquiry concluded that Israeli forces committed four of five acts defined as genocide under international law, including mass killings and deliberately creating unlivable conditions. UN officials cited Israeli statements as "direct evidence of genocidal intent." Despite an August UN declaration confirming famine conditions in Gaza City, Israel has maintained strict aid restrictions and halted previous tactical pauses in fighting. This week, Israel allegedly launched drone attacks on the Global Sumud Flotilla, an international aid convoy comprising boats from 44 countries, prompting Italy and Spain to dispatch rescue vessels.

Libya has signed a major deal with TotalEnergies and ConocoPhillips to expand the Waha Oil venture, aiming to more than double production capacity over the next 25 years. The agreement, signed Saturday in Tripoli during the Libya Energy & Economic Summit, could lift output to 850,000 barrels per day from about 350,000, according to Minister of State for Communication and Political Affairs Walid Ellafi. Total investment is expected to reach as much as $20 billion. The pact marks a renewed push into Libya’s vast oil reserves after nearly a decade of depressed production following the 2011 civil war. It will support development of four new fields and a broad exploration program across 19 concession areas. Libya says the project could generate more than $376 billion in revenue over its lifetime. The summit also produced other energy agreements, including a deal with Chevron on exploration and mature-field redevelopment in the Sirte basin, and an accord with Egypt on logistics and joint energy exploration and production. Despite political uncertainty, Libya’s oil potential continues to attract global firms.

# Libya Signs Major Oil Expansion Deal Libya has signed a significant agreement with TotalEnergies and ConocoPhillips to expand the Waha Oil venture, with projected investments reaching $20 billion over 25 years. The deal aims to increase production from approximately 350,000 barrels per day to 850,000 bpd, more than doubling current capacity. This agreement marks a major development following nearly a decade of minimal production due to Libya's civil war beginning in 2011. The project includes developing four new oil fields and launching exploration across 19 concession areas, expected to generate over $376 billion in revenues for Libya. The pact was signed during the Libya Energy & Economic Summit in Tripoli, signaling renewed international investor interest in Libya's substantial petroleum reserves. Additional deals were also concluded, including agreements with Chevron on exploration and investment opportunities, and with Egypt on energy cooperation. Despite ongoing political uncertainty, Libya's vast fossil fuel resources and investor-friendly reforms continue attracting global energy companies seeking to access cheaply produced crude and replenish reserves.

A new Mixed Migration Center report, affiliated with the IOM, says migrant departures from Libya to Europe fell by 25% in the first quarter of 2025. Even so, Libya remains a major transit and destination country, with 9,168 migrants arriving in Italy from January to March, 93% of them—about 8,500 people—having departed from Libyan shores. At the same time, the number of refugees and asylum seekers inside Libya continues to rise. Since the start of 2025, 88,283 refugees have been registered, a 12% increase from the end of 2024. The main driver is Sudan’s ongoing war, which has pushed about 256,000 Sudanese refugees into Libya since April 2023. Sudanese now make up 29% of refugees in the country, followed by migrants from Niger, Egypt, Chad, and Nigeria. IOM data put Libya’s total migrant population at about 824,131 in December 2024, up 17% year on year. The report also notes renewed irregular migration from eastern Libya toward Greece.

# Summary A Mixed Migration Center report reveals that migrant departures from Libya to Europe decreased 25% in early 2025, yet refugee populations within Libya are rising sharply. Approximately 9,168 migrants reached Italy between January and March 2025, with 93% departing from Libya. Meanwhile, 88,283 refugees were registered in Libya since 2025 began—a 12% increase from late 2024. Sudan's ongoing civil war is the primary driver, accounting for 29% of Libya's refugee population, with around 256,000 Sudanese refugees having fled there since April 2023. Other significant origin countries include Niger (23%), Egypt (20%), Chad (10%), and Nigeria (4%). By December 2024, Libya hosted approximately 824,131 total migrants—a 17% annual increase, concentrated mainly in western Libya (53%). The report also notes a resurgence of irregular migration from eastern Libya toward Greece, suggesting smugglers are adapting to increased Mediterranean enforcement.

The UN human rights office said civilian killings in Sudan rose sharply in the first half of this year, driven by intensifying ethnic violence, especially in western Darfur. The conflict between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), which began in April 2023, has caused mass displacement, ethnically targeted killings and what the UN describes as the world’s worst humanitarian crisis. According to a new report from the Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights, at least 3,384 civilians were killed between January and June, most of them in Darfur. That total amounts to nearly 80 percent of all civilian casualties documented in Sudan last year. The UN said counting casualties has remained difficult because health services have collapsed, fighting continues and communications are often cut off. OHCHR Sudan representative Li Fung said the office was receiving “more reports of horrors on the ground” every day. The report said most deaths resulted from artillery shelling and air and drone strikes in densely populated areas. It highlighted killings during the RSF’s offensive on El-Fasher, the last major stronghold of its rivals in Darfur, and attacks in April on the Zamzam and Abu Shouk camps for displaced people. The report also found at least 990 civilians were killed in summary executions in the first six months of the year. That figure tripled between February and April, largely because of a surge in Khartoum after the army and allied fighters retook the city in late March. A witness told the UN he saw children as young as 14 or 15, accused of being RSF members, summarily killed during SAF searches in East Nile. Fung said ethnicity was a key factor in the violence, with communities targeted because of perceived links to either side. Both the SAF and RSF deny deliberately attacking civilians. The International Committee of the Red Cross and Red Crescent said Sudan’s humanitarian situation is worsening, while the country is also facing its worst cholera outbreak in four years.

# Sudan Faces Significant Rise in Civilian Deaths, UN Reports Sudan has experienced a dramatic surge in civilian killings during the first half of 2024, according to the UN human rights office. At least 3,384 civilians were killed between January and June—nearly 80 percent of all documented civilian casualties from the entire previous year—primarily in the western Darfur region. The violence stems from the ongoing conflict that began in April 2023 between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF). The war has triggered ethnically-driven killings, mass displacement, and what the UN describes as the world's worst humanitarian crisis. Most deaths resulted from artillery shelling, air strikes, and drone attacks in populated areas. Significant casualties occurred during the RSF's offensive on El-Fasher city and attacks on displacement camps in April. Additionally, at least 990 civilians were killed in summary executions, with numbers tripling between February and April following the SAF's recapture of Khartoum in late March. Reports documented children as young as 14 or 15 being summarily executed. UN officials emphasized that ethnicity is a primary motivating factor for the violence, with certain communities targeted due to their perceived associations with SAF and RSF leadership, exacerbating decades of existing discrimination. The humanitarian situation continues deteriorating. Sudan faces its worst cholera outbreak in four years, with 2,500 cases reported in Khartoum since June. Both warring sides have denied deliberately attacking civilians, while casualty figures remain difficult to verify due to collapsed health services and communication breakdowns.

An Indian-origin South African family has honoured a World War II hero in New Delhi more than 80 years after his death. Jay Muckerdhooj and his wife Sham became the first descendants of Pilot Officer Dharamraj Aheer Goordeen to lay a wreath at the Delhi/Karachi 1939-1945 War Memorial inside the Delhi War Cemetery. Goordeen, who came from Dannhauser in the former Natal province of South Africa, died in service on April 21, 1942, at the age of 25 in Kohat, now in Pakistan. He had gone to India to study medicine, but instead joined the Royal Indian Air Force and served with the Allied Forces during World War II. At the time, both India and South Africa were under British rule. The Muckerdhooj couple, Goordeen’s third-generation descendants and residents of Meyerson, South Africa, said the visit was their first step in tracing their family roots in India. Their trip was arranged after Jay Muckerdhooj sought help from the South African Indian Legion of Military Veterans (SAIL). Brigadier General Kevin Moonsamy, the Defence Advisor at the South African High Commission in New Delhi, helped facilitate the visit and hosted the family at the embassy. Because the memorial is usually closed on weekends, special permission had to be obtained for the wreath-laying on Saturday. Moonsamy said this was the first such request his office had received from a family seeking to honour a forebear. SAIL said the occasion was significant because it continues to campaign for recognition of the military service of South Africans of Indian origin, many of whom were sidelined during apartheid. After the memorial visit, the Muckerdhooj couple traveled to Bihar to visit the ancestral village from which their family had migrated to South Africa over a century ago.

# South African Family Honors WW2 Hero After 82 Years An Indian-origin South African family recently paid tribute to their ancestor, Pilot Officer Dharamraj Aheer Goordeen, a Royal Indian Air Force officer who died during World War II. Jay Muckerdhooj and his wife Sham became the first descendants to lay a wreath at the Delhi/Karachi 1939-1945 War Memorial in New Delhi's Delhi War Cemetery on Saturday. Goordeen, from Dannhauser in Natal, South Africa, died in service on April 21, 1942, at age 25 in Kohat, Pakistan. Originally traveling to India to study medicine, he enlisted in the Royal Indian Air Force to fight alongside Allied Forces against Axis Forces. At that time, both India and South Africa were British colonies. The Muckerdhooj couple, third-generation descendants residing in Meyerson, South Africa, initiated this visit as their first step in tracing their ancestry in India. Brigadier General Kevin Moonsamy, Defence Advisor at the South African High Commission in New Delhi, facilitated the visit after the family contacted the South African Indian Legion of Military Veterans (SAIL) for assistance. SAIL, established six years ago, works to recognize the military contributions of Indian-origin South African citizens, who faced restrictions under apartheid but served their country with dedication. Following the memorial ceremony, the couple traveled to Bihar to visit their ancestral village, where their forebears originated before immigrating to South Africa over a century ago.

Sudan’s leading pro-democracy group, the Sudanese Professionals’ Association (SPA), sharply criticized the United Nations on Friday, accusing it of failing to protect Sudan’s democratic transition and of being too lenient toward the military leaders behind last year’s coup. The group rejected a UN Mission in Sudan initiative meant to bring civilian and military actors to the negotiating table, saying the mission had not explicitly condemned the coup and had effectively recognized the coup authorities through its actions. The statement came amid continued UN consultations led by Volker Perthes, head of the UN Integrated Transition Assistance Mission in Sudan (UNITAMS), in an effort to resolve the country’s political crisis. The SPA said involving the coup perpetrators in talks contradicted the Sudanese people’s aspirations and reaffirmed its opposition to any new partnership with the military. It insisted that the army must leave politics and allow a fully civilian government to lead the transition. Sudan’s path to democracy has been unstable since a 2019 popular uprising forced longtime autocratic president Omar al-Bashir from power after three decades of repression and isolation. That transition was upended by the October military coup. The situation worsened after Prime Minister Abdalla Hamdok, the civilian face of the transitional government, resigned on Jan. 2, following failed efforts to reach a compromise. He had previously been ousted in the coup and reinstated under international pressure. Since the coup, at least 79 people have been killed and hundreds wounded in protests, with mass arrests and allegations of sexual violence also reported.

# Sudan Pro-democracy Group Denounces UN Mediation Efforts Sudan's leading pro-democracy organization, the Sudanese Professionals' Association (SPA), has strongly criticized the United Nations for its handling of Sudan's political crisis. The group accused the UN Mission in Sudan of failing to protect the country's democratic transition and being lenient toward the military generals responsible for October's coup. The SPA rejected a UN initiative aimed at facilitating negotiations between civilians and the military, stating that the mission had "failed to explicitly condemn the coup" and that its actions implied recognition of the coup authorities. Sudan's democratic transition has been severely disrupted since the October military takeover, which reversed progress made after a 2019 uprising removed longtime autocrat Omar al-Bashir. The situation deteriorated further when Prime Minister Abdalla Hamdok resigned on January 2 after failing to broker a compromise between competing factions. The SPA directly challenged UN Integrated Transition Assistance Mission head Volker Perthes, arguing that including coup perpetrators in consultations contradicts the Sudanese people's wishes. The group insists the military must completely withdraw from politics and allow a civilian-led government. Since the coup, at least 79 people have been killed and hundreds wounded during crackdowns on protests. The UN has also documented mass arrests of activists and allegations of sexual violence during demonstrations.

Rwanda-backed M23 rebels entered Bukavu, the second-largest city in eastern Congo, on Friday, according to local and civil society leaders, marking a major new advance in their long-running fight with Congolese government forces. Jean Samy, vice-president of civil society in South Kivu, said the rebels had moved into the Kazingu and Bagira areas and were pushing toward the city center, where Bukavu’s population is about 1.3 million. He reported gunfire in parts of the city, and videos circulating online appeared to show rebels marching toward Bagira. The advance came only hours after the rebels said they had seized Kavumu airport, a second strategic airfield in the region, after a days-long offensive. The Associated Press could not immediately verify who controlled the airport, which lies about 30 kilometers, or 18.5 miles, from Bukavu, the capital of South Kivu province. Government officials and civil society leaders did not immediately comment on the airport’s status. The M23, backed by roughly 4,000 Rwandan troops, had already taken Goma, eastern Congo’s largest city, in late January. It is the most prominent of more than 100 armed groups operating in Congo’s mineral-rich east. The fighting around Goma has killed at least 2,000 people and displaced hundreds of thousands more, according to the U.N. and Congolese authorities. M23 spokesperson Lawrence Kanyuka said on X that the rebels took Kavumu airport and surrounding areas to “eliminate the threat at the source,” arguing that the airport endangered civilians. Congo’s Communication Ministry condemned the rebels for violating a ceasefire called for by regional leaders, saying they were “imposing an urban war” by attacking positions held by the Congolese army, known as the FARDC, which the ministry said was trying to avoid bloodshed in Bukavu. A civil society leader in Kavumu, speaking anonymously for fear of reprisals, said soldiers were seen abandoning their positions and heading toward Bukavu, which caused panic. Residents described widespread fear and disorder as the fighting spread. Some fled from Kavumu into Bukavu, while others left Bukavu for nearby towns. Many also rushed to buy food and basic supplies as economic activity appeared to grind to a halt. One resident, Chirimwami Alexis, said he left after seeing soldiers “dropping out and fleeing,” adding that people were running without preparation or food. The U.N. refugee agency said heavy shelling and looting had destroyed about 70,000 emergency shelters around Goma and Minova, leaving some 350,000 displaced people without roofs over their heads. It said many were now crowded into makeshift shelters, churches, schools, and hospitals. President Félix Tshisekedi, speaking at the Munich Security Conference in Germany, criticized the international community and Rwanda for failing to stop the offensive. African leaders are expected to meet in Ethiopia for an African Union summit, after a recent regional meeting called for a ceasefire but did not demand that M23 halt its advance.

# Rwanda-backed Rebels Advance into Eastern Congo's Second Major City Rwanda-backed M23 rebels have advanced into Bukavu, eastern Congo's second-largest city with approximately 1.3 million residents, according to local and civil society leaders. The rebels entered the city's Kazingu and Bagira zones on Friday while advancing toward the city center, with gunfire reported in various areas. Videos posted online showed rebels marching through the Bagira area. This latest advance represents a significant escalation in the yearslong conflict between the M23 rebels and Congolese government forces. Supported by approximately 4,000 troops from neighboring Rwanda, the M23 previously captured Goma, eastern Congo's largest city, in late January. The rebels are among more than 100 armed groups competing for control of Congo's mineral-rich eastern region. Hours before entering Bukavu, the M23 claimed to have seized Kavumu airport, located about 30 kilometers from Bukavu in South Kivu province. The M23 spokesperson Lawrence Kanyuka justified the airport seizure, stating the rebels took control to "eliminate the threat at the source" and remove "danger to the civilian population." However, the Associated Press could not immediately confirm control of the airport, and government officials did not immediately respond. The humanitarian toll continues to mount dramatically. The United Nations reported that 350,000 internally displaced people lack shelter after heavy artillery shelling and looting destroyed approximately 70,000 emergency shelters around Goma and Minova. The conflict has created the world's largest humanitarian crisis, with close to 6.5 million people displaced overall. At least 2,000 people have been killed in and around Goma alone. Congo's government has criticized the rebels for violating a ceasefire called for by regional leaders. The Communication Ministry stated that M23 forces were "imposing an urban war" while the Congolese military attempted to avoid bloodshed in Bukavu. The M23 had declared a unilateral ceasefire last week, which the government dismissed as false before the rebels resumed their advance, capturing several nearby towns including Katana. The escalation has caused widespread panic among residents. Some are fleeing from Kavumu toward Bukavu, while others are evacuating from Bukavu to neighboring towns. Residents are stocking household supplies as economic activities collapse. Local soldiers reportedly abandoned their positions, fueling community fear and prompting residents to flee with minimal preparation or food. President Félix Tshisekedi, attending the Munich Security Conference in Germany, criticized the international community's failure to stop the aggression, questioning the United Nations' effectiveness and suggesting it operates as a "two-tier organization" favoring powerful nations over weaker ones. African leaders are scheduled to gather in Ethiopia this weekend for an African Union summit. A recent meeting of eastern and southern African leaders called for a ceasefire but notably did not urge M23 to cease their advance.

A Libyan official said the Government of National Accord (GNA) is financing 28 militia and mercenary groups in the war, spending about $50 million per group each month. Imran Ambiou al-Qanash, a member of the Egyptian and Libyan People's Reconciliations Committee, said the money covers salaries, weapons and ammunition, operations, and travel. He named several GNA-aligned factions, including the Tripoli-based Libyan Protection Forces, al-Samoud brigade, Nawasi brigade, the joint deterrent and intervention force, Abu Salim Axis, Bab Tajura militia, and the Liberal Battalion. Al-Qanash also accused these groups of looting civilian homes in Tarhuna, southwest of Tripoli, and of carrying out field executions and detentions in Tarhuna and in areas south of the capital, including Bani Walid, al-Asaba, and Qasr bin Ghashir. He claimed the militias include extremists, ISIS members, and Syrian mercenaries, and said some leaders were tied to the Muslim Brotherhood, al-Qaeda, or had previously been held at Guantanamo. Turkey, which backs the GNA, has also been accused of sending Syrian mercenaries, weapons, ammunition, and drones.

# Summary Libya's Government of National Accord (GNA) funds 28 militia and mercenary groups engaged in the ongoing civil war, spending approximately $50 million monthly per militia group, according to an official citing tribal leaders. These expenditures cover salaries, weapons, supplies, operations, and travel. Named militia groups include the Libyan Protection Forces, al-Samoud brigade, Nawasi brigade, and others. According to Imran Ambiou al-Qanash, a member of the Egyptian and Libyan People's Reconciliations Committee, these militias have recently looted civilian homes in Tarhuna and allegedly conducted field executions and detentions in areas southwest of Tripoli, including Bani Walid and Qasr bin Ghashir. Al-Qanash claims the GNA militias include Libyan extremists, ISIS members, and Syrian mercenaries, led by Muslim Brotherhood and al-Qaeda members, plus former Guantanamo detainees. Turkey, which supports the GNA against the Libyan National Army, has been accused of supplying Syrian mercenaries, weapons, ammunition, and drones.

Pakistan announced the creation of a new missile unit, three months after its worst military confrontation with India in decades. On Independence Day, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif said the unit would strengthen conventional military power and allow Pakistan to strike in all directions, warning it would respond to any aggression. The move follows May 6–10 exchanges of missile strikes, drone attacks and artillery fire that killed more than 70 people, mostly civilians. Pakistan’s defense budget is estimated at $9 billion, up 20%.

# Summary Pakistan announced the creation of a new missile unit on Independence Day, three months after a severe military confrontation with India. Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif stated the unit can strike in all directions and enhance conventional capabilities. Pakistan's arsenal includes advanced missiles, Chinese fighter jets, and joint Pakistani-Chinese aircraft. In May, Pakistan and India exchanged missile strikes and artillery fire, killing over 70 people, mostly civilians. Pakistan's defense spending increased 20% to $9 billion this year, excluding salaries.

In Narathiwat’s Takbai district, an Islamic leader opened color games at Tadika school in Tabahile village, drawing more than 800 students and villagers. Mayuzo Ma Imam Musjid Dohzan chaired the ceremony, joined by Takbai police superintendent Pol. Col. Patcharapol na Nakhorn. The event took place on the first day of Muharram, the Islamic New Year, which fell on 2 October 2016. Color games were being organized across Tadika schools in the southernmost region to promote fun, unity, and closer ties between communities and authorities. Such activities had been suspended for about a decade because of unrest in the Deep South, but school committees and officials agreed to revive them to restore happiness for local residents. The games featured four color groups and playful contests such as sack running, blindfolded banana eating, musical chairs, tug-of-war, three-legged running, and balloon stepping. Mayuzo said the event aimed to strengthen society and remind youth of the new year’s meaning.

# Summary On October 3, 2016, an Islamic leader inaugurated color games at Tabahile Tadika school in Takbai district, Narathiwat, attended by over 800 students, villagers, and police officials. The event coincided with the Islamic New Year (Hijira 1438) on October 2. After being suspended for a decade due to unrest in the Deep South, Tadika schools throughout the region jointly revived the games to promote community unity and happiness. The competition featured four color teams (red, navy blue, yellow, and sky blue) participating in various fun activities including relay races, blindfolded challenges, musical chairs, tug-of-war, and balloon-stepping contests. Organizers intended the games to strengthen local society and educate young people about the significance of the Islamic New Year celebration.

Myanmar’s anti-junta forces sharply condemned the military regime’s planned election, calling it illegitimate, fraudulent, and a bid to entrench military rule. On Friday, the National Unity Consultative Council (NUCC) and the Ta’ang Land Council (TLC) both issued statements rejecting the vote after the junta’s election commission announced it would be held in phases, with the first round set for December 28 in 102 townships. The NUCC, which brings together hundreds of anti-coup groups including the civilian National Unity Government’s parliamentary wing, ethnic armed organizations, political parties, and civil society groups, said the military had no authority to organize an election because it seized power in violation of its own 2008 Constitution. It accused the junta of killing people, committing genocide, and using the election to hide its crimes, protect its interests, and preserve power. The coalition said the process would only deepen conflict and declared the election “completely illegitimate and fraudulent.” The TLC, the top political body in Ta’ang areas and a coalition involving the Ta’ang National Party, the Ta’ang National Liberation Army (TNLA), and Ta’ang civil society organizations, also opposed the vote. It said the election was intended to prolong dictatorship and maintain the military’s grip on power. The group urged both the public and the international community to reject the process and called on the UN and others to take immediate action to stop what it described as war crimes, crimes against humanity, and mass killings across Myanmar. The article noted that the regime has been bombing TNLA-controlled towns and villages in northern Shan State and Mandalay Region after the group refused to return liberated areas during China-brokered talks in late April. It added that civilians in TNLA areas have been killed by airstrikes and shelling. The election has also been denounced by the International Trade Union Confederation and by election watchdogs including International IDEA, Asian Network for Free Elections, and Club de Madrid, all of which said a credible vote is impossible under current conditions. Several anti-regime groups have warned they may target officials who help carry out the election.

# Myanmar's Anti-Junta Groups Condemn Regime's Election Myanmar's opposition groups have strongly denounced the military junta's planned elections as illegitimate and fraudulent. The National Unity Consultative Council (NUCC), representing hundreds of anti-junta organizations including ethnic armed groups and civil society organizations, issued a statement Friday condemning the elections scheduled to begin December 28 in 102 townships. The NUCC accused the junta of killing Myanmar's people and committing genocide, characterizing the regime as a terrorist organization that violated its own constitution during the 2020 coup. According to the coalition, the elections are merely an attempt to evade accountability for crimes committed, protect military interests, and maintain power—actions that will only deepen conflict. The Ta'ang Land Council, the highest political authority in Ta'ang state, similarly opposed the elections, stating they aim to prolong military dictatorship. The council urged the international community, including the UN, to take immediate action against the regime's alleged war crimes, crimes against humanity, and mass killings occurring daily across the country. International observers have joined the condemnation. The International Trade Union Confederation called the election a "cosmetic trick," noting the regime has banned independent unions and civil society organizations while criminalizing electoral criticism with prison sentences up to 10 years. Election watchdog organizations, including the International Institute for Democracy and Electoral Assistance and the Asian Network for Free Elections, rejected the election in a joint February statement. They emphasized that genuine elections are impossible given banned opposition parties, imprisoned political leaders, and suppressed press freedom. Meanwhile, the junta continues military operations against the Ta'ang National Liberation Army in northern Shan State and Mandalay Region after the armed group refused to surrender liberated territories during peace talks in April. Several anti-regime groups have warned they will target junta-appointed administrators supporting the electoral process.

Pakistan allegedly violated the ceasefire along the Line of Control in Jammu and Kashmir’s Poonch district, opening mortar shelling and small-arms fire in the Degwar sector around 3:45 p.m. One Indian Army jawan was killed and two others injured. In response, the Indian Army escalated firing and, according to sources, caused damage on the Pakistan side. Further details were awaited.

# Summary Pakistan initiated an unprovoked ceasefire violation in the Degwar sector of Poonch, Jammu and Kashmir, using mortar and small arms fire on Saturday. The attack killed one Indian Army jawan and injured two others. In response, the Indian Army escalated caliber firing and inflicted damage on the Pakistani side. The ceasefire violation occurred around 1545 hours.

The Israeli Cabinet has approved the first phase of a ceasefire agreement with Hamas, a move that includes a prisoner exchange and an Israeli withdrawal from part of Gaza. According to Al Jazeera on Friday, October 10, 2025, the exact way this initial deal fits into a broader framework for lasting peace remains uncertain. Hamas’ chief negotiator, Khalil al-Hayya, said the group had received assurances from the United States and mediators that the first phase means the war in Gaza “has fully ended.” The Israeli government’s ratification, confirmed in the early hours of Friday, is expected to bring a halt to fighting in Gaza within 24 hours. Under the arrangement, Hamas has 72 hours to release Israeli prisoners. The vote reportedly faced strong resistance from right-wing Israeli factions. National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir had earlier told Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu that he would not remain in any government “that would allow Hamas to rule in Gaza.” Even after the ceasefire deal was reached, Israeli attacks continued across Gaza on Thursday, killing nine Palestinians and injuring dozens, according to eyewitnesses and medical officials. Strikes hit northern, central, and southern areas of the territory, involving air raids, artillery fire, gunfire, and smoke bombs. In Gaza City, an attack on a house in the city center killed three people, including two women, while others were injured and many remained missing. Israeli fighter jets also bombed the Zeitoun, Sabra, and al-Nafaq neighborhoods, though no casualties were reported there. A drone strike on displaced people sheltering at Yarmouk School in western Gaza City injured several more. In the southeastern Al-Zaytoun district, four Palestinians were wounded in a shooting. Later, an Israeli bomber struck a house in Sabra, killing four family members and leaving about 40 people trapped under rubble, according to the Palestinian Civil Defense and medical sources cited by Anadolu. In central Gaza, Israeli gunfire wounded several Palestinians near the Nuseirat refugee camp as they tried to travel along Al-Rashid Street. In Khan Younis, Israeli forces bombed a civilian gathering in the Al-Biyuk neighborhood, killing one person, while artillery fire in the Hamd area killed a woman and injured others. Additional strikes near the Bani Suhaila roundabout also caused casualties. The violence came after a ceasefire announcement in the early hours of Thursday, following four days of indirect negotiations in Egypt’s Sharm el-Sheikh, mediated by Turkey, Egypt, Qatar, and the United States. The broader U.S.-backed 20-point plan unveiled by Donald Trump on September 29 calls for all Israeli prisoners to be released in exchange for about 2,000 Palestinian detainees, a permanent ceasefire, and a gradual Israeli withdrawal from Gaza. Later phases envision a new Gaza administration without Hamas, security forces involving Arab and Islamic troops, Hamas disarmament, and reconstruction funding from Arab and Muslim states. Arab and Muslim countries have welcomed the plan, though officials say many details still need negotiation. The article also cites Gaza death tolls of at least 67,194 Palestinians killed and 169,890 injured since October 2023, while 1,139 people were killed in Israel during the October 7 attacks, with about 200 taken hostage and only dozens still in Gaza.

# Summary: Israeli Cabinet Approves Gaza Ceasefire Amid Ongoing Violence The Israeli Cabinet has approved the "first phase" of a ceasefire agreement with Hamas, which includes prisoner exchanges and Israeli withdrawal from parts of Gaza. However, the alignment of this agreement with broader peace objectives remains unclear. Hamas's negotiation head, Khalil al-Hayya, stated that the group has received assurances from the United States and mediators that the first phase represents the complete end of the Gaza war. Israel's ratification, confirmed early Friday, October 10, 2025, is expected to halt hostilities within 24 hours, while Hamas faces a 72-hour deadline to release Israeli prisoners. The vote faced significant opposition from right-wing Israeli factions, with National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir declaring he would not support any government allowing Hamas to rule Gaza. Despite the ceasefire agreement, Israeli forces killed nine Palestinians and injured dozens throughout Gaza on Thursday. Attacks occurred across northern, central, and southern regions, involving airstrikes, artillery shelling, and drone strikes. In Gaza City, an Israeli attack destroyed a central house, killing three Palestinians, including two women. Fighter jets bombed multiple neighborhoods, while drones targeted refugee shelters at Yarmouk School. In Khan Younis, Israeli military bombed civilian gatherings and shelled populated areas, causing additional casualties. The ceasefire follows four days of indirect negotiations in Sharm el-Sheikh, Egypt, mediated by Turkey, Egypt, Qatar, and the United States. On September 29, President Trump unveiled a 20-point peace plan including the release of all Israeli prisoners in exchange for approximately 2,000 Palestinian detainees, a permanent ceasefire, and gradual Israeli force withdrawal from Gaza. The plan's second phase proposes new Gaza governance without Hamas participation, security forces comprising Palestinian and Arab/Islamic troops, and Hamas disarmament. It calls for funding from Arab and Muslim nations for reconstruction, with limited Palestinian Authority involvement. Arab and Muslim countries have welcomed the plan while noting that many details require further negotiation. Since October 2023, Israel's military operations have killed at least 67,194 Palestinian civilians, mostly children and women, and injured 169,890 others. Thousands are believed buried under destroyed buildings. The October 7, 2023 attacks killed 1,139 Israelis and captured approximately 200 people, with dozens remaining in Gaza.

Ahead of Xi Jinping’s speech at the annual United Nations General Assembly, Chinese state media portrayed him as a defender of the U.N. spirit and a champion of global cooperation. Xinhua and other commentaries emphasized China’s long record of supporting multilateralism and cast Xi as a calm, responsible voice on the world stage. But the article says that behind this messaging, China is entering a difficult and delicate moment in its rise as a global power. Analysts quoted in the piece argue that Xi faces a far more complicated international environment than China’s propaganda suggests. Mike Mazza of the American Enterprise Institute said Xi has “his work cut out for him” because of tensions with Europe over trade, investment, climate policy, and human rights, as well as the Trump administration’s confrontational stance toward China. He noted that Beijing has failed to exploit divisions between Europe and Washington, that hopes for better ties with Japan have stalled, and that relations with Australia have sharply deteriorated amid spying allegations, accusations of political interference, and demands for an inquiry into the coronavirus’ origins. Even the Philippines, which had been moving closer to Beijing than to Washington, pulled back from threatening to end a key military pact with the United States, another setback for China’s regional ambitions. The article says many of these troubles stem from China’s own actions. Beijing’s rapid military expansion and economic power have made it seem increasingly assertive to neighbors, while its broader rise now appears less inevitable and more fragile. China has also faced mounting criticism over the pandemic, which began in Wuhan late last year. Some observers accuse Beijing of initially trying to conceal the outbreak and later using its response for public relations gains. Other major sources of friction include the crackdown in Hong Kong, where China imposed a sweeping national security law that severely restricted civil liberties; allegations of mass detention and cultural repression in Xinjiang; and growing military pressure on Taiwan, which Beijing claims as its own territory. China’s push to control nearly the entire South China Sea has deepened tensions with the United States and Southeast Asian neighbors, and a longstanding border dispute with India turned violent this year, with deadly clashes and shots fired for the first time in decades. These developments, the article says, have weakened the case for engagement with China even as the trade war between Washington and Beijing continues. Steve Tsang of SOAS said many democracies that once supported China’s modernization are now uneasy about the direction Xi is taking. Ralph Cossa of the Pacific Forum argued that Beijing often refuses to admit its own role in creating problems and instead blames others. In prepared remarks for a meeting marking the U.N.’s 75th anniversary, Xi directly criticized what appeared to be a reference to the United States, saying no country should dominate global affairs, control others’ destinies, or act as the world’s “hegemon, bully or boss.” He declared unilateralism a dead end. The article notes that this message could also be seen as reflecting the concerns of China’s neighbors, who view Beijing’s foreign policy as increasingly aggressive. Brookings analyst Cheng Li warned that the United States and China are on a collision course that could lead to dangerous military conflict. At the same time, Xi is expected to highlight China’s support for multilateralism, pandemic recovery, climate action, and peacekeeping, while portraying the U.S. as absent from global leadership. Some countries may welcome China’s model of recovery from Covid-19, and others may value Beijing’s Belt and Road investment and debt relief.

# Summary: Xi Jinping Faces Complex International Challenges at UN Address Chinese leader Xi Jinping addressed the United Nations General Assembly at a delicate moment for China, despite state media portraying him as a champion of international cooperation and global reason. However, analysts suggest underlying unease as China navigates its complex military, economic, and political rise while confronting U.S. containment strategies and managing deteriorating relationships worldwide. **Regional Tensions and Setbacks** China faces significant diplomatic challenges across multiple regions. Relations with Europe have grown strained over trade, investment, human rights, and climate issues. A potential détente with Japan has stalled, while Australia relations have nosedived following espionage allegations and calls for coronavirus origin investigations. The Philippines recently backed away from canceling a military pact with the United States, representing another regional setback for Beijing's dominance aspirations. **Domestic and International Criticism** China confronts mounting criticism on multiple fronts. The coronavirus pandemic, which originated in China, sparked allegations that Beijing initially covered up the outbreak before exploiting its response for public relations. Hong Kong's civil rights restrictions following the national security law implementation have drawn international outrage. Widespread accusations of mass detentions and cultural genocide against Uyghur Muslims in Xinjiang have intensified global concern. Additionally, China's military pressure on Taiwan and claims to nearly the entire South China Sea have created friction with neighboring countries and the United States. A deadly border clash with India in 2020—the first military confrontation in decades between the rivals—further undermined China's international standing. These issues have weakened arguments supporting engagement with China amid the ongoing U.S.-China trade war. **Xi's Strategic Position** Xi attempted to position China as a multilateral advocate in prepared remarks, criticizing unilateralism and stating that no country should dominate global affairs or act as a hegemon. However, analysts note this criticism could equally apply to China's own aggressive regional behavior. Experts indicate Xi faces a "very mixed international environment." While some developing nations appreciate China's Belt and Road infrastructure initiative and pandemic assistance, many democracies previously supportive of China's development now feel uncomfortable with Xi's leadership direction. The U.S.-China relationship has deteriorated into what some analysts describe as a potential collision course with dangerous military conflict risks. **Strategic Goals** Xi's immediate objectives include showcasing China's commitment to multilateralism and global problem-solving—from pandemic relief to climate change and peacekeeping—while highlighting perceived American leadership vacuums. Some nations view China's COVID-19 recovery as a model superior to the U.S. response, potentially strengthening Beijing's appeal. Analysts emphasize that China's problems largely stem from its own actions. According to experts, Beijing struggles to acknowledge this reality, instead attributing difficulties to external sources. This defensive posture, combined with genuine international concerns about China's trajectory, creates the delicate diplomatic moment Xi navigates at the United Nations.

Margie Reckard, 63, was among the 22 people killed in the August 3 mass shooting at a Walmart in El Paso, Texas, leaving her husband, Antonio Basco, with no remaining family. Basco, who had been married to Reckard for more than two decades, described her as the happiest and luckiest part of his life and said he still expected her to come home. Because he had no other relatives, Basco asked the Perches Funeral Home to issue an open invitation for the entire town to attend Reckard’s funeral on Friday night. The invitation, posted on Facebook, drew widespread attention: the funeral home said it had been viewed more than 11,000 times, and more than 1,000 mourners were expected. Since the venue could hold only 250 people, organizers were discussing moving the service to a nearby church. The tragedy also prompted public support for Basco, who runs a mobile car wash business. A GoFundMe campaign raised more than $25,000 to help him. The fundraiser’s organizer said Basco’s story, especially that he was completely alone, moved him deeply. The shooting was carried out by Patrick Crusius, a 21-year-old white man who drove more than nine hours to El Paso. After his arrest, he said he had targeted “Mexicans.” Before the attack, he had posted a white supremacist manifesto online warning of a supposed “Hispanic invasion” of Texas. Critics of President Donald Trump have accused him of helping fuel such hatred.

# Summary Margie Reckard, 63, was killed in the El Paso Walmart shooting on August 3 that claimed 22 lives. Her husband of over two decades, Antonio Basco, was left without any other family members. Devastated by the loss, Basco invited the entire town to attend his wife's funeral on Friday night. He told CNN that Margie "made me the happiest man in the world" and expressed his grief, saying he still looks at the front door expecting her to walk in. The funeral home director reported that the Facebook invitation received over 11,000 visits, with more than 1,000 mourners expected to attend. Since the funeral home could only accommodate 250 people, organizers arranged to move the service to a nearby church. A GoFundMe campaign was established to support Basco, who runs a mobile car wash business. The fundraiser exceeded $25,000, with organizer Carlos Armendariz noting that Basco's story of being alone particularly moved him. The shooting was carried out by 21-year-old Patrick Crusius, who drove nine hours to El Paso specifically to target "Mexicans." Before the attack, Crusius published a white supremacist manifesto expressing fears of a "Hispanic invasion" of Texas. Critics have blamed President Donald Trump for stoking such hatred.

In his inaugural address, US President Donald Trump declared that “from this day forward” American policy would be governed by “America First,” a message that immediately unsettled allies and adversaries alike. The speech reflected Trump’s campaign promises to make America “great again” and to protect its borders from foreign countries that, in his words, were “making our products, stealing our companies, and destroying our jobs.” It portrayed the United States as a nation under siege, damaged by predatory states and in need of repair through protectionist policies. The article compares this “America First” stance to historical isolationism and to the idea of “Fortress Europe,” a term associated with Adolf Hitler’s defensive strategy on the Atlantic coast during World War II. It notes that American isolationism was once a major policy trend until President Woodrow Wilson sent troops to France in World War I, helping shift the country toward international engagement in the name of defending democracy. The Economist, in a Nov. 19, 2016 article, drew a contrast between Trump and Ronald Reagan. Reagan, it said, envisioned America as a “shining city on a hill” that looked outward toward others, while Trump promised to put America first and reject what he called the “false song of globalism.” According to the magazine, Reagan’s America was optimistic, whereas Trump’s was angry. It argued that Trump’s populism weakened civic nationalism and departed from the postwar tradition in which US presidents, while often skeptical of international bodies like the International Criminal Court and the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, still supported the broader rules-based world order. The article warned that when America turns inward, the result can be intolerance, suspicion of minorities, and political strains, including renewed allegations of anti-Semitism. The doctrine also caused concern in Asia. Reports from Tokyo said Asian leaders, while publicly offering congratulations and expressing hopes that Trump would strengthen alliances and shared interests, privately conveyed unease about the confrontational tone of his America First approach. That discomfort was echoed by public protests across the region. More than 10,000 people joined rallies in cities including Sydney, Melbourne, Wellington, Tokyo, and Manila to denounce the hate speech, xenophobia, and misogyny associated with Trump’s campaign. One Tokyo protester said people should speak out for fair treatment regardless of gender, skin color, or sexual orientation.

# Summary: Trump's "America First" Doctrine and Global Concerns In his inaugural address, President Donald Trump declared "America First" as his governing principle, immediately unsettling US allies and adversaries worldwide. As a billionaire businessman without prior political or military experience, Trump's announcement sparked global anxiety about America's future direction. During his campaign, Trump promised to restore American greatness by protecting borders from what he characterized as predatory nations stealing jobs and destroying American companies. He depicted America as a nation under siege requiring protectionist policies for recovery. This rhetoric echoed historical isolationism, specifically recalling Hitler's "Festung Europa" (Fortress Europe) concept during World War II. The article contrasts Trump's approach with previous American foreign policy. Historically, isolationism dominated until President Woodrow Wilson sent forces to France in World War I to promote democracy globally. More recently, Ronald Reagan in 1980 also promised renewal but envisioned America as an optimistic "city on a hill" looking outward toward others. The Economist noted that Trump's vision differs fundamentally—his America is "angry" rather than optimistic, rejecting what he calls "the false song of globalism." Critics warn that Trump's populist nationalism represents a departure from postwar American values. While previous presidents supported universal values and global institutions, Trump's doctrine threatens the rules-based international order that has promoted global prosperity and stability. The Economist cautioned that America's last inward turn after World War I had "calamitous" consequences, and warned that contemporary nationalism tends to produce domestic intolerance and feed suspicions about minorities' loyalties. The article notes that anti-Semitic allegations have infected American politics for the first time in decades. Asian leaders expressed particular unease. Despite offering congratulatory messages, their statements carried strong undercurrents of concern about Trump's confrontational approach. The doctrine provoked regional protests, with over 10,000 people rallying in cities including Sydney, Melbourne, Wellington, Tokyo, and Manila against the hate speech, xenophobia, and misogyny characterizing Trump's campaign. Demonstrators demanded fair treatment regardless of gender, skin color, or sexual orientation, reflecting widespread anxiety about the direction of American foreign policy and its implications for global stability.

The Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) said on March 29, 2022, that Russian authorities and Russia-backed forces must stop detaining Ukrainian journalists and ensure that reporters can work safely during the war. CPJ said at least two Ukrainian journalists had been injured by Russian shelling in separate incidents, while another journalist was taken to the Russia-backed separatist-controlled city of Donetsk after being detained. On March 25, Russian forces shelled a civilian evacuation convoy in the northern Chernihiv region, injuring Andriy Tsaplienko, a reporter for the Ukrainian broadcaster 1+1. According to media reports and a statement from his outlet, Tsaplienko suffered a minor thigh injury and was treated at a local hospital. The convoy was reportedly carrying civilians in a humanitarian evacuation, and one post cited by CPJ said shelling should not occur at such a location under “written and unwritten rules.” Journalists from TRT World were also present during the attack but were not hurt. Tsaplienko, who has covered wars around the world, has been reporting on the war in Ukraine. The next day, March 26, another Ukrainian journalist, Oleksandr Navrotskyi, a camera operator for Channel 24, was injured in shelling in the village of Lukyanovka in the Kyiv region. CPJ said he was filming while being escorted by the Ukrainian military when shrapnel from a Russian rocket strike hit his knee. Channel 24 executive producer Bohdan Tugushi told CPJ that Navrotskyi had undergone three operations by March 29, and doctors were still unable to say whether he would walk again because the knee injury was so severe. Tugushi said he needed at least two more surgeries. Navrotskyi had worked for Channel 24 for seven years and had prior war-reporting experience. Also on March 26, Russian forces detained journalist Iryna Dubchenko in Rozivka, in southeastern Ukraine, and took her to Donetsk, according to media reports and social media posts from her friends and relatives. CPJ said that by March 28, the Ukrainian military commandant’s office in Rozivka had told Dubchenko’s family that she had disappeared two days earlier and been taken to Donetsk. Her sister said Russian soldiers searched Dubchenko’s home and told her they “knew everything” about her journalism. Dubchenko has worked for several Ukrainian media outlets, including Depo.Zaporizhzhia, Subota, and UNIAN. Her sister said Dubchenko had been working throughout the Russian invasion. According to the family, Russian forces accused her of hiding a wounded Ukrainian soldier and took her for an “investigative action,” though CPJ said it could not independently verify that claim. The Ukrainian military administration in the Zaporizhzhia region later confirmed her abduction and said response measures were underway. CPJ also said it was investigating the alleged abduction of journalist Konstantin Ovsyannikov in Prymorsk on March 26. Reports on social media initially said he had been detained, then later claimed he had been released. CPJ said it had sought comment from Russian and Ukrainian defense ministries and the self-proclaimed Donetsk People’s Republic, but received no replies.

# Summary: Ukrainian Journalists Injured and Detained During Russian Invasion The Committee to Protect Journalists issued a statement on March 29, 2022, condemning Russian authorities for detaining Ukrainian journalists and targeting media personnel covering the ongoing war. The organization called for the immediate release of detained journalists and demanded that Russia ensure press safety and freedom from reprisal. The statement documented several incidents of violence and detention against Ukrainian journalists in late March 2022. On March 25, reporter Andriy Tsaplienko of the 1+1 television broadcaster was injured when Russian forces shelled a civilian evacuation convoy in the Chernihiv region. Tsaplienko sustained a minor thigh injury and received hospital treatment. The convoy was conducting humanitarian evacuations, making the attack particularly egregious under international humanitarian law. The following day, March 26, camera operator Oleksandr Navrotskyi of Channel 24 was severely injured during Russian shelling in the village of Lukyanovka near Kyiv. While filming alongside Ukrainian military escorts, Navrotskyi was struck in the knee by shrapnel from a Russian rocket strike. His injury proved serious, requiring three operations by March 29, with doctors uncertain whether he would regain the ability to walk. Medical professionals indicated he would need at least two additional surgeries. Also on March 26, journalist Iryna Dubchenko was detained by Russian forces in Rozivka and transported to Donetsk, a Russia-backed separatist-controlled city. Russian soldiers searched her home, claiming knowledge of her journalistic activities. They accused her of harboring a wounded Ukrainian soldier and took her for an "investigative action." Dubchenko had worked for several Ukrainian news organizations, including Depo.Zaporizhzhia, Subota newspaper, and the UNIAN news agency, and had reported extensively throughout Russia's invasion. Gulnoza Said, CPJ's Europe and Central Asia program coordinator, emphasized that journalists are civilians protected under international humanitarian law and should not be targeted in conflict. She demanded Dubchenko's immediate release and called on both Russian and Ukrainian authorities to protect press freedom in war zones. The Committee was also investigating the alleged abduction of journalist Konstantin Ovsyannikov in Prymorsk on March 26. Social media posts indicated he was detained but later released. Ovsyannikov had recently covered Ukrainian protests against Russian occupation. CPJ attempted to obtain responses from Russian and Ukrainian Ministries of Defense and the self-proclaimed Donetsk People's Republic but received no replies. The incidents highlighted the dangerous conditions facing journalists documenting the conflict and raised serious concerns about violations of press freedom and international humanitarian law during Russia's invasion of Ukraine.

A 49-year-old UK driver escaped serious injury after his vehicle overturned in a ditch near England’s southwest coast. Police say he claimed he swerved to avoid an octopus in the road, but officers found no octopus at the scene. He was arrested Tuesday on suspicion of driving under the influence of drugs. Authorities used the case to warn about drugged driving, while social media users mocked the bizarre explanation with octopus-themed jokes.

# Summary A 49-year-old UK driver crashed his vehicle into a ditch while allegedly swerving to avoid an octopus. Police found no evidence of the creature at the scene near England's southwest coast. The driver was arrested on suspicion of driving under the influence of drugs. Police noted the octopus would have had to travel over three miles across hills and fields to reach that location, making the claim implausible. The incident has sparked humor on social media.

Piraeus Bank in Kyiv said the ownership of the Lviv Macaroni Factory’s real estate was illegally transferred and the plant was later seized by unknown people. The bank said a state registrar in Lviv region re-registered 17 factory buildings and the property complex to Citycom Estate LLC on July 15. Four days later, unknown persons entered the factory grounds, forced guards to leave and blocked access. Piraeus Bank said the factory had been declared bankrupt in 2012, so any sale of its assets should occur only through bankruptcy auction procedures.

# Summary Piraeus Bank reported an illegal ownership change of Lviv Macaroni Factory's real estate. On July 15, the state registrar transferred ownership of 17 factory objects to Citycom Estate LLC without proper procedure. Four days later, unidentified individuals forcibly occupied the factory premises, expelling guards and restricting access. The bank emphasized that since the factory was declared bankrupt in 2012, any property sale must occur through official bankruptcy auction procedures, not private transfers.

John Chilcot, who heads Britain’s official inquiry into the Iraq war, defended the long delay in publishing its report, telling a parliamentary committee that the complexity of the investigation made the slowdown unavoidable. The inquiry, announced in 2009 and originally expected to take a year, missed its latest target, with Chilcot saying in April there was “no realistic prospect” of finishing before the 7 May general election. He said the inquiry covers decisions and consequences over nine years, not a single event, and that it had underestimated the time needed to analyze evidence from more than 150,000 government documents and 150 witnesses. The delay, including time for criticized figures to respond, has angered lawmakers and raised fears of a whitewash among some war victims’ relatives.

# Summary John Chilcot, head of Britain's Iraq war inquiry, defended significant publication delays before a parliamentary committee. Announced in 2009 and originally expected within a year, the report investigating the US-led invasion and its aftermath faced repeated postponements, with no completion before the May general election. The latest delay, allowing criticized parties to respond, sparked outcry from lawmakers and concerns about a whitewash from war victims' families. Chilcot attributed delays to the inquiry's unprecedented scope, covering nine years of decisions and their consequences. The investigation analyzed over 150,000 government documents and 150 witness testimonies. Diplomatic sensitivities regarding exchanges between President George W. Bush and Prime Minister Tony Blair further complicated publication. Britain was America's primary ally in the war despite significant public opposition.

The United States sharply rejected a North Korean proposal to temporarily halt future nuclear tests if Washington cancels joint military exercises with South Korea, calling the offer an “implicit threat.” State Department spokeswoman Jen Psaki said North Korea was “inappropriately” linking routine US-South Korean drills to the possibility of another nuclear test. She said any new test would be a “clear violation” of North Korea’s obligations under multiple UN Security Council resolutions. Psaki made the remarks on Saturday while traveling with Secretary of State John Kerry, who was en route to India and stopped over in Munich. North Korea’s official KCNA news agency said the proposal had been delivered to the US through a “relevant channel” on Friday. The message urged Washington to help ease tensions on the Korean peninsula by suspending all of this year’s joint military exercises in South Korea and nearby areas. KCNA also said that if the United States wanted clarification, North Korea was ready to meet “anytime.” Psaki said the US remained open to dialogue, but only if talks were aimed at returning to “credible and authentic negotiations” on denuclearizing the Korean peninsula. She urged North Korea to stop making threats, reduce tensions, and take steps toward denuclearization before negotiations could resume. The article notes that the United States keeps nearly 30,000 troops in South Korea and holds annual joint military exercises with Seoul. Washington describes these drills as transparent and defensive, while North Korea regularly condemns them as rehearsals for invasion and the main source of tensions on the peninsula. The two Koreas remain technically at war because the 1950–53 Korean War ended with a ceasefire, not a peace treaty. North Korea has already carried out three nuclear tests, the last in February 2013, and had recently threatened a fourth test after a UN resolution criticizing its human rights record. However, satellite imagery showed no signs of an imminent detonation. Analysts said the offer to trade a pause in nuclear testing for a halt to military drills suggested a more pragmatic approach than usual.

# Summary North Korea proposed suspending future nuclear tests if the United States cancels its joint military exercises with South Korea. The U.S. State Department rejected this offer, with spokeswoman Jen Psaki calling it an "implicit threat" that inappropriately linked routine military drills to the possibility of nuclear testing. Pyongyang conveyed its proposal through official channels on Friday, requesting that Washington suspend all 2015 joint military exercises in South Korea and surrounding areas to ease tensions on the Korean Peninsula. North Korea indicated it was prepared to engage in talks at any time to discuss the proposal. However, the U.S. firmly rejected the linkage between military exercises and nuclear testing. Psaki emphasized that any nuclear test would violate multiple UN Security Council resolutions and that the U.S. remains open to dialogue only if aimed at genuine negotiations on denuclearization of the peninsula. She called on North Korea to cease all threats and reduce tensions. The U.S. maintains approximately 30,000 troops in South Korea and conducts regular joint military exercises with its ally—a practice conducted openly for roughly 40 years. While the U.S. characterizes these drills as transparent and defense-oriented, North Korea consistently condemns them as provocative invasion rehearsals. The exercises are a persistent source of tension between the two Koreas, who remain technically at war following the 1950-53 Korean War, which ended in a ceasefire rather than a peace treaty. North Korea has conducted three nuclear tests, the most recent in February 2013, and previously threatened a fourth test. Analysts noted that North Korea's conditional offer suggested a more pragmatic approach than typical demands. However, satellite imagery showed no signs of imminent nuclear detonation. Experts estimated North Korea possessed approximately 12 nuclear weapons with capacity to produce four to six additional devices annually.

France has decided to back Ukraine’s possible accession to NATO as a way to encourage negotiations between Moscow and Kyiv, Le Monde reported. Citing a June 12 security meeting at the Élysée Palace, the paper said Paris views Ukraine’s Euro-Atlantic integration as a security guarantee that could prevent escalation and future aggression after the war. Meanwhile, NATO Secretary General Jens Stoltenberg said allies are not considering a formal invitation before the July 11-12 Vilnius summit, and Ukraine’s membership will not be discussed until the conflict with Russia ends. Kyiv applied for fast-track membership in September 2022.

# Summary France has decided to support Ukraine's potential NATO accession as a negotiation tool between Moscow and Kyiv, according to Le Monde. French officials believe Ukraine's Euro-Atlantic integration would serve as a security guarantee, potentially preventing future Russian aggression after the conflict ends. However, NATO Secretary General Jens Stoltenberg stated that allies are not discussing formal membership invitations ahead of the July Vilnius summit. He reiterated that Ukraine's NATO membership cannot be determined until the military conflict concludes. Ukraine applied for accelerated NATO membership in September 2022 following Russia's invasion.

NATO will continue supporting Afghan security forces after ending its 18-year military mission in Afghanistan, Secretary General Jens Stoltenberg said Friday. Speaking in Paris after talks with French President Emmanuel Macron, Stoltenberg said the alliance is entering “a new chapter” as it withdraws its troops in the coming months. Under the revised role, NATO would provide advice and capacity-building support to Afghan security institutions, along with continued financial assistance. Stoltenberg also said NATO plans to offer military education and training outside Afghanistan, with a focus on Afghan Special Operations Forces, though the location has not yet been determined. The announcement comes as the United States and its allies prepare to leave Afghanistan following President Joe Biden’s order to withdraw all American troops by September. U.S. military leaders are still working out how to complete the pullout while helping Afghan forces and tracking the threat that originally led to the U.S.-led invasion after the Sept. 11, 2001 attacks. European allies and Canada depend on U.S. logistics and transport support in Afghanistan, and their forces are also expected to leave. Many officials fear the Afghan government and military could be quickly overwhelmed by the Taliban once foreign troops depart. Questions also remain about who will protect international embassies in Kabul and secure the city’s airport, the country’s main gateway. Stoltenberg said NATO intends to fund services, including support for Kabul airport operations. Meanwhile, violence continues to rise in Afghanistan, with recent roadside bombings and a bus attack killing multiple civilians. The government blamed the Taliban, which denied involvement.

# NATO to Continue Afghan Training After Withdrawal NATO will maintain its support for Afghan forces after ending its 18-year military presence in Afghanistan, Secretary General Jens Stoltenberg announced Friday following discussions with French President Emmanuel Macron. Rather than completely withdrawing, NATO plans to shift to a new role focused on "advice and capacity-building support" to Afghan security institutions. The alliance will provide military education and training to Afghan Special Operations Forces outside the country, though the specific location remains undetermined. NATO will also continue providing financial support and fund services including Kabul airport operations. This announcement comes as U.S. military officials work to implement President Biden's order to withdraw all American troops by September. U.S. allies in Europe and Canada depend on American logistical support to operate in Afghanistan and must also withdraw their forces. Officials express significant concern about Afghanistan's stability following the withdrawal. Many fear the Afghan government and military will be quickly overwhelmed by the Taliban once international forces depart. The security situation remains precarious, with escalating violence including roadside bombings that killed 13 people Thursday and militant attacks resulting in three deaths. Critical questions remain unanswered regarding the protection of international embassies in Kabul and the security of the capital's airport, the main international gateway to Afghanistan. NATO officials indicated they are consulting on implementation details and next steps for maintaining these essential operations.

Poland’s president, Andrzej Duda, said Saturday that U.S. President Joe Biden’s upcoming two-day visit to Warsaw will have “world dimension” significance as it marks the anniversary of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. Biden is scheduled to arrive Tuesday and meet with leaders of NATO’s nine eastern flank countries, then deliver a speech on how the United States has rallied global support for Ukraine, according to the White House. Duda made his remarks at the Munich Security Conference in Germany, emphasizing that this will be Biden’s second trip to Poland in less than a year, underscoring Poland’s role as a major supporter of Kyiv with military and humanitarian aid.
