# Summary U.S. President Joe Biden will visit Warsaw on Tuesday to mark the one-year anniversary of Russia's invasion of Ukraine. Polish President Andrzej Duda stated the visit will have "world dimension" significance. During his two-day trip, Biden plans to meet with leaders of NATO's nine eastern flank nations and deliver a speech about how the United States rallied global support for Ukraine. This marks Biden's second visit to Poland in less than a year, highlighting the country's substantial military and humanitarian support for Ukraine. Secretary of State Antony Blinken emphasized Biden will make a "very significant speech" addressing the past year's developments and America's commitment to Ukraine's success. Ukrainian Foreign Minister Dmytro Kuleba predicted Biden's address will be more consequential than Russian President Putin's scheduled speech to Russia's legislature the same day. Since Putin's February 2022 invasion, Ukrainian resistance and Western weapons supplies have forced Russia to scale back its military objectives, though the war's diplomatic effects continue globally.

Abolhassan Banisadr, Iran’s first president after the 1979 Islamic Revolution and a one-time ally of Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini who later became one of the clerics’ sharpest critics, died Saturday in Paris at age 88 after a long illness, according to his family. Iranian state television also reported his death. Banisadr’s life and political career were closely tied to the upheaval that transformed Iran from a monarchy into an Islamic republic. He stood apart from the black-robed clerics who came to dominate the revolution’s aftermath: he wore Western-style suits, had a French intellectual background, and had once confided to philosopher Jean-Paul Sartre that he believed he would someday become Iran’s first president. At the same time, he described himself as a nationalist with a strong Shiite faith inherited from his cleric father, and he favored a socialist-style economic program. His rise, however, was shaped by forces he could not control. The U.S. Embassy hostage crisis and Iraq’s invasion of Iran deepened the turmoil after the revolution, while real power remained with Khomeini, the supreme leader. Banisadr had worked with Khomeini in exile in France and followed him back to Tehran, but the relationship deteriorated as Khomeini consolidated authority. Banisadr later compared Khomeini to a father slowly consumed by alcohol, saying “the drug this time was power.” Khomeini had been forced into exile by the shah and eventually arrived in France in 1978. Banisadr, already living there with his family, gave the cleric a place to stay after moving out of his own apartment. Khomeini settled in Neauphle-Le-Chateau, outside Paris, where Banisadr and a circle of associates helped shape and vet the messages Khomeini sent to supporters in Iran. Those taped and telephone-delivered messages helped build momentum for the revolution and Khomeini’s return after the shah fled in early 1979. After the revolution succeeded, Banisadr became a member of the Revolutionary Council and, just days after the Nov. 4, 1979 seizure of the U.S. Embassy in Tehran by hard-line students, was appointed foreign minister. He served only 18 days in that post before Khomeini replaced him with a hard-liner after Banisadr sought a negotiated end to the hostage crisis. Banisadr later denounced the hostage-takers as “dictators who have created a government within a government.” He remained influential for a time, helping push through the nationalization of major industries and former private holdings of the shah. In early 1980, after Khomeini had decreed that a cleric should not hold the newly created presidency, Banisadr won the office with about three-quarters of the vote. In his inaugural address he spoke of exporting the revolution and creating a new order in which the deprived would no longer remain deprived. But his presidency quickly became engulfed in crisis. Iran’s armed forces had been purged, and when Iraq invaded, the war that followed became an eight-year conflict. Khomeini named Banisadr commander-in-chief, but military setbacks and criticism from the Revolutionary Guard weakened him politically. He also survived two helicopter crashes near the front. His conflict with hard-line clerics intensified, and in June 1981 parliament impeached him for opposing clerical rule in politics. A month later, Banisadr fled Iran aboard an Iranian Air Force Boeing 707 with Massoud Rajavi, leader of the leftist militant group Mujahedeen-e-Khalq. Iranian media later claimed he escaped disguised as a woman; when he emerged, his trademark mustache had been shaved off. From exile, he accused Khomeini of bearing heavy responsibility for the country’s disaster. Born in Hamadan in 1933, Banisadr came from a religious family. His father was an ayatollah who opposed the shah’s father, Reza Shah. As a young man, Banisadr protested the shah, was jailed twice, supported Prime Minister Mohammad Mosaddegh, and was wounded during unrest in 1963 before fleeing to France. There he studied economics and finance at the Sorbonne, later taught there, and wrote on socialism and Islam. After leaving Iran, he and Rajavi formed the National Council of Resistance of Iran, though Banisadr left it in 1984 after the Mujahedeen-e-Khalq aligned with Saddam Hussein during the war with Iran. He spent the rest of his life near Paris under police protection because of threats from suspected Iranian assassins. Banisadr also became known for alleging, without evidence, that Ronald Reagan’s 1980 campaign had conspired with Iranian leaders to delay the hostage release in order to hurt Jimmy Carter. That claim helped popularize the idea of the “October Surprise.” U.S. Senate investigators later said there was no such deal, though the later Iran-Contra affair showed that U.S. arms did reach Iran through Israel after Reagan took office. Even in exile, Banisadr continued to argue that the clerics had used him and other democratic forces as tools. Looking back on the hostage crisis in 1991, he said he had told Khomeini that taking the Americans hostage was against Islam and democracy.

# Abolhassan Banisadr, Iran's First Post-Revolution President, Dies at 88 Abolhassan Banisadr, who served as Iran's first president following the 1979 Islamic Revolution, died Saturday at age 88 in a Paris hospital after a long illness. His death marks the end of a remarkable but tumultuous political career that exemplified the ideological conflicts that shaped post-revolutionary Iran. Banisadr stood out among Iran's revolutionary leadership for his Western education, French-style suits, and secular outlook—stark contrasts to the black-robed Shiite clerics who dominated the new Islamic Republic. Born in 1933 in Hamadan to an ayatollah father, Banisadr grew up in a religious family but developed socialist economic theories while studying at the Sorbonne in Paris. He authored books blending Islam and socialism, ideas that would later influence his political approach. His relationship with Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini proved crucial to his rise and fall. When Khomeini was exiled to France in 1978, Banisadr provided him housing in Paris and helped craft his revolutionary messages. These taped statements, distributed throughout Iran and Europe, helped lay the groundwork for Khomeini's triumphant return after Shah Mohammad Reza Pahlavi fled in early 1979. Following the revolution's success, Banisadr joined Khomeini's Revolutionary Council and briefly served as Foreign Minister. However, his attempt to negotiate an end to the U.S. Embassy hostage crisis—which began November 4, 1979—resulted in his removal after just 18 days, as hard-liners gained influence. Despite this setback, Banisadr remained in power and championed the nationalization of major industries and private holdings from the shah's era. In early 1980, after Khomeini decreed that clerics should not hold the presidency, Banisadr won three-quarters of the vote for the newly created office. His inaugural address reflected his revolutionary ideals: "Our revolutionary will not win unless it is exported. We are going to create a new order in which deprived people will not always be deprived." However, Banisadr never consolidated genuine power. True authority remained firmly with Khomeini, and events beyond his control undermined his presidency. Iraq's 1980 invasion launched a devastating eight-year war, during which Banisadr served as commander-in-chief. Battlefield failures and conflicts with the Revolutionary Guard became political liabilities. He survived two helicopter crashes near the front lines but could not overcome the mounting opposition from hard-line clerics in parliament. The conflict between Banisadr and the clerical establishment intensified over his fundamental opposition to clerics holding political power—an ironic stance given that Khomeini embodied exactly this theocratic model. In June 1981, a parliament controlled by hard-liners impeached him. One month later, Banisadr escaped Iran aboard an Iranian Air Force Boeing 707, fleeing to France with Massoud Rajavi, leader of the leftist Mujahedeen-e-Khalq militant group. He reportedly shaved his trademark mustache for the escape, with Iranian media claiming he disguised himself as a woman. Later reflecting on his relationship with Khomeini, Banisadr said: "I was like a child watching my father slowly turn into an alcoholic. The drug this time was power." From his Paris exile, Banisadr co-founded the National Council of Resistance of Iran, though he withdrew in 1984 after the Mujahedeen-e-Khalq aligned with Iraqi dictator Saddam Hussein. He lived under police protection, targeted by suspected Iranian assassins. Banisadr gained additional notoriety by alleging without evidence that Ronald Reagan's campaign colluded with Iranian leaders to delay the hostage release, damaging Jimmy Carter's reelection bid. This unsubstantiated claim birthed the "October Surprise" concept in American politics, though Senate investigators later found no evidence supporting it. Throughout his exile, Banisadr remained a vocal critic of Khomeini's theocratic system, arguing that the clergy had betrayed Islam and democracy. He spent his final decades in the Paris area, a symbol of the revolutionary ideals that were ultimately eclipsed by religious authoritarianism.

When Donald Rumsfeld died at age 88, many Iraqis reacted with anger rather than mourning, seeing him as one of the chief figures responsible for the destruction of their country. In Baghdad, Ali Ridha al-Tamimi told his wife and four children that Rumsfeld was “the person who ruined our country,” saying he would never forgive him for the suffering he caused. His feelings reflected a broader Iraqi view that Rumsfeld’s legacy is inseparable from the 2003 U.S.-led invasion that toppled Saddam Hussein and unleashed years of violence. Rumsfeld, who served as defense secretary under President George W. Bush, was one of the main architects and most vocal defenders of the invasion, which was justified by claims that Saddam possessed weapons of mass destruction. Those claims later proved baseless. Iraqis say the U.S. and its allies failed to plan for the aftermath of the invasion, and one of the first major decisions — dissolving Iraqi security forces — helped create a power vacuum that fueled sectarian conflict, extremist attacks, militia violence, and repeated car bombings. Rumsfeld is also remembered in Iraq for the Abu Ghraib prison scandal, where detainees in U.S. custody were abused and tortured in 2004. The prison, already infamous under Saddam for imprisoning and executing opponents, became a symbol of American humiliation and abuse after the scandal emerged. Rumsfeld later called Abu Ghraib his darkest hour as defense secretary. When news of his death broke in the United States on Wednesday, Iraqis took to social media to express bitterness and anger. Some posted “Rot in Hell,” while others called him a war criminal. For many, his death revived painful memories of the period after the invasion, which they associate with death, detention, torture, and national collapse. Al-Tamimi said he personally blamed Rumsfeld for his own arrest in 2006 on suspicion of anti-U.S. activity. He said he was held for two years in Camp Bucca prison in southern Iraq without conviction, while his son grew up barely knowing him. His son was just over a month old when he was detained. Al-Tamimi was eventually found innocent by an Iraqi court and released in 2008. He said of Rumsfeld, “He killed me while I was alive.” Other Iraqis echoed the same sense of betrayal. Journalist Muntader al-Zaidi, known for throwing his shoes at Bush in 2008, tweeted: “He is gone and Baghdad remains.” Political researcher Ihsan Alshamary called Rumsfeld “a black mark on the history of Iraq,” blaming him for the occupation and for policies that helped shape today’s political order. Baghdad resident Jawad al-Tai said he felt relief that one of those responsible for the deaths of thousands was dead, adding that Rumsfeld had not liberated Iraq but killed it. The article notes that some Iraqis were initially hopeful after Saddam’s fall, but that optimism faded as the U.S. struggled to manage the aftermath and Iraq descended into instability. Activist Sajad al-Rikabi said Iraq’s current corruption and broken political system stem from Rumsfeld’s policies, and that he would only say “Rest in Peace” if the U.S. dismantled the system he helped create.

# Summary: Iraqis React to Donald Rumsfeld's Death with Anger and Resentment When former U.S. Defense Secretary Donald Rumsfeld died at age 88, many Iraqis responded with hostility rather than sympathy, viewing him as responsible for their nation's destruction. The reaction reflects deep wounds from the 2003 U.S.-led invasion that toppled dictator Saddam Hussein and set Iraq on a devastating path. Rumsfeld served as a principal architect of the invasion, which was premised on claims that Saddam possessed weapons of mass destruction—allegations that proved baseless. Iraqi citizens hold him accountable not only for the invasion itself but for the catastrophic decisions that followed, particularly the disbanding of Iraqi security forces. This decision created a security vacuum that unleashed years of sectarian violence, extremist attacks, and car bombings that claimed thousands of lives. The Abu Ghraib prison scandal further cemented Rumsfeld's negative legacy in Iraqi memory. The facility, notorious under Saddam's regime for torture and executions, became infamous again in 2004 when American guards perpetrated shocking abuses against detainees. Rumsfeld later called this his darkest hour as defense secretary. Ali Ridha al-Tamimi, an Iraqi who was detained in 2006 on suspicion of anti-U.S. activities, exemplifies the personal suffering many experienced. Held for two years in Camp Bucca prison without conviction, he missed his son's infancy and early childhood. Though eventually found innocent and released in 2008, al-Tamimi said Rumsfeld "killed me while I was alive." He taught his children that Rumsfeld "ruined our country" and "destroyed many families." Upon learning of Rumsfeld's death, many Iraqis took to social media expressing anger. Some called him a war criminal and wished him to "rot in hell." Journalist Muntader al-Zaidi, famous for throwing his shoes at President Bush during a 2008 news conference in protest of the invasion, tweeted simply: "He is gone and Baghdad remains." Iraqi researchers and activists similarly condemned Rumsfeld's legacy. Ihsan Alshamary, a political affairs researcher, described him as "a black mark on Iraq's history," responsible for bringing corrupt politicians who continue controlling the country. Jawad al-Tai, a Baghdad resident, stated bluntly: "He didn't liberate us. This is a myth. He killed us and told us to thank him for it." The contrast between American and Iraqi perspectives on Rumsfeld is stark. In Washington, former colleagues remembered him as intelligent, patriotic, and skilled, though acknowledging the Iraq invasion's disastrous nature. President Bush praised his "steady service as a wartime secretary of defense." However, Iraqis view the consequences differently. While some initially welcomed Saddam's removal and hoped for positive change, that optimism evaporated as American uncertainty about post-invasion governance became apparent. The resulting power vacuum allowed violent Sunni extremist groups, militias, and Iranian-backed Shiite militias to flourish, destabilizing the nation for decades. Sajad al-Rikabi, a 38-year-old activist who participated in 2019 anti-corruption protests, encapsulates this perspective. He holds the U.S. responsible for Iraq's broken state and current political problems, stating he would only wish Rumsfeld "rest in peace" if America dismantled the system he created. For many Iraqis, Rumsfeld's death cannot bring closure to wounds that continue affecting their nation today.

The International Energy Agency said Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates could help steady oil markets by increasing crude production, as global supplies remain tight and spare capacity is limited. The warning came as Brent crude briefly climbed to $92.75 a barrel and later settled at fresh seven-year highs, reflecting persistent concerns about underproduction, recovering demand, and geopolitical risks. In its monthly oil report, the IEA said market risks with broad economic consequences could be eased if Middle Eastern producers with spare capacity made up for shortfalls elsewhere. Saudi Arabia and the UAE were identified as the producers with the largest available spare capacity. The agency also noted that if OPEC+ — the alliance of OPEC members and partners such as Russia — fully reversed its current production cuts, it could add 4.3 million barrels per day back to the market. But doing so would reduce effective spare capacity to just 2.5 million barrels per day by the end of the year, with most of that remaining capacity concentrated in Saudi Arabia and, to a lesser extent, the UAE. The IEA said OPEC+ continues to miss its monthly target of raising output by 400,000 barrels per day. In January, the gap widened to 900,000 barrels per day. Since the start of 2021, the bloc’s underperformance has effectively removed about 300 million barrels, or 800,000 barrels per day, from the market, the agency said. It added that a successful diplomatic agreement with Iran could eventually bring about 1.3 million barrels per day of Iranian oil back into circulation if U.S. sanctions were lifted. The agency said oil supply and demand may be roughly balanced in the first quarter, but could shift into surplus in the second quarter or later in the year. However, it stressed that immediate oversupply is unlikely because depleted inventories need to be rebuilt. OECD oil stocks fell by 60 million barrels in December to seven-year lows. Oil prices surged further on Friday as fears intensified that Russia might invade Ukraine, raising the prospect of disruption to energy supplies. Brent crude closed up $3.03, or 3.3 percent, at $94.44 a barrel, while U.S. West Texas Intermediate rose $3.22, or 3.6 percent, to $93.10. Both benchmarks reached their highest levels since late 2014 and posted their eighth straight weekly gain. The IEA also raised its 2022 demand forecast, saying global oil demand is expected to grow by 3.2 million barrels per day to a record 100.6 million barrels per day. The Biden administration said it had been speaking with major producers about increasing output and possible additional strategic releases. Meanwhile, indirect U.S.-Iran nuclear talks resumed this week, and U.S. drillers added 19 rigs, the biggest weekly increase in four years, bringing the total to 516, the highest since April 2020.

# Saudi Arabia and UAE Could Help Stabilize Oil Markets The International Energy Agency (IEA) reports that Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates could reduce oil market volatility by increasing crude production, as both nations hold the world's largest spare production capacity. Following the IEA's report of tight global supply, Brent crude oil futures surged to near seven-year highs, reaching $92.75 per barrel. The IEA raised its 2022 demand forecasts and confirmed that OPEC+ missed its January output targets by an even wider margin than previously reported. If OPEC+ completely unwound current output cuts, they could add 4.3 million barrels per day to the market. However, this would reduce effective spare capacity to just 2.5 million barrels per day by year's end, concentrated almost entirely in Saudi Arabia and the UAE. OPEC+ has consistently underperformed, missing its monthly target of 400,000 additional barrels per day. In January alone, the gap widened to 900,000 barrels per day. Since 2021, this prolonged underperformance has effectively removed 300 million barrels from the market. Potential relief could come from ongoing international negotiations with Iran. A successful deal lifting U.S. sanctions could gradually return 1.3 million barrels per day of Iranian oil to global markets. The IEA expects supply and demand to balance in the first quarter, then shift toward surplus in the second quarter or later in the year. Oil prices climbed 3 percent Friday, with Brent crude settling at $94.44 per barrel and U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude rising to $93.10—both reaching their highest levels since late 2014. This eighth consecutive week of gains reflects growing supply concerns amid recovering demand following the coronavirus pandemic. Geopolitical tensions significantly amplified price increases. Russia's military buildup near Ukraine prompted U.S. warnings of a potential major invasion and urged American citizens to leave within 48 hours. Fears of Russian supply disruptions and retaliatory sanctions on energy exports drove trading volumes to their highest in over two months. The IEA forecasts global demand will expand by 3.2 million barrels per day in 2022, reaching a record 100.6 million barrels per day. Depleted oil stocks in OECD countries, which fell to seven-year lows in December, require refilling, making immediate oversupply unlikely despite expected second-half surpluses. The Biden administration continues discussions with major oil producers about increased output and potential additional strategic petroleum reserve releases. Meanwhile, U.S. drillers added the most oil rigs in four years, with the rig count rising to 516—its highest since April 2020—suggesting future domestic production increases.

Eight people were killed Wednesday when a pickup truck and passenger bus collided on al-Bayda’s main road in central Yemen, according to state media. Several others were critically injured and taken to hospital. Residents blamed dangerous roads worsened by years of conflict and poor maintenance.

# Summary A pickup truck and passenger bus collided Wednesday in Yemen's central al-Bayda province, killing eight people and critically injuring several others. The accident occurred on the main road. Poor road conditions from Yemen's prolonged military conflict and lack of maintenance contributed to the deadly crash.

The Syrian Defense Ministry announced on Tuesday evening a four-day ceasefire with the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF), saying all firing by the Syrian Arab Army would stop from 20:00 local time. The ministry said the pause, which would last four days, followed understandings reached with the SDF and was intended to support national efforts to stabilize the situation. The SDF confirmed it had accepted the ceasefire and said it would not carry out military operations unless attacked. It also said it remained open to political dialogue, negotiated solutions, and implementing the January 18 agreement in a way that promotes de-escalation and stability. As part of broader efforts to integrate Kurdish forces into the Syrian state, the defense ministry said it had asked the SDF to name a candidate for the post of assistant to the defense minister in Damascus. The announcement came amid wider political contacts. Syrian President Ahmad al-Sharaa spoke by phone with Masoud Barzani, leader of Iraq’s Kurdistan Democratic Party, about regional developments and ways to strengthen stability and security. According to the Syrian presidency, both sides agreed to continue coordination and consultations to preserve peace and resolve differences in a way that serves all parties. Sharaa said Kurdish rights are guaranteed, including national, political, and civil rights, while Barzani voiced support for the agreement between Damascus and the SDF. Despite the ceasefire, the SDF soon accused government-allied factions of violating it. The group said heavy weapons were used in an attack on Tal Baroud, near the Abyad road south of Hasakah, and that Zarkan was under intense artillery fire. SDF spokesperson Farhad Shami also said Damascus-backed forces attacked al-Aqtan Prison north of Raqqa with five suicide drones and heavy gunfire. The ceasefire followed rapid government gains over the past several days, including the seizure of SDF-held territory in the biggest shift in control since Bashar al-Assad’s fall. The Interior Ministry said government forces had begun taking control of the al-Hol camp in northeastern Syria, which houses families of ISIL fighters and other displaced people. The SDF had already abandoned the camp. It still controls Hasakah and Kurdish-majority Qamishli, and Damascus said it would not enter those cities during the ceasefire. Under military pressure, the SDF also agreed to withdraw from the Arab-majority governorates of Raqqa and Deir Az Zor, including Syria’s main oilfields. Syria’s UN ambassador, Ibrahim Olabi, said the government hoped the ceasefire would hold and was working with U.S. partners to ensure that it does.

# Syrian Government and SDF Announce Four-Day Ceasefire The Syrian Defense Ministry announced a four-day ceasefire with the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) on Tuesday evening, effective from 20:00 local time. The ministry stated it would halt all firing across operational sectors, citing "understandings announced by the Syrian state with the SDF" and efforts to ensure success of national initiatives. The SDF confirmed acceptance and pledged not to engage in military action unless attacked, while affirming openness to political dialogue and implementation of a January 18 agreement. As part of integration efforts, the defense ministry requested the SDF nominate a candidate for assistant defense minister. Syrian President Ahmad al-Sharaa also spoke with Kurdistan Democratic Party leader Masoud Barzani, discussing regional stability and coordination. Sharaa emphasized guarantees of full Kurdish rights—national, political, and civil—while Barzani expressed support for the government-SDF agreement. However, the ceasefire faced immediate challenges. Shortly after taking effect, the SDF reported that government-allied groups attacked Tal Baroud village with heavy weapons, shelled the town of Zarkan with artillery, and launched five suicide drones and heavy gunfire at al-Aqtan Prison north of Raqqa. The ceasefire followed rapid Syrian government military advances and territorial gains from the SDF, marking President Sharaa's biggest success since former leader Bashar al-Assad's fall. The Syrian military seized control of the al-Hol camp, housing thousands of ISIS fighters' families and refugees, which the SDF had abandoned. The SDF retained control of Hasakah and Qamishli cities, which the government agreed not to enter during the ceasefire. Under military pressure, the SDF withdrew from Arab-majority governorates Raqqa and Deir Az Zor, containing Syria's primary oilfields. Syria's UN ambassador Ibrahim Olabi expressed hope the ceasefire would hold, noting coordination with the United States to ensure its success.

Turkey sharply escalated tensions with the United States by shelling Kurdish forces in northern Syria and signaling plans for a new cross-border offensive east of the Euphrates River. The Turkish Army fired artillery into areas held by the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF), which are allied with Washington in the fight against Islamic State. Turkish state media said the shelling killed ten Kurdish fighters. In response, the SDF said it reserved the right to retaliate, and Kurdish rebels said they destroyed a Turkish armored personnel carrier near the border. President Recep Tayyip Erdogan told lawmakers from his ruling Justice and Development Party that Turkey would destroy “terrorist structures” east of the Euphrates, a zone that had previously been off limits to Turkish forces. He later said Turkey had “finalised” its preparations and would launch a more comprehensive operation soon. Anadolu reported that Turkish bombardment of YPG positions began on October 28, and Erdogan described the shelling as the start of “active engagement” against what he called a terrorist organization. The United States expressed concern, especially because American personnel could be nearby. Deputy State Department spokesman Robert Palladino said unilateral strikes in northwestern Syria by any party were “of great concern” to Washington. The escalation came shortly after the United States and Turkey resolved a separate dispute over the detention of an American pastor in Turkey, a case that had badly shaken the Turkish currency. The deeper dispute remains Turkey’s hostility to the Kurdish People’s Protection Units (YPG), which Ankara considers a terrorist group and a threat to Turkish security. The YPG is the backbone of the SDF and has been a key US partner against ISIS. Turkey also opposes Washington’s continued support for the Kurdish forces and is simultaneously at odds with the US over Ankara’s planned purchase of a Russian missile defense system. According to pro-government Turkish media, Ankara’s longer-term goal is to create a 30-kilometer-deep “safe zone” running along the Syrian border from the Euphrates in the west to Iraq in the east. Turkey argues such zones are needed to repatriate some 3 million Syrian refugees who fled into Turkey during the war. Defence Minister Hulusi Akar said 260,000 refugees had already returned to Jarabulus since 2016. Critics, however, say Turkey is using refugee returns to alter the ethnic balance in Kurdish areas by resettling more pro-Turkish Arabs. The article notes that a major Turkish incursion could endanger around 2,000 US troops stationed in northern Syria to support and arm the YPG. At the same time, Turkey and the US have been trying to manage their rivalry through limited cooperation, including joint patrols in Manbij west of the Euphrates, where the YPG agreed to withdraw earlier this year. Erdogan’s announcement also followed a summit in Istanbul with the leaders of Russia, France, and Germany, which pushed for a truce in Idlib and a political process for Syria’s future without demanding that Bashar Assad leave power. Analysts said the meeting underscored broader international efforts to shape Syria’s postwar order while the United States pursues its own approach.

# Turkey Escalates Military Pressure in Syria Amid US Concerns Turkey has intensified military operations against Kurdish forces in northern Syria, creating significant tension with the United States and raising regional instability. Turkish artillery shelled Kurdish positions allied with America in the fight against ISIS, killing ten fighters according to Turkey's state news agency. President Recep Tayyip Erdogan subsequently announced plans for a major cross-border military operation east of the Euphrates River, a previously restricted zone. The US government expressed serious concern about the strikes, with Deputy State Department spokesman Robert Palladino warning that "unilateral military strikes into north-western Syria by any party, particularly as American personnel may be present or in the vicinity, are of great concern to us." The Kurdish-dominated Syrian Democratic Forces vowed to retaliate, claiming they destroyed a Turkish armored vehicle in response. The core dispute centers on Turkey's opposition to the Kurdish People's Protection Units (YPG), whom Ankara designates as terrorists despite their effectiveness against ISIS. Turkey views the YPG's control of Syrian border territory as a security threat, while the United States considers them vital allies, with approximately 2,000 American troops deployed in northern Syria supporting them. Erdogan declared that Turkey has "finalized our preparations, our plans, our programmes" for military action. Turkish media reports indicate Ankara plans to establish a 30-kilometer-wide corridor along the Turkish-Syrian border, effectively eliminating Kurdish presence in the region. Turkey justifies this by claiming safe zones are necessary for repatriating 3 million Syrian refugees, though critics argue the initiative actually increases pro-Turkish Arab populations in Kurdish areas. This escalation follows Turkey's recent resolution of a dispute with the United States over a detained American pastor, though tensions persist over other issues, including Turkey's intention to purchase Russian missile defense systems. The timing is significant, occurring three days after Erdogan hosted leaders from Russia, France, and Germany in Istanbul—notably excluding the United States. That summit focused on Syrian ceasefire efforts and political solutions, signaling increased international coordination that may undermine American interests in Syria. Analysts suggest the conference strengthened parties seeking American withdrawal from northern Syria. Joshua Landis, director of the Centre for Middle East Studies at the University of Oklahoma, stated that "Turkey, Syria, Iran and Russia want to drive the US out of North Syria and end its alliance with the YPG." However, some observers note potential for compromise. Turkey and the United States have begun joint military patrols in Manbij, a northern Syrian city, after the YPG agreed to withdraw. Professor Ilter Turan of Istanbul's Bilgi University suggested this arrangement demonstrates that direct confrontation between Ankara and Washington may be avoidable. Washington maintains that its YPG relationship is purely tactical and temporary, focused on defeating ISIS, while attempting to reassure Turkey without abandoning its Kurdish partners. This balancing act remains precarious as Turkey demonstrates increasing willingness to act unilaterally against Kurdish forces, potentially forcing a crisis between the NATO allies.

Taliban fighters in Afghanistan seized control of the Spin Boldak border crossing with Pakistan on Wednesday, marking one of their most significant gains as they rapidly advanced across the country during the U.S. troop withdrawal. The crossing lies in the town of Wesh in Afghanistan’s Spin Boldak district, opposite Chaman in Pakistan, and is one of the country’s most important trade routes. It is Afghanistan’s second-busiest entry point and a major commercial artery linking the southwest with Pakistani sea ports. Afghan government data say about 900 trucks use the route each day. Video released by the Taliban showed their white flag flying above the Friendship Gate at the crossing, replacing the Afghan flag. In the footage, a Taliban fighter declared that after “two decades of the brutality of Americans and their puppets,” the gate and the district had been captured, and said resistance had forced the enemy to withdraw. Afghan officials claimed government forces had pushed back the Taliban and were in control of the district, but civilians and Pakistani officials said the militants still held the crossing. A Pakistani security official said Wesh had been captured, while officials in Chaman said the Taliban had suspended all travel through the gate. The seizure of Spin Boldak came amid a broader Taliban offensive that has also taken other border crossings in Herat, Farah and Kunduz provinces. Analysts and business leaders said control of these posts gives the Taliban a new source of revenue. Shafiqullah Attai, chairman of the Afghanistan Chamber of Commerce and Investment, said border posts allow the militants to collect income. The Taliban, which ruled Afghanistan from 1996 until being ousted in 2001 after the U.S. bombing campaign following the Sept. 11 attacks, have been trying to topple the Western-backed government ever since. Their renewed momentum has been fueled by President Joe Biden’s decision to withdraw all U.S. troops by August, with American forces having left their main base two weeks earlier. Barry’s Bay is preparing to celebrate the opening of a redeveloped children’s park on its waterfront, and the park will bear the name of Mervin Olsheski. For some residents, especially those who remember him as a thin, scrappy boy growing up in Barry’s Bay in the 1960s, the honour may seem surprising. But a celebration of life held a week earlier at his pioneer farm in the Wilno Hills offered an answer: Olsheski was an extraordinary self-made man whose energy, business success, and larger-than-life personality left a lasting mark on his community and far beyond it. Mervin Wilfred Valentine Olsheski was born on Valentine’s Day eve in 1958, one of eight children in the Olsheski family. His siblings were Donald, Edgar, Gail, Connie, Wayne, Cynthia and Michelle. The article suggests that anyone who knew the Olsheski children in the 1960s would understand how unusual Mervin’s eventual life was: his rise from modest beginnings reflected intelligence, hard work and determination overcoming adversity and disadvantage, if not improbability itself. Olsheski died in Ukraine on June 22 of this year. The article says the details of how he came to be there, what he was doing there, and how his body was returned to Canada are known with certainty only to his wife, Wanda, a local schoolteacher, and their two children, Joseph and Kasia. What is clear, however, is that he had built a highly successful business career and accumulated great wealth. Yet those who gathered to remember him said that his money mattered far less than his personality, his loyalty to family and friends, and his appetite for life. At the celebration in the Wilno Hills, Robert Howe—his lawyer and longtime friend—served as master of ceremonies. Howe had first helped establish Merol Constructors Incorporated in 1981, after Olsheski graduated with a civil engineering degree. The event was anything but solemn in the usual sense. When Howe began by saying, “This is a celebration of Mervin’s life,” he was interrupted by applause, cheering, whistles, hoots, catcalls, and occasional swearing. That response, the article notes, was fitting for a man whose life was anything but ordinary. Howe described Olsheski as someone who packed “at least 100 years of living into his 66 years.” He said no one who spent even a few minutes with him could forget him. Beyond his boisterous personality, Olsheski was known for relentless work. While still in high school, he started a trucking business, hauling gravel and plowing snow. At age 23, after founding Merol Constructors, he won a government contract to install a series of beacons along the Distant Early Warning Line in the far north. He later built 25 CMHC houses in Renfrew County. In 1987, he created another company, Merol Power, and took on the rehabilitation of an old dam on the Mississippi River at Appleton near Carleton Place, where he established a hydroelectric power plant. He lived on the job site until the work was finished. After selling that project, he used some of the proceeds to go to Poland, where he completed three more similar dam projects under the name Merol Power Polska. He also purchased and refurbished an office tower in downtown Warsaw and later, with a partner, established a Swish Commercial Cleaning Products business there as well. Howe said Olsheski succeeded through “blood, sweat and tears” over the course of his life. He also praised his business judgment, saying Olsheski could tell what would work and what would not, and that he knew of no business failures. But Howe emphasized that Olsheski was not only a businessman; he was also deeply curious. Despite his hard work, he was always reading, analyzing, questioning and studying. He tried to anticipate the future, but he also looked to the past, believing that history offered lessons for the present and future. He was proud of his heritage and of the history of Poland and the Kaszuby region. That historical interest showed in several of his actions. He supported the creation of Wilno Heritage Park. He commissioned paintings of Poland and Kaszuby and displayed the work of local artists such as Al Burant and Michael Dombroskie. He also helped arrange for a stone from Kaszuby to be transported to Poland and placed at the Canadian embassy in Warsaw. Olsheski was also engaged with international affairs. Through extensive travel in Ukraine, Romania, Belarus, Russia and Kazakhstan, he developed first-hand knowledge of the region. In the late 1990s, he joined two Canadian trade missions to Poland. Howe said he even mingled with Russian oligarchs at Vladimir Putin’s hunting lodge. According to Howe, Olsheski predicted Russia’s invasion of Ukraine at least two months before it occurred. Locally, Olsheski served two terms on the former Sherwood, Jones and Burns Township council. Howe portrayed him as a complicated man: not humble, but modest; aware of his intelligence and usually confident in his conclusions; someone who disliked fools, but who trusted capable professionals such as doctors, lawyers and accountants when he respected their judgment. He was also willing to admit when he was wrong and to apologize. Other friends at the celebration echoed that assessment. Gerald Tracey, publisher of The Eganville Leader, Tony Yantha, a cousin and retired co-owner of the Barry’s Bay Dairy, and neighbor Mike Papania all said they valued him not for his wealth, which he did not flaunt, but for his exuberance, his adventurous spirit and his gift for storytelling. He turned business into adventure and was known for telling hilarious stories about himself and his life. Many said he would swear just as freely with the Pope or Queen as he would with anyone else, but would have them laughing within minutes. Howe said Olsheski never forgot his humble beginnings. He was generous without seeking attention for it. One example given was that he provided accommodation in Poland for Ukrainian refugees fleeing the Russian invasion. He was also described as a keen hunter, a hockey player in his youth, an accomplished downhill skier, and a decent golfer—especially if money was on the line. Whatever he did, Howe said, he gave it 100 percent or more, but he took calculated risks rather than reckless ones. A more personal tribute came from Lynn Howe, Robert Howe’s spouse, who had been Mervin’s smoking buddy and a close friend of Wanda. She said Olsheski could not easily be flattered or complimented, so for his 65th birthday she wrote him a poem instead of buying a gift. The poem captured his character in affectionate, humorous lines: “Mervin is the name, dams are his game,” it began, and went on to describe his swearing, his lack of pretension, his fairness, his long memory, and his deep knowledge of history. She called him “the best” of friends, while joking that she wished he would rest because, without him, no one else would tell the stories. The article closes by noting that Olsheski’s death in June is a profound loss for his family, friends and relatives. Yet his memory will endure not only in stories but also in the waterfront park in Barry’s Bay that will carry his name. For those who knew him, his legacy is that of a remarkable, self-made man whose wild, chaotic, generous, and unforgettable life was worth far more than money alone could measure.

American soldiers who fled to Canada instead of deploying to Iraq are pressing the Justin Trudeau government to stop legal proceedings against them and grant them permanent residency. At a Toronto news conference on Friday, the war resisters were joined by activists and Liberal backbencher Nathaniel Erskine-Smith, who said he was hopeful the government would act, though he offered no details. A Lowell, Michigan school librarian is suing a parent, alleging the woman led a yearslong harassment and smear campaign over the school library’s book collection. In the lawsuit, Beachler claims Boone posted numerous social media messages, texts and videos over the past five years calling her a “smut-peddling media specialist,” “groomer” and “pedophile.” Beachler says the accusations falsely portray her as engaging in criminal conduct and abusing children. She told News 8 the attacks have become severe enough that she has received death threats and now avoids going out in the community because she has been confronted there. Beachler said the controversy began after Boone, a member of the conservative group Moms for Liberty, challenged library books she believed were inappropriate. Boone has argued at school board meetings that schools should not expose children to sexually explicit material. Beachler said Lowell Area Schools has more than 75,000 books across six libraries, and only two titles have been challenged for mature content in the past five years. She said a committee and the school board read both books in full and decided to keep them. She also emphasized that library books are optional, not required curriculum, and noted that parents can restrict what their own children may access. Beachler is suing Boone for invasion of privacy and intentional infliction of emotional distress. News 8 said Boone and her attorney declined interview requests.

The United States urged Sudan’s army chief, Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, to join ceasefire talks that opened in Switzerland on Wednesday, even as only the rival Rapid Support Forces (RSF) took part at the start. The war in Sudan has raged since April 2023, pitting the Sudanese army, led by Burhan as the country’s de facto ruler, against the paramilitary RSF headed by his former deputy, Mohamed Hamdan Daglo. Because Burhan did not attend the opening session, US Secretary of State Antony Blinken called him directly and pressed him to participate. According to State Department spokesman Vedant Patel, Blinken stressed the “urgent need” for both sides to end the war and ensure humanitarian access for millions of Sudanese who are suffering. US special envoy Tom Perriello said after the session that it was “high time for the guns to be silenced.” The talks, expected to last up to 10 days, are being held behind closed doors at an undisclosed location in Switzerland. They are co-hosted by Saudi Arabia and Switzerland, with the African Union, Egypt, the United Arab Emirates and the United Nations forming a steering group. However, the Sudanese armed forces are unhappy with the format set by Washington. Sudanese Media Minister Graham Abdelkader said the government rejected “any new observers or participants,” after the US insisted that the UAE attend as an observer. The army has repeatedly accused the UAE of supporting the RSF, which the UAE denies. Humanitarian access is a central issue in the negotiations. Perriello said the goal was to secure a cessation of hostilities, improve aid delivery and establish enforcement mechanisms that produce concrete results. The conflict has created one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises: one in five Sudanese has been displaced, tens of thousands have been killed, and more than 25 million people—over half the population—face acute hunger. Doctors Without Borders said both sides had manipulated humanitarian access in violation of international law. MSF’s Sudan programme manager Vittorio Oppizzi argued that safe, unhindered aid access should not depend on a ceasefire or a political settlement. Analysts said Burhan faces internal divisions and mounting external pressure. Previous talks in Jeddah failed, and some experts argued Washington was trying to create momentum without having enough leverage. Meanwhile, fighting continued on the ground, with volunteer lawyers reporting increased RSF shelling of civilian areas, including attacks in El-Fasher and Omdurman on a school, a bus and a hospital. Outside UN headquarters in Geneva, about 100 protesters called for action and an immediate ceasefire, while Sudanese attendees said they wanted peace and justice for their country.

# US Presses Sudan Army Chief as Ceasefire Talks Open Ceasefire negotiations began in Switzerland on Wednesday with a significant absence: Sudan's army chief Abdel Fattah al-Burhan failed to attend, prompting urgent appeals from the United States. The talks opened with only the rival Rapid Support Forces (RSF) delegation present, highlighting deep divisions in efforts to end Sudan's devastating conflict. ## The Conflict War has devastated Sudan since April 2023, pitting the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) under de facto ruler Burhan against the paramilitary RSF, led by his former deputy Mohamed Hamdan Daglo. The conflict has created one of the world's worst humanitarian crises, forcing one in five people to flee their homes, killing tens of thousands, and leaving over 25 million Sudanese—more than half the population—facing acute hunger. ## Diplomatic Efforts US Secretary of State Antony Blinken telephoned Burhan directly, urging his participation and emphasizing the "urgent need" to end the war and ensure humanitarian access. Tom Perriello, the US special envoy for Sudan, stated it was "high time for the guns to be silenced." The talks, potentially lasting ten days, are co-hosted by Saudi Arabia and Switzerland, with the African Union, Egypt, the UAE, and UN as steering group members. ## Points of Contention The SAF objected to the talks' format, particularly Washington's insistence that the United Arab Emirates participate as an observer. The Sudanese government has repeatedly accused the UAE of backing the RSF, allegations the UAE denies. Sudan's Media Minister rejected "any new observers or participants." ## Humanitarian Concerns Medical charity Doctors Without Borders reported that both parties have "manipulated" humanitarian access in violation of international law. This week, increased indiscriminate artillery shelling by the RSF struck civilian areas including schools, hospitals, and buses carrying passengers. ## Analysis and Pressure Analysts suggest Burhan faces mounting pressure and internal divisions within his camp. Some supporters favor negotiations while others fiercely oppose talks. Alan Boswell from the International Crisis Group noted that Burhan could face severe consequences if viewed as "the main obstacle to ending the war." However, skeptics question whether the talks will succeed. Cameron Hudson from the Center for Strategic and International Studies argues the SAF won't negotiate without facing battlefield losses, diplomatic isolation, or economic devastation—pressures that don't currently exist. ## Public Sentiment Around 100 demonstrators gathered outside UN headquarters in Geneva, demanding immediate ceasefire and peace negotiations. Participants emphasized the urgency of ending the conflict and achieving justice for Sudanese victims. Previous ceasefire talks in Saudi Arabia's Jeddah proved unsuccessful, raising questions about whether these negotiations will achieve different results.

Congress is asking the Pentagon and State Department to produce a detailed assessment of whether the United States should expand its military presence in the Baltic states and what resources would be required to do so. The request is included in the conference report for the fiscal 2020 National Defense Authorization Act, which was still awaiting final passage when the report was released. The House passed the bill on Dec. 11, and the Senate was expected to vote Dec. 12. The three Baltic countries — Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia — have long sought a steadier and stronger American military presence as a deterrent to Russia. Since Russia’s annexation of Crimea in 2014, NATO and the U.S. military have already significantly increased their footprint in Eastern Europe. That buildup has included NATO rapid response forces, U.S. units embedded with Baltic forces, expanded equipment stockpiles, a rotational U.S. armored brigade combat team and combat aviation brigade, and more complex exercises. Baltic defense leaders say the enhanced forward presence battalions deployed in the region have lowered the risk of military conflict, but they still want further reinforcement, particularly from U.S. troops, to strengthen security against Russia. The legislation directs the Pentagon and State Department to jointly deliver a comprehensive report one year after enactment. The report must evaluate past and current efforts to improve the Baltic states’ defense capabilities and explain how those improvements can be achieved in the future, including resource needs and recommendations. Congress wants the analysis to cover rotational and forward U.S. presence, broader posture improvements, and the ability of the U.S. and NATO to respond quickly. Several specific areas are required. These include air defense systems, modern air-surveillance capabilities and counter-drone defenses, which are especially important to the Baltics given Russia’s military capabilities. Lawmakers also want recommendations on command-and-control improvements through secure and hardened technology, better capacity and coordination, and stronger intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance. The report must also address maritime domain awareness, cybersecurity and electronic warfare. Infrastructure and logistics are another priority, especially the transport of military supplies and equipment across the region. The report should also assess pre-positioned stockpiles, ammunition storage, and investments already made in those areas. In addition, Congress wants information on bilateral and multilateral training and exercises, cost-sharing arrangements with NATO allies, and possible host-nation contributions. The final report is to be submitted in unclassified form, though it may include a classified annex. It should also identify current funding sources for assistance, what additional funds may be needed, and how those funds could be obtained.

The Baltic nations have consistently expressed strong desire for increased and more permanent American military presence. Since Russia's 2014 annexation of Crimea, NATO and the U.S. have substantially expanded their Eastern European footprint through multiple initiatives: deploying NATO rapid response forces, embedding units under Baltic command, stockpiling equipment, rotating armored and aviation brigades, and conducting increasingly sophisticated exercises. The enhanced forward presence battalions currently deployed in the Baltics have significantly reduced military conflict risks, according to regional defense leaders. However, Baltic states continue prioritizing further American troop deployments to strengthen regional security. The legislation requires the Pentagon and State Department to jointly produce a detailed report within one year of enactment. This assessment must evaluate past and present defense improvement efforts, identify necessary improvements, and outline future resource requirements and recommendations. The report should specifically address several critical areas. Air defense systems and modern air-surveillance capabilities rank as top priorities for Baltic states facing potential Russian threats. The assessment must also cover counter-drone capabilities, command-and-control improvements through secure technology, intelligence and surveillance capabilities, maritime domain awareness, cybersecurity, and electronic warfare. Infrastructure and logistics improvements are essential, particularly regarding military supply transport. While equipment movement across the Baltics presents challenges, improvements are expected as countries upgrade rail lines from Soviet-era gauges. The report should account for pre-positioned ammunition stocks and storage investments. Additionally, Congress wants information on bilateral and multilateral training exercises, cost-sharing arrangements between the U.S. and NATO allies, and potential host country contributions. The report should describe current funding sources and identify additional resources needed. The House passed the NDAA on December 11, with Senate approval expected December 12. Congress has requested an unclassified version with potential classified annexes, ensuring public transparency while protecting sensitive information. The comprehensive assessment will inform future decisions about America's military commitment to the strategically important Baltic region.

A displacement camp in northwest Syria was hit by cluster bombs on Sunday, Nov. 6, 2022, at about 7 a.m. Damascus time, killing nine civilians, including three children and one woman, and wounding more than 75 others, according to the Syrian Civil Defense. The strike targeted the Kafar Jalis camp, which shelters thousands of displaced people. In a separate incident, artillery shelling injured two civilians on the outskirts of Areeha and in the village of Sarmin, south of Idlib. The attacks were described as the first major violence in a relatively calm year in Syria. UOSSM-Canada condemned the use of internationally prohibited cluster bombs against civilians and called for the international community to stop such attacks.

# Summary On November 6, 2022, a displacement camp in Kafar Jalis, northwest Syria, was attacked with cluster bombs, killing nine civilians including three children and one woman, according to the Syrian Civil Defense. Over 75 others were wounded in the attack on the camp housing thousands of displaced people. In a separate incident, two civilians were injured by artillery shelling near Areeha and Sarmin, south of Idlib. These attacks marked the first major violence in a relatively peaceful year in Syria. Dr. Anas al Kassem of UOSSM-Canada condemned the use of internationally prohibited cluster bombs on civilians, calling for the international community to intervene and protect innocent lives.

Slovak parliamentary leaders Tibor Gaspar and Andrej Danko said their January visit to Moscow was intended to encourage broader peace efforts over the war in Ukraine, not to shift Slovakia away from its EU and NATO commitments. Speaking in Bratislava, Gaspar said the delegation wanted to send a symbolic signal to other member states to begin discussing how negotiations to end the war could start, and to press political leaders in their own countries to pursue peace. Danko said Slovak MPs were the first parliamentary delegation to visit Russia since the conflict began. Danko said he discussed the possibility of peace talks with Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov, adding that any first step would have to come from Russia and the United States. He also said another trip to Moscow is planned for May, when the delegation will attend commemorations marking the end of World War II. He insisted Slovakia had not crossed any limits of its EU or NATO alignment, though he reiterated that the country has the right to discuss reforms within the EU. The talks also touched on gas supplies. Danko said Slovakia buys large amounts of liquefied gas that is Russian in origin and more expensive than before, partly because it no longer transits through Ukraine. Gaspar said Russia justified its actions by pointing to NATO expansion and concerns over treatment of the Russian minority in Ukraine. He argued Slovaks should hear both sides of the conflict, while also acknowledging the war has caused heavy casualties. Both men dismissed criticism of the trip as hysterical and rejected claims that it would drag Slovakia into Russia’s sphere of influence.

# Summary A Slovak parliamentary delegation visited Moscow in January to encourage peace negotiations regarding the Ukraine conflict. House Vice-chair Tibor Gaspar stated the delegation aimed to signal other member states to begin discussing how to end the war, while SNS leader Andrej Danko announced plans for another visit in May for World War II commemorations. Danko claimed Slovak MPs were the first parliamentary delegation since the conflict began and met with Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov. He stated both sides want resolution, with the U.S. and Russia needing to take the first steps. The delegation emphasized that Slovakia's EU and NATO membership remained unchanged, though they asserted Slovakia's right to discuss EU reforms. Discussions also covered gas supplies, with Danko noting Slovakia purchases Russian liquefied gas at prices four times higher than market rates due to supplies no longer transiting Ukraine. Gaspar explained Russia's perspective on NATO expansion, stating their arguments "seemed logical" to him. He called for objective information from both sides, noting Slovakia only hears the Ukrainian viewpoint. However, he acknowledged questions about whether military conflict was necessary. Both officials dismissed criticism of their trip, rejecting suggestions it would pull Slovakia toward Russian influence.

Belarus and Russia will hold their joint Union Shield 2019 military exercise deep inside Russian territory rather than near the border, Belarusian First Deputy Defense Minister Oleg Belokonev said in Minsk on Wednesday. He said the decision was deliberate and intended to avoid aggravating tensions in Europe, especially amid what he described as an increased number of NATO exercises in Eastern Europe near the borders of the Union State. The exercise is scheduled for September 13-19 at a firing range near Mulino in Russia’s Nizhny Novgorod region. Belokonev said it is the final stage of the two-year training cycle of the Belarusian and Russian armed forces and is held every two years, with the two countries alternating as hosts under a decision by their presidents. He said planners considered possible threats to the Union State and the risk of military conflict, including scenarios in which unrest begins with terrorists, separatists, or illegal armed groups supported from abroad. The exercise will focus on responding to such a scenario. Union Shield 2019 is expected to involve about 12,000 troops, up to 950 combat vehicles, and as many as 70 aircraft and helicopters. Belarus will contribute more than 4,000 troops, over 30 tanks, 80 armored vehicles, about 50 multiple rocket launcher systems, other weapons and mortars, and around 15 aircraft and helicopters. Belarusian forces are expected to return to their permanent bases by October 4.

Rustam, a 47-year-old Uzbek man living near Samarkand, illustrates the difficult balance many families in Uzbekistan face between migration, low wages, and poverty. After spending much of his adult life doing construction and other work in Russia, he returned home and tried to open a small roadside shop near Samarkand. He had already invested in flooring the shop and buying refrigerators for soft drinks, but he ran out of money before stocking them. As he told RFE/RL, “It was more expensive than I thought. Now I don’t have money for products.” Rustam’s experience reflects a broader reality in Uzbekistan: the economy has become more open in recent years, but many people still have very little disposable income. While he lived in Sochi, Russia, he regularly sent $100 to $400 a month to his elderly father. But in 2019 he was deported from Russia over a migration violation, which he says was unfair. He cannot return until at least the end of 2024. Back home, he says the work he can find pays far less than what he was able to save abroad. Repair and renovation jobs in nearby Nurobod bring him only about $15 a day, and even in Samarkand the rate rises only to around $25 a day, with a significant portion lost to transport costs because he does not own a car. Like many Uzbek families, Rustam and his wife are considering labor migration as a survival strategy. They have discussed sending her to Israel to work as a live-in nurse for the elderly, a job that is in high demand in Samarkand Province and could pay around $2,000 a month under a five-year placement. But he says local middlemen demand more than $15,000 upfront to secure such a job. Rustam, who has been married since 1999, said the couple has lived together for only four years in that entire time. Their son has also gone to work in Russia for the first time this year. The article places Rustam’s story against the backdrop of Uzbekistan’s changing political and economic landscape. Samarkand recently hosted the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development’s annual meeting, the first time the event had been held in Uzbekistan since 2003. President Shavkat Mirziyoev used the occasion to present Uzbekistan as a country that has moved beyond the isolation and state control associated with former president Islam Karimov. In his remarks, Mirziyoev said “today’s Uzbekistan is not yesterday’s Uzbekistan” and highlighted Samarkand’s historic role as a crossroads of trade and culture. There is some evidence of economic reform. Since Mirziyoev took office in 2016, Uzbekistan has improved its ranking in the Heritage Foundation’s Index of Economic Freedom, rising from 166th out of 178 countries to 109th out of 176. The government has pushed privatization, sought foreign investment, and reduced some regulatory burdens. Reforms have also included ending systemic forced labor in the cotton sector, making the som fully convertible, and easing travel restrictions to boost tourism. Yet the article emphasizes that these gains have not translated evenly into prosperity, especially in poorer regions like Nurobod district near Samarkand. The district’s administrative center, once known as Sovietobod, was historically supported by Soviet-era economic priorities, but today average salaries are well below the national average. Uzbekistan’s state statistics committee says the national average is around $300 per month, but many local wages fall short of that. Eric Livny, the EBRD’s lead regional economist for Central Asia, said he remained optimistic about Uzbekistan’s long-term prospects, but acknowledged that low wages are a structural issue. He explained that the country has a young and growing population and not enough decent jobs, which creates downward pressure on wages. In his words, for unskilled labor “it is a buyer’s market,” limiting consumption and demand. Still, he argued that living standards are gradually improving, pointing to rising sales of air conditioners and electronic goods as signs of growing consumer spending. The article notes that the central question for Uzbekistan-watchers is whether Mirziyoev can improve living standards fast enough in a system that still lacks real political competition and faces external uncertainty. The president is seeking another seven-year term in a snap July 9 vote that is expected to be uncontested. The International Monetary Fund has projected 6 percent growth for 2022, but it also warned of “exceptional uncertainty” and rising inflation, which was around 12 percent. A major pillar of household income remains remittances from migrants working abroad, especially in Russia. Uzbekistan sends more workers to Russia than any other country, including Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan, which are themselves heavily dependent on remittances. Last year, remittances doubled, helped in part by the strength of the Russian ruble after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. But the ruble has since fallen significantly, weakening that source of support. That uncertainty has made many Uzbek workers hesitant to return to Russia, especially as migrants there face the risk of military recruitment. Several taxi drivers in Samarkand told RFE/RL that the ruble’s instability was the main reason they were reluctant to go back, even though nearly all had worked there before. One of them, 25-year-old Daler, said he stays in Uzbekistan as the youngest son in a family of six, responsible for caring for his parents. He described friends who returned from St. Petersburg after President Vladimir Putin ordered mobilization in September, only to head back to Russia again once the immediate danger seemed to pass. Daler said the reason is simple: local wages are too low to allow saving. As a bus driver in Samarkand, he said, one can earn only 200,000 to 250,000 soms per day, roughly $17 to $22, enough to get by but not enough to build a future. The article ends by underscoring that this is the central dilemma facing many Uzbeks: even as the country opens up and grows, poverty and low wages continue to push people toward migration.

Uzbekistan Airways made its first flight to Tajikistan’s capital, Dushanbe, on April 11, the airline said. Russia flew two nuclear-capable strategic bombers over Belarus on Thursday for the second day in a row, in a show of support for Belarus amid a sharp dispute over migrants gathered at the Polish border. According to Belarus’s Defense Ministry, two Russian Tu-160 bombers carried out training flights and practiced bombing runs at the Ruzany firing range, about 37 miles east of the border with Poland. Belarusian fighter jets took part in the exercise by simulating an interception. The flights followed a similar mission on Wednesday, when two Russian Tu-22M3 long-range bombers patrolled Belarusian airspace and Belarusian air defenses practiced intercepting them. Belarus said such Russian bomber flights would now be carried out regularly. The Russian military said Thursday’s mission lasted more than four and a half hours and was meant to strengthen the two countries’ alliance, adding that it was not directed against any third country. The bomber patrols came as Russia openly backed Belarus during an escalating standoff with Poland and the European Union. Thousands of migrants and refugees, many from the Middle East, have been gathering on the Belarusian side of the border in hopes of entering the EU. Brussels has accused Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko of encouraging illegal crossings as a form of “hybrid attack” in retaliation for EU sanctions imposed after his disputed 2020 reelection and crackdown on dissent. Belarus denies those accusations, though it has said it will no longer prevent migrants and refugees from trying to enter the EU. On Thursday, Belarus’s Defense Ministry accused Poland of an “unprecedented” military buildup along the border, saying that 15,000 troops backed by tanks, air defenses, and other weapons were far beyond what migration control required. It said the buildup looked more like the creation of a strike force and justified Belarus taking action “both independently and within the existing agreements with our strategic ally,” meaning Russia. Lukashenko said the Russian bomber flights were a necessary response to the border tensions, remarking that despite the fact they were nuclear-capable, Belarus had “no other choice.” Russian officials and commentators echoed that line. Retired Col. Gen. Leonid Ivashov said the flights were intended to demonstrate Moscow’s support and help avert a wider military conflict. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the troop deployments on both sides of the border were deeply concerning and rejected Poland’s claim that Russia had helped create the crisis. He also said Putin remained in contact with Lukashenko. Separately, Aeroflot denied reports that it had helped transport migrants to Belarus, rejecting any suggestion that it had operated relevant flights and dismissing possible EU sanctions as based on false claims.

# Russia Sends Nuclear-Capable Bombers Over Belarus in Show of Support Russia deployed two nuclear-capable Tu-160 strategic bombers on a training mission over Belarus on Thursday, marking the second consecutive day of such flights. The bombers conducted practice bombing runs at the Ruzany firing range, located approximately 37 miles east of the Polish border, while Belarusian fighter jets simulated interception exercises. The Russian military stated the aircraft spent over 4.5 hours in the air and emphasized the patrol was not directed against any third countries. The Belarusian Defense Ministry announced that such Russian bomber flights would occur regularly going forward. These military demonstrations represent Russia's strong support for Belarus amid an escalating migration crisis at the Polish border. Thousands of migrants and refugees, primarily from the Middle East, have gathered on the Belarusian side of the border attempting to cross into Western Europe. This deployment prompted Belarus to respond through actions undertaken independently and in coordination with Russia under their union agreement. On Human Rights Day, December 10, a scientific-practical conference in Astana examined Kazakhstan’s progress in protecting human rights and the challenges that still remain. The event was organized by Kazakhstan’s Office of the Commissioner for Human Rights together with the UN Development Programme (UNDP) in Kazakhstan, the Commission on Human Rights under the President of Kazakhstan, the General Prosecutor’s Office, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and the Ministry of Culture and Information. Its purpose was to strengthen cooperation between state bodies and civil society in human rights work. Kazakhstan’s Human Rights Commissioner, Artur Lastayev, said the country has taken broad steps in recent years to improve citizens’ legal status and reinforce democratic institutions. He noted that Kazakhstan has recognized the competence of six UN treaty bodies on human rights, including the Human Rights Committee, the Committee against Torture, the Committee on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women, the Committee on the Rights of the Child, and the Committee on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities. Lastayev described the restoration of the constitutional court as a major development, saying it now allows citizens to file complaints directly to defend their constitutional rights. He also said the human rights institution itself was reorganized and strengthened, and that a separate article on it was added to the constitution. He pointed to recent legislation as further evidence of progress. This year, Kazakhstan adopted and implemented a law protecting women from domestic violence, criminalizing acts that civil society and international organizations had long urged the state to address. He also said the penalty for torture was sharply increased last year, with prison terms of up to 12 years. According to him, exclusive jurisdiction for investigating torture cases was established, which improved investigation effectiveness and led to a significant drop in torture complaints. Lastayev added that his office received more than 6,000 appeals in the first 11 months of 2024, a 15 percent increase compared with the same period in 2023. European Union Ambassador to Kazakhstan Aleska Simkic said the EU works closely with Kazakhstan on human rights and the rule of law. She noted that the two sides are linked by an enhanced partnership and cooperation agreement, the first of its kind in Central Asia, covering 29 areas of cooperation. She said discussions on rule of law and human rights have been productive, and that cooperation includes media freedom, freedom of association, the fight against gender-based violence, anti-torture efforts, and broader legal reforms. She also said Kazakhstan’s position in international forums such as the UN Human Rights Council and UN General Assembly is viewed positively by the EU. Police vehicles were deployed on the airstrip on the unilateral order of Mayor Cynthia Viteri, forcing the plane to divert to Quito.
