Argentina marked the April 2 anniversary of the 1982 Falklands War with the usual patriotic intensity, but President Javier Milei again found himself at odds with a national cause that has long united Argentines. For decades, Malvinas Day has been a moment when people across political lines rallied around Argentina’s claim to the islands, known internationally as the Falklands and controlled by Britain. Milei, however, has shown less interest in confrontational nationalism than in improving ties and trade with Britain, leaving many veterans and critics uncertain about where he stands. On Tuesday, Milei scaled back the commemoration in the name of austerity, canceling plans for a large Malvinas Day parade. At a memorial event in downtown Buenos Aires, he spoke warmly about Argentina’s soldiers but did not mention Britain or directly attack its sovereignty claim. Instead, he promised only an unspecified “roadmap for the return of Malvinas to Argentine hands.” He also used the occasion to criticize previous left-wing governments and argue that a “sovereign nation” must be active in international trade, a message that aligned with his broader push to lower trade barriers. The president’s approach has fueled skepticism, especially because of earlier gestures that angered patriots. During his campaign, Milei caused outrage by praising Margaret Thatcher, the former British prime minister who ordered the military response that defeated Argentina’s invasion in 1982. More recently, he met British Foreign Secretary David Cameron at the World Economic Forum in Davos to discuss possible investments in Argentina. Soon afterward, Cameron visited the Falkland Islands, becoming the first British foreign secretary in 30 years to do so and declaring the islands would remain British “forever.” Argentine provincial governors denounced the trip, but Milei remained silent. Veterans and nationalist figures reacted sharply to Milei’s tone and omissions. Carlos Retamozo, a former conscript who fought in the war at age 18, said he still could not tell what the president truly believes about the islands. Ramón Robles, head of the country’s main veterans association, accused Milei of “kneeling before the British empire” and subordinating sovereignty to business interests. Others said the day had become politicized. During the ceremony, supporters of Milei interrupted a wreath-laying with chants of “Long live freedom,” prompting veteran Daniel Pereira to lament that the commemoration had become “political propaganda.” Opposition leaders seized on the controversy as well. Buenos Aires province governor Axel Kicillof, a leading Peronist, condemned any admiration for Thatcher and insisted that sovereignty requires more than speeches. Yet some veterans preferred not to debate politics at all, saying the day should be reserved for honoring the dead and remembering the defeat. One veteran, Carlos Milock, reflected on the names of fallen comrades engraved on a memorial and said the pain of the war remained tied to “the greatest reason of all, the recovery of the Malvinas.”

# Argentina's Malvinas Day Amid Presidential Controversy On April 2, Argentina commemorated the anniversary of the 1982 Falkland War, a conflict that killed 649 Argentine and 255 British service members. However, President Javier Milei's approach to this traditionally unifying national holiday has sparked controversy and disappointed veterans who expected stronger nationalist rhetoric. ## Milei's Unconventional Stance Milei, a right-wing libertarian leader, has prioritized economic pragmatism over nationalist fervor regarding the Malvinas Islands—the Argentine name for the Falkland Islands, which Britain controls. Rather than attacking Britain's territorial claims, Milei has focused on expanding trade relationships with the British. This approach represents a dramatic departure from decades of Argentine tradition, where April 2 typically features patriotic denunciations of British occupation. Most controversially, Milei previously praised Margaret Thatcher, the former British prime minister who ordered military forces to retake the islands after Argentina's 1982 invasion attempt. This admission sparked outrage among nationalists, for whom admiring Thatcher constitutes a serious political transgression. ## Recent Diplomatic Developments Milei's diplomatic engagement with Britain intensified when he met with British Foreign Secretary David Cameron at the World Economic Forum in Davos. Shortly thereafter, Cameron became the first British foreign secretary in 30 years to visit the Falkland Islands, where he pledged the islands would remain British "forever." Argentine provincial governors condemned this visit as provocative, but Milei remained silent, instead advocating for a diplomatic solution respecting the islanders' wishes. ## Veteran and Political Reaction War veterans expressed confusion and disappointment about Milei's position. Carlos Retamozo, who fought as an 18-year-old conscript, stated he remained unclear about the president's stance on this "basic national issue." Ramón Robles, president of the main veteran association, accused Milei of "kneeling before the British empire." Notably, Milei cancelled plans for a grand Malvinas Day parade and delivered a speech targeting domestic political opponents rather than addressing British claims. He promised an undefined "roadmap for the return of Malvinas" but made no direct criticism of Britain. ## Political Polarization Milei's approach has weaponized Malvinas Day for partisan purposes. He invoked sovereignty arguments to support his free-trade agenda, criticizing previous leftist governments as "serial defaulters" unworthy of territorial claims. His left-wing opponents, including Buenos Aires Governor Axel Kicillof, seized the opportunity to attack Milei's perceived betrayal, declaring that "sovereignty is not just speech." The ceremony itself became fractious when Milei supporters interrupted the solemn wreath-laying with shouts of his campaign slogan, "Long live freedom!" ## Conclusion For decades, Malvinas Day united Argentines across political divides. However, Milei's pragmatic prioritization of trade relationships over nationalist posturing has transformed the commemoration into a battleground for political conflict. Some veterans expressed sadness that the day had become "political propaganda" rather than simple remembrance of fallen soldiers and commitment to recovering the islands.

Three months after Pope Francis formally suppressed the Peru-based lay movement Sodalitium Christianae Vitae (SCV) and its related branches, victims say the decision marked an important victory, but they are frustrated by the slow pace of justice and the lack of clear communication from Church authorities. SCV was founded by layman Luis Fernando Figari and eventually grew into a spiritual family made up of a branch of consecrated men, two branches of consecrated women, and an ecclesial movement. Francis took the rare step of suppressing the entire group earlier this year, shortly before his death, after ordering an extensive investigation in July 2023. That inquiry was led by two of his top Vatican investigators, Maltese Archbishop Charles Scicluna and Spanish Monsignor Jordi Bertomeu, both from the Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith. The investigation uncovered a wide range of alleged abuses across the SCV branches, including physical, psychological, spiritual and sexual abuse, some involving minors. Senior members have also been accused of financial wrongdoing, corruption, land trafficking, and persecution of a peasant farming community in Catacaos, in Peru’s Piura region. According to allegations, companies linked to or run by SCV members tried for years to force the farmers off ancestral land through intimidation, fabricated criminal accusations, and judicial harassment. The Catacaos community says it has faced at least 30 to 40 false criminal complaints over more than a decade, many supported by SCV-linked companies. The farmers have received legal backing from Peru’s National Coordinator of Human Rights (CNDDHH). On June 16, they won a major legal victory when the Fourth Criminal Court of Piura acquitted them of land usurpation charges brought by Constructora Keheda, a company tied to the SCV. According to the CNDDHH, the case dates to 2015, when the company allegedly tried to dispossess the farmers by falsifying communal land acquisition records, filing them with Peru’s public registry office, and then selling the land to private companies for agro-export development. The court, however, recognized that the Catacaos community had title deeds going back to the 1980s and found that the company’s witnesses had offered indirect and unsubstantiated testimony. The farmers maintain that the land belongs to their ancestors and has been communal property for roughly 400 years, meaning any transfer would require approval by a majority in an assembly. They say they have repeatedly lost land over the years and, when trying to recover it, have faced violence, including gunfire. One woman said her husband was killed by a criminal gang hired by an SCV-run company. Others say they were hit with false accusations of terrorism, usurpation, and invasion of private property. The CNDDHH called the court ruling a “precedent against the criminalization promoted by companies seeking to dispossess peasant communities of their lands,” describing it as “a victory for all who defend their territory against abuse.” Even so, former SCV members say their own search for justice remains stalled. On July 16, the Association for Truth, Justice and Fair Reparations (AVJR), made up of former members of all four SCV branches, issued a statement criticizing the slow liquidation of the suppressed group and calling on Pope Leo XIV to ensure quicker reparations. The association said many members had already filed complaints with two SCV-led investigative commissions in 2016 and 2017, as well as with the special papal mission sent in 2023 by Francis, Scicluna and Bertomeu. They stressed their independence from any political, civil or ecclesial body, and said they remain committed to truth, justice and fair reparation for victims. Members also said they had sent repeated communications to Church authorities, including Pope Francis, the Dicastery for Religious, and Bertomeu in his role as papal commissioner overseeing the liquidation of the SCV after suppression. In each case, they asked to be informed about victim assistance, the closure of the process, and coordination with the Catholic Church. They said none of those authorities had replied. While acknowledging the difficulty of managing such cases amid the transition from Pope Francis to Pope Leo XIV, the association said many victims have suffered not only harm, but also “revictimizations,” and that being ignored and made invisible is among the most painful experiences. They said the suppression of the SCV was just and important for the Church, but warned that in practice it has not yet brought meaningful healing. They urged full transparency about the process, those responsible, deadlines and procedures, saying this is necessary to deliver the care that both Francis and Leo XIV have promised.

Pope Francis initiated a comprehensive investigation in July 2023, led by Maltese Archbishop Charles Scicluna and Spanish Monsignor Jordi Bertomeu, Vatican officials specializing in abuse cases. The investigation uncovered widespread abuses across all branches, including physical, psychological, spiritual, and sexual abuse of members, some of whom were minors. Additionally, top-ranking members faced accusations of financial crimes, corruption, land trafficking, and persecution of peasant farmers. ## Landmark Court Victory for Catacaos Farmers On June 16, the Catacaos farming community achieved a significant victory when the Fourth Criminal Court of Piura acquitted them of land usurpation charges brought by Constructora Keheda, an SCV-connected company. The case originated in 2015 when the company allegedly falsified communal land records and attempted to dispossess the farmers of ancestral lands for agro-export development. The court recognized that the Catacaos community possessed legitimate title deeds dating to the 1980s and found the company's witnesses provided unsubstantiated testimony. The farmers assert their lands belong to their ancestors dating back 400 years and that any property transfers require community assembly approval. Over the years, the farmers have faced approximately 30-40 false criminal complaints from SCV-connected companies. They reported experiencing violence, including gunfire, and false terrorism allegations when attempting to reclaim control of their lands. The National Coordinator of Human Rights (CNDDHH) provided legal support throughout their ordeal. The CNDDHH hailed the ruling as "a precedent against the criminalization promoted by companies seeking to dispossess peasant communities of their lands." ## Frustration Among Abuse Survivors While the Catacaos farmers celebrated their milestone, former SCV members expressed considerable frustration. On July 16, the Association for Truth, Justice and Fair Reparations (AVJR)—representing survivors from all four SCV branches—issued a statement lamenting slow progress in the liquidation process and urging Pope Leo XIV (elected following Pope Francis's death) to expedite reparations. ## Communication Breakdown The AVJR noted that many members had filed complaints with SCV-led commissions in 2016 and 2017, as well as with the 2023 Special Mission led by Scicluna and Bertomeu. The association subsequently contacted various Church entities, including Pope Francis, the Dicastery for Religious, and Bertomeu in his capacity as papal commissioner overseeing the SCV's liquidation. They requested information about victim assistance processes, case closure timelines, and coordination mechanisms with the Church. The association reported receiving no responses from any Church authority contacted. ## Calls for Transparency and Action While acknowledging the complexities of transitioning papal leadership, AVJR members emphasized that survivors have experienced significant harm and "revictimizations," with many feeling "invisible and unheard." They stressed that the SCV's suppression, though just and exemplary, has not meaningfully contributed to healing. The association called for increased transparency regarding responsible parties, timelines, procedures, and concrete care measures that both Pope Francis and his successor promised to provide. They insisted on their independence from ecclesiastical, political, and civil entities while reaffirming their commitment to truth, justice, and fair reparations for all suppressed SCV family victims.

Venezuela’s government has moved to advance this year’s presidential election schedule while rejecting fresh U.S. sanctions threats and what it describes as interference in its internal affairs. In a speech on Wednesday at the Supreme Court in Caracas during the 2024 judicial opening ceremony, President Nicolás Maduro said “a new world has already been born” and no longer accepts “imperial tutelage” from the United States. He argued that Venezuela does not need Washington to attract investment, saying allied countries are ready to do business with the country. Maduro backed the idea of bringing the presidential vote forward and warned that the U.S.-supported opposition was trying to sabotage the process. He recalled earlier episodes of political violence, failed coup attempts, and the 2019 self-proclamation of Juan Guaidó as “interim president,” which Washington endorsed alongside sanctions on state oil company PDVSA and the seizure of CITGO. He warned that Venezuela’s next election, which he called a constitutional obligation, should not become “a new embarrassment.” His remarks came after the U.S. Treasury revoked a sanctions waiver for Venezuela’s gold sector and after U.S. State Department spokesperson Matthew Miller said the limited license for Venezuela’s energy sector, granted in October, would not be renewed in April unless opposition politician María Corina Machado were allowed to run for president. Miller repeated the threat two days later. On January 27, Venezuela’s Supreme Court rejected Machado’s appeal against her disqualification from public office, citing her role in supporting sanctions and other U.S.-backed regime-change efforts. Other opposition figures had their bans lifted. Machado, who has called for foreign intervention in Venezuela, said she would continue “all the way to the end” and refused to back another anti-government candidate. Washington says the court ruling violates the Barbados Accords signed between the Maduro government and the opposition. Caracas rejects that claim, saying the agreement does not require Machado’s ban to be lifted and only allows candidates selected by the parties if they comply with Venezuelan law. In response to the U.S. ultimatum, Venezuela’s National Assembly on Tuesday called for a national dialogue beginning February 5 to define an electoral route. Some analysts expect a May election, though no date has been announced. Assembly president Jorge Rodríguez urged broad participation from political parties, business groups, peasants and cultural workers to help draw up the calendar. Oil Minister Pedro Tellechea said Venezuela is ready for any scenario, including renewed sanctions on oil and gas, warning such measures would also hurt the United States. Since sanctions relief last year, Venezuela has re-entered international oil markets and increased exports, while major firms such as Chevron, Eni, Repsol and Maurel & Prom have expanded their activity there. Economist Francisco Rodríguez estimated that losing the waiver would cost Venezuela at least $1.6 billion in 2024. Vice President Delcy Rodríguez also threatened to suspend cooperation with Washington, including migrant repatriation flights that began in October, if the U.S. intensifies economic pressure.

President Nicolás Maduro declared that a "new world" no longer accepts American "imperial tutelage," asserting that allied nations wish to invest in Venezuela regardless of US pressure. At the border crossing between the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Rwanda in Goma, Bernadette Bita begins each day by screening travellers for Ebola. Armed with a thermometer and clipboard, she checks for symptoms before allowing people to continue their journeys. She says the work is part of a shared duty to protect both her own country and neighbouring states until Ebola is eradicated. Human Rights Watch said in its World Report 2024 that governments across Southern Africa increasingly targeted political opposition, activists, journalists, migrants, and refugees in 2023, deepening a regional decline in rights protections and democratic safeguards. The organization said problems long associated with the region—political instability, weak protections for freedom of expression and association, and limited equal participation—became more acute around elections, protests, and government efforts to restrict civic space. In its annual report, Human Rights Watch described 2023 as a year marked globally by human rights suppression, wartime atrocities, selective outrage, and transactional diplomacy, but also one in which governments were urged to uphold their obligations more consistently. In Southern Africa, the report said elections in Angola, Mozambique, Eswatini, and Zimbabwe should have strengthened democracy, the rule of law, and human rights, but instead were accompanied by serious abuses before, during, and after the voting. According to the report, parliamentarians, opposition figures, and human rights defenders were kidnapped, tortured, and killed in some cases. Zimbabwe was singled out for repression surrounding its August general elections and December parliamentary by-elections, which election observers said did not meet regional and international standards for democratic elections. Members and supporters of the Citizens’ Coalition for Change, the main opposition party, were reportedly targeted by assailants believed to be linked to covert state police operations, including a unit referred to as the “Ferret Team.” One activist, Tapfumeyi Masaya, was found dead on November 13 at Chabwino farm in Mashonaland East Province. In Eswatini, parliamentary elections were held in September, but the political environment remained tightly controlled. Human Rights Watch said Thulani Maseko, a leader in the Multi-Stakeholder Forum coalition of opposition parties and civil society groups, was assassinated hours after the king warned that those seeking democratic reform would be dealt with by mercenaries. Eswatini has banned political parties since 1973, and the king retains absolute power. Zambia also saw pressure on freedoms of assembly and association. Authorities used the Public Order Act to disrupt opposition activity, including by denying permission for meetings and rallies. Human Rights Watch noted that President Hakainde Hichilema had promised to repeal the NGO Act No. 16 of 2009, but his government had not done so. The law gives a government-dominated board broad control over nongovernmental organizations and civil society groups. In Mozambique, parliament amended a draft law that would have linked nongovernmental organizations’ work with counterterrorism financing and anti-money laundering rules in ways Human Rights Watch said would have enabled excessive government scrutiny and closure of organizations without judicial review. But security forces still used excessive force against civic groups and opposition members taking part in largely peaceful protests in October. The report also said civilians continued to be killed as violence in Cabo Delgado persisted. Angola’s security forces, Human Rights Watch said, have long carried out unlawful killings, excessive force against protesters, and arbitrary arrests of opposition activists. In 2023 alone, they were responsible for more than a dozen unlawful killings and numerous other serious abuses against political activists and peaceful demonstrators. The report also highlighted South Africa, where social and economic inequality contributed to anti-immigrant sentiment and xenophobia ahead of the 2024 general elections. The Department of Home Affairs issued a White Paper on Citizenship, Immigration and Refugee Protection that could lead South Africa to review or withdraw from the 1951 Refugee Convention and 1967 Protocol, with the intention of rejoining them with reservations. Vigilante groups such as Operation Dudula were reported to have violently targeted and harassed foreign nationals. Human Rights Watch criticized the government’s silence and inaction in the face of anti-immigrant hate speech, restrictions on access to health care, and raids and closures of businesses owned by foreigners, calling for investigations and accountability. In Malawi, refugees and asylum seekers were also affected by government actions. Since May 2023, the Homeland Security Ministry has detained and forcibly relocated 902 refugees and asylum seekers, including children, to Dzaleka refugee camp, saying they had not followed proper procedures. Human Rights Watch said the move violated rights to freedom of movement, education, and adequate living standards. Overall, the organization said Southern African governments had weakened checks and balances, restricted parliaments and judicial independence, and undermined freedoms of expression and association. It urged authorities to protect human rights, address abuses, and strengthen safeguards for refugees, migrants, internally displaced people, and other vulnerable groups.

# Southern Africa: Backsliding on Democracy Jeopardizes Rights Human Rights Watch's 2024 World Report documents a troubling deterioration in human rights protections across Southern Africa during 2023. Governments throughout the region systematically targeted opposition parties, activists, and journalists, undermining democratic principles and fundamental freedoms that are essential to functional democracies. ## Pattern of Abuses The report reveals a consistent pattern of serious human rights violations. Allan Ngari, Africa advocacy director at Human Rights Watch, emphasized that authorities must address "escalating cases of abduction, arbitrary detentions, torture and killings of opposition political activists." These abuses reflect a broader intolerance for political plurality and freedom of expression and association, indicating significant democratic backsliding. ## Electoral Violence and Suppression Elections in Angola, Mozambique, Eswatini, and Zimbabwe presented opportunities to strengthen human rights and democracy. Instead, the periods surrounding these elections were marked by systematic abuses. Zimbabwe's August general elections and December parliamentary by-elections failed to meet international standards. Opposition members from the Citizens' Coalition for Change were targeted by assailants allegedly connected to state police operations, including units known as "Ferret Team." Political activist Tapfumeyi Masaya was found dead in November following his activism. Eswatini's September parliamentary elections were preceded by the assassination of Thulani Maseko, leader of a multi-stakeholder coalition advocating for democratic reform. This killing occurred hours after the king warned that democracy advocates would face mercenary attacks. The country has banned political parties since 1973, with the king wielding absolute power. ## Civic Space Restrictions Multiple countries implemented legal mechanisms to suppress civic participation. Zambia's authorities used the Public Order Act to block opposition meetings and rallies. Despite President Haikande Hichilema's promises to repeal the restrictive NGO Act of 2009, his administration has failed to do so, allowing the government-dominated NGO Registration Board to continue limiting civil society activities. Mozambique initially faced similar threats when authorities attempted to conflate nongovernmental operations with counterterrorism financing. However, parliament members successfully revised the problematic draft law. Security forces nonetheless used excessive force against peaceful protesters in October, with numerous civilian deaths reported during ongoing conflicts in Cabo Delgado. Angola's security forces have committed over a dozen unlawful killings in 2023 and engaged in excessive force against protesters and arbitrary detention of opposition activists—a pattern spanning decades. ## Xenophobia and Refugee Crises Social and economic disparities have fueled anti-immigrant sentiment, particularly in South Africa ahead of 2024 elections. Vigilante groups like Operation Dudula have violently targeted foreign nationals while government officials remain silent, violating constitutional and international obligations. South Africa's Department of Home Affairs has proposed withdrawing from the 1951 Refugee Convention, potentially further restricting migrant protections. Malawi has forcibly relocated 902 refugees and asylum seekers, including children, since May 2023, violating their rights to freedom of movement, education, and adequate living standards. ## Conclusion The 34th edition of Human Rights Watch's World Report documents systematic erosion of democratic safeguards across Southern Africa. Governments have progressively dismantled checks on executive power, restricted parliamentary independence, and violated citizens' fundamental freedoms. Executive Director Tirana Hassan acknowledged 2023's human rights challenges while noting signs of hope for alternative paths forward. The report urges Southern African authorities to immediately cease abuses, uphold human rights obligations, strengthen judicial independence, and implement comprehensive reforms protecting all vulnerable populations, including refugees and internally displaced persons.

South Sudan’s President Salva Kiir and rebel leader Riek Machar have agreed once again to share power in a new attempt to end the country’s five-year civil war, officials said Wednesday. The deal was announced in Khartoum by South Sudan’s information minister, Michael Makuei Lueth, and is expected to be formally signed on Aug. 5, according to Sudan’s foreign minister. Under the agreement, Kiir will remain head of government during a transitional period, while Machar will return as first vice president. The new transitional administration will also include five vice presidents in total. The 11-page deal allocates 20 cabinet posts to Kiir’s camp, nine to Machar’s group, and six to other factions. The sides also agreed to share a 550-seat parliament, with 332 seats for Kiir’s side, 128 for Machar’s, and the remainder for other groups. Despite the announcement, negotiators and observers expressed caution. Manasseh Zindo, who has been involved in the talks for Machar’s side, said the opposition could “live with” the deal but warned it would fail unless early security arrangements are carried out. A similar power-sharing arrangement collapsed in July 2016 after fighting broke out in Juba, forcing Machar to flee on foot. The conflict began in December 2013 after tensions erupted between Kiir and Machar’s supporters. Since then, more than 2 million people have fled South Sudan, creating Africa’s largest refugee crisis since Rwanda in 1994, and millions more have faced hunger and near famine. Multiple cease-fires, including one described as “permanent,” have quickly broken down. A recent U.N. report accused government troops and allied forces of horrific abuses, including hangings, burnings, and widespread rape. The agreement came under heavy international pressure. The United States had already warned that another elite-level deal might trigger renewed conflict and said it would not fund or guarantee the process unless it included civil society, churches, women, and other excluded groups. The U.N. Security Council imposed an arms embargo earlier this month. Many South Sudanese remain skeptical. Wol Deng Atak, a journalist in exile, said relations between Kiir and Machar are at their lowest point and warned that another cycle of violence is possible.

# South Sudan's Leaders Agree to Power-Sharing Deal South Sudan's President Salva Kiir and opposition leader Riek Machar have agreed to share power again in another attempt to end the country's five-year civil war, officials announced Wednesday in Khartoum, Sudan. The agreement will be formally signed on August 5. Under the arrangement, Kiir will lead the government during a transitional period while Machar returns as first vice president—one of five vice presidential positions. The transitional government will include 20 ministers from Kiir's faction, nine from Machar's group, and six from other groups. Parliament will have 550 seats distributed similarly among the factions. However, this agreement faces significant skepticism. The U.S. State Department warned earlier this week that the deal "may sow the seeds of another cycle of conflict," refusing to fund South Sudan's government or guarantee the peace process unless it includes civil society, churches, women, and other excluded groups beyond the political elites. The civil war erupted in December 2013 between Kiir and his then-deputy Machar, killing tens of thousands and displacing over 2 million people—Africa's largest refugee crisis since the 1994 Rwandan genocide. Millions more face famine conditions. A critical concern is the history of failed agreements. A similar power-sharing deal collapsed in July 2016 when fighting erupted in the capital, Juba, forcing Machar to flee. Multiple cease-fires, including a "permanent" one signed weeks ago, have been violated within hours. Opposition negotiator Manasseh Zindo acknowledged the agreement could work only if early security arrangements are properly implemented. Meanwhile, both sides face accusations of atrocities, including hanging, burning, and sexual violence. The fracturing of South Sudan's opposition into multiple groups further complicates prospects, as some refuse to sign the agreement. Local observers remain deeply skeptical, with one exile editor noting that relations between Kiir and Machar are "at its lowest level ever."

UNHCR Egypt said the number of registered refugees and asylum seekers rose 208% from March 21, 2023 to January 31, 2025, reaching 902,700, including 32,081 registered in January 2025. Sudanese refugees and asylum seekers saw the sharpest increase, up 938% to 630,958, or 70% of the total. Syrians were next at 144,557, followed by South Sudanese, Eritreans, Ethiopians, Yemenis, Somalis and others. Women make up 53% and children 39%, with most refugees concentrated in Greater Cairo and several other governorates.

# Summary Between March 2023 and January 2025, UNHCR Egypt registered 902,700 refugees and asylum seekers, a 208% increase. In January 2025 alone, 32,081 were registered. Sudanese refugees comprise 70% of the total (630,958), with a 938% increase. Other major groups include Syrians (16%), South Sudanese (5%), and Eritreans (4%). Thousands of Somali refugees who left Kenya’s Dadaab camp under a UN-backed repatriation program are now stranded in harsh conditions on the outskirts of Kismayo, a port town in southern Somalia. The article describes a sprawling settlement of makeshift shacks built from sheet metal, branches, and cardboard on a grey sand dune above the Indian Ocean, where more than 16,000 people live with little shelter, sanitation, education, healthcare, or work. Children play among rubbish, and many families have no clear idea where they will go next. One of the returnees, Ahmed Mohamed Abukar, said he came back to his hometown in February after living for seven years in Dadaab with his wife and six children. He said worsening food and healthcare cuts in the Kenyan camp, along with pressure and threats from Kenyan authorities, left him feeling he had no choice but to return. Even so, he knew Somalia remained unsafe and underdeveloped. Standing in the sand with other returnees around him, he lamented that there is “nothing” in Kismayo and that the family lacks housing, schooling, health services, and work. The article explains that the returns are part of a “voluntary repatriation” agreement between UNHCR, the Kenyan government, and Somalia’s federal government. Under this arrangement, UNHCR spent much of 2016 transporting Somalis from Dadaab back across the border. According to UNHCR statistics, 30,731 Somali refugees had gone through the voluntary return process between December 2014 and September 2016, with 24,630 of them returning in 2016 alone after Kenya came under pressure to shut down the camp. Dadaab, which has hosted more than 400,000 Somali refugees for two decades, had been targeted for closure by Kenya, which described it as a security risk and an economic burden. Kismayo became a key arrival point because it is the first major town after the Dhobley border crossing and is relatively secure compared with much of southern Somalia. A UNHCR-supported reception centre there, run with Mercy Corps, was built in 2014 and was being expanded to handle up to 500 new arrivals a day in anticipation of more returnees. But in early September, Jubaland state authorities halted the return process, arguing that the situation was not safe or dignified. Jubaland’s justice minister, Adam Ibrahim Awhersi, said the state was overwhelmed and that returnees were arriving to find no food, no schools, no toilets, unsafe water, and little or no basic support. He accused UNHCR and Somalia’s federal government of misleading refugees with promises of assistance that could not be delivered. Somalia’s federal government responded that the number of returnees was too large and said more time was needed to prepare areas and services. Funding shortages compounded the problem. UNHCR had received only 27% of the $148.8 million it requested in 2016 to support the reintegration of Somali returnees. Meanwhile, Kenya briefly pledged to close Dadaab by the end of 2016, then backed away after the United States announced more than $146 million in extra aid for refugees, returnees, and drought victims in Kenya and Somalia. Of that amount, $59 million was earmarked for refugee assistance in Kenya and continued repatriation efforts. Critics argued that the returns were not truly voluntary. Ben Rawlence, an author and researcher familiar with Dadaab, said food ration cuts of one-third meant refugees were effectively choosing between starvation and the return package. Those who accept the package lose their refugee status and are promised about $2,400 per family of six over six months after arriving in Somalia, according to a Mercy Corps official. But many others returned spontaneously and were not registered, leaving them ineligible for any aid. The article stresses that Kismayo and its surroundings are already under strain, with about 40,000 internally displaced people in the area, along with refugees from Yemen and Ethiopia and an impoverished local population. No land was set aside for the returnees, and after the six-month support period, there is nothing further to help them rebuild. Somalia’s long war has devastated society and the economy, and large parts of the country remain battlegrounds between African Union and Somali forces on one side and al-Shabab on the other. Though Kismayo itself is relatively stable under local security forces, the countryside remains contested, and the federal government has little control in Jubaland. UNHCR defended the program, saying it provides information and support transparently and that the decision to return must be made freely and voluntarily. It also said reintegration requires cooperation from local authorities, UN agencies, and NGOs. But for people like Abukar, the reality is bleak. He appealed to Kenya not to abandon refugees abruptly after decades of hosting them, asking that it continue supporting them until Somalia is able to stand on its own.

# Refugees Stranded in Somalia After Kenya Eviction Over 16,000 Somali refugees have been left stranded in Kismayo, a port town in southern Somalia, living in makeshift shelters on the fringes of the community after being repatriated from Kenya's Dadaab refugee camp. The returnees face dire conditions with no adequate housing, education, healthcare, or employment opportunities, creating a humanitarian crisis in a region already devastated by decades of conflict. ## The Repatriation Program The UNHCR, Kenya's government, and Somalia's federal government established a "voluntary repatriation" agreement to return Somali refugees to their homeland. Between December 2014 and September 2016, approximately 30,731 Somali refugees from Dadaab were repatriated, with 24,630 of those returns occurring in 2016 alone as Kenya accelerated the process to close the camp. The returnees, like Ahmed Mohamed Abukar who arrived in February with his wife and six children after seven years in Dadaab, were motivated partly by food and healthcare cuts implemented in the camp and pressure from Kenyan authorities. ## Mounting Pressures Kenya, which has hosted over 400,000 Somali refugees for two decades, declared in May that it would close Dadaab by year's end, citing security threats and economic burdens. However, the government backed down in August after the United States pledged more than $146 million in additional aid. Critics argue that the repatriation process cannot truly be voluntary when refugees face starvation due to ration cuts of one-third, effectively forcing families to accept return packages. ## Local Resistance In early September 2016, Jubaland state authorities halted the returns process, with Justice Minister Adam Ibrahim Awhersi declaring the repatriation "neither safe, secure and definitely not dignified." He criticized the false promises made to refugees about support for resettlement, noting that families of five or six were living outdoors without schools, food, clean water, or toilets. Awhersi emphasized that no land had been set aside for returnees to settle and that Jubaland was overwhelmed, already hosting 40,000 internally displaced persons, plus refugees from Yemen and Ethiopia. ## Inadequate Support The returnees receive approximately $2,400 per family of six in allowances over six months, which proves insufficient given Somalia's devastated economy and expensive living conditions. After this six-month period ends, no further assistance is available. Many families have also returned spontaneously without registering with UNHCR, making them ineligible for any aid package whatsoever. Critically, UNHCR has received only 27% of the $148.8 million it requested from donors to support reintegration efforts in 2016, leaving a substantial funding gap. ## Precarious Security Situation Somalia remains unstable after 25 years of conflict. Al-Shabab insurgents continue mounting deadly attacks throughout the country, including in the capital Mogadishu, while swathes of the countryside remain battlegrounds between Western-backed African Union forces and militant fighters. Kismayo maintains only fragile peace through a local security force, while much of the surrounding countryside remains under al-Shabab control. The federal government cannot access semi-autonomous Jubaland and lacks control over the region, raising serious questions about whether returnees can receive adequate protection or justice. ## Disputed Voluntariness Researcher Ben Rawlence, who spent five years studying Dadaab, argues that ration cuts have effectively eliminated the voluntary nature of returns, with refugees choosing repatriation because they face starvation. UNHCR maintains that it provides transparent information and that decisions to return must be made freely and voluntarily, emphasizing that successful reintegration requires collective efforts from local administrations, UN agencies, and NGOs. Back in Kismayo's sandy camps, returnees like Abukar appeal to Kenya to maintain the care and support it provided for two decades, rather than abandoning them as their homeland struggles to establish stability and basic services.

Turkey says Greek forces continue to forcibly push back irregular migrants in the Aegean Sea, including women and children, into Turkish territorial waters. The Turkish National Defense Ministry shared video footage with Anadolu Agency showing Greek coast guards pointing guns at refugees, beating and shoving them, and dragging migrant boats back toward Turkey. The footage, taken at different times, also shows dangerous maneuvers intended to sink a boat, as well as shots fired into the air and around it. The report follows testimony from Somalian migrant Muna Hasim Dra, who said she and her friends were pushed into Turkish waters and showed visible beating wounds. Turkey, a major transit route for asylum seekers heading to Europe, and human rights groups have repeatedly condemned Greece’s pushback practice as illegal and dangerous, saying it violates humanitarian principles and international law.

Nearly 50 Somali migrants who survived a deadly boat disaster off Madagascar last month have returned to Somalia and were received by government officials in Mogadishu. The returnees, aged 17 to 50, arrived visibly relieved and wore clothing made from fabric in the colors of the Somali flag. Their repatriation followed a tragedy in which 25 people died in the Indian Ocean after the boat’s engine failed and the migrants were left stranded at sea. Survivors told The Associated Press they drifted for 13 days without food or water after the vessel broke down. Ahmed Hussein, who had been traveling with a cousin who died, said the group had hoped to reach Europe for a better life. The migrants said they survived by catching fish and rationing a few dates until those also ran out. Another survivor, Abdirashid Ibrahim, said people suffered swollen ankles, had nowhere to sleep, and were packed tightly together; some died from shock and others from starvation. Officials in Madagascar and Somalia had earlier said the boats capsized, but gave no detailed explanation. The boats had left a beach near Mogadishu on Nov. 2 with 73 people aboard and were believed to be heading for Mayotte, a French territory in the Indian Ocean about 1,600 kilometers away. Somali authorities said 48 survivors had been expected, but only 47 arrived, and one person’s whereabouts remained unclear. Abdulkadir Burgal, a Foreign Ministry official, said eight people involved in trafficking the migrants had been arrested. Maryan Yasin, the president’s special envoy for migration, said the returnees were happy to be home and promised they would not take such risks again.

# Migrants Survive Boat Tragedy, Return to Somalia Nearly 50 survivors of a migrant boat disaster that killed 25 people in the Indian Ocean off Madagascar have returned to Somalia. The survivors, aged 17 to 50, arrived in Mogadishu where government officials received them. Two boats carrying 73 migrants departed from a Mogadishu beach on November 2, intended for Mayotte, a French archipelago approximately 1,600 kilometers away. The vessels capsized after their engines failed, leaving survivors stranded at sea for 13 days without functioning propulsion, adequate food, or water. Survivor Ahmed Hussein described the harrowing experience: "We had no food or water, and the dates we had ran out during those 13 days. We survived by catching some fish." Another survivor, Abdirashid Ibrahim, reported that some people died from shock and starvation, while others developed severe swelling that prevented them from walking. The migrants were fleeing Somalia seeking better opportunities abroad, reflecting a broader pattern of irregular migration from Horn of Africa countries as people escape conflict and drought, according to UN agencies. Authorities initially reported 48 survivors, though only 47 arrived in Somalia, with one person's whereabouts remaining unclear. The Somali government arrested eight human traffickers involved in organizing the dangerous journey. Officials stated that survivors expressed commitment to avoiding such risks in the future. The government pledged a collective effort to address migration issues and prevent similar tragedies.

The Nigerian Civil Aviation Authority (NCAA) has inaugurated a National Facilitation Committee to implement Nigeria’s National Facilitation Programme, in line with a recommendation of the International Civil Aviation Organisation (ICAO). ICAO requires each contracting state to establish a national facilitation committee to help coordinate border-crossing formalities for international air travel. At the inauguration in Lagos, the Director of Consumer Protection Directorate, Adamu Abdullahi, who represented the acting Director-General, Benedict Adeyileka, said the committee brings together heads of relevant government agencies as well as chief executives of national bodies representing aircraft operators and airport operators. He added that, for practical work, members may also appoint middle-level management staff to represent them at working-group meetings. According to the NCAA spokesman, Sam Adurogboye, the primary responsibility for the National Facilitation Committee rests with the NCAA in Nigeria. The programme is intended to implement the Chicago Convention’s requirement that states facilitate border formalities for aircraft engaged in international operations, including passengers, crew and cargo. The committee, which will be chaired by the NCAA Director-General, includes representatives from the Aviation Ministry, Customs, Immigration, Police, Foreign Affairs, Agriculture/Environment, Security and Narcotics, Public Health, FAAN, NAMA, the Tourism Ministry, international airlines and the National Aviation Security Committee. Airport Facilitation Committees will be headed by airport managers and include similar agencies at airport level. Abdullahi said the committee’s duties include designating customs airports, creating procedures for scheduled and non-scheduled operators to request landing or departure permission, and arranging border inspection services. It is also expected to address document fraud, illegal migration, smuggling and touting, and to support border agencies in improving inspection systems and streamlining procedures. In addition, the committee will help prepare for the movement of large numbers of passengers, especially during holy pilgrimages, and review policies aimed at preventing the spread of contagious diseases by air, including aircraft disinfection and quarantine measures. The National Facilitation Committee will meet twice a year except in emergencies, while airport committees will meet quarterly. The NCAA will serve as secretariat. Abdullahi noted that the committee had now been inaugurated after being signed into law in 2007.

# NCAA Inaugurates National Facilitation Programme The Nigerian Civil Aviation Authority (NCAA) has inaugurated a National Facilitation Committee to implement the National Facilitation Programme, fulfilling an International Civil Aviation Organisation (ICAO) requirement that each contracting state establish such a committee. The committee, inaugurated in Lagos, comprises heads of government agencies and chief executive officers of national organisations representing aircraft operators and airport operators. Members may designate middle-level management staff to represent them at working group meetings. According to NCAA spokesman Sam Adurogboye, the programme implements the Chicago Convention mandate, which requires contracting states to facilitate border-crossing formalities for international aircraft operations, including procedures for passengers, crew, and cargo. The National Facilitation Committee, headed by the NCAA Director General, includes officials from the Aviation Ministry, Customs, Immigration, Police, Foreign Affairs, Agriculture/Environment, Security and Narcotics, Public Health, and representatives from FAAN, NAMA, Tourism Ministry, International Airlines, and the National Aviation Security Committee. Corresponding Airport Facilitation Committees, headed by Airport Managers, will comprise representatives from relevant agencies including Customs, Immigration, Quarantine, and State Security Service. The committee's responsibilities include designating customs airports, developing procedures for flight permissions, arranging border inspection services, and controlling security issues such as document fraud and smuggling. It will also coordinate passenger clearance during pilgrimages and establish policies preventing contagious disease spread through aviation, including aircraft disinfection and health screening measures. The National Facilitation Committee will meet bi-annually, except in emergencies, while Airport Facilitation Committees will meet quarterly. The NCAA will serve as the NNFC secretariat. Director Adamu Abdullahi noted that although the committee was signed into law in 2007, its formal inauguration had been delayed until now.

The 2024 World Press Photo contest has announced its winners, with Reuters photographer Mohammed Salem’s image of Palestinian woman Inas Abu Maamar holding the body of her niece Saly named Photo of the Year. Saly and four other family members were killed when an Israeli missile struck their home in Khan Younis, Gaza, on October 17, 2023. The jury said the photograph was composed with care and respect, conveying both the immediate and symbolic weight of profound loss. The contest drew more than 61,000 entries from nearly 4,000 photographers across 130 countries. Entries were first reviewed by six regional juries, and the final winners were selected by a global jury made up of the regional jury chairs and the global jury chair. Global jury chair Fiona Shields, head of photography at the Guardian, said the winning images were chosen for their ability to capture a specific moment while resonating beyond their immediate subject and time. She described Salem’s Photo of the Year as especially moving and as a powerful argument for peace. Several other projects were highlighted for their depth and human-centered approach. In Madagascar, Lee-Ann Olwage documented dementia through the relationship between 91-year-old Paul Rakotozandriny, known as “Dada Paul,” and his daughter Fara Rafaraniriana. The project explored local stigma around memory loss and reflected the Malagasy value of valim-babena, or children’s duty to care for aging parents. Alejandro Cegarra’s work focused on Mexico’s increasingly restrictive immigration policies. Drawing on his own experience migrating from Venezuela to Mexico in 2017, he offered a perspective centered on migrant agency and resilience. Julia Kochetova’s project on Russia’s war in Ukraine combined photography with diary-like storytelling, poetry, audio clips, and music to depict the conflict as a daily reality rather than a distant news event. World Press Photo Executive Director Joumana El Zein Khoury said the winning photographers were personally familiar with their subjects, which helped them bring greater understanding to audiences and foster empathy and compassion.

A Thai lawyer has petitioned a court to release 42 Uyghur men who have been detained in Thailand for more than 10 years and who rights groups fear may be deported to China, where they could face torture. The men, from China’s mostly Muslim Uyghur minority in Xinjiang, have been held on immigration charges at a Thai detention center since fleeing what they say was persecution by Beijing. Lawyer Chuchart Kanpai argued in a petition filed Thursday that the men have already effectively served any sentence they might have received through their prolonged detention. “They have been jailed from 2013 to 2025, more than 10 years. It is obvious that they have completed the sentence,” he said, adding that continued detention is unlawful. The court is scheduled to hear the case on Feb. 17, and Chuchart said witnesses, including representatives from the World Uyghur Congress, will testify. The petition comes amid renewed concern that Thailand may be preparing to send the men back to China. Justice for All said earlier this month that reports from 48 detained Uyghur asylum seekers suggested Thai authorities were pressuring them to sign forms in preparation for deportation. A Thai government spokesman denied on Jan. 23 that there was any policy to deport the Uyghurs, dismissing speculation that they would be forced back to China. International concern has also intensified. On Jan. 21, U.N. experts urged Thailand not to deport the men, warning they would likely face torture if returned. Uyghurs in Xinjiang have long faced severe repression, including mass detention in camps, allegations China denies. New U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio also said at his Jan. 15 confirmation hearing that the treatment of Uyghurs was “horrifying” and pledged to contact Thailand to prevent any repatriation. The detained men are part of a larger group of more than 350 Uyghurs who were previously in Thailand. Of those, 172 were resettled in Turkey, 109 were deported to China, and five died from inadequate medical conditions. Thailand’s 2015 deportations drew heavy international criticism. The country is not a signatory to the 1951 U.N. Refugee Convention and does not formally recognize refugees. Some Thai officials caution that the court process itself could be risky. Senator Angkhana Neelapaijit warned that if the court hears testimony from Chinese officials, it could conclude the men would be treated fairly in China, which she said would be dangerous.

# Thai Lawyer Seeks Release of 42 Detained Uyghurs A Thai lawyer has petitioned the court to release 42 Uyghurs who have been detained for over a decade on immigration charges. Some law enforcers have approached the Catholic Church and expressed a willingness to reveal their role in extrajudicial killings and summary executions, according to CBCP president Archbishop Socrates Villegas. In a statement Monday, Villegas said these officers had come to their spiritual leaders “to seek sanctuary, succor and protection,” adding that their consciences were troubling them. Villegas said the Church would first examine the sincerity of their motives and the truth of their accounts. If their stories check out, he said, the Church is prepared to provide them and their families with accommodation, shelter and protection. He cited the Gospel of Matthew in saying that what is done to “the least of our brethren” is done to Christ. The archbishop announced the opening of a Ministry of Mercy for law enforcers who need the Church’s hospitality. He said the Archdiocese of Lingayen-Dagupan would serve as a “loving teacher and mother” to police and other uniformed personnel seeking pastoral care, values formation, or protection. He also urged priests in his area to open their rectories, convents, seminaries, and other secure buildings to receive these potential witnesses. Villegas stressed that the Church would not force anyone to speak or make allegations, and would make sure no one else coerces them. He said any statements must be made with the help of independent counsel. If the officers chose to remain with the Church, he said, they would not be handed over to the state’s witness-protection program. He also asked for volunteer lawyers to assist the witnesses, while reminding priests not to discuss the contents of any testimony or deposition with them. He said any eventual testimony should be fair, accurate, and free from pressure. The statement followed earlier remarks by Villegas in August, when he said the country had descended into chaos amid the government’s war on drugs. He cited a week of police anti-drug operations that left at least 91 people dead, including 32 in Bulacan and Grade 12 student Kian Lloyd Delos Santos in Caloocan. He also criticized what he saw as the unequal treatment of the poor versus the powerful. The archdiocese had previously announced nightly bell-ringing from August 22 to November 27 to call for justice for the slain.

# Summary Archbishop Socrates Villegas, president of the Catholic Bishops' Conference of the Philippines, announced that law enforcers involved in extrajudicial killings and summary executions have approached the Church seeking spiritual guidance and protection. These officers are experiencing troubled consciences and wish to confess their participation in these killings to priests. The Church will evaluate the sincerity of their motives and the accuracy of their accounts before providing assistance. Villegas established the Ministry of Mercy to serve these law enforcers, offering them and their families accommodation, shelter, and protection. The Archdiocese of Lingaziuan Dagupan will provide pastoral counseling and values formation. Importantly, the Church will not compel officers to testify or make allegations. If they choose to remain with the Church rather than participate in state investigations, they will not be turned over to the government's witness-protection program. Any statements must be made with independent legal counsel present. Villegas called on priests to open rectories, convents, seminaries, and other secure buildings to accommodate these uniformed personnel. He questioned why only poor individuals are killed while the powerful receive preferential treatment. Police estimates place drug-related deaths at approximately 3,800, while human rights groups claim the figure reaches 13,000. The administration has disputed the higher estimates as exaggerated. Villegas previously ordered church bells in his archdiocese to ring nightly for 15 minutes to call for justice and awaken the nation's conscience regarding these killings.

Myanmar anti-coup activists who enter Thailand now face a serious risk of arrest and forced return to Myanmar, according to experts and rights groups, as the close relationship between the two countries’ militaries shapes border policy. The concern was highlighted after Thai authorities detained three members of a Myanmar anti-military group in the border town of Mae Sot and handed them over to the Myanmar junta. The three men — Ko Thiha, Ko Htet Nay Win and Ko Saw Phyo Lay — belong to Myanmar’s Lion Battalion Commando Column. They were arrested on April 1 on illegal entry charges. Local reports said they had crossed into Thailand for medical treatment after an altercation in which two of them were shot by Myanmar’s Border Guard Force. Instead of being treated as asylum-seekers or protected from return, they were transferred back to Myanmar authorities. Lalita Hanwong, a Southeast Asian history lecturer and social sciences instructor at Kasetsart University in Bangkok, said the move reflects the strong ties between the Thai and Myanmar militaries, especially after Myanmar’s 2021 coup and during the administration of Thai Prime Minister Prayut Chan-o-cha. She said Thailand does not want to openly damage its relationship with Myanmar’s military, known as the Tatmadaw, even if it cannot fully support it on the international stage. In practice, she said, Thailand can still assist the Myanmar military along the border by arresting or returning political refugees and other opponents of the regime. Thailand and Myanmar share a 2,414-kilometer border, making Thailand a major destination for people fleeing conflict in Myanmar. The United Nations says about 91,000 Myanmar refugees are currently in Thailand. But Thailand is not a party to the 1951 Refugee Convention and lacks a clear domestic legal framework for protecting urban refugees and asylum-seekers. Hanwong said the Thai government does not want a permanent refugee crisis and prefers to keep border camps temporary rather than recognize them as refugee camps. She said that if political refugees are found in Thailand, the government’s instinct is to send them back in order to please Myanmar’s ruling State Administrative Council. Sann Aung, executive director of the New Myanmar Foundation in Mae Sot, said the danger is greatest for people involved in the anti-junta resistance. He said such people are often forcibly returned without regard for their safety and may then be interrogated, extorted or otherwise harmed by Myanmar’s military. He argued Thai authorities should investigate detainees’ backgrounds before returning them and should not deport those involved in pro-democracy activity or resistance. Human Rights Watch also condemned the return of the three men, saying Thailand has worked with Myanmar to harass, arrest and forcibly return asylum-seekers. HRW Asia director Elaine Pearson said Thai officials colluded with the junta by unlawfully returning the activists despite clear threats to their lives and freedom. The group noted that Thailand has ratified anti-torture and anti-disappearance treaties, and that these protections were incorporated into a 2022 law banning deportation or extradition when a person faces torture or enforced disappearance. The National Unity Government, Myanmar’s shadow administration formed after the coup, said the return of the three men violated international policing procedures and raised concerns about their condition. Spokesperson Nay Phone Latt said the junta claimed all three were alive, but the NUG could confirm only two were alive based on photos and had received no further updates. Myanmar has been in crisis since the military overthrew the elected government, sparking armed resistance and a widening civil war. According to the Assistance Association for Political Prisoners, at least 3,408 people have been killed by military forces since the coup.

# Myanmar Anti-Coup Activists Face Arrest Risk in Thailand Myanmar's anti-military resistance members face serious danger if they cross into Thailand, as the Thai government increasingly collaborates with Myanmar's military junta to detain and forcibly return activists, according to experts and human rights organizations. The threat became concrete when Thai authorities arrested three members of Myanmar's Lion Battalion Commando Column in Mae Sot, a border town, on April 1 on illegal entry charges. Ko Thiha, Ko Htet Nay Win, and Ko Saw Phyo Lay had reportedly entered Thailand seeking medical treatment after two of them were shot by Myanmar's Border Guard Force. Thai authorities subsequently handed them over to the Myanmar junta, raising alarm among rights advocates. Lalita Hanwong, a Southeast Asian history lecturer at Kasetsart University in Bangkok, attributes this action to the strong military relationship between Thailand and Myanmar. She explained that Thailand's Prime Minister Prayut Chan-o-cha's regime has maintained close ties with Myanmar's military, particularly since Myanmar's 2021 coup. While Thailand cannot openly support the junta internationally, it can assist along the border by capturing and arresting political refugees. Thailand and Myanmar share a 2,414-kilometer border, making Thailand accessible to Myanmar refugees fleeing conflict. The United Nations reports approximately 91,000 Myanmar refugees are currently in Thailand. However, Thailand is not party to the 1951 Refugee Convention and lacks a domestic legal framework protecting urban refugees and asylum-seekers. The Thai government views these refugees as a burden rather than a responsibility. Officials call the border facilities "temporary camps" rather than "refugee camps" to avoid implying permanence. The government prioritizes maintaining friendly relations with Myanmar's State Administrative Council over protecting vulnerable populations. Sann Aung, executive director of the New Myanmar Foundation in Mae Sot, warned that resistance members face particular danger. Human Rights Watch has urged Thailand to end the detention of migrant and refugee children in immigration centers, arguing that the practice is arbitrary, harmful, and inconsistent with international law. In a report released in Bangkok, the New York-based rights group said Thai authorities process at least 4,000 children of migrant workers and refugee children through detention centers each year. According to the report, children are held for an average of nearly 10 months, and some remain detained for as long as two years. The group said the findings were based on interviews with more than 100 migrant children and adults, as well as Thai officials from the immigration department, police, and the Ministry of Social Development and Human Security. Human Rights Watch described detention facilities as severely overcrowded, with children often confined in cramped cells alongside adults. One case study cited a family sharing a cell with 100 others, where toilets were filthy, raw sewage was on the floor, and air quality was poor. The report also noted that Thailand has seen a rise in refugees and asylum seekers from countries including Syria, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, and Somalia, though most detainees are from neighboring Myanmar. Human Rights Watch said family separation in detention can expose children to psychological harm, poor nutrition, inadequate medical care, and limited access to education. Farmer said detention is especially damaging for young children and for refugees who have already experienced trauma during flight. The organization called on Thailand to adopt alternatives to detention and improve conditions in centers, following U.N. child-rights guidelines. It said children should not be detained in immigration facilities. Thailand responded that it is addressing problems in the camps and takes its duty to protect children seriously. The government also said many parents want their children to stay with them, and that release delays are often caused by legal-status problems in migrants’ home countries or slow U.N. asylum assessments.

# Summary: Human Rights Watch Calls for End to Thai Child Detention Policy Human Rights Watch has released a report urging Thailand to cease detaining migrant and refugee children in immigration detention centers, calling the practice arbitrary and illegal under international law. The New York-based organization advocates for alternative detention methods and improved conditions in existing facilities. According to the report, approximately 4,000 migrant and refugee children pass through Thai immigration detention centers annually. While the average stay lasts nearly 10 months, many children remain detained for up to two years. Researcher Alice Farmer emphasized that Thailand's system of indefinite detention violates international law, including the Convention on the Rights of the Child, to which Thailand is a signatory. The study, based on interviews with over 100 migrant children, adults, and government officials, documented severe overcrowding and poor conditions. One case study described 100 people sharing a single cell with filthy toilets, raw sewerage, and inadequate ventilation. The majority of detainees are from Myanmar, though Thailand has experienced increased numbers of refugees from Syria, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, and Somalia. Farmer noted that family separations cause psychological harm and expose children to inadequate nutrition, poor medical care, and limited educational access. Children fleeing traumatic conditions face additional trauma through detention. While the UN, non-governmental organizations, and foreign embassies provide some assistance, Human Rights Watch urges Thailand to align its practices with UN Committee guidelines on children's rights. The Thai government responded by stating it addresses detention camp problems seriously and protects children's welfare. Officials noted that many detainees lack legal status in their home countries or face delays in UN asylum assessments, contributing to extended detention periods.

ISIS briefly sowed confusion in Raqqa on Sunday by warning residents that the Tabqa Dam on the Euphrates was close to collapse, then later reversing that message and telling people not to flee. According to a technical source cited by AFP, fighting around the ISIS-held dam in northern Syria had already put it “out of service,” raising fears of dangerous water-level increases. At first, ISIS used loudspeakers to urge civilians to leave Raqqa, and thousands moved to the city’s outskirts. Later, the group’s police vehicles, known as the Hasba, drove through the streets telling residents to stay put and claiming the danger had passed. ISIS also set up checkpoints in northern Raqqa to stop people from leaving. Meanwhile, the US-backed Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) said they had made major gains near Tabqa. SDF spokesperson Talal Silo said his forces controlled 70 to 80 percent of the Tabqa military airport, located near the city on the Euphrates, and were still fighting ISIS inside and around the base. He said the airport could be fully captured within hours. Activist Abu Mohammad al-Raqqawi also said SDF forces were very close to the airport and only about 3 kilometers from the northern side of the dam. A military expert suggested ISIS may be using the dam threat to create flooding, obstruct a military advance, and trigger a refugee crisis affecting millions in the region.

# Summary As fighting intensified around Syria's Tabqa Dam, ISIS issued conflicting warnings to Raqqa residents on Sunday. The militant group initially used loudspeakers to alert citizens about the dam's potential collapse, prompting thousands to evacuate to suburban areas. However, ISIS later reversed course, sending police vehicles through the streets to assure residents the danger had passed and erecting military checkpoints to prevent further departures. A technical source confirmed to AFP that fighting at the ISIS-held dam had rendered it non-operational, creating risks of dangerous water level increases. Meanwhile, Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) made significant military progress in the region. SDF spokesperson Talal Silo reported that US-led coalition forces controlled 70-80 percent of the nearby Tabqa military airport and expected complete control within hours, despite ongoing intense clashes with ISIS militants. According to local activist Abu Mohammad al-Raqqawi, SDF forces were positioned just three kilometers from the dam's northern section. A Syrian military expert suggested ISIS may have deliberately issued the dam warning as a strategic tactic—potentially attempting to flood the surrounding area to hinder military operations and create a refugee crisis affecting the region's three million inhabitants, rather than demonstrating genuine concern for civilian safety.

French academic Jean-Pierre Filiu says he witnessed Israeli forces enabling the looting of aid in Gaza and attacking those guarding relief convoys. Filiu, a professor of Middle East studies at Sciences Po in France, spent more than a month in Gaza from December 2024, despite Israel’s ban on international media entering the enclave, and based a new book, *A Historian in Gaza*, on his experience. Filiu says his account supports UN allegations that Israeli attacks on Gaza’s police and security personnel helped looters operate at a time when widespread hunger threatened the territory. An internal UN memo reportedly described Israel’s approach as “passive if not active benevolence” toward looters. He describes one incident in which 66 aid trucks entering from the Kerem Shalom crossing, guarded by Hamas-linked security, came under Israeli attack. Filiu said Israeli quadcopters appeared to support looters assaulting the local security teams from nearby, killing two armed local notables who were protecting the convoy. As a result, 20 trucks were left unguarded and ransacked. Filiu argued that Israel’s goal was to discredit Hamas and the UN while allowing looters — some of whom were allegedly backed by Israel — to redistribute aid through their own networks or resell it for profit. He also described another Israeli strike on an alternative aid route that the World Food Programme had set up to avoid looting-prone areas, saying the bombing deliberately disabled the road. Speaking to *The Guardian*, Filiu said the war has erased much of Gaza’s infrastructure and called it a “universal tragedy” and a “laboratory” of a post-UN, post-Geneva Convention, and post-human-rights world. He added that Israel made no real effort to win hearts and minds, even though Hamas is deeply unpopular in Gaza. The article also notes that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has admitted Israeli support for the Popular Forces, an anti-Hamas group known for looting aid.

# Summary French academic Jean-Pierre Filiu, a Middle East studies professor at Sciences Po university, has documented witnessing Israeli military attacks on aid convoys and their security personnel in Gaza during a month-long visit in December 2024. Filiu describes a specific incident where 66 aid trucks entering through the Kerem Shalom border crossing, guarded by Hamas, came under attack by Israeli quadcopters. The assault killed two security personnel and left 20 trucks unguarded and ransacked. He notes that paradoxically, Hamas is likely most unpopular in Gaza itself, where residents understand Islamist rule's brutality firsthand. Prime Minister Netanyahu has previously acknowledged Israeli backing of the Popular Forces, an anti-Hamas group implicated in aid looting.

EU border agency Frontex said detected irregular crossings into the European Union fell 42% in the first nine months of 2024 compared with the same period last year, dropping to 166,000. The figures were released ahead of a Brussels summit where immigration is expected to be a major issue. The sharpest declines were on the Western Balkans route, down 79% to nearly 17,000, and the Central Mediterranean route, down 64% to 47,700.

# Summary Detected irregular crossings into the European Union dropped 42% in the first nine months of 2024 compared to the same period last year, according to EU border agency Frontex. The number fell to 166,000 crossings. The most significant decreases occurred along Western Balkans and Central Mediterranean routes, with 79% and 64% reductions respectively.
