Italy was scrambling on Monday to contain the fast-growing coronavirus outbreak that had turned the country into Europe’s main center of concern and triggered anxiety in neighboring countries and beyond. Police set up checkpoints around quarantined towns in northern Italy as authorities tried to stop the virus from spreading further, while travelers from Italy were already encountering restrictions abroad. A bus from Milan was stopped by police in Lyon, France, for health checks, and an Alitalia flight was held on the tarmac in Mauritius. Italian civil protection officials said 219 people had tested positive for COVID-19 and five had died, including two elderly men in northern Lombardy. Officials said the source of the outbreak still had not been identified, even as the virus spread to more than six regions. The rapid escalation prompted Austria to temporarily suspend rail traffic across its border with Italy. In Brussels, EU Health Commissioner Stella Kyriakides warned that the situation had changed quickly over the weekend and said governments must respond seriously without giving in to panic or misinformation. France tightened guidance for people who had visited Italy’s Lombardy and Veneto regions, advising them to wear face masks outdoors, avoid non-essential activities, and check their temperatures twice a day. The same advice was issued for travelers from China, South Korea, Singapore, and Macau. France itself had 12 confirmed cases and one death. In Lyon, French health authorities said they were evaluating the situation of Italians on the bus from Milan, but gave no details about whether anyone was suspected of infection. Italy’s neighbors Slovenia and Croatia held crisis meetings, with Croatia saying it would monitor travelers arriving from Italy, including children returning from school trips. Romania’s prime minister said anyone entering from affected regions would be quarantined for 14 days, though local reports said passengers were only being asked to fill out forms. Albania said it was monitoring about 5,000 passengers arriving by air, ferry, and land, with special attention to border crossings from Italy. Farther away, Mauritius blocked an Alitalia plane that had landed, and Italy’s foreign ministry said it was working to help the Italians on board. Mauritius had already begun quarantining passengers from Wuhan or those showing symptoms. Inside Italy, authorities canceled soccer matches, Masses, schools, theater performances, and even Venice’s famous Carnival. They also tried to reassure the public by noting that the virus’s mortality rate was low and that far more Italians had died from seasonal flu this year. Officials said the deaths so far involved elderly patients, some with serious underlying illnesses. Virologist Ilaria Capua said on state television that Italy’s high case count reflected the fact that the country was actively looking for infections, with more than 3,000 people tested, mostly those who had direct contact with confirmed cases. She predicted that more cases would likely be found but said many would be mild and comparable to what other European countries would eventually see. The most dramatic containment step was the effective sealing off of about a dozen towns in northern Italy, where more than 150 cases had been identified. In Codogno, southeast of Milan and near the location of the first hospitalized positive patient, police in face masks guarded checkpoints along the roads. Residents wearing masks and gloves lined up at a supermarket to stock up on food, only to find it closed by order of the mayor. The outbreak also disrupted Milan, Italy’s financial capital, where the final two runway shows of Milan Fashion Week scheduled for Monday were canceled. Some fashion houses had already moved to closed-door presentations streamed online. Civil protection chief Angelo Borrelli later said the total number of infections had risen to 219, with 167 in Lombardy. Five people had died and one had recovered. Health officials urged Italians to show civic responsibility and comply with the two-week containment measures in the north. The surge surprised Prime Minister Giuseppe Conte, who noted that Italy had already taken some of Europe’s strictest measures after the first cases in China, including a January 31 ban on flights to and from China, Taiwan, Hong Kong, and Macau, airport screening, and a state of emergency to free up funds. Until the previous week, Italy had recorded only three cases, including a Chinese couple from Wuhan who were hospitalized in Rome and recovering. The European Union’s health security committee met Monday, and a joint WHO-ECDC team was due to visit Italy. WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, speaking by video link, said the world was seeing how quickly a new virus could spread and cause fear and disruption. He said the WHO was especially concerned about Italy, South Korea, and Iran, where the death toll in Qom had reached 50.

# Italy Battles COVID-19 Outbreak as Europe Braces for Spread Italy has emerged as the epicenter of the COVID-19 outbreak in Europe, prompting urgent containment measures and triggering widespread concern among neighboring countries. Civil protection chief Angelo Borrelli reported 167 cases in Lombardy alone, with five deaths and one recovery. The WHO's health security committee convened to assess developments, with a joint WHO and European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control team preparing to visit Italy. WHO Director Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus expressed particular concern about Italy, South Korea, and Iran, where deaths in Qom reached 50. Ukraine further weakened its hold on the border with Russia on Friday after abandoning eight border posts that had come under repeated attack from separatist fighters. The Ukrainian State Border Guard Service said it withdrew its forces from the crossings because it could no longer protect local residents from the danger posed by the fighting. The posts had become increasingly isolated as combat spread away from the frontier and deeper into eastern Ukraine. Seven of the abandoned posts were in the southern Luhansk region, where pro-Russian rebels have recently strengthened their control despite a renewed Ukrainian military offensive aimed at crushing the insurgency. The eighth post was at Marynivka in Donetsk region, where heavy fighting erupted Thursday. According to the border service, the battle lasted for hours after an armored personnel carrier, seven vehicles carrying fighters, and four flatbed trucks fitted with machine-gun turrets approached the border positions from both sides. Video released by the border service showed the burned remains of one of the trucks on the Russian side of the border. Russia’s border guard service did not directly address the claim that attackers came from Russian territory, but said the Ukrainian post was nearly two miles inside Ukraine. It said the attack was repelled with help from Ukrainian airstrikes and that no munitions landed in Russia. The border clashes came amid a broader information battle over the humanitarian impact of the war. Moscow has increasingly portrayed Ukraine’s campaign in the east as a humanitarian crisis. Prime Minister Dmitry Medvedev said Thursday that the conflict had pushed thousands of Ukrainian civilians into Russia. Ukraine said it saw little sign of such a refugee surge, and its border service reported no noticeable increase in crossings into Russia. Russian lawmaker Vladimir Pligin later said Russia had received about 800 requests for refugee status from people arriving from Ukraine. Russia has also asked the U.N. Security Council to create safe corridors for civilians to leave the fighting zones, but Western governments have responded skeptically. The U.N. refugee agency said in May that while about 10,000 people had been displaced inside Ukraine, relatively few had sought asylum abroad.

Germany on Saturday was searching for possible accomplices of Anis Amri, the suspected Berlin Christmas market attacker, a day after he was killed in a shoot-out with Italian police in Milan. Authorities said hundreds of investigators would continue working through the Christmas holiday as pressure mounted on them to explain how the 24-year-old Tunisian was able to carry out the attack and then flee across Europe. Amri is believed to have hijacked a truck and driven it into holiday crowds at a Berlin market on Monday, killing 12 people in an assault claimed by the Islamic State group. After a four-day manhunt, his escape ended early Friday near Milan’s Sesto San Giovanni railway station, where police stopped him for a routine identity check. According to police, Amri pulled out a pistol, shouted “bastard police” in Italian, and fired at officers, lightly wounding one of them before being shot dead by 29-year-old rookie officer Luca Scata, who was later praised as a hero. German Chancellor Angela Merkel thanked Italy for ending the threat and said the danger of terrorism remained. She promised a “comprehensive” review of how Amri, already known to security services, managed to evade capture and warned that official procedures may need to change. German media and politicians have increasingly questioned whether enough was done to monitor him. Investigators are now focused on whether Amri had help from accomplices in planning the attack, carrying it out, or escaping afterward. Federal prosecutor Peter Frank said it was essential to determine whether a network supported him. Police said Amri had come to Italy from Germany via France, carrying only a few hundred euros and no phone. The Islamic State later released a video showing him pledging allegiance to its leader, Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi. Amri had first entered Europe in Italy in 2011 as a migrant, later spending four years in prison there for setting fire to a refugee center, during which he was apparently radicalized. He moved to Germany in 2015 using the Schengen zone’s open-border system. German security services began watching him in March, suspecting he was planning break-ins to fund weapons, but surveillance ended in September after he was viewed mainly as a petty drug dealer. The case has intensified debate over Merkel’s asylum policy, while Justice Minister Heiko Maas pledged stronger surveillance and faster deportations of illegal migrants.

Justice Minister Heiko Maas pledged to improve surveillance of potentially dangerous persons and expedite deportations of illegal migrants. Authorities deployed hundreds of investigators throughout the Christmas season to examine whether adequate procedures existed to monitor known jihadists and prevent such attacks.

Three people were killed and four others seriously wounded in a knife attack at a festival in the western German city of Solingen on Friday, police said. Authorities launched a major search for the suspect, who remained at large, and cordoned off a large area around the scene. Police deployed helicopters and emergency vehicles, and the public was urged to avoid the area. The attack took place during the first day of a three-day “Festival of Diversity,” part of Solingen’s celebrations for its 650th anniversary. The event was expected to draw up to 75,000 visitors and included music, street theatre, variety acts and comedians across the city centre and other locations. Solingen’s mayor, Tim-Oliver Kurzbach, said the city was in “shock, horror and great grief.” He thanked emergency workers and expressed sympathy for those who witnessed the attack, saying it was painful to think of the dead and injured. The city, which has about 150,000 residents and lies between Düsseldorf and Cologne, was left reeling by the violence. According to the Solinger Tageblatt newspaper, a co-organiser went on stage to announce that the festival was being cancelled and asked the crowd to leave the city centre. Thousands of attendees then cleared the area, with one journalist describing the scene as “ghostly.” Organiser Philipp Mueller said people left in shock but calmly. A witness, Lars Breitzke, said he was only a few metres from the attack and initially thought someone had drunk too much, before seeing people on the ground and pools of blood. The attack adds to a string of knife incidents in Germany over the past year. Interior Minister Nancy Faeser has already promised tougher action against knife crime. In May, a police officer was killed and five people were injured in a knife attack at a far-right rally in Mannheim.

A charity rescue ship from EMERGENCY rescued 76 migrants from an overloaded wooden boat in the Mediterranean and was heading to the southern Italian port of Naples, the group said on Saturday. The migrants were picked up in international waters in the Maltese search-and-rescue zone on Friday night. Among them were seven women and 24 children. The 12-meter boat had left Libya late on Thursday, and those rescued came from Egypt, Eritrea, Ethiopia and Syria. Italian authorities helped coordinate the operation, and the charity’s Life Support vessel was expected to arrive in Naples on Monday. Separately, another charity, Open Arms, said its Astral rescue yacht had arrived in Porto Empedocle in Sicily with 59 rescued migrants, including five children, two of them only a few weeks old. Open Arms said it had sought an Italian port after initially being told to return the migrants to Tunisia. The rescues came as crossings in the central Mediterranean increased. Italy has recorded nearly 95,000 sea arrivals so far this year, more than twice the figure for the same period last year. The route remains highly deadly, with more than 22,000 deaths or disappearances since 2014. Also on Saturday, a migrant boat capsized in the Channel, leaving at least six dead.

# Summary A charity rescue ship operated by EMERGENCY picked up 76 migrants from an overloaded wooden boat in the Mediterranean Sea on Friday night and was heading to Naples, Italy. The rescued individuals, including seven women and 24 children from Egypt, Eritrea, Ethiopia, and Syria, had departed Libya on Thursday. Simultaneously, another charity vessel, Open Arms, docked in Sicily with 59 rescued migrants, including five children. The organization had initially faced pressure to return migrants to Tunisia before Italian authorities assigned it a port. These rescues occur amid a significant surge in Mediterranean crossings. Italy has recorded nearly 95,000 sea arrivals this year—more than double the previous year's figure for the same period. The central Mediterranean remains one of the world's deadliest migration routes, with over 22,000 deaths or disappearances since 2014. Additionally, a migrant boat capsized in the English Channel on Saturday, resulting in at least six deaths and over 50 rescues.

Dutch police moved on Monday to end farmer protests that have disrupted traffic across the Netherlands. Farmers, angered by low produce prices, rising costs, cheap imports and EU environmental rules, have blocked highway exits with tractors and set fires along roads since last week. Social media images showed burning hay and tires in several locations. Police said they were trying to stop the protests and detain lawbreakers, but said they could not be everywhere at once. The Gelderland provincial police reported fires, fireworks and tractors on highways, warning of unsafe conditions. Earlier Monday, Belgian and Dutch farmers used dozens of tractors to block the Dutch-Belgian motorway border crossing between Maastricht and Liege, after similar border blockades on Friday. Similar farmer protests have also spread to other European countries in recent weeks.

# Summary Dutch police moved to end farmer protests on Monday as demonstrations escalated across the Netherlands. Farmers, angry over low produce prices, rising costs, cheap imports, and EU environmental regulations, blocked highway exits and set fires using hay and tires to disrupt traffic since the previous week. Police acknowledged difficulty managing the widespread disruption, stating their presence was needed simultaneously in multiple locations. Dangerous situations resulted from the fires, fireworks, and tractors on highways. Belgian and Dutch farmers also blocked the Dutch-Belgian motorway border crossing between Maastricht and Liege, continuing actions from Friday. Similar farmer protests have recently occurred throughout Europe.

A suicide blast and armed skirmish along the Saudi-Yemen border left several people dead and highlighted the persistent security threat posed by al-Qaeda-linked militants in the region. According to Saudi-owned Al-Arabiya TV, two suspected al-Qaeda fighters were surrounded inside a government building in southern Saudi Arabia early Saturday and blew themselves up as military operations were under way after an attack on a border post with Yemen. The channel did not provide details on additional casualties from that explosion. The violence followed an attack on Friday in which six people were killed, including the suicide bomber and two Saudi security personnel. Saudi security forces had been searching for armed al-Qaeda fighters who fled after that assault. Yemen’s state news agency, Saba, reported a related attack on the Yemeni side of the Wadia border crossing, where a suicide bomber drove a car packed with explosives into the crossing, killing himself and one soldier and injuring another. Yemeni security forces then chased the attackers, who escaped in two cars into the desert, according to a military source cited by Saba. A Yemeni official told Reuters that the same group of gunmen had crossed into Saudi Arabia after attacking the Yemeni post and identified them as al-Qaeda fighters. The attacks underscored Saudi Arabia’s long-standing concern over its 1,800-km border with Yemen, a country racked by conflict and home to al-Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula. Riyadh has spent years building a border fence, though the project has faced interruptions from local tribes. The kingdom has also recently intensified counterterrorism efforts, including the detention in May of 62 suspected al-Qaeda operatives.

# Summary: Suicide Blast Hits Saudi Border Post Two suspected al-Qaeda fighters detonated themselves inside a government building in southern Saudi Arabia on Saturday, according to Al-Arabiya TV. This incident followed an attack on a border post with Yemen on Friday that killed six people, including a suicide bomber and two security personnel. Saudi security forces had been pursuing al-Qaeda fighters who fled after the Friday attack. Separately, Yemen's state news agency reported that a suicide bomber drove an explosives-laden car into the Yemeni side of the Wadia border crossing, killing himself and one soldier while wounding another. Yemeni security forces subsequently chased the fleeing fighters into the desert. A Yemeni official indicated the same group of fighters was responsible for attacks on both sides of the border, identifying them as al-Qaeda members. The Wadia crossing, located in Hadramout province in southeastern Yemen, is situated in terrain that al-Qaeda exploits across the Middle East. Saudi Arabia has been constructing a security fence along its 1,800-kilometer border with Yemen since 2003 to deter armed groups and criminals, though construction has been interrupted by protesting tribesmen concerned about livestock access. The attacks underscore the security threat posed by armed rebels to both nations. Saudi Arabia, the world's largest oil exporter and a U.S. ally, previously overcame its own al-Qaeda uprising nearly a decade ago.

A migrant boat capsized off Yemen’s coast on Sunday, leaving dozens missing, Yemeni officials said. Khalid al-Subeihi, a coast guard official in the city of Mocha, said the vessel was carrying 75 migrants, mostly from the Horn of Africa. Twenty-six people survived, but at least 49 others remained missing. Lt. Co. Olwan al-Qameri said search operations were still under way on Monday. Yemen’s state-run SABA news agency, citing an unnamed coast guard official, reported that strong winds caused the boat to overturn and that all aboard, including women and children, fell into the water. The disaster is the latest in a series of deadly crossings by African migrants traveling through Yemen in hopes of reaching wealthier Gulf states. Each year, thousands undertake the dangerous journey from Ethiopia, Djibouti, and Somalia, fleeing poverty and insecurity in search of work.

# Migrant Boat Capsizes off Yemen A migrant boat carrying 75 people, primarily from the Horn of Africa, capsized off Yemen's coast on Sunday, leaving dozens missing. Yemeni coast guard official Khalid al-Subeihi reported that 26 people survived while at least 49 remain missing. According to Yemen's state news agency, strong winds caused the vessel to capsize, throwing all passengers—including women and children—into the water. Search and rescue operations continued Monday. This tragedy represents another maritime disaster involving African migrants attempting to reach oil-rich Gulf countries. Thousands of people annually undertake this dangerous journey from Ethiopia, Djibouti, and Somalia, seeking better economic opportunities and escape from poverty and insecurity in their home countries.

Turkish Coast Guard authorities said Friday they intercepted 36 irregular migrants in the Aegean Sea off Bodrum, in western Mugla province. The migrants were spotted on jet skis and rubber boats. Türkiye remains a major transit route for asylum seekers heading to Europe.

Saudi authorities arrested 18,836 people in one week for violating residency, work, and border security rules, the Saudi Press Agency reported. Of those, 11,710 were detained for residency violations, 4,239 for illegal border crossing attempts, and 2,887 for labor-related offenses. Among 1,741 people caught trying to enter the Kingdom illegally, 60% were Ethiopian, 39% Yemeni, and 1% from other nationalities. Another 46 were caught attempting to cross into neighboring countries, and 19 were held for transporting or harboring violators. The Interior Ministry warned facilitators could face up to 15 years in prison and fines up to SR1 million.

# Summary Saudi Arabia arrested 18,836 people in one week for violating residency, work, and border security regulations. The arrests included 11,710 for residency violations, 4,239 for illegal border crossing attempts, and 2,887 for labor-related offenses. Among 1,741 people caught attempting illegal entry, 60 percent were Ethiopian and 39 percent Yemeni. Additionally, 46 people were apprehended attempting to cross into neighboring countries, and 19 were arrested for transporting and harboring violators. The Ministry of Interior warned that facilitating illegal entry carries penalties including up to 15 years imprisonment, fines up to SR1 million, and asset confiscation.

Iran’s permanent representative to the United Nations, Majid Takht Ravanchi, said the international community should help Afghans overcome their current hardships, noting that Iran has already sent 30 aid convoys to Afghanistan. He made the remarks on Thursday at a virtual UN donor meeting co-hosted by the United Kingdom, Germany, and Qatar. Takht Ravanchi said Afghanistan’s humanitarian situation is worsening and described the country as facing “great challenges, opportunities, fears and hopes.” He argued that the world should support the Afghan people in overcoming difficulties and building a brighter future. He added that, as a neighboring country, Iran has stood by Afghanistan over the past four decades and has used its own capacities to help. According to the Iranian diplomat, Iran has hosted millions of Afghan refugees, who he said have received the least international assistance over the past 40 years. He said Iran has sent more than 30 shipments of humanitarian aid to Afghans in recent months, calling this only one example of Tehran’s support. Takht Ravanchi also said international financial support is essential for Afghanistan to get through its current crisis. He condemned the seizure of Afghanistan’s frozen assets as illegitimate and demanded their immediate and unconditional release. He stressed that hopes for the country’s future, especially among young people, depend on the formation of an inclusive government representing all parts of Afghan society, including different ethnic groups, men, women, and youth. Afghanistan has been in deep economic crisis since the Taliban returned to power on August 15 last year. A report published by Article18 and partner groups says Georgia is routinely rejecting asylum claims made by Iranian Christians, despite evidence that many face a real risk of persecution if sent back to Iran. The report was compiled with Christian Solidarity Worldwide, Open Doors, and Middle East Concern, based on interviews with migrants and their legal representatives. According to the findings, Iranian asylum seekers in Georgia are left in a precarious situation, with little chance of being recognized as refugees and few other routes to international protection. Some of those denied in Georgia had already spent years as refugees in neighboring countries, especially Turkey, where they say they experienced abuse, harassment, and fear of deportation. The report describes many as trapped in a “limbo” in which they no longer know where to go or how to secure safety. They are asking Georgian authorities to acknowledge their claims and urging the international community to create new safe and legal resettlement pathways. The report says that in 2023, Iranians made up about 20 percent of all asylum seekers in Georgia, and roughly 90 percent of them had fled after converting to Christianity. Yet over the past three years, Georgia’s immigration department has approved asylum for fewer than 1 percent of nearly 1,200 Iranian applicants, including those seeking protection for reasons beyond religious persecution. The authors argue that several factors may explain the pattern, including Georgia’s growing relationship with Iran and what they describe as intolerance toward forms of Christianity other than Georgian Orthodoxy. In most cases, officials reject applications by saying the person’s conversion is not genuine. However, the report says this rationale does not apply in the cases of Pastor Reza Fazeli and Amin Zangeneh Zad, whose Christian faith was accepted but whose asylum claims were still denied. The report highlights the emotional toll on applicants. Sasan Rezaee, who spent nearly a decade in Turkey before moving to Georgia, said he was so exhausted by the process that he had considered returning to Iran, even if it meant punishment. He said he could not stay in Georgia or Turkey and feared having no option but to go back home, adding that he sometimes thinks about suicide. Another asylum seeker, Iliya Rahnama, was forced to leave Georgia after his claim was rejected. He criticized what he sees as unequal treatment of Iranian Christians and pleaded for justice and recognition of religious freedom. The report calls on Georgia to improve refugee determination procedures, take seriously the diversity of Christian beliefs, and consult UN reporting on Iran when judging whether applicants face persecution. It also urges the international community to pressure Georgia, expand safe resettlement routes, and strengthen regional protection systems for Iranian Christians fleeing religious persecution.

A Syrian refugee family in Canada thanked the federal government on Thursday for helping them resettle after years of waiting and bureaucracy. The Al Dandashi family fled Syria in April 2012 and first went to Lebanon, where they registered with the United Nations High Commission on Refugees. Their case was submitted to Canadian officials in January 2014, and a week later the Canadian embassy in Beirut contacted them. Two weeks before the report, the family of five arrived in Laval, north of Montreal. The family said they had lived in difficult conditions in Lebanon and had worried about the future of their three sons, now 23, 21, and 13. Their eldest son, Mohamed, had been jailed for 40 days in Syria. Souhad Al Dandashi said she could now “see, God willing, a future” for her children. Jasem Al Dandashi, speaking on the eve of World Refugee Day, said he was not critical of Canada and felt “the steps were not too long.” The federal government has pledged to sponsor 200 refugees under UN protection by the end of the year and to allow the private sponsorship of 1,100 more, for a total of 1,300. However, refugee support groups have accused Ottawa of moving too slowly and imposing burdensome conditions on private sponsorships. Faisal Alazem of the Syrian Canadian Council said Canada should accept many more refugees, arguing that 200 was far too few given the scale of the crisis and pointing to a UN request last month for Canada to take in more than 5,000. Immigration Minister Chris Alexander pushed back, saying the UN High Commission was slowing the process and noting that it had not resettled 1,600 Syrian refugees worldwide across 16 countries, including Canada.

# Syrian Refugees Settle in Canada After Years of Waiting The Al Dandashi family, Syrian refugees who fled their country in April 2012, arrived in Laval, Quebec, two weeks ago after enduring years of bureaucratic processing. The family of five initially sought refuge in Lebanon, where they registered with the UN High Commission on Refugees. Their case was presented to Canadian officials in January 2014, and within a week, the Canadian embassy in Beirut contacted them. During their time in Lebanon, the family faced difficult conditions. Upon arriving in Canada, Souhad Al Dandashi expressed gratitude, saying she now sees "a future as I dreamed for them." He urged Canada to accept the UN's request for over 5,000 refugees. Mohamed Echkouna, a 24-year-old filmmaker from Mauritania, says film can shape emotions and perspectives like “brain surgery without opening up the brain.” Now studying visual effects at the Savannah College of Art and Design in Atlanta, he is using cinema to challenge what he sees as distorted international portrayals of Africa and to present Africans as the central characters in their own stories. Echkouna’s sense of identity was formed in the desert village where he was raised in Adrar, Mauritania, living with his mother while his father worked as a cameraman in Nouakchott. His childhood was semi-nomadic: the family moved among ancient Saharan settlements, and he spent his days tending hundreds of camels and sheep. In the village, only 13 families lived together, sharing responsibilities and creating a close-knit community. There, he identified as a Moor, speaking Hassaniya Arabic and learning local customs. He also developed a deep love for African music, including Senegalese, Nigerian and Malian sounds, and especially the kora, which he describes as almost heavenly. His ideas about identity changed after he moved to the city at age 10 to join his father. In Mauritania, he says, television offered little reflection of black Africa, and he began to notice how media shapes people’s sense of themselves. He says the country’s TV channels did not show Africans, and that Sudan was the closest thing to black Africa he saw on screen. Hollywood films introduced him to Africa, but in ways he found troubling. Movies such as Blood Diamond and Tears of the Sun showed him images of war, child soldiers and poverty, reinforcing negative stereotypes. This frustrated him and pushed him to explore his African identity more seriously. Seeking that connection, Echkouna applied to the African Leadership Academy in South Africa and later took a leap by enrolling at SCAD in the United States, despite lacking tuition money. The risk has paid off. With only two months left in his studies, he has already made a film, Trail of Hope, that has drawn critical praise and is being screened at the Cannes Film Festival’s Short Film Corner. Originally a class project, the film addresses women’s education, domestic violence and arranged marriage through the story of Mariam, a girl forced to leave school and marry a man who later kills her. Echkouna says the character is fictional but reflects the reality of many women in Mauritania and is intended to encourage discussion of women’s rights. He acknowledges that many African countries still face serious development challenges, but insists Africans should tell their own stories. “We need to be the hero,” he says. He now hopes to find talented actors across the continent and is planning a documentary on spiritual chanting, inspired by gospel music he heard in Xhosa-speaking churches in South Africa. Seeing himself as part of a new generation of African filmmakers, Echkouna says he is an African in the world, telling his story.

He believes film is a powerful tool to influence emotions and perspectives, describing it as "doing brain surgery without opening up the brain." His mission stems from a deep personal connection to Africa and frustration with how the continent is portrayed in international media. Echkouna's journey began in his mother's village in Adrar, Mauritania, where he spent his childhood in a semi-nomadic community of just 13 families. He herded camels and sheep while developing his identity as a Moor, speaking Hassaniya Arabic and learning local customs. This idyllic existence changed at age ten when he moved to the capital to live with his father, a cameraman. It was then that Echkouna began noticing media's influence on identity formation. Growing up in Mauritania, he observed that local television rarely featured African content. His introduction to Africa came through Hollywood films like "Blood Diamond" and "Tears of the Sun," which presented the continent through a deeply troubling lens. He was disturbed by the relentless negative imagery: war, child soldiers, and poverty. These portrayals clashed with his emerging sense of African identity and sparked his determination to tell different stories. Driven by this realization, Echkouna applied to the African Leadership Academy in South Africa, then took a significant risk by applying to the Savannah College of Art and Design in Atlanta despite lacking tuition funds. The gamble succeeded, and he is now completing his visual effects studies while already achieving critical recognition. His current goals include discovering talented actors across the continent and creating a documentary about spiritual chanting to illustrate global spiritual connectedness, inspired by experiencing gospel music in Xhosa during his time in South Africa. Representing a new generation of African filmmakers committed to preserving and sharing indigenous culture, Echkouna maintains his identity while studying in Atlanta. He views himself as "an African in the world, telling my story," determined to change how Africa and Africans are perceived globally through authentic, nuanced filmmaking.

The article argues that the real beneficiary of the first day of the Republican National Convention was Vladimir Putin, because the events in Cleveland showed how thoroughly Donald Trump and his allies had reshaped the GOP’s foreign policy posture toward Russia. The immediate trigger was a Washington Post report that Trump campaign aides had stripped a Republican platform plank of language endorsing lethal military aid to Ukraine. The original proposal would have supported “providing lethal defensive weapons,” but Trump’s team replaced it with the much vaguer phrase “appropriate assistance.” This mattered because Russia had invaded Ukraine in 2014, a move that ignited a war that has killed thousands and destabilized Eastern Europe. The article presents the change as evidence that Trump’s camp was willing to soften the party’s stance in order to avoid offending Moscow. That same day, the convention also gave a prime-time speaking slot to retired General Michael Flynn, who had previously been paid by Russian interests. The combination of the platform change and Flynn’s appearance was presented as proof that Trump’s influence over the party had become so strong that it could force the GOP to adopt a more Russia-friendly position. The piece places this in the broader context of Trump’s long-running praise for Putin. Trump has repeatedly described Putin as a strong, effective leader and has blamed tensions between Russia and the West on weak European leaders and President Barack Obama, whom he says failed to command respect. Trump has also spoken approvingly of Putin’s support for Syrian President Bashar al-Assad, even though Assad’s government has been linked to mass violence, the rise of the Islamic State, and the refugee crisis. The article argues that Trump’s supporters who admire authoritarianism, “traditional” values, and macho symbolism see Putin as a model because of his anti-LGBT policies, nationalist rhetoric, and public displays of strength. It suggests that the GOP’s shift reflects not only Trump’s personal views but also a larger transformation within the Republican base: many rank-and-file voters are now more skeptical of foreign intervention than the party’s traditional foreign policy establishment. The article compares this trend to far-right European parties that have developed close ties to Putin and echo Moscow’s claim that Western elites are pushing conflict for globalist or corporate interests.

The Washington Post revealed that Trump's team removed an anti-Russian provision from the GOP platform, specifically weakening language supporting military aid to Ukraine. Instead of endorsing "lethal defensive weapons" for Ukraine—a position aligned with Republican foreign policy consensus—the platform was altered to vague references to "appropriate assistance." This change occurred after Russia's 2014 invasion of Ukraine, which sparked an ongoing conflict resulting in thousands of deaths. Additionally, the convention featured a retired general with documented financial ties to Moscow in a prime-time speaking slot, further illustrating the campaign's Russian alignment. Ultimately, the article contends that Trump's campaign has consolidated enough control over the Republican Party to reshape its stance on a major foreign policy issue in Putin's favor, marking an unprecedented alignment between the GOP and Russian interests.

Two major refugee aid organizations, the International Rescue Committee (IRC) and HIAS, said Friday that they are ending their work with the Biden administration to help identify vulnerable migrants in Mexico who should be allowed into the United States to seek humanitarian protection. Their withdrawal is a setback for a government effort that relied on advocacy groups to refer especially at-risk people — including women with children and LGBTQ migrants — for exemptions from a Trump-era public health order that has largely shut down asylum at the border. The order, known as Title 42, was issued in March 2020 during the coronavirus pandemic. It allows U.S. authorities to quickly expel nearly all single adults and many families at the border without giving them a chance to request asylum. The Biden administration has kept the policy in place, despite pressure from advocates who argue that it is no longer justified on public health grounds. The administration has deferred to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, and the only major exception has been for unaccompanied children. The organizations said they had agreed to participate only until July 31, when the administration was expected to end the restrictions. But they said they have not been told that Title 42 will be lifted. HIAS spokesman Bill Swersey said the group did not want to support a system that, in its view, violates international human rights law. HIAS said it will continue working with the government until Aug. 31 to finish cases already underway. It said it had assisted 4,842 asylum-seekers as of July 23. IRC said it had helped 1,070 migrants as of July 27 and expected the total to reach about 1,500 once pending cases are completed. The group led the consortium’s work in Nogales, Arizona, and said its role will end Saturday. IRC regional vice president Meghan Lopez said the organization became involved because of the humanitarian crisis created by the backlog of cases at the border, but that the exemption process was never meant to be a long-term fix. She argued that Title 42 does not protect public health because asylum-seekers are tested for COVID-19 before entering the country, while the policy leaves thousands stranded in dangerous Mexican border cities. The Department of Homeland Security said its relationship with nongovernmental organizations was “fluid” and described the humanitarian exceptions as part of a phased effort to rebuild the immigration system. At the same time, the administration has increased efforts to deport Central American families quickly if they are caught at the border and do not claim fear of persecution. On Friday, DHS said it had resumed deportation flights to Guatemala, Honduras and El Salvador for families subject to expedited removal. HIAS has also been leading efforts in El Paso since early May and recently expanded to San Diego, according to the Women’s Refugee Commission. Its policy adviser, Ursela Ojeda, said the process should never have been necessary because many migrants remain stuck in Mexico with no way to seek protection. A separate but similar effort is being run by the American Civil Liberties Union, which has been forwarding requests for up to 35 families a day. The ACLU said about 2,000 people had been admitted through that process as of May, though it said the Biden administration will not allow a newer total to be released. Attorney Lee Gelernt said the exemption system has helped desperate families but cannot replace ending Title 42 and restoring a full legal asylum process.

# Advocacy Groups Withdraw from Biden Administration's Asylum Program Two major humanitarian organizations have ended their partnership with the Biden administration over its continued enforcement of Title 42, a Trump-era public health order that restricts asylum seekers at the U.S.-Mexico border. The International Rescue Committee (IRC) and HIAS announced their withdrawal from a consortium tasked with identifying vulnerable migrants—including women with children and LGBTQ individuals—who should be exempted from the public health restrictions while awaiting processing in Mexican border cities. HIAS will complete work through August 31, while the IRC's efforts ended Saturday. ## The Core Issue Title 42, named after a 1944 public health law and implemented by President Trump in March 2020, allows authorities to rapidly expel most single adults and many families without allowing them to seek asylum. Despite advocacy pressure arguing the emergency measure lacks public health justification, the Biden administration maintained it except for unaccompanied children, deferring to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The organizations agreed to participate only until July 31, when they expected the administration to eliminate Title 42 restrictions. However, no such announcement materialized, prompting their departure. ## Accomplishments and Concerns HIAS assisted 4,842 asylum-seekers as of July 23, while the IRC helped approximately 1,070 migrants, with estimates reaching 1,500 upon final processing. Despite these numbers, advocacy groups argue the exemption process was never intended as a permanent solution. "The reason IRC agreed to be engaged in this at all was we recognized the humanitarian crisis at the border due to the backlog of cases," said Meghan Lopez, IRC's regional vice president for Latin America. However, she emphasized that Title 42 doesn't protect public health since asylum-seekers must test negative for coronavirus before entering anyway. The policy instead forces thousands into dangerous Mexican border cities, increasing vulnerability. HIAS spokesman Bill Swersey stated: "The administration has not given any justification for keeping Title 42 in place, so we don't want to be supporting a system that violates international human rights law." ## Government Response and Broader Actions The Department of Homeland Security characterized its relationship with nongovernmental organizations as "fluid," describing humanitarian exceptions as part of a "phased approach to rebuilding our nation's immigration system." Simultaneously, the administration intensified deportation efforts, resuming flights to Central America for families subject to expedited removal—a legal process allowing deportation without immigration judge review. This contradictory approach has further alienated asylum advocates. The American Civil Liberties Union operates a separate exemption process, forwarding up to 35 family requests daily. The ACLU reported approximately 2,000 people admitted through its efforts to settle a lawsuit, though the administration refuses to release more recent figures. ACLU attorney Lee Gelernt emphasized that "the exemption process has been critical for desperate families but was never intended to be a substitute for ending Title 42, nor could a limited exemption process run by NGOs ever be an adequate substitute for a legal asylum process."

Beginning Feb. 1, Oklahoma air travelers who do not have REAL ID-compliant identification will have to pay a $45 identity-verification fee before reaching the TSA checkpoint. The fee pays for TSA’s new alternative screening process, called TSA ConfirmID, which provides a 10-day travel period. TSA says the system is intended to confirm a passenger’s identity and strengthen security. TSA Federal Security Director for Oklahoma Mathew Ketchum said travelers who do not want to pay the fee still have time to obtain a REAL ID-compliant driver’s license or another acceptable form of identification. He stressed that TSA’s job is to verify passengers’ identities and protect travelers and transportation systems. TSA listed many acceptable IDs, including REAL ID-compliant state driver’s licenses or photo IDs, Enhanced Driver’s Licenses, U.S. passports and passport cards, trusted traveler cards such as Global Entry and NEXUS, military IDs, permanent resident cards, border crossing cards, tribal IDs, HSPD-12 PIV cards, foreign passports, Canadian provincial licenses, TWIC cards, employment authorization cards, merchant mariner credentials, and veteran health identification cards. Travelers without acceptable ID are encouraged to use the TSA ConfirmID fee site before traveling on or after Feb. 1, 2026. TSA also directs the public to its REAL ID information page and AskTSA for questions.

# Summary Beginning February 1, 2026, Oklahoma airline travelers without REAL ID-compliant identification must pay a $45 fee for identity verification before reaching TSA checkpoints. The fee covers TSA ConfirmID, a modernized alternative verification system valid for 10-day travel periods. TSA Federal Security Director Mathew Ketchum encourages travelers to obtain REAL ID-compliant driver's licenses or acceptable identification instead. Numerous forms of acceptable ID exist, including REAL ID-compliant licenses, U.S. passports, DHS trusted traveler cards, military IDs, tribal IDs, and Canadian provincial driver's licenses. The TSA emphasizes that identity verification is necessary for security and passenger safety. Travelers without acceptable identification should pay the $45 fee through the TSA ConfirmID website before traveling. Additional information about REAL ID and acceptable identification is available on TSA.gov or through the AskTSA service.

U.S. Customs and Border Protection is considering cutting hours at the Danville border crossing in eastern Washington because vehicle traffic has declined over the past five years. The crossing, currently open from 8 a.m. to midnight, would operate from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. between Labor Day and Memorial Day, and from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. during the rest of the year. The proposal has worried Republic residents and businesses that rely on the crossing to reach Grand Forks, British Columbia.

# Summary U.S. Customs and Border Protection is considering reducing hours at the Danville border crossing in eastern Washington due to declining vehicle crossings over five years. The proposal would cut current hours from 8 a.m. to midnight to 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. during winter months and 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. during summer months. Toronto is launching a city-funded public education campaign this month to counter racist claims and hateful rumours about Syrian refugees. The effort comes as the city continues to resettle a large share of the refugees who have arrived in Canada since last fall: out of 26,166 total arrivals nationwide, 4,334 have settled in Toronto. City staff briefed council Monday on the resettlement effort. Coun. Joe Mihevc, a member of the Community Development and Recreation Committee, said the atmosphere has been difficult, pointing to images from Europe and anti-refugee rhetoric from some U.S. officials during the election season as factors that have intensified hostility toward “the other.” The campaign is titled the Ontario-wide Public Education Campaign Against Xenophobia, Islamophobia and Racism. It is being overseen by the Ontario Council of Agencies Serving Immigrants, whose executive director, Debbie Douglas, said the effort is aimed at a specific form of xenophobia tied to the arrival of Syrian refugees. She said the campaign will directly address anti-Arab and anti-Muslim sentiment, emphasizing that rumours and stereotypes are reinforcing pre-existing racist attitudes. The misinformation the campaign seeks to challenge includes claims that all Arabs and Muslims are terrorists, that refugees threaten Canada’s social systems, and that they are receiving government generosity at the expense of Canadians in need. Syrian-Canadian advocate Leen Al Zaibak, co-founder of Jusoor, said the campaign is badly needed because false information has been widespread and damaging. One of the most common rumours she has heard is that the government is spending more on Syrian refugees than on homeless people or veterans, which she said is untrue. The initiative will begin locally with posters directing people to a website designed to encourage discussion and self-reflection. It will then expand across Ontario through public service announcements and events. Starting in May, organizers plan to bring the campaign into schools, universities, business and landlord associations, and they also hope to work with police departments. Toronto city council approved $220,000 in February for the Newcomer Office’s Syrian Resettlement Program, with $90,000 set aside for the public education and anti-rumours campaign. Although polls have shown many Canadians oppose the scale of refugee resettlement, organizers say the goal is to provoke people into examining stereotypes and to build a broader anti-racism effort modeled on successful anti-smoking and anti-drunk-driving campaigns.

# City Launches Campaign to Combat Anti-Syrian Refugee Prejudice Toronto is launching a city-funded public education campaign this month to dispel racist claims and hateful rumors targeting Syrian refugees. The initiative comes as Canada continues welcoming Syrian refugees, with 26,166 arriving since last fall, of whom 4,334 have settled in Toronto. The campaign, called The Ontario-wide Public Education Campaign Against Xenophobia, Islamophobia and Racism, aims to counter specific misconceptions fueling anti-refugee sentiment. Common false claims include assertions that all Arabs and Muslims are terrorists, that they threaten Canada's social systems, and that they receive excessive government benefits at the expense of vulnerable Canadians. According to Debbie Douglas, executive director of the Ontario Council of Agencies Serving Immigrants, which oversees the campaign, xenophobic rumors feed pre-existing racist attitudes. The initiative will begin locally with poster campaigns directing people to a website designed to provoke discussion and reflection, then expand province-wide through public service announcements and events. Starting in May, the campaign will reach schools, universities, business associations, and landlord groups, with organizers hoping to collaborate with police departments. Toronto city council approved $220,000 in February for the Syrian Resettlement Program, allocating $90,000 specifically for the public education and anti-rumor campaign. Leen Al Zaibak, co-founder of Jusoor, a Syrian expatriate organization assisting refugee integration, emphasized the campaign's necessity, noting that misinformation is "destructive." She cited one prevalent rumor claiming the government spends more on Syrian refugees than on homeless people and veterans—a claim she identified as false. The campaign strategy deliberately aims to provoke thought, pushing Torontonians to examine their own stereotypes and prejudices. While the federal government strongly supports refugee resettlement, polls indicated most Canadians opposed accepting large numbers of refugees, particularly following the Paris terror attacks, which coincided with increased anti-Muslim incidents. The long-term goal extends beyond Syrian refugees to tackle all forms of racism broadly, emulating successful public health campaigns against drunk driving and smoking. Other cities, including Barcelona, have already implemented similar anti-rumor initiatives.

The Gordie Howe International Bridge, the second bridge linking Detroit and Windsor, Ontario, will not open for traffic until fall 2025, officials said, about 10 months later than originally planned. The delay stems from construction disruptions in both the U.S. and Canada caused by the COVID-19 pandemic. Construction began in 2018 and was previously expected to finish in 2024, with the deck still on track to be completed this year. The project’s cost has risen to CA$6.4 billion from CA$5.7 billion. # Bridge Opening Delayed to Fall 2025 The Gordie Howe International Bridge connecting Detroit and Canada will not open until fall 2025, officials announced Thursday. The project, which began in 2018, was originally scheduled for completion in 2024 but faced COVID-19-related construction disruptions in both countries. The bridge deck should finish this year, with a September 2025 opening target. The project cost increased from CA$5.7 billion to CA$6.4 billion. Named after the legendary Detroit Red Wings hockey player, the Howe bridge will serve as a second crossing alongside the Ambassador Bridge, currently the busiest U.S.-Canadian border crossing and critical to auto manufacturing trade.

Russian forces intensified their assault on the eastern Ukrainian city of Bakhmut on Wednesday, pressing their effort to secure a breakthrough in the year-old war, while a senior U.S. defense official said Russia was unlikely to make major territorial gains in the near term. Bakhmut, once a city of about 70,000 people, has been devastated after months of fighting and has become the main focus of repeated Russian attacks and stubborn Ukrainian defense. In a morning briefing, the Ukrainian military said Russian troops were continuing to advance toward the city and “do not stop storming” it. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said in a late Tuesday video address that the battle for Bakhmut was the “most difficult,” but that defending it remained essential. He said Russia “takes no account of people” and sends repeated waves of troops against Ukrainian positions, with the fighting growing more intense. Ukrainian military analyst Oleh Zhdanov said Russian forces had pushed a wedge between the villages of Berkhivka and Yahidne, north of Bakhmut, as part of an effort to encircle the city. He said the breakthrough on Bakhmut’s northern flank posed a clear threat. The Ukrainian military also said its forces had repelled 85 Russian attacks across different parts of the front line over the previous day, though Reuters said it could not independently verify battlefield claims from either side. Russian state media, meanwhile, aired a video clip from the area that it said showed Russian Su-25 fighter jets flying over Bakhmut. The clip included a man identified as a Wagner Group fighter saying the jets were welcome and helped “psychologically.” The Ukrainian military said its aircraft had carried out three strikes on concentrations of Russian forces on Tuesday night. The article described the battle for Bakhmut as part of a broader grinding struggle across the front. In Washington, senior U.S. defense official Colin Kahl told a congressional hearing that the war’s front lines were a “grinding slog” and that there was no indication Russian forces could sweep across Ukraine and achieve major territorial gains in the next year or so. His comments came during an oversight hearing on the nearly $32 billion in U.S. military aid sent to Ukraine since Russia’s invasion on Feb. 24, 2022. That assistance has included drones, long-range artillery systems, and air defense equipment. Ukraine has been seeking more weaponry to defend itself against repeated Russian missile and drone attacks, which in the winter damaged the power grid and other infrastructure, killed hundreds of civilians, and left millions without electricity or water. The International Criminal Court’s chief prosecutor, Karim Khan, was in Ukraine on Tuesday as part of an investigation into whether the attacks violated the Geneva conventions. Speaking in Vyshhorod, north of Kyiv, Khan said investigators were examining the scale, number, and breadth of attacks on Ukraine’s power grid and whether those targets were legitimate. Foreign ministers from around the world were set to meet in New Delhi on Wednesday and Thursday against the backdrop of the war in Ukraine and rising U.S.-China tensions. Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov, U.S. Secretary of State Antony Blinken, and China’s foreign minister, Qin Gang, were expected to attend. An Indian foreign ministry official said India did not want Ukraine to dominate the meeting, though it would be the main issue. On the diplomatic front, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov reiterated Moscow’s position that it was open to peace talks, but only if Ukraine and its Western backers accepted Russia’s annexation of Donetsk, Luhansk, Kherson, and Zaporizhzhia regions, which Russia claimed after referendums last September that most countries considered illegal. Despite setbacks, Russia still controls about a fifth of Ukraine’s territory. Zelenskiy’s government has ruled out negotiations under those terms and insists Russian troops must withdraw to Ukraine’s 1991 borders.

A large delegation from the European Parliament’s Delegation for Relations with Central Asia and Mongolia (DCAS) will visit Astana and Almaty this week to discuss bilateral cooperation with Kazakhstan. The group, led by newly appointed chair Giusi Princi, includes 11 members of the European Parliament and will take part in the 21st meeting of the Kazakhstan-EU Parliamentary Cooperation Committee. DCAS itself consists of 19 MEPs from different political groups and countries and works to strengthen inter-parliamentary ties and address issues of mutual concern. In comments to Kazinform, Princi said the trip is the largest delegation ever organized in the region and reflects a strong political message about the future of EU engagement with Central Asia, especially Kazakhstan. She thanked Kazakhstan’s embassy and parliament for helping prepare the visit. She also highlighted that Kazakhstan-EU relations are built on the Enhanced Partnership and Cooperation Agreement, which entered into force in 2020 and covers trade, human rights, energy, security and environmental protection. Princi said the EU is Kazakhstan’s biggest trading partner, accounting for roughly one-third of the country’s foreign trade, while Kazakhstan is an important supplier of oil and natural gas to Europe. She stressed that cooperation should expand beyond traditional areas into renewable energy, raw materials and connectivity. She also pointed to Kazakhstan’s reforms under President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, particularly in democratic governance, human rights and efforts to address domestic violence. According to Princi, the goal is to build a bridge based not only on trade and energy, but also on democracy, friendship and mutual respect. During the visit, the delegation is scheduled to meet ministers, human rights defenders, civil society representatives and a Kazakh university. The main discussions will center on the recent Kazakhstan-EU Cooperation Council meeting, implementation of the Enhanced Partnership and Cooperation Agreement, internal reforms, the rule of law and human rights. Other major topics include the Trans-Caspian transport corridor, which aims to improve transport links between Europe and Asia and reinforce Kazakhstan’s role as a logistics hub, as well as energy cooperation, climate action, hydrogen, renewables and critical raw materials. Princi said the talks will also address pluralism and press freedom. Princi also discussed EU migration and visa policy, saying the bloc needs a pragmatic approach that respects international law, strengthens external borders and builds partnerships with third countries on asylum processing, anti-trafficking efforts and returns. She welcomed ongoing talks to reduce visa costs and processing times for Kazakh citizens. First vice president Guillaume Peltier said strong partnerships in Central Asia are increasingly important in a turbulent multipolar world. He pledged to support deeper trade ties with Kazakhstan, especially those that promote energy independence, respect borders and expand diplomatic and economic exchange.

Ukraine and Slovakia may launch a direct international rail route between Kiev and Kosice in 2024, according to Ukrainian media citing the Restoration Ministry. Slovakia has approved the proposal, Slovak Transport Ministry Secretary of State Denisa Zilakova said. The train would travel from Kiev through the Pavlovo-Matovske Vojkovce border crossing to Haniska station near Kosice. Preparations include upgrading border and customs controls, adapting the Haniska platform, and arranging bus links to Kosice’s airport and rail terminal. Before launch, transport service contracts with Slovak Railway must be signed, while financing for the project is still being sought.

Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan have launched an Electronic Queue Management System (e-QMS) at the Dostuk border checkpoint, the main crossing between the two countries, to speed up processing for exporters and carriers. The system was officially introduced at a high-level event on the border and is designed to regulate vehicle flows by allowing users to reserve a crossing slot online or through a mobile app. Officials said this should reduce waiting times, ease congestion, improve predictability, and increase transparency, efficiency, and safety at the border. The platform was developed by the International Trade Centre (ITC) in cooperation with Kyrgyzstan’s State Customs Service and Ministry of Economy and Commerce. Kyrgyz Deputy Minister of Economy and Commerce Iskender Asylkulov said the system is an important step toward creating a better business environment, lowering costs for exporters and carriers, and supporting a broader digital transformation strategy aimed at improving the competitiveness of the Kyrgyz economy. The launch at Dostuk follows a successful pilot at the Kyzyl-Kiya checkpoint in November 2024. During the first six months there, more than 12,000 vehicles were processed, and the system reportedly reduced waiting times and received positive feedback from carriers. On the basis of that experience, the platform has now been expanded to Dostuk, one of the busiest and most strategically important border crossings with Uzbekistan. In 2024, more than 87,000 vehicles passed through Dostuk, including over 21,000 import shipments, nearly 8,000 export consignments, and more than 58,000 transit movements. Kyrgyz customs officials welcomed the shift toward a more service-oriented model. Medet Turzaliev, adviser to the chairman of the Kyrgyz State Customs Service, said the reform moves away from a traditional control approach toward one focused on the needs of businesses and carriers. EU officials also highlighted the project as an example of successful cooperation between Kyrgyzstan, the European Union, and ITC. The initiative is part of the four-year Ready4Trade Central Asia project, funded by the EU, which aims to improve the Trans-Caspian transport corridor, simplify border procedures, and strengthen SME competitiveness.

Kyrgyz Deputy Minister of Economy and Commerce Iskender Asylkulov emphasized that the system creates a favorable business environment by simplifying procedures, reducing costs, and supporting the country's digital transformation strategy. Cosimo Lamberti Fossati, Head of Programmes at the EU Delegation in Kyrgyzstan, highlighted how this digital innovation demonstrates cooperation between Kyrgyzstan, the EU, and ITC in accelerating trade flows and expanding export opportunities for Central Asian countries.

Amnesty International on Thursday accused Russia of helping Uzbekistan send back migrants, asylum seekers and other suspected opponents to face torture and unfair trials. In a new report, the rights group said Russia and Uzbekistan were acting as “partners in crime,” with Moscow prioritizing political and economic ties over its human rights obligations. The report said hundreds of Uzbeks have been abducted or forcibly returned from Russia since 2014. Amnesty said those returned to Uzbekistan face a “real risk of torture” and “manifestly unfair trials,” often followed by long prison sentences in harsh conditions. It added that detainees are typically held incommunicado and beaten or otherwise mistreated until they confess. Amnesty’s Europe and Central Asia director, John Dalhuisen, said Russian authorities were not merely ignoring abuses but were “lending a helping hand.” The group urged Moscow to stop extraditing or facilitating the removal of Uzbeks at risk of abuse. The report also claimed Russian officials, including the Federal Security Service (FSB), have been complicit in abductions and forced returns, even when European Court of Human Rights orders barred extradition. In one case, Amnesty said the FSB seized an Uzbek businessman in central Moscow and handed him over to Uzbek guards at an airport despite such a ban. Uzbekistan, ruled by Islam Karimov since 1991, denies using torture. But Amnesty cited testimony from relatives and survivors, including one account describing a returnee whose torturers had kicked out almost all his teeth. The report echoed wider criticism of Uzbekistan from Freedom House and the U.S. State Department over torture, abuse and denial of fair trials.

# Summary Amnesty International has accused Russia of being "partners in crime" with Uzbekistan by extraditing migrants and asylum seekers to face torture and unfair trials in the Central Asian nation. The rights group's report condemns Russian authorities for not only ignoring human rights abuses but actively facilitating forced removals to Uzbekistan, ruled by authoritarian leader Islam Karimov since 1991. According to Amnesty, hundreds of asylum seekers, refugees, and labor migrants have been abducted or forcibly returned from Russia to Uzbekistan since 2014. Those sent back face incommunicado detention, torture, and coerced confessions, followed by manifestly unfair trials resulting in lengthy prison sentences served in inhumane conditions. The report includes testimony from a relative describing severe torture inflicted on a forcibly returned asylum seeker. Amnesty alleges Russia has prioritized diplomatic relations with Uzbekistan over international human rights obligations, circumventing emergency orders from the European Court of Human Rights to prevent extraditions. The report documents cases where Russian Federal Security Service (FSB) officers were complicit in abductions when extraditions were refused. Despite overwhelming evidence of systematic torture, Uzbekistan denies using such practices. The country has been listed among the "Worst of the Worst" for political rights and civil liberties, with US State Department reports confirming security forces' torture and denial of due process. Amnesty urges Russia to cease extraditions and facilitate returns of Uzbeks facing real torture risks.

US Secretary of State John Kerry and UNDP Administrator Helen Clark opened the 2016 Social Good Summit in New York on 18 September, launching the first-ever Global Goals Week. The week is being organized by UNDP in partnership with Project Everyone, the United Nations Foundation and the SDG Action Campaign to mark the first anniversary of the adoption of the 17 Global Goals for sustainable development. The event is designed as a week of action, awareness and accountability, with a focus on showing how the Goals offer solutions to major global challenges, including the refugee crisis, disease, humanitarian emergencies, terrorism and war. Speaking at the summit, Kerry said, “There is a world to develop out there and that is what (Agenda) 2030 is about.” Helen Clark told the audience that world leaders had agreed last year on an ambitious plan to end poverty, address climate change and reduce inequality by 2030, but that achieving it would require people everywhere to work together. She said Global Goals Week was created so everyone could engage with these issues. Global Goals Week will now take place each September alongside the UN General Assembly, serving as an annual moment to reflect on the goals, celebrate progress and measure what remains to be done. The summit also announced that US Vice President Joe Biden would speak on Monday about global cooperation in the fight against cancer, alongside other speakers including singer Demi Lovato and Apple’s Lisa Jackson. Beyond New York, UNDP is hosting Social Good Summit events in more than 80 countries, including Gaza, Colombia and Mongolia. The annual summit, organized with Mashable, 92nd Street Y, the United Nations Foundation and UNDP, aims to broaden UN discussions by bringing in innovators, activists and entrepreneurs, and by using social media and technology to connect global citizens.

The International Olympic Committee has confirmed that a Refugee Olympic Team will compete at the Tokyo 2020 Games, following the team’s historic debut at Rio 2016. The decision was announced during the 133rd IOC Session in Buenos Aires, where delegates voted in favor of continuing the initiative. Before the vote, Yiech Pur Biel, a member of the Rio refugee team and a UNHCR High Level Supporter, urged IOC delegates to seize the “unique opportunity” to build on what had already been achieved and create a second Refugee Olympic Team for Tokyo. The first such team appeared in 2016, when refugees competed in the Olympics for the first time in modern history, joining more than 200 national teams that have taken part in the Games since 1896. The Rio team included 10 athletes from four countries: two swimmers, two judokas, a marathon runner, and five middle-distance runners. They competed under the IOC flag and became a symbol of resilience and of the IOC’s commitment to refugees. UN High Commissioner for Refugees Filippo Grandi welcomed the decision, saying the Rio team had captured the world’s imagination and revealed the human side of the refugee crisis through sport. He said it was admirable to give these young athletes another chance to compete at the highest level. The Rio athletes also met again in Buenos Aires this week at the IOC’s Olympism in Action Forum, their first reunion since 2016. There, they promoted sport as a force for peace and reflected on the hope their participation had inspired among refugees worldwide. Refugee Olympic athlete and UNHCR Goodwill Ambassador Yusra Mardini said the Tokyo decision would give refugees another chance to dream, and said she hoped to earn a place on the team again. IOC President Thomas Bach added that although an ideal world would not need a Refugee Team, the conditions that led to its creation still remain.

# Refugee Olympic Team Confirmed for Tokyo 2020 The International Olympic Committee (IOC) has officially approved a Refugee Olympic Team to compete at the Tokyo 2020 Games, continuing a groundbreaking initiative that debuted at Rio 2016. The confirmation came during the 133rd IOC Session in Buenos Aires, Argentina, on Tuesday. Yiech Pur Biel, a UNHCR High Level Supporter and member of the Rio Refugee Olympic Team, addressed delegates, urging them to build upon the previous achievement by fielding a second Olympic Refugee Team. In 2016, ten refugee athletes from four countries competed under the IOC flag in Rio de Janeiro for the first time in Olympic history. The team included swimmers, judokas, marathon runners, and middle-distance runners who competed with remarkable athletic prowess and resilience. UN High Commissioner for Refugees Filippo Grandi welcomed the announcement, noting that the Rio refugee team "captured the imagination of people around the world and showed the human side of the global refugee crisis through sport." He praised the decision to give these exceptional athletes another opportunity to compete at the highest levels. The decision was celebrated by Yusra Mardini, a Refugee Olympic Athlete and UNHCR Goodwill Ambassador, who expressed pride in the team's legacy and her determination to earn a spot on the Tokyo team. IOC President Thomas Bach acknowledged the bittersweet reality, stating: "In an ideal world, we would not need to have a Refugee Team at the Olympic Games. But, unfortunately, the reasons why we first created a Refugee Olympic Team before the Olympic Games Rio 2016 continue to persist." At the Rumichaca Bridge on the Ecuador-Colombia border, Venezuelans continue arriving in large numbers, many on foot and in desperate condition, as they flee the hunger, poverty and insecurity gripping their country. The article opens with the image of Fredy Ramon Castillo, a 60-year-old man in worn, soot-stained clothes, carrying a sleeping mat as he walks alone toward the bridge after traveling more than 2,000 kilometers from Valencia, Venezuela, in just eight days. He says his wages were not enough to buy medicine and that he left to help his mother, breaking into tears as he describes a hardship shared by thousands of others. The border crossing has become one of the main gateways for Venezuelans seeking survival and a better future. Officials and aid groups say that between 2,000 and 3,000 Venezuelans cross into Ecuador daily, with numbers reaching 5,000 on peak days. In 2018 alone, more than one million Venezuelans crossed this border, and more than 220,000 of them did not register their departure at official checkpoints, according to government figures. The exodus is rooted in Venezuela’s deepening economic collapse over the past five years. Severe shortages of food, medicine, basic goods and essential services such as electricity and potable water, combined with insecurity, have driven more than four million people to leave—described as the largest and fastest migration in recent Latin American history. Ecuador has become a major destination. It hosts more than 300,000 Venezuelans, and the foreign ministry in Quito says that number could rise to half a million by year’s end. Though it ranks fourth in total arrivals in Latin America behind Colombia, Peru and Chile, Ecuador has taken in the most Venezuelan migrants relative to its population. The article also describes the exhausting journeys many migrants endure. About 20 buses a day arrive from Colombia carrying Venezuelans, but many others travel by foot in groups or alone. One example is Edison Mendoza, who said he had been traveling for 19 days with his one-and-a-half-year-old daughter because “not having anything to eat” forced them to leave. He hopes to reach Lima, Peru, where relatives live. A World Migration Organization report cited in the article says that 54.4 percent of Venezuelans in Ecuador took one to seven days to reach the border, spending between $100 and $500. The migrant profile is also changing: more women are arriving, and many have at least a high school education. Ecuadorian officials say a small share, especially children, arrive without proper documents. Many newcomers first stand on street corners with signs saying, “I’m Venezuelan. I’m hungry. Please help me.”

The humanitarian disaster, characterized by widespread hunger, medicine shortages, and lack of basic services, is vividly illustrated through migrants crossing into Ecuador at the Rumichaca Bridge. Fredy Ramon Castillo exemplifies the desperation driving this migration. The 60-year-old traveled over 2,000 kilometers in eight days from Valencia, arriving emaciated and exhausted, unable to afford medicine in his homeland. His story reflects that of thousands crossing daily—between 2,000-5,000 Venezuelans per day at peak times, with over one million crossing in 2018 alone. Ecuador has become a critical refuge point, receiving the fourth-largest number of Venezuelan migrants in Latin America after Colombia, Peru, and Chile. The country currently houses more than 300,000 Venezuelan migrants, with projections suggesting the figure could reach half a million by year's end. Proportionally, Ecuador has absorbed more migrants relative to its population than any other Latin American nation. The migrant profile has evolved significantly. Initially dominated by family heads seeking economic opportunities, the movement now includes more women (44.7 percent) and entire families reuniting. Approximately 43.6 percent have completed high school education. Most migrants (54.4 percent) spend 1-7 days traveling, spending $100-$500 each. While 46.3 percent travel alone, 42.9 percent migrate with relatives. Destination preferences vary: 33.8 percent wish to stay in Ecuador, 52.3 percent target Peru, and 12.4 percent aim for Chile. Many arrive with minimal possessions, traveling by bus or foot, sometimes with young children. Upon arrival, desperate migrants often position themselves on street corners with signs reading: "I'm Venezuelan. I'm hungry. Please help me." Border authorities face challenges, including approximately 2.5 percent of arrivals lacking proper documentation, particularly children. Vladimir Velasco, Ecuador's Social Inclusion Ministry district director, notes that improved economic conditions among earlier migrants now enable family reunification, changing migration patterns. Ecuador's experience demonstrates both the severity of Venezuela's crisis and the strain mass migration places on neighboring nations, as desperate families seek survival and opportunity beyond their homeland's deteriorating conditions.

Venezuela temporarily closed its border with Brazil after a U.S. early-morning strike on Caracas, during which U.S. forces also said they had captured President Nicolás Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores.
