Violent turf wars among illegal armed groups worsened in January in Cúcuta, Colombia, a major border city with Venezuela, leaving 36 people dead in the metropolitan area that month alone, according to authorities and local organizations. Cúcuta, the capital of Norte de Santander province, sits at key border crossings and along numerous informal routes used for the movement of people, as well as the smuggling of goods, weapons, and drugs. Those corridors have long been contested by guerrillas, paramilitary groups, and criminal gangs that expanded from the Catatumbo region, one of Colombia’s largest coca-producing zones. The violence has helped make the Cúcuta metro area — which includes Cúcuta, Villa del Rosario, Los Patios, El Zulia, San Cayetano, and Puerto Santander, with about 1.2 million inhabitants — one of the country’s most homicide-prone urban areas, even exceeding cities such as Cali and Medellín. Metropolitan police chief Col. Carlos Andrés García said Cúcuta had long had a high murder rate and was once among the world’s 50 most violent cities. He identified armed actors in the area as the National Liberation Army (ELN), the Venezuelan Tren de Aragua gang, and dissident factions from the former FARC, along with four organized criminal groups fighting over drug sales points and local criminal activity. García said intelligence reports indicate that since December there has been a territorial dispute in Catatumbo, forcing armed members to hide in Cúcuta, where they are better organized than ordinary criminals and where clashes have intensified. At the same time, Cúcuta’s Citizen Safety Secretary Alejandro Martínez said that, despite the spike in killings, homicides through the third week of January were actually down 0.5% compared with the same period in 2022. He said the violence was concentrated in a nine-day stretch and that local police were gradually regaining control. Authorities also reported “extraterritorial” killings, in which people are murdered on the Venezuelan side in disputes over microtrafficking and their bodies are dumped in Colombia. García said there were 23 such murders last year, but only two this year, both near Puerto Santander. The article notes that diplomatic ties and judicial cooperation between Colombia and Venezuela were restored last year, helping efforts against cross-border crime. Still, Wilfredo Cañizares, director of the Progresar foundation, warned of a serious risk for rural residents in Cúcuta and Puerto Santander because of paramilitary expansion. He said more than 10,000 people in 35 communities face pressure from the Gaitanista Self-Defense Forces of Colombia, or Gulf Clan, which is pushing into the border zone despite being included in a six-month ceasefire that began Jan. 1.

The city, which serves as the primary crossing point between the two nations, has become a flashpoint for territorial conflicts among illegal armed groups competing for control of lucrative smuggling routes for drugs, weapons, and merchandise. The violence stems from expanding criminal activities originating in Catatumbo, one of Colombia's largest coca-producing regions. Armed groups, including guerrillas, paramilitaries, and criminal bands, have relocated operations to Cucuta's metro area—comprising six municipalities with approximately 1.2 million residents—where they are "better structured than common crime," according to police chief Col. Carlos Andres Garcia. The competing organizations include the National Liberation Army (ELN), currently engaged in peace negotiations with the Colombian government; the Tren de Aragua, a Venezuelan criminal group operating across South America; dissident FARC members; and local criminal organizations. These groups are fighting for control of drug distribution points, with four major criminal organizations identified as primary combatants. Historically, Cucuta ranked among the world's 50 most violent cities seven years ago and has since escalated beyond measurable comparison to other major Colombian cities like Cali and Medellin. Garcia noted that territorial disputes in Catatumbo forced armed group members to relocate to Cucuta, intensifying clashes there. However, officials presented conflicting assessments of the situation. Citizen Safety Secretary Alejandro Martinez reported a 0.5 percent homicide reduction compared to the previous year through mid-January, characterizing the January deaths as concentrated within a nine-day period. The Gaitanista Self-Defense Units (AGC), known as the Gulf Clan, continue expanding despite ostensibly participating in a government-proposed bilateral ceasefire beginning January 1.

Neiyerver Adrian Leon Rengel, a 27-year-old Venezuelan migrant, has vanished into the U.S. immigration system after being detained in Texas in March, and his family says neither the U.S. government nor Venezuelan authorities have given them a reliable account of where he is or what happened to him. The article traces Leon Rengel’s background as part of Venezuela’s “lost generation,” born in 1998 as Hugo Chávez came to power and the country began a long political and economic collapse. He grew up amid blackouts, food shortages, and failing institutions. For six years he lived in Colombia, where police said he had no criminal record. In 2023, hoping to earn a better future for his 6-year-old daughter, Isabela, who remained in Venezuela, he traveled north carrying his barber tools and entered the United States in June 2023 through a scheduled border appointment using a Biden-era digital portal designed to manage migrant arrivals. Once in the United States, Leon Rengel worked odd jobs and cut hair while saving money. In Dallas, he met Alejandra Gutierrez, another Venezuelan migrant. The two were together for more than a year, and she says he helped raise her daughter. They also had a dog named Princesa. His family and girlfriend describe him as a barber and a sports-loving, outgoing man who played baseball. Everything changed on March 13, his birthday, when federal agents detained him in the parking garage of the apartment complex where he lived in Irving, Texas, as he was leaving for a haircutting job, according to Gutierrez. She said the agents did not have an arrest warrant. They allegedly asked him to lift his shirt to inspect his tattoos, then claimed he was affiliated with the Tren de Aragua gang. Gutierrez said they took his documents and took him away. She says that was the last time she saw him. Leon Rengel was briefly held at East Hidalgo Detention Center, a private facility used by Immigration and Customs Enforcement in La Villa, Texas. After that, his trail went cold. His alien number, which could have been used to track him in ICE’s online system, disappeared two days later. ICE agents told Gutierrez he had been deported to Venezuela, but his family says he never arrived there. She says she has gone to ICE, contacted the FBI and the DEA, and heard the same answer each time: he had been deported, but no one could say where. The article says it is possible he was sent to a mega-prison in El Salvador, where the Trump administration has deported hundreds of Venezuelan men accused of gang ties, but there is no official record confirming that he was among them. Leon Rengel had no violent history and no serious criminal record. His only documented U.S. arrest came in November 2024, when he was a passenger in a car stopped by police. He was arrested for possession of drug paraphernalia, a non-jailable misdemeanor under Texas law, later pleaded guilty to marijuana possession, and agreed to pay a $492 fine. He received no jail time or probation. The article places his case in the broader context of the U.S. government’s targeting of Venezuelan men with tattoos, which officials have used as a basis to suspect Tren de Aragua membership. Experts in South America have warned that tattoos are not a reliable indicator of gang affiliation in Venezuela. Leon Rengel’s tattoos included the names of his mother Sandra and daughter Isabela, as well as images of a barbershop, a tiger, and a lion. The article also says Leon Rengel had applied for Temporary Protected Status in December 2024 after more than 18 months in the United States, and that his application is still pending. But TPS itself has become unstable, as the Trump administration has moved to end protections for more than 600,000 Venezuelans, a decision now facing legal challenge. His case, the article says, has become entangled in a larger national fight over deportation policy. The disappearance is framed as potentially more than a family tragedy. The article notes that, under Amnesty International’s standards, if Leon Rengel was removed without information, access to legal process, or confirmation of his location, the case could amount to an enforced disappearance, which is a serious violation of international human rights law. His family in Caracas has been deeply affected. One brother, Nedizon Leon Rengel, said their mother suffered a stroke last year and that her health has worsened under the stress. The family says they are overwhelmed and desperate for answers. The article then broadens to the Trump administration’s deportation campaign against Venezuelans. More than a month earlier, the first deportation flights from the United States to El Salvador carried over 200 Venezuelan men accused of belonging to Tren de Aragua. Those deportations were carried out after the administration invoked the Alien Enemies Act, a 227-year-old wartime law, arguing the gang was “invading” the United States. The U.S. Supreme Court has since temporarily blocked additional deportations to a third country under that law. Some families have been able to confirm that relatives are being held in the Salvadoran mega-prison CECOT after CBS News published a list of 238 names from the first flight. But Leon Rengel’s name does not appear on that list, and the identities of many people on later flights have not been disclosed. The article says at least three deportation flights have gone to El Salvador, though the full total remains unclear. On March 31, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on X that 17 people had been deported to El Salvador the previous day, but did not identify how many were Venezuelan or tied to each gang. The article also notes a recent proposal by Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele to return 252 Venezuelans held in CECOT to Venezuela in exchange for political prisoners held by the Maduro government, a move that human rights advocates condemned as a political trade. Meanwhile, the U.S. has not released the identities of all deportees, leaving families in painful uncertainty. The Miami Herald asked ICE for information about Leon Rengel on April 10 but had not received a response by the time of publication. Finally, the article highlights the diplomatic void that complicates these cases. Venezuela’s consular services in Miami have been closed since 2012, and diplomatic relations between the United States and Venezuela were severed in 2019. That leaves Venezuelan migrants with little protection or advocacy from their government and makes deportation cases harder to track. As of April 14, according to Venezuelan nonprofit Votoscopio, 2,580 Venezuelans had been deported to Venezuela from the United States and Mexico combined, but those figures do not say whether deportees were accused gang members or had criminal records. For Leon Rengel’s family, however, the central fact remains unresolved: they do not know where he is. His brother said the silence is unbearable, and his girlfriend said she lies awake at night wondering where he might be, still not knowing why he was arrested or whether he is safe.

Indian auto manufacturer Mahindra was named the fastest-growing brand in South Africa for 2022, according to a report by the National Association of Automobile Manufacturers of South Africa (NAAMSA). Mahindra SA boosted its sales volume by 78% compared with 2021, the highest growth among all vehicle brands that report to NAAMSA and more than five times the market average. The company’s growth was broad-based. In the passenger vehicle segment, sales rose 80% to 4,027 units in 2022. Light commercial vehicle sales, led by the Pik Up and Bolero ranges, increased 77% to 8,885 units. Overall, Mahindra averaged more than 1,000 sales per month, crossed the 10,000-unit annual mark for the first time, and finished the year with close to 14,000 total sales. This was the second time since 2019 that Mahindra was recognized as South Africa’s fastest-growing brand, and the fourth time in the past five years that it ranked among the country’s fastest-growing vehicle brands. Dimension Data has urged small and medium enterprises (SMEs) to rethink digital transformation by treating cybersecurity as a core part of business operations rather than an afterthought. The Nairobi-based systems integrator and managed services provider said many SMEs remain reluctant to invest in security, making them easy targets for cyberattacks that can severely disrupt operations at a time when small businesses can least afford downtime. The warning comes against a backdrop of growing losses in the financial sector. Dimension Data cited the Central Bank of Kenya’s Kenya Financial Sector Stability Report 2020, which showed that SACCOs, among the most active adopters of digital transformation, lost KSh106 million over 17 months to March 2021. The report attributed the losses to attackers exploiting weak system controls and minimal identity verification. Dimension Data said SMEs are following a similar digital adoption path and are therefore exposed to comparable cybersecurity risks. Speaking at the launch of a cybersecurity sensitisation campaign, Dimension Data East and West Head of Managed Security Services Dr. Bright Mawudor said there is a common misconception that cybercriminals focus only on large enterprises. In reality, he said, small businesses also hold sensitive and valuable data. He noted that SMEs often operate under tight IT budgets and lack the resources to hire and maintain in-house cybersecurity experts. As a result, security is often deprioritised, leaving businesses vulnerable to ransomware, internal threats and other attacks that have increased in recent months. Mawudor also pointed to findings from the 2021 NTT Global Threat Intelligence Report, which showed that 58 percent of organizations felt unprepared for a malware attack, while 83 percent had rethought their IT security due to pandemic-driven changes in working practices. He said Dimension Data’s campaign will include security workshops for SMBs, as well as practical guidance based on the Identify, Detect, Protect, Respond and Recover framework for managing cyber risks. The company said it will also demonstrate endpoint security, cloud posture and threat intelligence solutions through real-life demonstrations and proof of concepts to show how early detection and response can improve visibility across assets and applications. Together with its partners, Dimension Data plans to offer affordable, tailored managed security services covering security design, incident response, governance, risk and compliance, and cybersecurity assurance. According to Mawudor, this approach would help SMEs avoid the high costs of buying expensive tools, hiring specialists and training staff. Senior Cyber Security Solution Architect Henry Bett said SMEs are increasingly digitally transformed, with many relying on cloud services for finance and customer relationship management. He warned that business owners must understand the risks of non-compliance, especially now that Kenya’s Data Protection Act is in force and gives the Data Commissioner powers to penalize non-compliant firms. Bett added that SMEs should adopt a unified security architecture with centralized management and integrated controls. He said this would improve visibility, strengthen compliance, reduce risk and lower total cost of ownership while protecting workloads, workplaces and workforces across the organization.

A new Boston Consulting Group report says artificial intelligence is rapidly transforming cybersecurity and exposing serious weaknesses in corporate defences. Based on a global survey of 500 senior leaders, including 50 in Africa, the report finds that nearly 60% of African companies believe they faced an AI-powered cyberattack in the past year. Yet only half say they prioritise using AI to strengthen their defences, and just 29% have advanced AI cyber defence capabilities. BCG says the gap between attackers and defenders is widening as AI makes threats faster, more deceptive and more scalable. The report highlights AI-driven ransomware, phishing, voice cloning and deepfake video fraud as growing risks. Globally, only 7% of organisations have deployed AI-enabled defence tools, although 88% plan to do so. Meanwhile, just 5% of global companies and 3% of African companies have significantly increased cybersecurity budgets because of AI. The report also points to a major talent shortage: 69% of global firms and 82% of African firms struggle to hire AI-cybersecurity specialists. BCG executives warn that African businesses are already feeling the impact and cannot afford to rely on outdated tools and underfunded strategies.

A Cape Town woman, Vanessa Hartley, sparked outrage on social media after a post appearing under her Facebook name contained racist remarks about black people and Africans in Hout Bay. The post, shared on the Hout Bay Complete Facebook page, described black people as “stupid animals” and called for them to be tied to a rope, while complaining about “too many Africans flocking to Hout Bay.” Hartley later denied responsibility, saying her phone had been taken at a bar and that someone had used it to make the comments. She posted an apology on the group, claiming the remarks were made from her phone by someone who thought it was funny. Her partner, Ryno de Villiers, who runs The Eye of the Horus Security and IT where Hartley works, said the couple were overwhelmed by calls and inquiries. Hartley’s Facebook profile was deactivated around noon on Monday. De Villiers also reportedly blamed a “stupid drunk” for taking Hartley’s phone. Steve Blecher, the administrator and creator of the Hout Bay Complete page, said he received a call from someone claiming to be Hartley’s employer, who said the account had been hacked. He said the original comment was made in response to a photo of a local fisherman feeding seals. Blecher deleted Hartley’s apology after seeing a screenshot of the post and said he was shocked by the incident. He also stressed that the controversy could seriously damage the community-building work of the 4,000-member group.

# Summary A Cape Town woman named Vanessa Hartley faced backlash after racist comments appeared on her Facebook account on the Hout Bay Complete page. The posts, which included derogatory language about Black people and complaints about "too many Africans" in Hout Bay, sparked significant social media outrage on Monday. Hartley subsequently claimed her phone had been hacked. She initially apologized, stating her phone was taken at a bar where someone posted the offensive comments as a "joke." Her employer, Ryno de Villiers, supported this account, claiming a "stupid drunk" had accessed her phone and made the posts. However, the Facebook group's administrator, Steve Blecher, expressed skepticism about the hacking narrative. He noted the comments were posted in response to a photo of a community fisherman feeding seals. After seeing screenshots of both the original posts and Hartley's apology, Blecher deleted her apology from the group. The incident prompted complaints to the South African Human Rights Commission (SAHRC). Blecher expressed concern that the controversy could damage the 4,000-member Facebook group's mission to unite various Hout Bay communities, warning the negative impact could extend far beyond typical news cycles.

China’s Supreme People’s Procuratorate (SPP) said that in the first nine months of 2017, 710 people were charged with online crimes, up 80.7 percent from the same period a year earlier. During that time, 334 cases were indicted, an increase of 82.5 percent. The crackdown on cybercrime has intensified in China, especially after the widely publicized death of 18-year-old Xu Yuyu in August 2016. Xu died of cardiac arrest after losing 9,900 yuan, her university tuition, to telecom fraudsters. In July 2017, the main culprit in her case was sentenced to life in prison and had all personal property confiscated. SPP spokesperson Wang Songmiao said cybercrimes are becoming more complex, better organized, more concealed, and increasingly committed by young people. He said prosecutors are focusing on telephone scams, infringement of personal information, and the illegal manufacture, sale, or use of malicious base stations, radio equipment, and software. Zhang Xiangjun, deputy director of the SPP’s prosecution department, said these crimes are harder to combat because evidence is more difficult to gather, many illegal websites are overseas, and new forms of cybercrime do not always fit existing laws. He also noted a shortage of specialized talent. To address these problems, the SPP has issued guidelines to help prosecutors handle criminal review, arrests, and prosecutions.

# Summary China's Supreme People's Procuratorate reported charging 710 people with online crimes in the first nine months of 2017, representing an 80.7 percent increase compared to the same period in 2016. Of these cases, 334 were indicted, marking an 82.5 percent increase year-on-year. The crackdown intensified following the 2016 death of 18-year-old Xu Yuyu, who suffered cardiac arrest after losing her university tuition funds to telecom fraudsters. The principal culprit was later sentenced to life imprisonment with full asset confiscation. According to SPP spokesperson Wang Songmiao, cyber-crimes are becoming increasingly complex, better organized, and more disguised, with growing participation by young people and more severe consequences. Authorities are focusing on telephone scams, personal information theft, and illegal production or use of malicious equipment and software. However, officials acknowledge significant challenges in combating these crimes. Deputy director Zhang Xiangjun cited difficulties in obtaining evidence, proving crimes, and investigating cases involving overseas locations. Additionally, new crime types are difficult to classify under existing laws, and there is a shortage of specialized talent to identify and define cyber-crimes. The SPP has responded by developing guidelines to assist prosecutors in examining cases and approving arrests.

Rapper Jackson Makini, better known as Prezzo, has joined Wiper Democratic Movement and will reportedly seek the Kibra parliamentary seat on the party’s ticket in the 2022 general election. Wiper said party leader Kalonzo Musyoka received Prezzo and that, after discussions, they agreed he would not contest the Kibra by-election. The murder case against 42-year-old Nancy Majonhi was postponed in the Mankwe Magistrate’s Court in Mogwase on Tuesday because she was too ill to attend. The court heard that she was in hospital under police guard. At an earlier appearance, the court ordered that she undergo a mental examination before any bail application. Majonhi is accused of killing her husband, Prosper Chipungare, in July 2015 at a rented room in Ledig near Sun City after a fight. Police say she beat him with a hammer until he lost consciousness, then hacked his body with a spade and disposed of the remains in three pit toilets. She allegedly cleaned the scene afterward and reported him missing at the Sun City police station. According to North West police, Majonhi later returned to Zimbabwe, where she confessed to family members and in-laws that she had killed her husband. The families then came to South Africa, after which she handed herself over to police. Police searched the three pit latrines she identified and recovered a skull and bones, which will undergo DNA testing. The case was postponed to November 9.

# Summary A 42-year-old woman, Nancy Majonhi, accused of murdering her husband six years ago appeared in Mankwe Magistrate's Court in Mogwase, South Africa, but the case was postponed due to her hospitalization and ill-health. She is alleged to have beaten her husband, Prosper Chipungare, with a hammer in July 2015, then dismembered his body with a spade and disposed of the remains in three pit toilets. After cleaning the scene, she reported him missing to police. Following the incident, Majonhi fled to Zimbabwe where she confessed to family members. Both families subsequently arranged her return to South Africa, and she surrendered to authorities. Police recovered a skull and bones from the pit latrines identified by Majonhi, which will undergo DNA testing. The court previously ordered a mental examination before considering bail. Majonhi has been refusing food while in police custody. The case was adjourned to November 9.

The Bank of Punjab (BOP) has denied reports on social media and in some media outlets claiming it suffered a cyberattack, saying the incident was actually caused by a temporary technical glitch in its credit card system. The bank said the issue was discovered during routine monitoring, when it detected irregular credit card transactions. An internal review found that the glitch allowed a limited number of existing credit card holders to make unauthorised transactions. BOP stressed that the matter was not connected to any government scheme or special financing programme, including the Asaan Karobar Card, and affected only a defined group of credit card customers across its portfolio. It also rejected speculation that the problem was caused by a cyber breach, and clarified that a system update carried out on Friday, 2 January 2026, was unrelated to the incident. According to the bank, the technical issue has now been fully fixed and additional safeguards have been introduced. Recovery efforts are underway under standard procedures, and BOP said most affected customers have already contacted the bank and begun settling over-limit amounts. The bank described the situation as manageable and under control. BOP also dismissed claims about the scale of financial exposure as exaggerated and incorrect. It said all affected cardholders have been contacted directly, while unaffected customers do not need to take any action. The bank urged customers to stay alert to fraud and to deal only with verified bank representatives.

# Bank of Punjab Denies Cyberattack, Blames Credit Card Glitch The Bank of Punjab (BOP) has issued a formal statement refuting claims of a cyberattack on its systems, describing such reports as misleading and exaggerated. The bank confirmed that no cyber breach occurred. According to BOP, routine monitoring detected irregular credit card transactions among some existing cardholders. An internal review revealed these transactions resulted from a temporary technical glitch in the credit card system, which allowed a limited number of customers to make unauthorized transactions. The affected customers were not linked to any specific government initiative or scheme, including the Asaan Karobar Card. The bank categorically rejected cyberattack claims and stated that a system update on January 2, 2026, was unrelated to the credit card issue. The identified system gap has since been fully rectified with additional safeguards implemented. Recovery actions have commenced following standard procedures, with most affected customers already settling over-limit amounts. BOP dismissed circulating claims about the scale of financial exposure, calling reported figures speculative and exaggerated. All impacted credit card holders have been directly contacted and informed. The bank advised customers to remain vigilant against fraudulent approaches and engage only with authorized officials. Customers can contact the Bank of Punjab helpline at +92-42-111-267-200 for further clarification.

Malaysia has launched a Data Breach Notification system to require data users to report personal data leaks and hacking threats immediately, Deputy Communications Minister Teo Nie Ching said. The aim is to analyze incidents quickly, apply mitigation measures, and prevent further leaks so citizens are less likely to be targeted by scammers. Teo said the government wants to maintain public confidence in the country’s data management practices. She added that law enforcement agencies, regulators, and other organisations are stepping up public awareness, tightening regulations, and improving enforcement as digitalisation creates more opportunities for technology abuse and fraud. Malaysia has also established a National Scam Response Centre (NSRC) to help government and stakeholders coordinate anti-scam efforts, share information, review legal needs, and address the cross-border nature of fraud. Teo made the remarks during a two-day working visit to Bangkok, where she led a Malaysian delegation to the China Mobile South-east Asia Cooperation Conference. The delegation also visited True Digital Park, and Teo was scheduled to meet Thailand’s telecom regulator to discuss anti-scam measures.

# Malaysia Launches Data Breach Alert System Malaysia has introduced a Data Breach Notification system to combat scams and hacking threats, according to Deputy Communications Minister Teo Nie Ching. The system requires data users to immediately report personal data leakage incidents, enabling authorities to analyze information and implement swift mitigation measures to prevent further breaches. Queensland Police have charged five people over an alleged “boiler room” investment fraud that investigators say stole more than $3 million from about 300 victims. The scheme is alleged to have operated between 2018 and 2020, with detectives from the Financial and Cyber Crime Group making the arrests and laying charges in January after an extensive investigation. Police began probing the matter in 2019 after receiving complaints about a series of cold calls offering investment opportunities from business premises on the Gold Coast. In May 2020, officers executed multiple search warrants at homes and businesses across the region and seized a large amount of documents and equipment. Detectives say the materials showed the operation used several trading names, including Starbrite Traders Pty Ltd, Digital Sky Systems, New Vison Products and NPL. A 60-year-old woman has been charged with money laundering, fraud and personation in general – falsely represent. Two men, aged 43 and 42, have each been charged with money laundering and fraud. The woman is due to appear in Southport Magistrates Court on March 1, while the men are listed for March 19 and March 1 respectively. A 28-year-old woman and a 43-year-old man have also each been charged with fraud and are expected to face the same court on March 1 and March 5. Detective Inspector Kerry Lofdahl said the alleged fraud caused serious harm beyond financial loss, including damage to victims’ livelihoods, health and relationships. She warned that no reputable investment firm will cold-call people or contact them out of the blue through messaging apps or social media, and advised anyone who cannot clearly explain how an investment works to seek help from a registered financial planner. The case comes amid broader concerns about fraud in Queensland and Australia, with scam activity continuing to rise and authorities urging the public to check financial planners through the government’s Moneysmart website.

# Queensland Police Charge Five Over $3 Million Investment Fraud Queensland Police have charged five people in connection with an alleged "boiler room" investment fraud that defrauded at least 300 victims of approximately $3 million between 2018 and 2020. The Financial and Cyber Crime Group arrested and charged the suspects in January following a four-year investigation. The charges include a 60-year-old woman facing money laundering, fraud, and personation charges, two men aged 43 and 42 each charged with money laundering and fraud, and a 28-year-old woman and 43-year-old man each charged with fraud. A senior North Korean official who was widely reported to have been punished for the failed Hanoi nuclear summit has reappeared in state media, complicating claims of a purge and underscoring the difficulty of verifying developments inside the secretive country. On Monday, North Korean media showed Kim Yong Chol attending a concert near leader Kim Jong Un. In the images, Kim sat five seats away from Kim Jong Un in the same row with other senior officials at a musical performance by the wives of Korean People’s Army officers. The official Korean Central News Agency also listed Kim Yong Chol among the attendees, describing the event as one that highlighted the “ideological and mental features” of the officers’ wives. Kim Yong Chol has been one of North Korea’s top nuclear negotiators and the main counterpart to U.S. Secretary of State Mike Pompeo during the period when Kim Jong Un engaged in talks with Washington. He traveled to the United States and met President Donald Trump twice before the two leaders’ summits. The diplomatic process has been stalled since February, when the second Trump-Kim summit in Hanoi collapsed amid U.S. accusations that North Korea was demanding too much sanctions relief in exchange for only a partial surrender of its nuclear program. In the weeks after that failure, South Korea’s Chosun Ilbo reported, citing an unnamed source, that Kim Yong Chol had been sentenced to hard labor and ideological re-education. The same report said another envoy, Kim Hyok Chol, had been executed along with four other Foreign Ministry officials for allegedly betraying Kim Jong Un after being influenced by the United States. None of the officials reportedly executed have appeared in state media since then, but the new images of Kim Yong Chol prompted caution about the purge claims. South Korean officials said they could not confirm the report. The Unification Ministry in Seoul declined to comment on a “specific internal event in North Korea or its participants,” while the presidential Blue House warned against “hasty judgments or comments.” South Korea’s spy agency also said it could not verify the purge report. Pompeo said he had seen the report and that U.S. officials were trying to check it. Analysts noted that North Korea often uses harsh punishment for political failures, but many doubted that Kim Yong Chol had truly been purged. Some pointed out that if he were undergoing ideological re-education, he would not likely have appeared publicly so soon. Others argued it would be unusual for Kim Jong Un to execute a lower-ranking official like Kim Hyok Chol if Kim Yong Chol, a more senior figure, was the one most responsible for the Hanoi breakdown. One expert said extreme punishment would suggest North Korea was abandoning the talks altogether. Kim Yong Chol’s prominence in nuclear diplomacy had surprised many observers because he had previously handled inter-Korean affairs rather than U.S. negotiations. Before his diplomatic rise, he was known as a military intelligence chief linked to serious provocations, including deadly attacks on South Korea in 2010 and an alleged cyberattack on Sony Pictures in 2014. Both Seoul and Washington sanctioned him. The episode comes as North Korea has recently tested short-range missiles and issued hostile rhetoric, while Kim Jong Un has given the Trump administration until the end of the year to produce acceptable terms for a deal. Many experts believe Pyongyang is using calculated pressure to strengthen its bargaining position rather than fully collapse the negotiations. They expect seasoned Foreign Ministry officials such as Ri Yong Ho and Choe Son Hui to play leading roles if talks resume.

# Top North Korean Official Reappears After Purge Report A senior North Korean official reportedly sentenced to hard labor over failed nuclear negotiations with the United States has unexpectedly reappeared in public, casting doubt on earlier purge claims. Kim Yong Chol, North Korea's chief nuclear negotiator, was shown attending a concert near leader Kim Jong Un on Monday, according to state media. He sat five seats away from Kim Jong Un during a musical performance by wives of Korean People's Army officers, appearing alongside other top officials. The official Korean Central News Agency listed him among attendees at the event. The reappearance contradicts a report from South Korea's Chosun Ilbo newspaper published the previous week, which cited unnamed sources claiming Kim Yong Chol had been sentenced to hard labor and ideological re-education following the failed Hanoi summit in February. That same report alleged that senior envoy Kim Hyok Chol and four other Foreign Ministry officials were executed for allegedly being compromised by the United States. Kim Yong Chol has served as North Korea's lead nuclear negotiator since Kim Jong Un began talks with the United States last year. He met with U.S. President Donald Trump twice and traveled to Washington before Kim's two summits with Trump. Negotiations have stalled since February's second summit, when the U.S. rejected North Korean demands for extensive sanctions relief in exchange for only partial nuclear disarmament. South Korean officials have exercised caution regarding the purge allegations. The Unification Ministry declined to comment on the "specific internal event," while Seoul's spy service stated it could not confirm the report. The presidential Blue House warned against "hasty judgments." U.S. Secretary of State Mike Pompeo acknowledged awareness of the report but said officials were "doing our best to check it out." Experts express skepticism about the purge claims. Cheong Seong-Chang, an analyst at South Korea's Sejong Institute, noted that Kim Yong Chol's rapid public reappearance would be unlikely if he were undergoing political re-education. He also questioned why Kim Jong Un would execute the more junior Kim Hyok Chol while sparing the more senior Kim Yong Chol, who bore greater responsibility for the Hanoi failure. Cheong suggested that executing officials over negotiation failures would discourage future diplomats from engaging in talks with the United States. South Korea's government and media have mixed records tracking North Korea's elite, hampered by Pyongyang's strict information control. While North Korea has previously executed scapegoats for political failures, many experts doubt this report's accuracy. The purge allegations emerged during a delicate diplomatic period. North Korea recently tested short-range missiles and issued hostile rhetoric toward American and South Korean officials. Kim Jong Un declared in April that the Trump administration has until year's end to produce acceptable negotiation terms. Experts believe North Korea is employing measured brinkmanship to pressure Washington without collapsing negotiations entirely.

Freedom House has ranked China as the world’s worst abuser of internet freedom for the fourth year in a row, saying online censorship in the country has reached “unprecedented extremes.” In its annual report, based on a survey of 65 countries, the Washington-based human rights group warned that global internet freedom is continuing to decline as governments increasingly use social media to manipulate elections and monitor citizens, pushing technology toward “digital authoritarianism.” The report said China had the least free internet of all the countries surveyed, even more restrictive than Iran, Syria, Cuba and Vietnam. Researchers argued that the deterioration reflected Beijing’s tighter control over domestic information, especially ahead of the 30th anniversary of the Tiananmen Square crackdown in June and during nearly five months of increasingly violent anti-government protests in Hong Kong. The report also said China had stepped up efforts to influence election outcomes abroad and had become a major actor in spreading surveillance tools and information controls internationally. Adrian Shahbaz, a co-author of the report and research director for technology and democracy at Freedom House, said it was alarming to see China “weaponising its own content dissemination systems” to shape online discussion of sensitive issues such as the Hong Kong protests and the NBA controversy. That episode followed a tweet by the Houston Rockets’ general manager supporting Hong Kong protesters, which triggered boycott calls in China and official backlash. Shahbaz said Chinese media outlets and social media companies faced little accountability for censoring political, social and religious speech. He also said the group found numerous examples of disinformation about Hong Kong protesters circulating not only within mainland China and Hong Kong, but globally. Freedom House said Chinese authorities had developed a wide range of invasive surveillance tools, both low- and high-tech, to suppress behavior that does not conform to “Xi Jinping Thought.” The report described China as a leader in developing, using and exporting social media surveillance technologies. It noted that Beijing’s long-standing “Great Firewall” already blocks many overseas websites and slows cross-border internet traffic, but said control has intensified under President Xi Jinping, who has repeatedly emphasized the need for the Communist Party to tighten its grip on online communications in the name of social stability and “cyber sovereignty.” The report said politically sensitive topics such as the Tiananmen crackdown and the pro-democracy movement in Hong Kong are often scrubbed from Chinese internet platforms. It also said Beijing has further restricted digital activism by shutting down individual WeChat accounts that post “harmful” content and by using domestic companies to monitor users. Freedom House warned that big-data policing systems being developed by provincial governments could be used against ethnic minorities, including Muslim groups. Rights organizations estimate that more than one million Uygurs and other minorities are held in mass internment camps in Xinjiang, a claim China rejects, saying the facilities are vocational training centers for counterterrorism. The report also linked China and Russia to cyberattacks and information warfare abroad, including a February cyberattack in Australia ahead of elections there. It argued that while authoritarian governments are a major threat, the biggest social media platforms are based in the United States, and their misuse also reflects American neglect. Beyond China, Freedom House said internet freedoms declined in countries including Sudan, Kazakhstan, Brazil, Bangladesh and Zimbabwe. A record 47 of the 65 countries surveyed had arrested people for political, social or religious speech online. Freedom House president Mike Abramowitz said many governments now find propaganda more effective than censorship, and that authoritarian and populist leaders are exploiting social media algorithms to undermine fair elections.

Mozilla announced that Firefox is rolling out a major privacy update, centered on making anti-tracking protections easier to use and expanding several of its privacy tools. The headline change is that Enhanced Tracking Protection, a feature that blocks third-party tracking cookies from known advertisers and data brokers, is now being enabled by default for all new Firefox users. Mozilla said the move is intended to make it harder for more than a thousand companies to follow people’s activity across the web. The company framed the update as part of a broader effort to set a new privacy standard. Mozilla said that over the past year, technology companies have increasingly talked about privacy as users have become more concerned after several high-profile scandals. Firefox, Mozilla noted, had already been offering privacy-oriented tools before those issues became widely recognized, including tracking protection in Private Browsing mode. With public awareness rising, Mozilla said the time was right to strengthen protections for everyone. For new Firefox users, Enhanced Tracking Protection is included automatically in the browser’s “Standard” setting. It blocks known third-party tracking cookies based on the Disconnect list, and Mozilla said the feature is designed to be nearly invisible in normal use. Users will know it is active when they see a shield icon in the address bar next to the site URL, along with a small information icon. By clicking the shield and opening the Content Blocking section, users can see which tracking cookies are being blocked. Firefox also lets users disable blocking for a specific website if they choose. Existing Firefox users will receive the same protection by default in the coming months, without needing to change their settings. For those who want to enable it immediately, Mozilla provided instructions: open the browser menu, go to Content Blocking and privacy preferences, choose Custom, and make sure the Cookies option is set to block third-party trackers. Mozilla also pointed users to its privacy and security settings for more information about Standard, Strict, and Custom modes. Mozilla also announced an updated version of Facebook Container, one of its most popular privacy extensions. The add-on, which has been downloaded more than two million times, is designed to isolate users’ web activity from Facebook and make it harder for the company to track them across the internet. The new update goes further by preventing Facebook from tracking users on other websites that include Facebook features such as Like and Share buttons. Mozilla said that when users visit a news site or other page with embedded Facebook components, the extension blocks those connections to Facebook’s servers, limiting Facebook’s ability to build “shadow profiles” of people who are not even Facebook users. The extension is indicated by a purple fence badge. Another major update concerns password management. Mozilla introduced Firefox Lockwise, a desktop extension that expands its password tools across devices. The product family had previously included Firefox Lockbox for iOS, and earlier in the year Mozilla had announced versions for Android and iPad. Lockwise is intended to help users manage, edit, and access saved passwords more easily, with a consistent experience across desktop and mobile. Mozilla said the desktop add-on gives users another place to store and interact with logins and passwords, helping create a smoother transition between devices. Lockwise is now available on iOS, Android, and as a Firefox desktop add-on. Mozilla also updated Firefox Monitor, its free breach-notification service that tells users when an email address has appeared in a data breach. Since launch, more than 635,000 people have signed up for alerts. The new feature is a central dashboard for managing multiple email addresses, a request Mozilla said users had frequently made. The dashboard gives a summary of all registered accounts, shows how many known breaches may have exposed each one, and identifies whether passwords were leaked. Users can add new email addresses to their account and choose a primary address to receive notifications. Mozilla also added a verification step requiring each email address to be confirmed before it becomes active. Taken together, the updates reflect Mozilla’s continuing emphasis on privacy, tracking prevention, password security, and breach awareness. The company said these tools are meant to help users better control their personal information and understand where their data may be at risk.

A new Gemalto survey suggests consumers are increasingly willing to punish companies that fail to protect their data, with retailers seen as especially vulnerable. Surveying 10,500 consumers worldwide, the digital security company found that two-thirds of respondents (66%) said they would be unlikely to shop or do business with an organization after a breach involving financial or sensitive information. Retailers were judged most at risk from this backlash, with 62% saying they could suffer consequences, followed by banks at 59% and social media sites at 58%. The survey found that consumers are largely blaming businesses rather than themselves for data protection failures. Across all ages, 93% said companies should be held responsible, and 70% said the main responsibility for protecting personal data lies with the organization that holds it. This concern has made security a major factor in brand trust: 82% of respondents want organizations to have stronger online security measures, and 91% believe some of the apps and websites they use already put their personally identifiable information at risk. Social media platforms drew the greatest concern. Gemalto reported that 61% of consumers believe social media companies do not adequately protect consumer data, making them the most distrusted category in the survey. Banking websites were the next biggest concern at 40%. Despite expecting companies to do more, consumers said they do not believe businesses take data protection seriously enough. Only a quarter of those surveyed felt companies treat customer data security very seriously. Many consumers are responding by trying to hold businesses accountable directly: 35% said they have already given organizations feedback on their security methods, 19% have considered doing so, and 33% might do so in the future. Gemalto’s CTO for data protection, Jason Hart, said businesses have no choice but to improve security if they want to satisfy frustrated consumers, especially on social media. He warned that companies failing to respond to consumer concerns risk losing business as customers move elsewhere. The survey also highlighted how common the consequences of data breaches already are. A quarter of respondents said they had experienced fraudulent use of their financial information (26%), while 19% reported fraudulent use of their personal identifiable information and 16% said they had been victims of identity theft. Even so, 66% feared their personal information would be stolen at some point in the future. Although consumers worry about breaches, many are not changing their own online habits because they believe the burden should rest with companies. More than half of respondents (55%) said they still use the same password across different accounts. The findings also suggest younger consumers may be more likely to take action against companies. Among 18- to 24-year-olds, 67% said they would take fraudsters and breached brands to court, compared with 45% of those aged 65 and over. Another 28% of the youngest group said they were at least considering legal action. Hart said the results should serve as a wake-up call, warning that businesses risk damaging both revenue and reputation if they continue to appear careless about data security. He urged organizations to get the basics right and properly protect data with appropriate security controls.

Pope Francis made his first public appearance on Sunday since undergoing major intestinal surgery, stepping onto a balcony at Rome’s Gemelli Polyclinic hospital to greet supporters and thank them for their prayers. The 84-year-old pope stood for about 10 minutes outside his special hospital suite and delivered remarks after three hours of abdominal surgery on July 4 to remove part of his colon that had narrowed because of inflammation. The Vatican said he had been steadily recovering, though it did not specify when he would be discharged. A Holy See spokesperson had earlier said his hospital stay was expected to last about seven days, barring complications. Francis appeared shortly before noon, the time when he would normally have recited the Angelus from a window at the Vatican overlooking St. Peter’s Square. He told the crowd that he was glad to keep the Sunday appointment from the hospital and said he had felt the closeness of people’s prayers while recovering. At first his voice was somewhat weak, but he smiled broadly, waved, and thanked the faithful gathered below. Some hospital patients, well enough to leave their rooms briefly, joined the crowd in cheering him. Children who were also being treated at Gemelli stood beside him on the balcony. Reading from prepared remarks, Francis said his experience in the hospital had reminded him how important good health care is, especially when it is accessible to everyone. He praised health systems that are free and provide good service for all, saying such care is “precious.” He added that tenderness in caring for the sick is like “a caress” that helps ease pain and lift people up. He urged that this value not be lost, and suggested that even within the Catholic Church, health institutions should not be treated primarily as financial assets to be sold off when they are struggling. “The vocation in the church is not to have money, it’s to give service,” he said. The pope also thanked health care workers and expressed concern for the hospitalized children with him, asking why children suffer and calling that question one that touches the heart. He asked the public to pray for them. As is customary in his Sunday messages, Francis also spoke about world events and issues important to him. He reiterated his closeness to the people of Haiti after the assassination of President Jovenel Moïse and the wounding of the first lady, praying that Haiti could move toward a future of peace and harmony. He also again highlighted environmental concerns, urging people vacationing near the sea to protect the oceans and saying, “No plastic in the sea!” In another comment, he expressed hope that Europe would remain united in its founding values, a possible reference to tensions within the European Union over rights issues. He noted that Sunday was the feast of St. Benedict, patron saint of Europe. Francis ended by repeating his familiar request: “don’t forget to pray for me,” which drew strong applause. Later in the day, Vatican News showed him inside the hospital speaking with other patients while being wheeled down a corridor. In one video, he clasped the hand of a woman lying in a bed moved into the hallway for the occasion; she told him they were both 84 years old. The pope also had another reason to be cheerful: Argentina had just beaten Brazil 1-0 in the Copa America final, a result sure to please the soccer-loving pontiff, who supports San Lorenzo in his native Buenos Aires.

The platform runs on the Binance Smart Chain and uses the native DiFi token to enable instant payments. According to the company, users can trade files quickly without signups, and the system is designed to reduce hacking risks through decentralization and IPFS-based storage. The marketplace is intended for selling and buying a wide range of digital content, including videos, code, music albums, photo collections, games, databases, e-books, graphic designs, software utilities, and educational materials. Native, a specialist broker focused on digital assets, has launched the Native Risk Collective, a new underwriting partnership designed to give crypto and blockchain companies access to lower premiums and broader insurance coverage if they adopt approved security and risk-mitigation technologies. Announced in London on July 22, 2025, the initiative is presented as the first of its kind to directly connect vetted cybersecurity tools and operational safeguards to improved insurance terms. The framework is built around the idea that insurers should reward firms for reducing risk in measurable ways. Native and participating underwriters assess each technology vendor to determine how much it contributes to lowering exposure. Digital asset clients that use one or more approved vendors can then qualify for preferential rates through a panel of specialist insurers led by Lloyd’s of London underwriters Mosaic Insurance and Chaucer. In addition to lower pricing, those clients may gain access to a new insurance product tailored specifically to the technology, cyber, and crime risks faced by digital asset businesses. Several vendors have already joined the initiative, including Hacken, Circuit, BreachBits, Hypernative, and Station70, with more expected in the coming months. The approved technologies cover areas such as smart contract audits, onchain threat prevention, and disaster recovery. Native says the product will be available only to companies using vendors within the Risk Collective, meaning businesses are incentivized to choose pre-vetted providers that meet Native’s risk standards. The launch comes against a backdrop of long-standing frustration in the digital asset sector. Exchanges, custodians, wallet providers, and other crypto firms have often faced unusually high insurance costs because traditional insurers have viewed the industry as too risky and too difficult to underwrite with confidence. Even companies that have invested heavily in security infrastructure have typically seen little benefit in the form of better insurance terms. Native argues that the Risk Collective changes this dynamic by standardizing how mitigation measures are evaluated and incorporated into policies, making the sector easier for insurers to cover and expanding access to protection. Native’s co-founder and chief executive, Ben Davis, said insurers have avoided digital assets for years because of the perceived complexity and risk. He said the new framework gives underwriters a structure they can trust while linking them to vendors that are actively reducing risk “on the ground.” According to Davis, the model creates a win-win: customers receive more competitive premiums and better-managed risk, vendors can present their products as a route to improved insurance, and underwriters can support more secure businesses and potentially face fewer claims. Vendors participating in the program also framed the initiative as a shift in how Web3 security is valued. Hypernative’s Gal Sagie said the partnership sets a new standard by linking the use of advanced risk-mitigation technology to tangible benefits such as lower premiums and higher coverage. BreachBits’ J. Foster Davis said the same security principles used by Fortune 500 companies apply to Web3, but with added urgency because of the sector’s unique threats and the need for continuous adaptation. Hacken’s Denys Ivanov said the collective reflects a move toward proactive risk management, with real-time threat detection, automated response, and transparent defense becoming central to trust in Web3. Native describes itself as a global broker bridging traditional insurance markets and onchain capital for the crypto and blockchain industry. It says it combines consulting, insurance placement, and alternative risk transfer solutions, with access to Lloyd’s of London. Mosaic and Chaucer, the lead underwriting partners, are established specialty insurance groups with global reach and strong financial backing.

The article explains what a data breach scanner is, how it works, and why both individuals and businesses may need one to protect sensitive information from hackers. It opens by noting that data breaches can range from stolen credit card information on a laptop to major incidents such as hackers breaking into the Red Cross database and obtaining the personal data of 515,000 people. Citing Verizon’s 2022 Data Breach Investigation Report, it says that 80% of breaches happen because attackers either guess weak or reused passwords or find those passwords online. A data breach scanner is presented as a tool that checks whether your password or other personal data has already been exposed in a breach. Users simply enter a password, and the scanner searches the web for it. If the password appears in leaked data, the scanner warns that it has been compromised and should be changed. The article compares this to the way hackers use password-cracking programs, which scan the web for passwords and rapidly test hundreds or thousands of them in seconds. If the scanner cannot find the password online, the user’s account is considered harder to crack. The article says a capable breach scanner should do more than check passwords. It should also search for credit card numbers, email addresses, Social Security numbers, and other personal information. Ideally, it should also offer breach monitoring, meaning it continuously watches for signs that a user’s data has appeared in a new breach and sends alerts when that happens. However, because such monitoring requires the scanner to store personal information, the scanner itself must be secure. The article says at minimum it should use 256-bit AES encryption, which is described as an industry standard used in many systems, including U.S. government and military applications. It also highlights NordPass as a top choice, saying it uses stronger XChaCha20 encryption and zero-knowledge architecture, so even the company’s employees cannot access user data without permission. For individuals, the article recommends choosing a scanner that also functions as a password manager. Such a tool uses one master password to unlock a vault containing all online account credentials. It can generate long, random passwords made of letters, numbers, and special characters, then automatically fill them in when the user logs in. This reduces the need to reuse weak passwords and makes accounts much harder to hack. The article acknowledges that no tool is completely hacker-proof, but says this setup makes average users far less attractive targets because hackers are more likely to go after easier victims. For businesses, the article says the stakes are higher because companies often store large customer databases or manage third-party databases, making them more valuable targets. It also stresses the importance of limiting employee access to sensitive information on a need-to-know basis. A business-grade scanner should therefore include access management tools that let administrators control who can see what. It should also proactively scan company systems for breaches and notify affected employees so they can change credentials quickly. In addition, it should be easy for IT teams to use, with a simple dashboard and straightforward deployment and maintenance. The article concludes that the first step in protecting personal or business data is learning whether it has already been compromised. Data breach scanners can alert users when their information is exposed, and many also help prevent future breaches through password storage, breach monitoring, and strong encryption.

# Summary: Data Breach Scanners and Business Protection Data breaches represent a significant threat to both individuals and organizations, as demonstrated by incidents ranging from personal laptop compromises to large-scale attacks like the Red Cross breach affecting 515,000 people. According to the Verizon 2022 Data Breach Investigation Report, 80% of breaches occur because hackers exploit weak or reused passwords, either by guessing them or finding them online. Data breach scanners offer a solution by detecting compromised credentials and providing tools to prevent future breaches. ## How Data Breach Scanners Work Data breach scanners function by searching the internet for compromised passwords and personal information. Users input their passwords into the scanner, which searches online databases to determine if the credentials have been leaked. If a breach is detected, the scanner alerts the user to change their password immediately. Interestingly, hackers use similar technology in reverse—scanning the web for passwords and attempting thousands of combinations per second to crack security systems. The advantage of using a breach scanner is that if it cannot find your password online, hackers will face significantly greater difficulty accessing your accounts. ## Key Features Beyond password detection, comprehensive data breach scanners can identify compromised credit card numbers, email addresses, Social Security numbers, and other sensitive data. Advanced scanners offer passive breach monitoring, which continuously tracks personal information and notifies users immediately when breaches occur. However, this feature requires the scanner to store personal data, making the scanner itself a potential target for hackers. Security is therefore paramount. Reputable scanners employ 256-bit AES encryption, the industry standard used by government and military applications. Some providers, like NordPass, implement even stronger encryption such as XChaCha20 and zero-knowledge architecture, ensuring that even company employees cannot access user data without explicit permission. ## Individual Protection Features For personal use, ideal data breach scanners function as password managers. These tools use a single master password to access and manage all online accounts. Password managers generate long, random passwords containing special characters, letters, and numbers that are extremely difficult to crack. This approach eliminates the need for weak, easily remembered passwords while ensuring passwords are never repeated across accounts. While no system is completely hacker-proof, this level of security makes individual users significantly harder targets than average internet users. ## Business Requirements Businesses face different security challenges, particularly those maintaining extensive customer databases or accessing third-party data. Employees requiring access to sensitive information create additional vulnerability, making it essential to implement need-to-know access restrictions. Business data breach scanners should include access management features allowing administrators to limit employee access based on job requirements. Automated scanning of company databases with notifications to affected employees is crucial, as manual monitoring by individual employees is unreliable. Additionally, scanners should provide IT administrators with accessible dashboards for easy deployment, updates, and maintenance across networks of any size. ## Conclusion Determining whether data is already compromised represents the critical first step in cybersecurity. Effective data breach scanning software immediately alerts users to compromised information while offering password storage, scanning capabilities for various data types, and military-grade encryption protection. These tools provide essential defense mechanisms for both personal and business data security, helping prevent breaches before they occur and addressing compromises that have already happened.

European privacy regulators have warned WhatsApp over its new privacy policy, which would allow it to share users’ phone numbers with Facebook, its parent company. The EU’s Article 29 Working Party said it had serious concerns and asked WhatsApp to provide all relevant information quickly, urging it to suspend data sharing until proper legal safeguards are in place. WhatsApp said it is cooperating with authorities and remains committed to complying with the law. The watchdogs also sent a letter to Yahoo over two issues: a 2014 data breach that exposed the email credentials of 500 million users, and the company’s reported scanning of customers’ incoming emails for information requested by U.S. intelligence officials. Regulators asked Yahoo to explain the breach, notify affected users of possible harm, and cooperate with any investigations. They also requested details on the legal basis for the email-scanning practice and its compatibility with EU law. Both cases are due to be discussed by regulators in November.

# Summary European Union data protection authorities issued formal letters to WhatsApp and Yahoo on Friday, expressing serious concerns about their data-handling practices. Regarding WhatsApp, the EU watchdogs objected to the company's new privacy policy allowing it to share users' phone numbers with parent company Facebook. They requested WhatsApp provide relevant information and urged the company to pause data sharing until legal protections were established. The authorities also contacted Yahoo over a massive data breach affecting 500 million users and the company's scanning of customer emails for U.S. intelligence purposes. The EU demanded Yahoo communicate breach details, notify affected users, and cooperate with investigations. WhatsApp stated it was working constructively with authorities to address concerns. Both cases will be discussed by regulators in November.

The European Central Bank said its upcoming cyber resilience stress test will not change bank-specific capital requirements. The exercise, planned for the coming months, will involve 109 of the euro zone’s largest lenders and will simulate a successful cyberattack that disrupts normal operations. Rather than testing prevention, the ECB said it will focus on how banks respond, recover, activate emergency procedures, and restore business. Results are due in the summer, while individual bank findings will be discussed in the 2024 Supervisory Review and Evaluation Process. Twenty-eight banks will face an enhanced assessment requiring extra information. The ECB said the test will be mainly qualitative and will not affect capital through Pillar 2 guidance.

# ECB Cyber Stress Test Summary The European Central Bank announced its upcoming cyber resilience stress test involving 109 major banks will not affect individual capital requirements. Instead, it will serve as part of broader supervisory assessment. The test simulates a successful cyberattack disrupting daily operations and evaluates banks' response and recovery capabilities rather than prevention abilities. Banks will test emergency procedures and contingency plans to restore operations. Main findings will be released in summer, with individual results discussed during 2024 supervisory reviews. Twenty-eight banks will undergo enhanced assessment requiring additional information on attack preparedness. The ECB emphasized the test is primarily qualitative and will not impact capital through Pillar 2 guidance recommendations.

French police have dismantled a massive hacking operation that had infected more than 850,000 computers, mostly in Latin America, and remotely removed the malware from the devices. The operation began last spring after Czech antivirus firm Avast alerted authorities to Retadup, a worm being controlled from a server in the Paris region. France’s C3N cybercrime unit, working with the FBI, described the action as a “world first.” Investigators first copied the server used to coordinate the botnet, then hacked into it and took control. They then pushed instructions to infected computers to uninstall the malware. Police said the attackers had used the system to mine Monero cryptocurrency, and Retadup is also suspected in ransomware attacks and data theft. Cybercrime chief Colonel Jean-Dominique Nollet urged internet users to avoid suspicious emails and attachments and to keep antivirus software updated. Avast said nearly 85% of the infected computers had no antivirus protection or had disabled it.

The Digital Cooperation Organization (DCO) has called on major global technology companies to strengthen protections for user data, saying privacy safeguards must improve as digital services expand. In a joint statement issued Tuesday in Riyadh, the DCO’s member states — which together represent more than 500 million people — urged closer cooperation between tech firms and government institutions to raise privacy standards, improve terms of use, and ensure data is collected and used only with users’ knowledge and consent. DCO Secretary-General Deemah Al-Yahya warned that personal data was involved in nearly half of hacking incidents worldwide in 2021. She said stronger protection is essential if the internet and digital technologies are to reach their full potential and build public trust, especially among people who are less represented in the digital economy or more vulnerable to cyber threats. Al-Yahya said the DCO is promoting a new approach to data privacy based on cooperation between global technology companies and government leaders, with the goal of helping shape national policies and support developing countries as they build privacy systems and address related economic challenges. The statement also highlighted several privacy principles, including limiting data sharing with third parties that could compromise systems in member states, and giving users the ability to move or delete their data across platforms. It cited IBM’s 2021 Cost of a Data Breach Report, which found that 44% of breaches involved personal customer information and that such breaches were the most expensive, costing an average of $4.24 million each — a 10% increase from 2020. At the same time, the DCO emphasized the economic benefits of stronger digital governance and pointed to initiatives it has launched, including the Excellence Center for Data Flows, designed to improve cross-border data movement and develop data protection policies. The DCO includes Bahrain, Jordan, Kuwait, Nigeria, Oman, Pakistan, Rwanda and Saudi Arabia.

She called for technology companies to safeguard users against misuse of their personal information and stressed that building public confidence in data protection is essential to fully realize the internet's potential and create economic opportunities. The joint statement highlights several key privacy principles that technological companies should implement: obtaining explicit user knowledge and approval before using data, refraining from transferring data to third parties that could compromise security, and enabling users to move or delete their data from various platforms. The organization aims to accelerate digital economy growth while empowering women, youth, and entrepreneurs.

IBM Security, working with the Global Cyber Alliance and the Packet Clearing House, launched a free DNS service called Quad9 on Nov. 16. The service is built around the IP address 9.9.9.9 and is intended to make internet use safer by blocking access to known malicious domains. DNS, or Domain Name Service, is a core part of internet infrastructure because it translates domain names into IP addresses. Quad9’s network infrastructure is provided by the Packet Clearing House, while the Global Cyber Alliance supplies development capabilities. The service uses IBM’s X-Force Threat Intelligence database plus threat data from 18 other intelligence partners to build a blacklist of dangerous websites. According to Quad9 executive director John Todd, the system is not dependent on a single source of threat data; instead, it aggregates daily threat feeds from multiple partners that track malware and phishing activity. When a user tries to visit a site identified as malicious, Quad9 blocks the request and does not return a name resolution for that domain. The service is aimed mainly at organizations that do not maintain their own DNS blacklisting and whitelisting systems. Quad9 emphasizes that it is not a censorship tool: it only blocks domains associated with phishing, malware, and exploit kits, and does not filter content more broadly. Privacy is another major feature of the service. Phil Rettinger, president and COO of the Global Cyber Alliance, said Quad9 is designed to be privacy-sensitive and does not log the addresses that make DNS requests. The system keeps only geolocation data to help track the spread of requests tied to malicious domains, and the organization says it has no secondary revenue streams from personally identifiable data. Supporters believe Quad9 could demonstrate how much safer the internet and the Internet of Things can be when malicious sites are filtered at the DNS level. Users can enable the service by changing network settings, and Quad9 provides setup videos for both MacOS and Microsoft computers.

If successful, the service could significantly reduce cybercrime by eliminating spoofed websites at the DNS level, potentially transforming internet security practices.

SANS Institute has announced SANS Secure Middle East 2022, an in-person cybersecurity training program to be held at the Crowne Plaza Riyadh RDC Hotel & Convention Centre in Riyadh from March 19 to March 31, 2022. The program is designed to help participants build and strengthen essential information security skills for protecting critical assets both on-premise and in the cloud. The announcement comes amid rising cyber risk in Saudi Arabia and the wider GCC region, which SANS says has seen a surge in attacks since the start of the COVID-19 pandemic. Ned Baltagi, Managing Director for the Middle East and Africa at SANS Institute, said Saudi Arabia ranks second only to the United States as a global cybersecurity leader, but that rapid digitalization and pandemic-driven transformation have expanded the attack landscape. He cited a VMware report showing that 84% of 252 Saudis surveyed believed cyberattacks had increased because of remote working conditions. Baltagi said SANS emphasizes security strategies built around detection, response, and prevention, and described the event as an opportunity for professionals to improve their leadership and operational capabilities in managing security teams. The program will combine in-person instruction with live online streams and will be aligned with GIAC certifications. Courses will be taught by several cybersecurity experts, including Ian Reynolds for SEC401, Jason Jordaan for FOR508 and FOR500, Brian Ventura for MGT512, Mark Williams for MGT514, Bryce Galbraith for SEC504, Justin Searle for ICS410, and David Szili for FOR572. Classes will run daily from 8:30 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. AST, with breaks. Participants who register will also be eligible for an exclusive NetWars Tournament, which offers hands-on cybersecurity practice in a safe, monitored environment. In addition, attendees will have access to upcoming SANS Summits to expand their knowledge and professional network.
