Target announced a dramatic retreat from Canada, saying it will shut all 133 of its Canadian stores and take about $5.4 billion in pretax losses in its fiscal fourth quarter. The move, disclosed on Thursday, marks a major reversal for the U.S. discount retailer, which entered the Canadian market in March 2013 and had been trying to establish itself as a serious competitor to Wal-Mart Stores Inc. Shares of Target rose on the news, climbing more than 4 percent at one point and ending up 2.2 percent in afternoon trading. The losses will largely reflect the writedown of Target’s Canadian investment, along with exit costs and operating losses. The company had already sought creditor protection for its money-losing Canadian subsidiary. CEO Brian Cornell said the chain could not see a realistic path to profitability in Canada. He said that after reviewing the business, Target concluded it would need to commit billions more dollars without a reasonable expectation of an appropriate return, and that it did not expect the Canadian operation to become profitable until 2021 at the earliest. Target’s Canadian expansion had been troubled from the beginning. The company faced severe supply chain problems, including warehouse issues, poor communication with headquarters, and inexperienced staff. Those problems left many stores understocked and with limited merchandise, disappointing shoppers who had eagerly awaited Target’s arrival. Reuters reports from stores in Vancouver, Toronto, and Ottawa around Christmas found only moderate traffic, and Cornell said he had not seen the “step-change” in performance needed to justify continuing. The decision surprised some analysts, who had expected Target to close only its weakest stores and attempt to salvage the rest of the business. By the time of the shutdown announcement, Target had invested roughly $6 billion in Canada, according to Fitch Ratings, including about $2.5 billion in capital spending and $1.7 billion in cumulative losses. The company said leaving Canada would let it concentrate on the U.S. market, where it has been recovering from a major data breach during the 2013 holiday season. Target also said fourth-quarter comparable U.S. sales were likely to rise 3 percent, better than its previous 2 percent forecast, and it raised its adjusted earnings-per-share estimate to $1.43 to $1.47. Canadian retailers were expected to benefit from Target’s exit, and Target said it would continue pursuing growth in the United States, especially through smaller-format stores in big cities. But retail experts said the Canadian failure raised broader questions about Target’s long-term growth prospects, calling the expansion an avoidable implosion. Target said Canadian stores would stay open during liquidation and that, subject to court approval, employees would receive at least 16 weeks of compensation.

# Target Exits Canada with $5.4 Billion Loss Target Corporation announced it is closing all 133 of its Canadian stores and taking a $5.4 billion pretax loss in its fourth quarter, marking a dramatic retreat from the Canadian market less than two years after its launch. These challenges resulted in poorly stocked stores with limited selection, disappointing Canadian consumers who had eagerly anticipated Target's arrival in a market previously dominated by Walmart. Target raised its comparable U.S. sales forecast to 3 percent growth and increased adjusted earnings per share estimates to $1.43 to $1.47. Industry experts attributed the failure entirely to Target's execution. Retail consultant Antony Karabus stated: "Anything you could have gotten wrong in the playbook, they got wrong." Target plans to focus future growth on expanding smaller format stores in major U.S. cities. Target said stores would remain open during liquidation and committed to providing Canadian employees a minimum of 16 weeks of compensation with court approval. The company's Canadian failure raises significant questions about its long-term growth prospects and international expansion capabilities.

Sage, a provider of accounting, financial, HR and payroll technology for small and mid-sized businesses (SMBs), released a new global report on Oct. 12, 2023, examining how SMBs view cybersecurity and what obstacles they face. The study, titled *Cybersecurity for SMBs: Navigating Complexity and Building Resilience*, was conducted by Danebury Research across nine markets and was designed to show how businesses can better understand and manage cyber risks. The report’s central finding is that keeping up with new cyber threats is the biggest challenge for SMBs worldwide. Globally, 51% of SMB decision-makers identified staying on top of emerging threats as their top cybersecurity concern. Other leading issues included making sure employees understand cybersecurity expectations, educating staff about cyber risks, and figuring out what level of security investment is needed. A small Quebec municipality west of Montreal was briefly caught up in a wave of Islamic-themed cyberdefacements that has swept across the internet in the wake of the Charlie Hebdo attacks in Paris. Terrasse-Vaudreuil, a town of about 2,000 residents, saw its website’s home page hacked Thursday evening by a group calling itself the Middle East Cyber Army, or MECA. For roughly a dozen hours, visitors saw a message praising Islam and denouncing Charlie Hebdo, displayed over an image of the Qur’an. Town officials said the attack appeared to be random and unrelated to the municipality itself. Director-general Ron Kelley noted that many websites around the world have been infiltrated recently because of security vulnerabilities, and said the town was likely just one of many targets. Mayor Michel Bourdeau said provincial police had been notified and opened an investigation after receiving information about the hacking. He stressed that the incident had nothing to do with Terrasse-Vaudreuil and was “a combination of circumstances.” The mayor said he was alerted Thursday evening and that the site was restored early Friday. He also emphasized that only the town’s public homepage was compromised; residents’ personal information, which is stored on a separate server, was not accessed. The hackers’ message included the phrase “We are Muslims,” a reference to the Qur’an, and an insult aimed at Charlie Hebdo, along with the hashtag #OPFRANCE, which has been used in cyberattacks linked to the post-Charlie Hebdo backlash. French authorities have reported that thousands of websites were attacked in similar campaigns, and experts say MECA has been associated with defacing more than 1,000 sites worldwide, many of them unrelated to France. Despite the global context, local residents were mainly baffled. Community journalist Carmen Fabio said people did not see the hack as a direct threat, but were puzzled by one question above all: why Terrace-Vaudreuil?

# Summary Terrasse-Vaudreuil, a small Quebec municipality of approximately 2,000 residents west of Montreal, experienced a cyberattack on its website Thursday evening. The hacking group, calling itself MECA (Middle East Cyber Army), compromised the town's homepage for about twelve hours before it was restored Friday morning. The hackers displayed a message praising Islam and referencing the recent Charlie Hebdo attacks in Paris, ending with the hashtag #OPFRANCE. The defaced page featured Islamic imagery and text stating "We are Muslims. Quran is our book." Town officials, including Mayor Michel Bourdeau and Director-General Ron Kelley, expressed puzzlement about why their small municipality was targeted. They emphasized that the attack appeared random, resulting from a combination of circumstances and website security vulnerabilities rather than any connection to the town itself. Quebec provincial police opened an investigation following the incident. Officials confirmed that hackers only accessed the public homepage and did not compromise residents' personal information, which was stored on a separate, secure server. Residents were assured their data remained safe. The attack is part of a broader pattern. Experts note that MECA has defaced over 1,000 websites worldwide using similar messages, targeting sites with security weaknesses rather than specific organizations. According to researchers at Toronto's Citizen Lab, most defaced websites have no connection to Charlie Hebdo or France. French authorities reported approximately 19,000 French websites faced cyberattacks following the Paris magazine shooting. Reports indicate MECA's core membership consists of approximately ten teenagers, with ongoing recruitment efforts for additional hackers.

Toronto Raptors coach Nick Nurse is facing a rotation problem after forward Patrick McCaw was ruled out for at least four weeks following surgery to remove a benign mass from the back of his left knee. While the Raptors still managed to edge the Sacramento Kings 124-120 on Wednesday night at Scotiabank Arena, McCaw’s absence leaves a noticeable hole in the back end of Nurse’s bench. Nurse said before the game that he values McCaw’s basketball IQ and the way he “always makes things happen,” and acknowledged that someone else will have to absorb those minutes for the time being. The search for McCaw’s replacement has centered on three players: Terence Davis, Chris Boucher and Matt Thomas. Nurse said he is leaning toward Davis, while also expecting all three to receive more consistent playing time than they have been getting. The audition did not produce a clear answer. Davis, an undrafted rookie, had a rough night marked by foul trouble. In just over seven minutes of floor time, he was on the brink of fouling out after a series of early fouls, and Nurse said Davis simply needs more game experience. Nurse explained that Davis must learn to avoid holding fouls early in possessions and control his hands better on defense. Fred VanVleet offered similar advice, telling Davis to stop fouling and not to argue with referees, noting that rookies often get less benefit from the doubt. Boucher saw even less opportunity to make his case. He played about five minutes, though he did record an impressive block. His limited minutes may have been influenced by the fact that center Marc Gasol appeared to be regaining form and Serge Ibaka played well, but Nurse also seemed to be looking for a wing-type replacement for McCaw rather than another big man. Of the three candidates, Thomas made the strongest impression. He scored eight points on 2-for-3 shooting, all from three-point range, in nearly 11 minutes of action. He also showed scrappy, if imperfect, defense. Nurse said Thomas’s group was “okay,” noting that they were not great but at least held their own and contributed to an even stretch in the game. Still, Nurse stressed that the Raptors cannot realistically get through a four-week stretch using only a seven-man rotation. He will need one or more of these reserves to become a dependable eighth, ninth or even 10th man. Donald Trump’s acceptance speech at the Republican National Convention in Cleveland was greeted with loud enthusiasm from delegates, reinforcing the image of a party rallying behind its newly chosen nominee. In a 75-minute address on Thursday night, Trump offered a dark picture of American decline and promised that only he could restore the country. He pledged to defeat the Islamic State, revive jobs, stop “uncontrolled immigration,” and bring back law and order. The arena responded with repeated applause and chants, creating the appearance of Republican unity at the end of a highly contentious four-day convention. But the article makes clear that the unity was only partial and, in some ways, superficial. Several of Trump’s most prominent critics were absent from the arena, including Texas Sen. Ted Cruz and Ohio Gov. John Kasich, along with many other elected Republicans who refused to endorse him. Others in attendance remained silent or uneasy. The convention marked a larger transformation in the GOP: the older party associated with Ronald Reagan and the Bush family has given way to a new Republican Party dominated by Trump. That transition has been uneasy and incomplete, with reactions ranging from enthusiastic embrace to reluctant acceptance to outright rejection. The article describes a broad spectrum of Republican responses to Trump. Some party members, including first-time voters and former Democrats, were energized by his campaign and joined the party because of him. Others had supported rival candidates during the primaries but were willing to back Trump once he secured the nomination. Some still supported the party but were waiting to see whether he could prove himself as a potential commander-in-chief. Others continued to call themselves Republicans yet said they would not vote for him. A few had abandoned the party entirely and planned to vote for Hillary Clinton, a third-party candidate, a write-in, or not vote at all. Among convention attendees, Trump supporters were the most visible. Ann-Marie Villicana, an alternate delegate from Pasadena, California, said the party was “on the road to the new Republican Party” and argued that Trump was cleaning out an establishment that had ignored ordinary voters. She described a movement that would return the party to its roots and elevate “his people” in a Trump administration. Her friend Erik Laykin, also a pro-Trump alternate delegate from Los Angeles, called for a more inclusive Republican “big tent” focused on national security, taxes, jobs, the economy, and immigration rather than social issues. He said the party’s emphasis on religion and social conservatism had become divisive. That “big tent,” however, depends on perspective. For many Republicans, opposition to abortion and gay rights remains central. Trump’s politics are more culturally flexible than those of many social conservatives, and his convention speech included a first-of-its-kind Republican convention shout-out to the LGBTQ community. The appearance of openly gay tech entrepreneur Peter Thiel as a speaker also signaled inclusion. Yet Trump’s selection of Indiana Gov. Mike Pence, a prominent Christian conservative, reassured the party’s religious right. Christian conservative leader Gary Bauer praised Pence as an “outstanding” choice and said he expected the Trump-Pence ticket to perform at least as well as Mitt Romney did with “values voters” in 2012, perhaps even better. Bauer also defended Trump’s personal life, saying that while people are complicated, “you can’t fake good kids,” and expressing confidence in the children Trump raised. Ivanka Trump’s speech before her father helped reinforce that softer image. She delivered a polished, positive message about opportunity for women and described her father as a loving parent who encouraged her entrepreneurial success. Her remarks stood in sharp contrast to Trump’s darker, more confrontational tone. The article suggests that Trump’s family members, especially his adult children, may play an important role in reassuring voters who question whether his temperament is fit for the presidency. The article also shows how many delegates had moved through multiple candidates before landing on Trump. Christopher Harvey, a delegate from Harris County, Texas, said Trump was his fourth choice after Rick Santorum, Marco Rubio, and Ted Cruz. Once Trump clinched the nomination, Harvey said he was fully behind him and admired his refusal to be constrained by political correctness. Harvey, who is black, said he was not bothered by Trump’s handling of support from white supremacist David Duke, because he trusted Trump’s intentions. His comments illustrate how some delegates were willing to overlook controversies in favor of Trump’s appeal and anti-establishment posture. Cruz’s refusal to endorse Trump became one of the convention’s most dramatic moments. After Cruz delivered a speech that stopped short of backing the nominee, boos erupted from the crowd. The reaction underscored the party’s divisions even as it also showed how little support remained for Cruz in the hall. Cruz’s speech left the Texas delegation divided and raised questions about his own political future. Kasich’s absence was another sign of unresolved tension. As governor of Ohio, he would ordinarily have played a prominent role at a convention in his home state, but he declined to support Trump and instead held his own event that resembled a presidential campaign rollout. Ohio delegates reflected that ambivalence. Betty Montgomery, the state’s former attorney general, praised Kasich for taking a “principled stand” and said she remained uneasy about voting for Trump, though she would not vote for Clinton. Sarah Brown, another Ohio delegate, had no such hesitation and said she would vote for Trump simply because she wanted a Republican president. The article notes that changing allegiances can be difficult and personal. Henry Barbour, an RNC member from Mississippi, said “everybody moves at a different pace” as he described his own path from Rick Perry to Rubio and finally to Trump. At the start of the convention, the small “Never Trump” movement drew attention by trying to free delegates to vote their conscience, but that effort had already failed once Trump secured the nomination outright during the primaries. The floor chaos early in the week felt theatrical, with some opponents seeking publicity more than victory. A few “Never Trump” protesters in T-shirts circulated near the convention, but their influence was limited. In the end, most attendees seemed ready to accept Trump, however reluctantly, and move forward. They argued that he had won the nomination fairly and deserved the party’s support. Some also believed he had identified a real and neglected strain in the electorate: blue-collar and middle-American voters worried about economic insecurity and social change. Bauer argued that Washington think tanks had failed to address those anxieties and that Trump was the only candidate in a crowded GOP field whose message truly resonated with those voters. The article closes on that point, suggesting that Trump’s rise reflected not just party upheaval, but a deeper political vacuum he managed to fill.

Quebec non-profits that cannot afford even basic cybersecurity services are receiving free help through a pilot project led by Polytechnique Montréal. The initiative, called the “cybercitizen assistance network,” is run by IMC2, a cybersecurity institute connected to Polytechnique and other Quebec universities. It aims to help organizations that, as executive director Marc Gervais puts it, are below the “cybersecurity poverty line” and often lack the money or technical staff to buy training, audits, or other protections. The project trains students to identify weaknesses in non-profits’ digital systems while supervised by professors. Those students then conduct free cybersecurity audits and provide recommendations. Gervais said non-profits face the same kinds of threats as larger organizations—phishing, data breaches, ransomware, piracy, AI-linked fraud, and malware—but usually have no in-house expertise to respond. He noted that Quebec has tens of thousands of non-profits, many of which are vulnerable to the same kinds of cyberattacks that have hit government-linked systems and major institutions in the province. The pilot is funded by a $1.3-million Google grant announced in January 2024. The first organization to take part was the Institut du Nouveau Monde, a Montreal-based non-profit focused on citizen participation and democracy. Its operations director, Louis-Philippe Lizotte, said cybersecurity is not a natural priority for groups like his, but the risks are obvious. A former employee alerted the organization to the project, and it quickly accepted. At the Institut du Nouveau Monde, the audit was done online. Lizotte said the review was reassuring and showed the organization was not far from best practices. The recommendations included a few extra tools and better staff training. Gervais said the audits often uncover simple improvements to “basic cybersecurity hygiene” that can make a major difference. The project is also helping non-profits comply with Quebec’s 2021 privacy law, which tightened rules for all organizations handling personal information. The law requires explicit consent to collect or disclose data, a registry of confidentiality incidents, and reporting of breaches to the province’s access-to-information commission when requested. Violations can lead to significant fines. Project manager Fyscillia Ream said the online format allows the initiative to reach organizations across Quebec, though the current focus is on Montreal and Gatineau. After each audit, the institute provides a report and can offer follow-up training to help organizations become autonomous in managing cybersecurity. Gervais said the need is not just provincial but Canadian, and broader collaboration may eventually be necessary.

Onix Group LLC announced that it mailed breach notification letters to people affected by a cybersecurity incident involving its own systems and those of affiliates and service clients including Addiction Recovery Systems, Cadia Healthcare, Physician’s Mobile X-Ray, and Onix Hospitality Group. On March 27, 2023, Onix discovered a ransomware attack on its internal computer systems. Working with cybersecurity experts, the company determined that an unauthorized actor had accessed its network between March 20 and March 27, corrupted certain systems, and removed some files. The exposed files may have contained names, Social Security numbers, dates of birth, and scheduling, billing, and clinical information related to care at the healthcare providers. Some files also included human resources data such as names, Social Security numbers, direct deposit details, and health plan enrollment information. Onix said it mailed letters to affected individuals, opened a dedicated assistance line, and is offering free credit monitoring and identity theft protection. The company said it has strengthened its systems and will continue improving security measures. A toll-free call center is available at (866) 547-0496, Monday through Friday, 9:00 a.m. to 6:30 p.m. Eastern Time, excluding major U.S. holidays.

# Summary Onix Group LLC announced a data security incident affecting itself and four affiliated healthcare organizations on May 26, 2023. A ransomware attack occurred between March 20-27, 2023, compromising Onix's internal systems. Unauthorized access resulted in the removal of certain files containing sensitive personal information. Exposed data potentially included names, Social Security numbers, dates of birth, and healthcare-related information for patients. Onix immediately secured its systems and engaged cybersecurity experts to investigate. The company mailed notification letters to affected individuals and established a dedicated assistance line at (866) 547-0496, available weekdays 9:00 am-6:30 pm Eastern Time. Firan Technology Group Corporation (FTG) reported its financial results for the fourth quarter and full year ended Nov. 30, 2020, saying the business made a number of improvements during the year but was still hit hard by the COVID-19 pandemic, especially in its commercial aerospace-related operations. Overall annual sales fell 9% to $102.4 million from $112.7 million in 2019, a decline of $10.2 million. FTG said the pandemic reduced commercial aerospace activity and most affected sites tied to that market, notably Circuits Toronto and its facilities in China. For the fourth quarter, sales slipped 1.3% to $26.7 million from $27.1 million a year earlier. FTG said the weaker quarterly result reflected COVID-19-related pressure, partly offset by strong shipments in its simulator-related business, which is mainly tied to defense programs. The company also noted that its fourth quarter in 2019 had been hurt by a cyberattack, making the comparison more complicated. By segment, Circuits sales for the year dropped $5.6 million, or 8%, as Circuits Toronto experienced the biggest decline because of its heavier exposure to commercial aerospace. That weakness was partially offset by strong growth at Circuits Fredericksburg, where sales increased 140% because the site was included for the full year in 2020 but only about four and a half months in 2019. FTG also said Circuits Chatsworth underperformed in 2020, leading to organizational improvements in the fourth quarter and after year-end. A U.S. court sentenced Garrett Endicott, 22, of Warrensburg, Missouri, to 10 months in prison and ordered him to pay $121,549.37 in restitution for his role in a multi-million-dollar SIM hijacking scheme tied to an international hacking group known as “The Community.” Acting U.S. Attorney Saima Mohsin said Endicott pleaded guilty to cyber crimes connected to the operation and is the sixth and final defendant to be sentenced in the case. The Community specialized in SIM swapping, a form of identity theft in which hackers take control of victims’ phone numbers. Prosecutors said members of the group stole cryptocurrency from victims across the country, with cases linked to California, Missouri, Michigan, Utah, Texas, New York, and Illinois. The scheme often involved bribing cellphone company employees for access to targeted numbers or impersonating victims to convince carriers to transfer a number to a new SIM card. Once they controlled a victim’s phone number, the hackers could intercept emails, financial information, and two-factor authentication codes, giving them access to cryptocurrency accounts and other sensitive data. Law enforcement estimates that the cryptocurrency stolen from the sentenced defendants exceeded $9 million. Mohsin said the crimes caused millions of dollars in losses and, in some cases, wiped out victims’ retirement savings. Other defendants tied to the scheme were convicted in Florida, South Carolina, and Iowa, and one man from Ireland was also charged and sentenced by an Irish court to three years in prison. Because the case spanned multiple countries, Homeland Security Investigations led the probe with help from Irish law enforcement. HSI Detroit Acting Special Agent in Charge James C. Harris said the investigation disrupted a complex international cryptocurrency and identity theft operation and highlighted how vulnerable personal information can be. The article also noted that the FCC warned in September that about 80 percent of SIM hacking attempts are successful, and that U.S. authorities have recently increased efforts to combat cryptocurrency-related crime.

# Summary: Sixth Member of International Hacking Community Sentenced in SIM Card Scheme A U.S. court sentenced 22-year-old Garrett Endicott of Missouri to 10 months in prison for his role in a multi-million dollar SIM hijacking scheme. Endicott is the sixth and final defendant convicted in connection with an international hacking organization known as The Community. The group specialized in SIM swapping, an identity theft technique exploiting cell phone numbers to steal cryptocurrency from victims across multiple states including California, Missouri, Michigan, Utah, Texas, New York, and Illinois. Perpetrators typically bribed cell phone provider employees to access phone numbers or impersonated victims to request SIM card transfers to different devices, effectively hijacking their accounts. Once hackers gained access to victims' phone numbers, they could bypass security measures like two-factor authentication and access sensitive financial information, particularly cryptocurrency exchange accounts. Law enforcement estimates the total cryptocurrency theft exceeded $9 million across all sentenced defendants, with some victims losing their entire retirement savings. Endicott was ordered to pay $121,549.37 in restitution. Other convicted members were based in Florida, South Carolina, and Iowa, while an Irish defendant received a three-year sentence from an Irish court. The investigation involved collaboration between U.S. Homeland Security Investigations and Irish law enforcement authorities, highlighting the scheme's international scope. The Federal Communications Commission previously warned that approximately 80 percent of SIM hacking attempts succeed. This case reflects increased law enforcement focus on cryptocurrency crimes. The Department of Justice launched a dedicated cryptocurrency enforcement response team in October 2021, following major ransomware attacks that summer demanding cryptocurrency payments from U.S. companies.

President Donald Trump plans to sign an executive order as soon as Wednesday that would impose sanctions on foreign individuals or companies found to have interfered in US elections, according to two sources familiar with the matter. The move comes as US intelligence agencies, the military and law enforcement prepare to counter expected foreign interference in the Nov. 6 congressional elections, even as Trump continues to dismiss the special counsel investigation into Russian meddling in the 2016 election. Under the proposed order, sanctions could be applied to people or firms accused of election interference through cyberattacks or other methods. A US official said the administration wants to establish “a new norm in cyberspace” and make clear the US response to such behavior. The order is intended as a public warning and a first step in defining boundaries for foreign activity in US elections. The executive order would make the Office of the Director of National Intelligence the lead agency in determining whether meddling occurred, working with the CIA, the National Security Agency and the Department of Homeland Security. According to a draft reviewed by Reuters, any federal agency that becomes aware of foreign election interference would be required to report it to the intelligence director’s office. The order defines interference to include hacking attempts against election infrastructure, as well as coordinated digital propaganda campaigns or systematic leaks of private political information. The administration’s push is part of a broader effort to appear tough on election security ahead of November’s vote, which will decide whether Republicans keep control of the House and Senate. Congress was intentionally excluded from the drafting process, the official said, because the White House wanted to move ahead of pending legislation in both chambers dealing with similar issues. Lawmakers from both parties have criticized Trump’s perceived softness on Russia, especially after his July summit with Vladimir Putin, where he accepted Putin’s denials over the findings of US intelligence agencies. Congress has already passed a Russia sanctions bill, and the Treasury later imposed major sanctions on 24 Russians under that law.

An Amtrak passenger train traveling from Los Angeles to Chicago derailed Monday afternoon after colliding with a dump truck near Mendon, Missouri, according to Amtrak. Three passengers were taken from the scene to University Hospital in Columbia, though hospital spokesman Eric Maze said he did not yet have information on their conditions. Mendon is a small community of about 160 people, located roughly 84 miles northeast of Kansas City. The Associated Press later corrected the report to clarify that the train was traveling from Los Angeles to Chicago. No further details were immediately provided about the dump truck, the cause of the collision, or the extent of the injuries.

Fulton County’s ransomware crisis continued Friday after a deadline posted by the LockBit3.0 cybercriminal group passed without any public resolution. The group had threatened to release sensitive information about county agencies and Georgia residents unless Fulton County met its demands by 12:47 a.m., but by early morning the dark web post had been removed. It remains unclear whether the county paid a ransom or whether the hackers withdrew their demand. Despite the deadline, Fulton County is still dealing with disruptions from the Jan. 28 cyberattack. Residents cannot yet pay water bills online, the property tax website is only partly working, and county jails and courts are still relying on workarounds. Phone lines are gradually being restored. County leaders have not said whether any money was paid to the attackers. Board of Commissioners Chairman Robb Pitts said Wednesday that the situation is serious and will take time to resolve. A county source said officials are still trying to determine the full scope of the breach, which means they may not yet be able to negotiate with the hackers even if they choose to consider a ransom. Monday will mark three weeks since the incident was first reported, and the county will also host early voting at 36 locations for the presidential primary.

The hackers had threatened to publish sensitive information about Georgia citizens and county agencies if Fulton County didn't meet their demands. By Friday morning, the threat post had been removed from the dark web, though it remains unclear whether the county paid a ransom or the hackers withdrew their demands. Fulton County continues experiencing significant service disruptions stemming from the January 28 breach. Residents cannot pay water bills online, the property tax website is non-functional, and jails and courts rely on workarounds. County phone lines are gradually being restored. County officials remain largely silent on details. According to sources, the county is still assessing the full scope of the breach and cannot negotiate ransom terms until understanding the complete extent of compromised data. A county spokesperson could not confirm whether any ransom payment occurred. The cyberattack will mark three weeks since its initial discovery on Monday.

President Trump’s dismissive response to a sweeping cyberattack on U.S. government agencies and private organizations drew sharp criticism Sunday from lawmakers, incoming Biden aides, and cybersecurity experts, who said his refusal to clearly blame Russia was both misleading and dangerous. The controversy came as federal officials and investigators were still assessing the full damage from an intrusion described as one of the most sophisticated and far-reaching cyberespionage operations ever uncovered. Trump, however, used Saturday tweets to minimize the breach, calling it “far greater in the Fake News Media than in actuality” and saying “everything is well under control.” He also floated the possibility that China could be responsible and repeated baseless claims that hackers may have targeted voting machines, even though the attack was not tied to election equipment. His comments came one day after Secretary of State Michael Pompeo said in a radio interview that “we can say pretty clearly that it was the Russians that engaged in this activity.” Sen. Mitt Romney, one of the few Republicans willing to publicly criticize Trump on Russia, said on NBC’s “Meet the Press” that “Russia acted with impunity” and argued that Trump has “a blind spot when it comes to Russia.” Sen. Mark Warner of Virginia, the top Democrat on the Senate Intelligence Committee, said Trump’s reluctance to identify the adversary made the country less safe. Warner, who has been briefed on the hack, called the intrusion “extraordinarily serious” and said “all indications point to Russia” as the culprit. Security specialists said the attack was part of a broader espionage campaign in which hackers found weaknesses in software and products used by government agencies and companies, then infiltrated them. Investigators determined that hackers had compromised SolarWinds, the Austin-based software company, and inserted malware into an update distributed to more than 17,000 customers worldwide. Once the update was installed, the malware gave the attackers access to those systems, enabling them to exploit the backdoors for months. Experts said it could take weeks or months to fully determine the scale of the breach, and even longer to remove the intruders. Kevin Mandia, CEO of FireEye, the cybersecurity firm that first discovered the breach, said on CBS’s “Face the Nation” that the operation was “utterly clandestine,” comparing it to “a sniper round” fired from far away rather than a random attack. He said the method showed exceptional sophistication. Even some Trump-aligned Republicans urged a strong response, though without directly condemning the president’s comments. Sen. John Barrasso of Wyoming, the Senate’s No. 3 Republican, said on “Fox News Sunday” that the United States needed “a forceful, effective, punishing response” so attackers would “think twice” before striking again. He said the country had apparently been “blindsided.” Trump’s mixed messaging was also criticized by Ron Klain, Biden’s incoming chief of staff, who said the administration was sending conflicting signals by having Pompeo acknowledge Russia while Trump downplayed the attack. Klain said the U.S. response should come in “a clear and unambiguous voice,” and suggested Biden would take steps to reduce foreign actors’ ability to conduct such attacks. The question of retaliation, however, remains unsettled. Romney called for a response “of like magnitude or greater,” but Christopher Krebs, the recently fired director of the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, urged caution, warning against escalation. Other experts noted that because the attack appeared to be espionage rather than destructive sabotage, the United States would have a harder time justifying retaliation. Chinese President Xi Jinping wrapped up a three-day visit to Astana, Kazakhstan, on Wednesday after attending the second China-Central Asia Summit, where China and the five Central Asian countries reached a wide range of agreements on security, trade, development and regional cooperation. He also stressed that the countries should view each other as priority partners, share development opportunities, help one another in times of need, and work together to address risks and maintain regional security and stability. Former Kyrgyz foreign minister Alikbek Dzhekshenkulov said this spirit reflects the essence of China-Central Asia relations and will help drive future cooperation toward a closer community with a shared future. Tajik Foreign Minister Sirojiddin Muhriddin called the summit a “historic event” and said it opened a new chapter for a long-standing regional partnership. One of the summit’s key concrete outcomes was the launch of three cooperation centers and one cooperation platform under the China-Central Asia mechanism. These are the China-Central Asia poverty reduction cooperation center, the education exchange cooperation center, the desertification control cooperation center, and the smooth trade cooperation platform. Xi said China was ready to share development experience and technological advances with Central Asian countries, promote digital infrastructure connectivity, strengthen cooperation on artificial intelligence, and foster new quality productive forces. Muhriddin said these initiatives were very important and expressed hope for quick results. Belt and Road cooperation was another major focus. Xi urged the countries to promote high-quality Belt and Road cooperation and held separate bilateral meetings with the leaders of all five Central Asian states on the sidelines of the summit. With Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov and Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev, Xi highlighted the importance of advancing the high-quality construction of the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway, a project launched last year. In talks with Turkmen President Serdar Berdimuhamedov, he called for effective implementation of the strategic alignment between the Belt and Road Initiative and Turkmenistan’s strategy to revive the Great Silk Road. He also told Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev that high-quality Belt and Road cooperation should deepen China-Kazakhstan ties. Another major event at the summit was the signing by Xi and the five Central Asian leaders of the Treaty on Eternal Good-Neighborliness, Friendship and Cooperation. The treaty reaffirms support for each country’s independence, sovereignty, territorial integrity, sovereign equality and inviolable borders. It also commits the parties not to use or threaten force and to resolve disputes peacefully. Xi said the treaty would enshrine everlasting friendship in law and called it a new landmark in the history of relations among the six countries and a pioneering step in China’s neighborhood diplomacy. The summit also produced the Astana Declaration. In it, the six countries agreed to jointly combat terrorism, separatism and extremism, strongly condemning all three forces. They also pledged cooperation against cross-border infiltration by terrorist groups, drug smuggling, transnational organized crime and cybercrime, with the aim of protecting cooperation projects and responding jointly to security threats. Xi separately told Tajik President Emomali Rahmon that China and Tajikistan should deepen law enforcement and security cooperation and intensify efforts against terrorism, separatism and extremism. Xi also discussed broader international issues. In his talks with Mirziyoyev, he said China was ready to work with all sides to help restore peace and stability in the Middle East and called for rapid de-escalation to avoid further escalation. In his summit speech, he warned that “there is no winner in tariff wars or trade wars,” criticized unilateralism, protectionism and hegemonism, and said humanity should not return to “the law of the jungle” but instead build a community with a shared future. The leaders also decided that China will host the third China-Central Asia Summit in 2027. The mechanism was launched in May 2023 with the first summit in Xi’an, and the leaders agreed then to meet every two years, alternating between China and Central Asian countries. A secretariat was later established in Xi’an to further institutionalize the mechanism. Analysts said the platform has become an important vehicle for expanding cooperation and deepening political, economic and cultural ties between China and Central Asia.

Somali President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud told Arab News that Somalia’s long experience with war and instability has convinced him that violence cannot produce a lasting political settlement. Speaking after the Saudi-African Summit and the fifth Arab-African Summit in Riyadh on Nov. 11 and 12, he said the conflict between Israel and Hamas could not be resolved through force and that the only realistic path was a political agreement based on the two-state solution. Mohamud argued that Somalia’s own history made it a witness to the futility of violence. “As Somalis, we have been in an environment of violence for a long time,” he said. “We know where the violence ends up, and the consequences, and the result at the end of violence. No one can reach a political end by means of violence. It cannot happen.” He added that the world already recognizes a solution in which “two states, Palestine and Israel, living together side by side, peacefully” could exist, and asked why that path should not be pursued. He also described the situation in Gaza as a humanitarian catastrophe, saying it was “contrary to all human values.” He stressed that the issue was not only religious, Arab, or regional, but a matter of humanity, pointing to the suffering of children, mothers, and innocent civilians. His comments came amid the war in Gaza, which began after Hamas carried out an unprecedented cross-border attack on southern Israel on Oct. 7 that killed about 1,400 people, most of them civilians, and led to the taking of about 240 hostages. Israel’s response, including heavy bombardment and a ground offensive, has killed more than 11,000 people according to the Hamas-run health ministry and displaced more than half of Gaza’s population. He said the two countries share a long historical relationship rooted in geography, Islam, and cultural values, and that both face common threats from extremism and terrorism. He described Saudi Arabia as a country that has supported Somalia for decades through humanitarian aid, security cooperation, diplomatic backing, and assistance in global politics. Under King Salman and Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, he said, relations have continued to improve with “new progress,” “new confidence,” and expanding areas of cooperation. Security and counterterrorism were among the strongest areas of collaboration, Mohamud said. Somalia has been fighting Al-Shabaab, the militant group that has plagued the country for years, and he said Saudi Arabia’s own past experience with terrorism made it especially valuable as a source of advice and expertise. He praised the Kingdom as “the best place” to seek guidance in the struggle against violent extremism. The summit itself was presented as part of a broader effort to deepen Arab-African cooperation and recognize Africa’s rising importance in global trade and diplomacy. Mohamud said Africa is becoming “the destination” in the 21st century, not only for economic development but also for human capital, resources, and strategy. He said the era of colonial exploitation should give way to partnership and shared interests. He argued that Somalia is well placed to attract investment once security is fully restored. The country, he noted, has Africa’s longest coastline, a young and energetic population, untapped natural resources, and the potential to become a major logistics hub in the region. He said Somalia is now in the final stages of stabilization and security, and that defeating terrorist groups has created the conditions needed for investment. In his words, “Somalia is a white paper,” meaning that nearly every sector offers opportunity. Mohamud pointed to several areas of potential, including the blue economy, food security, minerals such as gold, uranium, copper, and cobalt, and rare natural elements. He also noted Somalia’s agricultural potential, saying it has close to 9 million hectares of arable land, two permanent rivers, favorable rainfall, and one of the world’s largest livestock populations. In his view, the country is largely untapped and “the sky’s the limit” for investors. The article also described Somalia’s long struggle against Al-Shabaab, which has been a major obstacle to development. The group, based in Somalia but active elsewhere in East Africa, has been linked to Al-Qaeda since 2012 and is suspected of ties to Al-Qaeda in the Islamic Maghreb and Al-Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula. Somalia, with international support, has fought the group through military operations, counter-radicalization efforts, and efforts to cut off its funding. Mohamud said the fight against Al-Shabaab takes place on three fronts. First is the military campaign, which he said has been strengthened. Second is the ideological struggle, because Al-Shabaab is an ideology-driven organization that misuses Islam, and Somali authorities are working to explain the “right path” of the religion to the public. Third is the economic front, since the group raises money from the population through what it calls zakat or charity. By restricting those revenue streams, he said, Somalia has been able to weaken the militants and make progress. Toward the end of the interview, Mohamud spoke briefly about himself, saying he remains healthy and committed to serving Somalia. He said he does not smoke or drink, keeps a disciplined routine, exercises, and is proud to have spent his life in public service. He has been president since May 2022, after previously serving from 2012 to 2017. Before entering politics, he worked as a civil rights activist and as a professor and dean at SIMAD University in Mogadishu. In 2013, Time magazine included him in its Time 100 list of the world’s most influential people for his work on reconciliation, anti-corruption, and reforms in Somalia’s security and economic sectors. Mohamud said his background in education and humanitarian service continues to shape his leadership, and that his greatest satisfaction comes from helping people.

Sudan’s Health Ministry has announced a national COVID-19 response plan as the country begins to confront confirmed coronavirus cases and broader public-health and humanitarian risks. According to the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) in Sudan, the government and humanitarian partners are taking measures to slow the spread of the virus while trying to maintain aid operations for vulnerable people. As of March 25, Sudan had confirmed three COVID-19 cases, including one death. Sixteen additional suspected cases were being monitored in isolation centers in Khartoum. In response, the Health Ministry unveiled a national plan worth $82 million, while state-level response plans were still being developed. Authorities in West Darfur closed the border with Chad on March 17, and in North Darfur the Health Ministry prepared isolation areas for suspected cases. The government has introduced a series of restrictions to limit transmission. These include a nightly curfew from 8 p.m. to 6 a.m. starting March 24 until further notice, a ban on inter-state bus travel from March 26 except for humanitarian, commercial, and technical shipments, and the closure of international and domestic airports until April 23, with exceptions only for humanitarian and cargo flights. Schools, universities, religious institutes, colleges, and higher institutes were closed for one month beginning March 14. Basic certification exams in all states were postponed until further notice, and all festivals, camps, sports events, and public gatherings such as weddings were banned. UN agencies and humanitarian partners continue to support Sudan’s response. UNICEF’s communication and risk-management team assisted the Health Ministry, media outlets, and the private sector with public-awareness efforts on prevention. This led to 105 mosques in Khartoum state promoting COVID-19 prevention messages and physical distancing during prayers. Private-sector partners printed up to 27,000 posters, reaching an estimated 540,000 people, and 86 orientation sessions at markets and other public places reached about 12,900 people. Humanitarian actors are also adjusting their operations to preserve essential services. They are developing scenarios, updating contingency plans, and shifting supplies from central warehouses to regional storage facilities. A medical shipment sent by Chinese businessman Jack Ma arrived in Khartoum on March 23, with logistical support from the World Food Programme and others. OCHA warned that measures such as physical distancing and alternate work arrangements are affecting humanitarian programming and operations. A task force has been created to assess the impact on front-line work and to prepare for possible larger outbreaks. The Humanitarian Aid Commission, which oversees humanitarian work in Sudan, placed all nonessential staff on leave until March 29. Some NGOs reported delays in administrative procedures, including approval of technical agreements needed to carry out projects. Sudan’s health system is particularly vulnerable because of years of underinvestment and economic crisis. The report notes that only one third of health facilities provide a complete basic package of care, and many are understaffed and underequipped for a large-scale outbreak, with shortages of essential medicines. To reduce crowding and maintain food access, partners in most locations plan to distribute food in advance starting in April, providing two to three months of rations at once. At the global level, the UN launched a $2 billion Global Humanitarian Response Plan for COVID-19 on March 25. The plan is intended to help the world’s most vulnerable countries in South America, Africa, the Middle East, and Asia, and to protect millions of people who depend on humanitarian aid. UN Under-Secretary-General for Humanitarian Affairs Mark Lowcock said the goal is to help countries prepare and continue supporting those who rely on aid, while equipping humanitarian organizations to fight the virus and contain its spread. The plan will be carried out by UN agencies, international NGOs, and NGO consortia, and will provide testing equipment, medical supplies, handwashing stations, public-information campaigns, and air bridges and hubs to move workers and supplies. The report also noted a separate humanitarian development in West Darfur, where people displaced by violence in and around El Geneina in late December 2019 have begun returning home. IOM estimated that 27,995 people, or 6,126 families, remained displaced in 35 sites in El Geneina, down by 9,913 people from the previous update. The earlier violence displaced about 40,000 people, including some 32,000 already displaced residents, and forced an estimated 10,000 others to flee into Chad. More than 50 people were reportedly killed and about 60 injured. Humanitarian agencies said they would continue supporting those still displaced.

Cambodia’s Ministry of Labor is launching a financial aid scheme with garment factory owners to support workers affected by the economic slowdown. The plan, announced on 7 March, follows a recommendation from Prime Minister Hun Sen and was discussed at a meeting chaired by Labor Minister Ith Sam Heng with employers’ associations from the garment and footwear sectors. Officials said export orders have been falling because of the global economic crisis linked to the Russia-Ukraine war, adding to the lingering impact of Covid-19. The ministry noted that more workers are being placed on suspended contracts, and it is unclear when conditions will return to normal. Production and export costs also remain high. Under the new programme, workers whose contracts are suspended by factories during the downturn will receive cash assistance starting in April 2023, modeled on support measures used during the pandemic. The government will provide $40 per worker, while factories will contribute $30 during the suspension period. Minister Ith Sam Heng thanked private-sector partners for cooperating during the previous ten rounds of Covid-19 relief measures. Employer representatives also praised the prime minister for supporting both businesses and workers during crises. The announcement comes as Cambodia’s apparel sector continues to face pressure. Earlier in the year, the Council for the Development of Cambodia approved three apparel-related investment projects expected to create up to 5,000 jobs. However, TAFTAC warned in January that footwear exports to the EU and US had not improved and could fall further, with orders potentially dropping by as much as 30% in the first half of 2023.

China’s economy grew 7.4 percent in 2014, the slowest annual pace in 24 years, according to official data released by the National Bureau of Statistics. The result was down from 7.7 percent in 2013 and marked the weakest performance since 1990, when growth was 3.8 percent. It was also the first time China missed its official annual growth target since 1998, falling just short of the government’s “about 7.5 percent” goal. The slowdown reflects pressure from weaker manufacturing and trade activity, along with falling real estate prices that have damaged the property sector, one of the main drivers of China’s economy. NBS chief Ma Jiantang said the economy had made “stable progress” under the country’s new normal, but warned that both domestic and international conditions remained complicated and that growth still faced difficulties and challenges. Growth in the final quarter of 2014 came in at 7.3 percent year on year, unchanged from the previous three months and slightly above economists’ expectations. The full-year figure was also a little better than the 7.3 percent median forecast in an AFP survey. The Shanghai stock market rose 1.80 percent after the data were released. Economists said the numbers were not alarming relative to expectations, but they still pointed to further slowing ahead. ANZ described the result as “not too bad,” while Nomura said growth would likely trend lower because of local government debt controls, the property correction, and broader deleveraging. For 2015, economists surveyed by AFP expect growth of 7.0 percent, while the IMF is even more cautious, forecasting 6.8 percent. Other indicators showed some late-year improvement: industrial production rose 7.9 percent in December, retail sales increased 11.9 percent, and fixed asset investment for the year climbed 15.7 percent. Despite the slowdown, Chinese authorities said they would continue shifting the economy toward consumer-led growth rather than heavy reliance on investment.

Cambodian Prime Minister Hun Sen has urged the public not to panic or rush to withdraw money from local banks following the collapse of two major U.S. lenders, Silicon Valley Bank (SVB) and Signature Bank. Speaking at a graduation ceremony in Phnom Penh, he said the failures of the banks do not pose a serious threat of contagion to Cambodia’s banking system and are unlikely to cause major damage to the global economy. SVB and Signature Bank were taken over by regulators earlier this month after facing massive withdrawal requests, a classic bank run triggered by fears about their stability. On March 13, U.S. President Joe Biden reassured Americans that the U.S. banking system remains safe and said his administration would strengthen regulations to prevent future failures. Hun Sen told depositors in Cambodia to trust the country’s regulators and banking institutions, saying banks have sufficient reserves to handle any problems. He said withdrawing funds out of fear would harm the common good. He also pointed to Cambodia’s past experience during the 1997 Asian financial crisis and the 2008 global financial crisis, noting that the Kingdom weathered those periods with limited damage. In response to the 2008 crisis, Cambodia increased its reserve requirement ratio to protect the system. According to the National Bank of Cambodia, reserve requirement ratios currently stand at 12.5 percent for foreign-currency deposits and 8 percent for domestic-currency deposits. The death toll from the 7.7 magnitude earthquake that struck Myanmar on March 28 has climbed to 3,645, with 5,017 people injured and 148 still missing, according to the State Administration Council’s information team. The country has also been hit by 98 aftershocks since the quake, ranging in magnitude from 2.8 to 7.5, the Department of Meteorology and Hydrology said. The earthquake caused widespread destruction across central Myanmar, with more than 80% of buildings damaged, especially in the townships of Sagaing, Mandalay and Magway. In Mandalay, UN Development Programme regional representative Titon Mitra said the health system is “completely overwhelmed,” with hospitals unable to handle the volume of patients. He added that medicines and medical supplies are in critically short supply. The UN humanitarian office (OCHA) said more than 500,000 people across the country have lost access to life-saving health care. Food shortages are also worsening. Mitra said markets in Sagaing and Magway are severely disrupted, many people have lost their incomes, and there are signs of hyperinflation. He also warned that because Myanmar is in the middle of an active civil war, aid distribution must be carefully coordinated to ensure it reaches areas outside military control as well. International assistance continues to arrive from the United Nations, India, the European Union, the United States and other organizations. India has taken a leading role through “Operation Brahma,” which New Delhi describes as part of its “Neighbourhood First” and “Act East” policies. Under the operation, India has sent tonnes of medical supplies, relief materials and food aid. Prime Minister Narendra Modi expressed condolences to Myanmar’s Senior General Min Aung Hlaing and reiterated India’s commitment to help. The two leaders met on April 4 at the BIMSTEC Summit in Bangkok, where they discussed the earthquake response and India’s ongoing relief efforts. India later delivered an additional 442-tonne shipment of food aid aboard the Indian Navy ship INS Gharial, which arrived at Thilawa port and was handed over to Yangon’s chief minister and local officials.

China is reacting to Robert Mugabe’s removal in Zimbabwe with little public regret, seeing his ouster as unlikely to damage Beijing’s interests. According to the article, Chinese officials and state media have treated the crisis cautiously but without offering any real support to Mugabe after the army seized power last week. Instead, Beijing called for a peaceful settlement within a legal framework and urged dialogue to resolve differences. On Wednesday, China’s Foreign Ministry said it respected Mugabe’s decision to resign and still regarded him as a “good friend” of China who had made “historic contributions” to Zimbabwe’s independence and liberation. That language reflected the long relationship between the two countries, which dates back to Zimbabwe’s liberation struggle, when China supported Mugabe’s side. Mugabe visited China many times over the years, including in January, when President Xi Jinping told him that China would “never forget its old friends.” But the article makes clear that China’s patience with Mugabe had worn thin. Zimbabwe’s economy had collapsed under years of turmoil, and China had little strategic dependence on the country. Unlike in places such as Zambia, Angola, or other African states where China has major access to copper or oil, Zimbabwe offered Beijing no crucial raw materials. Trade between the two countries was relatively small and falling: in 2016 it totaled $1.11 billion, down 15 percent from the previous year, far below China’s trade with South Africa. China even traded more with Tunisia and Senegal than with Zimbabwe. Chinese analysts said Beijing had no interest in propping up Mugabe. Shen Xiaolei, an Africa expert at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, said China would not interfere and was happy to let Zimbabweans make their own choices. He said the ruling party was fighting internally and that Mugabe’s economic policies and governance had created serious problems. He added that Zimbabwe’s regime was always headed for trouble, though he had not expected the collapse to come so quickly. The article contrasts Mugabe’s standing in Africa with his reputation in the West, where he is widely seen as a dictator whose violent rule and disastrous economic management ruined one of Africa’s most promising countries. Even so, China had once backed him on the world stage. In 2008, Beijing vetoed a Western-backed UN resolution that would have imposed an arms embargo and sanctions on Mugabe and other officials. Despite suspicions that Zimbabwe’s army chief, General Constantino Chiwenga, may have briefed Beijing before moving against Mugabe, China denied any advance knowledge. Its embassy in South Africa dismissed such claims as “complete nonsense.” At the same time, Chinese media began publishing increasingly negative coverage of Mugabe and his wife, Grace, linking Zimbabwe’s collapse to his policies. China also appears comfortable with Mugabe’s likely successor, Emmerson Mnangagwa, who has visited China often. Officials and state media portrayed him as a familiar figure unlikely to disrupt relations. Overall, the article suggests Beijing sees Zimbabwe’s political transition as an internal matter and expects continued friendly ties, regardless of who leads the country.

# China Shows Little Concern Over Mugabe's Ouster in Zimbabwe China has demonstrated minimal emotional investment in Robert Mugabe's removal from power as Zimbabwe's president, signaling relief rather than regret over the military-orchestrated transition. Despite decades of friendship dating to Zimbabwe's independence struggle, China's response has been notably restrained and pragmatic. Following the army's takeover last week, China deliberately avoided openly supporting Mugabe, instead calling vaguely for peaceful resolution through legal channels. The Foreign Ministry's Wednesday statement acknowledged Mugabe's resignation and described him as a "good friend" who contributed to Zimbabwe's independence, but notably offered no plea for his reinstatement or criticism of the military intervention. The cooling of China-Zimbabwe relations reflects economic realities. Trade between the nations dropped 15 percent year-on-year to $1.11 billion in 2016—a fraction of China's $35.3 billion trade with South Africa. Unlike strategic relationships with Zambia (copper) or Angola (oil), Zimbabwe provides no crucial raw materials vital to Chinese interests. Chinese analysts openly criticized Mugabe's governance. Shen Xiaolei from the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences noted the ruling party's internal conflicts and acknowledged that "Zimbabwe's regime was certainly going to get into trouble." China made clear it would not interfere, believing Zimbabwe's citizens should determine their own future. Chinese state media has recently aired unfavorable coverage of Mugabe and his wife Grace, with outlets calling her "a wanton squanderer" and blaming Mugabe's "extreme leftist, populist policies" for Zimbabwe's hyperinflation crisis. One commentary recounted a 1985 Deng Xiaoping meeting with Mugabe, suggesting Deng warned him about China's past mistakes and urged economic reforms—advice Mugabe apparently ignored. Interestingly, China denied foreknowledge of the military takeover despite General Constantino Chiwenga's recent Beijing visit. The Chinese embassy in South Africa dismissed suggestions of prior coordination as "complete nonsense," claiming this represented an attempt to smear China. However, China expressed confidence that Emmerson Mnangagwa, Mugabe's former vice-president and likely successor, will maintain friendly relations. State media noted Mnangagwa is a "known quantity" with frequent visits to China. Unlike Zambia, where anti-Chinese sentiment has emerged due to worker complaints about Chinese firms, Zimbabwe has experienced no such tensions. China's historical support for Mugabe included vetoing a 2008 UN resolution that would have imposed sanctions, arms embargoes, and travel restrictions. Yet this loyalty appears exhausted. The contrast between Mugabe's reviled status in the West—condemned as a despot whose economic mismanagement destroyed a promising African state—and China's pragmatic indifference is striking. Chinese officials now emphasize that broader China-Africa relations transcend individual leadership changes. Wang Wei from the Foreign Ministry's China Institute of International Studies stated that "China and Africa are all-weather friends," suggesting the relationship will continue developing regardless of Zimbabwe's political transitions, focused on mutual prosperity and development rather than personal loyalty to specific leaders.

Amid the banking turmoil triggered by the collapse of Silicon Valley Bank in the US, India’s International Financial Services Centres Authority (IFSCA) has set up an expert committee to prepare a roadmap for bringing Indian innovations and startups back onshore to Gujarat’s GIFT City. GIFT City, or Gujarat International Finance Tec-City, was originally designed as an integrated global hub for financial and technology services. According to an official release, the committee will be chaired by G Padmanabhan, former executive director of the Reserve Bank of India. Its members include representatives from major venture capital funds, startups, fintech companies, law firms, tax firms, and other experts. The panel has been asked to submit its recommendations within three months. The committee’s mandate is broad. It will examine what steps are needed to encourage Indian fintech firms and startups that are currently domiciled abroad to relocate to GIFT City. It will also identify key issues that must be addressed to develop GIFT City into a global fintech hub, and suggest ways to attract new fintech companies with international ambitions to establish a commercial presence there. In addition, it will look at the challenges and solutions needed to build an International Innovation Hub at GIFT IFSC. The release noted that India’s startup ecosystem is the third largest in the world, with 115 unicorns. Indian startups raised $44 billion in 2021, and more than $33 billion of that went into deals valued at over $5 million. It also pointed out that many Indian startups are incorporated outside India even though most of their market, workforce, and founders are based in the country. These “flipped” or externally domiciled startups make up a significant share of India’s unicorns. The move comes after Silicon Valley Bank collapsed on March 10 following a bank run, prompting US regulators to shut it down and place it under FDIC control. In response to the crisis, Union Minister Rajeev Chandrasekhar said Indian startups should prefer Indian banks and highlighted GIFT City’s special provisions as a fast and effective support mechanism. He also said more than $200 million in bank deposits had recently been transferred into GIFT City, which he described as a sign of the growing strength of India’s banking system.

WEF President Borge Brende similarly described the event as taking place against “the most complex geopolitical and geo-economic backdrop in decades,” warning that there is much at stake in avoiding global recession, low growth, high inflation, and high debt. The Ukrainian hryvnia (UAH), sometimes written hryvnya, is Ukraine’s national currency. It is divided into 100 kopiykas and uses a symbol based on the cursive Ukrainian letter He, resembling a backward “S” with two horizontal strokes, which are meant to suggest stability. The name “hryvnia” comes from an old medieval Slavic unit of weight. As of September 2020, one hryvnia was worth about US$0.035. The hryvnia became Ukraine’s official currency in 1996, after the collapse of the Soviet Union. It replaced the karbovanets at a rate of 100,000 karbovanets to 1 hryvnia, following severe hyperinflation in the 1990s that had made the old currency nearly worthless. At first, the hryvnia was introduced at an exchange rate of 1.76 UAH to US$1, but over time it lost substantial value, reaching nearly 28 UAH to US$1 by 2020. The currency is used throughout Ukraine except in Crimea, which has used the Russian ruble since Russia annexed the territory in 2014. The article also notes that a currency with the same name existed earlier, in 1917, when the region declared independence from the Russian Tsarist Empire. Between 1917 and 1920, the Ukrainian People’s Republic used karbovanets banknotes printed on ordinary paper, which were easy to counterfeit. During the occupations spanning the two World Wars, newer banknotes were issued, including later, more secure versions of the karbovanets. Ukraine’s broader economic history helps explain the hryvnia’s instability. Once one of the Soviet Bloc’s largest economies, Ukraine struggled after shifting to a market system. Many people turned to subsistence farming and barter to meet daily needs, while government reforms and the new currency only modestly improved conditions. The 2008 global financial crisis hit the country hard, leading to a US$16.5 billion IMF loan. By 2014, the hryvnia was among the world’s worst-performing currencies. The article says the currency’s outlook later showed some improvement, though Ukraine continued facing economic pressure from neighboring states and internal conflict, especially in the Donbas region. UNIAN reported calls for stronger Western and IMF support for Ukraine’s democratic institutions and anti-corruption reforms. Anders Aslund of the Atlantic Council warned that without IMF financing, Ukraine could face another major depreciation. World Bank data for 2019 showed 3.2% GDP growth and 7.9% inflation.
