The International Monetary Fund said Argentina’s debt is now “unsustainable,” citing the peso’s depreciation, a contraction in real GDP and other financial risks. The announcement came Wednesday after an IMF mission visited Buenos Aires from Feb. 12 to 19 and described its talks with Argentine officials as very productive. The Fund said Argentina’s authorities are taking steps to confront a severe economic and social crisis, including policies aimed at reducing poverty and stabilizing the economy. It added that the IMF and the government will keep cooperating closely. IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva is expected to meet Economy Minister Martin Guzmán at the upcoming G20 Finance Ministers meeting to discuss next steps. Argentina received a $50 billion IMF standby loan in June 2018, later raised to $56.3 billion, of which $44 billion was disbursed under former President Mauricio Macri. President Alberto Fernandez has said his government will not take the remaining funds and will review repayment terms.

# Summary The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has determined that Argentina's debt is unsustainable, citing peso depreciation, real GDP contraction, and other financial risks. Following a February 12-19 mission to Buenos Aires, the IMF acknowledged Argentine authorities' commitment to addressing economic challenges through poverty-reduction and stabilization policies. Despite these efforts, the Fund maintains that debt sustainability concerns remain. The IMF and Argentina will continue close cooperation, with Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva scheduled to meet Economy Minister Martin Guzmán at the upcoming G20 Finance Ministers meeting. Argentina previously received $44 billion of a $56.3 billion IMF standby loan approved in 2018. President Alberto Fernández's administration has declined the remaining funds and plans to review the repayment schedule.

Zimbabwe has a new leader for the first time in nearly 40 years, and the political change is being felt strongly among Central Indiana’s Zimbabwean community, which numbers more than 5,000 people by some estimates. On Friday, Emmerson Mnangagwa was sworn in after longtime ruler Robert Mugabe resigned following 37 years of oppressive rule. For Scholasticah Chidemo-Chinembiri, a Zimbabwe native who moved to the United States in 2000 with her children in search of better education and a better life, the news brought excitement and hope. She said conditions in Zimbabwe worsened sharply after 2000, when government policies helped trigger a collapse of the national currency and a severe economic decline. Once an agricultural country with relative prosperity, Zimbabwe later faced food shortages and hardship, especially in rural villages where families struggled to harvest enough to survive. Chidemo-Chinembiri responded to the crisis by founding the Healing Friends Foundation to support Zimbabwean families with food and money. She said the change in leadership could help her organization do more for people in rural areas and bring hope to friends and relatives back home. She described widespread relief among Zimbabweans who now believe they may be able to speak freely without fear of political retaliation or death. The interim president has promised reform, poverty reduction, and an end to corruption, and Chidemo-Chinembiri said Zimbabwe will need both international help and a new generation of leaders with fresh ideas. She also noted that her foundation still needs donations such as fans and medical supplies.

On June 27, 2017, more than 330 American Heart Association volunteers and staff from 46 states gathered in Washington, D.C., to urge Congress to strengthen federal support for cardiovascular disease research and to back legislation that would improve treatment access for heart and stroke patients. The delegation included Bob Harper, the personal trainer, survivor, and host of NBC’s “The Biggest Loser.” The advocates pressed lawmakers to prioritize National Institutes of Health funding for heart and stroke research, support bills expanding access to stroke telemedicine and cardiac rehabilitation, and oppose the Senate health care bill then under consideration. A central focus of the lobbying effort was the need for more NIH funding. Heart disease and stroke researchers and survivors met with legislators to highlight a recent American Heart Association report warning that cardiovascular disease will remain the nation’s most burdensome disease. The report projected that nearly half of Americans will face CVD and that related costs could exceed $1 trillion by 2035. Despite this outlook, the NIH devoted only 4 percent of its budget to heart research and 1 percent to stroke research, while its purchasing power had fallen by nearly 20 percent over the previous decade. Association volunteers planned to ask Congress to increase the NIH budget by $2 billion for 2018, arguing that insufficient funding would delay or prevent cures and treatments. American Heart Association President Steven Houser said the projections showed that “now is not the time to relax,” warning of a major health and economic crisis if investment did not increase. He argued that more NIH support was needed so Americans could receive future treatments and cures. The volunteers also sought support for two specific bills. One, the cardiac rehabilitation supervision bill (H.R. 1155/S. 1361), would allow physician assistants, nurse practitioners, and clinical nurse specialists to supervise cardiac rehab on a day-to-day basis. The association said this was needed because only about 30 percent of eligible patients use cardiac rehabilitation, and Medicare’s current direct-physician-supervision rule creates barriers, especially in rural areas where doctors are scarce. The second measure, the Furthering Access to Stroke Telemedicine (FAST) Act (H.R. 1148/S. 431), would expand Medicare reimbursement for telestroke services beyond rural areas. The association said broader telemedicine use could improve outcomes by increasing access to thrombolytic therapy and reducing stroke’s burden on patients and families. Finally, the advocates urged lawmakers to reject the health care bill, citing the Congressional Budget Office’s estimate that 22 million Americans would lose coverage by 2026 under the Senate’s Better Care Reconciliation Act. CEO Nancy Brown said the proposal would weaken Medicaid, raise premiums for older and low-income people, and reduce benefits. She said the association would not support repeal legislation unless it improved access to affordable, adequate coverage.

# American Heart Association Advocates for Heart Disease Research and Healthcare Access On June 27, 2017, more than 330 American Heart Association volunteers and staff members from 46 states gathered in Washington, D.C. to advocate for increased federal support for cardiovascular disease research and key legislation. The event included NBC's "The Biggest Loser" host Bob Harper, a personal trainer and heart disease survivor. The advocates urged Congress to prioritize National Institutes of Health (NIH) funding for heart and stroke research while supporting bills to expand stroke telemedicine access and cardiac rehabilitation services. They also encouraged lawmakers to oppose the proposed healthcare bill. **The Research Funding Crisis** According to the American Heart Association's recent report, cardiovascular disease will remain America's most burdensome disease. Nearly half the U.S. population is projected to face CVD, with costs exceeding $1 trillion by 2035. However, the NIH allocates only 4 percent of its budget to heart research and just 1 percent to stroke research—insufficient given these dire projections. Additionally, the NIH has lost nearly 20 percent of its purchasing power over the past decade. The association requested a $2 billion budget increase for 2018 to address this shortfall. American Heart Association President Steven Houser emphasized the urgency, stating that without adequate NIH funding, cures and treatments for CVD could be seriously delayed or never discovered. **Proposed Legislation** Volunteers advocated for two key bills: 1. **Cardiac Rehabilitation Supervision Bill (H.R. 1155/S. 1361)**: Currently, only 30 percent of eligible patients participate in cardiac rehabilitation programs. Medicare requires direct physician supervision, creating barriers—particularly in rural areas with physician shortages. The bill would allow physician assistants, nurse practitioners, and clinical nurse specialists to supervise these programs. 2. **Furthering Access to Stroke Telemedicine (FAST) Act (H.R. 1148/S. 431)**: Expanding telemedicine would increase patients receiving thrombolytic therapies and improve outcomes. However, Medicare currently reimburses telehealth services only in rural areas. The bill would eliminate this geographic restriction. **Healthcare Reform Opposition** The association also opposed the Senate's Better Care Reconciliation Act of 2017. The Congressional Budget Office reported that 22 million Americans would lose coverage by 2026 under the proposal. CEO Nancy Brown stated that the bill "significantly diminishes the existing Medicaid program, reduces access to quality coverage, raises premiums for older and low-income individuals and limits benefits." She warned the legislation "could have dire life-changing consequences for many heart and stroke patients." The American Heart Association adopted healthcare reform principles requiring any changes to current law to preserve and expand access to affordable, adequate health coverage. The organization pledged not to support any repeal bill without changes improving healthcare access for all Americans.

Chicago plans to close five migrant shelters housed in Park District fieldhouses over the coming weeks and relocate nearly 800 people, including families, so the buildings can reopen in time for summer camps, sports, and other community programming. The move is part of the city’s continuing effort to manage the influx of migrants arriving from the U.S.-Mexico border, while also responding to pressure from neighborhood residents who have objected to the shelters and from advocates who say city services remain insufficient. Mayor Brandon Johnson announced this week that the park-based shelters are “no longer necessary.” In a statement Monday, he said his administration and its partners had stepped up to provide shelter in park facilities when it was needed, and he expressed gratitude to alderpersons and communities that welcomed new arrivals. He said the buildings would return to their intended purpose for summer programming. Chicago says more than 37,000 migrants have arrived since 2022, when Texas Gov. Greg Abbott began sending buses of migrants to sanctuary cities. Many of the newcomers are from Venezuela, where a deep political, social, and economic crisis has driven widespread poverty. The city initially used police stations and airports as temporary holding sites before opening other shelters. Since last summer, some residents near the park fieldhouses have protested their use as shelters. A city dashboard showed that more than 10,000 people were still in city-run shelters as of Friday, down from nearly 15,000 in January. The city has not said exactly when all five park buildings will be emptied, only that the process will take several weeks. Volunteers working with migrants said residents of at least two of the facilities were told they would begin moving to other shelters on Saturday. Nearly 20 other temporary shelters remain open across Chicago, including churches, hotels, a library, and former warehouses. According to the city’s latest update, some of the largest shelters house more than 1,000 people, while smaller ones hold around 100. Officials said they are trying to move people to shelters closer to the park buildings, especially families with children enrolled in nearby schools. Chicago also began enforcing a 60-day shelter limit in mid-March, though many exemptions — including for families with school-age children — have meant few people have been forced out so far. The city says only 24 people have left shelters because of the cap. Those evicted can return to the city’s “landing zone” and reapply, though volunteers say that can result in people being sent back to the same shelter. Volunteers said they understand the desire to restore park facilities for summer use, but worry the relocations will disrupt migrants’ efforts to work and keep children in school. Some migrants said they had received little information about where they were going next and feared retaliation if they complained. The city says more than 15,000 people have already found other housing since data tracking began in 2022. Many have used state rental assistance, including more than 5,600 families, according to the Illinois Department of Human Services.

# Chicago to Close Migrant Shelters in Park Buildings for Summer Chicago announced plans to close five shelters housing migrants in park district buildings and relocate approximately 800 people, including families, to reopen these facilities for summer camps and community events. The closure represents the city's ongoing effort to manage the influx of migrants arriving from the U.S.-Mexico border while addressing community demands for park access. Mayor Brandon Johnson stated the shelters were "no longer necessary" and expressed pride in the city's efforts to welcome new arrivals. He emphasized that park facilities would return to their intended purpose for summer programming. The city initially used police stations and airports as temporary shelters before transitioning to park district fieldhouses, which have faced regular protests from nearby residents since last summer. Chicago has received over 37,000 migrants since 2022, when Texas Governor Greg Abbott began busing people to sanctuary cities. Many migrants originate from Venezuela, where economic and political crises have created severe poverty. The city's shelter population peaked at nearly 15,000 in January but has since declined to over 10,000 as of Friday. The relocation will occur over several weeks, with residents of at least two park buildings notified they would begin moving Saturday. The city aims to place people in other shelters closer to their current locations, particularly families with children enrolled in nearby schools. Nearly 20 additional temporary shelters remain operational across Chicago, including churches, hotels, libraries, and former warehouses, with the largest housing over 1,000 people. Chicago implemented a 60-day shelter stay limit in mid-March, though numerous exemptions—including for families with school-enrolled children—have limited actual evictions. Only 24 people have left shelters due to the caps. Evicted individuals can return to the city's "landing zone" and reapply for shelter, though volunteers report this sometimes results in people being sent to the same location. Volunteers working with migrants acknowledge the desire to restore park facilities but express concerns about the disruption. Volunteer Lydia Wong noted that forced moves complicate migrants' efforts to find employment and maintain children's school attendance, requiring them to navigate new routes and transportation methods. Several shelter residents reported receiving minimal information about relocation plans and declined to provide names, fearing retaliation from private agency employees managing the shelters. As of Wednesday, over 15,000 people have secured alternative housing since 2022. Additionally, more than 5,600 families have utilized state rental assistance programs to find permanent housing. The closure reflects broader challenges facing major U.S. cities, including New York and Denver, which have implemented similar shelter limits while requesting increased federal assistance to manage migrant arrivals. Chicago's approach attempts to balance community needs with supporting vulnerable populations, though critics argue the city prioritizes new arrivals over longtime residents, including unhoused individuals with similar needs.

A Latin American regional bloc known as the Lima Group agreed on Thursday that further steps may be needed to isolate Venezuela over President Nicolas Maduro’s alleged attacks on rights and democracy, Canadian Foreign Minister Chrystia Freeland said after a meeting in Toronto. Freeland said the group, which includes about 15 countries such as Canada, Brazil, Argentina, Peru and Mexico, has already condemned recent anti-democratic actions by Maduro’s government and may take “concrete steps” to increase pressure if needed. Canada is also considering a second round of sanctions against Venezuelan officials, following last month’s decision to target 40 senior officials for anti-democratic behavior, she said. The group criticized Venezuela’s recent regional election, in which the ruling Socialist Party won 18 of 23 governorships amid economic collapse, food shortages and soaring inflation. Freeland also noted that opposition protests have caused 125 deaths and thousands of arrests, and urged divided opposition groups to unite ahead of the Lima Group’s next meeting in Chile in January 2018.

# Summary The Lima Group, a regional Latin American alliance including Canada, met in Toronto to discuss further isolating Venezuela's President Nicolas Maduro, who faces accusations of undermining democracy and human rights. Canadian Foreign Minister Chrystia Freeland announced the group agreed that additional pressure on the Maduro regime may be necessary, including potential international isolation measures. Canada is considering imposing a second round of sanctions against Venezuelan officials, following initial targeted sanctions against 40 senior officials last month for anti-democratic behavior. The group previously condemned Venezuela's recent nationwide election, where the Socialist Party retained control despite widespread public anger over severe economic hardship, including food shortages and currency collapse. Opposition protests this year have resulted in 125 deaths, thousands of arrests, and significant property damage. Freeland emphasized the importance of opposition unity, urging Venezuelan opposition groups to work together to effectively represent their people's democratic aspirations.

Richard Kanyangu, a Zimbabwean-born pastor and psychiatric nurse living in Kamloops, Canada, says he plans to run for president of Zimbabwe in the 2018 election. He has already taken steps to get his name on the ballot and expects several other candidates, including at least three from the diaspora, to challenge President Robert Mugabe and Zanu PF. Kanyangu left Zimbabwe in 1995 to study in the United Kingdom and now lives in Canada with his wife and three sons. He works at Royal Inland Hospital and leads House of Destiny church. He said people around him, including coworkers, church members, and even his sons’ teachers, know about his political ambitions. He is also building a grassroots party, though he admits it has limited funding. Mugabe has ruled Zimbabwe for 36 years, and the country has suffered severe economic decline, including hyperinflation that once led to a 100-trillion-dollar banknote. Kanyangu said he hopes to mobilize Zimbabweans abroad, including an estimated 3.5 million living outside the country, for organization and fundraising. He plans to travel to Zimbabwe in June and remain there during the campaign period ahead of the election, though his family will stay in Canada because of safety concerns. He acknowledged that opposition supporters have faced violence from ruling-party-aligned gangs and said some in the governing party believe no one should oppose them. Despite the risks, Kanyangu says he has been thinking about the run for a long time and is now moving ahead publicly.

# Summary Richard Kanyangu, a 41-year-old Zimbabwean pastor and psychiatric nurse based in Kamloops, Canada, has announced his candidacy for Zimbabwe's presidency in the 2018 general elections. He becomes one of at least three diasporans challenging incumbent President Robert Mugabe and his Zanu PF party. Kanyangu left Zimbabwe in 1995 to study in the United Kingdom and has since built a life in Canada with his wife and three sons. He has taken the necessary steps to appear on the presidential ballot and expects approximately five or six candidates will run. Despite limited financial resources, Kanyangu has founded a grassroots political party and is spreading awareness through his workplace at Royal Inland Hospital, his church congregation, and local events in Kamloops and Vancouver. He plans to leverage the estimated 3.5 million Zimbabweans living abroad for organizational support and fundraising. Zimbabwe faces severe economic challenges, including hyperinflation and international sanctions, having issued a 100-trillion dollar note a decade ago. Mugabe has ruled for 36 years. Kanyangu plans to relocate to Zimbabwe in June to campaign during the election buildup, though he acknowledges the safety risks. Opposition supporters have faced violence from paramilitary gangs supporting the ruling party. He will not bring his family, recognizing the dangers of political opposition in the country.

U.S. regulators are growing more worried about Deutsche Bank’s health. According to The Wall Street Journal, the Federal Reserve last year classified the bank’s U.S. operations as being in “troubled condition,” one of the lowest possible ratings. The designation had not been made public before and caused Deutsche Bank shares to fall on Thursday. The Fed declined to comment when contacted by FOX Business. The rating system, known as CAMELS, evaluates capital adequacy, asset quality, management, earnings, liquidity and sensitivity on a scale from 1 to 5, with 4 and 5 indicating trouble. The Journal also reported that the FDIC placed Deutsche Bank on its list of “problem banks,” which includes institutions that receive a 4 or 5 from their primary regulator. The FDIC also declined to comment on specific institutions. Deutsche Bank has faced persistent difficulties in recent years, including three straight annual losses, repeated failures in Federal Reserve stress tests, and a recent decision by its new CEO to cut thousands of jobs and reduce U.S. operations. The bank said it is well capitalized with strong liquidity and is focused on fixing weaknesses in its control environment and infrastructure.

The upgraded badge was said to represent direct equity at a ratio of 0.001%, or one twenty-fifth of an AEX Shareholder Badge NFT. Holders would be entitled to standard shareholder rights, including annual dividends, quarterly financial report reviews, voting on decisions, and participation in shareholder meetings. So far, 710 badges had been issued in total: 600 through chain recharge activities, 60 through Texas activities, 10 through shareholder spokesperson activities, 30 through turntable activities, and 10 through GAT discount subscriptions. Los Angeles has approved a $1.87 billion, 10-year plan aimed at addressing its homelessness crisis and eventually ending the problem, city officials said Tuesday. The plan, adopted by the city council, calls for hiring more social workers, expanding access to quality housing, and building permanent housing for the city’s roughly 44,000 homeless residents. At the same time, Los Angeles County supervisors agreed to release $100 million over several years, including $42 million in the first 12 months, to support homeless housing efforts. County CEO Sachi Hamai called homelessness “the most serious humanitarian crisis confronting our county today.” However, the funding details still need formal approval, and the city is scheduled to vote on its budget in April. Councilman Jose Huizar, who co-chairs the Homelessness and Poverty Committee, acknowledged that earlier efforts to reduce homelessness had failed. The crisis has worsened sharply: between 2013 and 2015, homelessness in Los Angeles County rose 12.4 percent, while the number of people living on the street or in cars increased 85 percent. About 29,000 homeless people, or two-thirds, sleep outside or in vehicles. Officials blame the 2008–09 recession, rising housing costs, and the city’s mild climate and services, which attract homeless people. County officials spend about $1 billion annually on related care.

# Los Angeles Adopts $1.87 Billion Homeless Plan Los Angeles has adopted a $1.87 billion, 10-year plan to address homelessness affecting approximately 44,000 people in the county. The city council approved the initiative, which includes hiring social workers, providing quality housing, and constructing permanent housing units. Additionally, Los Angeles County supervisors committed $100 million over several years, with $42 million allocated in the first year. County CEO Sachi Hamai called homelessness "the most serious humanitarian crisis" facing the county. However, city councilman Jose Huizar acknowledged that previous homelessness reduction efforts had failed. Between 2013 and 2015, the homeless population surged 12.4 percent, with street homelessness increasing 85 percent. Of the 44,000 homeless individuals, approximately 29,000 (two-thirds) live on streets, in tents, or vehicles. The 2008-2009 economic crisis and housing inflation have exacerbated the problem, while Los Angeles's mild weather and available services attract homeless individuals. Notably, New York has a larger homeless population (57,000), but 95 percent utilize shelters. Los Angeles County currently spends approximately $1 billion annually on homeless-related medical, psychiatric, and social services. Officials argue that permanent housing is more cost-effective than jail or hospital care.

Iranian protesters who had been demonstrating against the Ali Khamenei regime over economic hardship, inflation, currency collapse, and unemployment are now also blaming U.S. President Donald Trump for the deadly unrest. The article says protests spread nationwide as Trump publicly encouraged demonstrators, warned the Iranian leadership, and said U.S. help was “on its way,” adding that America was “locked and loaded” if peaceful protesters were harmed. His comments raised hopes that U.S. military action against Iran might be imminent, reportedly emboldening more people to join the protests. According to the article, the Iranian authorities responded with a severe crackdown: internet shutdowns, mass arrests, and gunfire against crowds. Eyewitnesses described sniper fire and machine guns being used, and the piece cites estimates of the death toll that vary widely, from 3,090 according to the Human Rights Activists News Agency to 16,500 in a doctors’ report cited by The Sunday Times. But protesters say Trump betrayed them by suddenly reversing course. After initially sounding threatening toward Tehran, he later said Iranian leaders had assured him the killings and executions would stop and signaled that a U.S. strike would not happen. Several Iranians quoted in the article said they felt used and deceived, with one Tehran businessman claiming Trump was responsible for 15,000 deaths and another calling him worse than Khamenei.

# Summary Iranian protesters are blaming both their government and President Trump for thousands of deaths during recent unrest. While protests initially targeted the Ali Khamenei regime over economic crises including inflation and unemployment, death tolls have become a point of contention—ranging from 3,090 to 16,500 according to different sources. Trump's public statements initially fueled the demonstrations. He openly encouraged Iranian protesters, warned the Khamenei regime, and declared the US was "locked and loaded" if demonstrators were harmed, suggesting military intervention was imminent. These statements emboldened protesters to take to the streets. However, the Iranian government responded with a brutal crackdown, including internet shutdowns, mass arrests, and gunfire against protesters, resulting in significant casualties. Protesters feel betrayed after Trump abruptly reversed course, announcing that Iranian leadership had assured him killings would cease and that the anticipated US military action would not proceed. Iranian citizens interviewed expressed anger and a sense of manipulation, believing Trump had used them as "cannon fodder" before abandoning them. Some protesters view Trump's actions as worse than their own government's response, feeling deceived and abandoned after being encouraged to risk their lives based on false promises of American support.

# Canada Expands Venezuela Sanctions Canada expanded sanctions against President Nicolas Maduro's Venezuelan government on April 15, targeting 43 additional officials including high-ranking government members, regional governors, and those undermining democratic institutions. Digital Commodities Capital Corp. said it was issuing a clarification at the request of the British Columbia Securities Commission after the regulator raised concerns about two promotional articles published by aktiencheck.de AG on May 12 and June 4, 2025. The BCSC told the company that the articles overstated Digital Commodities’ exposure to digital assets and gold, omitted important facts, and included unsupported macroeconomic commentary that did not reflect the company’s own views or disclosures. The company clarified that its current investment policy limits digital and physical non-fiat investments to 25% of the value of its investment portfolio. It also said its current gold-related exposure consists only of an equity investment in Gold Finder Resources Ltd., an exploration-stage mining company. That position includes 10 million shares and 10 million warrants exercisable at $0.05 for two years, acquired for a total cost of $250,000. At the BCSC’s request, the two AG articles have been permanently removed from public circulation. Digital Commodities said it had retained AG on April 28, 2025, to support an initial awareness campaign in European markets, but it did not author, approve, or know in advance the specific content that was published. The company said it has since strengthened internal procedures and will review and approve all investor relations and promotional materials before publication in the future. Digital Commodities advised investors to rely only on its SEDAR+ filings and its website for company information.

Belarus’s Energy Minister Viktor Karankevich said the president’s decisions have been crucial to the development of the country’s energy system and to strengthening energy security. He made the remarks at a ceremony marking the commissioning of peaker energy generating devices at four energy facilities, an event held to coincide with the 30th anniversary of the institution of the presidency in Belarus. Karankevich said the energy sector has undergone large-scale modernization with state support and has become a reliable supplier of electricity for both the economy and households. He recalled the difficult 1990s, when industrial output, energy consumption, logistics, and supplies of raw materials and components all declined. After Aleksandr Lukashenko was elected president, Belarus overcame the crisis and restored growth in production and energy use, he said. The minister noted that since the early 2000s, two major state programs have guided the sector’s development. One focused on upgrading key energy facilities, saving energy, and increasing the share of local fuel in the energy mix through 2011. The second aimed to improve the energy system through 2016. During this period, efficient generating capacities were introduced, outdated equipment was removed, and major high-pressure stations were modernized. Over the past 30 years, installed generating capacity has grown 1.8 times to 12,000 MW. Electrical networks have expanded by 30,000 kilometers, while heating networks have nearly doubled in length. Electricity consumption also reached a record 41.1 billion kWh in 2023, and continued rising in the first five months of this year. Karankevich called the commissioning of the nuclear power plant a historic milestone. He said Belarus has fully stopped importing electricity and reduced its dependence on imported natural gas. Since the first unit was connected in November 2020, the plant has generated nearly 32 billion kWh, replacing 8.5 billion cubic meters of natural gas.

# Summary At a ceremony in Minsk marking the 30th anniversary of Belarus's presidency, Energy Minister Viktor Karankevich highlighted the country's significant energy sector development. He credited presidential decisions with ensuring effective energy system growth and enhanced energy security. The minister noted that Belarus endured difficult economic conditions during the 1990s, characterized by industrial decline and supply disruptions. Following Aleksandr Lukashenko's election as president, the country recovered from the economic crisis and restored production and energy consumption growth. Since the early 2000s, two major state programs have modernized the energy industry. These initiatives upgraded key facilities, promoted energy efficiency, increased local fuel usage, and replaced inefficient equipment with highly efficient generating capacities. Over 30 years, installed generation capacity has increased 1.8 times to 12,000 MW. Electrical grid infrastructure expanded significantly, with electrical networks growing by 30,000 kilometers and heating networks nearly doubling in length. Performance metrics have improved substantially. In 2023, electricity consumption reached a record 41.1 billion kWh, with 2.5 billion kWh added. Positive trends continued into 2024, with consumption rising 1.6 billion kWh over five months. Karankevich emphasized the nuclear power plant's historic importance. Since its first unit connected to the grid on November 3, 2020, the facility has generated approximately 32 billion kWh of electricity, replacing 8.5 billion cubic meters of natural gas. The country has achieved complete electricity self-sufficiency and significantly reduced natural gas import dependence.

Oil markets reacted with volatility after U.S. President Donald Trump moved against Venezuela by capturing President Nicolas Maduro on Jan. 3, creating uncertainty over future global supply and possible spillover effects for oil-exporting countries such as Kazakhstan. The article notes that the developments also drew criticism from governments and analysts who questioned the legal basis of the U.S. intervention, adding another layer of economic and political uncertainty. Experts quoted in the piece argue that any near-term effect on global oil supply is likely to be limited. Aruzhan Meirkhanova, a senior analyst at Outpost Eurasia, said Venezuela’s headline reserve figure of 303 billion barrels does not match production realities. She emphasized that the country currently produces less than 1% of global oil and that its extra-heavy crude is expensive and technically difficult to extract. In her view, Venezuela is unlikely to generate a substantial increase in global supply in the short term because the country would need massive, sustained investment to recover its industry. Trump said American companies would “go in, spend billions of dollars, fix the badly broken infrastructure,” but that optimism was not shared by the companies themselves. At a Jan. 9 meeting with industry executives, ExxonMobil Chairman and CEO Darren Woods described Venezuela as “uninvestable.” He said the company works in different political environments but does not approach opportunities with a short-term mindset. Meirkhanova said this reflected broader market sentiment. She cited Rystad Energy estimates that a meaningful recovery would require $8-9 billion in annual investment through 2040, and noted that major U.S. oil companies have publicly signaled they would need strong legal and contractual protections before returning. She concluded that short-term crude price effects from Venezuela should not be overstated. She also pointed out that unrest in Iran could have a more immediate influence on oil markets. If tensions there escalate, crude prices could rise in the short term, temporarily helping oil exporters. Kuanysh Beisengazin of the National Bureau of Economic Research described the Venezuelan episode as unprecedented in scale and said it could have broader implications for the global economy and investors, even though Venezuela accounts for only about 1% of world oil production. He said the use of direct U.S. military force in Latin America for the first time in decades increased geopolitical uncertainty and forced investors to reassess risk. In the immediate aftermath, he said, gold rose as a safe-haven asset and the U.S. dollar strengthened as capital moved toward perceived safety. Beisengazin added that Venezuela’s huge reserves could matter more in the long run if sanctions were lifted and Western companies returned. He also said the detention of a sitting head of state raised legal and institutional concerns, especially around sovereign immunity, a core principle of international law. He argued that the timing of the operation reflected favorable market conditions: oil supply in 2026 was relatively ample, U.S. production was rising, demand growth was slowing, and prices were already under pressure. He said Washington likely calculated that the move would not trigger fuel shortages in the U.S. or a politically damaging gasoline-price shock, especially because lower energy prices had helped bring down inflation. He also noted that Venezuela’s fiscal position had deteriorated sharply by 2025, with gold and foreign exchange reserves largely exhausted and hyperinflation controlled only through dollarization and external support. For Kazakhstan, the experts said the immediate impact appears limited, but the broader price environment remains a concern. Meirkhanova said Goldman Sachs has warned of a “wave of excess supply,” projecting average Brent crude at $56 per barrel in 2026 and possibly $54 in the fourth quarter. That is worrying for Kazakhstan, where oil production and exports rose last year thanks largely to the Tengiz expansion, but revenue gains have been reduced by lower prices. She said the 2026 budget assumes $60 per barrel, which is still below the fiscal breakeven level, meaning Kazakhstan must diversify its economy and prepare for tighter finances. Beisengazin said Venezuela’s developments have not yet pushed oil prices outside the range assumed in Kazakhstan’s budget. He said there is no immediate threat to budget revenues or the National Fund as long as prices stay roughly between $55 and $65 per barrel. However, he warned that a sharper escalation could lift prices to $70-$80 and temporarily boost Kazakhstan’s finances, while a gradual return of Venezuelan supply over one to two years could push prices lower. Prices near $50 would create problems for the country. The article concludes that these events mark a new phase in geoeconomics, where sanctions, military action, and markets are increasingly linked. Meirkhanova also said the possible return of Venezuelan oil would have only limited impact on the global energy transition, which is now driven not just by climate concerns but by economic and strategic competition. She argued that decarbonization has become sufficiently embedded in national strategies to withstand isolated supply shocks.

# Venezuela Crisis Shows Limited Oil Market Impact, Poses Challenges for Kazakhstan On January 3, 2026, U.S. President Donald Trump captured Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro, triggering oil market fluctuations and raising questions about global energy supply and geopolitical stability. While the action generated significant international debate regarding its legal basis, analysts suggest the immediate impact on global oil markets will be limited, though it carries important implications for oil-exporting nations like Kazakhstan. ## Venezuela's Minimal Role in Global Supply Despite Venezuela possessing the world's largest proven oil reserves at 303 billion barrels, experts emphasize that these figures don't reflect production realities. Currently, Venezuela accounts for less than 1% of global oil supply. According to Aruzhan Meirkhanova, a senior analyst at Outpost Eurasia, the country's extra-heavy crude is costly and complex to extract, limiting its practical contribution to world markets. Meaningful recovery of Venezuelan oil production would require sustained investments of $8-9 billion annually through 2040, a commitment major U.S. oil companies appear unwilling to make. During a January 9 meeting with industry executives, ExxonMobil Chairman Darren Woods described Venezuela as "uninvestable," noting that the company requires robust legal and contractual guarantees before entering any opportunity. These statements suggest that despite Trump's optimistic rhetoric about American companies investing billions to fix Venezuela's infrastructure, the private sector remains skeptical about the venture's viability. ## Broader Geopolitical Implications Kuanysh Beisengazin of the National Bureau of Economic Research characterized the episode as unprecedented in scale, marking the first direct U.S. military intervention in Latin America in decades. This action increased geopolitical uncertainty and prompted investors to reassess risk premiums. In the immediate aftermath, gold prices rose as investors sought safe-haven assets, while the U.S. dollar strengthened. The detention of a sitting head of state also raised significant questions about sovereign immunity, a cornerstone of international law protecting leaders from foreign jurisdiction. This legal uncertainty could have broader implications for global markets and investor confidence in the international system. ## Market Timing and Economic Factors Beisengazin noted that the operation's timing reflected specific cyclical conditions. The oil market entered 2026 relatively well-supplied, with rising U.S. production and slower demand growth keeping prices under pressure. This created a "window of opportunity" where military action wouldn't threaten fuel shortages or provoke domestic political backlash from rising gasoline prices. Additionally, Venezuela's fiscal constraints had reached critical levels by 2025, with the regime having exhausted its gold and foreign exchange reserves. ## Implications for Kazakhstan The developments pose particular challenges for Kazakhstan, a major OPEC+ member. While Kazakhstan increased oil production and export volumes last year through the Tengiz expansion, revenue returns have diminished due to lower average prices. Goldman Sachs has warned of excess global supply, projecting average Brent prices at $56 per barrel in 2026, potentially dipping to $54 in the fourth quarter. Kazakhstan's 2026 budget assumes a $60 per barrel baseline, which remains below the country's fiscal breakeven price. Meirkhanova emphasized that "the era of 'easy oil money' has come to an end," requiring Kazakhstan to accelerate diversification efforts and prepare for a more constrained fiscal environment. In the short term, provided oil prices remain within $55-$65 per barrel, the Venezuelan developments shouldn't significantly impact Kazakhstan's budget revenues or National Fund. However, risks exist on both sides: prices approaching $70-$80 could provide temporary relief, while further price declines toward $50 would pose serious challenges. ## Energy Transition Unaffected Finally, experts suggest that additional Venezuelan oil supply would minimally affect the global energy transition. The transition is no longer driven solely by climate concerns but by competition and economic resilience. Low-carbon energy systems have become sufficiently embedded in national strategies that isolated oil supply shocks are unlikely to reverse decarbonization efforts.

Western analysts have long assumed that Russia’s policy toward Ukraine was shaped mainly by the country’s business elite, the “oligarchs,” and that sanctions aimed at their wealth would therefore pressure President Vladimir Putin. But the article argues that this view no longer explains Kremlin behavior. Despite sanctions and falling oil prices hurting wealthy businessmen, Russian-backed rebels in eastern Ukraine continued their offensive and even spoke of creating a 100,000-strong reserve army. The reason, the article says, is that Putin’s inner circle is now increasingly dominated by the military-security establishment, or “siloviki,” rather than oligarchs. The siloviki include the armed forces, Interior Ministry troops, police, and the Federal Security Service (FSB). Military expert Alexander Golts says their influence is rising rapidly and that their core message—that Russia is surrounded by enemies and must defend itself from foreign aggression and internal subversion—has become a dominant theme in Russian media, especially on nightly television. According to the article, this climate of confrontation with the West has allowed the siloviki over the past decade to claim a larger share of the national budget, gain more access to the media, and increase their power inside the Kremlin. Their standing has been strengthened by the surge in patriotic sentiment after Russia’s bloodless seizure of Crimea in March 2014. Polls cited in the article suggest the military’s popularity has risen dramatically over the last decade. Among the most prominent siloviki are FSB chief Alexander Bortnikov, Interior Minister Vladimir Kolokoltsev, and Defense Minister Sergei Shoigu, who is also one of the country’s most popular public figures. Shoigu earned his reputation by successfully leading the Ministry of Emergency Situations before becoming defense minister in 2012. Although these officials tend to speak in bureaucratic language and reveal little about their personal views, hawkish ideas have become more visible in mainstream Russian discourse. The article cites Nikolai Patrushev, former FSB chief and current secretary of the Security Council, who recently argued that the West had revived a Cold War-style plan to destroy the USSR and was now applying it to Putin’s Russia. Analysts say Putin increasingly surrounds himself with leaders of state security structures, reinforcing a siege mentality that portrays Russia as a nation under constant threat. Experts quoted in the article believe Putin may genuinely fear a Western-backed “color revolution” in Russia, similar to the uprising that removed Ukrainian President Viktor Yanukovych. In response, the Kremlin is expanding internal security forces and giving them broader powers to detect and suppress dissent. Political analyst Alexei Mukhin says the government is especially focused on police reform and stronger security systems to prevent revolution before it starts. The article also points to the Kremlin budget as evidence of the siloviki’s growing clout. Russia’s military spending has risen sharply, reaching the equivalent of $80 billion this year, a 30 percent increase from the previous year. Unlike other sectors, defense was exempted from a general 10 percent government spending cut imposed during the economic crisis. This expansion has alarmed liberals, including former Finance Minister Alexei Kudrin, who resigned in 2011 over the uncontrolled growth of military budgets. Golts argues that the defense-industrial complex now supports roughly 10 million people, including families, making it Putin’s core constituency. Konovalov adds that the issue is not simply financial but political: as Putin becomes more estranged from big business, the siloviki provide him with a direct shield against threats to his rule.

The shift from oligarch influence to military-security establishment dominance thus reflects Putin's evolving assessment of where his security interests lie, fundamentally hardening Russia's foreign policy approach.

Russia is facing growing economic strain as its war-driven economy slows, raising fears of stagflation even though the country has so far withstood Western sanctions better than many expected. The article opens with the example of Oleg Ivanovich, a 67-year-old Moscow pensioner, who says bread prices have risen so sharply that he sometimes has to go without. Even so, he says he is willing to endure the hardship for the sake of Russia’s military offensive in Ukraine, using the Kremlin’s term “special military operation.” He expects prices to normalize once the war ends. The main economic problem is inflation. Annual inflation stood at just over 9 percent in August, reflecting broad price pressure after Russia sharply increased spending on its military campaign. Since sending troops into Ukraine in February 2022, Moscow has funneled billions of dollars into the armed forces, soldiers’ families, and weapons producers. That spending surge helped sustain growth and wages and frustrated Western hopes that sanctions would trigger an economic collapse. However, Russia’s Central Bank has recently begun warning about a different danger: stagflation, a combination of weak or stagnant growth and high inflation. Central Bank Governor Elvira Nabiullina said over the summer that labor shortages could slow growth even as stimulus continues to fuel inflation, describing this as a stagflation scenario that could only be stopped through a deep recession. The article says Russia’s economy is being distorted by war. Government spending has risen by almost 50 percent since the invasion, unemployment is at a record low, and consumer confidence is at a 15-year high. But these headline indicators mask serious structural weaknesses. Many workers—both skilled and unskilled—have left the country to avoid mobilization or joined the army, leaving millions of vacancies. At the same time, sanctions on Western technology have reduced productivity and disrupted supply chains. Economists quoted in the piece warn that these demographic and technological problems will likely produce very low growth in the long term. The central bank has already raised interest rates to 18 percent in an effort to contain inflation, and some analysts think rates could reach 20 percent by year’s end. That would echo the emergency hikes made at the start of the war to prevent a financial crisis and bank run. Higher borrowing costs are hurting private businesses outside the military sector and further limiting growth. A policy meeting on Friday is expected to offer clues about whether more tightening is coming. Russian President Vladimir Putin has portrayed military spending—he says it amounts to more than 8 percent of GDP—as a source of growth. But critics argue the economy is being “de-modernized,” with Russia shifting back toward Soviet-style models and standards while technological progress stalls. Despite these warnings, experts say Russia still has substantial room to continue financing the war. The country retains about $300 billion in reserves not frozen by the West, has low public debt of around 15 percent of GDP, and has announced tax increases to raise more revenue. For now, analysts say, there is little immediate economic pressure that would force Moscow to scale back its military campaign.

# Russia Faces Stagflation Threat as Growth Slows Russia is confronting a troubling economic scenario as it continues its military campaign in Ukraine: stagflation, characterized by stagnant economic growth combined with high inflation. This represents a significant challenge for the Kremlin, which has managed the economic fallout from the conflict better than many anticipated. ## Current Economic Pressures Annual inflation reached just over nine percent in August, causing hardship for ordinary Russians like pensioner Oleg Ivanovich, who sometimes skips meals due to soaring bread prices. The Central Bank has warned that the economy is overheating and may face stagflation, a potentially more severe problem than current conditions. Central Bank Governor Elvira Nabiullina cautioned that labor shortages could slow economic growth while stimulus measures accelerate inflation, creating a scenario "that can only be stopped at the cost of a deep recession." ## Mixed Economic Indicators Despite these warnings, Russia has achieved some positive short-term results through massive military spending. The regulator faces a dilemma: continuing rate increases could worsen stagflation, while relaxing policy might accelerate inflation. ## Structural Decline Critics argue Russia's economy is "de-modernizing," reverting to Soviet-era models while abandoning technological advancement. Military spending, which Putin claims exceeds eight percent of GDP, has become the primary growth driver—a situation one analyst describes as a "vicious circle of inflation and military Keynesianism." ## Long-Term Sustainability While many experts question the system's long-term viability, they see no immediate economic constraints on Russia's military capacity. Moscow commands approximately $300 billion in unfrozen reserves, maintains a low debt-to-GDP ratio of around 15 percent, and has announced substantial tax increases. Former deputy finance minister Sergey Aleksashenko estimates it will take a decade before Western technology sanctions become fully visible. Most analysts agree Russia has sufficient resources to sustain its military campaign at current intensity for several years, though perhaps not indefinitely.

Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro said this week that “de-dollarization” of world trade is inevitable and argued that Venezuela should join that process by reducing its reliance on the U.S. dollar. In a post on Twitter, he claimed the world is moving toward “a new world” free from “criminal sanctions and economic manipulations,” and he presented the shift away from the dollar as part of a broader, multipolar economic order. Maduro expanded on the theme during the latest episode of his weekly television program, *Con Maduro+* (“With Maduro Plus”). There, he pointed to Zimbabwe as a model worth studying. Zimbabwe recently introduced a gold-backed digital “token” as legal tender, and Maduro suggested that Venezuela could learn from such alternative monetary initiatives. He said his government should “insert ourselves there” in the global de-dollarization effort and eventually discourage, then expel, the U.S. currency from Venezuela. The article notes that Maduro’s remarks come after years in which his government has tolerated, and in many cases relied on, the use of U.S. dollars inside Venezuela. The bolivar, the national currency, has become nearly worthless after years of hyperinflation and economic collapse. Although the regime once tried to ban or heavily restrict dollar use, it later eased those controls because the economy had deteriorated so badly that many transactions were already being conducted in dollars. Maduro’s anti-dollar rhetoric also echoes moves by other leftist leaders in Latin America. The article cites Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, who signed an agreement with China in April to conduct trade in Chinese yuan rather than U.S. dollars, and former Argentine President Alberto Fernández, who signed a similar arrangement that same month. The piece recounts Venezuela’s long and unsuccessful efforts to break away from the dollar. Since 2017, the Maduro government has repeatedly tried to create alternatives. One early attempt was a “currency basket” exchange system tied to several foreign currencies, including the Chinese yuan, Russian ruble, euro, and Indian rupee. That initiative quickly faded. Maduro then launched the Petro, a state-backed cryptocurrency that also failed to gain meaningful adoption and is now used mainly to set fees for passports and other government documents. The article also reviews the regime’s earlier currency controls. Between 2003 and 2018, Venezuela imposed strict exchange controls that limited access to foreign currencies and, at one stage, made it illegal to mention unofficial exchange rates or trade foreign currency inside the country. Those controls were tightened so severely that violations could reportedly carry prison sentences of up to 15 years. But as Venezuela’s economy collapsed, the government relaxed the restrictions in 2018, allowing people to use foreign currencies more freely. That change led to an informal “dollarization” of the economy. Without any official decree, the U.S. dollar became the main reference for prices in shops and businesses, and it remains a key support for the country’s fragile economy. Maduro himself has used dollar values to calculate some payments distributed through a state social platform. In 2019, he even publicly thanked God for the dollarization of Venezuela, saying it gave the population and the economy some relief. Economist Asdrúbal Oliveros said Maduro’s new de-dollarization push would be very difficult to carry out. He argued that the dollar is deeply embedded in daily transactions, serves as a savings and reserve currency for many citizens, and anchors prices and expectations across the economy, making any attempt to replace it highly complex.

# Summary: Maduro Seeks to "De-Dollarize" Venezuela Following Zimbabwe Model Venezuelan socialist dictator Nicolás Maduro has renewed his push to eliminate U.S. dollar usage in Venezuela, declaring that the "de-dollarization of world trade is inevitable." Speaking on his new weekly television program Con Maduro+, Maduro identified Zimbabwe—which recently introduced a gold-backed digital currency as legal tender—as a potential model for Venezuela to follow in discouraging dollar use. Maduro instructed Vice President Delcy Rodriguez to study Zimbabwe's initiative, characterizing it as part of an accelerated global shift away from the dollar. He expressed intentions to "insert" Venezuela into this de-dollarization process and ultimately expel U.S. currency from the country, framing the effort as part of a broader multipolar world where multiple currencies would facilitate international trade and financial operations. This represents a dramatic reversal of policy for Maduro's regime. After 15 years of heavily restricting and penalizing foreign currency use, the government relaxed restrictions in 2018 following Venezuela's economic collapse. This shift inadvertently created an informal "dollarization" of the economy, wherein the dollar replaced Venezuela's devalued bolívar in everyday transactions without formal government decree. Ironically, Maduro himself has relied on the dollar to set stipend values distributed through the state's Fatherland platform and publicly thanked God in 2019 for dollarization, which provided economic relief to struggling citizens. The dollar has proven essential to sustaining Venezuela's devastated economy. Stores and businesses now reference dollar values to set prices, and the currency serves as both a payment medium and savings vehicle for citizens reluctant to hold the worthless bolívar. Maduro's de-dollarization rhetoric aligns with broader leftist trends in Latin America. Brazil's President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva signed an agreement with communist China in April to conduct trade using the Chinese yuan instead of dollars. Argentina's outgoing President Alberto Fernández signed a similar deal that same month. However, Maduro's previous attempts to move away from the dollar have consistently failed. Between 2003 and 2018, his regime enforced draconian currency controls, even imprisoning citizens for up to 15 years for discussing unofficial exchange rates or trading foreign currencies. The regime attempted launching a "currency basket" system featuring the Chinese yuan, Russian ruble, Euro, and Indian rupee, but the initiative collapsed quickly. Maduro subsequently created the Petro cryptocurrency, which failed to gain meaningful traction and now primarily anchors passport and document costs. Venezuelan economist Asdrúbal Oliveros cautioned that implementing de-dollarization would prove "complex and difficult." He identified three key obstacles: the dollar's widespread use as a payment method, its function as a savings and reserve currency for citizens reluctant to abandon it, and the fact that economic agents have anchored price expectations and costs in dollars, making currency switching extremely challenging. The fundamental contradiction in Maduro's position remains unresolved: the regime depends on dollar usage to maintain economic stability while simultaneously attempting to eliminate it, a paradox that has prevented previous de-dollarization efforts from succeeding.

In Cali, Colombia, agronomist Javier Gereda stands beside a row of high-tech fridges at a major seed bank and proudly points to a bean plant and its seedlings, calling them “my son and his siblings.” The plant is especially meaningful because it comes from a bean species that no longer survives in its original habitat in Costa Rica. According to Gereda, the seed bank is now the only place in the world where this extinct-in-the-wild species exists. The seeds that produced these plants are part of the Future Seeds gene bank, a vast collection preserved since the 1970s and now recognized as the world’s largest genetic library for beans, cassava, and tropical forages. The facility is operated by CGIAR’s Alliance of Bioversity International and the International Center for Tropical Agriculture (CIAT), and it sits amid sugarcane fields near Cali in southwestern Colombia. Scientists at the bank say its mission is increasingly urgent. As the global population grows and crop yields are threatened by degraded soils, hotter temperatures, and more extreme weather, researchers need crop varieties that can survive harsher conditions. The bank stores 67,000 samples in steel shelves, glass test tubes, and airtight packets kept in a giant refrigerator at minus 20 degrees Celsius. Geneticist Joe Tohme, who leads the Alliance’s crop research on nutrition and health, calls the collection “an insurance for the future.” The new facility has already received about $17.2 million in funding, including support from the Colombian government, and another $17 million donation from the Bezos Earth Fund. Its importance is underscored by the broader loss of agricultural diversity worldwide. Experts say humans once cultivated more than 6,000 different plants, but about 75% of crop diversity has disappeared in the last century. Today, roughly 40% of global calories come from just three crops: maize, wheat, and rice. That concentration leaves the food system vulnerable if climate change, conflict, or other disruptions damage harvests. The war in Ukraine, the article notes, exposed how fragile global food supply chains can be when interrupted, driving up prices and worsening hunger. The seed bank is meant to counter those risks by preserving genetic traits that can help farmers adapt to climate change, pests, diseases, and malnutrition. One in nine people still do not have enough food, and the world population is projected to reach 9.8 billion by 2050. Tohme describes climate change as the biggest threat to food security and an “existential threat,” arguing that the bank can help address both immediate and long-term challenges. Inside the laboratories, researchers inspect seeds under microscopes, selecting the healthiest ones for storage or study and discarding damaged samples. CIAT bean researcher Luis Guillermo Santos explained that scientists search the gene pool for special traits, such as the ability to withstand heat, drought, or excessive water. The bank also distributes seeds free of charge to researchers and farmers. Many of the requests come from cooperatives seeking varieties their ancestors once grew, or from farmers looking for crops better suited to local conditions. Santos said the bank receives about 100 requests a year for bean samples alone and has distributed more than 500,000 seed samples to 142 countries since 1973. Researchers say the collection has already produced important results. Seeds gathered decades ago from the Amazon regions of Ecuador and Colombia helped create a cassava variety resistant to brown streak disease, which has damaged harvests in parts of Africa. Other bean varieties with higher zinc and iron levels have been identified to help combat malnutrition. The bank is increasingly using modern tools to unlock the information hidden in its seeds. Scientists extract DNA, sequence genes, and combine genomics with big data and artificial intelligence to speed up the search for useful traits. Tohme described the collection as a library that needs translation, while biologist Monica Carvajal, who runs the digital side of Future Seeds, said it is like a “digital passport” and a bank of knowledge that gives access to biodiversity through data. The facility is also intended to train new scientists through partnerships with local and international universities. For Tohme and his colleagues, the challenge is not only to collect seeds, but to maintain them for generations. He said the work requires “a generational commitment” and must be preserved “for eternity.”
