Keiko Fujimori, daughter of jailed former President Alberto Fujimori, emerged as the leading candidate in Peru’s first-round presidential election, showing how powerfully her surname still shapes Peruvian politics. Her father is remembered by many as the man who defeated the Maoist Shining Path insurgency, restored security, curbed hyperinflation, and helped stabilize the economy, but he is also associated with authoritarian rule and human-rights abuses. That mixed legacy made the Fujimori name both an asset and a liability in the campaign. Despite widespread concern about her family’s history, Fujimori’s center-right Popular Force party won the most votes in the parliamentary and presidential races. However, she fell short of the majority needed to win outright and was forced into a June runoff against former Economy Minister Pedro Pablo Kuczynski, known as PPK. Polls had suggested Fujimori might win around 40 percent and possibly even surpass 50 percent, but the expected second-round opponent was leftist Verónika Mendoza. Instead, Mendoza finished with only 17 percent, while fears of the left in a country still haunted by the violence of the Shining Path helped Kuczynski reach the runoff with 24 percent. Analysts say Fujimori’s strongest support comes from working-class voters who credit her father with bringing order and prosperity. Her campaign also benefited from Peru’s electoral authorities disqualifying two candidates seen as potential rivals because of campaign irregularities. Her party’s broad grassroots organization and its parliamentary majority further strengthened her position. Still, Fujimori’s weakness lies in the darker side of her father’s rule, including the Barrios Altos and La Cantuta massacres, where 25 people were killed by right-wing gunmen. She also carries baggage from her previous presidential run, when she narrowly lost to outgoing President Ollanta Humala after suggesting she might pardon her father, a stance that mobilized her opponents. This time, Fujimori says she will not pardon Alberto Fujimori, will preserve the current economic model, and will focus on fighting crime. The June 5 runoff will decide not only Peru’s next president, but also how the country judges its past.

# Summary: Peru's Presidential Election and the Fujimori Legacy Keiko Fujimori, daughter of former President Alberto Fujimori, secured the most votes in Peru's first round of presidential elections but failed to win outright, forcing a June runoff against conservative former Economy Minister Pedro Pablo Kuczynski (PPK). Alberto Fujimori's 1990s presidency is remembered for suppressing the Shining Path Maoist insurgency and controlling hyperinflation, earning him both admiration and criticism for his ruthless methods. His legacy carries significant weight in Peruvian politics, comparable to Pinochet's controversial status in Chile. Despite predictions that her Popular Force party would capture 40% of votes, Fujimori received insufficient support for an immediate victory. The leftist Broad Front party, which many feared could advance to the runoff, garnered only 17%. This allowed the more palatable conservative candidate Kuczynski, with 24%, to face Fujimori in the second round. Fujimori's surname represents both her greatest asset and liability. Working-class voters credit her father with economic stability and defeating terrorism, potentially supporting her candidacy. However, her previous presidential campaign lost after she suggested pardoning her imprisoned father, mobilizing opposition voters. She now insists she will not pardon him and promises to maintain current economic policies while fighting crime. The 40-year-old, who became Latin America's youngest First Lady at 19, benefits from her party's strong parliamentary majority and grassroots structures. However, her weakness stems from her father's darker legacy, including massacres at Barrios Altos and La Cantuta that killed 25 people. Kuczynski's strategy involves uniting voters who fear the Fujimori name and oppose a return to authoritarian rule. The June 5 runoff will ultimately determine whether Peruvian voters prioritize economic stability and security associated with the Fujimori name or reject the family's controversial past.

A plane carrying 115 Venezuelan migrants from Chile landed in Caracas on Sunday, ending weeks of hardship for people stranded at the northern border with Peru. When the passengers disembarked, they were met with applause and cries of relief. One migrant, Gerardo Valladares, 22, said he would never leave Venezuela again and described being blocked for two weeks in poor conditions, with little information from Peruvian police. He said conditions improved only after UN human rights workers arrived around day 10. The repatriation flight was a private airline chartered by the government of President Nicolás Maduro. It came amid a broader border crisis in which hundreds of migrants, mostly Venezuelan but also Haitian, Colombian and Ecuadoran, were trapped in northern Chile after Peru refused them entry for lacking proper documents. Peru declared a 60-day state of emergency and sent troops to border checkpoints to stop undocumented crossings. Chilean President Gabriel Boric called the flight a “diplomatic triumph.” Venezuelan officials welcomed the returnees as part of the government’s “Return to the Homeland” program. The migration crisis reflects Venezuela’s severe economic and political collapse, which has driven about seven million people to leave the country.

# Summary A plane chartered by the Venezuelan government transported 115 stranded Venezuelan migrants from Chile to Caracas on May 8, 2023. The migrants had been trapped for weeks at the Chile-Peru border in difficult conditions, blocked by Peruvian authorities due to lack of documentation. Peru had declared a 60-day state of emergency and deployed troops to prevent undocumented workers from entering. The repatriation included migrants of various nationalities—Venezuelan, Haitian, Colombian, and Ecuadorian. UN rights workers' intervention around day 10 helped facilitate the process. Upon arrival in Caracas, passengers expressed relief and joy, with some vowing never to leave again, citing mistreatment abroad. Chilean President Gabriel Boric called the repatriation a "diplomatic triumph." Venezuelan officials welcomed the migrants as part of their "Return to the Homeland" program launched in 2018. The repatriation reflects Venezuela's severe economic and political crisis, which has driven approximately seven million Venezuelans abroad in recent years.

Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and Argentina’s Alberto Fernández will launch a plan of nearly 100 actions to revive their strategic alliance, Brazil’s Prensa Latina reported. Lula received Fernández in Brasília during his fourth visit to Brazil this year, as the two countries mark 200 years of diplomatic relations. Before the meeting, Lula said Brazil is working on an integrated financing line for Brazilian exports to Argentina and on “new and creative” measures to deepen financial integration and trade. Argentina is Brazil’s third-largest global trading partner, but is facing a severe economic crisis marked by currency devaluation, falling purchasing power, and high inflation.

# Summary Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and Argentine President Alberto Fernández announced plans to strengthen their strategic alliance through approximately 100 coordinated actions. Fernández's visit marks his fourth trip to Brazil this year, coinciding with the 200th anniversary of bilateral diplomatic relations. Lula announced the creation of an integral financing line for Brazilian exports to Argentina and emphasized implementing creative solutions for financial integration and trade facilitation. Argentina ranks as Brazil's third-largest trading partner globally, after China and the United States, though Argentina currently faces severe economic challenges including currency devaluation, reduced purchasing power, and high inflation. Fernández will meet with additional Brazilian officials before returning to Buenos Aires.

Banco do Brasil has asked Brazil’s solicitor general to take legal action against social media posts spreading false claims that the state-run lender could face U.S. sanctions because it serves a client sanctioned under the U.S. Magnitsky Act. In a document dated Friday and seen by Reuters, the bank warned that the posts could cause “undesirable consequences” if not quickly stopped, noting that clients had contacted it seeking clarification. It also said some of the messages came from federal lawmakers and urged steps to prevent damage to the national financial system. Brazil’s solicitor general said the matter had been referred to federal police for a criminal investigation into fake news, warning that such rumors could spark a bank run and harm the economy. Banco do Brasil later said it would pursue legal measures to protect its reputation after identifying “false and malicious” posts meant to fuel panic and suggest deposit withdrawals. The bank said Brazilian law allows prison terms of up to six years and fines for spreading false or incomplete information about financial institutions. The controversy comes amid worsening U.S.-Brazil relations, after President Donald Trump imposed tariffs on Brazilian goods and sanctions on Judge Alexandre de Moraes. Banco do Brasil shares fell 2.2% Monday after earlier losses.

# Summary Banco do Brasil has requested Brazil's solicitor general to take legal action against false social media claims suggesting the state-run bank faces U.S. sanctions because one of its clients—Judge Alexandre de Moraes—is sanctioned under the U.S. Magnitsky Act. The bank warned of potential economic consequences and reported that clients sought clarification amid widespread posts, including some from federal lawmakers. The solicitor general referred the case to federal police for criminal investigation into fake news distribution, cautioning that such misinformation could trigger a bank run and harm Brazil's economy. Banco do Brasil stated it would pursue legal action to defend its reputation against "false and malicious" posts intended to incite panic and deposit withdrawals. Under Brazilian law, spreading false information about financial institutions carries penalties of up to six years imprisonment plus fines. The situation stems from deteriorating U.S.-Brazil relations following President Trump's recent tariffs on Brazilian goods and sanctions against Judge Moraes, who oversees former President Bolsonaro's election plot case. Given the U.S. financial system's global reach, foreign banks often extend restrictions to sanctioned individuals to avoid secondary sanctions. Consequently, Brazilian bank shares have declined, with Banco do Brasil's stock falling 2.2% on Monday.

Spain says the crisis in Venezuela should be resolved by Latin American countries themselves, not by outside powers. Speaking in Santiago, Spanish secretary of state for international cooperation and Ibero-America Fernando García Casas said the region must find its own solution, whether through the Organization of American States or another forum. He cited a group of countries including Peru, Colombia, Mexico, Chile, Argentina, Brazil and Spain that agree urgent steps are needed to end Venezuela’s humanitarian crisis, release political prisoners, hold elections and stop the violence. García Casas argued that the Constituent Assembly is not a real solution because it does not lead to peace, democracy or reconciliation. He also said mediation efforts led by former presidents José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero, Leonel Fernández and Martín Torrijos have not produced all the results hoped for. García Casas stressed that democracy is one of Latin America’s strengths and said the region has improved significantly over the past two decades. He noted that the European Union engages with Latin America at several levels. During his visit to Chile, after meetings in Mexico on Central America and the OAS, he signed an agreement to make university degree recognition easier between Spain and Chile. He added that Spain has maintained aid and cooperation in the region despite economic cutbacks, and that Spanish companies have contributed investment, jobs, technology and corporate social responsibility.

# Spain Advocates Regional Solution for Venezuela Crisis Spain's secretary of state for international cooperation, Fernando Garcia Casas, has stated that the Venezuelan crisis must be resolved by Latin America itself rather than external powers. The humanitarian situation in Venezuela has resulted in 75 deaths during 80 days of protests. Garcia Casas emphasized that countries including Peru, Colombia, Mexico, Chile, Argentina, Brazil, and Spain agree that steps must be taken to end the crisis, free political prisoners, hold elections, and stop violence. He criticized Venezuela's Constitutional Assembly as ineffective for achieving peace, democracy, or reconciliation. The ongoing mediation efforts led by former presidents Jose Luis Rodriguez Zapatero, Leonel Fernandez, and Martin Torrijos have not achieved desired results, he acknowledged. Garcia Casas highlighted Latin America's democratic achievements and progress over the past two decades, noting the European Union engages with the region through multiple channels including bilateral relations and the Ibero-American Conference. During his visit to Chile, he signed an agreement facilitating university degree validation between Spain and Chile. Despite Spain's economic crisis, the country has maintained aid and cooperation levels in the region, with Spanish companies continuing to invest and create jobs.

Colombia on Thursday granted temporary legal status to more than 440,000 Venezuelan migrants, allowing them to remain in the country for two years and access social services. The decree, signed by President Juan Manuel Santos, applies to 442,462 Venezuelans who lack visas, stamped passports or other formal permission to stay in Colombia and who had registered in a recent two-month survey. The measure comes as Colombia has absorbed the largest share of the exodus from Venezuela, where hyperinflation, severe shortages of food and medicine, and rising crime have driven hundreds of thousands to leave. Estimates of the total number of Venezuelans who have fled under the governments of Hugo Chavez and Nicolas Maduro vary widely, with some opponents and academics putting the figure at 4 million, though Maduro has dismissed that as exaggerated. He blames an alleged “economic war” backed by opposition leaders and Washington, while critics say Venezuela’s crisis stems from currency and price controls and falling oil production. Colombia had asked undocumented Venezuelans to register so the government could assess social service needs. Many arrive with little money, and about 250,000 Colombians have also recently returned from Venezuela. Santos said Colombia would continue supporting both groups and called the decision “an international milestone in migration issues.” Under the plan, Venezuelans will receive emergency medical care, access to social security, prenatal care for pregnant women, continued school enrollment for children, and help finding work through public job centers. The government will also spend 20 billion pesos, or $6.9 million, to reimburse hospitals that treated migrants. Santos, who was leaving office on Tuesday, again criticized Maduro, and president-elect Ivan Duque has also sharply condemned the Venezuelan government.

# Colombia Grants Temporary Status to 440,000 Venezuelan Migrants Colombia has temporarily granted over 440,000 Venezuelan migrants permission to stay for two years and access social services, President Juan Manuel Santos announced Thursday. The decree targets Venezuelans without proper visas or documentation who registered during a recent two-month survey. Venezuela's severe economic crisis—marked by hyperinflation, food and medicine shortages, and crime—has driven massive emigration. While estimates of total Venezuelan emigrants range from millions (some opponents cite 4 million), President Nicolas Maduro disputes these figures, claiming his country faces an "economic war" orchestrated by opposition leaders and Washington. Critics attribute the crisis to government currency controls, price restrictions, and declining oil production. Colombia has absorbed the largest influx of Venezuelan refugees. The country conducted the survey to assess social service needs and help undocumented migrants. Under the decree, Venezuelan migrants gain access to emergency medical care, social security participation, prenatal care for pregnant women, and public school enrollment for children. Adults receive job-search assistance through Colombian employment centers. The government allocated 20 billion pesos ($6.9 million) to reimburse hospitals for treating migrants. Additionally, approximately 250,000 Colombians have recently returned from Venezuela. Santos, departing office Tuesday, criticized Venezuela's situation, highlighting the paradox of a nation with world's largest oil reserves facing widespread hunger and disease. His successor, Ivan Duque, has similarly condemned Maduro's policies and treatment of the opposition.

Brazilian President Dilma Rousseff won re-election in the closest presidential race in three decades, but the narrow victory left her Workers’ Party with its weakest mandate in years as it faces economic and political difficulties. Rousseff defeated center-right challenger Aecio Neves in a runoff on Sunday, winning 51.6 percent of the vote. Her win came after a bitter campaign that exposed deep divisions in Brazil between voters who wanted to preserve the social gains of the Workers’ Party and those who believed market-oriented policies were needed to restore growth. In her victory speech, Rousseff emphasized “dialogue” and national reconciliation as priorities for her second term. She said she understood public demands for a more efficient and less corrupt government and promised to become “a much better president” than before. But she now faces a more fragmented Congress and less political support, making it harder to push through political reform or revive a stagnant economy. She must also respond to widespread frustration over poor public services, which had fueled street protests a year earlier. The article notes that during the Workers’ Party’s time in power, Brazil enacted broad social programs that helped lift millions out of poverty and expand the middle class. Yet the economy, the world’s seventh largest, has slowed since 2011. Analysts warned that inflation had returned, the country was in technical recession, and public spending was out of control. Carlos Pereira of the Getulio Vargas Foundation said Rousseff had social inclusion on her side, but her first term’s macroeconomic policies had been weak, making it harder to combine social progress with economic stability. The campaign itself was highly combative, described as the most acrimonious since Brazil’s return to democracy in 1985. Neves attacked Rousseff over a widening corruption scandal at Petrobras, Brazil’s state-controlled oil company, where an informant told investigators that the Workers’ Party had directly benefited from a kickback scheme. Rousseff denied the accusations and warned voters that Neves’ victory would mean a return to the economic turmoil, hyperinflation, and high unemployment associated with the last period of Social Democratic rule. Supporters of Rousseff celebrated in Sao Paulo, where thousands gathered with banners and campaign music. One supporter said Brazil’s development had only just begun and praised the continuity her victory would bring. Neves, a former two-term governor of Minas Gerais with high approval ratings, thanked the more than 50 million Brazilians who voted for him. He said he had fought well, fulfilled his mission, and kept the faith.

# Brazil's Rousseff Wins Re-election with Slim Majority Amid Economic Challenges Brazilian President Dilma Rousseff secured re-election with just 51.6 percent of the vote in a runoff against center-right challenger Aecio Neves, marking the narrowest margin in three decades and delivering her left-leaning Workers' Party its weakest mandate. The victory comes as Brazil confronts significant economic and social challenges. In her victory speech, Rousseff emphasized "dialogue" and national reconciliation as priorities for her second term. She acknowledged public demands for a more efficient, less corrupt government, pledging to be "a much better president than I have been until now." However, she faces substantial obstacles: a stagnant economy, a fragmented congress where her support has diminished, and widespread frustration over inadequate public services that sparked major street demonstrations a year earlier. The Workers' Party's tenure has achieved notable social accomplishments, implementing expansive programs that lifted millions of Brazilians out of poverty into the middle class. However, Brazil's economy—the world's seventh-largest—has underperformed since 2011, raising concerns about sustainability of these social gains. Political analysts note the tension between Rousseff's social achievements and weak macroeconomic policies, with inflation returning, the country entering technical recession, and public spending spiraling out of control. The contentious campaign, considered the most acrimonious since Brazil's 1985 return to democracy, divided voters into two camps: those prioritizing social protection and inclusion versus those favoring market-friendly policies for economic growth. Both candidates claimed they could deliver both growth and social advancement, but the electorate remained skeptical. Neves, a two-term governor with a 92 percent approval rating, aggressively attacked Rousseff over a widening Petrobras kickback scandal, alleging the Workers' Party directly benefited. Rousseff denied the charges and warned that Neves represented a return to economic turbulence, hyperinflation, and unemployment from when the Social Democrats previously held power. Despite her narrow victory, Rousseff must now navigate a divided congress to implement political reforms and restart economic growth while maintaining social programs. The election results revealed a deeply polarized nation, with supporters like retired federal worker Liliane Viana celebrating continuity and feared backward movement, while Neves graciously conceded, thanking over 50 million voters who supported him and vowing he "kept the faith."

NEPI Rockcastle said it welcomed the Financial Services Conduct Authority’s decision to close an investigation into allegations that the JSE-listed property group had published false or misleading financial information. The FSCA announced on Monday that it had found no basis for claims that NEPI Rockcastle intentionally or negligently made false statements about its performance in its 31 December 2017 financial statements, and said it had closed the probe into a possible breach of the Financial Markets Act. The investigation followed last year’s wave of allegations from hedge funds and asset managers that wiped billions of rand off several real estate companies’ market value. American short-seller Viceroy Research had claimed it found inconsistencies in NEPI Rockcastle’s reporting and links to financial fraud, prompting calls for regulatory action. NEPI Rockcastle said the outcome confirmed its earlier statements to the market. Chief executive Alex Morar said the company follows strict corporate governance standards and that its board and management were satisfied with the integrity of its business practices. The FSCA said a separate investigation into possible prohibited trading in the company’s shares by third parties remained pending.

# Summary NEPI Rockcastle, a JSE-listed real estate investment firm, has been cleared by the Financial Services Conduct Authority (FSCA) of financial misconduct allegations. The FSCA closed its investigation into potential breaches of the Financial Markets Act, finding no evidence that NEPI Rockcastle intentionally or negligently published false statements in its 2017 financial statements. The investigation was triggered by American short-seller Viceroy Research, which alleged the company engaged in related-party deals and share price manipulation. Last year, NEPI Rockcastle and other real estate firms experienced significant losses following such allegations. The FSCA's only remaining investigation concerns possible prohibited trading practices in the company's shares by third parties, unrelated to NEPI Rockcastle itself. Chief Executive Alex Morar welcomed the conclusion, reaffirming the company's commitment to corporate governance and stating that allegations were groundless. NEPI Rockcastle emphasized its strong business performance and adherence to financial reporting best practices.

Police have launched a manhunt for two Turkish nationals, Abubekir Salim and Mehmet Selim Kaymak, accused of fraud involving a South African coal mining company. The pair are alleged to have illegally removed their countrymen, Huseyin Caliskan and Muhammed Caliskan, as directors of Root Mining, then siphoned millions of rand from the company to Mauritius. A fraud, forgery and theft case was opened against them last year. Sandton police reportedly tried to arrest the men on Monday but did not find them at their offices. They were expected to hand themselves over on Wednesday, but had not done so by Thursday. Police spokesperson Captain Granville Meyer confirmed that a warrant of arrest was issued on Monday and that the suspects remained at large. The case is linked to a larger dispute heard in the Pretoria High Court, where a draft order last week instructed Salim and Kaymak to repatriate more than R250 million from a Mauritius bank account to Londani Coal’s FNB account. The court said the money represented proceeds from coal sales mined by Londani, a subsidiary of Mpumalanga-based Sumo Coal. The draft order also seeks to freeze the men’s FNB accounts, believed to hold a combined R100 million. The Caliskan brothers say they were unlawfully removed from Root Mining, which has ties to Sumo Coal. Salim told The Star he was not a fugitive and claimed the matter had been put on hold.

# Summary Police have launched a manhunt for two Turkish nationals, Abubekir Salim and Mehmet Selim Kaymak, accused of defrauding over R250 million from a South African coal mining company. The suspects allegedly illegally gained control of Root Mining and fraudulently removed two Turkish directors, Huseyin and Muhammed Caliskan, from the company. They then siphoned millions of rand to a Mauritius bank account from Londani Coal, a subsidiary of Mpumalanga-based Sumo Coal. A fraud, forgery, and theft case was opened against them last year. Police attempted to arrest them on Monday but found them absent from their offices. An arrest warrant was issued, though the suspects failed to surrender as expected on Wednesday. When contacted by phone on Thursday, Salim claimed he was not a fugitive and that the matter had been suspended. Kaymak has been unreachable since Sunday. The Pretoria High Court recently issued a draft order requiring the suspects to repatriate the allegedly embezzled funds—believed to exceed R250 million—to Londani Coal's account. Additionally, their combined FNB bank accounts, estimated at R100 million, are to be frozen.

PayPal said it signed up “tens of thousands” of Nigerian customers in its first week of operating in Africa’s largest economy, with users already buying goods from Britain, China and the United States through its platform. A company official said the strong early uptake showed demand for online payments in a country where consumers previously could not easily buy directly from foreign merchants. Malvina Goldfeld, PayPal’s head of business development for sub-Saharan Africa, said in Lagos that the company had seen “great uptake” from Nigerians. PayPal launched in Nigeria and 10 other countries last month, expanding its global reach to 203 countries and offering online payment options through phones and computers in markets often affected by financial fraud. Before the launch, PayPal had secured deals with electronics suppliers in China and Dubai and partnered with Nigerian lender First Bank, which has more than 10.5 million customers. Goldfeld said the most popular purchases were from the United States, Britain and China, with electronics and fashion standing out as the main categories. PayPal previously launched in South Africa four years ago and Kenya last year, giving it access to shoppers across 40 sub-Saharan African countries. The company’s move comes as e-commerce grows rapidly in Africa, helped by retailers such as Jumia and a rising middle class. But Nigeria’s online shopping market still faces major obstacles, including weak infrastructure, port delays, supply-chain problems and low trust in online security. First Bank said 63 million Nigerians have active internet data subscriptions, but only about 1 percent make online transactions, even though purchases are expected to reach $1 billion this year.

# PayPal's Nigerian Launch Summary PayPal has successfully entered Nigeria, Africa's most populous nation, signing up tens of thousands of customers in its first week of operation. This marks a significant milestone as Nigerians can now purchase goods directly from foreign merchants for the first time. The platform launched simultaneously in 11 nations last month, bringing PayPal's total service coverage to 203 countries. According to Malvina Goldfeld, PayPal's head of business development for sub-Saharan Africa, the uptake has been impressive, with consumers already buying from retailers in Britain, China, and the United States. PayPal partnered with First Bank, Nigeria's largest lender with over 10.5 million customers, and secured deals with electronics suppliers in China and Dubai before launch. Electronics and fashion items dominate consumer purchases on the platform. Nigeria's e-commerce sector remains underdeveloped despite rapid growth. While 63 million Nigerians have internet data subscriptions, only 1 percent conduct online transactions. Online purchases are projected to reach $1 billion this year. Security concerns and fraud worries have historically hindered growth, though PayPal's entry is expected to boost confidence and development. PayPal's expansion follows successful launches in South Africa four years ago and Kenya last year, providing access to shoppers across 40 sub-Saharan African countries. Despite infrastructure challenges and supply chain issues, PayPal leadership believes the platform will accelerate e-commerce growth and logistics improvements.

At the Ninth Session of the Conference of the States Parties to the United Nations Convention Against Corruption (UNCAC) in Sharm El-Sheikh, Egypt, the Chairman of Nigeria’s Independent Corrupt Practices and Other Related Offences Commission (ICPC), Professor Bolaji Owasanoye, urged the United Nations and the wider global community to expose the real owners of artificial legal entities. He said doing so would help curb money laundering, illicit financial flows, and the concealment of stolen wealth. According to an ICPC statement, the conference brought together senior officials and anti-corruption agency heads from countries including the United States, United Kingdom, France, the Netherlands, Australia, Austria, Ukraine, India, the United Arab Emirates, Nigeria, Egypt, Burkina Faso, and Mali, alongside international organizations, civil society groups, and private-sector actors. Speaking on draft resolution L9, “Enhancing Access and Use of Beneficial Ownership Information to Facilitate the Identification, Recovery and Return of Proceeds of Crime,” Owasanoye argued that artificial legal entities are widely used to commit financial crimes and exploit developing countries. He said the world had already held enough meetings and debates on beneficial ownership and should now focus on action. In his words, authorities need to “lift the veil” on these entities to identify those behind them, trace assets, and recover hidden or stolen funds. He also noted that while charities play valuable roles, some are now being used to facilitate corruption. He called for greater information sharing and collaboration among intelligence agencies, saying a lack of transparency makes it difficult to uncover the people behind such crimes. In a separate panel appearance at a side event organized by the International Anti-Corruption Academy, Owasanoye said corruption threatens the achievement of the Sustainable Development Goals by worsening poverty and inequality. He stressed that global networking and information sharing are essential tools for fighting corruption and reducing social and economic disparities.

# Summary At the Ninth Session of the UN Conference of the States Parties to the UN Convention Against Corruption (CoSP9) in Sharm El-Sheikh, Egypt, Professor Bolaji Owasanoye, Chairman of Nigeria's Independent Corrupt Practices and Other Related Offences Commission (ICPC), called for immediate action to unmask the owners of artificial legal entities. Owasanoye argued that revealing beneficial ownership information is critical for combating money laundering, illicit financial flows (IFFs), and recovering stolen assets. He emphasized that artificial legal entities are being exploited to perpetrate financial crimes that disproportionately harm developing nations by depriving them of funds needed for development. Speaking on draft resolution L9 titled "Enhancing Access and Use of Beneficial Ownership Information to Facilitate the Identification, Recovery and Return of Proceeds of Crime," Owasanoye stressed the need to move beyond continued discussions to concrete action. He stated: "We need to lift the veil on these artificial legal entities" to enable asset tracing and recovery of hidden funds. The ICPC Chairman also warned that charitable organizations are increasingly being misused for corruption purposes. He advocated for enhanced transparency and information sharing among intelligence agencies to facilitate investigations and operations. Additionally, Owasanoye called for global cooperation and information sharing to achieve the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). He noted that corruption undermines development efforts by escalating poverty and increasing inequality, making international collaboration essential for addressing these challenges. The conference was attended by senior officials and anti-corruption agency heads from numerous countries including the United States, United Kingdom, France, Australia, India, and others, along with international bodies and civil society organizations.

Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua has praised the Competition Authority of Kenya for helping protect consumers, while urging it to strengthen public awareness so Kenyans are better shielded from unsafe and exploitative practices. He spoke on Wednesday at the Radisson Blu Hotel in Upper Hill, Nairobi, during the opening of the 2023 Consumers International Global Congress. Gachagua said consumer protection must keep pace with changing markets, especially as technology transforms trade and finance. He called for harmonisation of consumer protection laws across countries and for greater use of technology, including artificial intelligence, to detect and disrupt networks involved in consumer exploitation. He argued that because commerce is now increasingly global and digital, laws must be aligned across jurisdictions to remain effective, particularly in Africa where countries are at different stages of consumer protection. Citing a UN and Kenya Association of Manufacturers report, the Deputy President said Kenyan consumers remain exposed to exploitation. He noted that two out of five medicines on shelves are counterfeit, warning that such products endanger lives and undermine confidence in modern treatment. He also referred to a Kenya Anti-Counterfeit Authority report showing that 30 percent of counterfeit goods are locally manufactured, while 70 percent are smuggled into the country. Gachagua commended the Competition Authority’s enforcement record since its establishment in 2010. According to him, the agency has received 500 complaints and its interventions have affected more than 20 million consumers. He highlighted one major intervention involving disclosure and transparency practices by digital money lenders, which impacted over 30 million mobile money users. He said the Authority has worked with other regulators, including the Kenya Bureau of Standards, Communication Authority, Anti-Counterfeit Authority, Energy and Petroleum Regulatory Authority, Department of Weights and Measures, and Kenya Civil Aviation Authority, to strengthen consumer rights protections. The Deputy President also pointed to Kenya’s rapid digital growth, noting that 21 million internet users and 59 million SIM card subscribers rely on mobile phones for communication and payments. He warned that policymakers must stay ahead of online threats such as financial fraud, phishing, and ransom-related crimes. As digital commerce expands, he said, consumer-rights violations are also evolving, making outdated laws less effective unless regularly reviewed. He added that Kenya has made significant progress through e-transaction, cybercrime, data protection, and consumer protection laws. Gachagua was accompanied by senior officials from the Competition Authority, Consumers International, and COMESA Competition Commission, among others.

# Summary Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua commended the Competition Authority of Kenya (CAK) for protecting consumers while calling for enhanced efforts, particularly in public awareness campaigns. Speaking at the 2023 Consumers International Global Congress in Nairobi, he highlighted critical consumer protection challenges facing the nation. The DP emphasized that Kenyan consumers face significant exploitation, citing a UN and Kenya Association of Manufacturers report indicating that two of every five medicines on shelves are counterfeits—a situation that endangers lives and undermines confidence in modern treatment. He identified harmonizing global laws and integrating technology to combat illicit trade as essential steps for consumer protection. Since its establishment in 2010, CAK has received 500 complaints and impacted over 20 million consumers through enforcement efforts. A major intervention involved digital money lenders, affecting over 30 million mobile money service users by promoting disclosure and transparency practices. CAK collaborates with multiple sector regulators including the Kenya Bureau of Standards, Communication Authority, and Anti-Counterfeit Authority. Gachagua noted that Kenya's Anti-Counterfeit Authority reports 30 percent of counterfeit goods are locally manufactured, while 70 percent are smuggled into markets. He called for adopting artificial intelligence to track and suppress consumer exploitation networks globally. The Deputy President stressed that harmonizing consumer protection laws across jurisdictions is crucial, especially in Africa where countries operate at different development stages. As mobile banking and digital payments expand, relevant laws must evolve accordingly. Kenya has made substantial progress establishing e-Transaction Laws, Cybercrime Laws, Data Protection Privacy Laws, and Consumer Protection Laws. With 21 million internet users and 59 million SIM card subscribers relying on mobile phones for payments, protecting consumers from financial fraud, phishing, and ransomware is increasingly vital. Gachagua concluded that as digital technology evolves consumer rights violations, national and transnational legal provisions risk becoming obsolete without regular updates. Policymakers must stay ahead of emerging e-commerce threats to sustain safe online experiences for Kenyan consumers.

Nigerian authorities are stepping up their investigation into a major Flutterwave fraud case and plan to arrest 601 suspects linked to the scheme. The case stems from an October 2023 breach in Flutterwave’s point-of-sale system, which allegedly allowed 814 agents to carry out transactions beyond their account limits. That exploit led to 9,633 unauthorized transactions and the transfer of billions of naira into multiple bank accounts, including accounts at Polaris Bank, Stanbic IBTC, and Wema Bank. Court filings say Flutterwave’s total exposure was about ₦21.2 billion, though the company and partner banks managed to protect ₦7.2 billion by quickly restricting compromised accounts. In August 2024, the Federal High Court in Abuja refused a police request to reverse the transactions, saying due process and fair hearing had to be observed. After that ruling, police shifted their strategy toward freezing suspect accounts and prosecuting those believed to have received the stolen funds. Flutterwave first described the incident as a failed hacking attempt, but later investigations showed the fraud was far larger. The case has intensified concerns about cybersecurity and fraud risks in Nigeria’s fast-growing fintech sector.

# Summary Nigerian authorities are intensifying prosecution efforts in a major fraud case involving Flutterwave, a fintech company. Following an October 2023 breach in its Point-of-Sale system, the Nigeria Police Force plans to arrest 601 individuals accused of receiving fraudulent funds. The technical glitch allowed 814 agents to process transactions exceeding their account balances, resulting in 9,633 unauthorized transactions totaling ₦21.2 billion across multiple banks including Polaris Bank, Stanbic IBTC, and Wema Bank. Swift action by Flutterwave and partner banks preserved ₦7.2 billion by restricting compromised accounts. In August 2024, the Federal High Court in Abuja rejected a police request to reverse the transactions, citing due process requirements. Consequently, law enforcement has shifted focus to freezing suspect accounts and prosecuting suspected accomplices. Flutterwave initially attributed the breach to a failed hacking attempt, but investigations revealed the fraud's true scale. Authorities believe transaction recipients were aware of the illegal nature of the transfers. This case highlights vulnerabilities in Nigeria's fintech sector, prompting calls for enhanced cybersecurity measures and proactive monitoring systems.

Libya remains trapped in political paralysis more than a decade after the 2011 uprising and nearly ten years of civil war. The country is still split between rival power centers: UN-backed Interim Prime Minister Abdul Hamid al-Dbeibeh controls Tripoli and much of western Libya, while General Khalifa Haftar dominates the east. Despite repeated UN efforts to broker a settlement, no durable political agreement has been reached, and Libyans have still not been able to choose their representatives through free and fair elections. The article asks what role the international community can play in helping Libya move toward a rights-based democracy, and it presents the views of three Libyan civil society voices, in collaboration with the Atlantic Council’s North Africa Program and Lawyers for Libya Justice (LFJL). The first speaker argues that no meaningful international solution is possible unless the world treats Libya as a priority and stops approaching it in a fragmented, politicized way. He says Libya has been pushed to the margins of global attention, especially since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine shifted international focus elsewhere. He contrasts the swift global response to Ukraine — including sanctions and an International Criminal Court (ICC) arrest warrant for Vladimir Putin — with the much slower response to Libya’s years of violence, suggesting that there has been little genuine will to resolve the Libyan crisis. To illustrate the value of accountability, he points to the ICC arrest warrant issued for Mahmoud al-Warfali, a former Libyan general accused of war crimes, including murder and ordering the killing of non-combatants. According to him, the warrant had an immediate deterrent effect: abuses declined, videos of mass executions stopped circulating, and some militia leaders in the east disappeared from public view. He says the warrant made Haftar and al-Warfali’s forces anxious, proving that even a single decisive action by international actors can save lives. From this perspective, accountability and redress must come first. He calls for an end to human rights violations, an end to impunity, the rebuilding of Libya’s devastated judicial system, and the creation of a mechanism or independent court to prosecute atrocities. Without transitional justice and compensation for victims, he argues, there can be no solution. This position is attributed to Ali Alaspli, president of Libya Crimes Watch. The second speaker, Fatima Omar of Lawyers for Libya Justice, says the depth of Libya’s division, insecurity, and political deadlock makes a domestic solution nearly impossible. In her view, any settlement must be international in nature and supervised by the United Nations, rather than shaped by the competing interests of individual states. She criticizes foreign interference from countries including Egypt, Turkey, and the United Arab Emirates, saying their support for different armed factions — through weapons, ammunition, military vehicles, and other materiel — has prolonged the conflict. She notes that such interference violates UN Security Council Resolution 1973, which imposes a full arms embargo on Libya, as well as the commitments made at the Berlin Conference in January 2020, where participants pledged not to interfere in Libya’s internal affairs. Omar also identifies corruption as a central obstacle to peace. She says corruption is widespread across Libyan institutions and fuels the conflict because militias and armed groups compete for control of state resources and public funds. She urges the international community to use the UN Convention Against Corruption as a tool to combat these abuses through international cooperation, information sharing, prevention, asset recovery, and anti-money-laundering efforts. In her view, stronger international action under UN auspices could help deter corruption both inside and outside Libya. The third speaker focuses on elections and the role of civil society. This speaker says the international community should pressure all sides — political and military — to begin the electoral process and respect the results. # International Community's Role in Resolving Libya's Political Crisis Libya continues to endure severe political turmoil, now entering its twelfth year of instability following nearly a decade of civil conflict. The country remains fractured, with the UN-backed Interim Prime Minister Abdul Hamid al-Dbeibeh controlling Tripoli and western regions, while General Khalifa Haftar dominates the east. Despite sustained UN mediation efforts, meaningful progress toward resolution has remained elusive. The fundamental consequence of this prolonged deadlock is that ordinary Libyans have been denied their basic democratic right to freely elect their representatives through legitimate elections. To address this crisis, the Atlantic Council's North Africa Program has partnered with Lawyers for Libya Justice to amplify civil society voices and highlight pathways toward establishing a rights-based democracy. Three Libyan civil society representatives offered distinct perspectives on how the international community can constructively intervene. ## The Challenge of International Coordination One civil society representative emphasized that an international solution is problematic given the world's fragmented approach to Libya. The international community remains deeply divided and politicized, with decision-maker priorities shifting based on circumstances. Since Russia's invasion of Ukraine, Libya has been deprioritized on the global agenda, despite its thirteen-year conflict. This contrasts sharply with the swift international response to Ukraine, which has generated UN resolutions, sanctions, and ICC arrest warrants within a single year. However, this representative noted that targeted international action can prove effective. When the ICC issued an arrest warrant for Mahmoud al-Warfali, a former Libyan general accused of war crimes, observable improvements occurred: militia leaders disappeared, mass execution videos ceased circulating, and Haftar's forces became noticeably anxious. This single action demonstrably saved lives, illustrating that decisive international intervention can yield significant results. ## Prioritizing Accountability and Transitional Justice Ali Alaspli, president of Libya Crimes Watch, stressed that accountability and redress represent essential first steps toward any sustainable solution. Without these foundations, meaningful progress remains impossible. He urged the international community to prioritize Libya and pursue concrete measures including ending human rights violations, strengthening accountability mechanisms, dismantling impunity, restoring the judicial system, and establishing independent courts for prosecuting those responsible for atrocities. Transitional justice and victim redress must precede any political settlement. ## Enforcing International Agreements and Combating Corruption Fatima Omar, a Lawyers for Libya Justice partner and human rights advocate, argued that given Libya's domestic deadlock, solutions must be internationally overseen through the United Nations rather than determined by individual state interests. She highlighted how foreign interference from Egypt, Turkey, the United Arab Emirates, and others has exacerbated the crisis by supplying warring parties with weapons and military equipment, directly violating UN Security Council Resolution 1973 and the Berlin Conference Conclusions. Omar emphasized that combating widespread institutional corruption should become a priority. Militias and political factions are fighting primarily for control over state resources and public funds. The UN Convention Against Corruption provides mechanisms for international cooperation, information sharing, preventative measures, asset recovery, and money laundering prosecution that could effectively deter corruption if states strengthened their efforts. ## Strengthening Civil Society Participation Another representative advocated for pressuring all conflict parties to initiate elections and respect results. Critically, any political agreement must include provisions guaranteeing civil society genuine participation in dialogue processes aimed at political solutions. The representative highlighted a troubling deterioration in civil society conditions. Civil society actors increasingly face serious accusations including spreading moral deviance or spying for foreign powers, making their work increasingly dangerous. The international community must guarantee civil society representation in political dialogue meetings, strengthen and protect civil society through future agreements, and establish direct communication mechanisms between civil society and authorities regarding abuses. ## Conclusion These civil society representatives collectively emphasized that international support should not consist of temporary, ad hoc projects but rather strategic, long-term, cohesive plans. Through coordinated enforcement of existing international agreements, prioritization of accountability mechanisms, anti-corruption efforts, and genuine civil society inclusion, the international community can meaningfully contribute to resolving Libya's prolonged political crisis and supporting democratic development.

Chhattisgarh’s Economic Offences Wing (EOW) has registered a case against former chief minister’s principal secretary Aman Singh and his wife Yasmin Singh for allegedly accumulating disproportionate assets. The FIR was filed on Tuesday under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988, and IPC section 120B (criminal conspiracy), following a complaint lodged in November by Raipur-based RTI activist Uchit Sharma. According to an EOW official, the probe found that the couple had assets beyond their known sources of income, including immovable properties in Raipur and Durg in Chhattisgarh, as well as in Bhopal and Delhi. The officer also alleged that Aman Singh created shell companies that were used for money laundering. Yasmin Singh was said to have been appointed as Director of the Communication and Capacity Development Unit (CCDU) in the Rural Development Department in violation of government norms. Aman Singh, a former Indian Revenue Service officer, joined Raman Singh’s government on deputation in 2004, resigned from the IRS in 2010, and continued on contract during the BJP’s 15-year rule in Chhattisgarh. Yasmin Singh also worked on contract with state departments from 2005 to 2018. Both resigned after the Congress came to power in 2018. Aman Singh has denied the allegations, calling them a “political witch-hunt,” and has challenged the probe in the Chhattisgarh High Court. The EOW told the court on Wednesday that an FIR had been registered.

A high-profile dispute involving businessman Aravind Venkatesh Reddy (AVR Reddy) and a Kannada film actress has escalated after private photos, intimate MMS clips, and financial documents allegedly linked to the pair went viral on social media. The case, which has drawn major attention in the Sandalwood industry since late 2025, first surfaced publicly after Reddy was arrested at Kempegowda International Airport in November 2025. The controversy centers on conflicting accounts of a relationship that reportedly began at a cricket event in Sri Lanka in 2021. The actress, a former Bigg Boss contestant, has accused Reddy of stalking, sexual harassment, blackmail, and threatening her family after she tried to end the relationship. In her police complaint, she alleged that he morphed her photos to pressure her and said the harassment pushed her to attempt suicide. Reddy has strongly denied the allegations, insisting the relationship was consensual and describing it as a live-in arrangement. He has accused the actress of being a “serial fraudster” and claims she deceived him and other men for money. According to him, he spent more than ₹3 crore on her, including buying a luxury car. Việt Nam is moving toward creating a regulated digital asset exchange market, with officials and industry leaders saying trust, credibility and clear rules are essential if the country is to turn a fragmented trading scene into a competitive financial hub. The push comes amid strong domestic demand: more than 17 million Vietnamese are said to hold digital assets, and blockchain-related investment inflows reached over US$105 billion in 2023-24, a figure described as only “the tip of the iceberg.” Despite this activity, Việt Nam has yet to have a digital asset exchange that is legally recognised, widely trusted or transparent enough to fully support the market’s growth. A key turning point came with the approval of the Law on Digital Technology Industry, which is set to take effect on January 1, 2026. The law lays the groundwork for piloting digital asset exchanges as part of Việt Nam’s broader plan to build an international financial centre. Under this framework, the Ministry of Finance is drafting regulations that would license multiple exchanges. Analysts say this could legitimise a fast-growing investment channel, increase tax revenue, attract foreign capital and create new funding opportunities for technology start-ups. Phan Đức Trung, president of the Vietnam Blockchain and Digital Asset Association, said he expects about five domestic exchanges to be licensed in the pilot phase. He said these exchanges may connect with international markets to improve liquidity and competitiveness, and could support trading in major cryptocurrencies such as Bitcoin and Ethereum. At a talk show in HCM City on August 21, Trần Xuân Tiến, general secretary of the HCM City Blockchain Association, said the lack of a legal framework has long held the sector back. He argued that a clear legal environment would strengthen investor confidence and make the market more transparent. However, he warned that Việt Nam is in a race against time and could fall behind if exchanges are not opened within the next one to two years. At the same time, he cautioned that speed should not come at the expense of safety. He recommended building domestic exchanges to manage liquidity and data, while allowing international platforms to participate for competition and knowledge sharing. He cited models in Dubai, Singapore and South Korea, where bank-linked transaction accounts help improve transparency. Nguyễn Thế Vinh, CEO of Ninety Eight, said blockchain offers low-cost transactions, high liquidity and global connectivity. He argued that if Việt Nam develops the sector properly, it could attract foreign capital and build a fintech ecosystem comparable to global leaders. He also said domestic capability is important, but cooperation with major international platforms will be needed to tap their infrastructure and expertise. His message: act quickly, because the opportunity could disappear if delayed. Industry representatives stressed that transparency and investor protection must come first. Huỳnh Quốc Nam of OKX Global pointed to the collapse of a major global exchange as a warning, saying it failed because of misuse of customer assets. He called for exchanges to disclose trading volume and liquidity data, provide asset guarantees, and strengthen protections such as investor insurance, cybersecurity teams and strict know-your-customer checks to reduce fraud and money laundering. He also said Việt Nam should expand beyond basic trading into derivatives and margin products, which dominate global crypto markets, and test them in a sandbox environment. Lawyer Đào Tiến Phong of Investpush said regulators should impose strict licensing standards on virtual asset service providers, including requirements for custody, account guarantees, minimum capital and insurance. He said licensed exchanges should have a legal entity and physical presence in Việt Nam, and that personal data protection law will be important for safeguarding investors. He also supported allowing international exchanges to operate domestically while nurturing local platforms. The Việt Nam Blockchain Association said licensed exchanges could eventually offer up to 50 cryptocurrencies, including Bitcoin, Ethereum, USDT and USDC. The draft decree for the pilot is expected to be finalised later this month.

Thai cyber police have arrested seven Chinese nationals in Bangkok in a major crackdown on crypto fraud and money laundering under a “Trust No One” operation. The Cyber Crime Investigation Bureau (CCIB) first raided six suspected locations in the Sri Nakarin area, where officers detained two suspects: 31-year-old Xao Xian Su and 25-year-old Qi Yi Yee. Police said the pair used fake social media identities to lure victims into fraudulent crypto investment schemes, causing losses of more than 10 billion baht worldwide, including about 2.5 billion baht in Thailand. Investigators then expanded the probe and found more members of the gang still active. They later determined that other suspects were handling the laundering of the scam proceeds by converting the money into luxury assets in Thailand. In a second wave of raids, police searched 25 locations across Bangkok and arrested three more Chinese nationals: 54-year-old Zhang Han Lin, 29-year-old Zhou Lu, and Liu Jiayu. Zhang was reportedly wanted by Chinese authorities. Two were detained at a luxury hotel in Rama 9, while another was arrested in Soi Sukhumvit 101. Police seized 4 million baht in cash, condominium deeds, luxury cars, a bank account, a tablet, designer bags, and fake passports. Authorities said assets worth more than 600 million baht will be returned to victims.

# Summary Thai authorities conducted "Operation Trust No One" to combat cryptocurrency fraud, successfully arresting seven Chinese nationals in Bangkok. Initial raids in the Sri Nakarin neighborhood resulted in the arrest of two suspects, Xao Xian Su (31) and Qi Yi Yee (25), who used fake social media profiles to perpetrate investment scams. The scheme caused over 10 billion baht in global damages, with 2.5 billion baht within Thailand. Further investigation revealed additional gang members involved in money laundering, converting fraudulent proceeds into Thai luxury properties. Police conducted 25 raids across Bangkok, apprehending three more suspects: Zhang Han Lin (54), Zhou Lu (29), and Liu Jiayu. Zhang Han Lin faced an international arrest warrant from Chinese authorities. Officers recovered approximately 4 million baht in cash, three luxury condominiums valued at 44 million baht, luxury vehicles, fake passports, and other assets totaling over 600 million baht. Authorities plan to return all seized assets to victims both domestically and internationally.

JoAnn Pinkerton, a gynecologist and director of midlife health at the University of Virginia Medical Center, says menopause is still surrounded by a “don’t ask, don’t tell” stigma that leaves many women struggling unnecessarily. Speaking at a recent health briefing, Pinkerton said the biggest problem she sees is women “suffering in silence” after their concerns are dismissed or not fully heard by providers. At UVa, she said, clinicians try to listen carefully to determine whether the issue is bleeding, depression, relationship strain or another concern connected to midlife hormonal change. Pinkerton, who is also executive director emeritus of the North American Menopause Society, emphasized that it is important to distinguish between perimenopause and menopause. Perimenopause is the transitional period leading up to menopause, when the ovaries gradually produce fewer hormones and fewer eggs. Menopause itself is defined as 12 months without a menstrual period, assuming the woman is not pregnant. On average, women go through perimenopause and menopause between ages 45 and 55, though the timing and duration vary widely. She said the most common symptoms are hot flashes, night sweats and vaginal dryness. Hot flashes, also called vasomotor symptoms, are especially common: about 80% of women experience them, and some women have seven or more in a single day. Only about a quarter of those affected seek treatment, Pinkerton said. Treatment options have expanded significantly. Pinkerton contrasted today’s care with older advice that amounted to little more than using a fan or cold washcloth. She said menopausal hormone therapy is now the most effective treatment for hot flashes and can also improve sleep, mood swings, fatigue, bone aches, vaginal health and heart health. It is particularly important for women who enter menopause early, such as those whose ovaries are removed before age 40, because hormone therapy can help prevent major health problems linked to early loss of ovarian function. Pinkerton said the future of treatment looks promising because women now have several hormone therapy options, including FDA-approved identical hormones. These therapies can be delivered in multiple forms — oral, transdermal or vaginal — allowing treatment to be tailored to a woman’s health risks and benefits. UVa Medical Center is also studying a new drug, similar to neurokinin receptor antagonists, that targets brain circuits affected when estrogen levels drop during menopause. The medication is under FDA review and is designed to reduce the frequency and severity of hot flashes by dampening the relevant brain center. Pinkerton said early clinical trials have already shown benefits for hot flashes, night sweats, sleep and mood swings. For women who prefer not to use hormones, UVa also offers nonhormonal alternatives, including an FDA-approved low-dose paroxetine salt and other antidepressants. Pinkerton noted that menopause involves more than the three classic symptoms. Women may also experience loss of sex drive, sleep problems, increased belly fat, changes in breast size and shape, heart palpitations and brain fog. She said one of the most common concerns she sees at UVa’s Midlife Health and Gynecologic Specialties clinic is pain during sex, often after other symptoms have improved. In those cases, she urged women to seek help because UVa offers local vaginal treatments to address estrogen loss in the vagina. The clinic provides creams, tablets and ring suppositories, along with pelvic floor therapy and gynecology specialists. Pinkerton said the Midlife Health Center includes a credentialed menopause specialist and works closely with other departments, including mammography, bone specialists for osteoporosis care, and women’s health psychiatry for mood-related issues. She noted that depression can worsen during menopause. Pinkerton also warned that early menopause symptoms can resemble premenstrual syndrome, which may cause women to overlook the transition at first. Perimenopause can begin with subtle signs such as occasional missed periods before symptoms intensify over time. She encouraged women not to suffer in silence and recommended menopause.org as a resource for reliable information and for finding specialists by ZIP code.

The military-backed Union Solidarity and Development Party (USDP) used a Saturday campaign speech to urge voters to back it in Myanmar’s Nov. 3 by-elections, framing the contest as a battle to protect national sovereignty and territory. Speaking on state television and radio, USDP Secretary U Pike Htwe warned against “foreign intervention” and asked voters to support the party to ensure the country’s “perpetuation.” He said the party’s top priority was the “national interest” and vowed it would prevent “territorial loss” and “bullying from foreign countries.” The USDP, campaigning under the slogan “Time to Think,” has sharply criticized the government for including foreign experts on ad hoc bodies dealing with the crisis in Rakhine State, arguing that such involvement could threaten national security. The party has also previously warned that the Rakhine conflict could lead to territorial loss and accused the government of failing to defend the military’s operations there, which the United Nations and the United States have described as ethnic cleansing. The party has a controversial history. It was the political home of many retired military generals, came to power in the disputed 2010 elections, and was then heavily defeated by Aung San Suu Kyi’s National League for Democracy (NLD) in 2015. Some USDP figures have since been linked to embezzlement scandals from its time in office. In his speech, U Pike Htwe said the party would ensure Myanmar did “not lose an inch of land,” protect constitutional rights, and bring the peace process it began while in government to a successful conclusion. He also said the USDP had worked to develop politics, the economy, society, peace, the rule of law, and sovereignty while in power. Critics dismissed the messaging as nationalist scare tactics. Human rights activist Ko Moe Thway said the party’s talk of “territorial loss” and sovereignty was a recurring propaganda strategy. Political analyst U Yan Myo Thein argued that real peace and prosperity would require constitutional reform and a democratic federal union, but said the USDP was unlikely to lead such efforts. Thirteen national and regional parliamentary seats are being contested, with 69 candidates from 24 parties registered, including seven independents. The USDP is running in 10 seats, while the NLD is contesting all 13. U Pike Htwe urged voters to judge candidates by their qualifications and records, but analysts said even dissatisfied NLD supporters were unlikely to shift their votes to the USDP.

Prime Minister Hun Sen said on Saturday that Cambodia will bar online gambling from next year, arguing that the activity brings more harm than benefit to the country’s economy and security. Speaking at the opening of the 8th Sea Festival in Kampot province, he said the government’s goal is to eliminate gambling altogether. Hun Sen warned that continued reliance on online gambling could expose Cambodia to money laundering, organised crime and even terrorism financing. He said the country should not become a haven for criminal groups or illicit financial flows, and insisted that national security would be compromised if online gambling remained a major economic driver. According to him, Cambodia could lose major investors if the country became associated with criminal activity and money laundering, while legitimate investors would be more likely to stay if gambling were removed. The prime minister said he had heard criticism that the ban would hurt the real estate and construction sectors, but dismissed the idea that these industries should exist to support online gambling operations. He said the government had already acted in August by issuing a circular instructing ministries to stop granting licences for online gambling and to block renewals of existing licences. That decision, he said, followed “careful and extensive analysis.” Hun Sen also addressed concerns about the growing number of Chinese nationals in Cambodia, noting that some people worried the ban would force them to leave. He framed the issue as a choice between tolerating online gambling and protecting Cambodia’s sovereignty and safety. He added that gambling mainly benefits property owners who rent out buildings for gambling businesses, and urged them to find other uses for their properties. In his view, online gambling is not a sustainable source of national income and could lead to further criminal problems. Kim Heang, president of Keller Williams Cambodia, supported the ban. He said the real estate sector would feel short-term pain, including possible effects on hotels, casinos, guesthouses, staff and tax revenue, but argued that the long-term benefits would be greater. He said the policy would help prevent money laundering, anarchy, extortion and drug-related activity, and described online gambling as a “bubble” that would eventually burst.

Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi has moved quickly to congratulate US President-elect Joe Biden, signaling that New Delhi wants to preserve warm ties with Washington as Donald Trump prepares to leave office. The two leaders spoke by phone for the first time after Biden’s election victory, and Modi’s office also highlighted old photographs of the two men embracing in 2014 and 2016. Indian media has picked up on the idea of a long-running personal rapport between Modi and Biden, framing it as a possible “bromance” that could help keep the bilateral relationship on track. The gestures matter because the United States is India’s largest trading partner, and Modi’s government wants to avoid any disruption in relations after four years in which Trump and Modi appeared unusually close. Critics in India accused Modi of straying from diplomatic convention by seeming to favor Trump’s reelection, especially after the “Howdy Modi!” rally in Houston last year and the “Namaste Trump” event in Gujarat in February, where the two leaders appeared together on stage. Still, analysts quoted in the article argue that despite the visible camaraderie between Modi and Trump, a Biden presidency could actually be more advantageous for India, especially economically. The key difference, they say, is that Biden’s worldview is less focused on Trump’s “America First” approach and more open to using trade as part of a broader effort to rebuild alliances and stabilize global negotiations. That could mean a less confrontational tone and, potentially, a rollback of some tariffs that the Trump administration imposed on Indian goods. Biden could also restore India’s access to the Generalized System of Preferences, a trade program that had helped Indian exports. Such moves would be seen in New Delhi as a way to rebuild trust and improve diplomatic ties. But the article stresses that a friendlier tone does not mean trade disputes will disappear. India still maintains tariff and non-tariff barriers that frustrate American businesses, and these issues have persisted across administrations. Kashish Parpiani of the Observer Research Foundation said Biden would know these problems well and would continue to push India on them, but in a quieter, less public way than Trump did. In other words, the pressure may remain, even if the rhetoric changes. A major bilateral free trade agreement is unlikely to be an early priority for Biden, according to several analysts, because the new administration will be dealing with the economic damage caused by COVID-19 in the United States. Rupa Chanda of the Indian Institute of Management Bangalore said Biden would have to focus first on domestic unemployment and the concerns of labor unions. Amitendu Palit of the National University of Singapore went further, suggesting that a bilateral deal may not happen at all. Instead, he said, the Biden administration might try to revive a broader regional framework, possibly by renegotiating the Trans-Pacific Partnership to include India. Democrats have traditionally preferred multilateral trade arrangements over bilateral ones. The article explains the shifting regional trade landscape by contrasting the old TPP with newer agreements. The TPP had been a central part of Barack Obama’s “pivot to Asia,” designed as a 12-member pact that excluded China. Trump withdrew the US from it, and the agreement collapsed as a result. Meanwhile, China and 14 other Asia-Pacific countries recently signed the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership, or RCEP, which does not include either the US or India. India withdrew from RCEP last year, fearing that cheap imports from China and other members would hurt domestic producers. A successor to the TPP, the Comprehensive and Progressive Trans-Pacific Partnership, or CPTPP, could potentially offer both strategic and economic advantages to the US and India. Biden has not said whether he would rejoin it, but Palit argued that the pact could be reimagined as an anti-China economic bloc in the Indo-Pacific. That said, analysts remain divided over whether India would actually want to join such a multilateral arrangement. Priyanka Kishore of Oxford Economics said the Modi government has generally been reluctant to enter large trade pacts and prefers bilateral deals that it believes will better protect Indian manufacturers. Even if India joins a wider trade framework, some barriers are likely to remain. Access to India’s agricultural and dairy markets has long been one of the most contentious issues in trade talks. New Delhi is wary of upsetting small, independent farmers, who are politically influential, and it has also resisted US dairy imports on religious and cultural grounds because American cattle are fed blood-meal, a protein supplement derived from slaughtered animals. Kripalani of ORF noted that India is already close to self-sufficiency in dairy and that foreign companies would face extra certification requirements that would make their products too costly for Indian consumers. Such concerns could also trigger objections from other potential CPTPP members, including Australia and New Zealand. Still, Palit argued that exceptions and workarounds are common in multilateral trade deals and that India could benefit if access for US agricultural firms leads to investment in food processing, storage, and logistics. He pointed to India’s recent agricultural reforms as evidence that the country is trying to position itself as a regional export hub. In his view, allowing US companies into these sectors could help India attract capital and make any eventual trade deal easier to defend domestically. Another area where a Biden administration could help is digital trade. India currently requires companies handling sensitive consumer data to store and process that data within the country, a policy that creates complications for US technology firms such as Google and Amazon, as well as payment providers like Visa and Mastercard. The US trade representative had already criticized India’s rules in 2019 as “onerous” and warned that the country’s e-commerce policy could threaten the digital economy. Malachy Nugent of the US-India Strategic Partnership Forum said Biden would probably not reverse course entirely, but might prefer a multilateral approach that brings developed and emerging economies together to settle the issue. He also said data localization is inefficient and creates risks for consumers, including fraud and criminal misuse. The article also suggests that Biden’s return to global climate leadership could benefit India. As one of the countries most vulnerable to climate change, India stands to gain from renewed international efforts to reduce emissions. Biden has promised to rejoin the Paris climate accord and roll back Trump-era deregulation, which could revive global momentum on climate action. Chanda said this could encourage more investment in renewable energy and green technology in India, particularly from US companies, something that was less likely under Trump. Finally, the article notes that Biden’s handling of the COVID-19 pandemic may have indirect economic benefits for India. Nugent said global economies will not recover until the pandemic is under control, and a US administration that takes the virus more seriously could help restore confidence worldwide. Because the US remains a major engine of the global economy, stronger American performance would likely support India’s own recovery as well.

The article argues that Japan can no longer continue financing the United States the way it has for decades, and that this shift will make borrowing more expensive for Americans, from mortgages to credit cards to government debt. For roughly 40 years, the article says, the U.S. and Japan operated under a mutually convenient but unsustainable system. Japan exported goods to Americans, accumulated dollars, and then recycled those dollars into U.S. Treasury bonds. That arrangement helped keep U.S. borrowing costs low and allowed Americans to live beyond their means while Japan effectively financed the habit. The piece describes Japan as America’s “favorite ATM” and says the country is now no longer willing or able to keep playing that role. The immediate trigger for concern is a sharp rise in Japanese government bond yields. For years, Japanese bonds paid little or nothing, sometimes even negative returns, which pushed investors to look abroad. Now, for the first time in a long while, Japanese investors can earn meaningful returns at home. That change matters because Japan holds about $1.2 trillion in U.S. government debt.
