Over the past six years, 168 employees at South Korean banks and other financial firms embezzled a combined 178.92 billion won, or about $122.21 million, according to data from the Financial Supervisory Service (FSS). The stolen sums rose sharply from 5.67 billion won in 2018 to 15.69 billion won in 2021, then jumped to 82.76 billion won in 2022 before easing to 64.26 billion won last year. Despite the scale of the losses, only 17.45 billion won, or 9.8 percent, has been recovered. This year alone, 11 officials were caught stealing 1.51 billion won, with just 6.7 percent retrieved. The figures have intensified criticism of weak internal controls, especially after a Woori Bank employee was arrested for allegedly embezzling about 10 billion won. The FSS is now considering a law to make CEOs accountable for such crimes.

Japan has passed a law placing virtual currency exchanges under government regulation, following the fallout from the MtGox Bitcoin collapse and a major embezzlement scandal. The Tokyo-based exchange, once one of the world’s largest Bitcoin platforms and said to handle about 80% of global Bitcoin transactions, collapsed in 2014 after the suspected theft of nearly half a billion dollars’ worth of digital currency. MtGox later admitted that 850,000 coins, worth about US$480 million at the time, had vanished from its digital vaults, triggering bankruptcy protection and anger among investors. Under the new legislation, approved late Wednesday, all “virtual currency” exchanges must register with Japan’s Financial Services Agency. The law defines virtual currency as something with an “asset-like nature” that can be used to buy goods and services. Exchanges must now verify the identities of customers opening accounts. Japan’s Financial Services Agency said the measure is intended to address money-laundering risks and protect users. The move follows criticism that virtual currencies’ anonymity and weak oversight make them attractive to criminals. It also brings Japan in line with other G7 countries, which have either introduced or are considering similar rules after supporting “appropriate regulation” of virtual currencies in 2015. The MtGox case has remained a difficult one for Japanese authorities, who previously lacked laws specifically covering digital money. Prosecutors charged MtGox’s French-born head, Mark Karpeles, with embezzlement last year amid fraud allegations. He later said he had found about 200,000 of the missing coins in a “cold wallet.” Investors have urged court-appointed administrators to release the company’s data so experts can help determine what happened.

The new law, passed by Japanese lawmakers, requires all virtual currency exchanges to register with the Financial Services Agency and verify customer identities. The collapse left numerous angry investors demanding answers. The case proved challenging for Japanese authorities, as the country lacked specific digital currency regulations. Investors have urged court-appointed administrators to publicize MtGox's data for expert analysis. Japan's regulatory move aligns with other G7 nations, which have introduced or are developing similar legislation after expressing support for virtual currency regulation at a 2015 meeting. Critics argue that cryptocurrency's anonymity and lack of regulation make it attractive for criminal activities, while supporters contend virtual currencies offer efficient and anonymous fund transfers.

CryptoCloud, a cryptocurrency payment gateway based in Warsaw, Poland, announced a major platform update on May 21, 2024, aimed at making crypto payments faster, simpler, and more secure for businesses. The company said the changes are part of its broader effort to help merchants integrate cryptocurrency payments smoothly and take advantage of digital assets without sacrificing performance or security. One of the headline improvements is faster transaction confirmation for stablecoins USDT, USDC, and TUSD on the Tron network. CryptoCloud said it has introduced a search algorithm that speeds up confirmations while maintaining network security. As a result, these transactions are now confirmed in under a minute, which the company says should reduce checkout friction and cut down on customer support requests about pending payments. CryptoCloud also added payment instruction templates to its documentation to make crypto checkout easier for customers unfamiliar with digital currencies. Merchants can place these ready-made instructions on their websites or checkout pages to guide users through the payment process. The company says this should improve user experience and increase conversion rates, especially among first-time crypto users. To address price volatility, CryptoCloud introduced automatic conversion of incoming Bitcoin and Litecoin payments into USDT. This feature is designed to protect merchants from market swings by converting funds into a dollar-pegged stablecoin. The platform chooses the most favorable exchange rate from a network of more than 10 licensed operators, and merchants can enable the feature directly in project settings without extra configuration. The update also includes static wallets for businesses that handle recurring or repeated payments, such as account top-ups. Instead of generating a new invoice each time, customers can pay to a permanent address, and funds are credited immediately after an API response, streamlining the payment flow. On the security side, CryptoCloud added an AML transaction check to help merchants identify and stop high-risk transactions. The automated system scans each payment for signs of fraud or money laundering and can help businesses avoid exchange account suspensions. Like the other new tools, it can be turned on in project settings without changing the existing integration. Finally, the company released a guide for adding branded payment icons to websites. These icons signal that a merchant accepts cryptocurrency and are intended to attract crypto-friendly customers while strengthening brand recognition. Merchants can integrate them using HTML code or by uploading files from a provided archive. CryptoCloud said the update is only the beginning of further platform improvements.

Bavaria’s premier, Markus Söder, said he was “doubly disappointed,” and reports said Chancellor Angela Merkel told her party colleagues that Vienna’s position was “not good.” Austrian Chancellor Sebastian Kurz responded with a pointed line that was predictable in tone and politically effective: “We are not going to follow the German example.” Even Bild, the German tabloid that had often been favorable to Kurz, criticized him, with one editor urging him not to become “a heartless chancellor.” But Vienna bristled at what it saw as Germany singling it out. Austrian officials and commentators noted that Berlin’s energy seemed oddly concentrated on Austria rather than on other EU countries that also declined to take part. Of the EU’s 27 members, only nine agreed to participate in the German-led initiative, along with Switzerland. That made Austria’s treatment seem, from Vienna’s perspective, like another instance of German moralizing. Kurz’s refusal was politically astute, the article argues, because it shifted the debate away from refugees and onto German pressure. In a Europe where many want Berlin to show stronger leadership, the episode also showed how quickly German assertiveness can trigger resistance. More broadly, it revealed the complicated and often tortured relationship between Germans and Austrians, who share language, culture, and history, but have never fully meshed. The article traces this tension back through history. The dream of a Greater Germany, in which Austrians and Germans would be united, faded quickly after it became reality. The disappointment, the article suggests, may have had as much to do with Germans themselves as with Nazism or World War II. The war’s legacy still shapes perceptions: Germany is widely praised for confronting its past, while Austria long clung to the myth that it had been Hitler’s “first victim.” That narrative made Austria a convenient foil for Germans, who are often free to criticize or mock Austrians without provoking much international backlash. Privately, German politicians are said to regard Austrian counterparts with suspicion, sometimes seeing them as trying to “get away with something.” The article notes that this stereotype is not always unfounded, pointing to the Wirecard scandal, in which both main suspects were Austrian. It also recalls 2015, when then-Austrian Chancellor Werner Faymann urged Merkel to help relieve pressure caused by refugees crossing from Hungary into Austria. Merkel agreed and said, “Wir schaffen das” (“We can do it”), but Kurz, then foreign minister, later positioned himself as Merkel’s anti-migration opposite, a move that helped propel him to the chancellorship. Despite the political friction, Austria is deeply dependent on Germany economically. Germans make up more than 35 percent of overnight stays in Austrian tourism, German firms own or dominate major Austrian companies such as Rewe and Siemens, and Germany buys nearly one-third of Austrian exports. That dependence has long fed resentment, often expressed through satire and cultural jokes. The article cites “Die Piefke Saga,” a television miniseries about German tourists in Tyrol, as a classic example of Austrian mockery of Germans. The piece also explores the subtler cultural divide. The two countries are “divided by their common language,” and accents matter. In Germany, Austrian speech can prompt condescension; in Austria, a German accent can provoke quiet resistance. Austrian comedian and author Lisa Eckhart openly jokes about Germans and says Austrians still enjoy that kind of humor. Sports rivalry also fuels national feeling. Austria’s famous 3-2 win over Germany at the 1978 World Cup remains a defining football memory, and Dominic Thiem’s recent U.S. Open victory over Alexander Zverev stirred similar emotions. German indifference is part of the equation too. Germans may find Austrians amusing, but they generally do not think much about them, whereas Austrians often have strong opinions about Germans. One German comedian who moved to Austria said he had not expected that “every Austrian would have an opinion about Germans.” The article says some Germans have even sought business advice on how to navigate Austrian behavior, including reading between the lines, expecting rule-bending, and understanding that politeness can be deceptive. The article ends by noting that the cultural divide has not stopped migration: since 2010, the number of Germans living in Austria has risen by nearly 50 percent to around 200,000, about the same number of Austrians living in Germany. But even as the populations intermingle, old suspicions remain. As Waltz quips in the closing line, Austrians make life easier by being polite — but “they don’t mean it.”

# Germany and Austria: A Complicated Relationship Between Linguistic Cousins Germany and Austria maintain one of Europe's most complex and fraught bilateral relationships, despite sharing a common language and culture. This tension was recently illustrated when German politicians, including Chancellor Angela Merkel, Interior Minister Horst Seehofer, and Bavarian Premier Markus Söder, publicly criticized Austrian Chancellor Sebastian Kurz's refusal to participate in a European initiative to accept refugees stranded on the Greek island of Lesvos. The criticism prompted Kurz to respond defensively: "We are not going to follow the German example." The episode reveals deeper historical and cultural tensions that have defined German-Austrian relations for generations. Though they share linguistic and cultural roots and fought together in two world wars, Germans and Austrians have never truly meshed. Austrian fantasies of living together in "Großdeutschland" (Greater Germany) quickly dissipated once realized, with disappointment stemming less from Nazi ideology than from fundamental differences between the two peoples. The shadow of World War II continues to loom over the relationship. While Germany is regarded as a model for confronting its past, Austria clung for decades to the myth that it was Hitler's "first victim," positioning itself as a counter-example to German accountability. This disparity has created lasting friction, with Germany viewing Austria with suspicion—a sentiment that extends to modern times, as evidenced by the recent Wirecard scandal, where both main suspects were Austrian. A telling historical moment occurred in 2015 when then-Austrian Chancellor Werner Faymann pleaded with Merkel to accept refugees crossing the Hungarian-Austrian border. After Merkel agreed, foreign minister Kurz—now chancellor—repositioned himself as anti-Merkel on migration, a political maneuver that helped propel him to power. This reversal has left lasting resentment in Berlin, with Swiss observers noting that Merkel visibly displays discomfort around Kurz. Austria's economic dependence on Germany fuels quiet resentment that finds expression in dark comedy and cultural productions. Germany drives Austria's tourism industry, accounting for over 35 percent of overnight stays, and owns many of Austria's largest companies and employers, including supermarket giant Rewe and engineering group Siemens. Germany also represents nearly one-third of Austrian exports. This asymmetrical relationship creates an underlying power dynamic that Austrians find both frustrating and inescapable. The cultural divide manifests linguistically and socially. Austrians are as recognizable to Germans as Scots or Australians to English speakers. German accents in Austria trigger quiet resistance rather than the condescension Austrians encounter in Germany. Austrian author and comedian Lisa Eckhart has made German-baiting central to her act, claiming: "They love me as an Austrian because I cultivate what some Austrians have given up on—hatred of the German." This sentiment proves particularly potent in sports, where Austria's 3-2 victory over Germany in the 1978 World Cup remains seminal in Austrian football history. Similarly, Austrian tennis ace Dominic Thiem's recent U.S. Open victory over Germany's Alexander Zverev stirred comparable emotions. The asymmetry in attention is notable: Germans largely ignore Austrians, while Austrians obsess over Germans. German actor Dirk Stermann, who relocated to Austria, observed that he had no opinions about Austrians initially, "but what I didn't anticipate was that every Austrian would have an opinion about Germans." Some Germans feel so confused by hostile reception that a cottage industry has emerged advising German business executives on navigating Austrian mentality. Guides recommend reading between the lines, remembering that Austrians view rule-bending as normal, and understanding that Austrians prioritize jokes and politeness—though, as actor Christoph Waltz notes, "they don't mean it." Despite tensions, Germans increasingly relocate to Austria. Since 2010, the German population there has jumped 50 percent to 200,000, mirroring the approximately 200,000 Austrians living in Germany. The influx of German students in Austrian universities has fueled fears of "Germanization," though Austrians rarely voice such concerns directly to German guests. Ultimately, the refugee controversy exemplifies how German assertiveness, while increasingly necessary for EU leadership, remains fraught with historical baggage and cultural friction that make German-Austrian cooperation perpetually challenging.

Liliane Bettencourt, the billionaire heiress to the L’Oreal cosmetics empire and once the world’s wealthiest woman, has died at age 94, according to a statement from L’Oreal chief executive Jean-Paul Agon. She died in Neuilly, a suburb west of Paris; no further details were given. Bettencourt was the only child of L’Oreal founder Eugene Schueller and inherited about one-third of the company’s shares. Under her lifetime ownership, the Paris-based business grew from a small hair-dye supplier into the world’s largest beauty-products company, with more than 30 brands such as Lancome and Garnier sold in about 140 countries. In 2016, L’Oreal reported revenue of 25.8 billion euros, or about US$27 billion. Bloomberg’s Billionaires Index put Bettencourt’s net worth at US$42.5 billion. Born Liliane Henriette Betsy Schueller on Oct. 21, 1922, in Paris, she lost her mother at age five and later described the loss as leaving “an empty pit nothing could ever fill.” Raised by Dominican nuns, she said her childhood was dominated by a stern, workaholic father. At 15, she was sent to work at one of his factories gluing labels on L’Oreal bottles. Her father’s politics also troubled her: before and during World War II, Eugene Schueller supported the fascist group La Cagoule, which had links to the Nazi regime. After Eugene Schueller’s death in 1957, Bettencourt placed L’Oreal in the hands of his friend Francois Dalle, who led the company until 1984. Later, Lindsay Owen-Jones, who became CEO in 1988, helped transform it into the global giant it is today. Her grandson, Jean-Victor Meyers, joined the board in 2012. Bettencourt’s later years were marked by family conflict and scandal. After her husband, conservative politician Andre Bettencourt, died in 2007, she became embroiled in a legal dispute with her only child, Francoise Bettencourt Meyers, who claimed her mother was mentally unfit and manipulated by her entourage. In 2011, a judge placed Francoise and two grandsons in charge of Bettencourt’s interests. Secret recordings made by a former butler also triggered inquiries into possible illegal campaign financing tied to former President Nicolas Sarkozy’s 2007 election, though charges were later dropped in 2013. Bettencourt also lost money in Bernard Madoff’s Ponzi scheme.

The European Anti-Money Laundering Authority (AMLA), based in Frankfurt, is still in its early build-up phase, and Chair Bruna Szego says the agency is facing the typical difficulties of a startup. Speaking at the Frankfurt Financial Centre Talks, she said AMLA’s immediate priorities are rapid staff growth, the development of IT systems, and a communication strategy for engaging supervisory authorities and the public. She described the process as “flying an airplane while it is still being built,” while stressing that the goal is to avoid failure. Szego moved into her office in Frankfurt’s Messeturm in mid-February, and AMLA officially started work on July 1. The authority currently has 30 employees, but that number is expected to quadruple by the end of the year. By early 2028, AMLA is planned to be fully operational with 430 staff members. Once fully established, AMLA will have two main responsibilities: directly supervising about 40 cross-border financial service providers that pose high money-laundering risks, and coordinating national supervisory authorities across the EU. Among those national bodies are the Financial Intelligence Units (FIUs), which receive suspicious transaction reports from banks and other obliged entities, analyze them, and pass confirmed cases to law-enforcement authorities. Every EU member state must have an FIU. Szego said AMLA is intended to address the fragmented nature of anti-money-laundering efforts in Europe, particularly outside the financial sector, where criminals often exploit weaknesses. The agency is meant to improve coordination, strengthen cooperation between national supervisors and FIUs, and create a more coherent, risk-based system. She emphasized that AMLA will not replace national authorities but connect them. She also noted major differences among FIUs across Europe in staffing, funding, procedures, and institutional setup. Some are part of the police, others of administrations or intelligence services, which complicates information sharing because much of the data is highly sensitive. Despite these obstacles, Szego said AMLA is “on the right track” and should become a cornerstone of Europe’s financial system.

# AMLA: Europe's New Anti-Money Laundering Authority Takes Shape The Anti-Money Laundering Authority (AMLA), a newly established European regulatory body, is rapidly building its operations in Frankfurt under the leadership of Chair Bruna Szego. Officially commencing work on July 1, AMLA aims to strengthen Europe's coordinated response to financial crime. Szego outlined three immediate priorities: recruiting staff, developing IT infrastructure, and establishing communication channels with supervisory authorities and the public. She acknowledged the challenges of building the organization while simultaneously launching operations, comparing it to "flying an airplane while it is still being built." Currently operating with just 30 employees, AMLA plans to expand to approximately 430 staff members by early 2028. The workforce is expected to quadruple by year-end. Szego moved into her office in Frankfurt's Messeturm in mid-February. AMLA's primary responsibilities will include directly supervising approximately 40 cross-border financial service providers with elevated money-laundering risks and coordinating national supervisory authorities. This includes Financial Intelligence Units (FIUs), which operate in all 27 EU member states to analyze suspicious transaction reports from banks and forward confirmed cases to law enforcement. A major challenge lies in Europe's fragmented anti-money-laundering framework. FIUs vary significantly across countries in staffing, resources, operational practices, and institutional structures—some report to police, others to administrative or intelligence agencies. These differences complicate information sharing due to confidentiality concerns. Rather than replacing national authorities, AMLA seeks to connect them into a cohesive, risk-based system. Szego emphasized that both AMLA and financial institutions are essential for Europe's collective defense and maintaining a stable, trustworthy financial system. Despite considerable obstacles, Szego remains optimistic that AMLA will become a cornerstone of the European financial landscape.

Dutch authorities arrested Tornado Cash developer Alexey Pertsev in Amsterdam on Aug. 10, two days after the U.S. Treasury sanctioned the crypto mixing service. The Dutch Fiscal Information and Investigation Service said Pertsev was suspected of “involvement in concealing criminal financial flows and facilitating money laundering,” but authorities have not publicly specified which laws he allegedly broke. The arrest triggered strong backlash from the global crypto and open-source communities. In response, supporters launched a petition and awareness campaign arguing that Pertsev is being punished for publishing open-source software, not for any proven crime. The petition, hosted on Change.org, has surpassed 2,000 signatures, reaching 2,070 at the time of the report. Backers say the case could have a chilling effect on software development, with the petition warning that the accusations “threaten to kill the entire open-source software segment” because developers could be held responsible for how others use their code after it is released. The Dutch agency reportedly told the DeFi Education Fund that developing a tool is not illegal, but that making a tool available could be punishable if it was created specifically to commit criminal acts, such as concealing illicit money flows. Crypto advocates reject that framing, arguing that Tornado Cash was built as open-source technology for legitimate uses, especially privacy on the blockchain. Supporters have also taken the campaign offline and into the public eye. About 50 people protested Pertsev’s arrest in Dam Square in Amsterdam on Aug. 20. Prominent crypto figures, including Aave founder Stani Kulechov, have amplified the effort on Twitter, urging donations and petition signatures. Kulechov said arresting someone for writing privacy-preserving code was “out of line” and warned that the case could make privacy and encryption developers targets. According to the campaign website, Pertsev has not been formally charged and remains in custody on suspicion alone. Under Dutch law, he can reportedly be held for up to 110 days without charges.

# Summary Dutch authorities arrested Alexey Pertsev, a lead developer of Tornado Cash, on August 12 on suspicion of facilitating money laundering through the cryptocurrency mixing service. The arrest came two days after the U.S. Treasury Department sanctioned Tornado Cash. The crypto community has launched a campaign to secure Pertsev's release, with a Change.org petition garnering over 2,000 signatures. Supporters argue that arresting him for creating open-source code threatens the entire open-source software industry and that Tornado Cash was primarily designed for legitimate privacy purposes, not criminal activity. Dutch authorities claim Tornado Cash was created solely for money laundering, though they have not publicly disclosed the specific laws Pertsev allegedly violated. The Fiscal Information and Investigation Service stated that while developing a tool isn't prohibited, making one available that facilitates criminal activity may be punishable. Crypto advocates counter that publishing open-source code should not be criminalized. The petition warns that developers will be discouraged from creating privacy-focused software if they can be held responsible for how others use their tools. Influential figures in the crypto industry, including Aave founder Stani Kulechov, have voiced support for Pertsev, comparing privacy-preserving code to essential encryption technology. Approximately 50 protesters gathered in Amsterdam's Dam Square on August 20 to demonstrate against the arrest. Under Dutch law, Pertsev can be held in custody for up to 110 days without formal charges. He has not yet been charged with any crime and remains under arrest solely on suspicion.

Italian investigators have uncovered what prosecutors describe as a sprawling criminal network in Rome that infiltrated city government, public contracts, and even refugee services, prompting a national scandal and renewed doubts about Italy’s ability to confront corruption. At the center of the case is Massimo Carminati, a reputed mobster known as “The Pirate” and “The Blind One,” who lost an eye in a shootout years ago. In wiretapped conversations, Carminati was heard coaching an associate on how to deal with newly elected municipal officials after Rome’s city elections in 2013. He urged them to ask administrators what they needed, how they could make money, and what jobs the group could do for them—whether digging ditches or erecting billboards—so that no one else would get the work. Investigators say those intercepted conversations, along with many others, helped expose a two-year inquiry that led last week to Carminati’s arrest and the arrest of 36 others. The suspects are accused of using intimidation and corruption to win dozens of lucrative public tenders in the Italian capital. Prosecutors say the group infiltrated contracts for garbage collection, park maintenance, and a wide range of other municipal services. The charges include vote rigging, usury, extortion, and embezzlement. Rome’s chief prosecutor, Giuseppe Pignatone, told Italy’s anti-Mafia commission that more arrests and operations were expected. The scandal has shocked Italians not only because of its scale, but because it appears to have uncovered a new criminal ring at the heart of the capital, involving politicians from across the political spectrum. Prosecutors have dubbed the organization “Mafia Capitale,” comparing it to Italy’s traditional mob groups—the Mafia, Camorra, and ‘Ndrangheta—because of its use of coercion and its ability to penetrate public institutions. Italian newspapers, drawing from a nearly 1,200-page arrest warrant, have described the case in lurid detail and nicknamed it the “Middle-earth investigation,” referencing Tolkien’s fictional world and Carminati’s own “middle-earth theory” of society. In one wiretapped exchange, Carminati described a world divided between the living above and the dead below, with his group operating in the middle. Pignatone interpreted that as meaning Carminati’s organization connected the “world above,” or respectable society and institutions, with the “world below,” the criminal underworld, and served the former through the latter. The investigation also revealed alleged profiteering from Italy’s immigration crisis. Prosecutors say the gang muscled in on immigrant and refugee reception centers and Roma camps, turning a humanitarian emergency into a business. In one recording, Salvatore Buzzi, head of a social cooperative that managed services at reception centers, boasted that the money made from immigrants was more lucrative than drug trafficking. Buzzi claimed the operation was worth about $50 million to the organization. Among those arrested was a senior administrator who sat on the national board overseeing the immigrant emergency. Carminati was already known to law enforcement. He had been convicted years earlier for links to the Nuclei Armati Rivoluzionari, a far-right terrorist group active in the 1970s and 1980s, and to the Banda della Magliana, a notorious Rome gang. Prosecutors say that in this corruption scheme he operated without regard to ideology, profiting through contacts on the left, right, and center. The fallout has been political as well as judicial. Several politicians from different parties have resigned, including Rome’s former right-wing mayor Gianni Alemanno, who led the city from 2008 to 2013, the period during which prosecutors say the network flourished. Alemanno denies wrongdoing. After arrests involving members of his Democratic Party, Prime Minister Matteo Renzi placed the Rome party branch under emergency administration and vowed tougher anti-corruption laws, declaring that the corrupt would pay “until the last penny.” The case has also revived broader concerns about corruption in Italy. Transparency International recently ranked Italy among the worst in Europe for perceived public-sector corruption. Commentators said the Rome scandal exposed not only criminal activity, but also a wider culture of cronyism and the exploitation of public institutions for private gain.

Juventus, Italy’s most decorated soccer club, was handed a 15-point deduction on Friday after an appeal hearing at the Italian soccer federation over false accounting. The punishment could severely damage the club’s hopes of qualifying for Europe next season. Juventus had been third in Serie A, but the penalty drops it into midtable, leaving it 25 points behind league leader Napoli and 12 points outside the Champions League places. The club said it would appeal the ruling to Italy’s highest sports court within the Italian Olympic Committee. The decision came after the federation reviewed documents gathered by Turin prosecutors in an investigation into alleged false bookkeeping. Juventus had originally been cleared by the sports court in April, but the appeal reopened the case. Several former Juventus officials were also punished. Former president Andrea Agnelli and former CEO Maurizio Arrivabene each received two-year bans from soccer activities. The longest suspension, 2½ years, went to former sporting director Fabio Paratici, who is now Tottenham’s managing director. Current Juventus sporting director Federico Cherubini was banned for 16 months, while former player and board member Pavel Nedved received an eight-month ban. In total, bans were issued to nine Juventus staff members or former board members. The sanctions bar them from soccer-related activity in Italy and ask that UEFA and FIFA extend the bans internationally. Federation prosecutor Giuseppe Chiné had sought a nine-point deduction for Juventus, while eight other clubs named in the case — including Sampdoria, Genoa, Parma and Empoli — were all cleared. The ruling follows a turbulent period for Juventus. The club’s entire board resigned in November amid the investigation, and Gianluca Ferrero was named new president on Wednesday to lead a smaller five-member board. On the same day, Agnelli stepped down from his roles in family-linked businesses, including Stellantis and Exor. The penalty comes 17 years after the Calciopoli scandal, when Juventus was relegated to Serie B and stripped of two Serie A titles. Juventus has already been knocked out of the Champions League this season and has faced further scrutiny from UEFA and Italy’s market regulator, CONSOB. Prosecutors have questioned pandemic-era salary arrangements and alleged undisclosed payments, including to Cristiano Ronaldo. In September, Juventus reported a record loss of 254.3 million euros for 2021-22, its fifth straight annual loss. A preliminary hearing in the Turin criminal investigation is set for March.

For decades, Beirut’s Hamra Street symbolized Lebanon’s cosmopolitan identity: a lively boulevard of movie houses, theaters, cafes, luxury shops, and nightlife that drew intellectuals, artists, students, tourists, and political activists. In the 1960s and 1970s, it was widely seen as the elegant heart of the capital, often compared to Paris’s Champs Elysées. Colored holiday lights, Santa Clauses handing out candy, packed cafes, and performances by major Arab and international stars helped define its golden age. Even during Lebanon’s civil war, Hamra remained important, though it was scarred by violence, assassinations, militias, and the march of invading Israeli troops in 1982. Today, however, the street reflects Lebanon’s broader collapse. Many shops are shuttered, the sidewalks are crowded with impoverished Lebanese and Syrian refugees begging for money, trash accumulates in the corners, and electricity cuts leave streetlights dark. The avenue, once busy late into the night, now feels deserted before midnight, even during holiday periods. Business owners say high rents, soaring generator bills, and the loss of customers have forced many to close. The street’s decline mirrors the country’s economic crisis, which began in October 2019 and has been described by the World Bank as one of the worst financial collapses since the mid-19th century. The article centers on Michel Eid, an 88-year-old music shop owner who has worked on Hamra Street for more than 60 years. From his Tosca Music Shop and Electronic Supplies, Eid has watched the boulevard rise and fall through Lebanon’s postwar history. His store once sold records, clocks, calculators, and watches, but now he says business has fallen by 75% because so few customers remain. Eid says Lebanon has “hit rock bottom” and insists that nothing in the past—including the civil war—was as bad as the current situation. The collapse is rooted in Lebanon’s post-civil war political and economic order. After the war, former militia leaders became the country’s political class and held onto power. According to the article, they presided over an economy that periodically boomed but was effectively a corrupt, unsustainable Ponzi-like system. That system finally broke down in 2019. The Lebanese currency lost most of its value, bank deposits became inaccessible, salaries lost purchasing power, and prices soared in a country heavily dependent on imports. The United Nations estimates that 82% of the population now lives in poverty, and unemployment is around 40%. The crisis was further deepened by the COVID-19 pandemic and the massive 2020 explosion at Beirut’s port, which killed 216 people, wounded thousands, and devastated parts of the capital. Despite the severity of the economic collapse, the political system has remained largely unchanged. The same entrenched leadership continues to dominate and, according to the article, has done little to address the crisis. Basic reforms have been resisted, and negotiations with the International Monetary Fund have made no real progress. The story traces Hamra’s changing identity over time. After the civil war, Beirut’s commercial center shifted to a rebuilt downtown area, but Hamra received a facelift in the early 2000s, when new utility systems were installed and streets were repaved with cobblestones. That helped trigger a revival over the past 15 years. International chains such as Starbucks and Nike opened shops, restaurants expanded, and Syrian refugees fleeing their own civil war opened eateries, sweets shops, and shawarma stands. A new generation of young people, including many drawn by the spirit of the Arab Spring, brought energy back to the area’s bars and cafes. Yet this revival also displaced older landmarks. Famous establishments such as Modca cafe were replaced by banks, Faisal Restaurant gave way to a McDonald’s, and the Piccadilly Theater—once a cultural centerpiece where singer Fayrouz performed—was abandoned and later damaged by fire. Still, Hamra remained a daytime hub because of nearby medical centers and the American University of Beirut. Several longtime Hamra figures describe the street’s decline in personal terms. Hairdresser and clothing shop owner Elie Rbeiz, who has worked there since 1962 and once served wealthy clients including Saudi businessman Adnan Khashoggi, says his sales have plunged, though he remains determined not to give up. Newspaper and book vendor Naim Saleh says his business has been ruined, with foreign magazines now unaffordable for most customers and sales down from 50 books a day in the past to one or two a month. He says the growing number of beggars is a sign of how deep the suffering has become. Eid, too, refuses to leave. He says he will close his shop only when he stops working, and if his sons do not want his 4,500 records, he plans to donate them to the Lebanese National Higher Conservatory of Music. But unlike Rbeiz, he is not optimistic about Hamra’s future. He says the Gulf tourists who once sustained the street’s commerce will not return. Still, he insists that Hamra is inseparable from his life: “Hamra Street is the oxygen that I breathe.”

Lebanon’s caretaker prime minister, Najib Mikati, on Friday appealed to Iran to help secure a cease-fire in the war between Israel and Hezbollah, and appeared to be urging Tehran to press the militant group to accept a deal that could require it to pull back from the Israel-Lebanon border. The appeal came as Ali Larijani, a top adviser to Iran’s supreme leader, Ali Khamenei, visited Lebanon for talks with senior officials. Lebanese officials said an American cease-fire proposal had been passed to Hezbollah, with the aim of ending 13 months of cross-border fighting. Iran is Hezbollah’s main sponsor and has long funded and armed the group. Hezbollah began firing rockets into northern Israel the day after Hamas’ Oct. 7, 2023 attack on Israel triggered the war in Gaza, and exchanges between Israel and Hezbollah have continued since then. The conflict sharply intensified in late September, when Israel escalated its bombardment of Lebanon and said it intended to cripple Hezbollah and stop its attacks on Israeli territory. Lebanon’s Health Ministry says more than 3,400 people have been killed in Lebanon by Israeli fire, and that about 80% of those deaths occurred in the past month. According to Lebanese media, U.S. Ambassador Lisa Johnson delivered a draft cease-fire proposal to Nabih Berri, the Lebanese Parliament speaker, who has been leading negotiations on behalf of Hezbollah. A Lebanese official confirmed that Beirut had received a draft based on U.N. Security Council Resolution 1701, the measure that ended the last Israel-Hezbollah war in 2006. Under that resolution, only the Lebanese army and U.N. peacekeepers are supposed to operate in southern Lebanon, which would mean Hezbollah would have to withdraw from the area. That provision was never fully implemented. Lebanon accuses Israel of violating the same resolution by maintaining a presence in a small disputed border area and carrying out frequent military overflights over Lebanese territory. The Lebanese official did not provide details of the draft, saying only that Israel was insisting on certain guarantees. The U.S. Embassy neither confirmed nor denied the reports. Mikati said after meeting Larijani that Lebanon wanted the war to end and wanted Resolution 1701 implemented “in all its details,” according to a statement from his office. He also said Lebanon wanted Iran to help preserve national unity rather than take sides in domestic Lebanese politics. In recent weeks, Mikati has become more openly critical of Iran’s role in Lebanon. Larijani, after meeting both Mikati and Berri, said his visit was meant to show that Iran would stand with Lebanon’s government and people. When asked whether he was trying to undermine U.S.-led cease-fire efforts, he said Iran was not seeking to sabotage any initiative, but wanted to help solve the problem and would stand by Lebanon “whatever the circumstances.” Meanwhile, Israeli airstrikes continued across Lebanon on Friday. A strike on a home in the southern province of Nabatiyeh killed a mother, father and their three children, according to state media. Three additional strikes in Tyre province killed six people and wounded 32 more. Israeli forces also struck areas near Beirut, including three waves of air raids on buildings in the southern suburbs, known as Dahiyeh. In one earlier strike on the southeastern edge of Beirut, an Associated Press photographer captured a rocket hitting an 11-story residential building in Tayouneh, followed by a large blast that tore away part of the structure. There were no immediate reports of casualties in those Beirut-area strikes. In each case, the Israeli military had warned residents before the attacks, saying it was targeting Hezbollah facilities. Near Baalbek in eastern Lebanon, rescue workers ended their search for survivors after an Israeli strike hit a civil defense center, killing 14 civil defense workers and volunteers. The Israeli military did not immediately explain why that center was targeted. Lebanon’s civil defense is not affiliated with Hezbollah and provides essential rescue and medical services. Israel has broadened its operations in Lebanon while continuing its war in Gaza, saying it aims to destroy Hamas, which is also backed by Iran. On Friday, funerals were held for 11 Palestinians killed in Israeli airstrikes around Deir al-Balah in central Gaza. Two of the dead were children. At the United Nations, the Security Council’s 10 elected members circulated a draft resolution calling for “an immediate, unconditional and permanent cease-fire” in Gaza. Adoption of the measure depends on the United States, Israel’s closest ally, while the other permanent members — Russia, China, Britain and France — are expected to support it or abstain. The war in Gaza began after Palestinian militants attacked Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, killing about 1,200 people, mostly civilians, and taking roughly 250 hostages. Since then, Israel’s bombardment and ground operations have killed more than 43,000 people in Gaza, according to Palestinian health officials, who say more than half the dead are women and children.

A recent article argues that corruption has become entrenched in Turkey under President Recep Tayyip Erdogan’s rule, despite the ruling Justice and Development Party’s early promise to clean up politics and rescue the economy. The piece opens with the scandal involving former Trade Minister Ruhsar Pekcan, who was dismissed in April after it emerged that she had sold anti-COVID sanitizer produced by a company she co-owned with her husband to the ministry she led. A video circulated by investigative journalist Ismail Saymaz showed two people alleged to be Pekcan’s chauffeur and secretary straining the disinfectant through a sieve to remove fungus before rebottling it for sale. The footage quickly went viral and became a top trending topic on Twitter, provoking outrage and disgust. Pekcan has not responded publicly to the allegations. The article says Pekcan’s case is only one example of a wider pattern. In May, opposition lawmakers tried to launch a parliamentary inquiry into claims of nepotism and fraud against her, including allegations that she sold the product to the ministry above market value. That motion was blocked by lawmakers from the AKP and its ally, the far-right Nationalist Action Party. Critics say this reflects a broader culture of impunity. Erdogan and the AKP came to power in 2002 promising to end the longstanding web of corruption linking state officials, business interests, and organized crime, while also stabilizing an economy in crisis. The article notes that the economy is now in worse condition than when the party first took office. Berk Esen, a political scientist at Istanbul’s Sabanci University, is quoted saying corruption has become a defining feature of Turkey’s authoritarian system. He argues that the state still channels contracts, loans, and other benefits to insiders and business cronies, and that this has intensified as Erdogan has concentrated power over the past seven to eight years. According to Esen, the more personalized and authoritarian the regime becomes, the more corruption grows. The article recalls that in the AKP’s first decade, cheap credit and optimism about European Union membership helped drive growth and reduce poverty. But even early on, rumors of corruption circulated, including complaints from foreign investors that bribes were needed to gain access to Erdogan and secure business deals. Around the same time, the government began pressuring the media. The article cites heavy fines imposed on media mogul Aydin Dogan after his outlets reported on graft. Turkey’s standing on corruption has since worsened sharply. Transparency International currently ranks the country 86th out of 180 countries on its Corruption Perception Index, with a score of 40, a drop of 33 places and 10 points over seven years. The article then turns to a new wave of allegations from Sedat Peker, a fugitive organized crime figure broadcasting from Dubai since May. Peker has accused members of Erdogan’s government of crimes ranging from cocaine trafficking and extortion to murder and rape. The revelations have fed public concern about Turkey’s role in international drug flows; former AKP minister Ali Babacan said the country was now known abroad as a “narco state.” Peker has not directly accused Erdogan, but has targeted Interior Minister Suleyman Soylu and others, releasing screenshots, audio recordings, and other material he says is incriminating. In one of his latest Twitter threads, Peker shifted attention toward Erdogan’s inner circle. He alleged that Burhan Kuzu, a late AKP lawmaker and constitutional law professor who helped design the 2017 shift to an executive presidency, used the communications director’s office switchboard at the presidential complex to pressure bureaucrats into granting favors to shady businessmen and underworld figures. Kuzu had already faced prosecution for allegedly helping Iranian heroin trafficker Naji Sharifi Zindashti evade justice and was accused of receiving millions in kickbacks. After Kuzu’s death from COVID-19 in November, his aide Sinan Ciftci claimed in an interview that he had been murdered by having his ventilator disconnected. Ciftci also alleged that Kuzu used Erdogan’s son-in-law, former Economy Minister Berat Albayrak, Vice President Fuat Oktay, and parliament speaker Mustafa Sentop to further his schemes. Peker additionally said Kuzu was vulnerable to blackmail because of his weakness for women. The article says most of these accusations have not been independently verified, and only one case — involving a former Turkish general and the 1996 murder of a journalist in Turkish-occupied Northern Cyprus — has been investigated. By contrast, thousands of government critics have been prosecuted and jailed, according to Ahmet Sik, a lawmaker from the left-wing Turkish Workers’ Party. Journalist Timur Soykan says Erdogan must be aware of the allegations but is staying silent in hopes they will fade, as previous scandals have done. One earlier example was the corruption case tied to jailed businessman Reza Zarrab and an alleged sanctions-busting oil-for-gold scheme. Zarrab later became a witness in the U.S. case against Halkbank, the Turkish state lender accused of laundering money. This time, however, the article suggests public anger may be harder to contain because Turkey’s economy is in deep trouble and elections are due in 2023. Ahmet Sik argues that even if Peker’s claims are incomplete or partly fabricated, many people believe them to be true. In the end, the article says, Erdogan is trapped in a system of corrupt deals that now help sustain his power.

Thousands more have been wounded across both sides. The humanitarian situation in Gaza has deteriorated rapidly. On Wednesday, Gaza's only power station ran out of fuel and shut down, leaving residents dependent on scattered private generators for electricity. The U.N. reported Thursday that 423,000 people—nearly 18 percent of Gaza's population—have been forcibly displaced from their homes, representing a 25 percent increase in just one day. Gaza's only operational crossing with Egypt at Rafah has been rendered inoperable due to airstrikes, preventing the flow of desperately needed aid and fuel. A devastating strike Thursday afternoon in the Jabaliya refugee camp destroyed a residential building sheltering families who had fled bombing elsewhere. The al-Shihab family home was packed with relatives seeking shelter from the bombardment. Residents describe the situation as dire, with one neighbor, Khalil Abu Yahia, stating: "We can't flee because anywhere you go, you are bombed. You need a miracle to survive here." Hamas has indicated no willingness to release hostages while Israeli operations continue. In a video released Thursday, civilian Hamas figures defended the group's assault and condemned civilian deaths in Gaza resulting from Israeli airstrikes, though the tone differed markedly from the military wing's earlier triumphant messaging. The conflict has regional implications. Syrian state media reported that Israeli airstrikes Thursday rendered two Syrian international airports inoperable, raising concerns about broader regional escalation. Hamas militants have fired thousands of rockets into Israel in response to the bombardment. Diplomatically, the U.S. and Qatar reached an agreement Thursday that Qatar will not act on any Iranian requests to access $6 billion in unblocked Iranian funds from a recent prisoner exchange, addressing Republican criticism of the Biden administration's Iran deal. Hezbollah, Iran’s most powerful proxy and Lebanon’s dominant Shia militia for four decades, is described as entering one of the weakest periods in its history. The article says that September 2024 marked a dramatic low point when rescue workers recovered the body of Hezbollah leader Hassan Nasrallah from beneath the rubble in Beirut’s southern suburbs. It remains unclear whether he died from the force of Israeli air strikes or suffocated in his underground bunker, but his death exposed how fragile the movement had become. That fragility has deepened in recent weeks as unrest inside Iran, Hezbollah’s patron, and the regime’s harsh response have highlighted Tehran’s own vulnerabilities. Hezbollah’s role has long been to deter Israel and project Iranian power beyond the Islamic Republic’s borders, but now the group is under unprecedented pressure. Its military capacity and finances have both been reduced, and its remaining influence lies mostly in Lebanese politics rather than battlefield strength. The article describes a sharp squeeze on Hezbollah’s funding. One important revenue stream tied to organized crime and narcotics in Venezuela was disrupted after the removal of Nicolás Maduro, whose government had served as a hub for illicit Iranian oil exports, cocaine transit, and money laundering. Under Maduro, Caracas had also been part of a 20-year cooperation arrangement with Iran. After his removal, the United States cracked down on the network, and people who deal with Hezbollah say that money has largely dried up. Other pressures have mounted too. Israeli air strikes on Hezbollah targets continue. The group has lost control of Beirut airport, which had been an important route for moving people, weapons, and money between Lebanon and Iran. Meanwhile, the fall of Bashar al-Assad in Syria in 2024 disrupted another crucial corridor that Hezbollah had used to replenish its arsenal quietly and cheaply. The leadership has also been badly weakened. Even after a ceasefire with Israel, assassinations have continued. In November, Haytham Tabtabai, the commander in charge of rearmament, was killed in Beirut. The surviving leaders are described as old, infirm, and in hiding, avoiding meetings because any gathering could attract Israeli strikes. Politically, Hezbollah’s cover inside Lebanon has eroded. President Joseph Aoun, once cautious as army chief, has openly described weapons outside state control as “a burden,” a clear reference to Hezbollah’s arsenal. The once-taboo subject of disarmament is now discussed openly on television panels, showing how far the political climate has shifted. At the same time, Iran has tightened its grip on the organization. The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps now exercises direct authority over Hezbollah’s military structures. Whatever autonomy the militia once had effectively ended with Nasrallah’s death. Decisions on weapons, strategy, and escalation are now made in Tehran. Yet Hezbollah still retains power inside Lebanon, and resentment toward it is growing even among Shias, its traditional base. In southern Lebanon, villages remain in ruins after the 2024 war with Israel, with little reconstruction completed. The article recounts a case in which a Christian woman received a Hezbollah cheque that bounced at al-Qard al-Hassan, the group’s financial institution. Iran is still paying fighters’ salaries, according to local businessmen and analysts, but it is no longer funding reconstruction or welfare. Tehran’s priority is keeping Hezbollah capable of threatening Israel, not rebuilding Lebanon. Even so, Hezbollah is adapting. It is returning to the decentralized tactics that originally built its power: cells, tunnels, smuggling routes, and guerrilla warfare. It is studying Hamas’s experience in Gaza. The group has largely ceded territory south of the Litani River, allowing the Lebanese army to deploy there, but elsewhere it is consolidating. Since late 2025 it has been retrieving weapons left in Syria, reopening old smuggling routes, and relying more on tunnels in the Bekaa Valley. The article concludes that Hezbollah’s strength now lies in ambiguity: it is neither fully disarming nor openly fighting the state. That ambiguity helps it survive, because direct conflict with the Lebanese army would accelerate its decline. But disarmament would strip Hezbollah of its identity. As one activist says, weapons are the heart of Hezbollah. And as long as Iran survives, many believe Hezbollah will not disarm—though upheaval inside Iran makes its future increasingly uncertain.

# Iran's Most Powerful Proxy Humbled Hezbollah, Iran's dominant proxy militia that has controlled Lebanon for four decades, faces unprecedented challenges following the death of its long-standing leader Hassan Nasrallah in September 2024. Killed in Israeli airstrikes on Beirut's southern suburbs, Nasrallah's death exposed the organization's growing fragility at a moment when its patron Iran itself confronts mounting vulnerabilities. ## Financial Collapse and Military Losses The militia's financial situation has deteriorated dramatically. A primary revenue source—illicit activities conducted through Venezuela under Nicolás Maduro—has evaporated following Maduro's removal and subsequent American crackdowns. Venezuela had served as a crucial hub for Iranian oil exports, cocaine trafficking, and money laundering under a 20-year cooperation agreement signed in 2022. Additional military setbacks compound these financial pressures. Israeli airstrikes continue targeting Hezbollah positions. The group has lost control of Beirut airport, previously essential for moving personnel, weapons, and money between Lebanon and Iran. The 2024 fall of Bashar al-Assad in Syria disrupted supply routes that enabled Hezbollah to quietly and cheaply replenish its arsenal. ## Leadership Decimation Hezbollah's leadership has been systematically hollowed out. Beyond Nasrallah's assassination, the November killing of Haytham Tabtabai, the rearmament commander, further weakened the organization. Remaining leaders are aging, infirm, and in hiding, avoiding meetings due to fears of Israeli strikes. This leadership vacuum has forced Tehran to exercise direct control through the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, eliminating the autonomy Hezbollah previously enjoyed. ## Political Erosion in Lebanon The organization's political position within Lebanon has eroded significantly. President Joseph Aoun, formerly the army chief, has openly described weapons outside state control as "a burden" on Lebanon—an unmistakable reference to Hezbollah's arsenal. This represents a dramatic shift, as discussing Hezbollah's disarmament was previously taboo; Lebanese television now openly debates the topic. Resentment is mounting even among Shias, Hezbollah's traditional base. In southern Lebanon, where the group once prided itself on rapid reconstruction, villages remain in ruins following the 2024 war with Israel. The organization's financial institution, al-Qard al-Hassan, has issued bounced checks to Lebanese citizens, while Iran prioritizes maintaining Hezbollah's ability to threaten Israel over funding reconstruction and welfare programs. ## Adaptation and Uncertain Future Despite these weaknesses, Hezbollah remains a formidable domestic force capable of adaptation. The organization is reverting to earlier methods: decentralized cells, tunnels, smuggling routes, and guerrilla warfare. It has largely ceded territory south of the Litani River to the Lebanese army while consolidating elsewhere, recovering abandoned Syrian weapons and reactivating old smuggling paths through the Bekaa Valley. Hezbollah maintains ambiguous political positioning—neither fully disarming nor directly confronting the Lebanese state. This vagueness provides strategic advantage, as open conflict with the armed forces would accelerate its decline. However, the organization faces an existential dilemma: disarming would eliminate its raison d'être and claim to exceptionalism as a political party. Ultimately, Hezbollah's future remains uncertain. As long as Iran's regime survives, the militia likely will not disarm. Yet Iran's own convulsions suggest the militia's future grows increasingly precarious, regardless of its tactical adaptations.

Turkish police carried out “Cage-31” operations in 13 provinces, including Ankara, Istanbul, Izmir and Antalya, under the coordination of the Security Intelligence Directorate, Anti-Smuggling and Organized Crime Directorate, and the Interpol-Europol Department. Interior Minister Ali Yerlikaya said 42 people wanted on Interpol red notices or emergency notices were detained. The notices had been issued by Germany, Azerbaijan, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Iran, Sweden, Finland, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Egypt, Russia, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan. Authorities said the suspects were wanted for crimes including organized crime membership, illegal arms trafficking, drug trafficking, murder, migrant smuggling, fraud, robbery, theft, document forgery and tax evasion. Yerlikaya added that 114 red-notice fugitives have been captured in Cage operations since the start of the year.

# Summary Turkish authorities arrested 42 people wanted by Interpol across 13 cities during "Cage-31" operations coordinated by the General Directorate of Security Intelligence, Anti-Smuggling and Organized Crime Directorate, and Interpol-Europol Department. The suspects were wanted by 12 countries including Germany, Russia, Iran, and Azerbaijan for serious crimes including drug trafficking, illegal arms dealing, murder, human smuggling, fraud, robbery, and document forgery. Interior Minister Ali Yerlikaya announced that 114 red-notice wanted individuals have been apprehended since the year's beginning through these operations. Officials emphasized the state's commitment to combating terrorism, organized crime, and criminal activities.

A 64-year-old Manitowoc woman, Cherie Campion, was sentenced to 18 months in prison after pleading guilty in September to money laundering tied to a scheme that cost two companies more than $10 million. Prosecutors said she used a temporary staffing agency to submit thousands of fraudulent invoices, causing losses of $5 million and $5.38 million. Judge Lynn Adelman ordered her to pay over $10 million in restitution and noted her years of deception, including fake records, a false persona and a voice modulator. She will also serve three years of supervised release.

# Summary A 64-year-old Manitowoc woman, Cherie Campion, was sentenced to 18 months in prison for money laundering involving over $10 million. She pleaded guilty in September after submitting thousands of fraudulent invoices through a temporary staffing agency, causing two companies losses of $5 million and $5.38 million respectively. Campion created fake financial records, assumed false identities, and used a voice modulator to deceive victims. Judge Lynn Adelman ordered her to pay over $10 million in restitution and serve three years of supervised release.

Billionaire investor Mark Cuban lost about $870,000 in a crypto scam after suspicious transactions were spotted in a long-inactive MetaMask wallet labeled “Mark Cuban 2.” On-chain sleuth Wazz first noticed the activity on EtherScan and posted that the wallet, inactive for 160 days, had suddenly moved all its assets. Cuban later confirmed he lost five Ethereum tokens, along with other holdings including USDC, Polygon (MATIC), staked Ethereum (stETH), and tokens tied to SuperRare and Ethereum Name Service. Despite the theft, Cuban said he managed to move about $2 million in USDC from the wallet to Coinbase Custody, which likely prevented most of his assets from being stolen. He believes the breach happened because he downloaded a malicious version of MetaMask. Cuban said he had opened MetaMask for the first time in months, noticed the app crashed a couple of times, then locked his NFTs on OpenSea and removed his MATIC. This was not Cuban’s first crypto loss; he previously suffered losses in 2021 when Iron Finance’s TITAN collapsed. The article also notes that CoinEx separately reported a hot-wallet hack on September 12.

# Summary Billionaire investor Mark Cuban lost approximately $870,000 in a cryptocurrency scam on September 15. On-chain analyst Wazz discovered unusual transactions in Cuban's MetaMask wallet labeled "Mark Cuban 2," which had been inactive for over five months. Cuban confirmed losing five Ethereum tokens worth around $8,170, along with USD Coin, Polygon, Lido staked Ethereum, and other tokens. However, he successfully transferred approximately $2 million USDC to Coinbase Custody, preventing total asset loss. Cuban believes he downloaded a malicious version of MetaMask, stating the application "crashed a couple times" before the hack occurred. He subsequently locked his NFTs on OpenSea and removed MATIC from the account. This marks Cuban's second significant cryptocurrency loss. He previously lost unspecified assets when Iron Finance's TITAN stablecoin collapsed in a suspected rug pull in 2021. Additionally, cryptocurrency exchange CoinEx announced its hot wallets were hacked on September 12, with large amounts of Ethereum, Tron, and Polygon stolen.

The RCMP is investigating an alleged computer fraud scheme at VIA Rail after the Crown corporation referred the case following an internal probe by its ombudsman. QMI Agency previously reported that VIA fired a top computer department manager amid embezzlement allegations. A source said one or more IT companies may have overbilled for services, with losses reaching hundreds of thousands of dollars. QMI also reported the manager had a prior theft conviction from a Bombardier Aerospace case.

# Summary The RCMP is investigating alleged fraud at VIA Rail involving a top computer department manager who was fired in 2013. An internal investigation, assisted by the rail carrier's ombudsman, uncovered a suspected scheme where IT companies allegedly overbilled for services, totaling hundreds of thousands of dollars. The case was transferred to police. Notably, VIA Rail had hired the manager despite her prior 2010 conviction for stealing computers and monitors from Bombardier Aerospace.

The chairman of the House select committee investigating the Jan. 6 Capitol attack, Rep. Bennie Thompson of Mississippi, said Sunday that the panel has gathered “significant testimony” suggesting the White House “had been told to do something” while the insurrection was underway. Speaking on CNN’s “State of the Union,” Thompson said the committee is still working to verify the information before presenting it publicly in hearings and in its report, but he emphasized that it is “highly unusual for anyone in charge of anything to watch what’s going on and do nothing.” Thompson declined to say whether former President Donald Trump’s conduct during the attack would lead to a criminal referral to the Justice Department. “We don’t know,” he said, adding that the committee would make a referral only if its findings warranted one. His comments came just days before the first anniversary of the Jan. 6 attack, when a pro-Trump mob overran police, stormed the Capitol, and damaged the building in an effort to stop Congress from certifying the 2020 election. Several people died during or soon after the attack, and some officers who responded later died by suicide. The committee, which includes two Republicans, has been investigating the attack and the events leading up to it for months. Much of its work has been conducted privately, and an interim report is not expected until summer. Thompson also said the panel has “some concerns” about possible financial fraud involving Trump and his allies, saying investigators are looking closely at fundraising and spending tied to the post-election effort. He did not say whether the committee plans to subpoena Republican lawmakers such as Rep. Jim Jordan, a Trump ally. Instead, Thompson said he hoped members of Congress would cooperate voluntarily. The chairman said investigators are still examining testimony and documents related to the so-called “war room” at Washington’s Willard Hotel, where Trump allies Rudy Giuliani and Steve Bannon operated on Jan. 6. Thompson said the committee is seeking records about who paid for the operation, noting that former New York police commissioner Bernie Kerik has begun cooperating and that the hotel has been asked for information.

Bennie Thompson. Speaking on CNN's "State of the Union," Thompson emphasized the committee plans to verify all findings before presenting them publicly through reports and hearings. Thompson noted it would be "highly unusual" for anyone in leadership to witness the events and take no action. However, when asked whether former President Donald Trump's conduct warrants criminal referral to the Department of Justice, Thompson stated the committee remains uncertain and will make such referrals only if evidence supports them. The attack, which occurred one year before Thompson's comments, involved a pro-Trump mob that breached Capitol security, assaulted law enforcement officers, and damaged the building. Multiple deaths resulted from the violence that day, and several responding officers subsequently died by suicide. Thompson highlighted that former New York City police commissioner Bernie Kerik has begun cooperating with the committee. The panel is seeking hotel records and payment information related to the operation.

A San Antonio woman, Cindy Ellen McCarthy, also known as Cindy Wojtaszek, was sentenced to 33 months in federal prison for stealing more than $850,000 from a Castle Hills employer where she worked as a bookkeeper. Federal authorities said the 48-year-old used the company’s bank account to pay her personal credit card from November 2012 through July 2018, making about 200 transactions. She also altered bank statements to disguise the payments as vendor expenses. McCarthy pleaded guilty in October 2021 to one count of wire fraud. In addition to prison, she was ordered to pay $855,538.56 in restitution. The FBI and Castle Hills police investigated the case, and federal officials said she abused her position for personal gain.

# Summary A San Antonio woman, Cindy Ellen McCarthy, was sentenced to 33 months in prison for embezzling over $850,000 from her employer, a Castle Hills business. Working as a bookkeeper from November 2012 to July 2018, McCarthy made approximately 200 unauthorized transactions, using the company's bank account to pay her personal credit card. She concealed the theft by altering bank statements to disguise the payments as vendor transactions. McCarthy pleaded guilty to wire fraud in October 2021 and was ordered to pay $855,538.56 in restitution. The FBI and Castle Hills police investigated the case, highlighting the serious consequences of financial fraud and workplace embezzlement.

The FBI’s Denver Division is warning Coloradans about a growing wave of cryptocurrency scams as more people begin using digital currencies. Investigators say adults are increasingly being targeted, and the schemes often involve Tether (USDT) and USD Coin (USDC). In 2021, Coloradans reported losing about $25 million to these scams. According to FBI Denver, the fraud usually begins on social media, dating apps, or discussion forums, where a scammer approaches a victim with a supposed cryptocurrency investment opportunity. The pitch often includes promises of “zero risk” and claims that the victim can “make lots of money.” The scammer then asks for a link or phone number, saying it is needed to set up an investment account. Once the victim transfers money, the fraudster disappears. Investigators in Colorado say they are seeing two common versions of the scam. In one, a fake investment manager promises to grow the victim’s money, but only if the person buys cryptocurrency and sends it to an online account controlled by the scammer. In the other, an online romantic interest asks for money or cryptocurrency to help the victim invest. The FBI highlighted several Colorado cases from 2021, including a 52-year-old Aurora man who lost about $600,000 in a Tether fraud scheme, a 61-year-old Denver woman who lost about $1.3 million, a 62-year-old Evergreen man who lost about $350,000, a Parker couple in their late 40s who lost about $1.2 million, and a 53-year-old Timnath man who lost about $600,000 in a USD Coin scheme. Nationwide, the FBI said $575 million in crypto losses came from fake investment opportunities, and overall losses in 2021 were roughly 60 times higher than in 2018. Special Agent in Charge Mark Michalek said that as more people invest in cryptocurrency, more scams appear, and the best protection is to avoid becoming a victim in the first place. FBI Denver advises people to be skeptical of guaranteed profits, big payouts, and get-rich-quick offers, and to remember that legitimate investments do not promise sure returns. It also recommends researching any company or person online using terms like “review,” “scam,” or “complaint,” visiting websites directly instead of through links or QR codes, downloading apps only from official app stores, verifying that investment representatives use business email accounts, and resisting pressure to act quickly. Anyone who believes they have been scammed should report it to the FBI’s Internet Crime Complaint Center at ic3.gov.

# Colorado Residents Lost $25 Million to Cryptocurrency Scams in 2021 The FBI's Denver Division has issued a warning about the rising number of cryptocurrency scams targeting Coloradans, with losses totaling approximately $25 million in 2021 alone. As cryptocurrency adoption increases, so too does the prevalence of these fraudulent schemes, primarily involving Tether (USDT) and USD Coin (USDC). ## How the Scams Work Scammers typically initiate contact through social media, dating apps, or discussion forums, presenting fake cryptocurrency investment opportunities with promises of "zero risk" and substantial returns. They request personal links or phone numbers under the guise of setting up investment accounts. Once victims transfer funds, the fraudsters vanish with the money. Colorado investigators have identified two primary tactics: fake investment managers promising to grow victims' money in exchange for cryptocurrency transfers, and online romantic interests requesting funds for investment purposes. ## Notable Cases The FBI documented several significant losses in Colorado: - A 52-year-old Aurora man lost $600,000 - A 61-year-old Denver woman lost $1.3 million - A 62-year-old Evergreen man lost $350,000 - A Parker couple in their late 40s lost $1.2 million - A 53-year-old Timnath man lost $600,000 Nationally, $575 million of all cryptocurrency scam losses stemmed from fake investment opportunities, with 2021 losses approximately 60 times higher than 2018 figures. ## Prevention Tips FBI Denver Special Agent in Charge Mark Michalek emphasized that prevention is preferable to investigation. The agency recommends: - Avoiding investment opportunities guaranteeing profits or promising big payouts - Skepticism toward get-rich-quick schemes - Researching companies and individuals online before investing - Navigating to websites independently rather than using provided links - Downloading apps only from official app stores - Verifying investment advisors have legitimate business email accounts - Resisting pressure to make quick decisions Victims should file complaints with the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center at www.ic3.gov.

California Attorney General Kamala D. Harris, AARP California, and the District Office of Councilman Curren Price announced “Shred Fest 2016,” a free Los Angeles event on Saturday, April 30, designed to help consumers protect themselves from identity theft. Held at 4301 S. Central Avenue from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m., the event will provide secure shredding of sensitive documents and also offer information on how to avoid fraud and scams. The event is part of an ongoing partnership between Harris’s office and AARP to educate the public, especially seniors, about identity theft and financial fraud. It is also one of several Shred Fest 2016 events taking place nationwide and is connected to Money Smart Week, with support from AARP’s Fraud Watch Network and the AARP Foundation. Harris said her office must continue prosecuting those who target seniors while also teaching Californians how to reduce their risk of identity theft. Councilman Price noted that financial fraud costs millions of dollars each year and encouraged people to use the post-tax season period to clean out old financial records. Nancy McPherson, AARP California’s state director, said thieves often search trash and dumpsters for confidential information, making safe document disposal important. Experts recommend shredding materials such as papers containing Social Security numbers, birth dates, signatures, account numbers, passwords, or PINs; canceled or unused checks; deposit slips and ATM or credit card receipts after statements arrive; preapproved credit card offers; medical bills; investment statements; and expired ID cards like driver’s licenses, insurance cards, and passports. The article also notes that Harris and AARP have previously collaborated on tele-town halls, webinars, and consumer resources to help seniors and their families avoid scams. More information is available on the Attorney General’s identity theft website.
