Additional identity theft resources are available on the Attorney General's website.

U.S. authorities on Friday relaxed criminal-record restrictions in the coronavirus business payroll loan program, allowing some owners with older felony convictions to qualify. The Treasury Department and Small Business Administration cut the look-back period for non-financial felony convictions to one year from five, while keeping a five-year ban for felonies involving fraud, bribery, embezzlement and similar crimes. The move went further than Treasury Secretary Steven Mnuchin’s Wednesday suggestion of a three-year period. The change affects the Paycheck Protection Program, a major part of the nearly $3 trillion coronavirus relief package, which provides potentially forgivable loans to help businesses pay workers. Officials said the revision was made in the interest of criminal justice reform.

# Summary The U.S. Treasury Department and Small Business Administration have eased criminal record restrictions for the Paycheck Protection Program, a coronavirus relief loan initiative. The look-back period for non-financial felony convictions has been reduced from five years to one year, allowing some business owners with criminal records to access funds. However, felonies involving fraud, bribery, and embezzlement retain the five-year restriction. This change exceeds Treasury Secretary Steven Mnuchin's earlier suggestion of a three-year period. The modification was made to support criminal justice reform while administering the nearly $3 trillion pandemic relief package.

TD Bank has hired six senior bankers in New York from major rivals, including JPMorgan Chase, Goldman Sachs, Royal Bank of Canada, Bank of Montreal and Bank of Nova Scotia, as it works to strengthen its debt and equity capital markets businesses. TD Securities, the bank’s capital markets arm, brought in the managing directors between Oct. 31 and this month to expand coverage in leveraged finance, private credit and debt capital markets, according to TD executives speaking to Reuters. Grant Miller, TD’s head of global capital markets, said the bank sees broad opportunities to compete more aggressively and wanted to add external talent in areas that could support growth. Christopher Gerry, head of global debt capital markets, said the new hires will focus on sectors such as financial institutions, including regional banks and insurance, as well as natural resources, technology and infrastructure. He added that TD wants to be well positioned to finance fast-growing areas such as data centers. Among the new hires are Mark Trudell from BMO, who will lead industrials coverage for leveraged finance and private credit; Nadine Yang from JPMorgan, who will run U.S. equity capital markets coverage of technology; Sean McCarty from Scotiabank, who will lead U.S. energy coverage; Catherine Awong from RBC, who will co-manage the U.S. financial institutions debt capital markets practice; Tom Healy from Goldman Sachs, who will work alongside her; and Anthony Ragozino from RBC, who joined in October to lead regulatory advisory and capital solutions. The hiring push comes as Canadian banks seek U.S. growth. TD’s CEO Raymond Chun is aiming to increase fee-based income after a difficult period for the lender, including a 2024 anti-money-laundering fine tied to its U.S. personal banking business. TD has already expanded its capital markets franchise through its 2023 acquisition of Cowen.

# TD Bank Expands Capital Markets with Senior Banker Hires TD Bank has recruited six senior managing directors from major competitors including JPMorgan Chase, Goldman Sachs, and Royal Bank of Canada to strengthen its capital markets division in New York. These hires, who joined between October and November, will oversee leveraged finance, private credit, and debt capital markets operations. Grant Miller, TD's head of global capital markets, stated the bank aims to bolster external talent to compete effectively across all industries. Christopher Gerry, head of global debt capital markets, emphasized the bank's focus on emerging opportunities, particularly in financing data centers and other growth industries. The new hires include Mark Trudell from BMO to lead industrials coverage for leveraged finance and private credit, and Nadine Yang from JPMorgan to run U.S. equity capital markets coverage for technology. In debt capital markets, Sean McCarty joined from Scotiabank to lead energy company coverage, while Catherine Awong and Tom Healy were hired to manage the U.S. financial institutions practice. Anthony Ragozino joined in October from RBC to lead the regulatory advisory and capital solutions team. The expansion reflects Canadian banks' strategy to grow U.S. operations despite political uncertainties. TD, Canada's second-largest lender, is prioritizing fee-based businesses following regulatory challenges in 2024. The bank significantly expanded its capital markets presence after acquiring U.S. investment firm Cowen for $1.3 billion in 2023.

President Donald Trump’s Presidential Advisory Commission on Election Integrity is holding its first meeting Wednesday in Washington amid strong opposition from state election officials and a wave of legal challenges from privacy and civil rights groups. The commission was created by executive order on May 11 to “promote fair and honest Federal elections” and to examine “improper” and “fraudulent” voter registration and voting. Critics argue that the panel’s real purpose is to support Trump’s repeated, unsubstantiated claims that millions of people voted illegally in the 2016 election. They also warn that the commission’s work could be used to justify new voting restrictions that would suppress turnout nationwide. The commission is led by Vice President Mike Pence and Kansas Secretary of State Kris Kobach, both Republicans. Of its 12 members, seven are Republicans and five are Democrats. Wendy Weiser of the Brennan Center for Justice called it a “sham,” saying that while it is described as bipartisan, it is “led by Republicans, dominated by Republicans and stacked with the nation’s strongest proponents of voting restrictions.” The controversy intensified after Kobach sent a June 28 request to election officials in all 50 states asking for “publicly-available data from state voter rolls and feedback on how to improve election integrity” by July 14. The request prompted resistance across the country. According to the Brennan Center, election officials in 21 states and the District of Columbia refused to provide any data, citing privacy concerns. Eight states said they would not comply unless the commission paid for the information or used a formal request process. Seventeen states agreed to provide publicly available voter information. At least 14 lawsuits have been filed challenging the commission’s attempt to gather nationwide voter data, which is normally held by state and local authorities rather than the federal government. One of the plaintiffs, the Electronic Privacy Information Center (EPIC), sought a temporary restraining order in federal court in Washington, D.C. EPIC’s Marc Rotenberg said the commission had violated the constitutional right to informational privacy and posed an “imminent risk” to registered voters. The group argued that the commission’s request for detailed voter histories, its direction to send records to an unsecure website, and its proposal to publish partial Social Security numbers could expose people to identity theft and financial fraud. The administration responded in court that the data requested was already publicly available from the states and that the commission had taken reasonable steps to protect it by using a secure transfer method and storing it in White House systems. Still, on July 10 the commission asked states to pause submissions until a court rules in the D.C. case. Experts said a decision could come at any time. The dispute has also led to reports of voters withdrawing their registrations out of fear their personal information could be hacked or misused. In Denver, election officials reported a 2,800 percent increase in people unregistering after the commission’s request became public. Colorado officials said 3,394 people withdrew between June 28 and July 13. Similar reactions were reported in Vermont, Florida, and Alabama. # Summary: Trump's Election Integrity Commission Faces Significant Opposition President Donald Trump established the Presidential Advisory Commission on Election Integrity through an executive order on May 11, officially tasked with reviewing "improper" and "fraudulent" voter registration and voting practices. Led by Vice President Mike Pence and Kansas Secretary of State Kris Kobach, the commission held its first meeting on Wednesday amid substantial criticism and legal challenges. ## Structure and Criticism The commission comprises seven Republicans and five Democrats. However, critics argue the panel is fundamentally partisan despite claims of bipartisanship. Wendy Weiser from the Brennan Center for Justice characterized it as a "sham" designed to validate Trump's unsubstantiated claims that millions voted illegally in 2016. Opponents contend the commission's real purpose is establishing restrictive voting laws that would suppress voter participation nationwide. ## Data Request Controversy On June 28, Kobach requested that state election officials submit publicly available voter data by July 14. This unprecedented request sparked significant pushback. Of the states responding, 21 states plus Washington D.C. refused to submit any data citing privacy concerns, while eight states demanded payment or formal request procedures. Only 17 states agreed to comply with the request. ## Legal Challenges Fourteen lawsuits have been filed challenging the commission's data collection efforts. Privacy advocates argue the request violates constitutional rights and existing privacy laws. The Electronic Privacy Information Center filed for a temporary restraining order, claiming the commission poses "an imminent risk to registered voters" and that directing officials to send records to unsecure websites could enable identity theft and fraud. The administration countered that the requested data is already publicly available and that reasonable security measures have been implemented. On July 10, the commission asked states to suspend submissions pending a court ruling in the Washington D.C. case. ## Voter Registration Withdrawals The commission's data request triggered widespread voter anxiety. Hundreds of voters across the country withdrew their registrations from fear of hacking or data misuse. Denver experienced a dramatic 2,800 percent increase in unregistration requests, with 600-plus withdrawals recorded before July 14—compared to the typical eight per week. Colorado saw 3,394 residents withdraw between June 28 and July 13. Similar patterns emerged nationally. Vermont reported 372 withdrawal requests, while Florida's Seminole County received 15 unregistration calls. Alabama's Secretary of State received numerous "emotionally-charged responses" from concerned voters. ## Moving Forward State officials attributed voter concerns partly to insufficient information about the commission's intentions and data security measures. The Wednesday meeting was expected to include commission member swearing-in, introductions, discussions of objectives, expert presentations, and next steps. Experts anticipated a court ruling in the Washington D.C. case could arrive imminently, potentially clarifying the commission's authority to collect voter data and providing voters with needed information to make informed decisions about their registration status.

A federal grand jury in San Francisco indicted John Holdaway, 72, of Sandy, Utah, and Kevin Kyes, 68, of Campbell, California, on charges including conspiracy, wire fraud, and money laundering in connection with an alleged $7 million Ponzi scheme that targeted mostly Japanese investors from December 2012 through July 2015. According to the indictment, the two men operated a set of entities they called “Money Management Strategies,” or “MMS,” and pitched investors on the idea that their money would be used for currency or derivatives trading. They allegedly promised annual returns of 100% and claimed the investments were safe because the principal would remain in the bank accounts where it was deposited and any trading losses would be covered by MMS. Relying on those claims, investors wired or transferred funds to bank accounts in Northern California controlled by Holdaway and Kyes, sending about $7 million in total. Prosecutors say the money was not invested as promised. Instead, Holdaway and Kyes allegedly used it for their own spending, to make Ponzi-style payments to earlier investors, to repay people from previous investment programs they had run, and to support gold-related businesses. The indictment also alleges they falsely told investors they were receiving legitimate distributions or returns. To support those claims, the defendants allegedly created fake account statements and letters from an accountant. Holdaway is also accused of sending emails under false names to make it appear that several people worked for MMS, and of lying about traveling to Europe or elsewhere to manage investments. The grand jury charged both men with one count of conspiracy to commit wire fraud, 18 counts of wire fraud, one count of conspiracy to engage in monetary transactions involving criminal proceeds, and five counts of engaging in such transactions. Both defendants were arrested and made initial appearances in federal court, where they were released pending further hearings. Holdaway’s next court date was set for June 28, 2016, before U.S. Magistrate Judge Laurel Beeler, and Kyes’s for July 22, 2016, before U.S. District Judge Susan Illston. Officials emphasized that an indictment is only an आरोपation and that both men are presumed innocent unless proven guilty. If convicted, they face significant prison terms and fines, with wire fraud-related counts carrying up to 20 years each and money-laundering-related counts carrying up to 10 years each, along with possible restitution and supervised release. The case is being prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorney Benjamin Kingsley with help from Jessica Meegan and Daniel Charlier-Smith, following an FBI and IRS-Criminal Investigation probe.

Mueller has already brought charges against four former campaign or administration figures, including Paul Manafort and Michael Flynn. Flynn pleaded guilty to lying to FBI investigators about his Russian contacts and is assisting the probe. A new lawsuit filed Tuesday in Charlotte alleges that Diane Siskey, the widow of financier Rick Siskey, “actively participated” in her late husband’s Ponzi schemes, received millions of dollars in illicit gains, and is still concealing substantial money offshore. The suit was brought by a private equity fund formerly known as Siskey Capital and by two of its employees. It also accuses MetLife and its securities arm of ignoring warning signs about Rick Siskey’s conduct, despite what the complaint calls a clear warning that he was a “rogue broker.” Rick Siskey, 58, died by suicide in December, only days after court filings first suggested he was under fraud investigation. In January, an unsealed FBI affidavit alleged that he had been running a Ponzi scheme for years, defrauding investors of millions. Tuesday’s lawsuit is the first legal filing to directly accuse Diane Siskey of wrongdoing in the case. It follows an earlier suit this year that said MetLife knew about Rick Siskey’s activities. For years, Rick and Diane Siskey were associated with MetLife and worked for a firm operating under the name Wall Street Capitol. The couple was well known in Charlotte civic and social circles, and a YMCA branch carries their name. Since Rick Siskey’s death, no criminal charges have been brought against anyone else involved, though investors have forced four Siskey-related companies into federal bankruptcy court in Charlotte. According to the complaint, Charlotte businessman Marty Sumichrast formed Siskey Capital with Rick Siskey in 2013 but says he did not learn of his partner’s alleged illegal conduct until the allegations became public in December 2016. The company has since changed its name to Stone Street Partners, but the scandal has badly damaged the business, which is now being wound down, the suit says. The 32-page complaint includes claims of negligence and fraud against the Siskey estate, Diane Siskey, and MetLife, and seeks unspecified compensatory and punitive damages. Plaintiffs’ attorney Jim Smith declined to comment beyond the allegations in the filing. MetLife spokeswoman Kim Friedman said the company had only just learned of the suit and was reviewing it to determine next steps. Lane Williamson, a lawyer for the Siskey estate, said he was disappointed the estate would need to spend resources defending litigation that, in his view, would be better used to compensate investors. Diane Siskey and her attorneys did not respond to requests for comment. The lawsuit describes a “Siskey Team” that included Diane Siskey and other associates. Rick Siskey moved to Charlotte in the 1980s and built a business selling insurance and financial services. The complaint says the team began working with MetLife in the late 1990s. It alleges that Rick Siskey relied heavily on his wife and other team members to carry out his business decisions, and that MetLife helped establish him in a prominent SouthPark office building, lending his operation credibility through its brand. He operated under the Wall Street Capitol name because, according to the suit, the appearance of independence made his sales pitch more persuasive when recommending MetLife products. The complaint says that after joining MetLife, Siskey created a series of limited liability companies to carry out “several elaborate Ponzi schemes.” He allegedly promised clients fixed returns from safe investments, but instead diverted money into personal accounts to support a lavish lifestyle and pay earlier investors, a classic Ponzi structure. The suit estimates total investments exceeded $50 million. The complaint says Siskey hid the schemes from everyone except members of his team. It claims they worked in a separate section of MetLife’s offices, and that files related to the scheme were stored in locked cabinets in his assistant’s office. Siskey’s conduct first became public in 2004, when the National Association of Securities Dealers disciplined him for selling promissory notes in two funds without telling his employer. Those same transactions later led to a settlement with the U.S. Labor Department in 2011. Diane Siskey, the suit says, worked for MetLife and MetLife Securities from 2001 to 2016, managing the Wall Street Capitol office and serving as director of compliance. The complaint alleges she was deeply involved in Rick Siskey’s defense and settlement of the earlier securities and Labor Department issues. It also says a MetLife fraud investigator tried in 2015 to examine the couple’s activities, including millions of dollars in insurance policies they held on other people, but the company stopped the investigation after the Siskeys complained. The suit argues that if MetLife had maintained proper controls and completed a full investigation, the Ponzi scheme would have been discovered and stopped sooner. The filing further alleges that Diane Siskey personally helped form TSI Holdings, an entity central to the FBI affidavit on Rick Siskey’s alleged Ponzi scheme. It also says that from mid-2005 through mid-2013 there were 45 transactions totaling more than $47 million between her accounts and her husband’s, which the complaint characterizes as a conduit between his Ponzi entities and her finances. The plaintiffs say they became involved with Rick Siskey in 2013, when he approached Sumichrast about investing in public companies. After describing his achievements and presenting Diane Siskey as his business partner, he later proposed that they form a company together, and Sumichrast agreed. Dawn King and Paul Porter later joined the business, leaving well-paid jobs to do so. The suit says the three plaintiffs were shocked when FBI allegations surfaced in December 2016 and had no idea Siskey’s activities were illegal. About two weeks before his death, the complaint says, Rick Siskey visited the office and described the investigation as a minor technical issue, assuring employees that all investors would be repaid. Although Rick Siskey resigned from Siskey Capital on Dec. 14, 2016, the suit says Diane Siskey later texted Sumichrast to say her husband still owned a stake in the company. After his death, the complaint alleges, she demanded that Siskey Capital keep paying her health and auto expenses. It also says she is hiding significant funds offshore and that she showed no concern for defrauded investors, only for preserving her wealth. Meanwhile, Stone Street Partners and its employees have suffered from association with the scandal. The company has been unable to raise more capital and is being wound down, with existing investments being distributed to repay investors where possible. Past investments included expansion capital for Kure Corp., a vaping company. The lawsuit comes as claims are due this week against the estate and in bankruptcy court. Diane Siskey has pledged to set aside $37.5 million of the $47 million in life insurance proceeds from her husband’s death for investors. Additional money is expected from the sale of the couple’s home and from an estate auction. Bankruptcy trustee Joseph Grier has said he expects a “substantial distribution” to investors.

Kazakhstan’s financial monitoring agency, the Anti-Monopoly Service (AFM), has seized more than $10 million in digital assets linked to a large Ponzi scheme run through Amir Capital, a company that claimed to be a global investment fund. Authorities say the operation involved more than 40 suspects who collected Bitcoin, Ethereum, and Tether from Kazakhstani investors while promising monthly returns of up to 10%. Instead of investing the money in trading or mining, investigators allege the group used new deposits to pay earlier participants. The confiscated crypto was secured under a court order, and officials also froze a land parcel in the Almaty region. One alleged organizer, described as a woman closely tied to the scheme, has been placed in pre-trial detention for two months while the investigation continues. Complaints about Amir Capital first appeared in 2021, when customers said they could no longer withdraw their savings. The company blamed “technical difficulties,” but payouts never resumed. Authorities now say thousands of victims were affected and suffered significant losses. The AFM said more arrests and asset seizures are likely as investigators trace additional funds, and victims may later be able to file compensation claims. The case comes amid Kazakhstan’s broader push to tighten crypto oversight. The country has become a major crypto hub, especially after China’s mining crackdown pushed operators across the border. Recently, Kazakhstan launched a State Digital Asset Fund and introduced its own stablecoin, while related crackdowns on crypto fraud are also advancing in the United States.
