She has stated her willingness to be questioned in Brussels and expressed disbelief at the accusations against her sister, citing Eva's "morals and personality." Over the past five years, the sisters have frequently appeared together at technology events and collaborated on projects. Industry Commons, a lobbying group with Mantalena on its governing board, described her as "chief policy advisor and close employee" in Eva's office, though this description was removed from their website following the scandal. Mantalena claims she worked as an "assistant in Athens" under a special contract authorized for Members of European Parliament (MEPs), but her name never appeared on Eva's official advisory list. Eva Kaili's rise in Parliament was rapid. Elected in 2014, she became known as an influential digital policy legislator. She joined the Industrial Committee in July 2014 and helped evaluate the EU's €80 billion Horizon 2020 R&D program. In October 2014, she became the first vice-president of the Parliament's science and technology panel (STOA), assuming the chairmanship in 2017—becoming the first woman in that position until March 2022. Meanwhile, Mantalena, a lawyer, launched Made Group in August 2017 as a "non-profit platform" for communication strategy and social innovation. By 2021, she was listed as sole administrator. Notably, Matina Kanaki, who co-founded Made Group with Mantalena, became Eva's assistant in February 2020 and later became manager of a real estate company established by Eva and her partner Francesco Giorgi. Giorgi, an assistant to Italian MEP Andrea Cozzolino, was also detained in the investigation. Mantalena disputes the extent of overlap between Made Group and Eva's Brussels work, claiming their activities weren't explicitly following Eva's agenda. She emphasized that ELONtech received no financing and wasn't a legal entity or NGO. Other individuals named in the investigation did not respond to requests for comment.

Japanese authorities searched the home of former Nissan chairman Carlos Ghosn after his dramatic escape to Lebanon on December 31, Kyodo reported. Ghosn, who had been under house arrest in Japan on financial misconduct charges, said he fled “political persecution.” He was formally charged in January 2019 with financial fraud and abuse of power after earlier detention and release on bail. Prosecutors allege he used company funds to cover about $21 million in private investment losses and underreported his income. Ghosn claimed he received 7.8 billion yen, while prosecutors say it was 17 billion yen.

# Summary Carlos Ghosn, former Nissan chairman, fled Japan to Lebanon on December 31 while under house arrest. Japanese authorities subsequently searched his home following his escape. Ghosn faced charges of financial fraud and abuse of power, including allegedly covering $21 million in private investment losses using company funds and significantly underreporting his income. Prosecutors claimed he earned 17 billion yen ($156 million) during 2010-2018, contradicting his reported 7.8 billion yen ($71 million). Ghosn claimed he fled due to "political persecution." He had jumped bail while awaiting trial in Japan.

Gulnara Karimova, the imprisoned daughter of late Uzbek President Islam Karimov, has been sentenced to 13 years and four months in a new extortion and embezzlement case, Uzbekistan’s Supreme Court said. The term will count from August 2015, and five alleged accomplices were also convicted. Karimova, 47, was first sentenced in 2015 to five years and then jailed again in 2019 for violating house arrest terms. She recently appealed to President Shavkat Mirziyoyev for release, citing poor health and a need for surgery, while offering to stop challenging the state’s efforts to seize assets. She denies wrongdoing and says the government has already confiscated $1.2 billion from her.

# Summary Gulnara Karimova, daughter of late Uzbek President Islam Karimov, has been sentenced to 13 years and four months in prison for extortion and embezzlement. The 47-year-old was initially jailed in March 2019 for violating house arrest conditions following a 2015 five-year sentence. The Supreme Court also convicted five accomplices. The new sentence begins from August 2015. Last month, Karimova requested her release from successor President Shavkat Mirziyoyev, citing health concerns, and offered to cease legal challenges to asset confiscation worth $686 million in Switzerland. She claims the government has already seized $1.2 billion of her assets. Karimova denies wrongdoing.

Uzbekistan has set an ambitious goal of rising to 20th place in the World Bank and International Finance Corporation’s Doing Business ranking by 2022. The target is laid out in a presidential resolution titled “On additional measures to improve the ranking of the Republic of Uzbekistan in the annual report of the World Bank and the Doing Business International Finance Corporation.” Along with the resolution, the government approved a roadmap to improve the country’s position, developed with the participation of the World Bank and other international financial institutions. The resolution introduces a broad package of legal and administrative reforms, with many changes scheduled to take effect on 1 March 2019. Among the measures is a new rule allowing banks to remotely open accounts for legal entities founded by Uzbek residents and for individual entrepreneurs during state registration, provided remote identification requirements under Financial Action Task Force (FATF) standards are met. In land and construction regulation, the government is abolishing the former procedure for determining the exclusive purpose of land plots when they are sold through the E-IJRO AUKSION electronic trading platform. Instead, the auction documentation must include a full list of the types of structures that are prohibited or allowed on a given plot. Construction authorities will also take on the role of architectural and urban planning councils for approving design estimates, although approval will remain advisory for projects in historical areas, protected cultural heritage zones, and state-owned projects. The resolution also changes how construction-related costs are handled: if topographic and special surveys are needed after a building is sold through E-IJRO AUKSION, their cost will be covered from the proceeds of the land sale, without burdening land or property owners. In addition, the act of acceptance for completed buildings and structures will now be issued together with the certificate confirming state registration of property rights. Other reforms include economic sanctions for unauthorized disconnection of consumers from electricity, and allowing applications for state registration of property rights and cadastral registration to be submitted on an extraterritorial basis. Notaries handling real estate transactions will be required to send registration applications and related documents electronically to the state registration authority free of charge. Paper-based cadastral files will be replaced by electronic cadastral documentation. In corporate governance, shareholders will be able to hold supervisory board members liable for damages caused by major transactions or affiliated-party transactions equal to 10 percent or more of a company’s net assets. Disputes in limited and additional liability companies caused by deadlock will be resolved in court. Dividend payments on shares will be made through the Central Securities Depository or investment intermediaries. The resolution also expands trade and judicial procedures. The Chamber of Commerce and Industry will be able to issue certificates of origin alongside the Ministry of Investment and Foreign Trade, within one working day. From 1 March, pre-trial hearings will be introduced in economic courts, and a unified electronic system for collecting and paying court fees and other payments will be created. Government bodies will also be prohibited from demanding stamps on business documents, and the procedure for obtaining construction and installation permits will be replaced with a notification system for starting work.

# Uzbekistan Aims for 20th Place in World Bank's Doing Business Ranking by 2022 Uzbekistan has announced an ambitious plan to improve its position in the World Bank and International Finance Corporation's Doing Business ranking, targeting placement in the top 20 by 2022. This initiative is outlined in a Presidential resolution establishing a comprehensive roadmap developed in collaboration with the World Bank and other international financial institutions. The government has approved significant legislative amendments effective March 1, 2019, designed to streamline business operations and reduce bureaucratic obstacles. These changes span multiple sectors and administrative procedures. **Banking and Financial Services** Banks can now remotely open accounts for legal entities and individual entrepreneurs during state registration, provided remote identification requirements established by the Financial Action Task Force on Money Laundering are met. **Real Estate and Construction** The exclusive purpose requirement for land plots issued through electronic auction has been eliminated, with construction now permitted based on specified lists. Construction authorities have gained functions previously held by architectural councils, though historical and state sites retain advisory coordination requirements. Topographic survey costs are now funded from land sale proceeds rather than burdening property owners. Building acceptance certificates are now issued simultaneously with property registration documents. **Property Registration** Applications for property registration and cadastral registration can now be submitted remotely. Notary offices must electronically transmit registration applications to authorities without charging fees. Cadastral documentation now operates entirely in electronic form, eliminating paper requirements. **Corporate Governance** Shareholders can now hold supervisory board members liable for damages from major transactions involving 10 percent or more of company assets. Corporate disputes arising from insufficient votes are resolved through court proceedings. A new dividend payment mechanism through the Central Securities Depository or investment intermediaries has been introduced. **International Trade** The Chamber of Commerce and Industry now issues certificates of origin alongside the Ministry of Investment and Foreign Trade, with processing within one working day of application. **Judicial Procedures** Economic courts can now conduct pre-trial hearings for dispute resolution. A unified electronic payment system has been established for all court fees across criminal, civil, administrative, and economic courts. **General Business Operations** Government agencies can no longer require document stamps or stamp certification from businesses. Construction permission procedures have been replaced with a notification mechanism for commencement of work. Additionally, the government has introduced economic sanctions against unauthorized power supply disconnections. These comprehensive reforms demonstrate Uzbekistan's commitment to enhancing its business environment and international competitiveness through modernization of legal frameworks and administrative procedures.

Former Iranian welfare and social security minister Parviz Kazemi has been arrested on financial fraud charges, official media reported November 11. IRNA said he was taken to Tehran’s Evin prison on November 9. Kazemi resigned in 2006 after less than a year under President Mahmoud Ahmadinejad, citing political differences, and later worked in banking. In recent years, he became a critic of Ahmadinejad, whose allies have also faced jail and fraud-related cases.

# Summary Former Iranian welfare minister Parviz Kazemi was arrested November 9 and charged with financial fraud, according to Iran's IRNA news agency. Kazemi resigned in 2006 from his position under President Mahmoud Ahmadinejad due to political differences, later working in banking. He subsequently became critical of Ahmadinejad. Several of Ahmadinejad's allies face imprisonment on security and financial fraud charges, including close aide Esfandiar Rahim Mashaei, sentenced to six-and-a-half years in September.

A McClatchy and OCCRP investigation traces a sprawling money-laundering and political-exile network linking two prominent Kazakh families, the Khrapunovs and the Ablyazovs, to elite real estate in New York and to Donald Trump’s business orbit. The report argues that the case illustrates a broader pattern described in *Dictators Without Borders*: authoritarian elites and their associates use Western financial, legal, and political systems both to hide wealth and to protect themselves once they fall out with their home governments. The article centers on former Kazakh insiders Viktor Khrapunov and Mukhtar Ablyazov, both of whom rose to prominence under President Nursultan Nazarbayev before breaking with the regime. They are accused in multiple countries of financial crimes, though they and their families insist the charges are politically motivated. The report suggests that both claims may have some truth: the families may indeed be targets of political persecution, while also facing credible allegations of wrongdoing. According to McClatchy, the pressure is mounting on the Khrapunov family. Viktor Khrapunov lives in Switzerland, while Ukraine has reportedly sought the extradition of his son Ilyas, alleging he organized a hack against a law firm representing BTA Bank, the bank formerly associated with Ablyazov and central to many of the legal disputes. Ilyas is married to Madina Ablyazova, Mukhtar Ablyazov’s daughter. The couple reportedly held unusual diplomatic posts representing the Central African Republic in Geneva, and a source told McClatchy they were appointed by former Central African Republic ruler François Bozizé before he was overthrown. The article also revisits the 2013 deportation of Alma Shalabayeva, Ablyazov’s wife, and their six-year-old daughter from Italy. Italian authorities initially said the deportation was justified because Shalabayeva allegedly carried a fake Central African Republic passport. But the Financial Times later reported that the Central African Republic said the passport was valid. McClatchy further notes that Ilyas and Madina hold dual citizenship in St. Vincent and the Grenadines, which they obtained after a land purchase. Ilyas said the family had to seek secondary citizenship because Kazakhstan refused to renew their passports, leaving them unable to travel. The report warns that a Kazakh parliamentary bill aimed at stripping citizenship from people tied to terrorist groups could also be used against political opponents, since lacking a passport can effectively trap people abroad. Finally, the story stretches to the United States, connecting the Kazakh figures to New York and California properties and to Trump’s real estate empire through Bayrock, a firm owned by Kazakh businessman Tevfik Arif. The investigation raises questions about what Trump knew, and when, about possible laundering through properties bearing his name.

# Summary: Kazakhstan's Dirty Laundry: Money Laundering and New York Real Estate A joint investigation by McClatchy and the Organized Crime and Corruption Reporting Project reveals how Kazakhstani elites exploit Western financial systems to launder money and evade their government's reach. The report traces connections between two exiled Kazakh families—the Khrapunovs and Ablyazovs—and illicit real estate transactions in New York, including properties in the Trump Soho building. The case exemplifies a pattern documented in the book *Dictators Without Borders*: autocrats and their associates use Western financial, legal, and political systems to extend their power internationally while accessing wealth and legal protections unavailable in their home countries. They employ offshore companies and shell corporations to conceal ownership while purchasing luxury properties. Simultaneously, when these elites fall from favor with their government, Western legal systems sometimes shield them from extradition by citing torture concerns. Viktor Khrapunov and Mukhtar Ablyazov were once prominent figures in Kazakhstan under President Nursultan Nazarbayev but later fell out with the regime. Both face accusations of financial crimes across multiple countries. While they claim political persecution, courts in several nations have found evidence of serious financial misconduct—suggesting both narratives contain elements of truth. The investigation indicates authorities are closing in on the Khrapunovs. Viktor resides in Switzerland while his son Ilyas faces potential extradition to Ukraine for allegedly hacking a law firm representing BTA Bank, formerly owned by Ablyazov. Notably, Ilyas married Madina Ablyazova, Mukhtar's daughter, and the couple secured diplomatic posts representing the Central African Republic in Geneva—though these appointments came from a deposed ruler. The family obtained dual citizenship in St. Vincent and the Grenadines through property purchases, citing Kazakhstan's refusal to renew their passports. This lack of valid documentation effectively restricts international travel. Additionally, Italy's 2013 deportation of Ablyazov's wife Alma and their young daughter involved disputed claims about a Central African Republic passport's validity. The investigation also explores troubling links to Donald Trump's real estate empire through Bayrock, a development firm owned by Kazakhstani businessman Tevfik Arif, raising questions about what Trump knew regarding money laundering through properties bearing his name. Ultimately, the report demonstrates how Kazakhstani domestic politics extends far beyond its borders, with Western cities becoming venues for autocratic power struggles and financial crimes.

Ukrainian military intelligence says Russia is preparing a new disinformation campaign to weaken international support for President Volodymyr Zelensky. According to the agency, the Kremlin has approved plans to create an additional structure in Russia dedicated to discrediting Zelensky through coordinated provocations and propaganda aimed mainly at audiences in Western Europe. The goal, it said, is to shape public opinion against the Ukrainian leader and reduce sympathy for Ukraine. The agency said the campaign would center on a website already registered under the name “Zelensky Fund,” which would distribute Kremlin-produced material. Russia would then try to register the name across Europe and promote it through a large pan-European advertising effort. The supposed fund would reportedly operate in a manner similar to a pyramid or multi-level marketing scheme, where participants are rewarded for recruiting others. Ivana Stradner, a Washington-based expert on Russian disinformation, said this effort fits a long pattern of Kremlin attempts to undermine Zelensky. She argued that Moscow targets Western audiences by appealing to their values and has recently intensified claims about corruption in Ukraine and allegations that Ukraine is selling weapons on the black market. Stradner said Russia is frustrated by continued Western military support for Ukraine, even though it cannot stop weapons deliveries such as HIMARS, and therefore relies on disinformation to attack Zelensky’s credibility. She urged preemptive exposure of Russian narratives. The article also recalls the infamous Soviet-era MMM Ponzi scheme, which spread across former Soviet states before collapsing in 1994. It defrauded millions and led to tighter Russian laws against deceptive advertising.

# Summary Ukraine's defense intelligence agency has reported that Russia is launching a coordinated disinformation campaign to undermine international support for President Volodymyr Zelensky. According to the agency's Thursday social media announcement, the Russian presidential administration has approved plans to create a new structure designed to discredit the Ukrainian president through false information campaigns. The campaign will primarily target Western European audiences, aiming to shift public perception and discourage support for Ukraine. The centerpiece is a website called the "Zelensky Fund," which has already been registered. Russia plans to register this fund across Europe and promote it through extensive pan-European advertising. The fund would operate using a multi-level marketing model, where participants earn rewards by recruiting others into the scheme. Russian disinformation expert Ivana Stradner notes this represents an escalation of Russia's longstanding efforts to discredit Zelensky. Since February, Moscow has emphasized Ukrainian corruption allegations and launched campaigns claiming Ukraine sells weapons on the black market. Stradner explains that Russia, unable to halt Western military aid like HIMARS shipments, relies on disinformation to damage Zelensky's credibility with Western audiences. The article contextualizes this strategy by referencing the infamous MMM Ponzi scheme of the 1990s, which defrauded millions across former Soviet states using similar multi-level marketing tactics. Stradner emphasizes the importance of preemptively exposing Russian disinformation campaigns to counter their narratives effectively.

An Uzbek man wanted internationally for large-scale embezzlement was detained at Moscow’s Vnukovo Airport and extradited to Uzbekistan, Russia’s Interior Ministry said on 15 May. Investigators say he headed a private firm, obtained a bank loan of about US$9 million claiming it would be used to grow cotton, and later earned roughly US$20 million from agricultural sales but did not repay the loan. After fleeing abroad, he was located through an Interpol tip and handed over to Uzbek law enforcement the same day.

# Summary An Uzbek citizen wanted for large-scale embezzlement was arrested at Moscow's Vnukovo Airport and extradited to Uzbekistan on May 15. The suspect, who headed a private company, obtained a $9 million bank loan for cotton cultivation but failed to repay it despite earning approximately $20 million from agricultural product sales. He subsequently fled the country. Russian authorities detained him following a tip from Uzbekistan's Interpol National Bureau about his expected arrival and immediately extradited him to face local law enforcement.

Exiled former Bolivian president Evo Morales said in an interview published Sunday that he wants to return to Bolivia and run for a Senate seat in the country’s May elections. Morales fled Bolivia in December after the military withdrew its support amid violent protests over his disputed re-election to a fourth consecutive term. He is now living in Argentina and said he would like to go home despite an outstanding arrest warrant. Morales, Bolivia’s first indigenous president, ruled for nearly 14 years, but he is barred from running for president in the May vote. In an interview with Chile’s *La Tercera*, he said he left Bolivia with only a suitcase of clothes, some food, and a few thousand dollars, first traveling to Mexico. He again denounced his removal as a coup and said, “What we lost with the coup we will recover on May 3 in democracy.” He also called himself a “victim of the United States” and said he intends to run for the Senate. Morales also said he wants to return despite investigations linked to an audio recording in which he allegedly urged supporters to cut off food supplies to cities. Meanwhile, a Bolivian judge ordered six months of preventive detention for Patricia Hermosa, Morales’s former cabinet chief and legal representative, who was arrested Friday on sedition, terrorism, and terrorism-financing charges. Separately, Luis Arce, Morales’s movement’s presidential candidate, returned to Bolivia and was immediately subpoenaed over alleged embezzlement and breach of duties.

# Summary Exiled former Bolivian president Evo Morales announced his intention to return home and run for senator in May elections, despite facing an arrest warrant. Morales fled Bolivia in December after the military withdrew support during protests over his contested re-election bid for a fourth term. Now residing in Argentina, he is barred from running as a presidential candidate but plans to seek a Senate seat instead. In an interview with a Chilean newspaper, Morales described his departure as carrying minimal possessions and characterized his replacement by acting president Jeanine Anez as a coup. He expressed confidence that his party would recover losses through democratic means in the May elections and declared himself a victim of U.S. imperialism. Despite probes against him, including an audio recording allegedly showing him urging supporters to cut food supplies to cities, Morales stated he would return if possible, insisting Bolivians want his comeback. Meanwhile, a Bolivian judge ordered six months preventive detention for Patricia Hermosa, Morales's former cabinet chief and legal representative, on charges of sedition and terrorism. Additionally, the Movement for Socialism's presidential candidate Luis Arce faced legal subpoenas upon returning to Bolivia.

Two Brazilian footballers, Mayke of Palmeiras and Gustavo Scarpa of Nottingham Forest, say they were victims of a crypto scam after investing through a firm run by fellow player Willian Bigode of Fluminense. According to reports from Suno, Lance, and ESPN Brasil, Mayke and Scarpa have filed a lawsuit against WLJC, described as a consultancy and financial planning company operated by Bigode. They allege that WLJC advised them to put more than $2 million into a crypto-related investment in May last year, promising monthly returns of 3.5% to 5%. The expected profits never arrived, and the players say they were unable to recover their money when they tried to withdraw it. They also claim Bigode introduced them to the project and are asking the court to compel him to appear and to order repayment of their funds. The outlets reported that WLJC recommended an investment in Xland Holding. However, in October 2022, the Public Ministry in Brazil’s Acre state identified Xland as a possible financial pyramid scheme. Bigode’s legal team rejects any wrongdoing, saying he acted in good faith and is himself a victim of the Xland scheme. They say he lost about $3.4 million and only recommended the investment after being introduced to it by people he trusted. The team also stressed that WLJC is not a brokerage and cannot make investments for clients. The case comes amid wider crypto turmoil in Brazil, including the recent bankruptcy of Indeal, a company linked to a suspected $193 million pyramid scheme.

# Summary Two prominent Brazilian soccer players, Mayke (Palmeiras) and Gustavo Scarpa (Nottingham Forest), have filed a legal suit against a financial consulting firm called WLJC, operated by fellow player Willian Bigode (Fluminense). The dispute centers on a cryptocurrency investment made in May of the previous year. Mayke and Scarpa claim they invested over $2 million based on WLJC's recommendation, expecting monthly returns of 3.5% to 5%. They allege the promised profits never materialized and were unable to withdraw their funds when requested. The investment was directed toward Xland Holding, a platform later identified by Brazilian authorities in October 2022 as a possible financial pyramid scheme. Mayke and Scarpa claim Bigode personally introduced them to the project. In response, Bigode's legal team denies acting in bad faith, arguing that he is also a victim of the Xland scheme, having lost approximately $3.4 million himself. They contend that Bigode was introduced to the investment by trusted associates and that WLJC operates solely as a financial planning firm without brokerage authority. The case reflects broader concerns about cryptocurrency fraud in Brazil, following a recent bankruptcy declaration by Indeal, a company allegedly responsible for a $193 million crypto pyramid scheme.

Former Peruvian president Alberto Fujimori, who is serving a 25-year sentence for corruption and crimes against humanity, was taken from prison to a hospital after suffering high blood pressure and severe pain in his tongue. Prison officials said a doctor recommended the transfer. The 77-year-old has repeatedly been hospitalized in recent months for various ailments, including gastric problems, cataract surgery, and five operations for a cancerous tongue growth. The move came 12 days after his daughter Keiko narrowly lost Peru’s presidential election. Fujimori, president from 1990 to 2000, was jailed in 2007 and convicted in 2009 over death squad killings, as well as embezzlement and bribery. His family has sought a health-based reprieve, but President Ollanta Humala rejected it in 2013.

# Summary Alberto Fujimori, the 77-year-old former Peruvian president serving a 25-year sentence for corruption and crimes against humanity, was hospitalized for high blood pressure and severe tongue pain. Fujimori has experienced multiple health issues recently, including gastric problems, cataract surgery, and five operations for tongue cancer. Imprisoned since 2007 and convicted in 2009, he was originally jailed for his involvement in death squad killings targeting alleged Shining Path guerrilla members during the 1990s. He has also been convicted of embezzlement and bribery. His daughter Keiko recently lost Peru's presidential election to Pedro Pablo Kuczynski. His family has requested a presidential reprieve on health grounds, but President Ollanta Humala rejected this in 2013, deeming his condition insufficiently serious.

Raymound Guadalupe Felix-Perez, a man from Sinaloa, Mexico, was sentenced Tuesday in U.S. federal court in Missouri to 20 years in prison without parole for his role in a fentanyl conspiracy. He had pleaded guilty to conspiring to distribute more than 400 grams of fentanyl and to commit money laundering. Court records say he kept supplying fentanyl from Sinaloa to co-conspirators in several states before being arrested June 30, 2024, while trying to enter the U.S. in California.

# Summary Raymound Guadalupe Felix-Perez, a Sinaloa man, was sentenced to 20 years in federal prison for his role in a fentanyl conspiracy. He pleaded guilty to conspiracy to distribute over 400 grams of fentanyl and money laundering conspiracy. Felix-Perez distributed fentanyl to co-conspirators across Missouri, Iowa, Arizona, and Idaho. He was arrested June 30, 2024, while attempting to enter the United States in California.

Ecuadorian President Guillermo Lasso ended impeachment proceedings against him on Wednesday by dissolving the opposition-led National Assembly, which had accused him of embezzlement. Lasso, a right-wing former banker elected in 2021, denied wrongdoing and said the legislature was focused on destabilizing his government. Under Ecuador’s constitution, he can rule by decree for up to six months. The National Electoral Council must call presidential and legislative elections within seven days, and voting must take place within 90 days. The winners will serve out the remaining terms of Lasso and the lawmakers he removed, which were due to end in May 2025. Lawmakers had alleged that Lasso failed to stop a state oil transport contract they said was riddled with irregularities and would cost the country millions, an accusation he rejected. Lasso had defended himself before Congress on Tuesday, saying there was no proof of misconduct.

# Summary Ecuadorian President Guillermo Lasso dissolved the opposition-led National Assembly on Wednesday to halt impeachment proceedings against him for alleged embezzlement. Lasso denies wrongdoing and claims the assembly was destabilizing his government. Under Ecuador's constitution, he can govern by decree for up to six months while the National Electoral Council calls new presidential and legislative elections within 90 days. The assembly had accused Lasso of failing to intervene in an irregular state oil company contract with Amazonas Tankers that would cost millions. Lasso rejected these accusations, insisting there was no evidence of misconduct. The newly elected officials will complete terms originally scheduled to end in May 2025. The former banker, elected in 2021, has faced constant opposition from the 137-member assembly.

Argentina is tightening controls on money leaving the country as its economy comes under growing pressure. The Central Bank of the Argentine Republic has reportedly begun restricting individual purchases of Bitcoin, following new limits on how much U.S. currency people can buy. The measures are intended to slow the drain on the country’s shrinking foreign exchange reserves. According to Reuters, foreign-currency outflows surged after President Mauricio Macri was removed from office on October 30. Under the new rules, Argentines can buy only $200 per month in U.S. dollars through local bank accounts and just $100 per month in cash through the end of the year. That is far below the earlier $10,000 monthly cap introduced in early September 2019. Capital controls have intensified since Argentina elected a new government on Sunday, triggering a sell-off in the peso, bonds and equities and adding pressure on the national currency. Macri’s administration had already imposed restrictions on dollar purchases in an effort to stabilize markets, but foreign reserves have still fallen by more than $20 billion. The new controls also appear to affect crypto transactions. Juan Llanos, an anti-money laundering specialist and advisor to Metal Pay and Bitwage, said on Twitter that Argentine Bitcoin exchanges were not advertising their services, fearing further government regulation. Cointelegraph Brazil reported that the central bank has banned the purchase of Bitcoin and other cryptocurrencies with locally issued credit, debit and prepaid cards, leaving bank transfers as the only remaining option for such purchases. The central bank said the measures were meant to preserve reserves amid uncertainty. Meanwhile, newly elected President Alberto Fernandez must manage a fragile economy while relying on a $57 billion IMF financing agreement approved last year. The United States, which holds 16.5% of IMF voting power, says Argentina should honor its commitments. Treasury Secretary Steven Mnuchin said Washington wants Argentina to succeed, but expects the new government to uphold its IMF obligations or formally request changes through the Fund.

# Argentina Tightens Financial Controls Amid Economic Crisis Argentina's Central Bank is implementing strict restrictions on foreign currency and cryptocurrency purchases to stem the outflow of dwindling foreign exchange reserves. Following the election of a new government on October 30, the country faces severe economic pressure. The Central Bank has dramatically reduced US dollar purchase limits to $200 monthly through bank accounts and $100 in cash—down from the previous $10,000-per-month cap established in September 2019. Additionally, Bitcoin and cryptocurrency purchases via credit and debit cards are now prohibited; only bank transfers are permitted. These measures follow significant currency volatility after President Mauricio Macri's removal from office. The peso, bonds, and equities experienced sharp sell-offs, while Argentina's foreign reserves have declined by over $20 billion. The restrictions aim to preserve remaining reserves and stabilize markets. Newly-elected President Alberto Fernández faces mounting challenges including rising poverty, inflation, and depleting reserves. His administration depends heavily on a $57 billion IMF financing agreement approved last year to stabilize the economy. The United States, which controls 16.5% of IMF voting power, is closely monitoring Argentina's compliance. US Treasury Secretary Steven Mnuchin stated that America expects the new government to uphold its IMF commitment, though the IMF may consider modification requests as part of Argentina's broader economic plan. Meanwhile, Argentine Bitcoin exchanges have reportedly ceased advertising services, fearing additional government regulations on cryptocurrency operations. The financial squeeze reflects Argentina's desperate attempt to preserve its economic stability while navigating international obligations.

Brazil’s state-run oil company Petrobras has again become the center of political turmoil as rising fuel prices intensify pressure on President Jair Bolsonaro ahead of October’s election. Bolsonaro, who is seeking re-election, is widely blamed by voters for inflation, which has climbed above 11% in the past year, largely driven by surging petrol costs. Fuel prices in Brazil have risen 33% over the past year, reflecting international market trends and, more recently, the spike in crude prices caused by Russia’s war in Ukraine. Last week, Bolsonaro dismissed Petrobras CEO Joaquim Silva e Luna, accusing the company’s pricing of making petrol “unaffordable” and calling it a “crime” against Brazilians. Silva e Luna defended Petrobras’s approach, saying that changing pricing policy would be like “manipulating the law of gravity.” His removal followed a similar firing a year earlier of his predecessor, Roberto Castello Branco, for comparable reasons. Bolsonaro’s move was widely seen as a political sacrifice to appease voters angered by rising living costs. Economist Gesner Oliveira said Silva e Luna was “sacrificed” to satisfy Bolsonaro’s electorate. At the same time, Bolsonaro’s main challenger, leftist former president Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, has also promised to “Brazilianize the fuel price,” meaning to align it more closely with domestic realities. Lula currently leads opinion polls. The leadership change at Petrobras has proved difficult. Bolsonaro’s first choice to replace Silva e Luna, economist Adriano Pires, withdrew over a possible conflict of interest linked to his consulting work. Another nominee, Rodolfo Landim, also stepped aside to focus on his role as president of Flamengo football club. Several other candidates reportedly declined the job before the government nominated Jose Mauro Coelho, an official at the Ministry of Mines and Energy. His appointment could be approved on April 13, which would make him Petrobras’s 40th CEO in 68 years. Analysts say the company faces intense political pressure, but its listed status and Brazil’s dependence on imported oil limit how much pricing policy can be changed. Some suggest a stabilization fund could help soften price swings, but not fundamentally alter the system. Petrobras also remains under the shadow of possible privatization, which is supported by Bolsonaro and some of his allies.

# Rising Petrol Prices Fuel Crisis at Brazil's Petrobras Brazil's state-run oil company Petrobras faces mounting political pressure as fuel prices surge, creating uncertainty ahead of October's presidential election. President Jair Bolsonaro, seeking re-election, fired Petrobras CEO Joaquim Silva e Luna last week, blaming him for "unaffordable" petrol prices that constitute a "crime" against Brazilians. Fuel prices have risen 33 percent over the past year, while inflation nationwide has exceeded 11 percent. Polls show three-quarters of Brazilians hold Bolsonaro responsible for their economic hardship. Russia's invasion of Ukraine has further exacerbated crude price spikes. Silva e Luna's dismissal represents political sacrifice to appease voters, according to economist Gesner Oliveira. This marks the second CEO firing under Bolsonaro—his predecessor, Roberto Castello Branco, was similarly dismissed for fuel price concerns. Finding a replacement has proven challenging. Bolsonaro's initial choice, economist Adriano Pires, withdrew due to conflicts of interest with his energy consulting firm. His second nominee, Rodolfo Landim, also declined to focus on his Flamengo football club presidency. Several other candidates rejected the position, prompting the government to nominate Jose Mauro Coelho from the Ministry of Mines and Energy on Wednesday. His appointment could be approved at a shareholders' meeting on April 13, making him the 40th Petrobras CEO in 68 years. Bolsonaro's leftist rival, former President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, has also pledged to "Brazilianize the fuel price," adapting it to local conditions. Lula currently leads in election polls. Analysts warn the CEO position faces intense political pressure as an "easy political response to a complex economic problem." However, Petrobras' listing on international exchanges and Brazil's reliance on imported oil limit pricing flexibility. While stabilization funds could mitigate fluctuations, comprehensive tariff policy changes remain impossible. Petrobras recently recovered from the 2014-2021 Operation Car Wash corruption investigation and posted a record $20 billion net profit in 2021 despite pandemic impacts. The company now faces potential privatization, a policy favored by Bolsonaro and his allies, adding further uncertainty to its future.

Libyans on Wednesday marked the 10th anniversary of the 2011 uprising that toppled and led to the killing of longtime ruler Moammar Gadhafi, as hopes centered on a newly appointed interim government intended to steer the country toward elections later in the year and help reunify the fractured nation. Celebrations began late Tuesday in Tripoli, where people gathered in the main square under tight security. Streets and squares in the capital had been cleaned and decorated with banners and photographs commemorating the uprising. Similar events were held in other parts of the country, including the south and east. In Sabha, fireworks during the celebrations in the Mansheya neighborhood apparently killed a child and injured about 15 others, according to medical and city officials. The municipality called for an investigation into the explosion. In Benghazi, the eastern city regarded as the birthplace of the 2011 revolt, a small number of people gathered in the square despite unusually cold weather. Hassan Wanis, who heads Tripoli’s general authority for culture, said commemorations were planned across Libya’s three historic regions — Tripolitania in the west, Cyrenaica in the east and Fezzan in the southwest — and said people were especially eager to celebrate “in order to unify the country.” Libya’s uprising came amid the broader Arab Spring, after revolts in Tunisia and Egypt. But unlike those countries, Libya descended into prolonged instability after Gadhafi’s fall. The oil-rich nation has since become one of the region’s most difficult conflicts, plagued by armed groups, militant activity, looting and human trafficking. For years, Libya has been split between rival authorities: a weak U.N.-backed government in Tripoli, where armed factions wield significant power, and an eastern administration supported by Gen. Khalifa Hifter. Both sides have foreign backers. The latest major fighting began in April 2019, when Hifter, backed by the United Arab Emirates, Egypt and Russia, launched an offensive to seize Tripoli. That effort failed after Turkey increased support for the Tripoli-based government, sending troops and thousands of Syrian mercenaries. U.N.-led negotiations later produced an October agreement that ended hostilities and called for foreign fighters and mercenaries to leave within three months, along with compliance with the U.N. arms embargo. Those terms have not been fulfilled. The talks also led to the Libyan Political Dialogue Forum, which earlier this month selected an interim leadership: a three-member Presidential Council and a prime minister to guide Libya to elections scheduled for Dec. 24. The new leadership includes Mohammad Younes Menfi, a diplomat from eastern Libya, as chairman of the Presidential Council, and Abdul Hamid Mohammed Dbeibah, a businessman from Misrata, as prime minister. Dbeibah was still working on forming a Cabinet, which must be approved by the divided parliament. Menfi arrived in Tripoli on Tuesday and met with Dbeibah and other officials. U.N. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres, in calls with both men, urged them to ensure the elections proceed and the cease-fire deal is implemented, including the withdrawal of foreign forces. The U.N. says there are at least 20,000 mercenaries and foreign fighters in Libya. Amnesty International also used the anniversary to call for accountability for war crimes and serious human rights abuses committed over the past decade, warning that violence and impunity will continue unless those responsible are brought to justice rather than given power. Libya has also become a major transit route for migrants fleeing conflict and poverty, with traffickers sending people in unsafe boats across the Mediterranean. Many drown, while others are detained in harsh conditions.

# Libya Marks 10th Anniversary of 2011 Uprising Libyans celebrated the 10th anniversary of their 2011 uprising that toppled longtime dictator Moammar Gadhafi on Wednesday, with celebrations across the nation and hopes centered on a newly appointed government tasked with unifying the divided country through elections scheduled for December 24. Festivities began Tuesday evening in the capital, Tripoli, where crowds gathered in the main square under tight security as streets were decorated with banners and commemorative photos. Celebrations also occurred in other cities, though a fireworks accident in Sabha killed a child and injured approximately 15 people, prompting calls for investigation. Eastern Benghazi, birthplace of the 2011 uprising, also held observances despite cold weather sweeping the country. Hassan Wanis, head of Tripoli's general authority for culture, noted that celebrations were planned across Libya's three historic regions—Tripolitania, Cyrenaica, and Fezzan—emphasizing that people were particularly ready to celebrate "in order to unify the country." The 2011 uprising occurred amid the broader Arab Spring movement that toppled Tunisia's and Egypt's governments. However, Libya has since become one of the Middle East's most intractable conflicts, descending into chaos and becoming a haven for Islamic militants and armed groups engaged in looting and human trafficking. For years, Libya has been fractured between rival administrations: a weak UN-backed government in Tripoli, controlled by various armed factions, and an eastern government backed by strongman General Khalifa Hifter, each supported by foreign powers. In April 2019, Hifter launched an offensive to capture Tripoli, but his campaign collapsed when Turkey increased military support for the Tripoli administration with troops and Syrian mercenaries. UN-led negotiations resulted in an October ceasefire agreement calling for foreign force withdrawal within three months and adherence to an arms embargo—provisions not yet met. These talks established the Libyan Political Dialogue Forum, which appointed an interim government to lead the country toward elections. The interim government includes Mohammad Younes Menfi, a diplomat from eastern Libya, as Presidential Council chairman, and Abdul Hamid Mohammed Dbeibah, a businessman from western Misrata, as prime minister. Dbeibah is consulting on Cabinet formation requiring parliamentary confirmation. Menfi arrived in Tripoli Tuesday and met with officials, while UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres emphasized the importance of holding elections and implementing the ceasefire, including withdrawing approximately 20,000 foreign mercenaries and fighters currently in Libya. Amnesty International called for accountability for past war crimes and human rights violations, warning that without justice for perpetrators, "the violence, chaos, systematic human rights abuses and endless suffering of civilians that have characterized post-Gadhafi Libya will continue unabated." Additionally, Libya has become a major transit point for African and Middle Eastern migrants seeking escape from conflict and poverty. Traffickers pack desperate families into unreliable boats crossing the perilous Mediterranean route, where thousands drown or face detention in squalid conditions if captured.

Cape Town-based Premier Hotels & Resorts brand and marketing manager Alan Campbell says tourism is being reshaped by changing consumer habits, and he highlights several trends expected to influence the industry in 2017. One major shift is the move to mobile, as Google has confirmed that more searches now happen on mobile devices than on computers. This has made it easier for tourists to research, plan and book trips at any time, prompting the industry to respond with apps. Beyond review platforms such as TripAdvisor, hotels are also developing their own apps so guests can book stays, order room service, arrange spa appointments, request wake-up calls, have luggage collected and call taxis. Campbell also points to the rise of “bleisure” travel, where business trips are combined with leisure. He says these trips can help travellers work more effectively, reduce the stress of business travel and keep them more relaxed. Hotels that provide strong business and leisure facilities are therefore better positioned to attract this market. Another trend is the growth of intergenerational holidays, as families increasingly use group travel as a chance for grandparents, parents, children and extended relatives to spend time together. Properties that cater for both older and younger guests, including those offering joined suites, are benefiting. He also notes a surge in social media reviews, with platforms such as Facebook, Google Plus and Twitter becoming increasingly important sources of travel feedback, overtaking traditional review sites. Looking ahead, Campbell expects more South Africans to choose staycations and lesser-known destinations because of financial pressure. He also predicts reduced government travel spending as departments seek to cut expenditure by R1bn year-on-year. While optimistic about South Africa’s appeal to international visitors, he says the political climate could affect perceptions of the country.

# Tourism Trends to Watch in 2017 The tourism industry is experiencing significant shifts driven by changing consumer behavior, according to Alan Campbell, brand and marketing manager of Premier Hotels & Resorts. **Mobile Technology Dominance** Mobile devices now generate more searches than computers, enabling tourists to explore, plan, and book travel anywhere. Hotels have responded by developing apps that allow guests to book stays, order room service, arrange spa appointments, and request taxis. **Bleisure Travel Growth** "Bleisure" tourism—combining business and leisure—is increasingly popular, as travelers report improved work effectiveness and reduced stress. Hotels offering comprehensive business and leisure facilities are capitalizing on this trend. **Intergenerational Vacations** Multi-generational family holidays are rising in popularity as families seek quality time together. Accommodations offering connecting suites and facilities for various age groups are experiencing increased demand. **Social Media Reviews** Reviews have shifted from traditional platforms like TripAdvisor to social media sites including Facebook, Google Plus, and Twitter, which now surpass traditional review sites as traveler resources. **2017 Predictions** Campbell anticipates several trends for the coming year. South Africans will likely choose domestic staycations over international travel due to financial constraints and will explore lesser-known areas. Government travel spending is expected to decrease significantly as part of budget cuts. While Campbell remains optimistic about South Africa's appeal to international tourists, he expresses concern about how the country's political climate may influence visitor perceptions, hoping South Africa will generate positive media coverage.

The European Union’s CBRN Centres of Excellence and the African Union will hold a forum in Addis Ababa on December 12-13, 2023, to strengthen cooperation on chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear risk mitigation in Africa. The event comes amid growing concern over CBRN threats, highlighted by incidents such as the 2021 fuel tanker explosion in Freetown, Sierra Leone, and the Ebola outbreak. The EU CBRN CoE initiative, which includes 64 partner countries, 28 of them in Africa, supports countries in preventing, preparing for, responding to, and recovering from CBRN events at both strategic and technical levels. Its regional projects cover areas such as epidemic preparedness, chemical risk prevention, falsified medicines, and border control, while national support includes forming CBRN teams and drafting action plans. As the initiative enters its 14th year, the forum will bring together African Union officials, regional bodies, international organizations, and partner countries to align priorities and unlock synergies for a safer Africa.

# Summary The EU CBRN CoE - AU Forum, scheduled for December 12-13, 2023, in Addis Ababa, will address Chemical, Biological, Radiological, and Nuclear (CBRN) safety and security risks in Africa. Recent incidents like the 2021 Sierra Leone fuel tanker explosion and Ebola outbreak highlight the urgency of proactive measures. The EU CBRN CoE Initiative, with 64 partner countries including 28 from Africa, strengthens national capacities in preventing, preparing for, and responding to CBRN events. The initiative implements regional projects in epidemics, chemical risk prevention, falsified medicines, and border control, while supporting countries in establishing national CBRN teams and action plans. As the initiative enters its 14th year, the Forum aims to expand collaboration among African Union representatives, Regional Economic Communities, international organizations, and partner countries to effectively mitigate CBRN risks and enhance Africa's security.

The European Union’s foreign policy chief, Federica Mogherini, condemned the terrorist attack on Tripoli’s Corinthia Hotel, calling it a “reprehensible act of terrorism” that undermines efforts to restore peace and stability in Libya. The attack on Tuesday killed at least six people and injured three. It began with a car bomb explosion outside the luxury hotel, followed by an assault by three armed men; one attacker was arrested after a gunfight with security forces. According to security sources, three of the dead were foreign nationals shot by the gunmen, while the other three were security officers killed in the blast. Mogherini expressed EU solidarity with the victims, noting the hotel housed members of foreign diplomatic missions and Libya’s Tripoli-based Islamic Government chief, Omar al Hasi. She also reiterated EU support for UN-led talks among Libya’s rival political factions, as the country remains divided between competing governments in Tripoli and Tobruk since the 2011 ouster of Muammar Gaddafi.

# EU Condemns Terrorist Attack on Tripoli Hotel On January 27, a terrorist attack struck the Corinthia Hotel in Tripoli, Libya, killing at least six people and injuring three others. The assault began with a car bomb explosion outside the luxury hotel, followed by an assault by three armed gunmen. One attacker was arrested after exchanging fire with security forces. Three victims were foreign nationals shot by the terrorists, while three were security officers killed in the explosion. The hotel houses foreign diplomatic missions and was home to Libya's Islamic Government head, Omar al Hasi. EU High Representative Federica Mogherini condemned the attack as "reprehensible" and expressed solidarity with victims. She emphasized the EU's support for UN-supervised talks between competing Libyan political forces, aiming to resolve the country's internal conflict through dialogue and respect. Libya faces ongoing political instability with parallel government and parliament structures competing for power between Tripoli and Tobruk, stemming from Colonel Gaddafi's 2011 overthrow.

The death toll from a fuel truck explosion in Tanzania has risen to 100, officials said Wednesday, as more victims died from severe burns sustained in the 10 August blast near Morogoro, about 200 kilometres west of Dar es Salaam. Aminiel Aligaesha of the National Hospital said two people died during the day on Tuesday and another late that night, pushing the total to 100. The count had stood at 95 on Sunday, after two more deaths were reported Monday. At least 30 people died in the days after the accident, when a fireball swept through a crowd that had gathered around an overturned tanker to collect leaking petrol. Officials said the explosion began when a man tried to remove the truck’s battery, causing sparks that ignited the fuel. A doctor said most survivors had burns on more than 80% of their bodies and remained in critical condition. Many victims were motorbike taxi drivers. The disaster is the latest in a series of deadly fuel tanker explosions across Africa.

# Tanzania Fuel Truck Explosion Death Toll Reaches 100 A fuel truck explosion in Tanzania on August 10 has killed 100 people, with the death toll rising as victims succumbed to severe burns in subsequent days. The disaster occurred near Morogoro, 200 kilometers west of Dar es Salaam, when an overturned tanker ignited as crowds gathered to collect leaking petrol. Officials determined that a man attempting to remove the truck's battery created sparks that ignited the fuel. At least 30 victims died in the days following the explosion. Many of the deceased were motorbike taxi drivers who rushed to siphon fuel. Hospital officials report that most survivors suffered burns covering over 80% of their bodies and remain in critical condition. This tragedy represents the third major fuel tanker disaster in Africa this year, following incidents in Nigeria (45 deaths) and Niger (nearly 80 deaths). Previous catastrophes include a 2010 explosion in the Democratic Republic of Congo that killed 292 people and a 2015 incident in South Sudan claiming 203 lives.

At the ECA’s annual Adebayo Adedeji Lecture during the 54th Conference of Ministers of Finance, Economic Planning and Development in Dakar, Paul Tiyambe Zeleza of Case Western Reserve University argued that Africa must build high computing capacity and digitalize to succeed in the fourth industrial revolution. He said the new industrial era will affect all sectors, including education, technology, and health, and warned that Africa cannot afford to be marginalized again after being left behind in the previous three revolutions. Zeleza urged governments to promote digitalization, rethink capital spending, and develop holistic online curricula to support economic and digital transformation. He also called for integrated, inclusive, innovative, and sustainable institutions. According to him, African economies still rely heavily on primary commodity production and exports, a legacy of colonial structures. He linked the continent’s future to human capital, demographic growth, and effective policies, while stressing the need to close the gap between policy design and implementation.

# Summary At Africa's Conference of Ministers of Finance in Dakar, Senegal, Professor Paul Tiyambe Zeleza emphasized that Africa must develop high computing capacity to participate in the Fourth Industrial Revolution. Unlike previous industrial revolutions where Africa was marginalized, the continent must not fall behind this transformative shift affecting all sectors, including education, technology, and health. Prof. Zeleza advocated for digitalization, reformed capital expenditure strategies, and comprehensive online curriculum systems to achieve economic and digital transformation. He noted that African economies remain structurally dependent on primary commodity production since colonial times. He identified five key agendas of African nationalism: decolonization, nation-building, development, democracy, and regional integration. Regarding human capital development, he highlighted the importance of demographic structure, government policies for socioeconomic systems, and building capabilities. Population growth can either advance or hinder development depending on human capital quality, he concluded, while emphasizing the critical need to bridge the gap between policy design and implementation.

Russian media reported that North Korea will send 1,000 deminers and 5,000 military construction workers to Russia’s Kursk region to help with reconstruction, signaling a further deepening of military ties between Pyongyang and Moscow. The Russian state news agency RIA Novosti said the announcement came from Sergei Shoigu, a top Russian security official, during his visit to Pyongyang for talks with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. The report follows earlier cooperation in which North Korea has already sent troops and conventional weapons to support Russia’s war against Ukraine. In April, Moscow and Pyongyang officially confirmed for the first time that North Korean soldiers were fighting alongside Russian forces to repel a Ukrainian incursion into the Kursk border area. President Vladimir Putin thanked North Korea for its role and vowed not to forget its sacrifices. According to Russian state media, Shoigu and Kim also discussed rebuilding Kursk during a prior visit earlier this month. Russia’s Tass news agency said Shoigu returned to Pyongyang on Tuesday on a special mission from Putin, though North Korean media had not immediately confirmed the trip. U.S. and South Korean officials have warned that North Korea may be seeking Russian technology transfers in exchange for its support.

# Summary North Korea will send approximately 1,000 military deminers and 5,000 construction workers to Russia's Kursk region to support reconstruction efforts, according to Russian state media citing security official Sergei Shoigu. This announcement represents another expansion of military cooperation between the two nations. Shoigu made these comments during a visit to Pyongyang for meetings with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. The two officials had previously discussed rebuilding the Kursk region earlier in the month. North Korea has already deployed thousands of troops and conventional weapons to support Russia's war in Ukraine. The U.S. and South Korea have expressed concerns that North Korea may receive Russian military technology transfers in exchange, potentially strengthening its nuclear capabilities. In April, both countries officially confirmed North Korean troop deployment to Russia for the first time, with soldiers fighting alongside Russian forces against Ukrainian incursions into the Kursk border region. Putin previously thanked North Korea for its participation and pledged to remember their sacrifices.

In Bohol, Philippines, a fisherman demonstrated how dynamite fishing works by throwing a bottle bomb from an outrigger boat, triggering an explosion that killed or stunned fish and shattered coral below. The blast can devastate nearly everything within a 30- to 100-foot radius, rupturing fish organs, breaking spines and turning reefs into rubble, with little surviving from plankton to sharks. The Philippines, home to about 10,500 square miles of coral reef and a major center of marine biodiversity, has long struggled to curb illegal fishing and broader human damage. That challenge is now more urgent as climate change worsens ocean stress. A survey of Philippine reefs from 2015 to 2017 found no reefs in excellent condition, with 90 percent rated poor or fair. A 2017 UN report warned all 29 World Heritage coral reefs could die by 2100 without major cuts in carbon emissions.

# Dynamite Fishing Decimates Philippine Coral Reefs In the Philippines, dynamite fishing is devastating marine ecosystems with devastating efficiency. Fishermen use bottle bombs to kill fish indiscriminately, destroying everything within a 30- to 100-foot explosion radius, including coral, plankton, sea horses, anemones, and sharks. The Philippines contains 10,500 square miles of coral reef and represents a global center for marine biodiversity, yet the country has struggled to protect these ecosystems against illegal fishing and institutional neglect. A 2015-2017 survey published in the Philippine Journal of Science reveals the severity of the damage: no reefs remain in excellent condition, and 90 percent are classified as poor or fair. A 2017 UN report warns that all 29 World Heritage coral reefs, including one in the Philippines, will die by 2100 unless carbon emissions are drastically reduced. Stopping illegal fishing practices has become increasingly urgent as climate change threatens ocean ecosystems.

North Korea said Saturday that leader Kim Jong Un personally supervised another test-firing of a new multiple rocket launcher system, a weapon it says could improve its ability to hit targets in South Korea and U.S. military bases there. The announcement from the state-run Korean Central News Agency came one day after South Korea’s military reported that North Korea had fired projectiles twice into the sea off its east coast, marking the North’s third round of weapons tests in a little more than a week. According to KCNA, Kim expressed “great satisfaction” with Friday’s tests. The agency said the launches confirmed the system’s “altitude control level flight performance, track changing capability, accuracy of hitting a target and warhead explosion power of the guided ordnance rocket.” North Korea did not directly mention the United States or South Korea in its report. South Korean officials, however, said they and the U.S. military assessed the Friday launches as likely short-range ballistic missiles. South Korea’s military also said the weapons tested on Wednesday were ballistic missiles, despite North Korea’s claim that they were part of a newly developed “large-caliber multiple launch guided rocket system.” The South Korean Joint Chiefs of Staff said the Friday launches occurred at 2:59 a.m. and 3:23 a.m. from an eastern coastal area, and that the projectiles traveled 220 kilometers, or 137 miles. That range would be enough to reach the Seoul metropolitan area, where about half of South Korea’s population lives, as well as a major U.S. military base near the capital. The latest launches followed a July 25 test of two short-range ballistic missiles that South Korean officials said flew 600 kilometers before landing in the sea. North Korea said those tests were meant as a “solemn warning” to South Korea over its purchase of advanced U.S.-made fighter jets and planned joint military exercises with the United States, which Pyongyang calls invasion rehearsals. North Korea also tested short-range missiles on May 4 and May 9. The increased testing has been seen by experts as an effort to pressure Washington and Seoul amid stalled nuclear negotiations and upcoming U.S.-South Korea military drills. Analysts warn the North could intensify its weapons demonstrations in the coming months if diplomacy does not progress. The launches drew condemnation from Britain, France and Germany after a closed U.N. Security Council briefing. The three countries said North Korea’s ballistic activity violated U.N. sanctions and urged Pyongyang to enter meaningful negotiations with the United States on dismantling its nuclear weapons program. They said sanctions should remain until North Korea’s nuclear and ballistic missile programs are dismantled. In a separate KCNA report, an unidentified North Korean Foreign Ministry spokesperson rejected the criticism, saying the country has never recognized U.N. resolutions it views as a “grave provocation.” The spokesperson argued North Korea is not bound by any agreement limiting missile ranges and said its suspension of nuclear and intercontinental ballistic missile tests, announced by Kim last year during outreach to Washington, was voluntary and based on goodwill. President Donald Trump said Thursday he was not worried about the recently tested weapons, calling them “short-range missiles” and “very standard.” But the latest launches have dampened hopes raised after Trump’s June 30 meeting with Kim at the inter-Korean border, where they agreed to restart stalled working-level nuclear talks. No known follow-up meetings have taken place, and North Korea has said it will decide whether to continue its moratorium on nuclear and ICBM tests based partly on whether the planned August U.S.-South Korea exercises go ahead.

# North Korea Conducts Another Rocket Launcher Test North Korea announced Saturday that leader Kim Jong Un supervised another test of a new multiple rocket launcher system designed to enhance the country's capacity to strike targets in South Korea and U.S. military bases located there. This announcement followed South Korea's military detection of North Korean projectile launches into the sea off its eastern coast—the third weapons test in just over a week. The test occurred Friday, with launches detected at 2:59 a.m. and 3:23 a.m. from an eastern coastal area. The projectiles traveled 220 kilometers (137 miles), a range sufficient to cover the Seoul metropolitan area, home to approximately half of South Korea's population, and a major U.S. military base nearby. According to North Korea's state news agency KCNA, Kim expressed "great satisfaction" with the test, which confirmed the system's altitude control, track-changing capability, target accuracy, and warhead explosion power. However, South Korea's military assessed the Friday launches as short-range ballistic missiles, contradicting North Korea's characterization of them as a "large-caliber multiple launch guided rocket system." This discrepancy reflects ongoing disagreement over weapon classifications between the two nations. Experts attribute North Korea's increased testing activity to pressure tactics regarding stalled nuclear negotiations with the United States and planned U.S.-South Korea military exercises. Weapons demonstrations could intensify if diplomatic progress isn't achieved. The broader context includes a July 25 test of two short-range ballistic missiles that flew 600 kilometers, which North Korea claimed served as a "solemn warning" against South Korea's purchase of U.S. fighter jets and scheduled military drills. Additional tests occurred in May. International response came from the United Kingdom, France, and Germany, who condemned the ballistic activity as UN sanction violations and urged meaningful negotiations for nuclear disarmament. However, North Korea's Foreign Ministry spokesperson rejected these criticisms, asserting that North Korea never signed agreements limiting missile ranges and isn't bound by legal requirements. The spokesperson defended the weapons as rocket artillery and reaffirmed that any projectile follows a ballistic curve due to gravity. The spokesperson also referenced North Korea's previous unilateral suspension of nuclear and intercontinental ballistic missile tests as gestures of "goodwill" toward dialogue, suggesting these suspensions remain conditional on U.S. behavior. President Trump downplayed concerns Thursday, calling the tested weapons "very standard" short-range missiles. Nevertheless, recent demonstrations have dampened optimism following Trump's June 30 border summit with Kim, where leaders agreed to resume working-level nuclear talks that had stalled since February. No known meetings have occurred since that agreement. North Korea has warned that U.S.-South Korea military exercises scheduled for August would violate the summit agreement and indicated it will decide the fate of its diplomacy with Washington based on whether these exercises proceed.

Two employees of a cooking oil factory in Caloocan were left in critical condition after inhaling toxic fumes from a sewer while cleaning a grease trap, officials said. Limuel Ibe and Bobby Benitez reportedly lost consciousness after breathing in toxic hydrogen sulfide at Trans Asia’s plant in Barangay 167. Plant operations head Rodel Gomez said the men fainted after being overcome by a foul smell while descending into an open canal five feet deep, and denied any chemical or gas leak. He also clarified that 11 workers were not hospitalized for poisoning; nine were brought in only for precautionary checkups. The two victims remain confined at East Avenue Medical Center and were referred to a toxicologist.

# Summary Two employees at a Trans Asia cooking oil factory in Caloocan, Philippines, lost consciousness after inhaling toxic hydrogen sulfide fumes from a grease trap. Limuel Ibe and Bobby Benitez fainted while cleaning the five-foot-deep canal after washing it with water. The plant operations head denied chemical leakage, attributing the incident to foul odors. Additionally, nine other employees were hospitalized for preventive checkups. Both unconscious workers remain hospitalized at East Avenue Medical Center under toxicologist care. The company expressed openness to sanitation department inspections.

A month after a fiery tanker collision in the East China Sea, an unusual and largely hidden oil disaster has begun threatening some of Asia’s most productive fishing waters, from China toward Japan and potentially farther. The spill, caused by the sinking of the Iranian-owned tanker Sanchi, is being described by experts as unlike any major oil spill before because the petroleum involved is condensate, a toxic liquid byproduct of natural gas production. Unlike crude oil, condensate does not form thick black slicks or obvious surface masses that can be skimmed from the sea, so the damage has been difficult to see, track, and publicize. The accident began on the evening of Jan. 6, when the Sanchi, a Panamanian-flagged tanker owned by Iran, collided with the CF Crystal, a Hong Kong-flagged bulk carrier carrying grain from the United States to China. The collision occurred about 160 nautical miles east of Shanghai, in one of the world’s busiest shipping lanes. The Sanchi exploded, burned for more than a week, and eventually sank on Jan. 14. All 32 crew members are presumed dead. The Crystal was able to reach harbor and is now in a port in Zhoushan, China. What makes this spill especially alarming is the type of fuel released. Experts estimate that as much as 111,000 metric tons of condensate may have entered the sea, making it the worst tanker spill at sea since 1991 and likely the largest condensate spill ever recorded. Some of the condensate may have burned off during the fire, but the amount that entered the ocean is still uncertain. Because condensate evaporates or dissolves rather than clumping into visible patches, there is no easy way to remove it once it is in the water. It can remain toxic for some time while dispersing more quickly than crude oil. Scientists and environmental groups say the spill may already have reached a rich marine ecosystem around Zhoushan, an archipelago where the Yangtze River meets the East China Sea. That area alone produced about five million tons of seafood for China last year, including crab, squid, yellow croaker, mackerel and hairtail. Experts warn that if the contamination continues drifting east, it could eventually affect Japanese fisheries as well, including waters around Okinawa and, possibly, as far as Tokyo. Exposure to condensate is considered highly dangerous to humans, and while the effects of eating contaminated fish are not well studied, experts strongly caution against it. Paul Johnston of Greenpeace Research Laboratories at the University of Exeter said this was “an oil spill of a type we haven’t seen before,” adding that determining its impact may be “a huge task — probably next to impossible.” Katya Popova of the National Oceanography Center in England said the lack of a coordinated international response had worsened the scale of the disaster. Because the spill is not producing the kind of dramatic images associated with crude oil disasters, public attention has been limited, which may have slowed efforts to respond forcefully. China, as the country closest to the accident, has taken the lead in investigating and monitoring the spill. The government has also faced criticism for what some regard as a slow and insufficient response. Officials in Beijing announced on Feb. 1 that fish samples taken four to five nautical miles from the sunken vessel contained traces of petroleum hydrocarbons, indicating possible condensate contamination. They said testing would be expanded to a 90-mile radius and that fish entering markets would be closely monitored. Authorities also imposed a fishing ban in affected areas. Chinese officials have tried to present the government as actively managing the crisis, issuing regular statements and briefings and showing video of cleanup and monitoring operations. Han Xu, deputy director of the fisheries administration bureau at the Ministry of Agriculture, said the accident had had “a certain impact on the density of fishery resources,” though the full extent remained unknown. The wreck lies at a depth of 115 meters and is believed still to be leaking condensate and other fuel. Officials said they were still investigating pollution and fishery impacts. The spill has caused anxiety among people in the fishing and seafood trade around Zhoushan, though concerns are often voiced cautiously. At the International Aquatic Product City in Putuo, one fish wholesaler said the quality of seafood would decline because of oil in the water. Yet at the East River Fish Market, another seller dismissed questions by insisting, “Our fish are not from out there,” even though some likely were. The size of the affected area has fluctuated as the spill spread and dispersed. In January, three separate surface spills were spotted over an area of more than 128 square miles. But because condensate is hard to see and because the amount released remains uncertain, the true extent of the contamination is still unclear. China’s Ministry of Transportation first downplayed the possibility of a spill, then said 136,000 metric tons had been lost, before revising the figure downward to 111,000 tons. Even at the lower estimate, the disaster remains enormous. Some contamination may also have reached the air. Officials said they were testing air samples in provinces around Shanghai, since some of the fuel likely burned during the blaze. If oil washes ashore, cleanup may be possible in limited places using machinery or manual labor, but the larger challenge is that nobody knows how much of the high seas has been affected or where the pollution is now drifting. The spill is moving eastward toward Japan, though currents and winds make its path uncertain. The Japanese Coast Guard reported finding black globules on at least nine islands along the chain between Okinawa and Japan’s main islands. Those globules were not from the condensate itself, but may have come from other oil released by the Sanchi. Their appearance nonetheless raised concern that the contamination could already be affecting Japan’s third most important fishery, known for bonito and yellowfin tuna.
