Scientists have discovered a remarkably rich cache of 512-million-year-old marine fossils in southern China, revealing that deep-water animal life was thriving shortly after one of the earliest mass extinctions in Earth’s history. The fossils, found in mudstone at a single quarry in Huayuan county, Hunan province, belong to the Cambrian Period and preserve an exceptionally diverse ecosystem that researchers say rivals the famous Burgess Shale in Canada and Chengjiang biota in China. The team collected more than 50,000 specimens and analyzed 8,681 of them, identifying 153 species across 16 major animal groups. Of those species, 91 were previously unknown. The fossils are unusually well preserved, in some cases down to the cellular level, and reveal fine details such as legs, gills, guts, eyes and even nerves. The assemblage, named the Huayuan biota, includes invertebrates of many shapes and sizes, among them an apex predator with grasping appendages and other creatures covered in spines or resembling a cactus. According to lead author Han Zeng of the Nanjing Institute of Geology and Paleontology, the site represents a deep-water environment along the edge of the South China continental shelf. The fossils show a flourishing ecosystem with animals occupying different parts of the water column and seafloor, and using a variety of feeding strategies and forms of movement. The most common groups were arthropods, cnidarians such as jellyfish and corals, and sponges. The top predators were radiodonts, primitive arthropods equipped with raptorial appendages used to seize prey while swimming. Although all of the animals found were invertebrates, the site also contains abundant members of a group regarded as the closest relatives of vertebrates. The Huayuan biota is especially important because it offers the clearest view yet of marine life after the Sinsk event, a mass extinction about 513.5 million years ago that may have been triggered by volcanism and rapid climate change. That event interrupted the Cambrian explosion, the evolutionary burst during which most major animal groups first appeared. Senior author Maoyan Zhu said the fossils suggest the extinction affected deeper-water animals less severely than shallow-water species. The study also found surprising overlap with the later Burgess Shale, including species previously known only from Canada. Researchers say this may indicate that early animal larvae were already dispersing widely through ocean currents in the Cambrian seas.

# Chinese Fossils Reveal Thriving Marine Ecosystem Half a Billion Years Ago Scientists have discovered over 50,000 exceptionally well-preserved fossils in southern China dating back approximately 512 million years to the Cambrian Period. The fossils, collected from a single mudstone quarry in Hunan province's Huayuan county, represent a diverse deep-water ecosystem that flourished following the first major mass extinction event in animal history. Researchers examined 8,681 specimens and identified 153 species, with 91 previously unknown to science. The fossils span 16 major animal groups and are preserved so thoroughly that cellular details including legs, gills, guts, eyes, and nerves remain visible. This collection, termed the Huayuan biota, rivals two other significant fossil assemblages—Canada's Burgess Shale and China's Chengjiang biota—in revealing Cambrian marine life. The dominant organisms included arthropods (ancestors of modern crabs, insects, and spiders), cnidarians (jellyfish and corals), and sponges. The apex predators were radiodonts, primitive arthropods with specialized grasping appendages for capturing prey while swimming. The ecosystem contained diverse feeding habits and mobility patterns, with animals distributed throughout the water column and within marine sediment. The Huayuan biota existed in a deep-water environment at the continental shelf edge, following the Sinsk event—a mass extinction occurring 513.5 million years ago caused by volcanism triggering rapid climate change. This extinction interrupted the Cambrian explosion, when most major animal groups first emerged. Notably, the Huayuan fossils suggest that deep-water creatures survived this extinction better than their shallow-water counterparts. Significantly, the Huayuan biota shares several animal species with the Burgess Shale, located thousands of miles away. These shared taxa include arthropods previously found only in Canada. Paleontologist Han Zeng explained this distribution by proposing that early animal larvae could spread across oceans via currents during the Cambrian period. The study, published in Nature and led by researchers from the Nanjing Institute of Geology and Paleontology, provides unprecedented insights into how marine ecosystems recovered following the Sinsk event and demonstrates the remarkable geographic distribution of early animal life.

More than 130 countries have agreed to a major overhaul of international corporate taxation, including a global minimum corporate tax rate of 15 percent aimed at stopping multinational companies from shifting profits to low-tax jurisdictions. The agreement, announced Friday by the Paris-based Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development, involves 136 countries that together represent about 90 percent of the world economy. OECD officials said the plan could generate roughly US$150 billion in additional tax revenue for governments. The deal is meant to address how globalization and digital business models have outpaced existing tax rules. Under the new framework, countries would gain the right to tax some profits earned by companies operating in their markets even if those firms are based elsewhere. That includes revenue from online retail, web advertising and other digital activities, especially in cases where companies have no physical presence in the country where the sales or profits are generated. U.S. President Joe Biden has been a key supporter of the effort, which has gained momentum as governments seek new revenue after the COVID-19 pandemic. U.S. Treasury Secretary Janet Yellen called the agreement a “once-in-a-generation accomplishment for economic diplomacy,” saying it would end a “race to the bottom” in which countries compete by lowering corporate tax rates to attract business. She argued that the United States would instead compete through the skills of its workers and its capacity to innovate. The agreement still faces major obstacles before it can be implemented. In particular, the United States must approve related tax legislation proposed by Biden, and congressional rejection would create uncertainty for the whole project. Because the U.S. is home to many of the world’s largest multinational corporations, its participation is crucial to making the system effective. The deal also requires follow-up steps at the international and domestic levels before it can take full effect. Canadian officials welcomed the announcement. Deputy Prime Minister Chrystia Freeland said Canada strongly supports international efforts to ensure that all corporations, including the biggest global firms, pay their fair share. She called the agreement historic and said it would benefit the Canadian middle class and Canadian businesses. Freeland also said Canada’s social safety net depends on a strong national tax base. Canada has also been moving ahead with its own Digital Services Tax. Freeland said the Liberal government intends to finalize legislation for the tax by Jan. 1. Under the plan, the tax would take effect on Jan. 1, 2024, but only if the treaty implementing the global tax regime has not yet come into force. If that happens, the tax would apply beginning in 2024 to revenues earned from Jan. 1, 2022 onward. The world’s largest tech companies, including Google and Amazon, have supported the OECD negotiations in part because the new global system would replace a patchwork of country-by-country digital services taxes. In return for accepting a common international framework, countries would withdraw their separate digital taxes, leaving companies to deal with one coordinated regime instead of many different national rules. French Finance Minister Bruno Le Maire praised the agreement as a “tax revolution for the 21st century,” saying digital giants would finally pay their fair share in the countries, including France, where they generate value. Ireland’s decision on Thursday to join the agreement was another important step, since its low-tax policy has helped attract major firms such as Google and Facebook to base their European operations there. Even so, the deal is not universally accepted. Several developing countries, including Nigeria, Kenya, Pakistan and Sri Lanka, have signaled they will not sign on. Anti-poverty and tax fairness advocates say the arrangement would send most of the new revenue to wealthier countries, while offering less benefit to poorer nations that rely more heavily on corporate tax receipts. The G-24 group of developing countries said the deal would be “sub-optimal” and not sustainable without a larger share of reallocated profits. The agreement now moves to the Group of 20 finance ministers next week and then to G-20 leaders for final approval at a summit in Rome at the end of October. The system has two main parts: first, a diplomatic agreement allowing countries to tax profits earned in their markets by companies without a physical presence there, affecting around 100 global firms; and second, a 15 percent global minimum tax applying to companies with more than 750 billion euros in revenue. That minimum would be enacted through domestic laws based on OECD model rules, with a “top-up” mechanism ensuring tax avoided abroad would be paid at home. The deal’s effectiveness will depend heavily on major headquarters countries putting the minimum tax into force.

The G-24 group of developing countries expressed concerns that wealthier nations would capture the bulk of new revenue while developing countries, more dependent on corporate taxes, would receive insufficient benefits. Without a larger share of revenue from reallocated profits, the G-24 stated the deal would be "sub-optimal" and "not sustainable even in the short run." The agreement will be presented to Group of 20 finance ministers next week, followed by final approval from G-20 leaders at a summit in Rome at the end of October. Countries will sign a diplomatic agreement to implement the provisions according to model rules developed by the OECD. The deal requires that major headquarters countries implement the minimum tax for it to achieve its intended effects, though universal participation is not strictly necessary for effectiveness.

Shell has become the first major oil and gas company to cut its dividend in response to the collapse in oil prices and the economic shock from the Covid-19 pandemic. In a move not seen since the 1940s, the company reduced its first-quarter dividend by 66% to 16 cents per share from the previous quarter. During January to March, Shell still paid out $3.5 billion in dividends and completed one tranche of its share buyback programme, but it has already said it will not proceed with the next tranche. Chairman Chad Holliday said the board did not believe maintaining the current level of shareholder distributions was prudent given the risk of prolonged economic uncertainty, weaker commodity prices, heightened volatility and an unclear demand outlook. He said Shell would continue to weigh capital spending, balance-sheet strength and future returns to shareholders as conditions improve. The decision contrasts with BP, which said on 28 April that it would keep its dividend unchanged for the quarter despite rising net debt. Shell cut its payout even though it reduced net debt by $4.7 billion in the first quarter. Its net debt gearing fell slightly to 28.9% from 29.3% at the end of 2019. Shell’s first-quarter profit, excluding inventory effects, fell by half to $2.76 billion from a year earlier. The decline reflected lower realised oil, gas and LNG prices, weaker refining and chemicals margins, and lower sales volumes, partly offset by tax-related gains and lower operating costs. Production averaged 3.719 million barrels of oil equivalent per day, down 1% year on year, mainly because of asset sales, natural field decline and reduced output from the NAM joint venture with ExxonMobil, which operates the Groningen gas field in the Netherlands. Shell warned that second-quarter output would be much lower, forecasting 2.59 million to 3.14 million boe/d. Chief financial officer Jessica Uhl said about 40% of the drop would come from Opec+ production cuts affecting Shell’s equity stakes, with the rest due to assets being shut in for economic, logistical or other reasons. Refinery runs also weakened, falling 10% to 2.397 million b/d, and Shell expects utilisation of only 60% to 70% in the second quarter, down from 81% in the first. The company also warned that regulatory or infrastructure constraints could further limit production, LNG liquefaction and refining activity. Shell reiterated plans to cut 2020 capital spending to $20 billion or less and to reduce underlying operating expenses by $3 billion to $4 billion annually over the next year.

Poland’s Defense Ministry said Friday it has alerted prosecutors to suspected offenses by members of a special commission that investigated the 2010 plane crash in Russia that killed President Lech Kaczynski and 95 others. The commission, created in 2016 under the previous right-wing government, had advanced the claim that the crash was a Moscow-sponsored assassination, a theory that deepened already tense Polish-Russian relations. The ministry said a recent review by experts found 41 possible offenses linked to the commission’s work. According to the review, the commissioners lacked the qualifications needed to investigate aviation accidents and manipulated evidence and findings to support an unproven theory that an explosion had occurred aboard the plane. The review also said the inquiry cost the state about 81 million zlotys, or $20 million, and was marked by poor professionalism, lack of transparency, and unreliability. The review accused former Defense Minister Antoni Macierewicz, who led the commission, and his successor Mariusz Blaszczak of legal violations and abuse of power. Most of the notices sent to prosecutors concern those two men. Current Deputy Defense Minister Cezary Tomczyk said Macierewicz had “cynically” misled the public and could face up to 10 years in prison. Prime Minister Donald Tusk called him a “notorious liar.” Poland’s prosecutor’s office said only that the notices were being registered. Separate Polish and Russian aviation investigations had concluded the crash resulted from human error in heavy fog.

# Poland Alerts Prosecutors to Alleged Offenses in Presidential Crash Investigation Poland's Defense Ministry notified prosecutors Friday of 41 suspected offenses committed by members of a special commission that investigated the 2010 plane crash in Russia that killed President Lech Kaczynski and 95 others. Prime Minister Donald Tusk called Macierewicz an "instigator and notorious liar" acting on orders from Jaroslaw Kaczynski, the deceased president's twin brother. Professional aviation commissions in Poland and Russia previously concluded the April 2010 crash resulted from human error during landing in heavy fog.

A long-running dispute over Spain’s treatment of renewable energy investors is now reaching a London court, where investors from the Netherlands and Luxembourg are trying to recover about $125 million from the Spanish government. The case is part of a decade-old battle with major implications for clean energy investment across the European Union. The investors put money into a solar plant in southern Spain in 2011 after Spain had offered subsidies to encourage renewable energy development. But after the 2008 financial crisis, Spain cut those subsidies retroactively and without warning, saying it needed to reduce costs. Since then, Spain has been sued internationally more than 50 times over the changes. According to U.N. data, it has lost more than 20 of those cases but has still not paid out. The current lawsuit, being heard in London’s Commercial Court, is one of the latest attempts by investors to force payment. Their legal team argues that Spain’s refusal to honor awards is damaging confidence in Europe as a destination for clean energy capital, especially at a time when the United States is attracting investment through the Inflation Reduction Act, which offers strong incentives for domestic green technology. Experts say those U.S. incentives are already pulling investment away from EU countries such as Spain, making the bloc less competitive globally. The European Commission, which backs Spain in the dispute, says the Energy Charter Treaty does not apply in conflicts between EU member states such as Spain, the Netherlands and Luxembourg, because EU law takes precedence. The commission says it is still examining the arbitration award and has indicated that paying the investors could amount to illegal state aid. Spain’s Ecological Transition Ministry has taken the same position, saying the payments “may be contrary to EU law” and that Spain must wait for the commission’s decision before paying. The investors first brought their case in 2013 before the World Bank-backed International Centre for Settlement of Investment Disputes. In 2018, Spain was ordered to compensate them, and the total amount it has been told to pay in similar cases exceeds $1 billion. But Spain has refused, arguing that it cannot pay while EU state-aid rules are unresolved. Because the investors have waited so long, their lawyers are now trying a different tactic: seizing part of a $1 billion settlement awarded to Spain over a 2002 oil spill. Spain is arguing in London that the investors should not be allowed to take those assets instead of the compensation they have not received. The broader dispute has become a test of Europe’s credibility with investors. Spain ranks alongside Venezuela and Russia in a recent list of countries with the most unpaid debts from commercial treaty violations. Critics say the EU is undermining trust by supporting Spain’s refusal to pay, especially when it is also promoting the Green Deal, climate neutrality by 2050, and looser subsidy rules to support clean investment. Spain and the European Commission now say the best long-term solution may be to withdraw from the Energy Charter Treaty altogether, though that would not resolve existing cases. Lawyers for the investors and other critics warn that the unresolved disputes are sending a message that Europe may not reliably honor investment protections. That, they say, could push renewable energy money toward the United States instead of Europe, despite the need for more investment in cleaner energy.

# Spain's Renewable Energy Dispute Threatens EU Clean Energy Investment Spain faces a significant legal challenge in London's Commercial Court this week as renewable energy investors seek to recover $125 million in subsidies the Spanish government promised then abruptly cut. This decade-long dispute carries major implications for clean energy financing across the European Union and highlights growing concerns about investor confidence in European green technology initiatives. ## The Core Dispute In 2011, investors from the Netherlands and Luxembourg invested millions in a Spanish solar plant based on government subsidies designed to encourage renewable energy production. After the 2008 financial crisis, Spain controversially slashed these payments without notice to reduce costs. Spain has since been sued internationally over 50 times regarding these retroactive changes and has lost more than 20 cases without paying compensation, according to U.N. data on international investment disputes. Spain now ranks alongside Venezuela and Russia as countries with the most unpaid debts over commercial treaty violations. Most cases allege Spain violated the Energy Charter Treaty, a legally binding agreement between 50 countries protecting companies from unfair government interference in the energy sector. ## Broader Implications The dispute occurs as the U.S. Inflation Reduction Act draws clean energy investment away from EU countries, making the bloc less globally competitive. Experts worry that Spain's track record will further discourage renewable investment in Europe. Nikos Lavranos, an investment arbitration expert, argues the EU is "shooting itself in the foot" by supporting Spain, as it undermines investor confidence in European commitments to green energy. The contradiction is particularly stark given recent EU initiatives like the Green New Deal, which aims for carbon neutrality by 2050 and relaxed subsidy rules. Lavranos notes this inconsistency damages the EU's credibility on climate commitments. ## Legal Complexities The situation involves competing legal frameworks. In 2018, the World Bank-backed International Centre for Settlement of Investment Disputes ordered Spain to compensate investors over $1 billion. However, Spain refuses to pay, citing EU law. The European Commission argues that EU law supersedes the Energy Charter Treaty in disputes between member states and that compensation would constitute illegal state aid—a determination still under review. Investors' lawyers are attempting to seize part of a $1 billion settlement Spain received over a 2002 oil spill to secure compensation. The London court will hear Spain's arguments against asset seizure this week. ## Environmental Concerns Environmental campaigners have criticized the Energy Charter Treaty for protecting fossil fuel investments, allowing financiers to sue over policy changes aimed at reducing polluting projects. However, nearly all Spanish cases involve renewable energy, complicating this critique. ## Moving Forward The EU is considering coordinated withdrawal from the energy treaty, though this wouldn't affect pending disputes. Spain's Ecological Transition Ministry argues modernizing the treaty to align with Paris Agreement objectives is impossible. Meanwhile, investors' lawyer Nick Cherryman suggests the dispute will push capital toward the United States, where legislation offers favorable renewable investment conditions. He emphasizes that respecting investor commitments benefits everyone by accelerating the transition to cleaner energy. José Ángel Rueda, a Spanish arbitration lawyer, warns that Spain's reputation as a reliable state is at stake, contrasting its behavior unfavorably with other EU members like Germany and Hungary, which have honored similar awards.

Equinor has agreed to sell its South Riding Point oil terminal in the Bahamas to Estonian logistics and investment group Liwathon, the Norwegian company said Tuesday. Equinor bought the terminal in 2009 but said North American oil flows have changed and it now sells more crude to other regions, making a new owner better suited to develop the site. The company did not disclose the deal’s financial terms. The terminal was damaged by a 2019 hurricane and oil spill, though post-cleanup groundwater tests found no hydrocarbon deposits.

# Summary Equinor has sold its South Riding Point oil terminal in the Bahamas to Estonian company Liwathon Group. The Norwegian oil and gas producer acquired the terminal in 2009 but decided to divest as North American oil market flows shifted and the company increasingly sold crude to other global regions. Equinor believes a new owner is better positioned for the terminal's development. The sale price was not disclosed. A 2019 hurricane previously damaged the facility, causing an oil spill affecting nearby forests, though subsequent groundwater testing showed no hydrocarbon deposits.

Several Muslim sites in France were attacked overnight after the Charlie Hebdo killings, though no one was hurt. In Le Mans, three blank grenades were thrown at a mosque and a bullet hole was found in a window. Near Narbonne, shots were fired at a Muslim prayer hall after evening prayers, but it was empty. In Villefranche-sur-Saone, an explosion damaged a kebab shop near a mosque. Prosecutors called it a criminal act. France remains tense after Wednesday’s gun attack on Charlie Hebdo killed 12, and no link has been established between the incidents.

# Summary Following the Charlie Hebdo magazine attack in Paris that killed 12 people, several attacks targeted Muslim locations across France. Three blank grenades and a bullet were fired at a mosque in Le Mans, while shots were fired at a prayer hall in Port-la-Nouvelle, which was empty at the time. An explosion occurred at a kebab shop near a mosque in Villefranche-sur-Saone. No casualties resulted from any of these incidents. Prosecutors have not yet established connections between these attacks and the Charlie Hebdo shooting. France remains on heightened alert following the magazine's assault.

Pope Francis on Tuesday removed the leadership of Caritas Internationalis, the Vatican’s global charitable network, and installed temporary managers after an external review found serious problems at its headquarters. The Vatican said the investigation found no evidence of financial misconduct or sexual impropriety, but it did identify “real deficiencies” in management that badly damaged staff morale and team spirit. Ousted were chief executive Aloysius John, elected in a disputed 2019 vote, and the rest of the leadership team. The shake-up does not affect the 162 national Caritas organizations that form the international confederation.

The King Salman Humanitarian Aid and Relief Center (KSrelief), based in Riyadh, launched the Saudi Project to Dismantle Mines in Yemen, known as “Masam,” at a reception attended by princes, ministers, senior officials, diplomats, and representatives of international humanitarian organizations. The event opened with a documentary film explaining the project and its purpose. In his remarks, KSrelief Supervisor General Dr. Abdullah bin Abdulaziz Al-Rabeeah said Saudi Arabia has, since its founding, supported sisterly, neighboring, and friendly countries through charitable and humanitarian initiatives in line with Islamic teachings. He said Yemen has been a particular priority because of the close neighborhood, cultural, social, family, and religious ties between the Saudi and Yemeni peoples. Al-Rabeeah described the scale of the landmine problem in Yemen and the human suffering it has caused. He said authorities had found more than 600 landmines in liberated areas, in addition to 130,000 internationally prohibited anti-boat and anti-vessel sea mines, including 40,000 in Marib governorate and 16,000 on Mayon Island. Citing Yemeni government reports, he said that between December 2014 and December 2016, 1,539 people were killed or injured by landmine explosions, including more than 3,000 military personnel as well as civilians, women, and children, and that more than 900 of the victims suffered permanent disability. He also said later figures showed 615 killed, including 101 children and 26 women, and 924 injured, including 10 children and 36 women, along with 274 cases of total loss or amputation, including 18 cases of sight loss. He added that during one year alone, the National Program for Landmines Clearance recorded a large number of victims: 418 killed in Aden, Lahj, Abyan, and Taiz, and 1,775 injured, while in Al-Jawf and Marib there were 380 killed and 512 injured. He noted that these figures were likely lower than the actual number of incidents because many were never recorded by the national program. Al-Rabeeah said KSrelief’s Artificial Limbs Center in Marib had fitted 305 prostheses for more than 195 victims at risk of amputation. He said the mines disproportionately affect women and children, who make up the majority of victims, and that the center provided treatment and rehabilitation to many injured people aged between 12 and 72. He added that by 24 June 2018, the Marib limbs center had treated 11 women, 12 children, and 346 men in its first and second phases, with the second phase still ongoing. Other patients were being treated in Yemen and Saudi Arabia at KSrelief’s expense, while some were treated abroad, including 13 in Sudan, 45 in Jordan, and 106 in Jeddah, two of them children, bringing the total to 533. He also said Saudi Arabia had provided more than $11 billion in aid to Yemen over the previous three years, covering humanitarian relief, refugee support, development, support for the Yemeni Central Bank, and other assistance. He described Masam as one of several Saudi projects aimed at easing the suffering of the Yemeni people and said the Kingdom would continue such efforts to help restore stability, development, and well-being in Yemen. He concluded by thanking King Salman and Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman for their support of KSrelief and its humanitarian work. Yemeni Foreign Minister Khalid Hussein Al-Yamani, speaking on behalf of the Yemeni government and people, thanked Saudi Arabia and its leadership for launching the project to clear Yemeni territory of mines planted by Houthi militias. He praised KSrelief’s efforts in Yemen and said the planting of mines had created a major humanitarian catastrophe intended to punish the Yemeni people and increase their suffering. He said the practice violated international humanitarian law and related conventions. Al-Yamani also said the mines and improvised explosive devices came directly from Iran or were developed in Yemen by Iranian experts. He said early statistics indicated that Houthi militias had planted more than one million mines across Yemeni territory, causing more than 693 deaths and 704 injuries, including 216 children and 72 women. He stressed that landmines pose a serious threat to Yemen’s future and described the Saudi project as an important humanitarian initiative. The Secretary-General of the International Civil Defence Organisation (ICDO), Dr. Vladimir Kalashnikov, also addressed the gathering. He said the world was meeting to confront the threat of landmines, which have killed people not only in Yemen but also in countries such as Libya, Syria, and Iraq. He noted that the ICDO has long experience in mine-related work in countries including Serbia, Croatia, Sri Lanka, and Lebanon, and said Yemen has been an active member since joining the organization. He affirmed that the ICDO would not abandon Yemen and would support it through its partners and member states, including Saudi Arabia. He praised cooperation between the ICDO and KSrelief and expressed confidence that the Masam project would succeed.

He affirmed the ICDO's commitment to assisting Yemen through partnerships with member states like Saudi Arabia, expressing confidence in Masam's success and pledging continued cooperation with KSRelief to protect communities from mine-related disasters.

At least 18 Syrian soldiers were killed and 27 others wounded on Oct. 13 when an improvised explosive device hit a military bus in the al-Saboura suburb of Damascus, according to Syria’s state-run news agency SANA. SANA said the bus was struck in a “terrorist attack,” while a journalist for the government newspaper Tishreen later published a photo of the blast site. No group immediately claimed responsibility. A military source close to Syrian government forces said the bus belonged to the Fourth Armored Division, commanded by Maher al-Assad, the brother of President Bashar al-Assad. The source said al-Saboura has long been a stronghold of the division and has not seen major military operations since 2011, though it has experienced occasional explosions targeting the unit on nearby roads. The attack came amid a rise in Islamic State activity in the Damascus countryside in 2022, especially around al-Kiswah. In May, IS said it was behind bombings in the al-Dirkhbyeh area of al-Kiswah, which killed and wounded several people. After the bus bombing, both the Syrian government and Russia blamed IS. On Oct. 17, Russia’s state news agency TASS quoted Russian Maj. Gen. Oleg Yegorov as saying Russian and Syrian forces had killed 20 militants in a security operation in southern Syria against those suspected of carrying out the attack. However, Abu Muhammad al-Hourani, spokesman for the Horan Free League, said IS had not claimed the bombing. He said operations against IS cells in Jasim, in Daraa province, were being carried out by former Free Syrian Army fighters and groups from the Russian-backed Eighth Brigade, not by Russian or Syrian regime forces. A military official from the Eighth Brigade also said reinforcements sent to Jasim were not ordered by Damascus or Russian command, but were in response to appeals from local notables to help fight IS.

# Syrian Government Retaliates for Soldier Deaths On October 13, an improvised explosive device (IED) detonated on a military bus in al-Saboura suburb near Damascus, killing at least 18 Syrian soldiers and wounding 27 others. The Syrian state news agency SANA reported the incident as a "terrorist attack," though no group initially claimed responsibility. The targeted bus belonged to the Fourth Armored Division, led by Maher al-Assad, the president's brother. Al-Saboura has served as the division's stronghold for years and is considered a secured zone, though it has occasionally experienced sporadic explosions targeting military personnel. The attack coincided with escalating Islamic State (IS) violence in Damascus's countryside since early 2022, particularly in the al-Kiswah area. IS previously claimed responsibility for May bombings in al-Dirkhbyeh that killed several people. The Syrian government and Russia attributed the attack to IS. On October 17, Russian Major General Oleg Yegorov announced that Russian and Syrian forces killed 20 militants in a security operation in southern Syria targeting those responsible for the bombing. However, conflicting accounts emerged from local sources. Abu Muhammad al-Hourani, spokesman for the Horan Free League in Daraa province, stated that IS had not yet claimed responsibility for the bus bombing. He reported that ongoing operations against IS cells in Jasim were conducted by former Free Syrian Army (FSA) fighters and Russian-backed Eighth Brigade members—not Russian or Syrian regime forces, contrary to official claims. An Eighth Brigade official confirmed that military reinforcements to Jasim were not ordered by the Syrian government or Russian leadership, but rather sent in response to a request from local notables to combat IS. This suggests the retaliation operations may have involved more complex local dynamics than the official narrative indicated.

President Donald Trump and Saudi Arabia sharply escalated their warnings to Iran on Sunday amid rising tensions in the Middle East after a series of incidents involving Saudi oil facilities, tanker sabotage near the United Arab Emirates, and a rocket landing in Baghdad’s Green Zone. Trump issued a blunt tweet saying that if Iran wanted to fight, it would be the “official end of Iran,” adding, “Never threaten the United States again!” He did not provide further details. His comments came as Washington and Tehran were already locked in a broader confrontation over sanctions and the U.S. military presence in the Gulf. Saudi officials said they did not want war but warned that if conflict were forced on them, they would respond with full strength. Saudi Minister of State for Foreign Affairs Adel al-Jubeir said the kingdom was trying to prevent war, but if the other side chose it, Saudi Arabia would “respond with all force and determination” and defend its interests. King Salman also called for emergency Arab and Gulf summits in Mecca on May 30 to discuss the implications of the attacks. The immediate backdrop was a week of unrest. Saudi Arabia accused Iran of ordering drone strikes on two oil pumping stations in the kingdom, attacks claimed by Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthi movement. Two days earlier, four vessels, including two Saudi oil tankers, were sabotaged off the coast of the UAE. No one claimed responsibility for the sabotage, but U.S. officials and a Norwegian insurers’ report cited by Reuters said Iran or Iran’s Revolutionary Guards were highly likely to have facilitated the attack, possibly through the Houthis or Iraqi Shi’ite militias. Iran denied involvement in both incidents. In response to the maritime threats, Gulf Cooperation Council countries began “enhanced security patrols” in the Arabian Gulf’s international waters, according to the U.S. Navy’s Bahrain-based Fifth Fleet. The fleet said GCC states were increasing communication and coordination with each other, with navies and coast guards working alongside the U.S. Navy to improve maritime security. The tensions were further underscored by the rocket attack in Baghdad. Iraqi military officials said a Katyusha rocket fell in the Green Zone, the fortified district that houses government buildings and foreign embassies, without causing casualties. U.S. Central Command said there were no U.S. or coalition casualties and that Iraqi security forces were investigating. The Green Zone had been frequently targeted during the U.S. occupation of Iraq and has occasionally been hit since the American withdrawal in 2011. Iranian and Houthi officials rejected the accusations and struck a defiant tone. Iranian Foreign Minister Mohammad Javad Zarif said war was not inevitable and that no country had the “illusion it can confront Iran.” Revolutionary Guards commander Major General Hossein Salami said Iran was not seeking war but was not afraid of it. Meanwhile, a Houthi-controlled news agency quoted a military source saying the strike on Aramco facilities was only the beginning of future operations against 300 vital military targets in Saudi Arabia, the UAE, and their bases in Yemen. A senior Houthi official mocked the Saudi call for summits, saying the kingdom “only know[s] how to support war and destruction.” The United States has intensified sanctions on Iran in an effort to drive its oil exports to zero and has increased its military presence in the Gulf, saying it is responding to Iranian threats against U.S. troops and interests. Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman discussed regional developments and security with U.S. Secretary of State Mike Pompeo in a phone call on Sunday. The heightened atmosphere also produced precautionary measures elsewhere. Exxon Mobil evacuated foreign staff from an oilfield in neighboring Iraq, Bahrain warned its citizens against traveling to Iraq and Iran and told those already there to return, and the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration advised U.S. commercial airliners flying over the Gulf and Gulf of Oman to exercise caution. Saudi Arabia also said the crew of an Iranian oil tanker it had assisted earlier in the month remained in the kingdom and were receiving care.

# Trump and Saudi Arabia Issue Warnings to Iran Over Middle East Tensions The United States and Saudi Arabia have escalated their rhetoric toward Iran following a series of attacks in the Persian Gulf region, with President Donald Trump threatening that conflict with Iran would mean the "official end" of Iran. Saudi Arabia simultaneously warned it would respond with "all strength" if war erupted, while emphasizing its preference for peace. ## Recent Attacks Trigger Escalation The heightened tensions stem from several recent incidents. On Tuesday, drone strikes attributed to Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi group damaged two Saudi oil pumping stations. Earlier, four vessels, including two Saudi oil tankers, were sabotaged near the United Arab Emirates coast. Additionally, a Katyusha rocket struck Baghdad's heavily fortified Green Zone on Sunday, which houses government buildings and foreign embassies, though it caused no casualties. He emphasized that responsibility for avoiding war rests with Iran, saying "the ball is in Iran's court." ## Iranian Counterposition Iran has dismissed war prospects, with Foreign Minister Mohammad Javad Zarif asserting that Tehran does not want conflict and no country can confront Iran. Revolutionary Guards Commander Hossein Salami echoed this position, stating Iran is "not pursuing war but we are also not afraid of war." The Houthis, claiming responsibility for the oil facility attacks, threatened further operations against 300 vital military targets in Saudi Arabia, the UAE, and their Yemeni bases. The Syrian Observatory for Human Rights reported that the attackers used a booby-trapped car and an explosive-laden fuel tanker to blow up the prison gate. U.S.-led coalition helicopters reportedly fired near the prison and dropped light bombs to support ground forces searching for the escapees. In a separate alert the same day, police carried out a controlled explosion on gas canisters found in another suspicious package in Sefakoy. The incidents came as Istanbul remained on high security alert after a suicide bombing Tuesday in the Sultanahmet district, near major tourist sites, that killed a female bomber and a policeman. An extreme leftist group first claimed responsibility for that attack, then retracted it. Despite the conflict, Lebanese Shiite pilgrims have continued traveling to Syria, where the road from Lebanon to Damascus has remained relatively safe. March 1 marked one year since Louisville firefighters carried out the dramatic rescue of semi driver Sydney Thomas, whose truck was left dangling over the Clark Memorial Bridge. Firefighter Bryce Carden descended to reach Thomas, while other members of the crew backed him up and ensured the operation stayed safe and controlled. Captain Chad Rodgers, a 16-year veteran of the department, said the crew was fully prepared when they arrived and immediately understood what needed to be done. Although the scene appeared alarming to the public, he said it did not feel chaotic to the firefighters in the moment because of their constant training. Captain Michael Renn, who has been with Louisville Fire for 10 years, said the department already trained for bridge incidents because the Clark Memorial Bridge is known to be accident-prone. However, after the rescue, the department intensified its preparation. Renn said firefighters now do extra, more stressful training scenarios designed to push members further and help them improve. He added that the department has also incorporated new tools, including updated ropes and mechanical rope equipment, along with other devices they had not previously used. According to Renn, the rescue became a valuable lesson that led to hours of additional training and better equipment, which he viewed as a positive outcome. The incident also helped draw attention to the need for greater investment in Louisville Fire. In the months that followed, the city approved a contract that included historic raises for firefighters. Mayor Craig Greenberg also directed more than $6 million in budget surplus funds to the department for maintenance and new apparatus. Greenberg said the city will continue supporting firefighters financially and in terms of wellness in the years ahead. Greenberg praised Louisville firefighters as brave first responders whose work goes far beyond putting out fires. He pointed to several examples from the past year, including the Clark Memorial Bridge rescue, another rescue at a downtown construction site, the Givaudan explosion, and assistance sent to eastern Kentucky during flooding. He said the rescue that captured international attention was only one example of the many ways Louisville firefighters protect the community every day. For its part, Louisville Fire said it is proud of the work its members continue to do. The bridge rescue, officials said, not only tested their skill under pressure but also led to stronger training, better equipment, and renewed public recognition of the department’s broader role in the city.

Multiple emergency units responded Friday afternoon to a chemical leak at the Morgantown Industrial Park on the grounds of SI Group, Inc. The company said its Morgantown site experienced a leak of PCL3, or phosphorus trichloride, and that it immediately worked with the chemical’s supplier to stop the leak. SI Group also notified first responders and regulatory agencies as a precaution. MECCA 911 Executive Director Jim Smith said the call came in around 1:40 p.m. from SI Group representatives reporting a spill at the facility. Volunteers from the Granville, Westover, and River Road fire departments responded, along with company personnel. Smith said the spill was contained on site and the scene was cleared by midafternoon after about an hour. No injuries were reported. PCL3 is a colorless fuming liquid that reacts violently with water and can be highly corrosive to the skin, eyes, and lungs. SI Group said safety of employees and the community remains its primary concern.

# Chemical Leak at Morgantown Industrial Park On Friday afternoon, a chemical leak occurred at SI Group, Inc. in Morgantown Industrial Park. The company reported a leak of PCL3 (phosphorus trichloride), a highly corrosive chemical used in pharmaceutical and industrial applications. SI Group immediately notified first responders and regulatory agencies as a precautionary measure. Fire departments from Granville, Westover, and River Road responded after receiving a 911 call at approximately 1:40 p.m. The company successfully contained the spill on-site with assistance from local volunteers. The incident was cleared by mid-afternoon, with no reported injuries to employees or community members. PCL3 is a colorless fuming liquid that reacts violently with water, producing phosphoric acid and hydrogen chloride—both highly corrosive substances dangerous to skin, eyes, and lungs. SI Group emphasized that employee and community safety remained their primary concern throughout the incident.

The Supreme Court of Canada has declined to hear five appeals challenging the Trans Mountain pipeline expansion, removing another legal obstacle for the project. The cases were brought by environmental organizations and Indigenous groups from British Columbia, including B.C. Nature, the Raincoast Conservation Foundation, the Living Oceans Society, the Tsleil-Waututh First Nation, the Squamish First Nation and a group of four young people. The court gave no reasons for its decision, which was released Thursday. The appeals centered on the federal cabinet’s second approval of the pipeline expansion in June 2019. Opponents argued the government had violated the Species at Risk Act by approving the project despite its expected impact on the endangered southern resident killer whale population. The Federal Court of Appeal had previously overturned cabinet’s first approval in 2018, saying the government had not adequately consulted Indigenous peoples and had failed to properly consider the effects on marine animals. After that ruling, the federal government carried out another round of Indigenous consultations and took a second look at marine impacts before approving the project again. The same communities and environmental groups then launched new legal challenges. Last month, the Federal Court of Appeal dismissed appeals from Indigenous communities on the issue of consultation and refused to hear arguments from the environmental groups. The Supreme Court’s refusal to take up the cases now leaves those rulings in place. Conservation biologist Misty MacDuffee of the Raincoast Conservation Foundation said the law requires governments to protect endangered species, and she argued that the project would harm the fewer than 75 remaining southern resident killer whales through increased tanker traffic and underwater noise. She said no existing technology can eliminate those impacts, making the project incompatible with the Species at Risk Act. Environmental groups reacted with disappointment. EcoJustice lawyer Margot Venton said the decision means construction on the pipeline can proceed even though it could push an endangered population closer to extinction. She argued the case highlights a serious gap between the law’s promises and how species protection works in practice. Karen Wristen, executive director of the Living Oceans Society, said she was deeply concerned for the future of the whales, noting that only 73 remained as of last summer and that one more, L41, has since gone missing and is presumed dead. She pointed to multiple pressures on the population, including a shortage of Chinook salmon, vessel traffic, noise and pollution, warning that Trans Mountain-related shipping and the risk of an oil spill could further threaten survival. Alberta Energy Minister Sonya Savage welcomed the court’s decision as another step toward completing the project. She also used the occasion to criticize recent protests against a separate natural-gas pipeline in northern British Columbia, arguing that organized opposition to major infrastructure projects and disruptions to rail and road traffic could threaten future energy development.

# Supreme Court Clears Trans Mountain Pipeline Expansion Project The Supreme Court of Canada has decided not to hear five legal challenges against the Trans Mountain pipeline expansion project, clearing another significant hurdle for the controversial infrastructure development. The challenges came from environmental organizations and Indigenous groups in British Columbia who sought to overturn the federal cabinet's second approval of the pipeline in June 2019. These groups argued that cabinet violated the Species at Risk Act by failing to adequately protect endangered southern resident killer whales, which number fewer than 75 individuals and would be harmed by increased noise from oil tanker traffic. The pipeline's legal journey has been contentious. In 2018, the Federal Court of Appeal overturned cabinet's initial approval, citing insufficient Indigenous consultation and inadequate consideration of marine impacts. After conducting additional consultations and reassessing environmental effects, the government approved the project again in 2019. However, the same groups filed new appeals challenging this second approval. Last month, the Federal Court of Appeal dismissed Indigenous communities' appeals regarding consultation adequacy but declined to hear arguments from environmental groups. When these organizations appealed to the Supreme Court, Canada's highest court declined to review the cases without providing reasons. Conservation biologists and environmental advocates expressed deep concern about the decision. Misty MacDuffee from the Raincoast Conservation Foundation emphasized that existing legislation requires governments to protect endangered species populations. She noted that current technology cannot mitigate the harmful effects of marine vessel noise on killer whales, making the pipeline project incompatible with species protection obligations. Environmental groups reacted with disappointment. Margot Venton, a lawyer representing Raincoast, stated that the ruling allows construction to proceed despite pushing an already endangered population toward extinction. She criticized the apparent gap between the Species at Risk Act's strong language and its practical enforcement, questioning whether Canadian species protection mechanisms function adequately. Karen Wristen from Living Oceans Society expressed deep concern, noting that only 73 southern resident whales remained as of summer 2020, with one whale presumed dead since then. She highlighted multiple threats facing the population, including salmon shortages, ocean traffic, noise, and pollution, arguing that additional Trans Mountain-related shipping threats are unsustainable. Alberta's Energy Minister Sonya Savage welcomed the Supreme Court decision, stating it further enables project completion. However, she expressed concern about protests and blockades that disrupted transportation across Canada in February 2020, particularly those supporting Wet'suwet'en hereditary chiefs opposing a separate natural gas pipeline. Savage warned that "well-funded and organized groups" could obstruct future infrastructure projects and emphasized that the rule of law must be maintained to ensure projects proceed on schedule.

The Government of Canada has announced new funding to study how oil spills, especially diluted bitumen (dilbit), affect Pacific salmon. Fisheries, Oceans and the Canadian Coast Guard Minister Bernadette Jordan said the government is investing $349,948 over two years to the University of Guelph for research on Coho salmon in their early life stages. The project will examine how these young salmon are impacted when exposed to dilbit, a form of crude oil from oil sands mixed with a lighter diluent. The study builds on earlier University of Guelph research and is intended to close knowledge gaps about how salmon respond to oil exposure and recover afterward. It is being funded through the Oceans Protection Plan’s Fate, Behaviour, and Effects Initiative, which focuses on understanding how oil spills behave in marine environments and what biological effects they have. Officials said the research will improve scientific understanding of the risks posed by dilbit to aquatic species and ecosystems, while also helping inform spill response planning and preparedness. The government emphasized that Pacific salmon are important to the social, cultural, and economic well-being of many Canadians and Indigenous communities, and said the work will support conservation efforts and help protect these iconic fish for future generations.

The findings will enhance scientific understanding and help mitigate environmental risks.

Construction on St. Louis Street in downtown Mobile is set to begin Monday as part of a long-planned revitalization project that has been in development for about five years. The first phase will close the street from Springhill Avenue to Bayou Street, and work will then continue block by block over the next two and a half years. The $17 million project will replace aging infrastructure and add improvements including stormwater and drainage upgrades, new street lighting, landscaping, ADA-accessible features, and underground water and sewer lines. Mayor Sandy Stimpson said the goal is to make the street safer, more accessible, and more pedestrian-friendly. Local business and downtown leaders say the work will help match the recent private investment already seen on the street. Fred Rendfrey of the Downtown Mobile Alliance said the upgrades should make the area safer, more attractive, and more vibrant, encouraging further development. Business owners, including Braided River Brewery’s David Nelson, acknowledged the disruption but urged customers to keep supporting local businesses during construction. Most of the funding comes from the Restore Act, using money tied to the 2010 BP oil spill settlement. The city says it will keep residents updated as closures change.

As COVID-19 spread and governments shut down gyms, yoga studios, rec leagues, pickup sports and other group activities, many people turned to solo exercise instead. In Montreal and elsewhere, parks and bike paths filled with runners, walkers and cyclists trying to stay active while avoiding crowds. Running Room/Coin des Coureurs CEO John Stanton said the shift quickly boosted interest in running, with the company seeing a sharp rise in social media followers as people looked for ways to exercise during isolation. Stanton, who had returned from a business trip early in the pandemic and self-isolated for two weeks, even ran on his porch to maintain his routine. Running coach and marathoner Mia Phillips, who leads the Kahnawake group “The Runners,” said her Facebook activity increased as more people stayed home. She noted that many former runners were getting back into the sport, while regular participants were logging more kilometres than usual. For many, she said, running became a way to manage stress during an uncertain time. The popularity of outdoor exercise also created problems for public health officials. On a warm Saturday, too many people crowded places such as the Lachine Canal, Mount Royal Park and Île Notre-Dame, prompting the city to close some areas to limit gatherings. To give runners a competitive outlet after its stores closed, The Running Room launched a virtual race, joining other organizations and circuits that were doing the same. Stanton said the response was immediate, with 1,600 people signing up right away. The company later planned more virtual events, including a family walk and 10K. Across the internet, similarly themed races appeared with playful names such as “2020 Social Distancing 6K - We’re All In This Together, But Six Feet Apart,” “The Great Toilet Paper Chase of 2020,” and “The Sloth Run.” Ottawa’s Tamarack Ottawa Race Weekend, normally the country’s largest running festival and a key event in marathon season, was canceled, but organizers said they would hold a virtual race weekend instead. Phillips said she planned to run the Ottawa virtual marathon. Health ministers encouraged exercise as a way to reduce stress while maintaining social distancing, and social media reflected that advice with posts showing home workouts, improvised weights, and creative indoor exercises. Stanton predicted, however, that gyms, studios, pools and group fitness businesses would struggle to regain their pre-pandemic popularity once restrictions lifted. He also believed running clubs might not rebound fully, since many people would remain cautious about shared equipment and close contact. Although retail stores were closed, The Running Room continued some online sales from its Edmonton distribution centre and select stores. Still, the company had to cut its workforce from 800 employees to 130. Stanton said the layoffs were painful, but he hoped the business would recover. He added that while retail had taken a hit, the surge in interest in walking and running could have lasting benefits, with more people than ever going out alone to exercise in neighborhoods across Canada.

A pregnant Racine woman and a man from Racine have been charged after police say they were using drugs inside a hospital and that narcotics were found in their belongings. The Government of Canada says it is strengthening ocean protection through the Oceans Protection Plan by improving the Canadian Coast Guard’s ability to prevent and respond to marine pollution. On Sept. 7, 2018, Fisheries, Oceans and the Canadian Coast Guard Minister Jonathan Wilkinson announced in Victoria, B.C., the first delivery of new marine environmental response equipment for the Coast Guard’s Western Regional Headquarters. The equipment includes curtain boom, which can be deployed to form a temporary barrier and contain oil spills, and medium-sized portable skimmers, which collect and remove oil from the water’s surface. The new gear is part of the Environmental Response Equipment Modernization initiative and is intended to bolster the Coast Guard’s response to on-water environmental threats. Wilkinson said the plan is giving Coast Guard personnel innovative tools to improve responses to potential incidents and help keep Canada’s waters and coasts safe and clean for the future.

The article is a first-person account of a months-long storytelling and research project tracking the proposed Enbridge Northern Gateway Pipeline, which would move oil from the Athabasca oil sands in northern Alberta to the British Columbia coast. The writer has spent the first part of the project in Alberta, following the route from Fort McMurray, where the oil is extracted, to Fort Saskatchewan, where the pipeline would begin. The account emphasizes that the extraction end of the pipeline is as important to understanding the story as the transportation route itself, because the social, economic, and environmental consequences begin where the oil is mined. By late January, the writer has moved to Vancouver and plans to spend the next four and a half months in British Columbia, tracing the pipeline in reverse. Instead of starting inland, the journey will follow the tanker routes through the Hecate Strait between Haida Gwaii and the mainland coast, moving toward Kitimat, the pipeline’s proposed terminal. The writer will travel by ferry along the British Columbia coast, navigating islands and inlets in winter conditions, which are described as difficult and potentially rough. Friends warn about the weather and suggest antiemetics, but the writer intentionally wants to experience the coast at its most challenging time of year. This is meant to provide firsthand insight into the conditions oil tankers would face. The coast is portrayed as a complex, fjord-like landscape, often compared to Norway or southern Chile, and especially hard to navigate in winter. A major concern in the article is the risk of an oil spill. Opposition to Northern Gateway is led in part by Coastal First Nations, an alliance of Indigenous communities on the British Columbia coast. They argue that a spill would cause severe environmental and economic damage. Enbridge and some maritime experts, however, contend that the likelihood of a spill is lower than critics claim. The writer notes that the ferry route will not exactly match the tanker route, but there will be enough overlap to experience the same kinds of weather and coastal conditions that tankers would encounter. The article also places the pipeline debate in the context of falling global oil prices. Since the writer arrived in Edmonton in early October, crude prices have dropped sharply, and gasoline prices at the pump have fallen as well, from about $1.14 per liter to around 68 cents. While consumers benefit, the writer wonders how lower prices affect workers and how Enbridge is thinking about Northern Gateway in light of this market change. A visit to Fort McMurray in early December provides some answers. There, the writer stayed with a family originally from Cape Breton, Nova Scotia, and spoke with a host who has worked as an electrician in the oil industry for about a decade. The host said he had just finished a stretch of nearly a month without a day off. He explained that falling oil prices were affecting construction projects more than existing production, and that his own job remained secure because he worked on established projects. The worker also described broader changes in the oil industry over the past decade. He said there is now more demand for trades work and more interest among high school graduates in vocational education. He also observed that corporate behavior has become more restrained, with less of the rapid, uncontrolled expansion seen in the early 2000s. Projects are now developed in phases, and companies are more cautious rather than hiring thousands of workers at once. The writer is struck by how quickly global oil price changes can influence day-to-day work in the oil sands, even to the point of delaying new extraction projects indefinitely. In British Columbia, the writer sees a different relationship to the oil industry and a stronger public opposition to Northern Gateway. The contrast is not just about climate or geography, but also about how closely people’s livelihoods are tied to oil. In Alberta, the industry is more deeply woven into daily life. In British Columbia, opposition appears more intense. The writer cites a recent town hall-style event at the Vancouver Aboriginal Friendship Centre Society, where MP Nathan Cullen strongly opposed the pipeline and introduced Bill C-628, legislation aimed at blocking oil tanker traffic along the northern B.C. coast. The event drew roughly 250 people, filling nearly every seat and lining the walls of the gymnasium. The writer compares this with a Greenpeace-organized anti-pipeline talk in Calgary that drew only about 20 to 30 people, underscoring the difference in public engagement between the two provinces. At the same time, the writer resists drawing firm conclusions too early. The issue is described as increasingly complex the deeper the research goes. The writer initially saw the pipeline as a straightforward threat to pristine watersheds, fish-bearing streams, human communities, and wilderness areas. The concerns extend to Indigenous and non-Indigenous people, and to both human and non-human life that depends on those ecosystems. But the writer also notes a seeming contradiction: while Northern Gateway faces major resistance, liquefied natural gas pipelines are being proposed and approved in the same region. This raises the central question that will guide the rest of the journey: why does Northern Gateway provoke such intense controversy? The article ends by previewing the next phase of the project, which will involve DIY aerial photography and mapping using tools from the Public Laboratory for Open Technology and Science. The writer plans to use these grassroots tools to create aerial images of public areas along the pipeline route and to train local communities to generate their own cartographic data based on local knowledge. The next post will explain the technical and creative side of the project, including how kite-flying can produce useful data. The article closes with an invitation to a DIY Aerial Photography and Mapping Workshop in downtown Vancouver on January 31.

# Following the Oil Trail: From Alberta to British Columbia A journalist documenting the proposed Enbridge Northern Gateway Pipeline has completed four months of research in Alberta and is now transitioning to British Columbia to continue their storytelling project. The pipeline would transport oil from the Athabasca oil sands in northern Alberta to the British Columbia coast, and this investigation aims to explore both the extraction process and the transportation route, as well as the communities affected by this controversial infrastructure proposal. ## Alberta Phase: Understanding Oil Extraction During the first three months in Alberta, the journalist traveled from Fort McMurray, the oil boom town where extraction occurs, to Fort Saskatchewan, where the pipeline begins. This phase focused on tracing the pipeline's path and researching oil's presence and significance in the province. The timing of this research coincided with dramatic changes in global oil markets. Since the journalist's arrival in early October, crude oil prices have fallen substantially, with Canadian gas prices dropping from $1.14 per liter to 68 cents—a decline of 46 cents that benefits consumers but raises questions about industry workers' futures. To understand these impacts firsthand, the journalist interviewed a young electrician from Cape Breton, Nova Scotia, who has worked in Fort McMurray for a decade. He reported that falling oil prices are affecting construction projects rather than existing production operations. He also observed significant industry changes over his tenure: increased demand for trade workers, more vocational school interest among high school graduates, and a shift toward more conservative corporate practices. The rampant development of the early 2000s has given way to controlled, phased project development and smaller hiring cohorts rather than massive workforce expansions. ## British Columbia Phase: Different Landscape, Different Opposition Since early January, the journalist has been based in Vancouver and will spend the next four and a half months in British Columbia. Rather than following the pipeline route directly, they will travel in reverse, beginning with oil tanker routes through the Hecate Strait between Haida Gwaii and the mainland, then moving toward Kitimat, the pipeline's end terminal. This winter ferry journey along the British Columbia coast will provide firsthand experience of the challenging conditions—intricate shorelines, thousands of islands, and deep inlets—that make these waters comparable to Norwegian and Chilean fjords and particularly difficult to navigate in winter months. The contrast between Alberta and British Columbia opposition is striking. While the journalist attended an anti-pipeline talk in Calgary organized by Greenpeace that drew only 20-30 people, a town hall at the Vancouver Aboriginal Friendship Centre Society featuring MP Nathan Cullen, who introduced Bill C-628 to block oil tanker traffic along northern British Columbia's coast, drew approximately 250 people—the largest anti-pipeline crowd the journalist has witnessed in Canada since attending the Tar Sands Healing Walk in June 2014. This disparity reflects fundamental differences between the provinces. In Alberta, lives and livelihoods are complexly intertwined with the oil industry, creating economic dependencies that complicate opposition. In British Columbia, concerns focus on environmental and cultural impacts, particularly among Coastal First Nations, who fear catastrophic consequences from potential oil spills in ecologically sensitive regions. Enbridge and maritime experts argue that spill risks are lower than critics suggest, but the debate remains contentious. ## Unresolved Questions and Future Methodology The journalist grapples with a central question: why does the Northern Gateway Pipeline generate such intense controversy when liquefied natural gas pipelines are being proposed and approved in similar locations? Initially, the answer seemed straightforward—the pipeline threatens pristine watersheds, fish-bearing streams, and communities dependent on natural ecosystems. However, the selective opposition to Northern Gateway while accepting LNG infrastructure suggests deeper complexities worth exploring. ## Community-Centered Research Approach The project incorporates grassroots mapping tools from the Public Laboratory for Open Technology and Science (Public Lab) to create aerial images of areas along the proposed pipeline route. The journalist will lead training workshops enabling communities to generate their own cartographic data based on local knowledge, democratizing the research process and ensuring community voices shape the investigation's outcomes. The journalist is conducting a DIY Aerial Photography and Mapping Workshop on January 31st in downtown Vancouver, inviting community participation in this innovative documentation method. This hands-on approach reflects the project's commitment to community engagement and collaborative knowledge production as it continues unraveling the complex story of oil, pipelines, and their impacts across two Canadian provinces.

Tampa’s Vicente Nieto and Bros. Cigar Factory, a 100-year-old Ybor City building at 2708 N. 18th St., is set for restoration and a new use under the ownership of Liana Fuente, a member of the famed Fuente cigar family. Fuente bought the 7,000-square-foot property a year ago for $725,000 and estimates the renovation will cost about $1.5 million. She hopes to complete the project by next year. The building has deep family ties. In 1956, Fuente’s grandfather, Carlos Fuente Sr., purchased the factory and expanded it by about two-thirds so his father, Arturo Fuente Sr., could live on the second floor while cigar workers rolled cigars on the first. The family later sold the building and moved to a larger facility. Now, Liana Fuente says restoring it is a way to honor that history and give something back to Tampa. “I see this as my gift to the city from my family,” she said. Her plan is to preserve the exterior as it looked after the family’s additions while modernizing the interior for mixed use. The first floor is slated to include women-owned businesses: a bar, a florist, and event space. The second floor will hold five apartments, and the basement will remain storage for now. Fuente, 44, left her role as vice president of brand development for the family cigar company two years ago and says this is her first real estate project. She also plans to seek local historic landmark designation, which would help protect the building from future demolition or exterior changes. Inside, she intends to keep reminders of its cigar-making past, including family photographs, the old pulley system used to move tobacco between floors, and chalk names of cigar brands still visible on a second-floor wall. Fuente believes the handwriting may be her grandfather’s. The article traces the Fuente family’s cigar history back to 1912, when Arturo Fuente Sr. opened A. Fuente & Co. in West Tampa. A fire destroyed the business in 1924, and it took 22 years to rebuild it under the Arturo Fuente Cigar Co. name. The company later expanded in the 1950s, eventually moving rolling operations to the Dominican Republic, though its headquarters remains in Ybor City. Fuente said she persuaded her cousins, the Blancos, to keep the building in the family when it was put up for sale. “I get chills when I walk through it,” she said.
