A weekend fire in Lethbridge destroyed one garage, damaged another, and scorched the siding of a nearby house. Fire crews from three stations responded Sunday afternoon to the 1200 block of Fourth Avenue South after reports of a structure fire. Off-duty firefighter Dave Heatherington said he heard a loud bang that sounded like an explosion and went outside to find his neighbour’s garage on fire. Crews arrived to heavy smoke and flames from a single-car garage, and nearby homes on the south side of the street were evacuated as a precaution. Heatherington, who is also a platoon chief with Lethbridge Fire and EMS, helped connect a hose while crews battled the blaze. The garage where the fire began was completely destroyed in about 30 minutes. Owner Jim Day said the building was about 100 years old and had originally been a stable when his house was built in 1909. He said his wife had driven her car out and left less than 20 minutes before the fire started. Platoon Chief Shawn Folk said the wind helped push the fire south toward a house across the alley, scorching its siding. Day said he felt worst about the damage to his neighbours, including Heatherington’s garage, which had taken two years to build. Heatherington said no one was injured and all pets were safely removed.

# Fire Destroys 100-Year-Old Lethbridge Garage A weekend fire in Lethbridge destroyed a century-old garage and damaged neighboring properties. Fire crews from three stations responded Sunday afternoon to a structure fire in the 1200 block of Fourth Avenue S. after an off-duty firefighter heard an explosion-like noise and discovered his neighbor's garage ablaze. The single-car garage, originally built as a stable in 1909, was completely destroyed within 30 minutes. Owner Jim Day expressed relief that his wife had driven her car away just 20 minutes before the fire started. The fire spread to nearby properties. Wind conditions pushed flames toward a neighboring house across the alley, scorching and blistering its siding. An adjacent garage belonging to firefighter Dave Heatherington, who had spent two years building it with his brother-in-law, was also damaged. Fortunately, no injuries occurred and all pets were safely evacuated. Platoon Chief Shawn Folk noted that a north wind prevented worse damage—had the wind blown from the west, the consequences would have been more severe. An investigation into the fire's cause is underway. Despite the losses, residents emphasized that material possessions can be replaced.

ALBUQUERQUE, N.M. — The National Museum of Nuclear Science and History is unveiling a nearly full-scale replica of the Trinity Tower, the 100-foot steel structure that held the Gadget, the world’s first nuclear bomb to be detonated, before the July 16, 1945 test in New Mexico. The original tower and bomb were vaporized in the explosion, leaving behind little more than concrete footings, rebar, and melted sand that formed trinitite, a greenish glass. Museum executive director Jim Walther noted that workers had even placed mattresses beneath the Gadget as a precaution while it was being lifted into place, “just in case it fell.” The new replica, about 98 feet tall and made of 15,000 pounds of steel, stands prominently outside the Albuquerque museum. It took roughly two months to build. Most of the tower came from an old 1950s-era fire observation tower removed from a forest in Alabama. At the top is a small shed modeled on the original Trinity structure, which had an oak floor, corrugated iron on three sides, and a hatch underneath to receive the bomb. The replica’s shed is fully enclosed, with the open side and hatch painted on for appearance. A replica of the Gadget, donated by the props master of the canceled TV show “The Manhattan Project,” will hang from a pulley as if being raised into the tower before the test. Museum spokeswoman Jennifer Hayden said the project was made possible by local companies donating labor and equipment, and by Clay Kemper Perkins, a retired physicist, nuclear science enthusiast, and philanthropist who proposed the idea and funded it. Perkins, now 83, said the Trinity test and the later bombing of Nagasaki made a deep impression on him when he was 11 and inspired him to pursue physics. To mark the installation, the museum will host a Friday evening outdoor event featuring a screening of the History Channel’s “Modern Marvels: The Manhattan Project.” The museum will also be open, with food trucks on site. Doors open at 5:30 p.m., the movie begins at dark, and admission is $15. The first 100 attendees will receive a Trinity Tower water bottle and a museum-logo chocolate coin.

# Summary On July 16, 1945, the world's first nuclear bomb, nicknamed "the Gadget," was detonated atop a 100-foot steel tower in New Mexico. Workers had humorously placed mattresses beneath the tower as a precaution before hoisting the device. The explosion was so intense that it completely vaporized both the bomb and the tower, while the extreme heat melted surrounding sand into greenish glass fragments called trinitite. Today, little remains at the original Trinity site except concrete and rebar from the tower's foundation. The National Museum of Nuclear Science and History in Albuquerque now preserves artifacts and historical materials from this pivotal event. On Friday, the museum unveiled its newest exhibit: a nearly full-scale replica of the Trinity Tower, standing approximately 98 feet tall and constructed from 15,000 pounds of steel. The tower features a small shed at its top, modeled after the original oak-floored structure that had housed the Gadget. The original shed had three corrugated iron sides and a hatch for receiving the bomb, with the fourth side open toward a camera bunker. The replica took approximately two months to construct, incorporating materials from a 1950s-era fire observation tower salvaged from an Alabama forest. A replica of the Gadget itself, donated by the props department of the cancelled television show "The Manhattan Project," hangs from a pulley as if being hoisted into position. The project was conceived and funded by Clay Kemper Perkins, a retired physicist and nuclear science enthusiast. Perkins, now 83, was 11 years old when the Gadget detonated and witnessed the war's conclusion, an experience that inspired his physics career. Local companies contributed time and equipment to realize the vision. The museum is hosting a special outdoor event Friday featuring a screening of the History Channel's "The Manhattan Project" documentary, with food trucks available. Admission is $15 per person, and the first 100 visitors receive commemorative gifts.

Japan’s Mitsui O.S.K. Lines said its investigation found that human error caused the oil spill from the bulk carrier MV Wakashio off Mauritius. The company said the ship altered its course about two miles closer to shore than planned so crew members could get cellphone reception. It blamed the accident on inadequate nautical charts, weak navigation systems, poor risk awareness, and insufficient supervision and safety monitoring. According to the company, the chart lacked key depth information, and the crew on duty failed to make proper visual or radar safety checks. It also said the captain and crew were using cellphones while on duty. The Wakashio struck a coral reef on July 25 about a mile offshore. After nearly two weeks of pounding by heavy surf, its hull cracked and it began leaking fuel into a lagoon on Aug. 6, polluting protected wetlands and a bird and wildlife sanctuary. More than 1,000 tons of oil spilled into coastal waters, while about 3,000 tons remaining aboard were pumped into barges before the ship later broke in two. Mitsui O.S.K. Lines apologized and said it would spend about 500 million yen on electronic charts, training, and other safety measures. In September, it also offered 1 billion yen for environmental projects and support for Mauritius’s fishing community.

# Summary A Japanese shipping company's investigation revealed that human error caused the MV Wakashio oil spill off Mauritius. The bulk carrier deliberately shifted its course two miles closer to shore than planned so crew members could access cellphone signals. The investigation identified multiple failures: inadequate nautical charts lacking depth information, non-functional navigation systems, poor risk awareness, insufficient supervision, and crew members using cellphones while on duty. Safety checks were not conducted visually or by radar. The accident occurred on July 25 when the ship struck a coral reef. After two weeks of pounding by heavy surf, the hull cracked on August 6, leaking over 1,000 tons of fuel into a protected lagoon and wildlife sanctuary. Approximately 3,000 additional tons were pumped into barges before the ship broke apart. The environmental disaster severely impacted Mauritius, a tourism-dependent nation already struggling with coronavirus travel restrictions. Volunteers and environmental workers worked to contain damage, rescuing rare plants and seabirds. Mitsui O.S.K. Lines apologized and committed 500 million yen to safety improvements and 1 billion yen to support environmental projects and the local fishing community.

Murphy Oil has been fined $172,500 by the Alberta Energy Regulator after a pipeline spill in northwestern Alberta went undetected for 45 days. The regulator said the Arkansas-based company failed to properly maintain its leak detection system, allowing about 1.4 million litres of light oil to escape between January and March 2015 about 65 kilometres east of Peace River. The spill was caused by internal corrosion in a pipeline carrying condensate, a light oil used to dilute heavy oil so it can move through pipelines. AER pipelines director Ron Wagener said maintenance had not been carried out as required. He noted that most diluent meters at well pads had not been calibrated since October 2012. According to the regulator, if the end-point meters had been calibrated at least yearly and alarm settings adjusted properly, the system could have detected the leak earlier. The AER also faulted Murphy Oil for not reporting the release promptly or taking immediate remedial action. Murphy Oil said it has agreed to pay the fine and has made changes to prevent similar incidents. Craig Sinclair, the company’s director of health, safety and environment for Canadian operations, said it is now conducting pipeline integrity checks more often and training staff more extensively. The damaged five-year-old pipeline has since been purged and abandoned, with other pipelines now used to move condensate within the Seal heavy oilfield. The penalty is among the largest the AER has issued for a pipeline spill since 2013.

# Murphy Oil Fined for Undetected Pipeline Spill Murphy Oil has been fined $172,500 by the Alberta Energy Regulator for failing to maintain a pipeline that leaked for 45 days without detection. Between January and March 2015, approximately 1.4 million litres of light oil (condensate) spilled about 65 kilometres east of Peace River in northwestern Alberta due to internal corrosion. The regulator determined that Murphy Oil staff had not properly maintained the leak detection system as required. Specifically, most diluent meters at well pads had not been calibrated since October 2012, well beyond the required yearly interval. Had proper calibration and alarm adjustments been performed, the system would have detected the leak early. The company also faced criticism for delayed detection and failure to report the spill or take immediate remedial action promptly. Murphy Oil's Canadian operations director acknowledged the violations and stated the company has implemented significant changes, including more frequent pipeline integrity checks and enhanced personnel training. The company has since abandoned the five-year-old pipeline and rerouted condensate through alternative pipelines. The $172,500 fine ranks among the largest penalties issued by the Alberta Energy Regulator since its 2013 formation, though it remains below the $250,000 fine issued to Pengrowth Energy in 2014 for a similar undetected spill.

U.S. and Canadian authorities are examining whether criminal liability may arise from the Titan submersible disaster, in which all five people aboard were killed when the craft imploded during a deep-sea expedition to the Titanic wreck on June 18. The investigation is complicated by two major legal questions: which country should lead, and whether the 22-foot Titan qualifies as a maritime “vessel” under the law. The U.S. Coast Guard said it will conduct its highest-level investigation after the search-and-rescue effort recovered debris from the ocean floor in the North Atlantic near the Titanic site. Coast Guard Capt. Jason Neubauer said the inquiry will focus on “accountability aspects” of the implosion and could lead to recommendations for civil or criminal sanctions. At the same time, Canada’s Transportation Safety Board opened its own probe as parts of the submersible, operated by U.S.-based OceanGate, were brought to St. John’s, Newfoundland. The Royal Canadian Mounted Police also said it is assessing whether a criminal investigation is warranted. Legal experts say the case could expose OceanGate employees, operations managers, inspectors, or owners to liability, especially because OceanGate CEO Stockton Rush died in the disaster. Rush was piloting the Titan when it imploded. The other victims were British billionaire Hamish Harding, Pakistani businessman Shahzada Dawood and his son Suleman Dawood, and French diver Paul-Henri Nargeolet. Maritime defense lawyer George Chalos said anyone connected to the operation should immediately consider legal exposure. He said a criminal prosecution is possible, but the key question is where it could be brought. OceanGate is headquartered in Everett, Washington, the Titan was registered in the Bahamas, and it was launched from the Canadian ship Polar Prince out of St. John’s into international waters near the Titanic wreck. The passengers and crew were multinational, with Rush American and the others from Pakistan, France, and the U.K. French and British authorities are also investigating. Under U.S. law, prosecutors might rely on the Seaman’s Manslaughter Statute, an old maritime law that can apply to ship officers, engineers, pilots, owners, inspectors, and managers if negligence rises to the criminal level. But any U.S. case would first need to establish jurisdiction. Another hurdle is whether the Titan counts as a “vessel” under maritime law. Lawyers note that the submersible could not travel on the ocean surface, which may weaken the argument that the statute applies. Martin Davies of Tulane University said that despite the event feeling like a U.S.-centered operation, the facts may not support prosecution in any one country, and Canada appears to have the clearest jurisdiction. The article also notes that prior safety concerns about Titan could support civil suits by victims’ families and, if negligence was serious enough, criminal charges. The legal debate recalls the Deepwater Horizon case, where courts rejected attempts to use the Seaman’s Manslaughter Statute against BP employees because they were operating a drilling rig rather than a vessel. Chalos said that ruling shows the law is not a catchall for anything maritime-related.

# Summary: Titan Submersible Disaster Probes Face Tricky Test of Criminal Liability U.S. and Canadian authorities are investigating the June 18 implosion of the Titan submersible in international waters near the Titanic wreck, which killed all five people aboard, including OceanGate CEO Stockton Rush. The investigation faces significant jurisdictional and legal complexities that may complicate any potential criminal prosecution. The U.S. Coast Guard announced it will conduct its highest-level investigation, examining "accountability aspects" of the disaster and potentially recommending civil or criminal sanctions. Canada's Transportation Safety Board launched a parallel inquiry, with investigators dispatched to St. John's, Newfoundland, where submersible debris is being collected. France and Britain are also investigating since passengers included a British billionaire, Pakistani nationals, and a renowned French diver. Legal experts note that criminal prosecution is theoretically viable but face substantial obstacles. Maritime defense lawyer George Chalos emphasized that potential defendants should "lawyer-up immediately" given the liability exposure. If pursued, any U.S. criminal case would likely invoke the Seaman's Manslaughter Statute, a 19th-century law targeting ship officers, engineers, pilots, and company owners, inspectors, and managers. However, establishing jurisdiction presents a fundamental challenge. OceanGate is based in Washington state, but the submersible was registered in the Bahamas and deployed from a Canadian vessel in international waters. Legal experts disagree on which country has primary jurisdiction, with Tulane University maritime law director Martin Davies suggesting Canada has the "clearest" claim. Another critical obstacle involves whether the Titan qualifies as a "vessel" under maritime law. Legal experts are skeptical, noting the submersible could not navigate the ocean's surface. This distinction matters significantly because criminal charges under the Seaman's Manslaughter Statute require vessel status. A 2010 Deepwater Horizon case provides cautionary precedent: a federal appeals court rejected prosecutors' attempt to apply the statute to BP employees operating a drilling rig, ruling it wasn't a vessel. Pre-disaster safety concerns about the Titan offer potential grounds for civil negligence suits by passengers' families and could support criminal charges of gross negligence. However, the severity of negligence required for the Justice Department to pursue criminal prosecution remains unclear given the legal obstacles. OceanGate has not responded to requests for comment. Co-founder Guillermo Söhnlein, who left the company in 2013 but retains minority ownership, also declined comment. The Royal Canadian Mounted Police confirmed it's determining whether a criminal investigation is warranted but provided no additional details. The convergence of international jurisdictional questions, the vessel definition problem, and multinational involvement creates unprecedented legal complexity for prosecutors seeking accountability in what appears to be a case involving significant safety negligence.

Uzbekistan’s government has ordered a two-month inspection of the technical condition of vehicles fitted with gas cylinders, gas filling stations that service them, and other gas-powered equipment such as boilers and furnaces. Officials will then prepare a road map to prevent accidents involving natural gas use. The move follows a September 18 explosion in Kagan district, Bukhara region, when a gas cylinder on an Isuzu passenger bus exploded shortly after leaving a gas station, killing five people and injuring 21.

# Summary Uzbekistan's government has ordered inspections of gas-equipped vehicles and filling stations within two months, following a deadly bus explosion. On September 18, a gas cylinder on a passenger bus in Bukhara region exploded, killing five people and injuring twenty-one others shortly after leaving a gas station. The inspections will also cover boilers and furnaces using natural gas. Based on findings, officials will develop a safety roadmap to prevent future accidents involving natural gas equipment and vehicles.

Russia’s foreign ministry said police stopped three U.S. diplomats from entering a restricted area in northern Russia near a navy range where a secretive explosion briefly raised radioactivity levels. Spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said the Americans, described as military diplomats, had permission to visit Arkhangelsk but instead traveled to Severodvinsk and boarded a commuter train toward a nearby community. They were not detained. The Aug. 8 blast killed two servicemen and five nuclear engineers.

# Summary Russian police stopped three American military diplomats attempting to enter a restricted area near a northern naval range where an explosion caused radioactivity spikes. The diplomats had permission to visit Arkhangelsk but traveled instead to Severodvinsk and attempted boarding a train toward the naval facility. Russian officials said they were informed of the restricted zone and released without custody. The August 8 explosion killed two servicemen and five nuclear engineers.

A fireworks factory fire in Tanggerang, near Indonesia’s capital, has killed 47 people and injured 46 others, officials said. The blaze began around 8:30 a.m. local time after an explosion in a pickup minivan carrying raw materials for fireworks, according to Denny Hassan of the city’s disaster management agency. The death toll was confirmed by police and a medical institution. Rescuers said the bodies were badly burned and that crews were still searching the site for any additional victims. Firefighters said the fire has since been extinguished. The injured were taken to hospitals in Tanggerang and to a police hospital in Jakarta, while rescue teams from Jakarta assisted local responders at the scene.

# Fireworks Factory Fire in Indonesia A fireworks factory fire in Tangerang, near Indonesia's capital, has killed 47 people and injured 46 others. The disaster was triggered by an explosion in a pickup minivan loaded with fireworks raw materials. The fire began at 8:30 a.m. local time and has been extinguished. Authorities confirmed the death toll through police and medical institutions, though many bodies were severely burned. Rescue teams from Jakarta have been deployed to assist local firefighters in searching the scene for additional casualties. The injured are receiving treatment at hospitals in Tangerang and Jakarta.

Kazakhstan’s Energy Ministry said oil exports through the Caspian Pipeline Consortium (CPC) are continuing normally. This follows a Novorossiysk court ruling that suspended the CPC marine terminal for 30 days after a Rostransnadzor inspection found documentary violations in the oil spill response plan at hazardous facilities. Despite the suspension order, the ministry reported that Kazakh oil shipments via the pipeline system remain in regular operation.

# Summary Kazakhstan's Ministry of Energy confirmed that oil exports through the Caspian Pipeline Consortium (CPC) continue normally despite a Russian court's 30-day suspension of the CPC's marine terminal in Novorossiysk. The suspension was ordered to allow Russian transport authorities to inspect the facility's technical condition. The inspection identified several documentary violations related to the oil spill response plan.

Russian oil company LUKOIL said its oil spill response technology has received approval from the State Expert Review Agency, clearing the project for use. The system is designed for marine and freshwater ecosystems in the Arctic, where conventional containment and skimming methods are difficult because of harsh conditions. LUKOIL said the technology uses special strains of microorganisms and biological agents suited to marine, freshwater, and mesohalobiotic environments. According to the company, these biologicals do not create toxic compounds and are made without harmful substances. They can also treat polluted areas that are hard to access in extremely low temperatures, making them suitable for the Arctic and Atlantic Oceans.

# Summary Russian oil company LUKOIL received approval from Azerbaijan's State Expert Review Agency for its innovative oil spill response technology designed for Arctic marine and freshwater ecosystems. The technology utilizes specialized microorganism strains capable of functioning in harsh Arctic conditions where conventional containment and skimming methods prove ineffective. The biologicals work in marine, fresh, and brackish water environments without producing toxic compounds or requiring harmful substances in their production. This development enables contamination treatment in remote areas at extremely low temperatures, making it ideal for Arctic and Atlantic Ocean operations. LUKOIL, a major global oil and gas company, accounts for over 2 percent of worldwide oil production.

Azerbaijan’s State Oil Company (SOCAR) approved a plan on Sept. 3 to warn about and eliminate oil spills. In the near future, SOCAR will assess the technical condition of facilities with a high spill risk and review existing response capacities. The plan sets out mechanisms and specific measures to prevent spills, address their consequences, and restore the environment. It also calls for creating a cosmic monitoring system. SOCAR comprises the Azneft, Azerkimya, and Azerigas production unions, along with various processing, service, geophysical, and drilling enterprises.

# Summary Azerbaijan's State Oil Company (SOCAR) approved a comprehensive plan on September 3 to prevent and address oil spills. The initiative includes assessing the technical condition of facilities prone to spills and evaluating existing response capacities. SOCAR will implement specific measures to prevent spills, manage consequences, and restore the environment. The plan incorporates a cosmic monitoring system. Russia’s FSB said it foiled an alleged sabotage plot against the South Stream gas pipeline that it blamed on Ukrainian special services. According to the FSB Public Relations Center, several Russian citizens who helped prepare and support the attack were detained. Authorities seized four magnetic mines, four kilograms of plastic explosives, delayed-action fuses, 593,000 rubles, and phones containing communications with Ukrainian handlers. The messages reportedly included instructions for assembling and placing the bomb, money transfers, and the intended blast location in Volgograd region. The FSB opened a criminal case for preparing a terrorist act, involvement with a terrorist organization, and illegal explosives trafficking.

# Summary The Russian Federal Security Service (FSB) thwarted a terrorist attack on the South Stream gas pipeline allegedly orchestrated by Ukrainian special services. Russian citizens involved in preparing the attack were arrested, and authorities seized four magnetic mines, four kilograms of plastic explosives, delayed-action fuses, 593,000 rubles, and phones containing correspondence with Ukrainian services. Messages revealed instructions for assembling explosive devices, fund transfers, and target coordinates in Volgograd. The FSB initiated criminal proceedings for terrorism preparation, terrorist organization involvement, and explosives trafficking. The pipeline, comprising two lines with 15 billion cubic meters annual capacity, transports Russian gas to Turkey and Balkan countries.

A gas condensate pipeline blast in Ahvaz, southwest Iran, injured nine people, Fars reported. Authorities said corrosion caused the accident, and the fire was extinguished. The report follows a February gas pipeline explosion in southeastern Sistan and Baluchestan that killed two during technical tests.

# Iran Pipeline Explosion Summary A gas condensate pipeline explosion in Ahvaz, southwest Iran, injured nine people on August 8. Pipeline corrosion caused the accident, and firefighters extinguished the resulting fire. This incident follows a February explosion in southeastern Iran that killed two people during pipeline testing.

Nine people were killed Tuesday in an accidental explosion at an explosives factory in southern Brazil, authorities said. The blast struck around 6:00 a.m. near Curitiba, the capital of Parana state, leaving the site in ruins and scattering debris across a wide area. Six men and three women were initially missing, but officials later said there was no hope of finding survivors. Seven other people were injured and taken to nearby hospitals. Firefighters and security forces, using search dogs, combed the wreckage. Authorities said homes within about 1.5 kilometers suffered broken windows and structural damage from the shock wave, which was heard in several nearby towns. Enaex Brasil, the plant’s owner, said it was investigating the cause and would offer psychological support to victims’ families.

# Brazil Explosives Factory Blast Summary Nine people died in an accidental explosion at an explosives factory near Curitiba in southern Brazil on Tuesday morning around 6:00 am. The blast destroyed a large area, with debris scattered across the site. Six men and three women were killed in the incident. Seven others sustained injuries and received hospital treatment. The explosion's shock wave caused significant damage within a 1.5-kilometer radius, breaking windows and damaging structures in nearby houses. Security forces and dogs searched the debris for survivors. Enaex Brasil, the factory's owner, stated the cause was under investigation and offered psychological support to victims and families. Residents in several nearby towns reported hearing the explosion.

The White House is weighing whether President Barack Obama should visit Hiroshima during his late May trip to Japan for a Group of Seven summit, a US official said. The details of the visit have not been finalized, and a stop in Hiroshima has not been ruled out. Obama is already scheduled to attend the G7 summit in Mie prefecture in central Japan. Japan has long encouraged world leaders to visit Hiroshima and Nagasaki to witness the devastation caused by the atomic bombings and support nuclear disarmament. Japanese government spokesman Yoshihide Suga did not directly confirm the reports, but reiterated that Tokyo believes such visits help build momentum toward a world without nuclear weapons. The final US decision may come after Secretary of State John Kerry visits Hiroshima for a G7 foreign ministers meeting on April 10-11. In 2008, then-House Speaker Nancy Pelosi became the highest-ranking sitting US political figure to visit Hiroshima. The article also recalls that the United States dropped the first atomic bomb on Hiroshima on August 6, 1945, killing about 140,000 people, and a second bomb on Nagasaki three days later, killing about 74,000. The bombings remain controversial in the US.

Mexican authorities said Friday that they found about 600 migrants hidden inside two trailer trucks in the eastern state of Veracruz, according to the country’s National Migration Institute (INM). The migrants were discovered in closed box trailers traveling north toward the U.S. border. Officials said the group included 145 women and 455 men. The INM said the migrants came from 12 countries, though most were from nearby Guatemala, with roughly 400 people from there. Other significant groups were from Honduras, Nicaragua, and the Dominican Republic, as well as Bangladesh. The remaining migrants were reported to be from El Salvador, Cuba, Venezuela, Ecuador, Ghana, India, and Cameroon. After the discovery, migration officials began processing the migrants. The agency said it would notify child protection authorities in cases involving unaccompanied minors and families. Mexican authorities will then decide whether to repatriate the migrants to their home countries or allow them to remain in Mexico through a regularization process. The discovery comes amid a broader migration crisis affecting Mexico, the United States, and much of Latin America. In July, U.S. Customs and Border Protection reported 212,672 apprehensions at the U.S.-Mexico border, the highest monthly total in two decades. From October 2020 through June 2021, more than 1 million migrants were arrested at the border. The surge has led the U.S. government to broadcast radio ads in Central America aimed at discouraging people from migrating north. The article also notes the deadly toll of the crisis. In the 2021 fiscal year, U.S. Border Patrol recorded 557 deaths, the highest number since records began and more than double the 254 deaths reported in 2020. Migration from Central America has been driven by factors such as storms, violence, corruption, food insecurity, and limited economic opportunity, especially in countries like Honduras. Across Latin America, tougher immigration enforcement and the movement of Venezuelans and Haitians through the region have further strained migration systems. According to the International Organization for Migration, international migrants made up 2.6% of South America’s population in mid-2020, up from less than 1% in 2015.

Beyond Central America, Latin America faces additional migration pressures from Venezuelan exodus and Haitian migrants traversing the continent. Twelve people were injured and five vehicles destroyed Wednesday when a van carrying gas cylinders exploded on a residential street in Lima’s San Isidro district. Authorities said a fire, apparently triggered by a fault in the van’s ignition system, reached the cylinders and caused a major blast followed by smaller explosions. The shockwave was felt across several blocks. Driver Luis Echevarria and assistants escaped beforehand. Three victims were hospitalized and nine treated at the scene. Firefighters and police responded, and regulators opened an investigation.

# Gas Explosion in Lima Injures 12 A van carrying gas cylinders exploded Wednesday on a residential street in Lima's San Isidro district, injuring twelve people. A fire caused by an ignition fault ignited the cylinders, triggering a major explosion and subsequent smaller blasts felt across several blocks. The driver and assistants escaped before detonation. Five parked vehicles were destroyed and five others damaged. Three victims were hospitalized while nine received minor injury treatment on-site. Firefighters and police controlled the flames. Peru's mining and energy regulator launched an investigation.

Venezuelan state oil company PdV and Trafigura are discussing a long-term swap in which Trafigura would supply roughly 200,000 barrels per day of gasoline, diesel and base oils in exchange for a similar volume of Venezuelan crude, according to the energy ministry. The proposal underscores Venezuela’s worsening inability to meet domestic fuel demand despite its vast oil reserves. The crude volume under discussion would equal nearly 11% of Venezuela’s November output of 1.837 million b/d, based on official data reported to Opec. But the deal faces major hurdles. Venezuela’s production is falling quickly, and Trafigura would likely proceed cautiously because of US financial sanctions imposed on PdV and Venezuela in August 2017. Trafigura declined to comment. Fuel shortages are already widespread. Across Venezuela, motorists routinely line up for hours to buy rationed gasoline, and the fuel produced by PdV’s aging refineries is widely regarded as poor quality. Shortages of LPG have also forced many Venezuelans, especially in the interior, to cook with wood or, in urban slums, unsafe electric hot plates. PdV said an “international blockade” caused critical gasoline and diesel shortages in the second half of 2017 in up to 10 states, including Apure, Anzoategui, Amazonas, Barinas, Bolivar, Carabobo, Monagas, Tachira, Trujillo and Zulia. Service station operators in seven additional states reported worsening deficits, which they blamed on fewer weekly tanker deliveries from PdV. Union leader Ivan Freites rejected PdV’s explanation, saying the company’s refineries, with combined nameplate capacity of 1.3 million b/d, are only about 30% operational at best. He said the 940,000 b/d Paraguana refining complex is running below 15% of capacity, and noted that the Amuay refinery never fully recovered from a deadly 2012 explosion. PdV’s financial position is also deteriorating. Falling oil exports are not generating enough cash to pay for imports, and suppliers increasingly demand advance payment before unloading cargoes. Sanctions have further weakened PdV’s access to banking and trade finance. On the production side, Venezuela’s output fell by 248,000 b/d in October and November 2017 to 1.837 million b/d, nearly half the 3.3 million b/d the country produced in 1998. Output has dropped more than 930,000 b/d since Maduro took office in 2013, and further declines were expected in early 2018. Meanwhile, PdV management has been disrupted by anti-corruption investigations that have sent nearly 70 executives to jail since August.

# Summary: Trafigura and PdV Discuss Long-Term Oil Swap Venezuela's state-owned oil company PdV is negotiating a long-term agreement with Swiss trading house Trafigura to exchange approximately 200,000 barrels per day of Venezuelan crude oil for imported gasoline, diesel, and base oils. This discussion reflects Venezuela's severe inability to produce adequate fuel for domestic consumption despite possessing some of the world's largest crude reserves. The proposed crude volume represents nearly 11 percent of Venezuela's November production of 1.837 million barrels per day. However, significant obstacles threaten the agreement's execution, including Venezuela's rapidly declining crude production and U.S. financial sanctions imposed on both Venezuela and PdV since August 2017. Venezuela faces a critical fuel crisis. Citizens wait hours in line to purchase rationed gasoline of questionable quality, and millions have resorted to cooking with wood or dangerous electric hot plates due to LPG shortages. PdV blamed an "international blockade" for fuel shortages across ten states, though union leader Ivan Freitas disputed this claim, pointing instead to operational failures. PdV's refineries, with combined capacity of 1.3 million barrels per day, operate at only 30 percent capacity at best. The major Paraguana refining complex functions below 15 percent capacity, with the 635,000 b/d Amuay refinery still recovering from a devastating 2012 explosion that killed over 40 people and remains partially unrepaired. Financial constraints compound the crisis. PdV cannot generate sufficient revenue from declining oil exports to finance fuel imports, and suppliers now demand advance payment. U.S. sanctions have further deterred banks from conducting business with the company. Venezuela's crude production has collapsed dramatically. Output plunged to 1.837 million barrels per day in November 2017—the second-lowest level since 1952 and approaching half of the 3.3 million barrels per day produced in 1998. Production has dropped over 930,000 barrels per day since 2013. Further 200,000 b/d declines are expected through January 2018. Additionally, PdV's management faces paralysis from anti-corruption investigations that have imprisoned nearly 70 executives since August.

Peru’s state-owned PetroPeru is still unable to regain access to a section of its 100,000 b/d northern crude pipeline after protesters damaged it last month. The company halted pipeline operations on 27 November, and Canada’s Frontera Energy, which transports crude from block 192 in the northern jungle through the line, began shutting in wells on 3 December. Frontera produced about one-fifth of Peru’s 55,000 b/d of crude output in November, according to PeruPetro. The disruption is also affecting investment prospects. Felipe Cantuarias of the Peruvian Hydrocarbons Society said the conflict is not only reducing production but could deter future investors. That is especially relevant because Frontera’s block 192 contract expires in August 2019 and PetroPeru is seeking an investment partner. Environmental damage is mounting as well. Drone images show a large oil spill near the Mayuriaga indigenous community in Loreto, and PetroPeru says more than 8,000 barrels of heavy crude have spilled near the Morona pumping station along the 1,100 km pipeline. The protests began after local elections on 7 October, with residents accusing authorities of fraud. In mid-November, they first briefly kidnapped oil workers and then sabotaged the pipeline. President Martin Vizcarra sent negotiators, but leaders rejected them and demanded Prime Minister Cesar Villanueva instead. More than 100 police have been deployed, though officials fear renewed violence after a deadly 2009 pipeline-related clash. PetroPeru also said a second Loreto community was blocking another pumping station on 5 December.

# Peru Oil Pipeline Under Siege Peru's state-owned PetroPeru faces ongoing challenges accessing its 100,000 barrel-per-day northern crude pipeline, which was severed by protesters in November. PetroPeru suspended operations on November 27, prompting Canada's Frontera Energy to begin shutting in wells on December 3. Frontera, which produces roughly one-fifth of Peru's 55,000 barrels per day, is significantly impacted by the closure. Industry leaders warn that pipeline attacks may deter potential investment partners. The dispute has severe environmental consequences. Aerial photos reveal a major oil spill near the Mayuriaga indigenous community in Loreto region, with PetroPeru estimating over 8,000 barrels of heavy crude spilled near the Morona pumping station. Over 100 police officers have been deployed, though authorities exercise caution given a deadly 2009 clash between indigenous protesters and police that killed 33 people. A second community now blocks another pumping station, demanding government environmental remediation funds.

Floods in western Kenya have repeatedly destroyed rice crops, raising concerns about food insecurity in a country where demand for rice is rising fast, especially in cities. In Ahero, a rice-growing town in southwest Kenya, farmer Dennis Onyango was replanting his fields after his seedlings were wiped out by flooding for the third time in just a few months. Onyango, 35 and father of five, said the first flood came in early April when heavy rains hit Kisumu County. That flood flattened and waterlogged his young rice plants, forcing him to buy new seedlings and begin again. The same thing happened at the end of April, and then again three weeks before the report. He said he had now exhausted his money buying seedlings from other farmers. Onyango described the season as unlike anything he had experienced in his 15 years of rice farming. The repeated flooding has devastated not only his crop but also his finances, threatening his ability to support his family and pay school fees. He said that in a good year with two successful harvests, he can earn about 120,000 Kenyan shillings, or roughly $1,120. This year, however, he said the losses and the uncertainty of more flooding mean his situation is desperate. According to Joel Tanui, the western Kenya manager at the National Irrigation Board (NIB), the floods across Kenya’s rice-producing regions over the past two months could worsen food insecurity in a country already struggling to feed a rapidly urbanizing population. Climate scientists say such sudden, intense floods are becoming more common because of extreme weather linked to global warming. Tanui said the flooding has damaged rice harvests in several key production areas, including Kisumu, Homa Bay and Busia counties, which together account for up to 40% of Kenya’s rice output. Although rice needs plenty of water, he explained that floodwaters can be powerful enough to crush stalks and strip grains from the plants, while crops that remain standing can drown after being submerged for hours or days. The NIB said about 7,500 acres, or 3,035 hectares, of rice have been destroyed by floods since April. The agency manages many of Kenya’s main rice-growing projects, including Ahero. The article notes that rice is Kenya’s third most important food staple after maize and wheat, according to a 2014 Food and Agriculture Organization report. Rural Kenyans tend to eat less rice and rely more on maize and wheat, while city residents consume most of the rice. Demand is growing quickly: national rice consumption has been increasing at 12% a year, compared with 1% for maize and 4% for wheat. With more than a quarter of Kenya’s population now living in cities, the loss of domestic rice production could put additional pressure on food supplies. The food security situation is already fragile. The U.S. Agency for International Development said in April that about 1.3 million Kenyans, nearly 3% of the population, were facing crisis levels of food insecurity or worse. A mid-May European Commission humanitarian report said heavy rains had directly affected 1.26 million people across the Horn of Africa since March. The report also warned that the extreme weather is compounding locust invasions, increasing the number of people in need. Greenpeace Africa campaigner Amos Wemanya said extreme weather is damaging not just food production but other aspects of life as people are displaced and farmland is destroyed. He argued that farmers are being prevented from producing enough food for the country. He suggested agroforestry, or planting trees among crops, as one possible way to slow floodwaters and stabilize soil. Tanui said the government cannot easily rely on imports to replace the rice lost to flooding, especially because the COVID-19 pandemic has slowed or disrupted travel and farming activities globally. Kenya consumes about 600,000 metric tonnes of rice each year, and more than three-quarters of it is imported, mainly from Pakistan and Vietnam. But importing more rice would take time and could be difficult because many governments have restricted exports during the pandemic. Farmers in Ahero want government support to help them buy seeds and equipment and to waive loans from the Agricultural Finance Corporation, a state agency. Another farmer, William Otieno, said his rice seedlings were submerged before they could be transplanted into the main field, leaving them washed away or dead from prolonged soaking. He said the farmers had taken loans to plant this season and had already used their savings to replant. “The government should just help us,” he said.

# Kenya's Flooding Crisis Threatens Urban Food Security Kenya faces a serious threat to its food supply as devastating floods destroy rice crops across the country's major agricultural regions. The crisis is particularly alarming given the nation's rapidly urbanizing population's dependence on rice as a staple food. ## The Immediate Crisis In Ahero, a southwestern Kenyan town, rice farmer Dennis Onyango has replanted his fields three times since April after successive floods destroyed his seedlings. The 35-year-old, who has farmed rice for 15 years, describes the situation as "catastrophic" and unprecedented in his experience. Having exhausted his financial resources purchasing replacement seedlings, Onyango now faces an uncertain future as he lacks funds to replant again if flooding occurs. Since April, approximately 7,500 acres of rice have been destroyed by floods, according to the National Irrigation Board (NIB). The damage is concentrated in major rice-producing regions including Kisumu, Homa Bay, and Busia counties—areas that collectively supply up to 40 percent of Kenya's domestically grown rice. ## How Floods Damage Rice Although rice requires substantial water to grow, the force of intense flooding proves catastrophic. Floodwaters can crush rice stalks, strip grains from plants, and submerge remaining vegetation for extended periods, causing plants to drown. The combination of physical damage and waterlogging makes recovery extremely difficult. ## Vulnerability of Urban Populations Rice represents Kenya's third most important food staple after maize and wheat, according to a 2014 United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization report. Notably, rice consumption is concentrated in urban areas, with rural Kenyans preferring maize and wheat. National rice consumption is increasing at 12 percent annually—significantly faster than consumption of other staples. With over one-quarter of Kenya's population now living in cities, the flooding threatens to create serious food shortages. The NIB's Joel Tanui warns that the destruction of rice crops in major production hubs could worsen food insecurity in a country already struggling to feed its rapidly urbanizing population. ## The Import Problem Kenya consumes 600,000 metric tonnes of rice annually, with more than three-quarters imported, primarily from Pakistan and Vietnam. However, importing additional rice to compensate for flood losses presents significant challenges. The COVID-19 pandemic has disrupted global trade, with many governments restricting exports. Tanui notes that importing rice would take nearly as long as domestic production and faces practical obstacles during the pandemic. ## Broader Context Climate scientists attribute the increasing frequency of sudden, intense floods to extreme weather exacerbated by global warming. The flooding compounds existing challenges; the European Commission reported in mid-May that heavy rains had directly affected 1.26 million people across the Horn of Africa since March. Farmers face multiple threats simultaneously, including locust invasions alongside the flooding. The BBC this week launched new Igbo and Yoruba language services in Nigeria, expanding its local-language journalism in a country where digital media use is widespread and ethnic identity remains highly sensitive. The new services are digital-only and will go live online and on social media on Monday. They join the BBC’s Pidgin service, which began last year and has already drawn strong interest. Together, the three are part of 12 new language services being created worldwide with support from £291 million in British government funding. Peter Okwoche, who is overseeing editorial work for the launch, said Yoruba and Igbo were “the two final cogs in the wheel” for the BBC’s new West Africa services and insisted they were badly needed. He argued that original journalism in a local language can travel even further than English-language reporting. The BBC, he said, wants to strengthen African and Nigerian storytelling by helping people tell their own stories. The launch is aimed especially at Nigeria’s young, online population. The country has about 150 million mobile phone subscriptions and nearly 190 million people overall, with 62 percent of the population under 24. Okwoche said the services are also meant to reach business-minded men and women in the Igbo and Yoruba communities, both in Nigeria and abroad. He noted that foreign coverage of Nigeria often focuses narrowly on Boko Haram in the northeast, even though much more is happening across the country, including technology, business, entrepreneurship, and everyday urban life in places like Lagos. The timing is significant because Nigeria is experiencing renewed ethnic and regional tensions, particularly between the Igbo-speaking southeast and the Hausa-speaking north. In the southeast, the Indigenous People of Biafra (IPOB) has revived separatist sentiment decades after the original Biafra declaration helped trigger a devastating civil war. IPOB leader Nnamdi Kanu, who is on trial for treason in Abuja, has used populist rhetoric that has fueled clashes with the military and further propaganda on both sides. His separatist campaign has also encouraged similar calls from hardline Yoruba nationalists in the southwest. BBC Igbo is scheduled to air an interview with Kanu’s wife on Monday. Okwoche acknowledged the risks of reporting in such a charged environment, especially given Nigeria’s history of misinformation and strong regional loyalties. He said the BBC team had undergone months of rigorous training to report without emotional bias and to maintain credibility. He added that the BBC’s long-running Hausa service, which has served northern Nigeria for 60 years, showed it was “about time” other regions received similar coverage in their own languages.

The regulations would require inspections every five years for all occupied buildings above three floors and give professional construction bodies authority to enforce ethics in the sector. A multi-sectoral committee is already running a nationwide public awareness campaign on unsafe structures. Nyakiongora said the housing shortage is pushing developers to cut corners. He warned that Nairobi would suffer severe damage in a major earthquake. Unsafe buildings that cannot be rehabilitated will be demolished. In Kalehe territory in the Democratic Republic of Congo, the deadly floods and mudslides of May 2023 have prompted a local reforestation campaign that officials and residents hope will reduce the risk of future disasters. The effort is unfolding in the four villages worst affected by the catastrophe — Bushushu, Nyamukubi, Luzira and Chabondo — where many families are still mourning loved ones and struggling to recover from the destruction. The disaster struck after heavy rains caused four rivers in the area to overflow. The resulting floods and mudslides killed more than 440 people and left thousands missing. According to the Red Cross, around 1,200 homes were destroyed and more than 4,600 households were affected. The rains were not unusual for Kalehe, but the scale of the damage was unprecedented. U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres described the floods as “yet another illustration of the acceleration of climate change.” Residents say the human toll remains unbearable. Seventy-two-year-old Jérémie Lushambo still visits the Kabushungu River every day to pray for more than 50 relatives who disappeared in the water. He says he was able to recover some bodies, but others were swept away. His grief reflects the wider suffering in the area, where many families lost multiple generations in a single event. Environmental experts and local officials argue that deforestation played a major role in making the disaster worse. Agronomist Boris Hamuli says the hills around the villages had been stripped of trees for decades, leaving the soil exposed and vulnerable to erosion during the rainy season. Kalehe administrator Thomas Bakenga says the mountains and hills bordering Lake Kivu were once forested, but population growth and the need for survival pushed people to clear land for housing, farming, firewood and charcoal production. With few other job options, many residents depended on the forests for income and basic needs. In response, the local government launched a campaign in June 2023 to plant 1,000 trees on the bare hills above the flooded villages. So far, at least 150 volunteers, mostly young people aged 18 to 30 and supported by agronomists, have planted about 800 trees, including grevillea, casuarina and podocarpus. Bakenga says the campaign is meant to protect the environment and help prevent a repeat of the tragedy. For many participants, reforestation is also a personal act of healing. Simeon Rulinda, 47, lost two of his children and a cousin when a house collapsed during the floods in Bushushu. He says planting trees has become a form of therapy that helps him cope with grief while focusing on a better future. Similarly, 51-year-old Anaclet Mirindi, who lost uncles and cousins and narrowly survived because he and his family were away when the landslide struck, says planting trees is an investment in the safety of the next generation. The long-term scale of deforestation in Kalehe is severe. Data from Global Forest Watch shows that between 2015 and 2022 alone, the territory lost more than 420 square kilometers of tree cover, though the clearing began decades earlier. Across the Democratic Republic of Congo, which is often called the “second lung of the world” because of its vast tropical forests, deforestation remains a major problem. In 2022, the country lost more than 500,000 hectares of forest, with agriculture and charcoal production among the main drivers. Local environmental officials say the loss of trees weakened the soil over time until heavy rains triggered mudslides and devastation. Jackson Shamamba, an agronomist and engineer involved in the campaign, says preserving primary tropical forests is essential because they store carbon and release oxygen, helping regulate the planet’s climate. He argues that allowing plants to grow is a responsibility tied to human survival. The campaign is also changing attitudes in the community. Immaculée Maisha, 28, from Nyamukubi, says she grew up seeing elders cut trees for building and cooking and once accepted it as normal. But after the disaster, she says she now understands the importance of forests. Her memories of the flooding remain vivid and traumatic. She recalls huge boulders crashing down, crushing homes and killing people who could not run, including the elderly, children and the sick. She lost 26 relatives, including siblings, cousins, and her grandparents. The market-day disaster in Nyamukubi destroyed the market, 500 homes, a church, a mosque and many other buildings. The floods also destroyed crops and fields, leaving many survivors in extreme poverty and food insecurity. Germaine Mwavita, 52, says she left Bushushu after a landslide killed several family members and destroyed her home. She says food is scarce, aid from NGOs is insufficient, and she does not know whether recovery is possible. Rubambiza says nearly 500 families who lost their homes are expected to be relocated to areas where they can farm and raise livestock, reducing their dependence on cutting down trees for survival. Officials acknowledge that many residents still struggle to meet basic needs, but they hope the reforestation campaign will gradually build awareness and resilience. The trees will take between two and 10 years to fully grow, but participants and leaders say the project is already helping people understand the link between forests, livelihoods and disaster prevention.

Egyptian Minister of Irrigation Mohamed Abdel Ati visited Kampala, Uganda, on Sept. 26, 2018, to attend the closing ceremony of the first phase of the Averting Flood Risks Project in Kasese, a district that has suffered repeated flooding over the past two decades. The visit was part of broader technical cooperation between Egypt and Uganda in water resources and irrigation, and Abdel Ati was received by Ugandan Minister of Water and Environment Sam Cheptoris. During meetings at Uganda’s Ministry of Water, Abdel Ati reviewed the background of the Kasese project, explaining that the area had faced severe flooding caused by landslides in mountainous regions, which had damaged homes, farms, livestock, and poultry and caused major human and material losses. In response to Uganda’s request for help, Egypt quickly sent experts to assess the area, gather data, and identify high-risk zones. A memorandum of understanding for the project was signed in April 2016, and the work was divided into several phases. The first phase was carried out by El-Mokawloon El-Arab (Arab Contractors), a major Egyptian company operating in Uganda. It began on March 13, 2017, and was completed in February 2018. Cheptoris welcomed the cooperation and praised the technical expertise of Egypt’s water ministry, saying Egyptian specialists had helped turn floodwater into a useful resource instead of allowing it to be wasted and cause further damage. He also conveyed the gratitude of Kasese residents for Egypt’s support. Abdel Ati said he would visit the project site in Kasese on Sept. 27 with the Ugandan minister and the joint technical committees to review the results of their work. He emphasized that the meetings reflected the long-standing partnership between the two countries in irrigation and water resources. The article also noted that Egypt and Uganda have an existing memorandum of understanding from January 2010 covering several projects worth $4.5 million. These include drilling 75 boreholes in different parts of Uganda to provide drinking water, a project completed in December 2016. Egypt has also supplied heavy machinery for Ugandan water projects, including plans for containment dams to store rainwater for drinking purposes. The contract for those dams was signed with a Ugandan company in August 2017 and is expected to be implemented soon. Ahmed Bahaa el-Din, head of the Nile Water Section, said Egypt remains a source of technical support for Uganda, pointing to projects such as combating sea grass, controlling sea grass in Lakes Kyoga and Albert, and building tanks and boreholes while training Ugandan workers in water resources and irrigation.

Oil prices fell for a fourth straight day as OPEC ministers met in Vienna ahead of Thursday’s policy meeting, raising doubts that the group will agree on any production limits. Futures in New York dropped as much as 1 percent, extending recent declines and putting oil on course for its longest losing streak since April. West Texas Intermediate for July delivery fell to as low as $48.61 a barrel, while Brent for August delivery slipped to $49.36. Trading volume was below average. The market was pressured by signs that some supply disruptions were easing. Canadian oil-sand producers, including Suncor Energy, began restarting operations after wildfire threats subsided. At the same time, output losses in Nigeria and Libya continued to support prices. Despite the day’s weakness, oil had already risen about 85 percent from its 12-year low in February, helped by evidence that the global glut is shrinking. The UAE oil minister said in Vienna that the oversupply that drove prices down since 2014 is gradually correcting itself. He added on Twitter that OPEC’s strategy of allowing the market time to rebalance has worked, but needs more time. Still, analysts said expectations were low for any meaningful agreement this week, with Saudi Arabia expected to resist any supply freeze unless Iran joins in.

Experts warn that severe to extreme drought is expected to affect Cambodia, Laos, Thailand and Vietnam from now until January, threatening agriculture across the lower Mekong River Basin. The Mekong River Commission said water levels in the Mekong have fallen to their lowest in at least 60 years, and most of the basin has experienced exceptionally low flow since June. Thailand and Cambodia are expected to be hit hardest, while Laos and Vietnam may fare somewhat better. The commission attributed the drought to insufficient rainfall during the wet season, a delayed monsoon onset, an earlier-than-usual end to the rains, and El Niño conditions that have driven unusually high temperatures and evaporation. In a normal year, monsoon rains begin in late May and end in October, but this year they started nearly two weeks late and ended about three weeks early. Lam Hung Son, who heads the commission’s flood and drought centre in Phnom Penh, warned that prolonged dry weather could damage crop production and create water shortages for consumption. Conditions are expected to worsen from December into early January, with little or no rain across much of the basin.

# Cambodia, Laos, Thailand, Vietnam Face Severe Drought The Mekong River Commission warns that severe to extreme drought will affect Cambodia, Laos, Thailand, and Vietnam through January. Water levels have reached their lowest points in at least 60 years, with exceptionally low flow throughout the lower Mekong basin since June. Thailand and Cambodia face the most severe impacts. The drought stems from insufficient rainfall, delayed monsoon arrival, and early departure—occurring nearly two weeks late and three weeks early respectively. An El Niño event has contributed through abnormally high temperatures and evapotranspiration. Officials warn the drought threatens agricultural production and crop yields while potentially creating water shortages for consumption. Conditions are expected to worsen from December through early January, with minimal rainfall predicted across most basin areas. The Mekong River Commission, established in 1995, coordinates water resource management among the four affected nations.

At least 20 people were killed when a boat carrying wedding guests collided with a river barge at night in western Myanmar, authorities said, and several others remained missing as rescue teams continued searching. The accident happened Friday evening on a river in Pathein, a port city west of Yangon. Regional MP Aung Thu Htwe said the dead included 16 women and four men, and that about nine people were still unaccounted for. Around 30 people were rescued alive the night of the crash. Past disasters have killed dozens, including 73 people on the Chindwin River in October and 21 people off Rakhine in April.

The Vietnam Red Cross (VRC) held its first-ever all-level disaster response drill in Hanoi on August 17 as part of its annual conference on preparedness for natural disasters in 2016. The event brought together representatives from USAID, UNDP, UNICEF, international partners, and relevant agencies to review the VRC’s emergency response capacity and update preparedness plans. During the drill, participants simulated a storm as powerful as Super Typhoon Haiyan, which struck central Vietnam in 2013 and caused severe loss of life and property in Quang Binh, Quang Tri, Thua Thien-Hue, and Da Nang. The exercise covered damage assessment, reporting to central authorities, and activating response mechanisms before, during, and after the storm. It also included communication efforts to raise public awareness and mobilize domestic and international recovery resources. Earlier, on August 15-16, the VRC trained the National Disaster Response Force on standardized disaster prevention and response skills, including damage assessment, community needs evaluation, rescue, recovery, and international practices. As part of the Central Steering Committee for Natural Disaster Prevention and Control, the VRC has also promoted disaster awareness in communities and schools, planted mangrove forests, formed response teams at all levels, and assisted nearly 42,500 households affected by drought, salinity intrusion, and extreme cold.

Japan says the total cost of the Fukushima nuclear disaster will rise to 21.5 trillion yen, or about $188 billion, nearly double the 11 trillion yen estimate made three years ago. The figure includes compensation, decommissioning, and decontamination. It follows similar numbers reported by NHK and was developed by an expert panel deciding how costs will be shared among the government, plant operator Tokyo Electric Power (TEPCO), and others. The 2011 earthquake and tsunami killed or left missing more than 18,500 people and triggered meltdowns at three reactors. TEPCO faces decades of cleanup, including removing highly radioactive fuel rods.

# Fukushima Disaster Costs Double to $190 Billion Japan's government announced that total costs from the 2011 Fukushima nuclear disaster have nearly doubled to 21.5 trillion yen ($188 billion). This includes compensation, decommissioning, and decontamination expenses—significantly higher than the 11 trillion yen estimate from three years prior. An expert panel is determining how costs will be divided among the government, Tokyo Electric Power (TEPCO), and other parties. The March 2011 earthquake and tsunami killed over 18,500 people and triggered three reactor meltdowns at Fukushima, Japan's worst postwar disaster and most serious nuclear accident since Chernobyl. TEPCO must remove radioactive spent fuel and complete decommissioning over four decades while paying resident compensation. The government covers decontamination and contaminated debris storage costs.

Scientists are warning that Italy’s Campi Flegrei, or Phlegraean Fields, near Naples could erupt at any time, and volcanologist Giuseppe Mastrolorenzo says the danger is so severe that a major evacuation would be impossible under current arrangements. Speaking to Sputnik Italy, Mastrolorenzo of the Vesuvian Observatory said there is still no official, concrete evacuation plan for the millions of people living in the area. He described the risk around Naples as among the highest in the world because it combines the likelihood of a devastating eruption with the enormous number of people exposed. He estimated that about 3 million people could be affected if Mount Vesuvius or the Phlegraean Fields were to erupt. The Phlegraean Fields include supervolcanoes, which he said could produce an eruption hundreds of times larger than the one that destroyed Pompeii. Mastrolorenzo noted that in 2012 the volcanoes were placed under a yellow alert, the second of four warning levels, followed by orange and red. However, he argued that the system breaks down at the highest level: although a state of emergency could be declared, there is still no practical evacuation plan ready to move residents to safety. He said a recent emergency plan for the Phlegraean Fields exists, but in his view it is based on an average eruption scenario and does not adequately account for a large-scale catastrophe. He added that some plans envision relocating people to other parts of Italy, but not all mayors in the danger zone have prepared local evacuation arrangements. Mastrolorenzo said the public should be fully informed so people know where to go in an emergency, and he criticized repeated delays in approving a stronger plan. He compared the situation to past disasters such as the Indian Ocean tsunami and Hurricane Katrina, arguing that risks are often known but poorly prepared for. The situation is made more complicated, he said, by proposed geothermal power plants in the Ischia region and the Phlegraean Fields. These projects would drill deep into the ground and, according to Mastrolorenzo, could trigger earthquakes or even eruptions. Despite this, he said authorities have not blocked the projects. He urged that people adapt to nature by strengthening buildings, improving monitoring, and developing realistic emergency plans.

# Summary: Italy's Volcanic Crisis and Evacuation Concerns Italy faces an urgent volcanic threat that affects approximately 3 million people living near Naples, according to volcanologist Giuseppe Mastrolorenzo from the Vesuvian Observatory. The Phlegraean Fields (Campi Flegrei) and Mount Vesuvius represent the highest eruption risk in the world, yet no official evacuation plan exists despite the imminent danger. Mastrolorenzo emphasizes that the Phlegraean Fields contain super-volcanoes capable of eruptions "hundreds of times larger" than the catastrophic 1979 eruption of Mount Vesuvius that destroyed Pompeii. In 2012, these volcanoes were assigned a yellow threat code—the second-highest level on a four-tier warning system—but authorities have made limited preparations. A critical paradox exists: while emergency protocols theoretically exist at the highest red alert level, no concrete evacuation strategy can actually protect the population. Recent emergency plans developed for the region are inadequate, as they only account for average eruptions rather than large-scale disasters. Additionally, not all mayors in the danger zone have implemented evacuation procedures. Mastrolorenzo criticizes the repeated postponement of plan approval, attributing it to organizational optimism despite historical evidence. Past disasters like the Indian Ocean tsunami and Hurricane Katrina demonstrate that known risks are frequently underestimated during preparation phases. The situation worsens with plans to construct geothermal power stations in the Ischia region and Phlegraean Fields. These facilities would drill approximately 1 kilometer deep, potentially triggering earthquakes or volcanic eruptions in an already high-risk zone. Mastrolorenzo advocates for immediate action: informing all Italian citizens about evacuation procedures, constructing earthquake-resistant housing, and implementing proper monitoring systems. He stresses that humans must adapt to nature rather than imposing infrastructure on vulnerable geological zones, as eruptions could occur at any moment.

Ryan Patricia Kastl Miller, known as Tricia, died on August 10 in Metairie, Louisiana, at age 43. Born in Oklahoma City on May 19, 1978, she spent her childhood in New Orleans, Miami, and New York City. She graduated from the Academy of the Sacred Heart in 1996, then earned both bachelor’s and master’s degrees in communications from Loyola University New Orleans. She later received her Juris Doctor from Loyola’s College of Law, as part of one of the “Katrina” classes whose studies were disrupted by Hurricane Katrina. Her family said Tricia’s greatest joy was her four children, whom she loved above everything else. Though she was born with cerebral palsy, she did not let it limit her ambitions. Instead, her experiences with physical challenges helped shape her deep compassion and respect for others, especially people who were underserved or marginalized. While in law school, Tricia volunteered at the Loyola Katrina Clinic, which provided legal services to people affected by Hurricane Katrina. In recognition of her commitment to social justice, she received the Gillis Long Public Service Award in 2007. She continued serving her community through involvement with the Junior League of New Orleans, Court Appointed Special Advocates (CASA), Second Harvest Food Bank, and other organizations. Drawing on her own experiences with chronic medical conditions, she also became a strong advocate and source of support for others facing serious health challenges. Friends and family remembered her for her creativity, style, and love of fun. She enjoyed trips to see her favorite band, Depeche Mode, and took great joy in planning elaborate birthday parties for her children, including a wig-themed French Quarter party and themed sleepovers. She also loved trying new desserts, walking in the Krewe de Jeanne d’Arc, and even parasailing with her kids. Her fondness for mystery and suspense, especially Stephen King, was matched by her reputation for guessing plot twists long before they were revealed. She was also known for her love of pugs. Among her cherished memories was a visit to the Holy Land, including Petra and a baptism in the River Jordan performed by Father Harry Thompson. She also attended Camp Monterey in Tennessee for many years and treasured her friendships there. She is survived by her husband of 15 years, J. Matthew Miller III; their four daughters; her parents; brother; nephew; in-laws; sister-in-law; nieces; and many extended family members and friends. Visitation and a Catholic mass were scheduled for August 21 at Lake Lawn Metairie Funeral Home, with masks required. The family asked that donations be made to the Father Harry Thompson Center, Boys Hope-Girls Hope New Orleans, or the American Autoimmune Related Diseases Association.

Belgium has reached a major milestone in its transition to the F-35A Lightning II, joining a growing group of NATO allies operating the fifth-generation stealth fighter. The country’s third F-35A, AY-03, recently completed its first flight from Lockheed Martin’s facility in Fort Worth, Texas. The jet carried low-visibility Belgian markings, similar to the subdued national insignia used on some Danish and Polish F-35s. The flight came as Belgian pilots arrived at Luke Air Force Base in Arizona to begin training on the aircraft. Belgian Air Component Lt. Col. Pierre-Yves Libert called the arrival of the first jet at Luke AFB “a historic day,” saying the training program marked the start of a major new phase for the force. More F-35s are expected to arrive there in the coming months. Belgium plans to buy 34 F-35s in total, replacing its aging F-16 Fighting Falcons, which the country first adopted in 1979. Delivery of the new jets was delayed by the COVID-19 pandemic, but Belgium is still expected to receive its full order by 2030. The first Belgian F-35 rolled off the assembly line on December 10, 2023, and the first aircraft, AY-01, has already undergone extensive testing. The aircraft destined for Belgium will be fitted with the Technology Refresh 3, or TR-3, upgrade before they are delivered to Europe. TR-3 includes hardware and software improvements and is a key step toward the more advanced Block 4 configuration, which is expected to add dozens of new capabilities. Although TR-3 itself faced delays, the Pentagon earlier this year agreed to accept F-35s with a “truncated” version of the upgrade, allowing Lockheed Martin to resume deliveries to U.S. allies and partners. Belgium’s first operational F-35s are scheduled to arrive at Florennes Air Base next year, with a second squadron planned for Kleine-Brogel beginning in 2027. The new aircraft will support Belgium’s participation in NATO missions, including air policing, alongside other alliance members such as Denmark, Italy, the Netherlands, Norway, and the United Kingdom. Finland, Germany, Greece, and Poland have also ordered the fighter, and Lockheed Martin expects Europe to have about 500 F-35s by the end of the decade. As Belgium brings in the F-35, it will phase out its F-16 fleet. Some of those upgraded F-16s are being prepared for transfer to Ukraine, part of a broader NATO effort approved by Washington last year. Belgium, Denmark, the Netherlands, and Norway pledged to provide at least 79 Fighting Falcons to help Ukraine defend itself.
