A 5.1-magnitude earthquake struck northern Argentina on Sunday at 00:59 a.m. local time, approximately 63 kilometers west of San Antonio de los Cobres. The epicenter was located at a depth of 168.65 kilometers, according to the US Geological Survey.

President Bola Tinubu came under criticism after releasing ministerial portfolios on Wednesday, August 16, especially for assigning the Ministry of Defence to former Jigawa State governor Mohammed Badaru Abubakar and the Ministry of State Defence to former Zamfara governor Bello Matawalle. The appointments surprised many observers and drew backlash over what critics saw as putting national security in the hands of politicians with poor records on insecurity in their states. Aare Oladotun Hassan, president of the Yoruba Council Worldwide and secretary of the NBA Epe Branch, said the choice was “wrong and ill-timed.” He argued that the defence ministry should be led by experienced retired military generals rather than career politicians. According to him, giving such a sensitive role to former governors whose states were affected by terrorism amounted to “an own-goal against security” in Nigeria. He also warned that appointing people he considered unfit for such a vital ministry would seriously harm the country. A security expert and public affairs analyst, speaking anonymously, also dismissed the portfolio assignments as a “lacklustre team.” He said both men lacked relevant experience and track record, and went further to describe Matawalle as “a criminal.” Hassan urged Tinubu to reconsider the defence appointments and prioritize national interest over political considerations, stressing that Nigeria would not get the right security equipment and support if the wrong people were placed in charge. The article also noted that Matawalle, despite accusations of misusing public funds, reportedly donated N200 million for Sallah celebrations to supporters in Zamfara, according to the state APC chairman, Tukur Danfulani.

# Summary President Bola Ahmed Tinubu has faced significant criticism for appointing two former governors to sensitive defence positions. On August 16, Tinubu announced his 45-member ministerial list, assigning Mohammed Badaru Abubakar (ex-governor of Jigawa State) and Bello Matawalle (ex-governor of Zamfara State) to the Ministry of Defence and Ministry of State Defence respectively. Critics argue these appointments are problematic given both politicians' track records with security challenges in their former states. Aare Oladotun Hassan, President of Yoruba Council Worldwide and Secretary of the Nigerian Bar Association's Epe Branch, condemned the appointments as "wrong and ill-timed." He contended that defence positions should be held by experienced retired military generals, not career politicians, stating that assigning such roles to former governors whose states experienced militarization and terrorist activities amounts to an "own-goal against security." An anonymous security expert similarly criticized the appointments, describing the ministerial list as "lacklustre" and noting that both ministers lack relevant experience and track records. The expert alleged that Matawalle is "a criminal." Hassan urged President Tinubu to reconsider the defence ministry appointments based on national interest rather than political considerations, warning that unsuitable appointees could compromise security equipment procurement and perpetuate embezzlement issues. Additionally, Matawalle faces accusations of embezzling public funds. In June, the APC chairman reported that Matawalle donated N200 million to supporters for Sallah celebrations, raising further concerns about his suitability for the position.

The Democratic Alliance (DA) is launching its election manifesto in Johannesburg, with an expected 20,000 members gathering at Rand Stadium to hear leader Mmusi Maimane. KwaZulu-Natal leader and premier candidate Zwakele Mncwango said the manifesto is intended to appeal strongly to rural voters, as the party seeks to make inroads outside urban areas. Mncwango said the DA’s plan is built around five main priorities. The first is jobs, which he said matter in both rural and urban communities but are especially urgent in rural areas, where poverty and unemployment are widespread. The manifesto will also focus on crime, with the party arguing that rural areas need a better-trained police service and more resources to combat high levels of crime. Other priorities include border control and securing South Africa’s borders against illegal entry, as well as tackling corruption in forms such as embezzlement, “cash for jobs” and bribery. Service delivery is the fifth key issue, especially housing backlogs, sanitation and water shortages, which Mncwango said affect rural communities directly.

# DA Election Manifesto Summary The Democratic Alliance (DA) launched its election manifesto at the Rand Stadium, with party leader Mmusi Maimane addressing approximately 20,000 members. The party's KwaZulu-Natal leader, Zwakele Mncwango, emphasized that the manifesto targets rural voters and addresses five key points. The manifesto prioritizes job creation, as unemployment disproportionately affects rural communities living in poverty. Crime prevention is another focus, with the DA promising a dedicated, well-trained police force for rural areas, arguing that rural crime receives insufficient attention and resources despite rural residents paying taxes. Additional manifesto pillars include border control and securing the country against illegal immigration, combating corruption in all forms including embezzlement and bribery, and improving service delivery. The latter addresses critical rural issues including housing shortages, sanitation, and water access. The DA's strategy aims to make electoral inroads in rural areas by demonstrating how their policies directly benefit these communities.

The OECD has warned that companies mining and buying copper and cobalt from the Democratic Republic of Congo must do more to combat corruption and child labor. Congo is the world’s biggest cobalt producer and fifth-largest copper producer, and demand for both minerals has surged with the rise of electronics and electric vehicles. The OECD said in a report released Friday that child labor and other human rights abuses remain common at small-scale artisanal mining sites, where miners dig by hand. It also urged companies to pay closer attention to corruption risks involving Congo’s largest mining firms. Several major miners, including Glencore and Eurasian Resources Group, are already under investigation in the United States and Britain over alleged corruption in their Congo operations. Ben Katz, a report co-author, said companies should act proactively by improving working conditions in artisanal mining and addressing corruption in supply chains. The OECD said its guidance aims to help firms avoid contributing to conflict, bribery, or human rights abuses through mineral purchasing decisions.

# Summary The OECD has warned that companies mining and purchasing copper and cobalt from the Democratic Republic of Congo must intensify efforts to combat corruption and child labor. Congo is the world's largest cobalt producer and fifth-largest copper producer, holding nearly half of the world's known cobalt reserves. As demand for these minerals has increased due to growth in electronics and electric vehicles, concerns about mining conditions have escalated. The OECD report highlights that child labor and human rights abuses are prevalent in Congo's small-scale, artisanal mining operations where independent miners work by hand. While companies have attempted to address these issues, the OECD emphasizes they must also tackle corruption among major mining firms. Several major Congo-based miners, including Glencore and Eurasian Resources Group, face investigations in the US and UK for corruption allegations. The OECD recommends companies proactively improve working conditions in artisanal mining and address supply chain corruption, noting that artisanal production often mixes with industrial output.

Chief Justice David Maraga used a public lecture at the Oxford Union Conference to sharply criticize Kenya’s Executive and Legislature, saying their selective implementation of the Constitution is one of the biggest obstacles to constitutionalism in Africa. He argued that deep-rooted state capture and sectarian interests have slowed the reforms promised by Kenya’s 2010 Constitution. In his remarks, Maraga said that when left to themselves, the legislative and executive branches, dominated by politicians and elites, tend to apply the Constitution arbitrarily by choosing only the easier, less controversial provisions while protecting their own interests. He said this is exactly what has happened in Kenya. Maraga cited several examples of constitutional failure, including the inability to enforce the two-thirds gender rule, curb corruption, and eliminate electoral fraud. He pointed to Article 27(3), which guarantees equal opportunities in political, economic, and cultural spheres, and Article 81(b), which requires that no more than two-thirds of elective public bodies be of the same gender. Despite repeated efforts, bills intended to implement the gender rule have failed in Parliament. He also warned that corruption is draining nearly a third of Kenya’s annual budget through misappropriation and embezzlement, slowing economic growth. To illustrate the scale of the problem, he referred to global corruption estimates from the World Economic Forum, the World Bank, and Transparency International, which ranked Kenya 143rd out of 180 countries in 2017. Maraga further said political office has increasingly been used to accumulate economic power, turning elections into high-stakes contests that often lead to disputes and violence. He added that foreign data and ICT firms interfering in African elections pose a growing threat to democracy, stability, and security. According to him, Africa’s main problem is not election “divisiveness” but the lack of integrity in electoral management.

# Summary Chief Justice David Maraga has delivered his strongest criticism of Kenya's Executive and Legislative branches, asserting they have fundamentally failed to uphold the 2010 Constitution. Speaking at the Oxford Union Conference, Maraga identified selective constitutional implementation as the primary obstacle to constitutionalism in Africa. Maraga contends that politicians and political elites, left to their own devices, arbitrarily implement the Constitution while protecting personal and sectarian interests. He highlighted specific failures including non-enforcement of the two-thirds gender representation principle, persistent corruption, and electoral fraud. The Chief Justice pointed to Article 81(b), which mandates that no more than two-thirds of elective public bodies' members shall be of the same gender. Despite leadership support, multiple attempts to pass enabling legislation have failed in the National Assembly. Maraga emphasized that approximately one-third of Kenya's annual budget is lost through misappropriation and embezzlement, constraining economic growth. Global corruption costs an estimated $3.6 trillion annually, with Kenya ranked 143rd out of 180 countries in a 2017 Transparency International survey. The Chief Justice attributed Africa's electoral instability not to divisiveness but to poor electoral management integrity. He warned that electoral fraud and manipulation by foreign data firms pose serious threats to African democracy and security. Maraga also noted that the concentration of political power facilitates economic consolidation, transforming elections into high-pressure events with contested results and frequent violence. He advocates for improved electoral integrity and reduced foreign interference as essential for strengthening African democratic institutions.

Ethiopian prosecutors have formally charged 14 people, including two officers from the National Intelligence and Security Service (NISS), in connection with the alleged embezzlement of more than 7.7 billion birr from the Commercial Bank of Ethiopia (CBE). The case, filed at the Federal High Court’s Lideta Criminal Bench, follows an investigation by the Federal Police Crime Investigation Bureau. According to the indictment reviewed by Addis Standard, the suspects include CBE employees, government officials, private workers, and intelligence officers who allegedly conspired to divert public funds from three internal CBE accounts into dozens of private and fraudulent accounts. The scheme is said to have relied on unauthorized access to the bank’s internal system, obtained through the CBE’s Horro branch in western Oromia in April 2025. Prosecutors say the defendants abused access privileges to carry out a series of illegal withdrawals and transfers. Among the accused are three CBE employees, including the former manager of the Horro branch in Shambu, Oromia; two NISS economic intelligence officers; and several other individuals connected to government offices and private employment. The 14 defendants are currently in custody except for one, Negussie Emiru Gurino, of NISS’s Economic Intelligence Division, who remains at large. The charge sheet details several major transfers, including 4 billion birr allegedly split between two accounts under Israel Degefa Sime, 1 billion birr deposited into an account under Getachew Tegegn Abadama, and 2 billion birr into an account registered under Molla Shiferaw Ejigu, identified as the 10th defendant. In total, the fraudulent transactions are said to have amounted to 7.735 billion birr, with individual transfers ranging from 30 million to 500 million birr. The defendants also include employees of Addis Abeba city administration offices. In May, CBE had publicly denied reports that more than 7 billion birr had been stolen, calling the incident an “attempted theft” that was quickly detected and blocked by its internal controls. The new charges, however, present the case as a large-scale, coordinated embezzlement involving both banking and intelligence personnel.

# Summary Fourteen individuals, including two Ethiopian National Intelligence and Security Service (NISS) officers, have been formally charged with embezzling over 7.7 billion birr from the Commercial Bank of Ethiopia (CBE). The charges were filed at the Federal High Court's Lideta Criminal Bench following an investigation by the Federal Police Crime Investigation Bureau. The alleged scheme involved CBE employees, government officials, and private individuals who conspired to divert funds from three internal bank accounts into dozens of private and fraudulent accounts. The perpetrators exploited system access permissions obtained from the CBE's Horro branch in western Oromia in April 2025. The defendants include three CBE employees (among them the former Horro branch manager), two NISS economic intelligence officers, and various government workers from Addis Ababa City Administration. Of the 14 accused, all are in custody except for one NISS officer who remains at large. According to court documents, the fraudulent transactions involved substantial sums: 4 billion birr deposited into an account under Israel Degefa Sime, 1 billion birr under Getachew Tegegn Abadama, and 2 billion birr under Molla Shiferaw Ejigu. Additional transactions ranged from 30 million to 500 million birr. The case contradicts CBE's earlier public statement in May, when the bank claimed the incident was merely an "attempted theft" that was "detected early" and "thwarted within minutes" with no actual money withdrawn. The bank had denied any system breach and characterized the matter as under investigation. However, the detailed charges filed by federal prosecutors now suggest a sophisticated, premeditated embezzlement operation involving coordination between financial institutions and intelligence agencies, indicating the scope of the fraud was far more serious than initially disclosed.

The National Union of Somali Journalists (NUSOJ) has welcomed the United Nations’ call for Somalia’s proposed Official Information Bill (OIB) to be brought into line with international human rights standards. The issue was raised by Ms. Isha Dyfan, the UN Independent Expert on the Situation of Human Rights in Somalia, during her address to the 57th Session of the UN Human Rights Council. She described the bill as a promising development, but urged the Federal Government of Somalia to ensure it genuinely guarantees public access to information held by state institutions and avoids vague or overly broad clauses that could weaken the law’s purpose. NUSOJ also backed the unanimous adoption of Draft Resolution A/HRC/57/L.15, which seeks to support Somalia on human rights issues and renew the UN Independent Expert’s mandate. At the same time, however, the union joined growing international criticism of the OIB, warning that it could undermine Somalia’s democratic foundations if passed in its current form. The bill was approved by the Council of Ministers in March 2024 and is now awaiting parliamentary endorsement. Critics say it threatens the constitutional right to access information and could allow officials to classify too much material as confidential or linked to national security without adequate oversight or justification. The legislation has also been condemned for being drafted secretly, without public or stakeholder consultation, which opponents say weakens its legitimacy and risks entrenching secrecy and corruption in government. A coalition including the International Federation of Journalists, Reporters Without Borders, and the African Freedom of Information Centre has called on Somalia to withdraw the bill and start a more inclusive review process aligned with the African Union Model Law on Access to Information. With the government yet to respond, civil society groups and international actors are stepping up pressure, arguing that Somalia needs transparency-focused legislation that protects human rights and democratic accountability.

# Summary The National Union of Somali Journalists (NUSOJ) has praised the United Nations' call for Somalia's proposed Official Information Bill (OIB) to comply with international human rights standards. At the 57th Session of the UN Human Rights Council, UN Independent Expert Isha Dyfan acknowledged the OIB as a promising development but urged the Federal Government of Somalia to ensure it fully aligns with international human rights standards. She emphasized that all Somali citizens should have access to information held by public institutions and warned against overly broad provisions that could undermine the law's objectives. NUSOJ welcomed the unanimous adoption of Draft Resolution A/HRC/57/L.15, which provides human rights assistance to Somalia. However, the OIB has faced significant international criticism. Approved by the Council of Ministers in March 2024 and awaiting Federal Parliament endorsement, the bill is viewed as threatening Somalia's democratic foundations. Critics argue its broad exemptions could allow the government to classify information as confidential or related to national security without sufficient oversight or justification, restricting citizens' constitutional right to information access. A coalition including the International Federation of Journalists, Reporters Without Borders, and the African Freedom of Information Centre is urging the government to retract the bill and conduct a thorough, inclusive review process aligned with the African Union Model Law on Access to Information. The bill's secretive drafting without public or stakeholder consultation has drawn sharp criticism for undermining legitimacy and fostering governmental secrecy that could enable corruption. The international community and local civil society organizations are intensifying pressure on the government, with NUSOJ leading efforts to ensure proposed legislation promotes transparency and protects democratic principles and human rights standards.

African Global Operations, formerly Bosasa, has sold off more assets at a three-day auction in Krugersdorp as the insolvent company is wound up. Hundreds of bidders crowded into the sale, which followed liquidation after banks said they would close all the company’s accounts. Bosasa rose to prominence amid state capture allegations involving senior politicians. Auctioneer Clive Lazarus said the sale began Wednesday with motor vehicles and construction equipment, followed by properties and office furniture, and ended with smaller office and security items. Notable sales included late CEO Gavin Watson’s BMW X5, which fetched R590,000, and the company’s 8-hectare headquarters, sold for R14 million. Bosasa unsuccessfully tried to halt the auction through an urgent court application. Proceeds will go to creditors, especially the South African Revenue Service, which is owed more than R500 million.

# Summary African Global Operations (formerly Bosasa) concluded a three-day auction in Krugersdorp this week, selling assets from the company and its six subsidiaries. Hundreds of bidders competed for items including motor vehicles, commercial equipment, properties, and office furniture. The auction followed the company's liquidation after banks closed all accounts. Bosasa gained notoriety following corruption and bribery allegations involving senior politicians at the state capture inquiry. Notable sales included late CEO Gavin Watson's BMW X5 for R590,000 and the company's 8-hectare headquarters for R14 million. Despite attempting to halt the auction through an urgent court order, the company was unsuccessful. Auction proceeds will be distributed to creditors, with the South African Revenue Service being the largest creditor, owed over R500 million.

A civilian review panel of 13 South Korean citizens, including professors, school teachers, and two Buddhist monks, spent nine hours on Friday debating whether Samsung heir apparent Jay Y. Lee should be indicted on financial fraud allegations. Meeting in a government conference room in downtown Seoul, the panel heard arguments from both sides, then continued debating for two more hours before resorting to a secret ballot. The result was decisive: 10 members voted against indictment and only three favored it. One member said the group was “quite surprised” by the outcome, noting that the discussion had been heated but many participants had not fully revealed their views. Although the panel’s recommendation is not legally binding, it represents an important victory for Lee and Samsung. Lee had used a little-known civilian panel process, created in 2018 under reforms by the Moon Jae-in administration, to challenge the prosecutors’ case and gain a public airing of support. The decision immediately drew criticism from corporate governance activists and lawmakers, who urged prosecutors to indict Lee anyway. At the same time, prosecutors may be wary of ignoring the panel, since Samsung is widely seen as vital to South Korea’s economy, especially as the country looks for recovery after the coronavirus outbreak. The case is part of a broader clash between South Korea’s powerful chaebols and government efforts to curb their influence. The civilian panel system resembles a grand jury, except members are randomly selected from a pre-vetted pool by the Supreme Prosecutors’ Office. In this instance, the panel was seen as a test of both public opinion toward Samsung and confidence in the chief prosecutor, who is appointed by the president. Lee’s legal troubles began years earlier. South Korea’s special prosecutors indicted him in early 2017 on bribery and corruption charges tied to the scandal that helped bring down former President Park Geun-hye. Prosecutors alleged that Samsung provided horses and other benefits to a confidante of Park in exchange for support for Lee’s succession at the conglomerate. Lee was convicted, later released after his sentence was suspended, and the Supreme Court has since reversed that decision, creating the possibility of a retrial. The panel’s Friday discussion focused on a related case involving whether Lee and Samsung used illegal means to secure control of the conglomerate founded by his grandfather. The legal debate became highly technical, centering on Article 178 of the Financial Investment Services and Capital Markets Act, which prohibits unfair trading. Prosecutors suspect Samsung Biologics deliberately violated accounting rules to justify a merger ratio favorable to Cheil Industries and Samsung C&T, thereby boosting the value of Lee’s stake and strengthening his influence over Samsung Group. They also allege stock price manipulation during the 2015 merger, accusations Lee and Samsung deny. Panel members disagreed over whether prosecutors had enough evidence, with some saying there was no “smoking gun,” while others pointed to documents, phone records, and emails suggesting Lee knew about the scheme. The panel’s recommendation now leaves the decision with prosecutors, who have generally followed such advice in the past. If they move forward, Lee could face years more of legal proceedings.

# Samsung Heir's Fate Rests on Civilian Panel Decision A 13-member civilian panel in Seoul has recommended against indicting Samsung heir Jay Y. Lee on financial fraud charges, delivering a significant victory to South Korea's largest conglomerate in a case that has captivated the nation for years. The panel, comprising professors, teachers, and Buddhist monks, spent nine hours debating Lee's case on June 26 before voting 10-3 against indictment. Lee's legal team strategically invoked a rarely used option allowing civilian review of legal cases, gambling that public opinion would support the Samsung heir and undercut the government's prosecution. The decision immediately sparked controversy among corporate governance activists and lawmakers, who urged prosecutors to pursue indictment regardless. However, prosecutors face a dilemma: ignoring the panel risks angering a public that views Samsung as essential to South Korea's economic recovery following the coronavirus pandemic. Lee's case stems from a 2015 merger between Samsung subsidiaries that prosecutors allege was orchestrated to strengthen his control of the conglomerate. Specifically, prosecutors suspect Samsung Biologics intentionally violated accounting rules to justify a favorable merger ratio that benefited Cheil Industries, Lee's major holding company, and subsequently enhanced his influence at Samsung Group. Prosecutors also allege Lee manipulated stock prices during the transaction. The civilian panel system, created in 2018 as part of reforms under President Moon Jae-in's administration, operates similarly to grand juries. Panel members are randomly selected from a vetted pool by the supreme prosecutors' office. This marks the first time the system has reviewed such a high-profile case, making the decision particularly significant. During deliberations, panel members struggled with technical legal questions, particularly how to interpret Article 178 of the Financial Investment Services and Capital Markets Act regarding unfair trading practices. The panel divided on whether Samsung complied with financial law and whether Lee had clear motive to execute the merger. Some members argued prosecutors failed to produce a "smoking gun"—compelling evidence of criminal conduct—while others contended ample documentation existed, including phone calls and emails suggesting Lee's awareness of the alleged scheme. One panelist acknowledged the broader implications: "Apart from Lee's personal responsibility, I believe this should be a chance to uphold financial market law and order. Our society has to become transparent and fair for our future generations." Lee's legal troubles extend back to 2017, when special prosecutors first indicted him on bribery and corruption charges related to alleged payments to a confidante of former President Park Geun-hye in exchange for government support of his succession. He was initially convicted but released after serving approximately one year with a suspended sentence—a controversial decision the Supreme Court subsequently reversed, raising the prospect of retrial. Prosecutors have historically followed civilian panel recommendations, but this unprecedented high-stakes case may prove different. If prosecutors decide to proceed with indictment, Lee could face another three years of trials. The decision ultimately rests with prosecutors' office officials, who must weigh years of investigation against public opinion and the panel's recommendation.

South Korean business lobbies on Monday urged the government and parliament to quickly abolish the criminal breach of trust charge, saying it unfairly restricts normal management activities and should not be replaced with new regulations. Eight business groups, including the Federation of Korean Industries, said the law’s vague definition leaves companies vulnerable to criminal punishment for ordinary decisions. They argued that misconduct should instead be handled through fraud or embezzlement charges, or through civil lawsuits, as in the United States or Britain. In September, the government and ruling Democratic Party announced plans to scrap the charge, saying it had gone too far in limiting business activity. But the lobbies said there has been little concrete progress and called for prompt legislative action. They also opposed adding punitive damages or other supplementary measures after abolition.

# Summary South Korean business lobbies are urging the government and parliament to quickly abolish the breach of trust charge under criminal law without implementing replacement regulations. Eight business groups, including the Federation of Korean Industries, argue that the vague definition of breach of trust has exposed companies to criminal prosecution for normal business operations. Although the government and ruling Democratic Party announced plans to scrap the charge in September, no significant legislative progress has been made. The business lobbies advocate for unconditional abolition, with misconduct instead addressed through fraud, embezzlement charges, or civil lawsuits, following the U.S. and British models. They also oppose introducing alternative restrictions like a punitive damages system as a supplementary measure.

Former Thai Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra was indicted Tuesday on a royal defamation charge and then granted bail hours later, according to Thailand’s Attorney General’s Office. Thaksin, 74, reported to prosecutors in Bangkok in the morning and was formally charged in a case that has added to a string of court battles unsettling Thai politics. He returned to Thailand last year after years in self-imposed exile, served most of a corruption sentence in a hospital on medical grounds, and was paroled in February. Since then, he has remained highly visible and is widely seen as the influence behind the governing Pheu Thai party. Analysts say the prosecution may be a warning from conservative royalist opponents, who have long accused him of corruption, abuse of power, and disrespect toward the monarchy.

# Summary Former Thai Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra was indicted Tuesday on charges of defaming Thailand's monarchy and released on bail hours later. The 74-year-old voluntarily returned to Thailand last year after self-imposed exile and completed his corruption sentence in February on parole. Despite being ousted in a 2006 coup, Thaksin remains influential and is considered the unofficial power behind the ruling Pheu Thai party. He has maintained a high public profile with frequent appearances and political commentary that concerns Thailand's conservative establishment. Analysts view the lese majeste prosecution as a warning from his political opponents, who were historically staunch royalists, to reduce his political activities.

Indonesia’s Attorney General’s Office said it will auction assets seized from convicted tax fraudster Gayus Tambunan on Dec. 23. The open auction will allow anyone with a valid tax registration number (NPWP) to bid, according to AGO administration chief Murtiningsih. Items include a 260-square-meter plot with a luxury house in North Jakarta, an apartment in Central Jakarta, 31 gold bars, and two cars. Proceeds will go to the state. Gayus was sentenced to 30 years in prison in 2013 for bribery, tax evasion assistance, and passport forgery.

# Summary The Attorney General's Office will auction confiscated assets from convicted tax fraudster Gayus Tambunan on December 23. The open auction allows anyone with a valid tax registration number to bid. Items include luxury properties in Jakarta, an apartment, 31 gold bars, and two vehicles. Gayus, a mid-level tax official, received a 30-year sentence in 2013 for bribery, tax evasion assistance, law enforcement bribery, and passport forgery. Auction proceeds will benefit the state treasury.

Cambodian Prime Minister Hun Manet has ordered a nationwide ban on musical truck horns after social media videos showed people, especially youths and children, dancing on roadsides and even in the street as trucks played rhythmic tunes. Hun Manet instructed the Ministry of Public Works and Transportation and police to act immediately against any vehicle whose standard horn has been replaced with a melody horn, including removing the devices and restoring normal horns. He said provincial authorities had already begun enforcing the measure, but he announced it publicly to ensure it was applied across the country. In a Facebook post on Monday, he described the dancing as inappropriate and said it disrupted public order and created a traffic danger that could threaten lives, including those of the dancers. One video reportedly showed three young people dancing in the middle of a road as a large trailer truck approached playing music. The move follows Hun Manet’s rise to power last year after his father, Hun Sen, ruled Cambodia for 38 years.

# Summary Cambodian Prime Minister Hun Manet has ordered a nationwide ban on musical horns in vehicles, following viral social media videos showing people dancing on roads as trucks with tune-playing horns passed by. Hun Manet, who assumed office last year from his father Hun Sen after 38 years of rule, directed the Ministry of Public Works and Transportation and police to immediately remove musical horns and restore standard honking devices. The Prime Minister cited public safety concerns, stating that the dancing poses traffic hazards and threatens lives, particularly those of the dancers themselves. He noted that provincial authorities had already begun implementing the measure but wanted to announce it publicly to ensure nationwide enforcement. Hun Manet described the dancing as "inappropriate activity," especially among youth and children, that disrupts public order. One video showed three young people dancing in the middle of a road as a large trailer truck approached.

The Election Commission said it was satisfied overall with Thailand’s recent Senate election, even though the final announcement has been delayed until July 3, 2024. EC Secretary-General Sawaeng Boonmee announced that vote counting was completed on the morning of June 27 at IMPACT Forum in Muang Thong Thani and that he had submitted the names of the 200 elected senators and 100 alternates to the EC board. Under the law, the commission must spend five days checking the election for fairness and integrity, which pushed the announcement back by one day. Boonmee said the EC is gathering evidence on alleged irregularities, including collusion, block voting, self-promotion, and possible vote trading. He noted that some old regulations limiting self-promotion and vote solicitation have been revoked, so the EC must determine whether such behavior is now unlawful under current rules. He added that mutual support or vote trading without payment is not punishable, but any exchange of money or other benefits is illegal. The EC has received 614 complaints from the district to national levels. About 65% concern candidate qualifications and allegations of unfair practices, bribery, and benefit distribution, while around 3% involve claims of political influence behind nominations.

# Senate Election Summary The Election Commission (EC) expressed satisfaction with Thailand's recent Senate election, despite receiving 614 complaints about the process. EC Secretary-General Sawaeng Boonmee announced that vote counting was completed on June 27, 2024, with results for 200 elected senators and 100 alternates submitted to the EC board. The official announcement has been delayed to July 3 due to a mandatory five-day verification period required by law to ensure election integrity and fairness. Approximately 65% of complaints concern candidate qualifications, while 3% allege political influence in nominations. Other complaints involve unfair practices, bribery, and benefit distribution. The EC is investigating irregularities, including potential collusion and block voting among candidates. Officials clarified that with outdated regulations revoked, they must determine whether certain activities like self-promotion are now illegal. Vote trading without payment is not punishable, but any exchange involving monetary benefits constitutes an offense. The commission is gathering evidence and investigating hotel rental arrangements to identify illegal activities.

Former XPEC Entertainment chairman Aaron Hsu (許金龍) reported to prosecutors on Tuesday to begin serving a 10-year prison sentence for embezzlement. The case stems from a failed 2016 attempt by Japanese firm Bai Chi Gan Tou Digital Entertainment Co. to buy XPEC, which left about 30,000 Taiwanese investors with losses. Investigators later found Hsu had created the Japanese company as part of a fraud scheme. On Sept. 20, the Supreme Court rejected his final appeal, upheld a NT$60 million fine, and ordered confiscation of NT$1.2 billion in illegal profits. Hsu arrived on time at the Taipei District Prosecutors Office despite travel restrictions. He was originally sentenced to 18 years in 2018, but later rulings reduced the penalty.

# Summary Aaron Hsu, former chair of gaming company XPEC Entertainment Inc., began serving a 10-year prison sentence on September 26, 2023, for embezzlement. Hsu orchestrated a fraudulent scheme involving a Japanese firm's attempted acquisition of XPEC in May 2016, causing approximately 30,000 Taiwanese investors to lose money. The Supreme Court rejected his final appeals on September 20, confirming the sentence along with a NT$60 million fine and NT$1.2 billion in illegal profit confiscation. Originally sentenced to 18 years in 2018, subsequent appeals reduced both his prison term and fine. The investigation revealed involvement by Chinese and Japanese citizens, as well as government officials who served as XPEC directors.

Chou Ching-chun, the 77-year-old president of Taiwan’s Patriot Alliance Association, a pro-Chinese Communist Party group, died of COVID-19 on June 16, according to an announcement posted on Facebook by spokesperson Chen Li-ling. Chen said she became concerned after Chou did not answer her calls on June 15 and later learned from the group’s secretary-general, Chang Hsiu-yeh, that he was still being treated in a hospital. She said the news of his death came on Wednesday and expressed grief, while also implying government wrongdoing by writing, “I can only say the government killed him.” Chen also quoted Chang as saying Chou had fallen into a hypoxic coma around 1 p.m. and that attempts to resuscitate him at Taipei City Hospital’s Zhongxing Branch were unsuccessful. His family had already confirmed his death. Chou, whose original name was Chou Ching-tsuan, was an activist who supported unification between Taiwan and China. He served as president of the Patriot Alliance Association and also chaired the Chinese Democratic Progressive Party. He invested in agricultural and fishery businesses in China and reportedly had close ties with officials linked to China’s United Front work. In 2018, he reorganized the association into the Chinese Patriot Alliance Association and became its first chairman. In May 2021, Chou was convicted by the Taipei District Court for bribery related to the 2018 local elections and sentenced to three and a half years in prison. He had also attended a Beijing event in 2019 marking the 70th anniversary of the communist takeover of China. His organization has long been accused of attacking Falun Gong practitioners, especially near Taipei 101.

Poland said on Monday that it would seek Germany’s permission to send German-made Panther tanks to Ukraine, but would move ahead with other countries if Berlin refused. The announcement came amid growing pressure on Western governments to provide Ukraine with heavy armor as the war approaches its first anniversary. Ukraine has been asking for tanks for months, arguing they are needed to give its forces mobility, protection and firepower to break through Russian defensive lines and regain occupied territory. Kyiv wants the Panther 2, a widely used Western tank, to help it push forward in a planned spring offensive. Ukrainian officials say they need far more than a token number: Andriy Yermak, chief of staff to President Volodymyr Zelensky, wrote on Telegram that Ukraine needs “not 10-20, but several hundred” tanks to restore the country’s 1991 borders. Germany, which must approve any re-export of the tanks, has so far been cautious. Berlin says it does not want to take steps that could intensify the conflict, and has argued that other NATO countries have not formally requested permission to re-export their own tanks. But Germany’s stance appeared to soften on Sunday, when Foreign Minister Annalena Baerbock said Berlin would not stand in Poland’s way if it chose to send tanks to Ukraine. She later declined to clarify whether that reflected the position of the entire German government. Polish Prime Minister Mateusz Morawiecki said Poland would seek permission, but emphasized that even without approval it would still transfer its tanks if a small coalition of countries was formed. He said Poland’s condition was to build at least a limited alliance of states willing to act together. Latvia also signaled support, with Foreign Minister Edgars Rinkevics saying there were no good arguments against supplying battle tanks and dismissing the idea that such a move would escalate the war, since Russia was already escalating. The tank debate dominated recent Western meetings, including an EU summit in Brussels and a gathering of defense ministers in Germany. On Monday, EU foreign ministers also agreed to release 500 million euros in additional military aid for Ukraine. Other allies are also moving: Britain has pledged 14 Challenger 2 tanks, and France has said Ukraine has not ruled out sending Leclerc tanks. In the United States, lawmakers urged Washington to send M1 Abrams tanks, arguing that even that step would help push European allies to follow. The issue comes as fighting remains intense, especially around the eastern city of Bakhmut, where Russian Wagner mercenaries and Ukrainian troops are locked in battle. Both sides are thought to be preparing spring offensives as the war continues in a stalemate in eastern and southern Ukraine. Meanwhile, Zelensky’s government is facing a corruption scandal involving inflated food prices and bribery allegations, adding another complication for Kyiv. Russia reacted by saying divisions in Europe over tank deliveries showed anxiety inside NATO. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said countries sending weapons to Ukraine bear responsibility for prolonging the conflict. Ukraine, however, insists that restoring its territorial integrity is not negotiable.

# Poland Seeks Allied Support for Sending Panther Tanks to Ukraine Poland announced on Monday that it would request German permission to send Panther tanks to Ukraine, with a significant caveat: it will proceed regardless of Berlin's approval, provided other countries form a coalition to do the same. This declaration marks an escalation in Western military support discussions as Ukraine continues its conflict with Russia. The Ukrainian government has been actively seeking German-made Panther 2 tanks, considered among the most widely used Western tanks, to facilitate breakthroughs in Russian defenses and retake territory. However, Germany has maintained a cautious stance, citing concerns about potential escalation and noting that other NATO countries have not formally requested tank re-exports. Despite Germany's hesitation, Western nations have demonstrated substantial commitment to Ukraine's defense. The EU foreign ministers agreed Monday to release a 500-million-euro military aid package, and tank supply dominated discussions at both the EU summit in Brussels and a recent NATO defense ministers' meeting in Germany. Several European leaders have publicly challenged the escalation argument. Latvia's Foreign Minister Edgars Rinkevics stated that "the escalation argument doesn't work because Russia continues to escalate." Lithuanian Foreign Minister Gabrielius Landsbergis insisted tanks should not be withheld "one more day," while Luxembourg's Jean Asselborn warned that Russia could win if Europeans fail to provide necessary support now. Germany's position appeared to soften slightly when Foreign Minister Annalena Baerbock said Berlin would not prevent Poland from sending tanks, though she declined to clarify whether this represented official government policy. Polish Prime Minister Mateusz Morawiecki emphasized the importance of coalition-building, stating that even without German approval, Poland would transfer tanks to Ukraine if joined by other countries. Panther tanks offer strategic advantages over alternatives. Operated by approximately twenty countries, they are more widely available than British Challenger 2 or French Leclerc tanks, and they consume less fuel than turbine-powered U.S. Abrams tanks. Britain has committed to supplying fourteen Challenger 2 tanks, while France's President Macron indicated France had not ruled out sending Leclerc tanks. The timing reflects urgent military considerations. As the first anniversary of Russia's invasion approaches, both sides are preparing spring offensives to break the current stalemate. Fighting currently centers on the eastern city of Bakhmut, where Russian Wagner mercenaries and Ukrainian forces remain locked in battle. However, Ukraine faces complications beyond military concerns. President Zelensky confronts a corruption scandal involving inflated food prices for the military and bribery allegations against a deputy minister, potentially dampening Western support. Ukrainian officials have emphasized their substantial need, with Zelensky's chief of staff requesting "not 10-20, but several hundred" tanks. The Kremlin responded to European divisions over tank supplies by suggesting rising "anxiety" within NATO, though it acknowledged that all nations providing weapons bear responsibility for the conflict's continuation.

Glencore is facing a wave of investor lawsuits in the UK after pleading guilty earlier this year to bribery and market manipulation. Court records show that more than a dozen pension and investment funds, including Mubadala Investment Company, International Petroleum Investment Company, and funds linked to Phoenix Group, Standard Life and HSBC, have filed claims in London against Glencore and some of its executives. Another suit names abrdn Plc, Norges Bank and the Kuwait Investment Office as claimants. The exact allegations are not public, but sources familiar with the cases said they are linked to the more than US$1 billion fine Glencore paid in May. In that settlement, the mining company admitted to misconduct spanning more than a decade, including bribery and corruption in South America and Africa and price manipulation in US fuel-oil markets, ending investigations in the US, UK and Brazil. Glencore agreed to pay about US$1.1 billion to US and Brazilian authorities, while the UK penalty will be determined at a sentencing hearing in early November at Southwark Crown Court. The company had already set aside US$410 million for the UK fine. CEO Gary Nagle said the misconduct had no place in Glencore and pledged stronger ethics and compliance controls.

François Commeinhes, the mayor of Sète in southern France, has resigned after the Court of Cassation upheld his conviction for embezzlement of public funds. The final ruling, issued Wednesday, confirmed a sentence of one year in prison suspended, a five-year ban from holding public office, and a fine. Commeinhes, 75, announced his departure on social media shortly after the decision. The case centered on illegal salary increases granted between 2016 and 2019 to two senior city officials: Patrice Millet, the former director general of services, and the head of the city’s real estate division. According to the court findings, Commeinhes used his position to raise their pay by €99,000 and €44,000 respectively. He had initially been acquitted, but was later found guilty on appeal. His resignation triggered strong reactions in Sète and the wider Thau basin. Thierry Baéza, mayor of Mèze and vice-president of Sète Agglopôle Méditerranée, said the decision was Commeinhes’ own, but noted that justice left him little choice. He described it as courageous, while calling it a sad end to a political career. Opposition figures were more critical. Véronique Calueba of the “Together for Sète” group called it “the end of a reign,” blaming 24 years in power for what she described as a “drunkenness of power.” Her group said the ruling exposed a system built on clientelism, private interests, and opacity. Other local and regional politicians echoed those criticisms, saying the conviction marked the end of impunity and a clientelist political era. With the judgment now final, Commeinhes has stepped down from all elected offices.

# Summary François Commeinhes, 75-year-old mayor of Sète, France, has resigned following the Court of Cassation's final confirmation of his embezzlement conviction. The court upheld a sentence including a one-year suspended prison term, five-year ban from public office, and a fine. Commeinhes was convicted of illegally increasing salaries for two city officials between 2016 and 2019: former city services director Patrice Millet received an unauthorized €99,000 raise, while the real estate division head received €44,000. He initially was acquitted but later found guilty. The resignation, announced via social media, has generated reactions across Sète's political spectrum. Thierry Baéza, mayor of nearby Mèze, acknowledged the difficult decision while noting justice left little room for maneuver. Opposition members characterized the resignation as marking the end of Commeinhes' 24-year tenure. The "Together for Sète" opposition group stated the ruling sanctions a system based on "clientelism, private interest and total management opacity," noting additional cases remain pending against Commeinhes. Municipal councilors from various political backgrounds celebrated the verdict as ending "institutionalized impunity" and a "clientelist system." Deputy Sylvain Carrier called for Sète to shift toward "social and ecological policy" following the conservative administration's conclusion.

Europe’s monarchs have been pushed into an unusually visible role by the coronavirus pandemic, with several kings and queens stepping before their nations in televised or written messages meant to calm fears, encourage obedience to public-health rules, and project a sense of collective resolve. The article compares the moment to wartime, arguing that the crisis has temporarily restored a kind of public relevance to royal houses that are often viewed as ceremonial, outdated, or politically marginal. In Sweden, King Carl XVI Gustaf delivered a national address urging citizens to act responsibly and follow expert advice as the virus spread. Speaking as people worried about their health, relatives, and livelihoods, the 73-year-old monarch said the situation required responsibility from everyone. His message was especially aimed at older Swedes, who face the highest risk from the virus but had also sometimes resisted restrictions on their freedom. He and Queen Silvia said they were trying to follow the advice of authorities as closely as possible. Sweden’s response to the pandemic differed from much of Europe. Schools largely remained open, gatherings of up to 50 people were still permitted, universities were closed, workers were told to stay home when possible, and the elderly were urged to isolate themselves. Some academics criticized the strategy sharply, warning it amounted to a dangerous gamble. Against this background, the king’s speech was meant to reinforce public trust in the government’s approach and to show solidarity. Reaction in Sweden was mixed but not hostile. A columnist in the daily Aftonbladet called the speech “not brilliant, but a clear pass.” On the streets of Stockholm, however, some residents were dismissive. One 33-year-old art director said the king was largely irrelevant to people of his generation and often seemed like a comic-book figure. Public confidence in the Swedish royal family remains moderate rather than overwhelming, with a recent poll showing about half of respondents had a lot or quite a lot of confidence in the monarchy. Other European royals also addressed their populations in mid-March. The kings of Norway, Belgium, and the Netherlands spoke to their people, and Denmark’s queen did as well. In Britain, Queen Elizabeth II issued a written statement. Her son and heir, Prince Charles, later tested positive for the coronavirus but reported only mild symptoms and said he remained in good health. The article notes that royal messages are not only meant to reassure citizens emotionally. They also help frame the pandemic as a national emergency requiring sacrifice and unity, similar to wartime mobilization. Historically, such interventions have sometimes strengthened monarchies. The article cites King George VI’s wartime speech at the start of World War II, which warned of “dark days ahead,” as a powerful example of royal leadership. It also recalls Spanish King Juan Carlos’s televised denunciation of a coup attempt in 1981, which helped defeat it, and King Carl Gustaf’s role in Sweden after the 2004 Asian tsunami, when he became a symbolic “father of the nation.” Not every royal intervention was well received. In Spain, King Felipe VI’s speech was met with boos and the banging of pots from quarantined citizens on their balconies. The backlash was intensified by the royal family’s recent corruption scandal and by criticism that Felipe had been slow to respond compared with monarchs in less-affected countries. The article concludes that if the pandemic worsens and deaths rise sharply, monarchs may again be called upon to serve as symbols of national mourning and endurance. Yet the crisis could also expose the limits of their influence. For supporters, this may be a chance for royals to prove their continuing relevance; for critics, it may simply show how far removed they are from ordinary people.

# The Crown vs. Corona: European Monarchs Step Into the Spotlight During Pandemic As the coronavirus pandemic spreads across Europe, the continent's monarchs are experiencing a dramatic shift in their roles, emerging from routine ceremonial duties to deliver urgent messages to their nations—a level of national prominence not seen since World War II. ## Royal Addresses Across Europe Multiple European monarchs have recently addressed their people during the crisis. Sweden's King Carl XVI Gustaf delivered a speech emphasizing solidarity and the importance of social distancing, stating, "We are in a situation which demands people take responsibility." His message was aimed particularly at elderly citizens, who face the greatest health risks but have sometimes resisted new restrictions on their freedom. Similar addresses came from the kings of Norway, Belgium, and the Netherlands, the queen of Denmark, and Queen Elizabeth II of Britain, who released a written statement. Prince Charles tested positive for coronavirus but reported only mild symptoms. ## High Stakes for Monarchies The stakes for these royal interventions are exceptionally high. Success could transform antiquated institutions into sources of national strength and define a monarchy's relevance. Failure, however, could fundamentally undermine a royal house's purpose. As researcher Kristina Widestedt from Stockholm University explains, comforting messages help ease public anxiety during uncertain times, while royal appearances reinforce the collective sacrifice required during crises, comparable to wartime mobilization. ## Sweden's Unique Approach Sweden's pandemic strategy diverges significantly from most European nations. Schools remain largely open, gatherings of up to 50 people are permitted, and the government has resisted strict lockdowns—a controversial approach some academics warn resembles "Russian roulette." The government instead relies on voluntary compliance and targeted isolation of high-risk groups. ## Mixed Public Reception Public reaction to the king's speech in Sweden was cautiously positive in media circles, with columnist Lena Mellin calling it "not brilliant, but a clear pass." However, street-level responses proved less enthusiastic. Daniel Lindell, a 33-year-old Stockholm resident, dismissed the king as "kind of an irrelevance" and "a comic-book figure for many." Current polling shows approximately 50 percent of Swedes have "a lot or quite a lot of confidence" in the royals—steady but not overwhelming support. Responses elsewhere proved even more negative. In Spain, where the royal family recently faced corruption scandals, King Felipe VI's speech was met with pot-banging and jeering from thousands of quarantined citizens on their balconies. Many felt the king responded too slowly compared to monarchs in less-affected European regions. ## Historical Precedent for Royal Intervention Despite current mixed reactions, history demonstrates that royal speeches during crises can significantly boost national morale and enhance a monarchy's reputation. British King George VI's 1940 wartime address was galvanizing, Spanish King Juan Carlos's 1981 coup denunciation proved pivotal, and King Carl Gustaf's 2004 response to the Asian tsunami tragedy established him as a "father of the nation" figure. ## Looking Forward As the pandemic potentially worsens, European monarchs may be called upon to play increasingly significant roles in national mourning and recovery. Widestedt predicts the Swedish king may deliver longer, more personal speeches if death tolls and hospital strain escalate. For some monarchies, the crisis represents an opportunity to prove institutional relevance; for others, it may merely expose their powerlessness and distance from contemporary society.

LVMH, the French luxury giant behind Louis Vuitton and Moët & Chandon, reported record sales and net profit for 2014, though several underlying results fell short of market expectations. Sales rose 6 percent to a record 30.6 billion euros, while net profit reached a record 5.65 billion euros. However, that profit figure was boosted by a one-off 2.8 billion-euro gain tied to Hermes shares held by LVMH. Excluding that effect, net profit was under 3 billion euros, below analysts’ forecasts and also lower than the 3.4 billion euros reported in 2013. Operating profit declined 5 percent to 5.7 billion euros, and the operating margin slipped by 2 percentage points to 19 percent. Analysts had expected operating profit of 5.84 billion euros and adjusted net profit of 3.4 billion euros. Chief executive Bernard Arnault said the results showed LVMH’s ability to grow despite economic and currency uncertainty. Performance varied across divisions. Fashion and leather goods remained the strongest segment, with sales up 10 percent to 10.8 billion euros and a 2 percent gain in recurring net profit. By contrast, wines and spirits sales fell 5 percent, with net profit down 16 percent to 1.1 billion euros, mainly because cognac sales slowed in China amid the country’s anti-corruption crackdown on luxury gifting. Watches and jewellery also weakened, with net profit down 23 percent to 283 million euros. Selective retailing was the fastest-growing division, up 7 percent, helped by an exceptional year for Sephora. LVMH said it would propose increasing its dividend by 3 percent to 3.20 euros per share.

# LVMH Reports Record Sales and Profit Despite Mixed Results LVMH, the world's leading luxury company, announced record sales of 30.6 billion euros ($35.1 billion), representing 6 percent growth, and record net profit of 5.65 billion euros. However, when excluding a 2.8 billion euro gain from Hermès share distribution, net profit fell below 3 billion euros—significantly lower than analyst expectations and the company's 2013 profit of 3.4 billion euros. Operating profit declined 5 percent to 5.7 billion euros, with operating margins dropping 2 percentage points to 19 percent. While sales slightly exceeded analyst forecasts, operating profit fell short of expected 5.84 billion euros. CEO Bernard Arnault expressed confidence in LVMH's ability to progress despite economic and currency uncertainties. The company's fashion and leather goods segment led growth with 10 percent sales increases to 10.8 billion euros, achieving a 2 percent net profit gain—the only segment to do so. However, other segments underperformed. Wines and spirits sales dropped 5 percent, with net profit falling 16 percent to 1.1 billion euros, primarily due to declining cognac sales in China. The watches and jewellery segment saw net profit plummet 23 percent to 283 million euros amid weak retailer purchases. The selective retailing segment performed best, posting 7 percent growth, driven by exceptional results from Sephora perfume shops. Despite uncertainties, LVMH proposed increasing dividend payments by 3 percent to 3.20 euros per share, expressing confidence in maintaining growth momentum across all business groups in 2015.

The OSCE Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights (ODIHR) has condemned the sentencing of Azerbaijani human rights defender Anar Mammadli, who was given a prison term of five and a half years by a Baku court on 27 May 2014. ODIHR Director Ambassador Janez Lenarčič said the ruling was part of a broader campaign by Azerbaijani authorities to silence those defending fundamental freedoms and to intimidate others who might do the same. Mammadli, chair of the Election Monitoring and Democracy Studies (EMDS) centre, was detained on 16 December 2013 and charged with embezzlement, tax evasion, abuse of office, and forgery. Lenarčič argued that the charges and conviction were aimed at stopping Mammadli from defending voters’ rights and sending a warning to civil society in Azerbaijan. He said the actions of the authorities violated both Azerbaijan’s obligations to its citizens and its commitments as an OSCE participating State. The article says Mammadli and his organization had already faced sustained pressure. EMDS’s registration was revoked by the Ministry of Justice, and its predecessor had been deregistered by a district court in 2008, with that case still pending before the European Court of Human Rights. In the months before the charges, EMDS offices were searched, documents and computers were seized, and staff were questioned over allegations of foreign funding. In late November, Mammadli was barred from leaving the country to attend a European Union conference in Vilnius. EMDS had criticized major violations in the 9 October 2013 presidential election, and ODIHR observers reported many of the same problems.

# Summary On May 27, 2014, the OSCE Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights (ODIHR) condemned Azerbaijan's sentencing of human rights defender Anar Mammadli to 5½ years in prison. ODIHR Director Ambassador Janez Lenarčič characterized the conviction as part of a systematic campaign to suppress fundamental freedoms and silence dissent. Mammadli, chairman of the Election Monitoring and Democracy Studies (EMDS) center, was arrested on December 16, 2013, facing charges including embezzlement, tax evasion, abuse of office, and forgery. Prior to his arrest, authorities conducted office searches, seized documents and computers, and questioned staff about foreign funding allegations. The sentencing followed EMDS's critical assessment of Azerbaijan's October 2013 presidential election, where the organization documented extensive violations of fundamental freedoms. ODIHR observers independently reported similar findings. Lenarčič argued the conviction violated Azerbaijan's obligations as an OSCE participating state and contradicted the country's human rights commitments. He asserted the ruling was intended to intimidate other human rights workers and prevent Mammadli from defending voter rights. The EMDS organization's registration was revoked by the Ministry of Justice. It succeeded the Election Monitoring Centre, which was deregistered in 2008—an appeal regarding that decision remains pending at the European Court for Human Rights.

Spain’s interior minister, Jorge Fernandez Diaz, faced mounting calls to resign after leaked recordings suggested he had discussed with a Catalan anti-fraud official how to gather damaging information on political rivals. The conversations, published by the left-wing daily *Publico* just four days before Spain’s general election, appeared to show Fernandez Diaz and Daniel de Alfonso, head of Catalonia’s anti-fraud office, talking about possible investigations or leads involving pro-independence politicians in the region. In one recording, Fernandez Diaz allegedly said he could “intervene with the public prosecutor” to push for a probe that could then be leaked to the press. Another conversation published later the same day suggested he was willing to help launch an investigation that might be used politically. The revelations sparked a political storm during the final days of campaigning. Several opposition figures and police unions demanded his resignation. Podemos leader Pablo Iglesias said the interior minister, who should protect all citizens, seemed to be using his office to investigate political opponents, and called for an immediate resignation. Socialist leader Pedro Sanchez also accused Fernandez Diaz of using the state apparatus against rivals rather than tackling corruption inside his own party. Catalan regional president Carles Puigdemont said the leak confirmed suspicions of a “dirty war” against separatist politicians. Fernandez Diaz rejected the allegations, calling the leak a “conspiracy,” while acknowledging that the 2014 meeting had taken place. He said he remembered the general purpose of the meeting as one with the head of the regional anti-fraud office, whose role was to fight corruption. He also said it was “surreal” to suggest he was plotting against Catalan officials and said police had been asked to investigate how the conversation was recorded and leaked. Prime Minister Mariano Rajoy defended him, saying he had given a clear explanation and accusing critics of trying to exploit the scandal “four days before the end of the campaign.” The controversy erupted as the conservative Popular Party was expected to win Sunday’s election but fall short of the majority needed to govern, following months of political deadlock after the December vote.

# Spain's Interior Minister Faces Resignation Calls Over Leaked Conversations Spain's Interior Minister Jorge Fernández Díaz faced mounting pressure to resign Wednesday following leaked conversations that appeared to show him discussing ways to incriminate pro-independence political rivals with Catalonia's anti-fraud official. The online left-wing newspaper Público published recordings of conversations from 2014 in which Fernández Díaz and Daniel de Alfonso, head of Catalonia's anti-fraud office, discussed possible investigations against pro-independence politicians. A second conversation revealed the minister allegedly suggesting he could "intervene with the public prosecutor" to initiate probes that could be leaked to the press. The scandal erupted just four days before Sunday's general elections, igniting significant political controversy. Police unions and multiple political rivals, including leaders from the anti-austerity Podemos party and the Socialist party, demanded Fernández Díaz's resignation. Podemos leader Pablo Iglesias criticized the minister for "using his post to investigate political rivals," while Socialist leader Pedro Sánchez accused him of weaponizing state apparatus against opponents rather than combating corruption within his own party. Catalonia's pro-independence regional government head Carles Puigdemont called the behavior a "strategy of dirty war." Fernández Díaz acknowledged the 2014 meeting occurred but characterized the leak as a "conspiracy," claiming he merely discussed fighting fraud and corruption. He requested police investigate how the conversation was recorded and leaked. Acting Prime Minister Mariano Rajoy defended his minister, suggesting political opponents were "fishing in troubled waters" before elections. The controversy reflects ongoing tensions between Madrid and Catalonia's separatist politicians. The elections represent the second ballot in six months, following December's inconclusive results that left parties unable to form a coalition government.

Jihadists controlling Mosul are trying to turn their self-declared Islamic caliphate into a functioning state by introducing new services, enforcing order, and gradually imposing strict religious rules. According to local reports, the Islamic State has begun preparing to issue official documents such as passports and is seeking revenue through oil sales. The group is also presenting itself as fighting corruption and building a “fair” society, in an effort to win over residents who it now treats as citizens of the new caliphate. A bank employee in Mosul said the militants brought in accountants to inspect bank accounts and prevent embezzlement. Smaller private banks were given a phone number to call if anyone tried to withdraw money while falsely claiming to represent the Islamic State. Ordinary life has also been affected by the new emphasis on law and order. One resident, Ahmed, said people can no longer tip petrol station attendants, because such tips could be interpreted as bribes that might help them skip fuel queues later. Residents said the group has tried to ease its takeover by removing the checkpoints that had clogged the city under Iraqi government control. Some locals described the new situation as more free, with one saying it no longer felt like Iraq and that parking restrictions had disappeared. At the same time, the militants are slowly introducing their version of Islamic rule. When they arrived in Mosul last month, they distributed rule sheets stamped with the caliphate’s seal, saying the city would be governed by strict sharia and ordering women to cover up and stay home unless absolutely necessary. Activities seen as un-Islamic are being targeted as well. Pool and poker are being curtailed, and this week snooker clubs were reportedly shut across the city. Cigarettes have also become more expensive, with residents fearing a possible ban.

# Summary ISIS jihadists controlling Mosul, Iraq have begun implementing state services as part of their effort to establish a functioning Islamic caliphate. In an attempt to gain local support, they have launched an anti-corruption initiative and announced plans to issue official documents including passports and generate revenue through oil sales. The jihadists have introduced strict law-and-order policies affecting everyday life. Banks have been instructed to monitor withdrawals, and residents report even small gestures like tipping petrol station attendants are discouraged to prevent corruption. Some residents have responded positively to these changes, noting the removal of government checkpoints that previously restricted movement and describing a sense of newfound freedom in the city. However, ISIS is simultaneously implementing strict Islamic rules through a gradual approach. Upon arrival in Mosul last month, they distributed rule sheets stamped with the caliphate seal, mandating women cover up and remain home unless necessary. Activities deemed irreligious—such as snooker, pool, and poker—are being systematically shut down. Snooker clubs were closed this week, and residents anticipate further restrictions, with some bulk-buying cigarettes before they are potentially banned. This measured strategy represents a shift from ISIS's previous failed attempt to establish an Islamic state, when their harsh extremist policies prompted rejection by the population. By initially offering relief from government oppression while gradually introducing strict sharia law, ISIS aims to consolidate control over Mosul's residents and solidify their caliphate.

Hundreds of teachers across Iran staged protests on Thursday against changes to their pay and pension scales, saying the measures come amid worsening inflation and rising prices. In Gilan province on the Caspian Sea coast, about 150 teachers marched in Rasht and around 70 more in Lahijan. In Isfahan, Iran’s third-largest city, roughly 300 teachers demonstrated, while another protest took place in Chaharmahal-Bakhtiari province in the southwest. Social media also showed gatherings in Neyshabur, Kermanshah and Khorramshahr. Protesters chanted slogans such as “if embezzlement is reduced, our problems will be solved” and “we only heard promises, we didn’t see justice,” reflecting anger over corruption and unmet commitments. The demonstrations followed a reversal by President Ebrahim Raisi’s government, which changed course on a salary hike he had previously proposed while serving as judicial chief.

# Summary Hundreds of teachers across Iran protested on Thursday against changes to their pay and pensions amid soaring inflation. Demonstrations occurred in multiple cities, including approximately 150 teachers in Rasht, 70 in Lahijan, and 300 in Isfahan. Additional protests were reported in Chaharmahal-Bakhtiari, Neyshabur, Kermanshah, and Khorramshahr provinces. Protesters chanted slogans criticizing embezzlement and broken government promises, expressing frustration over unmet expectations. The demonstrations were prompted by new pay scales that exacerbate teachers' financial difficulties during a period of high inflation. Ultraconservative President Ebrahim Raisi, who took office in August, had previously proposed a salary increase while serving as judicial chief. An Israeli airstrike late Monday hit a densely populated residential neighborhood in central Beirut, striking the Zoqaq al-Blat area near major government and diplomatic sites, including the U.N. headquarters, Lebanon’s Parliament, the prime minister’s office and several embassies. Lebanon’s state-run National News Agency said two missiles landed in the area. Ambulance sirens were heard after the blast, and an Associated Press reporter at the scene described significant casualties on the street, though no official casualty count was immediately released. The Israeli army did not issue a warning before the strike, and the intended target was not immediately clear. The attack came as central Beirut, including Zoqaq al-Blat, has been sheltering many people displaced by fighting in southern Lebanon and Beirut’s southern suburbs. The strike also occurred near a Hussainiyeh, a Shiite mosque. It was the second straight day of Israeli strikes in central Beirut after a pause of more than a month. On Sunday, an Israeli strike in Ras el-Nabaa killed Hezbollah media spokesperson Mohammed Afif and six other people, including a woman. Later that day, another strike in the commercial district of Mar Elias killed four people. The target of that second strike also remained unclear. Minutes after Monday’s strike, Lebanon’s caretaker Prime Minister Najib Mikati called on “all countries and decision-makers” to stop what he described as “the bloody and destructive Israeli aggression on Lebanon” and to enforce international resolutions, especially U.N. Security Council Resolution 1701. Adopted in 2006, Resolution 1701 was meant to establish a buffer zone in southern Lebanon and end hostilities between Israel and Hezbollah, though its full implementation has remained incomplete. The resolution is again part of an American cease-fire proposal aimed at ending 13 months of cross-border fire between Israel and Hezbollah. Under the proposal, Israeli forces would withdraw completely, while the Lebanese army and UNIFIL, excluding Hezbollah, would become the only armed forces south of the Litani River. Meanwhile, Hezbollah fired dozens of projectiles at Israel on Monday. One rocket struck the northern Israeli city of Shfaram, injuring six people, one of them critically, and trapping a woman inside a building, according to Israel’s Magen David Adom rescue service. The Israeli military had no immediate comment on the Beirut strike.
