Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has recently enjoyed a series of political triumphs that have given him a rare reprieve from the corruption investigations hanging over him. Chief among them was US President Donald Trump’s May 8 decision to withdraw from the Iran nuclear agreement, a move Netanyahu had long opposed and had campaigned against even before the deal was signed in 2015. Netanyahu also celebrated the relocation of the US embassy from Tel Aviv to Jerusalem, after Trump recognized Jerusalem as Israel’s capital. The embassy opening was marked by a ceremony attended by senior US officials, including Ivanka Trump and Jared Kushner, and Netanyahu called it “a glorious day” and “history.” The celebrations came amid deadly violence on the Israel-Gaza border, where Israeli troops killed around 60 Palestinians during protests and clashes. Netanyahu defended the military’s actions, arguing that every country has a duty to protect its borders. For Netanyahu, these victories were not only personally vindicating but also useful politically, because graft probes remain a serious threat. Several investigations are examining his conduct, and the attorney general is expected to decide in the coming months whether to indict him in at least two cases. Police have already recommended charging him with bribery. Netanyahu, who has served about 12 years as prime minister over his career, denies all wrongdoing. His wife, Sara Netanyahu, is also facing possible trial over allegations of misuse of public funds, which she denies. Netanyahu’s mood appeared buoyed by another national success: Israeli singer Neta Barzilai won the Eurovision Song Contest just before the embassy opening, sparking widespread celebration. Netanyahu even mimicked her signature “chicken dance” gesture at a cabinet meeting and again when he met her later in the week. Public opinion also seemed to be improving for Netanyahu. A Maariv poll released in May showed his Likud party gaining strength, with support rising to 36 seats in the 120-member parliament from its current 30. This survey was conducted before Israel announced strikes on dozens of Iranian military targets in Syria, part of a broader effort to stop Iran’s military entrenchment there. Some analysts argued that these strikes, especially the well-planned operation codenamed “House of Cards,” won Netanyahu more respect than Trump’s actions. Israeli commentators said the corruption cases had temporarily receded from the headlines as the media awaited legal developments. But despite the current lull, the investigations have not gone away. The general expectation, according to one commentator, is that the attorney general may eventually indict Netanyahu on at least some counts.

# Netanyahu Basks in Victories While Facing Corruption Investigations Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has recently enjoyed a series of significant political victories that have temporarily overshadowed ongoing corruption probes threatening his political future. ## Major Foreign Policy Wins Netanyahu achieved two long-sought diplomatic victories in May 2018. Iraq’s parliament passed an amnesty bill last week, but the law is now facing mounting appeals and political criticism over its wording and drafting. The bill has sparked nationwide controversy because some of its articles are seen as vague and potentially open to legal loopholes and manipulation. In response, judicial authorities ordered the creation of six central committees to review criminal court rulings and convictions covered by the pardon. The review also extends to private complaints and to detainees or suspects arrested on security or military accusations. Cases to be reconsidered include detainees held more than three months without trial and suspects detained for more than 18 months without investigations being completed. Many political blocs have warned that the bill could lead to the release of terrorists and criminals. Legal experts say the language is loose, and critics note that politicians are included in an exception for those convicted of corruption or bribery. Former prime minister Nouri al-Maliki, leader of the State of Law Coalition, urged parliament to revisit the bill, calling the drafting process suspicious and suggesting backroom deals may have influenced its passage.

# Summary Iraq's recently passed amnesty bill faces significant political and legal challenges. The poorly drafted legislation contains potential legal loopholes that have sparked nationwide controversy. The judiciary has established six committees to review criminal convictions covered by the amnesty, including cases involving detainees held over three months without trial or suspects detained over 18 months without completed investigations. Multiple political blocs have expressed concern that the bill could release terrorists and criminals. Legal experts warn the vague language creates opportunities for misinterpretation and manipulation. Notably, the bill excludes politicians convicted of corruption or bribery. Former Prime Minister Nouri al-Maliki called for parliamentary review, citing suspicious circumstances surrounding the bill's passage. He criticized its non-traditional legal format and the unusual procedures preceding the vote, suggesting backroom deals facilitated the amnesty's approval. These concerns highlight deep divisions within Iraq's political establishment regarding the bill's implications.

The public, he said, wants stronger action against those who steal national wealth.

# Herat Custom House Achieves Record Revenue Collection Najeebullah Baidayee, chief of Herat Custom House, announced that the facility generated over 14.699 billion Afghanis in 1394 (2015-2016), exceeding the national ceiling and marking the highest revenue collection in a decade, excluding 1390. The National General Customs Houses initially set a revenue ceiling of 12.700 billion Afghanis for 1394. After the central customs and revenues department revised this to 14.566 billion Afghanis in September 2015, Herat Custom House surpassed even this adjusted target. Compared to 1393, revenues increased by 24 percent, generating approximately 3 billion additional Afghanis, with 166 million Afghanis donated to ARCS (Afghan Red Crescent Society). Economic experts emphasize that revenue collection is crucial for government operations. They note that Afghanistan's government has historically struggled with revenue collection over the past 15 years, with millions of dollars misappropriated by corrupt officials. However, recent anti-corruption efforts show promise. Expert Haroon Mir advocates for transparent revenue collection and investment in economic, educational, and health projects to address poverty and prevent corruption. He stresses that employing honest customs officials and utilizing digital equipment—recently installed by the Ministry of Finance—can enhance transparency and accountability. The public calls for continued transparent revenue collection and prosecution of officials who misappropriate national wealth.

The site described the post as “the type of thing that makes you remember how thankful you are for having been born,” and said it blamed Jews for bringing down his “Jew Father.” The post, titled “the Food Chain,” was widely criticized when it appeared on Friday for using imagery seen as anti-Semitic. It showed a figure in a black shawl with a “noticeably large” nose placing what looked like a bag of food before the faces of Ehud Barak, Eldad Yaniv and Meni Naftali. The post sparked a heated exchange between Yair Netanyahu and Barak, who called him crazy and suggested he needed a psychiatrist. Netanyahu responded by calling Barak a drunk needing retirement.

# Summary Yair Netanyahu, son of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, posted controversial social media content that has drawn widespread criticism in Israel and the United States. The post, titled "the Food Chain," features imagery that critics say evokes anti-Semitic tropes, including a figure in a black shawl with exaggerated features controlling other individuals and what appears to be George Soros orchestrating events from behind the scenes. The caricature targets Ehud Barak, Eldad Yaniv, and Meni Naftali—figures involved in protests against State Attorney Avichai Mandelblit regarding corruption investigations into Prime Minister Netanyahu and his wife Sarah. The post sparked significant backlash when the Daily Stormer, the largest neo-Nazi website in the United States, reposted and praised it, calling it evidence of Jewish infighting. The controversy escalated into a public exchange between Yair Netanyahu and former Prime Minister Barak, with Barak questioning whether the post reflected what the younger Netanyahu hears at home, suggesting either genetic or mental health issues. Yair Netanyahu responded with personal attacks, calling Barak a "constant drunk." Margaret Atwood’s long-awaited sequel to *The Handmaid’s Tale*, *The Testaments*, returns readers to Gilead 15 years after the events of the original novel and expands the dystopian world in several important ways. Published by McClelland & Stewart, the novel answers long-standing reader questions while also reflecting, with Atwood’s characteristic irony, “the world we’ve been living in.” The story is set in a more entrenched and complicated Gilead, where the totalitarian regime is no longer in its fragile early phase. Instead, it is weakened by war with the Republic of Texas, strained by shortages, and increasingly dependent on the most valuable resource it has: healthy babies. Espionage and defections are rising, with escape routes running through the underground “Femaleroad.” At the same time, the ruling elite is consumed by corruption, treachery, and purges, suggesting that the regime’s greatest danger may come from internal power struggles rather than outside enemies. Unlike *The Handmaid’s Tale*, which is told entirely through Offred’s limited perspective, *The Testaments* uses three narrators. Aunt Lydia returns as one of them, joined by two young girls who grow up on opposite sides of the Canada-Gilead border. Offred remains only indirectly present, but her influence still matters. This broader structure allows Atwood to reveal more about how Gilead functions and how its society has evolved. One of the biggest surprises is the new portrayal of Aunt Lydia. In the original novel, she was a cruel and authoritarian figure who helped enforce Gilead’s repression of women. In the sequel, however, readers learn that Lydia has been secretly documenting Gilead’s crimes, including her own role in building the system. Writing in one of the regime’s few remaining libraries, she recounts how she helped create its laws, uniforms, and naming system. The novel leaves it ambiguous whether her actions were driven by self-preservation, opportunism, or a change of heart. The book also gives a fuller look at Canada-Gilead relations. Canada, once mainly a refuge for escapees, becomes entangled in a major diplomatic dispute over baby Nicole, a child born to a handmaid and smuggled into Canada. Gilead demands the child’s return to her “legal” parents, and the Canadian government, under pressure, eventually agrees. But when Nicole cannot be found, she becomes a symbol on both sides of the border: a martyr in Gilead, and in Canada a rallying point for activists calling for stronger refugee protections and an end to ties with the regime. Anti-immigrant counter-protesters also emerge, demanding the border be closed. Finally, while *The Testaments* differs from the television adaptation of *The Handmaid’s Tale*, there is already interest in bringing it to screen. Hulu and MGM are reportedly developing the sequel, and Bruce Miller, the TV series’ creator and showrunner, is in discussions to adapt it, though it is not yet clear whether it will become part of the existing series or a separate project.

# Summary: Five Things to Know About Margaret Atwood's "The Testaments" Margaret Atwood's highly anticipated sequel to "The Handmaid's Tale," titled "The Testaments," was published by McClelland & Stewart. The novel was inspired by reader questions accumulated over 34 years and contemporary global events, delivering a dystopian narrative that functions as both a political thriller and allegory. ## Setting and Plot The sequel takes place 15 years after the original novel, depicting a more established and mature totalitarian regime. While the 1985 original focused on Gilead's early days of subjugating women as state property, "The Testaments" reveals a regime facing multiple internal and external crises. Gilead is weakened by war with the Republic of Texas, creating resource scarcity, particularly regarding healthy babies. Espionage increases as defectors escape through an underground network called the "Femaleroad." The greatest threat emerges from within the ruling class itself, plagued by treachery, corruption, and power struggles. ## Narrative Structure Unlike "The Handmaid's Tale," which presents only Offred's perspective confined within a commander's household, "The Testaments" employs three narrators. Aunt Lydia returns as a narrator, alongside two young girls raised on opposite sides of the Canada-Gilead border. This expanded viewpoint broadens readers' understanding of Gilead's operations. Offred appears only indirectly, though her legacy significantly influences the narrative. ## Aunt Lydia's Transformation The sequel reveals a dramatically different side of Aunt Lydia. Previously portrayed as a despotic authority figure wielding cattle prods and enforcing compliance, she is now shown secretly documenting Gilead's misdeeds in one of the regime's libraries. As a former judge, Aunt Lydia recounts her role in engineering the patriarchal system of laws and oppression. The narrative leaves ambiguous whether her actions stemmed from survival instincts or opportunism, inviting reader judgment. ## Canada-Gilead Relations While Canada served merely as a peripheral refuge in the original novel, "The Testaments" explores detailed bilateral relations. A central tension involves baby Nicole, born to a handmaid and smuggled into Canada. Gilead demands her return to her legal parents—a commander and his wife. Though Canada initially resists pressure, it eventually capitulates. When Nicole disappears, she becomes a symbol for opposing causes: Gilead elevates her to martyrdom with children praying for her return, while Canadian activists protest for refugee protection. While the first season closely followed the source material, subsequent seasons diverged into original stories. Atwood serves as consulting producer. Now, Hulu and MGM are developing "The Testaments" for television, with showrunner Bruce Miller reportedly in discussions to adapt the sequel, though it remains unclear whether it will continue the existing series or become a separate project.

The 132 cardinal electors who will choose the next pope are all in Rome, with the conclave scheduled to begin Wednesday. The article explains the centuries-old process by which the Roman Catholic Church selects its new leader and outlines who can take part. A conclave is the secret, ceremonial election in which cardinals vote repeatedly until one candidate secures a two-thirds majority and becomes pope. Before voting begins, the participating cardinals take a vow of secrecy and are not allowed to discuss the details of the election. The voting takes place in the Sistine Chapel. There is one ballot on the first day, followed by two votes in the morning and two in the afternoon on subsequent days. After each round, the ballots are burned. If no pope has been chosen, chemicals are added so the smoke turns black, signaling that the election continues. If a pope is elected, the smoke turns white, announcing success to the waiting crowds. There is no fixed time limit for a conclave. The longest papal election occurred before the modern conclave system was established, when it took three years to choose Pope Gregory X in 1271. That prolonged vacancy led Gregory X to formalize the sequestered process in order to prevent future delays. By contrast, the shortest conclave lasted only a few hours in 1503. Pope Francis was elected in two days after five rounds of voting. Technically, any baptized Catholic man can be elected pope, though for roughly the past 650 years the cardinals have chosen one of their own. Only cardinals under age 80 are allowed to vote. Of the Church’s 252 cardinals, 135 meet that age requirement, but only 132 will actually participate. The Vatican says two eligible cardinals are not traveling to Rome because of poor health, and a third will not take part because he was convicted of embezzlement and fraud. The article also notes the Canadian contingent. Canada has five cardinals, but only four can vote because Cardinal Marc Ouellet turned 80 last year. Ouellet remains eligible to be elected pope, but cannot be an elector. Cardinal Gerald Lacroix, Archbishop of Quebec and a member of Francis’s Council of Cardinals, is also named in an ongoing class-action lawsuit alleging sexual misconduct; both he and Ouellet deny wrongdoing, and the claims have not been tested in court. Cardinal Thomas Collins, former Archbishop of Toronto, is the only Canadian elector with prior conclave experience. Cardinal Francis Leo, the youngest Canadian cardinal, is 53, while Cardinal Michael Czerny, 78, serves in a senior Vatican role focused on migrants and environmental issues.

# Papal Conclave: What You Need to Know The 132 cardinals gathered in Rome are preparing to begin a conclave on Wednesday to elect the next pope, following a tradition that dates back centuries. ## The Conclave Process A conclave is the secret, ceremonial process through which cardinals select the new head of the Roman Catholic Church. All participating cardinals must take a vow of secrecy, preventing them from discussing election details. The process involves cardinals casting ballots in the Sistine Chapel until one candidate receives a two-thirds majority vote. The voting schedule includes one round on the first day, followed by two rounds each morning and afternoon on subsequent days. After each vote count, the ballots are burned. If no pope has been elected, chemicals are added to make the smoke black. White smoke signals a successful election. ## Timeline and Eligibility There is no official time limit for a conclave. Historically, the longest papal election took three years before Pope Gregory X was named in 1271, prompting Gregory to formalize the sequestration process to prevent lengthy elections. The shortest conclave lasted only hours in 1503. Pope Francis's election concluded in two days after five rounds of voting. While technically any baptized Catholic man can become pope, the College of Cardinals has exclusively chosen cardinals for the role over the past 650 years. Only cardinals under 80 years old can vote. Of 252 total cardinals, 135 meet this requirement, but only 132 are participating—two eligible cardinals are absent due to poor health, and one was convicted of embezzlement and fraud. ## Canadian Cardinals Canada has five cardinals, with four eligible to vote. Cardinal Marc Ouellet, a former front-runner for papacy, turned 80 and cannot vote, though he remains eligible for election. Cardinal Gerald Lacroix, 67, was appointed to Pope Francis's advisory council in 2023. Both Ouellet and Lacroix are considered long shots after being named in a 2022 sexual misconduct lawsuit, which both deny. The Vatican found no grounds to investigate Ouellet, and a church investigation found Lacroix's allegation unsubstantiated. Cardinal Thomas Collins, 78, is the only Canadian elector with previous conclave experience, having participated in Francis's 2013 election. Cardinal Francis Leo, 53, is Canada's newest cardinal, appointed just six months ago. Cardinal Michael Czerny, 78, serves as Prefect of the Dicastery for Promoting Integral Human Development at the Vatican.

Conservative Leader Andrew Scheer spent the second day of the federal election campaign in Toronto trying to focus attention on affordability, but he was again pulled into debate over abortion. Scheer and his wife, Jill, visited Chai Lifeline Canada, a Toronto and Montreal charity that supports families dealing with life-threatening illnesses. There, they painted and coloured with children and spoke with parents. Scheer joked that one child’s painting could someday be sold for a lot of money. He also talked about his own family, including one parent holding an infant, and highlighted a campaign promise to eliminate federal taxes on maternity and parental leave benefits through a tax credit. He said the measure could save parents about $4,000 a year at a time when expenses are rising and household income is falling. Scheer, who has five children aged 14 and under, said parents face major costs in those early months, including car seats, diapers, clothes, and even dry cleaning and carpet cleaning. The Parliamentary Budget Officer estimated the tax credit would cost $622 million in its first year and more than $1 billion by 2021, though the office said the estimate was uncertain because it relied on many assumptions. Scheer said the estimate was in line with Conservative expectations and said the party would explain how it would pay for the measure when its full platform was released. Scheer’s trip to Toronto was part of a broader Conservative strategy of campaigning aggressively in ridings the party hopes to win. He was in York Centre, where Conservative candidate Rachel Willson is trying to defeat Liberal incumbent Michael Levitt. Toronto’s Liberal dominance is strong: the party won every seat in the city in 2015, and York Centre had only briefly been held by the Conservatives from 2011 to 2015. The Conservatives have signaled for months that they intend to campaign offensively and do not see many of their 2015 seats as being in danger. But the campaign day was overshadowed again by abortion politics. Earlier Thursday, Toronto Liberal MP Carolyn Bennett shared a two-year-old video of Willson speaking at the March for Life on Parliament Hill. In the video, Willson said she was shocked that Canada has no legal restrictions on abortion, said she was working to have a monument to the “unborn” built in Canada, and described participation in a “no not this one” prayer campaign that involves trying to identify women considering abortion. Bennett used the video to question how Scheer could claim the abortion debate is closed in Canada while campaigning with a candidate she described as anti-choice. Scheer, a practising Catholic, has previously voted for anti-abortion bills and won support from social conservatives during the 2017 Conservative leadership race by pointing to that record and promising free votes for MPs on conscience issues. On Thursday, he denied Bennett’s accusations and called them “completely false.” He repeated his recent position that, if elected prime minister, he would vote against any abortion legislation. He also accused the Liberals of repeatedly trying to reopen the issue and “fearmonger” about it. Willson, who was with Scheer at the charity, said she supports his position and appreciates that the party does not force MPs to vote on moral conscience issues. She declined to say whether she would introduce abortion legislation herself, saying she is focused instead on what voters are telling her about affordability, security, and Liberal ethics. Scheer also spent much of Thursday preparing for the first leaders’ debate of his political career, though Liberal Leader Justin Trudeau would not be there. Trudeau chose to skip the Maclean’s and Citytv debate, saying he would only attend the two official debates in October. Scheer said Trudeau’s absence was unfortunate but not surprising, given the week’s events involving the RCMP’s investigation into possible obstruction-of-justice allegations tied to the SNC-Lavalin affair. The Globe and Mail reported that police were interviewing witnesses, including former justice minister Jody Wilson-Raybould, about whether Trudeau tried to interfere in the prosecution of the Quebec engineering firm, which faces foreign bribery and corruption charges. Just before the debate, the Conservatives also announced they had removed candidate Cameron Ogilvie in Winnipeg North over “discriminatory social-media posts.” The party said Ogilvie had hidden the posts during vetting earlier in the year. Ogilvie, who works in trucking and transportation, had been challenging Liberal incumbent Kevin Lamoureux. The Conservatives said they would name a replacement candidate.

Lundin Gold Inc. announced on May 8, 2025, that its board of directors has amended the company’s dividend policy and declared both a new special dividend and a higher quarterly dividend structure for shareholders. The Vancouver-based gold producer said it will pay cash dividends totaling US$0.45 per common share for the quarter, made up of a new variable quarterly dividend of US$0.15 per share and the existing fixed quarterly dividend of US$0.30 per share. In addition, the board declared a special dividend of US$0.41 per common share, or about US$100 million in total. The special dividend will be paid on June 9, 2025, to shareholders of record at the close of business on May 22, 2025. The quarterly dividends will be paid on June 25, 2025, to shareholders of record on June 10, 2025. Lundin Gold said both the quarterly dividends and the special dividend qualify as “eligible dividends” under Canadian income tax rules. President and CEO Ron Hochstein said the decision reflects the company’s strong financial position and operating performance, along with higher gold prices. He said the company’s debt-free balance sheet and robust operations made it possible to return additional cash to shareholders. According to Hochstein, the new structure is intended to combine a sustainable fixed dividend with a variable dividend that can rise during periods of strong free cash flow, while still leaving room to fund exploration and growth opportunities. Under the revised policy, the variable dividend will be determined at the board’s discretion and will be equal to at least 50% of the company’s normalized free cash flow for the preceding quarter, minus the fixed dividend already paid in that period. Lundin Gold said it defines normalized free cash flow by removing significant non-recurring items from its free cash flow calculation. For dividends expected to be paid in respect of fiscal 2025, the company said this normalization will include annual income tax and profit-sharing payments made in April, which totaled US$95.3 million. That amount will be spread evenly across the four quarters at US$23.8 million per quarter. The company said it will disclose more detail about its normalization approach in future years alongside year-end results. Lundin Gold said the new variable dividend for the first quarter of 2025 was calculated on that basis. Based on the company’s closing share price of CAD$59.39 on the Toronto Stock Exchange, the quarterly dividends of US$0.45 per share imply an estimated annual yield of about 4.2%. The company also explained how the dividends will be paid across its different trading venues. For shares trading on the TSX and OTCQX, the quarterly dividends will be paid in Canadian dollars on June 25, based on the exchange rate on the record date. For shares trading on Nasdaq Stockholm, payment will be made on June 30 in Swedish kronor under Euroclear procedures. To facilitate the quarterly dividend payment, Euroclear will impose a temporary administrative cross-border transfer closure from June 5 through June 10, during which shares cannot be transferred between the TSX and Nasdaq Stockholm. The special dividend will also be paid differently depending on the market. TSX and OTCQX shareholders will receive it in Canadian dollars on June 9, using the exchange rate on the special record date. Nasdaq Stockholm shareholders will receive the special dividend in Swedish kronor on June 12. For the special dividend, Euroclear will similarly close cross-border transfers from May 20 through May 22. Lundin Gold noted that payments to shareholders who are not residents of Canada will be reduced by any applicable Canadian withholding taxes. It directed investors to its dividend information page for more details. The company also included standard legal and regulatory disclosures. It said the release contains forward-looking information, including statements about dividend timing, amounts, and estimated yield, and warned that actual results could differ because of various risks. Those risks include instability in Ecuador, community relations, power supply reliability, tax changes, security, labor availability, mining operations, environmental compliance, illegal mining, infrastructure, government approvals, gold price fluctuations, dependence on a single mine, climate change, cyber security, legal claims, and other operational and regulatory factors. Lundin Gold said its expectations are reasonable but should not be relied upon as guarantees. The release also identified Lundin Gold’s business profile. The company, headquartered in Vancouver, owns the Fruta del Norte gold mine in southeast Ecuador, which it described as one of the highest-grade operating gold mines in the world. Lundin Gold said its board and management have extensive expertise and are committed to operating responsibly, maintaining transparency, following international best practices, and creating value for shareholders while also benefiting local communities, protecting workers’ health and safety, minimizing environmental impact, and continuing exploration to support long-term growth.

Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton said Friday that the State Bar of Texas is planning to sue him over his efforts to overturn the 2020 presidential election, adding another legal threat to the embattled Republican as he faces a close primary runoff. Paxton’s challenge to the election, based on false claims of fraud, had already been under review by the bar since last summer. The bar has not publicly filed a lawsuit against Paxton, but it did ask an Austin-area court on Friday to impose discipline on one of Paxton’s staff members, alleging professional misconduct connected to the election litigation. According to the bar’s complaint filed in Williamson County, Paxton’s top deputy, Brent Webster, was “dishonest” and made “false statements” in the petition asking the U.S. Supreme Court to block President Joe Biden’s victory. Because state law limits what it can say about investigations before a public complaint is filed, it declined further comment. The program also calls for drafting several new laws, including those on state service, public-private partnership, public procurement, legal information distribution, public control, protection of victims and witnesses in criminal proceedings, and administrative procedures. Other institutions, including the Supreme Court, the Supreme Economic Court, and parliamentary committees, also joined. The commission’s decisions will be binding on state bodies and other organizations.

# Uzbekistan Approves State Program Against Corruption President Shavkat Mirziyoyev of Uzbekistan has approved a state anti-corruption program for 2017-2018. The program aims to prevent corruption across government and society, detect and suppress corruption offenses, and eliminate their causes and conditions. Key initiatives include developing draft laws on state service, public-private partnerships, public procurement, legal information distribution, public control, and protection of witnesses in criminal proceedings. The program also emphasizes transparency in budget formation and spending. To coordinate anti-corruption efforts, Mirziyoyev established the Uzbek Republican Interdepartmental Commission, headed by Attorney General Ihtiyor Abdullayev. The commission includes representatives from major government agencies such as the Ministry of Justice, Internal Affairs, Tax Committee, Customs Committee, and the Supreme Court, among others. The commission's decisions are binding on all state bodies, public associations, and organizations in Uzbekistan, ensuring comprehensive implementation of anti-corruption measures nationwide.

UEFA President Michel Platini has postponed his decision on whether to run for FIFA president in 2015, saying he will first consult Europe’s 54 national federations during a series of regional meetings scheduled from September through December. Speaking to the UEFA Congress in Astana, Kazakhstan, Platini said he would “listen” to members and then make decisions together with them after the summer. He had previously said in 2013 that he would decide “during or after the World Cup in Brazil.” Platini’s delay comes as current FIFA president Sepp Blatter is widely expected to seek a fifth four-year term at the May 2015 election in Zurich. Blatter has said he would run if member associations asked him to, a possibility that could become clearer at FIFA’s congress in Sao Paulo on the eve of the World Cup opening match on June 11. Platini, a FIFA vice president and UEFA president since 2007, is long viewed as Blatter’s likely successor, though the two men have often disagreed despite describing each other as friends. At the UEFA gathering, both leaders exchanged polite but pointed remarks. Blatter noted that FIFA reforms, including the creation of independent ethics and audit committees, had not been fully adopted by other football bodies. Platini, in turn, reminded Blatter of his earlier promise that the current term would be his last, while also stressing Europe’s expectation that commitments made to UEFA should be taken seriously. Platini also used the occasion to press Blatter on third-party ownership of players’ economic rights, a practice UEFA wants banned because it distorts the transfer market and drains money from football. FIFA has not taken decisive action against it, despite its widespread use in parts of South America, Spain, and Portugal. Platini urged Blatter to show “political courage,” arguing that the sums involved in a single transfer can exceed FIFA’s entire annual $30 million solidarity budget. Beyond election politics, Platini outlined UEFA’s broader social agenda. He said UEFA would strengthen cooperation with the other continental confederations and create a children’s foundation to support youth programs worldwide. He also announced plans to help women and ethnic minorities move into football administration and said a conference in Rome in September would advance the educational side of UEFA’s anti-racism strategy.

# Summary UEFA President Michel Platini has delayed his decision on whether to run for FIFA president in 2015, pushing back his original deadline. Speaking at a UEFA Congress in Kazakhstan, Platini announced he would discuss the 2015 FIFA and UEFA elections during regional meetings with European football leaders scheduled between September and December, rather than deciding immediately. Platini had previously stated he would make his decision during or after the 2014 World Cup in Brazil. His potential candidacy is significant because he is widely viewed as the natural successor to 78-year-old FIFA President Sepp Blatter, who served as Platini's mentor. Blatter is expected to seek a fifth four-year term at the May 2015 election in Zurich, though he previously promised at the 2011 UEFA Congress that his current term would be his last. During their speeches, Platini and Blatter referred to each other as "dear friends" while also subtly criticizing one another. Platini appeared to remind Blatter of his earlier solidarity pledge to European football, while Blatter pointed out that FIFA's anti-corruption reforms had not been implemented by national associations and confederations. The most direct confrontation involved third-party ownership of players' economic rights. Platini made a "solemn request" to Blatter to ban the practice, which UEFA views as threatening transfer market integrity and draining substantial funds from the sport. Platini emphasized that money lost to third-party ownership exceeds FIFA's entire $30 million annual global solidarity program budget. Additionally, Platini outlined UEFA's expanded commitment to social issues, including establishing a new children's foundation to finance worldwide youth programs and initiatives to help women and ethnic minorities pursue management roles in football organizations. A planned anti-racism conference in Rome for September will develop UEFA's educational strategy on the issue. The UEFA presidential election will occur in March 2015 in Vienna, Austria.

Uzbekistan and Switzerland have agreed to return $131 million in assets seized from Gulnara Karimova, the imprisoned daughter of former Uzbek President Islam Karimov. Uzbekistan’s Justice Ministry said on August 16 that Justice Minister Ruslanbek Davletov and Swiss President Ignazio Cassis signed an agreement in Bern to place the confiscated money into a UN fund intended for sustainable development in Uzbekistan. Cassis said the fund would ensure the returned assets benefit the Uzbek population. The deal marks a significant step in Uzbekistan’s broader effort to recover about $1 billion in allegedly illicit funds held abroad, a process sometimes slowed by foreign governments’ demands for transparency in how the money will be used. Switzerland had frozen about 800 million Swiss francs, or $842 million, in 2012 as part of criminal proceedings against Karimova, who was once a pop singer and businesswoman and later fell out with her father. She is currently serving a prison sentence in Uzbekistan on embezzlement and criminal conspiracy charges. Earlier this year, Uzbekistan said it was working with Switzerland, the United States, France, Russia, and other countries to recover assets it described as earned through criminal activity. Uzbek officials said that assets worth around $131 million, confiscated in 2019, were ready to be transferred. In 2020, Switzerland said a framework agreement with Uzbekistan meant any returned assets must be used for the benefit of the Uzbek people. Karimova was once widely viewed as a possible successor to her father. She was put under house arrest in 2014, while he was still in power. After Islam Karimov died in 2016, Shavkat Mirziyoev became president. Investigators in several countries have linked Karimova to a long-running bribery scheme involving foreign telecom companies seeking access to the Uzbek market. She was sentenced in 2017, later placed under house arrest, detained again in 2019, and then received an additional 13-year sentence in 2020 after being convicted of extortion, money laundering, and related crimes.

# Swiss To Return Millions From Uzbek Leader's Daughter Uzbekistan and Switzerland have agreed to return $131 million in assets seized from Gulnara Karimova, daughter of late Uzbek President Islam Karimov. Uzbek Justice Minister Ruslanbek Davletov and Swiss President Ignazio Cassis signed the agreement in Bern on August 16. The confiscated funds will be placed in a UN-administered trust fund dedicated to sustainable development in Uzbekistan. This agreement represents progress in Tashkent's broader effort to recover approximately $1 billion in illicit assets from foreign jurisdictions. Switzerland had frozen around 800 million Swiss francs ($842 million) in 2012 during criminal proceedings against Karimova, a businesswoman and pop singer imprisoned on embezzlement and criminal conspiracy charges. Karimova, once considered a potential successor to her father, was placed under house arrest in 2014 while he remained in power. After Karimov's death in 2016, Shavkat Mirziyoev became president. Karimova was formally imprisoned in 2017. International investigators from Switzerland, the United States, Sweden, and the Netherlands linked Karimova to a massive bribery scheme involving foreign telecommunications companies seeking access to the Uzbek market. She received a 10-year sentence in December 2017, later commuted to five years of house arrest. In March 2019, she was detained for allegedly violating house arrest terms. Karimova attempted negotiating her release in February 2020, offering to return $686 million in exchange for dismissing domestic charges. However, a month later she received an additional 13-year sentence for extortion, money laundering, and related crimes. The returned assets will now benefit Uzbekistan's population through the UN fund.

Uzbekistan has begun a trial over the deaths of 65 children linked to contaminated cough syrups, far more than the 20 deaths it had previously reported. The medicines were produced by India’s Marion Biotech and imported into the country. Twenty-one defendants, including 19 Uzbeks and two Indians, face charges such as tax evasion, selling substandard or counterfeit medicines, abuse of office, negligence, forgery and bribery. They include former officials responsible for licensing imported medicines and executives of the importing company. India has canceled Marion Biotech’s manufacturing license and arrested some employees.

# Summary Uzbekistan began a trial Friday regarding 65 child deaths from contaminated cough syrups produced by India's Marion Biotech—significantly higher than the previously reported 20 deaths. Among 21 defendants are 19 Uzbeks and 2 Indians, including former senior officials responsible for medicine licensing and executives of the importing company. Charges include tax evasion, selling substandard medicines, abuse of office, negligence, forgery, and bribery. Azerbaijani investigative journalist Afgan Mukhtarli is at risk of torture after disappearing in Tbilisi on May 29 and reappearing in custody in Baku, Azerbaijan, following what he described as a cross-border abduction. Mukhtarli, who had lived in exile in Georgia since 2015 with his wife because of fears linked to his reporting on alleged corruption involving President Ilham Aliyev, is now held by Azerbaijan’s State Border Service investigative unit. According to his lawyer, Mukhtarli said he was seized in Tbilisi by plain-clothed men speaking Georgian, tied up, driven to the city’s outskirts, and beaten. The men allegedly changed cars twice before taking him across the border. Mukhtarli told his lawyer that 10,000 euros were planted in his pockets during the crossing so Azerbaijani authorities could accuse him of trespassing and smuggling. He also said he was mistreated after arriving in Azerbaijan. Amnesty International called the case deeply sinister and said Mukhtarli should be immediately and unconditionally released and protected from torture. The group said he appears to be a prisoner of conscience targeted for his journalism and suggested Georgian authorities may have been complicit. Amnesty urged Georgia to investigate promptly and hold everyone involved accountable.

# Summary Azerbaijani investigative journalist Afgan Mukhtarli disappeared from Tbilisi, Georgia on May 29 and resurfaced in custody in Baku, Azerbaijan. According to Amnesty International, Mukhtarli was abducted by plain-clothed men speaking Georgian who beat him, transported him across the border, and planted 10,000 Euros in his pockets to facilitate smuggling charges. Mukhtarli and his wife had fled to Georgia in 2015 after his investigations into President Ilham Aliyev's alleged corruption links. He now faces torture risks while detained by Azerbaijan's State Border Service Investigative Unit. Amnesty International claims Georgian authorities may have been complicit in the abduction and forced return. The organization demands Mukhtarli's immediate, unconditional release and calls for Georgia to investigate the incident and hold responsible parties accountable. Mukhtarli's family reported he had been under surveillance by Azerbaijani-speaking men in Tbilisi, suggesting premeditated monitoring.

A preliminary hearing in the criminal case against Azerbaijan’s former ambassador to Romania, Serbia, Montenegro, and Bosnia and Herzegovina, Eldar Hasanov, has been scheduled for August 27 at the Baku Court on Grave Crimes, where Judge Afgan Hajiyev will preside. According to investigators, Hasanov is suspected of crimes committed while serving as ambassador from 2010 to 2020. Authorities say that, allegedly with accomplices, he embezzled and spent more than 17.9 million manat in budget funds by falsely claiming they were needed to buy new embassy buildings and to carry out repair and construction work. He is also accused of laundering over 11.8 million manat, falsifying official documents, abusing his powers and causing major damage to state interests worth 327,373 manat, and misusing 192,387 manat in budget funds. Hasanov has been charged under several articles of Azerbaijan’s Criminal Code, including embezzlement, money laundering, abuse of power, budget misuse, and official forgery.

# Summary Azerbaijan's ex-Ambassador to Romania, Serbia, Montenegro, Bosnia, and Herzegovina, Eldar Hasanov, will face a preliminary trial on August 27 at the Baku Court on Grave Crimes. During his tenure from 2010 to 2020, Hasanov allegedly embezzled over 17.9 million manat (approximately 16.8 million euro) in state funds under the guise of purchasing embassy buildings and conducting repairs. He is also accused of laundering over 11.8 million manat obtained through criminal means and committing official forgery by falsifying documents.
