He faces multiple charges including embezzlement, money laundering, abuse of power, misuse of budget funds, and official forgery under Azerbaijan's Criminal Code.

GM Uzbekistan plans to raise car prices from Aug. 1, 2018, with an average increase of 14 percent, according to Uzavtosanoat JSC board chairman Shavkat Umurzakov, who spoke at the International Press Club. He said the company also intends to offer discounts to consumers. Umurzakov linked the price hike not simply to monopoly power but to low utilization at the Asaka plant. Although the factory has capacity to produce 290,000 cars a year, it is making only about 160,000, or roughly 50 percent of capacity. He argued that this raises production costs and hurts both buyers and the company’s export potential. The announcement triggered strong public backlash. Many critics said raising prices to address underproduction was illogical, and some called for a boycott of GM Uzbekistan products. The company and the broader Uzbek auto industry have faced growing criticism in the media in recent weeks. The article also places the price increase in the context of President Shavkat Mirziyoyev’s recent criticism of the sector. On July 24, he criticized the low localization level of Uzbek car production, saying the country still assembles cars while relying on imported spare parts and questioning why science and industry are not producing more domestic components. This was his second major public rebuke of the industry in a short period. Earlier, on June 26, Mirziyoyev had already sharply criticized the automobile sector, calling attention to falling production and exports, corruption, bribery, and nepotism. He also noted debts within Uzavtosanoat and said several company enterprises ended 2017 with losses, while exports had been sold below cost for years without meaningful efforts to reduce production expenses.

# GM Uzbekistan Price Increase Sparks Public Controversy Beginning August 1, 2018, GM Uzbekistan announced a 14 percent average price increase for its vehicles, though the company plans to offer consumer discounts. Chairman Shavkat Umurzakov attributed the rise to underutilization of production capacity rather than monopolistic practices. The Asaka plant operates at only 50 percent capacity, producing 160,000 cars annually despite having the ability to manufacture 290,000. This inefficiency drives up production costs, negatively impacting consumers and export competitiveness. The announcement triggered significant public backlash, with critics arguing that raising prices to combat underproduction is illogical. Some consumers have called for boycotts of GM Uzbekistan products. The price hike reflects broader problems within Uzbekistan's automobile industry. President Shavkat Mirziyoyev has recently criticized the sector twice, expressing dissatisfaction with its performance and structure. On July 24, he questioned why the industry merely assembles vehicles rather than manufacturing them, and noted that spare parts are still imported despite the factory's 20-year operation. Earlier on June 26, Mirziyoyev delivered harsh criticism regarding production and export declines, widespread corruption, bribery, and nepotism. He highlighted substantial debts within Uzavtosanoat JSC, the country's major car manufacturer, with several enterprises reporting 2017 losses. Additionally, cars were exported at prices below production costs without meaningful cost-reduction efforts. The controversy underscores systemic challenges in Uzbekistan's automotive sector requiring substantial structural reforms.

The Baku Grave Crimes Court has continued proceedings in the criminal case against former International Bank of Azerbaijan chairman Jahangir Hajiyev, his relative Ismayil Hidayetzade, former MP Dunyamin Khalilov, and others accused of embezzlement. The hearing, presided over by Judge Faig Ganiyev, included the defendants’ final statements from Hajiyev and Khalilov before the court recessed for a private meeting and postponed the case indefinitely. The state prosecutor asked the court to sentence Hajiyev to 17 years in prison, including an earlier sentence, and Khalilov to 15 years and 9 months, also taking into account his previous term. Six years was requested for Hidayetzade, while conditional sentences were sought for a long list of other defendants whose bank accounts had been opened in their names and later used to withdraw millions of manats. According to the investigation, Hajiyev allegedly directed illegal transactions involving promissory notes worth $3.4 billion and 987 million euros between 2001 and 2015. Prosecutors also said Khalilov and others misappropriated 4.7 billion manats. In addition, Hajiyev was accused of evading 1,752,000 manats in taxes through Aztorg LLC, which he and Khalilov jointly managed in 2011-2014. The court had previously sentenced Hajiyev to 15 years, Khalilov to 13 years, and Hidayetzade to 7 years. Later appeals reduced Khalilov’s term to 12 years and 9 months and Hidayetzade’s to five years.

# Summary The Baku Grave Crimes Court continued proceedings against former International Bank of Azerbaijan (IBA) head Jahangir Hajiyev and co-defendants accused of embezzlement. During the trial, defendants Hajiyev and ex-MP Dunyamin Khalilov presented final statements before the court recessed indefinitely. The state prosecutor demanded 17 years imprisonment for Hajiyev (including a previous sentence) and 15 years 9 months for Khalilov. Ismayil Hidayetzade, Hajiyev's relative, faced a six-year demand, while 19 other defendants with bank accounts used in the scheme received conditional punishment recommendations. Investigators found that between 2001-2015, Hajiyev allegedly orchestrated illegal transactions involving $3.4 billion and 987 million euros through promissory note contracts with foreign entities. Additionally, the defendants were suspected of misappropriating 4.7 billion manats and evading 1.752 million manats in taxes from their joint company, Aztorg LLC. Previously, the court had sentenced Hajiyev to 15 years, Khalilov to 13 years, and Hidayetzade to 7 years. Subsequent appeals reduced these sentences to 12 years 9 months and 5 years respectively.

A regional court in Russia on Wednesday upheld the embezzlement conviction of opposition leader and anti-corruption activist Alexei Navalny, handing him a five-year suspended sentence that will effectively bar him from challenging President Vladimir Putin, or Putin’s chosen successor, in the March 2018 presidential election. Although Navalny’s legal case has been unusually complicated, analysts say the political outcome is straightforward: the Kremlin has used the courts to neutralize its most serious potential challenger. Navalny stands out among Russia’s fragmented opposition because he has been able to appeal beyond liberal activists and attract broader anti-Kremlin sentiment. His strongest showing came in the 2013 Moscow mayoral election, when he was permitted to run against the Kremlin-backed incumbent, Sergei Sobyanin. Navalny won 27 percent of the vote, a result that surprised the political establishment and nearly forced a runoff. Experts say he was able to unite voters dissatisfied with the authorities in general, not just traditional liberals. His rise began during the mass protests that erupted in 2011 over alleged fraud in parliamentary elections. Navalny became a prominent figure in those demonstrations, was briefly jailed, and remained influential even after the protest movement faded. He built his reputation without a party or major public platform, instead turning anti-corruption campaigning into his signature political role. Through his blog and Twitter feed, he has repeatedly published investigations into the wealth and misconduct of Russia’s elite. The conviction at issue dates back to a timber-sales embezzlement case from 2009, when Navalny served as an adviser to the governor of the Kirov region. The case was dismissed at one point, then revived in 2013, when Navalny was convicted and initially sentenced to five years in prison. That sentence was later changed to a suspended term, which allowed him to run in the Moscow mayoral race. Analysts believe the authorities may have allowed that candidacy to create the appearance of competition. Navalny appealed to the European Court of Human Rights, which ruled a year ago that his trial had not been fair. Russia’s Supreme Court later overturned the 2013 conviction and sent the case back for review. Wednesday’s ruling reimposed the conviction and closed that legal loop, making it nearly impossible for Navalny to contest the presidential race unless the Supreme Court intervenes. Observers say Navalny’s influence has declined in recent years, especially after the surge of patriotic support for Putin following the Ukraine crisis and the annexation of Crimea. Polling reflects that weakness: the Levada Center says Putin enjoys overwhelming support, while Navalny registers only tiny levels of trust and backing. Even so, some analysts argue the ruling may preserve Navalny’s value as the Kremlin’s most visible political victim, keeping his credibility intact and making him an enduring irritant to the regime.

# Summary: Kremlin Uses Court Ruling to Block Navalny's Presidential Ambitions A regional court's Wednesday ruling upholding Alexei Navalny's embezzlement conviction and imposing a five-year suspended sentence effectively prevents Russia's most prominent opposition leader from running in the March 2018 presidential elections. This outcome represents a significant political victory for the Kremlin, as experts believe Navalny posed the greatest threat to President Vladimir Putin's continued rule. Navalny stands apart from Russia's fragmented opposition movement because he appeals to a broad coalition of anti-Kremlin voters, not just liberals associated with the unpopular 1990s. His political potential became evident during his 2013 Moscow mayoral campaign against the Kremlin's preferred candidate, when he captured an impressive 27 percent of the vote despite lacking an official political party or public platform. According to Nikolai Petrov of Moscow's National Research University, Navalny successfully consolidated voters across multiple demographics—liberals, creative professionals, and middle-class workers—through his anti-corruption message. The conviction illustrates how Putin's Russia employs courts to manage its carefully controlled political system. Navalny's legal troubles originated from charges of embezzling timber sales proceeds while advising the Kirov region governor in 2009. After initial dismissal, authorities revived the case in 2013, convicting him and sentencing him to five years in prison, later reduced to a suspended sentence. Notably, the Kremlin permitted Navalny to run for Moscow mayor—analysts suggest to create an appearance of genuine competition—but appears unwilling to risk allowing him in presidential elections. The European Court of Human Rights ruled a year ago that Navalny's trial was unfair. Russia's Supreme Court subsequently overturned the 2013 conviction, returning the case to the original court. Wednesday's new conviction effectively closes this legal loop, barring Navalny from presidential candidacy unless the Supreme Court intervenes. However, Navalny's political threat may have diminished. Following the Ukraine crisis three years ago, pro-Putin patriotism surged, and many former Navalny supporters embraced Putin's leadership and the Crimea annexation. Recent polling shows Putin commanding 56 percent trust while Navalny registers only 0.5 percent, with 61 percent of voters supporting Putin in presidential elections compared to less than 1 percent for Navalny. Experts note the Kremlin no longer needs to manufacture political competition. As a military leader, Putin expects overwhelming support rather than challenges. The broader opposition has lost appeal amid the political freeze of recent years. Nevertheless, the conviction may inadvertently benefit Navalny. Despite being barred from elections, he maintains credibility and status as the Kremlin's principal threat. The ruling demonstrates to international observers that Navalny is a regime victim, strengthening his position as what one analyst describes as "a pebble in Putin's shoe"—irritating enough to warrant attention but manageable for the Kremlin.

Brazil’s coronavirus crisis has laid bare deep weaknesses in its public health system, the SUS (Sistema Unico de Saude), which was launched in 1988 as a universal, free-care model inspired by Britain’s NHS. Created after the country’s military dictatorship, Brazil’s constitution declares health a universal right and a duty of the state. In practice, however, the system is buckling under the pressure of the pandemic and decades of underinvestment. As Brazil approached 100,000 COVID-19 deaths, becoming the second country after the United States to reach that grim mark, hospitals and clinics serving the public were struggling to cope. Doctors say the system lacks enough beds, staff and medicines. Fred Nicacio, an emergency room physician in Bauru, said the SUS looks ideal “on paper” but faces major real-world failures. He described exhausted, underpaid and undervalued frontline workers, some of whom have been infected and left out of service for weeks without replacements. He also pointed to corruption, ranging from embezzlement of funds by officials to abuse by patients seeking fake sick notes. Brazil has already been hit by several pandemic-related corruption scandals, including inflated prices for ventilators and field hospitals that were funded but never completed. Yet experts say corruption is only part of the story. Guilherme Werneck of ABRASCO said the core problem is chronic underfunding. An OECD report in 2019 found Brazil among the lowest public spenders on health, with per-capita investment 30% below the average for developed and emerging economies. Brazil devotes only about 4% of GDP to public health, far less than countries such as Germany, France and Britain. Researchers say health has never been a national priority since the SUS was created. Luciana Dias Lima of Fiocruz said President Jair Bolsonaro’s government has not done enough to coordinate public health services. She also noted a contradiction in Brazil’s system: while the state struggles to finance universal care, it also gives tax breaks that indirectly support the private health sector, money critics say should instead strengthen the SUS.

# Brazil's Public Health System Struggles Under Coronavirus Strain Brazil is approaching 100,000 COVID-19 deaths, becoming the second country worldwide to reach this milestone after the United States. The pandemic has exposed severe weaknesses in Brazil's public health system, the SUS (Single Health System), which was once considered among the world's most advanced. Established in 1988 following Brazil's transition from military dictatorship, the SUS was modeled after Britain's NHS and theoretically provides universal, free health care to all Brazilians. However, the system now faces critical challenges. An emergency room physician in Bauro reports severe shortages of hospital beds, staff, and medicines. Healthcare workers are demotivated, underpaid, and undervalued, with some colleagues infected and unable to be replaced. Systemic corruption compounds these problems, ranging from political leaders embezzling funds to patients fraudulently obtaining doctor's notes. Brazil has experienced numerous pandemic-related scandals, including over-billing for ventilator purchases and unbuilt field hospitals. The core issue, however, is chronic underfunding. A 2019 OECD report found Brazil among countries making the least public health investment, with per-capita spending 30 percent below developed and emerging country averages. Brazil allocates only four percent of GDP to public health—less than half the investment in Germany, France, and Britain. Researchers note that health has never been a strategic national priority since the SUS's creation. President Jair Bolsonaro's administration is criticized for insufficient coordination of public health services. Paradoxically, the federal government indirectly finances the private health system through tax breaks for private insurance holders—a practice unique among universal healthcare systems. Experts argue this diverted funding could strengthen the struggling public system instead, further highlighting how inequality persists even within Brazil's supposedly universal healthcare framework.

Chile’s Supreme Court ordered the seizure of more than $1.6 million from the estate of late dictator Gen. Augusto Pinochet, ruling the money had an illegal origin and could not be kept by his family. The court also sentenced three former military officers to four years in prison for embezzling public funds in a case tied to Pinochet, though they were allowed conditional liberty. Pinochet’s image as a corruption-free ruler collapsed after a 2004 U.S. Senate investigation into Riggs Bank exposed hidden wealth, with more accounts later found abroad. A court-ordered study concluded he amassed $21 million, but only $3 million was explained by his military salary. Pinochet died in 2006 under house arrest without trial.

# Summary Chile's Supreme Court ordered the seizure of $1.6 million from late dictator Augusto Pinochet's assets, ruling the money had illegal origins and could not remain with his family. The court also sentenced three former military officers to four years in prison for embezzlement, though they remained free under conditional liberty. Pinochet's reputation for austere governance was damaged after a 2004 U.S. Senate investigation revealed hidden wealth through Riggs Bank and accounts in Europe and the Caribbean. A court-ordered academic study determined Pinochet accumulated $21 million before his death, with only $3 million justified by his military salary. Pinochet died under house arrest in 2006 without facing trial for human rights violations or illegal enrichment, despite an estimated 3,095 deaths during his 1973-1990 dictatorship.

Brazilian police on Wednesday broadened the Car Wash corruption probe to examine about $8 million in alleged kickbacks tied to bunker fuel contracts Petrobras used for its tanker fleet. Searches were carried out in Rio de Janeiro, and investigators are targeting unnamed Petrobras officials over deals said to have taken place from 2009 to 2018. Prosecutors said they are also examining transactions in Brazil and Singapore, signaling that the long-running investigation into Petrobras dealings with major commodity traders such as Vitol, Glencore and Trafigura is widening beyond its earlier focus on Houston. Petrobras said it is a victim of corruption and has cooperated with authorities in dozens of criminal cases and 21 administrative probes. Prosecutors said there are indications Petrobras employees helped arrange a system with corrupt traders so that favorable contracts were awarded on a rotating basis. The Lava Jato probe began in 2014 and has become Brazil’s largest graft scandal, with about 200 convictions. Reuters previously reported suspicious activity in Petrobras’ Singapore trading unit dating back to 2012.

# Summary Brazil's Car Wash corruption investigation has expanded to examine alleged $8 million kickbacks involving bunker fuel contracts purchased by state oil company Petrobras for its tanker fleet between 2009 and 2018. Police conducted searches in Rio de Janeiro targeting unnamed Petrobras officials, while prosecutors investigated transactions in Brazil and Singapore involving major commodity trading firms including Vitol, Glencore, and Trafigura. Previously, the probe focused primarily on Petrobras' Houston operations. Petrobras stated it is corruption's victim rather than perpetrator, having assisted authorities with numerous criminal and administrative investigations. The Car Wash probe, launched in 2014, has become Brazil's largest graft scandal, resulting in approximately 200 convictions of businessmen, officials, and politicians. Prosecutors indicated Petrobras employees allegedly arranged a system with corrupt traders to award contracts on a rotating basis. In 2019, Reuters reported that Petrobras detected suspicious Singapore division transactions as early as 2012 but failed to halt them.

South America’s rollout of first Covid-19 vaccines has quickly turned from a source of hope into a wave of anger, as revelations of preferential access, cronyism, and corruption have shaken public trust in political leaders across the region. In Peru and Argentina, two ministers resigned after receiving or facilitating special access to scarce doses. In Ecuador, a minister is under investigation for the same kind of conduct, while prosecutors in Brazil and elsewhere are reviewing thousands of additional complaints involving politicians, their relatives, and allies cutting ahead in vaccination queues. The scandals are especially explosive because vaccines remain scarce. South America, like much of the developing world, has struggled to secure enough doses after wealthy countries bought up much of the global supply. That scarcity has intensified public outrage over elite privilege at a time when the region has been hit harder by the pandemic than almost anywhere else. South America accounts for nearly one-fifth of global Covid-19 deaths, with an official toll of about 450,000 despite estimates that the real number is at least twice as high. The virus has also overwhelmed health systems, driven millions into poverty, and deepened the region’s worst economic crisis in modern history. Although the pandemic initially boosted support for many governments because of emergency aid and calls for unity, analysts warn that the vaccine scandals may now erase that goodwill and fuel new instability. Public anger is likely to affect both street protests and upcoming elections, including Peru’s vote in April. As one Lima doctor said, politicians knew people were dying but still “vaccinated all their little friends.” The article describes several particularly brazen cases. In Peru, a deputy health minister received extra doses from a clinical trial, and his wife, sister, two children, nephew, and niece were also inoculated. In Ecuador, the health minister sent doses from the country’s first vaccine shipment, which was meant for the public sector, to a luxury private nursing home where his mother lives. In Argentina, a prominent journalist revealed on radio that he got vaccinated at the health ministry after contacting a friend who was then health minister, exposing what locals have dubbed a “VIP Immunisation Clinic” for government allies. In Brazil, prosecutors sought the arrest of the mayor of Manaus over allegations of preferential access for associates. In Suriname, the health minister gave himself the country’s first shot, saying he wanted to “set an example.” The fallout has already been severe. Doctors and nurses in Peru protested outside hospitals demanding vaccines as the scandal widened. Peru’s health minister and Argentina’s health minister both resigned, with the Argentine former official charged with abuse of power. Ecuador’s health minister faces both impeachment and criminal investigation. Peru has been hit particularly hard. Its official death toll exceeds 45,000, though excess mortality data suggest the true number is far higher. The scandal has also engulfed former President Martín Vizcarra, once popular for his anti-corruption stance, after it emerged that he secretly received a vaccine while still in office, before Peru had approved or purchased any doses, and then tried to conceal it. For many Peruvians, that betrayal has deepened a sense of hopelessness and distrust in the country’s leaders.

# COVID-19 Vaccine Scandal Rocks South America South America's initial hope surrounding COVID-19 vaccine arrivals has transformed into widespread anger as vaccination campaigns have become mired in scandal, corruption, and cronyism, destabilizing governments across the region. ## Government Officials Resign Multiple high-ranking officials have already resigned due to vaccine misconduct. Two ministers in Peru and one in Argentina stepped down after receiving preferential vaccine access or providing it to allies. Ecuador's health minister faces investigation for similar violations, while prosecutors in Peru, Argentina, and Brazil are examining thousands of accusations involving local politicians and their families circumventing vaccine queues. ## Widespread Corruption Cases The scandals reveal brazen abuses of power. In Peru, a deputy health minister received extra vaccine doses along with his wife, sister, two children, a nephew, and niece. Ecuador's health minister diverted doses from the public sector to a luxury nursing home where his mother resides. An Argentine journalist exposed what locals termed a "VIP Immunisation Clinic" after disclosing he received a shot through a connection with the health minister. Brazil's Manaus mayor faces arrest requests for allegedly giving allies preferential access, while Suriname's health minister allocated himself the country's first dose to "set an example." Former Peruvian President Martín Vizcarra, once praised for anti-corruption efforts, became entangled in scandal after secretly receiving a vaccine while in office, before Peru had even approved vaccines. He subsequently attempted to cover up the incident. ## Regional Impact and Consequences The vaccine scarcity amplifies public fury. South America, representing only 5 percent of the global population, has suffered nearly one-fifth of worldwide pandemic deaths—approximately 450,000 officially, though mortality data suggests the actual toll exceeds 900,000. The region's healthcare systems collapsed, millions fell into poverty, and economies experienced their worst crisis in modern history. Analysts warn these scandals could reverse the goodwill governments accumulated through pandemic relief efforts and calls for unity. As one pollster noted, "People find it much more difficult to tolerate corruption when health is at stake." ## Public Backlash Citizens across South America have mobilized through social media to denounce abuses and identify suspected line-cutters. Healthcare workers protested outside Peruvian hospitals demanding vaccines. The political ramifications could reshape upcoming elections, including Peru's April vote, in a region already volatile from public outrage over inequality and corruption. The vaccine scandals mirror similar incidents in Lebanon, Spain, the Philippines, and the United States, but Latin America's cases have proven particularly brazen. As one Lima resident whose husband died from COVID expressed, the scandals have shattered trust: "Who can we turn to? Who's left?"

Former Argentine President Cristina Fernandez de Kirchner went on trial Thursday in Buenos Aires on bribery charges linked to public works contracts approved during her presidency. The case, known as the “Notebooks” scandal, accuses Fernandez and 86 other former officials of taking part in an alleged kickback network in which businessmen paid bribes in return for lucrative government deals. Fernandez denies the accusations and called the proceedings a “show trial” on X, saying they were meant to keep pressure on her and distract public attention. Prosecutors began reading the indictment, opening what is expected to be a lengthy trial that may run through the end of the year and could take years more to resolve because of appeals. The case surfaced in 2018 after notebooks kept by a former official’s driver were discovered, allegedly documenting cash deliveries and meetings. Witnesses have also implicated Fernandez’s late husband, former President Nestor Kirchner, as a central figure. The trial, held virtually on Zoom, includes former ministers and business executives. It comes as Fernandez remains under house arrest after a separate fraud conviction, and follows a political boost for President Javier Milei after his party won midterm elections.

# Summary Argentine former President Cristina Fernandez de Kirchner went on trial Thursday on bribery charges related to public works contracts awarded during her administration. The "Notebooks" scandal involves 87 defendants accused of operating an illicit network that allegedly received bribes from businessmen in exchange for government contracts. Fernandez, who served as president from 2007-2015, has denied all charges and dismissed the trial as politically motivated. The case emerged in 2018 when notebooks belonging to a former official's driver surfaced, documenting alleged cash deliveries and meetings. Witnesses have implicated both Fernandez and her late husband, former President Nestor Kirchner, as central figures. Defendants include former ministers and executives from construction, energy, and transport companies. Several business leaders have testified as "repentants," revealing a kickback system allegedly used to finance the Peronist movement. Fernandez is currently under house arrest following a separate fraud conviction. The trial, conducted virtually via Zoom, is expected to continue through year-end, with final resolution potentially taking years due to appeals.

Brazilian police on Friday recommended corruption charges against former president Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva in connection with the massive Petrobras embezzlement scandal. The recommendation, seen in a filing by AFP, must first be reviewed by prosecutors and then approved by a judge before becoming formal charges. Lula and his wife already face corruption and money-laundering accusations. The case centers on claims that he owned a seaside apartment and a country house, with police alleging the apartment was renovated at the expense of construction firm OAS, which was implicated in Petrobras bribery schemes. The move came as Lula prepared to support President Dilma Rousseff’s impeachment defense.

# Summary Brazilian police recommended corruption charges against ex-president Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva on Friday, alleging his involvement in a massive Petrobras embezzlement scheme. The recommendation must be reviewed by prosecutors before becoming formal charges, with a judge ultimately deciding whether to accept them. Lula and his wife face corruption and money laundering charges related to alleged ownership of a seaside apartment and country house. Police claim construction company OAS, implicated in the Petrobras bribery scandal, paid for extensive apartment renovations. The development occurs as Lula's successor and protégé Dilma Rousseff faces Senate impeachment proceedings. Lula planned to support Rousseff in Brasilia on Monday.

A court in Buenos Aires has acquitted former Argentine President Carlos Menem of charges that he interfered with the investigation into the 1994 bombing of the Argentine Israelite Mutual Association (AMIA) Jewish center, which killed 85 people and remains Argentina’s deadliest terrorist attack. The three-judge panel also cleared 12 other defendants of the same accusation. The trial, ordered in August 2015, centered on allegations that Menem and other officials tried to divert the investigation away from a Syrian businessman who was a friend of the Menem family. After the verdict, Menem’s lawyer said there had been no evidence of illegal conduct by the former president and that Menem felt relieved. Relatives of AMIA victims strongly criticized the ruling. The group Active Memory said the evidence showed the Menem government knew an attack would occur and did nothing to prevent it or solve it, calling Menem one of the main figures responsible for impunity in the case. Menem, who was president from 1989 to 1999 and is now 88, likely would have avoided prison even if convicted because of his protections as a senator. No one has ever been convicted for carrying out the truck bombing, although prosecutors have implicated several former Iranian officials. Iran denies involvement and has refused to extradite suspects sought by Argentina. The bombing investigation itself was later found to have been marred by irregularities. In 2004, a court acquitted several people linked to an alleged local connection and ordered investigations into government and judicial officials for misconduct. While Menem was cleared on Thursday, other defendants were convicted on related corruption charges. Former federal judge Juan Jose Galeano, who led the original investigation, received a six-year sentence for embezzlement and malfeasance. Former intelligence chief Hugo Anzorrequy was sentenced to four years, and former prosecutors Eamon Mullen and Jose Barbaccia each received two-year terms for failing to perform their duties.

# Summary A court in Buenos Aires acquitted former Argentine President Carlos Menem on Thursday of charges that he interfered with the investigation into the 1994 bombing of the Argentine Israelite Mutual Association (AMIA), which killed 85 people in Argentina's deadliest terrorist attack. A dozen other defendants were also cleared of the same charge. The three-judge panel found insufficient evidence that Menem and other officials attempted to divert the investigation away from a Syrian businessman connected to the Menem family. Menem's lawyer expressed relief at the ruling, stating there was no justification for charges against the former president. However, victim advocacy groups rejected the decision, asserting that the Menem government knew about the attack beforehand and failed to prevent or clarify it, thereby enabling impunity in the case. While Menem was acquitted, several co-defendants received convictions on related charges. Former federal judge Juan Jose Galeano, who led the initial investigation, was sentenced to six years for embezzlement and malfeasance, specifically regarding $400,000 paid to an auto parts dealer to implicate police officers in a supposed "local connection" to the bombing. Hugo Anzorrequy, who headed Argentina's intelligence secretariat, received four years for embezzlement and concealment. Former prosecutors Eamon Mullen and Jose Barbaccia were each sentenced to two years for failing to fulfill their duties. Despite decades of investigation, no one has been convicted of the bombing itself. Prosecutors have implicated former Iranian officials, though Iran denies involvement and has refused to extradite suspects.

Venezuela’s oil minister and state oil company chief, Tareck El Aissami, abruptly resigned on Monday amid a widening anti-corruption investigation that has reached officials in the oil sector and other parts of government. His departure surprised many because he was considered a loyal ally of President Nicolás Maduro and a central figure in the government’s efforts to evade U.S. sanctions on the oil industry. El Aissami announced his resignation on Twitter just as authorities were intensifying probes into alleged graft. Maduro later said he accepted the resignation in order to “facilitate all the investigations” and allow the truth, punishment of the guilty, and justice to emerge. He described the government’s anti-corruption campaign as “bitter” and “painful.” The investigation was announced last week by Venezuela’s National Anti-Corruption Police and reportedly targets unnamed public officials in the oil industry, the justice system, and some local governments. Attorney General Tarek William Saab said Monday that at least six officials had already been arrested, including people linked to PDVSA, Venezuela’s state oil company, and that more arrests were expected. Among those detained was Joselit Ramirez, a cryptocurrency regulator who had already been indicted in the United States alongside El Aissami in 2020 on money-laundering charges. Corruption has long been widespread in Venezuela, a country with the world’s largest proven oil reserves, but officials are rarely held accountable. That reality is especially stark in a nation where most people survive on about $1.90 a day, the international extreme-poverty benchmark. Analysts said the government’s anti-corruption rhetoric may be partly political. Ryan Berg of the Center for Strategic and International Studies said the regime appeared to be using the probe to sideline someone it viewed as a threat, rather than to strengthen the rule of law. Oil is Venezuela’s economic lifeline. During the boom years under Hugo Chávez, high oil revenues financed expansive social programs such as subsidized food markets, public housing, free health clinics, and education initiatives. But falling oil prices and years of mismanagement, first under Chávez and later under Maduro, triggered a deep crisis that has driven millions into poverty and forced more than 7 million Venezuelans to leave the country. PDVSA’s production has also collapsed, falling from about 3.5 million barrels a day when Chávez took power in 1999 to roughly 700,000 barrels a day last year. David Smilde of Tulane University argued that the government’s actions are not simply about improving its image. He said the disappearance of billions of dollars matters to a government facing severe budget problems. Meanwhile, the Biden administration has recently eased some sanctions, including allowing Chevron to resume limited production in Venezuela, while Maduro’s government has been negotiating with U.S.-backed opposition figures in hopes of further relief. U.S. officials have long viewed El Aissami as a major obstacle. The Treasury Department designated him a narcotics kingpin in 2017, alleging he oversaw or helped own large cocaine shipments. He had previously served as interior minister under Chávez and later as governor, before becoming oil minister in 2020. Geoff Ramsey of the Atlantic Council said El Aissami was a key part of Maduro’s sanctions-evasion strategy and noted that if he is implicated further, it could affect the broader power structure. The resignation also follows earlier accusations against another former oil minister, Rafael Ramírez, whom Maduro’s government accused in September of involvement in a multibillion-dollar embezzlement scheme. Ramírez denied the allegations. Past investigations have also claimed billions went missing from PDVSA, and U.S. authorities have previously accused an Andorran bank of laundering money stolen from the company.

# Venezuela Oil Czar Tareck El Aissami Resigns Amid Corruption Investigation Tareck El Aissami, the powerful figure responsible for managing Venezuela's oil industry, unexpectedly resigned on Monday amid investigations into alleged government corruption. His departure shocked observers because El Aissami was considered a loyal ruling party member and a crucial player in the government's strategy to circumvent international economic sanctions. Venezuela's oil industry is fundamental to the country's survival, funding subsidized food programs and extremely cheap gasoline. However, the sector is widely regarded as deeply corrupt. The National Anti-Corruption Police announced investigations into unidentified officials across the oil industry, justice system, and local governments. Attorney General Tarek William Saab stated that at least six officials, including PDVSA-affiliated personnel, had been arrested, with more detentions expected. President Nicolás Maduro characterized the anti-corruption efforts as "bitter" and "painful," accepting El Aissami's resignation to "facilitate all the investigations." However, experts question the government's true motivations. Ryan Berg from the Center for Strategic and International Studies suggested the regime is using anti-corruption probes as cover to eliminate perceived political threats while continuing corrupt practices. Among those arrested is Joselit Ramirez, a cryptocurrency regulator indicted in the U.S. alongside El Aissami in 2020 on money laundering charges. El Aissami himself was designated a narcotics kingpin by the U.S. government in 2017, with the Treasury Department alleging he oversaw or partially owned narcotics shipments exceeding 1,000 kilograms on multiple occasions destined for Mexico and the United States. Corruption has plagued Venezuela for decades despite its position atop the world's largest petroleum reserves. Most citizens live on $1.90 daily—the international extreme poverty threshold—yet officials rarely face accountability. Scholars suggest the current crackdown reflects serious budgetary problems rather than genuine reform. David Smilde, a Tulane University researcher, noted that arresting high-ranking officials and accepting a powerful minister's resignation in a case involving $3 billion would not improve the government's image unless the missing money significantly impacts state finances. Venezuela's oil production has collapsed from 3.5 million barrels daily when Hugo Chávez took power in 1999 to approximately 700,000 barrels last year, caused by mismanagement and U.S. sanctions. Under Chávez, oil windfalls funded state-run food markets, public housing, free clinics, and education. However, subsequent price drops and governmental incompetence created a complex crisis pushing millions into poverty and forcing over 7 million Venezuelans to emigrate. The timing of El Aissami's resignation appears strategically connected to U.S. policy. The Biden administration recently loosened sanctions, allowing Chevron to resume production for the first time in three years. Maduro's government has been negotiating with U.S.-backed opponents primarily to lift sanctions. Congressional researchers viewed El Aissami as an impediment to these goals, with a November Congressional Research Center report warning that his continued presence could complicate oil sanctions relief efforts. Geoff Ramsey from the Atlantic Council emphasized El Aissami's significance, describing him as "a key player in the Maduro government's sanctions evasion strategy" who "knows where all the bodies are buried." His potential implication in wrongdoing could have serious consequences for the entire power structure. Previously, Maduro's government accused former oil minister Rafael Ramírez of involvement in multibillion-dollar embezzlement during the early 2010s. The 2016 opposition-led National Assembly reported $11 billion missing from PDVSA between 2004-2014 under Ramírez's tenure, while the U.S. Treasury accused an Andorran bank of laundering $2 billion stolen from PDVSA in 2015.

Brazilian federal prosecutors have formally charged Carlos Nuzman, the former head of the Rio de Janeiro Olympics, with corruption, money laundering, tax evasion and leading a criminal organization. The 75-year-old was arrested two weeks earlier and remains in prison. Prosecutors also charged Leonardo Gryner, Nuzman’s top aide on the Rio Olympic organizing committee. In their filing, prosecutors said the pair “promoted, formed, financed, and integrated a criminal organization” that sought to commit corruption and embezzlement against the state of Rio de Janeiro, Brazil’s Olympic Committee and the Rio 2016 organizing committee. They also alleged that Nuzman had undeclared assets in Switzerland, including 16 one-kilogram gold bars. Authorities in Brazil and France say Nuzman helped arrange a $2 million payment to Papa Massata Diack to secure votes for Rio’s successful bid to host the 2016 Games. Papa Massata Diack’s father, Lamine Diack, was then a powerful IOC member from Senegal with influence over African votes in the 2009 selection. Also charged were Papa Massata Diack, Lamine Diack, former Rio governor Sergio Cabral and businessman Arthur Cesar de Menezes Soares Filho. Nuzman resigned last week as president of the Brazilian Olympic Committee and denied wrongdoing, saying he was “unjustly implicated.” Prosecutors say there is strong evidence that his wealth increased in a way inconsistent with his declared assets and that public money meant for Olympic bodies was embezzled.

# Summary Carlos Nuzman, the 75-year-old head of Rio de Janeiro's 2016 Olympics, has been formally charged with corruption, money laundering, tax evasion, and running a criminal organization. Brazilian federal prosecutors filed the charges on Wednesday, two weeks after Nuzman's arrest. Prosecutors allege that Nuzman and his associate Leonardo Gryner created a criminal organization to commit corruption and embezzlement against Rio de Janeiro, Brazil's Olympic Committee, and the Rio 2016 organizing committee. The investigation centers on allegations that Nuzman helped pay $2 million to Papa Massata Diack to secure votes for hosting the 2016 Olympics. Lamine Diack, Papa Massata's father, was a powerful International Olympic Committee member from Senegal with influence over African voters during the 2009 host city selection. Additional charges were filed against Papa Massata Diack, Lamine Diack, former Rio governor Sergio Cabral, and businessman Arthur Cesar de Menezes Soares Filho. Prosecutors claim Nuzman has undeclared assets in Switzerland, including sixteen 1-kilogram gold bars. Nuzman resigned as president of the Brazilian Olympic Committee last week, denying wrongdoing and claiming he was "unjustly implicated." The IOC had awarded him a gold Olympic Order after the games concluded.

Claudia Díaz, Hugo Chávez’s former nurse and later Venezuela’s national treasurer, has been indicted in Miami federal court on money laundering charges tied to an alleged bribery scheme involving a billionaire media owner. Prosecutors say Díaz and her husband, Adrían Velasquez, received at least $4.2 million in payments that were routed from companies and bank accounts in Switzerland into their accounts in Miami in exchange for helping approve lucrative currency transactions while she held office. According to the charges, the money behind the scheme came from businessman Raúl Gorrín, owner of Globovisión, Venezuela’s last major private television network. Gorrín is already on U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s most-wanted list after being charged in 2017 in a separate $2.4 billion money laundering conspiracy. His network has also been sanctioned by the United States for allegedly helping prop up Nicolás Maduro’s government. Díaz, 46, rose from being a petty officer in Venezuela’s navy to becoming Chávez’s caregiver before his death from cancer in 2013. Chávez appointed her national treasurer in 2011, and she was replaced after Maduro took office. Díaz and Velasquez, a former security adviser to Chávez, now live in Madrid. They were briefly arrested there in 2018 on a Venezuelan warrant, but Spain’s Supreme Court denied extradition, saying they could be tortured if returned. The case is part of a broader U.S. effort to target corruption tied to Maduro-era officials and businessmen. Prosecutors say as much as $300 billion may have been looted from Venezuela’s state coffers over two decades of socialist rule. Díaz’s lawyer previously denied that she and her husband profited from their public positions. The indictment also follows earlier corruption findings involving Díaz’s predecessor, Alejandro Andrade, who agreed in 2018 to forfeit more than $1 billion in illicit proceeds from similar currency-dealing schemes. Prosecutors say Venezuela’s strict exchange controls created opportunities for officials to buy dollars at favorable official rates and resell them on the black market for huge gains.

# Summary Hugo Chávez's former nurse, Claudia Díaz, has been indicted in Miami federal court for money laundering. Díaz and her husband, Adrían Velasquez, are accused of accepting at least $4.2 million in bribes from businessman Raúl Gorrín, owner of Venezuela's last major private TV network, Globovisión. The bribes allegedly occurred when Díaz served as Venezuela's national treasurer, during which time she allegedly approved lucrative currency transactions benefiting Gorrín. Díaz, 46, was a former Venezuelan navy petty officer who cared for the ailing Chávez before his death from cancer in 2013. Chávez appointed her national treasurer in 2011, and she served until 2013 when Nicolás Maduro took power. She and her husband currently reside in Madrid, having been briefly arrested there in 2018 on a Venezuelan warrant. However, Spain's supreme court rejected Venezuela's extradition request, citing torture concerns. Gorrín, whose network faces U.S. sanctions, is on the Immigration and Customs Enforcement's most-wanted list for his alleged involvement in a $2.4 billion money laundering conspiracy. Payments to the couple came from Swiss companies and bank accounts to their Miami accounts. The case reflects broader U.S. efforts to prosecute Maduro-connected officials and businessmen. Venezuela's rigid currency controls enabled corruption, allowing privileged individuals to purchase hard currency at official rates and resell at black-market prices for profit. An estimated $300 billion has been raided from Venezuelan state coffers over two decades of socialist rule. Díaz's predecessor as treasurer, Alejandro Andrade, agreed in 2018 to forfeit over $1 billion in proceeds from similar currency deal approvals. Court records show Díaz allegedly purchased 250 gold bars valued at $9.5 million through a Caribbean company in 2014, later selling similar amounts through Swiss banks.

Peruvian authorities are being urged to investigate an explosive attack on the offices of Cadena Sur TV in Ica and protect the station’s journalists after a suspected dynamite blast damaged the building early on September 13, 2022. According to news reports and station owner and news director Gastón Medina, two men on a motorcycle arrived at about 4:30 a.m. and threw an explosive at the entrance of the independent television station. The blast destroyed the front door. Medina, who lives in the same building, said he was unharmed and had filed a police report. The attack was the latest in a series of threats and acts of vandalism directed at Medina and Cadena Sur. CPJ documented a death threat left at the station’s door on February 23. Later incidents included animal excrement smeared on the entrance on July 18, red paint sprayed on the door on July 27, and a dog carcass with its throat slit left outside on September 2. Medina believes the attacks are retaliation for the station’s reporting on alleged corruption by Ica governor Javier Gallegos, who is reportedly under investigation by the Attorney General’s office for alleged ties to organized crime. Gallegos’ office denied involvement in the explosion and said it respects the media and condemns attacks on press freedom. Neither Gallegos nor local police responded to CPJ’s requests for comment. CPJ warned that the threats could escalate if the perpetrators are not found and held accountable.

# Summary On September 13, 2022, an explosive device was detonated outside the offices of Cadena Sur, an independent television station in Ica, Peru. Two men on a motorcycle threw what appeared to be dynamite at the station's entrance around 4:30 a.m., destroying the door. Station owner and news director Gastón Medina was unharmed and filed a police report. This attack represents the latest in a series of incidents targeting Medina and Cadena Sur. Previous threats include a death threat left at the station's door in February, animal excrement smeared on the door in July, red paint sprayed on the entrance later that month, and a dog carcass with a slit throat left at the entrance in early September. Medina believes these incidents are retaliatory for Cadena Sur's reporting on alleged corruption by Ica Governor Javier Gallegos, who is under investigation for suspected ties to organized crime. Gallegos' office denied involvement in the attack and stated respect for press freedom. The Committee to Protect Journalists called for thorough investigation, prosecution of those responsible, and enhanced safety measures for the station's journalists. Neither Gallegos nor local police responded to requests for comment.

Chile’s national police chief, Bruno Villalobos, resigned on Monday after taking office under President Sebastián Piñera, as the Carabineros faced major corruption and evidence-tampering scandals. Piñera announced he had accepted the resignation at La Moneda palace, saying his government would pursue a more efficient fight against crime, drug trafficking and terrorism, and push a broad modernization of both the Carabineros and the Investigative Police (PDI). He said reforms would also target the intelligence system, coordination among police, prosecutors and judges, prison rehabilitation, and stronger municipal involvement in crime prevention. Villalobos had led the force since 2015, when he was appointed by former President Michelle Bachelet, and was originally expected to remain until 2019. His resignation comes amid “Pacogate,” a scandal that began in 2016 and has led to the arrest of 127 officers accused of embezzling about $44 million. The crisis deepened recently after prosecutors accused the Carabineros of tampering with evidence in cases involving Mapuche militants accused of arson in the Araucanía region. Julio Pineda, the deputy director, will serve as interim chief until a permanent replacement is named.

# Summary Bruno Villalobos, director of Chile's Carabineros national police force, resigned Monday following President Sebastian Piñera's inauguration. Piñera accepted the resignation as part of his crime-fighting agenda and pledged to modernize both the Carabineros and the Investigative Police (PDI), with emphasis on reforming intelligence systems and improving coordination among law enforcement, prosecutors, and judges. The resignation comes amid serious scandals plaguing the force. "Pacogate," which emerged in 2016, has resulted in 127 officers being arrested for embezzling approximately $44 million. The crisis intensified when the Attorney General's Office accused the Carabineros of tampering with evidence in cases against Mapuche militants accused of arson in Araucania. Villalobos, appointed by former President Michelle Bachelet in 2015, was expected to serve until 2019. Deputy Director Julio Pineda will assume the position temporarily until a permanent replacement is named. Piñera also outlined broader public safety initiatives, including prison reform and strengthened municipal involvement in reducing crime and drug trafficking.

Nairobi Governor Mike Sonko says he will reshuffle staff at the Nairobi Water and Sewerage Company next week to dismantle what he calls a cartel behind an artificial water shortage in the city. In a statement, Sonko said anyone found guilty would face consequences and that the reshuffle was inevitable as part of the fight against graft. Residents have recently complained of water shortages and urged county intervention.

# Summary Nairobi Governor Mike Sonko announced plans to reshuffle staff at Nairobi Water and Sewerage Company to combat cartels allegedly causing artificial water shortages. Sonko stated that those found guilty would face consequences and warned against corruption excuses. The reshuffle aims to dismantle the cartel and address residents' concerns about persistent water shortages affecting the city.

Sudan’s acting Minister of Justice, Mohamed Saeed Al-Hillu, said the government gives major attention to combating terrorism because of the threat it poses to international peace and security, and because Sudan rejects violence and extremism. Speaking at the International High-Level Conference on Human Rights and the Combat of Terrorism, held by the UN Office for Combat of Terrorism in Malaga, Spain, on May 10–11, he said Sudan is in a transitional period governed by the 2019 constitutional document, amended in 2020, which includes a comprehensive framework for human rights and basic freedoms. Al-Hillu said Sudan has adopted national laws to fight terrorism and prohibit its financing, and that it is party to several relevant international and regional agreements. The Economic Development Department will allocate R282 million of its R1.1 billion budget to the Competition Commission this year, Minister Ebrahim Patel told Parliament in Cape Town on Thursday. Patel said the funding is meant to help the commission continue its work to “open the economy for all,” after it had been described as under-resourced. He said competition authorities are expected to investigate about 100 cartel cases, assess 400 proposed mergers, and handle two more abuse-of-dominance cases. Patel also said he expects to table the results of three major market inquiries later this year into private healthcare, grocery retail — including shopping malls and spaza shops — and communication data costs. The commission has already investigated alleged abuse of dominance in sectors such as pharmaceuticals, ports, railways and school uniforms. In April, Competition Commissioner Tembinkosi Bonakele warned Parliament that financial strain would force the commission to reduce cartel investigations, including probes into automotive component manufacturers, set-top box service providers, edible fats and oils producers, and fresh produce and beef producers. During the debate after Patel’s speech, Elsie Coleman, chairperson of the portfolio committee on economic development, said the commission must be supported so small businesses can compete in South Africa’s economy. She said its market inquiries help expose unethical and anti-competitive conduct, and urged Patel to work with National Treasury to improve funding over the medium term. Patel also highlighted the draft Competition Amendment Bill, published for public comment in December. He called it a major reform of the 20-year-old Competition Act, designed to tackle economic concentration that excludes small businesses and black South Africans, and to give regulators stronger powers against excessive pricing, price discrimination and other abusive practices.

Sudan’s Sovereign Council on Monday inaugurated the country’s first gold shipment under a new state-controlled system, marking a major step in efforts to regulate the gold trade and curb smuggling. The ceremony, held in Khartoum, was attended by Prime Minister Abdallah Hamdok, several ministers, specialists, and representatives of the Forces for Freedom and Change. The shipment was managed through the newly created Strategic Commodities Portfolio, which was established last month to help secure imports of essential goods such as wheat, medicines, and fuel in exchange for regulated gold sales. The move comes after Sudan opened gold exports to the private sector in January in an attempt to reduce the long-running problem of gold smuggling and bring in much-needed foreign currency. For years, the Central Bank of Sudan had been the only legal buyer and exporter of gold, purchasing it at fixed prices from collection sites across the country. Officials say that system encouraged illegal trade. Under the revised rules, private mining companies were initially allowed to export up to 70 percent of their production if they deposited the proceeds in local banks, while the remaining 30 percent had to be sold to the central bank. In March, the split was changed to 50-50. Companies must also sell foreign currency earnings, unless needed for mining operations, directly to the central bank at the official exchange rate of SDG55 to the dollar, far below the parallel-market rate of around SDG150-160. In May, Sudan also established a gold stock market to align domestic gold prices more closely with international rates. Deputy chairperson of the Sovereign Council Lt Gen Mohamed Hamdan “Hemeti,” who also heads the High Committee for Economic Emergencies and commands the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces, welcomed the first “strategic shipment” of two tons of gold produced by more than 70 mining companies. He praised the government’s anti-smuggling measures and called for stronger monitoring of franchise mining companies and oil companies. Hemeti also said RSF officers recently seized 340 kilograms of plastic-packaged gold at Khartoum airport. Addressing allegations about the El Junaid company linked to his family, he said it produced 30-40 kilograms of gold monthly from Jebel Amer mines and supplied foreign currency to the central bank. He insisted the real problem was not the company, but a “mafia” trying to damage the economy and weaken the national currency. Hamdok, meanwhile, said the exchange-rate crisis and subsidies on basic commodities remain major challenges and must be discussed openly to build consensus on solutions. He stressed the need for detailed debate on sectoral policies and foreign trade, and said the government’s approach could shape relations with international financial institutions such as the IMF and World Bank. He also urged use of the outcomes of a current Khartoum University forum on state building in Sudan’s national development project. Sudan’s gold output was estimated at 93 tons in 2018.

South African stocks fell 1.6% on Friday as a sharp drop in oil prices intensified worries about slowing global growth. Brent crude sank to $71.12 a barrel after OPEC chose not to cut output despite a supply glut. Sasol, which earns about 40% of its annual revenue from oil, plunged 8.2% to R461.95, its biggest one-day fall in six years. Analysts said the lower oil price was increasingly being seen not just as a boost for consumers, but as a sign of weaker demand and slower economic activity worldwide. Other resource stocks also weakened: BHP Billiton dropped 5.7% to R262.10 and was the largest drag on the Top-40 index, cutting nearly 270 points. Trading was heavy, with 207 million shares changing hands, above last year’s daily average of 176 million.

The article describes how Tahrir Square in Cairo, once the symbolic heart of Egypt’s 2011 uprising, has been transformed under the influence of the army and anti-Muslim Brotherhood politics. Although the square still physically exists near the Nile, the Egyptian Museum, the Nile Hilton, and the Mogamma government building, the revolutionary atmosphere has largely vanished. In its place are street children, drug dealers, and other destitute people, while part of the square remains closed to traffic. Graffiti and old banners still linger, but the original revolutionaries are mostly absent. At the center of one traffic island stands a so-called “Museum of the Revolution,” but it presents a highly selective version of events. It displays photos of “martyrs” killed in clashes over the past year with the Muslim Brotherhood, while omitting those who died during the first anti-Mubarak uprising in early 2011, the Mohamed Mahmoud Street clashes in late 2011, and the Abbassia protests in 2012. Guarded by intimidating men, the museum mainly serves as anti-Brotherhood propaganda, showing caricatures of Brotherhood members as sheep and celebrating the Egyptian people and the army. Posters throughout the square glorify General Abdel Fattah al-Sisi, the army commander and defense minister, portraying him as the heir to Gamal Abdel Nasser and Anwar Sadat, while Hosni Mubarak has been erased from this new political narrative. The article then focuses on Mustapha El-Guindy, a veteran politician and businessman who has emerged as a key figure in this reoccupation of Tahrir. El-Guindy made his fortune in cruise tourism and later founded an NGO, Tourism for Development, in the late 1990s. He served as an independent member of parliament from 2005 to 2010 and later as vice-president of the Pan-African Parliament. Re-elected in 2011, he presents himself as a friend of the revolution and an ally of liberal and Nasserist opposition figures such as Mohamed El-Baradei and Hamdeen Sabahi. El-Guindy openly denounces the Muslim Brotherhood, calling it an international mafia that sought to alter Egypt’s identity. He claims to have personally defended Tahrir Square against them, saying he was nearly killed twice. He also portrays himself as a major supporter of Tamarod, the youth movement that gathered millions of signatures demanding President Mohamed Morsi’s resignation and helped organize the massive June 30 demonstrations that preceded Morsi’s removal. For El-Guindy, those events marked the beginning of a “great people’s revolution.” He argues that the revolution will succeed now because the people, the police, and the army are united. In his view, the earlier uprising was “aborted” because it produced an Islamist president who divided the nation instead of bringing bread, freedom, and dignity. He celebrates the return of national unity and insists that the army is the guarantor of Egypt’s protection from both foreign and internal enemies. The article also notes that on July 26, the anniversary of the 1952 revolution, El-Guindy returned to Tahrir with millions of others after General al-Sisi called on Egyptians to give him a mandate to fight Brotherhood “terrorism.” El-Guindy uses this mass mobilization to argue that Morsi’s ouster on July 3 was not a coup but a popular correction. Tahrir, once a space of individual freedom and pluralism, is now presented as a site of mass national revival. Elsewhere in the square, another tent displays anti-Obama and anti-Western media slogans, accusing them of leniency toward the Brotherhood. It is run by a small party called Al-Ahrar Al-Ichitakiyin, whose members likewise praise the army and al-Sisi as a new Nasser. El-Guindy says he does not rule out al-Sisi becoming a future presidential candidate and speaks of forming a center-left party with Nasser’s son, Abdel Hakim, and others. Its proposed platform would include a minimum wage, bread, clean water, and free electricity. He ends with a warning that the poor surround the square and could take it over if ignored.

Today, it is inhabited by street children, drug dealers, and destitute individuals, with half the esplanade remaining closed to traffic. A newly constructed "Museum of the Revolution" occupies the square's center, but its exhibits reveal a selective historical narrative. The museum displays photographs of young people killed in clashes with the Muslim Brotherhood, yet conspicuously omits those killed during the original 2011 revolution by Hosni Mubarak's troops, as well as victims from Mohamed Mahmoud Street and Abbassia protests. Instead, the museum functions primarily as anti-Muslim Brotherhood propaganda, featuring caricatures and glorifying the Egyptian army and General Abdel Fattah al-Sisi, who is portrayed as the successor to Gamal Abdel Nasser and Anwar Sadat. El-Guindy served as an independent parliament member and maintains connections to liberal and Nasserian opposition figures. He claims credit for organizing resistance to the Muslim Brotherhood during their presidency, asserting he "held the square with a handful of young people" against an organization he describes as an "international mafia." When massive protests erupted on June 30, 2013, leading to Morsi's July 3 overthrow, El-Guindy frames this as the beginning of a "people's great revolution"—distinct from the 2011 uprising, which he characterizes as "aborted" because it failed to deliver bread, freedom, and dignity. A significant shift has occurred in the composition of Tahrir's supporters. El-Guindy successfully reunited the revolution's original activists with the "couch party"—citizens who watched events on television—and even fouloul, supporters of the old Mubarak regime. He justifies this broad coalition by emphasizing national unity and the army's role as Egypt's protector against foreign and domestic enemies. The army, particularly General al-Sisi, has become the central unifying force. When al-Sisi called for a popular mandate to combat the Brotherhood's alleged "terrorism" on July 26, 2013, millions gathered in Tahrir Square. El-Guindy interprets this massive turnout as proof that Morsi's removal was not a military coup but genuine popular will. Currently, nationalist and populist sentiment dominates the square, with tents displaying anti-Western slogans and promoting al-Sisi as Nasser's reincarnation—a phenomenon described as "Nassermania." El-Guindy plans to establish a center-left party with Nasser's son and other figures, focusing on socio-populist policies including minimum wage, bread subsidies, clean water, and free electricity. El-Guindy's final warning proves prophetic: "The poor are there, all around us. If we don't take care of them, they will take over the Square." This statement underscores the underlying tensions beneath Tahrir's apparent stability, suggesting that unresolved economic grievances could reignite social unrest.

Congolese refugee Gilbert Kalenga, 31, has been denied bail on a charge of possessing dagga worth N$1.35 million. Swakopmund magistrate Conchita Olivier ruled on Friday that he was “not a good candidate for bail” and said releasing him would not be a risk the court was willing to take. Kalenga was arrested in June in Swakopmund after allegedly receiving 27 kg of compressed dagga from a courier service. He has maintained that he is innocent, saying he believed the package was chicken feed meant for a farm near Henties Bay. He also suggested he may have been framed by a drug cartel. Police are investigating whether four other suspects were involved in transporting the dagga from Otjiwarongo to Swakopmund. These include two men and a woman who allegedly delivered the consignment to the courier service in Otjiwarongo, as well as a contact known as “Mr Gabriel,” who allegedly instructed Kalenga to receive the supposed chicken feed and hand it over to a “farm worker” on the coast. Kalenga’s bail hearing has been ongoing since June. State prosecutor Beate Mwahi opposed bail, arguing that the charges were serious, the state had a strong case, and Kalenga might commit similar offences or abscond if released. She also said bail would not serve the public interest or the administration of justice. Olivier agreed with the state, saying that based on the evidence and testimony before the court, there was a likelihood the charges would be proved. She also noted that Kalenga has another pending drug case in Swakopmund, involving cocaine allegedly worth N$200, for which he is already out on bail. That, she said, supported the concern that he might reoffend. The magistrate further said Kalenga’s refugee status, lack of fixed assets in Namibia, and the possibility of a serious conviction increased the risk of abscondment. Although he told the court he would never flee because he considered himself Namibian, the court was not persuaded. Olivier added that drug offences are taken seriously because of their harmful effects on society. The case was postponed to October for further investigation.

Iron ore prices have fallen sharply in recent weeks, pressured by both immediate concerns about China’s economy and a longer-term challenge to the way the global market is priced. The benchmark 62% iron ore price for delivery to north China, as assessed by Argus, dropped to $121.95 a tonne on June 17, its lowest level since Jan. 1 and 24% below the 2022 peak of $160.30 reached on March 8. China’s domestic iron ore contract also weakened, ending last week at 838 yuan ($124.70), down 10.3% from its high for the year on June 6. The near-term decline has been driven mainly by falling profit margins at Chinese steel mills and a dimmer outlook for demand. Some mills are reportedly cutting output, while Sinosteel analysts estimate steel inventories rose by 316,700 tonnes last week to 22.2 million tonnes. Because China accounts for about 70% of global seaborne iron ore imports, any slowdown in steel demand quickly affects iron ore prices, since the mineral is a key ingredient in steel production. Broader economic worries are also weighing on sentiment. China’s continued zero-COVID policy and the possibility of more lockdowns are clouding the outlook for the world’s second-largest economy. The market is now caught between that negative mood and expectations that Beijing’s stimulus measures will help revive growth in the second half of the year. The direction of prices for the rest of 2022 will depend largely on how well China contains COVID-19 and how quickly stimulus spending boosts steel-intensive sectors such as housing, infrastructure, and vehicle manufacturing. Beyond the short-term demand slump, the article highlights a more structural threat: China’s effort to reshape iron ore purchasing and pricing. The current spot-based system dates largely to 2008, when BHP moved away from the old contract model and other miners followed. Now Beijing is reportedly seeking to create a central group to control iron ore imports by the end of the year, with the goal of forcing lower prices. The Financial Times reported that this plan is gaining momentum among major state-controlled steel mills. However, China’s leverage is limited by the concentrated supply side of the market. Australia and Brazil dominate seaborne iron ore exports, and China’s imports from those two countries in May totaled 83.7 million tonnes, or 87% of all seaborne arrivals, according to Kpler. Four companies — the big three Australian miners plus Brazil’s Vale — supplied 75.6% of China’s imports. China could diversify toward smaller suppliers such as South Africa and Canada, but those miners would have little reason to undercut Australian prices. With Ukraine’s exports disrupted by war and India banning exports, the market has become even tighter. The result may be a standoff over who gives in first.

Reports indicate some mills are reducing output while steel inventory surged by 316,700 tonnes to 22.2 million tonnes. China's continued zero-COVID policy and lingering lockdowns further dampen economic prospects, though stimulus measures may eventually revive demand in the second half of the year. Since China purchases approximately 70% of global seaborne iron ore, any steel-demand concerns directly impact prices. Beyond short-term challenges, the market faces a more fundamental threat. According to the Financial Times, China plans to establish a central buying group by year-end to control iron ore imports, aiming to leverage its dominant position as a buyer to force lower prices. While such proposals have surfaced previously, current momentum appears genuine among major state-controlled steel mills. However, China's negotiating position faces significant constraints. Although demand is concentrated among Chinese buyers, supply is equally concentrated. Australia and Brazil dominate production, supplying 87% of China's seaborne iron ore imports in May. Four major companies—Australia's top three producers plus Brazil's Vale—control 75.6% of China's imports. Additional supply concentration resulted from Ukraine's export losses since Russia's invasion and India's export ban. China's options are limited. While attempting to reduce Australian dependence by increasing Brazilian purchases might seem viable, miners in alternative countries lack incentive to undercut Australian competitors' prices. The handful of major suppliers exercise considerable market power, making coordinated pressure difficult. If China pursues ending the current spot pricing system established in 2008, the outcome likely depends on which side yields first. The concentrated supply structure means major producers can resist pressure, creating a potential stalemate. The iron ore market appears headed toward a confrontation between a dominant buyer attempting to restructure purchasing mechanisms and concentrated suppliers capable of resisting those efforts.

South Korean presidential candidate Sim Sang-jung is portrayed as a highly experienced, scandal-free politician whose candidacy nonetheless has little chance of success in Wednesday’s election. A four-term lawmaker, labor activist, and outspoken feminist, Sim stands apart from the two male front-runners, Yoon Suk-yeol of the opposition People Power Party and Lee Jae-myung of the ruling Democratic Party. But in South Korea’s deeply entrenched two-party, male-dominated political system, she remains a long shot, with approval ratings stuck in the low single digits. The article says Sim’s campaign highlights two major obstacles. First, she is a woman in a country where politics and society remain strongly patriarchal. South Korea has one of the world’s widest gender gaps: it has the highest gender wage gap among OECD countries, women hold only 18.6 percent of parliamentary seats, and just 3.6 percent of board members at major conglomerates are female. Experts quoted in the article say that female politicians face a steep climb to national leadership. Stanford sociology professor Gi-Wook Shin notes that South Korea is still a patriarchal society and that former president Park Geun-hye was an exception, largely benefiting from the legacy of her father, former dictator Park Chung-hee. Sim’s second disadvantage is party affiliation. She belongs to the small left-wing Justice Party, which holds only six seats in the National Assembly. South Korea’s first-past-the-post electoral system has long favored the country’s two major parties, and every president has come from that duopoly. The Justice Party advocates for climate justice, LGBT rights, and labor rights—positions still considered radical by many voters. As a self-described feminist, Sim sharply contrasts with Yoon, who has promised to abolish the ministry of gender equality and argues that women do not face systemic discrimination. Sim told AFP that “sexism clearly exists in South Korean society” and warned that campaign rhetoric encouraging hatred could damage democracy. She said Yoon’s proposals risk fueling misogynistic sentiment. The article also describes a bitter and scandal-ridden race among the leading candidates, which some media have dubbed “the election of the unfavourables.” Yoon has faced scrutiny over alleged links to shamans, while Lee has been dogged by allegations of mafia ties. Sim, by contrast, has kept a clean record. Her political roots lie in South Korea’s labor movement. She spent more than two decades fighting for workers’ rights, including going underground as a factory worker to help organize unions while still a student. In 1985, she helped lead a strike and was placed on the authoritarian government’s “most wanted” list. That background shaped her signature campaign promise: a four-day work week, an idea that would be highly unusual in a country known for extremely long working hours. Despite her limited prospects, Sim has found some support among women in their 20s and is admired by younger feminists for bringing women’s rights into the male-dominated labor movement. Still, analysts say she made strategic mistakes, including failing to distance herself from corruption allegations involving President Moon Jae-in’s administration. Sim herself says she could not persuade voters to imagine alternatives beyond the two dominant parties. Even so, scholars argue that her presence on the ballot is symbolically important because it challenges South Korea’s personality-driven, regionally rooted two-party politics.
