Government auditors have flagged a proposed P2.1-billion information technology project of the Philippine Health Insurance Corp. (PhilHealth) as riddled with irregularities, even though the project was supposedly meant to curb fraud and corruption inside the state insurer. According to reports by the Commission on Audit (COA) and PhilHealth’s own resident auditors, one major part of the proposal — the planned purchase of equipment worth P734 million — was not even included in the original budget request submitted by PhilHealth. Auditors said the project also contained overpriced items and vague procurement specifications that could allow suppliers to deliver equipment different from what the agency actually needed. In a report issued in May, COA auditors found that the budget for five “ICT resources,” including computers, scanners and related equipment, was inflated by about P98 million. PhilHealth’s internal auditors went further, saying some items and software programs were drastically overpriced. One example they cited was Adobe software, which normally cost P168,000 per unit but was listed in PhilHealth’s proposed budget at P21 million each — a 12,400-percent increase. They also said the budget for “application servers and licenses” was raised to P40 million from an original estimate of P25 million. The reports describe the IT project as part of PhilHealth’s effort to build an integrated system that would improve fraud detection and strengthen its operations. But the auditors said the proposal was full of inconsistencies. They noted that many of the equipment items PhilHealth wanted to buy were not included in its Information Systems Strategic Plan (ISSP) for 2018 to 2020, which had already been approved by the Department of Information and Communications Technology (DICT). The audit began in February and covered PhilHealth’s planned IT spending as reflected in its corporate operating budget for the year. The findings were presented to officials from the IT Management Department, Physical Resource and Infrastructure Department, and Comptrollership Department in a meeting on May 6. An Inquirer source said the reports were also submitted to PhilHealth president and CEO Ricardo Morales and Health Secretary Francisco Duque III, who chairs the PhilHealth board. The auditors said the discrepancies pointed to weaknesses in PhilHealth’s systems, policies and procedures. They stressed that ICT equipment is essential to the agency’s mission and must be properly controlled and accounted for. PhilHealth’s own auditors also said an integrated IT system is crucial because the corporation’s membership, collection and claims databases have remained fragmented despite years of spending on hardware and software. In their view, this fragmentation has allowed a “syndicate” to manipulate PhilHealth’s financial condition and carry out schemes disguised as public service. Although the reports did not identify the members of the alleged syndicate, a PhilHealth insider earlier told the Inquirer that a “mafia” of senior officials had long dominated the agency and prevented proper review of rates, overpayments and other questionable practices. The controversy over the IT project is believed to have contributed to the resignation of lawyer Thorrsson Montes Keith, PhilHealth’s antifraud officer. Sources familiar with the reports said the project triggered a “shouting match” among PhilHealth executives during an online meeting on July 22, a day before Keith submitted his resignation letter. In that letter to Morales, Keith cited “widespread corruption” as one of the reasons for leaving, though he did not elaborate. The latest scandal comes after earlier revelations that PhilHealth had lost P154 billion to various forms of fraud, including ghost dialysis reimbursements, overpayments, false claims and “upcasing” of ordinary illnesses. President Duterte had previously expressed anger over the losses, saying the government had been cheated out of money that could have been used for health care. He later removed PhilHealth’s top officials and appointed Morales, a retired army general, to clean up the agency. But more than a year later, the problems appear unresolved, even as PhilHealth remains responsible for health coverage for over 100 million Filipinos during the COVID-19 pandemic. Morales did not immediately respond to requests for comment. A separate COA audit query memorandum dated Jan. 31 also raised concerns about a P29-million procurement in 2016 for a “production database server” and “online services.” Auditors said the winning bidders had failed to comply with PhilHealth’s requirements, which they described as vague and potentially open to abuse. They also noted that delivery was delayed by 118 days and that no certification was issued showing PhilHealth personnel had been adequately trained to operate the system. The auditors further said PhilHealth’s IT unit initially sought P2.1 billion for the ISSP, but the board rejected it for lack of specific details. After “typographical errors” were corrected, the budget was reduced to P1.9 billion. Even then, PhilHealth’s internal auditors said the board had approved only about P25 million for a line subscription, while the full budget remained unapproved. Despite this, the board was later forced to approve a P328-million supplemental IT budget on March 15, 2020, after being told that “the entire PhilHealth system will collapse.” By that point, PhilHealth had already released P352 million for IT services even before the full proposal had been approved. In April, senior vice president and chief information officer Jovita Aragona sought approval to procure P750 million worth of IT equipment, and weeks later requested another P215 million. However, resident auditors said board members demanded an internal audit of existing hardware and software before approving the proposal. Aragona did not present the report, arguing that the items in her proposal were not covered by the internal review. Overall, the reports portray a procurement process marked by inflated costs, weak controls, delayed deliveries and unresolved questions about oversight inside one of the country’s most important public institutions.

Indonesia’s National Narcotics Agency (BNN) uncovered 14 international drug syndicates in 2024, according to agency head Commissioner General Marthinus Hukom. Speaking in Jakarta on Monday, he said the networks used multiple routes to smuggle narcotics into Indonesia, including air transport, ships, and land crossings. Hukom cited the Gregor Haas network, linked to the South American drug cartel system and the Sinaloa Cartel in Mexico, as one example of air-based trafficking. He also said smugglers exploited Indonesia’s maritime borders by using traditional wooden and synthetic-fiber boats, a method previously associated with a group from Tawau, Malaysia. On land, BNN and the Customs and Excise office, together with the Border Security Task Force, intercepted methamphetamine and ecstasy smuggling along the West Kalimantan border. The operation led to the seizure of about 100 kilograms of drugs and the arrest of six Indonesians and three foreigners. BNN also exposed drug smuggling allegedly controlled by Indonesians abroad, including wanted suspect Dewi Astuti, who remains overseas. Hukom said BNN is working with foreign and domestic law enforcement to pursue suspects. In addition, the agency uncovered 13 national syndicates operating across islands and provinces.

# Summary In 2024, Indonesia's National Narcotics Agency (BNN) identified 14 international drug syndicates, with Commissioner General Marthinus Hukom announcing the findings at a Jakarta press conference on December 23. These networks employed various smuggling methods, including air and sea transportation. Notable among them was the Gregor Haas network, linked to Mexico's Sinaloa Cartel. International traffickers exploited Indonesia's maritime boundaries using wooden and synthetic fiber ships, similar to tactics employed by Malaysian groups. The BNN successfully disrupted land-based smuggling along the West Kalimantan border, confiscating approximately 100 kilograms of crystal methamphetamine and ecstasy, while apprehending six Indonesians and three foreigners. Additionally, the agency uncovered narcotics smuggling operations controlled by Indonesians abroad, including wanted suspect Dewi Astuti. The BNN collaborated with international police narcotics departments and domestic agencies to pursue these individuals. Beyond international networks, the BNN also exposed 13 national drug syndicates operating across islands and provinces, with members from diverse backgrounds. Hukom appealed for public support to achieve national drug-control objectives.

Israel Folau says he is happy to cover his tattoos while in Japan, but he also wishes he had never gotten them at all. The Wallabies have spent four days in Tokyo adjusting to the cultural expectations of next year’s Rugby World Cup host nation, where visible tattoos can be sensitive because of their association with the Yakuza, the Japanese mafia. World Rugby has already warned teams and supporters to avoid openly displaying body art. On their previous tour of Japan, the Wallabies were surprised by rules requiring tattoos to be covered at gyms and swimming pools, but this time the issue has been less disruptive. Since arriving in Tokyo, players with tattoos have generally worn shirts instead of singlets in public. Folau, who has tattoos across his body and arms, still showed some of them when he attended a public signing event at sponsor ASICS on Wednesday, wearing a shirt that only covered part of his bicep. Despite that, he said he had not received any negative reactions from the public. Asked whether anyone had taken offence, Folau replied that he respected the culture and people of Japan. He said he was “happy to cover up the tattoos in respect of the people here and the culture,” adding that he loved Japanese culture and wanted to do whatever he could not to offend anyone. He described the Japanese people as “amazing” and “always embracing.” Folau then made a more personal admission, saying that if he had his time again, he probably would not have gotten any tattoos because of his faith and Biblical teaching. He said that was something he learned only later, and that he could not change the past. However, he also said he would not have his tattoos removed. For him, he said, faith is about internal change rather than undoing past actions, and he is simply grateful for where he is now and where he has come from. His teammate Samu Kerevi, who also has several tattoos, said his own interactions with Japanese people had been positive. He suggested the locals were more struck by the Wallabies’ size and physique than by their body art. Kerevi said he usually wears a long-sleeve shirt at lunch to cover his tattoos, and joked that the only real issue at the sauna was being given a small towel.

The team filmed the video during a training camp in Spain and spent the following weeks editing it. Still, he made clear that rapping is only a hobby and that cycling remains his job. He also suggested the team could make more videos if fans wanted them.

Punjab Inspector General of Police Muhammad Aamir Zulfiqar Khan on Friday took sweeping disciplinary and administrative action in Rawalpindi after a case in which an innocent citizen was wrongly implicated in a murder investigation. He removed SP Saddar Division Muhammad Nabil Khokhar from his post and suspended DSP Waqar Nisar and SHO Rawat Station SI Nadim Zafar. He also directed Regional Police Officer (RPO) Rawalpindi Nasir Mehmood Satti to begin strict departmental proceedings against the two officers and ordered the SSP Investigation to hold a formal inquiry and submit a report to the IG office. The IG went further, placing former SHO Ratta Amral Shakeel Ahmed under suspension and ordering a case to be registered against investigation officer SI Shabbir Ahmed for misuse of authority and conducting a flawed investigation. The action was presented as a response to serious police negligence and abuse of power. Aamir Zulfiqar Khan expressed deep concern over the rising street crime in Rawalpindi district, especially motorcycle theft, aerial firing, organized crime, drug trafficking, and land grabbing. He warned City Police Officer Syed Shehzad Nadim Bukhari to personally supervise a major crackdown on criminals or face consequences. He said officers who fail to meet crime-control targets, despite being provided with resources, should prepare for action against them. He also stressed that if any policeman is harmed because of the negligence of a supervisory officer, he would not hesitate to punish that officer. The IG issued these instructions while chairing a high-level crime meeting at the RPO Office and later meeting all DSPs and SHOs of the Rawalpindi region at Police Lines. During the sessions, he reviewed crime statistics and police performance. He told officers that the core duty of the police is to serve citizens and protect their lives, property, and dignity. He said officers must place themselves in the position of complainants when dealing with people at police stations, and that anyone who does not fulfill the oath taken at recruitment and training has no right to remain in the department. Among the operational directives, the IG ordered the establishment of CIA centers in all districts of the Rawalpindi region and said the CIA staff in Rawalpindi should be doubled and equipped with modern resources. He also directed Commandant Sihala DIG Ashfaq Ahmad Khan to conduct a six-day training course at Sihala College on modern scientific methods of custodial interrogation for CIA personnel. He instructed the CPO Rawalpindi to take zero-tolerance legal action against motorcycle theft and aerial firing, and to personally oversee operations against organized and professional criminals. Ten major Chinese companies making polysilicon, a key raw material for solar panels, have formed a new venture called Beijing Guanghe Qiancheng Technology in a sign that the industry is trying to address severe overcapacity. The company was set up in December and is backed by major producers including Tongwei, GCL Technology Holdings and Xinjiang Daqo New Energy, according to Chinese business registry data. Industry observers say it brings together nearly all of the leading Chinese polysilicon makers. The China Photovoltaic Industry Association says the venture is intended to serve as a platform for restructuring production capacity, with companies cooperating under state guidance to curb destructive competition upstream. The move comes after years of rapid expansion fueled by China’s subsidy-driven industrial policy and global demand expectations tied to carbon neutrality goals and, later, the 2022 energy price spike after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. But the sector expanded far faster than demand. China now accounts for about 95% of global polysilicon production capacity, and prices have collapsed. Polysilicon traded above $30 per kilogram in 2022, but by 2024 prices had fallen to roughly one-third of that level, with sale prices dropping below production costs around mid-2024. In response, Tongwei and Daqo announced domestic output cuts at the end of 2024, helping reduce average Chinese output in the second half of that year and again in early 2025. However, supply later rose again in the second half of 2025, weakening the recovery. The new venture has also drawn antitrust scrutiny: China’s market regulator reportedly warned some participants not to make agreements on output or prices. Analysts say tighter supply control could raise costs for solar panel makers, while a Trinasolar representative warned that reduced competition might also hurt product quality.

Manny Scott, one of the original “Freedom Writers,” told more than 3,000 Rowan-Salisbury Schools employees on Monday that one caring adult can change a child’s life. Speaking at Carson High School during a professional development day for teachers and a back-to-school conference for noncertified staff, Scott urged educators and school workers to recognize the power they have, even on difficult days. He said a teacher, coach, or cafeteria worker may be a student’s “last chance,” and encouraged the audience not to give up on children who are struggling. Scott, 40, shared a long and painful account of his childhood in and around Long Beach, California. He grew up in a broken home: his father was in prison and his stepfather was addicted to crack cocaine. Before he turned 16, Scott had moved 26 times and had slept in cars, on couches, in homeless shelters, and even on beaches. His family often had to beg or search through dumpsters for food. He also described a violent incident in which his stepfather slammed his mother’s face into a window, and when Scott rushed to help her, he was thrown from a second-floor balcony. He said those hardships followed him into school, where he was angry, withdrawn, and behind academically. At one point, his English skills were judged so weak that he was placed in English as a Second Language classes for Spanish speakers, even though English was his only language. Scott said his school years were filled with trauma and humiliation, not support. He recalled a sixth-grade teacher publicly criticizing his ragged clothes and then telling him in the hallway that he smelled and would end up like his father, who was in prison. Scott used that memory to challenge the Rowan County audience to think carefully about the effect their words and actions can have on vulnerable students. He asked them, “Do you enrich or impoverish the students under your care?” Scott also explained that poverty is not only a lack of money, but also a lack of access to caring people and helpful resources. By age 11, he was smoking marijuana, drinking alcohol, stealing, breaking into homes, and skipping large portions of school. He ended his freshman year with a 0.6 GPA. Feeling trapped by violence and instability, he eventually dropped out after his best friend was brutally murdered while trying to visit him. He spent his days wandering the streets until a chance encounter changed his direction. Sitting on a park bench in Long Beach, he met a crack addict who told him he saw himself in Scott and urged him to return to school. Scott went back to his high school and pleaded with the assistant principal to let him re-enroll. She agreed, but warned that catching up would be difficult. Over the next several years, Scott said, he encountered teachers and coaches who refused to give up on him. He described a math teacher who kept tutoring him until he understood, a science teacher whose passion inspired him, and coaches who became father figures. But the school environment remained tense, with a student body divided along racial lines and gang violence spilling into classrooms. It was in that environment that Scott and other students met Erin Gruwell, the new English teacher known to them as “Ms. G.” Gruwell, who came from a privileged background, made a point of trying to understand her students and experimenting with new approaches. She used cultural figures such as Tupac Shakur and Snoop Dogg to teach poetry and literary devices, and then introduced journals, telling students, “Everyone in this room has a voice, and I’m going to help you find it.” Scott said Gruwell’s example taught important lessons about persistence, humility, and listening to students. He urged the audience to keep trying new approaches and to “be a student of your students.” With Gruwell’s support and that of other teachers, Scott said he turned his life around, finishing high school with a 3.9 GPA and making the honor roll. Gruwell encouraged him to attend college, leading him to the University of California, Berkeley. After earning a bachelor’s degree, he said she kept pushing him to pursue graduate school and later a doctorate. He credited her with helping him believe in himself, saying that sometimes people must believe in someone else’s belief before their own confidence takes hold. Scott now travels and speaks about his experiences and is close to earning his Ph.D. He noted that all 150 students Gruwell taught earned high school diplomas and that many went on to successful careers. He emphasized that his story is not exceptional because of him, but because of the teacher who refused to give up. He ended by asking Rowan-Salisbury employees to renew their commitment to students, reminding them that even on their worst day, they could still be a child’s best hope, second chance, or last chance.

German companies are facing sharply rising cyber threats, according to two studies published Thursday. An EY survey of 450 firms found that the number of companies targeted by cyber attacks in the past three years has tripled compared with the three years to 2015, and 44 percent said they had been spied on. EY expert Bodo Meseke said many firms may not even notice attacks. Among larger companies with more than 1 billion euros in turnover, 67 percent of managers expect a significant further increase. They see Russia as the biggest threat, followed by China and the United States. Meseke said the danger is coming from multiple sources, including intelligence services, business rivals and organized crime. A separate Deloitte-backed Allensbach study found 27 percent of executives reported daily IT attacks, up from 12 percent four years ago, and 97 percent considered a major hacker attack at least probable.

After a wave of deadly prison riots in Ecuador, the country’s Catholic bishops have called for a thorough review and “humanization” of the prison system. At least 79 inmates were killed on Feb. 23 in coordinated violence in three prisons, with some bodies reportedly dismembered or beheaded in fighting between rival gangs. Church leaders said the killings were the result of a turf war that intensified after one of Ecuador’s most powerful gang leaders was murdered in December. In a statement released Thursday, the bishops said the crisis inside detention centers reflected “the prison crisis, social decomposition and collective indifference” facing the country. They urged authorities to conduct “a true evaluation of the prison system” and to develop “fully humane programs” that comply with Ecuador’s Constitution. They also offered Christian solidarity and prayer to the families of the dead and said the Church’s prison ministry was available to help de-escalate tensions and support those affected by the violence. Officials believe the unrest began in the maximum-security wings of the prisons, where rival gangs were fighting for control. Prisons director Edmundo Moncayo said the groups were seeking “criminal leadership within the detention centers.” Police and military forces later retook control of the facilities in three cities after large-scale raids, but authorities warned that mistrust remained high and that another revolt was still possible. The violence was described as unprecedented in scale, with reports of extreme brutality including beheadings and the removal of hearts. The crisis also exposed long-standing structural problems in Ecuador’s prison system, which is severely overcrowded. The system was built for about 27,000 inmates but currently holds around 38,000. Maximum-security units house prisoners linked to murder, drug trafficking, extortion and other serious crimes. Ecuador’s location between Colombia and Peru, the world’s two largest cocaine producers, has made it a key transit country for drug trafficking to the United States and Europe. In 2020, the country seized a record 128 tons of drugs, mostly cocaine. Government officials acknowledged the seriousness of the situation. Patricio Pazmiño, the minister responsible for the national police, said, “We are still living a time of crisis,” while General Patricio Carrillo, the police commander, said the prison system had “structural problems that we will not be able to solve now.” The riots left not only dozens of prisoners dead but also several prisoners and police officers injured. The bishops quoted Pope Francis’s 2019 remarks that prisons should become “more and more humane” and warned against allowing them to become places of violence and illegality. They pointed to Article 201 of Ecuador’s Constitution, which says the prison system should aim at comprehensive rehabilitation and reintegration into society while protecting the rights of detainees. The article also noted that Ecuador’s crisis fits a broader regional pattern. In Paraguay, seven people were killed on Feb. 16 in prison violence in Asunción, where inmates also kidnapped guards during a nearly 24-hour rebellion. Paraguayan bishops likewise condemned corruption, overcrowding and the lack of prison reform, urging more humane treatment and stronger efforts from the government, judiciary and legislature.

Two Indian-origin men in Britain, Anand Tripathi, 61, and Varun Bhardwaj, 39, have been jailed for a combined 34 years after a London trial found them guilty of running a major drug-smuggling and cigarette-duty evasion operation. Tripathi received a 15-year sentence, while Bhardwaj was handed 19 years. According to the UK Crown Prosecution Service, the pair used a freight company as a cover to clear shipping containers carrying illegal drugs and cigarettes. The containers were then diverted from their declared destinations to a warehouse they controlled, where organized crime groups unloaded the contraband. Prosecutors said Tripathi’s knowledge of importation and customs procedures, together with Bhardwaj’s day-to-day management of the business, helped the scheme operate for more than a year. The court heard that, between September 2021 and November 2022, the men imported 272.86 kilograms of cocaine and 2,503.36 kilograms of cannabis in four shipments. The drugs were concealed in legitimate cargo, including more than two tonnes of cannabis hidden among yams from Ghana and 49 kilograms of cocaine disguised with oranges from South Africa. The estimated street value of the seized narcotics was about £28.9 million. Police and border officials intercepted and destroyed the drugs before they could reach the market. The pair were also convicted over the smuggling of 18.6 million cigarettes, for which they failed to pay £9,774,220 in import duty and VAT. The cigarettes and drugs were seized at ports including Portsmouth, Felixstowe and London Gateway. Investigators said the men tried to avoid detection by setting up shell companies and keeping themselves at arm’s length from the shipments. Their operation was exposed after a failed diversion in Somerset in April 2022, when a container was mistakenly delivered to a farm instead of being redirected. Inside were plastic-wrapped blocks of cocaine worth about £15 million hidden among animal feed from Colombia. The farmer, suspicious of the packages, reported them to police. During a search of Bhardwaj’s home in Hounslow, west London, officers also found a kilogram of cannabis in a cupboard under the stairs. Bhardwaj claimed he was keeping it “as evidence,” but he was convicted of possession as well as other offences, including failing to disclose a phone PIN.

The European Union’s anti-fraud office, OLAF, is warning member states to be on guard against scammers trying to exploit the bloc’s slow COVID-19 vaccine rollout. In a statement Monday, OLAF said it had received multiple reports of fraudsters offering fake vaccines for sale to governments eager to speed up immunization campaigns. OLAF director-general Ville Itälä said the scams could take several forms: criminals might promise large vaccine shipments, deliver only a sample to secure an upfront payment, and then disappear; they might send counterfeit doses; or they might falsely claim to represent legitimate companies with access to real vaccines. “All of these claims have one thing in common: they are false,” he said. The warning comes as the EU has faced criticism for lagging behind countries such as Britain and Israel in vaccine distribution. The European Commission has signed six contracts for more than 2 billion doses, but only three vaccines have been approved so far, and deliveries have been disrupted by production delays. OLAF’s alert echoed a December warning from Europol about organized crime targeting vaccines, including attempts to sell dangerous counterfeits or steal genuine shipments. While the EU coordinates collective vaccine purchases, member states can also seek separate deals outside the bloc’s procurement system under certain conditions. Hungary has already moved in that direction, approving China’s Sinopharm vaccine and Russia’s Sputnik V after criticizing the pace of the EU rollout. OLAF said it has not seized any fake vaccines yet, but it is also tracking illegal trade in masks, test kits, and other pandemic-related goods. It said it has identified more than 1,000 suspected fraudsters and seized or detained over 14 million items, including fake test kits and substandard protective equipment.

The agency continues monitoring illicit trade of COVID-19-related products.

The scandals are also alarming potential allies such as Ciudadanos, whose leader Albert Rivera condemned the PP as resembling “a mafia system.” Within the PP, some figures, including spokesman Pablo Casado, called for a purge of corrupt members. Acting Interior Minister Jorge Fernandez Diaz, however, questioned the timing of the revelations.

The European Commission said on Tuesday that some of the biggest investment banks with past antitrust violations will be barred, for now, from participating in individual syndicated debt sales for the EU’s COVID-19 recovery fund, which could raise up to 800 billion euros. The banks will remain in the EU’s primary dealer network, but they will not be invited to bid on specific syndicated transactions until the Commission finishes reviewing whether they have taken enough remedial action and committed to preventing future misconduct. The Commission did not name the excluded banks, but it pointed to three cartel cases in the past three years involving 10 major primary dealers. In April and May, it fined banks including Bank of America, Credit Agricole, Natixis, Nomura, NatWest Markets, and UniCredit for taking part in bond cartels. Deutsche Bank was involved in one of those cases but escaped a fine because it reported the cartel to regulators. In 2019, Barclays, Citigroup, JPMorgan, and NatWest were fined for foreign exchange market rigging. These banks are among the EU’s 39 primary dealers, a group that helps manage syndicated debt sales, which are more lucrative than standard auctions and can encourage participation in the latter. The EU plans to begin debt auctions in September. The Commission said the banks would eventually return to syndications. The move came as the EU raised 20 billion euros in its first recovery-fund bond sale, which drew near-record demand and was led by BNP Paribas, DZ Bank, HSBC, IMI-Intesa Sanpaolo, and Morgan Stanley.

# EU Excludes Major Banks from Recovery Fund Bond Sales The European Union has temporarily excluded several major investment banks from participating in syndicated debt sales for its €800 billion COVID-19 recovery fund due to past antitrust violations. The European Commission announced it will conduct a careful assessment of whether banks previously found guilty of breaching antitrust rules have implemented necessary remedial measures. While these institutions remain part of the primary dealer network, they will not be invited to tender for individual syndicated transactions pending completion of the assessment. The excluded banks include those fined in April and May for participating in bond cartels, including Bank of America, Credit Agricole, Natixis, Nomura, NatWest Markets, and UniCredit. Deutsche Bank, which revealed the cartel to the Commission, avoided fines. Additionally, Barclays, Citigroup, JPMorgan, and NatWest were fined in 2019 for foreign exchange market rigging. The Commission did not specify which banks face exclusion but indicated the restriction affects approximately 10 of the EU's 39 primary dealers. These banks normally earn lucrative fees managing syndicated debt sales, which motivates their participation in less profitable debt auctions beginning in September. A Commission spokesperson stated the banks would eventually rejoin syndications. Meanwhile, the EU successfully raised €20 billion from its first recovery fund bond sale, led by BNP Paribas, DZ Bank, HSBC, IMI-Intesa Sanpaolo, and Morgan Stanley.

Six German men went on trial in Dresden over their alleged role in the 2019 theft of jewels worth more than €113 million from the city’s Green Vault museum, while the stolen treasures remain missing. The defendants, aged 22 to 28 and not publicly named under German privacy rules, are charged with aggravated gang theft and serious arson. Prosecutors say they broke into the Gruenes Gewoelbe in the early hours of 25 November 2019 and stole 21 pieces of jewellery containing more than 4,300 diamonds. Court spokesman Thomas Ziegler said prosecutors believe the men planned the robbery carefully, including scouting the site in advance and cutting part of a window grating beforehand so they could enter quickly. Authorities said earlier that the suspects had not commented on the allegations. Police have offered a €500,000 reward for information leading to the jewels. On Friday, Dresden prosecutor’s office spokesman Juergen Schmidt said there was still “no hot lead” on the location of the loot. He noted that even if convicted, the defendants cannot be compelled to testify about where the jewels are. The Dresden State Art Collections said there is no evidence the pieces were destroyed or sold, and museum spokeswoman Anja Priewe said the renewed publicity might help uncover new details. She pointed to other long-running recovery cases, including two Van Gogh paintings found more than 13 years after a Mafia theft. If convicted, four of the suspects could face up to 15 years in prison. The youngest defendants, twins, could receive up to 10 years in juvenile detention. Schmidt said all six are from the same family. The trial is scheduled to run until the end of October, with more than a dozen defense lawyers representing the men, who are in custody. Two other men have already been sentenced to four and a half years in prison for stealing the Big Maple Leaf, a 100-kilogram gold coin, from Berlin’s Bode Museum in 2017.

# Summary: Six Germans on Trial for €113 Million Green Vault Heist Six German men aged 22 to 28 appeared in court in Dresden on Friday, charged with stealing priceless jewels from the Green Vault Museum in November 2019. The defendants face charges of aggravated gang theft and serious arson in connection with the heist that netted 21 pieces of jewelry containing over 4,300 diamonds valued at more than €113 million. According to prosecutors, the defendants meticulously planned the crime by scouting the location beforehand, pre-sawing a window grating, and reattaching it to enable quick entry during the early morning heist on November 25, 2019. All suspects are family members and currently in custody, represented by more than a dozen defense lawyers. Despite the investigation, the stolen treasures' whereabouts remain unknown. Police offered a €500,000 reward for information about the jewels but have found no promising leads. Prosecutors noted that even if convicted, defendants cannot be compelled to testify about the items' location. Museum officials believe the jewelry sets have likely not been destroyed or sold. The trial is expected to continue until October. If convicted, four defendants could face up to fifteen years imprisonment, while the two youngest defendants—twins—face a maximum ten-year juvenile sentence. Two suspects previously received four-and-a-half-year sentences for stealing a 100-kilogram gold coin from Berlin's Bode Museum in 2017. The Green Vault collection, assembled in the 18th century by Augustus the Strong, survived World War II bombing but was taken as Soviet war booty. The treasures were returned to Dresden in 1958.

In eastern Germany, the return of wolves has become both an ecological issue and a political flashpoint, with anti-migrant politicians using the animal to stir fears that echo the rhetoric used against refugees. The article opens with a grisly scene near Förstgen, where a pack of wolves descended on a flock of sheep at dawn, leaving 55 animals dead and mutilated. Annett Hertweck, who runs a biosphere reserve and considers herself pro-wolf, arrived at the scene and described it as horrific. She noted that the wolves were descended from Polish forebears and that there are only a few hundred wolves in Germany, but some politicians and residents speak as if the country were facing an invasion. The wolf, long absent from Germany for nearly a century, has gradually returned by crossing from Poland and settling in rural areas. Its comeback has become entangled with Germany’s broader culture wars, especially the divide between urban and rural voters, west and east Germans, and those who welcome outsiders versus those who fear them. Hertweck argued that the wolf has become “the perfect scapegoat for our times,” cast as a dangerous foreign intruder, protected by elites. The article highlights how the far-right Alternative for Germany, or AfD, has made the wolf a political issue alongside immigration. Karsten Hilse, an AfD lawmaker from eastern Germany, explicitly compared the spread of wolves to the refugee crisis. He said the arrival of 1.2 million migrants since 2015 had brought crime and welfare dependence, and then added that “the same goes for wolves,” apparently referring to the public money spent on wolf protections and compensation for livestock losses. In the former Communist east, where wolves are most numerous and far-right politics are strongest, the issue has become central in regional election campaigns. One AfD activist in Saxony, Silke Grimm, has been campaigning to hunt wolves since 2014, when, she said, people mocked the idea. Now, she claims, others are adopting it. In her office near the Polish and Czech borders, she handed out two pamphlets: one arguing that Islam is incompatible with German culture, and the other claiming that the number of wolves is incompatible with Saxony’s “cultural landscape.” Like the AfD’s call for a ceiling on asylum seekers, the wolf leaflet demands a “ceiling” for wolves. It warns children not to go into the forest alone and depicts a wolf near a residential area with an abandoned teddy bear in the foreground. Grimm said wolves are dangerous, breed rapidly, and that official assurances they are under control are as unconvincing as government statements during the refugee crisis. Yet the article emphasizes that the facts do not support the panic. Vanessa Ludwig, a biologist with the regional government’s wolf information office, said there have been no reported cases of wolves killing humans in Germany in the past century, and the last known wolf-related human death in Western Europe occurred in Spain in the 1960s. German authorities count 73 wolf packs, 31 pairs, and three solitary wolves, or roughly 700 animals nationwide. Ludwig said there is no wolf crisis, and that the issue became politically charged in 2015 during the refugee crisis, after which it turned into a constant emotional storm. The story shows how fear spreads through local anecdotes. In the village of Uhsmannsdorf, two goats named Lolek and Bolek were killed by a wolf, and the incident helped persuade parents to keep children out of the nearby forest. Local mayor Heike Böhm said the story had reinforced the sense that wolves overrun the area, though she herself has never seen one. Even Chancellor Angela Merkel, when meeting conservatives in the region, acknowledged that wolves should be hunted “where necessary.” Her environment minister was considering a law to make it easier to shoot so-called “problem wolves.” Some people have acted on their own: a wolf was found dead in a lake, shot in the head and sunk with a cement block tied to its body, in what the article describes as a mafia-style execution. The article places this modern debate in historical context. In the 19th century, when the Brothers Grimm collected fairy tales, wolves were real threats to farmers and livestock, and they became the archetypal villain in stories such as “Little Red Riding Hood” and “The Wolf and the Seven Goats.” That folklore still shapes public imagination. Ludwig called it “Little Red Riding Hood syndrome,” explaining that fairy tales alone cannot erase the deep psychological associations attached to wolves in Germany. The wolf has also taken on symbolic meaning in the east, where some people feel disadvantaged by reunification. Under Communism, wolves crossing the border were shot; after reunification, they became a protected species under European Union law. For some eastern farmers, the wolf symbolizes a post-1989 order in which they feel they lost status, money, and even their children to the west. Hertweck, while sympathetic to their anger, said the wolf is blamed for grievances that have deeper political and social roots. The article ends with a counterpoint from Stephan Kaasche, a nature guide teaching children about wolves. Holding up a wolf skull, he told the children that the animal cannot swallow them whole. To him, the hysteria says more about human fears than about wolves themselves. He argued that people’s grievances are real, but unrelated to the animal, and that politicians exploiting the issue are “like a wolf in sheep’s clothing.”

Over the past century, no wolves have killed humans in Germany, and the last known wolf-caused human death in Western Europe occurred in Spain during the 1960s. Yet despite these reassuring statistics, emotions dominate the discussion. Ludwig pinpointed precisely when wolves became political: 2015, during the refugee crisis. Since then, she said, "it has been one big emotional storm." The parallel is clear—with both wolves and immigrants, emotions matter more than facts. ## Historical and Cultural Context The wolf's symbolic power runs deep in German culture. The Brothers Grimm, who collected fairy tales in this region, portrayed wolves as ultimate villains—the scheming predator in "Little Red Riding Hood" and "The Wolf and the Seven Goats." Ludwig calls this persistent anxiety "Little Red Riding Hood syndrome," explaining that the psychology is complex given the long history of wolves in German folklore. When a wolf killed both animals over two weeks, the incident reinforced local fears and changed community behavior—children no longer visit nearby forests. Local mayor Heike Böhm, who walks in the forest daily and has never seen a wolf, acknowledged that the story "has reinforced fears that the place is overrun with wolves." ## Government Response and Violence Chancellor Angela Merkel acknowledged that wolves should be hunted "where necessary," and the environment minister is considering legislation making it easier to shoot "problem wolves." Some haven't waited for legal authorization. Belgian prosecutors said dozens of people were arrested Tuesday in a Europol-coordinated operation across six European countries targeting an international drug-trafficking network. In Belgium alone, 30 people were detained, while “a small number of arrests” were also made abroad. Authorities carried out 109 searches in Belgium, Croatia, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands and Spain. The investigation, which began in Belgium at the end of 2020, focused on a network trafficking cocaine from South America. It was significantly advanced by the hacking of SKY ECC, an encrypted phone service widely used by organized crime groups. Belgian police said the case involved Eastern European traffickers based around Brussels and Southern European suspects linked to the so-called Limburg mafia. The probe started after Belgian police found a large quantity of acetone, several kilos of cannabis and counterfeit police clothing during a search in the Brussels region. Investigators later discovered the same network was already under scrutiny in Spain, prompting close cooperation between the two countries. Authorities said the group used multiple transport routes and methods, including container ships through the ports of Antwerp, Rotterdam, Le Havre and Hamburg, as well as road vehicles, cargo planes and private jets. Prosecutors said the case highlighted how criminal organizations now operate more like commercial joint ventures than traditional family clans. Belgium has become a major entry point for cocaine into Europe, with nearly 90 tonnes seized in Antwerp in 2021. Senior magistrate Ignacio de la Serna warned earlier this month that police were struggling to cope with the scale of the threat.

# Summary Police in Italy, Spain, and Germany arrested 32 people suspected of drug trafficking and money laundering linked to the Camorra crime syndicate. Nearly one ton of drugs and 5 million euros in cash were seized during the operation, coordinated by Eurojust, a European organized crime agency.

Israel Police said a long-running undercover operation has exposed a major smuggling, bribery, and money-laundering network operating through Ashdod Port, leading to the arrest of dozens of suspects in raids on Tuesday morning. The investigation, described as one of the most extensive undercover probes in Israel’s history, began in 2020 when the Tax Authority and police recruited an undercover agent nicknamed “Jack Sparrow.” For four and a half years, he posed as a customs inspector at the port, building trust with importers, customs officials, and other suspects. According to police, the agent was eventually drawn into helping manipulate container inspections and approve shipping manifests in exchange for bribes worth tens to hundreds of thousands of shekels. This allowed smugglers to evade taxes on valuable cargo. The network allegedly trafficked counterfeit luxury goods, high-end vehicle parts, and tobacco products, and investigators believe it also handled weapons, ammunition, dangerous drugs, and unauthorized pharmaceuticals hidden inside ordinary goods. The raids targeted homes and offices of dozens of suspects, including an employee of the Ministry of Transportation. Authorities seized more than one million shekels in cash, along with luxury vehicles, documents, and electronic equipment. Confiscation proceedings have already begun. Police said the case uncovered a network that extended deep into Israel’s business community and was linked to organized crime. Suspects are expected to face charges including smuggling, bribery of public officials, and money laundering. Investigators estimate the scheme caused losses of hundreds of millions, possibly billions, of shekels in unpaid taxes. Ashdod Port handles about 60% of Israel’s cargo and is a major hub for trade and humanitarian shipments.

Suspects face charges including money laundering, bribery of public officials, and smuggling. Ashdod Port, handling approximately 60 percent of Israel's cargo, was a critical target due to its importance in both commercial and humanitarian operations.

Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan on Monday accused social media companies of “digital fascism” and censorship, as his government kept Instagram blocked for a fourth day in a dispute that has affected millions of users and businesses in Turkiye. The US-owned platform, which has an estimated 50 million to 60 million subscribers in Turkiye, was ordered frozen by the country’s BTK communications authority on Friday, Aug. 2, without an explanation at the time. Government officials later said Instagram had failed to remove content they considered offensive or criminal. Company representatives were summoned to a government meeting on Monday, but the talks did not settle the dispute. Erdogan, speaking to officials from his ruling AKP party, said social media platforms “cannot even tolerate photos of Palestinian martyrs without immediately banning them.” He accused the companies of acting “like the mafia” and said they had “declared war” in the virtual world on the Palestinian cause. His communications director, Fahrettin Altun, had earlier accused Instagram of blocking condolence messages over the killing of Hamas political leader Ismael Haniyeh, who was killed in Tehran in an attack blamed on Israel. The transport and infrastructure minister, Abdulkadir Uraloglu, said Instagram had been suspended for ignoring demands to remove “criminal content,” including alleged insults to Ataturk, drug-related material and paedophilia. After the meeting with Meta representatives, Uraloglu said the government had “not got the results we wanted,” but would continue discussions. The ban has had major economic consequences. Emre Ekmekci of the e-commerce operators’ association said it was costing about 1.9 billion Turkish lira, or nearly US$57 million, per day in lost business. He noted that around 10% of online retail sales in Turkiye are conducted through social media. Other commentators said the shutdown would hurt advertisers, artists, small businesses, major brands, public institutions and the tourism sector. Turkish authorities have previously blocked access to platforms including Facebook, X and Wikipedia.

# Summary: Turkey Blocks Instagram Over Censorship Dispute Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan accused social media networks of "digital fascism" on Monday as his government maintained a four-day blockade of Instagram, which has 50-60 million users in Turkey. The Turkish communications authority (BTK) froze Instagram access on Friday without initial explanation. Government officials claim the platform censors content they deem acceptable while failing to remove posts authorities consider offensive. The dispute centers on Instagram's handling of posts related to Palestinian causes, particularly following the assassination of Hamas leader Ismail Haniyeh in Tehran. Erdogan's communications director alleged Instagram prevented users from posting condolences about Haniyeh's death. Erdogan criticized social media companies for respecting regulations in America and Europe while "deliberately ignoring them" regarding Turkish content standards. Instagram accounts for 10% of Turkey's online retail sales, equaling 930 million lira daily. Between 60-70% of Turkey's 85 million inhabitants use Instagram. Business owners, content creators, small enterprises, and major brands report substantial disruptions. The platform serves as crucial infrastructure for advertisers, artists, exporters, and the tourism industry. This blockade follows Turkey's history of temporarily restricting access to Facebook, X, and Wikipedia.

Carlos Medina, a 61-year-old handyman, has appeared in court in Los Angeles over the killing of Bishop David O’Connell, the Irish-born Catholic leader who was shot dead in his home last February. Medina, whose wife worked as the bishop’s housekeeper and who had previously done work at O’Connell’s house, has pleaded not guilty to one felony count of murder. He was arraigned at the Foltz Criminal Justice Centre on February 22, two days after his arrest, and a hearing later today is expected to set a trial date and outline the case. If convicted, he faces up to 35 years in prison. Bishop O’Connell, 69, was found dead on February 18 in east Los Angeles with a gunshot wound to the upper chest. A church deacon discovered him lying on his bed shortly before noon after he failed to attend a scheduled meeting. Police believe he was attacked while asleep, and there was no sign of forced entry. Medina was arrested within 48 hours after a lengthy standoff at his home in Torrance, not far from the bishop’s residence. The killing shocked Los Angeles, which held three days of mourning for the cleric, known as “The Peacemaker” for his work against gang violence and in support of vulnerable migrants. Born in Cork, O’Connell spent his ministry in Los Angeles, where he was widely known as “Bishop Dave” for his humility and dislike of ceremony. He played a role in peace efforts during the 1992 LA riots and often entered dangerous areas to speak with gang leaders directly. Ordained in Ireland in 1979, he was appointed auxiliary bishop of Los Angeles by Pope Francis in 2015. His requiem mass was led by Archbishop Jose Gomez, and a memorial mass was also held in Cork. O’Connell is survived by his brother, sister-in-law, nieces, and nephews.

The statement came after the US embassy said Washington would use all means, including military options, against drug-trafficking groups. The article describes this as part of a long pattern of US efforts to expand influence and military dominance in Latin America under the banner of fighting drugs. Although US officials have said no immediate operation is planned in Mexico, the possibility of even limited strikes is portrayed as a serious sovereignty threat. President Claudia Sheinbaum firmly rejected any US military presence and said any incursion would violate national sovereignty, promising to resist it. Legal experts, the article adds, warn such action would violate international law and could heighten regional tensions.

Syrian and Iraqi narcotics authorities carried out a joint security operation against an international criminal network involved in manufacturing, promoting and smuggling drugs, the Syrian Interior Ministry said. The operation, conducted through advanced intelligence coordination and regional security cooperation, followed systematic monitoring of the network’s structure, logistics routes and methods. Field action was synchronized across Homs province, Damascus Countryside and locations inside Iraq. Authorities arrested two suspects in Syria and a third in Iraq. They also seized about 2.5 million Captagon pills, which the ministry said dealt a major blow to the network’s operational and logistical capacity and cut off one of its main trafficking routes. The bust came about a month after another joint Syrian-Iraqi operation that intercepted nearly 200,000 Captagon pills being moved from Lebanon to Iraq via Syria.

# Summary Syrian and Iraqi authorities conducted a joint security operation against an international drug trafficking network, resulting in the seizure of approximately 2.5 million Captagon pills. The operation, coordinated between Syria's Narcotics Department and Iraq's General Directorate for Narcotics and Psychotropic Substances Affairs, targeted locations in Homs province, Damascus Countryside, and Iraq. Three suspects were arrested—two in Syria and one in Iraq. The bust resulted from systematic intelligence gathering, analysis, and operational coordination between the nations. Authorities described it as a major operation that disrupted the network's capabilities and severed a primary trafficking route. This operation follows a similar joint effort nearly a month earlier that seized approximately 200,000 Captagon pills being transported through Syrian territory.

When Club León was expelled from the 2025 Club World Cup, its supporters still showed up in force in Atlanta, turning what should have been their team’s tournament opener into a demonstration of loyalty, anger, and frustration. The scene at Mercedes-Benz Stadium on Monday was unusual from the start. The scoreboard listed LAFC as the home team and Chelsea as the visitor, even though many León fans had traveled expecting to see their club play. Among them was Israel Ornelas, a 35-year-old fan from Guanajuato, who arrived with his 10-year-old son wearing green León shirts. What was supposed to be a father-son trip had become, in his words, an exercise in helplessness. He described FIFA’s decision to remove León as a matter of “mafia and business” rather than football, saying the club’s place had been earned “on the field and not respected in the boardroom.” FIFA had kicked León out in March because the club is owned by Grupo Pachuca, which also owns fellow Liga MX side CF Pachuca. FIFA said León had violated the tournament’s multi-ownership rules. Pachuca was allowed to remain in the competition, but León was removed from the 32-team field. The decision infuriated fans and players alike. León’s star signing James Rodríguez called it “a grave injustice,” arguing that the team had qualified through sporting merit and that the punishment hurt both the club and its supporters. León appealed to the Court of Arbitration for Sport, but the ruling was upheld in May. To fill the vacancy, FIFA organized a one-game playoff between LAFC and Club América, with the winner taking León’s place in Group D. LAFC won 2-1 on May 31 and ultimately became the team that faced Chelsea in Atlanta. Chelsea defeated LAFC 2-0. Even without León on the field, several hundred León fans traveled to Atlanta to support the club’s cause. Outside the stadium before kickoff, they sang club chants such as “Dale, Dale León!” and shouted insults at FIFA, including “Pinche FIFA!” and “Robo!” Their anger reflected a broader feeling that the club had been unfairly denied a place in a tournament it had earned through performance. Some fans had planned the trip months in advance and decided to go anyway despite the team’s removal. Ornelas said he and his son had organized the journey six months earlier. They continued with the trip, he said, because the plans were already set and because they wanted to experience the city and attend the tournament, even if they ended up supporting Chelsea for the match. He said the situation felt deeply disrespectful to fans who had invested time, money, and hope in the club. Another pair of fans, Alexis Falcón and Alejandro Vargas, flew from León to Atlanta just hours before kickoff. They had bought tickets during the first presale and were upset that FIFA had not refunded them. Vargas said the issue had been lost in bureaucracy, emphasizing that fans were not responsible for the ownership dispute. Both men insisted that León had earned its place on the field. The expulsion also caused logistical confusion elsewhere. FIFA had designated Mercer University in Macon, Georgia, as León’s training site, and the school had spent about $1 million preparing a field to FIFA’s standards. Once León was removed, the university’s preparations suddenly seemed wasted, and FIFA simply replaced León with LAFC in its training and competition arrangements. LAFC then faced long bus rides and other inconveniences, though coach Steve Cherundolo said his team accepted the challenges because playing in the competition mattered more. For many supporters, the loss was especially painful because the Club World Cup offered León a rare chance to face elite international opposition and perhaps redeem an earlier disappointment. León had been eliminated by Urawa Red Diamonds in the second round of the previous seven-team edition in 2023. Still, the emotional investment was obvious among fans in Atlanta. A 16-year-old Chicago traveler, Estela González, said she felt León should have been playing and called the situation a robbery. Her godmother, Rosa Guerra, echoed that view, saying they had come because they did not want to lose what they had already spent. At a concession stand, Atlanta resident Ramiro Castillo stood alone in a León away jersey, disappointed that he would not see his team play as planned with family members. He said he had looked forward to the match since León won the Concacaf Champions Cup, but now was left with sadness and frustration. In the end, León was absent from the pitch but present in spirit, as fans used the match day to protest what they saw as an unjust exclusion from a tournament they believed they had rightfully earned.

Saudi Arabia, through the Saudi Oversight and Anti-Corruption Authority, has officially taken over the presidency of the Global Operational Network of Anti-Corruption Law Enforcement Authorities (GlobE Network) in a ceremony at the United Nations headquarters in Vienna. The Kingdom was elected unanimously to chair the network for the 2025–2027 term during a high-level meeting in Beijing, reflecting broad international confidence in its anti-corruption efforts. GlobE Network is the world’s largest platform for coordinating law enforcement agencies in the investigation and fight against cross-border corruption. It brings together more than 219 agencies from over 120 countries, along with several international organizations. The handover marked the transfer of leadership from Spain’s Chief Prosecutor of the Special Prosecutor’s Office against Corruption and Organized Crime to Dr. Nasser bin Ahmed Aba Al-Khail, Deputy of the Saudi Oversight and Anti-Corruption Authority for International Cooperation. The ceremony was attended by officials from the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime and representatives from member states. As the new chairman, Dr. Aba Al-Khail said Saudi Arabia aims to strengthen cooperation among member states in line with the UN Convention against Corruption. He said the Kingdom plans to develop new asset-recovery strategies and launch a secure communication platform to speed up information sharing, improve recovery of illicit assets, and help trace cross-border funds more effectively.

In a letter responding to Roger Cohen’s article on Israel and the Palestinians, Chris Maltas argues that the Middle East peace process should no longer be left to the parties directly involved. He says the United States, and by extension the European Union, are effectively principals in the conflict because they have long participated in peace efforts and earned trust from both sides. Since they understand what is needed to end the occupation while preserving Israel’s security, he contends that Western powers should set the terms of a peace agreement and impose them on Israel, Fatah and Hamas. Although those leaders would likely object that outsiders have no right to dictate conditions, Maltas says they would ultimately have to accept them, just as the world accepted the creation of Israel after the United Nations voted for it. He concludes that the status quo cannot continue. A second letter, by Greg Cundiff, shifts to U.S. corporate tax policy. He criticizes multinational corporations for threatening to move abroad unless the United States lowers corporate taxes, describing their behavior as arrogant and cartel-like. He argues that corporations have gained excessive influence over government through lobbying, campaign donations and control over policymaking, leaving their tax obligations shaped by market forces rather than public policy.

# Summary This article contains two letters to the editor addressing major political issues. The first letter argues that the United States and European Union should impose a Middle East peace settlement on Israel and the Palestinians rather than waiting for the parties to negotiate independently. The author contends that Western powers are already deeply involved in the conflict and possess sufficient knowledge to establish peace terms that would end the occupation while protecting Israeli security. He compares this approach to how the world accepted Israel's creation following a UN vote, suggesting the conflicting parties would similarly accept externally-imposed conditions. The second letter criticizes American corporate tax policy, describing corporations as having effectively captured the U.S. government. The author contends that corporations threaten the government with relocation unless tax rates are reduced, and that corporate influence permeates government agencies, Congress, and the judiciary through lobbying and campaign contributions. The letter characterizes this as an abuse of corporate power over American political and economic systems.

Two Edmonton men are on trial in Battleford after being arrested in a major drug bust tied to an organized crime investigation. Sahilpreet Grewal, 19, and Parminder Singh, 20, appeared in Court of King’s Bench on June 10. Grewal is out of custody, while Singh remains detained. Both have pleaded not guilty. Police say the case began on June 1, 2023, when the Saskatchewan RCMP Roving Traffic Unit stopped a westbound vehicle on Highway 16 near Maidstone as part of an Alberta RCMP Serious and Organized Crime Unit investigation. A search of the vehicle uncovered 90 kilograms of methamphetamine and 65 kilograms of cocaine, with the meth testing as high as 100 per cent purity and the cocaine up to 86 per cent. The men are charged with possession of methamphetamine for the purpose of trafficking and possession of cocaine for the purpose of trafficking. Justice J.P. Morrall is presiding over the judge-alone trial. On Tuesday, Crown prosecutor Kirsten Janis and defence lawyer Brian Beresh questioned RCMP Constable Kyle Castelin, one of the officers at the scene. Castelin confirmed the drug amounts and said the substances were found in duffel bags in the vehicle. The trial continues this week.

U.S. President Donald Trump has warned Canada that it will face a 100% tariff on all Canadian goods entering the United States if Ottawa completes a trade agreement with China. The threat, delivered on Saturday through Trump’s Truth Social account, sharply escalated already strained relations between Washington and Ottawa and added a new layer of tension to North American trade politics. The dispute centers on Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney’s recent outreach to Beijing. Carney visited China and described the outcome of his trip as a “new strategic partnership” with the Chinese government. That move was followed by what was described as a “preliminary but landmark trade agreement” intended to reduce tariffs between Canada and China. In Washington, the development was viewed with alarm, with Trump signaling concern that Canada could become a channel for Chinese products entering the U.S. market. Trump’s message was unusually blunt. He accused Carney of thinking he could turn Canada into a “drop-off port” for China to send goods into the United States, and said he would respond with immediate and severe economic punishment if the deal went ahead. In the post, Trump warned that “China will eat Canada alive,” claiming such an arrangement would damage Canadian businesses, social fabric, and way of life. He added that if Canada made a deal with China, it would be hit immediately with a 100% tariff on all Canadian goods coming into the USA. The warning reflects broader U.S. concerns about China’s economic influence and the possibility that closer Canada-China ties could weaken American leverage in the region. It also underscores how trade policy has become entangled with strategic and geopolitical rivalry, with the U.S. wary of any arrangement that might affect its own economy or the flow of goods across the border. The latest escalation comes against the backdrop of an increasingly hostile relationship between Trump and Carney. Carney’s speech at the World Economic Forum in Davos, where he spoke about a “rupture” in the global order, was widely interpreted as a criticism of Trump’s foreign policy. That speech further irritated Trump, who responded by withdrawing Carney’s invitation to join his self-styled “Board of Peace,” a proposed body meant to address international conflicts. Beyond the political rhetoric, the stakes for Canada are high because of its heavy dependence on trade with the United States. More than three-quarters of Canadian exports go to its southern neighbor, making the country especially vulnerable to punitive tariffs. Major Canadian industries such as automotive, aluminum, and steel have already felt the effects of U.S. tariffs, even though some of those pressures have been softened by broader free-trade arrangements. The timing is also sensitive. The United States, Canada, and Mexico are preparing to co-host the World Cup later this year, meaning the trade conflict could spill into broader diplomatic and public-facing cooperation among the three countries. Overall, the episode adds to a growing list of disputes that have strained U.S.-Canada relations since Trump returned to the White House, with both sides now facing mounting pressure to manage the fallout from a deepening trade and political confrontation.

Ryan Wedding, the former Canadian Olympic snowboarder accused of running a violent international cocaine trafficking network, pleaded not guilty on Monday in his first court appearance in California. The hearing took place in Santa Ana, where Wedding appeared calm, smiling often at a crowded gallery that included reporters from Canada and the United States as well as investigators involved in the case. Wearing jail-issued khaki clothing with an orange shirt, socks and Crocs, he confirmed his name, acknowledged that he understood his rights and said he had read the two indictments against him before entering his plea. Wedding is being represented by San Diego lawyer Anthony Colombo, a defense attorney known for handling major drug-trafficking cases, including the case of Rubén Oseguera, the son of Jalisco New Generation cartel leader Nemesio Oseguera. Colombo told reporters that the allegations against Wedding were merely “just accusations” at this stage and said his client was “in good spirits.” He also directly disputed the version of events promoted by Mexican officials, insisting that Wedding did not voluntarily surrender to U.S. authorities in Mexico City. “He didn’t surrender — he was apprehended,” Colombo said, adding that the Mexican government had put a “spin” on the arrest and that he would know how his client came into custody. The circumstances of Wedding’s capture have been unclear and politically sensitive, with contradictory accounts from Mexican and U.S. officials. On Friday, FBI Director Kash Patel said Wedding had been apprehended the previous night in Mexico City in a “high-stakes operation” involving the FBI’s hostage rescue team. Around the same time, Mexican security officials and the U.S. ambassador to Mexico said Wedding had surrendered. Then on Monday, Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum told reporters that Wedding had turned himself in to the U.S. Embassy in Mexico City days before Patel arrived in Mexico for meetings. Sheinbaum also said the two countries coordinate on security matters but do not conduct joint operations in Mexico, and she strongly rejected the idea of such cooperation. She later displayed an Instagram post showing an image of a man resembling Wedding and a caption announcing his surrender, suggesting it was proof of that account. However, reporting has indicated that the account claiming to be Wedding had previously posted fake, AI-generated images. Organized-crime journalist Ioan Grillo called Colombo’s denial “explosive for Mexico,” saying it was “like throwing out a grenade,” and added that he did not know whom to believe. Wedding’s courtroom appearance was the first step in what is expected to be a lengthy prosecution. As of Monday, the trial was scheduled for March, though Colombo said that due to the “voluminous evidence,” it would not proceed that early. Wedding, who had been on the run for a decade, was taken into custody last week and then flown to California the next day, where he was escorted off a plane by Patel and other agents. FBI footage showed the six-foot-four Canadian in handcuffs being led across the tarmac by a group of officers. Authorities believe Wedding spent the past 10 years in Mexico under the protection of the Sinaloa Cartel. Prosecutors allege he led a billion-dollar cocaine empire that moved large quantities of cocaine from Colombia through Mexico and Los Angeles into Canada, while also ordering violence against rivals and enemies. Those allegations include the assassination of a key FBI witness and the killings of an innocent couple in Caledon, Ontario. The investigation has already led to 36 arrests, including Canadians facing possible extradition to the United States. Among those charged are an uncle-nephew pair accused of managing the trafficking network, alleged hit men, a Toronto jeweller accused of money laundering, and a criminal defense lawyer from the Greater Toronto Area accused of advising Wedding to kill the confidential witness. Wedding faces more than a dozen charges in two indictments filed in 2024 and 2025, and if convicted, he would face a mandatory minimum sentence of life in federal prison.

The Government of Canada announced that Criminal Code amendments allowing single event sport betting will come into force on August 27, 2021. The announcement was made in Windsor, Ontario, by Labour Minister Filomena Tassi and Windsor—Tecumseh MP Irek Kusmierczyk on behalf of Justice Minister and Attorney General David Lametti. The amendments to paragraph 207(4)(b) received Royal Assent on June 29, 2021. The change will permit provinces and territories to conduct and manage single event sport betting within their own jurisdictions, either online or in physical locations. Betting on horse racing will remain federally regulated. The government said the measure is intended to support a safer, regulated gambling environment and to strengthen the economy by creating and protecting good jobs. Officials emphasized that communities with casinos and other gaming operations, especially those near the Canada-U.S. border, could benefit from the change, particularly as U.S. gambling laws have recently changed. The government also said revenues from single event sport betting could help provinces and territories fund public programs and services such as health care and education, similar to other lottery revenues. The federal government said it is continuing discussions with provinces, territories, and Indigenous nations, communities, and organizations about the future regulation of gaming in Canada. It said these talks are meant to better respond to calls for greater Indigenous participation in the conduct and regulation of gaming. In a quoted statement, Minister Tassi said legalizing single event sport betting would support workers in the gaming industry in Windsor, Southwestern Ontario, and across the country, while helping direct profits back into community growth. A statement from Minister Lametti said many Canadians already place such bets in unlicensed markets, sending money to organized crime instead of public services. He said the new law would bring sports betting into a safe, regulated system while protecting 2,500 jobs at Caesars Windsor and supporting cross-border tourism affected by the pandemic.

The International Organization for Migration said Thursday that more than 165,000 people have been internally displaced in Haiti because of gang violence, murders and kidnappings, which are also hampering aid delivery. The humanitarian crisis has been worsened by natural disasters, including severe flooding from torrential rains that affected more than 46,000 people and displaced over 13,000, as well as a 4.9 magnitude earthquake on June 6. IOM said nearly half of Haiti’s population, about 5.2 million people, now needs humanitarian assistance. It urged donors and other stakeholders to increase support for immediate needs and longer-term solutions, noting that Haiti’s Humanitarian Response Plan is funded at only 20%. The situation is unfolding amid a prolonged political and security crisis that intensified after President Jovenel Moise’s assassination in 2021, allowing armed gangs to expand their control over large parts of the country.

# Summary Over 165,000 Haitians are internally displaced due to gang violence, murders, and kidnappings, according to the International Organization for Migration (IOM). The humanitarian crisis has been exacerbated by natural disasters, including severe floods from torrential rains affecting 46,000 people and displacing 13,000, plus a 4.9 magnitude earthquake on June 6. Approximately 5.2 million Haitians—nearly half the population—require humanitarian assistance. The IOM is calling for increased international support, noting that Haiti's Humanitarian Response Plan is only 20% funded. The crisis stems from a socio-political emergency that intensified following President Jovenel Moise's assassination in July 2021, leading to unprecedented criminal gang activity controlling regions and engaging in extortion and kidnapping.

At a security conference in St. Petersburg on July 28, 2016, UNODC Executive Director Yury Fedotov warned that terrorism and violent extremism remain among the world’s biggest challenges. Speaking at the opening of the 15th Meeting of Heads of Special Services, Security Agencies and Law Enforcement Organizations at the Boris Yeltsin Presidential Library, he said the terrorism threat has changed over the past decade, becoming more decentralized and diffuse. He stressed that it now poses a greater danger to international peace and security than ever before. Fedotov pointed to the use of information technology to spread extremist ideology and the movement of foreign terrorist fighters across borders as major concerns. He cited Da’esh as a key example, saying the group has inspired attacks worldwide and attracted large numbers of foreign fighters from Europe, South Asia and South-East Asia. While some fighters have left conflict zones disillusioned, others remain radicalized and capable of carrying out attacks in their home countries or places of residence. He said UNODC is helping countries through programs in the Middle East, North Africa and the Balkans, expanding work on countering terrorist financing, and supporting extradition and mutual legal assistance. He also called for stronger action against youth radicalization and links between organized crime and terrorism.
