Moscow police have charged five former officers in connection with the case of Ivan Golunov, a prominent Russian investigative journalist whose 2019 arrest on drug charges sparked a major press freedom outcry. Golunov, who writes for the online outlet Meduza, was detained in June 2019 while reportedly on his way to meet a source in central Moscow. Police said they found mephedrone in his backpack and later claimed a large quantity of drugs had been discovered in a search of his apartment. From the outset, Golunov and his colleagues strongly denied the allegations and said the case was retaliation for his reporting on corruption in city government, business and criminal circles. His friends described him as cautious and sober, and they questioned the police evidence, including the refusal to allow him to take a hand swab test. They also disputed photos released by police that supposedly showed drug paraphernalia and laboratory equipment in his home. The arrest quickly triggered an unusually broad public response. Russia’s journalism community rallied around Golunov, major newspapers published identical front pages demanding his release, and hundreds of people protested in Moscow. Facing intense public pressure and widespread skepticism about the evidence, authorities dropped the charges and released him. Several officers involved in the arrest were dismissed in the immediate aftermath. However, Golunov and Meduza later complained that officials had not seriously pursued the question of who ordered the alleged frame-up or who tried to silence him. That changed this week when Russia’s Investigative Committee announced that five former officers “who initiated the illegal criminal investigation into Ivan Golunov” would face charges. Russian media later reported the former officers were accused of illegal drug purchase and possession, as well as fabricating evidence. Golunov welcomed the move, saying he had long sought such charges and hoped the case would now go to court. The article notes that Golunov’s case became a symbol for Russian civil society. In the year since, activists have borrowed the “I am/We are Ivan Golunov” slogan at protests over issues ranging from environmental disputes to arrests of journalists and illegal property seizures. But the piece also stresses that Golunov’s outcome was exceptional. Drug convictions remain common in Russia, accusations of police planting evidence are widespread, and many protesters have faced harsher treatment. Commentators cited in the article argued that Golunov was spared largely because the public mobilized on his behalf.

# Former Police Officers Charged with Framing Russian Journalist Moscow police have charged five former officers with fabricating evidence against Ivan Golunov, an investigative journalist for the online Meduza portal, in a case that became a symbol of press freedom in Russia. In June 2019, Golunov was arrested on drug possession charges widely suspected to be retaliation for his investigative reporting on corruption in government, business, and organized crime circles. Plainclothes officers claimed they discovered the drug mephedrone in his backpack, and police later alleged a large stash was found in his apartment. However, the case appeared fabricated from the start. Golunov's colleagues noted he was known for a cautious, sober lifestyle and was among Russia's most respected journalists. Police refused his offers to take hand swab tests for drug evidence, and photographs of alleged drug paraphernalia didn't resemble his actual apartment. Russia's journalism community mobilized quickly. Major newspapers published identical front pages demanding his release, and hundreds of protesters took to Moscow streets. Facing public pressure and weak evidence, authorities released Golunov within weeks and dropped all charges. Several officers involved were dismissed. However, Golunov and Meduza complained that authorities showed little interest in investigating who ordered the fabrication or attempted to silence the journalist. President Vladimir Putin promised action during a December press conference, and in January, Russia's Investigative Committee charged the five former officers with illegal drug possession, narcotics trafficking, and evidence fabrication. "The criminal charges, which I long sought and received with the help of the media and society, have been issued, and that's very good," Golunov told reporters, expressing hope the case would reach court. Golunov's case galvanized Russian civil society. Protesters at subsequent demonstrations—involving environmental issues, detained journalists, and property seizures—adopted banners stating "We are Ivan Golunov," substituting his name with their cause. The message implied: "If Golunov won, why can't we?" Yet observers cautioned that Golunov's victory remained exceptional. While he was spared, many other defendants faced convictions on similar charges, and demonstrators arrested during the summer's rolling Moscow protests received real sentences. Commentator Matvei Ganapolsky noted that Golunov succeeded because public support mobilized, but others in parallel courtrooms received harsh sentences. His point underscored that access to justice in Russia often depends on visibility and public backing rather than legal merit.

The European Union’s new Enhanced Partnership and Cooperation Agreement (EPCA) with Uzbekistan is intended to create a more modern and ambitious framework for deepening bilateral ties, according to Peter Stano, the European Commission’s lead spokesperson for foreign affairs and security policy. In an exclusive interview with Trend, Stano said the agreement is designed to support Uzbekistan’s ongoing reform agenda by encouraging cooperation and regulatory convergence in key sectors. Negotiations on the EPCA were completed in summer 2022, and the agreement is now being prepared for signature and entry into force. Stano said it covers a broad range of areas, including political dialogue and reforms, the rule of law, justice, freedom and security, human rights, migration, trade, and economic and sustainable development. It is also meant to improve the business and investment climate and expand cooperation on foreign policy and global issues such as climate change, corruption, and counterterrorism. Once implemented, the EPCA will allow the EU and Uzbekistan to broaden cooperation across political, economic, and security fields. Stano emphasized that the agreement places strong weight on shared values, including democracy, the rule of law, human rights, fundamental freedoms, and sustainable development. It also strengthens foreign and security policy cooperation, with attention to regional stability, non-proliferation of weapons of mass destruction, conflict prevention, crisis management, and international cooperation. The agreement also includes extensive provisions on justice, freedom, and security. These cover data protection, migration, anti-money-laundering efforts, the fight against terrorism, organized crime and corruption, the suppression of illicit drugs, judicial cooperation, and consular protection. In the economic sphere, Stano said the EPCA will improve the regulatory environment for trade in goods and services, state-owned enterprises, procurement, and intellectual property rights. It also expands cooperation in economic and financial affairs, energy, transport, environment and climate change, the digital economy, agriculture and rural development, employment and social affairs, culture, education and youth, and research. Stano highlighted the EU’s role in supporting Uzbekistan’s transition to a modern agri-food system. He said the EU is the main provider of grant funding to the sector, helping reforms that enable farmers to adapt to climate change, protect the environment, produce healthy food, and connect to local and global value chains. He noted that the EU has already provided 32.5 million euros for 2020–2023, with another 30 million euros planned for 2024–2027. He also recalled the EU’s January 2023 commitment at the Investors Forum for EU-Central Asia Transport Connectivity to invest 10 billion euros in sustainable transport links in Central Asia. These funds are intended to support 33 infrastructure needs and seven connectivity actions identified in a June 2023 study, strengthening trans-Caspian transport routes and boosting regional growth, including in Uzbekistan. Finally, Stano said green and energy transition cooperation is one of the EU Global Gateway flagship initiatives in Central Asia. Through a regional program on sustainable energy connectivity, the EU is supporting Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, Kyrgyzstan, and Turkmenistan in building a more sustainable energy mix through energy efficiency, renewable energy deployment, and investment-friendly conditions.

Hundreds of people marched through central Moscow on 15 July under the slogan “No to eternal Putin,” protesting constitutional changes approved in a 1 July referendum that would allow Vladimir Putin to remain dominant in Russian politics well beyond 2024. The unauthorized demonstration began at 7 p.m. from Pushkinskaya Square after organizers said they had formally requested permission from the Moscow authorities but received no response. Anticipating a police crackdown, protesters gathered in small groups and then moved along Tverskaya and Petrovka streets. Police arrested 140 people. Most were released the next morning after being ordered to report to police headquarters, while two activists, Anna Ljko and Aleksandr Dmitriev, were kept in solitary confinement. Among those detained were several prominent figures, including journalist Marina Litvinova, Open Russia executive director Andrei Pivovarov, Moscow State University professor Sergei Fedorov, and municipal deputy Yulia Galyamina, who was arrested along with her daughter. Galyamina said people should always do what they believe is right. As the procession moved through the city center, some participants chanted “Moscow, come out!” and urged passersby to join them. At one point, protesters staged a sit-in by lying on the ground and blocking traffic. Participants voiced frustration and anger, with one saying he felt like he was “banging [his] head against a brick wall,” while Pussy Riot member Maria Alyokhina described Russia as a “mafia state.” A similar protest took place in St. Petersburg, where about 1,000 people gathered on Malaja Sadovaja Street and signed petitions against the constitutional changes. Demonstrators also called for freedom for political prisoners and expressed support for Sergei Furgal, the detained governor of Khabarovsk, where protests were continuing for a sixth day despite police restrictions and coronavirus-related bans on public gatherings.

# Summary On July 15, Moscow witnessed significant anti-government protests against constitutional changes approved in a July 1 referendum. Hundreds of demonstrators gathered on central streets chanting "No to eternal Putin," opposing amendments that would allow Vladimir Putin to remain in power beyond 2024, when his current term limit expires. Police arrested 140 protesters, though most were released the following morning with requirements to sign reports at police headquarters. Two activists, Anna Ljko and Aleksandr Dmitriev, faced solitary confinement. The unauthorized demonstration began at 7 p.m. from Pushkinskaja Square after authorities failed to respond to the organizers' official authorization request. Demonstrators strategically formed small groups to circumvent restrictions, proceeding down central boulevards while chanting "Moscow, come out!" to recruit additional participants. The protest escalated when participants staged a sit-in, lying on the ground to block traffic. Notable arrests included journalists, academics, and political figures, including Pussy Riot singer Maria Aljokhina, who characterized Russia as a "mafia state" rather than a totalitarian regime. Concurrent demonstrations occurred in St. Petersburg, where approximately 1,000 people gathered on Malaja Sadovaja Street, collecting signatures against constitutional changes and demanding freedom for political prisoners, particularly Sergei Furgal, the arrested Khabarovsk governor. In Khabarovsk, residents continued their sixth consecutive day of protests against Furgal's arrest, while authorities used coronavirus concerns as justification for banning public gatherings.

Colombia is heading to a highly charged presidential runoff after no candidate won a majority in Sunday’s election, setting up a contest between conservative Iván Duque and leftist Gustavo Petro. Duque, a former senator and the chosen candidate of ex-president Álvaro Uribe, led the field with about 39 percent of the vote, according to nearly all quick-count results. Petro, a former rebel and ex-Bogotá mayor, finished second with 25 percent, narrowly defeating former Medellín mayor Sergio Fajardo, who received nearly 24 percent. Because no one crossed the 50 percent threshold, Duque and Petro will face each other in a June runoff. The result sharply split Colombia’s political landscape, with the two finalists offering starkly different visions for the country’s future as it tries to move beyond decades of conflict. Duque represents the right and is closely associated with Uribe, Colombia’s influential former president and the fiercest critic of the 2016 peace accord with the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia, or FARC. Duque says he does not want to dismantle the deal, but he wants to modify key parts of it. Among his priorities are making sure drug trafficking cannot be amnestied and blocking former guerrilla leaders from holding political office. He also favors forcibly eradicating coca crops rather than replacing them gradually. Petro, by contrast, has built his campaign on support for the peace accord and on an anti-establishment message that has resonated with younger voters and people frustrated by corruption and inequality. He has proposed ending Colombia’s dependence on oil exports and taxing large areas of unproductive land to encourage agricultural production. Critics have warned that his victory could push Colombia sharply left and unsettle financial markets. Petro has also been dogged by comparisons to Venezuela’s late socialist leader Hugo Chávez because of his past admiration for him, though Petro says he is a strong opponent of current Venezuelan president Nicolás Maduro and rejects claims that he would turn Colombia into an authoritarian state. In his speech to supporters Sunday night, Petro said the nearly 5 million votes he received represented youth and excluded Colombians who wanted to be heard. He argued that his proposals are not about authoritarian redistribution but about “democratization” of opportunity, especially through education and access to the middle class. His supporters celebrated with flags featuring the Soviet hammer and sickle and the symbol of the now-disbanded M-19 rebel group, which Petro belonged to in his youth. One supporter, street merchant Edilia Pinzon, said the campaign was “making history” because previous leaders had failed to deliver for poor Colombians. The election drew more than 19 million voters, the highest turnout in 20 years. Fajardo’s third-place finish was especially disappointing, since he had hoped to unify centrist forces. He had tried, unsuccessfully, to reach an alliance with Humberto de la Calle, the government’s chief negotiator in the peace talks. De la Calle’s roughly 2 percent of the vote would have been enough to push Fajardo into the runoff. Fajardo conceded defeat but did not endorse either remaining candidate, leaving his 4.5 million supporters as a potentially decisive bloc. The runoff is expected to turn on voters in urban areas and among the political center. Analysts said Duque may have a harder time attracting centrist and Fajardo supporters because of his hard line on the peace process, while Petro has tried throughout the campaign to present himself as a moderate despite his leftist background. Political analyst Leon Valencia said the winner will likely be whichever candidate can move closer to the center. The campaign has exposed deep fears on both sides. Duque’s opponents warn that he would amount to a third term for Uribe, who is still hugely popular for improving security and weakening armed groups but whose government was also marked by serious human rights abuses. Meanwhile, Petro’s critics invoke the specter of Chávez and fear a radical shift in economic policy. The dispute over the peace accord is central: many Colombians believe its terms are too generous because they allow former guerrillas involved in drug trafficking and violent crimes to avoid prison if they fully confess. The issue has been sharpened by recent drug-related arrests linked to former rebel figures. In his victory speech, Duque focused on law and order and said he wanted to unite the country rather than “govern with a rearview mirror.” He said he did not want to “tear up” the peace agreement, only to ensure “peace with justice” for victims. De la Calle, meanwhile, urged Colombians not to reverse the peace process, warning that after years of war, peace should not become the new source of division.

# Conservative and Leftist Head to Contentious Colombian Runoff Colombia is headed toward a polarizing presidential runoff between two ideologically opposed candidates following Sunday's election. Former Senator Ivan Duque, a conservative backed by ex-President Alvaro Uribe, secured the most votes with 39 percent, falling short of the 50 percent threshold needed to win outright. Gustavo Petro, a former guerrilla fighter and ex-Bogota mayor representing the left, finished second with 25 percent, narrowly edging out former Medellin Mayor Sergio Fajardo, who received nearly 24 percent and failed to advance to the runoff. The June runoff will pit candidates representing opposite ends of Colombia's political spectrum. Duque represents continuity with traditional conservative politics and is Uribe's handpicked successor, while Petro embodies an anti-establishment, populist movement that has galvanized youth voters frustrated by corruption and inequality. The stark contrast between them has sparked concerns on both sides of the political divide. Duque's platform centers on modifying Colombia's 2016 peace agreement with the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC). He promises to ensure drug trafficking remains a non-amnestied crime and prevent guerrilla leaders from holding political office. Uribe, though popular for improving security and weakening illegal armed groups, remains controversial for military human rights violations during his presidency. Critics worry a Duque victory would constitute an unconstitutional third term for Uribe. Petro supports implementing the peace accord and advocates for ending Colombia's dependence on oil exports while raising taxes on unproductive land to boost agriculture. His "Humane Colombia" platform promises to democratize opportunities through education and middle-class expansion. However, critics have drawn comparisons between Petro and Venezuela's late socialist leader Hugo Chavez, whom Petro once admired and brought to Colombia in 1994. Though Petro now opposes current Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro, these historical ties have haunted his campaign. Petro dismisses such comparisons as fear-mongering by a traditional political establishment unable to compete on substantive issues. The election achieved the highest turnout in two decades, with over 19 million voters casting ballots. Petro's supporters, including street merchants and youth from excluded sectors, view his candidacy as historic and transformative. In his victory speech, Petro emphasized that his nearly 5 million votes represented youth and marginalized Colombians demanding change and inclusion. Fajardo's failure to advance to the runoff proved especially significant. He fell less than two percentage points behind Petro despite unsuccessful negotiations to form an alliance with centrist Humberto de la Calle. De la Calle's 2 percent would have pushed Fajardo past Petro. Though Fajardo conceded, he has not indicated which candidate he will support, meaning his 4.5 million supporters will likely determine the runoff's outcome. The two candidates diverge fundamentally on critical issues. Regarding coca crop eradication, Duque favors forced eradication while Petro supports crop substitution programs. On international relations, Duque would maintain traditionally tight U.S.-Colombia relations, whereas Petro has criticized American assistance as ineffective. Concerning the peace agreement, their positions remain most contentious, with Duque advocating constitutional reforms addressing drug trafficking amnesty provisions and Petro supporting the accord's implementation. Analysts predict that urban voters dissatisfied with Colombia's polarized politics will prove decisive in the runoff. Political analyst Leon Valencia notes that whichever candidate successfully repositions toward the center will likely win. Duque faces a steeper challenge winning over centrist voters because his opposition to the peace process contrasts with Petro's moderate positioning throughout the campaign. Government peace negotiator de la Calle, while not explicitly endorsing either candidate, warned against backtracking on peace accord implementation, noting that eight years of war united Colombians while peace now divides them. The June runoff will ultimately determine whether Colombia continues its current trajectory or shifts dramatically leftward.

Donald Trump’s proposal to designate Mexican drug cartels as terrorist organizations has sparked a fierce debate in Mexico over whether the cartels’ extreme violence amounts to terrorism. While many Mexicans acknowledge the brutality of groups such as the Sinaloa cartel and Jalisco New Generation cartel, they broadly reject any suggestion that the United States should intervene. The issue gained urgency after the Nov. 4 attack on Mormon families in northern Mexico, when alleged members of the La Linea cartel ambushed three SUVs carrying 17 people, including 14 children. Three women and six children, including twin 8-month-old babies, were killed, and one vehicle was set on fire with occupants inside. In the aftermath, prominent members of the LeBaron family, who were among the victims, sent a petition to the White House calling on Trump to label Mexican cartels as terrorist groups. They argued that the cartels’ “unbridled acts of violence and murder” had created an international crisis and insisted, “They are terrorists, and it’s time to acknowledge it!” That appeal triggered a highly polarized reaction in Mexico. On social media, critics accused the LeBarons of betraying the country, while others supported the idea that narco-violence is terrorism because it is meant to instill fear in civilians. One supporter was Guanajuato Governor Diego Sinhue Rodriguez, who said the cartels’ public displays of mutilation and threats are designed to provoke terror. Experts, however, noted an important distinction between Mexican cartels and the foreign groups already on the U.S. terrorist blacklist, such as al-Qaida, Islamic State, ETA, FARC and others. Those organizations are defined by political or religious motives, whereas drug cartels are primarily profit-driven criminal enterprises. Former Mexican foreign minister Jorge Castaneda said cartels cannot be compared with groups like FARC because they lack any political component. Despite the debate, Mexicans have overwhelmingly bristled at Trump’s implied offer of help, especially any military intervention. Trump’s comments came in response to a question about whether he would consider using drones against cartels. Mexican officials quickly denounced the remarks as a violation of sovereignty, and President Andres Manuel Lopez Obrador responded that cooperation was acceptable, but interventionism was not. Analysts said the dispute is largely symbolic. Mexico and the United States already cooperate extensively on security and financial efforts against cartels, including DEA operations, U.S. personnel embedded with Mexican forces, and cross-border surveillance. As Castaneda put it, much of what Trump suggested is already happening, so a formal terrorist designation would likely change little on the ground.

# Summary: Trump's Plan to Designate Mexican Drug Cartels as Terrorist Organizations Donald Trump's proposal to designate Mexican drug cartels as Foreign Terrorist Organizations has sparked significant debate in Mexico, though Mexicans overwhelmingly oppose American intervention in the matter. The debate centers on whether cartels like the Sinaloa and Jalisco New Generation organizations should be classified as terrorist groups. While these cartels have committed horrific acts of violence—including grenade attacks, public executions, and massacres—experts argue they lack the defining characteristic of designated terrorist organizations: political or religious motivation. Unlike the 68 groups currently on the U.S. Foreign Terrorist Organizations list, Mexican cartels' primary objective is profit, not ideology. According to Jorge Castaneda, a former Mexican foreign minister, this would be the first time the U.S. has attempted to add mafia groups to the list. Trump's announcement was prompted by a November 4 massacre in northern Mexico, when alleged members of the La Linea cartel attacked three vehicles carrying Mormon families, killing three women and six children, including twin eight-month-old babies. The LeBaron family, prominent members of the affected community, petitioned the White House to designate cartels as terrorist organizations, arguing that their violence constitutes terrorism. This petition triggered a politically charged debate in Mexico. On social media, hashtags calling the LeBarons "traitors" went viral, though some, including Guanajuato's governor, supported the terrorism designation, arguing that cartels deliberately use violence to instill fear in civilians. However, Mexicans broadly rejected Trump's implicit offer of military assistance, including his suggestion to use drones against cartels. This rejection stems from deep historical grievances, particularly Mexico's loss of over half its territory to the United States in 1848. Any hint of U.S. military intervention is viewed as a violation of national sovereignty. Even President Andrés Manuel López Obrador, who maintains friendly relations with Trump, responded with "cooperation yes, interventionism no." Experts agree the debate is largely symbolic. Little would practically change, as the U.S. and Mexico already cooperate extensively against cartels through the DEA, which has maintained operations in Mexico for over 25 years, including embedded personnel with Mexican marines. The countries already collaborate on security and financial matters, making the formal terrorist designation relatively inconsequential for actual operations.

Colombia is undergoing a major anti-corruption and security purge, with strong backing from the United States, as part of a broader effort to make the post-FARC peace process work and to weaken the links between state institutions, drug trafficking, and paramilitary networks. The most dramatic development has been the arrest of Colombia’s top anti-corruption prosecutor, who was charged by a U.S. court last month with bribery offenses allegedly committed on American soil. He is now awaiting extradition. The article says the U.S. has taken a more aggressive role than the United Nations or European Union in targeting senior Colombian officials suspected of corruption or drug ties. That includes pursuing military and judicial figures and cracking down on paramilitary groups with connections to regional elites and state officials. Two former presidential security chiefs from the administration of former President Álvaro Uribe, whose family had close ties to the Medellín Cartel, are already serving prison terms in the United States. After the arrest of Colombia’s anti-corruption chief, Acting U.S. Assistant Attorney General Kenneth Blanco traveled to Colombia to meet Prosecutor General Néstor Humberto Martínez. The visit was meant to underscore Washington’s support for prosecuting corrupt officials. Blanco reaffirmed U.S. willingness to cooperate on investigations, information sharing, and asset seizures linked to illegal activity in both countries. Martínez, in turn, said both sides were committed to using extradition and other strong legal tools to deter corruption. His office said he would travel to Washington on July 18 to meet U.S. Attorney General Jeff Sessions and deepen ties between the two justice systems. The anti-corruption drive is tied to “Peace Colombia,” a bilateral initiative aimed at strengthening Colombia’s peace process and state institutions. The crackdown has been visible in recent weeks. In the Meta department, 21 people were arrested in the prosecutor’s office. At the Cartagena naval base, officials were investigated for allegedly embezzling $2 million from Military Logistical Agency funds. These actions followed an earlier purge in Nariño, where 15 prosecution officials were arrested over alleged ties to drug traffickers, guerrillas, and paramilitary groups. Fabio Ochoa, once one of Colombia’s most notorious drug lords and a key figure in the Medellín cartel, has been deported from the United States to Bogotá after serving 25 years of a 30-year prison sentence, and was quickly released by Colombian authorities. He arrived Monday on a deportation flight wearing a gray sweatshirt and carrying his belongings in a plastic bag. Immigration officials in bulletproof vests met him at the airport, took his fingerprints, and checked a database that showed he was not wanted in Colombia. The immigration agency later said on X that he was “freed so that he could join his family.” At the airport, Ochoa denied wrongdoing, saying, “I was framed.” He embraced his daughter, whom he had not seen in seven years, and said he planned to go to Medellín to live with his family. Calling his return “the nightmare is over,” the 67-year-old appeared relieved after decades of imprisonment. Ochoa and his older brothers built a vast fortune during the cocaine boom of the late 1970s and early 1980s, becoming wealthy enough to be listed by Forbes as billionaires in 1987. From Miami, Ochoa ran a distribution center for the cartel once led by Pablo Escobar, who was killed in 1993. Ochoa was first indicted in the United States over the 1986 killing of Barry Seal, a pilot who flew cocaine for the Medellín cartel and later became a DEA informant. In the early 1990s, Ochoa and his brothers surrendered to Colombian authorities under an arrangement that kept them from extradition to the US. They were released in 1996, but Ochoa was arrested again in 1999 for drug trafficking and extradited to the United States in 2001. In Miami, he was the only defendant among more than 40 accused in a smuggling conspiracy to go to trial; he was convicted and sentenced to 30 years, while others received lighter sentences after cooperating. Though his name has faded as Mexican cartels dominate today’s drug trade, Ochoa has recently reappeared in popular culture through Netflix series such as *Griselda* and *Narcos*. A former prosecutor said the family’s illicit wealth was never fully seized and predicted Ochoa would receive a warm welcome home.

Thirteen people have been killed over the past four days in violent clashes involving police and gangs in Porto Velho, the capital of Rondônia state in Brazil’s Amazon region, according to the state security department. Eight deaths were linked to attacks by criminal gangs, while five people died in confrontations with police since Tuesday morning. The violence escalated after criminals set fire to 20 buses, most of them school buses, apparently in retaliation for police action. In response, authorities restricted public transportation hours and deployed police escorts for city buses. The federal government sent national public security force troops to Rondônia for at least 90 days to help state police contain the unrest. Local police said the attacks were likely retaliation by the Comando Vermelho gang for operations against the faction in a housing complex it controls in the city. Although Comando Vermelho originated in Rio de Janeiro, it has become the most powerful criminal group in the Amazon in recent years. The article notes that crime is rising rapidly across the Amazon. A Brazilian Public Security Forum report found the region had 34 homicides per 100,000 people in 2023, nearly double the national average. Experts say the newer violence is tied less to land conflicts and more to gang battles over drug trafficking routes. Rondônia, which borders Bolivia, has become an important cocaine corridor, with police seizing 20 tons of cocaine there in the past decade.

Nobel Prize-winning economist Joseph Stiglitz said Panama’s commission investigating the country’s financial secrecy lacked the transparency it was meant to examine, and he resigned from the panel on Friday along with Swiss anti-corruption expert Mark Pieth. The committee had been formed after the April leak of more than 11.5 million documents from law firm Mossack Fonseca, known as the Panama Papers, which exposed offshore accounts and possible tax evasion by wealthy and powerful figures. Stiglitz and Pieth were part of a seven-member commission assigned to review Panama’s opaque financial and legal system. They said they repeatedly encountered resistance from the government and believed it was unwilling to support a genuinely open inquiry. Their main objection was Panama’s refusal to guarantee that the commission’s final report would be made public. Stiglitz said, “I thought the government was more committed, but obviously they’re not,” adding that officials had tried to undermine the effort. The Panamanian government responded that the commission was being managed autonomously and said the resignations were due to “internal differences.” It expressed regret over the departures and said it remained committed to transparency and international cooperation. According to Stiglitz and Pieth, the issue came to a head after the committee’s first full meeting in New York on June 4-5, where members agreed the government should promise to publish the report regardless of its conclusions. But they said a letter from Panama last week backed away from that commitment. Stiglitz suggested the government may be under pressure from those benefiting from the current system. The Panama Papers, spanning nearly 40 years, have also been linked to money laundering, arms and drug deals, and have increased pressure on Panama to reform.

# Summary Nobel Prize-winning economist Joseph Stiglitz resigned Friday from Panama's transparency investigation commission, criticizing the body itself for lacking transparency. Stiglitz and Swiss anti-corruption expert Mark Pieth, both seven-member commission members, quit after Panama refused to guarantee the committee's final report would be publicly released. Stiglitz stated the government was unwilling to support an open investigation, saying "It's amazing how they tried to undermine us." During the committee's first full meeting in New York in June, members reached consensus that the government must commit to publishing findings regardless of conclusions. The leak intensified pressure on Panama—known for lax financial laws—to implement reforms and increase financial transparency.

Rosario, Argentina, once best known as the birthplace of figures like rock star Fito Páez and soccer star Lionel Messi, is now making headlines for violent crime, drug dealing, and near-daily shootings and killings. She was pulled from the car, while three attackers restrained her son. Cejas confronted them after seeing his mother dragged out, and was shot at close range in the chest. A new generation of narcos is emerging in Mexico’s powerful criminal organizations, and with them has come a new musical style to glorify their lives and violence. In Sinaloa, in northwest Mexico, members of Grupo Flecha — an elite armed group that protects Sinaloa Cartel leader Ismael “El Mayo” Zambada — recently gathered in the mountains with speakers playing songs unlike the traditional narco-ballads associated with older traffickers. The older style, known as the narco-corrido, used guitars and accordions to tell stories of drug bosses, their killings, and those who died defending cartel territory. But that sound is increasingly being replaced by “Trapteño,” a blend of U.S. trap and Mexican norteño music. The new songs keep the same themes of cartel life, but the instrumentation has shifted to hip-hop drums, heavy bass, and synthesizers. One Flechas commander said the style grew out of the Sinaloa Cartel’s contacts in Atlanta, where trap music became popular, and argued that the criminal worlds of Atlanta and Culiacán are similar in their drugs, women, and mafia culture. The lyrics still focus on the same subjects: drug lords, violence, and the rise of bosses within the cartel hierarchy. Composer and singer Emmanuel Massú, known as “El Enfermo,” said the new generation needs a new way to tell old stories, even if the tradition remains rooted in the narco-corrido. He argued that people in Sinaloa live on the “frontlines” of the drug trade and need new forms of music to describe that reality. The Flechas commander also said the younger narcos see Trapteño as part of a broader modernization of cartel identity. Instead of the old image of traffickers in hats and boots, he said, they now dress in designer shoes, shirts, or military-style clothing. The music, in his view, helps present them as a more contemporary group. Juan Carlos Ramírez, a San Diego State University professor and expert on narco-corridos, said these songs matter deeply in cartel culture because they influence rival groups and even become targets during conflicts. According to him, one of the first things a criminal organization may do after fighting another group is order singers to stop mentioning enemies by name. He also said the songs can provide a more truthful account of Mexico’s criminal underworld than official narratives, which he called unreliable. At the same time, he warned that the newer style is reaching younger audiences, who may be drawn in by the music’s glamorization of drug bosses and cartel life. That concern comes amid evidence that cartels are recruiting more young people. REDIM, the Network for Children’s Rights in Mexico, estimates that as many as 30,000 children may already be working for cartels, with another 250,000 potentially recruitable in coming years. Tania Ramírez of REDIM said children can enter these organizations as early as age 9, beginning as lookouts or dealers before moving into more dangerous roles like trafficking or guarding stash houses. At the top of this new generation are the so-called “narco juniors” — sons and descendants of cartel bosses who are using family names to operate openly in Sinaloa. A cartel member in Culiacán said they are smarter but also more violent than previous generations, shaped by growing up around guns, killings, and power.

Stakeholders in Nigeria’s economy have called for stronger government investment in culture, arguing that the sector can generate substantial revenue if properly supported. The appeal was made during the two-day annual Ijakadi celebrations in Offa, organised by the Offa Descendants Union (ODU). The Olofa of Offa, Oba Muftau Gbadamosi, said both state and federal governments could earn more income if the nation’s cultural heritage and traditions are preserved and promoted. He stressed that culture should be treated as a viable business area, but only if it receives “due and unfettered support” from all levels of government. Describing this year’s celebration as more impactful than previous editions, he urged government backing for the festival and called on Offa indigenes to give it greater attention. He also encouraged people from the town to return home and identify with their roots. Waheed Olagunju, chairman of media, publicity, marketing and sponsorship, explained the significance of the annual rite and described culture as a way of life that remains relevant in modern society. He said communities should focus on creating value from cultural events and asked the federal government to consider how culture can be turned into a source of income. Comrade Lukman Afolabi, a cultural enthusiast and director of the Biohistocultural Resource Hub, said the Ijakadi festival symbolizes fairness, justice and equity. He added that the event should be better packaged to attract UNESCO recognition and align with Africa Union Agenda 2063, which emphasizes heritage protection and shared values through sustained investment.

A mixed-race Nigerian-European woman living abroad has described a painful family revelation involving her Nigerian father, her parents’ long separation, and a hidden child. She said her mother is European and her father is Nigerian, and that the couple separated more than 10 years ago but never officially divorced. According to her, the separation followed a serious incident in which her father did something severe to her mother, though she withheld details for privacy. She explained that in Europe, a spouse cannot simply be removed from the family home because of marital problems; only a court can force that in extreme circumstances. She said that about a year after the separation, her father began repeatedly begging her mother to reconcile with him. That pattern continued for years. At the same time, he was also involved with a Nigerian woman from his own tribe. Despite that relationship, he kept pressuring his estranged wife to take him back. Her mother refused, but the father did not stop trying. The situation came to a head on Christmas Day, when the father admitted through the family’s youngest daughter that he had a secret 9-year-old son he had hidden from everyone. He did not tell the family directly; instead, he asked the youngest sister to pass the message on. The daughter said this was especially shocking because the child was born roughly two years after the parents separated, meaning the father had known about the boy throughout the years he was asking his wife to reconcile. She added that the child lives in the same European country as the family but has been kept hidden. When she confronted her father by phone, he confirmed the child’s existence. He also said something that deeply disturbed her: that he feels no real affection for the boy and that the child will never replace his “real family,” meaning his European wife and their children. She described this as horrifying, especially because the child is his biological son and shares his Nigerian tribe. She also said it seemed especially painful given her father’s own childhood experience of suffering under a cruel stepmother. The woman said the child’s mother still wants to marry her father, and that he seems to keep her hopeful while also continuing to fantasize about reuniting with his legal wife. She and her mother concluded that if her mother had agreed to take him back, he could have legally returned to the home as her husband and later revealed the hidden child after regaining access, leaving her trapped in a marriage built on deception. She said the revelation has destroyed her respect for him and left her feeling disgusted, ashamed, and uncertain about trust, marriage, and cultural expectations. She is engaged to a loving European man and said the experience has made her fear repeating harmful patterns if she married a Nigerian man. While she said she still values Nigerian food, music, and culture, she no longer feels aligned with the way marriage and responsibility have been modeled to her. She ended by saying she no longer wants to be around her father and is seeking perspectives from people who understand Nigerian family dynamics.

# Summary: A Father's Hidden Child Reveals Deeper Betrayal A mixed-race woman living in Europe has shared her distressing discovery that her Nigerian father has been hiding a 9-year-old son from the entire family. The revelation emerged on Christmas Day 2025 when he confessed to her youngest sister rather than addressing the family directly. The backstory provides crucial context. The writer's parents legally separated over a decade ago following a serious incident that prompted the father's removal from the family home. Despite the separation, the father persistently pressured the mother to reconcile for years without success. Simultaneously, he was involved with a Nigerian woman and fathered a child approximately two years after the separation, yet concealed this entirely. What disturbs the writer most is the calculated deception. During all those years of begging his ex-wife to reunite, her father already knew about his other child living in the same European country. When confronted, he admitted everything and made a chilling confession: he feels no genuine affection for the 9-year-old and considers him replaceable, viewing only his original family as "real." This callousness is particularly shocking given the father's own traumatic childhood, which included suffering under a cruel stepmother. The writer expected him to identify with his hidden son's situation, but instead, he has completely compartmentalized the child from his life. The father's behavior suggests a pattern of manipulation. The child's mother still hopes to marry him, while he simultaneously fantasizes about reconciling with his legal European wife. He appears to maintain multiple parallel realities without commitment to any. A critical realization emerged: if the mother had agreed to reconcile, the father could have legally returned home. Once reestablished as her husband, he could have revealed the hidden child, effectively trapping her in a deceptive marriage from which she'd have no legal recourse to remove him again, as he claims he wouldn't repeat physical violence. The writer emphasizes cultural differences as fundamental to her disgust. In Europe, such secrecy violates core values of honesty and consent. She explicitly told her father that his Nigerian ex-partner might culturally accept such behavior, but her European mother operates under completely different relationship standards where trust and transparency are non-negotiable. This experience has profoundly damaged the writer's relationship with her father and shaken her confidence in shared family values. She feels shame explaining the situation to European friends and experiences a deep cultural dissonance. Engaged to a European man, she now harbors fears about marrying Nigerian men, worrying she might normalize behaviors she fundamentally rejects. While she doesn't reject her Nigerian heritage—appreciating its food, music, and culture—marriage, honesty, and responsibility represent values where she feels completely disconnected from what her father has modeled. She currently cannot bear being around him, as something fundamental has broken, and she struggles to rebuild respect where trust has been destroyed.

A Tokyo-based group is promoting high heels as a tool for improving women’s posture, confidence, and social presence, drawing both criticism and curiosity in Japan. The Japan High Heel Association (JHA) says many Japanese women “walk like ducks” because of the country’s traditional kimono culture and the legacy of shuffling in straw sandals. Its managing director, Yumiko, a former ballerina who runs a plush salon in Tokyo, argues that women should learn to stand tall and wear stilettos correctly in order to improve their gait and self-assurance. The association offers expensive etiquette and walking lessons, including classes focused on high-heel technique. Students pay 400,000 yen, or about $3,700, for a six-month course, and the organization says about 4,000 people have taken part so far. Similar schools have also begun appearing across Japan. Supporters of the movement say the lessons help women become more confident and better able to express themselves in a culture where women are often expected not to stand out. The campaign has also been met with ridicule and criticism. Some observers have called it sexist and absurd, especially in a society where women still contend with deeply rooted patriarchal expectations. Social commentator Mitsuko Shimomura dismissed the idea as “nonsense,” saying there is no connection between high heels and women’s power. Critics note that Japan has a long history of gender inequality, including past expectations that women walk behind men. Yumiko rejects the criticism, saying that while kimono culture may have shaped Japanese walking habits, most women no longer wear kimono all day and should learn how to wear Western-style heels properly. She also claims that women from China and Korea do not have the same posture issues. The article places this trend in a broader international context, noting that in the West there has been growing feminist resistance to dress codes that require women to wear heels. It cites Julia Roberts’ barefoot appearance at Cannes and a UK petition against workplace rules mandating high heels. JHA officials also argue that heels have a role in attracting men. Another director, Tomoko Kubota, said sexier-looking women could encourage Japanese men to “buck up their ideas.” The article mentions a 2014 French study suggesting men respond more positively to women in high heels, including being more likely to return a dropped glove. Meanwhile, students from across Japan continue to take JHA exams to qualify as high-heel instructors.

# Summary: Japan's High Heel Movement The Japan High Heel Association (JHA) is launching a campaign to encourage Japanese women to wear high heels, claiming the practice will improve their posture, confidence, and overall demeanor. JHA managing director Yumiko argues that Japanese women have poor walking habits, describing them as "waddling like ducks" with pigeon-toed gaits and poor posture—characteristics she attributes to Japan's traditional kimono culture and historical use of straw sandals. The organization offers expensive etiquette classes, charging 400,000 yen ($3,700) for six-month courses that teach proper walking technique in high heels. These classes have proven surprisingly popular, with approximately 4,000 participants to date, and similar programs are emerging nationwide. Yumiko contends that since most Japanese no longer wear kimonos daily, women should embrace Western fashion practices and learn proper heel-wearing techniques. The JHA argues that high heels provide psychological benefits beyond physical posture improvement. According to Yumiko, many Japanese women are culturally conditioned to be shy and avoid standing out. She believes wearing heels can boost confidence and encourage self-expression by helping women overcome these cultural constraints. JHA director Tomoko Kubota adds that attractive appearance benefits courtship, citing a 2014 French study showing men respond more positively to women wearing heels than flats. However, the campaign faces significant criticism. Social commentator Mitsuko Shimomura dismissed the idea as "nonsense," arguing there is no meaningful connection between footwear and women's empowerment. Critics characterize the initiative as sexist, particularly given Japan's ongoing struggles with patriarchal traditions that historically required women to walk behind men. The timing of this campaign contrasts sharply with global feminist movements. Western women are increasingly rebelling against dress code requirements mandating heels—Julia Roberts protested barefoot at Cannes Film Festival, and over 100,000 British citizens petitioned parliament to change workplace dress codes requiring women to wear high heels. These concurrent movements highlight diverging cultural attitudes toward women's fashion choices and autonomy. Historically, heels have existed for centuries, appearing in ancient Egyptian art dating back 4,000 years, and have alternately been fashionable for both men and women throughout history. Today, however, the JHA's promotion of heels as an empowerment tool stands in opposition to broader Western feminist efforts to eliminate mandatory heel-wearing and grant women freedom in choosing appropriate footwear.

Indian-American DJ and record producer KSHMR turned his performance at the Ola Sunburn music festival in Pune into a theatrical, India-themed musical narrative, blending high-energy EDM with Bollywood songs, live instruments and vivid visuals. Performing on the third day of the four-day festival at Oxford Golf Resort, Lavale, he framed the set as a story about two rulers fighting for a throne, unfolding it in fragments while matching the action with beats, rhythm and dramatic lighting. KSHMR, whose real name is Niles Hollowell-Dhar, mixed popular Indian tracks such as “Chardi jawani teri ankh mastani teri,” and EDM reworks of “Jimmy Jimmy aaja,” “Ek do teen char,” “Kajra re” and “Malhari,” prompting the crowd to dance. His set also included his own tracks “Power,” “Secrets” and “Islands,” along with the Ola Sunburn 2017 anthem “Shiva,” which he composed with The Golden Army. The performance featured a strong visual component, with blue, yellow and red tones, battle scenes, Indian art and sculpture, and even everyday images from Indian life, such as children playing outdoors and women sitting by a river. The DJ also highlighted his personal connection to India and Kashmir through track titles like “Delhi,” “JAMMU,” “Kashmir” and “Bazaar.” His show combined electronic music with live drumming and other instruments, creating what resembled a musical play more than a standard DJ set. At one point, he asked the audience to switch on their phone lights, further building the atmosphere. Visuals at the end summed up the performance with the message: “Yeh hai humari yatra (This is our journey). Yeh hai KSHMR (This is KSHMR).” After finishing, KSHMR returned to the front of the stage with the live musicians and dancers to thank them and the audience. He said the performers were among the most talented musicians he had ever met and asked the crowd to cheer for them. He also spoke emotionally about his family ties to India, saying he had grown up visiting the country and now felt as though he had “a million friends” there. He noted that his grandfather, whom he usually brings on stage, was unwell and asked the audience to pray for him. Meanwhile, the festival saw some tension when two brawls broke out, leading security to remove Indian flags from people near the “Empire of the Sun 2.0” stage. Security was tight throughout the event, with police and private agencies conducting checks for narcotics and monitoring for eve-teasing. The festival concludes Sunday with Dutch DJ Martin Garrix.

Meiji Yasuda Life Insurance Co. has released its annual survey of Japan’s most popular baby names, based on 6,312 boys and 6,193 girls born this year. For the first time, the top names in both categories ranked first: “Sui” for girls and “Minato” and “So” for boys, which are two readings of the same kanji. Among girls, the second-place name was a kanji pair read as either “Himari” or “Hinata,” followed by “Tsumugi.” For boys, “Iori” tied for second with another kanji pair read as “Yuito” or “Yuto.” The company said many of the leading names reflected hopes that children would grow into kind, sociable people who live “beautiful and happy” lives. It also noted that the kanji used for “Yuito/Yuto” has been the most common in boys’ names for five straight years, likely influenced by baseball star Shohei Ohtani’s name. For girls, the character meaning “love” has led for four years. Traditional, seasonal, and color-related characters were also popular.

# Summary Meiji Yasuda Life Insurance Co. released its annual baby names survey, showing that "Sui" was the most popular girl's name and "Minato"/"So" topped the boys' list—both leading their categories for the first time. Popular names like "Himari"/"Hinata" for girls and "Iori"/"Yuito"/"Yuto" for boys suggest parental hopes for children to exhibit positive qualities such as sociability and happiness. Japan’s auto industry is bracing for another major external challenge in 2026 as Taiwan’s Foxconn, the world’s best-known contract electronics manufacturer, intensifies its push into the Japanese market. After first focusing on Chinese electric vehicle makers, Foxconn is now turning its attention to Japan, raising a central question: will it become a partner to domestic automakers, a competitor, or both? The report focuses on Foxconn Technology Group’s EV strategy, led by former Nissan executive Jun Seki. Seki, once seen as a possible candidate for Nissan’s top job, left the company after internal power struggles and later joined Foxconn to lead its electric vehicle ambitions. Under his leadership, Foxconn has been studying Japanese automakers such as Toyota and Nissan while developing EVs of its own. It has already begun deploying electric buses and taxis and is now aiming at the passenger car market. Recent coverage of Foxconn Tech Day showed that cooperation with Japanese companies is progressing. The event featured new vehicle models and highlighted Foxconn’s growing mobility ambitions. At the same time, the company’s moves have already influenced the broader Japanese auto landscape. In December 2024, reports said Foxconn had approached Renault, Nissan’s largest shareholder, about buying its stake in Nissan. That reportedly helped accelerate talks between Nissan and Honda over a possible management integration, fueled partly by fears of foreign acquisition. Although those talks eventually collapsed, Foxconn’s maneuvering continued to cast a shadow over the sector. Financially, Foxconn remains extremely powerful. In the first half of 2025, it posted revenue of about 17 trillion yen, with operating and net profits both rising by double digits from the previous year. Its main business is still smartphone and electronics production, including iPhone assembly, but its fastest-growing segment is AI server manufacturing, which expanded by around 50 percent year on year. EVs remain part of its machinery and connector division, where sales are smaller but steadily growing. Analysts say Foxconn’s horizontal manufacturing model differs sharply from Japan’s traditional vertically integrated auto industry. Foxconn specializes in contract manufacturing, building products designed by others, while Japanese firms typically design, manufacture, and sell vehicles in-house. That model has made Foxconn dominant in global electronics, but its fit with Japan’s automotive culture remains uncertain. Still, Foxconn has shown it can revive struggling businesses, as seen in its acquisition of Sharp. Critics, however, say it lacks the brand-building and creative strengths prized by Japanese manufacturers. Meanwhile, the auto industry is changing rapidly as software, autonomous driving, and AI become central to vehicle development. Experts believe this shift could favor Foxconn’s modular, large-scale production strengths. At a November tech exhibition, Foxconn unveiled several EVs, including a compact electric bus and Model A, a new passenger vehicle priced at about 3 million yen. The company said it will supply EV buses to Mitsubishi Fuso Truck and Bus and may follow with passenger cars. Foxconn says it wants to build vehicles in Japan with local partners, though it is also considering its own production lines. It is additionally developing Level 4 autonomous driving with Nvidia and other partners, with robotaxis in mind. As Japan’s population declines and vehicle use shifts, Foxconn’s entry could have major consequences for jobs, industry structure, and technological leadership.

The number of Japanese restaurants overseas fell for the first time in 2025, according to a biennial survey by Japan’s Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries. The total dropped to about 181,000 from a record 187,000 in 2023. The main reason was a sharp decline in China, which still had the most Japanese restaurants abroad but saw its total fall by about 15,260 to 63,500, nearly 20% lower than two years earlier. The ministry linked the drop to China’s economic slowdown, including weak consumer demand, a property crisis, and high local-government debt. Even so, Japanese restaurants remained far more numerous overseas than in 2013, when there were about 55,000. The United States ranked second in 2025 with about 26,360 restaurants, followed by South Korea with 19,800 and Mexico with 7,430. Growth in other regions partly offset the decline in Asia, especially in Central and South America, where restaurant numbers rose about 20% amid interest in anime and Japanese pop culture. The Middle East also saw a roughly 20% increase, helped by growing health-consciousness.

# Summary The number of Japanese restaurants operating overseas declined for the first time in 2025, dropping to approximately 181,000 from a record 187,000 in 2023, according to a biennial Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries survey. China, which hosts the most Japanese restaurants globally, experienced the sharpest decline, falling nearly 20 percent to 63,500 establishments due to its economic downturn characterized by weak domestic demand, property crisis, and government debt issues. Despite this contraction, China remained the leading country for Japanese restaurants, followed by the United States (26,360), South Korea (19,800), and Mexico (7,430). Growth in other regions partially offset Asian declines. Central and South America saw approximately 20 percent increases, driven by anime and pop culture interest, while the Middle East experienced similar growth fueled by increased health consciousness. Overall, the 2025 figure remains substantially higher than the 55,000 restaurants recorded in 2013, reflecting sustained long-term expansion of Japanese cuisine globally.

Japan’s hot springs, or onsen, have long been central to the country’s culture, prized for relaxation, scenery and a sense of renewal. In recent years, they have also become increasingly popular with overseas visitors seeking a break from crowded sightseeing schedules. Among the most sought-after are “infinity onsen,” baths whose views seem to erase the boundary between the water and the sea, lake or sky. To highlight the country’s most striking examples, Nikkei asked a panel of experts to choose a top 10 from onsen across Japan. The result is a list of baths celebrated not only for their waters, but also for the landscapes surrounding them. The selected sites range from northern Aomori to southern Kagoshima, and each combines natural scenery, local character and distinctive bathing conditions. One featured bath is a seaside onsen in Aomori, on the northern tip of Honshu. Visitors feel the sea breeze while watching waves break in the distance, and the iron-rich hot spring water turns golden when exposed to the air, creating a vivid contrast with the sky over the Sea of Japan. Experts praised it for its rugged beauty, with one calling it a place everyone should experience at least once. The bath is also frequented by local fishermen from Fukaura’s tuna fleet after work. Dolphins are sometimes visible offshore. The spring is deep, murky and yellowish-brown, and flows naturally, which experts said satisfies serious hot spring fans. Non-guests may enter until 8 p.m., and bathing at night, with the sound of waves from the dark sea, can feel almost otherworldly. It is about 12 minutes by car from the Sakurajima ferry toll gate, and admission is 500 yen. The article explains that the ranking was created through a two-step selection process. The expert panel included Chihiro Akizuki, Kei Sugimoto, Kazuki Takahashi, Ishii, Uetake, Kawana and Kitade.

A Japanese government survey has found that the number of Japanese restaurants overseas fell for the first time in 2025, declining to about 181,000 from a record 187,000 in 2023. The drop was driven mainly by China, where the total number of such restaurants fell by roughly 15,260 to 63,500, a nearly 20% decrease, as the country’s economy weakened amid low domestic demand, a property crisis and heavy local-government debt. Even so, China remained the largest overseas market for Japanese restaurants, followed by the United States with about 26,360, South Korea with 19,800 and Mexico with 7,430. The overall figure was still more than triple the 55,000 recorded in 2013. Growth in other regions partly offset the decline, especially in Central and South America, where restaurant numbers rose about 20% on the back of anime and pop-culture interest, and in the Middle East, where health-conscious eating trends helped boost demand.

Japan’s ancient castles take on a particularly striking appearance in winter, when clear, dry air and snow make their outlines sharper and their historic features more dramatic. With snowfall this season expected to be about average, Nikkei asked a panel of experts to choose the country’s most spectacular castles to visit in winter. The resulting top 10 list spans Japan from Hokkaido in the north to Hyogo in the west, reflecting both the growing popularity of Japanese castles among international tourists and an ongoing “history boom” inside Japan. At No. 1 is Goryokaku in Hakodate, Hokkaido. Unlike most Japanese castles, Goryokaku is best known for its star-shaped fortification, which can only be seen in full from the air or from the 107-meter Goryokaku Tower. In winter, the entire structure is covered in snow, making its five-pointed outline stand out even more. Experts described the view as especially beautiful when the snow piles up in different ways, subtly changing the appearance of the star. The castle is illuminated only in winter after sunset, and when 2,000 lights around the moat are turned on, visitors reportedly cheer at the sight of the snow-covered star “floating” in the landscape. The design was originally intended for gun warfare, and the site also carries historical weight as the location of the last battle of the Boshin War, the civil conflict that ended Tokugawa rule in the late 1860s. The Hakodate Magistrate’s Office in the park is highlighted as a must-see for visitors interested in the era’s historical atmosphere. No. 2 is Matsumoto Castle in Nagano prefecture, one of Japan’s five castles designated as National Treasures. The castle has stood for more than 400 years, and in winter it is framed by the snow-covered Japanese Alps, creating what experts compared to a painting. The castle’s black clapboard exterior contrasts sharply with the white snow on the roof and surrounding mountains. It is also the only castle in Japan entirely coated in black lacquer. Visitors are encouraged to photograph the castle reflected upside down in the moat, and at night the site offers projection mapping, blending historical architecture with modern light displays. Aizuwakamatsu Castle, also known as Tsuruga Castle, ranks third. Its red-tiled roof is one of its defining features, but in snow the whole castle turns white, producing a striking seasonal transformation. The site becomes especially notable during the Aizu Painted-Candle Festival in February, when about 10,000 candles are placed around the castle. The event is described as a must-see, and the castle has also become popular with foreign tourists; in February of the previous year, about 80% of visitors were from overseas, according to the local tourism bureau. Hikone Castle in Shiga prefecture comes in at No. 4. Another National Treasure, it retains its Edo-period appearance and is praised for its elegant gables and the dazzling white effect created when its walls are covered by snow. Views from Genkyuen Garden are particularly admired, with the castle appearing to float in a silver-colored world. When the towers and gates are snow-covered, the scene can feel like stepping back into the Edo period. Tied for No. 5 are Hirosaki Castle in Aomori prefecture and Kanazawa Castle in Ishikawa prefecture. Hirosaki Castle is the northernmost of Japan’s 12 surviving original castle towers, and its snow-country surroundings make it especially distinctive in winter. Its gates and other structures are also admired for their sturdy construction. The nearby Snow Lantern Festival, held in February, features about 150 snow lanterns and miniature igloos and is considered family-friendly. Although heavy snowfall damaged one tower earlier in the year, restoration is underway and the main keep remains visible from outside, with the festival expected to proceed as scheduled. Kanazawa Castle is known for its stone foundation and for the way snow highlights details such as its silver lead roofing tiles, black slate grid pattern, and steel bars on the turrets. Its winter appeal is heightened by its proximity to Kenrokuen Garden, one of Japan’s three great gardens, whose snow-covered scenery creates a seasonal atmosphere unavailable at other times of year. No. 7 is Yokote Castle in Akita prefecture, a relatively modern reconstruction completed in 1965. Its appeal lies less in the castle itself than in the local winter traditions that surround it. Snow huts are built in front of the castle around the time of the first full moon after Lunar New Year. Inside the igloos, children roast rice cakes over braziers and serve them to visitors along with sweet, nonalcoholic sake. The castle’s interior tours are not offered in winter except during the festival dates, but the event is praised for allowing visitors to experience local culture and interact with residents. At No. 8 is Echizen Ono Castle in Fukui prefecture, often called a “castle in the sky.” In winter, when fog rises over the Ono Basin and snow covers the mountains, the castle can appear to float above a sea of clouds. A nearby vantage point about a kilometer west offers a well-known view of the castle shrouded in snow and mist. The tower itself is closed from December through March. No. 9 is the Takeda Castle ruins in Hyogo prefecture. This site has no remaining wooden buildings, having been abandoned about 400 years ago, but its stone walls and mountain-top foundations remain impressive. The ruins spread out like birds’ wings, and on mornings when temperatures shift sharply, fog often gathers, creating a famous “castle in the sky” effect. Snow and mist can make the ruins appear to float. Access to the ruins is prohibited until the end of February, and the best viewing point is Ritsuunkyo Gorge, opposite JR Takeda Station. Rounding out the list at No. 10 are the Yonezawa Castle ruins in Yamagata prefecture. Though the castle tower is gone, the site remains listed among Japan’s 100 fine castles. In winter, the snow-covered moat evokes the history of the Yonezawa domain and its hardships, including financial strain. The grounds also contain a shrine dedicated to the warlord Kenshin Uesugi, who is revered as a war god. During the Uesugi Snow Lantern Festival in February, the shrine is illuminated and snow lantern towers are built, creating a scene that experts said is moving partly because of its impermanence as the snow structures melt. The rankings were compiled through a survey in which 21 castles were first selected with the help of Yasutsune Owada and Sachiko Hagiwara. Seven experts then chose their top 10 based on factors such as snowy appearance and nearby events. The final panel included Kaori Inamoto, Yasuyuki Oka, Ineyuki Oshio, Toshihiro Takahashi, Kazuhisa Hatanaka, Owada, and Hagiwara.

# Summary: Alternative Protagonists for the Naruto Series The article, written by Suzail Ahmad, explores seven characters from the Naruto manga series who could potentially have served as better protagonists than Naruto Uzumaki himself. While acknowledging that creator Masashi Kishimoto crafted an excellent protagonist with compelling abilities, personality, and ideology that contributed to the series' popularity, the author argues that several other characters possess qualities that would have made them equally or more suitable for leading the narrative. ## The Seven Alternative Protagonists **Itachi Uchiha** ranks sixth on the list as a character "mature beyond his years." Despite his young age, Itachi experienced significant trauma and death, which shaped him into a pacifist who actively avoided conflict. His unique perspective differed substantially from Naruto's approach. Had Itachi been the protagonist, he would have lived longer and wouldn't have sacrificed himself fighting his brother Sasuke. Without his illness limiting him, Itachi could have fully utilized his Mangekyou Sharingan abilities against any threats, offering readers a fundamentally different narrative perspective. **Minato Namikaze**, the Fourth Hokage, ranks fifth. Minato earned the fear and respect of entire enemy armies during the Third Great Ninja War, with opposing nations issuing flee-on-sight orders for their ninjas when encountering him. His appeal as a protagonist stems from his compassion, exceptional intellect that allowed him to excel at the Academy, and his lack of a prestigious lineage—unlike most powerful ninjas in the story. Kishimoto has already released a one-shot featuring Minato, suggesting the author might consider developing a prequel centered on the Yellow Flash. **Neji Hyuuga** comes in fourth, described as "a genius born in the wrong family." Neji made an impressive impact during the Chunin Exams, dominating opponents with talent and ruthlessness, even defeating Naruto until the Nine-Tailed Beast intervened. Despite this strong introduction, Neji was subsequently sidelined. As the protagonist, his story could have explored the oppressive Hyuuga hierarchy, where branch family members like Neji were treated as inferior beings. His narrative could have naturally connected to the Otsutsuki Clan's storyline. **Hashirama Senju**, the First Hokage, ranks third as someone "born with one of the rarest powers." Hashirama possessed the Wood Release Kekkei Genkai, strong enough to stop tailed beasts, making him one of history's strongest ninjas. Even the legendary Madara Uchiha failed to defeat him in combat. As the protagonist, Hashirama would have received more screen time, allowing deeper exploration of his past and the early establishment of the Hidden Leaf Village. His story would likely have been shorter and more exciting. **Nagato Uzumaki**, ranked second, had "a more realistic approach" despite being a villain. Nagato was a phenomenal fighter and leader who elevated the Akatsuki organization. His ideology—that people cannot change without experiencing pain themselves—seemed radical yet proved accurate throughout the series, as evidenced by how the Hidden Leaf villagers treated Naruto despite his innocence. His strength and perspective would have made him an excellent protagonist. **Jiraiya** tops the list as "much more adventurous than Naruto." Known as the Toad Sage, Jiraiya served as mentor to many great ninjas while traveling across the world completing missions and interacting with diverse people. His travels broadened his perspective and deepened his understanding of the world. Had Kishimoto selected Jiraiya as the protagonist, the story would have featured multiple settings rather than focusing primarily on one location, allowing readers to explore the cultures of various ninja villages, both major and minor. The article suggests that while Naruto remains an excellent protagonist, these alternative characters possessed unique qualities, experiences, and perspectives that could have produced equally compelling or superior narratives had they been chosen to lead the series instead.
