Swedish actress Anita Ekberg, famed for her sensual role in Federico Fellini’s *La Dolce Vita*, has died in Italy at the age of 83. She died on Sunday in a hospital outside Rome, according to reports. Ekberg had spent her later years in a wheelchair after reportedly being knocked over by one of her Great Danes and breaking her hip. Born in 1931 in Malmö, Sweden, the sixth of eight children of a docker, Ekberg first drew attention as a teenager when she won Miss Sweden in 1950. Encouraged by her mother and friends, she entered beauty contests with hopes of becoming Miss Universe and soon traveled to the United States. Although she did not win the title, she was noticed by figures including filmmaker Russ Meyer, producer Howard Hughes and actor-producer John Wayne. She became a magazine pin-up and appeared in several comedy films, among them *Abbott and Costello Go to Mars* (1953), *Artists and Models* (1955) and *Hollywood or Bust* (1956), often cast in roles that emphasized her striking physique for comic effect. In 1954, while visiting a U.S. base in Greenland with William Holden and Bob Hope, Hope joked that her parents had been given the Nobel Prize for architecture. Ekberg later moved into Italian cinema, first appearing in King Vidor’s *War and Peace* (1956). Federico Fellini then cast her in the iconic fountain scene in *La Dolce Vita* (1960), where she wades through Rome’s Trevi Fountain opposite Marcello Mastroianni. The film won Fellini the Palme d’Or at Cannes, and the scene became one of the most famous images in film history. Ekberg went on to appear in other major Italian productions, including *Boccaccio ’70* (1962), *I Clowns* (1970) and *Intervista* (1987). In 2011, *La Stampa* reported that she had asked the Fellini Foundation for financial help. She later lived in a residence for the elderly near Rome. Her romantic relationships reportedly included Gianni Agnelli, Mastroianni, Errol Flynn and Frank Sinatra. She was married twice, first to actor Anthony Steel and later to actor Rik Van Nutter; both marriages ended in divorce and she had no children.

# Swedish Actress Anita Ekberg Dies at 83 Anita Ekberg, the Swedish actress best known for her iconic role in Federico Fellini's 1960 masterpiece "La Dolce Vita," has died in Italy at age 83. She passed away Sunday in a hospital outside Rome. Born in 1931 in Malmö, Sweden, Ekberg was the sixth of eight children. She rose to prominence after winning the Miss Sweden beauty pageant in 1950, which led to opportunities in the United States. During the 1950s, she became a celebrated pin-up and starlet, appearing in comedy films including "Abbott and Costello Go to Mars" and "Hollywood or Bust," where her striking physique was often central to the humor. Ekberg relocated to Italy in 1956 to appear in King Vidor's "War and Peace." Director Fellini subsequently discovered her and cast her in "La Dolce Vita," where she played the glamorous dream woman who tempts actor Marcello Mastroianni. The film's famous Trevi Fountain scene became one of cinema's most iconic images and won Fellini the Golden Palm at the 1960 Cannes Film Festival. She continued her Italian film career, starring in notable productions including "Boccaccio 70" alongside Sophia Loren and Fellini's "I Clowns" and "Intervista." Ekberg was married twice—to British actor Anthony Steel from 1956 to 1959 and American actor Rik Van Nutter from 1963 to 1975. Both marriages ended in divorce with no children. Her romantic liaisons reportedly included relationships with Gianni Agnelli, head of Fiat, as well as Mastroianni, Errol Flynn, and Frank Sinatra. In her later years, Ekberg faced hardship. After being knocked over by one of her Great Danes and breaking her hip, she spent several years in a wheelchair. By 2011, at age 80, she sought financial assistance from the Fellini Foundation and lived in a residence for elderly people near Rome.

Music helped define the emotion and symbolism of the Berlin Wall’s division and eventual collapse, according to this retrospective on songs and performances linked to the end of the Cold War in Germany. Thirty years after the Wall fell, the article traces a kind of unofficial soundtrack to peaceful revolution, showing how rock stars, classical musicians and pop hits captured the mood of a city and a country in transition. Among the most famous songs associated with the event is “Wind of Change” by the Scorpions. Although often treated as the anthem of the Wall’s fall, it was actually recorded in 1990, months after the barrier came down. Written by singer Klaus Meine after the band played a festival in the Soviet Union, its message of hope and freedom made it a defining song of the era and the best-selling single by a German band. Another iconic moment came from David Hasselhoff, who performed “Looking for Freedom” on New Year’s Eve 1989 in front of East and West Berliners gathered at a damaged section of the Wall. Wearing a light-up leather jacket, the “Knight Rider” and “Baywatch” star became a surprising pop symbol of reunification and remains popular in Germany. The article also recalls David Bowie and Bruce Springsteen. Bowie’s “Heroes” had already become an anthem for a divided Berlin, and during a 1987 concert in West Berlin he arranged speakers to face east so people beyond the Wall could hear. The crowd’s chants for the Wall to fall reportedly angered East German police. A year later, Springsteen performed in East Germany before a huge audience, telling fans he hoped barriers would one day be torn down. Classical cellist Mstislav Rostropovich gave a moving tribute two days after the Wall fell, traveling to Checkpoint Charlie to play Bach in memory of those who died because of the Wall. Pink Floyd’s “The Wall,” though not originally about Berlin, became linked to the event after Roger Waters staged a massive 1990 concert on the former “death strip,” where a 170-meter wall was built and destroyed during the show. The piece also mentions Udo Lindenberg’s satirical “Sonderzug nach Pankow,” which mocked East German leader Erich Honecker, and Kaoma’s “La Lambada,” a 1989 dance hit that became part of the jubilant atmosphere after reunification.

# Music and the Fall of the Berlin Wall Music played a pivotal role in capturing the emotion surrounding the Berlin Wall's collapse 30 years ago, with several iconic performances and songs becoming synonymous with this historic moment. **"Wind of Change" by The Scorpions** is widely remembered as the anthem of the Wall's fall, though it was actually recorded in 1990, months after the barrier's destruction. The melancholic rock ballad, inspired by a Soviet music festival, became the best-selling single by a German band, with its message of hope and freedom resonating globally. **David Hasselhoff's performance** became legendary when the Knight Rider actor performed "Looking for Freedom" on New Year's Eve 1989 at the crumbling Wall, wearing a distinctive light-studded leather jacket. The Baywatch star remains idolized in Germany, which even dedicated a museum to him. **David Bowie** had previously contributed to the Wall's symbolic demise. His 1987 West Berlin concert featured speakers deliberately facing east, allowing divided audiences to sing along. When crowds demanded "the Wall must go," East German police rioted in response. Upon Bowie's death in 2016, the German foreign ministry credited him with helping bring down the barrier. **Bruce Springsteen** performed for East Germans in 1988, declaring his hope that "all barriers will be torn down," further weakening communist resolve. Two days after the Wall's collapse, exiled Russian cellist **Mstislav Rostropovich** performed Bach at Checkpoint Charlie, with his impromptu performance broadcast worldwide as a tribute to those who died. **Pink Floyd's "The Wall,"** though written in 1979 about broader themes, became forever associated with Berlin after Roger Waters performed it before 350,000 people on the former "death strip" eight months post-collapse, complete with a 170-meter wall destroyed during the show. **Udo Lindenberg's 1983 song "Sonderzug nach Pankow"** mocked East German leader Erich Honecker, eventually earning the rocker permission to perform in the GDR, though notably not this particular song. Finally, **"La Lambada" by Kaoma** became the undisputed summer hit of 1989 in West Germany, with its hip-grinding dance moves providing an outlet for the unrestrained joy sweeping the reunified city.

The European Union is ready to help create a task force to protect cultural heritage sites in conflict zones and after natural disasters, EU foreign policy chief Federica Mogherini said Wednesday. In a note, she praised Italy’s initiative as a model for the international community and called defending cultural heritage a moral duty to future generations. The task force, which will include officers from Italy’s Carabinieri art squad, was established under an agreement between Italy and UNESCO last year as part of UNESCO’s “Unite4Heritage” campaign. Mogherini said the effort would support the fight against radicalization and terrorism by blocking illicit trade that can fund terror groups, while also preserving artworks worldwide.

President Trump said Saturday that he spoke with Swedish Prime Minister Stefan Lofven about jailed rapper A$AP Rocky and offered to personally vouch for his bail. In a tweet, Trump said the call was “very good” and that he assured Lofven Rocky was “not a flight risk.” Trump had already said Friday that he would intervene to try to help free the rapper, following appeals from the first lady and celebrities including Kanye West and Kim Kardashian West. After the call, Trump said the two sides agreed their teams would continue talking and that they would speak again within 48 hours. Swedish officials later confirmed the conversation. Prime Minister Lofven’s press secretary, Toni Eriksson, said the discussion lasted about 20 minutes and was “friendly and respectful.” She also stressed that Lofven emphasized the independence of Sweden’s courts and prosecutors and said the government could not and would not interfere with the legal process. She added that no follow-up call had been scheduled, though one might happen. Earlier Saturday, Lofven said he would be willing to speak with Trump but made the same point that Sweden’s judicial system operates independently and that everyone is equal before the law. A$AP Rocky, whose real name is Rakim May, has been held since early this month while Swedish police investigate an alleged fight in Stockholm before a music festival appearance. Videos posted on social media appear to show Rocky involved in a violent confrontation, though his lawyer says he acted in self-defense. Several other musicians, including Sean “Diddy” Combs, Justin Bieber, Shawn Mendes, Nicki Minaj, and Post Malone, have also spoken out in his support.

# Summary President Trump announced he had spoken with Swedish Prime Minister Stefan Löfven about jailed rapper A$AP Rocky, offering to personally guarantee his bail. Trump stated he assured the prime minister that Rocky was not a flight risk. Rocky, whose real name is Rakim May, has been in Swedish custody since early in the month following an alleged street fight in Stockholm. Iraq approved a new government on Monday after intense domestic and international pressure, clearing the way for the United States to expand military support against Islamic State militants. The vote took place during a tense, late-night parliamentary session in Baghdad, but several major posts, including the defense and interior ministries, remained unfilled because of disputes over who should hold them. Newly confirmed Prime Minister Haider al-Abadi said he would name candidates for those security positions within a week. The cabinet’s formation met a key U.S. demand for a more inclusive government that would bring Sunni and Kurdish groups into power-sharing after years of alienation under former Prime Minister Nouri al-Maliki. The Obama administration has tied broader military assistance to such inclusiveness. President Obama was expected to address the nation on Wednesday to present a wider strategy against the Islamic State, the al-Qaeda breakaway group that has seized territory in Iraq and Syria. On Monday night, Obama called Abadi and stressed the importance of close cooperation with Iraq and the international community to counter the militant threat. Abadi, in turn, pledged to work with all Iraqi communities and move quickly to address public grievances. Even so, the vote nearly collapsed before it began. Kurdish politicians withdrew from negotiations and went to Sulaymaniyah in the semiautonomous north, threatening to boycott the session over disputes about budget payments and oil sales. With Abadi under a 30-day deadline to form a government, U.S. official Brett McGurk and U.N. envoy Nickolay Mladenov traveled to Sulaymaniyah to persuade Kurdish leaders to return. Kurdish lawmakers eventually joined the session, but only after hours of uncertainty and with the warning that their participation was on a three-month trial basis. Tensions were visible inside parliament. Shiite lawmaker Mohammed Naji Mohammed criticized the removal of Hadi al-Amiri’s name from consideration for interior minister. Amiri, a former transport minister and head of the Badr Brigade, has been fighting Islamic State forces north of Baghdad, but Sunni politicians strongly opposed his nomination. Arguments also broke out during the opening religious recital, prompting Speaker Salim al-Jubouri to urge lawmakers to “respect the Koran.” The session opened with only 179 of 328 lawmakers present, just enough for a quorum, and the speaker complained that many members were in the cafeteria instead of the chamber. Eventually 289 lawmakers attended, and the cabinet was approved by a show of hands. The approved lineup reflected Iraq’s sectarian balance: Sunni politicians received the culture and finance ministries, while Shiites took the more powerful oil and finance portfolios. The Kurds, however, remained dissatisfied. Their chief grievance was nearly $8 billion in unpaid oil-sharing revenue they said Baghdad owed them since January. They also objected to receiving only three ministries, arguing that their population and political weight justified at least five. Another unresolved issue is whether Kurdish pesh merga forces will be integrated into Iraq’s national security forces. Former prime minister Maliki was voted in as vice president. Abadi shook his hand upon entering parliament, but Maliki did not visibly support the new prime minister’s agenda, which includes institution-building and anti-corruption efforts. The government vote came as U.S. jets and drones continued airstrikes near the Haditha Dam, where Iraqi officials said militants had been driven from the nearby town of Barwana. The dam has been under repeated attack since late June, as Islamic State fighters try to seize strategic infrastructure. U.S. Central Command said it had carried out 148 airstrikes across Iraq, with the operation near Haditha extending the campaign into western Anbar province, a region that was among the deadliest for U.S. troops during the Iraq war.

# Iraq Approves New Government, Expanding U.S. Military Role Iraq's parliament approved a new government on Monday, clearing the way for increased U.S. military support against Islamic State militants. The cabinet vote occurred during a contentious late-night session, with Prime Minister Haider al-Abadi sworn in despite significant controversies and last-minute political maneuvering. ## Government Formation and U.S. Involvement The new government meets U.S. demands for inclusivity, incorporating disenfranchised Sunni and Kurdish minorities—a condition the Obama administration linked to expanded military assistance. President Obama planned to address the nation Wednesday with a broader strategy against the Islamic State, the brutal al-Qaeda breakaway group destabilizing Iraq. The administration hopes an inclusive government can bridge sectarian divides and reduce support for extremists. Notably, key positions including defense and interior minister remained vacant during the vote. Abadi pledged to nominate candidates for these positions within a week. These ministries had remained unfilled under outgoing Prime Minister Nouri al-Maliki, who retained security portfolios himself. ## Political Tensions and Negotiations The voting session nearly didn't occur. Kurdish politicians initially withdrew to the semiautonomous north, threatening a boycott over demands regarding budget payments and oil revenue. With a 30-day deadline expiring Wednesday, U.S. Deputy Assistant Secretary of State Brett McGurk and UN Iraq Envoy Nickolay Mladenov traveled to persuade Kurdish leaders to participate. Friction also emerged over the interior ministry position. Shiite parliamentarians objected when Hadi al-Amiri's nomination was withdrawn. Sunni politicians had strongly opposed Amiri, head of the Badr Brigade militia, due to sectarian concerns. ## The Vote and Power-Sharing The session began with only 179 of 328 lawmakers present, prompting the speaker to criticize absent parliamentarians. After Kurdish lawmakers eventually returned from the cafeteria, the vote proceeded with 289 present. Sunni politicians received culture and finance ministries, while Shiites secured more powerful portfolios including oil. This financial squeeze left pesh merga fighters battling the Islamic State unpaid for months. Long-standing disputes persist over whether Kurds can independently negotiate oil company deals before sending proceeds to Baghdad. Questions also remain about incorporating pesh merga fighters into national Iraqi security forces. ## Symbolic Moments and Military Operations Notably, Maliki was voted vice president but didn't raise his hand supporting Abadi's agenda—which included institution building and fighting corruption. Abadi shook hands with Maliki upon his parliamentary arrival, suggesting diplomatic civility despite political differences. Meanwhile, U.S. military operations continued, with jets and drones conducting 148 airstrikes across Iraq. Recent operations expanded to Anbar province, historically deadliest for American troops during the Iraq war, with airstrikes near the strategically important Haditha Dam.

Aria, a 15-year-old Yazidi girl, is living with her family in a tent at the Khanke refugee camp near Dohuk in northwest Iraq, after fleeing ISIS captivity and violence. The camp, set up by the UNHCR just a month earlier, was created to shelter the huge number of Yazidis escaping ISIS’s advance from Sinjar. Aria told CNN that her family fled their home about six weeks earlier after hearing ISIS was approaching. They left in a neighbor’s car in the early morning, but were soon intercepted by ISIS fighters on the road. Armed men surrounded the vehicle, forced the family out, and separated the women and girls from the men, including Aria’s 19-year-old brother. Only the girls were taken away and packed into a minivan. She and her 14-year-old sister-in-law were driven about 120 kilometers to Mosul, which had become an ISIS stronghold after the militants captured Iraq’s second-largest city in June. There, Aria said, they were locked in a three-story house with dozens of other captured teenage girls. ISIS members tried to force the girls to convert and read the Quran, though many could not read. Aria described terrifying conditions and said that over three weeks in Mosul, a sheik came and took 20 girls, including her sister-in-law. She said the man forced himself on her sister-in-law and that many of her friends were raped. Aria said she was deeply traumatized by what she saw and heard, and that she still has nightmares. Sexual violence is highly taboo in her culture, and she did not say whether she herself was raped. A UNHCR official, Tanya Kareem, said girls and women in this situation often cannot speak openly about their abuse because of trauma and the shame it brings to their families in Yazidi society. Aria and another girl were later taken to Fallujah by two ISIS militants whom she identified as Abu Hassan and Abu Jaffar. She said the men were intimidating and filthy, with long beards, and forced the girls to marry them under threat of harm. The militants gave them a phone so they could call their families and say they had converted. Instead, Aria and her friend secretly contacted her friend’s uncle, who had connections in Fallujah. When the militants left, the girls escaped while dressed in niqabs. Unable to get direct help, they broke the door, walked for about an hour, and met people waiting to take them to a safe house. After Aria was reunited with her family in the refugee camp, she learned that her brother had been killed when ISIS captured them. She said he was shot in the head, and her mother spent the night beside his body. Aria now feels ashamed and unwelcome in the camp because people gossip about what happened to her. But she said her guilt is even greater because she later learned that ISIS raped other girls after her escape, as punishment for the girls’ attempted flight.

# Teenager Escapes ISIS: A Survivor's Story Fifteen-year-old "Aria" sits in a tent at the Khanke refugee camp in northwest Iraq, sharing her harrowing experience of captivity under ISIS. The camp was established just a month prior to accommodate Yazidis fleeing the militant group's assault on their hometown of Sinjar. ## The Capture Six weeks before the interview, Aria's family attempted to escape Sinjar after learning ISIS was approaching. While driving in a neighbor's car, they were intercepted by at least seven ISIS vehicles. The militants forcibly separated girls and women from men, including Aria's 19-year-old brother, and abducted the females in a minivan. ## Captivity in Mosul Aria and her 14-year-old sister-in-law were transported 120 kilometers to Mosul, ISIS's stronghold in Iraq's second-largest city. They were imprisoned in a three-story house with dozens of other teenage girls. The captors attempted forced religious conversion, demanding the girls read the Quran. During the three-week confinement, a sheik selected 20 girls, including Aria's sister-in-law, subjecting them to sexual abuse. "A lot of my friends were raped," Aria disclosed, visibly traumatized. She explained that discussing sexual assault is culturally taboo, making victims reluctant to acknowledge their experiences. The psychological toll manifests through nightmares and intrusive memories of the violence she witnessed. ## Forced Marriage and Escape Two ISIS militants, whom Aria identifies as Abu Hassan and Abu Jaffar, transferred her and a friend to Fallujah. The militants forced the girls into "marriages" under threats of harm and provided a phone for them to contact families and announce their supposed conversion. Using this phone, the girls secretly contacted her friend's uncle, who arranged assistance. When the militants left the house, the girls—wearing niqabs—escaped. They walked for approximately an hour to meet their uncle's associates, who transported them to a safe house in Fallujah before eventually reaching the refugee camp. ## Aftermath and Tragedy Aria's reunion with her family brought devastating news: her 19-year-old brother had been killed by ISIS during her abduction. She learned that militants shot him in the head, and her mother spent the night sleeping beside his body. ## Continuing Suffering Despite escaping physical captivity, Aria faces ongoing psychological and social challenges. Camp residents gossip about her and her circumstances, making her reluctant to venture outside. However, her personal shame is overshadowed by guilt and responsibility for other girls' suffering. When ISIS discovered Aria and her friend's escape, the militants punished the remaining captive girls through additional sexual abuse and intensified security measures, preventing further escapes. According to UNHCR Duhok director Tanya Kareem, trauma survivors from cultures with strict social codes struggle to discuss their ordeals. The combination of psychological trauma and cultural stigma creates profound barriers to healing and reintegration for victims like Aria.

Iraq’s President Abdul Latif Jamal Rashid signed the country’s accession to two international agreements aimed at protecting cultural heritage and recovering stolen artifacts. The signing took place in Baghdad on Friday, in the presence of Culture, Tourism and Antiquities Minister Ahmed Fakak Al-Badrani and Antiquities and Heritage Authority head Laith Majeed Hussein. The agreements are the 2001 Convention for the Protection of the Underwater Cultural Heritage and the 1995 UNIDROIT Convention on stolen or illegally exported cultural objects. Rashid also authorized the culture minister to deposit the necessary mandate and coordinate with Iraq’s diplomatic mission in Paris and its permanent representative to UNESCO. He said the move reflects Iraq’s commitment to safeguarding its heritage and reclaiming looted antiquities.

# Summary Iraqi President Abdul Latif Jamal Rashid signed Iraq's accession to two international agreements protecting cultural heritage. The first is the 2001 convention for protecting underwater cultural heritage, and the second is the 1995 Unidroit Convention addressing stolen or illegally exported cultural objects. Culture Minister Ahmed Fakak Al-Badrani attended the ceremony alongside the head of the Antiquities and Heritage Authority. The President authorized the Culture Minister to deposit the mandate with relevant international parties and coordinate with Iraq's diplomatic mission in Paris and UNESCO representative. The accession reflects Iraq's commitment to safeguarding its cultural heritage and recovering antiquities stolen or smuggled from the country.

Chaldean Patriarch Mar Louis Raphael I Sako has urged Iraq’s Christians to remain faithful to the Gospel and to their homeland despite ongoing persecution and violence. In a letter to the Christian community of Iraq, he said the land is not merely “dust” but part of their identity, language, customs, traditions, history, memory, and authenticity. “Land is sacred,” he wrote, stressing that Iraqi Christians, like their ancestors, are called to stay faithful to Christ and to their country. The patriarch’s message comes amid severe pressure on the country’s Christian minority, which has faced abuse, violence, and persecution from Islamic State militias. He pointed to the destruction of another symbol of Iraq’s ancient Christian heritage on Wednesday night, when terrorists blew up Tikrit’s Green Church after placing explosives inside the building. The same attackers also destroyed a mosque. Sako presented faith as the opposite of destruction and despair. Drawing extensively on the Gospels, especially the Gospel of John, he said the risen Christ lives and works through the Church, guiding believers’ steps. Faith, he said, is “a journey into the light” that can bring joy even in darkness because peace and resurrection remain possible. It frees people from fear, narrow judgments, and attachment to the past, and returns them to “God’s logic,” which looks toward the future. He compared faith to love: a deep loyalty that endures hardship, grows through generosity, and becomes a lamp that turns into light and joy. Acknowledging fears about the future and the mass exodus of Christians, he said those who remain are still “firm and strong in our vocation.” He described the Church’s mission in Iraq as bringing the Gospel of joy and hope to all. Sako also criticized laypeople and priests who claim there is no future for Christians in Iraq, urging everyone to listen to the Holy Spirit and live the Gospel in daily life. He concluded that believers need the Holy Spirit’s strength and consolation as they face the violence and injustice of the world.

# Summary Baghdad Patriarch Mar Louis Raphael I Sako has issued a letter urging Iraqi Christians to remain faithful to Christ and their homeland despite severe persecution. The patriarch emphasizes that land represents more than physical territory—it embodies identity, language, customs, traditions, history, and authenticity, describing it as sacred. The message comes amid intensifying violence against Iraq's Christian minority by Islamic State militants. Most recently, terrorists destroyed Tikrit's Green Church by detonating explosives planted inside the building, continuing a pattern of attacks targeting Christian symbols in the country. Sako frames faith as a journey toward light that can provide hope and guidance even during the darkest periods. He invokes Gospel teachings, particularly from John and Saint Paul, to convey that the Risen Christ lives and works through the Church, directing believers' steps toward peace and resurrection. The patriarch characterizes faith as a "deep loyalty" comparable to love, describing it as a lamp that burns to illuminate darkness with joy. Acknowledging threats to Christian presence in Iraq and widespread fears about the local Church's future, Sako criticizes those—both lay people and priests—who claim there is no future for Christians in Iraq. He calls them to remain "firm and strong" in their vocation despite mass exodus. The patriarch stresses that Iraqi Christians' 2,000-year presence has enriched the nation through wealth, culture, and pluralism. Their mission is to spread the Gospel of joy and hope to all people. He concludes that only through faith and the Holy Spirit can believers find consolation and courage to face violence and injustice, emphasizing that while believers' lives are not easy, they must confront new challenges with confidence.

Iraqi Deputy Foreign Minister Mouhammad Jawad Al-Doraky said on Monday that he hoped visa formalities between Iran and Iraq would soon be canceled. Speaking to IRNA after the seventh Iran-Iraq joint consular session in Baghdad, he said the two countries share deep historical, religious, cultural, and traditional ties, and that their borders “have no meaning” between such brotherly neighbors. He described the memorandum of understanding signed at the end of the meeting as important because it would help provide better services for the millions of people who travel between the two countries each year. Al-Doraky said bilateral relations could serve as a model for coexistence. He noted that Iran and Iraq have already signed four memoranda of understanding in legal and judicial areas, including extradition of convicts. One agreement also covers consular facilitation, solving citizens’ problems, 24-hour operation of border terminals, and consideration of Iran’s proposal to abolish visa requirements. Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister Hassan Qashqavi, who attended the session, said Iran was ready to remove visa formalities, but implementation depended on Iraq. He said about two million Iraqis visited Iran and 1.5 million Iranians visited Iraq last year, and predicted 750,000 Iranians would travel to Iraq for Arbaein on December 13.

# Summary At the conclusion of the seventh Iran-Iraq joint consular session in Baghdad, Iraqi Deputy Foreign Minister Mouhammad Jawad Al-Doraky expressed hope for eliminating visa requirements between the two nations. He emphasized the strong commonalities shared by Iran and Iraq, including borders, religion, culture, and traditions, suggesting that their bilateral relations could serve as a model for regional coexistence. The session resulted in a significant memorandum of understanding, which Al-Doraky described as a foundation for enhanced services to the millions of citizens who travel between the countries annually. The agreement includes provisions for facilitating consular affairs, solving citizen problems, operating border terminals 24 hours, and examining Iran's proposal to cancel visa requirements. Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister Hassan Qashqavi stated that Iran is prepared to lift visa formalities, though implementation depends on Iraq's cooperation. He noted that approximately two million Iraqis visited Iran last year and 1.5 million Iranians visited Iraq. Additionally, he predicted around 750,000 Iranians will visit Iraq in December for Arbaein celebrations.

The article describes the struggle to preserve the Sassoon Synagogue, the last surviving synagogue in Mosul, Iraq, amid war damage, political hostility toward Israel, and efforts to rebuild the city’s religious heritage. The synagogue, located in Mosul’s old Jewish quarter, is a rare remnant of a once-thriving Jewish community that numbered nearly 6,000 people before the creation of Israel in 1948. Its graceful arches and muted brickwork still hint at that past, even though the building has been badly damaged and neglected for years. After the U.S. invasion of Iraq in 2003, the synagogue was desecrated and repurposed: garbage was dumped inside, and its ritual bath, or mikveh, was turned into a horse barn. The situation worsened under ISIS, which occupied Mosul beginning in 2014 and left the city’s historic fabric in ruins. When Mosul was liberated in 2017 by a U.S.-led military campaign, cultural sites began to reappear from the rubble. UNESCO later estimated that 80% of the city’s cultural heritage, including the Jewish district, had been destroyed. Among the surviving landmarks was the Sassoon Synagogue, though it remained in poor condition. An effort to save the synagogue has been led in part by Iraqi Jews such as Edwin Shuker, who visited the site in 2019 and has continued to advocate for its restoration. Shuker argues that the synagogue is not only a Jewish landmark but also a symbol of coexistence in Iraq’s history. He says international organizations, including the Swiss-based International Alliance for the Protection of Heritage in Conflict Areas (ALIPH), had shown interest in funding reconstruction. However, progress has been blocked by a new Iraqi law passed in May 2022 titled “Criminalizing Normalization and Establishment of Relations with the Zionist Entity.” The law bans Iraqis inside and outside the country from engaging with Israelis or “Zionists,” with penalties that can include life imprisonment or death. According to Shuker, this has frozen the ALIPH-backed project because any involvement connected to Israel has become politically and legally dangerous. The article places this in the broader historical context of the destruction of Iraqi Jewish life. After 1948, most Iraqi Jews were displaced or forced out, and by the early 1950s only about 8,000 remained from a population that had once reached 150,000. Over time, Jewish heritage sites across Iraq were erased or repurposed. Shrines associated with the biblical prophets Ezra, Ezekiel, and Jonah were converted into mosques, and almost all synagogues disappeared, leaving only the Meir Toeg synagogue in Baghdad besides the Mosul site. The Sassoon Synagogue survived, but only as a damaged shell. The effort to recover this history is now politically fraught. The article notes that trying to revive Jewish memory in Iraq has become even more sensitive after the June kidnapping in Baghdad of Russian-Israeli researcher Elizabeth Tsurkov. Still, some Iraqis continue to support preservation. One is Omar Mohammed, a researcher at George Washington University and founder of the anonymous Mosul Eye blog. He recently completed an oral-history project on Iraqi Jews and said that Jewish history has been omitted from Iraqi textbooks and public memory. He stresses that Jews who once lived in Mosul had homes, property, and community life there, and deserve to be remembered. The article closes by contrasting the active reconstruction of Mosul’s mosques and churches with the silence around the synagogue. For Shuker, walking into the building feels like entering “a carpet filled with bullet holes.” The Sassoon Synagogue remains a sacred ruin, standing as a damaged but important witness to Mosul’s pluralistic past and to the city’s shared history among Muslims, Christians, Jews, and Yazidis.

# The Race to Save Mosul's Last Synagogue The Sassoon Synagogue, located in the old Jewish quarter of Mosul, Iraq, stands as the city's only remaining synagogue and a testament to a rich Jewish heritage now nearly lost to history. Once home to approximately 6,000 Jews before Israel's establishment in 1948, Mosul has seen its Jewish population almost entirely displaced. The synagogue itself, distinguished by graceful pointed arches and ornate brickwork in earth tones including azure blue and burnt sienna, has suffered tremendous neglect—serving as a garbage dump and horse barn since the 2003 U.S. invasion. Following Mosul's liberation from ISIS in 2017, efforts to preserve the city's cultural landmarks intensified. According to UNESCO, 80 percent of the city's cultural heritage was destroyed during the conflict. While international organizations have mobilized to reconstruct significant religious sites like the Great Mosque of al-Nuri and the Church of Our Lady of the Hour, the Sassoon Synagogue remains largely abandoned. Edwin Shuker, an Iraqi-born Jew, has emerged as a leading advocate for the synagogue's preservation. He emphasizes its importance as a symbol of the religious coexistence that historically characterized Iraq. The Swiss-based International Alliance for the Protection of Heritage in Conflict Areas (ALIPH) designated funds specifically for the synagogue's reconstruction, recognizing its cultural significance. However, a major obstacle has emerged that threatens to permanently derail preservation efforts. In May 2022, the Iraqi parliament passed the "Criminalizing Normalization and Establishment of Relations with the Zionist Entity" law, which forbids any Iraqi citizen from connecting with Israelis or Zionists. Violators face imprisonment or death sentences. This legislation has effectively frozen ALIPH's reconstruction project, creating an impossible legal situation for those attempting to save the synagogue. The historical context makes this law's impact particularly significant. Following Israel's 1948 establishment, Iraq's Jewish population plummeted from 150,000 to 8,000 by the early 1950s as systematic displacement and deportation occurred. The Iraqi government subsequently implemented state policies aimed at erasing Jewish memory and heritage spanning 2,600 years. Hundreds of synagogues vanished, with biblical prophet shrines converted to mosques. The Sassoon Synagogue's survival itself was miraculous. Despite these challenges, some Iraqis continue advocating for Jewish heritage preservation. Omar Mohammed, a George Washington University researcher and "Mosul Eye" blogger, recently completed a project documenting oral histories of Iraq's Jewish community. He discovered that most deported Mosul Jews remain alive, though they no longer reside in Iraq. Mohammed emphasizes the importance of restoring this omitted history to Iraqi consciousness. The situation remains precarious. The 2024 kidnapping of Russian-Israeli researcher Elizabeth Tsurkov in Baghdad underscores the dangers facing those promoting Jewish-Israeli connections. Meanwhile, the few remaining Iraqi Jews hide their faith and discuss their history only in secret. As Muslim and Christian religious monuments rise from Mosul's rubble through reconstruction projects, the Sassoon Synagogue sits quietly deteriorating. Its preservation would represent crucial acknowledgment of the religious pluralism and shared history among Muslims, Christians, Jews, and Yazidis that once characterized the region. Currently, however, parliamentary legislation effectively ensures the synagogue remains a sacred ruin, symbolizing both Mosul's lost Jewish heritage and the complex political realities preventing its restoration.

A month after the Islamic State’s advance triggered the mass flight of Christians, Yazidis and other minorities from northern Iraq, Chaldean Patriarch Louis Raphael I Sako warned that their suffering is worsening and that Iraq’s ancient pluralistic fabric is at risk of disappearing. In a written appeal to AsiaNews, the Baghdad patriarch described the displacement as a form of “genocide” against a people stripped of “religious, human, moral and national values,” and said the crisis is not only a tragedy for Christians but “a threat for all.” Sako said the exodus was not a solution for Christians, whom he described as the “leaven” of Iraq and bearers of hope. He argued that Iraq’s Christians should not abandon their homeland despite the danger and instability, but instead organize themselves, raise their voices, and work with others to build a new model of coexistence among Shiites, Sunnis, Arabs, Kurds, Turkmens, Christians and Yezidis. He also criticized both the Iraqi government and the broader international community for what he saw as hesitation and inaction in the face of Islamist violence. The patriarch’s letter was written against the backdrop of the Islamic State’s seizure of Christian and minority areas, which forced around 120,000 Christians from their historical homeland. He said the world had effectively turned away from the suffering, either because it approved of what was happening or because it was incapable of responding. In his view, ISIS was waging a ferocious war not only against people but against culture and diversity, threatening intellectual and social security as well. Sako portrayed the displaced as people who had lived in prosperity, pride and dignity in their hometowns until they were suddenly driven out, often on foot and in terror, in search of shelter. He said their children were traumatized, their towns seized and their homes looted, and that the scene recalled the darkest periods of history even though it was unfolding in the modern world. He called the violence a real genocide and a shameful stain on history. To underscore the human dimension of the crisis, he pointed to a 13-year-old girl appearing on Ishtar satellite channel who cried that she wanted to return to Qaraqosh and would rather die than continue living in humiliation. For Sako, her words were a plea to the world’s conscience. The patriarch also denounced the weakness of the Iraqi state, saying the government had failed to impose law and order as security deteriorated. He said this atmosphere of violence allowed extremist groups to expand. In Baghdad, he added, Christians and others were being kidnapped in broad daylight by armed men in tinted cars, threatened to leave their homes, and harassed in schools and public offices. He asked whether such behavior could continue without control or any effort at re-education. He also criticized political leaders for fighting over positions rather than uniting to identify the roots of extremism, violence and injustice, and to develop serious solutions before it was too late. He expressed hope that the new prime minister and government would recognize their historical, national and moral responsibility. Sako rejected emigration as the answer, saying many displaced Christians, robbed of everything including their documents and left with little trust in the authorities, were now waiting for an uncertain future and considering departure for Western countries. He said that in their own country, “only disasters prevail,” but insisted that leaving should not become the final solution. To avoid extinction, he said, Christians must remain active and courageous, preserve their role as a living witness, and pressure decision-makers at home and abroad to ensure a safe life in Iraq. He then outlined a series of practical proposals. These included forming competent Christian political and independent organizations; creating a crisis management team to document displaced families and seek compensation; setting up an education committee to track displaced students and help them continue schooling, including in Kurdistan; asking the UN and donor countries to build proper housing instead of tents for those unable or unwilling to return; and urging the UN Security Council to establish a peacekeeping force with Iraqi and Kurdish forces to liberate the Nineveh Plain and secure the return of residents. He also called for local police drawn from the communities of the Nineveh Plain, in line with a new law he said had been presented to the government, and for a UN Human Rights Council investigation into atrocities committed by the Islamic State, with those responsible brought to justice for crimes against humanity. At the broader ideological level, Sako urged resistance to extremism and the creation of a new mentality of living together in peace and harmony. He said the Islamic world must stop giving religious legitimacy and financial support to militants. Finally, he appealed to both the central Iraqi government and the Kurdistan regional government to promote openness, diversity, pluralism and equality against extremism, marginalization and backwardness. He said this transformation must begin with education, especially through changes in school and university curricula, because only education can build a society of equal citizens and a civil society that respects every religion and does not politicize faith for its own benefit.

# Baghdad Patriarch Warns of Christian Extinction in Iraq, Calls for Unity Against Islamism Mar Raphael I Louis Sako, the Chaldean Patriarch of Baghdad, has issued an urgent appeal describing the plight of Iraqi Christians and other minorities as a "genocide," warning that their continued existence in their homeland faces existential threat. He advocates for establishing a "new mentality of living together" among Shiites, Sunnis, Arabs, Kurds, Turkmens, Christians, and Yezidis in peace and harmony. This requires offensive action at the ideological level within the Islamic world to eliminate religious and financial legitimation of fundamentalism. Mar Sako's appeal represents both an anguished cry for immediate humanitarian intervention and a call for long-term structural transformation of Iraqi society. His emphasis on education, pluralism, and inclusive governance reflects conviction that extremism's roots run deep and require comprehensive solutions addressing ideology, governance, and social consciousness rather than merely military responses.

He asked God to protect Iraq and preserve it from evil, and framed the holiday as an opportunity to renew values of sacrifice, human dignity, and mutual respect. Sako said that Iraq cannot achieve freedom or dignity without honest relationships that recognize others as brothers and partners in the country. He called for genuine reconciliation, courageous dialogue, and effective political action to restore peace, security, and stability after years of conflict and war. Baghdad’s National Heritage Museum is reopening after being closed for 10 years, following its looting during the 2003 US-led invasion and the fall of Saddam Hussein. The museum, in Baghdad’s Al-Eskan district, has undergone extensive renovations under the Ministry of Culture, including the addition of traditional Baghdad shanasheel, or ornate oriental windows, and a design based on old Baghdad architecture and local building materials. Since the 2003 ransacking, museum staff, working with the ministry’s Fine Arts Department, have also been collecting rare antiquities for display in the restored Dome Hall. The new exhibits focus on everyday life in Iraq and the region over the past 200 years, including trade professions, coffeehouses, games, and traditions. Visitors will see handmade carpets, silver objects, traditional clothing for children and adults, and household items used by Iraqi families in the early 20th century. The collection also includes traditional guestrooms furnished with items made by skilled Iraqi craftsmen. Officials say the museum is an important national symbol and is expected to attract visitors and tourists interested in Mesopotamian civilization.

# Baghdad's National Heritage Museum Reopens Baghdad's National Heritage Museum has reopened after a decade-long closure following its looting during the 2003 US-led invasion that toppled Saddam Hussein. Located in western Baghdad's Al-Eskan district, the museum underwent extensive renovations featuring traditional Baghdad architectural elements, including ornate oriental windows and traditional building materials. Since its ransacking in 2003, museum staff coordinated with the Ministry of Culture's Fine Arts Department to acquire rare antiquities for the restored Dome Hall. The new collection showcases regional life over the past 200 years, including trade professions, coffeehouses, games, and traditions. Exhibits feature handmade carpets, silver objects, traditional clothing, and early 20th-century household items. A notable addition is a traditional guestroom displaying craftsman-made furnishings reflecting authentic Iraqi artisanship. Ministry officials describe the reopened museum as an important national symbol and cultural hub, positioning it to attract international visitors interested in Mesopotamian civilization and Iraqi heritage.

Oliver Laxe’s new film, *Sirāt*, has become one of the year’s most discussed titles since its prize-winning premiere at Cannes, and the director says the response has confirmed his belief that cinema should unsettle, not merely entertain. Speaking in Toronto during the fall film festival circuit, the 41-year-old French-born Galician filmmaker described the movie as a spiritual and existential journey designed to push viewers to look inward. *Sirāt* follows a father, played by Sergi López, and his 12-year-old son, played by Bruno Núñez Arjona, as they search for the father’s teenage daughter. Their search leads them to a remote rave in southern Morocco, where they fail to find her and instead join a small caravan of ravers crossing a vast desert. From there, the film expands into a stark meditation on impending catastrophe. A driving beat runs through the movie, but so do references to World War III on the radio and the effects of climate change on a parched landscape where water is scarce. The title means “path” or “way” in Arabic, and the film is unusually direct about the future it imagines for its characters and, by extension, for humanity. The film opens Friday for a one-week qualifying run in select theaters ahead of the Oscars, where it is Spain’s official submission. Neon will release it more widely in early 2026. It has already become a commercial success in Spain and France, and critics and audiences have compared it to *The Wages of Fear* and *Mad Max*. While the film has not been universally embraced, it has clearly made an impact. Laxe says that is the point. “For me, cinema isn’t about ‘I like it’ or ‘I don’t like it,’” he said. “My purpose is: Did it move something?” He described *Sirāt* as a “rite of passage” and said his aim was to provoke viewers into confronting their inner lives. In his view, much of modern audio-visual production is “made for destruction,” while people need to look inside if they are to become free and emancipated. He connected the film’s themes to climate change, artificial intelligence, and a broader human crisis of identity, saying the world is pushing people toward asking what it means to be human. Laxe also framed the movie as a kind of ceremonial experience rather than conventional entertainment. He said Cannes served as a test and noted that some people told him the film felt like “a ceremony.” He compared this to ancient Greek theater, which he said was meant to purge ghosts and serve society rather than simply amuse spectators. The director said the images for *Sirāt* began forming in 2011, after his first feature, a low-budget film made in Tangier with local neighbors. He later lived in a palm grove in southern Morocco, and additional inspiration came from trips to Senegal and Mauritania. The Moroccan desert and mountains, he said, feel like a “wounded landscape” where erosion and geological layers reveal the planet’s creation. He said the setting makes him feel small in a way that fosters humility rather than anxiety, and that he is always searching for transcendence. Laxe described himself as someone drawn to limits, and he linked art, rave culture, and spirituality to the experience of crossing dangerous thresholds without knowing where the path leads. He said the production was one of his easier shoots, though he acknowledged that filmmakers can be their own worst enemies by trying to say too much and thereby destroying the raw power of images. He also admitted to being frightened while making the film. Feedback from friends, including one who said, “We don’t want people to suffer,” made him question who he was making the film for. Still, he said he kept going because he knew he had to “jump into the abyss” and cross his own “minefield.” Some viewers, he said, are shaken by the movie, but later tell him they feel revived, as if the experience leaves them with more life.

Joanna Kulig, little known to many American audiences, is emerging as an international star thanks to her lead performance in Pawel Pawlikowski’s Polish drama “Cold War.” The film, expanding theatrically in the United States, centers on Zula, a singer played by Kulig, and Wiktor, a musician played by Tomasz Kot, whose passionate relationship spans years and borders in postwar Eastern Europe. Critics have praised Kulig’s screen presence, likening her to classic movie stars such as Jeanne Moreau and even Jennifer Lawrence. Kulig, 36, had already built a career in Polish film and television, appearing in projects such as “Elles” with Juliette Binoche and Pawlikowski’s earlier film “Ida.” But “Cold War” brought her a new level of attention after its premiere at the Cannes Film Festival, where it received an eight-minute standing ovation. Kulig said the response was overwhelming and unlike anything she had experienced before, noting that even stars like Julianne Moore and Benicio del Toro were moved to tears. Josh Gordon’s latest NFL suspension is presented as the result of his own repeated choices, not simply bad luck or overzealous enforcement by the league or the Cleveland Browns. The 23-year-old Browns receiver was suspended without pay for at least one year on Tuesday after again violating the NFL’s substance abuse policy, this time by failing an alcohol test. It was his third NFL suspension in three seasons, and the Browns had already disciplined him late last season for missing a team walk-through. The article argues that attempts to excuse Gordon’s behavior have failed and that he needs “tough love” rather than more enabling. Browns general manager Ray Farmer said the team was disappointed to once again be dealing with the situation. Farmer’s statement reflected frustration with a player whose talent has repeatedly been overshadowed by off-field problems. Gordon tried to explain the latest violation in an open letter published on The Cauldron. He said he had consumed two drinks and two beers on a flight to Las Vegas with teammates on Jan. 2, believing it was acceptable because the season was over. But the NFL had already imposed a zero-tolerance alcohol policy on him because of a DWI arrest the previous July and earlier substance-abuse issues. Gordon made matters worse by posting a video from the flight on social media, and when the plane landed he was notified that he had to report for a test within four hours. He failed that test. The piece places this incident in the context of a long pattern of substance-related troubles. Gordon had failed at least three marijuana tests in college and was expelled from both Utah and Baylor. In the NFL, he was suspended for two games in 2013, which he said stemmed from codeine in a prescribed cough syrup, and for 10 games in 2014, which he attributed to second-hand marijuana smoke. While NFL test results are confidential, the article notes that Gordon’s own explanations are unverified and likely contain some spin. Gordon’s letter also included a series of admissions and defenses. He wrote that he had failed himself by using marijuana regularly as a young teenager, by derailing his chance to play alongside Robert Griffin III at Baylor, by not checking whether his prescribed codeine medicine was permitted under NFL rules, by getting arrested for driving with an illegal blood-alcohol level, and by missing a late-season walk-through that led to his suspension for the final game of the year. At the same time, he insisted he was “not someone who deserves to be dissected and analyzed” as a cautionary tale, saying he was a human being with flaws who would persevere. The article is skeptical of Gordon’s self-description. It says his words about growth and responsibility are undermined by his actions. Browns sources reportedly said he had been late for meetings and other team obligations long before missing the final walk-through. The writer emphasizes that Gordon’s problems are not only about drugs or alcohol, but also about accountability and professionalism. Gordon also portrayed himself as someone who overcame poverty, violence, and lack of guidance in Houston, and who worked hard to escape a difficult environment. He said he had succeeded by avoiding crime, developing his football skills, and overcoming a long relationship with marijuana. Yet the article asks why, if that is true, he continues to risk everything. It suggests that immaturity may explain some of his behavior, but that recovery requires genuine willingness, not just need. In the end, Gordon insists he is neither a drug addict nor an alcoholic, but the Browns and the NFL no longer appear willing to accept that claim. Farmer said the team had repeatedly tried to help him and provide support, but those efforts had not worked. The Browns believe Gordon must make major changes if he is ever to fit the positive culture they are trying to build.

Canadian publishers are heading into the fall book season with what they describe as a particularly strong and wide-ranging lineup, anchored by major names in fiction, memoir, politics and non-fiction. The season is especially important for sales because, as Random House of Canada vice-president and associate publisher Scott Sellers notes, December and January remain the biggest months for buying books, and the fall release schedule feeds directly into the Christmas shopping period and the post-holiday market. Among the most attention-grabbing Canadian titles is a debut novel from filmmaker David Cronenberg. Best known for films such as *The Fly* and *A History of Violence*, Cronenberg is entering the literary world with *Consumed* (Hamish Hamilton Canada, Sept. 30), a novel about a young journalist investigating a grisly cannibalism murder in Paris. His publisher says the book has the same unsettling, provocative quality as his films and should not disappoint readers expecting something dark and twisted. Penguin’s Beth Lockley calls it a “riveting debut” that is “absolutely unapologetic,” sexually charged, provocative and “intoxicating.” Another major fall release comes from Margaret Atwood, whose *The Stone Mattress* (McClelland & Stewart, Sept. 9) marks her first short story collection since 2006’s *Moral Disorder*. The nine stories are described as inventive, rewarding and marked by Atwood’s trademark dark humour and playfulness. The publisher emphasizes that the collection is “deadly serious” while still displaying the wit and energy that have long defined her work. The season also includes high-profile autobiographical and political books. Liberal Leader Justin Trudeau’s *Common Ground* (HarperCollins Canada, Oct. 21) is presented as candid and thoughtful, offering insights into his life and his views on Canada’s future. HarperCollins publisher and editor-in-chief Iris Tupholme says Trudeau is known for speaking directly and honestly, and that readers can expect the same tone in the book. Hockey legend Gordie Howe’s *Mr. Hockey* (Viking Canada, Oct. 14) traces his life from Depression-era roots in a Saskatoon farmhouse to a five-decade career in hockey, along with his family relationships. Several other hockey figures are also publishing memoirs this fall. Jordin Tootoo’s *All the Way* (Viking, Oct. 21) recounts his experience as the first NHL player of Inuk descent, along with his struggles with addiction and the death of his brother. Clint Malarchuk’s *The Crazy Game* (HarperCollins, Oct. 21) addresses the anxiety, depression and obsessive compulsive disorder he dealt with during his playing career. Larry Robinson’s *The Great Defender* (FENN-M&S, Nov. 4) reflects on his 20 seasons in the NHL. Canadian fiction is especially prominent. Ann-Marie MacDonald returns after more than a decade with *Adult Onset* (Knopf Canada, Sept. 30), her first novel since *The Way the Crow Flies*. The book follows a semi-retired Toronto author whose old illness returns as tensions in her life intensify. David Bergen’s *Leaving Tomorrow* (HarperCollins, Sept. 16), his first novel since winning the 2005 Scotiabank Giller Prize for *The Time In Between*, centers on a small-town Alberta writer who moves to Paris. Johanna Skibsrud’s *Quartet for the End of Time* (Hamish Hamilton, Sept. 23), her first novel since winning the 2010 Giller Prize with *The Sentimentalists*, weaves together four characters during the 1932 Bonus Army Riots in Washington, D.C. David Bezmozgis’s *The Betrayers* (HarperCollins, now on shelves) follows a disgraced Israeli politician through a single day, while Michael Crummey’s *Sweetland* (Doubleday Canada, now on shelves) tells of a Newfoundland man refusing government compensation to resettle, a story about disappearing outport life and the hold of the past. Other notable fiction includes Kim Thuy’s *Man* (Random House, now on shelves), her follow-up to the Governor General’s Literary Award-winning *Ru*, about a woman who marries a Vietnamese restaurateur and becomes a chef in Montreal. Thomas King’s *The Back of the Turtle* (HarperCollins, out now), his first literary novel in 15 years, follows a scientist returning to his mother’s reserve only to find it gone. Publishers praise the book’s mix of Native mythology, Christianity and humour. Dionne Brand’s *Love Enough* (Knopf Canada, Sept. 30) brings together several intersecting characters. Carrie Snyder’s *Girl Runner* (House of Anansi Press, Sept. 6), about a centenarian former Olympic athlete, has already sold into nine territories. Russell Wangersky’s thriller *Walt* (Anansi, Sept. 13) follows *Whirl Away*. Emily St. John Mandel’s *Station Eleven* (HarperCollins, Sept. 9), about the aftermath of a stage star’s death, is another key release. The non-fiction list is equally broad. M.G. Vassanji’s *And Home was Kariakoo* (Doubleday, Oct. 14) explores his East African birthplace. Naomi Klein’s *This Changes Everything: Capitalism vs. the Climate* (Knopf Canada, Sept. 16) is billed as her most provocative book yet. Retired astronaut Chris Hadfield’s *You Are Here: Around the World in 92 Minutes* (Random House, Oct. 14) showcases photos he took from the International Space Station. The memoir section features Hazel McCallion’s *Hurricane Hazel* (HarperCollins, Oct. 21), Bruce Cockburn’s *Rumours of Glory* (HarperCollins, Nov. 4), Alan Doyle’s *Where I Belong* (Doubleday, Oct. 14), and Don Cherry’s *Straight Up and Personal* (Doubleday, Nov. 4). Publishers say the breadth of the season is the point: there is, in Lockley’s words, “a little bit of something for any reader out there.” Tupholme calls the list a “blockbuster” lineup with books across every category and says readers will find something for almost everyone.

Oliver Laxe’s “Sirāt” has become one of the most discussed films of the year since its prize-winning premiere at the Cannes Film Festival, and the director says that notoriety now follows him everywhere. “When I’m on a plane and things are going bad, I say, ‘Come on, you’re the director of ‘Sirāt.’ You cannot be scared,’” Laxe jokes. The 41-year-old, French-born Galician filmmaker has built a reputation for making spiritually charged, physically demanding films, and “Sirāt” has intensified that image. The film follows a father, played by Sergi López, and his 12-year-old son, played by Bruno Núñez Arjona, as they search for the father’s teenage daughter. Their search leads them to a remote rave in southern Morocco, where they fail to find her. From there, they join a small caravan of ravers moving across a vast desert landscape. What begins as a search party and a nocturnal subculture story gradually becomes something more severe and symbolic: a primal, existential journey toward apocalypse. The soundtrack pulses with a relentless beat, while the plot incorporates references to World War III on the radio and the harsh realities of climate change in a water-starved landscape. The title, “Sirāt,” is Arabic for “path” or “way,” and the film is unusually direct about the future it imagines for both its characters and the world beyond them. The movie opens in select theaters for a one-week qualifying run for the Oscars, where it is Spain’s submission. Neon will release it more widely in early 2026. It has already become a commercial success in Spain and France and has drawn comparisons to “The Wages of Fear” and “Mad Max.” Although the film has not won over everyone, it has clearly made an impact. For Laxe, that response is precisely the point. He says he is not interested in whether viewers simply “like” or “don’t like” a film. “My purpose is: Did it move something?” he says. At the Toronto International Film Festival, where he spoke with The Associated Press earlier this fall, Laxe discussed the film’s spiritual foundation and his belief that filmmaking must do something different now. He argued that most audiovisual production is made for “destruction,” and that people need to look inward if they want to become freer and more emancipated. In his view, “Sirāt” is a kind of rite of passage meant to force that inward gaze, even if what one finds there is uncomfortable. Laxe also suggested that the film’s broader idea is that everyone is, in a sense, a migrant. He said the future will push people to a border where they are forced to confront what it means to be human. Climate change and artificial intelligence, he argued, make that question unavoidable. Drawing on his study of psychotherapy, he said people are “broken” and disconnected from their wounds, which leads to fear and anguish. Despite the film’s bleakness, he described himself as optimistic, saying the coming era will be difficult but will compel people to look within. He also framed “Sirāt” as more than a conventional film, describing it instead as a ceremony. He pointed to ancient Greek theater as an example of art designed not for entertainment, but for purification and social renewal. In that sense, he sees cinema as something that should transform the audience, not merely amuse them. The origins of the film go back to 2011, when Laxe began developing its images after releasing his first feature, a low-budget film made in Tangiers with local neighbors. He later lived in a palm grove in southern Morocco, and also traveled in Senegal and Mauritania. The desert and mountain landscapes of Morocco inspired him deeply. He described them as wounded and layered, landscapes that make a person feel small in a humbling, not frightening, way. For a filmmaker seeking transcendence, they were the right setting. Laxe acknowledged that shooting “Sirāt” was physically demanding, with sandstorms and intense summer heat, but he said he likes to work near his limits. He connected art, rave culture, and spirituality through the idea of crossing minefields and venturing into the unknown. He also said this was one of his easier shoots, though he emphasized that filmmakers can undermine their own work by overexplaining it and “killing” its images. His goal, he said, is to preserve the raw, wild quality of the original vision from conception through production. Even so, he admitted he was afraid of the film’s reaction. Friends questioned whether audiences should be made to suffer, and he wondered who he was making the film for. But he kept going, saying he knew he had to “jump into the abyss” and cross his own minefield. Some viewers, he said, are shaken or frightened by the movie, but then tell him they feel revived when they leave the theater, as if they have more life.

Archeologists in Mexico have uncovered the ruins of a large Mayan palace in the Kulubá archaeological zone in Yucatán, about 160 kilometers from Cancún. The National Institute of Anthropology and History said the structure likely dates from 600 to 1050 A.D., during the Late Classic and Terminal Classic periods, when Mayan civilization was at its height. The palace measures about six meters high, 55 meters long, and 15 meters wide. Researchers are also studying nearby structures, including an altar, two possible residential buildings, an oven-like structure, and a burial site that may reveal more about the people who lived there. Lead archeologist Alfredo Barrera said the find is only the beginning and that protecting and restoring the site is a priority, with reforestation being considered to shield it from weather and sunlight. # Ancient Mayan Palace Discovered in Mexico Archaeologists have uncovered the ruins of a large palace in the Kulubá archaeological zone in Yucatan state, Mexico, approximately 160 kilometers from Cancún. The structure, measuring six meters high, 55 meters long, and 15 meters wide, dates back roughly 1,000 years to the Late Classic and Terminal Classic eras (600-1050 A.D.) of Mayan civilization. The site contains several additional structures, including an altar, two residential buildings, what appears to be an oven, and a burial site that researchers hope will provide insights into Mayan life. Lead archaeologist Alfredo Barrera emphasized that this discovery is just the beginning, with plans for protection and restoration of the cultural heritage through reforestation and other conservation methods. The Mayan civilization, considered one of the greatest in the Western Hemisphere, mysteriously declined before abandoning its cities. Scientists attribute this collapse to potential factors including climate change, drought, war, disease, and political instability.
