Vladimir Putin has spent nearly two decades as Russia’s dominant political figure, and the article portrays him as a leader who has carefully cultivated an image of reserve, control and distance. Unlike many Western politicians, and even unlike some Russian predecessors, Putin rarely reveals anything personal in public. His body may be familiar from photos of him horseback riding, fishing or otherwise posing in athletic settings, but his inner life remains largely hidden. The article argues that this emotional opacity is not just a matter of style; it may be central to who he is and how he rules. The piece opens by noting that after 18 years in power, with another six-year term expected after the March election, Putin does not display the appetites, vulnerabilities or spontaneity that often humanize politicians. If he experiences joy or sadness, it is kept private. Even in Russia’s political culture, which is often rigid and controlled, his restraint stands out. He has never shown the flamboyance of Boris Yeltsin, who once danced wildly in public, or the self-confessed rock enthusiasm of Dmitry Medvedev, who openly described himself as a Deep Purple fan. Some observers interpret Putin’s guarded nature as intentional self-protection. He may avoid revealing himself because he fears opponents could exploit any weakness. Others believe the lack of openness reflects his essence: a man so consumed by power that other interests are blurred. When George W. Bush once said he had gotten “a sense of his soul” after meeting Putin in 2001, critics mocked the idea, suggesting Putin had no soul at all. Mikhail Zygar, an editor and author of a book about the Kremlin, says Putin simply does not like people naturally and distrusts politicians who talk about values. Yet the article also presents a contrasting view from people who knew Putin earlier in life. Two of his former law professors in Leningrad, now St. Petersburg, describe him as warm, witty, sincere and open. Yuri Tolstoy, now 90, said Putin recently visited him after Tolstoy received Russia’s highest civilian honor, and that the meeting left him feeling better physically and energized. Another professor, Dzhenevra Lukovskaya, said Putin is charming and witty and that he meets Russia’s challenge of national self-definition. These reflections suggest that the private Putin may be more personable than the public one appears. The article then places Putin in a Russian historical and psychological context. Russia, it says, seems to be the object of Putin’s own self-identification: he may not be guided by a broad moral philosophy, but he appears to have an intense sense of being Russian, perhaps even embodying Russia itself. Zygar argues that Putin does not see himself as a dictator but as someone trying to save the country. He also describes Putin as tactical rather than strategic, good at responding to events rather than plotting grand designs. Russia’s military intervention in Syria is cited as an example of a reactive move shaped by frustration over international criticism of Russia’s support for separatists in Ukraine. The article traces Putin’s background to explain the origins of his drive for power. Born in 1952 in Leningrad to factory-worker parents, he grew up in a city haunted by memories of the nearly 900-day Nazi siege during World War II. One older brother died during the siege, and another died shortly after birth. Putin later described his childhood as harsh, spent in a bleak communal apartment. He said he became something of a “hooligan” and was one of the few students not admitted to the Communist Young Pioneers. As a teenager, he turned to martial arts, which he practiced seriously for many years. His path into the KGB began with youthful determination. He went to a local KGB office and asked to join, only to be told that the agency did not trust people who simply walked in off the street. He later said he waited through university for the KGB to remember him, and eventually an agent contacted him. His eventual posting was to Dresden in East Germany. Critics later dismissed his KGB career as unimpressive, since Dresden was in a Soviet ally rather than a hostile intelligence environment. Zygar argues that Putin’s real turning point came after the KGB, when he worked under Anatoly Sobchak, the reform-minded mayor of St. Petersburg. Sobchak embraced democratic procedures and lost an open election, which Zygar says was a formative lesson for Putin: never repeat the mistakes of free elections, open debates and influential opposition. That lesson, the article suggests, is relevant to the 2018 presidential race, in which anti-corruption campaigner Alexei Navalny is likely to be barred from running because of a felony conviction. The only notable alternative discussed is Ksenia Sobchak, the mayor’s daughter and a television personality, though she had not yet qualified for the ballot. Putin’s rise to national power was swift. In 1999, after being named prime minister by Boris Yeltsin, he was still relatively obscure. But his tough comments during the second Chechen war, especially the line about “wasting” terrorists “in the outhouse” if caught there, instantly projected a macho, ruthless image that has largely defined him ever since. Since then, public glimpses of tenderness have been rare: cuddling puppies from foreign leaders or kissing a child’s stomach. His family life is similarly hidden. He does not appear publicly with his two adult daughters, and his 2013 divorce from Lyudmila was handled in a highly staged televised announcement. The article ends by suggesting that Putin’s need for control may make it hard to imagine him simply retiring. If re-elected, he would be term-limited in 2024, but analysts quoted in the piece doubt he would step away from power. Dmitry Trenin of the Carnegie Moscow Center says Putin is more likely to shift into another role that would still allow him to oversee Russia from a different position.

# Putin: Public Man Who Remains Largely Mysterious Vladimir Putin has led Russia for 18 years and is poised to win another six-year term in a March election, yet he remains one of the world's most enigmatic political figures. Despite his shirtless public appearances and carefully cultivated image, Putin reveals remarkably little about his personal life or inner thoughts—a level of reserve that stands out even in Russia's rigid political culture. Unlike Western leaders who often display vulnerabilities or personal interests, Putin maintains an air of distance and shadow. He has never engaged in the uninhibited behavior of his predecessor Boris Yeltsin, who was known for spontaneous dancing, nor has he publicly championed personal passions like Dmitry Medvedev's love of rock music. This restraint may stem from Putin's calculated concern that opponents could exploit personal information, or it may simply reflect his singular focus on power. Observers offer conflicting interpretations of Putin's personality. Mikhail Zygar, editor at independent Dozhd TV and author of "All The Kremlin's Men," suggests Putin distrusts people naturally and dismisses politicians who speak about values. However, former law professors paint a warmer picture. Yuri Tolstoy, 90, describes Putin as easy-going, encouraging, and charming, claiming the president's recent visit improved his health. Another former professor, Dzhenevra Lukovskaya, calls Putin sincere, open, and witty. What emerges most clearly is that Russia itself appears to be Putin's primary identity. Rather than embracing a comprehensive ethical system, Putin seems to view himself as embodying Russia and saving the country from threats. Zygar characterizes him not as a grand strategist but as a tactical responder—citing the Syria military campaign as an example, launched partly out of exasperation with international criticism over Russia's Ukraine involvement. Putin's background illuminates his hunger for both visible and clandestine power. Born October 7, 1952, to factory-worker parents in Leningrad, he grew up in a city haunted by a nearly 900-day Nazi siege during World War II. Two of his older brothers died—one from diphtheria during the siege, another shortly after birth. The family lived in a dismal communal apartment with primitive facilities, an environment that shaped young Vladimir profoundly. Putin responded to these rough circumstances by becoming a childhood "hooligan," one of the few in his school barred from joining the Communist Young Pioneers. He later channeled his aggression into martial arts, practicing intensely into middle age. In a moment of youthful determination, he visited a local KGB office to inquire about joining the spy service. Though initially rebuffed, he eventually received a call years later from a mysterious man who recruited him. Putin's KGB career took him to Dresden in East Germany—a posting that critics later suggested demonstrated limited acuity in intelligence work. Zygar argues the KGB years were less significant than Putin's subsequent experience as deputy to Anatoly Sobchak, St. Petersburg's reform-minded mayor. Sobchak's fatal mistake, in Zygar's view, was holding free and fair elections and accepting defeat—a lesson Putin apparently learned well. This experience likely explains his approach to the 2018 election, where the only truly influential opposition figure, anti-corruption campaigner Alexei Navalny, faces near-certain ballot exclusion due to a felony conviction. Putin's meteoric rise to national prominence occurred with extraordinary speed. Before becoming Prime Minister in August 1999, he headed the Federal Security Service, an inherently low-visibility position. However, his comments about the second Chechen war made an indelible impression: "If we capture them in the toilet, then we will waste them in the outhouse." This adamant, macho, crude remark seemed to encapsulate Putin's essence, an image he has maintained consistently since then. Glimpses of Putin's private self remain rare. He makes no public appearances with his two adult daughters. His 2013 divorce announcement from wife Lyudmila was orchestrated with precision—the couple appeared on national television at an opera intermission, praised the performance, and announced their separation with theatrical control. Control appears fundamental to Putin's nature. Director of the Carnegie Moscow Center Dmitry Trenin suggests that if Putin wins re-election, he is unlikely to retire when termed out in 2024, instead taking another position from which to oversee Russian affairs. The question of how Putin would function without the presidency remains difficult to envision.

After contract verification, the buyer would send tokens to the specified address and receive either a download link or confirmation that services had been delivered. The seller would then receive the payment minus a platform commission, with the commission rate varying according to factors such as transaction type, user ratings, and total amount. Beyond payments, VRT tokens would also be used to reward participants for tasks such as content moderation and conflict resolution. The company said it would create a token fund for these incentives. Tokens could also be used to pay for content storage in a decentralized system based on IPFS, where users’ servers and hard drives would store platform content. Finally, VRT tokens would be used for entry into the company’s VR parks at a 20% discount, and they would be the only accepted payment for lump-sum franchise agreements. The article describes the contradictory place of Central Asian Muslims in Russia: they are widely mocked, discriminated against, and sometimes violently attacked, yet many also manage to build successful lives and careers there. It opens with the popular Russian TV comedy *Our Russia*, whose characters Ravshan and Joomshut are portrayed as bumbling labour migrants from ex-Soviet Central Asia. Their broken Russian, poor hygiene, and servile roles have turned their names into a slur and a symbol of negative Russian stereotypes about people from the mostly Muslim region. Sandjar Yanyshev, a Moscow-based Uzbek essayist and poet, says the comedy reflects a deeper fear of “darkies,” a racist term some xenophobes use for Central Asians and other Muslims. In his view, ridicule is a way of neutralizing fear: “What’s funny is not dangerous.” The article notes that millions of migrants from Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, and Kyrgyzstan work in Russia, usually in low-paid manual jobs. Xenophobia is common. A Levada poll from July found that 27 percent of Russians felt irritation, dislike, or fear toward Central Asians, and nearly one in five believed their presence in Russia should be limited. This hostility is not just verbal: hundreds have been killed and thousands injured in attacks by ultra-nationalists and skinheads. Migrants are also frequent targets of corrupt police, who extort money from them under threat of detention or deportation. Despite this environment, some Central Asians have risen to great prominence in Russia and beyond. The article highlights Alisher Usmanov, an ethnic Uzbek and Russia’s richest oligarch, with an estimated fortune of $15 billion. The son of a minor Soviet official, he controls steel businesses, co-owns Arsenal football club in Britain, and is said to be close to President Vladimir Putin. Other examples include Uzbek singer Nargiz Zakirova, whose unusual voice and appearance made her one of Russia’s most popular touring artists; rapper Jah Khalib and film director Timur Bekmambetov from Kazakhstan; and cosmonaut Salijan Sharipov, born in southern Kyrgyzstan, who spent more than 200 days in space and carried a copy of the Quran with him. The article emphasizes that Central Asians often have an advantage over migrants in Western Europe because they share historical and cultural ties with Russia and frequently speak Russian fluently. Khakim Ganiev, a chef and author of books on Uzbek cuisine, says many learned the language in school, which makes adaptation easier. Although they are often seen as a blue-collar workforce, many Central Asians in Russia work as software engineers, designers, doctors, and scholars. Yet success does not erase prejudice. The case of actor Aziz Beyshenaliev shows the limits of integration. An ethnic Kyrgyz who moved to Moscow in 1997, he first worked as a courier and loader before landing small film and television roles, often as terrorists, warlords, or historical figures. But in 2015 he left Russia after his son Seitek, then a schoolboy, experienced ostracism and repeated hate attacks because of his Asian features. Beyshenaliev said he could mentally detach himself from a hostile society, but his son could not. Seitek later flourished in a school in Almaty, Kazakhstan, while his father shifted into directing and theatre acting. The article places today’s migration in a long historical context. Central Asia and Russia have been linked for centuries through conquest, empire, and Soviet rule. Descendants of Mongol conqueror Genghis Khan ruled the Golden Horde, which later fractured and saw some nobles ally with Moscow and convert to Orthodox Christianity, contributing to Russian aristocratic lineages. Under the czars, Russia conquered Central Asia and the Caucasus. Soviet authorities then tried to sever Muslims from their religious and linguistic roots by replacing Arabic-based alphabets with Cyrillic, a legacy that still shapes the region. This explains why some migrants, such as a Tajik man in a village near Moscow, find it easier for their children to attend Russian schools. The article also recalls the Soviet period, when millions of Slavic civilians were evacuated to Central Asia during World War II and were warmly received. But Soviet economic policy also damaged the region. Moscow turned Central Asia into a cotton-producing zone, forcing the diversion of rivers and contributing to the drying of the Aral Sea, described by the United Nations as the largest man-made environmental disaster in history. After the USSR collapsed in 1991, industrial output fell sharply, and the region’s economies remained constrained by Soviet-style authoritarianism, weak reform, cheap Chinese competition, climate change, and water shortages. These pressures have driven migration. Remittances from workers in Russia are vital for Central Asian economies, accounting in 2016 for more than a third of Tajikistan’s GDP and a fourth of Kyrgyzstan’s. The article concludes that while xenophobia remains severe, the success of some Central Asians in Russia points to a broader and ongoing integration. About 800,000 have become Russian citizens, and their presence has added to the country’s ethnic diversity and economic life.

# Muslim Migrants Succeed in Russia Despite Xenophobia Central Asian migrants face significant xenophobia in Russia, yet some have achieved remarkable success despite widespread discrimination. These migrants, predominantly from Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, and Kyrgyzstan, represent over 60 million people from predominantly Muslim regions who have migrated to Russia seeking economic opportunities. ## Xenophobia and Cultural Stereotypes The negative attitudes toward Central Asians are pervasive in Russian society. A Levada polling agency survey found that 27 percent of Russians express "irritation, dislike or fear" toward Central Asians, while nearly one in five believe their presence should be restricted. Popular television shows like "Our Russia" perpetuate stereotypes by portraying Central Asian migrants as comedic characters with broken Russian, poor hygiene, and subservient roles, reinforcing derogatory attitudes. According to Uzbek-born essayist Sandjar Yanyshev, humor serves as a mechanism to overcome fear of the unfamiliar: "What's funny is not dangerous." The consequences of this xenophobia are severe. Hundreds of Central Asians have been killed and thousands wounded in hate attacks by ultra-nationalists and skinheads. Additionally, corrupt police officers routinely exploit migrants through extortion, threatening detention or deportation. ## Notable Success Stories Despite these obstacles, several Central Asians have achieved extraordinary success. Alisher Usmanov, an ethnic Uzbek, has become Russia's wealthiest oligarch with a net worth of $15 billion, controlling steel factories and co-owning Arsenal Football Club. He maintains close ties with President Vladimir Putin. Singer Nargiz Zakirova, an Uzbek with a distinctive three-octave voice and bold appearance, ranks among Russia's most popular touring artists. Rapper Jah Khalib and film director Timur Bekmambetov, both from Kazakhstan, have achieved significant success in their respective fields. Cosmonaut Salijan Sharipov, born in Kyrgyzstan, spent over 200 days in space conducting scientific experiments. Beyond entertainment and space exploration, many Central Asians work as software engineers, designers, medical doctors, and scholars. ## Advantages and Challenges Central Asian migrants possess certain advantages over Muslims in other European nations. They share cultural backgrounds with Russians and often speak Russian fluently from childhood, facilitating integration. Chef and author Khakim Ganiev noted that studying Russian since school makes adaptation easier. However, success does not guarantee freedom from xenophobia. Actor Aziz Beyshenaliev, an ethnic Kyrgyz who portrayed various roles including "Muslim terrorists" and medieval warlords, ultimately left Russia in 2015. His decision stemmed from his son Seitek's experiences with ostracism and hate attacks at school. Beyshenaliev explained that while adults can mentally distance themselves from societal prejudice, children struggle with constant external conflict. The family relocated to Almaty, Kazakhstan, where Seitek now thrives academically. ## Historical Context Russia's relationship with Muslims spans centuries. Descendants of Genghis Khan's Golden Horde, which once ruled southern Russia, embraced Islam in the 14th century before converting to Orthodox Christianity, establishing prominent Russian aristocratic families. Novelist Vladimir Nabokov traced his family lineage to Genghis Khan's son. Soviet policies significantly shaped Central Asian migration patterns. The USSR forced the region to focus on cotton cultivation, devastating the environment and economy. This agricultural focus diverted major rivers, drying the Aral Sea—the world's fourth-largest body of water—creating what the United Nations called "the largest man-made environmental disaster in history." The USSR's 1991 collapse decimated industrial infrastructure designed for a unified economy, pushing millions toward labor migration. ## Economic Significance Central Asian migrants play crucial economic roles in both Russia and their home countries. Their remittances are vital: in 2016, migrant earnings constituted more than one-third of Tajikistan's GDP and one-fourth of Kyrgyzstan's GDP. Approximately 800,000 Central Asians have become Russian nationals, contributing to Russia's cultural diversity and economic growth. Currently, Central Asia faces additional challenges including de-industrialization from cheap Chinese exports and climate change threatening water resources. Despite these obstacles, the success of prominent Central Asians suggests increasing integration possibilities for millions more migrants seeking better lives in Russia.

UNESCO’s Cluster Office in Almaty announced that its fourth ResiliArt debate would be held on Tuesday, 27 October 2020, from 16:00 to 18:00 Almaty time. The discussion would focus on the conservation and promotion challenges facing the cinema heritage of Central Asia. The ResiliArt movement was launched by UNESCO in response to COVID-19 lockdowns and confinement measures. It brings together artists and cultural professionals in a series of debates designed to highlight the pandemic’s impact on the cultural sector, give creative workers a platform to voice their concerns and needs, and help inform policy decisions and support mechanisms for the sector. UNESCO noted that Central Asian cinema has a history of about 100 years and has produced many films across different genres that reflect the region’s history and culture in varying political, economic, and social contexts. Over time, attitudes toward cinema from local communities and public authorities have shifted considerably. Today, preserving and promoting this heritage is seen as increasingly important, especially as new technologies make classic films easier to process, access, and watch. The debate was intended to address key questions: what the current condition of Central Asia’s film heritage is, which classic films remain available and where they can be viewed, how access for broader audiences can be improved, and how the COVID-19 crisis and related restrictions have affected the cultural sector and its preservation efforts. UNESCO said the event would provide a platform for sharing views and best practices on safeguarding and promoting cinema heritage at all levels. It was being organized within the ResiliArt framework and as part of the project “Strengthening Film Industries in Central Asia,” funded by the government of the Republic of Korea. The debate was also scheduled to mark World Day for Audiovisual Heritage. It would be conducted in English and Russian, with online simultaneous interpretation for panelists and viewers.

In an interview with the Russian news agency RIA-Novosti, Aleksandr Avdeev, Russia’s ambassador to the Holy See, argued that Moscow and the Vatican now have “broad” opportunities for cooperation in response to what he described as the erosion of the ethical and moral foundations of Christian civilization. He said both the Russian Orthodox Church and the Catholic Church view this as a serious danger, particularly because family life, marriage, and the upbringing of children are being undermined by norms that are not rooted in Christian tradition. Avdeev presented current relations between the two Churches as highly promising and emphasized the growing depth of their dialogue. He said this dialogue has been strengthened by Pope Francis’ statements in Rome on two long-standing points of division between Catholics and Orthodox. First, he noted, the pope condemned proselytism as a sin, which Avdeev called an unprecedented papal statement. Second, the pope stressed that cooperation and dialogue between Catholics and Orthodox must take place on the basis of equal dignity, with each side remaining itself. The ambassador linked this development to the historic February 2016 meeting in Cuba between Patriarch Kirill of Moscow and Pope Francis. In his view, the spirit of the Havana declaration is now being translated into practical cooperation. He pointed to joint humanitarian aid efforts in the Middle East and exchanges of experience in social work. He also said the Vatican is especially interested in Russia’s experience of coexistence between Christians and Muslims, arguing that five centuries of such coexistence have shown that relations are calmer where the two communities live together. At the same time, Avdeev said Russia values Catholic expertise in religious formation and in defending family values. He praised the Catholic Church’s recent synods on the family, saying they offered a detailed global analysis of social problems affecting families, children, and young couples. Avdeev also described the institutional framework for cooperation between the two Churches. He mentioned the council for collaboration, led by Metropolitan Ilarion and Cardinal Koch, and the Committee on Culture, headed by Bishop Tikhon and Cardinal Ravasi. He highlighted especially fruitful cultural cooperation, including planned exhibitions on twentieth-century new martyrs, ecclesiastical architecture, and the Russian painter Leonid Brailovskij, whose works preserved in the archive of the Congregation for Oriental Churches were to be shown in Russia for the first time. The ambassador said relations between Russia and the Holy See are now marked by growing trust. He cited President Vladimir Putin’s two visits to the Vatican and his telephone conversations with Pope Francis as evidence of personal trust between the leaders. Avdeev also said Russia and the Vatican often share positions on major international issues. He noted that despite its small size, the Vatican has global significance because it represents 1.2 billion Catholics. He identified Secretary of State Cardinal Pietro Parolin’s visit to Russia last August, including a meeting with Putin in Sochi, as the high point of official relations. Finally, Avdeev noted agreement between Russia and the Vatican in opposing Donald Trump’s decision to move the U.S. embassy to Jerusalem, saying the city should not be politicized because it is sacred to three Abrahamic religions. Asked about the possibility of a papal visit to Russia, he quoted Metropolitan Ilarion: “Each passing day brings us closer to this event.”

Marc Anthony delivered a highly energetic and emotional performance at the Viña del Mar International Song Festival in Chile, drawing enthusiastic reactions from the packed crowd at Quinta Vergara. O Cine & Vídeo Tarumã, em Manaus, exibirá nesta semana uma programação gratuita de filmes sobre costumes, histórias, crenças e a realidade africana, em homenagem ao Dia Mundial da África, celebrado em 25 de maio. A mostra temática, intitulada **“Conhecendo Traços Culturais da África no Cinema”**, acompanha o **I Seminário do Programa Nossa África – Diálogos Africanos: novos objetos, pesquisas e ensino**, promovido pelo Departamento de História da UFAM entre **23 e 26 de maio**. A programação começa na **terça-feira (23)** com **“Virgem Margarida”** (2013), de **Licínio Azevedo**, que retrata os campos de reeducação em Moçambique no período da independência, em 1975, onde prostitutas eram levadas para serem transformadas em “novas mulheres”. Na **quarta-feira (24)**, será exibido **“A Luz”** (1987), de **Souleymane Cissé**, um dos principais nomes do cinema africano. O filme, inspirado em lendas do povo bambara, mistura fantasia e drama e rendeu ao diretor o primeiro prêmio concedido a um cineasta africano em Cannes, o Prêmio do Júri. Já na **sexta-feira (25)**, encerra a mostra **“Le Président”** (2013), produção de Camarões dirigida por **Jean-Pierre Bekolo**, um falso documentário sobre a fuga de um presidente que está há 42 anos no poder, às vésperas de uma importante reunião eleitoral. # Summary Cine & Vídeo Tarumã, a free film screening project at UFAM in Manaus, is presenting a thematic week dedicated to African culture, history, and beliefs this week. The programming coincides with the World Africa Day (May 25) and the I Seminar on African Dialogues organized by the History Department, running from Tuesday (23) to Friday (26). The screenings feature three acclaimed African films: **Tuesday (23):** "Virgem Margarida" (2013), directed by Brazilian filmmaker Licínio Azevedo, depicts reeducation camps in Mozambique during its 1975 independence, where women were sent for "reeducation." **Wednesday (24):** "A Luz" (1987), directed by Souleymane Cissé, a pioneering African filmmaker who won the Jury Prize at Cannes—a historic first for an African director. The film blends fantasy and drama based on Bambara legends. **Friday (25):** "Le Président" (2013), a Cameroonian production by Jean-Pierre Bekolo, presents as a mock documentary about a president's escape from his palace after 42 years in power, on the eve of elections. The film was censored in Cameroon due to its resemblance to the actual president. All sessions are free and held at 12:30 PM at the Rio Negro Auditorium.

Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro on Friday accused actor Leonardo DiCaprio of helping finance fires in the Amazon rainforest, but offered no evidence for the claim. Speaking outside the presidential residence in Brasília, Bolsonaro mocked DiCaprio as “a cool guy” for allegedly “giving money to torch the Amazon,” echoing social media rumors that the environmental group World Wildlife Fund (WWF) had paid volunteer firefighters for images of blazes and then used those photos to solicit donations, including one supposedly from DiCaprio. The WWF denied receiving any donation from DiCaprio and said it did not obtain photos from the firefighters. DiCaprio also rejected the allegation, saying he had not donated to the WWF. In a statement, he praised “the people of Brazil working to save their natural and cultural heritage,” while stressing that “we did not fund the organizations targeted.” The dispute unfolded amid broader controversy over Brazil’s Amazon fires. Four members of the nongovernmental organization Alter do Chão Fire Brigade were arrested earlier in the week on police accusations that they had intentionally started fires in order to document them and attract donations. A judge ordered them released on Thursday. The arrests drew strong criticism from politicians and NGOs, who said the Bolsonaro government was trying to intimidate environmental groups. Scientists and activists say the fires are more likely being set by land speculators, farmers, and ranchers clearing land for agriculture. They argue that Bolsonaro’s pro-development, pro-farming rhetoric has emboldened deforesters. The Amazon is widely regarded as a crucial barrier against global climate change. Bolsonaro has repeatedly blamed NGOs and others for the fires. In an August Facebook live post, he said “everything indicates” NGOs were going to the Amazon to “set fire” to the forest, though he admitted he had no evidence. He later acknowledged that farmers could be illegally burning the rainforest, but subsequently accused the “lying media” of exaggerating the destruction. On Thursday, he repeated the DiCaprio allegation in a live webcast, claiming the WWF paid the firefighting NGO and that some of the money went to people setting fires.

The article argues that Medellín’s polished image hides a city still deeply shaped by crime and neglect. It opens by mocking the idea that Medellín is a “pretty girl” or a model of urban innovation, saying its concrete-heavy landscape, awkward historic center, and showy infrastructure projects reflect style without social purpose. The city’s leaders, the writer contends, have focused more on buildings and urban spectacle than on the needs of residents. Once associated with Pablo Escobar’s cartel, Medellín is described as having moved from drug-lord notoriety to a different but equally troubling reality: criminal control embedded in daily life. The city, together with nearby towns and suburbs, is said to be in the hands of an “industry called crime,” because its industrial economy has long since vanished. According to the article, gangs dominate entire neighborhoods, especially in comunas 1, 2 and 3, where groups such as Los Terribles, Los Triana and La 29 are said to operate openly. The mayor rejects claims that gangs share territorial control or maintain a “gun pact” to divide the city. Officials also point to a falling homicide rate as evidence of progress. But the article argues that lower killings do not mean safety, because extortion, protection payments, phone theft, and drug dealing remain widespread. It says there is effectively a parallel authority in Medellín, with gangs controlling territory from the downtown area to the suburbs. One especially alarming example is Villa Santa Fe de Antioquia, a public housing complex for poor families, where an armed gang allegedly sells drugs, extorts residents, and in some cases forces people from their homes. The article presents this as part of a broader pattern in Colombia of criminals creating internal displacement inside cities. Despite Medellín’s trams, trains, police presence, and reputation for calm, the piece says many neighborhoods are plagued by extortionists who collect money from shopkeepers and even enter homes to threaten residents. It also highlights neglect in the historic Prado district, where satirical posters advertise the area “for sale” to Mayor Aníbal Gaviria. The conclusion is bleak: Medellín may have a beautiful face, but its body and spirit are controlled by “dark, ugly interests,” much like in the era of local strongmen who ruled by force.

# Summary: Medellín's Deceptive Façade Medellín, Colombia presents an attractive exterior that masks serious underlying problems. While the city has shed its notorious association with Pablo Escobar's drug cartel and now markets itself as an innovative, high-tech urban center with modern infrastructure like colorful trams and overpasses, this carefully curated image conceals a darker reality. The city's leadership has prioritized architectural development over the welfare of its residents. Despite claims of progress, Medellín is fundamentally controlled by organized crime rather than legitimate governance. Criminal gangs such as "Los Terribles," "Los Triana," and "La 29" rule entire neighborhoods, particularly in Comunas 1, 2, and 3, operating with apparent impunity. Although city officials insist otherwise and point to reduced homicide rates as evidence of improvement, extensive criminal activity persists throughout the city. Extortion, mobile phone theft, and drug dealing remain rampant. Gangs have effectively divided the city into territories under their control, from downtown areas to suburban regions. A particularly troubling example is Villa Santa Fe de Antioquia, a public housing estate where armed gangs sell drugs, extort residents, and forcibly displace families. The criminal underworld operates a parallel authority system, with extortionists systematically targeting shops, kiosks, and private homes for protection payments. Police presence, while visible, appears largely ineffective, with officers often preoccupied rather than actively monitoring streets. The neglected historic Prado district, once home to the wealthy and declared a cultural heritage site, exemplifies official indifference. Anonymous posters sardonically advertise the area "for sale," reflecting public frustration with governmental abandonment of this neighborhood. Ultimately, despite Medellín's attractive surface appearance and modernization efforts, the city remains controlled by criminal interests rather than legitimate authority. The situation mirrors historical patterns of territorial control by powerful local bosses, suggesting little fundamental change from past decades. The city's true character—dominated by dark, ugly interests—contradicts its polished public image.

Brazil has chosen **“Bingo - The King of the Mornings”** as its submission for next year’s Foreign-Language Film Oscar. The decision was made by a commission of more than 200 film specialists and announced by the Brazilian Film Academy. The selection appears to have avoided the controversy that surrounded last year’s choice, when internal disputes over Cannes title **“Aquarius”** led three filmmakers to withdraw their films from consideration. Selected from **22 contenders**, “Bingo” is one of Brazil’s most anticipated films of 2017 and marks the first feature directed by **Daniel Rezende**, an acclaimed editor known for work on films including **“The Tree of Life,” “Elite Squad,”** and **“The Motorcycle Diaries.”** The film is also Brazil’s entry for the **2018 Spanish Academy Goya Awards**. Inspired by real-life actor and evangelical pastor **Arlindo Barreto**, who played Bozo the Clown in 1980s Brazil, the film follows Augusto, an artist who becomes a TV clown host and gains fame and fortune, but alienates his son in the process. The film comes from production company **Gullane**, which has now had three Oscar submissions in four years. It was written by **Luiz Bolognesi**, with cinematography by **Lula Carvalho**. Brazil’s last Oscar nomination was **“Central Station”** in 1999.

Four of five young people hospitalized after Buenos Aires’ Time Warp electronic music festival were in critical condition Sunday, the city Health Ministry said, while a minor continued to improve in intensive care. The most serious patient at Fernandez Hospital was on artificial respiration and suffering kidney failure, according to the hospital. Another man and a woman in intensive care also had kidney failure and were critical. The three worst cases were aged 19 to 23. The five were among festival attendees treated after five people, ages 20 to 30, died early Saturday at the Costa Salguero events center. Organizers canceled the festival’s second night after the deaths. Authorities are still investigating the cause, though medical sources suspect drug use. Police also reported that they stopped a minibus headed to the event and found 182 ecstasy pills, plus LSD, marijuana and cocaine.

One patient, on artificial respiration with kidney failure, is the most severely affected. Two others in the intensive care unit also suffer kidney failure and critical conditions. The three worst cases are aged 19-23; one minor is improving. The incident occurred Saturday at the Costa Salguero events center during the two-day festival. Five attendees aged 20-30 died early Saturday, prompting organizers to cancel the remaining show. The Time Warp festival, originating in Germany, was being held in Argentina for the third time. While the tragedy's cause remains under investigation, medical sources suspect drug use. Police discovered 182 ecstasy pills, LSD doses, marijuana, and cocaine in a minibus transporting festival attendees Friday.

South Africa and China have a strong political relationship that Pretoria says can support broader economic goals, International Relations and Cooperation Minister Maite Nkoana-Mashabane said on Tuesday. Speaking in Pretoria about President Jacob Zuma’s December 4-5 state visit to China, she said Beijing had agreed to help South Africa develop black industrialists who can take part in the mainstream economy as part of the country’s industrialisation drive. During the visit, the two governments adopted the China-South Africa Five-to-Ten Year Framework on Cooperation, designed to deepen and implement agreements first set out in the 2010 Beijing Declaration. China also agreed to speed up market-access talks for South African fresh produce, including maize and apples. Nkoana-Mashabane said the visit produced agreements and memorandums of understanding on human resource and capacity development, as well as support for South Africa’s industrial planning, including beneficiation and value addition for raw materials. China also committed to helping develop science and technology parks, industrial parks and the ocean economy. The leaders also discussed ways to boost tourism promotion and investment. Zuma and Xi Jinping further addressed the high-level Forum on China-Africa Cooperation, which South Africa will host and co-chair in 2015. South Africa will also host the 2015 Year of China, following China’s hosting of the Year of South Africa in 2014.

# Summary South African Minister Maite Nkoana-Mashabane announced that South Africa and China maintain strong political ties that provide a foundation for achieving economic objectives. During President Jacob Zuma's December 4-5 state visit to China, the two nations adopted a China-South Africa Five-to-Ten Year Framework on Cooperation to strengthen implementation of previous agreements since the 2010 Beijing Declaration. Key agreements reached include China's commitment to assist South Africa in creating black industrialists and supporting industrialization efforts. China agreed to expedite market access negotiations for South African agricultural exports, including maize and apples. The countries also concluded agreements on human resource development, industrial planning, and raw material beneficiation. Additionally, China committed to supporting Science and Technology parks and key sectors such as the Ocean Economy. Both nations discussed tourism promotion initiatives to boost investment and visitor numbers. Presidents Zuma and Xi Jinping discussed the upcoming 2015 Forum on China-Africa Cooperation (FOCAC), which South Africa will host and co-chair. South Africa will also host the 2015 Year of China, reciprocating China's hosting of the Year of South Africa in 2014.

Ethiopia earned about $2.63 billion from exports in the first five months of its current fiscal year, the Ministry of Trade and Regional Integration said. The amount represents 138.93% of the target set for the period, which began on July 8, and is 102.09% higher than in the same period last year. Ethiopia exported 612,499 tonnes of goods during the five months. Agricultural commodities brought in the largest share of revenue at 50.42%, followed by mining at 39.7%, manufacturing at 5.55%, and electricity and other products at 4.31%. The government has credited the increase in major agricultural exports to broad economic reforms and other enabling measures. In October 2024, Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed set an 8.4% growth target for the fiscal year, citing strong prospects in key sectors. The World Bank describes Ethiopia as one of Africa’s fastest-growing economies.

# Ethiopia's Strong Export Performance Ethiopia generated $2.63 billion in export revenue during the first five months of its 2024/2025 fiscal year, exceeding its initial target by 138.93 percent. The country exported approximately 612,499 tonnes of commodities, representing a 102.09 percent increase compared to the same period the previous year. Agricultural commodities led exports with 50.42 percent of total revenue, followed by mining (39.7 percent), manufacturing (5.55 percent), and electricity/other products (4.31 percent). The government attributes this growth to comprehensive economic reforms and enabling initiatives. Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed announced an 8.4 percent economic growth target for the current fiscal year, citing positive prospects across agricultural, manufacturing, and mining sectors. The World Bank recognizes Ethiopia as one of Africa's fastest-growing economies, with a population of approximately 126.5 million people.

A Cape Town ear, nose and throat specialist, Oliver Raynham, died in a freak boating accident on Thursday near the Hermanus lagoon. According to witness John Finch, owner of Stanford River Lodge, a sailboat with colorful sails was traveling down the river between Stanford and Hermanus when it struck a power line crossing the water, causing sparks to fly. Raynham was on board with three children and was reportedly holding the mast when it brushed the line. The children jumped off the boat and were rescued by nearby speedboats, and Finch initially believed everyone had survived. Raynham’s body was later found, but he could not be resuscitated. Finch also said the lagoon’s water level was unusually high this year because too little water had flowed into the sea.

# Summary A Cape Town ear, nose, and throat specialist, Oliver Raynham, died in a freak accident while supervising a pathfinders' camp near Hermanus. Witness John Finch observed a sailboat with colorful sails hit a power line crossing the river between Stanford and Hermanus. Raynham was holding the mast when it made contact with the live wire, causing sparks. Three children aboard jumped into the water and were rescued unharmed by nearby speedboats. Raynham's body was recovered and rushed to the hospital but could not be resuscitated. Finch attributed the accident partly to unusually high lagoon water levels that year.

Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Demeke Mekonnen praised Ethiopian ambassadors and diplomats for safeguarding the country’s interests and reflecting Ethiopians’ aspirations and heritage. He particularly commended ambassadors and diplomats for helping preserve national interests under difficult circumstances. He stressed that because many diplomatic issues do not have immediate or final resolutions and because global geopolitics remains unpredictable, Ethiopian diplomats must act proactively and in line with the Foreign Ministry’s reengagement strategy. Demeke called for stronger diplomatic capacity and more work tailored to Ethiopia’s specific situation and vulnerabilities. He urged diplomats to make maximum efforts to defend the country’s interests at every stage. State Minister of Foreign Affairs Ambassador Birtukan Ayano briefed the media on the retreat’s objectives. She said the ambassadors will review the challenges of 2022, assess the responses to them, and define the main engagement priorities for the coming year. She also noted that participants recently visited more than 10 institutions in Addis Ababa and Bishoftu to observe the results of reforms and understand how ambassadors can help strengthen institutional capacity. Over the two-week retreat, diplomats and mission heads will also discuss major national, regional, and international issues, and visit tourist destinations, industrial zones, and other sites. The opening was attended by foreign ministry state ministers, mission leaders, director generals, and officials of affiliated institutions.

The article argues that Somaliland should “Africanize” its foreign policy by shifting more attention from Western capitals to African states and institutions, which it says are ultimately more important to Somaliland’s recognition bid. It opens by noting that Somaliland and Eritrea were not invited to the recent U.S.-Africa Leaders meeting in Washington, D.C. The United States said Eritrea was excluded because of strained relations and Somaliland because it is not recognized as a sovereign state. Washington also said its invitations were consistent with the African Union’s position and with its own recognition of governments. The article treats this as unsurprising and as a reminder that Somaliland’s recognition question is still largely viewed through African diplomatic channels. The piece says this is a significant year for Somaliland’s international engagement, pointing to several developments that generated optimism: debate in the British House of Commons, President Muse Bihi Abdi’s visit to the United States, and the inclusion of the Somaliland Partnership Act in U.S. fiscal legislation. Even so, the author argues that Somaliland should reflect on whether its foreign policy has overemphasized Western lobbying while neglecting Africa, where the “real stakes” lie. The article stresses that while outreach to Western governments is useful, Somaliland’s case depends heavily on African capitals and African institutions. Looking back at Somaliland’s past administrations, the article says each government has pursued recognition and acceptance, but foreign policy has often been inconsistent, weakly institutionalized, and poorly coordinated. President Egal, it says, preferred direct personal diplomacy through letters rather than building a strong foreign service. Similar problems continued under Presidents Rayale, Silanyo, and Bihi. The article identifies the Rayale administration as the high point of Somaliland-Africa relations: Rayale toured African countries, presented Somaliland’s independence case, and met leaders such as Senegal’s President Abdoulaye Wade. During that period, an African Union fact-finding mission visited Somaliland and produced a report that captured the complexity of the Somaliland issue, which the author says was a missed opportunity for pushing recognition from within Africa. The article also mentions the late scholar Ali Mazrui’s visit to Somaliland and his later writings on the subject. Under the Silanyo administration and continuing under Bihi, the article says Somaliland shifted toward stronger ties with Arab and Gulf states. These relations brought investment, infrastructure projects, and especially the DP World expansion of Berbera Port, but also controversy, including a military base agreement with the UAE and Somaliland’s alignment in the 2017 Gulf crisis. However, the article argues that these engagements were often opaque, uncoordinated, and not sufficiently institutionalized. It says Somaliland gained strategic visibility through the Gulf relationship, but at the cost of neglecting Africa. The article then explains why Africa matters so much. African states, it says, are generally wary of new states emerging from existing ones because of their own histories of separatism and border disputes, and because they strongly defend the principle of not changing colonial borders. This makes Somaliland’s recognition struggle difficult, since it involves a border-related political claim without the approval of African states. At the same time, African states have influence in global institutions such as the United Nations, including through their voting power and their presence on the UN Security Council. Support from African governments, the article argues, would therefore be politically significant and could shape international debate. The author also says African states are direct stakeholders in Somaliland’s future because they would feel the effects of Somaliland statehood and regional integration. The modernization of Berbera Port and the Berbera corridor is presented as a major factor in regional connectivity, making stronger ties with neighboring and regional countries even more important. To build these ties, the article recommends opening diplomatic or liaison offices in key African hubs such as South Africa, Nigeria, Rwanda, and Ghana, citing their regional influence through blocs like SADC, ECOWAS, and COMESA. The article also warns that Somaliland’s internal political disputes, especially around elections and the arrests of journalists and opposition figures, damage its image as a democratic model. It says Somaliland should broaden its message beyond democracy and elections and instead emphasize cooperation, business, and opportunity, while still upholding human rights. Finally, it calls for a two-track diplomacy: one track should continue to press for recognition as an independent state, while the other should deepen economic and technical engagement with African governments, institutions, private sector actors, think tanks, and prominent individuals. The article suggests Somaliland should seek observer status in regional organizations and work with bodies such as NEPAD, even if its non-recognized status remains unresolved. Its core message is that Somaliland must rethink its Africa policy now, because changing regional dynamics create both opportunities and risks for its recognition ambitions and its role in the Horn of Africa.

# Summary: Why Somaliland Should "Africanize" Its Foreign Policy The recent exclusion of Somaliland from the U.S.-Africa Leaders Summit in Washington D.C. has prompted important reflection on Somaliland's approach to international engagement. While the United States justified this decision by citing lack of recognition and directing Somaliland's case to the African Union, the incident underscores a critical strategic oversight in Somaliland's foreign policy priorities. ## Current Foreign Policy Trajectory Somaliland's successive administrations have pursued inconsistent and poorly institutionalized foreign policies focused primarily on gaining Western recognition. President Egal relied on personal correspondence rather than developing robust foreign policy institutions. Subsequent leaders, including Rayale, Silanyo, and Bihi, perpetuated similar structural weaknesses. While these efforts produced some notable achievements—including parliamentary debate in the UK House of Commons and the passage of the U.S. Somaliland Partnership Act—they have largely neglected Africa's critical role in Somaliland's recognition. The Rayale administration represented a peak in African engagement, with the president touring African states and meeting heads of state, including Senegal's President Wade. However, this momentum was not sustained. Under Silanyo and continuing through Bihi's tenure, Somaliland shifted focus toward Arab nations, particularly Gulf states. This reorientation brought tangible benefits including infrastructure development and the DP World Berbera Port expansion, but occurred at the expense of African relationships and lacked transparency and institutional coordination. ## Why Africa Matters The author argues that African states represent Somaliland's most critical stakeholders for several compelling reasons. First, African nations are inherently sensitive to border changes and separatism, having long defended the principle of maintaining colonial boundaries. Consequently, African blessing is essential for Somaliland's recognition efforts. Second, African states possess significant institutional power through United Nations representation, including three permanent or non-permanent Security Council seats. Their support could substantially influence international recognition discussions. Furthermore, African nations will directly experience the consequences of Somaliland's statehood and represent major stakeholders in regional integration initiatives like the modernized Berbera port corridor. This geographic and economic proximity makes African engagement strategically indispensable. ## Recommended Strategic Shifts The commentary proposes establishing diplomatic and liaison offices in major African hubs including South Africa, Nigeria, Rwanda, and Ghana—nations wielding considerable continental political and economic influence within regional bodies like SADC, ECOWAS, and COMESA. Despite harboring their own separatist challenges, these countries maintain relationships with other aspiring states and could prove valuable allies. Somaliland should also recalibrate its diplomatic messaging. Rather than exclusively emphasizing democracy and elections—language that may alienate African political elites skeptical of democratic discourse—Somaliland should employ language emphasizing cooperation, business opportunities, and economic engagement. This represents not an abandonment of democratic principles but a pragmatic recognition that different audiences respond to different appeals. ## Two-Track Diplomacy Framework The author advocates adopting a two-track diplomatic strategy. The first track maintains emphasis on Somaliland's independence recognition, while the second promotes economic and technical engagement with African states without awaiting formal recognition. This approach enables Somaliland to function as an active regional participant through various channels including African institutions, private sector engagement, think tanks, and eminent personalities. Additionally, Somaliland should explore accessing regional institutions that accept "governments" rather than requiring state status, potentially securing observer status in regional economic communities or engaging with NEPAD initiatives. ## Internal Challenges The commentary notes that Somaliland's democratic reputation faces jeopardy from internal political disputes, including election controversies and journalist arrests. Continued democratic backsliding could significantly damage Somaliland's carefully cultivated image as a regional democracy beacon, further complicating international engagement efforts. ## Conclusion The author concludes that Somaliland faces a critical moment requiring fundamental foreign policy reassessment. Rather than continuing to prioritize Western capitals, Somaliland must recognize that its recognition pathway runs through African institutions and states. By establishing robust African diplomatic presence, employing strategic messaging focused on cooperation and opportunity, and implementing two-track diplomacy, Somaliland can position itself as an active regional participant while advancing its independence recognition agenda. This "Africanization" of foreign policy represents not abandoning Western engagement but rather restoring balance to Somaliland's international strategy.

Japan’s Ambassador to Ethiopia, Ito Takako, described a recent official delegation visit to Mekele, the capital of Tigray, as an important step toward peace in Ethiopia. The delegation, led by House of People’s Representatives Speaker Tagesse Chafo, included ministers, heads of service institutions, and National Dialogue commissioners. It spent a day in Mekele on Saturday. Takako said the visit could help strengthen the ongoing peace process by allowing the two sides to exchange ideas and feelings. She said Japan supports the Ethiopian government’s peace efforts and views the trip as a meaningful move toward stability in the country. She added that Japan will continue looking for ways to assist Ethiopia in implementing the peace agreement. The ambassador stressed that Ethiopia matters not only for its own stability but also for the wider Horn of Africa. She noted Ethiopia’s large population and strategic location, saying Japan seeks peace and stability in both Ethiopia and the region. Takako also said Japan wants to expand development cooperation with Ethiopia and continue humanitarian assistance for northern Ethiopia. She recalled the long history of Ethiopia-Japan relations, which began in the 1930s and were fully restored after World War II, with embassies established in both capitals in 1958.

The delegation, led by House Speaker Tagesse Chafo and including government ministers and National Dialogue commissioners, visited Mekele on December 26, 2020. Prime Minister Narendra Modi has dismissed India’s top diplomat, Sujatha Singh, and appointed the country’s ambassador to the United States, Subrahmanyam Jaishankar, as the new foreign secretary. The move came just a day after a successful visit by U.S. President Barack Obama and highlighted Modi’s growing control over foreign policy. The government said Singh was asked to step down with seven months left before retirement. Her removal was unusual: the last time the head of India’s elite foreign service was ousted was in the late 1980s. The decision drew criticism from the opposition Congress party, which had appointed Singh. Congress leader Manish Tewari questioned why she had been replaced so abruptly and said the government needed to explain. Since taking office last year, Modi has taken a highly active role in diplomacy, inviting regional leaders to his inauguration and holding high-profile meetings with leaders from the United States, China, Japan and Australia. Under Singh, India-U.S. ties had deteriorated sharply after a diplomatic dispute over the arrest of an Indian diplomat in New York. Modi has since moved quickly to repair relations with Washington, including a state visit to the U.S. and hosting Obama as guest of honour at India’s Republic Day parade, the first time a U.S. president received that role. Jaishankar said he would carry out the government’s priorities.

S. Jaishankar, India’s ambassador to the United States and a key figure in improving ties with Washington, took charge as foreign secretary on Thursday, a day after the government abruptly cut short Sujatha Singh’s tenure by seven months. The appointment, announced late Wednesday, was made by the Cabinet’s Appointments Committee headed by Prime Minister Narendra Modi. Singh’s two-year term was due to end later, but the government said her tenure was being “curtailed with immediate effect.” Jaishankar assumed office at South Block, where the Ministry of External Affairs is located, and later met External Affairs Minister Sushma Swaraj. The move triggered speculation in the media and on social media that Swaraj had been left out of the decision-making process. However, in a series of tweets that evening, Swaraj said she had been kept informed and had spoken personally to Singh before the change was made. She explained that because Jaishankar was due to retire on January 31, the government had to issue the appointment before that date. “Then I spoke to Ms Sujatha Singh personally. I told her that the Government wanted to appoint Dr. Jaishankar as Foreign Secretary,” she tweeted. Jaishankar, an Indian Foreign Service officer of the 1977 batch, said he was “honoured” to take on the responsibility and told officials at South Block that his priorities would be the government’s priorities. Singh was not present at his takeover ceremony. In a farewell email to colleagues, she stressed that the foreign secretary serves as the main interface with political leadership and said that “no individual is larger than institution.” The decision drew criticism from the Congress, which questioned why a fixed-tenure foreign secretary was being replaced so suddenly, especially just after US President Barack Obama’s three-day visit to India. Congress leader Manish Tewari suggested there may have been a connection between Singh’s handling of the Devyani Khobragade case and her removal. Khobragade, then India’s deputy consul general in New York, had been arrested and strip-searched by US authorities in December 2013, prompting a strong diplomatic response from India. The BJP defended the move, saying the government had every right to decide appointments and responsibilities. Party spokesperson Nalin Kohli said such decisions had been taken by previous governments as well. Jaishankar was widely credited with helping repair India-US relations after the Khobragade episode and with contributing to the smooth handling of Modi’s high-profile US visit in September. He had earlier been one of the officials involved in negotiating the nuclear deal with the US and had served as ambassador to China, Singapore, the Czech Republic, Sri Lanka, and Russia.

# Summary: S. Jaishankar Appointed Foreign Secretary, Replacing Sujatha Singh S. Jaishankar, India's ambassador to the United States, assumed office as foreign secretary on January 29, following a late-night government announcement that curtailed his predecessor Sujatha Singh's tenure seven months before its scheduled end. Jaishankar, an Indian Foreign Service officer from the 1977 batch who was set to retire on January 31, stated he was "honoured" by the appointment and pledged to make the government's priorities his own. The Cabinet's Appointments Committee, headed by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, announced Singh's tenure would be "curtailed with immediate effect." The surprise decision came one day after U.S. President Barack Obama concluded a state visit during which India and the United States announced a breakthrough on their stalled civil nuclear deal. Initial speculation suggested External Affairs Minister Sushma Swaraj had been excluded from the decision-making process. However, she issued evening tweets clarifying her involvement, stating she had personally informed Singh of the government's intention to appoint Jaishankar due to his impending retirement deadline. China’s new 13 per cent sales tax on condoms and other contraceptives, which took effect on January 1, 2026, has sparked public ridicule, online jokes and concern among health experts, even as Beijing tries to slow a sharp decline in births. The tax is part of a broader revision of China’s tax code that removes several exemptions dating back to 1994, when the country was still enforcing its strict one-child policy. In contrast to the new levy on contraception, services related to marriage, childcare and elderly care remain exempt from value-added tax, reflecting the government’s effort to encourage family formation and support an ageing society. The policy arrives at a moment of demographic strain. China, now the world’s second-largest economy, is struggling to persuade people to marry and have children as its population has fallen for three straight years. Official figures show that fewer than 10 million babies were born in 2024, roughly half the number recorded a decade earlier, when childbirth restrictions had already begun to ease. Beijing has already introduced a range of pronatalist measures, including longer parental leave and direct cash assistance for families, but the new condom tax has drawn particular attention because it appears to move in the opposite direction. Public health advocates warn that making contraception more expensive could have unintended consequences, including more unplanned pregnancies and a possible increase in HIV infections. The reaction online has largely been sarcastic rather than supportive. One retailer advised customers to stock up before prices rise, while social media users joked about buying a lifetime supply of condoms. Others pointed out that even a small increase in condom prices is trivial compared with the cost of raising a child over many years. That broader cost is central to the debate. A 2024 report from the Beijing-based Youth Population Research Institute ranked China among the most expensive places in the world to raise children, citing steep education costs, intense academic competition and the difficulty many women face in balancing work and motherhood. For many households, however, the main obstacle to having children is economic insecurity rather than the price of contraception. A prolonged slowdown, worsened by the property crisis, has reduced household savings and left many young people uncertain about the future. Some residents say the tax will have little effect on their own choices. A 36-year-old man in Henan province, who already has one child and does not plan to have another, compared the price increase to a small rise in metro fares, saying that people still use the metro because they need it. He said even if a box of condoms costs several yuan more, the annual increase would be manageable. Others fear the policy could create riskier behavior among vulnerable groups. A woman from Xi’an said contraception is a basic need and warned that students or financially struggling people might take chances if condoms become less affordable, calling that the policy’s most dangerous possible outcome. Experts are divided over the government’s motives. A demography scholar at the University of Wisconsin–Madison said expecting the tax to significantly raise fertility is unrealistic, and suggested fiscal pressures may be a bigger reason, as China seeks to broaden its tax base amid a weakening housing sector and rising government debt. He noted that value-added tax already provides nearly 40 per cent of total tax revenue. A researcher at the Center for Strategic and International Studies called the condom tax largely symbolic, saying it signals Beijing’s determination to respond to one of the world’s lowest fertility rates. She also warned that many family-support policies depend on heavily indebted provincial governments, raising doubts about implementation. Public support could weaken further if people feel the state is intruding into private life. Reports that local officials in some provinces have called women to ask about menstrual cycles and plans for children have already fueled such concerns, though a health bureau in Yunnan said the information was needed to identify pregnancies. Critics argue that China’s male-dominated leadership is missing deeper social changes behind the fertility decline, including women’s unequal childcare burden, falling marriage rates and even reduced interest in dating. Some say young people are increasingly turning inward, with booming sales of sex toys seen as another sign of detachment from relationships. In that context, the condom tax has become a symbol of a larger question: whether economic incentives and symbolic policies can address the deeper social fatigue shaping a generation’s choices.

After nine months of intensive German diplomacy aimed at easing the Ukraine crisis, Chancellor Angela Merkel concluded in mid-November that a different approach was needed. That effort came on Nov. 15 at 10 p.m. in the Brisbane Hilton, far from the fighting in eastern Ukraine. Merkel and Putin met on the hotel’s eighth floor. The discussion lasted nearly four hours, and around midnight Jean-Claude Juncker, the new president of the European Commission, joined them. Merkel’s goal was to get Putin, a fluent German speaker and former KGB officer, to drop his guarded tone and reveal his intentions. Instead, according to officials briefed on the talks, she received the same denials and dodges she had already heard for months. One official said Putin “radiated coldness,” adding that he had “dug himself in and he can’t get out.” The Brisbane meeting, along with another encounter in Milan a month earlier, convinced German officials that Merkel had reached a diplomatic dead end. In Milan, Putin had made promises about Russian conduct in eastern Ukraine that German officials say were broken within days. By then, Berlin’s patience was exhausted. Since February, when Ukraine’s pro-Russian president Viktor Yanukovych fled Kiev after the Maidan protests, Germany had taken the lead in trying to bring Putin into a negotiated settlement. Merkel had spoken to him by phone roughly three dozen times, and Foreign Minister Frank-Walter Steinmeier, from the traditionally Russia-friendly Social Democrats, had spent hundreds of hours seeking a deal. Yet German officials now said they had no new ideas for influencing the Russian leader. Communication would continue, but Berlin was preparing for a long standoff that some saw as resembling a second Cold War. German lawmakers and officials described the situation in bleak terms. Norbert Roettgen, who chairs the Bundestag foreign affairs committee, said Germany needed to prepare for “a prolonged conflict” in which Russia would use every means available. Another official said the country was in “a waiting game,” focused mainly on monitoring violence in eastern Ukraine and responding as needed. Merkel’s frustration became public two days after her meeting with Putin, when she delivered a sharply worded speech in Sydney. She accused Russia of violating international law through “old thinking” rooted in spheres of influence and warned that such behavior challenged the peaceful order established in Europe after two world wars and the Cold War. The next day, Steinmeier traveled to Moscow to assess the damage. Instead of progress, he was confronted by Putin with a long attack on the Maidan events and accusations that Europe had reneged on a deal to keep Yanukovych in power longer. Steinmeier later admitted that the visit had produced no breakthrough. With diplomacy stalled, German officials said their strategy had narrowed to damage control on three fronts. First was Kiev itself. Berlin was trying to prevent political rifts from widening between Ukraine’s President Petro Poroshenko and Prime Minister Arseniy Yatsenyuk. Yatsenyuk, a hard-line 40-year-old technocrat who emerged strengthened from October elections, risked making the more diplomatic Poroshenko appear weak. A split between them would complicate reforms and anti-corruption measures needed to secure Western aid, which would serve Moscow’s interests. German officials said they were working daily to avoid a repeat of the destructive feud that once split the Yushchenko-Tymoshenko government. The second front was a Kremlin propaganda campaign aimed at undermining the Western narrative of the Ukraine crisis, especially in Germany. Putin gave a carefully tailored interview to German public broadcaster ARD, striking a conciliatory tone while warning of alleged ethnic cleansing in eastern Ukraine by neo-Nazis. At the same time, Kremlin-funded RT launched a German-language channel, and German media reported being flooded with pro-Russian online comments that security sources believed were centrally organized. Analysts said Putin was trying to sway public opinion inside the EU and weaken support for Merkel’s line. Signs of that effort were already visible. Former SPD leader Matthias Platzeck broke ranks and urged Germany to recognize Russia’s annexation of Crimea. Russian officials and businessmen were also cultivating ties in Germany, especially in industrial regions like Stuttgart. Beyond Germany, Moscow was reaching out to former Eastern bloc EU members such as Hungary and Bulgaria, as well as Balkan states. In Europe more broadly, Russia appeared to be courting right-wing opposition parties; France’s National Front acknowledged receiving a 9 million euro loan from a Moscow-based bank. The third challenge was preserving EU unity on sanctions. The first round of EU sanctions was due to expire in March and would require renewal. German officials said Italy, Hungary, and Slovakia would be especially difficult to keep aligned. They feared Putin would try to peel countries away before then. For now, Berlin viewed any further tightening of sanctions as impossible unless Russian-backed separatists made a major military push, such as seizing Mariupol and creating a land corridor to Crimea. Merkel’s outlook was increasingly that the confrontation had shifted from a fast-moving crisis to a longer struggle in which the West would gradually squeeze Russia’s economy until Putin relented. As she said at an event at the church in eastern Germany where she was baptized, because Germany had ruled out war, some people might believe they could do whatever they wanted.
