# Germany's Failed Diplomatic Efforts with Putin Over Ukraine Crisis After nine months of intensive diplomatic efforts to resolve the Ukrainian crisis, German Chancellor Angela Merkel concluded in mid-November that her approach needed fundamental revision. Merkel had exhausted traditional diplomatic channels and decided to confront Russian President Vladimir Putin directly, meeting him alone with minimal staff at the Brisbane Hilton during the G20 summit in Australia on November 15. The nearly four-hour meeting, later joined by European Commission President Jean-Claude Juncker around midnight, represented a significant shift in strategy. Rather than challenging Putin's broken promises, Merkel sought to understand his actual intentions regarding Ukraine and other former Soviet territories. However, the encounter proved disappointing. Officials briefed on the conversation reported that Putin offered only the same denials and evasions Merkel had heard repeatedly. One official described Putin as radiating "coldness" and noted that "Putin has dug himself in and he can't get out." A month earlier, Merkel had met Putin in Milan, where he made promises about Russian behavior in eastern Ukraine that German officials claim were violated within days. These consecutive diplomatic failures pushed Berlin's frustration to unprecedented levels. Since February, when Ukraine's pro-Russian president Viktor Yanukovich fled Kiev amid violent protests, Germany had led Western diplomatic efforts to convince Putin to engage constructively. Merkel had spoken with Putin by phone thirty times, while Foreign Minister Frank-Walter Steinmeier, from the traditionally Russia-friendly Social Democratic Party, had invested hundreds of hours pursuing a negotiated settlement. German officials now admit they have exhausted their ideas for persuading Putin. Merkel's frustration manifested clearly in a Sydney speech two days after meeting Putin. Using unusually stark language, she accused Russia of trampling international law with "old thinking" based on spheres of influence, warning that this threatened Europe's peaceful order. Steinmeier subsequently traveled to Moscow, but Putin ambushed him with a tirade about the Maidan protests, accusing Europe of breaking commitments regarding Yanukovich. Steinmeier acknowledged no progress was achieved. Germany's strategy has now shifted to damage control across three fronts. First, Berlin works to prevent a split between Ukrainian President Petro Poroshenko and Prime Minister Arseny Yatseniuk, recalling how a similar rift between previous leaders Viktor Yushchenko and Yulia Tymoshenko nearly a decade ago weakened Ukraine. Such division would undermine economic reforms and anti-corruption measures necessary for Western aid, potentially serving Putin's interests. Second, Germany confronts what officials describe as a "massive propaganda campaign" by the Kremlin targeting Russian sympathizers throughout Europe. Putin's interview with German television station ARD, broadcast before Merkel's Sydney speech, struck an unusually conciliatory tone while expressing concerns about alleged neo-Nazi ethnic cleansing in eastern Ukraine. The Kremlin-funded broadcaster RT launched a German-language station to promote Moscow's narrative. German security sources report organized pro-Russian comment campaigns targeting German news websites, while analysts note Putin is effectively using propaganda tools to undermine the German narrative. Evidence of propaganda's effectiveness appears in cracks within German consensus. Former SPD leader Matthias Platzeck broke ranks urging recognition of Crimea's annexation. Russia is cultivating relationships with German businessmen and extending outreach to former eastern bloc EU members like Hungary and Bulgaria, plus Balkan states and right-wing European parties. France's National Front confirmed securing a nine-million-euro loan from a Moscow-based bank. The third challenge involves maintaining EU unity on sanctions. The first sanctions package expires in March and requires renewal, but German officials identify Italy, Hungary, and Slovakia as potentially difficult to retain. One official described keeping the EU united on Russia as a "Herculean task." Berlin currently views further economic sanctions as a "no go," though this position could change if Russian-backed separatists seize the strategic city of Mariupol, creating a corridor to Crimea. Merkel's confrontation with Putin appears to be evolving from a fast-moving dispute into a prolonged standoff reminiscent of a second Cold War. Germany will maintain communication channels but prepare for extended conflict. The Western strategy now centers on gradually squeezing Russia's struggling economy, hoping Putin eventually capitulates. As Merkel stated, despite ruling out military action, the West will not permit Russian aggression without consequences.

Azerbaijan’s leading investigative journalist and prominent government critic, Khadija Ismayilova, was arrested on December 5, 2014, in what Human Rights Watch described as a major blow to free expression in the country. The Sabail District Court in Baku ordered her held in pretrial detention for two months while authorities investigate allegations that she drove someone to attempt suicide. Human Rights Watch said the case appears to be part of a broader effort by the Azerbaijani government to silence dissent, and called for her immediate release. The arrest came one day after Ramiz Mehdiyev, head of the presidential administration, published an article denouncing nongovernmental organizations as a “fifth column” and accusing Ismayilova of treason. Little is known about the evidence behind the charges, because her lawyer signed a nondisclosure statement. Ismayilova had long expected retaliation and had urged Azerbaijan’s international partners to speak out publicly rather than rely on quiet diplomacy. She also encouraged fellow activists to continue defending human rights in Azerbaijan. Known for exposing government corruption and the business interests of the ruling family, she had already faced repeated pressure from the authorities. Beginning in February 2014, police questioned her several times as part of an investigation into the alleged leaking of state secrets, after pro-government media accused her of giving files on Azerbaijani opposition figures to supposed U.S. intelligence agents. The U.S. embassy denied the claim. She also faced a separate criminal defamation lawsuit over allegations that she published a document identifying a former opposition member as a government informer. Authorities had also restricted her movements: in October, customs officials stopped her from leaving the country for a conference, and earlier that month airport officials detained and searched her for hours upon her return from Strasbourg. In 2012, she was targeted by a smear campaign involving illegally obtained intimate images. Her arrest was the latest in a wider crackdown. Human Rights Watch said Azerbaijan had brought or threatened unfounded criminal charges against at least 50 activists, journalists, bloggers, and human rights defenders in the previous two and a half years, with many now imprisoned.

The article argues that U.S. sanctions and isolation policies have repeatedly failed to produce political change in authoritarian states, using Cuba as the clearest example and Russia as the likely next case. It opens with a hypothetical future speech by a U.S. president in 2064 about Russia, modeled closely on President Barack Obama’s recent announcement restoring diplomatic relations with Cuba and easing the long-standing U.S. trade embargo. The point of the imagined speech is to suggest that, just as Washington eventually acknowledged the failure of its Cuba policy, it may one day have to admit the same about Russia. The author recounts how the U.S. embargo on Cuba, imposed in 1960 and expanded by the 1996 Helms-Burton Act, was explicitly designed to weaken the Communist government and encourage democratic transition. Helms-Burton promised to help the Cuban people regain freedom and prosperity and to support a transition government or democratically elected government. Yet more than five decades later, Cuba remains ruled by the Communist Party, with no meaningful political opposition. Although its economy has become somewhat more flexible than under Fidel Castro, the country is still described as oppressive and heavily subordinated to state control. The author argues that this outcome is not despite the embargo, but partly because of it, since the policy gave the regime a powerful excuse to blame domestic hardship on an external enemy. To support this point, the article cites Canadian economist Archibald R.M. Ritter, who said the Helms-Burton policy reinforced Fidel Castro’s image as a defender of Cuba against foreign aggression, strengthened hardliners, silenced critics, and provided a pretext for internal failures. The author then draws a direct parallel to Western sanctions on Russia, suggesting they are producing the same effect by enabling Vladimir Putin to present himself as a protector against American hostility. The article notes that Putin used his annual press conference to avoid addressing his government’s failure to use Russia’s oil wealth effectively over the previous eight years, instead portraying himself as a barrier to U.S. aggression. This stance, the author says, is politically useful and popular, especially as Russia has become the most anti-American country in Europe over the past year. Although the U.S. has not officially said that sanctions are meant to bring down Putin, Secretary of State John Kerry has indicated they could be lifted quickly if Putin changed course. The author argues, however, that as long as Putin remains in power, he is unlikely to stop interfering in Ukraine or relinquish Crimea, which Russia annexed in March. German Chancellor Angela Merkel is cited as acknowledging that the West is engaged in an economic war of attrition against Putin. She compared the situation to East Germany in 1989, when economic collapse helped pave the way for reunification with West Germany after the Soviet Union weakened. But the article says Cuba offers a more relevant warning: sanctions there did not produce collapse or regime change. Instead, the embargo quickly destroyed the usefulness of Cuba’s U.S.-made industrial equipment, and when the Soviet Union later collapsed, Cuba adapted just enough to survive with limited market reforms and little public resistance. The author recounts a personal visit to Cuba, describing it as both ruined and strangely preserved by Communist rule. Ordinary goods such as decent food and gasoline were available only in “convertible pesos,” a tourist-linked currency exchanged at a harsh rate. Locals had little material comfort beyond cheap rum and salsa music, yet many spoke respectfully of the Castros, saying the leaders were not corrupt, were doing their best under the embargo, and were gradually allowing more private business. The author, aware that people in Communist societies may speak cautiously to outsiders, asked questions privately and over drinks, but still received similar answers. Cubans were not happy, but they had adapted to shortages, travel restrictions, and lack of internet freedom as if such conditions were normal. The author says he observed a similar mood in Moscow, where people complained about the economic damage caused by Russia’s self-isolation but were not ready to protest. Russians, he suggests, may not be able to endure Cuban-style austerity in the long term, especially given Russia’s harsh winters and less forgiving climate. For now, however, they remain cushioned by wealth accumulated during the oil boom years. The article concludes that Obama was right to admit the Cuba embargo was a failure, and that the same recognition should be applied immediately to sanctions on Russia. The author’s central warning is that trade, openness, and engagement are more effective than embargoes and isolation. Western leaders, he argues, should consider whether they really want to turn Putin’s Russia into a much larger and more dangerous version of Castro’s Cuba.

# U.S. Sanctions: A Failed Policy Repeated This opinion piece argues that Western sanctions against Russia are following the same counterproductive path as the decades-long U.S. embargo against Cuba, ultimately strengthening authoritarian leaders rather than promoting democratic change. The author opens with a satirical hypothetical scenario imagining a future U.S. president in 2064 announcing normalized relations with Russia after 50 years of isolation policy. The speech mirrors President Barack Obama's actual announcement in 2014 regarding Cuba, highlighting how both situations involve failed isolation strategies rooted in Cold War-era thinking. **The Cuba Precedent** The U.S. embargo against Cuba, initiated in 1960 and expanded through the Helms-Burton Act in 1996, explicitly aimed at regime change and democratization. However, after 54 years, Cuba remained under Communist Party rule with minimal political freedoms, despite economic liberalization. The author argues this outcome wasn't incidental to the embargo but largely caused by it. According to Canadian economist Archibald R.M. Ritter, Helms-Burton actually strengthened Fidel Castro's position by portraying him as a champion against external aggression. The sanctions reinforced hardliners, silenced critics, and provided convenient excuses for domestic failures. Rather than promoting freedom, the embargo became a tool that the regime used to justify restrictions on its people. **Russia Following the Same Pattern** The author observes that Western sanctions against Russia are producing identical results. Russian President Vladimir Putin uses Western pressure to portray himself as defending against American aggression—a popular narrative that made Russia the most anti-American nation in Europe. Secretary of State John Kerry claimed sanctions could be lifted within weeks or days if Putin changed course, yet both Kerry and other officials understood that Putin would never voluntarily cease involvement in Ukraine or return Crimea. German Chancellor Angela Merkel explicitly described Western policy as economic attrition against Putin, invoking East Germany's collapse in 1989 as a model. However, this comparison overlooks a crucial difference: Cuba's survival despite far harsher economic conditions. **Cuba's Resilience Under Embargo** The author's personal observations from Cuba reveal a country existing in perpetual economic hardship. U.S.-made capital became useless after the embargo; when Soviet support ended, the regime survived with minimal market reforms. Foreign tourists accessed goods through "convertible pesos" at unfavorable exchange rates, while locals endured shortages and restricted travel and internet access. Remarkably, despite these conditions, Cubans the author interviewed spoke respectfully of the Castros, crediting them with fighting the embargo and gradually improving conditions. Even when questioned privately over drinks, people maintained this perspective. They weren't happy but had accepted their circumstances as inevitable. **The Crucial Distinction** The author notes that Russians, though grumbling about economic costs from self-isolation, similarly show no protest inclination. However, Russia possesses advantages Cuba lacks: greater wealth from oil boom years and a larger, more powerful position. Russia could potentially endure longer under sanctions, yet Western leaders should question whether they truly want to create "Castro's Cuba—only far bigger and more dangerous." **The Path Forward** The author argues that Obama correctly admitted the Cuba embargo failed. If U.S. leaders possessed foresight, they would acknowledge Russia sanctions' failure immediately rather than waiting 50 years. The evidence suggests that trade, openness, and engagement prove more effective than isolation in influencing wayward nations. The central thesis is clear: isolation policies entrench authoritarian regimes by providing external enemies to blame for internal problems. Both Cuba and Russia demonstrate that sanctions strengthen leaders' control while offering populations convenient explanations for hardship. Breaking this cycle requires acknowledging failed strategies and pursuing diplomatic engagement instead.

Iraqi lawmakers and officials are seeking to move the case of four former Blackwater contractors, recently pardoned by US President Donald Trump, to international courts and the United Nations, according to Adnan al-Asadi, a member of Iraq’s parliament security and defense committee. Qassim Soleimani and militia leader Abu Mahdi al-Muhandis in January. A gradual coalition drawdown has been underway for months.

The United States invaded in 2003, withdrew in 2011, and returned in 2014 after the Islamic State group seized large parts of the country. Repeated attacks on the U.S. Embassy and on convoys carrying equipment for U.S. troops have prompted Washington to threaten to close its diplomatic mission in Baghdad. The incident also follows a Pentagon announcement that troop levels in Iraq would be reduced from 3,000 to 2,500. In mid-October, Iran-backed militias said they would temporarily stop attacks on American targets if U.S.-led coalition forces withdrew, citing a January Iraqi parliamentary resolution calling for their expulsion. That resolution followed the U.S. drone strike that killed Iranian Gen. Qassim Soleimani and Iraqi militia leader Abu Mahdi al-Muhandis near Baghdad airport. A gradual coalition drawdown has been underway for months, with Iraqi forces taking on more anti-Islamic State operations on their own.

# Summary Rockets struck Baghdad on Tuesday, with four landing in the heavily fortified Green Zone, killing a child and wounding at least five people. One rocket hit near Iraq's National Security Service, approximately 600 meters from the American Embassy. Some rockets were intercepted by a U.S. air defense system, while three additional rockets landed outside the Green Zone, hitting near Baghdad Medical City hospital and a public park. Two Iraqi security personnel were also wounded inside the Green Zone. The attack marks an end to an informal truce announced by Iran-backed militias in October, signaling renewed tensions. No group immediately claimed responsibility, though Iraq's military vowed "prosecution and accountability." This incident comes amid ongoing tensions between U.S. forces and Iran-aligned groups in Iraq. In October, Shiite militia groups had agreed to temporarily halt attacks targeting American presence, contingent on U.S.-led coalition troop withdrawal. This condition stemmed from a non-binding Iraqi parliamentary resolution passed in January, following the U.S. airstrike that killed Iranian General Qassim Soleimani and Iraqi militia leader Abu Mahdi al-Muhandis. The Pentagon recently announced plans to reduce U.S. troop levels in Iraq from 3,000 to 2,500. A gradual drawdown has been underway for months, with coalition forces withdrawing from several bases. U.S. officials support withdrawal but insist on a scheduled timeline, while most Iraqi officials favor gradual reduction. Iraqi forces have increasingly conducted anti-Islamic State operations independently, with coalition assistance now limited to high-level capabilities like surveillance and air support.

As the United States prepares to reduce its military presence in Iraq by another 500 troops, pro-Iranian factions have resumed attacks on the US embassy in Baghdad, ending a fragile truce that had briefly halted such violence. Late Tuesday, rockets struck the American diplomatic compound just as Washington announced the latest drawdown from its roughly 3,000-strong force. No group publicly claimed responsibility, but sources within the network of militias known as the “Islamic Resistance” told AFP they were involved. The attack marked a renewed escalation after a year of rocket and roadside bomb attacks on Western targets across Iraq, incidents that US and Iraqi officials have blamed on hardline groups aligned with Tehran. Analysts said the factions had recalculated their position as US troop levels fall, Donald Trump’s presidency nears its end, and Iraqi Prime Minister Mustafa Al Kadhemi remains firmly opposed to them. Hamdi Malik, an expert on Iraqi paramilitary groups, said the latest strike was more serious than earlier ones because it used heavier and more accurate Grad rockets rather than munitions meant to miss. He said the message was aimed at both the United States and Kadhemi, whom the militias view as too close to Washington. The US had already reduced its troop presence in Iraq from about 5,000 to 3,000 over the past year, arguing that the Islamic State threat had diminished. Iraqi Foreign Minister Fuad Hussein said Wednesday that the latest withdrawal had been planned and that the process was now in its final phase. Tehran has long demanded that US forces leave the region, a position it intensified after the January American drone strike that killed Iranian General Qassem Soleimani and Iraqi militia commander Abu Mahdi al-Muhandis. That attack was ordered by Trump as part of his “maximum pressure” campaign against Iran. Experts say the outgoing administration’s remaining months offer Iran a window to increase pressure. Ramzy Mardini of the University of Chicago’s Pearson Institute said the certainty that Trump will soon leave office gives Iran room to escalate and build leverage before Joe Biden takes over. Biden has signaled a desire to return to diplomacy with Iran, raising the possibility of sanctions relief. The earlier truce followed a warning from Secretary of State Mike Pompeo that the US would close its embassy if the attacks did not stop. Even during the calm, Iraqi officials said Washington was preparing evacuation plans for diplomats and considering possible strikes on Kataeb Hizhollah and other pro-Iran groups, along with new sanctions. A US official in Baghdad said the latest rocket attack could accelerate those plans and perhaps mark the breaking point for the embassy’s continued presence.

# Summary: Pro-Iran Factions Resume Iraq Attacks as US Troops Withdraw As the United States announced plans to withdraw an additional 500 troops from Iraq, reducing its presence to roughly 3,000 soldiers, pro-Iran militant factions have resumed attacks on American interests, breaking a month-long ceasefire. On Tuesday evening, rockets targeted the US embassy in Baghdad, marking a significant escalation in tensions. The attack was attributed to the "Islamic Resistance," a network of hardline groups aligned with Tehran, though no faction formally claimed responsibility. Experts note this represents a strategic shift—previous attacks used less accurate weapons suggesting deliberate misses to avoid retaliation. Tuesday's assault employed heavier Grad rockets, signaling serious intent. **Strategic Calculations** Analysts attribute the escalation to changing circumstances. With the Trump administration set to leave office in two months, Iraq's Prime Minister Mustafa Al Kadhemi perceived as pro-American, and US forces diminishing, pro-Iran factions recalculated their approach. The attack serves dual purposes: demonstrating power to both Washington and Baghdad's leadership while asserting that these groups will maintain influence even after American withdrawal. **Broader Context** The US has reduced troop levels from approximately 5,000 to 3,000, citing decreased threats from ISIS. However, Iran has long demanded complete American withdrawal, particularly following the January drone strike killing Iranian General Qassem Soleimani and a senior Iraqi paramilitary leader. The timing appears strategic. With Trump's departure guaranteed, Iran sees an opportunity to escalate before President-elect Joe Biden takes office. Biden has signaled interest in returning to diplomacy and potentially rejoining the nuclear deal Trump abandoned in 2018, which could lift sanctions on Tehran. **Potential Consequences** The rocket attack violated a truce established after Secretary of State Mike Pompeo threatened to close the US embassy if attacks continued. US officials in Baghdad suggest the new assault may trigger previously planned responses, including potential military strikes against pro-Iran factions and expanded sanctions on Iranian interests before the administration transitions. Experts suggest the escalation serves multiple purposes for Iran: gaining negotiating leverage with the incoming administration, establishing a hostile environment that complicates Biden's options for maintaining troops, and presenting the new administration with a fait accompli regarding troop withdrawals. The situation remains volatile, with the outgoing administration potentially preparing significant retaliation before leaving office, while pro-Iran groups attempt to consolidate power and influence during the transition period.

Ali Jayad al-Salhi, a veteran sniper in an Iraqi Shiite militia, was killed last year in fighting against the Islamic State group, but in death he has become a near-saintly figure among many Shiites in Iraq. Posters of al-Salhi now appear across Basra and other Shiite areas, his image is printed on cakes, poems celebrate his piety and bravery, and the rifle he is said to have used to kill nearly 400 militants is displayed in a museum in Karbala, the holiest Shiite city. His rise to legend reflects the growing political and military stature of Iraq’s Shiite militias, known as the Popular Mobilization Forces, or Hashed, after they helped defeat Islamic State. Backed by Iran in many cases, the militias have emerged from the war with a powerful aura among Iraq’s Shiite majority, who increasingly view them as a sacred force and potential pillar of post-ISIS Iraq. That reverence stands in sharp contrast to the view among many Sunni Muslims, who accuse the Hashed of abuses in areas seized from Islamic State and see the group as an instrument of Iranian influence in Iraq. For many Shiites, however, the Hashed embody long-standing religious themes of martyrdom, sacrifice and victory through death. Supporters compare the fighters to Imam Hussein, the grandson of the Prophet Muhammad who was killed at Karbala in the 7th century, and some even link the militias to Imam Mahdi, the hidden Shiite leader expected to return and lead a final battle against evil. The militias grew after Grand Ayatollah Ali al-Sistani called on volunteers in June 2014 to fight the militants. Tens of thousands answered, joining various factions. Since then, the Hashed have used funerals, posters, poetry and public mourning to elevate fallen commanders and fighters. Al-Salhi’s own funeral drew thousands to Najaf, where he was buried in the Valley of Peace cemetery near the shrine of Imam Ali.

Iraq’s president condemned a rocket strike on Baghdad’s heavily fortified Green Zone on Sunday night as a “terrorist act” that threatens civilians, the state’s sovereignty and the country’s international standing. According to the Iraqi military, eight rockets were fired at the area, which houses foreign embassies including the U.S. Embassy. At least one Iraqi soldier was injured when a rocket hit near a security checkpoint. Most of the rockets landed in the nearby Qadisiya residential neighborhood, damaging several buildings and cars. The U.S. Embassy said its compound suffered only minor damage and no embassy personnel were injured or killed. In a Facebook statement, the embassy said its defensive systems were activated during the attack. Witnesses in Baghdad said the C-RAM air defense system intercepted incoming rockets, and social media video showed tracers in the sky over the Green Zone. The embassy also said it had received reports of damage in surrounding residential areas and possible injuries to Iraqi civilians, and urged Iraqi leaders to prevent future attacks and hold those responsible accountable. The Iraqi presidency said in a written statement that attacking the Green Zone endangers innocent lives and property and damages Iraq’s foreign relations. It said targeting diplomatic missions undermines the country’s reputation and its efforts to preserve state prestige. The Iraqi military said an “outlaw group” launched the rockets from al-Rasheed camp in southern Baghdad. U.S. Secretary of State Mike Pompeo blamed Iranian-backed militias for the attack, saying the United States strongly condemned the latest strike on Baghdad’s International Zone. He said the attack caused at least one Iraqi civilian casualty and damaged civilian property, even though embassy staff were unharmed. Pompeo also argued that Iran-backed militias are obstructing Iraq’s recovery from the COVID-19 pandemic and economic crisis, while also stealing state resources, attacking protesters and activists, and fueling sectarian violence. The Green Zone has long been a frequent target of rocket attacks, often linked to opposition to the U.S. military presence in Iraq. Last month, seven rockets were fired at the area, killing at least one child and injuring five other civilians. The latest attack came as the Trump administration had announced plans to withdraw thousands more U.S. troops from Iraq and Afghanistan by January 15, 2021, leaving about 2,500 troops in each country. Earlier this month, CNN reported that some U.S. staff were being temporarily withdrawn from the Baghdad embassy amid concerns of retaliation around the anniversary of the killing of Iranian Gen. Qasem Soleimani.

The article looks back on the absurd, funny, and bizarre side of American politics in 2019, set against a deeply divided and painful political climate. It opens by noting that the year was dominated by impeachment, intense partisanship, and a Democratic presidential primary that often felt repetitive and exhausting. But alongside the seriousness, the NBC News Political Unit assembled a list of the year’s strangest political moments, presented in chronological order. One of the first examples was Beto O’Rourke, whose energetic and highly public online persona had helped make him a Democratic favorite after his close 2018 Senate race against Ted Cruz. His skateboarding, guacamole-eating, and other social media antics had once seemed charming, but his decision to post about a trip to the dental hygienist struck many as oversharing. The article suggests that this kind of unfiltered access to O’Rourke’s life did not age well, especially after he later declared, “Man, I’m just born to be in it,” only to exit the presidential race months later. Ted Cruz also earned a spot on the list for his response to an online meme that featured his photo and the caption “this man ate my son.” Instead of ignoring it, Cruz replied, “He was delicious!” The joke quickly sparked arguments online about whether the senator had been funny or simply alarming, with supporters and critics debating its meaning and who, if anyone, had “won” the exchange. The article then turns to John Delaney, described as having a “Very Serious Year” as he spent his own money campaigning for the Democratic nomination with little success. His earnestness and fitness-minded image were contrasted with his turn on the giant slide at the Iowa State Fair, which did not produce the carefree delight one might expect. The joke is that Delaney seemed too intense to enjoy even a simple fair attraction. Among the year’s most memorable political absurdities, the article highlights President Trump’s suggestion that the United States might buy Greenland from Denmark, comparing it to a “large real estate deal.” This sparked an international uproar and led to the cancellation of Trump’s planned state visit to Denmark. Another infamous Trump moment was his display of a doctored hurricane map, altered with a Sharpie, after a dispute with the National Weather Service in Alabama over storm projections. The article presents both episodes as the sort of thing future generations will hear about as emblematic of the Trump era. Sen. Mitt Romney also made the list for his secret Twitter identity. The article notes that he had used an alias account to lurk on the platform and later admitted that he was “Pierre Delecto,” a pseudonym that joined the ranks of memorable political alter egos. The comparison made is to Anthony Weiner’s “Carlos Danger,” underscoring how unusual Romney’s online secrecy seemed. Rudy Giuliani’s accidental phone calls became another source of political comedy. NBC News reporter Rich Schapiro received two butt-dials from Giuliani, during which the former New York mayor could be heard saying things like “the problem is we need some money.” The article notes that journalists were amused by the unexpected access, though the calls also underscored Giuliani’s chaotic role as Trump’s personal lawyer. The piece also mentions South Dakota’s meth-fighting slogan, “Meth. We’re on it.” Officials spent about half a million dollars on the campaign, and the article gently mocks the apparent lack of outside feedback before launching such a slogan. It acknowledges the seriousness of the meth crisis while still pointing out the awkwardness of the phrase. Another oddity involved Rep. Eric Swalwell, whose name became linked online to a viral discussion about whether a congressman had audibly passed gas during an MSNBC appearance. The article treats this as one of the internet’s enduring political mysteries, alongside more serious unsolved questions like the location of Jimmy Hoffa’s body and Area 51. Joe Biden also appears in the roundup for his habit of challenging people to push-up contests or footraces. He joked earlier in the year about doing so against Trump, and later, during a tense Iowa town hall, he angrily told an older man, “You’re a damn liar, man,” before again suggesting a physical contest. The article notes later debate over whether Biden also called the man fat. Andrew Yang likewise joked about challenging Trump to “any physical or mental feat under the sun,” later adding a joking exception about keeping a hot-air balloon from rising, saying Trump would be better at that because “he is so fat.” The article ends with a reference to Trump’s remarks about toilets, then closes with a short list of honorable mentions: teenagers running an 89-year-old’s presidential campaign, a gross prank Beto O’Rourke allegedly played on his wife, Marianne Williamson’s “Girlfriend” shoutout, Deval Patrick’s sparsely attended event, and Trump’s copyright dispute with Nickelback. It concludes by wishing readers happy holidays and a happy new year, and includes a correction noting that reporter Rich Schapiro’s name had been misspelled in an earlier version.

# A Year of Political Absurdity: 2019's Most Bizarre Moments As 2019 drew to a close, the NBC News Political Unit compiled a retrospective of the year's most ridiculous, laughable, and downright bizarre political moments—a necessary antidote to a year dominated by serious partisan divides and impeachment proceedings that left the nation split in half. ## Social Media Mishaps and Oversharing Beto O'Rourke's 2019 presidential campaign began with the promise of his viral social media presence and antagonistic 2018 Senate race against Ted Cruz. However, his decision to live-stream a dental hygiene appointment crossed the line from charming into uncomfortable territory, demonstrating that unfiltered access to a candidate's every moment doesn't always age well. Eight months after declaring "Man, I'm just born to be in it," O'Rourke had exited the race entirely. Senator Mitt Romney inadvertently revealed his secret Twitter alias, "Pierre Delecto," which he used as a "lurker" on the platform. The French-sounding pseudonym drew comparisons to Anthony Weiner's infamous "Carlos Danger" account, proving that older Republican men's relationships with technology continue to provide entertainment value. ## Presidential Eccentricities President Trump's most memorable 2019 moment may have been his suggestion to purchase Greenland—treating the ice-covered Danish territory as a potential real estate deal. The proposal sparked a transatlantic diplomatic incident that resulted in the cancellation of his planned state visit to Denmark, a moment future political historians will undoubtedly reference when discussing the Trump era. Equally absurd was Trump's response to criticism from the National Weather Service regarding Hurricane Dorian's projected path. The president displayed a doctored weather map that he allegedly altered himself with a Sharpie, demonstrating his willingness to engage in petty disputes with government agencies on social media. Trump also made headlines with unexpected comments about toilets, though the article doesn't elaborate on specifics—another entry in the year's collection of inexplicable presidential statements. ## Accidental Communications and Embarrassing Moments Rudy Giuliani, Trump's personal attorney, became famous for accidental "butt-dials" to NBC News reporter Rich Schapiro. In two separate incidents, Schapiro received unintended calls during which Giuliani could be heard discussing sensitive matters, including the phrase "the problem is we need some money." Schapiro wasn't alone; other prominent journalists reported receiving their own Giuliani butt-dials, though none quite as substantive. ## Campaign Trail Oddities John Delaney's serious Democratic presidential campaign, funded largely by his personal wealth, generated minimal political traction but plenty of awkward moments—including an unexpectedly grim appearance on the Iowa State Fair's giant slide that lacked the childlike joy such experiences typically inspire. South Dakota's state government made a questionable marketing decision when it spent half a million dollars on billboards promoting its methamphetamine awareness campaign with the slogan "Meth. We're on it."—a phrase that unintentionally suggested state endorsement of the drug. ## Confrontational Moments and Physical Challenges Joe Biden developed a peculiar habit of challenging critics to physical contests. When an 83-year-old Iowa man aggressively questioned Biden's age and his son Hunter's Ukrainian business dealings, Biden responded angrily, calling the man "a damn liar" and suggesting a push-up contest or footrace. Later disputes arose over whether Biden also insulted the man's appearance. Andrew Yang similarly mused about challenging Trump to physical or mental contests, though he acknowledged one exception: Trump would likely excel at keeping a rising hot-air balloon grounded because "he is so fat." ## Other Notable Absurdities The article mentions several additional bizarre moments: a congressman's apparent audible flatulence during an MSNBC appearance; Beto O'Rourke's alleged prank on his wife; Marianne Williamson's "Girlfriend" shoutout; a barely-attended campaign event for Deval Patrick; and Trump's copyright dispute with the band Nickelback. The compilation serves as a reminder that while 2019 featured serious political divisions and consequential debates about American values, the year also provided countless moments of unintentional comedy that offered welcome relief from the gravity of contemporary politics.

Japanese Prime Minister Shinzo Abe’s visit to Pearl Harbor was meant to commemorate reconciliation with outgoing U.S. President Barack Obama, but analysts said the trip was also carefully calibrated with Donald Trump in mind. Abe and Obama made a historic joint appearance at Pearl Harbor in Hawaii, where Abe praised the four years of progress in the Japan-U.S. relationship and underscored the importance of the alliance. His speech before war veterans highlighted forgiveness and cooperation between the two countries since World War II, but experts noted that Abe was just as notable for what he avoided saying. Unlike Obama, who used the occasion to warn against hatred, tribalism, and inward-looking politics, Abe did not mention any uncertainty created by Trump’s election. He only briefly referred to “now, and especially now” as a time to uphold the values of tolerance and reconciliation. Analysts said this restraint reflected Abe’s desire not to antagonize the incoming president, whose views on Asia and the U.S.-Japan alliance were still unclear. Brad Glosserman of the Honolulu-based Pacific Forum CSIS said the timing of the visit mattered because the Obama administration was ending and there was no guarantee Trump would share Obama’s priorities or perspective on the alliance. Obama had strengthened ties with Japan as part of his “pivot to Asia,” including support for concerns over China’s growing assertiveness in the region. By contrast, Trump’s policy toward Asia had not yet been articulated, and there was no clear sense of who would shape it. Abe had already become the first foreign leader to meet Trump after the election, visiting him at Trump Tower in New York, though little was revealed publicly about their discussion. With a possible rule change in Abe’s party potentially allowing him to remain in office until 2021, his legacy could depend heavily on how he manages relations with Trump as much as on his relationship with Obama. Other scholars said the Pearl Harbor visit gave Abe a useful opportunity to shape Trump’s view of Japan before a likely summit shortly after inauguration. Tosh Minohara of Kobe University said Trump’s interest in Japan appeared limited and that Abe’s visit let him make an impression before the January meeting. He described the atmosphere at Pearl Harbor as cordial but deliberately measured, suggesting Abe avoided overly emotional displays of closeness with Obama that might have irritated Trump. Fumiaki Kubo of the University of Tokyo said Abe had planned to visit Pearl Harbor eventually to reciprocate Obama’s historic trip to Hiroshima in May, but might have delayed it if Hillary Clinton had won the election. He argued that reconciliation would have been harder to explain to Trump, who sees foreign relations in transactional terms. The next major task for Abe is to brief Trump on Japan’s expanding security role under new legislation and on Tokyo’s support for countries resisting China’s claims in the South China Sea. Kubo said Abe will want Trump to reaffirm key Obama-era understandings, including U.S. support for Japan under Article 5 of the security treaty, which Obama confirmed applies to the disputed Senkaku Islands. Abe will also want Trump to continue backing freedom of navigation in the South China Sea. Analysts warned that China may test the new U.S. administration with more assertive moves in the region. Recent Chinese actions have included flights through the Miyako Strait and the seizure of a U.S. underwater drone near the Philippines. While Pearl Harbor may be remembered as a symbolic final chapter in the Obama-Abe partnership, the durability of the Japan-U.S. alliance now depends on how Abe handles the Trump era.

# Summary: Abe's Pearl Harbor Message Aims to Inform, Not Antagonize Trump Japanese Prime Minister Shinzo Abe visited Pearl Harbor with outgoing U.S. President Barack Obama in December 2016, marking a historic joint appearance at the site of Japan's 1941 attack that brought America into World War II. While the visit celebrated four years of progress in the Japan-U.S. alliance under Obama, experts suggest Abe was strategically positioning Japan for the incoming Trump administration. Abe's approach at Pearl Harbor was notably measured, reflecting awareness of the uncertain relationship ahead. His speech avoided references to Trump-related uncertainty, instead making only subtle allusions to the importance of maintaining tolerance and reconciliation. In contrast, Obama's remarks appeared to address Trump's campaign rhetoric, emphasizing the need to resist tribalism and hatred. According to Brad Glosserman of the Pacific Forum CSIS, the timing reflected concerns that Trump might not prioritize the U.S.-Japan alliance as Obama had through his "pivot to Asia" policy. The visit served multiple strategic purposes. Abe reciprocated Obama's historic May visit to Hiroshima, but the timing was crucial. Experts suggest Abe accelerated the visit because Trump's unclear Asian policy created uncertainty about future diplomatic opportunities. Trump's interest in Asia appeared limited, making the Pearl Harbor visit valuable for establishing rapport before their scheduled January meeting. Abe had previously met Trump at Trump Tower in New York following the election but revealed little to media afterward. The Pearl Harbor visit allowed Abe to make a positive impression before substantive policy discussions occurred. Kobe University professor Tosh Minohara noted the atmosphere was "cordial, but at a measured distance," reflecting Abe's caution about appearing too close to Obama. Several critical issues require Trump's confirmation. Obama had explicitly stated that the disputed Senkaku Islands in Okinawa Prefecture fall under the Japan-U.S. security treaty's Article 5, meaning America would defend them if attacked. Trump's commitment to this position remained unclear. Additionally, Abe needed assurance regarding freedom of navigation in the South China Sea, where China has been increasingly assertive. Recent Chinese military actions heightened concerns about regional stability. These included overflights of the Miyako Strait separating Okinawa islands and seizure of a U.S. underwater drone in international waters near the Philippines. Experts predicted China might test Trump's intentions through further assertive actions in coming months. Abe's political situation added urgency. A potential rule change in his Liberal Democratic Party could keep him in power until 2021, meaning his legacy would be defined significantly by his handling of Trump-era foreign policy. University of Tokyo professor Fumiaki Kubo suggested that if Abe had delayed the Pearl Harbor visit, explaining historical reconciliation to Trump—who views bilateral relations transactionally—would have become more difficult. The Pearl Harbor visit served as a final note on Abe-Obama cooperation while establishing groundwork for Trump relations. However, significant challenges remained in maintaining the Japan-U.S. alliance as the cornerstone of American foreign policy under the new administration. The success of Abe's strategy would depend on Trump's January confirmation of key security commitments made under Obama.

Prime Minister Shinzo Abe ended 2019 with an unusually busy round of diplomacy that highlighted the major foreign policy tests Japan would face in 2020. He first hosted Iranian President Hassan Rouhani in Tokyo on Dec. 20-21, the first visit to Japan by an Iranian president in 19 years. Soon after, Abe traveled to Chengdu for the Japan-China-South Korea summit, where he met Chinese Premier Li Keqiang, South Korean President Moon Jae-in, and separately Chinese President Xi Jinping. These meetings, the article argues, foreshadowed the difficult balancing acts Abe would have to manage in the year ahead. Iran is presented as the clearest example of that balancing act. Since the Trump administration withdrew the United States from the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action, tensions between Washington and Tehran have escalated. Although President Donald Trump has not ruled out his own summit diplomacy with Rouhani, the U.S. continues to push allies to take a harder line on Iran and to participate in security patrols in the Persian Gulf. Japan, however, has long maintained friendly ties with Tehran, and Iran is its third-largest oil supplier. As Abe’s government considers dispatching Self-Defense Forces to the Strait of Hormuz in indirect support of the U.S.-led Maritime Security Initiative, it must do so without damaging relations with Iran, requiring careful coordination with both Washington and Tehran. China poses an even more complex challenge. Japan is preparing for Xi Jinping’s state visit in the spring, and Abe and Chinese leaders agreed during the Chengdu meetings to work toward “a new era” in bilateral relations. But Abe drew criticism at home for not speaking forcefully enough about China’s human rights abuses and its assertive behavior, especially amid developments in Hong Kong. At the same time, although U.S.-China tensions eased somewhat after a preliminary trade agreement on Dec. 13, Washington remains deeply critical of Beijing on broader issues and continues to urge allies to take a similar stance. With calls growing in Japan to cancel Xi’s visit, Abe must balance improving ties with China against defending the universal values that have shaped postwar Japanese foreign policy. South Korea remains another difficult issue. Relations between Tokyo and Seoul have deteriorated sharply under the Moon administration, falling to their lowest point since diplomatic normalization in 1965. Abe’s Dec. 24 summit with Moon, the first between the two leaders in 18 months, was a modest step toward stopping the decline, but major disagreements remain unresolved and a quick turnaround appears unlikely. Still, Japan sees South Korea as an important partner because of the North Korean threat. Abe must therefore find a way to re-engage Seoul without making concessions on sensitive issues such as compensation for wartime Korean laborers. The U.S.-Japan alliance will also face pressure in 2020. The Defense Ministry announced on Dec. 25 that replacing U.S. Marine Corps Air Station Futenma in Okinawa will take 12 years, delaying relocation beyond 2030 and provoking renewed opposition from Okinawa’s prefectural government. Japan will also begin negotiations to renew its host nation support agreement with the U.S., likely facing demands for greater financial support, as seen in the U.S.-South Korea burden-sharing talks. Abe’s personal ties with Trump may again come under scrutiny if they fail to ease Washington’s stance. Combined with the burden of hosting the Summer Olympics, these issues make 2020 a demanding year for Abe as Japan’s top diplomat.

# Abe's Foreign Policy Challenges for 2020 Prime Minister Shinzo Abe concluded 2019 with intensive diplomatic engagements that foreshadowed the complex foreign policy challenges he would face in 2020. His year-end activities included hosting Iranian President Hassan Rouhani in December—the first Iranian presidential visit to Japan in 19 years—and attending a Japan-China-South Korea summit in Chengdu, where he met with Chinese Premier Li Keqiang, Chinese President Xi Jinping, and South Korean President Moon Jae-in. ## The Iran Balancing Act Iran represents Abe's most delicate diplomatic challenge. Following the United States' withdrawal from the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA), tensions between Washington and Tehran have escalated. While the Trump administration hasn't ruled out summit diplomacy with Iran, it continues pressuring allies to adopt a hardline stance and participate in Persian Gulf security operations. Japan faces a competing interest: Iran supplies Japan with significant oil resources, and Tokyo has cultivated a beneficial bilateral relationship with Tehran. Abe's government is considering dispatching Self-Defense Forces to the Strait of Hormuz as part of the U.S.-led Maritime Security Initiative, requiring careful coordination with both Washington and Tehran to avoid damaging relations with either party. ## China's Complications China presents an even more intricate challenge. Abe's government is preparing for Xi Jinping's state visit in spring 2020. During December meetings, both sides agreed to forge "a new era" in bilateral relations. However, Abe faced domestic criticism for not taking a stronger stance against China regarding human rights violations in Hong Kong and other regions. Additionally, while U.S.-China trade tensions temporarily eased following a preliminary trade agreement, the United States remains critical of Chinese behavior and urges allies to maintain a similar position. Growing calls in Japan for canceling Xi's state visit have placed Abe in a difficult position between improving Japan-China relations and upholding Japan's postwar commitment to universal values. ## South Korea's Persistent Problems South Korea presents equally complicated challenges. Japan-Korea relations have deteriorated significantly since Moon Jae-in's administration began, reaching their lowest point since 1965. Although Abe's December summit with Moon—their first meeting in 18 months—represented progress, fundamental disagreements remain on critical issues, offering little hope for immediate improvement. Japan urgently needs South Korea as a partner against North Korean threats, yet some observers note Japan has succumbed to "Korea fatigue." Abe must re-engage Seoul while avoiding compromises on sensitive issues like compensation for Korean laborers during World War II. North Korea's resurgence of provocative rhetoric adds urgency to this diplomatic challenge. ## U.S. Alliance Management Finally, Abe faces challenges managing the U.S.-Japan alliance. The Defense Ministry announced that constructing a replacement facility for the U.S. Marine Corps Air Station Futenma will take 12 years, pushing relocation beyond 2030. This triggered strong opposition from Okinawa's prefectural government. Additionally, Japan will negotiate renewal of its host nation support agreement with the United States, likely facing increased demands for greater financial contributions to U.S. military presence in Japan. With these multifaceted diplomatic challenges and the added responsibility of hosting the Summer Olympics, 2020 promised to be exceptionally demanding for Abe's diplomatic agenda.

The union representing fuel-service workers at Montreal’s two airports said negotiations with Swissport Canada would resume Thursday after two days of picketing, though there was some confusion late Wednesday over exactly when formal talks would restart. Union spokesman Michel Richer first said both sides had agreed to meet Thursday at 10 a.m. But Swissport later said mediators had told the company to “stand by” and that it would not be at the table at that time for the initial meeting with the union. A company representative, Nathalie Bergeron, said Swissport was ready to negotiate whenever called upon. Richer later said the “negotiation process is relaunched” and that the union would meet mediators in the morning before talks with the company were expected to continue. Meanwhile, striking workers returned to the picket lines for a demonstration at Montreal-Trudeau airport. Richer said the workers would remain on strike until a contract was signed. About 100 Swissport employees, who refuel aircraft at Montreal-Trudeau International Airport and the cargo airfield in Mirabel, walked off the job around 11 a.m. the previous day after rejecting a tentative contract. Swissport said it had brought in trained managers from across the country to keep fueling operations running and insisted there had been no flight delays because of the strike. The company said its continuity plan allowed it to continue servicing customers without interruption. The airport confirmed that delayed flights shown on the departures board were caused by weather conditions over the previous days, not the strike. The main issues in dispute are salaries and work-life balance. The workers had been without a contract since August. Last Friday, they rejected a tentative agreement by a 90 per cent vote. Swissport then asked the Canada Industrial Relations Board to suspend the strike, accusing the union of bargaining in bad faith. The board allowed the strike to continue but ordered the union back to the bargaining table. In its ruling, the board said the union had not informed Swissport of the vote result and instead served strike notice while making new demands that were estimated to be more than double those in the tentative deal. The board also ordered the union to drop those new demands as negotiations resumed.

Rex Tillerson, the longtime chief executive of ExxonMobil and President-elect Donald Trump’s nominee for secretary of state, is portrayed as an unusually experienced corporate diplomat whose career has been shaped by global negotiations, especially with Russia. Trump praised Tillerson’s “relationships with leaders all over the world,” suggesting that his international contacts would serve U.S. interests. The most sensitive of those ties is his long relationship with Vladimir Putin, which helped fuel concern over whether Tillerson could be confirmed by the Senate at a time when U.S. intelligence said Moscow had interfered in the election to help Trump. Critics from across the political spectrum quickly questioned the nomination. Senator John McCain, for example, denounced Putin as “a thug, bully and a murderer” and warned against softening that judgment. Environmental groups also objected to the idea of an oil industry veteran becoming America’s top diplomat, particularly because of the role the State Department plays in global climate negotiations. Tillerson, 64, was born in Wichita Falls, Texas, and joined Exxon in 1975 as a young engineer after college. He stayed with the company for his entire career, rising steadily through the ranks to become CEO in 2006. After spending about a decade overseeing Exxon’s operations in more than 50 countries, he had been expected to retire in March. Commentators have described Exxon as an organization that sees itself almost as a transnational power with its own foreign policy, and Tillerson as someone who helped run a “parallel quasi-state” by building relationships with foreign leaders in ways that sometimes diverged from official U.S. policy. One example cited was Exxon’s decision to pursue an oil deal in Iraqi Kurdistan despite objections from the State Department. The company also worked with authoritarian governments even while publicly supporting human rights. Still, investigative accounts have also described Tillerson as personally professional and disciplined in his management style. Tillerson’s ties to Putin were especially significant. The two first met in the 1990s when Tillerson was overseeing a project on Sakhalin Island, and their relationship deepened after Putin came to power in 1999. John Hamre of the Center for Strategic and International Studies said Tillerson had spent more face-to-face time with Putin than almost any other American besides Henry Kissinger. Their relationship was cemented by a major 2011 Exxon-Rosneft agreement to explore for oil in the Arctic and Siberia, a deal initially valued at $3.2 billion and potentially worth far more. That project was later suspended by Western sanctions on Russia. Tillerson has criticized sanctions, arguing they can cause broad collateral damage, raising questions about whether, as secretary of state, he might support easing sanctions in ways that could also benefit Exxon.

The two met in the 1990s during an oil project on Sakhalin Island and strengthened ties after Putin came to power. However, Western sanctions against Russia have stalled the deal. Tillerson has been a vocal opponent of sanctions as a foreign policy tool, arguing they cause "broad collateral damage." As Secretary of State, he would be positioned to advocate for easing sanctions, potentially benefiting his former employer. Despite these concerns, Coll's investigation credits Tillerson with professional integrity throughout his career. The central question remains whether he can prioritize American interests over the oil industry that shaped his entire professional life.

Melissa Roy, who helps organize events at the friendship centre, said the best part of her job is seeing people smile and that the holidays create a stronger sense of togetherness. He emphasized that language is a direct connection to ancestors, culture, and traditional teachings such as love, sharing, and hope.

Haitian Montrealers marked Jan. 1 not only as New Year’s Day but also as Haiti’s Independence Day by preparing and distributing traditional Joumou soup to people experiencing homelessness in Montreal. At Pikliz restaurant in St. Henri, Aly Acadia and about a dozen others cooked the “freedom soup,” which organizer Myriam Joseph said is meant to be shared. She explained that the soup carries deep historical meaning: during Haiti’s colonial period, enslaved Africans were forbidden to eat it, so after independence in 1804, Haitians celebrated by making and eating it. Restaurant co-owner Akim Acadia said the tradition remains important for Haitian families, who gather to eat soup every Jan. 1. Joseph said she wanted to extend that custom to people who cannot afford food, emphasizing that the effort should continue beyond a single day. Co-organizer Marilou Yoshimura said the group distributed 175 servings in total, sending some to homeless shelters and handing the rest directly to people on the street, with help from a social worker who knew where to find them. Joseph said the cause is personal as well: she knows four homeless women who are victims of violence, including one friend she regularly searches for. She and her fellow organizers hope to make the soup distribution an annual tradition and support homeless people throughout the year.

The soup, called Joumou, holds deep historical significance for Haitian culture. During colonial times, enslaved people were forbidden from eating soup. According to restaurant co-owner Akim Acadia, sharing soup remains central to Haitian identity: "When it's Jan. 1, we all have soup with family. It's a big thing for us." The volunteers distributed 175 servings of soup containing ground vegetables, meat, and pasta to homeless shelters and people on the streets, with assistance from a social worker familiar with the community. Joseph's motivation was personal—she knows four homeless women, including a friend, who are victims of violence. Moved by their struggles, she organized this event and plans to continue distributing soup annually while providing year-round support to homeless individuals.

In his final press conference of the year, outgoing U.S. President Barack Obama said he was proud of his record after eight years in office and believed he had performed well as president. Speaking in New York, Obama defended his administration’s handling of major domestic and foreign policy issues, including the economy, the Affordable Care Act, the war in Syria, and Russian interference in the U.S. election. Obama said he was “very proud of the work I’ve done” and argued that he was a better president at the end of his term than when he began. He described his presidency as a historic success despite a difficult start, pointing to the expansion of health coverage under Obamacare. When he entered office, he said, 44 million Americans were uninsured; by the end of his term, more than 20 million of them had gained coverage, and more than 90 percent of Americans were insured for the first time in U.S. history. He also highlighted the state of the economy when he took office in 2009, during the worst recession in decades. Obama recalled that unemployment was nearing 10 percent at the time, but had fallen to 4.6 percent, the lowest level in nearly a decade. He again cited the killing of al Qaeda leader Osama bin Laden and said he had brought 165,000 troops home. “What we’ve done works,” he said, adding that the country was better off than it had been in 2008. On foreign policy, Obama said Syria had been one of the hardest problems of his presidency. He described the suffering in Aleppo as horrific and said he felt personally responsible for trying to prevent such tragedies. He admitted that he had not been successful in ending the violence, but argued that a large-scale U.S. military intervention was not realistic given the strain on American forces. He said diplomacy remained the best available option, even though it could not solve everything. Obama also addressed criticism that he had reacted too slowly to reports of Russian cyber-meddling in the presidential election. He said his main concern was protecting the integrity of the election process without making the issue appear partisan. He said he had told Russian President Vladimir Putin to “cut it out” during a meeting in China in September and promised to respond to Russian actions both publicly and covertly before leaving office on January 20, 2017. The president criticized Republicans, the press, and what he called the coarsening of political culture. He also attacked Putin and Syrian President Bashar al-Assad for the “savage” assault on Aleppo, and dismissed Russia as a weaker country whose economy depended on oil, gas, and arms. Obama expressed frustration with Republican willingness to accept President-elect Donald Trump’s admiration of Putin, saying “Ronald Reagan would roll over in his grave.” He said the media’s coverage of Hillary Clinton during the campaign was troubling, but added that Democrats needed to connect more directly with communities where people were struggling. Obama denied any personal tension with Trump, but warned that campaigning was very different from governing and said Trump would soon face the sobering realities of the presidency. He added that China would not accept Trump’s suggestion that Taiwan could be used as leverage in relations with Beijing.

By the time of his remarks, it had dropped to 4.6 percent, the lowest in nearly a decade. On healthcare, Obama pointed to the passage of the Affordable Care Act as a historic success, noting that his administration had insured more than 20 million previously uninsured Americans, bringing the total insured population to over 90 percent for the first time in U.S. history. ## Foreign Policy and Military Decisions Obama defended his foreign policy decisions, including the elimination of al Qaeda leader Osama bin Laden and the withdrawal of 165,000 troops from overseas deployments. The report says investigators gathered evidence from search warrants, wiretaps, financial records and plea-bargain testimony that points to a criminal conspiracy led by Bolsonaro. It alleges that Bolsonaro “effectively planned, directed and executed” actions aimed at abolishing the democratic rule of law so he could remain in power, with coordination dating back to at least 2019. Police said Bolsonaro also had full knowledge of a plan to assassinate then president-elect Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and Lula’s running mate, Geraldo Alckmin. That allegation is based on conversations intercepted among conspirators and meetings held at the presidential residence. The report identifies eight major pieces of evidence supporting the formal accusation. Argentina’s legalization of abortion in 2020 was the result of a long, cumulative shift in public debate, political organization, and street activism rather than a sudden breakthrough. Just two years earlier, supporters of legal abortion had suffered a painful defeat when the Senate rejected a legalization bill after intense opposition from the Catholic Church. Yet that loss, activists and lawmakers said, helped change the terms of the debate and broaden support for abortion rights in the country. The article describes how the movement grew from a young, urban protest campaign into a national coalition that included older women, men, workers, professionals, and rural activists. Its modern form emerged in 2015 with Ni Una Menos, a women’s movement that began in outrage over the killing of women and quickly expanded to focus on the dangers of illegal, underground abortions. What had once looked like a narrow feminist cause became a broader social movement rooted in public health, social justice, and gender equality. Activists and officials said the movement drew strength from Argentina’s long tradition of mass mobilization. The article links the green handkerchiefs worn by abortion-rights supporters to the white handkerchiefs used decades earlier by the Mothers and Grandmothers of the Plaza de Mayo, who protested the disappearances and abuses of the military dictatorship in the 1970s and 1980s. That legacy helped normalize the idea that “the street,” as Argentines call public protest, can produce political change. Elizabeth Gómez Alcorta, the minister of women, gender and diversity, said street mobilization has a powerful effect in winning rights. The article also places the abortion debate within a broader sequence of progressive legal reforms in Argentina. In 2010, Congress approved same-sex marriage, making Argentina the first country in Latin America to do so. In 2012, it passed one of the world’s most advanced gender identity laws. Both reforms were propelled by public activism. Over time, women also gained greater influence inside Congress itself. A quota law in the 1990s reserved one-third of legislative seats for women, and later reforms expanded that to parity, giving female lawmakers a stronger role in shaping debate. The abortion issue had been discussed in feminist circles since the 1980s, but for many years it had little traction in mainstream politics. UNAMID said on 20 December 2018 that it had completed the closure and handover of 10 team sites to the Government of Sudan, ending with the Graida site in South Darfur. The handovers took place between October and December 2018 as part of the mission’s second-phase reconfiguration, ordered by UN Security Council Resolution 2429 of July 2018. The sites included El Sireaf, Um Baro and Korma in North Darfur; Labado and Shaeria in East Darfur; Mukhjar in Central Darfur; Masteri and Mournei in West Darfur; and Buram and Graida in South Darfur. UNAMID urged the government to use the former mission facilities for non-military civilian purposes that benefit local communities, as promised in the memoranda of understanding and handover documents. Joint Special Representative Jeremiah Mamabolo said the sites should support institutions such as universities, hospitals and schools to address urgent health and education needs. The sites were handed over under existing lease agreements.

The rallies began after noon prayers and were smaller than Thursday’s protests, when at least eight people were killed as thousands marched, some demanding the overthrow of President Omar al-Bashir. A government spokesman blamed “infiltrators” for turning peaceful demonstrations into “subversive activity.” The unrest was among the largest Sudan has seen in five years and could complicate efforts to amend the constitution, potentially allowing Bashir to stay in power into a fourth decade. The country’s economic crisis has deepened since South Sudan’s secession in 2011 cost Sudan three-quarters of its oil output, its main source of foreign currency. Smaller protests also broke out in at least eight Khartoum neighborhoods. Police increased security around major mosques, while many users reported internet disruptions, especially on Facebook, Twitter and WhatsApp. Some people believed the government was trying to slow the protests. Meanwhile, long lines formed at ATMs and bakeries, and the Education Ministry closed schools and kindergartens in Khartoum for safety.

China’s anti-poverty campaign has entered a new phase focused not on declaring victory, but on making sure that victory lasts. After the country announced in 2021 that it had eliminated absolute poverty, the Chinese leadership set up a five-year transition period at the end of 2020 to consolidate those gains, expand them, and connect poverty alleviation with rural revitalization. That transition period is now in its final year, but officials say the effort will continue without interruption. A central rural work conference held Monday and Tuesday in Beijing called for regular mechanisms to prevent rural residents from falling back into poverty. Xinhua’s article describes China’s approach through the acronym “SHIELD,” which stands for systematic and dynamic monitoring, human-centered ethos, industrial development, endogenous empowerment, layered and targeted support, and durable endeavor. Together, these elements are presented as the country’s main safeguards against poverty relapse. The first component is systematic and dynamic monitoring. China has built a long-term system to track signs that households may be slipping back into hardship, especially among groups that were previously lifted out of poverty. The system relies on regular checks and digital monitoring of warning indicators such as sudden medical expenses, job loss, and crop failures. The goal is to detect risks early and respond quickly. In one example from a remote village in Guizhou Province, a local Party secretary learned in April 2025 that a resident named Yang Xilong faced unusually high medical costs because of an eye disease. Within days, a simplified process involving village verification, township review, and district approval brought the family into targeted support, reducing the risk of medical-driven poverty. The article says this monitoring system combines digital tools with face-to-face verification, so that families are not missed because they have moved or live in hard-to-reach places. It also notes that some grassroots governments are adopting the DeepSeek model to analyze data and generate assistance recommendations automatically. In Shanxin town in Guangxi, this reportedly improved analytical efficiency by 50 percent compared with traditional methods. The second pillar is a human-centered ethos. The Chinese government says it treats people at risk of falling back into poverty not as abstract statistics but as individuals facing specific hardships such as illness, disability, or family tragedy. This approach is tied to the broader Chinese modernization concept, which is described as people-centered rather than capital-centered, and also linked to the Confucian ideal of “Ren,” or benevolence. Professor Hu Wen of the Sichuan Administration Institute said the five-year transition period is an important institutional innovation because it allows China to keep supporting people while also creating long-term, regular poverty-prevention mechanisms and encouraging self-reliance as rural revitalization advances. This people-centered system has produced measurable results. By the end of September, more than 7 million people at risk of returning to poverty had received targeted aid, according to the Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Affairs. Education and health indicators have also remained strong: children from households lifted out of poverty have maintained a dynamic zero dropout rate at the compulsory education level, basic medical insurance coverage has stayed above 99 percent, rural housing renovation and seismic retrofitting have continued, and rural tap water penetration has reached 94 percent. Industrial development is the third key element. The central rural work conference emphasized the need to build and expand county-level industries that create wealth and to give farmers more ways to participate in them. One example comes from a garment company in Guizhou, where more than 400 workers, many from relocated households, earn monthly wages of about 4,000 to 5,000 yuan, with top workers earning as much as 10,000 yuan. This has helped stabilize incomes in one of China’s poorest former regions. Across poverty-stricken counties, two to three specialty industries have been developed over the past five years, and their combined value has surpassed 1.7 trillion yuan. To support this progress, the government has invested 850.5 billion yuan in infrastructure and public services in formerly impoverished areas, including transport, water conservancy, education, and healthcare. The fourth pillar is endogenous empowerment, meaning helping formerly poor areas develop their own internal momentum. The article highlights Huawu Village in Guizhou, where Miao embroidery has evolved from a simple “fingertip skill” into a “fingertip economy,” and Zhaojue County in Sichuan, where a once-isolated “cliff village” has become a tourism destination. The idea is to use local resources, crafts, and culture to create sustainable growth. This approach combines poverty alleviation with confidence-building, skills, and knowledge, so residents can move from receiving help to driving their own development. By the end of 2024, 33.05 million people from previously impoverished households were employed, and rural disposable income in counties that escaped poverty reached 17,522 yuan last year, up 24.7 percent from 2021. Layered and targeted support is the fifth element. Instead of a one-size-fits-all model, China uses different forms of aid depending on a household’s needs and capacity. People able to work receive skills training, job placement, and microloans. Those with partial ability may get public welfare jobs. Families hit by illness or disaster can receive subsidies for healthcare, housing, education, and other needs. Those who cannot work at all are covered by the social assistance safety net. The article cites the case of Luo Linmei from Guizhou, whose family received a combination of support after her father died: her mother got a public welfare job and subsistence allowances, while Luo and her sister received education grants through high school and university, helping the family avoid relapse into poverty. The final pillar is durable endeavor. Looking ahead to the 2026-2030 period, China’s next five-year plan, the government says it will continue to consolidate and expand poverty alleviation achievements, strengthen support for key counties, and build regular mechanisms to prevent large-scale poverty relapse. Han Wenxiu, executive deputy director of the Office of the Central Committee for Financial and Economic Affairs, said the bottom line against large-scale relapse must be upheld persistently and permanently after the transition period ends.
