Chinese President Xi Jinping on Wednesday called for a “strong start” to China’s 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030), urging unity, sustained effort and coordinated action to advance Chinese modernization. Xi made the remarks at a New Year gathering hosted by China’s top political advisory body, the Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference (CPPCC). Extending New Year greetings to the Party and people of all ethnic groups, he said China should continue opening up new horizons in modernization and work together to ensure a solid beginning to the new planning period. Xi described 2025 as an extraordinary year in which China met its main economic and social development targets, showed strong economic resilience and vitality, and maintained overall social stability. He said the year also marked the successful conclusion of the 14th Five-Year Plan (2021-2025), during which China’s comprehensive national strength reached a new level. Looking ahead to 2026, he stressed the need for coordinated efforts across multiple fronts to secure a sound start to the next five-year cycle. He specifically said the CPPCC should focus its consultative and deliberative work on the formulation and implementation of the 15th Five-Year Plan, helping to rally broad support and collective strength for Chinese modernization. The same day, Xi also exchanged New Year greetings with Russian President Vladimir Putin, reaffirming the steady development of China-Russia ties. In his message, Xi sent warm greetings to Putin and the Russian people and noted that 2025 marked the 80th anniversary of the founding of the United Nations. He said China and Russia had jointly commemorated the 80th anniversaries of the victories in the Chinese People’s War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression, the Soviet Union’s Great Patriotic War, and the World Anti-Fascist War, sending a strong message that peace, justice and the will of the people will prevail. Xi said 2025 was a concrete step forward for the China-Russia comprehensive strategic partnership of coordination for a new era. He recalled two meetings with Putin during the year in Beijing and Moscow, where they discussed major issues of common concern. He cited the implementation of mutual visa exemption, progress in energy corridor construction, and growing cooperation in emerging sectors as signs of rising momentum in bilateral relations. He also said the two countries had strengthened mutual support at the United Nations and other multilateral forums, contributing to global governance reform. Looking ahead, Xi noted that 2026 will mark the 30th anniversary of their strategic partnership and the 25th anniversary of the Russia-China Treaty of Good-Neighborliness and Friendly Cooperation, and said the two sides will jointly host a “China-Russia Year of Education” in 2026-2027. Putin, in return, praised the continued sound development of ties and said the two leaders’ meetings had produced important consensuses. He highlighted expanded trade, progress on major projects, and visa exemptions that have boosted people-to-people exchanges. He also expressed readiness to stay in close contact with Xi on bilateral and international issues. On the same day, Chinese Premier Li Qiang and Russian Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin also exchanged greetings, with both sides emphasizing deeper cooperation and more tangible results in the year ahead.

The article describes a Hangzhou International Communication Center initiative that brought together 10 international “Hangzhou Seekers” and 10 Hangzhou representatives for a series of cross-cultural conversations titled **“Hangzhou and the World: 10 Paired Conversations.”** The project was launched alongside another event, **“Hangzhou, a Window to China’s 5000-Year Civilization,”** and was presented as part of Hangzhou’s effort to build an open, inclusive platform for dialogue between Chinese and global civilizations. According to the release, the 10 seekers came from **Spain, Italy, Egypt, Brazil, the United States, Thailand, Turkey, Greece, Canada, and Germany**. They included scholars, media professionals, artists, historians, and other cultural figures. The central idea of the project was that curiosity and enthusiasm for the world can make anyone an “in-depth explorer,” and that meaningful civilizational exchange should happen through conversation rather than one-sided narration. The article emphasizes that Hangzhou is using this project to connect East and West through shared discussion on culture, history, education, art, and technology. Each paired conversation centered on a distinct theme. One of the most prominent exchanges brought together **Remonda Fayez Michel**, curator of the **Grand Egyptian Museum**, and **Xu Tianjin**, director of the **Liangzhu Museum** and a renowned archaeologist. Their discussion focused on **innovative museum curation and civilization narration**. Xu, who has spent more than 40 years on Shang and Zhou dynasty archaeology and is known for engaging younger audiences through accessible content, argued that archaeologists should not only excavate relics and study history but also interpret culture and encourage public participation. The two discussed how museums can better present ancient civilizations to global audiences. In another conversation, **Francisca Molinero**, principal of a well-known international school in Spain, met **Ling Ran**, founding consultant of Yungu School, to discuss **cross-cultural education**. Francisca’s school brings together students from more than 45 countries, giving her extensive experience in multicultural teaching. The two explored how technologies such as AI can be applied in education, how to define the greatest value of education for children, and what educational goals should guide schools in East and West. Music was the focus of the pairing between **Kittiporn Tantrarungroj**, chairman of the Thailand Choral Association, and **Zhou Weiping**, artistic director of the Hangzhou Philharmonic Angel Choir. Their theme was **nationality and globality of music**. Kittiporn, who changed careers from doctor to conductor, has integrated Thai cultural elements into choral music and brought them to international stages. Zhou shared his own work combining local characteristics with a broader international choral perspective. The article notes that the two had first met at a Korean choral festival before reconnecting in Hangzhou. History as a bridge across cultures was the subject of the conversation between **David Ringo Miano**, an American historian and popular science blogger, and **Wang Chong**, director of the American Studies Center at Zhejiang International Studies University. Their theme was **the unique role of history in cross-cultural communication**. They discussed how historical narratives, patterns of civilizational rise and decline, and past interactions between civilizations can help people understand present-day misunderstandings and promote mutual understanding. The article also highlights a discussion on **youth and social change** between **Renato de Almeida Freitas Junior**, a Brazilian lawyer, and **Yang Rui**, a special host at the Hangzhou International Communication Center. Renato, visiting China for the first time, paid close attention to China’s technological development and how technology is used to benefit ordinary people. Their conversation touched on the relationship between Hangzhou and Curitiba, Brazil, which became sister cities in 2001, and compared the two cities in areas such as transportation, culture, and art. For the theme **“Generation Z Embraces Diverse Civilizations,”** **Angelina Hui Qing Zhang**, a Canadian social media strategy consultant with 7 million followers, spoke with **Daria**, host of Hangzhoufeel. They discussed how content creators can connect global youth culture through fashion, beauty, music, and other digital content, and how cross-cultural creativity thrives in the online ecosystem. Another pair, **Christina Papageorgopoulou**, a Greek anthropology professor, and **Guo Yi**, a professor at Zhejiang University’s School of Art and Archaeology, explored **archaeological science and the code of human civilization**. Christina’s work includes paleodietary studies, paleodemography, paleogenetics, and digital archaeology. The two discussed the development of Chinese archaeology, the role of youth participation, and the potential of ancient DNA and stable isotope analysis in studying civilizations such as Liangzhu. They framed archaeological science as a field that can drive methodological innovation and theoretical breakthroughs in understanding civilizations. The theme **“Let Stories Become History”** guided the exchange between **Leonardo Cinieri Lombroso**, an Italian documentary director, and **Gu Jiafeng**, a Chinese film producer. Leonardo recalled a documentary about a Chinese girl and her Roman landlady that had once sparked interest in China among Italian audiences. In Hangzhou, he approached his visit as a story-collecting journey. The two discussed how Chinese and Asian films tell stories and how directors and cameras can serve as a common language for cultural integration. Photography was the focus of the conversation between **Gunther Riehle**, a German photographer ranked among the world’s top 10, and **Wu Zongqi**, honorary chairman of the Zhejiang Photographers Association. Their theme was **cities and nature in images**. Gunther had previously won the Grand Prize at the Zhejiang International Photography Exhibition, creating a lasting connection with China. The article says Hangzhou offers rich inspiration for photographers, allowing artistic dialogue through images. Finally, **Tunç Akkoç**, founder and editor-in-chief of the Turkish media outlet Harici, met **Shen Zhixing**, director and professor at the Turkish Research Center of the Mediterranean Research Institute at Zhejiang International Studies University. Their theme was **the exploration of the coexistence of diverse civilizations**. Shen has spent more than 30 years teaching and researching Turkish language and literature, compiling a Turkish-Chinese dictionary and introducing works such as Orhan Pamuk’s *My Name Is Red* to Chinese readers. The two discussed China-Turkey relations and literary translation. The release concludes by stressing that civilization’s charm lies in **diversity rather than uniformity, and dialogue rather than monologue**. It says the content from **“Hangzhou and the World: 10 Paired Conversations”** has been published on Hangzhoufeel’s social media accounts.

Those pressures exposed deep divisions inside Scholz’s three-party coalition, which included his center-left Social Democrats, the environmentalist Greens, and the pro-business Free Democrats. After weeks of internal conflict over how to revive the economy, Scholz announced Wednesday night that he was dismissing Finance Minister Christian Lindner. Since Lindner’s party was essential to the coalition’s parliamentary majority, the firing effectively brought down the government. Scholz said he would seek a vote of confidence in parliament on Jan. 15. If he loses that vote, an early election could be held by the end of March, much earlier than the regularly scheduled September vote. Until then, Scholz said he would consult opposition leader Friedrich Merz, head of the center-right Christian Democrats, about possible steps to strengthen the economy and defense. But business leaders immediately pressed for faster action, saying Germany could not afford prolonged instability. Dirk Jandura, president of the wholesale trade association BGA, said every extra day with the current government was “a lost day” and demanded new elections as soon as possible. Other industry leaders echoed that view, warning that Germany needed a stable government capable of addressing its economic crisis. Siegfried Russwurm, president of the Federation of German Industries, said the country needed a “new, capable government with its own parliamentary majority as quickly as possible,” especially given the worsening global situation and Germany’s poor economic performance. The coalition collapse came at the same time European leaders were absorbing the implications of Trump’s election victory. Analysts and officials warned that a second Trump presidency could have serious consequences for Europe’s security and economy. Trump has threatened to weaken U.S. commitments to NATO, shift American support away from Ukraine, and impose tariffs of up to 20% on goods from the European Union, with even higher tariffs on Chinese products. Such measures could hit Germany particularly hard because its economy depends heavily on exports. Germany still has not recovered fully from the pandemic, and the energy shock caused by Russia’s invasion of Ukraine forced Berlin and other Western nations to cut themselves off from Russian gas and oil. At the same time, Chinese competition, including in electric vehicles, has intensified pressure on German carmakers, forcing production cuts and layoffs. Volkswagen recently announced plans to close at least three factories in Germany, the first domestic closures in its 87-year history. Economists said the political turmoil and Trump’s return could worsen the outlook. Carsten Brzeski of ING said the events of the last 24 hours had “further darkened” an already bleak short-term outlook. He noted that the U.S. takes about 10% of German exports and warned that tariffs on European cars could deepen trouble for the auto industry. Not everyone agreed that Trump would necessarily be bad for German carmakers. Some analysts argued that his protectionist policies toward China could indirectly help them by limiting Chinese electric vehicles in the U.S. market. Daniel Gros of the Institute for European Policymaking at Bocconi University said Trump could “save the German automotive sector” by keeping high tariffs on Chinese EVs, since the U.S. is one of the few major markets where German automakers do not face intense Chinese competition. Scholz blamed Lindner for refusing to compromise on economic policy, including tax increases or changes to Germany’s constitutional debt limits. He accused Lindner of publicly pushing tax cuts for a small group of high earners while proposing cuts to pensions for everyone else, calling that “not decent” and “not fair.” The dispute reflected the broader tensions in a coalition that had been formed in 2021 with ambitious goals of modernizing Germany across ideological lines. The government can point to some achievements: it helped Germany avoid an energy crunch after Russia cut gas supplies, began military modernization, and passed some social reforms. But for many Germans, the coalition became associated with dysfunction and paralysis. With the economic outlook worsening and the new U.S. administration approaching, business leaders and analysts alike said Germany urgently needs stable leadership and a clear direction.

# Germany's Economy in Crisis as Government Coalition Collapses Germany's largest economy is facing a critical juncture as Chancellor Olaf Scholz's three-party governing coalition collapsed Wednesday night, coinciding with mounting economic challenges and the impending return of Donald Trump to the U.S. presidency. ## The Coalition's Breakdown The immediate trigger for the coalition's collapse was Scholz's firing of Finance Minister Christian Lindner, whose pro-business Free Democratic Party was essential to maintaining the government's parliamentary majority. The dismissal came after weeks of internal disputes over how to address Germany's struggling economy. The coalition, formed in 2021 with ambitious progressive goals, had become increasingly dysfunctional as its three ideologically disparate members—Scholz's center-left Social Democrats, the environmentalist Greens, and the Free Democrats—could not find common ground on critical economic issues. The fundamental disagreement centered on how to stimulate the economy. The Social Democrats and Greens proposed massive state investments, while the Free Democrats opposed tax increases and rejected changes to Germany's strict debt limitations. Scholz accused Lindner of bad faith, pointing to the finance minister's proposal for billions in tax cuts for top earners while simultaneously cutting pensions for all recipients. ## Political Path Forward Scholz announced plans to seek a confidence vote in parliament on January 15, which could trigger early elections by the end of March if he loses. Germany's regularly scheduled election was not due until September. In the interim, Scholz said he would engage with opposition leader Friedrich Merz of the center-right Christian Democrats to discuss strengthening the economy and defense capabilities. However, German business leaders expressed frustration with this timeline, demanding immediate action to establish a stable government capable of addressing the crisis. ## Economic Troubles Germany's economic problems predate the coalition's collapse. The economy has been shrinking for two years following the coronavirus pandemic, Russia's invasion of Ukraine, and intensifying competition from China. The war in Ukraine forced Germany to sever ties with Russian energy supplies, eliminating the cheap and plentiful gas and oil that had long powered German industry. Meanwhile, Chinese electric vehicles are flooding global markets, forcing German and European automakers to reduce production and lay off workers. Volkswagen announced plans to close at least three domestic factories—the first closures in its 87-year history—underscoring the sector's distress. ## Trump's Return and Global Risks The timing of the coalition's collapse coincides with the certainty of Trump's return to the White House, creating additional uncertainties. Trump has threatened to withdraw NATO commitments, reduce support for Ukraine, and impose tariffs up to 20% on European Union goods and higher rates on Chinese products. These threats pose particular dangers for Germany, which depends heavily on exports to the United States, with approximately 10% of German exports destined for American markets. Analysts warn that Trump's tariff threats could devastate Germany's automotive industry, already struggling with Chinese competition. However, some experts suggest potential benefits: Trump's continuation of Biden's 100% tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles could protect German carmakers, as the United States remains one of the few major markets where German manufacturers face limited Chinese competition. ## European Implications The political instability in Germany carries broader implications for the European Union. European leaders note that a strong Franco-German alliance traditionally provides the EU with important counterweight during periods of international tension. With Germany now facing governmental uncertainty, this alliance is weakened at a moment when European security and economic interests face significant threats from Trump's anticipated policies. ## Business Community Demands German business leaders have called for rapid resolution of the political crisis. The wholesale lobby president stated, "Every additional day with this federal government is a lost day," demanding new elections as soon as possible. Industry federation leaders emphasized the need for a capable government with its own parliamentary majority before the U.S. government's inauguration in early 2025, when uncertainty is expected to increase further. The convergence of domestic political instability, persistent economic weakness, and looming international trade tensions has created what analysts describe as a "bleak short-term outlook" for Europe's largest economy.

Poland-based Filipino academics and students were encouraged to use their overseas education and research experience to help the Philippines, as they gathered in Warsaw on November 23 for an event co-organized by Filipino academics and the Philippine Embassy in Poland. The gathering highlighted the growing presence of Filipino scholars in Polish universities and the government’s effort to connect them with national development programs. Philippine Ambassador to Poland Leah Basinang-Ruiz told the attendees that they play a “critical and special role” in strengthening Philippine-Poland relations and should take part in embassy activities. She urged them to think beyond their personal academic goals and see themselves as representatives of the Philippines abroad. According to her, Filipino migrants and students can help embassies project the country’s economy, politics, society, values, and culture, while also staying engaged with fellow Filipinos and supporting the country’s progress. The ambassador’s remarks were followed by a presentation from First Secretary and Consul Alena Grace Borra on the Department of Science and Technology’s Balik Scientist Program (BSP). The program, launched by presidential decree in 1975, encourages Filipino scientists, technologists, and experts to return home and share their knowledge for scientific, agro-industrial, and economic development. It was later strengthened by Republic Act 11035, or the Balik Scientist Act, passed in June 2018. The law expanded incentives for returning experts, including relocation assistance, higher pay, housing or accommodation allowances, insurance coverage, and research funding. Borra said many BSP participants work in agriculture, aquatic, and natural resources, which account for 28.4 percent of the program, and in health, which makes up 27.9 percent. She also invited Poland-based students to consider joining the industry, energy, and emerging technology sector, which currently has the largest share of returning experts at 47.7 percent. She noted that although Poland is still a relatively new destination for Filipino academics and scientists, it is important to raise awareness of the program early. Several attendees welcomed the initiative. Jaime Bonifacio Jr., a 35-year-old public health student at Jagiellonian University in Krakow, said he had always planned to study abroad to gain the skills needed to become an effective public health leader. He is completing the Governance and Economics of Health Systems in Transition track under the Erasmus Mundus European Public Health Master program, after spending the first half of the course at the University of Sheffield in the United Kingdom. Bonifacio said he intends to return to the Philippines after finishing his degree because he loves the country and wants to contribute to its development. He described the Balik Scientist Program as a strong incentive for scholars and scientists to go home and help expand the country’s research capacity. Another postgraduate student, 25-year-old John Warren Tamor, praised the program but said the government must first address the difficulties faced by local researchers. He pointed out that many are underpaid and overworked, forcing them to take on multiple jobs and weakening both research and instruction. Tamor, who is studying in the Master of Science in Transition, Innovation, and Sustainability Environments program at the Poznan University of Economics and Business, said returning home could be a realistic option after his studies, but only if structural reforms create a better environment for scientists. The event was proposed by Lorico Lapitan Jr., an assistant professor at Warsaw University of Technology, after he spoke with Ambassador Basinang-Ruiz following a Filipino basketball tournament in Poznan in May 2024. Lapitan, together with co-organizers Jayson Pasahol and Hazel Kato-Caingles, invited 56 participants, including students, alumni, and visiting researchers from different Polish institutions. Other attendees also shared how studying in Poland had broadened their perspectives. Jess Raymundo, a 34-year-old master’s student in Teaching English to Young Learners at the University of Warsaw, said Poland had been an attractive destination for international students. A former preschool teacher in Japan, she said her training in content and language integrated learning would help her compare early childhood and primary education systems in the Philippines, Japan, and Poland. She said she would consider returning home only if there were similar programs for non-scientific professionals to share expertise, though she still planned to seek work in Poland. Like Tamor, she cited low compensation and the continuing brain drain in the Philippine education sector as major concerns. Still, she said she hopes to support Filipino teachers through virtual exchanges and collaboration. Throughout the gathering, the students emphasized pride in Filipino identity and encouraged others to pursue scholarships abroad. Bonifacio said overseas study can broaden perspectives and inspire people to serve the Philippines better, while Tamor urged Filipinos not to lose sight of what makes them uniquely Filipino despite frustrations with the country.

A UN independent expert has urged Poland to take “swift and decisive” action to protect lesbian, gay, bisexual, trans and other gender-diverse people from discrimination and violence. Graeme Reid, the UN Independent Expert on protection against violence and discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity, issued the call at the end of a 10-day visit to Poland from 18 to 29 November 2024. Reid said the slow pace of legal reform was frustrating for many of the 130 civil society representatives and government officials he met in Warsaw, Krakow, Lublin, Wroclaw and Poznan. He said he heard numerous distressing accounts, including a gay man who was denied access to his dying partner because Poland does not recognize legal partnerships, trans people forced to sue their parents to obtain legal gender recognition, and children excluded from their homes, bullied at school, and unable to access timely psychological support. He urged Parliament and the Government to adopt reforms that would bring Polish law into line with international human rights standards, especially on discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity. Reid said even small legal changes could make a major difference. The expert welcomed Poland’s December 2023 apology for past state-sponsored discriminatory rhetoric against LGBT people, and noted government acknowledgements that current laws and policies do not fully meet international standards. He also said authorities were working on better protection against hate crimes, the introduction of same-sex civil unions, and a clearer legal path to gender recognition. Reid warned that eight years of hostile rhetoric and policies had taken a serious toll on mental health, with reports of self-harm among LGBT youth linked to rejection, bullying, and poor access to support. He will present a full report to the Human Rights Council in June 2025.

# Summary UN Independent Expert Graeme Reid concluded a 10-day visit to Poland on November 29, 2024, urging the government to take immediate legislative action to protect LGBT people from discrimination and violence. During his visit, Reid met with 130 civil society representatives and government officials across five major cities. He documented serious human rights concerns, including cases of same-sex partners denied hospital access, transgender individuals forced to sue parents for legal gender recognition, and LGBT youth experiencing homelessness, school bullying, and inadequate mental health support. Reid emphasized that Poland's slow pace of legal reform has disappointed civil society advocates. He highlighted alarming mental health consequences from eight years of state-sponsored hostile rhetoric against LGBT people, including reports of self-harm among LGBT youth driven by family rejection, school bullying, and inadequate access to healthcare and psychological support. The expert called for swift legislative reforms to align Poland's laws with international human rights standards, specifically addressing discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity. He welcomed Poland's December 2023 government apology for past discriminatory rhetoric and acknowledged government recognition that current laws fall short of international standards. Reid noted positive developments, including government commitments to strengthen hate crime protections, enable same-sex civil unions, and establish clear legal pathways for gender recognition. The expert will present a comprehensive report to the UN Human Rights Council in June 2025.

Zimmer Biomet Holdings announced that it has received U.S. Food and Drug Administration 510(k) clearance for its OsseoFit™ Stemless Shoulder System, a new implant for total shoulder replacement. The company said the device is designed to replicate the natural anatomy of the humeral, or upper arm, bone in order to improve anatomical fit while preserving as much healthy bone as possible. The system broadens Zimmer Biomet’s shoulder-replacement portfolio and is intended to work with the company’s Identity Humeral Heads using Versa-Dial Technology, which allows infinite offset placement, as well as the Alliance Glenoid, giving surgeons a wide range of options to match a patient’s anatomy. Zimmer Biomet described OsseoFit as an anatomically shaped, stemless implant that supports bone conservation and stable initial fixation. It also uses the company’s OsseoTi porous metal technology to promote biological fixation. According to the company, the left- or right-sided anchor implants have fins that create a press-fit during insertion and include fully porous windows. Their fin geometry and anchor spacing are meant to help the implant orient properly within natural bone, avoid cortical impingement, and reach denser bone areas. The design also includes anterior reattachment suture holes to assist with subscapularis repair. Zimmer Biomet said the system comes in a single instrument tray, which is intended to improve workflow and sterile processing efficiency and make the product suitable for a range of care settings, including ambulatory surgical centers. A Mayo Clinic orthopedic surgery professor who was part of the surgeon development team said bone preservation is becoming increasingly important as younger and more active patients undergo shoulder replacement and may need revision surgery later. He said using a method that mimics the asymmetry of the natural humerus helps surgeons preserve native bone while optimizing fixation. The company said the OsseoFit Stemless Shoulder System is expected to be commercially available in the first quarter of 2025. The release also noted that Mayo Clinic has a financial interest in the technology and that any revenue it receives will support its nonprofit mission in patient care, education, and research. Zimmer Biomet, headquartered in Warsaw, Indiana, said it is a global medical technology company with a broad portfolio aimed at improving mobility and health through innovative products and integrated digital and robotic technologies. The announcement also included a standard caution that the release contains forward-looking statements subject to risks and uncertainties, and that actual results could differ from expectations.

Poland has pledged to double its support for the World Bank’s International Development Association (IDA), the fund that finances development projects in 78 low-income countries. Announced on 7 November 2024 in Washington and Warsaw, the new commitment marks an unprecedented IDA21 pledge of 37 million euros, reflecting Poland’s continued support for international development amid worsening global crises. IDA funds projects that promote economic growth, resilience, and improved living conditions through investments in areas such as education, health, clean water, sanitation, agriculture, infrastructure, business climate reform, and institutional strengthening. Poland said its larger contribution is intended to help tackle the fragility and vulnerabilities that keep the world’s poorest countries trapped in poverty and drive migration and brain drain. Polish Finance Minister Andrzej Domański said the pledge reflects belief in collective action for sustainable development and resilience, stressing that low-income countries urgently need support during a turbulent period. Deputy Finance Minister Paweł Karbownik added that IDA’s experience in implementing large-scale, repeatable projects can help countries reverse cycles of poverty and create jobs at home. He said Poland will propose a Council of Ministers resolution to approve EUR 37.54 million for IDA’s 21st replenishment, to be paid over nine years starting in 2026. The announcement comes as a World Bank report warns that the world’s 26 poorest countries, home to 40% of the most poverty-stricken people, are more indebted than at any time since 2006 and increasingly exposed to natural disasters and other shocks. World Bank Vice President for Development Finance Akihiko Nishio welcomed Poland’s increase, calling it a strong sign of solidarity that will help mobilize private capital, strengthen stability, build climate resilience, and lift millions out of poverty. IDA replenishments occur every three years, with the current round due to conclude in December 2024.

Charles Norman Howell, known as Norm, of Poland, died Saturday afternoon, Dec. 7, 2024, at The Inn at Poland Way. He was 96. Born March 25, 1928, in Youngstown, he was the son of Ray E. and Marion Griffiths Howell. Howell graduated from Poland Seminary High School in 1946 and went on to earn a bachelor’s degree in electrical engineering from Carnegie Tech. He began his career at Duquesne Lighting in Pittsburgh, then joined Ajax Magnethermic Corporation in Boardman, a company that later moved to Warren. He served as chief engineer there until retirement. On Sept. 10, 1949, he married his childhood sweetheart, the former Melva Jeannine Weckbacher. The couple shared 64 years together before her death in 2013. They raised three children and were later joined by seven grandsons and 11 great-grandchildren. Family was central to Howell’s life, and he was remembered as a devoted husband, father, grandfather and great-grandfather who took pride in providing for and caring for his loved ones. In retirement, he enjoyed using his skills to design and build home improvement projects for family members. He also liked playing bridge in several clubs, including the Southside Duplicate Bridge Club and the Canfield Duplicate Bridge Club, and spent time on jigsaw and crossword puzzles. Friends and family remembered him as a gentleman with kindness and a good sense of humor. Howell was a member of the Ohio Society of Professional Engineers and the Poland Kiwanis Club, where he once served as treasurer. He also served in the U.S. Army Reserve. He is survived by his companion, Margery Cooksey; his three children; seven grandsons; 11 great-grandchildren; and a sister-in-law. He was preceded in death by his wife and two brothers. A funeral service is scheduled for 1 p.m. Wednesday, Dec. 11, 2024, at Poland Riverside Cemetery.

The article describes the human toll of Yemen’s year-old war through the stories of four Yemenis living through displacement, poverty, trauma, and bureaucratic obstacles, amid hopeful reports of a possible nationwide ceasefire. By the time the article was written, more than 2.4 million Yemenis had been displaced internally, and more than 6,000 people had been killed in the conflict, about half of them civilians. The war began after Houthi rebels seized the capital, Sanaa, prompting fighting with supporters of Yemen’s ousted government, which has been backed by a Saudi-led military coalition. On Wednesday, reports circulated that the warring parties had agreed to a nationwide cessation of hostilities beginning the following month, raising hopes among many Yemenis that the fighting might finally ease. The first story is that of Ahmad Salim Abdul Manaa, who spent three decades living in Aden before fleeing with his family in late June of the previous year when fighting erupted between Houthi rebels and forces loyal to the government. He and his family had lived in Khour Maksar, one of the hardest-hit neighborhoods in the city. Abdul Manaa said they tried four times to leave Aden but were unable to get out because the main road toward Hadramout province was blocked by clashes. Eventually, he made it to Mukalla, the capital of Hadramout, where he now works as a taxi driver. His family, however, lives separately in the poor and remote village of Hajjar, where he was born. Saudi Crown Prince and Prime Minister Mohammed bin Salman, who also chairs the Board of Trustees of King Abdullah University of Science and Technology (KAUST), launched the university’s new strategy on Sunday, setting out a plan to turn research into economically valuable innovations and to align KAUST more closely with Saudi Arabia’s Vision 2030. The strategy is built around the Kingdom’s national priorities for research, development and innovation: Health and Wellness; Sustainable Environment and Essential Needs; Energy and Industrial Leadership; and Economies of the Future. It also aims to deepen KAUST’s partnerships with public and private sector entities so the university can play a larger role in national development and economic diversification. In remarks quoted in the article, the Crown Prince said KAUST has distinguished itself since its founding through its research, innovations and faculty, becoming one of the world’s leading research universities. He said the new strategy builds on the university’s scientific and academic achievements and marks “a new era” for KAUST to become “a beacon of knowledge and a source of inspiration and innovation” in line with Vision 2030. A central goal of the strategy is to increase the chances that research will become commercially useful and economically beneficial. To do this, KAUST will launch the National Transformation Institute for Applied Research, or NTI, which is intended to speed up technology development and commercialization in support of economic diversification. The university will also restructure its research centers to better match national RDI priorities. In addition, KAUST plans to create a $200 million deep-tech investment fund, Capital K, equivalent to SR750 million, to invest over five to eight years in early-stage technologies from KAUST, Saudi Arabia, or abroad. The fund is intended to fill unmet investment needs in high-tech firms and help create high-quality technical jobs. The strategy also emphasizes opportunities for researchers, faculty and students, with a focus on applying science to create sustainable global impact through stronger local and international partnerships. One highlighted example is the KAUST Reefscape Restoration Initiative, developed with NEOM. The project will focus on cultivating and restoring hundreds of thousands of coral reefs across 100 hectares on Shushah Island in the Red Sea. The article says this initiative is part of a larger marine destination centered on coral propagation, conservation and enhancement, with nurseries expected to produce 500,000 coral fragments per year. KAUST said it will continue working with major companies in Saudi Arabia and globally, including Aramco, SABIC, ACWA Power, IBM, Dow and Boeing. It also plans to strengthen international cooperation with leading academic institutions and technology innovators around the world. One specific area mentioned is new strategic agreements with academic and commercial institutions in Shenzhen, China, to collaborate on applied research in aerospace, robotics and microelectronics. According to the article, these efforts are meant to strengthen Saudi Arabia’s higher education ecosystem, nurture future scientific leaders, promote research and global innovation, and support the growth of advanced technology startups. Ultimately, KAUST expects the strategy to improve the competitiveness of the Saudi economy and raise the Kingdom’s standing as a global innovation leader. The article also highlights KAUST’s existing record. Since its establishment, the university has built a strong international reputation, ranking first globally for “citations per faculty” in the QS 2021 ranking. Its research output is said to appear in the top 25 percent of the world’s highest-ranked scientific journals. KAUST alumni and talent have gone on to leadership roles in major institutions such as NASA, MIT and NEOM. The university’s stated vision is to be a destination for scientific and technological education and research, using discovery to address global challenges and bridge people and cultures. Its mission focuses on advancing and disseminating scientific knowledge through collaborative research and graduate education, with special emphasis on food, water, energy and the environment.

The article argues for reconsidering the assumption that cement and high-rise construction are automatically superior to mud-based building. It opens by pointing out the irony of dismissing mud houses as primitive in a world that already has more than 100-storey buildings, including a reference to Shibam in Yemen, home to ancient mud skyscrapers. The piece suggests that modern building culture, especially in developing countries like India, often treats cement as the default “pakka” material and mud as “kachcha,” even though cement is a relatively recent industrial material with a short history compared with earth, which has been used for building since ancient times. The article frames this as part of a broader critique of centralized, industrial systems. As some developed economies begin to recognize the downsides of centralized ecosystems and seek more decentralized alternatives, the author argues that countries such as India may be causing harm by equating progress with cement and concrete construction. India, the article says, has a deep architectural tradition and extensive knowledge of local building materials, but that knowledge is often overlooked. It cites eco-architecture pioneers such as the late Laurie Baker and Didi Contractor, and introduces two contemporary advocates of earth construction, Biju of Thannal and Sourabh Phadke, who answer common questions about mud houses. In the FAQ, the first concern is structural strength. The answer emphasizes that earthen buildings are far stronger than many people assume. Mud, it explains, can be understood as a kind of concrete: when inert aggregates are bound together by a material, the result is concrete, and in earthen construction the binding agent is clay. Portland cement concrete is simply one type of concrete, not the definition of the term itself. The next question concerns durability. The article notes that some of the oldest surviving structures on Earth are earthen buildings thousands of years old, while the oldest cement concrete buildings are only a little over a century old. The point is not to dismiss cement, which the authors describe as an excellent material when used wisely, but to challenge unquestioned faith in modern construction habits. The article warns that when processes are not thought through, they can become rituals rather than rational choices. Earth construction, by contrast, is presented as a time-tested method. The FAQ then addresses weather resistance. The answer is simple: a mud house needs “a good hat and a good pair of shoes,” meaning a roof that protects the walls from direct rain and a foundation that prevents moisture from rising into the walls. Mud houses do not dissolve into puddles when it rains; instead, damage occurs mainly through surface erosion from rain striking exposed walls or from water wicking upward from the ground. With proper design, these problems are avoidable. When asked about multi-storey buildings, the article says that earth can indeed be used for several floors. It suggests first asking whether extra height is truly necessary, but if it is, two or three storeys can be built without much difficulty, provided the walls are strong enough to bear the load. The article adds that ancient civilizations built eight- and nine-storey structures entirely from raw earth, reinforcing the material’s potential. Cost is another major topic. The article says mud buildings are usually cheaper than conventional modern buildings, though the exact difference depends on the situation. More importantly, it argues that building should not be judged only in monetary terms. Instead, it proposes thinking in terms of energy use, since energy is a universal measure. Financial costs vary by location, currency, and subsidies, but energy costs remain comparable everywhere. The article also highlights how mud construction keeps money circulating locally: because earth building relies on local materials, local knowledge, and local labor, most of the spending stays within the community. It estimates that about two-thirds of the money goes to labor and one-third to materials, the reverse of industrial construction, and presents this as an investment in people. Finally, the article asks whether someone with no construction experience can build a mud house. The answer is yes. It notes that for centuries people around the world built their own homes without formal degrees in engineering or architecture, and that only recently have these professions become dominant. The article presents self-building as both possible and empowering, describing it as a life-changing experience. The piece closes by acknowledging a practical limitation: mud houses may not be realistic in dense cities like Delhi or Mumbai. Still, it says the broader purpose is to question assumptions about construction and to ask whether better materials, local sourcing, and simpler, more environmentally friendly processes are possible. The article ends by inviting readers to share ideas and experiences with the Slow Tech initiative.

It points out that cement, despite its current dominance, has only existed for about a century, whereas mud has been used for building since ancient times. The article cites Shibam in Yemen, which features the world's oldest mud skyscrapers, as evidence of mud's durability and structural viability. The author contends that as developed economies recognize problems with centralized systems, they're increasingly seeking decentralized alternatives. Meanwhile, developing countries like India actively discourage mud construction, teaching children that mud houses are "kachcha" (temporary) and cement structures are "pakka" (permanent). This cultural shift may be counterproductive, as it dismisses valuable indigenous knowledge in favor of newer materials with unknown long-term effects. ## Strength and Durability of Mud Structures In a question-and-answer format with eco-builders Biju of Thannal and Sourabh Phadke, the article addresses common misconceptions about mud houses. Regarding structural strength, the experts explain that earth is actually a type of concrete—specifically, earth concrete bound together by clay particles. This contrasts with Portland cement concrete, which is simply another concrete variant, not the only legitimate option. The durability question receives compelling evidence. The oldest standing structures on Earth are earthen buildings thousands of years old, while the oldest existing cement concrete buildings are only slightly over a century old. This historical record suggests that mud construction may actually outlast modern cement buildings, contradicting conventional wisdom. ## Maintenance and Weather Resistance A major concern addressed is whether mud houses deteriorate in rain. The experts dismiss the notion that mud structures turn into puddles, explaining that proper maintenance—specifically a good roof and foundation—keeps mud houses healthy. The experts encourage individuals to reclaim this responsibility, noting that millions worldwide continue building mud houses themselves. ## Urban Limitations and Future Questions While acknowledging that mud construction may not work in densely packed cities like Delhi or Mumbai, the article encourages questioning standard construction assumptions. It asks whether better materials exist locally, whether processes could be simplified, and whether environmental impacts could be reduced. The piece ultimately advocates for reconsidering automatic acceptance of cement construction, promoting sustainable alternatives that leverage local resources and knowledge.

At a debate in Idaho Falls on Thursday, Republican Rep. Wendy Horman and Rod Gramer, former president of Idaho Business for Education, presented sharply opposed visions of private school choice as Idaho prepares for another legislative session in which the issue is expected to be a major focus. About 95 people attended the Idaho Falls City Club event, where the two clashed over the cost of school choice programs, accountability for private schools, the role of parents, and the impact on public education. Horman framed private school choice as a fundamental equity issue. She called it the “civil rights issue of our time,” arguing that children should have access to the best education possible regardless of family income or where they live. Gramer, by contrast, described private school subsidies as an “existential threat” to public education and “the most expensive government handout in the history of the United States.” Their exchange reflected the broader national debate over vouchers, tax credits, and other programs that direct public money toward private schooling. A major point of contention was whether Idaho’s private school choice program should be capped and how much it might ultimately cost. Gramer warned that such programs tend to expand over time, citing Arizona and Indiana as examples. He argued that “out-of-state billionaires and their front organizations” continue pushing vouchers until they become universal and lack accountability. He pressed Horman to commit to never supporting spending above the $50 million annual cap she included in a bill last session. Horman resisted giving a firm long-term pledge. She said any growth in the program would require legislative action and insisted that she does not support “budget-busting bills.” When Gramer repeated his question, she said she had not come to debate him but to “speak my piece.” Under further pressure from moderator Karole Honas, Horman said she would evaluate future requests as they arise and would consider whether a large waitlist of families seeking aid might justify expansion. She also said many Idahoans support school choice and she wants to respond to public demand. Gramer estimated that a voucher-style program in Idaho could eventually cost as much as $300 million. He argued that public education is already underfunded, pointing to Idaho’s backlog of school facility repairs, low per-student spending, and the state constitution’s requirement to maintain a “uniform and thorough” system of public schools. In his view, the state should not divert money to other educational settings such as homeschooling, religious schools, or private schools. He compared the idea to a financially strapped business trying to buy three new businesses while unable to pay its existing bills. Horman countered that supporting school choice does not mean harming public schools or diverting their funding. She said she plans to sponsor a 2025 bill creating refundable tax credits that parents could use for private school tuition. Because the proposal would operate as a tax credit rather than a direct spending program, she argued, “there’s no pot of money to draw from.” The audience reacted with some laughter and snickers when she described it as a revenue reduction. The debate also focused on accountability. Gramer questioned how private schools would be held accountable if they were not required to administer standardized tests or publicly report results. Horman said many private schools likely already test students even without a mandate, but she rejected test scores as the best measure of success. She said standardized tests are heavily influenced by family income, zip code, and parents’ education levels, making them only a “snapshot in time.” In her view, a better accountability measure is whether families choose a school and continue enrolling their children there. Honas raised concerns about whether taxpayers would be forced to support schools with objectionable curricula, including schools that were satanic, denied the Holocaust, or promoted discriminatory views. Horman said taxpayers “would have to support that” under a choice system, though she argued that most parents would never choose such schools. She said she trusts parents to make the best decisions for their children and believes that, with rare exceptions, no one is better positioned than parents to decide on education. Gramer responded that he did not want to subsidize schools teaching Holocaust denial or discrimination, warning that once public money flows to private or religious schools, the state loses control over what children are taught. Horman also argued that Idaho already has public money going to private and religious education through Idaho Launch, a state-funded grant program for graduating seniors pursuing higher education. She said critics worried about a school choice bill being “the camel’s nose under the tent” should recognize that “the tent door is already wide open.” She pointed out that in the first round of Idaho Launch awards, 867 of 6,496 recipients—about 13 percent—attended private universities. The two also disagreed about access in rural areas. Horman said private schools exist in 24 of Idaho’s 44 counties, arguing that claims that rural students have no alternatives are inaccurate. She said competition would help public schools and that choice can be “life-changing” for children who need a different setting. Gramer replied that nearly half of Idaho counties still have no private school at all, and in places that do, only one option may exist. In closing, Horman said her policy motivation is Idaho’s most vulnerable students. She repeated that “school choice is the civil rights issue of our time” and told a personal story about meeting a child caring for younger siblings while his mother was away on a multi-day drug binge. For Horman, such cases show why some children need educational alternatives that their parents cannot afford. Gramer ended by emphasizing that public schools serve all students, regardless of race, gender, disability, or socioeconomic status, and that Idaho must not abandon its 314,000 public school students. He said every child deserves a great education under the state constitution, and public schools should remain the priority.

Historically low interest rates have been a major driver of the stock market’s strong rally, because cheap borrowing supports growth and pushes investors out of low-yielding bonds and into riskier assets such as stocks. But the article warns that this setup could be threatened if rates rise too quickly. The immediate concern came this week as the yield on the 10-year U.S. Treasury note climbed to 2.44%, its highest level since March, up sharply from 2.27% on October 16. Since bond prices move inversely to yields, that jump reflected a notable selloff in the bond market. Investors attributed the move partly to expectations of stronger economic growth, as well as worries that President Trump’s pick to lead the Federal Reserve might be more aggressive about raising rates than Janet Yellen. Some also feared that Trump’s proposed tax overhaul could overheat the economy and push inflation and rates higher. The sudden rise in yields prompted prominent bond investor Jeff Gundlach to warn that the 30-year bull market in bonds may be nearing its end if the trend does not reverse soon. Still, not everyone sees the move as a crisis. Mike LaBella of QS Investors said rates remain low enough to support stocks, though he warned that a faster climb toward 3% or 4% would become alarming. Art Hogan of Wunderlich Securities said the economy can handle slowly rising rates, but acknowledged that the recent jump was too abrupt to be considered normal. The article notes that the stock market has benefited enormously from the long era of ultra-low rates, which made bonds unattractive and encouraged investors to accept higher valuations in stocks. That means many investors may be unprepared for a rapid shift. The Treasury Department’s Office of Financial Research recently highlighted market risk as the biggest vulnerability in the financial system, specifically pointing to the possibility that markets are not ready for higher interest rates. Other possible pressures on bonds include tax reform, which could increase federal deficits or stimulate an already healthy economy, and possible changes in bond-buying programs by the Federal Reserve and European Central Bank. Even so, some strategists, including Guy LeBas of Janney Capital, argue it is premature to declare the end of the bond bull market, since Treasury yields are still low by historical standards and demographic trends should continue to support demand for safe income-producing assets.

However, recent developments suggest this foundation may be shifting, potentially destabilizing the market. This week, the 10-year Treasury yield jumped to 2.44%, its highest level since March, rising significantly from 2.27% on October 16. This bond selloff reflects expectations for faster economic growth and concerns that President Trump's Federal Reserve choice will raise rates more aggressively than Janet Yellen. Additionally, worries about Trump's proposed tax overhaul potentially overheating the economy have contributed to the rate increase. The sharp rate movement prompted prominent bond investor Jeff Gundlach to warn that the 30-year bull market in bonds may be ending, declaring "the moment of truth has arrived." Portfolio manager Mike LaBella suggests rates remain low enough to sustain the stock market rally, but warns that rates climbing above 3% or approaching 4% would be concerning. Experts acknowledge that gradually rising rates wouldn't necessarily harm markets—indeed, many welcome a return to normal rates after nearly a decade of ultra-low conditions. Banks, in particular, have struggled in the low-rate environment. However, the recent spike has been notably abrupt rather than gradual, catching investors off guard. The Treasury Department's Office of Financial Research identified market risk as the primary vulnerability in the financial system, specifically highlighting that markets are unprepared for higher rates. Several factors could push rates higher: Trump's tax reform could add to the federal deficit or overstimulate the economy, and both the European Central Bank and Federal Reserve may unwind emergency bond-buying programs more aggressively than anticipated. However, some experts remain optimistic about bonds. Guy LeBas argues it's premature to declare the end of the bull market, noting Treasury rates remain just above their five-year average. Bond advocates point to demographic trends—aging populations in major economies seeking safe, steady income—as supporting sustained demand for bonds. In summary, while rising interest rates pose a genuine risk to the stock market's continued rally, whether this represents an imminent threat or merely a market adjustment remains uncertain.

Bentonville School District Superintendent Debbie Jones has been named one of four finalists for national superintendent of the year, according to a Monday news release from AASA, The School Superintendents Association. The finalists will be introduced to the national education community at a Jan. 9 news conference at the National Press Club in Washington, D.C. The 2025 winner will be announced at AASA’s National Conference on Education, scheduled for March 6-8 in New Orleans. The award, co-presented by AASA, Corebridge Financial and Sourcewell, honors superintendents whose leadership and commitment have advanced public education in their communities. Jones, 58, was named Arkansas’ state superintendent of the year in September. She is in her ninth year leading Bentonville schools and has more than 25 years of education experience in Arkansas. Bentonville is the state’s second-largest school district. Jones said the recognition reflects the work of many people in the district. She pointed to efforts to provide affordable housing for teachers, expand student opportunities through parent choice schools and offer affordable child care for employees, saying the district’s team excels at creative problem-solving while maintaining academic excellence. No superintendent from Arkansas has ever won the national award, which began in 1988, according to AASA records. The other finalists are Sharon Desmoulin-Kherat of Peoria Public School District 150 in Illinois, Walter B. Gonsoulin Jr. of Jefferson County Schools in Alabama, and David K. Moore of the School District of Indian River County in Florida. The article notes that Bentonville continues to grow rapidly. Holyoke Mayor Joshua Garcia defended the city’s affordability on Tuesday even as property taxes are expected to rise by an average of $352 next year. In a statement, Garcia said Holyoke “remains one of the most accessible and affordable places to live and work in the region” for residents across income levels, and argued that the increase reflects broader budget pressures rather than a loss of affordability. Garcia said the tax hike is tied to the city’s need to fund municipal services and future capital projects. He noted that each half-percent change in the tax rate brings in about $600,000 in revenue. One of the biggest financial strains is Holyoke’s sewer system, which is facing a $1.21 million deficit. The city had previously built up enough excess cash to handle unexpected costs, but the sewer shortfall eliminated that cushion. Garcia said that without a new sewer rate, the deficit would keep recurring each year. He added that the city has now entered the first year of a long-term sewer operations contract, which he expects will reduce the chance of similar surprises, but he stressed that sewer operations still need to be self-sustaining rather than subsidized by taxpayers. At the same time, Garcia said some changes in the city’s tax structure will soften the impact. On Dec. 2, the City Council approved a new residential tax rate of $17.43 per $1,000 and a commercial rate of $38.16 per $1,000, both slightly lower than the prior year’s rates. Garcia said the average single-family home tax bill will increase by about $352 annually, or roughly $29 per month. He said that increase is being driven largely by rising home values and growing obligations in areas such as schools, transportation, insurance, and pensions. Holyoke’s required local school contribution under the Student Opportunity Act will rise 5.87%, or $773,886, to $13.96 million. After offsets, the net school cost will increase 5.23%, or $1.19 million, to nearly $23.9 million. Transportation costs rose 10.32%, adding $1.2 million; health insurance premiums increased 9%, or $661,859; and pension costs climbed 4.65%, or $584,545, to $13.15 million. Garcia said about $8 million of the pension total is helping the city move toward fully funding its retirement system by 2032. Garcia also argued that Holyoke remains affordable compared with nearby communities. He said the city’s median home price is lower than many surrounding towns, utility rates are among the lowest in the state, and residents benefit from free curbside trash pickup. He also pointed to Holyoke’s large share of subsidized housing, saying about 40% of rental homes are supported by government programs and that 19.34% of all homes are subsidized, the highest share in Massachusetts. Looking ahead, Garcia said the city will keep working to add housing, expand the tax base, and limit future tax increases through measures such as sewer-rate reform, zoning changes, and the Municipal Finance Modernization Act.

Millions of dollars in grant funding are now available for Lowcountry nonprofits through the Coastal Community Foundation, which is seeking applications from organizations that can show clear, measurable impact in their communities. Samuel Bellamy, the foundation’s director of grant programs and impact, said applicants should focus on the real-world results their work will produce. He noted that the more specific the application, the easier it is for review panels and community volunteers to understand the project’s value. Last year, the foundation received more than 100 applications and awarded about $37 million in grants, with some individual awards reaching $25,000. Other funds support neighborhood development, racial equity, harbor water quality, services for children with special needs, educational opportunities for underserved youth, and programs encouraging physical activity and healthy lifestyles. Foundation leaders say the grants are intended to help strong ideas move forward and make a tangible difference in the region.

Belarus hosted its first Vienna Ball in the history of independent Belarus on 28 December at the Palace of Independence in Minsk, according to BelTA. The event was attended by President Aleksandr Lukashenko, Prime Minister Sergei Rumas, Council of the Republic Chair Natalya Kochanova, Presidential Administration Head Igor Sergeyenko, senior officials, and diplomats. Yet the main attention was on the debutantes: more than 360 students and graduates of universities and vocational colleges who had been invited because of their achievements in study, art, sport, science, and public service. The ball was organized in keeping with long-established Viennese traditions, and its status as part of the world’s intangible cultural heritage was highlighted. It opened with a polonaise performed by the debutante girls in white gowns holding small bouquets, while the young men wore tailcoats. Lukashenko addressed the participants, praising their appearance and saying he was proud of the beauty of the Belarusian nation, which he said was reflected not only in outward appearance but also in intelligence, education, and hard work. The women wore gowns in soft colors such as rose, blue, beige, and light green. The men appeared in tailcoats, tuxedos, and uniforms. Officials acknowledged that the occasion was unusual and caused some nervousness. Kochanova said it was only her second New Year ball and that she had helped Sergeyenko prepare through rehearsals. Austria’s ambassador to Belarus, Aloisia Worgetter, called it a great honor to attend and said European ball traditions fit well into Belarusian cultural life while gaining a national character. Her gown was made by Belarusian designer Natalya Lyakhovets. She did not dance because of medical reasons, but said she hoped to return to the floor at the next ball. Participants performed polka, pas des patineurs, galop, and the Midnight Quadrille. When a traditional Viennese waltz was announced, everyone joined in to dance to Strauss music, including Lukashenko. The program also featured professional performers such as Vienna State Opera soloist Zoryana Kushpler and Belarusian Merited Artists Oksana Volkova and Vladimir Gromov. A choreographer from the Elmayer dance school gave master classes. Worgetter thanked the organizers for the evening and presented a symbolic gift: a glass ball made by Neman Glassworks filled with round Austrian sweets. She expressed hope that Viennese balls would become a lasting tradition in Belarus. Lukashenko responded positively, saying such traditions would eventually take root in the center of “Mother Europe,” and suggested holding the balls annually with Austrian assistance. Foreign Minister Vladimir Makei said culture and art unite nations despite political disagreements, and that Austrian participation would help strengthen ties between the two peoples. At the end of the evening, A1 presented a gift card to SOS Children’s Villages in Belarus. All participants received New Year gifts, and the president instructed that a video of the event be made.

At the ceremony, Council of the Republic Chairwoman Natalya Kochanova thanked Nedzelsky on behalf of Belarusian gifted young people. She said the Belarusian government supports talented youth and noted that President Aleksandr Lukashenko pays close attention to cultural development and international cultural ties, including with Ukraine. Nedzelsky said the harp, made in France in 2018, has strong acoustic qualities and high sound quality, and can suit any musical style. He said that in the hands of a skilled performer it can sound like a symphony orchestra. He also recalled participating in the Days of Ukrainian Culture in Alexandria in 2018, which left a strong impression on him. In his view, Belarus has many talented people who should become known both at home and abroad, and joint efforts could help the world discover Belarusian talent. Belarusian Culture Minister Yuri Bondar also thanked the Ukrainian musicians, calling them friends of Belarus. He said the gift would help Belarusian musicians work with a unique instrument and suggested a national harp school could be created. Bondar also pointed to the government’s broader program of supporting musical education, including the replacement and repair of thousands of instruments in educational and cultural institutions. During the master class, Bzhezhinska performed works from the 20th and 21st centuries as well as jazz, explained the harp’s features, and answered questions from students and schoolchildren. Born in Ukraine and now based in London, she teaches and performs internationally.

The first Vienna Ball in the history of independent Belarus was held on 28 December at the Palace of Independence in Minsk, BelTA reported. The event was attended by President Aleksandr Lukashenko, Prime Minister Sergei Rumas, Council of the Republic Chair Natalya Kochanova, Head of the Presidential Administration Igor Sergeyenko, other senior officials, and diplomats. Yet the main attention was on more than 360 debutantes — students and graduates of universities and vocational colleges — who received invitations for their achievements in studies, art, sport, science, and public work. The ball followed the traditions of classic Viennese balls, which are recognized as part of the world’s intangible cultural heritage. It opened with a polonaise performed by the debutante girls in white gowns carrying small bouquets, while the boys wore tailcoats. Lukashenko addressed the participants, saying he was proud of the beauty of Belarusian youth, which in his view was reflected not only in appearance but also in intelligence, education, and hard work. He said these qualities distinguish Belarusians. The participants wore elegant formal attire in soft colors such as rose, blue, beige, and light green, while the men appeared in tailcoats, tuxedos, and uniforms. Several officials admitted they were nervous because the event was unusual and significant. Kochanova said this was her second New Year ball and that she had helped Sergeyenko prepare for it through rehearsals. Austria’s ambassador to Belarus, Aloisia Worgetter, called it an honor to attend the Minsk Vienna Ball and said European ball traditions fit well into Belarusian cultural life while also taking on a national character. Her dress was made by Belarusian designer Natalya Lyakhovets. Although she did not dance because of medical reasons, she said she hoped to return to the dance floor by the next ball. The program included polka, pas des patineurs, galop, and the Midnight Quadrille. When the traditional Viennese waltz began, the dance floor filled to Strauss music, and Lukashenko joined the dancers. The evening also featured professional performers, including Vienna State Opera soloist Zoryana Kushpler and Belarusian Merited Artists Oksana Volkova and Vladimir Gromov. A choreographer from the Elmayer dance school conducted master classes. Worgetter thanked the organizers and presented a symbolic gift: a glass ball from Neman Glassworks filled with Austrian sweets. She said the event showed how Austrian traditions and a love of elegance had been embraced in Belarus and expressed hope that Viennese balls would become a regular tradition there. Lukashenko responded positively, saying such traditions should be adopted in the “center of Mother Europe” and suggested holding Viennese balls annually with Austrian assistance. Foreign Minister Vladimir Makei said culture and art unite people and countries despite political disagreements, and that Austrian participation could bring the two peoples closer. The event ended with a gift card from A1 for SOS Children’s Villages in Belarus, and all participants received New Year gifts. Lukashenko also instructed that a video be made about the ball.
