The article describes Venezuela’s socialist regime as one that has long treated television and radio not just as propaganda tools, but as stages for political performance, with dictators and senior officials cast as celebrities. The author, writing from Caracas, says she has lived under the “Bolivarian revolution” for 25 years and still cannot understand why regime figures are so obsessed with becoming TV stars when the country is facing severe crises including poverty, inflation, hunger, lack of health care and education, and a major migration exodus. The story traces this media culture back to Hugo Chávez, who launched his long-running broadcast “Aló Presidente” in May 1999, just months after taking power. The author recalls being 11 years old when the show began and remembers the public fuss around it. The program started as a radio call-in show in which ordinary Venezuelans were supposedly able to speak directly with Chávez. It later expanded to television, though the interactive premise largely disappeared. Instead, the show became a political spectacle with ministers seated in the audience and prominent leftist guests such as Fidel Castro and Evo Morales. According to the article, “Aló Presidente” was more than just a vanity project. It became a platform for major political decisions and public displays of power. Chávez used it to threaten Colombia after a Colombian attack on a FARC camp killed rebel leader Raúl Reyes, sending troops and tanks to the border in response. In 2002, during another broadcast, Chávez used a whistle on air to fire executives from the state oil company PDVSA and replace them with loyalists, a move that helped trigger a major crisis and marked the beginning of the collapse of Venezuela’s oil industry. Another episode in 2010 showed Chávez walking through Caracas’ Bolívar Square and pointing at historic buildings he ordered to be expropriated immediately. One of those, La Francia, had housed jewelers who were abruptly put out of work. The article says Chávez’s show inspired similar efforts by leftist leaders elsewhere in Latin America, including in Brazil, Argentina, Ecuador, Bolivia, and Uruguay. But “Aló Presidente” was inseparable from Chávez himself, and when he became seriously ill, the show faded. It went on indefinite hiatus in January 2012 as Chávez underwent treatment for cancer, and he died in March 2013. His successor, Nicolás Maduro, continued the tradition in a different style. The article says Maduro has launched several media projects, including a salsa radio show in 2016 and, more recently, “Con Maduro+,” which began in April. This newer program is presented as part of Maduro’s effort to “rehabilitate” his image and even cultivate a TikTok-friendly persona. Unlike Chávez’s more overtly political and sprawling broadcasts, “Con Maduro+” is described as closer to an afternoon talk show, with colorful suits, guest chats, and even an “Artificial Intelligence” sidekick. The visual style is deliberately less associated with the traditional socialist red. The article contrasts Maduro’s polished image-management with a more openly ideological and aggressive show, “Con el Mazo Dando” (“Hitting with the Mallet”), hosted by Diosdado Cabello, a powerful regime figure described as a strongman and suspected drug lord. This program is presented as the purest expression of the regime’s media culture. It features large images of Maduro and Chávez, along with Cabello’s signature club-like prop, and functions like a ritual of political punishment. Cabello uses it to insult, intimidate, and expose politicians, journalists, and others who are not aligned with the government. The article notes that in Venezuela people can be imprisoned for 20 years under “hate speech” laws, but those rules clearly do not apply to this show. A recurring segment called the “Cartelera,” or bulletin board, is singled out as especially revealing. Cabello pins printed headlines and social media posts to a cork board, then goes through them one by one, marking the ones he approves of and scribbling over those he rejects. The author treats this as a theatrical demonstration of state surveillance and control. The article says the regime actively monitors social media to suppress dissent, and “El Mazo” recently reinforced that point. In October, Cabello reacted on air to a tweet from a Venezuelan user who had nicknamed him “The Devil’s Gerber Baby” after quoting a news post about him. The author notes that the woman who made the joke has since left Venezuela and now lives in Argentina, like millions of other Venezuelans who have fled the country. For those still inside Venezuela, the message is clear: be careful. The piece concludes that lower-ranking regime members also host local radio and occasional television shows, but Maduro and Cabello dominate in reach and production value. The author ends with a bitter joke that if Chávez had chosen to be a television anchor rather than a military man and political leader, Venezuela might have had a better chance.

# Summary: Venezuela's Socialist Regime and Its Obsession with Television The author, a Venezuelan citizen who has lived under the socialist "Bolivarian revolution" for 25 years, examines the Venezuelan government's peculiar obsession with television programming despite the nation facing severe crises including poverty, inflation, hunger, inadequate healthcare and education access, and a massive migration crisis. The regime controls virtually all media in Venezuela, creating an extensive state-owned media empire that dominates over the few remaining private outlets. The phenomenon began with late dictator Hugo Chávez, who launched "Aló Presidente" in May 1999, just three months into his rule. This lengthy radio and television program allowed Chávez to discuss government and politics while ostensibly permitting ordinary citizens to call in and speak with him directly. The show later expanded to television, dropping the call-in format and instead featuring government ministers and regional leftist leaders like Fidel Castro and Evo Morales as guests. While occasionally featuring lighthearted moments, "Aló Presidente" served as the stage for some of Venezuela's most consequential and destructive political decisions. During one episode, Chávez threatened Colombia by deploying troops and tanks to the border in response to a Colombian military operation against FARC camps. In 2002, Chávez famously fired PDVSA oil company executives on live television using a whistle, replacing them with regime loyalists—an action that triggered a year-long crisis and initiated the collapse of Venezuela's oil industry, the country's primary source of revenue. In 2010, Chávez pointed to historic buildings in Caracas' Bolívar Square and ordered their immediate expropriation on air, leaving workers jobless on a whim. The show's success inspired similar programs across the region in Brazil, Argentina, Ecuador, Bolivia, and Uruguay. However, "Aló Presidente" was inseparable from Chávez himself, and the show went indefinite hiatus in January 2012 as Chávez underwent cancer treatment. He died in March 2013. Successor Nicolás Maduro has continued this tradition, launching his own programs including a salsa radio show in 2016 and "Con Maduro+" in April of this year. Unlike "Aló Presidente's" authoritarian tone, "Con Maduro+" presents itself as friendly and trendy, featuring Maduro in colorful suits chatting with guests and even accompanied by an "Artificial Intelligence" sidekick. This reflects Maduro's attempt to rehabilitate his image and become a TikTok influencer. However, a different program, "Con el Mazo Dando" ("Hitting with the Mallet"), hosted by socialist strongman and suspected drug lord Diosdado Cabello, represents the pure essence of the original Chávez-era show. This structured program features large images of Maduro and Chávez in the background and Cabello wielding his infamous prop club. The show functions as "socialist liturgy," with Cabello spreading regime propaganda, insulting and intimidating opposition politicians, journalists, and regime opponents while leaking private telephone conversations. A particularly notable segment called "Cartelera" involves Cabello presenting printed news headlines and social media posts pinned to a cork board, which he then judges by scribbling over dissenting content or marking approved stories with checkmarks. This ritual demonstrates the regime's active surveillance of social media to suppress dissent. In October, when a Twitter user nicknamed Cabello "The Devil's Gerber Baby," Cabello featured the tweet on his show, reminding Venezuelans of the dangers of public criticism. The woman who made the joke has since fled to Argentina, joining over 7.7 million Venezuelans who have emigrated. While lower-ranking regime members host their own local radio and television shows, Maduro's and Cabello's programs dominate in reach, scope, and production budgets. The author concludes that had Chávez pursued a career as a television anchor rather than military leadership, Venezuela might have avoided its current socialist catastrophe.

Six Venezuelan education activists were released from prison on Wednesday, their lawyer and one man’s wife said, amid a reported prisoner swap deal between Venezuela and the United States. The six had been convicted of conspiracy earlier this year and sentenced to 16 years, but maintained their innocence.

# Summary Six Venezuelan activists imprisoned on conspiracy charges were freed Wednesday as part of a prisoner swap deal. Venezuela reportedly agreed to release up to 36 people in exchange for a government ally held in the United States. The activists, education campaigners sentenced to 16 years, maintained their innocence.

Venezuela released dozens of prisoners, including Americans and opposition-linked detainees, in a major swap with the United States that returned Colombian businessman Alex Saab to Caracas. The deal, announced Dec. 21 and described by U.S. officials and Venezuelan sources, followed months of negotiations mediated by Qatar. Saab, a close ally of President Nicolás Maduro, had been held in federal jail in Miami after being accused by U.S. prosecutors of helping siphon roughly $350 million from Venezuela through the United States in a bribery scheme involving Venezuelan officials. He denied the allegations and had not yet been convicted. On returning to Venezuela, Saab thanked Maduro and the Venezuelan people, saying he felt proud to serve the country and its government. Maduro called the exchange a step toward a new era in relations with Washington. In return for Saab’s release, Venezuela freed all six Americans the U.S. government had classified as wrongfully detained, along with four other Americans, according to two U.S. officials. The officials said the released Americans were on their way home. The named U.S. detainees included Eyvin Hernandez, Jerrel Kenemore, Joseph Ryan Cristella and Savoi Wright. Hernandez and Kenemore were arrested near the Colombian border in March 2022, and Cristella was arrested in July 2023; all three were accused of entering the country illegally. Biden said in a written statement that he was grateful their ordeal was over and that the U.S. was ensuring Venezuela met its commitments. The swap also sent the fugitive Malaysian businessman Leonard Glenn Francis, known as “Fat Leonard,” back to the United States. Francis has been implicated in a major U.S. Navy bribery scandal, with prosecutors alleging he provided Navy officers with cash, luxury gifts, cigars, cognac and sex parties in exchange for contracts. He had escaped U.S. house arrest last year before sentencing and was later detained in Venezuela while facing extradition proceedings. Venezuelan legal group Foro Penal said it had confirmed 20 releases by late afternoon, including 15 Venezuelans. Among them were six education activists convicted earlier this year on conspiracy charges and sentenced to 16 years, as well as Roberto Abdul, a member of the opposition primary planning committee. Sources also said arrest orders were expected to be withdrawn for three people linked to opposition candidate María Corina Machado’s campaign. The prisoner exchange came amid U.S. pressure over Venezuela’s commitments to hold fair elections in 2024. Washington had tied continued sanctions relief to progress on political prisoner releases and the removal of bans on opposition candidates. Biden said Maduro had agreed to specific requirements for a democratic election.

# Venezuela Releases Dozens in Major Prisoner Swap Venezuela's government has freed at least 20 opposition-linked prisoners and 10 Americans in a significant prisoner exchange with the United States. The swap centers on the return of Colombian businessman Alex Saab, a Maduro ally who received clemency from President Joe Biden. ## The Deal The agreement, negotiated over months by Qatar, represents a major diplomatic development between the US and the OPEC member nation. US prosecutors had accused Saab of siphoning approximately $350 million from Venezuela through bribery schemes, charges he denies. Despite never being convicted, Saab's return to Venezuela was previously considered unlikely, making his release a victory for President Nicolas Maduro. ## American Detainees Released All six Americans classified by the US as wrongfully detained in Venezuela have been freed, along with four additional Americans. Named detainees include Eyvin Hernandez, Jerrel Kenemore, Joseph Ryan Cristella, and Savoi Wright. Hernandez and Kenemore were arrested near the Colombian border in March 2022 on charges of illegal entry, while Cristella was detained in July 2021. President Biden expressed gratitude for their release, stating he is "grateful that their ordeal is finally over." ## Venezuelan Prisoners Venezuelan human rights organization Foro Penal confirmed that 20 people were freed, including 15 Venezuelans. Released prisoners include six education campaigners convicted of conspiracy and sentenced to 16 years, who maintain their innocence, and Roberto Abdul, a member of the opposition primary planning committee. Three individuals associated with opposition candidate Maria Corina Machado's campaign had arrest orders withdrawn. ## Additional Returns The US also recovered fugitive Malaysian businessman Leonard Glenn Francis, known as "Fat Leonard," who fled US house arrest by cutting off his monitoring anklet. Francis faces charges related to bribing US Navy officers with cash, food, cigars, and hotel services in exchange for military contracts. He had been detained in Venezuela facing extradition. ## Context and Conditions The swap follows the White House's October announcement of sanctions relief in response to Venezuela's agreement to hold fair 2024 elections. However, Washington had set a November 30 deadline for progress on removing opposition candidate bans and releasing prisoners, threatening to reinstate sanctions if demands weren't met. Maduro characterized the exchange as marking "a step toward a new era of diplomatic relations" with the United States. Upon returning to Venezuela, Saab expressed pride in serving Maduro's government, while the Venezuelan president emphasized his commitment to the negotiated agreements.

Venezuela’s worsening humanitarian and economic crisis has been accompanied by a troubling rise in suicides, according to experts and civil society groups cited in this report. The article opens with the story of Ernesto, a 50-year-old man in Caracas who took his own life in early November after swallowing a cocktail of drugs and alcohol in the apartment where he lived alone. His family shared his final message with IPS. In it, he described the physical pain and despair he had been living with: he could not afford an ophthalmologist as his eyesight deteriorated, his molars were falling out, eating hurt, and he could no longer pay for dental care after years of being able to meet his expenses. He wrote that his dreams, plans, and goals were disappearing, and concluded that although he had done what he could for his family and country, he would not continue “being dead in life.” The article says Ernesto is a fictitious name used at the family’s request. His case is presented as one example of a broader pattern in a country where the collapse of living conditions has left many people without the means to cope with illness, poverty, and hopelessness. Gustavo Páez, a demographer with the Venezuelan Observatory of Violence (OVV), said the suicide rate doubled between 2018 and 2022 compared with 2015, and that the complex humanitarian emergency is likely a major factor. Venezuela, a country of just over 28 million people, saw its suicide rate rise from 3.8 per 100,000 inhabitants to 9.3 in 2018, before easing slightly to 8.2 in 2019 and 7.7 in 2022, according to OVV data. The annual average in the last four years has been 2,260 cases. Rossana García Mujica, a clinical psychologist and professor at the Central University of Venezuela, noted that while these figures are lower than the global average of 10.5 per 100,000 and lower than some regional rates, they may not tell the full story because underreporting is likely. She pointed out that Venezuela’s last official yearbook on the subject was published in 2014. In her view, the apparent decline in the rate could reflect a temporary economic improvement, but 2023 has been difficult and the numbers are unlikely to remain stable. The article places the suicide trend within the broader Venezuelan crisis. HumVenezuela, a platform of dozens of civil society organizations, defines the situation as a complex humanitarian emergency caused by the combined erosion of the economic, institutional, and social structures that support life, safety, freedom, and well-being. Since 2013, Venezuela has endured eight consecutive years of severe recession that wiped out four-fifths of its GDP, more than two years of hyperinflation, and the collapse of the national currency and wages. Health services and basic utilities have also deteriorated sharply in many parts of the country. The crisis has pushed more than seven million Venezuelans to migrate, according to United Nations figures. There was a slight economic recovery in 2021 and 2022, especially in consumption, helped in part by remittances sent by migrants. But that trend stalled in 2023. Páez said suicide rates move with the pace of the humanitarian emergency: as the macroeconomy worsens, families lose access to food, services, recreation, and medicine, which can lead to mental disorders linked to suicidal behavior. He also said family grief caused by migration is another factor contributing to frustration, depression, and self-harm. The report includes another case: R., a poor young woman who posted a video on social media describing her struggle to receive chemotherapy. She lived in the interior of the country and traveled monthly to Caracas to obtain treatment through medicine banks provided by the government. She said that on one recent visit she had been sent from one part of the city to another, and when she finally arrived, she was 15 minutes late and denied the chemotherapy because distribution had ended at 3 p.m. Exhausted, after sleeping at a relative’s house and climbing roughly 200 steps up a steep hillside neighborhood, she said in a quiet voice that she was tired, her legs hurt, and she no longer wanted to fight. Experts interviewed in the article say economic hardship is especially decisive for certain groups. Yorelis Acosta, a psychologist who works with people vulnerable to depression and fear and also teaches at UCV, said that for Venezuelans over 30, and especially men between 40 and 50, financial problems are often a determining factor. She linked self-harm and suicide to statements such as “I don’t have a job,” “I’m out of work,” or “I have a disease and I can’t afford my treatment.” She said suicides rise during economic crises. García Mujica said the most vulnerable groups include men between 30 and 64 and young people between 15 and 24. She said she has observed an increase in anxiety disorders and depression in adults, and in young people a rise in suicide, self-injury, and eating disorders. She added that self-harm can be a way of coping with emotional pain, sadness, anger, and stress, and suggested that social networks may intensify intolerance of frustration and the desire for immediacy. She also warned of a serious lack of face-to-face family communication, saying that family life increasingly happens on phones rather than in person, leaving adolescents more influenced by social media than real interaction. OVV media monitoring found that between 2019 and 2022, 81 percent of reported suicide cases involved men and 19 percent women. More than half were adults between 30 and 64. Venezuela’s socialist government said Monday that it has begun issuing Venezuelan identity and nationality documents to residents of the disputed Essequibo region, the vast territory that makes up most of Guyana. The move is the latest step in Nicolás Maduro’s escalating campaign to assert Venezuelan control over the area, a dispute that dates back to at least 1899 but was revived with new force in December when Maduro announced plans to annex the region. The document drive was one of the measures Maduro said would follow the December 3 referendum, which Venezuelan authorities claimed produced more than 10.5 million votes in favor of annexation. Independent images and reporting at the time, however, showed low turnout and largely empty polling stations. Maduro declared the referendum results “binding” and ordered a series of actions, including creating a new Venezuelan state in Essequibo, granting Venezuelan citizenship to the region’s roughly 125,000 inhabitants, and opening the territory to oil, gas, and mining exploration licenses. Most residents of Essequibo are members of Indigenous communities. On Monday, Interior, Justice, and Peace Minister Remigio Ceballos said the state identity agency SAIME had opened three mobile offices in the Venezuelan border city of Tumeremo, Bolívar state, to process nationality documents for Essequibo residents who want them. He said the offices are operating out of a “temporary administrative” center for a planned new state called “Guayana Esequiba,” and added that permanent SAIME offices would eventually be built there. Ceballos praised Maduro’s actions as a “great achievement” for the country. Rosalba Gil, head of Venezuela’s National Electoral Center, also said she had visited Tumeremo and that new registration units would be opened there. She urged “Essequibians” to come to the civil registry to fix documents and obtain identification cards. The government did not say how many people had actually received Venezuelan papers. The dispute concerns a territory of more than 61,600 square miles, administered by Guyana and representing about two-thirds of its land area. For years the issue was relatively quiet, but tensions rose sharply after Guyana discovered offshore oil and signed deals with Houston-based ExxonMobil for production. Maduro has accused ExxonMobil of being part of a U.S.-backed plot to colonize South America. The International Court of Justice ruled in 2023 that it has jurisdiction over the case, after Guyana asked the court to intervene in 2018. A final ruling is expected years from now. Venezuela says it does not recognize the ICJ’s authority in the matter. Maduro is scheduled to meet Guyanese President Irfaan Ali in Trinidad and Tobago on Thursday to discuss the dispute. Ali told AFP he would attend but maintained that the issue belongs before the ICJ and is not open to negotiation. Meanwhile, Venezuelan General Alexis Rodríguez Cabello, whom Maduro named as the “sole authority” for Essequibo, said he met with Indigenous representatives to advance a development plan focused on health, infrastructure, education, and culture. He described the government’s effort as part of a “harmonic development plan” and said it reflects Venezuela’s policy of peace, dialogue, and social action.

Venezuela’s prolonged economic collapse has driven more than 7.7 million people to leave the country over the past decade, creating one of the world’s largest displacement crises. For years, most Venezuelan migrants and refugees remained in South America, especially in Colombia, which has received nearly 3 million, and Peru, which has taken in more than 1.5 million. More recently, however, a growing share has begun heading north toward Central America and the United States, often by crossing the Darién Gap, a dangerous jungle corridor between Colombia and Panama. A September 2023 analysis by R4V, a platform created in 2018 by UN agencies and humanitarian organizations to respond to the Venezuelan crisis, shows how migration patterns shifted in 2022 and 2023. In the first ten months of 2022, arrivals to the north increased, but they fell sharply in late 2022 after the U.S. government announced a new immigration policy for Venezuelans that included expulsion measures for irregular migrants. In 2023, however, arrivals through the Darién surged again, partly because of changes to that policy. Panama recorded a historic 333,700 crossings in 2023, more than 60 percent of them Venezuelans and more than three times the number seen in the same period of 2022. The report says this has placed a historic strain on host countries’ capacities. The journey through the Darién is extremely hazardous. Migrants must pass through mountainous terrain covered by dense forest and vulnerable to flooding, where injuries are common. The dangers are not only environmental. The report says migrants face stabbings, gunshot wounds, human trafficking, and sexual violence. Médecins Sans Frontières reported 172 cases of sexual violence in the Darién in 2022. The growing flow of migrants has also created lucrative opportunities for criminal networks. A range of services has emerged along the route, including boat transport between points in the jungle, guides, and porters who carry food and equipment. Depending on the service, fees can range from tens to hundreds of dollars per person, creating a multimillion-dollar business tied to organized crime and, in some cases, local politicians and community leaders. At the same time, humanitarian funding is shrinking. R4V says its 228 partners have been severely affected by grave funding shortages in the first half of 2023. As of October 27, the 2023 regional response plan was only 16 percent funded, compared with 37.3 percent in 2022 and 41 percent in 2021. Much of the funding traditionally comes from governments, especially the United States, which provided around 80 percent in 2022, and from multilateral donors such as the European Union. Several governments contributed far less in 2023 than they had the year before. The funding gap limits support for millions of Venezuelan migrants and refugees who need help with health care, shelter, education, hygiene, transportation, food, employment, and protection. The International Organization for Migration said in September 2023 that more than 4 million Venezuelan migrants and refugees across the Americas were struggling to meet basic needs. Eduardo Stein of IOM and UNHCR has called for greater international support, especially for those crossing the Darién, where a separate study found that 57 percent of surveyed migrants said it was the place where they most needed assistance but did not receive it, especially food and water. UNICEF has also warned that many migrants are children, including many unaccompanied and under age 5.

The newly appointed CEO of the Ethiopia-Djibouti Railway S.C., Takele Uma, says he aims to turn the debt-laden railway into a profitable company within three years. He made the pledge on 28 August 2024 during a consultation with employees in Dire Dawa, where he also outlined ongoing internal changes and a new organizational structure. Dire Dawa mayor Kedir Juhar attended the meeting. Takele told staff that although the railway has been operating for six years, it has accumulated debt instead of delivering the expected national benefits. He said a three-year strategic plan and a revised organizational framework have been prepared to guide the turnaround. He expressed confidence that better operational management, organizational reform, and strategic planning could make the railway profitable within the target period. Over the past week, Takele has held consultations with workers at the railway headquarters and at stations in Meiso and Adama. In these meetings, he urged employees to work together to make the railway a stronger contributor to Ethiopia’s economy, especially by supporting export and import trade. He also stressed the urgent need to improve financial performance, create a better working environment, and transform the railway into a productive institution. Takele, formerly Ethiopia’s Minister of Mines and deputy mayor of Addis Abeba, was appointed by Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed in mid-July 2024. He replaced Abdi Zenebe, who has since become deputy executive director at the Institute of Foreign Affairs. Two weeks ago, Takele also met Chinese Ambassador Chen Hai to discuss serious operational and maintenance problems. He said only 15 of the railway’s 32 freight locomotives are functioning, reducing annual freight capacity from a designed 6.3 million tons to 2.4 million tons, or 38% of capacity. The 750-kilometer Addis Abeba-Djibouti railway was built as a $4 billion joint project involving Ethiopia, Djibouti, and China, with 70% financed by China Exim Bank. Construction began in 2011, and China Railway Construction Corporation managed operations from 2018 until May 2024, when control shifted to the Ethiopian and Djiboutian governments. Officials have long blamed theft and vandalism for revenue losses, including a reported 114 million birr loss in early 2020/2021.

South Africa will keep Africa, especially the Southern African Development Community (SADC), at the center of its foreign policy in 2019, International Relations and Cooperation Minister Lindiwe Sisulu said in a Christmas Eve message. She said regional stability is essential to socio-economic development in South Africa and across the continent, and pledged that the country would work with others to build an Africa free of conflict. Sisulu said South Africa will push for faster implementation of the African Union’s Continental Free Trade Area Agreement so that businesses across SADC and the wider continent can trade more easily. She said South Africa aims to position itself as the continent’s business capital and as a hub for transport and technology. Its developed financial and transport systems, she added, are already helping support infrastructure development in the region. She stressed that SADC needs stronger road, rail, air, technology and communications links to help business grow. She also noted that South Africa will begin a two-year term as a non-permanent member of the United Nations Security Council next year. Early in 2019, she plans to consult diplomats on South Africa’s priorities, including silencing guns in Africa, fighting extremism and terrorism, and protecting women, children and civilians in conflict zones. Looking back at 2018, Sisulu described it as an outstanding year for South African diplomacy. She highlighted the country’s roles in BRICS and IORA, as well as hosting major meetings. Going forward, diplomats will continue promoting South Africa as an investment and tourism destination, while supporting development, peace and security in Africa.

# Summary South African Minister of International Relations and Cooperation Lindiwe Sisulu announced that Africa and the Southern African Development Community (SADC) region will remain strategic foreign policy priorities for South Africa in 2019. Sisulu emphasized that regional and continental stability are essential for socio-economic development. South Africa aims to work with other nations to create an Africa free of conflict and expedite implementation of the African Union's Continental Free Trade Area Agreement to facilitate business across the continent. The country aspires to become Africa's business capital and a transport and technology hub. Sisulu highlighted that South Africa's advanced financial and transport sectors are crucial for developing SADC infrastructure, and improved road, rail, air, and technology connectivity is necessary for business growth. Beginning in 2019, South Africa will assume a non-permanent seat on the United Nations Security Council for two years. During this tenure, the country will focus on conflict resolution in Africa, combating extremism and terrorism, and protecting vulnerable populations in conflict zones. Reflecting on 2018, Sisulu noted it was an outstanding year for South African diplomacy, with the country chairing BRICS and the Indian Ocean Rim Association while hosting major regional summits. Looking ahead, South African diplomats will continue attracting investment, promoting tourism, and advancing development, peace, and security initiatives across Africa.

Severe thunderstorms in Limpopo and the Eastern Cape have raised South Africa’s death toll to seven, Cooperative Governance and Traditional Affairs Minister Zweli Mkhize said. Four people died from drowning in the Tzaneen and Sekhukhune areas, while three others were killed by lightning in Amathole. The heavy rain has also caused injuries and widespread damage to infrastructure. In Sebokeng in the Vaal area, homes and streets were flooded, with Evaton among the worst affected. Emergency support teams have been deployed to the hardest-hit areas. The Emfuleni Municipality said some homes were unusable and residents had been temporarily relocated. Mkhize expressed condolences to the bereaved families.

# Summary Severe thunderstorms in South Africa's Limpopo and Eastern Cape provinces have killed seven people over recent days. Four deaths occurred in Tzaneen and Sekhukhune from drowning, while three in Amathole were struck by lightning. Heavy rainfall has caused extensive injuries and infrastructure damage nationwide, with Sebokeng in the Vaal area experiencing severe flooding. Homes and streets are submerged, forcing residents into temporary relocation. The Emfuleni Municipality reports affected areas including Evaton, where houses are nearly destroyed. The government has deployed emergency personnel to affected regions, and the Minister of Cooperative Governance offered condolences to bereaved families.

Leclanché SA, the Swiss energy storage company listed on the SIX exchange, said it had completed more than 100MWh of stationary storage projects worldwide, reaching a milestone the company’s CEO, Anil Srivastava, had said earlier in December was expected by the end of 2018. The announcement framed the achievement as an important step for Leclanché as it entered 2019, with the company emphasizing rising demand for stationary storage systems that can help integrate renewable energy into electricity grids, as well as demand for grid-to-electric-vehicle storage solutions. A central example of this milestone was the Graciosa project in the Azores, which Leclanché highlighted as a landmark and replicable model for island power systems. The company said its lithium titanate cell (LTO)-based battery energy storage system was chosen for the project because of its long-life performance characteristics. According to Leclanché, those batteries are well suited to the repeated cycling and stress involved in a microgrid, and they help maximize wind-energy integration while supporting the long-term power purchase agreement tied to the project. Leclanché said the system has helped clean up Graciosa’s energy supply by enabling more than 70% renewable energy on the island’s grid and reducing reliance on diesel fuel. Srivastava said the Graciosa project demonstrated that renewable integration could be increased “today,” not just in the future, and said the solution could be replicated on other islands. He added that, together with partner HowardScott, Leclanché hoped to deploy the same type of storage solution across the Azores. He also argued that utilities, automakers, fleet operators, fast-charging infrastructure companies and AI applications all need smarter, faster and greener storage systems, and said Leclanché’s combination of cell technology and grid-to-EV expertise made it a unique partner. Dom Hughes, director of Graciolica, the project company, said the project had required patient investors and the efforts of a large international engineering team. He credited EDA, the customer utility, as well as Leclanché’s on-site team. He said Tractebel coordinated the project in 2018, working with Greensmith Energy, which provided the hybrid microgrid technology and solution, and Leclanché, which supplied the battery system. Hughes added that Greensmith’s GEMS controls platform is central to the plant’s operation. He said Graciolica would be able to provide 100% clean energy under the right conditions and fully automated grid-forming services to EDA. The article also included Leclanché’s broader company description, noting that it is headquartered in Switzerland and has more than 100 years of battery and energy storage innovation behind it. It positions itself as a pure-play energy storage company focused on stationary storage, e-transport solutions and specialty battery systems. The release closed with a standard disclaimer about forward-looking statements and cited Navigant Research projections showing rapid expected growth in global utility-scale energy storage installations through 2026.

Isabel dos Santos, widely described as Africa’s richest woman, has condemned an Angolan court order to seize about $1 billion of her assets, calling it a politically motivated attack. The 46-year-old daughter of former Angolan President Jose Eduardo dos Santos said the case was handled in secrecy and that she was denied the chance to respond to what she described as fabricated charges. According to Angola’s state news agency, a court on Dec. 23 ordered her bank accounts frozen and her shares in several local companies seized, including stakes in telecom firm Unitel, BFA bank and cement producer Cimangola. The action is part of President Joao Lourenco’s anti-corruption campaign, which has targeted figures linked to the former ruling family. Dos Santos, whose fortune Forbes estimates at $2.2 billion, said on Twitter that she would use all available Angolan and international legal means to challenge the order and prove the truth. She said her wealth came from her education and business skills, not from her father’s influence. She now lives outside Angola, saying she faces death threats at home. Her family had long benefited from Angola’s oil and diamond wealth, even as the country remained poor and underdeveloped. Jose Eduardo dos Santos ruled for 38 years, a period marked by corruption and missing state funds. Before leaving office in 2017, he appointed Isabel dos Santos to head state oil company Sonangol, but Lourenco later removed her. Her brother is also on trial in Angola over allegations he helped move $500 million out of the country.

# Isabel dos Santos Denounces Angolan Court Seizure as "Politically Motivated" Isabel dos Santos, Africa's richest woman with a $2.2 billion fortune, has condemned an Angolan court order freezing her bank accounts and seizing approximately $1 billion in assets as a "politically motivated attack." The 46-year-old daughter of former Angolan President Jose Eduardo dos Santos had her shares in major companies seized on December 23, including stakes in telecommunications firm Unitel, BFA bank, and cement company Cimangola. She claims the trial was conducted in "total secrecy" with fabricated charges and documents, and vows to use all available legal remedies to fight the order. The seizure is part of President Joao Lourenco's anti-corruption campaign following her father's 38-year presidency, during which billions in state funds disappeared. Since taking office in 2017, Lourenco removed dos Santos as head of Angola's state oil firm and initiated efforts to recover stolen assets. Dos Santos attributes her wealth to education and business acumen rather than family connections, though her father appointed her to lead Sonangol in 2016. She now resides outside Angola, citing death threats. Her brother, Jose Filomento dos Santos, currently faces trial for allegedly smuggling $500 million from Angola's Sovereign Wealth Fund, charges he denies. Angola possesses sub-Saharan Africa's third-largest economy through oil and diamonds, yet widespread poverty persists among its 32 million citizens.

The Chinese Railway Construction Corporation (CRCC) has officially handed over management of the Ethio-Djibouti Railway to the governments of Ethiopia and Djibouti, six years after commercial operations began. The transfer was marked by a ceremony in Addis Abeba on 10 May 2024. CRCC had managed the line since operations started in 2018. The Ethio-Djibouti Railway stretches more than 750 kilometers from Addis Abeba to the port of Djibouti and is Africa’s first electrified railway. It is one of the major infrastructure projects linked to China’s Belt and Road Initiative, launched in 2013 to strengthen links between Asia, Africa, and Europe and promote trade and economic growth. Construction of the railway began in 2011 by China Railway Group Limited and China Civil Engineering Construction Corporation, both Chinese state-owned firms. Freight services started in November 2015, followed by trial passenger and service operations on the Ethiopian side in October 2016 and on the Djibouti side in January 2018. The project cost $4 billion in total. Ethiopia’s section cost $3.4 billion, financed 70% by China Exim Bank and 30% by the Ethiopian government, while Djibouti contributed $878 million. At the handover ceremony, railway executive director Abdi Zenabi said the line had transformed cargo transport between the two countries by reducing transit times and improving trade opportunities. Since commercial operations began, the railway has completed 1,824 passenger trips carrying nearly 530,900 passengers and 6,133 freight trips transporting about 7.33 million metric tons of cargo.

# Ethiopia and Djibouti Assume Control of Ethio-Djibouti Railway After six years of operations, the Chinese Railway Construction Corporation (CRCC) has officially transferred management of the Ethio-Djibouti Railway to Ethiopian and Djiboutian governments in a ceremony held May 10, 2024, in Addis Abeba. The 750-kilometer railway, Africa's first electrified railway, connects Addis Abeba to Djibouti's port and was constructed as part of China's Belt and Road Initiative. Chinese state-owned enterprises began construction in 2011, with freight services commencing in November 2015 and full commercial operations beginning in 2018. The $4 billion project was financed through a partnership: China Exim Bank covered 70% of the Ethiopian segment's $3.4 billion cost, with Ethiopia providing 30%, while Djibouti contributed $878 million. Since operations began, the railway has transported nearly 531,000 passengers across 1,824 journeys and moved approximately 7.3 million metric tons of cargo in 6,133 freight trips. According to executive director Abdi Zenabi, the railway has significantly improved transportation efficiency and trade prospects between the two nations by reducing transit times and expanding commercial opportunities.

South African companies are increasingly embracing Managed Business Services (MBS), a model similar to “everything as a service,” because it helps them cut costs, simplify operations and avoid large technology investments during a difficult economic period. The article explains that, with budgets tight, businesses still need to maintain operations, improve efficiency and find ways to generate revenue, and IT departments are being pushed to support these broader goals. A recent 2018 ITWeb Brainstorm CIO Survey showed this shift clearly: nearly half of the CIOs surveyed said IT teams were being asked to prioritise efficiency and cost savings across the whole business, while a quarter said they were expected to help accelerate new business development. MBS is presented as a flexible, utility-based offering delivered on a per-seat, per-month basis. Companies can access services such as IT, security, communications and printing without buying and maintaining the underlying technology themselves. One key attraction is that MBS is treated as an operating expense, which is especially useful as accounting rules for rental agreements are changing and may force some off-balance-sheet arrangements to be reported. By using MBS, firms can obtain the services they need without the reporting burden associated with ownership or leasing. The article says demand is also being driven by growing concerns over cybersecurity and compliance. As South African businesses face more cyberattacks and a more complex regulatory environment, many find it easier to outsource sensitive workloads to trusted providers so they can focus on their core activities. Print management remains an important part of many MBS packages, despite the shift to digital work, because companies still spend heavily on printing. Print-as-a-service helps them track usage, reduce waste, manage costs and secure network printers. Overall, the article argues that MBS offers lower costs, provider-managed maintenance, access to the latest technology and faster deployment of new services, enabling businesses to respond more quickly to market changes.

# Managed Business Services Gaining Traction in South Africa Managed Business Services (MBS), the latest evolution in "as a service" offerings, is increasingly appealing to South African companies facing economic pressures and operational challenges. ## Key Drivers The 2018 ITWeb Brainstorm CIO Survey reveals that nearly half of CIOs surveyed report being pressured to prioritize efficiency and cost savings across their entire organizations, while a quarter are tasked with developing new revenue-generating business lines. These competing demands make MBS an attractive solution. ## How MBS Works MBS provides customizable, utility-based IT services—including IT support, security, communications, and printing—on a per-seat, per-month consumption model. Companies receive necessary services without making substantial technology investments, making it ideal for organizations with tight budgets. ## Financial and Regulatory Advantages MBS offerings are classified as operating expenses rather than capital expenditures, providing significant accounting benefits. This distinction becomes particularly relevant as new accounting standards for rental agreements take effect in 2019, requiring companies to report previously off-balance-sheet lease agreements on their balance sheets. MBS sidesteps these reporting complexities. ## Security and Compliance A major driver of MBS adoption is the growing need for data security and regulatory compliance. South African companies face increasing cybersecurity threats and complex regulatory requirements. Outsourcing these critical functions to trusted service providers allows companies to focus on core business operations while ensuring compliance. ## Additional Benefits Print management remains a significant MBS component, helping companies reduce printing costs, track usage, and secure network printers. Beyond cost savings and maintenance handled by providers, MBS ensures companies always have access to the latest technologies, can quickly deploy new services, and respond rapidly to market changes through continuous data and resource availability. The article concludes that organizations not exploring MBS risk missing a substantial opportunity to achieve faster, better, and more cost-effective operations.

Cape Town’s 2018 was marked by a series of major political, social and legal flashpoints, reflected in the Cape Argus front pages throughout the year. The city endured a severe water crisis, with the City of Cape Town and the DA struggling to manage both the shortage itself and the political backlash, before rain eventually eased fears that the army would have to man water stations. Metrorail also dominated headlines after arson attacks, vandalism and crime severely disrupted train services and left commuters stranded and frustrated. Gang violence on the Cape Flats remained a major concern, prompting President Cyril Ramaphosa to announce the rollout of an Anti Gang Unit in affected areas, with plans for it to expand nationally. Several high-profile court cases ended with heavy sentences, including Henry van Breda, Jason Rohde, and the killers of Matie student Hannah Cornelius, all of whom were convicted in shocking murder cases. Housing and social housing became increasingly contentious, especially in the wake of Patricia de Lille’s resignation after widespread opposition to her approach to moving people closer to the city. Her departure also triggered resignations by senior DA figures, including Brett Herron, who accused the party of blocking social housing projects. The article notes that the City owns more than 44,000 pieces of land, yet still cannot meet housing demand. It ends by noting that parents would face higher school fees in 2019.

# Summary 2018 was a significant year for Cape Town, marked by multiple crises and political developments. The city navigated a severe water shortage that threatened to require military intervention at water stations, though rainfall eventually eased the crisis. The Metrorail system faced crippling challenges from arson attacks, vandalism, and crime, severely affecting commuters. Gang violence on the Cape Flats prompted President Cyril Ramaphosa to announce the rollout of an Anti-Gang Unit in problem areas, with plans for national expansion. Several high-profile murder convictions dominated headlines, including those of Henry van Breda, Jason Rohde, and the killers of Matie student Hannah Cornelius, all receiving substantial sentences. Former mayor Patricia De Lille resigned following public disapproval of her social housing policies aimed at relocating residents closer to the city center. Her stance prompted resignations from senior DA councillors, including Brett Herron, who cited a "white cabal" blocking housing projects. Despite owning over 44,000 land parcels, the City struggled to address housing demand. Additionally, President Jacob Zuma stepped down, while the District Six saga continued unresolved. The year concluded with concerns about rising school fees affecting families in the coming year.

Japan’s Government Pension Investment Fund (GPIF), the world’s largest pension fund with 127.3 trillion yen in assets, announced a major overhaul of its investment strategy to seek higher returns. The fund said it will double its target allocation to both Japanese and overseas equities to 25 percent each, up from 12 percent apiece. At the same time, it will sharply cut domestic bonds to 35 percent from 60 percent. The new targets do not include short-term assets, which had been part of the previous allocation framework. GPIF also raised its target for foreign bonds to 15 percent from 11 percent and said it will invest up to 5 percent of total holdings in alternative assets such as private equity, infrastructure and real estate. These alternative investments will be counted within the broader asset classes rather than as a separate category. The shift came amid expectations that Japan’s long period of deflation is ending. GPIF President Takahiro Mitani said the fund’s previous strategy had been built on the assumption that prices would keep falling, while the new allocation is based on the expectation that consumer prices will rise. He also said the Bank of Japan’s large-scale bond buying had made it easier for GPIF to reduce its bond exposure. The announcement followed a surprise easing move by the Bank of Japan, which expanded its monetary base target and helped push Japanese stocks sharply higher. The Nikkei 225 rose 4.8 percent on the day, while the Topix index gained 4.3 percent, its biggest one-day rise since June 2013. Markets had already been buoyed by reports that GPIF’s announcement was imminent. Investors had been waiting for the revised strategy since a government panel said last year that the pension fund was too dependent on domestic bonds, especially as inflation began to return and pension payouts increased with Japan’s aging population. Analysts had generally expected GPIF to shift toward more equities, but the final allocations were somewhat different from market forecasts. GPIF also adjusted its risk limits, raising the deviation band for Japanese bonds to 10 percent from 8 percent and for Japanese stocks to 9 percent from 6 percent. Foreign equities will now be benchmarked against the MSCI All-Country World Index, which includes emerging markets, instead of mainly the MSCI Kokusai Index of developed markets. Mitani said the timetable for implementing the changes had not yet been decided. Market strategists said the pace of rebalancing would be crucial, with some estimating it could take around five years, but even a gradual shift would have a significant impact on Japanese and global markets.

# Japan's Pension Fund Announces Major Investment Shift Japan's Government Pension Investment Fund (GPIF), the world's largest pension fund with 127.3 trillion yen in assets, has announced a significant reallocation strategy aimed at achieving higher returns in response to changing economic conditions. The fund is dramatically increasing its stock market exposure, setting allocation targets of 25 percent each for Japanese and overseas equities, up from 12 percent previously. Correspondingly, domestic bond holdings will be reduced from 60 percent to 35 percent of assets. GPIF will also begin investing up to 5 percent in alternative assets including private equity, infrastructure, and real estate. Foreign bond allocations will increase to 15 percent from 11 percent. The new strategy reflects a fundamental shift in assumptions, as GPIF President Takahiro Mitani explained that the previous allocation was designed around expectations of continued deflation, while the new approach assumes rising consumer prices. The announcement came hours after the Bank of Japan unexpectedly expanded monetary easing, creating what analysts called a "double punch" for stock markets. The Nikkei 225 surged 4.8 percent on the day, while the Topix index rallied 4.3 percent—its steepest gain since June 2013. The revised strategy addresses longstanding concerns that GPIF was over-reliant on domestic bonds. A government panel had previously flagged this imbalance, noting that mounting pension payouts for Japan's aging population required more growth-oriented investments. The fund's new allocation targets slightly exceeded analyst expectations, which had predicted 24 percent for local stocks, 15 percent for global shares, and 40 percent for Japanese bonds. GPIF also adjusted its deviation limits, providing flexibility during the portfolio rebalancing process. The timing of the announcement, combined with the Bank of Japan's policy expansion, boosted investor confidence. Market strategists noted that increased GPIF allocation to Japanese stocks should support share prices, while expanded foreign investments may help weaken the yen. However, the timeframe for implementing these changes remains undetermined. Investment strategists suggest a five-year transition period would be typical, though the fund could potentially move faster. Regardless of the timeline, analysts expect the reallocation to have significant market impacts as GPIF gradually shifts its massive portfolio toward equities and alternative investments.

Japan’s Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism (MLIT) has approved SKY-System, a ballast-water management system developed by Nippon Yuka Kogyo Co. Ltd. of the NYK Group together with Katayama Chemical Industries Co. Ltd. Ballast water, taken on by ships to maintain stability, can carry marine organisms from one region to another and threaten local ecosystems when discharged. SKY-System treats ballast water by disinfecting organisms and bacteria, using Peraclean Ocean, a biodegradable biocide developed by Evonik Industries and Katayama Chemical Industries. According to the report, it is the first system able to reliably sterilize organisms regardless of ballast-water quality, including seawater, brackish water, freshwater, and ice-cold water. The system is described as energy-efficient, easy to maintain, compact, and installable on all vessel types without dry-docking. It can be fitted during operation with little or no off-hire time, helping reduce installation costs and making it a practical breakthrough in ballast-water treatment.

Ltd. and Katayama Chemical Industries Co. Ltd. Ballast water is seawater ships carry for balance, taken on at unloading ports and discharged at loading ports. The project also promises a range of amenities, including landscaped gardens, 24-hour power backup, a clubhouse, swimming pool, indoor and outdoor sports facilities, and a community hall. A 9-hole golf course and an international-standard clubhouse were highlighted as major attractions. Godrej City is being positioned as a strong investment opportunity because of its location in Panvel, which the company described as Mumbai’s next major investment destination. The township is near the proposed international airport, the Nhava Sheva Sea Link, major expressways, and planned metro lines. It is located between NH 4 and the Mumbai-Pune Expressway and overlooks the Matheran hills. Prices for the apartments are expected to range from INR 50 lakh to INR 1.1 crore. The article also notes Godrej Properties’ background as an established developer founded in 1990, with projects across 12 Indian cities and a record of awards for sustainability and innovation.

A Kobe University study warns that Japan could face a catastrophic volcanic eruption within the next century, potentially threatening nearly all of its 127 million people. Earth sciences professors Yoshiyuki Tatsumi and Keiko Suzuki said a “colossal” eruption could effectively leave Japan “extinct as a country.” Their analysis, based on volcanic activity over the past 120,000 years, estimated the odds of such an event at about 1 percent over the next 100 years. The researchers pointed to past examples showing that low-probability disasters can still strike. They noted that just before the 1995 Kobe earthquake, the chance of a major quake there had also been estimated at about 1 percent over 30 years. That quake, measuring 7.2 magnitude, killed 6,400 people and injured nearly 4,400. The study comes weeks after Mount Ontake erupted without warning, killing 57 people and leaving at least six missing, in Japan’s deadliest volcanic eruption in almost 90 years. The authors said the warning is especially serious because Japan contains about 7 percent of the volcanoes that have erupted in the past 10,000 years. They highlighted Kyushu as a major danger zone. A massive eruption there could bury an area home to 7 million people in lava and molten rock within two hours. Ash carried by westerly winds could then make much of Honshu uninhabitable and cripple transport and other infrastructure, leaving about 120 million people in major cities and towns with little hope of rescue. The study called for better technology to monitor deep magma reservoirs.

# Summary A Kobe University study warns that Japan faces approximately a one percent risk of a catastrophic volcanic eruption within the next century that could potentially destroy the nation and endanger its entire 127 million population. Professors Yoshiyuki Tatsumi and Keiko Suzuki analyzed volcanic eruption patterns over the past 120,000 years to reach their conclusion. They note that Japan contains about seven percent of the world's volcanoes that have erupted in the past 10,000 years, making it particularly vulnerable. The researchers warn that a major eruption on Kyushu, the southernmost main island, could bury seven million people under lava and molten rock within two hours. Volcanic ash carried by westerly winds would render most of Honshu uninhabitable by damaging critical infrastructure and transport systems, making it nearly impossible to save approximately 120 million people in major cities. The study references a massive eruption 28,000 years ago that created a 23-kilometer-wide crater in southern Kyushu as evidence of such catastrophic potential. The researchers compare their findings to the 1995 Kobe earthquake, which killed 6,400 people despite a calculated one percent probability—suggesting such disasters could occur unexpectedly. The study calls for developing new technology to monitor magma reservoirs beneath Earth's crust to better predict eruptions.

Toyota is preparing to make a cautious entry into the market for hydrogen-powered fuel cell vehicles, announcing that it will begin selling its first model, the Mirai, in Japan on Dec. 15, with sales in the United States and Europe scheduled for mid-2015. The launch will be small and expensive: Toyota plans to sell only a few hundred cars in the first year, with a target of 400 units in Japan and 300 elsewhere, and the Mirai will cost ¥6.7 million, or about $57,600, before taxes. The Mirai is a four-door, sporty-looking car that runs on compressed hydrogen stored in two tanks beneath the vehicle. Fuel cell cars emit no exhaust, although fossil fuels are still used to produce and pressurize the hydrogen. Toyota is entering a field that remains largely untested commercially, though Honda and Hyundai are also pursuing limited sales and leases of similar vehicles. A major obstacle is infrastructure. Only a few dozen hydrogen filling stations exist worldwide, making refueling difficult for early adopters. Governments are subsidizing station construction, but the future of the technology depends on both lower vehicle costs and a broader fueling network. Toyota executive Yoshikazu Tanaka said he expects it will take 10 to 20 years before Mirai sales reach the tens of thousands annually. He acknowledged the risk but said Toyota sees it as a challenge, comparing the situation to the early days of the Prius hybrid, which eventually became a major success after its 1997 launch. Toyota is trying to make the Mirai appealing by giving it a futuristic design and quick acceleration, especially from 40 to 70 kilometers per hour. In Japan, the government plans to offer a ¥2 million subsidy, which would reduce the effective price to ¥4.7 million. Still, sales will be limited to areas with fueling stations, mainly around Tokyo, Osaka, Nagoya, and parts of Kyushu. In the U.S., some stations have opened in California and more are planned in the Northeast, while Germany and the U.K. are among the European countries building or planning stations. Toyota expects early buyers to be wealthy consumers, as well as governments and companies seeking to reduce their carbon footprint. The Mirai can travel 650 to 700 kilometers on a tank, and Toyota believes hydrogen could eventually become cheaper to use than gasoline.

# Toyota Launches Hydrogen Fuel Cell Vehicle Toyota announced it will begin selling the Mirai, a hydrogen-powered fuel cell car, in Japan on December 15, with US and European launches planned for mid-2015. The world's largest automaker is taking its first step into the emerging market for emissions-free vehicles, though initial sales will be limited. The four-door Mirai will retail for ¥6.7 million ($57,600) before taxes in Japan, with a government subsidy reducing the effective price to ¥4.7 million. Toyota expects to sell 400 vehicles in Japan and 300 worldwide during the first year. Honda and Hyundai are also exploring fuel cell vehicle sales and leases. Fuel cell vehicles run on compressed hydrogen gas stored in tanks, emitting no exhaust. However, fossil fuels are used in hydrogen production and pressurization. The technology faces significant obstacles: high costs and minimal infrastructure. Worldwide, only a few dozen hydrogen filling stations exist, though governments are subsidizing construction of more. Sales will initially be limited to urban areas with fueling stations. In Japan, this includes regions around Tokyo, Osaka, Nagoya, and northern Kyushu. California has several stations, with plans for US Northeast expansion. Germany and the United Kingdom are developing infrastructure as well. Toyota's deputy chief engineer Yoshikazu Tanaka acknowledged the venture's risks but compared it to the company's successful Prius hybrid launch in 1997. He estimates fuel cell vehicles will reach tens of thousands in annual sales within 10 to 20 years. The infrastructure challenge resembles a "chicken and egg situation"—stations won't be built without vehicles, yet vehicles won't sell without stations. Initially, buyers will likely be affluent consumers seeking to reduce carbon footprints and environmentally-conscious governments and companies. The Mirai can travel 650 to 700 kilometers on two hydrogen tanks. While hydrogen fuel may initially be expensive, Toyota expects it to eventually become cheaper than gasoline as demand increases and competition grows.

The First Pacific Group is setting aside about P100 billion in capital spending for 2015 as it pushes further into infrastructure, utilities and services, though some tollway projects may be delayed because of unresolved tariff issues. Metro Pacific Investments Corp. (MPIC) chief finance officer David J. Nicol said the group will invest P96.6 billion next year, about P12 billion more than its 2014 budget. The largest item is the P36 billion capital program of Philippine Long Distance and Telephone Co. Maynilad Water Services, MPIC’s water unit, will spend P17.5 billion, while Manila Electric Co. will allocate P14.7 billion. Other planned spending includes about P9 billion for the Light Rail Transit Line 1 expansion, P1 billion for MPIC’s new sugar business, P2.3 billion for its hospitals group, and about P5.9 billion from Philex Mining Corp. Metro Pacific Tollways Corp. plans to spend P10.3 billion in 2015 to expand existing tollway operations, but president Ramoncito Fernandez said the figure is only tentative because the company has not been allowed to raise tariffs to secure fair returns. He said the firm will honor its commitments, but will not begin new ones until the tariff issue becomes clearer. MPTC is considering P30 billion to P40 billion in tollroad expansion, and Fernandez said delayed tariff approvals could affect plans and cause about P3.4 billion in lost revenue from 2012 to 2015. Meralco president Oscar Reyes said much of its capex will go to boosting distribution capacity and strengthening facilities against climate change. MPIC president Jose Ma. K. Lim said the group aims to double hospital capacity to about 5,400 beds within five years, at a cost of roughly P10 billion.

# First Pacific Group Sets P100B Capital Expenditure for 2015 First Pacific Group announced approximately P100 billion in capital expenditures for 2015, with Metro Pacific Investments Corporation (MPIC) allocating P96.6 billion—P12 billion more than 2014's budget. The company plans aggressive expansion across infrastructure, utilities, and services sectors. The largest allocation, P36 billion, goes to Philippine Long Distance and Telephone Company, followed by water subsidiary Maynilad Water Services (P17.5 billion) and Manila Electric Company (P14.7 billion). Other investments include P9 billion for Light Rail Transit Line 1 expansion, P5.9 billion for Philex Mining, P2.3 billion for hospitals, and P1 billion for sugar business operations. President Ramoncito Fernandez indicated their P30-40 billion tollroad expansion depends on resolving tariff adjustment issues with the government. He warned that further delays could impact expansion plans and noted projected revenue losses of P3.4 billion from 2012-2015 due to tariff approval delays. Việt Nam’s frozen IPO market is making it harder for the stock market to attract foreign capital, especially because the market remains heavily concentrated in banking stocks and lacks new large listings. After a strong IPO wave in 2017–19, when major names such as Petrolimex, Vinhomes, Vincom Retail, Techcombank, VPBank, Bình Sơn Refining and Petrochemical, and PV Power came to market, IPO activity has stalled for the past four years. A Deloitte Việt Nam report cited in the article said that in 2022 there were only eight successful IPOs in Việt Nam, raising a total of US$71 billion. By comparison, Thailand recorded 42 IPOs raising $3.6 billion, while Indonesia had 59 IPOs raising $2.3 billion. Since the COVID-19 pandemic, some new opportunities have emerged through the transfer of listings to the HCM City Stock Exchange (HOSE), including Đức Giang Chemicals, Việt Nam Rubber Corporation, Becamex, and Viettel Construction. However, these stocks generally had low free-float liquidity and were not attractive to foreign investors. Unlike the strong market conditions in 2018, recent IPOs have often failed to draw cash inflows and many have fallen sharply after listing. One major reason for the stagnant IPO market is the slow equitisation of state-owned enterprises. Large SOEs such as Agribank, VNPT, MobiFone, Vinataba, Vinachem, and HUD still have no clear completion dates for their equitisation plans. Nguyễn Duy Linh, general director of VPBank Securities, said valuation problems have caused SOE IPOs to remain stuck, creating a bottleneck for foreign indirect investment flows. Linh said foreign portfolio investors are likely to become more selective as US interest-rate cuts begin and emerging markets recover, and Việt Nam could benefit if it offers a compelling investment story. He argued that upgrading the market’s status, strengthening IPO activity, and accelerating divestment from SOEs in 2024–25 would help attract foreign capital. He also stressed that inflows depend on the quality of economic growth, stock quality, transparency, and whether companies meet investment criteria. Dragon Capital Việt Nam chairman Dominic Scriven said the market should not depend only on SOE IPOs. He urged greater promotion of private-sector listings, arguing that more diversified stocks would help foreign investors build portfolios. He noted that banking and real estate stocks dominate the market, limiting investment choices. Banking stocks alone account for nearly 40 per cent of HOSE’s capitalization, with Vietcombank and BIDV together making up 15 per cent. There are 14 banking stocks in the VN30 basket, and 16 of the 41 companies with market capitalisation above US$1 billion are banks. The article said several large private firms have planned IPOs in recent years, including Hưng Thịnh Land, CP Việt Nam, VSIP, Giao Hàng Tiết Kiệm, Bách Hoá Xanh, and Thaco. Việt Nam is currently classified as a frontier market by FTSE Russell and MSCI, though FTSE Russell placed it on a watch list in September 2023 for possible upgrade to secondary emerging market status.

# Vietnam's Frozen IPO Market Challenges Foreign Investment Attraction Vietnam's securities market faces significant challenges in attracting foreign capital due to a prolonged freeze in initial public offerings (IPOs) from new market entrants. After a robust period from 2017-2019 featuring major IPOs from companies like Vinhomes, Techcombank, and VPBank, the market has stagnated for four years. The disparity is striking: Vietnam recorded only eight successful IPOs in 2022, raising $71 billion, compared to Thailand's 42 IPOs ($3.6 billion) and Indonesia's 59 IPOs ($2.3 billion). While some companies have switched listings to Ho Chi Minh City Stock Exchange since the pandemic, these stocks typically feature low liquidity and limited appeal to foreign investors. Several factors contribute to this frozen market. Delayed equitization of state-owned enterprises (SOEs)—including Agribank, VNPT, MobiFone, and others—has created a bottleneck. Asset valuation problems have particularly hindered SOE IPOs, limiting foreign indirect investment flows. Additionally, recent IPOs have underperformed, with many stocks declining significantly after launch. The current market structure presents another obstacle: Vietnam's stock market is heavily dominated by banking and real estate stocks. Banks account for nearly 40 percent of Ho Chi Minh City Stock Exchange's capitalization, with Vietcombank and BIDV alone representing 15 percent. Banking stocks comprise 14 of the 30 companies in the VN30 index, and 16 of 41 companies valued above $1 billion are banks. This lack of diversity makes portfolio development difficult for foreign investors and funds. Industry experts emphasize that private sector IPOs offer a solution. Dragon Capital's chairman Dominic Scriven argues that relying solely on SOE IPOs is insufficient. Instead, promoting private enterprise listings would provide the stock diversity necessary to attract foreign capital. Multiple private companies—including Hung Thinh Land, CP Vietnam, VSIP, and Giao Hang Tiet Kiem—have announced billion-dollar IPO plans. VPBank Securities' general director Nguyen Duy Linh notes that with anticipated US Federal Reserve rate cuts and emerging market recovery, Vietnam could attract foreign investors if it improves market fundamentals. He recommends strengthening IPO activity, SOE capital divestment, and upgrading market status during 2024-2025. Currently classified as a "frontier market" by FTSE Russell and MSCI, Vietnam was placed on a watch list in September 2023 for possible reclassification to secondary emerging market status. Achieving this upgrade, combined with increased private sector IPOs and improved market transparency, could unlock significant foreign investment opportunities for Vietnam's securities market.

France said a global climate agreement must not undermine individual countries’ economic growth, as Paris tries to secure India’s backing ahead of the U.N. climate summit due in December. Speaking in New Delhi on Thursday, French Foreign Minister Laurent Fabius said any deal would fail if countries believed it would harm their development prospects. He stressed that the agreement must recognize each nation’s right to develop and said he understood “the constraints of India” as it pursues economic growth. India, the world’s third-largest greenhouse gas emitter, is seen as a key player in the talks because it often speaks for developing countries. It has long resisted binding emissions targets, arguing that rich nations should bear most of the burden and that strict limits could slow its economy. Instead, India has focused on expanding renewable energy and improving efficiency while still relying heavily on coal to meet rising energy demand. At the same event, India’s environment minister, Prakash Javadekar, said the country would build 100,000 megawatts of solar capacity by 2020, which he said would be 33 times its current level and two years ahead of an earlier target. Fabius said countries are expected to submit national emissions plans by an informal March 31 deadline to form the basis of the Paris deal. He also called for greater public and private financing for the U.N. green climate fund, saying that cutting emissions would require sustainable development support. The fund has raised more than $10 billion so far, but Fabius said annual financing must reach $100 billion by 2020.

# Summary France's foreign minister Laurent Fabius visited New Delhi to secure India's support for a global climate agreement planned for the December Paris summit. Fabius emphasized that any international deal must recognize each country's right to economic development, warning that nations believing the agreement would harm their growth prospects would reject it. India, the world's third-largest greenhouse gas emitter, plays a crucial role in climate negotiations as the voice of developing nations. Fabius acknowledged India's economic constraints and growth aspirations during discussions with Prime Minister Narendra Modi. Countries are expected to submit national emission-reduction plans by March 31 to form the basis of the Paris agreement. India has historically resisted binding emissions targets, arguing that wealthy nations should bear greater responsibility for emissions reductions. Instead, India has committed to expanding renewable energy and improving energy efficiency while continuing significant coal consumption to meet growing energy demands. India's environment minister announced an ambitious plan to build 100,000 MW of solar power capacity by 2020—33 times current levels and two years ahead of schedule. Fabius also called for increased public and private funding for the Green Climate Fund, a UN initiative helping developing nations address climate change. He noted the fund's initial capitalization reached $10 billion but emphasized the need for $100 billion annually starting in 2020 to achieve meaningful emissions reductions.
