Jordan and Japan issued a joint communique following King Abdullah II’s visit to Tokyo from November 18 to 21, 2014, during which he met Prime Minister Shinzo Abe on November 20. The statement marked the 60th anniversary of diplomatic relations between the two countries and reaffirmed their commitment to deepen longstanding ties, including the historical friendship between the Japanese Imperial Family and the Jordanian Royal Family. Both sides said they aimed to further develop their strategic relationship and continue working together for peace and stability. On bilateral issues, Abe thanked Jordan for supporting Japan’s bid for permanent membership on the UN Security Council and praised Jordan’s role as a non-permanent member representing the Asia-Pacific group. He also commended Jordan’s humanitarian support for Syrian refugees. Japan announced new aid for Jordan, including a grant of 2.238 billion yen for the rehabilitation and expansion of water networks in Balqa Governorate and 200 million yen in non-project grant aid for Japanese small and medium-sized enterprise products. King Abdullah thanked Japan for its assistance to Jordan, including a 12 billion yen Development Policy Loan provided in March 2014, and for Japan’s support for Syrian refugees and host countries, which had exceeded US$400 million. Jordan requested another Development Policy Loan for 2015. Abe said Japan would continue supporting Jordan, in coordination with the international community, given the difficult fiscal pressures caused by regional instability and the influx of refugees. Both sides also urged broader international help for Syrian refugees and host countries, describing the crisis as the worst humanitarian emergency in modern history. The two leaders discussed expanding high-level exchanges, strengthening policy consultations, and broadening defense ties through more visits between defense officials. They also highlighted cultural cooperation, with King Abdullah thanking Japan for grant aid to build the Petra Museum, due to open in 2016. Finally, he praised Japanese expertise in nuclear and renewable energy and encouraged greater Japanese business activity in Jordan.

# Summary: Jordan-Japan Joint Communique King Abdullah II of Jordan visited Japan from November 18-21, 2014, meeting with Prime Minister Shinzo Abe on November 20. The visit commemorated the 60th anniversary of diplomatic relations between the two nations, with both sides reaffirming their commitment to strengthening bilateral ties and promoting regional peace and stability. **Bilateral Relations and Support:** Prime Minister Abe expressed gratitude for Jordan's support of Japan's permanent UN Security Council membership and appreciated Jordan's representation of the Asia-Pacific group as a non-permanent Security Council member. Japan announced significant financial assistance to Jordan, including 2.238 billion Yen in Grant Aid for water network rehabilitation in Balqa Governorate and 200 million Yen in non-project grant aid for Japanese small and medium enterprises' products. **Refugee Crisis:** Both nations emphasized the humanitarian crisis created by Syrian refugees, with Japan acknowledging Jordan's humanitarian assistance efforts. Japan has provided over $400 million in support to Syrian refugees and host countries. Prime Minister Abe committed to continuing Japan's assistance to Jordan, recognizing the strain on the country's infrastructure, services, and employment from the refugee influx. Both leaders called on the international community to increase aid. **Cultural and Defense Cooperation:** The nations agreed to expand high-level exchanges and strengthen policy consultations between foreign ministers. Defense relations will be enhanced through increased visits between Japanese and Jordanian military officials. Japan provided 686.2 million Yen for constructing the Petra Museum, scheduled for 2016 inauguration. King Abdullah expressed interest in Japanese expertise in nuclear and renewable energy, encouraging Japanese corporate investment in Jordan.

France’s defense minister, Sébastien Lecornu, visited Kyiv on Wednesday to reaffirm French military support for Ukraine and discuss further assistance as the war with Russia continues. Lecornu traveled to the Ukrainian capital after a stop in Poland, where he announced a deal to sell Poland two French-made military satellites. In Kyiv, he laid a wreath at a monument honoring Ukrainians killed defending their country and was due to meet President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Defense Minister Oleksiy Reznikov, and senior army officials. France has generally spoken less loudly than the United States and Britain about its role in supporting Ukraine, but it has steadily supplied weapons since Russia’s invasion on Feb. 24. Paris also hosted two aid conferences for Ukraine this month. Still, many Ukrainians remain skeptical of France’s approach because President Emmanuel Macron has tried to keep communication open with Russian President Vladimir Putin and has repeatedly called for a negotiated settlement. Before the visit, Lecornu tweeted that France’s support for Ukraine had been “constant.” The trip came a week after Zelenskyy visited the United States and amid a battlefield situation that has changed little in recent weeks. Fighting remains concentrated in eastern Ukraine. Russian forces are trying to seize all of the Donbas by focusing on Bakhmut in Donetsk province, while Ukrainian forces are counterattacking near Kreminna in neighboring Luhansk province in an effort to regain territory and potentially split Russian forces. France has sent Ukraine a significant portion of its Caesar artillery systems, along with anti-tank missiles, Crotale air-defense batteries and rocket launchers. It is also training about 2,000 Ukrainian soldiers in France. Macron said last week that more weapons would be sent in early 2023. The war has also prompted new escalation from Moscow. On Tuesday, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov accused the United States and NATO of prolonging the conflict to weaken Russia. Also Tuesday, President Vladimir Putin signed a decree banning oil exports to countries that support the $60-per-barrel price cap imposed by the European Union and Group of Seven. The ban begins in February and will run through July, though the cap is above recent Russian oil prices, making its impact uncertain. Russia’s invasion, now 10 months old, has killed tens of thousands and displaced millions. Russian strikes on energy infrastructure have left many Ukrainians without heat and electricity. Recent shelling wounded at least eight civilians, including three in Bakhmut, and hit a maternity hospital in Kherson, damaging nearby buildings but reportedly injuring no one. The British Defense Ministry said Russia has likely reinforced positions near Kreminna to hold a strategically important line against Ukraine’s counteroffensive. Ukraine has said it wants a peace conference by the end of February, but major differences remain over any settlement.

The British Defense Ministry reported that Russia has reinforced positions near Kreminna under pressure from Ukrainian counteroffensives and will likely prioritize holding this logistically important area. Ukraine's foreign minister expressed hope for a peace conference by February's end, though negotiations remain complicated. 2022 was defined by war, political upheaval, social unrest and extreme weather across the world. The year began with Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine on February 24, the biggest attack in Europe since World War II. Millions of Ukrainians fled their homes as Russian forces advanced. The West responded with sweeping sanctions on Moscow and major military and financial support for Kyiv. Russia failed to seize the capital, Kyiv, or overthrow President Volodymyr Zelensky’s government. Instead, its troops captured much of Ukraine’s Black Sea coast, including Mariupol, which was devastated after a three-month siege. In April, Russian forces were accused of killing civilians in Bucha, near Kyiv. By September, Ukrainian troops had regained territory in the northeast and south, prompting Putin to hastily annex four partially occupied Ukrainian regions in a move condemned by the United Nations as illegal. In November, Russian troops withdrew from Kherson after eight months of occupation. By year’s end, Russia was pounding Ukraine’s energy infrastructure, causing widespread blackouts as winter approached. Zelensky’s first overseas trip since the invasion came in December, when he visited Washington to seek long-term U.S. support. Britain endured a turbulent political year. Boris Johnson was forced to resign after a series of scandals, and Liz Truss replaced him only to become the shortest-serving British prime minister ever, lasting just 44 days before quitting after a disastrous mini-budget. Rishi Sunak then became the country’s fifth Conservative prime minister in six years. The year was also marked by the death of Queen Elizabeth II at age 96, ending the reign of Britain’s longest-serving monarch. In the United States, the Supreme Court shocked the world in June by overturning Roe v. Wade, the 1973 decision that had guaranteed a constitutional right to abortion nationwide. The ruling returned abortion policy to the states, and Republican-led bans followed in 16 states, affecting 26.5 million women. The issue became a major factor in the November midterm elections, where voters in several states backed candidates who supported abortion access. China saw Xi Jinping secure a historic third term in November, cementing his authority as leader of the world’s second-largest economy. But public frustration grew over the government’s strict zero-Covid policy, with protests erupting in Beijing, Shanghai, Guangzhou, Wuhan, Urumqi and other cities. Some demonstrators even called for Xi to step down. At the same time, China sharply increased military pressure on Taiwan, sending more warplanes into the island’s air defence zone and holding its largest exercises in decades. In December, Beijing began easing zero-Covid restrictions, ending large-scale lockdowns and allowing some infected people to isolate at home, while also announcing that quarantine for overseas arrivals would be scrapped in the new year. Climate change drove record heat and destructive weather. Europe experienced its hottest summer on record, and Britain recorded temperatures above 40 degrees Celsius for the first time. Record temperatures also hit parts of the Arctic, Antarctic, China and the United States. In poorer countries, flooding in Pakistan, severe floods in Nigeria and drought in Somalia brought devastation and famine risk. At the COP27 climate summit in Egypt, wealthy countries agreed to create a “loss and damage” fund to help compensate poorer nations for climate harms. The war in Ukraine also triggered a global energy crisis, with gas and electricity prices surging. Britain’s energy bills doubled over the year. Rising prices contributed to Sri Lanka’s economic collapse and cost-of-living crisis, which forced President Gotabaya Rajapaksa to flee the country in August. Inflation rose sharply worldwide, leading central banks to raise interest rates aggressively and fueling fears of another debt crisis. Politically, the far right advanced in Europe. Italy elected Giorgia Meloni, its most right-wing leader since World War II. The Sweden Democrats emerged as key winners in Sweden, helping bring conservatives to power. In France, gains by the far right and hard left stripped President Emmanuel Macron of his parliamentary majority. By contrast, the political right weakened in Latin America: Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva returned to power in Brazil by defeating Jair Bolsonaro, while left-wing leaders also won in Colombia and Honduras. Iran was shaken by the death of 22-year-old Mahsa Amini after her arrest over alleged violations of the Islamic dress code. Her death sparked the country’s biggest protests in years, with women and girls publicly removing headscarves in defiance of the clerical establishment. Authorities responded harshly, sentencing protesters to death. Mohsen Shekari was executed on December 8, followed four days later by Majidreza Rahnavard. Iran Human Rights said at least 469 people had been killed in the protests by December 19, while the UN reported at least 14,000 arrests. On the field, however, the tournament delivered drama, culminating in Lionel Messi leading Argentina to a penalty-shootout victory over France in one of the greatest finals ever played.

# 2022: A Year of Living Dangerously 2022 was marked by geopolitical upheaval, climate crises, and significant political shifts across the globe. The year's defining moment came on February 24 when Russian President Vladimir Putin launched Europe's largest invasion since World War II, sending troops into Ukraine. The invasion triggered millions of Ukrainians to flee, prompted unprecedented Western sanctions against Moscow, and led to billions in aid flowing to Ukraine. Despite initial objectives, Russian forces failed to capture Kyiv or overthrow President Volodymyr Zelensky, though they secured much of Ukraine's Black Sea coastline, including the devastated port of Mariupol after a brutal three-month siege. The conflict escalated throughout the year. In April, Russian forces were accused of massacring civilians in the Kyiv suburb of Bucha. By September, Ukrainian forces began reclaiming territory, prompting Putin to hastily annex four partially-controlled regions—a move the UN declared illegal. In November, Russian forces retreated from southern Kherson after eight months of occupation. As winter approached, relentless Russian strikes damaged Ukraine's energy infrastructure, causing widespread power cuts. In December, Zelensky traveled to Washington to address Congress, appealing for sustained American support. In Britain, political turmoil saw three prime ministers. Queen Elizabeth II, the nation's longest-reigning monarch, died at 96. Boris Johnson resigned following numerous scandals, succeeded by Liz Truss, whose catastrophic 44-day tenure made her the shortest-serving British leader. Rishi Sunak took office in October as the fifth Conservative prime minister in six years. The United States experienced seismic judicial change when the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade in June, eliminating constitutional abortion protections and returning the issue to individual states. Republicans implemented abortion bans in 16 states affecting 26.5 million women. The decision significantly influenced November's midterms, with voters supporting abortion-access candidates in several states. China's President Xi Jinping secured an unprecedented third term in November but faced growing public discontent with the zero-Covid policy. Hundreds protested in major cities, with some calling for Xi's resignation. Beijing subsequently announced policy relaxations in December. Meanwhile, Chinese military exercises around Taiwan intensified regional tensions. Extreme weather dominated 2022. Europe experienced its hottest summer on record, with temperatures exceeding 40°C in Britain for the first time. Pakistan suffered catastrophic flooding, Nigeria experienced its worst floods in a decade, and drought-threatened Somalia faced famine conditions. At the UN climate summit in Egypt, wealthy nations agreed to establish a "loss and damage" fund compensating developing countries for climate impacts. The Ukraine crisis triggered an unprecedented energy crisis, with gas and electricity costs soaring globally. Britain's energy bills doubled yearly. This contributed to Sri Lanka's severe cost-of-living crisis, forcing President Gotabaya Rajapaksa to flee in August. Global inflation prompted aggressive interest rate increases, raising recession fears. Politically, Europe's far-right surged. Italy elected its most right-wing post-fascist leader since World War II in Giorgia Meloni, while Sweden's anti-immigration Sweden Democrats achieved significant gains. France's Macron lost his parliamentary majority as both far-right and hard-left parties gained ground. Conversely, Latin America trended leftward, with Brazil's Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva ousting far-right incumbent Jair Bolsonaro, while left-wing leaders ascended in Colombia and Honduras. Iran erupted in protests following 22-year-old Mahsa Amini's death after arrest for dress code violations. Women defiantly removed headscarves in unprecedented challenges to clerical authority. Authorities responded brutally, executing protesters and arresting thousands. By December 19, security forces had killed at least 469 people. Ethiopia's government and Tigrayan rebels reached a landmark peace agreement, allowing humanitarian aid to resume to the devastated northern region. The World Cup in Qatar proved controversial due to human rights concerns and migrant worker deaths, though alcohol bans and boycotts faded as play began. Lionel Messi finally achieved his elusive World Cup triumph, leading Argentina to victory against France in an epic penalty shootout.

Iran hosted more than 3.1 million foreign tourists in the first half of 2024, but arrivals remained well below pre-pandemic levels, according to updated UN Tourism data. The country received 3,129,449 international visitors between January and June, a 37% decline from 2019. Monthly arrivals fluctuated throughout the period: 494,696 in January, 506,313 in February, 396,772 in March, 497,469 in April, 443,282 in May, and a peak of 790,917 in June. The figures suggest an improvement over 2023, when fewer than 3 million tourists entered Iran in the first seven months, though the data does not identify the visitors’ nationalities. Iran’s Ministry of Cultural Heritage, Tourism, and Handicrafts said the totals also include Iranian expatriates traveling for tourism purposes. Officials say attracting more foreign visitors is vital for economic recovery and for developing the tourism sector. The drop in arrivals reflects the lingering effects of the COVID-19 pandemic. While global tourism was expected to recover to 98% of pre-pandemic levels by the end of 2024, Iran has continued to lag behind. Globally, international travel reached about 1.1 billion people in the first nine months of 2024. The Middle East led growth with a 29% increase over 2019, and Europe and Africa have already surpassed pre-pandemic levels, while Asia-Pacific is recovering more slowly. Iran is now trying to revive its tourism industry. Last month, Tourism Minister Seyyed Reza Salehi-Amiri said his ministry was working with the Foreign Ministry to remove barriers to international tourism. He also called for correcting what he described as false global narratives about Iran, proposed “tourist cards” to ease currency exchange for visitors, and urged the Central Bank to help. With more than 2,700 tourism projects underway, the government is also being pressed to reduce bureaucracy, improve infrastructure, expand international partnerships, and promote Iran’s heritage sites, including 28 UNESCO World Heritage listings.

# Iran's Tourism Recovery Remains Sluggish Iran welcomed over 3.1 million foreign tourists in the first half of 2024, representing a modest recovery but still falling 37% short of pre-pandemic 2019 levels, according to UN Tourism data. Monthly arrivals ranged from 396,772 in March to 790,917 in June, showing improvement compared to 2023 when fewer than 3 million visitors arrived in seven months. The figures include Iranian expatriates visiting for tourism purposes, though visitor nationality data was not specified. The persistent decline reflects lingering pandemic impacts, as global tourism was projected to reach 98% of pre-pandemic levels by end-2024. Notably, the Middle East experienced 29% growth compared to 2019, while Europe and Africa have surpassed pre-pandemic levels. Asia-Pacific, like Iran, continues gradual recovery. To revitalize the sector, Iran's Minister of Cultural Heritage, Tourism, and Handicrafts, Seyyed Reza Salehi-Amiri, announced initiatives to remove obstacles to international tourism. He emphasized correcting global perceptions damaged by "false narratives" in certain media outlets and promoting Iran's cultural heritage to younger generations. Key measures include issuing "tourist cards" to facilitate currency exchange and streamlining bureaucratic processes for over 2,700 tourism projects under development. The minister called for enhanced infrastructure and investor incentives while stressing the importance of global partnerships and targeted advertising. Iran possesses significant tourism assets, including 28 UNESCO World Heritage sites encompassing bazaars, museums, mosques, historical bridges, bathhouses, and madrasas, which officials hope will attract international visitors and generate economic benefits.

The Makkah Mashaer Metro (MMM), built by China Railway Construction Corporation (CRCC), has said that 70 percent of its locally recruited workforce is Saudi. CRCC’s operational data show a rapid rise in local hiring: about 1,000 staff in 2010, 2,000 in 2011, 4,000 in 2012, 5,500 in 2013, and 6,000 in 2014, in line with requirements from the Saudi Ministry of Municipal and Rural Affairs. However, the article notes that fewer than 50 Saudi employees hold senior or supervisory posts, such as third-party interface managers, deputy station managers, station masters, assistant station masters, and station control room agents. Deputy Stations Manager Taher Baghdadi said there are 50 Saudis in senior positions overseeing nine stations, while about 6,000 people are employed during Haj, including some contract workers trained specifically for the season. The SR6.6 billion project has been operating for five years and has carried 26 million pilgrims, moving them from Arafat to Mina in 13 minutes and from Arafat to Muzdalifah in seven minutes. Baghdadi said the metro has had no accidents since opening in November 2010 and has dramatically cut travel time between Arafat and Muzdalifah from six to eight hours to less than 20 minutes, describing it as a historic transportation achievement. Because the metro is a government service intended only for pilgrims, ticket revenue covers only about one-third of operating costs. The Ministry of Haj coordinates with Haj companies and sells around 400,000 tickets to them. Baghdadi said staff do not stop pilgrims who insist on boarding, except during peak hours when tickets are more strictly required. Arab News was given exclusive access to CRCC facilities, control rooms, stations, and senior executives, including Saudi officials.

# Makkah Mashaer Metro: Saudi Employment and Operations The Makkah Mashaer Metro (MMM), developed by China Railway Construction Corporation (CRCC), has achieved significant Saudi employment levels, with 70 percent of its locally recruited staff being Saudi nationals. The workforce has grown substantially since operations began, increasing from approximately 1,000 employees in 2010 to 6,000 by 2014, doubling annually through 2012 before continuing to expand to meet Saudi Ministry of Municipal and Rural Affairs requirements. However, fewer than 50 Saudi employees hold high-level supervisory positions, such as station managers and control room operators. According to Deputy Stations Manager Taher Baghdadi, these 50 Saudis supervise nine stations, with many employees hired seasonally during the Hajj pilgrimage after receiving extensive training. Since opening in November 2010, the SR6.6 billion project has operated safely without accidents, transporting 26 million pilgrims over five years. The metro dramatically reduces travel times: the Arafat-to-Mina journey takes just 13 minutes, while Arafat-to-Muzdalifah takes seven minutes—previously requiring six to eight hours. The metro operates exclusively for pilgrims, with ticket prices covering only one-third of operational costs. The Ministry of Haj sells approximately 400,000 tickets to operating agencies, though staff permit pilgrims to board without tickets outside peak hours, treating them as "guests of the country." Arab News received exclusive access to CRCC headquarters and operational control areas, becoming the only Saudi media organization granted firsthand information about the metro's operations.

Iran’s UN envoy Amir Saeid Iravani said Israel’s “clear confession” that it assassinated Hamas leader Ismail Haniyeh in Tehran justified Iran’s missile attack on Israel on October 1. In a letter to the UN Security Council, Iravani responded to remarks by Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz, who for the first time publicly admitted Israel killed Haniyeh on Iranian soil, according to Tasnim and Xinhua. Katz made the admission while warning Yemen’s Houthi rebels that Israel would destroy their infrastructure and “decapitate” their leaders. Haniyeh was killed in Tehran on July 31, shortly after Israeli strikes killed senior Hezbollah commander Fuad Shukr in Beirut. Hamas later named Yahya Sinwar as its military chief, but he was also killed in an Israeli operation in southern Gaza on October 16. Israel also killed Hezbollah chief Hassan Nasrallah, Katz said. At the commemoration event, Katz said Israel would strike Houthi strategic infrastructure in Hodeidah and Sanaa just as it had killed Haniyeh, Sinwar and Nasrallah. The article also notes Katz claimed Israel helped overthrow Bashar al-Assad’s government in Syria. Iran’s October 1 missile attack triggered Israeli warnings, with the IDF saying civilians were in bomb shelters as rockets were fired from Iran.

# Summary Iran's UN envoy Amir Saeid Iravani stated that Israel's admission to assassinating Hamas leader Ismail Haniyeh in Tehran justifies Iran's October 1 military attack against Israel. Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz publicly confirmed for the first time on Monday that Israel killed Haniyeh in Tehran. Katz also warned Houthi rebels from Yemen, stating Israel would destroy their infrastructure and eliminate their leaders, just as it did to Haniyeh, military chief Yahya Sinwar, and Hezbollah leader Hassan Nasrallah. Haniyeh was killed in July, hours after Israeli airstrikes killed Hezbollah commander Fuad Shukr in Lebanon. Sinwar was subsequently killed in October during an Israeli operation in Gaza, while Nasrallah was also eliminated by Israel. Katz additionally acknowledged Israel's involvement in overthrowing Syria's Bashar al-Assad regime. Iran responded to these killings by launching a missile attack on Israel on October 1, prompting Israeli civilians to seek shelter as rockets were fired at the country.

Iran and Tajikistan discussed expanding cooperation in tourism, culture, and handicrafts during a meeting Tuesday in Tehran between Iran’s Minister of Cultural Heritage, Tourism, and Handicrafts, Seyyed Reza Salehi-Amiri, and Tajikistan’s Ambassador to Iran, Nizomiddin Zohidi. Salehi-Amiri stressed the deep cultural, historical, religious, and linguistic ties between the two countries and said Iran gives priority to relations with neighboring states, including Tajikistan. He said a planned visit by Iran’s president to Tajikistan could open a “new chapter” in bilateral relations. The minister proposed producing multilingual films and other high-quality cultural works to highlight shared civilizational values, as well as organizing joint cultural events, research projects, restoration efforts, and cultural days featuring artists and intellectuals from both nations. He also said tourism between Iran and Tajikistan remains low despite their closeness, and called for better planning and agreements to make travel easier. He noted that Tehran alone has more than 3,000 travel agencies that could help promote tourism. Salehi-Amiri added that Iran wants to strengthen direct flights, mentioning Kish Island’s readiness to develop a health tourism city that could attract Tajik visitors via direct flights from Dushanbe. Zohidi welcomed the proposals and said closer ties are supported by the two nations’ common heritage. He said Tajikistan is eager to expand tourism links, including a possible direct Dushanbe-Shiraz flight. He also proposed removing visa requirements entirely. Salehi-Amiri said he would raise that idea with the government. The two sides further discussed joint handicrafts training and promotion.

# Summary Iran's Minister of Cultural Heritage, Tourism, and Handicrafts, Seyyed Reza Salehi-Amiri, met with Tajikistan's Ambassador to Iran, Nizomiddin Zohidi, to discuss strengthening bilateral relations in tourism and cultural cooperation. The minister emphasized shared cultural and historical bonds between the nations and proposed several collaborative initiatives. These include producing high-quality multilingual films showcasing their shared civilizational values, organizing joint cultural events featuring intellectuals and artists, and conducting collaborative research and restoration projects. Salehi-Amiri highlighted significant untapped tourism potential, noting that despite cultural and linguistic proximity, travel between the countries remains modest. He suggested better planning and agreements to facilitate tourism, mentioning Tehran's 3,000 travel agencies ready to promote travel. He also proposed strengthening direct flights between the countries and developing Kish Island as a health tourism destination. The Iranian government prioritizes relations with neighboring countries, with an anticipated presidential visit to Tajikistan potentially marking a new chapter in bilateral relations. Ambassador Zohidi welcomed the proposals, expressing enthusiasm for expanding tourism infrastructure and establishing a direct Dushanbe-Shiraz flight. He proposed eliminating visa requirements between the nations, which Salehi-Amiri promised to advocate for at the governmental level. Both officials also discussed increasing cooperation in handicrafts through joint training programs and promotion of artisanal traditions.

Iran’s Cultural Heritage, Tourism, and Handicrafts Directorate in Fars province has announced plans for a new 6-kilometer tourist route linking three major archaeological sites: Persepolis, Naqsh-e Rostam, and Naqsh-e Rajab. Mohammad Sabet-Eqlidi, the directorate’s head, said the route will be designed with three separate lanes for pedestrians, cyclists, and vehicles, creating a more integrated visitor experience. He described the project as part of a wider effort to improve Iran’s cultural tourism infrastructure and make its historic landmarks more accessible to domestic and international travelers. The route centers on Persepolis, the ceremonial capital of the Achaemenid Empire and a UNESCO World Heritage site built about 2,500 years ago. Known for its palaces, columns, and carved reliefs, Persepolis includes major structures such as the Apadana Palace and the Throne Hall. Nearby is Naqsh-e Rostam, a cliffside necropolis containing the tombs of four Achaemenid kings, widely believed to include Darius I, Xerxes I, Artaxerxes I, and Darius II. The site also features seven Sassanian bas-reliefs and the Ka’beh-ye Zardusht, an ancient square structure thought to date to the early 6th century BC. The third site, Naqsh-e Rajab, lies about three kilometers from Persepolis and preserves early Sassanid carvings. Though less famous, it offers important scenes of royal ceremonies and victories, complementing the historical significance of the neighboring monuments.

# Iran Plans New Tourist Pathway Connecting Ancient Sites Iran's Cultural Heritage, Tourism, and Handicrafts Directorate in Fars province has announced plans for a new 6-kilometer tourist pathway linking three major archaeological sites: Persepolis, Naqsh-e Rostam, and Naqsh-e Rajab. According to the directorate's director Mohammad Sabet-Eqlidi, the route will feature three separate lanes for pedestrians, cyclists, and vehicles, creating an integrated experience for visitors exploring these ancient landmarks. The initiative aims to enhance Iran's cultural tourism infrastructure for both domestic and international travelers. **Persepolis**, the ceremonial capital of the Achaemenid Empire built 2,500 years ago, is a UNESCO World Heritage site featuring grandiose palaces, towering columns, and intricate bas-reliefs depicting royal ceremonies and dignitaries. Key highlights include the Apadana Palace and Throne Hall. **Naqsh-e Rostam**, located near Persepolis, is a necropolis containing tombs of four Achaemenid kings carved into cliffs, accompanied by seven striking Sassanian bas-reliefs. It also features the Ka'beh-ye Zardusht, a sixth-century BC structure intertwining Achaemenid and Sassanian legacies. **Naqsh-e Rajab**, situated three kilometers from Persepolis, preserves early Sassanid petroglyphs and features elaborate stone carvings depicting regal ceremonies and triumphs, offering valuable insight into Sassanid history and art.

Israel intensified its military response to Hamas on Tuesday, pounding downtown Gaza City and widening its call-up of reservists to 360,000, according to Israeli media. The escalation came four days after Hamas fighters crossed into Israel, triggering gunbattles inside Israeli towns and marking the first such fighting there in decades. Israel’s military said Tuesday morning that it had effectively regained control of its southern region and the border area after the surprise assault. Officials vowed severe retaliation against Hamas, while Gaza residents faced worsening conditions and increasingly had nowhere to flee as strikes spread across the territory. The war’s death toll had reached at least 1,600 on both sides, with Israeli officials warning the number could rise significantly. Israel also said Hamas and other militant groups in Gaza were holding more than 150 soldiers and civilians hostage. The conflict appeared likely to broaden further. A major unanswered question was whether Israel would launch a ground offensive into Gaza, a narrow coastal enclave home to 2.3 million people and governed by Hamas since 2007. The article framed the situation as a rapidly escalating war with no clear end in sight, as Israel prepared for a larger military campaign and Hamas continued to hold hostages.

# Israel Escalates Military Response to Hamas Attack Four days after Hamas militants launched a major attack on Israel, killing residents and taking hostages, Israel has intensified its military response with extensive bombing campaigns in Gaza City and a significant expansion of its armed forces. Israel's military reported regaining effective control of its southern regions and border areas on Tuesday. The country mobilized 360,000 reservists, signaling preparation for a prolonged conflict. Israeli officials vowed punishing retaliation against Hamas, the militant group governing Gaza since 2007. The conflict has already resulted in at least 1,600 deaths on both sides, with potential for significantly higher casualties. Hamas and allied militant groups are reportedly holding more than 150 Israeli soldiers and civilians hostage. The bombardment of downtown Gaza City has left many Palestinian residents with limited options for safety in the densely populated territory of 2.3 million people. Israeli officials have not ruled out launching a ground offensive into Gaza, which could further escalate the conflict. Military analysts expect the conflict to intensify significantly in the coming days. The situation remains fluid, with ongoing operations and potential for expanded military action as Israel pursues its stated objective of retaliation against Hamas.

Alberta’s carbon levy rose on New Year’s Day, increasing from $20 to $30 per tonne, but the province’s NDP government says the higher tax is part of a broader strategy that is helping strengthen the economy. Deputy premier Sarah Hoffman argued that the carbon price introduced on January 1, 2017, was linked to the province’s improving economic outlook and to federal approval of major pipeline projects. She said Ottawa made clear that its support for the Trans Mountain expansion from Alberta to the B.C. coast was tied in part to Alberta’s climate policy and its pricing of carbon. Hoffman said the new rate would add about 2.5 cents per litre at the gas pumps. She acknowledged that 2017 was still a difficult year for Albertans but said the province had “definitely rounded the corner,” pointing to “tens of thousands of new jobs.” She also said the government had designed the policy to protect ordinary Albertans through rebates, while using revenue from the levy to support green infrastructure, energy efficiency, and renewable energy. According to the province, a couple with two children earning up to $95,000 annually will receive a rebate of $540. The Opposition United Conservative Party sharply criticized the tax. Leader Jason Kenney posted a video on New Year’s Eve showing him filling up his truck before the increase, repeating a stunt he used the previous year. Kenney said the carbon tax had already destroyed thousands of good-paying jobs, driven entrepreneurs out of business, and raised costs for families. In a statement Monday, he called it “all economic pain with no environmental gain.” Kenney also argued that the tax had not helped pipeline development, noting that since the NDP unveiled its climate plan, the Northern Gateway project was vetoed by the federal government, Keystone XL was rejected by former U.S. president Barack Obama, and Energy East was effectively killed by the National Energy Board. He added that the NDP government in British Columbia was also opposing Trans Mountain. In his view, no government or interest group had changed from opposing pipelines to supporting them because of Alberta’s carbon tax. Another long-running criticism from the opposition is that the NDP did not mention a carbon tax during the 2015 election campaign. Kenney said the party had told voters it would not impose such a tax, while UCP spokeswoman Annie Dormuth called it a “lie by omission.” Hoffman rejected that claim, saying the NDP had been clear it would take environmental leadership and was still developing the details of its plan during the campaign. She accused Kenney of misrepresenting reality and of wanting to portray himself as the only person capable of steering Alberta’s economy.

# Alberta's Carbon Tax Increase Sparks Economic Debate Alberta's carbon tax increased from $20 to $30 per tonne on January 1, resulting in an additional 2.5 cents per litre at gas pumps. The NDP government argues this increase will benefit the economy, while the opposition strongly disagrees. Deputy Premier Sarah Hoffman contends there is a direct link between Alberta's carbon pricing policy and pipeline approvals. She emphasized that the federal government explicitly stated its approval of the Trans Mountain pipeline expansion from Alberta to British Columbia was contingent on the province implementing carbon pricing and other climate policies. Hoffman noted that 2017 was difficult economically but that Alberta has "rounded the corner" with "tens of thousands of new jobs" created. The government plans to reinvest carbon tax revenue into green infrastructure, energy efficiency programs, and renewable energy. Additionally, low- and middle-income Albertans will receive increased rebates to offset the tax's impact. For example, a couple with two children earning up to $95,000 annually will receive a $540 rebate. Hoffman acknowledged the tax increases costs for residents but argued the government has protected ordinary Albertans while establishing an important environmental leadership profile necessary for long-term economic strength. Opposition Leader Jason Kenney of the United Conservative Party vehemently opposes the tax, calling it "all economic pain with no environmental gain." He posted videos on social media showing himself filling up his truck before the increase, similar to his actions the previous year. Kenney argues the tax has destroyed thousands of jobs, bankrupted entrepreneurs, and made life more expensive for families. Kenney also disputed claims that the carbon tax facilitated pipeline approvals. He noted that since the NDP announced its climate plan, the Prime Minister vetoed Northern Gateway, former President Obama vetoed Keystone XL, the National Energy Board effectively killed Energy East, and British Columbia's NDP government has opposed Trans Mountain. A contentious point involves the 2015 election campaign. Kenney claims the NDP promised not to introduce a carbon tax, calling the implementation "a lie by omission." Hoffman countered that the NDP clearly campaigned on environmental leadership and was developing a climate plan's details. The debate reflects fundamental disagreements about whether carbon pricing stimulates economic growth through environmental credibility and pipeline approvals or damages the economy through increased costs and job losses.

The pandemic triggered a huge surge in bicycle demand, leaving bike shops in Indianapolis and elsewhere overwhelmed with backorders. Jimmy Revard, owner of The Bike Line in Broad Ripple, said 2020 became the busiest year in his 41 years in business. At first, he and his staff feared the pandemic would hurt sales, but instead customers flooded in, eager for outdoor exercise and a safe way to get out of the house. Revard said the shop sold out of bikes, and many of the bicycles now arriving are already sold before they reach the store. He said the shop has never had to back-order bikes before, but now it routinely has more than 1,000 on order at once. Some customers are waiting as long as a year for delivery. One customer, Sherry Owensby, ordered six bikes in June and was still waiting for three of them, which were intended as Christmas gifts. She said she was shocked by the delay and expected them much sooner. Revard said the shortages are caused by pandemic-related disruptions at multiple stages, including parts production, manufacturing, distribution, and shipping. While customers are frustrated, he said the store is doing its best to manage the backlog.

# Bicycle Boom Creates Shop Backlog During Pandemic During 2020, bicycle shops experienced unprecedented demand despite pandemic-related challenges. The Bike Line in Indianapolis, owned by Jimmy Revard for 41 years, had its busiest year ever after initially fearing business closure. As COVID-19 emerged in spring, people sought safe outdoor activities, driving continuous bike purchases. The shop sold out of inventory and accumulated over 1,000 bikes on back-order at any given time. Most bikes now sell before arriving at the store. Customers face extended wait times, with some waiting up to one year for their purchases. Customer Sherry Owensby ordered six bikes in June but remained waiting for three by late 2020, having expected delivery by summer. Revard attributed delays to pandemic-related supply chain disruptions affecting parts manufacturers, distributors, and shipping across multiple layers. Despite frustrations from customers and staff, Owensby praised the shop's communication and customer service during the shortage. The bicycle industry's unexpected boom contrasts sharply with many struggling sectors, as people prioritize outdoor exercise and fresh air during lockdowns.

Canada’s 150th anniversary year was marked by weather setbacks, political tensions and occasional criticism, but Heritage Minister Melanie Joly says it was ultimately a success because it gave Canadians memorable shared experiences and helped advance reconciliation. Joly acknowledged the difficulties openly: torrential rain flooded Parliament Hill during the Canada Day celebration, and bitter cold forced the cancellation of many New Year’s Eve events, including planned musical performances on Parliament Hill. Still, she dismissed the weather as a minor part of the larger story. “We’re Canadians,” she said, adding that Canadians are used to dealing with Mother Nature. In her view, the real legacy of Canada 150 was the sense of gratitude and participation it generated across the country. The federal government spent heavily to make that happen. Heritage Canada budgeted $200 million for Canada 150 events and programming, while another $300 million went toward infrastructure projects such as upgrades to community ice rinks and public parks. Parks Canada spent about $76 million to allow free entry to national parks for the year. Joly said the aim was to create “moments Canadians will remember.” By the government’s account, the year reached a huge audience. Heritage Canada said 87 per cent of Canadians took part in at least one Canada 150 event, representing about 31 million participants. There were 5,800 events nationwide. Some drew massive crowds: La Machine, the French theatrical production featuring giant robotic creatures, attracted 750,000 people to downtown Ottawa over four days, far above expectations. Free access to national parks and historic sites brought in a record 27.3 million visitors. Other major events included the Walk for Reconciliation in Vancouver, tall ships celebrations in several provinces, and the largest National Acadian Day ever held. The celebrations also appeared to boost tourism. The New York Times and Lonely Planet both ranked Canada the top place to visit in 2017, and domestic and international tourism rose 3.1 per cent. Overseas visitors increased 7.1 per cent and American tourists 2.7 per cent, making it Canada’s strongest year ever for international tourism. Ottawa, which hosted many of the central events, saw overnight visits rise 5.5 per cent, the highest increase among Canadian cities. Kazakhstan, a major producer of natural resources, is under increasing pressure to adopt low-carbon technologies as global carbon regulations tighten. Because key parts of its economy—aviation, transport, metallurgy, and cement production—are highly emission-intensive, the country must speed up its decarbonization efforts to remain competitive. A World Economic Forum report, *High-Emission Sectors: Challenges and Opportunities for Low-Carbon Technology Providers*, says major structural changes in energy, transport, and industry will be needed. In aviation, the report identifies Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) as one of the most practical near-term solutions. SAF, made from renewable inputs such as vegetable oils, used cooking oil, agricultural waste, and even carbon dioxide, can cut life-cycle emissions by up to 80% compared with fossil fuels. Because it can be used in existing engines, it is considered a feasible option for airports. For Kazakhstan, which wants to become a regional aviation hub, investment in SAF production and storage could reduce emissions and potentially supply neighboring markets. But this would require substantial infrastructure spending, likely with support from development banks and private investors. The transport and logistics sector, which connects Europe and Asia, is another major emissions source. The report recommends electric and hydrogen-powered trucks, along with new charging and hydrogen refueling infrastructure. Expanding rail freight, which emits far less carbon than road transport, would also help. The government could further encourage adoption through tax breaks and subsidies for electric or hybrid vehicles, while aligning with international green corridor initiatives to attract foreign investment. Metallurgy and cement production are among Kazakhstan’s most carbon-intensive industries. The report says modernization, renewable energy use, and carbon capture and storage (CCS) are essential. Kazakhstan’s geology is well suited for underground CO2 storage, creating opportunities for CCS infrastructure at industrial sites. Partnerships with international technology companies, energy-efficient factory upgrades, and special economic zones with tax incentives could help attract investment and support the transition.

St. Petersburg Mayor Rick Kriseman ended his first year in office with a setback when the city council rejected a proposed agreement on Dec. 18 that would have allowed the Tampa Bay Rays to explore alternative stadium sites in Hillsborough and Pinellas counties. Kriseman had spent a year negotiating the deal and criticized the council for choosing a workshop instead of making a decision, saying, “That’s not leadership.” He then declined media interviews the next day and left for the holidays. Before that vote, Kriseman told FOX 13 News that his administration had made strong progress on several long-standing issues. Early in his term, he reopened the exterior areas of the St. Pete Pier to the public, and by year’s end eight design concepts had been submitted for the pier’s renovation or replacement. He also helped resolve a years-old dispute over emergency medical services funding with a newly appointed county administrator. Other accomplishments included ending red light cameras in a way that could allow their return, hiring a new police chief to restart community policing, raising the minimum wage for city workers to $10.10 an hour, and granting six weeks of paid leave to parents of newborns. Looking ahead to 2015, Kriseman said his main focus will be economic development in south St. Petersburg, where he wants more restaurants, grocery stores, and retail options. Replacing the city’s aging police station also remains a priority, while the stadium and Pier issues are expected to stay prominent.

On December 18th, the city council rejected a stadium agreement Kriseman had spent a year negotiating, which would have allowed the Tampa Bay Rays to explore alternative stadium sites in surrounding counties. The mayor expressed frustration with council members for scheduling a workshop instead of making a decision, calling it a lack of leadership. Despite this setback, Kriseman achieved several notable successes during his first year. He reopened the St. Pete Pier to the public and received eight design concepts for its renovation or replacement. He also resolved a long-standing dispute over emergency medical services funding, removed red light cameras while preserving options for their return, hired a new police chief to revitalize community policing, raised the minimum wage for city workers to $10.10 per hour, and implemented six weeks of paid parental leave. Private gardeners, horticultural associations, and government bodies in Kazakhstan are working to revive the aport apple, a once-famous national variety known for its deep red color, strong aroma, and distinctive flavor. The fruit was long associated with the mountainous areas around Almaty, where it once grew abundantly, but urban expansion has sharply reduced the number of orchards and put the variety at risk. According to Saule Kazybayeva, deputy chair of the Kazakh Scientific Research Institute of Fruit Growing and Viticulture, aport apples were historically transported by traders to Siberia and southern regions through railroad stations. The variety spread widely across southeastern Kazakhstan, especially in the Zailiyskiy Alatau foothills, helped by the Vernyi Horticultural School and by gardener Moiseyev’s large private orchard, which reportedly supplied more than 100,000 seedlings each year. Kazybayeva said the decline began as large-scale construction and commercial development replaced orchards with housing, business, and infrastructure projects, particularly in Almaty. She also noted that modern apple varieties such as Golden Delicious and Red Delicious became more popular because they are easier to transport, store longer, and are more suitable for mass production. By contrast, aport apples require special care and have a short shelf life, making them less profitable commercially. Despite these challenges, local growers continue to cultivate the apple. Roman Safarov, president of the Almaty Aport Producers Association, said the fruit is notable for its size: on average, aport apples weigh 250 to 400 grams, though some can reach up to 900 grams. He described the variety as having a unique aroma and a characteristic crunch when bitten. Safarov emphasized that the tree is difficult to grow, requiring specialized knowledge and patience, since it does not begin bearing fruit until its eighth or ninth year. Experts say high-quality aport apples can only be grown in orchards located at elevations between 850 and 1,250 meters above sea level, which limits suitable land mainly to the foothills of Almaty and the Almaty Region. The regional agriculture department told Kazinform that orchard areas have shrunk from 1,071 hectares to 446 hectares because the trees are vulnerable to disease. Safarov said producers currently receive no dedicated state subsidies, although the issue is being considered by the government. He argued that long-term, low-interest loans and insurance would be more useful than the current subsidy system, which covers only intensive horticulture. In response, the Ministry of Agriculture and the National Agrarian Scientific and Educational Center have launched a 2024-2028 program to restore the aport variety. The plan involves private investors and nursery farms and aims to green 110 hectares. The ministry said aport trees currently cover about 2,500 hectares in the Almaty and Zhetisu regions, with around 416,000 trees in total, and about 230 hectares in Almaty city itself. In 2024, seeds from Sivers apple trees were collected, and in 2025 planting is set to begin on a 10-hectare plot at the Talgar Kazakh Research Institute of Fruit and Vegetable Growing, which will serve as a mother and cuttings orchard for future nursery expansion.

# Gardeners Lead Revival of Kazakhstan's Legendary Aport Apple Private gardeners and agricultural associations in Kazakhstan are undertaking efforts to revive the aport apple, a nationally cherished fruit characterized by its rich red color and distinctive flavor. Once abundant in the mountainous regions near Almaty, these legendary apples now face extinction due to urbanization and changing agricultural practices. ## Historical Significance and Decline The aport apple has deep historical roots in southeastern Kazakhstan, particularly in the Zailiyskiy Alatau mountains. Traders once transported these unique apples across Siberia and southern regions via railroad stations. The variety spread rapidly thanks to the Vernyi Horticultural School and private orchards that supplied over 100,000 seedlings annually. However, large-scale construction and commercial development have decimated the once-flourishing aport gardens. According to Saule Kazybayeva, deputy chair of the Kazakh Scientific Research Institute of Fruit Growing and Viticulture, urbanization in major cities like Almaty transformed landscapes where orchards once thrived. Additionally, more productive and commercially viable apple varieties, such as Golden Delicious and Red Delicious, replaced aport cultivation because they are easier to transport and have longer shelf lives. In contrast, aport apples require special care and cannot be stored long-term, making commercial cultivation less profitable. ## Unique Characteristics and Growing Challenges Roman Safarov, president of the Almaty Aport Producers Association, highlights the aport apple's remarkable qualities. These apples typically weigh between 250 and 400 grams, with some reaching 900 grams. They possess a distinctive pleasant aroma and characteristic crunchy sound when bitten. However, cultivating aport apples presents significant challenges. The trees are delicate and demanding, requiring specialized knowledge and care. Most critically, aport trees only begin bearing fruit in their eighth or ninth year, discouraging most gardeners. High-quality aport apples can only be grown at altitudes between 850 and 1,250 meters above sea level, limiting suitable growing areas to Almaty's foothills and the Almaty Region. The situation has worsened recently, with aport orchard areas shrinking from 1,071 to 446 hectares due to disease vulnerability and declining apple quality. ## Government Support and Revival Program Currently, aport producers receive no specific state subsidies, though the Ministry of Agriculture is exploring amendments to subsidy rules. Safarov advocates for long-term loans at minimal interest rates and insurance options rather than direct subsidies. The Kazakh Ministry of Agriculture and the National Agrarian Scientific and Educational Center have developed a 2024-2028 program to revive aport cultivation, aiming to green 110 hectares. Currently, approximately 2,500 hectares of aport trees exist across Almaty and Zhetisu regions, comprising around 416,000 trees. The initiative's first phase collected seeds from Sivers apple trees, with seedling planting scheduled to begin in 2025 at the Talgar Kazakh Research Institute on a ten-hectare mother orchard, which will support expansion among private gardeners.

The United Nations said that 85 former FARC guerrillas have been killed in Colombia since the peace accord was signed two years ago, including 14 murders between September 26 and December 26 of this year alone. In his quarterly report on the UN mission in Colombia, Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said the killings were attributed by a state special investigation unit to illegal armed groups and criminal organizations. The UN said many of the cases were linked to the Gulf Clan drug-trafficking network, FARC dissidents, the ELN guerrilla group, and remnants of the disbanded EPL rebels. Guterres urged President Ivan Duque’s government to strengthen security plans for ex-combatants. He also expressed deep concern about violence against social leaders and human rights defenders, noting that the UN had verified 163 of 454 reported murders since the peace deal. Most of those killings occurred in areas abandoned by former FARC fighters and where the state has little presence. Colombia’s ombudsman estimates 423 activists were killed from 2016 through November. Although about 7,000 FARC members laid down their arms and the group became a political party, around 1,600 dissidents remain active. Colombia’s decades-long conflict has involved guerrillas, paramilitaries, drug traffickers and state forces, causing massive death and displacement.

Ecopetrol Group said its board of directors approved a 2023 general organic investment plan worth an estimated COP 25.3 trillion to COP 29.8 trillion, with individual projects to be reviewed later depending on their size and importance. The company said the plan is designed to advance the four pillars of its 2040 strategy and support Colombia’s energy transition, including investments in hydrogen, renewable power, transmission, energy efficiency, gas, and other low-emission initiatives. A central feature of the plan is the company’s commitment to energy transition projects. Ecopetrol said between COP 5.9 trillion and COP 6.8 trillion will go toward renewable self-generation, hydrogen, transmission and roads, and energy efficiency. Another COP 3.6 trillion to COP 4.1 trillion is set aside for gas self-sufficiency. A larger portion, between COP 15.8 trillion and COP 18.9 trillion, will be used to maintain energy security, financial sustainability, and support the country’s trade balance. The company said renewable self-generation, hydrogen, energy efficiency, carbon capture, and ISA’s transmission and roads business together account for about 23% of the 2023 plan. Within that transition spending, Ecopetrol said about COP 4.1 trillion over the next three years, including roughly COP 315 billion in 2023, will allow it to add 900 megawatts of renewable energy capacity, produce more than 50,000 tons of low-carbon hydrogen, reduce about 400,000 tons of CO2e emissions, and advance carbon capture and storage studies. Gas remains another important focus. Ecopetrol said gas investments in 2023 will range from COP 3.6 trillion to COP 4.1 trillion and should support production of 174,000 to 177,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day, equivalent to about 800 million cubic feet of natural gas plus white products. The goal is to maintain current supply and increase it through exploration, with 12 wells planned for 2023, mainly in Piedemonte, Caribbean Offshore, and Northern Colombia. The company said gas is being positioned as a transition fuel and as part of efforts to strengthen social gas and energy communities. ISA, Ecopetrol’s transmission and roads business, plans to invest about COP 6.3 trillion in 2023 and COP 19.8 trillion over the next three years. Around COP 5.4 trillion is expected to go toward building 9,657 kilometers of energy transmission lines by 2025, including 6,227 kilometers for non-conventional renewable energy transmission. Ecopetrol said this would consolidate ISA as a Latin American leader in energy transmission. Geographically, about 66% of the total 2023 investment is expected to be made in Colombia, while 34% will go to international operations. Those overseas investments are intended to secure long-term resources for the energy transition and continue low-emission investments, mainly in electricity transmission. The international spending will be concentrated in the United States, especially the Permian basin, as well as Brazil, Peru, and Chile. In upstream operations, the plan is expected to support organic production of 720,000 to 725,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day in 2023, with 76% oil and 24% gas and white products. Ecopetrol said it will focus on enhanced recovery technologies to maximize existing reserves and offset natural field decline. Between 2023 and 2025, the company expects to drill about 1,600 development wells, including 574 in 2023, and 25 exploratory wells in basins such as Llanos Orientales, Mid-Magdalena Valley, Piedemonte, and Caribbean Offshore. Midstream investments, equal to 5% of the plan, will emphasize infrastructure integrity and reliability through Cenit, Ocensa, ODC, and ODL, along with pipeline expansion to ensure domestic refined-product supply. Transport volumes are expected to exceed one million barrels per day. Downstream spending, representing 7% of the total, will focus on the Barrancabermeja and Cartagena refineries to improve reliability, availability, sustainability, fuel quality, and wastewater management. Combined refinery throughput is projected at 420,000 to 430,000 barrels per day. The company also set aside nearly COP 2.3 trillion for TESG-related value creation, including decarbonization, water management, fuel quality, and other initiatives. Social investment of COP 472 billion is planned for local development projects, such as road improvements, education, drinking water, and new gas connections. Another COP 405 billion will support science, technology, and innovation. Ecopetrol said the plan assumes self-funding, collection of receivables from Colombia’s Fuel Price Stabilization Fund, and low leverage. It expects a Brent oil price of USD 80 per barrel in 2023, ROACE above 10%, EBITDA margin above 40%, and transfers to the nation exceeding COP 40 trillion. President Felipe Bayón Pardo said the company’s strong 2022 results support the plan and that Ecopetrol will keep growing with the energy transition while creating value for society and shareholders.

Valparaiso marked Veterans Day with its annual ceremony at the Valparaiso Service Memorial, where residents, emergency responders and city leaders gathered to honor local service members and those killed in war. The memorial, located in a quiet corner of Foundation Meadows Park, is one of the city’s central places of remembrance and is used for ceremonies on both Veterans Day and Memorial Day. The memorial’s Duty and Sacrifice wall bears the names of 164 Valparaiso-area residents who died while serving in World War I, World War II, Korea, Vietnam and the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan. During Friday morning’s ceremony, all 164 names were read aloud. Mayor Matt Murphy said each name represented “a life, a family and a tremendous sacrifice,” and urged people to continue showing respect for veterans throughout the year, not only on Veterans Day. The memorial also includes a Charity wall, Hope wall and Friendship wall. Each of these stone slabs features quotes written by Valparaiso students. When the memorial was created in 2003, middle school students were asked to write essays about duty, sacrifice, charity, hope and friendship. Surrounding bricks are etched with the names of veterans, teachers, doctors, public safety officers, volunteers and neighbors, reinforcing the memorial’s broader message of community service. One of the ceremony’s speakers, Lenny Corso, said he honors those lost in combat every day. Corso, a Vietnam-era veteran who has lived in Valparaiso since the 1990s, said he lost four friends in Vietnam and described his involvement in veterans affairs as a way of honoring them. He enlisted in 1966 at age 20 and was recruited into the Army’s Green Beret Medic program after growing up in Logansport, Indiana. Corso described difficult memories from working in a burn center at Fort Sam Houston in Texas, where he treated soldiers injured by napalm. He explained how wounded troops were often evacuated by helicopter, stabilized in Japan and then brought to the United States for long-term care. He also said he lost two high school classmates, a Green Beret Medic classmate and his sergeant major during the war. In addition to remembering the dead and wounded, Corso emphasized the importance of recognizing veterans living with invisible injuries such as post-traumatic stress disorder. He said many young service members see traumatic things at ages 19 to 22 that most people never experience, and argued that society must do more to understand PTSD and help those affected. He pointed to statistics showing elevated PTSD, suicide and homelessness rates among veterans. Corso encouraged struggling veterans to seek help at the Adam Benjamin Jr. VA clinic in Crown Point or the Jesse Brown Medical Center in Chicago.

Haile Gebrselassie criticized the decision to hold the track and field world championships in Qatar, saying the heat made the marathon dangerously unsafe and could have caused deaths. Speaking to The Associated Press from Addis Ababa, the former marathon world-record holder called it “a mistake” to stage the event in Doha, especially the women’s marathon. The race began at midnight Saturday to avoid the worst heat, but humidity still made conditions feel like 105 degrees. Of the 68 women who started, 28 dropped out, 30 received medical checks, and one was briefly hospitalized. All three Ethiopian runners failed to finish, while Kenya’s Ruth Chepngetich won the race. Gebrselassie said the stadium events were manageable because they were held in the air-conditioned Khalifa International Stadium, but the marathon and race walks were exposed to the extreme weather. He argued the marathon should have been shortened or removed entirely. He also warned that poor experiences in such conditions could damage athletes’ morale. The men’s marathon was scheduled for Sunday, and other endurance events had already seen heavy attrition, including the 50-kilometer walks. The IAAF defended the Doha events, noting similar completion rates in past championships. Next year’s Olympic marathons in Tokyo are set for an early 6 a.m. start.

Paralympic swimmer Kat Swanepoel says her next major goal is the 2023 World Championships, as she continues building toward the Paris 2024 Paralympic Games. Eyewitness News spoke to the 35-year-old South African para-athlete about her journey, her achievements, and the challenges she has overcome while living with a severe degenerative condition. Swanepoel has primary progressive multiple sclerosis (PPMS), an autoimmune disease she developed in 2008 while in her fourth year studying occupational therapy. The condition attacks the central nervous system and has left her paralysed from the chest down, blind in one eye, and with little to no sensation or movement below her chest and through parts of her arms. She also experiences fatigue-related speech difficulties, and the disease has affected her brain, optic nerves and spinal cord. She has suffered a stroke, and seizures are not uncommon. Despite these setbacks, Swanepoel has remained deeply involved in sport. She said she has been active since childhood and was introduced to para-sport through her occupational therapy training. After becoming a full-time wheelchair user, she began playing wheelchair basketball about a year later, and later added wheelchair rugby. She has represented South Africa in both sports and earned her national colours through wheelchair basketball, making it the first of three sports in which she has competed at a high level. Swimming became her current focus shortly before the Covid-19 lockdown, when she started in December 2019. Swanepoel said the pandemic unexpectedly helped her career, because the postponement of the Paralympic Games gave her more time to qualify and prepare. Her recent results have been particularly strong. She represented South Africa at the Tokyo Paralympic Games and won medals as well as breaking African records at the World Para Swimming Championships in Madeira, Portugal, in June. Among her proudest moments, she listed wearing the green and gold for the first time in wheelchair basketball, singing the national anthem at her first world championships, being named best two-point player and rookie of the tournament at the Asia-Oceania Wheelchair Rugby Cup, and narrowly missing a bronze medal in the 50m backstroke final at Tokyo after taking 12 seconds off her personal best. Swanepoel credits much of her success to coach Theo Verster, as well as teammates, friends and family. Looking ahead, she says the 2023 World Championships are crucial because performances there will help South Africa earn competition slots for Paris 2024.

The Philippine men’s football team suffered a painful 1-1 draw against Vietnam on Wednesday, Dec. 18, at Rizal Memorial Stadium, leaving its hopes of reaching the ASEAN Mitsubishi Electric Cup knockout stage in jeopardy. The late goal denied the Philippines a chance to end a 12-year winless streak against Vietnam. The last Philippine victory over the Vietnamese came in November 2012, and the country’s most famous result in the rivalry remains the “Miracle in Hanoi,” when the Filipinos stunned Vietnam 2-0 in the 2010 AFF Championship. The draw meant the team came closer than it had in years to matching that historic upset on home soil. Goalkeeper Patrick Deyto said the team had defended well but was undone by one set piece. He noted that set pieces had become a major weakness, with three goals conceded from them in the tournament, and took responsibility for failing to secure the ball on the decisive corner after making two key saves in stoppage time. Despite the disappointment, Gayoso praised the team’s effort and resilience, saying everyone showed heart and worked hard. The Philippines had opened the tournament with draws against Myanmar and host Laos, and while the results have been frustrating, the performances have been stronger than earlier matches in which the team often trailed before rescuing late points. The Filipinos now travel to Solo City to face Indonesia on Dec. 21.

Loh Kean Yew’s rise to badminton stardom has been built on years of sacrifice, uncertainty and stubborn belief. In a recent interview in Bangkok, the 25-year-old Singaporean world No. 3 recalled how, at 18, he shocked his family by deciding to drop out of Republic Polytechnic to pursue badminton full time. He had no backup plan if the gamble failed, and the consequences became clear almost immediately. At the time, Singapore’s top men’s singles players were Derek Wong and Ryan Ng, and Loh had to compete in lower-tier tournaments where prize money was only in the hundreds of dollars. To support himself, he worked part-time as a coach while living on a modest allowance from the Singapore Badminton Association. The situation became even harder during his national service years, from 18 to 20, when he could not enter many competitions and had to use part of his $500 monthly allowance to help pay rent while living in Singapore with his brother, fellow national player Loh Kean Hean. His parents were in Penang, and he described those years as “rough.” Still, Loh says he never doubted his choice. After moving to Singapore at 13 and becoming a Singapore citizen in 2015, he was determined to make badminton his career. His resolve hardened further after winning bronze at the 2015 SEA Games. He wanted to commit fully without later regretting missed opportunities. Money, he said, was never his main motivation; improving as a player was. If he kept getting better, he believed the rest would follow. That attitude is what he now encourages in young athletes who hope to make it professionally. He says talent alone is not enough; one must also have belief, work hard and maintain the right mindset. The approach has paid off. Loh’s profile rose sharply after he became Singapore’s first badminton world champion in 2021, and his earnings have followed. After taking US$16,500 for finishing third in his group at the Badminton World Federation World Tour Finals on Friday, he ended the 2022 season with career-high prize money of more than US$71,582.50 before tax, up from US$60,550 in 2021. Even so, Loh is realistic about the financial realities of badminton. He notes that while his prize money is meaningful, it is small compared with what athletes in other sports earn. He points to football and tennis, saying badminton has room to grow commercially because the sport is fast and exciting. Top badminton players such as Viktor Axelsen can earn far more, while global stars in football and tennis make vastly larger sums. Loh is nevertheless grateful for the support he now receives. As a Sports Excellence Scholarship recipient, he gets backing from Sport Singapore, the Singapore National Olympic Council and the Singapore Badminton Association. His growing reputation has also brought endorsement roles with Seiko, HSBC, Li-Ning, Singapore Airlines and Grab. This has made travel and daily life easier; he no longer worries as much about food costs on tour, and he no longer has to choose the cheapest meal options as often as before. He still lives simply. He bought his first suit only recently, paying $300 for it to attend the Singapore Sports Awards in November, where he was named Sportsman of the Year and received $10,000. He says he does not spend much on branded clothing and still uses public transport or rides pillion to training at times. Although he hopes to own an apartment one day, he says that as a single 25-year-old he can only buy private property, which remains out of reach financially, so he continues saving. Those around him say fame has not changed him. National coach Kelvin Ho, who has coached Loh for a decade, describes him as the same hardworking, cheerful and respectful person, though more mature in handling pressure. Teammate Joel Koh says Loh remains humble and grateful, but is now even more focused and hungry to improve. Loh himself says that despite the extra commitments, the exhaustion and the pressure that come with success, he accepts them as part of his journey toward the top and his Olympic medal ambitions. He says he has grown in the past year, gained a broader perspective on life, and learned much — but insists, “I am still me.”

# Badminton Star Loh Kean Yew: From Struggle to Success Loh Kean Yew's journey to becoming Singapore's badminton champion was marked by sacrifice and unwavering determination. Still frugal, Loh considers spending $200 on two T-shirts extravagant and continues using public transport or riding pillion with his brother to training. ## Unchanged Character Despite his success, those closest to Loh report he remains unchanged. National coach Kelvin Ho, who has coached him for a decade, describes him as the "same boring guy"—maintaining a routine of eating, training, napping, and analyzing games. Three members of the Armed Forces of the Philippines’ Intelligence Service (ISAFP) were killed in an ambush in Basilan province on Monday evening, authorities said Tuesday. The Basilan Police Provincial Office said the attack happened around 6:25 p.m. in Barangay Baimbing, Lamitan City, about 15 kilometers from the city proper. The victims, based in Zamboanga City, were riding in a sport utility vehicle along the highway when unidentified gunmen opened fire. Their identities have not yet been confirmed. Police said the area has no cellular service, which delayed communication. Authorities are investigating to identify the attackers and determine the motive. Basilan was recently declared free of the Abu Sayyaf Group.

A group of gymnastics advocates has launched the Cebu Elite Gymnastics Club in Cebu City with the goal of developing the province’s next world-class gymnast, possibly even another Carlos Yulo. The club was founded by former national team member and national coach Joel Panugalinog, his wife Magie, and lawyer-sports advocate Jerome Abayon. They said the project was born from a long-held desire to return home and help build Cebu’s gymnastics program after years of working abroad, especially in Singapore, where they coached foreign athletes instead of local talent. At the club’s formal launching at the UP Cebu Graduate School on December 22, Magie Panugalinog said they had always hoped to retire from competition and move into coaching, but lacked opportunities to nurture Filipino gymnasts in their own province. Joel said it was painful to compete against Filipino gymnasts representing Singapore, and that experience motivated them to create a facility where Cebuano athletes could thrive. The club features a training center equipped with apparatuses that meet international standards and was built with an investment of nearly P3 million. Joel serves as head coach, Magie as administrative manager, and Abayon as club president. They are backed by other former Cebuano national team members who train children as young as 18 months old. National coach Allen Aldrin Castañeda, who attended the blessing, said he believes the club can produce athletes capable of reaching the national team. Since opening in August, the club has already won 169 medals in different competitions. It now has 92 members, including 10 scholar-athletes considered strong prospects for events such as the CVIRAA and Palarong Pambansa. The club serves children from 18 to 36 months old, ages 3 to 5, and ages 6 to 9. Its leaders said their aim goes beyond medals: they want to build future champions and raise Cebu’s profile in gymnastics, with hopes of eventually seeing a Cebuano athlete win Olympic gold.
