Vietnam’s pickleball boom has become both a sporting craze and a public nuisance, with the sharp pop-pop of paddles now echoing from before dawn until after midnight at newly built courts across Hanoi and other crowded cities. What began as a fast-rising pastime has turned into a source of frustration for many residents, who say the sport’s noise is disrupting sleep, work and daily life. Pickleball only took off in Vietnam about two years ago, later than in the United States and Canada, but its growth has been explosive. According to DUPR, a pickleball rating company, Vietnam is now the second-fastest-growing market in Asia after Malaysia. A regional professional circuit, PPA Tour Asia, says more than 16 million people in Vietnam have picked up a paddle, though that estimate is based on a survey of roughly 1,000 respondents. One earlier survey suggested that, per capita, more people in Vietnam had taken up pickleball than anywhere else in Asia. The sport’s rapid spread is most visible in Hanoi’s Long Bien district, now considered the capital’s pickleball center. State media says the district has more than 100 courts, up from 54 in less than a year. Clubs such as Pickleholic Club, Victory Pickleball and Pro Pickleball Vn sit within a five-minute walk of one another, with many more courts nearby. Across Hanoi, dozens of new courts have been built, often wedged into tight alleyways or placed beneath high-rise buildings, amplifying the sound for surrounding neighborhoods. That has sparked a wave of complaints. Residents say the noise is constant and unavoidable, especially in densely packed urban areas where one court can disturb thousands of people. Hoa Nguyen, 44, who lives with her family behind a multicourt complex on Hanoi’s northeastern outskirts, said the noise “drives me nuts” and that people play in the middle of the night. She said she had filed a complaint with local authorities. State media reports that most noise complaints filed through Hanoi’s iHanoi app are related to pickleball, and it has described the sport as an “acoustic hazard.” The problem is not limited to Hanoi. In Ho Chi Minh City, where there are an estimated 1,000 pickleball courts, workers and nearby residents are also struggling with the racket. Lam Thanh, 50, who manages a dormitory for workers near one of the courts, said the sound of paddles, cheering, shouting and joking is “extremely exhausting.” Another resident said the sound made it impossible to concentrate, describing it as deeply unpleasant. Beyond the paddle strikes themselves, complaints also include unruly crowds, honking horns and parking lots clogged by players and spectators. The article says the tension reflects both Vietnam’s enthusiasm for the sport and the pressures of rapid urban growth. The country’s cities have expanded quickly during years of economic boom, leaving little room between homes and sports facilities. In a nation where a nationwide noise ordinance is supposed to limit excessive late-night noise, residents say the rules are often not enforced at pickleball venues. Ho Chi Minh City already ranks among the loudest cities in Asia, according to the United Nations, and noise levels there are considered high enough to harm hearing. As frustration grows, pressure is mounting on authorities to respond. State media has begun publishing health warnings from doctors, with one report saying the constant bouncing of the pickleball can disturb sleep, trigger stress and increase cardiovascular risk. VTC News went so far as to say the sound is like “the ticking of a clock against the temples,” adding that many people are now “haunted” by it. Around the world, pickleball has already prompted protests and lawsuits over noise, but Vietnam’s case is especially intense because of how quickly the sport has spread into crowded urban neighborhoods. For some, it is a light, accessible game suitable for both children and adults. For others, it is an all-day and all-night acoustic battle that local authorities are struggling to contain.

Court-side noise frequently goes unchecked, leaving residents with limited recourse beyond filing complaints and petitions requesting restricted playing hours. The situation reflects a broader pattern observed globally, where pickleball's expansion has sparked outrage, protests, and legal action in various communities. Vietnam's unique circumstances—rapid urban growth driven by economic expansion combined with densely packed residential areas positioned near newly constructed courts—have intensified the conflict between the sport's enthusiasts and frustrated neighbors seeking peaceful living conditions.

At least 18 people, including six children, were injured in a Christmas Day accident in Carcar City, Cebu, after a multicab driver lost control of his vehicle around 4 p.m. on December 25, 2024. The multicab flipped and collided with another vehicle. The driver, identified as 40-year-old Ritchel Sergas Juanito of Bolinawan, Carcar City, is in police custody, while the injured passengers are confined in a hospital. The victims were relatives returning home from a beach outing in southern Cebu. Police identified the injured as Ernesto Villarin, Ginno Tulod, Ara Mae Villarin, Artemio Baclay Sr., Elvie Razaga, Reynaldo Coloyan Jr., Lyndon Canadalla, Joan Juanito, Romeo Baring, Rochelle Canayon, Vincent Patrick Razaga, Juanito, and six children aged one to 13. Investigators said Juanito admitted losing control of the multicab. Police are still investigating. Separately, a couple lost their 6-year-old daughter in another Christmas Day crash in Naga City, and the father later died in hospital on December 26.

# Summary On Christmas Day 2024, a multicab driver in Carcar City, Cebu lost control of his vehicle, causing it to flip and collide with another car at approximately 4 p.m. The accident injured 18 people, including six children, who were relatives returning from a beach outing. Driver Ritchel Sergas Juanito, 40, admitted to losing control and remains in police custody. All injured passengers were hospitalized. In a separate incident on the same day, a couple's 6-year-old daughter was killed when their motorcycle was struck by a sleepy driver's SUV in Naga City. The mother and father were injured; the father died from his injuries on December 26 while receiving hospital treatment. Police continue investigating both accidents.

Vermont skier Ryan Cochran-Siegle earned the first World Cup victory of his career with a surprise win in the super-G at Bormio, Italy, on the Stelvio course. The 28-year-old from Vermont beat Austria’s Vincent Kriechmayr by 0.79 seconds in his 101st World Cup start, giving the United States its first World Cup super-G win since Bode Miller in 2006. The margin was the largest in a super-G race in nearly five years. Cochran-Siegle said the result shocked him, adding that he had no expectations for the demanding course and simply tried to ski it as well as he could. His victory also appears to be the first by a Vermont-born skier on the World Cup circuit since his aunt, Marilyn Cochran, won a giant slalom in 1973. The win came less than two weeks after Cochran-Siegle’s previous career-best result, a runner-up finish at Val Gardena, another Italian resort. He also competed at the 2018 Pyeongchang Olympics, finishing 11th in giant slalom. A 2012 world junior champion in downhill and combined, he missed time after a knee injury in 2013 and returned to the circuit in 2016. A graduate of Mount Abraham Union High School, Cochran-Siegle is set to race again in the downhill, where he was the fastest in training.

# Summary Ryan Cochran-Siegle, a Vermont native and son of 1972 Olympic gold medalist Barbara Ann Cochran, won his first World Cup event in the super-G on Italy's iconic Stelvio course. Finishing 0.79 seconds ahead of Austria's Vincent Kriechmayr, Cochran-Siegle achieved the largest victory margin in the super-G discipline in nearly five years and became the first American to win a World Cup super-G since Bode Miller in 2006. The 28-year-old's triumph comes just two weeks after his first career World Cup podium finish at Val Gardena, marking his 101st World Cup start. His victory is believed to be the first by a Vermont-born skier on the World Cup circuit since his aunt, Marilyn Cochran, won a GS race in 1973. A 2018 Olympian who competed in the giant slalom, Cochran-Siegle has overcome significant challenges, including a knee injury from a 2013 crash that sidelined him until 2016. The 2012 World Junior champion in downhill and combined expressed surprise at his success, noting he didn't hold expectations for the race. He was scheduled to compete in the downhill event Wednesday morning.

Tuscan Holdings (NASDAQ:THCB) is rising sharply even though there is no new company-specific announcement, with the stock up nearly 20% on Wednesday as investors continue to focus on its planned merger with battery maker Microvast. Tuscan Holdings originally began as a cannabis-focused special purpose acquisition company, but in late November it pivoted toward electric vehicles and announced plans to take Microvast public. Microvast develops battery systems for electric vehicles, but unlike many EV companies that target passenger cars, it specializes in city transit applications such as buses and taxis. The company says it aims to produce high-power batteries with fast-charging capabilities and lower costs. Simone Biles was named The Associated Press Female Athlete of the Year for a third time after a remarkable comeback to gymnastics that restored her to the top of the sport and underscored how much her life has changed since the turbulence of the Tokyo Olympics. Biles’ return began in late July at a suburban Chicago arena, where she entered her first competition in two years with understandable nerves. She later admitted she had doubts too, but by the end of that meet she felt at home again. Over the following months, she went on to win the U.S. national championship in August and the world championship in October, adding to her already unmatched resume. By December, those achievements earned her AP’s top female athlete honor once again. Her 2023 comeback included a record eighth U.S. national title and a sixth world all-around gold medal. In AP voting by sports media professionals, she finished ahead of Iowa basketball star Caitlin Clark and Aitana Bonmati, the Ballon d’Or winner and a member of Spain’s World Cup-winning soccer team. Biles became only the sixth woman to win the AP award three times, having previously received it in 2016 and 2019. The article traces how different this return was from the end of the 2020 Tokyo Olympics, when Biles withdrew from several finals because of “the twisties,” a dangerous mental block that affects spatial awareness in the air. She later won bronze on balance beam, but the broader story of those Games centered on her decision to prioritize her safety and mental health. While many praised her for that choice, she also faced criticism online. Afterward, she stepped away from competition for two years, describing herself as being in a “protective shell” while she worked more deeply in therapy and considered whether and how she might return. Even after deciding to come back, Biles said self-doubt still surfaced. This time, though, she handled it differently. Rather than letting anxiety control her, she accepted it, took a breath and focused on performing. She said she did far better than she expected, which reflected both her resilience and the support system around her. The article also emphasizes how much Biles’ life has evolved since her first AP awards. In 2016, she was still a teenager fresh off her breakout performance at the Rio Olympics, living with her parents and centered almost entirely on gymnastics. By 2019, she was already the dominant figure in the sport, but her identity was still closely tied to competition. Now, at 26, she has made a conscious effort to keep gymnastics from defining her entirely. She married Green Bay Packers safety Jonathan Owens in the spring, spends time attending Packers games when possible, works with sponsors and corporate partners, and is involved in building a house with her husband. She says this shift has been both natural and intentional. In the past, she says, every bad practice or mistake felt like the end of the world. Now she approaches the sport more calmly, saying that if a day goes badly, she can simply return tomorrow and start again. Biles said she did not fully commit to the comeback until late spring, when coach Cecile Landi suggested over margaritas that it might be time to show the world what she had been working on. Biles agreed, though she still worried she might not be ready. But those around her believed in her long before she fully believed in herself. Once she returned, she quickly reminded the sport why she is considered the greatest gymnast of all time. Her routines were not only successful but astonishingly difficult, with sharp execution and high-risk skills across all four events. On vault, she became the first woman to perform a Yurchenko double-pike in international competition, a move now named among five elements in her honor in the sport’s code of points. She does not need to attempt such difficulty to win, but she does it anyway. Looking ahead, Biles is expected to have a chance for a third Olympics in Paris, though she avoids discussing it directly. The article closes by highlighting how her priorities have broadened: when she reflected on her best moment of 2023, she chose a photo from her wedding reception dancing with Owens rather than one from a podium. For Biles, gymnastics remains central, but it is no longer the only thing that defines her life.

Right-wing media and gender-critical commentators used the episode to vilify Van Leuven, portraying her as someone who had unfairly taken opportunities from women and did not deserve her victories. The article notes, however, that Van Leuven later lost that tournament 4-0 to Aildeen de Graaf. The story emphasizes that darts has been part of Van Leuven’s life since childhood. She says her family was “built on the back of darts.” Her parents met in a pub while playing darts, her father played on a local team, and her grandfather on her mother’s side also played. As a child, she often went with her parents to their local venue and watched her father play. By age 14, she had begun entering competitions herself, moving beyond simply “throwing three pointy things at a board.” Darts became a central part of family life, though she says her sister was never much interested in it. Van Leuven also speaks candidly about a difficult childhood. She says she was bullied relentlessly at school and struggled to find her place. One of the few places where she felt safe was her grandmother’s house. She visited often, helped with chores, cooked with her grandmother, and spent time talking with her. Her grandmother, she says, listened without judgment and offered a home close to where she lived but far enough away from the bullying. That time also helped shape her love of cooking. Today, Van Leuven works as a chef de partie at a local restaurant. She says the job is rewarding but stressful, especially when customers request changes to dishes late in the shift, forcing staff to work overtime. She particularly dislikes end-of-night orders for extras such as cappuccinos, hot chocolate with whipped cream, fresh pastries, and cookies after the kitchen has already been struggling to keep up. At the same time, she enjoys making desserts and experimenting with pastries and sweets. Recently, she has also taken up bouldering, or indoor free-form climbing. She joined a queer climbing group after finding an online WhatsApp community and eventually found the courage to attend. She describes the group as safe and welcoming, a place where people can either talk or keep climbing until they run out of energy. The sport appealed to her because it involves problem-solving, much like darts, but what kept her coming back was the community. She says they have seen her in difficult moments and helped her keep going. Van Leuven says confidence remains a challenge, and spaces like the bouldering group help her feel comfortable not only as a trans woman but as a human being. She says the signs of her gender identity were present from an early age, including playing dress-up with her sister and ending up in dresses and makeup. A Dutch documentary about trans people was the first time she felt truly recognized in others’ stories. She acted on those feelings at 17, and 12 years later says she has learned a great deal by accepting herself. Looking ahead, she hopes to give back by creating a safe space or community center for trans and queer people. In her downtime, she watches TV and reads, currently working through Grey’s Anatomy and a book called The Kitchen, along with autobiographies. The article closes by stressing that Van Leuven is being used as a target in a broader political battle, but that she is simply a person trying to live authentically. Her message is straightforward: she wants respect for who she is and insists that she is allowed to be herself.

He said the camp would help athletes practice relay baton exchanges, improve evaluation, and build team cohesion, while also reducing costs for Nigeria. Speaking to The Guardian, Okorie said that because nearly all of Nigeria’s top athletes live abroad, especially in the United States, it makes sense to organize preparation there. He noted that the 2024 season is especially important, with the African Games in March, the World Relays, and the Olympic Games in Paris. According to him, athletes based in the U.S. make up about 99.2 percent of Nigeria’s elite athletes, and he has already begun contacting athletes and coaches in the U.S., Europe, and Canada. Okorie, a former 400m hurdler and silver medalist at the 2003 African Games, also represented Nigeria at the 2003 World Championships and led the country’s team to the 2022 World Championships, where Tobi Amusan won gold and set a world record, and Ese Brume won silver. He said the plan can only succeed if the Federal Government provides urgent financial support. He appealed to the Sports Minister to strengthen the Performance Director’s office so Nigeria can prepare properly. The proposal follows criticism of poor baton exchanges that cost Nigeria medals at the 2023 World Championships in Budapest.

Iraq’s football association is finally set to hold long-delayed elections for its board on Saturday, after repeated postponements prompted FIFA to threaten the country with “immediate and indefinite suspension.” The vote, taking place at a central Baghdad hotel, will be conducted by a 75-member committee of club chiefs, provincial sports officials and other representatives, who are to choose a president, two deputies and an eight-member board. The main contest is between current president Najeh Hmoud and his deputy, Abdulkhaliq Massud. Hmoud had won disputed elections in 2011, but those results were later annulled by the Switzerland-based Court of Arbitration for Sport because of multiple irregularities. New elections were first expected in January, then postponed to April, and postponed again until Saturday. The delays and turmoil have reflected Iraq’s broader political dysfunction, with the football association long accused of chaos, malpractice and political interference. FIFA and the Asian Football Confederation warned that if the vote did not happen by the end of May, Iraq’s football body would face suspension. They also said an AFC representative received threatening phone calls during preparations for the April election. Despite the unrest, football remains hugely popular in Iraq, where cafes are often filled with fans watching the national team.

In Baghdad’s Sadr City, a neighborhood long scarred by sectarian violence, a once-unused patch of land has been turned into a full-size soccer field — but one that now stands as a symbol of both recovery and waste. Haider Jameel, a janitor by day and soccer coach by evening, has used the site as a neighborhood pitch for decades. It was abandoned only during the worst years of Iraq’s civil war, especially in 2006, when the Mahdi Army, a Shiite militia loyal to Muqtada al-Sadr, used the area to stage attacks and kidnapped people were often executed nearby. After the violence eased, the Iraqi government and the United States poured money into cleaning up Sadr City. As part of that effort, scrap was cleared and the field was built. A contractor, speaking anonymously for safety reasons, said the U.S. Army paid him $1.1 million for the project. Yet the field shows little evidence of that expense: it has no lights, bleachers, or showers, and players must use a nearby shop to wash. When it rains, the dirt surface floods, and local residents pool money to buy fresh dirt to repair it. The field still sees heavy use, but two similar soccer fields in Ghazaliyah, a mixed suburb in western Baghdad, were built under the same contract for nearly $1 million each and are now abandoned, serving as rubbish dumps filled with broken bottles and burning trash. The article places this waste in a broader context of frustration over how both U.S. aid and Iraq’s own oil wealth have been spent. Many Iraqis wonder why so much money has failed to improve daily life. At the same time, sectarian violence is rising again: violent deaths reached a five-year high last year, and soccer gatherings in Shiite neighborhoods have increasingly been targeted by attacks from the Islamic State of Iraq and Syria. Despite the hardships, young boys training on Jameel’s field speak hopefully of the future. But as their families contribute money to keep the pitch usable, they are reminded that Iraq’s oil-rich state cannot yet be relied upon to provide even basic amenities.

The situation grows more precarious as sectarian violence resurges. Last year marked the highest level of violent deaths in Iraq in five years, with attacks increasingly targeting crowds at soccer matches in Shiite neighborhoods by ISIS-affiliated groups seeking civilian casualties. Despite these challenges, the field remains in use and is named after Mohammed Kamil, a local resident killed during sectarian violence. Young players continue training there, hoping for a better future while collecting contributions from parents to maintain their million-dollar field's dirt surface.

Iran’s Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei on Sunday defended the government’s decision to raise gasoline prices, even as the move triggered widespread protests and violent clashes across the country. In a televised speech, he said the unrest was not driven by ordinary Iranians but by “hooligans,” “sabotage,” and “arson” carried out by the Islamic Republic’s enemies and foreign-backed opponents. He also urged officials to prevent similar increases in the prices of other goods. The protests erupted after the government announced a sharp fuel-price hike and rationing plan on Friday. Riot police and security forces clashed with demonstrators in Tehran and dozens of other cities on Saturday, according to Iranian media and social media reports. The unrest spread to more than 100 cities and towns, and the authorities said there were deaths and major property damage. Officials reported that one person died in the southeastern city of Sirjan on Friday, while state news agency IRNA said a police officer was killed on Saturday. Fars news agency said around 1,000 protesters had been arrested and about 100 banks were torched. Iran’s government says the price increase is intended to generate about $2.55 billion annually, money that would be used to expand subsidies for 18 million low-income families, or roughly 60 million people. Under the new system, regular gasoline rose to 15,000 rials per litre from 10,000 rials, with additional purchases priced at 30,000 rials per litre. Even after the increase, however, Iranian fuel remains among the cheapest in the world. Khamenei’s intervention appeared to settle the issue politically, at least for now. Iranian lawmakers who had planned to discuss forcing the government to revise the decision withdrew their motion after his remarks, state media reported. Meanwhile, the Intelligence Ministry said protest leaders had been identified and that “appropriate action” was underway. President Hassan Rouhani also acknowledged the right to peaceful protest but drew a line between demonstrations and violence, warning that the state would not allow “insecurity” through riots. The unrest comes amid deep economic strain in Iran, worsened by U.S. sanctions after Washington withdrew from the nuclear deal. The Trump administration voiced support for what it called peaceful protests, while condemning the use of lethal force and communications restrictions. The White House accused Iran’s leaders of pursuing nuclear and missile programs and supporting terrorism. Iranian authorities have also restricted internet access, apparently to limit coordination among protesters and the spread of video evidence. NetBlocks said connectivity had dropped to about 5% of normal levels. France warned its citizens in Iran to avoid public places, and reports said many shops in Tehran’s bazaar closed on Sunday after disturbances, though police reinforcements were later sent in.

Iran's clerical rulers sought to prevent escalation reminiscent of 2017 protests over poor living standards, when 22 people reportedly died across 80 cities. The White House condemned the "lethal force and severe communications restrictions" against demonstrators, while criticizing Iran's nuclear and missile programs. A late-night shootout in Baghdad highlighted the growing power of Shiite militias in Iraq and the difficulty the government faces in controlling them, even as they fight alongside state forces against Islamic State (IS). The clash began shortly after midnight, when heavy machine-gun fire broke the curfew silence in the capital. At first, residents feared it was an IS attack, as jihadists had been battling government troops on the outskirts of Baghdad for months. But the gunfire was instead tied to a confrontation between Iraqi police and members of Asaib Ahl al-Haq, one of the most hardline Shiite militias. According to police and army officers, the militia was holding Sara Hamid Niran, a businesswoman and cousin of Deputy Prime Minister Roz Nuri Shaways. Officials said she had been kidnapped in the southern port city of Basra the previous month and moved to a building in Baghdad’s Karrada district. Niran reportedly escaped by prying open a small window with a spoon and climbing into a neighboring house. She then ran to a nearby federal police checkpoint, shouting that she had been kidnapped and identifying her connection to the deputy prime minister. Police said Asaib Ahl al-Haq had demanded about two billion Iraqi dinars, or roughly $1.66 million, for her release. As police converged on the building, Niran was taken away in an armored Humvee. Officers initially believed they were dealing with an extortion gang, but reinforcements soon arrived and the situation escalated. Militiamen appeared in large numbers, blocked the street with sport utility vehicles, and threatened police, warning them to hand over the hostage or be killed. Police responded by sending in an armored personnel carrier to break through the roadblock, triggering a fierce exchange of gunfire. Despite the intensity of the clash, only four policemen were wounded. It was unclear whether any militia members were killed or injured, though police said two were detained. The incident alarmed Baghdad residents, some of whom initially feared IS had entered the city. One local man said he told his family to prepare to flee and complained that authorities had not explained what had happened. Police officers also described growing frustration and fear, saying militias increasingly ignore checkpoints and move freely with weapons despite official orders to stop them. The article notes that Asaib Ahl al-Haq, which has ties to Iran, has been fighting IS alongside Iraqi security forces, yet is also seen as one of the most aggressive militias and a challenge to state authority. Human rights groups have accused such militias of abuses including summary executions and torture. The problem may be worsening, the report says, because Iraq’s new interior minister, Mohammed al-Ghabban, comes from the Badr bloc, which is linked to another major Shiite militia.

Thousands of anti-government protesters in Baghdad turned Iraq’s 2-1 World Cup qualifying victory over Iran into a public celebration, using the match as a morale boost for a protest movement that has been weakened by a deadly security crackdown. Crowds gathered in Tahrir Square, the center of the demonstrations, to watch the game on a giant screen. Many waved Iraqi flags, chanted “Iran, out!” and lit fireworks as the national team scored early and then secured the win with a late goal. The match carried added significance because Iraq had originally been scheduled to host Iran and Bahrain in Basra, but unrest in the country forced the international soccer federation to require a different venue for security reasons. The Iraqi football association chose Amman, Jordan, instead. For protesters, the victory was more than a sporting result. Several said it could revive momentum in a movement that began in October and has demanded an end to Iraq’s sectarian political system, corruption, unemployment, poor public services, and Iranian influence in state affairs. Demonstrations in Baghdad and the Shiite south have left more than 320 people dead and thousands wounded. Protesters have refused government proposals for limited economic and constitutional reforms, instead demanding the resignation of the entire political leadership, including Prime Minister Adel Abdul-Mahdi. The government has recently tightened its response, pushing demonstrators back from bridges over the Tigris River toward the fortified Green Zone. Reports of disappearances and arbitrary arrests have also frightened many away from the streets. Protesters hoped the soccer win would encourage more people to return. Celebrations also took place in the southern city of Nasiriyah, where protesters watched the game in Haboub Square. Some framed the result as a symbolic defeat for Iran and its allies in Iraq. The U.S. ambassador to Iraq, Mathew Tueller, also posted support online, praising Iraq and sharing a photo of himself in the national team’s colors.

The Metropolitan Atlanta Rapid Transit Authority is beginning 2026 with a major systemwide modernization aimed at improving service before Atlanta hosts the 2026 FIFA World Cup this summer. MARTA is testing its new CQ400 railcars, which it says are the most technologically advanced trains in the country. The trains feature open gangways, charging stations and real-time service information, and multiple train sets are expected to be operating by the time the World Cup starts. The agency is also rolling out a new contactless fare system called Better Breeze, which will let riders tap bank cards or mobile wallets at faregates. A transition period will run from March 28 to May 2, during which both the old and new payment systems will work so riders can use up existing balances. Bus service is also being reshaped. MARTA plans to launch its NextGen Bus Network on April 18, which it says will triple the number of residents with access to 15-minute service. Before that, MARTA Reach, an on-demand transit service, will begin March 7 in 12 zones. The region’s first Bus Rapid Transit line, the MARTA Rapid A-Line, will connect downtown Atlanta to Summerhill and the Atlanta Beltline using dedicated lanes and off-board payment. Interim General Manager and CEO Jonathan Hunt called 2026 one of the most consequential years in MARTA’s history, saying riders and visitors will see a safer, cleaner and more reliable system. Other improvements include upgrades at Five Points Station, a new app combining MARTA’s current mobile tools, and multilingual messaging and increased security for World Cup visitors.

In an open letter addressed to Quebec Premier François Legault, Health Minister Christian Dubé, public health director Horacio Arruda and Education Minister Jean-François Roberge, representatives of competitive alpine skiing argue that the sport should be allowed to continue, even in red zones, because it can be part of the solution to the province’s health and youth-development challenges. The letter says ski racing is not widely understood by the public, but that the children and teenagers who practice it share the same goals as other young Quebec athletes: building confidence, staying mentally healthy and, for some, dreaming of reaching the Olympics. It emphasizes that alpine skiing is an outdoor, individual, non-contact sport practiced in a large natural environment, where athletes already wear goggles, gloves and face coverings as part of normal equipment. While recreational resort skiing was still permitted at the time, the authors warn that racing and even training would be compromised during the winter because current red-zone rules appear to prevent course training, even when done individually. They argue that this is unnecessary because young racers train on the same mountains as other skiers and only need occasional coaching from a distance. The letter stresses that health measures are easy to apply in ski clubs. Training groups are usually small, two-metre distancing is easy to maintain, and all activities take place outdoors. Coaches and athletes do not interact indoors, and outside they can communicate while staying apart. The authors also note that there is no equipment sharing, even among the youngest athletes, and that ski organizations already operate with strict safety protocols because the sport involves managing risks carefully. According to the letter, organized sport is widely recognized as beneficial for children and adolescents. The authors say young people need structured activities, especially as it becomes harder for parents to prevent them from doing anything beyond school. They argue that skiing is a safe and effective way to reduce isolation and support physical, mental and emotional well-being. The organizations behind the letter say they are ready to help health authorities develop a safe framework for continuing ski training. They ask the government to classify skiing as a priority organized sport that can restart immediately, and they urge officials to respond quickly so the sport can continue this winter.

# Summary: Open Letter on Competitive Skiing During Red Zone Restrictions An open letter addressed to Quebec's premier and health officials advocates for allowing competitive alpine skiing to continue during red zone COVID-19 restrictions. The letter, written on behalf of Quebec's ski racing community, argues that the sport should be exempted or adapted to permit training and competition for young athletes. The authors emphasize that competitive alpine skiing—including downhill, cross-country, and freestyle skiing—is fundamentally different from recreational resort skiing currently permitted in red zones. They highlight that the sport is practiced outdoors in natural environments and involves no physical contact between participants. Athletes already wear protective equipment including eye protection, gloves, and face coverings as standard practice, making additional sanitary measures easily implementable. The letter stresses the importance of skiing for young athletes' physical and mental health, noting that the sport builds self-confidence, provides structure, and offers some athletes pathways to elite competition and Olympic aspirations. The authors argue that current red zone restrictions unnecessarily prevent even individual training sessions and course work, potentially leaving young racers behind in their development. The ski community proposes that their sport meets safety criteria for continuation. They note that athletes train in small groups where two-meter distancing is easily maintained, all activities occur outdoors, coaches maintain distance from athletes, there is no shared equipment, and no indoor contact occurs between coaches and participants. The authors emphasize that their organizations already possess established safety protocols and coaching expertise in implementing strict guidelines. The letter concludes by requesting that health authorities recognize organized skiing as a priority sport that should be restarted immediately. The authors position themselves as willing partners with health officials, offering their expertise to create a safe framework for winter training. They argue that allowing competitive skiing would serve the broader public health goal of reducing youth isolation and maintaining mental and physical wellness during the pandemic.

South Dundas council has approved a fee policy that protects youth recreation users at municipal facilities while shifting higher costs onto adult recreation, junior hockey, and some out-of-area users. The decision came at the municipality’s Dec. 7 regular council meeting, where councillors rejected a broader set of recreation fee increases proposed by staff. Director of Environmental Services Danielle Watson presented the staff recommendation, which called for ice rental increases of between 15 and 26 per cent at the Morrisburg Arena, along with new charges for the first time to use municipal baseball diamonds. Watson said the arena’s budgeted ice rental revenue for 2020-21 does not even cover the labour costs of operating the facility, let alone maintenance. She argued the municipality should begin recovering more of those expenses in anticipation of future needs at aging recreation infrastructure, pointing specifically to the planned replacement of the arena stairs in 2021 or 2022. Watson also told council that South Dundas had the lowest ice rental rates in SDG Counties and that it did not currently charge for baseball diamond use. Council, however, made it clear it wanted youth sports and recreation kept affordable. Councillor Lloyd Wells said he did not want youth fees to rise, and Councillor Archie Mellan agreed. Councillor Donald Lewis said he preferred to see children in minor hockey or skating club rather than “causing havoc on the street,” and said he had no issue charging adults. Deputy Mayor Kirsten Gardner also supported leaving youth rates unchanged, noting that skating clubs already do substantial fundraising. Mayor Steven Byvelds said the arena has never made money and likely never will, adding that while it is wise to plan for future upkeep, substantial spending has already been made on the facility in recent years and future users will ultimately pay for a new arena. The final decision left youth recreation fees unchanged. Minor hockey and figure skating will continue to pay $95 per hour for ice time, and South Dundas youth baseball programs will not be charged to use municipal diamonds. Public skating will also remain free. The financial burden will instead be placed on adult recreation and junior hockey. Prime-time ice rental, including junior hockey games, will rise from $125 to $150 per hour in 2021-22. Non-prime-time adult ice use will increase by 18 per cent to $100 per hour. Council also approved a new non-resident team rate of $200 per hour for clubs and users from outside South Dundas, including tournament users such as the Leo Boivin AAA Classic Tournament from Prescott. School rental rates will remain at $85 per hour, and each school will still receive two free hours of ice time per season. On the baseball side, adult recreation users will be charged $20 per game for use of municipal diamonds, while practices will remain free. This includes leagues such as Blooperball. Council also scaled back staff’s proposed increase for some municipally run programs. Adult programs such as Yoga, Bootcamp, and adult Taekwondo will rise by 10 per cent rather than the 15 per cent suggested by staff. Youth Taekwondo and swimming lessons will not increase. Reactions were mixed. South Dundas Minor Hockey Association president Joyce Latulippe thanked council for supporting minor hockey and youth activities, saying the association’s ice fees help keep one of the area’s most affordable hockey programs running. Williamsburg Pioneers baseball president David Lapier also welcomed the decision not to charge youth teams for diamond use, calling recreation important for keeping children active. The Morrisburg Lions, South Dundas’ Junior C hockey club, were far less pleased. President and general manager Kevin Casselman said the club would have preferred a gradual increase spread over two years instead of a 20 per cent jump during the pandemic. He warned that many players had already been hit by reduced work hours and lost summer employment, and that higher fees could make post-secondary education costs even harder to manage. Casselman also noted that the National Capital Junior Hockey League caps player registration fees at $700 and ticket prices at $8, leaving clubs heavily dependent on sponsorships. He said the pandemic has made sponsorships much harder to secure because local businesses are struggling themselves. The meeting also clarified a point of confusion about minor hockey in South Dundas. Watson had described the South Dundas and North Dundas minor hockey programs as “amalgamated,” but Latulippe explained that the two associations remain separate organizations. They each have their own executives and run house-league teams independently, though they collaborate on rep-level teams. Those rep teams rotate between the two associations every two years. In 2019-20, South Dundas hosted Under-11 and Under-15 rep teams, while North Dundas hosted Under-13 and Under-18 teams. Players who make rep teams move to the host association for that season.

The Trudeau government has hired IBM Canada to help design and implement the federal buyback program for firearms that were recently prohibited. The contract is worth nearly $1.2 million, according to a federal award notice. In early May, the Liberal government banned about 1,500 models and variants of what it called assault-style firearms, arguing they were built for the battlefield rather than hunting or sport shooting. The ban means those guns can no longer be legally used, sold, or imported. At the same time, the government announced plans for a compensation program to allow current owners to turn in the firearms in exchange for payment. Public Safety Canada had invited 15 consulting firms, including IBM Canada, to propose “a range of options and approaches” for the buyback. Under the first stage of the contract, due to be completed by Feb. 8, IBM is to consult with other federal agencies, possibly other levels of government, and industry experts. The company will help develop options for compensation plans for each affected firearm, assess the risks and benefits of different models, and identify other factors that could affect whether each approach is workable. A second phase would involve reviewing and revising the design as needed, followed by implementation of the chosen option. Public Safety Canada said the goal is to provide fair compensation to affected owners and businesses while keeping implementation and management costs sustainable. Gun-control advocates welcomed the ban, but sport shooters, firearm-rights groups, and some Conservative MPs criticized the measures. PolySeSouvient, a prominent gun-control group, has urged the government to make the buyback mandatory so owners cannot simply keep the newly banned firearms. It also wants the prohibitions embedded in law rather than left in regulation, to make them harder for a future government to undo. Public Safety Minister Bill Blair has said the government intends to introduce legislation creating an evergreen firearms classification framework, replacing what he described as a rigid system that manufacturers had been able to work around. The Liberals have also promised to give provinces and cities more authority over handgun storage and use, and to take stronger steps to prevent people with mental health or criminal risk factors from obtaining firearms.

Connor McDavid is entering the Olympic season in exceptional form, and the Edmonton Oilers captain said Wednesday that he is “ramping up” his game as he prepares for the Milan tournament. The comments came on the same day Hockey Canada announced its 25-man Olympic roster, making McDavid the central figure in the hockey conversation even though the roster itself was the official news. McDavid is coming off the most productive month of his NHL career. He has collected 33 points in December alone and entered the Christmas break with 67 points, the highest league total at that point since Mario Lemieux and Jaromir Jagr in the 1995-96 season. With one game left in the month against Boston, he was on pace for 141 points, which would be the second-highest total of his career. Oilers coach Kris Knoblauch joked that if McDavid is already this hot and is still “ramping it up,” the rest of the league should be worried. McDavid explained that he wants to peak in February, when the Olympic tournament begins. He said players are used to moving from ordinary midseason NHL games into a short, high-pressure event that feels like playoff hockey, and that he is trying to make sure his game is in the right place by then. He also indicated that he was not fully satisfied with his performance at last winter’s 4 Nations event, even though he scored the tournament-winning goal. He believes he can contribute more consistently in a future best-on-best international competition. The forward, who turns 29 in two weeks, has long spoken about the disappointment of his generation being denied Olympic opportunities. He said the roster announcement made the Games feel real and added that he and teammate Leon Draisaitl are excited about the chance to compete at an event they have never played in before. McDavid said he has been looking forward to the Olympics since he was a child, and that the upcoming tournament is a major motivation. The article also notes that McDavid will likely leave Edmonton without several potential Team Canada teammates. Zach Hyman, Evan Bouchard and Ryan Nugent-Hopkins were all left off the roster. McDavid said he was disappointed for them, noting that they are all very good players who could have made the team in a different year or under different circumstances. The omitted Oilers players had arguments based on recent high-level experience. Hyman has returned from a dislocated wrist and produced 11 goals and 21 points in 21 games, which he said left him proud of his comeback even though he was disappointed by the selection. Bouchard’s case was hurt by early-season defensive mistakes, despite a stronger recent stretch. Bouchard said the decision is made and must be accepted, but added that he would be ready if injuries create an opening. Nugent-Hopkins was also considered a strong candidate because of his role in the Oilers’ recent deep playoff runs. The article concludes by noting that all of the Oilers players not chosen for the Olympic team will continue to undergo drug testing in case they are later added as injury replacements.

# Connor McDavid Preparing for Olympic Spotlight Connor McDavid is entering the upcoming Olympic Games in Milan with exceptional momentum, having just completed the most productive December of his NHL career with 33 points. The Edmonton Oilers captain enters the Christmas break with 67 total points this season—the highest total since Mario Lemieux and Jaromir Jagr achieved the same in 1995-96. Head coach Kris Knoblauch expressed concern about opposing teams facing an even more elevated version of McDavid, saying "If he's ramping it up even more, I'm afraid for the opposition." McDavid, 25, has made clear his intention to peak for the February Olympic tournament. He acknowledged that while he scored the tournament-winning goal at last year's 4 Nations competition, he felt his performance wasn't consistently strong enough. This time, he's determined to deliver more reliable contributions throughout the Games. "You've got to find a way to peak in February," McDavid explained, noting the unique challenge of transitioning from regular-season play to Olympic competition within days. "It's important that guys are ramping up their games." His current trajectory is remarkable. McDavid is on pace for 141 points this season, which would be his second-highest single-season total. His offensive dominance is evident in every shift, with Knoblauch describing him as "tenacious," "hungry to score goals," and constantly "driving the net" while maintaining focus at an elevated level. The Olympic roster announcement by Hockey Canada on Wednesday added urgency to McDavid's preparation. For the 29-year-old (turning 29 in two weeks), Olympic participation carries special significance. He's part of a generation of elite NHL players who have been denied Olympic opportunities, having missed two potential Games already. He and teammates like Nathan MacKinnon should have competed twice by now. "It's definitely getting real, with the team being announced today," McDavid said. "We're a month away from our break. It's getting here, and I'm excited about it." However, not all Oilers made the cut. Teammates Zach Hyman, Evan Bouchard, and Ryan Nugent-Hopkins were excluded despite their contributions to Edmonton's recent playoff success. The team has won six playoff series over the past two springs, reaching the Cup Finals twice. McDavid expressed disappointment for his teammates, acknowledging that "great players here that, different year, different situation, could easily be on the team" were passed over. The selection committee appeared to prioritize defensive reliability, particularly for a tournament where a single defensive lapse could determine medal outcomes. Hyman, who returned from a dislocated wrist to record 11 goals and 21 points in 21 games, accepted his exclusion gracefully. All non-selected Oilers will continue receiving Olympic drug testing in case injuries create roster openings.

The victory came after Galysheva had already earned silver on the first day of the same World Cup stage, when she scored 77.79 points and finished just 0.11 points behind Kauf. The International Ski and Snowboard Federation (FIS) has approved neutral-athlete status for three Russian skiers and six Belarusian skiers, allowing them to enter qualifying events for the 2026 Milan Cortina Winter Games. Their return to competition, after being excluded since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, could come as soon as this weekend at World Cup events in Davos, Switzerland. Among those cleared are former Olympic and world champions. Belarusian freestyle skier Hanna Huskova won Olympic gold in women’s aerials in 2018 and silver in 2022, while Russian freestyle skier Anastasia Tatalina was the 2021 world champion in big air and finished fourth in slopestyle at the Beijing Olympics. Russian cross-country skiers Savelii Korostelev and Dariya Nepryaeva also received neutral status. Korostelev had recently posted “debut this weekend” on social media. FIS said the athletes may compete only if they formally accept the conditions for Individual Neutral Athlete status, which requires them not to have publicly supported the war and not to have ties to military or state security agencies. The federation did not say whether any applications were rejected, though the Russian ski federation told TASS that six of its athletes had applied. The approvals still require final vetting by the International Olympic Committee before any athlete can be invited to the Winter Games, which open Feb. 6. IOC rules have kept Russian athletes out of team events and were used in the Paris Olympics last year. Last week, the Court of Arbitration for Sport ruled in favor of the Russian ski federation and athletes, forcing FIS to process their neutral-status applications. More decisions are expected in the coming days and weeks. Even so, visa issues could complicate entry to some host countries. The final Russian contingent in Italy is expected to be fewer than 20, far below the more than 200 who competed in Beijing in 2022.

Argentina’s World Cup victory in Qatar has triggered a nationwide tattoo craze, with studios across the country reporting surging demand and many artists working overtime. Fans are choosing designs that commemorate the triumph in personal ways: some are honoring promises made before or during the tournament, others are expressing gratitude, and many simply want to preserve on their skin a moment they consider unforgettable. Popular images include Lionel Messi holding or kissing the trophy and the three stars representing Argentina’s three World Cup titles. The trend is especially strong among Argentines under 30, many of whom had never seen their national team win the tournament. Argentina’s previous World Cup victories came in 1978 and 1986, and the long 36-year wait since Diego Maradona lifted the trophy has weighed heavily on fans in a country where soccer is followed with exceptional passion. The emotional impact of the win has also stood out because it came during a period of severe economic hardship. Argentina has been struggling with years of malaise, inflation approaching 100%, and poverty affecting nearly four in ten people. In Buenos Aires, 26-year-old Sasha Mortier spent nearly two hours in a tattoo chair to fulfill a promise he made before the tournament began: he got the World Cup trophy and the date of the final tattooed on his torso. Mortier said an entire generation had missed out on such a moment and that the victory brought needed happiness to a troubled country. He also still has another promise to keep: he and a friend vowed to tattoo a rock they picked up from the ground just before Argentina’s penalty shootout against the Netherlands, believing it brought luck. Others have sought more elaborate tributes. Sebastián Fernández went to a tattoo shop in a southern Buenos Aires suburb soon after returning from Qatar, determined to have Messi kissing the trophy permanently inked on his thigh. He said the image would be historic and wanted something that would help him relive the emotion of the tournament. The tattoo was done by César “Yeyo” Molina, a well-known artist in soccer circles, who said demand has been unlike anything he has seen before. He described the World Cup frenzy as “impressive” and said his shop cannot keep up. His hyperrealistic work is especially sought after, though his tattoos generally cost at least $300, a significant amount for many Argentines. For those with less money, cheaper tattoos have sometimes gone viral for poor quality, including one infamous Messi portrait that made the star look overweight and gave him a double chin. Still, many fans are willing to pay for quality. Santiago Aposto, an Argentine living in Mexico, traveled back to Buenos Aires to fulfill a promise made after Argentina’s shock opening loss to Saudi Arabia. He said living abroad made him feel even more Argentine and described Messi as a representative of his generation, much as Maradona was for their parents. Another popular figure is goalkeeper Emiliano Martínez, known as “Dibu,” who became a hero in Argentina’s penalty shootout wins over the Netherlands and France. Twenty-year-old Valentín Bobadilla chose to tattoo Martínez’s controversial Golden Glove celebration gesture, saying it caught his attention and reflected his growing affection for the goalkeeper after the team’s victories.

# Argentina's Tattoo Fever Following World Cup Victory Argentina is experiencing an unprecedented surge in tattoo demand following the nation's World Cup victory in Qatar, with tattoo artists across the country working overtime to fulfill the wishes of enthusiastic fans. The phenomenon reflects how profoundly the championship has affected Argentines, particularly younger generations who had never witnessed their country win soccer's most prestigious tournament before. Argentina previously won the World Cup in 1978 and 1986, leaving a 36-year gap that weighed heavily on fans in this soccer-obsessed nation. The victory comes at a time when Argentina faces significant economic challenges, including inflation near 100% and poverty affecting nearly 40% of the population. For many, the World Cup triumph has provided a much-needed emotional uplift during difficult economic times. The tattoo designs predominantly feature superstar Lionel Messi holding the trophy, often accompanied by three stars representing Argentina's three World Cup victories. The trend is most pronounced among people under 30, the generation that had never experienced such a triumph. Many fans are fulfilling promises they made before or during the tournament. Sasha Mortier, 26, spent nearly two hours getting a tattoo of the trophy and championship match date on his torso, fulfilling a pre-tournament pledge. He explained that his generation desperately needed this victory and the happiness it brought during their country's difficult period. Sebastián Fernández chose to immortalize an iconic image: Messi kissing the trophy. He traveled to renowned tattoo artist César "Yeyo" Molina, whose hyperrealistic designs are highly sought after. The intricate tattoo covering Fernández's entire thigh took two days to complete and cost at least $300—a significant sum for average Argentines. Molina reports unprecedented demand, stating he has never experienced such overwhelming business. "The madness over the Cup is impressive," he said. "Work wise, we're at an incredible time, we can't keep up." Beyond Messi, goalkeeper Emiliano Martínez, nicknamed "Dibu," has become another popular tattoo subject. His crucial performances in penalty shootouts against the Netherlands and France made him a local hero. Some fans, like 20-year-old Valentín Bobadilla, have even chosen to tattoo the goalkeeper's controversial gesture when he won the Golden Glove award. However, not all tattoo experiences have been successful. Some budget-conscious fans seeking cheaper alternatives have ended up with poor-quality results that have gone viral on social media, including an infamous unflattering Messi tattoo. Santiago Aposto, a 31-year-old Argentine living in Mexico, deliberately chose a reputable studio to fulfill his promise, getting a tattoo of Messi with the trophy. He noted that living abroad intensified his Argentine identity and connection to Messi, comparable to what previous generations felt toward Diego Maradona. The tattoo phenomenon vividly demonstrates how deeply the World Cup victory has resonated with Argentines, providing a tangible way to commemorate an unforgettable moment during challenging times.

Brazil’s Alison dos Santos upset the favorites to win the men’s 400m hurdles at the World Championships in Eugene, Oregon, setting a championship record. The race had been billed as a duel between Norway’s Olympic champion Karsten Warholm and American Rai Benjamin, but dos Santos pulled away on the final straight. Benjamin took silver, Trevor Bassitt bronze, and Warholm, returning from a hamstring tear, finished seventh.

# Athletics: Dos Santos Wins 400m Hurdles World Final Brazilian Alison dos Santos won the 400-meter hurdles world championship title on Tuesday, setting a championship record and denying Norwegian Karsten Warholm a third consecutive title. Despite pre-race focus on Warholm and American rival Rai Benjamin, dos Santos dominated down the final stretch. Benjamin secured silver, while American Trevor Bassitt claimed bronze. Warholm, recovering from a June hamstring injury and lacking recent race experience, finished seventh.

Venezuelan trap shooter Leonel Martínez will return to the Olympics in Paris at age 60, 40 years after his first appearance at the Los Angeles Games in 1984. His comeback marks the second-longest gap between Olympic appearances in history, behind only Japanese equestrian Hiroshi Hoketsu. Martínez, from Ciudad Ojeda in Venezuela’s western oil state of Zulia, was just 20 when he competed in Los Angeles and finished 41st out of 70. He had expected to continue to the 1988 Seoul Olympics, but life intervened. He focused on personal and business responsibilities, founded a company making disposable medical supplies, married Magaly Chacín, and raised two children. For years, he left the sport behind. Nearly three decades later, Martínez felt a renewed desire to return. He said “something awakened” in him and described a new spark in his life. He reentered competition in 2011, qualifying for the Pan American Games in Guadalajara, and gradually rebuilt his confidence through regional events. A major influence was Peruvian shooter Francisco Boza, a fellow South American and Olympic medalist, who encouraged Martínez to see age as a “state of mind.” Martínez was especially inspired when Boza won gold at the 2015 Pan American Games at age 50. Martínez earned his place in Paris by winning silver at the 2023 Pan American Games in Santiago, Chile, where he lost gold by one point to Guatemala’s Jean Pierre Brol, who was 41. Martínez said the lesson from his long career is perseverance: people fail to achieve their dreams because they give up too easily. He also credited his lifelong connection to the sport. His father, Alonso Martínez, who competed internationally, introduced him to shooting as a teenager. Martínez said he loved trap shooting from the start. Looking back, he said he competed in 1984 with uncertainty and nerves that hurt his performance. Now, he believes experience helps him manage those emotions more calmly. He sees trap shooting as a sport where mental strength matters more than physical power.

Venezuela has rejected the UNHCR’s method for including a Venezuelan national in the Olympic team under refugee status, saying he does not meet the international criteria to be classified as a refugee. In a statement issued Friday night, Caracas said the man was placed on the sports shooting team despite not qualifying under refugee rules. The government urged UNHCR and the International Olympic Committee to establish direct and ongoing communication with the relevant institutions to protect transparency and the rigor of high-performance sport and to correct the damage caused. It also stressed that UNHCR must respect principles of international and refugee law, including impartiality, objectivity, non-selectivity, and non-politicization. Venezuela said it supports inclusive policies for people displaced by persecution and war, but warned that political interference could harm Olympic qualification processes and the spirit of national teams competing for Paris 2024.

# Summary Venezuela rejected the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) method of including a Venezuelan national in the Olympic sports shooting team, arguing the individual does not meet international refugee criteria. In a statement released Friday, Venezuela called on the UNHCR and International Olympic Committee to establish better communication with relevant institutions to ensure transparency and maintain the integrity of competitive sports. Venezuela emphasized that principles of International Law and Refugee Law—including impartiality, objectivity, and non-politicization—must be respected. While recognizing the importance of inclusive sports policies for displaced persons, Venezuela warned that political considerations could negatively impact national teams qualifying for the Paris 2024 Olympics and global sports standards.

The participating groups agreed to maintain ongoing dialogue and cooperation to strengthen the coalition’s reach nationwide. UNFPA, which leads global efforts to support health, rights, and development, works in Venezuela with partners from the private sector and civil society on these issues.

Venezuelan teacher Raydis Franco, who now teaches Spanish at Nankai University in Tianjin, says marathon running helped him discover a sport that suited him after he struggled with ball sports as a child. Franco came to Tianjin in 2015 to study and stayed to work after graduating. He began running marathons in college in Venezuela after a friend invited and coached him, and he found the sport appealing because it requires little more than shoes and determination. Since then, he has used marathons as a way to explore China. After races, he often visits local museums to learn about regional history and culture, collecting souvenirs such as magnets. He recalled doing this in Xiamen in Fujian Province and in Anyang in Henan Province, which is known as the hometown of oracle bone script. Franco also enjoys the scenery along his running routes, especially the night view of Tianjin’s Hai River. He said South Cuiping Park reminds him of a hill near his hometown of Caracas. Looking ahead, he plans to keep running marathons in more Chinese cities as a way to travel across the country.

Rio de Janeiro is set to stage a glittering Olympic opening ceremony at the Maracana Stadium, launching the first Games ever held in South America. More than 70,000 spectators, 10,400 athletes and dozens of world leaders are expected at the event, which begins two weeks of competition running through August 21 and featuring stars such as Usain Bolt and Michael Phelps. The ceremony comes after a deeply troubled seven-year build-up marked by recession, unemployment, crime, drugs scandals, infrastructure problems and the Zika public health crisis. Brazil’s economy has slumped, and the usual excitement that accompanies an Olympic opening has been muted. Organizers are hoping the samba-filled spectacle will lift national spirits. Fernando Meirelles, one of the creative directors and the filmmaker behind “City of God,” said he hoped the ceremony would act as “a kind of anti-depressant for Brazil” and send a message of tolerance and environmental care to a tense world. President Dilma Rousseff has been impeached and will not attend; interim president Michel Temer will open the ceremony instead, likely to a hostile crowd. Brazilian media reported that music may be turned up immediately after he speaks to drown out any booing from protesters.

Flamengo have settled a $1.8 million debt with Brazil legend Romario, ending a 20-year dispute over unpaid wages from his three spells at the club in the 1990s. According to Globo Esporte, Flamengo had been paying him in monthly instalments due to run until 2022, but Romario accepted a lump-sum payment worth about a third of the total. The 1994 FIFA World Player of the Year retired in 2009, later became a federal senator, and still receives payments from Vasco da Gama over salary arrears.

Darwish also highlighted IHS Nigeria’s partnership with the Telecommunications and Technology Sustainability Working Group (TTSWG), which has reached more than 200,000 people through initiatives promoting sustainable practices across the ICT sector and the wider country. Beyond the SERAs, IHS Nigeria’s sustainability work has also earned recognition at several other 2023 awards, including honors from Africa Public Sector Conference and Awards, Top 50 Brands on Sustainability in Africa, World Sustainability Awards, Tech Innovation Award, CSR Reporters, CAHR Awards, and SOS Children’s Villages International.

Wema Bank Plc has announced a N1 billion loan scheme to help small and medium enterprises buy clean energy solutions such as solar panels, inverters and batteries. The financing will be provided in partnership with reputable renewable energy companies and service providers in Nigeria, who will also supply after-sales support and warranties of up to two years on products expected to last about 10 years. According to Dotun Ifebogun, Divisional Head of Retail Business, the initiative is meant to ease the burden of high energy costs on SMEs and support their role as key drivers of the economy. He said the bank wants to promote affordable alternative power options while educating businesses on the environmental benefits of solar energy. The programme also aligns with Wema Bank’s broader goal of advancing Nigeria’s energy transition and helping businesses adopt greener practices. Arthur Nkemeh, Head of SME Banking, added that beneficiaries will receive free technical assistance and capacity-building support in sustainability, energy efficiency and business management through the bank’s advisory services. Interested business owners can apply at any Wema Bank branch or contact the SME Banking team.

The initiative will be executed in partnership with reputable renewable energy companies that offer after-sales services and two-year warranties on products with approximately 10-year lifespans. At the UNCTAD E-Week 2023 conference in Geneva, the Nigeria Customs Service (NCS) urged developing countries to adopt stronger data governance systems, saying such frameworks are essential for digital transformation, privacy protection, and sustainable development. The NCS hosted a dedicated session at the Centre International de Conférences de Genève, represented by CSC DO Anikoh and CSC of Obieze, to promote discussion on implementing a data governance framework that matches international best practices. The session gathered public- and private-sector experts to examine key issues such as data accuracy, security, standardisation, and responsible sharing. DHL’s Steven Pope called for strict controls on data sharing to prevent misuse, while the Universal Postal Union’s Javier Garcia stressed that national frameworks should align with global rules and provisions. Participants also discussed fair compensation for data analysts, the role of analysts in specialized agencies, poor data quality and integrity, barriers faced by startups in accessing real data, and the use of private-sector data for policy-making. A major theme was the need for international regulation to curb data misuse. Speakers agreed that developing countries must manage data at macro, regional, and international levels, and that cooperation between private companies and regulators is vital. They also noted that private-sector data governance builds trust, supports innovation, and helps balance privacy with usability. For e-commerce and supply chain businesses, data governance was described as necessary to reduce risk and improve efficiency. The discussion also highlighted legal tools such as NDAs and trade agreements, and pointed to GDPR-style standards as useful for cross-border data flows. The session ended by recommending that developing-country regulators adopt data governance frameworks or seek support from bodies such as the WTO and WCO.

# Summary: NCS Champions Global Data Governance Framework The Nigeria Customs Service (NCS) emphasized the critical importance of robust data governance in developing countries during a pivotal session at the UNCTAD E-Week 2023 conference in Geneva. Represented by CSC DO Anikoh and CSC Obieze, the NCS facilitated dialogue among public and private sector experts on adopting data governance frameworks aligned with international best practices. Key discussion points included data accuracy, security, standardization, and fair compensation for data analysts. DHL's Steven Pope stressed the necessity of stringent controls on data sharing to prevent misuse, while the Universal Postal Union's Javier Garcia highlighted the importance of national frameworks aligning with global provisions. The session addressed multiple challenges, including data quality integrity, startup access to real data, and opportunities for accessing private company data for policy-making. International regulation to prevent data misuse emerged as a central theme. Participants concluded that data governance is fundamental to digital transformation and e-commerce supply chain efficiency. The discussion emphasized the vital role of data sharing between private and regulatory sectors while addressing privacy and security concerns. Legal frameworks like GDPR and NDAs were recognized as necessary safeguards. The session recommended that developing countries adopt comprehensive data governance frameworks balancing standardization, harmonization, and simplification, with assistance from international bodies like the WTO and WCO to facilitate responsible cross-border data flows and promote sustainable development.

Delta State Governor Sheriff Oborevwori has approved land for the take-off of the Federal University of Medical and Health Sciences in Kwale, Ndokwa West Local Government Area. State Commissioner for Lands, Surveys and Urban Development, Chief Emamusi Obiodeh, announced this in Asaba, saying the university will begin operations at the former site of the Delta State School of Marine Technology in Kwale. The governor approved 15 hectares, including existing facilities and infrastructure, while the school has relocated to its permanent campus. The new federal university will use the site temporarily until it moves to a permanent 100-hectare location at Umuseti-Kwale. Obiodeh said Oborevwori welcomed the federal government’s choice of Delta and reaffirmed the state’s readiness to partner with government and serious investors on impactful developments.

# Summary Delta State Governor Sheriff Oborevwori has approved a 15-hectare take-off site for the Federal University of Medical and Health Sciences in Kwale, Ndokwa West Local Government Area. The land, previously occupied by the School of Marine Technology, includes existing facilities and infrastructure. State Commissioner for Lands Emamusi Obiodeh announced the approval in Asaba on Friday. The university will temporarily operate from this site until relocating to its permanent 100-hectare location at Umuseti-Kwale. # Summary Nigeria's mobile revolution two decades ago saw the nation leap from 400,000 landlines to 80 million mobile lines, representing its largest developmental stride in 63 years. The National Directorate of Employment (NDE) has trained 25 unemployed youths in Adamawa State on solar power installation and maintenance as part of efforts to create employment opportunities. Speaking at the close of the weeklong programme in Yola, NDE’s Adamawa Coordinator, Malam Mohammed Jimada, said the training was designed to equip beneficiaries with practical skills for self-reliance. He urged them to apply what they learned so they could benefit from the programme and eventually become employers of labour. Jimada also said the Federal Government was making efforts to make young people productive, and he assured the trainees that each would receive a starter pack, though he did not explain why it was not distributed immediately. The Rector of Ogun State Institute of Technology (OGITECH), Igbesa, Dr Abiodun Oluseye, has said skill acquisition and practical training are essential for students to remain globally competitive and relevant in the job market. In an interview with The Guardian, he stressed that institutions must equip students with the competencies needed to succeed in today’s world. Oluseye said a conducive learning environment is necessary to attract modern academic programmes, while improved staff welfare is important for achieving strong results. He explained that his goal is to transform OGITECH into a leading centre of learning and a global hub of academic excellence. Drawing on more than 25 years of experience in the polytechnic sub-sector, he said development is central to realizing that vision. He also emphasized that polytechnic education should help solve societal problems through research. According to him, students need a broad education supported by well-equipped laboratories, qualified lecturers and exposure to industry. He said OGITECH intends to take advantage of its location in an industrial area, noting that the surrounding free trade zone hosts more than 200 companies and that the institution is the only one nearby. He said the school is already working to tap into those opportunities. Oluseye further raised concerns about discrimination in employment within the sub-sector. He recalled that when he assumed office, he found that some HND graduates with distinction were employed as instructors, which he considered unfair. After discussions with the governing council, he said such staff were moved to lecturer cadre, while those employed earlier were upgraded to assistant lecturers. He also lamented the financial burden of running technical institutions and said OGITECH is partnering with private organisations for support. Looking ahead, he said the institution is focused on practical skills and emerging technologies, including Artificial Intelligence, and plans to introduce new programmes such as Music Technology, Art and Design, and Agricultural Engineering.
