Tokyo stocks are expected to keep rising in 2026 and may challenge new record highs, helped by hopes that Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s expansionary fiscal policies will lift economic growth and corporate earnings. Market strategists said the Nikkei Stock Average could move toward 55,000, above its all-time closing high of 52,411.34 set in October, as optimism continues around artificial intelligence, semiconductors, and sectors favored by government investment policy. Analysts said AI- and semiconductor-related shares, which already led the market higher this year, should continue to benefit as the government pushes investment in strategic industries. Shipbuilding stocks are also seen as potential winners. Maki Sawada of Nomura Securities said policy support could sustain a positive cycle in which growth and price increases are accompanied by wage gains, helping corporate profits. Automakers are another sector expected to improve. Their shares were hurt this year by U.S. tariffs imposed under President Donald Trump, but analysts said the impact should ease next year after Japan and the United States reached an agreement in July to reduce the tariff rate. Masahiro Yamaguchi of SMBC Trust Bank said exporters, especially automakers, had been hit hard this year but could see a rebound in 2026, which would support the broader market. The biggest downside risk identified by analysts is a further plunge in the yen. If the currency weakens beyond 160 to the dollar, import costs would rise further, worsening inflation for households already facing high food and living expenses. That could hurt consumer spending and reduce support for the Takaichi government, which currently enjoys strong approval ratings. The yen has already stayed mostly above 150 in recent months, despite Bank of Japan rate hikes and U.S. Federal Reserve easing. It earlier reached a high for the year in the 139 range in April. Takuya Kanda of the Gaitame.com Research Institute said the narrowing interest-rate gap between Japan and the U.S. could help the yen strengthen somewhat, but he warned that recent trends suggest the rate differential alone is unlikely to determine the currency’s direction. He said yen-selling flows for both investment and non-investment purposes are likely to continue. Dealers also said concerns about Japan’s fiscal health under Takaichi are weighing on the currency, and a possible landslide election win for her Liberal Democratic Party next year could add to yen weakness. A sharp yen decline would also threaten consumer sentiment and real wages. Chisa Kobayashi of UBS SuMi Trust Wealth Management said that if inflation keeps rising, wage increases may not be enough in real terms, which could weaken government support and undermine expectations for growth, putting pressure on equities. Rising long-term Japanese interest rates are another concern, but analysts said the effect on stocks should remain limited unless the 10-year government bond yield climbs above 2.5 percent soon. The yield recently rose above 2.0 percent after the BOJ lifted its policy rate to a 30-year high of about 0.75 percent on Dec. 19, and it later reached 2.100 percent, the highest since 1999. Yamaguchi said higher rates could help bank shares, though they would become negative for stocks if they eventually slowed the economy. A further risk is disappointment in the AI sector. Analysts noted that concerns this year about whether massive AI investments would generate enough returns already caused several selloffs in technology and semiconductor shares. Masahiro Ichikawa of Sumitomo Mitsui DS Asset Management said Japanese stocks could fall if investors conclude that data center spending is excessive or profits are not meeting expectations.

Philstar.com’s Supreme section closed out 2018 by highlighting a group of “unsung heroes” whose work had a visible impact on their communities, industries, and causes. The feature focused on people and initiatives that may not have gotten widespread attention during the year, but which helped drive innovation, empowerment, and social change in the Philippines. One of the featured innovators was Engineer Rey Ramos, who worked with the Carlos Hilado Memorial State College DRRM Team in Talisay, Negros Occidental, with support from TUKLAS Innovation Labs, to develop the Bottle Net Life Jacket. The idea came from observing how people routinely discard plastic bottles after use. Ramos and his team saw those bottles as potential flotation devices, especially in coastal barangays where many families lack access to life jackets. The jacket uses recycled fishing net and plastic bottles, which are buoyant and do not absorb water, reducing resistance in the water. The bottles are lined with Styrofoam and plastic waste to help absorb impact from debris or collisions. The life jacket also includes practical survival features such as a waterproof phone pocket, whistle, and flashlight. Another disaster-response innovation featured was the Intelligent Flood Warning and Monitoring System created by robotics professor and electronics and communications engineer Jonathan Cartilla and his team in Carcar, Cebu. Also supported by TUKLAS Innovation Labs, the system uses a sensor to measure how quickly water is rising and can calculate when it is likely to overflow into surrounding areas. This gives communities advance warning and more time to evacuate. The system includes prerecorded announcements in the local dialect, and local government units can also customize the audio warnings and text blasts. Importantly, it is designed to keep working even when electricity is cut and mobile networks are down. The article also recognized actor Iyah Mina, whose Best Actress win at the 2018 Cinema One Original Awards marked a breakthrough for transgender representation in Philippine cinema. Mina emphasized that transgender people should portray transgender roles because representation matters and transgender identity is not a performance. Her win was presented as a meaningful challenge to industry norms and a step toward more authentic portrayals of transgender lives on screen. In literature, Segundo Matias Jr. was cited for the release of his young adult novel Mga Batang Poz, which tells the story of four teenagers living with HIV. The book drew controversy because of its subject matter and its challenge to religiously conservative attitudes, but it also earned strong praise from critics and writers. Notably, award-winning writer Ricky Lee described the novel as a “master class in storytelling,” underscoring Matias’ ability to bring marginalized narratives into mainstream discussion. The feature also turned to the hospitality industry, highlighting Nowie and Odette Potenciano of The Sunny Side Group in Boracay. When the six-month closure of Boracay was announced, the couple had little time to prepare and focused first on protecting their employees. With help from friends in Manila, they set up temporary pop-up versions of their restaurants in Makati and Alabang. They also arranged transport and housing for their 50 staff members so they would not be left without income during the island’s shutdown. The couple acknowledged the financial cost, but said doing nothing would have been harder to accept. In film production, Bianca Balbuena was recognized as a key force behind some of the year’s most notable local films, including Lav Diaz’s Panahon ng Halimaw, Dwein Baltazar’s Gusto Kita With All My Hypothalamus and Oda sa Wala, and Kenneth Dagatan’s horror film Ma. The article described her as a producer who learned how to secure funding for ambitious projects and who consistently helps bring challenging, unconventional films to life. The piece also highlighted Anthill Fabric Gallery, which works with weaving communities across the Philippines to preserve local textiles through contemporary, zero-waste design. The enterprise ensures that women weavers receive attention and fair opportunities, while also helping them through incentives, savings programs, and business systems that can support long-term livelihood and entrepreneurship. Proudly Promdi was included for promoting local spirits such as Tapuey and Bugnay rice wine, made in partnership with a small winemaking community in Adams, Ilocos Norte. The company aims to encourage households to buy local spirits, support craftsmanship, and sustain community livelihoods. Finally, the feature noted Kurvine Chua, founder of United Cassette Philippines, who helped revive interest in cassette tapes. Chua argued that cassettes are a more accessible format than vinyl and have practical appeal for people in niche and underground music scenes. Through his efforts, cassette releases by both local and international artists found new life, showing that an old format could still thrive for aesthetic and practical reasons.

State-owned gas utility GAIL India Ltd said it has commissioned India’s second-largest rooftop solar power plant at its petrochemical complex in Pata, Uttar Pradesh. The 5.76 MWp project has been installed over warehouse roofs and covers about 65,000 square meters. GAIL said the plant is expected to operate at a plant load factor of around 15% annually and generate more than 79 lakh kilowatt-hours of electricity each year for captive use at its gas-based petrochemicals facility. The company said the project will cut carbon emissions by about 6,300 tonnes per year and support India’s climate goals. GAIL chairman and managing director B.C. Tripathi said the initiative reflects the company’s effort to lower the carbon footprint of its installations and aligns with the “Make in India” campaign, with Indian vendors handling manufacturing, supply and execution. The article notes that Tata Power Solar commissioned a larger 12 MW rooftop project in Amritsar in December 2015. It also places GAIL’s project in the context of India’s broader renewable energy goals, including a target of 40 GW of rooftop solar by 2022 as part of 175 GW of non-hydro renewable capacity.

Assets held by the world’s sovereign wealth funds and public pension funds reached a record $31.9 trillion in 2021, boosted by rising U.S. stock prices and higher oil prices, according to an annual Global SWF report. Sovereign wealth fund assets rose 6% to $10.5 trillion, while public pension fund assets climbed 9% to $21.4 trillion. The report said state-owned investors were also more active than in any of the previous six years, deploying $215.6 billion across more deals, with sovereign wealth funds accounting for nearly half of that total. Singapore’s GIC was the most active investor, increasing dealmaking by 75% to $31.1 billion across 109 deals, with more than a third of its capital going into real estate, especially logistics. Venture capital remained a relatively small part of overall allocations, but rose by more than 80% to $18.2 billion, with Singapore’s Temasek contributing more than a quarter. The report also noted that investors were watching China closely amid the crackdown on technology firms, though most remained bullish on Chinese stocks. Germany has closed its last black coal mine, marking the end of an industry that helped fuel the country’s industrial rise and postwar recovery. At the Prosper-Haniel mine in Bottrop, seven miners emerged from deep underground carrying the final lump of coal ever to be brought up from the site. Dust-covered and emotional, they handed the football-sized piece to President Frank-Walter Steinmeier and offered the traditional miners’ farewell, “Glueck Auf,” meaning “good luck.” Steinmeier called the moment the end of “a piece of German history,” saying the country’s development over the past two centuries would have been unthinkable without coal. Prosper-Haniel and another mine in Ibbenbueren, about 60 miles north, were the last survivors of a once-dominant coal sector that employed about 500,000 people at its peak in the 1950s. Their output had long supported the Ruhr Valley’s steel mills, but the industry gradually declined as cheaper imported coal undercut German production. For decades, the mines survived only through heavy subsidies. In 2007, Germany decided to phase out the industry, promising early retirement or retraining for remaining workers. Since 1998, federal support for coal mining has exceeded 40 billion euros, with another 2.7 billion euros planned through 2022. Some of that money goes toward mine maintenance and environmental cleanup, including efforts to prevent parts of the Ruhr region from sinking as old tunnels collapse. Large sums have also supported redevelopment in the region, which has increasingly shifted toward universities, research centers and technology start-ups. Steinmeier encouraged miners and their families to look to the future while taking pride in the Ruhr’s history as a multicultural industrial region shaped by immigration from Poland, Italy and Turkey. The closure is also seen as a preview of larger energy challenges ahead. Germany still generates nearly two-fifths of its electricity from coal, and scientists say that must fall if the country is to cut greenhouse gas emissions. Lignite, or brown coal, remains in use and is even dirtier than black coal. A government panel is expected to propose a gradual lignite phaseout. Some Germans worry renewable energy will not fully replace coal and nuclear power, which the country plans to abandon by 2022. The ceremony also honored miners who died underground, underscoring the risks of the work. That danger was reinforced soon after, when a miner died in Ibbenbueren and 13 miners were killed in a Czech coal mine explosion.

# Germany Closes Its Last Black Coal Mine Germany marked the end of an era last Friday when the Prosper-Haniel mine in Bottrop closed, bringing deep-shaft black coal mining to an end in the country. Seven miners emerged from over 3,000 feet below ground with the final lump of coal, which they presented to President Frank-Walter Steinmeier with the traditional miners' greeting "Glueck Auf" (good luck). The ceremony symbolized the conclusion of an industry fundamental to Germany's industrial revolution and postwar economic recovery. The Prosper-Haniel mine and the Ibbenbueren colliery, located 60 miles north, were the last operating deep mines in a region that once employed half a million workers at its peak in the 1950s. These mines had sustained the Ruhr Valley's steel industry until cheaper foreign coal imports rendered German "black gold" uneconomical. The mines survived only through substantial government subsidies. In 2007, Germany decided to phase out coal mining, offering early retirement and retraining programs to remaining workers. Since 1998, the coal industry has received over 40 billion euros in federal funds, with an additional 2.7 billion euros allocated through 2022. These funds support mine maintenance, environmental cleanup—including preventing ground subsidence from tunnel collapse—and regional economic redevelopment. The Ruhr region has successfully diversified, developing universities, research facilities, and technology startups. The area's cultural heritage as a 19th-century melting pot, attracting Polish, Italian, and Turkish immigrant workers, was acknowledged by President Steinmeier. The closure of deep-shaft mining represents a significant test for Germany's planned phase-out of open-cast lignite (brown coal) mines. Currently, Germany generates nearly 40 percent of its electricity from coal, which scientists argue is incompatible with reducing greenhouse gas emissions. Lignite is dirtier than black coal but remains cheaper to extract. A government panel will deliver proposals in February for gradually phasing out lignite operations. Concerns persist about whether renewable energy sources alone can adequately power Germany's industrial economy, especially following the planned 2022 nuclear plant shutdown. Globally, over 400 coal mining regions face similar closure pressures in coming decades due to climate change mitigation efforts.

German Chancellor Angela Merkel is set to make her first-ever visit to the Auschwitz-Birkenau Memorial on Friday, near the end of her 14 years in office, and will bring a 60 million euro donation from Germany to support conservation of the former Nazi death camp site, according to the museum. The visit is notable because Merkel has long spoken openly about Germany’s responsibility for the crimes of World War Two, but she had not yet visited Auschwitz itself. Her trip will place her alongside previous German chancellors who visited the site before leaving office. Museum director Piotr Cywinski said Auschwitz is not only a museum but also “the biggest cemetery in the world,” stressing that remembrance is essential for shaping the present and future. Merkel is making the visit at the invitation of the Auschwitz foundation and will announce the donation during a ceremony marking the foundation’s 10th anniversary. The contribution is split evenly between Germany’s federal government and the country’s regional governments. It will make Germany the largest donor to the Auschwitz-Birkenau Foundation, which finances preservation work at the site where more than 1 million people were murdered in what was then Nazi-occupied Poland. The article notes that more than 3 million of Poland’s 3.2 million Jews were killed by the Nazis, representing about half of all Jews murdered in the Holocaust. The donation will help preserve 30 brick barracks in Birkenau, including structures such as an old kitchen and latrine. Cywinski explained that many of the buildings were never meant to last long and require ongoing maintenance. He said the foundation needs roughly 18 million to 20 million zlotys, or about $4.62 million to $5.13 million, each year for conservation. He also said the funding is intended as an investment in the future and in education, not as a way to single out any country’s past. The foundation’s endowment, which depends on bond payouts, has not generated as much as hoped, partly because of the 2009 financial crisis. Two years ago, Cywinski appealed to donor countries for more help, but Germany is the only one to respond so far. The United States and Poland had previously been major donors. Merkel has visited other concentration camp sites before and has met Auschwitz survivors.

Assets held by the world’s sovereign wealth funds and public pension funds reached a record $31.9 trillion in 2021, according to an annual report by Global SWF. The rise was driven by stronger U.S. stock markets and higher oil prices. Sovereign wealth fund assets increased 6% to $10.5 trillion, while public pension fund assets climbed 9% to $21.4 trillion. The report said state-owned investors also became more active, deploying more capital in 2021 than in any of the previous six years. They invested $215.6 billion across a record level of dealmaking, with nearly half of that coming from sovereign wealth funds. Singapore’s GIC was the most active fund, boosting its dealmaking by 75% to $31.1 billion across 109 deals, with more than a third of the money going into real estate, especially logistics. Global SWF noted that emerging markets attracted only 23% of deployed capital, one of the lowest shares in six years. Venture capital, though still a small portion of overall spending, rose more than 80% to $18.2 billion, with Singapore’s Temasek responsible for more than a quarter of that. The report said the pandemic shifted investment strategies toward healthcare, retail, consumer and technology sectors. Investors are also watching China closely amid regulatory crackdowns, though most remain bullish on Chinese stocks. Four new sovereign wealth funds were launched during the year, including Azerbaijan Investment Holdings, and several more are planned.

Iranian Kurdish exiles in Iraq say they support the protests sweeping Iran but reject accusations from Tehran that they are orchestrating the unrest. The exiles, members of banned Iranian Kurdish opposition parties based in northern Iraq, say their influence inside Iran is limited and that the demonstrations are being driven primarily by anger among ordinary Iranians, especially over the treatment of women after the death of 22-year-old Mahsa Amini in police custody. The article opens in Sulimaniyah, Iraq, where Dara Qureshi, an exile and activist, scrolls through phone contacts that use aliases to protect activists across the border in Iran. He is helping one contact, “Brwa,” figure out how to use Starlink after Elon Musk said the satellite internet service would be made available to Iranians affected by state internet restrictions. Qureshi says he tries to help, but there is only a brief window before the other person’s internet connection is cut off again. That kind of contact, the exiles say, reflects the limited and fragile role they play in the protests. Iranian authorities have blamed foreign-backed elements and Kurdish opposition groups for the unrest, which has spread to more than 40 cities. The exiles counter that the government is using them as scapegoats to distract from the broader public anger driving the protests. They say the demonstrations began after Amini, an Iranian Kurdish woman from the city of Saqqez, died after being arrested by Tehran’s morality police for allegedly wearing her mandatory headscarf improperly. In Kurdish communities, she is often called by her Kurdish name, Zhina. The protests have prompted a harsh response from Iranian authorities. This week, Iran launched three rounds of drone and missile strikes against Iraq-based Iranian Kurdish opposition bases in northern Iraq, killing at least nine people. The attacks were condemned by Iraqi officials and the wider international community, and Iran’s ambassador to Iraq was summoned by the Iraqi Foreign Ministry. Iran also announced the arrest of nine foreigners in connection with the demonstrations. Amnesty International said it obtained leaked documents showing that Iranian security forces were ordered to “severely confront” protesters and reported that at least 52 people had been killed since the unrest began. Iranian state television put the toll at at least 41 protesters and police killed and said hundreds had been arrested. The Kurdish opposition parties say their reach inside Iran is mostly confined to Kurdish-majority areas in the west. Rosaline Kamangir, an Iranian Kurdish women’s rights activist, said the parties may have issued calls for protests and strikes, but the people organizing on the ground are inside Iran. She said local activists are acting on their own beliefs, even if they sometimes agree with the parties’ views. The article notes that Iran’s Kurdish regions have long hosted a separatist movement that predates the 1979 Islamic Revolution and later became a low-level guerrilla insurgency against Iran’s Revolutionary Guard. But the current protests are not primarily nationalist. Instead, they have become part of a broader nationwide movement centered on women’s rights and opposition to repression. Women have burned their hijabs and cut their hair during demonstrations, turning Amini into a symbol of defiance. Residents described deep anger and fear. A woman in Bukan, identified as Nisreen, said she joined protests because Amini’s death made her angry and because women in Iran are oppressed and have few opportunities. She said the first protest she attended was peaceful before shootings and arrests began. The exiles also described the personal toll of the crackdown and the limits of their own activism. Kawser Fattahi of Komala said two cousins in Iran had disappeared after being taken away, and Qureshi said his uncle was detained during a protest in Bukan. Fattahi had to leave her party compound in Koya after it was hit in the Iranian strikes, and she and others dispersed to friends’ homes or mountain areas. Many activists keep two phones and rely on social media to encourage protests and strikes, but widespread internet outages in Iran have made communication far more difficult. Messages that once arrived constantly now come only in bursts every couple of days.

With widespread outages affecting social media access, the opposition parties' ability to coordinate has become severely limited. He said humanitarian aid alone is not enough unless the Houthis are also forced to stop politicizing humanitarian issues. He added that meaningful discussion of sustainable development is impossible in densely populated areas under militia control. He accused the Houthis of blocking life-saving vaccines from entering their territories, which he said has led to the return of deadly diseases that had been eradicated two decades ago. He also described severe damage across Yemen’s education, service, and economic sectors, saying millions of students have returned to school under harsh conditions and that the state protection network supporting education has collapsed. According to Alimi, the Houthis have destroyed Yemen’s economic achievements over recent decades. Alongside his UN appearance, Alimi held a series of meetings with UN and international officials to highlight the crisis and seek backing for peace efforts. He and PLC Vice President Aidrous al-Zubaidi met with US Secretary of State Antony Blinken, discussing Yemen’s situation and mediation efforts by Saudi Arabia and Oman to renew the truce and launch a comprehensive UN-led political process. Alimi also thanked the US for humanitarian help amid Houthi attacks on oil infrastructure and shipping. He later met UN Under-Secretary-General Vladimir Voronkov to discuss the wider security implications of the war, calling for support to rebuild state institutions, law enforcement, and counterterrorism capabilities. In a separate meeting with IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva, he discussed Yemen’s economic and humanitarian situation and expressed appreciation for IMF assistance, including Special Drawing Rights. Alimi also praised Saudi support for Yemen’s state budget and its role in stabilizing the country’s economy and services.

Yemen’s Huthi rebels, also known as Ansarallah, have sharply escalated attacks on ships in the Red Sea, saying they are retaliating against Israel’s military campaign in Gaza. The strikes have disrupted one of the world’s most important shipping lanes and raised fears that the Gaza war could widen into a broader regional conflict involving Iran-backed militias and outside powers. The Huthi movement emerged in the 1990s in northern Yemen around Hussein al-Huthi, who launched a religious revival movement called “Believing Youth” to defend Zaidism, a centuries-old branch of Shia Islam. Zaidis had once ruled Yemen for centuries, but were marginalized after the Sunni regime that took power following the 1962 civil war. Al-Huthi’s movement opposed radical Sunnism, especially Saudi-backed Wahhabi influence, and its followers became known as Huthis. At first, Yemen’s longtime president Ali Abdullah Saleh tolerated the movement, but as it grew more popular and more critical of the government, it became a threat. Tensions intensified in 2003, when Saleh backed the U.S.-led invasion of Iraq, a move many Yemenis opposed. Al-Huthi capitalized on public anger by organizing mass protests. After months of unrest, Saleh ordered his arrest. Al-Huthi was killed by Yemeni forces in September 2004, but the movement survived and expanded its military wing. The Huthis gained momentum during the Arab Spring in 2011, taking control of the northern province of Saada and calling for the end of the Saleh regime. Saleh eventually agreed to step down and transfer power to Vice President Abd-Rabbu Mansour Hadi, but the new government was also unpopular. In 2014, the Huthis seized parts of Sanaa, Yemen’s capital, and by early 2015 they had stormed the presidential palace. Hadi fled to Saudi Arabia, which then launched a military campaign against the Huthis in March 2015 at his request. What was expected to be a quick intervention turned into a long and devastating war. A ceasefire was signed in 2022, but it expired after six months, and the conflict has not returned to full-scale fighting. The United Nations says the war has become the world’s worst humanitarian crisis, with nearly a quarter of a million people killed. Since the ceasefire, the Huthis have consolidated control over most of northern Yemen and have sought a permanent settlement with Saudi Arabia that would solidify their rule. Iran has played a major role in strengthening the group. According to U.S. and independent assessments, Tehran increased support to the Huthis as the Yemeni war escalated and its rivalry with Saudi Arabia deepened. They have used drones and anti-ship missiles to attack commercial vessels, including ships not believed to have any link to Israel. The Red Sea is a critical global trade route stretching from the Bab-el-Mandeb strait near Yemen to the Suez Canal in Egypt. About 12% of global trade and 30% of container traffic passes through it. The article concludes that the Biden administration, already under pressure to push Israel toward winding down the Gaza war, may find itself drawn deeper into Middle East conflict because of the Huthis’ increasingly effective and disruptive campaign.

Iranian Kurdish exiles based in Iraq say they have been supporting protesters inside Iran but insist they are not organizing the unrest, despite accusations from Tehran that the demonstrations are foreign-backed and directed by Kurdish opposition groups. The protests began after the death of 22-year-old Mahsa Amini, an Iranian Kurdish woman who died in custody after morality police in Tehran arrested her for allegedly wearing her headscarf improperly. The unrest has spread to more than 40 cities and has become one of the biggest challenges to Iran’s authorities in years. The article opens in Sulimaniyah, Iraq, where Dara Qureshi, a member of an exiled Iranian Kurdish opposition party, is shown trying to help an activist in Iran who is asking how to access Starlink, the satellite internet service Elon Musk said he would make available to Iranians facing state internet restrictions. Qureshi knows the activist has only a few minutes of connectivity before the internet cuts out. This exchange illustrates the limited but real support Kurdish exiles provide through phone contacts, social media, and advice, even as they deny any central role in organizing the protests. Iranian officials have used that support to argue that the protests were orchestrated by outside forces. Kurdish exiles reject that claim, saying the anger driving the demonstrations is broad-based and domestic, rooted in outrage over women’s treatment and government repression. Rosaline Kamangir, an Iranian Kurdish women’s rights activist, said the Kurdish parties issued calls for protests and strikes in Kurdish areas, but the people actually organizing and taking to the streets are inside Iran. She said local protesters may agree with the parties politically, but they are acting on their own beliefs. The protests have not taken on a strongly Kurdish nationalist character. Although Amini came from Saqqez in Iran’s Kurdish region and many Kurds refer to her by her Kurdish name, Zhina, the demonstrations have instead centered on women’s rights and opposition to the Islamic Republic’s restrictions. Women protesters have burned their hijabs and cut their hair in public, turning Amini into a symbol of wider anger over repression. A woman in the Kurdish town of Bukan, identified as Nisreen, said she joined because Amini’s death made her angry and because women in Iran are oppressed and denied opportunities. She said the first protest she attended began peacefully but later turned violent when shooting and arrests started. The Kurdish regions of western Iran have long been home to separatist movements and low-level guerrilla conflict with Iran’s Revolutionary Guard. The main exiled Kurdish parties based in Iraq are the Kurdistan Democratic Party in Iran, Komala, and the Kurdistan Free Life Party, or PJAK. Their influence inside Iran is limited by geography, security, and the danger of crossing the border. Still, activists say nearly every family in the Kurdish regions knows someone linked to these parties or someone who has been arrested in the protests. Iran’s response has intensified sharply. This week it launched three rounds of drone and missile strikes against Iraqi bases used by Iranian Kurdish opposition groups, killing at least nine people and prompting condemnation from Iraqi officials and the international community. Iran’s ambassador to Iraq was summoned by the Iraqi Foreign Ministry. At home, Iran has also stepped up arrests, including nine foreigners detained over the demonstrations, according to state media. Amnesty International said leaked documents show authorities ordered security forces to “severely confront” protesters and reported at least 52 deaths since the unrest began, while Iranian state TV put the toll at 41 protesters and police, with hundreds arrested. For exiles like Kawser Fattahi of Komala, the protests are deeply personal. She said relatives in Iran have been detained or are missing, and her own family members are protesting. Because of internet shutdowns, communication is increasingly difficult, with activists relying on unregistered calls and brief bursts of online access. As the crackdown grows, Kurdish exiles say they remain connected to events in Iran, but only as supporters and intermediaries—not as the force behind the uprising.

U.S. crude oil production is climbing again, according to the Energy Information Administration. For the week ending Dec. 21, total U.S. output reached 11.697 million barrels per day, up 99,000 barrels per day from the previous week and 1.9 million barrels per day higher than a year earlier. Commercial crude inventories in the United States were essentially unchanged week to week, standing at 441.4 million barrels, about 7% above the five-year average for this time of year. Imports also rose, averaging 7.7 million barrels per day, an increase of 233,000 barrels per day from the prior week, though the four-week average remained 2.3% below the same period last year. Oil prices have been volatile. After jumping 8% on Wednesday, the biggest one-day gain in two years, prices fell 2% the next day. Even with that rebound and retreat, U.S. and global crude benchmarks have dropped more than one-third since early October and are on track to finish the year down more than 20%. In Kansas, crude at CHS in McPherson was quoted at $35.50 per barrel last Friday, more than $5 lower than the start of the month and roughly $20 below the end-of-October level. The article also highlights growing political uncertainty in New Mexico, where crude production has more than doubled over the past four years. Industry leaders are worried that the state’s shift to Democratic control in January will bring tighter regulation and lower revenues. The incoming governor and state land commissioner plan to limit new leasing on state lands where drillers had intended to tap freshwater aquifers, and they also want to crack down on methane waste from flaring. The new land commissioner will oversee 9 million acres of state land and wants to raise the production royalty by at least one-third, to match Texas’ rate and increase funding for schools and hospitals. In Louisiana, an offshore platform toppled by Hurricane Ivan in 2004 is still leaking oil into the Gulf of Mexico. The company involved, Taylor Energy, is challenging a Coast Guard order requiring it to design and install a containment system. A new estimate says the leak is releasing between 10,000 and 30,000 gallons of crude oil into the ocean each day. The October administrative order also included possible daily civil penalties of up to $40,000 for noncompliance. Environmental opposition is also growing in Alaska. Five conservation groups filed suit to block oil production from a proposed artificial gravel island in federal Arctic waters off Alaska’s north coast. They asked the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals to review approval of the Liberty project in the Beaufort Sea, arguing that the offshore production plan violates federal law. North Dakota reported another record for oil and gas production and for the number of producing wells, but its gas-capture performance worsened. Preliminary October figures showed more than 43 million barrels of oil produced statewide, equal to 1.39 million barrels per day and up more than 32,000 barrels per day from the prior month. At the same time, operators flared more than 20% of the natural gas produced at oil wells, about 2 percentage points worse than the previous month. The state recently said it was relaxing its anti-flaring goals, which have not been met for years. Rail traffic carrying petroleum continues to rise because pipeline bottlenecks persist. The Association of American Railroads said petroleum and petroleum products filled more than 30,000 rail cars, up more than 27% from a year earlier. The year-to-date total through Dec. 15 was nearly 584,000 rail cars, up more than 17%. Canada saw similar growth, with more than 11,000 tanker cars filled, up more than 31%, and a 22% increase for the year. In Canada, transportation constraints and weak crude prices have prompted new ideas and government support. Canadian National Railways says it is testing a method of mixing Alberta bitumen with plastic from grocery bags and then encasing it in more plastic, creating small pellets that can be shipped in grain hopper cars. The pellets are described as floating, sealed, and easier to clean up in a spill. Meanwhile, the Canadian government announced a $1.19 billion support package for the oil and gas industry, mainly in loans, to help firms find new export markets. Reuters reported that Canada recently hit record production of 4.9 million barrels per day but has struggled to move the crude to the United States because of transportation bottlenecks. Finally, Exxon-Mobil withdrew an export project in British Columbia from environmental review, effectively shelving the plan. The project had been expected to produce about 15 million tons per year of liquefied natural gas, with potential expansion to 30 million tons annually.

New Mexico’s space and creative technology sectors are in line for a potentially transformative federal investment, with two separate local coalitions named finalists for grants from the U.S. Economic Development Administration’s “Build Back Better Regional Challenge.” Each coalition could receive up to $100 million, meaning the state’s two proposals together could bring as much as $200 million into the region if both ultimately win. The two finalists are led by Central New Mexico Community College and the Albuquerque Hispano Chamber of Commerce. Their proposals were among 60 finalists chosen from 529 applications submitted nationwide. As finalists, each coalition will receive $500,000 to further develop its initial concept into a more detailed proposal for submission to the EDA in March. After that, the agency will choose between 20 and 30 coalitions for final awards. The funding comes from the $3 billion the EDA received last year through American Rescue Plan stimulus money to help communities recover from the COVID-19 pandemic. Of that total, $1 billion was set aside for the Build Back Better challenge, which is designed to strengthen regional industry clusters. The CNM-led proposal, called the Space Valley Coalition, includes New Space NM, the NM Trade Alliance and the NM Spaceport Authority. Its centerpiece is a proposed Space Valley Center in Albuquerque that would serve as a hub for New Mexico’s space industry. The facility would include a large auditorium for up to 750 people, breakout rooms for as many as 150, business offices and laboratory space for space companies. It is intended to become a central gathering and co-working location where companies, organizations and entrepreneurs can meet, collaborate, attend conferences and access accelerator and incubator services. Some workforce education and training programs would also be based there. Officials compared the concept to Rainforest Innovations at Innovate ABQ Downtown, which brings together public, private and academic partners to support entrepreneurship and startup growth. But in this case, the unifying force would be the space economy. The proposal’s backers say such a center could help elevate New Mexico’s profile nationally, attract conferences and businesses, and provide a dedicated site for government and industry meetings. A key feature would be a Sensitive Compartmented Information Facility, or SCIF, standard, allowing classified meetings for defense entities, government agencies and cleared companies. Supporters said such large SCIF-standard facilities are rare outside military bases, and that the center could become one of the country’s top venues for major classified space-related meetings. The CNM-led coalition is also seeking money for a multipurpose building at the vertical launch area of Spaceport America in southern New Mexico. That building would include rooms, labs, bays and storage space for rocket assembly, payload integration and processing, and mission control. In addition, the proposal includes new workforce development programs and the creation of a space-focused venture fund of up to $25 million, intended to invest in as many as 30 New Mexico companies over 10 years. A venture studio would provide business development support to those firms. If fully funded, the Mid-Region Council of Governments estimates the Space Valley proposal could generate $540 million in economic growth over 10 years, create at least 1,000 direct jobs and support thousands of indirect jobs. The second finalist, led by the Albuquerque Hispano Chamber of Commerce, is called Create New Mexico. That coalition brings together financial institutions, colleges, nonprofits and city governments with the goal of making Central and Northern New Mexico a leader in creative technologies such as animation, artificial intelligence, video games and 3-D modeling and printing. Create New Mexico would fund eight coordinated projects, each led by a different organization. Among them are a Santa Fe initiative to develop a mixed-use manufacturing and entrepreneurial hub and a Stagecoach Foundation program offering boot camps focused on creative technology in film and television. Grant Development Director Ryan Chavez said the coalition’s aim is to overcome the fragmentation that often keeps creative sectors isolated. The proposal seeks to build a sustainable cluster by bringing organizations together and aligning their efforts. Chavez said New Mexico, especially the Mid-Rio Grande and North Central regions, already has a higher-than-average concentration of jobs in these fields, but growth is limited by barriers such as weak broadband access, especially in rural and Native American communities. The coalition also pointed to a shortage of venture capital. To address that, organizations such as Santa Fe-based Creative Startups and Albuquerque-based DreamSpring would help support entrepreneurs. DreamSpring’s Metta Smith said her group would provide virtual and in-person technical assistance on credit, financial literacy and other basics for small business owners, many of whom are first-time borrowers. # New Mexico's Space and Tech Industries Compete for $200 Million in Federal Grants New Mexico's space and creative technology sectors are positioned to receive significant federal funding through the U.S. Economic Development Administration's "Build Back Better Regional Challenge." Two local community coalitions have been selected as finalists, each eligible to compete for up to $100 million in grants to develop their respective industries. ## The Competition and Timeline The Central New Mexico Community College and the Albuquerque Hispano Chamber of Commerce each led separate proposals that advanced to the finalist stage. These two proposals represent just 60 finalists selected from 529 grant requests submitted by organizations nationwide. Both coalitions will receive $500,000 each to develop more comprehensive plans for submission to the EDA in March. The federal agency will ultimately select between 20 and 30 coalition proposals for final grant awards. The funding originates from $3 billion allocated to the EDA under the American Rescue Plan as stimulus money to help states and communities recover from the coronavirus pandemic. The EDA designated $1 billion of this amount specifically for the Build Back Better challenge to develop and strengthen regional industry clusters across the country. ## The Space Valley Coalition Proposal The CNM-led "Space Valley Coalition," which includes the New Space NM industry alliance, the New Mexico Trade Alliance, and the New Mexico Spaceport Authority, proposes constructing a large "Space Valley Center" in Albuquerque. This facility would serve as a central hub for space industry development and collaboration. The proposed center would feature a 750-person auditorium, breakout rooms accommodating 150 people, business offices, and laboratory spaces for space companies. It would function similarly to the Rainforest Innovations building at the Innovate ABQ development zone downtown, but specifically dedicated to the space industry. The facility would host meetings, conferences, networking events, and collaborative initiatives while expanding space-focused business accelerators and incubator programs. A distinctive feature of the proposed center is its construction to Sensitive Compartmented Information Facility (SCIF) standards, allowing U.S. defense entities, government agencies, and cleared companies to conduct classified meetings and conferences. This would make it one of only a few large SCIF-standard facilities in the nation not located on a military base, addressing a significant gap in national infrastructure for classified meetings. Beyond the Albuquerque center, the coalition proposal includes funding for a multipurpose building at Spaceport America in southern New Mexico. This facility would support rocket assembly, payload integration, and mission control operations. The proposal also includes workforce development programs and establishment of a space-focused venture fund of up to $25 million to invest in approximately 30 New Mexico companies over ten years. If awarded the full $100 million grant, the Mid-Region Council of Governments estimates the projects would generate $540 million in economic growth over a decade, creating at least 1,000 direct jobs and thousands of indirect positions. ## The Create New Mexico Proposal The Hispano Chamber-led "Create New Mexico" coalition brings together financial institutions, colleges, nonprofits, and city governments to establish Central and Northern New Mexico as a leader in creative technologies. These technologies encompass animation, artificial intelligence, video games, and 3-D modeling and printing—fields combining creative and technical skills. The coalition proposes eight coordinated projects across the creative technology sector. Projects include Santa Fe's plan to establish a mixed-use manufacturing and entrepreneurial hub and the Stagecoach Foundation's boot camps for creative technology professionals in film and television. ## Addressing Regional Challenges The Create New Mexico coalition recognizes significant barriers to growth in the region. Poor internet access creates an urban-rural divide, particularly affecting rural and Native American communities. Additionally, venture capital funding shortages limit entrepreneurial opportunities. To address these issues, organizations like Creative Startups and DreamSpring will provide technical assistance, microloans, and a new seed fund supporting creative technology entrepreneurs, with 80 percent of loan recipients targeted to be women or ethnic minorities. Both coalitions view their $500,000 preliminary grants as opportunities to strengthen partnerships and develop more detailed proposals for March submission, positioning New Mexico to capitalize on federal economic development funding.

In Chandler, Arizona, a suburb near Phoenix where Waymo has been testing self-driving vans since 2017, public frustration with autonomous vehicles has at times turned into direct confrontation. Over the past two years, the city has seen at least 21 attacks on Waymo vehicles, ranging from tire slashing and rock throwing to dangerous attempts to force the vans off the road. The incidents, documented in police reports and first reported by The Arizona Republic, have made Chandler an early focal point for broader anxieties about driverless cars and the technology behind them. One of the most recent attacks took place one day in October, around noon, when a man emerged from a park and approached a Waymo van that was stopped at an intersection. Carrying an unidentified sharp object, he slashed one of the vehicle’s tires and then disappeared into the neighborhood on foot. Police identified him as a white man in his 20s. The episode was one of many in which residents or passers-by acted out against the vehicles, apparently motivated by anger, fear, or distrust. According to police records, some people have thrown rocks at the vans. Others have repeatedly tried to run them off the road. In one case, a woman yelled at a Waymo vehicle and told it to leave her suburban neighborhood. In another, a man pulled alongside a Waymo van and threatened the employee inside with a piece of PVC pipe. One of the most alarming incidents involved a man waving a .22-caliber revolver at a Waymo vehicle and the backup driver seated inside. He later told police he “despises” driverless cars and cited the death of a female pedestrian in nearby Tempe in March, when a self-driving Uber vehicle struck and killed her. Among the residents who have clashed with the vans were Erik O’Polka, 37, and his wife, Elizabeth, 35. Police warned O’Polka in November after multiple reports that his Jeep Wrangler had tried to run Waymo vans off the road, including one instance in which he drove head-on toward a self-driving vehicle until it had to stop abruptly. The couple said their hostility began after their 10-year-old son nearly was hit by one of the vehicles while playing in a cul-de-sac nearby. O’Polka said, “There are other places they can test,” and his wife said they had not consented to being part of a “beta test.” She also admitted that she may have forced one of the vehicles to pull over so she could yell at it to get out of the neighborhood. The article suggests that these attacks reflect a wider backlash against autonomous technology. Some analysts believe more of this behavior may emerge as the country debates the social consequences of driverless cars, including fears of job losses for human drivers and the idea that corporations are ceding mobility to machines. Media theorist Douglas Rushkoff argued that people are “lashing out justifiably,” comparing driverless cars to robotic “scabs” that replace workers who refuse to cross picket lines. He said many people believe the companies developing the technology do not have the public’s best interests at heart and that the human safety drivers inside these vehicles are effectively training systems that may eventually replace them. The relationship between Waymo and local police appears to have been complicated. In several incidents, emergency drivers told Chandler police that Waymo preferred not to pursue criminal charges against assailants. Officers also said the company was often reluctant to provide video evidence of attacks. In one case, a Waymo employee told police they would need a warrant to obtain footage recorded by the vehicles. Officer William Johnson described one incident involving a Chrysler PT Cruiser weaving between lanes and taunting a Waymo van. A Waymo manager showed him video images but would not let police keep them for a fuller investigation, saying the company did not want to pursue the matter and was concerned about disruptions to testing in Chandler. Waymo pushed back on the suggestion that it was downplaying the attacks. In a statement, spokeswoman Alexis Georgeson said the incidents represented only a small fraction of the more than 25,000 miles the company’s vans travel daily in Arizona. She said safety is the company’s top priority and that Arizonans have generally been welcoming and excited about the technology’s potential to make roads safer. Georgeson also said Waymo reports dangerous incidents and provides photos and videos to law enforcement when appropriate, and that it supports its drivers and does pursue cases of vandalism. Despite the hostility, Arizona officials have largely continued to welcome autonomous vehicle testing. Rob Antoniak, chief operating officer of Valley Metro, said the state still had “open arms” for driverless cars and warned that isolated criminals should not derail the future of transportation. Still, the opposition remains visible. In one August incident, Charles Pinkham, 37, stood in the street in front of a Waymo van in Chandler while heavily intoxicated. Officer Richard Rimbach wrote that Pinkham was alternately calm, belligerent, and agitated, and said he was tired of the vehicles driving in his neighborhood. The Waymo employee inside the van, Candice Dunson, declined to press charges and told police the company preferred to stop routing vehicles through the area. Pinkham received a warning, and the van moved on.

Boise-area customers will see higher utility bills in the new year after Idaho regulators approved rate increases for Idaho Power and Intermountain Gas, though both companies received less than they originally requested. Idaho Power, which serves more than 630,000 customers in southern Idaho, agreed to a settlement that will raise its annual revenue by $110 million, or 7.48%. The company had initially sought a much larger increase of $199.1 million, or 13.09%. According to the Idaho Public Utilities Commission, the average Idaho Power residential customer, using about 900 kilowatt-hours per month, will see a monthly bill increase of about $12.13. The new rates take effect Thursday, Jan. 1. The commission said Idaho Power needs the added revenue to help pay for investments in upgrading, replacing and building power lines, substations and other infrastructure, as well as wildlife resilience efforts. The commission said the settlement balanced customer concerns about limiting rate hikes with the company’s need to recover costs. Intermountain Gas, which has about 404,800 customers in southern Idaho, also won approval for a settlement that will increase rates by 6.02%, or about $2.45 a month, for the average residential customer. Its monthly residential customer charge will also rise by $3, to $11 a month. The company’s annual revenue will increase by $13 million, or 10.4%, less than the $26.5 million, or 22.2%, increase it originally requested. General service commercial customers will see monthly bills rise by 2.46%, or $4.42 a month, and their customer charge will increase by $8, to $23 a month. The new Intermountain Gas rates also take effect Thursday. The utility said the increase is needed for operational and maintenance costs and infrastructure investments. The commission said the settlement would allow Intermountain Gas to operate sustainably while avoiding a burden on customers. Adam Rush, a commission spokesperson, said both utilities met with intervenors earlier this year in an effort to reach agreement before a full hearing. He said the resulting increases were close to what the companies likely would have received anyway if the cases had been fully litigated. Intervenors in the Idaho Power case included the city of Boise, the U.S. Department of Energy, Micron, Kroger, Idahydro, the NW Energy Coalition, Clean Energy Opportunities and Industrial Customers of Idaho Power. In the Intermountain Gas case, Micron and the Alliance of Western Energy Consumers were among the intervenors. The commission held customer hearings for both cases in November. Separately, the commission approved Idaho Power’s application to buy power and energy storage capacity from Crimson Orchard Solar LLC, which is developing a large solar farm with battery storage in Elmore County near Mountain Home. The 20-year agreement begins June 1, 2027, and would provide Idaho Power with 100 megawatts of electricity and 100 megawatts of energy storage capacity. Crimson Orchard is a subsidiary of Clēnera, which is owned by Enlight Renewable Energy of Israel. Idaho Power said the project is needed because of system deficits and a lack of other viable energy options. The company also said electricity demand is expected to grow by 2.1% across all customer classes over the next two decades, driven not only by population growth but also by increased per-customer usage from electrification.

The City of Kelowna, B.C., is moving to protect a 147-year-old heritage log house after it was badly damaged by fire earlier this year. In a narrow vote last week, city council approved setting aside $29,000 to build a temporary roof for Fleming House, a measure intended to shield the structure from weather while longer-term decisions are made. Fleming House is a two-storey farmhouse built in 1871 by Frederick Brent, one of the region’s first European settlers. According to the city’s website, it was constructed from hand-hewn pine logs and is a rare surviving example from that period, when little building took place because of a recession. The logs are squared and substantial, measuring about 35 centimetres high and 17 centimetres thick. Brent also built the nearby Grist Mill, which the city describes as the oldest grist mill in British Columbia. Over the years, the house and mill changed hands several times. In 1900, John Dilworth modernized the house by adding milled siding, plaster walls, a rear storage shed with a shed roof, a porch and veranda, and two corbelled chimneys. The property was later bought by William Fleming in 1908. Both buildings were eventually moved to Kelowna’s Heritage Park in 2002. Don Knox of the Central Okanagan Historical Society said the structures are important links to the city’s past. He noted that the mill site was Kelowna’s first commercial enterprise and served as a gathering place where people from around the district would bring grain, socialize, and catch up on local news. The fire occurred over the summer when a cooking fire beside the house “got away” and spread to the building. Knox said the damage was severe, especially to the siding and interior. He also said the fire removed the later additions and left the house closer to its original form. A Dec. 3 report to council from the parks and building department, citing the Central Okanagan Heritage Society, recommended doing only the minimum needed to reduce current risks and preserve the building for possible future restoration. The report said a temporary roof would buy time for a more concrete heritage plan, especially as the nearby Okanagan Rail Trail attracts more pedestrians and cyclists. It also noted that Fleming House and the Grist Mill are not currently insurable because they lack fire suppression systems, and that fire remains a concern until additional protection, such as a hydrant, is installed. Knox said preserving the house matters because Kelowna has lost many of its oldest homes from the 1860s and 1870s, leaving few reminders of how the city once looked.

President Donald Trump on Monday urged Democratic lawmakers to cut short their holiday break and return to Washington to help pass funding that would reopen parts of the federal government, which had been shut down for 10 days. Trump argued that a “properly built” wall would sharply reduce illegal immigration and help stop drug and weapons trafficking. He dismissed Democrats’ criticism that a wall is outdated or ineffective, saying it would work “almost 100%” and calling it more immoral not to build one if people are dying. His remarks appeared to reference the deaths of two young Guatemalan migrants in December after being taken into custody by U.S. border agents. The shutdown began on Dec. 22 after Republican and Democratic negotiators reached an impasse over Trump’s demand for more than $5 billion for the wall. The funding lapse has affected agencies in 10 departments, including Transportation and Justice, as well as many national parks. About 800,000 of the 2.1 million federal workers are affected and will not receive pay during the shutdown. Officials and lawmakers have warned the closure could last into early January, when Democrats are set to take control of the House and could pass a budget without wall funding. This is Trump’s third government shutdown since taking office in 2017.

Belarus’s first remote Earth sensing satellite has generated economic benefits that, according to Sergei Zolotoi, director of the National Academy of Sciences’ Geoinformation Systems enterprise, exceed the cost of building the satellite and operating the entire system by more than $30 million. He made the remarks in BelTA’s YouTube project *After the Fact: Lukashenko’s Decisions*. Zolotoi said the value of the satellite system cannot be judged only by direct commercial returns, because optoelectronic surveillance satellites are now used primarily for national security tasks. He noted that in Western countries governments often make major advance commitments to satellite projects, guaranteeing a large share of output for state use. In his words, this model allows companies such as SpaceX to secure financing because most of the satellite’s capacity is already sold in advance, leaving only a small portion for commercial use. He recalled that when Belarus launched its first satellite in 2006, only two or three satellites with two-meter resolution were in orbit. At that time, scanning such imagery cost about $8 per square kilometer, while a satellite could cover roughly 100,000 square kilometers per day. Under those conditions, selling even 10% of the output would have allowed the project to pay for itself within two years. But by 2012, the market had changed dramatically: many more satellites were available, and the price of such scanning had fallen to around $0.30 per square kilometer, more than 20 times lower, while the cost of building a satellite remained largely unchanged. Zolotoi emphasized that despite the more competitive market, high-resolution foreign satellite data cannot always be bought when it is most needed. He said it is currently impossible to purchase such data over the territory of Ukraine or Belarus, meaning countries without their own satellites may simply not have access to it during critical situations. He argued that the project’s economic effect should also include indirect benefits, especially revenues from software, technologies, and devices created during the satellite program. According to him, those earnings alone surpassed the cost of the BKA satellite and the operation of the system by more than $30 million. Zolotoi also pointed to practical uses of the system. Belarus’s Emergencies Ministry receives information on temperature anomalies and fires, including in neighboring countries. He cited the 2019 Chernobyl exclusion zone fire, when Belarusian authorities were warned two weeks before the blaze approached the border. Belarusian firefighters worked near the border, and only four hectares burned on the Belarusian side, compared with thousands on the Ukrainian side. He also mentioned use of the data in Venezuela to assess coastal erosion.

# Economic Impact of Belarus's Remote Earth Sensing Satellite Belarus's remote Earth sensing satellite, launched in 2012, has proven economically beneficial despite initial skepticism about its commercial viability. According to Sergei Zolotoi, Director of Geoinformation Systems at the National Academy of Sciences of Belarus, earnings from selling technologies and devices developed through the project exceed the satellite's construction and operational costs by over $30 million. Zolotoi explained that evaluating such projects requires looking beyond direct commercial returns. He noted that Western governments typically guarantee purchasing 80% of satellite output, with only 15-20% available for commercial use. This model enables financing through loans and ensures sustainability. The satellite market has become increasingly competitive since Belarus's 2006 launch of its first satellite. When that first satellite operated, only 2-3 satellites with 2-meter resolution existed, with scanning costs at $8 per square kilometer. By 2012, the market had transformed dramatically—scanning costs dropped to approximately $0.30 per square kilometer, a 20-fold decrease, while satellite manufacturing costs remained relatively stable. Despite market challenges, Zolotoi emphasized the strategic importance of domestic satellite capability. High-resolution space data over Belarus and Ukraine cannot be purchased from foreign sources, particularly during critical situations. This autonomous data access proved invaluable during the 2019 Chernobyl exclusion zone fire, when Belarus's remote sensing system detected the emergency two weeks before it threatened the border, while Ukrainian authorities denied its occurrence. Belarusian emergency services used this information to prevent fire spread, limiting damage to four hectares on their side compared to thousands in Ukraine. The satellite system generates indirect economic benefits beyond direct sales. The Emergencies Ministry uses it for monitoring temperature anomalies and fires across borders. Additionally, technologies developed through the project have found international applications, including coast erosion evaluation work in Venezuela. Zolotoi concluded that while space technologies drive domestic production sector development, space data effectively addresses various national economy tasks. Therefore, assessing the satellite project's success requires considering both direct commercial effects and indirect benefits, including national security, emergency management, and technological advancement—factors that justify the initial investment beyond simple economic calculations.

Risebit announced a new generation of blockchain-based investment platforms designed to offer users lower interest rates, transparency, and security. The company said it will also launch its own cryptocurrency, Risecoin, which the community will use to vote on investment projects. A major feature of the platform is “intelligent arbitrage,” a system that scans exchanges to find the best conversion rate for crypto assets and then routes transactions to the exchange offering the most favorable price. Risebit said this approach is intended to evolve into a cross-chain solution rather than remain limited to a single decentralized exchange. The platform currently operates on BNB Chain, but the team said it is working to expand to other blockchains, including Ethereum, Avalanche, Polygon, and Moonbeam. Risebit also plans to add borrowing and lending services. According to the company’s whitepaper, users will post cryptocurrency as collateral in order to borrow BUSD, with interest rates expected to be lower than those charged by traditional banks. If collateral value falls below a set threshold, the platform will automatically sell the assets to restore liquidity and cover the loan, helping prevent losses from sharp market declines. Bitcoin, Ethereum, Cardano, Polkadot, Avalanche, and Solana were among the assets named as acceptable collateral. The company also outlined a governance system that will let users vote on projects, with voting expected to take one to two weeks before a winner is announced. Risebit described itself as a decentralized investment platform that also offers mining, staking, and other services, and said its native token will play a central role.

# Risebit Launches Next-Generation Investment Platform Risebit announced a new decentralized investment platform on November 21, 2022, offering users affordable interest rates, transparency, and security. The platform will introduce Risecoin, its native cryptocurrency, which community members will use to vote on investment projects. ## Key Features **Intelligent Arbitrage System**: Risebit employs an algorithm that searches across multiple exchanges to find the best conversion rates for cryptocurrency assets, automatically routing transactions to the optimal decentralized exchange (DEX). The system aims to become a cross-chain solution beyond single DEX limitations, providing users enhanced price discovery and options. Currently operating on BNB Chain, the team plans to expand to Ethereum, Avalanche, Polygon, and Moonbeam blockchains. **Lending and Borrowing Services**: The platform offers significantly lower interest rates than traditional banks. Users must post cryptocurrency as collateral to borrow BUSD. The system automatically liquidates collateral if its value falls below settlement price, maintaining liquidity and covering loan-related taxes. Accepted collaterals include Bitcoin, Ethereum, Cardano, Polkadot, Avalanche, and Solana. **Governance System**: Users gain voting control over platform decisions through a two-step workflow. Voting operations typically last 1-2 weeks before Risebit announces winning projects. Risebit positions itself as a comprehensive blockchain-based investment platform enabling safe, reliable returns through trading, mining, staking, and additional services.

U.S. Secretary of State John F. Kerry and Argentine Foreign Minister Susana Malcorra launched a High-Level Dialogue in Buenos Aires aimed at deepening the bilateral partnership between the United States and Argentina. The two governments said the dialogue would be built on shared values, principles, and interests, and would seek concrete results in areas such as inclusive economic development, trade and investment, labor, tourism, and educational exchange. It would also address broader regional and global issues, including democracy and human rights, peacekeeping, security cooperation, non-proliferation, the environment, climate change, and clean energy. The officials agreed that their teams would continue talks later in the year, with annual meetings planned afterward. The dialogue was accompanied by a working lunch hosted by Malcorra, where the sides discussed economic challenges, reform priorities, and cooperation to support Argentina’s reintegration into the international financial community and promote sustainable growth in both countries. The statement said the meeting built on the positive agenda created by President Mauricio Macri’s March 2016 visit from President Barack Obama to Argentina. On global issues, the two countries said they shared concern over the refugee crisis and the humanitarian tragedy it represents. Kerry praised Macri’s decision to accept 3,000 Syrian refugees and provide humanitarian aid to neighboring countries affected by the Syrian conflict. The United States said it would support Argentina’s efforts as part of a shared international responsibility. Kerry also welcomed Argentina’s pledge earlier in the year to strengthen its Intended Nationally Determined Contribution under the climate framework and emphasized the need for an ambitious revision. Both countries reaffirmed their commitment to bring the Paris Agreement into force in 2016 and to keep working toward an amendment to phase down hydrofluorocarbons by October 2016. Kerry also welcomed Argentina’s participation in the September 2016 Our Ocean conference in Washington. In addition, the two sides identified priorities for supporting Argentina’s contributions to UN peacekeeping, including the implementation of $1.2 million in U.S. assistance. In their discussion of the Western Hemisphere, Kerry and Malcorra restated their commitment to peace, democracy, and human rights in the Americas. They welcomed progress toward a final peace accord between Colombia and the FARC and reaffirmed support for Colombia’s efforts to secure a lasting peace. The United States praised Argentina for offering unarmed international observers for the future UN Political Mission, along with demining assistance, technical support, and humanitarian aid once a peace deal is signed. They also discussed Venezuela. The officials welcomed the National Electoral Council’s verification of the signatures needed to advance a recall referendum to the petition stage and urged Venezuelan authorities to set a timetable for the rest of the process. They voiced support for a timely, inclusive, and effective political dialogue to address the needs of the Venezuelan people. They also reiterated support for prior statements from the Organization of American States and for mediation efforts by UNASUR, former presidents of Panama and the Dominican Republic, and a former Spanish prime minister, all aimed at a peaceful, constitutional solution. The two sides also endorsed the international call for peaceful, transparent, and credible elections in Haiti so the country could elect a president as soon as possible. On human rights, both governments reaffirmed support for the Organization of American States and the Inter-American Human Rights System, and for cooperation in the UN and other forums. At President Macri’s request, and consistent with President Obama’s pledge to declassify more U.S. records on abuses committed by Argentina’s military dictatorship, Kerry delivered the first tranche of declassified documents to Macri. Economically, Kerry welcomed Argentina’s measures to restore sustainable growth and attract foreign investment, calling the settlement of the long-running dispute with holdout bondholders a critical step. He also praised Argentina’s efforts to rejoin the international financial community, including renewed consultations with the IMF and its commitment to chair the G-20 in 2018. The United States welcomed Argentina’s observer status in the Pacific Alliance and said both governments, along with the private sector, should work to remove trade barriers, improve market access, protect intellectual property, and identify new investment opportunities. The statement highlighted upcoming commercial engagement, including the first Trade and Investment Framework Agreement meeting in Buenos Aires on August 29 and the first Commercial Dialogue in Washington later in the year.
