The article argues that the most consequential event of 2019 was Hong Kong’s 235-day uprising against Beijing, which began on April 3 with the introduction of an extradition bill by Hong Kong authorities backed by China. Critics saw the bill as a tool that would allow Beijing to send political opponents and other inconvenient people into the mainland’s repressive legal system. What started as opposition to the bill grew into a much broader pro-democracy movement that, by late November, had shaken both Hong Kong and the Chinese Communist Party’s confidence. The protests culminated in the Nov. 24 district council elections, where pro-democracy candidates won a sweeping victory, surprising Beijing, which had expected voters to rebuke the demonstrators. The column places Hong Kong in a wider regional and historical context. It notes that Taiwan was heading into a presidential election in early 2020, after Xi Jinping made Taiwan a central focus of his New Year’s speech on Jan. 2, 2019. The article suggests that if Taiwan re-elected President Tsai Ing-wen, it would, like Hong Kong, be rejecting China’s “one country, two systems” formula as a path to the gradual loss of freedom. The piece also contrasts the end of the Cold War with the present. Thirty years after the fall of the Berlin Wall, the world still has roughly 1.5 billion people living under communist regimes, with China accounting for the overwhelming majority. The author stresses that China’s system remains rooted in Leninist principles, above all the insistence that nothing may challenge the party’s supremacy. The article then turns to China’s treatment of dissent and surveillance, citing revelations about mass detention camps in northwestern China, where perhaps a million or more Uighurs and other Muslims have been confined. It criticizes Western business leaders and politicians who have praised China or minimized its authoritarianism. Michael Bloomberg is singled out for saying that Xi Jinping “is not a dictator,” despite the evidence of repression. The column also mocks American self-censorship and “groveling” toward China, contrasting it with the defiance of the creators of “South Park,” who responded to China’s censorship with pointed satire. President Trump is portrayed as inconsistent toward China and other authoritarian leaders. The article quotes him saying he stood with both Hong Kong and Xi Jinping, and notes that his early decision to withdraw from the Trans-Pacific Partnership weakened a trade coalition that excluded China. It also mentions Trump’s friendly relationships with Vladimir Putin, Recep Tayyip Erdogan, and Kim Jong Un, while observing that North Korea resumed missile testing in 2019 and continued to seek concessions from Washington. The article closes by reflecting on the significance of restraint in the nuclear age, noting that 2019 marked 73 years since nuclear weapons were last used in war. Sometimes, it says, what does not happen—such as nuclear war—is itself momentous.

# Summary: The 235 Days That Rattled China and Shook the World This column examines 2019's most significant global developments, particularly Hong Kong's pro-democracy movement and its broader implications for China's authoritarian regime. The Hong Kong uprising began April 3 when Beijing-backed officials introduced an extradition bill threatening to expand mainland China's control over the territory. The movement culminated in November 24 elections where voters rejected the Chinese Communist Party's expected outcome, demonstrating resistance to the "one country, two systems" framework promised to Hong Kong. These 235 days of protests challenged the regime's assumption that prosperity could purchase political compliance. Taiwan faces similar pressures. President Xi Jinping identified Taiwan as central to his nationalist agenda, but the island's January 2020 presidential election likely will reelect Tsai Ing-wen, signaling another rejection of Beijing's governance model. The column notes a troubling historical irony: approximately 1.5 billion people lived under communist regimes thirty years ago when the Soviet Union collapsed, and the same number does today—though this represents a smaller percentage of global population. Critically, 89 percent of those currently under communist rule live in China's Leninist system, which permits no challenge to party supremacy. The author criticizes American business leaders and politicians for enabling this system. He specifically references Michael Bloomberg's pre-election comments praising Xi Jinping as a listener to the public and denying he is a dictator—comments made just 51 days before revelations about concentration camps in northwestern China holding potentially millions of Uyghurs. The column compares such appeasement to 1930s figures who romanticized fascist dictators. The author praises "South Park" creators for their defiant response when China banned their show, contrasting their principled stance with President Trump's contradictory approach to China. While Trump expressed support for Hong Kong, he simultaneously called Xi "a friend," undermining Hong Kong's cause. More problematically, Trump withdrew from the Trans-Pacific Partnership shortly after inauguration, eliminating a 12-nation coalition excluding China—a strategic error benefiting Beijing. The column extends criticism to Trump's relationships with other authoritarian leaders: Putin, continuing Ukraine's dismemberment; Erdogan, ignoring warnings about attacking Kurds; and Kim Jong Un, whom Trump claimed to "fall in love" with. North Korea resumed ballistic missile testing after a 522-day pause, with Kim demanding additional U.S. concessions by year's end to avoid "shocking punishment." The author concludes with a sobering observation: 2019 marked the 73rd consecutive year without nuclear weapons use since 1945. This absence itself represents something momentous, serving as a reminder of what remains at stake in international relations.

TC Energy announced that it will not redeem its Cumulative Redeemable First Preferred Shares, Series 5 and Series 6, on Jan. 30, 2026. Because the company is not exercising its redemption right, holders of the two preferred share series will be given the opportunity to convert between the two classes, subject to certain conditions and deadlines. For Series 5 shareholders, the options are either to keep their shares and continue receiving a fixed-rate quarterly dividend, or to convert any or all of those shares on a one-for-one basis into Series 6 shares and receive a floating-rate quarterly dividend. For Series 6 shareholders, the choices are the reverse: they may keep their shares and continue receiving a floating-rate quarterly dividend, or convert any or all of them one-for-one into Series 5 shares and receive a fixed-rate quarterly dividend. TC Energy said that Series 5 shareholders who retain their shares will receive a new annual fixed dividend rate of 4.501% for the five-year period beginning Jan. 30, 2026 and ending just before Jan. 30, 2031. Series 6 shareholders who retain their shares will receive a floating quarterly dividend rate of 3.732% for the three-month period beginning Jan. 30, 2026 and ending just before April 30, 2026. That floating rate will be reset every quarter. The same rates will apply to shareholders who convert into the other series: Series 5 shares converted into Series 6 shares will receive the floating quarterly dividend rate of 3.732% for the first quarter beginning Jan. 30, 2026, while Series 6 shares converted into Series 5 shares will receive the fixed annual dividend rate of 4.501% over the new five-year period. The company noted that the floating rate will be reset every quarter, while the fixed rate will remain in place for the five-year term. Beneficial owners who want to exercise their conversion rights must act through their broker or other nominee and follow the required instructions by 5 p.m. Eastern time on Jan. 16, 2026. TC Energy warned that notices received after that deadline will not be valid, and it advised shareholders to submit instructions well ahead of time so intermediaries have enough time to complete the process. If a beneficial owner does not provide notice or does not contact their broker by the deadline, they will keep their existing shares and receive the new dividend rate applicable to that series, assuming no automatic conversion condition is triggered. The company also set out two automatic conversion rules that could apply if one of the share series would otherwise have fewer than one million shares outstanding after Jan. 30, 2026. If TC Energy determines that fewer than one million Series 5 shares would remain outstanding, all remaining Series 5 shares will automatically convert into Series 6 shares on a one-for-one basis. If fewer than one million Series 6 shares would remain outstanding, all remaining Series 6 shares will automatically convert into Series 5 shares on a one-for-one basis. In either case, TC Energy said it will issue a news release no later than Jan. 23, 2026 to announce that outcome. The company added that holders of Series 5 and Series 6 shares will again have the opportunity to convert their shares on Jan. 30, 2031, and on Jan. 30 every fifth year thereafter, as long as the shares remain outstanding. TC Energy included a reminder that more detailed information on the terms and risks of the preferred shares is available in the prospectus supplement dated June 17, 2010, available through SEDAR+ and the company’s website. Ukraine’s DTEK Energo said its thermal power plants increased electricity output by 28% in May-August compared with the same period in 2022, according to Ukrainian media citing the company. In August alone, when summer demand reached record highs because of the heat, generation was 35% higher than a year earlier. From January to August 2023, DTEK’s thermal plants supplied about 9.9 billion kWh to the grid, enough to cover the average annual consumption of roughly 3.3 million households. DTEK Energy CEO Ildar Saleev said workers are repairing and restoring stations ahead of the autumn-winter period while also supporting the power system during peak demand. Last week, two power units with nearly 400 MW of capacity returned to service after maintenance.

# Summary Ukraine's DTEK Energo thermal power plants significantly increased electricity production in 2023. From May-August, output rose 28% compared to the same period in 2022, with August alone seeing a 35% increase due to record summer consumption from heat. Through January-August 2023, the plants generated approximately 9.9 billion kWh, sufficient to power about 3.3 million families annually. DTEK Energy's General Director stated the company is simultaneously repairing facilities and preparing for peak autumn-winter demand. Recently, two power units with nearly 400 MW combined capacity were returned to operation after maintenance. Currently, DTEK Energo operates six of its nine thermal power plants across Ukraine.

Ukraine has formed a delegation to negotiate accession to the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP, or TPP11), according to Ukrainian media citing the Economy Ministry. First Deputy Prime Minister and Economy Minister Yulia Sviridenko will lead the team. She said the ministry expects Ukraine to join the pact in early 2024, though accession could still happen this year. Sviridenko said membership would help Ukraine reduce non-tariff barriers in trade in goods and services with countries in the region, open new markets, and improve access to foreign investment. The ministry also plans to open at least ten trade missions in the Pacific region, including in South Africa, Nigeria, Egypt, and Ghana. The CPTPP was concluded in 2018 and has been ratified by ten countries.

# Ukraine Pursues Trans-Pacific Partnership Membership Ukraine has established a delegation to negotiate membership in the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP), led by First Deputy Prime Minister Yulia Sviridenko. The Economy Ministry targets accession in early 2024, with potential for joining by year's end. According to Sviridenko, CPTPP membership would allow Ukraine to eliminate non-tariff trade barriers and access new markets in the region. The agreement would also facilitate foreign direct investment from major economies including the United States, United Kingdom, and EU countries. Ukraine plans to open at least ten trade missions across the Pacific region, including in South Africa, Nigeria, Egypt, and Ghana. The CPTPP, finalized in 2018, currently includes ten ratified members: Australia, Canada, Chile, Japan, Malaysia, Mexico, New Zealand, Peru, Singapore, and Vietnam. Primary exports include electronics, machinery, automobiles, and mineral fuel.

Belarus President Alexander Lukashenko told representatives of the business community in Minsk on 22 December that relations between the state and business should be governed by a clear “standard formula.” He said officials at every level, from local council heads to ministers, must follow not only the letter but also the spirit of regulations: if the law allows assistance, they should provide it; if it does not allow help, they should not interfere; and if intervention is required, they must act. Lukashenko said all decisions aimed at liberalizing business conditions must be implemented quickly, and he ordered the Presidential Administration and the State Control Committee to create a system for monitoring how legal acts are carried out. If new by-laws are needed, he said, they should be adopted without delay. He also said the government is preparing a new decree on licensing that should comprehensively resolve licensing issues. According to the president, recent documents have laid the groundwork for a broader review of legislation affecting entrepreneurship, and he wants this work completed in 2018. He urged authorities and business leaders to inform the public about the new rules using all available communication channels, including the Internet. Lukashenko emphasized that Belarus has “one economy,” meaning business must also meet the government’s broader economic goals. He said the state has significantly reduced the number of requirements imposed on businesses, but managers and owners are now fully responsible for conditions at their enterprises. He noted that the government largely stays out of pricing, but warned firms not to raise prices unnecessarily. He said the Ministry of Antimonopoly Regulation and Trade, which he said had been strengthened, and the State Control Committee would monitor prices. He also called on business to ensure decent wages and employment for workers. If companies follow these principles, he said, the state will remain a reliable partner. Lukashenko added that the reforms should also boost the IT sector, so that capital, people and technology all work for the country’s benefit.

# Belarus President Outlines Business-Government Relations Framework On December 22, Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko met with business representatives to establish a standard formula for government-business interactions. He directed all officials, from local council chairs to ministers, to follow three principles: implement laws as written, provide assistance when legally permitted, refrain from interference when not required by law, and intervene when necessary. Lukashenko emphasized the importance of rapidly implementing business liberalization measures and establishing a monitoring system for regulatory compliance. He instructed the Presidential Administration and State Control Committee to develop necessary bylaws quickly. The president announced that the government is drafting a comprehensive decree on licensing to address all licensing issues systematically. He indicated that legislative revisions across entrepreneurship-related areas should be completed in 2018, with authorities obligated to communicate new working conditions to the public through all available channels, including the internet. Lukashenko stressed that business and government share responsibility for the economy's success. While the state has significantly reduced requirements for businesses, managers and owners now bear full responsibility for their enterprises' operations. Regarding pricing, the president noted minimal state interference but confirmed that the strengthened Ministry of Antimonopoly Regulation and Trade, alongside the State Control Committee, will monitor prices without disrupting business operations. The president outlined three expectations for businesses: maintain reasonable pricing, pay decent wages, and ensure employment. He promised that companies adhering to these rules would receive reliable state partnership and assistance. Finally, Lukashenko expressed confidence that these decisions would stimulate IT sector growth, emphasizing that capital, people, and technology should collectively benefit the entire country.

Belarusian Prime Minister Andrei Kobyakov has asked the Eurasian Development Bank (EDB) to prepare a separate cooperation strategy for Belarus, during a meeting on 27 December with EDB Board Chairman Andrei Belyaninov in Minsk. Kobyakov said the bank’s overall development strategy is being revised and expressed hope that Belarus would be included in it, but also proposed a dedicated EDB-Belarus strategy that would clearly define the main priorities for future cooperation. He noted that Belarus has used this approach with other international financial institutions. The prime minister also called for the resumption and expansion of project financing, saying the volume of cooperation had recently declined but that he expected improvement soon. He added that Belarus believes the EDB can help advance integration in the Eurasian region and said the country is ready to offer projects with strong integration benefits. Belyaninov said the bank intends to deepen ties with Belarus and suggested treating the meeting as a working conference to discuss future cooperation in detail. The EDB, founded by Russia and Kazakhstan in 2006, is a multilateral financial institution with six member states: Armenia, Belarus, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Russia, and Tajikistan.

# Summary On December 27, Belarusian Prime Minister Andrei Kobyakov met with Eurasian Development Bank (EDB) Chairman Andrei Belyaninov to discuss enhanced cooperation. Kobyakov requested that the EDB prepare a dedicated strategy for Belarus cooperation as part of its broader development strategy adjustments. He emphasized Belarus's desire to increase project financing volumes, noting that cooperation levels have recently declined. Kobyakov expressed confidence that the EDB's efforts would advance Eurasian integration and pledged Belarus's commitment to offering integration-focused projects. Belyaninov affirmed the bank's intention to strengthen relations with Belarus and proposed conducting their meeting as a working conference given the significant Belarusian delegation present. The EDB, established in 2006 by Russia and Kazakhstan, serves six member states: Armenia, Belarus, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Russia, and Tajikistan. With a charter capital of $7 billion, the organization aims to promote sustainable economic growth and expand mutual trade among participating nations.

Vitebsk plans to sign twinning and cooperation agreements with Lublin, Poland, and Kosice, Slovakia, in 2018, Mayor Viktor Nikolaikin said at a city council session. He added that the city is also considering similar deals with Estonia’s Tartu and Lithuania’s Panevezys. In 2017, Vitebsk already formed partnerships with Irkutsk, Volgograd, and Saratov in Russia. Overall, the regional center now works with 25 sister cities in 10 countries, including Russia, Latvia, China, Germany, Sweden, and Israel. Nikolaikin said these ties help expand contacts and support local businesses abroad. Currently, 670 Vitebsk enterprises and organizations conduct foreign economic activity, trading with partners in 90 countries. Russia still remains the main export market, though its share fell to 68.6%.

A Belarus-China trading house will be registered in the Shanghai free trade zone to market a broad range of Belarusian foods. Agriculture and Food Ministry official Aleksei Bogdanov said 2017 was a successful year for bilateral cooperation, with dairy exports to China rising tenfold and Belarus also entering the Chinese beef market.

Vitebsk’s merchandise exports are projected to rise by 25% in 2017, mayor Viktor Nikolaikin told the City Council of Deputies. About half of the city’s industrial output is exported. Foreign trade in services is expected to jump by nearly 200% compared with 2016, with especially strong growth in construction and transport services, both more than doubling. Together, goods and services trade should produce a surplus of more than $126 million in 2017. Nikolaikin said this was a major achievement for a city that had once hoped merely to reach balance. Vitebsk companies now export to 54 countries, with new markets in 2017 including Azerbaijan, Namibia, the UAE, Armenia, Moldova, Vietnam, and the United States.

Mrs. Lida Muir, 91, died peacefully at Pioneer Ridge on December 24, 2023, with her family at her side. Born Lida Lea DiBlasio in Befaro, Italy, on July 14, 1932, she emigrated to Port Arthur at age five with her mother, Guilia, joining her father, Anthony, who was already there. Over the following years, other extended family members also came to Canada. Lida worked as a bookkeeper at Bourke’s Drug Mart, where she met James Muir, the man she would marry on June 20, 1953. Together they raised two sons, Warren and Sheldon. While raising her family, she gave her time to volunteer work, including with the MS Society and at Dawson Court, a home for the aged, where she volunteered for more than 20 years and said she loved every moment. She was also active in Our Lady of Loretto Catholic Church and the Thunder Bay Catholic Women’s League. Her closest friendships included her lifelong “Gabby Group” — Emma Toivonen, Jeanette Gresko and Mary Spittle — who brought her laughter and companionship. The Muir family camp at Bolduc Bay on Dog Lake was a cherished gathering place for generations of family and friends. In her later years, she also lived with and delighted in her fourth grandchild, Layla, who brought her great joy. Lida was remembered as kind, honest, humorous, and deeply proud of her grandchildren, Courtney, Brandon and Brooklyn. She is survived by her son Sheldon and daughter-in-law Jessica, son Warren, grandchildren, brother Nino, nephew Jonathan, and many other relatives. She was predeceased by her parents, brother Aldo, and husband James. Funeral Mass will be held January 3, 2024, at Our Lady of Loretto R.C. Church, with virtual attendance available.

Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko on 22 December urged private businesses to expand more actively into small towns and rural areas, saying this was important for both economic development and the quality of life of people outside major cities. He made the remarks at a meeting with representatives of the Belarusian business community in Minsk, according to BelTA. Lukashenko said he was especially concerned that small and medium-sized private firms tend to concentrate in the capital and other large cities. He argued that while retail and service businesses naturally do better where there are more customers, manufacturing enterprises would be better placed in the regions, where labor is cheaper, land and resources are available, and businesses can benefit from tax preferences, lower customs duties, and easier export rules. He also pointed to the decline in rural commerce. Over recent years, the number of shops in the countryside had fallen, including a 10% drop in 2012–2015. He said many consumer service and catering outlets could not survive because of low customer numbers, leaving former shop and restaurant buildings empty. Lukashenko stressed that rural residents need access to everyday services such as home repairs, appliance repair, hairdressing, clothing services, and other basic needs, and said small business could provide them if conditions were favorable and prices affordable. The president referred to a decree on developing retail, catering, and consumer services, saying it already contains measures to reduce business costs in rural areas. These include exemption from value-added tax, a reduced profit tax rate of 6% compared with the general rate, and no land or real estate taxes. He emphasized that local authorities should carefully decide where these incentives apply, warning against creating a “tax haven” near Minsk or oblast capitals. At the same time, he said Belarus would benefit if foreign companies from nearby Russian, Lithuanian, or Ukrainian regions used the relaxed rules in remote Belarusian areas. Lukashenko also invited business representatives to suggest additional measures and noted that people can first test demand for their services without immediately registering as self-employed under a separate decree regulating individual activity.

# Summary On December 22, Belarus President Alexander Lukashenko met with business community representatives to encourage greater private business development in small towns and rural areas. He expressed concern that small and medium-sized companies concentrate primarily in the capital and larger cities, neglecting countryside opportunities. Lukashenko acknowledged that while services naturally gravitate toward population centers, manufacturing should relocate to regions offering cheaper labor, available land, and natural resources. He emphasized that rural areas also provide tax incentives, including lower tax rates, reduced customs duties, and relaxed export regulations. The president highlighted a concerning trend: rural shop numbers declined by 10% between 2012-2015, with many former retail and service establishments now abandoned. Low customer volumes make it difficult for businesses to remain profitable in these areas. Lukashenko stressed the importance of improving rural Belarusians' quality of life by providing essential services like home repairs, appliance maintenance, hairdressing, and tailoring. To support rural business development, a presidential decree on retail, public catering, and consumer services offers substantial tax benefits for countryside operations. These include exemption from value-added tax (which typically comprises 20% of prices), a 6% profit tax (three times lower than standard rates), and elimination of land and real estate taxes. Local authorities will determine where these regulations apply, though Lukashenko cautioned against creating tax havens near major cities. Lukashenko welcomed foreign companies utilizing these relaxed regulations in remote areas, viewing it as beneficial to the nation. He also noted that individuals need not immediately register as self-employed entrepreneurs; they can initially operate under less formal arrangements to test market demand for their services. The president invited business representatives to suggest additional measures needed to attract private enterprise to rural and small-town Belarus.

Venezuela’s only telecommunications satellite has drifted out of orbit and stopped working, leaving the country with an expensive communications gap. The Chinese-built satellite, launched in 2008 with great fanfare under President Hugo Chavez, was intended to symbolize national sovereignty and support what Chavez called “21st-century socialism.” Instead, it has failed three years before its planned 2023 expiration. The satellite, known as VeneSat-1 or the Simon Bolivar Satellite, had been used to provide internet access to rural areas lacking fiber-optic connections and to beam Venezuela’s state-run television channels into poor and remote homes without cable service. Its loss means the government will likely need to rely on international commercial satellite providers to continue distributing content to those areas, a move that could cost millions of dollars and may be complicated by U.S. sanctions. State television will still reach viewers through cable operators and old-style antennas, but access will be more difficult in places where telecommunications infrastructure is deteriorating. The problem was first detected on March 13, when ExoAnalytic Solutions, a California satellite-tracking company, reported that the satellite had moved away from its assigned position and was tumbling westward. That assessment was later confirmed by AGI, a Pennsylvania-based tracking firm. Venezuela’s Ministry of Science then confirmed on Wednesday that the satellite was no longer operational, though it gave no explanation. Experts say possible causes include overheating, component failure, micrometeorite damage, or a fuel shortage. Venezuelan analysts believe fuel depletion may have been likely, since the satellite was placed in an orbital slot that was not ideal for serving Venezuela and required extra fuel to keep in position. Telecommunications consultant Patrick Boza said many in the industry doubted it would last its full 15-year lifespan. Journalist William Peña argued that the satellite was placed in an orbit assigned to Uruguay for political reasons, calling it a product of “ideological arrogance.”

Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva has completed one of the most dramatic political comebacks in modern Brazilian history. He was widely seen as a blue-collar hero and one of the world’s most popular politicians. But his reputation was badly damaged by Operation Carwash, Brazil’s biggest corruption investigation. Lula was convicted of graft and spent 580 days in jail from April 2018 to November 2019. His absence from that race, combined with anger at his Workers’ Party, helped Bolsonaro rise to power. Bolsonaro’s presidency, however, quickly became unpopular. A Reuters investigation describes how, during Donald Trump’s four years in office, China expanded its influence across Latin America while the United States fell behind in trade, investment and diplomatic sway. The article says Trump made his position clear to the region: Latin American countries should avoid doing business with China. But that warning largely failed, and by the time President-elect Joe Biden prepared to take office on Jan. 20, Beijing had strengthened its presence in much of the resource-rich region long considered Washington’s political backyard. The report says Biden inherits a difficult challenge. He has promised to restore U.S. global leadership after Trump’s “America First” approach and has argued that declining U.S. influence in Latin America threatens national security. In March, Biden told Americas Quarterly that Trump’s “incompetence and neglect” in Latin America and the Caribbean would end on his first day in office. His team declined to comment for the Reuters story. The article says China has become the dominant economic partner for much of Latin America. Since 2018, if Mexico is excluded, China has surpassed the United States as the region’s largest trade partner. Beijing has been buying Andean copper, Argentine grains and Brazilian meat, while also expanding investment and low-interest lending for energy projects, solar farms, dams, ports, railways and highways. Former Bolivian President Jorge Quiroga told Reuters that South America’s reality is shaped by Brazil and China, saying he would rank Brazil first and China second as the region’s most important partners. Officials in Latin America said China will be difficult to dislodge because it offers money and market access that many indebted countries need, especially after the economic damage caused by the coronavirus pandemic. One Argentine government official said China has more interest in Argentina than the United States does, adding that Trump showed little interest and expressing hope that Biden would do better. China is now the top trade partner for Brazil, Chile, Peru, Uruguay and several other countries, and its trade with Argentina far exceeds that of the United States. Using U.N. Comtrade data, Reuters found that in 2019, trade between China and Latin America excluding Mexico topped $223 billion, compared with $198 billion in U.S. trade. The United States remains larger overall only because of Mexico, its biggest global trading partner. Some countries in the region viewed the Trump administration as mainly scolding them for growing closer to China, especially through Chinese financing and technology ties as the global race for 5G intensified. Former Obama adviser Mark Feierstein said Trump’s lack of engagement, along with the U.S. withdrawal from the Trans-Pacific Partnership trade pact, created a vacuum that China filled. He said Trump made China appear to be the better partner, and that Biden would try to reverse that. Analysts and former officials expect a Biden administration to give Latin America greater attention, though it will also have to deal with the pandemic recovery and repair U.S. ties elsewhere. Janet Napolitano, former Homeland Security secretary under Obama, said Biden sees strong relations across Central and South America as strategically valuable to the United States. Experts said Biden is likely to keep warning countries about the risks of getting too close to China, but may also offer more financial support and restore humanitarian aid cut under Trump. The article also says China used the pandemic to deepen its diplomatic reach by sending medical supplies such as ventilators and masks. In Argentina, recent cooperation with China has expanded to include vaccine trials, a currency swap extension, space cooperation, and a Chinese military studies course at the national defense college. Argentina has also discussed a possible state visit to China by President Alberto Fernandez and joining China’s Belt and Road Initiative. Margaret Myers of the Inter-American Dialogue said Chinese sovereign lending has slowed somewhat, but commercial bank financing has taken its place. She pointed to a $2.4 billion loan from China Exim Bank to Ecuador this year as an example of China’s economic diplomacy opening doors. The United States has tried to respond more aggressively in recent months, launching initiatives to compete with China, but some saw those moves as too late. A senior U.S. official said the rivalry is playing out globally, including in Latin America, and that Washington has a strategy to push back. State Department official Francis Fannon said the pandemic could push some countries toward China, but insisted the United States remains the “partner of choice.”

A British Columbia Supreme Court judge has upheld more than $343,000 in wildfire suppression costs imposed on Tolko Industries after a 2016 fire near Nazko, in central B.C., escaped from a debris pile at one of the company’s cut blocks. The blaze burned about four square kilometres after a contractor set the pile on fire, according to the court decision posted Monday. The case involved four “holdover fires” reported by Tolko to the BC Wildfire Service in spring 2016. These fires were said to have smouldered underground for periods ranging from six weeks to five months after they were believed to be extinguished. The Nazko fire was the only one that escaped the cut block. Tolko had originally succeeded at the Forest Appeals Commission, which overturned the cost-recovery order. The commission said the company was exempt under the Wildfire Regulation because it did not intend to start a fire and because the blaze resulted from forestry activity. But Supreme Court Justice Michael Brundrett ruled that the commission wrongly interpreted the law by treating “fire” as meaning “wildfire” and by separating the intentional lighting of the debris burn from the wildfire that followed. Brundrett said the law does not require a person to intend to start a wildfire that accidentally spreads from a deliberately lit controlled fire. He added that limiting cost recovery only to wilfully caused wildfires, such as arson, would make the scheme almost meaningless. The decision noted that timber harvesting produces large amounts of debris that are often burned later, and that holdover fires can occur when smouldering continues beneath the ground. Tolko had burned about 65,000 debris piles during the 2015-16 season. The company was originally issued a $15,000 administrative penalty plus the firefighting bill, and only challenged the cost-recovery portion.

Baseball’s 2016 home-run surge was on full display as the postseason opened in Toronto, where the Baltimore Orioles and Toronto Blue Jays, two of the most power-heavy teams in the league, met in the American League wild-card round. The Orioles led the majors with 253 home runs, while the Blue Jays ranked second among playoff teams. Baltimore had six players with at least 20 homers, as did Toronto. Orioles slugger Mark Trumbo led the majors with 47 home runs, but even that total did not approach a record. What made the season striking was not a single historic outlier, but the breadth of the power surge. Only one season in major league history had produced more home runs than 2016: the 2000 season, when teams hit 5,693. In 2016, the total reached 5,610. No player reached 50 homers, yet power was widespread. Just two years earlier, in 2014, only 11 players had hit 30 home runs. In 2016, 38 players did. Overall, hitters launched 701 more home runs than in 2015 and 1,424 more than in 2014. With numbers rising so quickly, many wondered whether the baseball itself had been altered. Others feared a return to a steroid-era problem. Commissioner Rob Manfred, in Toronto for Tuesday’s game, rejected the idea that the ball was to blame. He said baseball had tested the ball and was “absolutely convinced” that the spike was not caused by differences in the baseball. In his view, the increase reflected changes in how the game is played and how hitters are trained from a young age. The modern game has become increasingly home-run oriented. Alongside the rise in homers, strikeouts reached another record high in 2016, while sacrifice hits fell to a record low. Former Mets general manager Steve Phillips, now covering the series for TSN and MLB Network Radio, offered several on-field explanations. He said players now use leg kicks more often, even smaller hitters, and that the game has largely moved away from slap hitters. He also pointed to the bats, saying they are heavily lacquered and coated. Another factor, he argued, is the prevalence of high-velocity pitching: hitters have adjusted to more fastballs by changing their timing, and many pitchers with strong fastballs lack quality secondary pitches. Still, the backdrop to any discussion of power in baseball remains the steroid era. Baseball’s current performance-enhancing drug testing policy, which began in 2003, is regarded as strong, but the early phase was more complicated. In 2003, baseball conducted anonymous survey testing to decide whether stricter testing with penalties was needed. More than 100 players tested positive, including David Ortiz. Manfred noted on Sunday that at least 10 of those positives may not have been scientifically clear-cut. He said there were legitimate questions about whether those results were truly positive, but the cases were never fully examined because the league already had enough positives to trigger formal testing the next year. Manfred also addressed Ortiz’s Hall of Fame candidacy, saying there is a major difference between players who are caught and suspended and those whose names appear in ambiguous, never-intended-for-public results. Ortiz will first be eligible for the Hall of Fame ballot in 2021. The article then turned to a broader question: whether home-run power actually wins championships. The answer, historically, is not often. The Kansas City Royals won the 2015 World Series with only one home run in the Fall Classic, relying instead on contact hitting and relentless pressure. The San Francisco Giants won titles in 2010, 2012, and 2014 without a single 30-homer player on their rosters. Elliott Kalb of MLB Network examined every postseason since 1995, the first year with wild-card teams, and found that the regular-season home-run leader has rarely become champion. Only the 2009 Yankees won the World Series after leading postseason teams in homers; only the 1995 Cleveland Indians also reached the pennant. More than half the time, the top home-run team was eliminated in the division series, including the powerful 1997 Mariners, who were upset by Baltimore. The 2016 Orioles were especially dependent on the long ball, scoring 51.9 percent of their runs via home runs, second only to the 2010 Blue Jays at 53.1 percent. The 2016 Mets were close behind at 51.1 percent. Orioles manager Buck Showalter said teams must know what kind of club they are and adapt accordingly. The article closes with that larger uncertainty: more teams are embracing power again, but October will determine how well that style translates in the postseason.

The Winnipeg Blue Bombers opened the second half of their 2025 CFL season with a gritty 26-13 road victory over the Montreal Alouettes on Thursday night at steamy Molson Stadium before 20,310 fans. Demski, one of the offense’s most important players, and Sterns, another major contributor, both exited due to injuries, forcing Winnipeg to improvise. Joey Corcoran stepped in, and later in the game Chris Streveler was used at receiver as the Bombers pieced together a makeshift attack. Running back Brady Oliveira delivered another dominant performance, showing why he won the CFL’s Most Outstanding Player award a year earlier. He ran 16 times for 137 yards and a touchdown and also caught nine passes for 73 yards, finishing with 210 yards from scrimmage against one of the league’s top defenses. He emphasized that the Bombers battled through adversity and honored the players who went down by making the most of their opportunities. Middle linebacker Tony Jones had another steady outing, Willie Jefferson contributed key knockdowns, and kicker Sergio Castillo was perfect on four field-goal attempts. That was especially notable because protecting the football had been a problem at various points earlier in the season. Montreal, meanwhile, was dealing with major quarterback turmoil. The Alouettes were down to their fourth-string quarterback, Caleb Morgan, after injuries had already sidelined starter Davis Alexander and backups McLeod Bethel-Thompson and Caleb Evans. Morgan, a 28-year-old former New York Jets draft pick who played at Florida International, had some early success with big plays to Alexander Hollins and a touchdown pass to Tyler Snead. The key stretch came with Winnipeg leading 16-13 entering the fourth quarter. The Bombers then put together a 10-play, 81-yard drive that ended with Oliveira’s second touchdown of the season and second in as many games. Head coach Mike O’Shea said he was pleased with how the offense adjusted at halftime and how players filled unfamiliar roles, calling Streveler’s work running routes from the slot especially impressive. The main concern for Winnipeg was the health of Demski and Sterns, whose absences could significantly affect the offense heading into the Labour Day Classic. Auckland’s landmark mixed-use development The Orange, at 141–149 Newton Road in Eden Terrace, is being offered for sale for the first time. The property combines a heritage-listed character building, The Orange Hall, with a modern built-to-rent apartment complex and commercial space, making it one of the city fringe’s more unusual investment opportunities. The comprehensive freehold development includes 66 apartments, three office levels and two retail units. It generates about 65 per cent of its income from residential tenants and 35 per cent from commercial leases, which Colliers says gives it a split-risk profile that is relatively resilient in uncertain economic conditions. The property currently produces around $1.78 million in net annual rent, offering what the agents describe as secure and diversified income for a new owner. Colliers International has been appointed to market the property by deadline private treaty, closing at 4pm on Wednesday 25 November unless sold beforehand. Auckland Director of Investment Sales Gareth Fraser said the asset was a rare chance to buy a “trophy” property combining heritage character, modern design and long-term income potential. He said The Orange’s mix of quality, scale, location and income profile would appeal to premium property investors. The heritage centrepiece, The Orange Hall, has deep cultural significance. Completed in 1923, it was designed by Arthur Sinclair O’Connor and built by Fletcher Construction. Its name comes from William of Orange, King William III of England. Fraser said the hall has been an important part of New Zealand’s cultural and architectural history for nearly a century. During World War II, it operated six nights a week and drew crowds queuing along Newton Road. It helped launch the careers of performers including Dame Kiri Te Kanawa and Sir Howard Morrison. The building was primarily a jazz venue until 1987, when it was taken over by the Performing Arts School and repainted in its distinctive orange colour. The current owners transformed the property in 2015, according to Colliers International Director Richard Kirke. He said they redeveloped the 2,048-square-metre freehold site while retaining and restoring the heritage-listed hall. The new design, by Crosson Architects, won a New Zealand Architecture Award in 2016. The Orange Hall was fully refurbished and earthquake strengthened, with its brick north façade preserved and new full-height windows added to the west side facing a raised central plaza. Inside, it now provides three levels of character office space featuring exposed timber beams, sand-blasted walls, wood panelling and a character ceiling. The plaza includes basalt paving, planters, etched footprints and dancefloor chairs referencing the site’s past. Two new buildings wrap around the hall and plaza, fronting Newton Road and Dundonald Road. These contain 32 studio apartments, 24 one-bedroom apartments, five two-bedroom apartments and six two-level loft apartments, one of which is used as a commercial office. The development also includes two retail units, more office space, a lobby and two basement levels with 80 car parks. Colliers Strategic Advisory National Director Alan McMahon said the property highlights the growing relevance of built-to-rent investment in Auckland. He said there is strong pent-up demand for well-managed rental housing, while Covid-19 has worsened affordability and pushed more investors into residential property. At the same time, population growth continues, including returning New Zealanders, while supply remains constrained by high land and construction costs. In his view, demand will continue to exceed supply, making The Orange an attractive entry point into the BTR sector. The apartments are professionally managed by Crockers Property Management. Colliers said the complex has continued to perform through Covid, with 98 per cent of residential income collected in 2020. Beyond passive ownership, the property could also be adapted in several ways, including converting some commercial space to residential use, increasing rents or lease terms, forming a BTR fund or syndicate, converting lofts to office space, or subdividing and unit-titling the apartments for future sale and potential capital gain. Associate Director Jonathan Lynch said the location is another major strength. The property is about 2 kilometres from the CBD and close to cafes, hospitality venues and transport links, including motorway ramps and major bus routes. It will also be within walking distance of the new City Rail Link stations at Mt Eden and Karangahape Road. Nearby childcare and schooling options add to the appeal. Lynch said the Newton/Uptown precinct is well placed to attract strong tenant demand now and in the future.

Congolese national deputy Jean-Claude Kibala on Friday urged the government to assist victims of the earthquake that struck Kamituga, in South Kivu, on Wednesday. He called for the aid already provided to victims of the Nyiragongo volcanic eruption to be extended to the mining town’s residents. Kibala also appealed for stricter public standards and a contingency plan to better manage natural disasters in the Democratic Republic of Congo. He said he had already sent an assessment team to the area to organize emergency support. According to him, the quake damaged several key buildings, including Kagunzi Primary School in Kitemba, a dispensary in Essence, a private university, and the 8th CEPAC Pentecostal church. The disaster left 10 people injured and caused cracks in many homes. Kamituga, home to about 260,000 people, is an important mining and transport hub on National Road 2 and a major market for goods from Mwenga and Shabunda. The wider Kamituga economic zone, covering those territories, has more than 1.5 million inhabitants.

# Earthquake Strikes Kamituga in South Kivu On June 12, 2021, National Deputy Jean-Claude Kibala urged the Democratic Republic of Congo's government to provide humanitarian aid to victims of an earthquake that struck Kamituga in South Kivu province on Wednesday. The earthquake caused significant damage, destroying buildings including Kagunzi Primary School, a dispensary, a private university, and a Pentecostal church. The disaster resulted in 10 injuries and structural damage to numerous houses throughout the city. Kibala recommended extending the government assistance already provided for the recent Nyiragongo volcano eruption to earthquake victims. He also called for the implementation of strict building standards and a comprehensive disaster management contingency plan to mitigate future natural disaster impacts. The deputy dispatched assessment teams to the affected area for emergency assistance. Kamituga, a city of 260,000 residents, serves as a critical mining center and communication hub on the national road network. The region, part of South Kivu's western economic zone with over 1.5 million inhabitants, plays a vital role in the province's development.

More than a month after Super Typhoon Yutu struck the U.S. Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands, recovery is still underway. The storm hit Saipan and Tinian on Oct. 25 with winds over 180 mph, affecting more than 50,000 people. Abbra Firman, an eastern Montana disaster program manager for the American Red Cross, has been helping on the islands and said some roads have reopened. She praised residents for their resilience, generosity, and volunteer spirit, calling the people of Saipan “phenomenal.” Firman also said many are proud to be U.S. citizens and part of the U.S. Commonwealth. Yutu was the strongest storm of 2018 and the strongest ever to hit U.S. lands and territories.

# Summary Super Typhoon Yutu struck the U.S. Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands on October 25, affecting over 50,000 people with winds exceeding 180 miles per hour. More than a month later, recovery efforts continue on Saipan and Tinian. Abbra Firman, a Montana-based American Red Cross disaster program manager, praised the islanders' resilience and community spirit during reconstruction. Roads have begun reopening as recovery progresses. Yutu ranks as the strongest storm of 2018 and the most powerful ever to impact the U.S. and its territories.

The Coalition avenir Québec launched a website Tuesday evening, pl61.ca, to defend Bill 61 after the government’s economic recovery plan was quickly attacked by opposition parties. The site says it aims to separate “fact and fiction” amid what it calls false information circulating online, and urges Quebecers to help spread accurate information as the province tries to “revive the economy without reviving the pandemic.” The website was created by the CAQ party itself, not by the Quebec government. Metadata linked to the domain shows it was launched on behalf of Denis Joannette, a senior CAQ executive. The site presents a list of claims it labels false, along with statements it identifies as facts, but it does not say where the disputed claims came from or who made them. Opposition leaders quickly criticized the move. Québec solidaire co-spokesperson Gabriel Nadeau-Dubois called it “damage control,” while Parti québécois leader Martin Ouellet compared it to efforts by the Liberals to defend their reputation during the Charbonneau Commission. Ouellet said the CAQ should not give itself disproportionate powers to avoid repeating that era. The public committee monitoring Charbonneau recommendations also warned that the site could create conditions “extremely favourable” to corruption and collusion. Critics say the government is using the COVID-19 crisis to bypass the democratic process. The site also includes a section inviting citizens to review regional infrastructure projects.

# Summary The Coalition avenir Québec (CAQ) party launched a website called "pl61.ca" to promote Bill 61, the government's economic recovery plan, which has faced significant opposition criticism. The website aims to distinguish fact from fiction regarding the legislation, claiming to counter misinformation circulating on social media. The website was created by the CAQ party itself, not the government, as confirmed by domain metadata linking it to Denis Joannette, a senior CAQ executive. Opposition parties quickly criticized the initiative. Québec solidaire co-spokesperson Gabriel Nadeau-Dubois called it "damage control," while Parti québecois leader Martin Ouellet compared it to Liberal strategies during the Charbonneau Commission, warning against granting "disproportionate powers." The website lists statements deemed "false" and "true" but lacks attribution or sources for these claims. The public committee monitoring Charbonneau Commission recommendations warned that the website creates conditions favorable to corruption and embezzlement. Opposition parties argue the CAQ is exploiting the COVID-19 pandemic to circumvent democratic processes. The site also allows citizens to view preliminary government infrastructure projects for their regions.

South Carolina authorities say 34-year-old Kershaw County sheriff’s office employee Samantha Connell stole money collected from sex offenders when they registered. According to a State Law Enforcement Division warrant, she took all payments into the county’s fund for 16 months beginning in January 2015. She alone had the key to the cash drawer, and no deposits were made. She is charged with embezzlement of public funds under $10,000.

# Summary A 34-year-old South Carolina sheriff's office employee, Samantha Connell, is accused of stealing money from a sex offender registration fund in Kershaw County. According to an arrest warrant from the State Law Enforcement Division, Connell allegedly took all funds collected over 16 months beginning January 2015. As the sole keyholder to the storage drawer and with no deposits made during that period, she faces embezzlement charges for less than $10,000.

NDP Leader Jagmeet Singh promised a $100-million federal fund on Sunday to help steer young people away from gangs, saying the money would support after-school and mentorship programs. He said the pledge followed roundtables with experts, community organizers and front-line workers in Surrey and Toronto, who identified a lack of programming for youth as a major problem. The announcement came in Surrey, B.C., where gang violence has been a major concern in recent years. The backlash over that violence helped spur the creation in June 2018 of Wake Up Surrey, a parent-led Sikh community group pushing for stronger action from police and governments. The group has also criticized the RCMP for not prioritizing public safety and diversity training. Surrey’s mayor, elected last fall, has promised to replace the Mounties with a municipal police force, a move the group supports. Wake Up Surrey founding member Gurpreet Singh Sahota attended Singh’s town hall and said the group appreciates the attention from Singh and other federal parties, but wants to see real action rather than campaign promises. He noted that the Liberals previously pledged $327 million to fight youth gang violence during a byelection campaign, but the group has not seen the money materialize. Sahota said skepticism remains high, especially after another targeted shooting death in Surrey the day before, which police are treating as part of a gang war.

# NDP Promises $100 Million for Youth Gang Prevention Programs NDP Leader Jagmeet Singh announced a $100-million federal fund Sunday to help keep young people out of gangs, addressing gang violence that has plagued Surrey, B.C. Singh stated the funding would support after-school and mentorship programs, based on recommendations from experts, community organizers, and front-line workers he consulted in Surrey and Toronto. However, Gurpreet Singh Sahota, founding member of Wake Up Surrey—a parent-led community group created in June 2018 to combat gang violence—expressed cautious skepticism. While appreciating Singh's commitment, Sahota emphasized the group wants to see actual results, not just campaign promises. Sahota noted that the Liberals previously promised $327 million during a byelection campaign two years ago to combat youth gang violence, but the group has yet to receive any funding. Oil prices fell in thin trading after the Easter holiday break, which had closed many markets for up to four days, and after a US government report pointed to rising production. Brent crude futures were down 4 cents at $55.32 a barrel in early trading, after ending Monday 53 cents lower at $55.36. West Texas Intermediate (WTI) futures also slipped 4 cents to $52.61, following a 53-cent decline to $52.65 in the previous session. Both benchmarks had risen for three straight weeks before the holiday period. Analysts said the market may be due for a correction after a month of gains driven by speculators. Jonathan Chan of Phillip Futures in Singapore said Brent could test $54 and WTI $51.70. The main pressure came from expectations that US shale output will rise sharply in May. According to the US Energy Information Administration’s drilling productivity report, production was forecast to increase by 123,000 barrels per day to 5.19 million barrels per day. If realized, that would be the largest monthly increase since February 2015 and the highest output level since November 2015. A Reuters analysis also suggested more oil could come from US shale fields as financial firms invest heavily in production. Rising US output, now making the country the world’s third-largest oil producer, could increase pressure on Opec to deepen cuts. Opec is scheduled to meet on May 25 to consider extending output restraints beyond June, though Saudi Arabia’s energy minister has said it is too early to discuss that. Matt Stanley of Freight Investor Services said the market was uneasy because strong compliance and demand data were being offset by the threat of higher US production and exports.

# Oil Prices Slump Following Easter Break Oil prices declined in light trading following the Easter holiday break, which closed many markets for up to four days. Benchmark Brent crude futures fell 4 cents to $55.32 per barrel, while US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude dropped 4 cents to $52.61 per barrel, ending a three-week rally. An analyst at Phillip Futures in Singapore attributed the decline to speculators who had pushed prices upward for nearly a month, predicting a "healthy price correction" with Brent testing $54 and WTI reaching $51.70. The downward pressure intensified following a US government report indicating rising domestic production. US shale production in May was expected to post its largest monthly gain in over two years—a 123,000 barrel-per-day increase to 5.19 million barrels daily—marking the highest production level since November 2015. This anticipated production surge threatens to strain the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC), which agreed to curb output in late 2016. OPEC is scheduled to meet May 25 to consider extending production cuts beyond June, though Saudi Arabia's energy minister suggested it was premature to discuss extensions. Market participants remain concerned about the conflicting signals: strong Chinese economic data and rising demand against the significant threat posed by increasing US production and exports.

Ontario Provincial Police have gone to court to obtain audio recordings as part of an investigation into allegations that Ontario Liberals broke the law during the selection process for the Sudbury byelection candidate. The case centers on Andrew Olivier, the Liberal candidate in Sudbury in the last provincial election. Premier Kathleen Wynne asked him not to seek the nomination for the upcoming byelection because she preferred another candidate, Glenn Thibeault, a former NDP MP who switched to the Liberals. Olivier, who is quadriplegic and records conversations instead of taking notes, alleges that Liberals offered him a job or appointment in return for stepping aside. Olivier posted recordings of conversations with two Liberals, including Ontario Liberal campaign director Pat Sorbara, on YouTube. The Progressive Conservatives first asked the OPP to investigate, arguing the alleged conduct could violate Criminal Code provisions related to offering government advantages and securing appointments. After interviewing Olivier, police initially found no evidence of a criminal offence. But after the audio was made public, the Tories pushed for a second review. OPP Det.-Supt. Dave Truax said Olivier had previously chosen not to provide the recordings voluntarily, but police later obtained a production order. Elections Ontario is also investigating, having interviewed both Wynne and Sorbara. The New Democrats say the alleged conduct may breach the Election Act, which prohibits promising a job or appointment to induce someone to withdraw as a candidate. NDP MPP Gilles Bisson condemned the Liberals, calling the matter “attempted bribery.” The Liberals deny wrongdoing and say the recordings support their account. They argue the discussions were about possible ways Olivier could remain involved in the party or in accessibility-related work, but only after he had already been told he would not be the candidate. Olivier is now running in the byelection as an independent. The Sudbury seat was vacated in November by NDP MPP Joe Cimino, and the Liberals are eager to win back the riding.

# Summary: OPP Investigate Ontario Liberal Candidate Selection Process Ontario's provincial police have obtained a court order to secure audio recordings in an investigation into whether the provincial Liberal Party broke the law during the selection of a candidate for the Sudbury byelection. The controversy centers on Andrew Olivier, the Liberals' candidate in the previous general election, who alleged that Premier Kathleen Wynne asked him to withdraw from the byelection nomination in favor of Glenn Thibeault, a former NDP MP. Olivier claimed the Liberals offered him a job or appointment in exchange for stepping aside. Olivier, who is quadriplegic and records conversations for documentation purposes, posted audio of his discussions with Liberal officials, including campaign director Pat Sorbara, to YouTube. The Progressive Conservatives requested an OPP investigation, suspecting the actions violated Criminal Code sections regarding offering government advantages and securing appointments. Initially, police found insufficient evidence of criminal wrongdoing after interviewing Olivier. However, after he publicly released the recordings, the OPP reopened the investigation and obtained a production order for the audio files. Elections Ontario is also investigating, having interviewed both Wynne and Sorbara. The New Democrats argue the conduct violates the Election Act, which prohibits promising jobs or appointments to induce candidate withdrawal. The Liberals maintain the recordings vindicate them, showing discussions occurred only after Olivier was already informed he wouldn't be the candidate. Sorbara's recorded comments discuss potential roles in party work or board appointments. Olivier is now running in the byelection as an independent candidate. The Sudbury seat became vacant when NDP MPP Joe Cimino resigned after five months, and the Liberals are eager to reclaim the previously Liberal-held riding.

Polish activist groups campaigning for a restitution law have invited U.S. senators to visit Warsaw and see alleged abuses in the return of property seized, stolen or sold under duress during and after World War II. Last week, 59 senators urged Poland’s prime minister to pass legislation compensating heirs of former owners. Poland is the only central European country without such a law. Activists say weak regulation has enabled criminal schemes that transfer properties to the wrong people.

# Summary Polish restitution groups invited US senators to witness irregularities in property return cases. Fifty-nine US senators recently urged Poland's prime minister to pass legislation compensating heirs of those who lost property during WWII and communism. Poland lacks such a law, relying instead on court cases. Activists claim criminal activity has resulted in properties being transferred to unrelated individuals. Polish lawmakers combating this "restitution mafia" organized a Warsaw tour for senators to see affected sites.

Typhoon Mitag killed at least four people and left two others missing after battering South Korea’s southern and eastern regions overnight, authorities said Thursday. The storm made landfall Wednesday night in Haenam county in the southwest and moved east across the peninsula, weakening into a tropical storm before reaching the Sea of Japan/East Sea on Thursday morning. The dead included a 70-year-old woman in Pohang who was blown over by strong winds, a woman in Samcheok who was killed when a landslide triggered by heavy rain collapsed a house wall onto her while she slept, another victim in Yeongdeok in a similar landslide-related incident, and a 76-year-old man in Seongju who was swept or thrown by powerful winds. Officials said the typhoon brought record rainfall to some areas. Uljin county in North Gyeongsang recorded 104.5 millimeters per square meter per hour, the highest since such measurements began, while Donghae in Gangwon saw 67.4 mm/m2/h, its highest since 1992. The Korea Meteorological Agency warned that heavy rain would continue along the eastern coast and nearby islands even as the storm weakened. Mitag also hit southwestern and western Japan, causing flooding and heavy rain. In Kochi, floodwaters engulfed several parked vehicles near a river, though it was unclear whether anyone was inside.

# Typhoon Mitag Devastates South Korea Typhoon Mitag, the 18th of the Pacific season, struck South Korea on Wednesday night, killing at least four people and leaving two missing. The storm made landfall in southwestern Haenam county and swept eastward across the peninsula before weakening to a tropical storm as it reached the Sea of Japan Thursday morning. The confirmed deaths included a 70-year-old woman knocked down by strong winds in Pohang, two individuals killed by landslides triggered by heavy rains in Samcheok and Yeongdeok, and a 76-year-old man swept away by winds in Seongju village. Two people remain missing. This was South Korea's seventh typhoon this year and produced record rainfall in multiple regions. Ulijin county recorded 104.5 millimeters per square meter per hour—the highest measurement since the Korean Meteorological Agency began tracking such data. Donghae city experienced 67.4 mm/m² per hour, the highest since 1992. Despite the typhoon's downgrade to a storm, authorities warned that heavy rains would continue along the eastern coast and nearby islands. The typhoon also affected southwestern and western Japan, causing flooding that engulfed vehicles in Kochi.

Brazil’s Supreme Federal Tribunal (STF) has opened a new inquiry into former President Jair Bolsonaro and several members of his family and former administration over alleged wrongdoing in the handling of the COVID-19 pandemic. The case was authorized this week by STF Justice Flávio Dino, according to Brazilian media reports on Thursday. The probe targets Bolsonaro, his three oldest sons, Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, Congressman Eduardo Bolsonaro, and Councilman Carlos Bolsonaro, along with about 20 other people, including former officials, lawmakers, and journalists. It stems from a request by Brazil’s Federal Police, which in late 2024 asked the STF to allow an investigation based on a 1,180-page report produced by a Senate parliamentary inquiry commission in 2021. That Senate report accused Bolsonaro and others in his government of multiple crimes tied to the pandemic response. Among the offenses recommended for indictment were malfeasance, charlatanism, epidemic resulting in death, violation of preventive health measures, misuse of public funds, incitement to crime, forgery of private documents, crimes of responsibility, and even crimes against humanity, including extermination, persecution, and other inhumane acts. The commission argued that the alleged conduct was linked to denialism about the virus and vaccines, suspected corruption in vaccine procurement, and the promotion of scientifically unsupported COVID-19 treatments. Although the Senate CPI made those accusations in 2021, Brazil’s Prosecutor General concluded in July 2022 that there was not enough evidence to open a formal investigation at that time. Dino’s order said the legal requirements for a police inquiry were now present and stated that the parliamentary investigation had pointed to possible crimes against public administration, including contract irregularities, bid rigging, overbilling, embezzlement, use of front companies, and other illegal acts described in the report. Dino approved the Federal Police request and gave investigators an initial 60-day period to work on the case. The new inquiry is the latest in a long series of legal actions against Bolsonaro since he left office in January 2023. It comes only days after the STF sentenced him to 27 years and three months in prison for crimes against democracy, finding that he led a coup plot to overturn the 2022 election, which he narrowly lost to President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. Other recent developments have also added to Bolsonaro’s legal and personal troubles. A Brazilian federal court fined him about $188,750 for alleged “recreational racism” tied to remarks he made in 2021. Meanwhile, his doctor announced this week that he has been diagnosed with squamous cell carcinoma after skin lesions were removed. Bolsonaro is currently under strict house arrest and barred from commenting publicly. His son Flávio reacted angrily online, while Carlos Bolsonaro mocked the new probe on social media.

# Summary: Brazil Opens New Judicial Probe Against Bolsonaro Over Pandemic Response Brazilian Supreme Federal Tribunal Justice Flávio Dino has opened a new inquiry against former President Jair Bolsonaro and his three eldest sons, along with approximately 20 other individuals including former government officials, lawmakers, and journalists. The investigation concerns alleged irregular practices during the Bolsonaro administration's handling of the COVID-19 pandemic. The inquiry originated from a petition filed by the Brazilian Federal Police in late 2024, based on a 1,180-page report from a 2021 Parliamentary Inquiry Commission (CPI) in the Senate. That report alleged Bolsonaro and others committed multiple crimes related to pandemic management, recommending indictment on charges including malfeasance, epidemic resulting in death, violation of health measures, irregular use of public funds, incitement to crime, and crimes against humanity. The Senate commission's allegations centered on pandemic denialism regarding the virus and vaccines, suspected corruption in vaccine purchases by the Ministry of Health, and deaths allegedly caused by scientifically unsupported COVID-19 treatments. Despite these recommendations, Brazil's Office of the Prosecutor General determined in July 2022 that insufficient evidence existed to justify an investigation. Justice Dino's court order determined that legal requirements for initiating a police investigation were present. He emphasized that the parliamentary investigation had identified evidence of crimes against public administration, including contract irregularities, bid rigging, overbilling, and embezzlement. The Federal Police received a 60-day period to conduct initial investigations. This latest inquiry represents the most recent in a series of judicial actions against Bolsonaro since he left office in January 2023. It comes days after the Supreme Federal Tribunal convicted him to 27 years and three months in prison for "crimes against democracy," ruling he led a coup plot to overturn his 2022 election loss to President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. Additionally, a federal court recently imposed an approximately $188,750 fine for alleged "recreational racism." Bolsonaro cannot publicly comment on the new inquiry due to house arrest ordered by Justice Alexandre de Moraes in August, which also forbids him from issuing statements or using phones. His son Senator Flávio Bolsonaro responded with "Shame on you, Dino," while Councilman Carlos Bolsonaro posted on social media about the investigation. Recently, Bolsonaro's chief medical officer announced the former president was diagnosed with squamous cell carcinoma after eight skin lesions were surgically removed.

Former JPMorgan private client adviser Michael Oppenheim, 49, was sentenced by U.S. District Judge Analisa Torres to five years in prison for embezzling nearly $20 million from clients. He also must forfeit almost $20.2 million and pay restitution to JPMorgan after pleading guilty in November to embezzlement and securities fraud. Prosecutors said Oppenheim, who worked with about 500 wealthy clients in JPMorgan’s midtown Manhattan offices, stole money from 2008 to 2015 by convincing some clients to let him withdraw funds for supposed low-risk municipal bond investments and, in other cases, taking money without permission. His lawyer cited a long-standing gambling addiction and asked for leniency. JPMorgan said it alerted authorities and was angered by the breach of trust.

# Summary Michael Oppenheim, a 49-year-old former JPMorgan vice president and private client adviser, was sentenced to five years in prison for embezzling approximately $20 million from wealthy clients between 2008 and 2015. Operating from JPMorgan's Manhattan offices, Oppenheim managed about 500 clients and deceived them by falsely claiming he would invest their money in low-risk municipal bonds, while actually stealing the funds for himself. In some cases, he withdrew money without permission. Judge Analisa Torres ordered him to forfeit nearly $20.2 million and pay restitution to JPMorgan after his guilty plea in November. His defense attorney attributed the crimes to a "pathological gambling addiction."

Valentino’s first couture show after the funeral of house founder Valentino Garavani in Rome began in an atmosphere of mourning, then shifted into a highly theatrical presentation in Paris. VIP guests, including Sir Elton John, were led through darkness to their seats on simple stools placed inside circular pods with small viewing windows. Once the show started, the blinds rose and a soundtrack of classical music was abruptly interrupted by barking dogs. Models appeared behind glass like mannequins, so guests saw only fragments of each look at a time, reinforcing the sense of a controlled, almost clinical “peep show” of couture. The staging was stark and futuristic: white, sterile, and unsettling, with the presentation emphasizing a curated gaze and partial views rather than full reveals. Creative director Alessandro Michele, known for maximalist instincts, used restriction as part of the concept, rationing spectacle instead of overwhelming the room with it. The clothes themselves were often dazzling but, according to the report, did not always live up to the ambition of the set. Michele offered disco-inspired shine, with sparkle, gems, bedazzled headwear, and layered gold collars that carried a slight circus feel. There were also stronger moments, including dramatic sleeves that widened into leg-of-mutton shapes, sequined fabrics that caught the light with Valentino polish, and voluminous skirts that swamped the human figure. Still, the collection was described as comparatively restrained and at times cautious for a designer associated with excess. The front row underscored the event’s importance, with celebrities and fashion figures such as Dakota Johnson, Kirsten Dunst, and Tyla in attendance alongside ambassadors and other high-profile guests. The mood suggested a major brand moment, while the collection felt like a reset as Michele tested how far he could stretch Valentino’s couture language. Fashion critic Suzy Menkes said the emotional weight of the show was intensified by Garavani’s funeral, calling it “an end of an era.” She noted that although new designers are taking over many houses, Valentino’s departure felt especially significant because he was a widely understood, beloved figure with broad recognition beyond fashion insiders.
