UN experts say Yemen’s Houthi rebels are receiving drone parts and weapons with technical features similar to Iranian-made arms, in what may be a violation of the UN arms embargo on the group. In a report to the Security Council obtained by The Associated Press, the panel said the main smuggling route for both commercially available drone components and weapons appears to be overland from Oman and Yemen’s southern coast, passing through territory held by the internationally recognized government before reaching Houthi-controlled Sanaa. The experts also said a major seizure on Nov. 25 of a dhow in the Arabian Sea, which was carrying anti-tank missiles, shows that sea transport continues to be used in possible embargo violations. The report reviewed the state of Yemen’s civil war, which began when the Houthis seized Sanaa in 2014. A Saudi-led coalition backing the Yemeni government has fought the rebels since 2015. The conflict has killed thousands of civilians and produced the world’s worst humanitarian crisis, with widespread shortages of food and medical care and a continuing risk of famine. The panel said neither side made much progress in 2019 toward a political settlement or a military victory. The experts also accused both sides of economic warfare, saying they used financial and economic pressure to deprive opponents of funds and supplies, while profiteering from the war remained widespread. In the north, the Houthis were said to be tightening political and military control through pervasive intelligence services and harsh repression of tribal opposition and dissent. The panel reported a network targeting women who opposed the Houthis, including through sexual violence. It said it documented 11 cases in which women were arrested, detained, beaten, tortured or sexually abused because of their political activity or affiliations, and were threatened with prostitution or organized-crime charges if they continued. Militarily, the Houthis intensified attacks on Saudi Arabia during 2019 using a new unmanned Delta-design drone and a new land-attack cruise missile. The panel investigated the Sept. 14 attacks on Saudi Aramco’s Khurays and Abqaiq facilities, which disrupted global energy supplies and cut Saudi oil production in half. Although the Houthis claimed responsibility, the experts said the estimated range of the weapons made a launch from Houthi territory unlikely. They concluded the systems were probably imported illegally, not built in Yemen. The panel traced parts from Hong Kong to Muscat and from Japan to Abu Dhabi.

On August 13, 2017, Iran’s parliament approved a long-awaited amendment to the country’s drug law that would significantly narrow the range of drug offenses carrying a mandatory death sentence, according to Human Rights Watch. The change is seen as an important step, though it is less sweeping than a December 2016 draft that would have eliminated the death penalty for most nonviolent drug offenses. Iran has one of the world’s highest execution rates. Amnesty International reported that at least 567 people were executed in 2016, including at least two who were children at the time of their alleged crimes. When the revised draft was introduced, Hassan Noroozi, spokesperson for the parliamentary judicial committee, said around 5,000 people were on death row for drug offenses, most of them between the ages of 20 and 30. Human Rights Watch said the amendment could spare hundreds of people who should never have faced execution. Sarah Leah Whitson, the group’s Middle East director, said Iranian officials themselves have acknowledged that capital punishment does not effectively combat drugs, and urged parliament to go further by abolishing the death penalty for all drug offenses. The bill still requires approval by the Guardian Council, a 12-member body of Islamic jurists that must decide whether the law conforms to Iran’s constitution and its interpretation of sharia. Under the current law, even nonviolent offenses can trigger mandatory execution, including possession of as little as 30 grams of synthetic drugs such as methamphetamines, or trafficking, possession, or trade of more than five kilograms of opium or 30 grams of heroin. The approved amendment would replace the death penalty or life imprisonment for many of these offenses with prison terms of up to 30 years. However, the death penalty would remain in some cases, including when the accused or another participant used or carried weapons with intent to use them against law enforcement, when the defendant was a leader of a drug trafficking cartel, when a child was used in the offense, or when someone with a prior drug-related execution or long prison sentence commits another drug offense. After objections from Iran’s judiciary and the Interior Ministry’s drug control headquarters, parliament revised the bill to keep the death penalty for nonviolent offenses involving production, distribution, trafficking, and selling drugs, but only above higher thresholds: more than 50 kilograms of “traditional” drugs such as opium or two kilograms of synthetic drugs. The death penalty was also restored for possession, purchase, or concealment of more than three kilograms of synthetic drugs. Despite the reform effort, executions for drug offenses have continued. Human Rights Watch urged Iran on July 20 to stop these executions while the amendment awaited final approval. The group has also documented serious due process violations, torture, and coerced confessions in drug cases, including at Ghezel Hesar prison. It says these practices, along with Iran’s use of the death penalty for drug crimes, violate international law.

# Iran Raises the Bar for Drug-Related Death Penalties On August 13, 2017, Iran's parliament approved a significant amendment to its drug law that raises the threshold for mandatory death sentences, according to Human Rights Watch. This reform represents progress, though it falls short of a more ambitious December 2016 draft that sought to eliminate capital punishment for most nonviolent drug offenses. Iran executes people at one of the world's highest rates. Amnesty International documented at least 567 executions in Iran during 2016 alone, including two individuals who were children at the time of their alleged crimes. According to parliamentary spokesperson Hassan Noroozi, approximately 5,000 people currently face death row for drug offenses, predominantly between ages 20 and 30. Under Iran's previous drug law, possession of as little as 30 grams of synthetic drugs or trafficking more than five kilograms of opium carried mandatory death sentences. The approved amendment converts these offenses to prison sentences of up to 30 years. However, the death penalty remains for drug leaders, cases involving weapons intended against law enforcement, those who involved children in trafficking, and repeat offenders with prior execution or lengthy sentences. After pushback from Iran's judiciary and drug control authorities, parliament modified the amendment to maintain capital punishment for drug production, distribution, trafficking, and sales. The revised thresholds increased to more than 50 kilograms of traditional drugs like opium or two kilograms of synthetic drugs. Death penalty provisions also remain for possession or concealment of more than three kilograms of synthetic drugs. Sarah Leah Whitson, Human Rights Watch's Middle East director, stated that if enacted, the amendment could save hundreds from execution. She emphasized that even Iranian officials acknowledge capital punishment's ineffectiveness against drug trafficking and called for complete abolition of death penalties for all drug offenders. The amendment requires approval from Iran's Guardian Council, a 12-member body of Islamic jurists who determine constitutional and religious compliance. Human Rights Watch has documented serious due process violations in drug cases, including torture, forced confessions, and restricted legal representation in Iranian prisons. The United Nations Human Rights Committee has determined that drug offenses do not constitute "most serious crimes" under international law, making death penalties for such crimes violations of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, which Iran has ratified. Despite pending reforms, authorities have continued executing drug offenders. Human Rights Watch urged immediate cessation of these executions pending final approval and called on the Guardian Council to expedite reform implementation to address Iran's "execution epidemic."

Two years after Democrats were stunned by Donald Trump’s 2016 victory, many party operatives and candidates are approaching the 2018 midterms with a mix of confidence and deep unease, worried that another seemingly favorable election could still end in disappointment. The article opens by recalling the moment in October 2016 when Hillary Clinton’s campaign appeared to be cruising toward victory after the release of the “Access Hollywood” tape, in which Trump bragged about sexual assault. Jesse Ferguson, then deputy press secretary for Clinton’s campaign, remembers that period vividly — and also remembers the shock of what happened a month later. Now, with Democrats hoping to gain 23 House seats and win control of the chamber, Ferguson says he cannot tell whether his anxiety is a sign of lingering trauma or simply hard-earned caution. “Election Day will either prove to me I have PTSD or show I’ve been living deja vu,” he said. That feeling is widespread among Democrats who lived through 2016. Many are watching the final stretch of the 2018 campaign nervously, aware that the party is favored but not secure. Democratic leaders publicly insist this year is different, but even they acknowledge some unsettling parallels: President Trump remains unpopular and engulfed in controversy, Democrats lead in many polls, and some Republicans are openly pessimistic. At the same time, the memory of 2016 makes Democrats wary of believing too much in favorable polling or a coming “blue wave.” The article notes that FiveThirtyEight gives Democrats a 76.9 percent chance of winning the House one month before Election Day — a better-than-even likelihood, but not a certainty. That figure is actually higher than the 71.4 percent chance FiveThirtyEight gave Clinton in 2016, which only deepens the anxiety for some Democrats. Jesse Lehrich, who worked on Clinton’s campaign, recalled watching returns at the Javits Center in New York and receiving texts from reporters and operatives after Wisconsin had already been called for Trump. He said people were slow to accept the result because they had not seriously considered the possibility that Trump could win. Lehrich said he sees clear similarities between 2016 and 2018, but believes Democrats are more alert to the dangers this time and less likely to relax too soon. Not everyone agrees. Rep. Seth Moulton of Massachusetts said bluntly that Democrats are indeed overconfident. He warned that the party could win many seats or still fail to capture the House majority, and urged Democrats to remember that the election consists of many difficult races, not a guaranteed wave. One major lesson Democrats say they have internalized is the unreliability of polling. They argue that pollsters missed key elements of the 2016 electorate, especially rural Trump voters and the scale of support in red areas. Ben Ray Lujan, chairman of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, said last cycle’s polling was “off” and called the failure to capture the rural vote a “devastating mistake.” He said the DCCC has taken steps to improve its methods, but he stressed that winning the House would still require a hard-fought effort. A Democratic pollster quoted anonymously agreed that the party appears favored, but said the outcome is far from certain. The environment could produce a sweeping Democratic victory, or simply a good election year that still falls short of a majority. He warned that less likely outcomes can still happen and that Democrats should not assume the most favorable scenario is inevitable. Unlike in 2016, Democrats also have historical momentum on their side: the party in the White House typically loses ground in midterm elections. Several Democrats argue that Trump’s actual presidency, rather than the hypothetical prospect of it, has transformed the political environment. Former DCCC chairman Steve Israel said Democratic energy is “at nuclear levels” and that voters are highly motivated to turn out. He said most Democrats — and many Republicans — believe Democrats will win the House, with the only real question being the size of the majority. Still, Ferguson and others remain wary. He believes the effort to repeal the Affordable Care Act and the daily realities of Trump’s presidency have changed the race, but he remembers how much can happen in the final month of a campaign. In 2016, the last stretch brought both the “Access Hollywood” tape and FBI Director James Comey’s announcement that the Clinton email investigation had been reopened. Republicans now argue that the 2018 version of an October surprise has already occurred in the Brett Kavanaugh confirmation fight, which they say energized conservative voters. Ferguson’s conclusion is cautious: Democrats should not assume that what they see now will hold through Election Day, because they have already learned how quickly everything can change.

# Democrats Haunted by 2016 as Midterm Elections Approach Two years after Hillary Clinton's shocking defeat despite favorable polling and apparent momentum, Democratic operatives are experiencing anxiety as the 2018 midterm elections near. With control of the House at stake, party veterans who lived through the 2016 disappointment are nervously watching history unfold, uncertain whether their current optimism will prove justified or if disaster will strike again. ## The Parallels The similarities between 2016 and 2018 are striking. President Trump is unpopular and facing numerous scandals, Democrats lead in polls, and some Republicans are openly pessimistic about their prospects. FiveThirtyEight gives Democrats a 76.9 percent chance of winning the House majority—only slightly better than the 71.4 percent odds given to Clinton two years ago. Democrats need to gain 23 House seats to achieve a majority. Jesse Lehrich, a Clinton campaign veteran, recalls the shock of watching returns from the Javits Center in New York as the unthinkable happened. "They just called Wisconsin. We lost," he remembered saying. He observes similar patterns in 2018 but believes Democrats are more cognizant of the parallels and determined not to become complacent. However, not all Democratic leaders share this confidence. Representative Seth Moulton flatly acknowledged that his party may be overconfident, emphasizing that Democrats face "a lot of tough races that will be hard-fought victories" rather than an unstoppable wave. ## The Polling Problem If Democrats are universally nervous about anything, it's polling accuracy. While Clinton's polling wasn't actually as favorable as some remember, the failure to detect a wave of Trump supporters in rural areas was devastating. Ben Ray Lujan, chairman of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, called this "a devastating mistake" and emphasized that the DCCC has taken deliberate steps to understand rural voters better. One Democratic pollster acknowledged that while data suggests Democrats are favored to win the majority, it remains uncertain whether the political environment will create an electoral tsunami or merely a good year that still falls short. The pollster warned that even outcomes with only 20-30 percent probability can occur, as 2016 demonstrated. ## Reasons for Cautious Optimism History may work in Democrats' favor this cycle. The incumbent president's party typically struggles during midterm elections—an advantage Democrats didn't have in 2016 when they sought the presidency for a third consecutive term. Additionally, some argue that Trump's actual presidency, rather than the hypothetical concerns from 2016, fundamentally changes voter dynamics. Steve Israel, a former DCCC chairman, claims "Democratic energy is at nuclear levels," with supporters willing to "crawl over broken glass to vote." He believes most Democrats and many Republicans expect a Democratic House majority, with the real question being the margin of victory. ## Lingering Uncertainty Despite these positive indicators, Democratic operatives remain cautious. Ferguson acknowledges that Trump's presidency and healthcare concerns may motivate voters differently than 2016, but he remains wary of potential October surprises. The final month of 2016 brought the "Access Hollywood" tape and FBI Director James Comey's email announcement—shocks that upended expectations. Republicans counter that Brett Kavanaugh's confirmation fight already provided 2018's October surprise by motivating conservative voters. Ultimately, Democratic veterans of 2016 have learned that unexpected outcomes are possible. As Ferguson expressed, "We make a mistake if we assume that what we're seeing today is what we'll see for the entire month."

Ontario police have charged two Liberal insiders in connection with alleged bribery during the 2015 Sudbury byelection, including a new allegation involving current Energy Minister Glenn Thibeault. Pat Sorbara, who was then Premier Kathleen Wynne’s deputy chief of staff, was charged Tuesday with two counts under Ontario’s Election Act. Liberal operative Gerry Lougheed was charged with one count. Court records say one of Sorbara’s charges concerns Thibeault, who was a federal New Democrat MP for Sudbury before winning the provincial Liberal nomination and running in the February 2015 byelection. Thibeault denied that he was offered anything in exchange for switching parties or running for the Liberals. Speaking Wednesday, he said he had many conversations with Sorbara about whether he would run, what the party needed, policy issues, the byelection timeline and building a campaign team. But, he said, “in terms of offers being made, this was a choice that I made to do this.” His lawyer also said no inducement was made or accepted. Police allege that between Nov. 19, 2014, and the day after the byelection, Sorbara promised Thibeault “an office or employment” to persuade him to become a candidate. Investigators say the promise was made “knowingly,” which would increase the potential penalty from a maximum $5,000 fine to as much as $25,000 and/or up to two years less a day in jail. Sorbara has since resigned from her later role as the Ontario Liberals’ CEO and 2018 campaign director. She said she was shocked by the charges and believes they will not stand. The other allegations in the case stem from claims Sorbara and Lougheed offered Andrew Olivier, a former Sudbury Liberal candidate, a job or appointment in order to get him to step aside for Thibeault. Wynne has said those discussions were aimed at keeping Olivier in the party and that there was no quid pro quo because she had already decided to appoint Thibeault as the candidate before the conversations took place. The issue first became public in late 2014 when Olivier, who is quadriplegic and often records conversations instead of taking notes, released audio of his discussions with Sorbara and Lougheed. NDP deputy leader Jagmeet Singh said the new allegation about Thibeault is the first suggestion of impropriety involving Thibeault’s own candidacy, and the NDP has asked Elections Ontario to investigate whether he accepted anything in return for running. The Progressive Conservatives also pressed the issue in the legislature, briefly storming out of question period after rules limited their questioning. Sorbara and Lougheed are scheduled to appear in court in Sudbury on Nov. 21. Lougheed’s lawyer said his client denies wrongdoing.

# Summary: Ontario Liberal Bribery Allegations Ontario Premier Kathleen Wynne's former deputy chief of staff, Pat Sorbara, has been charged with two bribery counts under the provincial Election Act for allegedly offering inducements to secure political candidates. Liberal operative Gerry Lougheed faces one count. These charges represent the first allegations of impropriety directly involving Glenn Thibeault's candidacy in a 2015 Sudbury byelection. According to police allegations, Sorbara promised Thibeault, then a New Democratic MP, "an office or employment" between November 2014 and February 2015 to persuade him to run for the Ontario Liberals. The "knowingly" element of the charges increases potential penalties from a $5,000 fine to up to $25,000 and/or two years less a day in jail. Thibeault denied receiving any inducements, stating his conversations with Sorbara focused on policy discussions, campaign logistics, and team-building rather than offers. His lawyer confirmed no inducement was made or accepted. Sorbara expressed shock at the allegations and believes the charges will not succeed. The investigation also involves separate allegations that Sorbara and Lougheed offered Andrew Olivier, the previous Sudbury Liberal candidate, a job or appointment to step aside for Thibeault. Olivier, a quadriplegic who records conversations, released audio of his discussions with both officials. Premier Wynne characterized these conversations as efforts to retain Olivier in the party, claiming no quid pro quo existed since Thibeault was already selected before Olivier was approached. The scandal originated in late 2014 when Olivier publicly disclosed the alleged offers. NDP deputy leader Jagmeet Singh questioned whether the alleged inducement involved a cabinet position, calling it "a serious attack on the credibility of the cabinet and this premier." The NDP has requested Elections Ontario investigate whether Thibeault accepted anything violating the Election Act. Sorbara recently resigned from her positions as Ontario Liberals CEO and 2018 campaign director following the charges. Sorbara and Lougheed are scheduled to appear in Sudbury court on November 21, with trial potentially occurring near the June 2018 election. The bribery allegations are part of a broader scandal affecting the Ontario Liberals. Former premier Dalton McGuinty's top staffers, David Livingston and Laura Miller, face trial in September 2017 for breach of trust and mischief related to deleted emails concerning the cancellation of two gas plants, which cost taxpayers up to $1.1 billion. Police are also investigating financial irregularities at Ornge air ambulance service and alleged document destruction in a Trillium Power Wind Corp. lawsuit against the province. Lougheed had previously faced criminal charges of counselling an offence not committed and unlawfully influencing appointments, but those charges were stayed earlier this year. His lawyer maintains Lougheed did nothing warranting culpable findings.

Caroline Eden and Eleanor Ford’s *Samarkand: Recipes and Stories from Central Asia and the Caucasus* is presented as a richly atmospheric blend of travel writing, history, photography and cookery. The reviewer places it among a recent wave of books inspired by the ancient trading routes, but says Eden and Ford take a different, more vivid approach than standard historical accounts such as Peter Frankopan’s *Silk Roads*. Their book evokes the old spice and silk roads through evocative prose, traditional recipes and striking images that together create an almost three-dimensional sense of place. A recurring concern in cookery books is the difficulty of sourcing unusual ingredients, but the review notes that most of the recipes rely on items available in an ordinary supermarket, even if some ingredients such as barberries or Aleppo pepper may be harder to find. The exotic quality of the food is part of the appeal, reflecting the remote and culturally layered regions the authors visited. The review praises Eden’s storytelling, which combines historical research with close observation to portray life in places such as Samarkand and Tashkent. These names are described as conjuring images of mystery, architecture, fabrics and wandering travellers, but the book also shows the present-day realities of the region, where shifting borders, mixed cultures and religious and ethnic ambiguities remain central. The lives of local people are portrayed as shaped by migration and exchange, contrasting with the more rigid divisions of life in the West. The book is organized conventionally by food categories such as starters, meat dishes, breads and drinks, but the recipes are enriched by background notes on ingredients, history and the social customs surrounding how dishes are eaten. The reviewer particularly values the context around dishes like pilaf, including where and how the authors first tasted them. This makes the book more than a recipe collection: it becomes a cultural journey grounded in firsthand experience. The final impression is one of abundance, authenticity and temptation, leaving the reviewer torn between cooking plov at home or traveling to Tashkent to taste it in situ.

# Summary: Samarkand - Recipes and Stories from Central Asia and the Caucasus Caroline Eden and Eleanor Ford's new cookbook, *Samarkand*, takes a distinctive approach to exploring the ancient Silk Road by combining travel narratives with traditional recipes from Central Asia and the Caucasus. While numerous books have recently examined these historic trading routes, this work stands apart through its integration of evocative storytelling, stunning photography, and accessible culinary instructions. A notable strength of the book is its practical ingredient sourcing. Despite featuring exotic cuisines from remote locations, most recipes require only readily available supermarket items, making them achievable for average home cooks. The authors visited places far off the beaten path, so some effort in sourcing ingredients is expected and appropriate. The book's structure follows traditional cookbook organization, covering starters, meat dishes, breads, and beverages. However, what distinguishes it is the contextual information woven throughout—historical details about ingredients, cultural backgrounds, and personal accounts of how the authors first encountered each dish. This approach transforms simple recipes like pilaf into meaningful cultural experiences by explaining when, where, and how local inhabitants actually eat these foods. Eden, an experienced travel writer, combines historical research with keen observation to create an atmospheric portrait of life along the Spice Route. The photographs by Ford beautifully complement the text, capturing the richness of these cultures. Readers gain insight into how current inhabitants navigate shifting borders, blended cultures, and religious ambiguities—a reality quite different from Western life. The book's authenticity stems from the authors' dedication to experiencing food in its original context, whether consumed casually or in family homes. While readers cannot replicate this firsthand experience, the detailed accounts add layers of meaning to their own cooking attempts. Ultimately, *Samarkand* succeeds because context is paramount. The combination of compelling text, artful food photography, and cultural documentation creates a comprehensive portrait of a world defined by silks, spices, and vibrant colors, making it as inspiring to read as it is to cook from.

# Israel Braces for Rare 'Medicane' Storm Israel faces an unusual tropical storm this weekend, bringing heavy rainfall, flooding, and strong winds to Israel and Egypt. A "medicane"—combining Mediterranean and hurricane characteristics—is exceptionally rare this far east in the Mediterranean. More than 80 people were injured in Kerala, India, after villagers protesting the Adani Group’s $900 million Vizhinjam port project clashed with police, marking a sharp escalation in a months-long standoff. The protesters are largely from a Christian fishing community that says the port has damaged their livelihoods and caused coastal erosion. They have been blocking the site for more than three months, including by erecting a large shelter at the entrance. The unrest intensified over the weekend when police arrested some protesters who had blocked Adani construction vehicles from entering the site, despite a court order allowing work to resume. In response, hundreds of protesters, including Catholic priests, marched to a police station late Sunday night. According to police documents and local television footage, the confrontation turned violent, leaving police vehicles damaged. Protest leaders said dozens of protesters were hurt, while a senior police official said 36 officers were wounded. Another official said more than 600 police officers were deployed in Vizhinjam afterward to restore order. Police and protesters gave sharply different accounts of the violence. The police case document said protesters entered the station with “lethal weapons,” threatened to set it on fire, and held officers hostage. Protest leaders, meanwhile, accused police of throwing stones at them. The Adani Group said the port complies with all laws and cited studies saying it is not responsible for shoreline erosion; the Kerala government has also said erosion is due to natural causes. The company did not comment on the weekend clashes. The protests have continued despite repeated orders from Kerala’s top court to allow construction to restart. On Monday, the court again pressed state officials on why its order was not being enforced and asked for a response by Friday. The port, located on India’s southern tip, is intended to serve major East-West trade routes. Adani’s conglomerate is funding about one-third of the project, with the rest coming from state and federal governments, under a 40-year operating agreement.

# Summary: Adani Port Protests in Kerala Over 80 people were injured in violent clashes between police and protesters in Kerala, India, over the $900-million Vizhinjam port project developed by billionaire Gautam Adani's ports business. The protests, led by a mostly Christian fishing community, have halted construction for over three months. Villagers oppose the port development, citing coastal erosion and loss of livelihoods. They have blocked the construction site entrance with a 1,200-square-foot shelter. Ethiopia’s Agricultural Businesses Corporation (EABC) says a little over half of the fertilizer ordered for this year’s farming season has reached the Port of Djibouti. The shipment is meant to support both the current “Bega” dry season and the upcoming “Mehir” main harvest. In September 2023, Agriculture Minister Girma Amente announced a plan to procure 23 million quintals of fertilizer, almost double the 14 million quintals imported in the previous harvest season. According to EABC, 12 million quintals, or 52% of the total, have now arrived in Djibouti. Of that amount, 11.7 million quintals have already been moved into Ethiopia and are being distributed to farmers through agricultural cooperatives and unions. The first fertilizer consignments began arriving in late October 2023, and procurement and distribution started earlier this year than in previous seasons. However, reports say conflict in parts of the country, including the Amhara region, is hindering delivery to small-scale farmers. Tesfaw Batable, who heads the Amhara Disaster Prevention and Food Security Program Coordinating Commission, told Deutsche Welle that movement restrictions caused by the conflict are delaying both fertilizer and food grain distribution. Last year, shortages and late deliveries sparked protests nationwide, while farmers also struggled with high fertilizer prices, which reportedly reached 12,000 birr per quintal.

# Ethiopia Receives Over Half of Annual Fertilizer Order Ethiopia's Agricultural Businesses Corporation reports that 12 million quintals—52% of the 23 million quintals ordered for the current harvest season—have arrived at Djibouti Port. This represents a significant increase from the previous season's 14 million quintals. Of the arrived fertilizers, 11.7 million quintals have been transported into Ethiopia and are being distributed to farmers through agricultural cooperatives and unions. The initial shipments began arriving in late October 2023, marking an earlier procurement timeline than previous seasons. However, distribution faces substantial obstacles. Ongoing conflicts in regions like Amhara are restricting people's movement and delaying fertilizer delivery to small-scale farmers. According to the Amhara Disaster Prevention and Food Security Program Coordinating Commission, these disruptions are preventing timely access to essential agricultural inputs. Additionally, farmers struggle with affordability, as fertilizer prices reached 12,000 birr per quintal last year. Last year's fertilizer scarcity sparked widespread nationwide demonstrations, particularly in Amhara and Oromia regions, highlighting the critical importance of reliable agricultural input supply for Ethiopia's farming communities.

The Obama administration announced on Monday that U.S. military and civilian personnel had completed the destruction of Syria’s declared chemical weapons stockpile. President Barack Obama said the neutralization of the agents helps ensure that the Assad regime cannot use chemical weapons against the Syrian people and shows the international community will not tolerate such weapons. The operation was carried out with the ship Cape Ray, whose crew was congratulated by Defense Secretary Chuck Hagel for eliminating the stockpile in international waters. Obama thanked Denmark, Norway, Italy, Finland, Germany, and the United Kingdom for their contributions, and also noted support from Russia and China. Pentagon press secretary Rear Adm. John Kirby said the effort, supported by the Organization for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons and the United Nations, demonstrated what diplomacy can achieve when backed by a willingness to use military force. Secretary of State John Kerry said the destruction was completed “in record time” despite Syria’s civil war, but stressed that the work was not finished. He said there were still “discrepancies and omissions” in Syria’s chemical weapons declaration, suggesting the Assad government had not fully disclosed its stockpile. Kerry also expressed concern about the continued use of chlorine gas against Syrian civilians and reaffirmed U.S. support for moderate rebels in the conflict. The announcement came nearly a year after the August 21, 2013 sarin gas attack in the Ghouta suburbs outside Damascus, which killed more than 1,400 people and triggered international action to eliminate Syria’s chemical arsenal.

# Syria's Declared Chemical Weapons Stockpile Destroyed The Obama administration announced that U.S. military and civilian personnel successfully completed the destruction of Syria's declared chemical weapons stockpile. President Obama stated that neutralizing these chemical agents prevents the Assad regime from using them against Syrian civilians and demonstrates that the international community will not tolerate such weapons. Secretary of Defense Chuck Hagel congratulated the crew of the Cape Ray, the ship responsible for neutralizing the chemical weapons in international waters. President Obama thanked Denmark, Norway, Italy, Finland, Germany, and the United Kingdom for their contributions, while also acknowledging assistance from Russia and China. The effort was conducted with support from the Organization for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons and the United Nations. However, the administration acknowledged concerns that Syria may not have fully disclosed its entire chemical weapons stockpile. Secretary of State John Kerry emphasized that significant work remains, noting "discrepancies and omissions" in Syria's chemical weapons declaration. He also expressed concern about continued chlorine gas attacks against Syrian civilians by Assad's forces and reaffirmed U.S. support for moderate Syrian rebels, promising continued political and financial assistance. The announcement comes nearly one year after a sarin gas attack on August 21, 2013, in the Ghouta suburbs near Damascus killed over 1,400 people. The destruction of the declared stockpile represents a significant milestone, though complete elimination of Syria's chemical weapons program remains incomplete.

Tshwane Executive Mayor Dr. Nasiphi Moya has rejected claims that the City of Tshwane was slow to blacklist controversial businessman Edwin Sodi over the Rooiwal Wastewater Treatment Plant scandal. Responding to a report titled “No rush to blacklist Edwin Sodi,” Moya said the article gave the false impression that the city lacked urgency, when in fact officials were working through the required legal and administrative steps to ensure the process would stand up to scrutiny. According to Moya, Tshwane began acting against suppliers linked to the Rooiwal Joint Venture in 2023, and by 2024 had already made an initial submission to National Treasury. She said the city deliberately focused on building stronger internal controls before sending the matter to Treasury, rather than rushing a defective case that could be rejected. Those controls included creating a formal Standard Operating Procedure for supplier restrictions and blacklisting, setting up a Supplier Review Committee with approved terms of reference, and adding extra checks to make sure the process complied with all legislative and regulatory requirements. Moya acknowledged that the timeline was longer than ideal, but said the extra steps were necessary to produce a lawful and defensible submission. She argued that speed alone was not the right measure if the end result could be challenged or overturned. In her view, a flawed process that fails legal scrutiny does not help accountability, residents, or the rule of law. She also addressed criticism that city officials supposedly did not know where Sodi-linked company directors were located. Moya said this criticism misunderstood the legal distinction between knowing someone’s general whereabouts and formally serving legal notices on a corporate entity, which must be done according to prescribed procedures. The city, she said, made repeated attempts to serve notices through official channels and verified information using the Central Supplier Database and other systems. To strengthen the case, Tshwane also commissioned an independent legal review. Moya rejected the suggestion that the city had intentionally delayed the blacklisting effort or lacked urgency in pursuing accountability. She said the process is now moving forward: Tshwane’s Supplier Review Committee has completed its assessment and issued a final recommendation. The matter now awaits approval by the City Manager before being sent by the Chief Financial Officer to National Treasury for final decision-making. Once the file reaches National Treasury, responsibility for the matter shifts fully to the national department, which has the power to impose restrictions. Moya said the city should not take shortcuts simply to appear decisive, stressing that the current multi-party coalition government is committed to dealing with corruption and underperformance through lawful, transparent, and enforceable action. She reaffirmed that where wrongdoing is found, Tshwane will act, but in a way that produces durable outcomes rather than procedurally weak decisions.

A federal appeals court in San Francisco ruled 2-1 on Monday that the Trump administration may deport hundreds of thousands of immigrants who had been granted temporary protected status (TPS) for humanitarian reasons. The decision from a panel of the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals overturned a lower court injunction that had blocked the administration from ending TPS for immigrants from El Salvador, Haiti, Nicaragua and Sudan while the case was being litigated. The ruling affects about 300,000 immigrants and roughly 200,000 of their U.S.-citizen children. Many of the adults have lived in the United States for decades. The Trump administration had moved to revoke their protections in 2017 and 2018, arguing that conditions in their home countries had improved enough to make return safe. The immigrants and their children sued, and a federal judge in San Francisco blocked the administration’s action in 2018. Writing for the majority, Judge Consuelo M. Callahan said federal law does not allow courts to second-guess the Homeland Security secretary’s decisions about which countries’ citizens should receive protected status. She argued that the TPS statute limits, rather than expands, the secretary’s discretion. Judge Ryan D. Nelson joined the opinion. Judge Morgan Christen dissented, saying the administration had changed policy and practice without public review and describing the move as “an abrupt and unexplained change.” She also pointed to claims in the lawsuit that the deportation decisions were motivated by racial and ethnic bias, citing President Trump’s reported remarks about Haiti and El Salvador and his broader comments about immigrants from Mexico and Central America. Christen wrote that the statements were clear in their meaning and could not be dismissed. The Justice Department welcomed the ruling, saying the district court’s injunction had prevented the Department of Homeland Security from carrying out authority Congress had given solely to the secretary and that the 9th Circuit correctly recognized the plain language of immigration law. The ruling does not immediately strip TPS from the affected immigrants. According to the ACLU Foundation of Southern California, which represents them, TPS holders from the affected countries can keep their status until at least February, and those from El Salvador until at least November. The challengers said they would seek review by a larger, 11-judge panel of the 9th Circuit and, if necessary, take the case to the U.S. Supreme Court. The article also traced the history of TPS for each country. Sudan first received protection in 1997 because of civil war and later extensions tied to displacement, human rights abuses, famine and limited humanitarian access. Nicaragua was designated in 1999 after Hurricane Mitch, with later extensions based on drought, flooding and other disasters. El Salvador received TPS in 2001 after earthquakes displaced a large share of the population, and Haiti was designated in 2010 after a devastating earthquake, later receiving extensions because of natural disasters and a cholera outbreak. Supporters of the immigrants said many TPS holders are essential workers who continued working during the COVID-19 pandemic. The National TPS Alliance and ACLU said they would continue fighting the case and urged Congress to create a permanent path to residency.

# Appeals Court Rules Trump Administration Can Deport Immigrants with Temporary Protected Status A federal appeals court panel in San Francisco ruled 2-1 on Monday that the Trump administration may proceed with deporting hundreds of thousands of immigrants who held temporary protected status (TPS), overturning a lower court's protective injunction. The decision affects approximately 300,000 noncitizens and 200,000 of their U.S. citizen children from El Salvador, Haiti, Nicaragua, and Sudan—many of whom have lived in America for decades. The 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals majority, led by Judge Consuelo M. Callahan, determined that federal law does not permit courts to challenge the Secretary of Homeland Security's decisions regarding which countries' citizens qualify for protected status. Callahan, a George W. Bush appointee, wrote that the TPS statute constrains the Secretary's discretion only to prevent unwarranted designations or extensions. Judge Ryan D. Nelson, a Trump appointee, joined the majority opinion. Judge Morgan Christen, an Obama appointee, dissented strongly, arguing the Trump administration had abruptly changed policy without public review. She noted that the lawsuit alleged the deportation notices were motivated by racial and ethnic bias, referencing Trump's reported derogatory comments about Haiti and El Salvador as "shithole countries" and his characterization of immigrants from Mexico and Central America as criminals and "snakes." "We cannot sweep aside the words that were actually used," Christen wrote, emphasizing that the President's statements required no interpretation and some explicitly targeted people, not places. The Department of Justice expressed satisfaction with the ruling, stating that the district court's two-year injunction had prevented the Department of Homeland Security from exercising congressionally granted discretion. The DOJ called the accusations of racial animus "baseless." However, the decision will not immediately end TPS protections. Immigrants from Sudan, Haiti, and Nicaragua may maintain their status until at least February, while El Salvador's holders retain protection until at least November. The American Civil Liberties Union Foundation of Southern California, representing the immigrants, announced plans to appeal to a larger 9th Circuit panel. These countries received TPS designations due to humanitarian crises: Sudan in 1997 for civil war; Nicaragua in 1999 after Hurricane Mitch; El Salvador in 2001 following earthquakes; and Haiti in 2010 after a devastating earthquake. Previous administrations extended these protections multiple times based on ongoing natural disasters, human rights abuses, and other humanitarian concerns. The Trump administration revoked these protections in 2017 and 2018, prompting the lawsuit. A San Francisco federal judge blocked the administration's action in 2018, but Monday's appeals court decision reversed that protection. Paul Andre Mondesir, lead organizer for the National TPS Alliance, stated that over 130,000 family members were essential workers during the COVID-19 pandemic and pledged to exhaust all legal remedies, potentially appealing to the Supreme Court. ACLU senior counsel Ahilan Arulanantham argued that Trump's statements "made perfectly clear that his administration acted out of racial animus," asserting that the Constitution prohibits racism-driven policy.

Twelve rescued manatees were tagged with GPS trackers and released into Florida waters Monday, marking the largest single-day release on record, according to the Save The Manatee Club. Most were orphaned after their mothers died from starvation, which officials link to seagrass loss in the Indian River Lagoon. In response, wildlife officials are distributing lettuce to help supplement the manatees’ diets.

# Manatee Release Summary A record 12 rescued manatees were released into Florida waters Monday, marking the most released in a single day. The GPS-tagged manatees, mostly orphans whose mothers starved, were returned by the Save The Manatee Club. Officials attribute manatee starvation to seagrass loss in the Indian River Lagoon. Wildlife officials are now distributing lettuce to supplement manatees' diets.

He argued that if Armenia genuinely wants peace, it must abandon what he called an aggressive policy. Bayramov recalled that on the night of February 25–26, 1992, Armenian military formations, with support from the 366th motorized rifle regiment based in Khankendi, carried out the Khojaly massacre. According to the figures he cited, 613 people were killed, including women, children, and the elderly; eight families were wiped out; 1,275 people were taken hostage; and the fate of 150 remains unknown. He also listed five missile strikes on Ganja in October 2020. The attacks, on October 4, 5, 8, 11, and 17, killed and wounded civilians, with the deadliest raids on October 11 and 17. Bayramov said Armenian forces also struck Barda on October 28, 2020, using prohibited missiles and heavy artillery, killing 20 civilians and injuring up to 70.

# Summary On February 24, Azerbaijan's Foreign Minister Jeyhun Bayramov commemorated the 31st anniversary of the Khojaly genocide, accusing Armenia of continuing atrocities during the 2020 Karabakh war in Barda and Ganja. A Washington Free Beacon report says several major human rights organizations have refused to condemn Iran’s strike on Soroka Medical Center, a hospital in southern Israel, even though the attack injured at least 80 people and destroyed the hospital’s surgical ward. The strike was one of several Iranian air attacks on civilian targets after the conflict between Israel and Iran escalated earlier this month. The Free Beacon contacted more than a dozen groups that frequently criticize Israel, including Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch, Oxfam International, the American Friends Service Committee, CODEPINK, DAWN, Adalah, and others, seeking comment on the hospital bombing. Amnesty said it was “unable to comment at present” because its research team was still reviewing the incident. The article notes that Amnesty has not shown similar restraint in its criticism of Israel, continuing to accuse it publicly of imposing “genocidal conditions” in Gaza and condemning Israeli military operations in the region. It also cited Amnesty’s earlier description of Israel’s raid on Al Shifa Hospital in Gaza, which Israel said was being used as a Hamas command center, as “a devastating attack on human rights.” Two other groups, Nonviolence International and PAX for Peace, said they could not comment because of staff holidays. PAX, however, had earlier condemned Israel’s military action in Iran and circulated a petition calling for a complete arms embargo against Israel. The Canadian Foreign Policy Institute went further, effectively blaming Israel for the hospital strike. A board member said in an emailed statement that “Israel should not put civilian infrastructure near its military installations” and argued that Israel has bombed hospitals repeatedly in Gaza. The article says Iran claimed it was targeting an Israeli military command center, but that outpost was located about a mile from the hospital and was not hit. Only one organization, Churches for Middle East Peace, issued a statement that clearly condemned Iran’s attack, saying hospitals must be protected as places of healing. Even so, about half of its statement also criticized Israel’s actions in Gaza. Several other groups did not respond at all, including Human Rights Watch, the American Friends Service Committee, Adalah, DAWN, CODEPINK, the Euro-Mediterranean Human Rights Monitor, Oxfam International, the International Federation for Human Rights, Just Peace Advocates, and the European Council on Foreign Relations. The report also quotes NGO Monitor, a watchdog organization critical of anti-Israel NGOs, accusing these groups of selectively applying human rights principles to demonize Israel while ignoring abuses by Hamas and Iran. NGO Monitor president Gerald Steinberg said the “human rights” sector has long embraced a radical anti-Western, anti-Israel agenda and erases Israeli victims, including those killed in the Oct. 7 attacks and in Iranian missile strikes on civilians. According to the article, the same groups that declined to condemn the hospital bombing have been outspoken in denouncing Israel’s actions, including its strikes on Iran’s nuclear facilities, as “war crimes,” “aggression,” or “genocide.”

# Human Rights Groups Decline to Condemn Iran's Hospital Strike Several prominent human rights organizations have notably refused to condemn Iran's recent airstrike on Soroka Medical Center in southern Israel, which destroyed the hospital's surgical ward and injured at least 80 people. The Washington Free Beacon contacted over a dozen self-proclaimed human rights groups known for frequently criticizing Israel to request comment on the attack. Amnesty International stated it was "unable to comment at present as our research team is still looking into this incident." However, the organization has shown no such hesitation regarding Israeli actions, continuing to denounce Israel on social media and accusing it of imposing "genocidal conditions against Palestinians in occupied Gaza." When Israel previously raided Al Shifa Hospital in Gaza—identified as a Hamas command center—Amnesty International condemned the operation as "a devastating attack on human rights." Human Rights Watch, the American Friends Service Committee, Adalah, Democracy for the Arab World Now, CODEPINK, Oxfam International, and several other organizations did not respond to requests for comment. Two groups, Nonviolence International and PAX for Peace, cited staff holidays as reasons for their inability to comment, despite PAX having condemned Israel's military actions in Iran earlier in the week. The Canadian Foreign Policy Institute shifted blame to Israel, stating that "Israel should not put civilian infrastructure near its military installations." This argument appears contradicted by the fact that Iran's intended military target was located approximately one mile away from the hospital and was not hit in the strike. Only Churches for Middle East Peace provided a statement condemning Iran's attack, emphasizing that hospitals "must be protected as safe places." However, the organization balanced this by also criticizing Israel's actions in Gaza. In contrast, these organizations have been vocal in condemning Israeli actions. Human Rights Watch claimed that "Israeli authorities have starved, killed, and maimed thousands of Palestinian children in Gaza" and are responsible for war crimes and genocide. The American Friends Service Committee denounced "Israel's unilateral military attack on Iranian sovereign territory," while Adalah and Democracy for the Arab World Now called for military embargoes and sanctions against Israel. NGO Monitor, which tracks the anti-Israel nonprofit sector, criticized these organizations for having "weaponized the moral principles of human rights to demonize the Jewish state." President Gerald Steinberg stated that these groups have embraced a "radical anti-Western, anti-Israel agenda" for approximately 25 years, automatically characterizing Palestinians as victims while treating Hamas and Iran as beyond reproach. He argued these organizations erase Israeli victims, including those from October 7 attacks and Iran's missile strikes targeting civilians. The disparity in responses highlights what critics view as a double standard in how certain human rights organizations apply their principles when evaluating Israeli versus Iranian actions.

In Onitsha, Nigeria, Sister Dorothy Okoli of the Missionary Sisters of St John Paul II of Mary is leading a small but determined effort to help young women leave prostitution. On a recent sunny afternoon, she drove an unmarked Toyota Sienna from her convent to a hotel where girls are trapped in the sex trade, stopping first at a grocery store to buy food and other supplies. She said she sees the work as a calling and regularly brings gift items and cash to build trust with the women she visits. Okoli is the superior general of her religious institute in Anambra state. In July, her congregation launched the Save Young Girls Motherhood Foundation, and she and three other nuns began working to rehabilitate commercial sex workers. At first, Okoli expected only a few women would need help. Instead, she said they discovered a much larger problem, with many girls facing needs far beyond what the nuns can handle alone. She said the effort requires support from the government, churches, and private individuals. The sisters, who have backgrounds in guidance and counseling, economics, and education, rely on prayer before entering brothels or hotels. Okoli said many of the women are vulnerable to HIV and other serious illnesses. In Nigeria, HIV prevalence among sex workers is estimated at 27.4% for brothel-based female sex workers and 21.1% for those outside brothels. Although commercial sex work is illegal in Nigeria and is widely regarded as exploitative and violent against women, the trade continues, including in southern Nigeria where underage prostitution, pimps, and brothel ownership are prohibited. One of the women Okoli has met is 25-year-old Benita Ekwe, who entered brothel work after her mother lost her job in 2017, one year after her father died. Ekwe said she earns between $5 and $48 a day and sends money home for her siblings’ food and schooling. She said she is uncomfortable with the job and fears for her life, but hopes to continue only long enough to save money to start a small business and support her family. As the eldest of six children, she said she feels responsible for helping her younger siblings stay in school and wants to open a food stall for her mother. Ekwe and the other women pay hotel management $15 for their rooms, and if they do not earn enough, they must take money from their bank accounts to cover the cost. Okoli said this reflects the broader exploitation women face in prostitution, including poor living conditions and mistreatment by male clients. Since July, the nuns have spoken with more than 100 sex workers and helped two women begin tailoring businesses with housing. Okoli said the process of persuading women to leave the trade is slow and depends on having enough funds to help them start over immediately after rehabilitation.

# Nigerian Nuns Work to Rescue Women from Sex Trade In Onitsha, Nigeria, Sister DorothyOlogi and three other nuns from the Missionary Sisters of St John Paul II of Mary are conducting a compassionate rescue operation targeting women trapped in commercial sex work. Established in July, the Save Young Girls Motherhood Foundation represents their organized effort to rehabilitate sex workers through prayer, personal visits, and financial support. Sister Dorothy approaches her mission with deliberate dedication, regularly visiting hotels where young girls are exploited. She brings gifts and cash to build trust with the women, sometimes earning their affection so strongly that they resist her departure. Drawing on backgrounds in guidance, counseling, economics, and education, the nuns prepare themselves spiritually through prayer before each visit. The scope of the problem exceeds initial expectations. What the nuns anticipated as a modest undertaking revealed a massive crisis requiring government and community support. The women face severe health risks, with Nigeria's HIV prevalence among brothel-based female sex workers estimated at 27.4%, and 21.1% among non-brothel workers. Beyond disease, they endure exploitation, inhabit uninhabitable rooms, and face mistreatment from clients. Benita Ekwe, 25, exemplifies the desperation driving women into prostitution. After her father's death and mother's job loss in 2017, she entered a brothel to support her four younger siblings. Earning between five and forty-eight dollars daily, she pays fifteen dollars to the hotel management for room rental, sometimes depleting her savings on days with insufficient earnings. She dropped out of school due to financial constraints and hopes her siblings receive the education she missed. Despite recognizing the profession's dangers, Benita views it as temporary, planning to establish a food stall for her mother once she accumulates sufficient capital. Her situation illustrates the impossible choices facing impoverished families in Nigeria. Although Nigerian law prohibits commercial sex work, underage prostitution, pimping, and brothel operations—and Nigeria signed the UN Convention against Transnational Organized Crime—the illegal trade persists throughout the country. Since launching their foundation, the nuns have engaged with over 100 commercial sex workers and successfully established two women in tailoring businesses with housing support. However, funding limitations hinder expansion of their rehabilitation program, which requires resources to immediately establish women once they complete rehabilitation. Sister Dorothy emphasizes that rehabilitation demands gradual, sustained intervention. Benita remains in ongoing counseling, representing the patient, long-term commitment necessary for transformation. The nuns' work demonstrates that rescuing women from sexual exploitation requires not merely good intentions, but dedicated resources, community support, and comprehensive rehabilitation programs addressing both immediate needs and long-term economic independence.

A protest is planned for Sunday, International Women’s Day, outside the Montreal headquarters of MindGeek, the company that owns Pornhub. Organizers say the demonstration is meant to condemn Pornhub for allegedly profiting from sex trafficking and the sexual exploitation of women and children. The protest comes amid a series of controversies involving the site. Pornhub removed videos from the “Girls Do Porn” creators in October 2019 after the owner and employees were charged with sex trafficking. In November 2019, a man was sentenced to 18 months in jail for distributing intimate images of his ex-partner and three other victims without consent; one image was viewed more than 1.5 million times. This year, another woman alleged that a video of her being raped at age 14 appeared on Pornhub. A petition calling for the site to be shut down has collected more than 370,000 signatures, arguing that Pornhub lacks reliable age and consent verification. Senator Julie Miville-Dechêne is expected to attend, and the campaign has support from more than 75 advocacy groups and experts.

# Summary A demonstration is planned for International Women's Day at Mindgeek's Montreal headquarters, which owns Pornhub. Protesters accuse the platform of profiting from sex trafficking and sexual exploitation of women and children. The action follows several incidents: Pornhub removed content from "Girls Do Porn" creators after sex trafficking charges in 2019. A man received an 18-month sentence for distributing intimate images without consent, with one image viewed 1.5 million times. Additionally, a woman reported that a video of her rape at age 14 appeared on the platform. A petition to shut down Pornhub has collected over 370,000 signatures, citing the site's lack of age verification and consent verification systems. Senator Julie Miville-Dechêne, a member of anti-trafficking and feminist parliamentary groups, is expected to attend and has condemned the platform's hosting of exploitative content. The shutdown campaign has gained support from over 75 child protection, women's rights, and anti-trafficking organizations, plus survivors and experts in commercial sexual exploitation.

Carter Hastings scored twice and set up two more, Tyler Davis scored twice, and Tyler Brown chipped in one goal and five assists. The Kuwaiti Embassy in Baghdad urged Kuwaiti nationals, especially bird hunters, to obey Iraqi laws while visiting Muthanna governorate and other southern areas. Conservationists say decades of conflict, sanctions, and terrorism have made animal sightings increasingly rare, while reliable data on species loss remain limited because of ongoing instability. Nature Iraq says at least 31 bird species in the country are threatened or near extinction, and Baghdad Zoo’s director says Iraq’s wildlife has been greatly depleted.

# Summary The Kuwaiti Embassy in Baghdad has urged Kuwaiti nationals to comply with Iraqi hunting laws, particularly regarding bird hunting in Muthanna governorate and southern Iraq. The embassy warned visitors that violations could result in legal prosecution and harm. Pacific Gas & Electric Corp. spent nearly $10 million on California lobbying in 2018, making it the state’s top political spender in the year before the utility filed for bankruptcy. More than $5 million of that total went toward lobbying on wildfire-related proposals, including efforts to change the strict liability rules that can force utilities to pay for fires sparked by their equipment. Lawmakers did not ease that liability, but they did pass a measure allowing utilities to issue bonds more easily to cover wildfire damages and shift some costs to ratepayers. PG&E spokeswoman Lynsey Paulo said the company’s lobbying was aimed at protecting customers and employees, and that the money came from shareholders rather than ratepayers. PG&E, the nation’s largest utility, filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy on Tuesday as it confronts potentially tens of billions of dollars in wildfire liability tied to destructive fires in Northern California in 2017 and 2018. The bankruptcy could reduce payouts to wildfire victims and raise costs for customers. Paulo said worsening wildfires are among the company’s most serious challenges. The spending drew criticism from California Common Cause, which called the amount “shocking” and accused the utility of trying to buy influence in Sacramento while people’s homes and lives were at stake. According to a Thursday filing with the California secretary of state, about $9.6 million of PG&E’s lobbying went to general efforts, including hiring lobbyists, working through Sacramento firms, and paying for meals and other perks for lawmakers. From July through September alone, the company spent $6 million, including meals, event tickets for public employees, and more than $10,000 in campaign contributions to nine sitting lawmakers and one candidate. PG&E also spent about $350,000 lobbying the California Public Utilities Commission. The company is facing 750 lawsuits, its lawyer said in court Thursday. Investigators have not yet determined the cause of the deadly November fire that destroyed much of Paradise and killed at least 86 people, though PG&E has reported equipment problems near the ignition site. Other major California utilities spent less: Sempra spent about $1.4 million lobbying lawmakers and $167,000 on the CPUC, while Edison International spent just over $4 million on general lobbying and $191,000 on the commission. The Western States Petroleum Association was the state’s second-highest spender overall at nearly $7.9 million, followed by Chevron and subsidiaries at about $4 million.

# Summary: PG&E's Massive 2018 Lobbying Spending Pacific Gas & Electric Corp. spent nearly $10 million on California lobbying in 2018, the highest amount of any entity seeking to influence state government that year. This spending occurred just before the utility giant filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy, facing potentially tens of billions in liability from devastating Northern California wildfires in 2017 and 2018. More than half of PG&E's lobbying expenditure—approximately $5 million—focused on wildfire safety and response proposals, particularly efforts to reduce the strict liability utilities face when their equipment causes wildfires. Although lawmakers rejected reducing liability, they passed legislation allowing utilities to issue bonds to cover wildfire damages and pass some costs to ratepayers. PG&E's spokeswoman stated the spending was intended to benefit customers and employees, funded by shareholders rather than ratepayers. The utility argued that worsening wildfires represent the most critical issue facing both the company and California. However, critics view the spending negatively. Katie Phillips from California Common Cause called it "shocking," characterizing it as an attempt to "buy influence in Sacramento" while people's homes and lives were at stake. Of the nearly $10 million total, approximately $9.6 million went toward general lobbying activities, including hiring in-house and external lobbyists, and providing meals and event tickets to lawmakers. Between July and September alone, PG&E spent $6 million on lobbying, including over $10,000 in campaign contributions to nine sitting lawmakers and one candidate. The company also spent about $350,000 lobbying the California Public Utilities Commission. PG&E currently faces 750 lawsuits. Investigators have not determined the cause of the massive November fire that killed at least 86 people in Paradise, though PG&E reported equipment problems near where the fire started. Comparatively, other major California utilities spent significantly less: Sempra spent $1.4 million and Edison International spent just over $4 million on general lobbying in 2018.

Kenyan cult leader Paul Nthenge Mackenzie has gone on trial for manslaughter over the deaths of more than 400 of his followers in the Shakahola Forest massacre, one of the world’s deadliest cult-related tragedies. Mackenzie, a self-proclaimed pastor, appeared on Monday in a magistrate’s court in Mombasa with 93 other suspects, all of whom have pleaded not guilty to multiple manslaughter charges. Prosecutors say the case is unlike any other in Kenya and will be pursued under a law dealing with suicide pacts. Mackenzie is accused of persuading his followers to starve themselves so they could “meet Jesus.” He was arrested in April last year after bodies began turning up in the remote Shakahola forest near Malindi on Kenya’s coast. Since then, rescuers have spent months searching the area and have recovered about 448 bodies from mass graves. Autopsies showed most victims died from starvation, while others, including children, appeared to have been strangled, beaten or suffocated. Earlier court documents also said some bodies had organs removed. The current charge sheet names 95 defendants: 55 men and 40 women, including Mackenzie’s wife. One woman accused in the case has since died in police custody from complications linked to long-term illness and fasting. Prosecutors say they have prepared at least 420 witnesses, and the manslaughter hearings are scheduled to run for four days. Some testimony will be heard in private. This is not the only case against the suspects. They were also tried last month on terrorism charges connected to the massacre and face separate proceedings for murder and child torture and cruelty, with prosecutors saying the abuses occurred between 2020 and 2023. Authorities began returning identified victims’ bodies to relatives in March, after DNA testing. So far, 34 bodies have been released. Mackenzie founded the Good News International Church in 2003, later said he shut it down in 2019, and moved to Shakahola while predicting the world would end in August last year. The case has triggered outrage in Kenya and renewed debate over tighter regulation of fringe religious groups. A presidential commission has recommended a mix of self-regulation and state oversight, while other official reports say the deaths could have been prevented.

# Kenya Cult Leader on Trial for Mass Starvation Deaths Self-proclaimed pastor Paul Nthenge Mackenzie went on trial Monday in Mombasa, Kenya, for manslaughter in connection with the deaths of over 400 followers in what prosecutors describe as an unprecedented case. Mackenzie and 93 other suspects pleaded not guilty to multiple manslaughter charges related to the "Shakahola Forest Massacre." Mackenzie allegedly incited his followers to starve themselves to death to "meet Jesus." He was arrested in April 2023 after bodies were discovered in the remote Shakahola forest near Malindi. Rescue operations have since unearthed approximately 448 bodies from mass graves. Autopsies revealed most victims died from starvation, while others—including children—showed signs of strangulation, beating, or suffocation. Some bodies had organs removed. The charge sheet includes 95 defendants: 55 men and 40 women, including Mackenzie's wife. One female defendant died in police custody due to complications from prolonged fasting. Prosecutors have prepared at least 420 witnesses, with hearings scheduled through Thursday. Some testimony will be presented behind closed doors. Prosecutor Alexander Jami Yamina emphasized the case's uniqueness, stating they will charge defendants under Kenyan law dealing with suicide pacts. The suspects also face separate terrorism, murder, and child torture charges related to deaths occurring between 2020 and 2023. Mackenzie founded the Good News International Church in 2003 but claimed to have closed it in 2019, relocating to Shakahola to prepare for what he predicted would be the world's end in August 2023. The tragedy prompted government action. President William Ruto's investigative commission recommended a hybrid model of self-regulation and government oversight for religious organizations. Senate reports and human rights watchdogs concluded authorities could have prevented the deaths. Since March, authorities have returned 34 identified victims' bodies to families after DNA identification work. The case has sparked debate about regulating fringe religious denominations, though efforts face opposition from those citing constitutional protections for church-state separation.
