Pakistan has hosted more than 1.4 million Afghan refugees and 850,000 Afghan Citizen Card holders for four decades, despite facing economic and social strain, according to the article. It says Pakistan has maintained high standards of protection even during the COVID-19 pandemic and has extended substantial support to Afghans, including free enrollment in government primary schools, access to higher education through scholarships, bank accounts, and livelihood opportunities. The piece argues that, despite these humanitarian measures, Afghan and Indian media and other “disgruntled elements” continue to spread negative propaganda against Pakistan. It cites a recent controversy in which Afghan media allegedly tried to create a false impression about Pakistan after some Afghan refugees were arrested in Sindh province. Official sources said the individuals were detained by Sindh police because they lacked legal residence documents. A security analyst quoted in the article questioned why any country would tolerate undocumented migrants and said India’s criticism of Pakistan should be viewed in light of India’s own treatment of Afghans. The article claims that around 21,000 Afghans live in India, with about 11,000 registered only as asylum-seekers, and says they face hardship due to limited access to income, education, and health care. It also says India treats Afghan refugees as illegal migrants under its Foreigners Act and recently revoked Afghan student visas.

# Summary Pakistan hosts over 1.4 million Afghan refugees and 850,000 Afghan Citizen Card holders despite economic pressures, maintaining this humanitarian commitment for four decades. These refugees receive substantial benefits including free enrollment in government schools, higher education scholarships, bank accounts, and livelihood opportunities. However, Afghan and Indian media outlets have allegedly spread baseless propaganda against Pakistan. Recently, Afghan media misrepresented the arrest of Afghan refugees in Sindh province by local police for lacking legal residence documents—a standard enforcement measure any country would implement. A security analyst questioned why Pakistan should tolerate undocumented immigrants traveling illegally within its borders, noting that no country permits such irregularities. The analyst criticized India's treatment of Afghan refugees, highlighting that of 21,000 Afghans in India, only 11,000 are registered as asylum-seekers without official refugee recognition. Afghan residents in India lack access to income, education, and healthcare despite living there for 15 years. India officially classifies Afghan refugees as illegal migrants under its 1946 Foreigners Act, which denies them social services and protection from deportation. Additionally, India recently revoked visas for Afghan students despite their dependence on Indian universities.

Israel has long portrayed itself as a country that provides humanitarian assistance abroad, and the article says that principle has extended even to Syria, despite the two countries’ lack of diplomatic relations and their formal state of war. According to Maj. Efi Ribner, commanding officer of the Golan Israeli Liaison Office, the fact that Syria is an enemy state did not stop Israel’s government and the Israel Defense Forces from responding to the suffering of civilians caught in the Syrian civil war. Ribner said Israeli leaders quickly concluded that helping civilians was consistent with the values of a Jewish state and that it was wrong to stand by while people suffered on the other side of the border. Israel launched “Operation Good Neighbor” in June 2016 to provide medical and civilian aid to Syrians while maintaining its stated policy of non-involvement in the conflict. Ribner explained that the operation’s goal was not only to expand direct Israeli assistance, but also to coordinate with international humanitarian organizations and use existing infrastructure in Israel to channel aid efficiently. The article describes several outside partners involved in the effort. Rahma Relief Foundation donated medicine valued at $90 million, while Friend Ships Unlimited, a Louisiana-based organization, worked with the operation to build a field clinic just east of the Israel-Syria border. That clinic treats between 35 and 70 Syrian patients each day. International groups also helped establish a maternity hospital in a Syrian village near the border, with NIS 6 million in donations used to buy equipment such as machinery and beds. The first baby was delivered there the day after it opened. The relief base is located only a few kilometers from the border. On average, aid is delivered two to three times a day, either by allowing Syrians to cross into Israel for treatment or by sending supplies such as fuel and food across the fence into Syria. Since the operation began, the Israeli government has contributed about NIS 30 million, or $8.6 million, in humanitarian aid to Syrian civilians, while nongovernmental organizations have donated roughly NIS 350 million, or $100 million. Sgt. Ziv Fox, an IDF paramedic and commander at the Israeli Military Medicine Academy and training base, said the mission reflects his desire to save lives. He emphasized that the medical teams do not ask patients about their beliefs or political views, only treat their injuries. Many of the Syrians were raised amid years of hostility between the two countries, he noted, but now they need help and the Israeli teams can provide it. The article also explains how wounded Syrians arrive at a gate in the border fence at night, are checked to ensure they are unarmed, receive basic treatment, and are then taken by ambulance to Israeli hospitals. Depending on the seriousness of their condition, they may remain in Israel for days or months before being returned to a gate along the border, whose location changes for security reasons. Fox said that not all of them survive, and sometimes the soldiers later see them again only as bodies. Ribner and Fox have been touring the United States as part of a joint initiative by the IDF Spokesperson Unit and StandWithUs. They also recently met with Israel’s ambassador to the United Nations, Danny Danon, who praised the soldiers and officers involved and said they represent the true face of Israel and the IDF.

# Israel's Humanitarian Aid to Syria Despite Decades of Conflict Israel has established a remarkable humanitarian initiative in Syria, one of its enemy states, demonstrating that compassion transcends political boundaries and military conflict. Despite having no diplomatic relations and existing in a state of war since Israel's establishment, the Israeli Defense Forces (IDF) have committed substantial resources to assist suffering Syrian civilians. ## Operation Good Neighbor In June 2016, Israel launched "Operation Good Neighbor," a comprehensive humanitarian program designed to provide medical and civilian aid to Syrians while maintaining Israel's non-involvement policy in Syria's civil war. According to Maj. Efi Ribner, commanding officer of the Golan Israeli Liaison Office, the Israeli government and IDF quickly recognized that humanitarian crises transcend enemy-ally distinctions. The decision reflected core Jewish values that compel assistance when civilians suffer and help is available. ## Scope and Impact The operation has achieved significant results through both government and non-governmental contributions. The Israeli government has provided approximately NIS 30 million ($8.6 million) in humanitarian aid, while NGOs have donated roughly NIS 350 million ($100 million). International organizations have partnered with Israel to expand relief efforts, including the Rahma Relief Foundation's $90 million medicine donation and Friend Ships Unlimited's field clinic construction. The field clinic, located immediately east of the Israel-Syria border, treats 35 to 70 Syrian patients daily. Additionally, a maternity hospital was established in a Syrian border village using NIS 6 million in donations, delivering its first baby immediately after opening. ## Daily Operations Operating from bases a few kilometers from the border, the relief effort delivers humanitarian assistance two to three times daily. Syrians cross the border at night through designated gates for medical evaluation and treatment. After security checks to ensure they are unarmed, patients receive basic care and are transported by ambulance to Israeli hospitals for more serious conditions. Hospital stays range from days to months depending on injury severity. Patients are then returned to the border gate, which frequently changes locations for security purposes. ## Personal Perspectives Sgt. Ziv Fox, an IDF paramedic and commander at the Israeli Military Medicine Academy, exemplifies the operation's spirit. He joined the IDF to save lives and views Operation Good Neighbor as fulfilling that mission beautifully. Fox emphasizes that his team provides care based solely on medical need, regardless of patients' backgrounds or beliefs, despite decades of hostility between nations. He acknowledges the emotional toll, noting that some patients do not survive their injuries. ## Recognition and Advocacy Ribner and Fox have toured the United States as part of a joint IDF and StandWithUs initiative to raise awareness about this humanitarian work. They met with Danny Danon, Israel's UN ambassador, who praised their efforts as representing the true face of Israel and the IDF. Danon highlighted the contrast between Syria's regime violence and Israel's consistent provision of medical care to Syrian civilians. This initiative demonstrates how humanitarian principles can bridge even the deepest political divides, providing hope amid regional conflict.

Oxfam warned that as many as 20 million people in South Sudan, northern Nigeria, Yemen and Somalia were at risk of starvation in 2017 and urged donor governments to act immediately with both humanitarian aid and political pressure. The organization said famine had already been declared in parts of South Sudan, while northern Nigeria was likely already experiencing famine conditions in areas cut off from aid. Somalia and Yemen, it said, were on the brink. According to Oxfam, the main cause of these crises is conflict, except in Somalia, where drought is driving the emergency. The group criticized donor countries for failing to do enough to resolve the conflicts and, in the case of Yemen, for contributing to the war through arms sales. Oxfam said governments had a moral duty to fully meet the $4.4 billion needed for a humanitarian response and to address the political causes of the collapse in these countries. Nigel Timmins, Oxfam’s humanitarian director, said famine does not happen suddenly but follows months of ignored warnings and delayed action. He described it as a slow, agonizing process shaped by national politics and international indifference. He argued that half-hearted responses to UN appeals had already weakened the aid effort and warned that without a major influx of cash, the humanitarian system would be overwhelmed and many more people would die. The article said hunger crises can deteriorate quickly, with malnutrition and deaths rising sharply once a tipping point is reached. Aid, including feeding and health centers, must arrive before people become too weak and exhaust their ability to feed their families. Oxfam’s figures showed the scale of the crisis: in Somalia, 2.9 million people faced acute food insecurity and could tip into famine if rains failed and support did not arrive; in Nigeria, more than 5 million were already in food crisis, with 400,000 possibly in famine-like conditions and the number potentially rising to 800,000; in South Sudan, 100,000 people were facing starvation and another 1 million were on the brink; and in Yemen, over 7 million were one step away from famine while another 10 million were severely hungry, with wheat stocks expected to run out in April. Oxfam said it was already assisting more than a million people in Yemen, over 600,000 in South Sudan, and more than 200,000 in Nigeria.

# Summary: The Threat of Four Famines in 2017 In 2017, Oxfam issued an urgent humanitarian crisis alert, warning that approximately 20 million people across four countries faced imminent starvation. Famine had already been declared in parts of South Sudan, while northern Nigeria, Yemen, and Somalia stood on the brink of catastrophic food shortages. **The Crisis by Country:** South Sudan faced the most immediate threat, with 100,000 people already starving and 1 million more on the brink of famine in Unity State. In Nigeria, over 5 million people faced acute food insecurity, with projections reaching 5.7 million by June 2017, and approximately 400,000 people already experiencing famine conditions. Somalia had 2.9 million people in acute food crisis, vulnerable to tipping into famine if April-June rains failed. Yemen experienced the world's largest hunger emergency, with over 7 million people one step away from famine and 10 million severely hungry; the UN reported wheat stocks would be depleted by April. **Root Causes and Responsibility:** Oxfam identified conflict as the primary driver in South Sudan, Nigeria, and Yemen, while drought caused Somalia's crisis. The organization criticized donor countries for inadequately supporting conflict resolution efforts and, in Yemen's case, fueling conflict through arms sales. This failure created a moral obligation to address the humanitarian emergency. **Call for Action:** Oxfam's Humanitarian Director Nigel Timmins emphasized that famine results from prolonged neglect rather than sudden occurrence, describing it as "the ultimate betrayal of our common humanity." He stressed that immediate action was essential because hunger crises deteriorate exponentially after reaching critical tipping points, making rapid intervention crucial. Oxfam demanded $4.4 billion in humanitarian funding and called for immediate political and diplomatic action alongside aid delivery. The organization was already operating in these regions, assisting over 1 million people in Yemen, 600,000 in South Sudan, 200,000 in Nigeria, and conducting assessment missions in Somalia. Without urgent funding and intervention, the organization warned that mortality rates would surge catastrophically across all four nations.

Mahat’s story is one of flight, survival, and gradual rebuilding after years of violence and detention. He grew up in Mogadishu, Somalia, and by his early 20s had a stable job. He says he never originally imagined leaving for Europe, but the worsening violence in Somalia changed everything. He describes a climate in which people around him were being killed almost daily, including relatives and friends, and says he eventually feared for his own life. The turning point came in 2015, when his father was killed by the militant group Al-Shabaab. The murder devastated his family, and when Al-Shabaab later targeted Mahat himself, he decided he had no choice but to run. According to Mahat, Al-Shabaab told him he must either work with them or be killed. He escaped before they could carry out the threat. After leaving, he later learned that his family home had been burned down. From Somalia he moved on to Libya, hoping to find a route to safety, but instead entered another period of abuse and uncertainty. In Libya, asylum-seekers are widely exposed to unlawful detention, violence, and exploitation by smugglers and traffickers. Mahat was detained in northwest Libya for almost two years. He describes overcrowded, suffocating conditions: extreme heat, no proper ventilation, only one toilet for hundreds of people, and food provided just once a day. Disease spread easily, including scabies, and medical care was effectively reserved for those with money. Like many detainees, Mahat was also subjected to abuse by smugglers who tried to extort money from him through family members. When he said he had none, he was beaten with a metal object and sometimes shocked with electricity. Despite the brutality, Mahat says returning to Somalia was not an option. He and others remained in detention because they still hoped to reach safety one day. Before the conflict, Mahat had worked as a midwife in Somalia, and that experience became crucial in Libya. Pregnant women in detention were especially vulnerable and often received no medical attention at all, so Mahat stepped in to help. Over time, he became an unofficial midwife in the centre and says he helped deliver 15 babies. One of the most detailed examples he gives took place in February 2018. A Somali woman, already about six months pregnant when she was brought into detention, went into labour two months later. Other detainees told her that Mahat would help, and women brought her to him. He worked with two others, including a qualified doctor from Eritrea, to assist the delivery. The detention centre provided only the most basic supplies, and even that came only after Mahat requested them. He informed the guards the day before the birth, wrote down what he needed, and was eventually given a small separated area with blankets for privacy. In those harsh conditions, a baby boy named Abubakar was born safely. Mahat says the mother and child later survived and were eventually rescued by the Lifeline and relocated from Malta to Portugal. He remains in contact with them. In total, he says he helped bring 15 babies into the world in Libya. Mahat’s own escape came on the night of 20 June, when he was put onto a flimsy boat with around 130 other people. He knew the crossing was dangerous and understood that many people die at sea. He says smugglers offered no real protection, only the chance to board a boat and hope for survival. After a night in darkness, the group spotted a vessel in the distance. Panic broke out because some feared it was a Libyan boat that would return them to danger. Some even wanted to jump into the sea rather than be taken back. When they realized it was a rescue vessel, relief spread through the boat. They were brought aboard the Lifeline, where Mahat recalls being greeted kindly, given water, food, and medical care. He says he was deeply grateful to be saved. The Lifeline was eventually allowed to dock in Malta on 28 June, after delays caused by worsening weather and disagreements among EU member states over where the rescued people should disembark. Mahat says he had never heard of Malta before arriving there. He was later granted Subsidiary Protection. Since then, he has been trying to rebuild his life. He works in Malta as a Somali cultural mediator for an organization that supports refugees and asylum-seekers, a role he values because it allows him to help others in similar situations. At the same time, he hopes to continue his education and eventually become a doctor. He has started studying science at Mcast, lives in a shared house with other refugees, and spends his free time exploring Valletta and other parts of the island. Though he carries the trauma of Somalia and Libya with him, Mahat says he is looking ahead with hope, determination, and a desire to reach a place of peace.

# From Conflict to Safety: One Man's Journey to Peace Mahat's journey to safety represents the harrowing experiences faced by countless asylum-seekers fleeing violence and persecution. His story begins in Somalia, where he lived a relatively stable life working as a midwife in Mogadishu. Everything changed in 2015 when his father was killed by Al-Shabaab, the armed militant group that has terrorized Somalia for years. The tragedy devastated his family, and when Al-Shabaab later targeted Mahat himself, demanding he either join their ranks or face death, he made the only choice available to him: escape. After fleeing Somalia, Mahat learned that his family home had been burned to the ground. With nowhere else to turn, he made his way to Libya, a decision that would trap him in a different kind of nightmare. What he encountered there was a system of unlawful detention characterized by inhumane conditions and widespread human rights abuses. For nearly two years, Mahat was imprisoned in northwest Libya, experiencing the brutal reality of a detention facility designed to extract money from desperate people. The conditions were appalling. Hundreds of detainees were crammed into spaces without adequate ventilation, forced to share a single toilet among approximately 800 people. Food was rationed to once daily, and disease spread rapidly through the facility. Smugglers employed torture as a standard practice, forcing detainees to call family members abroad and extort money from them. When Mahat could not pay, he was beaten with metal objects and subjected to electrical torture. Despite these horrors, returning to Somalia remained impossible, making the detention center a trap with no apparent exit. However, Mahat's professional background as a midwife became invaluable in this desperate situation. Pregnant women in the detention center were among the most vulnerable detainees, yet they received no medical attention or care. Drawing on his experience, Mahat began providing essential support to expectant mothers, eventually becoming the facility's unofficial midwife. During his nearly two-year detention, he delivered fifteen babies, often under the most difficult circumstances imaginable. One particularly memorable case occurred in February 2018 when a woman who had been pregnant when brought to detention went into labor. Word spread through the facility that "Mahat will help you," and women brought the expectant mother to him. With assistance from a qualified doctor from Eritrea and basic supplies Mahat had to specifically request, he managed to create a makeshift delivery area using blankets for privacy. Despite the cramped, unsanitary conditions, he successfully delivered a healthy baby boy named Abubakar. Over a year later, Mahat maintained contact with Abubakar's mother, eventually learning that they had been rescued and relocated to Portugal to start fresh. Mahat's own escape came on June 20 when smugglers placed him on a flimsy boat with approximately 130 other people. The crossing was extremely dangerous—smugglers offered no guarantees of safety, only the grim reality that passengers might die at sea. After a terrifying night in complete darkness, a boat appeared on the horizon. Initial panic seized the refugees, who feared it might be a Libyan vessel that would return them to face further violence and certain death. Their relief was overwhelming when they discovered it was the Lifeline, a rescue ship whose crew greeted them with warmth and immediately provided medical attention, water, and food. The Lifeline reached Malta on June 28, and Mahat set foot in a safe country for the first time. He was eventually granted Subsidiary Protection status, allowing him to begin rebuilding his life. Today, he works as a Somali cultural mediator for an organization serving refugees and asylum-seekers in Malta, a position that allows him to support others facing similar struggles. Despite his difficult past, Mahat maintains ambitious dreams for his future. His ultimate goal is to become a doctor, a path that requires starting nearly from scratch despite his existing qualifications and experience—a common challenge for refugees forced to leave everything behind. He has enrolled in science studies at Mcast, a higher education institute in Malta, and lives independently in a shared house with other refugees. In his spare time, he explores the island, gradually building a new life. Over a year after his rescue at sea, Mahat continues moving forward with optimism, hope, and determination, slowly but steadily working toward the peace and respect he seeks.

Canadian distributor LMPI says 1,500 copies of the latest Charlie Hebdo issue will be available across Canada on Friday, a major increase from the usual weekly distribution of about 100 copies. Director of sales Louis-Philip Vermeersch said the magazine’s wider release is meant to meet strong public interest, though he warned it still may not satisfy demand. The satirical French magazine is normally sold only in Quebec and at one store in Toronto, but this time it will be distributed to 135 stores nationwide, mostly in Quebec. Ontario will have seven outlets carrying it, including five in Toronto and two in Ottawa. British Columbia will have three stores participating, in Vancouver and Victoria, while Calgary, Fredericton, Moncton and Halifax will each have one retailer offering copies. Vermeersch said stores will receive an average of 10 copies each, and he expects the issue to be on newsstands by noon Friday. Interest in the issue follows last week’s deadly attack on Charlie Hebdo’s Paris headquarters, where two gunmen killed 12 people. The magazine had long faced threats because of its depictions of the Prophet Muhammad, which many Muslims consider blasphemous. On Tuesday, surviving staff unveiled the new cover at a press conference in Paris. It shows a caricature of Muhammad crying and holding a sign reading “I am Charlie,” with “All is forgiven” above him. The issue also mocks other religions and includes a spread on the massive Paris march that drew more than a million people in protest against terrorism. Charlie Hebdo’s publisher has said the magazine will increase production to three million copies worldwide, but LMPI says there is no confirmation that any additional copies will reach Canada.

A legal challenge in Britain is seeking to force the government to ban smartphones in schools, arguing that allowing them during the school day fails to protect children from harm. The case is being brought by four plaintiffs: Flossie McShea, now 17, and two fathers and a mother. McShea says her own experience shows why the issue matters. She got a smartphone at age 11 and, within months, was exposed at school to violent and sexualized material shared by classmates during lessons and breaks. Students would show her extreme videos face-to-face, send them through group chats, or share them by AirDrop. She also says classmates took “mugs,” or mugshot-style photos of her, and posted them online. She says she quickly became addicted to social media and that the phone changed her life. The lawsuit comes amid growing alarm across Britain about children’s use of smartphones and social media. The government has warned that the issue requires “urgent attention,” pointing to risks such as sexual exploitation, bullying-related distress, and even premature death. Campaigners often cite tragic cases of teenagers who died by suicide after encountering distressing content online. The plaintiffs are asking for a judicial review, arguing that the state has a duty to safeguard children during school hours and that this duty is breached if smartphones are allowed in classrooms. Their claim is narrower than a general ban on phones in society, but it could become a powerful test of the government’s responsibility toward children while they are at school. The case is unfolding as European governments increasingly intervene in children’s digital lives. France banned smartphones in primary and middle schools in 2018 and is now considering a social media ban for children under 15. Italy introduced school phone restrictions years ago and expanded them later. Denmark has moved toward making schools phone-free for most children ages 7 to 16 and is also planning to restrict social media access for those under 15. Britain is now debating all of these issues at once: phone use in schools, social media restrictions, and broader design changes to make platforms less addictive. Last week, the U.K. government opened a three-month consultation on a package of possible measures, including an Australia-style social media ban, tighter school phone rules, and changes to reduce the addictive nature of platforms. The move came after pressure from within Prime Minister Keir Starmer’s Labour Party, where more than 60 lawmakers wrote to him warning that successive governments had failed to protect young people from “unregulated, addictive social media platforms.” Meanwhile, the House of Lords has backed a proposal to ban under-16s from social media and is due next month to debate banning smartphones in schools. The debate is complicated. Some analysts and charities warn that age-based social media bans might be hard to enforce or could drive teenagers toward less regulated parts of the internet. Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy said in December that enforcement is the key issue and questioned whether the country really wants to prosecute under-18s for using social media. Others argue that the focus on age verification misses the deeper problem, saying governments should instead require platforms to change the content and algorithms that keep children hooked. McShea’s case asks a different question: what does the state owe children during the school day? British schools already have a legal duty to “safeguard” pupils, similar to a duty of care. Because of that framework, Britain is one of the few countries where a court can be asked to treat smartphones in schools as a child-protection issue. In the United States, similar debates are usually framed around parental choice, school rules, and free-speech concerns. In Britain, most secondary school students bring phones to school. The government has not imposed a nationwide ban, leaving decisions to individual principals. Updated guidance from the Education Department says schools should have policies preventing pupils from using phones during lessons, breaks, and lunchtime, but the guidance is not mandatory. McShea and other campaigners want a full national ban during the school day. Some school leaders support stronger rules. Kirsty Rogers, principal of a secondary school near Oxford, introduced a phone ban at her school last year, using locked pouches paid for from the school’s own budget. She said the change “helped turn the school around,” with older students asking for sports equipment during breaks and fewer pupils leaving lessons to go to the bathroom. But she said the government later asked her to help provide case studies showing schools’ flexibility in managing phone policies, and she declined. In her view, if phones are harmful, the government needs a firmer national position rather than leaving thousands of schools to figure it out on their own, without funding or clear direction. Researchers caution that school bans alone may not solve the broader problem. Evidence is limited and mixed. A U.K. study found no major difference in mental health or educational outcomes between schools that allowed phones and those that banned them, though the sample was small. Victoria Goodyear, who led the research at the University of Birmingham, said the crucial issue is total phone time, not just where it happens. The study suggested school bans could reduce use during the school day by about 40 minutes, but overall phone use still averaged four to six hours a day. She argued that policy must address phone use both in and out of school. That has pushed the debate beyond classrooms and toward the design of social media platforms themselves, especially features such as infinite scrolling and algorithms that amplify extreme content. As governments hesitate, some parents are taking matters into their own hands. One fast-growing initiative is Smartphone-Free Childhood, a British nonprofit co-founded by Daisy Greenwell. It encourages parents to delay smartphones until age 14 and social media until 16, and more than 170,000 children worldwide have been signed up to the pledge. Greenwell said many parents would prefer not to give an 11-year-old a smartphone, but peer pressure and “network effects” make it difficult when other children have them. Parents, she said, are trying to resist systems larger than any one family. McShea believes the risks extend beyond school, but she sees schools as the clearest place to begin. She says her Devon school introduced a full smartphone ban, and she noticed the difference. In her first year of secondary school, she recalls, students seemed to stop talking almost overnight, absorbed in screens. Now, she says, younger children on her bus actually talk to each other. For her, that small change captures why the issue matters: smartphones shape not only academic life but also children’s social and emotional development.

Kazakhstan has started building a DNA database for people convicted of serious crimes, according to Inkar Tazhigulova, head of the biological and chemical examination laboratory at the Astana Institute of Forensic Expertise. She said the country adopted the Law on Dactyloscopic and Genomic Registration at the end of last year, and it will take effect in 2021. Under the law, all people convicted of grave and especially grave crimes will be genotyped. Preparatory work is already underway, including entering genetic material collected from crime scenes and from unknown persons into the database so law enforcement can automatically compare it with samples from suspects or convicts in the future. Tazhigulova said the system should save time and improve crime-solving. She noted that the United Kingdom created the first such database in 1995, and she studied Britain’s experience during a Bolashak Programme internship last year. After returning to Kazakhstan, she joined the working group that helped draft the law and is now involved in preparing the regulatory documents. The Institute of Forensic Expertise already conducts molecular-genetic studies in civil and criminal cases, including paternity disputes, murders, rapes, unidentified remains, drug trafficking, theft and other offenses. Tazhigulova also said genetic passports may be useful for people in high-risk professions such as police, military personnel, pilots and journalists.

Japan has long been known for exceptionally clean streets despite having very few public trash cans, but that approach is being reconsidered as tourism rebounds and litter increases. In Osaka’s tourist-heavy Dotonbori district, about 20 new “smart” garbage cans called SmaGO were installed this week. The solar-powered bins can detect when they are filling up and compress trash by about 20%, while also sending data through a smartphone app to alert workers before they overflow. The bins are distributed in Japan by startup Forcetec, whose chief executive, Yohei Takemura, said more local governments are realizing that adding trash cans may be the only practical solution. He said cities are increasingly willing to test them as a way to stay cleaner. Public trash cans largely disappeared from many parts of Japan after the 1995 Aum Shinrikyo sarin gas attack in Tokyo, though they remain in some high-traffic places such as major train stations. Osaka’s Environment Bureau said the city had removed them entirely in response to overflowing garbage and complaints from residents. The issue has become more urgent as inbound tourism officially exceeded pre-pandemic levels in October. Prime Minister Fumio Kishida’s October anti-overtourism package even includes subsidies for smart trash cans, alongside efforts to steer visitors toward lesser-known destinations. Japan’s popular street food culture adds to the problem, since many tourists buy snacks such as takoyaki and fish-shaped sweets but are unfamiliar with Japan’s strict waste-sorting habits and often do not want to carry trash around. Takemura said Japanese people traditionally carry their own rubbish home. Forcetec imports the bins from U.S.-based Bigbelly, which introduced them nearly two decades ago. After some early reluctance, Tokyo’s Omotesando shopping street installed them in 2020, and more than 200 now stand in tourist areas including Kyoto’s Arashiyama bamboo forest.

Former Chilean President Michelle Bachelet was presented on Wednesday with the Indira Gandhi Prize for Peace, Disarmament and Development in New Delhi. The award was conferred by Sonia Gandhi, chairperson of the Indira Gandhi Memorial Trust and Congress Parliamentary Party chairperson. Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge and jury chairman Shiv Shankar Menon were also present at the ceremony. In her remarks, Sonia Gandhi highlighted Bachelet’s personal and political journey, noting that she had endured loss, oppression, torture and exile in her early life before breaking barriers to become Chile and Latin America’s first woman Defence Minister. She also recalled that Bachelet made history by serving twice as President of Chile. Sonia Gandhi said Bachelet’s influence extended well beyond Chile and Latin America, especially after she became the first director of UN Women in 2010 and later the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights. Sonia Gandhi praised Bachelet’s work on women’s rights, gender equality, public health and social welfare. She said Bachelet had reformed Chile’s healthcare system, expanded access to primary care, supported victims of sexual abuse, improved conditions for women in the military and police, and introduced tax reforms that strengthened pension schemes and social protection for women and children. She also credited her government with advancing quotas to boost women’s political participation and legislation promoting equality and freedoms. Bachelet, in her acceptance remarks, spoke warmly of India’s cultural richness, history and diversity, saying tradition and modernity coexist there. She said Indira Gandhi believed nations prosper through harmony, and argued that no country can face today’s conflicts alone. Bachelet said Gandhi inspired her to enter politics to improve people’s welfare, and stressed that peace and progress are essential to human dignity. She also underlined the need for stronger multilateralism and daily cooperation across nations, generations and differences.

Congress Parliamentary Party Chairperson Sonia Gandhi, who heads the Indira Gandhi Memorial Trust that awards the prize, presented the honor alongside Congress President Mallikarjun Kharge and jury Chairman Shiv Shankar Menon. Alberta’s Court of Appeal has unanimously rejected the extradition appeal of Faruq Khalil Muhammad “Isa,” also known as Sayfildin Tahir Sharif, clearing the way for his transfer to the United States to face terrorism-related charges tied to the deaths of five American soldiers in Iraq. The Edmonton man, a dual Canadian-Iraqi citizen, was arrested by the RCMP in January 2011 after being identified by U.S. security forces, and he has fought extradition for three years. The charges against him stem from a 2009 suicide bombing in Iraq. U.S. authorities allege that Isa conspired to murder Americans abroad, provided material support to terrorists, and aided and abetted the murder of Americans abroad. According to the allegations, he communicated by phone and email with an aspiring suicide bomber, advised him on hiding Internet and email activity, encouraged others to join terrorist groups, and helped plan the transfer of money to support terrorists. A lower court had already ruled that Isa should be sent to New York for trial, and the Court of Appeal upheld that decision this week. The editorial argues that Isa will likely now seek leave to appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada, and says he should do so. It contends that because terrorism cases are politically charged, extradition decisions must be carefully reviewed to protect due process and keep justice separate from political pressure. The article notes that Canadian officials appear to have obtained a U.S. promise that Isa will not face the death penalty. Even so, he could still face a sentence more severe than what he might receive in Canada, including the possibility of life imprisonment without parole. The Court of Appeal also considered claims that three men, including Isa’s brother, were tortured into giving investigators information against him. The extradition judge had dismissed those claims. While the court found that one man’s torture allegations had an “air of reality,” it concluded that even if that evidence were excluded, the remaining evidence on the conspiracy charge was still overwhelming. At the same time, the editorial stresses that little of the evidence has been made public in Canada, aside from references to wiretaps and hard drives. Because extradition hearings do not require proof beyond a reasonable doubt, only enough credible evidence to justify a trial abroad, the piece concludes that the Supreme Court should review the case before Isa is sent to face another country’s justice system.

# Summary: Alberta Court Upholds Extradition in Terrorism Case An Edmonton man faces extradition to the United States after Alberta's Court of Appeal unanimously rejected his appeal challenging the decision to send him to trial in New York. Faruq Khalil Muhammad 'Isa, a dual Canadian-Iraqi citizen arrested in January 2011, has been fighting extradition for three years and is expected to appeal to Canada's Supreme Court. 'Isa is accused of involvement in a 2009 suicide bombing in Iraq that killed five American soldiers. The charges against him include conspiracy to murder Americans abroad, providing material support to terrorists, and aiding and abetting murder. Specifically, he allegedly maintained phone and email contact with an aspiring suicide bomber, offering advice on concealing digital activity, encouraging others to join terrorist forces, and plotting to send money to support terrorists. The Court of Appeal addressed concerns that torture may have been used to extract information from three men, including 'Isa's brother. While the court acknowledged torture allegations had an "air of reality" regarding one interrogated individual, it concluded that even excluding such evidence, "the remaining evidence for committing on the conspiracy charge was overwhelming." However, little of this evidence has been made public in Canada, with details drawn primarily from wiretaps and hard drives. The editorial argues that the Supreme Court must review this case before 'Isa is extradited to face potential lifetime imprisonment without parole in the United States—a sentence more severe than he would likely receive in Canada. The piece emphasizes that while terrorism is serious, justice must not become politicized. It notes that terrorism cases have previously involved political statements from Canadian officials, as exemplified by the Omar Khadr case. The editorial contends that 'Isa appears to be "low-hanging fruit" and a minor player who primarily communicated online from his apartment, rather than a significant terrorist threat. It stresses the importance of rigorous judicial process to protect all Canadians from political manipulation of the justice system. While Canadian officials secured a promise that 'Isa will not face the death penalty, the editorial argues the Supreme Court should carefully assess the credibility of charges before allowing extradition to another nation's justice system.

French satirical weekly *Charlie Hebdo* will publish a special edition next week mocking God to mark the 10th anniversary of the jihadist attack on its Paris offices that killed eight staff members. The paper is using the occasion to signal defiance toward the gunmen who stormed its newsroom on Jan. 7, 2015, and shouted that they had “killed Charlie Hebdo.” Editor-in-chief Gerard Biard said the attackers did not destroy the publication, adding that he wants it to endure “for a thousand years.” The attack was carried out by two Paris-born brothers as revenge for the magazine’s repeated publication of cartoons lampooning the Prophet Muhammad. The massacre of some of France’s best-known cartoonists became a defining moment in modern French history and was followed by a wave of Al-Qaeda and Islamic State attacks in France and across western Europe that killed hundreds. Next week’s issue will present the results of a competition launched in November to find the “funniest and meanest” depictions of God. The edition is aimed, according to the paper, at people tired of a society shaped by religion, moral absolutes, and religious leaders dictating daily life. Commemorations will be held Tuesday at the site of the attack, as well as at the location of a linked assault on a Jewish supermarket. President Emmanuel Macron and Paris Mayor Anne Hidalgo are expected to attend. The killings shocked France and triggered an enormous show of solidarity, including the slogan “Je Suis Charlie,” in support of the magazine and its slain contributors, among them Cabu, Charb, Honore, Tignous and Wolinski. At the same time, the magazine’s aggressive, often crude style of satire also sparked anger and debate. Since its founding in 1970, *Charlie Hebdo* has repeatedly pushed against French hate-speech rules, which protect minorities but permit blasphemy and ridicule of religion. Supporters of free speech view the magazine’s right to mock religion as a hard-won liberty. Critics, however, accuse it at times of crossing into Islamophobia, especially in cartoons that appeared to link Islam with terrorism. Riss, the director and survivor of the 2015 attack, has said the point of the magazine is to publish material that makes people question assumptions and resist ideology. The attack transformed *Charlie Hebdo* from a marginal publication into a globally recognized symbol of free expression. More than three million people marched in France after the killings, and about 40 world leaders came to Paris in a show of support. A special post-attack issue sold more than eight million copies, and donations poured in, giving the paper an unexpected financial boost. Subscriptions later fell from a peak of more than 200,000 to around 30,000, though weekly sales remain above pre-attack levels. The magazine now has about 12 cartoonists working in a secret, heavily protected office. Yet controversy continues: recent front pages and cartoons have prompted legal complaints and public outrage. The paper’s first anniversary issue in 2016 featured a bearded God-like figure carrying a Kalashnikov, underscoring its continuing commitment to provocation.

Khartoum’s resistance committees say they are moving ahead with plans to establish local Legislative Councils in the city’s districts, a step they present as the basis for creating a broader national Legislative Council. Ahmed Esmat, spokesperson for the Khartoum City Resistance Committees, said the committees have already formed groups to set up councils in neighbourhoods across the capital. The initiative comes after years of frustration over the failure to create the Transitional Legislative Council (TLC) promised under the Juba Peace Agreement. According to the article, the TLC was never formed partly because the Forces for Freedom and Change (FFC) could not agree on a list of members. Many revolutionary groups viewed that failure as a betrayal of the revolution’s goals. Two years ago, Shamson Yohanna of the El Salama resistance committees in southern Khartoum warned that the council would not truly represent ordinary people, arguing that the largest share would go to the FFC, which he said did not reflect youth, women, or members of armed struggle movements. Esmat said the current effort is based on the resistance committees’ unified charter and is intended to lead to a parallel government whose legitimacy comes from neighbourhood committees organized in general assemblies. He also said the new councils would “restrict all the work of the tax system,” though the article does not explain how. The resistance committees are also preparing to sign the Revolutionary Charter for Establishing People’s Power, a document that sets out their political framework. Esmat said the charter is in its final form and would be announced within two days, then presented to all political groups and committees that reject the Framework Agreement. That agreement was signed by Sudan’s military junta and a coalition of civilian parties led by the FFC-Central Council. A unified version of the charter was already signed four months earlier after the committees worked to merge two separate drafts, one from Wad Madani and one from Khartoum. Most Khartoum resistance committees support the charter, but some in the Southern Belt of Khartoum, Haj Yousef, Khartoum North (Bahri), Sharg en Neel, and Central Khartoum have not yet signed. Esmat said organizers are still trying to persuade them to join the project and take part in forming local Legislative Councils. The article places this effort within the broader history of Sudan’s resistance committees: decentralized, youth-driven grassroots groups that emerged during the December 2018 revolution and played a major role in the pro-democracy movement. After the June 3, 2019 massacre at the Khartoum sit-in, they became watchdogs over other opposition forces, insisting that revolutionary ideals not be traded away for power.

A ferry crew discovered 25 migrants hidden inside a refrigerated container aboard a cargo vessel traveling from the Netherlands to Britain on Tuesday, according to Dutch emergency services. The ship, bound for Felixstowe, turned back to the Dutch port of Vlaardingen near Rotterdam after the stowaways were found. Medical teams treated the migrants at the port, and two were taken to hospital for further care because of possible hypothermia. The other 23 were taken to a police facility after being checked. Emergency officials said no one had died. DFDS Seaways, which operates the ferry, said the migrants had apparently boarded on a lorry trailer, and the truck driver was arrested, according to Dutch newspaper De Telegraaf. The group was described as mainly male, and some were wrapped in silver thermal blankets. Their nationalities were not immediately known. The incident came a month after 39 Vietnamese migrants were found dead in a refrigerated truck in Britain, underscoring the dangers of illegal routes into Europe. Vlaardingen Mayor Annemiek Jetten said desperate people were still attempting the crossing despite those deaths, though it was unclear whether fears of tougher post-Brexit immigration rules were also driving the attempts.

The ship immediately returned to the Dutch port of Vlaardingen near Rotterdam. All migrants received medical attention at the port, with two hospitalized for suspected hypothermia. No deaths were reported. The stowaways had boarded via a lorry trailer, and the truck driver was arrested. She suggested uncertainty about tougher UK immigration laws following Brexit may be driving the surge in attempted illegal border crossings.

Mevlude Genc, who became a symbol of reconciliation after a racist arson attack killed five members of her family in Germany, has died at 79, authorities in North Rhine-Westphalia said Sunday. Genc and her husband, Turkish immigrants living in Solingen, lost two daughters, two granddaughters and a niece when far-right extremists set fire to their home in 1993. Seventeen others were seriously injured. Four young Germans were later convicted of murder and attempted murder and sentenced to 10 to 15 years in prison. The attack, along with others around that time, raised fears of resurgent neo-Nazi sentiment after German reunification. Despite her loss, Genc urged Turks and Germans to reject hatred and live together in peace. State governor Hendrik Wuest praised her as embodying faith in human goodness and said her legacy would endure.

# Summary Mevlude Genc, a Turkish-German woman who advocated for reconciliation after a tragic racist attack, has died at 79. In 1993, far-right extremists firebombed her Solingen home, killing five family members—two daughters, two granddaughters, and a niece—and injuring 17 others. Four perpetrators received 10-15 year sentences for murder and attempted murder. Despite her devastating loss, Genc championed unity between Turkish and German communities, famously stating that her family's death should inspire friendship and coexistence. Her message of compassion resonated widely during a period marked by rising neo-Nazi sentiment following German reunification in 1990. State Governor Hendrick Wuest praised her as embodying "the belief in the goodness of human beings," noting her legacy will endure.

Poland’s Internal Security Agency said on Tuesday that a 27-year-old Colombian national acted on behalf of Russian intelligence in a series of arson attacks in Poland and the Czech Republic. According to the agency, he set fire in May 2024 to two construction supply depots in Poland after being trained by a person linked to Russian intelligence services. Officials said he was taught how to make incendiary devices and Molotov cocktails, and how to record the attacks for use in propaganda. Polish authorities said Russian-language media later used photos and videos from the fires for disinformation, including a false claim that one blaze hit a logistics center in Radom storing military equipment supplied to Ukraine by European countries. After the attacks in Poland, the suspect allegedly traveled to the Czech Republic, where he burned a bus depot and was later detained while preparing another attack on a shopping mall. He has already been sentenced to eight years in prison in the Czech Republic for terrorism-related acts, and in Poland he could face up to 10 years or life imprisonment. Russia’s embassy denied the accusations.

# Summary Poland's Internal Security Agency announced that a 27-year-old Colombian national, acting under Russian intelligence direction, carried out arson attacks in Poland and the Czech Republic in 2024. The suspect received training from Russian operatives in preparing incendiary devices and documenting attacks for propaganda purposes. In May 2024, he set fire to two construction supply depots in Poland. Russian-language media subsequently used photographs and videos from these attacks to spread disinformation, falsely claiming one fire targeted a logistics center storing military aid for Ukraine. Following the Polish attacks, the Colombian traveled to the Czech Republic and set fire to a bus depot. Czech authorities arrested him before he could attack a shopping mall. He was sentenced to eight years in prison in the Czech Republic and faces up to 10 years or life imprisonment in Poland. Polish officials characterize these incidents as part of Russia's "hybrid warfare" campaign against Ukraine-supporting nations, employing sabotage, arson, and cyberattacks. Russia has denied involvement in such attacks.

Chile’s President Sebastián Piñera announced a $24 million plan on Monday to ease the long-running conflict between the state and the country’s indigenous Mapuche population in southern Chile. The package is the latest in a series of efforts to address tensions rooted largely in disputes over ancestral lands. Piñera’s center-right government said it wants to improve relations with the Mapuche by boosting indigenous representation in government and speeding up the creation of a ministry for indigenous people. The plan also includes housing subsidies, infrastructure upgrades, and 12 new hospitals for the Araucanía region. Piñera said the proposal is not a final solution but something civil society can review and improve. About 600,000 Mapuche live in Chile, mainly in Araucanía and Biobío, where poverty is widespread and arson attacks on forestry and other businesses have risen in recent years.

# Summary Chilean President Sebastian Pinera announced a $24 million investment plan to resolve the longstanding conflict between the state and indigenous Mapuche population in the south. The initiative addresses disputes over ancestral lands and includes increased indigenous government representation, creation of a ministry of indigenous affairs, housing subsidies, infrastructure improvements, and twelve new hospitals for the Araucania region. Approximately 600,000 Mapuche live in Chile's southern forested provinces, among the country's poorest communities. The Mapuche claim the state and private companies have seized their ancestral lands, exploited natural resources, and used excessive force against them. Recent years have witnessed increased arson attacks against forestry companies, often attributed to disgruntled Mapuche groups. Pinera characterized the plan as a proposal requiring further analysis and input from civil society rather than a final solution.

Serbian producer Firefly is shaping its adaptation of the true-crime-inspired novel *Gorilla* with the controversy around Netflix’s *Baby Reindeer* in mind. The 6×55-minute series is based on Dusan Savkovic’s 1976 novel, which fictionalizes two real unsolved crimes: the 1966 deaths of Serbian-born US actor Milos Milos and Barbara Ann Thomason in Mickey Rooney’s Los Angeles home, and the 1968 Marković affair in France, centered on the death of Stevan Marković, a friend of Milos and bodyguard to Alain Delon. At Content Warsaw, Firefly co-founder, COO and producer Ivana Miković said the company wants to avoid the legal and reputational issues that have followed *Baby Reindeer*, which has faced threats of legal action over its claims of being a true story and its depiction of real people. Firefly’s approach is to use Savkovic’s book and the historical crimes as inspiration, but to fictionalize the material more heavily. The pitch bible says the goal is to free the story from the “constraints of reality” and focus on the human tragedy behind the events. Miković said Firefly will change names and the setup, and add new storylines and characters to give the drama more depth. She emphasized that the project is not a documentary and needs creative expansion. Firefly is also working on other projects, including *Constantine’s Crossing*, *Children of Evil*, and several book-based series currently being offered to international partners at the event.

# Summary Serbian production company Firefly is developing a true crime drama adaptation called *Gorilla*, deliberately learning from controversies surrounding Netflix's *Baby Reindeer*. *Gorilla* is based on a 1976 Serbian novel by Dusan Savkovic that fictionalizes two real unsolved crimes: the 1966 deaths of Serbian-American actor Milos Milos and Barbara Ann Thomason (Mickey Rooney's estranged wife) found in Rooney's Los Angeles home, and the 1968 Marković affair—a French political scandal involving blackmail and alleged orgies connected to future French president Georges Pompidou. To avoid legal issues faced by *Baby Reindeer*, which has been threatened with lawsuits over its "true story" portrayal of real individuals, Firefly plans significant changes. Producer Ivana Miković stated they will alter character names, settings, and add fictional storylines and new characters while maintaining the source material's essence. Miković emphasized: "It's not a documentary, you need to add to it," explaining their strategy to explore deeper human themes without documentary constraints. This announcement comes after Firefly recently completed the WWII series *Constantine's Crossing* at its new Serbian studio complex and worked with Germany's Beta Film on *Children of Evil* for Max. At Content Warsaw, Firefly is seeking international partners for multiple book-based series, including English-language titles *Rabies* and *Fatal Ally*.

Israeli Consul-General Paul Hirschson said antisemitism in Canada has sharply worsened since Hamas’s Oct. 7 attack on Israel, and that many Canadian Jews are now thinking about moving to Israel. In an interview with JNS in his Montreal office, Hirschson said the violence and hostility have forced Jews to reassess the people and communities around them. “Since Oct. 7, we have seen where our friends, colleagues and neighborhoods stand,” he said. “Some of them stood where we thought they would. Many didn’t and we can’t unsee it.” He pointed to a surge in hate crimes and incidents immediately after the Hamas assault. Montreal police recorded 63 hate crimes against Jews and 41 hate incidents from Oct. 7 to Nov. 14. Those included the firebombing of a Jewish community center and synagogue in Dollard-des-Ormeaux and a shooting attack on the Yeshiva Gedola elementary school. Hirschson said more attacks followed: in May, police responded to a shooting at a Jewish school in Côte-des-Neiges-Notre-Dame-de-Grâce; in June, a Jewish-owned restaurant in Mile End was hit by projectiles believed to have been fired from an airsoft gun; and last month a Jewish tombstone at Montreal’s Kehal Israel cemetery was desecrated with a swastika made from stones placed on graves. He said most of the attacks happened at night and few involved direct physical assaults, suggesting the goal was to terrorize rather than injure. In his view, that strategy has succeeded. “Members of the community are not happy. They feel threatened and insecure,” he said, adding that the number of Jews considering aliyah is increasing. He said he personally wants all Jews to move to Israel, but not because of antisemitism; rather, because “Israel is the greatest place.” Hirschson also said a recent email threat to bomb more than 100 Jewish sites across Canada could not simply be dismissed. Even if officials doubted it was real, he said, the proper response was to shut down the sites and let police investigate. He argued that antisemitism must be condemned directly and not folded into broad comparisons with Islamophobia. In his view, treating the two as morally equivalent turns a real threat into an abstract debate and ignores the pain people are experiencing. While saying Canada has traditionally been a friend of Israel, Hirschson said Jerusalem is disappointed with Ottawa’s response since Oct. 7. He noted that Canada is among the few G7 countries whose leader has not visited Israel since the Hamas attacks, and that Ottawa was among the first of Israel’s friends, along with Australia and New Zealand, to back a ceasefire at the United Nations. He also criticized Canada’s decision to halt arms sales to Israel, which drew a sharp rebuke from Israeli Foreign Minister Yisrael Katz in March. Hirschson said real friendship is tested in hard times, and he expected stronger support after Israel was attacked by what he called a terror organization that raped, kidnapped and murdered civilians. He also criticized Ottawa’s response to Israel’s preemptive strike on Hezbollah in southern Lebanon, saying Canada immediately referred back to Gaza even though the immediate threat came from Hezbollah. He accused Canadian officials of repeatedly linking Israel’s actions to the Palestinians through what he called “moral equivalence.” He said domestic politics also shape Canadian policy, citing the influence of Muslim communities in Canada and Montreal’s large Arab population. He argued that in some academic and public settings, Israel is seen in black-and-white terms: if Jews are no longer victims, then they are cast as perpetrators. Still, he said Israel and Canada stand together as liberal, democratic societies, and warned that if Israel fails in the current conflict, Canada, the United States and Europe will also suffer.

The Uttar Pradesh government has directed all 75 districts to take part in the main event of the upcoming Global Investors Summit (GIS), which will be held in Lucknow from February 10 to 12. According to an official statement from the Chief Minister’s office, this will be the first time that investment-related activities will be organized simultaneously across all districts in a single day. District-level programs will be used to invite local entrepreneurs and investors, with the aim of highlighting business opportunities across the state. Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath discussed the summit and other administrative issues during a cabinet meeting on Saturday. The meeting also covered law and order. The government said that, after earlier outreach efforts under the “Sarkar Aap Ke Dwaar” initiative, in-charge ministers are now being appointed for every district for the next year. The chief minister instructed these ministers to stay updated on district affairs, visit their assigned districts regularly, and spend at least 24 hours during each tour. He also asked them to involve public representatives in meetings, review government schemes, and assess law and order. Yogi Adityanath further directed ministers to make surprise visits to at least one development block and one tehsil in their districts. During these visits, they are to review women’s safety, prosecution in SC/ST cases, police patrolling, child sexual abuse concerns, problems faced by businessmen, action against gangsters, traffic management, and revenue collection efforts. He also emphasized continuous monitoring of aspirational development blocks and interaction with youth linked to the Chief Minister’s Fellowship Scheme. The chief minister stressed that senior field officials, including divisional commissioners, district magistrates, police commissioners or superintendents, and chief development officers, should regularly review development projects with local public representatives. He also urged ministers to promote Millets Year by organizing millet-based dinners for public representatives and intellectuals and by raising public awareness about the importance of coarse grains.

China has launched two trade barrier investigations against US practices, in what officials and analysts described as a measured response to fresh American trade probes aimed at China and other economies. The Ministry of Commerce announced the investigations separately on Friday, saying they were “reciprocal countermeasures” to two new Section 301 probes initiated by the United States. # Summary: China-ROK FTA Needs Digital Modernization The China-Republic of Korea Free Trade Agreement, which entered into force in 2015, requires urgent modernization to address the dramatic shift toward digital commerce that has occurred over the past decade. While the agreement successfully governed traditional trade in physical goods, it is now dangerously outdated for an economy increasingly dominated by digital services and technology. ## The Scale of Digital Trade Global digitally delivered services reached $4.78 trillion in 2024, with China and the ROK both serving as major players in this expanding sector. Bilateral online shopping between the two countries continues to grow rapidly, with the digital corridor becoming a primary engine of their trade relationship. South Korea's gaming and fintech sectors are rapidly entering the Chinese market, while China's e-commerce applications have become integral to Korean digital life. This represents far more than business as usual—it constitutes an accelerating digital merger between two of the world's most technologically advanced populations. ## The Fundamental Problem Despite this dramatic transformation, the current FTA remains anchored in an outdated framework focused on traditional tariffs for physical goods. This creates a critical mismatch between regulatory reality and actual trade patterns. While physical ports between the countries remain open, the digital highway connecting them is obstructed by regulatory barriers and inconsistent rules. ## Critical Gaps in Current Framework The 2015 agreement lacks a dedicated chapter on digital trade. Its existing e-commerce chapter contains only nine articles consisting of largely symbolic, noncontroversial statements. Crucially missing are provisions addressing the heavy hitters of modern digital commerce: cross-border data transfers, server localization requirements, and artificial intelligence governance. The agreement provides no clear rules regarding when governments can restrict data movement or mandate domestic servers. The issue extends beyond mere omission. Modern commerce increasingly integrates products with data—one cannot export a humanoid robot without the massive data streams powering its AI, nor can modern medical services function without cross-border sensitive data transfers. These transactions currently exist in a legal gray zone, as the 2015 framework could not anticipate the data-driven reality of 2026. ## National Security Complications Perhaps most problematically, national security—a concept now permeating every commercial sector and constantly redefined with technological breakthroughs—lacks clear definition in the agreement. This absence creates a collision between national sovereignty and free trade principles. Without modern mechanisms to address these concerns, the framework invites endless tit-for-tat trade barriers. ## The Path Forward Following a January Beijing summit, both nations have renewed negotiations on lingering issues. Once resolved, China and the ROK must immediately pursue a comprehensive digital upgrade of their bilateral FTA. This modernization should establish critical balance between data security and seamless marketplace access, potentially serving as a reliable benchmark for other nations navigating similar challenges. The author argues that attempting to govern modern commerce with a decade-old rulebook is dangerously obsolete. When regulatory rules remain unclear, innovation stalls—particularly for small startups that represent growth engines but hesitate when confronting confusing, defensive regulations. A modernized FTA would align with broader international cooperation themes and address the digital revolution fundamentally reshaping global trade definitions. The digital upgrade represents not merely an update but a necessary transformation enabling both nations to build a high-speed lane for future commerce.

China’s latest trade policy signals, unveiled during the recently concluded “two sessions,” are being viewed by African analysts and officials as a potential boost for African exporters. In its Government Work Report on March 5, China said it would keep the volume of foreign trade stable while improving its structure, expand the cross-border use of the renminbi, promote cross-border e-commerce, increase trade in intermediate goods, and advance digital and green trade. Observers say this reflects a shift from sheer trade volume toward higher-quality, more value-added exchanges. Stephen Nduvi, a research fellow at the Global Centre for Policy and Strategy in Nairobi, said the policy points to a more predictable Chinese market and greater opportunity for African suppliers in agribusiness, green products and processed commodities. He noted that China-Africa trade reached $348 billion last year, and while demand for raw materials remains strong, China is increasingly seeking higher-value and semi-processed imports. That trend, he argued, could encourage African countries to invest in local processing and industrial capacity so they can move up the value chain. Nduvi said African exporters could diversify into horticulture, textiles, cocoa derivatives and eco-friendly products. He added that small and medium-sized enterprises are especially well placed to benefit if they have digital readiness, traceable supply chains and strong branding. The growth of cross-border e-commerce and overseas warehouse networks in China, he said, could help African businesses scale more easily through platforms such as Tmall, JD Worldwide and Alibaba’s cross-border channels. These platforms can allow firms to test consumer demand and expand efficiently, while overseas warehouses shorten delivery times and lower logistics costs. However, he also pointed to obstacles such as regulatory compliance, weak digital literacy and difficulties integrating with Chinese payment systems. Maged Refaat Aboulmagd, an Egyptian diplomat and member of the Egypt-China Friendship Association, said China’s emphasis on digital and green trade is especially promising because services are among the fastest sectors for job creation and require relatively limited capital. He said services account for more than half of new jobs in African societies, and young people are best positioned to fill them. He urged African governments to invest in infrastructure for green trade and sustainable supply chains, and to work with Chinese companies, UN agencies and financial institutions to obtain the capital and expertise needed to process exports locally and join global supply chains. He also called for stronger industrialization, agro-processing, rural development, green energy, technical education, banking integration and regulatory reform, alongside a more effective African Continental Free Trade Area. Humphrey Moshi of the University of Dar es Salaam said Africa’s dependence on raw material exports and imports of manufactured goods leaves it disadvantaged through low export values, expensive imports, job losses and missed technological gains. He said China’s plan to expand trade in intermediate goods supports Africa’s industrialization goals by adding value, diversifying economies, creating jobs and promoting technology transfer. He also welcomed China’s push to use the renminbi more widely in trade, saying it could reduce exchange risks and offer African countries an alternative to the dollar, whose scarcity and rising value have worsened inflation and living costs.

Amid growing pressure on the US dollar-centered global monetary system, experts and business leaders said renminbi internationalization is becoming increasingly important for both China’s economic development and global financial stability. The comments were made on Monday at the China Development Forum 2026 in Beijing. Zhu Min, former deputy managing director of the International Monetary Fund, said promoting the renminbi, or yuan, as an international currency is now not only a domestic economic need for China but also a broader requirement for the international financial system. He argued that as China pursues high-quality development, a stronger RMB is increasingly necessary to support innovation-led growth, industrial upgrading, green transformation and the overseas expansion of Chinese companies. Zhu said the global dominance of the US dollar is weakening because the US no longer has the economic weight to support a single-currency system. He noted that the US share of global output has fallen from 45 percent to about 25 percent, while its share of world trade has declined from 25 percent to roughly 13 percent. He also pointed to the “weaponization” of the dollar, trade conflicts and other policy actions as factors that have reduced confidence in the currency, along with concerns over the independence of the US Federal Reserve. According to Zhu, these shifts are visible in financial markets, where countries are increasing gold reserves and holding more non-major reserve currencies, including the RMB, as alternatives to the dollar, euro, yen and pound. He described this as evidence of “dollar avoidance” and declining trust in the US currency. Zhu said renminbi internationalization has accelerated in recent years. The RMB’s share in cross-border financial activity has risen from 20 percent to 63 percent, while its share in China’s trade payments has climbed from 10 percent to 35.4 percent over the past decade. The European Parliament is due to vote on Thursday on whether to implement a trade agreement between the United States and the EU, after several delays. US Ambassador to the EU Andrew Puzder warned that rejecting the deal would be “economic malpractice,” while saying the signs ahead of the vote were encouraging. He also cautioned that if the agreement is not approved, the EU should expect higher US tariffs. The vote concerns a revised version of the political deal first reached last summer, not the original understanding struck in July between Donald Trump and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen in Scotland. That original arrangement was criticized in Europe as too favorable to Washington, since it tripled levies on European goods while reducing tariffs on US industrial products to zero. The version now before lawmakers includes changes made by the European Parliament, such as an expiration date, a sovereignty-related trigger, and automatic snapbacks on steel tariffs. Parliamentary sources told Euronews the package is not ideal but is likely to pass because most political groups intend to support it. The EU had paused adoption of the deal after the US Supreme Court struck down the administration’s broad tariff measures last month and after Washington threatened to annex Greenland. At the same time, the EU is moving ahead with a separate trade agreement with Australia, finalized in Canberra on Tuesday after nearly a decade of negotiations. Puzder said the US does not view that pact as harmful, arguing that trade deals between close allies help the world. The Australia-EU agreement will remove tariffs on both sides, including Australia’s 5 percent duty on EU imports, and open wider trade in sectors such as critical minerals, manufactured goods, and dairy.

Finland’s President Alexander Stubb said Canada is making the right strategic choices in a turbulent global environment by broadening its trade relationships beyond the United States while still maintaining ties with Washington. The Finnish president’s visit reflected growing ties between Ottawa and Helsinki under Prime Minister Mark Carney. Stubb said he and Carney exchange text messages almost daily. Carney has promoted what he calls “principled pragmatism,” meaning Canada should defend human rights and international law while also expanding trade and investment, including with countries governed by autocratic regimes, and while avoiding direct confrontation with Washington and Beijing. Stubb has described a similar idea as “values-based realism.” Carney even referenced Stubb in a January speech at the World Economic Forum, where he spoke about a rupture in the world order. Stubb said the two leaders are now trying to bring together Carney’s idea of rupture and his own idea of transition. A major part of Stubb’s remarks focused on Russia and the war in Ukraine. He said he had once been more hopeful about the possibility of a ceasefire or peace deal with Moscow, but now sees what he called “classical Russian delay tactics.” Because of that, he said Ukraine’s allies should begin preparing for “the next winter” in the conflict. Stubb also argued that smaller countries such as Canada and Finland can still have significant influence in a shifting world order. He said small states have “a lot of agency” if they are willing to use it. On multilateralism, Stubb said Canada is right to try to preserve the international system by engaging more with developing countries. He suggested reforms to the United Nations and the global financial lending system so they better reflect the concerns of the Global South, while still allowing those institutions to respond effectively to Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. In a more lighthearted moment, Stubb said Canada joining the European Union would be “a marriage made in heaven,” joking that such negotiations would be faster than Finland’s accession to NATO. She suggested expanding cooperation beyond Arctic icebreakers to other types of vessels, and building similar partnerships in satellites and quantum technology.
