Authorities are probing allegations that the individual diverted funds from 110 U.S. government contracts—totaling $46 million—into a private operating entity. Rubrik is reportedly cooperating fully with the investigation and aims to resolve the matter by the end of March to keep its IPO timeline on track. Founded in 2014, Rubrik provides cloud-based ransomware protection and data-backup services to over 5,000 clients, including Nvidia and Home Depot. The firm reports annual recurring revenue exceeding $600 million. Despite the firm's strong financial standing, the IPO comes during a period of subdued activity in the U.S. market, where recent offerings from companies like Amer Sports and BrightSpring Health Services have struggled to meet their initial price expectations.

The Law Society of Manitoba has issued an urgent warning to its members following ransomware attacks on two provincial law firms. The firms were targeted by “MAZE,” a malicious software that encrypted their systems, blocking access to essential files, email, accounting software, and cloud-based backups. The attackers are demanding a substantial ransom for data restoration. The Law Society believes the breach originated from staff clicking on deceptive COVID-19-themed links or attachments. Examples included fraudulent outbreak maps, seminar registrations, and fake vendor communications. Consequently, the organization has cautioned members to exercise extreme vigilance regarding suspicious emails and unverified links. Currently, the affected firms are collaborating with IT professionals and cyber insurers to recover their compromised data. However, the Law Society remains uncertain if full access will be regained. While the identity of the impacted firms remains undisclosed, the incident serves as a stark reminder of the escalating cyber threats exploiting pandemic-related anxieties.

This edition of the *Taipei Times* sports briefs covers a variety of notable events across professional golf, baseball, and the intersection of sports and politics. In professional golf, Taiwan’s C.T. Pan started the AT&T Byron Nelson in Dallas strong, finishing the first round tied for 13th with a five-under-par 66. He sits three strokes behind leader Denny McCarthy. Meanwhile, former NFL quarterback Tony Romo, competing via a sponsor’s exemption, struggled to a five-over 76 despite an impressive early eagle. In Major League Baseball, Los Angeles Angels slugger Albert Pujols reached a historic milestone, recording his 2,000th career RBI with a third-inning solo home run against the Detroit Tigers. Pujols joins legends Alex Rodriguez and Hank Aaron as the only players in MLB history to achieve this feat. Angels manager Brad Ausmus praised the achievement, calling Pujols one of the greatest hitters to ever play the game. Controversy emerged regarding Mariners pitcher Yusei Kikuchi, who was spotted with a mysterious dark substance—likely pine tar—under his cap during a win against the New York Yankees. Despite the speculation, MLB issued no penalties. Yankees manager Aaron Boone declined to comment, and crew chief Dana DeMuth noted that the umpires observed no suspicious behavior, as pitchers often use such substances to improve grip. Finally, the Boston Red Sox visited the White House to celebrate their World Series title. The event was marked by the absence of manager Alex Cora and about a dozen players of color, who boycotted the visit to protest the Trump administration’s policies, specifically the response to Hurricane Maria in Puerto Rico. The White House also faced embarrassment for errors on its website, which misspelled the team’s name and misidentified the event as the "World Cup Series."

Auckland’s landmark mixed-use development, "The Orange," located at 141-149 Newton Road in Eden Terrace, has officially hit the market for the first time. Representing a unique blend of heritage preservation and contemporary urban design, the property is being marketed by Colliers International through a deadline private treaty process, with offers closing on November 25. The Orange is a sophisticated integrated development situated on a 2,048-square-meter freehold site. It is anchored by the historic Orange Hall, a cultural icon completed in 1923 that once hosted legendary performers like Dame Kiri Te Kanawa and Sir Howard Morrison. Following a 2015 redevelopment led by Crosson Architects—which received a 2016 New Zealand Architecture Award—the site now features a striking juxtaposition of the original brick-facade hall and modern, curved architecture with bold orange accents. The property serves as a high-performing, split-risk investment, generating approximately $1.78 million in net annual rent. This income stream is diversified between residential and commercial sectors, with 65 percent derived from 66 high-quality apartments and 35 percent from three levels of character office space and two retail units. The residential component, which includes a mix of studios, one-bedroom, two-bedroom, and loft apartments, represents a rare opportunity to enter the burgeoning built-to-rent (BTR) sector. According to Alan McMahon of Colliers, the BTR model is particularly timely given Auckland’s ongoing housing supply constraints, population growth, and the high demand for professionally managed, quality rental accommodation. The commercial and residential tenancies are currently managed by Crockers Property Management, ensuring operational stability. The asset has proven resilient even amidst the challenges of the Covid-19 pandemic, with the residential portion recording a 98 percent rent collection rate in 2020. Beyond its current status as a passive investment, the property offers a new owner significant flexibility. Potential value-add strategies include converting commercial space to residential units, reconfiguring lofts for office use, or pursuing unit-titling and subdivision to realize future capital gains. The site’s appeal is further bolstered by its location in the Newton/Uptown precinct. Situated just two kilometers from the Auckland CBD, the development offers excellent connectivity, including immediate access to motorways, major bus routes, and proximity to the forthcoming City Rail Link stations at Mt Eden and K'Road. The area provides robust local amenities, including reputable schools and diverse hospitality options, which continue to drive strong tenant demand. The redevelopment of the site prioritized both aesthetics and functionality. The refurbished Orange Hall now offers modern office environments featuring exposed timber beams and original paneling, while the central plaza integrates historical elements, such as etched dancefloor chairs, into a contemporary basalt-paved space. The broader complex also provides extensive infrastructure, including 80 basement car parking spaces. Gareth Fraser and Richard Kirke of Colliers describe the property as a "trophy asset." By combining the historical prestige of the Orange Hall with the modern, income-generating capacity of its BTR apartments and commercial offices, The Orange stands as a distinct opportunity for investors looking to secure a foothold in one of Auckland’s most dynamic city-fringe locations. With its combination of secure, diversified returns and long-term development potential, the property is positioned as a premier addition to any significant property portfolio.

On June 12, 2021, National Deputy Jean-Claude Kibala appealed to the Democratic Republic of the Congo’s government to provide urgent humanitarian aid to victims of a recent earthquake in the mining city of Kamituga, South Kivu. Kibala, who represents the Mwenga territory, urged authorities to extend support similar to that provided following the Nyiragongo volcano eruption. He also stressed the necessity of establishing rigorous building standards and a comprehensive national contingency plan to mitigate future natural disasters. The earthquake, which struck on Wednesday, caused significant structural damage, including the destruction of the Kagunzi Primary School, a local dispensary, a private university, and the 8th CEPAC Pentecostal Church. Additionally, numerous homes sustained cracks, and 10 individuals were reported injured. Kibala confirmed that he has already dispatched an assessment team to the disaster site to coordinate immediate relief efforts. Kamituga is a vital economic hub for the region, serving over 260,000 residents and supporting a broader population of 1.5 million across the Mwenga and Shabunda territories. The deputy’s call highlights the critical need for systemic disaster management in this essential mining and communications center.

Over a month after Super Typhoon Yutu devastated the U.S. Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands on October 25, recovery efforts continue. With winds reaching 180 mph, the storm—the strongest of 2018—severely impacted over 50,000 residents on Saipan and Tinian. Abbra Firman, a disaster program manager for the American Red Cross based in Montana, is currently assisting in the relief operations. She reports that infrastructure, such as roads, is slowly being restored. Firman expressed deep admiration for the local community’s remarkable resiliency, strong family spirit, and immense pride in their American citizenship, describing her experience supporting the ongoing recovery as truly inspiring.

The Coalition Avenir Québec (CAQ) recently launched a website, "pl61.ca," to advocate for Bill 61, the government’s controversial economic recovery plan. The site, established by the political party rather than the government, claims its purpose is to debunk "false information" circulating on social media regarding the legislation. The homepage asserts that the party aims to revive the economy while preventing the spread of misinformation during the pandemic. However, the initiative has faced swift backlash from opposition parties. Québec solidaire’s Gabriel Nadeau-Dubois dismissed the site as "damage control," while Parti Québécois leader Martin Ouellet compared the strategy to the former Liberal government’s reputation-management tactics. Critics argue that the CAQ is attempting to bypass democratic processes under the guise of pandemic recovery. Furthermore, the public committee overseeing the Charbonneau Commission’s recommendations warned that the bill could foster an environment conducive to corruption and collusion. Despite these concerns, the website continues to promote the government’s agenda, featuring a list of "facts" and "falsehoods" without citing sources, while encouraging citizens to view infrastructure projects in their respective regions. The site reflects a deepening divide between the CAQ and opposition leaders regarding transparency and executive power.

Samantha Connell, a 34-year-old Kershaw County sheriff’s office employee, faces embezzlement charges for allegedly stealing sex offender registration fees. Authorities claim Connell, who held the only key to the secure drawer, siphoned all incoming funds over a 16-month period beginning in January 2015. She is charged with embezzling public funds totaling less than $10,000 following an investigation by state officials.

NDP Leader Jagmeet Singh has pledged a $100-million federal fund aimed at preventing youth involvement in gangs. Announced during a town hall in Surrey, B.C., the funding is intended to bolster after-school and mentorship programs. Singh stated the initiative follows consultations with community organizers, experts, and front-line workers in Surrey and Toronto who identified a critical lack of resources for at-risk youth. The promise arrives amid persistent gang violence in Surrey, which recently saw another targeted shooting death. Public frustration regarding this issue led to the formation of "Wake Up Surrey" in 2018, a group advocating for increased public safety and a transition from RCMP to a municipal police force. Gurpreet Singh Sahota, a founding member of the group, acknowledged the NDP’s proposal but expressed significant skepticism toward election-season rhetoric. Sahota noted that the Liberal government previously promised $327 million to combat youth gang violence during a byelection two years ago, yet the community has yet to see those funds materialize. While residents are desperate for solutions to the ongoing “gang war,” Sahota remains wary of whether any political party will move beyond campaign promises to deliver tangible, long-term action once the election concludes.

Following the extended Easter holiday, oil prices experienced a decline in light trading as markets reopened. Benchmark Brent crude futures dipped to $55.32, while US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude fell to $52.61 per barrel. This downward trend follows a three-week period of consecutive gains, leading some analysts to suggest that the market is undergoing a necessary price correction after recent speculative growth. The primary catalyst for the slump is a report from the US Energy Information Administration indicating a significant surge in domestic production. US shale output is projected to climb by 123,000 barrels per day in May, reaching its highest level since November 2015. This expansion, fueled by increased investment, signals a robust return to drilling as prices remain above the $50 threshold. This rise in American production creates significant pressure on OPEC, which previously agreed to output cuts to stabilize global prices. With an OPEC meeting scheduled for May 25 to discuss extending these production limits beyond June, the surge in US shale presents a major challenge to the cartel’s efforts to reduce the ongoing global supply glut. Market participants remain cautious, balancing signs of rising demand and strong Chinese economic data against the looming impact of increased US exports and production capacity.

The Ontario Provincial Police (OPP) have secured a production order to obtain audio recordings as part of an investigation into allegations that the provincial Liberal Party broke the law during the selection of a candidate for the Sudbury byelection. The controversy centers on Andrew Olivier, who served as the Liberal candidate in Sudbury during the previous general election. Olivier alleges that Premier Kathleen Wynne and campaign director Pat Sorbara pressured him to step aside to make room for Glenn Thibeault, a former NDP MP recruited by the Liberals. Olivier, who is quadriplegic, routinely records conversations for note-taking and subsequently released audio of his discussions with party officials on YouTube. The Progressive Conservatives filed an initial complaint with the OPP, arguing that the alleged offers of jobs or government appointments in exchange for withdrawing from a race may violate the Criminal Code. While an initial police review found no evidence of criminal activity, the release of the recordings prompted the OPP to reopen the case and seek a court-ordered production of the files. Simultaneously, Elections Ontario is conducting its own investigation into potential violations of the Election Act, which prohibits offering inducements to influence a candidacy. The Liberal Party maintains that the recordings actually vindicate them, asserting that they were merely discussing potential future roles for Olivier within the party or government after he had already been informed he would not be the candidate. The Sudbury seat became vacant following the surprise resignation of NDP MPP Joe Cimino. Olivier is now contesting the seat as an independent candidate, while the opposition parties have characterized the incident as a display of political entitlement.

Polish activists and lawmakers have invited U.S. senators to Warsaw to witness firsthand the systemic irregularities in property restitution. This follows a letter from 59 senators urging Poland to pass legislation compensating heirs for property seized during World War II and communism. Poland remains the only Central European nation lacking such laws, forcing cases into courts where activists allege a "restitution mafia" illegally transfers properties to unauthorized individuals, highlighting the urgent need for formal regulatory reform.

Typhoon Mitag, the 18th typhoon of the Pacific season, struck South Korea this week, resulting in at least four deaths and two individuals remaining missing. Making landfall in Haenam on Wednesday night, the storm swept across the peninsula toward the Sea of Japan, dumping record-breaking rainfall along the way. The fatalities occurred due to severe weather conditions: two elderly individuals were killed by powerful wind gusts in Pohang and Seongju, while two women died in Samcheok and Yeongdeok after landslides caused by torrential rains collapsed residential walls. Authorities reported that Uljin county experienced unprecedented rainfall intensity, reaching 104.5 millimeters per hour, while Donghae recorded its highest rainfall levels since 1992. Although Mitag has been downgraded to a tropical storm, the Korea Meteorological Agency warned that heavy rains would persist across the eastern coast and nearby islands. This event marks the seventh typhoon to impact South Korea this year. Meanwhile, the storm system has moved toward Japan, causing significant flooding in the city of Kochi, where floodwaters engulfed vehicles near a river. Rescue efforts and damage assessments continue in both nations as the region grapples with the aftermath of the severe weather event.

Brazilian Supreme Federal Tribunal (STF) Justice Flávio Dino has authorized a new judicial inquiry targeting former President Jair Bolsonaro, his three eldest sons—Senator Flávio, Congressman Eduardo, and Councilman Carlos—and approximately 20 other individuals, including former government officials, lawmakers, and journalists. This investigation centers on allegations of irregular practices during the Bolsonaro administration’s handling of the COVID-19 pandemic. The inquiry originates from a 1,180-page report produced by a 2021 Parliamentary Inquiry Commission (CPI) in the Brazilian Senate. That report accused the former president and his associates of numerous crimes, including malfeasance, "charlatanism," the use of scientifically unsupported treatments, corruption in vaccine procurement, and crimes against humanity. Although the Office of the Prosecutor General previously dismissed these allegations in 2022 due to insufficient evidence, Justice Dino has now determined that there is sufficient legal basis to initiate a formal police investigation. He has granted the Federal Police an initial 60-day period to examine claims of administrative misconduct, bid rigging, embezzlement, and the use of "front" companies. This development marks the latest in a series of legal challenges against Jair Bolsonaro since he left office in January 2023. The new probe follows closely on the heels of an STF ruling that convicted Bolsonaro of leading a "coup" plot to overturn the 2022 presidential election results, sentencing him to 27 years and three months in prison. Furthermore, a federal court recently imposed a substantial fine on the former president for remarks characterized as "recreational racism." Amid these mounting legal battles, it was also revealed that Bolsonaro has been diagnosed with squamous cell carcinoma, a form of skin cancer, following the surgical removal of several lesions. Bolsonaro is currently unable to comment on the new inquiry. In August, STF Justice Alexandre de Moraes placed the former president under strict house arrest, prohibiting him from issuing public statements or using communication devices. While the former president remains silent, his sons have reacted critically to the news. Senator Flávio Bolsonaro expressed his disdain on social media, while Councilman Carlos Bolsonaro sarcastically remarked on the frequency of the investigations against him. The younger Bolsonaro also highlighted that previous judicial and prosecutorial bodies had previously archived investigations related to the same COVID-19 allegations, questioning the current necessity of reopening the case. As the investigation proceeds, the legal pressure on the former president and his family continues to intensify within the Brazilian judiciary.

Michael Oppenheim, a 49-year-old former JPMorgan vice president, has been sentenced to five years in prison for embezzling $20 million from wealthy clients. Between 2008 and 2015, the Manhattan-based adviser deceived approximately 500 clients by falsely claiming he would invest their funds in low-risk municipal bonds, while in other instances, he simply stole their money without authorization. Following his guilty plea to embezzlement and securities fraud last November, U.S. District Judge Analisa Torres ordered him to forfeit $20.2 million and pay full restitution. Oppenheim’s defense attorney attributed the crimes to a severe, long-standing gambling addiction. JPMorgan, which alerted authorities to the scheme, expressed deep anger over the breach of client trust regarding the firm’s fiduciary responsibilities.

Valentino’s first couture show since the funeral of founder Valentino Garavani was a study in contrasts, blending a somber, transitional atmosphere with a provocative, high-concept theatrical experience. Held in Paris, the event marked a poignant turning point for the legendary fashion house, signaling the end of an era for a brand that, as fashion critic Suzy Menkes noted, transcended the industry to become a globally recognized cultural icon. Creative director Alessandro Michele, typically known for maximalism, opted for a restrained and clinical staging. Guests, including stars like Elton John and Dakota Johnson, were seated in darkness around circular, sterile-white pods. When the show began, blinds lifted to reveal models behind glass, turning the presentation into a curated, fragmented "peep show" accompanied by an unsettling soundscape of barking dogs. This clever use of restriction forced attendees to view the collection in slices rather than as a whole, highlighting Michele’s ability to command a room through tension and showcraft. The collection itself served as a "reset," with Michele cautiously testing the boundaries of Valentino’s established codes. While he incorporated signature "disco sheen"—featuring sequined surfaces, bedazzled headwear, and dramatic, billowing silhouettes—the couture remained surprisingly restrained. It lacked the untethered excess often associated with Michele’s work, suggesting a designer carefully calibrating his vision to honor the house's heritage while establishing his own path. The emotional weight of the show was undeniable. With industry veterans like Menkes reflecting on the passing of Garavani, the event felt like more than just a seasonal debut; it was a memorial to a specific type of legendary, larger-than-life designer. As the industry navigates a new generation of creative leadership, this show underscored the difficulty of replacing the distinct character of the past, even as Valentino moves forward into a futuristic, albeit tightly controlled, new chapter.

A new report from a United Nations panel of experts has revealed that Yemen’s Houthi rebels are obtaining drone components and weaponry that share technical characteristics with arms manufactured in Iran. This activity potentially violates the UN arms embargo currently in place. Investigators identified a primary smuggling route that traverses overland from Oman and Yemen's southern coast, moving through government-controlled territory toward the Houthi-held capital, Sanaa. Additionally, maritime routes remain a significant concern, evidenced by a November seizure of anti-tank missiles from a dhow in the Arabian Sea. The conflict in Yemen, which began with the 2014 Houthi takeover, has devolved into a protracted stalemate between the rebels and a Saudi-led coalition. As the fighting continues, the nation remains mired in the world’s worst humanitarian crisis, teetering on the edge of famine. The UN experts noted that both sides have engaged in economic warfare, while corruption and profiteering have become systemic. In the north, the Houthis have solidified their control through pervasive intelligence networks and the brutal suppression of dissent. The panel specifically documented a disturbing campaign of sexual violence, torture, and detention targeting women who participated in political protests or opposed Houthi rule. Throughout 2019, the Houthis intensified aerial strikes against Saudi Arabia, deploying new land-attack cruise missiles and Delta-design drones. While the Houthis claimed responsibility for the high-profile September attack on Saudi Aramco oil facilities, the UN panel concluded that the weapons used lacked the range to reach the targets from Houthi-controlled territory, casting doubt on the rebels’ claims. However, the panel confirmed that the Houthis have utilized similar sophisticated weaponry in other regional attacks. Investigators believe these advanced systems were not manufactured within Yemen but were imported in breach of the arms embargo. By analyzing debris and seized cargo, the panel traced shipments of components to addresses in Oman and the United Arab Emirates. Despite these findings, a conclusive military victory or political settlement remains elusive, leaving the Yemeni population to endure ongoing instability and humanitarian suffering.

On August 13, 2017, the Iranian parliament passed a significant amendment to the nation’s drug laws, marking a pivotal, albeit limited, shift in how the country handles nonviolent drug offenses. Iran, which maintains one of the world's highest execution rates, saw at least 567 individuals put to death in 2016 alone. According to Hassan Noroozi, spokesperson for the parliamentary judicial committee, approximately 5,000 individuals, many in their twenties, currently face death sentences for drug-related crimes. The amendment serves as a response to the widely acknowledged failure of capital punishment to deter drug trafficking. While the reform is less expansive than a 2016 draft that aimed to abolish the death penalty for almost all nonviolent drug offenses, it nonetheless represents a meaningful step toward reducing executions. Under existing law, mandatory death sentences apply to relatively small quantities of drugs, such as 30 grams of synthetic substances or five kilograms of opium. The new amendment replaces many of these mandatory death sentences with prison terms of up to 30 years. However, the bill retains the death penalty for specific circumstances. Executions remain mandatory for offenders who carry or use weapons against law enforcement, leaders of drug cartels, those who exploit children in trafficking, or repeat offenders with significant prior drug convictions. Furthermore, following opposition from the judiciary and the Interior Ministry, the parliament adjusted the threshold for capital punishment to apply to larger quantities—specifically, over 50 kilograms of traditional drugs or two kilograms of synthetic substances. For the legislation to take effect, it must be ratified by the Guardian Council, a body of 12 Islamic jurists tasked with ensuring the bill aligns with the Iranian constitution and sharia law. Human Rights Watch has urged the Council to approve the reforms immediately, citing that the current use of capital punishment for drug offenses violates the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, which limits the death penalty to the "most serious crimes." Beyond the legal thresholds, Human Rights Watch has repeatedly highlighted systemic abuses within the Iranian justice system, including torture, forced confessions, and the denial of adequate legal representation. By raising the bar for the death penalty, the amendment offers a glimmer of hope for hundreds currently on death row. Nevertheless, rights advocates continue to push for the total abolition of capital punishment in Iran, arguing that the practice is inherently inhumane and irreversible.

The article explores the lingering trauma and pervasive anxiety within the Democratic Party as the 2018 midterm elections approach. Two years after Hillary Clinton’s unexpected 2016 loss, many Democratic operatives are struggling to reconcile favorable polling data with the painful memory of a victory that seemed certain but ultimately slipped away. The primary objective for Democrats in 2018 is to capture 23 House seats to secure a majority. While FiveThirtyEight currently grants them a 76.9 percent chance of success—a figure higher than the probability assigned to Clinton at a similar point in 2016—this statistical optimism has failed to soothe the nerves of those who lived through the 2016 cycle. Veterans of the Clinton campaign, such as Jesse Ferguson and Jesse Lehrich, describe a sense of "deja vu" or "PTSD." They recall how, in 2016, the political establishment was slow to process the reality of a Donald Trump victory because they had never considered it a viable possibility. This apprehension is not universal, as many party leaders insist that the current cycle is fundamentally different. Unlike the 2016 presidential race, the 2018 midterms follow the historical trend of incumbent presidents facing significant headwinds in their first midterms. Steve Israel, a former chairman of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee (DCCC), argues that "Democratic energy is at nuclear levels," suggesting that voters are far more galvanized today than they were previously. Furthermore, supporters of the current Democratic outlook emphasize that the political landscape is no longer hypothetical; voters are reacting to the daily reality of the Trump presidency rather than just campaign rhetoric. However, skepticism remains. Democratic Representative Seth Moulton openly warned that the party might be overconfident, cautioning that they are facing a series of tough, hard-fought races rather than an unstoppable "blue wave." A central point of concern for Democrats is the reliability of polling data. Many acknowledge that pollsters committed a "devastating mistake" in 2016 by failing to account for rural voters and overestimating Clinton’s strength in key states. Ben Ray Lujan, the current DCCC chairman, noted that the committee has taken deliberate steps to better understand data models and rural demographics this time around. Despite these improvements, anonymous pollsters emphasize that uncertainty remains. They warn that even if a Democratic majority is the most likely outcome, there is always a statistical possibility of an alternative result, and failing to account for that possibility would be a repeat of the hubris seen in 2016. The article highlights that the final month of a campaign is notoriously volatile. In 2016, the release of the "Access Hollywood" tape and the late-stage announcement from FBI Director James Comey regarding the Clinton email investigation fundamentally altered the race's trajectory. While some Republicans argue that the recent confirmation battle over Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh has already served as the 2018 "October surprise" by energizing the conservative base, Democrats remain wary of the unknown. Ultimately, the piece captures a party caught between historical trends favoring a victory and a profound fear of history repeating itself. While Democrats are more prepared and cognizant of the risks than they were two years ago, the trauma of 2016 ensures that no one is taking a majority for granted until the final votes are counted.

The National Water Command Centre has issued a flood warning for nine provinces across Thailand’s North and Northeast regions. From May 12 to 14, residents should prepare for potential flash floods and runoff caused by isolated heavy rainfall. This weather pattern is driven by a low-pressure system in the Bay of Bengal, which is expected to intensify into a tropical storm. Affected provinces include Kalasin, Khon Kaen, Chaiyaphum, Maha Sarakham, Yasothon, and Ubon Ratchathani. Authorities have urged local agencies to closely monitor water levels, implement flood mitigation strategies, and keep the public informed to ensure safety during this period of severe weather.

The political landscape in Ontario has been shaken by bribery charges filed against two prominent Liberal operatives. Pat Sorbara, the former deputy chief of staff to Premier Kathleen Wynne, and Gerry Lougheed, a well-known party operative, have been charged under the provincial Election Act. These allegations stem from a long-running controversy surrounding the February 2015 byelection in Sudbury, Ontario. The charges against Sorbara include two counts of bribery, one of which specifically concerns Glenn Thibeault, the current Ontario energy minister. Police allege that Sorbara "knowingly" offered Thibeault—who was a New Democrat Member of Parliament at the time—employment or an office to induce him to switch parties and run as the Liberal candidate in Sudbury. Because police allege these actions were committed knowingly, the potential penalties are significant, including fines of up to $25,000 and possible jail time of nearly two years. Thibeault has publicly denied these allegations, maintaining that his decision to join the Ontario Liberals was a personal choice rather than the result of any improper inducement. His legal counsel echoed this sentiment, asserting that no bribes were offered or accepted. Sorbara, who recently resigned from her roles as the party’s CEO and 2018 campaign director, has expressed shock at the charges and remains confident that she will be vindicated in court. The broader scandal originated in late 2014, when Andrew Olivier, a previous Liberal candidate in Sudbury, released audio recordings of conversations with Sorbara and Lougheed. Olivier alleged that the pair attempted to persuade him to step aside for Thibeault by offering him a job or political appointment. Premier Wynne has consistently defended these interactions, arguing that the party was merely attempting to keep Olivier within the Liberal fold and that no *quid pro quo* arrangement existed, as the decision to appoint Thibeault had already been finalized. Opposition parties have reacted sharply to the news. NDP deputy leader Jagmeet Singh has raised concerns regarding the integrity of the cabinet, questioning whether a potential cabinet seat served as an inducement for Thibeault. Meanwhile, Progressive Conservative members staged a walkout during the legislature’s question period, frustrated by procedural rules that limited their ability to grill the government on the matter. Sorbara and Lougheed are scheduled to appear in a Sudbury court on November 21. This legal battle adds to a series of scandals involving the Ontario Liberal party, including ongoing investigations into the Ornge air ambulance service and the upcoming trial of former staffers regarding the deletion of emails related to the cancellation of two gas plants.

*Samarkand: Recipes and Stories from Central Asia and the Caucasus*, authored by Caroline Eden and Eleanor Ford, offers a unique and immersive exploration of the ancient Silk Road. Departing from purely historical accounts, the authors blend travelogue with traditional culinary practices, resulting in a work that feels remarkably vivid and three-dimensional. A standout feature of the book is its accessibility. While readers may occasionally struggle to source specific ingredients like barberries or Aleppo pepper in standard supermarkets, the vast majority of recipes are straightforward. The authors argue that the slight effort required to locate niche items is part of the charm, reflecting the remote, off-the-beaten-path locations they visited to compile their collection. The book is structured traditionally, categorizing meals into starters, meat dishes, breads, and drinks. However, it distinguishes itself by interspersing these recipes with rich historical context, cultural insights, and personal anecdotes. Eden, an experienced travel writer, provides evocative narratives that bring to life the mysterious allure of places like Samarkand and Tashkent. Through these stories, the authors highlight the region's shifting borders, cultural blending, and the enduring migratory traditions of its people, contrasting these fluid identities with the more rigid structures of life in the West. Ultimately, the strength of *Samarkand* lies in its authentic storytelling. By sharing the specific circumstances under which they first sampled dishes—whether in local family homes or while traveling—the authors imbue simple recipes like pilaf with profound meaning. The combination of high-quality photography, well-researched text, and a genuine commitment to culinary exploration creates a compelling portrait of a region defined by its vibrant history and diverse flavors. It is a work that serves as both a practical guide for the kitchen and an inspiring invitation to explore the legendary spice routes, leaving the reader torn between attempting a new recipe at home or embarking on a journey to experience these dishes in their place of origin.

Israel is bracing for a rare weather phenomenon known as a "medicane," a hybrid storm combining Mediterranean and tropical characteristics. Forecasters expect the system to bring intense rainfall, flooding, and powerful winds to Israel and parts of Egypt this weekend. While meteorologists note that these storms are becoming more frequent, the UK Met Office emphasized that a medicane occurring this far east in the Mediterranean remains an incredibly unusual and extreme meteorological event.

In Kerala, India, a long-standing dispute over the $900-million Vizhinjam port project escalated into violent clashes between police and local demonstrators, resulting in over 80 injuries. The protests, led by a local Christian fishing community, have stalled construction for three months. Villagers argue that the port development, spearheaded by billionaire Gautam Adani’s conglomerate, is responsible for severe coastal erosion and the loss of their livelihoods. The latest unrest began over the weekend after police arrested protesters who blocked construction vehicles, defying a court order to allow work to resume. In response, hundreds of demonstrators, guided by Catholic priests, marched on a local police station on Sunday night. The confrontation turned violent, leaving at least 46 protesters and 36 officers injured, while several police vehicles were damaged. Authorities have since deployed over 600 officers to the area to bolster security. Official accounts from the police allege that protesters arrived with weapons, held officers hostage, and threatened to burn the station down. Conversely, protest leaders claim that police initiated the violence by pelting the crowd with stones. The Adani Group, which is Asia’s wealthiest business entity, maintains that the port project adheres to all legal requirements and asserts that scientific studies link coastal erosion to natural causes rather than construction. While the project is viewed as a vital economic hub capable of rivaling ports in Singapore and Dubai, it has faced significant public backlash similar to the opposition Adani encountered during his coal mining ventures in Australia. As the standoff continues, the Kerala state High Court has demanded an explanation from the state administration regarding its failure to enforce court orders that would allow construction to proceed. With the state and federal governments subsidizing two-thirds of the project's costs, the court has ordered officials to provide a formal response by Friday.

The Ethiopian Agricultural Businesses Corporation (EABC) has confirmed that over half of the country’s fertilizer order for the current agricultural cycle has arrived at the Port of Djibouti. To support the "Bega" and "Mehir" seasons, the government procured 23 million quintals of fertilizer—nearly double the 14 million quintals imported last year. As of now, 12 million quintals (52% of the total order) have reached the port, with 11.7 million quintals already transported into Ethiopia for distribution via agricultural cooperatives. While procurement and arrival timelines are significantly improved compared to previous years, logistical success remains hampered by regional instability. Conflicts, particularly in the Amhara region, have restricted movement and delayed the delivery of these essential inputs to small-scale farmers. These distribution challenges echo last year’s difficulties, which saw widespread protests fueled by fertilizer scarcity and soaring costs, with prices reaching 12,000 birr per quintal. Although the government initiated the procurement process earlier this year to avoid a repeat of past crises, ongoing insecurity continues to threaten the timely arrival of supplies to the farmers who need them most, potentially impacting national agricultural output.

The Obama administration announced on Monday that U.S. military and civilian personnel have successfully destroyed Syria’s declared chemical weapons stockpile. This operation, overseen by the Organization for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons and the United Nations, involved neutralizing the agents aboard the vessel *Cape Ray* in international waters. President Obama praised the achievement as a testament to the power of diplomacy backed by the threat of military force, while extending gratitude to international partners, including Denmark, Norway, Italy, Finland, Germany, the United Kingdom, Russia, and China. The destruction of these weapons follows the devastating August 2013 sarin gas attack in Ghouta, which claimed over 1,400 lives. Pentagon press secretary Rear Adm. John Kirby hailed the mission as a significant milestone, noting it was accomplished despite the ongoing Syrian civil war. However, U.S. officials cautioned that the work remains incomplete. Secretary of State John Kerry highlighted persistent "discrepancies and omissions" in Syria’s initial declarations, suggesting the regime may not have fully disclosed its entire arsenal. Furthermore, Kerry expressed grave concern regarding the continued use of chlorine gas against Syrian civilians by forces loyal to President Bashar al-Assad. Reaffirming the United States' commitment to the region, Kerry stated that the U.S. will continue providing support to moderate rebels, emphasizing the need to oppose both the Assad regime and the violent extremists who have exploited the country’s instability. The destruction of the declared stockpile marks a vital step, but significant challenges regarding Syria's compliance remain.

Tshwane Executive Mayor Dr. Nasiphi Moya has formally pushed back against allegations that her administration intentionally delayed the blacklisting of controversial businessman Edwin Sodi. These accusations, which emerged following reports of a stalled process regarding the Rooiwal Wastewater Treatment Plant scandal, suggested that the city lacked urgency in holding Sodi accountable for his role in a project linked to a devastating cholera outbreak. In a detailed response, Mayor Moya rejected the narrative of administrative negligence, asserting that the city’s pace was dictated by a commitment to procedural integrity rather than a lack of political will. She emphasized that the administration prioritized building a legally sound case that could withstand rigorous judicial scrutiny, rather than rushing a flawed submission that might ultimately be rejected by the National Treasury. To ensure the blacklisting process was enforceable, the city implemented several institutional safeguards. This included establishing a formal Standard Operating Procedure for supplier restrictions, creating a dedicated Supplier Review Committee with clear terms of reference, and incorporating additional internal compliance checks. Moya acknowledged that while the timeline extended beyond what many stakeholders deemed ideal, these steps were essential to ensure that the city’s actions were durable and fully compliant with South African legislative requirements. The Mayor also addressed public criticism regarding the city's purported inability to locate Sodi-linked company directors. She clarified that there is a significant legal distinction between a general awareness of a person’s location and the formal service of legal notices on corporate entities. The city, she explained, followed prescribed legal channels, utilizing the Central Supplier Database and other official systems to attempt service. To further bolster the legitimacy of these efforts, the city commissioned an independent legal review. Moya confirmed that the city’s Supplier Review Committee has now completed its evaluation and issued a definitive recommendation. This documentation is currently awaiting final sign-off from the City Manager before it is forwarded to the National Treasury, which holds the ultimate authority to impose nationwide restrictions on suppliers. The Mayor warned against the dangers of taking legal shortcuts, arguing that a hasty process prone to failure does not serve the residents of Tshwane, the interests of justice, or the rule of law. She reaffirmed the current multi-party coalition government’s pledge to eradicate corruption and underperformance through transparent, lawful, and decisive governance. By focusing on consequence management, the administration aims to ensure that when wrongdoing is identified, the resulting actions are not only punitive but also legally unassailable. Ultimately, Mayor Moya’s stance underscores a shift toward prioritizing sustainable accountability over the optics of immediate, yet potentially fragile, bureaucratic actions.

In a significant 2-1 decision, a panel of the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals has ruled that the Trump administration may proceed with plans to deport hundreds of thousands of immigrants currently residing in the United States under Temporary Protected Status (TPS). This ruling overturns a previous injunction that had successfully blocked the administration’s efforts to revoke humanitarian protections for citizens from El Salvador, Haiti, Nicaragua, and Sudan. The legal battle centers on the Trump administration’s 2017 and 2018 decisions to terminate these protections, arguing that the home countries of these individuals had recovered sufficiently to be considered safe. The court’s decision affects approximately 300,000 noncitizens and their 200,000 U.S.-born children, many of whom have built lives in the United States over several decades. Writing for the majority, Judge Consuelo M. Callahan, an appointee of President George W. Bush, asserted that federal law does not grant the judiciary the authority to challenge the discretion of the Secretary of Homeland Security regarding TPS designations. She argued that the statute governing TPS is designed to limit, rather than expand, the government's obligations. She was joined in this opinion by Judge Ryan D. Nelson, an appointee of President Donald Trump. The decision prompted a sharp dissent from Judge Morgan Christen, an appointee of President Barack Obama. Judge Christen argued that the administration’s policy reversal lacked transparency and failed to undergo necessary public review. Crucially, she highlighted the plaintiffs' claims that the deportations were motivated by racial and ethnic bias. She pointed to President Trump’s past derogatory remarks regarding Haiti, El Salvador, and other nations, noting that the court should not ignore the clear implications of the President’s own words. The Department of Justice welcomed the ruling, stating that the court correctly recognized that the administration’s actions were within the scope of its statutory authority and were not subject to judicial interference. Conversely, legal advocates—including the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) of Southern California—vowed to continue the fight. They maintained that the administration’s policies were driven by racism, which is unconstitutional. Despite the ruling, the affected immigrants will not be deported immediately. TPS holders from El Salvador are protected until at least November, while those from the other three nations retain their status until at least February. The challengers have announced their intention to appeal the decision to a larger, 11-judge panel of the 9th Circuit. Should the case proceed, it could eventually reach the U.S. Supreme Court. For now, advocates emphasize that many of these immigrants are essential workers who have served on the front lines during the COVID-19 pandemic, and they are calling on Congress to provide a permanent legislative solution for those facing the threat of deportation.

On Monday, Florida officials released 12 rescued manatees back into the wild, marking a record number for a single day. Most of these animals were orphans whose mothers perished due to starvation caused by seagrass loss in the Indian River Lagoon. To combat this ongoing crisis, wildlife authorities are actively supplementing the manatees' diets by distributing lettuce throughout the affected Brevard County region.

During a commemorative event marking the 31st anniversary of the Khojaly genocide, Azerbaijani Foreign Minister Jeyhun Bayramov condemned Armenia’s history of military aggression. He stated that Armenia continued its "atrocious crimes" beyond the 1992 massacre during the 2020 second Karabakh war, specifically citing missile attacks on Ganja and Barda. Bayramov emphasized that for sustainable peace, Armenia must renounce its aggressive policies. The Khojaly genocide, occurring on February 25-26, 1992, remains a central tragedy for Azerbaijan, resulting in 613 deaths, including many women and children, with 1,275 people taken hostage. Bayramov further highlighted the toll of the 2020 conflict, noting that Ganja was bombed five times in October, leading to numerous civilian casualties. Additionally, an October 28, 2020, missile attack on Barda killed 20 civilians and injured 70 others. By linking these events, the Foreign Minister underscored the long-standing impact of these conflicts on the Azerbaijani population and reiterated the necessity for Armenia to move toward a peaceful future.

A recent report by *The Washington Free Beacon* highlights a notable silence from several prominent human rights organizations regarding an Iranian airstrike that hit the Soroka Medical Center in southern Israel. The attack, which destroyed the hospital’s surgical ward and injured at least 80 people, occurred during a period of escalating conflict between Iran and Israel. While Iran maintained it was targeting a nearby military command center, the facility was located a mile away and remained untouched by the strike. The *Free Beacon* reached out to over a dozen self-proclaimed human rights groups—many of which are frequent critics of Israeli military policy—to solicit comment on the bombing of the medical facility. The responses, or lack thereof, revealed a stark contrast to how these same organizations typically address Israeli military actions. Amnesty International, which has previously accused Israel of committing "genocidal conditions" and characterized Israeli raids on hospitals in Gaza as "devastating attacks on human rights," declined to condemn the Iranian strike, stating they were still "looking into the incident." Similarly, groups like Nonviolence International and PAX for Peace cited staff holidays as the reason for their inability to provide comment. Notably, PAX had issued a condemnation of Israel earlier in the week regarding its own military actions, even calling for an arms embargo against the Jewish state. The Canadian Foreign Policy Institute took a more provocative stance, effectively shifting the blame to Israel. A board member for the group suggested that Israel should not place civilian infrastructure near military installations, drawing a parallel to Israel's own military operations in Gaza. Of the organizations contacted, only Churches for Middle East Peace issued a condemnation of Iran, though the organization’s statement also included criticisms of Israeli actions in Gaza. Many other high-profile groups, including Human Rights Watch, Oxfam International, and CODEPINK, did not respond to requests for comment. Gerald Steinberg, president of the watchdog group NGO Monitor, argued that this pattern of silence confirms that many human rights organizations have "weaponized" their platforms to promote a radical, anti-Israel agenda. According to Steinberg, these groups operate under a framework where Palestinians are viewed exclusively as victims, while the actions of Iran and its proxies are rarely held to the same standard of scrutiny. This discrepancy in advocacy is further evidenced by the organizations' continued, vocal condemnation of Israel for alleged "war crimes" and "aggression" in the region. Even as they remained silent on the hospital strike, many of these same groups continued to issue statements calling for U.S. sanctions and arms embargoes against Israel in response to its operations against Iranian targets.

In Anambra state, Nigeria, Sister Dorothy Okoli and her congregation, the Missionary Sisters of St. John Paul II of Mary, are engaged in a challenging mission to rescue women from the commercial sex trade. Recognizing that the industry is rife with exploitation and violence, the sisters established the Save Young Girls Motherhood Foundation in July. Led by Okoli, the group uses their backgrounds in counseling, economics, and education to reach out to women trapped in local brothels, offering them a path toward rehabilitation and a new life. The work is both dangerous and emotionally taxing. To build trust with the women, Okoli frequently visits these establishments with food, provisions, and cash gifts. She emphasizes that this ministry requires immense dedication and constant prayer, noting that the reality of the situation far exceeds her initial expectations regarding the number of women in need. The prevalence of HIV and other life-threatening health risks among these sex workers underscores the urgency of the sisters' intervention. While Nigerian law prohibits the operation of brothels and the trafficking of women, the trade remains a pervasive issue driven by poverty and a lack of economic opportunity. A poignant example of the individuals the sisters serve is 25-year-old Benita Ekwe. After the death of her father and her mother’s subsequent job loss, Ekwe entered the sex trade to support her five younger siblings, sacrificing her own education to ensure theirs. She characterizes her work as high-risk and deeply uncomfortable, expressing a desperate desire to leave the trade once she has saved enough money to open a food stall for her mother and secure her family’s future. Like many others, she faces severe exploitation, including high "rent" fees paid to hotel management just to secure a space to work. Since the foundation’s inception, the nuns have interacted with over 100 women. While they have successfully transitioned two women into independent tailoring businesses with housing, the process is inherently slow. Okoli notes that the primary obstacle to their progress is a lack of sustained funding. The rehabilitation process requires significant financial resources to ensure the women have immediate alternatives to the sex trade once they decide to retire. Despite these hurdles, Sister Okoli remains committed to the long-term intervention process, advocating for greater support from the government, the church, and the community to help these women escape the cycle of poverty and exploitation.

A protest is scheduled for International Women's Day outside the Montreal headquarters of MindGeek, the parent company of Pornhub. Demonstrators intend to denounce the platform for allegedly profiting from the sexual exploitation and trafficking of women and children. Public criticism has intensified following several high-profile incidents, including the hosting of content from "Girls Do Porn" creators charged with sex trafficking and the viral distribution of non-consensual intimate images. Furthermore, recent allegations involving a video of a minor being raped have fueled outrage. Critics argue the site lacks robust age and consent verification systems. A petition calling for the platform’s closure has surpassed 370,000 signatures, supported by over 75 advocacy organizations. Senator Julie Miville-Dechêne, a vocal advocate against human trafficking, plans to attend the demonstration. She has publicly condemned Pornhub for hosting content involving underage girls, insisting the company must implement stricter measures to ensure all uploaded content is free from exploitation and trafficking.

The Wallaceburg Red Devils dominated the Point Edward Pacers with a 16-7 victory, led by Marshall Powless’s impressive 10-point performance. With this win, the Far West Division leaders moved to 16-2 in the Ontario Jr. 'B' Lacrosse League. The team received strong offensive contributions from Kyle Dawson, Sidney Powless, and Carter Hastings, while goalies Cecil Jacobs and Brayden Bell combined for 40 saves. The Red Devils now face crucial matchups against the Windsor Clippers and Six Nations Rebels, aiming to secure first place in the Western Conference. In international competition, Chatham’s Hokey Langan netted a hat trick to help Canada defeat the United States 6-1 in the opening game of the World Ball Hockey Federation women’s championship in Moscow. Rachael Tricker also scored for Canada as they began their title defense. Elsewhere in sports, Dylan Bonner was officially confirmed as the Mini Mods' feature winner at South Buxton Raceway following a successful technical inspection. On the basketball court, Alec McGregor of Chatham played for London’s Team Compass, falling 64-58 to Gators Elite in the Canadian Youth Basketball League’s Grade 12 final. McGregor had been instrumental throughout the tournament, scoring double digits in both the quarter-final and semifinal rounds. In beach volleyball, Chatham athletes excelled at an Ontario Volleyball Association tournament in Grand Bend. Elliot Cowan and Lauryn Lahey captured gold in the 14-and-under girls' premier division, while four other Chatham duos reached the quarter-finals in their respective categories. Finally, Marshall Powless capped off a successful week by winning a gold medal with Caledonia McKinnon Park at the OFSAA 'A/AA' lacrosse festival in Ottawa, contributing four assists in the championship victory over St. Catharines Holy Cross.

The Kuwaiti Embassy in Baghdad has issued an urgent advisory urging its citizens to strictly adhere to Iraqi hunting regulations, particularly within the Muthanna governorate and southern regions. This directive aims to protect Kuwaiti visitors from potential legal consequences and physical harm. The appeal comes amidst a broader environmental crisis in Iraq, where decades of conflict, sanctions, and instability have severely depleted the nation's wildlife. Conservation experts and organizations like Nature Iraq report that dozens of bird species now face extinction. With scientific data scarce, officials emphasize that Iraq’s once-abundant biodiversity has been devastated by years of war, necessitating stricter conservation efforts.

In 2018, the year preceding its Chapter 11 bankruptcy filing, Pacific Gas & Electric (PG&E) emerged as the top lobbying spender in California. The utility giant poured nearly $10 million into efforts to influence state government, a figure that has drawn sharp criticism from transparency advocates. The bulk of this expenditure—over $5 million—was directed toward issues concerning wildfire safety and response. PG&E specifically lobbied to reduce the strict liability standards utilities face when their equipment ignites wildfires. While lawmakers ultimately rejected those attempts, they did pass legislation allowing utilities to issue bonds to cover wildfire-related damages, with the costs potentially passed on to ratepayers. PG&E spokeswoman Lynsey Paulo defended the spending, asserting that the funds came from shareholders rather than customers and were intended to address the critical challenges posed by worsening wildfires. The disclosure, filed with the California secretary of state, reveals that $9.6 million went toward general lobbying, including hiring firms and providing perks like meals and event tickets for public officials. Additionally, the utility spent $350,000 lobbying the California Public Utilities Commission. These figures dwarf the lobbying expenditures of other major utilities; for comparison, Edison International spent just over $4 million, and Sempra spent roughly $1.4 million. The only entity approaching PG&E’s spending was the Western States Petroleum Association, which spent nearly $7.9 million. PG&E’s aggressive lobbying occurred against a backdrop of mounting legal peril. The utility is currently facing 750 lawsuits related to devastating wildfires in 2017 and 2018. While investigations into the deadly November fire in Paradise are ongoing, PG&E has acknowledged equipment issues near the fire’s origin. Critics, including California Common Cause, condemned the spending as an attempt to "buy influence" at a time when the company’s actions directly impacted the lives and homes of Californians. The utility’s bankruptcy filing now threatens to limit payouts to victims while potentially increasing future costs for customers.

Gold prices (XAU/USD) are hovering in a narrow range above the $2,030 mark, trading near $2,035 during early Asian hours on Thursday. The precious metal is currently supported by safe-haven demand stemming from persistent geopolitical instability in the Middle East, specifically following recent US military airstrikes in Iraq, Syria, and Yemen in response to regional attacks on US troops and commercial shipping in the Red Sea. Market sentiment remains heavily influenced by the Federal Reserve's stance on monetary policy. Several Fed officials—including Adriana Kugler, Susan Collins, Neel Kashkari, and Thomas Barkin—have echoed Chair Jerome Powell’s recent message, indicating no urgency to cut interest rates. Policymakers are waiting for more definitive evidence that inflation is sustainably trending toward the 2% target before adjusting rates from their current two-decade highs. Consequently, investors have largely abandoned expectations for a March rate cut, shifting their focus toward a potential reduction in May. While the "higher-for-longer" interest rate environment typically weighs on gold because it is a non-yielding asset, the geopolitical tensions act as a counterbalancing force, limiting significant downside. Meanwhile, the US Dollar Index has dipped to 104.00, and 10-year Treasury yields have edged down to 4.11%. Looking ahead, market participants are bracing for key economic updates, including China’s January Consumer and Producer Price Indices, as well as US weekly jobless claims and further commentary from Richmond Fed President Barkin.

Paul Nthenge Mackenzie, the leader of the Good News International Church, has gone on trial in Mombasa, Kenya, facing manslaughter charges linked to the “Shakahola Forest Massacre.” This unprecedented legal proceeding involves 94 suspects accused of orchestrating the deaths of over 400 followers, making it one of the deadliest cult-related tragedies in modern history. The case centers on allegations that Mackenzie incited his followers to starve themselves to death to “meet Jesus.” The ordeal came to light in April 2023 when authorities began discovering mass graves in the remote Shakahola forest. To date, 448 bodies have been unearthed. While autopsies confirmed starvation as the primary cause of death, forensic evidence also revealed signs of strangulation, blunt force trauma, and, in some instances, the removal of organs. The trial, which is expected to be a complex legal undertaking, involves 95 original defendants, though one woman recently died in custody. Prosecutors have prepared testimony from at least 420 witnesses, some of whom will provide evidence in closed-door sessions. This manslaughter trial is one of several legal battles facing Mackenzie; he and his co-defendants also face separate charges of terrorism, murder, and child cruelty related to activities occurring between 2020 and 2023. The tragedy has prompted significant national soul-searching regarding the regulation of religious institutions in Kenya. Although Mackenzie had a history of extremism and prior legal trouble, he was able to operate his sect largely unchecked. Official reports from the Kenyan senate and human rights watchdogs have suggested that authorities could have intervened to prevent the loss of life. In response, President William Ruto established a commission to investigate the massacre and propose stricter oversight for religious bodies. However, these efforts face ongoing challenges due to constitutional protections regarding the separation of church and state, leaving the nation to grapple with how to balance religious freedom with public safety.

Saudi newspapers, including *Al-Riyadh* and *Al-Yaum*, recently highlighted the significance of King Salman bin Abdulaziz’s Eid al-Fitr address. The editorials emphasized the Kingdom’s steadfast commitment to global stability, prosperity, and international cooperation, particularly during the ongoing pandemic. The papers lauded Saudi Arabia’s leadership of the G20 summit, noting how the Kingdom effectively guided global efforts to navigate the health crisis. Furthermore, the King reiterated the government’s dedication to serving pilgrims, noting that recent protective measures were essential to ensuring safety during these challenging times. Beyond international relations, the editorials addressed critical domestic security concerns. *Al-Yaum* reported a stern warning from the Presidency of State Security regarding illegal charitable donations. Authorities cautioned that funds collected by unknown entities via social media are often funneled into terrorism, money laundering, and human trafficking. Consequently, the public was reminded that the King Salman Humanitarian Aid and Relief Center (KSRelief) remains the sole authorized channel for distributing Saudi humanitarian aid abroad to ensure security and transparency.

For over four decades, Pakistan has demonstrated unparalleled hospitality by hosting more than 1.4 million Afghan refugees and 850,000 Afghan Citizen Card holders. Despite facing significant economic pressures, Pakistan provides these individuals with access to primary and higher education, bank accounts, and various livelihood opportunities, even maintaining these standards throughout the COVID-19 pandemic. However, the article notes that Pakistan frequently faces baseless propaganda from Afghan and Indian media. Specifically, recent reports attempted to misrepresent the arrest of Afghan citizens in Sindh province. Officials clarified that these individuals were detained solely for lacking legal residency documents, questioning which nation would tolerate illegal migration. In contrast, the piece highlights the poor treatment of Afghan refugees in India. While hosting approximately 21,000 Afghans, India does not officially recognize them as refugees, treating them instead as illegal migrants under the Foreigners Act of 1946. Consequently, these individuals are denied access to essential social services, healthcare, and education. Furthermore, the report criticizes India for recently revoking the visas of Afghan students. Pakistan maintains that its humanitarian efforts remain consistent, despite the negative narratives propagated by external media outlets regarding its enforcement of immigration laws.

Despite being in a state of war with Syria since Israel’s founding, Israel has consistently demonstrated a commitment to humanitarian aid, extending its reach to Syrians suffering amidst their country’s brutal civil war. According to Maj. Efi Ribner, commanding officer of the Golan Israeli Liaison Office, the decision to assist stems from a fundamental moral imperative. Even though Syria is considered an enemy state, Israel’s leadership and the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) determined that standing by while civilians suffer is incompatible with the values of the Jewish state. In June 2016, Israel formalized these efforts by launching "Operation Good Neighbor." This initiative provides medical and civilian aid to Syrian refugees while maintaining Israel’s strict policy of non-involvement in the Syrian internal conflict. The operation serves two primary functions: increasing direct assistance from the IDF and coordinating with international non-governmental organizations (NGOs) to channel aid through Israeli infrastructure. The impact of this cooperation is significant. Organizations like the Rahma Relief Foundation have provided $90 million in medicine, while Louisiana-based Friend Ships Unlimited partnered with the IDF to establish a field clinic near the border that treats between 35 and 70 patients daily. Furthermore, international aid helped fund a maternity hospital in a Syrian village near the border, which saw its first delivery just a day after opening. The logistics of the operation are rigorous. Located just kilometers from the border, the relief effort facilitates the transfer of supplies—including food and fuel—or the transport of patients into Israel multiple times a day. Since the operation’s inception, the Israeli government has contributed approximately NIS 30 million ($8.6 million) in aid, complemented by roughly NIS 350 million ($100 million) in donations from NGOs. For the soldiers involved, the mission transcends political animosity. Sgt. Ziv Fox, an IDF paramedic, describes the work as the realization of his goal to save lives, emphasizing that Israeli personnel do not inquire about a patient’s background or political beliefs. Instead, they provide care based solely on medical need. Syrians seeking help arrive at the border fence at night, where they undergo security screenings before being transported to Israeli hospitals. Depending on the severity of their injuries, these patients may remain in Israel for days or months before being returned to the border. While the outcomes are not always positive—some patients unfortunately succumb to their injuries—the IDF remains committed to providing care to those in desperate need. Recently, Major Ribner and Sgt. Fox toured the United States to share the story of "Operation Good Neighbor" in a joint initiative between the IDF and the nonprofit StandWithUs. During their visit, they met with Israel’s UN Ambassador Danny Danon, who praised the soldiers as the "true face of Israel." He contrasted the IDF’s humanitarian efforts with the actions of the Syrian regime, highlighting the contrast between the ongoing slaughter of Syrian citizens and Israel’s dedication to providing life-saving care to its neighbors.

In 2017, the international aid organization Oxfam issued an urgent appeal for global intervention to prevent a catastrophic humanitarian disaster. At the time, as many as 20 million people across South Sudan, Nigeria, Somalia, and Yemen faced the immediate threat of starvation. Oxfam declared that famine had already emerged in parts of South Sudan, while approximately 400,000 individuals in northern Nigeria, isolated from aid, were likely suffering from famine conditions. Meanwhile, Yemen and Somalia were teetering on the brink of similar crises. The primary drivers of this widespread suffering were identified as violent conflict and, in the case of Somalia, severe drought. Oxfam’s Humanitarian Director, Nigel Timmins, criticized the international community for its "procrastination and ignored warnings," arguing that these famines were not sudden events but the result of political indifference. Furthermore, the organization condemned donor nations for failing to fully fund UN humanitarian appeals and, in the case of Yemen, for exacerbating the conflict through continued arms sales. Oxfam emphasized that famine is an agonizing, predictable process that accelerates exponentially once a tipping point is reached. To prevent mass mortality, the organization called for an immediate injection of $4.4 billion in humanitarian aid, coupled with decisive diplomatic action to resolve the underlying political conflicts. The scale of the crisis was staggering: 2.9 million people in Somalia faced acute food insecurity, with the situation expected to worsen if seasonal rains failed. In Nigeria, projections suggested that up to 800,000 people could face famine-like conditions by the end of 2017. South Sudan saw 100,000 people already starving, and Yemen—the world’s largest hunger emergency—had over 7 million people on the verge of famine, with national wheat stocks expected to run dry by April. Oxfam stressed that while the situation was dire, it was not yet inevitable. With rapid, large-scale support and political resolve, the international community could still prevent a total humanitarian collapse and save millions of lives.

The story of Mahat, a Somali refugee now residing in Malta, serves as a harrowing testament to the desperation that drives individuals to flee their homelands and the extraordinary resilience they display in the face of systemic cruelty. His journey from a stable life in Mogadishu to a new beginning in Europe is a narrative defined by trauma, human rights abuses, and a persistent, life-affirming commitment to helping others. Mahat’s life in Somalia was once defined by professional stability and community. However, his world fractured in 2015 when his father was murdered by the militant group Al-Shabaab. The tragedy was compounded when the same group targeted Mahat, presenting him with a lethal ultimatum: join their cause or be killed. Choosing survival, Mahat fled, later learning that his family home had been burned to the ground. His attempt to find safety led him to Libya, a country where he would endure two years of brutal detention. The conditions within the detention centers were inhumane: overcrowded, stiflingly hot, and lacking basic sanitation, with one toilet serving 800 people. Disease was rampant, and medical care was reserved exclusively for those who could afford it. Mahat describes a environment of systematic extortion where smugglers tortured detainees, often using electricity or metal objects, to coerce their families into sending ransom money. Mahat, having no such resources, suffered these violent beatings repeatedly. Yet, amidst this darkness, Mahat’s background as a midwife in Somalia became a beacon of hope for his fellow captives. Recognizing that pregnant women in detention were utterly neglected, Mahat stepped into the role of an unofficial, on-call midwife. Despite the lack of medical supplies and the hostility of the detention staff, he successfully delivered 15 babies. He recalls the case of one mother, who, with the help of a fellow detainee and a qualified Eritrean doctor, gave birth to a boy named Abubakar in a makeshift space partitioned by blankets. Mahat’s intervention ensured that these children entered the world safely despite the surrounding squalor. He remains connected to the mother and child, who have since been relocated to Portugal. The turning point in Mahat’s journey came on June 20, 2018, when he and 130 others were placed on a flimsy, dangerous boat. The crossing was fraught with terror; the passengers feared interception by Libyan authorities, which would have meant a return to the torture they had escaped. When they were eventually spotted, the relief of discovering a rescue vessel—the *Lifeline*—was immense. The crew provided immediate care, and after a tense standoff regarding international port access, the ship was permitted to dock in Malta on June 28, 2018. Upon his arrival, Mahat was granted Subsidiary Protection, marking the beginning of his quest to rebuild a life that had been systematically dismantled. The path to stability, however, is not without challenges. He currently works as a Somali cultural mediator, assisting other refugees and asylum-seekers in Malta. While he finds fulfillment in this role, his ambitions remain high; he aspires to become a doctor, a goal that requires him to start his education almost from scratch, as many refugees must do when their credentials are not recognized in their new countries. Currently, Mahat is studying science at the Malta College of Arts, Science and Technology (MCAST) and living independently. Although he carries the heavy burden of the trauma he witnessed and endured, he possesses a forward-looking mindset. His story is not merely one of survival, but of the triumph of human dignity. By acting as a midwife in the most degrading of circumstances and now dedicating his life to supporting his fellow refugees, Mahat has turned his own suffering into a source of hope for others. Despite the obstacles that remain, he approaches his future in Malta with a profound sense of optimism and determination, seeking, above all, the peace that eluded him for so long.

Following the tragic terrorist attack on the Paris headquarters of the satirical magazine *Charlie Hebdo*, which left 12 people dead, Canadian distributor LMPI is significantly increasing the local availability of the publication's latest issue. While the magazine typically distributes only 100 copies weekly in Canada—primarily in Quebec and one Toronto location—director of sales Louis-Philip Vermeersch announced that 1,500 copies will be available this Friday. This expanded distribution will reach 135 stores nationwide. While the majority of these retailers remain in Quebec, the magazines will also be available at select locations in Toronto, Ottawa, Vancouver, Victoria, Calgary, Fredericton, Moncton, and Halifax. Despite this increase, Vermeersch warned that supply will likely fall short of intense public demand. Although the publisher has boosted global production to three million copies, those are primarily earmarked for the French domestic market, and further Canadian shipments remain unconfirmed. The controversial cover of the new issue features a weeping Prophet Muhammad holding a sign that reads "I am Charlie" under the headline "All is forgiven." The publication, which has long faced threats for its depictions of the Prophet, also includes content condemning the recent terrorism and illustrating the massive solidarity marches in Paris. The attack on the magazine sparked a three-day terror spree that claimed 17 lives in total. All three gunmen, who claimed affiliations with Middle Eastern extremist groups, were ultimately killed by security forces. Canadian newsstands are expected to carry the issue by Friday at noon.

Bobby Ray Parks is poised to rejoin the Gilas Pilipinas national team for the upcoming FIBA Asia Cup in Jakarta, scheduled for July 12–24. His inclusion follows an invitation from Barangay Ginebra PBA Governor Alfrancis Chua, who previously managed Parks during the player’s tenure with Alab Pilipinas. Parks, 29, recently completed a successful rookie campaign with the Nagoya Diamond Dolphins in Japan’s B.League, where he averaged 10.4 points and 3.6 rebounds across 46 games. Despite his commitment to continue playing in Japan, he has accepted the call to represent the Philippines once more. His international experience includes appearances in three SEA Games and the 2016 Olympic Qualifying Tournament. In contrast to Parks, 7-foot center Greg Slaughter declined an invitation from head coach Chot Reyes to join the national squad, citing existing commitments.
